## [The Complete Works of St. Cyprian]

[Col. 0009]

## [Cyprianic Dissertations]

# First Dissertation on St. Cyprian’s Eighth Letter, by Dodwell: On Visions, and on the Manner in Which the Ancients Confirmed the Credibility of Their Visions, etc.

[Col. 0009A] § 1. Visions and prophetic gifts continued from the times of the Apostles down to Cyprian, according to the author of the Apocalypse and Hermas.—§ 2. Clement of Rome and the author of the Apocryphal Esdras.—§ 3. Ignatius.—§ 4. Quadratus, Philip’s daughters, Ammia of Philadelphia, and Polycarp.—§ 5. Justin Martyr.—§ 6. Melito of Sardis, Alexander the Phrygian, Attalus, and others.—§ 7. Irenaeus.—§ 8. Perpetua and Saturus. They were not Montanists.—§ 9. It is not true that the Church surrendered to the Montanists the claim to prophecy.—§ 10. On the contrary, after the reign of Commodus the Catholics refuted the Montanists’ prophecies by the very argument that the gift of true prophecy would remain perpetually in the Church, whereas the Montanists’ gift had already become extinct.—§ 11. Thus Asterius Urbanus and Epiphanius.—§§ 12, 13. The author of the Acts of Perpetua [Col. 0009B] and Felicity.—§ 14. The visions of Natalis and Potamiaena, and the appointment of Alexander at Jerusalem and Fabian at Rome as bishops.—§ 15. Origen acknowledges prophecies.—§ 16. The testimony of Gregory of Nyssa concerning St. Gregory Thaumaturgus is declined.—§ 17. A vision of Dionysius of Alexandria.—§§ 18, 19, 20, 21. Visions of Cyprian himself.—§ 22. Another vision of Dionysius of Alexandria.—§ 23. Visions were customarily announced publicly, and this before their fulfillment.—§ 24. How provision was made against fraud under the pretext of visions.—§§ 25, 26, 27. On the arguments by which the credibility of visions was proved, especially intrinsic arguments. The gift of disclosing thoughts.—§§ 28, 29, 30. The gift of predicting future events. According to the principles of that age, future events which would not otherwise exceed created powers nevertheless could not be predicted by anyone other than God. [Col. 0009C]—§ 31. It comes to the same thing whether they were revealed immediately by God himself or through some created intermediary.—§ 32. The agreement of this hypothesis with the phenomena is an argument for its truth.—§ 33. How they established the credibility of some prophecies from the credibility of others.—§ 34. Not everything said or done by true prophets was prophetic.—§§ 35, 36, 37. Certain errors on the part of prophets are compatible with true prophecy, and which errors these are.—§ 38. The truth of a prophecy was proved from the unity of the communion to which the prophet had attached himself.—§ 39. The credibility of those whose prophecies were all obscure could not be commended in any way except from the unity of their communion. [Col. 0010A]—§ 40. Visions were especially characteristic of the young.—§§ 41, 42. What is to be thought of those who have held the prophecies of the ancients up to ridicule.

§ 1.—The reader should not expect here a compilation drawn from the rabbis or from others who dealt with prophecy and prophetic visions. We shall select only those matters which, so far as I know, have been omitted by scholars or have not yet received sufficient attention, but which nevertheless appear to possess some importance for the history of the age with which we are concerned.

Scholars therefore do badly when they refer what they read in the authors of that age concerning visions to Montanus and the Montanists, as though visions had ceased in the Church from the very time of the Apostles, every claim to them had been regarded with suspicion [Col. 0010B] and condemned in the Church, and they had been left to the Montanists alone. There is no reason whatever to think so. Rather, throughout that entire interval, from the Apostles down to Cyprian, visions were continuously in use and were always approved by the Church. Near the end of the first century the work which we possess as the Apocalypse was written, whether by the Apostle or perhaps by John the Presbyter; yet its entire subject matter consists of visions. At approximately the same time Hermas wrote his *Shepherd*, for it is clear from Book I of the *Visions*, no. 2, that he wrote under Clement. Nor need we linger over the later testimonies of the *Pontifical*, of the poems *Against Marcion*, or of the letters to Justus of Vienne that bear the name of Pius, all of doubtful credibility. Since the work of Hermas consists of three books, the first bears the title *Visions* [Col. 0010C] and is wholly devoted to that subject. In the second he also expressly discusses the distinction between true and false prophets and spirits (*Mandates* 11, 12). To what purpose, unless he believed that the gifts of true prophets had continued in the Church down to that time? Blondel calls him a masked prophet and dreamer, “an abyss of Montanist superstitions” (*Apologia pro Sententia Hieronymi*, pp. 16–17). Yet in the same place, following his custom, he amassed highly honorable encomia from Fathers who thought otherwise—and indeed from men utterly alien to Montanist superstitions. [Col. 0011A] Thus the Fathers who were were contemporaries of the Montanists, and who were the first to condemn those superstitions, could find nothing Montanist in him. Let the reader who loves antiquity (*philarchaios*, φιλαρχαῖος) judge which party deserves greater trust.

§ 2.—We have said that Clement of Rome was a contemporary of Hermas and likewise a defender of prophetic gifts. For it may readily be gathered from these words of his that gifts of this sort were those in which the authors of the schism took pride:

> “Let someone be faithful; let him be capable of uttering knowledge; let him be wise in the just judgment”—or, as Clement of Alexandria reads, “discernment,” and more correctly—“of words”  
> (*First Epistle to the Corinthians* § 48; also from Asterius Urbanus, Book V, ch. 17).

These terms refer to nothing other than the prophetic gifts of those times. The “faith” (*pistis*, πίστις) in which they could glory was none other than the miraculous faith which the Apostle calls “the word of faith” (*logos pisteōs*, λόγος πίστεως), in the passage where the gifts of the Holy Spirit are called “words” (*logoi*, λόγοι) by him. [Col. 0011B] “Knowledge” (*gnōsis*, γνῶσις) was not knowledge of just any kind, but that knowledge of mysteries which the same Apostle calls “knowledge falsely so called” (*pseudōnymos gnōsis*, ψευδώνυμος γνῶσις) in heretics who boasted under that name. The same applies to “wisdom” (*sophia*, σοφία), which he also calls “the word of wisdom” (*logos sophias*, λόγος σοφίας). “Discernment of words” (*diakrisis logōn*, διάκρισις λόγων) is the same as “discernment of spirits” (*diakrisis pneumatōn*, διάκρισις πνευμάτων), in the sense in which we have said that the gifts of the Holy Spirit were called “words.” Unless perhaps we understand “words” (*logōn*) as “thoughts” (*logismōn*, λογισμῶν), in which case we shall also interpret “discernment of spirits” as the revelation of thoughts. The author of the books of the Apocryphal Esdras may perhaps have been contemporary with these times; visions and revelations of this kind constitute by far the greatest part of those books.

§ 3.—Ignatius comes next. These faultfinders of antiquity criticize in him precisely the fact that he is more favorable to these prophetic gifts than they would wish. [Col. 0011C] In § 7 of his *Epistle to the Philadelphians*, he records a prophecy of his own and calls God himself as witness that it was truly revealed to him:

> “For even if some wished to deceive me according to the flesh, nevertheless the Spirit is not deceived, since it is from God. For it knows whence it comes and where it goes, and it exposes hidden things. While I was among you I cried out; I spoke with a loud voice: ‘Attend to the bishop, the presbytery, and the deacons.’ But they suspected me of saying these things because I had prior knowledge of the division of certain persons. Yet he in whom I am bound is my witness”—or, more correctly, according to the interpolated edition, supported also by Ussher’s ancient translator: “But if you suspect me of saying these things because I had learned beforehand of the division of certain persons, he in whom I am bound is my witness”—“that I did not learn it from human flesh. But the Spirit proclaimed these words: ‘Do nothing apart from the bishop,’” etc.

The same man speaks of gifts of this kind belonging to himself in § 4 of his *Epistle to the Trallians*:

[Col. 0011D]

> “Am I not able to write to you about heavenly things? But I fear that I might cause harm to you, since you are infants. Bear with me, lest, being unable to contain them, you should be strangled. For although I am able to understand heavenly things, the stations of the angels, the musterings of the rulers, and things visible and invisible, I am not on that account already a disciple.”

Nor, as will be clear from other monuments of that age, was Ignatius singular in this matter.

§ 4.—Quadratus immediately followed Ignatius; he dedicated an apology for the Christians to Hadrian. Eusebius writes that he, together with Philip’s daughters—whom St. Luke calls prophetesses—was himself distinguished by prophetic grace (*Ecclesiastical History* III.37). Indeed, from what Polycrates wrote to Victor, it is probable that [Col. 0012A] those daughters of Philip survived until these times. Ammia of Philadelphia, herself also a prophetess, continued the succession (*diadochē*, διαδοχή) from Quadratus down to the rise of Montanus (Asterius Urbanus in Eusebius, cited above). The Smyrnaeans themselves, in the letter concerning Polycarp’s martyrdom which they sent to the Philomelians, are witnesses above all exception that a prophetic vision of his martyrdom was granted to Polycarp. They call this Apostolic Teacher also prophetic, and acknowledge that nothing was predicted by him which was not confirmed by its fulfillment (*in* Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.15):

> “For every word that he uttered from his mouth both has been fulfilled,” they say, “and will be fulfilled.”

Our most learned Chester scholar holds, with the greatest probability, that he suffered in the year 147.

[Col. 0012B] § 5.—Eusebius says the same of Justin Martyr:

> “He writes that even down to his own time prophetic gifts continued to shine forth”  
> (*Ecclesiastical History* IV.18).

And rightly so. These are Justin’s words to Trypho:

> “For among us prophetic gifts exist even to the present day. From this you yourselves ought to understand that the gifts which formerly existed among your people have been transferred to us”  
> (*Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 308B).

Later he used the same argument against the Jews: after Christ’s advent there had been no prophets among the Jews, and on this point he calls their own perception as witness:

> “Prophets will no longer arise among your people according to the ancient custom. This is something that you can see with your own eyes. For after him no prophet at all has arisen among you”  
> (pp. 314C–D).

But he confirms, by the testimony of the same senses, that such persons continued among the Christians of his own time, [Col. 0012C] using the same word “to see” (*idein*, ἰδεῖν):

> “And among us one may see both women and men possessing gifts from the Spirit of God”  
> (p. 315B).

It was therefore as manifest that the Christians had prophets as it was that they had ceased among the Jews. Both facts were so manifest that they could serve as an argument against an opponent. The Apostle used the same form of argument in Galatians 3:2, for by “the Spirit” the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit are meant.

§ 6.—Toward the end of Marcus’s reign we have this encomium of Melito of Sardis by Polycrates: that, inspired by the Holy Spirit, he conducted his entire life—“he who ordered his whole conduct in the Holy Spirit” (*ton en hagiō pneumati panta politeusamenon*, τὸν ἐν ἁγίῳ πνεύματι πάντα πολιτευσάμενον; in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.24). During the same persecution Alexander the Phrygian is said to have been “not without a share in the apostolic gift” (*ouk amoiros apostolikou charismatos*, οὐκ ἄμοιρος Ἀποστολικοῦ χαρίσματος; from the *Letter of the Churches of Lyons and Vienne*, [Col. 0012D] in Eusebius V.1). We have already seen, from the similar passage of the Smyrnaeans concerning Polycarp, where these two things are joined together, that this prophetic gift must be included in that apostolic grace (in Eusebius V.3). The Church of Gaul records a revelation made to Attalus concerning Alcibiades. Eusebius states that the frequent prophecies of others in various churches lent credibility to the Montanists’ claims concerning prophecy:

> “Accordingly, very many wondrous works of divine grace were still being performed at that time in various churches, and these gave many people confidence that those persons also prophesied”  
> (Eusebius, ibid., ch. 4).

Thus this claim was not yet peculiar to the Montanists, as scholars have hitherto supposed.

[Col. 0013A] § 7.—Irenaeus says the same of that age—that is, his own—whose Greek words Eusebius has preserved for us:

> “Others also possess foreknowledge of things to come, visions, and prophetic utterances”  
> (Irenaeus II.58; in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.7).

He presses this as an argument against the heretics. Elsewhere he likewise says:

> “Where the Church is, there is also the Spirit; and where the Spirit of God is, there is the Church and every grace”  
> (Irenaeus III.40).

He denies that any count can be made of the gifts exercised by the Church in his own time:

> “It is impossible to number the gifts which the Church throughout the whole world, having received them from God, performs each day in the name of Jesus Christ, who was crucified under Pontius Pilate, for the benefit of the nations”  
> (Irenaeus II.58; in Eusebius, ibid.).

From this we also understand how common they were. And lest we suspect that Irenaeus might have been deceived here, [Col. 0013B] he further adds that he reported them not merely on another’s testimony, but as things he himself had heard with his own ears:

> “We also hear many brethren in the Church who possess prophetic gifts, who speak through the Spirit in languages of every kind, bring the hidden things of human beings into the open for their benefit, and expound the mysteries of God”  
> (in Eusebius, ibid.).

What could have been said more explicitly?

§ 8.—I do not cite Tertullian’s testimonies because Rigaltius renders him suspect of Montanism, though he does not deny that examples of prophetic visions occur quite frequently in Tertullian. There is also another testimony contemporary with Tertullian which certainly must by no means be omitted: the *Acts of Perpetua and Felicity*. There we have the visions of Perpetua and Saturus; indeed, they were committed to writing by the martyrs’ [Col. 0013C] own hands. They too are African and were composed entirely after the pattern of the Cyprianic visions. We also have the preface of a contemporary author, in which he proves and commends the occurrence of visions of this kind from Joel’s prophecy. It is astonishing that the most learned editor infers from this that both the writer and even the martyrs themselves favored the Montanists. If that had been true, it is not at all probable that they would have been numbered among the martyrs or that their memory would have been venerated in the Catholic Church. For the distinguished Chester scholar proved from Tertullian himself that the position which denied the status of martyrdom to schismatics was not introduced by Cyprian, but had been accepted in Africa from the time of Tertullian himself. Indeed, we shall shortly show that the passages which [Col. 0013D] learned men refer to this matter were composed against the Montanists rather than in accordance with their opinion.

§ 9.—For it is not true that the Church surrendered to the Montanists the claim to prophecy. The Catholics had neither regarded Montanus and his women as true prophets nor believed that the succession of prophets would ever fail in the Church. The Catholics taught both points against the Montanists, and the Montanist writers can most easily be distinguished from them by either point. They attributed the Montanists’ prophecies not to a good spirit but to an evil one; hence Montanus’s complaint in Eusebius that he was regarded as a wolf although he was a lamb (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.16, from Asterius Urbanus). Accordingly, when Maximilla first pretended to prophesy, Apollonius says that [Col. 0014A] Zoticus wished to act as an exorcist and to treat her as demon-possessed, had he not been restrained by others (in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.18). Aelius Publius Julius, Bishop of the colony of Debeltum, bears the same witness concerning Sotas in a passage quoted by Serapion and preserved by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.19. Asterius Urbanus says the same concerning the aforementioned Zoticus, Bishop of Comana, and Julian of Apamea, in Eusebius V.16 (ibid., chs. 16–18).

The Catholics inferred this from various marks by which true prophets were to be distinguished from enthusiasts: that Montanus had smeared cosmetic dye upon his eyebrows and hair; that he had established salaries for his prophets and a kind of commerce under that pretext; that his women had left their husbands when they assumed the office of prophetesses; that these women were likewise wholly intent upon avarice and upon scraping together money by any conceivable means; [Col. 0014B] that they had taught “contrary to the custom handed down by tradition and by the succession of the Church from above” (*para to kata paradosin kai kata diadochēn anōthen tēs ekklēsias ethos*, παρὰ τὸ κατὰ παράδοσιν καὶ κατὰ διαδοχὴν ἄνωθεν τῆς ἐκκλησίας ἔθος); and, above all, that their profane spirit had driven them into madness, something which the Catholics never believed had befallen true prophets. This argument in particular occasioned Tertullian’s writing *On Ecstasy* against Apollonius.

§ 10.—But the Catholics also employed against them the other argument we have mentioned, taking their occasion from the following circumstance. Maximilla had predicted concerning herself that after her there would be no other prophetess, but the consummation. Her words in Epiphanius are:

> “After me there will no longer be a prophetess, but the consummation”  
> (*Met’ eme prophētis ouketi estai, alla synteleia*, Μετ’ ἐμὲ προφῆτις οὐκέτι ἔσται, ἀλλὰ συντέλεια; Epiphanius, *Heresies* XLVIII.2).

These words certainly persuade me to agree with Blondel’s position—[Col. 0014C] not that all the Sibylline oracles extant today were fabricated by the Montanists, but that at least some of them were. For in those oracles this *synteleia*, or consummation, is deferred to the reign of Marcus. Now it is highly probable that Maximilla died toward the end of his reign. Since Asterius Urbanus counts thirteen or fourteen years, inclusively, from her death to the year in which he was writing (in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.16–17), scholars think that this date can most suitably be referred to no reign other than that of Commodus.

The Catholics, on the contrary, thought that even from this fact the Montanists’ claims to prophecy should be convicted of falsehood: their prophecy, even by their own admission, would at some point come to an end, whereas true prophecy would be perpetual and would in fact continue until the consummation of the world. This, unless I am mistaken, was how they understood [Col. 0014D] the Apostle in Ephesians 4:11–13; and so too the prophets, especially, I think, the passage of Joel already mentioned. By this reasoning they were so far from denying the prophecies of their own times that any church in which there were no prophets was not even to be regarded as a church.

§ 11.—Thus Asterius Urbanus argued:

> “For if, as they say, after Quadratus and Ammia of Philadelphia the women associated with Montanus succeeded to the prophetic gift, let them show which of their people succeeded Montanus and the women. For the Apostle holds that the prophetic gift must exist throughout the entire Church until the perfect coming”  
> (in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.17).

Thus Epiphanius:

> “For if gifts must be received, [Col. 0015A] and if there must be gifts in the Church, why do they no longer have prophets after Montanus, Priscilla, and Maximilla? Has grace then ceased to operate? But grace does not cease to operate in the holy Church. Far be it! But if those who prophesied prophesied only until a certain time and now prophesy no longer, then neither did Priscilla nor Maximilla prophesy after”—the manuscript reads “according to”—“those prophecies which, through the holy Apostles, were approved in the holy Church”  
> (*Heresies* XLVIII.2).

These words plainly do not suit the age of Epiphanius, by which time it was already admitted that these gifts (*charismata*, χαρίσματα) had not continued until then. I therefore suppose that he copied these words unskillfully from some earlier writer.

§ 12.—The ancient author of the *Acts of Perpetua and Felicity*, whoever he was, a contemporary of the martyrs, argues according to the same pattern. After citing the passage of Joel, [Col. 0015B] he proved that the prophecies of the New Testament were so far from falling short of those of the Old Testament that, on the contrary, even greater prophecies should be expected under the New Testament. He then adds the following in support of the position I have mentioned:

> “And so we also, who both acknowledge and honor new visions just as we do the prophecies equally promised to us, and who reckon the other powers of the Holy Spirit among the instruments of the Church—to which the same Spirit was sent, administering every gift in all persons just as the Lord distributes to each—necessarily set them down in order and celebrate them by public reading to the glory of God. We do so lest any weakness or despair of faith should suppose that the grace of the Divinity dwelt only among the ancients, whether in the condescension shown to martyrs or in that shown through revelations; since God always performs what he has promised—as testimony for unbelievers and [Col. 0015C] as a benefit for believers”  
> (*Preface*).

The whole of that discussion is directed precisely to preventing the later visions from being discredited because God had deigned to reveal them in the last times of the Church. To prevent this, he undertook to prove that they were to be expected especially in the last times, and always down to the consummation. These statements might perhaps seem to have been directed against the pagans; they might also have been directed against the Montanists. I should rather believe that they were directed against the Montanists, because he confirmed what he had said by the testimony of the Scriptures. It is certainly evident that the propositions he advanced here were acknowledged among his own people—something that could not possibly have been written by a Montanist.

§ 13.—For it should first be noted that these words were written by the author in the year of the Lord 202, [Col. 0015D] that is, approximately twenty-three years after the death of Maximilla; for we have said that she died in the last year of Marcus, namely AD 179. But if she had been a true prophetess, no other prophet was thereafter to be expected. Therefore, the man who still expected others, and believed that they must always be expected, cannot possibly have regarded her as a true prophetess and accordingly could not have been a Montanist. For although that heresy was later divided into various sects, all nevertheless agreed on this point: those first women were to be acknowledged as prophetesses.

Second, it should be noted that even if we interpret Maximilla’s words in the most favorable sense, understanding them of female prophetesses rather than male prophets, this preface still could not have been written by a Montanist. For its author was about to include the visions of the prophetess Perpetua, [Col. 0016A] although it is certain that this interpretation cannot be accommodated to Maximilla’s meaning. For when she said that after her there would be the *synteleia*, the consummation, it necessarily excluded absolutely every subsequent exercise of prophecy.

Third, since Asterius Urbanus had employed this very argument at least ten years earlier in refuting that sect, who could believe that a defender of the sect would employ the same argument?

Fourth, it is also clear from Urbanus himself that in actual fact they terminated the entire succession of their prophets with Maximilla and admitted no successor whatever after her. Epiphanius, who employed the same argument (*Heresies* XLVIII.2), confirms that after her death no one else was acknowledged by the Montanists down to his own times. It is therefore impossible that [Col. 0016B] a Montanist should have enrolled Saturus and Perpetua in the register of prophets. The reader must at least concede from the reasoning of those other writers that anyone who argues in this way ought not on that account to be regarded as a Montanist. Yet the learned men who think otherwise produce no other argument.

For my part, I readily acknowledge and freely concede that the ancients went astray throughout this entire argument concerning the perpetuity of prophecy; nor does our recognition of this kind of error, or of other frequent errors on their part, diminish their authority. They had no other foundation for their opinion than the texts we have mentioned. Whether they reasoned correctly from them is not a question concerning their testimony, but concerning their judgment—a matter in which their antiquity affords them no protection. But what I infer from their argument—namely, that they in fact acknowledged prophecies in their own age—[Col. 0016C] concerns a matter of fact, regarding which their testimony concerning their own age is entirely certain.

§ 14.—But to return to the point from which the discussion digressed: in the same persecution under Severus in which Perpetua and Felicity suffered, other examples of visions also occurred (the unknown author *Against the Heresy of Artemon*, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.28). First was the vision of Natalis the confessor, under Zephyrinus, the Roman pontiff, by which he was recalled from the heresy of Artemon to the Catholic Church (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.5). Then there were other visions of Potamiaena, by which not only Basilides but also several other Alexandrians were converted to the Christian faith.

There were, moreover, other revelations and visions: by the first Alexander was commanded to migrate from Cappadocia to Palestine (Eusebius, ibid., ch. 11); [Col. 0016D] in the second and third, together with what the Jews call a heavenly voice, the people of Jerusalem and their bishop were admonished to admit the same Alexander to the episcopate. Under Maximinus or Gordian, Fabian was made bishop by a divine revelation (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.29), the Holy Spirit descending upon him in the form of a dove, in precisely the same manner as he had descended upon the Savior.

§ 15.—Under Gordian, or perhaps rather under Philip, Origen appears to have written his volumes *Against Celsus*. For the “dissension” (*stasis*, στάσις) which he mentions on p. 120 should not be referred to the state (*Against Celsus* III), as the translator supposed, but rather to the sects of Christians. [Col. 0017A] By that time Christians had not suffered persecution “for a considerable period” (*chronō pleioni*, χρόνῳ πλείονι), and he even says that it had occurred “long ago” (*palai*, πάλαι). He appears clearly to designate the long peace mentioned by Cyprian (*On the Lapsed*), namely, the interval between the persecution of Severus and that of Decius.

That prophetic gifts flourished among Christians at this time is attested by Origen himself, a witness of the highest credibility concerning his own age, who summarizes the whole subject of prophetic gifts in a few words:

> “Neither have those alien to the faith done anything resembling the prophets, nor is it recorded that any of the later Jews, after the coming of Jesus, prophesied. For it is acknowledged that the Holy Spirit abandoned them after they acted impiously toward God and toward the one who had been prophesied by the prophets among them”  
> (Book VII, p. 337).

Justin Martyr said the same above concerning the Jews. [Col. 0017B] Origen continues:

> “At the beginning of Jesus’ teaching, and still more after his ascension, signs of the Holy Spirit were manifested in greater number; later they became fewer. Nevertheless, even now traces of him remain among a few persons whose souls have been purified by the Word and by conduct in accordance with it.”

When he says that in his time only traces remained, he undoubtedly had in view those first beginnings of Christian worship at Pentecost. The prophetic gifts we have discussed, which under the Apostles had once been common among Christians of every rank, had by then become peculiar only to illustrious Christians of the highest merit.

§ 16.—The life of Gregory Thaumaturgus, Origen’s disciple, written by Gregory of Nyssa, would by itself furnish ample evidence here, [Col. 0017C] were I not afraid of detracting from the credibility of monuments of greater certainty by also amassing more uncertain ones. Gregory of Nyssa drew his account not from contemporary records, but chiefly from oral tradition, and that tradition derived from an interval of at least one generation. If he had received those accounts directly and had represented the event to posterity exactly as it occurred, without enlarging it by his own reasonings and conjectures, I certainly would not see why assent should be denied to Gregory of Nyssa, or indeed to any man of established credibility. Such, however, are the materials we have hitherto advanced and those which we shall advance below.

§ 17.—Let his place therefore be supplied by another fellow disciple under Origen, Dionysius of Alexandria. Near the end of Philip’s reign, when a persecution arose at Alexandria through the impending assault of a populace raging against the Christians, Dionysius was commanded by a divine warning to flee, and God opened for him, [Col. 0017D] contrary to expectation, a path of escape. He himself says so in his letter to Germanus:

> “When God commanded me to depart and wondrously made a way for me,” etc.  
> (in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.40).

He calls God himself as witness that these things were true:

> “I speak in the presence of God, and he himself knows that I do not lie. I did not undertake my flight on my own initiative, without divine sanction.”

What are we to do here? Shall we refuse to believe a most holy man even when he gives his oath?

§ 18.—We have now come to Cyprian’s own times. If we consult his testimony alone, there will certainly be no reason to doubt either that there were visions and other prophecies or that they were entirely truthful. In the very letter with which we are dealing he recalls a vision shown long before the tempest of that devastation arose, [Col. 0018A] which he had already understood would come. Indeed, the vision concerning the lack of unanimity was of the kind described by the Apostle, by which even the hidden things of hearts were made manifest.

There was also another revelation which he says had been entrusted to “the least servant”—by which phrase he undoubtedly designated himself:

> “Tell him,” it said, “to be confident, because peace is coming.”

They were still far removed from any hope of peace when Cyprian wrote this. Yet for that reason he did not think that it should be concealed; rather, he directed that this very letter be read to the brethren. It is therefore clear that he was so certain of the fulfillment that, nevertheless, what had been promised would come to pass.

When the persecution began, he withdrew. Just as we have shown that Dionysius did this, so it is clear that Cyprian likewise did it at God’s direction:

> “And you will hear everything,” he says, “when the Lord, who [Col. 0018B] commanded me to withdraw, has restored me to you”  
> (*Letter* X).

He says the same in *Letter* XV, and Pontius says it many times in his *Life* of Cyprian.

The presbyters had rashly granted peace to the lapsed without consulting him. Concerning what he should do in this matter, he likewise had God as his instructor:

> “And so divine judgment does not cease to rebuke us by night or by day. For besides the visions of the night, even during the day the innocent age of children among us is filled with the Holy Spirit; in ecstasy it sees with its eyes, hears, and speaks those things by which the Lord deigns to admonish and instruct us.”

It is everywhere clear from his letters what disturbances were caused him by the five presbyters who supported the lapsed. This too had previously been revealed to him by the Lord in a heavenly vision:

> “This is a persecution,” he says, “another and still another trial; and these five presbyters are nothing other than those five leading men who had recently been associated with the magistrates [Col. 0018C] in the edict”  
> (*Letter* XL).

Pamelius understood this correctly, as it appears:

> “He seems to me to allude to some vision in which five leading men appeared together with the magistrates, jointly publishing an edict against the bishops.”

§ 19.—They had already learned by divine revelation of the second persecution of their time, under Gallus and Volusian, and they judged that the people should be warned of it in letters which are still extant. Thus Cyprian writes to the people of Thibaris:

> “For since, by the condescension of the Lord who instructs us, we are repeatedly impelled and more fully admonished, we must also convey to your conscience the anxious concern of our warning. For you ought to know, believe with certainty, and hold fast that the day of pressure has begun to hang over our heads”  
> [Col. 0018D] (*Letter* LVI), etc.

Then, after a few intervening words:

> “Nor should we suppose that the things now coming are of the same kind as those which have passed. A more grievous and more savage struggle is now impending,” etc.

Again, Cyprian writes with the synod to Cornelius:

> “But since we see that the day of another assault has again begun to approach, and since by frequent and continual manifestations we are admonished to be armed and prepared for the contest which the enemy declares against us, let us also prepare by our exhortations the people entrusted to us by divine condescension,” etc.  
> (*Letter* LIV).

Later:

> “For obedience must be rendered to righteous manifestations and warnings, so that the sheep may not be abandoned by their shepherds in time of danger,” etc.

Again:

> “It has pleased us, at the suggestion of the Holy Spirit and with the Lord admonishing us through [Col. 0019A] many manifest visions—because the enemy is announced beforehand and shown to be threatening us—to gather the soldiers of Christ within the camp,” etc.

Atheists will perhaps not believe these things. But what grounds do they have for judging them unworthy of belief? Here we have visions which were not merely numerous but also manifest; they were not fabricated after the event, but announced beforehand and confirmed by the event. Nor was this attested by the obscure credibility of some private individual, but committed to writing with the consenting judgment of an entire synod; and had they been false, these writings would have remained as perpetual monuments to the affair—writings, as Jerome says, clearer than the sun. I do not see what more they could desire to establish the factual truth of the matter, provided that they wished to judge impartially and not deprive human beings of absolutely all credibility.

[Col. 0019B] § 20.—Visions of this sort were so familiar to Cyprian that he received them even in the exercise of ecclesiastical discipline and expected still others thereafter. Thus, concerning Florentius Pupianus, he says that if he “had made the fullest satisfaction, they could take account of his communion”; yet, he continues:

> “The consideration and fear of divine judgment still remain among us, so that I must first consult my Lord whether by his manifestation and admonition he permits peace to be given to you and you to be admitted to the communion of his Church. For I remember what has already been shown to me—or rather, what was commanded by divine and dominical authority to a servant who obeys and fears. Among the other things which he deigned to show and reveal, he also added these words”—they were undoubtedly words of Christ in the vision which follows—“and so, he who does not believe Christ when he [Col. 0019C] appoints a priest afterward begins to believe him when he avenges the priest”  
> (*Letter* LXIX).

Divine revelations were so frequent in that age that Cyprian did not dare to promise what judgment he would pronounce even concerning the repentant Pupianus, lest perhaps something different should be commanded by God. He therefore intimated that God must first be consulted, so that he might await God’s punishment upon the rebel—punishment plainly of the kind which learned men admit to have accompanied apostolic censures.

Again, concerning the presbyters who had communicated with the lapsed without consulting him, Cyprian says:

> “I shall employ the warning by which the Lord commands me that, for the present, they be prohibited from offering,” etc.  
> (*Letter* X).

§ 21.—It is therefore clear that all matters of greater importance which concerned the public condition of the Church were foretold by visions of this kind. Celerinus the confessor was appointed reader [Col. 0019D] by Cyprian (*Letter* XXXIV). Since, out of humility, he hesitated to give his consent to the Church, he was compelled by God’s own admonition and exhortation in a vision during the night not to refuse.

Nor was the most holy man left without a warning concerning his own martyrdom: it was indeed a dream, but a prophetic and altogether unmistakable one. On the first day that he stayed in his place of exile at Curubis, his death—and even the very manner of his martyrdom—was represented by a prophetic symbol. He asked for and received a delay of one day, so that he might arrange his affairs in due order, perhaps those of the Church. In the prophetic idiom of Daniel and the Apocalypse, that day signified a year. The event corresponded with the utmost exactitude. Pontius reports that [Col. 0020A] after the completion of a year Cyprian was crowned on the very day on which this had been shown to him a year earlier (*Life of Cyprian*).

What do we doubt here? The dream? Pontius, a member of his household and his companion in exile, received the account from Cyprian himself. Pontius? But the matter had already become known to everyone before the day of the martyrdom, so that Pontius could not have invented anything even if he had wished to do so:

> “For in the intervening time,” he says, “his impending suffering was known with certainty by everyone”  
> (Pontius, ibid.).

Moreover, Pontius published these things while Cyprian’s memory was still fresh, when many of Cyprian’s enemies still survived who were hostile to his name—pagans, the lapsed, rivals, and even heretics themselves. Do they think it probable that these men would have remained asleep and allowed the account of the event to pass unchallenged, if it were false and so easy to refute?

Do we therefore doubt [Col. 0020B] the credibility of the dream? Yet its fulfillment, most manifest and beyond every objection, confirmed it. Accordingly, even if those other explicit testimonies we have examined concerning the occurrence of visions had been lacking, the Cyprianic visions alone would nevertheless have sufficed to establish their own credibility and thereby to commend the cause of the entire Christian religion.

§ 22.—In Cyprian’s final years, namely during the pontificate of Xystus, that Dionysius of Alexandria whom we mentioned above records a vision through which, he says, he was confirmed in reading the books of heretics. For he writes as follows in his letter to Philemon, a presbyter of the Roman Church: “A divinely sent vision came to me and strengthened me; and a word addressed to me expressly commanded me, saying: ‘Read everything that may come into your hands, for you are capable of correcting and testing each thing, [Col. 0020C] and from the beginning this has been for you the cause of your faith’” (in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VII, 7). Eusebius dates the beginning of his own times from the end of the period of this Dionysius (*Ecclesiastical History*, VII, 32). Since he thought it worth recording in his history how long the succession of prophetic gifts continued, he plainly implies that by his own time it had ceased. Accordingly, only after the time of Constantine did teachers first inquire into the reason for its cessation, although even then they did not acknowledge that those gifts had ceased altogether. But I believe that before Constantine there was no one who thought that they had ceased, much less anyone who considered it necessary to investigate the reason for their cessation.

§ 23.—Another point must also be observed, one that contributes greatly to commending the visions of that age [Col. 0020D]: although they were generally presented at night and to persons asleep, they were nevertheless not kept within the private confidence of individuals alone, but were openly proclaimed before the face of the Church at the first opportunity. It is clear that this practice was observed from the very times of the apostles. Those prophecies mentioned in the Epistle to the Corinthians belonged entirely to ecclesiastical assemblies. Hence the great confusion in those gatherings: several spoke at the same time and did not wait for their turns to prophesy; they exercised gifts by which the Church could not be edified, as when those possessing the gift of tongues used it without the gift of interpretation; and even women—prophetesses, of course—prophesied in gatherings of men contrary to the decorum of their sex, [Col. 0021A] and without veils, perhaps with disheveled hair, after the manner of Sibyls. Nor was it otherwise when Agabus foretold the worldwide famine that occurred under the emperor Claudius. Warned by that prediction, even before the famine itself occurred, they immediately provided monetary assistance, in precisely the same manner as we have already seen Cyprian taking measures against a similarly predicted persecution that was still in the future (Acts XI, 28–30). For public calamities, or at least events concerning public persons, were generally the subject matter of prophecies of this kind. Agabus foretold these bonds of St. Paul (Acts XXI, 10–11). Other disciples also foretold them, v. 4; “the Spirit in every city” (*pneuma kata polin*) foretold them as well, ch. XX, 23—that is, as I judge, the “spiritual persons” (*pneumatikoi*) of the individual churches, which even in that age were distributed city by city. [Col. 0021B] So too, finally, the errors of the last times were foretold (I Tim. IV). In that passage also I understand “the Spirit” to mean the prophets of the assemblies. When it says that they foretold these things “expressly” (*rhētōs*), it plainly implies that these things were foretold in explicit words, contrary to the usual manner of prophecies, which were generally wrapped in symbols extremely difficult to understand. It is at least highly probable that no prophecies of private persons were accepted unless those persons had proved themselves under public examination. We have certainly seen Ignatius exercising his office publicly. The prophets of that same age—St. John, pseudo-Esdras, who wished to assume the person of a true prophet, and Hermas—were commanded to write their prophecies for public use. In Cyprian’s time also they communicated their visions openly and before the face of the Church. We have already shown that the vision granted to Cyprian himself [Col. 0021C] in exile became known to everyone, as did those concerning the approaching persecution. This can also be inferred from the exceedingly abrupt manner in which the visions are mentioned, both in this letter, in Epistle XL concerning the five presbyters, and in Epistle LXIX concerning Florentius Pupianus. For he merely touched upon them and never set out any one of them in sequence (*kathexēs*), as though recalling a matter already very well known to everyone and therefore requiring no narrative.

§ 24.—Since this was so, it appeared that excellent provision had been made against any deceit of impostors being imposed upon the faithful. First of all, no one could be admitted to this office unless he enjoyed the highest reputation and his life was entirely free from every suspicion of fraud and cunning. Thus it came about that, once every suspicion concerning the prophet had been removed, judgment had to be passed solely upon his prophecy. [Col. 0021D] Moreover, so that this duty of judgment might be performed with the greatest possible accuracy, excellent safeguards were available in public. Other prophets were present, as were judges of prophets, endowed with the gift of discerning spirits and doubtless themselves of wholly unimpeachable reputation. If a prophecy conflicted with any one of these, then, since it was acknowledged that the same Spirit of God could not contradict himself, it plainly followed that there was now room for suspicion. For although it was certain that all gifts of the divine Spirit were equally infallible, it was nevertheless also certain—with respect to what are called the grounds of credibility—that there were stronger reasons for believing one person inspired than another, and that it was just for the less credible person to be judged by the more credible. As regards the suspicion of fraud, moreover, [Col. 0022A] nothing was more foreign to it than the age of children, whom, as we have already seen, prophesied in Cyprian’s century.

§ 25.—Fraud having thus been excluded, other arguments were nevertheless available by which it could be proved that a prophecy had proceeded from God as its author. Either the prophet confirmed that he had been sent by God through the performance of another miracle—what the writers of the Old Testament call the “sign of the prophet”—or he proved by arguments intrinsic to the prophecy that it had emanated from God. If he wished to establish his authority by a miracle, he would necessarily possess another gift; this, however, is not necessary under the economy of the Gospel. There were two kinds of intrinsic arguments intended especially to prove that the revelation surpassed the powers of nature and therefore had to be attributed to the author of nature alone. Prophets revealed either the hidden [Col. 0022B] thoughts of human beings or contingent future events. Both of these, especially according to the principles of that age, belonged to God alone and surpassed every power of created beings. The former certainly did, because God alone is the “knower of hearts” (*kardiognōstēs*), the searcher of things and hearts, before whom all things are naked and “laid open” (*tetrachēlismena*). Consequently, no one could search the hidden things of God except the Spirit of God (I Cor. II, 11). The Apostle also calls the Spirit a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart (Heb. IV, 12). Therefore, when a person revealed the thoughts of another, once every suspicion of fraud had been removed, he was believed to have been inspired by no spirit other than the divine Spirit.

§ 26.—That there were among the “spiritual persons” (*pneumatikoi*) of the Church some who were also endowed with this gift is clear from the Apostle, I Cor. XIV, 24–25: “But if,” he says, “all prophesy, and an unbeliever or unlearned person enters, he is convicted by all and judged by all. For the secrets of his heart are made manifest; and so, falling upon his face, he will worship God, declaring that God is truly among you.” In the case of this unbeliever it was certain that nothing could have been arranged by collusion; it was therefore absolutely certain that whoever thus disclosed his thoughts had learned them only through the inspiration of the divine Spirit. This grace is frequently mentioned in the history of the Savior (Matt. IX, 2, 4; XII, 25; Luke V, 22; VI, 8; XI, 17), from whom the Church received “grace in place of grace” (*charin anti charitos*). St. Peter employed the same gift in the cases of Ananias and Sapphira, and also in that of Simon Magus. Concerning Simon he says: “Your heart is not right before God” (Acts VIII, 21). Again: “For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness [Col. 0022D] and the bond of iniquity.” St. Paul did so even more clearly in the case of Elymas the magician (Acts XIII, 9–10). For, being full of the Holy Spirit, he rebuked not only what Elymas had done but also his deceitful disposition, although Elymas had previously been unknown to him. We have seen Ignatius employ it as well, when he was the first to bring the secret counsels of the schismatics to light. Indeed, I do not know whether this may perhaps have been the gift of the “discernment of spirits” (*diakrisis pneumatōn*) mentioned by the Apostle. The sacred writers certainly used related words in this very matter of the Spirit. He is called “discerning of thoughts” (*kritikos enthymēseōn*), etc., Heb. IV, 12, and “one who examines” (*anakritikos*), I Cor. XIV, 24; and indeed the use of “spirit” to mean the heart and its thoughts is too frequent for the reader to require instruction on the point.

[Col. 0023A] § 27.—There were, moreover, two classes of persons whose thoughts were thus disclosed. Prophets might reveal the thoughts of other prophets with whom they themselves had no communication, from which a powerful confirmation of the predicted matter arose. Thus, concerning Timothy, there was not one prophecy but many mutually concordant prophecies; and so too there were the prophecies concerning St. Paul by “spirits city by city” (*pneumatōn kata poleis*), as we saw above. Greater faith had to be placed in these persons because they appeared to know not merely human secrets but divine mysteries as well. There were, however, two kinds of human thoughts that might be manifested by this gift: those of the faithful and those of unbelievers. If an unbeliever had infiltrated ecclesiastical assemblies with malicious intent—whether in order to betray them, expose them to ridicule, or gratify some worldly attachment—the fact itself was disclosed by revelation of the Spirit. Hence it came about that, if he belonged to the class of persons whom the Greeks call “fair-minded” (*eugnōmonountes*), he would not so much grow angry at those who exposed him as be carried away in admiration of them, as is implied in the passage of the Epistle to the Corinthians cited above. The thoughts of the faithful, on the other hand, were disclosed if some were to be enrolled among the clergy, as in the example of Timothy; if they had committed some fraud, as in the case of Ananias and Sapphira; if they had laid an ambush, as the Lord himself exposed Judas when he was plotting against him; or, finally, perhaps if they had committed any other secret crime. For this is precisely what St. Peter reproved in Ananias and Sapphira (Acts V, 4, 9): that they had dared to lie not to men but to God, and that they were putting the Spirit of the Lord to the test. It was as though he had reproached them because, although they had joined themselves [Col. 0023C] to assemblies in which they themselves acknowledged the gifts of the Spirit—including, among the others, the gift by which secrets were revealed—they nevertheless hoped that their hidden crimes could remain concealed and that they would commit them with impunity. This undoubtedly struck them with a great fear even of secret crimes, when they understood that thereafter no hiding places would be secure, v. 5. Nor is there anything in this very form of reasoning that even atheists could justly censure.

§ 28.—There was, however, another argument, and one intrinsic to the gift of prophecy itself, by which the ancients confirmed the credibility of their prophecies: namely, the prediction of contingent future events. Such a prediction was understood to be certain and to have God as its author once the event itself had confirmed it. This line of argument [Col. 0023D] was entirely certain according to Christian principles. God himself issues this challenge in Isaiah (Isa. XLI, 23). Nor, according to Christian principles, could this foreknowledge of contingent future events in fact be attributed to anyone other than God. For even if we grant that there are many events that do not exceed the powers of created beings, nevertheless, given the providence maintained by Christians, there were certain events that had no cause determined by nature from which they could be known beforehand. Indeed, events arising not from any single cause but from the agreement and combination of them all—as was true of most events concerning the public—were rendered uncertain either by the failure of a single cause or by the intervention of a single cause. Consequently, [Col. 0024A] they could be known as future only through that cause to which the combination of all other causes was in fact subject. Christians believed that cause to be none other than the first, best, and greatest God.

§ 29.—First, they believed that the world had not been made by chance, as the Epicureans maintained, but by a definite providence, and that it continued to be governed by the same providence by which it had been made. Second, they believed that free will was subject to no other cause except God alone. Consequently, they entirely rejected all notions of fate distinct from the decree of the supreme God: whether the Epicurean conception derived from the influence of material causes, or the astrologers’ conception deduced from either the motion [Col. 0024B] or the causal power of the heavenly stars. If, therefore, they made free will subject to God alone, it plainly follows that the certainty of those events which depended either upon free will itself or upon some condition to be posited by free will had in fact to be derived from God alone. As for events arising from material causes, they could acknowledge some mechanical force belonging to the universal motion. Yet they did not acknowledge it in such a manner that any created being with whom we have dealings could either know contingent future events from that universal concurrence of motion or disclose them to us. Certainly none could disclose them unless it were an intellectual being, whom we Christians call an angel. But they assigned the angels who deal with us to definite provinces of created things, and believed the *Logos* to be the presiding power over all provinces. Consequently, none of the angels with whom we deal, as I have said, [Col. 0024C] was placed over the universal motion in such a way that he could judge from his own causal sphere concerning the occurrence of contingent future events. Nor did Christians acknowledge them to be so incorporeal that they could behold all created things in the mirror of the Creator. They did not believe that angels knew all created things, except those that God had deigned to reveal to them; nor did they believe that God had in fact deigned to reveal all things to them. The Apostle testifies that the angels learned from the Church the mystery of the Incarnation (Eph. III, 10). We also have Ignatius as our authority that three things remained hidden from the devil before the Incarnation (Ignatius, *Epistle to the Ephesians*, § 19). But there is no leisure to dwell upon each of these matters.

§ 30.—Meanwhile it is clear that, given this hypothesis, no one can know contingent future events—whether dependent upon free will or upon the universal [Col. 0024D] motion—unless the supreme God reveals them. But even if they had known that universal motion, they could not in that way have judged with certainty concerning events of this sort. For they did not believe that the entire world was governed by God so mechanically that God neither wished nor was accustomed to intervene sometimes against that universal motion, and more often apart from it: against it, certainly, in miracles; apart from it, whenever he wished to hear even the ordinary prayers of the elect. For the prayers of the devout, especially for temporal goods, would generally be futile if God could accomplish nothing outside the universal course of nature without a miracle. Miracles of this kind would then have to be performed as often as the prayers [Col. 0025A] of the good were to be heard. But if God both wills and is accustomed to accomplish many things apart from that universal motion, it follows that, even if the latter were perfectly known, nothing certain could be pronounced concerning contingent future events.

§ 31.—But even if these matters did not by their nature surpass created powers, and yet could not be known by a creature unless God revealed them, this alone is abundantly sufficient to ensure that, whenever they became known to human beings, they should rightly be attributed to the supreme God. For the question to be asked is not whether God himself revealed them to human beings, or some creature subject to him did so at his command and with his permission, but whether some opposing power could do so against his will. For in this lies the danger of error. Yet, given the hypothesis we have set forth, it was certain [Col. 0025B] that revelations of this kind could not come from any opposing power. For there was no creature that could know them against God’s will; nor was it probable that God would reveal to hostile angels—who were bitter enemies of him and his people—things that were not owed to their nature and could not be known unless he revealed them. It follows, therefore, that if he employed the ministry of angels in making a revelation known to human beings, he would certainly employ none but good angels. Nor was there any reason to fear that they would not discharge the office entrusted to them with the greatest diligence and fidelity. Thus it was established that these true revelations concerning contingent future events could have no author except God.

§ 32.—Although the truth of the hypothesis from which, as we have said, these just and legitimate consequences follow was proved by the authority of those who taught it—an authority itself commended by other miracles—nevertheless, the very probability of the consequences, and their apt coherence with one another and with the phenomena, also contributes something to establishing the truth of the premises. For in causes of this sort, which no reasoning of ours can reach *a priori*, people seek only to frame for themselves some hypothesis that suitably agrees with the phenomena, and they seek no other proof of it than that suitable agreement with the phenomena; they judge that hypothesis truer which corresponds more aptly and to a greater number of phenomena. Thus they judge concerning the motions of the heavenly spheres, the seas, and the winds, concerning the nature of the magnet, and concerning all other things of this kind. Yet the principle of providence is no less hidden from us [Col. 0025D] than the principle of the heavenly spheres. Nor does this Christian hypothesis concerning providence agree less aptly with the phenomena than does that of Ptolemy, or even that of Copernicus, or of any other astronomer, with the phenomena of those motions. On the contrary, even the Christians most ignorant of nature were far more certain in their prophecies concerning contingent future events than even the most learned astrologers were in their judgments. From this it also followed that it was far more probable that these things came from God than that they should be traced back to any concurrence of natural causes.

§ 33.—Once the truth of past prophecies had thus been proved by their fulfillment, the authority of the prophet then supplied grounds for similarly expecting the fulfillment [Col. 0026A] of his other prophecies. The more frequently events corresponded to his prophecies, the more certainly it was established that these things were to be attributed not to chance but to definite causes. There were, however, two kinds of prophecy: some were clear and easy to understand, so that no doubt could arise concerning the prophet’s true meaning; others, according to the customary idiom of prophecy, were wrapped in symbols and riddles, so that it was difficult to understand what the judgment of the prophet or of the divine power might be. The latter were to be judged most securely from the truth of the former. If all had been obscure, as in the oracles of Loxian Apollo and in the ravings of our present-day enthusiasts, there would have been no intrinsic grounds of credibility; and unless perhaps extrinsic grounds supplied their place, however true they might have been, [Col. 0026B] they certainly possessed no mark of truth by which they could be distinguished from falsehoods, and therefore imposed no obligation upon others to believe them true. But if some were perspicuous, it was then easy to judge what should be held concerning the rest. If the event had failed to correspond to even a single perspicuous prophecy, it plainly followed that the rest were not to be trusted either; rather, they were to be attributed either to natural enthusiasm or to some other spirit, more likely diabolical than divine.

Thus Asterius Urbanus refutes the prophecies of Maximilla (in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, V, 16). She had predicted that “wars” (*polemoi*) and “disturbances” (*akatastasiai*) were imminent; yet after thirteen full years had already elapsed, there had been neither a particular nor a universal war anywhere on earth, and Christians had continued to enjoy a firm and stable peace. From this he concludes that all credibility must be denied her. But if the things predicted had occurred, then the prophet’s credibility was established to a greater or lesser degree according to the frequency of such fulfillments. This line of argument was altogether most sound, and I do not see what the buffoons among today’s atheists can censure in it, much less ridicule; nor what similar evidence the fanatics born yesterday or the day before can offer for the prophecies they now hawk about—whether they belong to those who are classed under the common name of Protestants, or to those whom papist theologians call mystics. Neither group employs extrinsic arguments: either miracles performed openly, publicly, and before the eyes of unbelievers, or the testimonies of other prophets whom we also acknowledge. Neither group employs intrinsic testimonies: either the disclosed secrets of unbelievers’ hearts or predictions of contingent future events clearly made and published long before their fulfillment.

§ 34.—Meanwhile, readers must be warned that not everything belonging to prophets is therefore to be attributed to the prophetic spirit. I do not believe that even the Jews taught this concerning their prophets, nor the Greeks concerning the Pythian prophetesses, nor other pagans—the Phoenicians and Egyptians—concerning their prophets, nor indeed any people who acknowledged prophets. Elisha did not know of the Shunammite woman’s misfortune. The most holy Apostle also uttered some things by a human spirit. A prophet’s credibility, therefore, must not be called into doubt if some statements spoken in a merely human manner escaped him—that is, in matters which he himself attributed not to the Spirit of God but rather to his own spirit. Thus, if the Apostle had erred in those matters in which he warned that he, and not the Lord, was giving counsel, [Col. 0027A] this ought not to prejudice his other prophecies. Nor is the distinction between these two as uncertain as the profane author of the *Theologico-Political Treatise* wished. Where the sacred writers had inserted a qualification, that very qualification was a sign that only the matters to which the qualification applied were to be excepted, while the remainder were to be understood as coming from another spirit. Thus, because the Apostle had thought it necessary to warn explicitly in his written epistles whenever he set forth something from his own spirit, it plainly follows that the divine Spirit must be held to be the author of the remainder. Conversely, because Ignatius expressly declared the Spirit to be the author of those things that he uttered with the divine Spirit as their author, it likewise follows that, excepting these, the remainder must be attributed to Ignatius’s private spirit.

[Col. 0027B] § 35.—Some also believe that true prophets inspired by the Spirit of God were left to their own spirit in communicating what had been revealed, so that they might announce it to others according to their own capacity, which was more cultivated and polished in one person than in another. If, therefore, in matters noted only incidentally and contributing nothing to the principal purpose of the prophecy, they erred either through a lapse of their own memory or while accommodating themselves to the mistaken but nevertheless accepted preconceptions of their hearers—preconceptions more suitable for their arguments than the revealed matters themselves, since the latter were to be proved and the former could be used as concessions—if, I say, they went astray in such things, not even that error should be imputed to the prophetic spirit. Thus, when the Evangelist cites Jeremiah instead of Zechariah; when the Apostle assigns 450 years to the Judges [Col. 0027C] and forty to Saul; when St. Luke records an uncertain number of stadia, and St. Paul an uncertain number of persons baptized—these cases plainly imply that details of this kind were left to the writers’ human capacities, and that there is consequently no reason to refer them to the divine Spirit.

§ 36.—There is also another instance in which errors could creep in not only among those who heard prophecies, but even among the prophets themselves: namely, in the interpretation of obscure prophecies. For certain prophecies were, by a definite purpose of the Spirit, so obscure that they could not be understood without another revelation; thus the first revelations seemed to have been given for no other purpose than to arouse the curiosity and diligence of the holy prophets in obtaining [Col. 0027D] the second. We see this especially in Daniel, where second visions are frequently mentioned as interpretations of the first. If, therefore, before receiving the second visions he had ventured to interpret the first, an interpretation of that kind would have had to be attributed wholly to a human and not a divine spirit; consequently, any error in it would have been most unjustly referred to the Holy Spirit.

§ 37.—The ancient Christians held the same view concerning written prophecies as well: wherever they were obscure, they could by no means be understood with certainty unless the same Spirit by whom they had been dictated revealed their meaning anew. We should not therefore be surprised at the errors of the ancients concerning the nearness of the end of the world. For the Spirit had not revealed it in explicit words. They inferred it rather from the frequent mention of “the last times” in Old Testament prophecies whenever evangelical matters were mentioned, although those expressions could quite appropriately be understood of the final period of the Jewish economy. It is altogether inequitable for us to impute to the Spirit those human errors which the Spirit himself had not undertaken to correct, and which those inspired by that Spirit did not themselves assert that the Spirit had undertaken to correct. Meanwhile, the sufficiently certain rule of judgment that we have described was available. For if the reliability of even those prophecies that were perspicuous, offered no escape through obscurity, and were presented by the “spiritual persons” (*pneumatikoi*) in the name of the Spirit was invariably established and nowhere contradicted itself, this was in itself a sufficiently manifest proof both that those who predicted them were inspired by a spirit and that this spirit was most truthful and therefore divine. Consequently, they were likewise to be believed in other manifest matters expressly presented in the name of the Spirit. If, by contrast, the event had disproved the credibility of the perspicuous prophecies, that was sufficient to abolish the credibility of all the remaining prophecies of the same kind.

§ 38.—Thus far, unless I am mistaken, we have rightly confirmed the credibility of obscure prophecies from manifest ones when those obscure and manifest prophecies belonged to the same prophet. But the reader may perhaps ask, and not without reason, how obscure prophecies were to be confirmed from manifest ones when the prophecies belonged to different persons—so that one prophet had manifest prophecies, while another had only obscure ones and none manifest. [Col. 0028C] A doubtful prophet could indeed be commended by the testimony of an unquestioned prophet. Yet there was also another mode of proof, derived from the common unity of the Spirit. For according to the principles of that age it was legitimate to argue thus: those who belonged to one and the same communion possessed one spirit, derived from the same sacraments—that is, the same channels of grace—and through the power of the same institution.

They concluded that the spirit of a single communion was one, not merely on the general ground that it had been conferred upon them in like manner through the same sacraments. Since these sacraments were the symbols of certain definite and lawful covenants concerning the conferral of that very Spirit, they could certainly bind only those whose symbols they were. Thus an evil spirit could not enter human beings unless they in turn had entered into a covenant with it; [Col. 0028D] nor could human beings enter into a covenant with it through symbols instituted by the good Spirit. They also concluded it because the Spirit itself was the bond of unity within the same communion. Therefore, just as internal communion was to be presumed from that external communion, so it also followed that those who participated in the same sacraments participated equally in one and the same Spirit.

Given, therefore, some preternatural motion which could proceed neither from a bodily affection nor from natural enthusiasm, but had plainly to be attributed to some spirit, it had first to be supposed that this was no other spirit than the one operating in the other members of the same communion. Thus one could rightly judge [Col. 0029A] the spirit of this member also from the operations or “energies” (*energeiai*) of the other members. If the spirit was good in the others, it certainly could not be evil in this one. The arguments perhaps lacking in this member, by which it could be distinguished whether he should be numbered among the good or rather among the evil, were nevertheless not lacking in other members of the same mystical body. Thus one ultimately had to conclude that all the gifts of the other members—and not only their gifts, but also the arguments by which this very gift had been authenticated in others—had likewise to be brought forward in support of this person’s credibility, however destitute he might be of arguments of his own.

§ 39.—Yet this also followed: prophecies of this obscure kind possessed no support except within the unity of the Church. [Col. 0029B] For just as they had nothing in themselves by which they could be commended, so, once unity had been violated, those extrinsic arguments I have mentioned did nothing to establish their credibility. If a prophet had called another prophet as a witness, even that witness was not held competent outside unity. As for the gifts and manifestations of others, they had no bearing upon a prophet outside unity. Indeed, according to these principles, every prophecy outside the Church was suspect for that very reason: it could not come from the good Spirit because it was outside unity.

For since God had instituted the sacraments as means of conferring the Spirit, it was necessary that he should will that whoever refused to employ the means instituted by him would not obtain the benefits attainable through those means. [Col. 0029C] If he had not willed this, there would have been no obligation to employ the means. And since those means instituted by God are nothing other than symbols of unity—for we are baptized into one body and, by partaking of that one bread, grow together into one body—he seems thereby to have indicated that he is unwilling to confer his Spirit upon any except those established in unity. However that may be, it is certain that this opinion actually prevailed among the ancients: the Spirit of God belonged to none but those united within the Church. Thus, in this very argument concerning spiritual gifts, they inferred that the spirit present among those who were not united was not that Spirit of God who is the bond of unity. We observed the Apostle employing this very line of argument in the second, as yet unpublished, part of our work on schism. They call baptism, through which the Spirit is conferred, the laver of regeneration. Who could doubt [Col. 0029D] that among those who have not been reborn there is no principle of spiritual life? Indeed, somewhat later Christians applied exorcisms to those about to be baptized, thereby plainly implying once again that the spirit among those outside unity was altogether diabolical.

Would that those who today entertain such exalted opinions of their own spirit outside unity would seriously weigh these matters. At least they would see that, in their pretenses concerning the Spirit, they possess none of that affinity with the earliest Christians which they so loudly boast and advertise. There is just reason to suspect that those who employ means of conferring the Spirit other than those instituted by God possess a spirit other than the divine Spirit, especially when the arguments intrinsic to prophecy itself that I have mentioned are lacking. So much for the credibility of ancient prophecies; in these I see nothing [Col. 0030A] that modern atheists can justly censure.

§ 40.—Concerning visions, however, another point should be observed in passing—one which I do not know whether others have noticed—namely, that they were proper to the young. I infer this from that celebrated passage of Joel: “Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy; your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions” (Joel II, 28). Dreams are plainly assigned to old men just as visions are to the young. That violent agitation of the bodily humors, of course, could be endured only in the vigor of youth. For in visions there threatened an exceedingly great terror arising from the things seen; even now, those who have dealings with apparitions experience this terror so powerfully that wasting and pallor overtake them and gradually reduce them to an extremely diseased condition of body.

In addition there is the extremely violent contortion of the state of possession (*katochē*) [Col. 0030B]: a savage countenance, burning eyes, foaming mouths, and the exceedingly labored gasping of heaving breasts. Such, indeed, was the condition among the prophets of the nations: in Lucan the Pythian priestess approached the tripod most unwillingly, and some prophetesses were killed by the very violence of the agitation. Thus Lucan writes (*Civil War*, book V, v. 116):

> For if a god enters beneath the breast,  
> Untimely death is either the punishment  
> Or the price of receiving the divine power; for under the goad  
> And surge of frenzy, the human frame gives way,  
> And the assaults of the gods convulse frail souls.

And Valerius Maximus says concerning the Delphic oracle: “Thus, although sure responses are sought from it by those who consult it, an excessive draught of the divine Spirit proves fatal to those who render them” (Book I, ch. 8, Roman Example 10).

The agitation of pseudo-prophets and enthusiasts [Col. 0030C] was indeed far more violent, so that from this very feature Catholics judged that true prophets should be distinguished from those of the Montanists. There was no madness in true prophets, no such violent convulsion of possession (*katochē*). Rather, they remained self-possessed and uttered their predictions prudently and knowingly. Nevertheless, the terror caused by the things seen was difficult for the frailty of human nature to endure. Daniel’s spirit shuddered (Dan. VII, 15); he collapsed to the ground (VIII, 19); “no strength remained in him, and his appearance was changed within him, and he withered away, nor did he retain any strength” (X, 8); “he lay prostrate upon his face, and his countenance clung to the ground” (ibid., 9); “he stood trembling” (ibid., 11); “in the vision his bodily frame was dissolved, and no strength remained in him, and even his breath was stopped” (ibid., 17). The terror described in Job (Job IV, 13–14) and in Abraham (Gen. XV, 12) is likewise none other than the terror of a prophetic vision. There is therefore no reason to wonder that these experiences were more tolerable to the young than to the old. Accordingly, even among the pagans Tiresias teaches that possession (*katochē*) belongs to the young. For in Seneca he says (*Oedipus*, v. 29):

> If I possessed the vigor of youth . . . .

And were my blood warm, I would shake God from my breast.

Our Cyprian, having distinguished nocturnal visions, which should rather be classed as the dreams of old men, from daytime prophecies, ascribed the latter to the innocent age of children (Epistle X): that is, plainly, possession (*κατοχή*), [Col. 0031A] for this is what his words transcribed above imply—to be filled with the Holy Spirit and carried away from the senses, a condition called ecstasy (*extasis*) in those disputes of the Church against the Montanists. Accordingly, just as we learn from Pontius that dreams were presented to Cyprian near the end of his life, so, if any of the visions he mentions were revealed to Cyprian himself, it will follow that he experienced, not long after his youth, when his age was already declining toward old age, what is certainly most probable. For if he had reached advanced old age, it could scarcely have happened that he would not have become known to Tertullian himself, although we nowhere read that Cyprian did more than study his books.

§ 41.—I readily admit that even in Cyprian’s age there were people who treated dreams and visions as objects of ridicule. But what sort of people they were he himself discloses in his letter to Florentius [Col. 0031B] Pupianus. “Although,” he says (Ep. LXIX), “I know that dreams seem ridiculous and visions foolish to certain people—but surely to those who prefer to believe accusations against priests rather than to believe a priest.” He plainly implies that those who thought in this way were ill-disposed toward the Church. That such people should think so was certainly not surprising.
