For virtually contemporary with prophecy itself there existed that class of people whom Scripture describes, who attempted through laughter and jokes, mockery and biting remarks, to expose religion to ridicule when they could never accomplish the same thing by arguments. And indeed the prophets exhibited gestures somewhat foreign to ordinary human practice, which ridiculous men could readily portray as though the prophets themselves were also ridiculous. Joseph’s brothers called him a dreamer [Col. 0031C] (Gen. XXXVII, 19), a fact which Cyprian himself had also observed. The commanders of the army called mad the prophet who had been sent by Elisha and had promised Jehu the kingdom of Israel; yet they did not disregard the oracle he delivered. Thus, although they had called him mad in name, they nevertheless judged that he should by no means seriously be regarded as mad. And those frequent cautions, even in apostolic times, against despising or extinguishing prophecies sufficiently imply how prone people were to do the very thing against which they so often had necessarily to be warned. Nor, certainly, was anything else to be expected in those times, when the prophets were so stiff-necked and so disruptive of public order: when several spoke at once; when prophetesses preached in assemblies [Col. 0031D] of men, even with their heads uncovered, contrary to the modesty of their sex; when prophets displayed their gifts without any regard for edification or usefulness, and at last had to be restrained by ecclesiastical discipline from continuing to act in this way in the future. These things were certainly to be charged as faults against the prophets themselves, not against their prophetic gifts. For the spirit which they possessed is said to be subject to them [Col. 0032A], lest those things be said to have occurred through its irresistible impulse. Yet we experience today, among a similar class of adversaries, how readily contempt for officeholders is transformed into contempt for the office; how readily and eagerly they seize upon such minor peculiarities as may occur elsewhere contrary to common opinion—opinions which are certainly most unfair standards of what is good and honorable, to say nothing harsher—in order to bring contempt upon persons whose consciences are troubled by the reverence properly owed to their office; and likewise how readily they allow themselves to be swept aside in this manner, so that they do not think the merits of the cause itself should even be investigated whenever they have formed a less honorable opinion of the persons of the prophets. No one, however, will concede that such people are impartial judges.

§ 42.—But if, even in the times of those prophets [Col. 0032B] who had produced the most certain proofs of their prophecies, there were nevertheless critics of this sort, it is certainly unsurprising that such people should also have appeared in Cyprian’s time, when the Epicureans had already gained influence among the philosophers and treated everything beyond the natural order with ridicule. This one point was sufficient: if any who had understood more deeply the prophecies we have mentioned—and who had no interest in having them judged false—existed, none of them called those prophecies into doubt. We have seen, moreover, that Cyprian’s contemporaries acknowledged prophetic gifts in the Church, men who were considered the most learned of that age and the most experienced in ecclesiastical affairs. Nor is it probable that such strict discipline could have prevailed in the Church unless the immediate presence of the divine power in the Church had been established by the clearest signs. [Col. 0032C] For if they could convict that claim to the prophetic spirit of falsehood, the credibility of all the rest would at once have begun to collapse, and there would have been no reason for them to seek the Church’s communion through the so unwelcome penance of many years—especially when there was no magistrate to compel them, while, on the contrary, there was one who supported the rebels and strove by every means to entice them into rebellion. As for the atheistic Epicureans, it has always been, and still is today, their disposition to remain content with their general hypotheses and to think that particular examples are not even worth investigating. How unfamiliar they were with ecclesiastical affairs is evident from the example of Celsus alone. Although he boastfully claimed that everything was perfectly well known to him, in matters concerning the Church he rarely hits the mark. Indeed, [Col. 0032D] it is nearly his constant practice that, although he wished to strike the Church, the charges by which he believed the Church’s cause could be undermined scarcely ever apply to anyone except heretics cast out of the Church. An excellent critic of the Church indeed, who could not even distinguish the Church from the assemblies of heretics most bitterly hostile to it!

## SECOND DISSERTATION ON THE TWENTY-FOURTH EPISTLE OF SAINT CYPRIAN, BY DODWELL: ON PRESBYTER-TEACHERS, THE TEACHER OF THE HEARERS, AND ECCLESIASTICAL EMBASSIES

[Col. 0033]

[Col. 0033A] § 1. Presbyter-teachers earlier than Cyprian, of the highest dignity in the Church.—§ 2. Contemporary with the Apostles, and derived from the Jewish Scribes and teachers.—§ 3. Their office founded upon an extraordinary gift.—§§ 4, 5, 6. That duty of teaching did not belong to all presbyters, as is commonly believed.—§ 7. In approving a teacher of the hearers, Cyprian consulted the presbyter-teachers alone.—§ 8. The hearers were the same as the catechumens.—§ 9. They also used the word “catechumens.” The origin of the name “hearers.”—§ 10. The instruction of catechumens corresponded to the mysteries.—§ 11. In Cyprian’s time the teacher of the hearers was a subdeacon. On Pantaenus, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen as catechists in the Alexandrian school.—§ 12. In Cyprian, ministers of the lower orders are sometimes included under the common name of clergy and sometimes [Col. 0033B] excluded.—§ 13. All Cyprian’s embassies, and others mentioned in his Epistles.—§ 14. In Cyprian’s age embassies were conducted by clerics, generally two at a time, and rarely by persons above the rank of subdeacon.—§ 15. Other embassies earlier than Cyprian: those of Clement of Alexandria and Irenaeus.—§ 16. The embassies of the Church of Smyrna, of Polycarp, and of Ignatius were more honorable than those of Cyprian.—§ 17. Embassies of the Apostolic age.—§ 18. Modeled upon the customs of the law of hospitality.—§ 19. Traveling apostles were received by the Churches in the same manner as provincial governors customarily were by their provincials.—§ 20. The embassies of that age were highly honorable.

§ 1.—“Or when, together with the presbyter-teachers, we carefully examined the readers [Col. 0033C], we appointed Optatus from among the readers as teacher of the hearers.” This office of the presbyter-teachers must be noted, for it did not first arise in Cyprian’s time, but was in fact handed down from the Apostles to his own day. Tertullian, who was earlier than Cyprian, mentions it (*Prescription against Heretics*, ch. 3): “What then,” he says, “if a bishop, if a deacon, if a widow, if a virgin, if a teacher, if even a martyr, has fallen away from the rule—will heresies therefore appear to possess the truth?” [Col. 0034A] Here he mentions this gift in such a way as plainly to distinguish it from the ecclesiastical offices of the episcopate and diaconate. For the items that follow are gifts belonging to persons, not to offices; and these very gifts are distinguished from one another by rank in such a way that the teacher occupies the rank immediately below the martyr and is superior in dignity not only to widows but also to virgins. The same author says later: “Is there, then, some brother who is a teacher, endowed with the grace of knowledge?” etc. Saturus the martyr, a contemporary of Tertullian, mentions Aspasius, a presbyter-teacher who was at variance with Bishop Optatus (*Acts of Perpetua and Felicity*, in the *Vision of Saturus*). Hermas mentions them in various places. Book I, Vision 3: “Those square and white stones which fit together at the joints are the apostles, bishops, teachers, and ministers who entered in the clemency of God, exercised the episcopate, taught, and ministered [Col. 0034B] in holiness and modesty to God’s elect, both those who have fallen asleep and those who still remain; and they always agreed with them, maintained peace among themselves, and listened to one another.”

It is remarkable that Blondel should infer from this passage that the bishops and teachers were the same persons, as though the words “exercised the episcopate” were to be referred to the teachers and not rather to the bishops who had just preceded them—especially since the words “and taught” also occur there and correspond most appropriately to the teachers. That bishops were, for the most part, equipped with this gift is certainly very probable, because of the Apostle’s precept that a bishop must be “apt to teach” (*διδακτικός*), I Tim. III, 2; II Tim. II, 24; and consequently that the presbyter known to be endowed with that gift was especially likely to be advanced to the honor of the episcopate. [Col. 0034C] Yet we have already seen examples of presbyter-teachers as well, and therefore it is not necessary that anyone who was a teacher should also be a bishop. Blondel refers us in vain to those authors who flourished after the gift of the teaching office had died out in the Church.

But let us return to our Hermas. The same author says again, Book II, Mandate 4: “Even now, Lord, I have heard from certain teachers that there is no other repentance,” etc. Book III, Similitude 9: “The forty, however, are apostles and teachers of the preaching of the Son of God.” [Col. 0035A] Later: “And he said: Because these Apostles and teachers who preached the name of the Son of God, after dying in possession of his faith and power, preached to those who had died before them.” Again: “Concerning the eighth mountain, on which there were very many springs from which every kind of God’s creature was watered, these are those who believed the Apostles whom the Lord sent throughout the whole world to preach; and certain teachers who preached and taught chastely and sincerely,” etc. From all of these passages we also understand what that teaching was from which the teachers received their name: namely, the duty of preaching, as Hermas puts it; and also that their dignity was so great that they are generally joined with the Apostles.

[Col. 0035B] § 2.—These teachers are also frequently mentioned in Holy Scripture: Acts XIII, 1, “prophets and teachers”; I Cor. XII, “first Apostles, second prophets, third teachers,” before the other extraordinary gifts (*χαρίσματα*) of the Spirit, vv. 28, 29; Eph. IV, 11, “Apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors, and teachers.” Evangelists and pastors are inserted here; these were gifts peculiar to the New Testament and should not be dated from Pentecost, when the Spirit was poured out. For evangelists were necessary at the time when the Gospel had to be carried to foreigners. I do not know whether this occurred before the account of Cornelius; it can certainly scarcely have preceded the death of Stephen and the persecution stirred up on that occasion. The office of pastors became necessary when the Church’s alms had to be [Col. 0036C] distributed among the poor. For this very distribution is “to shepherd” (*ποιμαίνειν*), I Pet. V, 2, in accordance with what we have argued above. Thus it follows that the place immediately after the prophets must be assigned to teachers among the original gifts.

For the model of this office was transferred from the synagogue itself to the Church. The Jews likewise had their own rabbis—“guides” (*καθηγηταί*), “disputants of this age” (*συζητηταὶ τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου*), Scribes, “lawyers” (*νομικοί*), and “teachers of the Law” (*νομοδιδάσκαλοι*), for they are distinguished by all these titles—who are also called simply “teachers” (*διδάσκαλοι*), Luke II, 46. That this office was highly honorable among them is clear from Rom. II, 18–21. It was therefore necessary for the Savior to warn his disciples against aspiring to that title. Yet there is reason to suspect that this ambition, together with the office itself, also crept in among Christians, James III, 1.

[Col. 0035D] § 3.—Just as all offices of the Church in those earliest beginnings were administered through the extraordinary assistance of the Holy Spirit, it is certain that the same occurred in this office as well. This is implied by the word “gave” (*ἔδωκε*) in Eph. IV, 11, which must be referred to the passage quoted from Ps. LXVIII, 19, v. 8: “He gave gifts to men” (*Ἔδωκε δόματα τοῖς ἀνθρώποις*). Teachers, therefore, must also be counted among those “gifts” (*δόματα*). Accordingly, among the gifts (*χαρίσματα*) of the Spirit we find “teaching” (*διδασκαλία*), Rom. XII, 6, 7; “prophecy” (*προφητεία*) and “teaching” (*διδαχή*), I Cor. XIV, 6, in precisely the same form in which we saw “prophets” (*προφήτας*) and “teachers” (*διδασκάλους*) joined above. Again, in the same chapter, “teaching” (*διδαχή*), v. 26.

That the situation of the African teachers was no different is shown by the passages we cited above from Tertullian (*Prescription*, ch. 14), in which he says that the man he calls a teacher [Col. 0036A] was endowed with the grace of knowledge. For we have proved that gifts (*χαρίσματα*) of the Spirit of this kind continued down to the time of our Cyprian. I readily admit that in that age extraordinary gifts were also employed in the administration of ordinary offices. Yet we infer that this office of teachers was no less extraordinary than the gift of teaching itself, because, when gifts of this kind failed, the office itself also gradually fell into disuse. For there is no mention of it in the canons of later centuries. Nor is it anywhere joined in the New Testament with the ordinary offices of bishop, presbyter, or deacon, but rather with those extraordinary offices and powers of Apostles, prophets, and miracles, which all admit have long since ceased. Nor do the Fathers of the fourth [Col. 0036B] century and later possess even faint traces, drawn from the established customs of their own age, from which to write about the teachers’ office; rather, just like us, they conjecture from the text alone and from the writings of the ancients. Let the Independent brethren therefore consider on what grounds they judge that this office should be continued, although they themselves will not deny that the gifts upon which we have proved it rested have ceased.

§ 4.—It must also be observed that, when Cyprian mentions presbyter-teachers, he simultaneously implies that there were certainly others within the presbyterate who were not teachers. For there was no need for the bishop who wrote these words to distinguish presbyter-teachers from bishops who were likewise teachers. Nor did any persons other than presbyters have a place in the examination of those who were to be promoted into the clergy. The same is true when Saturus calls Aspasius a presbyter- [Col. 0036C] teacher. Since, therefore, we have learned from Hermas that the duty of teaching was the same as that of preaching, it plainly follows that it was not the role of every presbyter to preach in the Church, still less that it was so essential to the presbyteral office—as modern schismatics believe—that anyone who did not perform that duty should not even be regarded as a presbyter.

Nor should this be attributed to an error of more recent centuries. That the same arrangement prevailed even under the Apostles is clear from I Tim. V, 17, although some wrongly infer that those “presbyters who rule” (*προεστῶτας*) and were distinct from those “who labor in word and teaching” (*κοπιῶσιν ἐν λόγῳ καὶ διδασκαλίᾳ*) were laymen. For this inference they have no support either from the text or from the accepted customs of that age. It follows, therefore, that not even the Apostles required that gift as a prior qualification in those being ordained, and that it had no place among the gifts (*χαρίσματα*) conferred [Col. 0036D] by the laying on of hands itself. Nor did God himself—by whose direction all things were then conducted and who would undoubtedly not fail the Church in matters necessary—establish this office in such a way that this gift was absolutely necessary for its administration.

§ 5.—Furthermore, since Christians generally borrowed their own customs from the accepted practices of their age, I think there was scarcely any precedent in which the duty of teaching was necessarily joined with the priesthood. We have said that the Jews had Scribes and rabbis, undoubtedly from the priestly tribe. Yet it was very far from being the case that the whole priestly family consisted of Scribes or rabbis. The Jews perhaps [Col. 0037A] received the order of Scribes from the Egyptians. For the Egyptians had their own “sacred scribes” (*ἱερογραμματεῖς*), men most expert and learned in sacred matters, so that it is extremely probable that they were priests. Yet not all priests were on that account sacred scribes; indeed, this dignity seems to have belonged only to a few, although a third part of the Egyptian people belonged to the priestly order. The same conclusion must be reached concerning the “sacred scribes” (*ἱερογραμματεῖς*) and “sacred recorders” (*ἱερομνήμονες*) of the Athenians and other nations. Thus, if Christians had judged that these two offices, so different from one another, must nevertheless be joined together, they would necessarily have had no precedent for doing so. Yet there were very few practices, if indeed there were any at all, which Christians introduced without precedent.

§ 6.—Since, therefore, we have proved that not all presbyters were endowed with the gift [Col. 0037B] of teaching, whether by original institution or even in actual practice, it plainly follows that those who lacked that gift were not bound to teach; rather, they ought to have refrained from the duty of teaching. For this is what the Apostle exhorts: that each person should devote himself exclusively to the gift with which he had been equipped, Rom. XII, 6–8, etc.; that “a man should think with sober judgment, each according to the measure of faith which God has apportioned,” v. 3; and that God distributed gifts according to a definite plan, so that no person should himself possess them all, but each should supply what another lacked, and thus all should be mutually necessary to one another, so that there should be no “SCHISM in the body” (I Cor. XII, 18, 24, 25). If, therefore, all who lacked some gift ought not even to have exercised it, it follows that those to whom the gift of teaching had been denied ought not to have taught.

Meanwhile, we acknowledge that, [Col. 0037C] according to the Apostle’s intention, if any are endowed with both gifts—“leadership” (*προστασία*) and “teaching” (*διδασκαλία*)—they are deservedly worthy of the double honor of which he speaks. Nor have we argued these points with the intention of defending idleness, if anyone is not occupied with other duties necessary to the Church. We do not think that the Apostle or the primitive Church intended any such thing. I would rather think it a cause for joy and congratulation if any Church possessed presbyters all of whom could fulfill this duty of teaching in such a way that they neither performed it unbecomingly nor neglected their other duties. Yet the adversaries make it a pretext for schism if men destitute of this gift are admitted to holy orders, or are equally occupied with other necessary cares of the Church, so that they cannot devote themselves exclusively to this one duty. Indeed, under the pretext of this single duty they [Col. 0037D] neglect all the rest—daily public prayers, visitation of the faithful, instruction of catechumens, celebration of the sacraments, viaticum for the dying—and do not leave themselves even enough free time to discharge their remaining duties. Such practices are certainly so far from apostolic and so far from conformity with primitive Christianity that they should not even be approved.

§ 7.—We see further that, in examining this teacher of the hearers, Cyprian consulted no presbyters other than the teachers. It is certainly highly probable that he observed the same practice in other matters also, so that in whatever field each person excelled, Cyprian judged that he should be consulted in that field. Accordingly, when [Col. 0038A] he recalls that everything he had done from the very beginning of his episcopate was conducted with the common counsel of the presbyters, this should be understood to mean that in each particular matter he excluded from his counsel no one whom that matter concerned, and that he admitted them all whenever a matter concerned them all. This was indeed required by that apostolic rule concerning gifts which we have just mentioned: that each person should devote himself exclusively to exercising the gift with which he had been endowed and should not involve himself in other matters having no relation to his gift. It also follows that the gift by which the hearers were taught was the same as that by which the faithful were taught, because Cyprian consulted the presbyter-teachers when appointing the teacher of the hearers.

§ 8.—There were indeed other “hearers” among the ranks of penitents, who, after they had heard the Scriptures and the “teaching” (*διδασκαλία*), [Col. 0038B] had to be dismissed from the assemblies. And these indeed were contemporaneous with our Cyprian, if Gregory Thaumaturgus’s canonical epistle is to be believed. But, so far as I know, no trace of them exists in the African Church, especially in that age. Nor did they have teachers other than those of the faithful, for the hearings which they attended were common to all the faithful. According to the usage of the African Church, moreover, no others were called hearers except catechumens. We have already seen above that those whom the Roman clergy called catechumens in Ep. III are the same persons whom Cyprian calls hearers in Ep. XIII. This is also clear from Tertullian, than whom no one is a better interpreter of Cyprian. In Tertullian the hearers are contrasted with the “dipped,” in the sense in which “to be dipped” in the same author means to be baptized (*On Repentance*, chs. 6, 7). He calls the same persons auditors and mentions their initial training, [Col. 0038C] so that no one may doubt that they are none other than catechumens.

§ 9.—Indeed, this very name “hearers” seems to have been extremely common. Yet even in that age there is no lack of examples in which the same persons are called catechumens, even among Latin writers. We have already said that the Roman clergy used this name “catechumens.” Cyprian himself also used it in *Testimonies*, Book III, ch. 98; and Tertullian in *On the Soldier’s Crown*, ch. 2, and *Prescription*, ch. 41. It was only in the fourth century, the age of St. Augustine, and thereafter that this name finally prevailed by itself.

As for the name “hearers,” I think it was derived entirely from the sacred text—namely, from those passages in which faith itself is so often called “hearing” (*ἀκοή*), a word which even the ancient translators rendered *auditus*. Thus: “Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word,” [Col. 0038D] Rom. X, 17; “the hearing of faith,” Gal. III, 2, 5; “the word of the hearing of God,” I Thess. II, 13. The Apostle, moreover, derived this usage from the Old Testament, Isa. LIII, 1: “Who has believed our hearing?” For this is how the translators of both Tertullian and Cyprian read that passage. The Apostle referred us to that passage of Isaiah in the clearest words, Rom. X, 16. The commonplace pagan “auditions” (*ἀκροάματα*), which were generally entertainments, are irrelevant here. Those philosophical teachings which were entrusted only to candidates for initiation, according to the pattern of the mysteries, may perhaps be relevant.

§ 10.—The entire method of instructing catechumens certainly reproduced that pattern of the mysteries. Those who were to be initiated adopted a new manner of life (Meursius, [Col. 0039A] *Eleusinia*, ch. 17). And Clement of Alexandria’s oldest catechetical work now extant, namely the *Paedagogus*, is wholly occupied with it. In the Petroma there were also ritual books that candidates for initiation first had to read and then to copy (ibid., ch. 10). Cyril of Jerusalem and others likewise discuss in their *Catecheses* the rites of baptism, the “assent” (*σύνταξις*) and “renunciation” (*ἀπόταξις*), the turning toward the east and west, and so forth.

§ 11.—Finally, it must be observed that this teaching office for the hearers belonged to the office of subdeacon. The teaching of the hearers assigned to Optatus was equivalent to the reading assigned to Saturus when he was to be promoted to the rank of reader: namely, a preliminary trial of his future office. In the Alexandrian school (*διδασκαλεῖον*) of catechesis (*κατήχησις*), or of sacred discourses (*ἱεροὶ λόγοι*), the same office was perhaps sometimes assigned to presbyters. Pantaenus [Col. 0039B] is generally thought to have been a presbyter, although I do not know whether any of the ancients actually calls him so (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, V, 10; VI, 3, 6). Alexander, Bishop of Jerusalem, calls Clement, Pantaenus’s successor in that office, a presbyter (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VI, 11). But when Alexander wrote that letter, Origen seems already to have succeeded Clement in his position, and therefore it is not certain whether Clement was a presbyter while he discharged that office.

That office was not, however, necessarily attached to the presbyterate, as is clear from the fact that Origen was promoted to it by Demetrius when he was only eighteen years old. At that time it is not established that he had been initiated even into those lower orders which are regarded as sacred. It is certain that he did not receive the presbyterate before his journey to Achaia [Col. 0039C] under Alexander Severus. This arrangement was perhaps instituted with the intention that, since the faithful had already been received into the bosom of the Church, they should accordingly have a teacher who, at least in the Church’s estimation, was a priest. For that grace of knowledge with which Tertullian said a teacher ought to be endowed belonged to priests, as is also clear from the prescription of the Old Law, Mal. II, 7. In that passage the very word “knowledge” was used not only by the old translator in current use but also by Cyprian himself.

For the instruction of catechumens, however, who were situated outside the Church, even a layman was sufficient, although, as a mark of honor, they chose one who stood next to the clergy. This is especially so because, from what we have argued above concerning their opinion, it is clear that even the ordinary body of Christians so excelled all outsiders [Col. 0039D] in holiness that, by comparison with them, Christians deserved to be regarded as priests.

§ 12.—It must further be observed from this same passage of Cyprian that readers and subdeacons were also included under the general title of clerics. He certainly implies this when he says that it was necessary for him to write to the Roman clergy through clerics, and for this very reason says that Saturus had been appointed reader and Optatus subdeacon. In a similar example, Felicianus the acolyte is called a cleric in Ep. LV. The same is also clear with regard to readers, although that rank was lower than the subdiaconate, from Cyprian’s letters concerning Aurelius and Celerinus, whom he promoted to the honor of the readership.

Concerning Aurelius he writes as follows, Ep. XXXIII: “In clerical ordinations, dearly beloved brothers, we are accustomed to consult you beforehand,” etc. Aurelius was therefore both a cleric and ordained. “Such a man,” he says, “deserved the lower ranks of clerical ordination.” [Col. 0040A] This, therefore, was also a rank of clerical ordination. Again: “Know, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, that he has been ordained by me and by the colleagues who were present—an action which I know you both gladly embrace and desire to see repeated in the ordination of many such persons in our Church.”

Concerning Celerinus he says in Ep. XXXIV that he was worthy “that he who had so sublimely confessed Christ should afterward adorn Christ’s clergy by ecclesiastical ministries.” Again, he says that “our brother Celerinus, glorious alike in virtues and conduct, has been joined to our clergy, not by human favor but by divine condescension.” Yet in the very epistle now before us Cyprian says that [Col. 0040B] Optatus the reader was merely next to the clergy and counts him among those who were being prepared for the clergy. Moreover, in Cyprian’s letters either issued in the name of the clergy or addressed *To the Clergy*, no mention ever occurs of anyone other than presbyters and deacons. Who does not see that, following the custom of his age, he uses the name “clergy” sometimes more broadly and sometimes more strictly, so that those who in one sense are called clerics must, when compared with others, be counted among the laity? We could observe the same phenomenon in the later canons of the Church. At present, however, we have resolved to deal with the times of Cyprian, or even earlier times.

§ 13.—The custom of that age concerning ecclesiastical embassies is also worthy of observation. For such embassies were extremely attentive to the dignity both of those by whom and of those to whom [Col. 0040C] they were sent.

Cyprian’s first embassy to the Romans was sent through the subdeacon Clementius; we have mention of it in Epp. III, IV, and XV.

The second is the present embassy to the Roman clergy, through Saturus the reader and Optatus the subdeacon. It is mentioned in this very Epistle and in Epp. XXIX and XXXII.

The third was to the same clergy through the subdeacon Fortunatus, Ep. XXX.

The fourth was Novatian’s embassy to Cyprian concerning his ordination, through Maximus the presbyter, Augendus the deacon, and also a certain Machaeus and Longinus, whose orders are not established, Ep. XLI.

The fifth was sent by Cyprian together with the synod to investigate the ordination of Cornelius, through the bishops Caldonius and Fortunatus, Epp. XLI, XLII, and XLV.

The sixth was sent by Cyprian privately to Cornelius through the presbyter Primitivus, Ep. XLI.

The seventh was sent by Cyprian to the same man [Col. 0040D] through Mettius the subdeacon and Nicephorus the acolyte, Epp. XLII, XLIII, and XLIV.

The eighth was sent by Cornelius to Cyprian through Augendus the confessor, Ep. XLVIII. It is unclear, however, what position he held in the Church.

The ninth was sent by Antonianus to Cyprian through Quintus the presbyter, Ep. LII.

The tenth was sent by Cornelius to Cyprian through Saturus the acolyte, Ep. LV.

The eleventh was sent by Cyprian to Cornelius through Felicianus the acolyte, in the same Epistle.

The twelfth was sent by Bishop Pomponius to Cyprian together with the synod, through Paconius the brother, Ep. LXII; but his dignity is not mentioned either.

The thirteenth was the embassy of the Churches of Asturica and Emerita through their bishops Felix and Sabinus, Ep. LXVIII, in the case in which the episcopate itself had been disputed. For these men [Col. 0041A] had been substituted in place of Martialis and Basilides, who were *libellatici*.

The fourteenth was sent by Quintus, Bishop of Mauretania, to Cyprian the primate, through Lucianus, perhaps a presbyter, Ep. LXXI.

The fifteenth was Cyprian’s, but apparently in the name of the whole African Church, to Firmilian, apparently the chief bishop of Cappadocia, through Rogatianus the deacon, Ep. LXXV.

The sixteenth, and finally the last, was sent by Cyprian himself, now in exile, to his fellow bishops who were likewise laboring in the mines, through Victor Herennianus the subdeacon and the acolytes Lucanus, Maximus, and Amantius, Epp. LXXVIII, LXXIX, and LXXX.

§ 14.—Cyprian’s words must be noted: “And because it was necessary for me to write through clerics,” etc. From these words it is clear that, according to the custom of that age, ecclesiastical embassies [Col. 0041B] were to be entrusted to none but clerics. This was perhaps done so that greater credibility might attach to the messages carried back and forth. Cyprian certainly took it very badly when, in Ep. III, he regarded the letter of the Roman clergy as suspect, because the credibility of a clerical letter was thereby impaired and it might perhaps have been corrupted by some falsehood and fraud. I readily recognize that the letter could be called “clerical” either because it had been written by the Roman clergy (Ep. IV), or because it was entrusted to the envoy Clementius the subdeacon, who was himself also a cleric. Yet in this passage it was only the envoy’s credibility, not that of the writers, that was called into question.

Those envoys whose rank is not otherwise established were therefore clerics as well. And if acolytes and any other ministers of the lower orders conducted embassies, it necessarily follows from this very argument that they too were counted [Col. 0041C] among the clergy.

It should also be noted that very many embassies, especially those sent overseas, were entrusted to two envoys. Novatian’s sending four envoys was probably done to gain goodwill. Perhaps the same conclusion should be reached concerning the embassy to the martyrs: either those four envoys were sent in honor of the martyrs, or because the martyrs were situated in various places, or so that more witnesses of good faith might be present during the distribution of the Church’s alms. For even in that otherwise golden age there were examples of bad faith in financial matters. Such, even within the African Church itself, had been the presbyter Novatus, Ep. XLIX. Such was Felicissimus, Ep. XXXVIII. Such, finally—who would believe it?—was Nicostratus himself, a deacon and confessor, Epp. XLVIII and XLIX.

It is also worthy of notice [Col. 0041D] that the principal envoy was generally a subdeacon and did not rise above that rank. So it was in the first, second, third, seventh, and sixteenth embassies. If a person of higher rank was ever sent, this generally occurred when only one envoy was dispatched, so that the deficiency in number might be compensated by the person’s dignity. So it was in the ninth, fourteenth, and fifteenth embassies. Although in other instances we possess only the names of individual envoys, even of lower order, it is nevertheless not certain that only single envoys were dispatched.

The same practice prevailed not only in overseas embassies but also in those sent by provincial bishops to their province’s primate, such as the fourteenth embassy. Bishops themselves undertook embassies [Col. 0042A] only very rarely and for reasons that were otherwise of the utmost gravity. In the thirteenth embassy, the reason is manifest; in the fifth it is also easy to discern. For a decision had to be made between the bishops Cornelius and Novatian. Provision also had to be made for the future issuance of letters of communion, the entire exchange of which belonged to none but bishops.

Furthermore, envoys were sent both by an African synod and to a synod—that is, to the bishops of the province, to whom the ordination of the Roman bishop belonged. For the name “synod,” as it passed from pagan usage to Christians, designates any colleges or fraternities of priests, whether in assemblies or even individually. Nor is the Church without examples of this meaning, if that were the matter presently under discussion.

[Col. 0042B] § 15. Such, then, was the state of embassies in Cyprian’s age. There were also some embassies earlier than Cyprian organized according to the same pattern. Clement of Alexandria, a presbyter, was sent—though alone—as an envoy by Alexander, bishop of Jerusalem, to the Church of Antioch, the chief Church of all Syria (to which Judaea also belonged) (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, VI.11). This was plainly patterned on the fourteenth embassy. Irenaeus, a presbyter, was the envoy of the martyrs of Lyons and Vienne to Eleutherus, the Roman pontiff—and there is no reason to make him a bishop at that time, as Blondel does—and he likewise went alone (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, V.4). We have, I think, no examples of other embassies as far back as the times of Polycarp and Ignatius (see Valesius, *Notes* on this passage of Eusebius). Let us therefore examine [Col. 0042C] how those embassies were constituted.

§ 16. The letter of the Church of Smyrna to the Philomelians concerning the martyrdom of Polycarp was written through a certain brother named Marcus, after the pattern of the twelfth embassy; the old Latin translator calls him Martianus, but nothing is known of his rank in the Church. There is a similar silence concerning the rank of Crescens, whom Polycarp himself employed as messenger for the letter he sent to the Philippians. Ignatius’s letters (*Epistle to the Smyrnaeans*, § 12; *to the Ephesians*, § 12) to the Smyrnaeans, Ephesians, and Philadelphians appear to have been entrusted to Burrhus the deacon, who had been sent to Ignatius in the common name of the Smyrnaeans and Ephesians. To whom the remaining letters were entrusted is unknown, but it is certainly very likely that they too were entrusted to Burrhus. For Ignatius’s words in the *Epistle to the Smyrnaeans* [Col. 0042D] must be noted: ὃν ἀπεστείλατε μετ’ ἐμοῦ, “whom you sent with me.” Burrhus, therefore, was sent not merely to Ignatius but with him (see *Epistle to the Ephesians*, § 2), to be his traveling companion and a messenger for carrying out embassies. I think that the other Ephesians as well (*Epistle to the Romans*, § 10)—Crocus, Onesimus, Euplus, and Fronto—were sent in the same capacity, and indeed that none other than they carried the letter to the Romans. Philo, a Cilician deacon, also performed the same office (*Epistle to the Philadelphians*, § 11).

Nor did deacons alone perform embassies in the time of Ignatius; others superior to deacons did so as well. “The cities and Churches of Asia honored the saint,” say the authors contemporary with Ignatius’s martyrdom, “through bishops, presbyters, and deacons” (Ussher’s ed., p. 5). This very custom of embassies [Col. 0043A] certainly has the character of Ignatius’s own century, not of some later age. Ignatius himself is the most authoritative witness that the Magnesians did this (*Epistle to the Magnesians*, § 2): not only Damas their bishop, but also the presbyters Bassus and Apollonius and the deacon Sotio were with him at Smyrna.

He repeatedly asks the Churches to send some envoy to strengthen his see of Antioch, then deprived of its bishop. He calls this envoy now θεοδρόμος, “God’s runner” (*Epistle to Polycarp*, § 7), and now θεοπρεσβευτής, “God’s ambassador” (*Epistle to the Smyrnaeans*, § 11); Polycarp also mentions him in his *Epistle to the Philippians*. What persons those Churches appointed as envoys is shown by the same most holy martyr Ignatius in his *Epistle to the Philadelphians*: Αἱ ἔγγιστα, he says, ἐκκλησίαι ἔπεμψαν ἐπισκόπους, αἱ δὲ πρεσβυτέρους καὶ διακόνους, “The nearest Churches sent bishops, while others sent presbyters and deacons” (*Epistle to the Philadelphians*, § 10). In the aforementioned [Col. 0043B] *Epistle to the Philippians*, Polycarp himself deliberates whether he should undertake the embassy himself or rather send another envoy. Thus it was not incompatible even with episcopal rank for bishops themselves to discharge the office of envoy.

From this it is also incidentally evident that in that century the office of bishop was not so fixed as Salmasius supposed. Rather, the very name “bishop” was taken from the office of those who traveled about in Greek cities. And the Canons call rural bishops περιοδευταί, “itinerants,” whose office in the countryside was the same as that of bishops in cities. Moreover, περίοδος, “circuit” or “journey,” is the very word by which, as Salmasius himself observed, the apostles’ travels are denoted in the more ancient monuments of the Church. Nothing therefore prevents the same persons from having been both apostles and bishops, from having been able both to travel and nevertheless to preside over particular Churches. [Col. 0043C] This is especially so because the travels of the other apostles ought not to be judged from the example of St Paul. The others certainly confined themselves for the most part within particular provinces toward the close of that century, when Churches had already been established and bishops placed in those Churches.

St James seems not to have traveled far from Jerusalem, if we believe authentic records, including those of Acts. Polycrates and Clement of Alexandria suggest that Philip did not go far from Hierapolis, nor John from proconsular Asia. Within these bounds nothing in the discipline of the primitive Church prevented other bishops also from traveling. Moreover, when St Paul contends that he surpassed the other apostles in labor (1 Cor. 15:10), he certainly and manifestly implies that the labors of the other apostles are not to be assessed from his example alone. That he surpassed each individual one is too clear to admit of doubt. [Col. 0043D] His words may also be understood to mean that he left all the labors of them all, even taken together, far behind him. If that is true, bishops could equal the labors of the other apostles.

Polycarp perhaps equaled them when, under Anicetus, he journeyed from his own Smyrna to Rome, and perhaps from there proceeded into Gaul to establish that colony of Christians at Lyons and Vienne. Certainly no indubitable monuments of the primitive Church suggest that this one man’s labors were inferior to those of the other apostles. Yet he was very far from exceeding the bounds of the episcopal office, nor did any of the ancients censure him on that account. Since matters stood thus, [Col. 0044A] it was entirely fitting that they should employ no persons other than those of the higher orders for embassies, since those ministers of inferior orders whom the Church employed in Cyprian’s age had not yet been introduced into the Church.

§ 17. These practices of Ignatius’s time plainly reproduced the very latest traces of the apostolic age. The apostles’ principal labor was devoted more to spreading Churches than to governing them. It was therefore fitting that the most honorable envoys possible should be chosen, especially since the very office of propagating the Gospel belonged chiefly to those who occupied the foremost rank in the Church, such as the apostles themselves, the evangelists, and so forth.

Accordingly, besides those apostles of Christ who bore the primary title, the Churches also had their own men [Col. 0044B] whom they likewise called apostles, apparently because they were ordinarily sent as messengers to represent the Churches by which they were sent. For the very name “apostleship” seems in that age to imply precisely this. These apostles are called ἀπόστολοι ἐκκλησιῶν, “apostles of the Churches” (2 Cor. 8:23). Thus Epaphroditus was the apostle of the Philippians (Phil. 2:25). Moreover, the benefits conferred upon them were believed to redound not to them alone but εἰς πρόσωπον τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν, “to the person of the Churches,” because, as I have said, they represented those Churches.

From this we understand how far Walo Messalinus departed from the apostle’s meaning in his explanation of these apostles, when he supposes that these secondary apostles were sent by the primary apostles to the Churches, rather than conversely by the Churches to the apostles. If that had been true, the honor paid to them could not have pertained ad πρόσωπον ἐκκλησιῶν, [Col. 0044C] “to the person of the Churches,” but rather to the apostles by whom they had been sent. Furthermore, the interpretation seems altogether harsher according to which those were to be called ἀπόστολοι ἐκκλησιῶν, “apostles of the Churches,” who had been sent to plant Churches, rather than those who had been sent by the Churches themselves. Those are certainly called apostles of God and of Christ who are sent, not to God or Christ, but by them; thus the contrary expression would be entirely novel and unsupported by any example.

Rather, the origin of the primary apostles too seems to be derived from this representation of the sender’s person. Those are called the attendants of princes whose office it is to be personally present to princes and always to appear in their sight. Hence they are said to behold the countenances of princes and to proceed from their countenances. What [Col. 0044D] the Latin translators call “countenances,” the Hebrews express in accordance with their own idiom; the Greek translators render that word πρόσωπον, “face” or “person.” In keeping with this custom of princes, the majestic presence of God is likewise veiled in Scripture under metaphors of countenance and face. The bread of the Presence is called the bread of faces, proper to those, namely, who became table-companions of princes. The “angel of the Presence” in the prophet is the same as the one who is said in the Gospel to behold the face of God.

Moreover, just as an affront to princes was to be judged according to the dignity of their messengers, and was the more serious the more honorable the messenger had been, so the highest degree of honor belonged to one who was most constantly in the sight of princes. Therefore, if anyone treated with less than due honor a person who was said to have gone out from the prince’s countenance, [Col. 0045A] it was as though he had despised the prince himself acting and present in person. Accordingly, when the Lord declares that honor and contempt will be common to himself and the apostles, he thereby implies that they are to be numbered among those messengers who are ἀπὸ προσώπου, “from the presence.” The same judgment must therefore be made concerning these apostles of the Churches: that they came, as it were, from the countenances of the Churches, since both honors and affronts redounded alike to both parties—to the Churches themselves and to the apostles sent by the Churches—as though both sustained one and the same person.

But if Salmasius’s contention were true, that these secondary apostles of the Churches belonged to the Churches for no other reason than that they were sent to plant Churches, there would certainly be no reason why they could be distinguished by that title alone [Col. 0045B] from the primary apostles. For those very apostles of Christ were also sent and appointed by Christ for this same office of planting Churches (Eph. 4:11–13). They too had definite κανόνες, “spheres” or “assigned fields,” by agreement, lest we suppose that these secondary apostles were in this respect inferior.

What office properly belonged to Epaphroditus’s apostleship can easily be gathered from that same *Epistle to the Philippians* (Phil. 4:18): “But I have all things, and abound: I am full, having received from Epaphroditus the things which you sent,” etc. That embassy therefore concerned money. This should not, however, be understood as though, once that commission had been performed, they immediately returned to their own people. Those who had been sent in this way afterwards undertook other embassies in the name of the person to whom they had been sent, even to distant [Col. 0045C] regions whenever this served the public interest of the catholic Church. Thus Paul commends to the Corinthians those apostles of the Churches, whom he had doubtless sent there himself (2 Cor. 8:24). Thus Ignatius seems to have dispatched to Rome the Ephesians who had been sent to him (*Epistle to the Romans*, conclusion). For they were sent with precisely that purpose whom the apostle mentions in the cited passage (2 Cor. 8:19) as χειροτονοθέντας ὑπὸ τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν συνεκδήμους, “appointed by the Churches as traveling companions.”

From this we understand who the apostles called συνέκδημοι, “fellow travelers,” were, of whom we read in Acts 19:29: none other, certainly, than these whom we have called apostles. The same persons are called συνέποντες, “accompanying” (Acts 20:4); συνεξελθόντες, “going out together” (Acts 16:3); and συνελθόντες, “going together” (Acts 15:38). It belonged so closely to their office to minister to those leading men that, if any withdrew, they were regarded as having failed in their duty. The apostle sometimes complains in his letters that he was deserted by such men. The same persons are called διακοῦντες, [Col. 0045D] “ministering” (for the supply of alms was properly called διακονία, “ministry”) (Acts 19:22), and ὑπηρέται, “assistants” (Acts 13:5). Indeed, there were very many who ministered to St Paul in this way: some were taken up by Paul himself, some delegated to him by the Churches, and some voluntarily devoted and dedicated themselves.

The apostles themselves likewise observed the practice of employing as envoys in matters of the greatest importance none but those who excelled the rest. Thus it was done at the Council of Jerusalem, when the apostles’ decree concerning the necessity of circumcision had to be sent to the Church of Antioch. They did not appoint just any chance persons who voluntarily offered themselves, but men chosen from their own number to discharge this office: [Col. 0046A] Ἔδοξε, etc., ἐκλεξαμένους ἄνδρας ἐξ αὐτῶν πέμψαι, etc., “It seemed good … to choose men from among themselves and send them,” etc. (Acts 15:22); and this they actually did, v. 25.

Nor did the Jews act otherwise, from whom the precedent seems to have passed to the Christians. They too delegated ἄνδρας ἐκλεκτούς, “chosen men,” throughout the whole world, λέγοντες αἵρεσιν ἄθεον Χριστιανῶν πεφηνέναι, “saying that a godless sect of Christians had appeared,” as St Justin Martyr testifies in more than one place (*Dialogue with Trypho*, pp. 234 E, 335 C).

§ 18. Nor should it be surprising that the Churches rendered these services to apostles, since they rendered the same even to ordinary Christians whenever the latter were engaged in matters concerning the public Christian cause. For no small part of communion consisted in the right of hospitality. To this also belong the very many letters of commendation of the ancients, in imitation of which ecclesiastical letters were likewise formally drawn up and composed. [Col. 0046B] Guests who remained were supplied with expenses free of charge; those departing were given ξένια, “guest-gifts”; and, if necessary, traveling companions were added if they were to proceed farther.

These practices are evident from the most ancient scenes of hospitality in Homer and later passed into the customs of more recent Greeks. The apostles repeatedly commend this φιλοξενία, “hospitality to strangers”; and the primitive Christians assigned it such importance that wealthy private persons sometimes dedicated themselves and all their possessions to receiving holy persons traveling from every quarter. Such appears to have been Gaius, not merely St Paul’s private host but host of the whole Church as well (Rom. 16:23). He is commended under the same title by St John in his Third Epistle, vv. 5–8. Such also was Philemon (*Epistle to Philemon*, vv. 5–7), and Mnason the Cypriot (Acts 21:16).

Nevertheless, this seems ordinarily to have been a public office of the Churches. [Col. 0046C] For we read that even entire cities of those times exercised this reciprocal right of hospitality toward one another. Cicero has some examples, unless I am mistaken, in the *Verrines*. Thus the practice could very easily have passed to Churches which, according to the custom of that century too, embraced whole cities, and which are therefore compared with cities by Origen (*Against Celsus*, III). This is especially likely because even before the birth of Christianity the Jews of Jerusalem had performed the same offices toward provincial Jews of the διασπορά, “Dispersion.” Not to go farther afield, I infer this from Acts 28:21.

Because these duties of hospitality belonged particularly to those appointed to public offices in the Church, the apostle writes thus concerning the widows of the Church (1 Tim. 5:10): “If she has received strangers, if she has washed the saints’ [Col. 0046D] feet, if she has ministered to those suffering tribulation.” Concerning the bishop: “For a bishop must be blameless, the husband of one wife, sober, prudent, respectable, modest, hospitable” (1 Tim. 3:2). Again concerning the same: “But hospitable, kindly, sober” (Titus 1:8), etc. For he was πᾶσι τοῖς ἐν χρείᾳ οὖσι κηδεμών, “guardian of all who were in need,” according to the testimony of St Justin Martyr (*Apology*, II).

§ 19. These, therefore, were the common duties of the Churches toward all travelers, and we certainly have no reason to doubt that they were performed even more diligently toward the apostles themselves. I know of nothing by which illustrious men were customarily received, according to the usage of that century, that [Col. 0047A] the Churches did not likewise observe in receiving apostles and the leading men of the Church; and they did so with an even readier spirit, because they believed that they were earning the favor not only of those to whom they rendered these services, but even of God himself, in whose work those men were engaged, and that they too would become participants in their works.

When the apostle came to Rome, the brethren streamed out to meet him as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns (Acts 28:15). In Ignatius’s case, however, as he hastened toward martyrdom, they went out as far as the harbor. The Maltese “honored” him as he departed “with many honors, and when they sailed, they put on board the things that were necessary” (ibid., 28:10). These were doubtless their ξένια, “guest-gifts.” The Ephesians accompanied him as far as the ship when he departed (Acts 20:38). This was the προπομπή, “escort,” which the apostle himself also mentions in very many places.

According to the custom of that age too, [Col. 0047B] this pertained to the honor of the visitor: the more illustrious a person was in dignity, the more illustrious also were those sent to meet him. This was also observed in receiving provincial governors: embassies from the cities, consisting of the leading men in each city, were sent to whatever place they first landed in the province. The same was also observed by neighboring cities on journeys. Since Christians imitated this practice in the travels of apostles and leading men of the Church, it is likely that they also imitated the custom of ensuring that the envoys were not unequal to the dignity of those arriving.

For [Col. 0047C] although the apostles banished worldly pomp far away, they nevertheless observed and tenaciously retained propriety. This certainly seems to have been St Paul’s character and disposition. Nor was this without reason. For although, particularly in those centuries of persecution, there was no danger of ostentation in persons received in this manner, nevertheless these morally indifferent observances contributed greatly toward inspiring respect and reverence in their subjects. They certainly were not to be neglected, especially since these services were not commanded but were rendered through the subjects’ entirely free and most ardent devotion.

§ 20. From this we conclude that, even if we could not learn from another source what rank in the Church was held by those appointed to undertake these embassies, we should nevertheless have no reason to doubt that it was highly honorable. In that earliest history of the apostolic age, [Col. 0048A] mention of the ordinary ministries of the Church—namely bishops, presbyters, and deacons—occurs more rarely. The extraordinary ministers—apostles, evangelists, pastors, teachers, and prophets—were more frequent and altogether better known and more celebrated.

It is indeed probable that the earliest, primary, and very simple administration of the Church belonged to these men; and then, when they had found that administration more disturbed and disorderly, those ministers whom we retain today—the ordinary ministers—gradually succeeded in their place, and the extraordinary ministers were gradually made subject to the ordinary ones in accordance with the discipline of the assemblies. Therefore, whenever these extraordinary ministers discharged the duties of the assemblies, we shall look in vain for mention of the ordinary ministers. This alone is sufficient: they held not merely the highest dignity but also [Col. 0048B] the highest place in the administration of the Church, and therefore, if they undertook any embassies, those embassies must have been highly honorable.

When at length, on account of the discipline of the assemblies, they were subjected to the ordinary ministers of the assemblies, they nevertheless still retained, beyond doubt, the highest honor. For they were not attached to particular Churches, but were rather common to the whole catholic Church. And in that age, doubtless, when the work of the supreme ministers consisted more in disseminating Christianity widely than in governing Churches already founded and established, it is scarcely possible that their office was not preferred to that of persons belonging only to individual Churches.

Those appointed as envoys appear to have belonged to this number of extraordinary ministers. The apostle acknowledges that those very [Col. 0048C] gifts of theirs were given for the sake of unbelievers rather than believers, and would therefore be more useful if employed in converting unbelievers rather than in confirming believers. This was especially so because they were sent with the express purpose not merely of receiving those who arrived, but also of being companions and συνεργοί, “fellow workers,” of those traveling and journeying abroad.

But the Church of that age required an altogether different method of administration from that of later ages. Those, therefore, are wholly mistaken who permit nothing in the Church today unless it conforms to the example of that apostolic Church. Circumstances must certainly be considered and prudence employed—a prudence which the apostles undoubtedly exercised in many matters.

# THIRD DISSERTATION ON THE SECOND BAPTISM OF MARTYRDOM, BY DODWELL

[Col. 0047]

§ 1.—Why we assign a separate dissertation to this subject.—§ 2. This opinion has descended from the earliest times of the Church to our own.—§ 3. Baptism by water and external union with the Church are prerequisites for the baptism by the blood of martyrdom.—§ 4. The ancients preferred baptism by blood to baptism by water.—§§ 5–6. Cyprian’s passage on this subject is explained.—§ 7. This opinion of the ancients is defended.—§ 8. The passages of Scripture from which they inferred it. [Col. 0048]—§ 9. First observation: legitimate argument proceeds from the Lord’s deeds, especially deeds of the kind that the ancients employed in this matter.—§§ 10–11. Second observation: it is established not only by the Lord’s deeds but by his very words that martyrdom must be regarded as baptism.—§ 12. Third observation: the affinity between baptism and martyrdom is not merely verbal, but belongs also to the things themselves. The occasion of the passages in which the ancients believed baptism by blood to be treated [Col. 0049A] was martyrdom. The Lord’s baptism was his martyrdom, and in the ecclesiastical sense.—§§ 13–16. Heretics contemporary with the apostles denied martyrdom. St John refuted their pseudo-Christs by an argument from the coming of the true Messiah through water and blood. That entire argument is explained.—§ 17. Fourth observation: in that very rite of initiation and expiation to which the ancients attributed cleansing from sins, the use of blood was as frequent among them as the use of water, and indeed the blood proper to those being initiated.—§ 18. This custom prevailed not only in initiations but also in covenants, according to the most ancient customs.—§ 19. Just as they readily conceded to blood the principal role in this matter of expiation, so they acknowledged human blood to possess by far the greatest power [Col. 0049B], even in comparison with other kinds of blood.—§ 20. Fifth observation: this baptism by blood pertains to the sacrament of baptism itself, and pertains to it in such a way that it completes its principal part.—§ 21. First, the baptismal covenant must be explained according to the customs governing covenants among the ancients.—§ 22. Second, as in other covenants, so also in our baptismal covenant, the duties of the different parties must be distinguished from one another: some are God’s, others ours.—§ 23. Third, every legal right which we obtain by benefit of the covenant must be derived from God’s promises upon the performance of our duty.—§ 24. Fourth, the conditions incumbent upon us in this baptismal covenant, to be fulfilled on our part, must be inferred from the meaning of its solemn symbols.—§ 25. Fifth, the solemn sacramental symbols of our baptism [Col. 0049C] signify not only baptism by water, but also baptism by blood; and they signify them in such a way that both are understood to belong to one and the same baptism.—§ 26. This is in fact the case.—§§ 27–28. The reason for the fact is given.—§§ 29–30. Sixth, baptism by blood is so foreshadowed in the very symbol of baptism by water that it is plainly implied that baptism by water has no efficacy unless it is referred to baptism by blood.—§§ 31–32. Seventh inference: not only by the law of the baptismal covenant but also by its equity, all the benefits to be furnished by Christ as his part of the baptismal covenant may be claimed in baptism by blood.—§§ 33–34. Eighth inference: full remission of all preceding sins must [Col. 0049D] be granted to martyrdom just as to baptism.—§ 35. It is in no way inconsistent with the nature of baptism that baptism by water and baptism by blood should be separated from one another by an interval of time.—§ 36.—Ninth, the ancients regarded the martyrs’ blood as Christ’s blood.—§ 37. Tenth, especially if, following Christ’s example, it had been shed for the public cause of souls.—§ 38. The ancients are defended.—§ 39. We pledge ourselves to martyrdom in the other sacrament also, the Eucharist.—§ 40. In martyrdom we obtain a right to the benefits of baptism, both privative and positive.

§ 1.—We said in the preceding dissertation [Note: [Col. 0049D] Its title is: *On the Extraordinary Courage of the First Martyrs and Its Causes*. We had at first intended [Col. 0050D] to include it in this volume, but because it contained much that gave offense, it had to be omitted.] that among the [Col. 0050A] martyrdoms of the earliest times, the doctrines received by that primitive Church concerning the dignity of martyrdom held the foremost place among the forms of divine assistance—above all, the doctrine by which they claimed for martyrdom the function and benefits of a second baptism.

Because I know that this is foreign to the opinions of more recent writers, who prefer their own interpretations of Holy Scripture—however weak and unsupported by any certain reasoning—to the reasonings of the ancients; and because this entire method of mystical argumentation, which by a certain right is peculiar to mystical Scripture in general, and especially to this subject of the sacraments, has nevertheless been scorned or neglected by most of the most celebrated interpreters of our time; and because the Roman Catholic writers who defend this ancient opinion today nevertheless put forward only [Col. 0050B] the authority of the ancients, entirely unconcerned with their reasonings—whether they inferred it rightly from Scripture, in a manner suited to the understanding of primitive Christianity (to which alone, as we have proved elsewhere, the Holy Spirit had regard in composing the Scriptures: in the *Prolegomena* to Dominus Stearn, *On Obstinacy*), and therefore solidly—we consequently judged it most advisable to assign this agreeable and useful subject its own separate dissertation.

§ 2.—Accordingly, this opinion concerning a second baptism of martyrdom was derived from the earliest times of the Church and the most recent memory of the apostles, and was commonly received in the Church. The author of the *Acts* writes thus concerning Felicitas (*Acts of Perpetua and Felicitas*, pp. 29–30, Oxford ed.): “Likewise Felicitas, rejoicing that she had safely given birth so that she might fight the beasts, was to be washed after childbirth in a second baptism with blood, from the midwife to the net-fighter.” [Col. 0050C]

The cry of the pagans concerning Saturus also bears on the same point. When his whole body was drenched in his own blood by a single bite from the leopard, they cried, “Well washed! Well washed!” The author of the *Acts* interprets this as an allusion, made even by crowds who did not understand it, to the second washing of martyrdom. Thus among Christians there had already become established a manner of speaking by which a person was said to be washed in the baptism of martyrdom no less than in baptism by water.

Furthermore, Tertullian used the expression “second immersion” for martyrdom (Tertullian, *On Patience*, ch. 13; *On Baptism*, ch. 16), which elsewhere he also designates by the name “second laver,” namely the baptism of blood. Origen does not speak otherwise. From the very function of baptism he rightly infers that martyrdom may properly and deservedly be distinguished by the name “baptism,” because it provides remission of sins just as [Col. 0050D] baptism does, lest his opponents suspect that here only the name itself is being considered (Origen, *On Matthew*, p. 416, Huet’s ed.):

> Καθὸ ἄφεσιν λαμβάνει ἁμαρτημάτων ὁ ὑπομείνας βάπτισμά ἐστιν· εἰ γὰρ τὸ βάπτισμα ἄφεσιν ἁμαρτημάτων ἐπαγγέλλεται, καθὼς παρειλήφαμεν περὶ τοῦ ἐν ὕδατι καὶ πνεύματι βαπτίσματος, ἄφεσιν δὲ λαμβάνει ἁμαρτημάτων καὶ ὁ τὸ τοῦ μαρτυρίου ὑπομείνας βάπτισμα, βάπτισμα τὸ μαρτύριον εὐλόγως λέγοιτ’ ἄν, etc.
>
> “Insofar as the person who endures it receives remission of sins, it is a baptism. For if baptism promises remission of sins, as we have received concerning baptism in water and Spirit, and the person who endures the baptism of martyrdom also receives remission of sins, martyrdom may reasonably be called baptism,” etc.

The same Adamantius states the same doctrine frequently in other places as well (Origen, *Homilies on Judges*, hom. 7; *On John*, tome VIII, p. 133, Huet’s ed.). Our Cyprian does so frequently too (Cyprian, *Epistle* LIV; *On the Lord’s Prayer*; *Exhortation to Martyrdom*; *Epistle* LXXIII), [Col. 0051A] as do very many later Fathers after Cyprian, whom it would be wearisome to enumerate individually here. For this opinion, approved by the concurring votes of Greeks and Latins, has consequently descended even to our own times.

§ 3.—It is furthermore worthy of notice that the ancients compared these two baptisms, of water and of blood, with one another in such a way that they sometimes placed this second baptism of blood after the first baptism of water, and conversely sometimes preferred it, according, namely, to a different relation and consideration.

With respect to that function of baptism by water through which we are united with Christ and the Church—although we have already shown in the preceding dissertation that the ancients conceded that baptism by blood also possessed a power at least to increase and advance this very union [Col. 0051B]—they nevertheless made that concession in such a way that meanwhile they acknowledged no power in it to advance the union of those who had not yet been joined to the Church by some prior and at least incipient bond of union, whether through communion in the Eucharistic office, or through baptism actually received, or at least desired in intention, as was the case with catechumens who were *competentes*; and, again, they acknowledged no power in it to obtain the benefits of martyrdom for those not yet united.

For they attributed no benefit to martyrdom if anyone suffered outside unity; nor did they recognize as one of its benefits that, by that very fact, anyone should be regarded as united by some invisible unity merely because he had suffered martyrdom. Accordingly, they believed that the martyrdoms of heretics and schismatics—that is, of those who had been cut off from unity [Col. 0051C] either by some act of their own or by an act of the Church—belonged neither to persons united with the Church nor, consequently, possessed any value before God.

They judged the case of catechumens more favorably. These were not so much separated from unity as they had not yet attained that unity; their not yet being united was therefore not to be imputed to them as a fault, but rather it was to their praise that they had observed the laws of ecclesiastical discipline. They were certainly already united by both their own intention and that of the Church; and because they had subjected themselves to ecclesiastical laws, by that very fact they professed themselves members of political unity, since they did not dare to seize mystical unity, however highly they valued it, but awaited the time when they might duly attain it through the laws of ecclesiastical polity.

It was therefore equitable that the benefits of unity should be granted to those [Col. 0051D] already joined by that unity which was lawful, and who were prevented by no fault of their own from attaining that other unity which was not yet lawful for them. According to the judgment of those centuries, moreover, the fruit of martyrdom was to be numbered among the benefits of unity. Our Cyprian argues this case of the catechumens in his epistle to Jubaianus (*Epistle* LXXIII).

That he condemned the martyrdoms of heretics and schismatics is too well known to require any proof. That Cyprian did not stand alone in this matter, but condemned them with the assent of the universal Church, is clear from St Augustine himself. Although Augustine most vigorously opposes our martyr in the controversy concerning the baptism of heretics, he nevertheless everywhere [Col. 0052A] approves Cyprian’s judgment concerning the martyrdoms of heretics and schismatics. It is also clear from the practice of the catholic Church itself: although it has always shown the greatest reverence for true martyrs, it has nevertheless never numbered heretics or schismatics among them, admitted none of their names into its calendars, and instituted no solemn commemoration of them.

§ 4.—Although, therefore, that prior baptism of water is necessary for the subject’s proper disposition, so that one may receive the fruit of baptism by blood, nevertheless, if we wish to make this comparison correctly and judge the benefit of each baptism, we must further ask which baptism confers the greater benefit upon a properly disposed subject.

With respect to this benefit, Origen and our Cyprian preferred baptism by blood to baptism by water. “The baptism of blood,” [Col. 0052B] says Origen (*Homilies on Judges*, hom. 7), “is the only baptism that renders us purer than the baptism of water rendered us.” A little later he explains this as follows:

> “I fear that this baptism is more excellent than the baptism bestowed through water. For after receiving the latter, very few are so blessed that they have been able to preserve it unstained until the end of life. But whoever has been baptized with this baptism can no longer go on to sin. And if it is not presumptuous to venture some assertion in such matters, we may say that through the former baptism past sins are cleansed, but through the latter even future sins are destroyed. There sins are forgiven; here they are excluded.”

In complete agreement with this opinion, our martyr calls this “the most glorious and greatest baptism of blood,” because, namely, the benefits of baptism by blood [Col. 0052C] are more glorious and greater than those which a properly disposed subject may expect through baptism by water. For he writes as follows in his *Exhortation to Martyrdom*:

> “Only let us, who by the Lord’s permission have bestowed the first baptism upon believers, prepare each person for the other as well, intimating and teaching that this baptism is greater in grace, more sublime in power, more precious in honor: a baptism in which angels baptize; a baptism in which God and his Christ rejoice; a baptism after which no one sins any longer; a baptism which brings the growth of our faith to completion; a baptism which, as we withdraw from the world, immediately joins us to God. In the baptism of water remission of sins is received; in that of blood, the crown of virtues. It is a thing to be embraced and desired, and to be sought with all the prayers [Col. 0052D] of our petitions, so that we who are servants of God may also be his friends.”

Here in this testimony of our Cyprian we find much in common with the passage from Origen, matters which cast reciprocal light both upon the common assertion and upon one another.

§ 5.—He estimates the magnitude of the grace chiefly from this consideration: after the baptism of water, when we sin again and lose baptismal grace, there remains in the baptism of blood no fear of future sins. Through it, therefore, we are rendered secure concerning future sins as well as past ones, whereas in the baptism of water only past sins are expiated. Origen had already observed this before Cyprian, as did, after our Cyprian, the most holy martyr Pelagia in Ambrose, book III, *On Virgins*. [Col. 0053A]

He further considers it pertinent to the magnitude of the grace that, whereas the Apostle referred the baptism of water to an “elementary doctrine” (*ἀρχῆς λόγον*) and a “foundation” (*θεμέλιον*) (Heb. 6:1–2), this baptism of blood serves to bring the advances of our faith to completion; that, whereas in the baptism of water, upon renouncing the world, we nevertheless await the enjoyment of God only from afar, through the baptism of blood we are immediately united to God; that, whereas there we obtain the remission of sins, here we may also expect a reward and a crown; and that there we profess ourselves servants of God—or at least his freedmen (*ἀπελευθέρους*)—whereas here we are also acknowledged as God’s friends.

Moreover, he calls this baptism of blood “more exalted in power,” because in the baptism of water we employ a human being as minister, whereas in the baptism of blood we are initiated through the ministry of angels. For just as that baptism of the martyrs is entirely invisible—at least as regards the part that concerns God himself—so, according to the principles of mystical philosophy, we have said that this invisible ministry (*λειτουργία*) must certainly be referred to God himself. Now in the mystical priesthood there were two offices corresponding exactly to those of the visible priesthood: one superior office, which they called “improving” (*βελτιωτικόν*) or “perfecting” (*τελειωτικόν*), undoubtedly proper to Christ himself in this mystical ministry (*λειτουργία*); and another, inferior or “ministerial” office (*ὑπηρετικόν*), which we have no reason to doubt was proper also to the angels. So too, unless we are mistaken, we have elsewhere proved that the function of baptism belonged to that inferior ministry. [Col. 0053B]

For in the outward administration of the baptism of water, the apostles generally employed ministers of the lower order. Accordingly, the same judgment must be made about that invisible and mystical baptism, so that it may correspond exactly to outward baptism: here too there was employment of ministers (*ὑπηρετῶν*), who, according to the understanding of those ancient writers, could have been none other than angels. For ancient writers—Jewish, ecclesiastical, sacred, and canonical alike—attribute to angels the symbol of the divine presence, which the Jews call the *Shechinah*; and an appearance which in one place they attribute to God they elsewhere assign to angels. We read that God appeared to Moses in the bush, yet St. Stephen calls him an angel (Acts 7:35). God promulgated the Decalogue on Mount Sinai, yet the Apostle says that this same law was promulgated by angels (Heb. 2:2). [Col. 0053C]

Indeed, in the entire business of the heavenly mysteries performed through the mysteries of the visible ecclesiastical hierarchy, Clement of Alexandria assigns to the angels the same office that is performed by the ordinary ministers of the Church, both that “improving” office (*βελτιωτικόν*) which I have mentioned and also the “ministerial” office (*ὑπηρετικόν*): “Both these ministries,” he says (Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, VII, beginning), “are discharged for God by angels, according to the administration of earthly affairs, and also by the Gnostic himself” (*ταύτας ἄμφω τὰς διακονίας ἄγγελοί τε ὑπηρετοῦνται τῷ θεῷ κατὰ τὴν τῶν περιγείων οἰκονομίαν, καὶ αὐτὸς ὁ γνωστικός*), etc. [Col. 0053D] But let us return to our Cyprian.

§ 6.—Finally, he adds that this mystical baptism of blood is more precious in honor. These words should perhaps be referred to the fact that, whereas in the baptism of water we are enrolled merely as servants, here in the baptism of blood we are adorned with the far more honorable title of friends. Perhaps they also refer to the outward pomp and ceremonial of this divine contest, namely that in it God [Col. 0054A] and his Christ rejoice.

The Lord teaches that there is rejoicing in heaven over the conversion of a sinner. They may perhaps have referred this conversion to the baptism of water and understood that rejoicing in heaven as the rejoicing of the angels. For “heaven” is contrasted with God (St. Luke 15:21), and heaven is joined with “those who dwell in it” (*τοῖς κατοικοῦσι*) (Rev. 12:12), something that certainly cannot so suitably be understood of the Triune God.

Thus they believed God to preside over this baptism of blood because, after comparing martyrdom to athletic contests or theatrical games, they made God the director of the contest and, as it were, a consul watching from the orchestra. In this connection Octavius uses the very word “spectacle,” borrowed from the theaters (Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, p. 358): “What a beautiful spectacle it is for God,” he says, “when a Christian enters into combat with suffering,” [Col. 0054B] etc. And our Cyprian writes (Epistle LVI): “Christ watches his soldier fighting everywhere.” And later: “Behold a sublime and mighty contest, glorious with the prize of a heavenly crown: God watches us as we contend. God watches us as we do battle and fight in the conflict of faith; his angels watch, and Christ also watches.” Elsewhere too (Epistle IX): “Oh, what a spectacle that was for the Lord—how sublime, how great, how acceptable in God’s eyes because of the sacramental fidelity and devotion of his soldier,” etc.

Nor is it surprising that Christians so often employed this same comparison, since the philosophers themselves—Seneca (*On Providence*, ch. 3) and Epictetus (*Letter to Arrian*)—had also employed it. Yet it is likely that the comparison was derived from a still higher source, namely from those visions in which God had appeared as present to those who were suffering. Thus Christ appeared to St. Stephen (Acts 7:55).
