During Polycarp’s contest, moreover, the Smyrnaeans record that a voice was sent forth from heaven: “Be strong, Polycarp, and show yourself a man” (*ἴσχυε Πολύκαρπε, καὶ ἀνδρίζου*) (*Epistle to the Philomelians*, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.15). [Col. 0054C] And rightly indeed did they regard this favorable presence of God as the highest honor.

They may perhaps have preferred the ceremonial of this baptism of blood in this respect: whereas Holy Scripture records that there is joy in heaven over the conversion of a sinner—one, that is, expiated by the baptism of water—they understood by “heaven” the heavenly creatures, namely the angels; here, however, they represented God himself and his Christ as applauding.

§ 7.—I am not unaware how little regard the despisers of antiquity will have for these reasonings of the ancient Christians. Because the ancients honored martyrdom with the title of a second baptism; because they did not bestow upon it merely the bare title but also attributed to it all the benefits of the first baptism; and because, not content even with that, they made it superior to the very baptism instituted by God—the despisers of antiquity will undoubtedly regard these things as nothing but the delusions and inventions of the martyrs. [Col. 0054D] They will furthermore be indignant and cry out that this audacity is intolerable: that the ancients attributed so much to their own inventions that they dared even to compare their fictitious baptism with the baptism instituted by Christ, much less prefer it.

Let us therefore ask whether the ancients held this opinion deservedly or otherwise. Meanwhile I ask and entreat our critics to set aside their passions for a time while we explain why the earliest Christians thought as they did. In this way they will both be fairer to us and take the best counsel for themselves, if they refrain from becoming rash judges of those heroes, who were undoubtedly most dear to Christ. [Col. 0055A]

Let us therefore see first whence the ancients inferred this second baptism. From that we shall understand whether their inference was sound and solid, and then whether the conclusions which, once those earlier principles had been granted, they built upon a comparison of the two baptisms were likewise solid.

§ 8.—It is manifest that the more recent writers received this doctrine from the more ancient. The former, therefore, should not be included in our present reckoning. Our martyr referred to this passage (St. Luke 12:50): “Of this,” he says, “the Lord also spoke when he said that he had another baptism with which to be baptized” (Epistle LXXIII, to Jubaianus). Origen also referred to it. Tertullian is more copious in proving the point:

> “We have indeed also a second washing, itself unique: namely, that of blood, concerning which the Lord says, ‘I have a baptism with which to be baptized,’ although he had already been baptized. For he had come through water and blood, as John wrote, so that he might be baptized in water and glorified in blood. Accordingly, to make us called through water and chosen through blood, he sent forth these two baptisms from the wound of his pierced side. For those who believed in his blood were to be washed with water, and those who had washed with water were also to drink blood. This is the baptism which supplies the washing when it has not been received and restores it when it has been lost.”  
> (Tertullian, *On Baptism*, ch. 16)

[Col. 0055B]

Because the Lord called his Passion another baptism; because he came in water and blood; and because on the cross he sent forth blood together with water from the wound of his pierced side—from these things they infer that the Lord had a twofold baptism. Yet from St. Matthew 20:22 they could infer that it was not peculiar to the Lord, for in that passage the Passion of the apostles must also be understood under the name of baptism. Let us therefore see whether this argument proceeds correctly and legitimately. [Col. 0055C]

§ 9.—First, therefore, we must recall what we also observed above [Note: [Col. 0055D] In the dissertation entitled *On the Principle of Unity*, etc., which it was not appropriate to append to the present volume]: not only the sayings of our Lord, but also his deeds—those, at least, which we now possess as committed to writing—are prophetic and were recorded for the perpetual use of the Church. Consequently, argumentation from deeds of this kind is not futile, as is commonly supposed, but solid.

Tertullian therefore concludes correctly from the fact that the Lord came through blood as well as through water that blood as well as water is beneficial to Christians. He likewise reasons correctly from the fact that Christ sent forth blood as well as water from the wound in his side that this blood too would be of use to the Church. [Col. 0055D]

But to prevent excessive license from being permitted in arguments of this kind, it must first be observed that the examples of the Lord which Tertullian produced here were not extraordinary but ordinary. In ordinary matters, our opponents will readily admit that the Lord’s life is an example for Christians. No one should doubt that his coming through blood as well as through water is something in which we can imitate him; this is precisely what we mean by the word “ordinary.” Moreover, physicians will also concede that the flowing of water together with blood from the wound in his side was not extraordinary, if it is understood as the fluid of the pericardium. [Col. 0056A]

Second, it must be observed that the Christian life is described in the New Testament as though whatever Christ did literally must be performed by us mystically. Thus we must die with him, be crucified with him, bear disgrace with him, be buried with him, rise with him, and ascend with him into heaven.

Third, it should be noted that these things must be understood principally, or at least primarily, of Christ’s sufferings. Although he did some things which perhaps surpass our capacity for imitation, we must nevertheless suffer the same things that he suffered.

Fourth, it should be noted that the meaning of a prophecy can best be judged when the prophetic type alludes to a known reality in the practice of the Church which is represented by it. For in prophetic representations it is certain that God intended the type to represent, not itself for its own sake, but the antitype; and it is likewise certain that this antitype must be sought nowhere other than in the Church. [Col. 0056B] Consequently, whenever a suitable antitype is found in the Church which corresponds exactly to the type, and there is no question of some other reality being expressed by it more vividly, there can be no doubt that God intended that very thing. Nor does this method of argument permit any latitude to wanton ingenuity.

This method is certainly entirely consistent with all the practices of the ancients who engaged in interpreting prophetic symbols. The writers of the New Testament kept before their eyes that the entire economy of the New Testament was antitypical, having been foreshadowed in the entire economy of the Old Testament. Consequently, whenever they found something similar in both economies, they also admitted here what they admitted nowhere else: that in similarities of this kind, reasoning from the prototypical likeness to the antitypical is sound and legitimate. [Col. 0056C]

They acknowledged an argument of this kind to possess a degree of certainty compatible with the obscurity that is generally characteristic of symbolic and prophetic style: a certainty sufficient at least to leave room in the meantime for the free choice of human beings, yet sufficient to enable sensible people to regulate their conduct prudently.

Thus, wherever in the Old Testament we find any mention of water, the sacred writers also refer all such passages to the baptismal water of the New Testament and infer from them the duties that must be observed in our baptism. So too, in the famous Athenian oracle concerning the wooden walls, Themistocles, considering that it had been issued for the sake of the Athenians, most prudently inferred that it must accordingly be understood with reference to Athenian customs. [Col. 0056D] Since the oracles of Loxias—that is, the Delphic Apollo—like the prophecies of the Jews, were to be explained not literally but symbolically, he therefore judged that one must ask whether there was anything in the already established Athenian commonwealth having some affinity with wooden walls. The oracle did not indicate walls that were to be newly constructed; and in a city flourishing in strength and maritime commerce there was nothing of which those walls could be more suitably understood than ships. Nor can anything be objected to the contrary concerning the uncertainty of this method of argument, since such uncertainty has been common to virtually all prophecies and oracles from the very beginnings of both. [Col. 0057A]

§ 10.—All these arguments, therefore, will proceed with the greatest force if it is assumed, fifth, that the realities represented by the prophetic types pertained to the perpetual use of the Church. For it is absolutely certain that those things which were to continue perpetually are matters of concern to God, and that they especially needed to be established by some definite decree; they must therefore be considered to have belonged to God’s principal design in the prophetic symbols. Accordingly, whenever something corresponds to them with complete exactness, it must be attributed not to fortuitous chance but to the most certain counsel of Providence.

Therefore, since what we read about the Lord’s coming through [Col. 0057B] water and blood, and about water and blood flowing from the wound in his side, fulfilled the function of symbols according to the idiom of prophetic style; since these things correspond most aptly to these two baptisms of the Church; and since there is no reason to doubt that both were to be perpetual—it plainly follows that the Lord is most suitably understood in this manner.

This is especially so if it is observed, sixth, that unless we refer the Lord’s types to this purpose, as foretelling the state and constitution that he willed for the Church, there is certainly nothing else from which it may be established that the Church’s discipline was constituted by him. For nowhere do we read that the Lord expressly prescribed it. Moreover, this method of delivering teaching through symbols was so approved by the Lord that he delivered everything to the multitude, and even most things to the disciples, through symbols; [Col. 0057C] and indeed, in accordance with the testimony of the ancient prophecies concerning him, this was how he was to teach.

This manner of communicating things was especially suitable when future realities were being communicated for which the hearers’ understanding was not yet mature. For when the Savior communicated such things, he instructed even the disciples through symbols, deliberately ensuring that they would not be understood until the event had confirmed their truth. Now the baptism of the Spirit, which was indeed the principal part of the sacrament, was nevertheless not communicated before the Resurrection; accordingly, he too foretold it, not in express words, but under the symbol of water (St. John 7:38–39).

But if he judged that the baptism of the Spirit, which contributed so greatly to his glory, should nevertheless be enveloped in obscure riddles, then by much stronger reason that baptism of blood and martyrdom had to be concealed from those who could not yet comprehend it at all. [Col. 0057D] For they had not believed that the Lord himself had to undergo that baptism of blood and virtually relapsed into unbelief when, contrary to their expectation, they discovered that it had truly happened (St. Luke 24:21). They would therefore have suffered far more serious scandal if, while they were not yet mature enough, they had learned that they too must undergo the same baptism.

Consequently, although the Lord sometimes mentioned the things that the disciples were to suffer on his account, lest, when they occurred, they should suspect that he had been unaware of them or that they had occurred contrary to his design, he nevertheless did so very cautiously and in accommodation to the understanding of the weak—far from mentioning explicitly the baptism of blood, which was a state of suffering.

[Col. 0058A] § 11.—It must therefore be observed, second, that it also cannot be denied that the Savior called his Passion a baptism, and that, in his reckoning, the apostles’ suffering for his name amounted to their being baptized with the baptism with which he himself was baptized (St. Matt. 20:22). For this is what we have in the Greek and in other very ancient versions. Those words are nevertheless absent from the Latin Vulgate, with Hilary, Ambrose (Hilary, canon 30 on Matthew), Jerome (Jerome, book III, *Commentary on Matthew 20*), and even Origen himself supporting that omission, whatever Grotius may intimate to the contrary (Origen, *On Matthew*, vol. XVI, p. 415 of Huet’s edition).

The most ancient Syriac interpreter, however, agrees with the Greek manuscripts. And even if we were to concede that the words should be expunged here, no one doubts that they must nevertheless be read in St. Mark [Col. 0058B] 10:38–39. Accordingly, we have no reason to fear for the argument.

Our opponents, however, will understand here a different meaning of the word “baptism” from that which we use when speaking of the sacrament. Let them therefore show another meaning in the authors of that age besides one pertaining to expiation and sanctification. All the baptisms then in use, I think, certainly aimed at that purpose: not only the baptisms of human beings, by which they were enrolled in the discipline of the Pharisees or of John, but also those of vessels and sacred utensils.

Therefore, when the Lord applies to martyrdom a word of known meaning, he must have intended that the same result would come from martyrdom as was expected from those baptisms: namely, that his followers would be cleansed and expiated from their impurities by blood as well as by water. [Col. 0058C]

If they say that the Lord nowhere indicated that these fruits were to be expected from martyrdom, they might likewise observe that the Savior never taught this even concerning the sacrament of baptism. There is certainly no mention of the expiation of sins in his institution of it in St. Matthew, nor in the account of its practice in St. John. Yet we have proved elsewhere from the apostles’ writings that this is the fruit of sacramental baptism.

It is therefore altogether likely that the apostles derived what they taught from the familiar meaning of the word at that time, as I have said, and from the contemporary practice of the thing itself among those from whom the Christians received it—unless our opponents think it preferable, without any necessity whatever, to have recourse here to a new revelation made to the apostles. But if the apostles inferred from the familiar meaning of the word that this power of expiating sins must be attributed to sacramental baptism, why should we not infer in the same manner, from the meaning of the same word, that the same purifying power must likewise be attributed to the baptism of blood? [Col. 0058D]

§ 12.—But lest anyone think that our sole support rests upon the meaning of the word itself, come, let us see whether the matter itself establishes that the Savior was correctly understood here by the ancients.

It must therefore be observed, third, that the most probable occasion of those passages which the ancients believed to concern the baptism of blood was martyrdom. No one should doubt that the other baptism with which the Lord said he was to be baptized must be understood of his Passion on the cross. Yet that very Passion, in accordance also with the usage of the sacred writers, is called a martyrdom. Hence the Lord himself is called “the faithful and true witness” (*μάρτυς ὁ πιστὸς καὶ ἀληθινός*) (Rev. 1:5; 3:14), and is said “to have borne witness to the good confession under Pontius Pilate” (*μαρτυρῆσαι ἐπὶ Ποντίου Πιλάτου τὴν καλὴν ὁμολογίαν*) (1 Tim. 6:13). [Col. 0059A] All these expressions, according to the idiom of the primitive Church, designate martyrdom.

Moreover, lest we suppose that anything here was fabricated by ecclesiastical writers, Holy Scripture itself employs the word “martyr” in its ecclesiastical sense. Thus Stephen is a “martyr” (*μάρτυς*) (Acts 22:20), as is Antipas, “the faithful martyr” (*μάρτυς ὁ πιστός*) (Rev. 2:13)—the same words which, as we have seen, the author of the Apocalypse had earlier attributed to the Lord. No one, therefore, should be surprised that the ancients understood the word “martyr,” when applied even to the Lord, in its ecclesiastical sense.

Indeed, some of the martyrs in Eusebius so far from believing this meaning of the word foreign to the Lord virtually made the title “Martyr” proper to the Lord alone (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.2). [Col. 0059B] But if the Lord’s Passion was a martyrdom and must likewise be honored with the name of baptism, what new or incongruous thing do we say if we affirm the same concerning the martyrs of the Church?

§ 13.—It is certainly probable that the occasion of the other passages points in the same direction. When the apostle St. John wrote, there appear already to have arisen heretics who were indeed earlier than the Valentinians, yet were their parents and origins. For the Valentinian system was not entirely new. Rather, Valentinus “reshaped the inventions of earlier heretics according to his own distinctive character” (*πρὸς ἴδιον χαρακτῆρα μεθήρμωσε*), as Irenaeus says of him (Irenaeus, book I, ch. 5); he was born from the seeds of a certain ancient opinion, according to Tertullian (Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, ch. 4). [Col. 0059C]

Just as the Valentinians divided Jesus from Christ, following the example of earlier heretics who were contemporaries of the Apostle—on whose account the Apostle devotes so much attention to precisely that argument in his First Epistle—so it is probable that those heretics contemporary with the Apostle, like the Valentinians themselves, also abolished martyrdoms. The Apostle’s arguments will certainly fit that position perfectly, as our Hammond observed before us.

These heretics were antichrists or, what amounts to the same thing in the Apostle’s usage, false Christs, because they assumed for themselves the person of the Christ promised to the Jews. Accordingly, the Apostle intimates that the whole purpose of his Gospel was that people should believe that Jesus was the Son of God (John 20:31)—the title, namely, which the Jews of that age asserted to belong to the Messiah on the basis of Psalm 2:7—and not that those leaders of the heretics were the Son of God. [Col. 0059D]

Therefore, among the other arguments by which the Apostle refutes that false claim to be Christ, he also employed the argument concerning the true Christ’s coming through water and blood: “This is he,” he says, “who came through water and blood, Jesus Christ; not in water only, but in water and blood” (1 John 5:6).

He argued, that is, from the signs of the true Messiah which were agreed upon among the Jews, or at least among the Christians of that age, both to prove that our Jesus was the true Messiah and to disprove those false Christs by the very title of baptism. “He came,” the Apostle says, “through water and blood.” [Col. 0060A]

Among the other titles of the Messiah by which they understood him to be designated in Scripture, the foremost—or at least a principal one—was “the Coming One” (*ὁ Ἐρχόμενος*). Thus we find it in St. Luke 7:19–20 and elsewhere. Perhaps they derived it from the celebrated passage Genesis 49:10, or from Psalms 50:3; 94:13; 98:9, or from other similar passages of Scripture in which the Messiah is said to be coming.

Therefore, since the Messiah was called “the Coming One,” the signs of the Messiah amount to the same thing as the signs of the Advent. Thus the disciples say of the true Messiah, “What will be the sign of your coming?” (St. Matthew); and the Apostle says of the false Messiah, “Whose coming is according to the working of Satan, with all power and signs,” etc. (2 Thess. 2:9). To come through water and blood, therefore, means the same as to prove oneself the true Messiah through water and blood.

§ 14.—The one who was to come into the world was the same one who was to be sent and sanctified by the Father (St. John 10:36). What kind of sanctification this was understood to be we shall best infer from the holiest office of the Jews, namely the high priesthood. It is established that in the high priest’s sanctification both water and blood had a place: water in Exodus 29:4 and Leviticus 8:6; blood in Exodus 29:20–21 and Leviticus 8:23–24.

For in this very matter the Apostle applied to the Messiah, as the mystical priest of the evangelical covenant, the example of the Jewish high priest, because the Messiah too was to be sanctified through his Passion. The Apostle employed the word “perfection” or “consecration” (*τελείωσις*) (Heb. 2:10–11; 5:8–9), a term that was mystical and proper to the sacred administration of the mysteries. [Col. 0060C]

Yet the Apostle compares Christ’s priesthood with the Jewish priesthood in such a way that, after showing that blood was employed in the consecration of both, he makes Christ’s priesthood pre-eminent in this respect: Christ was consecrated solely by his own blood, whereas the Jews employed only the external blood of animals in the consecration of their priests (Heb. 9:25–26). He repeatedly presses the same point elsewhere, teaching that Christ was initiated not with the blood of bulls or goats, but solely with his own true blood.

Thus the Apostle agreed with the Jews—to whose principles he adapted his argument here—that Christ would be a high priest foreshadowed by the supreme high priest of the Jews. Consequently, the one who was to be the true Messiah was both to be cleansed with blood as well as water—or, to use the evangelical expression, baptized with them—and was himself to cleanse others with those same elements. [Col. 0060D]

That this was an accepted belief concerning the baptism of water is established by the Pharisees’ very question, by which they thought to investigate whether John was presenting himself as the Messiah: “Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?” (St. John 1:25).

The Lord’s words to the disciples intimate the same concerning the baptism of blood: “O foolish and slow of heart to believe all that the prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary that the Christ should suffer these things and so enter into his glory?” (St. Luke 24:25–26). He inferred this, namely, from those Scriptures whose meaning he afterward explained to the disciples, when he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures. These were passages which, either on the basis of premises conceded in those ages or by certain accepted reasonings of that age, had to be understood of the Messiah and which foretold the Messiah’s future Passion. [Col. 0061A] Writers not only of the New Testament but also Fathers of subsequent centuries whose disputations against the Jews survive today—Justin, Tertullian, Eusebius, etc.—adduce very many such passages.

§ 15.—Those Scriptures, therefore, which according to the understanding of that age were interpreted as referring to the Messiah’s Passion could serve as arguments among those who, just as they differed from the orthodox by denying that Jesus was the Christ, differed in turn from the Jews by nevertheless believing that the Christ whom they had imagined, whatever sort of Christ he might be, had already come.

Thus the Apostle confirmed that Jesus was the Christ because he had come through blood as well as through [Col. 0061B] water. He placed the emphasis and force of the argument precisely in this: that Jesus came not in water only, but in water and blood. For not even the false Christs had rejected that claim of coming in water; they had merely failed to include blood among the signs of their coming, since those antichrists themselves had given their disciples neither an example nor even an institution of suffering. For that very reason the Apostle proves that they must be excluded from the name of Christ, since anyone bearing that name was bound to employ both signs.

§ 16.—Nor do I think that the sign in the Gospel concerning the water and blood flowing from the wound in Christ’s side on the cross should be referred to anything else. The Apostle thought it necessary to confirm that sign so forcefully, as though it had been the subject of the greatest doubt:

> “And he who saw it has borne witness, and his testimony is true. And he knows that he speaks the truth, so that you also may believe” (St. John 19:35).

[Col. 0061C]

Had there not been a controversy among Christ’s rivals which had to be settled by the reasoning I have described, the Lord’s other miracles would certainly have confirmed with sufficient fullness that he had been sent by the Father. Yet the Apostle produced no witnesses for those miracles, much less confirmed them with so great an asseveration as he employed here.

Moreover, the words “so that you also” possess a certain extraordinary emphasis. The other miracles, that is, were both performed for the sake of unbelievers and committed to writing; this one miracle, however, was intended for entirely different adversaries—namely, the defenders of those antichristian rivals for whose sake the Gospel had been written.

Tertullian was therefore correct to refer to the same subject both this emission of blood and water from Christ’s side and this twofold baptism of water and blood. [Col. 0061D] Since the Apostle wrote both passages against the same adversaries, it is certainly probable that they must be referred to the same subject.

Furthermore, since the Apostle (1 John 5:8) compares blood with the baptisms of water and the Spirit in such a way that it completes a triad with them, it plainly follows that the character of baptism was common to blood and water. And because from the emission of water and blood he refutes the antichrists in the Gospel in the same manner as he had refuted them in the Epistle through the coming in water and blood, it follows further that, if the baptism of blood is meant by “blood” in the Epistle, then the baptisms of water and blood must likewise be understood in that emission of water and blood recorded in the Gospel. [Col. 0062A]

Thus, from the occasion of the passages which Tertullian—and, undoubtedly, the ancient Church together with Tertullian—referred to this subject when mentioning water and blood, we infer that no other blood than baptismal blood is to be understood.

§ 17.—But you will say that the character of baptism common to water, blood, and the Spirit was common only equivocally; consequently, we should not infer from this common character of baptism that the same fruits are to be expected from the baptism of blood and the baptism of water.

To prevent this objection, we observe further, fourth, that in the very rite of initiation and expiation to which the ancients attributed that cleansing of sins, the use of blood was as frequent among them as the use of water. Everyone will readily concede that sacrifices played a part in both Jewish [Col. 0062B] and Gentile initiation.

Among the Jews, the rabbinic observation is also well known according to which they say that three things must be observed in proselytism: circumcision, sacrifice, and baptism. Moreover, we have already proved that, in the judgment of the ancients, martyrdom took the place of sacrifice.

Besides sacrificial blood, it was not foreign to the common practice of initiations for people also to employ their own blood for their expiation. Circumcision among the Jews is a clear example. We also learn from Tertullian that blood was shed in the initiations of Bellona (*Apology*, ch. 8):

> “Today, in that place, the consecrated blood of Bellona, caught in the palm of the hand from a slashed thigh, is given to her marked initiates.”

Other writers also mention the same rite. [Col. 0062C] Yet when Lampridius writes thus in his life of Commodus—“He ordered the servants of Bellona actually to cut their arms”—Casaubon infers that the wounds of the Bellonarii were usually only feigned and simulated. Later enthusiasts may perhaps have reached that conclusion through their more indulgent little interpretations.

But from the passage of Tertullian quoted above, as well as from Vegetius and most of the other writers who mention this rite, we infer that the shedding of blood introduced by the ancients was real, as was that practiced by soldiers initiated into the rites of Bellona.

Indeed, very many passages of Scripture establish that this custom of purification through bloodletting was extremely ancient: Leviticus 19:28; Deuteronomy 14:1; 1 Kings 18:28; Jeremiah 16:6. Thus did the worshipers of Baal; thus the Galli—whose sacred day, the ninth day before the Kalends of April, which they also called the Day of Blood, is mentioned in the *Life of the Divine Claudius* by Trebellius Pollio. Casaubon wrongly referred to Bellona what Trebellius himself referred to the Great Mother. [Col. 0062D] Thus too did the devotees of Isis and the Luperci, grievously punishing themselves with scourges or blows to the breast until they drew blood. They followed, that is, the same example by which even witches are said today to seal their covenants with demons in their own blood.

Source/review notes: The supplied Latin has an inherited lacuna after “appellatum” in § 18: the designation said to occur at Exodus 4:26 is absent. The draft’s “bridegroom of blood” therefore cannot be retained from the supplied text alone; the edit marks the gap explicitly.

§ 18.—Nor did baptism merely take the place of initiation rites; it also served the function of a covenant. Now it was also the custom of parties entering a covenant to ratify their agreements with one another by their own blood. This was how the Jews understood their circumcision. Hence Medus and Gregory—and, before them, Schindler in his *Lexicon*—observed, with reference to Exodus 4:26, that one who had been initiated into the Mosaic covenant by blood was called, in accordance with accepted Jewish customs, [by a designation absent from the supplied source]. [Col. 0063A]

The same practice obtained in the covenants of the Gentiles, even in the most ancient of them, some memory of which we indeed retain to this day. Concerning the Medes and Lydians, Herodotus is our authority in *Clio*: “These nations make sworn covenants in the same manner as the Greeks; and, in addition, when they have cut their arms, they lick up one another’s blood where it flows together.” Concerning the Scythians, in *Melpomene*: “The Scythians make sworn covenants with those with whom they are contracting in the following manner: after pouring wine into a large earthenware bowl, they mingle with it the blood of those who are making the covenant.” Solinus writes as follows concerning the same Scythians and the Medes: “By drinking one another’s blood they ratify a covenant, following not only their own custom but also the established practice of the Medes” (*Polyhistor*, ch. 20). [Col. 0063B] More recent historians, moreover, have also mentioned other barbarian peoples among whom this custom was received.

Our writers against the Socinians have shown that the Gentiles understood the same thing even in those sacrifices of brute animals: those slaughters of animals stood in the place of human beings, who called down similar treatment upon themselves if they should break faith. Accordingly, that sacrificial blood, although animal blood, was nevertheless a substitute for human blood and was to be regarded in precisely the same way as if the person himself had pledged his own blood.

And although this twofold purification by water and by blood, undertaken for the expiation of sins, was received among both Jews and Gentiles, greater efficacy was nevertheless ascribed to blood than to water. For the offenses believed to be expiated by the sprinkling of water were comparatively light. All the graver offenses regarded as *piacula*, or ἄγη (*polluting transgressions*), had to be cleansed by blood. [Col. 0063C] The ancients numbered homicide among such polluting offenses, because it branded the earth itself with a stain that could be washed away by no cleansing fluid other than blood. If the perpetrator was known, they expiated the pollution with his own blood; but if he remained unknown, with the blood of a heifer to be sacrificed at the place.

Nor was killing alone involved: the legal impurity contracted through contact with dead bodies also had to be cleansed by the ashes of the red heifer. Indeed, the sins of the whole Israelite people were cast by imprecation upon the scapegoat (Lev. XVI), to be atoned for, as the Rabbis maintain, by its death. Nor was the opinion of the Greeks concerning their own καθάρματα (*purificatory victims*) any different, as we learn from the scholiast on Aristophanes (*Aristophanes, scholium on Plutus*).

And this purification of sins by blood was so universal that the Apostle admits no exception here: “Without,” he says, “the shedding of blood there is no remission” (Heb. IX, 22). [Col. 0063D] It was therefore consistent with the doctrines of those times that, although they regarded both expiation by blood and expiation by water as baptism, they nevertheless acknowledged a greater power in the baptism of blood than in the baptism of water.

§ 19.—And just as they readily assigned the chief part in this work of expiation to blood, so they recognized by far the greatest power in human blood above every other kind of blood. From this arose that monstrous ἀνθρωποθυσία (*human sacrifice*) which prevailed among the ancients, because human blood appeared most suitable for expiating human transgressions.

When some especially grave calamity from an angered deity threatened a country—one that portended the widespread destruction of many—the lives of the many had to be redeemed by the blood of a few, whether that blood was to be drawn in sacrifice or in some other manner. [Col. 0064A] The author commonly believed to be the very ancient Pseudo-Sanchuniathon, in Philo of Byblos, gave this explanation of ἀνθρωποθυσία among the Phoenicians (apud Eusebius, *Praeparatio evangelica*, I, 10; IV, 16; Porphyry, *De abstinentia*, II, 56).

Mythographers give the same explanation for why Phrixus and Helle were marked out for sacrifice when the barrenness of the earth threatened famine—for so Ino persuaded Athamas. They give the same explanation for the daughters of Leos, for Andromeda, and even, among the later Romans, for Curtius and the two Decii devoting themselves to destruction in order to preserve or increase their country. Agamemnon sought to preserve the army’s safety by sacrificing his daughter Iphigenia; and he also sought to preserve it by sacrificing Polyxena, an enemy. [Col. 0064B]

Many examples tending to the same conclusion provide ample proof of how much power they attributed to human blood in expiating human crimes, and how greatly they preferred it to purifications by water. Among the Jews, circumcision itself performed the function of an entirely blood-based expiation—or a baptism, if one prefers to call it so with the Lord—and one, moreover, to be performed with the human blood of the person being initiated.

Accordingly, since the one thing that properly belongs to the nature of baptism is that sins are expiated in it; and since, in this mode of expiation, the Lord had before him the examples both of the Jews and of the Gentiles, who attributed this benefit to blood no less than to water, who attributed it even to the human blood of the person being initiated, and who granted a greater efficacy to purification by blood than even to purification by water: it was surely not consistent that Christians alone should lack that greater power of expiation in blood than in water of which others boasted among themselves. [Col. 0064C]

This is especially so because, as we have already said, virtually the whole argument of the New Testament is devoted to proving that whatever privileges either Jews or Gentiles possessed and boasted of belonged to Christians in a superior and more excellent manner. It was not consistent that, when both the Lord himself and the writers of the New Testament employed the word “baptism” in this same connection, they should nevertheless have understood by it a meaning other than the universally known and accepted meaning of expiation. It was not consistent that those who thought in this way should nevertheless speak otherwise than we have already observed our martyr speaking: namely, that the expiatory power of the baptism of blood should be regarded as far superior to that of the baptism of water. [Col. 0064D] So far are we from being obliged to regard this manner of speaking as harsh and alien both to the dignity of the sacraments and to the intention of the Lord, as our adversaries consider it to be.

§ 20.—We have thus shown how aptly, consistently, and coherently all these things fit together according to the doctrines of that age, if we understand the Lord himself and his Apostles in this way. It follows that a presumption should rather be made in favor of this sense—or, if we prefer Tertullian’s term, it should be laid down as a preliminary rule—unless clear arguments arise from the matter itself showing why it should be understood otherwise.

But so far are we from having contrary arguments in the matter itself that nothing contributes more to the confirmation of our position than a deeper examination of the matter itself. [Col. 0065A] It must therefore be observed, fifthly, that this baptism of blood belongs to the sacrament of baptism itself, and indeed belongs to it in such a way that it completes its principal part. Once we have proved this, no one, I think, will fail readily to concede that the principal fruit of baptism may rightfully and deservedly be expected from it.

Nor, I think, does that comparison of the Apostle tend to any other conclusion, in which he brought water, blood, and the Spirit together into one, so that, just as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one, so water, the Spirit, and blood are “unto one”—because they all perform and complete one and the same office. We have observed that the water and the Spirit must be understood as baptismal; accordingly, this baptism of blood must complete that sacramental baptism. [Col. 0065B]

Origen himself observed this before us, lest anyone suspect that our interpretation is insufficiently consistent with the doctrines of the ancients. Nor is it an objection that those same ancients called this baptism of blood a “second” baptism. For they must be understood in this sense: although sacramental baptism cannot be renewed a second time, nevertheless in martyrdom its benefits are to be expected anew, without any renewal of that baptism itself; and the new sins of adult believers, which had not been remitted in the baptism of water, are here remitted fully and entirely, according to the manner and measure of baptismal remission. Since this is a second remission, it will certainly not be surprising if it seems also to be attributed to a second baptism. [Col. 0065C] But, setting aside the Apostle’s testimony, come: let us explain the matter itself from the proper nature of this sacramental baptism.

§ 21.—Let us therefore recall first of all that this whole business of baptism is a kind of covenant between believers and God and can be explained from nothing more correctly than from the received customs of covenants.

For the following propositions are so manifest from the reasonings of the New Testament that it is astonishing that there are people today who doubt our assertion: that the Gospel is a καινὴ διαθήκη, a “new covenant,” different, of course, from that which belonged to the Jews and to the Mosaic law; that under the Gospel there is not only a testament but also a covenant, and that this twofold meaning of διαθήκη is applicable even to the times of the Gospel; that under mystical Israelitism there are exactly the same covenantal benefits that formerly belonged properly to literal Israelitism, so that the Most High God is enrolled as our own God, while we in turn [Col. 0065D] are enrolled as his own people; and not only this, but also that this confederation of ours with God is external and must be understood in such a way that some external bond of political union exists, common both among ourselves and between God and us, by which we profess ourselves to be in covenant with God and are also recognized by others as being in covenant with him—precisely in the same manner in which Israel according to the flesh could once be recognized, above the nations of the whole world, as the people in covenant with God.

If, I say, we acknowledge these propositions as true, it plainly follows that the external solemnities by which we are enrolled in the political society of Christians are solemnities of the covenant. [Col. 0066A] And who would doubt that it is the proper office of baptism that through it we are initiated into the sacred rites of Christians and enrolled in the Christians’ own society?

It is further consistent with this that the Spirit conferred in Christian baptism is called in the New Testament an ἀρραβών, a “pledge” or “earnest”—which Roman writers also call *arrha*. For under Roman law an earnest was proper to covenants, especially marriage contracts. The Apostle intimates in Ephesians V that the mystical unity with the Church corresponds to marital unity. An earnest, moreover, properly belongs to the time when we first enter into the covenant. It follows from this that it cannot be understood of any conferral of the Spirit other than the baptismal one.

Finally, the baptismal forms used in the primitive Church also agree with this:

“Do you believe?”

“I believe.”

“Do you renounce?”

“I renounce.” [Col. 0066B]

For these too were modeled upon the forms of Roman contracts, again especially marriage contracts:

“Do you give?”

“I give.”

“Do you pledge?”

“I pledge.”

From this, at least, it necessarily follows that the earliest Christians regarded baptism as a covenant.

§ 22.—From this it follows, secondly, that just as in other covenants, so also in our baptismal covenant, the obligations of the different parties must be distinguished from one another: some belong to God and others to us.

To God belong the promises by which provision is made for bestowing the benefits of baptism: both those to be bestowed in the present—expiation of all sins, the gift of the Holy Spirit, mystical union with Christ, at least externally, and so forth—and those concerning the future rewards of our duty.

To us belong the things that we in turn pledge to perform as our part of the baptismal covenant. [Col. 0066C] For although we admit that promises made outside covenants may quite properly be understood without an obligation on the part of another party, nevertheless promises that constitute one side of a covenant altogether require reciprocal obligations from both parties. The very nature of a covenant necessarily presupposes this. For promises that presupposed no corresponding obligations on the opposite side might perhaps be said to have been given, but certainly not covenanted.

§ 23.—It follows, thirdly, that every legal right which we obtain by the benefit of the covenant must be derived from God’s promises on the basis of the performance of our obligation. For this is common to all covenants: the promises contained in them are understood as conditional and are not owed until the conditions of the promises have been performed by the other party. [Col. 0066D]

But in the kind of covenants which, on one side, include only benefits to be bestowed upon others and no benefits in turn to be received from them—such as covenants common to God and human beings must necessarily be—everyone will admit that it is equitable that there can be no right to the benefits unless the conditions to be performed by the other party have first been fulfilled.

At present, however, we are treating of legal right, not of equity alone. There may perhaps be some equity in allowing a person who intended to fulfill a condition sometimes to obtain the benefit attached to that condition, even though he has not yet fulfilled it in fact, when through no fault of his own he is prevented from fulfilling it in fact. Nevertheless, it is entirely certain that anyone who has not fulfilled the condition in fact lacks, at least, a legal right, whatever course of events may have prevented him. [Col. 0067A]

This argument applies with still greater force to covenants whose conditions are not merely conditions imposed at the will of the imposer, but also dispositions necessary on the part of the subject. Since, therefore, no benefit from this covenant accrues to God, it follows that whatever God requires from us is necessary for our sake, so that unless we perform what is required, we are rendered unfit and indisposed for obtaining the very benefits promised.

§ 24.—Fourthly, therefore, in order to understand what conditions incumbent upon us are to be fulfilled as our part of this baptismal covenant, we must attend to the symbols to be employed by us in the covenant’s solemnities themselves, and to what those symbols signify by God’s own institution and according to the laws of symbolic signification prevailing at least in that age. [Col. 0067B]

For symbols employed in the solemnities of a covenant are instituted not merely to signify but also to bind. Just as all sacraments, or mysteries, are to be understood as sacred covenants between human beings and God, so it is characteristic of all sacred intercourse that its terms should be understood symbolically rather than literally, and that the obligations binding the parties transacting with one another should be represented not so much by words as by things—things, however, which are symbols of other things.

Accordingly, by virtue of the baptismal covenant we are regarded as promising that we will thereafter perform what is signified by the baptismal symbols; and when these things have been performed by us, they give us the resulting right to claim the divine promises by virtue of that same evangelical covenant. [Col. 0067C]

§ 25.—Fifthly, in the solemn symbols of our sacramental baptism, not only the baptism of water but also the baptism of blood is denoted. It is denoted, however, in such a way that both are indicated by one and the same symbol, by one and the same element, so that they are therefore understood to belong, as we have said, to one and the same baptism.

For when water is employed, we promise the abandonment of sins and a future holiness of life, which is represented quite aptly by the external symbol of water. Likewise, when we descend into the water and in turn emerge from it, we represent Christ’s death, burial, and resurrection; and we also pledge ourselves as participants in all these things, prepared, namely, to endure for his sake, even unto death, whatever he may bring upon us. [Col. 0067D]

By the same symbol, insofar as it refers to Christ, we understand that Christ will reckon our sufferings as his own, and that he will reward our sufferings with the same recompense that he himself claims from the Father under his covenant with the Father.

It will thus be clear by what right our sufferings claim for themselves the name of baptism, since they serve to complete the very nature of sacramental baptism. It will also be clear by what further right they claim the benefits of that same baptism, since they too are represented by symbols instituted by God and instituted with this very purpose: to represent and pledge our sufferings. These symbols are also promissory symbols belonging to God as he covenants with us; [Col. 0068A] by the reciprocal right of the covenant, they bind him to perform what is represented by the symbols—to acknowledge our sufferings as his own, and to compensate them by his merit and his reward.

§ 26.—Indeed, if we gather the various assertions of the several passages of Scripture into one bundle, it will readily become clear that this entire argument was framed with the utmost precision according to the intention and principles of our Lord.

First of all, the Apostle teaches plainly enough in Romans VI that our suffering and death with Christ are represented in baptism; and not merely represented, but represented in such a way as somehow to unite our sufferings with Christ’s suffering and make both common to each.

That our suffering and Christ’s are one is clear from his words:

“We have died with Christ,” v. 8;

“Our old man was crucified together with him,” v. 6;

“We were buried together with him,” v. 4. [Col. 0068B]

And the following words intimate that this entire union is accomplished by a kind of vivid representation:

“We have been planted together in the likeness of his death,” v. 5.

Nor is it accomplished by any office other than that of baptism:

“Do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? For we were buried together with him by baptism into death,” vv. 3–4.

This must not, however, be regarded as a bare union alone, constituted wholly in human imagination and estimation. We have said that the nature of a promissory symbol is such that it brings with it a certain legal obligation, by which the parties covenanting with one another are bound to perform what they represented by the symbols. Hence, although the reality could not be produced by mere likeness, from this representation itself there nevertheless arises for us a certain right to the reality, by which we may claim the internal and mystical union itself and its benefits. [Col. 0068C]

Reasonings of the following kind rest upon this very principle:

“For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be so in his resurrection,” v. 5;

“But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live together with Christ,” v. 8 [the source gives v. 6].

For we have already shown that the death under discussion here is none other than the typical and symbolic death represented in baptism. The Apostle took it as established that those to whom he thus argued had already undergone that symbolic death, since they had employed the symbols of death in baptism. From this, as from a commonly acknowledged principle, the argument proceeded legitimately, provided we also understand that symbols employed in making a covenant are themselves promissory.

Nor, as I judge, does the following reasoning of the same Apostle, although in another place, rest upon any different hypothesis:

“Therefore, if you have risen together with Christ,” he says, “seek the things that are above,” and so forth (Col. III, 1).

“Mortify, therefore, your members,” and so forth (v. 5). [Col. 0068D]

His supposition that they had already risen can refer to nothing other than their emergence from the baptismal water, which was the symbol of resurrection. Thus, in the forensic idiom of covenants, they were considered to have risen when they employed the symbol of resurrection.

From this he rightly infers the duties of the Colossians, provided only that the principles which we have already shown must necessarily be presupposed. For by that symbol of death—namely, immersion—they pledged that they would undertake the mortification of their members; and by the symbol of resurrection they likewise pledged that they would rise to a new and heavenly life. From this everyone can see how soundly and prudently he argues when, on the basis of their covenant and promise, he exhorts them not to fail in their duty or break faith. [Col. 0069A] Such consequences would, however, be exceedingly weak and barren if he were exhorting them from an empty symbol of death and resurrection to mystical death and resurrection.

§ 27.—It is thus established as a matter of fact that the baptism of blood cannot be excluded either by the institution of the baptism of water itself or from the benefit of the baptismal covenant.

If we inquire further into the rationale of this fact, it must, unless I am mistaken, be derived at a deeper level from two principles in particular: first, that Christ’s death was to be crowned with the reward of the blessed resurrection; and second, that it must be numbered among the chief benefits of baptism that, by virtue of baptism, our death too is reckoned to Christ.

We have already shown above, even from the Old Testament, that this reward of resurrection was owed to Christ by the very title of his death. [Col. 0069B] It was owed under that earlier covenant concerning the whole business of redemption and the incarnation which he concluded with the Father.

For Christ’s resurrection is attributed not so much to his own proper and native Deity as to the Father. Moreover, in this affair the Father acted not precisely in the person of a father, but of a judge; he had regard not to his own στοργή (*affection*) toward the Son, but rather to Christ’s merit in his suffering. Christ, furthermore, is to be considered here not according to his equality with the Father, but plainly as a subject, and he regarded the reward of exaltation as bestowed by the Father for the merit of his obedience.

All these things, I say, plainly prove that Christ here assumed not his own person but another’s, and indeed one very different from his own. [Col. 0069C] Indeed, the very nature of the person he sustained necessarily requires some covenant and a mutual agreement with the Father.

For by the name of Christ there is understood not one individual person, as the schools say, but a political and public person who within his scope embraces all the faithful of every age and every place. The benefits of this person are understood to belong to them all.

Christ’s merits might perhaps have obtained some reward for himself by a right of equity. But the facts that he claims that reward not merely on equitable grounds but as a debt of justice, and that it is owed by the Father not only to himself but to all his people, cannot possibly be understood without a covenant by which the Father also accepted the constitution of that political person. [Col. 0069D]

For, antecedently to the covenant, this was so completely discretionary that, unless it had been so agreed, no equity would have bound the Father to pay the reward of Christ’s merits to the faithful, especially since he would already have paid it to Christ himself in his own proper person.

And it was entirely consistent with the Platonic doctrines of that age that this αἰώνιος διαθήκη, the “eternal covenant” of the Gospel—which was nevertheless terrestrial—should have another corresponding covenant, προαιώνιος, “before the ages,” in heaven, to whose power the efficacy of the terrestrial covenant must also be attributed.

We have thus proved the existence of this covenant. Although more recent writers also assert it, they do not prove it at all, nor will those who admit no proof except explicit testimonies of Scripture ever be able to prove it. [Col. 0070A]

§ 28.—Two things, therefore, had to be attributed to this heavenly covenant: first, that a reward for his merits was owed to Christ even by legal right; and second, that all the faithful constituted with Christ one person in law. For we do not read that provision for either of these things was made in the terrestrial covenant.

Yet this covenant did not descend to individual human beings so as to make it possible to know which persons belong to this political person of Christ and can therefore claim for themselves the benefits of that heavenly covenant.

Accordingly, besides this heavenly covenant of the Father with Christ, another covenant was also necessary: one between Christ and human beings, and one external in a manner suited to human capacity and to be celebrated with external symbols, so that it might be known who those are whom Christ acknowledges as his own. [Col. 0070B]

As this covenant belongs to the sacraments generally, so it belongs more nearly and especially to baptism, which all acknowledge as the single sacrament of initiation. For we properly call that a covenant by which we first acquire the right of the covenant and its benefits, not that by which we increase and consummate the same right once acquired.

In the same manner, therefore, in which we have shown that martyrdom belongs to the consummation of baptism, it will also be judged to belong to the evangelical covenant and the benefits of that covenant. Thus no one may interpret this communion of baptism with martyrdom as a sharing of the name alone, but not also of the reality signified by the name.

§ 29.—For it must be observed, sixthly, that martyrdom is foreshadowed in baptism not only in that general manner in which all the other duties of the baptized person are foreshadowed. Rather, the very symbol of the baptism of water represents what we have called our baptism of blood in such a way that the baptism of water has absolutely no efficacy unless it is referred to the baptism of blood. [Col. 0070C]

Insofar as immersion in water denotes the mortification of animal life, and emergence from that same water pledges a new and spiritual life, it represents these through the promissory meaning of the symbol which I have described. I admit that there is no duty of the Christian life that cannot be referred to one or the other of these, since all such duties concern either κάθαρσις (*purification*) or τελείωσις (*perfection*), to speak with the Pythagoreans: the latter are similarly to be referred to the new and mystical life, and the former to the new and mystical death.

Yet we do not therefore claim the benefits of a new baptism for each individual duty of the Christian life, or even for all such duties collected together. [Col. 0070D] For since we have said that the principal purpose of baptism was for us vividly to represent the image of Christ dying and rising again, and that we derive all hope of baptismal benefit from that very representation, it follows that the principal purpose of baptism must consist in that life and death by which we most precisely express Christ, and that the benefits of baptism are to be expected chiefly from those same realities.

But both the death and the resurrection of Christ, to which we profess ourselves conformed in baptism and whose images we bear there, were bodily—as the Apostle too speaks in the case of the bodily resurrection (1 Cor. XV). If only a mystical resurrection were pledged in baptism, the whole of that argument of the Apostle would collapse. [Col. 0071A]

Indeed, it is highly probable that the error of those who denied the resurrection arose from their understanding the symbolic resurrection of baptism as referring only to the mystical resurrection of the soul and not also to the body.

But since it is manifest from that entire discussion of the Apostle that the principal purpose of baptism was to introduce into the baptismal covenant promises of the greatest possible certainty concerning that very matter about which the faith of that age especially wavered, it plainly follows that it is Christ’s resurrection, none other than bodily resurrection, that is exhibited in baptism, and that our corresponding resurrection is also principally bodily.

As for mystical death and resurrection, so far are we from being able through them to φορεῖν εἰκόνα, “bear the image,” of Christ, that Christ himself was never truly dead or raised in that sense. [Col. 0071B] He could not die to sin, for he had never lived to sin. He had no need to mortify the flesh, for he never experienced any rebellion of the flesh. Nor did he rise to a new and spiritual life, for he had never lived any life other than a spiritual one.

Mystical death and resurrection must therefore have been secondary, not the primary representation in baptism, insofar as they—although they themselves denote no conformity with Christ—at least dispose us toward that conformity of our souls with Christ which, I admit, is itself most pleasing to Christ.

§ 30.—Since, therefore, we have proved that this representation of death and resurrection in baptism must be referred first to our bodies, it follows that the primary purpose of baptism is that we devote our bodies to Christ and pledge ourselves ready and prepared to meet bodily death for Christ’s sake. [Col. 0071C]

From this we conceive and receive the most certain possible hope of all the other benefits of baptism. First among them is that of the blessed resurrection—namely, of the body—which corresponds most precisely to bodily sufferings. Just as this was for most people, especially in that age, the chief reason for embracing Christianity, so it was the most difficult of all to believe. It was therefore fitting that it should be commended by altogether certain arguments.

Then we also promise that mystical death and resurrection which are denoted by the secondary meaning of our immersion and emergence in baptism. And insofar as these same symbols are employed on Christ’s side as well, he simultaneously pledges that his own assistance will not fail us. [Col. 0071D]

It is thus established that martyrdom is contained in the primary signification of baptism. It is further established that this pledge of martyrdom is given by us in such a way that it constitutes the condition to be performed on our side, upon which the remaining benefits of baptism depend.

It thus follows from the right conferred by this covenant that all the benefits of baptism are owed to martyrdom, at least in intention. It follows that martyrdom belongs to the consummation of baptism in the same way as martyrdom actually undergone belongs to the consummation of martyrdom existing merely in intention.

§ 31.—Lest I seem excessively intent upon seizing the minutiae of the baptismal covenant, I infer, seventhly, that all the benefits which Christ must perform as his part of the baptismal covenant may be claimed in the baptism of blood not only under the law of that covenant but also under its equity. [Col. 0072A] Thus nothing may seem to remain that could cause us to doubt whether the ancients rightly inferred these things and did so according to the intention of Christ.

For we have already shown that the condition to be performed by us in order to acquire that right to Christ’s promised benefits is precisely this devotion of our body for Christ. Nevertheless, Christ grants the benefits of baptism even to those who, newly baptized, are taken away by a bloodless death. The reason is not that they have performed the condition to which those benefits are due under the equity of the covenant, but that the first benefits of the covenant are granted freely and entirely without any condition—especially to those who, because of an incapacity in the subject, were not yet subject to an actual obligation or to the performance of a condition in fact. [Col. 0072B]

The case of adults is altogether different. A condition they are not yet able to perform they could at least have the will to perform, so that the intention itself is regarded by God as equivalent to the deed.

Yet the grounds of equity by which someone is excused from performing a condition of the covenant are very different from those by which someone is judged to have fulfilled that same condition of the law—not according to the letter of the law, perhaps, but according to the lawgiver’s intention, provided that an equitable interpreter of the law is employed.

Thus martyrdom existing in intention, although according to the letter of the law it is in reality something different, will nevertheless be judged equivalent to martyrdom actually undergone according to equitable interpretation. It will thus come about that all the benefits of baptism are owed solely to martyrdom, at least in intention.

But if, even in baptized persons who are not martyrs, the entire right to the benefits of baptism which they obtained in baptism is nevertheless owed solely to martyrdom in intention, who does not see that it must with still greater reason be attributed to actual martyrdom? [Col. 0072C] For actual martyrdom is the very condition of the law, not some other thing requiring an equitable interpreter of the law in order that it may be regarded as the condition itself.

Therefore, even if it were nowhere else established by explicit words of the evangelical law that the benefits of baptism are owed to martyrdom, we could nevertheless readily infer it from the consequence of this same reasoning.

§ 32.—For in every legislation, including human legislation, that mode of argument is approved by which we make provision for cases omitted from the laws on the basis of parity of reasoning. It arises from those general canons according to which legislators desire provision to be made for all cases, wish reason to be followed everywhere as a guide, and would approve in other similar cases the same rationale they had approved in one case. [Col. 0072D]

Hence it follows that provisions established in this way are regarded not merely as the counsels of prudent persons but as possessing the force of laws. It follows from this that, even if divine legislation were to be framed only after the example of human laws, parity of reasoning would have to be understood as possessing the force of divine law.

But there is certainly greater reason why this argument should hold in divine legislation than in human legislation. For human legislators make mistakes even in their reasoning and do not foresee all consequences, even legitimate ones. Therefore, even when we reason correctly from their principles, it may still be doubted whether they themselves would have approved our conclusions. [Col. 0073A]

God, however, can err neither in principles nor in consequences. It will therefore be certain that whatever rationale he has approved in one case he will also acknowledge in other cases. It will be certain that if he grants such great benefits in baptism for the sake of martyrdom, he will with much greater reason grant them to martyrdom itself. It will be certain that if he recompenses even the intention of martyrdom with so great and abundant a reward, there is no reason for us to fear that he will deny the same reward when the vow has been fulfilled. Finally, it will accordingly be certain that if baptized persons obtain a full remission of sins, complete in all its parts, martyrs too will assuredly obtain that same remission.

§ 33.—For I add, eighthly, that this common right of baptism and martyrdom is not to be understood in such a way that in [Col. 0073B] baptism sins are indeed remitted by virtue of that martyrdom which, in intention, we profess at baptism, but only those sins which preceded baptism, and not likewise those committed between baptism and martyrdom. The ancients understood martyrdom to be equal to baptism in this very respect also: just as in baptism all sins are remitted—namely, those preceding baptism, not only original but also actual sins—so the same is to be held concerning martyrdom as well; that is, it effaces the offenses of an entire life, so that nothing further remains to be expiated.

They rightly reasoned thus from the principles just explained. For if, on account of that intention of martyrdom, full pardon of past sins is granted, we shall certainly expect, as I have said, equal pardon all the more once that same intention has been fulfilled. But such pardon cannot be equal if baptism, whenever it is received, nevertheless effaces all past sins, while in martyrdom no sins are effaced except those which preceded baptism, although baptism may be separated from it by so great an interval—an interval to which there must necessarily correspond an accumulation of sins not yet remitted.

Certainly, according to the equity of a covenant, the more fully we perform the conditions required of us on our side of the covenant, the stronger the right to the reward to be rendered by God consequently becomes and grows for us; and, conversely, the greater becomes God’s own obligation to render the reward that he promised. Accordingly, under the terms of the covenant, we may also claim for ourselves a greater measure of God’s favor. Indeed, even if the consideration of the covenant is set aside, we may at least expect that favor of God which I have mentioned with confidence proportionately greater as we furnish more manifest proof of our goodwill toward God. But no one should doubt that the person who has shed his blood for God has given far clearer proof of his goodwill toward God than one who merely possessed a ready and prepared disposition to shed it. And since we regard it as an act of special favor when someone construes the will as equivalent to the deed, this is assuredly a sign that the deed itself comes closer to the standard of justice—and far closer still whenever the consideration of a covenant is also involved. It is therefore entirely consonant both with the nature of a covenant and with right reason that the plenary pardon of sins which we grant to baptism should not, in our judgment, be denied to martyrdom.

§ 34.—Furthermore, according to accepted covenantal practice, everyone acknowledges this also to be equitable: whenever, after an agreement has first been entered into, certain first installments of the reward are delivered into the claimant’s hands, the fullness of the reward nevertheless awaits the fulfillment of the agreement and the performance of the covenant’s condition, and it will be all the more abundant in proportion as those first installments were greater. Marriage contracts place earnest-money in the hands, but not yet the dowry, unless the marriage has been consummated. The same custom also prevails in other covenants relating to goods and undertakings. Yet it is especially evident in covenants entered into by guardians in the name of those who have not yet reached adulthood. The very inception of the agreement invests them with a certain inchoate right. Until, however, they have become adults, advanced to an age capable of performing the conditions, and able to consummate the covenant in their own name as well, they are not considered to possess with a full and perfected right even what they have already obtained, much less to possess so firm a right to the covenant’s future rewards. What purpose would this serve unless conditions already performed were valued more highly than conditions merely undertaken, however firm the pledge that they would be performed? It is therefore fitting that the pardon belonging to baptism consummated in martyrdom should be fuller than that belonging to baptism merely begun. Consequently, if past sins are washed away in baptism by water, there is no reason for us to doubt that they will likewise be washed away in baptism by blood.

§ 35.—The fact that baptism by blood follows baptism by water after an interval of time is certainly no reason for us to regard it as foreign to the nature of baptism. As we have seen, the Apostle distinguished three parts of baptism: water, Spirit, and blood. Yet those who were cleansed by baptism in water did not always receive the baptismal Spirit at one and the same time, as we have proved elsewhere. The Apostles were bathed in baptismal water while the Lord was still alive, although none received the Spirit until after his resurrection. Philip the deacon cleansed the Samaritans with water, but no one except the Apostles could confer the Spirit upon them.

What, then? Shall we attribute to water alone that power of expiating past sins? It would then follow that a new expiation was required for sins committed after baptism by water. For just as, in the mysteries of the Gentiles, the purificatory elements (*kathartiká*, καθαρτικὰ) were believed to prepare the way for initiation or perfection (*teleiōsei*, τελειώσει), [Col. 0074D] so that nothing impure might remain when they sought admission to the more sacred rites, so cleansing by water undoubtedly ministered to the Spirit, lest any impurity of the vessel prevent him from being received in a manner worthy of himself. It was therefore wholly incompatible with his holiness that anyone should receive him while impure. Consequently, it was necessary that the Spirit himself take the place of water in expiating sins more recent than baptism by water. But if we grant that power to the Spirit, there will certainly be no reason to regard it as foreign to blood.

Under the terms of the covenant, that power was rather to be expected from blood, because blood concerns our duty and disposition, which are usually taken into greater account in the law of covenants than God’s gratuitous gifts. This view is further supported by the Platonic doctrines of that age—by which this entire symbolic theology must altogether be explained. Since all the power of symbols or antitypes was believed to be derived from their prototypes, they nevertheless explained the efficacy of symbols in such a way that the symbols themselves contributed nothing to the effect in their own right; they merely indicated to whom the native power of the prototypes was to be applied. Thus all that power—whether natural or also a matter of legal right—was to be expected from the prototypes themselves.

And since the status of the contracting parties must be equitable when they are joined to one another by that legal transaction, it is surely fitting that the same force which we concede to divine symbols with respect to God’s obligation should in turn be conceded to our symbols with respect to our obligation; and that, by the same covenantal right by which God inflicts punishment upon transgressors, he should be bound to render a reward to those who have performed the condition. If, therefore, even the profession of martyrdom effects the remission of sins by virtue of martyrdom while it is still absent, then martyrdom itself, when present, must certainly and necessarily effect that same remission.

This agrees most precisely with what we cited above concerning the martyrs being said to have washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb. For this could not so suitably be understood of the washing of baptism, which was common to all the faithful, but rather of the washing proper to sufferers; nor merely of the expiation of those sins which preceded that great tribulation and had, namely, been expiated in baptism by water, but also of those sins which were to be expiated in that very tribulation.

§ 36.—Nor will there be any reason to wonder that the ancients assigned so great a power to the martyrs’ baptism by blood if we also recall, ninthly, that the blood of the martyrs was attributed by the ancients to Christ himself—and attributed to Christ in such a way that it was believed not to belong to the martyrs, nor to have served merely the martyrs’ own advantage, but rather that of the universal Church. We have proved this opinion of the ancients elsewhere, and have likewise shown how far it was from conflicting with Scripture and the principles of the sacred writers.

If these points are granted, we shall now understand how soundly and prudently they gathered all this efficacy of baptism by blood from Scripture. For no one doubts that this expiation of sins belongs to the blood of Christ. Yet the name “Christ” is very often understood of the whole mystical body of Christ. Why, then, should we not ascribe that sin-cleansing power to Christ understood in this way? There is surely no reason why, whenever Holy Scripture teaches that the blood of Christ washes and cleanses our sins, we should understand it solely of his personal blood. Indeed, the very rationale of the name suggests rather that this power is common to Christ and his mystical body. For he shared his name with us precisely for this purpose: that the rights corresponding to the name should also be understood as common.

Thus, in the unity of marriage—which the Apostle employs here to explain Christ’s mystical unity with the Church—the name common to man and woman also makes the legal rights of each common to both. So also, when the blood of the martyrs is regarded as the blood of Christ, it is fitting that this occurs so that the rights of each blood may in turn become common to both. Yet there is no reason to doubt that any symbol of Christ is nevertheless surpassed by his true and original blood. We have said, however, that it comes to the same thing whether Christ acknowledged the martyrs’ blood as his own, or through the mystical union of the two kinds of blood applied the power of his own blood through martyrdom. That very application must certainly have been all the more efficacious, the more closely it touches the blood of Christ and presents it in a more living representation.

§ 37.—It is still more fitting to judge that the ancients reasoned correctly here, and in accordance with the equity of the case, because, tenthly, they assigned so great a power not to every suffering or death of the faithful, but only to those by which they approached more closely to the example of Christ’s death—namely, when they offered themselves for the public cause of the Church and of the brethren.

Every death of all the saints is indeed precious in the sight of the Lord. Still more precious is the death of the innocent, that is, of those oppressed by the violence of unjust men. Nor is there any reason to doubt that the death by which those persons fall for whom every duty is dearer than life itself, and who choose death rather than sin, is also dear to God. This very death is also akin to the baptismal obligation and should not be thought wholly foreign to baptism’s rewards and privileges. Nor, undoubtedly, is that death displeasing to God which the pagans extol with such praises—the death by which someone spends his life for his fatherland and, by his single death, redeems the deaths of many; nor is such a death foreign to Christ’s example.

Yet of all deaths, that one approaches far most closely to Christ’s most illustrious example in which someone meets death for the sake of souls—and indeed for the common cause of many, or even of all the faithful everywhere; if someone dies for the common faith, for the common body of the faithful, for their common unity and the common bond of that unity, so that he may preserve the mystical body of Christ in its integrity and further enrich it by the new accession of those who return to their senses.

This is to bear “the same sufferings” (*tà autà tōn pathēmátōn*, τὰ αὐτὰ τῶν παθημάτων); this is to bear the “image” (*eikóna*, εἰκὸνα) of Christ—and specifically of Christ suffering; this is to supply what was lacking in Christ’s sufferings for the Church; this is to die, be crucified, and be buried with him, since we both suffer the same things and suffer them for the same cause, sharing with Christ both the suffering and its cause. All these expressions plainly imply a certain mystical union shared by us with Christ in the very cause of these sufferings, so that both sets of sufferings are considered to belong to one and the same aggregate of sufferings.
