In these reasonings concerning mystical unity, the Apostle recognizes canons of this kind, and indeed universal ones: what belongs to the head is also common to the members; what belongs to the firstfruits belongs also to the whole mass. Had those canons of which we have spoken not been universal, the Apostle would certainly have had to add why they were to be recognized in this particular case rather than in any other. For here the Apostle assumed the role of one presenting an argument, not of one issuing a decree merely on his own authority.

Thus, therefore, the same expiation of sins which belongs to the head belongs also to the members; what belongs to the firstfruits of this blood will likewise belong to the whole mass. In this way, namely, the Lord wished to encourage us to undergo death for the brethren with a willing and steadfast spirit, so that in this very cause we might imitate him: just as he laid down his life for us, so we too should lay down our lives for the brethren, 1 St. John 3:16. Thus the disciples were ready to lay down their lives for the Apostle, and he in turn for the disciples. Thus Ignatius wished to be the “life given in exchange” (*antípsychos*, ἀντίψυχος) for those who adhered to the bishops, because, namely, he wished to redeem their “lives” (*psychás*, ψυχὰς) with his own “life” (*psychēi*, ψυχῇ)—lives with life. Hence arose that great love of Christians for one another, by which Tertullian records that they were famous and conspicuous even in his own age. The story of Damon and Pythias is by far the most celebrated among the Pythagoreans. The Essenes among the Jews emulated them, and the Christians emulated the Essenes, though they surpassed all of them by a great distance. Thus even the practice of the earliest Christians corresponded exactly with these principles. Thus the Lord, the lawgiver by far the most expert of all, supported that most generous practice with principles that were also most prudent.

§ 38.—Since these things are so, we now easily understand that there is no reason for the earliest Christians to be spoken ill of in this matter. They honored martyrdom with the title of baptism. They did so neither rashly nor merely according to their own judgment. They had Christ himself as the author whom they followed. Yet together with the title they also attributed to martyrdom the rights of baptism, and specifically of sacramental baptism instituted by God himself.

This would undoubtedly have been an enormous crime if they had ascribed to inventions of their own those things which God was required to perform under the sacramental covenant, while relying upon no promise of God and upon no lawful representative of God who could at least act in God’s person and promise in God’s name those things which God himself would be bound to perform because of a lawful delegation. But the ancients were far removed from that crime of using God’s name as a pretext for their own institutions without divine authority.

Yet it was certainly not impious for them to expect the conditions to be performed by God in the baptismal covenant instituted by God himself. It was not impious to infer from the purpose of sacramental baptism whatever further element appeared to be included in the baptismal covenant. It was not impious to infer this very thing concerning martyrdom if they could do so by a legitimate argument proper to the sacraments. Finally, it was not impious if, after proving this concerning martyrdom, they also ascribed to it the rights of baptism.

But they not only compare martyrdom with baptism; they even prefer it to baptism. They would indeed have done wrong if it had already been established that they dared to set their own human institutions in rivalry with divine institutions. Yet from what has been said it is clear that the matter stands otherwise. Since the ancients proved that martyrdom was included in the baptismal covenant, their opponents certainly classify martyrdom among human institutions without justification. They are no longer comparing human institutions with divine ones, but divine institutions with divine ones—or perhaps rather one part of a divine institution with another part of the same institution.

Nothing, however, prevents one divine institution from being more excellent than another; indeed, this is rather necessary whenever they are directed toward the same end, but with some subordination. For that which approaches the end more closely will necessarily be more excellent in the capacity of a means. Yet a subordination of this kind cannot be separated from symbolic covenants, which all acknowledge the sacraments to be. For although symbols are employed to represent duties utterly different from the symbols themselves, and thereby to pledge those very duties—so that each serves in turn as a means—it is nevertheless clear that the duty possesses a far higher standing than the symbol, and confers a much greater and stronger right to the reward promised by God.

Finally, however, it may be said that both the symbol of our profession in baptism and the condition which, through that symbol, we promise to perform on our side of the baptismal covenant, although employed in a covenant instituted by God, nevertheless concern human duties and that part of the covenant which pertains to human beings. Thus divine things will not be compared with human things; rather, certain human duties will be compared with other duties that are likewise human, so that some may be regarded as better than others and more pleasing to God.

I readily acknowledge that the right of these duties to a reward must be referred entirely to the divine covenant and institution. Yet this is true in such a way that, although God does not render the reward because of works, the recompense is nevertheless made according to works. Consequently, the more excellent each of our duties is in itself and the more pleasing to God, the more strictly is it required by God as a contracting party and the more abundant is the reward with which it is crowned.

§ 39.—Although in this dissertation we have considered baptism alone, what we have asserted concerning baptism could also have been asserted concerning the other sacrament, the Eucharist: namely, that our martyrdom for Christ is represented here and thereby pledged, so that the martyrs may consequently claim the rewards of this Eucharistic covenant as well.

For the Lord’s body is represented in the broken Eucharistic bread only as having suffered, been broken, and been crucified; and his blood in the poured-out wine only as itself having been poured out. Who does not see how manifestly these things must be referred to Christ’s sufferings? Accordingly, when through that one bread we profess that we are one body with Christ, 1 Cor. 10:17, what we pledge by this manifestly symbolic rite of pledging is that we shall share with Christ not only in the body but also in the body’s very sufferings, so that we too present ourselves as ready to suffer and be crucified with him.

Moreover, when it is said that this blood is poured out for many, we further promise that, following Christ’s example, we too shall approach suffering with a spirit all the readier, the more people we understand will have their salvation advanced by our death. For in this way we shall represent more vividly the example of the suffering Christ. The things, therefore, which we have thus far discussed concerning the rewards of martyrdom are probable and entirely consonant with the divine purpose, since we see that the covenants of both sacraments aim at this same end.

§ 40.—Although we have also thus far treated only that one benefit of baptism—the remission of sins, which is itself privative, and from which exemption from punishment, itself likewise privative, also follows—there is nevertheless no reason for us on that account to deny that the martyrs possess a right to the positive benefits of baptism. For if we suffer with Christ, we shall also reign with him. Thus the Apostle argues from the canon proper to these mystical arguments. Thus the ancients also argued when, as we have shown, they ascribed to the martyrs the foremost seat in Christ’s kingdom. And they did so rightly.

For if a reward was set before Christ when he was about to suffer, then, once the condition of the covenant had been performed, that great reward was certainly owed to him. If we also sustain in our own suffering the same person of the suffering Christ—and sustain it with the express purpose that the rights accruing to the suffering Christ under the divine covenant might likewise accrue to us when we suffer—it follows that this immense reward has also been laid up for us who suffer: a reward as great as that which, by right of this covenant, was owed to Christ, and owed by the same right of that same covenant. Thus all the benefits of baptism, both negative and positive, will be owed to the martyrs.

[COMPLETE WORKS OF SIXTUS II]

[Col. 0079]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE CONCERNING SIXTUS II, TWENTY-THIRD ROMAN PONTIFF

[Col. 0079B] **On the years of Sixtus II’s pontificate.**—Sixtus was ordained in Stephen’s place on August 24 in the year 257; the catalogues of the Roman pontiffs report that he was Greek by nationality and an Athenian philosopher. How many years he held the pontificate, however, cannot be determined, for ancient and more recent chronologists are divided into opposing camps. Eusebius himself assigns him eight years in the *Chronicle*, but eleven years in the *History* [Note: [Col. 0079D] Eusebius, *Chronicle*, p. 752; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chap. 27]. The other catalogues of pontiffs, by contrast, allow Sixtus scarcely two years, or even one [Note: [Col. 0079D] Anastasius the Librarian, vol. I]. From Cyprian’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0079D] Cyprian, Epistle LXXX], it is known that he was crowned with martyrdom in the following year. Therefore, since he assumed the pontificate in August 257, it follows that he occupied the Roman see for eleven months and some days, as many learned men demonstrate, even against the catalogues of pontiffs [Col. 0079C] [Note: [Col. 0079D] Pagi, *Critique*, at the year 257, no. 2, and at the year 258, no. 3; Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. IV, p. 16; Coutant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, p. 258; Mansi, notes on Baronius’ *Annals* at the year 261, p. 92; Basnage, at the year 258, no. 6; Pearson, at the year 257].

Perhaps Eusebius had written in the *History* that he presided for eleven months, which months were afterward changed into years by another hand; for it seems wholly inconsistent with Eusebius’ diligence that he should have erred so disgracefully in the chronology of the pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0079D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chap. 5]. We do not dwell on what is read in the *Chronicle*, where eight years are attributed to Sixtus, since we know that Eusebius’ *Chronicle* has been interpolated throughout.

When Dionysius of Alexandria heard that Sixtus was administering the Roman Church, he addressed a letter to him: “This is the second concerning baptism, in which he sets forth the opinion and judgment both of Stephen and of the other bishops.” Another letter of Dionysius shows him to have been a most prudent man; in it Dionysius asks Sixtus’ counsel concerning an old man who, having been baptized by heretics, was entreating for the Catholic sacrament of regeneration with prayers and tears, affirming that the baptism of heretics had nothing in common with that of the Church. These are Dionysius’ words [Note: [Col. 0080C] In Eusebius, at the passage cited, chap. 9]: “I need your counsel, brother, and I seek your judgment, lest perhaps I myself should err.”

Learned men infer from three letters sent to Sixtus by the same St. Dionysius of Alexandria, fragments of which Eusebius quotes [Note: [Col. 0080C] Eusebius, at the passage cited, chaps. 5 and 9], that under the pontificate of Sixtus the controversy concerning baptism continued which had begun to be debated under his predecessor [Note: [Col. 0080C] Tillemont, passage cited; Sandini, *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 47, quarto edition]. The words of Pontius the Deacon [Note: [Col. 0080C] Pontius, *Life of St. Cyprian*] show that St. Sixtus did not approve of his predecessor’s unyielding harshness, for Pontius calls Sixtus “a good and peaceable priest.” From this the profoundly learned Tillemont infers [Note: [Col. 0080C] Tillemont, passage cited] that the most holy pontiff settled the aforesaid dispute by his extraordinary gentleness and tireless effort.

[Col. 0080C] Nearly everything else that he did during his pontificate has passed out of memory. From the *Short List of the Depositions of the Martyrs*, Pearson relates [Note: [Col. 0080D] Pearson, *Cyprianic Annals*, at the year 258, § 2] that he transferred the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul “to the Catacombs, as the fury of persecution grew daily more savage, so that the stations might be held there more safely [Note: [Col. 0080D] Petavius, in his notes on Epiphanius, p. 356, understands a ‘station’ to mean that religious observance by which the faithful, assembling for the synaxis on appointed days, persevered until the ninth hour; hence the term is also sometimes used for the multitude itself and its assembly. Du Cange says that a ‘station’ was a gathering or assembly of the faithful, especially one held on Sunday; he judges, moreover, that it was called a ‘station’ by a metaphor drawn from soldiers, who, when they establish a garrison in a certain place, are said to ‘make a station’].”

**St. Sixtus II is crowned with martyrdom on August 5, 258.**—Sixtus, however, consecrated the memory of his name by the most illustrious deed of all, when he entered the contest of martyrdom for the faith. St. Cyprian indicates the day and place of his martyrdom in his letter to Successus with these words: “You should know that Sixtus was executed in the Cemetery on the eighth day before the Ides of August, and Quartus with him.” Among the Latins the word used in this passage signifies punishment of any kind, but according to Brissonius, Calvin, and other jurists it signifies a stroke of the sword, or beheading.

Regarding the year also, most scholars adopt Pagi’s opinion: namely, that he suffered in the year of the Lord 258, the same year as St. Cyprian, as Pontius states in the *Life of Cyprian*. [Note: [Col. 0081D] Bianchini, in his edition of Anastasius, and Monsieur Le Beuf, in the *History of the Church of Auxerre*, place the martyrdom of St. Sixtus II one year later, namely in 259.] Coutant [Note: [Col. 0081D] Coutant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, p. 158, no. 4], by restoring a mutilated passage in the Bucherian Catalogue, confirms Pagi’s opinion. For the Bucherian Catalogue reads: “He suffered—Sixtus—on the eighth day before the Ides of August, from the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus until the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus.”

To dispel the darkness from this passage, Coutant advises that, from the Fossatensis manuscript, the words “the presbyters presided” should be supplied before “from the consulship [Col. 0081B] of Tuscus and Bassus.” With the aid of this supplement we learn that the Roman clergy administered the Roman Church from August of the year 258 until July 21 of the year 259, when Aemilianus and Bassus held the consulship.

This sheds light upon the Corbie and Fossatensis Catalogues, in which Sixtus is assigned one year, ten months, and twenty-three or twenty-four days, perhaps reckoning from Sixtus’ ordination to the election of his successor Dionysius. In the Fossatensis Catalogue and that of the Queen of Sweden reproduced by Bollandus, the pontificate is said to have been vacant for two years—understand this as part of the year 258 and another part of the following year. In the *Pontifical Book*, where the years of St. Sixtus’ tenure of the see are discussed, astonishing carelessness is revealed, as the aforementioned Coutant observes.

[Col. 0081C] Isidore ascribes two letters to Sixtus II. The first is addressed to a certain Bishop Gratus and was, Binius contends, written on account of Sabellius, Noetus, Ebion, and Cerinthus. The letter shows that condemned bishops are permitted to approach the Apostolic See. It is dated on the Kalends of September, in the consulship of the illustrious Valerian and Decius.

The second was sent to bishops established throughout the provinces of Spain. It contains five headings. First: how should one proceed if someone has a case against bishops or administrators of the Church? Second: concerning bishops despoiled of their property or driven from their sees. Third: that no bishop may retain, ordain, or judge another bishop’s parishioner. Fourth: concerning bishops unjustly condemned and restored by apostolic authority. Fifth: that excommunicated persons cannot accuse bishops. It is dated the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of the most illustrious Valerian and Decius.

Even if we remain silent, anyone at all is capable of taking these letters away from Sixtus. First, the notation of the consuls is utterly false. During Sixtus’ tenure, Valerian’s colleague in the consulship was not Decius but Gallienus. Furthermore, the superscriptions show that the decretals were written in the same year. But in the year 258 Sixtus, who suffered on August 6, could not write to Gratus on the Kalends of September. He could indeed have done so in the preceding year, but it is impossible that he sent the letter to the Spaniards on July 16, 257, when he had not yet entered upon the pontificate.

Next, since a most severe persecution weighed upon the Roman Church throughout Sixtus’ entire episcopate, it is utterly absurd that Sixtus should have composed letters of this tenor, in which there is no mention of the Church’s affliction and no exhortation to bear crosses with a patient spirit. In the first letter, the impostor inserts an entire page taken from Idacius Clarus’ *Against Varimadus*. Compare it with p. 730 of the *Greatest Library of the Fathers*, vol. V. The second steals the opening of Leo the Great’s fifty-fourth letter: “By the great gift of God’s mercy, the joys of the whole Catholic Church have been multiplied.”

[Col. 0082B] **On the Sayings of Xystus: whether they belong to Pope Sixtus.**—There are 430 sayings of Xystus, a pagan philosopher, which were translated into Latin by Rufinus and have sometimes been ascribed to Pope Sixtus. Augustine, who had fallen into this error, afterward committed the following words to writing in book II, chapter 42, of his *Retractions*: “In the book *On Nature and Grace*, I defended certain words which Pelagius had presented as those of Sixtus, Roman pontiff and martyr, as though they truly belonged to that same Sixtus; for so I had thought, but I afterward read that they belonged to Xystus the philosopher and not to Sixtus the Christian.”

Saying 120 certainly does not sound Christian: “Do not ask of God that which, once you have it, you will not possess perpetually.” Thus neither peace of mind, nor the tranquility of the Church, nor bodily health should be sought by prayer. Saying [Col. 0082C] 125 is also repugnant to the faith: “Whatever does not contribute to the blessedness of God should not befit the man of God.” Thus the resurrection of the body would not be part of the saints’ felicity, since it is incompatible with the glory of the immortal God. Nor is saying 184 sufficiently pious: “Regard disparaging a wise man and disparaging God as equal sins.”

When Rufinus, with glittering embellishment, placed the name of Pope Sixtus the martyr upon the sayings of Xystus the philosopher, he received deserved punishment from Jerome. On this subject there is a notable passage in the letter *Against Pelagius, to Ctesiphon* [Note: [Col. 0082D] Jerome, Letter XXXIII to Ctesiphon, p. 476, vol. IV, Benedictine edition; and on chapter XXII of Jeremiah and chapter XVIII of Ezekiel]:

“But who could explain in fitting words that rashness—or rather madness—of his, whereby he changed the name of the book of Xystus the Pythagorean, a man without Christ and a pagan, and gave it the title of Sixtus the martyr and bishop of the Roman Church? In it, according to the doctrine of the Pythagoreans, who make man equal to God and say that he is of God’s substance, many things are said about perfection, so that those who do not know the philosopher’s volume may drink from Babylon’s golden cup under the martyr’s name. Finally, in that volume there is no mention of the prophets, none of the patriarchs, none of the Apostles, and none of Christ, so that he would have us maintain that a bishop and martyr existed without faith in Christ.”

Let the sayings be examined, especially 248, which reeks of pure and unadulterated Pelagianism, and 265, which approves Origen’s deed in amputating his genitals for the sake of continence.—Pope Gelasius placed this [Col. 0083A] work, falsely attributed to St. Sixtus, pope and martyr, among the apocrypha [Note: [Col. 0083A] In Mansi, *Councils*, vol. VIII, p. 151], or regarded it as a work composed by heretics.

These sayings of Sixtus were printed in volume III of the *Library of the Fathers*, and separately together with Rufinus’ preface to Apronianus: at Basel, 1520; Cologne, 1522; Louvain, 1618; Amsterdam, 1688; and in the *Mythological, Physical, and Moral Opuscules* [Col. 0084A] of Thomas Gale, Leipzig, quarto, 1725, by Sieber the German, who also maintains that these sayings truly belong to Pope Sixtus the martyr. Two canons are also erroneously cited by Gratian under the name of Sixtus II [Note: [Col. 0084A] Gratian’s *Decretum*, Cause 2, Question 6; and Cause 3, Question 17].

[Col. 0083]

## DOUBTFUL LETTERS OF POPE SIXTUS II. (S)

[Note: [Col. 0083D] [[Col. 0083] This note is printed at the foot of column 83, but its callout number, (1), does not appear in the text.] **Letter.** The very opening of the letter indicates that this letter was written to Bishop Gratus on account of the followers of Sabellius, Noetus, Ebion, and Cerinthus. For Sabellius, the founder of a heresy, having emerged from the underworld during this pontificate, abolished every distinction of persons in God; the others said that Christ was nothing before the Incarnation. Therefore, in order soundly to refute their errors and instruct the bishop who had consulted him on this matter, he writes this letter to him, proving by explicit testimonies of Scripture that Christ, in respect of his divine nature, is the eternal Son of the eternal Father; that he is a person distinct from the Father in the Godhead; and that he has always existed without any beginning in time. The remaining matters that appear worthy of note both here and in the following letter have been annotated in connection with the preceding letters of the preceding pontiffs.]

## FIRST LETTER  
### TO A CERTAIN BISHOP GRATUS

That accused or condemned bishops are permitted to appeal to, or approach, the Apostolic See, without whose authority their cases ought not to be concluded.

[Col. 0083B]

Bishop Sixtus to Gratus, his fellow bishop: greetings.

I rejoiced and was exceedingly glad in Christ Jesus our Lord (Leo, Epistle 31) because of the letter from your Charity, which clearly shows how greatly you love the catholic faith and how greatly you detest the error of corrupt men. For every heresy is exceedingly impious and hostile to the truth of the Gospel: it seeks not merely to injure some particular part, but to tear up the very foundations of the Christian religion. For I am mindful [Col. 0083C] that I preside in the name of that Church whose confession has been glorified by our Lord Jesus Christ, and (St. Leo, Epistle 31) whose faith never deceives anyone, but indeed destroys all heresies. I understand, moreover, that I am permitted no other course than to devote all my efforts to that cause in which the salvation of the universal Church is under attack.

Acknowledge, dearest son (Ithacius, *Against Varimadus*, ch. 12), that the Son of God was born neither in time nor after the ages, but was ineffably begotten from the Father’s womb before all ages, as God the Father himself says through the prophet: “In the splendors of the saints, from the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Psalm 109). The prophet Isaiah also clearly expressed this judgment for the doubtful and unbelieving, when he showed [Col. 0084B] that the Son was ineffably born from none other than the Father: “In his humiliation,” he says, “his judgment was taken away. Who shall recount his birth?” (Isa. 53). And in the book of Job he says: “Where will you find the wisdom of God? For it is hidden from the eyes of men and concealed from the birds of heaven” (Job 28).

Awaken for a moment, and, if you possess within yourself any measure of the light of knowledge, you will discover that he whose birth could not be recounted by the prophet could not have been begotten in time—or, as you yourself attempt to maintain, could not have been begotten at all. “In the beginning,” says John the Evangelist, “was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1). And again: “He was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world” (ibid.). Therefore, if in the expression “was” you wish to seek for a point in time, [Col. 0084C] you will not find one, because from the moment the Father is, from that moment the Son also is; and what the Father is, that the Son also is. Solomon says:

“I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature. I caused an unfailing light to arise in heaven, and like a cloud I covered the whole earth. I dwell in the highest places, and my throne is in a pillar of cloud. I alone encompassed the circuit of heaven and penetrated the depth of the abyss. I stood throughout the whole earth, and among the people I held primacy” (Ecclus. 24).

Likewise, in the same place:

“When he prepared heaven, I was present with him, and when he marked out his throne; when above the strong winds he made the clouds on high, and when he established sure springs beneath heaven; when he made firm the foundations of the earth, I was with him, arranging all things, and I was the one in whom he delighted, as he rejoiced over the completed world” (Prov. 8).

And in Psalm 101: [Col. 0084D]

“You, Lord, founded the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; and like a covering you will change them, and they will be changed. But you are the very same, and your years will not fail.”

For there was no age or period of time before the Son was born from the Father, since he who established all times by his own power could not have been born in time or after the ages.

[Note: [Col. 0084D] Thus far are the words of Ithacius, from which Mangi’s fraud is most clearly exposed.]

With these few statements I have briefly answered your questions, dearest brother. For the rest, I admonish your Charity to strive to convert all whom you know to be in error to the catholic faith and to the unity of those who believe rightly, and [Col. 0085A] never yourself to depart from the apostolic path. But if they do not listen to you and persist in their errors—which God forbid—inform us about them as quickly as you can. Do not delay, so that by apostolic authority they may either speedily be converted to the Church or be separated from the Church.

We have also heard that certain men in error, together with those who agree with them, are troubling you and the other fellow bishops, and are drawing some bishops of your province along with them in order to defame and condemn you.

For this reason, it was established long ago in this holy see by many bishops, and has now once again been confirmed for the assistance of you and the other brethren, that all bishops who are assailed or accused in certain more serious cases may, whenever necessary, freely appeal to the Apostolic See and [Col. 0085B] flee to it as to a mother, so that by it—as has always been the case—they may be piously supported, defended, and delivered. Ancient authority—the authority of the apostles, their successors, and the canons—reserved to its determination all major ecclesiastical cases and judgments concerning bishops, because bishops are held blameworthy when they have acted toward their brethren otherwise than the popes of that same see have judged proper.

It was therefore decreed that a bishop accused or judged by the bishops of his province in any case may freely appeal to and approach the pontiff of the Apostolic See (Council of Sardica, canons 4, 5, 7). The pontiff shall arrange, either personally or through his vicars, for the case to be reconsidered. While the pontiff conducts the case in a second trial, no other bishop is to be installed or ordained in the appellant’s place; for although [Col. 0085C] the bishops of the province may investigate the case of an accused bishop, they are not permitted to decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff, since it was said to the blessed apostle Peter by none other than the Lord himself: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16 and 18).

And if anyone believes himself to be oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the primate of the diocese (Hadrian, Collection, ch. 6), or before the pope of the universal Apostolic Church. For the apostle James says: “Judgment without mercy will be given to him who has shown no mercy. But mercy exalts itself above judgment.”

Therefore, in all things (St. Gregory, Epistle 45, book VIII), dearest son, guard your heart, as it is written: “With all vigilance guard your heart, because life [Col. 0085D] proceeds from it” (Prov. 4). I have written these things briefly as a reminder. But I ask that you pray for me, so that almighty God may deign to guard me both from malignant spirits and from corrupt men; for in this pilgrimage of my life many evils surround me all at once, so that I may rightly say with the Psalmist: “Your wrath has passed over me, and your terrors have troubled me. They have surrounded me like water all day long; they have surrounded me together” (Psalm 87).

May heavenly grace protect both us in the cities and you everywhere, because the ancient enemy is not excluded from any region of the earth in his work of temptation. For if he struck down a human being in paradise (Gen. 3), what place outside paradise can there be into which he is unable to penetrate the minds of men? The eyes of the ancient enemy—through whose envy death entered the world (Wis. 2)—are [Col. 0086A] always watchful to ensnare human souls; and he who by his own malice fell from glory into misery desires to drag many others with him into perdition through his wickedness. We must therefore trust solely in the protection of our Creator and cry to him from the depths of our hearts: “Be to me a protecting God and a fortified place, that you may save me” (Psalms 30 and 70).

Given on the Kalends of September.

[Note: [Col. 0086D] The chronological indication is false.]

In the consulship of the most illustrious Valerian and Decius.

## EPISTLE II

### CONTENTS

I. How anyone who has a case against bishops or the administrators of the Church is to conduct himself.  
II. Concerning bishops despoiled of their property or driven from their sees.  
III. That no bishop is to retain, ordain, or judge another bishop’s parishioner.  
IV. Concerning bishops unjustly condemned and restored by apostolic authority.  
V. That excommunicated persons cannot accuse bishops, nor can those who do not accept bishops in their own accusation; and that a superior cannot be judged or condemned by an inferior.

[Col. 0086B]

Bishop Sixtus, to his most beloved brethren established throughout the provinces of Spain: greetings in the Lord.

Through the great gift of God’s mercy (St. Leo, Epistle 54), the joys of the whole Catholic Church are multiplied when the condition of the churches flourishes under the order established for it by the apostles and their successors. But [Col. 0086C] when we learn that it is being disturbed by the cunning of the ancient enemy, we are saddened by no slight grief.

For this reason, brethren, we exhort, admonish, and implore you not to depart in any way from the path of apostolic institution or dissent from the head, but to hold without hesitation the faith and order established by the apostles and apostolic men. For if the pillars of some great house collapse, the house itself will by no means remain standing afterward. So too, if you, who are the pillars of the Church, begin to be shaken, the holy Church governed through you will waste away and fall. These two things, brethren, are greatly to be feared, weighed with the utmost moderation, and guarded against lest they occur. For Truth itself said: “You are the salt of the earth; but if the salt loses its savor, with what shall it be salted?” and so forth (Matt. 5; Rom. 1).

Therefore, dearest brethren, [Col. 0086D] I admonish you, because I am indebted to you and love you greatly. When I hear good reports about you, I rejoice exceedingly; conversely, when I hear of adversity, I am greatly troubled. Although I am separated from you by long distances across the earth, I am nevertheless wholly united with you in heart (St. Gregory, Epistle 36, book IV). I therefore have complete confidence in your Blessedness’s disposition toward me, because when you love me in return, you are not far from me.

Hence we give still greater thanks to that mustard seed (Matt. 13; Mark 4; Luke 13) which, though appearing as a small and contemptible seed, has spread everywhere [Col. 0087A] as branches rise from the same root and extend themselves, so that all the birds of heaven nest in them (Matt. 13). Thanks also be to that leaven which, in three measures of flour (Luke 13), mingled the mass of the whole human race into unity; and to the little stone cut from the mountain without hands, which occupied the whole face of the earth (Dan. 2). By assuming for this purpose the nature of our flesh and the form of a servant’s condition, he humbly extended himself everywhere, so that, when the entire human race had been gathered into unity, he might bring to completion the one body of the whole Church, and so that this partial distinction of members might contribute to the well-being of that joined structure.

Thus we too are not far from you, because in him who is everywhere we are one. Let us therefore give thanks to him who, abolishing enmity in his flesh, brought it about that throughout the whole world there should be one flock and [Col. 0087B] one fold under one shepherd. Let us always remember the admonition of the preacher of truth: “Take care to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4). For no one preserves the bond of peace while he troubles another or persecutes him in words or deeds.

Brethren, we have placed these matters first because we have heard that accusations are being pursued among you, and that bishops driven from their sees or despoiled of their property are being brought to judgment.

### I

For this reason it has been decreed that if anyone believes that he has a personal case against a bishop or against the administrators of the Church (Hadrian, Collection, ch. 2, from the Fifth Council of Orléans, canon 17), he is not to approach the judges before first having recourse to them in a spirit of charity, so that, admonished in familiar conversation, they may remedy the matters that have been made the subject of complaint. If he acts otherwise, let him be [Col. 0087C] deprived of communion.

### II

Henceforth, let no pontiff presume to excommunicate or judge any bishop who has been despoiled of his property or driven from his see, because one who has already been stripped bare has no privilege left by which he can be despoiled (the same in the decretal of Pope Alexander and in the decretal of Pope Julius).

### III

Let no bishop presume to retain, ordain, or judge another bishop’s parishioner without that bishop’s consent; for just as such an ordination will be invalid, so too will the judgment (Hadrian, Collection, ch. 16). We hold that no one is bound by the sentence of any judge other than his own (Anianus on the sole constitution of title 16, book IV, *Theodosian Code*). For one who had no authority to ordain him will likewise have no authority whatever to judge him. We command you to observe these provisions henceforth and to assist one another as brethren [Col. 0087D] (the same in the decretals of Sixtus I, and likewise in the decretals of Pope Julius).

### IV

As for the brethren whom you unjustly condemned through earthly fear, know that they have justly been restored by us. By the authority of Saint Peter and of the apostolic office, we command that everything taken from them be restored to them in its entirety, unless you wish yourselves and your princes to be separated from our college and from the members of the Church.

For by God’s just judgment sinners are often given power to persecute his saints (Prosper, *Sentences* 23, and St. Augustine on Psalm 118), so that those who are aided and guided by the Spirit of God may be made more illustrious through the trials of their labors. Nevertheless, those who do this will in no way escape punishment, for, as the Lord says: “Woe to him through whom the stumbling block [Col. 0088A] comes” (Matt. 18). And although, according to the Savior’s declaration, it is necessary that stumbling blocks come, nevertheless, woe to the person through whom they come.

For rashly judging another person’s hidden thoughts is a sin (Prosper, *Sentences* 21, and St. Augustine on the same Psalm); and it is unjust to censure on suspicion someone whose works appear to be nothing but good, since God alone is the just judge of matters unknown to man, for he is the true examiner. Hence it is written: “Let us not judge uncertain matters until the Lord comes, who will both illuminate the things hidden in darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Cor. 4) (in the decretal collection of Ivo, book IV). And even if such things are true (St. Isidore, *Synonyms* II, ch. 16), they are nevertheless not to be believed unless proved by certain indications, unless demonstrated by an evident judgment, and unless made public through judicial procedure.

[Col. 0088B] No one, therefore, may be condemned by human examination whom God has reserved for his own judgment (Hadrian, Collection, chs. 51 and 67; and Constantine the Great to the Fathers of Nicaea). All these dangers must be guarded against with the utmost care, lest we appear presumptuous.

An accusation against bishops is not to be readily accepted, for the Lord says: “You shall not receive a lying report” (Exod. 23). And the Apostle says (1 Tim. 5) that an accusation against a presbyter is not to be received without two or three suitable witnesses. See Epistle II of Pope Julius, stained with the same mark of spuriousness (*notheia*, νοθεία). If these precautions must be taken regarding presbyters or the rest of the faithful, how much more regarding bishops?

From these facts it is evident that you desire to lord it over your brethren rather than to take counsel for them or support them, because honor inflates pride, and what was provided [Col. 0088C] for concord turns toward harm. In accordance with the foregoing rules, if they had done anything contrary to their order, you ought to have reported it to us and awaited what we would write in answer to your inquiries. This applies to such an extent that, even if they committed something grave and intolerable, our judgment was to be awaited, so that you would decree nothing beforehand and nothing other than what you knew to be pleasing to us, and would depart from the established rules neither through negligence nor presumption.

Let such conduct cease, and let there be no harmful machinations by those who refuse to accept us in their complaint or accusation, for we can by no means endure such devices patiently, since it is fitting that we be diligent guardians of the ordinances of the fathers. The matter rightly concerns us if by our silence we favor error.

### V

[Col. 0088D] It has furthermore often already been decreed by our holy predecessors that no one under anathema is to be accepted in an accusation before us. With our authority having been brought to bear, let such presumption be checked; let persons of this sort be summoned, since we know that we have been appointed over them by the Lord, not they over us. And just as a superior cannot be judged by an inferior, neither can he be bound by one, because everything great is rare.

Let us bear the burdens of all who are oppressed—or rather, the blessed apostle Peter bears them in us, whose office we discharge as his legates and by whose rule we are formed—so that, supported by his aid, we may be protected from every adversity, now and forever.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August.

[Note: [Col. 0088D] The chronological indication is false.]

In the consulship of the most illustrious Valerian and Decius.

# DECREES OF SIXTUS II

[Col. 0089A]

## FROM GRATIAN  
*(Cause 2, Question 6, and Cause 3, Question 6)*

[Col. 0089A] If anyone believes himself to be oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the pope of the universal Apostolic Church.

## FROM THE SAME, AS ABOVE

On an appeal, judges of another province ought not to hear the case.

[Col. 0090A]

If any cleric is accused of any crimes whatever, let him conduct his case in the province in which the person accused resides; and let his accuser not suppose that he may drag him elsewhere or farther away to stand trial.

[Col. 0089]

# LETTERS RELATING TO SIXTUS II, POPE AND MARTYR

## LETTER I: FRAGMENTS OF DIONYSIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, TO POPE SIXTUS

[Note: [Col. 0089] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Note: [Col. 0089C]

**“Previously, indeed, letters.”** Eusebius prefixes the following: “To this Xystus, Dionysius wrote a second letter concerning Baptism, in which he sets out the opinion and judgment both of Stephen and of the other bishops, writing as follows concerning Stephen.” Here this letter is called not the second to Xystus, but the second concerning baptism, because Eusebius had previously mentioned one written by the same Dionysius to Stephen on the same subject. — Coustant.

**“Concerning Helenus and Firmilian.”** Rufinus, book VII, ch. 4, renders this “to Firmilian and Helenus,” and omits the words appended to this letter. Firmilian, in Epistle 75 to Cyprian, includes the bishops of the aforesaid provinces under the single designation “the Easterners,” and says that Stephen had broken peace first with the Africans, who were in the south, and then with the Easterners. — Coustant.

**“It was decreed.”** Namely, at councils held at Iconium and Synnada, as is explained below, in addition to those celebrated in Africa. — Coustant.

**“First instructed in doctrine.”** Valesius’s interpretation, “that they should first become catechumens,” is unsatisfactory because it leads the reader to suppose that, in the judgment of those who rebaptized, persons coming from heresy had to perform the duties of catechumens [Col. 0090C] before receiving baptism. Certainly, in the Third Council of Carthage, over which Cyprian presided, we have the judgments of eighty-six bishops; but although they all decree that persons coming from heresy must be baptized, no one demands that they first become catechumens. Lucius of Thabeste alone said: “I judge that heretics must be execrated, and therefore must be exorcized and baptized”; and in ch. 37 Vincentius of Thibaris said: “First, through the imposition of hands in exorcism, and second, through the regeneration of baptism, they can then attain the promise of Christ.” He interpreted as exorcism that imposition of hands which, with Stephen’s own agreement, was to be applied to them. These Africans likewise say nothing about imparting instruction; but there was no need for any command on that subject, since other laws teach that a heretic is not to be received unless he professes the catholic faith. — Coustant.

**“Concerning all these persons.”** That is, Firmilian, Helenus, and their associates, so that Stephen would not separate them from his communion. — Coustant.

**“They had written to me concerning the same.”** Valesius added “matters” here, although that word is absent from the Greek and does not appear to need expression in Latin. It is more appropriate [Col. 0091C] to understand “concerning the same” as referring to Firmilian and Helenus, whom the presbyters Dionysius and Philemon, agreeing with Stephen, thought should be separated from communion. — Coustant.

**“For since concerning the doctrine . . .”** [Col. 0091D] Rufinus, with his customary freedom, translated this entire fragment into Latin as follows:

“Since concerning that doctrine which recently arose at Ptolemais, a city of the Pentapolis—a doctrine full of blasphemies against God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, denying that he is truly the Son of the Father or the firstborn of every creature, and likewise abolishing the understanding of the Holy Spirit—both parties came to me concerning these matters and, in the presence of the brethren, discussed the issues that had been raised, I also pursued the matter in writing, insofar as God granted ability to my littleness, and wrote an exact and careful exposition of every particular. I have sent you copies of these writings.” — Coustant.]

Dionysius recalls letters that he had written both to Pope Stephen and to the presbyters Dionysius and Philemon concerning the baptism of heretics and the Sabellian heresy.

[Col. 0089B]

### 1. Latin Version

Previously, indeed, Stephen had written letters concerning Helenus and Firmilian and all those established throughout Cilicia, Cappadocia, and all the neighboring provinces. He declared that for this same reason he would withdraw from their communion: because they rebaptized heretics.

Consider the gravity of the matter. For in fact, as I hear, it was decreed in very great councils of bishops that those who come from heresy should first be instructed in [catholic] doctrine and should then be cleansed through baptism from the defilements of the old and impure leaven. I sent him a letter beseeching and imploring him concerning all these persons.

[Col. 0090B]

### Greek Version

Previously, then, Stephen had also written concerning Helenus and Firmilian and all those from Cilicia, Cappadocia, Galatia, and all the neighboring nations adjoining them, saying that he would not maintain communion with them either, for this same reason: “Because,” he says, “they rebaptize heretics.”

Consider the magnitude of the matter. For decisions concerning this have in fact been made in the greatest councils of bishops, as I understand: namely, that those who come from heresy, after first being catechized, should then wash themselves and be cleansed from the defilement of the old and impure leaven. I wrote to him, beseeching him concerning all these persons.

[Col. 0089]

A little later Dionysius continues:

[Col. 0089B]

### 2. Latin Version

I also replied to our beloved fellow presbyters Dionysius and Philemon, who had previously agreed with Stephen and had written to me concerning the same persons—[Col. 0089C] formerly in a few words, but now at greater length.

[Col. 0090B]

### Greek Version

I also wrote to our beloved fellow presbyters Dionysius and Philemon, who had previously agreed in judgment with Stephen and who were writing to me concerning the same matters—[Col. 0090C] formerly briefly, but now at greater length.

[Col. 0091]

In the same letter, says Eusebius (*History*, book VII, ch. 6), he informs Xystus in the following words about the Sabellian heretics, since they were then becoming prevalent.

[Col. 0091A]

### 3. Latin Version

For concerning the doctrine recently raised in Ptolemais, a city of the Pentapolis—a doctrine that is impious and full of blasphemy against almighty God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, full of unbelief and faithlessness toward his only-begotten Son, the firstborn of every creature, the Word made man, and one that abolishes the understanding of the Holy Spirit—when letters had been brought to me from both sides and brethren had come to debate the matter, I wrote certain letters, explaining it more clearly insofar as I was able by God’s gift. I have sent copies of them to you.

[Col. 0092A]

### Greek Version

For concerning the doctrine now raised at Ptolemais in the Pentapolis—a doctrine that is impious and contains much blasphemy concerning almighty God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, contains much unbelief concerning his only-begotten Son and the firstborn of all creation, the Word who became man, and displays insensibility concerning the Holy Spirit—when both preliminary letters and brethren who were to debate had come to me from each side, I wrote certain things, setting the matter out more instructively insofar as I was able, God granting it. I sent you copies of them.

## LETTER II: FRAGMENTS OF DIONYSIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, TO PHILEMON, A PRESBYTER OF SIXTUS

[Note: [Col. 0091] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Note: [Col. 0091D]

**EPISTLE II.** Eusebius immediately appends this passage to the fragments of the preceding letter with these words: “In the letter to Philemon, a Roman presbyter, which is the third among those he wrote concerning baptism”—*en tē tritē tōn peri baptismatos* (ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ τῶν περὶ βαπτίσματος)—“the same Dionysius relates the following.”

Thus the first is reckoned as the letter to Stephen, the second as the preceding letter to Xystus, and this as the third. By this ordering Eusebius indicates [Col. 0092C] that this letter to Philemon was not earlier than the preceding one to Xystus. Consequently, the opinion of Baronius, who thinks this fragment was excerpted from a letter written under Stephen, cannot be defended. Yet neither is the preceding letter to Xystus [Col. 0092D] later than this one, since Dionysius mentions the present letter in that very letter, no. 2. We therefore judge that both were sent at the same time. Nor do we think that he mentioned this letter in that one for any reason other than that it might be communicated to Xystus. This letter, therefore, also pertains in some manner to Xystus; and consequently it appears consistent with our undertaking to present here the fragments of it transmitted to us by Eusebius. We present them all the more willingly because they contribute considerably to clarifying the question of baptism. — Coustant.

**“Be skilled money-changers.”** Very many Fathers—collected with the utmost diligence by Cotelier in book II of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, ch. 36—cite these words as those of Christ or of an apostle. They are nevertheless absent from our manuscripts, whether Greek or Latin. In their place Rufinus—whom Cotelier therefore accuses of enormous audacity—did not hesitate to substitute: “Read everything; retain what is good,” that is, the manner in which Augustine cites Paul’s statement in 1 Thess. 5:21 in *On Nature and Grace*, ch. 39. — Coustant.

[Col. 0093B] **“Those who from heretics . . .”** Dionysius appears to establish three classes of persons here. The first consists of those who, [Col. 0093C] born among heretics and baptized by them, came to the Church. The second consists of those who returned to the Church after openly abandoning it. The last consists of certain persons who, although they had not ceased attending the Church’s assemblies, nevertheless secretly met with heretics and listened to them as teachers.

If this is so, what Jerome writes concerning Dionysius of Alexandria in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 79, cannot stand: “Agreeing with the doctrine of Cyprian and the African synod, he sent numerous letters to various persons concerning the rebaptism of heretics.” For this prelate declares that, following the example of his predecessor and teacher, he received every one of the persons just mentioned who came to the Church without repeating the baptism of any of them.

The conclusion of this fragment, however, appears to require that both it and the preceding statements be referred only to those who had defected from the Catholic Church to heresy. However that may be, on this subject the authority of Basil, bishop of Caesarea, [Col. 0093D] is no less than Jerome’s testimony. In his canonical epistle to Amphilochius, ch. 5, Basil teaches that Dionysius of Alexandria accepted the baptism of heretics; and he says that he marvels at how so great a bishop, endowed with knowledge of the canons, did not reject even the baptism of the Pepuzenes, although they baptized in the Father, the Son, Montanus, and Priscilla.

Basil does not speak in this way because the Montanists administered baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, Montanus, and Priscilla, but because they were believed to understand Montanus and Priscilla by the designation “Holy Spirit,” since they proclaimed that through them the Holy Spirit had spoken and had been given more perfectly. Basil is following the steps of his predecessor Firmilian, by whom the same heretics are accused of believing that the Spirit spoke through Montanus and Priscilla—in Cyprian the name is given as Prisca—and consequently that this was not the Spirit of truth but of error.

Finally, the following fourth letter of Dionysius to Xystus will demonstrate how greatly Dionysius recoiled from repeating baptism, that is, from the doctrine of Cyprian and the African synod. — Coustant.

**“To the assemblies of the faithful.”** Valesius translates both the preceding word *synagesthai* (συνάγεσθαι) as “to communicate with the brethren,” and the present *synēgagen* (συνηγάγεν) as “he admitted them to communion.” Both words signify assemblies, either those which someone attends or [Col. 0094C] those with which he is joined. Accordingly, this *synēgagen* could be rendered “he joined them to the assemblies,” with “catholic” understood. In harmony with this manner of speaking, Siricius says in Epistle 1 to Himerius, ch. 1: “These persons, through the invocation of the sevenfold Spirit alone and the imposition of the bishop’s hand, we associate with the assembly of Catholics.” And Leo says in Epistle 2 to Rusticus, ch. 18: “Through the imposition of hands, with the power of the Holy Spirit invoked—the power they could not receive from heretics—they are to be joined to the Catholics.” — Coustant.

**“By no means asking this of them.”** In Valesius: “By no means thinking that they needed a repeated baptism.” — Coustant.

**“They had received from him.”** That is, from Heraclas, who is understood to have conferred baptism upon them. Even to those baptized among heretics the Holy Spirit can in a certain sense [Col. 0094D] be said to have been conferred—namely, for the reception of the sacrament, not for the attainment of the sacrament’s grace, which even those Fathers who accept the baptism of heretics deny can be attained from heretics.

For the sacrament received, once the obstacle of error by which its efficacy had been held in suspense has been removed, and once what was lacking has been supplied—as the Anonymous author already praised more than once puts it in Labbe, vol. I of the *Councils*, p. 775—that is, to use the same author’s words, once the faith has subsequently been made sincere and thoroughly purified, at last attains its integrity. — Coustant.

**“Earlier bishops.”** Cyprian, in Epistle 71 to Quintus and Epistle 2 to Stephen, acknowledges that it was introduced by Agrippinus. Firmilian, however, in Epistle 75 to Cyprian, teaches that in the East it was confirmed at Iconium, a place in Phrygia, when bishops from Galatia, Cilicia, and the other neighboring regions assembled there.

Since Eusebius inserted this passage of Dionysius into his *History*, he cannot have regarded Cyprian as the first author of the opinion that heretics should be rebaptized, although his words in book VII, ch. 2, may appear to suggest this. — Coustant.]

[Col. 0091B]

### Latin Version

I applied myself to reading the books of heretics and learning their traditions. For a time, indeed, I defiled my mind with their utterly accursed opinions; yet I derived this benefit from them: that I refuted them within myself and detested them much more intensely.

When a certain brother from the order of presbyters tried to deter me and feared that I might become mingled with the same mire of wickedness—for he said that my mind would be contaminated, and he spoke truly, as I myself perceived—I was strengthened by a divinely sent vision. A word addressed to me expressly commanded me, saying: “Read everything that comes into your hands, for you are capable of correcting and testing each matter; and this was for you from the beginning the cause and occasion of believing.”

I accepted this vision as agreeing with the apostolic voice, which addresses those endowed with greater strength in this way: “Be skilled money-changers” (1 Thess. 5:21).

[Col. 0092B]

### Greek Version

I encountered both the writings and the traditions of the heretics. For a short time I stained my soul with their utterly defiled thoughts, but I nevertheless derived this benefit from them: that I refuted them within myself and detested them much more intensely.

Then one of the presbyter-brethren tried to restrain me and frightened me with the prospect that I might become mingled with that very mire of wickedness—for he said that I would corrupt my own soul, and he spoke truly, as I perceived. But a divinely sent vision came to me and strengthened me. A word addressed to me commanded me expressly, saying: “Read everything that you may take into your hands, for you are capable of setting each matter right and testing it; and this was for you from the beginning the cause of your faith.”

I accepted the vision as agreeing with the apostolic voice that says to those of greater strength: [Col. 0092C] “Become approved money-changers.”

[Col. 0091]

Then, says Eusebius, after discussing certain matters concerning all the heresies, he adds:

[Col. 0091C]

### Latin Version

I received this rule and pattern from our blessed pope Heraclas. For when persons came from the heresies—even if they had defected from the Church, or rather, even if they had not defected but, while appearing to attend the assemblies of the faithful, had been accused of visiting teachers of perverse doctrine—he expelled them from the Church and did not receive them despite their many entreaties until they had openly and publicly recounted everything they had heard from the adversaries. Only then did he admit them to the assemblies of the faithful, by no means requiring them to receive baptism again, since they had previously received the Holy Spirit from him.

[Col. 0092C]

### Greek Version

I received this rule and pattern from our blessed pope Heraclas. For those who came from the heresies—even though they had departed from the Church, or rather, had not even departed but appeared to attend its assemblies, yet had been reported for visiting one of those teaching other doctrines—he expelled from the Church. When they pleaded, he did not receive them until they had publicly related everything that they had heard among those who held the opposing position. Then he joined them to the assembly, without requiring another baptism from them, for they had previously received the Holy Spirit from him.

[Col. 0093]

Again, after discussing this question fully, he adds:

[Col. 0093A]

### Latin Version

I learned this as well: that it was not only now among the Africans that this custom was introduced, but that long before, in the time of the bishops preceding us, it had also been approved in the most populous churches, in synods of the brethren held at Iconium and Synnada, and among very many others. I am unwilling, by overturning their judgments, to cast them into disputes and contentions. For it is said: “You shall not move your neighbor’s boundaries, which your fathers established” (Deut. 19:14).

[Col. 0094A]

### Greek Version

I have learned this too: it was not only now that those in Africa introduced this practice; rather, long before, under the bishops preceding us, it was approved in the most populous churches, in the synods of the brethren at Iconium and Synnada, and among many others. I cannot bring myself, by overturning their resolutions, to cast them into strife and contentious rivalry. For it is said: “You shall not move your neighbor’s boundaries, which your fathers established.”

## LETTER III: A FRAGMENT OF DIONYSIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, TO DIONYSIUS, THEN A PRESBYTER OF XYSTUS AND AFTERWARD HIS SUCCESSOR

[Note: [Col. 0093] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Note: [Col. 0094D]

**Fragment of Dionysius.** From the words of the preceding letter [Col. 0095C] it may be gathered that, at the very time when Pope Stephen wrote that heretics were not to be rebaptized, the presbyters Philemon and Dionysius sent letters to Dionysius of Alexandria on the same subject. Dionysius of Alexandria also replied to both of them, first briefly and afterward—when Xystus had already succeeded Stephen—at greater length. He wrote to them separately, as is established by the fact that the letter written in reply to Philemon is called by Eusebius the third concerning baptism, while the letter to Dionysius is called the fourth.

Concerning the latter, Eusebius introduces it as follows: “The fourth of his letters concerning baptism [Col. 0095D] was written to Dionysius, who was then a presbyter of the city of Rome but was appointed bishop of the same city a little later. From this letter it is possible to learn, through the testimony of Dionysius of Alexandria, that this Roman Dionysius was a most learned and altogether admirable man.” After this preface he appends the following fragment. — Coustant.

**“He holds the laver invalid.”** Hence in Cyprian’s Epistle 73 to Jubaianus we read that the Novatianists rebaptized those whom they enticed away from us. And in the appendix to Augustine, vol. III, the ancient author of *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, question 102, says concerning Novatian himself: “He is so angry with us that he denies that we are Christians”—and therefore considers that our baptism must be repeated—“although he knows that we were initiated in that faith on which he himself relies.”

This agrees with the statement in the commonly circulated Ambrosian commentary on 1 Corinthians, ch. 1: “For they were like the Novatianists and Donatists are now, who claim baptism for themselves while rejecting those baptized by our people.” — Coustant.]

[Col. 0096C] **Even if there remains some hope.** The Greek word ἔλπις (“hope”) is sometimes used in the sense of “opinion.” Here, indeed, its construction with a verb in the past tense seems to require that we understand it in that sense. Nor do we, with Valesius, interpret this passage as referring to those who had lapsed into idolatry, but rather to Catholics led astray by Novatian. By repudiating their baptism, he drove away the Holy Spirit, which they had received through the gift of this sacrament before they were led astray, although it is credible that in some of them the Holy Spirit had either remained through innocence or—as Valesius understands it—had returned through repentance. [Col. 0096D] Thus there is no need for us to ask: “How can the Holy Spirit remain in those who have lapsed?” COUSTANT.]

**He teaches that Novatian is rightly opposed because of his schism, his impious doctrine, and his repetition of baptism for those who came over to him.**

[Col. 0093B] For we rightly abhor Novatian, who has torn the Church apart [Col. 0095A] and drawn some of the brethren into impiety and blasphemies; who has introduced throughout the world an utterly profane doctrine concerning God and slanders our most gracious Lord Jesus Christ as though he were merciless. In addition to all these things, he treats the sacred washing as invalid and rejects it; he overturns the faith and confession that precede baptism, and utterly drives the Holy Spirit away from them, even if there remains some hope either that he had continued in them or that he had returned to them.

[Col. 0094B] For we rightly abhor Novatian, who has torn the Church apart [Col. 0096A] and drawn some of the brethren into impieties and blasphemies; who has brought in an utterly profane doctrine concerning God and slanders our most gracious Lord Jesus Christ as though he were merciless. In addition to all these things, he rejects the holy washing and overturns both the faith and the confession that precede it, utterly driving the Holy Spirit away from them, even if there was some hope that he had remained or returned to them.

## LETTER IV: FRAGMENT OF DIONYSIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, TO POPE SIXTUS II

[Note: [Col. 0093] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Note: [Col. 0096D]

**A fragment of Dionysius of Alexandria.** Eusebius introduces this letter as follows: “There is also extant a fifth letter of his to Xystus, bishop of the city of Rome, in which, after discussing many matters against the heretics, he relates that something of the following kind occurred in his own time.” In it Dionysius relates what had recently happened when he had administered baptism publicly and solemnly. From this it is inferred that the letter was written shortly after Easter, or at any rate Pentecost, in the year 258. COUSTANT.

**The baptism by which he had been initiated among the heretics.** Rufinus rendered this as follows: “That he had received baptism from the heretics in a different manner; yet, in comparison with what he now saw being administered by us, he did not consider it baptism at all, because that entire confession was filled with blasphemies.” From this passage it is plainly established that, in the time of Dionysius and his predecessors, the accepted practice in the Church of Alexandria was to receive heretics without repeating baptism. [Col. 0097A] It must also be noted [Col. 0097B] that the man’s scruple concerning his baptism arose not because he had received it from heretics, but because, as he believed, he had received it under a different form. For baptism administered with words or actions other than those prescribed by Christ has never been regarded in the Church as Christ’s baptism, and therefore not as true baptism. Dionysius’s predecessor held no different opinion, although he may perhaps deserve blame for neglecting to ask the man who came from heresy how he had been baptized. To prevent an inconvenience of this kind thereafter, the Council of Arles in 314 decreed in canon 8: “If anyone comes to the Church from a heresy, let them question him concerning the Creed; and if they ascertain that he was baptized in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, let a hand merely be laid upon him so that he may receive the Holy Spirit. But if, when questioned, he does not answer with this Trinity, let him be baptized.” COUSTANT.

**With words and actions.** Valesius has “with words and ceremonies.” Here he is reluctant to depart even slightly from the Greek. Everyone would wish, however, [Col. 0097C] that Dionysius had explained who those heretics were and what the actions and words were with which they administered baptism. But perhaps he himself had been unable to learn anything except general statements from the man who was uncertain about his baptism. COUSTANT.

**Reception and grace.** Christophorson: “reception into the Church.” Musculus simply: “reception”; Valesius declares in his notes that he prefers this interpretation, because in baptism God receives us as sons. In his text of Eusebius, however, he prefers: “and most true adoption.” We think that this passage should be understood as though we read: “so that he might be endowed not only with the reception in which he rejoiced when admitted into the Church, but also with the grace of which he grieved to be deprived.” From Rufinus’s interpretation—“For this reason he begged to be washed and purified by ecclesiastical baptism, so that he might also obtain the grace of the Holy Spirit”—it is clear that he read παραδοχῆς χάριτος (“reception of grace”), without the intervening conjunction καί (“and”). If that reading is correct, the Latin should be translated “reception of grace.” COUSTANT.

[Col. 0097D] **Responded, “Amen.”** The following words of Justin Martyr, *Apology* I, agree with this: “When he [the priest] has completed the prayers and the Eucharist, all the people present acclaim, saying, ‘Amen.’” Οὗ συντελέσαντος τὰς εὐχὰς καὶ τὴν εὐχαριστίαν, πᾶς ὁ παρὼν λαὸς παρευφημεῖ λέγων, Ἀμὴν: “When he has completed the prayers and the Eucharist, all the people present acclaim, saying, ‘Amen.’” For this reason Emperor Justinian says in *Novel* 137, chapter 6: “We command all bishops and presbyters to perform the divine oblation . . . not in secret, but in a voice that may be heard by the most faithful people.” And shortly afterward: “If you bless only in spirit, how will the person occupying the place of the unlearned append that holy ‘Amen’ to your thanksgiving?” Above, on page 157, note b, we already observed that the faithful formerly customarily answered “Amen” to the priest who delivered the Eucharist to them and said, “The Body of Christ,” or “The Blood of Christ.” But the course of Dionysius’s argument makes it clear that he is speaking here of the response “Amen” appended to the words of consecration. He certainly says that it was spoken by the man whom he afterward brings to the altar to receive the Eucharist. Now it is not for a private person [Col. 0098A] to revive a custom that has fallen into disuse; rather, a man devoted to humility [Col. 0098B] and peace will always prefer the alternative now established by long usage. It will be enough, when he reaches that place in the sacred liturgy where the ancients used to respond “Amen,” to affirm with sincere inward conviction the faith that they expressed by that word, so that, following Ambrose’s counsel in *On the Mysteries*, chapter 9, what the mouth formerly uttered by saying “Amen”—that is, “It is true”—may now be confessed by an attentive mind. COUSTANT.

**And extended his hands to receive.** This practice too, by which the faithful customarily received the body of Christ in their hands, has fallen into disuse, but we do not read that it was abolished by any law. Our Mabillon, *Gallican Liturgy*, book I, chapter 5, no. 25, infers from Gregory of Tours, book X, chapter 8, that it continued in Gaul at least into the sixth century. COUSTANT.

**I would not have dared to renew him.** Whether Xystus replied to Dionysius and removed his scruple is unknown to us. Perhaps the persecution and his death, which followed not long afterward, deprived this pope of the opportunity to reply. But the canon of the Council of Arles cited above, [Col. 0098C] canon 8, clearly decides that someone who had not been baptized with the words prescribed by Christ must be baptized. For that reason the Council of Nicaea, canon 19, also required Paulianists coming to the Church to be baptized, because, as Innocent says in Letter 16 to the Macedonians, chapter 10, those heretics did not baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit; and therefore such a baptism was no baptism at all. “For who,” says Augustine in *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, book VI, chapter 25, “does not know that it is not Christ’s baptism if the Gospel words of which the Creed consists are lacking?” Christ’s general precept nevertheless is: “Unless one is born again of water,” etc.; and, since the preaching of the Gospel, the Church judges that salvation is not to be hoped for by anyone unless he has fulfilled this command in fact or in desire. No matter how often someone has attended gatherings of the faithful and there partaken of Christ’s body and blood, no one can be more certain that he has received the grace of the Holy Spirit than Peter was certain that this gift had been bestowed upon Cornelius and his companions. Nevertheless, he did not hesitate to require all those whom he saw filled with the Holy Spirit [Col. 0098D] to be baptized, “so that nothing might appear to have been omitted,” says Cyprian in Letter 2 to Stephen, no. 1, “whereby the apostolic teachings might observe in every respect the divine commandment and the law of the Gospel.” Nor, in my judgment, should it be doubted that Dionysius himself understood this. His distress therefore arose rather from the fact that, since the man who said he had been baptized with different actions and words could furnish no certain proof of this, Dionysius feared repeating baptism contrary to apostolic teaching. He experienced in his own person that horror of repeating baptism which Augustine later testified was implanted in the minds of the faithful, in *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, book V, chapter 5. Tossed about in this uncertainty, he preferred to think concerning the man in question what Cyprian, in Letter 73 to Jubaianus, said that he thought concerning others who had not been baptized in the Church: “The Lord is able in his mercy to grant pardon and not to separate from the gifts of his Church those who, having been admitted to the Church in simplicity [without baptism], have fallen asleep in the Church.” Leo later relieved a fear of this kind in Letter 115 to Neon, [Col. 0099A] where he begins: “First of all, therefore, we must take care lest, while preserving a certain appearance of caution, we incur the loss of souls that are to be regenerated.” He then indeed admits that it is an inexpiable crime to undergo twice the washing once bestowed for regeneration; but immediately afterward he nevertheless adds: “But in this case [of one whom no one knows to have been truly baptized] nothing similar is feared, since that which is entirely unknown to have been done cannot incur the guilt of repetition.” Now concerning the baptism about which Dionysius thought it necessary to consult Xystus, it was certainly established that it had been conferred by heretics. [Col. 0100A] Nor is there any doubt that if the man so baptized had approached Cyprian and those who assembled with him in the African synod, they would immediately have decreed that he must be baptized. From this too it is confirmed that Dionysius by no means agreed with them. It is at least clear from this that the man, who had been baptized by heretics, had been admitted into the Church by Heraclas without a new baptism. Dionysius himself expressly declares that, in receiving heretics, he followed the practice of Heraclas. COUSTANT.]

[Col. 0095]

**Concerning a man who desired to be initiated by the Church’s baptism, since he said that among the heretics he had received baptism with different words and actions.**

[Col. 0095B] Indeed, brother, I truly need counsel and ask your judgment, lest perhaps I be mistaken, concerning a matter of the following kind that has befallen me. One of the brethren who assemble at the church, long regarded as a believer, and who before my ordination—and, unless I am mistaken, even before the episcopate of Heraclas himself—had shared in the gathering of the faithful, was present at the baptism of those who had recently been baptized and heard the questions and answers. He then approached me weeping and lamenting his own condition. Falling at my feet, he began to confess and solemnly swear that the baptism by which he had been initiated among the heretics was not of this kind and had absolutely nothing in common with ours, for it had been full of impiety and blasphemy. He said [Col. 0095C] that his soul was pierced by an exceedingly bitter sense of grief and that he did not dare even to raise his eyes to God, [Col. 0097A] because he had been initiated with those profane words and actions. He therefore implored that he might receive this most pure washing, together with reception and grace. I did not dare to do this, but told him that his long-standing communion was sufficient for that purpose. For one who had heard the thanksgiving, who had responded “Amen” together with the others, who had stood at the sacred table, extended his hands to receive the holy food and taken it, and who had for a very long time partaken of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—such a man I would not have dared to renew all over again. I therefore instructed him [Col. 0099A] to take courage and to approach the Holy Things with firm faith and a good conscience and become a partaker of them. But he does not cease mourning; he shudders at approaching the table, and only with difficulty, when entreated, can he bear to be present at the prayers.

[Col. 0096B] Indeed, brother, I truly need counsel and ask your judgment, since a matter of the following kind has come before me and I fear that I may perhaps be mistaken. One of the brethren who assemble with us, long regarded as a believer and having shared in the congregation before my ordination—and, I think, even before the appointment of the blessed Heraclas—was present with those who had lately been baptized and heard the questions and answers. He approached me weeping and lamenting himself. Falling at my feet, he confessed and solemnly swore that the baptism with which he had been baptized among the heretics was not of this kind and had absolutely nothing in common with this one, for that baptism had been filled with impiety and blasphemies. He said that his soul was now deeply pierced and that he did not even have the confidence [Col. 0096C] to lift his eyes toward God, on account of those profane words and actions. [Col. 0098A] For this reason he begged to obtain this most pure purification, reception, and grace. I did not dare to do this, saying that his long-standing communion was sufficient for him in this matter. For one who had heard the thanksgiving, joined in pronouncing the “Amen,” stood at the table, extended his hands to receive the holy food and accepted it, and who for a considerable time had partaken of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—I would not dare now to reconstruct him anew from the beginning. I instructed him to take courage and to approach participation in the Holy Things [Col. 0100A] with firm faith and a good conscience. But he neither ceases mourning nor is free from dread at approaching the table; and only with difficulty, when entreated, can he bear to stand together with the others at the prayers.

[Col. 0099]

## NOTICE OF CERTAIN WRITINGS PERTAINING TO SIXTUS

[Col. 0099B] 1. Dionysius also wrote another letter to Sixtus, which Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 9, considered it sufficient to indicate in these words: “There is also a fifth letter of the same Dionysius concerning baptism, written in his own name and that of the church which he governed, to Sixtus and the church of the city of Rome, in which he undertook a very lengthy discussion of the question proposed.”
