II. Pontius has the following in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*: “Word had already come concerning Sixtus, the good and peaceable priest and therefore most blessed martyr. The executioner’s imminent arrival was now expected.” The Oxford editor summarily renders these words as follows: “Sixtus, the Roman pontiff, warns Cyprian of the persecution that was to follow.” [Col. 0100B] Accordingly, if he has grasped Pontius’s meaning, it must be said that Sixtus, when his martyrdom was near, sent Cyprian letters informing him of the impending persecution. But Pontius means only that persecution was raging at Rome, that news of Sixtus’s martyrdom and death had already arrived, and that at Carthage the executioner was expected from day to day. For here this deacon briefly touches upon what Cyprian explains in Letter 82 to Successus: namely, that the men whom he himself had sent to Rome to ascertain the truth had returned; from them he learned both that Valerian had issued a rescript to the Senate against the Christians, and that Sixtus had been executed, and that the officials placed in charge of this persecution in the City were pressing it forward daily. D. COUSTANT.

## [THE COMPLETE WORKS OF POPE DIONYSIUS]

[Col. 0099]

# PROLEGOMENA ON SAINT DIONYSIUS, ROMAN PONTIFF

## ARTICLE I. The History of His Life

[Col. 0099B]

[Col. 0099C] Dionysius is commonly believed to have been Greek by descent and Calabrian by birth. [Note: [Col. 0099C] Cave, *Historia litteraria*, vol. I, p. 133; Johann Georg Walch, *Historia Ecclesiastica*, p. 1001. The *Liber Pontificalis* relates that he was a monk, which is altogether false.] We have no certain knowledge of his activities before the year of Christ 256. At that time he served as a presbyter of the Roman Church and was addressed in letters by Dionysius of Alexandria. From the letter that was the fourth on Baptism [Note: [Col. 0099C] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 7; and in Gallandi, vol. III, Letter 8, p. 523, note 5], “it is possible to learn, from the testimony of Dionysius of Alexandria, that this same Roman Dionysius was a most learned and altogether admirable man.”

Dionysius had supported Stephen, since he and Philemon, together with Pope Stephen, judged that Firmilian and Helenus, who rejected the baptism of heretics, should be excluded from communion. [Col. 0100B] [Note: [Col. 0100C] See Coutant’s note 6 on Letter 6, which is the second letter on Baptism to Sixtus II, above in this volume.] But he later departed from Stephen’s position, either because he judged with Cyprian that heretics must be baptized [Note: [Col. 0100C] Launoy indeed thinks so, vol. VIII, p. 603. But “I believe,” says the distinguished Maran in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*, §30, p. 100, Venice edition, 1758, folio, “that very few will fail to reject Launoy’s conjecture”], or because he disapproved of Stephen’s harsh action [Col. 0100C] in either excommunicating the Africans or at least threatening them with excommunication.

This is taught by the letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Sixtus, the predecessor of Dionysius of Rome, which is the second letter on Baptism: “But I have also written to our dearest brothers and fellow presbyters Dionysius and Philemon, who previously held the same opinion as Stephen—formerly in brief, but now at greater length.” We therefore believe, says the distinguished Maran, [Note: [Col. 0100C] Maran, passage cited, p. 101] and not without reason, that through the wisdom of these two presbyters of the Roman Church, [Col. 0101A] Stephen’s decree against those who rebaptized was moderated.

**The time at which Saint Dionysius became pontiff.**—After Sixtus II, or Xystus, was slain in Valerian’s persecution, our Dionysius succeeded to the Roman see. Scholars dispute when Saint Dionysius began his pontificate and how long he occupied it. As the most learned Pierre Coustant notes, [Note: [Col. 0101D] Coustant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 269 ff.] the common text of Anastasius, or the *Liber Pontificalis*, is inconsistent with itself. It places Xystus’s beheading on the eighth day before the Ides of August and Dionysius’s ordination on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, yet nevertheless states that the Roman see was vacant for only thirty-five days after Xystus’s death.

But from the Bucherian Catalogue and other sources we learn more correctly that, because Valerian’s persecution prevented a successor from being appointed to Xystus, the see remained vacant from the eighth day before the Ides of August in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus until the twelfth day before the Kalends of August in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus—that is, from 6 August [Col. 0101B] 258 until 21 July 259—and therefore for eleven months and fifteen days. During this interval the presbyters of the Roman Church administered it together with the deacons, as was customary. Afterward, in the year 259, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August—that is, Friday, 22 July—Dionysius was elected bishop of the city of Rome; while Xystus was pontiff, he had been eminent among the presbyters of that Church.

“To copy the words of the Bucherian Catalogue, he held office in the time of Gallienus, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus, until the seventh day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Claudius and Paternus”; accordingly, from 22 July 259 until 26 December 269. It follows that [Col. 0101C] he governed the Church for ten years, five months, and four days, excluding the day of his death. [Note: [Col. 0101D] Pagius arranges the chronology of Saint Dionysius’s pontificate in this way in his *Critique on Baronius’s Annals*, at the year 271, p. 9; Basnage, at the year 259, in the *Political-Ecclesiastical Annals*, p. 400; and the Benedictines in *The Art of Verifying Dates*, p. 243. For other opinions, see the different editions of the *Pontifical* in Schelstrate, pp. 434–435, vol. I of *Ecclesiastical Antiquity Illustrated*.]

From this the *Liber Pontificalis* is also proved false, for although it transcribes the preceding words of the Bucherian Catalogue, it nevertheless says that Dionysius occupied the see for six years, two months, and four days. Nor is the Bucherian Catalogue itself free of error, since it assigns the same pope only eight years, two months, and six days. In the very ancient register of the burial of the Roman bishops published by Bucherius on page 267, the deposition or burial of Dionysius is recorded as follows: “On the sixth day before the Kalends of January, Dionysius in the Cemetery of Callistus.”

The Acts of Saint Lawrence, near their conclusion [Col. 0102A] in Surius under 10 August, state that Dionysius was consecrated by Maximus, bishop of Ostia. [Note: [Col. 0101D] Baronius, at the year 261, §11.] Saint Augustine, in the *Summary of the Conference with the Donatists*, is indeed the authority for the ancient custom by which the Roman bishop was consecrated by the bishop of Ostia. [Note: [Col. 0101D] These are Augustine’s words in the aforementioned *Summary of the Conference*, day III, chapter 16: “Nor is the bishop of the Roman Church ordained by any metropolitan bishop, but by the neighboring bishop of Ostia.” As Mabillon teaches in chapter 18 of the *Commentary on the Roman Order*, p. 119, this must not be understood as though the latter were the sole consecrator, but rather as the principal consecrator of the Roman pontiff in the place of a metropolitan.]

Hence he assigned churches to presbyters, [Note: [Col. 0101D] Baronius, at the year 263, §§31, 33, 34, 51] and established cemeteries, parishes, and dioceses. [Note: [Col. 0102C] The *Liber Pontificalis*, whose words Baronius explains at the year 270, §17, as follows: “It was the work of Dionysius to divide again and distribute appropriately the parishes which his predecessors had marked out with fixed boundaries and assigned to presbyters, but which Valerian’s persecution had disrupted, [Col. 0102D] and to assign cemeteries to each.” See Blanchini’s notes on Anastasius the Librarian, vol. II, pp. 230–231.]

To this pontiff the bishops of the Pentapolis accused Dionysius of Alexandria of holding the same opinion concerning the Son of God that Arius afterward held. When Dionysius heard them, he wrote both against the followers of Sabellius and against those who held the opinion which Arius later advanced and for which he was expelled from the Church. [Note: [Col. 0102D] Saint Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book IV, §12: “Sabellius says that the Son is himself the one who is also the Father.”] He also sent a letter to Dionysius of Alexandria to indicate the matter of which he had been accused by them. [Note: [Col. 0102D] Saint Athanasius, *Letter on the Opinion of Dionysius*, §13, p. 252 in Montfaucon’s Paris edition, vol. I, part I, p. 198 in the Padua edition of 1777, folio.]

He then held a council at Rome, in which the same Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, disclosed his position by letter [Col. 0102B] and cleared himself of the charge brought against him; by a great consensus he was declared free from all blame. [Note: [Col. 0102D] In Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, vol. I, p. 1015. Hardouin records this Roman synod under the year 260 in his index of councils.]

The same pontiff is believed to have held a synod in that city [Note: [Col. 0102D] Baronius, at the year 265, §§4, 10] against Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, who denied Christ’s divinity. Pagius, at the year 264, §4, teaches that those who believe this are misled by a passage of Saint Athanasius that has not been correctly understood.

Hardouin also maintains that under this pontiff, around the year 262, a council was held in Africa at which it was decreed that heretics were not to be rebaptized, as Jerome testifies in the *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, chapter VIII, in these words: [Note: [Col. 0102D] Jerome, *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*, no. 23, p. 196, Venice quarto edition of 1767, vol. II.] “Finally, those very bishops who had decreed with him [Cyprian] that heretics must be rebaptized, returning to the ancient custom, issued a new decree.” But [Col. 0102C] we learn this only from Jerome; nowhere else will one find any mention of this new decree. Indeed, the controversy between the Donatists and Saint Augustine knows absolutely nothing of the kind. Pamelius adduces Saint Dionysius of Alexandria as a witness to this event, but, in the judgment of the latest editor of Saint Jerome’s works, he is mistaken along with Baronius.

The most holy pontiff Dionysius departed this life in the year of the Lord 269, on 26 December, according to Pagius, Basnage, and the authors of *The Art of Verifying Dates*. The highly learned Father Berti, [Note: [Col. 0102D] Berti, *Ecclesiastical History, or Historical Dissertations*, vol. II, Dissertation I, *On the Roman Bishops of the Third Century*, §18, p. 330, Augsburg edition, 1761, octavo] following Baronius, [Note: [Col. 0102D] Baronius, at the year 272, §21] believes that Dionysius first departed to the majority—that is, died—in the year 271. He is led by Baronius’s [Col. 0103A] argument that the second synod against Paul of Samosata was celebrated at Antioch only after the death of the emperor Claudius, who died and was succeeded by Aurelian. We, however, judge that the synod’s letter to Dionysius of Rome and the other bishops was written in 269, while Claudius was still alive. [Note: [Col. 0103C] See Pagius’s observations in his *Critique*, at the year 271, no. 2 ff.; and Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, vol. I, p. 1090 ff.]

**Eulogy of Saint Dionysius of Rome.**—The praise of singular learning which Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 7, attributes to our Dionysius on the strength of Dionysius of Alexandria’s testimony—calling him “a most learned and altogether admirable man”—is sufficiently, indeed abundantly, secured for him by the fragment of his writings that survives. In it, while striving to overthrow Sabellian inventions, he simultaneously anticipates and overturns the tenets of Arius and of the tritheists, and sets forth in advance the faith which the Council of Nicaea would later [Col. 0103B] follow and decree that all others should follow.

In this matter he also revealed his prudence, because he neither said nor did anything harsh against Dionysius of Alexandria, however gravely the latter had been accused. Without concealing the gravity of the charge brought against him, he nevertheless waited patiently until that bishop had given ample satisfaction and entirely dispelled the suspicion cast upon him.

Moreover, Saint Basil calls [Note: [Col. 0103C] “We ask for nothing entirely new, but for what was customary in former times among the other blessed men beloved by God, and especially among you [the Roman pontiffs; Saint Basil is addressing Pope Damasus]. For we know from the succession of memory, having questioned our fathers and also learned from letters still preserved among us, that Dionysius, that most blessed bishop who shone among you both for orthodox faith and for his other virtues, visited our church of Caesarea, consoled our fathers by letters, and sent men to redeem the brethren held captive” (Saint Basil, Letter 70, otherwise 220, p. 164, Paris Benedictine edition). The highly learned editor Julien Garnier observes on this passage of Saint Basil that what Basil relates concerning the beneficence of the Roman bishops toward other churches is confirmed by the testimonies both of Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 23, and of Dionysius of Alexandria, book VII, chapter 5, and even of Eusebius himself, who declares in book IV, chapter 23, that this custom was preserved by the Romans during the final persecution. The calamity mentioned by Basil occurred under Gallienus, when the Scythians devastated Cappadocia and the neighboring regions, as Sozomen testifies in book II, chapter 6. From such great evils God drew this great good: Christians carried away by the barbarians captured their victors and brought them to Christ. Hence Basil says in Letter 164 that the first seeds of piety among the Goths sprang from Cappadocia through the labors of the blessed Eutyches.] our Saint Dionysius most renowned both for his faith and for his other distinguished virtues. He is especially commended by many for his works of charity and mercy toward captives. For he revived Asia Minor, which had been devastated by the barbarians’ first incursions, not only by his letters but also with money, by which very many Christians were restored to freedom. [Col. 0103C] [Note: [Col. 0103D] Saint Basil also employs the authority of Saint Dionysius of Rome to confirm the principal truths of religion in *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter XXIX, no. 72, p. 60, Paris Benedictine edition.]

Saint Athanasius numbers him among [Col. 0104A] those Fathers whose doctrine—and indeed whose phrases and words—the Council of Nicaea employed. [Note: [Col. 0104C] Athanasius, *Letter on the Synods*, no. 43, Padua edition, vol. I, part II, p. 605 A–B; and Montfaucon’s Paris edition, [Col. 0104D] vol. I, p. 737.]

## ARTICLE II. On the Writings of Saint Dionysius, Roman Pontiff, Both Genuine and Spurious, and Especially on the Fragment of the Letter to Saint Dionysius of Alexandria—or, Rather, Against the Sabellians

To the great loss of the Church, nearly all the writings of Saint Dionysius, bishop of Rome, have perished through the ravages of time. He published a book *On the Twofold Heresy*. [Note: [Col. 0104D] Basnage, *Political-Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. II, at the year 259, no. VIII, p. 400, cites no author or ancient monument for this book of Dionysius *On the Twofold Heresy*. Perhaps this book is nothing other than the letter to Dionysius of Alexandria in which Dionysius of Rome refuted the twofold heresy of the tritheists and of Sabellius.]

Athanasius mentioned the writings of this great man more than once: “From the works of Dionysius of Rome,” he says, [Note: [Col. 0104D] Athanasius, *Works*, vol. I, Paris edition, 1627, pp. 558 and 918; Padua edition, 1777, vol. II, part I, *On the Opinion of Dionysius*, p. 198 ff., no. 13, and part II, no. 43, p. 605], “against those who assert that the Son of God is a work, it is shown that the heresy of the Arians was condemned by everyone long ago.” He also cites the words of Dionysius in the book *On the Decrees* [Col. 0104B] *of the Council of Nicaea*, vol. I, p. 275 of the old edition, and in the Paris Benedictine edition, §26, p. 231 ff.

**Notice of Letter I of Pope Dionysius to Dionysius of Alexandria. Its cause and occasion are set forth from Athanasius.**—When Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, heard that the heresy of Sabellius, which confounded the persons of the Holy Trinity, had arisen at Ptolemais, a city of the Pentapolis, he hastened to inform Pope Xystus of it and to send him certain letters that he had composed on that account. According to Eusebius, Dionysius of Alexandria wrote “letters against Sabellius to Ammon, bishop of Berenice in the Pentapolis: one to Telesphorus, another to Euphranor, and yet another to Ammon and Euporus.” Certain persons, however, were moved particularly by his letters to Ammon and Euphranor [Col. 0104C] and denounced him to the Roman pontiff. Dionysius of Rome regarded the matter as sufficiently grave that, after first holding a council, he did not delay in admonishing the Alexandrian.

Athanasius sets forth the cause and occasion of that letter in the *Letter on the Opinion of Dionysius*, no. 13, as follows: [Note: [Col. 0104D] Athanasius, *On the Opinion of Dionysius*, no. 13, p. 198 ff., cited Padua edition.] “When Dionysius of Alexandria, moved by zeal for religion, had written against the heresy of Sabellius to Ammon and Euphranor, certain brethren from the Church, men indeed of sound doctrine, but without asking him [Dionysius of Alexandria] why he had written in that manner, went to Rome [Note: [Col. 0104D] Julius I afterward, in Letter I, no. 22, reproached the Eusebians because they had condemned Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, without his knowledge, in these words: “But why, especially concerning the Church of Alexandria, was nothing written to us? Do you not know that this is the custom: that first there should be correspondence with us, and that from here what is just should be decided?” We do not know whether this custom was older than the time of Dionysius. Here, at any rate, Athanasius does not blame the accusers of the bishop of Alexandria for bringing his name before the Roman pontiff, but because they had neglected first to inquire what his true opinion was.] and [Col. 0105A] accused him before Dionysius, the bishop of Rome who bore the same name.”

For, as Athanasius also reports in the same work, no. 4, Dionysius had said in the aforementioned letter, no. 4: “The Son of God is a work and a created thing, not proper to the Father by nature but foreign to him in substance, as a vine-grower is to the vine and a shipwright to a boat; for since he is a created thing, he did not exist before he was made.”

“When he heard these things,” says Athanasius, no. 13, “Dionysius, bishop of Rome, wrote [Note: [Col. 0105C] The Greek reads: ἐπέστειλε δὲ καὶ Διονυσιῷ δηλῶσαι περὶ ὧν εἰρήκασι κατ᾽ αὐτοῦ, “and he also wrote to Dionysius to explain the matters they had spoken against him.” Pearson conjectures that δηλώσας, “making known,” should be read in place of δηλῶσαι, “to explain”; accordingly, Dionysius of Rome wrote to the Alexandrian in order to make known to him what had been said against him. This conjecture agrees sufficiently well with Athanasius’s narrative and seems all the more probable because Dionysius of Alexandria did not know what had been alleged against him and could have learned it only from writings sent from the City. But because Dionysius of Rome took care to inform the Alexandrian of the allegations against him for no other reason than that he might explain his mind and opinion concerning them, there is no danger whichever reading one follows. What Dionysius of Alexandria subsequently did—refuting the charges brought against him—in some measure confirms the common reading], both against the followers of Sabellius and against those who held the opinion [of which Dionysius of Alexandria was believed to be an advocate] for which Arius was afterward expelled from the Church. He also wrote [Note: [Col. 0105D] Athanasius, *On the Synods*, no. 43, vol. I, part II, p. 605, Padua edition] a letter to Dionysius [of Alexandria], so that he might explain the matters concerning which he had been accused by those men [the brethren mentioned above].”

[Col. 0105B] Concerning the same letter, Athanasius recorded the following in *On the Synods*, no. 43: “When certain persons had reported to the bishop of Rome concerning the Alexandrian that he affirmed the Son to be a created thing and not consubstantial with the Father, the Roman Synod [Note: [Col. 0105D] From this is confirmed the practice, constant down to the present, whereby the Roman pontiffs customarily pronounced nothing concerning matters reported to them without a synod. Athanasius also confirms the custom whereby the same pontiffs were accustomed to send and make known synodal decrees in their own names, since he attributes to Pope Dionysius the letter sent from the synod to the bishop of Alexandria.] took the matter with indignation; and the bishop of Rome, in a letter written to his namesake, made known to him the opinion of everyone concerning the matter.”

### The Words of Athanasius Examined. Baronius’s Opinion, Distinguishing the Work of Dionysius of Rome against Sabellius from His Letter Addressed to Dionysius of Alexandria, Is Preferable

Baronius judges that the work mentioned by Athanasius in the first place must be distinguished from the *Letter to Dionysius* which he mentions immediately afterward; others have doubts on this matter.

> **Note [Col. 0105D].** See Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. IV, p. 142, *sur S. Denis, pape*, Brussels ed.; Ceillier, *Hist. génér.*, vol. III, p. 327, note a.

But Baronius’s opinion [Col. 0106A] seems preferable to us. First, Athanasius designates the work of Dionysius of Rome against the Sabellians by the simple verb ἐγράψε, “he wrote”; and then adds, ἐπέστειλε δὲ καὶ Διονυσίῳ, “and he also sent a letter to Dionysius.” Here the particles δὲ καί indicate something distinct; the verb ἐπέστειλε properly means “he wrote a letter”; and the following word Διονυσίῳ indicates the person to whom that letter was addressed.

The very requirements of propriety—and indeed of fairness—also demanded that the Roman pontiff make known by a private letter, rather than by a public work, both the accusations made against the prelate of so great a see as Alexandria, a man of such merit and so closely bound in friendship to the Roman bishops as Dionysius was, and Rome’s judgment concerning them. Moreover, in the work against the Sabellians Dionysius of Rome addresses not one particular bishop but several. [Col. 0106B]

Finally, the opening of the fragment appended below does not at all fit either Dionysius of Rome or Dionysius of Alexandria individually. There Dionysius of Rome first states that certain persons introduce three Godheads, and immediately adds: “For I hear that some of those who proclaim and teach the divine Word among you are instructors in this opinion.” He would not have reproved his friend with vague and general words of this kind; rather, he sent him particular propositions excerpted from his writings and admonished him to explain them.

### Account of Letter II—or of the Fragment of Pope Dionysius’s Work against the Sabellians

> **Note [Col. 0106D].** In our edition this letter has been made the first, since the letter presented as the first by Dom Coustant is itself discussed at the beginning of Article II here.

We owe to Athanasius an important fragment of the letter written by Dionysius of Rome against the Sabellians. Athanasius cites it as follows in his *Letter on the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea*, no. 26:

> **Note [Col. 0106D].** Athanasius, vol. I, part I, *De Decret. Nic.*, no. 26, p. 182, Padua ed.

[Col. 0106C] “Dionysius also, Bishop of Rome, writing against the Sabellians, expresses his indignation in these words against those who dare to say such things …”—namely, that the Word was made and created.

This is an excerpt from the work which the same Athanasius, in his *Letter on the Opinion of Dionysius*, no. 13, says was written against the Sabellians and against those who held the opinion for which Arius was afterward expelled from the Church. We demonstrated in the account of the preceding letter that this work must be distinguished from the letter of the same pontiff sent at the same time to Dionysius of Alexandria.

In this work Dionysius refutes the doctrine of the tritheists, toward which the Alexandrian prelate seemed favorably disposed, in such a way that he simultaneously rebuts the opinion of the Sabellians, which that same bishop was opposing. This method of proceeding provided the Church’s defenders with an important lesson [Col. 0106D]: that they must contend against heresies with such prudence that they not only guard against contrary errors but also defeat both at once.

The style of this fragment has the character of a letter composed in the manner of a rather extensive treatise and disputation. Dionysius of Alexandria, writing to Xystus, teaches that the letters which he had sent against the nascent heresy of Sabellius were of this kind. It was probably sent either to the churches of the Pentapolis, where Sabellius’s heresy had arisen and spread; to the Alexandrian church itself, over which Dionysius presided; or to his accusers. [Col. 0107A] Together with the preceding letter, it appears to belong to the beginning of Dionysius’s pontificate, since its occasion was supplied by the accusation arising from the letters sent to Pope Xystus.

Thus far the very learned Father Coustant, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Maur, vol. I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 272 ff.

### Editions of This Fragment of Dionysius’s Letter

Father Mansi caused the fragment of Dionysius’s letter or work against the Sabellians, edited by Coustant, to be reprinted in vol. I of his *Amplissima collectio conciliorum*, together with the observations of that most learned Benedictine monk, pp. 1009–1016.

The indefatigable Gallandi likewise inserted the fragment into vol. III of his library of the ancient holy Fathers and, in editing it, resolved to follow the distinguished Coustant. [Col. 0107B]

Christian Friedrich Rösler presents the cited fragment of Dionysius in Greek alone, adding certain observations in the vernacular language. He took it from Athanasius’s *Letter on the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea*, according to Montfaucon’s Paris edition of 1698, in his *Bibliotheca veterum patrum*, part II, Leipzig, 1777, octavo, pp. 381–384.

Finally, the indefatigable Father Dominicus Schramm caused the aforesaid fragment to be reprinted in Latin alone in vol. VI of his *Analysis Sanctorum Patrum*, printed at Augsburg in 1784, pp. 415–417.

### The Lost Letter of Dionysius of Rome to the Caesareans in Cappadocia

Saint Basil, cited a little above, testifies that Pope Dionysius wrote a letter to the church of Caesarea in Cappadocia [Col. 0107C] to console it concerning the incursion of the barbarians by which it had been afflicted. Basil had seen with his own eyes its autograph (αὐτόγραφον), preserved with great care in that Church’s archive; but we lament that it was lost in later times.

Two letters adorned with the illustrious name of Pope Dionysius circulate. The first, addressed to the prefect Urbanus, exhorts him “wisely to arrange and judge the matters entrusted to him.” It is dated the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the consulship of the most illustrious Aurelian and Bassus.

The latter is written to Bishop Severus concerning parish churches: each is to be assigned to an individual presbyter, and no one is to encroach upon the boundaries or jurisdiction of another’s parish. It is dated the fifth day before the Ides of September, in the consulship of the most illustrious Claudius and Paternus.

Both their style, unworthy of so learned a man as Dionysius, [Col. 0107D] and their inscriptions demonstrate that the letters were falsely attributed to him. Aurelian and Bassus entered office in the year 271, by which time Dionysius had already died. Dionysius could indeed have written a letter during the consulship of Claudius and Paternus; nevertheless, he did not write it to Severus. This is clear because the author who masqueraded under his name did not know that Paternus’s colleague Claudius was the emperor—a fact that could not have been unknown to the real Dionysius.

Leo’s Letter XXIV supplied the impostor with the opening of the letter: “Long ago and from the beginning we received such confidence from blessed Peter, the prince of the apostles.” He also inserted passages from Gregory the Great. Consult book IV, Letter 52, and book VII, Letter 113, of the letters of Saint Gregory the Great.

Both letters appear in Mansi’s most recent *Collection of Councils*, vol. I, pp. 1004–1008. [Col. 0108A] They may be seen convicted of falsity in Blondel’s *Pseudo-Isidore*, p. 349 ff., and in Schelstrate, *Antiquitates illustratae*, vol. II.

### Other Works Wrongly Ascribed to Saint Dionysius

Louis Jacob of Saint-Charles,

> **Note [Col. 0108D].** Ludov. Jac., *Bibliothec. pontific.*, book II, p. 62,

ascribes various minor works to Dionysius of Rome. On the authority, namely, of the fragments of the fictitious Liutprand of Pavia, he assigns him a book *On the Situation of the World*. But the error is sufficiently evident when a book on the situation of the world is attributed to him, since Dionysius Periegetes, the pagan whose distinguished Greek poem on this subject survives, differs from Bishop Dionysius as widely as heaven from earth and by more than a century in time.

Similarly, it cannot be accepted that the same author attributes to Pope Dionysius “A Commentary against the Arian Heresies,” since in his time the name of the heretic Arius had not yet been heard; it first began to be known in the year 316. [Col. 0108B]

Nor did Pope Dionysius write “against Paul of Samosata,” as the aforesaid writer thinks; it was Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria, who did so, as I see Cave has already correctly noted.

> **Note [Col. 0108D].** Cave, *Historia litteraria*, vol. I, p. 133.

## ARTICLE III  
### The Doctrine of Saint Dionysius, Roman Pontiff

### § I.—On the Most Holy Trinity

#### The Tritheists and Marcionites Are Refuted by Saint Dionysius. The Three Divine Persons Are Inseparable Because of the Unity of Nature

Just as the Marcionites in some fashion established three Gods by partitioning the holy Unity into three alien substances entirely separated from one another, so Saint Dionysius calls this doctrine vain and diabolical:

> “For Marcion’s vain doctrine,” he says, “is … diabolical.”

> **Note [Col. 0108D].** Dionysius of Rome, in Saint Athanasius, *On the Decrees of the Council*, vol. I, pp. 231–232, Montfaucon ed., Paris, 1698; and vol. I, part I, p. 182, no. 26, Padua ed., 1777; likewise in Mansi, *Concilia*, vol. I, p. 1011 ff.; and Gallandi, *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. III, p. 538 ff.

He then adds that this is not the doctrine of Christ’s true disciples or of those who assent to the Savior’s precepts:

> “For these”—that is, Christians—“are not unaware that the Trinity is proclaimed in divine Scripture; but neither the Old nor the New Testament teaches that there are three Gods.”

“Therefore,” the holy Pontiff concludes, “the wondrous and divine Unity must not be separated into three Godheads.”

A little earlier the same Saint Dionysius teaches that the divine Word is united to God the Father, that the Holy Spirit remains and dwells in God, and that the Trinity is brought back and gathered into the one almighty God, the Lord of all:

> “For it is necessary that the divine Word be united to the God of all, and that the Holy Spirit remain and dwell in God, [Col. 0108D] and, finally, that the divine Trinity be brought back and gathered into one … almighty God of all.”

These words show most plainly that the one God is distinguished into three Persons; consequently, according to the doctrine cited, the three divine Persons are of the same essence and the same nature.

The cited words [Col. 0109A] of Saint Dionysius could be twisted into confirmation of the Sabellians’ error only by a wholly perverse interpretation, since it is certain and beyond doubt that he was no less exact when discussing the Trinity of Persons than when discussing the Unity of nature:

> “Thus,” he says, “the proclamation of the divine Trinity and of the holy Monarchy will be preserved entire.”

> **Note [Col. 0109C].** Dionysius of Rome, passage cited, at the end of the fragment against Sabellius.

He then calls the doctrine of Sabellius impious, since Sabellius said that the Father was the Son, and conversely:

> “His—Sabellius’s—impiety consists in this: that he says the Son is the Father, and conversely.”

No doubt, therefore, can arise concerning this holy pontiff’s orthodox faith in regard to the mystery of the most holy Trinity.

### § II.—On the Consubstantiality of the Word

#### The Word Is Consubstantial with the Father

[Col. 0109B] By the same reasoning, no one can doubt this pope’s Catholic faith concerning the consubstantiality of the Word, since one who transmits Catholic doctrine concerning the Trinity simultaneously transmits Catholic doctrine concerning the consubstantiality of the Word.

But so that we may perceive the proposed truth ever more clearly, Saint Dionysius proves what he had taught above concerning the Son’s union with the Father by two sayings of Saint John the Evangelist, taken from his Gospel:

> “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30);

and:

> “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10).

These are the considerations by which Saint Dionysius was moved to write that the Word is united to the Father by an inseparable union, so that these two Persons are one and the same Godhead.

> **Note [Col. 0109C].** Dionysius of Rome, fragment against the Sabellians, no. 2, p. 1013, in Mansi.

#### The Word Was Not Formed or Made, but Begotten from All Eternity

[Col. 0109C] Once this truth is established, no one can assert without fault that the Son of God was made or created,

> “since divine Scripture testifies that he was begotten … and not formed and made.”

> **Note [Cols. 0109C–0110C].** In harmony with these words, the Council of Nicaea professes in its creed that the Son was “begotten, not made.” Athanasius, moreover, in his *Letter on the Opinion of Dionysius of Alexandria*, no. 13, rightly proves from this that this profession was not devised for the first time by that council. “For since,” he says, “Dionysius, Bishop of Rome, also wrote against those who say that the Son of God is a created and made thing, it is perfectly clear that the Arian heresy of Christ’s enemies was not now for the first time, but long ago, condemned by all with anathema.”

“Therefore, it is not a slight but the greatest impiety [Col. 0110A] to say that the Lord is in some fashion made by hand. For if the Son was made, there was a time when he was not.”

> **Note [Col. 0110C].** Here too Dionysius condemns in advance Arius’s celebrated declaration and anticipates the Council of Nicaea, which at the end of its creed anathematized τοὺς λέγοντας· Ἦν ποτε, ὅτε οὐκ ἦν, “those who say, ‘There was once a time when he was not.’” Thus, when Valens cried out in the church at Rimini, “If anyone says, ‘There was a time when the Son was not,’ let him be anathema,” then, Jerome says in the *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, “all the bishops and the whole Church together received Valens’s declaration with applause and a kind of exultation,” naturally supposing that by these words he was entirely renouncing the Arian heresy, which maintained that the Son was created.

“But he always existed, if indeed he is, as he himself declares, in the Father, and if Christ is the Word, Wisdom, and Power.”

Surely no one can defend the eternity, divinity, and consubstantiality of the Word with greater precision. Catholics can only find it exceedingly gratifying to behold these fundamental truths of religion asserted clearly and with the utmost force by Fathers of the Church who flourished before the rise of the Arian heresy.

#### The Divinity of the Holy Spirit

Moreover, Saint Dionysius, Bishop of Rome, also defended in particular the divinity of the Holy Spirit, since Saint Basil the Great cites his authority to prove that divinity against those who attacked it.

> **Note [Col. 0110C].** Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 29, no. 72.

Basil, however, quotes no text of Saint Dionysius of Rome. Yet the same divinity of the Holy Spirit may be inferred from two passages of the often-cited fragment against the Sabellians. First, he says that “the Holy Spirit remains and dwells in God.”

> **Note [Col. 0110C].** Dionysius of Rome, fragment against the Sabellians, no. 1, in Mansi, p. 1012.

He then lays down:

> “One must believe in God the Father almighty, and in Christ Jesus his Son, and in the Holy Spirit.”

> **Note [Col. 0110C].** Ibid., no. 3, p. 1016.

Finally, it should be observed that Saint Dionysius of Rome interprets the passage Proverbs 8:22, ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησέ με, “in the beginning he made me,” in this manner:

> “The Lord made me ruler; he set me over … his works.”

> **Note [Col. 0110D].** Ibid., no. 2.

In this manner of interpretation he departed entirely [Col. 0110C] from the customary exposition of this passage among the ancient Fathers.

[Col. 0109]

## LETTER I, OR A FRAGMENT OF POPE DIONYSIUS’S WORK AGAINST THE SABELLIANS

> **Note [Col. 0110].** The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.

[Col. 0109D]

### 1

It would now be proper to argue against those who destroy the “Monarchy,” that most august proclamation of the Church of God, by dividing and cutting it into three particular powers, separate [Col. 0111A] hypostases, and three Godheads (*Athanasius, Letter on the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea*, no. 26).

> **Note [Cols. 0111B–0114C]: “Monarchy.”** At the very end of the fragment below, the author has τὸ ἅγιον κήρυγμα τῆς μοναρχίας, “the holy proclamation of the Monarchy.” It is well known that Theophilus of Antioch used the word Τριάς, “Trinity,” even in the Church’s second century. Before Theophilus, Athenagoras had written the following in his *Embassy for the Christians*: “Who, then, would not be at a loss on hearing that people who speak of God the Father, God the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and who demonstrate both their power in their UNION and their DISTINCTION in order, are called atheists?” (§10). See also the parallel statements in §11. **ROUTH.**
>
> **“Hypostases.”** Our Dionysius here, together with the entire school of secular writers—to use the words of Jerome’s Letter 10 to Damasus, no. 4—understands *hypostasis* as nothing other than *ousia*, and, together with the whole Church, abhors the sacrilegious proclamation of three substances, insofar as the Latin word *substantia* corresponds to the Greek οὐσία.
>
> Even by that time, however, it had become customary in the Church, at least in Alexandria, for the term ὑπόστασις to be employed to signify a person. This may certainly be inferred from Origen’s words in *On John*, tractate 2: “We believe that the Father, the Son, and the Spirit are three persons (τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις).” Likewise, in book VIII *Against Celsus*, he affirms that the Father and the Son are “two realities in hypostasis” (δύο τῇ ὑποστάσει πράγματα).
>
> Dionysius of Alexandria himself says, in the fragments of the third letter below, no. 15, εἰ τῷ τρεῖς εἶναι τὰς ὑποστάσεις, “if by the fact that the hypostases are three,” in the same sense.
>
> Hence there is a suspicion that what Dionysius of Rome now discusses is directed against Dionysius of Alexandria. The latter, because he proclaimed in God τρεῖς ὑποστάσεις, “three hypostases,” began to hear himself described as an advocate of three divine substances or essences and three Godheads, and as a destroyer of the Monarchy. At this point the source is syntactically defective—apparently lacking a governing verb—and continues: “that he might clear himself of this opinion.” Indeed, Basil, Letter 41, teaches that he had previously posited a diversity of *ousia*, or essence, among the divine Persons.
>
> But when it became established that the Greeks understood “person” by the term ὑπόστασις, the Latins also did not hesitate to adapt the word *substantia* to the same sense, as is especially clear concerning Augustine, *On the Trinity*, book VII, ch. 5, no. 9. **COUSTANT.**
>
> More accurate than these remarks, however—even though the terms οὐσία and φύσις were similarly customarily used by the ancients for ὑπόστασις, a subsisting person, as I noted above from Photius—is what the distinguished Maran later wrote concerning Dionysius of Rome’s position in his preface to vol. III of the *Works of Saint Basil the Great*:
>
> “Saint Basil, in *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 29, cites that statement of Dionysius: εἰ τῷ τρεῖς εἶναι τὰς ὑποστάσεις, etc., ‘if by the fact that the hypostases are three,’ etc. Dionysius of Alexandria therefore admits three hypostases, but refutes those who contended that, because they are three, they are divided, as though there were not one essence in the three.
>
> “This must be carefully observed so that we may understand how undeservedly two distinguished writers, Petavius, book IV *On the Trinity*, ch. 1, and Peter Coustant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 290, suppose Dionysius of Rome to be in conflict with Dionysius of Alexandria.”
>
> That is, in connection with the fragment of Dionysius of Alexandria, as I have already noted. Add to these writers Tillemont, *Mémoires ecclésiastiques*, *Life of Dionysius of Alexandria*, §15, at the end.
>
> “There is certainly no difference of opinion between the two Dionysii. Both censure divided hypostases; nor can one hypostasis be imputed to the Roman Dionysius, since he says precisely the same thing as the Alexandrian. Rather, from the fact that he refutes three divided hypostases, it follows with some clarity that he would have found nothing to censure if one essence in three hypostases had been admitted” (p. VI).
>
> Maran is correct here, unless I am mistaken. There is, moreover, another fragment of Dionysius of Alexandria adduced by Basil the Great in the same place, consisting of these few words: Θειοτάτη γὰρ διὰ τοῦτο· μετὰ τὴν Μονάδα καὶ ἡ Τριάς, “For on this account the Trinity also, after the Monad, is most divine”; below, p. 128, no. 15. **ROUTH.**
>
> **“Saying that the Son is the Father, and conversely.”** The Arians in Athanasius, *On the Councils*, no. 16, express this heresy of Sabellius in a single word, saying that he proclaimed a ὑιοπάτωρ, “Son-Father.” Hilary, *On the Trinity*, book IV, no. 12, translates it into Latin: “He said that the one who is the Father is himself the Son.” **COUSTANT.**
>
> **“Marcion’s doctrine.”** Marcion’s heresy, in which he imagined two principles, one of good and the other of evil, is better known. Cyril of Jerusalem, however, although in Catechesis 6, no. 16, he notes this doctrine of his and says that Marcion established different Gods—one good and the other just, that is, one harsh and severe in punishment, the other kind and inclined to mercy—nevertheless says beforehand concerning Marcion’s disciples in Catechesis 16, no. 4: “We proclaim three Gods; let the Marcionites be silent.” Then, in no. 7, he adds concerning the master himself: “The most impious Marcion was the first to assert that there are three Gods.”
>
> Epiphanius, *Heresy* 42, no. 3, explains in what manner this was asserted by him. But a certain Rhodo, nearly contemporary with Marcion, first writes in Eusebius, book VII, ch. 13: “Others, just like Marcion, introduce two principles”; and a little later adds: “Still others, as though driven from these positions by a storm into something worse, posited not merely two but three natures; their leader and standard-bearer is Syneros.”
>
> Augustine, however, in *On Heresies*, ch. 22, summarizes the positions of Epiphanius and Eusebius as follows: “Although Epiphanius says that he—Marcion—asserted three principles, the good, the just, and the evil, Eusebius writes that a certain Syneros, not Marcion, was the author of the three principles and natures.” **COUSTANT.**

For I have heard that some of those who proclaim and teach the divine Word among you are instructors in this opinion. They are diametrically opposed, so to speak, to the opinion of Sabellius. For he blasphemes by saying that the Son himself is the Father, and conversely; but they in some fashion proclaim three Gods by dividing the holy Unity into three alien hypostases entirely separated from one another.

For it is necessary that the divine Word be united to the God of all, and the Holy Spirit must remain and dwell in God; and therefore it is altogether necessary that the divine Trinity be summed up and gathered into one, as though into a kind of summit—by which I mean the almighty God of all.

For the doctrine of foolish Marcion, which cuts and divides the Monarchy [Col. 0111B] into three principles, [Col. 0113A] is assuredly diabolical, and not the doctrine of Christ’s true disciples or of those who are pleased with the Savior’s teachings.

> **Note [Cols. 0113B–0114C]: “Into three Principles.”** Above, indeed, Dionysius distinguishes the three divine Persons in such a way that he appears to attribute the designation “God of all” to the Father. But presently, when explaining his meaning, he openly teaches that the divine Trinity converges in the unity of nature, by which it comes about that there is one God of all.
>
> Since this is so, and since the same holy pontiff rejects three principles, he sufficiently indicates what he means by “Monarchy”: namely, that the Church believes in a single principle of all things. Nor does Tertullian differ from this position when he says in *Against Praxeas*, ch. 3: “I know that Monarchy signifies nothing other than a singular and unique dominion.” Dominion is unique precisely because the principle is unique.
>
> It should be noted how Tertullian reconciles and harmonizes the proclamation of the Monarchy with faith in the Trinity. Praxeas had reproached him for destroying the Monarchy. Tertullian replied:
>
> “Since I derive the Son from no other source, but from the SUBSTANCE OF THE FATHER, doing nothing without the Father’s will and having received all power from the Father, how can I be destroying from the faith the Monarchy which, delivered by the Father to the Son, I preserve in the Son? Let this be said by me also concerning the third degree, because I consider the Spirit to be from no other source than from the Father through the Son. See, therefore, whether it is not rather you who destroy the Monarchy.”
>
> From this passage it is clear that both Tertullian and Praxeas charged one another with destroying the Monarchy, while both were persuaded that the faith was utterly destroyed by anyone who destroyed the Monarchy.
>
> A recent writer is therefore gravely mistaken when, from a misunderstood passage of *Against Praxeas*, ch. 10, in which Praxeas and his followers are called “most empty-headed Monarchians,” he maintains that the defenders of the Monarchy are to be regarded in precisely the same way as heretics, and that Tertullian so regarded them.
>
> Tertullian does not blame them for professing to maintain the Monarchy, but because, after casting aside the true faith concerning it, they profess it in the emptiest fashion. This is much as one might properly call people who arrogate the Christian name to themselves while leading a life alien to Christian morals and faith “false and most empty-headed Christians,” without thereby being thought to blame or reject the Christian name. Likewise, one who censures false prophets does not condemn the Prophets.
>
> But enough on this subject here. Certainly, for our Dionysius the Monarchy is the most august proclamation of the Church of God. A book by Justin Martyr, *On the Monarchy of God*, cited by Eusebius and Jerome, survives. Irenaeus too, according to the same Eusebius, *History*, book V, ch. 20, had entitled his letter to Florinus *On the Monarchy*.
>
> Tatian, in his *Oration against the Greeks*, among the many considerations by which he teaches that the truth of the divine Scriptures was proven and indubitable to him, also recalls that they established “the single monarchy of the universe” (τῶν ὅλων τὸ μοναρχικόν).
>
> Not even Apelles, Marcion’s disciple, dared deny this doctrine of the Monarchy, or of the single principle, in the conversation which he held with Rhodo. For, as Rhodo himself testifies in Eusebius, book V, ch. 13, Apelles said that there was one principle, just as our religion also teaches.
>
> Athanasius similarly proves in *Oration IV against the Arians*, no. 1, that Monarchy properly exists in God. And in the *Oration against the Greeks*, he teaches with sufficient clarity in the following words that anyone who denies the Monarchy must be regarded as atheistic: Ὥσπερ ἐλέγομεν τὴν πολυθεότητα ἀθεότητα, οὕτως ἀνάγκη τὴν πολυαρχίαν ἀναρχίαν εἶναι, “Just as we said that polytheism is atheism, so it necessarily follows that a plurality of principles is absence of principle.”
>
> Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 18, sets out to prove how we profess Persons in God without allowing the proper doctrine of the Monarchy to fall away: καὶ τὸ εὐσεβὲς δόγμα τῆς μοναρχίας οὐ διαπίπτει, “and the pious doctrine of the Monarchy does not fall away.”
>
> The same doctrine is found in Gregory of Nazianzus, both in Oration 23 and in Oration 37, where he resolves the following objection: εἰ Θεός, καὶ Θεός, καὶ Θεός, πῶς οὐ τρεῖς θεοί, ἢ πῶς οὐ πολυαρχία τὸ δοξαζόμενον; “If God, and God, and God, how are there not three Gods? Or how is that which is glorified not a plurality of principles?”
>
> Gregory of Nyssa likewise admonishes in his *Catechetical Oration*, ch. 3, that the dominion of the Monarchy must not be sundered by being cut into different Godheads.
>
> Cyril of Jerusalem agrees with these statements in Catechesis 6. Epiphanius says in *Heresy* 62, no. 3: “In proclaiming the Monarchy we do not go astray, but proclaim one Trinity.”
>
> I pass over the testimonies of others concerning this matter. To those cited I add only Augustine’s statement in *Against Faustus*, book XX, ch. 19: “Let Faustus, therefore—or rather those who delight in his writings—learn that we do not derive our belief in the Monarchy from the Gentiles,” etc. **COUSTANT.**
>
> **“That the Lord was made.”** Valens seemed to the Fathers of the Council of Rimini to have professed the faith opposed to this blasphemy—which Arius afterward impiously defended—and openly to have rejected the Arian doctrine when, according to Jerome, *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, he craftily cried out: “If anyone says that the Son of God is a creature as the other creatures are, let him be anathema.”
>
> But when Valens and his associates began to boast that he had not denied that the Son was a creature, but only that he was like the other creatures, the bishops who had been deceived by this fraud and were being represented as heretics without their knowledge rightly protested that they had suspected nothing evil in his declaration of faith:
>
> “We supposed,” they said, “that the meaning agreed with the words; nor did we fear that in the Church of God, where there is simplicity and pure confession, one thing was concealed in the heart and another uttered by the lips.” **COUSTANT.**
>
> **“That he was begotten.”** In harmony with these words, the Council of Nicaea professes in its creed that the Son was “begotten, not made.” Athanasius, moreover, in his *Letter on the Opinion of Dionysius*, no. 13, rightly proves from this that this profession was not devised for the first time by that council:
>
> “For since,” he says, “Dionysius, Bishop of Rome, also wrote against those who say that the Son of God is a created and made thing, it is perfectly clear that the heresy of the Arians, Christ’s enemies, was not now for the first time, but long ago, condemned by all with anathema.” **COUSTANT.**

For Christ’s disciples know well that the Trinity is indeed proclaimed in divine Scripture, but neither the Old nor the New Testament teaches that there are three Gods.

### 2

No less blameworthy are those who suppose that the Son is a work and imagine that the Lord was made like one of the things that truly came into being, when the divine oracles testify that he was begotten, as is fitting and proper, and not fashioned or made.

It is therefore not a slight but the greatest impiety to say that the Lord is in some fashion made by hand. For if the Son was made, [Col. 0115A] there was a time when he was not.

> **Note [Cols. 0115D–0116D]: “A time when he was not.”** Here too Dionysius condemns in advance Arius’s celebrated declaration and anticipates the Council of Nicaea, which at the end of its creed anathematized τοὺς λέγοντας· Ἦν ποτε, ὅτε οὐκ ἦν, “those who say, ‘There was once a time when he was not.’”
>
> Thus, when Valens cried out in the church at Rimini, “If anyone says, ‘There was a time when the Son was not,’ let him be anathema,” then, Jerome says in his *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, “all the bishops and the whole Church together received Valens’s declaration with applause and a kind of exultation,” naturally supposing that by these words he was entirely renouncing the Arian heresy, which maintained that the Son was created. **COUSTANT.**
>
> In the same passage it is clear from Jerome that Valens himself also uttered many other propositions—and assented when Claudius uttered them—which I would find it difficult to reconcile with doctrines alien to the Catholic faith. For example, Valens himself says: “If anyone says that the Son is from things that did not exist and not from God the Father, let him be anathema.”
>
> Valens also assented when Claudius declared: “If anyone says that the Son of God indeed existed before all ages, but not before absolutely all time, thereby placing something before him, let him be anathema.” **ROUTH.**

But he always existed, if indeed, as he himself declares, he is in the Father (John 14:12). And if Christ is the Word, Wisdom, and Power—for the divine Scriptures teach that Christ is these things, as you yourselves know—these are assuredly powers of God.

Consequently, if the Son was made, there was a time when these did not exist; and therefore there was a time when God was without them—which is utterly absurd.

But why should I discuss these matters at greater length among you, men full of the Spirit and thoroughly understanding the absurdities that follow from the opinion which asserts that the Son was made? The leaders of this opinion seem to me not to have attended to these things at all, and for that reason to have strayed completely from the truth when they explain otherwise than divine and prophetic Scripture intends the passage:

> “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways” (Proverbs 8:22).

[Col. 0115B] For, as you know, the verb “created” does not have only one meaning. In this passage “created” means the same as “set me over the works made by him”—made, I say, through the Son himself. Here “created” must not be understood as equivalent to “made,” for “to make” and “to create” differ from one another.

Moses says in the great Song of Deuteronomy:

> “Did not that very Father of yours possess you, and make you, and create you?” (Deuteronomy 32:6).

Thus someone might also rightly rebuke them:

> O rash and reckless men! Is the firstborn of all creation (Colossians 1:15), begotten from the womb before the morning star (Psalm 109:3), a thing that was made—the one who, as Wisdom says, was begotten before all the hills (Proverbs 8:28)?

Finally, anyone who reads the divine oracles will find that in many passages he is said to have been begotten, but that the Son is nowhere said to have been made. From these texts those who dare to call his divine and inexplicable generation a making are openly convicted [Col. 0115C] of holding a false opinion concerning the Lord’s generation.

### 3

The wondrous and divine Unity must therefore neither be separated into three Godheads, nor the dignity and supreme greatness of the Lord diminished by the term “making.” Rather, one must believe in God the Father almighty, in Christ Jesus his Son, and in the Holy Spirit.

The Word, moreover, must be united to the God of all, for he says:

> “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30);

and:

> “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John 14:10).

Thus the divine Trinity and the holy proclamation of the Monarchy will be preserved entire.

[Col. 0110D]

Next, I might properly speak against those who divide,

> **Note [Cols. 0109D–0110D].** The Royal Codex reads καταδιαιροῦντας, “subdivide.” Montfaucon. On the authority of this codex, I have admitted into the text the article which was absent from the printed editions. **ROUTH.**

cut apart, and abolish the most venerable proclamation of the Church of God—the Monarchy—by dividing it into three particular powers, apportioned hypostases, and three Godheads. [Col. 0112A]

For I have learned that some of those among you who catechize and teach the divine Word are guides of this way of thinking. They are diametrically opposed, so to speak, to the opinion of Sabellius. For he blasphemes by saying that the Son himself is the Father, and conversely; but they in some fashion proclaim three Gods by dividing the holy Monad into three alien hypostases entirely separated from one another.

For it is necessary that the divine Word be united to the God of all; and the Holy Spirit must abide and dwell in God. It is therefore altogether necessary that the divine Trinity be summed up and gathered into one, as though into a kind of summit—by which I mean the almighty God of all.

For the doctrine of foolish Marcion, involving a cutting and division of the Monarchy into three principles, [Col. 0112B]

> **Note [Col. 0111].** Perhaps the text should read τομὴ καὶ διαίρεσις, “a cutting and division,” with the verb ἐστί, “is,” understood after δίδαγμα, “doctrine.” **ROUTH.**

is a diabolical teaching, and not the teaching of Christ’s true disciples or of those who are pleased with the Savior’s lessons. [Col. 0114A] For they know clearly that a Trinity is proclaimed by divine Scripture, but that neither the Old nor the New Testament proclaims three Gods.

Nor would one blame any less those who believe that the Son is a work [Note: [Col. 0113B] Reg.: “those who believed.” Basil: “those who believe.” And in another hand: variant, “those who believed.” [Col. 0114B] Montfaucon.], and who suppose that the Lord came into being as though he were one of the things that truly came into being; for the divine oracles testify concerning him to the generation appropriate and fitting to him, and not to some fashioning and making. It is therefore no ordinary blasphemy, but indeed the greatest, to say that the Lord was in some manner made by hand. For if the Son came into being, there was a time when he did not exist [Col. 0116A]; but he always existed, since [Note: [Col. 0115D] Thus Reg., as the sense also requires. The editions and other manuscripts have “but if.” Montf.] he is in the Father, as he himself says. And if Christ is Word and Wisdom and Power—for the divine Scriptures say that Christ is these things, as you know—and these are powers of God, then, if the Son came into being, there was a time when these did not exist. There was therefore a time when God was without them; but this is utterly absurd.

And why should I discuss these matters with you at greater length—you who are Spirit-bearing men and clearly understand the absurdities that arise from saying that the Son is a work? Those who introduced this opinion seem to me not to have attended to those absurdities [Note: [Col. 0115D] Thus Reg. The others and the editions omit “this.” Shortly afterward Reg. has ᾗ instead of ἢ. Montfaucon. But in this latter place ταύτῃ should apparently be changed to αὐτῇ. Routh.], and for that reason to have strayed altogether from the truth by understanding otherwise than the divine and prophetic Scripture intends [Note: [Col. 0115D] Perhaps αὐτῇ. Routh.] the words, “The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways.” For, as you know, “created” does not have only one meaning. Here “created” must be understood [Col. 0116B] in the sense of “appointed over the works brought into being by him”—works brought into being through the Son himself. “Created” cannot here be used in the sense of “made” [Note: [Col. 0115D] Thus the manuscripts and the Commelin edition. Moreover, ἐπί here has the same meaning [Col. 0116D] as ἀντί, the reading of the earlier edition. Shortly afterward we restored τὸ κτίσαι, absent from the Commelin edition, from the Regius and Basiliensis manuscripts; Nannius and Ambrosius Camaldulensis also read this expression. Montfaucon. But τὸ κτίσαι also appears in the earlier Paris edition. Routh.]; for “to create” differs from “to make.” Moses says in the great song in Deuteronomy: “Is not this your father who acquired you, and made you, and created you?”

Someone might also say to them: “O reckless men! Is the firstborn of all creation a work—the one begotten from the womb before the morning star, the one who says as Wisdom, ‘Before all the hills he begets me’?” In many places in the divine oracles one may find it said that the Son was begotten, but not that he came into being. By these passages those who entertain false notions [Note: [Col. 0116D] Reg. and Basil.: “false things.” Montfaucon.] about the Lord’s generation are manifestly refuted—those who dare to call his divine and ineffable generation a making.

[Col. 0116C] Therefore one must neither divide the wonderful and divine Monad into three Godheads, nor diminish [Note: [Col. 0116D] Should κολούειν, “curtail,” perhaps be read instead of κωλύειν, “hinder”? Routh.] through making the dignity and surpassing greatness of the Lord. Rather, one must believe in God the Father almighty, and in Christ Jesus his Son, and in the Holy Spirit; and the Word must be united with the God of all. For he says, “I and the Father are one,” and, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” In this way both the divine Trinity and the holy proclamation of the monarchy will be preserved.

These passages are extant in St. Athanasius, *Letter concerning the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea*, [Col. 0116D] chapter XXVI, p. 231, Benedictine edition.

[LETTERS]

[Col. 0117]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FRAGMENTS BELOW

### I

The work from which the fragments below were copied is frequently cited by Athanasius in *On the Councils*, no. 44; the *Letter concerning the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea*, no. 25; and the *Letter concerning the Opinion of Dionysius*. The same work is mentioned by Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 29, and by Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 79. These two Doctors, however, describe it differently. Jerome teaches that it was divided into four books, whereas Basil presents certain words from it as taken from a second letter to Dionysius, his namesake.

In fact, Athanasius establishes both that it was divided into books and that the designation “letter” properly belonged to it. In the same *Letter concerning the Opinion of Dionysius*, no. 13, he says: “Dionysius immediately published books in order to clear himself, which he entitled *Refutation and Defense*”; and in no. 14 he speaks of the same writing as follows: “He entitled his letter *Refutation and Defense*.” It was therefore a letter divided into four books, and consequently one of those which Dionysius describes as having been dictated by him at greater length and in the manner of a treatise—διδασκαλικώτερον ὑφηγούμενος, “expounding it in a more didactic fashion” (*Letter* 1, to Xystus).

It was not sent by him immediately after he was informed of the accusation against him. For, lest he appear to neglect the charge if he delayed too long in replying to the Roman pontiff, he first sent him a letter that Dionysius himself mentions below, no. 6, while addressing Dionysius of Rome, in these words: καὶ σοι δι᾿ ἄλλης ἐπιστολῆς ἔγραψα, “and I wrote to you in another letter.” Consequently Basil did not improperly call it both a *Letter* and a second letter to Dionysius, his namesake.

At the same time, it is also a *Refutation and Defense*: a refutation of Dionysius’s adversaries and accusers, who are exposed and refuted in this work; and a defense of Dionysius himself, who endeavors in it to clear himself of the errors charged against him. Since he accomplished this successfully, Athanasius rightly charges the Arians with shameless calumny because they did not blush to pass off as Dionysius’s opinions things that he had openly and explicitly rejected.

### II

This defense of Dionysius is of all the greater importance because it gives us an example of what the other Fathers before the Council of Nicaea would have done—those from whom certain statements escaped that appeared akin to Arian impiety—if a similar necessity had compelled them to explain their meaning more clearly. From this one is readily led to believe that not one of them would have failed, like Dionysius, to condemn that same unbelief.

Athanasius, no. 14, explains in the following manner which portions of this work he thought should be copied and which omitted:

> “Omitting, because of the length of the books, very many of his statements in which he examines the matters brought into question, draws conclusions from the arguments presented, refutes his adversaries by questioning them, or accuses his detractors, I shall present only those passages that appear necessary for dispelling the charges.”

In the passages he does copy, however, he does not preserve the order of the books. Instead, as the matters under discussion required, he presents now one fragment and then another from the first book, afterward another from the second, then again a fourth from the first, to which he joins another from the fourth. But since the purpose of our undertaking is to collect accurately the remains of this work, as one written to the Roman pontiff, it seemed preferable to present the individual fragments in the order maintained among the books from which they were copied.

Finally, if we consider the sequence of events preceding this work, we may in some measure determine the period in which it was composed. Several letters of Dionysius of Alexandria against the Sabellians, published while Xystus was pontiff, gave occasion for the accusation against him. Moved by them, certain Catholics, without the knowledge of the Alexandrian prelate himself, hurried to Rome and reported to the Roman pontiff what displeased them in his writings. Dionysius of Rome immediately admonished Dionysius of Alexandria. The latter sought to satisfy him first by a brief letter and soon afterward by a longer one, “immediately,” as Athanasius remarks. Accordingly, nothing prevents us from assigning this defense of Dionysius to the year 262. The learned Tillemont likewise thinks that it may be referred to the end of that year. **COUSTANT.**

[Col. 0117]

## LETTER II OF DIONYSIUS, BISHOP OF ALEXANDRIA, TO DIONYSIUS OF ROME

### Or, Fragments of the Work Entitled *Refutation and Defense*

[Note: [Col. 0118] The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### From the First Book

1. For there was no time when God was not Father.

And in what follows, Athanasius says, he professes that Christ always exists, since he is Word and Wisdom and Power.

2. God did not first exist without having begotten these things and afterward beget the Son; rather, the Son has his being not from himself but from the Father.

A little later he says concerning the Son himself:

3. Since he is the radiance of eternal light, he himself is necessarily eternal. For since the light always exists, it is evident that the radiance always exists. Light is understood to be light precisely because it shines, and it is impossible for light not to give light. Let us return again to examples. If the sun exists, its radiance also exists, and so does day. If none of these exists, it is far from possible that the sun should be present. If the sun were eternal, day too would never cease. As things now stand, however—for such is not the case—day begins when the sun begins and ends when it ends. But God is eternal light, which neither began nor will ever cease. Therefore the eternal radiance shines before him and coexists with him; existing without beginning and always begotten, it shines forth before him. It is the Wisdom who says: “I was she in whom he rejoiced, and I delighted daily before his face at all times” (Prov. VIII, 30).

A little afterward he continues his discourse concerning the same subject as follows:

4. Since the Father is eternal, the Son also is eternal, light from light. For where there is a begetter, there is also offspring. If there is no offspring, how and of whom can one be a begetter? But both exist, and they always exist. Since, therefore, God is light, Christ is radiance. And since God is spirit—“God,” he says, “is spirit” (John IV, 24)—Christ is correspondingly also called vapor: “For he is,” it says, “a vapor of the power of God” (Wis. VII, 25).

Again he says:

5. But the Son alone, always coexisting with the Father and filled with him who is, himself also is, since he is from the Father (from Athanasius, ibid., no. 17).

[Col. 0118]

1. For there was no time when God was not Father.

“And he knows this,” Athanasius says immediately afterward, “in the following passages: that Christ always exists, since he is Word and Wisdom and Power.”

2. For God did not first exist barren of these things and afterward beget a child; rather, the Son has his being not from himself but from the Father.

“And a little later,” Athanasius continues, “he again says concerning the same Son”:

3. Since he is the radiance of eternal light, he himself is necessarily eternal. For since the light always exists, it is evident that the radiance always exists. Indeed, that it is light is apprehended by its shining, and light cannot exist without giving light. Let us return again to examples. If the sun exists, day exists; if none of these things exists, it is far from possible that the sun should be present. If, then, the sun were eternal, day too would be unceasing. But as things now stand—for it is not eternal—day began when the sun began and ceases when it ceases. God, however, [Col. 0120B] is eternal light, which neither began nor will ever cease. Therefore the eternal radiance lies before him and coexists with him; it is without beginning and always begotten, shining forth before him. This is the Wisdom who says: “I was she in whom he rejoiced; and I delighted daily before his face at all times.”

“And again, a little afterward,” Athanasius says, “he adds concerning the same subject”:

4. Since, therefore, the Father is eternal, the Son also is eternal, being light from light. For when there is a begetter, there is also offspring; but if there were no offspring, how and of whom could one be a begetter? Yet both exist, and they always exist.

Then, Athanasius says, he again adds the following:

Since God is light, Christ is radiance. And since God is spirit—“God,” he says, “is spirit”—Christ is correspondingly also called vapor: “For he is,” it says, “a vapor of the power of God.”

“And from the second book,” Athanasius says, “he again says”:

5. But the Son alone, always coexisting with the Father and filled with him who is, himself also is, since he is from the Father.

These passages are cited in an uninterrupted sequence by St. Athanasius in the *Letter concerning the Opinion of Dionysius*, no. 15, p. 253, Benedictine edition.

### From the Same First Book

[Note: [Col. 0119D] Athanasius explains as follows the purpose for which Dionysius introduced the ensuing statements: “In the first book he again refutes his accusers, who falsely claimed that he had said the Son was one of the things made and was by no means consubstantial with the Father, in these words.” It is therefore evident that the charges made against the Alexandrian Dionysius had been refuted in the preceding letter of Dionysius of Rome. For those who suppose that the Lord was made like one of the things made are refuted in that letter, no. 2.

It should also be noted that the faith by which we believe the Father and the Son to be of one substance, or consubstantial, was always so firmly implanted in the minds of the faithful that, when the Alexandrian bishop was thought to deny it, Catholic men immediately denounced him to the Roman pontiff, and he did not delay in demonstrating himself entirely alien to such an opinion. Nor is this less worthy of observation: so many years before the Council of Nicaea, the faithful indignantly refused to tolerate the rejection not only of the reality signified by the word ὁμοούσιον, “consubstantial,” but in some manner of the word itself. **COUSTANT.**]

[Col. 0119]

[Col. 0119D] 6. Nevertheless, when I said that certain created things and products were to be considered, I presented examples of such things only in passing, as less suitable, when I said: “Neither is a plant the same thing as the farmer, nor a vessel the same thing as the shipwright” (from Athanasius, ibid., no. 18). I then dwelt at greater length upon examples that were adequate and more closely fitted to the nature of the subject, and explained more fully those that were truer, devising various arguments, which [Col. 0121A] I also set forth to you in another letter. In these I exposed as false the charge they bring against me, namely that I do not affirm Christ to be consubstantial with God.

For although I say that I have nowhere found or read this term in the sacred Scriptures, the other arguments I immediately added—which they have suppressed—are in no way inconsistent with this understanding. For I presented human offspring as an example, since it is certainly of the same kind as its begetter; and I said that parents are in reality distinguished from their children only in that the parents are not themselves the children, or else it would necessarily follow that there were neither parents nor children.

Because of present circumstances, however, I do not have the letter in my possession, as I said before. Otherwise I would have sent you the very words I wrote at that time—indeed, a copy of the entire letter—and I shall send it whenever I am able to obtain it. I know and remember, moreover, that I added several analogies drawn from things related by nature. I said that a plant growing either from a seed or from a root is distinct from that from which it sprang, although it is altogether of the same nature as it. Similarly, a river flowing from a spring assumes another form and name: the spring is not called a river, nor the river a spring, but both exist; the spring is, as it were, the father, while the river is water from the spring.

But they pretend, as though blind, not to see that these and similar things were written. Instead they attempt from a distance to strike me with two unconnected little expressions, as though with stones, failing to observe that examples which are unlike—and sometimes even contrary—often shed light upon matters that are unknown [Col. 0121C] and require interpretation if they are to be understood.

[Note: [Col. 0121C]

**“I set forth to you in another letter.”** Athanasius, both in the *Letter concerning the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea*, no. 25, and in *On the Councils*, no. 44, contents himself with briefly summarizing the earlier words of this testimony and begins his quotation with: Καὶ δι᾿ ἄλλης ἐπιστολῆς ἔγραψα, ἐν οἷς ἤλεγξα κτλ., “And I wrote in another letter, in which I refuted,” etc.; there the word σοι, “to you,” is absent. But since it is absent here from no ancient manuscript, whether written or printed, and since it is safer to judge the integrity of a sentence from passages in which it is presented more fully and completely than from those in which it is less complete or abbreviated, there is no reason to doubt that a previously written letter to Dionysius of Rome is mentioned here—especially since Basil calls this one the second. **COUSTANT.**

**“Are in no way inconsistent.”** That is: they demonstrate that I hold concerning Christ the same thing that those who proclaim him consubstantial understand. **COUSTANT.**

**“The letter, however.”** Some letter of Dionysius appears to be mentioned here from which the occasion for accusing him was taken. From it, as he soon complains, his opponents had brought forward his statement that he had nowhere read the expression “of one substance,” or *homoousios*, in the Scriptures, while suppressing the arguments [Col. 0122C] or examples by which he affirmed the reality signified by that expression. Accordingly, it seems that one should agree with Tillemont, who believes that the letter to Ammonius [Col. 0122D] and Euphranor is indicated here.

From this one may also infer that Dionysius composed this work in a troubled period, when he did not even have his own writings in his possession. For although Valerian’s persecution ceased when that emperor was defeated and captured in the year 260, Dionysius’s own festal or paschal letters testify that the city of Alexandria remained unsettled until the year 262. **COUSTANT.**

**“Two unconnected little expressions.”** In attempting to demonstrate the distinction between the Father and the Son, Dionysius had used the insufficiently precise analogies of a plant and a farmer, and of a vessel and its builder. **COUSTANT.**

**“The mind, however.”** That is, the thought which is sent outward by means of the voice. This same analogy, by which Dionysius here illustrates at once the unity and the distinction of the Father and the Son, afterward became familiar to Augustine in explaining the mystery of the incarnate Word. Thus he says in Sermon 119, new edition, no. 7: “Just as my word was uttered to your perception and did not depart from my heart, so that Word was uttered to our perception and did not depart from his Father. My word was with me and proceeded into sound; the Word of God was with the Father and proceeded into flesh.” **COUSTANT.**]

[Col. 0120D] 6. Nevertheless, when I said that certain created things were to be considered, I presented examples of such things in passing, as less useful. For I said that neither the plant was the same as the farmer—one should supply “the same”—nor the vessel the same as the shipwright. Then I dwelt upon more adequate and more closely fitting examples, and treated at greater length those that were truer, devising various additional arguments. These I also wrote to you in another letter; in them I exposed as false the charge they bring against me, namely that I do not say Christ is *homoousios* (ὁμοούσιον), “consubstantial,” with God.
