For even though I say that I have not found this term or read it anywhere in the holy Scriptures, nevertheless my other ensuing arguments, which they have suppressed, are in no way discordant with this understanding. For I presented human offspring as an example, clearly because it is of the same kind. I said that parents are necessarily distinct from their children only because they themselves are not the children; otherwise it would necessarily follow that there were neither parents nor children.

As I said before, because of present circumstances I cannot produce the letter. Otherwise I would have sent you the very words I wrote then—indeed, a copy of the whole letter; and I shall do so whenever I can obtain it. I know and remember that I added several analogies drawn from kindred things. For I also said that a plant growing from a seed or from a root is distinct from that from which it sprouted, yet is altogether of the same nature as it. I said also that a river flowing from a spring assumes a different form and name: the spring is not called a river, nor the river a spring, but both exist; the spring is, as it were, the father, while the river [the Greek text erroneously reads “father”] is water from the spring.

But they pretend not even to see that these and similar things were written, acting as though blind. With two unconnected little expressions, as though with stones, they attempt to strike me from a distance, not knowing that, in the case of matters unknown and requiring explanation, not merely dissimilar but often even contrary examples serve to disclose the things being investigated.

(These passages are adduced by St. Athanasius in the *Letter concerning the Opinion of Dionysius*, no. XVIII, p. 255.)

They do not understand that the Father, insofar as he is Father, cannot be alienated from the Son; for that name is manifestly the ground of cohesion and conjunction. Nor can the Son be separated from the Father, for the designation “Father” signifies communion. How, then, could I, who use such names, suppose that these are separated from one another and divided altogether?

### Around the Middle of the Work

[Note: [Col. 0127D] Basil preserved for us the three following fragments. Presenting the last of them first, he prefaces it by saying that he is giving the very words with which Dionysius of Alexandria, in his second letter to his namesake, concluded his discourse περὶ ἐλέγχου καὶ ἀπολογίας, “concerning refutation and defense”—that is, completed and closed the work with which we are concerned. Then, appending what we place first, he cites it as follows: “The same author also speaks against the Sabellians around the middle of the writing.”

It is therefore evident that the work which Athanasius notes was divided into four books was by no means divided by Basil into four letters; otherwise that Doctor would have cited the conclusion of the entire work from the fourth, not the second, letter. By indicating that the testimony of Dionysius given below occurred around the middle of “the writing,” he also confirms that he regarded the whole work as one writing or one letter, not as several.

It is more important to observe the distinction with which the two men named Dionysius employ the same word ὑπόστασις. By this word the Roman understands substance or essence, *ousia*, and on that account refuses to admit three hypostases in God. For the Alexandrian, however, *hypostasis* means nothing other than what the Latins call *persona*, “person.” Accordingly, he proclaims three hypostases in a Catholic sense. For to Dionysius and others who opposed Sabellius, the proclamation of three persons seemed insufficient, because Sabellius too readily acknowledged three *personae* in God, of the kind that one and the same man can represent in the theater.

Basil of Caesarea, however, in Letter 41 to Maximus the Philosopher, writes that Dionysius at one time posited in God not only ἑτερότητα ὑποστάσεως, “difference of hypostasis,” but also οὐσίας διαφοράν, “difference of essence”; that he likewise at first rejected ὁμοούσιον, “consubstantial,” and afterward admitted it in the defense sent to his namesake. “Hence,” he says, “he was found variable and inconsistent in his writings.” Baronius thinks, however, that Basil would have spoken differently if he had then read Athanasius’s *Letter concerning the Opinion of Dionysius*. **COUSTANT.**]

## LETTER IV

Eusebius, *History*, book VII, chapter 9, mentions a letter of Dionysius of Alexandria to Dionysius of Rome concerning Lucian; nothing else about this letter is known to us from any other source. The Lucian in question, about whom—or on whose behalf—the letter was written, is believed to have been Cyprian’s successor, whom Optatus mentions in book I in these words:

> “The altar stood in its place, upon which the peaceable bishops of former times offered sacrifice: Cyprian, Lucian, and the others.”

A learned man therefore reasonably believes that the letter was written so that peace might be preserved inviolate between the successors of Stephen and Cyprian. For just as God had earlier raised up at the same time both Victor, to defend the apostolic tradition concerning the date of Easter, and Irenaeus, to establish peace among the churches at variance, so too it was not without God’s providence that Stephen [Col. 0129B] presided over the Roman Church and Dionysius over the Alexandrian Church at the same time: the former was to be the defender of the divine tradition concerning baptism, while the latter was to mediate ecclesiastical peace. The conjectures concerning this letter require that it be assigned to the beginning of the pontificate of Dionysius of Rome.

## V

The letter of Dionysius, bishop of Rome, to the Church of Caesarea in Cappadocia is lost. Basil, bishop of that same city, testifies that it was preserved at Caesarea and was famous within the memory of their ancestors (Basil, Letter 220; Damasus, Letter 2, no. 3). Together with this letter, by which he consoled the afflicted Caesareans, Dionysius sent delegates to secure the release of their brethren who had been redeemed from captivity.

It is conjectured that this captivity of the Caesareans occurred after the year 260, in which Valerian was defeated and captured by the Persians. From that point onward the neighboring Roman provinces began to lie open to barbarian incursions. Philostorgius, book II, chapter 5, relates specifically that around the year 264 the Scythians—that is, the Goths—raided the cities of Cappadocia and carried many captives away with them.

## VI

In Eusebius, book VII, chapter 30, one reads a letter of the Council of Antioch addressed “to Dionysius of Rome, Maximus, who had succeeded Dionysius of Alexandria, and all fellow bishops, presbyters, and deacons everywhere throughout the world, and to the universal Catholic Church.” It announces that Paul of Samosata had been deposed from the episcopate and Domnus appointed in his place.

Eusebius transcribes almost the entire letter; but since, apart from its address, it contains nothing specifically pertaining either to Dionysius or to his see, it is sufficient for us merely to mention it. Eusebius, book VII, chapter 29, says that the Council of Antioch from which it was written was held “in the time of the emperor Aurelian,” who succeeded Claudius II in the year 270, around the month of April. It is therefore believed to have been composed not long before the death of our Dionysius—or even after his death, but before news of it had reached Antioch.

## VII

Isidore Mercator falsely attributed two letters to Pope Dionysius, one to Urban the prefect and the other to Severus the bishop. They are to be published in their proper place with the remaining productions of that same fabricator.

[Col. 0129]

## ROMAN COUNCIL IN THE CASE OF DIONYSIUS OF ALEXANDRIA, ACCUSED OF SABELLIANISM

### Held in the Year 263, during the Pontificate of Dionysius

[Note: [Col. 0129D] The year is uncertain.]

[NOTE]

[Col. 0129D]

The Roman Council. This council was celebrated at Rome under the authority of Pope Dionysius, in the year of the Lord 263, for the following reason. The Sabellian heresy, which had arisen and spread under its author Sabellius, abolished the distinction of persons in the most glorious and adorable Trinity. Dionysius of Alexandria, judging it his duty to refute a Libyan under his jurisdiction, wrote certain treatises against him. In the unfavorable judgment of the people of the Pentapolis, however, these maintained a distinction and diversity not only of persons but also of the divine nature. The people of the Pentapolis therefore accused this same Dionysius of Alexandria before Pope Dionysius, alleging that he did not hold orthodox views concerning the faith and the Trinity. The pontiff summoned this assembly of bishops, cited Dionysius of Alexandria [Col. 0130D] before the council, and ordered him to declare in writing what he believed concerning the nature and ineffable substance of the most glorious Trinity: whether the divine nature subsisting in the three persons was one and the same, or diverse. The bishop of Alexandria, having been accused calumniously, obeyed the pontiff’s decree and sent a letter setting forth his mind and clearing him of the charge brought against him—which is extant in Baronius under this year, no. 34—together with four apologetic books written in his defense, which were to be delivered shortly thereafter. Once these had been received, and after the case of the accusing Pentapolitans and of Dionysius defending himself had been debated long and extensively, following mature prior deliberation Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, was acquitted of the accusers’ calumny [Col. 0131A] by the opinion and judgment of all the bishops who attended this council, as Athanasius testifies in the treatise he wrote *On the Opinion of Dionysius against the Arians* [Col. 0132A] (see Baronius, year 263, nos. 30–50).

## THE ALEXANDRIAN SYNODS OF DIONYSIUS, FROM THE *SYNODICAL BOOKLET*

[Note: [Col. 0131] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.] (S)*

[Col. 0131]

[Col. 0131A] A divine and holy particular synod, assembled at Alexandria by Dionysius the Confessor, its archbishop, which repudiated Sabellius, the enemy of the divinity.

A divine and holy provincial synod, assembled at Alexandria by the same Dionysius, which condemned and, after their deaths, repudiated Nepotianus, bishop of Egypt, and Cerinthus, because they asserted—and involved [Col. 0131B] very many others in the same error—that Christ’s kingdom would be in the earthly Jerusalem, taught a millennium of years, and furthermore required sacrifices of oxen and the slaughter of sheep as lawful observances.

A divine and holy local synod, assembled at Alexandria by the aforementioned Dionysius, which condemned and repudiated after their deaths Nepotianus, bishop of Egypt, and Cerinthus, as men who made confident assertions [Col. 0132B] and deceived a great many people, maintaining that Christ’s kingdom would be in the earthly Jerusalem and dogmatizing about the millennium; and, in addition, legislating sacrifices of oxen and the slaughter of sheep.

## LETTER I OF POPE DIONYSIUS TO THE PREFECT URBANUS

[Note: [Col. 0131D] This letter and the following are alike regarded as spurious (*νοθεύεται*).]

He exhorts him to love and investigate wisdom, so that he may reasonably and wisely arrange and judge the matters entrusted to him.

[Col. 0131B]

Dionysius the bishop, to Urbanus the prefect, greeting.

The highest good is to love those who love one; and, conversely, there is no worse evil than for citizens to envy their fellow citizens. We therefore give thanks for your charity, because you receive and assist the faithful of Saint Peter well. Hence [Col. 0131C] you should know that you are loved by us and ours, and that we have no small concern for you and yours. We therefore exhort your affection never to delay completing the good work you have begun [Note: [Col. 0132D] The text of the letter is the same as that of Letter 2 of Felix IV, likewise forged.], because it is not the beginning but the end that is praised.

We also exhort you to love and investigate wisdom, so that you may reasonably and wisely arrange and judge the matters entrusted to you, as the Lord says through the prophet: “Be instructed, you who judge the earth” (Ps. 2). “Therefore fear God and keep his commandments” (Eccles. 12). And love him with all your heart, and your neighbor as yourself (Mark 12).

“The Most High God created wisdom in the Holy Spirit” (Eccles. 1), and saw, numbered, and measured her. He poured her out over all his works and over all flesh; [Note: [Col. 0131D] “Flesh according to his gift, and he bestows,” Labbe.] he bestowed her as his gift upon those who love him. The fear of the Lord is glory, [Col. 0131D] gladness, and a crown of rejoicing. The fear of the Lord will delight the heart and give happiness and joy through length of days. It will be well at the end for one who fears God, and on the day of his death he will be blessed. The love of God is honorable wisdom. Those to whom she appears in a vision love him [Note: [Col. 0131D] “her,” Labbe.] in that vision and in the recognition of his mighty works.

The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. It was created together with the faithful in the womb; it walks with chosen women and is recognized among the righteous faithful [Note: [Col. 0131D] “the righteous and faithful,” Labbe.]. The fear of the Lord is the religious observance of knowledge. Religious observance will guard and [Col. 0132B] justify the heart and will give delight and joy. It will be well for the one who fears God, and in the days of his consummation [Note: [Col. 0132D] “consolation,” Labbe.] he will be blessed.

The fullness of wisdom is to fear God, and it brings fullness from her fruits. The crown of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, filling one with peace and the fruit of salvation; and he saw and numbered her. Both knowledge and understanding are gifts of God. Wisdom will apportion herself to prudence [Note: [Col. 0132D] “Wisdom will apportion knowledge and understanding to prudence,” Labbe.], and she exalts the glory of those who hold her fast. The root of wisdom is to fear God, for her branches are long-lived.

In [Col. 0132C] the treasures of wisdom are understanding and the religious observance of knowledge; wisdom, however, is an abomination to sinners. The fear of the Lord drives away sin, for one who is without fear cannot be justified. The wrath of his vehemence is his destruction. A patient man will endure until the appointed time, and afterward joy will be restored to him. Good sense will conceal his words until the appointed time, and the lips of many will recount his understanding.

In the treasures of wisdom is the signification of discipline; but the worship of God is an abomination to the sinner. Son, if you desire wisdom, preserve justice, and God will bestow her upon you; for wisdom and discipline are the fear of the Lord, and what is pleasing to him is faith and meekness, and he will fill his treasures. Do not be stubborn and unbelieving toward the fear of the Lord, and do not approach him with a double heart. Do not be a hypocrite in the sight of men, [Col. 0132D] and do not be ensnared by your lips. Pay heed to them, lest perhaps you fall, place a stumbling block before your soul, bring dishonor upon yourself, and God reveal your hidden things.

Brother, always contend for faith and justice and for the salvation of your soul, and act courageously in assisting the brethren, so that you may receive a reward from the Lord. For it is written: “Son, preserve the proper time and avoid evil” (Eccles. 4). For your soul’s sake, do not be ashamed to speak the truth. For there is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that brings glory and grace. Do not show partiality against [Col. 0133A] yourself, nor accept a lie against your own soul. Do not defer to your neighbor when you fall, and do not withhold a word in a time of salvation. Do not hide your wisdom in its beauty. For wisdom is recognized by the tongue, while understanding, knowledge, and teaching are recognized in words of truth [Note: [Col. 0133D] “in the word of a sensible man,” Labbe.], and steadfastness in works of justice.

Do not contradict the truth in any way, and be ashamed of the falsehood arising from your lack of instruction. Do not be ashamed to confess your sins, and do not subject yourself to a man on account of sin. Do not resist the face of the mighty, nor strive against the current of a river. Struggle for justice on behalf of your soul, and contend for justice even to death; and God will fight your enemies for you and overthrow them mightily.

Do not be hasty in your speech, or useless and negligent in your works. Do not be [Col. 0134A] like a lion in your house, overthrowing your household and oppressing those subject to you. Do not let your hand be extended to receive but closed when it is time to give.

Supported by these authorities of Scripture, always remain so upright, and do not turn aside from the path of truth, that you may continually obtain God’s grace and continually enjoy the friendship of good men. Let your mind depart from the love of this world all the more readily in proportion as it is impelled when called. For we desire to see you when present and, when you are absent, long to converse with you at least by letter. We therefore pray that blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, may happily lead you to his thresholds, so that, in the grace of the Almighty, we may deserve to enjoy your presence.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of February, in the consulship of the most illustrious men Aurelian and Bassus. [Note: [Col. 0133C] The year 271. But if one reads “Fuscus and Bassus,” it will be the year 258.]

## LETTER II OF POPE DIONYSIUS TO BISHOP SEVERUS

Concerning parochial churches: that each should be assigned to an individual presbyter, and that no one should invade the boundaries or jurisdiction of another’s parish.

[Col. 0133]

[Col. 0133B] Dionysius the bishop, to Severus the bishop, greeting.

Long ago and from the beginning (St. Leo, Letter 24), we received such confidence from blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that, with the Lord’s help, we possess authority to assist the universal Church and, by apostolic authority, to correct and amend whatever is harmful. For it was to this end that the providence of the divine [Note: [Col. 0133C] St. Gregory, Letter 52, Book IV, with only slight alterations.] dispensation established distinct ranks and diverse orders: so that, while inferiors showed reverence to their superiors and superiors bestowed affection upon their inferiors, one harmonious fabric might be woven from diversity, and the administration of the respective offices might be properly produced. [Col. 0133C] The whole could not subsist by any other arrangement unless so great an order of distinctions preserved it.

Since creation cannot be governed or live in one and the same equality, the example of the heavenly armies instructs us: since there are angels and archangels, it is evident that they are not equal, but, as you know, one differs from another in power and rank. If, therefore, this distinction is acknowledged to exist among those who are without sin, what man would refuse willingly to submit himself to this arrangement? From this, peace and mutual charity embrace one another in turn, and the sincerity of concord remains firm in reciprocal love pleasing to God; for each office is then performed beneficially [Col. 0134B] when a single superior has been appointed to whom recourse may be had. [Note: [Col. 0133D] “May be cared for,” Labbe.]

Concerning the parochial [Note: [Col. 0134D] “parish,” Labbe.] churches, then, regarding which you wished to consult the Apostolic See—how they should be maintained throughout [Note: [Col. 0133C] Córdoba was subject to Seville in the time of Pope Dionysius; but around the year 790, under the Moors, it was the capital of the Spanish kingdom.] the province of Córdoba and divided among the priests—we think nothing better can be communicated to your charity than that you should follow what we are known recently to have done in the Roman Church.

We assigned individual churches to individual presbyters, divided parishes and cemeteries among them, [Note: [Col. 0133C] “We assigned individual churches to individual presbyters and divided parishes and cemeteries among them.” That this distinction of parishes was first made not by Dionysius but by Evaristus is evident from what we said above in the notes to the life of that same Evaristus, at the words “He established titles.” But when, during the persecution of Valerian, presbyters were driven [Col. 0134C] from the churches by the public edict discussed above in the notes to the life of Sixtus, and Christian assemblies in cemeteries were forbidden, confusion among parishes, churches, and cemeteries undoubtedly resulted. Once peace was granted to the Church and free access to the cemeteries was restored, Dionysius, the Roman pontiff, assigned to others parishes deprived of their presbyters by exile or martyrdom, divided anew those confused during the persecution, distributed them according to due proportion, and once more entrusted cemeteries to individuals, as certain predecessors had done before him (see Baronius, year 270, no. 17).—SEVERINUS BINIUS.] and decreed that each should possess his own jurisdiction. Thus no one is to invade another parish’s lands, boundaries, or jurisdiction; rather, each is to be content with his own boundaries (St. Leo I, Letter 89) and so guard the church and people entrusted to him that, before the tribunal of the eternal Judge, he may render an account for everything [Col. 0134C] entrusted to him and receive for his deeds not condemnation but glory.

It is fitting, dearest brother, that you and all bishops should follow this rule. You are to make what is written to you known to everyone you can, so that this precept may become not particular but universal.

As for the crimes which you say are alleged against bishops, do not permit this in any manner through intermediaries, but only through the very persons who bring the accusations—provided, however, that they themselves appear worthy and irreproachable and have demonstrated in public records that they are entirely free [Note: [Col. 0134C] Council of Arles I, canon 13; *Decretum*, 15, q. 3: “No one except.”] of suspicion and enmity, and that they lead an irreproachable life of faith. For no one who has confessed against himself can be believed concerning another’s crime, since his confession concerning himself and every matter [Col. 0135A] (“profession,” thus in the manuscript) is dangerous and (Hadrian’s Collection 64; and the ancient interpretation of Constitution 12, title I, book IX of the Theodosian Code; *Decretum*, 3, q. 4, “Another’s”) ought not to be admitted.

Similarly, we neither can nor ought to receive an accomplice in another’s error, one who voluntarily departs from the path of his own commitment, or one who obstructs the sacred rules and constitutions of the Fathers. Nor do we permit attacks upon those who believe rightly or obey the ordinances of the holy Fathers, because we judge all those infamous who transgress either their own law or the Christian law, or willingly set aside apostolic or canonical authority.

These things, [Note: [Col. 0135B] St. Gregory, Letter 113, Book VII, whose words and style everyone will immediately recognize.] therefore, dearest brother, which we have bestowed out of affection for the priestly name and honor, we command you, your subjects, and everyone to observe, and to announce and preach [Col. 0135B] to others, so that piety may serve their benefit and love may bear fruit. Accordingly, by rebuking, exhorting, persuading, soothing, and consoling [Note: [Col. 0135B] “Counseling,” Labbe.], let us hasten to benefit everyone we can. Let our tongue be a balm to the good and a goad to the wicked. Let it restrain the timid [Note: [Col. 0135B] “the proud,” Labbe.], soothe the angry, [Col. 0136A] sharpen the sluggish, inflame the idle by exhortation [Note: [Col. 0135B] “exhorts,” Labbe.], persuade those who shrink back, soothe the harsh, and console the desperate, so that, because we are called teachers [Note: [Col. 0136B] “rulers,” Labbe.], we may show the path of salvation to those who walk upon it.

Let us remain vigilant on guard and take anxious care to fortify the entrance against the enemy’s snares. If at any time error has led astray a lost [Note: [Col. 0136B] “through byways,” Labbe.] sheep from the flocks entrusted to us, let us strive with all our effort to recall it to the Lord’s fold, so that from the name of shepherd which we bear we may obtain not punishment but reward.

Since in all these matters the assistance of divine grace is necessary, let us beseech the mercy of almighty God with continual prayers, that he may both give us the will to perform them and grant us the power, and may direct us, with the fruits of good works, along that path of which he testified that he is the Shepherd of shepherds, [Col. 0136B] so that through him, without whom we can do nothing [Note: [Col. 0136B] “We rise to do nothing,” Labbe.], we may be able to accomplish all things.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of September [Note: [Col. 0135B] The year 269.], in the consulship of the most illustrious men Claudius and Paternus. [Note: [Col. 0135B] According to the testimony of Saint Athanasius in his book *On the Decrees of the Nicene Synod*, this same Pope Dionysius wrote an outstanding letter against the Sabellians, in which he admirably confirmed the unity of God in the Trinity and the Trinity in unity. Would that it were now available to refute the new and ancient Arians and Sabellians!]

# THE COMPLETE WORKS OF FELIX I

[Col. 0135]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE CONCERNING SAINT FELIX, ROMAN PONTIFF

[Col. 0135C]

### Felix Becomes Roman Pontiff in the Year 269, on December 28 or 31

Felix, a Roman by birth and son of Constantius, was appointed in Dionysius’s place on December 28, or on the last day of the year 269. [Note: [Col. 0135D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapters 30 and 32; Pagius, at the year 274, no. 2; *L’Art de vérifier les dates*, p. 243; Saccarelli, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. IV, p. 128.] Following in his predecessor’s footsteps, he considered nothing more urgent than to overthrow the heresies rising against the Church.

Accordingly, since the wound inflicted upon catholic truth by Paul of Samosata was fresh, and the scar left by Sabellius’s error had not yet closed, he wrote to Maximus, bishop of Alexandria [Col. 0135D] and successor of Dionysius, concerning the divinity and likewise the humanity of the Son of God, and the two natures distinct in one Person. With this letter, as with a double-edged sword, he struck down both heresies with a single blow: by showing the divine nature in Christ to be indivisibly united to his humanity, he condemned Paul’s heresy; by preaching that the human nature in the same Christ was distinct in its proper character from the divine, and by demonstrating the subsistence of the divine substance in three persons, [Col. 0136C] he refuted Sabellius.

The *Liber Pontificalis* reports that the rite of offering sacrifices above the tombs or memorials of the martyrs [Note: [Col. 0136C] Bona, book I, *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 19, §5. Anastasius writes of Felix I, Supreme Pontiff: “He decreed that Masses should be celebrated above the tombs or memorials of the martyrs,” perhaps because he issued a law on the matter so that it could not be done otherwise. I would judge that the custom of consecrating altars with the relics of martyrs arose from this. Baronius, at the year 275, §2, writes: “The Church claims an institution of this kind from long before the time of Pope Felix.... Felix’s decree, therefore, appears to have established what had previously been observed merely by tradition, without a written canon.” Tillemont also holds this opinion.

Moreover, Bertius notes in his *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. II, p. 333, §19, *Dissertation on the Roman Bishops of the Third Century*, that the words of Revelation, chapter 6, pertain to this very rite: “Therefore I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those slain because of the Word of God.” This is gathered from Ambrose, Letter 22, otherwise 54, who says: “Let the triumphant victims take their places where Christ is the sacrificial victim: he, however, above the altar, who suffered for men; they beneath the altar, who were redeemed by his suffering.” See also Sermon 11 among the Augustinian sermons *On the Saints*, now relegated to the appendix.

The antiquity of this rite is confirmed by the ancient custom of the Roman pontiffs of celebrating the sacred mysteries over the tombs of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Hence Jerome says against Vigilantius, the despiser of the saints’ relics: [Col. 0137A] “The Roman bishop therefore does wrong when, over what according to us are the venerable bones of the dead men Peter and Paul, but according to you are worthless dust, he offers sacrifices to the Lord and regards their tombs as Christ’s altars?” Also relevant are those carefully constructed monuments of the martyrs, set out like chapels or altars, which Paulus Aringhius and Boldetti describe in *On the Cemeteries*, book I, chapter 8.

That this ancient custom—suited and useful not only to the devotion of the faithful but also to the constraints of the nascent Church and the times [Col. 0137B] of persecution—continued in subsequent centuries is demonstrated by the sermons of the Fathers delivered at the tables of the martyrs. Among them is Augustine’s Sermon 113, *On Various Subjects*, entitled *At the Table of Cyprian*, which contains the following:

> As those of you who know Carthage are aware, in the very place where Cyprian’s blood was shed for the name of Christ, a table was constructed for God. It is nevertheless called Cyprian’s table, not because Cyprian ever dined there, but because he was sacrificed there; and because by his own sacrifice he prepared this table—not one at which he might feed or be fed, but one at which sacrifice might be offered to God, to whom he himself was offered.

To this pertain the verses of Saint Paulinus, *Birthday Poem* IX:

> From the windows above they behold all the altars,  
> Beneath which, within, the bodies of saints have their resting place.  
> For apostolic ashes, laid beneath the heavenly table,  
> Amid the sacred libations render up the odor, pleasing to Christ,  
> Of sacred dust that breathes.

Likewise Prudentius, Hymn XI, *On the Crowns* (*περὶ Στεφάνων*):

[Col. 0137C]

> Beneath such coverings Hippolytus’s body is committed,  
> Near where an altar dedicated to God has been placed.  
> That table which bestows the sacrament, and is also set there  
> As the faithful guardian of its own martyr,  
> Preserves his bones in the tomb in hope of the eternal Avenger,  
> And likewise feeds the people of the Tiber with holy fare.

The most learned Cardinal Bona, in the aforementioned chapter 19, and, in their works on Felix I, Emmanuel Schelstrate, Franciscus Pagius, and Antonius Sandinus, observe that from this ancient custom of constructing altars over the memorials of martyrs arose the practice whereby the consecrating bishop deposits sacred relics beneath those same altars.] [Col. 0137A]

After Felix had presided over the catholic Church for five years, he died a martyr during the ninth persecution against the Christians, which Aurelian had begun in the year 272. [Note: [Col. 0137C] Eusebius and Jerome in the *Chronicle*, and likewise Orosius, book VII, chapter 23, call it the ninth persecution. Some, as related by Baronius at the year 273, §4, believe it to be the one which Saint Leo, Sermon 74, chapter 6, makes the eighth and calls famous because of the countless thousands of martyrs. Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 6, says: “Aurelian, although by nature mad and impetuous, and although he remembered Valerian’s captivity, nevertheless forgot his crime and punishment and provoked God’s wrath by cruel deeds.” Thus persecution was not merely threatened by Aurelian, as Dodwell thought, but, as Pagius says and proves at the year 272, §9, was put into execution.

Eusebius therefore writes in book VIII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 4, that the devil, as though lulled to sleep, did not disturb the Church’s peace from the times of Decius and Valerian until Diocletian, “because,” as the same Pagius says, §11, “the persecution stirred up by Aurelian was exceedingly brief, whereas the persecutions of both Decius and Valerian had been prolonged. For the same reason he also makes no mention of Numerian and Maximian Herculius, who nevertheless harassed the Church before Diocletian’s persecution, as is evident from the annals.”]

### When and for How Long Did Felix Occupy the See?

Eusebius relates that Felix governed the Church for five years. [Note: [Col. 0137D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 32: “At that time, after Felix had governed the Roman Church for five years, Eutychian succeeded in his place.” P. 230 of the Turin edition.] [Col. 0138A] The Bucherian Catalogue, the other catalogue belonging to the Queen of Sweden, the Fossatensis manuscript, and the *Liber Pontificalis* agree with him insofar as they teach that he was pontiff in the times “of Claudius and Aurelian, from the consulship of Claudius and Paternus to the consulship of Aurelian II and Capitolinus,” that is, from the year 269 to 274. From this agreement there appears no room to doubt that Felix succeeded Dionysius in the very year in which Dionysius ceased to live, and thus after December 26 of the year 269.

The authority of those same codices, however, does not make it so easy to determine the day or month on which this pope died. For if we consult the Bucherian Catalogue, he held the pontificate for five years, eleven months, and twenty-five days; accordingly, he would have to be said to have remained pontiff not merely until the consulship of Aurelian II and Capitolinus, but until that of Aurelian III and Marcellinus, that is, until the year 275. [Col. 0138B]

In the codex of the Queen of Sweden, the Fossatensis manuscript, and the *Liber Pontificalis*, it is written that he occupied the see for four years, three months, and twenty-five days, and was buried on the third day before the Kalends of June in his own cemetery on the Via Aurelia. Even now, according to the martyrologies of Bede, Ado, Usuard, and the Roman Martyrology, the feast of Saint Felix, Pope and Martyr, is celebrated on the third day before the Kalends of June.

In the Bucherian list of the burials of Roman bishops, [Note: [Col. 0138D] In Schelstrate and Bucherius, *Doctrine of Times*, p. 269.] however, his burial is recorded on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the cemetery of Callistus. That reading could conveniently be brought into agreement with the former, since it can easily happen among copyists that they write “the third day before the Kalends of January” in place of “the third day before the Kalends of June.” But the former cannot likewise be reconciled with the preceding data, since from the end of December, when it is agreed that Felix was ordained, [Col. 0138C] to May 29, only five complete months intervene.

Antonius Pagius thinks that “five years” crept into the Bucherian Catalogue in place of “four years”; and, once this error is corrected from the other books, he holds that “four years, eleven months, and twenty-five days” should be retained. From this catalogue, thus emended, the other books may in turn be corrected, since it is not unusual for copyists to write II in place of X, and consequently “three months” in place of “eleven months.”

The aforementioned Pagius [Note: [Col. 0138D] Pagius, *Critical Commentary*, at the year 274, no. 2.] therefore judges that Felix was ordained on December 28, 269, and died on December 22, 274. The Bucherian list of the burials of the Roman bishops does indeed support him, if we grant that “the third day before the Kalends of January” crept into it in place of “the eleventh day before the Kalends of January,” through an error which, as we have said, was common among copyists. Moreover, the period assigned to Felix’s successor supports the conclusion that Felix lived until [Col. 0138D] December of the year 274.

### Was Saint Felix a Martyr?

This same pope is honored with the title of martyr by the Ephesian synod, Cyril, and others. Nor is it an objection that he is listed by Bucherius in the aforementioned register under the heading “Burials of Bishops,” since under the same heading we also read of Lucius, who was crowned with martyrdom beyond doubt, according to Cyprian’s testimony. Indeed, the most distinguished catalogues, the *Liber Pontificalis*, the Roman Martyrology, and other martyrologies likewise attest Saint Felix’s martyrdom.

Papirius therefore rightly and wisely addresses Felix as follows: [Col. 0139A]

> You were a man distinguished in faith, life, and knowledge, and fit to undergo martyrdom, as the event demonstrated. For under Aurelian—something that cannot be denied—a harsh, savage, and, to use the word of Flavius Vopiscus, bloodthirsty ruler and most bitter enemy of the Christian name, you most steadfastly suffered this for Christ, as befitted the son of Constantius, for that was your father’s name. Thus it is not without reason that Cyril of Alexandria and Vincent of Lérins, who lived under Celestine I, call you a holy martyr. And that other bishop brought you forward as a witness and called you a teacher of the Roman Church, saying: “The opinion of Felix, most holy Roman bishop and martyr, concerning the Incarnation of the Word and the Faith.”

By these words Papirius alludes to Saint Felix’s letter to Maximus, bishop [Col. 0139B] of Alexandria, against the heresies of Sabellius and Paul of Samosata.

### The Encyclical Letter of the Antiochene Synod, Addressed to His Predecessor Dionysius, Was Delivered to Felix

It is known from Eusebius [Note: [Col. 0139D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chapter 30.] that the encyclical letter of the Council of Antioch was addressed by name to Dionysius, bishop of the city of Rome. Through it he was informed that Paul of Samosata had been deposed from the see of Antioch because of his perverse doctrine and depraved conduct, and that Domnus had been appointed in his place.

“We therefore,” says the synod, [Note: [Col. 0139D] In Eusebius, at the passage cited, and in Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, vol. I, p. 1100.] “make this known to you so that you may write to him (Domnus) and receive letters of communion from him. But let this man (Paul) write to Artemas, and let those who follow Artemas communicate with him.”

Since this letter could not be delivered [Col. 0139C] to Dionysius because death intervened, it was at least delivered to his successor, as is known always to have been done subsequently whenever the same thing occurred.

### Emperor Aurelian’s Judgment, Glorious for the Roman See

Meanwhile Paul, although condemned by so celebrated a synod—which Hilary relates to have consisted of eighty bishops [Note: [Col. 0139D] Hilary, *On the Synods*, no. 86.]—long refused to leave the residence of the Church of Antioch and surrender it to Domnus. Consequently, “when Emperor Aurelian was appealed to, he decided the matter most correctly, in Eusebius’s judgment, [Note: [Col. 0139D] Eusebius, at the passage cited.] ordering that the house be delivered to those to whom the prelates of the Christian religion in Italy and the bishop of Rome should write.”

Aurelian could not have been appealed to in this case until, after defeating Zenobia, ruler of the East and Paul’s patron, he recovered Antioch; learned men note that this occurred [Col. 0139D] toward the end of the year 272.

So celebrated a judgment required Felix to assemble as soon as possible with the other bishops of Italy and thereafter to write with them to Domnus, declaring that he ratified his ordination and confirming Paul’s condemnation. There appears no room to doubt that Felix performed what belonged to his office in this matter. His predecessors had always followed the custom of communicating to synods every matter referred to them from the various churches and then giving their replies; and his successors did not cease to imitate that custom for many centuries. Who, then, could believe that Felix neglected a matter for which the judgment of a pagan emperor, so useful to the whole Church and so glorious specifically for the Roman Church, called? [Col. 0140A]

Felix was then given a suitable occasion to defend the divinity of Christ and refute Paul, who, by reviving the impiety of Artemas, was, as the Antiochene Fathers say, declaring war on God—“setting himself against God” (*ἀντιτασσόμενον αὐτὸν τῷ Θεῷ*)—because he denied Christ’s divine nature.

Whatever Felix wrote on that or other occasions has so completely perished that scarcely a small fragment bearing his name has reached us. Yet this is a substantial argument that he became celebrated for his writings: when the Apollinarians sought to support their fabrications with suitable authority, they attempted to attribute various works not to obscure figures but to the more distinguished writers of the Church; they therefore decided to fabricate certain writings under this pope’s name as well. [Col. 0140B]

Nor did the Ephesian Fathers neglect to defend the faith by his authority. Among the testimonies of the Fathers, they expressly cite [Note: [Col. 0140D] Council of Ephesus, act I, p. 512.] a fragment of “Felix, most holy Bishop of Rome and Martyr, to Maximus, Bishop of Alexandria, and the Alexandrian clergy.” Cyril also inserted it into his *Apology against the Easterners*, on Anathema VI, and Marius Mercator [Note: [Col. 0140D] Marius Mercator, pp. 178 and 240, Baluze’s edition.] translated it into Latin.

### The Authenticity of This Fragment Is Established

There are nevertheless some who deny that this fragment belongs to our Felix and think it should be attributed to the Felix whom Emperor Constantius substituted for Liberius. But the argument that led them to an opinion of this kind is altogether weak. They rely solely upon the fact that in the Council of Ephesus, as also in Cyril, this fragment is placed after the testimony of Pope Julius.

If that reasoning were valid, Cyprian would have to be said to be later than Julius and Felix, since he is cited after them in that council; conversely, Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, would have to be regarded as earlier than Felix and Julius, since he is placed before them in the cited work of Cyril.

But Vincent of Lérins [Note: [Col. 0140D] Vincent of Lérins, *Commonitory*, chapter 42.] and Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, in the conference with the Acephali, where they mention the same testimonies, place Felix before Julius, as the chronological order requires. Moreover, everyone sees [Col. 0140D] that it would have been utterly unworthy of so great a synod to use, for establishing the faith, the authority of a man intruded by the Arian faction into the place of a catholic prelate.

Nor does the title “most holy Bishop of Rome and Martyr,” with which Cyril and the Ephesian Fathers adorn Felix, befit such a man. Finally, the very inscription bearing the name of Maximus of Alexandria does not allow us to doubt that Cyril and the Ephesian synod cited the appended fragment as the testimony of Felix I. For the encyclical letter of the Antiochene synod, addressed jointly to Dionysius of Rome and Maximus [Col. 0141A] of Alexandria, teaches us with certainty that this Maximus, Dionysius of Alexandria’s successor, was a contemporary of our Felix.

### Le Quien’s Contrary Opinion Is Refuted

For a different reason, however, Michel Le Quien, in his learned dissertations on John Damascene, judges that nothing now remains to prevent us from denying this fragment not only to our Felix but from ascribing it to heretics. After proving that several letters had been fabricated by the Apollinarians under the name of Pope Julius, he finally adds: [Note: [Col. 0141D] Le Quien, *Dissertations on Damascene*, II, §7.] “Hypatius and Liberatus testify that in a letter circulated under the name of Felix of Rome, one nature was asserted; no room therefore remains for doubt that it proceeded from the same source as the others I have mentioned.”

Yet if the learned man is willing to abide by the words of Hypatius and Liberatus which he himself cites, he will have to admit as Felix’s genuine offspring the testimony produced by the Council of Ephesus and Cyril. For Hypatius distinguishes two testimonies of Felix: one produced by Cyril in the Ephesian synod and elsewhere; the other cited by the Acephali from heretical writings or from works corrupted by heretics. He is content to reject the latter as spurious, while freely and gladly acknowledging the former as genuine. Let us examine his words.

Source/review notes: The supplied source itself is incomplete: although its heading announces four doubtful letters, it includes only three and ends partway through Letter III.; The transition immediately before [Col. 0151A] is corrupt in the supplied Latin (“Quod … mus”); the draft appropriately flags the corruption and reconstructs the evident Romans 5 wording.

### The Words of Hypatius, Bishop of Ephesus, and Liberatus the Deacon, Examined Concerning the Same Fragment

The Acephali, or Severians, at the conference held in the imperial city in 533 by order of the emperor Justinian, charge the holy fathers of the Council of Chalcedon with transgression, [Col. 0141C] “because [Note: [Col. 0141D] Labbe, *Concilia*, vol. IV, p. 1766, and Mansi, *Collectio Conciliorum*, vol. VIII, p. 820.] although the blessed Cyril and the blessed Athanasius, bishops of the city of Alexandria, as well as Felix and Julius of the Roman Church, Gregory the Wonderworker, and Dionysius the Areopagite had defined one nature of God the Word after the union, the Chalcedonian fathers transgressed against them all and presumed to preach two natures after the union.”

Hypatius answers them:

> “Those letters or testimonies of which you speak are false to such a degree that the blessed Cyril was unwilling to mention even one of them, either in the letters he wrote to Nestorius or among the [Note: [Col. 0141D] Understand this as though “testimonies” were to be read immediately afterward.] testimonies that he produced against Nestorius’s blasphemies at the holy Synod of Ephesus, when he had the greatest reason to produce them; nor did he do so in his exposition of the Twelve Chapters against Theodoret and Andrew … nor in his work against the Eastern [Note: [Col. 0141D] That is, in the *Apology against the Easterners*.] [Col. 0141D] council.”

He then defends the authenticity of the testimonies produced by Cyril at the Synod of Ephesus, expressly including that of Felix, and contrasts them with the others in this manner:

> “We also say this: when the blessed Cyril produced at Ephesus the testimonies of twelve glorious fathers against the blasphemies of Nestorius—namely, of Saint Peter, bishop of Alexandria and martyr; Saint Felix, bishop of Rome and martyr; Cyprian, bishop of Carthage and martyr; the blessed Athanasius and the blessed Theophilus, bishops [Col. 0142A] of Alexandria; Julius, bishop of Rome; Ambrose and Basil; Gregory, the other Gregory, Amphilochius of Iconium, and Atticus of Constantinople—he produced no testimony of theirs concerning one nature.”

The Acephali reply: “Why do you suspect us of having falsified them?”—that is, the letters which they produced under the names of Felix and others.

Hypatius answers them in these words:

> “We do not suspect you, but the ancient Apollinarist heretics.”

Then, when those same heretics press the matter and say, “We can show that the blessed Cyril used these testimonies in his books against Diodore and Theodore,” Hypatius answers:

> “Now you are especially rendering those books against Diodore and Theodore doubtful as well, since you say that they were fictitiously produced against dead men who could not refute [Col. 0142B] the falsehood. For if they were produced against the dead, Cyril had much greater reason to produce the same testimonies against Nestorius and those who wrote against his Chapters. But it now appears that heretics falsified the books by adding them.”

Liberatus, for his part, first mentions this conference with the Acephali in chapter 9, and then, in chapter 10, after briefly reviewing what we have just transcribed from it, adds:

> “Cyril wrote four books: three against Diodore and Theodore, as though they were the authors of the Nestorian doctrine, and another book on the Incarnation. These contain corrupted testimonies of the ancient fathers”—

so reads the old Corbie manuscript, whereas the printed editions incorrectly read “uncorrupted”—

> “namely, those of Pope Felix, Dionysius the Areopagite, bishop of the Corinthians, and Gregory [Col. 0142C] surnamed the Wonderworker (*thaumatourgos*, θαυματοῦργος). Against these, the Catholic defenders of the truth answered the Acephali that those books were not Cyril’s, since he did not use against the living Nestorius, or in any of his letters, the testimonies which he is said to have placed in them against dead men. They therefore say that Cyril neither dictated nor published those books.”

Since it is evident that Liberatus is speaking in accordance with Hypatius’s judgment, the testimony of the two must be regarded as a single testimony. From it the conclusion follows that under the name of one and the same Felix both genuine letters and false or adulterated ones were circulated: the genuine letters were cited at the Council of Ephesus, whereas the false or corrupted ones were cited by the Acephali.

### Although Its Integrity May Be Called into Question, Its Teaching Is Nevertheless Catholic. All Doubt Is Removed by the [Col. 0142D] Authority of the Ancients

Nevertheless, I confess that this consideration moves me not to regard as indubitably genuine even the letter of Felix cited at the Council of Ephesus and by Cyril: Cyril, in his letter to Succensus and elsewhere, professes “one incarnate nature of the Word.” For he appears to have been led to such a profession from no other source than his belief that writings forged by the Apollinarists under the names of illustrious men genuinely belonged to those whose names they bore.

Hence Flavian too, in the confession that he sent to the emperor Theodosius, says: “We do not deny [Note: [Col. 0142D] Council of Chalcedon, part [uncertain], ch. V, and Liberatus, ch. 11.] that one must speak of one nature of God the Word, yet incarnate and made human, because from both there is one and the same [Col. 0143A] Lord Jesus Christ.”

However that may be, if that fragment inscribed with the name of Felix is the work of a heretic, it is the work of one who, while striving to appear Catholic, borrowed his expressions from the orthodox faith. Certainly, since Cyril and the Synod of Ephesus judged it not unworthy of the most holy pope and martyr Felix, and since Marius Mercator, Vincent of Lérins, Hypatius, bishop of Ephesus, and other Catholics afterward accepted it as his, so long as nothing else is established, religious scruple forbids us to remove it from his works. Indeed, anyone may safely present as orthodox what is supported by such great authority.

### Moreover, the Heresy of Apollinaris Is Refuted by the Same Fragment

The heresy of Apollinaris, which maintained that Christ assumed a human body deprived of soul or mind, and therefore an imperfect [Col. 0143B] human being, is refuted by the final words of this fragment. Accordingly, even on this ground the suspicion that it might be the production of some Apollinarist would be entirely removed, if the devices and frauds of those heretics were not known.

But, as the learned Michael Le Quien prudently observed, and as Epiphanius [Note: [Col. 0143C] Epiphanius, *Heresies* LXXVII, §23.] recorded, Vitalis, a disciple of Apollinaris, did not hesitate to proclaim that Christ was an altogether perfect man, while nevertheless unhesitatingly denying that Christ had assumed a mind. When asked how he reconciled these claims, he answered:

> “We say that he was a perfect man insofar as we assign divinity to him in place of a mind and add flesh and soul, so that a perfect man exists from flesh, soul, and divinity, the last serving [Col. 0143C] in place of a mind.”

But wickedness lies to itself. For one who believes that Christ lacked the principal part of humanity calls him a perfect man only in mockery.

Thus far Coutant.

Just as Gallandi followed Coutant in editing the other letters of the ancient Roman pontiffs, so too he prepared his edition of this fragment attributed to Felix according to Coutant’s text. He also inserted Coutant’s judgment concerning this fragment and his defense of it into chapter 14 of the prolegomena [Col. 0144A] to volume III of his *Library of the Ancient Fathers*.

Three further letters are assigned to Felix I by Pseudo-Isidore. The first, addressed to Bishop Paternus, contains six chapters:

1. That supporters of enemies be excluded from accusing a bishop.
2. That superiors not be assailed by accusations from inferiors.
3. That no definite judgment be rendered in a doubtful matter.
4. That clerics prosecute their own actions.
5. How primates ought to conduct themselves toward an accused bishop.
6. That judges of the Church not pronounce sentence in the absence of the person whose case is being tried.

It is dated on the Nones of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious Claudius and Aurelian.

The second letter, concerning the authority of the Apostolic See and accused bishops, was sent to all the bishops established throughout Gaul. It is dated on the fifth [Col. 0144B] day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of the most illustrious Claudius and Paternus.

Finally, the third letter, addressed to Bishop Benignus, deals with two matters. It condemns both those who contend that the Son does not see the Father and those who affirm that the Son is less than the Father. It is dated on the Nones of February, in the consulship of the most illustrious Claudius and Paternus.

But this Felix in disguise spreads his deceitful net for the learned in vain. The subscription of the first letter is utterly false. During Felix’s pontificate there was no consulship of Claudius and Aurelian. Its opening—“I have been caused to rejoice exceedingly and to exult in the Lord”—and many of the words that follow are found in Leo’s Letter XXXI.

The subscription of the second exposes the impostor. Dionysius was still alive on the Ides of August in the consulship of Claudius and Paternus. What Felix, then, could at that time have sent his decretal to the [Col. 0144C] bishops of Gaul? Leo also supplied the opening of this decretal in Letter XXXII: “Of good works and spiritual pursuits,” etc. Nor was this counterfeit Felix content with this one theft: he borrowed words from the letter of Peter, bishop of Ravenna, to the presbyter Eutyches. See the *Great Library of the Fathers*, vol. VII, p. 979, and Mansi, *Amplissima Collectio Conciliorum*, vol. I, pp. 1103–1114. Blondel likewise exposes these letters of Felix I as fraudulent in his *Pseudo-Isidore*, p. 353 and following.

[Col. 0143]

# FOUR DOUBTFUL LETTERS OF SAINT FELIX I, POPE AND MARTYR (G, S)

## LETTER I. TO BISHOP PATERNUS

### Concerning the Trials, Accusations, and Defenses of the Sacred Orders

I.—That detractors and supporters of enemies be excluded from accusing a bishop.  
II.—That inferiors not be assailed by accusations from superiors.  
III.—That no definite sentence be rendered in a doubtful matter concerning those [Col. 0145B] who bring any action against a cleric in the province.  
IV.—That clerics prosecute their own actions.  
V.—How primates ought to conduct themselves toward an accused bishop.  
VI.—That judges of the Church not pronounce sentence in the absence of the person whose case is being tried, and that neither the calumny nor the voice of a traitor be heard.

Felix, bishop, to his dearest and most beloved fellow bishop Paternus: greeting in the Lord.

Your Charity’s writings have caused me to rejoice exceedingly (*Saint Leo, Letter* 31) and to exult in the Lord, for they clearly show how greatly you love the Catholic faith and how greatly you detest heretical error. [Col. 0145C] That heresy is indeed exceedingly impious and hostile to the truth of the Gospel: it attempts not merely to injure some particular portion, but to tear up the very foundations of the Christian religion.

For whomever [Note: [Col. 0145D] Labbe reads: “Wherever it creeps.”] it draws to itself, it causes to fall not only into this vice but into many others; and, at the instigation of the ancient enemy himself, they become persecutors not only of the Church but also of her priests. Let us therefore take care with one mind to correct and pursue such people, and let us strive to free the Church, her faithful, and the Lord’s priests from their enemy.

Our almighty Redeemer will grant strength to charity and justice (*Saint Gregory, Letter* 36, book IV). Though we are far apart, he whose workmanship constructed the Church like an ark, with the four sides of the world, with timbers joined together so as not to decay, and bound fast with the pitch of charity, will himself grant us the unity of his Spirit, so that it may be disturbed neither by any adverse wind nor by the swelling of any wave approaching from without. But just as, under the governance of his grace, we must ask that no wave coming upon us from without disturb us, so, dearest brother, we must pray [Col. 0145D] with our whole heart that the right hand of his providence drain away the accumulated bilge-water within us.

For the adversary, the devil, who rages against the humble and prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (1 Peter 5), no longer, as we see, merely circles the sheepfolds, [Note: [Col. 0145D] Labbe reads “circles.”] but sinks his teeth so forcefully into certain indispensable members of the Church that no one can doubt [Col. 0146] that, unless by the Lord’s action the whole provident company of pastors comes together with one accord, he will quickly tear apart the entire flock—which God forbid.

### I

Therefore we exclude detractors, who by divine authority must be rooted out, and supporters of enemies from bringing accusations against a bishop.

### II

Likewise, let none of the highest rank be assailed or destroyed by accusations from inferiors (Hadrian, col. 19).

### III

Nor shall a definite [Col. 0146B] sentence be rendered in a matter (*Saint Gregory, Letter* 30, book VIII), nor shall any judgment be valid unless conducted in due order.

### IV

If anyone believes that a cleric ought to be prosecuted on any charges whatsoever, he shall prosecute his action in the province in which (Hadrian, col. 8) the person being prosecuted resides, [Note: [Col. 0146D] Labbe reads *exerat*, “prosecute.”] and the accuser shall not suppose that he may be dragged elsewhere or farther away for trial. If the person prosecuted considers the judges suspect, he shall be permitted to appeal to the primates.

### V

When the primates investigate an accused bishop, they too shall not pronounce a sentence of condemnation before, relying upon apostolic authority, either he confesses himself guilty (*Anonymous in the Constitutions*, book IX, title 40; *Theodosian Code*; Decretum, cause 11, question 3, “That the condemnation of bishops is invalid”), or he is duly convicted by trustworthy witnesses who have been canonically examined. [Col. 0146C] Otherwise, we judge the condemnation of bishops invalid and unjust and therefore subject to review by a synod, so that those who have been oppressed by anyone may receive assistance in every cause.

### VI

The judges of the Church must take care (*Fourth Council of Carthage*, canon 28) not to pronounce sentence when the person whose case is being tried is absent, because such a sentence will be invalid; for they themselves will also render an account in person for their treatment of their brethren. Neither the calumny nor the voice [Note: [Col. 0146D] Labbe reads: “The voice of a calumniator shall never be heard.”] of a traitor shall be heard. For no one can know a debtor better than the person who endured his injury (*Theodosian Code*, constitution 3, title 10, book X) and wickedness.

All who wish to live devoutly in Christ must therefore suffer reproaches from impious people unlike themselves, and be despised as foolish and insane (*Prosper, Sentence* 32, from Augustine on Psalm 122), because they surrender present goods in order to acquire those that are invisible and future. Yet the contempt and mockery of such people will recoil upon those who persecute them, because their abundance will turn to poverty and their pride to disgrace. Whatever adversity or evil [Col. 0146D] is inflicted upon the righteous is not punishment for crime but a test of virtue. Just as gold becomes better the more thoroughly it is refined, so the righteous person becomes much purer and dearer to God the more he is afflicted, provided that he bears the affliction patiently. Hence Truth itself says (Matthew 5): “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

[Note: [Col. 0148D] [[Col. 0148] This note is printed at the foot of column 148, but its callout number, (1), does not appear in the text.] “Observe the false consuls, whichever way you turn.”]

[Col. 0147A] The Lord speaks of such people through Isaiah, saying (Isaiah 66):

> Hear the word of the Lord, you who tremble at his word. Your brethren who hate you and cast you out on account of my name have said, “Let the Lord be glorified, and we shall see your joy”; but they themselves shall be put to shame. A voice of the people from the city, a voice from the temple, the voice of the Lord rendering recompense to his enemies. Before she was in labor, she gave birth; before her labor came, she bore a male child. Who has ever heard such a thing, and who has seen anything like it? Shall the earth give birth in one day? Or shall a nation be born [Note: [Col. 0147D] Labbe reads “shall be born.”] all at once, because Zion went into labor and bore her children? Shall I, who cause others to give birth, not myself bring forth? says the Lord. Shall I, who grant generation to others, be barren? says the Lord your God.
>
> Rejoice with Jerusalem, and exult in her, all you who love [Col. 0147B] her. Rejoice with her in universal joy, all you who mourn over her, so that you may suck and be filled from the breast of her consolation, so that you may draw milk and overflow with delights from the fullness of her glory. For thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall turn toward her as a river of peace, and as an overflowing torrent the glory of the nations, which you shall suck. You shall be carried at the breasts, and they shall caress you upon the knees. As a mother caresses someone, so shall I console you, and in Jerusalem you shall be consoled.
>
> You shall see, and your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall spring up like grass. The hand of the Lord shall be known to his servants, and he shall be indignant against his enemies. For behold, the Lord shall come in fire, and his chariot [Note: [Col. 0147D] Labbe reads “chariots.”] like a whirlwind, to repay his wrath with indignation and his rebuke with a flame of fire. For in fire the Lord judges [Note: [Col. 0147D] Labbe reads “shall judge”], and by his sword he judges all [Col. 0147C] flesh, and those slain by the Lord shall be multiplied.
>
> Those who sanctified themselves and thought themselves pure in the gardens, behind the inner door, who ate swine’s flesh, the abomination, and the mouse, shall be consumed together, says the Lord. But I come to gather their works and their thoughts together with all nations and tongues; and they shall come and see my glory, and I shall place a sign among them.
>
> I shall send some of those who have been saved to the nations: to the sea, to Africa, to Lydia [Note: [Col. 0147D] Labbe reads “Libya”], to those drawing the bow; to Italy and Greece; to the distant islands; to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory. They shall proclaim my glory among the nations, and they shall bring all your brethren from every nation as a gift to the Lord, on horses, in chariots, in litters, on mules, and in wagons, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says [Col. 0147D] the Lord, just as the children of Israel bring an offering in a clean vessel into the house of the Lord.
>
> I shall take some of them as priests and Levites, says the Lord. For just as the new heavens and the new earth that I make shall stand before me, says the Lord, so shall your offspring and your name stand. And month shall follow month, Sabbath shall follow Sabbath, and all flesh [OCR: *scaro*] shall come to worship before my face, says the Lord.
>
> They shall go out and see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and [Col. 0148A] their fire shall not be extinguished, and they shall be a spectacle unto satiety for all flesh.

What else do detractors do (*Saint Gregory, Letter* 45, book VIII), except blow upon the dust and stir up earth into their own eyes? The more strongly they blow their detraction, the less truth they see.

Such people must nevertheless be endured and corrected, dearest brother, because they are blind and leaders of the blind (Matthew 15). In response to your inquiries, dearest brother, I have briefly answered these matters, which we command you and all bishops to observe in accordance with canonical order. Yet we admonish your Prudence, brother, to strive with all your strength for the welfare of the Church and her priests; to observe in everything the order of the holy Roman and Apostolic Church; and not to permit the decrees of the saints to be violated. Instruct all whom you can, so that you may present fruitful sheaves [Col. 0148B] to the Lord.

Farewell.

Given on the Nones [Note: [Col. 0147D] Labbe reads “the ninth day before the Kalends.”] of June, in the consulship of the most illustrious Claudius and Aurelian [Note: [Col. 0148D] Labbe reads “Marinianus.”].

## LETTER II. CONCERNING THE AUTHORITY OF THE JUDGE OF THE APOSTOLIC SEE AND ACCUSED BISHOPS

[Note: [Col. 0148D] Labbe adds: “And concerning memorials of the martyrs.”]

Felix, bishop, to all the bishops established throughout the provinces of Gaul: greeting in the Lord.

There is no doubt that God is the author of good works and spiritual pursuits (*Saint Leo, Letter* 32), since he incites minds toward them and assists the deeds. Your writings therefore caused me to rejoice because of your good zeal and the integrity of your devout faith; but they saddened me greatly because of your affliction and distress.

Being sorrowful, I read your sorrowful letter (Peter Chrysologus, *Letter to Eutyches*), [Col. 0148C] and with due grief I went through your mournful writings. For just as hearing of the peace of the churches, the concord of their priests, and the tranquility of the people causes [Note: [Col. 0148D] Labbe reads “to approach.”] us joy [Note: [Col. 0148D] Labbe reads “causes us to rejoice with heavenly joy”], so fraternal affliction grieves and casts us down.

Nevertheless, do not be greatly saddened (*Saint Gregory, Letter* 45, book VIII), because Truth itself says: “If you were of this world, the world would love what was its own; but because you are not of this world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15)—that is, the lovers of the world hate you. Whatever they may say or do against you, always preserve your faith intact and keep your conscience pure, so that your spirit and soul may be preserved entire on the day of the Lord (1 Thessalonians 5).

For your support, we have summoned more than seventy of our brethren and fellow bishops, [Col. 0148D] with whom we have decreed that the provisions inserted below are to be treated in accordance with canonical order. For after your letters—which, as you know, contained your many complaints and accounts of oppression—had been read in everyone’s hearing, together with the decrees concerning accusations against bishops, the holy synod [Col. 0149A] [Note: [Col. 0149D] Hadrian, collection, ch. 5, calls it a Roman synod, but which synod it was and when it was held is not yet clear. Nothing can be inferred from this letter, since it is spurious.] said:

> These are the provisions that, henceforth, because of the snares of evil men who rage indiscriminately against the Church and ecclesiastical persons, we desire to be most firmly preserved for all time.
>
> If any bishop is accused by accusers who are eligible to be received, after they have charitably admonished him that he ought to amend and correct the matter, and he has refused to correct it, only then—and not before—shall his case be canonically referred to the highest primates. At a suitable place within the province and at a suitable time [Note: [Col. 0149D] Hadrian reads: “at a time predetermined by the Nicene canons.” This reveals the interpolator’s fraud.], namely in autumn or summer, they must summon a council in due order, so that the case may be heard there by all the bishops of that province.
>
> The accused himself, having been duly summoned, must also attend unless illness (*Theodosian Code*, book IX, title 1, constitution 10; Decretum, cause 3, question 2, “If a bishop shall have been …”) [Col. 0149B] or another grave necessity detains him; for no one has permission to summon an accused person beyond the boundaries of the province before a hearing is requested.
>
> For if he has been despoiled of his own property or that of the church entrusted to him, or—God forbid, for this ought to be alien to all the faithful—has been driven from his own see, or has been held in some form of detention and separated from his flock, then, in accordance with the canons, he can neither be summoned nor judged before he has been restored to his former condition with every privilege of his office and all his possessions taken from him through his enemies’ plots have been legally restored. The sole exception is if, for his own necessity, he voluntarily chooses to appear, though even then he must by no means be judged.
>
> Therefore he shall in no way be required [Note: [Col. 0149D] Labbe reads “compelled.”] by anyone to answer before absolutely everything he had lost through his enemies’ allegations has been restored to his control by an honorable council and according to legal procedure [Note: [Col. 0149D] Third Roman Council under Symmachus]. The prelate shall be restored with every honor to his former position; and after he has long been able freely and securely to arrange and order his affairs, then, within four, five, or seven [Note: [Col. 0149D] Labbe reads “six, or …”] months, according to his ability, and not before, he shall be duly summoned at the appointed time to a lawful and canonical council, shall come to plead his case, and, if it thus appears just, shall answer the propositions of his accusers.
>
> The greatest care must be taken that he not be compelled to answer before these things have been done, because contention must always be avoided. For no Christian can rightly believe that a bishop’s episcopate may be taken from him (*African Council*, canon 87) before the outcome of his case is known, because such presumption is sacrilege, and the author of such acts is sacrilegious.
>
> If the bishop is ill (Decretum, cause 3, question 3, “If he is ill”), or some grave necessity detains him, he shall send a representative to the synod on his behalf. A person charged with a crime shall not be suspended [Col. 0150A] from communion (*Third Council of Carthage*, canon 7), unless, having been summoned by letter to plead his case on the day appointed by the chosen judges, he fails to appear—that is, unless some necessity overtakes him within the period of the aforesaid months, or longer, as the case may require.
>
> But if both parties come to plead the case—for one must not be heard without the other—the court must inquire into the character, faith, and possible bias of the accusers, and the intention with which they act. They must not be admitted unless they are men of good conduct and right faith, free from every suspicion, distinguished by a good life, and not infamous.
>
> If the persons of the accusers appear culpable in the trial of bishops (Decretum, cause 3, question 10, “If the persons of the accusers”; likewise the Council of Carthage), [Col. 0150B] they shall not be admitted to make accusations, unless they wish to assert their own non-criminal causes or ecclesiastical causes. An infamous person (Decretum, cause 3, question 7, “An infamous person”) can be neither an attorney nor a legal representative.
>
> When the opposing party is absent (Decretum, cause 3, question 9, “When the opposing party is absent”), the accuser shall not be heard; nor shall a sentence pronounced by a judge in the absence of the other party possess any validity (see Anianus on the *Sentences of Paul*, book V, titles 2 and 5). An absent person can neither be accused through another nor bring an accusation (Decretum, cause 3, question 9, “An absent person through another”), nor shall anyone related to those persons be admitted.
>
> No one, therefore, should be summoned from one province to another (see Novel 3 of book III, Anianus, and *Theodosian Code*, constitution 4, book II, title 1), or to the imperial court, except upon the report of the judge to whom an appeal has been made; that is, the plaintiff must always follow the defendant’s forum. If anyone considers the judge hostile to him, he shall lodge an appeal, which ought to be denied to no one. (Thus far chapter 5 of Hadrian’s collection, though certain passages have been inserted.)
>
> By a general enactment we prohibit foreign tribunals (Decretum, cause 3, question 6, “Foreign tribunals”), because it is unworthy that one who ought to have as judges his fellow provincials (Hadrian, collection 17, from constitution 10, title 1, book IX of the *Theodosian Code*) and persons chosen by himself should be judged by outsiders.

These things, brethren, were unanimously decreed in the synod for your aid and defense and that of all our fellow bishops. Thus, if perhaps some fools (*Second Council of Hispania*, canon 13), deceived by the error of diabolical deception, wish to accuse you, they may recover their senses upon reading or hearing these provisions and return to the concord of unity; and what formerly served for vengeance will pass into glory.

For undoubtedly there are many who, in the Apostle’s words, having itching ears, turn their hearing away from the truth and turn instead to fables (1 Timothy 4), and turn to the injury of honors [Note: [Col. 0150D] Labbe reads “good people.”]. The same Apostle says (the same council cited above) of the ignorance of unbelievers: “Had they known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians 2). Likewise, if these people had perfectly known and loved the Lord, they would never have troubled his servants or persecuted them by words or deeds.

For [the text is corrupt at the transition] [Col. 0151A] when we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son (Romans 5); why, then, do we persecute our brethren? Why do we disturb the condition of God’s Church and afflict those who ought to serve him?

The martyrs suffered (the same council cited above), yet their souls were not slain when their bodies suffered, as the mouth of Truth attests: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matthew 10). From this it must be recognized that, if the souls of the martyrs cannot be destroyed by torments when their bodies have been slain, neither should the souls of preachers and teachers be persecuted or disturbed and turned away from God’s service, because they do not perish together with their bodies.

Such disturbers of the Church not only commit the evils mentioned above but also execrate the memorials (*memoriae*) of the martyrs (*Council of Gangra*, canon 20, Dionysius’s interpretation). [Col. 0151B] We have therefore decreed in the aforesaid synod, and command you and all churches to observe and carry out, that Masses be celebrated over the memorials of the martyrs, so that their memory cannot be extinguished by such people nor their veneration prevented.

But you, brethren, do not be greatly disturbed or distressed; rather, be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his glory (Ephesians 6). Meanwhile, possess these decrees, enacted by apostolic authority, as your protection. Know that we are always prepared, even to death if necessary, to accomplish with the Lord’s assistance whatever may be necessary for you. Yet they, by God’s agency, will perish, and you will stand—provided that your labor is not empty but full of faith and charity.

“Woe,” says the prophet, “to him who gives his friend a drink, pouring in [Col. 0151C] his gall” (Habakkuk 2). And again, the wisest Solomon says (these words also occur in the letter of Felix II to the Egyptians):

> He who speaks wicked things cannot remain hidden, nor will reproving judgment pass him by. Inquiry shall therefore be made into the thoughts of the ungodly. The hearing of his words shall reach the Lord, for the correction of his iniquities. For the ear of zeal hears all things, and the tumult of murmurings shall not be concealed. (Wisdom 1)

For if they had wished to embrace these things with sound judgment of their own, they would by no means have fallen into a reprobate mind. Guarding their words through fear of God, they would surely have preserved the devout definition of the holy fathers without any presumptuous act of injury. For sacred Scripture says: “Good counsel shall preserve you, and a good mind shall guard you” (Proverbs 2).

Such accusations and detractions do not proceed spiritually [Col. 0151D] from the saving fountains toward the acquisition of eternal life. Accordingly, the blessed Apostle Paul suitably warns us in advance that one ought “not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly” (Romans 12), persevering within the definition of piety.

Those who transgress these things have not only suffered injury by falling from their own stability, but have left in their households a memorial of their folly, so that they could not remain hidden in the very matters in which they sinned. For “glory [Col. 0152A] and dishonor are in speech” (Sirach 5), and a man’s fall is in the speech of his tongue [Note: [Col. 0151D] Labbe reads: “in a man’s tongue.”].

It is therefore fitting that this demonstration of their censures be inserted into our acts, so that you may no longer suffer such things while they sow weeds and scandals, but may deserve to rejoice in your offices and teachings. Let them therefore be ashamed and hasten to withdraw such things and blasphemies of this sort, unless they wish to be separated from our priestly college and torn away from the fellowship of the whole Christian people.
