Although we could have said and written many further and very necessary things concerning these matters, which are found established in the decrees of the Apostolic See by the apostles and their successors—namely, our predecessors—it seemed better to us to close the letter with a prayer.

May almighty God and his only-begotten Son, [Col. 0152B] Christ our Savior, grant you this impulse: that you assist with all your strength all our brethren and fellow bishops laboring under any tribulations whatsoever; that, suffering together with them, you bear the cross of the same Lord and Savior; and that you appear before everyone as his true disciples, so that both you and those who are with you may possess, here and in the future, the better things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have they entered into the human heart, which God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2).

Through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom and with whom be glory to almighty God for ever and ever. Amen.

I pray that you remain well, dearest brethren.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of the most illustrious Claudius and Paternus (A.D. 269, while Dionysius was not yet dead).

## LETTER III. TO BISHOP BENIGNUS

[Col. 0152C]

I. Those who contend that the Son does not see the Father err, on the ground that no one has ever seen God.  
II. Those who affirm that the Son is less than the Father err, because the Father is invisible whereas the Son is visible.

Felix, bishop, to his most beloved brother Benignus, bishop: greeting in the Lord.

Having received the letters of your Fraternity (*Zacharias, Letter* V), in which you questioned me concerning teachings of the faith that were understood by some otherwise than the mysteries of the true faith maintain, we have not refused, insofar as the Lord has enabled us, to answer out of fraternal love.

For doubtful and more important affairs have always customarily received their definitive resolution from this [Col. 0152D] holy See, from the time of the apostles who instructed it by their teachings. You therefore acted rightly in wishing both yourself and the others to be strengthened and instructed by the responses of this holy See.

I.—For your letter, and that of your brethren, stated that certain persons say that the Son cannot properly see the Father, because it is written: “For no one has ever seen God.” And others fabricate this claim: “The Son is therefore less than the Father, because the Father bears witness to him.” Others, moreover, prattle that he is less than the Father because [Col. 0153A] the Father himself is said to be invisible (John 1; Matt. 17; Mark 9; Luke 9; 1 Cor. 4; Col. 1; 1 Tim. 1), whereas the Son is shown to be visible. For these men, ignorant of the principles of the divine Scriptures and of the apostles, fashion such claims out of their own understanding, or a corrupted one, and seek to lead the hearts of the faithful astray.

[Note: [Col. 0153D] See Ithacius, *Against Varimadus the Arian*, chs. 18, 19, and 20, and their headings, and from this recognize the fraud.]

Let us, however, return to the very source of the fountain, from which we demonstrate, by the clearer testimonies contained in the writings of the Old and New Testaments, that the Son has always been able, and is able, to see the Father. Solomon says: “With you is Wisdom, who knows your works, who was present with you when you made the world, and she herself knows what is pleasing before your eyes.” And the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.” And again: “No one has [Col. 0153B] ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known.” And again he said to the Jews: “You do not know him, but I know him. And if I were to say that I do not know him, I would be like you, a liar.” Likewise in the same place: “He who is from God knows him.” And again: “I know him, because I am from him.”

See, we have demonstrated that the Son always sees the Father. How do they maintain that he cannot see the Father, in whose bosom he is known to abide? If you examine the divine Scriptures with an unclouded understanding, you will find not only the Father bearing witness to the Son, but the whole inseparable Trinity bearing witness together, as the Lord himself declares when he says: “I am he who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John 8). And again: “If I bear witness concerning myself, my [Col. 0153C] testimony is true, because I know whence I came and where I am going” (*ibid.*). And concerning the Holy Spirit: “When the Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, comes, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15). Consider, I beg you, consider: where one power of bearing witness is shown, none is judged either greater or inferior to another.

II.—We have already said this quite often: according to the form [Note: [Col. 0153D] Ithacius, ch. 20, where you see mention made of the foregoing.] of man, the Son is said to be visible; but according to the substance of the Godhead, he is proclaimed invisible, as the apostle Paul attests: “O the depth,” he says, “of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11). And in Isaiah: “To whom do you consider him similar, since he himself is invisible?” (Isa. 40). Likewise the Apostle says: “To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given among the nations, [Col. 0153D] to proclaim the unsearchable riches of Christ and to enlighten everyone as to the dispensation of the mystery hidden from the ages, in whom he created all things” (Eph. 3). Likewise he himself says: “Who is the image of the invisible God” (Col. 1). And to the Colossians: “I, Paul, am a minister, who now rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up in my flesh what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ for the sake of his body, which is the Church. Of this Church I was made a minister according to God’s dispensation, in the ministry of Christ, [Col. 0154A] which was hidden from ages and generations” (*ibid.*). Likewise there: “That their hearts may be consoled in charity, unto all the riches of the fullness of understanding, unto the knowledge of the mystery, which is Christ, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. 2).

And in Psalm 76: “Your way is in the sea, and your paths in many waters, and your footprints will not be known.” And in Solomon: “Who will search out the Wisdom of God that precedes all things?” (Ecclus. 1). Likewise there: “To whom has the root of wisdom been revealed, and who has recognized her subtleties?” (*ibid.*). Likewise there: “To whom has the discipline of wisdom been made manifest, and who has understood the multiplicity of her entrances?” (*ibid.*). Likewise there: “For the works of the Lord alone are wonderful, glorious and hidden, and his works unseen by men” (Ecclus. 2).

See: just as the Father is invisible, [Col. 0154B] so the Son also is found to be. How, then, is he judged inferior to the Father by those who say what you reported, merely because he deigned to let himself be seen by us in the flesh? Do not believe such people, and teach others to turn away from their opinion.

“Therefore serve the Lord in fear, and exult before him with trembling” (Ps. 2). “Embrace discipline, lest you perish from the righteous way.” This, moreover (24, q. 1, *A recta ergo fide*), is the living tradition of the apostles; this is true charity, which must be preached, truly loved and fostered, and confidently held by all. This holy and apostolic mother of all the churches (Agatho, Letter to Emperor Constantine, act 4 of the Sixth Ecumenical Council), the Church of Christ, which by the grace of almighty God is proved never to have strayed from the path of apostolic tradition, nor to have succumbed so as to be corrupted by heretical [Col. 0154C] innovations, but remains undefiled to the end, just as at the beginning it received the rule of the Christian faith from its founders, the princes of Christ’s apostles—this in accordance with the divine promise of the Lord and Savior himself, who spoke in his Gospels to the chief of his disciples, saying: “Peter, behold, Satan has demanded to sift you as one sifts wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22).

Let your excellent prudence therefore consider how good it is to persevere in the stewardship entrusted to you and in the right faith, to resist heretics and Christ’s adversaries, and never to turn aside from the path of truth. For the Lord and Savior of all, whose faith it is, who did not hesitate to die for us and redeemed us with his own blood, promised that the faith of blessed Peter [Col. 0154D] would not fail, and admonished him to strengthen his brethren. It has always been known to everyone that the apostolic pontiffs, the predecessors of my insignificance, confidently did this. My own littleness also, although unequal to them and the least of all, nevertheless desires, by reason of the ministry received through divine condescension, to follow in their footsteps.

For woe will be to us who have undertaken the burden of this ministry if we neglect to proclaim the truth of our Savior Jesus Christ, which the apostles proclaimed. Woe will be to us if by silence we suppress the truth which we are commanded to distribute to the money-changers—that is, to instill in and teach the Christian peoples. What shall we say at Christ’s future judgment if we are ashamed to proclaim the truth of his words? [Col. 0155A] What will become of us when Christ our God, the just Judge, demands a strict account concerning the souls entrusted to us and the office we have undertaken (1 Cor. 9; Matt. 25)?

Therefore, brethren, I exhort your charity (St. Leo, Letter against the Manichaeans), I adjure and admonish you to keep watch, with all the diligence you can and ought to exercise, to seek out heretics and enemies of God’s holy Church; and lest this plague spread more widely, remove them from sound minds with all the severity [Col. 0156A] that lies within your power and strength. For just as the person who has more diligently carried out whatever advances the salvation of the people entrusted to him will receive from God the reward of a worthy recompense, so before the Lord’s tribunal no one who has refused to guard his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will be able to excuse himself from the charge of negligence.

Given on the Nones of February, in the consulship of the most illustrious Claudius and Paternus (269, before Felix had yet been elected).

## LETTER IV

[Note: [Col. 0155B] A fragment of this letter survives in the Council of Chalcedon, first session, and in Cyril’s *Apology*. Certain very learned men have thought that it was written by Felix II, because in both places the aforesaid fragment is appended after the letter of Pope Julius. But the subject and title of the letter most firmly refute that opinion. For if it was written, as the title indicates, to Maximus, bishop of Alexandria and successor of Dionysius, it could have been written not by the second Felix, but by the first: for Felix, successor of Dionysius as Roman pontiff, presided over the universal Church at the same time that Maximus, after Dionysius, governed the Church of Alexandria.

The occasion for writing this letter was as follows. When Paul of Samosata had recently inflicted a wound upon Catholic truth, and the scar left by the error of Sabellius had not yet closed, Pontiff Felix wrote this letter to Maximus, bishop of Alexandria, concerning the divinity and, equally, the humanity of the Son of God, and concerning the two natures distinguished in one person, so that the successors of both Dionysii might vigorously continue the war against Sabellius and the Samosatene that their two predecessors had begun. Accordingly, with this letter, as though with a double-edged sword, he pierced both heresies with a single stroke: by showing the divine nature in Christ indivisibly united to his humanity, he condemns the heresy of Paul; while by demonstrating that the human nature in the same Christ is distinct from the divine nature, and that the divine substance subsists in three persons, he refutes Sabellius.

The fact that, in the Council of Chalcedon and in Cyril at the places mentioned above, it is listed after Julius’s letter resulted from their having paid no attention to chronology when arranging these texts. Vincent of Lérins, however, in *Against Heresies*, ch. 42, correctly understanding that in the time of Felix II no bishop named Maximus presided over the Church of Alexandria, observes the chronology and names Felix first, and then Julius. The same Vincent adds that this very letter of Pope Felix and martyr was read among other testimonies of the Fathers at the Council of Ephesus. See Baronius, year of Christ 273, nos. 11, 12, and 13. Severinus Binius.]

### TO MAXIMUS, BISHOP, AND THE CLERGY [Note: [Col. 0155C] “Clergy” in Labbé.] OF ALEXANDRIA

A fragment concerning Christ’s divinity and humanity.

[Note: [Col. 0155] The Latin and Greek versions of the following texts are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0155]

[Col. 0155A] Concerning the incarnation of the Word and the faith, we believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, because he himself is the eternal Son of God. For the Son of God did not assume a man so that there might be another besides himself; rather, while existing as perfect God, he became at the same time perfect man, incarnate of the Virgin. [Col. 0155B]

[Col. 0156A] Concerning [Note: [Col. 0156C] We present the Greek text from the first session of the Council of Ephesus, in which Peter, an Alexandrian presbyter and chief of the notaries, read selected testimonies from the holy Fathers concerning the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ; and from chapter 2 of part 3 of the same council, that is, the *Apologetic* of St. Cyril, patriarch of Alexandria, in defense of the twelve chapters against the Eastern bishops. Labbé.] the incarnation of the Word and the faith, we believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, who was born of [Col. 0156B] the Virgin Mary, because he himself is the eternal Son and Word of God, and not a man assumed by God, so that he might be someone other than him. For the Son of God did not assume a man so that there might be another besides himself; rather, while being perfect God, he became at the same time perfect man, incarnate of a virgin.

# COMPLETE WORKS OF POPE EUTYCHIAN

[Col. 0155]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE CONCERNING SAINT EUTYCHIAN, POPE

[Col. 0155D] **Eutychian was ordained pope on 5 January 275 and died in the year 283.**—Eutychian, son of Marinus or Martinus, an Etruscan and a native of Luna, succeeded Felix in the final days of 274 or the first days of the following year, 275. He was ordained on 5 January, a Tuesday, which in that year coincided with 5 January.

[Note: [Col. 0155D] Pagi, *Critica*, at the year 274; Baronius, at 275, no. 5, and at 283, no. 9; Coustant, *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, vol. I, p. 298.]

He presided over the Roman Church for eight years, eleven months, [Col. 0156D] and three days, and died in 283 on the seventh day before the Ides of December, as is recorded in the Bucherian Catalogue: “From the third consulship of Aurelian and that of Marcellinus to the second consulship of Carus and that of Carinus”—that is, from 5 January 275 to 7 December 283, or to the eighth, on which date Eutychian’s name is read in the short list of episcopal depositions: “On the sixth day before the Ides of December, Eutychian, in Callistus”—namely, in the cemetery of Callistus.

Eusebius must therefore be corrected, since he writes that Eutychian held the Roman pontificate for only ten months; and, as Valesius notes, he subtracted from Eutychian the eight years that he had added to Sixtus. The author of the *Pontifical* ascribed to Damasus erred even more shamefully: he extends Eutychian’s pontificate from the third consulship of Aurelian and that of Marcellinus to the second consulship of Carus and that of Carinus, yet reports that he occupied the see for one year, one month, and one day. [Col. 0157A]

**Concerning the heresy of the Manichaeans and Manes.**—During Eutychian’s pontificate, the insane heresy of the Manichaeans arose, to the common injury of the human race.

[Note: [Col. 0157C] Eusebius, *Chronicle*, p. 760, vol. VIII of Jerome.]

Although it was no less infamous than ridiculous, it nevertheless became the most celebrated among all the heresies that raised their heads during the first three centuries of the Church, and it raged with very great breadth throughout the world. The leader of this sect was a slave of Persian nationality, who changed his own name, Cubricus, to that of Manes or Manichaeus. He was sent to prison because he had hastened the death of the son of Varanes, king of the Persians, whom he had promised to cure through prayer. Escaping from there by flight, he came to Mesopotamia, and there disseminated his errors and dreams around the year 277. [Col. 0157B]

He was defeated more than once in public disputations by Archelaus, the most learned archbishop of Mesopotamia. Returning thence once more into Persia, he was discovered by Persian guards, arrested, and brought before the king. The king reproached Manes with the killing of his son and with his escape from prison and chains, and in the year 278 ordered that he be flayed according to Persian law and that the remainder of his body be given to wild beasts to devour. His skin, however, which had contained such great wickedness, was to be hung like a wineskin before the gates.

[Note: [Col. 0157C] Epiphanius, heresy 66; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* VI; Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, bk. I; Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Archelaus; Zacagni, *Monuments of the Latin and Greek Church*; Valesius, *Notes on Socrates*; [Col. 0157D] Ceillier, *Bibliothèque*; Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, vol. II; Walch, *History of the Heretics*, vol. I, p. 713.]

[Col. 0157C] **Should Eutychian be numbered among the martyrs?**—Baronius, both in his notes on the *Martyrology* and in his *Annals*, relates that Eutychian died by martyrdom; Blondel follows him.

[Note: [Col. 0157D] Blondel, *Pseudo-Isidore*.]

Yet, as Pagi says, he appears to deserve inclusion among the confessors:

[Note: [Col. 0157D] Pagi, note 10 at the year 283.]

first, because the author of the Bucherian Catalogue enrolled him in the short list of episcopal depositions, but not that of the martyrs; and second, because his death occurred at a time when, according to Eusebius,

[Note: [Col. 0157D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, bk. VIII, ch. 1.]

the Church of Christ enjoyed the most profound peace.

**What did St. Eutychian decree?**—This holy pontiff is to be commended [Col. 0158A] for the singular devotion with which he honored the martyrs. For, according to the author of the *Pontifical*, he buried 342 martyrs with his own hands, and established that no one should bury a martyr without a dalmatic or purple *colobium*.

[Note: [Col. 0158C] Blanchinus, in his notes on Anastasius the Librarian, vol. II, part II, p. 244, writes: “Promoting the concern to vindicate the martyrs, the cautious pontiff prudently commanded that certain proofs of martyrdom be added at their burial. He ordered that a *colobium* or dalmatic—not just any such garment, but one dyed purple—be used to wrap the martyrs, whom the Church also customarily calls ‘purple-clad’ in the hymn for All Saints: ‘You purple-clad martyrs.’ Before this decree of Eutychian, Christians customarily buried the sacred bodies of the martyrs with linen cloths sprinkled with their blood. [Col. 0158D] Nevertheless, very many martyrs both before and after Eutychian’s decree were interred in tombs wrapped in white linen cloths, perhaps after the example of our Restorer, as the distinguished Laurentius Berti observes in *Dissertation I on the Roman Bishops of the Third Century*, vol. II, §21, p. 337.”]

By a new decree he confirmed a custom that had otherwise already prevailed: that produce, beans, and grapes should be blessed upon the altar. He perhaps did so in order to oppose the error of the Manichaeans, who detested created things as having originated from an evil principle.

**Letters attributed to Eutychian.**—Under Eutychian’s name, Isidore the Sinner, or Mercator, fabricated two letters. The first is addressed to John and all the bishops of the province of Baetica, concerning faith in the Lord’s incarnation. The second, addressed to the bishops established throughout Sicily, comprises three subjects: [Col. 0158B] 1. The manner of admitting an accusation against clerics. 2. Who are not to be admitted as accusers of religious persons. 3. The manner of proceeding in ecclesiastical cases, since one must not proceed according to a secular manner.

The author nevertheless affixed to his decretals identifying marks that do not fit Eutychian. The letter to the bishops of Baetica is dated on the second day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious Aurelian and Marcellus. Yet the true Eutychian would have written “Marcellinus,” not “Marcellus,” and would, according to custom, have added the numeral identifying Aurelian’s consulship. Nothing can surpass the impostor’s impudence: he inserted into his decretal an entire chapter from Hilary which survives also in Leo the Great’s Letter 97 to Emperor Leo, ch. 3. The words “We also admonish your fraternity,” etc., are likewise taken from Gregory the Great’s [Col. 0158C] Letter 25, book II. The latter letter quotes Scripture from a version compounded from the Old Latin and Hieronymian versions. It interpolates decrees of Hadrian I issued in favor of Ingelram, bishop of Metz, as Blondel has already learnedly observed. Lumper.

[Col. 0157]

## CONCERNING THE DECREES ATTRIBUTED TO EUTYCHIAN

(Extracted from Dom Coustant.)

[Col. 0157D] **SUMMARY.**—1. Two decrees. The grounds on which Baronius supports the first decree.—2. The grounds on which the second may be supported.—3. [Col. 0158D] The ancient use of the dalmatic in the Church.—4, 5. The beginning of this usage is wrongly attributed to Sylvester.—6–15. [Col. 0159A] Two letters forged by Isidore. Ten decrees attributed to Eutychian.

1. In the *Pontifical Book*, Eutychian is said to have ordained “that produce, beans, and grapes should be blessed upon the altar,” and also “that whoever among the faithful buried a martyr should under no circumstances bury him without a dalmatic or purple *colobium*.” But the false claims made in this book both about other pontiffs and specifically about Eutychian detract from the authority of these statements. Baronius nevertheless accepts and defends both. He considers the first decree to have been appropriately issued by this pope to fortify the faithful against the nascent heresy of Manichaeus, which execrated produce and other material things as having been created by the evil principle.

Furthermore, in support of his opinion he cites Apostolic Canons 3, 4, and 5, which nevertheless, especially according to the translation of Dionysius Exiguus, seem rather to oppose it. Canon 4, namely, provides that “nothing may be offered at the altar except new ears of grain, grapes, oil for the lamps, and incense.” [Col. 0159B] It must therefore be conceded that these canons at least forbid the offering upon the altar of beans, which the commonly reported decree of Eutychian established were to be blessed upon the altar. Canon 5 then ordains “that all the remaining fruits—or all other fruits—be sent home as firstfruits to the bishop and presbyters, and not offered upon the altar.” Thus we hear that these canons prohibit what Eutychian’s decree commands to be offered upon the altar.

2. As for the other decree, the same father of the *Annals* proves that from it, under the pretext of devotion, the practice was introduced not only toward martyrs but also toward sacred ministers. [Col. 0159C] He does so both from book IV, chapter 40, of the *Dialogues* of Pope St. Gregory, where Gregory relates that the dalmatic of the deacon Paschasius was laid over his bier, and from the acts of the Roman synod held in 513, in which the same pope first declares:

“A custom surpassing their merit has arisen for the rulers of this see: when their bodies are carried out for burial, they are covered with dalmatics, and the people tear those same dalmatics into pieces to distribute them out of reverence for their sanctity.”

The modest pontiff then forbids that custom in these words: “By the present decree I ordain that the bier upon which the body of the Roman pontiff is borne for burial shall be covered with no cloth.” At the same time, he indicates the source of that usage when he adds among these words: “Although there are many coverings from the sacred bodies of apostles and martyrs,” etc. It is as though he were saying: [Col. 0159D] “This honor, rightly rendered to the bodies of apostles and martyrs, has undeservedly been transferred to those whose sanctity is not equal to theirs.” One can moreover conceive the following reason why Eutychian might have decreed this honor for the martyrs: the Manichaeans rejected the veneration of the holy martyrs as though it were idolatry.

3. Nor should it be denied that the terms *colobium* and “dalmatic” are ancient. In the *Life of St. Cyprian* written by Pontius, we read: “And when Cyprian had removed his dalmatic and handed it to the deacons, he stood in his linen garment.” An ancient author of the *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, in the Appendix to Augustine, vol. III, ch. 49, reproaches the deacons of the Roman Church as follows: “As though deacons today are not clad in dalmatics like bishops.” There [Col. 0160A] he notes both that the use of dalmatics properly belongs to bishops, and that it was arrogantly usurped by Roman deacons.

Cyprian, bishop of Toulon, also writes in his *Life of St. Caesarius, Bishop of Arles*, that at the very time Pope Symmachus “adorned Caesarius with the specially granted privilege of the pallium, he also caused his deacons to be distinguished by wearing dalmatics after the fashion of the Roman Church.” Gregory testifies in book IX, Letter 107, that Aregius requested permission for himself and his archdeacon to use dalmatics. Gregory did not “rashly and suddenly” permit this as something “new”; but when he later granted it, he also sent the dalmatics themselves to Aregius through the agency of Abbot Cyriacus. In the library of Fleury, the following is read in a letter from Pope Zacharias to Austrobert, bishop of Vienne: “We have sent a dalmatic for your use, so that, because your church received from this see both the doctrine of the faith and the custom of priestly attire, it may also receive from it the adornment of honor.” [Col. 0160B]

4. From this one may gather how much credence is owed to the commonly circulated Anastasius when he writes concerning Sylvester: “And he ordained that deacons should use dalmatics in the Church”—especially if this decree is understood to refer not only to Roman deacons but to deacons everywhere. It also refutes what others say: that the use of dalmatics was first introduced into the Church by Sylvester, whereas priests had previously used *colobia*.

It likewise refutes the narrative in the *Life of Sylvester* published by Combefis: namely, that Euphrosynus, bishop of Pamphylia, came to Rome bringing with him the *colobium* of St. James, the brother of the Lord; [Col. 0160C] that he performed the sacred rites clothed in it; that this caused Roman priests to use *colobia*; but that the *colobia* were afterward changed into dalmatics in order to cover the nakedness of the arms. The same applies to the tradition reported by Anselm of Lucca, as cited by Du Cange: “The use of *colobia* began with St. Sylvester and his presbyters, and Marcus, Julius, and Liberius used them in succession. After them, however, the *colobia* were changed into dalmatics.” From this it would follow that not Sylvester but Damasus I should be said to have introduced the use of dalmatics into the Church.

Yet what we have said concerning Cyprian’s dalmatic from his *Life* written by Pontius establishes that its use in the Church is older than both Damasus and Sylvester; just as the testimonies cited immediately above prove that the same usage was commonly believed to be [Col. 0160D] more recent than that of the *colobia*.

5. *Colobia*, like dalmatics, were ankle-length tunics. Dalmatics differed from tunics and *colobia* in that dalmatics had broad sleeves, tunics narrow sleeves, and *colobia* either no sleeves or short ones. Concerning *colobia* with short sleeves, we have the following from Cassian, *On the Habit of Monks*, ch. 5: “Clad also in linen *colobia*, which scarcely reach the beginnings of their elbows, they leave the remainder of their arms bare.”

Dorotheus, however, in Instruction 1, asks why the monks’ *colobium* lacks sleeves, when everyone else’s has them. Likewise, after adding, “Our *colobium* bears a purple emblem,” he again asks: “What does the purple emblem signify?” and answers: “Everyone who serves as a soldier of the king bears purple on his cloak.” This explanation can indeed be applied to the decree we are examining, which provides that no one should bury a martyr without a purple *colobium*. Accordingly, I have not regretted discussing these matters at somewhat greater length, since they cast light upon the proof of either the authenticity or the falsity of certain decrees. [Col. 0161A]

6. In editions of the councils, after two spurious letters of Eutychian that came from the workshop of Isidore Mercator and that will be published by us together with the other productions of that same workshop, ten other decrees are appended, collected from various compilations of canons. The first is quoted from Gratian, II, question 3, chapter 91, as follows:

“If any bishop or abbot orders his presbyter or monk to sing Masses for heretics”—other collectors add “who are dead”—“it is neither lawful nor [Col. 0161B] expedient for them to obey.”

But this is a small portion of a longer decree, which Anselm, book II, according to the German manuscript, ch. 117; Burchard, book XIX, ch. 105; and Ivo, part 13, ch. 117, likewise present as attributed to Eutychian, in the following form:

“If anyone has given or received communion from the hand of a heretic and does not know that the Catholic Church forbids it, then, upon learning this afterward, he shall do penance for one year. But if he knows and disregards it, and afterward performs penance, he shall do penance for ten years; others judge that he should do so for seven, and others, more leniently, for five.

“If anyone permits a heretic to celebrate his Mass in a Catholic church, and does not know, he shall do penance for forty days. If he does so out of reverence for him, he shall do penance for one year. If he does so in condemnation of the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0161D] ‘And of the custom of the Romans’ does not occur in the text attributed to Jerome.] and of the custom of the Romans, he shall be cast out [Col. 0161C] of the Church as a heretic, [Note: [Col. 0161D] ‘Unless he has repented’ in the text attributed to Jerome.] unless he has done penance; if he has done so, he shall do penance for ten years.

“If anyone has departed from the Catholic Church for an assembly of heretics, has persuaded others to do so, and afterward has performed penance, he shall do penance for twelve years: four years”—three in Anselm—“outside the church, six years”—seven in the same author—“among the hearers, and two more outside communion. Concerning these it is stated in the [Note: [Col. 0161D] ‘In the synod’ in the text attributed to Jerome.] canon that in the tenth year they are to receive communion without an offering.

“If a bishop or abbot orders his monk to sing Masses for dead heretics”—these are the words cited by Gratian—“it is neither lawful nor expedient for him to obey.

“If it happens to a presbyter that, where he has sung Mass, another person recites the names of the dead and [Note: [Col. 0161D] ‘And if he names a single heretic’ in Anselm.] names heretics [Col. 0161D] together with Catholics, then, if he learns of it after Mass, he shall do penance [Note: [Col. 0162D] ‘He shall fast’ in the text attributed to Jerome.] for a week; if he has done this repeatedly, he shall do penance for a complete year.

“If anyone has arranged a Mass for the death of a heretic, so that, in accordance with his religion, [Note: [Col. 0162D] ‘He has made relics from him there, because he fasted a great deal, and afterward’ in the text attributed to Jerome.] he has kept his relics there, and does not know the difference between this and the Catholic faith, then, after he learns of it and performs penance, he must burn the relics there with fire and do penance for one year. But if he knows and has disregarded it, then, when moved to penance, he shall do penance for [Note: [Col. 0162D] ‘forty’ in the text attributed to Jerome.] ten years.

“If anyone has departed from the [Col. 0162A] Catholic faith without any necessity, and afterward has accepted penance with his whole heart, he shall do penance for three years outside the church—that is, among the hearers—then, according to the Council of Nicaea (canon 11), for seven years in the churches among the penitents, and for two further years outside communion.”

In the German manuscript containing Anselm’s collection, we read next: “He shall do penance for three years outside the church, one among the hearers, according to the Council of Nicaea.” This reading at first seemed preferable, because the hearers entered the church and there listened to the readings and sermons together with the other faithful. But the cited Council of Nicaea does not permit this reading, for the compiler of this decree rashly added the words “outside the church” to the council’s wording.

Even if I pass over in silence the repeated use of the term “Mass” in this decree and other features that savor of an age later than Eutychian’s, the Council of Nicaea cited in it, which was celebrated forty-two years after Eutychian’s death, plainly discloses the falsity of its attribution. Nor is Gratian consistent with himself: for he attributes the greater part of the same text to Julius at XXIV, question 1, chapter 41. But the whole passage was copied from chapter 2 of the *Penitential* attributed to Jerome, except for the variants that we have noted in the margin. [Col. 0162B]

7. The second decree, “Nevertheless also,” etc., by which an abbess is prohibited from veiling a maiden, whether a virgin or a widow, was copied from Gratian, XX, question 2, chapter 3. It is also cited by Burchard, book VIII, ch. 17, and Ivo, part 7, ch. 38, as coming from chapter 13 of Eutychian’s decrees. It belongs, however, to book I, chapter 43, of the Sixth Council of Paris, held in 829.

[Col. 0162C] 8. The third decree, “It must also be preached that the faithful should beware of perjury,” etc., was taken from Gratian, XXII, question 1, chapter 17. Gratian indeed followed the earlier collectors of canons: Anselm, book II, according to the German manuscript, ch. 58; Burchard, book XII, ch. 14; and Ivo, part 12, ch. 71. Among them it is likewise cited as coming from chapter 26 of Eutychian’s decrees. It belongs, however, to Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, chapter 26, in Sirmond, vol. II of *Councils of Gaul*, p. 217.

9. To these is appended the fourth decree:

“If anyone has carried out mutilations of limbs or burnings of houses, ordered them to be carried out, or consented to someone carrying them out, he shall know himself deprived of communion with the Church until, before the bishop of the city and the other citizens, he has made legal and amicable amends to each person for these acts. But if, after a second and [Col. 0162D] third summons, he has not made amends for everything of which he is accused, he shall be separated from the entire fellowship of Christians as a heathen and a publican.”

Although Gratian, XXIII, question 8, chapter 31, following Ivo, part 13, ch. 40, and Burchard, book XI, ch. 30, attributes this decree to Eutychian, it nevertheless appears with good reason to be more recent than he.

10. Gratian, XXVIII, question 1, chapters 2 and 3, supplies the fifth decree, “If any gentile has put away a gentile wife before baptism,” and the sixth, “Likewise, if one of the spouses has been baptized and the other is a gentile.” [Col. 0163A] Burchard, book XI, chs. 59 and 60, and Ivo, part 8, chs. 195 and 196, had anticipated him in this. Both were copied from the *Penitential of Theodore of Canterbury*, chs. 13 and 45, as may be seen in Petit, vol. I, p. 11, and D’Achery, *Spicilegium*, vol. IX.

11. What is copied in the seventh place from Gratian, XXXV, question 6, chapter 7, concerns the synodal oath and begins:

“The bishop, sitting in the synod, after a suitable exhortation, ought to summon into their midst seven men from the people of that parish, or more, as he sees fit—men of greater maturity, honor, and truthfulness,” etc.

It is quoted in the same manner in Anselm, book VI, according to the German manuscript, ch. 146. It also survives in Burchard, book I, chs. 91 and 92, as though taken from chapter 9 [Col. 0163B] of the decrees of Pope Eutychian. But in Burchard, chs. 92 and 93, there follow eighty-eight headings concerning the matters about which, as though by command of the same Eutychian, those who have first bound themselves by the synodal oath are to be questioned.

Moreover, all those collectors agree upon the following formula of the oath, in which, “when the pledges of the saints have been brought forward,” the person swearing is required to declare:

“That neither because of affection, nor because of fear, nor because of reward, nor because of kinship will you in any way conceal anything from the bishop, or from his delegate whom he has ordered to investigate this, whenever he questions you concerning it. So may God help you, and these relics of the saints.”

Similar to this is the formula for questioning reported by Gratian in the same place, chapter 5, as follows:

“Concerning this kinship which they say exists between that man N. and his wife N., whatever you know about it or have heard from your neighbors or from your older relatives, you will not by any device conceal from your bishop, or from his delegate whom he has ordered to investigate this, whether because of affection, fear, reward, or consanguinity, whenever he questions you concerning it. So may God help you, and these relics of the saints.” [Col. 0163C]

Yet this last formula—which in Burchard, book VII, ch. 25, and Ivo, part 9, ch. 61, also lacks a heading, for the citation from Gregory and the Roman Council prefixed to the preceding decrees does not, as the Pithou brothers supposed, pertain to this formula—is cited by Gratian as coming from the *Roman Order*. It is therefore probable that the preceding decree was also taken from that same *Order*.

[Col. 0163D] 12. It must nevertheless be acknowledged that a custom of this kind was introduced into the Roman Church only in later centuries, [Col. 0164A] and that in Rome, as also in the East, at least down to the sixth century, the prevailing practice was that those about to give testimony touched the Gospels placed before them, without any mention of sacred relics. Evidence for this is supplied by Pope Vigilius’s Letter 15, no. 2; fragment 44 of Pelagius I, addressed to Decoratus; the acts of the Synod of Mopsuestia incorporated into session 5 of the Fifth General Council; and the Sixth General Council, session 14, p. 977. The command to use the foregoing formula, or to swear over relics, is found in Baluze, vol. I of the *Capitularies*, in Capitular IV of the year 803, or the Law of the Ripuarians, ch. 57, p. 398, and in Sirmond, vol. II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 246, in these words:

> “Every oath is to be sworn in a church or over relics; and what is to be sworn in a church is to be sworn either with [Col. 0164B] six chosen men, or, if there must be twelve, with such men as he can find. And he shall swear as follows: ‘So may God and those saints whose relics these are help him, that he may speak the truth.’”

A command and practice concerning the same matter may be seen in the aforesaid Baluze, p. 60, in Capitular II of King Dagobert, from the year 630, or the Law of the Alamanni, ch. 7, where it is decreed:

> “These oaths must be sworn in such a way that the co-swearers place their hands upon the reliquary, while only the man whose case is under inquiry pronounces the words and places his own hand upon the hands of them all: ‘So may God or those relics help him,’ etc.”

See the Council of Frankfurt, held in 794, canon 9, where the practice of swearing either by touching the Gospels or in the presence of relics set out before the swearer is indicated.

13. The decree *The Great Evil of Drunkenness*, [Col. 0164C] which was published from book XIV, ch. 2, of the collection in sixteen books, and which we find in Burchard, book XVI, ch. 2, and Ivo, part 13, ch. 71, is canon 46 of the Council of Mainz held in 813.

14. What follows this—“Bishops and ministers of God must not devote themselves to excessive feasting and drunkenness”—is likewise presented by Burchard, book XVI, ch. 3, and Ivo, part XIII, ch. 70, as copied from the same collection, at the same place, ch. 3. It pertains no more to Eutychian than does the preceding item, but belongs to the Second Council of Reims, held in 813, of which it is canon 18.

15. The final decree, *It Must Be Observed by Us*, which prescribes with whom the ministers of God may dine, was taken from book XIV, ch. 10, of the collection in sixteen books, and is cited on the same basis by Burchard, book XVI, ch. 10, and [Col. 0164D] Ivo, part 11, ch. 78. It is chapter 13 of the Capitular of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans.

[Col. 0163]

## EXHORTATION OF POPE EUTYCHIAN TO PRIESTS, FROM AN ANCIENT VATICAN CODE. (S)\*

[Col. 0163D] Brothers and priests of the Lord, you are fellow workers of our order. We, though unworthy, hold the place of Aaron; you hold the place of Eleazar and Ithamar. We discharge the office of the twelve apostles; you correspond to the seventy-two disciples. We are your shepherds, and you are the shepherds of the people entrusted to you. [Col. 0164D] We shall render an account of you to the supreme Shepherd, our Lord Jesus Christ, and you shall render an account of the people entrusted to you: we for you, the shepherds, and you for the sheep, that is, for the congregations committed to you. Therefore, dearly beloved sons, let us look ahead to the danger inherent in so great an office entrusted to us.

Accordingly, we admonish and beseech [Col. 0165A] your brotherhood to commit to memory what we suggest for your salvation and ours. First of all, we admonish you that your life and conduct must be irreproachable: namely, that your dwelling should be beside the church and that you should have no women in your houses. Rise every night for Nocturns; chant your office at the appointed hours; conduct the celebrations of Mass reverently; receive the body and blood of the Lord with fear and reverence. Let no one occupy himself with chess or games of dice. Wash and wipe the sacred vessels with your own hands. Let no one sing Mass unless fasting; let no one sing who does not receive Communion; let no one sing without amice, alb, stole, maniple—that is, *fanon*—and chasuble. These vestments must be clean and must not be used for any other purposes. Let no one sing Mass in an alb that he uses for his own ordinary purposes. [Col. 0165B] Let no one dare to celebrate Mass with a wooden or glass chalice. Let no woman approach the altar or touch the Lord’s chalice. Let the corporal be perfectly clean. Let the altar be covered with clean linens.

Nothing is to be placed upon the altar except reliquaries, relics, and the four Gospels, or a pyx containing the Lord’s body as viaticum for the sick; everything else is to be stored in a clean place. Everyone is to have a complete missal, a lectionary, an antiphonary, and the book of forty homilies. A place is to be prepared in the sacristy or beside the altar where the water used to wash the sacred vessels may be poured away, and where a clean vessel containing water is to hang so that the priest may wash his hands after Communion. The churches are to be well roofed and vaulted, and the churchyard is to be securely enclosed on every side.

[Col. 0165C] Let no one sing Mass outside a church, in private houses, or in places that have not been consecrated. Let no one sing Mass alone. Every priest is to have a cleric or scholar who will read the Epistle or lesson, make the responses to him at Mass, and sing the psalms with him. Visit the sick, reconcile them after confession, anoint them with holy oil according to the Apostle, and give them Communion with your own hand. Let no one presume to give Communion to a layman or woman to carry to a sick person. Let no one sell the sacred chrism. Let none of you demand any reward, price, or [Col. 0165D] gift for baptizing infants, reconciling sinners or the sick, burying the dead, or consecrating churches; nor is anyone to use money or any fraudulent device to seize the churches of others. See to it that no infant dies without baptism through your negligence.

Let none of you be a drunkard or quarrelsome. Let no one bear weapons in a disturbance, but only the word of the Lord. Let no one devote himself to the sport of dogs or birds; let no one eat and drink in taverns. Let each of you, to the extent of his understanding, proclaim something from the Gospel, the Epistle, or another passage of divine Scripture to his congregation on Sundays and feast days. Let him care for the poor, strangers, and orphans, providing them with lodging and refreshment so that they may have support. Let him restore those at variance to harmony and defend widows, so that in these and other such matters he may offer an example of every good work.

Every Sunday before Mass let him make holy water, sprinkle his congregation and the dwellings of the faithful, keep one vessel solely [Col. 0166A] for this purpose, and go in procession around his courtyard or around the church. Do not give sacred vessels or priestly vestments as security to a merchant or any secular person. Let none of you, for the sake of anything whatsoever, bring to reconciliation a person who is doing penance unworthily or bear testimony that he has been reconciled. Let none of you charge interest or become the collector of his own loan. Know that the goods and property you acquire from the day of your ordination belong to the church to which you have been appointed or which you serve.

Let no one acquire and possess a church without the bishop’s knowledge and consent. Let no one hold a church through the power of secular persons. Let no one abandon the church to which he has been appointed and move to another. Let no one [Col. 0166B] have several churches without the assistance of other priests. Under no circumstances is one church to be divided among several men. Let no one receive another priest’s parishioner at Mass, except while the person is traveling or if this has been agreed upon. Let no one sing Mass in another man’s church or parish without the consent and invitation of its own priest. Let no one receive a tithe belonging to another church. Let no one invite a penitent to eat meat and drink wine unless alms are given for him at that time.

Let no one presume to baptize except on the vigils of Easter and Pentecost, unless necessity or danger of death requires it. Each priest is to have a stone font; if he cannot have one of stone, let him have another vessel prepared for this purpose, in which nothing else is done. See to it that you impart the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer [Col. 0166C] to all your parishioners. Instruct your congregations that the fasts of the Ember Days, the Rogations, and the Greater Litany must by every means be observed. On the Wednesday before Lent, invite the people to confession and impose penance upon them according to the character of their offense—not from your own judgment, but as it is written in the penitential.

At three times in the year—that is, at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost—admonish all the faithful to receive Communion in the body and blood, except penitents who have been forbidden to do so. Exhort married persons to abstain from their wives at appointed times: that is, from the Advent of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany has passed; from Septuagesima until the octave [Col. 0166D] of Easter has passed; and from the Rogations until the octave of Pentecost has passed. In addition, they are to abstain on every Saturday until Monday, and on the vigils of Saint Mary, Saint John, and the apostles, as well as on the appointed vigils and feasts of other saints. On Sundays after Mass, distribute blessed bread (*eulogiae*) to the people.

Let no priest travel without an orarium, that is, a stole. Let none of you be dressed in lay clothing or clothing of various colors. Let no one presume to sell, exchange, or by any device alienate any object, property, or bondservant belonging to the church.

Teach the people to celebrate the Lord’s Day and other festivals from evening to evening without servile work. Forbid women’s songs and dances, entertainers’ games, and songs from being performed in the church or churchyard. Under solemn appeal to almighty God, forbid the diabolical songs which the common people [Col. 0167A] customarily perform over the dead during the hours of the night, as well as the loud laughter in which they indulge.

Do not associate with the excommunicated. Let no one presume even to sing Mass with them, and announce this also to the congregations entrusted to you. Let none of you attend weddings. Announce to everyone that no one is to take a wife unless the marriage has been publicly celebrated. Let no one take another man’s betrothed. Forbid weddings from the Advent of the Lord until the octave of Epiphany has passed, from Septuagesima until the close of Easter has passed, and from the Rogations until the octave of Pentecost has passed.

Prohibit abduction in every way, and anathematize anyone who approaches a woman closely related to him by blood, or any relative within the seventh generation. Admonish everyone to make all his shepherds and other servants [Col. 0167B] come to church on Sundays and feast days. Let godparents impart the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer to their spiritual children, or have them taught these things. Let the chrism be kept under seal or lock because of certain unbelievers.

Concerning the mystery entrusted to you, we are concerned to admonish you that each of you should, if possible, possess a written exposition of the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer according to the tradition of the orthodox fathers. He should understand it fully and from it constantly instruct the people entrusted to him by preaching. If he does not understand it, let him at least retain and believe it. He should also understand well the prayers of the Masses, the prefaces, and the canon; and if he cannot do so, he should at least be able [Col. 0167C] to pronounce them distinctly and from memory. He should be able to read the Epistle and Gospel well, [Col. 0168A] and would that he could explain their literal sense! He should know how to recite from memory, according to rule and with the customary canticles, the verses and divisions of the Psalms. He is to memorize the discourse of Bishop Athanasius beginning “Whoever wishes” (*Quicumque vult*) and chant it every day.

He should be able and know how to pronounce distinctly the exorcisms and prayers for making a catechumen and consecrating the baptismal font, as well as the other prayers over a male or female, whether singly or in groups. Each priest is to possess and prudently understand the rite of baptism for emergency use with the sick, the rite of reconciliation according to the authority of the canons, and the rite for anointing the sick. When invited to visit and reconcile the sick, he is to hasten willingly and attend to their need—not for earthly gain, [Col. 0168B] but because of that love with which Christ loved us. He is to take care to chant the prayers and the seven special psalms around them.

Likewise, he is to know by heart the rite for conducting the obsequies of the dead, the intercessions, the exorcisms of salt and water, and the night and day offices. If he does not know the greater computation, let him at least know the lesser—that is, the epacts, concurrents, regular limits, and, if he can, the other matters. He should understand the martyrology and the penitential. Let everyone possess this little book and read it frequently, lest he consign to oblivion the things he is required to observe.

Dearly beloved brothers, may almighty God deign to grant us the ability to retain these things in memory and carry them out for our salvation. His kingdom and dominion endure without end [Col. 0168C] forever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0167]

## DOUBTFUL LETTER AND DECREES OF SAINT EUTYCHIAN, POPE AND MARTYR. (G, S)

## LETTER I

[Note: [Col. 0167D] This first letter of Eutychian contains an antidote prepared against the poisons of Paul of Samosata. For it teaches that Christ the Lord, whom Paul said to be a mere man, is the true and eternal Son of God, incarnate [Col. 0168D] in time in the womb of the Blessed Virgin Mary through the power of the Holy Spirit, and that through this the divine nature was in no way changed. SEVERINUS BINIUS.]

### TO JOHN AND ALL THE BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCE OF BOEOTIA

On faith in the Lord’s Incarnation. How Christ existed as true God and true man, while the proper character of each nature was preserved.

[Col. 0167D]

To his dearly beloved brothers, John and all the bishops established throughout the province of Boeotia, Eutychian the bishop: greetings in the Lord.

The justice of your request prompts us gladly to grant the desire of your brotherhood (Symmachus, Letter 5, to St. Caesarius) [Note: [Col. 0167D] “Intimate,” Labbe.] and to reply briefly to your inquiries. [Col. 0168C] And although I know that your love is devoted to every good work (St. Leo, Letter 46), nevertheless, so that it may become more effective toward those whose understanding is unsound, we instruct you how you ought to teach them concerning the incarnation of our Savior.

This, then, is the one immovable foundation, [Col. 0168D] this the one blessed rock of faith confessed by the mouth of Peter: “You are,” he says, “the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16). It contains within itself as many proofs of truth as there will be questions raised by perversity and accusations by unbelief (St. Leo, p. 97, from St. Hilary’s books *On the Trinity*, which he cites). In all the other matters, let there now be the dispensation of the Father’s will.

Therefore the birth and the body, and afterward the cross, death, and the underworld, are our salvation [Note: [Col. 0167D] “The Virgin, the birth, and the body; afterward the cross, death, and the underworld are our salvation.” This is unquestionably how the passage must be read.]. [Col. 0168D] For the sake of the human race the Son of God was born from the Virgin and the Holy Spirit. The Spirit himself [Col. 0169A] served him in this operation, and he, overshadowing her by his own power—that is, the power of God—wove together for himself the beginnings of a body and established the first elements of flesh, [Note: [Col. 0169D] “Constructed,” Labbe.] so that, having become man from the Virgin, he might receive in himself the nature of flesh. Through the fellowship of this union, the body of the whole human race would be sanctified in him. And just as all were created in him through his willingness to become bodily, so he in turn would be brought into relation with all through that which in him is invisible.

The invisible image of God, therefore, did not refuse the abasement of a human beginning, but passed through conception, birth, crying, the cradle, and all the humiliations of our nature. What, in the end, shall we repay that is worthy of such loving condescension [Note: [Col. 0169D] “Worthy of such loving condescension,” in the dative, Labbe.]? The one only-begotten God, whose origin from God is beyond description, grows within [Col. 0169B] the womb of the holy Virgin after being implanted in the form of a human body. He who contains all things, within whom and through whom all things exist, is brought forth according to the law of human birth. He at whose voice archangels and angels tremble, and heaven and earth and all the elements of this world are dissolved, is heard crying in infancy. He who is invisible and incomprehensible, not to be encompassed by sight, sense, or touch, is wrapped in swaddling clothes in a cradle.

If anyone reflects that these things were unworthy of God, he thereby confesses himself obligated by an even greater benefaction, in proportion as these things were less suited to the majesty of God. He through whom man was made had no need to become man; but we needed God to become flesh and dwell in us—that is, through the assumption of flesh, for the one who dwells within all flesh to inhabit it. His humility is our nobility; his humiliation is our honor. What he is—God subsisting in flesh—[Col. 0169C] this we in turn become, renewed from flesh into God. Certainly [Note: [Col. 0170D] “For certainly thus,” Labbe.] the person who does not know Christ Jesus to be true God and likewise true [Note: [Col. 0170D] “Not thus,” Labbe.] man does not know his own life. And it is a matter of the same danger either not to believe Jesus Christ or the Holy Spirit to be God, or to deny in Christ the flesh of our body (the same St. Leo, in the same place, from the same St. Hilary).

“Therefore,” he says, “everyone who acknowledges me before men, I also will acknowledge before my Father who is in heaven; but whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 10). The Word made flesh was saying these things (John 1), and the man Jesus Christ, the Lord of majesty, was teaching them. He was himself established in his own person as mediator for the salvation of the Church; and in that very mystery of mediation between God and men, he existed as one from both sides, [Col. 0169D] since he himself, from both natures united into one, is the same reality of each nature. Yet this is so in such a way that he lacks neither while existing in both, lest perhaps, by being born as man, he cease to be God, or conversely, by remaining God, he not be man.

This, therefore, is the true faith of human blessedness: to proclaim God and man, to confess Word and flesh; neither to fail to recognize that God is man, nor to ignore that the flesh is the Word. The only-begotten God, therefore, was born as man from the Virgin (the same author, in the same letter, from the same [Col. 0170A] St. Hilary), and, according to the fullness of time, being in himself destined to advance man into God, he maintained this manner throughout the whole Gospel discourse: that he taught himself to be believed as the Son of God, while proclaiming and declaring himself the Son of Man. As man he spoke and did all the things that belong to God; and then, as God, he spoke and did all the things that belong to man. Yet in this very discourse concerning both kinds, he never spoke without signifying both man and God.

This [Note: [Col. 0170D] “Hence,” Labbe.] gives heretics their opportunity to deceive the simple and ignorant: they falsely claim that the things spoken by him according to his humanity were spoken according to a weakness of the divine nature. And because it is one and the same person who speaks everything he says concerning himself, they contend that he spoke everything about his divinity. We certainly do not deny that the whole discourse [Col. 0170B] belonging to him pertains to his nature. But if Jesus Christ is both man and God; if he did not first become God when he became man; if, when he is both man and God, he is not therefore no longer God; and if, after the assumption of man into God, he is wholly man and wholly God—then it is necessary to say that his mystery is one and the same; the phrase *quod generis* (“as regards kind”?) is textually uncertain.

When, therefore, you distinguish in him man from God according to time, then distinguish the discourse of God from that of man. When you confess God and man in time, then discern what was said in time by God and by man. But when he exists as man and God, understand once again that the time belongs to the whole man and now to the whole God. For if something was said to indicate a time, adapt to that time the things that were said. Thus, since God before becoming man is one condition, man and God another, and wholly man and wholly God after becoming man [Col. 0170C] and God another, you must not confuse by times and kinds the mystery of the dispensation. According to the character of the kinds and natures, one mode of discourse was necessarily used, within the mystery of the man, while he was not yet born; another while he was still going to die; and another when he was eternal.

For our sake, therefore, Jesus Christ did all these things and was born as the man of our body. He spoke according to the customary condition of our nature, yet without ceasing to possess his own nature as God. For although in birth, suffering, and death he carried out the reality belonging to our nature, he nevertheless performed all those realities by the power of his own nature. Do you see how God and man are so proclaimed that death is assigned to the man, but the raising of the flesh to God [Note: [Col. 0170D] The same St. Leo, in the same place, from the same St. Hilary. From these passages the reader may judge how far this purple differs from cheap and everyday scraps of a merchant’s cloth.]? Yet this does not mean that the one who died is different from the one through whom the dead man rises. For when stripped of the flesh, [Col. 0170D] it is Christ who died; and again, the one who raises Christ from the dead is the same Christ who strips himself of the flesh. Understand the nature of God in the power of the resurrection; recognize the dispensation of the man in death. And although both acts were performed in accordance with their respective natures, remember nevertheless that he who is both is the one Christ Jesus.

These things [Col. 0171A] therefore had to be demonstrated by me in a few words, so that we might remember that the form of each nature must be considered in our Lord Jesus Christ: for he who, while remaining in the form of God, assumed the form of a servant, did not in any way lose his divinity.

For the rest, brothers, we exhort you to admonish them to turn to him. [Note: [Col. 0171D] From this point onward, the interpolator, according to his custom, inserts certain material and attaches longer patches from the Bible and other sources.] Hence it is written:

> Son, do not delay in turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day. For his wrath will come suddenly, and in the time of vengeance he will destroy you. Do not be anxious over unjust riches; they will profit you nothing on the day of calamity and vengeance. Do not winnow yourself before every wind, and do not walk along every path, for thus the double-tongued sinner is exposed. Be steadfast in the way of the Lord and in the truth of your understanding and knowledge, and let the word of peace and justice follow you.
>
> Be gentle in hearing the word of God, so that you may understand, [Col. 0171B] and give your answer with wisdom. If you possess understanding, answer your neighbor; but if not, let your hand be upon your mouth, lest you be caught by an undisciplined word and put to shame. Honor and glory are found in the discourse of a sensible man, but the tongue of the imprudent is his ruin. Do not be called a whisperer, and do not be caught by your tongue and put to shame. Shame and repentance lie upon the thief, and the worst condemnation [Note: [Col. 0171D] “Devouring,” Labbe.] upon the double-tongued; but hatred, hostility, and disgrace lie upon the whisperer.
>
> Do justice to the small and the great alike. Do not become your neighbor’s enemy for the sake of a friend. For the wicked man will inherit reproach and disgrace, as will every envious and double-tongued sinner. Do not exalt yourself in the thought of your soul like a bull, lest your strength perhaps be shattered through foolishness; it will consume your leaves and destroy your fruit, [Col. 0171C] and you will be left like a withered tree in the wilderness. For a wicked soul destroys the person who possesses it, hands him over to the delight of his enemy, and brings him into the lot of the ungodly.  
> (Ecclus. 6)

Brothers, admonish one another with such exhortations; always pursue good and avoid evil. For with great diligence (Gelasius, Letter 9), according to the blessed Apostle, care must be taken lest the faith and discipline of the Lord be blasphemed (1 Tim. 6). Even if those things which by themselves cannot cause harm, provided that the integrity of the other matters is secure, must sometimes be tolerated, those things must nevertheless be guarded against with the utmost care which cannot be accepted without manifest discredit. But if regard for circumstances and times, or concern for an expedited provision, excuses those very things which are sometimes believed capable of being permitted without any injury, how much more must those things [Col. 0171D] in no way be impaired which neither any necessity nor any ecclesiastical advantage whatsoever compels us to impair?

For this reason, brothers, we have set these things before you: those kinds of offerings which, according to the ordinance of the apostles and their successors (Apostolic Canons 3, 4, and 5, from the translation of Dionysius Exiguus), may not be offered upon the altar are to be carried to the priests’ house, blessed by the priests, and, once blessed with a simple blessing, finally received by the people. Only beans and grapes, and the other things which the apostles [Col. 0172A] prescribed, are to be offered upon the altar.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, we desire (St. Gregory, Letter 52, book IV), and with all our prayers beseech almighty God, that he may cause your love to grow more and more fervent in steadfast love of him, and grant you to remain in one harmony within the peace of the Church. We also admonish your brotherhood (St. Gregory, Letter 25, book II) to keep diligent watch over the souls entrusted to you and to attend more to the gain of souls than to the advantages of the present life. Be diligent guardians in preserving and administering ecclesiastical property, so that when the coming Judge comes to judge, he may approve that you have worthily discharged in every respect the pastoral office you undertook.

May almighty God keep you under his protection (St. Gregory, Letter 50, book [Col. 0172B] IV), grant you to preserve by your conduct the honor bestowed upon you by God, and help you to lead the souls entrusted to you, with abundant fruit, to the eternal pastures and to present them worthily to him; and may he deign to place you among his saints and elect.

Given on the second day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of the most illustrious Aurelian and Marcellus [Note: [Col. 0171D] “Marcellinus,” Labbe.]. [Note: [Col. 0172D] In the year 275, while Felix was not yet dead.]

## LETTER II. TO THE BISHOPS ESTABLISHED THROUGHOUT SICILY

[Note: [Col. 0172D] Merlin and certain others wrongly read “Ciciliam.” Labbe.]

I. On the manner of receiving an accusation against clerics.  
II. Those who are not to be admitted as accusers of religious persons.  
III. On the manner of proceeding in ecclesiastical affairs, since one must not proceed according to the secular manner.

[Col. 0172C] To all his most beloved brothers, the bishops established throughout Sicily, Eutychian.

Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us (Eph. 1, from a version combining the Old Latin and Jerome’s translation) with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and immaculate before him in love. He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ unto himself, according to the purpose of his will, for the praise of the glory of his grace, by which he bestowed grace [Note: [Col. 0172D] “He made us acceptable,” Labbe.] upon us in his beloved Son. In him we have redemption through his blood, the remission of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which he caused to abound in us in all wisdom and prudence, so that he might make known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, [Col. 0172D] which he purposed in him for the dispensation of the fullness of times: to restore in Christ all things in heaven and on earth, in him.

In him we also were called by lot, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we who first hoped in Christ might exist for his praise and glory. In him you also, when you had heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation, and had believed in him, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of our inheritance, unto the redemption of the possession, [Col. 0173A] for the praise of his glory.

Therefore I also, hearing of your faith in the Lord Jesus Christ and your love toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you and making mention of you in my prayers, that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, with the eyes of your heart enlightened, so that you may know what is the hope of his calling, what are the riches of the glory of his inheritance among the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of his power toward us who have believed, according to the working of his mighty power. He worked this in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, above every principality, authority, power, dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the age to come. He subjected all things beneath [Col. 0173B] his feet and gave him as head over the whole Church, which is his body and his fullness: he who fills all things in all. [Note: [Col. 0173D] “Is filled,” Labbe.]

And when you were dead in your offenses and sins (Eph. 2), in which you once walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of this air, the spirit who now works in the children [Note: [Col. 0173D] “In the children,” accusative, Labbe.] of unbelief, among whom we too once conducted ourselves in the desires of our flesh, doing the will [Note: [Col. 0173D] “The wills,” Labbe.] of the flesh and of our thoughts, we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest.

But now, brothers, because by his grace and freely given mercy God has made us his children from being children of wrath—and because we who were not worthy servants have been made his sons, not through any preceding merits but by his grace, as we have said—in him we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. 8). Let us follow his examples, being at once children of mercy, [Col. 0173C] justice, and love, so that with his help we may be both called and truly be children of God, laying aside, according to the Apostle Peter, all malice, all deceit, hypocrisies, envies, and all detractions (1 Pet. 2).

Those who do such things are shown to be not children of God but rather children of wickedness, as the Apostle Paul says:

> The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, wantonness, idolatry, sorcery, hostilities, contentions, jealousies, outbursts of wrath, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.  
> (Gal. 5)

The statement is grave, brothers, and exceedingly dreadful: “Those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.” And [Col. 0173D] Truth itself says: “What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, but suffer the loss of his soul?” (Matt. 16).

The things we have set forth are exceedingly grave and must be avoided with the utmost care. For those to whom the kingdom of God is closed are undoubtedly denied the Church as well. Concerning them, the Lord in the Gospel, proclaiming the authority of the apostles and their successor, says: “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and those whom you bind shall be bound” (John 20; Matt. 18). That is: those whom you exclude from the Church, unless they have been reconciled through satisfaction, [Col. 0174A] will also find the gate of the heavenly kingdom closed to them.

### I

Therefore, guarding against these things (*Causa* 2, question 6, *Not Thus in Ecclesiastical Matters*) and foreseeing the dispositions of fools, we decree, with pastoral care and together with all the bishops and the faithful of both orders of the holy Roman and universal Church, that ecclesiastical cases must not be conducted in the same manner as secular cases. For under secular laws, after someone who has been summoned has appeared and begun to contend in court, he is not permitted to withdraw before the case has been completed. In ecclesiastical proceedings, however, he is permitted to withdraw after stating his case, if this should be necessary or if he sees that he is being unduly burdened.

As for the procedure of accusation, [Note: [Col. 0174D] Hadrian, collection 7, from the Theodosian Code, book IX, title 1, law 2, the final constitution, as Antonius Augustinus sagaciously divined.] we both declare [Note: [Col. 0174D] “To be,” Labbe.] and command [Note: [Col. 0174D] “We have learned,” Labbe.] that the following procedure be observed: if any cleric becomes entangled in a criminal charge, a man who [Col. 0174B] could be accused is not for that reason immediately to be regarded as guilty, lest we render innocence suspect.

Rather, whoever he is (*Causa* 1, question 8, *Whoever That Man Is*) who brings the charge must come into court, state the defendant’s name, accept the bond of formal inscription, and observe the law of equivalent punishment. He is nevertheless to receive consideration appropriate to his rank, lest perhaps [Note: [Col. 0174D] Other reading: “lest perhaps he suffer”; another: “let him suffer. Lest perhaps,” Labbe.] he think that he possesses a license to lie, since the law of reciprocal punishment demands vengeance against false accusers.

For all heretics, suspected persons, excommunicates, murderers (Hadrian, collection 63), criminals, thieves, perpetrators of sacrilege, robbers, poisoners, adulterers, those who have committed abduction or given false testimony, and those who resort to diviners and magicians are under no circumstances to be admitted as accusers.

### II

No person of ill repute whatsoever (*Causa* 3, question 4, *No Person of Ill Repute Whatsoever*), nor any sacrilegious person, is permitted in any matter [Col. 0174C] to give testimony against a devout Christian, even if that Christian is a person of humble and servile status; nor may such a person assail a Christian concerning any matter, action, or formal accusation.

The right to accuse or testify is likewise to be denied to all who have disregarded the dignity of the Christian religion and name, the norm of their own law or profession, or matters regularly forbidden to them (Anianus, on Constitution I, title 7, book X of the Theodosian Code).

### III

Likewise, we forbid ecclesiastical judges to hear any cases that are not covered by the laws or are known to be prohibited. Not only ecclesiastical laws but also secular laws command that these provisions be observed. [Note: [Col. 0174D] By which emperors were they enacted in favor of ecclesiastics? In the time of Eutychian and his predecessors?]

For an accusation against priests ought not to be made indiscriminately and at random (Second Council of Carthage). For if it were readily admitted, far too few would be found free of accusation, because [Col. 0174D] all who desire to live devoutly in Christ suffer persecution. Blessed, however, are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake. Hence Truth itself says (I Tim. 3; Matt. 5; John 17):

> Father, I have revealed your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world. They were yours, [Col. 0175A] and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word. Now they know that everything you have given me is from you, because the words you gave me I have given to them, and they have received them. They have truly known that I came forth from you, and they have believed that you sent me.
>
> I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours. All that is mine is yours, and yours is mine, and I have been glorified in them. I am no longer in the world, but they are in the world, and I am coming to you. Holy Father, preserve in your name those whom you have given me, that they may be one, just as we are.
>
> While I was with them, I preserved them in your name. I guarded those whom you gave me, and not one of them perished except the son of perdition, that Scripture might be fulfilled. But now I am coming to you, and I speak these things in the world so that they may have my joy fulfilled within themselves.
>
> I have given them your word, and [Col. 0175B] the world has hated them because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. I do not pray that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil. They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.
>
> Sanctify them in truth. Your word is truth. Just as you sent me into the world, so I have sent them into the world. For their sake I sanctify myself, that they too may be sanctified in truth.
>
> Yet I pray not only for them, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one, and that the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory that you gave me I have given them, that they may be one, just as we are one: I in them and you in me, that they may be brought to completion in unity, so that the world may know that you sent me and that you loved them just as you loved me.
>
> Father, I desire that those whom you have given me may also be with me where I am, so that they may see my glory, [Col. 0175C] which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world. Righteous Father, the world has not known you, but I have known you, and these have known that you sent me. I have made your name known to them, and I shall make it known, so that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.

And the same John, apostle and evangelist, speaks in his First Epistle, saying (I John 4):
