> Most beloved, let us love one another, because love is from God, and everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.
>
> In this the love of God was revealed among us: that God sent his only-begotten Son into the world so that we might live through him. In this is love—not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as propitiation for our sins.
>
> Most beloved, if God so loved [Col. 0175D] us, we too ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God. If we love one another, God remains in us, and his love is perfected in us.
>
> By this we understand that we remain in him and he in us: because he has given us of his Spirit. And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son as Savior of the world. Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him and he in God.
>
> And we have seen and believed the love that God has for us. God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God in him. In this, love is perfected with us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, because as he is, so [Col. 0176A] are we in this world.
>
> There is no fear in love; rather, perfect love casts fear outside, because fear entails punishment. Whoever fears has not been perfected in love. Let us therefore love God, because God first loved us.
>
> If anyone says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar. For how can one who does not love his brother, whom he sees, love God, whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from God: that whoever loves God should also love his brother.
>
> Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God. And everyone who loves the one who begot also loves the one who was born from him. By this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God and carry out his commandments. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments; and his commandments are not [Col. 0176B] burdensome (I John 5).

And through the prophet the Lord admonishes that his disciples and their successors are not to be harmed, saying (Ps. 32, from St. Jerome’s version, which he combines with the Old Latin and the Itala):

> The angel of the Lord encircles those who fear him and will rescue them. Taste and see that the Lord is good. Blessed is the man who hopes in him.
>
> Fear the Lord, all you his saints, because those who fear him suffer no want. Lions have been in need and have gone hungry, but those who seek the Lord will lack no good thing.
>
> Come, children, listen to me; I shall teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man who desires life and loves to see good days? Guard your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it.
>
> The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears attend to their cry. But the face [Col. 0176C] of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy the memory of them from the earth.
>
> The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard them and delivered them from all their afflictions. The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and will save those crushed in spirit.
>
> Many are the afflictions of the righteous man, but the Lord will deliver him from them all. The Lord guards all his bones; not one of them will be broken.
>
> Wickedness will slay the impious, and those who hate the righteous will be held guilty. The Lord will redeem the souls of his servants and will deliver them.

You, therefore, brothers (Ps. 54), place your hearts upon the Lord, and he will sustain you, because he will never allow the righteous to be shaken. But God our Lord will bring our enemies down, according to the prophet’s words, into the pit of destruction, because men of bloodshed and deceit will not live out half their days. Yet always hope in the Lord and place your confidence [Col. 0176D] in him, because he himself will deliver us. For he is blessed from age to age, and of his kingdom there will be no end (Luke 1).

Issued on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October [19 September] (in the year 283), in the consulship of the most illustrious Carus for the second time and Carinus. [Note: [Col. 0176D] “The thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, under Carus,” etc. This confirms what we said above in the notes to the *Life of Eutychian*, at the words “the eighth day before the Kalends of August”: that it is more accurate to say that Eutychian died on the sixth day before the Ides of December [8 December], rather than on the eighth day before the Kalends of August [25 July]. For this letter was written after August, in the month of September; it is therefore entirely certain that, at least according to what the Pontifical says, he did not depart this life in July. SEVERINUS BINIUS.]

# DECREES OF POPE EUTYCHIAN—IF, INDEED, THE NAME OF EUTYCHIAN ITSELF IS NOT AN ERROR—WHICH ARE NOT CONTAINED IN THE PRECEDING MATERIAL, TAKEN BY LABBÉ FROM GRATIAN, IVO, AND OTHERS

[Col. 0177]

## FIRST  
### One must not obey a bishop who orders Mass to be celebrated for heretics

[Col. 0177A]

If any bishop or abbot orders his priest or monk to celebrate Masses for heretics [Note: [Col. 0177D] The other compilers add “who are dead”; for [Col. 0178D] it is lawful to pray even for the living and for other evil persons, including by a special prayer. LABBÉ.], this is not permitted. For it is not expedient to obey them.

## SECOND  
### An abbess who presumes to veil a virgin or widow is to be excommunicated

We have likewise found in certain places an unusual practice, full of folly and contrary to ecclesiastical authority: namely, that some abbesses and certain nuns presume, contrary to divine law, to impose the veil upon widows and young virgins. Consequently, some women who have been unlawfully veiled suppose that they may [Col. 0177B] more freely serve their carnal desires and fulfill their own wishes.

We therefore decree that if, after this ruling, an abbess or any nun whatsoever should break forth into such audacity as to presume to veil either a widow or a young virgin, she is to be subjected to canonical judgment until she makes satisfaction. (*In the Decrees of Ivo*, book III; 20, q. 2, *Statuimus ut si abbatissa*.)

## THIRD  
### One who refuses to perform penance for perjury is to be deprived of fellowship with the faithful

It must also be preached that the faithful should beware of perjury and abstain from it with the greatest care, knowing that it is a grave crime, prohibited in the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel (Lev. 6; Josh. 9; Mal. [Col. 0177C] 3; Matt. 5).

We have heard, however, that some make light of this crime and impose a comparatively lenient measure of penance for acts of perjury. They ought to know that the same penance must be imposed for perjury as for adultery, fornication, homicide committed voluntarily, and the other criminal vices.

But if anyone, after committing perjury or any other criminal sin, refuses to come to confession because he fears a lengthy penance, he is to be excluded from the Church—that is, from the communion and fellowship of the faithful—so that no one may eat with him, drink with him, pray with him, or receive him into his house.

## FOURTH  
### One who mutilates limbs or burns houses without judicial authority is to be excommunicated

[Col. 0177D]

If anyone has mutilated limbs or burned houses, [Col. 0178A] has ordered these things to be done, or has consented to the person doing them, let him know that he is deprived of the Church until he has made lawful and amicable amends to each person for these acts before the bishop of the city and the other citizens. But if, after a second and third summons, he has not corrected all the matters of which he is accused, he is to be separated from the entire fellowship of Christians as a heathen and a tax collector.

## FIFTH  
### After baptism, a believer has the choice of taking back the wife whom he had previously dismissed

If a gentile has dismissed his gentile wife before baptism, after his baptism it will lie within his power either to take her back or not to take her back.

## SIXTH  
### A believer is not compelled to follow an unbeliever who departs

[Col. 0178B]

Likewise, if one of a married couple has been baptized and the other remains a gentile and is unwilling to follow, it is as the Apostle says: “If the unbeliever departs, let the unbeliever depart” (I Cor. 7).

## SEVENTH  
### The synodal oath

A bishop presiding in a synod, after a suitable address, should call forward seven men from the people of his [Note: [Col. 0177D] “His own,” Labbé.] parish—or more, as he sees fit—who are more mature, honorable, and truthful. When the sacred relics have been brought forward [Note: [Col. 0177D] “Having been brought forward,” Labbé.], he should bind each of them by an oath in the following form:

> From now onward [Note: [Col. 0177D] “Previously,” Labbé.], whatever you know or have heard, or [Col. 0178C] may subsequently inquire into, that has been done or will be done in this parish contrary to the will of God and right Christianity—if it occurs in your days—provided that it comes to your knowledge in any way whatsoever; if you know, or if it has been reported to you, that it is a synodal matter and pertains to the bishop’s ministry, you shall in no way conceal it from the bishop, or from the agent whom he has ordered to investigate it, whether from affection, fear, reward, or kinship, whenever he questions you about it. So may God and these relics of the saints help you.
>
> And that [Note: [Col. 0178D] Burchard reads “this” and prefixes the heading *The Oath of the Others*.] oath which he duly [Note: [Col. 0178D] “This man,” Labbé.] swore concerning a synodal matter, you shall observe on your own part, insofar as you know or have heard anything, or shall inquire into it from this day onward. So may God help you.

## EIGHTH  
### From the decree consisting of sixteen books, book fourteen, chapter two: The evil of drunkenness is to be avoided entirely

[Col. 0179A]

We command Christians to guard by every means against the great evil of drunkenness, from which all vices spring. We have decreed that anyone who refuses to avoid it is to be excommunicated until he makes suitable amendment.

## NINTH  
### From the same work, chapter three: Bishops and ministers of God ought not to be weighed down by drunkenness

Bishops and ministers of God ought not to indulge in excessive feasting and drinking, but should consider the Lord’s declaration: “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness” (Luke [Col. 0179B] 21; I Thess. 3). They should take food in moderation [Col. 0180A] and only the necessary sustenance, so that, according to the Apostle, they may be sober and ready for the service of God.

## TENTH  
### From the same work, chapter ten: With what kinds of persons priests ought to share meals

We must take care that you abstain from drunkenness and preach that the people subject to you should likewise abstain. You are neither to go about drinking or eating in taverns, nor to wander through houses or villages out of any idle curiosity, nor to hold banquets with women or with any impure persons.

An exception may be made if some head of a household invites you to his home and wishes, together with his wife and his people, to rejoice with you in spiritual gladness, to receive the refreshment of your words, and to furnish you with bodily refreshment as a service of charity. For whenever any of the faithful refreshes you with bodily food, he ought in turn to be refreshed [Col. 0180B] by you with spiritual food.

[Col. 0179]

# THE MESOPOTAMIAN SYNOD OF ARCHELAUS

[Note: [Col. 0180] The Latin and Greek versions of the following text are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0179B]

The divine, holy, particular synod assembled in Mesopotamia by Archelaus, bishop of Carchar, and Diodorus the priest, against the infernal Manes and the presbyter Diodonades; after refuting them in many ways, it repudiated them.

[Col. 0180B]

**Greek version:** The divine and holy particular synod assembled in Mesopotamia by Archelaus, bishop of Carchar, and Diodorus the priest, against Manes the gloomy and the presbyter Diodoriades; after refuting them in many ways, it repudiated them.

# [THE COMPLETE WORKS OF POPE CAIUS]

[Col. 0179]

# HISTORICAL ACCOUNT OF ST. CAIUS, ROMAN PONTIFF

[Col. 0179C]

### The pontificate and death of Pope Caius

St. Caius—whom the *Pontifical of Damasus* reports to have been Dalmatian by nationality, of the family of Diocletian, and the son of a man named Caius—was appointed to succeed Eutychian in the year of the Lord 283, on Monday, 17 December, according to Coustant, whom the authors of *L’Art de vérifier les dates* follow. [Note: [Col. 0179D] Coustant, *Epistolae Romanorum pontificum*, vol. I, p. 306; Mansi also agrees with him in his notes on the annals of Baronius.]

He was a man of great prudence and great virtue, as stated in the *Acts of St. Sebastian*. [Note: [Col. 0179D] *Acta Sanctorum*, in the Bollandist edition, 20 January, chap. 18.] He is said to have confirmed the Church’s ancient institution that clerics should advance toward the episcopate through the seven grades of orders, giving proof of themselves along the way. [Note: [Col. 0179D] The number of orders as seven appears in the Epistle of Pope Cornelius in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chap. 43.]

Whatever else he accomplished while serving as pontiff for twelve years, four months, and five days lies hidden, buried in the darkness of antiquity. He ceased to live on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April], in the consulship of Diocletian for the sixth time and Constantius [Col. 0179D] Caesar for the second time, as is stated in the Bucherian Catalogue. The short list of depositions likewise adds concerning him: “On the tenth day before the Kalends of May, Caius in the cemetery of Callistus.”

Moreover, if the catalogues of the Roman pontiffs are to be trusted, Caius fled Diocletian’s persecution, lived in the crypts, and died as a confessor. [Col. 0180C] Nevertheless, his memory is recorded among the martyrs in some martyrologies. Nor is this surprising, since that title was sometimes also bestowed upon those who, although they contended for faith in Christ, did not exchange life for death, yet during their lives suffered persecutions, mockery, and hardships for their devotion and then died in peace. There can be no doubt that this happened to Pope Caius, who held the pontificate under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian.

The chronology of Eusebius is also less than accurate [Note: [Col. 0180D] Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, chap. 32.] when he says that Caius occupied the Roman See for approximately fifteen years, almost down to Eusebius’s own time; for it is established that Caius scarcely reached his thirteenth year.

### The decretal attributed to Caius

Isidore assigned to Caius, the Roman [Col. 0180D] pontiff, a single decretal addressed to Bishop Felix and comprising six chapters.

The first states that pagans and heretics cannot accuse Christians. The second states that a bishop is not to be accused before secular judges. The third concerns the accusation of a bishop, priest, deacon, or other cleric before bishops. The fourth concerns those who deny the incarnation of the Word of God. The fifth states that the hope of eternal life cannot be attained except through Jesus Christ, the mediator between God and humanity. The sixth concerns ecclesiastical orders.

[Col. 0181A] It is dated on the Kalends of March [1 March], in the consulship of the most illustrious Diocletian for the sixth time and Constantius for the second time. This subscription alone betrays the fraud. But the impostor’s foolishness rivals his dishonesty, since he appropriated an entire chapter of Leo the Great—the second chapter of Epistle 97—and inserted it word for word into the decretal.

If Caius had lent these words to Leo the Great, Pope Leo would undoubtedly have numbered him among the ancient witnesses by whose authority it is established that the epistle was addressed to Emperor Leo. For he ought much more to have mentioned Caius, both his predecessor and a more ancient author, than Athanasius, Ambrose, and Augustine, whose authority he employs to defeat the heretics.

LUMPER.

[Col. 0181]

# ON THE SINGLE DECREE CONCERNING THOSE TO BE ORDAINED WHICH IS ATTRIBUTED TO CAIUS

[Col. 0181B]

1. Not only has no genuine letter of this pope been transmitted to us, but none is mentioned anywhere. It is said only in the *Pontifical Book* that he decreed:

> That all should ascend through the orders in the Church as follows: if anyone deserved to become a bishop, he should first be a doorkeeper, reader, exorcist, acolyte, then subdeacon, deacon, and priest, and thereafter be ordained bishop.

2. If this decree is understood to have established that it is fitting for everyone to ascend through those ecclesiastical offices to the episcopate, rather than by a precipitous leap, Cyprian provides assurance that this practice had already been accepted before the time of Caius. For he proves from this that the ordination of Cornelius had been legitimate (*Cornelius*, ep. 10, no. 7):

> He did not arrive at the episcopate suddenly, but was advanced through all the ecclesiastical offices; and, having often earned God’s favor in divine ministries, he ascended through every grade of religious service to the lofty summit of the priesthood.

Cornelius himself [Col. 0181C] teaches us what those grades were when he records that at that time his church had (Ep. 9, no. 4):

> Forty-six priests, seven deacons, the same number of subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, and fifty-two exorcists and readers together with doorkeepers.

I would not venture to affirm, however, that Cornelius performed the duties of every one of those grades without exception.

3. But if the decree quoted above is regarded as an ecclesiastical law from which no one could be exempted except by the person who enacted it, it can easily be demonstrated from numerous examples that it is far more recent than Caius.

The Council of Sardica is later than this pope, since that council was held in 347 and enacted in canon 10—or canon 13 in Isidore Mercator—

> That if anyone from the forum, whether a wealthy man or a scholar, is considered worthy to become a bishop, he is not to be appointed before he has fulfilled the ministry of reader, deacon, and priest. [Col. 0181D]

It further requires:

> That he should hold the grade of each order for a period of no inconsiderable length, through which both his faith and the uprightness of his conduct . . . may become known.

The Greeks add the subdiaconate to these three grades, for they recognize only these four grades of orders together with the episcopate, as is evident from various records, and expressly from the following provision of the Eighth Synod, act 10, chap. 5:

> If anyone . . . is found to have passed through all the ecclesiastical grades with a blameless life for the prescribed periods—so that he has completed one year in the office of reader, two as subdeacon, three as deacon, and four in the priesthood—he is to be raised to the honor of the episcopate.

It therefore remains for us to prove that even in the Latin [Col. 0182B] Church, and specifically in the Roman Church, it was not required of everyone that they first pass through the seven aforementioned grades before they could be elevated to the episcopate.

4. Siricius, in Epistle 1 to Himerius, nos. 9 and 10, and Zosimus, in Epistle 9 to Hesychius, nos. 2 and 5, define the grades through which each person was to be advanced to the dignity of bishop or priest. They command that “the rudiments of divine service”—to use Zosimus’s words—be learned, not in the office of doorkeeper, but “first in the grade of reader.”

Indeed, when Siricius rules concerning one who is baptized at an advanced age that, if he hastens to enter sacred service, he should immediately—after receiving baptism—“be associated with the number of the readers or the exorcists,” he appears to require not both grades from him but only one or the other. Zosimus, in agreement with him, decrees concerning the same sort of person:

> After baptism, if he desires [Col. 0182C] to be assigned to the divine service, he is immediately to be placed either among the readers or among the exorcists.

This passage of Zosimus may, however, be explained so that “either among the readers or among the exorcists” means for him the same as “first among the readers and then among the exorcists,” especially since he prefaces it with these words:

> Let him become accustomed to the Lord’s camp, learning the rudiments of divine service first among the readers; nor let him consider it beneath him to become, in due order, an exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, and deacon.

What is remarkable is that although Siricius and Zosimus describe with such precision in the cited letters the individual grades through which they wish one to reach the summit of the priesthood, they consistently say nothing of the doorkeeper. They certainly would not have passed over it in silence if the decree quoted above had been promulgated by Caius.

The admittedly spurious but nevertheless ancient *Constitution of Sylvester*, [Col. 0182D] or Second Roman Council under Sylvester, agrees with them on this matter. In chapter 11 it decrees:

> That no one should be raised from the lay state, through the rank of acolyte [Note: [Col. 0181D] Perhaps “the rank of the acolytate,” Galland.] up to the episcopate, unless he had first been a reader for thirty years, then an exorcist for one day, and afterward assumed the burden of an acolyte and served ten years in that order of acolytes, so that he might assume the burden of a subdeacon and remain in the subdiaconate for five years, etc.

Just as no further mention of the doorkeeper is made here, neither is it mentioned in the following provision of the same *Constitution*, chap. 7:

> That all, from the subdeacon down to the reader, should be subject to the cardinal deacon of the city of Rome; that only the priest represents honor in the Church, while priests, subdeacons, deacons, acolytes, [Col. 0183A] exorcists, and readers represent obedience to the pontiff in every place.

The same constitution or council nevertheless mentions the doorkeeper in chap. 3, where we read:

> That no priest is to bring any accusation against a bishop, no deacon against a priest, no subdeacon against a deacon, no exorcist against a subdeacon, no reader against an exorcist, and no doorkeeper against a reader.

Accordingly, one must by no means infer from the silence of Siricius or Zosimus that they were unaware of the grade of doorkeeper, which Cornelius, as we have said, recognized. It can nevertheless be gathered from this that they did not consider service as a doorkeeper in any way a necessary requirement for those entering the clergy.

Certainly, infants whom they wished to enroll in the sacred service, although they could soon perform the office of reader, [Col. 0183B] did not so quickly become strong and capable of fulfilling the duties of doorkeeper. For it was the doorkeepers’ duty to repel from the church entrance those unworthy to enter.

Augustine, in his book *On Pastors*, now Sermon 46, no. 31, describes how among the Donatists the doorkeeper, “standing or sitting at the door” of their basilicas, questions those who wish to enter and casts out those who do not belong to the same communion. Infants were incapable of performing this duty.

Long after the time of Siricius [Col. 0184A] and Zosimus, Gelasius, in Epistle 11, chap. 2, although he recognizes the grade of doorkeeper, nevertheless prescribes in the same passage:

> If anyone trained in a religious vocation and in monastic disciplines enters clerical office . . . he is immediately to be made a reader, notary, or else defender; after three months he is to become an acolyte, especially if his age also supports this, and in the sixth month he is to receive the title of subdeacon.

Thus he permits not only the grade of doorkeeper but also that of exorcist to be omitted.

There is no need to present here examples of persons who attained the episcopate after omitting one, or even several, of the seven aforementioned grades. Therefore the decree under discussion seems no more to belong to Caius than the following decree belongs to Sylvester, although it was published [Col. 0184B] under the title of the Third Roman Council under that pope:

> If anyone desires to earn admission to the clergy, it is right that he should be a doorkeeper for one year, a reader for twenty years, an exorcist for ten years, an acolyte for five years, a subdeacon for five years, and a deacon for five years; and if he advances to the honor of the priesthood and serves in that order for six years . . . he is then to be chosen by the whole Church for consecration as bishop.

COUSTANT.

[Col. 0183]

# LETTER [Note: [Col. 0183D] Falsely attributed by Isidore. LABBÉ.] OF POPE CAIUS TO BISHOP FELIX: THAT PAGANS CANNOT ACCUSE CHRISTIANS; CONCERNING THE ACCUSATION OF A BISHOP AND HIS ACCUSERS; CONCERNING DESPOILMENT OR EXPULSION; AND CONCERNING THE INCARNATION OF THE LORD. (S)

[Col. 0183C]

I. That pagans and heretics cannot accuse Christians.  
II. That a bishop is not to be accused before secular judges.  
III. Concerning the accusation of a bishop, priest, deacon, or other clerics before bishops.  
IV. Concerning those who deny the incarnation of the Word of God.  
V. That the hope of eternal life cannot be attained except through Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and humanity.  
VI. Concerning ecclesiastical orders.

Caius to his most beloved brother, Bishop Felix.

[Col. 0183D]

We have gratefully received the letters sent to us by your Charity (Vigilius, Epistle 2), letters full of anxious concern for Catholic inquiry, and we bless the mercy of our Lord because he deigns to provide his sheep, even in the remotest parts of the world, with such shepherds. Through them the sheep may both abound in saving pastures and be preserved from the ravenousness of the wicked wolf [Note: [Col. 0183D] “Ancient enemy,” Labbé.], so that they may not fall victim to the snares of his stealthy encroachment.

Hence it is certain that the grace of the promised blessedness attends you, since you seek with such eager zeal the perfection of heavenly teaching. For it is written: “Blessed are those [Col. 0184C] who search his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart” (Ps. 118).

Therefore, most beloved brother, as we consider with our whole mind the purpose of your consultation, we trust that this disposition also proceeds from you, since you strive to maintain the rule of the Catholic faith in the same paths upon which you know it to have been founded in the Apostolic See.

And although the sound of the apostles has gone out through the whole world and their words have extended to the ends of the earth (Ps. 18, from Jerome’s version), and have proved the hearts of your Charity faithful to Christ, nevertheless, if anything in the Church entrusted to your governance with the Lord’s help has not yet become clear in the full light, you return to the same source from which that saving water flowed. This is something we have embraced with due charity, because you have confidently wished to be confirmed by our reply concerning those matters whose observance among you, you said, remained [Col. 0184D] uncertain.

Therefore, greeting your Charity in the Lord, we believe [Note: [Col. 0184D] “We have believed,” Labbé.] that you should be instructed point by point concerning what the authority of the Apostolic See maintains in accordance with Catholic discipline, with some chapters from the rules of the saints also appended.

### I

First, you should know that pagans [Note: [Col. 0184D] Baronius, in his notes for 31 January in the year 351, says that Optatus was the first to use this word, followed by Prudentius, Augustine, etc., and that it was not used before the period of the Christian emperors.] and heretics (2, q. 7, *Pagani et haeretici*) cannot accuse Christians or raise a defamatory charge against them.

[Col. 0185A]

### II

Next, let no one ever presume to accuse a bishop or other clerics before secular judges.

### III

And if any bishop, priest, deacon, or clerics of any rank are accused before bishops—for an accusation ought not to be made elsewhere—by any person who may properly be received as an accuser (these and similar provisions are taken from the Theodosian Code and Anianus; Hadrian, chap. 22), whoever he may be, whether a man of exalted honor or of any other rank, who undertakes this kind of blameworthy prosecution, let him know that he must produce documentary proofs.

Therefore, if anyone brings unproved allegations against persons of this kind, let him understand that, by the authority of this decree, he is to suffer the loss of his good name, so that through damage to his reputation and the forfeiture of his standing he may learn that, at least henceforth, he is not permitted to plot with impunity against another’s honor.

For we believe that the following matters have been sufficiently established by the apostles, their successors, and our predecessors: [Col. 0185B] how one is to come before a council; how those who have been despoiled of their possessions (3, q. 1, *Episcopus suis rebus expoliatus*) or expelled from their own sees are to proceed; which accusers are to be received and which are not; how everything taken from those who have been expelled and despoiled is to be restored to them according to law; that no charge can be brought against them before this has been done; how, after complete restitution, they are to be granted an interval of one year or six months; and how they ought to be permitted to arrange all their affairs lawfully and peacefully, without any person’s serious interference, and to avail themselves of the counsels of their friends and of the fathers of the Church.

I do not think there is any need to discuss these matters further at present, unless questions arise that are not yet clear. But if you do not possess their decrees, send the most trustworthy scribes, who may copy them in the presence of reliable witnesses and, under formal guarantee, bring them back to you.

## IV

Moreover, to satisfy your inquiries concerning the incarnation and reality of the Word: whoever those persons may be [Note: [Col. 0185D] “Whoever those persons may be.” Surius noted in the margin of this epistle that these words—in which the opinion of Paul of Samosata and of other heretics who deny the incarnation of the Son of God is most learnedly convicted and refuted from Scripture—from here to the end of the epistle are found in the first epistle of Leo to the Emperor Leo. (SEVERINUS BINIUS.)], they are so blinded [Note: [Col. 0185D] St. Leo, Epistle 97, from which certain passages have already been excerpted above in the first epistle attributed to Pope Eutychianus. See p. 914, C.] and so estranged from the light of truth that, from the time of the Incarnation onward, they deny the reality of the Word of God. Let them show in what respect they claim the Christian name for themselves, and by what reasoning they agree with the Gospel of truth, if from the blessed Virgin’s childbearing either flesh without deity was born, or deity without flesh.

For just as it cannot be denied, since the Evangelist says so, that “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1), so it cannot be denied, since the blessed apostle Paul proclaims it, that “God was in [Col. 0185D] Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5). But what reconciliation could there have been, by which God might again be made gracious toward the human race, if the mediator between God and humanity had not taken up humanity’s cause? And in what way could he have fulfilled the reality of the mediator unless he who, in the form [Col. 0186A] of God, is equal to the Father (Phil. 2), had in the form of a servant also become a participant in our condition, so that the bond of death, incurred through the transgression of one, might be broken by the death of one—of him who alone owed nothing to death?

For the outpouring of Christ’s righteous blood was so rich as a ransom that, if the whole company of captives believed in its Redeemer, the devil’s bonds would hold none of them; for, as the Apostle says, “Where sin abounded, grace also abounded beyond measure” (Rom. 5). And since those born under the sentence of sin have received the power to be reborn unto righteousness, the gift of freedom has become stronger than the debt of servitude.

What hope, then, do those leave themselves in the protection of this mystery who deny the reality of a human body in our Savior? Let them say by what sacrifice they have been reconciled; let them say by what blood they have been redeemed. [Col. 0186B] Who is it, as the Apostle says, “who delivered himself up for us, an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling savor” (Eph. 5)? Or what sacrifice was ever more sacred than that which the true and eternal high priest placed upon the altar of the cross through the immolation of his own flesh?

Although “precious in the sight of the Lord was the death of the righteous” (Ps. 115), the slaying of no innocent person was the redemption of the world. The righteous received crowns; they did not bestow them. From the fortitude of the faithful arose examples of endurance, not gifts of righteousness. For the deaths of individuals concerned those individuals alone, nor did anyone discharge another’s debt by his own end, since there has been only one Son of Man, our Lord Jesus Christ, who truly was the spotless Lamb, in whom all were crucified, all died, all were buried, and all were also raised. [Col. 0186C] Of these he himself said: “When I have been lifted up from the earth, I shall draw all things to myself” (John 12).

For faith, which justifies the ungodly and creates the righteous, when brought back to participation in humanity, obtains salvation in him in whom alone humanity finds itself innocent, possessing through God’s grace the freedom to glory in the power of him who, having engaged the enemy of the human race in the humility of our flesh, bestowed his victory upon those in whose body he triumphed.

Therefore, although in the one Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and of man, there is one person of the Word and the flesh, who inseparably and indivisibly shares common actions, the qualities of the works themselves must nevertheless be understood; and by the contemplation of an uncorrupted faith it must be discerned to what the humility of the flesh is raised, and to what the [Col. 0186D] loftiness of the deity inclines: what it is that the flesh does not do without the Word, and what it is that the Word does not accomplish without the flesh.

For without the power of the Word the Virgin would neither conceive nor give birth; and without the reality of the flesh, infancy wrapped in swaddling-clothes would not lie there. Without the power of the Word, the Magi would not adore the child revealed by the guiding star; without the reality of the flesh, the child would not be ordered to be taken into Egypt and withdrawn from Herod’s persecution. Without the power of the Word, the Father’s voice sent from heaven would not say, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him” (Matt. 3 and 17); and without the reality of the flesh, John would not testify: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

Without the [Col. 0187A] power of the Word, the restoration of the weak and the vivification of the dead would not take place; and without the reality of the flesh, neither food for him when fasting nor sleep for him when weary would be necessary (Matt. 4; John 11; Mark 4; John 10 and 14). Finally, without the power of the Word, the Lord would not profess himself equal to the Father; and without the reality of the flesh, the same Lord would not say that the Father was greater than he, since the catholic faith accepts and defends both, and, according to the confession of the blessed apostle Peter, believes that the one Christ, the Son of God, is both man and the Word (Matt. 16).

Therefore, although from that beginning when the Word was made flesh in the Virgin’s womb (John 1), there was never any division between the two forms, and throughout every stage of bodily growth the acts of the whole period belonged to one person, nevertheless, [Col. 0187B] so to speak, we do not confound by any commingling those very things that were done inseparably; rather, from the character of the works we perceive what belongs to each form.

Let those hypocrites, therefore, who with blinded minds refuse to receive the light of truth, say in which form Christ, the Lord of majesty, was fastened to the wood of the cross; what lay in the tomb; what flesh, after the stone of the sepulcher had been rolled away, rose again on the third day; and in what flesh, after his resurrection, he reproved certain unbelieving disciples and refuted the hesitation of those in doubt when he said: “Touch and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have” (John 19; Matt. 28); and to the apostle Thomas: “Put your hand into my side, and see my hands and feet; and do not be unbelieving, but faithful” (Luke 24; John 20). [Col. 0187C] By this manifestation of his body, indeed, he was already destroying the lies of the heretics, so that the whole Church of Christ, which was to be renewed [Note: [Col. 0187D] “Instructed,” Labbe.] by these teachings, would not hesitate to believe what the apostles had undertaken to preach.

## V

But if, amid so great a light of truth, heretical obstinacy does not abandon its darkness, let them show from what source they promise themselves the hope of eternal life, which cannot be reached except through the mediator between God and humanity (1 Tim. 4), the man Jesus Christ. For, as the blessed apostle Peter says, “There is no other name given to men under heaven by which we must be saved” (Acts 4); nor is there redemption from human captivity except in the blood of him who gave himself as a ransom for all and who, as the Apostle proclaims (1 Tim. 2; Phil. 2), although he was in the form of God, did not [Col. 0187D] consider being equal to God an act of robbery, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in human likeness and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and bestowed upon him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.

Therefore, since there is one Lord Jesus Christ, and in him the entirely one and identical person of true deity and true humanity, we nevertheless understand the exaltation by which, as the teacher of the Gentiles said, “God exalted him and bestowed upon him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2), to pertain to that form which was to be enriched by so great an increase of glorification. [Col. 0188A] For in the form of God the Son was equal to the Father (John 10), and between the Begetter and the Only-Begotten there was no distinction in essence and no diversity in majesty; nor through the mystery of the Incarnation had anything departed from the Word that had to be restored to him by the Father’s gift.

But the form of a servant, through which the impassible deity fulfilled the mystery of great godliness, is human humility, which was raised into the glory of divine power and, from the Virgin’s very conception, joined to deity in such unity that divine acts were not performed without the man, nor [Col. 0188B] human acts without God. Therefore, just as the Lord of majesty is said to have been crucified, so he who from eternity is equal to God is said to have been exalted; for, while the unity of the person remains inseparable, one and the same person is entirely the Son of Man because of the flesh and entirely the Son of God because of his one deity with the Father.

Whatever, therefore, Christ received in time, he received according to his humanity, to which those things it did not possess were conferred. For according to the power of the deity, the Son possesses without distinction everything the Father possesses (John 5); and the very things he received from the Father in the form of a servant, he himself also bestowed in the form of God. For according to the form of God, he and the Father are one (John 10); but according to the form of a servant, he came not to do his own will, but the will of him who [Col. 0188C] sent him (John 4, 5, 6).

According to the form of God, “as the Father has life in himself, so he also gave the Son to have life in himself” (John 5); according to the form of a servant, “his soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. 26). And one and the same person is, as the Apostle proclaims, both rich and poor (2 Cor. 8). Rich, because the Evangelist says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1). Poor, however, because for our sake “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid.).

But what is his emptying, and what his poverty, except the assumption of the form of a servant, through which, with the majesty of the Word veiled, the dispensation of human redemption was fulfilled? For because the original bonds of our captivity could not be broken [Col. 0188D] unless there came into being a man of our race and our nature whom the judgments incurred by sin did not bind, and who with his immaculate blood would wash away the deadly bond written against us, so, just as it had been divinely ordained from the beginning, it was accomplished in the fullness of time, so that the promise, signified in many ways, might attain its long-awaited fulfillment, and there could be no ambiguity concerning that which had always been proclaimed by continuous testimonies.

The impiety of the heretics reveals that they are engaged in great sacrilege when, under the appearance of honoring the deity [Note: [Col. 0188D] “By honoring the appearance of deity,” Labbe.], they deny the reality of human [Col. 0189A] flesh in Christ; and they think it a pious belief to say that, in our Savior, that which saves is not real. Yet, in accordance with the promise preceding [Note: [Col. 0189C] “Running through,” Labbe.] all ages, the world was reconciled to God in Christ (1 Cor. 5) in such a manner that, unless the Word had deigned to become flesh, no flesh could be saved.

For the whole mystery of the Christian faith is darkened by a great obscurity—as the heretics would have it—if the light of truth is thought to have lain hidden beneath the falsehood of a phantom. Therefore, let no Christian think that he should be ashamed of the reality of our body in Christ, because all the apostles and the apostles’ disciples, and all the distinguished teachers of the churches who deserved to attain either the crown of martyrdom or the glory of confession, shone in the light of this faith, everywhere thundering forth in harmonious declarations [Col. 0189B] that in the Lord Jesus Christ one person of deity and flesh must be confessed.

By what analogy of reason, or by what passage of the divine books, does heretical impiety think itself supported when it denies the reality of Christ’s body, although neither the Law ceased to testify to it, nor the prophet to foretell it, nor the Gospels to teach it, nor Christ himself to demonstrate it? Let them search through the whole sequence of the Scriptures for a place to which they may flee from their darkness, not for one by which they may obscure the true light; and through all the ages they will find the truth flashing forth so brightly that they will see that this great and wondrous mystery, which was completed at the end, was believed from the beginning.

Since no part of the sacred writings is silent concerning this, it is enough to have set forth certain mutually consonant signs of the truth, [Col. 0189C] by which the diligence of faith may be directed into the most radiant breadth of understanding and, by the light of an uncorrupted comprehension, may perceive that Christians should not be ashamed of the Son of God, who unceasingly professes himself the Son of Man and a man, but should glory in him with the utmost constancy; for, as the blessed Apostle says (1 Tim. 3): “Great is the mystery of godliness, which was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, [Col. 0190A] was preached among the Gentiles, believed in the world, and taken up in glory” [Note: [Col. 0190B] Thus far the words of St. Leo, from which you may see that the offspring have a different scent.].

## VI

Concerning the ordinations of bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the clerics who follow them, we know that the holy apostles and their successors—and especially Anacletus (Epistle 2, which has no credibility among learned men), as well as others—made sufficient provision; and therefore it is unnecessary now to repeat [Note: [Col. 0190C] “For us to repeat, except,” Labbe.] anything except what they did not establish.

Nevertheless, in laying down the following provision [Note: [Col. 0190B] “Nevertheless, we.” What is said here and above in the Life of Caius concerning the ecclesiastical hierarchy as established and instituted by Pope Caius must by no means be understood as though he were the first to institute the rule that one who was to ascend to the highest order should climb to the summit of the priesthood through the grades of the lower orders; for it has been related in many places above that an order of hierarchy of this kind had been established in the Church in the times of the apostles. Caius’s decree, therefore, appears to have established nothing other than that no one should be advanced to the episcopal throne unless he had ministered in each of the lower orders for the due and customary period. See Baronius, year 296, no. 2. SEVERINUS BINIUS.], we command you and everyone else to observe it: those who deserve to be ordained are to ascend to the ecclesiastical orders in the Church in this manner; that is, if anyone deserves to be a bishop [Note: [Col. 0190C] The words of the *Pontifical*.], he is first to be a doorkeeper, then a reader, afterward an exorcist, then he is to be consecrated an acolyte, thereafter a subdeacon, then a deacon, and afterward [Col. 0190B] a presbyter; and thereafter, if he deserves it, he is to be ordained a bishop.

And the districts, just as we have done in this city, are to be divided among deacons in each populous city. And whatever difficult questions arise throughout the individual provinces (Innocent, Epistle II) are always to be referred to the Apostolic See (St. Leo, Epistle LXXXIV, ch. 7; Vigilius, Epistle II).

Farewell, brother, and pray for us.

Given on the Kalends of March, in the sixth consulship of Diocletian [Note: [Col. 0190C] A.D. 296] and the second of Constantius, most illustrious men.

# THE COMPLETE WORKS OF COMMODIANUS OF GAZA

[Col. 0189]

# PROLEGOMENA ON COMMODIANUS OF GAZA, AN AFRICAN BY ORIGIN

## ARTICLE I. A Summary of His Life

[Col. 0189D]

### What did the ancients record concerning Commodianus?

Gennadius is the first of the ancients to mention Commodianus, and he expressed his character reasonably well in these words [Note: [Col. 0189D] Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 15.]:

> “Commodianus,” he says, “while reading our literature as well as secular literature, received an occasion for faith. Having therefore become a Christian, and wishing to offer Christ, the author of his salvation, some gift from his studies, he wrote, in unpolished language and something resembling verse, a book against the pagans. [Col. 0190D] And because he had touched upon only a little of our literature, he was better able to demolish their doctrines than to establish ours. Hence, in arguing against them concerning the divine promises, he employed a sufficiently mean and crude understanding, so to speak, striking them with astonishment and us with despair, while following Tertullian, Lactantius, and Papias as authorities [Note: [Col. 0190D] And certainly he follows Papias when he affirms the doctrine of the thousand years in the final chapter, and Tertullian in many of the things he discusses concerning the gods of the Gentiles. I am indeed doubtful about Lactantius, says the very learned Albert Fabricius in *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. I, p. 406, Padua edition, 1754, although Rigaltius also at first agreed with Gennadius in this respect—for in his second thoughts [Col. 0191C] on Instruction XXXIII he himself attached little weight to this opinion. Rigaltius did not hesitate to claim that Pope Sylvester is mentioned in Instruction XXXIII, v. 5; for he read the verse thus: “Enter Sylvester’s stalls, to the Shepherd’s manger.” Compare Barthius, *Adversaria* LIII, 5.]. He treated moral doctrine very well, and especially the love of voluntary poverty, and impressed it upon his students.”

Thus Gennadius; from him Honorius of Autun also derived a few remarks [Note: [Col. 0191C] Honorius of Autun, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, bk. II, ch. 15.]. But after the presbyter of Marseilles, Gelasius, the Roman pontiff, also mentioned Commodianus, listing his work among the apocrypha in his decree.

### The author calls himself “of Gaza”; but why?

To what country this author belonged is wholly unknown, since the ancient writers are silent concerning his homeland. Some assign him to the Italians and Romans. Those who think him an African employ a conjecture that is not altogether contemptible.

He does indeed call himself “of Gaza” (*Gazaeus*) [Note: [Col. 0191C] Commodianus, Instruction LXXX.]; but who could safely affirm that this derives from Gaza, the city of Palestine? Learned men, however, consider it more likely [Note: [Col. 0191C] He calls himself *Gazaeus*, not from some city called Gaza, but from *gazum*, or the treasury of the Church, just as he was called Commodianus from *commodum*, “provision” or “benefit.” The latter name belonged to him as a pagan; the former he adopted after becoming a Christian, perhaps for no other reason than that, after becoming poor following his conversion, he was supported from the Church’s common treasury. Hence he also calls himself Christ’s beggar. Cave, *Historia litteraria*, vol. I, pp. 136 and 237.] that he so designated himself because, after being admitted into the Christian congregation, he received his livelihood from the *gazophylacium*, or treasury of the Church. He is thought to confirm this conjecture himself when he calls himself “Christ’s beggar,” as we discover from the initial letters of the final Instruction when they are read upward in reverse order.

### He is considered an African

However the matter stands, Dodwell conjectures that Commodianus was an African [Note: [Col. 0191D] Dodwell, *Dissertation on the Age of Commodianus*, § 9.], because his Instructions have many things in common with St. Cyprian. Rigaltius, moreover, had preceded him in the same opinion [Note: [Col. 0191D] Rigaltius, Preface to Commodianus.]. In his judgment, the author’s style savors of the rusticity of African fierceness, although it nevertheless frequently recalls the pointed expressions of Tertullian, Cyprian, and Minucius. In Cave’s judgment [Note: [Col. 0191D] Cave, at the place cited.], further support seems to be provided by the words he employs—*Zabulus*, *Zacones*, and others—which are almost peculiar to African writers.

[Col. 0191C]

### Converted from pagan superstition to the faith of Christ, he composed a little book entitled *Instructions against the Gods of the Gentiles*

That he was a pagan by birth and upbringing he himself sufficiently indicates, both in his preface [Note: [Col. 0191D]

> I likewise went astray for a long time,  
> Frequenting temples, with my parents themselves unaware;  
> At last I withdrew myself from them by reading about the Law.  
>   
> (Commodianus, Preface, vv. 4–6.)]

and when elsewhere he addresses the Gentiles in these words [Note: [Col. 0191D] Commodianus, Instruction XXXIII, v. 491, and Instruction XXXVI, v. 374:

> I too lived as a pagan, lingering with a perverse mind. [Reading *fui* for the evident OCR *sui*.]

]:

> And I, who now admonish you, was once the same, wandering in ignorance.

Then, in Instruction LXI, he says that he was lifted out of the sewer—that is, out of the world and out of idolatry.

Therefore, while Commodianus was still without the Christian religion, still devoted to pagan superstition, and living in the darkness of superstitious and impious peoples, it came about by God’s gift that, as he devoted himself to examining the sacred writings, through reading them he gradually emerged from that night and, illuminated by heavenly light, gave his name to Christ [Note: [Col. 0192D] Commodianus, Preface, vv. 4–6.]. We know well from their writings that the same thing also happened to Justin Martyr, Tatian, and others.

Thus strengthened by saving doctrine and kindled with zeal for the faith, he turned first to the overthrow of the errors of the enemies of divine truth and devoted his effort to refuting their errors. For the sake of this purpose, therefore, he composed a little book under the title *Instructions against the Gods of the Gentiles, on Behalf of Christian Discipline*. In it he assailed the false divinities and corrupt cults of the Gentiles; and although excellence of talent and art is less evident here, he nevertheless displayed a quite exceptional holiness and a true and unfeigned love toward God.

### The period in which Commodianus flourished is investigated

Learned men do not agree concerning the age in which Commodianus lived. Rigaltius [Note: [Col. 0192D] Rigaltius, Preface to Commodianus.], Dupin [Note: [Col. 0192D] Dupin, *Bibliothèque des auteurs*, vol. I, pp. 326 and 328, in the notes to the Latin Cologne edition.], and Ceillier [Note: [Col. 0192D] Ceillier, *Histoire générale*, vol. IV, ch. 6, p. 179.] think that he flourished during the reign of Constantine the Great and the pontificate of St. Sylvester, whom Commodianus is commonly held by learned men to have mentioned in his writings.

Dodwell, however, judged him to have been earlier, either contemporary with Cyprian or only slightly later [Note: [Col. 0192D] Dodwell, *Dissertation on the Age of Commodianus*, Oxford, 1698, octavo.]. For this reason Cave, although in the first edition of his commentary on ecclesiastical writers he had listed Commodianus among the writers of the fourth century, was moved by Dodwell’s conjectures in the later Oxford edition and adopted the same opinion. Sebastian Pauli [Note: [Col. 0192D] Sebastian Pauli, *Dissertation on the Poetry of the Holy Fathers*, p. 180.], a regular cleric, assigns him to the period when the second century was drawing toward its close, in a dissertation published in Italian at Naples in 1714, in octavo, concerning the poetry of the Greek and Latin Holy Fathers in the earliest centuries of Christ’s Church.

### Gennadius examined

If, however, we listen to Gennadius, it would seem necessary to conclude that Commodianus lived, at the latest, in the fourth century; for he says that Commodianus followed Tertullian, Lactantius, and Papias as authorities. Most scholars have indeed thought that this was Gennadius’s opinion. But if his words are examined more deeply, they perhaps ought not to be understood as referring to the date of our writer, but rather to certain tenets which Commodianus is in fact found [Col. 0192D] to have shared with those authors.

Otherwise, one would have to say that the presbyter of Marseilles believed Papias to have been later than Tertullian and Lactantius, since he places Papias after those writers—something I certainly would not dare to affirm. Consequently, in my own judgment, Gennadius appears by those words to have suggested only that Commodianus at certain points followed doctrines which Papias first, then Tertullian, and afterward Lactantius taught with insufficient correctness.

[Col. 0193A]

### The opinion of Rigaltius is less satisfactory

However the matter stands, Rigaltius, apparently moved by the authority of Gennadius and taking his words as referring to the age of Commodianus, attempted in addition to confirm that date from the author’s own Instructions [Note: [Col. 0193D] Rigaltius, on Instruction XXXIII, v. 494.]. He believed, that is, that he had discovered a chronological indication by which he could establish that Commodianus was a contemporary of the Roman pontiff Sylvester and therefore of Constantine the Great. Nearly all learned men thereafter adopted this opinion of Rigaltius.

### Dodwell’s opinion seems preferable

But Henry [Col. 0193B] Dodwell, a most acute investigator in the examination of antiquity, first restored to its true reading, though with Sirmond as his precursor, a passage of Commodianus that had been tampered with by Rigaltius in his search for support for his own case. Then, after surveying the whole work, he perceived that it had been composed while persecutions of the Church were still raging; and thus he demonstrated that Commodianus belonged closer to Cyprian’s time than to Sylvester’s.

Indeed, most of that critical scholar’s arguments are of such a kind that they seem to possess very great power to compel assent. It is therefore my intention to present at least a concise account of them, since the dissertation *On the Age of Commodianus*, which that most distinguished man appended to his *Velleian, Quintilian, and Statian Annals* at Oxford in 1698, in octavo, is unavailable to very many readers.

[Col. 0193C]

### Dodwell’s opinion summarized by Cave

The very learned Cave summarizes Dodwell’s opinion as follows [Note: [Col. 0193D] Cave, *Historia litteraria*, p. 137, second Oxford edition, 1740.]:

> “It should first be noted, therefore, that Commodianus reckons only two hundred years from Christ. In Instruction VI, v. 2, he addresses the Gentiles as follows:
>
> > And if infancy perceived this, why for two hundred years  
> > Have you remained infants? Surely you will not always remain so?
>
> It must be admitted that the two hundred years in this passage are not to be understood strictly, as though there had not been a few more. For writers who lived before an exact epoch for the Christian era had yet been devised, when calculating the years from Christ’s birth down to their own age, generally speak in round numbers; they stop at the end of the century that has most recently elapsed and omit the additional period, whether greater or smaller. Arnobius sometimes expresses himself in this way, book I, [Col. 0193D] p. 9: ‘It is approximately three hundred years, a little less or a little more, since we began to be Christians.’ Nor did Ennius speak differently long ago: ‘It is seven hundred years, a little more or less.’
>
> “But they never did this when the years extending beyond the stated number occupied the complete span of the century in question, much less when they also embraced another century. Therefore, even though Commodianus could have said ‘two hundred years’ before the third century had fully ended, those words cannot by any reasoning be extended beyond the passing portion of that current century. By an altogether invincible argument that no sophistry can evade, our author must be confined within the limits of the third century.
>
> [Col. 0194A]
>
> “Commodianus wrote either when peace had only just been restored and was not yet complete, or when persecution was shortly expected. Hence he calls the peace ‘treacherous’ in Instruction LXV, and says that persecution is at hand: ‘the contest is exceedingly near,’ Instruction LIII, v. 10. He admonishes the faithful to assist the martyrs—or, to use his own word, to ‘co-martyr’ (*admartyrizare*)—in Instruction LVIII, v. 19. There he also describes the struggle with sorrow, and the palm bestowed upon victory, Instruction LXII.
>
> “He treats those who openly displayed a desire for martyrdom in Instruction LX, v. 1: ‘If the shepherd has made confession’—that is, according to Rigaltius’s interpretation, if, when questioned concerning the Name, he clearly and steadfastly answered, ‘I am a Christian’; and if, when ordered to place incense upon the pagans’ censer, he cried out in courageous refusal, ‘I will not do it’—‘he has doubled the contest.’
>
> “And, [Col. 0194B] not to accumulate further examples, he calls Caesar a tyrant in Instruction XXIII, v. 14. These and many other things are entirely appropriate to the third century, when, after the Decian persecution had ceased, the peace restored under Gallienus—weak and unstable as it was—was soon interrupted by persecution under Aurelian; but they cannot be reconciled with the time of Sylvester. For after Constantine gained control of affairs in the West, everything was quiet and peaceful, and there was no fear of persecution by the pagans. Christians lived safely under his protection, fortified by laws, adorned with privileges, enriched with wealth and dignities, and everywhere found the magistrates, following the emperor’s example, favorable and benevolent.
>
> “The whole manner of writing reflects the character, customs, and discipline of Cyprian’s age. He frequently uses almost the same modes of expression as Tertullian and Cyprian, as Rigaltius notes throughout. He appears to censure the schism of Novatus in Instruction XLII. In Instruction LXI, he reproves those who, while their brethren labored under arms against a hostile world, were themselves stuffed with wealth and neither fought nor presented themselves beside those who did; and who, when they saw a brother excluded because of schism, nevertheless desired peace in the camp—that is, the granting of indulgence to the lapsed before peace was restored to the Church.
>
> “In Instruction LVII, he contends that discipline must not be relaxed through excessive indulgence. In Instruction LII, he establishes two classes of deserters: ‘There is one wicked man,’ namely, one who sacrifices to an idol; ‘another partially withdraws,’ one who offers the governor a certificate and the extortioner money so that he will not be dragged to the Capitol to sacrifice. Rigaltius says that he has in view the *thurificati*, those who offered incense, and the *libellatici*, those who procured certificates; and the latter are scarcely mentioned in any age [Col. 0194D] other than that of Cyprian.
>
> “I should become endless if I were to list everything he has in common with Cyprian concerning penitents, zeal for martyrdom, flight during persecution, the designs of schismatics, the pomp of funerals, the duty not to mourn children who died during persecution, the Jews, and so forth.
>
> “Throughout this whole little book there is no mention—not even the slightest—of Constantine’s recently obtained victory over Maxentius; none of the sign of the cross miraculously appearing in heaven; none of Constantine’s glory and good fortune, or of the immunities granted to the Church. Yet this could rightly have been expected from a man burning with boundless zeal for his religion. I admit that this is a negative argument, [Col. 0195A] but among equitable judges of the evidence it possesses no small weight and authority.
>
> “Having set these matters forth, it remains for us briefly to examine the common opinion concerning the period of Pope Sylvester. Its sole basis and foundation is a passage of Commodianus as it appears in the printed texts, Instruction XXXIII, v. 5, where he invites the Gentiles to the Church:
>
> > Enter Sylvester’s stalls, to the Shepherd’s manger.
>
> “But these words are not Commodianus’s own; they are instead a fabrication of Rigaltius’s ingenuity, and the original words appear to refer to something quite different. In the Sirmond manuscript, from which Rigaltius made his copy, the words, by his own admission, read as follows:
>
> [Col. 0195B]
>
> > Enter the woodland stalls, to the bull’s mangers.
>
> “He is addressing the Gentiles as persons endowed with bestial minds and habits. Hence, in the preceding verse, he speaks of ‘savage and exasperated hearts’; in Instruction XXXV, v. 1, ‘You are wild like deer’; v. 5, ‘Do not be a wild beast’; v. 17, ‘Wandering like a beast.’ He therefore invites these people, who wander through woods and fields like bulls, to enter the Church’s stalls and approach Christ’s manger, where, as he says in the words immediately following, they might remain safe from robbers beneath a royal roof.
>
> “I therefore have no doubt that, with the distinguished Dodwell, we should read with a slight alteration:
>
> > Enter, woodland bulls, the stalls at the mangers.
>
> “*Sylvestres* is plural for *sylvestreis*, for the ancients wrote it in either fashion.”
>
> Thus far Cave, and perhaps more than enough from that most learned man.

Here I merely add the observation that Sirmond read:

> “Enter, steadfast ones, your … to the bull’s mangers” (*Intrate stabiles vestra ad praesepia tauri*; the transmitted wording is materially uncertain).

But the copy had:

> “Enter … into Sylvester’s stalls, to the bull’s mangers” (*Intrate stabilis Sylvestri ad praesepia tauri*; the transmitted wording is materially uncertain).

Finally, I observe that the distinguished Schroeckh, in part IV of his *Christian History*, p. 489, and the distinguished Oelrichs [Note: [Col. 0195D] Commodianus is wrongly relegated to the fourth century. Oelrichs, *Commentaries on the Latin Ecclesiastical Writers of the First Six Centuries*, p. 44.] adopt Dodwell’s opinion.

## ARTICLE II. Concerning the Little Book Composed by Commodianus

### The work’s division and purpose

The little work of Commodianus entitled *Instructions against the Gods of the Gentiles* contains eighty [Note: [Col. 0195D] Schurtzfleisch, Preface to Commodianus.] chapters in all. The first thirty-six are directed chiefly to persons alien to the Christian religion; after demonstrating to them the vanity of the impious divinities, he exhorts them to embrace the religion of Christ.

Those that follow, down to the forty-fourth, concern the Jews, whom the author earnestly invites into the fellowship of the Christian name; there he speaks at the same time about Antichrist, the judgment, and the resurrection. The remaining chapters are directed chiefly to the instruction of catechumens, devout worshipers of God, and penitents in particular, lest, forgetting the duties of Christians, they return to worldly things.

### The author’s style

“Commodianus wrote in unpolished language, something resembling verse,” says Gennadius. That is to say, as Rigaltius [Col. 0196A] explains [Note: [Col. 0196D] Rigaltius, at the place cited.]:

> “In composing verses he observes neither rules nor measures; everywhere he gives more attention to the acrostic than to the meter. The acrostics are formed from the titles of the respective short poems, with a letter allotted to each verse in such a way that, beginning with the first verse of each poem, the poem’s entire title runs downward through the initial letters of the verses.”

In certain places, however, this rule fails, as learned men have noted in the appropriate passages [Note: [Col. 0196D] In the final chapter, the acrostic is to be read not, as in the others, from the first verse to the last, but from the last to the first; it yields the words: “Commodianus, Christ’s beggar.”].

The verses of Commodianus are so arranged that the rhythm of hexameter verse is preserved throughout, while syllabic quantity is disregarded, as in St. Augustine’s trochaic psalm against the Donatist party, which is prefixed to his writings against Donatus in volume IX of his works; or as in other examples in the illustrious Scipione Maffei’s dissertation *On Rhythmic Verse* (*Sopra i versi ritmici*), appended to his *Diplomatic History*, p. 186 ff.; and in the hexameters prefixed to a Latin biblical codex from about A.D. 750, published by Cardinal Gregorio in Giusto Fontanini’s appendix to *The Silver Votive Disc*, p. 86; or as is customary in the political verse of modern Greece; or like the Greek hexameter poem from the Murbach manuscript Psalter published by the celebrated Montfaucon in his *Greek Palaeography*, p. 220.

As regards his manner of writing, it is indeed rather harsh, because unfamiliar words are employed throughout in Latin; but in compensation the author intersperses uncommon pieces of learning from Greek and Latin antiquity, as learned men have observed.

### The value and critical assessment of the work

Moreover, in this monument of ecclesiastical antiquity one sees above all its ancient piety [Col. 0196C]. For its author everywhere reveals himself as a good man, truly Christian, removed from all ostentation of worldly glory, and an outstanding practitioner of the charity that particularly befits a Christian. Yet it must not be concealed that the little book is sprinkled with several blemishes that Commodian shares with some of the earlier Fathers. Such are the accounts of the deserting angels, from whom the giants were born [Note: [Col. 0196D] Commodian, *Instructions* III]; of chiliasm, the first resurrection, earthly felicity, and so forth [Note: [Col. 0196D] Id., *Instructions* XVIII, XLIV]. These doctrines seem indeed to have been the reason why the work was numbered among the apocrypha by Gelasius, just as Clement of Alexandria, Arnobius, Lactantius, Sulpicius Severus, and other most distinguished authors were likewise assigned to that category because of their own blemishes.

Gelasius’s judgment, however, should not be understood as meaning that works of this kind by earlier writers are to be rejected altogether—as though that supreme pontiff had wholly proscribed them from the Church, says the great Baronius [Note: [Col. 0196D] Baronius, at the year 31, § 60]—but only that they should be denied public reading in the Church. “On this subject we remember having made several observations elsewhere, drawing on the distinguished Fontanini” [Note: [Col. 0196D] Fontanini, *Literary History of Aquileia*, book V, ch. 11, § 8, p. 354], writes [Col. 0197A] the very learned Gallandius [Note: [Col. 0197D] Gallandius, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. III, Prolegomena, ch. 18, no. 2, p. XLVIII], from whom we have taken these remarks.

### The distinguished Dupin’s judgment concerning the style, the author’s character, and the value of the work

The very learned Dupin’s critical judgment [Note: [Col. 0197D] Dupin, *Library of Authors*, vol. I, p. 327, Latin ed., Cologne] concerning Commodian and his little book differs little from Gallandius’s assessment. “His style,” he says, “is harsh, his words barbarous, and his thoughts humble. The author seems to have been good, simple, humble, beneficent, most ardently aflame with love for Christ, wholly devoted to his religion, austere in conduct, fiercely hostile to vice, holding all the goods of this world in contempt, and one who would have made an excellent monk, as Rigaltius observed. Yet he was not unlearned or ignorant, for his work contains much erudite material pertaining to secular knowledge; indeed, it includes some rare and recondite information about the gods of the gentiles. He appears to have possessed a sound and keen mind [Col. 0197B], thoroughly instructed in Christian moral precepts.”

### Synopsis or analysis of this work

This little work may be divided into three parts. The first, containing thirty-six stanzas, is addressed to the gentiles, whom he exhorts to embrace the Christian religion after demonstrating that the gods they worship are fictitious. The second is addressed to the Jews, whom he likewise exhorts to embrace the Christian faith, showing that the Law was figurative. He discusses Antichrist, the Last Judgment, and the resurrection. The final part is addressed to Christian catechumens, the faithful, and penitents, to whom he gives excellent moral precepts; it begins with stanza forty-six.

Most of the errors of the ancients are found in this author. He teaches that demons are angels corrupted by love for women [Col. 0197C], from whose intercourse with them giants were born; that the world will end after six thousand years; that Nero is Antichrist; and that there will be a twofold resurrection: the resurrection of the good before the thousand-year kingdom, and the general resurrection that will occur at the Last Judgment. After the first resurrection, the good will remain on earth for a thousand years; afterward all human beings will be judged, the wicked cast into the fire, and the entire face of nature transformed.

His moral precepts are outstanding. He urges catechumens to lead lives free from sin; penitents to pray day and night and to conduct their lives with the utmost strictness in order to obtain pardon for their transgression. He exhorts the faithful to avoid evil and put away hatred [Col. 0197D], affirming that martyrdom would not profit them if they hated their brothers. He sets before apostates the enormity of their sin. He admonishes all Christians that, since they are soldiers of Christ, they must fight continually against their passions. He forbids attendance at profane spectacles. He urges Christian women to be modest and to shun luxury and magnificence in dress.

He gives excellent precepts to pastors and presbyters: that they discharge their ministry properly, lead blameless lives free from avarice, and above all come to the assistance of the poor. He tells the rich [Col. 0198A] not to become mentally conceited because of their wealth, but to distribute it to the needy, help them, visit the sick, and feed those in want. He says that the death of children and relatives should not be lamented. He condemns funeral processions and sumptuous funerals. He sharply reproves those who do not observe silence in church:

> “The priest of the Lord said,” he writes [Note: [Col. 0198D] Commodian, *Instructions* LXXVI: “When the priest of the Lord commands ‘Lift up your hearts,’ as the prayer is about to be made, so that you may keep silence, you answer clearly, yet you do not abide by what you have promised. He entreats the Most High on behalf of the devout people, lest anyone perish, while you turn to idle stories; you smile there, or disparage your neighbor’s reputation; you speak without discipline, as though God, who made all things, were absent and neither heard nor saw”], “‘Lift up your hearts to God.’ You answer that you have them raised to him, and immediately depart from your promise. He prays to God for the people, while you exchange idle stories among yourselves, laugh, slander another’s reputation, and scatter thoughtless words—as though God, who made all things and sees and hears them, were absent.”

He tells those who pray to God to purify their hearts before applying themselves to prayer. In a word, the final part of these *Instructions* contains outstanding exhortations [Col. 0198B] by which Christians are urged to pursue virtue and flee vice, as well as admonitions against the corrupted conduct of Christians and the crimes of that age, which were almost identical with those of our own. Thus far the very learned Dupin.

## ARTICLE III  
### On the editions of Commodian

### On Rigaltius’s edition

This treatise of Commodian long lay hidden in darkness and was first brought to light in the last century, after Father Sirmond had copied it from an ancient manuscript [Note: [Col. 0198D] Gilbert Gaulmin mentions this copy while it was still unpublished and emends two passages in his notes on Eustathius’s *The Loves of Ismenias and Ismene*, pp. 17 ff.]. Rigaltius had this copy printed in 1649—or rather, in 1650.

Rigaltius himself declares in the following words [Col. 0198C] how much care and labor he devoted to Commodian:

> “I possessed only a copy of the old exemplar of this little book,” he says [Note: [Col. 0198D] Nicolas Rigaltius, Preface to Commodian], “given me by the excellent Jacques Sirmond, but corrupted almost everywhere by hideous errors. Either Sirmond himself possesses the old manuscript, or he does not deny knowing where it may be obtained. I certainly agree strongly with those who think that license in conjecturing is futile and deceptive—indeed, in this branch of letters often pernicious. Yet the copies of this little book establish that the ancient manuscript itself had long since become extremely corrupt. Accordingly, as is customary in desperate cases, I resolved to make an experiment upon poor Commodian—not because I regard the matter itself as poor, since I consider no small value to attach to a Christian whom Gennadius numbered among illustrious men—to see whether, by some exercise of industry, this little book by a most ancient writer might be corrected and restored in our edition [Col. 0198D].
>
> “Moreover, whatever Commodian may prove to be, he was cited first by Gennadius and afterward by Gelasius. At last, in this century, he appeared in Sirmond’s hands, squalid [Col. 0199A], as though emerging from chains and from long neglect among the barbarians, and demanding vindication. He certainly could not have wished for a more excellent champion than Sirmond. For once displayed by him and shared with friends, he began to be received and fostered kindly. Nor would I have him hope for anything else from this edition than that, when presented once more to Sirmond, he may at last come forth under his full and lawful manumission, cleansed and polished in liberal attire.
>
> “Meanwhile, while that is being hastened, I desire to secure a manumitter of great authority; and, in reliance upon that man’s kindness, I trust that he will take in good part the few hours I have devoted to a man intensely concerned with establishing Christian piety and discipline. Thus he may appear beside Cyprian today, just as Minucius recently stood beside Tertullian; and now each teacher may rejoice in his own follower, and each minister likewise serve his own master or priest.
>
> “This man chastises his age, utterly defiled by evil conduct, as an everywhere vehement and forbidding monitor. As though in prophetic frenzy, he pours forth the sounds of verse, careless of order, careless of elegance, with asyndeta and anacolutha everywhere—yet in such a way that even amid the negligence there emerges care, ability, and a certain force of expression.
>
> “In my observations I have chiefly endeavored to append material from writers close to Commodian’s age that might cast light upon obscure passages. I have proposed such conjectures as no one should offer without ancient exemplars, though one need not be at all ashamed to employ them so long as the exemplars do not contradict them.”

Thus far Rigaltius.

### Survey of the editions of this little book

Nicolas Rigaltius was therefore the first to edit Commodian from Jacques Sirmond’s exceedingly corrupt copy, at Toul in Lorraine, through the royal printers S. Belgrand and J. Laurent, in 1650, quarto [Note: [Col. 0199D] The distinguished Rémy Ceillier, vol. IV of the *Histoire générale*, p. 6, p. 181, records a Paris edition of Commodian from 1648, while Gallandius records the Toul edition as 1649], adding learned notes.
