It was next appended to Cyprian, Minucius, Arnobius, and Julius Firmicus, who appeared with elucidations prepared by the same Rigaltius and Philippe Priorius, Paris, 1666, folio. It was then printed without Rigaltius’s notes in volume XXVII of the *Library of the Fathers*, Lyon, 1677, folio. After that it was reprinted at Wittenberg in 1705, quarto, with Rigaltius’s observations, Dodwell’s dissertation, and a preface by Heinrich Leonhard Schurtzfleisch. A supplement of notes on this writer, taken from Ezechiel Spanheim’s library, together with the aforementioned Schurtzfleisch’s glossary and index, was printed separately at Wittenberg in 1709, quarto.

In the later edition of his Minucius Felix, the distinguished John Davies likewise appended Commodian, elucidated with his own and Rigaltius’s notes, Cambridge, 1711, octavo. The Pesaro collection of Latin poets also includes this writer, in volume VI, in the year 1756.

Finally, Commodian was reprinted at Venice in 1767 in volume III of the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, pp. 621–653. Gallandius modeled his own edition on Rigaltius’s later Paris edition, placing Rigaltius’s notes and Davies’s observations beneath the text [Col. 0200A], and occasionally adding observations of his own. The distinguished Father Dominicus Schramm, a Benedictine of Banz, followed Gallandius’s edition in his *Analysis of the Holy Fathers*, vol. VI, Augsburg, 1784, pp. 483–518.

Baluze emended certain passages of Commodian from the manuscript codex of Saint-Aubin at Angers in his notes on Cyprian, pp. 454, 455, and 458. Cave [Note: [Col. 0200D] Cave, *Literary History*, vol. I, at the year 270, p. 138] closes his account of this little work with these excellent words of Rigaltius:

> “The use and efficacy of this little book will be an unwavering and perpetual love of Christ; a spirit courageous for martyrdom; and the greatest devotion toward the poor. It teaches, moreover, that the vices which still dishonor the Church are of the greatest antiquity; that the multitude of those disputing about divine matters has always been infinite, but the number of Christians very small.”

## ARTICLE IV  
### On Antonius, author of the *Poem against the Gentiles*

[Col. 0200B]

### The *Poem against the Gentiles* appended to Commodian; wrongly attributed to Paulinus of Nola

Because of the similarity of its subject, the very learned Gallandius appends to Commodian a *Poem to the Gentiles*, which Ludovico Muratori brought to light under the name of Saint Paulinus of Nola toward the end of the preceding century. John Liron, a Benedictine, was the first to observe correctly that this poem does not recognize Paulinus as its author, but another man named Antonius, converted from pagan superstition to faith in Christ. He did so in a work published at Paris in 1717 under the French title *Les Aménités de la critique, ou dissertations et remarques nouvelles sur divers points* [Col. 0200C] *de l’antiquité ecclésiastique et profane* (“The Pleasures of Criticism, or New Dissertations and Remarks on Various Points of Ecclesiastical and Profane Antiquity”). On this matter, besides the author of the *Historical and Critical Library of the Writers of the Congregation of Saint-Maur* [Note: [Col. 0200D] *Bibliothèque historique et critique des auteurs de la Congrégation de Saint-Maur*, p. 201], see the Paris *Journal des Savants* [Note: [Col. 0200D] *Journal des Savants*, 1717, June, pp. 654 ff.].

### Inquiry into who this Antonius was

Who this Antonius, the author of the poem, actually was, I cannot determine. Had he written in Greek, one might perhaps readily encounter among the Greeks someone to whom the poem could be attributed. But the author must be sought among the Latins.

### Fabricius’s conjecture concerning Antonius of Fussala rejected

Fabricius, on the verso of the title page of his selection of arguments published at Hamburg in 1725, attributes the poem under discussion to a certain Antonius of Fussala, without giving any reason why he should think so. But if he had in mind that Antonius of Fussala [Col. 0200D] whom Saint Augustine mentions [Note: [Col. 0200D] Augustine, Epistle 209, formerly 261, nos. 3 ff., *Works*, vol. II, p. 777, Benedictine ed.], the learned man would have strayed far from the truth. For we know from various passages that our Antonius, before giving his name to Christ, had been devoted to the impious worship of false divinities.

First, at the very beginning he says (*Poem*, verse 1):

> I, Antonius, confess that I examined every sect.

[Col. 0201A] Then, after a lengthy intervening passage in which he relates the fables of the gods, he adds (*ibid.*, verses 151–154):

> All these things I formerly believed, until the holy Church,  
> When I had gained the bright light, received me—  
> No longer uncertain and driven through so many storms—  
> Into the harbor of salvation, and after wandering waves  
> Established me in a tranquil abode.

And presently afterward (*ibid.*, verses 161–162):

> So may he who has now taken error from our mind  
> Open the light of paradise upon a better path.

But Augustine’s Antonius, bishop of Fussala, is said to have been born to Catholic parents. For the holy Father says of him [Note: [Col. 0201B] Augustine, Epistle 209, formerly 261, nos. 3 ff., *Works*, vol. II, p. 777, Benedictine ed.]:

> “Fussala [Note: [Col. 0201B] Augustine, *loc. cit.*, nos. 2–3] is the name of a fortified town bordering the territory of Hippo. Previously there had never been a bishop there. Without their having requested him, I offered them a certain Antonius, who was then with me and had indeed been raised by us in the monastery from a very young age.”

[Col. 0201B]

### By what right is the author identified as the Antonius known to Jerome?

The highly distinguished authors of the French *Literary History*, members of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, adopted [Col. 0202A] another opinion, putting forward another Antonius who is mentioned in Jerome’s correspondence [Note: [Col. 0202B] *Histoire littéraire de la France*, vol. II, p. 193]. Yet their opinion too is mere conjecture, supported by no foundation.

### What care did Gallandius employ in reprinting it?

Gallandius based his edition of Antonius’s poem upon Muratori’s later edition of 1736, printed at Verona, together with Muratori’s notes. Into these he also incorporated the learned observations that Cornelius Vonck had published to elucidate the same poem of Antonius (Vonck, *Critical Specimen*, pp. 1–10, Utrecht, 1744). Nor did Gallandius think that he should omit the remarks [Col. 0202B] made by an anonymous author in the Leipzig *Acta Eruditorum* in a review of Vonck’s *Critical Specimen* (*Acta Eruditorum*, Leipzig, 1746, pp. 215 ff.).

[Col. 0201]

# COMMODIAN’S INSTRUCTIONS AGAINST THE GODS OF THE GENTILES, FOR CHRISTIAN DISCIPLINE: THROUGH THE INITIAL LETTERS OF THE VERSES

[Note: [Col. 0201C]

**THROUGH THE INITIAL LETTERS OF THE VERSES.** Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, whose works Jacques Sirmond edited, wrote two epitaphs through the initial and final letters of their verses. GALLANDIUS.

**A favorable visitation.** The translators of the Septuagint call “visitation” *episkopēn* (ἐπισκοπὴν), that is, a visitation either of divine grace or vengeance; of blessing unto eternal life or of cursing unto Gehenna. The Wisdom of Solomon promises a favorable visitation to the just and holy in chapter 3: “And in the time of their visitation they shall shine forth” (*Kai en kairō episkopēs autōn eklampsousi*, Καὶ ἐν καιρῷ ἐπισκόπης αὐτῶν ἐκλαμφούσι). RIGALTIUS.

**By reading from the Law.** Here and commonly elsewhere he calls the books of both Testaments “the Law.” RIGALTIUS.—Minucius does likewise in *Octavius*, ch. VII: “Look in the books.” On that passage Davies observes that this manner of speaking is familiar to African writers, and especially to Tertullian. Commodian himself uses it below in *Instruction* XLVII, verse 745:

[Col. 0202C]

> I admonish the faithful: brothers, put away hatred.

DAVIES.

**I grieve for the civic multitude! Unaware that it perishes.** The punctuation presented by Dodwell in his *Dissertation on the Age of Commodian*, § IX, is preferable:

> I grieve for the civic multitude.

He grieves, Dodwell says, for people of his own condition, his associates in their former error. Thus *Instruction* XXII, verse 277:

> Alas, I grieve, fellow citizens, that you are thus stupefied by the world.

Davies takes the same view and thinks that immediately afterward *perit* (“it perishes”) should more correctly be read instead of *perdit* (“it destroys”). DAVIES.

**I instruct the ignorant in the truth.** Hence the title of the work, *Instructions*—namely, instructions in Christian piety. We also possess, under the same title *Instructions*, two books addressed to Salonius by Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, from the age of Theodosius the Younger. RIGALTIUS.]

(C)

## I.—PREFACE

[Col. 0201C]

Our preface shows the way to one who wanders,  
And a favorable visitation when the world’s boundary comes:  
To become eternal—a thing that ignorant hearts disbelieve.  
I likewise wandered for a long time,  
[Col. 0202C] Frequenting temples, while my parents themselves were ignorant.  
At last I withdrew from there by reading from the Law.  
I call the Lord to witness; I grieve for the civic multitude,  
Which, unaware that it perishes, persists in seeking vain gods.  
Therefore, thoroughly instructed, I instruct the ignorant in the truth.

[Note: [Col. 0203B]

**They prayed to dying gods.** In his notes on Cyprian’s *On the Vanity of Idols*, Baluze reads from the manuscript codex of Saint-Aubin at Angers: “They prayed to dead gods.” That reading indeed seems to be confirmed by *Instruction* XX, verse 262: “For in your folly you worship those who have died an evil death.”

**The resurrection too is taught.** In the Law of the Lord the resurrection of bodies is taught; the hope of life to be lived again in the age is also taught. From this point the author now begins to construct his doctrine of millennial felicity. RIGALTIUS.—**The resurrection is taught in the Law itself.** The Chiliasts indeed distorted several passages of Genesis in order to establish their opinion, but they also relied upon certain *rhēseis* (ῥήσεις, “sayings”) of the prophets and especially upon the Apocalypse of John. See Justin Martyr’s *Dialogue with Trypho*, p. 239; Irenaeus, book V, chs. XXX ff.; and Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book III, ch. 24. DAVIES.

**And fortunate in hope.** Tertullian had written a book expressing this thought, *On the Hope of the Faithful*. Agobard, bishop of Lyon, formerly possessed this book in his codex of Tertullian, as is declared by the index of the ancient exemplar preserved in the royal library. RIGALTIUS.

**To live again in the age.** “In the age” means on the earth, in this world. RIGALTIUS.

**THE WORSHIP OF DEMONS.** The things related in this *Instruction* about the apostate or deserting angels, from whom the giants were born, and about the demons born from the giants as authors of images and idolatry, are almost peculiar to Commodian. Yet I would not deny that what ancient Christians transmitted on this subject had its origin in the apocryphal Book of Enoch, from which Paul himself nevertheless cited something. But everyone has invented such varied and divergent accounts of these matters, and all disagree so greatly both with their source and with one another, that it is very uncertain what ought to be treated as a tradition—apart from this one point: that it is extremely rash for a mortal to assert anything about divine matters beyond what has been disclosed by our Lord himself. RIGALTIUS.

**When almighty God adorned the nature of the world.** *Kosmon kekosmēkas* (κόσμον κεκόσμηκας), “you have adorned the world,” with stars and angels. *Kosmos* (κόσμος): the Greeks designated it by a word meaning “ornament”; “and we too, from its finished and absolute elegance, call it the World,” says Pliny at the beginning of his second book. RIGALTIUS.—**The nature of the world:** the world itself. See below, *Instruction* VII, verse 89, § 2.

**He wished the earth to be visited by angels.** Moses did not say “angels,” but “sons of God,” concerning whom we have observed something at *Instruction* XXXVI. RIGALTIUS.

**Whose ordinances they despised.** That is, commands and laws.

**So great was the beauty of the women.** Justin, Athenagoras, Tertullian, Cyprian, Lactantius, Sulpicius Severus, and others transmitted similar things from that apocryphal Book of Enoch. Joseph Scaliger published its very words in his notes on the Greek passages of Eusebius’s *Chronology*, where he discusses the Watchers. RIGALTIUS.—This opinion arose from a misunderstanding of Genesis 6:2. Josephus, *Jewish Antiquities*, book I, ch. III, no. 1: “For many angels of God, having intercourse with women, begot insolent children” (*Polloi gar angeloi Theou gynaixi symmigentes, hybristas egennēsan paidas*, Πόλλοι γὰρ ἄγγελοι Θεοῦ γυναιξὶ συμμιγέντες, ὑβριστὰς ἐγέννησαν παῖδας). Likewise the author of the *Testaments of the Patriarchs*, in the *Testament of Reuben*, ch. V. Pamelius indicated passages from other writers in his notes on Tertullian’s first *Paradox*. DAVIES.

**Return to heaven.** That is, into heaven. VIRGIL, *Aeneid* XI, 191:

> The cry and the blare of men’s trumpets rise to heaven.

Likewise “received into heaven” in Phaedrus, book IV, fable XI, line 3. See Thomas Muncker on Hyginus, fable XV. DAVIES.

**From them the arts on earth.** The ancients derived this opinion from the pseudo-Enoch. Tertullian, *On the Dress of Women*, book I, ch. 2, will supply much on this subject. See also book II, ch. 10. DAVIES.

**Did not judge that they should be received.** Lactantius, book II, ch. XVI: “Then, not being received into heaven because of the sins in which they had immersed themselves, they fell to earth.” RIGALTIUS.

**They overthrow many bodies.** This is believed to occur in those subject to falling sickness, that is, epileptics. Augustine, *On the Happy Life*, p. 213: “These people suffer from the falling sickness; among us this is the popular name given to those whom the comitial disease overthrows.” We have commented on the words of Tertullian, *To Scapula*: “when he was cast down by a demon.” ID.

**When does he grow old?** Read *quomodo* (or *quo modo*), “how does he grow old?” Commodian is not asking at what time Saturn, who was regarded as a god, grows old. DAVIES.

**Why did he devour his children?** The familiar fable says that Saturn devoured his sons when he heard that his son would drive him from his kingdom, and that his wife, when Jupiter was born, offered the voracious father a stone in place of the infant. Servius on book XIII of the *Aeneid*. RIGALTIUS.

**He swallowed a stone in place of his son.** And a stone that certainly gave him colic. RIGALTIUS.]

## II.—GOD’S INDIGNATION

[Col. 0203A]

In the Law the Lord of heaven, earth, and sea commanded:  
“Do not,” he says, “worship empty gods  
Made by your own hands from wood or gold,  
Lest my indignation destroy you for these things.”  
Before Moses, the uncultivated nation lived without the Law  
And, not knowing God, prayed to dying gods,  
Making vain idols after their likenesses.  
When the Lord had brought the Jews out of the land of Egypt,  
The Almighty afterward imposed the Law and commanded this:  
That they should serve him alone, and not those gods.  
The resurrection too is taught in that Law,  
And the hope of being fortunate by living again in the age,  
If vain idols are abandoned and not worshiped.

## III.—THE WORSHIP OF DEMONS

[Col. 0203B]

When almighty God adorned the nature of the world,  
He wished this earth to be visited by angels.  
Those who were sent despised his ordinances:  
So great was the beauty of the women who seduced them  
[Col. 0204A] That, once defiled, they could not return to heaven.  
From that time the rebels uttered words against God.  
The Most High therefore passed sentence upon them;  
From their seed the giants are said to have been born.  
From them the arts were brought forth upon the earth;  
They taught people to dye wool and to do all that is practiced.  
Mortals also set up images to them after they had died.  
But because they sprang from wicked seed, the Almighty  
Did not judge that they, once dead, should be received back from death.  
Hence they now wander and overthrow many bodies—  
Above all, those whom you worship and invoke today as gods.

## IV.—SATURN

And old Saturn—if he is a god, how does he grow old?  
Or if he was a god, why did he devour his children,  
[Col. 0204B] Driven by terror? But because he was no god,  
In monstrous madness he consumed his children’s flesh.  
He was a king on earth, born upon Mount Olympus;  
He was not divine, but declared himself a god.  
He lost his reason and swallowed a stone in place of his son.  
Thus the god escaped: he is now called Jupiter.

[Note: [Col. 0205C]

**The smith Pyracmon had made his scepters.** One of the Cyclopes. Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, verse 424:

> In a vast cavern the Cyclopes worked the iron—  
> Brontes and Steropes, and Pyracmon with limbs bare.

Hesiod, however, gives another account in the *Theogony*, verse 140. Apollodorus agrees with him, *Library*, book I, ch. I, § 2. DAVIES.

**Not that Jovis.** Thus in the following *Instruction*: “Jovis thunders.” He frequently afterward employed *Jovis* in the nominative case, a practice also followed by much earlier authors. RIGALTIUS.

**ON THE THUNDERBOLT OF JOVIS HIMSELF.** Only this appears in the copy. But in the acrostic Commodian added “listen”—that is, listen in mockery, since throughout the poem he teaches that Jovis is not a god, does not thunder, and is not heard thundering. RIGALTIUS.

**And if childhood thought so.** Cujas, in his note on law 2, *On Patrimonial Estates*, which belongs to Constantine, and on law 1, *On Fugitive Tenant-Farmers*, which belongs to Gratian, observed that persons under twenty-five years of age were called “children.” Commodian lived near that period and employed the language of his century, which is also used by the ancient translator of Holy Scripture. RIGALTIUS.

**Why for two hundred years?** He counts two hundred years from the age of Christ, while the third century was still in progress. RIGALTIUS.

**Childhood changed into maturity.** The Old Latin version of Paul, 1 Corinthians 13:11: “When I was a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things of a child.” Apollonius in Philostratus, book I, ch. XIII, p. 23: “When I was a youth, I used to inquire; but now one should not inquire, but teach what one has discovered” (*meirakion ōn ezētēka, nyn de ou chrē zētein, alla didaskein ha heurēka*, μειράκιον ὢν ἐζήτηκα, νῦν δὲ οὐ χρὴ ζητεῖν, ἀλλὰ διδάσκειν ἃ εὕρηκα). RIGALTIUS.

**You believe that he thunders.** The old glosses: *Tonitruum, tonitru*, “thunder”; Greek *brontē* (βροντή). Other manuscripts have *brontē*, “thunder”; *brontō* (βροντῶ), “I thunder”; *brontaios* (βρονταῖος), “thunderable.” One should read *tonitrualis*. Lucretius, book I:

> Lest the thundering temples of heaven collapse from above.

RIGALTIUS.

**On goat’s milk.** Some identify Amalthea as the goat, others as the goat’s mistress. See Ovid, *Fasti* V, verse 113; Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book I, ch. XXI; and Hyginus, *Poetical Astronomy*, book II, ch. XIII. DAVIES.

**The lover of Ganymede.** The copy reads *erme*, with *medis Festus* written above it. They used *catamitus* for Ganymede, who was Jupiter’s concubine. RIGALTIUS.

**The lover of Alcmena.** So reads Rigaltius’s Paris edition of 1661, followed by the Wittenberg edition of 1705. But Davies, in his Cambridge edition of 1712, reads “the lover of Ganymede,” perhaps at Rigaltius’s suggestion, since Rigaltius expressed this reading in his note.

**And you say that they are heavenly.** For Ganymede too is said to have been carried off into heaven by the eagle. See Eusebius’s fourth minor work, Sirmond’s ed., pp. 198–199. RIGALTIUS.

The very learned Rigaltius has gone astray. Commodian is not now treating Ganymede, but censuring all the gods of the gentiles. DAVIES.

**ON THE SEPTIZONIUM.** *Septizonium*, *septemzonium*, and *septizodium* were names given to every sevenfold arrangement: masses constructed one upon another, gigantic complexes. Thus the Septizonium of Severus. Ammianus Marcellinus XV: “the Septizonium, a nymphaeum of ambitious workmanship.” Joseph Scaliger, *Observations on Eusebius’s Chronicle*, p. 209. GALLANDIUS.

**Driven out by Jove.** The copy reads: “He fled, driven out by Jove.” The verb “fled” is superfluous; once it is removed, both the verse and the acrostic stand correctly. For he is to be believed either driven out by Jove or present as Jovis in the star. *Jovis* is nominative, as in *Instruction* V: “not that Jovis.” RIGALTIUS.

**Who arranged the stars of the pole, and creator of the earth.** The text seems to require this emendation, so that it mocks Jove as the creator of the earth as well as of the pole, although he created neither earth nor pole. GALLANDIUS.

**He loved nurturing Venus.** We have thus emended the copy’s “he loved a mortal bird.” That is corrupt, and the story of Leda transformed into a swan would be irrelevant. But the poets’ inventions are full of Jupiter’s lust for Venus. RIGALTIUS.

**Among the stars themselves.** In heaven itself. RIGALTIUS.

**Or Mars caught with her.** He points to Mars caught with Venus.

**With her.** With Venus, who is in heaven and indeed numbered among the stars. This confirms the conjecture just offered. RIGALTIUS.

**Through a husband’s jealousy.** The jealousy of Vulcan, Juno’s son. Ovid, *Fasti* IV.

**You who believe those born of Maia come from the stars.** The copy reads *marhos*, consistently so everywhere; but without doubt one must read *Maios*, that is, “those born of Maia,” daughter of Atlas. RIGALTIUS.]

## V.—JUPITER

[Col. 0205A]

This Jupiter was born to Saturn on the island of Breta [sic];  
When he had grown up, he deprived his father of the kingdom.  
Thereafter he seduced the wives and sisters of noblemen.  
Furthermore, the smith Pyracmon had made his scepters.  
In the beginning God made heaven, earth, and sea;  
But this terrible being was born midway through time,  
Emerging as a young man from a cave and secretly reared.  
Recognize that God is the author of creation, not that Jovis.

## VI.—ON THE THUNDERBOLT OF JOVIS HIMSELF

You say, fools, “Jovis thunders; he hurls the lightning himself.”  
And if childhood thought so, why for two hundred years  
Have you remained infants? Will you always remain so?  
Once childhood has changed into maturity, life cannot contain  
[Col. 0205B] Childish play. Childhood has passed; let your hearts likewise withdraw.  
Your counsels ought to correspond to mature conduct.  
So, foolish man, you believe that Jove thunders,  
Though he was born on earth and nourished with goat’s milk.  
Therefore, if Saturn had devoured him,  
Who would have sent rain in those days after his death?  
Especially if a god is believed to be born from a mortal father:  
Saturn grew old on earth and there failed.  
No prophet foretold that Jupiter would be born.  
Or, if he himself thunders, the Law would have been given by him.  
[Col. 0206A] Tales invented by poets lead you astray.  
But he reigned in Crete and there came to his end.  
The lover of Alcmena has been made almighty by you;  
If he lived, he would now love living persons in the same way.  
You worship the impure and call them heavenly,  
Though born from mortal seed, from those giants.  
You hear and read that he was born on earth:  
How did the seducer deserve to ascend to heaven?  
It is also said that the Cyclopes made his thunderbolt;  
For an immortal obtained his weapons from mortals.  
Though guilty of so many crimes, a murderer even of his own kin,  
By your authority you have raised him on high.

## VII.—ON THE SEPTIZONIUM AND THE STARS

The circle of the zodiacal belt deceives you through your ignorance,  
And perhaps for that reason you conclude that Jove must be invoked.  
Saturn is said to be there, but only as a star; for that man,  
Driven out by Jove, is believed to be present as Jovis in a star—  
He who arranged the stars of the pole and was creator of the earth,  
Who made war upon the Trojans and loved nurturing Venus;  
Or Mars was caught with her among the stars themselves  
Through a husband’s jealousy, though the young man is called a god.  
O utter fools, who believe that those born of Maia govern from the stars  
Those who are being born, or the whole nature of the world!  
They are exposed to wounds and themselves live beneath fate—

[Col. 0207A] [Note: [Col. 0207C]

**Obscene, inquisitive.** Curiosity is indeed sometimes classed as a vice, but it has nothing to do with the matter Commodian is discussing. One must certainly read: “obscene, furious.” DAVIES.

**And just as many mortal sons.** That is, sons mortal in the same fashion. RIGALTIUS.

**And finally they pass into the fishes.** For the popular verses encompassing the twice-six signs of the zodiac end thus: “the Goat, the Water-Jar, the Fishes.” Commodian continues mockingly: “And you will prove it in the kitchen.” Aquarius precedes; “you will prove” or “discover” that they are not gods, and the kitchen itself will prove it. RIGALTIUS.

**Although they are immediately present to us.** He calls the sun and moon “immediately present” stars because, of all the heavenly bodies, they are perceived by us most distinctly; they are the most effective, powerful, and conspicuous. Thus Virgil speaks of “present deities”; in him Nisus says to the Moon:

> You, goddess, be present to aid our undertaking.

*Aeneid* IX, 404. RIGALTIUS.

**You err because you believe, as I did before, that they must be invoked.** A little word wholly necessary to the sense has fallen out. Read: “You err because you believe, as I did before, that they must be invoked.” DAVIES.

**They promise nothing concerning life.** That is, immortal, eternal life. RIGALTIUS.

**Promise.** Horace: “What belongs to physicians, physicians promise.” Juvenal: “His eyes abandoned, while the physician promised nothing.” RIGALTIUS.

**With his *saraballum*.** Jerome, on Daniel, says: “Aquila and Theodotion used the word *saraballa*, and not *sarabara*, as the corrupt reading has it.” Hesychius: “garments worn about the shins” (*ta peri tas knēmidas endymata*, τὰ περὶ τὰς κνημῖδας ἐνδύματα). Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, where he discusses Alexander: “He died in captive *sarabara*.” The same author, *To the Martyrs*: “God, of course, would not hear people wearing cloaks, although he heard the three saints praying in the furnace of the Babylonian king with their *sarabara* and their tiaras.” The Old Latin version of Daniel 3:94 has *saraballa*, although the Greek retains *sarabara* (σαραβάρα). Isidore, *Origins* XIX, cites Publius: “Why, then, did the Parthians suspend *sarabara* upon your belly?” Jerome translates the word into Latin as *braccas*, “breeches,” which seems the truer rendering and better suited to the meaning of Publius, Tertullian, and Commodian. RIGALTIUS.

**Painted gods upon a panel.** Rigaltius takes *axis* here in the sense in which Virgil says, *Aeneid* IV, 481:

> Where mighty Atlas  
> Turns upon his shoulder the axis fitted with blazing stars.

Thus “upon the axis” would mean “in heaven,” for the axis is *anastros* (ἄναστρος), “starless.” SER.

The very learned Rigaltius has strayed far from Commodian’s meaning. Here *axis* denotes not heaven but a wooden board. Festus, under the relevant entry: “A sawn plank is called an *axis*.” Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book II, ch. XII: “In those most ancient laws of Solon, which at Athens were engraved upon wooden tablets.” DAVIES.

**If you do not know how to live.** That is, if you lack wisdom leading to Christ, the author of eternal life. RIGALTIUS.]]

Go on dwelling with the beasts. He alludes to the beasts and the ζῴδια (*zōdia*, “zodiacal signs”) customarily depicted in the Zodiac: the ram, bull, and lion.

Not he, together with Apollo, for the Trojans. See Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* II.610:

> Neptune shakes the walls and the foundations,  
> torn up by his mighty trident.

He did not beget the monstrous Cyclops. He means Polyphemus. See Homer, *Odyssey* I.70. Consult also Hyginus, *Fabula* CXXV, and Servius on *Aeneid* III.678. Some authors, however, relate that this Cyclops was born of other parents. See the distinguished Joseph Barnes on Euripides’ *Cyclops*, v. 644. DAVIS.

You make Apollo a lyre-player. Eusebius, IV, among the minor works edited by Sirmond, p. 199: “And is not that respectable fellow also a lyre-player? First of all, why should we count lyre-players among the gods?” etc.

By the function of a wether. By the function of a haruspex who had inspected the entrails of a wether. RIG.

Double-hearted. Cunning, deceitful. He calls her “double-hearted” because she had two hearts and deceived her lover. With one heart she promised Apollo her embraces so that she might learn from him the art of divination; with the other she was faithless, for after she had learned it, she denied what she had promised. *Bicors* means “of divided heart”; Hesychius: διψυχία, ἀπορία, “double-mindedness, perplexity.” Commodian would have said *bicordia*; and in the epistles of Barnabas and Clement occur δίψυχος, δίγνωμος, δίγνωσσος, “double-minded, divided in judgment.” RIG.]

Obscene, inquisitive, warriors of an impious life;

And they made for him just as many mortal sons,

All terrible, foolish, mighty in the seven-zoned heaven.

If you worship the stars, worship also the twelve signs:

Then the ram, the bull, the twins, and the savage lion.

And at last they pass among the fishes; by that too you will prove it.

Your lawless law is flight: whatever it wishes to be, it will prevail.

It wishes to be wanton; it seeks to live without restraint.

You will be whatever you wish, while praying to gods and goddesses.

Thus I too worshipped while I was in error—the very thing I now condemn.

## VIII.—THE SUN AND THE MOON

Although the sun and moon are present here with us,

You err, as I did before, in thinking that they should be worshipped.

They are indeed among the heavenly bodies, but do not move of their own will.

When the Almighty first created all things,

He placed them there among the stars on the fourth day.

[Col. 0207B] The ancient error, indeed, when ***  
[The text is materially defective.]

And in the Law he commanded that no one worship them.

You pray to so many gods who promise nothing concerning life.

Their law does not exist on earth, nor were they themselves foretold.

But a few priests lead you astray,

Saying, though they themselves are destined to die, that some divinity can be of benefit.

Come near, read, and learn the truth.

## IX.—MERCURY

Let your Mercury be depicted wearing *saraballa* trousers.

With a helmet or a winged cap, but naked otherwise.

[Col. 0208A] I see a wondrous thing: a god flying with a little purse.

Run, poor wretches, with your laps outspread wherever he flies,

So that he may empty his purse; from that moment be ready.

Look at the painted figure, since from on high he will thus

Scatter coins for you; then you may leap about without anxiety.

Foolish man, are you not insane—to worship gods painted on a plank?

If you do not know how to live, go on dwelling with the beasts.

## X.—NEPTUNE

You make Neptune a god born from Saturn;

And he carries a trident so that he may spear fish.

From that equipment it is evident that he is a marine god.

Did he not, together with Apollo, build walls for the Trojans?

How, then, was that needy mason made a god?

Did he not beget the monstrous Cyclops? And could not even that greater being

Live on his own resources?—for he practised the building trade.

[Col. 0208B] Thus one begotten begot another, though he himself had long since died.

## XI.—APOLLO, A FALSE DIVINER

You make Apollo a lyre-player and a diviner.

First, born of Maia on the island of Delos,

And afterward, for an agreed wage, acting obediently as a builder,

He constructed the walls for Laomedon, king of the Trojans.

He hired himself out—the one whom you, in your delusion, regard as a god.

The marrow of his bones burned with love for Cassandra,

But the maiden cunningly mocked him, and the diviner was deceived.

By inspecting a wether he ought to have recognized the double-hearted woman.

[Col. 0209A] [Note: [Col. 0209B]

The maiden terrified him with her beauty. Read *Torruit*, “The maiden inflamed him with her beauty.” RIG.

She first, who ought to have. From him she desired to receive such efficacious knowledge. RIG.

Nor could he overtake her in the race. Julius Firmicus: “Yet from that company of corrupted women, one maiden both escaped and defeated the god who loved her. For although the god could divine and foretell the future, he could neither find Daphne nor rape her.” Eusebius, cited above: “What an outrage! The maiden flees for the sake of chastity, while the so-called god pursues her out of lustful passion and fails to catch her,” etc. And shortly afterward: “But perhaps some facile poet, speaking thoughtlessly, falsely attributed such things to the gods, and the lyre-player did not pursue the maiden,” etc.

For they lived on a wretched diet. The copy reads *bizo*, a corruption of *victu*. RIG.

Wretched. Dreadful, miserable, harsh, or cruel. RIG.

Admetus’ flocks as well. Baluze, in his notes on Cyprian’s *On the Vanity of Idols*, observes that the manuscript copy of Commodian from Saint-Aubin of Angers reads *a primitia* in place of *Admeti*. DAVIS.

Father Liber, certainly twice-born. Julius Hyginus, *Astronomica* CLXVII, relates a similar story: [Col. 0209D] “Liber, son of Jupiter and Proserpina, was torn apart by the Titans. Jupiter crushed his heart and gave it to Semele in a drink. When she had become pregnant from it, Juno changed herself into Beroe, Semele’s nurse, and said: ‘My foster-child, ask Jupiter to come to you just as he comes to Juno, so that you may know what pleasure there is in lying with a god.’ Incited by her, Semele made this request of Jupiter and was struck by a thunderbolt. Jupiter took Liber from her womb and gave him to Nysus to be reared. From this he was called Dionysius and was named “Twice-Mothered.” The same author, no. CLXXIX. Nonnus, *Dionysiaca* VIII, at the beginning. RIG.

Jupiter’s second Maia. Here *Jovis* is in the nominative case, as above. The Glosses of Isidore: “*Maia*: physician, midwife.” RIG.

First from Jupiter and Proserpina. A word has dropped out. Read: “first from Jupiter **and** Proserpina.” DAVIS.

From this, being twice-born, he is called Dionysus. This is a poetic etymology of the name. Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius* II, gave another: Νύσιος γὰρ ὁ Διονύσιος ἀπὸ τῆς ἐν Ἰνδοῖς Νύσης, “For Dionysus is called Nysian from Nysa in India.” Arsaces, king of Armenia, dedicated a leopard with the inscription: “KING ARSACES TO THE NYSAEAN GOD.” Stephanus: Αεγται καὶ νυκεκ [corrupt; probably λέγεται καὶ Νυσεύς, “he is also called Nyseus”]. From Philostratus, then, it may be gathered [Col. 0210B] that Nysa is, as it were, the thigh of the Caucasus; that this region was planted with the vine sacred to Bacchus-Dionysus; and that from this arose the fable of Jupiter carrying Bacchus in his thigh, ἐν μηρῷ. Land-surveyors, just as they spoke of the peaks and brows of mountains, also used the terms thigh, calf, ledge, strap, and foot. Hence the poets said that Dionysus was inserted into Jupiter’s thigh. RIG.

Or reckless adventurers. The ancient Glosses: Ριφοκινδυνοκ [i.e. ῥιψοκίνδυνος], “reckless, venturesome.” Others used *parabolus* and *parabolanus*. Paul to the Philippians: παραβολευσάμενος τῇ ψυχῇ, “having risked his life.” The Old Latin manuscript version has: “having hazarded his soul.” RIG.

[Col. 0210C] And cobblers of Mimnermus. So the copy reads. Commodian may perhaps have written *Mimnermomerique sutores*: γελωτοποιοί ῥαψῳδοί, “comic rhapsodists,” who sought laughter in the theatres by stitching and arranging passages from the poems of Mimnermus and Homer into a different meaning. See Athenaeus, book XIII, p. 620, where he discusses singers of comic songs and comic tragedies. RIG.

Living in like fashion. As above in this very Instruction, “they revel in deeds of the same kind.” Juvenal says, “they live Bacchanalia.” Or he used *simile* adverbially, whence *simillime*. RIG.

Stirred by wine. They are moved after drinking well—after drinking deeply. *Motari* means “to be repeatedly moved,” that is, to dance. Horace: “As a matron is commanded to move on festival days.” RIG.

Which he first pressed out. Bacchus is said to have been the first to reveal the use of wine in India. Hence he is called both the planter of the vine and the discoverer of vines. GALL.

In his revel. In the games, the triennial orgies. RIG.

Invictus. Arnobius, book V, *Against the Nations*, relates from Timotheus the Theologian the story of this Invictus, who was the son of the Great Mother and grandson of the rock Agdus on the borders of Phrygia, and who possessed a savagery unheard of in every respect. Our Commodian had this story in view; the illumination needed for this Instruction must be sought nowhere else. Timotheus’ account, however, differs greatly from what is reported about this same Agdestis in Pausanias’ *Achaica*, p. 223. RIG.—“Invictus, born from a rock.” *Deus Invictus*, “the Unconquered God,” is a perpetual epithet of the Sun; therefore the figure meant is not Agdestis but Mithras. See Gruter’s *Inscriptions*, p. 33 ff. Indeed, everything Commodian relates concerning INVICTUS is attributed by the ancients to Mithras. For he was said to have been born from a rock. Jerome, *Against Jovinian* I, col. 149, Benedictine edition: “The fables of the nations also relate that MITHRAS and Erichthonius were generated either in ROCK or in the earth, solely from the heat of lust.” He was also regarded as a thief, whence Porphyry calls him βουκλόπος, “cattle-thief,” *On the Cave of the Nymphs*, p. 292. DAVIS.

Invictus, born from a rock. Arnobius, book V, near the beginning: “He possessed unconquerable strength and an untamable ferocity of spirit, and a mad and furious lust toward both sexes; to ravage by violence what he had seized, to destroy and lay waste, to go in his savagery wherever inclination led him; to care for neither gods nor human beings, and to believe nothing more powerful than himself,” etc. Mithras was also called the Unconquered God, the name by which the Persians call the sun, as is repeatedly found in ancient inscriptions. Indeed, the rites of Agdestis and Mithras sometimes appear to have been confused, especially in Christian writings; and Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, relates that Mithras was a man who drove away cattle. Hence Statius also said: “Indignant to follow Mithras as he twists the horns.” Commodian charges Agdestis with the same deed. RIG.]

For the diviner withdrew from there, rejected.

The maiden inflamed him by her beauty, though he should have inflamed her.

She first ought to have loved the god,

Yet in his lust he began to love Daphne thus;

And he nevertheless pursues her, wishing to violate the girl.

The fool loves without reward and could not overtake her in the race.

Or, if he was a god, he should have overtaken her through the air.

She reached shelter first, while the diviner was left behind.

A race of human beings deceives you, for they lived on a wretched diet.

He is also said to have tended the flocks of Admetus.

During games, as he threw the discus high into the air,

He could not stop it when it slipped: he struck his friend down.

That was the last day of his companion Hyacinthus.

If he possessed divination, he would have foreknown his friend’s death.

## XII.—FATHER LIBER, BACCHUS

[Col. 0209B] You yourselves say that Father Liber was certainly twice-born,

First born in India from Jupiter and Proserpina.

[Col. 0210A] Warring against the Titans amid bloodshed,

He died, just like any one of mortals.

Then, restored by his fate within another womb,

Semele receives him again, as Jupiter’s second Maia.

Her womb was cut open when she died near childbirth;

He was taken out and given as a foster-child to Nysus to be reared.

From this, being twice-born, he is called Dionysus,

Whose false religion is practised in emptiness.

His followers too rave like Bacchants, as they themselves now appear to be,

Either reckless adventurers or cobblers of Mimnermus;

They conspire in wickedness and perform a prelude with counterfeit madness,

So as to deceive the others, who will say that the divine presence is at hand.

From this you plainly see people living in like fashion,

Stirred by the wine which he was the first to press out;

In his revel they gave him honour.

## XIII.—INVICTUS

[Col. 0210B]

If Invictus, born from a rock, is regarded as a god,

[Col. 0211A] [Note: [Col. 0211B]

Now, then, go back and tell us which of these was prior. The copy reads: *Nunc ergo reticeo*, “Now, therefore, I am silent.” I see that some have consequently constructed this reading, but we judge it entirely foreign to Commodian’s meaning. His intention is this: You say that Invictus was born from a rock; tell us, therefore—that is, recount—whence these two, Invictus and the Rock, derived their race and origin. For whoever is shown to have existed earlier as their parent or creator was unquestionably prior, superior, and greater. He then adds from the story of Timotheus or Arnobius: “The rock defeated the god.” To this Commodian replies: If the rock defeated the god, the creator of that rock from which your god Invictus was born must be sought. RIG.

The rock defeated the god. Arnobius, book V, near the beginning, speaking of the stones thrown into the empty world by Deucalion and Pyrrha: “From these stones, together with the others,” he says, “that figure called the Great Mother was formed and divinely animated. She was given rest and sleep on the very summit of the rock. Jupiter sought her with incestuous desires; but when, after a long struggle, he could not obtain what he had promised himself, he discharged his lust upon the stone, defeated,” etc. Behold Jupiter defeated by a rock. RIG.

Moreover, you continue to portray him as a thief. Thus Instruction LIII: “And he consecrates him as his personal attendant.” And the following Instruction on Silvanus: “From what source did Silvanus appear, in turn, to be a god?” RIG.

Since, if he were a god, ever. One might prefer: “Since, if he were a god, he certainly would not have lived by theft.” But this particle *utique*, “certainly,” will occur again in the very next verse. RIG.

Monster-devouring nature. I approve the emendation *monstruosa*, “monstrous”: “lion-faced.” RIG.

And he kept driving away other men’s cattle. Thus this Invictus, like Mithras, was a cattle-rustling robber, “indignant to follow those who twist the horns,” as we noted above from Statius. Lactantius Placidus confirms this on *Thebaid* I. Julius Firmicus: “Worshipping a man who drove away cattle, they transfer his rites to the nature of fire.” RIG.

In caves. Read “into caves.” See below, Instruction XXIV, verses 326–327; Arnobius, book II, p. 6 of the Plantin edition: “who introduced true religion **in the world**.” Again, p. 68: “Others say that souls are everlasting and cannot degenerate **in nature** into something mortal.” Recent critics have corrupted these passages. Thomas Muncker, that most diligent scholar, collected further examples of similar expressions in his note on Hyginus, *Fabula* L, p. 92. DAVIS.

Silvanus. The ancient Glosses: “Silvanus, Pan, Θεὸς ὑγαῖος [corrupt; probably Θεὸς ὑλαῖος, ‘woodland god’]. *Syrinx*: pipe.” From this they invented the story that Syrinx was a maiden loved by Pan. Servius on *Georgics* III: “Pan, a rustic deity.” RIG.

You purchased a lord who was for sale. Commodian seems to have written: “You purchased a **god** who was for sale.” Similarly, Instruction XVI: “And those who are manufactured you call gods for yourself.” RIG.

When you have bought it for him. Namely, the pipe: without it he would not be regarded as a god. RIG.

Are you not ashamed, fool, to worship such panels? Should you not also be ashamed to worship other fables or panels, even if more artistically fashioned? RIG.

Who may “diat” life after death. What if Commodian wrote *duat*, an archaic form meaning “may give,” just as *fuat* means “may be,” and in Festus *duit* means “may give”? The ancient Glosses: “*Duit*, δοίη, ‘may he give’; *duint*, δοῖεν, δωσώσιν, ‘may they give.’” In the copy, an emendation is supplied: “who teaches one to live after death.” [Col. 0212C] RIG.—Beyond doubt read *vivere DICIT*, “says that one will live.” Thus below, Instruction XXI.272:

> Seek rather the righteousness of the Law: it brings  
> The aid of salvation and says that one will become eternal.

The very form of the letters supports and confirms our emendation. DAVIS.—I prefer Rigaltius’ emendation. Davis’ conjecture is not established by verse 272 of Instruction XXI: the Law indeed “says,” but God “GIVES” life. Still less pleasing is Vonk’s proposal *vivere sciat*, “may know how to live,” in *Lectiones Latinae* I.9, p. 74.

Those who have become *biothanati*. By *biothanati* Commodian means idolaters who, after completing the course of their lives, plunge headlong into eternal death; Christians, by contrast, are called from death to immortal life. The discussions in Tertullian, *On the Soul*, concerning *aori* and *biothanati*, or *biaiothanati*, are irrelevant here. RIG.

The monster of the Aventine hill. He means Cacus. Ovid, *Fasti* I.551:

> Cacus, the terror and disgrace of the Aventine wood.

In Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.267, he is called half-beast. See Livy I.7 and Dionysius of Halicarnassus IV.39. DAVIS.

The rustic mind of men. The copy reads “the rustic race of men.” RIGALTIUS.—There was no reason for Rigaltius to reject the manuscript reading, *gens hominum*, “race of men”; it is entirely sound and genuine. Our author above, Instruction XI.147: “A RACE OF MEN deceives you.” Ovid, *Amores* II, Elegy XIV.10:

> The race of men was destined to perish through its vice.

So too Tertullian, *Apology* XXVI. DAVIS.

To the absent Thunderer. That is, to the dead Jupiter.

They vowed victims. Commodian offends against historical accuracy. For it was not the Aborigines, but Hercules himself, who sacrificed a victim to Jupiter. See Ovid, *Fasti* I.579, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I, chapter 39. DAVIS.

And you say that the *geneses* are the fates. γενέσεις, “nativities,” that is, horoscopes. RIG.]

Now, then, go back and tell us which of these was prior.

The rock defeated the god; the rock’s creator must therefore be sought.

Moreover, you continue to portray him as a thief;

For if he were a god, he would never have lived by theft.

He was certainly earthly, and monstrous in nature.

He continually drove other men’s cattle into caves,

As did Cacus, that son of Vulcan.

## XIV.—SILVANUS

From what source did Silvanus appear, in turn, to be a god?

Perhaps he finds favour because the pipe plays well,

Since he supplies the wood; otherwise perhaps he would not exist.

You purchased a lord who was for sale when you bought the pipe for him.

Look—the wood gives out. What is owed to him then?

Are you not ashamed, fool, to worship such panels?

[Col. 0212A] Seek the one God, who may give life after death.

Withdraw from those who have become *biothanati*, “doomed to eternal death.”

## XV.—HERCULES

Because Hercules struck down the monster of the Aventine hill,

Who had been accustomed to steal Evander’s herds,

The rustic and also unlearned minds of men, by way of praise,

When they wished to give thanks to the absent Thunderer,

Foolishly vowed victims as if praying to a god,

And erected altars dripping with milk as a memorial for themselves.

From this it came about that he is worshipped according to ancient custom.

Yet this man is not a god, although he was mighty in arms.

## XVI.—GODS AND GODDESSES

You say that beings manifestly bloodstained are gods,

And you say that horoscopes assign fates to you.

[Col. 0213A] [Note: [Col. 0213B]

You call them lords for yourself. Thus Instruction LIII: “And he consecrates him as his personal attendant.” RIG.

Faria. The copy reads *Furiam*, “Fury.” Arnobius also counts Laverna, Bellona, the Discords, and the Furies among the goddesses. Some call this heavenly goddess the Moon, others Atargatis or Astarte, and still others the Syrian Goddess. RIG.—Faria together with Caelestis, the virgins. The reading of the copy should not be abandoned, provided that the passage is suitably punctuated. Write: “Fury, together with Caelestis, the virgins.” Thus in Gruter, CCCXVIII.4: “to the incomparable priest of CAELESTIS.” Tertullian, *Apology* XII: “We are driven to the beasts—the very beasts, of course, which you assign to Liber, Cybele, and CAELESTIS.” See also chapter XXIV and Thomas Reinesius on Inscription XXIX of the First Class. DAVIS.

For whom your wives sway their loins. Broken by luxury and lust, they undulate by writhing their loins. Hence Persius said that lascivious poems enter the loins. From this also come *delumbati* and *elumbes*, “weak-loined.” RIG.

Which even now cannot be counted. Pliny, *Natural History* II: “We also find innumerable divinities among these: even the lower regions are divided into classes, as are diseases and many pestilences, because in trembling fear we desire them to be appeased.”—They are carried on the neck. As amulets, περίαπτα, “things fastened around one”; or rather they are carried upon the shoulders. Thus he soon says: “They ought rather to be exported to the farthest lands.” RIG.

While they seek to scrape together their livelihood. Thus Horace, *Satires* I.3: “From whatever source he scrapes together his fee or coins.” The ancient Glosses: “*Extricare*, ἐκποδίσαι, ‘remove from the way’; *expedi*, ἔκπλεξον, ‘disentangle.’” Bibaculus, on Valerius Cato: “Able to solve every question, but finding it difficult to settle a single account.”

They induce others to believe that falsehood lies beneath the mysteries. That is, by frauds and impostures they so deceive the eyes of the common people that the falsity, covered and obscured by mystery, is not detected. The Galli of the Great Mother belonged to this class of impostors. Livy, book XXVIII, chapter XIX, says that when the Romans had crossed the river Sangarius by a bridge, the Galli met them with their sacred emblems, “prophesying in a frenzied chant that the goddess granted the Romans the power of war and victory.” That Livy wrote “the power of war and victory,” not “the road of war,” as all printed editions have it, is evident from Polybius: Φάσκοντες προσαγγέλλειν τὴν θεὸν νίκην καὶ κράτος, “claiming to announce that the goddess granted victory and power.” Livy calls the objects “emblems of impostors”; Polybius calls them προστήθια καὶ τύπους, “breast-ornaments and images.” RIGALTIUS.—The meaning devised by Rigaltius cannot be extracted from these words. Perhaps one should read:

> They induce others to believe that something sacred lies beneath the mysteries.

That is, they falsely persuade others that something holy and divine lies hidden beneath the mystery. DAVIS.

[Col. 0214B] And they weary themselves beneath a guise. “Beneath a guise” means under an assumed role, falsely, by pretence. Publilius Syrus: “An heir’s weeping is laughter beneath a mask.” RIG.

You have often seen the Dindymarians. The Dindymarians are the flock of Dindymene Cybele. Catullus’ Attis says to his Gallae: “Come, go together, Gallae, to Cybele’s lofty groves. Go together, wandering flock of the Dindymenian mistress.” Martial XI.82: “The eunuch Dindymus.” RIG.

Or when they batter their own backs. Writers differ concerning the tricks of these rogues. Lucian, *On the Syrian Goddess*: τέμνονται τε τοὺς πήχεας, καὶ τοῖσι νώτοισι πρὸς ἀλλήλους τύπτονται, “They cut their forearms and beat one another upon the back.” Apuleius, book VIII: “Stripping their arms bare up to the shoulder, they raise huge swords and axes, cry out ecstatically, and leap about, the music of the pipe inciting their frenzied dance.” And shortly afterward: [Col. 0214C] “At last, with the double-edged blades they carried, they cut their own arms.” And after some further remarks: “Seizing a scourge . . . they lash themselves with its many-knotted blows, fortified by a wondrous contempt for the pain of the wounds.” RIG.

They batter their own filthy backs with a double axe. The copy reads *parca bipenne*, “sparing with the double axe.” Commodian appears to be reproaching the effeminate Galli here with something disgracefully obscene. The ancient Glosses: ἰσχίον, “hip,” *dorsum*, “back,” *lumbi*, “loins.” Other Glosses: ὀσφύες, ἰσχία, “loins, hips.” Apuleius: “You would indeed have seen the ground grow wet with the filth of their effeminate blood beneath the advance of the swords and blows of the scourges,” etc. RIG.

They preserve with their teaching what they heal with blood. That is: in vain they preserve by their teaching, and likewise fail to heal by their blood. RIG.

They seek such devices so that they may collect contributions. Above in the same Instruction he said: “While they seek to scrape together their livelihood.” That such were already the devices of wandering charlatans in his own age is attested by the author of the book *On the Sacred Disease*, commonly attributed to Hippocrates: Ἄνθρωποι βίου δεόμενοι πολλὰ καὶ παντοῖα τεκταίνονται καὶ ποικίλλουσιν, “People in need of a livelihood contrive many varied things and embellish them.” RIG.

They seek such devices. Similarly in Tertullian: “devices of adornment,” “devices of punishment,” “devices of the arts,” etc. RIG.

They cast a shadow over the people. They deceive them by placing a cloud and shadow before them—that is, by frauds. RIG.

It arose from antiquity. Ovid, *Fasti* IV:

> Antiquity is accepted as a weighty witness;  
> refrain from disturbing the belief received.

GALL.

So that the diviner may be believed when he produces falsehoods. Perhaps the words have been transposed: “producing falsehoods.” RIG.

Yet no majesty of theirs has spoken. Commodian says this concerning the images of the nations, on the basis of the pronouncement of Psalm 113: “They have mouths and will not speak.” “No majesty of theirs”—namely, of the images that form the subject of this Instruction—“has spoken” means that it has said nothing and uttered no oracles. RIG.]

Tell me now, then, to which of them the sacred rites should first be offered.

Between the two paths an untimely death wanders.

If horoscopes assign your fates, why do you pray to a god?

Foolish man, you are deceived when you seek to pray to the dead,

And you call manufactured objects lords over you.

Or you pray as goddesses to certain females—I know not whom:

Bellona and Nemesis as goddesses, Fury together with heavenly Caelestis,

The Virgins, and Venus, for whom your wives sway their loins.

There are, moreover, other demons in the shrines

Which even now cannot be counted and are carried upon the neck,

Though they cannot render an account even of themselves. These plagues

Ought rather to be exported to the farthest lands.

## XVII.—THEIR IMAGES

[Col. 0213B] A few wicked, empty prophets make fools of you.

[Col. 0214A] While they seek to scrape together their livelihood,

They induce others to believe that falsehood lies beneath the mysteries.

Then, pretending to be shaken by some divine power,

They proclaim its majesty and weary themselves beneath an assumed guise.

You have often seen the Dindymarians, and with what uproar

They engage in debauchery while seeking to feign madness,

Or batter their filthy backs with a double axe.

Through their teaching they preserve what they heal with blood.

Observe: no divine power compels them [the Latin is uncertain];

They themselves first pierce themselves while of sound mind.

But they seek such devices so that they may collect contributions.

From this, see that everything is fictitious.

They cast a shadow over the simple people, claiming that they will perish unless they believe.

Once established in vanity, the practice advanced through antiquity,

So that the diviner may be believed when he produces falsehoods.

[Col. 0214B] Yet no majesty of theirs has ever spoken.

[Note: [Col. 0215C]

ON AMMUDATES. I shall be grateful to anyone who can point out another author who mentions this divinity. The ending indicates a Persian word, as in *Mithridates, Orondates, Tiridates,* and *Meherdates*. Procopius, in the *Persian Wars*, mentions Ἀμμούδιος, Ammodius, a not insignificant estate, Δάρας μέτρον εἴκοσι σταδίων ἀπέχων, “twenty stades distant from Dara,” where the Persians encamped against the Romans. In Hesychius, moreover, Datis is the name of a Persian commander. Yet how empty these observations are unless they are confirmed from another source! RIG.

THE NEMESIACS. The profane writings of the nations also discuss, without clear distinction, the Galli of Cybele, the Idaeans, Bellonarii, Isiacs, and Nemesiacs. Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VIII, describes a Nemesiac: “He began with loud prophecy, and with an invented lie commenced to assail and accuse himself, as though he had committed some offence against the law of the sacred religion; and furthermore he demanded with his own hands the just punishment for his guilty deed. Finally seizing a scourge,” etc. We made the same observations above concerning the Dindymarians, at Instruction XVII, where Commodian speaks of the uproar with which they engage in debauchery and feign madness. That uproar and madness also belonged to the Nemesiacs, as may be seen in the following words of Apuleius: [Col. 0215D] “From the very moment of their entrance they filled the air with discordant howls and flew about in a frenzy,” etc. Catullus therefore said in an epigram to Licinus that Nemesis was a violent goddess: “Lest Nemesis exact penalties from you. She is a violent goddess; take care not to injure her.” Babrius, quoted by the Suda: Παρῆν δ’ ἡ Νέμεσις, ἥ τ’ ἄδικ’ ἐποπτεύει, “Nemesis too was present, she who watches over unjust deeds.” Other passages of this kind, cited there from ancient writers, express the same thought. Ammianus Marcellinus XIV: “These and innumerable deeds of this kind are performed by Adrasteia, the avenger of impious crimes and rewarder of good deeds, whom by a second name we also call Nemesis,” etc. Finally Apuleius, *On the World*, says that she is Necessity, the inescapable force of retribution. RIG.

Is it not disgraceful? Isidore, book IV, final chapter, where he discusses punishments established by law: “disgrace and infamy.” RIG.

He feeds his own entrails. Apuleius: “They attack their own muscles with bites and cut their arms.” RIG.—Rigaltius is entirely mistaken. Commodian means that when the Nemesiac acts with apparent severity—that is, when he tears his body with scourges and sword—he is seeking a livelihood for himself. Hence Instruction XVII, [Col. 0216C] v. 213:

> While seeking to feign madness,  
> Or battering their filthy backs with a double axe . . .  
> They cast a shadow over the simple people, claiming that they will perish unless they believe.

Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VIII, p. 173: “At last, when wearied, or at least sated with their own mutilation, they gave their butchery a rest; and, while many eagerly offered them contributions of bronze and even silver, they received them in the broad folds of their garments,” etc. DAVIS.

He befouls the citizens. He pollutes them with abuse and reproaches and, as it were, sprinkles them with dung. The Glosses of Isidore edited by Vulcanius: “*Scurra*: one who is befouled. *Scurrula*: one who befouls.” Learned men long ago showed from Dio and Suetonius that *scurrae*, “buffoons,” were so called from the Greek word κόπριος, “dung-man.” The Suda: κόπριος ἀνὴρ ὡς ἀπὸ δημοῦ, λέγει δὲ τὸν κοπρολόγον, “a ‘dung-man,’ as though from the people; it means a speaker of filth.” The copy reads *incopiat*. RIG.

He spins, rotating by himself. That impostor uses a piece of wood crossed and bifurcated to spin himself around, so that the ignorant common people may suppose him possessed by a divine power—whirled around by epilepsy, sudden collapse, or dizziness as if by a divine force or on a divine axis. But discerning people laugh at the impostor and shout: “Find a stranger!” and “Let someone who does not know you carry you away!” RIG.

With a forked piece of wood. Land-surveyors used *bifurcium* for a boundary marker and *ungula bifurca* for a cloven hoof. RIG.

You call the Titans your Tutani. “The Moors worship Titans as kings.” Arnobius, book I.

You pray beneath your roof to the savage, silent ones. So many household gods. Is the reading of the manuscript perhaps: “Or mute, silent ones”? Rigaltius has departed too far from it. Perhaps read: “Thus you pray beneath your roof to MUTE, SILENT goddesses. So many Lares.” For the Lares are the sons of the goddess Muta. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* I.20: “They say that this Muta is she from whom the Lares were born.” See Ovid, *Fasti* II.572, 583 ff. Immediately afterward, however, *aediculae*, “little shrines,” must be read, as the rules of Latin usage demonstrate. DAVIS.

You should rather melt them down. It would be more useful if you melted and liquefied those bronze objects, so that they might be made into small jars, basins, a frying pan, and dishes. Juvenal, *Satire* X.64. RIG.

You even call mountains gods. The copy reads *Monte ses deos dicitis*, which seems to approach “the Montensian gods.” They are mentioned in an inscription in Gruter, p. XXI.3, where we read that an altar was erected to Jupiter the Lightning-Bringer at the command of the Montensian gods. Nevertheless, we judge that the text should read: “You even call mountains gods,” so that for Commodian the Montensians are those who believed that certain divine powers inhabited mountains. Hence he says: “Let them rule in gold, darkened by evil and helping with an alien mind.” He condemns the greed of those who placed the highest human happiness in money and an accumulation of gold, which is the incitement to every evil. These gods, he says, may rule in gold, darkened by evil—as if he were describing those gods, the Manes who guard metals, beneath the dark and innermost caverns of the mountains. They begrudge mortals who are excessively greedy for treasure. If these gods perhaps assist the avaricious who dig into the mountains’ hidden places, they do so unwillingly, as reluctant beings, and with an alien mind—that is, assisting with an entirely hostile disposition. Accordingly, they should not be said to have given what can be taken only by plunder: namely, by an assault that brings not merely the excavation but the ruin of the mountain, dug through and shattered with much fire and vinegar. Pliny, *Natural History* XXXIII, at the beginning of the book: “We pursue every vein of the earth and see mountains hollowed out, wondering that the earth sometimes gapes open or trembles—as though this too could not be understood as an expression of our sacred parent’s indignation. We enter her entrails and seek riches in the abode of the Manes. The things she concealed and sank beneath the earth drive us toward the lower regions. If only gold could be banished entirely from life—that accursed hunger, as the most celebrated authors have called it, assailed with reproaches by all the best men and discovered for the destruction of life!” And chapter IV: “It has surpassed the work of the Giants.” And shortly afterward: “Frequent arches are therefore left to support the mountains. Flint blocks the way; they shatter these with fire and vinegar.” And after some further remarks: “The Manes are dragged up among human beings so as to import vice.” RIG.]

## XVIII.—AMMUDATES AND THE GREAT GOD

[Col. 0215A]

We have already said much about accursed superstition,

Yet we continue, lest we be said to have passed anything over.

Worshippers used to venerate their Ammudates according to custom.

He was great in their eyes so long as there was gold in his temple.

They bowed their heads beneath the divine presence as though it were present.

Matters reached the point where Caesar removed the gold.

The divine power failed, or fled, or passed into the fire.

The originator of this crime is clearly the man who fashioned that same image;

Prophesying falsely, he leads so many great men astray.

And now the one who was accustomed to be a diviner has fallen silent.

Voices used to burst forth as though his mind had been altered,

As though that wooden god were speaking into his ear.

Tell me now yourselves: are these not false divinities?

How many did that prophet destroy by means of this prodigy?

[Col. 0215B] The one who formerly prophesied has now forgotten how to prophesy.

Such portents are entirely fabricated by wine-drinkers,

Whose damnable audacity invents divine powers.

They used to carry it, and that image dried up;

For it too is silent, and no one at all now prophesies concerning it.

But you yourselves wish to perish.

## XIX.—THE VAIN NEMESIACS

Is it not disgraceful for a sensible man to be led astray,

And to worship such a thing, or call a piece of wood Diana?

[Col. 0216A] Early in the morning you believe a drunken, brutal man destined to perish,

Who by his craft falsely says whatever he pleases.

While acting with severity, he feeds his belly.

One detestable man befouls all the citizens.

He has attached to himself others, forming a fellowship of the same kind,

With whom he fabricates a story so as to adorn a god.

He cannot divine for himself, yet dares to do so for others.

He lifts the image onto his shoulders whenever he pleases and sets it down whenever he pleases.

He spins, rotating by himself with a forked piece of wood,

So that you might suppose him inspired by the divinity of the wood.

You do not worship the gods about whom they falsely prophesy;

You worship the priests themselves, fearing in vain.

But if your heart is vigorous, flee now from the sanctuaries of death.

## XX.—THE TITANS

You call the Titans your Tutani.

[Col. 0216B] You pray beneath your roof to savage, silent beings:

So many Lares, little shrines, and images fashioned for Titan.

For in your folly you worship those who died an evil death,

Without reading their law; nor do they themselves speak.

And you dare to call cast-bronze objects gods.

You should rather melt them down into little vessels for yourselves.

## XXI.—THE MONTENSIANS

You even call mountains gods: let them rule in gold,

Darkened by evil and helping with a mind alien to yours.

[Col. 0217A] [Note: [Col. 0217D]

For what you follow among vain things rejoices through the ages. Read: “For you rejoice through the ages because you follow EMPTY gods.” Commodian, Instruction II.12:

> Do not, he says, worship empty gods.

Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* II.1: “For I am eager, after convicting the EMPTY gods”—other manuscripts read “the MANES”—“to assert the majesty of the one God.” DAVIS.

Another inspects a hand. I believe the text should read:

> With the blood of bleating victims poured out, another summons the Manes.

For they used the blood of beasts to evoke the dead, as is evident from Homer, *Odyssey* XI.36, and Isidore, *Origins* VIII.9, to mention no more. Indeed, they sometimes did not abstain from human blood. See Jan Broukhusius on Tibullus I, Elegy II.45. DAVIS.

Where are all the leaders and kings who consulted it concerning life? Julius Firmicus, a practitioner of this astrological art, preferred in book II, final chapter, through the prudence of courtly flattery, to betray his own discipline rather than endanger himself by declaring what power it possessed regarding royal government or the horoscopes of emperors. “Take care,” he says, “never to answer anyone who questions you about the condition of the commonwealth or the life of the Roman emperor. For it is neither proper nor lawful that we learn anything about the condition of the commonwealth through impious curiosity. Nor has any astrologer been able to determine anything true concerning the emperor’s fate. The emperor alone is not subject to the courses of the stars, and his is the only fate over which the stars possess no power of decision,” etc. RIG.

To have known their own portents. Portents by which something concerning themselves is signified and foreshown. The ancient Glosses: “*Portendit*, σημαίνει διὰ τέρας, ‘he signifies by means of a portent.’”

Demons wander in the world. Baluze, in his notes on Cyprian, *De idolorum vanitate*, p. 571, Paris ed. 1726, attests that an old manuscript of Saint-Aubin of Angers reads *daemones in mundo vagi*, “demons wandering in the world.” Thus Commodian himself, *Instruction* III, v. 36:

> Hence they now wander about and overthrow many bodies.

You have entered upon two ways. H. Menard and J. B. Cotelier collected much concerning the two ways [Col. 0218D] in their notes on the *Epistle of Barnabas*, ch. XVIII. In what follows read: *condiscite rectam*, “learn the right one.” DAVIS.

And as though sociable. In the copy it is uncertain whether one should read *communis*, “sociable,” or *comis*, “affable.” He said, “a commonplace and frivolous disposition.” Terence. RIG.

In the barbarian manner. By “barbarian customs” he means the rites and religions of peoples who are not Christian at all—the rites of the secular world, not of the Church. RIG.

You hymn yourself. The copy reads *hymnificis*, as though Commodian were alluding to the neighing of a beast of burden and, in a Greek turn of phrase, had said, “You yourself neighingly sing to yourself.” Nevertheless, in *Instruction* LX he will speak of the “hymned choir,” meaning the Church, which customarily delights in hymns and praises of God and our Lord. The Latin version of Isaiah 10:30 reads: “Neigh with your voice, daughter of Gallim.” RIG.

Meager in your own house. Frail and excessively sparing in your own home.

Ready for banquets. Those of the powerful, even when food sacrificed to idols is served. RIG.

And to shun the precepts. The precepts of Christ the Lord, whether those of ecclesiastical discipline or of the *agapae* of Christian charity. RIG.]

For if your spirit remained pure and your mind serene,  
You yourself ought to reason with yourself about those things.  
You are a senseless man if you think that they can save you,  
Whether they rule or diminish anything. If you seek anything sound,  
Seek rather the righteousness of the law: it bears  
The aid of salvation and bids one become eternal.  
For what you pursue among vanities gives pleasure only for a time.  
For a brief while you rejoice, and afterward you lament in the depths.  
Withdraw from them if you wish to rise with Christ.

## XXII.—THE DULLNESS OF THE AGE

Alas, fellow citizens, I grieve that you are thus being stupefied by the world!  
One man hastens to lots, another observes birds,  
Another, after the blood of bleating animals has been shed, examines a hand,  
And, credulous, desires to hear empty answers.  
Where are all the leaders and kings who consulted concerning their lives,  
[Col. 0217B] Or what benefit was it to them to have known their own portents?  
Learn what is good, I beg you, fellow citizens; beware of images:  
Seek everything in the law of the Almighty.  
Thus it pleased the Lord of lords on high,  
For our testing, that demons should wander in the world;  
[Col. 0218A] And yet, from the other side, he sent commandments beforehand  
That those who abandon their altars should become heavenly.  
Therefore I do not undertake to debate this in a little book:  
The law teaches and summons in the midst: take counsel for yourselves.  
You have entered upon two ways; learn the right one.

## XXIII.—ON THOSE WHO ARE READY EVERYWHERE

While you serve your belly, you say that you are innocent,  
And, as though merely sociable, make yourself ready everywhere.  
Woe to you, foolish man! You yourself look about for death.  
You seek to live without law, in the barbarian manner;  
You hymn yourself, even “neighingly” singing concerning the Word,  
You who pretend to be simple: “I live straightforwardly with this man.”  
You believe that you are living while you desire to fill your belly.  
You remain meager in your own house, perversely;  
[Col. 0218B] Ready for banquets, yet shunning the precepts.  
Or perhaps you disbelieve that God will judge the dead;  
Foolishly, you make yourself ruler of heaven in his place.  
You look to your belly as though you were its providence.  
At one moment you seem profane, at another holy.

[Col. 0219A] [Note: [Col. 0219C]

You come forward as a suppliant of God. That is, you pray to Christ while kneeling before an image of Jupiter. RIG.

Under the gaze of the tyrant. By “the tyrant” he means a non-Christian Caesar, an image of Jupiter, or the devil. RIG.

Stripped of the Law. Deprived of the works enjoined by the Christian law. RIG.

You go before. Christians who have been released to the Lord in the peace of the Church are said to have “gone before.” RIG. Read *procedis*, “you proceed.” DAVIS.

Why in the syn.—do you run to the Pharisees? The copy reads: *decurris saepe bifarios*, “you often run down in two directions.” RIG.

You are led to a malignant place. To the bad Christian he says, “you are led to a malignant place”; to the true Christian, “you are led to a benign place.” Apart from these two orders, Saint Ephrem the Syrian, who lived near Commodian’s time and was praised by Jerome in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, teaches that there is no intermediate order. He then says: “I speak of one place above and the other below, between which lies the intervening diversity [Col. 0219D] of differences in recompense.” The same author says a little later: “To escape Gehenna is itself to enter the kingdom of heaven, just as to fall away from that kingdom is to enter Gehenna.” Gerard Vossius translated these passages into Latin from Greek works not yet published; and, as Vossius himself judged in his edition, they do not in any way prejudice the doctrine of Purgatory. Tertullian, *To the Soul*: “We affirm that you remain after the discharge of life, await the day of judgment, and according to your deserts are assigned either to torment or to refreshment, each everlasting.” RIG.

To those to whom that delightfulness clings. He means the delightfulness of the Millenarians. RIG.

For you doubters, punishment without a body. The eternal fire, which torments even souls stripped of the body. RIG.

It causes him to cry out to a brother. By “brother” he means a believer, a Christian. “It causes him to cry out to a brother” means to call upon a brother’s aid, as did [Col. 0220C] that rich man clothed in purple, crying out to Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water. Luke 16:24. RIG.

The torturer’s order. The order of the tempter, the devil, who reproaches the condemned man with the cause of his condemnation, so that he may add this insult also to the condemned man’s punishment. RIG.

Enter now, after having been invited so often. *Instruction* XXXIII: “Enter steadfastly, to the shepherd’s manger of Sylvester.” RIG.

The time likewise made ready. *Totidem* is used for “also,” “in like manner,” as above. RIG.

It is God’s first law. The Old Testament displayed beforehand the shadows and sacraments, or mysteries, of the New. RIG.

Nor are the threats from him. From God, that is. For God wishes you to be saved. Therefore, by establishing the law, he showed you the way of salvation; if you abandon it through your perversity, the way itself now threatens you with destruction. RIG.

Be stupefied now. Varro, in his books *On Agriculture*, said: “They made me blaze up,” and forms such as “make accustomed” and “make endure” [Col. 0220D] are formed in the same way. Ennius, moreover, had said: “I shall cause the brow to be smashed with a rock.” RIG.

The guilty man will be defeated. That is, he will be convicted.

In the second death. After the death of the body, the soul is consigned to the punishments of eternal death. Apocalypse 2: “He who conquers will not be harmed by the second death.” Tertullian, in his book *On Flight in Persecution*: “In the lake of sulfur and fire, which is the second death.” RIG.

Of heavenly discipline. Divine and Christian discipline. RIG.

Do those things not remind you that you are a man destined to die? Does the thought of death not restore you to yourself? Does it not call you back to your own self and to a sound mind? Perhaps, however, one should read *Terrebunt*, “They will terrify.” Will that thought not terrify you—that the time is approaching, or that within a few days you will be in the condition of a dead man whose soul will be seized by a demon and tortured? RIG.

Or a light one attacks. One must certainly write *seu levis invadit*, “or a light illness attacks,” illness being understood. DAVIS.]

You come forward as a suppliant of God beneath the tyrant’s gaze.  
You will learn in your fate whose law now gives you aid.

## XXIV.—TO THOSE LIVING BETWEEN THE TWO

Thinking that by living doubtfully between the two you can remain safe,  
Stripped of the law, worn out by luxury, you go forward.  
You look ahead so vainly—why do you seek wicked things?  
And why suppose that whatever you have done will thereafter remain with the dead?  
Look back, fool: you did not exist, and behold, now you are seen.  
You do not know whence you came forth, nor whence you are nourished.  
You flee the Most High God, the benefactor of your life,  
And your ruler, who would prefer that you live.  
You turn your face away and present your back to God.  
You plunge yourself into darkness while thinking that you dwell in light.  
Why do you run about in the synagogue among the Pharisees,  
[Col. 0219B] So that he whom you freely deny may become merciful to you?  
You go out from there and once again seek sound things.  
You wish to live between the two, but thereby you will perish.  
Moreover, you say: “Who is there who has redeemed anyone from death,  
So that we may believe him that punishments are carried out there?”  
Ah, malicious man, it is not as you suppose.  
For after burial, the man who lived rightly receives benefit.  
But when you soon die, you will be led to a malignant place,  
Whereas those who believe in Christ are led to a benign place,  
And that delightfulness caresses those to whom it clings.  
But for you doubters there is punishment without a body,  
And the torturer’s order causes you to cry out to a brother.

## XXV.—THOSE WHO FEAR AND WILL NOT BELIEVE

How long, foolish man, will you refuse to acknowledge Christ?  
[Col. 0220A] You avoid the rich field and scatter seed upon barren ground.  
You seek to remain in the forest, where the robber dwells.  
You say, “I too belong to God,” yet you wander outside.  
Enter now into the hall, after having been invited so often.  
The harvest is already ripe; the time likewise is ready.  
Look, reap now. What? Do you not repent? From there,  
Now, if you have nothing, gather: the vintage is wine.  
The time for life is present—the time to believe before death.  
God’s first law is the foundation of the later law.  
It indeed marked you as one who would believe under the second law.  
Nor are the threats from him, but from the law itself, powerful against you.  
Be stupefied now; swear that you believe in Christ,
