For the Old Testament proclaims him.  
For it is necessary only to believe in him who died,  
So that you may be able to rise again and live forever.  
[Col. 0220B] Therefore, if anyone disbelieves that these things will occur,  
Provided that the guilty man will be convicted in the second death,  
I shall sing briefly in this little book of what is to come.  
For it is possible to know where hope must be placed above all.  
Nevertheless, I urge you to believe in Christ as quickly as possible.

## XXVI.—TO THOSE WHO REBEL AGAINST THE LAW OF CHRIST, THE LIVING GOD

Unhappy man, you reject the goodness of heavenly discipline  
And rush into death while wishing to wander without restraint.  
Luxury and the brief pleasures of the world destroy you;  
For this you will be tormented beneath the infernal regions for all time.  
The pleasures in which you foolishly delight are empty.  
Do those things not remind you that you are a man destined to die?

[Col. 0221A] [Note: [Col. 0221C]

Certainly in twofold fashion, if you are ill. If you grow weak, if you are consumed by some prolonged illness; thus he said above, “if you are held by a long illness.” Hence the saying: “It is a kind of mercy to be killed quickly.” RIG.

A glass-like life. What an ancient writer said of fortune may most truly be said of human life: “Our life [Col. 0221D] is made of glass: just when it shines, it breaks.” RIG.

Joyous days. “Days of joy,” “gladdening days,” “happy days.” The formation of this word is highly suspect to me, and nothing can be pronounced with certainty unless the ancient manuscript is inspected. The Old Latin translator of the work called the *Epistle of Barnabas* renders Greek *εὐφροσύνη* (*euphrosynē*, “gladness”) as *laetatio*, “rejoicing.” The Paris edition incorrectly reads *legationes*, “embassies.” RIG.

He denied it. For he answered, “I do not know.” He denied knowing what he knew with absolute certainty, for he was still fresh from the murder of his brother. By lying thus to God, upon whom ignorance cannot fall, he most shamelessly denied God; and by a sacrilegious lie he attempted to steal away and, as it were, murder God’s knowledge. He wished divinity, *τὸ Θεῖον* (*to Theion*, “the divine nature”), to be taken from God. RIG.

And when you recalled the world. By rebelling against the law of Christ, you recalled the world; you recalled the devil whom you had renounced. RIG.

YOU WILL NOT OUTDIE GOD. You will not die in such a way that even when dead you escape God’s hands, as though God could no longer do anything with you once you were dead. RIG.

[Col. 0222C] You are defeated, senseless man. Even against your will, you are held fast by foolishness. RIG.

Whose ordinances proclaim. By “ordinances” he means the laws and commandments of Christ: discipline preserved through faith. RIG.

That the dead live. That is, they are called to eternal life.

[Col. 0222D] Extinguished in the fates. “Extinction,” that is, death. DAVIS.

That the deeds of the dead have been forgotten. That the things each dead person formerly did while living in the body have been consigned to oblivion.

Fool, you who think that you put yourself off. You who think that through death you are stripped away so completely that you are now nothing and nothing of you remains any longer.

Know him as one to be desired. Namely, God the Father and our Lord. RIGALTIUS.

It is laid away. In the tomb.

You. Your soul, the most principal part of you. RIG.

Hither. It directs itself hither. ID.

Will not be able to be equated. With divine eyes.

Concern for one’s conduct. Above he said, “concerning former conduct.”

They torment the accursed with punishments. Thus, concerning Christ himself, *Instruction* XXXVI says, “the accursed one through the cross.” The old glosses give: *Dirus*—*Θεοχόλωτος, δεινός* (*Theocholōtos, deinos*: “the object of divine wrath, terrible”); *Diritas*—*Δεινότης* (*deinotēs*, “terribleness”). Other glosses give: *δεινός*, “malicious, wicked, savage, fierce, harsh, atrocious”; [Col. 0223C] *δεινοποιῷ*, “harshly, severely.” Elsewhere: *Θεοχόλωτος*, “one who has incurred wrath”; the manuscript reads “one at whom God is angry.” And in Festus: “*Dirus*: born from the wrath of a god.” Juvenal: “begotten by those angry gods.” RIG.]

Can thirty years not yet make you wise?  
If at first you erred unknowingly, look back upon your gray hair.  
You now think that you enjoy a happy life here  
Amid injuries; yet here are the losses of your possessions,  
Wars, unspeakable frauds, and thefts accompanied by blood;  
The body is tormented by ulcers, and groans and lamentations arise;  
Either a light illness attacks, or you are held by a long disease,  
Or you are bereft of your children, or mourn a lost spouse.  
Everything is abandoned. Alas! Honors fall from on high  
Through vice and poverty—certainly doubly so if you are ill.  
And you call it life, when mortal life is made of glass?  
Look at last and see that this time is futile;  
But in the future you have the hope of living without deceit.  
Surely little children who were snatched away wished to live,  
And youths deprived of life perhaps wished to grow old;  
[Col. 0221B] They were preparing to enjoy joyous days themselves,  
And yet against our will we surrender everything to the world.  
I too was a Gentile and lingered with a perverse mind,  
And I thought the life of this age was the true life.  
Like you, I judged that when death came,  
Once the spirit had departed, the dead person’s soul had perished.  
But these things are not so, for the founder and creator of the world  
Demanded from the brother the brother who had been slain.  
“Impious man,” he said, “tell me: where is your brother?” He denied it.  
“For your brother’s blood has cried aloud to me on high.”  
You are tormented, I see, where you thought you would feel nothing.  
But he lives and occupies the places at the right hand;  
He enjoys the delights you have lost, wicked man.  
You recalled the world, while he went on before;  
He will be immortal, but you will lament beneath Tartarus.  
[Col. 0221C] Surely God lives, who has caused the dead to live,  
So as to render worthy rewards to the innocent and good,  
But cruel Tartarus to the mad and impious.  
Begin to understand God’s judgments, deluded man.

## XXVII.—FOOL, YOU WILL NOT OUTDIE GOD

[Col. 0222A]

Fool, you will not outdie God, nor, once dead, escape the Most High.  
Although you may determine that when dead you will feel nothing,  
You are defeated, senseless man: God, the founder of the world, lives,  
And his ordinances proclaim that the dead live.  
But while you rush headlong and seek to live without God,  
You judge that a person is extinguished in death and believe this extinction fated.  
The eternal God has not arranged matters as you suppose,  
So that the deeds formerly done by the dead should be forgotten.  
Ruling us now, he has made receptacles for the dead;  
But after we are ashes, we shall see those things.  
Fool, you who think that through death you are stripped away and cease to be,  
You have made your ruler and Lord powerless.  
But death does not end in nothingness, if you reconsider in your heart.  
Know him as one to be desired, for too late you will feel his presence.  
[Col. 0222B] You were the ruler of your flesh; surely your flesh did not rule you.  
Once freed from it, the flesh is laid away, but you go hither.  
A mortal human being is rightly separated from the flesh;  
Therefore mortal eyes will not be able to equal the divine.  
Thus our abyss stands, by God’s secret counsel.  
Therefore, while you dwell in fragile mortality, give honor to God,  
And believe that Christ will restore you living from the dead.  
You ought to render praises to the Almighty in the Church.

## XXVIII.—THE RIGHTEOUS RISE AGAIN

Righteousness and goodness, peace and true patience  
Cause one to live after death, together with care for one’s conduct.  
But a deceitful mind—harmful, treacherous, and depraved—  
Withdraws to its own region and remains in savage death.  
Impious man, hear now what you gain through your evil deeds.  
[Col. 0222C] Look at earthly judges, who now, while in the body,  
Torment the accursed with punishments: either punishments by the sword  
Are prepared for their deserts, or lamentation in a long imprisonment.  
In the end, do you hope to mock the heavenly God,  
The ruler of the firmament, through whom all things were made?

[Col. 0223A] [Note: [Col. 0223C]

Who brought you forth without your knowing. Read: “Who brought you forth while you were unknowing.” DAVIS.

In the golden age. In the golden Jerusalem, namely, in that millennial course of undisturbed felicity. RIG.

In God’s secret counsel. Above he said: “Thus our abyss stands [Col. 0223D] by God’s secret counsel.” RIG.

There are always lamentations. Weeping and gnashing of teeth. RIG.

The poor man cries, *εὕρηκα*. The copy reads: *Vixit et extinxit pauper Ebrea clamor*. The brilliant emendation is: *Vixit, et extinxi. Pauper εὕρηκα clamat*—“He lived, and I extinguished him. The poor man cries, ‘I have found it!’” In the preceding verse Commodian says: “Alas, wretched men! Let those of moderate means flee far away from you”—that is, from the rich. He then introduces the rich man speaking tauntingly at the poor man’s funeral, as though the poor man had been troublesome and excessively importunate while alive: “At last I have driven away a great nuisance from myself. That filthy Lazarus lived; I extinguished the wretch.” He then speaks of the poor man’s soul, stripped of the body and already taken up into heaven. “The poor man,” Commodian says, “cries *εὕρηκα* (*heurēka*), ‘I have found it!’”—that is: “I have found what I desired, what I asked from the Lord. I possess the way by which one goes to heaven.” Thus Stephen, even while being stoned, says: “I see the heavens opened,” etc. RIG.

To the Furies of Charybdis. To Satan’s angels in the chasm of hell, where there is no solid ground but an unswimmable depth. RIG.

You worked. That is, “he worked.” *Ἀχαϊκῶς* (*Achaïkōs*), “in the Achaean manner,” or, if you prefer, barbarously. With similar license he said in *Instruction* XXXI, v. [Col. 0224C] 466: *Intuite dicta Salomonis*, “Look upon the words of Solomon.” Again, in *Instruction* XXXIX, v. 481: *Bacchent aulica semper*, “Let courtly things always revel.” DAVIS.

Observe now, barren man. Barren Christians will be discussed in *Instruction* LV. RIG.

Do you do good? I am here. This is spoken in the person of God, who offers mercy and presents grace and most immediate aid to the penitent—namely himself, the author of every form of felicity. RIG.

[Col. 0224D] How gifts and presents corrupt judges. Commodian is referring, as I believe, to Ecclesiastes 3:16. On that passage Jerome writes as follows, vol. V, p. 10, Victor ed.: “The meaning is plain, but it is wrapped in the cloud of translation. Beneath this sun, he says, I sought truth and judgment, and I saw that even upon the judges’ own benches it was not truth that prevailed, but gifts.” See Psalm 81:2. DAVIS.

Victory carries off the case for the wicked party. The copy reads: *victoria tollit iniquam*, “victory carries off the wicked woman.” RIG.

Solomon openly utters blasphemy. Thus the copy reads, just as above it has *ignominium* and *infamium* in *Instruction* XIX. ID.

The belly is God. Commodian had Philippians 3:19 in mind. DAVIS.

Be a new judge. That is, having obtained a new magistracy.

By whose excellence. God’s, who bestows so much upon you with so liberal a hand. RIG.

The Lord’s cruciarius. Thus the copy reads: *Cruciatum Domini*, “the Lord’s torment,” the cross of Christ, Christ crucified: *Τὸν μέγαν ἐκεῖνον τὸν ἐν τῇ Παλαιστίνῃ ἀνασκολοπισθέντα*—“that great one who was impaled in Palestine.” In place of *cruciarius*, the Greeks used *Martyrium*, “Martyrion”; Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, relates in his little book *On the Site of the City of Jerusalem* that the basilica magnificently adorned by Emperor Constantine was called by that name. From Eucherius’s account in the Vatican manuscript, [Col. 0225B] the most learned Jacques Sirmond observed that another basilica built by the same Constantine was called by the proper name *Anastasis*, “Resurrection.” Latin writers could surely call this “Resurrection” by the same right by which the Greeks called the cross “Martyrion,” the name of that basilica [Col. 0225C] especially mentioned by Eucherius. Furthermore, our Commodian transferred that word, *ἀνάστασις* (*anastasis*), meaning the resurrection of the faithful itself, into his Latin in *Instruction* XLIII. Yet no one would therefore deny that it was also the name of a basilica.

But a coin struck under Constantine, whose obverse displays the face of a man without any name and whose reverse displays the structure of a temple between two soldiers, will not be proved to bear the likeness of Christ the Lord by any better argument than that Christ himself said that he would destroy this temple—indicating himself—and restore it after three days, thereby signifying that he himself would rise again. Without that meaning, anyone arguing against those who might deny that the face is Christ’s will proceed on far weaker conjectures.

Now, if we believe that the coin presents a true image of Christ and that the fidelity of the original was preserved for three hundred years, why is something that all Christians should contemplate with such zeal and devotion kept hidden for so long? Why, moreover, did it remain hidden for so long among those who now wish [Col. 0225D] Christ to be depicted as handsome? For Sirmond, who saw the coin, says only that the face is lively and grave. Elsewhere I called it austere, so as to detract as little as possible from the traditions of the Fathers nearest to that first age of Christ, who did not regard as shameful, deceptive, or hateful *τὸ δύσ­ειδες, τὸ ἀειδές, τὸ εὐτελές καὶ τὴν ὄψιν αἰσχράν*—“an ill-favored appearance, shapelessness, lowliness, and ugliness of countenance.” RIG.]

You rage, you rave, and now disparage even the name of God;  
Therefore you will not escape: he will impose punishments according to your deeds.  
Now I wish you to be cautious, lest you enter the heat of the fire.  
Hand yourself over to Christ now, so that your good deeds may follow you.

## XXIX.—TO THE EVIL, UNBELIEVING RICH MAN

You delay, rich man, while gazing excessively upon all your possessions,  
To which you still seek insatiably to cling.  
“After these things,” you say, “I do not hope to live once dead.”  
Ungrateful to the Most High God, since you judge God to be such!  
He brought you forth while you were unknowing, and then nourished you.  
He himself governs your meadows, himself your vineyards,  
Himself your flock of cattle and whatever you possess.  
Yet you pay no attention to these things—or perhaps you govern everything?  
He who made this heaven, the earth, and the salt seas  
[Col. 0223B] Has determined to restore us ourselves in the golden age;  
And now, if you believe, life is lived within God’s secret counsel.  
Learn of God, fool, who wishes you to stand present as an immortal,  
So that in the contest you may render him everlasting thanks.  
His law teaches this, but because you seek to wander,  
You disbelieve everything, and therefore will go into Tartarus.  
Soon you surrender your soul and are led where you regret being.  
There spiritual and eternal punishment pours over you;  
There are always lamentations, and you will not outdie it,  
Proclaiming the Almighty God there, when it is already too late.

## XXX.—RICH MEN, BE HUMBLE

Learn, mortal man, to show yourself good to everyone.  
Why do you make yourself out to be different amid the people?  
You go where you do not know, and depart from here in ignorance.  
Impiously you behave, though you share the same bodily nature;  
You thirst continually for riches and raise yourself excessively on high,  
And exhibit arrogance, nor do you look upon the poor of your own accord.  
You do not feed those now subject to you, nor even your own relatives.  
Alas, wretched men! Let those of moderate means flee far away from you.  
[Col. 0224A] “He lived; and I extinguished him.” The poor man cries, *Εὕρηκα*—“I have found it!”  
Soon, as you yourself perish, you are driven to the Furies of Charybdis.  
So undisciplined are you rich men.  
You give laws to those people, but prepare none for yourselves.  
Rich man, strip yourself of such evils, though perverse toward God,  
So that perhaps what you have now done may indeed come to your aid.  
Be companions of the divine power while you have time,  
And love the lowly as the elm loves the vine.  
Now observe, barren man, the law terrible to the wicked  
And equally benign to the good; remain protected in prosperity.  
Rich men, cast off hearts of fraud and take up hearts of peace.  
And behold your own evil. Do you do good? I am here.

## XXXI.—TO JUDGES

Look upon the words of Solomon, all you judges:  
How, with a single word, he disparages you.  
[Col. 0224B] How gifts and presents corrupt judges! From this  
The judgment follows: you always love the givers;  
And when a case arises, victory carries it off for the wicked party.  
Thus I am innocent and, though lowly, do not accuse you,  
Because Solomon openly utters the reproach.  
But for you the belly is God, and rewards are your laws.  
Paul the apostle declares this, not I, a double-dealer.

## XXXII.—TO THOSE WHO PLEASE THEMSELVES

If place or occasion favors you, or rank has promoted you,  
Be a newly appointed judge: why are you now puffed up by it?  
Untaught, you blaspheme him by whose excellence you live,  
Never reflecting upon such great fragility.  
Through ranks and profits, greedy for fortune, you grow presumptuous.  
There is no law for you, nor do you recognize yourself in prosperity.  
Though courtly things be valued in gold, let them always revel;  
[Col. 0224C] If you have not worshiped the Lord’s crucified one, you have perished.  
Both place and occasion and rank are now granted to you,  
If only you believe; but if not, you will fear on that account.

[Col. 0225A] [Note: [Col. 0225D]

Conform yourself to Christ. Obey Christ; order your life according to Christ’s laws and commandments. RIG.

TO THE GENTILES. To everyone, certainly, but especially to those who were still raging against Christians here and there throughout Italy and at Rome, or who hated and mocked the name or discipline of Christ. RIG.

Assume the likeness of your Lord. Put on Christ the Lord. Paul, Romans 13:14 and Galatians 3:27: “In baptism you put on Christ.” Assume Christ’s form or character—that is, keep his commandments and precepts. Christ himself, Matthew 11:29: “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart.” Hence Commodian adds: “Raise up your savage hearts.” RIG.

[Col. 0226B] Raise up your hearts. He alludes to the solemn formula *Sursum corda*, “Lift up your hearts.” RIG.

Enter steadfastly. The copy reads: *Intrate stabilis silvestri ad praesepia tauri*. The emendation readily presented itself: *Intrate stabiles Silvestri ad praesepe pastoris*, “Enter steadfastly, to the shepherd’s manger of Sylvester.” These words contribute considerably to the preeminence of the Roman Church. RIG.

Rigaltius certainly seems to have departed too far from the reading of the copy, which, by his own testimony, reads:

[Col. 0226C] *Intrate stabilis silvestri ad praesepia tauri.*

Sirmond, as cited by Fabricius in *Delectus argumentorum*, p. 229, read:

> *Intrate stabiles vestra ad praesepia tauri.*  
> Enter steadfastly to your bull’s mangers.

This is more pleasing than Dodwell’s:

> *Intrate stabula silvestres ad praesepia tauri.*  
> Enter the stalls, wild creatures, to the bull’s mangers.

Davies nevertheless agrees with Dodwell, who defends his emendation of this passage at greater length in his dissertation *On the Age of Commodian*, §§ 6 and 9.

Beneath the royal roof. In Christ’s Church, beneath Christ the King. RIG.

Take refuge beneath the cave. In the crypts of the Christian Church. Perhaps he alludes to the time when Sylvester is believed to have hidden with his clergy on Mount Soracte. RIG.

To be filled with coarse pods. Horace, *Epistles* II.1: “He lives on pods and second-rate bread.” RIG.

[Col. 0226D] A useful mare is tamed. Philostratus relates that Apollonius’s brother was corrected by his younger brother by this example: *Κἀκεῖνον μὲν ὥσπερ οἱ καταψόντες τοὺς δυσ­ηνίους τε καὶ μὴ εὐαγωγοὺς τῶν ἵππων ἐς πειθὼ ἤγαγε καὶ μετερρύθμισε τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων*, etc.—“And he brought that man to obedience and reformed him from his errors, just as those who soothe horses that are disobedient and not easily managed,” etc., book I, ch. 10.

Enter under arms. Enter the camp of the Christians; become a soldier of Christ; enter Christ’s Church. RIG.—This expression cannot mean what Rigaltius wishes. The passage seems corrupt to me, and with a slight alteration I would emend it thus:

> *Tu te ipsa doma sapiens, et intra sub antro.*  
> Tame yourself, wise creature, and enter beneath the cave.

He addresses the Gentiles as beasts that must be driven from the forests into caves. Above, *Instruction* XXXIII, v. 496:

> Wolves are in the forest; therefore take refuge beneath the cave.

DAVIS.

Beast-man. From *bestia*, “beast,” he formed the masculine *bestius*. RIG.—Read: *Sed sic, quasi bestius, erras*, “But you wander thus, like a beast-man,” as the sense itself shows. DAVIS.

The golden age mentioned beforehand. Here too he introduces the fable of the Millenarians, or of the golden and jeweled Jerusalem. RIG.]

Conform yourself to Christ, and bow your neck to him.  
For him honor remains, together with complete assurance concerning all things.  
When the times flatter you, be more cautious.  
If you fail to foresee what awaits you at the final limits of fate,  
You can never return to life without Christ.

## XXXIII.—TO THE GENTILES

Fierce people without a shepherd, cease now to wander.  
I too, who warn you, was the same—ignorant and wandering.  
Therefore, now assume the likeness of your Lord.  
Raise upward your savage and embittered hearts.  
Enter steadfastly, to the shepherd’s manger of Sylvester,  
Remaining safe from robbers beneath the royal roof.  
Wolves are in the forest; therefore take refuge beneath the cave.  
You fight and rage, nor do you consider where you dwell.  
Believe in the one God, so that, though dead, you may be able to live,  
[Col. 0225B] And rise in the kingdom when the resurrection of the righteous occurs.

## XXXIV.—AGAIN, TO IGNORANT GENTILES

The untamed neck refuses to bear the yoke of labor;  
[Col. 0226A] Then it delights to be filled in the fields with coarse pods.  
And yet, though unwilling, the useful mare is tamed,  
And, once first thoroughly subdued, becomes less fierce.  
Gentile, human being, my brother, do not be a wild beast.  
At last tear yourself free and reconsider within yourself.  
Surely you are not cattle or a beast, but were born a human being.  
Tame yourself wisely and enter under arms.  
You who follow idols pursue nothing but the vanity of the age.  
Your frivolous hearts destroy you when you are almost set free.  
There gold, garments, and silver are measured by the ell.  
There warfare is waged, and afterward Love is sung instead of psalms.  
Do you think it is life where you play or gaze upon such things?  
Ignorant man, you cast lots; you seek dead and golden things.  
You will not escape the plague thereby, though you yourself be a diviner.  
You do not seek the grace that the Lord sent to be read upon earth,  
[Col. 0226B] But wander thus like a beast-man.  
The golden ages mentioned beforehand will come to you if you believe,  
[Col. 0227A] [Note: [Col. 0227B]

ON THE TREE OF LIFE AND DEATH. In this *Instruction* an acrostic is not maintained, but rather the sequence of the letters of the alphabet. The same occurs below in *Instruction* LX, though there the letter X is missing.

Adam, the first to fall. He alludes to the first-formed man. RIG.

Belias the tempter. The devil; “beast” in place of “serpent.” Thus *Instruction* LIII: “Moreover, do not spare yourself against Belias.” RIG.—[Col. 0227C] In the *Testaments of the Patriarchs*, the *Sibylline Oracles*, and many other ancient writings, the devil is called *Βελιάρ* (*Beliar*), just as Commodian calls him *Belias*. Both spellings, however, are wholly incorrect. The true name is *Belial*. See Ussher’s note on ch. 11 of the epistle to the Philippians ascribed to Ignatius. DAVIS.

Leader of the offspring of birth. The middle word is idle and disrupts the sense. Read: *Dux nativitatis*, “Leader of birth”—that is, the first of all to be born, or the first-formed man. DAVIS.

Beware now of the life-giving fruits, believers. In the preceding verse Commodian signified Christ when he said: “Life hangs upon the tree, bearing fruits—the commandments.” Why, then, does he now warn us to beware of the life-giving fruits? One must certainly read: *Capite nunc vitalia poma credentes*, “Take now the life-giving fruits, believers.” Thus shortly afterward, v. 533: “Now stretch out your hand and take from the life-giving tree.” DAVIS.

Of the primordial law. Tertullian used the phrase “primordial law” in *Against the Jews*, ch. 2. RIG.

The excellent subsequent law of the Lord. The second law: the New Testament, the Gospel. RIG.

[Col. 0227D] Render yourselves to the second law. Thus above, *Instruction* XXVI: “Do those things not restore you?” RIG.

The fates of demons. The oracles of idols and the impostures of idolaters. RIG.—Servius, in his note on *Aeneid* V.703, indeed observes that *fata* can mean “oracles.” But Commodian is not dealing with the responses of the gods. At my own risk I read: *Templorum culturas, daemonum fana vitate*, “Avoid the worship of temples and the shrines of demons.” DAVIS.

*Xanta Dei lex est.* That is, *Sancta*, “Holy is God’s law.” Thus *Xantones* for *Santones*. Elias Vinetus on Ausonius, epistle XI. RIG.

The Zabolic law. Thus below, *Instruction* LIX, v. 922: “All things belonging to the pomp of Zabulus.” And *Instruction* LXVIII has *Zacones* for *Diacones*, “deacons.” Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, ch. XVI: “After those nine most glorious battles in which Zabulus was conquered by you, he did not dare to engage with you any further.” Other ecclesiastical writers are also known to have used the same manner of speech: Hilary on Matthew 26; Jerome in his translation of Origen’s Homilies I, III, VI, IX, and XI on Ezekiel—to omit the rest. Concerning the change of the particle *διά* (*dia*) into Aeolic *ζᾶ* (*za*), it is best to consult the observations of learned men [Col. 0228B] on the most recent edition of Hesychius, under *ζαβάλλειν* (*zaballein*), but especially Huet’s *Dissertations*, edited by Tilladet, vol. I, pp. 93–95. See also Rigaltius below, on the title of *Instruction* XXXVII. DAVIS.

ON THE FOLLY OF THE CROSS. Either it must be read as a compound word, *crucistultitia*, Greek *σταυρομωρία* (*stauromōria*, “cross-folly”), or [Col. 0228C] a verse is missing from the acrostic.

But the cross has become foolishness. Paul to the Corinthians: *Ἕλλησι μωρία* (*Hellēsi mōria*), “foolishness to the Greeks.” Here, however, Commodian addresses universally all peoples who worship idols, so that by the “adulterous people” he means the race of Cain.

The dreadful one overshadows through the cross. As above: “They overshadow the simple people.” Through his cross Christ regarded the wise of this age as fools and madmen. He overshadowed them through the dreadfulness of the cross, accomplishing such marvelous deeds of divine majesty. RIG.—Anyone who calls our Savior *dirus*, “dreadful” or “accursed,” is guilty of blasphemy. Read:

> *Rex aeternitatis per crucem diros adumbrat,  
> Ut sibi non credant.*

> The King of eternity overshadows the accursed through the cross,  
> So that they do not believe in him.

Thus *Instruction* XXVIII, v. 419: “They torment the accursed with punishments.” DAVIS.—If this emendation is adopted, Commodian will have had in view Luke 8:18: “So that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand.” Compare also Matthew 13:13, and see shortly below, v. 577.

Hence Enoch, Cain’s offspring. The copy reads: *Inde Nohel suboles Cananaei*, “Hence Nohel, offspring of the Canaanite.” Concerning this Enoch, Eusebius says [Col. 0228D] in the first book of his *Chronicles*, published by Scaliger: “This is the other Enoch, not the one who was translated so that he should not die; for the latter is the son of Jared, seventh from Adam.” RIG.—See Genesis 4:17. Josephus calls him *Ἐνῶσος* (*Enōsos*) in *Antiquities* I.3, and some copies of the Septuagint translation do indeed do likewise. DAVIS.

He returned with peace. I confess that I do not see the meaning of these words. Perhaps one should read: *Et inde secunda terribilem legem primo cum pace revincit*—“And from there the second law, with peace, overcomes the first, terrible law.” ID.

But the race of Abel. Rather, the race of Seth, whom Adam himself—or rather Eve herself—says was appointed to her by God as another offspring in place of Abel, whom Cain killed. Luke traces Christ’s genealogy to Seth, not to Cain—or Abel. The accounts concerning the *mialgamia*, “mixed marriage,” of the sons of men with the sons of God, who are also commonly called *Egregori* in ancient writings, are so entangled [Col. 0229B] in fabulous inventions that even the most perceptive cannot clearly discern what may be confidently affirmed. See Suidas under the word *Μιαιγαμίαι* (*Miai­gamiai*, “mixed marriages”), together with Scaliger’s excerpts from book I of Enoch and Petavius’s collections in his volume *On the Angels*. RIG.]

And you will begin again to live immortally forever.  
This also is granted you: to know what you formerly were.  
Make yourself subject to God, who governs all things.

## XXXV.—ON THE TREE OF LIFE AND DEATH

Adam, the first to fall, sought to evade God’s commands.  
Belias was the tempter, through envy of the palm of victory.  
What he did, whether good or evil, he transmitted also to us.  
The leader of birth—the first-born—we therefore die through him,  
Because he withdrew from the divine Word and became an exile.  
When six thousand years have been completed, we shall be immortal.  
When the fruit of the tree was tasted, death entered the world.  
Through this tree of death we are begotten for the life to come.  
Life hangs upon the tree, bearing fruits—the commandments.  
Take now the life-giving fruits, believers.  
The law from the tree was given as an object of fear to the first human being;  
[Col. 0227B] From it death arose when the primordial law was neglected.  
Now stretch out your hand and take from the life-giving tree.  
The excellent subsequent law of the Lord proceeded from the tree.  
The first law was lost; hence one is permitted to taste.

Whoever worships forbidden gods embraces the evil pleasures of life.

Reject the taste; it will suffice to know what it was.

If you wish to live, submit yourselves to the second law.

[Col. 0228A] Avoid the cults of temples and the decrees of demons.

Turn yourselves to Christ, and you will be companions of God.

Holy is God’s law, which teaches the dead to live.

The Lord commanded that a hymn be offered to him alone;

Avoid the diabolical law altogether.

### XXXVI.—ON THE FOLLY OF THE CROSS

I have spoken of the twofold sign, whence death proceeded,

And likewise, repeatedly, life proceeds from it.

But the cross has been made folly to an adulterous people.

The King of eternity, dread, is foreshadowed through the cross,

So that they might now believe in him—O fools who live in death!

Cain killed the younger and was found wicked;

From him Enoch and the Cainite offspring are said to have been born.

Thus an unrighteous race increased in the world, which never

Directs its mind toward God: belief in the cross

[Col. 0228B] Becomes an object of horror, and they say that they live rightly.

The first law was upon wood, and from it came the second.

The law was terrible at first; it returned with peace.

In their pride they rushed into empty transgressions:

They refuse to acknowledge the Lord pierced with nails;

When his judgment comes, there they will recognize him.

But Abel’s race now believes in kindly Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0229C]

**WHO JUDAIZE AS FANATICS.** *Judaizant* [“they Judaize”]. In the most ancient manuscripts of Cyprian’s Council of Carthage, *Exorcidiare* occurs for *Exorcizare*. So too in Instruction XXXV, *Zabolicam legem* for *Diabolicam legem*, and frequently *zacones* for *diacones*. RIG.

**You yourself were blind.** Without doubt it should be read: “You yourself wander blind.” DAVIS.

**They are funerals.** He alludes to the common saying, Δὶς κραμβὴ θάνατος, “Cabbage served twice is death”: “Cabbage repeated kills the wretched schoolmasters.” RIG.

**Or because the heaped-up soil of the plough encloses the field.** The form of the acrostic admits no more. RIG.

**From so great a crime.** He means the crime of the Jews, who crucified their king, our Lord. RIG.

**He himself, bloodstained, recoiled.** Upon the cross itself, when Christ had completed everything that the Father had commanded, he renounced the ungrateful people and turned himself toward the foreign nations. Here he calls him “bloodstained,” whom above he called “dread.” RIG.—Far be it that the most gracious Redeemer of the human race should be called “bloodstained.” Read: “From so great a crime he himself recoiled from the bloodstained”; that is, after so great a crime he turned away from those blood-soaked Jews—in the same sense as above, verse 547. DAVIS.

**You do not wish to be overcome.** So above, Instruction XXVII: “You are overcome, foolish man.” But when a foolish man allows himself to be overcome, he comes to his senses. The Jews, who kick against the goad, refuse to be overcome. RIG.

**What you mock.** Read *quam*, namely, “the law.” DAVIS.

**Look upon Leah.** Justin, Tertullian, Cyprian, and other Christian Fathers use these arguments in disputation against the Jews.

**With such weak eyes.** Cyprian: “Leah, the elder, with weaker eyes.” Sulpicius Severus: “Leah, less comely in her eyes.” Commodian says that this Leah was a type of the Synagogue, but Rachel, the younger and more beautiful, a type of the Christian Church. This comparison certainly casts down the arrogance of the Jews, who preferred the narrowness of the Synagogue to the breadth of the Church. Jerome, Letter 126 to Dardanus.

[Col. 0230B] **Whom Jacob received as a sign.** She was substituted for Rachel, whom he loved.

[Col. 0230C] **As a sign.** As a mystery and figure of the Old Testament.

**For the beloved younger one.** In the manuscript, “for the lesser offense.” Cyprian incorrectly has: “The younger, beautiful one, as a type of the Church.” RIGALT.

**Consider fully what was spoken from heaven to Rebecca.** The author has in view Genesis 25:23: Καὶ εἶπε Κύριος αὐτῇ (Ῥεβέκκῃ)· Δύο ἔθνη ἐν τῇ γαστρί σου εἰσί· καὶ δύο λαοὶ ἐκ τῆς κοιλίας σου διασταλήσονται· καὶ λαὸς λαοῦ ὑπερέξει, καὶ ὁ μείζων δουλεύσει τῷ ἐλάσσονι: “And the Lord said to her—Rebecca—‘Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples shall be divided from your belly; one people shall surpass the other, and the elder shall serve the younger.’” See also St. Paul, Romans 9:12–13. DAVIS.

**Resembling another woman.** Virgil: “Made to resemble Camers in appearance.” RIGALT.

**By the law of those who cry aloud.** By the writings of the Prophets. So in Instruction LVI: “If the prophet had only cried aloud into the cloud.”

**The Most High.** He who is also the Highest. RIGALT.

**And the Most High despises your sabbaths and thirtieth-day observances.** Commodian points to Isaiah 1:13–14: “Offer sacrifice in vain no longer: incense is an abomination to me. The new moon and the sabbath and other festivals I will not endure: your assemblies are wicked. My soul has hated your calends and your solemnities.” In place of “new moons” and “calends,” Commodian said “thirtieth-day observances.” So too Horace, *Satires* I.9.69:

> Today is the thirtieth-day sabbath: would you  
> Insult the circumcised Jews?

On this matter see Scaliger, *Canones Isagogici*, book III, pp. 223, 264. DAVIS.

**To have perished by an unjust death.** That is, to have died, to have been removed from human affairs. He speaks in a human—or rather pagan—fashion. For one who rose again from the dead on the third day ought not to be said to have perished. RIGALT.—**To have perished by an unjust death.** Rigaltius understood these words as referring to Christ. Yet, upon examination of the scriptural text that Commodian evidently had in view, the author appears to have spoken not of Christ but of the unbelieving Jews, whom he says perished by an unjust or evil death. Compare Isaiah 8:14–15 with Matthew 21:42, 44.]

### XXXVII.—WHO JUDAIZE AS FANATICS

[Col. 0229A]

What? Half a Jew—do you wish to be half a pagan?

When dead, you will not thereby escape the judgment of Christ.

You yourself were blind, and you enter among the blind, foolish man:

Thus one blind man leads another blind man into a pit.

You go where you do not know, and depart from there still ignorant;

Let learners go to the learned and depart learned.

But you go to those from whom you can learn nothing.

You go outside the gates, and from there you go also to idols.

First ask what has been commanded in the law;

Let them tell you whether worship of gods has been commanded.

For they are ignorant of precisely that whereby they might have power.

But because they are themselves guilty through this very offense,

They relate nothing of God’s commandments except what is marvelous;

[Col. 0229B] Yet then, blind as you are, they lead you with themselves into the pit.

They are corpses; it is too much to repeat familiar things about them.

Or because the heaped-up soil of the plough encloses the field.

The Almighty did not will that they should understand the King;

From so great a crime he himself recoiled from the bloodstained.

He delivered himself to us when the law was supplemented;

Hence they now hide among us, abandoned by the King.

But if you think there is hope in them,

You are altogether mistaken if you worship both God and shrines.

### XXXVIII.—TO THE JEWS

Ever wicked, stiff-necked, and kicking against the goad,

You refuse to be overcome; thus you will be heirs.

[Col. 0230A] Isaiah said that you were thickened in heart.

You behold the law that Moses dashed down in anger.

And the same Lord gave him a second law:

In that law he placed hope, but you reject it with mockery.

For this reason you will not be worthy of the kingdom of heaven.

### XXXIX.—AGAIN, TO THE JEWS

Look upon Leah, who was a type of the Synagogue,

With such weak eyes, whom Jacob received as a sign;

And yet he served again for the beloved younger one:

A true mystery and a type of our Church.

Consider fully what was spoken from heaven to Rebecca,

So that, resembling another woman, you may believe in Christ.

Then consider Tamar’s bearing of the twins;

Turn your attention to Cain, the first tiller of the earth,

[Col. 0230B] And to Abel the shepherd, who was without blemish,

An offerer sacrificed by his brother in his brother’s destruction.

Understand, therefore, that the younger ones are approved by Christ.

### XL.—AGAIN, TO THE SAME

There is no unbelieving people but yours, unrighteous men,

Rejected in so many places and so often by the law of those who cry aloud.

The Most High despises your sabbaths and thirtieth-day observances;

He wholly rejects all your observances derived from the law,

Although it had commanded you to make sacrifices to him;

He who said that he would cast a stone to be your stumbling block.

Those who would not believe were to perish by an unjust death,

And the beloved were to be saved through other laws; hence

[Col. 0231A] [Note: [Col. 0231B]

**Isaiah said.** What follows is not found in Isaiah, so that from this point the author’s preface—“I have said nothing in an orderly fashion”—is entirely true. Yet Isaiah does contain a passage about the New Jerusalem, cited by Justin Martyr against Trypho in support of that period of one thousand years. It is chapter 65 of the prophecy. RIGALT.—Rigaltius suffered a lapse of memory when he asserted that what follows was not in Isaiah; for it is found in chapter 14, verses 16–17: “Is this the man who disturbed the earth, who shook kingdoms, who made the world a wilderness?” and so forth. What the prophet had said of the king of Babylon, Commodian transfers to Antichrist. DAVIS.

**Who moves the world, and as many kings.** “He moves the world and likewise the kings.” We have often observed already that the particle *totidem* has this meaning here.

**He will have divided the world among three rulers.** If the manuscript reading is sound, Commodian truly expressed this carelessly. For Antichrist was not to divide the world among three rulers, but to overcome three kings. See Daniel 7:24; Irenaeus, book V, chapters 25–26; and Lactantius VII.16. Perhaps it should read:

> By defeating three rulers, he will have subdued the world;

that is, by fighting against three emperors he will have subjugated the world. DAVIS.

[Col. 0231D] **Nero raised from hell.** So in Instruction LXI, “raised from the sewer.” The manuscript is most corrupt here: “Herod raised from hell.” RIGALT.

**Nero will occupy half.** Sulpicius Severus, *History* II.28, says that “many accepted the opinion that he himself would come as Antichrist.” RIGALT.—**He will reign for three and a half years.** Irenaeus, book V, chapter 25: “He—Antichrist—will be given into his hand until a time, times, and half a time; that is, three years and six months, during which, when he comes, he will reign over the earth.” See also chapters 28 and 30 and Lactantius, book VII, chapter 17. Jerome and other ancient writers held the same opinion. DAVIS.—Or should it read “in three”?

**Then Babylon the harlot.** In John’s Apocalypse she bears upon her forehead the name “Mystery: Babylon the Great, mother of the fornications and abominations of the earth.” Tertullian, in his book *Against the Jews*: “Babylon in our John is a figure of the city of Rome, and accordingly of one that is great, proud, and a vanquisher of the saints.” The authors of *De finibus regundis* called Rome Babylon; there too [Col. 0232B] we noted what pertains to this subject, pp. 271 and 313. RIGALT.

**And the Latin victor.** Irenaeus, book V, chapter 25: “But the name LATEINOS also has the number six hundred and sixty-six. This is very probable, since the final kingdom bears this name; for those who now reign are Latins. Yet we shall not glory in this,” etc. How different this Latin is from that Sylvester to whose manger he summons all Christians in Instruction XXX! RIG.

**The first believers, deceived.** So in Instruction XXXV: “the first man.” RIG.

**The image will speak.** Revelation 13:15. This is also related of the image of Apollonius of Tyana. ID.

**Recapitulating the Scriptures from it.** Hesychius: ἀνακεφαλαιοῦται, συμπληροῦται, ἐπαναλαμβάνει—“it is summed up, completed, taken up again.” Irenaeus frequently uses this verb in book V, chapter 15, of Christ himself: “Recapitulating,” he says, “in himself all things that are in heaven and on earth.” And shortly afterward: “These things, therefore, he recapitulated in himself, uniting man to the Spirit,” etc. Tertullian, book V *Against Marcion*: “As that word sounds in Greek, to recapitulate—that is, to bring back to the beginning, or to review all things from the beginning in Christ.” 4 Esdras 12:25: “Those who will recapitulate his impieties, and those who will complete his last things.” RIG.

[Col. 0232D] **Living among nine tribes.** Read: “Living among nine **of the tribes**.” So shortly afterward, verse 638: “Two and a half of the tribes left behind.” DAVIS.

**I judge it more fittingly for you.** I would correct these words by a slight change: “I declare it more openly to you.” Commodian professes that he will explain the obscure scriptural statements concerning the nine and a half tribes, Antichrist, and certain other matters. RIG.

**A choir of holy prophets.** A synod of bishops. RIGALT.

**The foul men whom the horses.** He attacks the crimes of Novatus and Novatian, who, after being suspended and cast out of the Church, inflamed the people against their bishops. See Cyprian, Letter 49. RIG.

**Nor would the band rush rashly toward peace at some time.** This concerns the history of the lapsed and the schismatics, who by factional canvassing pressured the bishops to grant peace even to the unworthy and against their will. RIG.

**From the crime of two brothers.** Formerly brothers, today apostates. RIG.]

You do not believe in the Life suspended upon the wood,

Though God himself is Life: he himself hung there for us.

But with hardened heart you mock that same one.

### XLI.—ON THE TIME OF ANTICHRIST

Isaiah said: “This is the man who moves the world,

And as many kings, under whom the earth will be made desolate.”

Listen, for the prophet foretold concerning him.

I have said nothing in orderly composition, but carelessly.

Then, indeed, the world will end when he appears.

He will have divided the world among three rulers.

But when Nero has been raised from hell,

Elijah will first come to mark the beloved.

In the events that the region of Africa and the northern nation endure, the whole

Earth will tremble on every side for seven years;

But Elijah will hold half the period and Nero half.

[Col. 0231B] Then Babylon the harlot, burned into ash,

And thereafter he will proceed to Jerusalem, the Latin victor.

Then he will say: “I am the Christ for whom you have always prayed.”

And indeed the deceived first believers praise him together.

His false prophet performs many signs

So that they may believe him; above all, the image will speak.

The Almighty permits him to become such a being.

[Col. 0232A] The Jews, recapitulating the Scriptures from this,

Cry aloud together to the Most High that they have been deceived.

### XLII.—ON THE HIDDEN HOLY PEOPLE OF ALMIGHTY CHRIST, THE LIVING GOD

The hidden final holy people will be longed for,

And indeed we do not know where it dwells,

Living among nine and a half tribes, while for us

O . . . . . . . . . . . .

He commanded them through the ancient law to live;

Let us all now live: a new tradition of the law is delivered.

As the law itself teaches, I declare it more openly to you.

Two and a half of the tribes were left behind. Why

Was half a tribe left with these? So that they might be martyrs

When he brought war throughout the world against his chosen ones;

Or certainly so that a choir of holy prophets

[Col. 0232B] Might rise up before the people and impose a bridle upon them—

The foul men whom the horses slaughtered with unrestrained hoof—

And so that the band might not at some time rush rashly toward peace.

These tribes have been set apart, and all the mysteries of Christ

Are fulfilled through them throughout the whole age.

They arose, however, from the crime of two brothers,

Under whose auspices they followed the wicked deed.

[Col. 0233A] [Note: [Col. 0233C]

**Bloodstained.** Savage, dread, atrocious. RIG.

**On account of the mysteries of Christ.** In the manuscript: “on account of the mysteries, chaste.” RIG.

**The things related by the law are hastening to fulfillment.** Quintus Julius Hilarianus used this manner of speaking and, around the year of Christ 360, wrote things about Antichrist and the end of the age consonant with Commodian: “If we listen to God’s command, which is trustworthy, we must accept whatever the divine law has faithfully related to us,” etc. RIG.

**Or swellings in the nose.** In the manuscript, incorrectly, “breasts for the son.” He means an ozena, or rather a polyp. An ozena is a malignant ulcer in the nose named after the polyp fish; it is καρκινῶδες, “cancerous,” and constricts and chokes the nostrils. RIG.

**Resting in bed.** An ancient inscription at Milan reads: “AURELIUS, EUSEBIUS, TO THEIR MOTHER. CONTRARY TO THEIR WISH. FAITHFUL. SHE RESTS.” Gruter, p. 1050, no. 9. RIG.

**They are commanded to pass over to the Lord.** So in an ancient inscription at Vienne in Gaul: “HE PASSED OVER ON THE DAY . . . ORBIS. FAUSTUS. A DISTINGUISHED MAN. C.—CONSULS.” RIG.

**They hasten to defend their captive mother.** He means Jerusalem. See Instruction XLI, verse 623. DAVIS.

**They are laid low by the soldier of heaven.** See Revelation 19:19. The manuscript reads: “The soldiers of Eli are laid low.” RIG.—**They are laid low by the soldier of heaven.** Rigaltius’s emendation makes the sentence ungrammatical, for “tyrant,” singular, preceded it. Read: “Those soldiers are laid low,” namely, the soldiers of Antichrist. See Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book VII, chapters 17 and 19. DAVIS.

**False prophet.** Revelation 19:20.

**The leading men and commanders are commanded to serve.** Below, in Instruction LXXX, he will say: “Beneath a servile yoke let them carry provisions upon their necks.”

**The Lord will begin to administer judgment through fire.** Tertullian, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chapter 25: “Thereafter, when fire has also been sent, the assize of the universal resurrection will be judged from the books.” RIGALT.

**ON THE END OF THE AGE.** Tertullian called it “the conclusion of the times” in his book *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*. Elsewhere: “the conclusion of sacrifice and of worldly glory.” RIG.

**When the lion has been removed.** Christians believed this lion would be Nero. Sulpicius Severus, *Dialogues* II.14, concerning what the angel had announced to blessed Martin: “When we asked him about the end of the age, he said to us that Nero and Antichrist must come first,” etc. And shortly afterward: “Finally, Nero is to be killed by Antichrist,” etc. RIG.

**In a flame of fire.** Paul, 2 Thessalonians 1:8, ἐν πυρὶ φλογός, “in flaming fire”; Revelation 19:12, φλὸξ πυρός, “a flame of fire.” RIG.

**So that he may be overtaken by fire.** Read *occupetur*, “may be overtaken”; Latin usage itself requires it. DAVIS.

**Amen, Amen, blazes.** That is, the Word of God, by which the Lord himself is designated: ὁ πιστὸς καὶ ἀληθινός, ἡ ἀρχὴ τῆς κτίσεως τοῦ Θεοῦ, “the faithful and true one, the beginning of the creation of God.” Revelation 3:14. Just as Commodian says in this Instruction, “Amen blazes,” so Jerome, in the preface to book II of his commentary on Galatians, said that through the Roman Church “Amen” resounds like heavenly thunder. See Isidore, *Origins* VI.19. RIG.

**As the hidden things of John report.** The manuscript reads: “As the bodies bear for the saints,” which is undoubtedly corrupt. We emend: “As the hidden things of the saint report,” or rather, “the hidden things of John.” Ancient glosses give: *Opertum*, ἀπόκρυφον, “hidden, apocryphal.” The Latins called the Apocalypse “Revelation.” Sulpicius Severus, *Ecclesiastical History* II.31, counts the Apocalypse of John among doubtful works. Jerome, Letter 129 to Dardanus, no. 4, speaking of Barnabas’s Epistle to the Hebrews, says: “We receive both”—namely, the Epistle to the Hebrews and the Apocalypse. That Revelation certainly presents us with mysteries that are deeply veiled and hidden. RIG.—Rigaltius is much too cursory here concerning the αὐθεντία, “authority,” of the Apocalypse. He is mistaken when he writes that Sulpicius Severus counted the Apocalypse among doubtful works. For Sulpicius says in *Ecclesiastical History* II.31: “Domitian, son of Vespasian, persecuted the Christians. At that time he banished John the Apostle and Evangelist to the island of Patmos, where, after hidden mysteries had been revealed to him, he composed and published the book of the holy Apocalypse—which indeed is rejected by many either foolishly or impiously.” DAVIS.

**A city descends from heaven.** Tertullian, book III *Against Marcion*: “We confess that a kingdom upon earth has been promised to us, but before heaven and in another state, namely, after the resurrection for a thousand years, in Jerusalem, the city of divine workmanship, brought down from heaven, which the Apostle also designates as our mother above.” A little later in the same work: “It is established even by pagan witnesses that in Judea, for forty days, at moments in the morning, a city hung down from heaven,” etc.]

Not without reason were those bloodstained people themselves scattered;

They will assemble again on account of the mysteries of Christ.

Then the things related by the law hasten to fulfillment.

Christ Almighty descends to his chosen ones,

Who were hidden from us for so long a time;

Made into so many thousands: that is the true heavenly nation.

No child there dies before his father, nor do they feel pain

In their bodies, or swellings in the nose.

Resting in their beds, they depart at a ripe age,

Fulfilling all things in the law; and therefore they are protected.

They are commanded to pass over to the Lord on the right-hand side;

He dries up the river for them, and they cross as before.

The Lord himself proceeds with them no less;

He crosses over to our lands; they come with the heavenly King.

What can I say of what God will bring forth along their journey?

[Col. 0233B] Mountains sink down before them, and springs burst forth;

Creation rejoices to see the heavenly people.

Here, however, they hasten to defend their captive mother.

But when the unrighteous king who holds her hears of it,

He flees toward the north and gathers everyone.

But when the tyrant strikes himself against the army of God,

By heavenly terror they are laid low through the soldier of heaven;

He himself is seized together with the unspeakable false prophet.

By the Lord’s decree they are delivered alive to Gehenna.

Thereafter the leading men and commanders are commanded to serve.

Then the saints will enter the bosom of their ancient mother.

But so that those whom he wickedly persuaded may also find relief,

He will torment in various punishments those who believed him.

The end has arrived, when stumbling blocks are removed from the world.

The Lord will begin to administer judgment through fire.

### XLIII.—ON THE END OF THIS AGE

A trumpet gives the signal in heaven when the lion has been removed,

And suddenly darkness comes amid the crashing of heaven.

The Lord casts down his eyes so that the earth trembles;

He cries aloud so that all throughout the world may hear:

“Behold, I have long been silent, enduring your deeds for so long a time.”

Together they cry aloud, lamenting and groaning too late;

They howl and weep, and no respite is given to the unrighteous.

What will a mother do for her nursing infant when she herself is burned?

In a flame of fire the Lord will judge the unrighteous;

But the fire will not touch the righteous—rather, it will lick them.

They remain beneath one fire, but one party has wept under sentence.

[Col. 0234B] So great will be the heat that the stones themselves will melt;

The winds gather into thunderbolts; heavenly wrath rages,

So that wherever the impious man flees, he is overtaken by fire.

There will be no help, nor any seagoing ship.

Amen sets the nations ablaze, and the Medes and Parthians burn

For a thousand years, as the hidden things of John report.

For afterward, when the thousand years have passed, they are delivered to Gehenna

And are burned together with the structure whose inhabitants they were.

### XLIV.—ON THE FIRST RESURRECTION

The city will descend from heaven at the first *anastasis* [resurrection];

There is something for us to relate concerning so great a heavenly structure.

[Col. 0235A] [Note: [Col. 0235B]

**At the first resurrection.** Revelation 20:5. Tertullian, in his book [Col. 0235C] *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “When the devil has been banished into the abyss, the privilege of the first resurrection is arranged from the thrones.” Following the teaching of the millenarians, he establishes two resurrections: the first, of those rising to that earthly happiness of a thousand years; the second, the universal resurrection, when God sends the fire that will consume the whole world for the assize of the final judgment. And yet Tertullian himself elsewhere repeatedly affirms that the souls of martyrs are taken up to heaven immediately in the crown of martyrdom; but for others, including the faithful themselves, he posits a delay of resurrection, so that in the underworld they expiate every minor offense through a shorter or longer delay before rising. These opinions are certainly perplexed and tangled, as the opinions of mortals generally are when they inquire too curiously into God’s counsels or press into them with too little reverence. See *On the Soul* 24 and *Scorpiace* 12; observations on Cyprian, Letter 52. RIG.

**They will be incorrupt.** Read: “We shall be incorrupt.” DAVIS.

**And they themselves beget children.** This was certainly exceptionally foolish in that fable of the millennial period. Lactantius VII.24: “Throughout those same thousand years they will beget an infinite multitude, and their offspring will be holy and dear to God,” etc. RIG.

**No sieges.** Below he will say: “He perishes through being besieged.” RIG.

**The evil one in anguish.** By “the evil one” he means the dragon, serpent, devil, Satan—the πονηρός, “evil one.” RIG.

**Anguish.** Constriction, torment.

Perhaps one should read: “Fire will exercise dominion,” that is, will lay waste all things. DAVIS.

**Completing their journey.** Completing their allotted span of life on earth, or dwelling upon the earth. RIG.

**Yet avoiding.** As above, Instruction XLIII: “But the fire will not touch the righteous.” RIG.

**Both the stars and these things are changed.** Perhaps it should be restored as: “Even the stars themselves are changed.” Whatever the case, it is plain to anyone that the received reading is not sound. DAVIS.

**They will be cast into the second death.** The first is the death of the body; the second, that of the soul, which is eternal death, eternal fire. See Instruction LII. RIG.

[Col. 0236B] **But the righteous are placed in the inner dwellings.** For the saints are said to enter, or go into, the kingdom of God and eternal life. The wicked, by contrast, are cast out, driven away, and sent into the outer darkness. RIG.

**TO THE CATECHUMENS.** The acrostic shows that this word was commonly written in this form in the age of Commodian. They are the καθηχούμενοι, “those receiving oral instruction”; the Hearers, the Competents, the διδασκόμενοι, “those being taught.” RIG.

[Col. 0236C] **Take care that you do not sin as before.** That is, do not live the sort of life that you lived before you were called to the Christian faith. So in the following Instruction: “Hence you will not escape sin if you follow the former ways.” One follows the former ways when, after professing the name of Christ, one returns to his vomit and lives a life dissolute with the vices of the age, adopting the behavior that he practiced before giving his faith to Christ. RIG.

**In baptism the coarse impurity of your birth is washed away.** The manuscript reads: “In baptism for you, only the things of birth are held.” At first sight it seemed preferable to read “birth-giving baptism,” in the sense in which Cyprian said to Donatus that “with the aid of the birth-giving water, the stain of the former age was wiped away.” Commodian’s meaning would thus have been that a new birth is given to us in Christian baptism, by which we are reborn after putting off the filth of the old Adam. For we are all born from him, and his sin, propagated as it were through successive transmissions over a long series, has passed down into us. But we are reborn in Christ, namely, through birth-giving baptism. That meaning is certainly good and true. But what is to be done with the words that follow in the manuscript—“only are held,” or “only are washed”? I therefore thought the meaning was that only the sins belonging to birth are washed away in baptism, not those committed after baptism when faith in Christian discipline has been violated. This meaning likewise appears suitable enough, if “sin belonging to birth” means the sin that each person brings with him from his origin. Yet, to conceal nothing, the reading that “only sins belonging to birth are washed away in baptism” displeased me, since its very ambiguity provokes laughter. Accordingly, upon more careful reflection another reading of this kind occurred to me: “In baptism the birth-stain, *solox*, is washed away for you.” Although this reading does not entirely remove the ambiguity, it nevertheless corrects it and emphasizes the necessity of the birth-giving bath, so that the coarse stains of original sin, which we believe are washed away by baptism, may now be called *solox genitale*. *Solox*, a word used by Tertullian in *On the Pallium*, comes readily under Commodian’s style, as do many other words we have observed throughout. Festus notes that it means coarse wool: οἰσύπειον, ἔριον ῥυπαρὸν προβάτων, “greasy wool, the filthy wool of sheep.” From it grammarians also derived “solecism,” as well as any coarse or gross, dishonorable, and shameful thing. RIG.]

We who were devoted to him shall rise again,

And we shall be incorrupt, then living without death;

Nor will there be any pain or groaning there.

Those who prevail under Antichrist, winning mighty martyrdoms, will also come;

They too will live throughout the whole period.

They receive good things because they suffered evil things,

And for a thousand years they themselves marry and beget children.

All the revenues of the earth are gathered there,

Because the renewed earth pours forth exceedingly and without end.

There is no rain there, nor cold in the golden camp,

No sieges, as now, nor acts of plunder.

That city has no need of the light of a lamp;

It shines from its Creator, who also appears there.

It extends twelve thousand stadia in breadth, in length, and likewise in height;

Its foundation is on earth, but its summit reaches heaven.

[Col. 0235B] Outside the city gates, however, the sun and moon will shine.

The evil one is enclosed in anguish so that the righteous may be sustained.

But after the thousand years God will destroy all things.

### XLV.—ON THE DAY OF JUDGMENT

I add something about the day of judgment for the sake of unbelievers.

[Col. 0236A] Once more God’s fire will be released and granted power.

The earth utters a true groan, then, at the final end,

As all complete their journey, and then all the unbelieving;

Yet the fire avoids the camps of his saints.

All nature is transformed in a single flame:

The earth is burned from its depths, and the mountains melt;

Nothing remains of the sea: it is overcome by mighty fire.

This heaven and the stars perish, and these things are changed.

Another new and everlasting heaven and earth are fashioned.

Then those who deserve it are cast into the second death;

But the righteous are placed in the inner dwellings.

### XLVI.—TO THE CATECHUMENS

All who believe in Christ after abandoning idols,

I admonish briefly for the sake of your salvation.

[Col. 0236B] If in former times you practiced anything through error,

Once pledged to Christ, abandon all such things.

And when you have known God, be a good and proven recruit;

Let virginal modesty dwell with you in the Lamb.

Let the mind keep watch over good things; take care that you do not sin as before.

In baptism the coarse impurity of your birth is washed away.

[Col. 0237A] [Note: [Col. 0237B]

**For if any catechumen sins.** Cyprian, book III *To Quirinus*, article 98: “That a catechumen ought no longer to sin.” In testimony for this article he cites Romans 3: “Let us do evil so that good may come.” It is as though certain persons in the catechumenate said: “Let us play; let us indulge our pleasures and appetites as much as we please, for baptism will wash away whatever sin we commit.” There were, indeed, people so impious that they postponed baptism until the very end of life so that they might enjoy their wickedness longer, confident of the efficacy of that washing even at the last moment. This was charged as a fault against the baptism of Emperor Constantine. Far wiser and safer is that confession of Prosper of Aquitaine: “Though I was once born under the law of sin and held captive by the ordinary condition of death transmitted to me from my parents, lest I be detained under the right of so savage a master for a long time, you, merciful and compassionate Lord, set me free at the very beginning of my life. I found the tyrant-slayer before I understood my slavery,” etc. RIG.

**A penalty is assigned.** Shortly he will say: “but not without loss”—namely, because the term of his catechumenate is prolonged. Concerning catechumens who had fallen, the fathers of the Council of Nicaea decreed in canon 15 that they should be separated from the catechumens’ prayer for three years and afterward received again. RIG.

**Let that one live among the standards.** We think it should read: “Let him live among the standards.” “Among the standards,” namely, the Christian standards, as in a military camp.

**The sum for you.** As though he said: “Let this, in summary, remain fixed in your mind and memory.” RIG.

**I admonish the faithful brothers to remove themselves from hatred.** Rigaltius argues that it should be “I admonish the faithful not to destroy brothers through hatred.” Tertullian argued most earnestly against these hatreds and dissensions among Christians in his little work *To the Martyrs*: “Above all, therefore, blessed ones, do not grieve the Holy Spirit,” etc. People destroy brothers through hatred when they overthrow brotherhood through their animosities; they turn not merely friends but brothers into enemies. One should therefore write: “I admonish the faithful not to destroy brothers through hatred.” RIG.—Rigaltius’s emendation is uncalled for. So in Instruction XXII, verse 277:

> Alas! I grieve, fellow citizens, that you are thus dulled by the world.

And in Instruction I, verse 6:

> By reading from the law.

See the annotations on that passage. DAVIS.

**It is taught that evil cannot be expiated even by the shedding of blood.** Commodian has 1 Corinthians 13:3 in view. DAVIS.

**The law is given to the unrighteous.** By “the unrighteous” he means one who is not a Christian. RIG.—Here, however, the author had 1 Timothy 1:9 in mind. See also Galatians 5:23. DAVIS.

**So that he may be able to restrain himself.** So too he will say in the following Instruction:

> The law has been given to man, and the teaching of life must be read,  
> From which he is reminded how he may live cautiously. RIG.

**Hence you will not escape sin if you follow the former ways.** This is what he said above: “sinning as before.” Whether one reads “following sin in the former manner,” as in the manuscript, or “following the former ways,” matters little; the sense is the same. RIG.

**You have been washed once; can you possibly be immersed again?** You have lost baptism, which is one and unrepeatable. Prosper’s declaration of faith is admirable: “Although I have withdrawn from your gifts, your gifts have nevertheless remained in me.” RIG.

**For these enchantments, to whom the loss of mind has been delivered.** The word *incantamentis* [“enchantments”] has been split apart, with the result that the verse itself also appears broken. Eugenius of Toledo played similarly in addressing a certain John who disliked linked verses:

> O Io—hannes, you who despise linked verses,  
> Receive them, if you are skillful and know how to join the divided things.

Such were the verbal artifices of that age. The tmesis gives: “For these enchantments, to whom the loss has been delivered”; that is, things laid out here and there and carelessly to deceive birds and beasts. By “enchantments” he means sophisms, every kind of deceit used to capture birds and beasts. Why, moreover, should he not have called “enchantments” such tricks set out or exposed to deceive unwary birds and beasts? This tmesis is no harsher than that of Ennius: *Saxo cere comminuam brum*—the split form of *saxō cerebrum comminuam*, “I shall crush his brain with a stone.” RIG.

**And profitable things deceive those who pursue them, like bait.** Written above the line in the manuscript is: “Golden things deceive.” The true reading may perhaps have been: “And pits deceive those who pursue them, like bait.” The “pits” are holes covered with brushwood and foliage to bring down beasts pursuing hunters. RIG.

**And his own place.** “He is reminded” must be repeated from what precedes. The law given to man causes him to remember to live cautiously; it causes him to remember his own place—that is, heaven if he lives cautiously and rightly, hell if wickedly. The same law also causes him to avert the things that belong to death: to pray that God avert the eternal death he may perhaps have deserved by sinning. RIG.

**The bait of the mousetrap.** This seems the proper emendation of the corrupted manuscript reading: “And the bait of the mousetrap, where death and long life.” Ancient glosses give: *Muscipulum*, μυάγρα, “mousetrap”; *muscipula*, παγίδες, “traps”; and in the feminine singular, *muscipula*, παγίς, “snare.” Phaedrus, book V, fable 1: “He who had often escaped snares and mousetraps.” RIG.

**To possess the willing for martyrdom.** So it is read in the manuscript; it means nothing other than “to take up, or possess, the will for martyrdom”: to desire martyrdom, to wish to become a martyr. RIG.—**To possess the willing.** That is, “to possess the will for martyrdom.” The infinitive is used as a substantive. So Persius, *Satires* V.53:

> Each person has his own willing, nor do all live by one desire.

We have collected many similar passages from ancient writers in our notes on Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, chapter 34. DAVIS.]

For if any catechumen sins, a penalty is assigned;

Let him live among the standards, but not without loss.

The sum for you is this: always avoid grave sins.

### XLVII.—TO THE FAITHFUL

I admonish the faithful brothers to remove themselves from hatred.

Impious hatreds are reckoned against martyrs for the fire;

A martyr whose confession is of such a kind is destroyed;

It is taught that evil cannot be expiated even by the shedding of blood.

The law is given to the unrighteous so that he may restrain himself.

Hence he ought to be free of deceit; and so should you.

You sin twice against God when you prolong quarrels with a brother;

Hence you will not escape sin if you follow the former ways.

You have been washed once; can you possibly be immersed again?

### XLVIII.—FAITHFUL, BEWARE OF EVIL

[Col. 0237B] Birds and the beasts of the forests are deceived in the woods

[Col. 0238A] By these enchantments, to which the loss of mind has been delivered.

Profitable things also deceive those who pursue them, like bait;

They do not know how to avoid evil, nor are they bound by law.

The law has been given to man, and the teaching of life must be read,

From which he is reminded how he may live cautiously,

And of his own place, and how he may avert the things that belong to death.

He condemns himself grievously who sins against the King:

Either bound in iron, cast down from his rank,

Or deprived of life, he loses what he ought to have enjoyed.

Warned by this example, do not commit grave sin.

Having been transformed by the washing, cherish love all the more.

Keep far away from the bait of the mousetrap, where death lies.

There are many martyrdoms that take place without the shedding of blood:

Not to covet what belongs to another, to desire to possess the will for martyrdom,

To restrain your tongue, to render yourself humble,

[Col. 0238B] Not to inflict violence unprovoked, nor to repay violence done to you.

[Col. 0239A] [Note: [Col. 0239C]

**If you have been a patient mountain.** What “a patient mountain” (*mons patiens*) might mean entirely escapes me. Read: “if you have been patient in mind” (*mens patiens fueris*). Commodianus has put the mind, which is the better part of a human being, for the whole person. See above, Instruction XXVII, v. 406. DAVIS.

**You have become a penitent.** You have been admitted to penance. For they sought to have a place of penance granted to them through a lengthy demonstration of repentance. Penance was granted only with difficulty to one who had transgressed in such a way as to expose the Church to reproach for retaining in her company so disgraceful a sinner—one who had deserved to be expelled, excluded, and barred from the Church, and who by his transgression had caused the Church to blush. Yet that same Church did not begrudge penitents their conversion to God, with whom she did not despair of obtaining pardon. RIG.

**Do not depart from your mother.** From the Church, our lady and mother, at whose breasts we are nourished. RIG.

**I myself felt the fall.** I felt myself dying; I felt from what height I myself had fallen. In the transcript: “that I had felt the fall” (*sensisse ruinam*). RIG.—Read *sensisse ruinam*, as it stands in the transcript, whose authority Rigault rashly abandoned. “I confessed,” says Commodianus, “that I had felt the fall.” DAVIS.

**And to roll among stones.** In the transcript: “and to roll sufficiently” (*volutarique satis*). The penitent’s condition is the harsh treatment of his own person: to dwell apart from joy, amid the roughness of sackcloth and the horror of ashes, estranged from every enjoyment of life. Tertullian speaks of one “rolling in sackcloth and ashes, begrimed and reconciled.” RIG.

**Lest perhaps you perish from among the people.** That is, from the Church: from the multitude of the faithful, from the people of Christ, from the holy people. For at that time the Church consisted of the bishop, presbyter, deacon, and people, or laity. RIG.

**Than to pass under a barbarian king.** By “barbarian king” he means a non-Christian king. RIG.

**If you surrender your hands.** If you put incense into the censer. RIG.

**Make yourself secure on every side.** Commodianus differs from Tertullian here, but agrees with Cyprian. During persecution he counsels flight or concealment. Indeed, he teaches that there is martyrdom in concealment and flight. He wholly forbids anyone to rush into danger or offer himself up. Finally, he says that the Christian who discloses himself to the enemy is his own betrayer. If, however, he falls into the enemy’s hands or is overwhelmed by the persecutors, he must then be utterly steadfast for the name of Christ. For if he buys back his life by denial, he will perish together with that very life. RIG.

**Then he refused to live.** The man who showed too little courage before the governor or tyrant—who offered incense to the idol or denied Christ—refused to live the eternal life: he renounced eternal life in order to preserve a momentary one. RIG.

**If anyone is destitute of the Lord.** That is, simply a pagan. He says “destitute of the Lord” in the same form as, concerning Saturn, “he comes destitute of understanding,” Instruction IV. RIG.

**Or profaned by the enemy.** Overcome by the persecutors of the Christian name, from whom he returned as a denier. RIG.

**Made sounding bronze.** 1 Corinthians 13:1: χαλκὸς ἠχῶν, “sounding bronze.” RIG.

**Or like deaf asps.** Those who stop their ears against the wisdom of God.—He alludes to Psalm 58:5. DAVIS.

**They ought to pray sufficiently.** That is, until they deserve to obtain from the bishop the opportunity for penance, after the Church, which they dishonored by denying Christ, has been appeased through a long and pitiable public confession (*exomologesis*). RIG.

**Or such persons should hide themselves.** So that henceforth they may nowhere be seen in the Church’s camp. RIG.

**Concerning infants.** The meaning is clear; it was only necessary to establish the text of the Instruction in the form in which we have now arranged for it to be published. RIG.

**And before they could flee, the little ones.** In the transcript: “And before he could flee, he seized the helpless little ones.”

**And let them be born as though anew.** He took the metaphor from John 3:3–4. DAVIS.

**Let them flee the terrible law.** In the transcript: “Fleeing the terrible law.” “Let them flee,” he says, “that terrible pagan law which commands sacrifice to idols, the worshipers of which law are destined for eternal flames.” RIG.

**Deserters.** He establishes two kinds of deserters: those who offered incense and those who obtained certificates of sacrifice. RIG.

**There is another who is wicked.** One who sacrifices to an idol, which in God’s sight is the principal crime. RIG.]

If you have been patient in mind, understand that you are a martyr.

### XLIX.—TO PENITENTS

You have become a penitent: pray by night and day.

Yet do not depart far from your mother,

And then the Most High may be merciful to you.

The confession of guilt will not come to nothing; accordingly,

Learn openly to weep over your state of guilt.

If you have a wound, seek the herb and the physician.

Yet amid your punishments you will be able to lessen your losses.

For—I will indeed confess it—I stand here as one of you,

And terror must be left behind: I myself felt the fall.

Therefore I admonish the wounded to walk more cautiously:

To disfigure beard and hair in the dust of the earth,

To roll in sackcloth, and to make supplication to the highest King.

He will come to your aid, lest perhaps you perish from among the people.

### L.—THOSE WHO HAVE APOSTATIZED FROM GOD

[Col. 0239B]

When war is being waged or the enemy presses in,

He who can conquer or remain concealed wins great trophies.

But unhappy will be the man who is captured by them.

He loses country and king who refused worthily to fight

For truth, for his country, and for his life.

He ought to have died rather than pass under a barbarian king

And seek the servitude that one submits to lawless enemies.

If you die fighting for the king, you have conquered.

But if you surrender, though physically unharmed, you have perished under the law.

Let the enemy cross the river; hide yourself in concealment.

[Col. 0240A] Or if he can enter—whether he can or not—do not cease:

Make yourself and your own secure on every side; you have conquered.

And act vigilantly, lest anyone rush into those dangers.

It will be a disgraceful thing if anyone discloses himself to the enemy.

The fool who does not know how to conquer, yet runs out to surrender himself,

Has left no glory either to himself or to his country.

Then he refused to live, since life itself will perish.

If anyone is destitute of the Lord or has been profaned by the enemy,

Made sounding bronze, or deaf like asps,

Such persons ought to pray sufficiently, or else hide themselves.

### LI.—CONCERNING INFANTS

The enemy’s sudden assault came flooding in,

And before they could flee, it seized the helpless little ones.

They must not be reproached, although they appear to have been captured;

[Col. 0240B] Yet I do not indeed excuse them: perhaps because of their parents’ sins

They merited this, and God therefore handed them over.

Nevertheless, I exhort them, once grown, to return to arms

And to be born as though anew from their mother’s womb.

Let them flee the terrible and ever-bloodstained law,

Impious, untaught, and living the life of a beast.

For when another war must perhaps be waged,
