He who can conquer—or at least now knows how to take precautions—

S . . . . . . . . . . . . .

### LII.—DESERTERS

For “deserters” are not so called from only one kind.

One is wicked; another withdraws only in part;

[Col. 0241A] [Note: [Col. 0241B]

**Another withdraws only in part.** To avoid being dragged to the Capitol to sacrifice, he makes an arrangement by presenting a certificate to the governor and money to the extortioner. RIG.

**True judgments are decreed.** Here, as also in the best authors, *verum* bears the force of “just” or “equitable.” See Broukhusius on Propertius, Book III, Elegy XIII, 11. DAVIS.

**Service is rendered to Christ, just as Caesar is obeyed.** Service is rendered to Christ, who forbids sacrifice to an idol and punishes those who sacrifice—even after death—with eternal punishments; Caesar is obeyed when he orders those who do not sacrifice to an idol to die, but has nothing he can do to the dead. For those who died in this way for Christ—who obeyed Caesar in such a way as courageously to meet death for Christ’s name—live the eternal life. RIG.

**If you have been an offender.** By *delictor* he means a sinner; we have observed Cyprian also speaking in this way. RIG.

**When the camps have been reestablished.** That is, when the camps have again been established against the Church, you yourself, having been restored to the Church’s camp after receiving penance, must no longer be a deserter. RIG.

**Let ceasing to sin be an immense deed for you.** Similar is Instruction XLIII: “The sum for you is this: always avoid grave sins.” RIG.

**Then therefore begin to abandon your former deeds.** Above he said: “Take care not to sin hereafter,” Instruction XLVI. Here he contrasts “abandoning former things” with the “pursuing old things” of Instruction XLVII. “Old” or “former” things are those committed before faith, sins of the kind committed by pagans or profane persons. RIG.

**At the king’s command.** Understand Christ, the head of the Church. [Col. 0241D] RIG.

**So that you may daily stand ready before your superior.** We have emended what had been corrupted in the transcript as “before your purpose” (*ut tuo proposito*). He calls him the *praepositus*, whom Justin and others call the προεστώς, “presiding officer,” and Tertullian the *praesidens*, “president”; Tertullian also called him both the superior of the Church and the superior presiding over baptism. RIG.

**Assume that the contest is near.** *Sume*, “assume” or “anticipate”: understand that the festive and solemn contest is close at hand, from which the road to heaven lies open. The Romans called the day of competition “agonal” and the festive contests *Agonalia*, which were earlier called *Agonia*, as Ovid testifies in *Fasti* I:

> And ancient speech formerly called them *Agonia*. RIG.

**At the desired one who is to rule because of hope.** It appears that one should write: “at the one who, beyond expectation, is to fight” (*praeter spem dimicaturum*). The king who is to come—that is, Christ—will preside over the martyrdom, the contest. “Watch therefore, soldiers of Christ, because at an hour you do not expect, the Son of Man will come” (Luke 12:40). RIG.

**And appoints him to be his own attendant.** He said *satellem* for *satellitem*, and “appoints him to be his own” means steadfast, firm, and courageous. In the transcript I noticed, beneath an erasure, a trace of the old reading *deduat*, which we consider entirely unsuitable here. RIG.

**Moreover, do not spare yourself against Belial.** The transcript had read: “Moreover, do not spare yourself amid transgressions.” That reading could be accepted and explained, had not the person who reviewed the transcript advised us that the old hand had written “against Belial” (*in Belian*). That is: Beware lest, through your idleness or negligence, while perhaps flattering yourself too much, you fail yourself in the struggle against Belial, or the devil; lest Satan—the evil and wicked one—steal upon you while you are unprepared. RIG.

**Rather, be energetic.** Far be it that Belial should bring destruction upon you through his temptations; indeed, win renown from them instead, so that you may be an example to the brethren of most diligently maintained discipline and faith. RIG.

**Concerning fugitives.** The transcript reads “concerning places of refuge” (*de refugiis*), and before the penultimate verse there appears a mark of a lacuna, as though Commodianus had used *refugia* for *refugi*, as he used *servitia* for *servi*. We do not think anything is missing, and have entitled the Instruction “Concerning Fugitives”; thus the mark of a lacuna will have been superfluous. RIG.

**Begotten from this one.** That is, from this Belial, mentioned in the preceding Instruction. RIG.

**They return again to their own.** To their own pagans and idolaters. RIG.

**The Cainite root.** Or rather *Cainaea*, as above in Instruction XXXVI. The transcript incorrectly reads “Canaanite root” (*radix cananaea*). RIG.

[Col. 0242D] **Under a barbarian king.** Just as above he called Christ simply “the king,” so here he calls Belial, Satan, or Antichrist the “barbarian king.” RIG.

**On the appointed day.** On the decisive, censorial day—the day of judgment, the day of inspection, at the examination and inspection of souls. RIG.

**If they refuse to live, they ought to be regarded by idols.** The transcript reads: *Sydere volunt*. Following these traces one should write: “If they wish to see what gods they worship, yet refuse to place faith in the true God because they do not see him, and instead trust in their images of bronze and wood, let them at least gaze upon them as much as they please: they have eyes of bronze and wood, yet do not see. Therefore the makers and worshipers of such gods make themselves superior to their own divinities and mock the blind eyes of their gods; and so, because of their impiety, they themselves deserve to be rejected by their gods.” But if we love the truth, this reading should be preferred: “If they refuse to live, they ought to be regarded by idols.” For the whole philosophy of Commodianus concerns eternal life. If these men refuse to live it, he says, they deserve to be regarded by idols—that is, by Satan’s ministers, who nest in the hollows of images. RIG.]

Yet true judgments are decreed for both.

Behold, service is rendered to Christ, just as Caesar is obeyed.

Seek the king’s refuge if you have been an offender;

Implore him; prostrate yourself and confess to him.

He whose are all things, including all that is ours, will forgive everything.

When the camps have been reestablished, take care not to sin any further.

Do not wander long, soldier, through the dens of beasts.

Let ceasing to sin be an immense deed for you.

### LIII.—TO THE SOLDIERS OF CHRIST

When you have enrolled for military service, you are held by the bridle.

Then therefore begin to abandon your former deeds.

Avoid indulgence, since the toil of arms is imminent.

The king’s command must be obeyed with every excellence,

If you wish to reach the joyful last days.

As a good soldier, always await the rewards to be enjoyed.

[Col. 0241B] Do not flatter yourself; put idleness wholly aside,

So that you may daily stand ready before your superior.

Be watchful; rise early and inspect the standards.

When you see war, assume that the contest is near.

[Col. 0242A] This is the king’s glory: to see his soldier prepared.

The king is at hand, the longed-for one, who will reign because of our hope.

He prepares gifts; rejoicing over the victory,

He looks upon the soldier and appoints him to be his own attendant.

Moreover, do not spare yourself against Belial.

Rather, be energetic, so that he may yield renown in exchange for death.

### LIV.—CONCERNING FUGITIVES

The souls of the condemned deservedly separate themselves.

Begotten from this one, they return again to their own.

The Cainite root, an accursed seed, breaks forth

And, among a servile race, flees beneath a barbarian king.

The eternal flame will torment them on the appointed day.

The wandering fugitive wishes to stray without discipline,

To range through the defiles of the roads, released from law.

Such men, therefore, whom no punishment has constrained—

[Col. 0242B] If they refuse to live, they ought to be regarded by idols.

### LV.—CONCERNING THE SEED OF DARNEL

Concerning the seed of darnel: those who stand intermingled in the Church.

[Col. 0243A] [Note: [Col. 0243B]

**Concerning the seed of darnel.** The parable of the darnel is found in Matthew 13:24. DAVIS.

[Col. 0243C] **The law is our field.** The parable of the field signifies for us the law of Christ. Christ himself says: “I am the true vine” (John 15:1).

**Sterile Christians.** Unfruitful, ἄγονοι (“barren”), eunuchs, sterile in good works. RIG.

**The accursed fig tree.** See Matthew 12:19. DAVIS.

**You prepare no gift for the treasury.** By *gazum* he means the sacred treasury, the *corbona*, the Church’s treasury, or the treasury-chest. Instruction LXXII says: “Moreover, you ought to put something from your earnings into the treasury.” Tertullian had called it the chest; others, the basin. Commodianus therefore calls those Christians “sterile” who contributed none of their resources for the use of the poor. Cyprian calls this sterility sacrilegious in his book *On Works and Almsgiving*. Paulinus, Epistle XXXIV, called the hands of those who neglected the table established in the Church by the Lord for the needy “dry hands.” The same author says: “This, then, is the table of the heavenly banker, building up the treasure of life and putting God’s capital to work in order to purchase the pearl.” RIG.

**TO THE DISSEMBLER.** To the hypocrite, who pretends to be a Christian while living in an antichristian—that is, worldly and satanic—fashion. RIG.

**Had proclaimed into a cloud.** This reading is entirely absurd. I think one should read, “had proclaimed to the world” (*declamasset in orbem*), as shortly below at v. 865. Commodianus means that it would have been enough if even a single prophet had announced the Lord’s laws to the world. DAVIS.

**Thus with the same heart you wish to see good things.** With the same disposition by which you desire to be affected by God’s blessings and benefits, you also desire to become rich through slanders and deceits from the spoils of your brother. RIG.

**The Almighty seeks the gentle.** Matthew 5:5: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” Peacemakers, εἰρηνοποιοί.

**But the ungentle.** In 2 Timothy 3, Paul’s ἀνήμεροι (“savage”) and ἀφιλάγαθοι (“not lovers of good”) are opposed to the kindly. RIG.

**You know where he submerged them.** In the lake of fire, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. RIG.

**WORLDLY THINGS MUST BE FLED ENTIRELY.** That is, there must be no dissembling, for the Church has nothing in common with the world. The Church is Christ’s; the world is Satan’s. Thus the offspring of the Most High must not be mingled with the devil’s children, nor discipline relaxed through excessive indulgence by pastors, whether from favoritism or filthy gain. RIG.

[Col. 0244C] **Teachers.** Teachers, superiors, presidents, pastors, bishops. RIG.

**With the troop of the Evil One.** “The Evil One,” that is, Satan. RIG.

**Where Satan works amid the din of the circus.** Tertullian, in his book *On the Spectacles*: “Since frenzy, therefore, is forbidden us, we are removed from every spectacle, including the circus, where frenzy properly presides,” etc. RIG.

**Works in the circus.** The transcript had read: “Where Satan was compared with the din.” RIG.

**Those former things which you renounced.** By “former things” he means what was called above “previous” or “old”: those things that preceded faith. These, indeed, are the devil, his pomp, and his angels. See Tertullian throughout his work *On the Spectacles*. RIG.

**What will one man accomplish?** Read: “What will the Anointed One accomplish?” (*quid proderit unctus*), that is, Christ, who was fastened to the cross in order to draw human beings away from the devil’s power and make them his chosen people. Thus Instruction LXXII, v. 1151.

**Or if it was granted because of weakness.** If spectacles were permitted to you by those excessively lenient and accommodating teachers in order to refresh or revive the strength of your failing spirit. RIG.

**Do not love the world.** 1 John 2:15.

**Nor what it encompasses.** That is, everything enclosed and contained by the world. John said, “the things that are in the world.” Tertullian and Cyprian called it “the pomp of the devil.” RIG.

**You observe a human commandment.** He distinguishes between God’s commandments and human commandments or traditions. We have shown that Cyprian did this very frequently, following Paul’s precepts. RIG.

**By which teachers’ mouths are closed.** And they become mute, unable to bark. RIG.

**As I speak the truth … look to the Highest.** Did Christ’s beggar, then, call himself the highest? Read: “As I speak the truth, look to the Highest, as you are bound to do.” Guided by my warning, dedicate yourself to God, as is fitting. DAVIS.

**Look to the Highest.** The Most High, God best and greatest, who is the supreme Teacher. RIG.]

When the season of harvest has been completed, there is separated from the fruit

The darnel that sprang up, which the Lord did not sow.

The farmer gathers and separates all that darnel.

The law is our field: whoever does good within it,

The Ruler himself assuredly provides us

True rest; for the darnel is burned with fire.

If, therefore, you think that because they dwell beneath one roof

They are the same, you err: I designate you as sterile Christians.

The fig tree without fruit was accursed

At the Lord’s word, and immediately it withered.

You perform no works; you prepare no gift for the treasury.

And, being empty, do you think you will thus earn the Lord’s favor?

### LVI.—TO THE DISSEMBLER

Do you dissemble concerning the law proclaimed with so great a heralding,

Crying out in the heavenly voice of so many prophets?

[Col. 0243B] If only one prophet had proclaimed it to the world,

The Lord’s voice sent through him would assuredly have sufficed.

Throughout the volumes of so many prophets, the Lord’s law proclaims aloud;

No one abandons his wickedness: thus with the same heart

You wish to see good things, yet seek to live by fraud.

Why, then, did the law itself proceed with such great labor?

You abuse the Lord’s commandments, yet claim yourself as his son.

[Col. 0244A] If you are such a man, you will be found without a defense, I say [text uncertain].

The Almighty seeks the gentle to be his sons,

Upright in a good heart and devoted to the divine law;

But you already know where he submerged the ungentle.

### LVII.—WORLDLY THINGS MUST BE FLED ENTIRELY

If certain teachers, while awaiting your gifts

Or fearing influential persons, relax every rule for you,

I do not merely grieve, but am compelled to speak the truth:

You proceed with the troop of the Evil One to empty spectacles,

Where Satan works amid the din of the circus.

You persuade yourself that anything you please is permissible.

Offspring of the Most High, mingled with the children of the Devil,

Do you wish to look back upon those former things which you renounced?

You are again occupied with those very things: what will the Anointed One accomplish?

Or if it was granted because of weakness—something that, profane fool,

[Col. 0244B] I . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Do not love the world, nor what it encompasses:

So mighty is God’s voice, and it seems authoritative to you.

You observe a human commandment and avoid God’s;

You trust in the gift by which teachers’ mouths are closed,

So that they remain silent and do not tell you the divine commands.

As I speak the truth, look to the Highest, as you are bound to do:

[Col. 0245A] [Note: [Col. 0245C]

**In pagan fashion.** As a pagan. Thus Paul in Galatians 2.

**Your offspring to chatter.** Juvenal, Satire V, spoke of a “talkative nest.”

**To enjoy that life.** Do you think that he enjoys that life which God promises to his faithful? RIG.—**To enjoy that life.** The acrostic requires the reading: “While you think you enjoy life, you err in your improvidence” (*Dum vita frunisci putas, improvidus erras*).—*Frunisci* means “to enjoy.” See Festus and Nonius, chapter 2. DAVIS.

**THAT A CHRISTIAN SHOULD BE SUCH.** Not a hypocrite, not a dissembler, not one who pursues worldly things. RIG.

**To eat bread amid groaning.** He alludes to Genesis 3:19. DAVIS.

**You will then be a stranger to him.** Not Christ’s coheir, not God’s son, not a citizen of that eternal city. RIG.

**Refreshed by food, the children rose to play.** Moses, Exodus [Col. 0245D] 32:6. Saint Paul cites the passage in 1 Corinthians 10:7. DAVIS.

**Those who departed voluntarily.** The circumcised Jews, mutilated, λειπόδερμοι (“lacking foreskin”), circumcised men. RIG.

**Hope comes with labor.** Hope accompanies labor. Hope sustains the farmer. RIG.

**Assist the martyrs.** Stand beside the martyr; go to the martyrs who are in prison. Aid their necessities according to your means; foster and kindle their steadfastness with warnings and exhortations. Commodianus himself says in Instruction LXI:

> Certainly, if one does not himself fight, let him at least provide support for them.

An ancient inscription at Rome on the Ostian Way reads:

> DEVOTED TO THE SERVICE OF THE MARTYRS, I, MANDROSA, PASSED THROUGH THE LIFE OF THIS FALSE WORLD.

In Gruter, p. MLV. RIG.

**All of the Devil’s pomp.** So also in the following Instruction, v. 958. See the notes above on Instruction XXXV, v. 543. DAVIS.

**So that your hair may remain black at every season.** Even when, with old age approaching, it grows whiter. RIG.

**For the woman who believes from the heart, it should suffice to be approved by her husband.** It should suffice for a woman who believes from the heart to be approved by her husband—not through adornments, but through a good disposition. RIG.

**You put a bogey upon yourself.** So it reads in the transcript. Hesychius: Μομμώ· ὃ ἡμεῖς Μορμὼ φαμεν, τὸ φοβητρὸν τοῖς παιδίοις, “Mommō: what we call Mormō, the thing used to frighten children.” The *Etymologicum*: Μορμώ, ὄνομα γυναικός· μεταφορικῶς ἐκ ταύτης τὰ πρὸς κατάπληξιν τυπωθέντα προσωπεῖα ἐκάλουν μορμολυκεῖα, “Mormō, the name of a woman; metaphorically, from her they called masks fashioned to cause terror *mormolykeia*.” *Momar* is a Sicilian expression meaning a blameworthy and shameful mode of dress. See Festus and Isidore in the *Glosses*. Commodianus therefore says that Christian matrons who adorn themselves indecently put a “bogey” upon themselves when dressed in a more shameless or wanton fashion and ornament. RIG.

**You put upon yourself.** You surround or clothe yourself with it. RIG.

**Raised up by the widows’ prayers.** He touches upon the story of Tabitha. Moved by the widows’ prayers, Peter prayed to God to raise Tabitha from death, and she was raised when Peter cried, “Tabitha, arise” (Acts 9). Cyprian, *On Works and Almsgiving*. RIG.

**Not by coiffures.** In the transcript, “not by companions” (*non comitibus*), with “adornments” written above it. Lucretius I: “surrounded by maidenly coiffures.” RIG.

**She-wolves.** In the transcript, *Lupans*. *Lupanae*, λύκαιναι, “she-wolves.” The glosses give: Πόρνη, “brothel-woman, prostitute”; Πορνεῖον, “brothel.” RIG.

**Hear the voice.** The verses of this Instruction are composed in an abecedarian or alphabetical sequence. RIG.—Here the acrostic pattern is not observed, but the sequence of the letters of the alphabet is, as above in Instruction XXXV. Nevertheless, the letter X is missing here. DAVIS.

**Blessed Paul commands.** He alludes to 1 Timothy 2:9. See also Titus 2:3. DAVIS.

**“Exalted,” he says, etc.** The substance of these words is found in Isaiah 3:16–24. DAVIS.

**It is not permitted in God’s sight.** Commodianus also derives this from Tertullian, as well as what follows in the remainder of this Instruction. RIG.]

Assign yourself as a dependent to him whose son you were.

If, faithful man, you seek to live in pagan fashion,

The world’s pleasures remove you from Christ’s grace.

Without discipline, you presume that something trivial is permissible,

And you seek beloved actors and musical songs;

Nor do you care that your offspring chatter in such madness.

Do you think that he enjoys life? In your improvidence, you err.

The Most High commands, yet you avoid his righteous precepts.

### LVIII.—THAT A CHRISTIAN SHOULD BE SUCH

Since the Lord says that bread must be eaten amid groaning,

Why, then, do you now act as you do, desiring to live joyfully?

You seek to annul the sentence sent by the supreme God

Against the first-formed man; you wish to betray the law’s restraint.

If almighty God commanded us to live by sweat,

You who delight yourself will then be a stranger to him.

[Col. 0245B] Scripture says that the Lord was indignant with the Jews:

Refreshed by food, the children rose to play.

Why, then, do we now follow those who departed voluntarily?

We must beware of the very things through which they perished.

The greater part of you stands devoted to indulgence.

You transgress the law when you stain yourself with cosmetics; against you

The apostle cries out—indeed, God cries through him:

“Your own license,” he says, “destroys you in that very license.”

Be, therefore, such as Christ wishes you to be:

Gentle and joyful in him, though sorrowful toward the world.

Run, labor, sweat, and fight with sorrow.

Hope comes with labor, and the victor’s palm is bestowed.

If you desire refreshment, assist the martyrs.

Await the future rest in the passage through death.

### LIX.—TO THE MATRONS OF THE CHURCH OF THE LIVING GOD

[Col. 0245C] Christian woman, do you wish to be a matron like the ladies of the world?

[Col. 0246A] You surround yourself with gold or a silken garment, chaste woman;

You cast the law’s terror from your ears upon the wind.

You pursue empty things, all of the Devil’s pomp.

You adorn yourself before the mirror, with curls swept back over your forehead;

You also apply false cosmetics to your cheeks,

And antimony to pure eyes, with perverse beauty;

Or you dye your hair so that it may remain black at every season.

God is the inspector who penetrates every heart;

But modest women have no need of these things.

Pierce your breast with a chaste and modest disposition.

God’s law testifies that such practices must depart.

For the woman who believes from the heart and is approved by her husband,

It should suffice to be so not through adornments but through a good disposition.

Put on garments as cold and summer heat require,

Or the excessive heat of the sun, provided only that you are proven modest;

[Col. 0246B] And among God’s people display the gifts of your resources.

You, once most illustrious, put a bogey upon yourself.

She who lay lifeless was raised by the widows’ prayers:

Through giving she merited to be raised—not through coiffures.

You good matrons, flee the adornment of vanity.

Such adornment suits prostitutes (*lupanae*, literally “she-wolves”).

Conquer the Evil One, modest women of Christ.

In giving, display all your riches.

### LX.—AGAIN, TO THE SAME WOMEN

Hear the voice, you who wish to remain a Christian:

How blessed Paul commands you to be adorned;

Likewise Isaiah, the heaven-speaking teacher and author.

For he detests those who pursue the world’s depravity.

“Exalted,” he says, “the daughters of Zion shall lie low.”

[Col. 0246C] It is not permitted in God’s sight for a Christian believer to be so adorned.

[Col. 0247A] [Note: [Col. 0247B]

**That such women are unjust.** They are unjust because they condemn God’s hands; they reproach God for not having adorned them differently. They affect what God did not will; they make themselves other than God made them—which is unjust and shameless. Thus Tertullian denies that a color compounded through the adulteration of colors is legitimate. God is the author of nature; Satan, its falsifier. See Book II of *On the Dress of Women*. RIG.

**You smear your eyes with soot.** With the black powder by which the outlines of the eyes are extended. RIG.

**You raise your little locks.** Juvenal, Satire VI:

> With so many structures she builds  
> Her head still higher. RIG.

**Strand by strand.** With the hair divided into separate locks. By *grani* understand the individual strands of hair. The old translator of the history of Judith says: “She parted her hair,” that is, she arranged it in locks. And in the Council of Braga: “It was decreed that readers should not let down locks of hair in the pagan fashion.” The old glosses give *granitum*, κοκκωτόν, “granulated.” Isidore, *Origins* XI: “The locks and cinnabar of the Goths.” See Jacques Sirmond and Jean Savaron on Sidonius Apollinaris, Book I, Epistle II. Another arrangement of the hair consists of tiers and rings over the whole coiffed head. Quintilian XII.10. RIG.

**You treat your cheeks with cosmetics.** Tertullian: “They assault the skin with cosmetics; they stain the cheeks with rouge.” RIG.

[Col. 0247D] **Hands worthy of God.** Hands which you ought more worthily to extend toward God in prayer. RIG.

**You bind with an evil omen.** For it is an omen of condemnation, whose formula appears in Matthew: “Bind his hands and feet and cast him into the outer darkness.” RIG.

**With the hymn-singing choir.** The Church of Christ. RIG.

**And please the Christ who was pleasing.** Of him the Father says from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” RIG.

**Raised from the sewer.** From the world, from idolatry. Above, Instruction XLI: “Nero, raised from hell.” RIG.

**No one crowned in the contest.** Cyprian also lamented this. RIG.

**Deformed remnants of the fallen, you rebuke the disaster.** Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*. RIG.

**O belly, swollen with indulgence.** In the transcript: “O triumphantly accomplish through indulgence” (*ovanter efficite luxu*). RIG.

**Nor do you stand beside the combatant.** To strengthen him by exhortation, counsel, and example; to revive him with material assistance. RIG.

[Col. 0248B] **You see a brother excluded.** Excluded because of schism. RIG.

**To fight with the enemy.** To stand against the Church alongside the enemy and other schismatics. RIG.

[Col. 0248C] **You desire peace in the camp.** Before peace was granted to the Church, you desired that peace be granted prematurely to the excluded man. Cyprian. RIG.

**Outside, he fights against it.** The lapsed or excluded man despises the Church or opposes the Church. RIG.

**Be merciful.** Be most tender-hearted, dutiful, and beneficent toward the poor. RIG.

**Look to the meals provided by Tobit.** A reading closer to the traces in the transcript would be: “Look to the meals provided by Tobit” (*Prandia ab eo prospisce Tobo*). Thus, in the preface written in gold letters to Theodulf’s Bible, “the book of Tobit” is *liber Tobi*; and in the ancient Canon of Scriptures preserved by Anastasius, Patriarch of Constantinople, “Tobit and Tobias” are *Tobe et Tobias*. In Greek, Τώβιτ καὶ Τωβίας. And in the *Suda*: Τώβιτ, ὄνομα κύριον, καὶ Τωβίας ὁμοίως, “Tobit, a proper name, and likewise Tobias.” The father was called Τωβήτ or Τώβιτ; the son, Τωβίας. In the transcript: “look from him to the urn” (*ab eo prospice Lurna*). Above was written *Jobba*. In Book III of his *Testimonies*, Cyprian included the piety toward the poor commended in the sacred pages concerning Tobias. RIG.

**Who may feed you in return.** Luke 14.

**Who is preparing to be laid out.** *Componi*: to be buried; one who is thinking about burial, who counts himself fortunate if he may be laid out as soon as possible. Horace: “I have laid them all away. Fortunate men! Now I alone remain—finish me.” Acro explains: “I have laid them all away”: “I have buried them all in urns.” RIG.

**If he has not previously pledged himself.** If he has not promised himself to someone else who invited him, to whom he has agreed to make himself available for dinner. RIG.

**Call forth a poor man from the crowd.** In the transcript: “Shake out” (*Excute*). This passage indicates that in Commodianus’ age, *agapae*, or love-feasts, were in use in the Church on Sundays. RIG.

**Your hope lies in the tablets.** In the tablets of the New Testament. RIG.

**When Christ has been fed.** Christ himself says in Matthew 25:35: “For I was hungry, and you gave me food,” etc. RIG.

**Stephen, who loves an upright life, chooses it as his path for the journey.** Without doubt one should write:

> He who chose what is right chose the right road for his journey.

See Acts 6–7.

**First conquer the Evil One.** Satan, who in the sacred Scriptures is ὁ πονηρός, “the Evil One.” RIG.

**That king of yours.** Christ.]

Do you seek to go forth in pagan fashion, holy woman of God?

God’s heralds condemn such women, crying aloud in the law

That women who adorn themselves in this way are unjust.

You dye your hair and smear your eyes with soot;

You raise your little locks strand by strand, with your forehead painted;

You treat your cheeks with cosmetics beneath a coating of rouge;

And earrings hang with a most oppressive weight.

You overwhelm your neck with necklaces, gems, and gold;

You bind hands worthy of God with an evil omen.

Why should I mention your garments, or all the Devil’s pomp?

You reject the law when you desire to please the world.

You dance in houses; instead of psalms, you sing love songs.

Though you may be chaste, you do not clear yourself by following sinister things.

Christ therefore ranks such women as you with the pagans.

Please the hymn-singing choir and the Christ who was pleasing;

Burning with zeal, offer fragrance to Christ.

### LXI.—IN THE CHURCH, TO ALL THE PEOPLE OF GOD

[Col. 0247B]

I am not righteous, brothers, but one raised from the sewer.

I do not exalt myself; rather, I grieve for you, since I see

That out of so great a people no one is crowned in the contest.

Certainly, if one does not himself fight, let him at least provide support for them.

You rebuke the disaster; O belly swollen with indulgence!

Your brother toils under arms while the world opposes him,

And, stuffed with wealth, you neither fight nor stand beside the combatant?

[Col. 0248A] Fool, do you not understand that one man fights for many?

The whole Church depends upon such a man, if he conquers.

You see a brother excluded and fighting with the enemy.

You desire peace in the camp; outside, he fights against it.

Be merciful, so that before all else you may be saved.

Do you not fear the Lord, crying aloud through so great a proclamation,

Who commands that food be provided even to enemies?

Look to the meals provided by Tobit, who always

Ate with a poor man on every single day.

Do you seek to feed, fool, someone who may feed you in return?

Do you wish that man to obey me who is preparing to be laid out?

The brother crushed by want and wasting away nearby cries out

Against the man sumptuously fed, his belly distended.

What do you say concerning the Lord’s Day? If a man has not previously pledged himself,

Call forth a poor man from the crowd to take to dinner.

[Col. 0248B] Your hope lies in the tablets concerning Christ when he has been fed.

### LXII.—TO ONE WHO DESIRES MARTYRDOM

Since you desire martyrdom, my son, listen.

Be such as Abel was, or as Isaac himself was, or

As Stephen, who loves an upright life as his path for the journey.

What you desire is indeed a thing suited to the blessed.

First conquer the Evil One by good deeds and upright living.

When that king of yours sees this, be confident.

[Col. 0249A] [Note: [Col. 0249B]

**The time belongs to him.** The time of persecution and of peace. RIG.

**And let us conduct ourselves in both.** Let us serve Christ himself [Col. 0249C] in peace and in war. RIG.

**If war is absent.** If persecution ceases. RIG.

**In peace they will go as martyrs.** As above, “Martyrs without blood”: though tortures were lacking and though a tyrant was lacking, they did not lack a spirit strong against every kind of torture. RIG.

**While the Evil One remains, they refuse to conquer.** While the Wicked One remains, they refuse to conquer: they fail, do not persevere in faith, are overthrown, and are cast down from the faith. RIG.

**Through the siege the Wicked One perishes.** Through a prolonged siege around the most steadfast Christian, Satan is finally wearied and broken. RIG.

**But the lawful combatant.** The most steadfast Christian, the true athlete, thoroughly faithful, is not conquered and does not feel the punishments; he overcomes the tortures themselves. RIG.

**And with wailing and zeal, strike your breast with blows.** He will chastise his wailing with blows, and in his zeal and love for the Lord he will be zealous for death. Wisdom 1:12. RIG.

**Martyrdom.** To undergo martyrdom, to become a martyr. The ancient Latin translation of Eusebius of Caesarea speaks in this way in the first treatise *On the Resurrection*: “To him who is killed, and to him who takes up martyrdom.” RIG.]

Daily Warfare. Human life is military service, a place of trial (*πειρατήριον*). Job 7:1. Arrian develops this thought at length in his discourses on Epictetus, III, chap. 24: “Each person’s life is a kind of military service, and one both long and varied,” etc., p. 174. So speaks that pagan philosopher, who had encountered our writings. But the wisdom of Christ is far more perfect, as found in Eusebius, in the seventh of the minor works published by Sirmond in an ancient Latin translation—the Greek texts, if they have not already perished, still remaining concealed—p. 255:

> “There is always persecution, always an invisible war; always a crown, always self-denial. Do you wish to see the contests of religious devotion? Sometimes a man has boiled over in anger against someone subject to him; but, remembering the Lord, he has laid aside his bitterness. For it is harder to resist the heat of blazing anger than an external flame of fire. Therefore, just as the man who withstands the outward flame for God’s sake is a martyr, so too is he a martyr—[Col. 0250B] and truly a martyr—who extinguishes the inward conflagration of envy for the sake of the Lord Jesus.”

And shortly afterward: [Col. 0250C]

> “These, therefore, are the daily contests that confront us by day and by night.”

He then adds examples. RIG.

You seek to wage war. Rashly and furiously you rush toward martyrdom, restless and turbulent. RIG.

Restrain your fury. Do not rage back against an adversary whose mind is raging; do not curse one who curses you, nor bite one who bites you. RIG.

With sincere zeal. In the transcript: *sincero perseclo* [a corrupt reading]. RIG.

Idle for Christ. One who is occupied with none of the works contained in Christ’s commandments. RIG.

While you seek to fall upon him. To fall upon him as though upon prey. RIG.

If you return. To yourself. RIG.

Fool, this night you are summoned. Luke 12:20: “This very night they demand your soul from you” (*Ταύτῃ τῇ νυκτὶ τὴν ψυχήν σου ἀπαιτοῦσιν ἀπὸ σοῦ*). Cyprian, *On Works and Almsgiving*: “Fool, this night your soul is demanded of you; whose, then, will the things you have prepared be?” Martial VII.44: “Seize, heap up, carry off, possess: it must be left behind.” [Col. 0250D]

At the top of the house. Luc.: “into the storerooms.” RIG.

Daily life will supply each person with the Lord. The passage is corrupt, but it can easily be restored. Read:

> The Lord will supply each person with daily sustenance.

See Matt. 6:31; Luke 12:29. Commodian uses *vita* (“life”) for *victus* (“sustenance”). Donatus on Terence’s *Phormio*, Act I, Scene III, 12: “*Vita* signifies conduct, the soul, food, the span of living, and the fortune that befalls the living.” The Greeks employ *βίος* similarly. DAVIS.

So that you may jingle in the crossroads. That you may go about with a little bell in order to win the favor of the common people. RIG.—The pronoun should be deleted, and the reading should be: “So that you may jingle in the crossroads.” See Matt. 6:2. DAVIS.

One must be exceedingly careful not to be naïve. You must temper the simplicity of the dove with the prudence of the serpent. RIG.]

The time is his, and we conduct ourselves for either condition:

So that, if war is absent, martyrs may advance in peace.

Many indeed go astray, saying, “By our blood

We have conquered the Evil One,” though, while he remains, they refuse to conquer.

He perishes through siege, and therefore the Evil One feels it;

But the lawful combatant does not feel the pains inflicted.

And, crying out in zeal, strike your breast with your fists.

Now, if you conquer through good deeds, you are a martyr in that contest.

You, therefore, who seek to take up martyrdom by your profession,

Clothe yourself with good works in time of peace, and be secure.

### LXIII.—DAILY WARFARE

You seek to wage war, fool, as though wars had ceased.

From the day of the first-formed man, battle is waged for you until the end.

Lust casts you headlong: there is war—fight against it.

Luxury urges you on: reject its use, and you have won the war.

[Col. 0249B] Abstain from abundant wine, lest through it you go astray.

Restrain the tongue with which you adore the Lord from cursing.

Restrain your fury; make yourself peaceable toward everyone.

Take care not to crush inferiors already oppressed by misery.

Offer yourself merely as a protector, and do no harm.

Lead yourselves on the straight path with sincere zeal.

Amid your riches, make yourself gracious to the little ones.

Give from your labor; clothe the naked: thus you will conquer.

Set traps for no one, you who serve God.

Look to the beginning, from which the envious enemy perished.

[Col. 0250A] I am no teacher; rather, the law itself teaches by crying aloud.

You utter so many words in vain, when in a single moment,

Idle for Christ, you seek to take up martyrdom.

### LXIV.—ON THE ZEAL OF COVETOUSNESS

While you covet, through that very thing you perish; while you burn with envy of your neighbor,

You extinguish yourself when you kindle yourself inwardly.

Envious man, you envy another who labors under evil,

And you desire to become his equal in so great a fortune.

The law does not regard matters thus: while you seek to fall upon him,

Hanging upon every outcome, you live in a fever for gain.

And since you are guilty before yourself, you condemn yourself with yourself as judge.

The covetous gaze of the eyes is never satisfied.

Now, therefore, if you return to yourself and reflect, your desire is vain.

C. . . . . . . . . . . . . .

Hence God cries: “Fool, this night you are summoned!”

[Col. 0250B] Death rushes upon you from behind: whose will those talents be?

Storing unjust profits at the top of the house.

The Lord will supply each person with daily sustenance.

Let another heap things up; you seek to live well.

And with a heart conscious of God, you will live victorious over all things.

For I do not tell you to jingle in the crossroads

As you remain watchful for your own day, living without fraud.

A bird perishes through bait, or, unwary, sticks fast in birdlime.

Consider that you must be exceedingly careful not to be naïve.

Let others pass beyond the limit; you always look ahead.

[Note: [Col. 0251B]

Those who give from evil. Ignatius to the Trallians: “One of the ancients gives this admonition: Let no one be called good who mingles good with evil” (*παραῖνεῖ τις τῶν παλαιῶν, Μηδεὶς ἀγαθὸς λεγέσθω κακῷ τὸ ἀγαθὸν κεραννύς* [text uncertain]). RIG.

[Col. 0251C] Gifts of the unjust. Ecclesiasticus 34.

You will burst forth against the wretched. As above: “You seek to fall upon him, hanging upon every outcome.” Instruction LXIV.

The hundredth doubles the coin. From money placed at interest, you have exacted one percent each month, as with Pollio in Juvenal, who, prepared to pay threefold interest, goes about but finds no fools; and in Horace, *Satires* I.2: “One who exacts fivefold returns on the principal.”

The hundredth. 2 Esdras 5: “Restore their fields to them, and indeed also the hundredth part of the money.” The Greek of the Sixtine edition has only: “And from the money, bring out for yourselves the grain, the wine, and the oil” (*καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀργυρίου τὸν σῖτον καὶ τὸν οἶνον, καὶ τὸ ἔλαιον ἐξενέγκατε ἑαυτοῖς*). Something appears to be missing. The Latin translator adapted his Latin wording to the usage of his own age. Chrysologus: “The world’s interest is one for a hundred; Christ’s interest, a hundred for one.”

Candidate. By “candidate” he means a petitioner, supplicant, beggar, and perhaps also a candidate for baptism, whom Tertullian calls “God’s candidate.”

An opportunity for profiteers. For scourgers of the grain supply. RIG.

The people are presently your enemy. They now detest your greed; but in the future you will also have God as avenger. RIG.

You, unjustly holy through the price. These words are utterly contradictory. Read: “You, made unjust through the price.” DAVIS.

From profit on merchandise. Merchandise shamefully acquired and still more shamefully stored and held back, in order to profit from a shortage of grain. RIG.

The appointed time. A time of treacherous peace. The age was thus ordered by God. Cyprian had described such a period in his book *On the Lapsed*: “A long peace had corrupted the discipline handed down to us by God. Every individual devoted himself to increasing his patrimony,” etc. RIG.

Of the headlong people. The people who rashly wished peace to be granted to the lapsed, who were hastening toward reconciliation. RIG.

Establish the law of the city. The law and discipline of the city of God, the Church. Cyprian, Epistles 10, 11, 12, 13, 14. RIG.

You perceive the splinter. This refers to Matt. 7:3 or Luke 6:41. DAVIS.

And in the foretold slaughter. Jeremiah 48:15 and 1:27.

[Col. 0252B] You praise treacherous peace. You walk over fires concealed beneath deceptive ash. RIG.

I warn certain readers. Those who lacked the degree of expertise that Cyprian required in ordaining them. Epistles 24, 32, and 34. RIG.

Merely to recognize. *ἀναγνῶναι*, “to read,” which Commodian transfers to the simple recognition of the forehead, face, and countenance. RIG.

To flee conflict. Contentions and quarrels. RIG.

To suppress terror. Not to be threatening. RIG.

Render the rightful services of the wicked. To bishops and also to others, indeed even to secular authorities. RIG.—It should read:

> Abandon rightful services even to the wicked.

For the structure of the Latin language rejects the received reading. DAVIS.

Lilies of the field. “Lilies of the field” (*κρίνα τοῦ ἀγροῦ*). Matt. 6:28.

When you deliver edicts. Edicts that lead to the crown of martyrdom. RIG.

You are flowers among the people. Ecclesiasticus 39:19: “Blossom like the lily, you flowers.” But in what sense were readers “among the people,” when even Cyprian so carefully established them in a rank, with the people being either consulted or giving their approval to the ordination? For among the readers there was also a teacher of the hearers, or catechumens. The reader was therefore in clerical ordination, though not in priestly ordination, which, beginning with the bishop as highest priest, did not extend beyond the deacon or subdeacon. Thus the reader blossomed among the people, as one destined soon to approach the priesthood or the priestly order. See the letters of Cyprian cited above. That the Scriptures, or sacred codices, were entrusted to the reader is taught by the *Acts of the Purging of Caecilianus and Felix*, under the consulships of Constantine and Constantius.

You are Christ’s lamps. For readers read the Scriptures in church from the ambo and pulpit.

Deacons, the mystery of Christ. The same Ignatius, to the Trallians: “The deacons, being ministers of the mysteries of Christ Jesus, must be pleasing in every respect,” etc. (*Δεῖ δὲ καὶ τοὺς διακόνους ὄντας μυστηρίων Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ κατὰ πάντα τρόπον ἀρέσκειν*). RIG.

*Zacones*. Deacons, in an abbreviated Greek form: *διακονοῦντες*, “ministering.”

The mystery of Christ. The sacrament of Christ. In many churches the deacons administered the body [Col. 0253B] of Christ. This was later forbidden by the First Council of Arles, canon 15:

> “Concerning deacons whom we have learned to offer in many places, it has been determined that this ought by no means to be done.”

Arles II, canon 15:

> “A deacon is not to sit among the presbyters in the sacristy, nor, when a presbyter is present, is he to presume to administer the body of Christ.”

It follows that they had administered it when the presbyter was absent. [Col. 0253C] Commodian wishes this mystery to be performed chastely. RIG.—See the observations above on Instruction XXXV, verse 543.]

### LXV.—THOSE WHO GIVE FROM EVIL

[Col. 0251A]

Why do you pretend to be good through another’s injury, madman?

From the source of your generosity another person weeps each day.

Do you disbelieve that the Lord sees these things from heaven?

“The Most High does not approve the gifts of the unjust,” he says.

You will burst forth against the wretched once you have gained a position.

One man gives gifts so as to leave another empty-handed.

Or, if you have lent at interest, and the hundredth has doubled your coin,

You wish to give alms so that, as though purging evil by evil, you may cleanse yourself.

The Almighty utterly rejects such works.

You have given from tears; that “candidate,” crushed by thankless

Interest, laments, reduced to poverty.

Furthermore, having found an opportunity for profiteers, the people

Are presently your enemy; you, made unjust through the price,

Wish also to atone for yourself from the profit on your merchandise.

[Col. 0251B] You deceive yourself, not another, unjust man.

### LXVI.—ON TREACHEROUS PEACE

The appointed time has come upon our people: there is peace in the world,

And ruin at the same time presses down as the age flatters.

You rush the people headlong, whom you have driven into schism.

Either establish the law of the city, or depart from it.

You perceive the splinter lodged in our eyes,

But in your own eyes you refuse to see the beam.

[Col. 0252A] Treacherous peace has come upon you, while persecution blazes.

Wounds are not visible, and thus you fall without slaughter.

War is waged in secret, hidden beneath peace itself;

Scarcely one among you has conducted himself cautiously.

O badly defended men, caught in the foretold slaughter!

You praise a treacherous peace, one unjust to you.

Having become soldiers of another, not of Christ, you have perished.

### LXVII.—TO READERS

I admonish certain readers merely to recognize,

And to provide others, by their example, with material for living well;

To flee conflict and avoid quarrels and all such disputes;

To suppress terror and never be proud.

Render rightful services even to the wicked.

Make yourselves like Christ the teacher, little children;

Through good deeds be lilies among those of the field.

[Col. 0252B] You have become blessed when you encounter the edicts [of persecution].

You are flowers among the people; you are Christ’s lamps.

Preserve what you are, and you can remember it.

### LXVIII.—TO MINISTERS

Deacons, perform the mystery of Christ chastely;

Therefore, as ministers, fulfill the teacher’s precepts.

Do not play the part of an impartial judge;

Fulfill your office, thoroughly instructed in all things,

[Col. 0253A] [Note: [Col. 0253C]

Directing your attention upward. Consult Rigault below on Instruction LXXVII, verse 1204.

In diverse circumstances. I am well aware that the ancients used “diverse” to mean “contrary,” but I do not remember reading “diverse circumstances” in that sense. It should be written: “Prepared to give an example in adverse circumstances.” DAVIS.

If a shepherd has confessed. If, when questioned about the Name, he has answered clearly and steadfastly, “I am a Christian”; if, when ordered to place incense upon the pagans’ censer, he has cried out with courageous refusal, “I will not do it.” RIG.

Observing secular things. One who still involves himself in secular affairs. By “secular things” he means things opposed to Christ, things antichristian. Christ and the age—that is, Satan—are opposites. Christ shows no partiality toward persons; the age, or Satan, speaks of nobility, high birth, and offices of state. Christ speaks of simplicity and holy poverty; the age, of riches. Christ speaks of kindness, mercy, [Col. 0253D] and piety; Satan, of kingdoms, vengeance, treachery, plunder, conflagrations, and triumphs. We have demonstrated more concerning these matters in the letter prefixed to our edition of Cyprian; they appear to have reached their greatest increase beginning in Commodian’s age. RIG.

Woe to the unhappy people, who waver because their front is uncertain. Commodian says that the shepherds—bishops and presbyters—are the front line of the Christian people; therefore, as in a battle line, the strongest soldiers must be placed in the foremost ranks, to serve as an example to the rest. Tertullian, *On Flight*:

> “But when the leaders themselves—that is, the deacons, presbyters, and bishops themselves—flee, who from the rank and file will hold firm when they exhort him to fix his position in the battle line?” etc.

RIG.

But one who is devoted. That good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. RIG.

Holds together. He holds the whole sheepfold upon the track of steadfast faith. RIG.

Swarms rejoice beneath suitable kings. For swarms of bees are said each to have their own king or leader. Cyprian, Epistle 69. RIG.

[Col. 0254B] TO THE HIGHBORN. Such were the leading men, patrons, and wealthy persons who received poorer men into their clientele. RIG.

“I alone, though solitary, will surround the Lord’s altar as though I were many,” says Tertullian against the most vaunted multitude of the psychics, in *On Modesty*. RIG.

Often by one man. Phaedrus [Col. 0254C] Augustus tells a fable to this effect in book IV, fable 3:

> There is often more good in one man than in a crowd.

In this instruction Commodian censures the faults of those who possessed authority among the Christians of his age. Yet throughout all his instructions he discusses neglected discipline with such heartfelt concern and zeal that he instills despair of salvation into the Christians of his time. Gennadius, bishop of Marseille, recognized the truth of this oracle. He did not remove the sadness of the prophecy or complaint; rather, by transmitting Commodian himself to posterity, he rendered him remarkable by this distinction.

Nevertheless, this was not Commodian’s complaint alone. A little earlier Cyprian had denounced the Church’s treacherous peace in his work *On the Lapsed*. Later Sulpicius Severus concluded his books of *Sacred History* with this truly lamentable complaint:

> “And now,” he says, “when everything was most visibly being disturbed and confounded by the dissensions of bishops, and when through them all things had been corrupted by hatred or favoritism, fear, inconstancy, envy, faction, lust, [Col. 0254D] greed, arrogance, sleep, and idleness, the majority finally contended against the few who offered sound counsel, employing insane counsels and obstinate pursuits.”

RIG.

The tempter of all . . . Satan. Here Commodian certainly instills despair into bishops. RIG.

Because truth incurs hatred. That is, produces or brings hatred upon itself. Thus elsewhere Commodian said “to take up martyrdom,” meaning to accomplish and carry off the glory of Christian martyrdom. RIG.

No one acts for nothing. You sell your patronage at a high price. RIG.

Your embezzlement. So it reads in the transcript. If the reading is genuine, *peculantia* means embezzlement or plunder (*διαρπαγή*). RIG.

And you feed upon them. You devour them. RIG.

The foundations of the earth. The underworld. The passage of Isaiah 14:15 reads thus according to the Septuagint: “But now you will descend into Hades and into the foundations of the earth” (*Νῦν δὲ εἰς ᾅδην καταβήσῃ καὶ εἰς τὰ θεμέλια τῆς γῆς*). Aquila and Theodotion said, “into the pit” (*εἰς λάκκον*). The Old Latin version: “into the foundations of the lake.” Ancient glosses: “*Λάκκος*: hollow, lake, [Col. 0255B] cistern.” Likewise: “Muddy places” (*πηλώδεις τόποι*). Tertullian said “a lake of fire and sulfur” in *On Flight*. RIG.]

Directing your attention upward, always devoted to the Most High God.

Render to God the sacred ministries of the altar in safety,

Prepared to give an example in adverse circumstances.

Bow your own heads to the shepherds.

Thus it will come about that you can be approved by Christ.

### LXIX.—TO GOD’S SHEPHERDS

If a shepherd has confessed, he has doubled the contest.

The Apostle, moreover, commands teachers to be such as these:

Let the ruler be patient; let him know when to loosen the reins.

Let him first inspire fear and afterward anoint with honey.

And first let him take care to do himself what he says.

A shepherd who observes secular things is held at fault,

To whose face you would dare to say anything.

At the reports of this, Gehenna itself boils in the underworld.

Woe to the unhappy people, who waver because their front is uncertain.

If such a shepherd is present, the flock stands almost lost;

But a devoted shepherd holds it together by governing rightly.

Swarms rejoice beneath suitable kings.

In such men there is hope, and the whole Church lives.

### LXX.—I SPEAK TO THE HIGHBORN

The present time requires me alone to tell you the truth.

Often one man gives the warning that many refuse.

I wish to turn your hatred upon me alone,

So that the hearts of all may fear the tempter.

Consider the saying that truth incurs hatred.

I have already foretold how many things would arise from treacherous peace.

While it flattered you, alas, the deceiver crept in unnoticed.

Because you did not know that snares were threatening, you fell.

You swallow what is utterly bitter, though it belongs to the age itself.

No one for whom you intercede acts without payment.

The man who fled from the fire acts in the abyss through your agency;

Then, stripped by you, the wretched man begs for aid.

The judges themselves now recoil from your embezzlement.

S . . . . . . . . . . . . .

On a shorter heading I would not plow so many lines,

You observe the teachers toward whom you advance of your own accord:

[Col. 0254B] You feast together with them, and you feed upon them.

For these things you are already almost entering the foundations of the earth.

### LXXI.—VISIT A SICK PERSON IN THIS WAY

If a brother is sick—I am speaking of a poor man—

[Col. 0255A] [Note: [Col. 0255B]

To visit such a person as he lies ill. A bedridden patient, one confined to a pallet. [Col. 0255C] RIG.

A poor man, always hated. The poor are commonly troublesome and hateful to the rich, and even to their neighbors and friends. “Friends will hate poor friends” (*φίλοι μισήσουσι φίλους πτωχούς*). Prov. 14:20. RIG.

From which he may recover himself. From which he may take something to alleviate his poverty and obtain a little money to procure the necessities whose denial causes nature pain, and so at length recover his strength. RIG.—“From which he may recover himself,” etc.: regain his strength. The French similarly say *se reprendre*. See the glossary of Charles du Fresne. DAVIS.

To carry provisions. Commodian himself will say in the final Instruction: “Let them carry provisions upon their necks.”

TO THE HEALTHY POOR. In the preceding Instruction he spoke of the sick and bedridden; now he speaks of those who are strong and healthy, though needy, who can nevertheless obtain the means of supporting themselves by practicing their craft. He wishes even these people to contribute something from the resources of their craft to their sick brothers. RIG.

Healthy poverty. Ecclesiasticus 30:14: “A poor man who is healthy and strong in constitution” (*πτωχὸς ὑγιὴς καὶ ἰσχύων τῇ ἕξει*).

A poor man answering from on high. One who answers as though looking down upon another. Prov. 18:25: “The poor man speaks with entreaties.”

For gentle speech. Gentle speech often has great power among angry people, and by its graciousness causes the angry man’s crest to subside and his heat to diminish; it cools the heated spirit of the angry man. Thus Lucilius said: “When the bronze cauldron boils, a small ladle cools it.” RIG.

Softens. It loosens rigidity, softens, melts, and liquefies. Plautus used *dirigere* in the same sense in the *Curculio*: “When an armed man pierces an elephant with his sword”—that is, so cuts or transfixes it that, its blood poured out, the rigid bulk of the beast is dissolved or falls divided. Glosses: “I straighten or direct” (*ἀπευθύνω*), *derigo*. RIG.—Commodian is referring to Prov. 15:1.

You know the proverb. Ancient glosses: “Theology” (*θεολογία*), “the proverbs of God.”

Furthermore, into the treasury. Above, Instruction IV: “You do not prepare a house with treasure.” Glosses: “Treasure” (*gaza*): “money, in the Persian language” (*χρήματα, Περσίδι διαλέκτῳ*). [Col. 0256B] Cyprian: “And do you believe that you celebrate the Lord’s rite, when you pay no attention to the Corban?” Commodian LXI: “What do you say concerning the Lord’s day?” etc. RIG.

[Col. 0256C] That solitary woman. A widow, one living alone.

The Anointed One. Christ. Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. 3: “The name Christian, so far as its meaning is concerned, is derived from anointing—a name composed from sweetness or kindness.” RIG.

To appear in black. As was presently the custom of peoples by no means Christian. Julius Paulus, *Sentences*, book I, title *On Tombs and Mourning*: “A person in mourning must abstain from banquets, ornaments, purple, and white clothing.” Black clothing, a color suited to mourning, is a more sorrowful dress. They had no hope of resurrection; they mourned their dead as lost, as though they no longer existed.

But Christians, who said that their faithful brothers had migrated to eternal life, departed, or gone before them, did not appear in black, “for black is death-bearing” (*τὸ γὰρ μέλαν θανατῶδες*). Thus they rejected all omens of death. For they denied that the black and funereal theta upon tombs, or growing old in black clothing, had any relevance to Christians, since they were certain of eternal life after departure. RIG.

In the Solomonic book. The book is entitled *Ecclesiasticus, the Wisdom of Jesus Son of Sirach*. Commodian calls it a “Solomonic book” because it contains maxims or sayings after the model of Solomon. RIG.

When the week is complete. Ecclesiasticus 22:13: “Mourning for the dead lasts seven days.” We learn that this custom was extremely ancient from the story of Jacob, Genesis 50:10, and from the observations that learned men have made on that passage and on Sirach, drawing from Philo and Ammianus Marcellinus. RIG.

To lament like pagans. In the manner of the nations. Paul to the Thessalonians, I: “As also the rest, who possess no hope” (*καθὼς καὶ οἱ λοιποί, οἱ μὴ ἔχοντες ἐλπίδα*)—namely, the hope of resurrection. RIG.

Because you are less than the nations. It should read: “In what respect are you less than the nations?” DAVIS.

You cry out that they are extinguished. As above, Instruction XXX: “He has lived,” and “I have extinguished.” Pagans called the dead “extinguished”; Christians called them those sent ahead, transferred to God, or summoned by the Lord. RIG.

Nor did the father lead his son to be sacrificed at the altar in grief. Ennodius, bishop of Pavia, cited these examples of Abraham and David in connection with the general theme that sons must not be mourned, in Epistle 1 of book II. There Sirmond was the first to identify these verses of Commodian—and indeed Commodian’s very name, which had been unknown since the age of Gennadius and Gelasius. Eusebius, in his work *On the Resurrection*: “Do not ask whether Isaac was actually slain; from the moment the father resolved upon it, Isaac was dead to his father,” p. 51 of Sirmond’s edition. RIG.]

Do not visit such a person lying ill with empty hands.

Do good under God; render service by means of a coin.

Through it he recovers; or, if he has collapsed,

Let the poor man be restored, since he has no means from which

To repay you; but the Creator and Maker of the world will repay you for him.

Or, if you are reluctant to go to the poor man, always regarded with hatred,

Send money and something from which he can recover himself.

Likewise, if a poor sister lies sick in bed,

Let your matrons begin to carry provisions.

God himself cries: “Break your bread for the needy.”

Visiting requires not words but good deeds.

It is unjust for a brother, overcome by poverty, to lie sick.

Make an effort: he requires food and drink, not words.

Look after such people—those who are truly disabled

And cannot sustain themselves; give to them repeatedly.

I pledge that the Lord will give you fourfold.

### LXXII.—TO THE HEALTHY POOR

[Col. 0255B]

What is healthy poverty, if riches are not present?

Certainly, if you have a craft, then share with your brother as well.

Ensure this one thing for yourself: do not let yourself be called proud.

I promise you this, since you live more securely than a rich man:

Receive into your ears the teaching of the great Solomon.

God hates a poor man who answers from on high;

Therefore humble yourself, and render honor to the powerful.

[Col. 0256A] For gentle speech—you know the proverb—will soften him.

He is overcome by service, even if his anger is long-standing.

If the tongue remains silent, you have found nothing better.

But if you have no craft by which your life may be sustained,

Then offer your labor, or run an errand, at a powerful man’s command.

Do not be ashamed or reluctant, while healthy, to run ahead.

Furthermore, you must place something earned from your labor into the treasury,

Just as that solitary woman did, whom the Anointed One preferred.

### LXXIII.—SONS MUST NOT BE MOURNED

Although the death of sons may leave the heart as a vessel of pain,

It is nevertheless unlawful to appear in black or to lament.

The law prudently says to grieve in spirit, without outward display,

In the Solomonic book, when the week is complete.

Having forgotten the Lord and the promised resurrection,

If you have made your sons martyrs, will you bewail them with such cries?

[Col. 0256B] Are you not ashamed to mourn your children unrestrainedly, like a pagan?

You tear your face, beat your breast, and rend your garments,

Yet do you not fear the Lord whose kingdom you desire to see?

Mourn as is lawful, but do not go astray on their account.

In what respect, then, are you less than the nations?

Through the devil’s offspring you behave like the crowds born from it.

You cry out that they are extinguished. By what favor? Falsely—you have perished.

Nor did the father lead his son to be sacrificed at the altar in grief;

Nor did the prophet mourn in grief for his dead son.

[Col. 0257A] [Note: [Col. 0257C]

Devoted to God. Glosses: “Most devoted” (*καθοσιώτατος*): prepared to suffer and do all things. RIG.

You know the proverbs. Thus Emperor Julian says to a certain Dionysius: “You have heard the tale” (*Μῦθον ἀκήκοας*), and “You know the story” (*Ἱστορίαν ἐπίστασαι*). RIGAULT.

He wished to be carried through the forum. Like that Gargilius in Horace, who:

> Early in the morning ordered nets, hunting spears, and slaves  
> To pass through the crowded forum and the people.

RIG.

You who seek funeral guilds for these things. The guild of Libitinarian funeral workers, who conducted funerals according to pagan ritual, with a magnificent display, a very large crowd following the funeral, and ancestral images. RIG.

You seek guilds. That is, you summon them. Thus in Instruction XIX he said, “to form a guild”: “when a similar guild had been formed.” RIG.

Under Vejovis. Under idols. The transcript reads: “under vigor.” RIG.

[Col. 0257D] It is fitting at Easter, the most blessed day, on which we received the pledge and earnest of resurrection into eternal life. RIG.

Those who beg when the divine things have been completed. So it reads in the transcript, where “those who beg for divine sabbaths” is written above it. Neither reading seems probable to me. The following, however, would produce a meaning most suitable to this instruction: “Let those also rejoice who beg beneath the completed divine rites.” Piety toward the poor is commended, especially toward those who ask and beg the faithful for help and kindness at the time when the assembly is dismissed on Easter Day—the time when the Mass, or Easter dismissal, is customarily pronounced; the time when the faithful are dismissed after the solemnities, mysteries, and divine rites have been completed. RIG.

Consider from what source these things may be remembered on your behalf. In the transcript: “You will reject, perhaps, from which they may be remembered.” These words are thoroughly corrupt. RIG.

When you yourselves do not act. Above, in Instruction LXIX, he said: “And first let him take care to do himself what he says.” Apollonius: “A lawgiver must make the things he himself has done into commandments for the multitude” (*Δεῖ γὰρ νομοθέτην ἃ πεποίηκεν ἑαυτόν, ταῦτα ἐπιτάγματα ἐς τοὺς πολλοὺς ποιεῖσθαι*). Horace: “If you wish me to weep, you must first grieve yourself.” It is characteristic of the Pharisees to speak but not act—to impose upon the people burdens that they themselves are unwilling to touch even with a finger. RIG.

Thus blasphemy concerning you often afflicts many. Commodian says this of the clergy of his age; at that time the term “clergy” also included the priesthood. Jerome likewise testifies concerning his own age in Epistle XXII to Eustochium, section 16:

> “The clergy themselves,” he says, “who ought to hold the office of teaching and instilling fear, kiss the heads of matrons and extend a hand which, unless you knew better, you might think they wished to use in blessing them—but they are receiving payment for the greeting. Meanwhile, those women, when they see that priests require their protection, are lifted up in pride,” etc.

How far had Antichrist already advanced through the churches in those times? The leaders themselves now required the protection of an admonisher; and those who had undertaken the pontifical office of governing the people through their admonitions were themselves abandoning their own protection through evil transgression. RIG.

ON TALE-TELLERS. Chatterers and gossips. RIG.

The house of the stomach. The breast. RIG.

Of the stomach. Of the heart, mind, or conscience. RIG.

[Col. 0258D] For the daily offense. The transcript reads “divine.” “The daily offense” means the assaults of every day. RIG.

You debauch your lips. You profane, violate, and loosen your lips through excess and wickedness. Just as *luxuriari* is derived from *luxuria*, so *luxari* is derived from *luxus*. “I behave dissolutely” (*ἀσωτεύομαι*), “I indulge in excess” (*luxo, luxurior*). Festus: “*Luxantur* is derived from *luxus*; that is, they indulge in excess.” RIG.

As though they were beginning at the baths. As though they were commencing the bath. And in the following verse: “And they constrict the house of God as though making it a marketplace.” RIG.—The sense, unless I am mistaken, requires the reading: “They crowd together and make the house of God into something like a marketplace.” DAVIS.

Like a marketplace. “A house of trade” (*οἶκον ἐμπορίου*). John 2:16. RIG.

The Lord certainly terrified the house of prayer. When he drove out the money changers with a twisted whip. John 2:15. RIG.

Lift up your hearts. An ancient formula requesting attention and silence. Ancient glosses: “Up” (*sus*), *ἄνω*; “upward” (*sursum*), *ἐπάνω*. Likewise: “Above, below” (*ἄνω, κάτω*), “upward, downward.” RIG.

For the devout people. For the whole brotherhood. RIG.

I set no limit for the drunkard, but prefer a beast. The transcript reads: “I set no limit for the drunkard, but a beast worse.” From the first reading, indeed, the emendation immediately suggested itself: “The drunkard sets no limit for himself; rather, a greater beast sets one.” The meaning therefore appeared to be: one devoted to drunkenness sets no limit for himself and does not listen to anyone admonishing him to do so; rather, a greater beast, a greater glutton, sets a limit for his drinking companion, whom drunkenness, having disordered his mind, has cast down unconscious—no longer master of mind or reason, and therefore a beast. But this is too elaborate [Col. 0259C] and forced an exposition. Accordingly, the following simpler text is preferred: “I set no limit for the drunkard, but prefer a beast.” RIG.]

For he did not conduct the Almighty’s child to burial weeping;

Rather, devoted to God, he swiftly conducted the funeral.

### LXXIV.—ON FUNERAL DISPLAY

You who seek to concern yourself with funeral display

Go astray, still seeking, as God’s servant, to please even in death.

Ah! That a lifeless, death-stricken body should be adorned!

O true vanity, to desire honor for the dead!

The mind remains captive to the world, not devoted to Christ even in death.

You know the proverbs: he wished to be carried through the forum.

You live with minds so savage and so like his

That at death you wish to possess an auspicious and happy day,

So that the people may gather and behold praise joined with mourning.

You do not foresee where you may deserve to go after death.

Behold, they follow the funeral; but perhaps you are already being burned,

Reduced to punishment. What will the display profit the dead man?

[Col. 0257B] You will be accused, you who seek funeral guilds for these things.

You desire to live under Vejovis; you deceive yourself.

### LXXV.—TO THE CLERGY

It is fitting at Easter, our most blessed day,

That those who beg when the divine rites have been completed should also rejoice.

Let what is sufficient—wine and food—be distributed to them.

Consider from what source these things may be remembered on your behalf.

With so small an expense, you fail to make a gift to Christ.

When you yourselves do not act, how can you persuade such people

To practice the justice of the law—even once a year?

[Col. 0258A] Thus blasphemy concerning you often afflicts many.

### LXXVI.—ON TALE-TELLERS AND SILENCE

While it appears trivial to each person and is not avoided,

And while, as though harmless, it rushes forth because you misuse it,

Stories intervene at the place to which you came to pour out prayers

Or to strike the house of your heart in repentance for the daily offense.

The heralds’ trumpet cries while the reader reads,

So that ears may open, but you close yours all the more;

You debauch the lips with which you ought to groan.

Shut your breast against evils, or resolve them within your breast.

But because money gives the rich a bold front,

Everyone therefore perishes when they trust themselves most.

Women likewise gather as though beginning at the baths;

They crowd together and make the house of God into something like a marketplace.

The Lord certainly terrified the house of prayer.

[Col. 0258B] When the Lord’s priest has commanded, “Lift up your hearts,”

So that silence may prevail while prayer is being made,

You answer clearly, yet do not restrain yourself in accordance with your promises.

He entreats the Most High for the devout people,

That no one may perish, while you turn aside into stories;

There you smile to yourself, or disparage your neighbor’s reputation.

Without discipline you speak as though God were absent—

God, who made all things, as though he neither heard nor saw.

### LXXVII.—TO DRUNKARDS

I set no limit for the drunkard, but prefer a beast.

[Col. 0259A] [Note: [Col. 0259C]

You grow proud through drinking. The transcript reads: “heavenly things” or “higher.” RIG.

Holding the authority of a ruler among the Cyclopes, fool. That is, among the Cyclopes of Polyphemus. RIG.

Hence in the stories. In the myths, in the *Odyssey*. Glosses: “In a history” (*ἱστορίᾳ*), “records.” Hesychius: “He narrates” (*ἱστορεῖ*), “he tells a myth” (*μυθεύει*); “history” (*ἱστορία*), “testimonies and similar things” (*μαρτύρια, καὶ τὰ ὅμοια*). RIG.

For me, it is best to drink. Commodian adds this in his own person; he means to drink eternal life through the Gospels, the commandments, and Christ’s examples. RIG.

You extinguish Gehenna for yourself. He alludes to the story of the rich man clothed in purple, whose tongue was burned in the underworld with such fiery torment that he longed, as the greatest relief, for the tiniest drop of water to be dripped upon it from Lazarus’s finger. Luke 17.

TO A HOST. A giver of a banquet (*ἑστιάτωρ*). RIG.

The poor man who does not repay you. Instruction LXI. RIG.

You lend to the Most High. Cyprian, *On Discipline*: “Lend your patrimony to God; feed Christ.” [Col. 0259D] RIG.—Solomon, Prov. 19:17: “He who shows mercy to the poor lends to God,” as the ancient translator has it in Cyprian’s *Testimonies to Quirinus*, book III, chap. 1. DAVIS.

From the hidden places. From the innermost recess of the heart, from the sanctuary of your mind. RIGAULT.

So that, taking pity on the needy, you may pray. Paulinus, Epistle XXXIV: “It is one thing when you alone pray for yourself, and another when a multitude trembles before God on your behalf.” RIG.

THE NAME “GAZAEUS.” That is, Commodian: from *gaza* comes *Gazaeus*, as from *commoda* comes *Commodianus*. *Commoda* means resources, riches, treasure. Ancient glosses: “Advantages, profitable things, money” (*Commoda, λυσιτελῆ, χρήματα*). RIG.

Hold fast to the beginning. I have no doubt that the author was referring to David’s words in Ps. 109:4: “With you is the beginning on the day of your power.” Clearly “beginning” (*ἀρχή*) means sovereign power. Suetonius also used *principium* in this sense, as the most learned Bishop Bossuet of Meaux observed on the cited passage of the Psalm.]
