[Col. 0260B] **And those whom fire consumed in this age.** Under the imperial laws concerning punishments, death by fire was the supreme penalty. Christians, however, recoiled from funeral pyres and tomb-fires even for the bodies of the dead, through a foreboding dread of that eternal fire. Their first concern, therefore, was to strengthen the spirits of those destined for martyrdom against the torments of fire. In 1 Peter 4:12, Peter exhorts Christians not to be terrified if martyrdom comes through fire and the burning of the body, and not to recoil from it as something strange, unheard-of, unprecedented, or foreign to Christians: “Do not regard as strange the fiery trial among you” (*mē xenizesthe tē en hymin pyrōsei*). Cyprian, Epistle LVI: “Do not be astonished at the burning that comes upon you, which takes place for your testing,” etc.; on this passage we too have made some observations. And so this Christian parody would run:

> O how great the heat, how great the labors you will suffer,
>
> If fires are something strange to you!

**When six thousand years have been completed.** Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho the Jew*, p. 307, declares that he believes this together with most other Christians who are entirely sound in judgment: “I, and any others who are entirely orthodox Christians, believe in the resurrection and in a thousand years in Jerusalem,” etc. Quintus Julius Hilarianus—whom the compilers of the *Library of the Fathers* published from the library of Pierre Pithou—believed that this period of six thousand years would reach its completion around A.D. 369:

> From the Passion of the Lord Christ—from the time when the Son of God promised resurrection to those who believed in him—four hundred and seventy years must be completed, so that the total of six thousand years may be concluded. At the beginning of the seventh millennium, those who believe with true faith will be delivered from the world. For then the first resurrection of the saints will take place. Of the four hundred and seventy years from the Passion of the Lord to the consulship of Caesar and Atticus, three hundred and sixty-nine years had passed on the ninth day before the Kalends of April. One hundred and one years therefore remain until the six thousand years are completed, etc.

RIG.

**When the thousandth year has been completed.** The Epistle attributed to Barnabas, p. 54: “Therefore, children, in six days—that is, in six thousand years—all things will be brought to completion.” The old Latin translator: “From this you ought to know that in six thousand years all things will be brought to completion.” RIG.

**Speaking to the mountains themselves.** Luke 23:30: “Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall upon us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’” Hosea had foretold this at 10:8; see Revelation 6:16. RIG.

**All flesh is restored together with its deed.** Each person is given back and restored together with his own deeds and works, so that, according to what each has done, he may be sent to the crown or to Gehenna. RIG.]

By drinking you become arrogant, and inwardly you depart from soundness of mind,  
Foolishly maintaining the rule of a sovereign among the Cyclopes.  
Hence, in the histories, you say: “While dead, I do not drink.  
For me the best thing is to drink—and to be wise at heart.”  
Supply instead—why seek to abuse your means any further?—  
The poorest little pauper, and you will both be refreshed.  
If you do this, you extinguish Gehenna for yourself.

### LXXVIII.—TO A PASTOR

You who seek to feed others, and have prepared what you could,  
Have done rightly by feeding them continually.  
Yet invite the poor man who cannot feed you in return.  
Then your table will be approved by the one God.  
The Almighty especially commanded that such people be fed.  
When you feed them, look upon the weak, and you lend to the Most High.  
The Lord willed that you should prove yourselves in this matter.

### LXXIV.—TO ONE WHO PRAYS

[Col. 0259B]

If you desire your prayer to be heard from heaven,  
Break the bonds of wickedness from their hidden recesses.  
Or if, moved by pity for the needy, you pray through good deeds,  
Do not doubt that what you have asked will be granted to you as you pray.  
But if, destitute of good works, you worship God,  
By no means offer prayers so foolishly.

### LXXX.—THE NAME OF GAZAEUS

[Col. 0260A]

Future inhabitants of heaven with Christ our God,  
Who holds sovereignty and sees all things from heaven:  
Let simplicity and goodness dwell within your body.  
Do not be angry without cause against a devoted brother,  
For you will receive from him whatever you have done.  
This pleased Christ: that the dead should rise—yes, indeed,  
With their own bodies, even those whom fire consumed in this age—  
When six thousand years have been completed and the world has ended.  
Meanwhile heaven is transformed, its course having been changed,  
For then the impious are burned by divine fire.  
The wrath of the supreme God blazes while creation groans.  
Those held more worthy, born of an illustrious lineage,  
And noble men, when Antichrist has been defeated,

[Col. 0260B] By God’s command will live again in that age,  
For a thousand years, indeed, to serve the saints and the Most High  
Under the yoke of slavery, carrying provisions upon their necks,  
So that they may be judged again when the kingdom has ended.  
Those who reduce God to nothing, when the thousandth year is complete,  
Will perish by fire, speaking to the mountains themselves.  
In funeral pyres and tombs, all flesh is restored together with its deed;  
They are plunged into hell and endure punishments forever.

They are shown these things, and read the deeds from heaven,  
Recorded in ancient memory, according to what is owed and what is deserved.  
The reward forever, according to their deeds, comes from the Sovereign.

[Col. 0262A] I cannot encompass everything in a little book.

*[THE COMPLETE WORKS OF ANTONIUS.]*

## THE POEM OF ANTONIUS AGAINST THE PAGANS. (C, G, S)\*

[Col. 0261B] [Note: [Col. 0261C]

**Antonius.** Who can tell me whom Paulinus is addressing here? Vossius, *On the Art of Grammar*, Book IV, chapter 5, shows that the ancients employed the nominative in place of the vocative. MURATOR.

**I unfold such things in verse.** Cornelius Valerius Vonck, a distinguished man, presents observations on this poem by Antonius in his *Critical Specimen*, pp. 1–10. Some of these are reviewed by the anonymous Leipzig scholar in the *Acta Eruditorum* for 1746, p. 215ff. From them I intend to excerpt the more important observations that help elucidate this poem. Here, therefore, Vonck reads: “I unfold such things in song.” This is more elegant [Col. 0261D] than the author’s age and style permit. GALLAND.

**He called upon the lyre with melodious voice.** Perhaps with greater license than is proper, the critic changes *chelyn*, “lyre,” to *Deum*, “God.” Why might the author not have written: “David himself called upon the lyre”? He was evidently referring to Psalms 56:9 and 107:3: “Arise, my glory; arise, psaltery and harp.” VONCK.

**To be drowned.** Unless Paulinus employed poetic license, something is wanting for the meter. Perhaps *mersos*, “the drowned,” should be read in place of *mergi*, “to be drowned.” MURATOR.—The distinguished Muratori, to assist the faltering meter, substituted *mersos* for *mergi*. Vonck proposed: *qui mergi funestos*, “who saw the deadly men drowned.” Yet neither emendation is necessary. Virgil likewise employs such a hiatus, *Eclogues* III, verse 6:

> And the juice is taken from the flock, and the milk from the lambs.

The best poets do this very frequently. Our author does the same shortly afterward, in verse 15. A. LIPS.

**And a spring.** Here too the verse labors somewhat. I would write:

> For whom manna came from heaven, for whom, O spring, etc.

MUR. To restore the meter of this line, the editor rewrites it as “For whom manna came from heaven, for whom a spring”; the critic, more easily, transposes “spring and.” But the anonymous Leipzig scholar rightly thinks that nothing should be changed here, because of the poet’s license. GALLAND.

**He fashions them from bronze.** Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 13, reproached the pagans with the same thing:

> The household gods whom you call Lares you treat by household authority, pawning them and sometimes transforming Saturn into a chamber pot, sometimes Minerva into a ladle, according as each has been broken and battered through being worshiped for a long time, or according as each master has found domestic necessity more sacred. You similarly disgrace your public gods by public law, keeping them taxable at the auctioneer’s stand. If one resorts to the Capitol or the vegetable market, under the same auctioneer’s proclamation, beneath the same spear, and under the same quaestor’s entry, divinity is awarded to the bidder and leased out.

The *cacabulum* mentioned by Tertullian, a vessel used for filth, is modestly indicated by Paulinus in these words:

> Or rather often transform it into shameful forms.

MUR.

**Let him send the fabricated thing.** Read: “let him send the shattered pieces to the mint.” VONCK.

**The minds of the gods.** The pagans foolishly sought the intentions of the gods in the entrails of slaughtered animals. Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book V:

> A diseased entrail too had disclosed signs of the truth  
> And warnings from the gods....

[Col. 0263A] Seneca, himself a pagan, condemned this same error of theirs in *Natural Questions*, Book II: [Col. 0263B]

> You make God excessively idle and the attendant of a petty matter if he arranges dreams for some and entrails for others, etc.

Consult Caesar Bulenger’s book *On Magic*, etc. MURATOR.]

I, ANTONIUS, confess that I have examined every sect;  
I have investigated a great many things and run through every particular,  
But I have found nothing better than believing in Christ.  
I have determined to set these things down in gentle verse;  
And lest it displease anyone that I unfold such things in poetry,  
David himself called upon the lyre with melodious voice.  
Following his example, we shall sing humble verses on great themes,  
Declaring what must be shunned, pursued, and cultivated,  
Provided that in every case both the fact and the cause are proved.

First, even the Jewish people failed to recognize  
The wondrous grace of God. For although it had then been rescued from the wicked Pharaoh,  
And had crossed the sea on foot, with a fiery pillar  
As its guide, and had seen the hostile horsemen drowned;  
And although it lacked nothing even in the deserted fields—

[Col. 0261C] Manna came to it from heaven, and a spring flowed from the rock—

[Col. 0262B] Afterward it denied the very God who had bestowed such blessings.  
And while, with a deranged heart, it sought another divine power,  
It destroyed in blazing fires the gold that it had contributed.

Likewise, the pagan worships the stones he himself has carved,  
And makes for himself the very thing that he himself must fear.  
Then he worships images, which he fashions from bronze in such a way  
That, whenever he pleases, he may send the fabricated thing to the mint,  
Or rather often transform it into shameful forms.  
Then he slaughters wretched animals, and seeks the minds of gods  
Whom he imagines to be angry in a still-warm lung,  
And begs for a human life by means of an animal’s death.  
Why does one who makes his request with blood ask that pardon be granted?  
What sort of thing is that? How foolish? How deserving of censure?

[Col. 0262C] Although Almighty God once fashioned man,

[Col. 0263A] [Note: [Col. 0263B]

**He even sells him.** The words we recently quoted from Tertullian again apply to this. Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, chapter 16:

> The god was sold so that he might benefit the purchaser, and the purchaser worshiped as a suppliant whatever he had shortly before seen put up for auction.

MURATOR.

**Am I to believe that philosophers possess any reason?** St. Eucherius wrote elegantly on this subject in his *Exhortation to Valerian*. Among other things, he says:

> It will quickly become clear to you how greatly these teachings of ours—that is, the precepts of piety and truth—ought to be preferred to the precepts of the philosophers. In their teachings there is either a shadow of virtue or false wisdom; in ours, however, complete righteousness and solid truth are contained. Hence it may be said that others have appropriated the name of philosophy, but we its life. For what manner of precepts for living can be given by men who do not know its cause?

MUR.

**There are Cynics.** These philosophers were commonly called *kynikoi*, that is, “canine,” *apo tou kynos*, “from the dog.” Diogenes Laertius says this in his *Life of Antisthenes*: “He was the first to inaugurate Cynicism”; that is, he founded the Cynic sect and was its leader. Hence Ausonius sings of him:

> I am the first founder of Cynicism. What reasoning is this?  
> Alcides is said to be far earlier.  
> Once I ranked second, with Alcides as my teacher;  
> Now I am first among Cynics, while he is a god.

Laertius, however, in his *Proem*, asserts that the Cynics were so called by way of reproach: “And from terms of abuse, as in the case of the Cynics.” Suetonius, in his *Vespasian*:

> When he encountered Demetrius the Cynic on the road after the latter’s condemnation, and Demetrius did not deign either to rise or to greet him, but even barked out something or other against him, Vespasian was content merely to call him “dog.”

Augustine too writes elegantly in *The City of God*, Book XIV, chapter 20:

> Those canine philosophers, that is, the Cynics, failed to see this, when, in opposition to human modesty, they put forward nothing other than a canine—that is, an unclean—opinion.

MURATOR.

**And those who follow Plato’s uncertain doctrine.** Plato for the most part adhered to Socrates and is therefore numbered among the Socratics by Laertius in the *Prolegomena*. Yet because he “established the Old Academy,” he laid the foundations of a new sect. Hence arose the sect of the Platonists. Strictly speaking, however, they were called Academics. Laertius, in his *Life of Plato*:

> He was buried in the Academy, where he had spent most of his time philosophizing; hence the school that descended from him was called Academic.

Augustine, *The City of God*, Book VIII, chapter 12:

> Since Speusippus, the son of Plato’s sister, and Xenocrates succeeded him in his school, which was called the Academy, they and their successors were therefore called Academics.

More recent and highly distinguished philosophers, however, who chose to follow Plato, did not wish to be called Peripatetics or Academics, but Platonists.

[Col. 0264A] **Uncertain doctrine.** Prudentius in the *Apotheosis*:

> Consult the ravings of bearded Plato;  
> Consult also the shaggy Cynics whom he imagines, and those whom  
> Aristotle enveloped in a twisted whirl of sinews.

[Col. 0264B] **For a long time the soul’s....** The verse labors somewhat. I would write:

> Whom the substance of the soul, long investigated, confounds.

MUR.

**Which, beyond its title....** Plato’s book in which he addresses the immortality of the soul is certainly excellent and very celebrated; but if it is compared with Christian assertions and the entirely certain proofs of our faith, it contains nothing certain within. For a pagan man situated far from true religion, it was a great marvel of wisdom to pronounce an opinion not altogether deserving ridicule concerning the soul’s perpetuity. Yet it is not my task here to investigate how many errors he committed in that opinion, but only to warn that most things in the book are advanced as uncertainties. Theodoret, a most learned writer, in his fifth *Discourse against the Greeks*, examines this opinion of Plato very acutely and repeatedly finds it wavering. He then adds:

> Although the most wise Plato delivered a great many arguments concerning the immortality of the soul, he did not persuade even his pupil Aristotle to accept this position.

[Col. 0264C] Acciaiuoli translates it thus: “Plato indeed, the most wise, who delivered many discourses on the immortality of the soul, did not persuade even his pupil Aristotle to accept that position.” MURATOR.

**There are also Physicists.** The Greek *physis* means *natura*, “nature,” in Latin; hence “Physicists,” or natural philosophers. Laertius in the *Proem*: “Some were called Physicists because they wrote about the nature of things.” MURATOR.

**For one of them had a staff.** Laertius, in his *Life of Diogenes*:

> Once, on seeing a child drinking with his hands, Diogenes threw the cup out of his wallet.

The whole company of writers attributes this deed to Diogenes, especially Seneca in Epistle 90 and St. Jerome in *Against Jovinian*, Book II. In agreement with Paulinus, they say that Diogenes’ teacher was not a child, as Laertius has it, but a peasant. Yet since Diogenes was a pupil of Antisthenes, the leader of the Cynics, and followed Cynic [Col. 0264D] philosophy, thereby deserving the designation “Cynic” above all others, I certainly wonder why Paulinus, after clearly distinguishing the Cynics from the Physicists, afterward attributes this deed of Diogenes to one of the Physicists. Nor may it be answered that the ancients cultivated a threefold philosophy and therefore that physics, which was one of its three parts, also belonged to the Cynics; for the Cynics rejected this branch of philosophy and devoted themselves to ethics alone. These are the words of Laertius in his *Life of Menedemus*:

> It is therefore their doctrine—the Cynics’—to abolish the logical and physical branches and to attend only to ethics.

What Paulinus adds, moreover, is entirely appropriate to the Cynics, not the Physicists. MURATOR.

**They drink no wine.** Laertius explicitly records this of the Cynics in his *Life of Menedemus the Cynic*: “Most use vegetables and nothing but cold water.” And in the *Life of Diogenes* he says:

> At home he also taught his attendants to be content with light and inexpensive food and to drink water.

[Col. 0265A] MURATOR.]

Man dares to fashion a god. Lest any crime be lacking,  
Its owner even sells this god, and a purchaser acquires him for himself.  
Am I to believe that philosophers possess any reason,  
When they lack reason and their wisdom is empty?  
There are Cynics, like dogs, as their name reveals.  
There are also those who follow Plato’s uncertain doctrine,  
Whom the substance of the soul, long investigated, confounds:  
Always discussing it, yet unable to reach a determination.  
Hence they love to copy out Plato’s book *On the Soul*,  
Which, beyond its title, contains nothing certain within.

There are also Physicists, named after Nature,  
[Col. 0264A] Who delight in an ancient, crude, and uncultivated life.  
For one of them once carried a staff and an earthenware vessel,  
Thinking that these alone were useful and alone ought to be possessed:  
The one to serve as an aid, the other as a means of drinking.  
But when he saw a farmer standing and scooping up with cupped hands  
Water that he meant to drink, he broke the earthenware vessel.  
Casting it far away, he said that superfluous things must be discarded:  
The peasant had taught him that he could despise even that.

These men drink no wine, nor are they nourished on a diet of bread.

[Col. 0265A] [Note: [Col. 0265A]

**Nor do they recline on beds.** The celebrated jar of Diogenes the Cynic is still known, in which that philosopher reclined by night and day. Other Cynics imitated him. Cresollius, *Mystagogus*, Book IV, chapter 20, section 3, says of them:

> For the sake of the emptiest glory, the Cynics slept upon grassy couches or the bare earth, so that by this harshness of life and counterfeit endurance they might turn everyone’s eyes upon themselves.

They were also accustomed to lie upon a cloak spread beneath them, as Martial indicates in Book IV, Epigram 52, when speaking of a Cynic:

> Whom the cloak of the bare pallet covers as a wife.

An *abolla* was a cloak. MURATOR.

**Nor the cold.** The Cynics lacked only those garments that serve to ward off the cold; for, being without a tunic, they used a cloak alone. St. Cyprian censures them for the shameless ostentation of a bare and half-naked breast. See Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XIV, chapter 20. MUR.

**And ungrateful to God.** Seneca rightly says in *On the Shortness of Life*, chapter 14, that the Cynics “go beyond human nature.” All the bodily hardships sought by these philosophers were marvels of pride rather than of true wisdom. Diogenes once declared that he was trampling upon Plato’s pride, to which Plato replied: “Yes, with another kind of pride.” On these matters consult Tatian the Assyrian in his most elegant *Oration against the Greeks*. MURATOR.

**What the Capitols are.** Here we encounter a mutilated passage, not easily disentangled and lacking punctuation—as does the entire manuscript codex. I would nevertheless add a second *est*, and punctuate it thus:

> What are the Capitols? First,  
> Here is a god, and the god’s wife; and this very woman  
> They also claim to be his sister, etc.

So Muratori. Vonck, however, reads and punctuates thus:

> What the Capitols are: the first  
> God among these....

**This very woman also to be his sister.** Virgil, whom Paulinus recalls here, introduces Juno speaking of herself in *Aeneid*, Book I:

> But I, who advance as queen of the gods, and as Jupiter’s  
> Sister and wife....

Gregory Nazianzen, Oration I *Against Julian*: “Hera, sister and wife of great Zeus.” Augustine reproaches the pagans for this shamelessness in *The City of God*, Book IV, chapter 10. Minucius likewise says: “You worship incestuous gods joined with mother, daughter, and sister.” MURATOR.

**Vergilius.** Thus the codex. Politian, *Miscellanies*, Epistle 2, chapter 77, and Book V, Epistle 3, demonstrates by explicit evidence that *Vergilius*, not *Virgilius*, should be written. Many inscriptions and the most ancient books have it so. Caelius Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings*, Book VII, chapter 4, and Manutius in his *Orthography* defend the contrary opinion by adducing other examples. Their arguments may be reviewed in Dausquius’ *Orthography*, according to whom *Virgilius* sounds more correct. MURATOR.

**Violated his own daughter.** Everyone will acknowledge that no one other than Proserpina is meant here, the daughter of Jupiter by Ceres, since she was later given in marriage to Pluto. But who affirmed that Jupiter violated her? Eusebius of Caesarea, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book II, has the following:

> Demeter gives birth; the daughter is reared; and Zeus, who fathered her, afterward has intercourse with this very Persephone, his own daughter, after her mother Deo, forgetting his earlier pollution; and he has intercourse with her after becoming a dragon.

That is: Ceres gave birth, and her daughter was brought up. After Ceres, Jupiter again coupled with Proserpina, the daughter whom he himself had fathered, forgetting his former crime; assuming the form of a dragon, he violated her.

Eusebius drew this account, in almost the same words, from Clement of Alexandria’s *Exhortation to the Pagans*. You may add Arnobius, who treats the matter at length in *Against the Pagans*, Book V. This will also illuminate a passage in Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book VI. Enumerating Jupiter’s adulteries, he says:

> How, as gold, he deceived Danaë; as fire, the daughter of Asopus;  
> As a shepherd, Mnemosyne; and as a many-shaped serpent, the daughter of Deo.

Here *Deois*, “the daughter of Deo,” is Proserpina, the daughter of Ceres by Jupiter. In Greek, Ceres is called *Dēō*, from *dēō*, “I find”; from this the patronymic designation *Deois* was applied to Proserpina. Orpheus—or whoever the author may be—says that Liber was born from this unspeakable union, and Diodorus Siculus, *Historical Library*, Book III, agrees. MUR.

**Now a serpent.** Jupiter assumed the form of a serpent when, as we have just seen, he coupled with Proserpina; that of a bull when he carried off Europa; that of a swan when he deceived Leda; and finally that of a tree—unless perhaps *aurum*, “gold,” should be read here in place of *arbos*, “tree”—when the wicked adulterer lay with another woman. Ovid expresses these and other transformations in *Metamorphoses*, Book VI:

> She made Leda recline beneath a swan’s wings;  
> She added how Jupiter, concealed beneath the form of a satyr,  
> Filled beautiful Nycteïs with twin offspring;  
> How he was Amphitryon when he captivated you, woman of Tiryns;  
> How, as gold, he deceived Danaë; as fire, the daughter of Asopus;  
> As a shepherd, Mnemosyne; and as a many-shaped serpent, the daughter of Deo.

A certain Greek also played wittily upon the theme in these two lines:

> Zeus became a swan, a bull, a satyr, and gold, for love  
> Of Leda, Europa, Antiope, and Danaë.

Nazianzen mocks this lewdness of Jupiter in his *Oration against Julian*: “Jupiter becomes anything whatsoever because of impurity and lust,” etc. Seek further examples in Arnobius, Lactantius, Clement, and other most ancient Fathers. MUR.

**More shamefully than these, he fashioned himself as an eagle.** By means of an eagle Jupiter abducted Ganymede. Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book III:

> Whom the swift bearer of Jupiter, swooping from Ida,  
> Snatched aloft with hooked talons.

Some, however, make Jupiter himself the perpetrator of this abduction after being transformed into an eagle. There is a Greek verse:

> Zeus came as an eagle to godlike Ganymede.

Ovid likewise, *Metamorphoses*, Book X:

> The king of the gods once burned with love for Phrygian Ganymede,  
> And something was found which Jupiter preferred to be  
> Rather than what he was. Yet he deigned to be changed into no bird  
> Except the one that carries his thunderbolts to earth.

This is the meaning of our Paulinus in this passage. MUR.]

They neither recline on beds nor ward off the cold with clothing;  
And, ungrateful to God, they reject what he has provided.

What shall I say of their various rites? Shall I speak of the temples  
Built for gods and goddesses—what the Capitols are? First,  
Here is a god and the god’s wife, whom they also claim

[Col. 0266A] That he even violated his own daughter and gave her to his brother;

Now he was a serpent, now a bull, now a swan, now a tree.  
By transforming himself, he himself reveals what sort of being he was:  
Another’s form pleased him more than his own.  
More shamefully than these, he fashioned himself as an eagle and entered  
The impious embraces of a boy. What does the multitude of his worshipers say?

[Col. 0267A] [Note: [Col. 0267A]

**Either let it deny that he is Jupiter.** St. Justin Martyr, in the *First Apology*—which until now has been regarded as the second—speaks thus (§21):

> Far be such a conception of the gods from a temperate mind: that the very ruler and father of all, Zeus according to them, was both a parricide and the son of such a father; and that, overcome by lust for wicked and shameful pleasures, he approached Ganymede and the many women whom he defiled by adultery.

Lactantius, after recalling the abduction of Ganymede, adds: “Whether the one who did these things was greatest, we shall consider; he certainly was not best.” See further Augustine, *The City of God*, chapter 9, and Arnobius, *Against the Pagans*, Book III.

**He certainly has a name.** Since Jupiter’s outrages are so numerous—since, indeed, he torments households through acts of sexual violence and the pagans frequently have Jupiter as their enemy without cause—the poet says that the name *Jovis*, “Jupiter,” does not suit this god. Or, as Lactantius thinks in *Divine Institutes*, Book I, chapter 2:

> Cicero explains that Jupiter and Juno were so named from *juvando*, “helping,” and that *Jupiter* means, as it were, *juvans pater*, “helping father.” This name is by no means appropriate to God, because helping belongs to a human being who confers some assistance upon one who is separate from him, and it denotes a limited benefit.

He then proceeds to show how little that designation befits the supreme God. MUR.

[Col. 0267C] **And they say, “Jupiter Most Excellent.”** Pliny in the *Panegyric* says: “The father of men and gods is worshiped under the name first of Most Excellent, and then of Greatest.” This was Jupiter’s principal title, and it occurs very frequently among ancient writers. Relevant to our subject are Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book I, chapter 10:

> What of Jupiter, the father of all these, who in the solemn prayer is called Most Excellent and Greatest?

And below:

> Whether the one who did these things was greatest, we shall consider; he certainly was not best.

Arnobius likewise, *Against the Pagans*, Book I: “Although Jupiter is held by you to be both Most Excellent and Greatest.” MUR.

**Father Janus.** As Brissonius teaches in *On Formulae*, Book I, the ancients began their prayers with Janus. Martial, Book X, Epigram 28, speaking of this divine power:

> Most beautiful begetter of the years and of the shining world,  
> Whom public vows and prayers invoke first.

Aurelius Victor, *Epitome of Roman History*:

> In all sacred rites they assigned the first place to Janus, to such an extent that even when sacrifice was offered to other gods, once incense had been placed upon the altars, Janus was named first, with the additional title “Father.”

Paulus, the epitomator of Festus, under the word *Chaos*:

> Hence Janus is so named, with the aspirate removed, because he was first of all and was the first to whom supplication was made.

Arnobius, speaking of him in Book III:

> And so among you he is believed to bear the name of God, since you place him first in all your prayers.

Hence Ovid, *Fasti*, Book I:

> Why, although I appease the divine powers of others,  
> Do I first bring incense and unmixed wine to you, Janus?

Consult Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 9; Horace, *Epistles*, Book I, Epistle 16; Servius on *Aeneid* VII; etc. MURATORI.—Vonck appears rightly to have conjectured: “but Father Janus.” Shortly afterward, in verse 70, he rewrites *hunc*, “him,” as *hinc*, “hence”: “Hence they depicted him with a double form”—quite correctly.

**Janiculum.** Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, speaking of Saturn, says: “When Saturn had been driven into exile, Janus received him as a guest; the Janiculum was named after Janus.” Solinus, *Polyhistor*, chapter 2; Arnobius, Book I; and Augustine, *The City of God*, Book VII, chapter 4, assert the same. Virgil too, Book VIII:

> Father Janus founded this citadel, and Saturn that one:  
> This was named Janiculum, and that Saturnia.

Minucius:

> Accordingly, because he had safely lain concealed, he preferred to call his hiding place Latium, and the city Saturnia after his own name; and Janus likewise left the Janiculum to posterity as his memorial.

I am surprised that Dionysius of Halicarnassus, otherwise so careful a writer on Roman antiquities, committed to writing that Romulus, the son of Aeneas and brother of Ascanius and Remus, founded “the city called Aeneia after his father, which was later named Janiculum.” MUR.

**Who, since he could look upon many future things.** This too is the opinion of others, who assert that Janus was represented with two faces because he looked back upon the past and foresaw the future. Ovid, however, in *Fasti*, Book I; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I; Augustine, *The City of God*, Book VII, chapter 8; and others devised different explanations, and their volumes are readily available to anyone who wishes to review them. Macrobius, however, in the cited book and especially chapter 7, supports Paulinus. MUR.

**Twin Janus.** Numa was the first of all to dedicate the Twin Janus. Velleius, Book II, calls it by this name: “Certainly the closing of the Twin Janus provided a sign of peace.” Pliny, Book XXXIV, chapter 7: “In addition, the Twin Janus was dedicated by King Numa.” The same author, Book XXXIII, chapter 2: “The bronze coin bore Twin Janus on one side and a ship’s beak on the other.” The following verses of Paulinus refer to this. See also Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book IV; Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 14; and Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 9. MUR.

**A coin was first struck in his honor.** Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, writes on this matter:

> Why did the ancient coin have on one side an image of two-faced Janus, and on the other the stern or prow of a ship engraved upon it? Was it—as most people say—in honor of Saturn, who crossed over to Italy in a ship?

Plutarch himself says that this explanation is not altogether to be approved; yet highly reputable authors accepted it. Ovid, conversing with Janus in *Fasti*, Book I, sings:

> But why is a naval shape stamped on one side of the bronze,  
> And a two-headed form on the other?

Janus replies:

> The reason for the ship remains: the sickle-bearing god came by ship  
> To the Tuscan river, after wandering through the world.  
> But a grateful posterity fashioned the stern upon the bronze,  
> Attesting the coming of the divine guest.

Yet Paulinus appears to disagree with others, since he attributes the arrival in Italy to Janus himself, whereas the others refer it to Saturn. Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, Book XV, asserts that such coins were used not only in Italy but also in Greece:

> Many cities in Greece and in Italy stamped upon their coinage a two-headed face, and on the other side either a raft, a crown, or a ship.

The accompanying Latin rendering reads: “Many cities in Greece, Italy, and Sicily strike coinage impressed with a two-headed face, and on the other side either a raft, a crown, or a ship.”

Similar coins can still be seen among lovers of antiquity, especially in the collection of the distinguished Count of the Holy Roman Empire Francesco Mezzabarba Birago. He possessed a very extensive numismatic treasury and in past years published a highly praised work on imperial coins, by which he wonderfully enlarged Occo’s work. But alas, our misfortune! This most learned man was taken from the living this year, A.D. 1697, and left learned men greatly mourning his loss. MUR.]

Either let it deny that he is Jupiter, or acknowledge this disgrace.  
He certainly has a name that cannot be justified by reason.  
They perform rites for Jupiter and say, “Jupiter Most Excellent”;  
They petition him, yet place Father Janus first in order.

This Janus was a king, a prudent man, who gave his own name  
[Col. 0268A] To the Janiculum. Since he could look upon many future things,  
They depicted him with a double form.  
And the ancient Latins called him the Twin Janus.  
Because he came by ship to the Ausonian shores,  
A coin was first struck in his honor in such a form  
That one side engraved his head and the other a ship.

[Col. 0269A] [Note: [Col. 0269B]

**Nomismata.** Both *numisma* and *nomisma*, “coin,” are used. The first occurs in Horace, *Epistles*, Book II, Epistle 1, and Martial, Book I, Epigram 40. The second occurs in ancient glossaries and in authors of the highest standing. It certainly conforms better to the Greek spelling, which is *nomisma*. MUR.

**Heads and ships.** Among Italian children there is a game called *giocare a testa, o arma*, “to play head or arms,” or *a testa, o croce*, “head or cross”; among the French, *jouer à croix ou pile*, “to play cross or reverse.” It is the very game played among the ancients. Accept this testimony. Aurelius Victor—or whoever the author may be—in the book *On the Origin of the Roman People* says:

> Janus is also said to have introduced this practice of marking bronze and stamping it into the form of coinage. On one side his head was impressed, and on the other the ship in which he had traveled.

Observe how this author agrees with Paulinus concerning Janus’s arrival. He adds:

> Hence gamblers, after placing and covering a coin, give their fellow players the choice of declaring what they think lies beneath, a head or a ship; the common people now corruptly call this *naviandi*.

Correct this word *naviandi* [Col. 0269C] and substitute *navia*. Macrobius agrees with this in *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 7:

> When Janus first marked bronze, he preserved his reverence for Saturn even in this: since Saturn had been brought by ship, an image of Janus’s own head was stamped on one side and a ship on the other. That bronze was marked in this way is understood even today from the game of chance, when boys toss coins into the air and cry “heads” or “ship”—a game that bears witness to antiquity.

Andreas Schott says that here *naviam*, not *navim*, should be read in full, on the authority of four Pithou manuscripts. I, however, would prefer to read *navia* or *navium*, as the meter of Paulinus’s verse establishes beyond dispute. Certainly Johannes Isaac Pontanus reads *navia* in his 1597 edition of Macrobius. MUR.

**Second to the king.** Before his son Jupiter, Saturn was king. Afterward, once expelled, he left the reins of either the heavenly or earthly kingdom to his son. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book I, chapter 11:

> I see that one god was king in the earliest times and another in later times. It can therefore happen that yet another will be king hereafter. But divine sovereignty is either always immutable or, if it is mutable—which cannot be—then surely it must always be mutable.

Hence the “Saturnian kingdoms,” and the golden age is attributed to Saturn’s reign. MUR.—The distinguished scholar wrongly understands “to the king” as referring to Saturn, since Janus is meant. Above, in verse 67, Paulinus had said that Janus enjoyed precedence over Jupiter in prayers. The following verse 78 confirms this. Also relevant is the passage from Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 134, in addition to the authors cited by Muratori on verse 67:

> Before you sacrifice the sow, offer the sacrificial cake to Janus as follows: “Father Janus, in presenting this sacrificial cake to you, I pray with good prayers.”

Then afterward:

> Present a cake to Jupiter and sacrifice with these words: “Jupiter, in presenting this cake to you, I pray with good prayers,” etc.

VONCK.

**And in sacrifices.** He repeats what he had indicated above: that the pagans’ prayers and vows began with the invocation of Janus and then turned to Jupiter—something certainly never befitting the greatest of the divine powers and ruler of them all. MUR.

**He also has a mother.** Rhea, or Cybele, the mother of Jupiter, became passionately enamored of the shepherd Attis. When he refused to comply with the shameless goddess, he was castrated. Ovid speaks of this in *Fasti*, Book IV:

> A Phrygian boy, remarkable for beauty in the lofty woods,  
> Joined the turret-bearing goddess in chaste love, etc.

This deed of the goddess is reproached against the pagans by Minucius in the *Octavius* [Col. 0270B]:

> “As for Cybele’s Dindyma—one is ashamed to say it—she castrated her ill-fatedly beloved adulterer because, being herself ugly and old, as befitted the mother of so many gods, she could not entice him to debauchery, and did so, of course, to make the eunuch a god.”

Augustine, *City of God*, book VI, chapter 7:

> “These are the rites of the Mother of the Gods, in which Attis, a handsome youth beloved by her and mutilated through womanly jealousy, is mourned through the wretched condition of mutilated men themselves, whom they call Galli.”

MUR.

**For the shepherd is earlier.** The theology of the Gentiles consists of such labyrinthine obscurities and contradictions that no one can easily extricate himself from it. Eusebius of Caesarea, *Preparation*, book II, chapter 4, where he discusses Phrygian theology, says that Cybele was seized by love for Attis before the marriages of the gods. But as many heads, so many opinions.

**Or Jovis himself.** *Jovis* is correctly used in the nominative case, as Priscian attests. Among the ancients, *Jovis* alone was said, from *juvando* (“helping”); with another word added, he was called Jupiter, as though *Jovis pater* (“Father Jovis”), or, as [Col. 0270C] Lactantius more plausibly thinks, *Juvans pater* (“the Helping Father”). *Jovis* occurs in the nominative in Hyginus’ *Book of Fables*, in Nonius Marcellus, and in other authors whom you may consult. A certain exceedingly severe critic, Natalis Alexander Galius, denies Augustine’s authorship of the four books *On the Creed for Catechumens*, because their style seems to him alien to Augustine’s—indeed, even to the doctrines of the grammarians. Among his examples he adduces this: “There it is imagined that this same Jovis has Juno as both sister and wife”; and he censures the use of the name *Jovis* in the nominative case. But he is mistaken, since this use of the name is found in authors of the highest authority and therefore would not be unworthy of Augustine. Content with these observations, we proceed to other matters. MURAT.—Perhaps better: *aut Jovis ipso*. Here *aut* is written for *haut* or *haud* (“not”). He says that the shepherd is earlier than Jove, not that Jupiter is earlier than the shepherd, as the poets babble to no purpose. Scholars know that the ancients very often wrote *aut* in place of *haut*. VONCK.

**But better.** Would not *magis* be preferable? But perhaps *melior*? MUR.

**Half-men.** These are the Galli, priests of the Mother of the Gods, [Col. 0270D] whose male organs were amputated in memory of the emasculated Attis. Lactantius, book I, chapter 17:

> “The Mother of the Gods both loved a handsome youth and, when she caught him with a rival mistress, cut away his male organs and made him a half-man. For that reason her rites are now celebrated by priests called Galli.”

After exposing Cybele’s impurity, Minucius adds:

> “Because of this fable the Galli, her half-men, worship her by punishing their own bodies. These are no longer sacred rites; they are tortures.”

See Juvenal, satire 2, and Paulinus himself, *Natal Poem* XI. MUR.

**Nor are there lacking men.** Augustine’s entire purpose in book VI of the *City of God*, and elsewhere, is to refute this pagan vanity and subterfuge. They commonly objected that old women’s fables abounded in inward mysteries and that philological truths lay concealed within them; but they were confounded by their own arguments. “Furthermore,” says the holy Doctor in chapter 8, “if those sacred rites, which are proven to be more shameful than the obscenities of the stage, are excused and purified on the ground that they possess their own interpretations, why are poetic tales not likewise excused and purified? etc.” Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 1 against Julian, after enumerating certain pagan superstitions, adds:

> ταῦτα ἐπεισκυκλείσθω τοῖς θαυμαστοῖς τῆς θεολογίας ἀκροαταῖς· εἶτ᾽ ἐπινοείσθω τούτοις ἀλληγορήματα καὶ τερατεύματα, καὶ τῶν προκειμένων ἐκπίπτων ὁ λόγος εἰς βάραθρα χωρείτω, καὶ κρήμνους θεωρίας οὐκ ἐχούσης τὸ στάσιμον.
>
> “Let these things be thrust upon the distinguished and admiring hearers of theology; then let allegories and monstrous interpretations be devised for them, and let discourse, straying from the matters proposed, advance into chasms and over the precipices of a speculation possessing no solid footing.”

MUR.]

In memory of him, whatever coins they now stamp  
They call “heads” and “ships,” from that ancient event.

What do they hope for from Jove, who ranks second after the king  
And is invoked in sacrifices by the mouths of those who pray?

He too has a mother, seized by love for a shepherd:  
For the shepherd is earlier than Jupiter—or Jovis himself.

[Col. 0270A] Yet better was the shepherd who wished to preserve  
His chaste modesty and spurned the goddess; she savagely  
Cut off his male parts, lest he should ever touch  
Another’s marriage-bed—he who refused to enter hers.

Was this, then, the just judgment of the gods:  
That he who did not become an adulterer should never become a husband?

Even now the half-men bewail their shameful mysteries:

[Col. 0271A] [Note: [Col. 0271B]

**And submits to male intercourse.** I suspect that a verse is missing here, for the sense remains uncertain. Certainly the word *abscindi* (“to be cut off”) is absolutely necessary here, so that the meaning would be: “and submits to his male parts being cut off.” MUR.—Nothing is missing here, despite Muratori’s suspicion. It is truly astonishing that so great a man hesitated over so small a matter. Antonius is in fact denouncing the perverse chastity of Cybele’s priests: they avoid intercourse with women but, far more wickedly, submit to intercourse with men. That the Galli, the sacrificial priests of the Great Mother, were infamous for such crimes is evident from Ambrose, *On Virgins*, book I, chapter 4:

> “What am I to say about the Phrygian rites, in which unchastity is a discipline—and would that it were only the unchastity of the weaker sex!”

VONCK.

**The stage provokes laughter.** Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, chapter 13, has these lucid words:

> “O grim consolation for criminal lust! O lamentable delusion of mankind! You have made heaven into a stage and, through sheer precipices, led wandering minds into cruel ruin.”

And below:

> “Transfer your temples instead to the theater, so that the secrets of those religions may be handed down upon the stage and, lest impiety omit anything, actors may readily become priests.”

I pass over Augustine, Letter 5 to Marcellinus and *City of God*, book VII, chapter 26, and Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 15.

**Saturn.** Hesiod relates the story at length in the *Theogony*, Natalis Comes in *Mythology*, book II, and the other authors who treated pagan theology in their writings.

[Col. 0271D] **And they call him Chronos.** It should have been written *Cronon*, for Saturn in Greek is Κρόνος (*Kronos*). But because he is said to signify time, he is also called χρόνος (*chronos*, “time”). Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 22; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Antiquities*, book I; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II; and others discuss this. Arnobius, however, utterly rejects this designation in book III *Against the Nations*:

> “For if time is signified by this name, as Greek interpreters suppose, so that what is *Chronos* may be taken for *Cronos*, then there is no divine Saturn. For who is so insane as to call time a god? etc.”

**What it creates, it consumes.** He has elegantly rendered into Latin a verse on Saturn from the hymn of Orpheus, or Onomacritus:

> Ὃς δαπανᾷς μὲν ἅπαντα, καὶ αὔξεις ἔμπαλιν αὐτός.
>
> “You who consume all things and, in turn, increase them all yourself.”

Or:

> “You who bring forth all things consume all things again.”

For *promittit* (“promises”) I would read *remittit* (“sends back” or “restores”).

**And Latium for that reason.** Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VIII, speaking of Saturn [Col. 0272B]:

> And he preferred it to be called Latium,  
> Since he had lain safely hidden upon these shores.

**The evil of the Latiarian rite.** This was an exceedingly cruel expiatory sacrifice of paganism. To Jupiter, whom they called Latiaris, a human victim was sacrificed. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 9, reveals the fact:

> “Behold, in that most religious city of the pious descendants of Aeneas, there is a certain Jupiter whom at his games they drench with human blood.”

Cerda illustrates the passage admirably. Minucius:

> “Even today Jupiter Latiaris is worshiped by the Romans with homicide and, as is worthy of Saturn’s son, is fattened on the blood of a wicked and guilty man.”

And elsewhere:

> “When Latiaris is drenched in blood.”

Porphyry, book II, *On Abstinence from Animate Food*:

> Ἀλλ᾽ ἔτι καὶ νῦν τίς ἀγνοεῖ κατὰ τὴν μεγάλην πόλιν τῇ τοῦ Λαπαρίου Διὸς ἑορτῇ σπαζόμενον ἄνθρωπον;
>
> “Indeed, even in our own age, who does not know that in the great City a man is sacrificed at the festival of Jupiter Latiaris?”

[Col. 0272C] Prudentius, book I *Against Symmachus*:

> Human blood is poured out in the rite of Latiaris.

Saint Athanasius, *Oration against the Gentiles*:

> Καὶ οἱ πάλαι δὲ Ῥωμαῖοι τὸν καλούμενον Λαπάριον Δία ἀνθρωποθυσίαις ἐθρήσκευον.
>
> “The ancient Romans too worshiped the so-called Jupiter Latiaris with human sacrifices.”

Tatian, *Against the Greeks*:

> Εὑρὼν δὲ μὲν Ῥωμαίοις τὸν Λαπάριον Δία λύθροις ἀνθρώπων, καὶ τοῖς ἀπὸ τῶν ἀνδροκτασιῶν αἵμασι τερπόμενον.
>
> “Among the Romans likewise, Jupiter Latiaris is appeased with human gore and delights in blood shed through murders.”

Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, book IV, commemorates these rites performed for Jupiter Latiaris, though he does not mention this victim. Hence learn that *Jovem Latiarem* is a better expression than *Latialem*, although some deny it. MUR.

**And the Invincible.** When I communicated these two verses to the most distinguished and learned knight Prospero Mandosio, so that he might unlock their secret learning for me, he replied that both he and the illustrious Ciampini greatly approved the opinion of the very learned Abbot Filippo Buonarroti, whose skill in the science of ancient coins we shall shortly admire. Buonarroti maintained that this passage concerns the sacrifices of Mithras, which acquired the greatest renown among the pagans. Having therefore profited from such eminent men, I shall touch upon the matter briefly and explain this notable piece of learning.

The Persians, above all peoples, practiced the worship of the sun. They called it Mithras and added to it the epithet *Invictus* (“Invincible”). In Gruter, p. 33 and following, and in Reinesius, many inscriptions occur dedicated “To the Invincible God,” “To the Invincible God Mithras,” “To the Sun Mithras,” “To the Invincible Sun,” and “To the Invincible Sun Mithras.” Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, chapter 5, asserts that Jupiter is divided into two powers, one of which—the male one—is called Mithras. Herodotus, book I, speaking of the Persians:

> Θύουσι δὲ οὐρανίῃ Ἀφροδίτῃ, ἣν καλέουσι Μίθραν.
>
> “They sacrifice to celestial Aphrodite, whom they call Mithras.”

Nicetas, on Nazianzen’s *Invective*:

> Τὸν Μίθραν οἱ μὲν τὸν ἥλιον, οἱ δὲ τὸν νεφρὸν τοῦ πυρός, ἄλλοι ἰδικήν τινα δύναμιν ὑπολαμβάνουσι.
>
> “Some hold Mithras to be the sun, others the kidney (*nephros*) of fire, and others a certain distinctive power.”

[Col. 0273A] Accordingly, since I see that Mithras signifies not only the sun but something else, I can easily explain the inscription in Gruter, p. 22, no. 12. It reads:

> D. I. M. ET. SOLI. SOCIO SAC.

That is:

> “Sacred to the Invincible God Mithras and to his companion, the Sun.”

Here Mithras must be understood as a divinity distinct from the sun, not as the sun himself regarded as a foreign deity, as Reinesius rather incorrectly supposes on inscription 48, class I.

[Col. 0273B] Ancient inscriptions also read:

> NANNAE. SEBECIO DEO. MITHRAE

Caesar Bulenger, *On Permitted and Ancient Magic*, book I, chapter 4, thinks that all these words refer to the sun Mithras. I, however, believe the stone was dedicated to three gods: that NANNA is the name of Diana Nannaea, mentioned in 1 Maccabees 6, 2 Maccabees 1, Jerome, and Josephus; that SEBECIUS is to be understood as Jupiter Sabazius, of whom Orpheus, or Onomacritus, says in a hymn:

> Κλῦθι πάτερ, Κρόνου υἱέ, Σαβάζιε κύδιμε δαῖμον.
>
> “Hear me, Father, son of Saturn, Sabazius, glorious divinity.”

For I do not know on what authority Heinsius, in *Sacred Aristarchus*, called Bacchus also Sabazius. But this is more than enough. MUR.

**Caves.** The word σπήλαιον (*spēlaion*) is Greek; in Latin it is called *spelunca*, “cave.” Yet Ausonian ears tolerated the Greek name. Virgil, *Eclogue* 10:

> I am resolved to dwell in the woods, amid the caves of beasts, etc.

[Col. 0273C] Claudian, *On the Gothic War*:

> The fearsome caves  
> Of beasts . . .

The sacrifices of Mithras were performed in the most secret caverns. There the mysteries received by his worshipers were preserved in religious silence. Indeed, those who wished to be initiated into those rites underwent testing through many torments. Hence the Suda, under the word *Mithras*, says:

> Οὐκ ἂν οὖν εἰς αὐτὸν δυνήσαιτό τις τελεσθῆναι, εἰ μὴ διά τινων βαθμῶν παρελθὼν τῶν κολάσεων δείξει ἑαυτὸν ὅσιον καὶ ἀπαθῆ.
>
> “No one can be initiated into it unless, after passing through certain degrees of punishment, he shows himself holy and immune to passions.”

The same is confirmed by Nazianzen, Oration 3; Lampridius in his *Commodus*; and Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 15. Tertullian’s words are:

> “Blush, you Roman fellow-soldiers of his, who are no longer to be judged by him but by some soldier of Mithras, who, when he is initiated in the cave, etc.”

Saint Justin Martyr, in the *Dialogue with Trypho*, twice says that the rites of Mithras are performed [Col. 0273D]:

> ἐν τόπῳ ἐπικαλουμένῳ παρ᾽ αὐτοῖς σπηλαίῳ
>
> “in a place that among them is called a *spēlaion*, that is, a cavern.”

See Jerome, *Letter to Laeta*; Reinesius, *Inscriptions*, class I, no. 48; Bulenger, *On Permitted and Ancient Magic*, book I, chapter 4; Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, Syntagma I, chapter 6; Salmasius on the *Augustan History*, fols. 349, 382, etc.]

Nor are there lacking men whom this contagion transforms,  
Who inwardly worship some supposedly greater mystery.

They call it holy; if a chaste man wishes to approach it,  
He will be profane. Thus the stricter priest himself  
Avoids intercourse with women, but submits to intercourse with men.

O blinded minds of men! Their sacred rites always  
Provoke laughter on the stage, yet they do not abandon this error.

They declare that Saturn is Jove’s father and that he devoured  
His own earlier-born children, and soon from his belly vomited  
The abominable feast; but afterward, through his wife’s cunning,  
He swallowed a stone substituted for Jove:

Had she not done this, Jupiter would have been consumed.

[Col. 0272A] They call him Chronos—and falsely Chronos—because time  
Consumes what it creates and restores what it has consumed.

Why, then, do they disguise the name obliquely as “time”?  
They say too that, because he often feared for himself on account of his offspring,

He was cast down from heaven by Jove and lay hidden throughout  
The fields of Italy, which was therefore then named Latium.

A great god each of them! One lies hidden on earth;  
The other could not discover where on earth he was concealed.

Hence the ancient Romans established the evil Latiarian rite,  
So that a slaughtered man might satiate an empty name.

What darkness possesses their minds? What improvident hearts are these?  
What is worshiped is nothing, yet bloody rites are performed.

[Col. 0273A] [Note: [Col. 0273D]

**And what they read.** It seems preferable to write *quemque tegunt tenebris* (“and whom they cover in darkness”). Nevertheless, the existing sense is satisfactory. MUR.

**Conceals.** *Celo* in the sense of *lateo* (“I lie hidden”) is an unusual verb. I find it used only with the meaning “to cover” or “conceal.” Yet the very learned Michele Maddi, worthy offspring of the distinguished Carlo M. Maddi, informed me that in Plautus’ *Bacchides*, act 3, scene 2, one reads:

> However you may behave, I warn you: you will not escape notice.

The scholiast Lambinus explains it thus: “You will not deceive; you will not lie hidden.” Certainly, if you insist that the pronoun *te* must be understood there, I in turn shall understand the pronoun *se* in Paulinus’ verse. [Col. 0274A] If someone wished to emend it, I would read:

> *Celet in infernis ni se horum causa malorum.*
>
> “Unless the cause of these evils hides itself in the infernal regions.”

Indeed, the manuscript codex has *malorum*, not *malarum*. MUR.—Muratori is certainly ingenious here, but we can readily dispense with every emendation if we punctuate the passage correctly:

[Col. 0274B]

> Who would secretly worship the light, and conceal  
> The heavenly star?—unless it is the cause of evil things, dwelling in hell.

Who, he asks, is so stupid as to worship the light secretly and hide the heavenly star—the sun, that is—in gloomy caves, when only the author of evil dwells in the infernal regions? After *malarum* something must be understood, as everyone can see. The passage could otherwise be explained, while retaining the common punctuation, in another sufficiently appropriate sense, if someone should tell Antonius that his meter is defective; since so many earlier poets often neglected its laws, there is no reason why we should regard the same practice as foreign to our poet. Whoever prefers may therefore interpret it thus: “And would he conceal the heavenly star in hidden or infernal places, except for the sake of evil things?” In this way *causa* is taken in the ablative, not the nominative. VONCK.

**The Isiac.** In the rites of Isis, sistra were shaken and the dog’s head of Anubis was displayed. Lucan, book VIII, includes both:

> The demigod dogs and the sistra commanding grief.

Ausonius, writing to our Paulinus, Letter 25:

> Mareotic sistra stir Isiac tumults.

Anubis was furthermore also called Cynocephalus, a name expressing his form. Athanasius, *Oration against the Greeks*:

> ὁ παρ᾽ Αἰγυπτίοις Κυνοκέφαλος Ἀνούβις
>
> “the dog-headed Anubis among the Egyptians.”

Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book IX:

> With her were barking Anubis,  
> The sistra, and Osiris, never sought enough.

On the sistra consult Lorenzo Pignoria, *The Isiac Table*, and the excellent dissertation of the most learned and distinguished Benedetto Bacchini. MUR.

**Something or other.** Paulinus reproduced a passage of Minucius:

> “Soon, when the little child is found, Isis rejoices, the priests exult, and Cynocephalus, the finder, glories; nor do they ever cease, year after year, either to lose what they find or to find what they lose.”

Julius Firmicus, [Col. 0274D] chapter 2:

> “You find nothing here except what you must either seek again or mourn again.”

Paulinus himself, *Natal Poem* XI:

> For what, I ask, is more blind than those  
> Who seek one who was not lost, and discover one  
> Who exists nowhere? . . .

**What has Serapis deserved?** I readily confess that I am stuck here. Paulinus mentions some festival day on which Serapis was compelled to assume many forms, but I find no trace of it anywhere. Certainly Macrobius and Plutarch, in the book *On Isis and Osiris*, present Serapis in no other form than the human:

> πανταχοῦ ἀνθρωπόμορφον Ὀσίριδος ἄγαλμα
>
> “Everywhere the image of Osiris is shown in human form.”

A solution must therefore be awaited from more learned men. MUR.—It is well known from the histories what the Egyptians handed down concerning Osiris, who is identical with Serapis: namely, that he was killed by Typhon and torn into fourteen parts. The Egyptians represented this in their rites. Plutarch refers to it in *On Isis and Osiris* when he writes [Col. 0275A] that Isis established rites in memory of her husband Osiris, mingling with the most sacred sacrifices images, signs, and representations of the events that had befallen them. VONCK.]

Why, too, do they hide the Invincible One beneath dark caverns,  
And dare call “the sun” the one whom they cover in darkness?

Who would secretly worship the light and conceal  
The heavenly star in the infernal regions, unless it were the cause of evil?

Why do they not similarly hide the Isiac sistrum  
And the dog’s head, but display them in public places?

[Col. 0274A] Surely they seek something or other, and rejoice when it is found;  
Then lose it again, so that they may seek it once more.

What wise man could endure this—that the former, as it were, shut up the sun,  
While the latter openly display the monstrosities of their own gods?

What has Serapis deserved, that he is thus torn apart by them

[Col. 0275A] [Note: [Col. 0275A]

**Here, finally, he is always made a beast, etc.** I should indeed think that Antonius, knowing that the Egyptians worshiped many [Col. 0275B] images in the forms of various animals, believed that all of them should be referred to the one Serapis. Paulinus agrees in *Natal Poem* XI, verse 98. See Martianus Capella, *The Marriage of Philology*, book II, p. 43. VONCK.

**Now a man, now bread.** This verse seems corrupt. It should read:

> *Nunc homo, nunc sanus, nunc corpore languidus aegro.*
>
> “Now a man, now healthy, now languishing in a sick body.”

For the Poet says that Serapis is represented in human form, now healthy and now languishing with sickness. See Marsham, *Chronicle*, age XI, p. 319. VONCK.—Excellent. This restoration also greatly pleases the anonymous Leipzig scholar. GALL.

**Why should I speak also of Vesta?** Some believed Vesta to be the earth itself; others, the guardian of every home; still others thought that through her the pure fire of the ether was signified. Hence Orpheus said that she inhabited not the regions of Sicily but the ether:

[Col. 0275C]

> Ἑστία εὐδυνάτοιο Κρόνου θύγατερ βασίλεια,  
> Ἣ μέσον οἶκον ἔχεις πυρὸς ἀενάοιο μεγίστου.
>
> “Vesta, queenly daughter of mighty Saturn,  
> You who dwell in the central region of the vast, ever-flowing ethereal fire.”

Others gave other explanations; hence it is no wonder that our poet affirms that even her priest does not know what she is.

**Why is fire female?** You have seen above from Orpheus that Vesta is taken to mean fire. I now add Ovid, *Fasti*, book VI:

> Understand Vesta as nothing other than living flame.

Yet he had earlier said:

> Vesta is also the earth . . .

Augustine, *City of God*, book IV, chapter 10, speaks thus:

> “They hold that the same earth is Ceres and also Vesta, although they more frequently declare Vesta to be nothing but fire.”

He repeats the same in book VII, chapter 16. See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* and book II *On the Laws*, Diodorus, and others. Paulinus therefore wonders and laughs at why fire should be called a woman. MUR.

[Col. 0275D] **Hyginus.** Julius Hyginus was Augustus’ freedman and a friend of Ovid. He wrote a book of fables that still survives. Yet I could not find there the passage cited by Paulinus. He also wrote books of *Genealogies*; a book *On the Penates*, praised by Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book III, chapter 14; a book *On the Attributes of the Gods*, likewise attested by Macrobius, book III, chapter 8; and *Miscellaneous Questions*, mentioned by Fabius, Gellius, and Diomedes. The voracity of time has deprived us of all these. Our Paulinus doubtless drew the learning here proposed from those books. MUR.

**As Hyginus records.** Read *commentat* (“records”) rather than *commendat* (“commends”); the usage, though rarer, is nevertheless established. VONCK.

**They hang them for the Sun.** The Vulcanalia were festivals in honor of Vulcan. They are mentioned in the most ancient calendars in Gruter, pp. 133, 134, and 135, and in another similar calendar in Dempster, *Roman Antiquities*, in the *Supplement* to book IV, chapter 4. They were celebrated on the tenth day before the Kalends of September. Columella agrees, *On Agriculture*, [Col. 0276A] book II, chapter 3: “Moreover,” he says, “in August, around the Vulcanalia, comes the third sowing.” Varro also mentions them in *On the Latin Language*.

Ancient idolaters customarily hung garments as offerings to false gods. Aristophanes, *Birds*:

[Col. 0276B]

> . . . . . . Τίς δὲ θεὸς  
> Πολιοῦχος ἔσται, τῷ ξανοῦμεν τὸν πέπλον;
>
> “But what god will be guardian of the city, for whom shall we weave the robe?”

That is: “For which god shall we hang up garments?” Apuleius, *The Golden Ass*, book VI:

> “You see splendid gifts and strips of cloth embroidered with gold, fastened to tree branches and doorposts.”

Alexander ab Alexandro, book III, chapter 18:

> “In other mysteries the custom is handed down that each person should dedicate to the temples and divinities the garment in which he was initiated.”

Pinto Ramírez collects these and other testimonies in *Sacred Gleanings*, treatise I, chapters 2 and 22, §15. But I had been unable to find in any author garments dedicated specifically to the Sun, when the very learned Abbot Bianchini, to whose care the library of Cardinal Ottoboni was entrusted, informed me through the distinguished Ciampini that a passage concerning this exists in Herodotus. It is in book II, where he treats King Necho:

> Ἐν τῇ δὲ ἐσθῆτι ἔτυχε ταῦτα κατεργασάμενος ἀνέθηκε τῷ Ἀπόλλωνι πέμψας ἐς Βραγχίδας τὰς Μιλησίων.
>
> “Since he had been successful in these deeds while wearing that garment, he dedicated it to Apollo, sending it to the Branchidae of the Milesians.”

MUR.

**Adonis is carried.** There were among the Gentiles the Adonia, that is, festivals sacred to Adonis, mentioned by Aristophanes in the *Peace* and by Ovid in *Metamorphoses*, book X, in this verse spoken by Venus:

> It shall annually enact an imitation of my grief.

According to Natalis Comes, *Mythology*, book V, chapter 16, the ceremonies of Adonis were celebrated with particular fervor at Alexandria, where his image was carried with great pomp. But it is evident that another occasion is meant here, on which the image of Adonis was carried—namely, during the Vulcanalia themselves; for the poet says: “Then Adonis too is carried.” The story of Venus and this youth is famous. MUR.

**Then they throw dung.** The gods of the Gentiles were customarily dishonored with dung. The very learned Abbot Bianchini, prefect of the Ottoboni Library, directed my attention through the distinguished Giovanni Ciampini to a verse of Orpheus, or Onomacritus, concerning a similar rite. It occurs in Nazianzen, [Col. 0276D] *Invective* 1 against Julian:

> Ζεῦ κύδιστε, μέγιστε θεῶν, εἰλυμμένε κόπρῳ.
>
> “O Jupiter most glorious, greatest of the gods, smeared with dung.”

Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, Syntagma II, chapter 5, recites the same verse, but considers the phrase εἰλυμμένος κόπρῳ (“smeared with dung”) no more relevant to Jupiter Stercoreus than Virgil’s words about Jupiter:

> And mind, infused throughout its limbs,  
> Animates the whole mass and mingles with its mighty body.

He would have Jupiter described in both places as enveloped in the mysteries of nature. But the Latin verses have nothing to do with the Greek, and the κόπρος (“dung”) with which Jupiter is said to be smeared is incompatible with such an explanation. There were, moreover, Dung Gods; and, as Selden notes in the same place, *Beelzebul* means “Lord of Dung.” Rabbi Abraham Ben Kattun explains Exodus 23:33 thus: “You shall not permit those who worship foreign or dung-gods to dwell among you.”

[Col. 0277B] But why did Adonis have to endure dung? I think I have found the reason. Some held that Adonis was the seed of wheat; among them the scholiast on Theocritus says:

> Ἄδωνις, ἤγουν ὁ σῖτος, ὁ σπειρόμενος ἓξ μῆνας ἐν τῇ γῇ ποιεῖ ὑπὸ τῆς σπορᾶς, etc.
>
> “Adonis—that is, the grain—when sown, spends six months beneath the earth after sowing, etc.”

Dung is therefore as appropriately applied to Adonis as to wheat. Moreover, because enmity existed between Vulcan and the lovers of Venus, Adonis was treated badly while Vulcan’s rites were being celebrated. [Col. 0277C] These, then, I judge to be the more immediate reasons why he was compelled to endure such shameful treatment during the Vulcanalia. MUR.]

Through various shameful places? Here, finally, he is always  
Made a beast, made a dog, made the foul carcass of an ass,

Now a man, now bread, now languishing in a sick body.  
While they do such things, they confess that he feels nothing.

Why should I speak also of Vesta, whom her own priest denies  
That he knows what she is? Yet in the innermost sanctuary

An ever-unextinguished fire is imagined to be preserved within.  
Why is she a goddess, not a god? Why is fire said to be female?

[Col. 0276A] This woman, indeed, as Hyginus records,  
Was once the first to weave a garment from newly spun thread,

Named from her own name; she herself gave it  
To Vulcan, who had then shown her how to guard

The covered hearths. He, again delighted by the gift,  
Offered it to the Sun, through whom he had earlier discovered

Mars’s adultery. Now the entire credulous crowd  
Hangs garments for the Sun during the Vulcanalia;

And, to stigmatize Venus, Adonis too is then carried.

[Col. 0277A] [Note: [Col. 0277C]

**They pelt him with dung.** Read: *ipsum, pro! stercore jactant*—“they pelt him—shame!—with dung.” Here *pro* indicates indignation at the matter and does not function as a preposition, but as an interjection. VONCK.

**Five-year banquets.** Since the true explanation of these verses escaped me, Giovanni Ciampini, a distinguished man and a supreme ornament of the City, advised me to seek the solution in Lipsius, chapter 10, *On Vesta and the Vestals*. I had indeed consulted this author before, but through inattention this piece of learning escaped me. He says:

> “What is read in certain *Acts of Sylvester* lies in obscurity or a cloud: that he closed the mouth of a dragon and consigned it to perpetual imprisonment, and that provisions had customarily been supplied to it on each Kalends by the Virgins of Vesta. For which of the ancients records any such thing? I see that it is therefore despised or rejected as false by great men. While I was uncertain, I wondered whether Tertullian had not looked to this in *To His Wife*, chapter 6, in these words: ‘At Rome, those women who tend the image of that inextinguishable fire, caring for the omens of their punishment together with the Dragon himself, are deemed virgins.’”

Thus Lipsius. But observe, if you please, how much weight Paulinus adds to all this. I confess, however, that I have not yet understood why he calls them “five-year banquets.” Our codex indeed has *quenquennis*, but neither meter nor sense permits that reading; it was written in place of *quinquenneis*. MUR.

**Those who worship what must be abandoned.** A similar passage occurs in Minucius: “Is it not ridiculous either to mourn what you worship or to worship what you mourn?” MUR.

**I previously considered all these things.** No one will deny that one or more verses are missing here, for the preceding words remain uncertain and require a similar thought to complete them: “I previously pondered all these things with a doubtful mind and did not know how to approve them, when I obtained the clear light, etc.” MUR.—The distinguished Muratori thought that something was missing here. The learned Vonck read *clarus sum lumen adeptus* (“I became enlightened after attaining the light”) or *clarum cum lumen adeptum* (“when the clear light had been attained”). Yet I prefer the conjecture of the anonymous Leipzig scholar:

> “What,” he says, “if you read *clarum QUAM lumen adeptus*—‘before I attained the clear light’? Then everything would flow well. Antonius says: ‘I considered all these things before I had attained the clear light and before the holy Church received me.’”

GALL.

**Church.** Paulinus elsewhere pronounces this word in the same way for metrical reasons. In the *Epithalamium*:

> The great sacrament whereby the Church is wedded to Christ.

[Col. 0278C]

> May that love bind you by which the Church binds Christ.

Likewise in *Natal Poem* IV and elsewhere. The Anonymous author of book I *Against Marcion*, among the poems attributed to Tertullian, also used it so:

> Thus too the Church proceeds according to the apostolic word.

MUR.

**Just now.** He indicates the time when he was committing these things to writing, namely the year 395; for Paulinus had recently moved to Nola to devote himself there to a religious and pious manner of life. See what I discussed in the preface to this poem. MUR.

**Here by a better way, etc.** Muratori punctuated thus:

> Here, happy by a better way, may he open  
> The threshold of paradise. Our faith, dedicated to one certain being . . .

But with learned men the passage should be punctuated as below. There should not be a stop after the name *Felix*, nor should that word be referred to what precedes, as though it were the name of a martyr celebrated by Paulinus. VONCK.

[Col. 0278D] **And apportioned heaven to its places.** Muratori considers it a matter worthy of investigation that the author distinguishes sea, lands, air, and heaven as elements, and gives no thought whatever to fire. But I do not think Antonius is acting as a philosopher here; perhaps he imitated the words of the sacred writer in Genesis 1, where no mention of fire occurs. Prudentius too does not recognize fire as an independently existing element but as something generated from another, *Against Symmachus*, book I, verse 395:

> Whatever the earth, the sea, or wondrous heaven produces,  
> They made into gods—hills, straits, rivers, flames.

**These four beginnings it drew from various things.** Read *auxit* (“increased” or “enriched”), for *hausit* (“drew”) is wholly meaningless. VONCK.

**Thus the elements.** There will scarcely be anyone to whom Paulinus’ view does not appear novel. He plainly distinguishes sea, lands, air, and heaven under the name of elements, and gives no thought whatever to fire. It is a fine question and worthy of investigation.]

Then they throw dung; they pelt him—shame!—with dung.  
If you inquire into everything, it appears still more laughable.

Another practice is added here: you hear that those whom they call  
The Virgins of Vesta carry five-year banquets to a Dragon,

Which either does not exist or, if it does, is the devil himself,  
The ancient adversary and tempter of the human race.

And they worship the one who now, at the name of Christ,  
Both trembles and hangs helpless, confessing all his deeds.

What madness possesses men, that they proclaim falsehoods as truths—  
Worshiping what should be abandoned and abandoning what should be worshiped?

It will now be enough for us to recount these empty terrors.  
I considered all these things before I attained the clear light;

And not long afterward the holy Church received me—uncertain  
And driven through so many storms—into the harbor of salvation,

And after my wandering upon the waves placed me in a tranquil abode,  
So that now, once the cloud of evils has been wiped away,

I may hope at the appointed time for serene light.

[Col. 0277B] Now that former salvation, which forgetful Adam lost—  
Then through the persuasion of evil, but now with Christ as helmsman—

Rescued from the rocks, will rise again, to endure forever.

[Col. 0278A] For our Ruler governs all things on every side in such a way  
That he who has just now taken error of mind away from us

May here, by a better path, open the gates of paradise.  
Happy is our Faith, dedicated to the one sure God.

For God is one; the Son is one substance;  
One is in both, one vigor, one power.

For Christ, the Word of God, flashed forth from the Father’s breast,  
And he who was not born, as it were, but proceeded from his mouth,

Always existed; he removed that empty chaos  
And took away the shapeless gulf of the interwoven night,

And apportioned sea, lands, air, and heaven to their places.  
When darkness had been driven away, he gave them the twin light.

But when all things marveled to see a new sun arise,  
He enriched these four first principles with various things.

Human beings are upon the lands; stars have been added to heaven;  
The bird hangs in the air, the fish swims in the liquid sea.

Thus he adorned each element with its own forms,

[Col. 0278B] Bound together these things though diverse, joined them though distinct,  
And distinguished them though joined; divided as they now are, they cohere.

For the ocean encloses the earth, the sea is enclosed, and it itself—

[Col. 0279A] [Note: [Col. 0279B]

**It is enclosed in the middle by—** Far be it from our Paulinus to have admitted that imaginary sphere of fire which Aristotle and his followers cleverly devised and still approve. Hence he affirms that the air is enclosed not by those fictitious flames but by the ether or heaven. MUR.

**And after the seven thrones.** It must certainly be admitted that not merely seven but nine heavens were situated beneath the empyrean. Seven of them contain the wandering stars, as the little verse has it:

> Cynthia, Mercury, Venus, and the Sun, Mars, Jove, Saturn.

The eighth is occupied by the fixed stars; the ninth is the *primum mobile*, which is followed by the empyrean. Nevertheless, Paulinus explicitly believes that seven heavens exist before the empyrean. You ask on what grounds? I answer: by poetic license. For among poets the dwelling of the supreme God is placed in the eighth heaven, that is, in the starry heaven. Virgil, *Aeneid*, book X:

[Col. 0279C]

> The father of the gods and king of men calls  
> The council to the starry dwelling . . .

Sidonius Apollinaris, in the *Panegyric to Avitus*, speaking of the council of the gods:

> The very pavement consists of stars; now the Father,  
> Serene, seats himself upon his golden throne . . .

Euripides, in the *Ion*, calls it:

> Διὸς πολύαστρον ἕδος
>
> “the many-starred dwelling of Zeus.”

Add Chrysostom, Oration 2 *On the Nature of God*, and others. This was also the opinion of ancient Christians. Philastrius, bishop of Brescia, catalogs an imaginary heresy concerning the diversity of the heavens in chapter 46 and says:

> “Therefore, whether one wishes to accept seven heavens according to David and this firmament as the seventh, he does not err. For Solomon speaks of three heavens, thus: ‘heaven and the heaven of heaven.’ Paul the Apostle likewise confesses that he was caught up to the third heaven. Therefore, whether one accepts seven with David, or three, or two, he does not err.”

MUR.

[Col. 0279D] **Whence from afar.** He imitates Virgil, who sings thus in *Aeneid*, book X:

> The father of the gods and king of men calls  
> The council to the starry dwelling, whence from on high  
> He surveys every land and the camp of the descendants of Dardanus . . .

Let us also hear here the foremost of the Italian poets, book I of *Jerusalem Delivered*:

> When from his lofty throne the eternal Father,  
> Which stands in heaven’s most limpid region,  
> Turned his eyes downward and, in a single point  
> And single glance, beheld all that the world contains.

**Embraces within the City.** The poets made the boundaries of the Roman Empire the same as those of the world. Rutilius, in his *Journey*, elegantly writes:

> And while you offer the conquered a share in your own law,  
> You have made a city of what formerly was the world.

The scholiast on Dionysius, *Description of the World*:

> ὅπερ δὲ πόλις τοῖς αὐτῆς ὁρίοις καὶ χώραις ἐστί, τοῦτο ἥδε ἡ πόλις τῆς [Col. 0280B] ἁπάσης οἰκουμένης, ὥσπερ αὐτῆς χώρας ἄστυ κοινὸν ἀποδεδειγμένη.
>
> “What any city is to its own boundaries and territories, this city, Rome, is to the provinces of the whole world, having been appointed, as it were, the common capital of the entire inhabited earth.”

Hence Rome is called by Claudian the city “which pours forth dominion over all.” Thus Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 5, called Rome the single fatherland of all nations throughout the whole world. For more, consult Bulenger, *On the Roman Empire*, book II, chapter 5. MUR.

*Hinc ita.* I would prefer: *Hunc ita.* MUR.
