**Cosmon from ornament.** Greek *κόσμος* means “ornament.” Paulinus believes that the name of the world, which the Greeks call *κόσμος* (*kosmos*), is derived from this meaning, because the world is in truth a beautiful arrangement of ornaments. Others derive the etymology of this name *ἀπὸ κόσμου*, from *kosmos* meaning “order” or “measure,” since the world is truly the ordered condition of things linked together. Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book I, agrees with our poet: “Accordingly, to say something about this world, though it be unworthy of it [Col. 0280C]: among the Greeks its very name denotes ornament and adornment, not filth.” MUR.

**Mundum from light.** Honorius of Autun, *On the Image of the World*, chapter 1; Isidore, *Origins*, book III, chapter 28, and book XIII, chapter 1, suppose that *mundus* was so called as though from *movendus* (“that which must be moved”), because it is in perpetual motion. But Varro, Cicero, Pliny, the jurist Paulus, and others more correctly maintain that it was named from *mundities* (“cleanness, elegance”). Paulinus adopts this etymology when he says that *mundus* is named from light.

**Here is God.** That is, the divine Word and Son of God, through whom, as he sang above, all things were made, and without him nothing was made that was made. The manuscript reads: “Here God from the heart.” I supplied the verb *is*. Yet the verse still limps; I could add a second *is*: “Here is the Spirit of the mouth.” MUR.—Muratori supplies, because of the caesura: “Here God IS from the heart of God.” And this is sufficiently correct. Moreover, Virgil too disregarded elision before *hic* in *Aeneid* I.20:

> Cherishing it above Samos, which she had set aside. Here were her arms.

[Col. 0280D] Similarly, above, verse 54, the manuscript had:

> Here God, and the wife of God, and his own sister.

There likewise the distinguished editor adds *is* twice: “Here God is, and the wife of God is.” But since so many places occur in this poem where, if you consult the manuscript—and what authority could be safer?—a caesura is lacking or elision is not admitted, I can scarcely believe that all those passages were corrupted by accident. Perhaps Antonius sinned against meter in most of them, something hardly unusual among poets of the period to which our author shows himself to belong. For we have absolutely no reason to disregard the manuscript’s authority in all these cases. VONCK.

**The workshop of things.** Sipontinus taught that *fabrica* is properly used for a workshop. Perhaps the word should be understood in that sense here. In my opinion, however, either an error has crept into the manuscript or a line is missing. MUR.

**Nor let the pagan.** For more about this name, consult Baronius, the great father of the *Annals*, in the *Martyrology* for January 31; Gothofredus on book VI of the *Theodosian Code*, title 10, *On Pagans*, etc.; and other writers. In the fourth century after Christ this name began to be applied to the Gentiles, since, after being driven from the cities, they still practiced their profane religion in the villages (*pagi*) and countryside. MUR.]

Beneath the ethereal axis, midway, air is enclosed.

This too is a heaven, which we behold on high;

it lies beneath six others rising at equal intervals.

Beyond the seven thrones, beyond so many heavenly realms,

is all the remaining region, which towers above them all,

which rises beyond them, which stretches everywhere on high,

which lies open without end and which no mind can comprehend:

the dwelling of inaccessible light and the holy seat

of mighty God, whence from afar he sees subjected beneath him

the things he made. Thus all things stand, while spirit encompasses all.

These same things, whose use is granted to us,

which the lower pole embraces within the great City,

[Col. 0280A] though all stand far apart, are held together in a single peace.

Finally, they possess one name: all things are the World.

The Greeks of old also called it *Cosmos*;

hence, distinguishing what was thus composed, each language

named *Cosmos* from ornament, and *Mundus* from light.

For all the region in which the sun now shines lay foul in shadow,

and the example remains whenever night disfigures everything

and teaches, by contrast with darkness, what grace has been given in light.

He who made so many good things, who thus worked everywhere—

this is God from the heart of God, this the Spirit of his mouth,

the Word of the holy Father, the workshop of so great a universe.

Nor let the pagan boast, if he avoids idols,

[Col. 0281A] [Note: [Col. 0281C]

**If he avoids.** The manuscript read: “If anyone avoids idols.” I emended it. MUR.

**Divine power.** I chose to write *numine* (“divine power”) in place of *nomine* (“name”), as the manuscript has it. MUR.

**The Savior turned.** The word *versus* (“turned”) scarcely pleases me. Perhaps *verus* (“true”) should be written. MUR.

**Living power.** I leave the correction of this error to others. MUR.—The phrase *living power* is altogether lifeless here. Muratori leaves the correction of the error to others; Fabricius conjectured *conquered*. Unless I am mistaken, the genuine reading is *power once seen*. When, the poet says, the supreme Deity reveals the signs of his majesty, every kind of creature fears destruction; but as soon as his power is seen, or appears, it will cease, and at the same time he clears the sky, formerly encircled by black clouds, and consoles the sorrowful minds of human beings with renewed brightness. What precedes and follows sufficiently supports this interpretation, so that we need add no more. VONCK.—The Anonymous Leipzig critic adds his vote to Vonck’s emendation.]

and suppose it sufficient that he believes in one divine power.

How will that man worship God if he does not worship his Word?

If he does not venerate his Power with equal honor?

And whoever confesses that God is invisible

and incomprehensible, if he reflects upon Christ as well,

will find the same to be true, since no one can comprehend

the Word and no one can see him; only his works are seen.

For the Son was born in the Father, and in the Son the Father made all things;

and whatever he bestowed by his power he preserves by his loving-kindness.

Thus he was, and may the Savior, turned toward us, stand forever,

who removed errors, who made true things visible,

and, after appeasing the Father, restored the perishing world to him.

Nor is it strange that he who created all things governs all things,

who brought the whole from nothing, preferred light

to darkness, and commanded day to follow night;

and, because he was in the flesh, forgives the sins of the flesh.

[Col. 0281B] For he sees that the frail readily fall into transgressions,

and though he rebukes them, he will grant one pardon to all.

(I shall say something extraordinary, nor shall I regret having said it:)

he will be more merciful than just. For if, in the end, he chooses

to be just, no guilty person will escape punishment:

for the just one condemns evils, but the merciful one forgives them all.

This ensures that the gifts of the life to come are secure,

and that indulgence restores once more what guilt removed.

If these gifts were not granted to the people when they ask,

[Col. 0282A] then scarcely anyone would be free of every transgression.

Who could deserve to take possession of the promised light?

Then it will be a joy for the blessed to reach the kingdoms of heaven;

then death itself will be able to die, since throughout all time

life will be everlasting, because then, in the blessed abode,

there will be no opportunity for sin, where there is no desire.

So great a glory remains reserved for the faithful people.

He grants more than this and has given this still greater gift:

a sinner who repents of having fallen before

you do not cause to be numbered among the sinful crowd.

Indeed, it is punishment enough when one’s own guilt causes sorrow;

fear is its own penalty, and the one who confesses

that he has deserved punishment already suffers, as it were, the torments of guilt.

What could be better, or what could be more moderate?

He judges, investigates, chastises, spares, and honors—

he who conquers all things and is not himself conquered even by anger.

[Col. 0282B] We already perceive in the present what is to come:

for when he often gathers threatening and dreadful clouds,

flashes with fearsome holiness in intensely ruddy fire,

and thunders amid gloomy rains and black clouds,

every kind of creature fears destruction; but power, once seen,

will cease, and at the same time he clears both sky and minds.

He thereby commands us to hope for this then also—he who now proves

that he can destroy all things, if he refuses to will their destruction.

Thus salvation to be renewed is revealed for the age to come,

and the eternal loving-kindness of the eternal God will remain.

**THE COMPLETE WORKS OF VICTORINUS OF PETTAU**

[Col. 0281]

# PROLEGOMENA ON SAINT VICTORINUS, BISHOP OF PETTAU AND MARTYR

## ARTICLE I. A Synopsis of His Life

[Col. 0281D]

**When did he flourish? Various testimonies concerning him from Jerome. What did Optatus of Milevis say before Jerome?**—Cave appears to have inferred with sufficient confidence from the evidence supplied by Jerome that Victorinus was of Greek origin, or was at least born near the borders of Greece [Note: [Col. 0281D] Cave, *Literary History*, vol. I, p. 147.]. He was bishop of Pettau [Note: [Col. 0281D] Launoy, a Frenchman, demonstrated that this is the correct reading in a special and learned dissertation published at Paris in 1653, octavo, and in his collected works, vol. II, part I, p. 634 ff. He thereby completely eradicated the longstanding error according to which Baronius, at the year 303, no. 16, and many others called Victorinus bishop of Poitiers in Aquitaine, Gaul. For Launoy demonstrates that in five passages of St. Jerome in which Victorinus is mentioned—twice in the *Catalogue*, chapters 74 and 101; once *Against Vigilantius*; once *Against Helvidius*; and finally once in the thirty-sixth chapter of *Ezekiel*—the ancient editions read *Petabionensis*, *Petavionensis*, *Pictabiensis*, or *Pictabionensis*. The same forms of the name occur in the ancient martyrologies of Usuard, Ado, and others, as well as in Merlin’s first edition of the councils and in the edition [Col. 0283B] of the commentary on the Apocalypse attributed to this author. From so many testimonies and the various arguments he presents, the learned man finally concludes that this Victorinus was not bishop of Poitiers but of a city in Pannonia formerly called Petabio or Petavio, but now Petau. Petau was the colony and town in the Carnic region—on the borders of Styria and Slavonia—mentioned by Tacitus; and, according to the more recent territorial division, it is now a town in the Austrian district of the duchy of Styria, belonging to the archbishopric of Salzburg, or Juvavum. [Col. 0283C] Launoy further adds that Fortunatus, a priest of Poitiers who celebrated numerous bishops of Gaul in his poems, would certainly have praised all the more a martyr who had been the first among the people of Poitiers to consecrate the Christian religion by his blood. Nor did Gregory of Tours say a single word about Victorinus either in his *History* or in the work he composed about martyrs. By this profound silence the alleged episcopate of Victorinus at Poitiers is buried.], in Upper Pannonia beside the River Drava. [Col. 0282D] He became a bishop after having been an orator, as Cassiodorus teaches us in more than one place [Col. 0283A] [Note: [Col. 0283C] “Concerning this book, Ecclesiastes, Victorinus too, who became a bishop after having been an orator, discussed several matters.” Cassiodorus, *Institutions of Divine Literature*, chapter 5, vol. II, p. 512; chapter 7, p. 513; and chapter 9.]. According to the aforementioned Cave he flourished around the year 290, but according to Sixtus of Siena [Note: [Col. 0283C] Sixtus of Siena, *Sacred Library*, book IV, p. 308.], around the year 270. According to the common opinion, he is said to have suffered martyrdom during Diocletian’s persecution in the year 393 [as printed] [Note: [Col. 0283C] Cave, *Literary History*, cited passage; Pagi, at the year 303, note 9; Basnage, at the year 303, no. 16; Tillemont, *Memoirs*, vol. V, p. 133.]. Ceillier notes, however [Note: [Col. 0283C] Ceillier, *General History*, vol. III, p. 345.], that the time at which he suffered martyrdom cannot be determined exactly. It does indeed appear probable that he was crowned with martyrdom under Diocletian at the beginning of the fourth century, since, when enumerating his illustrious men, St. Jerome [Note: [Col. 0283C] Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 74.] places our Victorinus immediately before the priest Pamphilus, who is known to have suffered martyrdom under Maximinus in the year 309, as Tillemont correctly observed [Note: [Col. 0283D] Tillemont, *Memoirs*, vol. V, part II, p. 215; Brussels edition, p. 133.]. His feast is celebrated in the martyrologies on the fourth day before the Nones of November. Ado’s words for this day are: “The feast of St. Victorinus [Col. 0283B], Bishop of Pettau, who was crowned with martyrdom in the persecution of Diocletian.”

Although the greatest Doctor numbers Victorinus among the Latin Fathers [Note: [Col. 0283D] Jerome, preface to the commentaries on Matthew, p. 7, vol. VII, Venice edition, 1769, quarto: “I confess that I have read works on Matthew . . . and, among the Latins, the short works of Hilary, Victorinus, and Fortunatian.”], he calls him a pillar of the Church [Note: [Col. 0283D] “If Rufinus wished to place authorities at the head of his work, showing whom he followed, he had readily at hand Hilary the confessor . . . he had Ambrose . . . and the martyr Victorinus, who proves his guilelessness by plotting against no one. He is silent about all these and, passing over what may be called the pillars of the Church, pursues me alone, a flea and a man of no account.” Jerome, *Apology Against Rufinus*, book I, p. 351; and Venice edition, vol. II, no. 2, p. 459.]. Jerome also says that Victorinus translated Origen’s treatises not as a translator but as the author of a work of his own [Note: [Col. 0283D] Jerome, Letter 41, p. 346; and Venice edition, Letter to Pammachius and Oceanus 84, no. 7, vol. I, p. 529.]. Yet he says [Note: [Col. 0283D] The same, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 74, p. 914.] that Victorinus knew Latin less well than Greek, and therefore his works, though grand in their ideas, appear comparatively poor in their verbal composition [Col. 0284A]. Writing to Paulinus in the same vein [Note: [Col. 0284C] The same, Letter 49 to Paulinus, vol. IV, p. 567; and Venice edition, Letter 58, no. 10, vol. I, p. 326.], he says: “Victorinus, renowned and crowned with martyrdom, cannot express what he understands” [Note: [Col. 0284C] From these passages the very learned Lardner, *Credibility of the Gospel History*, part II, vol. III, p. 186, conjectures that Victorinus wrote most of his short works in Latin, since it was the vernacular of the region in which he was bishop, though he had acquired little mastery of its idiom and elegance. For, as Cave notes, the language of the Greeks, among whom he had spent much of his time, excessively corrupted, as commonly happens, his style when writing Latin. Hence his works were excellent in ideas but obscure in expression, as the distinguished Beati observes, vol. II, *Ecclesiastical History*, dissertation IV, §24, p. 480, Augsburg octavo edition, 1761.]. Elsewhere he says: “The martyr Victorinus, of holy memory, could say with the Apostle: ‘Even if unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge’” [Note: [Col. 0284D] Jerome, prologue to the *Commentary on Isaiah*, vol. IV, p. 5.]. Again: “Although learning is lacking in the martyr Victorinus’s books, the will to learn is nevertheless not lacking” [Note: [Col. 0284D] The same, Letter to the orator Magnus, §5, vol. I, p. 427.]. From the argument of the letter itself, Sixtus of Siena [Note: [Col. 0284D] Sixtus of Siena, *Sacred Library*, book IV, p. 486.], Possevino [Note: [Col. 0284D] Possevino, *Sacred Apparatus*, vol. II, p. 523.], Launoy [Note: [Col. 0284D] Launoy, cited passage, p. 645 ff.], and Gallandi [Note: [Col. 0284D] Gallandi, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. IV, Prolegomena, chapter 2, p. 5, no. 1.] conclude that this statement of Jerome must be understood as referring to education in secular disciplines. If their opinion is correct, says the distinguished Schoenemann [Note: [Col. 0284D] *Latin Library of the Fathers: Literary History*, chapter 3, no. 8, p. 143.], what are we to do with Cassiodorus [Note: [Col. 0284D] Cassiodorus, cited passage.], who writes that Victorinus became a bishop after having been an orator? Was Victorinus merely a common pettifogger? For [Col. 0284B] although the orator’s profession could easily lack a more refined education, it nevertheless required more than merely a desire for learning. Nor indeed do I see how he could have possessed merely a slight tincture of those resources without which that art could not exist at all, if Jerome was able to find his writings wholly wanting in learning. But since so little survives of this Victorinus, and not even that little is certain, it will scarcely be possible to settle this question.

Before Jerome, however, Optatus of Milevis had mentioned Victorinus [Note: [Col. 0284D] Optatus of Milevis, *On the Donatist Schism*, book I, chapter 9, p. 8, Amsterdam edition.], placing him in the register of defenders of the Catholic Church by whom Marcion, Praxeas, Sabellius, Valentinus, and the rest down to the Cataphrygians were defeated in their respective times—namely by Victorinus of Pettau, Zephyrinus of Rome, and Tertullian of Carthage. Jerome agrees with him, testifying that the holy [Col. 0284C] martyr sharpened his pen against all heresies [Note: [Col. 0284D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, in the *Catalogue*, chapter 74.].

## ARTICLE II. On the Authentic Writings of St. Victorinus, Bishop and Martyr

**Catalogue of the works of St. Victorinus.**—According to Jerome’s testimony [Note: [Col. 0284D] The same, cited passage.], the holy bishop and martyr Victorinus wrote [Col. 0285A] commentaries on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Isaiah, Ezekiel, Habakkuk, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, and the Apocalypse of John; a work against all heresies; and many other works. Almost all of these appear to have perished through the ravages of time. Nor does Trithemius [Note: [Col. 0285D] Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 46.] enlarge the catalogue of St. Victorinus’s works, but merely lists his short works in a different order. We nevertheless believe it worthwhile to discuss these works more distinctly.

The first work of St. Victorinus the martyr mentioned by St. Jerome in his *Catalogue* is a commentary on the first book of Moses, or an exposition of Genesis. Elsewhere St. Jerome [Note: [Col. 0285D] “Since, however, we promised to add what it signified figuratively as well, let us quote the words of the martyr Hippolytus, from whom our Victorinus does not differ greatly—not because he treated everything more fully, but because he can provide the reader with an opportunity for a broader understanding.” Jerome, to Damasus, Question III, p. 569, in Benedictine vol. II; otherwise Letter 125; and in the latest Venice quarto edition, vol. I, Letter 36, no. 16, p. 169.], in connection with a question proposed by Pope Damasus—why Isaac, a just man beloved by God, was deceived [Col. 0285B] and mistakenly blessed not the son whom he wished to bless but the one whom he did not—cites a certain writing of St. Victorinus on Genesis 27.

**The treatise *On the Fabric of the World* appears to be an excerpt from the commentaries on Genesis.**—Cave and Lardner believe that a fragment survives which was apparently excerpted from his commentary on Genesis [Note: [Col. 0285D] Cave, *Literary History*, vol. I, p. 147; Lardner, *Credibility*, part II, vol. III, p. 189; and Gallandi, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. IV, Prolegomena, chapter 2, p. 6.]. In the manuscript copy it bears this title: “Here begins the treatise *On the Fabric of the World* by St. Victorinus.” William Cave published it from an ancient manuscript in the Lambeth Library of the Archbishop of Canterbury, copied about eight hundred years earlier. It was subsequently revised once more against the same manuscript, the only one extant, with conjectures by several learned men—Henry Maurice and John Batteley—placed in the margin. But because Cave’s edition seemed to have been insufficiently collated with the manuscript exemplar, [Col. 0285C] J. Walker edited the short work for a third time and added several critical annotations, as the recent editor of Cave’s *Literary History* informs us [Note: [Col. 0285D] Cave, cited passage, p. 149.].

**This fragment is a genuine work of St. Victorinus.**—Concerning the fragment’s authenticity, the very learned Gallandi says that there is assuredly no legitimate reason for anyone to doubt it [Note: [Col. 0285D] Gallandi, cited passage, p. 6.]. Whether one considers the manuscript’s venerable antiquity; the name of Victorinus appearing at the head of the manuscript copy; the subject of the work, which the ancients report Victorinus to have treated in his exposition of Genesis; the author’s rough and unpolished style, as we learn from Jerome; or especially the chiliasts’ doctrines asserted here [Note: [Col. 0285D] Victorinus, *On the Fabric of the World*, section IV.], which the same Jerome authoritatively reports Victorinus to have followed [Note: [Col. 0285D] Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, in the *Catalogue*, chapter 18.]—all these considerations openly proclaim that this [Col. 0286A] little book, or a certain *ἀποσπασμάτιον* (“small excerpt”) from the commentaries on Genesis, must be assigned to Victorinus of Pettau. But I should like you, Gallandi continues, to compare especially what the author says in §5 about the seven Churches to which the apostle Paul sent his letters with what Victorinus explains about those same seven Pauline Churches in his scholia on Apocalypse 1:16, which will be discussed shortly.

Nothing whatever from the commentaries on the second and third books of Moses, Ezekiel, Habakkuk, and the Song of Songs has reached us; all perished through the ravages of time.

St. Jerome mentioned the exposition of the prophet Isaiah in the prologue to his own commentary on that prophet, in these words [Note: [Col. 0286D] Jerome, prologue to Isaiah, p. 3; and Venice edition, vol. IV, p. 5.]: “To undertake an explanation of the entire book of Isaiah is a work of great labor and effort, for on it the intellects of our predecessors—to wit, the Greeks—have toiled. Among the Latins, however, there is profound silence, apart from the martyr Victorinus of holy memory, who could say with the Apostle: ‘Even if unskilled in speech, yet not in knowledge.’” Elsewhere he cites the mystical interpretation given by our holy martyr Victorinus to the text of Isaiah 6:2 as follows [Note: [Col. 0286D] Jerome, to Damasus, vol. III, p. 518, Benedictine edition; otherwise Letter 142; and Venice edition, vol. I, Letter 18, no. 6, p. 50, *On the Seraphim*.]: “Six wings belonged to the one, and six wings to the other. Our Victorinus interpreted them as the twelve apostles.”

It will not be pointless, the very learned Gallandi observes [Note: [Col. 0286D] Gallandi, cited passage, p. 5, no. 2.], to note here that Victorinus did indeed write commentaries on Isaiah, but not according to four editions—that is, those of the Septuagint, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion—down to the vision of the beasts in the desert, as Launoy [Note: [Col. 0286D] Launoy, cited passage.] and Hody [Note: [Col. 0286D] Hody, *On the Original Text of the Bible*, book III, part II, chapter 1, §4, p. 345.] inferred incorrectly from St. Jerome’s prologue [Col. 0286C] to the exposition of Isaiah. For it is clear from the context itself that the holy Doctor reported this not of Victorinus but of Origen, as the learned Grabe correctly perceived [Note: [Col. 0286D] Grabe, *On the Faults of the Septuagint Translators*, chapter 2, §12, p. 66.].

**Victorinus’s commentaries on Ecclesiastes.**—In his own commentary on Ecclesiastes, St. Jerome cites St. Victorinus’s exposition of Ecclesiastes 4:13 in these words [Note: [Col. 0286D] Jerome, *Commentary on Ecclesiastes*, vol. II, p. 741 at the end; and Venice edition, vol. III, p. 425 C–D.]: “Origen and Victorinus held views that did not differ greatly from one another. After that general interpretation, which is evident to everyone—that a poor and wise young man is better than an old and foolish king; and that it often happens that the former, departing by his wisdom from the king’s prison, rules in place of the corrupt sovereign, while the foolish king loses the authority [Col. 0286D] he possessed—they interpreted this passage as referring to Christ and the Devil, maintaining that the poor and wise boy [Col. 0287A] was Christ.”

Cassiodorus also mentions St. Victorinus’s commentary, saying [Note: [Col. 0287D] Cassiodorus, *Institutions of Divine Literature*, chapter 5.]: “Concerning this book, Ecclesiastes, Victorinus too . . . discussed several matters.” From Cassiodorus’s manner of speaking, it appears probable that Victorinus explained only certain passages of Ecclesiastes.

**On St. Victorinus’s commentary on Matthew.**—In his *Catalogue*, St. Jerome makes no mention of an exposition of Matthew by St. Victorinus. But in the prologue to his commentary on this Evangelist he says [Note: [Col. 0287D] Jerome, prologue to Matthew, p. 8; and Venice edition, vol. VIII, p. 7.]: “I confess that I have read . . . and, among the Latins, the short works of Hilary, Victorinus, and Fortunatian.” Cassiodorus [Note: [Col. 0287D] Cassiodorus, ibid., chapter 7.] expressly says: “Concerning Matthew, Victorinus, who became a bishop after having been an orator, discussed several matters.” The very learned Lardner therefore conjectures [Note: [Col. 0287D] Lardner, cited passage, p. 191.] that St. Victorinus’s short work [Col. 0287B] comprised either only brief observations or explanations of individual passages of that Gospel.

Both St. Jerome and Cassiodorus mention commentaries on the Apocalypse of St. John composed by our holy martyr. Cassiodorus writes of them as follows [Note: [Col. 0287D] Cassiodorus, cited passage, chapter 9.]: “Concerning this book, the Apocalypse, Victorinus, the bishop mentioned so often, briefly treated certain extremely difficult passages.” In Cave’s judgment [Note: [Col. 0287D] Cave, cited passage, p. 147.], by these words Cassiodorus indicates that Victorinus did not so much elucidate the entire Apocalypse in a commentary as treat certain more difficult passages. More generally, the illustrious Ceillier observes [Note: [Col. 0287D] Ceillier, cited passage, pp. 345–346.] that it is uncertain whether St. Victorinus composed complete commentaries or whether he expounded the sacred books [Col. 0287C] from beginning to end. For Cassiodorus asserts quite plainly that the holy bishop explained only certain passages of Ecclesiastes, St. Matthew, and the Apocalypse.

**On St. Victorinus’s scholia on the Apocalypse of John.**—The second of Victorinus’s writings to have reached us is his scholia on the Apocalypse. Basil Millanius, a monk of Monte Cassino, was the first to publish them from a manuscript in the library of Monte Cassino. They appeared at Bologna in octavo, from the press of Antonio Giaccarello and Pellegrino Bonardo, in 1558. This first editor of the scholia complained that the manuscript he used had been so corrupted by the ignorance of copyists that he could often arrive at the correct meaning only by conjecture.

[Col. 0287D] Concerning the work, its author, and the care he devoted to elucidating it, it may perhaps be worthwhile to hear the editor himself address his reader in these words:

> “Friendly reader,” he says, “I took diligent and careful precautions to ensure that there should be no point on which you might charge me either with complete negligence or even with rashness. For I read this short work [Col. 0288A] with the greatest care; and although I could disapprove of many statements in it as contrary to correct principles of writing, I nevertheless altered almost nothing in the text itself. Instead, I noted the passages, whatever their quality, so that they might stand or fall by your judgment rather than mine.
>
> “The little book is certainly of such a kind that it will bring both great benefit to pious and religious persons who delight in writings of this sort and, indeed, much assistance toward understanding those matters hidden beneath the exceedingly profound meanings of the Apocalypse. Although its style is very far removed from the ancient brilliance and purity of the Latin language—reflecting both the character of an age in which literary culture had already declined, if it had not wholly collapsed together with the majesty of the empire, and the foreign quality of the Gallic nation, which at that time had not yet been cultivated, as it is now, either in intellect or in knowledge of the noblest [Col. 0288B] arts—this author nevertheless accomplished so much through his brevity that the usefulness of his subject can abundantly compensate for the unusual character of certain words.
>
> “Since we ourselves follow not the words—which he repeatedly uses improperly and in senses far removed from correct usage—but the meanings themselves, we certainly did not wish to appear more learned than the author himself in matters of wording. Following in his footsteps, therefore, we note below the points that seemed especially worthy of observation.”

Thus far the distinguished editor Basil Millanius. Had the passage from Jerome’s *On Illustrious Men* mentioned above occurred to him, he would neither have supposed that Victorinus was a Gaul, or bishop of Poitiers, nor have lamented so greatly his unpolished style.

[Col. 0288C] Gallandi says that we considered it necessary to reproduce these statements from our editor chiefly because this edition of the short work—the only one and indeed extremely rare—had until now escaped every single scholar known to have written about ecclesiastical authors either in the present or in the preceding century [Note: [Col. 0288D] Gallandi, cited passage, p. 6.]. For if they had examined it, I do not doubt that they would have accepted such scholia as a genuine work of Victorinus and would at the same time have recognized as altogether spurious, being extraordinarily interpolated, the commentary on the Apocalypse circulated under his name in the libraries of the Fathers.

First, we learn from Cassiodorus [Note: [Col. 0288D] Cassiodorus, cited passage, chapter 9.] that Victorinus briefly treated certain extremely difficult passages in the book of the Apocalypse. This description is known to agree perfectly with our scholia [Col. 0288D] and to be foreign to the widely circulated commentary, as will become evident to anyone who compares the two works. Secondly—and this is the principal point—the doctrine of the millennial kingdom appears in our scholia [Note: [Col. 0288D] Victorinus, *Scholia on the Apocalypse*, 1:15; 20:6.]; we learned above from Jerome that Victorinus certainly acknowledged this doctrine in common with other early writers.

It must not, however, be concealed that Victorinus concludes his scholia with these words: “Therefore no heed must be paid to those who assert that the kingdom of the thousand years is earthly, for they share the opinion of the heretic Cerinthus.” [Col. 0289A] Concerning these words, I would first say with Sixtus of Siena [Note: [Col. 0289D] Sixtus of Siena, *Sacred Library*, book VI, annotation 348.] that Victorinus’s absurd opinion was perhaps corrected in this way by another hand and that the statement now found there was inserted in its place. But I would then prefer to suppose that words of this kind were actually written by Victorinus so that, although he had once been imbued with that opinion concerning an earthly kingdom, he might exclude from it whatever particularly corrupt elements the doctrines of Cerinthus had introduced. Justin Martyr acted no differently, for although he embraced the same opinion, he says [Note: [Col. 0289D] Justin Martyr, *Dialogue with Trypho*, chapter 139.]: “Those who believe in Christ and acknowledge the truth of what was handed down both by him and by the prophets know that they will be with him in that land and will receive eternal and incorruptible goods as their inheritance.”

## ARTICLE III. On the Doubtful or Spurious Works of St. Victorinus

[Col. 0289B]

**The widely circulated commentary on the Apocalypse must be denied to Victorinus.**—A commentary on the Apocalypse exists in the libraries of the holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 0289D] In the Paris *Library*, vol. I; Lyon edition, vol. III, p. 414. Other editions of this commentary are listed in Jacques Le Long, *Bibliotheca Sacra*, p. 1003.] under the title: “By Victorinus, Bishop of Pettau.” Whether it is genuinely his work, however, is still disputed among the learned. The very learned Cave writes [Note: [Col. 0289D] Cave, cited passage, p. 147.]:

> “It must either not be his or have been extraordinarily interpolated and altered. For Jerome expressly reports [Note: [Col. 0289D] Jerome, *Catalogue*, chapter 18, and preface to Victorinus’s *Commentary*.] that in his commentary Victorinus favored the error of the chiliasts; yet the author of this commentary vigorously attacks it [Col. 0289C] and ascribes that doctrine to the heresiarch Cerinthus. He also cites Theodore, the compiler of an ecclesiastical history under Justinian, whose collections we possess today—to omit other points. From this it is most evidently concluded that, if the work is Victorinus’s, it has suffered remarkable interpolations and assumed an entirely different appearance from the one it had when it first left Victorinus’s hand.”

Basnage pronounces upon the aforementioned commentary of Victorinus on the Apocalypse in the following manner [Note: [Col. 0289D] Basnage, at the year 303, no. 16.]: “That book is filled with many fables. He believes that Jeremiah has not yet departed this life; that Nero will be the Antichrist and will come at the end of the world. The most illustrious Dupin inclines to the view, in his new library, that the commentary is Victorinus’s: *il y a apparence qu’il est de lui*—‘there is reason to believe that it is by him.’ Nevertheless, we believe that it must be denied to Victorinus, and we offer Jerome as judge (*On Papias*, chapter 18, in the *Catalogue*): ‘He is said to have produced a Jewish δευτέρωσις (*deuterōsis*, “repetition” or “second exposition”) concerning the thousand years; he was followed by Irenaeus and Apollinaris and the others [Col. 0290A] who say that after the resurrection the Lord will reign in the flesh with the saints. Tertullian also, in his book *On the Hope of the Faithful*, and Victorinus of Poetovio and Lactantius, are led by this opinion.’”

Yet the commentary ascribed to Victorinus strikes down the opinion of the millenarians [Note: [Col. 0290D] Victorinus, *Commentary*, in *Bibliotheca magna patrum*, vol. III, p. 421.]: “I do not think that the kingdom of a thousand years is a fixed term. . . . As the capacity of my understanding perceives the matter to be set forth, since the number ten signifies the Decalogue, while the number one hundred represents the crown of virginity, whoever has preserved inviolate the resolve of virginity and faithfully fulfilled the commandments of the Decalogue . . . is truly a priest of Christ; and, completing the number one thousand, he is believed to reign with Christ in perfect integrity, and for him the devil is rightly bound.”

The most learned Lampe [Note: [Col. 0290D] “This is all the less consistent, since it is very probable that this book is falsely ascribed to Victorinus. . . .” Lampe, *Prolegomena on John*, book I, chapter 4, no. 12, p. 66.] judges it highly probable [Col. 0290B] that this commentary is falsely ascribed to Victorinus. By contrast, the learned Dupin, after adducing various arguments on both sides, finally concludes [Note: [Col. 0290D] Dupin, *Bibliothèque des auteurs ecclésiastiques*, vol. I, p. 194; and Latin ed., Cologne, p. 301.]: “It must not therefore be asserted that this commentary is falsely ascribed to Victorinus; indeed, it is more likely that it is his genuine offspring.”

The most judicious Tillemont [Note: [Col. 0290D] Tillemont, *Mémoires ecclésiastiques*, vol. V, p. 218 and note 2; Brussels ed., p. 134.], in his customary manner, treated this question modestly and carefully. He first acknowledges that, on the strength of various considerations, the γνησιότης (*gnēsiotēs*, “genuineness”) of that commentary on the Apocalypse is called into doubt by no small number of scholars; but he then asserts that, in his view, far more arguments remain which induce us to believe that this short commentary should be regarded as a certain ἀπόσπασμα (*apospasma*, “surviving fragment”) from among the many works and labors of this holy martyr. [Col. 0290C] At the same time, however, it must also be conceded that passages once occurring in it in favor of chiliasm underwent alteration in later times [Note: [Col. 0290D] Id., ibid.].

Furthermore, the illustrious Tillemont elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0290D] Id., ibid., note 3, p. 444; Brussels ed., p. 312.] also supplies certain considerations from which it may be understood why the passages now found in the aforementioned short commentary concerning chiliasm are either corrupted or interpolated. These passages occur at the end of the aforesaid little work, and at first glance anyone can readily recognize that their style differs greatly from that of the preceding passages. In addition, we may quite readily believe that various ancient holy Fathers underwent alterations of this kind concerning the same doctrine [Note: [Col. 0290D] Id., vol. II, “Les Millénaires,” p. 251. There he adduces Sulpicius Severus’s dialogue entitled *Gallus* and the last five chapters of St. Irenaeus’s book V *Against Heresies*, in which the error of the millenarians was omitted.].

Our conjecture in the present case is still further confirmed by the fact that, in this very exposition, certain traces of the millenarians’ opinion [Col. 0291A] are still encountered, since it is asserted there [Note: [Col. 0291C] “Where they—that is, the apostles—first stood, they established the Church, namely in Judaea, where all the saints are to assemble and worship their Lord.” [Col. 0291D] Victorinus, *On the Apocalypse*, p. 415.] that all the saints are to assemble and worship our Lord Jesus Christ.

But whether the aforementioned short commentary is Victorinus’s or not, various marks of antiquity are nevertheless found in it. To these Tillemont refers the author’s manner of speaking about the Roman Senate [Note: [Col. 0291D] “And I saw,” he says, “the woman drunk with the blood of the saints. By decree of that Senate, consummate in wickedness, he himself issued throughout all nations the decree against every preaching of the faith, even after indulgence had been granted.” Id., ibid., p. 420 H.], namely, that at that time it decreed persecutions against Christians in its own name and by its own authority.

Next comes what he writes about Nero [Note: [Col. 0291D] Id., ibid., p. 420 D; and he has similar statements in the scholia on Apocalypse, chapter XIII, p. 61, in Gallandius.], in the following manner: “By the statement that one of the heads was slain unto death and that its mortal wound was healed, he means Nero. For it is well established that, when the cavalry dispatched by the Senate was pursuing him, he cut his own throat. God will therefore send him after raising him up—a king worthy of the worthy, and a Christ of the kind the Jews have deserved.” This opinion was more common in the early [Col. 0291B] centuries of the Church than in later ones.

Third, when he enumerates the Epistles of the divine Paul, there is profound silence concerning the Epistle to the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0291D] Id., ibid., p. 415 E.]. Now, in the age of our St. Victorinus, the prevailing opinion among Western Christians was that the Epistle to the Hebrews did not have the divine Paul as its author.

It is likewise worthy of notice in this commentary that, when the prophet who is to come with Elijah is mentioned, no reference is made to Enoch; it is merely reported that some had thought Moses or Elisha to be meant in his place [Note: [Col. 0291D] “Many think that he is Elijah, or Elisha, or Moses; but both of the latter are dead. Jeremiah’s death, however, is not found recorded, because all our ancient authorities handed down that he is Jeremiah.” Id., ibid., p. 418 D. Similar statements occur in the scholia on Apocalypse, chapter XI, p. 59, in Gallandius, vol. IV.]. As for the author’s own opinion, he thought it was Jeremiah, precisely because his death is not commemorated in Scripture.

All these things may be regarded as reasonably suitable indications of the antiquity of the aforementioned commentary. Finally, the style observed in this work agrees very well with the characterization [Col. 0291C] of Victorinus’s manner of writing made by St. Jerome: namely, that it was rough and unpolished, and that Victorinus’s works seem great in their ideas but rather poor in their verbal composition.

Thus does the most learned Tillemont judge concerning the commentary on the Apocalypse, although at the same time he also observes that the safest course would be to leave the question of its true author undecided [Note: [Col. 0291D] Tillemont, loc. cit.]. The highly learned Lardner endorsed this judgment wholeheartedly [Note: [Col. 0291D] Lardner, loc. cit., p. 195.]. By contrast, the Most Reverend Ceillier does not hesitate to affirm that this commentary is rightly ascribed to St. Victorinus, bishop and martyr of Poetovio [Note: [Col. 0291D] Ceillier, loc. cit., p. 346.]; but in confirmation of his opinion [Col. 0292A] he adduces no arguments other than those which we noted above from Tillemont.

In our own age, however, the most learned men Gallandius [Note: [Col. 0292B] Gallandius, loc. cit., p. 6, in the prolegomena, chapter III. I quoted his words at the end of the preceding article while discussing the scholia of St. Victorinus on the Apocalypse.], Oelrichs [Note: [Col. 0292B] “Nor is the commentary—on the Apocalypse—which is usually found in the Libraries of the Fathers genuine.” [Col. 0292C] Oelrichs, *Commentarii de scriptoribus ecclesiasticis Latinis*, Leipzig, 1791, p. 46.], and Schoenemann [Note: [Col. 0292C] “As for the *Commentary on the Apocalypse* now extant under his—Victorinus’s—name in the *Library of the Fathers*, vol. III, we learn from Jerome’s censures of him that it is not his, or at least that it has been wretchedly mutilated and interpolated. Jerome says that the author favors the opinion of the chiliasts, whereas the present commentary attacks it instead and calls it the heresy of Cerinthus. This commentary would be convicted of fraud still more strongly if we were permitted to use what Cave thought he had plainly detected in Cassiodorus—*On Divine Readings*, chapter 9—namely, that Victorinus did not so much elucidate the entire Apocalypse in a commentary as treat certain more difficult passages.” Schoenemann, *Bibliotheca historico-literaria Patrum Latinorum*, vol. I, chapter III, no. 8, p. 145 ff., Leipzig, octavo, 1792.] deny the commentary on the Apocalypse to Victorinus.

For my part, I am greatly pleased by the judgment of that most acute man and supreme critic, Jean de Launoy, who expresses the following view concerning the author of this commentary [Note: [Col. 0292C] Launoy, *Works*, vol. II, part I, p. 646 ff.]: “As regards Victorinus’s commentary on the Apocalypse, which we possess in the *Library of the Fathers*, it is possible—if Cassiodorus is to be believed—that it is partly his and partly another’s: his, in those portions containing the explanation of difficult passages; another’s, namely that of the person who supplied the exposition of the remaining passages. In short, this entire matter has been brought to such a state that it is certain that there is nothing certain which can be stated truly and affirmatively.”

[Col. 0292B] Moreover, following the illustrious Ceillier [Note: [Col. 0292C] Ceillier, loc. cit., p. 347.], we encounter in the aforementioned commentary the following points worthy of notice.

First: “Paul taught that all the churches throughout the whole world are seven, being named in groups of seven, and that they are one catholic Church” [Note: [Col. 0292C] St. Victorinus, *Commentary on the Apocalypse*, in the Lyons *Library of the [Col. 0292D] Fathers*, vol. III, p. 415. Similar statements occur in the scholia on Apocalypse, chapter II, p. 53, in Gallandius.].

Second, that baptism removes sins [Note: [Col. 0292D] “The reproach is the former sin, which is removed in baptism, and the person begins to be called a Christian; this is the meaning of: ‘Let your name be invoked over us.’” Id., ibid.].

Third, that the Nicolaitans received their name from Nicolas the Deacon; and that they taught that food sacrificed to idols could lawfully be eaten after it had been exorcised, and that peace—that is, ecclesiastical reconciliation—was to be granted to fornicators on the eighth day after their fall [Note: [Col. 0292D] “The Nicolaitans, however, were at that time false and pestilential men who, under the name of Nicolas the minister, fashioned a heresy for themselves, teaching that food offered to idols should be exorcised and could then be eaten, and that anyone who had committed fornication should receive peace on the eighth day.” Id., ibid. Similar statements occur in the scholia of St. Victorinus on Apocalypse, chapter II, in Gallandius, vol. IV, p. 54.].

Fourth, the author enumerates twenty-four books of the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 0292D] “Now the books of the Old Testament which are received are twenty-four; you will find them in the *Epitomes of Theodore*.” Id., ibid., p. 417. Compare Victorinus’s scholia on Apocalypse, chapter IV, p. 56, in Gallandius.], relying on the tradition of a certain Theodore [Note: [Col. 0292D] Who this Theodore was is not easy to determine. [Col. 0293B] Was he a Latin or a Greek of the first three centuries? Perhaps Gregory Thaumaturgus, adorned with this name by St. Jerome in the *Catalogue*, chapter 65; or Theodotus, cited by St. Clement of Alexandria in the *Excerpts*, pp. 794 and 795. The highly learned Dupin, who does not doubt that the aforementioned commentary is older than the age of Justinian, thinks it more credible that the citation [Col. 0293C] of Theodore was added by some would-be scholar. See Tillemont, vol. V, p. 313; Dupin, loc. cit., p. 301.].

From the same [Col. 0293A] short commentary it is evident that the Apocalypse was at that time fully acknowledged [Note: [Col. 0293C] This is clear from the formulas with which the author of this little book cites the Apocalypse. For example, *Library of the Fathers*, vol. III, p. 419: “The opened book is the one that John saw.” After a few intervening words he calls this John an apostle: “But because it says that John was going to write down all that the thunders had spoken—that is, whatever things in the Old Testament were obscure and had been foretold—he is forbidden to write them, but commanded to leave them sealed; for he was an apostle, and the grace of a subsequent rank ought not to be placed in the first.” He further discusses the time when the Apocalypse was written and comments as follows on Apocalypse 10:11: “This means that, when John saw this, he was on the island of Patmos, condemned to the mines by the emperor Domitian. There, therefore, he saw the Apocalypse. And when, now an old man, he thought that he would obtain his reception through martyrdom, Domitian was killed, all his judgments were annulled, and John was released from the mines. Thus afterward he handed down this same Apocalypse, which he had received from [Col. 0293D] the Lord. This is the meaning of: ‘You must prophesy again.’” And in the same work, p. 420: “It is necessary to understand the time at which the writing of the Apocalypse was published, since Domitian was emperor at that time. ‘One remains,’ under whom the Apocalypse was written—namely Domitian.” Compare Victorinus’s scholia on Apocalypse, chapter XIII, p. 61, in Gallandius.].

Finally, this commentary also takes account of the Epistle to the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0293D] For example, p. 418: “Thus heaven is understood as the golden altar.”]. In the appendix to the third volume of the Maurist edition of the works of the divine Augustine there is printed an anonymous author’s commentary on the Apocalypse, for the greater part drawn from the one that bears the name of St. Victorinus of Poetovio [Note: [Col. 0293D] See the Maurists’ *Notice concerning the Exposition on the Apocalypse Which Follows*, vol. XVI of the works of the divine Augustine, Venice ed., quarto, p. 618.].

A preface of the Fathers [Note: [Col. 0293D] Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, vol. III, p. 414.] is prefixed to this commentary on the Apocalypse and ascribed to Jerome; in it Victorinus is said to have held the same opinion as Papias and Nepos. But, in the judgment of a most learned man [Note: [Col. 0293D] Lardner, loc. cit., pp. 195–196.], that prologue, or letter to Anatolius, is ascribed to the divine Jerome without any foundation whatsoever; and no critic, so far as I know, accepts it as genuine.

[Col. 0293B] **Other Works Falsely Ascribed to St. Victorinus.**—Two poems are also attributed to our St. Victorinus; they are contained in Fabricius’s collection of sacred poets, one concerning Jesus Christ as God and man, while the other is entitled *The Tree of Life*. But the conjecture is wholly uncertain and, as Cave says [Note: [Col. 0293D] Cave, loc. cit.], appears to me false; the most illustrious pair of scholars Oelrichs and Schoenemann agree with him [Note: [Col. 0293D] Oelrichs and Schoenemann, loc. cit.].

Tillemont observes [Note: [Col. 0293D] Tillemont, loc. cit., p. 134.] that in various manuscripts [Col. 0294A] the *Hymn on the Holy Cross*, or *On Easter*, or *On Baptism*, included among the works of the divine Cyprian [Note: [Col. 0294D] *On the Cross of the Lord*, p. 4 of the appendix to Cyprian’s works.], is attributed to St. Victorinus, bishop and martyr of Poetovio. Our venerable Bede likewise cites this hymn under Victorinus’s name [Note: [Col. 0294D] Bede, *On the Holy Places*, chapter 2, p. 317, Cambridge, 1722.] in these words: “Led by this opinion, Victorinus, bishop of the Church of Poitiers, begins as follows when writing about Golgotha”:

> There is a place at the center of all the world we behold,  
> Which the Jews call Golgotha in their ancestral tongue.

This poem is exceedingly distinguished and, when the style of our author is considered, too elegant for it to be capable of, or properly liable to, attribution to him. From this poem, as Tillemont reports [Note: [Col. 0294D] Tillemont, loc. cit., p. 134.], we learn that many people in that age wished to profess the Christian religion but did not even remain steadfast in it as far as baptism.

[Col. 0294B] Tillemont, already cited many times, seeks to vindicate for Victorinus the poem, or verses, by an uncertain author against Marcion, customarily published among Tertullian’s writings [Note: [Col. 0294D] Id., ibid.]. Although we are unwilling to make this opinion our own, since it rests upon a slight conjecture [Note: [Col. 0294D] Namely, because the statement made by the divine Jerome concerning St. Victorinus’s limited command of the Latin language is very well suited to this little work.], we nevertheless do not hesitate to assign that work to the third century, as its treatment shows, and especially the list of Roman bishops which it contains.

The author of this composition accepted the Epistle to the Hebrews among the disputed books, as is clear from the following verses [Note: [Col. 0294D] Among Tertullian’s works published at Paris in 1634, p. 804; and Venice ed., 1744, p. 636.]:

> For with the blood of a calf, mingled with water,  
> He sprinkled the people, all the vessels together,  
> The priests [reading *sacerdotes* for OCR *sacerdotis*], and the written volumes of the Law.  
> *(Compare Hebrews 9:19.)*
>
> This our Lord, who redeemed us by his death,  
> [Col. 0294C] Willed to suffer outside the camp  
> The violence of an unjust people.  
> *(See Hebrews 13:12.)*
>
> Hence also John, the disciple, the ineffable author  
> Of the new covenant, bears witness that beneath the altar  
> He saw souls who had suffered for the Name,  
> Crying out for God’s vengeance for the slaughter committed by the powerful one.  
> *(See Apocalypse 6:5.)*

And in the same place, p. 805 of the Paris edition of 1634 and p. 637 of the Venice edition of 1744:

> Thus also John; thus the Spirit reveals to him  
> So many in number: elders upon white thrones [or: white-clad elders upon thrones; the Latin is ambiguous].  
> *(See Apocalypse 4:4.)*

St. Jerome [Note: [Col. 0294D] Jerome, *Against Rufinus*, book I, chapter 16, p. 459, Venice ed., 1766.] cites a commentary by Victorinus on the dialogues of Marcus Tullius Cicero; but a subject of that kind is better suited to Victorinus Afer, who was a professor of rhetoric.

## ARTICLE IV  
### Theological Observations on the Genuine Short Works of St. Victorinus, and a Survey of Their Editions

[Col. 0295A]

**The Teaching of St. Victorinus concerning the Four Gospels, etc.**—In the fragment *On the Creation of the World*, in which he discusses the work of the seventh day, St. Victorinus observes, among other things worthy of notice, the four living creatures before the throne of God, the four Gospels, and the four rivers flowing in paradise [Note: [Col. 0295D] Victorinus, *On the Creation of the World*, chapter II, in Gallandius, vol. IV, p. 49; in Cave, vol. I, p. 148; and in this Paris edition, this volume, p. [page number absent].].

The Gospel of St. John is adduced in the same treatise in this manner [Note: [Col. 0295D] Id., ibid., chapter IV, p. 50; and in Cave, p. 149.]: “John the Evangelist says as follows: ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.’”

In his scholia on the Apocalypse of blessed John, he discusses those same four Gospels as follows [Note: [Col. 0295D] Victorinus, scholia on Apocalypse, from chapter IV, p. 55, in Gallandius.]:

“The four living creatures are the four [Col. 0295B] Gospels. ‘The first living creature was like a lion, the second like a calf, the third had a face like a man, and the fourth was like a flying eagle. . . .’ The reason that the living creatures differ in appearance is this: the living creature like a lion represents Mark, in whom the voice of a lion roaring in the wilderness is heard. Matthew, however, endeavors by the human figure to set forth for us the lineage of Mary [Note: [Col. 0295D] Observe that Victorinus teaches that Matthew describes for us the genealogy of Mary, not of Christ, contrary to what the majority of theologians now suppose.], from whom Christ received his flesh. Therefore, when he enumerates the line from Abraham to David and down to Joseph, he spoke as though concerning a man. For that reason his proclamation displays the figure of a man. Luke, because he narrates the priesthood of Zechariah as he offers a sacrifice for the people, and the angel appearing to him, took the image of a calf on account of the priesthood and the account of the sacrifice. John the Evangelist, like an eagle, takes up [Col. 0295C] wings, hastens toward the heights, and discusses the Word of God.

“Mark the Evangelist begins thus: ‘The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: The voice of one crying in the wilderness’; he has the figure of a lion. Matthew, however, begins: ‘The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the Son of David, the Son of Abraham’; this is the face of a man. Luke said: ‘There was a priest named Zechariah, of the division of Abijah, and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron’; this is the image of a calf. But when John begins, ‘In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,’ he displays the likeness of a flying eagle [Note: [Col. 0295D] Similar statements occur in St. Victorinus’s commentary on the Apocalypse, in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, vol. III, p. 416.].

“Not only the Evangelists, but also the very Word of God the almighty Father—that is, his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ—bears the same images during his advent. When he preaches to us, he is like a lion and a lion’s cub; [Col. 0295D] and because, for the salvation of humankind, he became man in order to overcome death and set everyone free, and because he offered himself as a sacrifice to the Father on our behalf, he is called a calf. And because he overcame death and ascended [Col. 0296A] into heaven, spreading his wings and protecting his people, he is named a flying eagle. These proclamations, therefore, although they are four, are nevertheless one, because they proceeded from one mouth. That those living creatures have eyes within and without signifies, in the proclamation of the New Testament, spiritual providence, which both looks into the secrets of the heart and sees the things that are to come—the things within and without.”

In this passage of St. Victorinus we find all four Gospels and the beginning of each—or at least matters occurring immediately after the beginning in each of them. Hence this passage must be held by us in the highest esteem.

**At What Time and on What Occasion Was John’s Gospel Written?**—St. Victorinus records not only the time at which St. John composed his Gospel, but also the occasion that moved him to do so. He composed it, namely, after John had been banished to the island of Patmos, with the purpose of refuting and destroying the heresies that had arisen at that time [Note: [Col. 0296D] Victorinus, scholia on Apocalypse, chapter XI, p. 59, in Gallandius.].

“The reed shown, resembling a rod”—these are St. Victorinus’s words—“is this very Apocalypse, which he afterward presented to the churches; for he also afterward wrote the Gospel of our perfect faith for the sake of our salvation. For when Valentinus, Cerinthus, Ebion, and the others belonging to the school of Satan had spread throughout the world, all the bishops from the neighboring provinces assembled before him and compelled him to compose his own testimony as well.”

Statements not greatly dissimilar occur in Victorinus’s commentary on the Apocalypse [Note: [Col. 0296D] Victorinus, *On the Apocalypse*, p. 418 C, in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*.].

**The Acts of the Apostles Cited by St. Victorinus.**—St. Victorinus mentions the Acts of the Apostles twice [Col. 0296C] in these scholia on the Apocalypse. He does so when he writes [Note: [Col. 0296D] Id., scholia on Apocalypse, chapter XII, p. 60, in Gallandius and in this volume. The same occurs in the commentary on Apocalypse, p. 419 A, in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*. Compare Acts 1:9–11.]: “And we read in the Acts of the Apostles how, while speaking to his disciples, he was caught up into heaven.”

Elsewhere he writes [Note: [Col. 0296D] Id., ibid., chapter I, p. 53, Gallandius. Compare Acts 2:33. Similar words occur in the commentary on Apocalypse, p. 415.]: “As Peter cried out to the Jews: ‘Exalted by the right hand of God, he poured out the Spirit received from the Father, this Spirit whom you see.’”

**On the Epistles of the Divine Paul.**—In the fragment *On the Creation of the World*, first published by Cave, the following example appears among Victorinus’s meditations on the seventh day, on which God rested from all his labor, concerning this noteworthy number: “And the seven Churches in Paul” [Note: [Col. 0296D] Victorinus, fragment *On the Creation of the World*, in Cave, *Historia litteraria*, p. 149 A; and in Gallandius, *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. IV, p. 50 B, §5.]. Here the margin of Cave’s edition has “Apocalypse” in place of “Paul,” but incorrectly; “Paul” is right. For Cyprian, *On Exhortation to Martyrdom*, p. 125 of the Amsterdam edition and p. 179 of the Bremen edition, says: [Col. 0296D] “The apostle Paul, who makes mention of this lawful and fixed number, writes to seven Churches.” See also [Col. 0297A] the other material in the same place illustrating this passage.

That Victorinus understood these to be the seven Churches to which the same number of Epistles in the Pauline collection was directed is manifestly clear from two passages of our author, one in the scholia on the Apocalypse and the other in his commentary on the Apocalypse. Both contain the following [Note: [Col. 0297D] Victorinus, scholia on Apocalypse, chapter II, p. 53, in Gallandius; and *Commentary on the Apocalypse*, p. 415 D–E, in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*.]:

“These seven stars are the seven Churches to which he wrote Epistles—not because these alone are Churches or the principal Churches, but because what he says to one he says to all. Hence Paul also taught that all the Churches throughout the whole world, named in groups of seven, are seven and are one catholic Church, by writing to seven Churches: to the Romans, Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, and Thessalonians. Afterward he wrote to individual persons, lest he exceed the measure [Col. 0297B] of seven Churches. And, condensing his proclamation into a brief statement, he says to Timothy: ‘That you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the Church of the living God.’”

**The First Epistle of the Apostle Peter Cited by Victorinus.**—It is clear from both his scholia and his commentary on the Apocalypse that St. Victorinus acknowledged the first Epistle of the divine Peter. For, on these words of Apocalypse 1:6, “And made us a kingdom and priests” [Note: [Col. 0297D] Id., scholia on Apocalypse, chapter I, p. 52 B; and commentary on Apocalypse, p. 414 H, in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*.], he says: “That is, the Church of all the faithful, just as Peter the Apostle also says [Note: [Col. 0297D] 1 Peter 2:9.]: ‘A holy nation, a royal priesthood.’”

**The Apocalypse Is Expressly Attributed to John the Evangelist.**—In the fragment of St. Victorinus’s little work *On the Creation of the World*, express mention is also made of the Apocalypse of John. For at the end of that fragment the following words are read [Note: [Col. 0297D] Victorinus, fragment *On the Creation of the World*, in Cave, p. 149; and in Gallandius, no. VI, p. 51; but not in this volume.]:

“Accordingly, without doubt, there are twelve angels of the day [Col. 0297C] and twelve angels of the night, corresponding, namely, to the number of hours. For these are the twenty-four witnesses of the days and nights, who sit before the throne of God with golden crowns upon their heads, whom the Apocalypse of John, apostle and evangelist, calls elders.”

**The Time and Place at Which the Apocalypse Was Written.**—In these scholia St. Victorinus, bishop and martyr, records the time at which the Apocalypse was written by St. John the Apostle, when he says on chapter 13:10:

“It is necessary to understand the time at which the written Apocalypse was published, since Domitian was emperor at that time. Before him, however, had been his brother Titus, and Vespasian, Otho, Vitellius, and Galba. These are the five who have fallen. ‘ONE REMAINS,’ under whom the Apocalypse was written—namely Domitian [Note: [Col. 0297D] Victorinus, scholia on Apocalypse, p. 61 C, in Gallandius and in this volume, p. [page number absent].].”

And a little earlier, on chapter 10:11, he writes [Col. 0297D] [Note: [Col. 0297D] Id., ibid., p. 59.]:

“He says this because, when John saw these things, he was on the island of Patmos, condemned to the mines by the emperor Domitian. There, therefore, he saw the Apocalypse. [Col. 0298A] And when, now an old man, he thought that he would obtain his reception through martyrdom, Domitian was killed, all his judgments were annulled, and John was released from the mines. Thus afterward he handed down this same Apocalypse, which he had received from God.”

Compare Victorinus’s *Commentary on the Apocalypse*, vol. III of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, p. 420 C and G.

**The Number of the Books of the Old Testament.**—The following points concerning the Old Testament must be noted in our St. Victorinus. He counts twenty-four books of the Old Testament when he says [Note: [Col. 0298D] Id., ibid., p. 55.]:

“The twenty-four elders are the twenty-four books of the prophets and the Law, which bear witness to the judgment. . . . ‘SIX WINGS’ are the testimonies of the books of the Old Testament. Therefore, six multiplied by four makes twenty-four, as many as there are elders [Col. 0298B] sitting upon the judgment seats. . . . Now the books of the Old Testament which are received are twenty-four; you will find them in the *Epitomes of Theodore* [Note: [Col. 0298D] Id., ibid., p. 56 A. Like many other monuments of this Theodore, they have perished. Concerning him, Gallandius says in note 1: “I have nothing that I can report to you with certainty; for chronological considerations prevent me from affirming that he is either Theodore of Heraclea or Theodore of Antioch.”].”

Almost the same words occur in Victorinus’s *Commentary on the Apocalypse*, in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, vol. III, p. 417.

**The Connection of the Old Testament with the New.**—The holy martyr and bishop further teaches that the new covenant ought to possess its faith and foundation in the old covenant, upon which it rests and is, as it were, built. For he writes [Note: [Col. 0298D] Victorinus, scholia on Apocalypse, p. 55 D. Compare Victorinus, commentary on Apocalypse, p. 417 A, in the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, loc. cit.]:

“And the proclamation with the ‘new’ signifies the Christian people singing a new song—that is, publicly declaring its own formation. It is new that the Son of God should become man; new, that he should ascend bodily into heaven; new, that he should grant forgiveness of sins to humankind; new, [Col. 0298C] that he should seal people with the Holy Spirit; new, that he should receive the priesthood of sacred observance and await the kingdom of the boundless promise.

“The lyre, and its string stretched upon wood, signifies Christ’s flesh joined to the wood of the Passion; the bowl signifies confession and the propagation of the new priesthood. The praise of the many angels—indeed, of all—is the salvation of all and the testimony of the whole creation, offering thanksgiving to our Lord for humankind’s deliverance from the calamity of death. The unsealing of the seals is the opening of the Old Testament and the foretelling by the prophets of the things that will occur at the last time [Note: [Col. 0298D] Id., ibid., p. 56 D–E; in this volume, p. [page number absent]; and commentary on Apocalypse, p. 417 F.].”

Concerning Jesus Christ our Lord, St. Victorinus teaches [Note: [Col. 0298D] Id., ibid., p. 59 A.] that he is the Son of God, begotten with the Father before the beginning of the age, made man in a true soul and [Col. 0298D] flesh—made man for our salvation [Note: [Col. 0298D] Id., ibid., p. 55 C.]:

“We say”—these are [Col. 0299A] St. Victorinus’s words [Note: [Col. 0299D] Victorinus, scholia on Apocalypse, p. 55 D. Compare the commentary, p. 417, and the commentary on Apocalypse, p. 59 A.]—“that we confess the Father to be almighty, and Christ to be his Son, begotten with the Father before the beginning of the age, made man in a true soul and flesh; that, after both misery and death had been overcome, he was received bodily into heaven by the Father; and that he poured out the Holy Spirit, the gift and pledge of immortality.”

**The Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit.**—In the fragment *On the Creation of the World*, he discusses the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit in the following manner [Note: [Col. 0299D] Victorinus, *On the Creation of the World*, nos. 5 and 6, in Gallandius, p. 50, and in this volume.]:

“These seven Spirits are the names of the Spirit who rested upon Christ of God—Isaiah 11. The highest heaven, therefore, is that of wisdom; the second, understanding; the third, counsel; the fourth, might; the fifth, knowledge; the sixth, piety; and the seventh, fear of God. Thus, when this Word made light, he is called wisdom; when he made heaven, understanding; [Col. 0299B] when earth and sea, counsel; when the sun and moon and the other things, manifest might; when he calls forth the things of earth and sea, knowledge; when he fashioned man, piety; when he blessed and sanctified man, he bears the name fear of God.”

**Fasting on the Day of Preparation. Celebration of the Lord’s Day, and the Sabbath Changed into the Lord’s Day.**—St. Victorinus also mentions the celebration of the Lord’s Day and the Sabbath’s change into the Lord’s Day, when he speaks as follows [Note: [Col. 0299D] Id., ibid., p. 49, nos. 2 and 3.]:

“And, to explain the matter more fully: behold the four living creatures before the throne of God, the four Gospels, the four rivers flowing in paradise, the four generations of peoples—from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, from Abraham to Moses, and from Moses to Christ the Lord, the Son of God.

“On the fifth day the earth and water brought forth their offspring. On the sixth day [Col. 0299C] the things that were lacking were created, and thus God fashioned man from the soil as lord of all the things that he had created upon the earth and upon the water. Yet he first created the angels and archangels. This sixth day is called the *Parasceve*, that is, the preparation of the kingdom. He therefore completed his works before creating the angels and fashioned man afterward, lest perhaps they falsely claim that they had been his helpers. On this day also, on account of the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ, we either keep a station before God or fast.

“On the seventh day he rested from all his works, blessed it, and sanctified it. Therefore, so that on the Lord’s Day we may proceed to the bread with thanksgiving and may not appear to observe the Sabbath with the Jews, we customarily join the *Parasceve* and the Sabbath together. Christ [Col. 0299D] therefore abolished the Sabbath in his body. Joshua the son of Nun likewise abolished the Sabbath; for on the Sabbath day he commanded the children of Israel to march around the walls of the city of Jericho with trumpeters and to declare war against the Philistines. Mattathias, the leader of Judah, also abolished the Sabbath; for on the Sabbath he killed an officer of the former king of Syria and subjected the Philistines by his pursuit. Accordingly, that true Sabbath is the seven thousand years in which Christ is to reign with his elect.”

[Col. 0300A] Editions of the works of St. Victorinus of Poetovio.—The treatise of St. Victorinus *On the Creation of the World* was first published by Cave, vol. I of the *Literary History of Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 103, London, folio, 1689; it was reprinted with several critical notes by the distinguished Walker at Oxford in 1740 and at Basel in 1741, pp. 148–151, in Cave’s *Literary History*. Gallandi followed this latter edition when reprinting the present fragment of Victorinus in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. IV, pp. 40–52; in his customary manner, he divided it into several sections and enlarged it with a number of observations.

The *Scholia of St. Victorinus of Poetovio on the Apocalypse*, first published at Bologna in octavo by Basilio Millanio in 1558, were included by Gallandi in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*, vol. IV, pp. 52–64. [Col. 0300B] The indefatigable Fr. Dominicus Schramm provides an analysis of these two little works in vol. VIII, pp. 24–56.

The *Commentary of St. Victorinus on the Apocalypse*, whose first edition remains unknown to me (so writes the distinguished Albert Fabricius, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. VI, book 20, p. 295, Mansi’s edition, Padua, quarto, 1754), was subsequently included in the collections of the Fathers: the Paris edition of 1644, vol. I, from p. 507; and the Lyons edition, vol. III, pp. 414–421.

Two poems—one *On Jesus Christ, God and Man*, and the other entitled *On the Passover*, or *The Tree of Life*—were printed on p. 761 of Gregor Fabricius’s *Christian Works of the Ancient Ecclesiastical Poets*.

Among these little works falsely ascribed to Victorinus belongs [Col. 0300C] the edition produced at Gotha by the press of Reyher, through Johann Michael Schallius, 1652, octavo: *The Sacred Remains of Two Victorini: One, Victorinus of Poitiers, Bishop and Martyr; the Other, the African Gaius Marius, First a Roman Rhetorician and a Most Distinguished Man of Consular Rank Converted to the Faith, and Subsequently a Most Subtle Disputant; That Is, Their Christian Writings in Prose* (the printed *prorsa* should be attributed to a typographical error) *and Verse: Namely, the Former’s Commentary on the Apocalypse of John, and Three Most Elegant Poems on Jesus Christ, God and Man, on His Passover or Cross, and on the Seven Maccabean Brothers and Martyrs; and the Latter’s*, etc. *Each and Every Work, with Notes and a Preface by Dr. Andreas Rivinus (Professor at Leipzig), Who Had Them Printed at His Own Expense.*

On the men named Victorinus.—By way of conclusion, it must be noted here, [Col. 0300D] first, that the most learned Launoy observes in his second, shorter dissertation [Note: [Col. 0300D] Launoy, *Works*, vol. II, p. 945 ff.] that five different authors were distinguished by the same name, namely Victorinus. The first was a defender of Praxeas’s opinion, mentioned by Tertullian [Note: [Col. 0300D] Tertullian, *On the Prescription of Heretics*, ch. 53]; the second was the Victorinus discussed thus far. A certain Roman rhetorician, of whom Augustine speaks [Note: [Col. 0300D] Augustine, *Confessions*, book VIII, ch. 2], is counted third. The fourth was the man of Marseille mentioned by Gennadius [Note: [Col. 0300D] Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 60. Compare Sidonius, *Letters*, book V, letter 21. In Cave’s judgment, this Victorinus of Marseille flourished in the year 434]. Finally, the last, or [Col. 0301A] fifth, was an orator surnamed Lampadius, whom Photius mentions [Note: [Col. 0301A] Photius, *Library*, codex 101, p. 276]. See this dissertation.

Second, Pope Gelasius of Rome included the little works of Victorinus among the apocrypha in his decree [Note: [Col. 0301A] Labbe, *Councils*, vol. IV, p. 1261, and Mansi, *Collection of Councils*, vol. VIII, col. 152], perhaps because they were tainted by the error of the millenarians, as Jerome testifies in several places. But in the judgment of the most learned Christian Friedrich Schmidt [Note: [Col. 0301A] Chr. Frid. Schmidt, *Ancient History and Vindication of the Canon*, p. 335, note], we would by no means call the passages from Jerome beyond exception. For although it can rightly be affirmed that the writers whom Jerome censures held chiliasm and, in describing it, departed here and there from John’s Apocalypse, it is nevertheless utterly false that those same men were devoted to the gross opinions which the ancients were accustomed to ascribe to Cerinthus, and which Lardner, with excessive credulity (*The Credibility of the Gospel History*, vol. II, part II, p. 649 ff.), supposes that the orthodox teachers shared with that Cerinthus. LUMPER.

[Col. 0301]

FRAGMENT OF ST. VICTORINUS, MARTYR AND BISHOP OF POETOVIO, WHO FLOURISHED TOWARD THE END OF THE THIRD CENTURY. (C, S)

[Note: [Col. 0301B]

Victorinus’s Treatise *On the Creation of the World*. William Cave explains his reason for publishing this short commentary in the following words, *Literary History*, vol. I, p. 147:

> “I possess a hitherto unpublished treatise of Victorinus *On the Creation of the World*, which the distinguished Henry Maurice, S.T.P., domestic chaplain to the lord archbishop, copied from an ancient manuscript in the Lambeth Library and kindly communicated to me. And now, for a second time, the most learned and candid John Batteley, doctor of theology and chaplain to the same archbishop, has collated it through to the end of the manuscript codex. The manuscript does not say who this Victorinus was. Both the style [Col. 0301C] and the subject itself, however, openly proclaim that it is our Victorinus, especially since the error of the Chiliasts is plainly defended in it, an error which Jerome reports that our Victorinus cherished (*On Illustrious Men*, ch. 18). This little book appears to be a certain fragment (*ἀποσπασμάτιον*, ‘small extract’) taken either from a commentary on Genesis or from one on the Apocalypse. I shall therefore append it here, both because of its venerable antiquity and because of the fame of this most celebrated martyr. Thus, then, the Lambeth codex reads, though it is certainly corrupt in several places, which occasionally render the meaning less clear. We have placed in the margin certain conjectures supplied by the aforesaid scholars.”

Thus far that most excellent man. Subsequently, however, the learned editor of that new edition of Cave’s *History* not only arranged for this little work to be reprinted, but also added another carefully made copy of the Lambeth codex, together with the following account of it:

> “This manuscript codex, which Henry Maurice copied and John Batteley subsequently collated—each being domestic chaplain to the lord Archbishop of Canterbury—is a parchment quarto codex in the Lambeth Library, [Col. 0302B] numbered there as no. 90. It is certainly ancient, being approximately eight hundred years old. Among various treatises by other authors it contains this work of Victorinus *On the Creation of the World*, beginning on p. 71. It cannot be sufficiently cleared of corruptions without the assistance of another codex, as has also happened with other books resting upon a single manuscript codex, such as Velleius Paterculus, Minucius, and Arnobius. Since, however, it had previously been copied and collated with little accuracy, the distinguished J. Walker, S.T.P., collated it once again against the manuscript codex and, for the reader’s benefit, added some brief critical notes.”

Comparison with the [Col. 0302C] manuscript codex sufficiently proved to me that this last recension was exceedingly accurate. At my request the comparison was undertaken by Henry John Todd, a man most highly deserving of his native language and humane letters, who is keeper of the lord archbishop’s library. Finally, I resolved to add my own contribution to the corrections of the distinguished Walker—whose services to Cicero are sufficiently well known through John Davies—so that the discourse of the holy martyr might emerge in a purer, if not entirely clarified, form. In vol. IV of his *Library of the Fathers*, Gallandi reproduced both Walker’s copy and his notes, and himself divided the little work into sections. ROUTH.

“And reflecting together with my mind.” I have ventured to supply the particle *et* (“and”). ROUTH.
