“This is the speed of that creation.” This wording is at least rather harsh; it should not, however, be tampered with, since the entire discourse is rough and scarcely Latin. ROUTH.

“Creation” (*conditione*). *Old Glosses*: *Conditio*, κατάστασις (“constitution, condition”). In this passage, indeed, the word is employed for the act of creation; among ecclesiastical writers, it is more commonly used for a created thing. [Col. 0302D] ROUTH.

“On the seventh . . . consecrated.” The manuscript reads: *septimo quibus laborem* [Col. 0303B] *benedictione ::: consegravit*, with *c* written above *g*. The words *quibus laborem* have been struck through with a small line by a recent hand. From the traces of the older writing I restore it thus: *septimo quievit a labore et benedictione consecravit* (“on the seventh he rested from labor and consecrated it with a blessing”). So below: “On the seventh day he rested from all his works and blessed it.” WALKER.—If these corrections by the distinguished man ought to be admitted into the text, I for my part would think that, [Col. 0303C] since a space was left in the manuscript before the word *consecravit*, *eum* (“it”) should be added. But, to tell the truth, these words appear to depart widely from the shapes of the letters; I would therefore prefer to substitute *quietus* (“at rest”) for *quibus* and add *sua* (“his”) after *benedictione*. ROUTH.]

HERE BEGINS VICTORINUS’S TREATISE ON THE CREATION OF THE WORLD

[Col. 0301B]

AS I REFLECT [Note: [Col. 0301B] Manuscript: *Cogitante*; Gallandi] and [Note: [Col. 0301B] Perhaps *et* should be added; Routh], together with my own mind, consider the creation of this world in which we are kept enclosed, such too is the speed of that creation, as is contained in the book of Moses [Col. 0302B] which he wrote concerning its creation and which is called Genesis. God brought forth that entire mass in six days as the adornment [Note: [Col. 0301B] Perhaps *Ornamentum*; Routh] of his majesty; on the seventh, at rest [Note: [Col. 0302B] Perhaps *Quietus*; Routh], he consecrated it with his [Note: [Col. 0302B] Perhaps *Sua* should be supplied; Routh] blessing. Accordingly, since heavenly and earthly things are governed by the sevenfold number of days, I shall begin by measuring from this week the reckoning of all weeks, and [Col. 0303A] [Note: [Col. 0303C]

“The seventh . . . regions.” The manuscript reads: *septimam ad omnium septimarium regionum*. I read: *de hac septimana omnium septimanarum rationem metibor* (“from this week I shall measure the reckoning of all weeks”). Below: “which is to pass beyond the order of the week’s arrangement.” WALKER.

“The day of power unto that completion.” Perhaps it should be restored as: *virtutis divinae consummationem* (“the completion of divine power”). Below, at p. 306, line 2, you have: “God . . . completed his works.” ROUTH.

“I shall attempt.” Gallandi says: “Walker read *conamur* (‘we attempt’). But the preceding *metibor* (‘I shall measure’), *prout potuero* (‘as far as I can’), favor the reading *conabor* (‘I shall attempt’). So below, §6: ‘As far as my small understanding can, I shall attempt to show.’” In the manuscript, however, the letter *u* is written above the second *o* in *conamor*; it was not added or substituted by Walker. Cave’s copy has *conabor*. ROUTH.

“Twelvefold.” The manuscript has *duodecinario*. Cave’s copy had corrected it. ROUTH.

“Rest . . . would bring on.” Walker correctly reads *requietis* (“of rest”) for *requies* (“rest”); Cave’s copy supplies *superduceret* (“would bring on”) in place of the manuscript reading *superdoceret*. ROUTH.

“Thus it . . . might be moderated.” Walker’s corrections were: *Hac se alterna vice labor quietis refoveretur* (“by this alternating succession labor would be refreshed by rest”), and *ac sic* (“and thus”), and *quiete noctis* (“by the rest of night”). You have *ac sic* below at p. 305, line 6. ROUTH.

“Greater and lesser . . . night.” Thus Cave’s copy corrected the manuscript reading *majus ut minus ut alterum praecessit diei alterum noctis* (“greater as lesser as one preceded the day, the other the night”); and immediately afterward it likewise substituted *caeteraque* (“and the other things”) for the manuscript’s *citheraque*. ROUTH.

“And the hours by their fixed intervals.” The manuscript reads *et horis praestationes*. I admit the conjecture appended in Cave’s margin. ROUTH.

“The fourth day, the *tetras*, etc.” Among the ancient Christians, the *stationes*—that is, religious worship [Col. 0304B] and fasting—were customarily held both on the fourth day, which was called the *tetras*, and on the sixth, called *parasceve*. They lasted until the ninth hour or even until evening. When, however, the time was prolonged, they were called fasts, not *stations*, as the author says below, p. 306, line 5: “On this day also—the sixth—we undertake either a station for God or a fast.” Indeed, as St. Victorinus shows, the fast of the fourth day was sometimes extended into the following day; this is a “superposition.” See the note above on St. Dionysius’s letter to Basilides, vol. II, p. 419. *Aut* (“or”) should be added before “until evening.” ROUTH.

“The fourfold number of seasons.” Walker advises deleting *temporum* (“of seasons”), since it was transferred here from what follows. Cave’s copy had substituted *tetradem* for *tetrade*. ROUTH.

“From that fact.” So excellently, says Walker, the learned men wrote in the margin of Cave’s edition instead of *ex aere*. I have therefore adopted it. ROUTH.

“Four generations of peoples, from Adam,” etc. I do not understand what Victorinus had in mind here, unless he found as many origins of nations in each of those four genealogies. ROUTH.

“And four living creatures,” etc.—That is, in Revelation 4:6. The *Commentary on the Apocalypse*, Paris *Library of the Fathers*, vol. I, p. 1249, ascribed to our Victorinus, maintains that these living creatures signify the four evangelists. Professors of the art of painting, when depicting the evangelists, were accustomed to place those same animals beside them as symbols or signs. Indeed, Irenaeus, book III, ch. 11, pursuing two parallel lines of argument, attempted to show that precisely four Gospels had to exist for this reason. Judge from John’s vision whether the word *similia* (“like”) has dropped out after *animalia* (“living creatures”) in Victorinus. ROUTH.

“Euphrates. Man.” Walker wishes to read: “and Euphrates. And Man.” In the first place, however, the conjunction would be superfluous, although in the second it would not be objectionable. Shortly afterward, following the manuscript as the distinguished Todd advised, I printed *auctor* in place of *autor*. ROUTH.

“On the fourth day, by the impious.” Here and a little below the manuscript has *tetradem*. Both Cave’s copy and Walker corrected it. I confess that I can scarcely understand how Christ is said to have been arrested on the *tetras*, or fourth day. Epiphanius, however, has a parallel statement in *Exposition of the Catholic Faith*, §22:

> “The assemblies (*συνάξεις*) appointed by the apostles are held on the fourth day, on the day before the Sabbath, and on the Lord’s Day; and on the fourth day and the day before the Sabbath with fasting until the ninth hour, since, as the fourth day was dawning, [Col. 0305B] the Lord was arrested,” etc.

But these words must be interpreted as referring to the impious counsel then formed by the Jews for carrying out their criminal deed; compare Mark 14:1. I note in passing that the distinguished Montfaucon wrongly placed these words of Epiphanius among the “unedited” texts (*ἀνέκδοτα*) of the Coislin Library. See the preface to the catalogue, fol. 3 verso, and p. 112, where they are cited as though they belonged to Athanasius. But, leaving this aside, my interpretation is confirmed by the final canon of St. Peter of Alexandria, which teaches the following:

> “No one will accuse us for observing the fourth day and the Preparation, on which we have reasonably been commanded by tradition to fast: the fourth day because of the counsel taken by the Jews for the betrayal of the Lord, and the Preparation because he suffered for us; for the Lord’s Day is a day of rejoicing,” etc.

The canon should be restored thus, as others too have advised, from the most ancient manuscripts. On the observance of the fourth day and the Preparation, [Col. 0305C] I shall make further observations in that same place on St. Peter of Alexandria. ROUTH.]

as far as I am able, I shall attempt to express the day of divine power in relation to that completion.

In the beginning God made light and divided it into the twelvefold measure of the hours, into day and night. This was plainly so that night, as a place of rest, might follow upon the day devoted to human labors, and day in turn might overcome it; and thus, by this alternating succession, labor might be refreshed by the rest of night, while rest in turn might be moderated by the activity of day. On the fourth day he made two luminaries in heaven, the greater and the lesser, so that one might govern the day and the other the night (Gen. 1:16–17), namely the sun and the moon. He also placed the other stars in heaven, so that they might shine upon the earth and distinguish seasons, years, months, days, and hours by their fixed intervals.

The rationale of the truth is now disclosed: why the fourth day is called the *tetras*; [Col. 0303B] why we fast until the ninth hour, [Col. 0304A] until evening, or why a “superposition” is made until the next day. This world, then, consists of four elements: fire, water, heaven, and earth. These four elements therefore constitute a fourfold number. The sun and moon likewise produce four seasons over the course of the year—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—and these seasons constitute a fourfold number. And, to develop the matter further, behold: four living creatures before the throne of God (Rev. 4:6); four Gospels; four rivers flowing in Paradise (Gen. 2:10); four generations of peoples, from Adam to Noah, from Noah to Abraham, from Abraham to Moses, and from Moses to Christ the Lord, the Son of God; four living creatures (Rev. 4:7), namely the man, calf, lion, and eagle; and four rivers (Gen. 2:11), Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, and Euphrates. The man Christ Jesus, the author of the things [Col. 0304B] we have mentioned above, was arrested by the impious on the fourth day, [Col. 0305A] [Note: [Col. 0305C]

“On the fourth day because of majesty.” The manuscript has *tetradem*, in place of which Walker substitutes *tetrade*; but I would read *tetrade*, etc. ROUTH.

“And the seasons . . . run their course.” Walker says that the conjunction *et* (“and”) should be deleted and, in his opinion, *decurrunt* (“run their course”) should be written for *decurrant* (“may run their course”). I would, however, prefer to read *ut* (“so that”) in place of *et*, and *humanitati* (“for humanity”) in place of *humanitatis* (“of humanity”). ROUTH.

“Therefore we undertake either [a station or] a superposition.” See what I observed a little above at col. 304. According to Walker’s copy, the manuscript reads *ideo aut superstitionem facimus* (“therefore we undertake either superstition”). In Cave’s margin *autem* is corrected for *aut*, while in the copy itself *superpositionem* was placed in lieu of *superstitionem*, which, according to Walker’s collation, is read in the manuscript. The facts are otherwise, however, according to the distinguished Todd. Because of what shortly follows at line 2, p. 306—“On this day also . . . we undertake either a station for God or a fast”—I have ventured to add what you see in the text. ROUTH.

[Col. 0305D] “And thus God [formed] man.” In the manuscript codex these four words are placed before “on the sixth day”; but, as Walker advises, everything becomes clear when the words are restored to the present order in Cave’s copy. ROUTH.

“Than” (*quam*). This conjunction seems rightly to have been added in the copy. A little later it is maintained that angels were created neither before the world was established nor on the days preceding the sixth, but only on the sixth day. Different persons, however, hold different opinions concerning a matter which either does not occur at all in Holy Scripture or is at least not clearly signified there. ROUTH.

“Earth.” So the manuscript reads, and *creavit* (“created”) is supplied in the margin of Cave’s copy; but I prefer Walker’s correction. Meanwhile, from the beginning of Genesis itself I infer something different from this doctrine of Victorinus. Light was indeed created on the first day, before the heavenly luminaries made on the fourth day, but not before heaven and earth. Julius Africanus wrote in his *Chronicle*, above at vol. II, p. 124: “still unorganized” (*ἀδιοργάνιστον*); “for the time being [on the first day], the first-created light, poured abroad” (*τέως τὸ πρωτόκτιστον φῶς καὶ κεχυμένον*). [Col. 0306B] ROUTH.

“The preparation, that is, of the kingdom.” That is, of the great Sabbath, or the kingdom of Christ, concerning which you will see something below. ROUTH.

“Whom.” In Cave’s margin they add: “The words ‘was created on the sixth day’ are missing.” But with a slight alteration I read: “For Adam he completed in [his] image . . .” deleting *quem* (“whom”). WALKER.

“They might assert.” I have recorded this emendation of Walker. The manuscript has *asseverant* (“they assert”); Cave’s copy, *asseverent* (“they may assert”). A little above, the manuscript has *crearet* (“might create”) for *creavit* (“created”), which was corrected in the copy. ROUTH.

“We undertake either a station for God or a fast.” In this passage of Victorinus, *statio* is used not only for what is called an assembly but also for abstinence, and it was of shorter duration, as I said above, than a fast. [Col. 0306C] The latter lasted until evening and, unlike a station, did not end at the ninth hour. Thus the author states above that on the fourth day it was customary to abstain from food either until the ninth hour or until evening, p. 303, line 17. ROUTH.

“On this day we customarily make a superposition.” Council of Elvira, canon XXXVI: “It was resolved that the error be corrected, so that on every Sabbath day we may celebrate the prolongation of the fast.” Tertullian, however, disapproved of this custom of fasting on the Sabbath, which the Roman Church at least, together with other Christians, embraced. In *Against the Psychics*, ch. 14, he writes: “Even if you [Catholics] sometimes prolong the Sabbath fast, you never fast on it except at Easter, according to the reason given elsewhere.” Thus he writes. Victorinus, however, continues: “And let a superposition be made on the Preparation, lest we appear in any way to observe the Sabbath with the Jews.” I interpret these words as follows. Since all feast days customarily began at sunset, Christians had to prolong the fast of the sixth day, which lasted until evening, [Col. 0306D] lest they appear to celebrate and observe the Sabbath as a feast together with the Jews, who were accustomed to keep the Sabbath as a holiday. Above, Victorinus had said of the fourth day: “Why we fast until the ninth hour or until evening, or why a superposition is made until the next day.” Nevertheless, the Greeks and other Eastern Christians, who in accordance with the ancient custom of observing the Sabbath were accustomed not to fast on that day except at Easter, later attempted to reverse the accusation and charge the Latins with Judaizing. Thus Matthew Blastares, in the *Alphabetical Syntagma*, letter A, p. 9, writes the following about Sabbatius, leader of the Sabbatians:

> “But out of ambition for what was worse, he chose to observe the Sabbath in Jewish fashion, practicing a fast on it and doing the other things similarly to them, as the Latins too do at the present day.”

This is in Beveridge’s *Synodicon*. There the practice of fasting on the Sabbath is censured, not because the Jews customarily fasted on that day—for, on the contrary, they feasted—but because Sabbatius and the Latins observed the seventh day, like the unbelieving Jews, as though it were sacred. [Col. 0307B] ROUTH.]

Therefore, on the fourth day, because of his arrest and because of the majesty of his works, and so that the seasons may run their course beneficially for humanity, fruitful in crops and calm in weather, we undertake either a station or a superposition.

On the fifth day earth and water brought forth their offspring. On the sixth day the things that were still lacking were created; and thus God formed man from the soil, as lord of all the things that he had created upon the earth and upon the water. Yet he created angels and archangels before he fashioned man, giving spiritual things precedence over earthly things. For light came before heaven and earth. This sixth day is called *parasceve*, that is, the preparation of the kingdom; for Adam he completed in his own image and likeness. He therefore completed his works before creating the angels and fashioning man, lest perhaps they falsely assert that they had been his assistants. On this day also, because of the Passion of the Lord Jesus Christ, we undertake either a station for God or a fast. On the seventh day he rested from all his works, and blessed and sanctified it. On this day we customarily make a superposition, so that on the Lord’s Day we may come forth to the bread with thanksgiving. And let a superposition be made on the Preparation, lest we appear in any respect to observe the Sabbath together with the Jews, which Christ himself, the Lord of the Sabbath, declares through his prophets [Col. 0307A] [Note: [Col. 0307B]

“Which Sabbath.” The manuscript reads *quod sabbato* (“which on the Sabbath”). I read: *quod sabbatum corpore suo resolvit* (“which Sabbath he abolished in his body”). So below. WALKER.—See the passage of the Apostle at Ephesians 2:14–15.

“Which day.” Walker advises writing *dies* (“day”) for *die* (“on the day”), though there is reason to doubt this emendation. John 7:23 is indicated, where the following occurs: “Therefore Moses gave you circumcision—not because it is from Moses, but from the fathers—and on the Sabbath you circumcise a man.” Here the author used *plerumque* (“generally”) for “often,” unless the following passage of Epiphanius, *Heresies* XXX, no. 32, persuades you otherwise:

> “For it is shown that those who circumcise the newborn child on the Sabbath, if they wish to observe the eighth day with precision and find that it falls on the Sabbath, perform a work by circumcising him and abolish the Sabbath; but if they postpone it so as not to abolish the Sabbath, they then perform the circumcision on the ninth day and abolish circumcision and the commandment’s prescribed limit of eight days.”

Thus Victorinus may be understood to have said that circumcision is generally performed on the Sabbath if that day is the eighth after the child’s birth. ROUTH.

“We were reading,” etc. “All these words,” says Walker, “are exceedingly corrupt.” In the margin of Cave’s copy it is noted: “Perhaps *quod* is missing before *ante ipsum*, and perhaps *praelioque* should be read for *praelio quae*.” The passage is plainly difficult to correct; I must attempt it according to my ability. Unless I am mistaken, Victorinus is referring to Exodus 17, where it is related that after Moses had said to Joshua, “Choose men and go out to fight against Amalek . . . when Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but if he lowered them a little, Amalek prevailed . . . and Joshua routed Amalek and his people by the edge of the sword.” The holy man Victorinus inferred that this happened on the Sabbath, perhaps from the stages in the journey of the people of Israel, [Col. 0307D] or perhaps he followed some Jewish tradition. Light will be shed upon the passage by Tertullian’s exposition of Moses’ words in book III *Against Marcion*, to omit other authors:

> “Now Moses, only at that particular time when Jesus [Joshua] was fighting against Amalek, prayed while seated with hands outspread. Yet when the situation was so critical, he ought surely instead to have entrusted his prayer to God on bent knees, with hands beating his breast and face lowered to the ground, unless it was because, where the name of the Lord Jesus was fighting—he who would one day fight against the devil—the posture of the cross was also necessary, through which Jesus would gain the victory,” ch. 18.

Thus Tertullian. Then the apostle Paul speaks as follows in Colossians 2:14: “Erasing the written record of the decree that stood against us and was contrary to us, he removed it from our midst, fastening it to the cross.” Moreover, as Sabellicus relates the matter from 1 Maccabees 2 in his *Sacred History Extracted from His Enneads*, book VI, p. 279, London edition, the pagans “attempted to bring the Jews down from the mountains. But since they could be moved by neither exhortation nor threats, on the Sabbath day, when the Jews were forbidden by their ancestral custom to fight, the enemies entered the mountains and, with no one resisting them, cruelly killed more than a thousand in the caves by sword and fire. A law was then first enacted permitting them to fight on Sabbaths against enemies in defense of their lives.” Victorinus is referring to this, unless I am again mistaken, in the latter part of the sentence. Why, then, should the discourse not proceed well enough as follows?

> “Moses, foreseeing the hardness of that people”—Israel, hostile both to Christ and to the new law, and therefore rejected—“accordingly raised his hands on the Sabbath day, and thus fixed him to the cross. And on the Sabbath they were sought in battle by foreigners, so that they might be captured and, as it were, be shaped by the severity of the law for avoiding discipline,”

that is, the ceremonial law. For after the other examples cited, there follows this statement, set in opposition to the ancient Sabbath: “so that the true and [Col. 0308C] righteous Sabbath might be observed in the seventh millennium of years,” p. 309, line 8. In the manuscript, moreover, an *i* is written above the second *e* in *devetando*. ROUTH.

“On the eighth day.” In the margin of Cave’s copy it is noted: “The title of Psalm 6 is ‘concerning the eighth’ (*ὑπὲρ τῆς ὀγδόης*).” Bede writes in his *Hexaemeron*:

> “For in the title of the Psalm it is said, ‘Unto the end, among hymns, a psalm of David concerning the eighth.’ The entire text of the following Psalm shows that this was written concerning the day of judgment. In it the prophet, fearing the wrath of the judgment to come, cries out: ‘Lord, do not accuse me in your judgment, nor rebuke me in your fury,’” etc.

See p. 21, vol. IV, of Bede’s works published at Basel. And long before him Basil the Great had written as follows in *On the Holy Spirit*, ch. 27, concerning the Lord’s Day, or “the first day of the week” (*τῇ μιᾷ τοῦ σαββάτου*):

> “This same day is therefore both the first and the eighth, revealing through itself that truly first and genuine eighth day which the psalmist too recalled in certain titles of the Psalms: the state after the present age, the unceasing day, the day without evening, the day without successor, that endless [Col. 0308D] and ageless age.”

See p. 56 of the Benedictine edition. Asterius likewise writes in his *Homily on Psalm 6*, in Cotelier’s *Monuments of the Greek Church*, vol. II: “Singing the psalm concerning the eighth day and the resurrection of the dead, he prayed,” p. 56. Most interpreters, however, have understood this title differently. Meanwhile, compare the Fourth Council of Carthage on the eighth day itself, or the future age. This doctrine concerning an eighth age had indeed become prevalent among the ancients from the very beginnings of Christianity. ROUTH.

“Which is to pass beyond the order of the week’s arrangement,” etc. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VII, p. 866, Potter’s edition:

> “After the final excellence attained in the flesh, always changing for the better in accordance with what is fitting, he hastens through the holy seven-day period to the paternal court, to that which is truly the Lord’s Day alone.”

In Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 37, and in Theodoret, *Interpretation of the Psalms*, p. 640, Schulze’s edition, the *ogdoad*, or eightfold period, signifies the kingdom of heaven, which is to follow the final judgment. ROUTH.

“Jesus [Joshua] son of Nun,” etc. The proof cited here, together with the other examples and arguments advanced by Victorinus for the future abolition of the Sabbath, may all be found, if I remember correctly, both in Justin Martyr and in Tertullian’s works. The latter, however, in book IV, ch. 12, *Against Marcion*, distinguishes in the commandment of the Decalogue between human work, or “your work,” and divine work; and he therefore maintains that the Sabbath was not abolished even by the carrying of the ark around Jericho. ROUTH.]

that he hates in his soul (Isa. 1:13–14); this Sabbath he abolished in his own body. Earlier, moreover, when he himself commanded Moses that circumcision should not pass beyond the eighth day—which often falls on the Sabbath—as we read written in the Gospel (John 7:22), Moses, foreseeing the hardness of that people (Matt. 19:8), therefore raised his hands on the Sabbath day and thus fixed him to the cross (Exod. 17:9, 12; Col. 2:14). And on the Sabbath they were sought in battle by foreigners (1 Macc. 2:31–41), so that they might be captured and, as it were, be shaped by the severity of the law for avoiding discipline.

And therefore, in the sixth Psalm, concerning the eighth day, David asks the Lord not to accuse or judge him in his wrath or fury (Ps. 6:1). For this is truly the eighth day of that future judgment, which is to pass beyond the order of the week’s arrangement. Jesus [Joshua] son of Nun, Moses’ successor, likewise abolished the Sabbath; for on the Sabbath day he commanded the children of Israel (Josh. 6:3) to go around the walls of the city [Col. 0309A] [Note: [Col. 0309C]

“Of Antiochus.” Since the margin of Cave’s copy advised that this should be read in place of *antiqui* (“of the ancient”), I have adopted it. ROUTH.

“Isaiah too, and the rest of his colleagues.” Where are Isaiah and the other prophets said to have abolished the Sabbath? Yet I cannot explain how *Isaiah* intruded in place of *David*. In St. Matthew 12:3, Jesus asks the Pharisees: “Have you not read what David did when he and those who were with him were hungry?” See also St. Mark and St. Luke. The manuscript has *collegi* (“I gathered”), from which the distinguished Walker wishes to read *collegii* (“of the college”); but in this instance I have followed Cave’s copy. ROUTH.

“So that the true.” The manuscript has “and the true.” But I have followed the conjecture of the learned men who annotated Cave’s copy. ROUTH.

“Each.” Perhaps *singulis* (“for each”) should be read. Chiliasts customarily cite this passage from Psalm 89. ROUTH.

“I have the eyes of the Lord.” In Cave’s margin: “Perhaps, ‘the Lord has eyes.’” But *habeo* (“I have”) is correct, that is, “I hold” or “I find.” WALKER.—Zechariah 4:10: “These seven are the eyes of the Lord, which range throughout the whole earth.” ROUTH.

“And seven thousand years.” The manuscript has *millia*. It seems that one should read “is,” or “will be, in the seventh millennium,” or rather, as a little above, “in the seventh millenary of years.” Walker, however, advises only that the conjunction *et* (“and”) be deleted. Moreover, Victorinus, following several other Fathers, assigns the seventh millennium to the kingdom of Christ, which is hereafter to be celebrated together with his saints; it is to be followed by the final judgment and the ogdoad. That same ogdoad, however, was referred by others to the time of the Messiah, or the first coming of Christ. ROUTH.

“Are.” Walker advises deleting this. Concerning the seven heavens about which Victorinus speaks foolishly, what Origen says in book VI *Against Celsus*, no. 21, is true: “The Scriptures current in the churches of God do not proclaim seven heavens, or indeed any determinate number of them.” The same is also said by Origen at the end of no. 23. ROUTH.

“These seven spirits.” I have thought that these words should be distinguished from what follows. Nor would I, with the learned men who made several annotations in Cave’s margin, change *eorum spiritus* (“their spirit”) to *eorum spirituum* (“of their spirits”). ROUTH.

“Spirit of fear.” The manuscript has *spiritu timoris* (“by the spirit of fear”), but Walker says that it should be corrected as above in accordance with the text of Isaiah. ROUTH.

“The thunders bellow, the rivers are extended.” In Cave’s margin: “Perhaps ‘lightning bolts.’” I read: “lightning bolts are kindled.” WALKER.—Pliny, *Natural History*, book II, ch. 38: “Hence clouds, thunders, and other lightning bolts.” “From this, therefore,” etc.—that is, from the heaven of the fear of God. ROUTH.

“Fires mass together.” I am uncertain whether it should be rewritten as “fires mass themselves together,” or whether the author uses the verb *conglobo* in this sense, although the expression would be more elegant if understood in the sense of administration or expiation. See Gesner in the *Thesaurus of the Roman Language*. ROUTH.

“The care of a dreadful head of hair will be undertaken.” Perhaps it should be written: “care is taken concerning a dreadful comet.” Samuel Crell, however, conjectured that it should be restored as: “dreadful heads of hair run.” ROUTH.

“Sometimes the sun also approaches and is seen together with the moon.” I would read: “Sometimes it happens that the sun and moon are also seen together” (*invicem*, that is, “simultaneously”). Furthermore, in the words that follow, perhaps *aspectus* (“appearances”) should be restored in place of *aspectu* (“by an appearance”), and *efficiant* (“may produce”) in place of *efficiunt* (“produce”). ROUTH.]

But Jesus is the author of the whole creation. The manuscript reads: “they produce the authority of the whole creation, righteous,” etc. Hence I read: “they produce. But the author of this whole creation”—“Word” is his surname. Or: “But Jesus is the author of the whole creation.” Thus above: “The man Christ Jesus, their author.” See [Col. 0310D] Artemonius—that is, Samuel Crell—*Preface*, p. 21, before the beginning of the Gospel of John, etc., perversely dragging these words into his own hypothesis and corrupting them. WALKER.—Thus the Word of God is called “the father of the human race” by Irenaeus, or perhaps even by some Christian earlier than he. See Irenaeus, book IV, ch. 31, otherwise 51, p. 259, Massuet’s edition. The words “the authority of the whole creation” are joined to the preceding words in Cave’s transcript. And the distinguished P. Wesseling, *Probabilia*, ch. XIV, p. 117, when that excellent conjecture of Walker had not yet been published, concluded that *juste* (“justly”), or *justius* (“more justly”), had originally been written in place of *justus* (“righteous”). But because of Victorinus’s words found above at p. 305, I have judged Walker’s latter emendation preferable and have not hesitated to place it in the text here. If, however, anyone should prefer the other reading, “but the author of this whole creation,” it would seem to me that *auctori autem* should be restored in place of *auctoritatem*. Crell indeed wished to restore *istius* in place of *justus*, so as to emend the passage: “The Word is his surname,” that is, the Word of whom we have spoken above has “Word of God” as his surname. For since Victorinus adduces John 1:1 to prove that Christ is called the Word of God, it would follow that he read: “and the Word was of God.” Baraterius, in his *Anti-Artemonius, or The Beginning of the Gospel of John Vindicated*, part I, ch. 16, § III, p. 110, informed me, before I had seen Crell’s book, that Crell had reconstructed and argued the passage in this way; there he himself proposes the reading: “Of this Word, ‘God’ is the surname.” ROUTH.]

To go around Jericho with trumpeters and declare war against the foreigners. But Mattathias, the leader of Judah, relaxed the Sabbath; for on the Sabbath he killed the prefect of Antiochus, king of Syria (1 Macc. 2:26, 40, 41), and subdued the foreigners through his persecution of them. And we read in Matthew: Isaiah also, and his other colleagues, relaxed the Sabbath (Matt. 12:3), so that the true and righteous Sabbath might be observed in the seventh millennium of years.

For this reason the Lord assigned one thousand years to each of these seven days; for thus it is ordained: “In your sight, O Lord, a thousand years are as one day” (Ps. 89:4). Therefore, in God’s sight, the individual millennia have been established, for “I have the seven eyes of the Lord” (Zech. 4:10). Consequently, as I have recalled, that true Sabbath, and [Col. 0309B] seven thousand years [Note: [Col. 0309B] Perhaps: “It will be in the seventh millennium of years,” as above. Routh.] in which Christ is to reign with his elect [Col. 0310A]. There are also seven heavens [Note: [Col. 0309B] Perhaps “there are” should be deleted. Walker.], corresponding to those days; for thus it is ordained: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the spirit of his mouth all their power” (Ps. 32:6).

These are the seven spirits. Their names are the spirits that rested upon God’s Christ, as is ordained in the prophet Isaiah: “And there shall rest upon him the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of God filled him” (Isa. 11:2–3). The highest heaven, therefore, is that of wisdom; the second, of understanding; the third, of counsel; the fourth, of might; the fifth, of knowledge; the sixth, of piety; the seventh, of the fear of God.

From this, therefore, thunders roar, rivers are extended [Note: [Col. 0309B] Perhaps: “lightning bolts are kindled.” Walker.], fires mass together, burning beams appear, stars shine, a dreadful head of hair will be tended [Note: [Col. 0310B] Perhaps: “The dreadful comet is attended to.” Routh.]. Sometimes there also approaches [Note: [Col. 0310B] Perhaps: “It sometimes happens that.” Routh.] [Col. 0310B] the sun and moon visit one another [Note: [Col. 0310B] Perhaps: “are seen together.” Routh.]; and those still more fearsome things, [Col. 0311A]

[Note: [Col. 0311C]

“My heart has uttered a good word”; the Septuagint has Ἐξερεύξατο ἡ καρδία μου λόγον ἀγαθόν, “My heart uttered a good word.” The Vulgate indeed has: “My heart uttered a good word.” Nevertheless, whether Victorinus—who, according to Jerome above at p. 234, knew how to write Greek better than Latin—used *eructatum est* in place of *eructavit*, or rather understood that the heart had uttered, others may judge. ROUTH.

“Therefore the first was made,” etc. In Cave’s margin, *Dominus* (“Lord”) is substituted for *hominis* (“of man”). I embrace the emendation, but would wish to read the whole passage thus: “Therefore the first made is a creature; the second man is the Lord of the human race, as the Apostle says.” Namely, in 1 Corinthians 15:43, 47. Shortly afterward, at line 3, p. 240, occur the words: “that he might re-form that Adam over the course of a week and come to the aid of his whole creation.”

“This Word, therefore”–“bears the name Fear of God.” According to Walker, the words that follow had been written thus in the manuscript, while Cave’s transcript emended them: *coelu* for *coelum*, *terra* for *terram*, *sole et luna* for *solem et lunam*, *cum terrae ac maris* for *cum terram ac mare*, and *homine* for *hominem*. But the distinguished Todd attests that in the codex itself a later hand had written the letter *m* above most of these words. Meanwhile, I would prefer to read *timoris* in place of *timor*. ROUTH.

“Horns.” The manuscript has *cornuta* (“horned things”); I corrected it to *cornua* (“horns”) following Revelation 5:6. ROUTH.

“In Paul.” In place of *Paulum*, the margin of Cave’s edition has “Perhaps Revelation,” but wrongly; *Paulum* is correct. Cyprian, *On Exhortation to Martyrdom*, p. 125, Amsterdam edition: [Col. 0312B] “The Apostle Paul, who makes mention of this lawful and certain number, writes to seven churches.” See also the other material there that illustrates this passage. WALKER.—The fragment *On the Canon of Holy Scripture*, first published by the distinguished Muratori in his *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, has the following: “Since the blessed Apostle Paul himself, following the order of his predecessor John, writes by name to only seven churches, in the following order: to the Corinthians,” etc. ROUTH.

“Seven deacons.” Compare the note on the fragments of Cornelius concerning the number of deacons. Concerning the form *diacones*, Vossius writes in his book *On Faults of Speech*: “*Diacones* and *diaconibus* occur frequently in ecclesiastical writers, even ancient ones. But we regard these men as teachers of piety rather than of Latin. More elegant writers, therefore, always say *diaconus*, as the Greek has διάκονος.” Book I, ch. 20, p. 82. Tertullian and Cyprian, however, so far as I remember, almost always have *diaconi*, although, I admit, the situation is otherwise in the headings of Cyprian’s letters and where Cyprian relates, in the letter to Successus that is [Col. 0312D] Letter 80 or 82: “The emperor Valerian wrote back to the senate that bishops, presbyters, and deacons should immediately be punished.” Hence the noun *diacones* appears to have been more usual and common at that time. ROUTH.

“In the house of Solomon.” Walker advises that this be read in place of “into the house of Solomon.” Those who maintain that there are seven sacraments in the Church customarily bring forward many of these groups of seven, to note this in passing, either to confirm or to illustrate the matter. ROUTH.

“That Adam,” etc. I have followed Walker’s advice that these words should be joined with what follows—“through the birth of his Son,” etc.—rather than with what precedes; he further wishes to restore *subvenerit* in place of *subveniret*. Cave’s transcript had corrected *nativitatem* to *nativitate*. Clement of Alexandria commanded that one must proceed through the holy week, or through the various advances in goodness; see above at p. 250. ROUTH.

“On that day the angel Gabriel [announced the good news] to Mary,” etc. It is scarcely worth anyone’s effort to show how Victorinus, like other ancient commentators and chronologists, assembled these and other things of this kind. Shortly afterward Cave’s transcript has *mundasse* (“cleansed”) in place of *inundasse* (“flooded”). ROUTH.]

shining with light in the battle line at the sight of him [Note: [Col. 0311B] Perhaps: “at their sight.” Routh.], produce them [Note: [Col. 0311B] Perhaps: “may produce.” Routh.].

The authority of the whole creation, righteous [Note: [Col. 0311B] Perhaps: “But Jesus is the author of the whole creation.” Walker.]; “Word” is his surname, for his Father says thus: “My heart has uttered [Note: [Col. 0311B] Perhaps: “My heart uttered.” Routh.] a good word” (Ps. 45:1). John the Evangelist says thus: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:1–3).

Therefore the first was made “of creation” [Note: [Col. 0311B] Perhaps: “a creature.” Routh.]; the second, “of man” [Note: [Col. 0311B] Perhaps: “the man, the Lord.” Routh.] of the human race, as the Apostle says (1 Cor. 15:45, 47). This Word, therefore, when he made light, is called Wisdom; when he made heaven, Understanding; when he made land and sea, Counsel; when he made the sun and moon and the other bright bodies, Might; when he stirs the land and sea, Knowledge; when he fashioned man, Piety; when he blesses and sanctifies man, he bears the name Fear [Note: [Col. 0312B] Perhaps: “of the Fear.” Routh.] [Col. 0311B] of God.

Behold: the seven horns of the Lamb (Rev. 5:6); the seven eyes of God (Zech. 4:10); the seven eyes (Rev. 5:6), of tin [Note: [Col. 0312B] Perhaps: “are those of the Lamb,” in Cave’s margin. Walker judges that “seven eyes” should be deleted.]; the seven spirits (Rev. 4:5); the seven burning torches before God’s throne (Rev. 4:5); the seven golden lampstands [Col. 0312A] (Rev. 1:13); the seven ewe-lambs (Lev. 23:18); the seven women in Isaiah (Isa. 4:1); the seven churches in Paul (Acts 6:3); the seven deacons; the seven angels (more than once in Revelation); the seven trumpets [Note: [Col. 0312B] Perhaps: “trumpets” in the nominative. Routh.] (Josh. 6, or Rev. 8); the seven seals of the book (Rev. 5:1); the seven weeks by which Pentecost is completed; the seven weeks in Daniel (Dan. 9:25); likewise the forty-three weeks in Daniel; with Noah, seven of every clean creature in the ark (Gen. 7:2); the sevenfold vengeance for Cain (Gen. 4:15); the seven years for remitting a debt (Deut. 15:1); the lamp with seven openings (Zech. 4:2); the seven pillars of Wisdom in the house [Note: [Col. 0312B] Perhaps: “in the house.” Walker.] of Solomon (Prov. 11:1).

Now, therefore, you may see mention made of the unerring glory of God in providence; nevertheless, as far as my small mind is able, I shall attempt [Col. 0312B] to demonstrate it. That he might re-form that Adam over the course of a week and come to the aid of his whole creation [Note: [Col. 0312B] Perhaps: “might have come to the aid.” Walker.], this was accomplished through the birth of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord.

Who, therefore, instructed in God’s law and filled with the Holy Spirit, does not perceive in his heart that on the day when the dragon deceived Eve, Gabriel [Col. 0313A]

[Note: [Col. 0313C]

“On that day [he was] transformed into flesh, on which he made the land,” etc. This would not agree with the statement at line 13, “on that day [he was] transformed into flesh, on which he formed man from the soil”—which the book of Genesis shows to have occurred on the sixth day, whereas the land and water are said to have appeared on the third day—unless one were to say that the former statement must be understood of Christ’s incarnation in the womb of the Blessed Virgin. Compare the words shortly above at line 9 and the note on Fragment I of Africanus’s *Chronicle*, vol. II, p. 239. ROUTH.

“On which land and water brought forth their offspring.” At p. 236, line 28, this is said to have occurred on the fifth day. But water is indeed related to have brought forth its offspring on the fifth day, whereas the land did so on the sixth. ROUTH.

“On that day [he] suffered, on which Adam fell.” Almost everyone holds that Adam fell on the very day on which God created him. ROUTH.

“Decline.” This word is sometimes used of death. ROUTH.

“He knows these to be.” Perhaps one should write “and he withdrew.” For the word “withdrew” is customary for the Old Latin translator. For example: “But when Jesus had heard that John had been handed over, he withdrew (ἀνεχώρησεν) into Galilee” (Matt. 4:12). But in Cave’s margin it is conjectured that *spicas* (“ears of grain”) should be read in place of “these.” Shortly afterward I think *cervical* (“cushion”) should be read in place of *cervicalem*, and “stormy seas” in place of “seas or a storm.” ROUTH.

“Instructs the blind in eloquence.” The manuscript has *eloquentiam*, and the archaic *clodos* for *claudos*. Immediately before “instructs the blind in eloquence,” he had said “restores the lame.” Here, however, on account of the number seven, about which Victorinus has so much to say, I scarcely doubt that he had added something of this kind: “makes the deaf hear and restores the dead.” Compare Luke 7:22. Meanwhile, Melito of Sardis writes as follows in a fragment of his book *On the Incarnation of Christ*: Θεὸς γὰρ ὢν ὁμοῦ τε [Col. 0314D] καὶ ἄνθρωπος τέλειος ὁ αὐτὸς, τὰς δύο αὐτοῦ οὐσίας ἐπιστώσατο ἡμῖν· τὴν μὲν Θεότητα αὐτοῦ διὰ τῶν σημείων ἐν τῇ τριετίᾳ τῇ μετὰ τὸ βάπτισμα, τὴν δὲ ἀνθρωπότητα αὐτοῦ, ἐν τοῖς τριάκοντα χρόνοις τοῖς πρὸ τοῦ βαπτίσματος: “For, being at once God and perfect man, the same person confirmed to us his two natures: his divinity through the signs during the three-year period after baptism, and his humanity during the thirty years before baptism.” ROUTH.

“Is proclaimed to be the Lord of the same. By the number twelve, ‘to say.’” You may emend this exceedingly corrupt passage thus: “Proclaims to the same people. The day, in the number twelve.” For the author sends the reader to the beginning of his little commentary, at p. 303, line 5. ROUTH.

“Are reckoned,” etc. The manuscript has: “are reckoned have been established. Therefore, without doubt, however, of the day.” I therefore think that Walker—who punctuates the words differently from one another, writes *constituti*, and deletes “however”—should be followed rather than the learned men in Cave’s margin, who add the particle “and” before “have been established.” ROUTH.

“Whom in.” Walker says that “in” should be deleted. Cave’s transcript less correctly has *Apocalypsi*. ROUTH.

“Six wings,” etc. Victorinus—whom Jerome calls “our own” here for that reason—[commented on] Ecclesiastes among other books of Holy Scripture, as the same Jerome says in *On Illustrious Men*, prefixed by me to this fragment. [The supplied Latin is defective here.] ROUTH.

“The old man,” etc., etc. Since it is not established to which of the two these words belong, Origen or Victorinus, I refrain from transcribing more here. ROUTH.]

the angel announced the good news to the Virgin Mary; that on the day when he made light, the Holy Spirit flooded the Virgin Mary; that on the day when he made land and water, he was transformed into flesh; that on the day when he made the stars, he was transformed into milk; that on the day when land and water brought forth their offspring, he was transformed into blood; that on the day when he formed man from the soil, he was transformed into flesh; that Christ was born on the day when he fashioned man; that on the same [Note: [Col. 0313C] Perhaps: “on that.” Walker.] day on which [Note: [Col. 0313C] Perhaps: “on which,” feminine. Walker.] Adam fell, he suffered; and that on the day when he made light, he rose [Note: [Col. 0313C] Perhaps: “he rose,” infinitive construction. Walker.] from the dead?

He also completes his humanity in a sevenfold number: birth, infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, mature age, and decline [Note: [Col. 0313C] Perhaps: “decline,” nominative. Walker.]. He also showed his humanity to the Jews in these ways: when he hungers and thirsts, and gives food and drink; when he walks, “he knows these to be” [Col. 0313B] [Note: [Col. 0313C] Perhaps: “and he withdrew.” Routh.]; when he slept upon a cushion [Note: [Col. 0313C] Perhaps: “cushion,” rather than “upon a cushion.” Routh.] (Mark 4:38); but when he walks with his feet upon the seas or a storm [Note: [Col. 0313C] Perhaps: “upon stormy straits,” with “or” deleted. Routh.], commands the winds, heals the sick, restores the lame, and instructs the blind in eloquence [Note: [Col. 0314C] Perhaps the words “makes the deaf hear and restores the dead” have fallen out. Routh.], see that he is proclaimed to be the Lord of the same [Note: [Col. 0314C] Perhaps: “proclaims to the same people.” Routh.].

By the number twelve, “to say” [Note: [Col. 0314C] Perhaps: “the day.” Routh.], as I recalled above, is divided in two ways into twelve hours of light and twelve of night; for by these hours months, years, seasons, and ages are reckoned. Therefore, without doubt, there have been appointed [Note: [Col. 0314C] Perhaps: “appointed.” Walker.]—however [Note: [Col. 0314C] Walker says “however” should be deleted.]—twelve angels of the day and twelve angels of the night, corresponding, that is, to the number of hours. For these are the twenty-four witnesses of the days and nights (Rev. 4:4), who sit before God’s throne with golden crowns upon their heads, whom the Apocalypse of John, Apostle and Evangelist, calls elders—because [Col. 0314A] they are older than both the other angels and human beings.

**HERE ENDS VICTORINUS’S TREATISE ON THE CREATION OF THE WORLD.**

[**NOTES.**]

William Cave first published it from the Lambeth manuscript in the *Historia Litteraria*, vol. I, p. 148.

St. Jerome, in his letter to Damasus, vol. III, p. 518, Martianay’s edition, recalls the following interpretation of Isaiah 6:2:

Our Victorinus interpreted the six wings of one of the Seraphim and the six wings of the other (Isa. 6:2) as the twelve apostles.

Concerning St. Victorinus’s interpretation of Ecclesiastes 4:13, St. Jerome writes as follows in his *Commentary on Ecclesiastes* at that passage, vol. II, p. 741:

[Col. 0314B] Origen and Victorinus held opinions that did not differ greatly from one another. After that general interpretation, evident to everyone, that a poor and wise youth is better than an old and foolish king, and that it frequently happens that the former, even after leaving the king’s prison, rules through his wisdom in place of the perverse sovereign, while the foolish king loses the dominion he had held, they interpreted this passage with reference to Christ and the Devil. By the poor and wise boy they understand Christ as the boy, in accordance with the words, “It is a great thing for you to be called my boy” (Isa. 49:6); as poor, because “he became poor although he was rich” (2 Cor. 8:9); and as wise, because “he advanced in age and wisdom and grace before God and men” (Luke 2, final verse). He was born in the kingdom of the old man, etc.

[Col. 0315A] [Note: [Col. 0315A]

“I assert this concerning Victorinus,” etc. While Helvidius was attacking the perpetual virginity of St. Mary, he had adduced certain words of Victorinus. ROUTH.]

[Note: [Col. 0315B]

Victorinus wrote a commentary [ [Col. 0315D] Although we have admitted the Victorinian scholia which our present commentator rejects here, we nevertheless thought it best to record what Routh judged concerning the scholia on the Apocalypse.] on John’s Apocalypse, as Jerome reports above in *On Illustrious Men*, p. 233. As for the treatise published under Victorinus’s name in volume I of the Paris *Library of the Fathers*, we must say, with Tillemont, *Mémoires ecclésiastiques*, vol. V, note 2, on St. Victorinus, and Lardner, *On Gospel Faith*, part II, book I, ch. 56, p. 196, etc., that the work was indeed interpolated and altered in several places, but that the greater part of it was nevertheless genuinely written by Victorinus. This is all the more likely because in many respects that commentary agrees admirably [Col. 0315C] with the fragment *On the Creation of the World*, published formerly by Cave and now here. Compare also Ceillier, *Histoire générale des Auteurs sacrés et ecclésiastiques*, vol. III, ch. 21, § 3, p. 346.

Moreover, certain shorter *Scholia of Victorinus on the Apocalypse*, as though now restored after a kind of exile, have been brought back by Gallandi; they had first been published from a Monte Cassino manuscript by Basilius Millanius, a monk of Monte Cassino, at Bologna in 1558. Gallandi says in volume IV, p. 6, of his *Library of the Fathers* that he had no doubt that, if the learned had been acquainted with this sole and therefore exceedingly rare edition of the little work, “they would have received the *Scholia* as the genuine offspring of Victorinus, and would at the same time have recognized as wholly spurious, because astonishingly interpolated, that *Commentary on the Apocalypse* which circulates under his name in the Libraries of the Fathers.”

So Gallandi. Yet although traces of more ancient teaching may occasionally be detected in these shorter scholia, they nevertheless seemed to me to have been interpolated by some ill-employed person, assuming that they truly belonged to Victorinus, a writer of the third century. In them, at comment [Col. 0316B] 14 on Revelation 1, “But his head and hair were white,” etc., this interpretation occurs: “In the white hair is the multitude of abbots.” Again, at comment 18 on chapter 13, “The number of it is the name of a man, and its number is six hundred and sixty-six,” after many other remarks, this has been added: “Likewise another Gothic name of his”—that is, of Antichrist—“which will be clear in itself, namely Γενσηρικός (*Genseric*), which, calculated in the same way in Greek letters, has γʹ, three; εʹ, five,” etc. Genseric, king of the Vandals, is meant; he persecuted Catholics in Africa in the fifth century.

I pass over other things, but let the reader note, I ask, that in the same little work there is not only what is written at the end against the chiliasts, but also scholia throughout [Col. 0316C] the whole of chapter twenty opposed to their position; although, as Cave observed long ago while discussing the other commentary, Victorinus favored the error of the chiliasts in his commentary—as Jerome expressly reports—and undoubtedly did the same in the surviving fragment *On the Creation of the World*. But enough of this.

Of the poems that some have attributed to Victorinus, none enjoys testimony equal to that brief poem still extant, entitled *On the Cross of the Lord*, or *On the Passover*. The Venerable Bede attributed its first two verses to Victorinus in his little book *On the Holy Places*, ch. 3, p. 489, vol. III, Basel edition:

> “Led by this opinion,” says Bede, “Victorinus of Poitiers, bishop of the Church, begins as follows when writing about Golgotha:
>
> There is a place we believe to be the center of the whole world;
>
> The Jews call it Golgotha in their native tongue.”

Nevertheless, I do not oppose the judgment of those who, because of the difference in style, wish to deny the poem to Victorinus. For the author of the poem appears to speak Latin—a claim that can scarcely be made of Victorinus in his treatise *On the Creation of the World*. For, as Jerome testifies in several places, the ability to write in pure and correct Latin was not added to the sum of the holy martyr’s praises.]

St. Jerome writes as follows concerning Victorinus in *Against Helvidius*, vol. IV, p. 141:

I assert concerning Victorinus what I also assert concerning the Evangelists: that he called them the Lord’s brothers, not Mary’s sons; brothers, moreover, in the sense explained above—by kinship, not by birth.

Concerning a certain opinion of Victorinus and others, St. Jerome writes as follows in *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 18:

He—Papias—is said to have published a Jewish δευτέρωσις (*deuterōsis*, “secondary exposition”) concerning a thousand years. Irenaeus, Apollinarius, and the others who say that after the resurrection the Lord will reign in the flesh with the saints followed him. Tertullian also, in his book *On the Hope of the Faithful*, Victorinus [Col. 0315B] of Pettau, and Lactantius are guided by this opinion.

[Col. 0316A] Concerning the same opinion St. Jerome writes as follows in his *Commentary on Ezekiel*, ch. 36, vol. III, p. 952:

For we do not, in accordance with the Jewish fables that they call δευτερώσεις (*deuterōseis*, “secondary expositions”), await a jeweled and golden Jerusalem from heaven; nor are we to suffer anew the injury of circumcision, or offer sacrifices of bulls and rams, or sleep in the idleness of the Sabbath. Yet many of our own writers promise this, especially Tertullian’s book entitled *On the Hope of the Faithful*, the seventh volume of Lactantius’s *Institutions*, the frequent expositions of Victorinus, bishop of Pettau, and, recently, our own Severus in the dialogue to which he gave the title *Gallus*. And, to name the Greeks and join the first with the last: Irenaeus and Apollinarius.

[Col. 0317]

# SCHOLIA OF SAINT VICTORINUS, BISHOP OF PETTAU AND MARTYR, ON THE APOCALYPSE OF BLESSED JOHN

[Note: [Col. 0317C] These *Scholia* of St. Victorinus were first published at Bologna in 1558 by Basilius Millanius, a monk of Monte Cassino, from a manuscript codex of the Monte Cassino library; he also added annotations. We have caused this first edition of all to be printed, since the texts found in the Libraries of the Fathers are astonishingly interpolated. GALLAND.]

(C, S)*

## THE EXPOSITION BEGINS

## FROM CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0317A]

**1. “The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ, which God gave him and showed to his servants—things that must happen soon—and he signified it. Blessed are those who read and those who hear the words of this prophecy, and keep the things that are written.”** The beginning of the book promises blessedness to the person who reads, hears, and keeps it, so that, by applying himself to the reading, he may learn works from it and observe the commandments.

**4. “Grace to you and peace from him who is, who was, and who is to come.”** He “is,” because he endures. He “was,” because he made all things with the Father and has now taken his beginning from the Virgin. He “is to come,” certainly, to judge.

**“And from the seven spirits who are in the presence of his throne.”** We read of the sevenfold Spirit in Isaiah (Isa. 11:2), namely the spirit of wisdom and understanding, of counsel and fortitude, of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord.

**5. “And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead.”** In the humanity he assumed, he bore witness in the world; in it he also suffered, released us from sin by his blood, defeated hell, and rose first from the dead. “Death will no longer have dominion over him” (Rom. 6:9); and when he reigns, the kingdom of the world is destroyed.

**6. “And he made us a kingdom and priests to God and his Father.”** That is, the Church of all the faithful, as the apostle Peter also says: “A holy nation, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9).

**7. “Behold, he will come with the clouds, and every eye will see him.”** For he who at first came hidden in the humanity he assumed [Col. 0317C] will shortly come manifestly, in majesty and glory, to judge. But what does he say?

**12. “And turning, I saw seven golden lampstands, and in the midst of the seven golden lampstands one like a son [Col. 0318A] of man.”** He says “like” because, after death had been vanquished and he had ascended into heaven, the power that he received from the Father was united in his body with the Spirit of his glory.

**13. “Like a son of man, walking amid the golden lampstands.”** He means amid the churches, as it is said in Solomon: “I shall walk amid the paths of the righteous” (Prov. 8:20). His antiquity is immortality and the origin of majesty.

**“Clothed in a long robe.”** In the long robe—that is, the priestly garment—the flesh that was corrupted [Note: [Col. 0317C] “The flesh that was corrupted.” Unless someone offers something better, I would wish to emend this passage thus: “The flesh that was not corrupted in death and possesses [Col. 0317D] the priesthood through suffering is most plainly declared.”] unto death and possesses the priesthood through suffering is most plainly declared.

**“And he was girded at the breasts with a golden girdle.”** His breasts are the two Testaments, and the golden girdle is the choir of the saints, like gold tested by fire. Alternatively, the golden girdle fastened around the breast indicates a conscience refined in the furnace and a pure and spiritual understanding, which has been delivered to the churches.

**14. “But his head and hair were white, like white wool and like snow.”** Brightness is shown in the head, for “the head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11:3). In the white hair is the multitude of abbots [Note: [Col. 0317D] “The multitude of abbots.” The little work is certainly learned and useful if you consider it as a whole, and you may willingly confess that you love its author and owe him a great deal. [Col. 0318C] But in some places it becomes so feeble that you would scarcely consider it worthy of a learned man and would call its authorship into doubt, because at times it seems to savor of the composition of some more recent and not especially learned person—as here in the designation “abbots.” For in the period when Victorinus flourished, Antony, the first abbot, had lived only a little earlier, unless someone should say that people had embraced monasticism so ardently by that time that a great many abbots had arisen. Moreover, I have even found *abbatorum* (“of abbots”) written. Perhaps someone might judge that *albatorum* (“of those clothed in white”) should be read. It will suffice for me to have indicated this suspicion, since amid such ignorance of the matter and of the corrupt exemplar I cannot assign any certain rationale.], like wool because of the guileless sheep, and like snow because of the innumerable multitude of white-robed persons instructed from heaven.

**“His eyes were like a flame of fire.”** They are God’s commandments, which provide light to believers but a conflagration to unbelievers.

**16. “But in his face was brightness like the sun.”** By saying “brightness,” he meant that appearance of his by which he spoke with human beings face to face. The sun’s glory, however, is less than the Lord’s glory. Yet because of its rising and setting [Col. 0318C] and rising again—signifying that he was born, suffered, and rose—the Scripture supplied the comparison, likening his face to the sun’s glory.

**15. “His feet were like fine brass, as though refined in a furnace.”** By the feet he means the apostles, who, refined through suffering, preached his word throughout the whole world. Because the proclamation advanced through them, he rightly called them feet. Hence the prophet also anticipated this when he said: “We shall worship in the place where his feet stood” (Ps. 131:7). For where they first stood and established the Church—that is, in Judaea—all the saints are to assemble and worship their Lord.

**16. “And from his mouth proceeded a sword sharpened on both sides.”** By the twice-sharpened sword flashing from his mouth, it is shown that he himself is the one who both now brought forth the word of the Gospel and formerly, through Moses, brought knowledge of the Law to the whole world. But because through the same word he is to exact judgment upon the whole [Col. 0319B] human race, of both the New and the Old Testament, it is consequently described as twice sharpened. For the sword arms the soldier, kills the enemy, and punishes the deserter.

And to show the apostles that he was announcing judgment, he said: “I did not come to send peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10). After he had finished the parables, he said to them: “Have you understood all these things?” And they said, “Yes.” He added: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of God is like a householder bringing forth from his treasure things new and old” (Matt. 13:51–52): the new things are the apostles’ words of the Gospel; the old, the commandments of the Law and the prophets. He testified that these proceeded from his own mouth.

But he also said to Peter: “Go to the sea and cast a hook; take the fish that first comes up, and when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater”—that is, two denarii—“and you shall give it for me and for yourself” (Matt. 17:26). David similarly said through the Spirit: “God has spoken once; these two things I have heard” (Ps. 61). For God decreed once, from the beginning, what would happen until the end.

Finally, since he was appointed judge by the Father because of his assumption of humanity, and wished to show that human beings would be judged by the word of preaching, he said: “Do you think that I shall judge you on the last day? No; but the word,” he says, “which I have spoken to you—that will judge you on the last day” (John 12:48). And Paul says of Antichrist to the Thessalonians: “Whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the spirit of his mouth” (2 Thess. 2:8). And Isaiah says: “With the spirit of his lips he will kill the wicked” (Isa. 11:4). This, therefore, is the twice-sharpened [Col. 0319D] sword proceeding from his mouth.

**15. “And his voice was like the voice of many waters.”** [Note: [Col. 0319D] “And his voice was like the voice of many waters.” You will not be surprised that here, and in several other places besides, the Apostle’s words are read in a reversed order, since shortly afterward you will hear this author of ours declare that, in interpreting this book, the reader must follow neither the order of the words nor the sequence of the text, but the understanding of the subject matter.] The many waters are understood to be peoples, or the gift of baptism, which he sent forth through the Apostles, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

16. And he had seven stars in his right hand. He said that there were seven stars in his right hand [Col. 0320A] because the Holy Spirit of sevenfold power was given into his authority by the Father. As Peter exclaimed to the Jews: “Exalted by the right hand of God, he poured out this Spirit, received from the Father, whom you see and hear” (Acts 2:33). John the Baptist had also anticipated this, saying to his disciples: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure. The Father,” he says, “loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” (John 3:34–35). These seven stars are the seven churches that he names by their own names and calls those to which he addressed letters. It is not because they alone are churches or preeminent, but because what he says to one he says to all. For they differ in no respect such that, on this ground, someone should rank a few similar ones above the greater number. Paul taught that throughout the whole world all the churches, named seven by groups of seven [Col. 0320B], are seven and are one catholic Church. And first, so that he himself might preserve the type of the seven churches, he did not exceed the number. Rather, he wrote to the Romans, the Corinthians, the Galatians, the Ephesians, the Thessalonians, the Philippians, and the Colossians. Afterward he wrote to individual persons, lest he exceed the number of seven churches. And, compressing his preaching into a brief statement, he says thus to Timothy: “That you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the Church of the living God” (1 Tim. 3:15).

We read that this type was also proclaimed by the Holy Spirit through Isaiah, concerning “the seven women who took hold of one man” (Isa. 4:1). The one man is Christ, not born from seed; the seven women [Col. 0320C], however, are the seven churches, receiving their own bread and clothed in their own tunics, who ask that their reproach be taken away, provided only that his name be invoked over them. The bread is the Holy Spirit, who nourishes unto eternal life, evidently promised to them through faith. Their own tunics, however, with which they desire to be covered, are the glory of immortality, concerning which the apostle Paul says: “For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53). They ask that their reproach be taken away—that is, that they be cleansed from sins; for the former sin is a reproach, which is taken away in baptism, and people begin to be called Christians. This is what is meant by: “Let your name be invoked over us.”

> **Note [Col. 0319D]: “They ask that their reproach be taken away.”** We added the word *ask* from the preceding reading in order to make the expression clearer. Nor will it be necessary for us immediately to give a reason wherever we have emended something, when the matter is so firmly established and self-evident that no one could doubt that it ought to be written so; for to pursue every instance would be almost endless, so thoroughly were nearly all the individual words disordered and corrupted. [Col. 0320D]

Therefore, in these seven churches are the faithful of the one catholic Church, because [Col. 0320D] one Church exists in the seven through the character of faith and election. Or he writes to those who labor in the world, live on the modest yield of their labors, and are patient; and when they see certain people in the Church who are wasteful and pestilential, they bear with them lest dissension arise. Nevertheless, he admonishes them concerning love, so that wherever their faith is deficient, they may repent.

> **Note [Col. 0320D]: “Work.”** I would believe that the author used this verb in place of *live*, and said *dispensatores* (“stewards”) for *dissipatores* (“wasteful people”), and likewise *portant* (“carry/bear”) for *ferunt* (“bear”), the two expressions that immediately follow.

Or he writes to those who inhabit cruel places among persecutors, that they may remain faithful. Or to those who, under the pretext of mercy, commit illicit sins in the Church and teach others to commit them. Or to those in the Church who are easily swayed. Or to those who are negligent and are Christians in name alone. Or to those who have been humbly instructed, that they may persevere steadfastly in the faith. Or to those who devote themselves to the Scriptures and labor to understand the mysteries of preaching, but are unwilling to do God’s work—that is, mercy and love. To all he declares repentance; to all he announces judgment.

## FROM CHAPTER II

2. “I know your labor, your works, and your patience.” In the first letter he speaks thus: I know that you labor and work; [Col. 0321B] I see that you are patient. Do not suppose that I remain far from you.

“And that you cannot bear evil people, and those who say that they are Jews and are not, and you have found them to be liars; and you have patience for my name’s sake.” All these things pertain to praise, and no slight praise. Such men, such a class, and such people of election must certainly be admonished, lest, after these good things of God have been granted them, they be deprived of them. He said that he had these few things against them:

4–5. “And you have abandoned your former love; remember whence you have fallen.” Whoever falls, falls from a height; therefore he said “whence,” because the works of love must be practiced to the very end, for this is the chief commandment. Finally, unless this is done, he threatened to move the lampstand [Col. 0321C] from its place—that is, to scatter the congregation.

6. “Thus you too have it in you to hate the works of the Nicolaitans.” But because you yourself also hated those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans, you may expect praise. To hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which he himself also hated, pertains to praise. The works of the Nicolaitans at that time belonged to deceitful and pestilential men who, under the name of Nicolas the minister, had made a heresy for themselves: namely, that food offered to idols might be exorcised and eaten, and that whoever had committed fornication might receive peace on the eighth day. Therefore he commends those to whom he writes, and to such great men he promised the tree that is in the paradise of his God.

> **Note [Col. 0321D]: “Food offered to idols.”** Here and elsewhere he used *delibatum* for *idolothyton*, that is, what was sacrificed to idols. *To exorcise*, however, appears to be understood as “to expiate from the guilt of a desecrated or polluted religion” [Col. 0322D], which is contrary to the proper meaning of the word; for Greek *ἐξορκίζειν* (*exorkizein*) means “to bind under an oath” rather than “to release from a religious bond.”

The following letter discloses the conduct and customary practice of the next, distinct class. Thus he says:

[Col. 0321D] 9. “I know your tribulation and poverty, but you are rich.” For he knows that riches are stored up with him for such people. He also knows the slander from those Jews who, though denying, say that they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan, since they are gathered by the Antichrist. To them he says:

10. “Be faithful unto death.” That is, let them persevere in faithfulness unto death.

11. “Whoever conquers will not be harmed by the second death.” That is, he will not be punished in hell.

The third class of saints shows that there are men who [Col. 0322A] are strong in faith and do not dread persecution; but because among them there are also some who are inclined toward illicit unions, he says:

14, 16. “You have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat and to fornicate; so you too have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans, but I shall fight against them with the sword of my mouth.” That is: I shall declare what I commanded, and compare it with what you have done. For the teaching of Balaam (Num. 2) taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the eyes of the children of Israel, to eat food offered to idols, and to fornicate—something known to have happened long ago. For he gave this counsel to the king of the Moabites, and they caused the people to stumble. Thus, he says, you have among you people who hold such a teaching, so that under the pretext of mercy you corrupt others.

[Col. 0322B] 17. “Whoever conquers, I shall give him the hidden manna, and I shall give him a white stone.” The hidden manna is immortality; the white gem is adoption as a son of God; the new name written upon the stone is “Christian.”

The fourth class signifies the nobility of the faithful who work daily and accomplish ever greater works. But he also shows that there are there people easily disposed to grant illicit terms of peace and to heed novel prophecies. He reproves them and forewarns the others who disapprove of this and recognize the opposing wickedness, through which it seeks to bring evils, sufferings, and dangers upon the heads of the faithful. Therefore he says:

24. “I place no other burden upon you.” That is: I have not given you laws, observances, and burdens—which would be another burden.

[Col. 0322C] 25–26. “But hold fast what you have until I come; and whoever conquers, I shall give him authority over all nations.” That is: I shall appoint him a judge among the other saints.

28. “And I shall give him the morning star.” That is, the first resurrection. He promised the morning star, which puts night to flight and announces the light—that is, the beginning of the day.

## FROM CHAPTER III

The fifth class, the assembly or manner of life of the saints, reveals negligent people who perform in the world occupations other than those they ought to perform, and who are Christians in name alone. Therefore he exhorts them, in the hope that somehow, having turned back from negligence, they may be saved. Thus he says:

[Col. 0322D] 2. “Be watchful and strengthen the things that remained, which were about to die; for I have not found your works complete before God.” It is not enough for a tree to be alive and not bear fruit, just as it is not enough to be called a Christian and to confess Christ, yet not possess him in one’s deeds—that is, not to carry out his commandments.

The sixth class is the manner of life of the finest elect. The customary practice of the saints is revealed—namely, of those who are humble in the world, unlearned in the Scriptures, and hold the faith immovably, and who, utterly unbroken by any [Col. 0323A] circumstance or fear, are not drawn back from the faith. Therefore he says to them:

8. “I have set before you an open door, because you have kept the word of my patience”—despite such little strength.

10. “And I shall preserve you from the hour of temptation.” This is so that people of this kind may know their glory: they are not even permitted to be handed over to temptation.

12. “Whoever conquers will become a pillar in the temple of God.” For just as a pillar is the adornment of a building, so whoever perseveres will attain nobility in the Church.

The seventh assembly of the Church likewise reveals people who are wealthy and placed in positions of dignity, but who believe as the wealthy do. Among them the Scriptures are indeed discussed in private chambers, but outwardly they are faithful and are understood by no one; namely, they boast and say [Col. 0323B] that they know everything, endowed with confidence in their learning, but devoid of works. Therefore he says:

15. That they are “neither cold nor hot.” That is, neither unbelievers nor faithful, for they are all things to all people. And because one who is neither cold nor hot, but lukewarm, causes nausea, he says:

16. “I shall vomit you out of my mouth.” Although nausea is hateful, it nevertheless harms no one; so it is also when people of this kind have been cast out. But because there is time for repentance, he says:

18. “I counsel you to buy from me refined gold.” That is, how you may be able to endure tribulations and sufferings for the name of the Lord.

“And anoint your eyes with eye salve.” This is so that you may strive also to perform in deed what you gladly learn through Scripture. And because, if by these means people return from a great fall to great repentance, they are useful not only to themselves but can also benefit many others, he promised them no slight reward—namely, to sit upon the throne of judgment.

## FROM CHAPTER IV

“After these things I saw, and behold, a door opened in heaven.” The open door in heaven proclaims the New Testament.

“And the first voice that I heard, like a trumpet speaking with me, saying, ‘Come up here.’” When it is shown to be open, it is evident that it had formerly been closed to human beings. It was sufficiently and fully opened when Christ ascended bodily into heaven to the Father. But when he says that the first voice he had heard [Col. 0323D] spoke with him, he incontrovertibly refutes those who say that one being spoke in the prophets and another in the Gospel, since rather he who came is the very one who spoke in the prophets. For John was of the circumcision, and that whole people who had heard the preaching of the Old Testament had been edified by that voice.

That same voice, he says, which I had heard—it said to me: “Come up here.” That is, the Spirit whom, shortly before, he declares that he saw walking like a son of man among the golden lampstands [Col. 0324A]. And now from that point he recalls the things that had been foretold in figures through the Law; by means of this Scripture he joins together all the earlier prophets and opens the Scriptures. And because, after our Lord invited into heaven all who believe in his name, he immediately poured out the Holy Spirit, who was to carry them to heaven, he says:

> **Note [Col. 0323D]: “Who was to carry.”** We say *ferturus* instead of *laturus*, even if this does not accord with grammarians’ usage, just as shortly above we also have *odire* instead of *odisse*. Nevertheless, we were unwilling to alter the reading of an ancient manuscript, especially one venerable for its age. [Col. 0324D]

2. “Immediately I was in the Spirit.” And since the mind of the faithful is opened through the Holy Spirit, and what was also proclaimed to those of old is disclosed to them, he speaks meaningfully:

“And behold, a throne had been set in heaven.” What is the throne that has been set, if not the throne of the judge and king?

3. “And above the throne one was sitting, similar in appearance to jasper and sardius.” He says that he saw above the throne the likeness of jasper [Col. 0324B] and sardius. Jasper has the color of water; sardius, of fire.
