> **Note:** [Col. 0347D] The same, ibid., book II, chap. 3, p. 165.

“Magnetes, a most ancient ecclesiastical writer, says in books II and V, which he wrote against the pagan Theosthenes, who falsely alleged against us a discrepancy among the Evangelists and other things in the Gospel: Because [Col. 0347C] one of the Evangelists said—

> **Note:** [Col. 0347D] Mark 15:36.

—‘putting the sponge around a reed,’ another said—

> **Note:** [Col. 0347D] John 19:29.

—‘putting it around hyssop,’ because of the plant’s resemblance, although, he says, ‘reed’ ought to have been said.

> “Likewise, what one Evangelist called ‘wine’—

> **Note:** [Col. 0347D] Mark 15:23.

> —was again called ‘vinegar’ at the cross—

> **Note:** [Col. 0347D] Matt. 27:48; Luke 23:36; John 19:29.

> —for they drew it from the same vessel that had been placed there, both when they reached Calvary and upon the cross, especially,” he says, “since the Evangelists observed the law of history and wrote nothing beyond what was then being said amid that uproar and frenzy. For they considered that the history would thus be free from every suspicion, εἰ μὴ περιεργότερον ἀλλ᾽ ἄπλαστον εὑρεθείη τῆς ἱστορίας τὸ γράμμα”—that is, “if the written account of the history were found to be not over-elaborate, but unadorned.”

And elsewhere:

> **Note:** [Col. 0347D] Turrianus, passage cited, book II, chap. 13, p. 211.

“The same Magnetes, whom I mentioned above, [Col. 0347D] in book IV of his *Apologies against Theosthenes*, the slanderer of the Gospels, explains why Paul here numbered himself, though still living, among the dead: [Col. 0348A]

> Οὕτω γὰρ ἄν τις Φιλαίτερος καὶ τῶν ὁμοστοίχων ἀγαπῶν τὴν συγγένειαν δοκεῖ.

> ‘For in this way,’ he says, ‘it happens that someone seems to love the friends among whom he numbers himself and those who belong to his own rank.’”

These passages from Magnes cited by Turrianus, Gallandi says, must be added to those that we have reproduced below in their proper place.

## ARTICLE II. A Fragment of Magnes from Book III of the *Apology of the Gospels against the Pagan Theosthenes*, in Francisco Turrianus’ *Treatise on the Most Holy Eucharist against the Pole Wolan*, p. 93, Florentine edition, 1575

### I

“That this is not ξένον καὶ φρικῶδες—that is, strange and dreadful, or unheard-of and horrifying—may be understood by considering an infant child: unless it eats its mother’s flesh and blood, how does it live? For milk is, in truth, blood by nature. To speak more clearly, I shall recount something natural, lest you think this a fable.

According to the body, we were born from the earth, and in a certain manner we are nourished by its flesh and blood—that is, by grain and wine. Listen now attentively. In the beginning the Son of God created the earth; from the earth he formed the human being; from the human being he himself assumed flesh. If, therefore, [Col. 0348B] the earth is predicated of the body by reason of its ancient origin; and if the earth, by reason of creation, was Christ’s own creature; and from it bread and wine came into being, and from it in turn the human body; and Christ put on this body: then rightly, when he had taken bread and wine, he said, ‘This is my body’” (Matt. 26:26; 1 Cor. 11:34).

> **Note:** [Col. 0348C] *That this is*, etc. Turrianus prefixes the following to this splendid fragment: “I shall translate here from the Greek what Magnetes, an ecclesiastical and very ancient author, wrote in book III of his *Apologies against Theosthenes*, the slanderer of the Gospels. This man was therefore saying the same thing as those people of Capernaum: ‘This saying is hard; and who can hear it?’ Magnetes replies: ‘That this is,’ etc.”

> **Note:** [Col. 0348C] *If, therefore, concerning the body.* From these words to the end, Coccius copied Turrianus while suppressing his name: *Thesaurus Catholicus*, vol. II, p. 607 ff.

### II

He then adds:

> Οὐ γὰρ τύπος σώματος οὐ δὲ τύπος αἵματος, ὥς τινες ἐῤῥαψώδησαν πεπηρωμένοι, ἀλλὰ κατ᾽ ἀλήθειαν αἷμα καὶ σῶμα Χριστοῦ.

> “For it is not a figure of the body, nor a figure of the blood, as certain people, obtuse in mind, have composed their idle tales; rather, it is truly the blood and body of Christ.” [Col. 0348C]

> **Note:** [Col. 0348C] *Οὐ γὰρ … Χριστοῦ.* Turrianus repeats this same passage at the end of his comments on book V of the *Clementine Constitutions*, chap. 13; and from him, as it seems, Bulengerus repeats it in *Diatribe* III on Casaubon’s *Exercises*, p. 164. The distinguished Le Quien likewise quotes the same words from the passage of Turrianus cited above, in his comments on John Damascene’s *On the Orthodox Faith*, book IV, p. 271. There he observes that the books of Macarius Magnes against the pagan Theosthenes were very well known in Damascene’s age. Nor may one pass over the notable testimony of Zacharias of Crete in his *Responses to the Most Reverend Claude de Guise, Cardinal of Lorraine*, which the most learned Giovanni Lami published not long ago with Nicetas’ exposition of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, part I, p. 72 ff. Thus Zacharias writes on p. 77:

> Ὁ δὲ Μάγνης διδάσκαλος ἀρχαῖος ὢν, οὕτως ἐν ἀπολογίᾳ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου πρὸς Θεοσθένην φησὶ, Ὅτι ἡ εὐχαριστία ἀληθῶς σῶμα, καὶ αἷμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ· οὐ τύπος σώματος καὶ αἵματος, ὥς τινες ῥαψωδήσαντες πεπηρωμένοι τὸν νοῦν ἔλεγον.

> “Magnes, who is an ancient teacher, speaks as follows in his *Apology of the Gospel against Theosthenes*: ‘The Eucharist is truly the body and blood of Christ, not a figure of the body and blood, as certain people, composing fables and blinded in mind, used to say.’” [Col. 0348D]

That is: “For it is not a figure of the body or blood, as certain people babbled with a stupefied mind, but rather truly the body and blood of Christ.” [Col. 0349A]

He continues his philosophical argument:

“Since,” he says, “the body comes from the earth, and bread and wine come from the earth, how is it that no other person dared to say, ‘My flesh is truly food; my blood is truly drink’ (John 6:56)? Surely because none other than this one is the creator of the earth; the earth is the creature of none other than the Son of God.

Therefore he said: ‘This is my body.’ For the earth is my creature and not another’s. All others were born after the earth, receiving their body from me; but I existed before the earth and did not receive it from anyone. From the earth—that is, from my own creature—I received a body, assuming flesh. From what is mine, therefore, I set before you a gift of grace (*charisma*).

From the earth bread came into being to nourish you; but the earth [Col. 0349B] is my creature. From the earth the body likewise came into being, and this bodily mass is mine. Therefore, by virtue of the union by which I, the holy one, was united with what is earthly, I give bread and wine, commanding them to be my body and blood.”

### III

“For if Abraham or any other just and holy man had said, ‘My flesh is food, and my blood is drink,’ he would have dared to utter a very great falsehood; or if he had said, ‘This is my body; this is my blood,’ the substance would not have been his own but another’s, nor, when eaten, would it have given life to those who ate it.

For that which does not have the living Word united with the body that was earthly would not lead those who eat to eternal life. Christ, therefore, gave his own body and blood to believers, introducing into them the life-giving medicine [Col. 0349C] of the divinity.”

He then adds:

> Ἄρτον γοῦν λέγων τὴν σάρκα καὶ οἶνον τὸ αἷμα, ἐπαίδευσεν ἡμᾶς εὐλόγως ἐκ γῆς εἶναι τὸ σῶμα.

That is: “Therefore, by calling that which is flesh ‘bread,’ and that which is blood ‘wine,’ he fittingly taught us that the body, like bread, comes from the earth, and that the substance in the body and in the bread belongs to one kind.”

### IV

“But ordinary bread, produced through the cultivation of the earth, although it is a kind of flesh of the earth, does not promise to furnish eternal life. Rather, it grants brief relief to those who partake of it, and it is quickly extinguished, being without the divine Spirit.

But the bread prepared in the blessed earth of Christ, through the power of the united divinity, brings immortality to a person by the mere tasting of it. For the mystical bread has the Father’s inseparable blessing—I mean the blessing effected in [Col. 0349D] his body and blood—and unites the one who eats it to the body of Christ and makes him a member of Christ.

For just as a written sheet conveys to the pupil the power it has received through the teacher’s letters and through it unites him with the teacher, so the body that is that mystical bread and the blood [Col. 0350A] that is that wine confer upon the participant the immortality of the undefiled divinity αὐτόθεν—that is, from their own source, or from themselves—and through it lead him back to the incorruptible dwelling of the Creator.

For the flesh of the Savior, when eaten, is not corrupted, nor is this blood consumed when drunk. Rather, the one who eats advances in strength; but that which is eaten cannot be consumed, because every act of consumption is in some manner akin to nature.”

> **Note:** [Col. 0350C] *For the flesh of the Savior, when eaten.* Allatius presents the Greek of this passage in his *Exercises against Creyghton*, p. 563:

> Οὔτε σὰρξ τοῦ Σωτῆρος τρωγομένη φθείρεται, οὔτε ἐξαναλίσκεται τὸ αἷμα πινόμενον, ἀλλ᾽ ὁ τρώγων μὲν εἰς αὔξησιν θείων δυνάμεων αἴρεται· τὸ δὲ τρωγόμενον ἐστὶν ἀδαπάνητον, ἐπειδὴ τοῖς ἀδαπανήτου φύσεως λόγῳ τινὶ συγγενὲς ὑπάρχει καὶ ἀχώριστον.

> “Neither is the flesh of the Savior corrupted when eaten, nor is the blood exhausted when drunk; rather, the one who eats is raised to an increase of divine powers, while that which is eaten is inexhaustible, since it is in some manner akin to, and inseparable from, the things of an inexhaustible nature.”

> “Nor indeed is the flesh of the Savior corrupted when eaten, nor is the blood consumed when drunk; rather, the one who eats grows in divine powers, while that which is eaten cannot be consumed, because it is in a certain way akin to a nature that can be consumed and is in no way separable from it.” [Col. 0350D]

Le Quien repeats the same passage from Allatius in the place cited, p. 273.

The indefatigable and most learned Reverend Father Dominikus Schramm had this same fragment reprinted in volume VI of his *Analysis of the Works of the Holy Fathers and Ecclesiastical Writers*, published at Augsburg in 1784, pp. 418–420. He nevertheless omitted Gallandi’s notes drawn from Allatius, Zacharias of Crete, and Le Quien. [Col. 0350B]

It would otherwise be desirable for the complete work of Macarius Magnes’ *Apocritics* someday to become public property. One might reasonably hope that the documents of this most ancient writer would shed great light upon orthodox faith and ecclesiastical discipline.

In the last century, however, the distinguished Albertinus attacked this work as well and denied both the antiquity and the authenticity of its author:

> **Note:** [Col. 0350D] Albertinus, *On the Sacrament of the Eucharist*, book II, p. 400.

He wrote as follows:

> “But truly, let such finery be offered to the common people. For who among the ancients—or indeed even among the more recent writers over the course of nine or ten centuries—has so much as mentioned the name of this Magnes? He is an entirely fictitious author, or at least some new and recent petty Greek, the whole reliability of whose writings rests with Turrianus, a man of little judgment and highly suspect fidelity. Yet our adversaries dare, without shame, to bring forth rubbish of this sort as monuments of the ancients. O the faith of God and humankind!” [Col. 0350C]

How rash Albertinus’ judgment was in this matter is observed both by the highly learned Cave and abundantly established by what has been said thus far.

> **Note:** [Col. 0350D] Cave, *Historia litteraria*, vol. I, p. 135.

# THE COMPLETE WORKS OF ARNOBIUS THE AFRICAN

[Col. 0349]

# HISTORICAL NOTICE CONCERNING ARNOBIUS THE AFRICAN

## SUMMARY

[Col. 0349D]

I. Arnobius, a celebrated rhetorician at Sicca in Africa under Diocletian. Devoted to pagan superstition, he is divinely called to the Christian religion.

II. Jerome’s passage concerning Arnobius is examined.

III. The date at which he composed the seven books *Against the Nations* is investigated. From the author himself it is shown that this occurred in the year 304 or the following year.

IV. The value of Arnobius’ work is explained. The author is judged to have attacked pagan superstition much more clearly than he taught Christian truth.

V. On the principal editions of the work. The Leiden edition is superior, although it is not free from faults and errors. What labor has been contributed toward preparing our edition.

## I

From Jerome (*On Illustrious Men*, chap. LXXIX) we learn that Arnobius taught rhetoric with the greatest distinction at Sicca, a city of inland Africa, under the emperor Diocletian. At that time he was devoted to the worship of idols, as he himself laments in these words:

> “Only recently—O blindness!—I worshiped images.... [Col. 0351B] Now, having been led into the paths of truth by so great a teacher, Christ, I know what all those things are; concerning things deserving judgment, I judge as they deserve” (Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, book I, chap. 13).

How it came about that he embraced the Christian religion is related elsewhere by Jerome as follows:

> “Arnobius, a celebrated rhetorician in Africa..., while training young men in the city of Sicca for declamation, was still a pagan when dreams impelled him toward belief. When he could not obtain from the bishop the faith that he had always opposed, he labored through the night to compose most eloquent books against his former religion; and at last, as though by giving certain hostages, he obtained a covenant of piety” (Jerome, *Chronicle*, at the year 2342, p. 181).

Arnobius was therefore granted so great a light—and was indeed so powerfully struck by dreams divinely sent—that he renounced his former impiety and embraced the true worship of God. For he teaches that Christ, “not through empty dreams, but under the appearance of pure simplicity” (Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, book I, chap. XVI), was still accustomed to appear in his own time. The author wrote this, Dodwell says, because he had himself experienced it; hence he could truly say that he had been “led into the paths of truth by Christ himself, so great a teacher” (Dodwell, *Dissertation on Irenaeus* II, § 57, p. 199). [Col. 0351C]

What Arnobius did afterward, however, or in what year he departed this life, is entirely unknown to us.

## II

Nor should anyone infer from Jerome’s words just quoted that our author lived at least until the year 326, merely because the holy Doctor wrote them immediately after noting Constantine’s twentieth anniversary, celebrated in that same year of Christ, 326. For from those same words of Jerome it would then have to be inferred that Arnobius was converted to faith in Christ in that very year and that shortly before it he composed his books *Against the Nations*, by which, as though by certain hostages, he obtained a covenant of piety. Yet, on the contrary, it is manifest from Arnobius himself, as we shall shortly see, and is moreover not obscurely apparent from Jerome himself (*On Illustrious Men*, passage cited), that those books were written by the author during the reign of Diocletian. [Col. 0351D]

Therefore, in order that Jerome may be consistent with himself, it is important to observe, with the most learned scholar (Nourry, *Apparatus to the Library of the Fathers*, vol. II, p. 283), that at that place in Eusebius’ *Chronicle* the great Doctor did not indicate Arnobius’ true period. For in the *Chronicle*, after Eusebius’ notice of Constantine’s twentieth anniversary, Jerome himself immediately adds:

> “Thus far Eusebius, the companion of Pamphilus the Martyr, writes the history; we have appended the following matters to it.”

He then continues at once: “Arnobius, a rhetorician,” etc. Therefore, to avoid interrupting Eusebius’ narrative, Jerome appended the words concerning Arnobius—of whom there is no mention in that bishop of Caesarea—to the preceding material from Eusebius. Later, in his own work *On Illustrious Men*, he clearly published his judgment concerning the same writer. [Col. 0352A]

### III

We must now examine more closely at what precise time Arnobius composed his seven books *Against the Nations*. In his work, then, three indications appear, two chronological and the third historical; from these it may in some measure be possible to determine what we are seeking. [Col. 0352B] First, the author speaks as follows: “It is nearly three hundred years, a little less or more, since we began to be Christians and to be counted as such in the world” (Arnobius, *Against the Nations*, book I, chap. 6). Here the three hundred years, to speak with Dodwell (Dodwell, *Dissert. II Iren.*, § 56, p. 197), if reckoned from the forty-second year of Augustus according to the chronology of those times, end in the year 298 of the common era.

Next we encounter these words of Arnobius: “At what age is the city of Rome stated in the annals to be? It has reached one thousand and fifty years, or not much less than that” (Arnobius, book II, chap. 34). Now the year 1050 from the founding of the City, according to the Varronian reckoning, corresponds to the year 297 of the common era; according to the Capitoline reckoning, however, it falls in the year of Christ [Col. 0352C] 298. Thus the author appears, up to this point, to be approximately consistent with himself. But since in the former passage he adds, “a little less or more,” and in the latter, “or not much less than that,” a doubt arises whether in both places he made his calculations precisely.

Setting aside, therefore, both chronological indications, we must have recourse to another, historical one, which appears more certain. The author continues as follows: “Why indeed did our writings deserve to be given to the flames? Why were our meeting places savagely destroyed?” (ibid., book IV, chap. 18). Arnobius certainly wrote these words after the year 303, when the persecution of Diocletian began to rage. “For then,” says Eusebius, “we saw with our own eyes sacred buildings leveled to the ground and utterly overthrown, and the sacred books of the divine Scriptures burned in the middle of the marketplace” [Col. 0352D] (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chap. 8).

Baronius was the first of all to embrace this more probable judgment concerning the time when Arnobius was writing (Baronius, at the year 302, § 17); he was afterward followed by Dodwell (Dodwell, loc. cit.), Pagius (Pagi, at the year 302, § 15), and others, although Tillemont attempted in some degree to weaken it (Tillemont, *Mémoires*, vol. IV, p. 767, note). Yet although Arnobius appears to speak with greater certainty in this last passage, there is no reason for us to judge, with certain learned men, that he was inconsistent with himself in his other calculations. For the author certainly did not write out all seven of his books with a single stroke of the pen. Thus, when writing the first two, he may first have accurately calculated the years from the founding of the City, and then the years of the Christian era, allowing “a little more” or [Col. 0353A] “not much less”; but when he reached book IV, at which time the Diocletian persecution was raging, he disclosed to us the date of his writing by more certain indications. On these premises, Arnobius appears finally to have completed his entire work in the year 304, or perhaps in the following year.

### IV

We may now speak of the value of Arnobius’s work in the words of a learned man, who explains his judgment approximately as follows:

> “This treasury of recondite wisdom, by which the insane religion of the nations is refuted and the true religion confirmed, is beyond all praise. For who, when he reads through its vigorous eloquence, the weight of its arguments, and its exquisite reflections, is not carried away into love and longing for so great an author? Everywhere his most flourishing style triumphs, and the pagans themselves are slain [Col. 0353B] with their own sword. That pen pierced and finished off, all at once, all the silent gods of the nations. In a word: Arnobius the African, writing *Against the Nations*, is an author of profound learning, subtle, eloquent, pre-eminent in genius and fluency, and a most valiant conqueror of paganism.”

(*Preface to Arnobius*, Leiden edition, 1651.) Such are his words.

Since Arnobius, in composing his seven books, set himself a twofold task—namely, to prove both that the religion of the pagans was false and that of the Christians true—he appears to have attacked the impiety of pagan superstition far more lucidly than he demonstrated the truth of the Christian faith. Hence St. Jerome says:

> “I think that Origen, because of his learning, should sometimes be read in the same way as Tertullian, Novatus, Arnobius, Apollinaris, and certain ecclesiastical writers, Greek and Latin alike: so that we may choose what is good in them and avoid what is contrary to it, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: ‘Test all things; hold fast what is good’” (1 Thess. 5:21).

(Jerome, Epistle LXII, otherwise LXXVI, to Tranquillinus, § 2.) [Col. 0353C]

Nevertheless, the mysteries of the Christian religion were not so unknown to Arnobius that he failed to discuss correctly the principal articles of faith, as the most learned Nourry (Nourry, *Apparatus to the Library of the Fathers*, vol. II, pp. 290, 296 ff.), Maran (Maran, *The Divinity of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, book III, chap. 4, § 5, and book IV, chap. 22, § 1, pp. 326, 534), and others have clearly demonstrated against certain excessively severe critics. It will therefore be worthwhile to consult them.

[Col. 0353D]

### V

But to conclude our discussion of the author and his work: from the sole surviving manuscript codex in the Vatican Library, written in an elegant hand more than eight hundred years ago—which afterward passed into the Royal Library at Paris—the first Roman edition of Arnobius’s work was published in 1542 through the efforts of Fausto Sabeo. This was followed by several editions refined through the scholarship of learned men—Canter, Ursinus, Elmenhorst, Stewechius, Heraldus, and others. The most accurate of them all is considered to be that published at Leiden in 1651, based upon the recension of a most celebrated scholar and accompanied by the complete commentaries of all the editors. The Paris edition of 1666 was afterward conformed to it, adorned with the notes of Priorius and selections from those of others, and appended to the works of Cyprian.

Although [Col. 0354A] the Leiden edition is rightly regarded as distinctly superior to the others, it nevertheless suffers from a considerable number of blemishes caused by the typesetters; indeed, in some places entire words are found to have been omitted altogether. The Paris edition, which reproduced it, consequently abounds in these errors and in others still more serious.

Therefore, under the particular guidance of the illustrious Nourry, who devoted very great labor to purifying and elucidating the books of Arnobius (Nourry, *Apparatus to the Library of the Fathers*, vol. II, pp. 257–570), we applied ourselves to polishing our own edition. We compared the more select notes of learned men, primarily for the correction of Arnobius’s text, and interwove such observations of our own as they were. Then, so that the reading of the author might henceforth be more useful, and at the same time that we might alleviate the readers’ [Col. 0354B] weariness and labor, we have for the first time divided the books of Arnobius—which until now had appeared as a continuous and unbroken discourse—into chapters or sections. We have further supplied an analysis of these in the index appended to the work.

Thus far Gallandi. But now let us examine the individual editions with Schoenemann.

## SIXTEENTH CENTURY

### 1543

Rome, at the press of Franciscus Priscianensis of Florence, folio: *Eight Books of Arnobius’s Disputations Against the Nations, Now First Published*. At the end: Rome, in the house of Franciscus Priscianensis, 1542.

This first edition of Arnobius is owed to Fausto Sabeo [Col. 0354C] of Brescia, at that time custodian of the Vatican Library, a learned man and especially a distinguished composer of verse. He dedicated it to Francis I, king of the French, in a letter dated at Rome, from the Palatine Library, on the Kalends of September 1543. It is useful to excerpt some material from it for the reader’s convenience. For we have discovered that, although many have spoken about this edition, very few have actually seen it, a circumstance that has everywhere given occasion to various errors.

The principal matter that may appear worthy of anyone’s attention is surely this: Sabeo says that Arnobius was his by right of war, since he had rescued him from the midst of barbarism, not without loss and danger. If one considers these words more attentively, while also recalling what we read as having been handed down concerning Sabeo’s life and activities, he appears to mean that he had discovered a codex of Arnobius—the only one, as it later proved—in remote lands—perhaps in regions of Germany or Belgium—and had brought it into the Vatican Library. For, as concerns the first part of this conjecture, he repeatedly speaks in his verses of fierce and savage peoples and the midst of barbarism, from which, at the greatest danger and labor, and even at his own expense, he brought forth ancient codices; he had been sent to search for these by Pope Leo and then by Leo’s successors.

That this same codex was deposited by him in the Vatican is suggested both by the responsibilities of the office entrusted to him and, furthermore, confirmed by the explicit words of Fulvius Ursinus—himself also an editor of Arnobius—inserted in the dedicatory letter to Gregory XIII prefixed to the second Roman edition, in which he testifies that Arnobius was first brought to light from the Vatican Library. [Col. 0355A]

At one time Ludovicus Carrio held the following opinion:

> **Note [Col. 0355D].** In *Emendations*, book I, chap. 9, fol. 18, Paris edition, 1583, quarto. What is written in the *Scaligerana* (Cologne edition, 1695, octavo, p. 33) concerning this codex of Arnobius appears neither to have been considered carefully enough by its excellent author nor to have been read correctly by the person who transcribed it.

This opinion was afterward approved by the unanimous agreement of learned men: that the codex of Arnobius now preserved in the Royal Library at Paris was the very one from which Sabeo brought Arnobius to light. This is established by the fact that a displacement of several pages into the wrong location, which occurs in the first Roman publication of these books, is finally found to occur in this codex itself. Carrio therefore suspects that this codex was presented to Francis together with the text printed by Priscianensis. If he is to be thought correct in this conjecture—as is also rendered probable by the fact that Fulvius Ursinus, editor of the second Roman edition, makes no mention of a codex that he used—this transfer must have been made by order of Pope Paul III.

Certainly, from that time onward the Royal Codex [Col. 0355B] was regarded as unique and was judged, as the safest standard of Arnobian textual criticism, worthy of repeated examination by learned men.

But let us return to Sabeo. He begins his dedicatory letter as follows:

> “For a long time now, students of the liberal arts who regard me with no ordinary affection have assailed me with daily remonstrances and almost with abuse, because, although I could and should support the study of letters and our divine faith, I continued day after day to contrive delays. The reason was that I was suppressing Arnobius, the destroyer of the old religion, and claiming him for myself. I replied, on the contrary, that he was exceedingly full of many and manifold blemishes and errors, greatly changed from what he had once been, and that he shrank from the sight of learned men [Col. 0355C] and blushed with shame.
>
> “Then they, uniting all their labor and zeal toward a single purpose, took measures to ensure that he should come forth before the public complete and cleansed. And because his treatment was being drawn out at length—for it was difficult to find and assemble at a prescribed hour many men hindered by different occupations—Hieronymus Ferrarius and Franciscus Priscianensis, most learned men of the keenest intelligence and judgment, undertook the commission of correcting and printing Arnobius. They accomplished it so successfully that they rescued him from his many enormous faults and errors; then, having printed him in elegant and most beautiful type, they brought him forth into the arena, while releasing me from accusations and vexations.”

Such are his words. From these, anyone may easily reconcile the differing and mutually contradictory statements that he will find written everywhere by various persons about this edition; I have neither the leisure nor the inclination to devote labor to refuting them.

Let us add that this edition is most splendid in the elegance of its typography and paper. We are therefore altogether astonished, along with the cardinal who wrote *Literary Brescia* (vol. II, p. 192), that a man who had nothing more frequently on his lips than “I am faint and hungry”—

> **Note [Col. 0355D].** See all the examples he produced from his epigrams.

—could have supplied the expense for so large and handsome an edition. For this is explicitly [Col. 0356A] affirmed in the privilege granted to him by Paul III and printed on several pages near the beginning. There, through a typesetter’s error, the date was falsely printed as 1562 instead of 1542—the eighth year of Paul’s pontificate.

Three copies of this edition survive in the Royal Library at Paris: one with corrections and variant readings written by the hand of Jacques Dalechamps; another with notes and corrections copied by Nicolas Rigault; and a third with a glossary by François Pithou and an index of subjects and words, together with manuscript restorations and marginal conjectures by Jean Passerat. See *Catalogue*, vol. I, p. 367.

### 1546

[Col. 0356B] Basel, at Froben’s press, octavo: *Eight Books of Arnobius’s Disputations Against the Nations, Now at Last Made So Accurate That They May Be Read by Scholars Without Any Offense and With Greater Profit from the Labor of Reading. With an Index of Matters Worthy of Note.*

Sigismund Gelenius, in his dedicatory letter to Gilbert Cousin, canon of Nozeroy, after drawing a comparison between Lactantius and Arnobius, continues:

> “But we leave this judgment to the critics; we have undertaken nothing except the labor of correction. For just as the Romans deserved praise for generosity in sharing and for fidelity in transcription, so it cannot be denied that they employed no one practiced in reading ancient characters. As a result, it very frequently happened that they transmitted not so much the authentic reading as traces of it, [Col. 0356C] by means of which we could scarcely reach the truth step by step. You will admit that our claims are not empty if you care to make the experiment on any single gathering of sheets and determine whether this edition of ours is clearer than the other. For the difference is enormous—greater than you would easily believe unless you had sampled the earlier edition.”

Besides the index praised on the title page, there was also added a short index of authors cited by Arnobius.

### 1560

Basel, at the press of Hieronymus Froben, octavo: *The Commentaries of the African Arnobius on All the Psalms, as Corrected by Desiderius Erasmus. To Which Are Added the Eight Books of Disputations Against the Nations by the Same Arnobius, as Revised by Sigismund* [Col. 0356D] *Gelenius*. *Catalogue de la Bibliothèque Royale*, vol. I, p. 367.

### 1580

Paris, at the press of Michel Julien, folio: *The Eight Books of Arnobius, First Issued in a More Correct Form by Sigismund Gelenius and Then by R. Laurentius, Together with Tertullian. R. Laurent de La Barre.*

The chief merit of this edition lies in the summaries prefixed to each book, then in the marginal notes and the index of memorable matters. Since the editor himself says absolutely nothing about the method by which he revised the text, one could scarcely describe it without diligently comparing the edition with that of Gelenius. The scholia printed below the text are not of great value.

### 1582

Antwerp, from the press of Christophe Plantin: *The Seven Books of Arnobius the Divine Against the Nations, Revised and Enlarged. From the Library of Theodorus Canter of Utrecht, Whose Notes Have Also Been Added.*

[Col. 0357A] Canter, being as destitute of manuscript codices as Gelenius, understood that he had to rely upon his own ingenuity. Supported partly by the authority of the Roman codex—that is, the first edition—which he maintains served him in place of a manuscript and contained illustrious traces of the ancient text, and partly by the aid of Clement of Alexandria, from whom our author is shown to have borrowed many passages almost word for word, he accomplished in this edition whatever was achieved.

He says:

> “We have inserted no conjectures into the text, however true and certain they might be; rather, whatever was changed and added by us was done on the authority and credit of the Roman codex. But where we had nothing better to substitute, we followed the reading of Gelenius [Col. 0357B]—who, though otherwise a most learned man and one who rendered excellent service to literature, allowed himself altogether too much liberty in correcting this author—even when it was sometimes false and far removed from every trace of the truth. In a very great number of passages, however—if I may say so without offense—we rejected his deceptive and adulterated reading and restored the true and genuine text.”

Would that he had fulfilled what he promised concerning his future study of this author:

> **Note [Col. 0357D].** In the preface to the reader before the notes, and again in the notes on the sixth book. How great an expectation of this work existed among learned men even at that time may be shown by the words of Meursius, who, when presenting his *Arnobian Critic* to readers, says: “‘What!’ you may perhaps exclaim, ‘before Canter?’ Before him indeed, but with his consent—nay, even at his command. Do not spitefully keep declaring that I have thrust my sickle into his harvest.”

He had promised to prepare a very extensive commentary on Arnobius. Certainly no one would have felt the need expressed by Salmasius. For the notes that Canter added in the present edition do no more than explain the grounds of his corrections or serve to compare passages from Clement of Alexandria. Yet Canter not infrequently appeals to conjectures by Joseph [Col. 0357C] Scaliger, Turnebus, Lipsius, and Muretus.

He dedicated Arnobius to Valentin Guellius Pimpontius, senator in the Parlement of Paris, in a letter dated at Utrecht on the Ides of November 1581. Finally, it must not be overlooked that the editor divided the text into definite chapters or sections. I do not know how it happened that subsequent editors again abandoned so excellent a practice.

### 1583

Rome, from the printing house of Domenico Basa, quarto: *The Seven Books of Arnobius’s Disputations Against the Nations—The Octavius of Marcus Minucius Felix. The Second and More Correct Roman Edition.*

It is difficult to speak of Ursinus’s work without using [Col. 0357D] his own words. We therefore prefer to appear excessive rather than, through economy of paper, risk omitting anything worth knowing.

Take, then, the following:

> “It is now the fortieth year,” he says, “since this pious writer first came forth into the light from the Vatican Library of the Holy Father—not disfigured by the condition and squalor in which he had long lain hidden, but cleansed by the industry of learned men from the almost innumerable stains with which he was befouled. Although by intelligence and learning, so far as they could in those times, [Col. 0358A] they removed almost countless blemishes from this writer—

> **Note [Col. 0358D].** He writes this, of course, on Sabeo’s authority; he by no means inspected the codex itself. One grows weary of this absurd rhetorical habit affected by all Italian authors of this age.

> “—they could not restore the entire body completely to its original splendor. Accordingly, after the book had now been published at Rome and widely circulated among men, not only Italians—many of whom then flourished in keenness of judgment and intellect—but also men beyond the Alps began to polish Arnobius with more diligent care.
>
> “Among the Italians, to omit the naming of the rest, one especially distinguished himself. He was also the first to work after the publication of the printed copy: Giovanni Battista Sighicelli of Bologna, who was afterward made bishop of Faenza by Pope Pius IV. In this writer he corrected and restored many passages that demanded no ordinary learning and no mediocre intellect, and healed others that were nearly beyond hope. But, imitating Cinna’s treatment of his *Smyrna*, never, as they say, taking his hand from the tablet and with the publication of his corrections being the last thing on his mind, he delayed; meanwhile the Germans published their own Arnobius. [Col. 0358B]
>
> “If, in return for all their wit and abuse directed against the Romans, they had displayed in transcribing the copy the same fidelity, and in correcting it the same scrupulousness, as the Romans had employed, they would undoubtedly have earned greater gratitude from all students. But as it is, while they think it lawful to correct according to their own pleasure and judgment anything they consider corrupt—adding, removing, and changing material so as to extract some meaning—they have altered so much in Arnobius that in countless passages not even a trace of the ancient reading has been left.
>
> “When Pedro Chacón, a Spaniard of great [Col. 0358C] intelligence and judgment refined by learning, observed this defect in Arnobius, he began, at the urging of that most distinguished man Cardinal Antonio Carafa—who was exceedingly eager that ancient sacred writers should be polished in every respect—to compare more carefully the printed copies available from every quarter [the text is slightly uncertain here], and to correct them both learnedly and ingeniously. He had brought the projected work to such a point that he would shortly have published Arnobius, elucidated by his industry with many excellent corrections. But when the correction of the book had been nearly completed, though not yet polished, he was carried off by an untimely death. By his will he left such corrections to that illustrious man upon whom the entire undertaking depended, to be published if the latter thought fit.”

Carafa therefore entrusted to Ursinus the task of polishing and publishing the work. [Col. 0358D] Ursinus collected into one body and carefully examined the corrections of those whom we have just named from his account, together with those of other learned men that circulated in various places concerning Arnobius. He affirms that he admitted into the text only those that appeared both to have been approved by the judgment of many and to be true beyond all dispute. Those that did not appear sufficiently certain to be admitted safely he had printed, marked by their own numbers, in the margins of the pages; and he added notes, where any existed, that had been written in confirmation of the conjectures. To all these he also added some observations of his own, noticed in passing while reading.

Finally, from Ursinus [Col. 0359A] we learn that at almost the same time as the eighth book of Arnobius was restored in Germany to its proper author, Cardinal Sirleto detected the same misattribution. It was indeed through his persuasion that the *Octavius* of Minucius was first published in Italy in this edition.

### 1586

Antwerp [from the press of Christophe Plantin], octavo: *The Seven Books of Arnobius, with the Selections of Godescalcus Stewechius.*

I have not myself seen this first edition of Stewechius, nor have I found it mentioned in any catalogue; but I cite it on the authority of Fabricius:

> **Note [Col. 0359C].** In the *Selection of Arguments and Catalogue of Writers for the Truth of the Christian Religion*, p. 226. From him, in turn, Lipenius, *Bibliotheca theologica*, I, 734, and the *Great Ecclesiastical Library of Cologne*, p. 623, cite it.

The prefaces of Stewechius inserted into the edition of 1604 appear to lend Fabricius’s statement some credibility. For there appear there two dedicatory letters and an address to the reader. [Col. 0359B] The materials prefixed to the *Selections* are dated 1586; the dedicatory letter prefixed to the text, however, is dated 1587. The preface to the reader lacks a date, but Stewechius says there that:

> “He had come very close to publishing separately two years earlier the *Selections*, which had sprung solely from his own modest talent, for the assistance of Arnobius; but Franciscus Modius had dissuaded him, and through Modius’s work it had indeed been made possible for him also to correct and restore the text.”

I do not sufficiently understand to what these statements should be referred. On the other hand, most of those who have discussed editions of Arnobius—including the exceedingly diligent Nourry—

> **Note [Col. 0359C].** *Apparatus to the Great Library of the Ancient Fathers.*

—are entirely silent about this edition. Moreover, the approbation prefixed to the Antwerp edition of 1604 appears to contradict its existence, since it says not that Arnobius was being reprinted, but that he was only then at last being committed to type:

> **Note [Col. 0359D].** To encourage learned men all the more to investigate more carefully the alleged first edition of Stewechius, let the following be added here: “This restoration of Arnobius by Godescalcus Stewechius can bring much benefit to the studious reader. I therefore judge it worthy of being committed to type. Antwerp, 24 January 1604. Egbert Spitholdus, canon and parish priest of Antwerp.”

Accordingly, although I would not now venture to determine the matter, [Col. 0359C] I nevertheless confess myself more inclined toward the view that Arnobius as edited by Stewechius was not printed before 1604. The authority of Aubertus Miraeus also supports this conclusion; he writes as an established fact:

> **Note [Col. 0359D].** In the notes on Jerome’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Fabricius edition, 1718, p. 165. Fabricius himself says no differently in the same place, and likewise Franciscus Sweertius in *Athenae Belgicae* (Antwerp, 1628, folio, p. 294), where, while reviewing the writings of Stewechius, he simply records: “*Selections on Arnobius*, printed by Trognaesius.” Add the fact that Caspar Schoppe, in his *Art of Criticism*, where he praises Stewechius’s writings, is entirely unaware of both Arnobius and the *Selections* upon him. From all these considerations I would say with some confidence that those prefaces marked with the years 1586 and 1587 misled Fabricius.

Miraeus states that Plantin printed at Antwerp in 1604 the seven books of Arnobius with the notes of Theodorus Canter, and Trognaesius printed them with the notes of Godescalcus Stewechius.

### 1597

The *Great Ecclesiastical Library* [Col. 0360A] of Cologne cites an edition by Heraldus at Geneva, but I would not venture to guarantee the statement.

### 1598

Leiden, from the press of Joannes Balduinus: *Joannes Meursius’s Arnobian Critic, Divided among Seven Books. Also the Minucian Hypocritic and Excerpts from the Manuscript of the Royal Library at Paris, in Which Arnobius Against the Nations and Minucius Are Variously Corrected in More than Six Hundred Passages, as Are Other Writers.*

Although it cannot be denied without unfairness that in this hastily composed work Meursius displayed a splendid keenness of intellect—one that blossomed from, and almost overflowed with, an abundance of every kind of learning—it will nevertheless be rightly judged that this work pertains no more to Arnobius and Minucius than to the whole of antiquity and to a very large number of writers.

[Col. 0360B] For whenever he touched upon Arnobius and Minucius, he showed himself wonderfully skilled in detecting and thoroughly healing wounds. He acutely perceived many things to which earlier editors had been altogether blind, and removed many blemishes with the lightest remedy; but these services were rendered by him much more lavishly to all sorts of other writers than to Arnobius and Minucius.

“At the beginning,” he says, “I had resolved to annotate nothing, being intent solely upon restoring the author’s health. Yet I could not restrain myself from occasionally making excursions, especially when invited by an opportunity to correct another passage.” In all such cases he carefully and conscientiously endeavored to claim nothing belonging to another, not to waste time reporting other men’s corrections or refuting their errors, but simply to set forth his own views.

Furthermore, you would, I think, have conceded even without his assertion that everything he accomplished in Arnobius proceeded from his own ingenuity and not from ancient books. [Col. 0360C] Yet you may perhaps be surprised that the first edition was so rare in those regions that Meursius says he wished Canter had reproduced more variants from the Roman codex, since this would have furnished an opportunity for making further discoveries.

Finally, there were appended to this work excerpts from the Royal Manuscript, taken from the book of Joseph Scaliger, who had once collated it at Paris with the Royal Manuscript. Meursius appended his own judgment to each reading, and sometimes more extended observations as well. “In general,” he says:

> “I have seen from this collation that several passages may usefully be enlarged, that some of my conjectures are confirmed, and that occasion is likewise given for discovering not a few new ones—although, in truth, I very often found coals instead of the treasure for which I had hoped, and nothing but a dunghill; [Col. 0360D] yet from it, unless my judgment deceives me egregiously, I extracted a few little gems, so to speak.”

These excerpts, moreover, are dedicated to his friend Petrus Scriverius, whom he himself describes as most dearly beloved. No one should hesitate to count among fables what Adrien Baillet (*Des Antiscripteurs*, vol. II, p. 299) handed down concerning Scriverius’s *Anticritic*.

## SEVENTEENTH CENTURY

### 1603

Hanau, octavo: *Arnobius … with Notes by Geverhard Elmenhorst, Dedicated to the Illustrious Joseph Scaliger, Easily the Foremost Scholar of His Age.*

Thus Fabricius (*Delectus*, p. 226), and after him the *Great* [Col. 0361A] *Ecclesiastical Library*, present Elmenhorst’s first edition. Nourry handled a copy of it.

Paris, octavo: *Arnobius … with Observations by Desiderius Heraldus.* Fabricius cites this in the passage indicated; I doubt whether correctly.

### 1604

Antwerp, at the press of Joachim Trognaesius, octavo: *Arnobius … with the Selections of Godescalcus Stewechius.* Compare what was said above under the year 1586.

Stewechius devoted repeated labor to his Arnobius. He first composed the *Selections*, in which undertaking he admits that he relied solely upon his own ingenuity. Then, when variant readings from a manuscript codex had been supplied to him by Franciscus Modius, he took up anew the labor he had already completed. By means of these readings, he affirms, he not only improved the *Selections* but also interpolated, [Col. 0361B] corrected, and enlarged Arnobius’s text itself in countless places by filling lacunae of great importance. We shall present our judgment concerning this codex in its proper place.

As regards the *Selections*—for we must hear about these before there is occasion to speak of the recension of the text itself—Stewechius says that he decided to call them by this name because, from the very many passages he found corrupt or obscure, he selected those that were to be corrected or illustrated from his own ingenuity and from parchment codices. This effort, generally and almost everywhere based on the ancient usage and distinctive character of Roman speech, as well as on rites traditionally observed among the ancients, by no means turned out unsuccessfully for him, and so forth.

Just as Varro provides very great assistance toward the elucidation of Arnobius, so these *Selections* of Stewechius, in my [Col. 0361C] judgment, provide excellent assistance in understanding Varro and all earlier linguistic learning. The synopsis of contents prefixed to them also contributes considerably to this end.

Yet neither from these materials nor from the edition itself that I hold in my hands can I confess myself sufficiently able to discern how he refashioned the text according to his own or other men’s conjectures. The text certainly presented by the Trognaesius edition of 1604 does not differ greatly from that of Ursinus; yet it cites Stewechius’s readings in the margin all the more frequently, and sometimes in such a fashion that one cannot tell whether these printers issued a recension differing in some way from that of Stewechius.

If our conjecture has been made somewhat too hastily, and the Antwerp edition of 1604 was in fact printed according to Stewechius’s own copy, one may perhaps praise the modesty of the man, who preferred to fill the margins of the book with corrections and conjectures [Col. 0361D] rather than admit even the most certain correction into the continuous text. Whether, as matters stand, he can be said to have interpolated, corrected, and produced a more complete text itself, let others decide.

For although, in the same preface from which we quoted the preceding statements, he claims concerning his work in preparing the text that, with the utmost candor, he wrote everywhere in their proper places—and even in the margin itself—the names of those who before him had extended helping hands to Arnobius, and that he would have done the same in the case of the material supplied by Ursinus, had the latter not mixed everything together, his own with that of others; nevertheless, because of this diligence regarding variant readings, he could not regard himself as the savior of the text itself.

### 1605

Paris, at the press of Marc Orry, in the Rue Saint-Jacques, at the sign of the Leaping Lion, octavo: *The Seven Books of Arnobius … The Octavius of Marcus* [Col. 0362A] *Minucius Felix. A New Edition, Printed after the Roman Edition, but Enlarged and Corrected in Certain Places from the Royal Manuscript. Observations and Corrections by Desiderius Heraldus on the Seven Books of Arnobius.*

By “Roman” understand the most recent Roman edition. The more ancient readings it restored, the more excellent it appeared to Heraldus and the more frequently it was praised by him. Consequently, in a number of passages where that edition had followed Gelenius, he abandoned it and either embraced Canter’s opinion or introduced certain material of his own.

He delivered judgment on individual readings in his observations, though in very few words. The remaining observations serve either to explain the meaning or to illustrate matters of every kind. Although various materials in them are drawn from every branch of ancient learning, he by no means forgot what was appropriate, what was irrelevant, or what was commonplace. [Col. 0362B]

It was also an excellent arrangement that the text of Arnobius should be presented separately with its own special index of subjects, and then that the observations of Heraldus themselves should be presented with indexes both of the authors who are variously illustrated or corrected and of the subjects discussed.

Finally, it deserves notice that this work was undertaken for recreation and brought to completion within the space of two months. It should also be noted that the dedicatory letter, which entirely serves in place of a preface, is dated at Paris on the Kalends of March 1605. Thus it scarcely appears probable that the work of Heraldus was published before that year.

### 1610

Hamburg, folio: *The Seven Books of Arnobius … Geverhard Elmenhorst Revised Them by Collating Various Codices and Illustrated Them with Observations*—so the title reads.

[Col. 0362C] Elmenhorst to the reader: “So that you may understand the method of my undertaking, know that in preparing this new edition of Arnobius I relied principally upon the old text of Francesco Sabeo of Brescia, printed at Rome in 1542. Wherever it was corrupt or defective, I had recourse to manuscript excerpts and the emendations of learned men, selected the best of them, and—though rarely—inserted them into Arnobius’ text, as reason itself dictated. I also added a collection of variant readings, in which I name those whose emendations I approve and follow. In my observations I chiefly sought to expound the meaning of the author whom I undertook to edit, and, wherever it was obscure, to elucidate it briefly and plainly. Certainly I have freed this most learned writer from innumerable [Col. 0362D] blemishes of the foulest errors and, as I trust, have applied wholesome remedies to countless passages in his work that were in a diseased condition. I do not, however, conceal the fact that many false and corrupt readings still remain which cannot possibly be understood or corrected without the aid of a better manuscript. I deliberately passed over these without touching them and left them to be corrected by more gifted minds. Etc.”

You now know the manuscripts whose impressive display makes the title-page boastful. If you ask about Elmenhorst himself, he certainly lacked maturity and diligence, if not ability. The text was copied almost word for word from the second Roman edition. Consequently, he also took all the conjectures and emendations that Ursinus had placed in the margin without naming their authors, cited them under Fulvius’ name, and, intermingling others with them, appended them at the end of his observations, rarely interposing a judgment of his own. [Col. 0363A] Nor, indeed, were the annotations composed in such a way that they could greatly please the learned men whom his age produced. Apart from material heaped up abundantly from every ancient writer concerning individual words or subjects, you will look in vain for anything else. Nevertheless, this edition was printed quite handsomely, in clear and splendid type; and although it lacks a division into chapters, a number is conveniently marked in the inner margin for every ten lines of each page. Three indexes were also added to the text—of subjects, words, and expressions—and two to the annotations: one of authors whose passages are cited, and one of subjects and terms. In the copy of this edition preserved by the Royal-Academic Library, certain notes and emendations were added by Heumann, who formerly owned it.

[Col. 0363B] Toulouse, 1612, octavo: Julius Caesar Bulenger of Juliodunum, *Book One of Selections on Arnobius*.—A worthless work.

## 1634

Douai, octavo: Stewechius’ *Selections*, with *Paratitla*, or summaries, by Leander of St Martin.

## 1651

Leiden, from the press of Johannes Maire, quarto: *The Seven Books of Arnobius . . . . ., with the recension of a most celebrated man and the complete commentaries of all commentators. The newest and most accurate edition of all.*

“As regards this edition of our Arnobius, which we here present in a most accurate form,” says the printer, “some years ago we obtained a copy emended by the hand of a most celebrated man, [Col. 0363C] whose learning and reputation hold, as it were, the foremost place in those arts that take their name from humanitas. We subsequently entrusted its care to another learned man, so that he might bring forward whatever could be collected to enhance the distinction of this edition. We have therefore brought together all the commentators—and indeed their complete works, with no part abridged—into a single body, so that the rationale of the edition may be derived from them, and so that it may lack nothing that one could even desire in one’s fondest wishes.”

Salmasius is thought to have been the author of this recension, and his commentary is likewise said to have been cut short by his death. So far as we have learned by comparison—for absolutely no record of the alterations appears, I suppose lest the typographical elegance be impaired—the recension is certainly not unworthy of him. It therefore differs altogether from its predecessors, although it adopted many of those readings [Col. 0363D] which, as we have indicated, Ursinus had proposed in the margin of his edition; and thus perhaps Salmasius made his principal offering to Ciacconius’ genius.

There is no need to instruct readers at greater length concerning the other merits of this edition. They will find the commentaries of Canter, Stewechius, Elmenhorst, and Heraldus copied word for word. They might at least have served the convenience of scholars by appending a comprehensive index. For the rest, Antonius Thysius, jurisconsult, is said to have been partly responsible for preparing this edition—namely, for ensuring that the annotations of the individual commentators were correctly transcribed—as is also shown by his epigram on Arnobius on the page immediately following the dedication. Nourry complained especially that this otherwise most elegant edition teems with compositors’ errors, and very ugly ones at that.

## 1666

[Col. 0364A]

Paris, published by Jean Dupuis, folio, together with the works of Cyprian, from Rigault’s edition as prepared by Priorius. From the Paris journal of this year [Note: [Col. 0364D] *Journal des savants*, February, page 41: “The whole accompanied by observations from various authors.”] we have learned that all the authors published here in addition to Rigault’s Cyprian were furnished, as in the earlier edition, with excerpts from the notes of various scholars. The text was reproduced from the Leiden edition, together with all its errors, which were likewise augmented.

## 1677

Lyon, published by the Anissons, folio, in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, vol. III, pp. 430–514. A reprint of Priorius’ edition. The notes are for the most part Elmenhorst’s, with occasional notes by Heraldus, Stewechius, and others, among which Priorius interspersed his own.

# THE EIGHTEENTH CENTURY

## 1715

[Col. 0364B] Paris, published by Jean-Baptiste Delespine, folio, in Nicolas Le Nourry’s *Apparatus to the Bibliotheca Maxima Patrum Published at Lyon*, vol. II, pp. 257–570.—A dissertation on Arnobius in which, after analyses of the individual books, he discusses the author, the date, purpose, subject, and treatment of the work, its style, learning, and other merits, the arrangement of the work, the integrity of the books, and the corruption of the text; the errors of Arnobius; the various manuscripts and editions of these books; and the notes and observations upon them. He treats these matters at length, in his customary fashion but excellently, from p. 257 to p. 296. Finally, from p. 296 to p. 570, he presents new observations on Arnobius, in which either the individual arguments employed by Arnobius both to establish the truth and to refute his opponents’ [Col. 0364C] errors are examined, or the more important monuments of antiquity are elucidated.

## 1768

Venice, from the printing house of Giovanni Battista Albrizzi, folio, in Gallandi’s *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, etc., vol. IV, pp. 133–224. The text of the Leiden edition is presented, cleansed of blemishes and polished through the use of Nourry’s contributions. It had also been resolved to add a selection of the more important notes, especially those concerned with emending the text, but here we miss diligence as much as judgment. To what purpose, I ask, are Priorius’ notes, which you will see thrust upon every page? The singular merit by which this edition surpasses the preceding editions of Arnobius—and perhaps its greatest merit—is its division into chapters of the text that, with the sole exception of Canter, all previous editors had [Col. 0364D] presented in one uninterrupted sequence. An analysis of these chapters, appended at the end, offers what amounts to an epitome of the entire author.

## 1783

Würzburg, at the Stahel bookshop, octavo: *The Seven Books of Arnobius Afer Against the Nations, and Julius Firmicus Maternus, vir clarissimus, On the Error of Profane Religions*, etc.

The same works under the title: *Works of the Holy Latin Fathers*, volume five.

# THE NINETEENTH CENTURY

## 1816

Leipzig, at the expense of Friedrich Christian Wilhelm Vogel, [Col. 0365] two volumes, octavo, bearing the title: *The Seven Books of the Disputations of Arnobius Afer Against the Nations*.—Edited and elucidated with [Col. 0366] selected notes by earlier interpreters, by others, and by the editor himself, Johann Conrad Orelli.

[Col. 0365]

# PRELIMINARY DISSERTATION ON THE SEVEN BOOKS OF ARNOBIUS’ DISPUTATIONS *AGAINST THE NATIONS*

(BY DOM LE NOURRY)

## CHAPTER ONE  
Analysis of These Books

[Col. 0365A]

### ARTICLE I  
Analysis of the First Book

At the very beginning of his work Arnobius declares that he undertook it in order to repel the old and frequently repeated calumny by which the pagans, because the Christians had renounced and rejected the worship of false gods, accused them—no less falsely than rashly—of being the cause and authors of every public calamity and evil. The graver this accusation was, the more, he professes, he was impelled to refute it, while nevertheless setting aside partisan zeal, lest, if all Christians remained silent, it should either appear true to some [Col. 0365B] or the pagans should boast that they had won their case.

He therefore makes it clear that, from the rise of the Christian religion down to his own times, nothing had been either altered, weakened, or dissolved in the qualities of the elements, the entire fabric of the world, the courses of the stars, the alternation of seasons, days, and nights, the fertility of the earth and animals, the private and public affairs of mankind, or the customary manner of life.

Nor does he allow the pagans to object that, because the gods had been offended by the Christians’ impiety, crimes, and contempt, the world was being overwhelmed by pestilence, hailstorms, barrenness, wars, and other calamities. For from the pagans’ own histories and annals we know that, before the name of Christians had ever been heard, [Col. 0365C] mankind was afflicted by the same calamities or by still more frequent and greater disasters—the printed Latin has the apparently corrupt *claribus*, probably *cladibus*—including rains of stones, earthquakes and chasms in the earth, flood, fire, the savagery of wild beasts, the venom of serpents, and the overthrow and destruction of entire cities. It is likewise certain that cruel wars were formerly waged by the Atlanteans, Assyrians, Bactrians, Persians, Greeks, Trojans, and Romans—by Ninus, Zoroaster, Xerxes, Alexander the Great, and others—and that wars diminished after the birth of Christ.

“Why, then,” the pagans asked, “is the world oppressed by so many and such great evils, and all but crushed beneath them?” “What is that to me?” Arnobius replies. “It is not my office,” he says, “to disclose those hidden causes, since I applied myself to writing [Col. 0366A] solely in order to vindicate the Christian religion from the most unjust calumnies.” “But what,” he continues, “if these things must be referred to natural causes: to the sharp and violent impact of the elements, the various motions of the stars, and fixed cycles of events from which good and evil flow, ebb, and alternate?” Moreover, things that appear evil to human beings, who measure everything by their own convenience, are certainly beneficial to nature as a whole and to the world. Our author confirms this by Plato’s authority and by various examples involving sailors, the sun, a torrent, rain, winter, summer, hellebore, wolves, and serpents. From this he concludes that it is the mark of an arrogant man to investigate these hidden causes unless he has first learned who [Col. 0366B] he himself is, whence he comes, and why the world was created.

He further shrewdly convicts the pagans of the perversity of clamoring that all evils must be laid at the door of Christians, who had arisen only about three hundred years before: for in the intervening years and periods following their appearance, innumerable victories had been won, the boundaries of the Roman Empire extended, and the food supply had been extraordinarily abundant.

The pagans nevertheless countered that during those very periods, because of the gods’ corresponding hatred for the Christians, fields had sometimes been devastated by barrenness and wars had occasionally ended unsuccessfully. “What then?” says our author. “Can the gods, with truly astonishing inconstancy, be said [Col. 0366C] to remember and forget by turns the injuries inflicted upon them by Christians?” Moreover, Christians lived throughout the whole world, intermingled with every nation. By what right, then, can it be asserted that, in vengeance upon them, the Alamanni, Persians, and Scythians were defeated by the Romans; that Asia and Syria were gnawed bare and consumed by mice and locusts, but not Spain and Gaul; that the Gaetulians and Tinguitanians suffered a shortage of grain, while the Moors and Nomads were enriched by an exceedingly abundant harvest; or, finally, that some were killed by famine while others in the same city enjoyed an abundance of everything? For if the gods possessed any fairness and justice, all those peoples among whom Christians lived in equal measure should certainly have shared one and the same lot and fortune.

[Col. 0367A] Arnobius next demonstrates by various arguments that anger cannot possibly befall the immortal gods. What, then, could be more absurd to say than that they were so inflamed with anger by the injuries inflicted upon them by the Christians that they exacted punishment for them indiscriminately both from the Christians themselves and from the innocent pagans, as the latter claimed? For they could easily have afflicted the guilty separately with punishments and the deserving with benefits. If there are any heavenly gods, they can neither be mollified by the pagans’ flattery nor grieve and grow angry because of the Christians’ contempt. Our author therefore concludes that these ridiculous charges were fabricated solely by the greed of soothsayers, diviners, and prophets.

With no less effrontery, the pagans objected that the gods raged against mankind because the Christians had introduced throughout the entire world certain forms of worship hitherto [Col. 0367B] unheard of. For Christians revere, worship, love, and daily invoke the one true God, the Lord of all things, who knows the innermost thoughts of our hearts. Whoever condemns the worship of this true God—whether he be called Jupiter, Apollo, or anything else—does not deserve the name of god. But because the time had not yet come to disclose who these and the other pagan gods were, our author there openly declares the sum of the whole Christian religion: to worship and adore, with sincere mind and prostrate body, that true and only God, as Christ taught; and, with prayers joined together, to ask from him true and honorable goods and innocence of life and conduct. [Col. 0367C] Who could deny that the cause of these worshipers is better than that of those who adore and revere Grandules, Aii Locutii, Limentini, Fauns, Fatuae, the guardian spirits of cities, Pausi, and Bellonae? Yet the gods tolerate these worshipers without punishment and permit public rites to be performed for prostitutes and courtesans and magnificent temples to be erected for cats, dung beetles, and heifers; while, incensed with anger against the Christians, they forbid them to adore the supreme Father, from whom those very gods of the pagans must themselves have received whatever divinity, power, and immortality they are believed to possess.

But to make this still more evident, Arnobius proves from the effects that the true God is the maker of all things, older than Apollo, Mercury, and all the other fictitious divinities, infinite, unbegotten, immortal, eternal, and circumscribed by no place or bodily [Col. 0367D] form. Accordingly, just as it is unsurprising that one should not know what sort of being he is or how great he is, so it is the height of madness to call into doubt whether he actually exists. There have nevertheless been philosophers who either denied this or continually investigated it, as well as those who thought that everything was fashioned by chance events and the collisions of atoms. But since it is an even greater folly to contradict foolish assertions, Arnobius passes over these claims and asserts that it has been implanted by nature in everyone to acknowledge this supreme king and governor of all. Indeed, he confidently maintains that even animals and stones themselves, if they happened to be able to speak, would proclaim it openly and publicly. The pagans therefore proclaim Jupiter the supreme god in vain. For the supreme God is unbegotten and eternal. [Col. 0368A] Yet who does not know that Jupiter not only had brothers but also grandfathers and grandmothers, a father and mother, from whom he was born in the ordinary human manner? If the pagans, therefore, did not worship this Jupiter, but their religion and that of the Christians were one, there would no longer be any anger on Jupiter’s part—or, if there were, it would expose his divinity as false.

The pagans nevertheless insisted that their gods were hostile to the Christians, not indeed because the Christians revered almighty God, but because they maintained that a man who had been born and put to death by the infamous punishment of the cross was God, and adored him with daily supplications. Arnobius asks these same pagans who the gods were who took offense at Christ’s being worshiped by us. “Not Janus,” he says, “not Saturn, [Col. 0368B] Fauna, Bona Dea, the Indigetes, Aesculapius, Liber Pater, Mercury, Diana, Apollo, Venus, Ceres, Proserpina, Hercules, the Titans, the Bocores, Apis or Serapis, Isis, and the sons of Ops,” whom the most ancient pagan histories record as having been born in the human manner, lived just like other human beings, and died. Did they themselves wish to be worshiped by the pagans and, forgetful of their former condition, prove unable to endure without the greatest fits of anger that Christians worshiped Christ?

But if it was right for the pagans to enroll certain persons among the gods because of the benefits which, as they believed, those persons had conferred upon them—Liber for the invention of wine, Ceres for bread, Aesculapius for medicinal herbs, Minerva for the olive, Triptolemus for the plow, and Hercules for [Col. 0368C] conquering monsters—how much more should Christ receive divine honor from mankind? For he most abundantly bestowed upon them benefits far greater and infinite in number: by imbuing us with true knowledge of God, breaking our pride, and leading us away from false opinions and the impious worship of the gods to the true religion, as Arnobius himself had learned through saving experience.

“But he,” the pagans said, “perished affixed to the gibbet of the cross.” What follows from that? For Christ’s death no more detracted from his teaching and outstanding deeds than did the deaths of Pythagoras or Socrates from theirs. Moreover, what infamy of death can ever brand an innocent man, such as Aquilius, Trebonius, or Regulus? And what is more worthy of ridicule than this argument of the pagans, who honored with superstitious worship and temples Liber Pater, [Col. 0368D] who was torn limb from limb by the Titans; Aesculapius, who was struck by lightning; Hercules, who was burned alive; Attis, who was mutilated; and Romulus, who was killed by the senators?

Furthermore, Christ, sent to us by the supreme King, is proved as certainly as evidently to be the true God by the innumerable miracles he performed. He did not accomplish them by magical power, as some most shamelessly lied. By his word and name alone he healed every kind of disease, drove out demons, calmed the violent surges of winds and storms, walked upon the sea with dry feet, raised others and himself from the dead, and afterward presented himself to the sight of very many people. He gave his disciples the ability to speak in every language, even those unknown to them; suddenly filled the whole world with his teaching; [Col. 0369A] imposed silence upon prophets and soothsayers; and utterly crushed the arrogance of magicians.

Nor could one oppose to these deeds the cases of ill health among certain people supposedly cured by the pagans’ gods. Even if this is granted for the moment without proof, it remained certain that no pagan god had ever restored health to sick people, as Christ had, merely by applying a hand or uttering a word. Arnobius also freely concedes that some god might have been able to heal one or two sick persons with certain medicines. “But,” he says, “there are many thousands of people who, though they very frequently prostrated themselves in temples and wearied Aesculapius and the other gods with repeatedly offered prayers and vows, nevertheless found not even the slightest [Col. 0369B] relief and indeed were afterward in an even worse condition.”

Nor does he permit another pagan to object that the gods bring assistance not to evil people but only to good and pious ones. For Christ assists all evil persons equally with the good. Furthermore, if the gods gave aid only to the good, this must undoubtedly be attributed not to divine power but to some chance occurrence.

Our author further demonstrates the truth of Christ’s miracles from that wholly marvelous power which Christ gave even to men of the lowest common rank—fishermen, craftsmen, and peasants—to perform every kind of wonder merely in his name. For neither Jupiter nor Zoroaster, Armenius, Pamphilus, Apollonius, Damigerus, Dardanus, Velus, Julianus, Bebulus, nor anyone else ever performed anything resembling these wonders; indeed, none even healed a pustule [Col. 0369C] in the same manner as Christ and his disciples. And truly, the greatness and power of Christ himself—God on high and from his innermost root, though formerly unknown to mankind—was demonstrated with the utmost clarity even by the miracles that occurred at his death alone.

Nor were the pagans to be heard who, with utterly intolerable audacity, clamored that these things were false. For witnesses of the greatest credibility, and not readily credulous, handed these events down to posterity; and unless they had been clearer than light itself, those witnesses would surely not, by proclaiming them, have willingly incurred the universal hatred of mankind for no reason. And if these miracles were indeed false, by what fateful desperation, I ask, and at what certain peril to their lives, were they proclaimed by Christ’s disciples? How was the Christian religion established and confirmed by them and accepted throughout the entire world in the briefest [Col. 0369D] span of time?

No one could ever say, except with the greatest absurdity, that these same miracles were either falsely recorded or excessively exaggerated by our writers. For they had not committed to writing and memory every event that might have led the pagans into still greater astonishment or disbelief. If any writings are found to have been corrupted or adulterated, Arnobius ascribes this to the malice of demons, who sought by these corruptions to weaken the truth of events that had actually occurred. Yet the things written about Christ in our books are as true as the things handed down by the pagans concerning their gods are false.

“But our writings,” they insisted, “are older and therefore truer.” As if, says Arnobius, that [Col. 0370A] antiquity had not been the mother of so many and such great errors and fables as fill the books of those same pagans! Moreover, falsehood can be detected by everyone far more easily in recent writings than in the most ancient ones.

The pagans insisted that the Christians’ books had been composed by uneducated men in rough and unpolished language and were everywhere foully defiled by solecisms and barbarisms. “Granted,” Arnobius replies. “For that very reason they must surely be accorded greater trust, because they proceeded from a simple mind ignorant of seductive embellishment.” Truth does not pursue the reputation, pomp, and ornaments of elegant and polished discourse, which must be left to the forum. Moreover, this very truth, amid defects of language, benefits mankind always, like good fruit among brambles and thorns. [Col. 0370B] Furthermore, when matters far removed from display are being discussed, attention must be paid to what is actually said, not to how it is said. Accordingly, certain devotees of wisdom, although they could have spoken correctly and ornately, nevertheless rejected every refinement of discourse. Finally, as Arnobius proves, no form of speech is defective by its own nature, but only by human convention.

Since the pagans could not deny these things, they asked the Christians why Christ, if he was God, assumed human form and was killed in the human manner. Arnobius easily answers them, saying that because Christ could never be seen by any human being, nor could he die, in his original and incorporeal nature, he therefore assumed human form, by which he might make himself visible to them, live among them, and at last be able [Col. 0370C] to undergo death. Arnobius admits, however, that there were hidden reasons why Christ assumed human rather than some other nature—reasons which the pagans’ obstinate unbelief and stubbornness did not permit to be explained.

But they again objected that it was wholly incredible, and more obscure than Cimmerian darkness, that Christ, being God and man, had appeared only in human nature and ended his life affixed to a gibbet. But this rebuttal, says Arnobius, is futile. For if the Sibyl, Bacis, Helenus, Martius, and the other prophets of those same pagans had been impiously killed, would they say that those through whom they believed their gods had spoken were killed because of their own crimes? Besides, Arnobius continues, Christ’s death belonged to the human being assumed, not to Christ himself; to what was carried, not to the bearer. He adds that Christ died voluntarily because of most profound mysteries, [Col. 0370D] since no one could ever have inflicted even the slightest violence—much less laid violent hands—upon him by whom so many miracles had been performed. Christ therefore allowed himself to be killed by the impious in order to heal and instruct mankind, with as much gentleness as freedom.
