Arnobius consequently rebukes the pagans sharply: although they bestowed divine honors upon tyrants polluted by every kind of impiety and crime, extolled the authors of satirical books with the highest praises, and presented them with statues, they nevertheless persecuted Christ alone—the herald of the greatest and most salutary truths—with the most unjust and implacable hatred. For what could be more unjust and cruel than continually to assail with the bitterest warfare the lord of all virtues and destroyer of death, who, by permitting his own death, gave everyone certain hope for the future salvation of our souls, provided that we live piously?

[Col. 0371A]

### ARTICLE II  
Analysis of the Second Book

After requesting leave to depart briefly from his subject, Arnobius asks the pagans why they hated Christ, who was guilty of no offense against them, so intensely that, merely upon hearing his name, they immediately blazed with anger. Even if he were not worthy of being believed by anyone, he still should not have been despised, precisely because he showed everyone the way to heaven and blessed immortality. The pagans replied that he was the object of their utmost [Col. 0371B] hatred because he had expelled from the entire world all worship of the gods and the entire religion of their ancestors. “Is Christ impious, then,” says Arnobius, “because, after overthrowing an impious religion, he introduced the true one and taught us that only the true God must be worshiped—the God whom we naturally know and attest to be the source of every good, the creator of all things, and therefore actually existent?”

Then, postponing to another occasion a discussion of the pagans’ various superstitions, he shows that they were wholly unjustified in refusing to believe Christ’s words merely because he did not prove to us by actual delivery that he would one day give what he promised. “But,” says Arnobius, “if no certain proof of future things can be offered, is it not better to believe those who offer some hope than others who [Col. 0371C] offer none?” He then shows that we possess many by no means wholly uncertain proofs concerning what Christ promised. First, his teaching and religion were disseminated within a brief span of time through every part of the world, even among the more barbarous nations, just as he had promised. Second, however harsh and austere this teaching might appear, it was nevertheless eagerly sought by orators, grammarians, rhetoricians, jurisconsults, physicians, and philosophers endowed with great ability. Third, his followers could not be compelled by absolutely any punishments, even the most severe, to abandon it; instead, their number continually increased through those very punishments. Since these things, previously promised by Christ, had occurred, there was no reason to doubt the fulfillment [Col. 0371D] of the other things he had also promised.

Nor could so many people initiated into the Christian religion throughout the whole earth appear to others to be dull, obtuse, and foolish unless those others boasted that they alone were endowed with wisdom and knowledge. “But with what sort of wisdom and knowledge?” asks our author. “Grammar, poetry, rhetoric, logic, and dialectic?” How empty the display of these disciplines is becomes evident from the fact that a human being cannot know by himself either divine or obscure things; what he himself is, as Socrates says; whence, by whom, and for what reason he was created; why he is oppressed by so many miseries and evils; what he does in dreams; what difference there is between dreaming and waking; how sight or smell occurs; or why the mind, though immortal, is foolish in infants and weary in the old. Finally, although [Col. 0372A] a person may sometimes pronounce something true, he still does not know even that with certainty.

The pagans, therefore, since they were in no respect more learned than others, wrongly reproached the Christians for believing their divine teacher. For without antecedent faith no undertaking at all is begun by travelers, sailors, or farmers. Without faith no one enters marriage; no sick person summons a physician; no soldier wages war; no pupil listens to a teacher; nor does any pagan invoke his gods. Indeed, the pagans believed the opinions of philosophers, who nevertheless put forward nothing certain or established about the first principles of things or other subjects and continually battle among themselves. Is it not therefore more reasonable to believe Christ, who confirmed his teaching by such great miracles, than Plato, Cronius, Numenius, [Col. 0372B] or any others, however worthy of praise for their moral integrity and their knowledge of eloquence, logic, arithmetic, music, and geometry, who could never perform the least thing resembling these miracles? Certainly, if Christ had used only human subtleties and arguments, everyone would have denied him the belief which they were compelled to grant because of the miracles performed by him and his disciples among the Indians, Seres, Persians, Medes, Arabs, Egyptians, Galatians, Parthians, and Phrygians, and in Asia, Syria, Achaea, Macedonia, Epirus, and everywhere in East and West—most especially at Rome, where Simon Magus was cast down from the heights of the air by Peter and fell to the ground with his legs broken.

What more need be said? The faith of the Christians certainly ought not to have been assailed by the pagans but praised [Col. 0372C] by them, because Christians shared with the leading philosophers opinions concerning God, the resurrection of bodies, the salvation of souls, and the future punishments of the impious, although these matters were explained differently by the philosophers and by Christians. At this point Arnobius expounds the nature of our soul, the source from which it proceeds, and why it becomes subject to various passions and vices.

He then rebuffs the arrogance of those who insolently boasted that our soul shares the same immortality and nature as God the Father. For we are born, live, and are undone by disease and old age in the same manner as animals. In addition, some have thought that after death the souls of the wicked migrate into the bodies of beasts.

[Col. 0372D] “But,” they said, “the soul of man is divine, since man surpasses the other animals in reason.” “Very well indeed,” says Arnobius, “if man always made good use of this reason of his.” But where is the excellence of the human soul? Is it because human beings build houses and cities? Yet if living creatures had hands capable of practicing the arts, they too could certainly erect similar buildings. For other things are made by them which human beings have never been able to imitate. Do human beings surpass beasts because they know how to procure clothing, household furnishings, and other necessities for sustaining human life? Yet all these things are not the gifts of knowledge but inventions of direst necessity.

Furthermore, since all human arts and branches of knowledge, acquired through labor and experience, contain nothing greatly marvelous [Col. 0373A] in themselves, and since not everyone knows everything, it must surely be regarded as settled and certain that human souls, neither divine nor instructed in all knowledge, did not fly down from heaven into this world. From this also collapses the error of Plato and certain other philosophers, expressed merely in different words, whereby they dreamed that knowledge is the recollection of things known by a person before he was born. Arnobius overthrows this false opinion with still other arguments. First, because then all human beings would possess the same knowledge, recollection, and judgment. Second, suppose that some boy is born in an utterly desolate and inaccessible wilderness and is raised there in total silence by a mute nurse; that he subsequently lives upon some exceedingly simple food and never hears anyone speak. Let him then, after thirty or forty years, be brought out from that place and appear in public. Duller than a stone, [Col. 0373B] he will be entirely unable to answer when questioned about any subject whatever; he will know nothing of natural things or of those things believed necessary for human use, comfort, and pleasure, which our author enumerates. Finally, he will not utter any articulate and distinct sound. Is it not clearly established from this that his soul did not come into the world instructed in every branch of knowledge?

Arnobius then brilliantly refutes Plato’s opposing argument, drawn from questioning a boy about numbers. For if you were to ask not only this boy but even the forty-year-old man just described anything about multiplying or dividing numbers, or about triangles and squares, he would be completely mute; or he would answer, not from Plato’s fictitious memory of things once known, but from what he had learned through daily practice. Human beings are indeed instructed by their teachers’ training, just as animals are trained by practice and habituation. The human soul, therefore, did not come here instructed in all knowledge. For it should teach rather than be taught.

Nor should you say that when the soul is joined to the body it forgets its former knowledge and, as they say, from being learned becomes elementary—that is, needing instruction in the first elements. For, first, according to the teaching of those same philosophers, the soul is a simple and incorporeal substance. When joined to the body, therefore, it cannot lose anything belonging to its spiritual nature and former knowledge. [Col. 0373D] Otherwise it would become mortal and corruptible. Second, while it animates the body, it remembers things that it did and heard more than eighty years before; it should therefore remember all the more those things which it knew before its union with the body. Finally, if this union causes its former knowledge to fall from the soul, how can they say that it knows itself to be incorporeal, immortal, and once imbued with every kind of knowledge, but then to have forgotten everything it knew?

Finally, from the arguments thus set forth, Arnobius concludes that man—a proletarian (proletarius), a census-class citizen (classicus), one counted by head (capite census), and altogether destitute—is not to be assigned to the first order, that is, the divine, nor is the same immortality to be attributed to him as to God. Otherwise, being exposed to no accidental misfortunes [Col. 0374A] and fearing no punishments in the underworld, he will cast himself headlong and with impunity into every kind of pleasure and wickedness, in contempt of the virtues.

By the same reasoning, moreover, Arnobius attacks and utterly overthrows the contrary opinion of Epicurus, who prattled that our soul is mortal. For if that opinion is true, there will no longer be any reason why we should cultivate our minds through philosophy, devote ourselves to the virtues, and flee from vice.

Concerning our soul, then, our Arnobius determines as follows: it is a substance of a certain intermediate nature between the mortal and the divine, and by God’s beneficence is made long-lived and immortal. Therefore Christians, leading a pious manner of life in this world, hope that after death [Col. 0374B] they too will migrate back to heaven—as the pagans boasted of their own return thither—and, in addition, obtain from God the reward of eternal happiness promised by Christ, with the most certain pledge of his miracles.

“But how,” they asked, “can the soul ever become immortal, if it is of that intermediate quality?” Arnobius replies that it is enough for us that omnipotent God, whom nothing can withstand, has made us certainly assured of the immortality of our soul. And what of the fact that the pagans themselves were compelled to acknowledge that their gods, or angels and demons, were of an intermediate quality of this kind? For they believed that these beings, having at some point been born, were afterward made immortal [Col. 0374C] by the supreme will of God the Father, as Plato teaches.

Our soul, therefore, was created by some supreme power, but it is neither of divine offspring nor a daughter of the highest God. For had it possessed so great a perfection, nothing further could be desired in it; nor would human opinions differ, nor would any human soul have wished to be sent from the abodes of the blessed into a body.

Arnobius does not allow it to be objected that the world would be imperfect without man, and that God therefore sent into a human body each soul begotten from himself. By a twofold and lengthy induction, he attempts to make plain that man was created not for the perfection of the world—which could indeed have existed without him—but for man’s own private benefit and advantage. From these considerations he concludes that the soul is not divine, nor was it subsequently [Col. 0374D] sent by the highest God into some body.

“But,” they say, “it came into the world of its own will, not at God’s command.” “Why, then?” Arnobius replies. “Is it because, if God had commanded it to come, God himself would be said to be the cause of all the calamities by which man is oppressed in this world, and also of all the crimes he commits?” But this argument, he says, carries no weight. For because God does not prevent man, as he is able, from coming into this world, he would no less have to be called the cause of those same crimes and calamities. Yet this cannot be pronounced of him without the greatest impiety.

The pagans pressed the point: “Tell us, then, whence the soul was begotten or brought forth.” But this, Arnobius says, we may be ignorant of, just as we are ignorant of many other things, although we know that the soul [Col. 0375A] is neither divine nor the offspring of God. For we know that nothing could ever be made by the highest God unless it were perfect in every respect. We know no less certainly that human beings are nothing other than souls bound to bodies, which are corrupted by every kind of vice. For although some are blameless and excellent in character, these are certainly very few, and the whole human race must not be judged by the small number of those whom Arnobius adduces. “Who, then,” he continues, “are the perfect human beings? The philosophers, perhaps?” Yet these, struggling daily with desires and the various passions of the mind, demonstrate that their soul is weak and prone to vice. Therefore neither their soul nor that of others is divine.

[Col. 0375B] Nor is there any reason for the pagans to laugh if we acknowledge that it is unknown to us how the soul was created. For no one deserves ridicule merely because he does not know something, or because he admits that he does not know what he does not know. But one who thinks that he knows what is obscure and surpasses human knowledge is rightly to be ridiculed. Moreover, those who believed that souls descend from the supreme King himself into the human body advanced nothing certain and ascertained, but only suspicions and conjectures, which are nothing other than uncertain opinion and ignorance of the matter itself.

Furthermore, the pagan philosophers themselves did not know whence, or of what kind, are the souls of elephants, deer, lions, and other animals—indeed, not even those of locusts, mice, shrews, and other little creatures of that sort; and surely no one would say that these arose from Plato’s imaginary mixing-bowl. [Col. 0375C] Nor is there any greater agreement among the philosophers as to by whom and from what primary substances our souls were made. But if they think that Plato piously and reverently asserted that souls were created, not indeed by the highest God, but by certain lesser powers, why should we not be permitted to assert, with far greater certainty, that they are of an intermediate quality and that, although they were not brought forth by the principal powers and are subject to the laws of death, they are nevertheless endowed with immortality by God?

Nor should you say that absolutely nothing happens without God’s will. Take care lest it be concluded from this that God is the author of all the many and great evils by which human beings are overwhelmed, and which are not known to arise from the imbalance of the elements. Nor should you inquire too curiously whence those evils arise and why God permits them. For it matters little whether we know or do not know this, provided that we hold it as entirely certain [Col. 0375D] that nothing evil, vicious, or harmful is done by the true God, and that nothing done by him fails to be beneficial to all and utterly full of love and joy. Nor should our ignorance of so many other matters seem remarkable to anyone. For who does not know that there are such great disputes among everyone, and especially among philosophers, concerning every subject—the origin and destruction of the world, the first beginnings of things, the gods, and the constitution of our soul—that nothing is asserted by anyone which cannot immediately be demolished and refuted by another?

Therefore, even if Christians were ignorant by whom and from what our soul was created, whence evil arises, or why God permits it, the pagans could accomplish nothing against them on that account, since far more things remain unknown [Col. 0376A] to the pagans themselves: the world’s origin, place, and position; snow, the sun, the moon, and the stars; rain, wind, the alternation of storms; the saltiness of the sea; certain soils that are sweet, bitter, or cold; and the composition of the human limbs. Nor do they know any better what purpose is served in the world by owls, immissuli (small birds of uncertain identification), ants, thornbushes, darnel, and other similar things; why wheat, spelt, barley, and the other crops suited to human use have this shape rather than another; or, finally, what odor, taste, and other qualities of that kind actually are. Rightly, therefore, does Christ, the true God speaking under human form, command us, after leaving aside all these and other similar questions, to raise ourselves with our whole mind to the Lord of all things and to maintain a perpetual remembrance of him. Although he cannot be comprehended, [Col. 0376B] no one but a madman doubts that he alone is God. The pagans, therefore, who do not acknowledge him are awaited by savage torments after death, however much the Magi, the Etruscans, or others may promise them that, if they have lived piously, heaven lies open to them after death. For it lies within the power of that God alone—not of others, however much they may be called gods—to confer immortality. For this reason Christ was sent by him to free us from destruction and ruin.

“What, then,” the pagans objected, “became of the souls of those who died before Christ’s coming?” Christ himself, Arnobius says, taught us that at the appropriate time they were preserved and liberated by him, just as from him alone we learned when the human race began to exist on earth, when souls were first bound to bodies, and who was the creator of man. [Col. 0376C]

The pagans pressed further: “Why, then, does he not liberate all souls with equal beneficence?” “He calls all equally,” Arnobius replies, “and has given them the power to come to him.” Therefore, it is our fault, not God’s, if we do not obtain his beneficence. He confirms this by Plato’s authority, and adds that God, who has no need of our salvation, imposes compulsion upon no one.

They persisted: “If God is powerful and merciful, why does he not cause human beings to believe his promises even against their will?” Such force, Arnobius says, would not be grace but injustice, since it would extort from unwilling persons what they do not want and reject, but may obtain if they wish.

“Therefore,” the pagans said, “only a Christian can obtain blessed immortality through Christ’s aid and assistance.” [Col. 0376D] “Correct,” Arnobius says. For to the Christian alone is this power granted by God the Father. Nor ought this to have seemed strange to the pagans, who believed that certain distinctive powers had been given to each of their gods.

Arnobius then turns to the pagans’ old and frequently reiterated complaint, in which they protested that the religion of the Christians was novel and that their ancient ancestral rites should not be exchanged for barbarous and foreign ones. By various arguments, however, he shows that human beings have always found it advantageous to prefer good and useful things to bad and useless ones through beneficial change. Therefore, it is not the mere alteration of something, but always the reason for the alteration, that must be investigated. Then, if changing ancient institutions is imputed as a crime, Arnobius proves the pagans guilty [Col. 0377A] of this crime by a lengthy enumeration of foods, customs, laws, and sacred rites that they themselves had changed.

Moreover, even if the Christian religion had been disseminated only a few days before, did not all human institutions, arts, sciences, and disciplines—some of which our author enumerates—have a beginning? Did not even their gods, Jupiter and the others whom he names individually, begin to exist, as the pagans themselves acknowledged? Therefore, if the Christian religion did not exist four hundred years ago, they could not deny that even two thousand years ago none of their own gods existed.

“But it is agreed,” they said, “that our religion is far older than the Christian religion, and is therefore truer.” [Col. 0377B] Arnobius, however, charges this inference with falsehood, because both religions are said to have had a beginning, and two thousand years ought not to be regarded as a long time when compared with the still earlier ages of the past. Furthermore, nothing is older than the omnipotent and eternal God; and thus what is worshiped in him is not new or recent. But even if we learned this late, and only in the time of Christ, nothing could be established from that fact against the Christians or in favor of the pagans, who had themselves adopted the name of Serapis, Isis, and Apollo, and the rites of the Phrygian Mother and of Ceres, at no very remote date.

The pagans, however, demanded why Christ had been sent by God so late. Arnobius in turn asks them why winter, summer, and rain sometimes recur not always at a fixed [Col. 0377C] and appropriate time, but later; and why Hercules, Aesculapius, Mercury, and others entered the company of the gods, and came to our knowledge, so late. Thus, although the reason why something was done cannot be given, it must not on that account be denied that it was done. Besides, what can be late or premature in eternity? What if the worsening condition and weakness of humankind, greater in later than in earlier ages, required it? Finally, every event came about in the manner and at the time established by God’s immutable decree.

Finally, the pagans asked why the God whom the Christians served, if he is omnipotent, permitted them to be harassed and oppressed by every kind of persecution, penalty, and torture. Arnobius in turn asks them why their gods permitted their own worshipers to be overwhelmed by similar hardships and [Col. 0377D] calamities. But Christians, he says, to whom nothing has been promised in this life, have been taught willingly to endure punishments, tortures, and every hardship, and know with complete certainty that these bring them not some evil but true liberation, through which they will obtain eternal salvation. After exhorting the pagans to secure that salvation, Arnobius brings the book to an end.

## ARTICLE III. Analysis of the Third Book

Although the Christian religion had long since been more than sufficiently vindicated by distinguished defenders, and, requiring no advocate whatever, stood by itself wholly unshaken against every assault of its adversaries, Arnobius nevertheless judged it worth the effort [Col. 0378A] to answer the pagans, who continually asked why Christians neither cultivated nor worshiped the gods. He therefore replies that in God, the creator and governor of all things, Christians cultivate and worship whatever ought to be cultivated and worshiped. If, then, there are any gods, they derive their origin from him and are worshiped in him. But the pagans could never prove that they truly were gods, for it was always unknown to them either whence their gods received their names or how great their multitude was.

He proceeds still further and demonstrates with the greatest clarity, from the things the pagans proclaimed about their gods, that no such gods exist. First, they worshiped male and female gods. Yet he plainly establishes that the divine nature is capable not merely of no distinction of sex but of no sex at all, both by Cicero’s testimony [Col. 0378B] and from the fact that sexual difference was given for the generation of offspring. Although the word “God” is masculine in gender, the gods of the pagans can neither beget nor be begotten. For since they are imagined as immortal and not subject to old age or other infirmities, if they could beget, their number would already be infinite. Furthermore, they would be contaminated by shameful pleasures and desires. Finally, the goddesses would undergo the disgraceful conditions of pregnancy and childbirth, and the other discomforts of women. There is therefore no reason whatsoever why the pagans should take offense when Christians reject such begotten and begetting gods.

Second, those same pagans, like the Sadducees, were persuaded that the gods were formed and composed in a corporeal and human shape. Yet surely whatever consists of a body [Col. 0378C] must necessarily be mortal. Moreover, after enumerating the human limbs, Arnobius shows that the gods cannot be composed of them. Added to this is the fact that the gods would have to be said to be either like or unlike one another. Not the former—for who could distinguish one from another? Nor the latter—for some, as the pagans represented them, would have large heads, others large foreheads; some would be children, youths, or old men; some would be formed with these features and others with different ones, some with this shape and others with another. Yet this is no less absurd than attributing the forms of animals to them, as the Egyptians indeed did and the other pagans rightly ridiculed.

Nor should certain among them be heard when they reply that human form is assigned to the gods merely as a mark of honor. For it is a worse error and a greater insult [Col. 0378D] to ascribe to gods forms which they are not believed to possess. Arnobius adds, not without wit, that if beasts were at some point endowed with reason and wished to honor human beings, would human beings patiently endure being painted and exhibited in bestial form? God, therefore, can have no appearance or shape, although he hears, sees, and understands; or, if he has any, we are wholly ignorant of it. We know one thing: there is nothing bodily, nor any human features or passions, in God, whose nature cannot be explained in any mortal speech.

Third, the pagans represented each individual god as instructed in some art and branch of knowledge, and as presiding in separate portions over human duties, occupations, and other affairs, whether good or evil, honorable or shameful—all of which are carefully enumerated here by Arnobius. But no one will ever persuade Christians of these things, however much they are called impious and atheists. [Col. 0379A]

Fourth, Arnobius clearly demonstrates that the pagans’ gods are entirely fictitious from their various opinions concerning Janus, Saturn, Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, Neptune, Mercury, the Great Mother, Vulcan, Diana, and others. For since there can be only one eternal God—whom some vainly believed to be this world—the falsity of all the rest of those called gods is shown with the utmost clarity by this variety of utterly ridiculous opinions.

Fifth, therefore, Arnobius establishes the same point no less effectively from the pagans’ perpetual and absurd disputes and disagreements concerning the origin and number of their gods—namely, the Muses, the Novensiles, [Col. 0379B] the Penates, and the Lares. For amid so many disagreements no pagan was able to determine which of them was the true God, which ought to be invoked and honored, or which could ever bring aid to those who sought it.

## ARTICLE IV. Analysis of the Fourth Book

Arnobius continues the argument he had begun against the gods of the pagans and plainly shows that Piety, Concord, Safety, Honor, Virtue, Happiness, and other divinities of this kind, for whom those same pagans had built magnificent temples, cannot be said—whether in jest or sport, or seriously and affirmatively—to possess divine power [Col. 0379C] and to be enrolled among the gods. Precisely the same judgment must be made concerning Victory, Peace, and Equity. For all these, like their opposites, subsist in human actions and passions. No less perversely, certain beings, as the pagans dreamed, were brought forward as gods because of benefits rendered: Luperca, Praestana, or Panda, or Pantica, Pellonia, and other hosts of unknown divinities. For benefactors are not thereby gods; there is only one true God, the creator of all things.

Who could hear without indignation those who prattled that certain gods presided over the regions on the left and were enemies of those on the right? For since the world is spherical and round, its parts can be called left and right, east and west, the south wind and the south, only with reference to us when we are at rest. The same pagans also imagined with utter foolishness [Col. 0379D] that certain gods were placed in charge of some things, and others of different things: namely Lateranus, or Genius, over hearths; Venus Militaris over military debaucheries and the violation of boys; Perfica, Pertunda, and Tutunus over obscene matters; Puta over the pruning of trees; Nemestrinus over groves; Patellana and Patella over doors to be opened or already opened; Nodutis over the joints of grain, and Terensis over their threshing; Vibilia over wanderings from the road; Orbana over parents bereaved of children; Naenia over the ends of life; Ossilago over the knitting together of bones; Peta, Puta, and Patella over bees; Mellonia over honey; the Lucrii over profit; Libentina and Liburnus over lust; Limentinus and Lima over thresholds; Limus over crookedness; Saturn over sowing; Montinus over mountains; Murcida over the slothful; and the goddess Pecunia over money and wealth. For if these and many other gods, whom our author omitted lest he weary the reader, [Col. 0380A] preside over individual things, why are certain gods not similarly appointed over gourds, turnips, kitchens, cress, figs, beets, cabbages, nails, hair, and other parts of the body? He clearly shows that one notion is no less remote from truth, and no less disgraceful to the gods, than the other.

Nor may anyone object that they are gods because, when summoned by haruspices, they immediately come and give certain responses. For even if this were gratuitously conceded, who has ever seen Mellonia or Limentinus inserted into another creature’s entrails in order to give responses? What if the responses were given by deceit and fraud, or by the craft and deceptions of demons? Furthermore, since the pagans put forward so great a multitude of gods, they could not know [Col. 0380B] whether a single god alone might not be substituted for all the others whom they invoked. They ought not, however, to ask who the true God is, since the Egyptians, Persians, Indians, and all other peoples acknowledged him.

But Arnobius presses the point and makes it plain that the pagans produced utterly absurd monstrosities among their gods: namely, three Jupiters; five Suns, and as many Mercuries, Minervas, and Dionysuses; three Dianas and three Aesculapiuses; four Vulcans and four Venuses; three races of Castors and of Muses; six Herculeses; teams of three Cupids; and teams of four bearing the name Apollo. Yet all these gods cannot be gods of the same name, or else it is wholly unknown which among them is the true God. Then, if a sacrifice is made to one—Minerva, for example—without her being called by her particular name, will not the others attempt, in foolish rivalry, to claim it as offered to themselves? [Col. 0380C]

But if anyone says that it is unknown to him whether theologians or others wrote in their books things they knew and had ascertained, or false and fictitious things according to their fancy: “What is that to us?” Arnobius asks. It is enough that all the things said about the gods are convicted of falsehood. Therefore, those ancient books of theologians, pontiffs, and others must be removed from circulation, or the pagans must disclose to us which things found in them are true.

Yet how could anything true be indicated in books in which those same gods are everywhere and indiscriminately assailed with the greatest insults? For there the gods are proclaimed to have been born just like human beings, after marriages had first been celebrated, or from adultery and incest, as Jupiter and his children; or from eggs, like Castor and Pollux; or from the foam of the sea, like [Col. 0380D] Venus. Therefore, should not the public calamities of the human race be ascribed to those same pagans who obstinately asserted these things and impiously worshiped such monstrous divinities, rather than to Christians, who detest them with the horror they deserve?

Nor did the insane opinion of the pagans stop there. In their books they further advertised Saturn in chains; the infant Jupiter saved by the Curetes, occupying the kingdom of the father whom he had expelled, and unwittingly fed on human flesh; Vulcan the smith, lame in one foot; Aesculapius struck by lightning; Apollo enriched by false oracles; Mercury and Laverna as thieves; the Muses as the little maidservants of Megaclo; Venus as a prostitute; the Palladium made from the remains of Pelops; the homeland and chains of Mars, and his adultery with Venus; [Col. 0381A] the hired servitude of Hercules, Apollo, and Neptune; Minerva as bearer of the lamp in marital intimacies; the wounds of Mars, Venus, Pluto, and Juno; the burials of Jupiter, Saturn, Castor, and Pollux, and the latter two alternately living and dying; Hercules consumed by fire; the unbridled lust of Neptune and Apollo for women whom our author calls by name; Jupiter’s various transformations for the same purpose; and the frenzied wantonness of him and of other gods and goddesses toward males. Yet all these things are either false or true. If the former, the gods ought to have avenged such great and shameless slanders by the death of all pagans. If the latter, those same gods are proved to have been wretched, infamous, and utterly criminal human beings.

Moreover, their human nature is most plainly [Col. 0381B] established not only by the testimony of Euhemerus, Nicagoras, Leo, Theodorus, Hippo, and Diagoras, but also by the deeds performed by Jupiter, the wars of Minerva and Diana, Liber’s attempt to seize the kingdom of the Indians, and the condition, work, trade, and marriages of the others. Arnobius declares, however, that he did not undertake to prove this, easy though it was, but rather that the gods are treated more insultingly by no one than by the pagans.

He continues to demonstrate this both from the solemn and established rites, mysteries, ceremonies, and games held in honor of those same gods—which certainly could not be called inventions of the poets—and also from their already enumerated debaucheries, crimes, wounds, and wars. For the injustice of the pagans [Col. 0381C] was all the greater because they punished with the utmost severity of the laws the authors of any defamatory saying, poem, or pamphlet, yet endured with the greatest patience the writing and chanting of such great reproaches and disgraces against the gods. Indeed, they listened with the greatest pleasure to those who wrote them, and even to actors and mimes who represented them in theaters and public spectacles, and rewarded them with praise and prizes.

What room for doubt remained, then, that public calamities had arisen from so great a mockery and derision of the gods? Therefore, no person of sound mind will ever deny that the writings of the pagans ought to have been burned rather than the books of the Christians, and their theaters demolished rather than the Christians’ meeting places. For in Christian meeting places and assemblies [Col. 0381D] the true God is entreated; peace and pardon are sought for all, whether living or dead; and nothing is heard except what makes human beings humane, gentle, modest, self-restrained, and chaste. Therefore, if the gods are inflamed with anger, as the pagans believed, they ought to have been angry not with the Christians, but with the pagans themselves, who displayed the gods’ disgrace and shame before everyone’s eyes. If, however, the gods are free from anger, they are said in vain to be angry with the Christians.

## ARTICLE V. Analysis of the Fifth Book

Arnobius comes to another argument against the gods of the pagans and derives it from stories which, since the pagans preserved them in daily observance, celebrated them at annual festivals, and represented them in images, they evidently regarded as entirely true. The first is the story of Numa Pompilius, who was said to have obtained from Jupiter Elicius, after deceiving him by tricks and contrivances, the ritual means of averting a thunderbolt. From all the circumstances of this story, our author makes it manifest to everyone that nothing more remote from truth and divinity could be imagined. [Col. 0382A]

The second is the story of Acdestis and Atys, which everyone knows was notorious for the utterly shameful crimes of Jupiter, the Mother of the Gods, Nana, and Ia; for Atys’s ignominious castration; for his death and Ia’s; and for the other circumstances attached to it. Arnobius therefore argues against it in precisely the same way as against the others and plainly shows that the pagans could not convict it of falsehood. For it had been handed down by their most ancient writers and was customarily celebrated with the greatest pomp and solemnity at the pagans’ annual festival of the Mother of the Gods. [Col. 0382B] There could have been no reason for so great a solemnity unless they believed that all those things had actually happened. But if there was some other obscure reason for it, that reason must certainly have been utterly obscene and shameful, since the greatest indecencies were enacted at that festival.

Arnobius declares that he passes over many other similar stories, deterred by their execrable foulness. Nevertheless, he briefly touches upon Fauna, or the Good Goddess, beaten with rods; the shameful origin of Servius; and the utterly foul and unspeakable acts customarily performed in the Omophagia, the rites of the Corybantes, the Bacchanalia, and the Phrygian rites and mysteries. On their account, however, he shrewdly observes that so many and such great adulteries and other crimes are related of Jupiter [Col. 0382C] that he seems to have been born for no other purpose than that all the filth of infamy and of every most loathsome misdeed and crime might be channeled into him. He then proceeds to other rites—namely, the Thesmophoria, Eleusinia, and Halimuntia—in which there was no less lust and wantonness than in the others. After placing these before the eyes and sight of all, he asks the pagans whether Christians ought to be compelled, even by every kind of most dreadful torture, to perform these rites; and whether the pagans themselves wished to be like the gods whose crimes and outrages were commemorated in those mysteries, or to set them before their children or spouses as examples. He therefore says that it seems astonishing to him that anyone who denies or doubts that these are gods should be called by them [Col. 0382D] an atheist and sacrilegious. Finally, from all these things he concludes that gods of this kind ought to have been hostile not to the Christians who rejected them, but to the pagans who proclaimed such great crimes of theirs.

Arnobius next shows the pagans’ response to be futile and empty when they contended that all these stories were to be understood only in an allegorical sense. For to refute them, it is entirely sufficient that they cannot be interpreted in their natural sense without impiety. Then why were they handed down by writers to posterity with such seriousness if they were not to be explained in their natural sense? Did those writers ever testify anywhere that they were to be understood solely in a mystical and allegorical sense? But if there can be several allegorical parts and hidden meanings within the same story, where did they reveal to anyone precisely in what sense [Col. 0383A] those parts ought to be understood? Are all the parts of a single story to be explained allegorically, or only some? Surely not all. For the pagans would have to interpret allegorically every deed, place, region, house, nation, and other thing included in these stories, and demonstrate that they cannot be understood otherwise. They would also arbitrarily imagine that some parts of a single story are to be understood in that allegorical sense and others in the natural sense. For in the story of Summanus and Proserpina, or of Jupiter and Ceres, what part rather than another can be assigned as requiring explanation in an allegorical or natural sense? What reason can be given why, in explaining certain parts of the story of either Jupiter or Summanus, it is necessary to make a transition [Col. 0383B] from the natural to the allegorical sense?

Therefore, everything contained in one and the same story must be understood in one and the same sense, whether natural or allegorical. Yet in this second, allegorical meaning, all the elements of one and the same story cannot be explained, any more than in a narrative of the Trojan War or the battle of Cannae. For the things concerning the gods that we read recorded in writing are proved thereby to have actually and truly happened, because solemn festivals concerning them were celebrated at fixed times. These festivals had to have a constant and definite origin; they were not instituted without some reason.

Yet grant, if you wish, that in the description of any story something altogether different is signified from what the words express. Certainly that will no less redound to the gods’ disgrace and insult. [Col. 0383C] For what greater injury can be done to the gods than to signify, for example, the earth moistened by rain through the impious intercourse of Jupiter and Ceres? Would it not have been far better for a person to be mute than to designate honorable and natural things by the most shameful crimes of the gods? Tell me, please: what prevented each natural thing from being signified by its own proper name rather than by some crime of the gods?

Nor should it be said that the gods were unwilling for their mysteries to be made public, and that their stories were therefore written in allegorical circumlocutions. For although the stories wrapped in allegorical darkness were known only to a few, the gods’ crimes were set forth with the greatest clarity before everyone; and these gave human beings, already far too inclined toward vice, an opportunity to commit the same deeds. [Col. 0383D] Moreover, to what human being did the gods ever declare that they wished the most obscene crimes ascribed to them to be advertised beneath the obscurity of allegorical interpretation? Who doubts that they would always have preferred honorable rather than shameful things to be said of them? Furthermore, if they designated the sun by the name of Atys, what became of the man whom the stories report was born in Phrygia and performed the many deeds represented in theaters and commemorated in annual solemnities? What, moreover, had the sun done to deserve being called by the name of the castrated man Atys? Finally, our author shows that many things are repeatedly read in the stories of the gods which cannot be explained allegorically. From these considerations he concludes that it is altogether impious for the gods—if the pagans were persuaded that they truly existed—to be called by the pagans [Col. 0384A] names utterly shameful and wholly unworthy of divine majesty.

## ARTICLE VI. Analysis of the Sixth Book

In this and the following book, Arnobius refutes another accusation made by the pagans, by which they charged Christians with the greatest impiety because they had no temples or images of the gods and never offered them any sacrifices. He begins with the temples of the gods and openly acknowledges that Christians have none—not out of contempt for the gods, if indeed any such beings exist, but because, since gods must always be beneficent, utterly perfect in every kind of virtue, and incapable of anger or disturbance, they hold all temples in great contempt. [Col. 0384B] For temples can be of no use to them, although, being fashioned by the limited ingenuity of human beings, they seem supremely magnificent to those same human beings alone. Phoroneus, or Merops, or Aeacus is said to have been the first of all to build them. Yet however magnificently they were constructed afterward, what could be more injurious and insulting to the gods than rashly to assert that Jupiter, or any other god, is enclosed within a temple, little hut, chamber, and cell?

“But,” the pagans said, “we build temples for the gods so that, being in some fashion in their presence, we may address them with great reverence and, invoking them at close range, be more readily heard by them.” “But wrongly,” Arnobius says. For the true God knows all things, even the silent thoughts of our minds; he hears all things equally, [Col. 0384C] is absent nowhere, and does not, like Jupiter, go to dine among the Ethiopians. In a word, he is everywhere present through his immensity and never moves from place to place.

Added to this is the fact that very many of the gods’ most costly and august temples are nothing other than tombs of the dead. Such, indeed, are reported to have been the monuments and common burial places of Cecrops, Acrisius, Erichthonius, Daira and Immarus, the maidens of Celeus, Hyperoche and Laodice, Clearchus, Leucophryne, Tesmessus, Cinyras, and very many others. Finally, the Capitol received its name from the head of Tolus that was discovered there. From this Arnobius concludes that temples are built for the gods in vain and contrary to their dignity.

There is surely no better reason for worshiping their images. For if the gods dwell in heaven, prayers must be poured forth to them, not to their images. [Col. 0384D] But if it is doubtful whether they dwell there, an image of a doubtful object is fashioned in vain. Moreover, whoever believes that the gods exist has no need of images to make their presence manifest.

Then Arnobius confronts those who maintained that through images they worshipped and prayed to the gods. For if that were the case, they would never worship the gods if no images of this kind existed. What, moreover, could be more absurd than that, although the pagans believed they could supplicate their gods themselves, they should ask something of them through a lifeless effigy, as though through an intermediary acting on trust? For what else is this than to recognize that the god is one thing and to entreat an image wholly devoid of sensation?

[Col. 0385A] Moreover, an image of any object must resemble that object itself; otherwise it will not be an image. Yet no pagan can know whether any particular god truly is such as his image represents him. But we certainly know that the gods cannot be such as the sun, moon, winds, and others were represented, with a lion’s face or some other countenance. The pagans rightly and deservedly ridiculed the ancient people who worshipped as gods a river, a sword, a stone, a shapeless piece of wood, or something similar. Yet those very pagans are no less deserving of ridicule when they portray Ammon with ram’s horns, Saturn with a sickle, Venus naked, Vulcan with cap and hammer, Apollo with plectrum and lyre, and Neptune with a trident. Who does not see how far these things depart from the gods’ true form? Moreover, if these are the peculiar attributes of each particular god, then, when you take his own attribute from one and give it to another, [Col. 0385B] neither will any longer be distinguishable.

Nor did the pagans merely give their gods attributes unworthy of them, but also the forms and features of certain human beings, and even of prostitutes. For they fashioned Mercury after the likeness of Alcibiades, and Venus after those of Cratina and Phryne. What of the fact that Phidias, indulging his lust, inscribed upon the finger of the Olympian Jupiter that he had made the name of Pantarkes, a boy whom he loved? He reached this degree of wantonness and audacity because he knew that through his service and artistry Jupiter was worshipped by human beings. Arnobius therefore exhorts the pagans to return to a sounder mind and at last understand that the images they worshipped with such great honor were bones, stones, bronze, silver, gold, and very often the vilest material, which had served the most shameful [Col. 0385C] uses. For who could bring himself to believe that the one whom he had himself fashioned from such material was a god?

Arnobius presses the argument that no one is so insane as to worship and adore the separately arranged parts of an image. Why, then, did the pagans venerate those parts when joined together? Certainly they possess no greater divine power when joined than when divided. In addition, if anyone were to enter the innermost parts of the image of Olympian Jupiter, or of any other image, what would he see except sheets of metal, or pieces of wood and stone, bound together and joined by poured lead, chains, hooks, and rings? Would he not see the head, belly, and other parts hollow, empty, and unfinished within? But even if he is not permitted to see these things, does he not see the image’s external parts discolored by [Col. 0385D] greasy smoke and soot, collapsing from neglect, rust, decay, or age, and fouled and defiled by mice, cockroaches, spiders, swallows, and other little creatures?

“You are mistaken,” the pagans said. “We do not worship the material of the images, but the gods dwelling within the images after their sacred dedication.” “But you yourselves,” Arnobius replies, “O pagans, are entirely mistaken.” For who could possibly believe that the gods abandon their celestial abodes to dwell in images, and are compelled by some dedication of those images to inhabit them? Furthermore, if they always remain within them, nothing could be more wretched than such a dwelling. If they sometimes depart from them, it will surely be uncertain when the images ought to be worshipped. But come now: [Col. 0386A] do the gods contract their bodies within small consecrated images and extend them within large and immense ones? Can a single god—Vulcan, for example—remain in all his images, wherever among the nations they have been set up and consecrated, either multiplied or undivided?

What more need be said? If the gods truly dwell in these images of theirs, why do the pagans protect them with barriers, keys, bolts, dogs, and geese, and guard them most diligently, lest they suffer some injury? Why did Jupiter and Aesculapius so patiently endure the plundering of their images by Antiochus and Dionysius? If you say that the gods cared nothing about such things, surely Venus ought to have repelled the incredible wantonness of Pygmalion and of another depraved man toward her images. Should not Capitoline Jupiter, Argive Juno, Serapis, Diana of Ephesus, [Col. 0386B] Apollo, and the others also have preserved untouched from fire and other disasters the images and shrines in which they dwelt?

The pagans’ final bulwark for retaining images was the claim that the ancients were not unaware of all these things, but that by this worship of images the ignorant populace had to be kept in duty and religion. But this position collapses and overthrows itself. For what is there to frighten even the most ignorant common people in images of the gods that have been despoiled or pillaged? What is to be feared in Saturn’s sickle, the toothed key of two-headed Janus, Jupiter’s tinder, Juno’s girdle, Minerva’s helmet, Ceres’ breasts, and the other ridiculous insignia of the gods of this kind? What could these things, and others far more shameful, contribute toward preserving religion among human beings? So far, indeed, was this [Col. 0386C] from happening that to this day people could not be restrained from crimes and outrages by any fear of the severest laws or by any punishments. Finally, Arnobius indicates that sacrifices must next be discussed, and brings the book to an end.

## ARTICLE VII. Analysis of the Seventh Book

At the beginning of this book Arnobius proves, first by the authority of Varro and then by reason, that no sacrifices should be made to the gods. For whether the gods are said to be true gods, or composed of corporeal matter, or made by human hand and skill, they desire no sacrifices. If there are any true gods, they must be such as Christians declare the Lord of all things to be: omnipotent, [Col. 0386D] and unbegotten God. Those who are such receive absolutely nothing from earthly matter by which they might either be nourished or delighted. No reason, therefore, can be given for making sacrifices to the gods. They are not nourished by these sacrifices, since everything that is nourished is mortal. And what of the fact that nothing from what is brought to the altars reaches the gods?

Nor are victims slaughtered for the gods’ pleasure. For whoever is affected by pleasure of this kind is still mortal. What enticement to pleasure can the gods find in the slaughter of harmless animals, from which even human beings often recoil?

It was indeed the popular and common opinion that the anger of the gods was appeased by sacrifices. But an impulse of anger, which is unworthy of the gods, [Col. 0387A] cannot arise in an immortal mind. Grant, nevertheless, that the gods are struck by anger: victims should surely not be sacrificed to them before their minds have been seized by it. For morsels and food should not be offered to them as to wild beasts and animals, lest their anger and fury be aroused. Nor should they be offered after the gods have become inflamed with anger because of an offense committed by insignificant mortals—if such a thing can happen. For apart from the fact that the gods have never decreed anything about the matter, no one will be persuaded that, when some animal has been slaughtered and offered, they either put aside their anger or forget the injuries done to them, or that through such sacrifices, as though for an agreed payment, they grant pardon for sins committed against them. For the multitude of sinful people would increase if the forgiving favor of the gods were thus for sale. To this is added the apparent injustice of killing an innocent animal for a guilty [Col. 0387B] and sinful human being.

Nor is there any basis for arguing that victims are sacrificed to the gods so that they may bestow prosperity and remove adversity. For apart from the fact that the most learned philosophers among the pagans believed that everything happens by fate, if it is indeed in the gods’ power to bestow favorable and unfavorable circumstances upon human beings, why do they so ungratefully allow the many—indeed, almost innumerable—people who burden their altars with continual sacrifices and victims to be reduced to the utmost distress? Furthermore, it is absurd to say that the gods sell their benefits for the price of sacrifices. For a rich man who slaughtered many victims ought to receive more benefits from the gods, while a poor man who offered a little incense should receive none or very few. Moreover, if two peoples contending in war made entirely identical sacrifices to the gods, [Col. 0387C] the gods could assist neither of them, nor indeed either one, without injustice.

Nor is there any better reason for asserting that sacrifices are made to the gods for the sake of honoring them and increasing their power. For why should the same not be said about all other human actions? And what of the further fact that the increase of honor and power pertains to human beings, as weak and ambitious creatures, but not to the gods?

Arnobius nevertheless admits that honor should be paid to the true God, who, just as he does not burn with anger, neither rejoices in honor conferred upon him nor is indignant when it is withheld, nor believes that he becomes greater through the flatteries of others. Add that no honor comes to the gods from slaughtered animals, whose smoke soils their images, and whose blood and stench defile their temples and altars.

[Col. 0387D] But if you nevertheless continue to contend that the gods are honored by the blood of animals, why are elephants, camels, lions, eagles, storks, and very many other animals not sacrificed to them? Nor does it help to reply that the gods are honored only by the things that they benignly supply for our nourishment. For cumin, cress, turnips, and everything else useful to us would then also have to be offered in sacrifice to those same gods. Furthermore, if dogs or other animals were imagined to have received the use of reason, and to offer and sacrifice to human beings, as to their gods, the things upon which they themselves feed, would human beings not consider this to have been done as an insult to them rather than as an honor?

Arnobius presses the further point that, just as the gods are of one kind, so they ought to be of one mind; why, then, is one victim [Col. 0388A] sacrificed to one god and another to another? Is one pleasing to this god and another unpleasant to that one? Why are males sacrificed to one and females to another, when there is no distinction of sex among the gods? Why is a white-colored victim slaughtered for the gods above, but a black one for those below? Can one color be more pleasing to the gods than another? What of the fact that the infernal gods, like the Manes, do not exist at all? But let us grant that they exist: if black victims please them, why are the teeth, bones, and flesh of those same victims—and incense, milk, oil, and other things that are not black—offered to them? Nor does Arnobius wish to be answered that different victims are sacrificed to different gods by some custom. For the question is not whether human beings, but whether the gods decreed that some victim was more suitable to one god than to another, and whether those gods themselves divided among themselves by pact [Col. 0388B] and agreement the animals to be sacrificed.

Moreover, on what grounds is it said that a pregnant sow is suitable for Mother Earth and a virgin heifer for the virgin Minerva? By the same reasoning it will be concluded that musicians are suitable for Apollo, physicians for Aesculapius, craftsmen for Vulcan, and eloquent men for Mercury, and that these people should therefore be sacrificed to those gods, just as the sow is sacrificed to Earth and the heifer to Minerva.

The pagans objected that sacrifices should be made to good gods so that they might benefit people, and to evil gods so that they might not harm them. Arnobius replies that all gods ought by nature to be good. Therefore, since no god is evil by nature, even if he receives no honor from human beings, he will nevertheless be unable for that reason to treat them badly or harm them. To this is added the fact that, if this pagan opinion is true, [Col. 0388C] it follows from it that a good god becomes evil if the victim owed him is not slaughtered, while an evil god becomes good when a sacrifice is made. But what person of sound mind would say that the nature of God is changed?

Furthermore, even if it could be lawful for bulls and other animals to be sacrificed to the gods, how could they benefit from the innumerable kinds of sausages, porridges, sacrificial cakes, and fritters enumerated by our author, which were employed in the pagans’ mysteries and sacrifices? Are all these foods, called by obscure names so that they might seem more august, pleasing to the palates of the gods and useful to their languishing stomachs? Why are they served either separately, or sometimes raw, sometimes boiled, or roasted?

There is no better reason for burning incense upon their altars. [Col. 0388D] For that rite is recent and was unknown in ancient times. It must therefore either be regarded as useless, or the ancient people, who are known never to have practiced it, must have sinned. And what of the fact that it is vainly boasted that some honor is given to the gods by presenting incense? For incense is nothing but a resin flowing from the bark of certain trees. Why, then, is the resin that forms on other trees not likewise burned for them? Is it because it does not smell as sweet? What follows from that? Are some odors pleasing to the gods, just as to human beings, while others are disagreeable and unpleasant? Certainly not. For, as the philosophers admit, the gods are incorporeal, have no nostrils, and cannot be soothed by any scent of incense or anything else.

Vainly, and equally without reason, [Col. 0389A] did the pagans also pour out unmixed wine in their sacred rites as the companion of incense. For the use of wine is plainly useless to gods who suffer neither thirst nor hunger and need no nourishment. The pagans were also mistaken in believing that it was poured out either in honor of the gods or to make them propitious, since it weakens the sinews of every virtue, is hostile to chastity, modesty, and shame, and, if consumed too eagerly, hurls the mind into frenzy and madness. What could be more foolish than pouring a libation of some wine with prescribed words, lest any other wine become sacred and be withdrawn from human use? Is not a law and condition thus imposed upon the gods, so that they may receive no more wine—and therefore no more honor—than human beings please?

Arnobius shows that it is no less impious to say that the gods are delighted or honored by garlands, wreaths, flowers, cymbals, drums, [Col. 0389B] instrumental music, and songs. In similar fashion, he demonstrates that the pagans were altogether deserving of ridicule and pity, for it was their custom to celebrate the bathing of the Mother of the Gods, as though she became dirty; Jupiter’s banquet, as though he needed food; Aesculapius’ vintage, as though he cultivated vineyards; Venus’ ceremonial couch, as though she needed a bed; and Earth’s birthday, as though at some time she had first come into life.

After this he assails most sharply those same pagans’ sacred rites, and the Floral and Megalensian games instituted in honor of the gods, by which they babbled that the gods were appeased. He also proves that nothing is more foreign to right reason than to believe that the gods are delighted, [Col. 0389C] soothed, and reconciled by the shameful and ridiculous comedies and tragedies then performed and by the impious and utterly obscene gestures of mimes.

He makes it plain that so many and such monstrous opinions arose because the pagans were entirely ignorant of the nature of the true God, and were falsely persuaded that their gods were of the same substance as themselves, were composed of the same limbs and the same body, and consequently, like human beings, were born, rejoiced, suffered pain, were cleansed, gathered vintages, and were afflicted by the same diseases. There our author compares with one another, and sets in mutual opposition, the opinions of pagans and Christians; from this he concludes that Christians are pious, while the pagans are truly guilty and conscious of the senseless impiety with which they reproached them.

He next proceeds to overthrow the pagans’ final and, as it seemed, stronger bulwark, by which [Col. 0389D] they endeavored to prove from various accounts of miracles, as they called them, that the gods, offended by human sins, had blazed with anger, but were afterward appeased by human satisfaction. For, first, they related that before the circus games dedicated to Jupiter had begun, a certain slave was beaten with rods through the middle of the circus arena and punished by carrying the *patibulum*. Then those games were celebrated, by which Jupiter was profoundly offended. In vengeance for so great a crime, as they said, a plague ravaged the city. But when, at that same Jupiter’s command, the games had been duly repeated, the pestilence ceased.

Second, they claimed that it was handed down in memory that the Capitol was struck by lightning and the image of Jupiter thrown down from its seat. But when, in accordance with the soothsayers’ response, [Col. 0390A] it had been placed on a higher site facing the rising sun, hidden matters were then disclosed and the guilty were punished as they deserved.

Third, during the most calamitous period of the republic, a dreadful plague was raging, and the Romans had nearly been defeated by their enemies. But after gods had been brought from nations across the sea—namely, the images of Aesculapius from Epidaurus to the island in the Tiber, and of the Mother of the Gods from Phrygian Pessinus to the city—and after magnificent temples had been constructed for them, the plague was immediately calmed, the enemy driven from Italy, the city’s honor restored, and the boundaries of the empire extended far and wide; and, after many illustrious achievements at home and abroad, the name and majesty of the Roman nation were established with unshaken firmness.

Arnobius replies to all these claims that they were indeed handed down in writings, [Col. 0390B] but merely presented the appearance of miracles. For by carefully examining every circumstance of each of these accounts, he demonstrates most clearly that nothing could ever be imagined more unworthy of the gods’ supreme grandeur, dignity, majesty, and even their very name; nothing more contrary to truth or less deserving of belief.

## CHAPTER II. On the Author and Date of These Books, and the Manner in Which He Composed Them

### ARTICLE I. Who Was the Author of These Books, and at What Time and for What Reason He Applied His Mind to Composing Them

[Col. 0390C] It is the certain and settled opinion of everyone that Arnobius was the true author of these seven books. They are indeed attributed to him by Jerome in various passages soon to be cited, and afterward by other writers with so great and unanimous a consensus that the point seems no longer to need any proof.

From the same Jerome we also learn that Arnobius was a native of Sicca, a city and colony of inland Africa; that there he was devoted to the impious religion of the pagans; and that he taught rhetoric during the reign of Diocletian. Jerome’s own words are these: “Arnobius, under the emperor Diocletian, taught rhetoric with great distinction at Sicca in Africa, and wrote against the nations the volumes that are commonly extant” (Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, § 89), which he published as pledges of the religion he had adopted. [Col. 0390D] Arnobius himself laments that he had been enslaved to the impious worship of gods and idols (the same author, *Chronicle of Eusebius*, at the year 2342); and he testifies in these words that not long before writing these books he had been led, under Christ’s instruction, to the light of truth:

> “Only recently I used to worship—O blindness!—images freshly brought from furnaces, gods produced on anvils and fashioned by hammers, and elephants’ bones. If ever I caught sight of paintings, fillets upon age-worn trees, a smooth stone smeared with olive oil, I flattered it, addressed it, and asked favors of it as though an active power were present, although it was an insensible block of wood. I inflicted grave insults upon those very deities whom I had persuaded myself existed, since I believed them to be wood, stones, [Col. 0391A] and bones, or to dwell in material of this kind. Now, led into the paths of truth by so great a teacher, I know what all these things are; I hold worthy opinions about worthy beings; I do no dishonor to the divine name; and with unshaken gradations and authorities I assign to each person or dignity what is due to it” (Arnobius, Book I, pp. 22–23).

Endowed, therefore, with so great a light and so great a grace of Christ, and also impelled by dreams, he sought from the bishop of Sicca permission to renounce his former errors and profess the Christian religion publicly. But because, as Jerome says, he had always previously attacked it in his public schools, the bishop at first refused to admit him to its profession until he had been made entirely certain of Arnobius’ sincere repentance. Arnobius, therefore, impatient of delay [Col. 0391B] and wishing to obtain his desire as quickly as possible, set his mind to writing these books; when he had presented them as so many public pledges of his faith, he was permitted to make publicly the greatly desired profession of the Christian religion, and was initiated into our sacred mysteries by the same bishop. But it is better still to hear Jerome relate these matters:

> “Arnobius the rhetorician is regarded as distinguished in Africa. While he was training young men in declamation in the city of Sicca, and while still a pagan was driven by dreams toward belief, he could not obtain from the bishop the faith that he had always opposed. He therefore composed most splendid books against his former religion and at last, as though by furnishing certain pledges, obtained a covenant of piety” (Jerome, *Chronicle*, at the year 2342).

What he did afterward has been withheld from us either by the injury of time or by the negligence of writers. [Col. 0391C] Yet certainly, because he embraced the Christian religion with such ardent zeal, there seems to be no room whatever to doubt that he fully discharged every duty of a true and pious Christian.

The precise time at which he wrote these books is disputed and debated by the most learned writers of our age. The words of Jerome that we have quoted occur in the Eusebian Chronicle immediately after the record of Constantine’s *vicennalia*, which, as they say, were celebrated at Nicomedia in the year of Christ 326. On the other hand, the same Jerome, in other words that we previously cited, seems to indicate quite clearly that Arnobius published these books while Diocletian was ruling the Romans. Yet [Col. 0391D] Diocletian is said to have reigned for approximately twenty years, namely from the year of Christ 284 to 304. Did Jerome not therefore believe that Arnobius published these books before Constantine’s *vicennalia*, or the year 326? It nevertheless seems to us that Jerome can easily be reconciled with himself. For in the Eusebian Chronicle, after recording Constantine’s *vicennalia*, he added: “Up to this point Eusebius, the companion of the martyr Pamphilus, writes the history; we have appended the following material to it.” He then continues immediately: “Arnobius the rhetorician,” and so forth. Can it not be said that these words of his were appended to the foregoing words of Eusebius so that he would not interrupt Eusebius’ discourse, and that he did not there indicate Arnobius’ true period? If anyone should object that Jerome there, as [Col. 0392A] afterward, marks the chronological order, he—and indeed everyone else—will certainly admit that Jerome did not contradict himself and that greater reliance should be placed upon the words he wrote in his own work than upon those written in the work of another.

But because in his own catalogue *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he did indeed say that the books of our Arnobius were published under Diocletian, but not in which year of that reign, we must investigate the matter more accurately. This can be ascertained from no better source than the books of our author himself. At the beginning of the first book he speaks as follows: “It is nearly three hundred years, a little more or less, since we Christians began to exist and to be counted in the world” (Arnobius, Book I, p. 9). From this it is manifestly inferred, as everyone readily concedes, that these books were written by him [Col. 0392B] around the year of Christ 300. But no definite date for them is yet designated there. Some therefore believe that it can be determined from these words of Arnobius himself: “Why did our writings deserve to be given to the flames? Why were our meeting places savagely destroyed?” (Book IV, p. 152). For when Eusebius discusses the period when Diocletian was raging against the Christians, he says: “Then we saw with our own eyes the sacred buildings leveled to the ground and utterly demolished, and the sacred books of the divine Scriptures burned in the middle of the forum” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VIII, chap. VIII, p. 293). These things occurred, as we have noted elsewhere, during the ninth consulship of Diocletian and the seventh of Maximian—or, as some judge, the eighth of Diocletian and the sixth of Maximian—that is, in the year of Christ 303 or 302 (*Dissertation on Lucius Caecilius*, chap. 8, art. 3). [Col. 0392C] For a law was then enacted that the sacred books of the Christians—or, as we read in the *Life of Felix, Bishop of Thibiuca*, the “divine books” (*libri deifici*)—should be consigned to fire and flame (Optatus of Milevis, new ed., p. 227), and that their churches, or, as our author likes to call them, meeting places, should be destroyed. From these facts, which Augustine and Theodoret confirm, some think it can be concluded that Arnobius was engaged in composing his books in that very year (Augustine, *On Baptism, Against the Donatists*, Book VII, chap. 2, p. 187; and *Abridgment of the Conference with the Donatists*, chap. 15, pp. 569, 573; Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chap. 39, p. 248).

Others object, however, that Arnobius made no mention of a law issued against Christian meeting places and books, but only of books burned and meeting places destroyed. [Col. 0392D] Yet grant, they say, that he referred to that law: had there not previously been a similar protest by the martyr Justin to the pagans about the proscription of our sacred books?

> “By the agency and instigation of evil demons,” he says, “the penalty of death has been established against those who read the books of Hystaspes, the Sibyl, or the prophets, so that through fear people may be deterred from reading those writings and acquiring a knowledge of good things from them, and instead may be kept in slavery to the demons” (Justin Martyr, *First Apology*, p. 82).

What, moreover, of the fact that Origen recorded that churches had been burned before the time of our Arnobius, during the reign of Maximinus in the year 235, and that, therefore—to use our author’s words—the Christians’ [Col. 0393A] meeting places had been destroyed?

> “We know,” Origen says, “that among us an earthquake occurred in certain places and that certain ruins were produced, so that the impious who were outside the faith said that the Christians were the cause of the earthquake; on this account the churches both suffered persecutions and were burned” (Origen, *Tractate VIII on Matthew*, p. 88).

What, then, prevents Arnobius from being understood as referring to things that had occurred long before, and more than once?

Nor do those make much progress who attempt to establish that opinion by these words of Arnobius: “What age is the city of Rome declared to have in the annals? It has endured for one thousand and fifty years, or not much less than that” (Book II, p. 94). In the first place, he there establishes no certain and fixed point in time. [Col. 0393B] Then, in complete silence, he omitted who or what sort of annals these were, and what method their authors followed for calculating the years from the foundation of the city.

“But,” you will say, “he could not have been ignorant of the year in which the foundations of Rome were laid. For he knew very well that, not long before he began writing his books, the thousandth year of that royal city had been celebrated under the rule of Philip—that is, as they say, in the year of Christ 247 or 248. When, therefore, he says, ‘or not much less than that,’ he indicates quite clearly that he issued these books to the public in the year 296 or 297.”

Others, however, infer that the books were not published until after the three-hundredth year of Christ from the fact that elsewhere he introduces the pagans as arguing against the Christians in these words: [Col. 0393C] “Four hundred years ago your religion did not exist” (*ibid.*). For if these books had been completed before the three-hundredth year of Christ, he would undoubtedly have said in them that the Christian religion had not existed three hundred, rather than four hundred, years earlier. We are well aware that some have thought that through a copyist’s carelessness “four hundred” was substituted for “three hundred.” But this conjecture is confirmed by the testimony and authority of no manuscript codex or writer. What if the pagans preferred, as is customary, to put forward a larger rather than a smaller number of years? In that case, certainly, nothing definite could be concluded from it.

We have set before you these divergent opinions concerning the date of the books, together with the weight of the reasons upon which they rest, so that you may give your assent to whichever seems nearer [Col. 0393D] the truth. For our part, nothing more certain and established has so far occurred to us than that Arnobius, in the words cited above and in others concerning the cruel persecution of Christians, the burning of their books, and the destruction of their churches, was alluding to the aforementioned edict of Diocletian, and that his books were therefore made public around the year of Christ 303. We nevertheless dare pronounce nothing with certainty, and leave the matter entirely to the judgment of others.

### ARTICLE II. On the True Title and Subject of These Books; Whether Arnobius Treats That Subject Properly; His Style and Learning; and the Division of the Entire Work into Books and Chapters

No title is now prefixed in the royal manuscript codex of these books of Arnobius, [Col. 0394A] from which the first page has been torn away. But at the end of the first, third, fifth, and seventh books we read: “Here ends the book of Arnobius.” At the end of the fourth, however: “Here ends the fourth book of Arnobius the orator.” Finally, at the close of the second: “Here ends the second book of Arnobius *Against the Nations*.” In their first and second Roman editions, and in the Basel, Antwerp, Stewechius, Paris, and Heraldus editions, they are entitled: *The Seven Books of Arnobius Against the Gentiles*. In the last edition, published at Leiden: *The Seven Books of Arnobius the African Against the Gentiles*. We have no doubt that this last title was taken from Jerome, who supplies the same heading more than once (Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, § 89; and Letter 84, *To Magnus*). Yet in the royal manuscript codex, and [Col. 0394B] in another mentioned by Stewechius, the wording is *Against the Nations*. But the reading *Against the Gentiles* seems preferable, since Jerome had undoubtedly read it in far older manuscript codices.
