In any event, because the meaning of the two titles is the same, it would be entirely useless and superfluous to spin out a longer discussion of it.

From both of these titles we readily understand that the subject of these books, and Arnobius’ purpose and end in composing them, was nothing other than to demonstrate that the pagans’ religion was false and that of the Christians true. Nor are many arguments needed to prove this, since it ought to be perfectly evident to everyone from the analysis of those books that we have supplied.

[Col. 0394C] Some, however, think that Arnobius accomplished these two tasks with unequal success. For, they say, he showed the falsity of pagan religion far more successfully and effectively than the truth of Christianity. They believe the reason for this was that it was much easier for Arnobius and other pagans very recently brought to the Christian faith to overthrow completely the impious and absurd rites and errors that they knew thoroughly than to demonstrate the truth of Christian doctrine, whose mysteries they did not yet know sufficiently.

But what prevents those to whom our sacred mysteries have not yet been revealed from establishing and demonstrating the truth of the Christian religion most conclusively by general arguments, or, as the scholastics say, by “motives of credibility”? [Col. 0394D] Below, moreover, we shall demonstrate that our author defends it with the most powerful arguments, which he draws from the true miracles of Christ and his disciples, from the truly marvelous and almost incredible constancy of innumerable martyrs, and from the extremely rapid propagation throughout the whole world of the Christian religion, which had long before been promised by the sacred prophets. In any case, not all the mysteries of the Christian religion were so unknown to Arnobius that he did not correctly discuss, as will be stated in the proper place, the true nature of God, Christ the true Son of God and our Savior, and certain other doctrines and teachings of that religion. Without doubt it was for this reason that Jerome calls his books “most splendid,” because he establishes [Col. 0395A] the truth of the Christian religion no less splendidly than he destroys the falsity of the pagan religion (Jerome, *Chronicle*, at the year 2342).

But the more highly Jerome extols these books of our author for the force and weight of their arguments, the more severely he criticizes his manner of writing and speaking. For he wrote the following to Paulinus: “Arnobius is uneven and excessive, confused through lacking a division of his work” (Letter 49, p. 567). This judgment of Jerome displeased a certain more recent heterodox writer, who, after citing Jerome’s words, delivers the contrary verdict as though from a tripod: “Arnobius seems to me an eloquent author, and one who treated his argument against the pagans so accurately and elegantly that I can scarcely see how better things could be said against them than [Col. 0395B] those so well argued by the ancients” (Hoornbeeck, *Theological Exercises*, Book I, chap. 1, § 11, p. 131).

But tell us, please, learned theologian: where did Jerome say that Arnobius had not treated that argument accurately and elegantly? Why does he call his books “most splendid,” unless because he most abundantly accomplished his purpose of establishing the Christian religion? Can you truly deny that in his books he is “confused through lacking a division of his work”? Does that confusion not occur everywhere throughout the first and second books? We acknowledge that in the third book the arguments are distinguished fairly elegantly and accurately. Yet in all of them a clearer division is surely wanted. I appeal as witnesses to everyone who has read these books; and unless they acknowledge this confusion, we shall admit that those Aristarchuses of ours possess eyes keener than a lynx. [Col. 0395C]

Let the theologian praised by us further explain what he understands by the term “eloquent.” If he means learned and expert, we readily concede to him that Arnobius is eloquent; if he means one who speaks clearly and elegantly, or a good model of Latin style, we deny it. For his manner of writing is not only uneven, excessive, and redundant, but also unrefined, rough, unpolished, and, because of its very many obsolete words, harsh and grating. Some offer a twofold explanation for this ungroomed and unadorned diction. First, because Arnobius was an African by birth, he all the more readily followed the African manner of speaking, since he wished to complete his books quickly and to offer them, as we have already noted, as pledges of his faith. Second, this very haste to finish them more quickly [Col. 0395D] plainly prevented him from attending everywhere to elegance and purity of expression. It cannot, however, be denied that very many passages occur throughout which are expressed aptly, gracefully, elegantly, and rhetorically, and are adorned and illuminated with most weighty words and thoughts.

Most scholars extol with great praise the profound learning scattered everywhere throughout these books. Yet it must be admitted that, in the manner we have described, this learning concerns secular rather than sacred subjects, as will become sufficiently evident from everything discussed below.

The entire work was divided by Arnobius himself into seven books. This is most clearly proved both by the authority of the manuscript codex and by that of Jerome. For we have already seen this division made in the old royal codex [Col. 0396A]. Jerome, moreover, wrote of our Arnobius in his letter to Magnus: “He composed seven books *Against the Nations*, and his pupil Lactantius the same number” (Jerome, Epistle 83, p. 656).

These books, however, were never divided into chapters or sections. Yet this method of writing in a connected and continuous discourse seems to have contributed not a little to the confusion we noted shortly before. Therefore, if in some new edition of these books anyone should divide them—which is not so difficult—into chapters or sections, he will surely both remedy this confusion and greatly relieve the reader’s weariness and labor.

## ARTICLE III. On the Integrity of These Books and the Corruption of Their Text; Whether, and from Whom, Arnobius Borrowed Numerous Passages; Whether He Cited Certain Testimonies of Sacred Scripture

[Col. 0396B]

This work of Arnobius has not come down to us intact and entirely complete. Learned men have already observed that something is missing at its end—either cut away, omitted through the negligence of copyists, or rendered no longer legible because it had been effaced by the foul corruption of earlier codices. We ourselves have already observed that the first page of the royal manuscript codex had been removed. That something was likewise omitted or torn away at the end of the entire work may be inferred from the fact that Arnobius there refutes at length and invincibly various pagan stories which they advertised as full of miracles; nevertheless, he gives no answer at all [Col. 0396C] to the objection he himself had raised from the Capitol being struck by a thunderbolt and the statue of Jupiter being cast down (Book VII, p. 245). For although in his answer to the preceding story he signifies clearly enough that all the others are thereby utterly overthrown, nevertheless, because he refutes individually all the others he has proposed, it will scarcely seem probable to anyone that he left this one alone entirely untouched and passed it over without any answer.

Moreover, after dissolving and overthrowing the pagans’ arguments drawn from stories of this sort, he is accustomed to draw some conclusion against them and in favor of the Christians. But if this ought ever to have been done anywhere, it certainly ought to have been done at the place where, by refuting what the pagans regarded as their strongest argument, he brought his books to an end. [Col. 0396D] Nevertheless, if anyone contends that this escaped Arnobius while he was hastening to finish his books, we shall not resist him, provided that he proves it properly. But he must first remember that Arnobius would certainly not have required much delay or hesitation to draw there the conclusion arising from what he had said.

Furthermore, at the beginning of the second book we read a long fragment extending over two pages or more, from the words *And not from love of all virtues* to the words *may bestow upon those who will believe* (Book II, p. 43), which had been transposed in the manuscript codex and the old editions. For everything contained there is in no way connected with Arnobius’s text at that point. Hence, in the latest editions, the individual passages [Col. 0397A] appear to have been restored quite suitably to their proper places, with the exception of these words: “so that he might not extend the light and span of life to all, and remove the danger of ignorance”; no one, perhaps, will deny that these words, omitted in some editions, were inserted in the latest edition in a place still foreign to them. Is this not a by no means obscure indication to us that the disorderly restoration of that fragment was made on the editors’ own authority by those who supervised the latest editions of these books?

Another passage, moreover, before the end of the seventh book, from the words *We do not deny* up to and including the words *After they had been brought*, etc., is presented in the royal manuscript codex and the oldest editions; in it, several things previously said in scattered places are copied out again in exactly the same words. Therefore [Col. 0397B] Stewechius, in his edition of these books of Arnobius, relegated all of them to the end of the work. In the later editions, however, they were omitted entirely. But this omission ought to have been noted, or at least some reason for it given.

Someone may perhaps ask why a copyist ventured to thrust so absurd a fragment into Arnobius’s text. But it is extremely difficult to state the cause of rashness of this sort. Might it not, nevertheless, reasonably be said that in an earlier codex of Arnobius, from which the first copyist transcribed his own, there was some lacuna, or words effaced by age or some other accident, which he wished to supply in whatever way he could, so that he might sell his codex for a higher price and persuade everyone that it was complete? However that may be, it is enough to have warned that these words are not [Col. 0397C] Arnobius’s.

Very many passages also occur throughout the same text of Arnobius that were foully corrupted by a careless and ignorant copyist. But to enumerate them one by one would doubtless be as easy for us as it would be tiresome for others. We therefore now abstain all the more willingly from so long an enumeration, since below we shall repeatedly have a more suitable opportunity to correct and amend the principal errors.

Meanwhile it is worth observing that neither few nor obscure authors are cited by Arnobius in these books. But especially from two—Cicero and Clement of Alexandria, the first of whom he cites somewhere expressly by name, while suppressing the name of the second—he borrowed numerous passages. How much he excerpted from Cicero you may learn from these words of Jerome [Col. 0397D] to Magnus: “If you wish to read those books of Arnobius, you will find in them an epitome [ἐπιτομήν] of Cicero’s dialogues, namely *On the Nature of the Gods*” (Jerome, Epistle LXXXIII, to Magnus, p. 656). What our author drew from Clement of Alexandria he borrowed from the latter’s *Exhortation to the Greeks*. Since, however, the individual passages which he transferred from each writer into his own books are to be set forth by us below, we have thought it best to refrain from enumerating them now, lest we repeat the same material.

In these books, however, he produced no express testimonies of Sacred Scripture, either by citing the author’s name or otherwise, except for this one, which he indicates as deriving not so much from any sacred writer as from a common saying: [Col. 0398A] “Has that widely current saying never brushed your ears: ‘The wisdom of man is foolishness with God’?” (Arnobius, Book II, p. 46). For it will seem, not without reason, to some to have been taken from these words of Paul to the Corinthians: “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (I Corinthians 1:19). However the matter may stand, you will scarcely find any other testimony in all the books of Arnobius cited from Sacred Scripture in its very words or under the author’s name. He was therefore unwilling to contend against the pagans by invoking the manifest authority of Sacred Scripture, although others had used it successfully in disputations against them. For he doubtless feared that he would waste his effort against men who despised it.

Consequently, nearly all Christ’s miracles described [Col. 0398B] in the books of the New Testament he presents as established not so much from those books as by certain, constant, and public report and by universal acknowledgment. Yet in one place—to observe this in passing—he speaks as follows of the loaves multiplied by Christ: “He satisfied five thousand who followed him with five loaves; and lest those unbelieving and hardened men should think that these were illusions, he filled the folds of twice six baskets with a heap of leftover fragments” (Book I, p. 26). But in the Gospels of Matthew and Mark we read: “Seven loaves . . . and they took up what remained of the fragments, seven baskets full.” In Luke, however: “Taking the five loaves . . . and what remained to them was taken up, twelve baskets.” Finally, in John: “They therefore gathered them up, and filled twelve baskets with fragments from the five barley loaves” [Col. 0398C] (Matt. 15:34 ff.; Mark 8:6 ff.; Luke 9:17; John 6:13). Yet seven large baskets (*sportae*), as some have noted, held more than twelve small baskets (*cophini*). Consider, therefore, whether Arnobius, when writing this, through a lapse of memory placed the term *sportae* there instead of *cophini*.

## ARTICLE IV. On Certain Errors Ascribed to Arnobius

It certainly ought to seem surprising to no one that Arnobius, not yet instructed by a complete knowledge of divine Scripture and the sacred mysteries of our religion, should have struck against certain reefs of error when he was composing these books. Whether, however, he is accused of them justly or unjustly must be weighed. Let Jerome therefore be the first brought forward [Col. 0398D], who wrote these words to Tranquillinus: “I think that Origen, because of his learning, ought sometimes to be read in the same way as Tertullian, Novatian, Arnobius, Apollinaris, and certain ecclesiastical writers: so that we select what is good in them and avoid what is contrary, according to the Apostle’s saying: ‘Test everything; hold fast what is good’” (Jerome, Epistle 56, to Tranquillinus, p. 589). Thus that distinguished man modestly warned us that certain things in the books of our Arnobius, as also in those of certain others, must be avoided.

But certain more recent writers, less favorably disposed toward our ancient authors than Jerome was, boldly affirm that Arnobius fell not merely into errors of some ordinary kind, [Col. 0399A] but into the gravest of all. Heraldus condemns him for utterly intolerable ignorance and error because, in disputing against the pagans, he confesses that he does not know who the true gods are. These are Arnobius’s words to the pagans: “‘Who,’ you ask, ‘are the true gods?’ To answer you in a common and simple phrase: ‘We do not know’” (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 211). On this passage Heraldus says: “Indeed, this ignorance is not tolerable, and from this it appears that Arnobius, when he wrote these books, was a stranger even to the principal articles of the faith.” Could Arnobius really have erred, while composing these books, not merely concerning one of the chief articles of religion, but concerning the first and foundation of them all? What else, I ask you, is he doing throughout this entire work except demonstrating that the gods of the pagans are false [Col. 0399B], and that there is only one God, whom Christians adored after utterly rejecting all those fictitious deities? Does he not thereby show most evidently that Christians are treated by the pagans with complete injustice for this reason, and subjected even to every kind of most dreadful punishment?

Then, when the pagans ask who the true gods are, Arnobius answers that he does not know, and immediately gives the reason: because he had never seen them. Yet he admits that he had heard from the pagans that they were very numerous. These gods, if they exist anywhere, as the pagans supposed, or if they are true, as Terentius—undoubtedly Varro—believes, must certainly be such as they are called: unbegotten, eternal, desiring no earthly pleasure, and such as almighty God is, [Col. 0399C] whom all Christians know and understand. What, then, does this argument against the pagans and this explanation of the divine nature contain that is intolerable, or characteristic of a man wholly unacquainted with the principal articles of faith? Is not that conception, explanation, and description of almighty God true? Moreover, we shall clearly show below that our author’s opinion concerning God and the divine nature is sound.

But, you will say, he says that he does not know who the true gods are; what, therefore, could be less tolerable than this ignorance? Yet who does not see that this is, as they say, a rhetorical figure? For, in the manner of rhetoricians, from the adversaries’ own admission he proves that the pagan gods are false and are no gods at all, and consequently that their divinity—which could have no existence—was known neither to anyone else nor to himself.

[Col. 0399D] There are indeed many other errors of which Arnobius is accused, namely concerning the supreme God, his anger, the human soul, sin, the resurrection of the flesh, the punishments of the impious, the cause of public calamities, and other teachings of the Christian religion. But whether he is justly and deservedly, or undeservedly, charged with all these errors, we shall examine below with our customary candor, when a more suitable place presents itself for us to discuss those same dogmas and arguments of our sacred religion.

## ARTICLE V. On the Various Manuscript Codices and Editions of These Books

Only one manuscript codex of these books remains to us. It is preserved [Col. 0400A] in the most richly furnished library of our Most Christian King and was formerly marked there with the number 1344, but is now numbered 3975. In it, the *Octavius* of Minucius Felix is appended to the seven books of Arnobius as though it were Arnobius’s eighth book. We have discussed both this matter and the antiquity of this manuscript codex sufficiently in the preceding dissertation (*Dissertation on the Octavius of Minucius*, chap. 2, art. 2). We also observed there that numerous errors of a copyist wholly ignorant of Latin occur throughout this codex. But they are far more frequent in these books of Arnobius, and that unlearned scribe erred more often and more grossly especially in transcribing proper or less commonly used names. It would be a useless labor to unfold here the exceedingly long series of his errors. For many of those errors are noted in the annotations of various scholars [Col. 0400B], and many more in the collection of variant readings published in the latest edition of these books. Others omitted there have nevertheless presented themselves to us as we read the same books with greater care, and we shall indicate them later when the opportunity arises.

Besides this manuscript codex, Stewechius testifies that another, ancient and of very good quality (Stewechius, Letter to the Reader), was once in the possession of Flacius Illyricus and afterward of Henricus Petraeus. Stewechius states that from its variant readings, collected by Franciscus Modius of Bruges, jurist, and sent to him, he corrected Arnobius’s text in countless places and supplied lacunae of great importance. But concerning the antiquity and elegance of this book, which we have not been permitted to see, we can establish nothing with certainty. Nevertheless, from a collation of Stewechius’s edition and the other editions [Col. 0400C] of this work, we have discovered that this codex was not much more correct than the other, royal codex which we used; that it nearly always abounded in the same errors, was disfigured by transpositions and additions, and was defective and gaping with lacunae.

From the earlier royal manuscript codex, the first edition of these books of Arnobius was prepared at Rome in 1542 through the efforts of Faustus Sabaeus of Brescia, and from it nearly all later editions derived. The second was printed at Basel by Froben in 1546 under the supervision of Sigismund Gelenius, who declares that he corrected numerous errors intruded into Arnobius’s text in the previous edition by persons unpracticed in reading ancient characters. Since, however, he is silent as to whether [Col. 0400D] he emended the text from any manuscript codex, may it not be inferred that he attempted to apply a healing hand to it solely through his own conjectures? These books of Arnobius were again issued to the public from the same Froben presses in the same city in 1560, and afterward at Paris in 1570.

Theodorus Canterus subsequently made public a new edition of them, printed by Plantin at Antwerp in 1582, which, as he says, had been corrected according to the authority of the royal manuscript and with the aid of Clement of Alexandria. He admits, however, that sometimes, when no better readings were available, he followed various readings of Gelenius, whom he nevertheless accuses of indulging excessively in conjecture.

[Col. 0401A] Then, forty years after the first edition of these books was published at Rome—that is, in the year of Christ 1583—Fulvius Ursinus caused another to be brought to light in the same city. He openly declares that, assisted by the emendations of Joannes Baptista Sighicellus and the Spaniard Petrus Chaconius, he corrected in it numerous corruptions and alterations made by the Germans, who had corrupted Arnobius’s text in countless places according to their own whim and judgment. He nevertheless testifies that he admitted nothing into the author’s text unless it was most manifestly and indisputably true and had been approved by the judgment of many. Those readings, however, which did not appear so certain he marked in the margins of the pages, adding certain brief observations to confirm the conjectures.

[Col. 0401B] Gebhartus Elmenhorstius published two editions of this work of Arnobius, one at Hanover in 1603, the other, in larger type and format, at Hamburg in 1610. In the earlier edition he informs us (Letter to the Reader) that, while still a young man, he devoted his labor to publishing these books and, after diligently collating his copy with the edition of Fulvius Ursinus, rendered them more polished. But he is wholly silent about what sort of copy that was. In the notice prefixed to the second edition, however, he declares that in reviewing it he used the old codex of Franciscus Sabaeus of Brescia, published in Roman type in 1542. Where that text was corrupt, he says that he had recourse to manuscript excerpts and the emendations of learned men, and asserts that with these aids he cleansed the books of Arnobius of innumerable blemishes, yet in such a way [Col. 0401C] that he rarely inserted anything into the text. Nevertheless, he openly declares that many false and corrupt passages still remain; since they cannot be understood without the aid of a better codex, he left them untouched, to be corrected by more fortunate talents. But he does not tell us which codices supplied those variant readings. By the terms “manuscripts” and “learned men,” however, he appears without doubt to have meant nothing other than the codex of the royal library, the editors of the previous editions, and the authors of certain observations.

We owe another edition of the same books, published at Antwerp in 1604, to the labor of Godeschalcus Stewechius (*In the dedicatory letter*, Trier, 1587). He declares that, by means of the variant readings of the old manuscript [Col. 0401D] sent by Modius, as we have observed, he made it not only fuller in many places but also better through the correction of innumerable errors. He entered the differing readings, whether of the handwritten book or of other editions, in the margins of the pages. He would have done the same, as he notes, with those passages which Ursinus’s edition presents as properly restored, if only Ursinus had distinguished the work of others from his own and had not appropriated everything on the same footing as his own. In 1634, Leander of Saint Martin, a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict and president general of the English congregation of that order, caused the same edition of Stewechius to be reprinted in new type at Douai. But he added nothing to it except *paratitla*, or brief [Col. 0402A] summaries, by which Arnobius’s obscure text is explained and his errors noted.

Through the work and care of Desiderius Heraldus, a new edition of these books was published at Paris in 1005 [probably 1605], corrected, as he puts it, according to the Roman edition and enlarged and emended in certain places from the royal manuscript. But he devoted greater effort to writing notes than to emending Arnobius’s text. He informs us that he was moved to this because very many in his time had devoted effort to restoring humane letters with a success proportionate to the greatness of their labor, but had expended either very little or none at all on illustrating sacred and ecclesiastical literature. He was therefore persuaded that it was a far more useful labor to turn his attention to publishing and explaining the writings of the ancient Fathers of the Church. At first [Col. 0402B] he considered publishing and emending the books of Tertullian. But, deterred by the magnitude of the labor, he preferred to make trial upon Arnobius: “And,” he says, “I so began the undertaking that, as the month ran its course and the work I had undertaken proceeded favorably, I found myself brought to the end of the book” (dedicatory letter).

Later, in 1651, these seven books of our author were published at Leiden with the recension, as the title states, “of a Most Celebrated Man,” and with the complete commentaries of all previous scholars. Although this man’s name is withheld, Thysius is nevertheless said to have been partly responsible for this edition. Yet however much it is advertised as the most accurate of all, we have detected in it not only numerous printers’ errors, but also certain words omitted entirely.

[Col. 0402C] The last edition of these books was appended by Prieur to the works of Cyprian in 1666. But since this edition, like the preceding one, was prepared solely from the old editions, it is doubtless sprinkled and stained with the same errors, as well as with other new faults introduced by the printers.

Although, therefore, each editor greatly extols the edition he supervised and boldly asserts that he washed away the countless blemishes of others, it is nevertheless established that none has come down to us entirely perfect and complete in every respect. Such an edition can never be produced unless, besides the codex of our Most Christian King mentioned by us, and perhaps the other manuscript codex, still others written more accurately by their copyists are found. If any can be unearthed somewhere from the shelves of libraries, they must be collated most diligently with the printed editions; and, so that the confusion of the text may be removed as far as possible, it must be divided into chapters and sections, and clear summaries of the chapters and sections must be provided.

## ARTICLE VI. On the Notes and Observations of Various Scholars upon These Books

Several editors of Arnobius’s books, and other learned men as well, published notes and observations upon them. First, Latinus Latinius left a few variant readings as well as observations and notes upon them (*Sacred and Secular Library of Latinius*, p. 98). But he presents us with nothing other than his own conjectures and those of certain others. Meursius then, in the nineteenth year of his life and in the year of Christ 1598, published his *Arnobian Critic*, printed by the Elzevir press at Leiden. He informs us that he had been unwilling to anticipate Canterus, who was contemplating the same undertaking, without the latter’s permission, lest he be accused of putting his sickle into another man’s harvest. In that work, moreover, he aimed at scarcely anything other than emending the errors of Arnobius’s text without any unpublished codex, but by his own powers and youthful talent. He nevertheless admits that, while intent upon the labor and spurred on by it, he could not prevent himself from sometimes ranging beyond his proposed limits. How successfully he accomplished this is surely proved by the many learned writers who afterward, with the aid of manuscripts, attempted to heal the countless defects and wounds in our author’s text, but were compelled to leave it still disfigured by very many errors [Col. 0403B].

Accordingly, that *Arnobian Critic* composed by Meursius did not deter Theodorus Canterus from publishing notes and observations on Arnobius’s books, which, as we have said, he had previously resolved to publish. In them he gives an account of the Arnobian text as emended by him or requiring emendation, and indicates many passages which Arnobius took especially from Clement of Alexandria. He explains only a few passages, however, and admits that very many others remain which require a fuller interpretation. For this reason, he promised that he would shortly publish a very extensive commentary on these books of Arnobius. But whether he fulfilled his pledge, or why he did not keep his promise, has thus far remained unknown to us.

[Col. 0403C] Stewechius also wrote observations of two kinds on our author’s books, the first of which he calls a *Syllabus of Select Passages*, and the second *Select Passages*. In the latter he strives, to the best of his ability, either to emend and elucidate many of Arnobius’s words and statements from conjecture and from parchment codices, as he says, or to confirm them by the authority of other writers. The *Syllabus of Select Passages*, however, is, as its title states, an abridgment of the entire work, though it presents nothing other than explanations of certain words and some matters worthy of note in these books of Arnobius.

Just as Elmenhorstius made public two editions of the same books of Arnobius, so he undertook the burden of illustrating each with various notes. [Col. 0403D] In the first edition, by very brief annotations he indicates variant readings of Arnobius’s text, or attempts to corroborate Arnobius’s statements, often by citations of other authors’ books and rarely by their words. Therefore, in the second edition, he published a different set of notes, omitting nearly all of these. He informs his reader that in those new observations his principal aim was to explain and interpret the author’s meaning, wherever it is more obscure, as briefly and clearly as possible (*In the notice to the Reader*). Yet although he professes to have pursued brevity, it is nevertheless evident that those observations contain much that is superfluous and useless, in which matters perfectly clear and well known are explained and confirmed without any necessity. You will also find many things [Col. 0404A] outside the bounds and purpose of the author, and not a few that concern grammar alone and in which words similar to Arnobius’s are sometimes presented. Nor does he sometimes hesitate to accuse our author of error; whether deservedly or unjustly, we shall see later. Finally, he candidly admits that he omitted many passages which are false, corrupt, and obscure.

Heraldus, however, is more lengthy in his observations and notes, but departs from the author’s purpose more frequently than Elmenhorstius. For in them, taking occasion from some writer whom he has cited, he strays excessively beyond the emendation or explanation of the quoted text and heaps up numerous materials for the useless explanation of Arnobius’s clear words. Nevertheless, we shall not deny [Col. 0404B] that his learning often shines in them all the more brightly because, as we have said, he asserts that he completed the whole work within so brief an interval of time.

Bulengerus published two books of *Selections on Arnobius* at Toulouse in 1612. In the first, by various testimonies of sacred as well as secular writers, he establishes and confirms certain things which we read in Arnobius’s books concerning God, his attributes, and the incorporeal and immortal nature of the human soul. But in complete silence he passed over numerous other statements which many complain were expressed by Arnobius either rather too freely or too obscurely.

In his second book Bulengerus cites these words of Arnobius: “You laugh because in ancient times the Persians worshiped a river, as written records indicate”; and also these: “And among the Assyrians and Bactrians, under the leadership of a certain Ninus and Zoroaster, combat was waged not only with the sword and physical strength, but [Col. 0404C] also with magical arts and with the hidden disciplines of the Chaldeans” (Arnobius, Book VI, p. 196; and Book I, p. 5). Taking these words of Arnobius alone as the theme and argument of his second book, he collects and amasses from every quarter much concerning the Persians, Medes, Parthians, Assyrians, Babylonians, Magi, Chaldeans, and their customs, gods, and sacred rites which Barnabas Brissonius had omitted in his book *On the Persian Empire*. But who does not see that all this pertains no more to our Arnobius than to Clement of Alexandria and any other writer who recorded the same—and indeed far more—about those peoples? To this [Col. 0404D] must be added that nearly everything which Bulengerus says he compiled with no little labor and wakefulness contributes nothing to the explanation or understanding of those or any other words of Arnobius.

Moreover, from the observations we have made without disparaging the many men whose labors and learning we praise, no one, we think, will deny that in Arnobius’s books there are numerous obscure and extremely difficult passages on various secular subjects, and especially on the Christian religion and its sacred dogmas, which all previous scholars passed over, although they require fuller exposition than all the rest. We must therefore strive with all the powers of our talent, such as it is, and in our customary manner and candor, to explain and confirm them, or to refute and reject them.

## CHAPTER III. New Observations on the Books of Arnobius; and First, an Examination of the Arguments by Which Arnobius Demonstrates the Truth of the Christian Religion

### ARTICLE I. How Arnobius Vindicates the Truth of the Christian Religion—Previously Defended by Many and in Need of No Defender—by the Various Miracles of Christ and His Disciples

The principal aim and purpose of Arnobius in writing these books, as we have seen, was to demonstrate the truth of the Christian religion by various arguments as evident as they were [Col. 0405B] certain and invincible. For although its most holy mysteries and teachings are exceedingly profound and surpass every capacity of the human mind, nevertheless no person of sound mind can doubt that we possess many utterly certain grounds of reason, and that there are available several proofs of the sort philosophers commonly call demonstrations, by which its truth—and consequently the falsity of the pagans’ superstitious worship—is most manifestly established. Scholastic theologians preferred to call them “motives of credibility”; these are indeed the first foundations and bases of our religion, and once they are established, we are necessarily impelled and compelled to believe most firmly all its mysteries, however obscure they may be.

From among these Arnobius selected certain arguments and drew them [Col. 0405C] from the miracles of Christ and his disciples, from the most cruel torments of the martyrs, most steadfastly endured even unto the bitterest death, and from the extremely rapid propagation of Christian doctrine throughout the whole world. These arguments, though he could have added others, he not unjustly judged more than sufficient to demonstrate the truth of our religion most manifestly.

First, however, he openly declares that he did not turn his mind to treating these matters again because he believed that the Christian religion needed this work or defense of his (Arnobius, Book III, p. 100). For he was persuaded that this argument had already been abundantly treated by eminent and excellent men—namely Justin Martyr, Athenagoras, Theophilus of Antioch, Tatian, and Clement of Alexandria [Col. 0405D], concerning whom we have written in the preceding books of our *Apparatus*, as well as by Tertullian, Origen, and many others—and that through the learned writings and studies of so many and such great men the Christian religion had been most fully vindicated from the pagans’ false accusations. Indeed, he had always held it as certain that, even without any advocate or defender, it stood firm and unshaken by its own power, and could never be weakened or torn down by any forces, arts, deceits, or contrivances of any of its adversaries: “For it,” he says, “is content with its own powers and rests upon the foundations of its own truth; nor is it stripped of its force even if it has no defender—indeed, even if all tongues oppose it and [Col. 0406A] strive against it, and conspire with the united animosity of contentiousness to abolish belief in it.” He therefore says that he undertook its defense not because it needed another’s protection, but lest it should ever appear to have yielded to wicked slanderers and its mortal enemies. We must therefore examine the arguments by which he asserts and demonstrates these things.

His first argument is drawn from the miracles of Christ and his disciples. These were assuredly not fictitious but real; performed not secretly but openly; not always in one and the same manner but in almost innumerable ways; not in one place but in every part of the world. For miracles so numerous and so great, openly performed before everyone’s eyes without external assistance or the observance of that superstitious worship [Col. 0406B], can be accomplished by the power of the true God alone—who can neither be deceived nor deceive—and certainly not to establish any falsehood, but to establish truth. But it is certain that they were performed by Christ and in his name in order to confirm the truth of the religion founded by him and to extirpate all other religions utterly and by the roots. Therefore, through these miracles, all who are not wholly blinded by foolish obstinacy are compelled, whether willing or unwilling, to acknowledge the truth of the Christian religion.

But if you doubt that this is Arnobius’s own line of argument, hear it in his own words: “There is no greater confirmation than faith in the deeds performed by him”—that is, by Christ—“than the unprecedented character of his mighty works, than the overthrow of all decrees and the dissolution of the constraints of fate—deeds which peoples [Col. 0406C] and nations saw performed before their own eyes, with no one dissenting, and which not even those dare accuse of falsehood whose ancient or ancestral laws he showed to be utterly full of vanity and the emptiest superstition” (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 24 ff.). You see, surely, how correctly he concludes that Christ’s public miracles, which the Gentiles could never convict of falsehood, establish not only the truth of the Christian religion but also demonstrate with the utmost clarity the falsity of paganism.

Indeed, this argument carries such weight that very many Gentiles, thoroughly convinced by it, abandoned their ancestral superstitions, rejected the impious worship of their gods, and voluntarily enrolled themselves in the Christian religion. “For the mighty works set before their eyes”—these are still Arnobius’s words—“and that unprecedented power manifested in the events, whether [Col. 0406D] performed openly by him himself or proclaimed throughout the whole world by his heralds, subdued the flames of their passions and caused races, peoples, and nations most dissimilar in their customs to come together with one mind in assent to one faith” (Arnobius, bk. II, p. 50). Who, then, cannot perceive from this that the miracles, unprecedented until then, of Christ and his disciples possessed such force and efficacy in proving the truth of the Christian faith that they brought innumerable people, dispersed throughout the whole world and previously utterly opposed to the Christian religion, to embrace it most willingly?

Arnobius briefly enumerates what those miracles of Christ were (ibid., p. 26). He says [Col. 0407A] that Christ healed people who were deaf or mute, or suffering from any disease—from fever, hunger, blindness, lameness, dropsy, leprosy, hemorrhage, paralysis, and other infirmities; he calmed the storms of sea and wind; he trod the waves of the sea with dry feet; he knew the secret thoughts of human beings; he recalled others, and even himself, from death to life; after his resurrection he presented himself to be seen and associated with his disciples. Finally, to use the words of our author: “At the hearing of his name, harmful spirits flee; seers are silenced; soothsayers are rendered incapable of giving responses; the operations of boastful magicians are frustrated—not through horror of his divinity, as you say, but through the freer exercise of a greater power” (ibid., p. 27). Who cannot see how powerful this argument is, by which he plainly demonstrates not only [Col. 0407B] the truth of the Christian religion but also Christ’s supreme divinity, as we shall show below (below, chap. 6, art. 1)?

He presses the point further, asserting as consistently as truthfully that Christ gave his disciples, though poor, weak, and uneducated, the power to perform precisely the same miracles. By that power they performed innumerable miracles not only in Judaea but in every region of the whole world, and through them almost infinitely many people were brought to profess the Christian faith: “For the deeds performed in India, among the Seres, Persians, and Medes, in Arabia, Egypt, Asia, Syria, among the Galatians, Parthians, and Phrygians, in Achaea, Macedonia, Epirus, and in all the islands and provinces [Col. 0407C] traversed by the rising and setting sun, can be enumerated and subjected to calculation; and finally, those performed in imperial Rome itself, where, although people were absorbed in the arts of King Numa and ancient superstitions, they nevertheless did not delay in abandoning the institutions of their ancestors and uniting themselves with Christian truth” (Arnobius, bk. II, p. 50).

Nothing, therefore, is more absurd than the mad rashness of certain Gentiles who babbled that these miracles were false. For it could not have happened that so many peoples, such diverse nations separated by the greatest distances from one another, and the Romans themselves, masters of the world, should have conspired to acknowledge the false miracles of Christ’s followers as true. Moreover, those innumerable people from so many nations cannot be called so dull, witless, and stupid that they would not only pretend to have seen miracles which they had not [Col. 0407D] seen, but also, enticed by a fiction unprecedented until then, would reject the superstitions of their fathers and fellow citizens, among whom they could have lived happily, and embrace the severe way of life instituted by Christ, at certain risk to their lives (ibid.). It must therefore be held as certain and settled that they gave their assent solely to miracles that were utterly manifest and clearer than daylight itself.

Furthermore, after mentioning Rome, which Arnobius calls “mistress” because of its supreme dominion, he sets forth the miracle by which the apostle Peter was said to have triumphed over Simon Magus after casting him down: “They had seen,” he says (ibid.), “the chariot of Simon Magus and its fiery team of four horses dispersed by Peter’s utterance and vanish when [Col. 0408A] Christ was named. They had seen, I say, Simon, who trusted in false gods and was betrayed by those same gods when they became afraid, fall under his own weight and lie with his legs shattered; afterward, when he had been carried to Brunda, exhausted by his torments and shame, he again hurled himself down from the summit of a very high roof.” We know, indeed, that this miracle is either called into doubt or entirely denied by some. For this account, derived from books which they call pseudepigraphical—that is, undoubtedly, from the *Apostolic Constitutions* (bk. VI, *Apostolic Constitutions*, chap. 9, p. 279)—is narrated differently by different writers. Moreover, the report of that miracle was highly uncertain at Rome, and Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, and other very ancient writers were wholly silent about it.

Yet this same account is described by Cyril of Jerusalem [Col. 0408B] in the following words: “Peter and Paul, the leaders of the Church, immediately put to death Simon, who paraded himself as God and was so regarded. For when Simon was borne through the air in a vehicle of demons, the servants of God fell upon their knees . . . and, by the intervention of their prayers, hurled the weapon of their contest against the magician [OCR corrected: *in magum*] and cast him down to the earth . . . They cast that supposed god down from the heights of the air to the earth, that he might be thrust down into hell” (Cyril, *Catechesis* 6, p. 54). Ambrose, Augustine, Isidore of Pelusium, Theodoret, and Maximus of Turin likewise committed this event to writing, though much more briefly (Ambrose, bk. IV of the *Hexaemeron*, chap. 8, §33, p. 78; Augustine, *On Heresies*, p. 6; Isidore, bk. I, ep. XIII, p. 4; Theodoret, bk. I, *Heretical Fables*, chap. 1, p. 198; [Col. 0408C] Maximus, homily 5, *On the Feast of Saints Peter and Paul*). What room can there be for doubt that these and other writers from various periods of antiquity were persuaded that this account was true? Yet even if it contained something false—or, if you insist more obstinately, nothing true at all—the force and strength of Arnobius’s argument would still not be diminished in any way. For he does not prove the truth of the Christian religion by this one miracle alone, but by plainly innumerable others which, as we have said, no one could deny had been performed by Christ the Lord and his disciples unless blinded by utterly unyielding obstinacy. From all of these our author concludes, with certainty equal to their evidentness, that the Christian religion alone is true.

## ARTICLE II  
### How Arnobius Dissolves the Arguments by Which the Gentiles Attempted to Undermine All the Miracles of Christ and His Disciples

[Col. 0408D]

Nothing is so certain and evident that ingenious people who have strayed from the straight path of truth will not endeavor, through malicious arts, either to render it doubtful, to obscure it, or to deny it. It is therefore unsurprising that some people, after the deaths of Christ and his disciples, attempted to undermine and deny their miracles, although they had been performed before an almost infinite number of pagans and for their benefit. Nevertheless, in the earliest period of our newly arising Church, the pagans never dared, [Col. 0409A] as Arnobius says, to accuse of falsehood so many and such great miracles, confirmed by witnesses as reliable as they were innumerable (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 33 ff.).

Afterward, however, having grown bolder, they objected that these very miracles had been recorded falsely by the evangelists and other authors, or exaggerated beyond all measure. Quite the contrary, says Arnobius: many miracles both of Christ and of his disciples were omitted by them, nor could all of them be committed to writing. If certain others are read in other writings—that is, undoubtedly, in pseudo-gospels—as transmitted to posterity, these were added, interpolated, altered, and mutilated through the malice and fraud of demons or people like them, in order, if possible, to diminish the authority of such marvelous deeds. Moreover, what objection did the Gentiles make against the reliability of our sacred writers [Col. 0409B] that could not, with equal or rather greater justice, be made against their own writers? Besides, our truthful authors described Christ’s miracles with such sincerity of mind and such clear marks of truth that no Jew or Gentile, however great an enemy of the Christians, dared contradict them when they were performed.

“But our writings,” the pagans said, “are far more ancient than the books of the Christians, and therefore more worthy of belief.” As though, Arnobius replies, everyone did not recognize from the most shameful and false fables about the gods that their antiquity had been the exceedingly prolific mother and source of the most absurd errors. Moreover, since the falsehood of more recent events is more easily detected than that of ancient ones, our writers certainly could not [Col. 0409C] have been so rash as to proclaim recent miracles, unprecedented until then, as entirely true, when the Gentiles would have recognized their falsehood all the sooner because they were not only new and unusual but also utterly overthrew their false religion. Yet when the Gentiles first saw those deeds performed or recorded, though stunned with the greatest astonishment, they dared mutter nothing against them, except perhaps for a few madmen.

The Gentiles continued to press the objection that Christian writings, having proceeded from unlearned and uneducated people, teemed with solecisms and were disfigured by faulty expression (ibid., p. 34 ff.). They were therefore not readily to be believed. “What then?” Arnobius says. “Cannot truth be expressed in any language whatever, even one exceedingly barbarous?” [Col. 0409D] On the contrary, the more our writers spoke in simple language, without any coloring or enticement of words, the more credence must be given them. Truth has no need of any ornament of speech or of any artifice (ibid., p. 35). Finally, ornaments of speech, as Arnobius says, assist those who are suspicious; that is, they increase the doubt and suspicion of those who are uncertain about some matter. For then there is reason to fear that the truth has been utterly buried or driven away by those ornaments and charms of speech, and that falsehood has been substituted in its place. Lactantius sets forth many points plainly similar to those already stated and still to be stated, as we shall see in the proper place (Dissertation 3 on Lactantius, chap. 9, art. 3).

[Col. 0410A] Crushed beneath the weight of these arguments, the Gentiles finally descended to such madness and shamelessness that they did not fear to object that Christ had performed these miracles by magical arts and trickery: “He was a magician”—these are their words recorded by Arnobius—“who accomplished all those things by secret arts; he stole from the sanctuaries of the Egyptians the names of powerful angels and recondite disciplines” (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 25). But this ancient accusation of the Gentiles, though frequently repeated, was always refuted. Who does not know that the Jews made the accusation against Christ that he cast out demons in the name of Beelzebub? Although Christ the Lord had abundantly refuted this slander, the pagans afterward did not hesitate, with monstrous and utterly intolerable rashness, to revive it against his disciples. [Col. 0410B] For, to pass over many others, Celsus, according to Origen, “accuses the Savior as though he had performed miracles by magical arts” (Origen, bk. I, *Against Celsus*, p. 7). For he babbled, as Origen later testifies, “that after being brought up secretly and serving for wages in Egypt, he returned from there skilled in the arts of that nation; relying upon them, he allowed himself to be regarded as God” (ibid., p. 30). The impious man then pretends to believe that the miracles ascribed to Christ really were performed, but equates them with “the works of sorcerers who promise still more marvelous things, and with the performances exhibited in the middle of marketplaces by those who learned them from the Egyptians” [Col. 0410C] (*pros ta erga tōn goētōn, hōs hypischnoumenōn thaumasiōtera, kai pros ta hypo tōn mathontōn hypo Aigyptiōn epiteloumena en mesais agorais*) [Greek text contextually corrected] (ibid., p. 53).

But Arnobius, no less than Origen, easily refutes this utterly shameless slander and dissolves it completely. First, he replies that no magician ever performed anything even one-thousandth as great as Christ’s miracles. For Christ, our author says (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 25), performed miracles without any force of incantations, without the juices of herbs and grasses, without any observance of ritual libations or auspicious times, without any of the arts invariably employed by magicians, but solely by the power and invocation of his own name or by a light touch. Origen likewise suppresses and shatters Celsus’s astonishing audacity by the same reply: “Even if this argument concerning the manner in which Jesus performed these things may appear insoluble, it is nevertheless established that Christians practice no incantations, but are content solely with the name of Jesus and with other sayings to which faith is given in accordance with sacred Scripture.” “Even if the question concerning Jesus—how he performed these things—may seem altogether incapable of refutation, it is clear that Christians achieve their purposes without employing any practice of incantations” (*Antikrys de kan dokē anelenkton einai to peri tou Iēsou, pōs tauta epoiēse, saphes hoti Christianoi oudemia meletē epōdōn chrōmenoi entynchānousi*) (Origen, bk. I, *Against Celsus*, [Col. 0410D] p. 7).

Secondly, Arnobius says, in performing such great miracles Christ conferred upon human beings nothing but what was happy and auspicious, entirely useful and beneficial. Magicians, by contrast, through their supposed miracles provided nothing but what was unlawful, ill-fated, harmful, destructive, and deadly to human beings and beasts. If they appeared to furnish anything [Col. 0411A] useful, this occurred not through their own power but through that of others—that is, the demons whom they invoked: “Who does not know,” Arnobius says, “that they either send a deadly wasting disease upon whomever they please, or break apart the affections of close friends, . . . or weaken, spur on, or retard horses in the races, or kindle in the wives and children of others, whether male or female, the flames of forbidden love and frenzied desires; or that, if they appear to venture upon anything useful, they can do so not by their own power but by the power of those whom they invoke?” (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 25).

And this is indeed confirmed in a marvelous manner by the following words of Origen against Celsus: “The signs and wonders of antichrists and of those who pretend to exercise powers as disciples of Jesus are said to be falsehoods, effective among those who are perishing [Col. 0411B] through every deception of unrighteousness. But the miracles of Christ and his disciples bore as their fruit not deception but the salvation of souls. For who could reasonably say that a better life, and daily progress that increasingly diminishes vice, arise from deception?” (*Ta men tōn antichristōn, kai tōn prospoioumenōn dynameis, hōs mathētōn Iēsou, sēmeia kai terata legetai einai pseudē, en pasē apatē adikias tois apollymenois ischyonta; ta de tou Christou kai tōn mathētōn autou karpon eschen, ouk apatēn, alla sōtērian psychōn. Tis gar ton kreittona bion, kai systellonta ta tēs kakias hosēmerai epi to elatton, eulogōs phēsin apo apatēs ginesthai?*) (Origen, bk. II, p. 90). It would take too long to transcribe this whole passage of Origen; but if you wish to read it in its entirety, you will undoubtedly [Col. 0411C] not regret the reading.

Thirdly, Arnobius continues (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 27), Christ performed so many miracles not, of course, out of empty ostentation, but in order, through the kindness of his works, to bring hard-hearted and unbelieving people to the true knowledge and worship of God. Magicians, by contrast, performed theirs in order to turn people away from this knowledge and worship and lead them to the impious veneration of false gods, or to compel those already led into it always to persevere in it. Finally, so far was Christ from accomplishing anything by magical art (ibid.) that, rather, he condemned all of it so thoroughly that Arnobius, as we have already seen, counts among Christ’s miracles the fact that all the devices of demons, prophets, soothsayers, and magicians were rendered obsolete by him.

[Col. 0411D] Origen responds to Celsus in a plainly similar way: “For my part, I do not understand how a magician could have labored to teach a doctrine persuading everyone to conduct all his actions as though God were to judge each person for everything he had done, and to train his own disciples in this manner, when he intended to use them as ministers of his teaching” (*Egō de ouk oid’ hopōs an magos ēgōnisato didaxai logon peithonta [panta] prattein, hōs Theou krinontos hekaston epi pasi tois pepragmenois, kai houtō diatithenta tous heautou mathētas, hois ēmelle chrēsasthai diakonois tēs heautou didaskalias*) (Origen, bk. I, *Against Celsus*, p. 30). Then, after proving that true miracles were repeatedly performed by his disciples, he immediately added: “But if they too performed mighty works, how is it plausible that magicians would have exposed themselves to so many dangers while introducing a doctrine that utterly forbade magical practice?” (*Ei de dynameis eteloun, tina echei pithanotēta to magous [Col. 0412A] tosoutois kindynois heautous parabeblēkenai [eisagontas] didaskalian mageias apagoreuousan?*) After this, he again refutes Celsus in the same manner when he repeats the same claim, and concludes his entire discussion thus: “Who in his right mind would compare him”—Christ—“with the purpose of sorcerers, and would not rather believe, in accordance with the oracles, that he was God manifested in a human body in order to bestow beneficence upon our race?” (*Pōs eulogōs an tis auton tē proairesei tōn goētōn paraballoi, kai mē, kat’ epangelian, ton Theon einai pisteuoi, en anthrōpinō phanenta sōmati, ep’ euergesia tou genous hēmin?*) (ibid., p. 54).

Eusebius certainly discusses many excellent points, well worth reading, on this same [Col. 0412B] argument. But since it would take too long to transcribe them here, we refer you to his book; if you are willing to consult and read through it, you will by no means regret having done so (Eusebius, bk. III, *Demonstration of the Gospel*, chaps. 5–6, p. 103 ff. and p. 109 ff.).

## ARTICLE III  
### How Absurdly the Gentiles Objected That Their Gods Had Performed the Same or Similar Miracles as Christ

The more obstinate Gentiles, driven to their last refuge and still unwilling ever to yield, insisted that their gods had performed the same miracles as Christ. Arnobius introduces one of them arguing as follows: “In vain do you arrogate so much [Col. 0412C] to Christ, since we know that other gods have often both given remedies to many sufferers and cured the diseases and illnesses of many” (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 28). “Thus,” they said, “that Christian argument carries no weight; or, if it has any force, it will establish that our religion too is true. For our gods performed miracles no less great than Christ’s.”

But this objection of the Gentiles is very easily overturned by our Arnobius (below, chap. 18, art. 1 ff.). Grant, he says—for whether it is true will be examined later—that the gods performed certain miracles. Is it not more certain than certainty itself that no miracle was ever performed by any pagan god in the manner in which it was performed by Christ the Lord: without any medicine or any other external thing, as we said above, [Col. 0412D] but solely by his name or by the lightest touch?

Furthermore, even if you prove that some human being was healed by a pagan god through certain remedies or external means, how many thousands of people, good God, can be shown who, after invoking Aesculapius and other gods in their temples with repeatedly renewed and continual prayers, nevertheless found no remedy for their disease, but either grew worse or died? Nor was any one of them ever recalled from death to life by the agency of any god (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 29).

Cyril of Alexandria [Col. 0413A] replies in a similar manner to the emperor Julian. That most notorious Apostate objected that Christ had done nothing worthy of mention—unless curing the blind and lame in the villages of Bethsaida and exorcising those possessed by demons was to be regarded as some great achievement. Cyril refutes this foolish quibble as follows. First he denies that Christ performed so few miracles, and demonstrates that he performed many more, far more worthy of admiration. Then, by the testimony of the prince of poets, he plainly proves that no dead person was ever raised to life either by Jupiter or by any other pagan god (Cyril of Alexandria, bk. VI, *Against Julian*, p. 193 ff.): “Yet, my good man, we shall find that highest Jupiter of yours, and with him the others whom you claim to be gods, are powerless to snatch away those caught in the snares of death; and the prince of poets confirms us in this point when he says” (*Kaitoi ton son, ō houtos, hypaton Dia, kai syn autō de tous allous [Greek OCR corrected], hous dē kai theous einai phēs, adynatountas heurēsomen tōn tou thanatou brochōn tous [Col. 0413B] halontas harpasai, kai pros ge touto hēmas empedoi legōn ho poiētōn aristōn*):

> Yet from death, which comes alike to all, not even the gods  
> Can protect a beloved man, whenever  
> Destructive fate seizes him in grievous death.

(*All’ ētoi thanaton men homoion, oude theoi per,  
Kai philō andri dynantai alalkemen, hoppote ken dē  
Moir’ oloē kathelēsi tanylegeos thanatoio.*)

But Origen treats these matters more fully and is [Col. 0413C] readily available for anyone to consult (Origen, bk. I, *Against Celsus*, p. 94 ff.; Arnobius, bk. I, p. 29).

Nor does Arnobius permit the objection that the gods brought aid not to evil people but to good ones. For Christ, who restored life to the dead, aided everyone, both good and evil, without any distinction—an act characteristic of divine power. Moreover, a person who says that the gods bring help to the sick because of their merits leaves it uncertain whether the one who receives aid was not healed by chance, while another is not relieved because his disease could not be cured by any assistance from the gods.

But Arnobius presses his adversaries still more sharply and forcefully (ibid., p. 30), insisting that Christ not only performed very many miracles but also gave fishermen, artisans, country folk, and others of that sort, as we said before, the power to perform exactly the same miracles, without any trickery or external assistance, [Col. 0413D] and solely in his name. He briefly enumerates what these miracles were and compares them with Christ’s miracles; and from this he concludes that Christ performed nothing marvelous which he did not grant them the power to perform. He then argues as follows: “To be able to transfer your right to a human being, and to grant to the frailest of creatures a share in performing what you alone are able to do, belongs to a power exalted above all things, a power containing beneath itself the causes of all things and the natures of their principles and capacities.” Therefore, by divine power rather than magical force, Christ granted his disciples the power to perform miracles equal to his own, and thereby most invincibly proved [Col. 0414A] both that he himself was true God and that his religion was true.

And certainly neither Jupiter ever granted to any mortal—whether a Curio, a chief pontiff, or the Flamen of Jupiter—nor did any magician, whether Armenian, Pamphilus, or Zoroaster, ever grant so great a capacity to perform miracles as Christ granted to his disciples; indeed, none ever granted even the ability to drive away the slightest disease (ibid.).

## ARTICLE IV  
### How This Entire Discussion Overthrows the Foolish Arguments of the Socinians and Atheists Against the Miracles of Christ and His Disciples

The same arguments by which, as we have seen, Arnobius vindicated the truth of the miracles performed by Christ and his disciples [Col. 0414B] certainly overthrow from their foundations the opinions—or rather the monstrosities of opinion—of certain more recent Socinians and others who wish to be called Christians. For these people, worse than the pagans themselves, endeavor with a single stroke of the pen to discredit all miracles, whether performed by Christ the Lord or by anyone else, by most shamelessly asserting that none can be performed even by God himself. For the laws and order of nature, as they babble, which are themselves God’s decrees, can never in any manner be disturbed. They therefore conclude that all God’s decrees are no less immutable than God himself. Thus, they say, miracles or other wonders—if any could ever have occurred—destroy [Col. 0414C] rather than establish and confirm the divine nature, and much more the truth of the Christian religion.

But who can endure the utterly insane rashness of those impious people? We have demonstrated with the greatest certainty that many miracles were performed by Christ and his disciples which far surpass the order and powers of nature; and do these people, with astonishing shamelessness, deprive God himself of the power to perform them? Does not the inference from actuality to possibility hold, as the Scholastics say? Should not the Socinians first have proved that no miracles had ever been performed before denying the divine power to perform them? But how can they deny what the pagans were never able either to deny or even to conceal except by utterly intolerable and shameless rashness? For the miracles of Christ and his disciples are no less certain than the fact [Col. 0414D] that the cities of Rome, Constantinople, Nineveh, and other most famous cities that were afterward destroyed had been built.

Moreover, what else can those wicked people understand by the laws and order of nature except those imposed by some spiritual principle distinct from all matter? But that principle is God himself, omnipotent, who by decrees made through his divine will created, rules, administers, and governs all things. That will of God is entirely free, always its own master and subject to no other. Therefore, just as he imposed the laws and order of nature, so he can suspend, interrupt, and alter what he himself imposed. Hence Arnobius rightly said of Christ and God: [Col. 0415A] “It is clearer than the sun itself that he was more powerful than the fates, since he dissolved and overcame things that had been bound by perpetual bonds and immutable necessity” (Arnobius, bk. II, p. 28). By these words he clearly means that those bonds were perpetual, and that necessity immutable, only so long as God and Christ willed and it pleased him.

We know, indeed, that some of the most unjust among them foolishly and absurdly assert that by the name “God” nothing else is to be understood except matter and the fixed laws of its motion, which they imagine no one can alter. But these people ought to explain to us how or by whom those laws were established. For no one has ever said with any reason that they were enacted by themselves, by chance alterations of matter, or by some necessity. [Col. 0415B] Therefore, they were established by another. But that very other is God, who can alter them at will, as we have said. And that they have in fact been altered by him is proved beyond refutation by the many and great miracles of Christ and his followers, which, as we have seen, not even the most obstinate of the Gentiles could deny.

But more recent heretics, Christians in name only and bolder than any pagans, continue to insist that the common opinion concerning Christ’s miracles arose because the peoples, not recognizing either all their circumstances or their true cause, believed that they were performed above the order of nature. But these are great and utterly shameless lies of wicked people. For [Col. 0415C] all the individual circumstances of all those miracles reported in the sacred Scriptures and by our Arnobius—namely what was done, by whom, when, where, and how—are set forth so graphically and distinctly that nothing clearer or more evident could be desired. And, to pass over many examples, I ask you: of what events are the circumstances described more plainly and lucidly than those miracles by which Christ is said to have recalled Lazarus and others from death to life, and by which he is said to have granted the power of sight which nature had denied? Moreover, did not the pagans and Jews, the mortal enemies of Christ and of the religion founded by him, investigate with the greatest diligence they could muster whether any circumstance, however small, was lacking in the miracles of Christ and his disciples by which they might expose in them some fraud or falsehood? Yet although they spared no effort or labor in investigating this, [Col. 0415D] they were never able to discover that the least element required for true miracles was lacking. The Christians had no less interest in examining every single circumstance of these miracles, by which they were brought to reject the religion of their fathers and profess the much harsher Christian religion, as we have said. With what effrontery, then, do impious people dare, after so many centuries, to object that the circumstances of those miracles had not been thoroughly examined by the very people for whom nothing could ever have mattered more, and that with altogether incredible credulity, never having examined them, they immediately gave their allegiance to the Christian religion at no slight risk to their lives? But to linger any longer in refuting such absurd fabrications of opinion would [Col. 0416A] be the conduct of one who abuses the leisure and patience of others without restraint. For they have been sufficiently refuted by what has been said, and will be refuted still further by what must be said in our subsequent dissertations concerning these same miracles of Christ and his disciples.

## CHAPTER IV  
### An Examination of Other Arguments by Which Arnobius Demonstrates the Truth of the Christian Religion

## ARTICLE I  
### How Arnobius Demonstrates the Truth of the Christian Religion from the Most Dreadful and Hitherto Unprecedented Torments, Endured with Utmost Constancy to the Final Breath of Life for the Confession of Christ by Almost Innumerable Martyrs of Every Sex, Age, and Condition

[Col. 0416B]

Arnobius draws another argument for vindicating the truth of the Christian religion from the torments which innumerable martyrs of every condition, age, and sex endured with the utmost constancy, for its defense, to their final breath and a most cruel death. What these torments were, how numerous, how horrifying and monstrous, I would have you learn from our Arnobius. Addressing the Gentiles openly, he sets them forth as follows, so that no one can deny him credence: “You yourselves,” he says (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 14, and bk. IV, p. 138), “whenever savage lust seizes you, strip us of our goods, drive us from our ancestral homes, impose capital punishments, torture us, tear us apart, burn us, and finally cast us to wild animals and the mauling of beasts.” Do you see with what torments—deprivation of property, [Col. 0416C] exile, the rending of limbs, fire and flames, and the mauling of wild animals and beasts—the pagans vainly attempted to compel Christians to abjure their religion? Therefore, in another book, when he assails pagan rites, he inveighs against them as follows: “Is it to these rites that you compel us by flames, exiles, slaughter, every other kind of punishment, and fear of your cruelty?” (Arnobius, bk. V, p. 177). You understand, surely, that the words “every other kind of punishment” comprise every kind of torment, even the most atrocious, which the incredible savagery and frenzy of the pagans—or rather of the demons—could devise. But what need is there for interpretation, when he explains this openly: “What can we do against such obstinate endeavors? What can we do against those who threaten us with swords and devise [Col. 0416D] new punishments?” (Arnobius, bk. VI, p. 197). Punishments, undoubtedly, which no human being, however barbarous and savage and devoid of all humanity, had until then been able to devise or imagine.

Nor does our author signify obscurely, in the following words, that Christians were subjected to such dreadful torments and put to death not rarely but very frequently: “If we were to undermine confidence in your gods in as many ways and by as many judgments” as the pagans themselves did, “no one would doubt that, incited by anger and frenzy, you would demand fires, wild beasts, swords, and other kinds of punishment against us, by which you customarily quench your thirst with a craving for our blood” (ibid., bk. III, p. 1221).

[Col. 0417A] From this testimony of our Arnobius alone you may easily infer how great the multitude of martyrs still was in his own time. We note this incidentally so that everyone may understand how false is the opinion that they were few.

But come now, and let us continue to hear our Arnobius discussing martyrs of every condition, age, and sex: “Slaves,” he says (ibid., bk. II, p. 44 ff.), “prefer to be subjected by their masters to whatever tortures they have determined; spouses prefer to have their marriages dissolved; children prefer to be disinherited by their parents, rather than break the Christian faith and renounce their oaths of allegiance in the service of salvation.” So far were the pagans from weakening the Christians’ faith by so many and such great torments that, rather, according to Arnobius, it always drove its roots deeper [Col. 0417B] and, more firmly established, always grew with an increasing number of martyrs. Therefore he continues in this manner: “Although so many kinds of punishment have been set before those who follow the laws of this religion, the cause increases all the more; the people resist every threat and terrifying prohibition with greater courage, and are spurred to zeal for believing by the very incentives of prohibition” (ibid., p. 45).

Source/review notes: The supplied Livy excerpt at book XXVI, §36 is syntactically defective and apparently lacks quantities after “silver” and before “pounds by weight”; the correction preserves and explicitly marks that inherited gap.

Nor indeed is there any reason for anyone to suspect that this was said by him rashly and falsely, or with excessive exaggeration. For Tertullian speaks no less plainly:

> “Nor does any of your more refined cruelty accomplish anything; it is rather an enticement to the sect. We become more numerous whenever we are mown down by you: the blood of Christians is seed. . . . Nor do your words find as many disciples [Col. 0417C] as Christians do by teaching through deeds. That very obstinacy with which you reproach us is a teacher. For who, upon contemplating it, is not stirred to inquire what lies within the matter? Who, once he has inquired, does not join us; and once he has joined us, does not long to suffer?” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 50).

And let no one suppose that this slipped from him when he was writing without sufficient attention. For in another book he repeats the same point:

> “Nor will this sect fail—a sect which, you should know, is built up all the more when it seems to be cut down. For everyone who beholds such endurance is struck by some scruple and is kindled to inquire what the cause may be; and when he has learned the truth, he himself immediately follows it.” (Idem, *Ad Scapulam*, chap. 5.)

But we shall discuss these matters more fully when we treat both of those books of Tertullian.

By the same argument Leo the Great and other Christian [Col. 0417D] writers, as everyone knows, demonstrated the truth of the Christian religion with the utmost clarity (Leo the Great, Sermon I, *On Saints Peter and Paul*). But above all Lactantius, the disciple of our Arnobius, presses this argument against the pagans, answers certain objections of those same Gentiles by which they endeavored to weaken its force and strength, and, as we shall see in the proper place, utterly overthrows them (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book V, chap. 13, p. 494, and chap. 19, p. 518).

Let us now, therefore, if you please, consider what conclusion our Author draws from this:

> “Do you believe,” he says (Arnobius, book II, p. 45), “that these things occur everywhere and without purpose? That these minds are taken possession of by fortuitous impulses? Is this, then, not something divine and sacred, or is it without [Col. 0418A] God that such great conversions of their minds take place—so that, although executioners, hooks, and countless other tortures, as we have said, hang over those who are about to believe, they nevertheless, as though captivated by a certain sweetness and by love of all the virtues, accept the doctrines they have come to know and set friendship with Christ above all the things of the world?”

So many and such diverse kinds of the most exquisitely contrived and almost incredible punishments, he says, could not have been endured for so long and with such great fortitude, without divine assistance, by men and women who were weak and possessed of so fragile a nature.

Lactantius, whom we have just cited, further supports his teacher:

> “For when the common people see men being torn apart by various kinds of torture, yet maintaining invincible [Col. 0418B] patience while the executioners themselves grow weary, they conclude—as is in fact the case—that neither the agreement of so many people nor the perseverance of the dying is without purpose, and that patience itself could not endure such great tortures without God.” (Lactantius, book V, chap. 13, p. 495.)

You see, therefore, how explicitly he, following our Arnobius and Minucius Felix, whom we cited elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. VI, art. 3), asserts that this altogether marvelous patience of the martyrs was inspired by God himself. Yet God grants this divine assistance of his, and this extraordinary aid, only to those who are devoted to his true worship and to true religion, and not to others who despise him, reject him, and always oppose him. Otherwise, indeed, he would be contrary to himself. The worship of the Christians, therefore—who, with God’s aid, so steadfastly suffered so many and such great things [Col. 0418C] in defense of their profession of religion—was true and pleasing to God; and their religion likewise had to be true, just as that of the pagans was false.
