## ARTICLE II. How Arnobius Further Vindicates the Truth of the Christian Religion from Its Doctrine, Which Was Most Rapidly Embraced throughout the Whole World by Innumerable People Devoted to the Worship of the Gods

Arnobius most clearly demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion by a third argument, drawn from its doctrine and from its remarkably swift propagation throughout every part of the world. For what, he asks, is its doctrine? It teaches that there is only one God, and that he is the supreme lord [Col. 0418D] and ruler of all things, and that for this reason he is to be prayed to and worshiped solely for our sake. It teaches that nothing is to be asked of him except what is just, honorable, and worthy of his hearing. It teaches that nothing is to be conceded to the unjust greed and lust of human beings, but that both must always be resisted; that unremitting attention must be given to innocence and moral integrity; and that we must purify ourselves from every stain by cutting away all offenses:

> “We Christians are nothing else,” in Arnobius’s words, “than worshipers, under Christ as our teacher, of the supreme King and Ruler; if you consider the matter, you will find nothing else practiced in this religion. This is the sum of all our conduct, this the appointed goal of our divine duties, this their end. Before him we all customarily prostrate ourselves; [Col. 0419A] him we worship with our united prayers; from him we ask things that are just, honorable, and worthy of his hearing. It is not that he desires us to be suppliants, or loves to have us prostrate ourselves and—or, according to the variant reading, “or”—to behold the reverence of so many thousands. This is for our benefit and has regard to our advantage. For because, through the defect of our innate weakness, we are prone to faults and to the various appetites of lust, he permits himself always to be present in our thoughts, so that while we pray to him and strive to deserve his gifts, we may receive the will to innocence and purify ourselves from every stain by cutting away all offenses.” (Arnobius, book I, pp. 14–15.)

Finally, the Christians proclaimed that all the gods of the Gentiles were false; they rejected every impious rite of theirs, their superstitious mysteries, sacrifices, and festivals; and they plainly and utterly condemned their corrupt morals.

Yet the truer, more dutiful, more powerful, and more just the Christian religion was—as he continues to say—the more difficult and laborious it certainly was to persuade the Gentiles of this very fact. For how great, I ask you, [Col. 0419B] was the labor and effort required of Christ’s inexperienced, uneducated, and uncultivated disciples to draw those same Gentiles away from the most ancient worship of gods and idols, and from other superstitions which for so many centuries they had imbibed with their nurses’ milk as though they were pious observances? How much labor and difficulty was involved in bringing countless thousands of people to profess the Christian religion, which they believed to be new and impious? How great an exertion of mind was needed to lead them away from the soft, luxurious, and lustful manner of life which they thought permissible, and toward another that was altogether hard, austere, severe, and utterly opposed to the natural appetite of human beings? Finally, how arduous and laborious it was, after breaking and overcoming the almost incredible obstinacy of people of this kind, to induce them to believe that the teachings of the Christian faith concerning Christ’s supreme divinity, his human birth and death, and the other matters we shall discuss below were true! [Col. 0419C]

Nevertheless, these same followers of Christ, however uncultivated and ignorant, however destitute of human assistance—and indeed resisted by every sort of person, commoners and nobles, princes, kings, emperors, priests, and high priests, with every force and impetus of spirit, skill, strength, and fury—spread this very religion throughout the whole world, by their preaching alone and by the [Col. 0419D] power of miracles, within the briefest interval of time. Moreover, they brought to it not merely certain women or ignorant men, but also orators endowed with great talents, grammarians, rhetoricians, jurists, physicians, and philosophers. It is surely better, however, to hear our Author himself speaking on these matters:

> “Do not at least these arguments,” he says, “give you grounds for belief: that already throughout every land, in so brief a span of time, the mysteries of this immense name have been diffused? That there is now no nation of such barbarous customs and such ignorance of gentleness that, converted by love of him, it has not softened its harshness and, after assuming tranquillity, passed over to peaceful dispositions? That orators endowed with such great talents, [Col. 0420A] grammarians, rhetoricians, jurists, physicians, and even philosophers who probe hidden things, seek these teachings after despising those in which they formerly trusted?” (Arnobius, book II, p. 44.)

Indeed, he repeatedly states that the whole world had thus been filled with followers of the Christian religion (Idem, book I, p. 33; book II, p. 50); and we have already observed that he accurately and carefully enumerates various regions situated toward the rising and setting sun which professed this religion of ours (above, this chapter, art. 1).

But how, I ask, did so many people, separated by such great distances, outstanding in exceptional talent and learning, and so obstinately attached to their opinions and prejudices—which were diametrically opposed to the Christian faith—cast them aside in so short a time and, of their own accord and by their own judgment, embrace this faith, which at that time brought with it scarcely anything in this world except punishments and certain death? Is not the truth of the Christian religion demonstrated by this supreme miracle of divine providence no less certainly, plainly, and effectively than by any clearer argument devised by human intelligence? [Col. 0420B]

# CHAPTER V. The Arguments of the Pagans against the Truth of the Christian Religion Are Examined

## ARTICLE I. How Absurdly the Pagans Objected That the Christian Religion Was to Be Rejected Because It Was New, and That Ancestral and Hereditary Rites Were to Be Preserved—Rites Which They Themselves Had Altered or Abolished in the Classes of the People, in Observations of the Sky, in Obnunciations, Assemblies, Signals from the Citadel, Fetial Ceremonies, *Clarigatio*, Auspices from *Acumina* (“Points”), the Annarian, Cincian, and Censorial Laws, and the Inner Sanctuaries of *Coligo* [uncertain reading]

[Col. 0420C]

Although the pagans left no stone unturned and employed every engine in order to overthrow the arguments we have thus far adduced to establish the truth of the Christian religion, they nevertheless brought forward almost nothing except, as the saying goes, reheated cabbage: an objection frequently repeated, endlessly recited, and always overthrown. For they cried out that the Christians’ religion was new and had arisen scarcely a few days before, whereas their own, handed down to them by their parents from remote antiquity, could not justly and rightly be abandoned and repudiated by them:

> “You are accustomed,” Arnobius says, “to object to us that our religion is new, born scarcely a few days ago, and that you could not abandon the ancient religion of your country and be transferred to barbarous and foreign rites.” [Col. 0420D] (Arnobius, book II, p. 90.)

In the preceding dissertation we showed how this customary and now long-obsolete argument was pressed by the pagans and refuted by Minucius (*Dissertation on Minucius Felix*, chap. 14, arts. 1–2). But because it is overthrown in different ways by different authors, we must now investigate the arguments by which Arnobius destroys it.

He therefore makes plain how much futility and extreme frivolity this argument contains. For it is implanted and innate in the minds of all people that they should prefer and substitute good things for bad, and [Col. 0421A] useful things for useless (Arnobius, book II, p. 90). It is therefore not the change itself, but the reason for the change, that must be weighed. Yet the Gentiles could not deny that, from the most remote age of mankind onward, they had made very many alterations in both human and divine affairs. For in the earliest and most ancient centuries, our Author says, after grain and clothing had been discovered and the construction of houses devised, human beings abandoned the former use of acorns, arbute-berries, skins, huts, and caves. Here, indeed, he appears to have aimed at the verses of Juvenal, Lucretius, and other poets, which anyone may easily read in their books (Juvenal, satire 6, beginning; Lucretius, book V, lines 937 ff. and 957 ff.). Yet no one ever said that these changes [Col. 0421B] were bad or to be condemned.

Furthermore, if every alteration of ancient customs and rites is a crime, the Romans are undoubtedly guilty of this crime, as Arnobius proves by an enumeration that is brief, certainly, but may seem insufficiently clear to many (Arnobius, book II, p. 91). For this reason, the obscurities there must be explained in a few words.

First, then, he relates that the Roman people were once divided into five classes. How certain this is, and what those classes of the Roman people instituted by Servius Tullius were, we are taught by Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and Aulus Gellius. Some, however, judge that in the text of Gellius, as in that of our Arnobius, *six classes* should be read (Livy, book I, §43, and book IV, §4; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, [Col. 0421C] *Roman Antiquities*, book IV, p. 221 ff.; Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book X, chap. 28, p. 573). But Lipsius observes that the sixth class was formerly exempt and inactive (Lipsius, vol. III, *On the Roman Army*, book I, dialogue 2, p. 15). Whether this is sufficient to untie the knot of this difficulty must be left to the judgment of others. Whatever the case may be, it is sufficiently established that these classes were altered by the Romans.

Arnobius then continues:

> “Do you still have magistrates elected by the people? Do you know what the military, urban, and common assemblies are?” (Arnobius, book II, p. 91.)

He reproaches the Romans because these institutions had not merely been altered by them but almost consigned to oblivion. There were various kinds of assemblies: some, as Livy reports, were *curiate*, which dealt with military affairs; others were [Col. 0421D] *centuriate*, in which consuls and military tribunes were elected (Livy, book I, §60, and book V, §52). Dionysius of Halicarnassus clearly relates how these were first instituted and thereafter conducted under the consuls (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, book IV, p. 224, and book VII, p. 474 ff.). Aulus Gellius explains from Felix and Labeo what the curiate and centuriate assemblies were, as do Manutius and Nicolas Gruchius, who published books about them (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book IV, chap. 27; Manutius and Gruchius, vol. I, *Roman Antiquities*). Alexander ab Alexandro and Tiraquellus also make numerous observations about these assemblies; you may consult them, as well as many others (Alexander and Tiraquellus, *Genial Days*, book IV, chap. 3).

[Col. 0422A] Meanwhile, let us follow Arnobius:

> “Do you still make observations from the sky,” he says, “or do you render proceedings idle by obnunciations?”

To *observe* (*servare*) is to announce something on the basis of an observation of the sky. What *to obnunciate* (*obnuntiare*) means you may learn from these words of Donatus on Terence:

> “One who announces something bad *obnuntiates*; one who announces something good *annunciates*. For augurs are properly said to *obnuntiate* when they have seen something of evil omen and inauspicious. Thus I *obnuntiate* an impending evil, as though I were announcing an omen. From this, indeed, comes the etymology (*ἐτυμολογία*) of this word.” (Donatus on Terence, *The Brothers*, act 4, scene 4.)

Cicero uses both words, and the first quite frequently, especially where he writes the following to Atticus:

> “He announced that on every day appointed for assemblies he would make observations from the sky. . . . Yet the substance of the matter is this: had Gaius Appius not obstructed Milo by an adverse augury, [Col. 0422B] the assemblies would have taken place.” (Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, book IV, letter 3, p. 239, line 42.)

Elsewhere, speaking of auspices:

> “But as for observing the sky, do you suppose that those who took the auspices were not themselves accustomed to do it? Now they give orders to the keeper of the sacred chickens, and he reports back.” (Idem, *On Divination*, book II, p. 289, line 44.)

Before our Arnobius, however, Lucan complained in these verses about the complete neglect or obsolescence of that earlier custom (Lucan, book VI, lines 426 ff.):

> None cared to ask what the nurturing Dodona  
> Proclaimed from Jupiter’s mouth concerning the first fruits;  
> Who could learn fate from entrails, who disclose it through birds,  
> Who could observe the lightning of heaven  
> And scrutinize the stars with Assyrian care.

Arnobius continues:

> “When you prepare wars, do you display the signal from the citadel, or perform the fetial rites? Do you reclaim stolen property through *clarigatio*?”

Here he mentions three practices [Col. 0422C] for preparing or declaring war. First, there was the signal or standard displayed from the citadel, concerning which Virgil writes (*Aeneid*, book VIII, line 1):

> When Turnus raised from the Laurentian citadel  
> The signal for war . . .

For, as Servius remarks on this passage:

> “A standard was customarily placed on the citadel as a visible sign that an army had been levied.”

We also read the following concerning this custom in Festus (under the word *Justi*):

> “The thirty days during which the army had been levied and the standard placed on the citadel were called regular days.”

You will find more concerning this custom in Dio Cassius and Lipsius (Dio Cassius, book XXVII, p. 47; Lipsius, *On Rural Affairs*, book I, chap. 2, p. 18 ff.).

Second, Arnobius mentions the fetial law, because the fetials declared war in the name of the Roman people, as may be learned from Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, [Col. 0422D] Gellius, and Lactantius (Livy, book I, §§24 and 32; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book II, p. 130; Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book XVI, chap. 4; Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book VI, chap. 9, p. 572). Concerning these rites and the *clarigatio*, which our Author names in the third place, Servius writes the following in his already-cited commentary on Virgil:

> “When the Romans wished to declare war, the *pater patratus*, that is, the chief of the fetials, proceeded to the enemy’s borders and, after reciting certain solemn formulas, said in a loud voice that he was declaring war for specified reasons: either because they had injured Rome’s allies, or because they had returned neither the stolen animals”—or “the seized property,” as Arnobius says—“nor those liable to surrender. This was called *clarigatio* from the loudness (*claritas*) of the voice. After this *clarigatio*, [Col. 0423A] a spear was cast into their territory, and the beginning of hostilities was thereby declared.” (Servius on *Aeneid*, book IX, line 53.)

Yet, when commenting on the following book of Virgil, where he relates several similar matters, Servius adds:

> “*Clarigatio* is either named from the loud voice used by the *pater patratus*, or from *ἀπὸ τῆς κλήρου*, that is, ‘from the lot,’ for they invaded the enemy’s fields by the lot of war.” (Idem, on book X, line 14.)

Pliny, moreover, committed to writing the following information about *clarigatio* that bears upon our subject:

> “Whenever envoys were sent to the enemy to perform the *clarigatio*—that is, loudly to demand the return of property carried off—one of them was always called the *verbenarius*.” (Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXII, chap. 2, p. 179.)

Brissonius made further observations on *clarigatio* and the fetials, which it would by no means be a useless labor for you to read (Brissonius, *On Formulas*, book IV, p. 383 ff.).

[Col. 0423B] Arnobius proceeds:

> “When you enter the hazards of war, do you derive hope for the battle and take auspices from the points (*acumina*)?” (Arnobius, book II, p. 91.)

Cicero had previously reproached the Romans more than once for rashly altering these customs. His exact words are:

> “Our ancestors would not allow military affairs to be conducted without taking auspices. How many years has it now been since wars began to be conducted by propraetors and proconsuls, who possess no auspices? Accordingly, not all of them cross over after taking auspices, nor do they take auspices from the sacred feeding. As for those taken from points (*acumina*)—which are wholly a military form of auspice—even Marcus Marcellus, five times consul, omitted them altogether, though he was both a commander and an excellent augur.” (Cicero, *On Divination*, book II, p. 290, line 14.)

In another book he testifies that this practice had been omitted through the negligence of the nobility [Col. 0423C] (Idem, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, p. 215, line 5).

What these auspices taken from *acumina*—“points” or “tips”—actually were has not yet been sufficiently ascertained, and authors hold various opinions about them. Some suspect that in Cicero’s text *agminibus* (“battle-lines”) should be read in place of *acuminibus* (“points”). But every manuscript both of Cicero and of our Arnobius contradicts this exceedingly slight conjecture. For this reason, some think that the *acumina* were mountain peaks, which it was customary to climb in order to take auguries. Others understand them as the sharp points or beaks of birds, which were observed in connection with the *tripudium solistimum*, the favorable feeding-omen. Yet both opinions appear to contradict Cicero’s preceding words, in which he asserts that the auspice from *acumina* was wholly military.

Others therefore suppose that the points of javelins, darts, and swords are meant: if they glittered [Col. 0423D] with a certain awe-inspiring radiance, they foretold a happy outcome of the battle; but if they were blunt, dirty, or covered in rust, they foretold an unhappy one. They think it can be proved from the following words of Dionysius of Halicarnassus concerning the battle of the Romans against the Sabines that Arnobius had this in view:

> “From the javelins fixed in the ground before the tents—these are Roman weapons which they hurl when they first engage at close quarters—from these javelins, I say, flames blazed around the tips of their pointed heads, and throughout the entire camp there was a radiance, just as though from torches, which lasted far into the night. From this apparition they understood—as the interpreters of such prodigies declared, and as anyone could easily conjecture—that the deity portended for them a swift and splendid victory, since everything yields to fire and there is nothing that is not consumed by the force of fire.”

> [Col. 0424A] *Ἐκ τῶν καταπεπηγμένων παρὰ ταῖς σκηναῖς ὑσσῶν· ἔστι δὲ ταῦτα βέλη Ῥωμαίων, ἃ συνιόντες εἰς χεῖρας ἐξακοντίζουσι . . . ἐκ τούτων δὴ τῶν ὑσσῶν περὶ τοῖς ἄκροις τῶν ὀβελίσκων φλόγες ἀνήπτοντο, καὶ δι’ ὅλου τοῦ στρατοπέδου σέλας ἦν, ὥσπερ ἀπὸ λαμπάδων, καὶ κατέσχε τῆς νυκτὸς ἐπὶ πολύ· ἐκ τούτου κατέλαβον τοῦ φάσματος, ὥσπερ οἱ τερατοσκόποι ἀπέφαινον, καὶ πᾶσι ἀνθρώποις συμβάλλειν οὐ χαλεπὸν ἦν, ὅτι νίκην αὐτοῖς ταχεῖαν καὶ λαμπρὰν σημαίνει τὸ δαιμόνιον· ἐπειδήπερ ἅπαν εἴκει πυρί, καὶ οὐδὲν ὅ τι οὐχ ὑπὸ τοῦ πυρὸς διαφθείρεται.*  
> (“From the javelins fixed beside the tents—for these are Roman missiles, which they cast when they come to close combat . . . from these javelins flames were kindled around the tips of the little spikes, and a radiance spread throughout the whole camp as though from torches, lasting far into the night. From this apparition they understood—as the interpreters of prodigies declared, and as it was not difficult for anyone to infer—that the divine power signified for them a swift and brilliant victory, since everything yields to fire, and there is nothing that is not destroyed by fire.”)  
> (Dionysius, *Roman Antiquities*, book V, p. 3123.)

It is not altogether improbable that Arnobius had this ancient custom in view—if Dionysius had said that it was a solemn custom, and one as frequently as publicly practiced.

[Col. 0424B] Some, however, regard it as more probable that these were the points of military standards, which were mounted upon longer poles and terminated in an iron tip. For if, when the camp was moved, the standard-bearer easily pulled them from enemy soil, this furnished a favorable omen and the promise of certain victory; but if he extracted them only with difficulty, an adverse prediction was made and a by no means uncertain defeat was foreshown. Yet anyone inclined toward this opinion must certainly note that Servius attributes the following practice to the fetials:

> “After the thirty-third day from their demand that the enemy restore the property, the fetials cast a spear.” (Servius on *Aeneid*, book IX, line 53.)

Arnobius, however, plainly distinguishes this from the auspices taken from *acumina*. Consequently, if anyone prefers this last explanation, he must certainly say that Arnobius is speaking of commanders entering enemy territory, whom, as Servius observes there after Varro, “for the sake of the omen they sent into that territory first, to occupy a site for the camp.” [Col. 0424C] You may now consider and decide whether this opinion or another is to be preferred to the rest.

Arnobius proceeds, and thus rebukes the frivolity and inconstancy of the pagans:

> “When assuming offices, do you observe the Annarian laws; in gifts and presents, the Cincian laws; and in restraining expenditure, the Censorial laws?” (Arnobius, book II, p. 91.)

The Annarian law was so called because it had ordained that new magistrates be appointed every year (Festus, under *ANNARIA*). A similar protest by Cicero concerning the abolition of this law may be read alongside that of our Arnobius (Cicero, *Philippic* I, p. 565). But who, unless wholly a stranger and foreigner to Roman history, can fail to know how [Col. 0424D] often these laws were despised and ruined? See Robertellus, *On the Magistracies of the Empire* (Robertellus, vol. III, *Roman Antiquities*, p. 38).

The Cincian law was enacted by Marcus Cincius, tribune of the plebs, in the year of the city 549. By it, as Cornelius Tacitus says, provision had anciently been made that no one should receive money or a gift for pleading a case (Cornelius Tacitus, *Annals*, book I, near the beginning). It was undoubtedly concerning this law that Pliny wrote the following to Rufus:

> “Appended to the edict was this decree of the Senate: everyone who had any case was commanded, before proceeding with it, to swear that he had given, promised, or guaranteed nothing to anyone in return for legal advocacy. By these words, and a thousand more besides, the selling and purchasing of advocacy were forbidden. [Col. 0425A] Once the cases had been concluded, however, it permitted the giving of no more than ten thousand sesterces.” (Pliny, book V, final letter, to Rufus.)

Livy, moreover, writes:

> “What aroused the Cincian law concerning gifts and presents, unless it was because the commons had already begun to become tributary and liable to payment to the Senate?” (Livy, book XXXIV, §4.)

By the Censorial laws, which were also called sumptuary and dietary laws, the excessive expenditure and luxury of dinners and banquets were restrained. One of these was the law which Livy, just cited, records as having been proposed by Oppius, tribune of the plebs (ibid., §1). In addition, Aulus Gellius and Macrobius enumerate the Orchian, Fannian, Didian, Licinian, Cornelian, Sullan, Lepidan, Antian, and Julian laws, as well as the edict of the emperor Augustus—or of Tiberius, as Gellius notes (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book II, chap. 4; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book III, chap. 17). Suetonius, however, [Col. 0425B] writes that the sumptuary law was enacted or revised by Augustus. See the books on laws by Manutius and Antonius Augustinus (Suetonius, book II, *Augustus*, chap. 34; Manutius, *On Roman Laws*, chap. 18; Antonius Augustinus, *On Laws*, book I, chap. 18).

Before our Arnobius, however, Tertullian had interrogated the pagans who reproached Christianity for its novelty in these words:

> “Where have those laws gone which suppressed expenditure and ostentation? Those which commanded that no more than one hundred asses be entered for a dinner, and that no more than one hen be served, and that one not fattened? . . . For I see dinners costing hundreds—now to be reckoned not in hundreds of asses but in hundreds of thousands of sesterces—and whole mines of silver worked into serving-dishes; and it would be too little if these belonged merely to senators rather than to freedmen, or even to men still breaking the whips with which they were flogged.” (Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chap. 6.)

[Col. 0425C] But we shall discuss these matters in their proper place (*Dissertation on This Book*, chap. 19, art. 2).

After this Arnobius says:

> “Do you keep perpetual hearth-fires burning in your inner sanctuaries and *coligines*?” (Arnobius, book II, p. 91.)

Certain printed editions read: “in the inner sanctuaries of Vesta.” In the latest edition, however, the conjunction *and* was removed. But no one has told us by what authority these changes were made. Lipsius, having been alerted by Rosweyde, observes that a certain manuscript codex reads: “*In pene impenetralibus et colignis*” (Lipsius, *Treatise on Vesta and the Vestals*, vol. III, p. 619). The royal manuscript codex certainly has simply: “*Impenetralibus et colignis*.” It is therefore no wonder that this corrupt passage has greatly tormented learned men.

[Col. 0425D] Lipsius believes that it can be explained in two ways. First, these words of Arnobius are not to be referred to Vesta, but to a certain private rite by which fire was anciently preserved and tended in the innermost part of houses and in the kitchen. To confirm this conjecture he adduces these words of Varro: “It is called *culina* (‘kitchen’) because there they tended (*colebant*) the fire.”

Second, he says that the words can still be understood of the public Vesta, and that *in culignis* should be written there, so that Arnobius’s meaning would be that fire was formerly placed in *culignae*, or earthenware vessels, just as it is even now customarily preserved beneath ashes. But the first explanation is opposed by the fact that Varro is speaking of the ordinary and promiscuous use of fire, whereas Arnobius speaks either of sacred fire or at least of a fire whose use [Col. 0426A] the Gentiles had abolished. The second is opposed by the fact that, as Lipsius himself admits, the noun *culigna* in Varro, Festus, and Livy instead denotes a drinking vessel in which wine was offered at sacrifices. Furthermore, what purpose would the mention of Vesta serve there, when no trace of it appears in Arnobius’s text?

The entire difficulty of this obscure saying of Arnobius lies chiefly in the single word *coliginis*. For we learn from these verses of Catullus (*Epigram to Marcellus*), concerning Troy, that there were inner hearths:

> To which, it is said, the Greek youth then hastened together  
> From every side, abandoning their inner hearths.

Servius likewise observes that the *penetralia* in Virgil (*Aeneid*, book VI, line 71) mean the hidden recesses of temples, namely in this verse:

> [Col. 0426B] Great inner sanctuaries in our realms await you too.

And who would not readily persuade himself that perpetual hearth-fires existed in them?

It remains only, therefore, to determine whether some word should be restored in place of *coliginis*. But, you will ask, why not read *in culinis* (“in kitchens”)? For Vossius, following Scaliger, shows from an ancient inscription that there were kitchens in the shrines of Hercules, where those about to travel abroad offered sacrifice. That would perhaps be no bad conjecture, if you could prove that perpetual hearth-fires were once kept there. Yet may one not add in support of this conjecture that, as we shall say below, the pagans regarded the hearths of the *genii* as gods, and that for this reason fire was once preserved for their worship and honor in kitchens and hearths, as the cited [Col. 0426C] Varro noted—but that this custom, having become more troublesome and inconvenient to their descendants, was neglected by them?

There are, moreover, some who wish to retain the word *coliginis*, which they believe to be derived from the verb *colo*, that is, “I inhabit” (Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, pp. 270, 587, and 914). They have therefore thought that the word *coligo* signifies “house,” “dwelling,” or “habitation” in our Author. But the conjunction *and* would have to be removed from the text of Arnobius, and it would have to be proved by at least some example that anyone ever used the noun *coligo* in this sense. Consider, therefore, whether the word *culinis* (“kitchens”) seems to agree better with Arnobius’s purpose. For without the aid of some more accurate manuscript we do not venture to determine anything certain on the matter.

[Col. 0426D] Arnobius then continues:

> “Do you make your tables sacred by setting out saltcellars and images of the gods?” (Arnobius, book II, p. 91.)

The saltcellar was a small vessel in which salt was customarily placed for use at table and in sacrifice. Porphyrion, the ancient interpreter of Horace, says:

> “Properly speaking, the *salinum* is a small dish in which first fruits were offered to the gods with salt.” (Porphyrion on Horace, book II, ode 16.)

You plainly see why Arnobius called tables sacred on account of the setting out of this saltcellar.

How sacred and dear it was to the pagans you will undoubtedly learn from these words of Livy:

> “Those who have wives or daughters are to leave a single ounce by weight of gold for each; of silver, those who have sat in the curule chair; the trappings of a horse, and pounds by weight, so that they may possess a saltcellar and a small dish [Col. 0427A] for the sake of the gods.” [The supplied Latin is syntactically defective after “silver” and before “pounds by weight.”] (Livy, book XXVI, §36.)

Valerius Maximus, moreover, infers that there was silver in the homes of Gaius Fabricius and Quintus Aemilius Papus because each possessed a dish for the gods and a saltcellar (Valerius Maximus, book IV, chap. 4, §3, p. 217). Hence that irony of Persius (satire 3, line 25):

> You have a little meal and a pure, unstained saltcellar:  
> What need you fear? And a dish securely tending the hearth.

For more on the saltcellar, see Lipsius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chap. 2, vol. III, p. 484. Arnobius added “and images of the gods,” under whose protection, undoubtedly, either the sacred tables stood or those other tables at which the pagans reclined after first invoking the gods. Is not one of these gods the one of whom Statius sings (*Silvae*, book I, poem 6, *On Hercules the Protector*, line 31):

> [Col. 0427B] The genius and guardian of the chaste table.

And a little later (ibid., line 50):

> The Pellaean  
> Ruler shall possess it, a divinity revered at joyful tables.

Yet the pagans afterward rejected these practices as old women’s superstitions.

## ARTICLE II. On Other Changes Made by the Pagans in Arranging the Marriage-Couches of Brides and Invoking the *Genii* of Husbands; in Dressing the Brides’ Hair with a Celibate Spear; on Carrying Girls’ Little Togas to Maiden Fortune; on Women’s Wool-Working and Abstinence from Wine; on White Bulls Slain upon the Alban Mount; on Entrails Offered Thoroughly Cooked or Half Raw; and on the Sacrifice of Human Heads

Arnobius continues and censures other changes made by the pagans in matters likewise of no slight importance. [Col. 0427C] To expose their great inconstancy more and more, he addresses them as follows:

> “When you enter into marriage, do you spread the little couches with the toga and invoke the *genii* of the husbands?” (Arnobius, book II, p. 91.)

Those little couches, as Servius observes, “are properly the *genial couches* which are spread for girls who are marrying, so called from the begetting of children” (Servius on *Aeneid*, book VI, p. 431), or, as Festus says, “in honor of the *genius*” (Festus, under *GENIALIS*). For the pagans were persuaded, as Augustine records from Valerius Soranus (Augustine, *City of God*, book VII, chap. 13, p. 172), and as Servius notes, that each human being had been allotted his own *genius*, who also possessed the power of producing things. It was customary to sacrifice to this same *genius*, and also to Tellus and Juno, the guardians of these matters, as Servius further says [Col. 0427D] (Servius, loc. cit., pp. 440 and 323). They observed this especially in the solemnities of marriage, and then invoked the husband’s *genius*, so that the marriage might be happy and auspicious and children might be born. Hence Juvenal assails in these verses those who violated the genial bed—and undoubtedly the husband’s *genius* as well (Juvenal, satire 6, lines 21–22):

> It is an ancient and long-established practice, Postumus, to shake  
> Another man’s bed and despise the *genius* of the sacred frame.

Concerning the genial couch and the customary manner of spreading and adorning it, see Apuleius, Lipsius, and others (Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book X, near the end; Lipsius, *Electa*, book II, [Col. 0428A] chap. 17, p. 264, vol. I). But the pagans afterward scorned and repudiated these customs.

It was also an ancient custom of theirs, as Arnobius says (Arnobius, book II, p. 91), to stroke—or dress—the hair of women entering marriage “with the celibate spear” (*hasta caelibaris*); that is, as Plutarch writes (*Roman Questions*, p. 285), they parted it with the point of a spear, or with a curved spear, as Ovid sings (*Fasti*, book II, p. 497):

> Nor for you, who will seem ripe to an eager mother,  
> Shall the curved spear arrange your maiden hair.

Plutarch and Festus offer various explanations of this custom, whose alteration Arnobius noted; consult them (Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, p. 285; Festus, under the word *CAELIBARIS*).

Source/review notes: The supplied source itself ends in the middle of Horace’s quotation; the draft faithfully translates the surviving fragment and does not invent the missing continuation.

[Col. 0428B] It had also once become customary for girls to carry their little togas—these are Arnobius’s words—to Fortune of Maidenhood (*Fortuna Virginalis*) (Arnobius, book II, p. 91). Plutarch, whom we cited just above, has recorded that Servius, who was said to have exalted the divine power of Fortune more than anyone else, founded various temples for her, one of which was dedicated to the Fortune of the Maiden, “another to the Maiden” (ἄλλο Παρθένου) (Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, p. 281). Elsewhere he says: “At the spring called Mossy there is still a shrine of the Fortune of the Maiden” (Παρθένου Τύχης ἱερὸν ἔστι) (the same author, *On the Fortune of Rome*, p. 322 ff.). This is thought to be the goddess of whom our Author speaks. Nor are there lacking those who think that she is the same as the goddess called *Virginensis* by Augustine, whom it was customary to invoke [Col. 0428C] when the girdle of a newly married virgin was loosened (Augustine, book IV of *The City of God*, ch. 11, p. 97).

Matrons, moreover, as Arnobius goes on to say, once worked in the atria of their houses and were commanded to abstain from wine (Arnobius, book II, p. 91). He adds that, in order to verify this abstinence, their relations by marriage and blood relatives had the right to kiss them. That women not merely of the lowest but even of the highest rank devoted themselves to wool-working and the making of clothes is clear from what Suetonius relates concerning Augustus Caesar: “He rarely wore any clothing other than that made at home, produced by his wife, sister, daughter, and granddaughters” (Suetonius, book II, *Life of Augustus*, ch. 73). Earlier, however—and this is more pertinent to our purpose—he had said of Augustus: “He brought up his daughter and granddaughters in such a way that he even accustomed them to wool-working, and forbade them to say or do anything except openly and of such a kind that it could be entered in the daily [Col. 0428D] records” (the same author, ch. 64). It was doubtless for this reason that Virgil sang in the following verses of Aeneas’s cloak woven by Dido:

> And the cloak hanging down from his shoulders  
> Glowed with Tyrian purple—a rich gift that Dido  
> Had made, interweaving the fabric with fine gold.

(Virgil, book IV of the *Aeneid*, lines 262 ff.)

In the preceding book he mentions a Phrygian cloak woven by Andromache’s own hands and given to Ascanius with these words:

> Take these things also, boy, that they may be  
> Memorials to you of my hands, and bear witness  
> To Andromache’s enduring love.

(The same author, book III, lines 486 f.)

Finally, to omit many other examples, Alexander the Great is said to have told Sisygambis, the mother of King Darius: [Col. 0429A] “Mother, you see that this garment which I am wearing is not only the gift but also the handiwork of my sisters.” Arnobius accordingly censures those matrons who no longer performed any wool-work in the atria of their houses. Tiraquellus has more on these matters, and you may consult him if you wish (Quintus Curtius, book V, well after the beginning; Tiraquellus, on law 10, *Connubium*, § 38 ff., pp. 202 ff.).

Dionysius of Halicarnassus attests that Romulus forbade women the use of wine. Polybius, Plutarch, Pliny, and Gellius observe that, in order to test whether they had drunk wine, it was laid down—as Arnobius says—that their relatives should kiss them. Tertullian, moreover, as we shall show in the proper place, reproaches the pagans for having abolished this custom requiring women to abstain from wine (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book II of *Roman Antiquities*, [Col. 0429B] pp. 95 f.; Polybius in Athenaeus, book X of the *Deipnosophists*, pp. 440 ff.; Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, p. 265; Pliny, book XIV of *Natural History*, ch. 13, p. 142; Gellius, book X of *Attic Nights*, ch. 23; Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 6, p. 7; *Dissertation on Tertullian*, ch. 18, art. 5).

Arnobius presses the matter further and objects against the pagans that, although in ancient times they had been permitted to sacrifice only white bulls on Mount Albanus, it was later prescribed by a decree of the Senate that reddish ones should thereafter be slaughtered. Livy relates that, under Tullus, king of the Romans, stones rained down on Mount Albanus, and then, he says, “They seemed to hear a mighty voice from the summit, commanding the Albans to perform their rites according to their ancestral custom—rites which they had consigned to oblivion, as though they had abandoned their gods together with their homeland” (Arnobius, book II, p. 91; Livy, book I, ch. 31). Elsewhere he represents Camillus [Col. 0429C] as addressing these words to the Romans: “See what a difference there is between us and our ancestors. They left us certain rites to be performed on Mount Albanus and at Lavinium” (the same author, book V, ch. 52). We also read it recorded by Dionysius of Halicarnassus (book IV, p. 250) that, so that the treaty made by Tarquin with the Volscians and Hernici might be perpetual, it was unanimously decreed that festivals should be celebrated every year on the high mountain overlooking Alba, where rites were to be performed for Jupiter Latiaris and a bull was to be slain as the common victim of them all. Does Arnobius not imply that this bull had been white and complain of the alteration of this rite?

He accuses the same pagans of another change in these words: “When, during the reigns of Romulus and Pompilius, the entrails were offered to the gods thoroughly cooked and steeped in moisture, did you not, under King Tullus, begin to offer them half-raw and only lightly heated?” (Arnobius, book II, p. 91). Yet Livy, immediately after describing Scipio’s prayers, added: “After these prayers, when the victim had been slain, he offered its raw entrails into the sea, as was customary” (Livy, book XXIX, ch. 27). And Virgil:

> The entrails  
> I shall offer into the salt waves.

(Virgil, book IV of the *Aeneid*, line 133.)

We note these passages because they concern the entrails of victims and because both writers use the verb *porricere* in the sense of “to sacrifice.” Macrobius has more on this verb, and you may read him (Macrobius, book II of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 2). [Col. 0430A] From the cited words of Livy you will understand that the Romans offered or sacrificed entrails neither thoroughly cooked, as under Romulus and Pompilius, nor half-raw, as under Tullus, but completely raw.

Finally, Arnobius says: “Before the arrival of Hercules in Italy, when, at Apollo’s prompting, supplication was made to Father Dis and to Saturn with human heads, you similarly changed this custom by a clever deception and an ambiguity of words” (Arnobius, book I, p. 91). Macrobius reveals and explains this entire deception in the following words:

“When for a long time they believed that they appeased Dis with human heads and Saturn with male victims, on account of the oracle which ran:

> And send heads to Hades [variant: to the son of Cronus], and lights to the Father.  
> Καὶ κεφαλὰς ἵδῃ (al. Κρονίδῃ) καὶ τῷ πατρὶ πέμπετε φῶτα.

Hercules, they say, when subsequently returning to Italy [Col. 0430B] with Geryon’s cattle, persuaded their descendants to replace ill-omened sacrifices with auspicious ones: they brought to Dis not human heads but *oscilla*, artistically fashioned in the likeness of human beings, and honored Saturn’s altars not by slaughtering men but by lighting lamps, because φῶτα means not only ‘men’ but also ‘lights’” (Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 2, p. 207).

Not content to have said this once, he repeats it later in the same book (the same author, ibid., ch. 11, p. 225).

Lactantius, however, who noted the ambiguous meaning of this word (Lactantius, book VI of the *Divine Institutes*, ch. 2, p. 546), relates the story somewhat differently, as does Dionysius of Halicarnassus. For they, like Ovid as cited by Lactantius himself, make mention only of Saturn; nevertheless, the argument of Arnobius, and its force and weight, always remain [Col. 0430C] unshaken (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I of *Roman Antiquities*, p. 30; Lactantius, book I, ch. 21, p. 114; Ovid, book V of the *Fasti*, p. 642).

Who, then, does not see from what has thus far been discussed how absurdly the pagans reproached Christians with the novelty of their religion and with altering antiquity, when they themselves stood accused of so many and such great changes in both human and divine affairs? Indeed, as Tertullian rightly argues—and as we shall observe in the proper place (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 6, p. 7; *Dissertation on This Book*, ch. 18, arts. 1 ff.)—in clothing, food, furnishings, property, and even speech, they had renounced their forefathers; and with astonishing fickleness they praised the institutions of their ancestors which they themselves despised and no longer observed. In like [Col. 0430D] manner, Ambrose turns back upon the pagan Symmachus himself, and upon the other pagans, the weapon that Symmachus had hurled (Ambrose, letter 18, pp. 837 ff., vol. II). But our Arnobius crushes and restrains their insolent obstinacy with still other arguments. Let us therefore, if you please, hear and follow him.

## ARTICLE III

The same argument of the pagans is further weakened by the fact that, just as the Christian religion had a beginning in time, so too did disciplines, arts, and sciences; and in particular haruspicy began after Tages—where the Acherontic books are discussed—and astrology after Theuth and Atlas, the prop and supporting column of heaven; likewise because the gods were born; because things ancient were once new; because the religion of the Romans did not exist before two thousand years ago, just as the Christian religion did not exist before four hundred years ago—where the first kings of the Latins are discussed; and finally because Christians worship nothing new.

[Col. 0431A]

Because the pagans never ceased objecting to the novelty of the Christian religion, Arnobius, in order, if possible, to stop their mouths completely, further makes it plain that, even if this were true, nothing could ever be inferred from it in their favor or against the Christians. For what is there, he asks, in human affairs, arts, disciplines, and sciences that did not at some time have a beginning and origin? Before the Etruscan Tages, Arnobius says, no one either knew or cared to know [Col. 0431B] “whether anything was signified by the fall of thunderbolts or by the veins of entrails” (Arnobius, book II, p. 92). Tages, according to Festus (Festus, under the word *TAGES*), was said to be the son of a Genius and grandson of Jupiter, who, while still a boy, gave the discipline of haruspicy to the twelve peoples of Etruria. Cicero handed down the following account of him to posterity:

“A certain Tages is said suddenly to have emerged in the territory of Tarquinii while the earth was being plowed and the furrow had been driven unusually deep, and to have addressed the man who was plowing. This Tages, according to the books of the Etruscans, is said to have appeared in the form of a boy but to have possessed the wisdom of an old man. When the plowman was astounded by the sight of him and raised a loud cry of amazement, people rushed together, and in a short time all Etruria assembled at [Col. 0431C] that place. Then Tages spoke at length in the hearing of many, who took down all his words and committed them to writing. His entire discourse contained the discipline of haruspicy; this was later enlarged by the discovery of new matters and their being referred back to those same principles” (Cicero, book II of *On Divination*, pp. 285 f.).

Ovid sang of this in the following verses:

> The Tyrrhenian plowman saw, amid the fields,  
> A fateful clod first move of its own accord,  
> With no one stirring it; then soon assume  
> A human shape and cast away the form of earth,  
> And open newborn lips to tell of coming fates.  
> The natives called him Tages, who was first  
> To teach the Etruscan people to disclose  
> The events that were to come.

(Ovid, book XV of the *Metamorphoses*, lines 553 ff.)

[Col. 0431D] Lucan, however, says:

> May the gods favor what has been seen,  
> And let no trust be placed in entrails; rather,  
> Let Tages, founder of the art, have invented these things,  
> As thus the Etruscan, wrapping everything in obscurity  
> And hiding much beneath ambiguity, used to prophesy.

(Lucan, book I, lines 635 ff.)

Servius, in his notes on Virgil (Servius, on book II of the *Aeneid*, p. 259), proves from verses of Lucretius that haruspicy was discovered by Tages in Etruria. You see, therefore, that this Tages—whom some report to have been an obscure man, others a plowman—is not without reason called the inventor in Etruria of haruspicy, which we have discussed elsewhere (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 2, ch. 21, art. 1, p. 1187).

Someone, however, may perhaps ask us whether [Col. 0432A] the books which Cicero calls the books of the Etruscans are the same as those called by Arnobius a little earlier the Acherontic books, when he said: “Etruria promises in the Acherontic books” (Arnobius, book II, p. 87). For Servius, in his commentary on the same Virgil (Servius, on book VIII of the *Aeneid*, p. 511), observes that Tages is said “to have composed books on haruspicy and Acherontic rites.” By these words he certainly appears to distinguish these works of Tages. But whether they were the same or different, Arnobius’s opinion is certainly sufficiently confirmed by this observation.

He adds: “When did knowledge of the movements of the stars or of the system of genethlialogy begin? Was it not after the Egyptian Theuth, or after Atlas, as some report—that bearer, carrier, prop, and supporting column of heaven?” [Col. 0432B] (Arnobius, book II, p. 92). We have discussed both Theuth and Atlas elsewhere (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 543, 1131, and 1188). There we observed that some ascribe to Atlas the invention of the former science, namely the movements of the stars, while others ascribe to him the first observation of the genethliacal system, that is, of birthdays.

Accordingly, we shall note only that by these four epithets—bearer, carrier, prop, and supporting column of heaven—Arnobius signifies one and precisely the same thing. For *tibicen* (“prop”), according to Paulus (in Festus, under the word *TIBICINES*), is sometimes used for a pillar or support by which some building, house, or other structure is upheld. Juvenal certainly used it in this sense:

> We inhabit a city supported by a slender prop.

[Col. 0432C] (*Satires* 3, line 293.)

Ovid likewise:

> She was only just sweeping the villa, which stood supported by a prop.

(Ovid, book IV of the *Fasti*, p. 598.)

The noun *destina* (“supporting column”) is used with the same meaning by Corippus the African in this verse:

> And Thomas, the supporting column of tottering Libya.

(Corippus, book I of *In Praise of the Emperor Justin*.)

Some cite in this connection the following words of Isidore of Seville: “The ruin of adultery is received by the supporting column of marriage” (Isidore, book II of the *Sentences*, ch. 40, p. 449). But printed editions read *destinatione*; some manuscripts have *conditione*, and others *doctrina*. Therefore, we do not think that this passage of Isidore should be pressed further than is proper.

[Col. 0432D] Arnobius, however, admits that these matters are slight and presses far weightier arguments against the pagans. For although the pagans proclaimed certain gods immortal (Arnobius, book II, pp. 92–93)—Jupiter and his brothers, Juno, Liber, Venus, Diana, Minerva, Apollo, and others—they nevertheless acknowledged that all these had at some time begun to exist and had been begotten by others, as will be stated below (below, ch. 9, arts. 3 ff.). What, then, could be more absurd and unjust than for the novelty of the Christian religion to be censured by men who were compelled to recognize and confess that same novelty among themselves?

But the pagans insisted that their own religion was extremely ancient, while that of the Christians was new and recent. Arnobius replies that nothing is more frivolous [Col. 0433A] or feeble than this argument (Arnobius, book II, pp. 93–94). For if what Christians do is new, it will become old, just as what is old among the pagans was once new. What of the fact that a religion must be judged not by the time at which it began, but by God himself, whom it worships (ibid., p. 94)?

The pagans, therefore, must no longer be heard shouting again that before four hundred years ago there had been no profession of Christianity. For who does not see that this claim has already been completely overthrown by what has been said? Accordingly, our Author replies only by way of superabundance that two thousand years earlier—as it was very easy to prove—none at all of the gods of those same pagan Romans or Latins had existed.

[Col. 0433B] For Saturn, the son of Heaven and Hecate, begot Jupiter and Picus; Picus begot Faunus, and Faunus Latinus (ibid.). How true this is may be gathered from various writers, and especially from these verses of Virgil:

> King Latinus, now advanced in age,  
> Ruled the fields and peaceful cities in long-lasting peace.  
> We learn that he was born to Faunus and the Laurentian nymph Marica;  
> Faunus’s father was Picus, and he traces his parentage  
> To you, Saturn: you are the ultimate source of his bloodline.

(Virgil, book VII of the *Aeneid*, lines 45 ff.)

Yet, as Arnobius argues, no more than a span of 360 years of time and life can be granted to these three men—Picus, Faunus, and Latinus. There can be no doubt that he extended this [Col. 0433C] interval beyond what was necessary, lest the pagans dare utter a word in reply. For in Eusebius’s *Chronicle* it is reduced far more, in these words (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, books I and II, at the year 838): “Aeneas was the first king of the Latins after the capture of Troy. Before him Janus, Saturn, Picus, and Faunus reigned for approximately 150 years”; that is, no fewer than 150 years less than Arnobius gratuitously conceded to the pagans. On these first kings of the Latins, see Dionysius of Halicarnassus, the Author of *The Origin of the Roman People*, Lactantius, Augustine, and others (Dionysius, book I of *Roman Antiquities*, pp. 24 and 34; Author of *Origins*, p. 596; Lactantius, book I, ch. 22, p. 127; Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, ch. 15, p. 499).

Arnobius continues that Ascanius and his other [Col. 0433D] successors reigned at Alba for nearly 420 years (Arnobius, book II, p. 94; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, at the end). In Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, however, 452 years are counted, and Clement of Alexandria counts 422. Finally, from the founding of Rome to his own age, our Author reckons approximately 1,050 years, while the author of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* says that 1,146 had elapsed. We also made some observations on all these matters in the chronology of Clement of Alexandria. But there is no need to pursue them more fully or to name numerous other chronographers individually. Arnobius does not follow a method of chronological computation exact in every detail; rather, content to cite the very writers of annals accepted by the pagans themselves, he concedes to them even more than they could have desired. From these facts, therefore, he demonstrates with the utmost clarity that their gods had not existed two thousand years earlier and that they could not justly [Col. 0434A] reproach the Christian religion for its novelty.

What of the fact, Arnobius continues (Arnobius, book II, p. 95), that the greatest pagan mysteries, customarily celebrated in honor of Serapis, Isis, the Mother of the Gods, and others—matters which we have treated elsewhere (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 758 f.; *Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 17, art. 1, and ch. 20, arts. 1–2), and which must still be treated below—are far more recent than their gods? Therefore, if those same pagans had wished to remain consistent with their own principles, these mysteries ought never to have been admitted by them, but always rejected.

“But at least,” the pagans said, “it follows most clearly from what has been conceded that the religion of our gods is far older than the Christian religion, and therefore truer.” [Col. 0434B] Arnobius first denies the inference. For it is enough that both religions began at some time for the reasoning to be equal on both sides. What contribution can two thousand years, when compared with all the ages that had elapsed before them, make toward the truth of any religion?

He then emphatically denies that Christians worship anything new or more recent than the religion of the pagans (Arnobius, book II, p. 95). For they worship God almighty, who is not only most ancient but also unbegotten and eternal, and the source and origin of all things. Christians therefore introduced nothing new into the world, but only what they had learned late from Christ, who dispelled the wretched blindness of human beings who worshiped false gods and did not know the true God.

Arnobius did not set forth more there concerning the other [Col. 0434C] doctrines of the Christian religion, both because what he had said was entirely sufficient to repel the accusation of a new religion and because a little earlier he had demonstrated the supreme divinity of Christ, while elsewhere he demonstrates other tenets of that same Christian religion, as we shall show later.

## CHAPTER VI

Another argument of the pagans against the Christian religion, drawn from public calamities, is answered.

## ARTICLE I

The pagans’ argument against the truth of the Christian religion, drawn from the various disasters and calamities by which the human race was formerly afflicted, is set forth; and it is shown by which writers it was formerly dissolved and refuted.

[Col. 0434D]

Another argument against the truth of the Christian religion, repeated by the pagans very often and to the point of nausea, was the notorious and utterly absurd slander by which they proclaimed, as Arnobius writes (Arnobius, book I, pp. 1 ff.), with equal falsity and audacity, that Christians—because they had rejected and repudiated the worship of the gods—were the cause of all the public disasters and calamities by which the human race was afflicted. For, as they boasted, the gods, justly angered by the impiety of the Christians, had entirely abandoned their care of earthly affairs, and all the evils by which people everywhere were accustomed to be consumed and oppressed had therefore been brought upon the whole world.

If you wish to know how frequent this complaint [Col. 0435A] and accusation of the pagans was, listen, if you please, to Tertullian:

“The pagans conspire in hatred of the good and upright, and clamor for innocent blood, putting forward, of course, in defense of their hatred that further absurdity that they consider Christians the cause of every public disaster and every misfortune of the people. If the Tiber rises to the walls, if the Nile does not rise over the fields, if the sky stands still, if the earth moves, if there is famine, if pestilence—at once the cry is: ‘The Christians to the lion!’ So many to one?”

(Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 40, p. 36.)

He repeats the same things in his book *To the Nations* (the same author, book I of *To the Nations*, ch. 9, p. 54). But we must say more about him in the proper place.

Origen likewise attests that the pagans abused this same [Col. 0435B] false accusation both in earlier times and still in his own:

“When these things happen to the world, it follows that, because people are abandoning the worship of the gods, they say that wars, famines, and pestilences occur because of the multitude of Christians. For the pagans, and all who thought as the nations do, have frequently blamed Christians for famine; and they have also attributed the causes of pestilences to the Church of Christ. We know that in our own region an earthquake occurred in certain places and that some buildings collapsed, so that the impious who were outside the faith said that the Christians were the cause of the earthquake. On this account the Churches suffered persecutions and were burned. Nor did they alone say this; even those who appeared wise said such things publicly: that the most severe [Col. 0435C] earthquakes occur because of the Christians.”

(Origen, Tractate 28 on Matthew, vol. II, p. 88.)

Lactantius is another witness that the pagans sang the same refrain even in his time, when he turned their accusation concerning public disasters and miseries back upon them in this way:

“Learn that all evils grow heavier upon human affairs daily for this reason: because God, the maker and governor of this world, has been abandoned; because impious religions have been adopted, contrary to divine law; and finally because you do not permit God to be worshiped even by a few.”

(Lactantius, book V, ch. 8, pp. 479 f.)

For if he alone were worshiped, with his laws observed, as is right, there would not be, he says, dissensions, wars, frauds, robberies, adulteries, and the other evils by which the human race destroys itself.

We have noted what Emperor Maximinus, [Col. 0435D] most hostile to Christians, replied to the unjust petitions of the cities against them (*Dissertation on Lucius Caecilius*, ch. 13, art. 3, p. 346). Yet in the letter he wrote to those cities, according to Eusebius, he boldly asserted that the harsher calamities:

> occurred because of the ruinous error of the utterly empty vanity of those lawless men, at the time when that error was rampant in their souls and, one might almost say, overwhelmed the whole inhabited world everywhere with shameful deeds.  
> Διὰ τὴν ὀλέθριον πλάνην τῆς ὑποκένου ματαιότητος τῶν ἀθεμίτων ἀνθρώπων ἐκείνων ἐγένετο, ἡνίκα κατὰ τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν ἐπεπόλαζε, καὶ σχεδὸν εἰπεῖν τὰ πανταχοῦ τῆς οἰκουμένης αἰσχύναις ἐπίεξε.

“They occurred because of the pestilential error of the utterly empty vanity of those wicked men, at the time when that error sprouted in their minds and filled almost the whole world with disgrace and dishonor” (Eusebius, book II of *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 7, p. 353).

[Col. 0436A] Later still, Symmachus did not hesitate to attribute the barrenness of the earth and the public famine to the denial of the privileges of the Vestal Virgins and pagan priests:

“Let no one think that I defend only the cause of religions: from deeds of this kind have arisen all the misfortunes of the Roman race. . . . Public famine followed this act, and a sickly harvest disappointed the hope of all the provinces. These are not defects of the soil. . . . The year withered because of sacrilege; for it was necessary that everything should perish which was denied to the religions.”

(In Ambrose, vol. II, pp. 831 ff.)

How frequent, nearly daily, and long-lasting that foolish complaint of the pagans was may further be inferred from the fact that they always had it on their lips from the beginning of the Christian religion down to Augustine’s time. [Col. 0436B] Listen, I ask you, to that holy teacher himself:

“When you hear blasphemers babbling and saying that afflictions abound in Christian times—for you know that they love to say this—and the proverb, though old, began in Christian times: ‘God does not send rain—go after the Christians.’ Although earlier people said this, people now say it even when God sends rain: ‘Go after the Christians.’”

(Augustine, on the title of Psalm 80, § 1, p. 857.)

He not only pursues this subject more fully there but also repeats it in another book in the following manner:

“Remember that, in recounting these things, I am still arguing against the ignorant, from whose ignorance arose that common proverb as well: ‘If rain is lacking, the Christians are the cause.’ For there are some who, educated in their liberal studies, are fond of history, from which [Col. 0436C] they know these things very easily; but in order to make the ignorant masses extremely hostile to us, they pretend not to know them and strive to confirm among the common people the claim that the disasters by which the human race must be afflicted at fixed intervals of place and time occur because of the Christian name, which is spreading throughout the world with immense renown and most illustrious celebrity in opposition to their gods.”

(The same author, book II of *The City of God*, ch. 3, p. 33.)

To repel and utterly suppress this importunate and false accusation, repeated by them so long and so often, the most learned defenders of our religion repeatedly published both treatises and books. For when Demetrianus barked that Christians were the cause of public calamities, Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, at first thought that his clamorous cries [Col. 0436D] and foolish reproaches ought to be despised. Yet, like our Arnobius (Arnobius, book I, p. 1), lest it be said that he had been overcome by the clamor of a man impiously railing against God and that the Christians had lost their case, he restrained that man’s utterly senseless rashness by publishing a treatise against him. At the beginning of this work he speaks as follows:

“But since you say that very many complain that wars arise more frequently, that pestilence and famine rage, that long stretches of clear weather hold back showers and rains, and that this is imputed to us, it is no longer right to remain silent. Otherwise, the fact that we are silent may begin to be regarded not as modesty but as lack of confidence, and while we disdain to refute the accusations, we may appear to acknowledge the charge. I therefore reply [Col. 0437A] both to you, Demetrianus, and to the others whom you have perhaps stirred up against us—sowing hatred by your slanderous words and making many companions for yourself, shoots sprung from your own root and origin—although I believe that they will nevertheless admit the reasonableness of our discourse.”

(Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 186.)

Augustine, of whom we spoke a little earlier, openly declares that for the same reason he composed his books *The City of God*, in the first five of which he expressly refutes this slander of unbelieving men. These are his own words on the subject:

“Meanwhile Rome was overthrown by an incursion of the Goths, acting under King Alaric, and by the force of a great disaster. The worshipers of many false gods, whom by customary usage we call pagans, attempted to attribute its overthrow [Col. 0437B] to the Christian religion and began to blaspheme the true God more bitterly and harshly than usual. Therefore, burning with zeal for the house of God, I undertook to write the books *The City of God* against their blasphemies and errors. . . . Of these books, the first five refute those who desire human affairs to prosper in such a way that they consider the worship of the many gods whom pagans have customarily worshiped necessary for this purpose, and contend that because this worship is prohibited, these evils arise and abound.”

(Augustine, book II of the *Retractions*, ch. 43.)

Nor was it enough for Augustine to have composed these books, excellent and outstanding though they were: he also impelled Orosius to write annals by which he might demonstrate publicly [Col. 0437C] that throughout every age of the centuries, and before the rise of the Christian religion, the world had suffered public calamities and human beings had been afflicted by common disasters, miseries, and hardships. Orosius himself states this in the preface to his histories. Since it would take too long to transcribe his words in full here, we have thought it preferable to direct every curious reader to his books. Before Orosius and Augustine, however, our Arnobius, in the books with which we are dealing, undertook—as we noted above—to suppress this same pagan slander fully and completely. Let us now therefore see, if you please, what his arguments are and how strong they are.

## ARTICLE II

The individual arguments of Arnobius are examined, by which he utterly overthrows the absurd accusations of the pagans, who never ceased proclaiming that Christians were the cause of all public disasters and calamities; and it is shown how clearly he demonstrates that from the very beginning of the Christian religion down to his own age nothing had changed contrary to the fixed laws of nature, either in heaven or on earth; but that before Christian times nations had often been consumed by famine, and destructive hailstorms, showers of stones, dried-up rivers, most deadly plagues, crops consumed by mice and locusts, and the greatest chasms and earthquakes had occurred.

[Col. 0437D]

Arnobius candidly admits that the pagans’ argument would be truly weighty and of the greatest importance, that Christians ought to be held in universal hatred, and that their religion should even be rejected and exterminated, if they were the cause of public evils and all calamities. But he demonstrates first that this is utterly false (Arnobius, book I, pp. 2–3), because from the very beginning of the [Col. 0438A] Christian religion down to his own age nothing had changed contrary to the fixed laws of nature: neither in the elements; nor in the course of the sun, moon, and stars; nor in the four seasons of the year; nor in the customary fertility of the earth and animals; nor in public human affairs and disciplines. Yet perhaps many would think that he had amplified the earlier public calamities a little too much by a rhetorical figure, had he not doubtless been persuaded that the slander so often repeated by the pagans, as we have said, had to be refuted by so many examples that they would be driven to silence, or at least to shame. Tertullian therefore likewise spends much time on a long enumeration of those same disasters that occurred before the birth of Christ, and afterward concludes, just as our Author does:

“If we compare the disasters of former times, lighter ones occur now, since the world received Christians from God. For from that time innocence has tempered the iniquities of the age, and intercessors before God have begun to exist.”

(Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 40.)

But he treats these matters—we shall discuss him in the proper place—more fully in another book (the same author, *On the Pallium*, ch. 27).

The pagans nevertheless objected: “The gods bring pestilences,” [Col. 0438B] these are Arnobius’s words, “and droughts, wars, scarcity of crops, locusts, mice, hailstorms, and other harmful things by which human affairs are assailed, because they have been provoked by the wrongs and offenses of Christians” (Arnobius, book I, p. 3). But this reasoning seemed to Arnobius so slight and trivial that he was entirely persuaded that it collapsed of itself without any refutation. For how, he asks, could the pagans have learned the names of these calamities after the beginning of the Christian religion unless they had occurred previously? And that all of them had indeed occurred earlier is demonstrated most clearly from the annals of those same pagans. He shows this by enumerating those disasters, just as Augustine did later (Augustine, book III of *The City of God*, ch. 17, pp. 73 ff.). We have already observed that Orosius, at Augustine’s urging, published seven books of histories to make this manifest to everyone. How correctly Orosius proved it will, God willing, be examined by us later in the proper place. Meanwhile, we must explain more clearly those matters which Arnobius does not set forth with sufficient clarity.

[Col. 0438D] He first relates that nations were often consumed by famine. Yet there is no one who does not know how many and how great examples of famine occur in the histories of the pagans. If you wish a few to be produced from among the many, then, passing over the famine in the time of the patriarch Joseph (Genesis, chs. 41 ff.), you will learn from Livy that, during the consulship of Proculus Geganius Macerinus and Lucius Menenius Lanatus, there was so great a famine and scarcity of grain that “many of the common people, having abandoned hope, wrapped their heads and threw themselves into the Tiber rather than prolong their lives in torment” (Livy, book IV, ch. 12). Augustine therefore aptly asks the pagans where at that time were the gods who gave no aid to people most devoted to their worship (Augustine, book III of *The City of God*, ch. 17, p. 74). Dionysius of Halicarnassus likewise writes, on the testimony of Herodotus, that when one part [Col. 0439A] of the Maeonians had long suffered from famine and were at last excessively oppressed by it, they departed from their ancestral fields and came to Umbria (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I of *Roman Antiquities*, p. 21). Finally, to omit further examples, in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, at the year 2022, the eighth year after the birth of Christ, it is noted that “so great a famine arose at Rome that five *modii* were sold for twenty-seven and a half denarii.” At that time the Christian name had not yet been heard either there or elsewhere.

Arnobius next objects that very frequent hailstorms, and even showers of stones, had occurred earlier. Horace certainly sang in the following verses of many storms, and specifically of an altogether dreadful hailstorm, which he believed had arisen not to avenge anything done by Christians but to avenge Caesar, slain by pagans:

[Col. 0439B]

> Already enough snow and dreadful hail  
> Upon the earth—
[…] of hail the Father sent; and, with his glowing

Right hand, having hurled [thunderbolts] at the sacred citadels,

He terrified the world, etc. (Horace, Book I, Ode 2.)

Arnobius then says: “In the ancient records, we see it included and set down that showers of stones have often shattered entire regions” (Arnobius, Book I, p. 4). Yet Cicero records showers of stones before Christian times: “What of the fact,” he says, “that a shower of stones has often fallen, sometimes of blood, occasionally of earth, and once even of milk?” (Cicero, Book II, *On Divination*, p. 271). Livy, moreover, relates that after the disaster at Cannae it rained stones: [Col. 0439C] “There were dreadful storms,” he says. “On the Alban Mount it rained stones continuously for two days. Many things were struck from heaven: two temples on the Capitol, the rampart in the camp at many points above Suessula; and two sentries were killed; at Cumae the wall and certain towers were not only struck by thunderbolts but even demolished. At Reate, a huge rock was seen flying through the air; the sun was redder than usual and resembled blood” (Livy, Book XXV, ch. 7). He also attests that the Sibylline books were consulted because stones had fallen from the sky more frequently than once in the same year. A little earlier he had said that a nine-day religious observance was held because stones had fallen from the sky. If you desire more, consult Tibullus, Valerius Maximus, Strabo, Solinus, and Salmasius’s annotations on the latter’s book [Col. 0439D] (Livy, Book XXIX, ch. 10; Tibullus, Book II, Elegy 5, v. 68; Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 6, § 5; Strabo, Book IV, *Geography*, p. 82 ff.; Solinus, ch. 2, p. 12).

To these things our author adds: “Mighty rivers have dried up when their beds became parched” (Arnobius, Book II, p. 4). Virgil, among others, certainly confirms this in the following verses:

You may see even the rivers dry;

The field is parched, and the dying grass thirsts through the corruption of the air.  
(Virgil, *Eclogue* 7, v. 56 ff.)

Most pertinent to our purpose, however, is the fact that Seneca attributes the drying-up of rivers not to the impiety of Christians, as other pagans did, but to natural causes (Seneca, Book III, *Natural Questions*, ch. 10 ff., p. 430).

The contagions of pestilence also, as Arnobius puts it, [Col. 0440A] have scorched and depopulated the human race (Arnobius, loc. cit.). Who, I ask you, could be ignorant of this if he has so much as touched with the tips of his fingers the writings of ancient authors—Livy, Eusebius, Orosius, and others? Augustine likewise presses the pagans with the same line of argument and confronts them with several pestilences taken from the Livy already cited by us. Nor can this weapon be hurled against them with much less force from the Seneca just quoted, who also attempts to explain the natural cause of pestilence (Livy, Book I, ch. 31; Book III, p. 6; Eusebius, *Chronicle*; Orosius, Book II, chs. 12, 13, etc.; Augustine, Book III, *City of God*, ch. 17, p. 74, and ch. 31, p. 88; Seneca, Book VII, *Natural Questions*, chs. 27 and 28, p. 463).

Moreover, our author insists that locusts and mice [Col. 0440B] have gnawed away and consumed every kind of crop (Arnobius, Book I, p. 4). We read in Livy that such great clouds of locusts were suddenly carried by the wind from the sea into Apulia that their swarms covered the fields far and wide, and that Gaius Licinius, the praetor-designate, was sent to remove this scourge from the crops (Livy, Book XLII, ch. 10, and Book XXX, ch. 2). He relates further that the whole countryside around Capua was filled with another immense multitude of those same locusts, though it was far from clear whence they had come. But Augustine should be heard, for from this calamity of the locusts and the earlier calamity of pestilence he argues against the pagans in precisely the same manner as Arnobius:

“They have recorded in writing that a multitude of locusts in Africa resembled a prodigy, when Africa was already a province of the Roman people [Col. 0440C]: after consuming the crops and the leaves of the trees, the immense and incalculable cloud of them is said to have been driven into the sea. When they had died, been cast back upon the shores, and thus corrupted the air, so great a pestilence arose that in the kingdom of Masinissa alone eight hundred thousand people are reported to have perished, and far more in the lands near the coasts. . . . Such, therefore, is the folly that we endure and are compelled to answer: who among them would not attribute such events to the Christian religion if he saw them occurring in Christian times?” (Augustine, Book III, *City of God*, ch. 31, p. 88).

Orosius reports the same things concerning these locusts; consult him, as well as Cornelius Tacitus on other such matters, and also Bochart, who discusses locusts at greater length (Orosius, Book V, ch. 11; Cornelius Tacitus, [Col. 0440D] Book XV, near the beginning; Bochart, Book IV, *On the Animals of Sacred Scripture*, ch. 1 ff.).

Arnobius continues (Book I, p. 4) and adds that cities and communities have been shaken by extremely powerful earthquakes and swallowed by enormous chasms in the earth. Pliny is our witness to these events; he writes as follows concerning earthquakes: “Let earthquakes be passed over in silence, and whatever occurs where at least the tombs of cities remain; let us call them marvels of the earth rather than crimes of nature” (Pliny, Book II, *Natural History*, ch. 92, p. 239)—and far less crimes of the Christians, as our author rightly argues. Earlier, however, the same Pliny had written of both earthquakes and fissures in the earth: “The earth is shaken in various ways,” he says, “and wondrous effects are produced: in one place walls are overthrown, in another things are swallowed by a deep chasm” (the same author, in the same book, chs. 79 and 80, p. 231 ff.). There he committed to writing many further things concerning them, [Col. 0441A] which you may read (same author, book cited, ch. 84, p. 234). He asserts that the greatest earthquake within human memory occurred during the reign of Tiberius, since twelve cities of Asia were overthrown by it. Strabo and Suetonius also recalled this earthquake, while Tacitus relates in the following words the fissuring of the earth that accompanied it:

“In the same year twelve celebrated cities of Asia collapsed in an earthquake at night, which was all the more unforeseen and destructive. Nor did the usual means of escape in such a disaster—rushing out into the open—afford any help, because people were swallowed as the earth split apart. It is related that immense mountains subsided, that places formerly level were seen raised aloft, and that fires flashed amid the ruins” (Strabo, Book XII, *Geography*, p. 578; Suetonius, *Life of Tiberius*, § 49; [Col. 0441B] Tacitus, Book II, *Annals*, § 7).

In Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, however, these events are assigned to the seventh year of Tiberius, and thirteen fallen cities are named there individually. Mention is also made there of numerous earthquakes that had occurred in earlier ages.
