Finally, to omit many examples, Cicero, citing Coelius as his witness, relates that “at the very time” when Flaminius was fighting against Hannibal, “such great earthquakes occurred among the Ligurians, in Gaul, on several islands, and throughout Italy that many towns collapsed, landslides occurred in many places, rivers flowed in opposite directions, and the sea flooded in on all sides” (Cicero, Book I, *On Divination*, p. 268, line 40 ff.). He later enumerates other calamities no less severe (ibid., p. 271, line [Col. 0441C] 27 ff.). Hence Apuleius says: “We have often learned that the ground has split apart through excessive earthquakes and that cities, together with their inhabitants, have been swallowed up.” Tertullian, moreover, refuting the pagans by precisely the same argument, confronts them with the Corinthian Sea’s having been drained away by an earthquake (Apuleius, *On the World*, p. 408; Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 40).

So far is it from being possible to establish anything against the truth of the Christian religion from these and similar irregular occurrences that, on the contrary, Cleanthes, as reported by Cicero, concludes from them that conceptions of the gods and of a certain celestial and divine power have been formed in human minds (Cicero, Book II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 215). He would undoubtedly have spoken better had he said “conceptions of the one perfectly just and omnipotent God.” But on this passage of Cicero consult Lescalopier’s observations; and on earthquakes and fissures, their effects and causes, consult Seneca’s books, and also Strabo, who supplied a great many of the examples that have been mentioned (Seneca, Book VI, *Natural Questions*, p. 454 f., and ch. 21 ff., p. 451 ff.; Strabo, Book I, *Geography*, p. 58 ff., and elsewhere).

## ARTICLE III

### By what other examples Arnobius shows that numerous public calamities occurred before the rise of the Christian religion: fires, floods—with discussion of the island of Atlantis and the computation of the years from the beginning of the world—likewise battles with wild beasts, and the very great wars between the Assyrians and Bactrians under the leadership of Ninus and Zoroaster, as well as the other wars of Alexander and the Romans; and that after the birth of Christ affairs proceeded far more prosperously

The examples of public calamities [Col. 0442A] that we have related thus far demonstrate more than sufficiently that the pagans could have invented nothing more absurd than the claim that the world was being afflicted by these calamities as punishment for the Christians. But Arnobius, in order to restrain more forcefully the unbridled insolence of these raving men, judged that the same point should be proved by still other examples (Arnobius, Book I, pp. 4–5). He therefore insists that before Christian times the world had been consumed by fire, cities had been covered by the waves of the sea, the human race had been swallowed by floods, and—as Plato relates—ten thousand years earlier a great multitude of people had erupted from the island of Atlantis and utterly defeated and destroyed innumerable nations.

This passage of Plato occurs in his *Timaeus*, where, on the authority of ancient writers, he relates that an invasion by immense forces took place from that island of Atlantis, [Col. 0442B] which he says was larger than Libya and Asia, and that various nations were thereby reduced to slavery (Plato, vol. III, *Timaeus*, pp. 24–25). But afterward, through the violence of floods and earthquakes, that entire warlike people, together with the island itself, was swallowed by the waves of the sea in the space of only one night and day, and thereafter absolutely nothing of them appeared except remnants of mud. This same passage of Plato is cited not only by Pliny and Strabo but also by Tertullian, who uses it, as does Arnobius, to refute and overthrow the absurd argument of the pagans. We know, indeed, that to some these accounts appear closer to fables than to truth (Pliny, Book II, *Natural History*, ch. 90, p. 238; Strabo, Book II, *Geography*, p. 101; Tertullian, *Apology*, [Col. 0442C] ch. 40; Book I, *To the Nations*, ch. 9, p. 54; and *On the Pallium*, ch. 2). Yet Plato’s authority ought always to have carried weight among the pagans, and it is by no means without justification that it is set against them.

Seneca then calls Thucydides as a witness that the same island was submerged, in the following words: “Thucydides says that around the time of the Peloponnesian War, the island of Atalanta was submerged either entirely or certainly for the greatest part.” Ammianus Marcellinus likewise supports him (Seneca, Book VI, *Natural Questions*, ch. 24, p. 894; Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVII, ch. 7, p. 169). But if you are still unwilling to trust both of them, listen, if you please, to Seneca as he recounts other similar events: “Believe,” as he said, “that the same thing happened at Sidon. Nor is there need of witnesses for this. For we ourselves remember that, when lands [Col. 0442D] were torn apart by an internal convulsion, places were rent asunder and plains disappeared” (Seneca, Book IV, *Natural Questions*, ch. 32, p. 299; Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVII, ch. 7, p. 269).

Anyone who desires more should listen to Seneca speaking elsewhere: “The sea entirely engulfed Helice and Buris”—or, as Marcellinus says, “Helice and Bura.” “. . . Ships now sail above two towns. But these are only two that we know, whose memory, preserved in writing, has brought them to our knowledge. How many other places have been submerged in other regions! How many peoples have either the earth or the sea enclosed within itself!” (Seneca, ibid., ch. 23, p. 894). Earlier he had cited Callisthenes as his authority. Strabo records the same things about Sidon and other inundations; anyone may readily consult him, as well as Ovid, and again Seneca and Pliny (Strabo, Book I, *Geography*, p. 58; Ovid, Book XV, *Metamorphoses*, v. 261 f.; Seneca, [Col. 0443A] book cited, ch. 29, p. 897; Pliny, Book II, chs. 93–94, p. 238 f.).

But someone will ask: by what reasoning could Arnobius have said that the events he relates concerning the island of Atlantis occurred ten thousand years ago? Did he not know that Christians calculate a much shorter span of years from the creation of the world? The difficulty is easily resolved. For Arnobius was setting forth there not his own opinion, but that of Plato, whom he cites in the same place and who introduces a priest speaking thus to Solon (Plato, *Timaeus*, vol. III, p. 23):

Τῆς καὶ ἐνθάδε διακοσμήσεως παρ’ ἡμῖν ἐν τοῖς ἱεροῖς γράμμασιν ὀκτακισχιλίων ἐτῶν ἀριθμὸς γέγραπται· περὶ δὲ τῶν ἐννακισχίλια ἔτη γεγονότων πολιτῶν σοι δηλώσω διὰ βραχέων.

[Col. 0443B] “As for the ancient ordering of our affairs here, a period of eight thousand years is recorded in our sacred writings; but I shall briefly explain to you the history of those citizens who lived nine thousand years ago.”

Tertullian, moreover, reproaches the pagans with the conflagrations of the world, and especially those of Sodom and Gomorrah, as we shall demonstrate in the proper place. Not only Josephus mentions this conflagration; Cornelius Tacitus himself also appears to do so in these words: “I would grant that the cities of the Jews were once consumed by fire from heaven” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 40, and *On the Pallium*, ch. 2; Josephus, Book I, *Jewish Antiquities*, ch. 22, and Book V, *Jewish War*, ch. 5; Tacitus, Book V, *Histories*, near the beginning).

[Col. 0443C] Arnobius proceeds and says that before the Christians “wars were waged with wild beasts, and battles with lions” (Arnobius, Book I, p. 5). If in that passage you desire a witness to battles fought against wild and savage beasts by an organized army of men, Aulus Gellius will immediately supply Tubero, who committed to writing that Regulus, when encamped beside the River Bagrada in Africa, “fought a great and fierce battle against a single serpent dwelling there, a creature of extraordinary monstrousness; it was long assailed, in a great struggle by the whole army, with ballistae and catapults, and after it was killed, its skin, one hundred and twenty feet long, was sent to Rome” (Gellius, Book VI, *Attic Nights*, ch. 3, p. 368). Valerius Maximus relates the same story from Livy, as does Pliny, who asserts that the event was well known; [Col. 0443D] likewise Seneca, Orosius, Florus, and others (Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 8, § 19, p. 77; Pliny, Book VIII, *Natural History*, ch. 14, p. 153; Seneca, Letter 82, p. 156; Orosius, Book IV, ch. 8; Florus, Book II, ch. 2).

But if Arnobius is speaking of contests in which gladiators and athletes entered the arena to fight against lions and other wild beasts, he should perhaps be understood as referring to the spectacles given by Sulla, Pompey, and others. Besides what we have discussed elsewhere concerning these spectacles, see Pliny, Cassius Dio, and above all Seneca (*Dissertation on Minucius’s Octavius*, ch. 9, art. 2; Pliny, Book VIII, *Natural History*, ch. 16, p. 160; Cassius Dio, Book XXXIX, *Roman History*; Seneca, *On the Shortness of Life*, chs. 13–14, p. 707), who denounces this cruelty as follows:

“Would you permit anyone to concern himself even with the fact that Lucius Sulla was the first to exhibit lions at large [Col. 0444A] in the circus, whereas they had previously been exhibited in chains, with javelin-throwers sent by King Bocchus to kill them? Or is it relevant to any good purpose that Pompey was the first to stage in the circus a battle of eighteen elephants, setting condemned men against them in the manner of a regular battle? The foremost man of the state, and one renowned, as tradition reports, for outstanding goodness among the leaders of old, thought it a memorable kind of spectacle to destroy human beings in a new fashion. They fight to the death—it is too little; they are torn to pieces—it is too little. They are crushed beneath the enormous bulk of animals. It would have been better for these things to pass into oblivion, lest some powerful man afterward should learn of them and envy an act utterly devoid of humanity. O how great a darkness immense good fortune casts over human minds! He then believed himself to be above the natural order, [Col. 0444B] when he threw so many companies of wretched men before beasts born beneath another sky, when he arranged a war between such unequal creatures, and when he shed much blood in the sight of the Roman people—though he himself would soon be compelled to shed still more.”

If anyone nevertheless contends that Arnobius should be understood as referring not to this but to the earlier contest of men against beasts, we shall not strongly oppose him.

Arnobius then disposes of the pagans’ final argument, drawn from the frequency of wars, first by observing (Arnobius, Book I, p. 5) that immense hosts of men emerging from the island of Atlantis routed and destroyed innumerable nations. But we spoke of these events shortly before.

Secondly, therefore, Arnobius confronts the pagans with the fact that [Col. 0444C] a battle was once fought between the Assyrians and the Bactrians, under the leadership of Ninus and Zoroaster, not only with iron weapons and physical strength but also with magical arts (ibid.). Eusebius is our witness that Zoroaster the magician then ruled the Bactrians while Ninus reigned among the Assyrians (Eusebius, Book X, *Preparation for the Gospel*, ch. 9, p. 484). In Eusebius’s *Chronicle* we read the following words, which seem relevant to our subject: “Zoroaster the magician, king of the Bactrians, is held to have been famous; Ninus fought against him.” This is confirmed by the authority of Pompeius Trogus, Augustine, Jerome, and Orosius (*Chronicle*, at the year 7; Trogus, Book I; Augustine, Book XXI, *City of God*, ch. 14, p. 634; Jerome, on Hosea 2:2, p. 1251, new ed.; Orosius, [Col. 0444D] Book I, ch. 4).

Nevertheless, Diodorus Siculus appears directly to contradict them, for in describing Ninus’s expedition against the Bactrians he calls their commander not Zoroaster but Oxyartes (Diodorus Siculus, Book II, *Library*, p. 66 ff.). Moreover, he observes nothing magical or extraordinary at all in that battle, but only the skill and ingenuity of Oxyartes, who drew part of Ninus’s army into certain narrow passes, engaged them in battle, routed the enemy, and killed a hundred thousand of them. But he was later defeated by Ninus.

To this may be added that, as Pliny, the *Suda*, and others observe, several men bore the name Zoroaster. Scaliger, moreover, attempts to prove from the testimony of Laertius (Scaliger, on Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, p. 15) that the man who was a magician lived later than Xerxes and was therefore many centuries later [Col. 0445A] than Ninus. Cotelerius, however, believes that Zoroaster the magician was one and the same man, whose name was variously given as Zarus, Nazaratus, Zabratus, Zarates, Zares, Zoroadus, and Zarades (Cotelerius, note on Book IV of the *Clementine Recognitions*, p. 368).

There are differing opinions concerning his date. Eudoxus and Aristotle, according to Pliny’s testimony, reported that he lived six thousand years before Plato; Hermodorus, as cited by Laertius, and Plutarch placed him five thousand years before the destruction of Troy; while Xanthus, as cited by the same Laertius, reported that he lived six hundred years before Xerxes’ crossing (Pliny, Book XXX, *Natural History*, ch. 1, p. 725; Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, vol. II, p. 369; Laertius, Proem, § 2). But this diversity of opinions did not prevent Eusebius, Augustine, and [Col. 0445B] Jerome, as we have seen, from supporting our Arnobius. The *Suda*, moreover, considers a second Zoroaster, an astronomer, to have been a contemporary of Ninus (*Suda*, s.v. Ζωροάστρης, “Zoroaster”). What wonder is it, then, if this magician—indeed, as they say, the inventor of magic—was said by many to have fought against Ninus by magical art?

However that may be, no one can doubt what Arnobius asserts in refutation of the pagans: that wars and battles were fought between the Assyrians and the Bactrians many centuries before the Christian religion.

It is no less certain that the Trojan War was concluded still much earlier, because, as our author says, Helen was abducted with the gods as leaders and instigators (Arnobius, Book I, [Col. 0445C] p. 5). Augustine discusses that war more fully and urges it against the same pagans by the same reasoning as Arnobius (Augustine, Book III, *City of God*, chs. 2–3, pp. 60–61). Since these events can be unknown to no one and are related by Homer and a great many other writers, it is superfluous to pursue them at greater length.

Likewise, no one is unaware of Xerxes’ war against the Greeks, which Arnobius next justly sets before the same pagans. When Xerxes was about to wage this war, Arnobius says that he sent the sea into the lands—by cutting through Mount Athos, of course—and crossed seas on foot (Arnobius, Book I, p. 5). Lucan celebrated these things in the following verses:

Tradition sings that swelling Xerxes over the waters

Built roads like these, daring greatly with his bridges,

[Col. 0445D] And brought Europe close to Asia, and Sestos to Abydos;

He marched across the strait of the swift Hellespont,

Fearing neither Eurus nor Zephyrus, though he brought sails and ships

Through the midst of Athos.  
(Lucan, Book II, *Pharsalia*, near the end.)

Jerome puts it more briefly: “That most powerful king Xerxes, who overturned mountains and paved the seas.” But Herodotus, Diodorus Siculus, Pliny, Justin the historian, Juvenal, and others have more concerning these matters (Jerome, Letter to Heliodorus, p. 275; Herodotus, Book VII, § 19 ff.; Diodorus, Book II, *Library*, p. 243 ff.; Pliny, Book IV, *Natural History*, ch. 10, p. 435; Justin, Book II; Juvenal, Satire 10, v. 173 ff.).

And who does not know and clearly recognize what Arnobius adds: “One young man, arising from the borders of Macedonia, subjected the kingdoms and [Col. 0446A] peoples of the East to captivity and servitude”? For no one fails to recognize that these words designate Alexander the Great and—to use Augustine’s words—his “most lavishly displayed and least enduring power, by which he subdued all Asia, indeed nearly the whole world, partly by force and arms, partly by terror” (Arnobius, Book I, p. 5; Augustine, Book XVIII, *City of God*, ch. 42, p. 524). Among the many other works concerning him, the books of Plutarch on both his life and his fortune, Arrian on his expedition, and Quintus Curtius on his history should especially be read. Finally, Arnobius says that before the birth of Christ the Romans laid waste and depopulated all nations (Arnobius, Book I, p. 5).

[Col. 0446B] But in order to restrain their mad ferocity still further, following Tertullian he asks them whether anyone can deny that after Christ’s death wars had diminished and that, during the intervening periods that subsequently elapsed, innumerable victories had been won, the boundaries of the empire extended, and such an abundance of provisions obtained that all marveled at it in astonishment (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 4, and *On the Pallium*, ch. 2; Arnobius, Book I, p. 9). Do we not also, he says (ibid., p. 6), owe countless other instances of prosperity and favorable outcomes to Christ’s laws and institutions, which prohibit the repaying of evil for evil, command injuries inflicted upon us to be borne patiently, and bid us shed our own blood rather than another’s? It is therefore as false [Col. 0446C] that Christians are the cause of public calamities as it is most certain that those calamities may with perfect justice be laid to the impiety of the pagans who worship fictitious gods.

This is made still more evident by the fact that not only the true God but even the pagans’ own gods were treated by them with contempt and the greatest ridicule (ibid., p. 15 ff.). For, as we shall see below following Arnobius, by shamelessly proclaiming their gods’ mortal origin, adulteries, and other crimes and outrages intolerable even among human beings, they could not be punished by those gods with penalties and calamities sufficiently severe. But Tertullian must also be heard on these matters in the proper place.

## ARTICLE IV

### A reply to the pagans who ask what the cause of evils or public calamities may be; proof that what is good for one may be evil for another; and that the defeated Alemanni, the Getuli and Tingitani killed by hunger, are vainly adduced on account of the Christians dwelling among them, while it is far more absurd to assert that the gods were angry with those same Christians and that this falsehood was fabricated by certain mendicant pagans

[Col. 0446D]

Such was the blindness of the pagans that, although they openly and insistently accused their own gods of the greatest crimes, they nevertheless remained persuaded that human beings had been harassed by public disasters and calamities not out of hatred for themselves but out of hatred for the Christians. They therefore pressed the matter and importunately demanded what could have been the cause and origin of so many such great evils, if the Christians had not caused them. But what has this to do with us? Arnobius replies (Arnobius, Book I, pp. 6 [Col. 0447A]–7). It is quite enough for us to have repelled the false calumny of those who attribute every evil to the Christians. But what if these things arise from the disturbance of the elements, the movements of the stars, and the dregs of matter exhaling extremely harmful and pestilential vapors, as Seneca teaches? (Seneca, Book VII, *Natural Questions*, p. 463.)

Furthermore, things that seem evil to human beings, who measure everything by their own convenience, are in reality good for the world itself (Arnobius, ibid.). For floods and conflagrations of the world are regarded by Plato not as the destruction of the world but as its purification, just as Origen and we ourselves have observed elsewhere (Plato, *Timaeus*, vol. III, p. 22, and Book III, *Laws*, vol. II, p. 676 ff.; Origen, Book IV, *Against Celsus*, p. 173; above, [Col. 0447B] *Dissertation on Minucius’s Octavius*, ch. 1, art. 4).

What, moreover, of the fact that the moderate heat of the sun, as Arnobius says, benefits many, though some voluptuary, accustomed to being roasted by it, complains that it is too temperate or has been entirely taken away from him? Here Arnobius alludes to the custom by which effeminate pagans of old used to exercise before eating and afterward be anointed in the sun, before a fire, or at the bath. Hence Persius:

His delicate skin tended by the constant sun.

And a little later:

But if, anointed, you remain idle and fix the sun upon your skin.  
(Persius, Satire 4, vv. 18 and 33.)

Juvenal, moreover:

Let our contracted skin drink the springtime sun

And escape the toga; you may go even now to the baths

Without loss of dignity.  
[Col. 0447C] (Juvenal, Satire 12, near the end.)

Thus the sun’s heat afforded these men as much pleasure as another regarded it as harmful to himself.

Arnobius continues that it is not known to us whether pestilences, diseases, famines, and other calamities of that kind may not occur in order that those things which appear to be superabundant in the world may be removed from it (Arnobius, Book I, p. 8). Tertullian, indeed, writes without hesitation: “In truth, pestilences, famines, wars, and the engulfing of cities ought to be reckoned as remedies, like the pruning of the overgrowing human race” (Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 30).

Our author adds that it is wrong to conclude that *veratrum*—that is, as Pliny says, hellebore—ought not to have grown merely because it is poisonous to human beings (Arnobius, Book I, [Col. 0447D] p. 8; Pliny, Book XXV, *Natural History*, ch. 5, p. 391). For though poisonous to man, it benefits goats and quails, as Lucretius sings:

Moreover, hellebore is acrid poison to us,

But it increases the fat of goats and quails.  
(Lucretius, Book IV, near the middle.)

If you seek the explanation, Ambrose will give you this: “Experts say that hellebore is the food and nourishment of quails, because through a certain natural balance in the constitution of their bodies they escape the harmful force of that food” (Ambrose, Book III, *Hexaemeron*, ch. 9, § 39, p. 48). Dioscorides, moreover, and his interpreter Mattioli teach that white hellebore is [Col. 0448A] a medicine for many diseases (Dioscorides, Book IV, ch. 146, and Book VI, ch. 33). Why poisonous things were created we shall see elsewhere.

Finally, Arnobius says that there is no defect in nature if the wolf lies in wait for sheepfolds and wool-bearing animals, and if a serpent kills a man by its bite (Arnobius, Book I, p. 8). Consider whether Arnobius was not aiming there at the following verses of Virgil:

And like a wolf that has lain in wait for a full sheepfold.  
(Virgil, Book VI, *Aeneid*, v. 59.)

And in another book:

If the wool-bearing flock is your concern.  
(Book III, *Georgics*, v. 384.)

By the single term “wool-bearing flock” (*lanicium*), each author includes sheep, lambs, and wethers. Arnobius further asserts that it is the mark of a proud and excessively [Col. 0448B] arrogant man to impose this condition upon God: that whatever pleases each individual, God must immediately do.

But the obstinate pagans, still yielding nothing, insisted that not only before but also after the Christian religion had been disseminated—and because Christians were intermingled with others—wars had been waged unsuccessfully, fields left uncultivated through barrenness, and human beings killed by hunger. Yet so feeble an argument is easily demolished by Arnobius. For, as he acutely argues, if the Alemanni, concerning whom Eusebius and others write, were defeated by the Romans because Christians dwelt among them, then for precisely the same reason the Romans themselves, among whom Christians were intermingled, ought to have been defeated (Arnobius, Book I, p. 9 ff.; Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at the years 1277 and 1316). If mice and locusts at some time [Col. 0448C] infested Asia and Syria, why did they not also infest Spain and Gaul, where many Christians similarly lived? If the Getuli and Tangitani—who, as Mela, Strabo, Pliny, Sallust, and others relate, were peoples of Africa—were grievously afflicted, some by drought and aridity, others by famine, why did the Moors, the Nomads, and others who shared a common life with Christians harvest the most abundant crops? Ambrose uses the same argument to refute the pagan Symmachus when he raises the same objection (Mela, Book I; Strabo, Book XVII, *Geography*, p. 829; Pliny, Book II, ch. 2, p. 627, and Book XXI, ch. 13, p. 13; Sallust, *Jugurthine War*, well after the beginning; Ambrose, Letter 18, § 19 ff., p. 838).

Nothing, therefore, could be devised more contrary and repugnant to the truth than that absurd pagan accusation [Col. 0448D] by which they ceaselessly cried out that these calamities had been inflicted by gods inflamed with anger against the Christians. But these considerations were not enough for Arnobius, and with two further arguments he refutes this foolish opinion (Arnobius, Book I, p. 9). For although it were true—something that, as we shall soon see, he maintains to be false—that the gods were inflamed with anger because of injuries received from the Christians, they would certainly be most unjust if, in avenging those injuries, they punished without any distinction not only the Christians but also the pagans—that is, according to their view, the guilty and innocent alike. For if they were true gods, they could surely heap every good upon their own worshipers and punish, afflict, and kill only the Christians who were hostile to them, imposing every calamity upon them according to their deserts. To punish them, therefore, they ought not to have awaited the assistance of those same pagans, which was far slighter and weaker:

“Surely they [the Christians] do not rage [Col. 0449A] against you,” Arnobius asks (ibid., p. 11), “so that, provoked as though by inward wounds, you rise up to take vengeance upon them? Do the gods, then, seek human protection; and unless they are defended by your vindication, are they themselves incapable of repelling and defending themselves against the insults offered to them? Indeed, if it is true that they burn with anger, leave them power over their own affairs; let them defend themselves, and in vengeance for their offended majesty let them display and put to the test their inward powers.”

Heraldus, however, judges this argument to be extremely weak [Col. 0449B] and entirely without force, and treats it with complete disdain. But for what reason, do you suppose? Because, he says, while God reserves for himself the punishment of perjury, he wills that human impiety be punished by human beings themselves. Yet if this argument is entirely feeble and carries no weight, Cyprian must be reproved, for he assails Demetrianus and the other pagans in precisely the same and an even sharper manner:

“If your gods possess any divinity and power,” he says, “let them themselves rise up to avenge themselves; let them defend themselves by their own majesty. Or what can they provide for those who worship them, when they cannot avenge themselves upon those who do not worship them? For if he who avenges is of greater worth than the one who is avenged, you are greater than your gods. But if you are greater than those whom you worship, you ought not to worship them; rather, they ought to worship and fear you as their master. If your vengeance defends them when they have been injured, just as your guardianship watches over them when they are shut up lest they perish, [Col. 0449C] be ashamed to worship those whom you defend; be ashamed to hope for protection from those whom you yourself protect” (Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, p. 191).

Lactantius, Arnobius’s disciple, must likewise be condemned, for he argued in the same manner that the pagans vainly expected protection from gods who were unable to protect themselves. And a little later he says: “When the pagans punish those caught committing sacrilege, they themselves show distrust in the power of their gods. For why do they not leave to the gods themselves above all the opportunity to avenge themselves, if they believe that those gods have any power?” (Lactantius, Book IV, pp. 154 and 158.) Will Heraldus, then, accuse these and other most learned Fathers of the Church of such ignorance or blindness that they failed to perceive how much weight this argument [Col. 0449D] carries?

Did Heraldus himself not see that they were arguing, as they say, *ad hominem*, from the pagans’ own opinion, by which they taught that their gods were in reality so inflamed against the Christians with anger—that is, with the desire to avenge themselves—that because of the Christians they afflicted both them and the pagans themselves together with the greatest calamities? Does Arnobius not rightly conclude from this that, if the gods were so angry, they ought, in the violence of this supreme wrath, to exact punishment by their divine power from the Christians alone, who despised them, and not entrust the task of avenging themselves to feeble human beings?

Nor should anyone object that this argument could have been turned against the Christians, whom God permitted not only [Col. 0450A] to be afflicted by public calamities but also to be tortured and killed by pagans. For Christians and pagans did not hold the same opinion concerning the anger of God. Moreover, Christians were very different from the pagans, for they acknowledged that nothing had been promised to them for this life: “For nothing,” Arnobius says (Book II, p. 98), “has been promised to us for this life,” but rather for the future life, which we await in blessedness. From this he concludes: “Therefore, that harshness of persecution of which you speak is our deliverance, not persecution; its torment will not inflict punishment, but will lead us forth into the light of freedom.” Tertullian’s answer is likewise the same, as we shall show in the proper place (*Dissertation on Tertullian*, ch. 16, art. 3). The anger of the gods alleged by the pagans could therefore establish [Col. 0450B] nothing against the Christians.

Finally, our author openly and expressly declares that it is altogether absurd to say that the gods, as those same pagans babbled, were truly angry (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 11). For they attributed to their gods unseemly impulses of anger, unjust and altogether like those of beasts. Yet if the gods had been blessed and immortal, they surely could not have been inflamed by these wholly blameworthy impulses of anger. For those who are agitated by emotions of this kind are fickle—now calm, now angry, and often unjust when they injure innocent persons, while at the same time they are also angry with others who are guilty. Moreover, the entire force and weight of this argument lies not in what Arnobius himself maintained concerning the true God—on which see below (following chapter, art. 3)—but in what the pagans proclaimed concerning the anger of their gods. [Col. 0450C]

For this reason, he indicates that he can scarcely bring himself to believe that this was the opinion of the more prudent pagans (ibid., p. 13). He therefore regards it rather as a foul lie contrived by soothsayers, diviners, fortune-tellers, prophets, and fanatics, lest, once their temples and sacred rites had been abandoned, they should lose the contributions that they were accustomed to exact from those who consulted them or from others (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 13). For these had begun to diminish and were being paid by very few pagans after the number of Christians had increased beyond measure. Those who complained most of all about this very great loss were procurers—as Tertullian says (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 43)—pimps, panderers, assassins, poisoners, magicians, soothsayers, fortune-tellers, and astrologers, whom we shall discuss in the appropriate place. [Col. 0450D] No one, moreover, will deny that the pagans placed greater trust in these latter persons, who boasted that they foretold the future or delivered the answers of the gods. Hence they readily believed them when they falsely claimed that the world was being overwhelmed by the greatest calamities because the Christians, through the novel superstitions of their religion, as they advertised them, had provoked the anger of the gods.

From what has thus far been said, however, it ought, we think, to be sufficiently evident to anyone that this shameless lie of the pagans, and the other charges brought by them against the Christian religion, are utterly overthrown by Arnobius, and that he demonstrates by the most irresistible arguments that this religion of the Christians alone is true. Let us now see what proofs [Col. 0451A] he offered for it, and how he presented and defended them.

## CHAPTER VII  
### The proofs of the Christian religion asserted by Arnobius are examined, beginning with God

## ARTICLE I  
### By what arguments Arnobius demonstrates that God exists; what he maintained concerning God’s nature; how clearly he demonstrates that it is altogether incorporeal; and how one of his answers has undeservedly been criticized by certain writers

The first and undoubtedly principal proof upon which the whole religion of the Christians is founded and by which that of the pagans is destroyed is that there exists only one almighty [Col. 0451B] God. Arnobius demonstrates this most evidently from God’s effects (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 16, and bk. II, p. 43), from the idea and recognition of him innate in all human beings, and from the inward consciousness of everyone. For this conception is so deeply implanted—or rather, innate—in the minds of individuals that they readily recognize that they have received from the true God not only their existence as human beings and the fact that they live, breathe, and move, but also that the whole world, the sun, the moon, the elements, the earth, and everything else were created by him and are ruled and administered by his providence. To confirm this argument, Arnobius judiciously adds that none of these things can be attributed to the fictitious gods of the pagans. For everyone professed that all these gods, like the world itself, had come into being at some definite time.

[Col. 0451C] He judges that this argument possesses such force, evidence, and clarity that, although all human beings may be ignorant of who, what kind of being, and how great God is, nevertheless no person of sound mind can call into doubt whether he exists. In our earlier dissertation on Minucius Felix’s *Octavius* (ch. 3, art. 5), we have already shown that not only Minucius, but also Cyprian, Tertullian, Lactantius, and even the pagan Cicero demonstrated by this same reasoning, as certainly as evidently, that there is only one God, by whose infinite power all things were created and by whose marvelous providence they are governed. Something more, however, must be said below concerning Lactantius and Tertullian. Furthermore, Arnobius elsewhere declares without hesitation that, if it were possible for animals and even creatures devoid of sensation to utter some sound of voice, they would immediately, with nature as their teacher and guide, cry out that there is one God, the sole creator of all things (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 18). Indeed, if we believe Clement of Alexandria, Xenocrates and Democritus—as we have observed elsewhere—taught that even mute animals possess some awareness and knowledge of God (*Apparatus*, vol. II, bk. III, diss. 2, ch. 6, art. 1, p. 848).

Arnobius says that this awareness is so innate in all human beings that everyone naturally invokes God and calls upon him as a witness:

> “We all know him naturally,” he says, “whether when we exclaim, ‘O God!’ or when we appoint God as witness against the wicked and, as though he saw us, raise our faces toward heaven” (Arnobius, bk. II, p. 43).

How true this is will be shown by Cicero, whom we have already cited and who wrote somewhere:

> “All judge that there is a divine power and nature. This belief is not produced by human conversation or agreement; the conviction has not been established by institutions or laws. In every matter, however, the agreement of all nations must be regarded as a law of nature” (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, bk. I, p. 119, penultimate line and following; and *On the Laws*, bk. II, p. 325, line 22).

Nor should you think that he said this thoughtlessly, for you will find it repeated by him elsewhere. Hence Arnobius elsewhere declares without hesitation that anyone who doubts that God exists is insane and foolishly desperate; that it is enough for a person, even if he knows nothing else, to recognize God; and that this is the highest knowledge:

> “Of all the things contained within the obscurity of the august divinity, God alone is beyond doubt, alone true, and one concerning whom no one can doubt unless he is insane and possessed of a mad despair. It is enough to know him, even if you know nothing else, and so to have attained true and supreme knowledge, fixed upon God as the head of all things and upon the knowledge of him.”

But since we proved these points above, it does not now appear necessary to pursue them at greater length (Arnobius, bk. II, p. 86; *Apparatus*, vol. I, p. 688; and dissertation on Minucius, ch. 3, art. 5).

You certainly see how clearly God is there called by Arnobius the head of all things and the only true God (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 13). Elsewhere, no less expressly, he calls him unbegotten, immortal, eternal, [Col. 0452C] incorporeal, devoid of quality and quantity, uncircumscribed, immeasurable, without position, motion, or configuration, the place and space of all things, the first cause, the source of things, the sower of ages and times, the Father, Lord, creator of all things, and almighty—one who can neither be seen nor explained by human beings (ibid., pp. 17, 19; bk. II, pp. 43, 67, 74, 75, 95; bk. III, p. 101). Even if we said nothing, who would fail to recognize from this how rightly he explained the divine nature and with what diligence and zeal he enumerated virtually each and every attribute of God?

Since we have discussed these matters more than once elsewhere, it will suffice to direct attention to the argument by which our author maintains and defends the catholic doctrine concerning the incorporeal or spiritual nature of God: [Col. 0452D]

> “Our judgment concerning this matter,” he says (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 107), “is as follows. Every divine nature that did not at some time begin to exist and will never come to the end of its life is devoid of bodily outlines and possesses no configurations of form by which an external boundary of limbs ordinarily confines an articulated structure. For whatever is of this kind we judge to be mortal and perishable; nor do we believe that anything constrained within outer limits and necessarily enclosed by an extremity possesses perpetual duration.”

Nothing, surely, could be stronger or more eloquent than this reasoning for establishing the incorporeal nature of God. For Arnobius rightly lays it down as certain and fixed that whatever is corporeal, or is composed of bodily outlines and form, is extended and consequently enclosed and circumscribed by its own boundaries and outermost parts. But whatever is enclosed in this way must, by that very fact, be mortal. God, however, is not merely immortal but also eternal, and is therefore incorporeal and of a spiritual nature.

How firmly Arnobius was persuaded of this is further established by the fact that, when the pagans attempted to confirm the corporeality of their gods by some testimony of the Jews and Sadducees, he answered in this manner:

> “And let no one at this point oppose to us Jewish tales and those of the Sadducean kind, on the ground that they assign forms and a face to God. For this is thought to be said in their books, so that the claim may, as it were, be confirmed by fact and authority. These writings either have nothing to do with us and have nothing whatever in common with us in any respect; or, if they are, as is believed, allied with ours, then you pagans must seek teachers of a higher understanding, through whom you may learn in what ways it is proper to disperse the clouds and unfold the coverings of those writings” (ibid., p. 106).

Some more recent critics, however, brand several things in this passage with the mark of censorious severity. First, they charge Arnobius with speaking too confusedly and even dangerously. For if he is speaking of the books of the Old Testament, this, they say, is undoubtedly impious and dreadful; but if he is speaking of rabbinical writings, it is entirely pointless, since everyone admits that these teem with fables. Second, he appears, they say, to betray the greatest ignorance when he asserts that the Jews believed and proclaimed God to be corporeal. For Origen answers Celsus that the Jews are numbered by Numenius the Pythagorean among those [Col. 0453C] who considered God to be altogether incorporeal (Origen, *Against Celsus*, bk. I, p. 13).

But these critics of our author ought to have observed somewhat more attentively that in this passage, as we have said, he was answering pagans who endeavored to establish against the Christians the corporeal nature of their gods by the authority of the Jews and Sadducees. He teaches, however, that their writings and literature are of two kinds. Some were undoubtedly of the sort produced by the Sadducees, who, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, “say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit” (Acts 23:8), and consequently that all things, not even God excepted, are corporeal. But their writings had nothing in common with Christian doctrines and therefore could not be used as an objection against Christians. Other writings, however, belonged to the Jews [Col. 0453D] and were believed to be allied with ours; such, certainly, are the books of the Old Testament. Because bodily members are attributed to God in those books, the pagans derived from them an argument for confirming that their own gods were corporeal. Arnobius replies, however, that the pagans should seek teachers of a higher understanding—readily accessible to all and not unknown even to the pagans themselves—who clearly demonstrated that those words of the Old Testament must be understood in the appropriate ways, that is, in an allegorical, metaphorical, and mystical sense, not a literal one. What, then, is there in these answers and statements of Arnobius that deserves criticism, that is contrary to the authority and dignity of the sacred Old Testament, or that was not also asserted by other orthodox Fathers of the Church? Surely no one [Col. 0454A] can fail to see with the greatest ease that by these answers of Arnobius, and by the other arguments we have reported, the spiritual and incorporeal nature of God is plainly asserted and vindicated.

## ARTICLE II  
### How rightly Arnobius asserts that the form of God cannot be explained; how he teaches what God’s immensity and infinite knowledge are; and how God has nothing resembling human beings

It may perhaps seem remarkable to someone that, when the pagans asked Arnobius what God’s form was, he frankly replied:

> “If you wish to hear the true judgment: either God has no form, or, if he is formed in some fashion, we certainly do not know what that form is” (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 110).

What then, someone may ask? Did he not know that the nature of God is not corporeal [Col. 0454B] but purely spiritual? He knew this perfectly well, as is evident from what has just been said; but he freely and sincerely admits that the perfection of the divine nature and of all its properties and attributes is so great that it can neither be comprehended by the feeble human intellect nor explained in any human words. He gives the true and certain reason for this: since the weakness of the human mind is such that it conceives whatever it perceives only in its own imperfect and finite manner, it cannot therefore conceive or express a perfect idea of the infinite nature of God. Hear, I ask you, his splendid words:

> “Whatever you say concerning God, whatever you conceive in the thought of your silent mind, passes over into a human meaning and is corrupted; and what is expressed in our words—words fashioned for human affairs—does not bear the mark of its proper meaning. The one most certain understanding a human being can possess concerning the nature of God is to know and perceive that nothing concerning him can be expressed in mortal speech” (ibid., p. 111).

For this reason, in the same place he declares without hesitation that we are so far from attributing to God any outlines of any sort of body that we are instead afraid to ascribe to him even the human virtues of our minds: knowledge, understanding, wisdom, temperance, uprightness, constancy, and others. For these virtues and these human goods are appraised by people, according to the capacity of their feeble minds, only by contrast with their opposing vices—something that cannot be said of God.

There is nothing in this doctrine of our Arnobius that is not altogether sound and orthodox. For we read Theophilus of Antioch, like Arnobius, writing (Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, bk. I, p. 71):

> Τὸ μὲν εἶδος τοῦ Θεοῦ ἄῤῥητον, καὶ ἀνέκφραστον, καὶ μὴ δυνάμενον ὀφθαλμοῖς σαρκίνοις ὁρασθῆναι.

> “The form (*eidos*) of God is ineffable and inexpressible—hidden from us and incapable of explanation—and cannot be seen by bodily eyes.”

Many ancient Fathers of the Church openly deny that οὐσία (*ousia*), or, as they say, essence and substance, properly applies to God; rather, he rises so far above all essences and intelligences that whatever is understood by the human mind must be denied of him, since he far surpasses all such things. We have seen this lucidly explained by Clement of Alexandria and by the author of the book *On the Divine Names*, which is ascribed to Dionysius the Areopagite. It would indeed be easy to accumulate here many testimonies of other Fathers of the Church; [Col. 0455A] but because Petavius, Thomassin, and others have already done so, we have judged that we should refrain from presenting them (*Apparatus*, vol. I, bk. I, diss. 10, ch. 1, § 3; and bk. III, diss. 2, ch. 6, art. 1, p. 948; Petavius, *Dogmatic Theology*, bk. I, ch. 6, § 10 and following, pp. 45 ff.).

We may nevertheless further observe that Arnobius’s assertion—that although God is circumscribed by no boundary or place and is immeasurable, he is nevertheless the place and space of all things—is admirably confirmed by these words of Tertullian:

> “God is almighty, he who grasps the whole world in his hand as though it were a nest; heaven is his throne and the earth his footstool; every place is in him, while he himself is not in a place; he is the outer boundary of the universe” (Tertullian, *Against Praxeas*, ch. 16, p. 648).

[Col. 0455B] Earlier still, and with no less precision, Theophilus of Antioch had written these words to Autolycus (Theophilus, *To Autolycus*, bk. II, p. 81):

> Θεοῦ δὲ τοῦ ὑψίστου καὶ παντοκράτορος, καὶ τοῦ ὄντος Θεοῦ, τοῦτ’ ἔστι μὴ μόνον τὸ πανταχόσε εἶναι, ἀλλὰ καὶ πάντα ἐφορᾶν, καὶ πάντων ἀκούειν, ὅτι μὴν μηδὲ τὸ ἐν τόπῳ χωρεῖσθαι· εἰ δὲ μή γε, μείζων ὁ χωρῶν τόπος αὐτοῦ εὑρεθήσεται, μεῖζον γάρ ἐστι τὸ χωροῦν τοῦ χωρουμένου. Θεὸς γὰρ οὐ χωρεῖται, ἀλλ’ αὐτός ἐστι τόπος τῶν ὅλων.

> “It is, as it were, proper to the most high and almighty God, the God who truly exists, not merely to be everywhere, but also, being present, to behold all things and hear all. Moreover, he is not contained in a place; otherwise the place containing him would be found greater than he, for that which contains is greater than that which is contained. God, then, is by no means circumscribed by place; rather, he himself is the place of all things.”

For this reason, when Autolycus objected that God, as sacred Scripture testifies, walked in paradise, Theophilus replied that this was said of the divine Word, by whom the person of the Father was also represented and all things were created. But, he says:

> Θεὸς καὶ πατὴρ τῶν ὅλων ἀχώρητός ἐστι, καὶ ἐν τόπῳ οὐχ εὑρίσκεται, οὐ γάρ ἐστι τόπος τῆς καταπαύσεως αὐτοῦ.

> “God, the Father of all things, is not contained by place, nor is he found in a place, for there is no place in which he may rest.”

What clearer or more appropriate statement could be desired for establishing the true and orthodox doctrine of our Arnobius? Elsewhere he also consistently declares it proper to the true God to fill all things by his power, “not partially anywhere,” as he says—that is, never divided—or, as he says elsewhere (Arnobius, bk. VI, pp. 192 and 204), “partially and divided into members,” but wholly everywhere, in such a way that he is neither present nor absent; rather, being present everywhere, he hears all who speak from every part of the world and, by antecedent knowledge, perceives the unspoken thoughts of their minds.

Furthermore, Arnobius teaches that the correct judgment, one worthy of God and constitutive of religion, is this: we believe that God has nothing resembling a human being; that he awaits nothing arriving from outside himself; that he is moved by no emotion of anger, pleasure, honor, ambition, or desire for reward, nor by any disturbance of mind; and that, as is proper to him, he knows himself by his own power—that is, perfectly and through his own power he knows himself as he is, in all his greatness and character (bk. VII, pp. 222 and 242). And rightly so: for God, who is the cause [Col. 0456A] of all things, by knowing himself knows each and every thing, past, present, and future. Who would deny that this knowledge is infinite and belongs to no other? Indeed, it is so proper to him that certain very learned Fathers of the Church believe his divine Word to proceed from this very knowledge. A more suitable occasion for discussing this opinion will be afforded elsewhere.

## ARTICLE III  
### Whether Arnobius’s doctrine concerning the anger of God is sound

Arnobius’s entire discussion of the anger of God appears to some insufficiently orthodox. For against the pagans, who, as we have seen (preceding chapter, art. 4), continually cried out that their gods were inflamed with implacable anger against the Christians, he argues as follows:

> “Why, when you assert that those most august gods [Col. 0456B] are angry with Christian peoples, do you not perceive or see what shameful emotions, what unseemly madnesses, you attribute to divine powers? For what else is it to be angry than to be mad, to rage, to be carried into a lust for vengeance, and, through the estrangement of a brutalized heart, to revel in another’s painful torture? . . . For wherever there is any emotion, as the wise hold, there must necessarily be passion. Where passion is situated, disturbance must consequently follow. Where there is disturbance, there are pain and distress. Where there are pain and distress, there is already room for diminution and corruption. If these two cause affliction, destruction is close at hand, and death brings all things to an end” (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 10).

But this, Heraldus says, is precisely the opinion of the Stoics, whose falsity Lactantius exposed in such a way that he appears to have censured this doctrine of his teacher Arnobius. For although Lactantius asserts somewhere that anger is unbecoming to a serious and wise person, elsewhere he nevertheless shows that God truly becomes angry.

But this accusation by Heraldus is wholly frivolous and rests upon a childish equivocation. Anger is understood in two ways. In the first, Cicero defines it as “the desire to punish one who appears to have inflicted an injury” (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, bk. IV, p. 166, line 8). If you ask him what “desire” is, he says: “It is an immoderate appetite for what is thought to be a great good, disobedient to reason” (ibid., bk. III, p. 151, line 40). Hence Seneca calls anger the foulest and most rabid of all emotions, wholly aroused in an impulse of pain, and one that “certain wise men have called a brief insanity” (Seneca, *On Anger*, bk. I, ch. 1; bk. II, ch. 35; and bk. III, chs. 3 and 4). More than once, moreover, he describes its most wicked and dreadful effects. Augustine added something further to Cicero’s preceding definition:

> “The ancients defined anger itself as nothing other than the desire for vengeance, although a person sometimes becomes angry even with inanimate things, where there is no possibility of vengeance” (Augustine, *City of God*, bk. XIV, ch. 15, p. 367).

There is no reason to doubt that this anger is evil and must be condemned. For, as Ambrose rightly teaches:

> “To the powerful their anger is burdensome; to the wicked, their malice; to the righteous, the weakness of their condition” (Ambrose, *On Job’s Complaint*, bk. II, [Col. 0457A] ch. 6, § 16, p. 632).

Hence scholastic theologians call it a passion that always implies at least some imperfection. Arnobius is undoubtedly discussing this very anger, which the pagans were not ashamed to attribute to their gods. Do you wish this to be proved to you from other words of his? We shall quote them at once:

> “And if we hold fast to that definition which it is proper for us stubbornly always to remember—that all emotions of mind are unknown to the gods—it follows that we must believe the gods never become angry. Indeed, no emotion is further removed from them than that which is nearest to wild and savage beasts, agitates those subject to it with storms, and leads them into danger of destruction. For whatever is afflicted by the movement of some thing is established to be passible and fragile; whatever is subject to passion and fragility must necessarily be mortal; anger, moreover, afflicts those subject to it and dissolves them. Therefore, that which is subject to the passions of anger must be said to be mortal” (Arnobius, bk. VII, p. 214).

What falsehood or defect is there in this argument, which is drawn from those things the pagans continually advertised concerning the anger of their gods against the Christians and its grossly unjust impulses?

There is, however, another kind of anger, which the ancient Fathers of the Church and, later, the scholastic theologians teach to be nothing other than the equitable avenging of an offense and injury received, without disturbance of mind, or the just judgment by which due punishment is inflicted. They freely admit that God is angry in this manner. For, Augustine says:

> “The anger of God is not a disturbance of his mind, but the judgment by which punishment is imposed upon sin” (*City of God*, bk. XV, ch. 25, p. 409).

Earlier, when Celsus objected that anger and other human emotions are attributed to God in our sacred Scriptures, Origen replied that their authors speak according to the human manner and for humanity’s benefit, but that a spiritual person can readily discern the true meaning of the writers. He then immediately added (Origen, *Against Celsus*, bk. IV, p. 211):

> Ὀργὴν οὖν ὀνομάζομεν Θεοῦ, οὐ πάθος δ’ αὐτοῦ αὐτὴν εἶναί φαμεν, ἀλλά τι παραλαμβανόμενον εἰς τὴν διὰ σκυθρωποτέρων ἀγωγῶν παίδευσιν, τοῖς τὰ τοσάδε καὶ τοιάδε ἡμαρτηκόσι.

> “Therefore, when we speak of the anger of God, we do not say that it is a passion in him, but something employed for the correction, through a more severe course of discipline, of those who have committed sins so many and of such a kind.”

We could introduce many others who speak similarly, such as Ambrose (Ambrose, *On Noah*, [Col. 0457D] ch. 4, § 9, p. 231). But because that would be too lengthy, we shall add only these words of Hilary:

> “The punishment appointed is believed to be the anger of God—not because that unchangeable and tranquil nature of God grows hot through the impulse of a turbulent movement, but because the person who, by the determination of a penalty, remains under punishment, perceives the author of this determination to be angry with him. For the punishment of the sufferer is believed to be the anger of the one who decrees it. And thus God is angry when those who are punished, through the pain of their punishment, perceive against themselves the anger of the decree. This anger was not stirred from placidity into anger by a change in the divine nature, but, from the determination of punishment, is anger for those who are to be punished” (Hilary, *Treatise on Psalm 2*, § 17, p. 35).

Nor did he say this only once; rather, he says further concerning the anger of God (ibid., on Psalm 68, § 19, [Col. 0458A] p. 225):

> “We have often explained that it signifies the determination of punishment, not a movement of mind blazing forth in vengeance.”

Arnobius, however, speaks of anger not in this latter sense but only in the former, in which the pagans babbled that their gods were inflamed. In this very sense, he elsewhere asserts that God, “as has often been said,” he says, “does not blaze with the flames of anger” (Arnobius, bk. VII, p. 222). He is right to declare that this anger cannot apply to God and that those who were said to blaze with it were not truly gods.

For when, as we noted a little earlier, he had said that becoming angry was nothing other than going mad, raging, being carried into the lust of vengeance, and reveling wildly, he immediately added:

> “Do the great gods, then, know, undergo, and experience what wild beasts experience, what savage animals experience, what deadly nurse-serpents contain in their venomous tooth” (that is, serpents that pour venom into water, of which Cicero, Lucan, and others speak), “what is frivolous in a human being, what is blameworthy in an earthly animal? That surpassing nature, established in the firmness of perpetual virtue, is asserted by you to know”—another reading has “to experience”—“these things” (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 10; Cicero, *Academic Questions*, bk. IV, p. 33; Lucan, bk. IX, line 772).

That is, this is asserted by you pagans, who attribute to your gods every evil that anger is known to possess in human beings and beasts. What in this entire argument can be censured as unsound or unorthodox? Against the pagans, Arnobius teaches and strives with all the powers of his intellect to demonstrate that vicious anger and its depraved impulses and effects cannot apply to the true God. But he never denied [Col. 0458C] that there is in God that anger which is a right judgment imposing punishment and the just avenging of some offense. What the Lactantius cited by Heraldus taught concerning the anger of God we shall investigate in the appropriate place.

## ARTICLE IV  
### Whether Arnobius believed God to be the author of every evil, both of punishment and of guilt

We seem to hear certain persons boldly accusing Arnobius of a most serious error in his discussion of God’s omnipotence. For does he not, they say, introduce someone objecting to him that, if all things happen by God’s will and nothing can happen without it, it follows that God is the author of all the evils by which human beings are daily tormented? After [Col. 0458D] considering this most attentively, Arnobius declares himself persuaded that those evils arise neither from the elements nor from their inequality (ibid., bk. II, pp. 80 ff.). For he thinks it impossible that things possessing neither sensation nor judgment should be harmful and malicious. What, then, does he afterward answer to these objections? Nothing, certainly, except that it matters little whether we know or are ignorant of the cause of evil. For he considers it enough for us to know that nothing harmful, destructive, or deadly proceeds from God, and that nothing is done by him unless it is salutary, sweet, desirable, pleasing, and most delightful to all.

But does not Arnobius, they say, grope and stumble blindly throughout this entire discourse by failing to distinguish the evil of guilt from the evil of punishment? For who who is not altogether a stranger and foreigner to our sacred Scriptures could fail to know that the devil is the author of the evil of guilt, with God permitting it, while God himself, by an entirely just judgment, is the author of the evil of punishment inflicted upon sinners? Could he not also have learned this from Tertullian, who, when arguing against Marcion’s error concerning an evil god as the author of evils, judiciously distinguishes these two evils?

> “We,” he says, “after applying a distinction between the two forms, separating the evils of transgression from the evils of punishment, and the evils of guilt from the evils of penalty, assign to each part its own author: the devil as the author of the evils of sin and guilt, but God the Creator as the author of the evils of retribution and punishment. Thus the former part is attributed to malice, the latter to justice, which establishes penal evils as judgments against the evils of transgression. It is therefore of these evils, which are appropriate to a judge, that the Creator professes himself the author. These are indeed evils to those upon whom they are repaid; in themselves, however, they are goods, insofar as they are just, defend good people, oppose transgressions, and in this order are worthy of God” (Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, bk. II, ch. 14, p. 464).

Origen, Augustine, and a great number of other Fathers of the Church, with a common consensus, support Tertullian as he pursues and asserts these points at greater length; but there is no need to cite them here on a matter unknown to no one (Origen, *Against Celsus*, bk. VI, p. 324; Augustine, *Against Adimantus*, ch. 26, etc.). Did Arnobius, then, not know these things? Or, if he did know them, why did he not resolve the difficulty with a brief explanation or by distinguishing the two kinds of evil? Was he persuaded of what we read in the Origen just cited: [Col. 0459C]

> “If any other topic among human affairs that requires investigation is difficult for our nature to track down, the origin of evils may deservedly be numbered among them” (Origen, *Against Celsus*, bk. IV, p. 207)?

He speaks thus in Greek:

> Εἴπερ οὖν ἄλλος τις τόπος τῶν ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἐξετάσεως δεόμενος δυσθήρατός ἐστι τῇ φύσει ἡμῶν, ἐν τούτοις καὶ ἡ τῶν κακῶν ταχθείη ἂν γένεσις.

> “If, then, any other subject among human affairs that calls for examination is difficult for our nature to apprehend, the origin of evils may also be ranked among such subjects.”

This explanation may perhaps not appear wholly inept to you if you consider for a moment that Arnobius regarded this question concerning the origin of evil as one of those over which human beings contend with one another while admitting that they themselves can establish nothing certain. Consequently, lest he be compelled to draw out the thread of his argument any further and to wander too long beyond the question concerning the soul that he had there proposed, he thought it enough openly to declare to all the pagans this one thing known with certainty by Christians: God is neither the cause nor the author of evil. Nevertheless, we cannot deny that this investigation concerning the author of evil could have been explained more clearly by him there, since in this same passage he digresses at length into other matters less worthy of knowledge and no more conducive to his intended discourse concerning the soul.

You should not, however, suppose that he leaves the matter altogether untouched. For he afterward openly asserts that although God is almighty, he never imposes force upon anyone to believe or act (Arnobius, bk. II, pp. 88 ff.). If he compelled an unwilling person to do something, this would undoubtedly not be grace, but force and injustice, by which necessity would be imposed upon a free will to do that which it does not will and from which it recoils. [Col. 0460A] Thus God, like Christ, compels no one, but calls everyone equally and gives all the power to come to him. If anyone therefore does not come, the fault is certainly that person’s, not God’s. From this reasoning it is evidently inferred that Arnobius believed the evils of guilt, transgression, and malice to proceed not from God, but from the free and depraved will of the human being; the evils of punishment, however, as has been said, are indeed inflicted by God, but under the compulsion of the sinners’ malice, which he cannot leave unpunished.

Someone will nevertheless object, by contrast, that Arnobius consistently denied that any cause of calamity could ever be brought upon human beings by God himself. For he expressly declares:

> “Whatever is capable of bringing about a cause of calamity must first be examined to determine what it is, and must be set apart at the greatest possible distance from the name of God” (ibid., bk. VII, p. 228).

But does he not by these very words stumble directly into Marcion’s error, according to which Marcion babbled that God is indeed the author of good things, but that all evils whatsoever flowed from some other evil principle?

Yet whoever argues in this manner has plainly failed to attend sufficiently to the fact that Arnobius is there refuting the opinion of the pagans. They foolishly maintained that some gods were good and favorable by their very nature, while others were evil and hostile; and that the latter were the authors of all evils and calamities—things that appeared to the pagans to be true evils—though in such a way that, when appeased by victims, sacrifices, and other superstitious rites, these gods became good instead of evil, or at least did not harm human beings. Although Arnobius admits [Col. 0460C] that Christians are overwhelmed by the same calamities as pagans and, with God permitting it, are tormented and slaughtered by pagans with the most atrocious punishments because they confess him, he nevertheless asserts, as we saw above, that these are certainly not evils but goods by which Christians are led forth into the light of eternal liberty (ibid., bk. II, p. 98; preceding chapter, art. 4).

Quite rightly, you will say—if, in refuting the pagans’ error, Arnobius had kept within the boundaries of truth. But he offers this general assertion, circumscribed by no limitation:

> “Whatever is by nature mild and placid is far removed from the practice and thought of doing harm” (Arnobius, bk. VII, pp. 228 ff.).

Indeed, in the same place he added that it is no more possible for one who is good by nature to harm another and bring some evil upon him than it is for fire to be changed into cold. Therefore, he truly believed that God, being good by nature, could create no evil of punishment, calamity, or torment for anyone, nor be its cause and author. This certainly relapses into Marcion’s error.

Yet, however general that proposition of Arnobius may appear, it applies only to the pagans and their false opinions. They laid it down as certain that the gods were by nature either good or evil in such a way that, at their pleasure and without any cause, they indiscriminately overwhelmed pious and impious people, the upright and the wicked, with calamities and miseries. Moreover, Arnobius is also speaking of punishments and afflictions that befall good and pious people, and that bring with them not evil but always some good, as we said just above. For no one would deny that the punishments inflicted upon the impious and criminal are good effects of divine justice punishing them. What, then, occurs in our author’s entire argument that is not altogether sound, orthodox, and utterly foreign to Marcion’s errors? If anyone should nevertheless insist more stubbornly and prove that Arnobius, swept away by the heat of argument, either failed to distinguish the true God from the false gods of the pagans with sufficient accuracy or truly fell into some error, we shall condemn him at once. But scarcely—indeed, hardly at all—will anyone persuade us that a man who, as we have shown, reasons so rightly concerning the supreme nature of the one God fell into an error wholly opposed to this orthodox doctrine.

## ARTICLE V. Whether Arnobius Believed That Certain Animals Were Not Created by God, That Man Is Subject to Evils through Natural Weakness, and That He Does Not Sin by the Choice of His Own Will

[Col. 0461B]

Heraldus presses the matter and thinks that our Arnobius fell into the error of the Marcionites and of others who denied God to be the Creator, in the passage where he proves that it can neither be known nor determined from whom our souls derive their origin, or by whom other than God Himself they were created, using this argument:

> “For if we deny that flies, scarab beetles, bedbugs, *nitedulae* [small vermin], weevils, and moths are the work of the omnipotent King, it does not follow that we should be required to say who made and fashioned them.”  
> (Arnobius, book II, p. 75.)

But is not this the very error that Jerome attacks in these words?

> “But if they do not think that small things belong to Him to whom great things also [Col. 0461C] belong, they must introduce for me, after the manner of Valentinus, Marcion, and Apelles, one creator of ants, gnats, and locusts, and another of heaven and earth, the sea and angels.”  
> (Jerome, preface to Paul’s Epistle to Philemon.)

Whether this was in fact the error of Valentinus and Marcion matters little at present; we have discussed them sufficiently in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, book II, dissertation I, chap. 5, § 3).

Heraldus might also have added Origen, Ambrose, and others to Jerome, and above all Augustine, who rightly and explicitly asserts that even among the lowest little animals there is no nature that was not created by God:

> “There is,” he says, “no nature, even among the most extreme and lowest little animals, which was not constituted by Him from whom come every measure, every form, and every [Col. 0461D] order, without which no existing thing can be found or conceived.”

And elsewhere:

> “Nor is it lawful to believe or say that the creator of any nature, however small and mortal, is anyone other than God.”  
> (Origen, book IV, *Against Celsus*, p. 202; Ambrose, book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, chap. 6, § 38, p. 125, and book V, chap. 2 ff.; Augustine, book II of *The City of God*, chap. 15, p. 284, and book XII of *The City of God*, chap. 24, p. 322.)

That Arnobius neither denied this nor was guilty of the error censured by Jerome may be gathered from the fact that he did not expressly say that scarab beetles and other little animals of this kind had not been made by God. Rather, he said that if this were denied, one should not therefore be required immediately and necessarily to prove by whom they were made.

Heraldus insists that in the same place Arnobius defines, with sufficient clarity, [Col. 0462A] that we may remain wholly blameless while ignorant of who gave origin to these useless little animals:

> “And maintain that they were not brought forth by a higher God.”  
> (Arnobius, book II, p. 75.)

But who, asks Heraldus, is this “higher God,” if not Marcion’s good god? Yet certainly no one—not even Heraldus himself—could ever say that Marcion or anyone else erred because he asserted that God was good, but because he asserted that there was an evil God and that this evil God was the creator of corporeal things. No one will ever be able to prove that Arnobius maintained this error.

Someone will press the point that God cannot be called “higher” unless another is called “lower.” Yet God cannot be called lower than another without serious error. What, then? Does not Arnobius teach with the greatest possible clarity, as we have seen and [Col. 0462B] shall show further below, that there is only one omnipotent God, the Creator of the world and of all things? God, therefore, is called “higher” by Arnobius in the same sense in which we later read:

> “He is the head of divinity itself,” as Arnobius puts it (*ibid.*, book III, p. 101), “from whom the very divinity of all the gods is derived”—

that is, of those gods whom foolish paganism had wrongly invented. Accordingly, when he called God “higher,” he was accommodating himself to the customary manner of speaking among the pagans; nothing can therefore justly or rightly be inferred from this against the doctrine he asserted concerning the one and only God.

But if you trust Elmenhorstius, although Arnobius may be shown not to have been infected by Marcion’s error, which absurdly proclaimed one good God and another evil one, [Col. 0462C] he nevertheless fell into another impiety surpassing, as Elmenhorstius says, every sacrilege. Is that truly so? Yes, says Elmenhorstius. For Arnobius himself openly and clearly asserts that man was created not by God but by certain lower powers, whoever they may be. For when discussing the salvation of souls, he taught the following in these very words:

> “So far is God from being believed the author of these things that whoever conceives man to have been begotten by Him falls under the charge of sacrilegious impiety: man, an unhappy and miserable thing, who grieves that he exists, who detests and laments his condition, who understands that he was begotten for no other reason than that evils might not lack material through which to spread themselves, and that there might always be miserable beings upon whose torments some [Col. 0462D] hidden force and cruelty hostile to humanity might feed.”  
> (*Ibid.*, book II, p. 75.)

In this passage, however, according to Elmenhorstius, Arnobius advances two errors of equal impiety. First, he utterly and completely denies that man was created by God. Second, he holds that man’s condition is so wretched and unhappy that man perceives himself to have been created for no other reason than that, through an importunate cruelty, he might be made subject to innumerable diseases and evils. For in the preceding book, when discussing Christ’s miracles, Arnobius had similarly said:

> “He was accustomed to heal by word and command every kind of disease that some importunate cruelty willed human bodies to endure.”  
> (*Ibid.*, book I, p. 28.)

Yet this delirious notion, says Elmenhorstius, was drawn by Arnobius [Col. 0463A] not from our sacred writers but from the pagans, and specifically from Pliny and Plutarch; it is rightly attacked by Lactantius. He could undoubtedly have added Clement of Alexandria to them, who, as we have seen, brought forward many other pagan writers lamenting man’s miserable condition (Pliny, book VII of the *Natural History*, preface; Plutarch, book *On Fortune*, p. 927, vol. II; Lactantius, book III, chap. 28, and *On the Workmanship of God*, chaps. 3 and 4; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 2, chap. 18, art. 1, p. 1137; above, this chap., art. 1).

There is, however, considerable reason to doubt whether our author was actually led by these absurd errors. For we have already made it clear that Arnobius declared in the most explicit words not only that the world was created by [Col. 0463B] God, but also that man himself owes it to God that he exists, that he is called a man, and that he breathes and lives. Since, therefore, no one can plausibly believe that Arnobius contradicted himself so disgracefully, may it not rightly be said that, in the earlier words cited, he is slaying the pagans with no sword other than their own and assailing them from the false opinions with which they were imbued? For they taught that our souls were of divine stock and had been sent by God into this world, where, wholly forgetful of their former and supreme dignity, they are tormented and overwhelmed by calamities of every kind. Who, therefore, would find it difficult to persuade himself that Arnobius is there arguing against the pagans from their own false opinion, but elsewhere, as we observed just above, explained his own view and openly asserted that man [Col. 0463C] was truly created by God?

As for man’s miserable condition, the Apostle too laments it insofar as it inclines us toward sin. But this propensity flowed not from God but from the sin of the first man. Moreover, Arnobius does not there mention vices and sins, but hardships and afflictions. Although these issued from the first sin of man, they nevertheless are not true evils, as we demonstrated above from Arnobius himself (above, chap. 4), but can even produce an eternal good for those who use them well.

Nevertheless Elmenhorstius and Heraldus rise again and object that Arnobius asserted that man sins through natural weakness, not through the choice of his will. For he proves that Christ assists both good and evil people [Col. 0463D] in this manner:

> “This is proper to the true God and to royal power: to deny His kindness to no one and not to reckon who deserves it and who does not, since natural weakness makes man a sinner, not the choice of the will, or of judgment” (the Royal manuscript reads *sed*, “but,” rather than *seu*, “or”).  
> (Arnobius, book I, p. 29.)

Heraldus thinks that by these words Arnobius signifies that man neither wills nor chooses evil, but through natural blindness judges to be good what is in reality evil. Is Arnobius, therefore, not rightly accused of falling into that error of certain ancient philosophers which Lactantius censured in these words?

> “They say that those who appear evil do not sin of their own accord, nor choose evil in preference to good, but, deceived by the appearance of good, [Col. 0464A] fall into evil while remaining ignorant of the distinction between good and evil.”  
> (Lactantius, book VI of the *Institutes*, chap. 14, p. 595.)

But whether this or some other meaning and judgment belongs to our Arnobius is all the more difficult to say because this passage is not entirely intact, but has been corrupted and depraved through the great ignorance of the copyist, which is detected everywhere throughout the work. For he wrote *sed* (“but”) in place of *seu* (“or”), as we have already noted. Some, however, consider this reading so alien to Arnobius’s meaning that they have not hesitated to substitute the word *seu* in the text on their own authority. Others think that the two words *naturalis infirmitas* (“natural weakness”) were intruded into the text and should be excised. But they offer no reason for this correction.

We, therefore, who wish nothing to be altered in the text of authors without the authority of some manuscript or an entirely certain and evident [Col. 0464B] proof, suspect that, if these words of Arnobius are uncorrupted, their meaning is altogether different. Indeed, we shall willingly adopt the opinion of those who prove that Arnobius uses the noun *peccatorem* (“sinner”) not to signify a man who does something contrary to divine law and commits sin properly so called, but a man who through natural weakness is inclined toward sin and vice. That this was his meaning may be inferred from the fact that, as we noted shortly before (above, this chap., art. 4), he most explicitly asserted that God inflicts compulsion on no one, that absolutely everyone is equally called and delivered by Christ, that no one is excluded from His mercy, and that a free power of action has been given to all. Therefore he rebukes the erring man in these words: [Col. 0464C]
