> “You who desire to be transformed and to suffer compulsion, so that you may do and seize, under coercion, what you do not wish—why do you refuse to accept voluntarily that which you desire to accomplish once transformed and changed? ‘I do not wish it,’ he says, ‘and I have no will for it.’ Why, then, do you accuse God as though something were lacking to you? You desire Him to bring you aid, though you not only spurn His gifts and favors but call them empty words and pursue them with mocking jests.”  
> (Arnobius, book II, p. 89.)

Can these possibly be the words of one who asserts that man sins through the necessity imposed by his weak nature? Quite the contrary: they are the words of an orthodox writer who utterly banishes this error. Since, therefore, it is improbable that Arnobius should be wholly at variance with himself, the words of his objected to by Elmenhorstius must undoubtedly be brought back to the sense in which he called man [Col. 0464D] a sinner because man is inclined toward sin through natural weakness.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Supreme Divinity of Christ and the Mystery of His Incarnation

### ARTICLE I. With What Powerful Arguments Arnobius Asserts and Vindicates the Supreme Divinity of Christ

Arnobius asserts the supreme divinity of the Son of God, Christ the Lord, with such clarity and evidentness that it could never be denied by anyone unless he were out of his mind or blinded by utterly incredible obstinacy. How deeply this principal [Col. 0465A] doctrine of the Christian religion was fixed in his mind may plainly be gathered from the fact that he seems never to think that he has sufficiently stated and inculcated it, either to Christians or even to the pagans themselves. For the pagans boldly objected, as he declared more than once, that their gods were hostile to Christians not because they “worshiped the omnipotent God, but because they believed that a man who had been born and put to death by the punishment of the cross both was God and still survived” (Arnobius, book I, p. 19), and because they worshiped Him daily. Nor did they merely impute this to them as a fault; on account of this confession they also tortured and slaughtered them with every kind of punishment.

Consider seriously with us, therefore, what Arnobius answers those who ceaselessly cry out these accusations as though from placards, and you will immediately understand how openly and certainly he proclaimed the true [Col. 0465B] divinity of Christ. For what, I ask you, would have been easier or more readily available to him than to answer that Christ was believed and called God by Christians not truly and properly, but metonymically and improperly? By that obvious response he would have completely stopped the mouths of the pagans. But so far is he from employing it that he proves from the following consideration that Christ Himself is true God (*ibid.*, p. 21): namely, that He conferred the greatest and innumerable benefits equally upon all men.

> “For this,” he says (*ibid.*, p. 29), “is proper to the true God and to royal power: to deny His kindness to no one and not to reckon who deserves it and who does not.”

He briefly mentions what these benefits are, and recalls especially that Christ brought men over from errors and false religion to the true religion, and taught them by whom the world and these very men were created, and what state awaits them after death. Then, immediately, [Col. 0465C] he drew this conclusion:

> “Shall Christ, then, not be regarded by us as God? Shall He not be honored with that worship of divinity which is the greatest that can otherwise be conceived—He from whom we have already received such great gifts while living, and from whom we expect still greater ones when the day comes?”

What could have been stated more expressly and clearly to assert the supreme divinity of Christ? The pagans were persuaded that Christ was believed to be true God by His followers, and they imputed this to them as the greatest crime. Arnobius, however, replies to those same pagans when they reproach every Christian with this conviction, not only that it is in fact the belief of Christians but also that its truth is proved and established by various arguments. [Col. 0465D] Indeed, he steadfastly asserts that Christ must be honored with the greatest divine worship that can be conceived. He therefore openly and clearly affirms not only that the pagans were not unjustified in believing that true divinity was attributed to Christ by Christians, but also that this was the Christians’ own sure and public doctrine, from which no punishments could ever tear them away.

But come now, and observe how Arnobius repeats this (*ibid.*, p. 24), and establishes and confirms it by a new and no less explicit form of expression. “You worship a man who was born,” the pagans said. See, indeed, the same reproach once again laid before Christians. I should like you to hear what our Arnobius again answers it: [Col. 0466A]

> “Even if,” he says, “that were true, nevertheless, as was said in the passages above, because of the many and so generous gifts that have proceeded from Him and are present in us, He ought to be called God. But since He is God in certain fact, without the ambiguity of any doubt whatsoever” (so it reads in the Royal manuscript), “do you think that we will deny that He is worshiped by us above all and is called the guardian of our body? ‘Then,’ someone will say, raging, angry, and agitated, ‘is that Christ God?’ ‘He is God,’ we shall answer, ‘and God of the inward powers; and—what torments the faithless with the bitterest anguish all the more—He was sent by the supreme King for a matter of the greatest importance.’”

You see, surely, how he repeats twice and three times, and inculcates, that Christ is true God—not merely in name and appellation, but in certain fact and without any doubt or ambiguity [Col. 0466B]—the guardian of our body and the God of our inward powers, that is, of our soul and all its faculties. To whom, I ask you, do all these things belong except to the supreme God?

As for his addition, “He was sent by the supreme King for a matter of the greatest importance,” by these words he certainly does not signify that Christ is inferior, but that He is one and the same supreme God with the Father, though distinct in person. Moreover, that matter of the greatest importance for which He is said to have been sent by Him is nothing other than that He might save men after leading them, as we have said, from the impious worship of idols and the false religion of the pagans to the true worship of God and true religion, and after freeing them from their sins by His death. Arnobius asserts that this was intolerable to the pagans (the same author, book II, p. 87 ff.) and, as he himself says, tormented them with the bitterest anguish. [Col. 0466C] But however much they might be tormented by this public confession of Christ’s divinity, he nevertheless does not fear to affirm steadfastly, even at the risk of his own life, that Christ is the supreme God.

He did not consider it sufficient to declare the supreme divinity of Christ in such clear and open words, or to prove it from His great benefits to men and from His divine teaching; he also demonstrates that same divinity most evidently from the innumerable miracles performed by Christ Himself and by His disciples.

We made clear above what these miracles were, how great, how genuine, and more certain than certainty itself (above, chap. 3, art. 1). No less clearly did we show how they were performed without any external assistance and without either medical or magical art, but by a word alone or a light [Col. 0466D] touch—something never granted to any god of the pagans or to anyone else. Accordingly, after Arnobius had related at length those miracles of Christ and His disciples, he argues as follows from the power Christ granted them to perform such acts:

> “To be able to transfer your own right to a man, and to grant to the frailest being that which you alone are able to do, sharing with him its performance, belongs to a power set above all things, which contains beneath itself the causes of all things and the natures of their principles and capacities.”  
> (Arnobius, book I, p. 31.)

But to whom, I ask you, except to God alone, the best and greatest, belongs this power set above all things, which contains beneath itself the causes of all things and the natures of their principles and capacities? Yet Arnobius most steadfastly asserts that Christ the Lord was endowed with this power [Col. 0467A] and demonstrates it by the strongest arguments. He was therefore entirely persuaded that Christ is true and supreme God.

But hear further, I pray, how he again infers this from Christ’s own miracles and pronounces it in the most explicit terms:

> “Nothing,” he says (*ibid.*, p. 32), “as you imagine, was magical in Christ, nothing human, deceptive, or treacherous; no fraud lay hidden in Him. Though you may mock as usual and abandon yourselves to wanton bursts of laughter, He was the sublime God, God from His innermost root, God sent as Savior from unknown kingdoms and by the Prince of all. Neither the sun itself nor any stars, if they possess perception, nor the governors, nor the princes of the world, nor finally the great gods, nor those who, pretending themselves to be gods, terrify the entire race of mortals, were able to know or even suspect whence or who He was.”

You have surely heard how Arnobius rightly infers from the miracles performed by Christ through an altogether divine power that He was the supreme God—or, as Arnobius says, the sublime God—not through some external designation or appearance, but “from His innermost root,” that is, God by His own nature and of such loftiness and excellence [Col. 0467B] that no earthly creature, nor the gods invented by the pagans, were ever able to comprehend it or know His origin. Who except one wholly persuaded of Christ’s supreme divinity ever spoke or argued in this manner?

Arnobius regarded it as so important to proclaim the supreme divinity of Christ to the pagans and to impress it upon both their ears and their minds that he never seemed to himself to have said it often enough. Therefore, elsewhere he addresses [Col. 0467C] the pagans as follows:

> “Christ, against your will, is God—God, I say, is Christ; for this must be said often, so that the hearing of the unbelieving may burst and be torn apart—speaking by command of God the Prince, beneath the form of a man.”  
> (Arnobius, book II, p. 85.)

But, someone will say, Christ is there called by Arnobius not the first and supreme God but only a second and lesser God. What else do these words of his mean: “speaking by command of God the Prince”? Who is this God the Prince by whose command Christ speaks? Undoubtedly it is God the Father and the supreme God, who is therefore called “Prince.” But whose Prince is He, unless Christ’s, whom He commands to speak and to whose command Christ submits? Christ, therefore, is a God lesser than Him at whose command He speaks, and inferior to Him; consequently, He is God not properly and by His own nature, but improperly and merely by name. Nor does Arnobius call Him only “God the Prince,” but [Col. 0467D] often also the “first God,” the “supreme God,” and “Father”:

> “For us,” he says, “the first God is sufficient—the first God, I say—the Father and Lord of things, the Founder and Governor of all. In Him we worship everything that is to be worshiped; we adore everything that it is fitting to adore; we earn His favor through acts of veneration in all the obedience that reverence demands.”  
> (*Ibid.*, book I, pp. 13, 18, and 19; book II, pp. 43 and 68; book III, p. 101 ff.)

Did Arnobius, then, acknowledge and believe only this God to be supreme, while Christ was a lesser God?

But nothing is more completely alien to or more remote from Arnobius’s thought. [Col. 0468A] For if this had been his opinion, he could easily have persuaded the pagans of it by explaining it clearly, as we have already observed, and would not have found so many of them resisting him so obstinately. On the contrary, with all the strength of his mind and discourse he declares, asserts, teaches, repeats, proves, inculcates, and demonstrates that Christ is true and supreme God, possessed of divine and infinite power and therefore also of a divine nature. Since, moreover, he everywhere asserts and proves against the error of the pagans that there is only one God and that there cannot be several, it follows with the utmost clarity that nothing was more deeply fixed in his mind than that Christ is one and the same God with His eternal Father.

Why, then, you will ask, does he call Christ’s Father both the “first God” and “God the Prince”? We answer that Arnobius sometimes calls Him this when accommodating himself [Col. 0468B] to the common speech of the pagans, who acknowledged that all their gods, whether greater or lesser, had once not existed and had been born at some definite time. Once this was posited, Arnobius argues that, if these gods were such as the pagans thought, they received from God the Prince the fact that they were born, that they lived, and that they possessed their divinity—if any such divinity could have existed—and their immortality. Hence Arnobius rightly concludes against those same pagans that these gods are false and fictitious, and that God Himself is the first and the Prince and therefore the supreme and unique God, and may be so called. For immediately after the words objected against him, he added:

> “Since we hold fast to the head of divinity itself, from whom the very divinity of all the gods, whoever they may be, is said to derive . . . whoever [Col. 0468C] these gods are whom you set before us as existing, if they are a royal offspring, they arise from the principal head . . . and this indeed would have been put forward by us in this manner, provided only that it is clear and established that, besides the King and Prince Himself, there are still other heads, which, distributed and separated by number, constitute something like a people belonging to the common multitude.”  
> (*Ibid.*, book III, p. 101.)

Earlier, however, he had said:

> “Since all the gods—whether those who are true, whoever they may be, or those who are said by report and opinion to be immortal and everlasting—exist through His will and by the gift of His beneficence, how can it be possible that they should be able to bestow on others that which they themselves are, since they possess it as something belonging to another and lent to them by a greater power?”  
> (*Ibid.*, book II, p. 87.)

[Col. 0468D] Who does not now see that God is called “the Prince” and “the first” by Arnobius because he had in view the pagans’ opinion concerning their gods, and that, even with this opinion posited, he concludes and demonstrates that these gods are false and that He alone is true God? For only He can be true God who, unbegotten and eternal, has no beginning.

These expressions, therefore, do nothing against the divinity of the divine Word and of Christ the Lord, which we have seen asserted by Arnobius more clearly and evidently than the light itself. Furthermore, what prevented Arnobius, when directing his mind to the Word Himself and the Son of God, from saying that the eternal Father is the first God and God the Prince—He who, because He begot this Son of His from eternity, is therefore rightly called the first, the Prince, and the fountain and origin of divinity?

[Col. 0469A] You will press the objection: Christ is said by Arnobius to speak “by command of God the Prince.” Therefore He is subject to Him and lesser than He. But if you notice that Arnobius immediately adds in the same place, “beneath the form of a man,” you will recognize that nothing is weaker than this argument. For who denies that Christ, insofar as He is man, is subject to God the Father and obeys His will?

### ARTICLE II. How Clearly Arnobius Taught That Christ Was as Truly Man as He Was True God

Arnobius does not permit the pagans to object that Christ cannot be called God (Arnobius, book I, p. 21 ff.) because He was born and ended His life through the punishment of the cross. For apart from the fact that the pagans themselves babbled that men who had been born, [Col. 0469B] died, and suffered punishments were gods, Christ’s divine teaching and the miracles performed by Him, as we have said, while living, dying, and dead, most clearly demonstrated that He was as truly God as man and that He participated in both the divine and the human nature. What wonder is it if, after receiving a human nature—or assuming a human body, which, as Arnobius says (*ibid.*, book I, p. 32), was but a small part of Him—He lived and lost a human life like other men? But it is better to hear Arnobius himself, so that you may understand how correctly and clearly he explains the human and divine nature of Christ and the most holy mystery of His Incarnation, as theologians now commonly call it.

For when the pagans asked, “If Christ was God, [Col. 0469C] why was He seen beneath the form of a man and killed in the manner of a man?” Arnobius answers as follows:

> “Could that invisible power, which possesses no bodily substance, have introduced and accommodated itself to the world, taken part in the assemblies of mortals, in any other way than by assuming some covering of more solid matter—one that could receive the gaze of the eyes and upon which the beholder’s sight could most sluggishly fix itself? For what mortal could have been able to see Him, who could have discerned Him, if He had willed to present Himself to the earth such as He is in His original nature, and such as He Himself willed to be in His own quality or divine power? He therefore assumed the form of a man and enclosed His power beneath the likeness of our race, so that He might be seen and beheld, might speak and teach, and might carry out all those things [Col. 0469D] which He had come into the world to perform, while preserving the command and ordinance of the supreme King.”  
> (*Ibid.*, p. 37.)

Could the supreme divinity of Christ and its conjunction with human nature have been stated in clearer words? Who, even after the Council of Nicaea and the other general councils, explained His two natures in a more lucid discourse? Yet in this passage Arnobius discloses not merely his own opinion but the common belief of all the Christians of his age. Who, therefore, would dare deny, or justly call into any doubt, whether before the time of that same Nicene Council they believed what was determined at that council and later councils concerning Christ’s divinity and the human nature assumed by Him?

Come now, if you please, and let us hear him further as he explains how death in no way impaired Christ’s divinity. The pagans objected: “He was killed in the manner of a man.” What does our Arnobius answer? [Col. 0470A]

> “Not He Himself,” he says (*ibid.*), “for the event of death cannot befall divine things, nor can that which is one and simple, and not compacted from the combination of any parts, collapse through the dissolution of destruction. Who, then, was seen hanging on the cross? Who died? The man whom He had put on and carried with Himself.”

He then shows that this should be credible to the pagans, who believed that, when prophets and Sibyls died, the being by whose inspiration they appeared to have uttered oracles did not die. After explaining these matters, he addresses the same pagans in these words:

> “That death of which you speak belonged to the man assumed, not to Him Himself; to that which was carried, not to the One carrying it. [Col. 0470B] Nor would He have submitted to suffer even that death unless so great a work had to be accomplished and an inexplicable principle of destiny, concealed in closed mysteries, had to be disclosed.”  
> (*Ibid.*, p. 38.)

Who has tasted, even with the very edge of his lips, the writings of the theologians and the ancient Fathers of the Church and does not know that they later answered heretics who raised the same objections in precisely a similar manner? Indeed, an infinite number of their testimonies could be adduced. But since the many passages cited by Theodoret and Gelasius (Theodoret, at the end of book III of the *Dialogue, The Impassible*; Gelasius, *Dialogue on the Two Natures*), and handed down by numerous others, are known to everyone, we shall omit them and report only these words of Ambrose, which are recited and transcribed in an epistle of Leo the Great and in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon:

> “As for what has been read,” says that eminent man (Ambrose, book II of [Col. 0470C] *On the Faith*, chap. 5, § 58, p. 481), “that the Lord of Majesty was crucified, we should not think that He was crucified in His majesty; rather, because the same One is God and man—God through divinity, man through the assumption of flesh—Jesus Christ, the Lord of Majesty, is said to have been crucified because, sharing both natures, that is, the human and the divine, He underwent suffering in His human nature, so that the One who suffered may without distinction be called both the Lord of Majesty and the Son of Man who, as Scripture says, descended from heaven.”

See what we have annotated on this passage of Ambrose, as well as the acts of the Council of Chalcedon cited by us there and Augustine’s first book *On the Trinity*.

Moreover, our Arnobius teaches that no one could ever have laid violent hands upon Christ, who had performed so many miracles, [Col. 0470D] if He had not wished to die, but that He died of His own accord and will.

> “Do you see? If He had not wished anyone to lay hands upon Him, would He have needed to strive with the greatest exertion to ward off His enemies by turning His power against them? He who had restored sight to the blind—if He had needed to do so, could He not have made others blind? . . . He allowed savage men to stretch out their hands against Him.”  
> (Arnobius, book I, p. 38.)

He died, therefore, because, as our author further says:

> “The Lord of all powers and the destroyer of death itself permitted His man to be killed.”  
> (*Ibid.*, p. 41.)

By these words Arnobius signifies that Christ was killed, when He willed it, only according to His human nature, yet in such a way that by dying He revealed His divine nature through new [Col. 0471A] and utterly astonishing miracles:

> “Stripped of the body,” he says (*ibid.*, p. 32), “which He carried about as a small part of Himself, after He allowed it to be seen and His greatness to become known, all the elements of the world, terrified by the novelty of the events, were thrown into confusion: the earth was shaken and trembled; the sea was poured out from its depths; the air was enveloped in masses of darkness; and the fiery orb of the sun grew rigid as its heat grew lukewarm.”

One must surely be blinder than a mole, or a man of inflexible obstinacy, not to see and acknowledge that Arnobius correctly distinguishes Christ’s two natures, divine and human, and thoroughly and properly attributes and explains to each what belongs to it.

But, you will ask, what does he mean when he says that there was a “simulated man” in Christ? For he says: [Col. 0471B]

> “The supreme King could not accomplish the things He had determined to do in the world without a simulated man.”  
> (*Ibid.*, p. 37.)

Did Arnobius perhaps think that Christ’s human nature was not real but fictitious and simulated? Did he not go completely astray with those heretics who foolishly asserted that Christ was not a true man, but, as they said, a phantom of a man and an illusory man? By no means whatsoever. For from the statements we have recalled concerning Christ’s life and death, it is proved more clearly than the noonday light that Arnobius believed with the utmost certainty that a true human nature and a true human body had been assumed by Christ. Accordingly, by the words *homine simulato* (“a simulated man”) he means the same as if he had said “a man represented and exhibited,” in such a way that the man whom He represented and exhibited was a true man. We cannot deny, [Col. 0471C] however, that Arnobius speaks improperly and less than accurately in this passage. But what rigorous critic would not readily pardon such an insufficiently polished manner of expression in a man who very frequently uses barbarous and obsolete words and does not write in a pure and correct style?

### ARTICLE III. Why Christ Became Man; Why He Came So Late and Not Long Before; What Happened to Those Who Died Before His Birth; and Concerning Men of Gigantic Body and the Stentorian Cries of Infants
If you ask Arnobius why Christ became man, he will give you this reason: because “he brought us over from false religions to the true religion; from lifeless images fashioned out of the vilest clay he raised us to the stars and heaven, and enabled us to mingle words of supplication and the discourse of prayers [Col. 0471D] with God, the Lord of all things.” (Arnob., bk. I, p. 22.) Therefore he openly declares the following about himself, not without a full expression of gratitude: “Now, having been led into the paths of truth by so great a teacher, I know what all these things are; I entertain worthy thoughts about worthy beings; I do no injury to the divine name; and I assign to each person or rank what is due to it, according to distinct degrees and authorities.” (Ibid.)

The pagans, however—nothing being more characteristic of them than infecting all that is best with the deadly poisons of their errors—attempted on this ground to attack the most sacred mystery of Christ’s incarnation. For they objected to the Christians (Ibid., bk. II, p. 96) that, if the matter were so, no reason could be given why Christ had been sent to us by [Col. 0472A] God the Father only after so many generations and ages of mankind; or what the earlier ages before his birth had deserved; or what had been done with the souls of ancient and exceedingly remote mortals (Ibid., p. 87). The very same argument, later revived against the Christians by Porphyry and other pagans, was thus submitted for solution to Augustine by a bishop named Deogratias: “What did the people of so many ages before Christ do? . . . What was done with those innumerable souls, which were guilty of no fault at all, since he in whom they might believe had not yet bestowed his advent upon humankind?” (Augustine, Epist. 102, p. 276.) You see, undoubtedly, that they attack the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and the truth of the entire Christian religion in precisely the same way.

[Col. 0472B] But hear also how Arnobius, and Augustine after him, thoroughly weaken and dissolve this argument. First, in objecting that no reason could be given why Christ became man after so many ages, the pagans were cutting their own throats with their own sword. For they themselves, says our author (Arnob., bk. II, p. 96), could give no reason, not only why winter, summer, autumn, rain, and other things of this kind repeatedly fail to occur at the proper and appropriate time, but especially why Hercules, Aesculapius, and others whom they believed to have been born for the benefit of humanity had appeared in the world so late. In precisely the same way Augustine sharply refutes them from the first origin of the mysteries instituted by them—which comes to the same thing:

“Let them themselves,” he says (Augustine, loc. cit.), [Col. 0472C] “tell us whether people were benefited by the rites of their gods, which admittedly were instituted at definite times. If they deny that these rites contributed anything to the salvation of souls, they join us in destroying them and confess that they are empty. . . . But if they defend them and assert that they were instituted wisely and beneficially, I ask what was done with those who died before these rites were instituted; for they were surely deprived of this salvation and benefit. But if they could be purified in some other way, why did that same method not continue among their descendants? What need was there to institute novel consecrations that had not existed in antiquity?”

They could not reply that no reason for these things could be given. By that very fact they were shown to be demanding from Christians, unjustly, some explanation [Col. 0472D] of Christ’s late advent. But if they offered any explanation, Christians would offer the same. Hence our Arnobius says: “You will say that there was some reason. There was therefore a reason here too why the Savior of our race should come, not recently, but today.” (Arnob., loc. cit.) Augustine likewise asks: “Why do they force this question upon the Christian religion, when they themselves either cannot answer it on behalf of their gods, or, if they can, by that very answer also answer on behalf of our religion?” (Augustine, loc. cit.)

They therefore had to admit that it is not lawful for a human being to scrutinize the counsels of God, who knew the appropriate time at which he ought to assist the human race (Arnob., ibid.). Augustine likewise answers this question in a similar manner: “Since they confess that the times do not glide by fortuitously [Col. 0473A] but are ordered by divine providence, what is fitting and appropriate for each time surpasses human judgment and is apportioned from that source from which providence itself takes thought for all things.” (Augustine, ibid., p. 277.) To this may also be added Ambrose, who, in a sermon on these words of Psalm 118, “It is time to act, O Lord,” similarly said: “It was a time not for commanding but for acting, because not an envoy or messenger, but the Lord himself was to save his people. He indeed knew the time and was not delaying, but we did not know at what time he could better come to our aid.” (Ambrose, Serm. 16 on Ps. 118, v. 126, p. 1181.)

Arnobius proceeds and offers another reason why Christ had not come into the world earlier, expressed in these [Col. 0473B] words: “It may be that the omnipotent Lord sent forth Christ only when the race of humanity had become more broken and our nature weaker.” (Arnob., bk. II, p. 97.) Ambrose again supports our Arnobius. When speaking of the patriarch Joseph’s blessing, he cites these words of Genesis: “Jacob loved him because he was the son of his old age,” and immediately adds:

“This is also referred to Christ. For when the world was growing old and already sinking toward its end, the Son of God shone upon it and came late through the Virgin Mary’s giving birth, as though he were the son of its old age. According to the mystery, he who had always existed with the Father before the ages assumed a body.” (Ambrose, *On the Blessings of the Patriarchs*, ch. 11, §48, p. 527.)

The pagans could not deny, says Arnobius, [Col. 0473C] that the human condition had varied according to the diversity of the times, that the form of the ancients differed from that of more recent people, and that the former possessed greater strength than the latter (Arnob., bk. II, p. 97). Their writings, indeed, handed down that demigods and heroes of enormous or gigantic stature had once existed, that infants had uttered Stentorian cries, and that bones of such great size had been unearthed in various regions that they could scarcely be believed to be human. Besides Herodotus, Pliny, and Solinus, Aulus Gellius committed to writing the following concerning these bones, which bears upon our author’s purpose:

“Herodotus, a teller of tales, wrote in the first book of his *Histories* that the body of Orestes was discovered beneath the earth and measured seven cubits in length, which make twelve and one-quarter feet—unless, as Homer believed, the bodies of ancient human beings were broader [Col. 0473D] and taller, while now, as though the world were already growing old, both things and human beings are diminishing.” (Herodotus, bk. I, §68, p. 27; Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. VII, ch. 16, p. 35; Solinus, ch. 10, p. 236; Aulus Gellius, bk. III, ch. 1, p. 9.)

Indeed, this lament occurs frequently in Homer’s *Iliad*, and is also noted by Pliny and Juvenal (Pliny, loc. cit.; Juvenal, *Satire* 15, v. 69).

In the royal manuscript, however, *centenarian cries* (*centenarios vagitus*) is read in place of *Stentorian cries* (*stentoreos vagitus*), doubtless through the customary carelessness of the copyist, who was entirely ignorant of what “Stentorian cries” and many other expressions meant. [Col. 0474A] They are called Stentorian cries because Homer represents Stentor as having so powerful a voice that it equaled the shout of fifty men (Homer, *Iliad* 5, near the end). For precisely this reason Juvenal sang somewhere:

> You, poor wretch, shout so as to surpass Stentor.  
> (Juvenal, *Satire* 13, v. 22.)

We note these things so that everyone may understand with what justification Arnobius said that, by the pagans’ own admission, human strength had diminished, and that Christ perhaps became man at the time when human nature was more broken and weaker, and stood in greater need of his assistance.

Arnobius moreover gives yet another reason why Christ did not assume humanity earlier: [Col. 0474B] namely, that he came into this world at the very time fixed by the immutable decree of God, of whom, since he is eternal, nothing can be said to be premature or late. For, as he says (Arnob., bk. II, p. 97), the unbounded sequence and continuation of the ages—that is, their continuation without measure and without beginning or end—possesses no time.

Christ was therefore sent into the world when God judged that he ought to become man. “For nothing,” as Arnobius further says (Ibid.), “compelled God not to await the necessary measures of the times.” Was this not also Augustine’s view, which he explained in these words?

“What I said—that Christ willed to appear to human beings and to have his teaching preached among them at the time and place where he knew [Col. 0474C] there would be those who would believe in him—may also be expressed thus: that Christ willed to appear to human beings and to have his teaching preached among them at the time and place where he knew there would be those who had been chosen in him before the foundation of the world.” (Augustine, Epist. 102, p. 278, and *On the Predestination of the Saints*, ch. 9, p. 803.)

As for those who died before Christ, Arnobius briefly replies: “What if the ancients had to be assisted in one way, while provision had to be made for later people in another?” (Arnob., loc. cit.) But what he either did not wish to explain or, perhaps because he had not yet been fully instructed in the whole of Christian doctrine, could not explain, is set out more clearly and fully by the theologians, and especially by Augustine [Col. 0474D] in the letter cited by us. There, among many other things, Augustine wrote:

“From the beginning of the human race, whoever believed in him [Christ], understood him in whatever manner they could, and lived piously and justly according to his commandments—whenever and wherever they lived—were undoubtedly saved through him. For just as we believe in him both as abiding with the Father and as having now come in the flesh, so the ancients believed in him both as abiding with the Father and as destined to come in the flesh.” (Augustine, Epist. 102, p. 277.)

Anyone desiring further arguments should consult the theologians on Book III of the *Sentences*, distinction 1; St. Thomas, I–II, q. 98, art. 6, and III, q. 2, arts. 5 and 6; Petavius, vol. IV, [Col. 0475A] *Dogmatic Theology*, ch. 17, p. 198 ff.; and the ancient Fathers of the Church cited by them.

# CHAPTER IX. On the Human Soul

## ARTICLE I. Which False Opinions of the Ancients Concerning the Nature, Origin, and Immortality of the Human Soul Arnobius Enumerates, and Whether He Refutes Them Correctly

It undoubtedly seems remarkable to some that Arnobius so explicitly asserts that Christ taught “what the human soul is; whether it flew to us of its own accord, or was sown and begotten together with the very entrails; [Col. 0475B] whether it lives subject to death, or has been endowed with the perpetuity of immortality.” (Arnob., bk. I, p. 22.) For he would not have dared to affirm so confidently that Christ taught these things unless he had read or known what Christ transmitted to us concerning the soul’s origin, nature, and immortality. But, they will say, if he read or knew these things, why is he accused of striking upon various reefs of error concerning that same soul? Before we examine whether he is censured justly or unjustly, it is useful to observe from Jerome what opinions and errors formerly existed concerning the origin of souls. In his letter to Augustine, Jerome enumerates them in these words:

“Concerning the condition of the soul, I remember your little question—or rather, the greatest question in the Church: whether it fell from heaven, as the philosopher Pythagoras, all the Platonists, and Origen think; whether it is derived from [Col. 0475C] God’s own substance, as the Stoics, Manichaeus, and the Spanish heresy of Priscillian suppose; whether souls, created long ago, are kept in God’s treasury, as certain ecclesiastical writers trust with foolish conviction; whether they are made by God each day and sent into bodies, according to what is written in the Gospel, ‘My Father works until now, and I work’; or whether they are certainly propagated by transmission, as Tertullian, Apollinaris, and the greater part of Westerners believe, so that, just as body is born from body, soul is born from soul and subsists under a condition similar to that of brute animals.” (Jerome, Epist. 165, p. 582.)

We have related these things because they will cast a useful light upon what must be said.

[Col. 0475D] Arnobius reports that there were formerly three opinions among the ancient philosophers concerning the condition of souls:

“One man,” these are his words (Arnob., bk. II, p. 82), “believes both that they are everlasting and that they survive the death of mortals; another does not believe that they survive, but that they perish together with the bodies themselves. A third holds that they do not immediately suffer extinction, but that after the human being has been laid to rest something of life is granted to them, after which they pass under the dominion of mortality.”

Elsewhere we have noted that the various opinions of those same philosophers concerning the soul are explained more distinctly by Cicero, Justin Martyr, Tertullian, Ambrose, and Augustine (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. II, diss. 2, ch. 7, §29, p. 436; Justin, *Exhortation*, p. 8, and the other passages cited in the *Apparatus*). Accordingly, [Col. 0476A] we shall add nothing else here except what the Latin Orator committed to writing and what is especially useful for explaining and confirming the position of our author. In the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, Cicero writes:

“There are those who think that the soul’s departure from the body is death. There are those who hold that no departure occurs, but that soul and body perish together, and that the soul is extinguished with the body. Among those who think that the soul departs, some believe that it is immediately dispersed, others that it remains for a long time, and others that it remains forever.” (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, bk. I, p. 118, line 4.)

He then explains the individual philosophers’ opinions concerning the nature of the soul. After reporting the views of Plato, Socrates, and Cato on the soul’s immortality, he says that the Epicureans, and especially Dicaearchus, contradicted them and taught that souls [Col. 0476B] are mortal: “The Stoics, however,” he continues (Ibid., p. 127), “grant us their use, as though we were quails. They say that souls will remain for a long time, but deny that they will remain forever.” Who does not see that Cicero, Jerome as already cited, and our Arnobius bring forward the same philosophical opinions concerning the soul and indicate who originated and defended them?

Our Arnobius refutes the absurd opinion of Epicurus and his followers with the force of these arguments:

“If souls approach the gates of death, as Epicurus’ doctrine determines, there is still no adequate reason why philosophy ought to be pursued, even if it is true that souls are purified by it and rendered clean from every vice. For if they perish indiscriminately, and their vital sensation fails and is extinguished in the very bodies, [Col. 0476C] it is not merely the greatest error but foolish blindness to bridle innate appetites, to confine life within narrow limits, to grant nothing to nature, and not to do what desires command and incite one to do, since no rewards for so great a labor await you when the day of death arrives and you are released from bodily bonds.” (Arnob., bk. II, pp. 64–65.)

That Epicurus’ assertion concerning the mortality of the soul was of this kind is evident from Laertius (Laertius, bk. X, *Life and Doctrines of Epicurus*, §63 ff.) and Lucretius, whose manner of expression Arnobius imitated from this verse:

> The gate of death, therefore, has not been barred against the mind.  
> (Lucretius, bk. III, v. 829.)

No one is so blind as not to see how powerful the argument is with which Arnobius refutes [Col. 0476D] this impious error. Certainly, who does not know that it possesses such force and weight that the Apostle Paul himself comprises the whole argument in these fewer words: “What does it profit me, if the dead do not rise? Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” (1 Cor. 15:32.)

Another error concerning the soul, as we have already seen from Jerome, was that souls derive from God’s own substance, or are a part of God, as Augustine rightly warns, or are divine, or even God himself, as we learn from these words of Cicero: “The soul, which—as I say—is divine, is, as Euripides dares to say, God.” (Augustine, Epist. 166, p. 584; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, bk. I, p. 125.) [Col. 0477A] Arnobius therefore undoubtedly marked this opinion as false when he denied that souls are daughters of the supreme King. (Arnob., bk. II, p. 68 ff.) He assails it with this argument:

“But if souls were, as rumor has it, the sovereign Lord’s offspring and the principal progeny of his power, nothing would have been lacking to their perfection, since they were begotten by the most perfect power. They would all have possessed one understanding and one agreement; they would always inhabit the royal palace and would not, after abandoning the seats of blessedness in which they had known and retained the most exalted teachings, imprudently seek these earthly places, so that, enveloped in dark bodies, they might live amid phlegm and blood, amid these wineskins of dung and the most obscene jars wrapped in sacks.”

Does Augustine not openly crush and overthrow the Manichaeans, who babbled that [Col. 0477B] the soul was a part of God, by a similar mode of argument? These are his words in writing to Jerome concerning the soul:

“The soul is not a part of God. For if it were, it would be entirely immutable and incorruptible. And if it were so, it would neither decline toward what is worse nor advance toward what is better; nor, as far as its own affections are concerned, would it begin to possess in itself anything that it did not possess, or cease to possess anything that it did possess. There is no need of external testimony to show how differently the matter actually stands: anyone who attends to himself knows it.” (Augustine, Epist. 166, p. 584.)

Our author also accuses of the greatest rashness those who taught that souls were begotten by God and sent here by him, so that beings of a divine and wholly incorporeal [Col. 0477C] nature might be thrust down into human bodies (Arnob., bk. II, p. 53). He endeavors to refute this opinion by almost the same arguments as the preceding one. No one, he says (Ibid., p. 70 ff.), will find it credible that those souls were sent by God into the world so that, being born from women, they might be subject to all the miseries, afflictions, calamities, accidents, losses, hardships, depraved affections of the mind, vices, sins, crimes, shameful deeds, evil acts, and other evils of infancy and subsequent stages of life, which he recounts at great length.

Nor will he permit the reply that they came here by their own will, not at God’s command. (Ibid., p. 73 ff.) For if that is so, the omnipotent God foresaw, yet did not prevent—as he could have done—those offspring of the first divinity [Col. 0477D] from falling into so many and such grave crimes and shameful deeds and from suffering so many and such great losses, adversities, and injuries. Yet surely whoever can prevent evils but does not, and instead permits them, is their cause. It is impious to say that the supremely wise and benevolent God is the cause of so many and such great evils, and that, because he did not prevent it although he could have done so, souls that had formerly been happy and free from every human contamination were sent and reduced to the miserable human condition, inclined toward every kind of crime. Does God not make all things perfect and capable of preserving the measures of their integrity—*mansiones* (royal manuscript: *mensiones*), or dimensions, as Arnobius says and as is confirmed from Cicero? (Cicero, *Orator*, p. 268.) Nor did Arnobius say this merely once or as though in passing; [Col. 0478A] he repeats and emphasizes the same proof at length, though in other words. (Arnob., bk. II, p. 76 ff.)

Some, however, think that this argument belongs to those who denied that humankind was created by God. But for them to make that observation correctly and judiciously, they should have shown us how Arnobius misuses that argument, as did the defenders of that impious error. For if he wished there to refute only the error of those who babbled that human souls were both divine and, as he puts it, the Lord’s offspring or daughters of God, he perhaps did not attack them badly with these arguments, just as Augustine did. For nothing except what is most perfect can proceed from God. But because he seems there to have undertaken to prove by this very argument that our souls are begotten [Col. 0478B] not by omnipotent God but by certain other powers, his proof is undoubtedly no less defective than his opinion is false. Whether he truly held this view concerning the origin of the soul we shall investigate in the following article.

With arguments of still greater weight he also strikes down the error according to which our souls were said to belong to a divine race (Ibid., p. 56 ff.); and another, according to which those same philosophers undoubtedly babbled that souls had existed long before the body and flown into this world most fully instructed in every science, discipline, and art, so that human knowledge, as Plato imagined, was nothing other than a recollection of former things (Plato, *Phaedo*, vol. I, p. 72 ff.; *Meno*, vol. II, p. 81 ff.; Cicero, [Col. 0478C] *Tusculan Disputations*, bk. I, p. 124). For if human souls were divine and had once known all things, no disagreement about anything could exist among human beings. Yet who in possession of his faculties would ever deny that this is utterly false?

Plato nevertheless attempts to confirm this opinion, however absurd and, as Lactantius thinks, derived from the fictions of poets, by the example—as Cicero also observes—of a little boy who, when questioned about geometrical measurement, answers as though he had learned geometry without a teacher (Plato, *Meno*, vol. II, p. 82 ff.; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, bk. I, p. 124, line 24). But that fictitious opinion is demolished by our Arnobius with another similar but far more effective example. Suppose, he says (Arnob., bk. II, [Col. 0478D] p. 57 ff.), that a boy were born in the most secluded place, exceedingly remote from every human habitation, and were brought up and nourished continuously in silence, without any clothing, and on only one kind of food and water alone, until the thirtieth or fortieth year of his life. Then let him come forth into human society and be questioned about his father, his upbringing and home, the various kinds of clothing and food, the sun, the moon, the earth, geometry, like Plato’s little boy, or any other discipline whatsoever. Would he not be ignorant of them all and more mute than a fish? If he were compelled to utter any sound, he would produce one that was entirely inarticulate.

As for Plato’s little boy, Arnobius maintains [Col. 0479A] that if he answers the questions correctly, he gives his answers not from things he recognizes through recollection, but from other things he had learned through daily experience. Our author therefore concludes that Plato was wholly mistaken (Plato, *Timaeus*, vol. III, p. 41) in believing that human souls, divine and imbued with all knowledge, issue into this world from living mixing-bowls. It must nevertheless be admitted that in this argument Arnobius is much more lengthy than he should have been, through his enumeration of many things that contributed little to it.

He therefore presses Plato more closely and sharply in this way. If the soul came into the world educated in every kind of learning, it ought to teach rather than learn (Arnob., bk. II, p. 61). Nor could Plato and his followers [Col. 0479B] reply that, when it is bound about by the body, it changes from learned to elementary—that is, as may be understood from Seneca, into something requiring instruction in the first elements (Seneca, Epist. 306, p. 102). For how could it be discerned whether it was recollecting former things or being taught new ones?

Furthermore, an incorporeal and immortal soul, such as they assert it to be, cannot forget everything it previously knew because of any impediment from the body. For if so great a change occurs within it, it will lose something of its integrity and will thus be capable of corruption, and will no longer be immortal.

Moreover, if the body causes the soul to forget all its former knowledge and understanding, how can the soul know that it had previously been instructed in the sciences but, because of the body’s obstruction, [Col. 0479C] had forgotten them all?

Finally, if the soul of an old man, enclosed within the body for eighty—or, if you wish, ninety or more—years, remembers deeds performed fifty or sixty years earlier, although the body does not impede it at all, why do they so persistently assert that everything the soul is said to have known perfectly before it was sent into the body afterwards escaped it?

These, then, are Arnobius’ arguments. Although they are not all of equal weight, no one will deny that, taken together, they completely and thoroughly destroy Plato’s error. Before we undertake to explain Arnobius’ own opinion concerning the human soul, it is useful to note certain expressions [Col. 0479D] that he borrowed from Lucretius in this discussion. For he writes that if souls yield to bodily assaults: “Life has been granted to them for use, not delivered into ownership.” (Arnob., bk. II, p. 62.) Lucretius had said:

> Life is given to no one in ownership, but to all for use.  
> (Lucretius, bk. III, v. 984.)

That is, no one is given proprietorship of life, but only its use.

Again Arnobius says: “It takes away the *repetentia* of former things,” that is, the capacity to revisit them (Arnob., bk. II, p. 63). Thus Lucretius had said in the poem previously cited by us:

> When once our capacity to revisit has been interrupted.  
> (Lucretius, bk. III, v. 864.)

Some, however, read *repentia nostra* there, while others read [Col. 0480A] *retinentia nobis*. But the former reading appears to be confirmed by the authority of our Arnobius. In that passage *repetentia* signifies the same thing as recollection.

## ARTICLE II. Whether Arnobius Was Right to Say That the Origin of the Human Soul Is Uncertain; Whether He Fell into the Error of Simon Magus, Saturninus, Carpocrates, and the Seleucians, Who Affirmed That It Was Created by Someone Other than God; and Whether Original Sin Was Unknown to Him

No one will deny that what Arnobius teaches is true: that all human souls flowed from one and the same source (Arnob., bk. II, p. 53). But he explains what this source is, from which they flowed, in such a way that he is not altogether undeservedly called to account for the very serious error whereby he signifies that it is uncertain.

[Col. 0480B] First, he introduces pagans who ask him by whose agency souls were begotten, how they were produced, and whether God is their parent and creator (Ibid., p. 75 ff.). What do you suppose he answers them? Quite plainly and candidly, he confesses that this is unknown not only to us but also to all the powers that exist in the world, and that it surpasses all their knowledge and ours.

But the pagans pressed him: If Christians join you in denying that souls were created by God, it is at least incumbent upon you to disclose by whom they were begotten. But he denies this too entirely. For, he says, we can without any blame be ignorant of the origin of souls and yet know that they are not God’s offspring [Col. 0480C] and were not begotten by him. Certainly, those who believed that they were made by God and came into human bodies said nothing definite and ascertained, but only what they had attained through conjecture and suspicion. Yet what, Arnobius asks, is the difference between suspicion and conjecture, uncertain opinion and ignorance?

Why, moreover, should it be surprising, he continues (Ibid., p. 78 ff.), if the origin of the human soul is unknown to us, when we have no clearer understanding of the source from which the souls of animals arise? For these are said to derive their origin not from Plato’s fictitious mixing-bowl, which he mentions in the *Timaeus*, but from the elements (Plato, *Timaeus*, vol. III, p. 41). Yet concerning which elements they come from, or how they are made, the philosophers are engaged in very great controversy, as they are concerning many other questions. [Col. 0480D] From this he concludes that there is no advantage in knowing these things and no harm in not knowing them, and that they should be left to God.

If Arnobius had confined himself within these limits, that moderation of his mind certainly ought not to have been blamed at all. For Augustine repeatedly and sincerely professed that the soul’s origin is exceedingly obscure and may remain hidden without danger. Indeed, in the first book of his *Retractations*, which he wrote when already an old man, he declares most openly that he had not yet discovered anything wholly certain and indubitable about it:

“As regards,” he says, “the origin of the soul, whereby it comes to be in the body—whether it derives from that one soul which was first created when the human being was made a living soul, or whether [Col. 0481A] individual souls are similarly made for individual persons—I did not know then, nor do I yet know.” (Arnob., bk. II, p. 86; Augustine, Epist. 102, p. 587; Epist. 119, p. 701; *Retractations*, bk. I, chs. 45 and 56; *Literal Commentary on Genesis*, bk. X, ch. 3; *On the Origin of the Soul*, bk. IV, chs. 5 and 11; bk. III, ch. 10; *Against Julian*, bk. LV, ch. 104; *Retractations*, bk. I, ch. 1.)

But our author, proceeding further, is accused of striking the reef of a false opinion and error. For he declares neither ambiguously nor hesitantly that we have learned from Christ that “souls are not daughters of the supreme King,” that is, of the highest God, “nor, as is said, were they begotten by him, began to know themselves, and were spoken of in the essential meaning of their own name” (the royal manuscript reads: “to exist within the meaning of their own name”); “but that they have some other progenitor, [Col. 0481B] separated from the Emperor”—that is, from God—“by a very great many degrees of dignity and power, yet belonging to his court and noble through the exalted splendor of his birth.” (Arnob., bk. II, p. 68.)

There he reveals his opinion concerning the origin of our souls with no obscurity at all. First, he rejects the opinion of those discussed in the preceding article, who believed that they were daughters of the supreme God, begotten by him, and had begun to know themselves before they were infused into the body. Second, he asserts that they were begotten by some progenitor who belonged to the court of that same supreme God and was noble through the splendor of his birth, but was separated from God himself by very many degrees of dignity and power.

[Col. 0481C] Nor should you suppose that he said this incautiously or hesitantly. For elsewhere he confidently declares it more than once. In one place he says: “We observe that human beings—that is, the souls themselves (for what are human beings but souls bound to bodies?)—by the innumerable savagery of their vices reveal that they are not of patrician stock, but were begotten from families of middling rank.” (Ibid., p. 75.) Elsewhere he says: “Not absurdly or vainly do we believe that human souls are of an intermediate quality, since they were produced by beings that are not principal.” (Ibid., p. 79.) What then? He accuses of impiety anyone who says that the soul was created by God: “Whoever conceives that the human being, an unhappy and wretched thing, was begotten by him [God], incurs the charge of sacrilegious impiety.” Who, therefore, will deny that Arnobius held this opinion as settled and certain, when he transmitted and asserted it so often, so clearly, and so consistently? It rests upon [Col. 0481D] no other foundation than his complete conviction, as we have seen, that human beings—or souls bound to human bodies and subject to so many vices—were not created by God, the supremely good and great, who can make nothing that is not altogether perfect and whole.

But Elmenhorst and Heraldus brand this opinion of Arnobius not only as false and erroneous, but also as madness, horrendous impiety, and blasphemy. They think that he drew this error from the school of Simon, Saturninus, Carpocrates, Marcion, the Seleucians, and the Hermians, notorious heretics. They attempt to prove this by the authority of Tertullian, who in his book *On the Prescriptions Against Heretics* (Tertullian, *On the Prescription of Heretics*, ch. 46) [Col. 0482A] writes that Simon Magus taught: “The world was fashioned by his angels”; that Saturninus taught (Ibid., ch. 48), “Angels far removed from God made the lower world”; and that Carpocrates said: “Powers far removed from the higher powers established this world in its lower regions.” But these things were written in the forty-sixth chapter of that book and in the subsequent chapters. We have observed elsewhere that those chapters were added to it by some impostor (vol. IV, *Apparatus*, pp. 8 and 15). Indeed, in the latest edition of Tertullian’s works it is noted that all these things are absent from the exceedingly ancient Agobard manuscript.

We are certainly aware that the same Tertullian, in his genuine book *On the Soul*, committed the following account of Saturninus to writing: [Col. 0482B]

“He affirms that the human being was made by angels and that, at first, the work was futile, feeble, and unstable, and writhed upon the ground like a worm because it lacked the strength to stand upright. Then, through the mercy of the supreme Power, in whose image—though an image not fully perceived—it had been rashly constructed, it received a little spark of life, which roused and raised it, gave it a firmer animation, and after the departure of life was itself to return to its original matrix.” (Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 23, p. 335.)

But no one can fail to see how greatly this error differs from the opinion of Arnobius explained above.

Furthermore, we observed in another book (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. II, diss. 1, ch. 3, art. 1, p. 286; art. 3, §2, p. 292; and ch. 5, §3, p. 317) that Saturninus taught that the human being and all other things were made by [Col. 0482C] angels without the Father’s knowledge; Carpocrates, that they were made by angels far inferior to the supreme Parent from whom they had defected; and Marcion, that they were created by another God. These monstrous opinions were undoubtedly rejected rather than adopted by Arnobius.

According to Augustine’s testimony, moreover, the Seleucians “do not attribute the soul to God as its Creator, but maintain that angels are the creators of souls from fire and spirit.” (Augustine, *On Heresies*, §56.) But these heretics appear to have lived after Arnobius. We make these observations for the benefit of those who rightly desire the writings and opinions of the ancient Fathers of the Church to be discussed accurately, and do not wish foreign errors—of which they never entertained any thought—to be ascribed to them.

Moreover, it matters little to know whether, and from which [Col. 0482D] heretics, Arnobius drew his opinion. For it is enough for us to know that it is deservedly condemned as false and erroneous. Augustine, indeed—to say nothing of others—rejects it in these words:

> “Those who believe their Plato that all mortal living beings were made, not by that supreme God who fashioned the world, but by other lesser beings whom he himself had created, acting with his permission or at his command—and that among these man would hold the chief place, one akin to the gods themselves—will readily rid themselves also of the error of this opinion if they rid themselves of the superstition by which they seek grounds for appearing justified in offering rites and sacrifices to those beings as though to their creators. For it is not right to believe or say that the creator of any nature, however small and mortal, is anyone but God, even before this can be understood.” [Col. 0483A] (Augustine, *On the City of God*, book XII, ch. 24, p. 322.)

Epiphanius and others demonstrate this same point from various sure testimonies of Holy Scripture. (Epiphanius, *Heresy* 23, § 5, p. 65 ff.)

Furthermore, although Arnobius seems so stubbornly to deny that human souls were created by the supreme God, it may perhaps be urged, not inappropriately, in his defense that he openly taught, as we have seen above (previous chapter), that the supreme God is the creator of all things, and specifically of the sun, the moon, and man himself. These, indeed, are his very words:

> “Do we not all owe to him, first of all, the very fact that we exist, that we are called human beings, that, whether sent forth by him or fallen away, we are confined in this bodily blindness? Does not the fact that we walk, breathe, [Col. 0483B] and live come to us from him, and does not the very power of living cause us to exist and to be moved by animal activity?” (Arnobius, book I, p. 16.)

But if the supreme God, about whom he is speaking there, is the creator of all things; if we owe to him the fact that we are human beings; if from him comes the fact that we exist and live—then it certainly follows that he is also the author and creator of our souls. For human beings, as we have observed him defining them (ibid., book II, pp. 52 and 56), are nothing other than souls enclosed in, or bound to, bodies.

What, then? Must he be said to have been inconsistent with himself and to have contradicted himself absurdly? But what prevents him from having maintained, without any instability or fickleness of mind whatever, that souls were created not by almighty God himself as their proximate cause, but by some other being among the higher powers, with God as only their remote cause and the first cause of all? Yet this does not appear to have been his opinion, because it is overturned by the same arguments with which, as we have said, he himself attempted to prove that souls, being subject to vices, could not have been created by the supreme God. Is it not therefore more likely that, carried away by the heat of argument, he pressed and pursued his argument beyond its proper limits? If, however, anyone should prove to us with certainty that he believed human souls to have been created not at all by the supreme God but only by certain inferior powers most noble by the splendor of their birth, we shall immediately admit that he erred, and we shall not follow him in his error.

Yet perhaps someone will not fail to suggest to us [Col. 0483D] that Arnobius fell into this error because he was not acquainted with the stain of original sin, by which man was made subject to so many miseries, weaknesses, and unlawful desires. But how could Arnobius have been ignorant of original sin, when we read that he wrote:

> “Because, through the fault of an inborn weakness, we are prone to sins and to the various appetites of lust, God permits himself always to be conceived in our thoughts, so that, while we pray to him and strive to deserve his gifts, we may receive the will to innocence and, by the removal of all offenses, cleanse ourselves from every stain.” (Ibid., book I, p. 15.)

What, I ask you, is that “fault of an inborn weakness” (*ingenitae infirmitatis vitium*) if not original sin itself? Indeed, even heterodox writers frankly and unequivocally acknowledge this. [Col. 0484A] (Hoornbeeck, *Theological Exercises*, book I, § II, p. 130.)

Why, then, you will say, does he strive with such great labor, such great effort, and such lengthy discourses to prove that the soul of man, who is subject to so many and such great miseries, could not have been created by God? Could he not have explained the matter merely by an exposition of original sin, or simply by mentioning its name? Certainly he could. But I would have you observe that he is arguing against the pagans, who had dreamed that our souls were divine, or divine offspring, or a part of God, and who had never so much as dreamed of original sin. What, then, if he refuted them solely from their own principles and argued *ad hominem*, as they say, and thought that original sin should be mentioned not there, [Col. 0484B] but elsewhere? And what can be established by a negative argument against something that we have asserted?

## ARTICLE III. What Arnobius’s true opinion was concerning the nature and immortality of the human soul, and whether he fell into some error concerning it

We must still diligently inquire what Arnobius thought concerning the nature of the human soul itself and its immortality, and whether, in defining it, he once again fell into error, as some suppose. Heraldus accuses him of having taught that the soul is corporeal and mortal. But this grave charge undoubtedly requires examination.

First, therefore, Heraldus thinks that our author regarded human souls [Col. 0484C] as corporeal because he supposed them to be affected by the sensation of pain. But where in the world did he set this down in writing? Where Arnobius speaks about Plato, Heraldus says, he uses these words:

> “He undertakes an insoluble problem: although he says that souls are immortal, everlasting, and devoid of bodily solidity, he nevertheless says that they are punished and subjects them to the sensation of pain. But what human being does not see that what is immortal and simple can admit no pain, while that which feels pain cannot possess immortality?” (Arnobius, book II, p. 52.)

Arnobius, however, is not explaining his own mind and opinion there; rather, he shows that Plato was in conflict with himself when he asserted that souls, although immortal and incorporeal, were affected by the sensation of pain. For whatever is affected by pain, he says, must plainly be mortal. What, then, is there in this refutation that deserves condemnation?

But, you will say, he in fact taught most openly that our souls are mortal. For shortly afterward, in the same passage, he added:

> “They are of an intermediate quality, as has been learned on the authority of Christ, and are capable of perishing if they have been ignorant of God; but they may be delivered unto life and freed from destruction if they apply themselves to his threats (the royal manuscript reads: ‘seeds’) and acts of mercy.” (Ibid.)

Later, moreover, he refutes the opinion of the philosophers—undoubtedly the Platonists—who asserted that souls are immortal (ibid., p. 63 ff.), on the ground that, if this were true, anyone, despising the virtues, would securely and fearlessly [Col. 0485A] plunge headlong into every kind of pleasure and crime. For he would be restrained by no fear of the supreme power:

> “One,” he says (ibid., p. 64), “who has been persuaded that he is as immortal as the first God himself.”

For then he would know himself to be so incorruptible that he could be struck and disturbed by no pain or agitation of mind whatever, nor polluted by the foulness of any shameful act. Indeed, as he says (ibid.), one who has no corporeal substance cannot be contaminated by any stain of sin. He says that this is why the intermediate and equivocal nature of souls gave philosophy occasion to assert that rewards await the good and punishments the wicked. By this conviction each person is kept within his duty. Hence he concludes:

> “Since these things are so, and since we hold it as handed down by the supreme author that [Col. 0485B] souls are not situated far from the chasms and jaws of death, yet may be made long-lived by the gift and favor of the supreme prince, provided only that they attempt and strive to know him . . . and then, having put aside savagery and inhumanity, resume gentler dispositions, so that they may be prepared for that which will be given—why are we judged by you to be brutish and foolish, if because of these fears we have surrendered and bound ourselves to God as our deliverer?” (Ibid., p. 65.)

He also shows that this opinion concerning the intermediate condition of souls cannot be rejected by the pagans, because they believed that their gods, by whatever name they called them, were of the same intermediate nature:

> “You who do not believe,” he says (ibid., p. 67), “that souls are of an intermediate quality and are confined upon the middle boundary between life and destruction—are not absolutely all those whom opinion supposes to be gods, angels, demons, or whatever other name they bear, themselves also of an intermediate quality and mutable in the condition of an uncertain lot?” [Col. 0485C]

There he reported Plato’s meaning, not his actual words, which you will find in the philosopher’s *Timaeus*, the work he undoubtedly cited, and quoted by Athenagoras, Cicero, and others. (Plato, *Timaeus*, vol. III, p. 41 ff.; Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 6; Cicero, *On the Universe*, in the fragments, vol. II, p. 29.)

Finally, Arnobius explained this opinion of his concerning the nature of our soul in these very clear and entirely unambiguous words:

> “Not incongruously or without reason do we believe that human souls are of an intermediate quality, since they were produced by beings that are not primal, are subject to the law [Col. 0485D] of death, and, though their powers are slight and perishable, may be endowed with perpetuity if they refer their hope of so great a gift to God, the supreme ruler, who alone has the power to bestow such things with corruption excluded.” (Arnobius, book II, p. 79.)

Is it not, then, proved sufficiently clearly from what has been said thus far that Arnobius held the opinion that human souls possess a certain quality and nature intermediate between mortality and immortality? He teaches that this intermediate condition consists in the soul’s being mortal by its own nature and becoming immortal solely by the gift and favor of God. Accordingly, he later declares still more plainly (ibid., p. 87):

> “No one but almighty God can preserve souls, nor is there anyone else who can make them long-lived and supply them with the spirit [Col. 0486A] of perpetuity, except him who alone is immortal and everlasting and is bounded by no limitation of time.”

Here observe in passing that, according to Petavius, by the term “long-lived” he means the same thing as if he had said “eternal.” (Petavius, vol. I, *Dogmatic Theology*, book III, ch. 3, p. 191.) This, then, appears to be the genuine opinion of our Arnobius concerning the nature of the human soul—an opinion which, as you see, he explained neither only once nor obscurely.

But on this account he is accused of several errors. First, he decides that souls are immortal through the favor of God alone, but mortal by their own nature and subject to death, from which they are rescued by God alone. Yet whatever is mortal must undoubtedly be corporeal. And who does not know that this is the error of certain ancient writers, [Col. 0486B] condemned long ago and not without ignominy?

Secondly, Arnobius thinks that human souls become immortal only by God’s favor, provided that they have acknowledged him and merited this benefit. But from this it further follows that he was persuaded that the souls of the impious and unbelieving perish and are not endowed with immortality by God. This second error, moreover, has deservedly been branded with a mark of censorial severity no less grave than the first.

As regards the first error, however, it is certainly not easy to say whether Arnobius fell into it unless it is first established what he understood by the expression “a nature intermediate between the mortal and the immortal.” Although he did not define this plainly and distinctly, it is nevertheless certain that he declared it for this reason: he consistently believed what we read as asserted by the Apostle (1 Timothy 6:16), that God alone is truly immortal. For what could be clearer and more explicit than these words of our author, to omit the rest?

> “Is not he alone unbegotten, alone immortal and everlasting?” (Arnobius, book II, p. 95.)

Indeed, he asserts that God alone is incorporeal:

> “Unbegotten,” he says (ibid., book I, p. 17), “immortal, everlasting, alone delineated by no bodily form and bounded by no circumscription.”

But if Arnobius denied that the soul is immortal only in the sense that it is immortal in a manner different from God’s, he certainly advanced nothing but what is sound and orthodox:

> “The human soul,” says Augustine, [Col. 0486D] “is immortal according to a certain manner proper to it. For it is not so in every respect, as is he of whom it was said: ‘Who alone possesses immortality.’” (Augustine, letter 146, p. 584.)

He then explains how the soul can be called both corporeal and incorporeal:

> “That the soul is incorporeal,” he writes to Jerome (ibid. ff.), “although this may be difficult to persuade slower minds, I nevertheless confess that I myself am persuaded of it. But lest I either create an unnecessary controversy over a word or rightly incur one—for when the matter is agreed upon, there is no need to quarrel about the name—if every substance or essence, or whatever that which exists in some way in itself is more aptly called, is a body, then the soul is a body. Likewise, if it is thought proper to call incorporeal only that nature [Col. 0487A] which is supremely immutable and wholly present everywhere, then the soul is a body, since the soul itself is not such a thing. But if nothing is a body except that which is so situated or moved through spatial extent in length, breadth, and height that a greater part of it occupies a greater place and a smaller part a smaller place, and it is less in the part than in the whole, then the soul is not a body. For throughout the entire body that it animates it extends, not by local diffusion but by a certain vital intensity. . . . Accordingly, if the soul is to be called a body, it certainly is not a body such as an earthly body, nor such as a watery, airy, or ethereal body. . . . Hence it is understood that the soul, whether it is to be called a body or corporeal, possesses a certain nature proper to itself, created with a substance more excellent than all these elements of the material mass of the world, [Col. 0487B] which cannot truly be conceived through any mental image of corporeal things such as we perceive through the senses of the flesh, but must be understood by the mind and felt by life.”

Augustine therefore acknowledges that, according to various modes of speaking, the human soul can be called corporeal and incorporeal, mortal and immortal. What, then, if Arnobius called it corporeal in the first sense, and for the same reason mortal, because it received its immortality from God himself, by whom it was created, as we noted concerning Tatian? (Vol. I, *Apparatus*, book II, dissertation 5, ch. 2, § 4, p. 539.) Will you deny that he is thereby vindicated from error?

And can it not be established that this was his mind and opinion from the words in which he himself proposes the following question?

> “And how can bodies unite themselves with incorporeal beings, or things made by God the supreme ruler be handed over by weaker causes to the dishonors of vice?” (Arnobius, book II, p. 53.)

I would have you attend to what he answers to that question. In turn he asks the pagans (ibid.) whether, laying aside the disdain and arrogance of their minds, they claim to share one and the same immortality with God the Father. Later, once again refuting the same error of the pagan philosophers, he says:

> “But if human beings [Col. 0487C] thoroughly knew either themselves or received some breath of an apprehension of God, they would never claim for themselves the divine and immortal nature.” (Ibid., p. 56.)

Can it not be inferred from this, not altogether inappropriately, that Arnobius’s opinion was that the human soul is immortal not in the same manner as God, but in an entirely different manner—namely, with an immortality which it does not possess from itself but has received from God, and which depends upon his power? But if this is his mind and opinion, and if he acknowledged no other intermediate condition of our soul than that by which it may be called intermediate between the immortal and incorporeal nature of God and other mortal and corporeal natures, it must be admitted that he was not altogether in error. For Petavius proved, from the authority of several ancient Fathers of the Church, that God alone is immortal for this reason: he did not receive immortality from another and is utterly immutable. (Petavius, vol. I, *Dogmatic Theology*, book III, ch. 4, § 10 ff., [Col. 0488A] p. 90 ff.) But whether this very opinion is Arnobius’s true opinion, I would have you consider and judge. Meanwhile, however, let us see whether he really thought the human soul to be altogether immortal.

## ARTICLE IV. Whether Arnobius taught that the souls of the impious are eventually to be reduced to nothing, or denied the future resurrection of our bodies

We seem to hear certain persons, together with Heraldus and some others, vehemently pressing against the opinion concerning the immortality of the human soul that we have ascribed to Arnobius, and asserting that he really believed the souls of the impious to die and, although not immediately extinguished, nevertheless to be consumed by the torments of a very long period. For he spoke of them not obscurely but clearly and openly:

> “They are cast into rushing rivers [Col. 0488B] of flames and, reduced to nothing, vanish away in the frustration of perpetual destruction.” (Arnobius, book II, p. 52.)

Nor do they allow it to be objected that in this passage he reports Plato’s opinion no less than his own. For he added the following in the same place:

> “And, to make plain what is unknown, this is the true death of man, this is the death that leaves no remainder.
