For that which is seen before our eyes is the separation of souls from the body, not the final end of annihilation. This, I say, is the true death of man: when souls that do not know God are consumed through the torment of a very long time by savage fire, into which they will be cast by certain beings who are cruelly fierce, unknown before Christ and disclosed by him who alone knew them.”

Does he not, they say, himself clearly and openly declare there that the souls of the impious and of those ignorant of God are to be tormented for only a very long interval of time, with their torments eventually to end, and are finally to be reduced to nothing? [Col. 0488C]

What, moreover, of the fact that he later expressly taught:

> “In this manner immortality is the gift of God the giver with regard to the gods brought forth, and in this manner he will deign to endow souls with immortality, although savage death may seem able to extinguish them and, once they have been reduced to nothing, to destroy them by an irreversible annihilation.” (Ibid., p. 68.)

But in this latter passage he seems to imply nothing other than that our souls, however incorporeal and spiritual in substance they may be, can—which no one denies—be utterly destroyed and reduced to nothing by God, their creator. The whole difficulty, however, turns upon whether [Col. 0488D] he believed that the souls of wicked human beings would really perish after they had been tortured by fire for a very long period. Yet because he thinks, as we have said, that the souls of faithful and pious human beings become immortal solely by God’s favor, it certainly follows that he thought the souls of unbelievers, deprived of this gift of immortality, would truly perish at some time and be altogether extinguished. Accordingly, he addresses the pagans in these words:

> “Your state is poised in uncertainty—I mean the salvation of your souls—and unless you apply yourselves to the knowledge of God the supreme ruler, savage death awaits you when you have been released from bodily bonds: a death that does not bring sudden extinction, but consumes through the course of time by the harshness of tormenting punishment.” (Ibid., p. 86.)

[Col. 0489A] He is therefore speaking of the punishments to be suffered after death by pagans—that is, unbelieving human beings—as though those punishments were not eternal but were eventually to come to an end together with their souls.

Nevertheless, he teaches no less plainly and clearly that there are certain unquenchable fires by which those souls of the impious are tormented. For he addresses the pagans who mocked this Christian opinion as follows:

> “You dare to mock us when we speak of Gehenna and of certain unquenchable fires into which we have learned that souls are cast by their enemies and adversaries.” (Ibid., p. 52.)

Elsewhere also he expressly speaks of “the unquenchable flames of Gehenna.” (Book IV, p. 159.) Nor should you reply that he indeed calls the fires unquenchable, but passes over in silence whether the souls of the impious [Col. 0489B] are to be tormented by them always and forever. For he asserts that those fires are kindled precisely so that the souls of the impious may be cast into them by their enemies, that is, by demons. But if those fires are everlasting while the souls are nevertheless eventually to be reduced to nothing, then surely the fires would be useless after all those souls had ceased to exist. Who will persuade us that Arnobius adopted so absurd an opinion and contradicted himself so absurdly? If, however, anyone should prove correctly that he asserted this, we shall immediately yield and admit that he erred disgracefully.

But Arnobius is accused—if it please God—of an even graver error by Elmenhorst and Heraldus where he argues as follows against the pagans concerning the resurrection of our bodies:

> “You dare,” he says (Arnobius, book II, p. 51), “to mock us because we say that there will be a resurrection of the dead. We confess that we do indeed say this, but you understand us otherwise than we mean. What does Plato say in the *Statesman*? When the world begins to rise from the western regions and to turn toward the axis belonging to the rising sun, does he not write that human beings will again burst forth from the bosom of the earth—old, gray-haired, and decrepit—and that, when their years begin to grow longer, they will pass through the same stages by which people now grow and finally arrive at the cradle of infancy?”” [Col. 0489C]

This passage of Plato, whose meaning rather than words Arnobius presents, is indeed found in the cited *Statesman*. (Plato, vol. II, *Statesman*, p. 170.) There is no need to quote the words themselves here, for doing so would require a longer undertaking, and there can be no controversy whatever concerning them.

Yet it is truly astonishing how great a brand of infamy—not merely of error, but of madness and frenzy—is thereby stamped upon our author. For if we believe Elmenhorst:

> “He raves with the frenzied men Marcion, Basilides, and Origen, who believed in a resurrection not of the flesh but of the body, and specifically of a spiritual body.”

These are the exact words of one who accuses Arnobius as gravely as he does rashly. We have transcribed them so that no one may think our statement of the matter unworthy of belief. But what greater rashness could there be than boldly to accuse a most ancient author of error, madness, and frenzy, yet offer no reason for the accusation? Elmenhorst offers none, [Col. 0490A] and we shall soon show that not even the slightest reason can be offered.

With Heraldus, however, the matter sticks fast: he appears hesitant and uncertain of precisely what error concerning the resurrection of bodies he should accuse Arnobius. For he reproaches him sometimes for approaching Origen’s false opinion, sometimes for approaching a still graver error, sometimes for approaching Marcion’s madness, and sometimes for neither teaching nor discovering anything certain about the resurrection.

But both his and Elmenhorst’s censures and accusations are utterly unjust and trifling. For Arnobius is not there expressly discussing the return of dead human beings to life. He is arguing against the pagans, who, although they conducted no affairs without faith and although they placed faith in the tenets of philosophers, which sometimes bore some resemblance to ours, nevertheless mocked Christians for believing both [Col. 0490B] Christ and all the articles of his teaching. While surveying the various articles of this teaching, he comes to the one concerning the resurrection of our bodies. There, by an argument *ad hominem*, as they like to say, he merely shows that the accusation made by the pagans was utterly foolish, because Christians placed due faith in the absolutely certain words of the Apostle writing to the Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 4:12 ff.), whereas pagans placed undue faith in Plato’s thoroughly doubtful account of souls returning to life. What in this argument can be accused of error, madness, or frenzy? What, I ask you, could be more unjust than to accuse Arnobius of the very error that he condemns and repudiates? Nor should you object that he did not explain his own opinion there. For no inference may properly be drawn against [Col. 0490C] him from his silence. Moreover, this was not the place for explaining his own opinion, since there he only repels and assails, as we have said, the foolish mockery and accusations of the pagans concerning the faith of Christians. But we must now discuss that Christian faith more fully.

# CHAPTER X. On the Faith, Hope, Churches, Holy Scriptures, Altars, Images, Synaxes, and Prayers Even for the Dead among Christians

## ARTICLE I. On the Faith of Christians and Its Necessity, Their Sure Hope of the Life to Come, and How Greatly It Is Opposed to the Opinions of the Pagans

[Col. 0490D]

Since Arnobius demonstrated the supreme divinity of Christ the Lord by various weighty arguments, as we have seen, it is certainly no wonder that he most firmly asserts that everyone must place faith in Christ’s words as divine. For he shows that Christ spoke the truth and must be believed by precisely the same arguments by which he asserts and vindicates his supreme divinity. But because the pagans were accustomed to mock this faith of the Christians, our author therefore proves by a brief induction that even human faith is so necessary (Arnobius, book II, p. 47) that the pagans themselves are compelled not only to place it in their own authors and philosophers, but also do not presume to undertake any affairs—voyages, cultivation of the land, [Col. 0491A] marriages, wars, and other matters, whether human or divine—unless faith goes before them.

Rufinus afterward used the same argument in such a way that he seems to have drawn it from our author himself. For he took the same examples and argued from them in this manner:

> “So that the way to understanding may lie open to you, you rightly profess that first of all you believe, because no one enters the sea and commits himself to the fluid and deep element unless he first believes that he can be saved. Nor does the farmer bury seed in the furrows and scatter crops upon the earth unless he believes that rains will come and that the warmth of the sun will also be present, by which the earth, being warmed, may bring forth crops with multiplied fruit and nourish them as the winds blow. In short, nothing can be done in life unless belief has gone before it. What wonder is it, therefore, [Col. 0491B] if, when approaching God, we profess first of all that we believe, since without this not even ordinary life itself can be conducted? We have set these points forth at the beginning because the pagans are accustomed to object to us that our religion, because it lacks rational arguments, consists solely in the persuasion to believe. We have therefore shown that nothing can either be done or remain established unless the power of believing has preceded it. Finally, marriages are contracted because it is believed that offspring will follow; children are entrusted to instruction in the arts because it is believed that the learning of their teachers will be transmitted to the pupils; and one man assumes the insignia of imperial power because he believes that peoples and cities, and even an armed army, will obey.” (Rufinus, *Commentary on the Creed*, shortly after the beginning, p. 171.)

Before him, Origen used the same argument and the same examples in refuting Celsus, and Eusebius used them in refuting pagans generally and proving the necessity of faith. [Col. 0491C] (Origen, *Against Celsus*, book I, pp. 9–10; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book I, ch. 5, p. 14 ff.) They pursue these points still more abundantly. It would therefore be too lengthy an undertaking to transcribe all their words, which everyone may read in their books, readily accessible to anyone. Whoever wishes to consult them may perhaps find the effort worthwhile and will do us a kindness if he can discover and indicate whether one of them culled his material from another. We have discussed the necessity of faith elsewhere. (Vol. I, *Apparatus*, book II, dissertation 2, ch. 11, art. 2, p. 1025 ff.)

From the same assertion of Christ’s divinity it follows that the hope and expectation of Christians concerning eternal salvation and the things Christ promised are wholly firm and certain. For he certainly cannot be God who does not fulfill his promises. Nor does Arnobius permit the pagans to object that the hope of Christians is vain and empty (Arnobius, book II, p. 44), or that the things Christ had so often promised were not fulfilled and given by him. For he kept his promises at the appointed time; and his miracles and the other things divinely performed by him are a pledge and confirmation of his other promises, neither doubtful nor uncertain.

Arnobius shows in addition how greatly Christians and pagans differed from one another concerning the hope of the future salvation of souls after death. The pagans, he says (ibid., book II, p. 66), placing the salvation of their souls in themselves, [Col. 0492A] believed that by their own effort alone they became gods; Christians, by contrast, distrusting the powers of their weak nature, awaited it from the mercy of almighty God. The pagans believed that they would acquire wings after death, with which they would fly up into heaven. Indeed, they dreamed that there were certain powers which, softened by the superstitious observances of secret arts and the commendatory prayers of magicians, gave easy access to heaven to those striving toward it. (Ibid., pp. 52 and 87.) On this matter one should read Plato in his genuine or spurious works, Servius, and Porphyry as quoted by Augustine. (Plato, *Phaedo*, vol. I, p. 107, and *Axiochus*, vol. III, p. 371; Servius, on *Aeneid* VI.758; Augustine, *On the City of God*, book X, chs. 9–10, p. 246 ff.)

For Christians, however, it is uncertain whether they may eventually merit to receive immortal life. [Col. 0492B] Finally, the pagans believed that of their own accord, with no one preventing them, they would return to the Lord’s abode as though it were their own proper dwelling. Christians, by contrast, did not hope that this could occur without the Lord of all things—that is, unless almighty God and Christ the Lord of immortality bestowed grace and the reward of eternal blessedness upon those who merited it, in the manner we explained above (previous chapter, art. 4). Do you wish to hear our Arnobius himself speaking? Here are his words:

> “Through him alone is there entrance to the Light; nor is it otherwise granted either to creep in or to force an entry, since all other approaches are closed and fortified by an impregnable citadel. Therefore, although you may have been pure and cleansed from every contamination of vice, and although you may have won over and bent those powers so that, when you return to heaven, they do not [Col. 0492C] close the roads and obstruct your passage, you will be able by no exertions to attain the reward of immortality unless you receive it through the bestowal of Christ, who creates immortality itself, and are admitted to true life.” (Arnobius, book II, p. 90.)

The madness of the pagans was therefore extreme, since they expected blessed immortality from some powers or other, or from themselves. By contrast, the hope of Christians is entirely certain: provided they are worthy, they trust that they will receive this blessed immortality from almighty God, its sole giver.

## ARTICLE II. On the Churches, Holy Scriptures, and Synaxes of the Christians; the Rite by Which They Prayed to God in Them; and What They Asked of Him

[Col. 0492D]

To proceed to other matters that likewise concern Christians: when the pagans objected that Christians had built no sacred edifices, Arnobius replied in such a way that he seems by no means to deny it. (Arnobius, book VI, p. 189.) What, then? Did Christians really have no sacred edifices, houses, churches, or temples in his time, in which they might all assemble together and pray to God? By no means. For they had many, which the Apostle calls “churches,” Eusebius calls προσευκτηρίων τοὺς οἴκους, “houses in which they prayed,” and Arnobius himself calls “meeting places” (*conventicula*). (Paul, First Epistle to the Corinthians, ch. XV, v. 15; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, ch. 2, p. 293; Arnobius, book [Col. 0493A] IV, p. 152.)

But Arnobius complains, with a sense of grief as bitter as it was just, that these had been destroyed by the pagans, just as the writings of the Christians had been consigned to the flames:

> “Why indeed,” he says, “did our writings deserve to be given to the flames? Why were our meeting places, in which the supreme God is prayed to, savagely destroyed?”

Just as no one could ever deny that Christians possessed their own writings and the sacred books of divine Scripture, so no one can deny that, before Arnobius’s time and during it, they possessed their own churches—or, as he preferred to call them, meeting places—where these had not been destroyed by the pagans. We have discussed above his reference to their destruction and to the burning of the sacred books. (Above, ch. 2, art. 1; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 731 ff.; dissertation on Minucius, ch. 12, art. 2.) Elsewhere [Col. 0493B] we have also explained why Arnobius seems to admit that the Christians had no churches, or no temples such as the pagans had, even though he declares most openly that they had built meeting places. Since no person of sound mind can deny this, no one can deny that Christian synaxes were held in these meeting places, by whatever name they may be called.

If you wish to know what they did in them, hear it in the very words of Arnobius himself:

> “The supreme God is prayed to; peace and pardon are requested for all—for magistrates, armies, kings, relatives, and enemies.” (Arnobius, book IV, p. 152.)

Cyril of Jerusalem joins him as a supporting witness and speaks somewhat more fully. (Cyril of Jerusalem, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 5, p. 539):

> Παρακαλοῦμεν [Col. 0493C] τὸν θεὸν ὑπὲρ κοινῆς τῶν Ἐκκλησιῶν εἰρήνης, ὑπὲρ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου εὐσταθείας, ὑπὲρ βασιλέων, ὑπὲρ στρατιωτῶν, καὶ συμμάχων, ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐν ἀσθενείαις, ὑπὲρ τῶν καταπονουμένων, καὶ ἀπαξαπλῶς, ὑπὲρ πάντων βοηθείας δεομένων.
>
> “We beseech God for the common peace of the Churches, for the stability of the world, for kings, for soldiers and allies, for those in sickness, for those who are afflicted, and, in sum, for all who stand in need of help.”

He adds that all Christians then invoked the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and martyrs, so that through their intercession God might hear their prayers and grant what they requested. But before either of these authors, Tertullian said more on these matters, as we shall see in the proper place. (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 40.)

But Arnobius explains as follows what, and by what rite and custom, the Christians there [Col. 0493D] prayed to God:

> “Before Him we all customarily prostrate ourselves; Him we adore with our prayers joined together; from Him we ask what is just and worthy of His hearing—not because He desires us to be suppliants or loves to see the veneration of so many thousands prostrated before Him. This is for our benefit and has regard to our own advantage.” (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 14 ff.)

Tertullian, however, when contending against Marcion’s error concerning two gods, says:

> “Toward another’s heaven one stretches out to another god; upon another’s earth one prostrates oneself before another god.” (Tertullian, bk. I, *Against Marcion*, ch. 24.)

Someone will undoubtedly tell us that this last word, “prostrates oneself” (*sternitur*), is explained by some as referring to those performing public penance, in accordance with this statement by the same Tertullian:

> “Confession (*exomologesis*) [Col. 0494A] is a discipline of prostrating and humbling a person.” (The same, *On Penance*, ch. 9.)

But it is already conceded that this must be understood of a plurality of Christians. Nor is it any less certain and evident that Arnobius spoke generally of all Christians (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 15), who in their assemblies prayed to God while prostrate and, as he says, adored Him with their prayers joined together. Are these not the joined prayers of which Tertullian elsewhere says:

> “We are a body through our shared consciousness of religion, the unity of our discipline, and the covenant of faith. We assemble before God so that, as though forming a band, we may surround Him with prayers. Such force is pleasing to God.” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 39, p. 34.)

Indeed, by this host of people praying they applied a force pleasing to God, so that they might obtain from Him, Arnobius continues (ibid.), [Col. 0494B] the will to innocence and purification from every stain of every transgression.

It is therefore no wonder that he openly asserts that absolutely nothing was heard in the assemblies

> “except what makes people humane, except what makes them gentle, modest, decent, chaste, generous sharers of their possessions, and bound to all by the bond of a firmly united brotherhood.”

(The same, bk. IV, p. 152.)

For this reason Augustine said more briefly, to be sure, but no less clearly:

> “The people flock to the churches in a chaste gathering, with an honorable separation of the two sexes, where they may hear how well they ought to live here for a time, so that after this life they may deserve to live blessedly and forever.”

(Augustine, bk. II, *The City of God*, ch. 28, p. 57.)

But we have discussed elsewhere what took place in Christian assemblies, and [Col. 0494C] all these matters mentioned by Arnobius will be explained still more clearly in our dissertation on Tertullian’s *Apology* (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 23 and 411; Dissertation on Tertullian, ch. 15, art. 2 ff.).

## ARTICLE III. On Christian Prayers for the Dead

In their sacred assemblies Christians prayed publicly to God not only for the living but also for the dead. For in them, Arnobius says,

> “the supreme God is entreated; peace and pardon are sought . . . for those still passing their lives and for those released from the bonds of their bodies.”

(Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 152.)

These words are so transparent and explicit that certain heterodox writers have been unable to obscure their clarity. [Col. 0494D] Yet the clearer they are, the more they have stirred black bile in others, who see perfectly well that from them it may be inferred with no uncertainty that there is some purgatory, or some place—by whatever name it may be called—where the souls of the righteous who die stained by certain blemishes of lighter sins are purified. But however much they gnash their teeth and employ every device, they will never diminish the authority of Arnobius. For why, I ask you, does he mention these prayers—which he could have omitted without in the least weakening the force of his argument? Why does he so boldly confront the pagans with them, unless because he knew with absolute certainty that it was an ancient, common, and pious custom of Christians to pray to God for the dead?

[Col. 0495A] And indeed, that this was the practice and custom of Christians contemporary with Arnobius and of those before him is most explicitly attested not only by writers of Arnobius’s own age, but also by very many earlier authors of unimpeachable credibility. For Tertullian writes the following against those who marry twice:

> “Nor will you be able to hate your former wife, for whom you preserve an even more religious affection now that she has been received by the Lord: you pray for her spirit and make annual offerings for her.”

(Tertullian, *Exhortation to Chastity*, ch. 2, p. 671.)

Again, in the following book he says:

> “A wife prays for the soul of her husband, asks meanwhile for refreshment for him and fellowship in the first resurrection, and makes an offering on the annual days of his falling asleep.”

(The same, *On Monogamy*, ch. 10, p. 682.)

[Col. 0495B] Nor is there any reason for a heterodox opponent to object that, when Tertullian composed these books, he had already defected to the party of the heretics and had drawn this doctrine from Montanus. For before he fell into that heresy, when briefly recounting the sacred rites of Christians, he is found to have taught precisely the same thing:

> “We make offerings for the dead and for their birthdays on their annual day.”

(The same, *The Soldier’s Crown*, ch. 3.)

Thus, so far is his testimony concerning these prayers from being weakened by the heterodox reply that it instead demonstrates more fully that this was a constant and certain teaching among heretics as well as Catholics.

The very ancient author of the *Apostolic Constitutions* exhorted Christians to pray to God for their dead brethren [Col. 0495C] as follows:

> “Let us pray for our brethren who have fallen asleep in Christ, that God, the lover of humanity, who received the soul of the deceased, may forgive him every voluntary and involuntary sin; and, becoming gracious and merciful to him, may place him in the region of the devout, who rest in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, together with all who from the beginning of the world have pleased God and done His will, whence pain, sorrow, and groaning have fled away.”

(*Apostolic Constitutions*, bk. VIII, chs. 40–41, p. 769 ff.)

He then directs that the third, ninth, fortieth, and anniversary days after their death be observed with prayers poured forth in the same manner.

Cyprian, moreover, writes the following to the people of Furni:

> “Our predecessor bishops decreed that [Col. 0495D] no brother should appoint a cleric as guardian or curator; and that, if anyone did so, no offering should be made for him, nor should the sacrifice for his falling asleep be celebrated.”

(Cyprian, Epistle 1, p. 2.)

We have indeed cited these words elsewhere, where, by the authority of Ambrose and other Fathers of the Church, we defended this position against the foolish quibbles and frivolous replies of the heretics (*Notes on Ambrose, Consolation on the Death of Valentinian*, p. 1194; and above, pp. 1121 and 1135).

Let Cyril of Jerusalem also come forward. In the preceding article we heard him discussing Christian prayers for all kinds of living people; now let us hear him speak of prayers for the dead (Cyril, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 5, p. 539):

> Δεόμεθα πάντες [Col. 0496A] ἡμεῖς ὑπὲρ πάντων, ἁπλῶς τῶν ἐν ἡμῖν προκεκοιμημένων, μεγίστην ὄνησιν πιστεύοντες ἔσεσθαι ταῖς ψυχαῖς, ὑπὲρ ὧν δέησις ἀναφέρεται τῆς ἁγίας, καὶ φρικωδεστάτης προκειμένης θυσίας.
>
> “We all pray for all, quite simply, who among us have previously fallen asleep, believing that the greatest benefit will accrue to the souls for whom supplication is offered while the holy and most awe-inspiring sacrifice lies before us.”

Eustratius, a presbyter of the Church of Constantinople, cited these words of Cyril in the book he composed around the middle of the sixth century on these same Christian prayers for the dead, in which he attributed these and other catecheses to Cyril. Who, then, after hearing these words of his, will not marvel at the Protestants who seriously reply that these prayers were once poured forth by Christians as a token of faith, hope, and charity, but not as aid for souls or as refreshment from purgatorial fire?

[Col. 0496B] We likewise cannot sufficiently marvel at Elmenhorst, who, in his observations on this passage of our Arnobius, boldly asserts that Augustine, in his book *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, candidly admits that prayers composed for the dead rest solely on ancestral tradition and are not confirmed by Holy Scripture. Yet these are Augustine’s very words, which Elmenhorst did not quote and had perhaps read not with his own eyes but with another’s:

> “In the books of the Maccabees we read that sacrifice was offered for the dead. But even if it were nowhere at all read in the ancient Scriptures, no small authority belongs to the universal Church, which is conspicuous in this custom, whereby the commendation [Col. 0496C] of the dead also has its place in the priest’s prayers, which are poured forth to the Lord God at His altar.”

(Augustine, *On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead*, ch. 1, vol. 6, p. 616.)

Does he not openly and candidly acknowledge there that these prayers are mentioned in the books of the Maccabees, which he regarded as canonical? But although you may deny that these books should be included in the canon of Holy Scripture, you cannot deny that they are venerable for their antiquity. Even if nothing whatsoever concerning these same prayers were read in the genuine books of Holy Scripture, Augustine nevertheless maintains that the custom of the ancient Church possesses no slight authority. But tell us, please, Elmenhorst: when someone expressly affirms that something is found in the books of the Maccabees and is sufficiently proved from elsewhere, even though it were not read in the ancient Scriptures—has that very person therefore denied [Col. 0496D] that it is found in Holy Scripture? Who has ever argued in this fashion unless blinded by prejudices born of error? But tell us further, please: is the authority and consensus of the universal Church in Augustine’s age—and for several centuries before him, as we have seen—really of such little weight? And whence did it flow, if not from the disciples of the Apostles and from the Apostles themselves?

The same Elmenhorst strays no less from the point when he insists that Epiphanius likewise denied that prayers for the dead are established by any testimony of Holy Scripture (Epiphanius, Heresy 75, §§3 and 7). For in our already cited observations on Ambrose (*Notes on Ambrose*, vol. II, p. 1193), we plainly showed that Epiphanius [Col. 0497A] defends the Catholic position and places the contrary position among the errors and heresies of Aerius. By what right, then, can one who denies that prayers should be poured forth for the dead be called a heretic, unless because his opinion is opposed to Holy Scripture and the constant tradition of the Church?

## ARTICLE IV. On Christian Altars, Sacrifices, and the Use of Incense; Whether Arnobius Spoke of Catechumens, of the Sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist, and of the Necessity of Divine Grace

The pagans further charged Christians (Arnobius, bk. VI, p. 289) not only with having, as we have said, no temples or sacred buildings, but also [Col. 0497B] no sacrificial altars (*arae*), no altars (*altaria*), no sacrifices, no images, and no use of incense. Arnobius does not appear to deny this altogether; indeed, he seems openly to declare that Christians performed no sacrifices and ought not to perform them. For he begins his sixth book with these words:

> “What then, someone may say: do you think that absolutely no sacrifices should be made? To answer you with the opinion not of ourselves but of your own Varro: none.”

(Arnobius, bk. VII, p. 211.)

But there is no one who will not very easily understand, from the authority of Varro cited by Arnobius and from the arguments subsequently advanced against sacrifices, that Arnobius is there discussing sacrifices performed according to pagan custom, and for that reason denies that they should be offered to the gods. Yet Heraldus accuses him there of ignorance and stupidity because, while attacking pagan sacrifices, [Col. 0497C] he made no mention of the sacrifices of the Israelite people. For in the first of his critical observations on Arnobius’s seventh book he censures him as follows:

> “I would nevertheless have wished Arnobius to say something about the sacrifices of the Israelite people, which constituted the sacramental sign of that great sacrifice whereby the spotless Lamb, sacrificed for our sins before the creation of the world, cleansed our sins. But we have sufficiently exposed Arnobius’s lack of instruction in religion above.”

But there we ourselves detected Heraldus’s own lack of instruction—to use his word—or rather his unfair disposition in reading and properly understanding the books of our Arnobius. For Arnobius had no other purpose in that book than to show that no sacrifices should be offered to the gods of the pagans and that Christians rightly and deservedly rejected them. Now [Col. 0497D] it is evident from our analysis of this book, and from what will be said below, that he demonstrated this by arguments of the greatest force. Who, then, in his right mind will deny that this was sufficient for him, even if he had remained completely silent about the sacrifices of the Israelites?

What, moreover, of the fact that he most explicitly proclaims that when pagans were asked the reason for their sacrifices, they vainly assigned their antiquity and customary observance as the explanation? For both had originated from human beings. No sacrifice can be performed rightly unless instituted by divine law:

> “But when I ask that the reason be brought forth for me,” he says, “I desire to hear of something that has descended from heaven.”

(Ibid., p. 227.)

Who, I ask you, will doubt that [Col. 0498A] this was the difference between pagan and Jewish sacrifices: that the former were sanctioned by human laws, but the latter by divine laws?

Furthermore, where Arnobius attacks and rejects pagan sacrifices, he also expressly teaches there (ibid., p. 215) that nothing was established by the pagans’ own gods concerning the manner in which they wished to be worshiped by human beings and honored with sacrifices. Here are his own words, if you care to hear them:

> “Did the gods,” he says, “ever enact any laws for mortals, and was it ever established by them what people ought or ought not to do; what ought to be consecrated and what avoided; or at least by what rites they wished themselves to be worshiped? . . . In my opinion nothing was ever established or enacted by them, since they were never seen; or, if they were seen, they could not with the clearest knowledge [Col. 0498B] be recognized.”

(Ibid., p. 215.)

Does he not, therefore, by this reasoning also reject pagan sacrifices while plainly and completely approving all the other things which God had commanded the Jews to perform? Yet even if he had said absolutely nothing about them, that silence is wrongly imputed to him as a fault. For besides the fact that the Jewish sacrifices had by then been abrogated, the subject under discussion was certainly not, as we have said, those sacrifices, but the impious sacrifices of the pagans, which were offered to fictitious and false gods and were rightly and deservedly detested by Christians.

Moreover, in precisely the same sense in which Arnobius denies that sacrifices should be offered to the gods, he likewise denied altogether that sacrificial altars and images should be erected and fashioned for them. But we have discussed these matters sufficiently in the preceding dissertation on Minucius’s *Octavius* (Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 12, art. 29). For [Col. 0498C], as will be sufficiently evident from what is said below, Arnobius argues against the pagans about them in no other manner than Minucius does.

As for the use of incense, Arnobius refutes the pagans who charged Christians with despising it (Arnobius, bk. VII, p. 231) by pointing out that among the pagans themselves it was not ancient, as will also be shown below. Tertullian, whom we shall discuss more fully in the proper place, admits somewhere that Christians burn no incense; nevertheless, elsewhere he testifies that they use it when burying the bodies of the dead and when the odor of some place is offensive. But not, he says, with the same rite, in the same ceremonial guise, or with the same equipment as is employed before idols. You see, therefore, that neither he nor Arnobius condemns every use of incense, but only that whereby incense was burned by pagans to idols. We have treated this elsewhere [Col. 0498D] (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. I, diss. 10, ch. 16, p. 198), and shall treat it again below.

Heraldus thought that Arnobius was speaking of the sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist where he teaches that our souls can become

> “long-lived,” or immortal, “provided only that they attempt to know God and then, laying aside servility and inhumanity, resume gentler dispositions, so that they may be prepared for that which will be given.”

(Arnobius, bk. II, p. 65.)

But on what reasoning, do you suppose, did Heraldus think that the earlier words signified the sacrament of Baptism and the later ones the Eucharist? Listen, please, and you will marvel. The most ancient Fathers of the Church, he says, not only adopted the pagans’ words that they used in explaining their mysteries, [Col. 0499A] but also adapted them to the Christian sacraments and transferred pagan rites into the Church. Now Arnobius, he says, excerpted the words cited by us for this purpose from the following passage of Cicero:

> “While your Athens seems to me to have produced and contributed many exceptional and divine things to human life, nothing among them is better than those mysteries by which we were cultivated and softened from a rustic and savage way of life into humanity; and through the initiations, as they are called, we have in truth learned the beginnings of life.”

(Cicero, bk. II, *On the Laws*, p. 339, line 31.)

From this Heraldus concludes that, by aiming at this passage of the Latin orator, Arnobius was speaking in his earlier words about Baptism and in his later words about the Eucharist. What a truly excellent inference! As if Arnobius could not have borrowed something from those words of Cicero [Col. 0499B] unless he were speaking of these Christian sacraments.

Yet nothing could be further from his intention. He is in fact discussing only the blessed immortality of our soul, which we cannot obtain unless we acknowledge the true God and lay aside the savagery of vice and inhumanity of conduct. Why, then, introduce Baptism there, when it was not under discussion? And apart from Heraldus, to whom could it have occurred that Arnobius’s final words—“so that souls may be prepared for that which will be given,” namely the reward of blessed immortality—signified the Eucharist? But observe the marvelous acuity of his intellect. Arnobius, he says, speaks of it obscurely and timidly, since he was a catechumen. Was he not more keen-sighted than Lynceus, seeing something that Arnobius had stated not merely [Col. 0499C] obscurely, as he claims, but in no way whatsoever, and had not intended to state? For, as we have noted, Arnobius said nothing other than that souls will not share in blessed eternity unless they acknowledge God and are prepared to attain it through purification from vice. Away, then, with these and similar annotations by certain writers, which they heap together solely in order to hunt after idle scraps of ill-digested learning.

It is therefore much more certain that our author acknowledged the necessity of divine grace, or divine assistance, for undergoing martyrdom in confession of the Christian religion. For, he says, they could not without God have steadfastly endured so many and such dreadful torments, even unto a death by torture. But since this was explained and demonstrated by us above [Col. 0499D] (above, ch. 4, art. 11), there is no need to prove it at greater length.

# CHAPTER XI. Examination of Arnobius’s Earlier Arguments Demonstrating That the Religion of the Pagans Is False

## ARTICLE I. Examination of the Arguments Arnobius Draws Against Pagan Religion from the Pagans’ Inability to Explain Where Their Gods Live, by Whom Their Names Were Imposed, and How Great Their Number Is; Together with an Assessment of Arnobius’s Judgment on Cicero’s Books, Especially *On the Nature of the Gods*, and Finally with the Testimony of Euhemerus, Nicagoras, Leon of Pella, Theodorus, Hippo, and Others

As we have shown, this entire work of Arnobius [Col. 0500A] against the pagans, divided into seven books, has only two parts: the first demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion, and the second the falsity of pagan religion. We have now examined the weight of the arguments by which he strives to demonstrate the truth of the Christian religion and of its principal doctrines, the holiness of its sacred mysteries and rites, and the integrity of the conduct of those who sincerely followed it, and by which he vindicates all these matters from the frequently repeated calumnies of the pagans. It remains for us to examine in a similar manner the other arguments which he advanced in the second part of his work to overthrow completely the pagans’ vain religions, impious cults, and utterly ridiculous and absurd superstitions.

First, then, our author proves by numerous arguments [Col. 0500B], as clearly as invincibly, that all the gods whom the pagans venerated with a cult no less impious than ancient were altogether false and fictitious. He began his discussion (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 102), as though with a preliminary skirmish, from the fact that the pagans were never able to explain where in the world their gods lived or how great their number was. For they cannot affirm with certainty that the gods dwell in heaven and are the same there as those worshiped on earth. No pagan ever flew up there and beheld their countenance and form.

Nor was the origin of the names by which the gods were called, and the persons by whom those names were devised and assigned, any better ascertained among them. Who, Arnobius asks, would dare to assert whether the gods imposed those names upon themselves on their days of purification? [Col. 0500C] In the royal manuscript the reading is *ludibriis* (“mockeries”); in the old editions, *ludicris* (“games”); in the latest, *lustricis* (“purificatory”), and this last is preferable. For, as Macrobius says (Macrobius, bk. I, *Saturnalia*, ch. 16, p. 307), the *lustricus dies* is the day on which infants are purified and receive a name: the ninth day for boys and the eighth for girls, as Servius also observes. But the gods, whom the pagans admitted to have been born just like other human beings, could not then have assumed names for themselves (Festus, *On the Meaning of Words*, p. 307). Nor were names given them by human beings. For their multitude was so great and utterly innumerable that a large proportion of them, as we shall show following Tertullian, was unknown even by name to most of the various nations and peoples.

I should like you to consider whether our author, in [Col. 0500D] writing these things, did not draw something from the following passage of Cicero, where Cotta presses this argument more sharply and demonstrates that the pagans’ gods do not exist:

> “Come then: do we make them gods by the names by which we call them? But first, there are as many names of gods as there are human languages. For Vulcan is not the same in Italy, Africa, and Spain, as you, Velleius, are the same wherever you go. Next, the number of names is not large, not even in our pontifical books, while the gods are innumerable. Are they, then, without names? That is indeed what you are compelled to say. For what point is there in having several names when there is a single appearance? How much better it would be, Velleius, to admit that you do not know what you do not know, instead of making me sick by pouring out such nonsense! Do you think [Col. 0501A] that God resembles me or you? Surely you do not.”

(Cicero, bk. I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 207, line 29.)

You certainly see that Cicero’s argument is the same as that of our Arnobius, by which he rightly and deservedly rejects the divinity of fictitious deities.

Nor is it only there that our author closely follows in the Latin orator’s footsteps. Elsewhere he frequently reproduces either Cicero’s words or his meaning. He drew them especially from Cicero’s three books *On the Nature of the Gods*, as everyone will understand from what is said below. Before proceeding further, therefore, it will undoubtedly be useful and worthwhile to observe what judgment our author passes upon these books of Cicero and why he refutes the pagans primarily on their authority.

Concerning Cicero himself as he speaks in these books, [Col. 0501B] Arnobius pronounces as follows:

> “Before all others Tullius, the most eloquent man of the Roman race, fearing no accusation of impiety, showed frankly, steadfastly, and freely, and with greater piety, what he thought about such a belief,”

namely, belief concerning the pagans’ gods.

> “If you were to proceed to derive your views from him, adopting what was written in accordance with the truth of his judgment, this case would already have been fully argued, nor would it demand from us, mere inarticulate speakers, a second pleading, as the expression goes.”

(Arnobius, bk. III, p. 103.)

For this reason, he continues, quite a few people recoiled from reading Cicero’s books *On the Nature of the Gods* and in no way whatever wished even to admit them to their hearing; others thought that they should be abolished by senatorial decree and removed from circulation. Cardinal Baronius thought that this was done by the edict of Diocletian mentioned by us above, and that Cicero’s books were in fact burned [Col. 0501C] together with Christian writings (Baronius, under the year 302, § 19, p. 723). But we fear that this most learned man did not sufficiently attend to the fact that Optatus and Eusebius, whom we cited elsewhere while discussing the same decree of Diocletian, mentioned only the sacred books of Holy Scripture, that is, our divinely inspired books.

Lactantius explains here in the following words how completely Cicero overthrew in these books the impious worship of the gods and all the false religions of the pagans, and what he thought about those same gods:

> “The leading figure of Roman philosophy, endowed also with the highest priesthood, refutes the invented and fictitious gods. He testifies that their rites are superstitions almost fit for old women, and laments that human beings are entangled [Col. 0501D] in false opinions and turbulent errors. For the whole third book *On the Nature of the Gods* utterly overthrows and destroys all religions. What more, then, is expected from us? Can we surpass Cicero in eloquence? Certainly not. But he lacked confidence because he did not know the truth. For he says that he can more easily state what a thing is not than what it is—that is, that he understands what is false but does not know what is true.”

(Lactantius, bk. I, *Divine Institutes*, ch. 17, p. 90.)

Lactantius, therefore, and very many other highly learned writers believed that the false religion of the pagans was utterly overthrown by these books of Cicero, even though Cicero was unable to reveal and establish another, true religion.

After quoting certain passages from Cicero’s second book, Augustine says that Cicero is indeed indignant at the institution of images and at the false [Col. 0502A] opinions of the pagans, but that

> “while fearing the custom of the state, he attempts to praise the religion of the ancestors and wishes to separate it from superstition, but cannot discover how he might do so.”

(Augustine, bk. IV, *The City of God*, ch. 30, p. 110.)

Then in the following book Augustine says that, since Cicero saw it to be the most evident madness

> “to confess God and deny His foreknowledge of the future, he attempted to affirm what is written: ‘The fool has said in his heart, There is no God,’ but not in his own person. For he saw how offensive and troublesome that would be; and therefore in his books *On the Nature of the Gods* he made Cotta argue on this subject against the Stoics, and preferred to cast his vote for Lucilius Balbus, to whom he had assigned the defense of the Stoic position, rather than for Cotta, who maintained that no divine nature exists.”

(The same, [Col. 0502B] ibid., bk. V, ch. 9, p. 121.)

But if Cicero in these books utterly abolished every religion, and if, to ward off resentment and trouble, he asserted the existence of gods only verbally and without sincere conviction, by what right, you will ask, does Arnobius affirm so emphatically (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 104) that these very books of Cicero are those

> “by which the Christian religion is confirmed and the authority of antiquity is crushed”?

It may reasonably be answered that by the name “Christian religion” Arnobius means its teaching concerning the true and sole God and His providence, which governs all things. Once that is asserted, the authority of antiquity, which had invented manifold and infinite gods, as we have said, is crushed. Now Cicero in his books *On the Nature of the Gods* demonstrates this as openly as he demonstrates that all [Col. 0502C] the religions of the pagans who worshiped any gods whatever are false. Once their falsity had been demonstrated, Arnobius thought it possible to conclude necessarily that the Christian religion alone is true and, with the other ancient religions rejected, ought to be embraced by everyone.

Besides Cicero, our author asserts that he could cite a thousand others—some of whom he names—who did not hesitate publicly to proclaim and prove in their writings that the gods of the pagans were altogether false and merely human:

> “We can indeed show that all those whom you introduce and call gods were human beings, either by reopening the case of Euhemerus of Acragas, whose little books Ennius translated [Col. 0502D] into the Italian tongue so that the matter might become clear to everyone, or by citing Nicagoras of Cyprus, Leon of Pella, Theodorus of Cyrene, or Hippo and Diagoras of Melos, or a thousand other authors, who with the care of scrupulous diligence brought hidden matters to light with candid freedom.”

(The same, bk. IV, p. 147.)

How true this is appears sufficiently from what we discussed concerning the writers praised by him in the first volume of our *Apparatus* and in the preceding dissertation on Minucius’s *Octavius* (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. 1, ch. 11, art. 5, p. 785 ff.; Dissertation on Minucius’s *Octavius*, final chapter and article). No one, moreover, as we think, has any room to doubt that Cicero and the others whom Arnobius named individually are the very persons of whom he said elsewhere:

> “We hear that certain people [Col. 0503A] devoted to the study of philosophy partly deny that there is any divine power, and partly inquire daily whether there is one.”

(Arnobius, bk. I, p. 18.)

With these points established, let us proceed to the other arguments by which he assails the absurd opinions of the pagans concerning their gods, and consequently their entire false religion, drawing his attack from the very sources upon which it seemed to them to have been founded and constructed. For he derives the force of his reasoning from the things which the pagans everywhere openly proclaimed concerning their gods as certain and entirely beyond doubt. In recounting and examining them, we shall follow, so far as possible, the order he adopted. But lest we occasionally repeat the same matters together with him, we shall treat together [Col. 0503B] and only once all the things that bear upon one and the same subject, even if he addressed them in various places.

## ARTICLE II. How Arnobius Demonstrates the False Divinity of Those Who Were Declared Gods Either Because of Benefits Conferred upon Humanity—Liber for the Invention of Wine, Ceres of Bread, Aesculapius of Medicinal Herbs, Minerva of the Olive, and Triptolemus of the Plow—or Because of Certain Distinguished Deeds, as in the Cases of Hercules and Romulus, Who Was Torn Apart by the Hands of the Senators

We have already disclosed and shown the various origins and thoroughly corrupt sources of idolatry and the impious worship of the gods (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 432 and 717 ff.; preceding Dissertation, ch. 14, art. 3): it flowed especially from the fact that ancient and benighted people enrolled among the gods those from whom they believed themselves to have received very great benefits, or who, they thought, had performed certain [Col. 0503C] distinguished deeds. For this reason Arnobius addresses those mad pagans in these words:

> “You enrolled Liber among the company of the gods because he discovered the use of wine; Ceres because she discovered bread; Aesculapius because he discovered medicinal herbs; Minerva because she discovered the olive; Triptolemus because he discovered the plow; and finally Hercules because he overcame and subdued wild beasts, thieves, and the nurses of many-headed monsters.”

(Arnobius, bk. I, p. 21.)

But what, I ask you, follows from this except that they were human beings, or at least that at some point they began to be gods, and consequently that divinity was attributed to them altogether falsely? For true divinity must be eternal and can never have had any beginning.

Nor should you say that these things were wrongly devised and gratuitously [Col. 0503D] invented by Arnobius. First, Diodorus Siculus, assuredly a most substantial witness in this matter, taught most explicitly that the use of wine was discovered by Dionysus, that is, Liber or Bacchus (Diodorus Siculus, bk. I, pp. 9–10; bk. III, p. 142). He had earlier narrated the matter more fully, when, after recalling certain other benefits Dionysus conferred upon humanity, he added the following (ibid., pp. 137–138):

> Ἀνθ` ὧν εὖ πάθοντας ἀπονεῖμαι τιμὰς ἰσοθέους ἀυτῷ καὶ θυσίας, προθύμως ἁπάντων ἀνθρώπων, διὰ τὸ μέγεθος τῆς εὐεργεσίας ἀπονειμάντων τὴν ἀθανασίαν.
>
> “In return for these things, those who had benefited bestowed upon him honors equal to those of the gods and sacrifices; all humanity, because of the greatness of his benefaction, eagerly conferred immortality upon him.”

Through these immense benefits he won such favor for himself that, consecrated to immortality by the eager devotion of all, he received both exceptional worship and solemn sacrifices as a god.

The invention of wine [Col. 0504A] is likewise attributed to Bacchus by Euripides and others (Euripides, *Bacchae*, line 277 ff.; preceding Dissertation, ch. 14, art. 4). Concerning him and Ceres, whom we discussed in the preceding dissertation, Lucretius has these verses:

> “For Ceres, it is said, established grain for mortals,  
> And Liber the liquid drawn from the vine-born fruit.”

(Lucretius, bk. V, line 14 ff.)

That same Ceres, the inventor of bread, is said by Diodorus Siculus to have taught Triptolemus how to sow crops and the whole method of harvesting from which bread is made, on condition that he share it with all humanity (Diodorus Siculus, bk. III, *Library*, p. 232). Hence Virgil sings:

> “Ceres was the first [Col. 0504B] to teach mortals to turn the earth with iron,  
> When acorns and arbutus berries already failed in the sacred woods  
> And Dodona denied them sustenance.”

(Virgil, *Georgics*, bk. I, line 147 ff.)

Ovid sings in agreement with Virgil:

> “Ceres was the first, when humanity was called to better things,  
> To exchange acorns for more useful food.  
> She compelled bulls to offer their necks to the yoke;  
> Then for the first time the sun beheld the plowed-up earth.”

(Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. IV, p. 548.)

Diodorus, whom we have already praised, further narrates that because of this benefit conferred upon them, the goddess Ceres was honored by the Athenians with offerings of victims and the Eleusinian initiations (Diodorus, bk. V, *Library*, p. 200).

Moreover, Diodorus, and Eusebius and Lactantius, who transcribed his words, declare most explicitly that Aesculapius [Col. 0504C] was believed to be the discoverer not only of medicinal herbs but also of medicine as a whole. We discussed him in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (Diodorus, bk. V, p. 235; Eusebius, bk. V, *Preparation for the Gospel*, ch. 2, p. 57; Lactantius, bk. I, ch. 19, p. 98; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1192).

Diodorus further bears witness that Minerva handed down the planting and cultivation of olive trees and the pressing of oil (Diodorus, loc. cit.). For although this kind of tree, mingled among wild trees, had existed before the birth of this Minerva, no method of cultivating or using it had yet been discovered. Hence Virgil:

And Minerva, discoverer of the olive,

And the boy who first revealed the curved plow. [Col. 0504D]  
(Virgil, *Georgics*, book I, verse 18.)

By the latter words some think that Osiris is designated, others Triptolemus, whom our Arnobius mentions. But see Servius’s commentary on these and the preceding verses of the Latin poet. Pliny, however, said (Pliny, *Natural History*, book VII, ch. 56, p. 99) that the invention of the plow was attributed to the Athenian Buzyges or to Triptolemus. But Ovid expressly introduces Ceres speaking of the latter as follows:

He indeed shall be mortal, but he will be the first to plow,

And sow, and reap rewards from cultivated soil.  
(Ovid, *Fasti*, book IV, p. 592.)

There, therefore, Triptolemus is expressly called the inventor of the plow, just as, in the passage of Diodorus Siculus cited shortly before, [Col. 0505A] he was instructed in the whole science of agriculture. On the invention of the plow and of the other things mentioned by Arnobius, see Polydore Vergil and other writers on the inventors of things (Diodorus, book I, pp. 11–12, passage cited; Polydore Vergil, *On the Inventors of Things*, book I, ch. 21, and book III, chs. 2–3).

From what we have related, one can readily understand what Arnobius writes elsewhere (Arnobius, book II, p. 90): that the earliest human beings used no food other than acorns or little fruits from wild branches [*buculos*, an uncertain reading], and no clothing other than bark and skins. This is further established and confirmed by the testimony of Diodorus Siculus, Ovid, Lucretius, and others (Diodorus, book I, p. 5; Ovid, *Fasti*, book I, near the end; Lucretius, book V, verse 951 ff.).

After these our author names Hercules [Col. 0505B] and speaks of his so-called labors. But to whom could these labors be unknown? Yet if any curious reader is unacquainted with them, he will find them explained by Diodorus Siculus and very many others (Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, book IV, p. 145 ff.). Concerning Hercules, Liber also—or Bacchus—and others who, because of distinguished deeds and benefits bestowed upon humankind, were proclaimed gods, Horace, in addition to Lactantius (Lactantius, book I, ch. 19, p. 98 ff.), sang as follows:

Romulus and Father Liber, and Pollux with Castor,

Were received into the temples of the gods after mighty deeds,

While they tended the earth and the race of men, brought harsh wars

To an end, allotted fields, and founded cities.

. . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

He who crushed the dreadful Hydra

Discovered that envy is overcome only at life’s final end. [Col. 0505C]  
(Horace, *Epistles*, book II, epistle 1, verse 5 ff.)

But Arnobius rightly reproaches the Romans because they enrolled this Romulus, whom Horace names first, among the gods on account of his distinguished deeds and the benefits he conferred. For he had been torn to pieces and killed by the hands of the senators. “Do you not say,” Arnobius asks (book I, p. 24), “that Father Romulus himself, torn apart by the hands of a hundred senators, is Mars’s Quirinus? Do you not honor him with priests and sacred couches, worship him in magnificent temples, and, after all this, swear that he ascended into heaven?” Although Livy tries to conceal the fact that Romulus’s life was so cruelly taken from him by the senators, Valerius Maximus, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and others openly and plainly acknowledge it [Col. 0505D] (Livy, book I, ch. 12; Valerius Maximus, book V, ch. 3, §1; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, book II, p. 18). In the preceding dissertation we showed how, through Proculus’s perjury, he was enrolled among the gods (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 15, art. 2).

Who, then, unless he is plainly insane, would call this man and the others whom we have mentioned gods, whatever false or genuine benefits they are said to have bestowed, or whatever distinguished deeds they are reported to have performed? For they were mere human beings, and indeed exceedingly wicked ones. Yet even if they had been as holy as they were criminal and shameful, never did all of them together secure for themselves, as Christ did, admiration through so many such astonishing deeds [Col. 0506A], or affection and grateful remembrance through so many benefits, as we have seen above. If, therefore, the pagans had remained consistent with their own principles, they certainly could not have denied Christ’s divinity, rejected his religion, or raged with such fury against his followers. Who, then, does not see how futile and empty that argument is? We have already seen how Minucius Felix overthrew this error, and below we shall show how it was refuted by Lactantius and Tertullian (ibid., art. 1; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 30, art. 5; and *On Tertullian*, ch. 25, art. 3).

## ARTICLE III. Another argument of Arnobius against the religion of the pagans is examined, drawn from the fact that the pagans called their gods male and female and said that, after celebrating marriages in the human manner, or by another and more shameful method, they begot children; with a discussion of seven-month pregnancies, *chalcidica*, the Hellespontian Priapus, the many-breasted Ceres, marriages of the gods celebrated by *usus*, spelt, and *coemptio*, betrothals, Fescennine songs, the royal offspring of Ops, the infamous birth of the Cytherean Venus, and the little prostitute Venus enriched by the king of Cyprus

[Col. 0506B]

Arnobius derives a very powerful argument against the pagans from the fact that they proclaimed their gods male and female, and acknowledged as much in their public prayers. “For in your customary prayers,” he says (Arnobius, book III, p. 139), “you say, ‘Whether you are a god or a goddess.’ The qualification expressing this doubt itself makes clear, by its disjunction, that you assign sex to the gods.” In Varro, moreover, we read how those prayers were customarily made: “A sacred grove,” he says (Varro, *On Agriculture*, p. 139), “must be cleared in the Roman manner as follows. Offer a pig as an expiatory victim. Frame the words thus: ‘Whether you are a god or a goddess to whom this place is sacred.’” [Col. 0506C] Brissonius proves these matters more fully (*On Formulas*, ch. 60), and we have touched upon them elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 15, art. 1).

Nor does Arnobius permit some thoughtless person to object that Christians also believe God to be male, since the word *Deus* (“God”) is masculine in gender. For by that term it is not sex but, according to linguistic usage, the meaning “God” that is expressed. It is therefore not God, but his name, that signifies the masculine gender.

Arnobius proves as follows that gods cannot be male and female. They cannot be such, he says (Arnobius, book III, p. 104 ff.), without possessing those parts and members by which the two sexes are distinguished and which were made for propagating offspring. Yet, if those bodily parts and members existed in the gods, they could not have been useless, as Cicero also says (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, p. 208 ff.). [Col. 0506D] So great a multitude of immortal gods, who never grow old or become weakened in bodily strength, ought consequently to have been begotten that everything would by now be full of them, nor could they any longer be contained even by innumerable heavens. We have already shown that Minucius and others also employed the same argument (*Dissertation on Minucius’s Octavius*, ch. 16, art. 2).

Arnobius briefly explains how many absurd, obscene, and god-unworthy consequences follow from their different sexes (Arnobius, book III, p. 104). [Col. 0507A] From this, he says, must arise the goddesses’ menstruation, pregnancies, miscarriages, customary labor pains, and seven-month pregnancies—that is, goddesses giving birth in the seventh month. From this also follow gods and goddesses naked in *chalcidica*—that is, as Turnebus and Scaliger observe, upper rooms and large buildings—and the horrifying indecency of the infamous Hellespontian Priapus, concerning whom see Natalis Comes, Vossius, and Huet (Turnebus, book XVIII, ch. 34; Scaliger, on Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, at the year 2104; N. Comes, *Mythology*, book V, ch. 15; Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, book II, ch. 7, p. 73 ff.; Huet, *Demonstration*, p. 109 ff.). From Iacchus also came the many-breasted Ceres, our author says, employing, as Lucretius declares, this very verse:

But the twin-breasted, many-breasted Ceres herself comes from Iacchus. [Col. 0507B]  
(Lucretius, book IV, verse 1161.)

Cicero, however, presses all these points more sharply: “Since you say,” he observes (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, p. 209, line 19), “that the gods are both male and female, you see what follows. For my part, I cannot wonder enough how that leader of yours arrived at such opinions”—namely Epicurus.

But why, someone may ask, do Arnobius and Tully not refute the ridiculous reply of Epicurus and his followers, in which they babbled that the gods do not indeed possess body and blood, but something like body and blood? The reason is certainly easy and obvious to everyone. Tully plainly and clearly showed that no one could ever understand that invention of Epicurus (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. [Col. 0507C] 202, line 43). Furthermore, the pagans actually boasted that their gods were endowed with real bodies and blood and, driven by an unbridled and ruinous lust for pleasure, devoted themselves to begetting children. Since Arnobius had sufficiently marked this point, he did not think that more time should be spent refuting that insane fabrication of the Epicureans.

How certainly the pagans believed that their gods were constituted with genuine human bodies, male and female, is evident from the fact that they themselves, as Arnobius rightly argues, transmitted to posterity as matters admitting no doubt numerous stories about their solemn marriages and the children born from them. For in almost all their books they had proclaimed that their gods’ marriages were contracted in the human manner [Col. 0507D] and on human terms, as Arnobius says (Arnobius, book IV, p. 140), and celebrated by *usus*, spelt, and *coemptio*. All these, according to Servius (on Virgil’s *Georgics*, verse 30), belonged to the ancient rites of marriage:

“For among the ancients marriages were contracted in three ways: by *usus*, if, for example, a woman had lived with a man for a year, even without legal formalities; by spelt, when they were joined through the chief pontiff and the Flamen Dialis by means of grain and salted meal, whence this was called *confarreatio*, and from marriages of this kind children whose father and mother were both living were born; and by *coemptio* and entry into the husband’s authority, when the woman assumed the position of a daughter and the husband that of a father, so that if either died first, the other would have the right of inheritance.” [Col. 0508A]

See the same Servius on *Aeneid* IV, verse 103; Brissonius, *On the Ancient Rite of Marriage*, in *Roman Antiquities*, vol. XIII, p. 1016 ff.; and, in the same volume, p. 1128 ff., Holmann’s *On the Ancient Rite of Marriage*, ch. 20 ff. These writers explain in their treatises the ancient rites, as well as what Arnobius added concerning proposals, agreements, betrothed persons, and Fescennine songs. The Fescennine verses, Festus says, were so called either because they were brought from the city of Fescennia or because they were believed to ward off the evil eye (*fascinum*) (works cited, pp. 1012, 1047, 1112, 1124; Festus, *On the Meaning of Words*). Accordingly Arnobius, jesting wittily with the pagans, says that because the goddesses had not participated in Fescennine songs, “they threw everything into confusion through discord” (Arnobius, book IV, p. 140). Various writers, and especially [Col. 0508B] Homer on several occasions, record that the gods attended the marriages of others and their celebration (Homer, *Iliad* XXIV).

By a brief enumeration Arnobius proves that, by the pagans’ own admission, the gods begot children not only in solemn wedlock but in another, far more shameful manner. What more powerful argument could be advanced to reveal, more clearly than the sun itself, the false and fabricated nature of their divinity? First, therefore, our author relates (Arnobius, book II, pp. 92 and 94; book IV, p. 143) that the pagans handed down the tradition that Saturn was born of Caelus and Hecate, and that from Saturn himself and Ops, as we have noted elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 15, art. 2), were born Jupiter and his brothers Neptune and Pluto, his sister Juno, and others; and that Jupiter was preserved by the Curetes so that he would not be devoured by his father, as we have likewise already observed. Doubtless for this [Col. 0508C] reason Arnobius calls them “the royal offspring of Ops” (Arnobius, book II, p. 20). And indeed we read in Diodorus Siculus (book V, p. 232):

> Κρόνου καὶ Ῥέας λέγεται γένεσθαι τὴν δὲ Ἑστίαν, καὶ Δήμητραν, καὶ Ἥραν· ἔτι δὲ Δία, καὶ Ποσειδῶνα, καὶ Ἀδῆν.

“From Saturn and Rhea, who among the Latins is Ops, Vesta, Ceres, Juno, Jupiter, Neptune, and Pluto are said to have been born.”

Hesiod, the author of the book *On the Universe*, and many others concur with this by broad agreement (Hesiod, *Theogony*, verse 453 ff.; Cicero, *On the Universe*, Appendix).

What, however, could have been imagined more shameful and foul than the infamous birth of the Cytherean Venus—a matter that ought to have been condemned to perpetual silence, yet which the pagans, casting aside all modesty, made public? Our Arnobius reproached them in these words: “Is it we,” he asks (Arnobius, book [Col. 0508D] IV, p. 143), “who say that the gleaming whiteness of the Cytherean Venus coagulated and took form from the foam of the sea and the severed genitals of Caelus,” whom we mentioned shortly before? Clement of Alexandria, however, presses the same pagans somewhat more fully and freely, so that they might be suffused with some salutary shame, if that were ever possible (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 10):

> Ἀγορεύω δὲ ἀναφανδὸν τὰ κεκρυμμένα, οὐκ αἰδούμενος λέγειν ἃ προσκυνεῖν οὐκ αἰσχύνεσθε· ἡ μὲν οὖν ἀφρογενής τε καὶ κυπρογενής, ἡ Κινύρα φίλη, τὴν Ἀφροδίτην λέγω, τὴν Φιλομηδέα, ὅτι μηδέων ἐξεφάνθη, μηδέων ἐκείνων τῶν ἀποκεκομμένων Οὐρανοῦ, τῶν λάχνων τῶν μετὰ τὴν τομὴν τὸ κῦμα βεβιασμένων· ὡς ἀσελγῶν ὑμῖν μορίων ἄξιος Ἀφροδίτη γίνεται καρπὸς ἐν ταῖς τελεταῖς.

“I openly proclaim the hidden things, not blushing to speak of what you are not ashamed to worship. She, then, who was foam-born and Cyprus-born, the beloved of Cinyras—I mean Aphrodite, *Philomēdēs*, because she appeared from the genitals, from those lustful genitals, I say, which had been cut from Uranus and which, after their severance, violated the wave—as a fruit worthy of your licentious parts, Aphrodite comes into being in the mysteries.” [Col. 0509A]

Macrobius, when discussing Saturn, says: “They say that he cut off the private parts of his father Caelus; when these were cast into the sea, Venus was born and received the name Ἀφροδίτη (*Aphroditē*) from the foam out of which she coagulated.” Consult also Cicero, who calls her the second Venus. If you wish, consult Hesiod, Servius, Gregory of Nazianzus, and others as well (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, ch. 8, p. 209; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, [Col. 0509B] p. 248, line 27; Hesiod, *Theogony*, verse 195 ff.; Servius on Virgil’s *Georgics* I, p. 113; Gregory, *First Oration against Julian*, near the end).

Arnobius appears to have drawn from the same Clement of Alexandria what he added: that this same little prostitute Venus was enriched by Cinyras, king of Cyprus, and consecrated among the number of the gods. You will also find this confirmed by Julius Firmicus (Arnobius, book IV, p. 143; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 10; Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 15). We have briefly touched upon her elsewhere (*Apparatus*, vol. I, p. 729).

## ARTICLE IV. How Arnobius demonstrates the falsity of Jupiter’s divinity from his adulteries: with Hyperion, from whom came the golden Sun; with Latona, from whom came Apollo and Diana, the bow-bearers wandering upon drifting islands; with Leda, from whom came the Castors, the Tyndarids or Dioscuri, the offspring of eggs, one of whom was a horse-tamer and the other a boxer invincible with the *caestus*; likewise from Jupiter’s other adulteries—with Alcmena, from whom came Hercules; with Semele, from whom came Bacchus, or Bromius, Nysius, and Evius, cast out from his mother’s womb by a thunderbolt and born a second time from his father’s seed; likewise Jupiter’s union with Maia, from whom came Mercury; with Electra, from whom came Dardanus; and with Laodamia, from whom came Sarpedon; with a discussion of Minerva’s birth from Jupiter’s brain, Jupiter’s transformations into various animal forms, and the words “Tisianes,” “Bocores Mauri,” and “babecali youths”

[Col. 0509C]

Jupiter celebrated an incestuous marriage with his sister Juno, as Arnobius, and before him Tertullian, [Col. 0509D] and others have observed (Arnobius, book IV, p. 143; Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 14). Yet that great and exceedingly lustful god, our author says, was not content with this wife, although through the majesty of her countenance and the whiteness of her arms—or, as Homer and Gregory of Nazianzus call her, λευκώλενος (*leukōlenos*), “white-armed”—and her extraordinary beauty of form, she was lovelier than all others (Arnobius, book IV, p. 141; Homer, *Iliad* I, verse 14 and elsewhere; Gregory of Nazianzus, *Third Oration against Julian*, p. 257). For he is said to have begotten children by various mistresses and prostitutes, and therefore through just as many adulteries. Nor did the pagans dare deny it. Arnobius therefore addresses them in these words: “From Hyperiona as mother,” he says (Arnobius, book IV, p. 141), “and from Jupiter, the hurler of the thunderbolt, was born the golden and most blazing Sun.” Elsewhere he says (ibid., p. 135): “The second Sun likewise was the son of Jupiter and is reported to have had Hyperiona as his mother.” But he plainly disagrees with [Col. 0510A] Hesiod, who sang that the Sun was born from his mother Theia and his father Hyperion. Cicero also enumerates the fathers of three Suns, one of whom, he says, was born from Hyperion; but he says nothing further there about this Sun. This is not at all surprising, since other writers differ concerning Hyperion (Hesiod, *Theogony*, verse 371 ff.; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, p. 247, line 45).

Arnobius agrees admirably with both Hesiod and Cicero, however, in what he immediately adds: “From Latona and the same Jupiter came the bow-bearing Delian and Diana, huntress of the forests” (Arnobius, book IV, p. 141). Or, as he had said in another book: “Diana and Apollo, bow-bearers, carried about during their mother’s flights and scarcely safe upon wandering islands” (ibid., book I, p. 20; Hesiod, *Theogony*, verse 917 ff.; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, [Col. 0510B] p. 248, line 17; Homer, *Iliad* XIV, verse 323 ff.; Strabo, *Geography*, book X, p. 483; Catullus, *Secular Hymn to Diana*; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book XV, fable 9). For these are Hesiod’s verses on the matter:

> Λητὼ δ’ Ἀπόλλωνα καὶ Ἄρτεμιν ἰοχέαιραν,  
> Ἱμερόεντα γόνον περὶ πάντων Οὐρανιώνων,  
> Γείνατ’ ἄρ’, Αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς φιλότητι μιγεῖσα.

Latona bore Apollo and Diana, who delights in arrows,

Lovely offspring beyond all the heavenly gods,

After joining in love with aegis-bearing Jupiter.

Tully, moreover, says: “The third Apollo was born of the third Jupiter and Latona, and is said to have come from the Hyperboreans to Delphi.” Besides Homer, Strabo, Catullus, and others, Ovid agrees with these writers when he introduces Apollo speaking:

[Col. 0510C]

The Delphic land serves me,

And Claros, and Tenedos, and the royal house of Patara;

Jupiter is my father.

From Herodotus, moreover, you will learn why this same Apollo and Diana are said by Arnobius to have been “carried about during their mother’s flights and scarcely safe upon wandering islands.” For Herodotus relates that Apollo and Diana were hidden and preserved by Latona on the island of Chemmis, which afterward floated upon the water (Herodotus, book II, §156, p. 151; Arnobius, book I, p. 20).

Our author again agrees with Cicero when he next reports that the Castors were also born from Jupiter himself: “In Greek,” he says (ibid.; book IV, p. 141), “their name is Dioscuri.” Cicero had indeed previously committed these words to writing: “The Διόσκουροι (*Dioskouroi*) are likewise called by many names among the Greeks.... The second pair, Castor and Pollux, were born from the third Jupiter [Col. 0510D] and Leda” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, p. 147). Theocritus, the Greek poet, joins in support of both with these verses (*Idyll* 22):

> Ὑμνέομες Λήδας τε καὶ Αἰγιόχῳ Διὸς υἱώ,  
> Κάστορα, καὶ φοβερὸν Πολυδεύκεα πὺξ ἐρεθίζειν,  
> Χεῖρας ἐπιζεύξαντα μέσοις βοέοισιν ἱμᾶσιν.

We celebrate in song the sons of Leda and aegis-bearing Jupiter:

Castor, and terrible Pollux when roused to box,

Who bound his hands with straps of oxhide.

See also Homer’s hymn to the sons of Jupiter and Theodoret (*Discourse 2, On Angels and Demons*, p. 511).

Arnobius calls both brothers by the single name “Castors,” “because,” Servius says [Col. 0511A] (on Virgil’s *Georgics*, verse 88, p. 125), “both are freely called Polluxes as well as Castors. For their games, temple, and stars are called those of the Castors.”

In his first book Arnobius had said: “The Tyndarid Castors” (the royal manuscript reads: *Tunc dari de Castores*), “one accustomed to taming horses, the other a good boxer and invincible with the rawhide *caestus*; the Titans and Bocores, Moors” (the royal manuscript reads: *Tisianes et Bucures, Mauri*), “and the offspring of eggs, the Syrian Gods” (Arnobius, book I, p. 20). You see how foully this passage has been corrupted by the copyist’s ignorance. We shall therefore attempt, so far as possible, to cast some light upon it.

First, both here and elsewhere Castor and Pollux are called “the Tyndarid Castors” by Arnobius, merely “the Tyndarids” by Cicero, and “the Tyndarid brothers” by [Col. 0511B] Ovid (Arnobius, book II, p. 93; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, p. 214, and book III, p. 24; Ovid, *Fasti*, book V, near the end). They received that name because they were believed to have been born from Tyndareus, king of Oebalia, and his wife Leda, although they were born from Jupiter’s illicit union with Leda after he had been transformed into a swan. For Leda bore Jupiter two eggs, from which not only Castor and Pollux, but also Helen and Clytemnestra, were said to have emerged. For this very reason the Dioscuri were surnamed Διόσκουροι (*Dioskouroi*), as we have said, from Διός (*Dios*), “of Jupiter,” and κόροι or κοῦροι (*koroi* or *kouroi*), “sons.” Some therefore conjecture that in Arnobius’s text *Dioscuri* should be read in place of *Dii Syri*, “Syrian Gods.” Selden, however, published a separate book *On the Syrian Gods*.

[Col. 0511C]

From what we observed shortly before, it is readily understood why Castor and Pollux are called by Arnobius (book I, p. 120) “the offspring of eggs,” and Jupiter “the begetter of shining-white eggs” (ibid., book IV, p. 142); concerning these see Vossius, among others. Horace admirably confirms both this point and what our author added in the same place—that one was accustomed to taming horses and the other was a good boxer—in this verse:

Castor delights in horses; he who was born from the same egg,

In boxing.  
(Horace, *Satires*, book II, verse 25.)

Elsewhere he repeats the point and calls them Leda’s sons in these verses:

I shall sing also of Alcides and Leda’s sons,

The one renowned for conquering with horses, the other

With fists. [Col. 0511D]  
(Horace, *Odes*, book I, ode 12, verse 25.)

Ovid and Propertius agree beautifully with Horace (Ovid, *Fasti*, book V; Propertius, book III, elegy 13).
