What the *caestus* is, with which Pollux is said to have been invincible, you will learn from Servius on this verse of Virgil, which our author perhaps had in mind:

Or if he trusts himself to enter battle with the rawhide *caestus*.  
(Virgil, *Aeneid*, book V, verse 68.)

Servius makes the following observations there:

“With the rawhide *caestus*: either ‘cruel’ or ‘hard,’ so that it is a simple expression, because the *caestus* is made of hard leather; or, when spelled with a diphthong, it signifies the weapons of boxers. It has a plural number and belongs to the fourth declension. For *cestus, cesti*, used only in the [Col. 0512A] singular and without a diphthong, signifies the girdle of Venus.”

Accordingly Theocritus, as we saw shortly before, sang that Pollux’s hands were bound with βοέοισιν ἱμᾶσιν (*boeoisin himasin*), “straps of oxhide,” as his translator rendered it—that is, with *caestūs*. To these may be added Seneca, who said somewhere:

Pollux, more skilled with the *caestus*,

Will yield together with his Castor.  
(Seneca, *Medea*, act I.)

We have made some observations about the *caestus* in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 2, p. 1193 ff.).

The greater difficulty, therefore, lies in Arnobius’s penultimate words: “Titans and Bocores, Moors,” or, as the [Col. 0512B] royal manuscript reads, “Tisianes and *bucules mauri*” (Arnobius, book I, p. 20), which Heraldus freely admits cannot be explained. Stewechius suspected that the reading should be: “marine fires and flashes,” because Castor and Pollux are stars favorable to sailors. He could have supported this with the testimony of Seneca, Pliny, and others (Seneca, *Natural Questions*, book I, ch. 1, p. 405; Pliny, *Natural History*, book II, ch. 37). But Stewechius’s conjecture was by no means pleasing to others. Meursius was more attracted by Grotius’s conjecture that one should write, “born from Tisianira and Bucerus.” For Tisianira is Nemesis, or Leda, and Jupiter is Bucerus, since he was once transformed into a bull. *Bucerum pecus* and *bucera armenta* mean the same as cattle. Yet even if Jupiter’s surname had been Bucerus, it would still have to be proved [Col. 0512C] why Arnobius should mention here Jupiter’s transformation into a bull rather than into a swan, under whose form he violated Leda, who is under discussion in that passage. To restore the true reading of Arnobius’s text, therefore, another uncorrupted manuscript is certainly required.

Arnobius continues (book IV, p. 141) and presses the pagans concerning Jupiter’s other adulteries as follows:

“From Alcmena and the same Jupiter was born that Theban Hercules, protected by his club and skin; from Semele and Jupiter himself came Liber, who is called Bromius and was born a second time from his father’s seed; again, from Jupiter himself and Maia came Mercury, eloquent in speech and bearer of the gracious serpents”—that is, the snakes upon the caduceus, by which the end of war and beginning of peace were announced.

[Col. 0512D]

But to whom could these things be unknown? Concerning the threefold adultery of Jupiter, through which he is said to have fathered the same number of sons by three women, Hesiod sang as follows (Hesiod, *Theogony*, verse 937 ff.):

> Ζηνὶ δ’ ἄρ’ Ἀτλαντὶς Μαίη τέκε κύδιμον Ἑρμῆν,  
> Κήρυκ’ ἀθανάτων, ἱερὸν λέχος εἰσαναβᾶσα.  
> Καδμείη δ’ ἄρα οἱ Σεμέλη τέκε φαίδιμον υἱόν,  
> Μιχθεῖσ’ ἐν φιλότητι, Διόνυσον πολυγηθέα,  
> Ἀθάνατον θνητή· νῦν δ’ ἀμφότεροι θεοί εἰσιν.  
> Ἀλκμήνη δ’ ἄρ’ ἔτικτε βίην Ἡρακληείην,  
> Μιχθεῖσ’ ἐν φιλότητι Διὸς νεφεληγερέταο.

To Jupiter, then, Maia, daughter of Atlas, bore glorious Mercury,

Herald of the immortals, after mounting his sacred bed.

And Semele, daughter of Cadmus, bore him a splendid son,

After joining with him in love: Dionysus, rich in joy—

A mortal woman bore an immortal; now both are gods.

And Alcmena bore the mighty strength of Hercules

After joining in love with cloud-gathering Jupiter. [Col. 0513A]

Concerning this offspring of Alcmena, Cicero says: “The sixth Hercules was born from Alcmena; Jupiter begot him, but it was the third Jupiter.” If you wish, you may read more in Diodorus Siculus, Hesiod, Plautus, and Vossius. Following Clement of Alexandria, our author adds that the same Jupiter spent nine nights with Alcmena. Concerning this and the other adulteries of Jupiter mentioned by our Arnobius, see Homer (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, p. 205, final line; Diodorus, *Library*, book IV, p. 157; Hesiod, *Shield of Hercules*; Plautus, *Amphitryon*; Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, book I, ch. 14, p. 162; Arnobius, book IV, p. 145; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 20; Homer, *Iliad* XIV, verse 316 ff.).

You will also find explained what Arnobius writes [Col. 0513B]: that Liber, or Bacchus, was born from Jupiter and Semele and then born again from his father’s seed or thigh; or, as he says elsewhere, that he was cast from his mother’s womb by a thunderbolt (Arnobius, book I, pp. 20 and 24; book IV, p. 141). For Diodorus relates that Semele, whom Jupiter passionately loved, extracted from him by her entreaties a promise that he would come to her when she was pregnant by him with the same majesty with which he approached Juno—that is, armed with thunder and lightning (Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, book XL, p. 138, and in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book II, ch. 2, p. 52). But since she could not endure so great a force of flashing light and thunderous noise, she immediately died and miscarried. Jupiter then sewed the infant into his thigh and, after giving birth to him at the appointed time, carried him to Nysa, a city of Arabia. There he was reared by the Nymphs and received the name Dionysus from his father and from the place [Col. 0513C] where he was born. If you wish other witnesses to be supplied, we shall promptly give you Homer, Nonnus, Ovid, and Cicero, whom you may easily consult whenever you please (Homer, *Iliad* XIV, verse 233 ff.; Nonnus, *Dionysiaca*, book I, beginning; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book III, §3, p. 102 ff.; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book I, p. 119).

Meanwhile observe that Liber is called by our author not only *Semeleius*, that is, the son of Semele, but also Bromius, Nysius, and Evius. “Βρόμιον δὲ,” says Diodorus Siculus, whom we cited, “ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ τὴν γένεσιν αὐτοῦ γενομένου βρόμου”: “He was called Bromius from the crash of thunder produced around the time of his birth.” Nysius, however, was named not from the already mentioned Arabian city of Nysa, as it seems, but rather from his father Nysus. For Cicero, after whom our author enumerates five [Col. 0513D] Dionysi, or Libers, expressly asserts that the fifth was born from Nysus and Thione. Finally, some think that the surname Evius was given to Bacchus because, after being transformed into a lion and killing each of the Giants, he was surnamed by his father Jupiter *Evhion*, or “good son.” Others suspect that this name arose from the word *Evoe*, or Εὐάν (*Euan*), with which the Bacchants openly acclaimed Bacchus in their mysteries, as we have noted elsewhere (Arnobius, book IV, p. 141, and book V, pp. 176–177; Diodorus Siculus, passage cited, *Library*, book III, p. 149; and in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book II, ch. 2, p. 54; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, p. 248, line 25).

From the Cicero cited shortly before you will doubtless [Col. 0514A] acknowledge that our author also took what he added next: that Mercury was born from the same Jupiter and Maia (Arnobius, book IV, p. 136; vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 3, ch. 9, art. 2, p. 757). For the Latin orator is recorded as having committed these words to writing: “The third Mercury was born from the third Jupiter and Maia; from him and Penelope they say Pan was born.” Diodorus Siculus, moreover, says: “Atlas had seven daughters.... Maia, the eldest, through Jupiter’s embrace bore Mercury,” the discoverer of many arts (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, p. 248, line 6; Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, book III, p. 135). Besides Macrobius (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, ch. 12, p. 122), Virgil supported both writers in these verses:

Mercury is your father, whom fair Maia,

Having conceived him on Cyllene’s icy summit, brought forth.

[Col. 0514B]

But Maia—if we put any trust in what we hear—

Was begotten by that same Atlas who holds aloft the stars of heaven.  
(Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VIII, verse 138 ff.)

On these verses see Servius’s observations.

The infamous Jupiter, moreover, robbed a thousand other virgins and women of their chastity, as Arnobius records elsewhere (Arnobius, book V, p. 172). There he expressly names Electra and Laodamia. Electra was a nymph, the daughter of Oceanus and Tethys, who, after being violated by Jupiter, bore Dardanus according to Ovid, or, according to Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Dardanus and Iasus (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, book I, p. 49). Ovid’s verses on the matter are:

Dardanus would not know himself born from Electra, daughter of Atlas,

Had Electra, of course, not lain with Jupiter. [Col. 0514C]  
(Ovid, *Fasti*, book IV, verse 49.)

By Laodamia, daughter of Bellerophon, the same Jupiter begot Sarpedon, king of Lycia, as Homer sings (*Iliad* VI, verse 197 ff.):

> Λαοδαμείῃ μὲν παρελέξατο μητίετα Ζεύς,  
> Ἡ δ’ ἔτεκ’ ἀντίθεον Σαρπηδόνα χαλκοκορυστήν.

With Laodamia lay Jupiter, lord of counsel,

And she bore godlike Sarpedon, the bronze-helmeted warrior.

Arnobius asserts that Jupiter’s lust was so great, so shameful, and so ruinous—as we have discussed elsewhere (Arnobius, book IV, p. 145; vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 753, 805, 1242 ff.)—that in order to satisfy it, if ever he could, he was not ashamed to transform himself into gold, a satyr, a dragon, a bird, a bull, and an ant. Ovid set these matters forth somewhat more clearly [Col. 0514D] in the following manner:

The Maeonian woman portrays Europa deceived by the likeness

Of a bull.

. . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

She fashioned Asterie held fast by the struggling eagle;

She fashioned Leda reclining beneath a swan’s wings;

She added how, concealed in the shape of a satyr,

Jupiter filled the lovely daughter of Nycteus [Note: [Col. 0514D] Antiope, daughter of Nycteus] with twin offspring;

How he was Amphitryon when he captivated you, Tirynthian woman [Note: [Col. 0514D] Alcmena];

How, as gold, he deceived Danaë; as fire, the daughter of Asopus [Note: [Col. 0514D] Aegina is the daughter of Asopus, king of Boeotia];

As a shepherd, Mnemosyne; as a spotted serpent, Deo’s daughter.

Later Gregory of Nazianzus wrote (Gregory of Nazianzus, vol. II, poem 61, p. 142):

[Col. 0515A]

> Ἄθρει δὴ πρώτιστον ὅσ’ ἔπλετο μαργοσύνῃσι,  
> Ταῦρος, κύκνος, χρυσός, ὄφις, πόσις, ἄρκτος, ἅπαντα  
> Ὅσσα μιν ὠκὺς ἄνωγεν ἔρως, κοῦρός τ’ ἀλαπαδνός,  
> Ὡς αὐτοί γ’ ἐνέπουσι θεῶν πλαστῆρες ἀκιδνῶν.

Behold for me how many forms the foremost of them assumes

While he is consumed by the fire of burning Venus:

Now a bull, now a white swan, now gold, now a dark-blue serpent,

Now a husband, now a bear; in short, whatever

Love and the feeble boy desire—as you yourselves say,

Who delight to fashion weak divinities with your hand.

We have touched elsewhere on this same Jupiter’s ridiculous transformation to violate Eurymedusa (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 1, ch. 9, art. 1, p. 752). On some of those abominable transformations of Jupiter see also Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, Epiphanius, Julius Firmicus, Vossius, [Col. 0515B] and others (Justin, *Exhortation to the Greeks* 2, p. 38; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 23 ff.; Epiphanius, *Ancoratus*, p. 108; Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religion*, p. 15; Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, book I, ch. 14; Arnobius, book II, pp. 93 and 118).

Perhaps it will appear less shameless to some that Arnobius, following Apollonius Rhodius, Nonnus, Lucian, Pausanias, Ovid, and many others, relates that Minerva was born from Jupiter’s brain (Apollonius, *Argonautica*, book IV, verse 1309 ff.; Nonnus, *Dionysiaca*, book I, verse 9 ff.; Lucian, *Dialogues of the Gods*, p. 73 ff., and *On Sacrifices*, p. 183; Pausanias, book I, p. 22; Ovid, *Fasti*, book III, near the end; Arnobius, book IV, p. 141 ff.). Yet no one, surely, will deny that even this was wholly unworthy of the supreme father of the gods. [Col. 0515C] For does it not necessarily follow from it that Jupiter was a human being, composed of a brain and other human members; that Minerva had not previously existed; and that she is wrongly enrolled among the goddesses?

Who, then, does not understand how rightly Arnobius concludes from all the matters we have thus far related that Jupiter could never have been assailed with any greater insult than by those who openly and everywhere shamelessly proclaimed his abominable adulteries? For what is more insulting to the gods than to arraign them on a charge of adultery, which human laws, as is evident from Justinian’s Code and Theodoret and as we have noted elsewhere, decreed should be punished by death? (*Code of Justinian*, book IX, title IX, *On the Julian Law concerning Adultery*; Theodoret, *Discourse 3, On Angels and Demons*, p. 154; vol. I, [Col. 0515D] *Apparatus*, p. 805 ff. and p. 1241 ff.)

Finally, in the same place our author added that this same Jupiter burned with such blind and untamed lust as *babecali* youths are accustomed to do. This is indeed how the royal manuscript reads, though it appears thoroughly corrupted by the copyist’s customary ignorance. Accordingly, for *babecali* some have conjectured that *vagari* (“to roam”) should be read, while others propose *bacchari* (“to revel frenziedly”); the latter is better insofar as it comes closer to Arnobius’s purpose. For Arnobius there assails Jupiter’s lack of restraint and shows that, although old and gray-haired, he burned with no less lustful ardor for women than young men do (the same author, ibid., p. 713; Arnobius, book IV, p. 141).

## CHAPTER XII. How Arnobius Shows That the Religion of the Pagans Is False from the Adulteries and Crimes of Other Gods and Goddesses

[Col. 0516A]

### ARTICLE I. How Irrefutably Arnobius Proved the Pagans’ Opinions About Their Gods to Be Absurd from Saturn’s Adultery with Philyra; Mars’s with Venus; Hercules’s with the Fifty Daughters of Thestius; Neptune’s with Amphitrite, Amymone, and Alope; Apollo’s with Arsinoe, Arethusa, Hypsipyle, Marpissa, Zeuxippe, Prothoe, Daphne, and Sterope, and Also with Coronis, from Whom Was Born Aesculapius, Struck by Lightning on Account of His Avarice

The chastity and modesty of the other gods were no greater than Jupiter’s. For Saturn, as Arnobius says (Arnobius, book IV, p. 145), although worn out by old age, [Col. 0516B] is nevertheless “shown in the songs” of the poets “to have been caught by his wife in adultery, to have assumed the form of a wild beast, and to have flown away under the appearance of a farm animal, uttering neighs.” With these words he marks the well-known tale celebrated by Apollonius of Rhodes (Apollonius, book II, *Argonautica*, vv. 1335 ff.), in which Saturn is said to have fallen in love with Philyra, daughter of Oceanus. While he was coupling with her, he changed himself into a horse so that he would not be recognized by the arrival of his wife Ops, or Rhea. From that intercourse was born the centaur Chiron, who had the appearance of a man in the front part of his body and a horse in the rear. Hence Ovid’s verse:

> How Saturn, as a horse, begot the two-formed Chiron.

(Ovid, book IV, *Metamorphoses*, § 3, p. 204.) You will find more in Natalis Comes (Natalis Comes, [Col. 0516C] book III, *Mythology*, ch. 12).

Now, in our preceding dissertation we noted what Arnobius recounts about Mars: while assailing another man’s genitals, he was caught entangled in snares—that is, discovered in adultery with Venus and bound in chains by Vulcan, as Gregory Nazianzen also writes and as we have noted elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 18, art. 4; Arnobius, book IV, p. 144, and book V, p. 186; Gregory, Oration 3, or 1 *Against Julian*, p. 258; *Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 17, art. 4).

Who, moreover, was more intemperate and wanton than Hercules? “The holy god,” as our author wittily jokes, “thoroughly taught the fifty daughters of Thestius in a single night both to relinquish the name of virginity and to bear the burdens of motherhood.” [Col. 0516D] (Arnobius, book IV, p. 145.) Tatian, Clement of Alexandria, Gregory Nazianzen, and Theodoret similarly reproached the pagans with this immoderate and hitherto unheard-of wantonness of Hercules (Tatian, *Oration Against the Greeks*, p. 159; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 20; Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 3, or 1 *Against Julian*, p. 263; Theodoret, Discourse 8, *On the Martyrs*, pp. 594 ff.). Among pagan writers, Pausanias reports what the opinions of earlier authors were on this matter; Ovid alludes to them and addresses Hercules himself thus:

> The crowd of Teuthrantian sisters will not be a reproach to you,  
> Of whose whole company not one was left untouched by you.

(Ovid, *Heroides*, Epistle 9, p. 89.)

[Col. 0517A] The king of the sea, Arnobius continues (book IV, p. 144)—that is, Neptune—was polluted by not merely one adultery: through the ardor of frenzied desire he deprived Amphitrite, Hippothoe, Amymone, Melanippe, and Alope of their virginal chastity. He borrowed this material from Clement of Alexandria, who added three further women to these (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 20):

> Κάλει μοι τὸν Ποσειδῶ, καὶ τὸν χορὸν τὸν διεφθαρμενόν ὑπ᾽ αὐτοῦ, τὴν Ἀμφιτείτην, τὴν Ἀμυμώνην, τὴν Ἀλόπιν, τὴν Μεναλίππην, τὴν Ἀλκυόνην, τὴν Ἱπποθόην, τὴν Χιόνην, τὰς ἄλλας τὰς μυρίας, ἐν αἷς δὴ καὶ τοσαύταις οὔσαις, ἔτι τοῦ Ποσειδῶνος ὑμῶν ἐστενοχωρεῖτο τὰ πάθη.
>
> Call Neptune for me, and the whole chorus corrupted by him: Amphitrite, Amymone, Alope, Melanippe, Alcyone, Hippothoe, Chione, and the [Col. 0517B] countless others. And although these women were so very numerous, the passions of your Neptune were still hemmed in within too narrow a space.

But Arnobius omitted the last three, as well as Clement’s countless others, because he judged those whom each author calls by name sufficient for his purpose. For the same reason, surely, Julius Firmicus names only Amymone, Alope, Melanippe, Chione, and Hippothoe. Concerning these and the others violated by Neptune, consult Natalis Comes and Vossius (Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 16; Comes, book II, *Mythology*, ch. 8, p. 166; Vossius, book I, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, ch. 15, p. 63).

Arnobius continues his irony and pleasantly mocks Apollo as follows: “Apollo Latonius, that immaculate, most chaste and pure god, lusted after the Arsinoes, Aethusas, [Col. 0517C] Hypsipyles, Marpissas, Zeuxippes, Prothoes, Daphnes, and Steropes with the heats of an unreflecting heart.” But earlier Clement of Alexandria, from whom Arnobius likewise sampled these things, said (Arnobius, book IV, p. 144; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 20):

> Κάλεί μοι καὶ τὸν Ἀπόλλω, Φοῖβός ἐστιν οὗτος, καὶ μάντις ἁγνὸς, καὶ σύμβουλος ἀγαθός· ἀλλ᾽ οὐ ταῦτα ἡ Στερόπη λέγει, οὐδὲ ἡ Αἴθουσα, οὐδὲ ἡ Ἀρσινόη, οὐδὲ ἡ Ζευξίππη, οὐδὲ ἡ Προθόη, οὐδὲ ἡ Μάρπισσα, οὐδὲ ἡ Ὑψιπύλη· Δάφνη γὰρ ἐξέφυγε μόνη καὶ τὸν μάντιν, καὶ τὴν φθοράν.
>
> Call Apollo for me as well. This is Phoebus, a chaste prophet and a good counselor. But Sterope does not say so, nor Aethusa, nor Arsinoe, nor Zeuxippe, nor Prothoe, nor Marpissa, nor Hypsipyle. Daphne alone escaped both the prophet and [Col. 0517D] violation.

Although Daphne escaped violation, this does not weaken the force of Arnobius’s argument; on the contrary, it proves most clearly that Apollo was driven by blind and unbridled lust for her and was shamefully inflamed. Ovid sang of this tale. In addition, you may read Julius Firmicus on her and on other women desperately loved by Apollo; and, if you still have leisure, consult Natalis Comes (Ovid, book II, *Metamorphoses*, fable 10, pp. 27 ff.; Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 762; Comes, book IV, *Mythology*, ch. 10, p. 342).

Aesculapius was undoubtedly the son of Apollo and grandson of Jupiter, and our Arnobius says more than once that he was born of Coronis (Arnobius, book I, p. 20, and [Col. 0518A] book VII, p. 249). Diodorus Siculus, whose words Eusebius transcribed, testifies somewhere that he was indeed the son of Apollo and Phoronis—Φορωνίδος; better in Eusebius, Κορωνίδος, “Coronis”—or, as Theodoret observes from Apollodorus, of Arsinoe. When he healed many people who were in desperate health, Jupiter, resenting it, struck him with a thunderbolt (Diodorus, book IV, *Library*, p. 189; Eusebius, book II, *Preparation for the Gospel*, ch. 2, p. 57; Theodoret, Discourse 8, *On the Martyrs*, p. 595).

Arnobius therefore left this written about him elsewhere: “Was it not because of greed and avarice, as the Boeotian Pindar sings, that Aesculapius was pierced by the weapon of the thunderbolt?” Tertullian likewise says: “There is also that lyric poet—I mean Pindar—who sings that Aesculapius was condemned by the thunderbolt as the due reward of his avarice, because he practiced medicine harmfully. Jupiter is evil, if the thunderbolt is his; impious toward his grandson, envious of the craftsman.” [Col. 0518B] (Arnobius, book IV, p. 143; Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 14, p. 15.) Clement of Alexandria had reported this earlier, citing verses on the matter not only from Pindar but also from Euripides. See, moreover, Cyril of Alexandria likewise arguing against Julian the Apostate, together with the points noted by us elsewhere and those to be discussed later in the following dissertation (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 18; Cyril, book VI *Against Julian*, pp. 200 ff.; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 754; *Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 15, art. 3).

To the writers cited we may add [Col. 0518C] one more, Gregory Nazianzen, who described these and other wholly unspeakable and execrable crimes of the gods in these few verses (Gregory Nazianzen, Poem 61, p. 142):

> Ψεύστας, ἀνδροφόνους, σκολιοὺς, ἐπίορκον ὀμοῦντας,  
> Ἅρπαγας, ἀνδρογύνους, μοιχοὺς, ἐπιβήτορας ἀνδρῶν.
>
> Liars, men bound in the blood of slaughter, crooked men,  
> Swearing falsely, plunderers, androgynes,  
> Breakers of the marriage-bed’s laws, and men who in unspeakable frenzy  
> Couple with boys and the male sex.

But concerning this wholly execrable love of boys, let us hear our Arnobius, if you please.

### ARTICLE II. How Clearly Arnobius Further Proved the Pagan Gods False from the Boys Catamitus, or Ganymede, Hylas, Hyacinthus, Pelops, and Chrysippus, Whom They Most Shamefully Loved and Violated

[Col. 0518D]

It was too little for the utterly insatiable lust of the gods to have committed so many detestable adulteries with women; blinded in addition by a most shameful love of boys, they inflicted upon them—horrible to say—those violations which the pagans were not ashamed to publish in their histories. For by Jupiter himself, whom they called the Best and Greatest God, “the boy Catamitus,” says Arnobius (Arnobius, book V, p. 172), “was stripped of the honor of his modesty.” And, as he had said in another book (the same author, book IV, p. 145), “The boy Catamitus is carried off to become his darling and keeper of the cups.” If you ask who this Catamitus was, Festus will answer (Festus, *On the [Col. 0519A] Meaning of Words*): “They used *Catamitus* for Ganymede, who was Jupiter’s catamite.” For this reason he is said to have been carried up to heaven, and Ovid celebrated the story in these verses:

> The king of the gods once burned with love  
> For Phrygian Ganymede, and something was found  
> That Jupiter preferred to be rather than what he was.  
> Yet he deigns to be changed into no bird except one  
> Capable of bearing his thunderbolts. Without delay,  
> Beating the air with deceitful wings, he carries off  
> The descendant of Ilus, who even now mixes the cups  
> And serves nectar to Jupiter, against Juno’s will.

(Ovid, book X, *Metamorphoses*, § 4, pp. 563 ff.) It is therefore no wonder that Arnobius reproached the pagans, once and again, with that monstrous and wholly detestable crime (Arnobius, book V, p. 187).

[Col. 0519B] Cicero, however, thinks it was perversely fabricated by Homer, who transferred human things to the gods. For somewhere he committed the following to writing: “Nor do I listen to Homer, who says that Ganymede was carried off by the gods because of his beauty so that he might serve cups to Jupiter—no just cause for so great an injury to be done to Laomedon. Homer invented these things and transferred human qualities to the gods; I should have preferred him to transfer divine qualities to us.” (Cicero, book I, *Tusculan Disputations*, p. 125, line 27.) But this did not prevent Arnobius and Julius Firmicus from rightly and deservedly reproaching the pagans for so great a crime, believed and proclaimed by nearly all of them (Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 15). Consult Vossius, if you wish (Vossius, book I, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, p. 61), who therefore argues that Cicero’s memory failed him there because [Col. 0519C] he called Ganymede the son of Laomedon. The same Vossius discusses the name Catamitus elsewhere (the same author, *Etymologies*; Arnobius, book IV, p. 145).

What our author added to these words—“And so that Fabius may be called Jupiter’s chick, he is burned in his tender parts and branded on his buttocks”—is explained a little more clearly by these words of Festus: “Fabius, whose surname was Eburnus, was called Jupiter’s chick because of his fairness, since his buttocks had been struck by lightning. The ancients called a boy whom someone loved that man’s *chick*.” (Festus, under the word *Pullus*.)

But let us proceed with our Arnobius to other matters. He addresses the pagans themselves as follows: “Why, not content to attribute concern for the female sex to the gods, [Col. 0519D], do you also add males as sexes beloved by them? Someone loves Hylas; another is engrossed by Hyacinthus; that one burns with desire for Pelops; this one sighs still more ardently for Chrysippus.” (Arnobius, book IV, p. 145.) You may readily understand from the following words of Clement of Alexandria that Arnobius took these things from him:

> Οὐδὲ γὰρ παίδων ἀπέσχοντο οἱ παρ᾽ ὑμῖν θεοί· ὁ μέν τις Ὕλα· ὁ δὲ Ὑακίνθου· ὁ δὲ Πέλοπος· ὁ δὲ Χρυσίππου.
>
> For certain gods among you did not even abstain from boys: one loved Hylas, another Hyacinthus, another Pelops, another Chrysippus.

(Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 21.)

Hylas was the son of Theodamas, king of the Dryopians, and was certainly very beautiful. Hercules killed his father, carried the boy off, and took him along to Colchis [Col. 0520A] when he sailed there with the Argonauts. He later sent him to draw water from the river Ascanius, or the spring of Calciamnus; but the nymphs, captivated by his beauty, carried him away. When Hercules had searched for him in vain, he instituted rites in his honor at which the name of Hylas was solemnly shouted. Hence Virgil:

> To these he adds Hylas, and the spring beside which  
> The sailors, having lost him, cried aloud, until the whole shore  
> Resounded: “Hylas! Hylas!”

(Virgil, *Eclogue* VI, v. 43.) On these verses see the observations of Servius, as well as Strabo, Apollonius, Theocritus, and others (Strabo, book XII, *Geography*, p. 564; Apollonius, book I, *Argonautica*, vv. 1207 ff.; Theocritus, *Idyll* 13).

[Col. 0520B] Ovid sang that Hyacinthus, son of King Amyclas, whom Arnobius next mentions, was desperately loved by Apollo and Zephyrus (Ovid, book XII, *Metamorphoses*, fable 5; Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, pp. 15 ff.); nor can this be unknown to anyone. Julius Firmicus reported about him, Hylas, and the other two, Pelops and Chrysippus, the same things as our Arnobius, though a little more clearly. From them he argues against the pagans as follows: “If someone delights in the embraces of boys, let him seek Ganymede in Jupiter’s lap; let him see Hercules searching for Hylas with an impatient love; let him learn that Apollo was captivated by desire for Hyacinthus. Let another look to Chrysippus, another to Pelops, so that he may say that, through the example of his gods, whatever is today most severely punished by Roman laws is permissible to him.”

[Col. 0520C] Tatian appears to indicate in the following words who loved Pelops, about whom the same Julius speaks elsewhere (ibid., p. 20; Tatian, *Oration Against the Greeks*, p. 162):

> Παρ᾽ ὑμῖν ὁ Πέλοψ δεῖπνον τῶν θεῶν γίνεται, καὶ Ποσειδῶνος ἐρώμενος.
>
> Among you Pelops is served at the banquet of the gods and is—or, “although he is”—a boy beloved by Neptune.

Pindar, however (Pindar, Olympian Ode I, vv. 38 ff.):

> … Τοῦ μεγασθενὴς  
> Ἐράσσατο γαίαοχος Ποσειδῶν.
>
> Him mighty Neptune,  
> Encircler of the earth, loved.

Finally, Athenaeus transmitted the following concerning Chrysippus and the love of boys (Athenaeus, book XIII, pp. 602 ff.): [Col. 0520D]

> Ἄλλοι δὲ φασι τῶν τοιούτων ἐρώτων κατάρξασθαι Λάιον, παρὰ Πέλοπι, καὶ ἐρασθέντα τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ Χρυσίππου, ὃν καὶ ἁρπάσαντα καὶ ἀναθέμενον εἰς ἅρμα, εἰς Θήβας φυγεῖν. Πραξίλλα δὲ ἡ Σικυωνία ὑπὸ Διὸς φησὶν ἁρπασθῆναι τὸν Χρύσιππον.
>
> Others say that Laius originated such forms of love while he was staying with Pelops. He fell in love with Pelops’s son Chrysippus, abducted him, placed him in a chariot, and fled to Thebes. Praxilla of Sicyon, however, says that Chrysippus was abducted by Jupiter.

See Aelian as well, if you are so inclined, though he does not mention Jupiter there (Aelian, book XIII, *Various History*, ch. 5). But who would not shudder to call gods those who burned with a love so execrable that no fires could ever suffice to expiate it?

### ARTICLE III. How Arnobius Shows the Divinity of the Goddesses to Be False from Their Unchaste Love for Men: Aurora’s for Tithonus, the Moon’s for Endymion, the Nereid’s for Aeacus, Thetis’s for the Father of Achilles, Proserpina’s for Adonis, Ceres’s for the Rustic Jasion, and Venus’s for Vulcan, Phaethon, Mars, and Anchises; and Why Venus Is Called “Dionean” and the Mother of the Trojan Man

[Col. 0521A]

How great the unchastity of the goddesses was Arnobius, following Clement of Alexandria, plainly demonstrates by these examples: “Is it not recorded in your writings that Tithonus was loved by Aurora; that the Moon burned for Endymion; the Nereid for Aeacus; Thetis for the father of Achilles; Proserpina for Adonis; his mother Ceres for some rustic or other named Jasion; and that after Vulcan, Phaethon, and Mars, that very Venus—the mother of the descendants of Aeneas [Col. 0521B] and founder of Roman dominion—entered into marriage with Anchises?” (Arnobius, book IV, pp. 145 ff.).

Clement of Alexandria had earlier reproached the same pagans with these things (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 21):

> Ἠὼς ἐπὶ Τιθωνῷ, Σελήνη Ἐνδυμίωνι, Νηρηὶς ἐπὶ Αἰακῷ, καὶ ἐπὶ Πηλεῖ Θέτις· ἐπὶ δὲ Ἰασίωνι Δημήτηρ, καὶ ἐπὶ Ἀδώνιδι Φερεφάττα· Ἀφροδίτη δὲ ἐπ᾽ Ἄρει κατῃσχυμμένη, μετῆλθεν ἐπὶ Κινύραν, καὶ Ἀγχίσην ἔγημεν· καὶ Φαέθοντα ἐλόχα, καὶ ἤρα Ἀδώνιδος.
>
> Aurora was inflamed for Tithonus; the Moon for Endymion; the Nereid for Aeacus; and Thetis for Peleus. Ceres was inflamed for Jasion, and Proserpina for Adonis. Venus, disgraced through Mars, passed on to Cinyras and married Anchises; she laid snares for Phaethon and loved Adonis.

[Col. 0521C] Tithonus, brother of Laomedon, king of the Trojans, was, as Servius says (Servius, on the passage of Virgil about to be cited), loved and carried off by Aurora because of the excellence of his beauty. He was conveyed in her chariot to Ethiopia and there begot Memnon by her. Hence Virgil sang:

> Or when pale Aurora rises,  
> Leaving Tithonus’s saffron bed.

(Virgil, book I, *Georgics*, v. 446.) And again in another book:

> And now first Aurora was sprinkling the earth with new light,  
> Leaving Tithonus’s saffron bed.

(The same author, book IV, *Aeneid*, v. 584.) Hesiod says more on these matters (Hesiod, *Theogony*, v. 904), as does Propertius (Propertius, book II, elegy 18; the same author, elegy 15), who wrote these verses about Endymion:

[Col. 0521D]

> Even naked Endymion is said to have captivated  
> Phoebus’s sister and to have lain with the naked goddess.

He was a shepherd, the son of Athlius. The Moon, captivated by love for him, hid him in a cave on Latmus, a mountain of Caria, and, as Cicero says, kissed him while he slept. Do you wish his words to be presented to you? Here they are: “Endymion, if we wish to listen to fables, fell asleep at some unknown time on Latmus, a mountain of Caria, and in my opinion has not yet awakened. Do you therefore suppose that he troubles himself when the Moon is eclipsed—the Moon by whom he is thought to have been put to sleep so that she might kiss him while he slept?” (Cicero, book I, *Tusculan Disputations*, p. 130, line 36.) If you wish to hear several authors who do not reject these things as old women’s tales unworthy ever to be heard, you may consult Theocritus, Ovid, [Col. 0522A] Pliny, and others (Theocritus, *Idyll* 3; Ovid, *Heroides*, Epistle 18, p. 199; book III, *Art of Love*, p. 473; Pliny, book II, *Natural History*, ch. 9, p. 152).

By the name “Nereid,” our Arnobius, still following Clement of Alexandria as we have already seen (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 21), means Psamathe, daughter of Nereus, by whom Aeacus, as Hesiod relates, begot Phocus (Hesiod, *Theogony*, v. 1004):

> Ἤτοι μὲν Φῶκον Ψαμάθη τέκε δῖα θεάων,  
> Αἰακοῦ ἐν φιλότητι, διὰ χρυσῆν Ἀφροδίτην.
>
> Psamathe, excellent among goddesses, indeed bore Phocus,  
> Through golden Venus, in love with Aeacus.

Ovid has much about Aeacus and Phocus, which you may read when you please (Ovid, book VII, *Metamorphoses*, § 24 ff.).

[Col. 0522B] The man whom Arnobius next calls the father of Achilles is rightly named Peleus by Clement of Alexandria; he begot Achilles by Thetis (Clement, loc. cit., p. 21). For Hesiod, whom we have already cited, sang (Hesiod, *Theogony*, v. 1006):

> Πηλεῖ δὲ δμηθεῖσα θεὰ Θέτις ἀργυρόπεζα,  
> Γείνατ᾽ Ἀχιλλῆα.
>
> The goddess Thetis of the silver feet, subdued by Peleus,  
> Bore Achilles.

But you will find this celebrated at length by Ovid (Ovid, book II, *Metamorphoses*, § 7).

It is reported that Proserpina and Venus, both desperately in love with Adonis, came before Jupiter for judgment so that he might pronounce to which of the two Adonis should be granted. [Col. 0522C] Jupiter appointed Calliope arbiter and judge of the dispute; she determined that each should possess him for half of the year. Read, if you wish, Hyginus, Apollodorus, and Giraldus (Hyginus, *Poetic Astronomy*; Apollodorus, book III, *Library*; Giraldus, *Syntagma 13 on the Gods*, p. 396).

Our author calls Jasion merely some rustic or other; Nonnus, however, calls him a farmer and the husband of Ceres. Others call him a son of Jupiter and Electra, and some a son of Menois and Phronia (Nonnus, book XLVIII, vv. 969 ff.). Hesiod says that he begot Plutus by Ceres (Hesiod, *Theogony*, v. 969):

> Δημήτηρ μὲν Πλοῦτον ἐγείνατο, δῖα θεάων,  
> Ἰασίῳ ἥρωϊ μιγεῖσ᾽ ἐρατῇ φιλότητι.
>
> Ceres, excellent among goddesses, bore Plutus,  
> [Col. 0522D] Mingling in delightful love with the hero Jasion.

Consult also, if you wish and have leisure, Theocritus and Ovid (Theocritus, *Idyll*, v. 50; Ovid, book IX, *Metamorphoses*, § 11).

But unchaste Venus burned with a most wicked love not only for Jasion, but also for Vulcan, Mars, Phaethon, and Anchises. We discussed Mars shortly above, and Phaethon—or rather Phaon—in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 767).

It is worth observing here, however, that Cicero distinguishes three Venuses, of whom “the third,” he says (Cicero, book III, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 248, line 28), “born of Jupiter and Dione, married Vulcan,” who burned for her, as our author said. This is confirmed by Servius [Col. 0523A] in his observations on these verses of Virgil:

> But Venus, the mother, not needlessly terrified in spirit,  
> Moved by the threats of the Laurentines and the harsh uproar,  
> Addresses Vulcan and begins these words in her husband’s  
> Golden chamber, breathing divine love into her speech.
>
> . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
>
> She had spoken; then, embracing him on either side  
> With snow-white arms, the goddess warmed his hesitation  
> With a soft embrace, etc.

(Virgil, book VIII, *Aeneid*, vv. 370 ff.)

Finally, if anyone wishes to have it proved that Venus also married Anchises and that Aeneas was born from this union, let him hear Hesiod among the Greeks (Hesiod, *Theogony*, v. 1008):

> Αἰνείαν δ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ἔτικτεν ἐϋστέφανος Κυθέρεια,  
> Ἀγχίσῃ ἥρωϊ μιγεῖσ᾽ ἐρατῇ φιλότητι.
>
> Fair-crowned Cytherea bore Aeneas,  
> Mingling in delightful love with the hero Anchises.

Let him also hear Virgil among the Latins, if he wishes:

[Col. 0523B]

> Are you indeed that Aeneas whom nurturing Venus bore  
> To Dardanian Anchises beside the waters of the Phrygian Simois?

(Virgil, book I, *Aeneid*, vv. 621 ff.) On these verses let him read Servius’s annotations. Let him also turn through the books of Ovid (Ovid, book IV, *Fasti*, § 1), who celebrated this in his *Fasti*, and in another book, where he mentions in the following two verses other adulteries of the goddesses recorded not only by Arnobius but also by Lactantius (Lactantius, book I, *Institutes*, ch. 17, p. 92):

> Anchises has Venus, the Latmian hero  
> [Note: [Col. 0523D] That is, Endymion.] the Moon,  
> And Jasion has Ceres, to whom he may be referred.

(Ovid, book II, *Tristia*, vv. 301 ff.)

A little earlier, however, we observed from Cicero that the third Venus was the one born of Jupiter and Dione who married Vulcan. It was about her that Arnobius had said (Arnobius, book [Col. 0523C] I, p. 20): “Venus, Dione’s offspring, the matronly mother of the Trojan man and the publisher of his inward grief”—that is, Venus was the daughter of the nymph Dione, concerning whom Virgil writes:

> I was offering sacred rites to the Dionean mother and the gods.

(Virgil, book I, *Aeneid*, v. 19.) That is, says Servius, to Venus, named after her mother Dione according to Homer. She was the mother of the Trojan man—that is, Aeneas—as we noted above; and the publisher of the inward grief of that same Aeneas, because she made public his unhappy misfortunes and his intimate and domestic sorrows, which Virgil celebrated (the same author, book VIII, vv. 379 ff.). Our author, however, did not distinguish this Venus from the others because he thought it sufficient for his purpose, whether there was one or several, to demonstrate that none of them could be called a goddess, since she had cast off every sense of human modesty.

Arnobius therefore rightly concludes from the matters discussed thus far that Christians, who denied that this Venus and absolutely all those other men and women stained by such great crimes and enormities were gods, were entirely undeserving of being called impious by the pagans. On the contrary, it must be established that those very pagans who proclaimed such things about their gods were to be condemned for the greatest impiety. For if those adulteries and crimes are true, those who committed them cannot be gods. But if they are shown to be false, the gods certainly ought to have destroyed all the pagans because of such shameless and utterly [Col. 0524A] intolerable slanders and because so many shameful deeds had been falsely attributed to them.

## CHAPTER XIII. How Clearly Arnobius Proves That the Gods of the Pagans Are False and Nonexistent from Their Native Lands, Forms, Figures, Disciplines, and Arts, to Which the Pagans Boasted That the Gods Devoted Themselves or over Which They Presided

### ARTICLE I. How Irrefutably Arnobius Demonstrates the Falsity of Their Divinity from the Native Lands, Forms, and Figures Assigned to the Gods by the Pagans

Although Arnobius had shown more than sufficiently that the gods of the pagans were false from their most shameful origins and execrable crimes, he demonstrates it again by other lines of reasoning no less certain and evident. One of these he derives from the assigned native lands of the gods and the places where they died, which the pagans themselves took pains to identify for us. From this it follows with the greatest possible certainty that those gods had at one time not existed and therefore could be neither everlasting nor endowed with a divine nature.

[Col. 0524B] First, Ceres, as Arnobius says (Arnobius, book I, p. 20; *Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 20, art. I), was asserted by the pagans to have been “born within the bounds of Trinacria and occupied in gathering flowers” before Proserpina was carried off by Pluto, as we explained elsewhere. By the name Trinacria, Arnobius undoubtedly means Sicily. For we learn from Diodorus Siculus and Servius (Diodorus, book V, *Library*, p. 199; Servius, on book VI of Virgil’s *Georgics*, p. 265) that this island was first called Trinacria, or Trinax, from its shape; later Sicania, from its inhabitants the Sicanians; and finally Sicily, from the Sicels. Diodorus adds that he had learned from the Sicilians, who had received the account through a long tradition from their ancestors, that this island had once been consecrated to Ceres and Proserpina. Cicero reported more on this matter, and you may readily consult him (Cicero, Fourth Oration *Against Verres*, p. 179).

What the pagans transmitted concerning Apis—who was called Serapis in the Peloponnese—and Isis in Egypt, and what our author records concerning them, has already been sufficiently explained by us; the leisure of others should not be abused by repeating it (Arnobius, book I, p. 20; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 1090).

We have also made clear that Arnobius excerpted from Clement of Alexandria what he relates about Mars’s native land and chains. There we examined whether Hervetus rightly or wrongly charges him with error. There likewise seems no room to doubt that Arnobius also drew from the same Clement what he added about dogs and asses sacrificed to Mars (Arnobius, book IV, p. 143; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 18; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 753).

Arnobius declares how base and unworthy of divine majesty were the forms which the pagans attributed to their gods in these words addressed to the pagans themselves (Arnobius, book III, [Col. 0525A] p. 107): “It is not enough that you encompass the gods by the measurement of forms, by a human thread and human boundaries, and—what is far more unworthy—confine them within the outlines of earthly bodies.” That is, you limit and circumscribe your gods by the measurement of forms—that is, by dimension or measure—and by human *thread*, or texture and lineaments, as well as by the *outline*, or outer boundary, of earthly bodies. Cicero used the first word (Cicero, *Orator*, p. 268, line 2), while the latter two appear to have been taken from Lucretius. He employs them in various passages, from which we shall cite the following:

> There are, then, obscure traces of forms  
> Which fly about everywhere, endowed with a subtle texture.

(Lucretius, book IV, vv. 85 ff.) [Col. 0525B] Elsewhere:

> They seem confused in appearance  
> By the very slightest line.
>
> . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
>
> Sometimes they seem to change a very slight line  
> In one direction or the other.

(Book V, v. 581 and vv. 588 ff.) In another book he uses the noun *circumcaesura* (“outline”) as follows:

> Yet the outer outline of the limbs  
> Keeps itself intact.

(Book III, v. 220.) And again:

> The outer outline of the limbs confines it.

(Book IV, v. 651.)

[Col. 0525C] Arnobius demonstrates through numerous supporting arguments that the gods can neither be such beings nor consist of bodily form or human figure and appearance. Nearly all of this material, adapted by Arnobius to his own manner, was excerpted from Cicero’s first book *On the Nature of the Gods*, where Cotta the Academic refutes Velleius the Epicurean (Arnobius, book III, pp. 107 ff.; Cicero, book I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, pp. 206 ff.). But, as we believe, this will become clearer to everyone from what is about to be said.

By a brief enumeration of bodily members, therefore, Arnobius first makes it evident that the gods can be composed neither of these members nor of any bodily shape whatever. He conducts this survey in his own inflated and turgid style, using certain unusual words which are therefore neither familiar nor wholly clear to everyone and ought not to be passed over without some explanation. He teaches that, in addition to the head, ears, feet, and the other parts of the body known to everyone, the gods cannot possibly have [Col. 0525D] “the projecting roof-tile of the nostrils, passable for mucous discharges and for the passage of breath” (Arnobius, book III, p. 107)—that is, the channel of the nostrils through which mucus and fluids flow down from the head and breath is conducted.

He adds: “Teeth of three kinds, arranged for three functions” (ibid.)—that is, the first, sharp teeth, which cut food; the broad molars, which grind it; and the canine teeth, whose nature is intermediate between the other two. See Aristotle, Pliny, and Isidore. Cicero, however, appears to recognize only two kinds of teeth: namely, the sharp front teeth and the innermost teeth, or molars (Aristotle, book III, *On the Parts of Animals*, ch. 1, vol. I, p. 999; Pliny, book II, *Natural History*, ch. 37, p. 553; [Col. 0526A] Isidore, book II, *Origins*, ch. 1; Cicero, book I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 234, lines 49 ff.).

Our author adds: “the little membranes of the omenta, and gullets” (Arnobius, loc. cit.). The omentum, called ἐπίπλοον (*epiploon*) by the Greeks, is a thin, fatty membrane which envelops the coils of the intestines and covers the lower parts of the abdomen. Hence Pliny says: “The stomach and intestines are covered by a fatty, thin omentum, except in egg-laying animals.” Isidore agrees with Pliny. Juvenal somewhere sang as follows of the use of omenta in sacred rites:

> And the white  
> Omenta of a pig.

And Persius:

> Though so many omenta of heifers melt for you in the flame.

[Col. 0526B] Finally, the gods fabricated by the pagans had to possess windpipes, says Arnobius. Isidore describes the windpipe as follows: “It takes its name from the throat, and its passage extends to the mouth and nostrils. It contains the route by which the voice is transmitted to the tongue so that it may strike words together; hence we also speak of chattering.” (Pliny, book II, *Natural History*, ch. 37, p. 574; Isidore, loc. cit.; Juvenal, Satire 13, v. 118; Persius, Satire 2, v. 45; Isidore, book II, *Origins*, ch. 1, and book XII, ch. 8.)

Yet if the gods have bodies, says Arnobius, they must also possess these and the other most repulsive parts of bodies. But nothing could be more absurd to say. If, however, they lack those members, their bodies will be inflated like wineskins, but entirely empty and hollow. [Col. 0526C] More briefly and lucidly, though somewhat differently, Cotta argues as follows against Velleius the Epicurean in Cicero: “God will therefore have a tongue and will not speak; teeth, palate, and throat with no use; and those organs which nature attached to the body for the purpose of procreation God will possess in vain. The external organs are no more purposeless than the internal ones—the heart, lungs, liver, and all the rest. Once their utility has been removed, what beauty do they possess? Since you maintain that these exist in God for the sake of beauty.” (Cicero, book I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 208, line 46.)

Arnobius’s second argument is contained in this dilemma: if these gods have any appearances, forms, and figures, they are either identical and mutually similar, or multiple and dissimilar. But if the figure and face of all the gods is one and the same, they certainly do not recognize or distinguish one another. If they are multiple and diverse, [Col. 0526D] “then,” Arnobius argues, “it must be said that some are big-headed, others pug-nosed, others large-browed, still others thick-lipped; among them some are long-chinned, mole-marked, or big-nosed; some have distended nostrils, others upturned noses; some have swollen cheeks, or, from the bulging of their cheeks, are pouch-cheeked; some are dwarfs, tall, or of middle stature, lean, fat, or corpulent; some have little curls formed by the twisting of their hair, while others are bald or shaved smooth by loss of hair.” (Arnobius, book III, p. 108.)

Who will doubt that these things were excerpted from Cicero, if Arnobius ever read these words of his? “I return to the gods. Do we suppose that none of them, if not actually cross-eyed, are at least squinting? That none has a mole? That none is pug-nosed, flap-eared, large-browed, or big-headed, as people among us are? Or have all such defects been corrected in them? Let that be granted to you. [Col. 0527A] Is there, then, a single face common to them all? For if there are several, one must necessarily be more beautiful than another. . . . For if there is no difference between one god and another, there is among the gods no recognition and no perception.” (Cicero, book I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 207, line 5.)

*Labeones* (“thick-lipped men”), concerning whom Pliny (Pliny, book II, *Natural History*, ch. 37, p. 553) and others speak, were so called from their excessively large lips. Consider, however, whether *silunculi* and *naevii* are those whom Cicero described as *sili* (“pug-nosed”) and as “having a mole.” We fear, nevertheless, that these words are corrupt in the text of Arnobius. For in the royal manuscript we read *cilunculos* and *naevimos*. The word *saccibucces* (“pouch-cheeked”) is no less corrupt. In the same royal manuscript it is written *sacrivoces*; others conjecture that *acrivoces* should be written. [Col. 0527B] But without the aid of some more accurate manuscript, who could determine with certainty what the true reading is?

Arnobius presses the point that the pagans cannot deny that the gods fashioned by their people are such as we have described. For their very “workshops,” as he says, “both disclose and reveal this. For when you make and give shape to gods, you fashion some with long hair, others smooth-faced, old men, young men, boys, swarthy, gray-eyed, tawny, half-naked, uncovered, or—lest the cold discomfort them—draped all over with a covering of flowing garments.” (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 108.) These words too were drawn from the same book of Cicero. For after the words of his that we cited, he continues the discourse he had begun as follows: “Perhaps we recognize Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo, and the other gods, if they come before us, as you say, by the appearance [Col. 0527C] that painters and sculptors have chosen for them—and not only by their appearance, but also by their adornment and clothing. . . . For in that manner one may say that Jupiter is always bearded, Apollo always beardless, that Minerva’s eyes are gray, and Neptune’s blue.” (Cicero, bk. I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 207, line 12.) Does it not follow clearly enough from this that the workshops of the pagans, as Arnobius calls them, are precisely those of the painters and sculptors, as Cicero says, who were accustomed to fashion images, statues, and likenesses of the gods in the manner described by both authors? Both therefore rightly conclude from this that nothing more unworthy of God or more insulting could ever be imagined.

But Arnobius deals still more closely with the pagans (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 109), and says that it is the height of folly [Col. 0527D] for them to ridicule the enigmas of the Egyptians, who enrolled the vilest animals among the number of the gods and honored them with solemn ceremonies and rites. For the pagans themselves were not ashamed to worship and venerate human beings furnished with certain animal attributes as the true likenesses of their gods. Yet these things were again sampled from the same Cicero (Cicero, bk. I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 207, line 19), who explains them more clearly in this fashion: “What then do you think? Does not that Apis, the sacred bull of the Egyptians, appear to the Egyptians to be a god? By Hercules, just as much as our Juno Sospita does to you—whom you never see, even in your dreams, except with a goatskin, a spear, a small shield, and shoes [Col. 0528A] with upturned toes,” that is, curved upward. Who indeed will not admit that both authors demonstrate with the utmost clarity that the madness of the Romans and other pagans, who worshiped gods represented with a human face and the attributes of some animal, was no less than that of the Egyptians, who venerated the animals themselves as gods?

Arnobius, however, assails and demolishes that madness with yet another battering ram (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 109 and following). If little asses, he says, dogs, and pigs possessed some degree of human intelligence for learning the arts, and, in order to honor us, made statues and images resembling themselves, would we not feel it utterly insulting, and resent it, that we were represented in the shape of beasts? Would not the pagans themselves be indignant if Romulus were represented [Col. 0528B] in the shape of an ass, Numa in that of a dog, and Cato—or Cicero, or anyone else—in that of a pig? We have already seen that Clement of Alexandria used this same argument against the pagans in the books of the *Stromata*, and that for the same purpose he, as likewise Eusebius and Theodoret, cited the verses of Xenophanes (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. 2, ch. 14, art. 1, p. 1089).

But the gods, as Arnobius assumes, ought to take it as a greater indignity that men depict them in human form than men would if beasts depicted them with brutish faces. For the difference between gods and human beings is far greater than that between human beings and beasts. “What beauty,” Arnobius asks, “is there in a human being? What, I ask, is admirable or becoming, except what some author or other chose to make common also to the *clurinum pecus* [ape-kind]?”—so reads the manuscript codex and the latest [Col. 0528C] edition. (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 110.) In Plautus, to be sure, we read *clusirum pecus*; but Vossius thinks that he wrote *clurinum pecus*, and that apes are meant by this term (Plautus, *Comedies*, *Truculentus*, act 2, scene 2; Vossius, *Etymology*, under the word CLURA). At any rate, Arnobius seems to use it in this sense; and in the words “some author or other,” Ennius is being cited. For when Arnobius wrote this, he undoubtedly had in mind the following passage of Cicero (Cicero, bk. I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 209, line 37): “But what relevance has that resemblance itself which so greatly delights you? What? Is not a dog like a wolf?” And, as Ennius says:

> How like us is the ape, that most hideous beast!

[Col. 0528D] A greater insult is therefore inflicted upon the gods when they are fashioned like human beings than upon human beings if they were represented as resembling apes and other beasts.

Nor does Arnobius allow the pagans to answer him that the forms and appearances of the gods are indeed different from those of human beings, but are adapted to them for the sake of honor (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 109). For this error is far worse than the former one. The more certainly the pagans knew these “divine formations,” as he calls them, to be false and more unlike their gods, the greater the disgrace they inflicted upon those gods by means of them. For the man who unwittingly attributes to the gods something false, which he nevertheless believes to be true, sins less than another who knowingly and deliberately ascribes falsehoods to them. *Formamenta* means the same [Col. 0529A] as figures and forms, as is clear from these verses of Lucretius, whom our author often follows:

> All the formations of the first elements  
> Can exist in any kind of splendor.

(Lucretius, bk. II, verse 818.)

## ARTICLE II. How fictitious are the gods whom the pagans declared to be skilled in, or set over, various arts: concerning Apollo the prophet, who foretells the future; Aesculapius the physician; Vulcan the smith; Tritonia or Tritogenia and Arachne the weavers; and the offspring of Atlas, namely Calypso, more eloquent than the other gods; concerning others who were imagined to preside over arts or sciences, such as Portunus over navigation, Pales over herds and flocks—whence the Palilia—Inuus or Pan over animals, Pythius over diviners, enriched by the treasuries of kings, and the Tutelary gods set over the protection of human beings.

Arnobius draws another argument against the false divinity of those whom the pagans worshiped [Col. 0529B] from the fact that the pagans proclaimed them craftsmen and patrons of the arts and sciences. For, as he says in addressing the pagans: “You introduce gods to us, some as smiths, others as physicians, wool-workers, sailors, lyre-players, flute-players, hunters, shepherds, and—what alone remained—farmers.” (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 111.) Nor could the pagans deny these things, which their own writers had celebrated again and again. For, to pass over a great many of them, Hesiod sang of these matters in the *Theogony*. Virgil himself, when invoking them, acknowledges rural gods and shepherd gods (Virgil, beginning of bk. I of the *Georgics*).

What could be more opposed to the divine nature than these absurd inventions of opinion? Are there, our author asks, fields in heaven for the gods to cultivate; [Col. 0529C] mountains and forests in which they may hunt; sick persons for them to heal; or other places in which they may practice the other arts? What greater folly and arrogance could there be than seriously to say that one god is trained in some art which another must not know? What could be more offensive than to assert that one goddess can bring aid to another who is in labor or ill, when the latter could not bring it to herself?

In vain, therefore, Arnobius continues (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 112), did the pagans imagine that the Latonian prophet—namely Apollo, born, as we have said, of Jupiter and Latona—was filled by another god, that is, by Jupiter himself, and foretold to the other gods things that they did not know. For an ancient poet once sang:

> Στέλλειν ὅπως τάχιστα· ταῦτα γὰρ πατὴρ  
> Ζεὺς ἐγκαθεῖ Λοξίᾳ.

> Come here with all possible speed; for such things  
> Father Zeus puts into Apollo’s mouth as he speaks.

[Col. 0529D] See Natalis Comes on this matter (*Mythology*, bk. IV, ch. 10, p. 359).

They also falsely proclaimed that the Epidaurian—that is, Aesculapius, whom we have already discussed more than once—healed the diseases and wounds of others (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 754 and 1193, and above, ch. 9, art. 2). Arnobius further states (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 113, and bk. IV, p. 143) that Vulcan manufactured weapons, or, as elsewhere, practiced smithcraft on the island of Lemnos. This was undoubtedly taken from the following words of Cicero: “The third Vulcan, born of the third Jupiter and Juno, is said to have presided over the forge at Lemnos.” [Col. 0530A] We have already shown from the verses of Virgil cited above that the arms of Aeneas were fashioned by him. This is also the same Vulcan under whose guardianship, our author elsewhere asserts, fire was placed. But we have treated him in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (Cicero, bk. III, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 248, line 2; Virgil, bk. VIII, *Aeneid*, verse 370 and following; Arnobius, bk. III, p. 114; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 776, and below).

The goddess who spun for the gods and, without burden, put upon them three-ply garments—that is, garments made from three threads of various colors—is called Tritonia by our Arnobius (Arnobius, bk. II, p. 112, and bk. VII, p. 228; below, ch. 14, art. 3). She is Pallas, or Minerva, who was therefore called Tritonia, Tritonis, or Tritogenia, either because she sprang from Jupiter’s brain, or, as Lucan and Servius after him say, from Triton, a lake in Africa [Col. 0530B] beside which she is said to have been born (Lucan, bk. IX, verse 341 and following; Servius, on bk. II of the *Aeneid*, p. 232). If Ovid is to be believed, however, she wove cloth and taught girls the art of weaving. Hear, I pray, his verses:

> When Pallas has been appeased, soften the wool, girls;  
> Learn now to unload the full distaffs.  
> She also teaches you to run the shuttle through the upright warp  
> And with the comb to close the loosely woven work.  
> Worship her, you who remove stains from damaged garments;  
> Worship her, whoever prepares bronze vessels for fleeces.

(Ovid, bk. III of the *Fasti*, near the end.) He also sang of the contest between the same Pallas and Arachne in wool-working and weaving, and of what each of them did (same author, beginning of bk. VI of the *Metamorphoses*, p. 187 and following). Finally, Julius Firmicus, when discussing the various [Col. 0530C] Minervas, says: “There was another in Egypt, the daughter of King Nile, a mistress of the art of weaving.” (Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 20.) But the pagans could never prove this.

Finally, the “offspring of Atlas” (the royal manuscript reads *Alantea*), who, as Arnobius says (Arnobius, bk. II, p. 112), is reported to have won first place in eloquence—is she not Calypso, the daughter of Atlas, as Homer and Tibullus observed (Homer, *Odyssey* V; Tibullus, bk. IV, elegy 1, verse 77), with whom the shipwrecked Ulysses stayed for six or seven years, and from whom he afterward departed at Jupiter’s command, as the same Homer sings? Ovid and others mention her more than once (Ovid, bk. II of the *Amores*, elegy 17, p. 336; bk. II of the *Art of Love*, p. 442; and epistle 10, p. 353). Was Calypso, then, more eloquent [Col. 0530D] than the other gods or goddesses?

What did the pagans reply to this? “We say that the gods are not workmen or craftsmen, but teachers of the arts and sciences.” Yet the vanity and worthlessness of this answer are evident from what has already been said, by which we have shown how positively the pagans declared that the arts were practiced by them. Grant, nevertheless, that the gods and goddesses merely presided over the arts. Tell me, then, how they could have taught them unless they had first been trained in them and had been the first practitioners. Moreover, since there is no place for arts among the heavenly beings, why did the pagans vainly babble that certain gods excelled only in this or that art and science? For the true God must necessarily know all things and be utterly ignorant of nothing.

[Col. 0531A] Nor indeed did those advance matters by the slightest degree who thought that gods truly presided over the arts, so that through their care and administration everything might turn out successfully for us. For Arnobius proves this to be utterly false (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 113). How many and how great shipwrecks, he says, do men suffer, although Portunus is said, on Virgil’s testimony, to preside over navigation? For Virgil sang of him:

> And father Portunus himself, with his mighty hand,  
> Propelled him on his way.

(Virgil, bk. V of the *Aeneid*, verse 240.) Ovid, however, says:

> He whom his own tongue calls Palaemon, but ours Portunus—  
> Be favorable, I pray, each of you, to our shores.

(Ovid, bk. VI of the *Fasti*, verse 490.) For Portunus was called Palaemon in Greek, and also Melicertes, [Col. 0531B] and, as Servius notes on the cited verse of Virgil and elsewhere, he was a marine god who presides over harbors. Varro mentioned him, his temple, and the festivals established in his honor (Servius, on bk. I of the *Georgics*, p. 91; Varro, bk. I, *On the Latin Language*, p. 50). But we shall discuss these matters in the following dissertation on the books of Lactantius.

Nor, Arnobius says (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 113), did Pales and Inuus—whom the pagans believed to preside over herds and flocks—ward off plagues and contagions from livestock. Pales was imagined to be the goddess of shepherds, or, as Solinus says, the Pastoral Goddess (Solinus, *Polyhistor*, ch. 1, p. 2). Hence Ovid, when writing of the Palilia, or the festival customarily held in joyous commemoration of this goddess on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, as Servius notes, celebrated it in these words:

> And when the year comes round, let us too make  
> Great cakes for Pales, mistress of shepherds.

[Col. 0531C] (Ovid, bk. IV of the *Fasti*, p. 602.) Virgil also sings of her:

> Pales herself has left the fields, and Apollo himself as well.

(Servius on Virgil, bk. III of the *Georgics*, verse 1, p. 120.) Again, when about to speak of animals, he begins with her as follows:

> You too, great Pales, . . . we shall sing.

(Virgil, *Eclogue* V, verse 4.) On these verses, and especially the latter, Servius observes that she was also the goddess of pastures, whom some called Vesta and others the Mother of the Gods. Varro, moreover, is said somewhere to have added his support to both Ovid and Virgil in these words: “The Palilia are named from Pales, because [Col. 0531D] festivals are held for that goddess.” Festus, however, endorsed them in the following fashion: “Pales was called the goddess of shepherds; her festivals were called the Palilia, or, as others maintain, the Parilia, because sacrifices were made to her on behalf of the delivery of livestock” (Festus, under the word PALES).

Servius, whom we have already cited, wished everyone to be advised that Pales is called a goddess in the feminine gender by Varro, but masculine by others: “this Pales,” he says (Servius on bk. III of the *Georgics*, verse 1). Nevertheless Caesius, afterward cited by our author, distinguishes from this goddess “Pales—but not,” he says (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 123), “that female whom common opinion accepts, but some minister and steward of Jupiter, of the masculine gender.” See Aulus Gellius, [Col. 0532A] Lilius Giraldus, Turnebus, and others (Gellius, bk. XIII of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 22; Giraldus, *Syntagma* 1, p. 42, and *Syntagma* 17, p. 525; Turnebus, bk. XIX of the *Adversaria*, ch. 11, p. 140).

Inuus, whom our author still mentions, was, according to Macrobius, the same as Pan; or, as Servius observes: “In Latin he is called Inuus, in Greek Πάν [Pan]; the same is ἐφιάλτης [ephialtēs, ‘nightmare’] in Greek and Incubus in Latin. He is likewise Faunus, likewise Fatuus and Fatuellus. He is called Inuus from *ineundo*, ‘going in to’ all animals indiscriminately.” (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 113; Macrobius, bk. I of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 22, p. 278; Servius, on bk. VI of the *Aeneid*, p. 441.) Do you hear what a charming god he is, and how worthy of a god his office is?

What more need be said? Arnobius says: “Pythius”—namely Apollo—“bestows [Col. 0532B] knowledge of divinity upon soothsayers; and why, then, does he so often give and furnish replies that are oblique and doubtful, submerged in a mist of obscurity?” (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 114.) Quite rightly so; for Chrysippus, as Cicero relates (Cicero, bk. II, *On Divination*, p. 296), had filled an entire volume with the oracles of Apollo—some false, some true by chance, some evasive and obscure, requiring an interpreter, and some ambiguous and needing to be referred to dialectic. The Latin Orator himself demonstrates this most clearly by certain examples involving Croesus and Pyrrhus. These are undoubtedly the two kings about whom our author afterward recorded, without naming them, the following: “Apollo, having been made rich, deceived [Col. 0532C] by the ambiguity of his response those very kings by whose treasuries and gifts he had been enriched.” (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 133.) Lucian had said much the same thing in these words (Lucian, dialogue *Juno and Latona*, p. 81):

> Ὁ δ᾽ Ἀπόλλων προσποιεῖται μὲν πάντα εἰδέναι, καὶ τοξεύειν, καὶ κιθαρίζειν, καὶ ἰατρὸς εἶναι, καὶ μαντεύεσθαι· καὶ καταστησάμενος ἐργαστήρια τῆς μαντικῆς, τὸ μὲν ἐν Δελφοῖς, τὸ μὲν ἐν Κλάρῳ, καὶ ἐν Διδύμοις, ἐξαπατᾷ τοὺς χρωμένους αὐτῷ, λοξὰ καὶ ἐπαμφοτερίζοντα, πρὸς ἑκάτερον τῆς ἐρωτήσεως ἀποκρινόμενος, ὡς ἀκίνδυνον εἶναι τὸ σφάλμα· καὶ πλουτεῖ μὲν ἀπὸ τοῦ τοιούτου· πολλοὶ γὰρ οἱ ἀνόητοι, καὶ παρέχοντες αὐτοὺς καταγοητεύεσθαι.

> Apollo pretends that he knows everything, that he can shoot the bow and play the lyre, that he is a physician, and that he can prophesy. Having established workshops of prophecy—one at Delphi, another at Claros, and another at Didyma—he deceives those who consult him by replying in oblique terms that lean both ways, toward either side of the question proposed, so that any error carries no risk for him. From this he makes a profit and grows rich; for there are many fools who offer themselves to be deluded by his sorcery.

[Col. 0532D] Lucian confirms these matters elsewhere, as do others (same author, *Zeus Tragoedus*, pp. 682 and 693).

But here the pagans rose up and replied: If those gods, and the other Tutelary gods, fail in their office and duty, the blame must be laid not upon them, but upon the human beings who did not supplicate them. By the name of Tutelary gods—to explain the term—Arnobius means (Arnobius, bk. V, p. 114) those whom Varro, according to Augustine (Augustine, bk. VI of *The City of God*, ch. 9, p. 156), said had been appointed over all matters pertaining to the protection of human life, from conception through extreme old age [Col. 0533A] and death. But more will be said about these shortly (below, art. 5). Arnobius shows briefly and clearly that nothing could be more frivolous and feeble than this reply. For who does not know that the kindness and beneficence of the gods toward human beings ought to be entirely gratuitous and never mercenary? And certainly the true God supplies seasons, winds, rains, and crops equally to all human beings, both good and evil. Moreover, the pagans privately assigned every sordid and base service unworthy of a freeborn person—as is already evident from what has been said and will become still clearer from what is to follow—to each of these fictitious Tutelary gods and to the others individually. They might, however, have deemed it somewhat more reasonable that the god Consus should preside over our thoughts and trustworthy counsels. But that fictitious god, whom they dreamed to be intent upon this [Col. 0533B] task alone, does not prevent, as Arnobius says, outcomes contrary to human counsels, or their sudden and unexpected alteration. Since we treated this god in the preceding dissertation (Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 16, art. 2), let us proceed, if you please, to others.

## ARTICLE III. Concerning still other gods similarly appointed over particular matters: Juno Lucina over childbirth, Unxia over anointings, Cinxia—or the goddess Virginensis—over the unfastening of girdles, and Victua and Potua over food and drink.

The pagans had falsely and absurdly introduced yet other gods as the special patrons of other particular matters. Arnobius therefore rightly rebukes them (Arnobius, bk. III, pp. 106, 112, and 114) because they did not hesitate to affirm that Juno [Col. 0533C] Lucina had been set over women’s childbirth. For although she was invoked by countless women in labor, she never brought assistance. How fair and just this rebuke is you may learn from Cicero, who ridicules that superstitious credulity in these words: “As among the Greeks they invoke Diana—and her as Light-Bringer—so among our people they invoke Juno Lucina in childbirth; this same Diana is called the all-wandering goddess. . . . She is invoked at childbirth because births reach maturity sometimes in seven, but generally in nine, courses of the moon. . . . Timaeus, neatly as he often does, after saying in his history that on the night Alexander was born the temple of Diana of Ephesus burned down, added that this was by no means surprising, because Diana, wishing to be present at Olympias’s labor, had been away from home.” [Col. 0533D] (Cicero, bk. II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 224, line 19.)

Not without reason, therefore, does Augustine often assail the pagans with the same argument. Somewhere he reproves them, not without mockery, as follows: “What need was there,” he asks, “for women in labor to invoke Lucina, since, if Felicity were present, they would not only give birth successfully, but would give birth to good children as well?” (Augustine, bk. IV of *The City of God*, ch. 12, p. 102.) Elsewhere—to avoid reciting everything he said—he states: “Nor did the Jewish women invoke Lucina, when God himself delivered and preserved their offspring from the hands of the Egyptians who persecuted them and wished to kill all their infants, [Col. 0534A] so that they might multiply in marvelous ways and that nation might increase beyond belief.” (Ibid., ch. 34, p. 114, and previously ch. 11, p. 97.) If anyone requires still other witnesses concerning that ridiculous goddess, let him consult Macrobius, Horace, Terence, Plautus—who mentions her rather often—and many others whom it would be superfluous to name here (Macrobius, bk. VII of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 16; Horace, bk. III of the *Odes*, ode 22; Terence, *The Brothers*, act 3, scene 4).

Arnobius continues: “Unxia presides over anointings,” he says (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 115), “and Cinxia over the unfastening of girdles.” To understand this, it must be observed that there was an ancient pagan custom by which, before a new bride was brought to her husband’s house, they adorned its doorposts with woolen bands and anointed and smeared them either with pig fat, as Pliny says, or with oil or wolf’s grease, as Servius notes (Pliny, bk. [Col. 0534B] XXVIII of the *Natural History*, ch. 9, p. 604; Servius, on bk. IV of the *Aeneid*, p. 343). On this custom see Donatus, Isidore, Giraldus, and the fuller discussion in Brissonius, who confirms the opinion of our Arnobius by the following words of Martianus Felix, in which he introduces Philology speaking with Juno as follows: “Since, unviolated in sex, I have suffered no bodily contact, mortal maidens ought to summon Iterduca, Domiduca, Unxia, and Cinxia to their weddings, so that you may protect their journeys, lead them into the homes they desire, and, when they anoint the doorposts, fasten there a favorable omen.” (Donatus on Terence’s *The Mother-in-Law*, act 1, scene 2; Isidore, bk. IV of the *Origins*, ch. 8; Giraldus, *History of the Gods*, *Syntagma* 3; Brissonius, *On the Marriage Rite*, near the end.)

They believed that Cinxia presided over the unfastening of girdles, [Col. 0534C] and therefore invoked her when the bridegroom, as Festus writes (Festus, under the words CINGUL. and CINXIA), untied the new bride’s girdle, which was bound with the Herculean knot. For precisely this reason Theocritus sang (*Idyll* 17, verse 60):

> Ἔνθα γὰρ Εἰλείθυιαν ἐβώσατο Λυσίζωνον.

> For there she called upon Eileithyia the Girdle-Loosener.

The accompanying Latin paraphrase reads: “For there they invoke Lucina the Girdle-Loosener (*Lysizona*).”

Although Festus, cited immediately above, asserts that Cinxia is a name of Juno, she is nevertheless called the goddess Virginensis by Augustine (Augustine, bk. IV of *The City of God*, ch. 11, p. 97; and bk. VI, ch. 9, p. 157). For where he discusses the offices of the individual gods, he says: “And certainly the goddess Virginensis is present so that [Col. 0534D] the maiden’s girdle may be loosened.” But who does not know that this and other goddesses and gods had numerous names? And certainly from the words of Cicero quoted shortly above we learn that she who among the Latins was called Juno Lucina was called Diana the Light-Bringer among the Greeks. Read further, if you wish, the already cited Giraldus and Brissonius, Vossius, and others (Vossius, bk. II, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, ch. 26, p. 219 and following).

In addition: “The most sacred Victa and Potua,” Arnobius says, “provide for food and drink.” (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 115.) Donatus, however, explains this in his notes on Terence: “We read in Varro that boys are initiated to Edulia, Potica, and Cuba, divinities of eating, drinking, and lying down, as soon as they have passed beyond [Col. 0535A] milk and the cradle. Hence Virgil says: ‘No god deemed him worthy of his table, nor goddess of her bed.’ Probus noted this.” (Donatus on Terence’s *Phormio*, act 1, scene 1.) Augustine, however, calls them Potina, who provides drink, and Educa, who provides food (Augustine, bk. IV of *The City of God*, ch. 11, p. 97). But he rejects both of these ridiculous divinities because the Israelites in Egypt took food and drink without Educa and Potina. Later he says: “If anyone employed two nurses for an infant, one of whom gave it nothing but food and the other nothing but drink, just as these people employed two goddesses for this purpose, Educa and Potina, he would surely appear to be a fool and to be staging something like a mime in his own house.” (Same author, bk. VI, ch. 9, p. 156.) These are undoubtedly the very same goddesses whom our Arnobius calls Victa and Potua—provided [Col. 0535B] that his text does not conceal the by no means unusual error of a copyist. But with no less contempt and mockery than Augustine, and certainly with justice, he condemns and rejects them.

## ARTICLE IV. Concerning other fictitious gods who were no less absurdly placed over other matters: Bellona over wars; Discord and the Furies over dissensions; Mars over battles; Mercury over *ceromata*, boxing matches, and wrestling; Pellonia over the expulsion of enemies—whose failure to favor the Romans is proved by the battle at the Caudine Forks, the battle at Lake Trasimene, and the disasters at Cannae; nor can it be said that gods preside over the left-hand side and oppose the right. Likewise concerning Pausus, who was opposed to wars; Praestana and Panda, or Pantica; and Titus Tatius, introduced into the Capitol.

If we take a step toward other matters, the farther we advance, the worse and far more degraded we shall surely find them. [Col. 0535C] For the pagans were not ashamed to include among the number of their gods those whom, as our Arnobius reports (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 115), they imagined, in their savage and cruel nature, both to delight in human misfortunes and to be set over them. He judged these notions so absurd that, passing over Bellona, Discord, the Furies, and the left-hand divinities, he came immediately to Mars, who was placed over wars and battles and, as they foolishly thought, ruled in them. He passes over Bellona because, if Mars cannot be the god of wars, as we shall shortly see, much less could a woman preside over such cruelty and the many crimes that battles bring with them (ibid., bk. I, p. 15, and bk. III, p. 115). Nevertheless, at Rome, near the Carmental Gate, a temple to this warlike goddess had been built by Appius, as Augustine and others noted, and dedicated on the day before the Nones of July [Col. 0535D] (Augustine, bk.
