III of *The City of God*, ch. 25, p. 82, and bk. IV, ch. 11, p. 96). Ovid celebrated this concisely in the following words:

> On this day Bellona is said to have been consecrated  
> In the Etruscan war, and she is ever propitious to Latium.  
> Appius was her founder; when he refused peace to Pyrrhus,  
> He saw much in his mind, though deprived of physical sight.  
> From her temple a small open space overlooks the upper Circus;  
> There stands a small column of no small renown.  
> From here a spear is customarily hurled by hand, heralding war,  
> Whenever it is resolved to take up arms against a king or peoples.

(Ovid, bk. VI of the *Fasti*, § 4.) This temple and meetings of the senate held within it are frequently mentioned by Livy and others, especially the poets Lucan, Horace, and Tibullus. Giraldus [Col. 0536A] offers more; consult him if you have leisure (bk. X, ch. 19; bk. XXVI, ch. 21; bk. XXVIII, ch. 9; Lucan, bk. VII, p. 847; Horace, *Sermones* 2, satire 3; Tibullus, bk. I, elegy VI; Giraldus, *Syntagma* 10, p. 309 and following).

Virgil, however, mentions in one and the same passage Bellona, Discord, the Furies, and Mars, of whom our author speaks:

> Mavors rages in the midst of the conflict,  
> Engraved upon the steel, and the grim Furies from the upper air;  
> Discord strides exultantly in her rent robe,  
> Followed by Bellona with her bloodstained scourge.

(Virgil, bk. VIII of the *Aeneid*, verse 700 and following.) The same Virgil again mentions Discord, as do Lucan, Augustine, and others (same author, bk. VI of the *Aeneid*, verses 280–281; Lucan, bk. VII, p. 287; Augustine, bk. III of *The City of God*, ch. 25, p. 82).

[Col. 0536B] Cicero teaches that the Furies, whom the Greeks called Eumenides or Erinyes, must be deleted from the register of goddesses: “But if Hecate is a goddess, why are not the Eumenides? If they are goddesses—and they have a shrine both at Athens and among us, since, as I interpret the name Furina, the Furies are goddesses—they are, I suppose, the observers and avengers of crimes and wicked deeds.” (Cicero, bk. III, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 246, line 33.) On this passage, read Lescalopier’s observations. See also, if you wish, Lilius Giraldus and Natalis Comes, by whom you will find many writers cited (Giraldus, *Syntagma* 6, p. 215 and following; Natalis Comes, bk. III of the *Mythology*, ch. 10, p. 215 and following).

That Mars was placed over battles by the pagans is so well known that it requires no proof. [Col. 0536C] We shall therefore offer only the following lines celebrated by Ovid:

> Mars was to be revered in Latium because he presides over arms;  
> Arms will give both wealth and a god to that savage nation.

Augustine therefore rightly turns this into a reproach and charge against those same pagans: “Since they could find no element or part of the world for Mars in which he might perform any sort of work of nature, they said that he was the god of war, which is a work of human beings and not something desirable for them. If, therefore, Felicity granted perpetual peace, Mars would have nothing to do.” (Ovid, bk. III of the *Fasti*, verse 85 and following; Augustine, bk. VII of *The City of God*, ch. 14, p. 173.) Who, therefore, would not resent the pagans for imagining, invoking, [Col. 0536D] and honoring so inhuman and cruel a god—and much more Discord and the Furies—as goddesses?

But come now, and, if it is still not burdensome to you, consider with us, I pray, how savage and cruel in nature was that other god of the pagans concerning whom Arnobius says: “Mercury takes care of the *ceromata* and presides over boxing matches and wrestling” (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 114), in which athletes mutually destroyed one another. Yet such was this god’s weakness that he could not prevent one side among the boxers and wrestlers from being defeated by the other or suffering some injury. Was it really permissible, then, to invent gods of this sort?

But, someone will ask, what does the word *ceromata* mean? It has a twofold meaning. *Ceroma* is an ointment made from oil, softened wax, and mud, [Col. 0537A] with which athletes and others were anointed. How common and widespread it once was may be learned from this single verse of Juvenal—unless he intended to denote some other similar and costly substance:

> A woman’s *ceroma*—  
> Who does not know it?

Martial also mentions it, and Pliny does so repeatedly (Juvenal, satire 6, before the middle; Martial, bk. XIV, epigram 19; Pliny, bk. XXVIII of the *Natural History*, ch. 4, p. 575; bk. XXIX, ch. 1, p. 672; and bk. XXXV, ch. 13, p. 247).

In another sense, *ceroma* signifies the place where those same athletes were anointed. For in the same Pliny you will find it written: “They adorn the wrestling-schools with images of athletes, and their own *ceromata*.” Seneca, however, says: [Col. 0537B] “In the *ceroma* . . . a spectator of boys quarreling sits.” (Same author, bk. XXXV, ch. 2, p. 171; Seneca, *On the Shortness of Life*, ch. 2, p. 367.) Arnobius appears to use *ceroma* in this second sense. For he writes that the pagans had been persuaded—though in vain—that the *ceromas*, or rather *ceromata*, were cared for by Mercury. His additional statement that Mercury presided over boxing matches and wrestling can be proved by these verses of Prudentius:

> Then, against scourge-bearers and boxers anointed with oil  
> And trained in the art of the gymnasium, the Etruscan soldier fought;  
> Nor could Mercury, distinguished by his broad-brimmed hat,  
> Save his own wrestling-schools from ruin when Sparta was captured.

(Prudentius, bk. II, *Against Symmachus*, § 4.) Pellonia, moreover, was believed to be a goddess powerful in driving away enemies, as Arnobius later relates (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 128). Hence Augustine asked, if [Col. 0537C] Felicity truly were a goddess: “Why should the goddess Fessonia be invoked on account of the weary, or the goddess Pellonia on account of enemies to be driven away?” (Augustine, bk. IV of *The City of God*, ch. 21, p. 103.) Arnobius, however, casts down her false divinity by another argument. For each of the two sides fighting against the other, he says, ought to have driven the other away through the protection of this goddess of theirs.

Nor could the Romans reply that this goddess was theirs and not other peoples’ (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 129). For it cannot be said that the goddesses were theirs—and this one in particular—in so exclusive a manner that they did not also belong to certain other nations. Furthermore, this benevolent goddess not only very often failed to drive away the enemies of the Romans, but also calmly permitted them to be afflicted and overthrown by the greatest disasters. For where, Arnobius asks (ibid.), was that goddess Pellonia [Col. 0537D] “when the public honor was brought beneath the yoke at the Caudine Forks?” The Caudine Forks—or Forks or Passes—were named from Caudum, or Caudium, a Samnite town in Italy near Beneventum, and are renowned for a signal Roman disaster. There the Roman forces, under the consuls and commanders Titus Veturius Calvinus and Spurius Postumius, were surrounded on every side by their enemies and reduced to such straits that, after laying down their arms, they were sent beneath the enemy’s yoke, as Livy relates more fully (Livy, beginning of bk. IX, and bk. XXV, ch. 6). Augustine therefore refutes the pagans, like Arnobius, by this same example and argument: “Where were the gods,” he asks, “when both consuls and their army [Col. 0538A], hemmed in at the Caudine Forks by the Samnites, were compelled to make a treaty with them, so that six hundred Roman knights were given as hostages, while the rest, having lost their arms, been stripped of their other possessions, and been deprived of their coverings, were sent under the enemy’s yoke wearing a single garment each?” (Augustine, bk. III of *The City of God*, ch. 17, p. 75.)

Nor was that the Romans’ only slaughter, despite Pellonia’s failure to prevent it. Rather, “at Lake Trasimene too,” our author continues, “torrents of blood ran” (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 129). This lake lies in the territory of Perusia, where the Roman army, under the consul and commander Flaminius, was routed and destroyed by Hannibal. Livy relates the history and afterward speaks of it in this manner: “This is the famous battle at Trasimene, remembered as one of the few great Roman disasters. [Col. 0538B] Fifteen thousand Romans were slain in the battle line; ten thousand, scattered in flight throughout all Etruria, made for Rome by different routes.” But concerning this disaster one may read Polybius, Valerius Maximus, Ovid, and others cited by us in the preceding dissertation. (Livy, bk. XXII, § 7; Polybius, Histories, bk. III, p. 233 ff.; Valerius Maximus, bk. I, ch. 6, § 6; Ovid, Fasti, bk. VI, p. 685; Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 17, art. 3.)

Finally Arnobius adds that Pellonia was not present “when the plains of Diomedes were heaped with Roman corpses” (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 129). He is undoubtedly speaking of the battle and disaster at Cannae, which Livy writes was foretold by Marcius, the celebrated prophet, in approximately these words: “Roman, offspring of Troy, flee the river Canna, [Col. 0538C] lest foreigners compel you to join battle on the plain of Diomedes. But do not believe me until you have filled the plain with blood and the river carries many thousands of your slain from the fruitful land into the great sea, and your flesh becomes food for the fish, the birds, and the wild beasts inhabiting the earth. For thus has Jupiter declared to me” (Livy, bk. XXV, § 12). Livy added: “Those who had served in those places recognized both the plains of Diomedes the Argive and the river Canna, just as they recognized the disaster itself” (ibid., ch. 6; and earlier, bk. XXII, ch. 43 ff.). But he treats these matters more fully both there and elsewhere, as do Polybius, Florus, Augustine, and others. The plains were called the plains of Diomedes because, after wounding Venus and abandoning his native land, he is said to have settled in Apulia, as Servius and very many others attest. [Col. 0538D] (Polybius, Histories, bk. III, p. 256 ff.; Florus, bk. II, ch. 6; Augustine, City of God, bk. III, ch. 19; Servius, on Aeneid VIII, p. 487.)

What did the pagans say to this? They replied that the gods presided over things on the left and were hostile to those on the right. Nor should you say that our Author gratuitously invented this answer because it was easier to refute. For we read that Varro committed the following to writing: “Things on the left are regarded as favorable auspices. Hence, when the assemblies or some other matter are proclaimed, one is told that there is a bird on the left; this usage comes from the Greek, because they call the left σκαιάν [skaián, ‘left’].” Servius, moreover, says: “‘Left’ means prosperous, because it is celestial. In matters of augury, however, *sinistrum* derives from *sinendo* [‘permitting’], because it permits us to act. Hence elsewhere: [Col. 0539A]

> If the deities on the left permit anyone.

The discipline of the augurs agrees that the left-hand regions are northern; and thunderbolts from that quarter are therefore more significant, since they are higher and nearer the dwelling of Jupiter.” (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. VI, p. 88; Servius, on *Aeneid* II.693.)

Yet the more certainly and insistently the pagans asserted these things, the more forcefully our Arnobius refuted them. For the entire world, as he argues, is spherical and round, and therefore has neither a right nor a left side. A part is called left or right only in relation to us and to our position, and only while we remain still. For each side changes with every movement of our body. Furthermore, what had the left and right sides done to deserve that the latter should have no divine guardians [Col. 0539B], while gods were said always to attend the left with favor and good fortune? Certainly nothing more absurd could have been devised.

Moreover, opposed to the aforementioned gods of war was Pausus, whom Arnobius seems particularly to set against Bellona when he said of the pagans: “They revere the Pausi and the Bellonae” (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 15). Vossius believes that Pausus was named from *pausa* [“pause”] (Vossius, *Etymologies*), and thus that he was the god of pause, rest, and peace and, as Turnebus observes, an adversary of wars and of Bellona (Turnebus, *Adversaria*, bk. XV, ch. 21). Whether he was Janus, whose temple was closed in time of war, must be left to the judgment of others. But what sane person, I ask, would not be moved to laughter or indignation [Col. 0539C] by these mutually opposed deities?

The divinity of Praestana and Panda could certainly be proved no more successfully. Arnobius, turning his discourse against the pagans themselves, rejects them in these words: “Praestana, as you report, was so named because Quirinus, or Romulus, surpassed (*praestiterit*) everyone in strength when casting the javelin; and because she was permitted to spread and open (*pandere atque aperire*) a road for Titus Tatius to seize the Capitoline hill, the goddess was called Panda, or Pantica” (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 128). Some have thought that the goddess Panda is mentioned in two poems of Varro cited by Aulus Gellius, which are disgracefully corrupt in his edition and which various writers have attempted to emend according to the sharpness of their ingenuity (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, bk. XIII, ch. 22). Turnebus and others, however, suspect that she is the deity who in an ancient lexicon is called εἰρήνης θεός [“god of peace”], that is, “goddess of peace,” [Col. 0539D] and that the name Panda was imposed upon her from the opening and throwing open of city gates in time of peace (Turnebus, *Adversaria*, bk. XIX, ch. 11). But Arnobius is certainly speaking neither of the goddess of peace nor of Ceres, in whose temple bread was given to those who had fled into it as into an asylum, as Nonius observes from the cited passage of Varro (Nonius, *On the Properties of Words*, ch. 1, s.v. PANDERE). He appears instead to be discussing a warlike goddess, one said to have opened a road for Titus Tatius to capture the Capitoline hill and therefore to have obtained the name Panda.

Vossius admits, however, that he could not recall the source from which Arnobius derived this etymology. Yet if Vossius lacked an authority for the etymology, there is by no means [Col. 0540A] a wholly feeble argument for it. For it is recorded in the writings of Livy, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Valerius Maximus, Propertius, Ovid, and others how Tatius and the Sabines were admitted onto the Capitoline hill, as Arnobius says, by Tarpeius’s virgin daughter (Livy, bk. I, § 11 ff.; Dionysius, bk. II, p. 105 ff.; Valerius Maximus, bk. IX, ch. 6, § 1; Propertius, bk. IV, elegy 4; Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. I, § 3). Dionysius of Halicarnassus further added that the maiden was honored with burial where she had fallen and that the Romans annually offered funeral rites to her. Is it not therefore sufficiently probable that she was for this reason enrolled among the goddesses under the name Panda or Pantica? Was not Praestana likewise admitted to the company of goddesses for the same reason, since they wrongly believed that with her assistance Romulus surpassed the others [Col. 0540B] in casting the javelin? For we learn from Augustine, to be cited later, that it was the pagans’ custom to call their gods by the name of the function which they thought them to perform or to have performed.

Whatever may be true concerning the etymologies of Panda or Pantica and Praestana, Arnobius utterly overthrows the fictitious divinity of each on the ground that neither was a goddess before Tarpeia and Romulus. For, as he says: “Had Romulus not secured the Palatine by the casting of a spear, and had the Sabine king been unable to capture the Tarpeian rock, there would be no Pantica and no Praestana” (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 128). Who, unless he were wholly foolish, would call those beings true gods who once were not gods and were made gods by none but human beings through some chance event? But let us now pass with our author from those whom the mad pagans fabricated as gods because of the terror of arms and wars [Col. 0540C] or the blessing of repose and peace, to others whom they made gods on account of the most contemptible services.

## ARTICLE V

### How Arnobius pursues his argument and demonstrates that the pagans wrongly fabricate the god Lateranus as presiding over unbaked bricks; a Genius over the hearth and other places; Aius Locutius over the protection of Rome; Fauns and Fatuae over the prediction of future events; Puta over the pruning of trees; Peta over things sought; Nemestrinus over groves; Patellana and Patellus over things opened or to be opened; Nodutis over the nodes of crops; Terensis over the threshing of grain; Saturn over sowing; Flora over flowers; Montinus over mountains; Vibilia over wanderings from the road; Limentinus over thresholds and Lima over their protection; Limi over crooked places; the Lucrii over the acquisition of profits; and the goddess Pecunia over wealth

If the imaginary jurisdictions of the gods clearly demonstrate their false divinity, then those by which the pagans everywhere proclaimed them [Col. 0540D] to preside over the most contemptible and abject things undoubtedly demonstrate that same falsehood still more effectively and plainly. For what could be more foolish and absurd than to advertise a certain Lateranus as the genius and god of hearths? Yet the pagans decided that he was called by this name “because that kind of furnace is built by men from unbaked bricks (*laterculis crudis*),” as Arnobius says (Arnobius, bk. IV, pp. 130 and 133; Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. XXXV, ch. 14, p. 248). Pliny, however, thought that no one was unaware that the latticework of walls was plastered and that buildings were constructed from unbaked bricks.

No one ought to be surprised that the pagans believed that some genius presided [Col. 0541A] over hearths. For the ancients called a “genius,” as Servius says (Servius, on *Georgics* I, p. 85, and on *Aeneid* V, p. 367), the natural god of each particular place, thing, or person. Elsewhere he also testifies that among the pagans no place was without a genius. If you desire other witnesses, you will immediately have Virgil, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Tertullian, and Prudentius, who say much about the geniuses presiding everywhere, especially those whom Arnobius elsewhere records as the geniuses of cities, customarily worshiped by those same pagans (Virgil, *Aeneid* V.95 and VII.135; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, bk. VIII, p. 513; Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, ch. 4; Arnobius, bk. I, p. 15; Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, bk. II, § 3). These are Prudentius’s verses:

> [Col. 0541B] Yet why do you fashion for me a single genius of Rome,  
> When you are accustomed to assign their own geniuses  
> To gates, houses, baths, and stables, and throughout every member  
> And place of the city to fabricate many thousands of geniuses,  
> Lest any corner be without its own attendant shade?

There he refutes what Symmachus prattled about gods who guarded cities, just as Cyril of Alexandria completely refuted other fictions of this kind which Julian the Apostate had uttered concerning the same gods (Symmachus, in Ambrose, vol. II, p. 830; Cyril of Alexandria, beginning of bk. IV *Against Julian the Apostate*, p. 115 ff.). Arnobius makes plain how insulting it is to the divine majesty to proclaim a god appointed over hearths and kitchens, running about through them and taking care that foods and stews are properly cooked and seasoned. Indeed, it is undoubtedly the act of a foolish and utterly deranged person [Col. 0541C] to invent a god who presides over hearths and furnaces—not over them all, however, but only over those constructed in one particular way, from unbaked bricks and no otherwise.

Perhaps the Aii Locutii should be cast into the aforementioned herd of geniuses or gods who kept watch over the protection of the city of Rome, and whom the pagans still customarily worshiped, as Arnobius reproaches them for doing (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 15). For Greek and Latin writers—Plutarch, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Cicero, Livy, Aulus Gellius, and others—have handed down to posterity that a voice was once heard, though disregarded, warning that precautions should be taken lest Rome be captured by the Gauls; and that, after the enemy had been repelled and defeated, a temple and altar were built in the New Road to Aius Locutius in commemoration of this event [Col. 0541D] (Plutarch, *Life of Camillus*, p. 144, and *On the Fortune of the Romans*, p. 319; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, bk. V, p. 290; Cicero, *On Divination*, bk. I, pp. 272 and 289; Livy, bk. V, near the end of chs. 50 and 52; Gellius, bk. XVI, ch. 17). Cicero ridicules that superstition no less wittily than Arnobius. The Orator attacks it thus: “A voice was heard warning that precautions should be taken lest Rome be captured by the Gauls. Consequently an altar was consecrated on the New Road to Aius Loquens. What then? This Aius Loquens, when no one knew him, spoke (*aiebat*) and talked (*loquebatur*), and from that obtained his name; but after he had obtained a dwelling, an altar, and a name, he fell silent” (Cicero, *On Divination*, bk. II, p. 289; Arnobius, bk. I, p. 15).

[Col. 0542A] Nor is it wholly without reason that Arnobius associates the Fauns and Fatuae with the fictitious gods believed to foretell the future, since the pagans similarly revered them as gods. Dionysius of Halicarnassus raises the question whether the voice which they said was divinely uttered belonged to some hero or to Faunus. Varro and Servius, moreover, think that Faunus was named from *fando* [“speaking”]; or, because, as Gaius Bassus in Lactantius and others supposed, she who was said to sing women’s fates, just as Faunus did those of men, was called Fatua. Virgil indeed praised the responses of Faunus. Cicero, however, although he said that the voices of Faunus were often heard in battles and times of disturbance, nevertheless, when he introduced Cotta answering Balbus, denied that he himself had ever heard such a voice of Faunus (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, bk. VI, [Col. 0542B] p. 290; Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. VI, p. 78; Servius, on Virgil, *Georgics* I.10–11 and *Aeneid* VII.45 ff.; Lactantius, bk. I, ch. 22, p. 127; Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.103; Cicero, *On Divination*, bk. I, p. 272; *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. II, p. 214, and bk. III, p. 24). See Isidore, *Origins*, bk. VIII, ch. 2; Natale Conti, *Mythology*, bk. V, ch. 9; Lilio Giraldi, *History of the Gods*, Syntagma 15, p. 427; Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, bk. I, ch. 12; Huet, *Demonstratio Evangelica*, proposition 4, ch. 9, § 4, p. 136 ff.; Alexander ab Alexandro and Tiraqueau’s notes, *Genial Days*, bk. VI, ch. 8, p. 648.

There was, moreover, another herd and assembly of gods whom the pagans falsely thought appointed over other things. Arnobius (bk. IV, p. 131) gathered [Col. 0542C] no small crowd of them, but Augustine a still larger one; their names and functions could reveal nothing but what was wholly unworthy of the divine nature. Arnobius mentions Puta as presiding over the pruning (*putationibus*) of trees (ibid., pp. 131–132), just as Peta presided over things sought (*petendis*), Nemestrinus over groves (*nemoribus*), Patellana undoubtedly over the opened husks of crops and Patella over those to be opened, Nodutis over the nodes of produce, Terensis over the actual threshing of grain, Saturn over sowing, and Montinus over mountains. You will undoubtedly laugh at this troop of gods and goddesses, whom the utterly blind pagans believed to preside over the cultivation of fields, the fruits of the earth, and mountains.

Augustine, however, enumerates some of these and many others [Col. 0542D] whom he represents as appointed to the same duties as Arnobius does. His own words should be compared with those of Arnobius:

> Nor did they think that the service of the fields should be entrusted to any single god. Instead, they appointed the goddess Rusina over the countryside, the god Jugutinus over mountain ridges, the goddess Collatina over hills, and Vallonia over valleys. They could not even find a single Segetia of such a kind that they might entrust the crops to her once and for all. Rather, they wished the goddess Seja to be appointed over the grain while it was sown beneath the earth; when it had emerged above the earth and formed a crop, the goddess Segetia; and over the harvested grain they appointed the goddess Tutilina. . . . They appointed Proserpina over sprouting grain, the god Nodotus over the joints and nodes of the stalks, [Col. 0543A] the goddess Volutina over the coverings of the husks, and the goddess Patelana when the husks open so that the ear may emerge. . . . I do not mention everything, because I am weary of what does not weary them.

(Augustine, *City of God*, ch. 8, p. 93 ff.)

You see clearly that he, like Arnobius, expressly includes Patelana and Nodotus—or Nodutis, as our author says—within this number of gods. It will therefore seem entirely probable to everyone that the others whom Arnobius mentions must be numbered among those whom Augustine and our Arnobius were weary of naming, and whom we likewise ought to be weary of naming.

Elsewhere, however, that most learned man made the same reference to Saturn as our author: “Saturn,” he says, “is one of the principal gods, in whose hands lies dominion over all sowing.” Earlier, however [Col. 0543B]: “Saturn, on account of the seed itself.” And shortly afterward: “Saturn possesses power over all seeds.” These statements were undoubtedly drawn from Varro. For in one of his books we read: “Saturn was named from sowing (*satu*).” But dominion over sowing belonged no more to him than dominion over flowers belonged to Flora, says our author. For they did not prevent flowers from being scorched by cold or heat. In the preceding dissertation, however, we discussed Flora and the games mentioned by Arnobius as celebrated in her honor (Augustine, *City of God*, bk. VII, ch. 13, p. 172; ibid., ch. 2, p. 163, and ch. 3, p. 164; Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. IV, p. 16; Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 113; Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 16, art. 3).

Moreover, although Arnobius calls Nemestrinus the god of groves and Montinus the god of mountains, Diana [Col. 0543C] is nevertheless called by Horace:

> Virgin guardian of mountains and groves.

(Horace, *Odes*, bk. III, ode 22.)

Faunus and Picus, moreover, proclaim the following about themselves in Ovid:

> We are rustic gods, who rule  
> Upon the lofty mountains.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. III, § 3, p. 532.)

But what prevents the pagans from foolishly believing Diana the guardian of groves and Nemestrinus their god? What also prevents Faunus or Picus from having been identical with Montinus, but called by different names? Concerning these gods, consult, if you wish, Tertullian, Giraldi, and Vossius (Tertullian, *On the Shows*, ch. 8, p. 93; Giraldi, *History of the Gods*, Syntagma 1, p. 89; Vossius, *On Pagan Theology*, bk. V, ch. 48, p. 89 ff.).

[Col. 0543D] Our author, like Augustine, also ridicules the pagans who dreamed that the goddess Mellonia was appointed over the production of honey. As though honey could never have been produced without her! Hence Augustine rightly says of the Jews: “Without Segetia they more happily received their crops, without Bubona their cattle, without Mellona their honey, without Pomona their fruit, and indeed from the one true God everything for which the Romans thought they must supplicate such great crowds of false gods” (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 131; Augustine, *City of God*, bk. V, ch. 14, p. 114).

What of the fact that the pagans had invented other gods appointed over roads, thresholds, and doors? For it was not without irony and rebuke that Arnobius said: [Col. 0544A] “Does the goddess Vibilia rescue people from wanderings on the roads?” (Arnobius, ibid.) Is she not the very one concerning whom Varro writes: “Venilia is named from coming (*veniendo*) and from that wind of which Plautus said: ‘What was said by the man who sailed with a favorable wind over a calm sea: I rejoice at the wind’” (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. IV, p. 18)? Augustine, moreover, cites the same Varro as saying elsewhere: “Venilia is the wave which comes to the shore.” Yet does Augustine not depart from him when he discusses infants and says: “From the hope which comes (*venit*), Venilia”? Servius reports that some said Venilia was so named because she grants pardon (*veniam*) to those who demand it (Augustine, *City of God*, bk. VII, ch. 22, p. 178; ibid., bk. IV, ch. 11, p. 97; Servius, on *Aeneid* X, p. 577). But if the words of Varro cited by us are more relevant to our author’s purpose, perhaps you doubt whether Arnobius’s text should read [Col. 0544B] *Venilia* rather than *Vibilia*. Yet what would you dare decide where there is so great a multitude of fictitious gods?

The pagans further believed that Limentinus presided over thresholds and that their protection was assigned to Lima. “But who could believe,” Arnobius argues, “that Limentinus or Lima guards thresholds and performs the duties of doorkeepers, when every day we see the thresholds of temples and private houses torn up and demolished, and when disgraceful traffic to brothels does not take place without them?” (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 132.) Arnobius mentions this Limentinus elsewhere (ibid., bk. I, p. 15), as does Cyprian in one place (Cyprian, *On the Vanity of Idols*, p. 13). In one of Tertullian’s books, which is mutilated throughout and gapes with lacunae, we read the following words, which nevertheless confirm our author’s statements quite clearly: [Col. 0544C]

> I pass over the gods Forculus, named from doors, and Cardea . . . . . . nibus, and Limentinus of thresholds, or whatever other doorkeepers are worshiped among neighboring . . . . num. For what is remarkable in this, when they also have them in brothels, kitchens, and the lowest dungeon?

(Tertullian, *To the Nations*, bk. II, ch. 15, p. 78.)

In another, more complete and intact book he also wrote:

> We ought to be certain—even if some are unaware of it through ignorance of secular literature—that among the Romans there are even gods of doors: Cardea, named from hinges (*cardinibus*); Forculus, from doors (*foribus*); Limentinus, from the threshold (*limine*); and Janus himself, from the doorway (*janua*). And we assuredly know that, although their names are empty and fabricated, nevertheless, when they are brought into superstition, they attract demons and every unclean spirit to themselves through the bond of consecration.

(Idem, *On Idolatry*, ch. 15.) [Col. 0544D]

Augustine mentions these same gods and wittily asks the pagans why Forculus and Limentinus are called male gods, while Cardea, a female, presides over the hinge (Augustine, *City of God*, bk. IV, ch. 8, p. 94; and bk. VI, ch. 7, p. 153). Did those holy gods, appointed over the thresholds and doors of brothels, also open them for the wanton and lustful?

Quite so, you will say. But in none of these passages is there any mention of the Lima named by Arnobius. They therefore suspect that the name is corrupt and that *Limentina*, *Janus*, or *Jana* should be read in its place. What if we were to read *Cardea*, concerning whom the authors just cited speak, or *Carna*, about whom Ovid sang at greater length (Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. VI, § 2, p. 652 [Col. 0545A] ff.)? But since, as has been said, the number of gods of this kind was infinite, we do not dare determine what was written in Arnobius’s text. Servius indeed observes somewhere that the threshold was consecrated to Vesta (Servius, on *Aeneid* VI, p. 414).

More corrupt still appear the words of Arnobius that follow: “Who [believes] that the Limi are overseers of crooked places?”—but in the royal manuscript the word is very badly written as *Lemons* (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 132). Since only this one manuscript of these books remains to us, copied by a most incompetent scribe, it is exceedingly difficult to say what the true reading of our author may be. We would not be reluctant to approve restoration of the word *Lemures*, concerning whom we have spoken elsewhere, as has Ovid, already cited by us (Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. V, § 5, p. 632 ff.). Nevertheless, [Col. 0545B] unless assisted by another, more accurate manuscript, we think that nothing certain can yet be established on this matter. Whatever the truth, what honorable and liberally educated man, I ask, would ever wish to perform the office of such a god?

Nor does Arnobius find it any more credible that “the gods Lucrii preside over the acquisition of profits, when profits very frequently arise from disgraceful causes and always consist in losses to others.” If you desire to know who these gods were, you may learn it from the Suda. For it says (Suda, s.v. Κερδῶος):

> Κερδῶος θεὸς ὁ Ἑρμῆς ὡς κέρδους ποιητικὸς καὶ ἄγγελον δὲ αὐτὸν καλοῦσι, καὶ κλῶπα, διὸ καὶ μάρσυππον αὐτὸν ποιοῦσι βαστάζειν, καὶ ἔφορον αὐτὸν τοῦ λόγου, καὶ τῆς κλοπῆς, καὶ ἐμπολείων, ἤγουν κέρδους ἔφορον.

> Hermes is the profitable god (*Kerdōos*), as the producer of profit or gain. They also call him a messenger and a thief, and therefore represent him carrying a purse; they make him overseer of speech, theft, and commerce—that is, overseer of gain.

Therefore [Col. 0545C] Gregory Nazianzen writes the following against Julian the Apostate: “Whenever I behold your Lucrius, Logius, and Enaegonius, I cover my eyes and pass by your god in shame at the spectacle” (Gregory Nazianzen, Oration IV, *Against Julian*, p. 309). On this passage Nonius observed: “The Greeks call the god Mercury Lucrius, as the originator of gain. Hence the comic poet Aristophanes too, in the *Plutus*, being uncertain by what name Mercury should be called, says: ‘Let us establish him as ἐμπολαῖον [Empolaios],’ that is, as president over commerce and gain.”

Gregory, however, appears to call not only Mercury but also Apollo the god Lucrius. For in the preceding oration [Col. 0545D] he had said:

> How will Lucrius be established among them, and the purse brought forward, and the thievish power and capacity of the god honored? And there is also this saying: “Without money Phoebus does not prophesy,” and, “Nothing is more excellent than an obol.” For these are their solemn and venerable maxims.

(Gregory Nazianzen, Oration III, *Against Julian*, p. 262.)

From this also comes that well-worn iambic verse among the Greeks:

> Ἄνευθε χαλκοῦ Φοῖβος οὐ μαντεύεται.

> Without money, the oracles of Phoebus are mute.

Giraldi further reminds us that Apollo, no less than Mercury, was surnamed Κερδῶος (*Kerdōos*), Lucrius, or Lucrio by the pagans (Giraldi, *History of the Gods*, Syntagma 7, p. 218).

It would be far more difficult to persuade any sensible person [Col. 0546A] that Pecunia [“Money”] is a goddess, although pagan literature indicates that she was regarded as a supreme deity, as Arnobius says (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 132). This goddess is frequently mentioned by Augustine. He informs us that the pagans invoked her so that they might become wealthy and obtain the money which they vainly imagined was bestowed by her (Augustine, *City of God*, bk. IV, ch. 20, p. 103, and ch. 24, p. 106; bk. VII, ch. 3, p. 165).

We know indeed that Juvenal declares that in his day no temple had been built to Pecunia and no altars erected to coins. For we have seen these verses of his:

> Although deadly Money does not yet  
> Dwell in a temple, and we have erected no altars to coins.

(Juvenal, Satire I.111 ff.) [Col. 0546B]

But that did not prevent Pecunia from being regarded as a goddess by the pagans before Arnobius’s time, or from being invoked by those greedy and eager for gain, whether in some temple of hers or elsewhere. Consider whether the following verses of Epicharmus, cited by Stobaeus, may be adduced in confirmation of this judgment:

> Ἐγὼ δ᾽ ὑπέλαβον χρησίμους εἶναι θεοὺς,  
> Τ᾽ ἀργύριον ἡμῶν, καὶ τὸ χρυσίον.

> But I consider our silver and gold  
> To be useful gods.

(Stobaeus, Discourse 89, *On the Praise of Wealth*, p. 533.)

Whatever judgment you make about these verses, who will not confess with our Arnobius that the gods mentioned by us are refuted by the very naming of their base and shameful functions?

## ARTICLE VI

### On other gods and goddesses whom the pagans asserted to preside over human vices and other things: Laverna, goddess of thieves, and Murcida, goddess of the slothful; Venus Militaris over the most shameful outrages; Perfica, Pertunda, and Tutinus or Mutinus over obscene pleasures; Libentina and Liburnus over the guardianship of lusts; Orbona and Naenia as ridiculous guardians of life’s end and of funerals; and also on registered prostitutes, Acca Laurentia, Flora, and Leaena

[Col. 0546C]

To anyone, however little impartial an assessor of things he may be, provided that some spark of right reason remains in him, nothing whatever will appear more alien to the divine nature, justice, and holiness than to fabricate gods who not only favor human vices but are actually appointed over them. Nevertheless, the pagans invented gods of this kind—and no small number of them—with astonishing [Col. 0546D] impiety that can never be condemned sufficiently. Gregory Nazianzen therefore addresses them in these verses (Gregory Nazianzen, vol. II, poem 61, p. 142):

> Ἄλλους δ᾽ αὖτ᾽ ἄλλοισι κακοῖς ἐπὶ κάρτος ἔχοντας,  
> Ὡς μὴ μοῦνον ἄτιτον ἅπαν κακὸν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐσθλὸν  
> Ἐμμέναι, ὡς ῥᾷ Θεῷ κεχαρισμένον, ὃς τόδ᾽ ἔτισε.

> You even have deities consecrated to unspeakable guilt,  
> And a different one presiding over every vice,  
> So that every crime may not merely go free of avenging punishment,  
> But may even obtain praise and honor,  
> As something pleasing and acceptable to the God who established it,  
> And worshiped by that same God.

But let us hear our Arnobius recount these infamous gods and their most disgraceful jurisdictions. They announced, he says, “Laverna as the goddess and guardian of thieves” (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 115) and robbers, especially, as others have observed, [Col. 0547A] those who stole secretly and covertly. Varro indeed attests that an altar was built at Rome to this goddess Laverna, from which the Lavernal Gate received its name (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. IV, p. 40). That those thieves supplicated her as their patroness is proved by these verses of Horace:

> Fair Laverna,  
> Grant that I may deceive; grant that I may appear just and holy;  
> Cast night over my sins and a cloud over my frauds.

(Horace, *Epistles*, bk. I, epistle 16.60 ff.)

You may see more in Festus, Nonius Marcellus, and Lilio Giraldi (Festus and Nonius, s.vv. LAVERNIONES and LAVERNAE; Giraldi, Syntagma 1, p. 50; Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 132).

With no less impiety those same pagans advertised Murcida—undoubtedly the opposite of Laverna—as the goddess of the slothful, [Col. 0547B] as Arnobius reproaches them for doing. He did not invent so insane a fiction of human superstition. Augustine relates, and plainly marvels, that the Romans, who assigned individual gods to almost every movement of human beings, instituted public rites for the goddess Murcia, “who,” in his words, “would not move beyond due measure, or who would make a person, as Pomponius says, *murcidus*—that is, excessively sluggish and inactive” (Augustine, *City of God*, bk. IV, ch. 16, p. 100). Livy, moreover, bears witness that Ancus Marcius, after defeating the Latins who had called him an indolent king of the Romans, returned to Rome. He then added: “After many Latins had been admitted into citizenship, places of residence were assigned at Murcia, so that the Aventine might be joined to the Palatine” (Livy, bk. I, §§ 32–33).

[Col. 0547C] Do you still desire another witness? Here is Tertullian, who records that a shrine was built to this same goddess: “Consus,” he says, “lies hidden underground by the turning-posts. The Murciae too they made into an idol. For they regard Murcia as the goddess of languor (*marcoris*), to whom they vowed a shrine in that quarter” (Tertullian, *On the Shows*, ch. 8, p. 93). We are well aware that some have thought *amoris* [“of love”] should be read there instead of *marcoris* [“of languor”]. For they persuaded themselves that Tertullian was speaking of Venus, who, as Pliny writes, was first named Myrtea and afterward Murcia. They could have added that Varro, Plutarch, and others also mention her (Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. V, ch. 19, p. 212; Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. IV, pp. 37–38; Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, vol. II, p. 268). But since we read *marcoris* in the more accurate [Col. 0547D] text of Tertullian, will it not appear highly probable that he should be understood as speaking of the same goddess Murcida as the writers cited by us? If anyone should rightly prove that this Murcida, goddess of the slothful, is none other than Venus Myrtea or Murcia, goddess of love or languor, we shall concede to him all the more gladly, because Arnobius’s position would thereby be established still more firmly.

Would you like something to be brought forward to the greater shame and everlasting disgrace of the pagans, and thus to the certain ruin and overthrow of their religion? Nothing could be easier. For at hand are those gods who, without any blush of shame, were worshiped by those blind pagans and appointed over unlawful and utterly disgraceful acts and vices. [Col. 0548A] It is unnecessary here to name, with our Arnobius (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 15), Venus—“that mother of desires,” he says, appointed over loves and the ardor of lust. For who does not know these things? It is therefore enough to say with Lactantius:

> Why should I speak of the obscenity of Venus, prostituted to the lusts of everyone—not only gods, but also human beings? . . . She was the first, as the sacred history records, to institute the harlot’s art, and she was responsible for commanding the women of Cyprus to make a public profit from their bodies. She ordered this so that she alone among women might not appear unchaste and desirous of men.

(Lactantius, *Institutes*, bk. I, ch. 17, p. 92.)

But because the pagans proclaimed several Venuses notorious for unchastity and lust, Arnobius attacks one in particular [Col. 0548B]—assuredly worse than the others—in these words: “Does even Venus Militaris preside over the abductions committed in military camps”—the royal manuscript reads *plagiis*, while the old edition has *flagitiis*, “outrages”—“and over the violation of boys?” (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 131). What, I ask, could have brought the pagans greater disgrace and reproach, if they had ever been capable of blushing, than the cult and veneration of that infamous goddess? But you will undoubtedly ask who that Venus Militaris was, since she is mentioned less frequently than the other Venuses. Nevertheless, Pausanias more than once mentions Venus Armed, and thus Venus Militaris (Pausanias, bk. II, p. 48; bk. III, pp. 97 and 106), particularly in these words:

> Κύθηρα δὲ ἡ πόλις ἀναβάντι ἀπὸ Σκανδείας, στάδια ὡς δεκά· τὸ δὲ ἱερὸν τῆς Οὐρανίας ἁγιώτατον, καὶ ἱερῶν, ὁπόσα Ἀφροδίτης παρ᾽ Ἕλλησίν ἐστιν, ἀρχαιότατον· αὑτὴ δὲ ἡ [Col. 0548C] θεὸς ξόανον ὡπλισμένον.

> From Scandea one ascends to the city of the Cytherans, a journey of about ten stades. There stands the temple of Uranian Venus, the holiest and most ancient of all the sanctuaries dedicated to Venus among the Greeks. The image of the goddess is armed.

Nonnus also sings of Venus as more powerful than Mars (Nonnus, *Dionysiaca*, bk. XXXV, v. 175 ff.):

> Μὴ Σπάρτης ἐπίβηθι, μαχήμονες ἧχι πολῖται  
> Χάλκεον εἶδος ἔχουσι κορυσσομένης Ἀφροδίτης.

> Do not enter Sparta, where its warlike citizens  
> Possess a bronze image of armed Venus.

[Col. 0548D] Lactantius relates (bk. I, ch. 19, p. 109) that these same Spartans built a shrine and statue to Venus Armed in memory of the women who met them after the Messenians had been put to flight and had intercourse with them. Finally Hesychius mentions: “Ἔγχειος Ἀφροδίτη, Κυπρίοις—Venus with the spear, among the Cypriots.” What act was so shameful and obscene that this Venus was not believed to preside over it? Arnobius therefore rightly and deservedly ridicules the pagans, because they thought Venus herself presided over the most disgraceful outrages of human beings, yet were not ashamed to proclaim and venerate her as military, armed, and spear-bearing, appointed over weapons just as over loves and outrages.

Arnobius continues (Arnobius, book IV, p. 131), and again asks the pagans whether they seriously believe that Perfica, Pertunda, and Tutunus preside over those obscene pleasures which they themselves publicly proclaimed and which he enumerates. For who, unless he has cast aside all sense of shame, would not be ashamed to worship—or even to mention—such divinities? We [Col. 0549A] are well aware that Lucretius used the name Perfica as though it were an epithet of nature when he sang:

> Until at last creative nature brought all things  
> To the perfect end of their growth.  
>
> The opening word is *Donicum* (or *donec*), “until.”  
> (Lucretius, book II, verses 1125 ff.)

But Arnobius said that Perfica was she who was reputed to bring the most shameful pleasures to their conclusion and completion. Still more shameful were the functions of Pertunda and Tutunus—also called Tutianus, Tutinus, or Mutinus—who, as Augustine observes, was called by the Greeks the infamous Priapus. Tertullian and Lactantius also say something about these beings, whom one is ashamed even to name, had not the pagans compelled us to do so; this will be discussed in the dissertations that follow (Augustine, *City of God*, book IV, ch. 11, p. 97, and book VI, ch. 9, p. 156; Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25, and [Col. 0549B] *To the Nations*, book II, ch. 11; Lactantius, book I, ch. 20, p. 110).

With no less blindness and madness, the Gentiles believed that Libentina and Liburnus, as Arnobius further relates, “presided over the guardianship of lusts.” Elsewhere we read in Varro’s writings: “From *libendo*, ‘desiring,’ come *libido*, ‘lust,’ *libidinosus*, ‘lustful,’ and other words in the same way, such as Libentina”—without doubt the goddess of whom our author speaks. For Augustine later said: “The goddess Libentina, whose name derives from lust.” Consider, however, whether she is the Libentina Venus of whom Cicero speaks: “The names of Desire, Pleasure, and Lubentina Venus have been consecrated—names of vicious, not natural, things.” (Arnobius, book IV, p. 132; Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book V, p. 57; Augustine, *City of God*, book IV, ch. 8, p. 93; Cicero, [Col. 0549C] *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, p. 223, line 7.)

As for Liburnus, his name appears to be corrupt. In the royal manuscript it reads *Burnus*. Since this was thought to have been corrupted through the copyist’s ignorance, editors made *Liburnus* out of it. But they did not trouble to tell us who this Liburnus was. Meursius therefore thought that *Liberus* should be read, whom Augustine attests was appointed by the pagans over lust (Augustine, *City of God*, book VI, ch. 9, p. 156, and book VII, ch. 2, p. 163). We would readily subscribe to this conjecture if, instead of *Libentina*, we were to read *Libera*, who, again according to Augustine, was likewise believed to preside over lust. But since Augustine there also teaches that the pagans considered her to be Venus, may it not be inferred from this that she was the same as Libentina? [Col. 0549D] Nevertheless, since, as we have said, the pagans possessed so many and such varied gods of this kind, we cannot state with certainty what the true reading of Arnobius is.

What more remained for exposing to everyone the everlasting disgrace and dishonor of pagan religion, except that these utterly shameless people should perform rites for prostitutes and harlots just as they did for their other gods? Yet “in the greatest cities,” says our author, “and among the more powerful peoples, public rites are performed for women who were once prostitutes for hire and exposed themselves to common lust” (Arnobius, book I, p. 15). By these words he undoubtedly refers to Acca Laurentia and Flora, whom we discussed in the preceding dissertation [Col. 0550A] (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 16, art. 2). That Laurentia is certainly the woman whom Arnobius elsewhere calls the goddess Luperca:

> Because, when the infants—Romulus, that is, and Remus—had been exposed, a she-wolf, though not gentle, spared them, she was called the goddess Luperca, on Varro’s authority.

(Arnobius, book IV, p. 128.) Hence Lactantius also says in the passage already cited: “The she-wolf who nursed Romulus was honored with divine honors.” But enough was said about her in our preceding dissertation.

The third of these notorious prostitutes was Leaena of Athens, whom Clement of Alexandria mentions, as do other writers cited in our dissertations on his works (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 2, ch. 24, art. 3, p. 1250). In Athenaeus, moreover, Demochares is said to have recorded that, in order to flatter Demetrius Poliorcetes, the Athenians [Col. 0550B] constructed temples to Leaena and to Lamia Aphrodite (Athenaeus, book VI, p. 252).

Moreover, although Orbona and Naenia might appear more honorable and modest than those two, they were no less false and fictitious divinities. The pagans believed, as Arnobius says (Arnobius, book IV, p. 131), that parents bereft of their children were under the protection of the former, and that people at the end of life were placed under the patronage of the latter. In Tertullian’s mutilated book, which gapes everywhere with lacunae, we read: “May Orbana, who sows into bereavement, extinguish”—an uncertain and evidently defective reading (Tertullian, *To the Nations*, book II, ch. 15). We have in addition the pagan Pliny as a witness that a shrine of Orbana had been built near the temple of the Lares (Pliny, *Natural History*, book II, ch. 7, p. [Col. 0550C] 142). A chapel had also been consecrated outside the Viminal Gate to the goddess Naenia, who presided over the final moments of life or over funerals, as we learn from Paulus and Festus.

What has been said concerning this goddess and the other gods and goddesses whom we have thus far seen named by Arnobius can further be supported by Varro’s testimony, which Augustine presented as follows:

> Varro began to recall and enumerate the gods from the conception of a human being, and carried that sequence down to the death of a decrepit old man; and he concluded the gods pertaining to the human being himself with the goddess Naenia, whose song is sung at the funerals of the aged. He then began to set forth other gods who pertain not to the human being himself, but to the things that belong to a human being, such as [Col. 0550D] food, clothing, and all other things necessary for this life, showing in each case what the function of each god was and why supplication should be made to each.

(Augustine, *City of God*, book VI, ch. 9, p. 158.)

No one can fail to perceive easily, from everything that we have discussed thus far, how rightly Arnobius concludes that all those gods are altogether false and, indeed, entirely nonexistent. For it has been proved more than sufficiently either that they never existed; or that at some time they had their origin and beginning; or that they did or suffered things utterly incompatible with divine majesty and nature, and very often entirely unworthy even of a person possessing the smallest degree of modesty and shame. Finally, if certain others are again brought forward by our Arnobius, an opportunity to speak of them will be given below [Col. 0551A] (Arnobius, book III, p. 113).

## CHAPTER XIV  
### Another Argument of Arnobius Against the Gods of the Gentiles, Derived from Their Servitude, Chains, Wounds, Death, and Tombs, Is Examined

### ARTICLE I  
#### How Forceful Arnobius’s Argument for Destroying the Gentiles’ Belief Concerning Their Gods Is, Being Drawn from the Servitude of Hercules, Apollo, and Neptune; the Degrading Service of Minerva; the Bondage of the Muses; the Chains of Mars and Saturn; Saturn’s Expulsion from His Kingdom; and the Wounds of Mars, Venus, Pluto, Juno, Minerva, and Hercules

The pagans degraded their own gods—than whose majesty nothing more sublime or excellent ought to have been conceived—so far that they everywhere proclaimed and advertised, with astonishing shamelessness, their servitude, chains, wounds, [Col. 0551B] and death. For they had handed down to memory, says Arnobius:

> That the gods served as hired slaves: Hercules at Sardis, because of love and wantonness; Delian Apollo under Admetus; Jupiter’s brother under Laomedon of Troy; the Pythian god under the same man, but together with his uncle; and Minerva as a provider of light and superintendent of lamps for those engaged in the private acts of marriage.

(Arnobius, book IV, p. 144.)

But Arnobius, according to his usual practice, excerpted these things from Clement of Alexandria (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 22), who fights against the pagans with the same argument and presses it upon them not merely more clearly and explicitly, but with several further examples that Arnobius deliberately omitted:

> Εἰκότως ἄρα οἱ τοιοίδε ὑμῶν θεοί, δοῦλοι παθῶν [Col. 0551C] γεγονότες, ἀλλὰ καὶ πρὸς τῶν Εἱλώτων καλουμένων τῶν παρὰ Λακεδαιμονίοις· δούλειον ὑπεισῆλθεν ζυγὸν Ἀπόλλων Ἀδμήτῳ ἐν Φεραῖς, Ἡρακλῆς ἐν Σάρδεσιν Ὀμφάλῃ· Λαομέδοντι δὲ ἐθήτευε Ποσειδῶν, καὶ Ἀπόλλων, καθάπερ ἀχρεῖος οἰκέτης, μηδὲ ἐλευθερίας δήπουθεν δυνηθεὶς τυχεῖν παρὰ τοῦ προτέρου δεσπότου· τότε καὶ τὰ Ἰλίου τείχη ἀνῳκοδομησάτην τῷ Φρυγί. Ὅμηρος δὲ τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν οὐκ αἰσχύνεται παραφαίνειν λέγων τῷ Ὀδυσσεῖ, χρύσεον λύχνον ἔχουσαν ἐν χερσίν.

> Rightly, therefore, are such gods of yours slaves of passions—and even of those whom the Lacedaemonians call Helots. Apollo submitted to the yoke of slavery under Admetus at Pherae, and Hercules under Omphale at Sardis. Poseidon and Apollo served Laomedon for hire, Apollo behaving like a useless household slave who apparently could not obtain freedom from his former master. At that time the two of them also rebuilt the walls of Troy for the Phrygian. Homer, moreover, is not ashamed to portray Athena lighting the way for Odysseus, holding a golden lamp in her hands.

Thus the Latin translator renders it:

> Your gods, therefore, are rightly such as were slaves of vices—and even of those whom the Lacedaemonians call Helots. Apollo submitted to the servile yoke under Admetus at Pherae, and Hercules under Omphale at Sardis. Neptune and Apollo were hired servants under Laomedon, Apollo behaving like a useless slave who could not obtain freedom from his former master. At that time they also restored the walls of Troy for the Phrygian. [Col. 0551D] Homer, moreover, is not ashamed to say that Minerva went before Ulysses with a golden lamp in her hands.

Both Clement and Arnobius cite the following lines of Homer (Homer, *Odyssey*, book XIX, verses 33 ff.):

> . . . . . Παροίθε δὲ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη  
> Χρύσεον λυχνὸν ἔχουσα φάος περικαλλὲς ἐποίει.

> Before them Pallas Athena,  
> Holding a golden lamp, shed most beautiful light.

(Homer, *Odyssey*, book XIX, verses 33 ff.)

We have discussed sufficiently elsewhere this absurd and ridiculous servitude of their gods (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 15, art. 3, and *Apparatus*, vol. I, p. 1090).

[Col. 0552A] Arnobius also drew from the same source, Clement of Alexandria, what he added there concerning the Muses:

> Is it one of us who has Myrtillus as his authority, who declares that the Muses were the daughters of Macar and the little slave girls of Megaclo?

(Arnobius, book IV, p. 145.)

For Clement relates, from the same Myrtillus—or Myrsillus of Lesbos—that while the Muses were slaves, they were purchased by Megaclo, daughter of Macar, king of the Lesbians, and that she afterwards built columns and temples for them. But we briefly touched on them in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 19; *Apparatus*, vol. I, p. 820).

Chains are undoubtedly harsher than servitude, yet the Gentiles believed that their gods had been most unworthily bound in them. For what is further removed from divinity than what they boasted:

> That Saturn, because of parricide—

these are Arnobius’s [Col. 0552B] words (Arnobius, book IV, p. 143)—

> was bound, and on appointed days was washed and relieved of the shackles of his chains?

Some printed editions read *suis*, “his own”; the royal manuscript, *tantis*, “such great.” The same royal manuscript reads *elevari*, “raised,” instead of *levari*, “relieved.”

Arnobius clearly alludes to what Macrobius explains more clearly from Apollodorus. On his authority he reports “that Saturn is bound throughout the year with a linen bond and released on the day sacred to him, that is, in the month of December” (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, ch. 8, p. 209). From this it can readily be inferred that in Arnobius’s text—unless one should read “only on feast days”—the same fact was expressed by another word of equivalent meaning. Why Lipsius wished to correct it to “only on his own days” is not sufficiently clear to us. Concerning the chains of Mars subsequently mentioned by our author, read, if you please, Homer and what we have noted in this dissertation [Col. 0552C] and elsewhere (Lipsius, book III, letter 15, vol. I, p. 180; Homer, *Iliad*, V, verse 385; above, ch. —; *Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 15, art. 2).

If the gods were reduced to servitude and cast into chains, what remained but that, after receiving blows, they should be said to have been injured and wounded? Yet the pagans certainly proclaimed precisely this everywhere and repeatedly:

> Is he not your own poet—

for thus Arnobius addresses the pagans (Arnobius, book IV, p. 144)—

> who represented Mars and Venus as wounded by mortal hands? Is not Panyassis one of you, who records that Father Dis and Queen Juno were wounded by Hercules? Do not the writings of your Polemo declare that the warrior-maiden was struck, bloodied, and maltreated by Ornytus? Does not Solibius affirm that Hercules himself was tormented by the sons of Hippocoon, and describe the inflicted wound and pain?

[Col. 0552D] These words were again sampled from the following passage of Clement of Alexandria (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 23):

> Τεκμηριοῖ Ὅμηρος μάλα ἀκριβῶς Ἀφροδίτην ἐπὶ τῷ τραύματι παρεισάγων ὀξὺ καὶ μέγα ἰάχουσαν· αὐτόν τε τὸν πολεμικώτατον Ἄρη ὑπὸ τοῦ Διομήδους κατὰ τοῦ κενεῶνος οὐτασμένον διηγούμενος. Πολέμων δὲ καὶ τὴν Ἀθηνᾶν ὑπὸ Ὀρνύτου τρωθῆναι λέγει, ναὶ μὴν καὶ τὸν Ἀϊδωνέα ὑπὸ Ἡρακλέους τοξευθῆναι Ὅμηρος λέγει, καὶ τὸν Ἤλειον Αὐγέαν Πανύασσις ἱστορεῖ· ἤδη δὲ καὶ τὴν Ἥραν τὴν ζυγίαν ἱστορεῖ ὑπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ Ἡρακλέους ὁ αὐτὸς οὗτος Πανύασσις ἐν Πύλῳ ἠμαθόεντι. Σωσίβιος δὲ καὶ τὸν Ἡρακλέα πρὸς τῶν Ἱπποκοωντιδῶν κατὰ τῆς χειρὸς οὐτασθῆναι λέγει.

> Homer supplies exceedingly precise evidence when he introduces Aphrodite crying out sharply and loudly because of her wound, and when he relates that the most warlike Ares himself was wounded in the flank by Diomedes. Polemo says that Athena too was wounded by Ornytus. Homer also says that Aidoneus was struck with an arrow by Heracles; and Panyassis relates the story of Augeas the Elean. This same Panyassis further relates that Hera, goddess of marriage, was wounded by that same Heracles at sandy Pylos. Sosibius says that Heracles too was wounded in the hand by the sons of Hippocoon.

The Latin translation reads:

> [Col. 0553A] Homer indicates plainly enough that Venus, because of her wound, cried out in a sharp and loud voice, and he relates that the most warlike Mars was wounded by Diomedes in the belly. Polemo says that Minerva too was wounded by Ornytus. Homer also relates that Pluto was wounded by Hercules, just as Panyassis relates concerning Augeas the Elean; Panyassis also relates that Juno, goddess of marriage, was wounded by that same Hercules in sandy Pylos. Sozibius says that Hercules too was wounded in the hand by the sons of Hippocoon.

You plainly see how Arnobius irrigated his own little gardens from the fountains of Clement of Alexandria—to use Cicero’s words when speaking of Epicurus and Democritus (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 212, line 44). It must also be evident to you that through this argument and these examples both writers establish most clearly [Col. 0553B] that those whose wounds could scarcely ever be without blood—and, what is worse, pus and corruption—or be healed without medicines, are neither gods nor immortals. We have discussed these gods’ wounds elsewhere: the blows suffered by Mars and Venus in the preceding dissertation, and the wounds of Minerva and Hercules in the first volume of our *Apparatus* (preceding dissertation, ch. 15, art. 3; *Apparatus*, vol. I, pp. 762 and 816). The cited verses of Homer concerning Juno and Pluto will be found in the fifth book of his *Iliad* (Homer, *Iliad*, V, verse 357).

Arnobius likewise excerpted from Clement of Alexandria what he related concerning the lame Vulcan and Aesculapius, who was struck by a thunderbolt. We have treated both elsewhere (Arnobius, book IV, [Col. 0553C] p. 143; *Apparatus*, vol. I, p. 754; and *Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 15, arts. 2 and 3).

### ARTICLE II  
#### How the Same Point Is Proved by the Examples of Jupiter, Who Unknowingly Ate Human Flesh; by His Death and Burial; by the Tombs of the Brothers Castor and Pollux, of Saturn, and of the Tyrian Hercules; and by the Theban Hercules, Who Was Consumed by Fire

Weakness and ignorance of mind must undoubtedly be judged worse than bodily wounds. Yet in Jupiter there was so great an ignorance of affairs and so great a facility for being deceived that, as Arnobius observes, “when invited to share a meal, he unwittingly ate Lycaon’s offspring instead of the entrails of a pig” (Arnobius, book IV, p. 143). But Arnobius, as usual, took this from Clement [Col. 0553D] of Alexandria and related it more briefly. For in Clement’s *Exhortation to the Gentiles* we read the following (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 23):

> Μετέλαβε δὲ καὶ τραπέζης ἀνθρωπίνης παρὰ τοῖς Αἰθίοψιν, ἀπανθρώπου δὲ καὶ ἀθέσμου, αὐτὸς ὁ Ζεὺς, παρὰ Λυκάονι τῷ Ἀρκάδι ἑστιώμενος, ἀνθρωπείων γοῦν ἐνεφορεῖτο σαρκῶν, οὐχ ἑκών· ἠγνόει γὰρ ὁ θεός, ὡς ἄρα Λυκάων ὁ Ἀρκάς, ὁ ἑστιάτωρ αὐτοῦ, τὸν παῖδα κατασφάξας τὸν αὐτοῦ, Νύκτιμος ὄνομα αὐτοῦ, παραθείη ὄψον τῷ Διί.

> Zeus himself also shared a human table among the Ethiopians—and an inhuman and unlawful one when he was entertained by Lycaon the Arcadian. For he filled himself with human flesh, though not willingly. The god did not know that Lycaon the Arcadian, his host, had slaughtered his own son, whose name was Nyctimus, and served him to Zeus as meat.

The Latin rendering states:

> Jupiter himself also partook of a human table among the Ethiopians, and then of an inhuman and unlawful one when he was entertained at a banquet by Lycaon the Arcadian; for, though unwillingly, he filled himself with human flesh. The god did not know that Lycaon the Arcadian, who was entertaining him, [Col. 0554A] had killed his own son, whose name was Nyctimus, and would set him before Jupiter to be eaten.

See Ovid, Hyginus, and Apollodorus concerning this and the other examples enumerated thus far (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book I, tale 7, p. 12 ff.).

What else remained, finally, for proving the mortal nature of Jupiter and the other false gods, except to make clear to everyone that they died in the human manner and were subsequently buried, and that none of them was recalled from the grave to life? Yet, Arnobius says, “We are told that Jupiter was delivered over for burial on the island of Crete” (Arnobius, book IV, p. 144). From whom this report came you may learn from Clement of Alexandria, whose footsteps Arnobius again follows. For these are Clement’s own Greek words (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, [Col. 0554B] p. 242):

> Ζήτει σου τὸν Δία, μὴ τὸν οὐρανὸν, ἀλλὰ τὴν γῆν πολυπραγμόνει· ὁ Κρής σοι διηγήσεται, παρ’ ᾧ καὶ τέθαπται. Καλλίμαχος ἐν ὕμνοις·  
>   
> . . . . Καὶ γὰρ τάφον, ὦ ἄνα, σεῖο  
> Κρῆτες ἐτεκτήναντο.

> Seek your Zeus; examine not heaven but earth. The Cretan, among whom he also lies buried, will tell you. Callimachus says in his *Hymns*:  
>   
> “For the Cretans, O lord, fashioned  
> A tomb for you.”

The Latin translator rendered it thus:

> Seek your Jupiter; do not search heaven, but earth. The Cretan among whom he is buried will tell you. Callimachus says in his *Hymns*:  
>   
> “For the Cretans constructed  
> Your tomb.”

But we have already observed with how much justice and reason our Arnobius reproached the pagans with this, and by what authority of other witnesses [Col. 0554C] he did so (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 14, art. 3).

Arnobius also made a summary of the same Clement’s words concerning other gods, although here either his memory appears to have failed him or his text has been corrupted. For he writes as follows (Arnobius, book IV, p. 144):

> In the territories of Sparta and Lacedaemon—

supply, “Do we say that”—

> the brothers, joined together in their cradle—

Castor and Pollux, that is—

> were buried? Is that author one of ours who is identified in the titles of his writings as Patrocles of Thurii, and who records that the tomb and remains of Saturn are contained in Sicilian earth? Is Plutarch of Chaeronea—

the royal manuscript reads “Hieronymus”—

> shown to belong to our party, who related that Hercules, after the collapse caused by epileptic fits, was reduced to ashes upon the heights of Oeta?

[Col. 0554D] Clement of Alexandria, however, writes (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 18):

> Φιλόχορος δὲ . . . . Κρόνον ἐπικεῖσθαι ἐν Σικελίᾳ, καὶ ἐνθαῦτα αὐτὸν τετάφθαι. Πατροκλῆς τε ὁ Θούριος, καὶ Σοφοκλῆς ὁ νεώτερος ἐν τρισὶ τραγωδίαις ἱστόρειτον τοῖν Διοσκούροιν  
>   
> (the royal manuscript reads: ἱστόρειτον τὼ Διοσκούρὼ περὶ)·  
>   
> Ἀνθρώπω τινὲ τούτω τὼ Διοσκούρω γενέσθην, εἴ τῳ ἱκανὸς πιστώσασθαι Ὅμηρος τὸ λελεγμένον·  
>   
> . . . . Τοὺς δ’ ἤδη κάτεχεν φυσίζοος αἶα,  
> Ἐν Λακεδαίμονι αὖθι, φίλῃ ἐνὶ πατρίδιῃ γαίῃ.

(Homer, *Iliad*, III, verse 243.)

> Philochorus says . . . that Cronus lies in Sicily and was buried there. Patrocles of Thurii and Sophocles the Younger, in three tragedies, relate concerning the Dioscuri that these two Dioscuri were mortal men, if Homer is sufficient to confirm the statement for anyone:  
>   
> “But them the life-giving earth already held  
> There in Lacedaemon, in their beloved native land.”

The Latin rendering reads:

> Philochorus says . . . that Saturn lies in Sicily and was buried there. Patrocles of Thurii and Sophocles the Younger write concerning Castor and Pollux that they [Col. 0555A] were human beings subject to death and fate. If Homer can convince anyone of this, let what is written be heard:  
>   
> “But these the life-giving earth already held  
> There in Lacedaemon, in their beloved native land.”

Clement then relates what the philosopher Hieronymus and Dicaearchus said about Hercules’ bodily and facial appearance, and immediately adds (Clement, ibid.):

> Οὗτος οὖν ὁ Ἡρακλῆς, δύο πρὸς τοῖς πεντήκοντα ἔτη βεβιωκὼς κατέστρεψε τὸν βίον, διὰ τῆς ἐν Οἴτῃ πυρᾶς κεκηδευμένος.

> This Hercules, therefore, after living fifty-two years, ended his life and received his funeral rites by means of the pyre on Oeta.

But in citing his witnesses, Arnobius appears to differ considerably from Clement. For Arnobius proves from the testimony of Patrocles of Thurii that Saturn was delivered over for burial [Col. 0555B] in Sicily, whereas Clement proves it from Philochorus. Moreover, Arnobius cites no one to show that Castor and Pollux were mortal human beings and were buried in Lacedaemon; Clement, however, cites three authorities—Patrocles of Thurii, Sophocles the Younger, and Homer. Finally, Clement reports the form and appearance of Hercules—and, as it seems, the manner of his death—as related by the philosopher Hieronymus and Dicaearchus; Arnobius, however, attributes it to the man of Chaeronea, or, as we have said the royal manuscript reads, “Hieronymus Plutarch.”

There is, however, no very great disagreement between our two writers if Arnobius cited no witness to the burial of Castor and Pollux, while Clement cited several and Homer foremost among them. But someone might perhaps wonder [Col. 0555C] why Arnobius made no mention of this prince of the Greek poets, who is praised not only by Clement but also by Cicero, in these very words:

> Homer, who lived not long after their time, says that they—

Castor and Pollux—

> were buried at Lacedaemon.

(Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, p. 241, line 30.)

For Arnobius frequently follows in the footsteps of these writers.

He differs more markedly from Clement in confirming Saturn’s burial from the testimony of Patrocles, whereas Clement confirms it from that of Philochorus. If they did not intend to produce different guarantors, consider, please, whether Arnobius’s memory failed him or whether the error should be blamed upon a copyist’s carelessness or ignorance. Such carelessness is certainly still more evident in the copied names “the man of Chaeronea” or [Col. 0555D] “Hieronymus Plutarch.” For if Arnobius was following Clement there, as elsewhere, the text should read “the philosopher Hieronymus,” who related that Hercules burned himself alive upon Mount Oeta.

Moreover, our author had already said in his first book concerning the death of this Hercules and of the other Hercules:

> The Theban or Tyrian Hercules: the latter was buried in the territory of Spain, the former consumed by the flames of Oeta.

(Arnobius, book I, p. 20.)

The first of these was the Hercules about whom Pausanias committed the following to writing (Pausanias, book V, p. 175):

> I heard at Thasos that he was the Tyrian Hercules whom the Thasians had worshipped from the beginning; but when they afterwards joined themselves to the Greeks, they also began to pay honors to the son of Amphitryon.

> Ἤκουσα δὲ ἐν Θάσῳ [Col. 0556A] τὸν αὐτὸν σφᾶς Ἡρακλέα, ὃν καὶ Τύριοι, σέβεσθαι· ὕστερον δὲ ἤδη τελοῦντας ἐς Ἕλληνας, νομίσαι καὶ Ἡρακλεῖ τῷ Ἀμφιτρύωνος νέμειν τιμάς.

> I heard at Thasos that they worshipped the same Heracles as the Tyrians; but later, when they had come to be counted among the Greeks, they decided also to assign honors to Heracles the son of Amphitryon.

It is related that, while the affairs of the Tyrians were favorable and prosperous, they sent a colony to Spain under the leadership of the Tyrian Hercules, and that Hercules himself eventually died and was buried there. Mela writes concerning the island of Gades:

> The temple of the Egyptian Hercules, illustrious for its founders, religion, antiquity, and wealth, was founded by the Tyrians. The reason why it is sacred is that his bones are laid there.

(Mela, book III, ch. 6.)

But Mela is censured on this point by Arrian and others because he improperly confused the Egyptian and Tyrian Hercules, whom Cicero and others distinguish (Arrian, *Expedition of Alexander*, book II, p. 125). Concerning the Tyrian Hercules who was worshipped in Spain, besides [Col. 0556B] Pausanias and Arrian, already cited, one may consult Quintus Curtius and Vossius (Arrian, loc. cit.; Q. Curtius, book VII; Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, book I, ch. 34, p. 131 ff.).

The Theban Hercules, moreover, although born—as we previously observed (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 15, art. 3)—from the adultery of Jupiter and Alcumena, was nevertheless regarded as the son of Amphitryon, a Theban and the husband of that same Alcumena, and was therefore called “the Theban.” Why and how he was burned alive on Mount Oeta we have also explained elsewhere. From that account you will also understand what our author says again shortly afterwards:

> In Sophocles’ *Trachiniae*, Hercules, the offspring of Jupiter, entangled in the snare of a deadly covering, is represented as uttering pitiable lamentations, broken by the violence of pain, [Col. 0556C] and wasting away to final dissolution through the torment of his disintegrating entrails.

(Arnobius, book IV, pp. 151 ff.)

Cicero, however, had said it earlier and more clearly:

> Let us look at Hercules himself, who was then broken by pain when he sought immortality through death itself. What cries does he utter in Sophocles’ *Trachiniae*? After Deianira had clothed him in the tunic stained with the Centaur’s blood, and it had adhered to his entrails, he says: “O many . . .,” etc.

(Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book II, p. 138, line 42.)

The verses of Sophocles transcribed by Cicero are in fact found in the tragedy he cites (Sophocles, *Trachiniae*, verses 1057 ff.).

How forceful this argument of Arnobius is may also be gathered from Cicero himself. After saying that Euhemerus demonstrated both the deaths and the burials of the gods, [Col. 0556D] Cicero concludes that he thereby utterly abolished religion—not, certainly, any religion other than that of the pagans (Cicero, at the end of *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 212).

## CHAPTER XV  
### How Arnobius Proved That the Pagans Wrongly Blamed the Poets for Everything Recorded About the Gods, and That the Gods Were Dishonored in the Games Instituted in Their Honor and Stripped of the Divinity Attributed to Them

### ARTICLE I  
#### It Is Shown That Everything Said About the Gods Was Wrongly Shifted onto the Poets, and That the Pagans Ought to Have Passed Sentence Against Them as Against Those Who Murmured Against Royal Power and Authority and as Against Slanderers, and to Have Proscribed Along with Them Actors, Mimes, and Pantomimes; with a Discussion of the Fifteen Laureled Men

[Col. 0557A] So that the pagans might weaken, or at least evade in some manner, the arguments of such weight that we have set forth, they answered that all those utterly shameful deeds, deaths, and burials of the gods were fictions of the poets, composed by men of unsound mind for lust and pleasure, by means of which they deceived the ignorant populace. But who will find it credible, asks Arnobius, that poets of the most remote antiquity reached such a degree of shamelessness that they disseminated infamous and utterly obscene tales about the gods in blind frenzy, and feared no punishment either from the gods themselves or from human beings? (Arnobius, book IV, pp. 148 ff.)

Then again, granted that they invented these things contrary to all law, human and divine, why did they not suffer, under the severity of the laws, the penalties due for so great a crime? Is it not an extremely serious offense to injure someone’s reputation, and much more that of a god? [Col. 0557B] Is it not a greater insult to accuse someone of a false crime than to cast that crime in his teeth? [The transmitted comparison is uncertain.] What of the fact that the pagans, who allowed learned men to advertise such shameful deeds of the gods with impunity, were guilty of no lesser offense than the poets themselves?

What crimes, sacrileges, chains, wounds, and deaths of the gods the poets sang can readily be understood from what has already been said and from what will be said below. Here Arnobius especially presses the charge ascribed to Jupiter:

> That very Jupiter, whose name—

he says—

> you ought not to have uttered without fear and a trembling of the entire body, is described as being caught by his wife while playing the lover, confessing his faults, and, like a madman unaware of himself, hardened in shamelessness, [Col. 0557C] publicly declaring which girlfriends he preferred to his spouse and which mistresses to his wife.

(Arnobius, book IV, p. 150.) The royal manuscript reads *amasius*.

There he undoubtedly alludes to those verses of Homer in which Jupiter tells and confesses to Juno that he had been seized by love for Ixion’s wife, Dia, as well as for Danae, the daughter of Phoenix, Semele, Alcmene, Ceres, and Latona (Homer, *Iliad*, XIV, verses 314 ff.).

Therefore, Arnobius continues (Arnobius, book IV, p. 150), the unbridled license of Homer and the other poets ought to have been restrained by pagan laws and plebiscites with no less severity than that applied to those who had murmured against kings and were consequently prosecuted for treason. In these words he plainly refers to the Julian law of treason, which Theodosius the Great later mitigated. See in the Justinian and Theodosian Codes [Col. 0557D] the laws concerning insults directed against the ruler, and Gothofredus’s observations upon them (Justinian Code, book I, titles 7 and 8; and Theodosian Code, vol. III, p. 42 ff.). These laws also confirm what Arnobius adds: that penalties were decreed against one who brought a magistrate or senator into contempt or pursued him with abuse. With how much greater severity, therefore, ought those guilty of offenses against divine majesty to have been treated? Why, then, did they grant the poets pardon and impunity?

But let us proceed, if you please. Our author adds:

> You were unwilling to allow the composition of an evil song, by which another person’s reputation and life might be stained, to go unpunished under the ordinances of the Ten Men; and, lest anyone should strike your ears with excessively wanton abuse, you established legal actions [Col. 0558A] for grievous injuries.

(Arnobius, book IV, p. 151.)

If anyone wishes to have this proved by some authority, let him hear Cicero:

> The Twelve Tables declare that even then it was customary to compose songs; and the laws ordained that it should not be permitted to do so to another’s injury.

(Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book IV, p. 163, line 23.)

Augustine, moreover, testifies that he copied the following word for word from the now-lost fourth book of Cicero’s *Republic*:

> Although our Twelve Tables established capital punishment for very few offenses, they nevertheless thought that this offense too should be punished: if anyone had sung an abusive song against another or composed a song that brought disgrace or dishonor upon him. Excellently done. For our lives ought to be submitted to the judgments of magistrates and lawful proceedings, not to the inventions of poets; nor ought we to hear reproach [Col. 0558B] except under a law that permits us to answer and to defend ourselves in court.

(Augustine, *City of God*, book II, ch. 9, p. 38.)

Augustine further confirmed this by the testimony of Seneca (ibid., ch. 12, p. 40). Finally, Horace sang:

> Indeed, a law  
> And penalty were enacted, forbidding anyone  
> To be portrayed in an abusive song.

(Horace, *Epistles*, book II, epistle 1, verses 152 ff.)

Shortly before, Horace had mentioned the tablets sanctioned by the Twelve Men. Consult him, if you please, and Gothofredus’s notes on the title concerning defamatory writings (Theodosian Code, vol. III, p. 237 ff.).
