With what great unfairness and injustice, therefore, did the pagans avenge injuries and slanders against human beings by such severe laws, while patiently tolerating—indeed, [Col. 0558C] extolling with the highest praise—the poets by whom the gods themselves were harassed with countless abuses and insults?

Yet the same license was given not only to poets but also to pantomimes, mimes, stage actors, comic actors, and tragic actors (Arnobius, book IV, p. 151). For in the theaters they all represented those same crimes of the gods—of Venus, Cybele, Hercules, and others—and their shameful and cruel deeds, with still greater shamelessness and no less impunity. The Gentiles—not merely the soft and effeminate among them, but the whole people, the senators, the colleges of priests and magistrates, the chief pontiffs, the curiones, the priests of Jupiter, the flamines, the augurs, and the fifteen laureled men—listened to them with great applause and pleasure. [Col. 0558D] Those fifteen men were the guardians of the Sibylline books; Servius observes that they were first two in number, then ten, and later fifteen. If you wish to know more about them, consult Cicero, Valerius Maximus, Aulus Gellius, Pliny, Suetonius, Tiraquellus, and Lactantius, whom we have cited elsewhere (Servius on *Aeneid* VI, verse 73; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, p. 225; Valerius Maximus, book I, ch. 1; Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book I, ch. 19, p. 86; Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXVIII, ch. 2, p. 557; Tiraquellus on Alexander ab Alexandro, *Days of Generation*, book III, ch. 16, p. 269; *Apparatus*, vol. I, p. 254).

So far were the pagans from punishing, as they deserved, mimes, stage actors, and other people of the same sort who represented such infamous [Col. 0559A] deeds of the gods, that they instead granted them, as our author rightly says, “gifts and rewards, exemption from public duties, immunity, freedom from service, together with crowns” (Arnobius, book IV, p. 152). For Theodoret said plainly:

> Τραγῳδίας μὲν καὶ κωμῳδίας ὑποκριταὶ ἔχουσιν εἰς ὃ βλέποντες τὴν τέχνην μετίασι, καὶ τῇ τῶν στεφάνων ἐλπίδι τῶν πόνων ἀνέχονται.

> Performers of tragedies and comedies have a prize in view for which they practice their art, and they endure their exertions in hope of crowns.

(Theodoret, discourse 9, *On Providence*, pp. 429 and 434.)

He adds that statues were decreed and erected for tragic actors, just as for army commanders, athletes, boxers, and charioteers, portraying them in the costume in which they had won.

Arnobius therefore rightly and deservedly condemns such great injustice. Together with Tertullian and Augustine, [Col. 0559B] he shows most clearly that divine majesty could never be offended, injured, and violated more atrociously than by these comedies and tragedies (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 35; Augustine, *City of God*, book II, ch. 8 ff.). Lactantius therefore wrote quite rightly and aptly on this point:

> Can anyone behave worse than those very people who, although they say that they worship the gods, nevertheless publicly and shamefully mock them, and even permit mimes about them to be performed amid laughter and pleasure? What sort of religion is this, or how great can that majesty be considered which is adored in temples and mocked in theaters? And those who have done these things do not pay the penalties for violating the divine power, but even depart honored and praised.

(Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, book III, ch. 20, p. 526.)

The already cited Augustine no less sharply rebukes and assails the foolishness of the pagans who prattled that the poets had invented the shameful deeds [Col. 0559C] of the gods:

> What are Mercury’s thefts, Venus’s wantonness, and the adulteries and shameful acts of the others in comparison with this evil? We would quote these things from books if they were not sung and danced in the theaters every day. But what are they in comparison with so great an evil, whose enormity belonged to the Great Mother alone—especially since those things are said to have been invented by the poets, whereas these were pleasing and acceptable to the gods? That they should be sung and written might be the audacity or wantonness of the poets; but that they should be added to divine rites and honors at the command and compulsion of those same divine powers—what is that but a crime of the gods, or rather a confession of demons and a deception of the wretched?

(Augustine, *City of God*, book VII, ch. 26, p. 182; and [Col. 0559D] book IV, ch. 10, p. 96.)

Indeed, even these crimes of the gods would have been unbelievable had they not been watched with the greatest delight in theaters instituted in their honor.

### ARTICLE II  
#### How Arnobius Demonstrates That the Gods of the Gentiles Are False from the Solemn Games Presented in Their Honor, Especially the Floralia and the Megalensian Games; the Renewal of Certain Games; the Comedies, Tragedies, and Atellan Farces Performed in Them; the Shaven Heads of Fools; the Noise of the *salepitae* [reading uncertain]; and the Redness of Phallic Amulets
The fictitious nature of their gods, their counterfeit majesty, and their superstitious worship were demonstrated still more clearly by those public games which the pagans themselves, Arnobius says, regarded as sacred, and by which they believed that the gods were honored and appeased, as though by solemn religious observances, and, after laying aside their hostility, reconciled to them (Arnob., book VII, [Col. 0560A] p. 238). Livy, and subsequently Valerius Maximus and Augustine, recorded that, during the consulship of T. Sulpicius Peticus and C. Licinius Stolo, when a very severe plague had not been allayed by a *lectisternium*, stage plays were instituted to appease the anger of the gods (Liv., book VII, beginning; Val. Max., book II, chap. 4, § 4; August., book I *On the City of God*, chap. 32, p. 29). Then afterward shameful stories and the indecent performances of actors were introduced into them. Hear, I ask you, the words of Augustine (book II *On the City of God*, chap. 17, p. 75; book IV, chap. 26, p. 106; and book VIII, chap. 13, p. 201): “Stage plays, exhibitions of obscenities, and the license of vanities were instituted at Rome not through the vices of men, but at the commands [Col. 0560B] of your gods. It would have been more tolerable for you to render divine honors to that Scipio than to worship gods of such a kind.” For this reason he afterward declares without hesitation that through these games a more serious plague was introduced into morals than into bodies, although they were said to have been instituted for the purpose of curing the bodily plague.

Earlier, however, Lactantius had said: “The celebrations of games are festivals of the gods, since they were instituted either for their birthdays or for the construction of new temples. Originally, indeed, the hunts that are called *munera* were assigned to Saturn; stage plays to Liber; and circus games to Neptune. Gradually, however, the same honor began to be accorded to the other gods also, and the several games were consecrated to their divinities, as Sisinnius Capito teaches in his books *On Spectacles*. Therefore, if anyone [Col. 0560C] attends spectacles at which people assemble for religious purposes, he has departed from the worship of God and gone over to the gods whose birthdays and festivals he has celebrated” (Lactan., book VI *On True Worship*, chap. 20, p. 621).

Tertullian pursues these matters at much greater length in an entire book *On Spectacles* (Tertull., *On Spectacles*, p. 89 ff.). For there he demonstrates with the utmost clarity that all those solemn games of the pagans belonged, by their origin, titles, and ceremonial apparatus, so completely to idolatry that no Christian was ever permitted to attend or watch them. Arnobius therefore said that the pagans counted them among religious duties by which they believed their gods were honored (Arnob., book VII, p. 238). But how, I ask you, could gods be honored by games in which the most shameful obscenities were performed?

[Col. 0560D] Our author, however, names only two specifically, the Floralia and the Megalensia, because it would have taken too long to enumerate them individually, and because everyone could easily understand from their example what judgment should be made about the others.

The Floral Games, or Floralia, as Macrobius observed, were games and festivals that derived their name and origin from a notorious prostitute. She had previously been called Chloris, as we have noted elsewhere, and desired these games to be instituted with money amassed through the shameful commerce of her body (Macrob., book I *Saturnalia*, chap. 4; *Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. 18, art. 3). But so that the memory of such an infamous origin might more easily be erased, they changed her name, called her Flora, and invented the fiction that she presided over flowers. Nevertheless, they were wholly unwilling to abandon [Col. 0561A] the licentiousness of their scandalous foundress, which was so pleasing to them. If you doubt whether we should be believed, you will surely not deny credit to Ovid, whose verses on the institution of these Floralia are as follows:

> The Fathers assembled, and, that the year might bloom prosperously,  
> They vowed annual festivals to our divinities.  
> We assented to their vows; the consul Laenas, together with his fellow consul  
> Postumius, discharged the obligation of games to me.  
> I was trying to discover why greater licentiousness  
> And freer jesting prevailed in these games.  
> But then it occurred to me that the name was not severe,  
> And that the goddess bears gifts suited to pleasures.

(Ovid, book V of the *Fasti*, § 3.)

There he describes the various kinds of licentiousness permitted at these games, which you may read if you have leisure. The consuls identified by him are Postumius Albinus and M. Popilius Laenas, by whom these games were first presented. [Col. 0561B] If you further ask why, at whose command, and in what year from the foundation of the City they were instituted, and on what day of the year they were held, you will learn from these words of Pliny: “They instituted the Floralia on the fourth day before the Kalends of the same month”—May—“in the 514th year of the City, in accordance with the Sibylline oracles, so that everything might shed its blossoms successfully. Varro fixes this date when the sun occupies the fourteenth degree of Taurus. Therefore, if the full moon falls within this four-day period, the crops and everything that is in flower must necessarily be harmed” (Plin., book XVIII *Natural History*, chap. 19, p. 527). In the calendrical *Fasti*, however, they are marked on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, and in the Rural Calendar near the end of the month of May. If you desire more information about those games, which were celebrated with the greatest obscenity and licentiousness, you may consult Varro, Cicero, Suetonius, Martial, Valerius Maximus, and especially Lactantius, [Col. 0561C] who is nevertheless charged with a certain error by Vossius; whether rightly or unjustly, we shall consider in its proper place (Varro, book IV *On the Latin Language*, p. 18; *On Rural Matters*, book I, chap. 1; Cic., fourth oration *Against Verres*, p. 194; Suet., *Life of Galba*, 6, § 6; Val. Max., book II, chap. 10, § 8; Martial, book I, epigrams 3 and 36; August., book II *On the City of God*, chap. 27, p. 57).

The Megalensian Games, however, had been decreed in honor of the Mother of the Gods after consultation of the Sibylline books. They are said to have been called by that name because at Pessinus, from which that goddess—or her image—was carried to Rome, there stood her most celebrated temple, which, as Varro attests, was called the *Megalesion*. “The Megalensia,” he says, “were so called from the Greeks, because she was summoned from Attalus, king of Pergamum, in accordance with the Sibylline books, [Col. 0561D] near the wall the *Megalesion*, where the temple of that goddess stood, whence she was conveyed to Rome” (Varr., book V *On the Latin Language*, p. 49). Scaliger, however, is persuaded that Varro’s words *prope murum* (“near the wall”) are corrupt and that one should read *Pessinunte* (“at Pessinus”) or ἀπὸ μητρὸς μεγάλης, “from the Great Mother,” although he inclines more strongly toward the former reading.

Of these games, which Livy and others mention quite frequently, Cicero spoke as follows: “Why should I speak of those games which our ancestors wished to be performed and celebrated on the Palatine, before the temple and in the very sight of the Great Mother, during the Megalensia? In customary practice and established usage they are the most chaste, solemn, and religious of games. At these games P. Africanus the Elder, when consul for the second time, first gave the senate a place before the assembled people. . . . . . . . Thus [Col. 0562A] those games possess so great a religious sanctity that it came when summoned from the remotest lands and established its seat in this city; they alone are not even designated by a Latin word, so that their very name declares both that a foreign cult was sought out and that it was received under the name of the Great Mother. Yet these games were performed by slaves and watched by slaves; indeed, while this man was aedile, the Megalensia belonged entirely to slaves” (Liv., book XXIX, chap. 7; Cic., oration 30, *On the Response of the Haruspices*, p. 432, lines 36 ff.).

The great religious devotion—or rather superstition—with which these and the other solemn games were performed by the pagans is evident not only from these words of Cicero, but especially from the fact that, if they were believed to have been polluted by even the slightest fault, they afterward had to be repeated with greater care and anxiety. Arnobius therefore addressed these words to the pagans themselves: “In your ceremonies and divine rites, [Col. 0562B] there is a place for your *postuliones* [a disputed term], and an offense is said to have been contracted requiring expiation if, through a lapse of inadvertence, anyone has made an error either in a word or with the *sympuvium*; if a fault has been committed during the race in the solemn games and divine chariot contests, you all immediately cry out that sacred obligations have been violated; if the player has stopped, or the flute-player has suddenly fallen silent; or if that boy who is called *patrimus* has through ignorance dropped the rein or has been unable to keep hold of the ground” (Arnob., book IV, p. 149). If anyone asks us where he obtained these details, the answer is readily available: they were excerpted from Cicero’s already cited oration. For there Cicero says: “If the player has stopped, or the flute-player has suddenly fallen silent, or if that boy whose father and mother are both living has not kept contact with the ground, or has dropped the sacred car or its rein, or if the aedile [Col. 0562C] has erred in a word or a gesture, the games have not been duly performed; those errors are expiated, and the minds of the immortal gods are appeased by repeating the games” (Cic., oration 30, *On the Response of the Haruspices*, p. 432, line 26). Some have informed us, however, that in this text of Cicero certain manuscripts have *aut sympulo aberravit*, “or erred with the *sympulum*,” in place of *aut si nutu aberravit*, “or if he erred in a gesture.” Arnobius nevertheless seems to have read *aut sympuvio deerravit*, “or erred with the *sympuvium*,” but with the same meaning. For *sympulum* and *sympuvium* signify an earthenware cup from which wine was customarily poured as a libation during sacrifices. Some may perhaps doubt whether the word *postulionibus* in Arnobius’s own text has been corrupted and whether *postulationibus* should be read instead. For Cicero, shortly before the words of his that we cited, had said: “Petitions were decreed for Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune, Tellus, and the heavenly gods,” [Col. 0562D] and afterward also: “A petition is owed to Tellus” (Idem, ibid., line 8; and p. 434, line 10; Guther., book IV *On Pontifical Law*, chap. 15). Guther, however, approves Arnobius’s reading *postulionibus* and, in order to remove every scruple, maintains that *postulationes* were made to the gods above and *postuliones* to the gods below, through which they requested that a man be devoted to them. Yet even if the matter were so, by what argument can it be established that Arnobius was speaking there of the gods below rather than those above? For if, as we have said, he excerpted anything from Cicero, he was undoubtedly speaking of the same gods as Cicero—that is, the gods above. We may add, if you wish, that nothing would have been easier for an unskilled or hurried copyist than to omit the two letters *at* when writing the word *postulionibus*. We are indeed aware [Col. 0563A] that Varro somewhere used the noun *postulio*, writing: “To demand a *postulio* of the gods of the dead, that is, that the bravest citizen be sent to the same place” (Varr., book IV *On the Latin Language*, p. 35). But Scaliger judges that the words “that is” should be deleted there and that the noun *postulio* signifies the same thing as *postulatio*.

Whatever judgment you make, Arnobius still seems to have taken from the same words of Cicero what he later related about the repetition of other games because of a slave who had been beaten with rods and killed in the circus (Arnob., book VII, p. 244). But we must explain these matters below in a more appropriate place.

Moreover, the greater the worship and religious devotion with which these and the other aforementioned solemn games were celebrated by the pagans, the more clearly it is thereby shown that the gods worshiped in them were [Col. 0563B] false and fictitious, and that the religion of those same pagans was wholly depraved and corrupt. For in these games, besides many other things utterly unworthy of gods, cruel tragedies and shameful comedies were performed, concerning which we discussed a little earlier. Arnobius specifically identifies Sophocles’ *Women of Trachis*, Euripides’ *Hercules*, and Plautus’s *Amphitryon* (ibid., pp. 238 ff.); these plays, having been printed more than once, are in everyone’s hands. In addition, four comedies of Terence are recorded as having been performed at the very Megalensian Games that we have explained. Who does not know how greatly the majesty of the gods—if they could ever have existed—was injured and mocked in them?

Our author further adds that Atellan [Col. 0563C] comedies or farces were also performed at public games (ibid., p. 239). If you wish to know what they were and why they were so named, you will easily understand from these words of Livy: “The young men took possession of this kind of entertainment, which had been received from the Oscans, and did not permit it to be polluted by professional actors. Hence the rule remains that performers in Atellan farces are neither removed from their tribe and perform military service as though they had no part in the theatrical profession” (Liv., book VII, chap. 2). Atella was a town of Campania, now Aversa; the Oscans were a people of Campania who very frequently employed shameful words. Hence the term *obscene* was derived to signify something shameful. Their comedies, therefore, when brought to Rome, were tempered, because they were more indecent, by Roman—or, as Valerius Maximus says, Italian—severity [Col. 0563D] (Val. Max., book II, chap. 4, § 4). Donatus, however, vainly attempts to excuse their obscenities in these words: “Atellan farces are composed of witty sayings and jokes, which contain nothing except charming elegance.” For Arnobius rightly maintains that these farces and comedies were neither more chaste nor more honorable than the others, and that the gods were treated no less unworthily in them than elsewhere.

He therefore sharply rebukes the pagans, who wrongly believed that the gods rejoiced in these solemn games and comedies, were honored and appeased by them, laid aside anger and hostility, and were reconciled to the people by whom they had been offended. For what joy could flood the gods, and what other pleasant emotions could affect them, at the sight of so many and such great obscenities in comedies—as has already been said and will be said again below—[Col. 0564A] the ridiculous and infamous representation of their own persons, and furthermore, as Arnobius puts it, “the shaven heads of fools, the sound of slap-makers, and the redness of enormous phalluses” (Arnob., book VII, p. 239)? In these stage games, that is, certain mimes and actors played the ridiculous roles of foolish men with shaven heads, and were reminded of their duty by the sound of the *salapitae*, that is, by resounding blows of the hand. Tertullian accordingly mocks and assails the mad recklessness of these utterly shameless men as follows: “Will the man who alters his countenance with a razor be pleasing? Faithless toward his own face, he is not content to make it resemble Saturn, Isis, and Liber, but also exposes it to the insults of slaps, as though he were playing at obedience to the Lord’s command. [Col. 0564B] Evidently the devil too teaches one patiently to offer the cheek to be struck!” (Tertull., *On Spectacles*, chap. 28). Julius Capitolinus, moreover, relates how a certain fool on the stage, in the presence of Antoninus the Philosopher, called the adulterer of Antoninus’s wife by his own name (Capitolin., near the end of the *Life of Antoninus the Philosopher*). But nothing was more shameless than the phallus, which should never have been mentioned by anyone except such writers as Augustine and our author, when pleading the Christian cause against the pagans who gloried in the infamous sexual immorality of their gods (August., book VI *On the City of God*, chap. 9, p. 157).

Who, then, would not admit that Arnobius rightly concludes from this that the pagans were seized by utterly astonishing blindness (Arnob., book V, pp. 176 and 184), since they believed that the gods rejoiced in, [Col. 0564C] were worshiped through, and were appeased by such infamous games and comedies? He judges that their opinions, absurd to such a degree, arose from no other cause than their complete ignorance of what God is, or what his nature, attributes, and qualities are. Whoever desires to know more about these games, comedies, and tragedies, which we have already discussed (*Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. 13, art. 1), should read the commentaries upon them by Lilius Giraldus, Scaliger, Camerarius, Casalis, Albericus Gentilis, Fabricius, and others. From what has been said, however, everyone understands clearly enough that even these facts alone utterly overthrow the gods of the pagans and their entire religion.

## CHAPTER XVI

### How Varied the Pagans’ Opinions Were Concerning Each of Their Gods, and How Rightly Arnobius Demonstrates from This That the Divinity of Each Is False

[Col. 0564D]

### ARTICLE I

#### Arnobius’s Argument Against the Gods of the Pagans Is Examined—an Argument Drawn from the Fact That a God Whom Some Said Was Begotten by Parents Was Affirmed by Others to Be Some Natural Object—Especially Janus, Saturn, Jupiter, Juno, Fluviona, Pomona, Ossipagina, Februtis, Populonia, Cinxia, and Caprotina

Arnobius drew another argument—no less effective and forceful than the others—against the absurd errors of the pagans concerning their gods from their varied and mutually conflicting opinions concerning one and the same god. For how, he asks, can you induce people to recognize and worship a god when you yourself [Col. 0565A] do not know what the god whom you worship is like, and have never been able to learn it from others? Were there not nearly as many opinions concerning one and the same pagan god as there were heads?

Our author, indeed, demonstrates this with the utmost clarity, still following his customary method of induction: “Let us begin solemnly,” he says, “with Janus, and likewise with the father whom some of you have declared to be the world, others the year, and some the sun” (Arnob., book III, p. 117). Do not suppose that he said this rashly. For we read the following in the writings of Servius: “Some hold that Janus is lord of the day, within which are sunrise and sunset. . . . . . . . Others hold that he is lord of the entire year, which is known to be divided into four seasons. That he is god of the year is proved by the fact that the first part of the year is named after him. For January [*Januarius*] is named from Janus. [Col. 0565B] . . . . . . Others understand Janus as the world, whose gates are therefore closed in time of peace because the world is closed on every side; in time of war they are opened in order to seek assistance, so that access may lie open” (Serv., on book VIII of the *Aeneid*, verses 605 ff., p. 474). He adds that Janus, or Eanus, was said by some, including Cicero (Cic., book I *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 224), to derive his name from *eundo*, “going,” and to be Mars himself; others believed him to be the air; and others called him Clusivius, Patuleius, Iazonius, and even Quirinus.

Macrobius, however, shows that some, including Nigidius, said that this same Janus was identical with the sun and Apollo; others said that he was the world and heaven; and still others called him by the same names that Servius enumerates, especially Janonius, “as though,” he says, [Col. 0565C] “he governed the entrances not only of the month of January but of all the months” (Macrob., book I *Saturnalia*, chap. 9).

But if this is so, Arnobius argues (Arnob., book III, p. 117), then certainly there will be no Janus whom the pagans represented as begotten by Caelus and Hecate, husband of Juturna, son-in-law of Vulturnus, father of Fontus, founder of the Janiculum, king of Italy, and the deity who, as is clear from Ovid, must always be placed first in every prayer and, as Cicero notes, in every sacrifice (Ovid, book I of the *Fasti*, § 3; Cic., book II *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 224). Augustine argues in an entirely similar manner: If Janus, he says, is the world, why did the pagans falsely assert that the beginnings, ends, and limits of things were referred to him? Why did they fashion him with two faces, as though the world had only two parts, or with four faces, [Col. 0565D] as though both he and the world were twofold? Why did they claim that the first things, or the beginnings of deeds, were in his power, while their highest consummations belonged to Jupiter, as though Jupiter were king of all? What, then, has become of this Jupiter, king of men and gods, if Janus is said to be the world? (August., book VII *On the City of God*, chaps. 7 ff., pp. 168 ff.; *Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. 15, art. 1.)

By another line of reasoning Arnobius further shows that no divinity can be attributed to this same Janus if he is the year. For what is a year except a certain span of time bounded by a fixed number of days and months? Who will persuade himself that something which passes and slips away possesses divine power? (Arnob., book III, p. 117).

[Col. 0566A] By precisely the same force of reasoning he establishes that Saturn possesses no divinity, since Saturn is said to have been time—*tempus* in Latin and χρόνος (*chronos*) in Greek—or, as Augustine says, the duration of time. Not only Macrobius and Plutarch expressly handed this down, but Cicero too did so in exactly these words: “They intended Saturn to be the one who governed the course and cyclical return of spaces and times. This god has in Greek the very name of the thing itself. For he is called Κρόνος (*Kronos*), which is the same as χρόνος (*chronos*), “a span of time.”” Arnobius again infers from this that Saturn, said to have been born from Caelus as his father, must be removed altogether (August., book IV *On the City of God*, chap. 10, p. 95; Macrob., book I *Saturnalia*, chap. 8; Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, vol. II, p. 363; Cic., book II *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 223, line 28).

[Col. 0566B] What, furthermore, of the fact that Jupiter, the son of this same Saturn and Ops, who was buried within the territory of the Cretans, must likewise be said never to have existed? For some maintained that he was the sun, others the ether. Macrobius proves by various testimonies of ancient authors that he was in fact the sun (Macrob., book I *Saturnalia*, chap. 23). Cicero, however, openly informs us that Chrysippus considered him to be the ether, and that Ennius—who is cited for the same reason by Varro also—said with universal assent:

> Look upon this  
> Shining vault on high, which all invoke as Jupiter.

(Cic., book I *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 201, line 34; and book II, p. 214, line 12; ibid., p. 223, line 37; Varr., book IV *On the Latin Language*, p. 16.)

Cicero produces Euripides as another witness, who, as he adds, expressed this succinctly, as he did many things [Col. 0566C] admirably (Cic., loc. cit.):

> You see the boundless ether spread on high,  
> Which enfolds the earth in a tender embrace:  
> Hold this to be the highest of the gods; declare this to be Jupiter.

Eusebius, however, wished us to be informed that, according to Orpheus—if Porphyry is to be trusted—Jupiter is said to be the whole universe, and the ether to be its soul (Euseb., book III *Preparation for the Gospel*, chap. 9, pp. 100 ff.).

The divinity of Juno is therefore also false, since, as Arnobius argues (Arnob., book III, p. 118), most said that she was the air, especially the Stoics, whose opinion Cicero explains in these words: “The air, moreover, as the Stoics maintain, lies between the sea and heaven and is consecrated under the name of Juno, who is the sister and wife of Jupiter, because it resembles the ether and is united with it in the closest possible conjunction. They made the air feminine and attributed it to Juno because nothing is softer than it” (Cic., book II *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 223, line 47).

Before Augustine, Macrobius expressed his agreement with the orator as follows: “Juno is called the sister and wife of Jupiter. Juno, however, is the air; she is called his sister because the air was produced from the same seeds as heaven, and his wife because it lies beneath heaven” (August., book IV *On the City of God*, chap. 10, p. 95; and book VII, chap. 16, p. 175; Macrob., book I *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, chap. 17). Porphyry, however, had committed the following words to writing, which Eusebius transcribed thus (Porphyr., in Euseb., book III *Preparation for the Gospel*, chap. 11, p. 108):

> Τὴν δὲ Ἥραν σύνοικον τῷ Διὶ πεποιήκασιν, τὴν αἰθέριον καὶ ἀέριον δύναμιν [Col. 0567A] Ἥραν προσείποντες· ἔστι γὰρ καὶ ὁ αἰθὴρ, ἀὴρ ὁ λεπτομερέστατος.

“They fashioned Juno as the wife of Jupiter because they called the ethereal and aerial power Juno. For the ether too is air of the subtlest and finest kind.”

He adds that she was called Juno, Ἥρα, ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀέρος, “from the air.” Finally, Macrobius, whom we cited a little earlier, relates elsewhere that Juno is the lowest air, as we shall observe shortly (Macrob., book III *Saturnalia*, chap. 3).

From this Arnobius argues as follows: “If she is the air, as you are accustomed to jest and repeat, deriving the term from the austerity of the Greek name, then no sister and wife of almighty Jupiter will be found, no Fluviona, no Pomona, no Ossipagina, no Februtis, Populonia, Cinxia, or Caprotina” (Arnob., book III, [Col. 0567B] p. 118). For the pagans had invented so many other Junos, and even more names and divine powers belonging to her. We have already discussed Cinxia a little earlier. Festus teaches who Fluviona was: “Women worshiped Juno Fluviona,” he says, “because they believed that she restrained the flow of blood during conception” (Festus, s.v. FLUVIONEM). Augustine confirms this designation on Varro’s authority as follows: “The goddess Mena presides over menstrual flows; although the daughter of Jupiter, she is nevertheless obscure. Yet in his book on the select gods, the same author, Varro, assigns this province of menstrual flows to Juno herself, who is also queen among the select gods; and here, as Juno Lucina, she presides over the same blood together with that same Mena, her stepdaughter” (August., book VII *On the City of God*, chap. 2, p. 163). You will find this repeated by Augustine a little [Col. 0567C] later, though more briefly, and treated by Vossius (ibid., chap. 3; Voss., book VI *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, chap. 26, p. 221).

Although Varro admits that the origin of Pomona’s name is obscure, he, Ovid, Servius, Augustine, and very many others nevertheless attest that the pagans proclaimed her the goddess of fruits and gardens (Varr., book VI *On the Latin Language*, p. 80; Ovid, book XIV *Metamorphoses*, § 17; Serv., on book VI of the *Aeneid*, p. 457; August., book IV *On the City of God*, chap. 34, p. 114; Fabric., in *Description of the City of Rome*, vol. III of *Roman Antiquities*, p. 432). How she could have been called Juno, however, is not readily apparent. Some therefore suspect that this name was corrupted by a copyist’s carelessness and that *Sororia* should be substituted for it, since Juno was said to be Jupiter’s sister and [Col. 0567D] wife. In confirmation of this opinion one may add that a temple was built at Rome for Juno beside the Sororian Beam, and was therefore called the temple of Juno Sororia. But if we may add another conjecture to this one, which is supported by the testimony of no manuscript, we shall say that, because fruits and produce belong to the earth or soil, it may have happened that Juno—who was believed to be the earth and to govern earthly things—was called Pomona, just as she was called by so many other names. Varro, with whom Augustine agrees, informs us in the following words that Juno was considered the earth: “Juno is the wife of Jupiter; he is heaven and she is earth, which is likewise Tellus. She is called Juno because together with Jupiter she assists—*juvat*—and queen because she rules all these earthly things” (Varr., [Col. 0568A] book IV *On the Latin Language*, p. 17; August., book VII *On the City of God*, chap. 16, p. 174). But let others judge this conjecture of ours.

Some also believe that the following name of the same Juno, by which Arnobius calls her Ossipagina, has been corrupted, and they would emend it to Opigena, of whom Festus speaks in this manner: “Matrons worshiped Juno Opigena because they believed that she brought aid to women laboring in childbirth” (Festus, s.v. OPIGENA). But this does not establish clearly enough whether she is the same as Ossipagina, who, as Arnobius later wrote, was a “solidifier of bones” and was thought to harden and solidify the bones of infants (Arnob., book IV, p. 131). Vossius readily agreed with Stewechius, who believed that *Ossipaga* or *Ossipanga* should be restored [Col. 0568B] (Voss., in *Etymologies*, s.v. *os*). For he judges that she was so named because she fastens—*pangit*—or, as the ancients used to say, *paget*, the bones of children.

Februtis, however, or Juno Febralis, was also surnamed Februta or Februalis by the Romans, as Festus further observes (Fest., s.v. FEBRUARIUS). She received that name from the month of February, during which her rites were customarily performed; and, as Festus likewise says, the Lupercalia were a festival on which women were *februated*, that is, purified and cleansed, by the Luperci with Juno’s little cloak—that is, a goatskin. You may read Varro, Augustine, and Lilius Giraldus (Varr., book V *On the Latin Language*, § 3; August., book VII *On the City of God*, chap. 7, p. 168; Girald., *Syntagma* 3, p. 119).

[Col. 0568C] P. Tertius, in Macrobius, mentions Juno Populonia and a temple dedicated in her honor: “In Papirian law,” he said, “it is clearly reported that a dedicated table can serve in place of an altar; thus, he says, a table was dedicated in the temple of Juno Populonia” (Macrob., book III *Saturnalia*, chap. 11). They say that this name was given to her because Juno was believed to preside over the union of male and female, from which new peoples are created. Seneca, however, in Augustine, mentioned a certain widow Populonia, and did not wonder that she lacked a suitor (August., book VI *On the City of God*, chap. 10, p. 160). But she was undoubtedly not Juno Populonia. On this goddess, and likewise on Februtis, Martianus Capella, book II *On the Marriage of Philology*, should be read.

[Col. 0568D] Women once sacrificed to Juno Caprotina—or, as others prefer, Capratina—because the chastity of maidens and matrons had been preserved and the people of Fidenae, who wished to take it from them, had been defeated. Varro speaks of this sacrifice as follows: “The Nones of Caprotina are so called because on that day in Latium women sacrifice to Juno Caprotina; they do so beneath a wild fig tree and employ a branch from the wild fig tree” (Varr., book V *On the Latin Language*, p. 50). Macrobius related the cause and institution of this sacrifice and of the festival called the Festival of the Maidservants. Plutarch and others also mention it. Furthermore, as Servius says, there were still more divine manifestations of Juno, such as Curis and Lucina, which Arnobius preferred to pass over in silence because he had already mentioned enough (Macrob., book I *Saturnalia*, chap. 11, p. 223; Plutarch, *Parallel Stories*, [Col. 0569A] vol. II, p. 313; Serv., on book I of the *Aeneid*, verses 12 and 13).

Since the pagans therefore had so many Junos—or, as Servius says, divine manifestations of Juno—our author certainly concludes from this that none of them, including the very one who was everywhere proclaimed the sister and wife of Jupiter, can be called a goddess if Juno, according to the etymology of the Greek name and the opinion of many, was the air. For air cannot be a god; therefore no Juno is a goddess.

### ARTICLE II

#### How Arnobius Shows from the Pagans’ Various Opinions That Minerva Is Not Truly a Goddess: She Who Was Born from Jupiter’s Brain and Was the Daughter of Mind and Victory; with a Discussion of the Etymology of the Name Minerva

Arnobius comes to Minerva and, on the testimony [Col. 0569B] of Granius, proves that Aristotle taught that she was the moon. Others, however, departed from this opinion and openly asserted that she was the summit of the ether and, as Arnobius says, the highest point of that height. Others held that she was memory: “Whence,” he says, “the name Minerva was formed, as though it were *Meminerva*” (Arnob., book III, p. 118). Porphyry approached Aristotle’s opinion more closely, as is clear from his words transcribed by Eusebius as follows (Euseb., book III *Preparation for the Gospel*, chap. 11, p. 113):

> Ὅπερ δὲ Ἀπόλλων ἐν ἡλίῳ, τοῦτο Ἀθήνη ἐν σελήνῃ, ἔστι γὰρ τῆς φρονήσεως σύμβολον, Ἀθηνᾶ τις οὖσα.

“What Apollo is in the sun, Minerva is in the moon; for the moon is a symbol of prudence, being, as it were, a Minerva.”

Augustine explains [Col. 0569C] in this manner the two opinions defended and asserted by different people: “Because they placed Minerva over the human arts and found no star in which to place her, they said that she was either the highest ether or even the moon.” And a little later: “Minerva is the highest ether, and Minerva is likewise the moon, which they believe to stand at the lowest boundary of the ether” (August., book VII *On the City of God*, chap. 16, p. 174). Diodorus Siculus, however, where he discusses Egyptian theology, recorded that the name Minerva was given to the air and that this was the reason why she was said to be a virgin born from Jupiter’s head, and was called Tritogeneia and Glaucopis. If you wish to read Diodorus’s words, you will find them transcribed by Eusebius as follows (Diod. Sicul., book I *Library*, p. 8; Euseb., book III *Preparation for the Gospel*, chap. 3, p. 89):

> Τὸν δὲ ἀέρα προσαγορεῦσαί φασιν Ἀθηνᾶν, μεθερμηνευομένης τῆς λέξεως· καὶ Διὸς θυγατέρα νομίσαι ταύτην, καὶ παρθένον [Col. 0569D] ὑποστήσασθαι διά τε τὸ ἄφθαρτον εἶναι φύσει τὸν ἀέρα, καὶ τὸν ἀκρότατον ἐπέχειν τόπον τοῦ σύμπαντος κόσμου· διόπερ ἐκ τῆς κορυφῆς τοῦ Διὸς μυθολογηθῆναι συνέβη ταύτην γενέσθαι· ὠνομάσθαι δὲ αὐτὴν Τριτογένειαν, ἀπὸ τοῦ τρὶς μεταβάλλειν αὐτῇ τὴν φύσιν κατ’ ἐνιαυτόν, ἔαρος, καὶ θέρους καὶ χειμῶνος· λέγεσθαι δὲ αὐτὴν καὶ γλαυκῶπιν, οὐχ ὥσπερ ἔνιοι τῶν Ἑλλήνων ὑπέλαβον, ἀπὸ τοῦ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς γλαυκούς—τοῦτο μὲν γὰρ εὐηθὲς ὑπάρχει—ἀλλ’ ἀπὸ τοῦ τὸν ἀέρα τὴν πρόσοψιν ἔχειν ἔγγλαυκον.

“They say that the air was called Athena—that is, Minerva—through an interpretation of the word; that she was regarded as the daughter of Jupiter and represented as a virgin because air is by nature not subject to corruption and occupies the highest place in the entire universe. Hence arose the myth that she was born from Jupiter’s head. [Col. 0570A] She was called Tritogeneia because her nature changes three times in the year: in spring, summer, and winter. She was also called Glaucopis, not, as some Greeks supposed, because she had gray-blue eyes—for that is foolish—but because the air has a gray-blue appearance.”

Let us add Servius, who wrote in his commentaries on Virgil’s *Aeneid*: “Powers are either terrestrial or aerial; but because the ether is fire, there is fire in the temples of ethereal powers, so that an image of their own element may be rendered to them. It is in the temple of Jupiter because he is the ether, and in Minerva’s [temple] because she is above the ether [punctuation contextually restored]. Hence she is said to have been born from her father’s head” (Serv., on book IV of the *Aeneid*, p. 326). Finally, Macrobius relates that those who, as he thought, investigated the truth more diligently gave the following reason why Minerva was called the highest summit of the ether: [Col. 0570B] “They maintain,” he says, “that the middle ether is Jupiter, that the middle ether together with the earth is Juno, and that the highest summit of the ether is Minerva. As their argument, they cite the fact that Tarquinius, son of Demaratus of Corinth, having been mystically initiated into the Samothracian rites, joined the divinities just mentioned in a single temple and beneath the same roof” (Macrob., book III *Saturnalia*, chap. 4). But consider, I ask you, how much force this argument possesses.

Vossius, moreover, believes that by the name Minerva the pagans understood the power of the ether and of God in the human being, and especially memory and its offspring, prudence (Voss., book II *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, chap. 42, p. 273). He believes that this interpretation, and also Arnobius’s statement that this same Minerva was called the daughter of Mind, can be confirmed by these verses of Afranius in Aulus Gellius, [Col. 0570C] in which he represented Wisdom as the daughter of experience and memory:

> Experience begot me; Memory, my mother, gave me birth.  
> The Greeks call me *Sophia*; you call me Wisdom.

(Gell., book XIII *Attic Nights*, chap. 8.)

Nevertheless, although Porphyry, as we saw a little earlier, said that just as Apollo is in the sun, so Minerva is in the moon, the symbol of prudence, Macrobius produces another testimony of his, in which he indicated that this same Minerva is a power of the sun that bestows prudence upon human beings. For these are the words of Macrobius: “Porphyry attests that Minerva is a power of the sun which supplies prudence to human minds. For this reason the goddess is said to have sprung from the head of Jupiter—that is, to have [Col. 0570D] issued from the highest region of the ether, whence the sun takes its origin” (Macrob., book I *Saturnalia*, chap. 17, p. 262).

The pagans therefore varied as much concerning the etymology of this name as they did concerning Minerva herself. For some, as Arnobius says, wished the name to be derived from *memory* (*memoria*), as though it were *Meminerva*. Cicero, however, thinks she was so called because she either *diminished* (*minueret*) or *threatened* (*minaretur*); Isidore, because she was, as it were, the goddess and gift (*munus*) of the various arts that were proclaimed to have been invented by her (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, p. 224, line 20; Isidore, *Origins*, VIII.11). Finally, Festus derives it from the fact that she gives good counsel (*bene moneat*). “For,” he says, “the pagans used her to represent wisdom. Cornificius, however, thinks that she was so named because she is fashioned and depicted threatening with weapons” (Festus, s.v. *MINERVA*). [Col. 0571A] Cornificius’ etymology is indeed the same as Cicero’s, but is explained by him.

Vossius, however, inclines more toward Festus’ opinion and judges that the verb *moneo* was derived from the older *meneo*, and that from *meneo* came *mentio*, *memini*, *memor*, and *reminiscor*; thus the name *Menerva* was formed, and afterward *Minerva* (Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, II.42, p. 271 ff.). There he also assembled many arguments by which the statements that we have seen made by Arnobius are clearly elucidated and established.

Indeed, even if we were to remain entirely silent, who, I ask, does not see how rightly our Arnobius concludes from this that there was no Minerva at all—no daughter of Mind or Victory, none born from Jupiter’s brain, no inventor of the olive tree, nor one [Col. 0571B] placed in charge of and instructed in various arts and disciplines—but merely a natural entity, which certainly cannot be a goddess? (Arnobius, III, p. 118.)

Yet the more clearly it is established from what has thus far been said that the pagans believed her to be the daughter of Mind and born from Jupiter’s brain, the more difficult it is to prove the grounds upon which Arnobius calls her the daughter of Victory. For Dionysius of Halicarnassus relates (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, I, p. 26):

> The Arcadians tell the myth that Victory (*Nikē*) was the daughter of Pallas, the son of Lycaon, and that she obtained the honors she now possesses among human beings at Athena’s wish, because she had been brought up together with that goddess. For Athena, immediately after her birth, had been entrusted by Zeus to Pallas and was brought up in his household until she reached maturity.

By these words [Col. 0571C] he plainly shows that Minerva was not the daughter of Victory, but was merely brought up together with her. Nevertheless, Arnobius had Pausanias as an earlier supporter of his opinion, for Pausanias had said (Pausanias, I, p. 40):

> There is also another sanctuary there of Athena, surnamed Victory (*Nikē*).

Moreover, in a certain hymn ascribed to Orpheus she is called *nikēphore daimōn*, “divine spirit who bears victory” (Orpheus, *Greek Poets*, I, p. 509). Arnobius’ account would, however, be fully confirmed by this if his text were read: “There is therefore no daughter of Mind, no Victory.” But if [Col. 0571D] the reading must be “No daughter of Victory,” consider, I ask, whether this opinion gained currency because she was surnamed from her own temple, in which she was called Victory, or because those who fought with her aid were said to carry off victory.

It is, moreover, far more commonly and widely known that she was said, as we have shown elsewhere (above, chap. 9, art. 2), to have invented the olive tree and, as Diodorus Siculus testifies, very many other arts. Hence he concludes: “From these things she is called *Erganē*” (Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, III, p. 142, and V, p. 235), that is, “Worker” or “Craftswoman.”

But who does not immediately perceive how much weight and force there is in this argument of Arnobius [Col. 0572A], by which he rejects Minerva and the other gods fabricated by the pagans? This is also clearly demonstrated by Eusebius and Augustine, who show from the pagans’ same varying opinions about Saturn, Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva that they were never gods (Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, III.10, p. 107; Augustine, *City of God*, IV.10, p. 95).

## ARTICLE III. How Arnobius further demonstrates this from Neptune, brother of the Stygian god, lord of sea-monsters, and mover of small sea-fish and surging waters; likewise from Mercury the Caduceus-Bearer, the Cyllenian, inventor of words and names, and regulator of markets, merchandise, and trade; and also from Ceres, who was called Earth, the Great Mother, Vesta, Ops, and the wife of Saturn. Here also concerning the etymology of the names Neptune, Mercury, Ceres, and Vesta.

[Col. 0572B] As we follow Arnobius in his enumeration of the other gods of the pagans, we next encounter Neptune, whom, he says, the pagans called by this name because water “veils” (*nubat*) the earth (Arnobius, III, p. 118). This etymology certainly did not lack an advocate and defender. For although Cicero wishes the name Neptune to be derived from swimming (*nando*), with a slight alteration of certain letters; Isidore from a cloud (*nube*), as though from thundering; and others even from the Greek verb *niptein*, “to wash, to cleanse”; Varro nevertheless expressly said: “Neptune is so called because the sea veils the lands, as a cloud veils the sky, from *nuptus*, that is, covering, as the ancients said; from this also come *nuptiae* and *nuptus*” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, p. 224; Isidore, *Origins*, VIII; Varro, *On the Latin Language*, IV, p. 18).

[Col. 0572C] But if this is true, says Arnobius, the god Neptune assuredly collapses—the one called by the pagans the brother of the Stygian god, that is, Pluto, and the full brother of Jupiter, whom we have already discussed. Our author adds ironically: “Armed with a trident, lord of sea-monsters and small sea-fish, king of the salty surges” (Arnobius, loc. cit.), that is, of sea and ocean, as is clear from these verses in which Virgil represents him as speaking:

> Not to him was dominion over the sea and the savage trident  
> Assigned by lot, but to me.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, I.142 ff.)

A *pistrix* is a large fish or sea-monster, which some believe to be a whale. There is much concerning the *pistrix* in Aratus’ *Phenomena*, from which [Col. 0572D] we have selected the following:

> Yet, spying Andromeda, the savage sea-monster  
> Goes on seeking her, and tracks her position as far as the mighty  
> Blasts of the north wind, blue though fixed in the regions of the south.

(In Cicero, *Fragments*, p. 33 ff.)

The *maena* is likewise a sea-fish, called *mainis* in Greek and *maenola* by the Romans today. Cicero mentions it in these words: “Those who despise pleasure itself may say that they do not prefer a sturgeon to a *maena*” (Cicero, *On Ends*, II, p. 66, line 34). Athenaeus also mentions it, as does Pliny more frequently; Pliny teaches us for which illnesses, and how, remedies are prepared from this fish (Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, VII, p. 313; Pliny, *Natural History*, XXVI.4, p. 448; XXVII.104, [Col. 0573A] p. 542; and XXXII.8 ff., p. 858 ff.). See Rondelet, V.13, Aldrovandi, and others concerning these two fish, the *pistrix* and the *maena*.

Arnobius therefore ridicules the pagans not without wit when he calls Neptune lord of sea-monsters and *maenae*, lord of the salty surges, and mover of the trembling brine, because those insane men seriously called him king of the ocean and sea. For besides the cited verses of Virgil, we read the following written by Cicero: “The other realm, the entire maritime realm, was assigned to Neptune, the brother of Jupiter, as they would have it; and the name is derived, just as *Portunus* is from *portus*, so *Neptunus* from *nando*, with the initial letters slightly altered” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, p. 224, line 1). What a splendid [Col. 0573B] god, then, who swims through the waves of the sea and rules only its domain!

Arnobius then continues as follows: “Mercury too was named as though he were a certain *medicurrius*, and because speech runs between two speakers and passes back and forth, the character of this name was contrived” (Arnobius, III, p. 118). Augustine supports Arnobius and explains the matter somewhat more fully: “Mercury,” he says, “is said to have been so called as though *running in the middle* (*medius currens*), because speech runs as an intermediary between human beings; hence he is called *Hermēs* in Greek, because discourse, or interpretation—which certainly pertains to discourse—is called *hermēneia*. Hence also he presides over merchandise, because discourse passes as an intermediary between sellers and buyers” (Augustine, *City of God*, VII.14, p. 173). [Col. 0573C] Isidore afterward copied these words of Augustine when explaining the etymology of the name. Festus, however, thinks that this name was imposed upon Mercury from merchandise (*merces*). Servius gives a different account: “Others,” he says, “maintain that the Latins called Mercury *medicurrius* because he is always running between heaven and the underworld” (Isidore, *Origins*, VIII.11; Festus, s.v. *MERCURIUS*; Servius on *Aeneid* VIII.138 ff.). Servius made these observations upon the following verses of Virgil, which explain what our author adds next. For the poet sings:

> Mercury is your father, whom fair Maia,  
> Having conceived him on Cyllene’s icy summit, brought forth.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, VIII.138.)

But what else, as Arnobius adds in the passage cited, follows from this variety and disagreement of opinions [Col. 0573D], except that the staff-bearing Cyllenian, brought forth upon an icy mountain, is abolished and extinguished, as is evident from the verses of Virgil just cited, toward which Arnobius may rightly be said to have aimed? He was called *caducitor*, or more properly *caduceator*, the Caduceus-Bearer, because, as Servius and very many others observe: “The caduceus is assigned to him by the god because, through the mediation of good faith, he brings enemies into friendship. This staff is therefore entwined with serpents so that, just as they come together after forgetting their venom, so enemies, having scorned and laid aside their hostilities, may return to friendship” (Servius, loc. cit.).

Our author adds that this same Mercury was the “contriver of words and names.” For, as Cicero observes [Col. 0574A] (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, III, p. 248, line 9), he was said to have transmitted laws and letters, a matter we have discussed elsewhere. Finally, he was “the regulator of markets, merchandise, and trade,” because the pagans, as we noted shortly before from Augustine and Isidore, believed that he presided over merchandise. Hence Servius says: “He is also the god of trade” (Servius, loc. cit.). Indeed, Festus, cited by us shortly before, thinks that his name was formed from this and gives the following reason: “For they believed him to be the god of all business dealings” (Festus, s.v. *MERCURIUS*). Moreover, from the former etymology and the pagans’ opinion Augustine draws the same conclusion as Arnobius: “If, therefore,” he says, “Mercury himself is speech, [Col. 0574B] as even they confess, he is not a god” (Augustine, *City of God*, V.12, p. 173).

By an entirely similar argument our author thus overturns the divinity of Ceres: “Some of you,” he says, “have declared Earth to be the Great Mother because she supplies nourishment to all living creatures; some declare this same being to be Ceres, because she bears a crop of health-giving seeds; others call her Vesta, because she alone stands still in the universe, while its other parts are established in perpetual motion” (Arnobius, III, p. 119). That Ceres is Earth must be observed a little below, and may now be proved by these words of Cicero, which confirm the etymology of Ceres adduced by Arnobius: “The Mother,” he says, “is Ceres from bearing crops (*gerendis frugibus*), as though *Geres*, [Col. 0574C] with the first letter likewise changed by chance, just as among the Greeks. For among them too she is called *Dēmētēr*, as though *Gē-mētēr*, ‘Earth-Mother’” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, p. 224). Concerning the name Vesta, he has the following a little later in the same passage: “The name Vesta comes from the Greeks, for she is the one whom they call *Hestia*” (ibid., line 13). Pharnutus says (*Ceres and Vesta*) that she was so named in Greek by the ancients *apo tou estanai*, “from standing or remaining stationary,” because she stands throughout all things. Ovid too indicated this in the following verses:

> Earth stands by its own power; from standing by her power Vesta is named,  
> And this may be the reason for the Greek name as well.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, VI.331.)

There he confirms not only the etymology of Vesta, but also that she is identical with the earth or soil. He had already said this [Col. 0574D] in the following verses:

> Vesta is the same as Earth; a watchful fire lies beneath them both;  
> Earth and hearth each signify their own fixed abode.

And below:

> Earth and Vesta are one and the same divine power.

(Ibid., verse 271.)

Servius and Augustine come forward in support of Ovid; you may readily consult them, and likewise Giraldi, Lipsius, and Vossius (Servius on *Aeneid* IV.297; Augustine, *City of God*, VII.16, p. 174; Giraldi, *Syntagma* 6; Lipsius, *On Vesta*, chap. 1; Vossius, *Progress of Idolatry*, II.59). Among many other things, they cite these verses of Euripides:

> And Mother Earth—the wise among mortals call you  
> Vesta, seated in the very aether.

[Col. 0575A] Yet by the authority and testimony of these writers, and also of Lucretius, whom you may consult (Lucretius, II.597 ff.; 995 ff.), it is clear that the proposition assumed by Arnobius is entirely true: these three divinities do not exist, since by them only the earth is signified, and the earth is certainly not of a divine nature.

For this reason our Arnobius rightly and properly added the following immediately afterward: “Nor can the Mother of the gods herself, whom Nigidius maintains to have been married to Saturn, rightly be called a goddess, since all these are names of one earth” (Arnobius, III, p. 119). Is not the same thing also asserted by Varro in these words? [Col. 0575B] “Earth is Ops, because all work (*opus*) is done here, and because we have need (*opus*) of her for living; hence she is called Mother Ops, because the earth nourishes. For she has brought forth all nations from the lands and receives them back again; she gives food, as Ennius says; and because she bears (*gerit*) crops, she is Ceres” (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, IV, p. 16). Who, moreover, does not know what we also noted above (above, chap. 9, art. 3), that Ops was called Saturn’s wife by the pagans?

But by whatever name she may be called, if she is the earth, she is not—and cannot be—a goddess. Augustine therefore rightly, after proving from other words of the same Varro that Earth, the Great Mother, and Ops are the same, concludes together with our Arnobius: “If, therefore, she is one goddess—although, when truth is consulted, she is not even that—why meanwhile is she divided into many?” (Augustine, *City of God*, VII.24, [Col. 0575C] p. 180). Nor does he permit the reply that the pagans did not absurdly consider them to be several goddesses, since several things may exist in one and the same goddess. For he immediately meets them with these words: “I grant,” he says, “that several things exist in one human being; are there therefore several human beings? So too several things may exist in one goddess; are there therefore several goddesses? But let them, as they please, divide, combine, multiply, unfold, and entangle” (ibid.). For the more they wish to multiply her, the more certainly they will overthrow the divinity of such a being.

## ARTICLE IV. By what reasoning Arnobius shows the divinity to be false of Vulcan, who is fire; of Venus, who is Proserpina; of the Sun, who is Liber and Apollo; of Diana, who was called Ceres and the Moon; and of all other divinities, because many pagans believed that the world was a certain living creature and a god. Here also concerning the etymology of the names Vulcan and Venus, and Apollo as the destroyer of mice.

[Col. 0575D]

By the same kind of argument Arnobius clearly proves that three other divinities of the pagans—Vulcan, Venus, and Proserpina—must be erased from the register of the gods (Arnobius, III, p. 119). They asserted, indeed, that Vulcan was fire. Do you wish this to be proved for you by at least some witnesses? Here is Varro, whose very words are: “From the greater force and violence of fire Vulcan was named” (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, IV, p. 18). Servius adds his testimony, stating it still more explicitly: “Vulcan is fire, and is called Vulcan, as though *Volcianus*, because it flies (*volet*) through the air. For fire [Col. 0576A] is born from the clouds. Hence Homer too says that he was hurled from the air down to the earth, because every thunderbolt falls from the air” (Servius on *Aeneid* VIII, p. 512). Isidore follows him, repeating almost all his preceding words. What of the fact that the same Servius had said earlier: “We very often use Vulcan to mean fire”? Augustine, moreover, says: “They maintain that Vulcan is the fire of the world” (Isidore, *Origins*, VIII.11; Servius on *Aeneid* I, p. 180; Augustine, *City of God*, VII.16, p. 164).

Nor is what our author adds—that Venus was so named “because she comes to all” (*ad cunctos veniat*)—more difficult to prove (Arnobius, III, p. 219 [read: 119]). It seems to have been taken from Cicero, who expressly declares: “Her who came to all things our people named Venus; [Col. 0576B] and *venustas* is derived from Venus, rather than Venus from *venustas*” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, p. 224, line 27). Others, however, held different opinions concerning the etymology of this word. Varro derives it from the old verb *viere*, or “to bind,” because Venus does not wish to conquer (*vincere*) but to bind and be bound (*vincire et vinciri*), namely by shameful bonds (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, IV, p. 12). Isidore, however, says: “Venus is so called because without force (*vi*; another reading, “without a man,” *viro*) a woman does not cease to be a virgin” (Isidore, *Origins*, VIII.11). But perhaps not without reason Cicero’s opinion appeared more probable to Arnobius.

Yet the more closely Arnobius approaches Cicero there, the further he seems to depart from him in what he adds: that Proserpina received her name because crops spring forth (*proserpunt*) into the light [Col. 0576C] (Arnobius, III, p. 119). For the Latin orator maintains that Proserpina is a Greek name. “She is,” he says, “the one called *Persephonē* in Greek, whom they believe to be the seed of crops, hidden and sought by her mother” (Cicero, loc. cit., line 6). Nevertheless, Arnobius had other followers and supporters of his opinion. For we read the following recorded by Varro: “Proserpina is so called because, like a serpent, she moves broadly, now toward the right and now toward the left. They said that *serpere* and *proserpere* were the same, as Plautus writes: ‘like a beast creeping forward’” (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, IV, p. 17). Isidore states it more briefly, but more clearly and in a manner better suited to our author’s meaning: “Proserpina, because crops spring forth (*proserpant*) from her.” Augustine had previously said: “Proserpina is named from creeping forth (*proserpendo*)” [Col. 0576D] (Isidore, *Origins*, VIII.8; Augustine, *City of God*, VII.20, p. 177). The opinion of these writers has pleased some people—even those who always admire Cicero—more than Cicero’s own.

Together with the same Augustine, Arnobius therefore cleverly infers from this that three of the pagans’ divinities are removed from existence (Arnobius, III, p. 319 [read: 119]): Vulcan, whom all regarded as the element of fire; Venus, whom they represented as lust diffused through all living creatures; and Proserpina, by whom they proclaimed that crops and growing shoots were set in motion. For whatever divergent opinions others might hold concerning them, nothing could be more false than to endow with some supreme divinity those whom they themselves called created things.

[Col. 0577A] Arnobius continues (ibid.) and presses the point that the pagans everywhere boast that the Sun, Liber, and Apollo are the same. Macrobius attempted to prove this not only by the testimony of Euripides and Aeschylus, but also by various arguments (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, II.18, p. 263). Servius recorded that it was asserted by the Stoics and Porphyry: “The Stoics,” he says, “call the same being the Sun, Liber, and Apollo.” Earlier he had said: “According to Porphyry’s book entitled *The Sun*, it is established that Apollo’s power is threefold, and that the same being is the Sun among the gods above, Father Liber upon earth, and Apollo in the underworld” (Servius on *Georgics* I.17, p. 59; on Virgil’s fifth *Eclogue*, verse 64, p. 27).

From this widespread conviction of the pagans [Col. 0577B], therefore, Arnobius plainly concludes that they diminish the number of the gods, and that there never existed in the nature of things either Liber, born of Semele, as we said above, or Pythian Apollo, the “destruction of mice,” as our same author calls him—a subject we have treated elsewhere (vol. II, *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation, chap. 9, art. 1, p. 754). From the same opinions of the pagans Augustine concludes that they fashioned several gods out of one and the same natural entity, but that these gods were plainly false and fictitious.

Why say more? Men who were not unlearned, as Arnobius says (Arnobius, III, p. 119), taught among the pagans that Diana, Ceres, and the Moon were not three persons distinct from one another, but that the Moon was called by this threefold name. Those learned men were undoubtedly [Col. 0577C] the Stoics, concerning whom Servius relates: “The Stoics call the same being the Sun … likewise they call the Moon the same as Diana, Ceres, Juno, and Proserpina; following them, Virgil invoked Liber and Ceres in place of the Sun and Moon” (Servius on *Georgics* I.7). Macrobius too observed this final point. Augustine, moreover, says: “They declared Apollo to be the Sun, and Diana, his full sister, likewise to be the Moon and the guardian of roads” (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, I.18, p. 266; Augustine, *City of God*, VII.16, p. 174).

But if Diana and Ceres really are that heavenly body called the Moon, Arnobius argues most correctly from this that not only Ceres—the supposed inventor of crops, as we have noted elsewhere [Col. 0577D] (*Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. 15, art. 1)—must be utterly extinguished and entirely abolished, but also Diana, Apollo’s full sister, as Augustine, cited shortly before, observes. For only the heavenly body called the Moon remains, and it cannot be a god. That Diana must also be removed from existence “whom,” as Arnobius says, “the horned hunter once beheld washing the impurities from her limbs in pure springs, and so incurred the penalty for his curiosity” (ibid., p. 120). By these words he plainly alludes to the story of Actaeon, who was said to have been changed into a stag because he had seen Diana bathing. See Ovid, Diodorus Siculus, Pausanias, Natale Conti, and others (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, III, fable 2; Diodorus Siculus, [Col. 0578A] IV, p. 195; Pausanias, IX, p. 283; Natale Conti, *Mythology*, VI.24).

Finally, by another general argument Arnobius strikes down and destroys all the errors of the pagans concerning their gods that we have now mentioned (Arnobius, III, p. 120). For the most learned philosophers, he says, both believed and defined the world to be a rational and intelligent living creature. But someone may ask: Is that really so, and who were those philosophers? Tell us. Nothing is easier to say. For this was not only the genuine opinion of Plato, as is clear from Cicero’s books, but also the constant opinion of Zeno and his Stoic followers, as we learn from Cicero, Lactantius, Laertius, Lipsius, and others (Plato, *Timaeus*, III, p. 0; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, I, p. 199; likewise Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, [Col. 0578B] p. 216 ff., and III, p. 243; Lactantius, II.5, p. 166; Laertius, VII, §142 ff.; Lipsius, Dissertation 10, *On Stoic Physics*, IV, p. 569 ff.).

But if the world is a rational living creature, it necessarily follows that the Sun, Moon, Earth, and other parts of the world—whether called by their own names or by another name, as we have seen—are falsely and pointlessly enrolled by them among the gods. For how can the world, if it is one living creature, like any individual human being, be divided into various parts and different limbs, each of which is itself a living creature distinct from the others and, as they would have it, one individual god? Lactantius argues similarly: “If the world is a god, then all the things within it are not gods, but limbs of a god; and these certainly cannot receive the name belonging to God alone. For no one could correctly say that the limbs of one human being are many human beings.” [Col. 0578C] Indeed, Cicero too completely overturns this error. Read, if you wish, what he—and, if you are so inclined, Eusebius—argued on the subject (Lactantius, II.5, p. 168; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, p. 243; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, III.10, p. 103 ff.).

## CHAPTER XVII. How Arnobius further overturns the vain fictions of pagan beliefs concerning the gods from their other disagreements about those same gods.

## ARTICLE I. Arnobius’ argument, drawn from the pagans’ diverse and contrary opinions concerning the parentage, condition, and number of the Muses, and concerning the Novensilian and Indigete gods, is examined; here also concerning the death of Aeneas.

[Col. 0578D]

The pagans’ great disagreements about one and the same divinity supply our Arnobius with another most evident argument, by which the false divinity of them all is once again most invincibly demonstrated. For what, I ask, do such great dissensions prove except that those same pagans possessed no certain and ascertained knowledge concerning any of their gods? By what right, therefore, could they worship, pray to, and adore them as true gods when they openly professed that they had never received any clear and indubitable information about them? Who, moreover, will not marvel at the magnitude of their divisions, conflicts, and disputes concerning, for example, the parentage, [Col. 0579A] condition, and number of the Muses?

For Mnaseas, as Arnobius says (Arnobius, III, p. 121), related that they sprang from Heaven and Earth; others said from Jupiter and Memory or Mind. Some called them virgins, others mothers. Ephorus numbered them as three, Mnaseas as four, Myrtillus as seven, Crates as eight, and Hesiod as nine, whose names he enumerates one by one. Servius, however, reduces all these divergent opinions chiefly to three: “Many,” he says, “have said that there are nine Muses, many eight, and many seven.” Cicero teaches more explicitly that the first four sprang from the second Jupiter; the second group from the third, or Cretan, Jupiter and Mnemosyne; and the third group from the third Jupiter and Antiope. These last, he says, the poets commonly call the Pierides and Pierian Muses (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, III, p. 247, line 41). But this question [Col. 0579B] is treated far more fully by Lilio Giraldi in a special *Syntagma on the Muses* (Giraldi, *Syntagma on the Muses*, p. 531 ff.). We have already touched upon them elsewhere. Yet you can certainly see how writers of no mean but rather of eminent reputation fought among themselves concerning the number, parentage, and condition of these Muses (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 820). Since, therefore, these and others did not adequately know the Muses, how could they both call them goddesses and invoke them?

No less serious, certainly, was their controversy concerning the Novensilian gods, their designation and number, and consequently their divinity. Some thought that they were so named from the number nine, which, as Varro, cited by Arnobius, related (Arnobius, III, p. 122), was considered most powerful in setting things in motion; [Col. 0579C] others derived the name from the novelty of the things over which they believed them to preside; and others from another kind of newness, namely because they were transported by conquerors—such as the Romans, as we have seen elsewhere (*Dissertation on Minucius*, chap. 16, art. 2)—into their own cities and temples and were dedicated with a new consecration. But Vossius and others discuss the etymology of this name at greater length (Vossius, *Etymologies*, s.v. *NOVEM*).

Arnobius presented various supporters of these widely divergent opinions. First was Piso, who “believes,” as Arnobius says, “that they are nine, established among the Sabines near the Trebia” (Arnobius, loc. cit.). The Trebia is a river not far from Placentia, which, as Strabo wrote, flows from the Apennines into the Po. At this river, moreover, Hannibal inflicted a devastating defeat upon the consul Scipio, as Polybius relates (Strabo, *Geography*, V, [Col. 0579D] p. 217; Polybius, *Histories*, III, p. 220 ff.). Hence these verses of Lucan (Lucan, II.48 ff.):

> O youth of wretched destiny, that we were not born  
> In the Punic age of Cannae and the Trebia!

Concerning the Novensilian gods, Varro, cited by our author, wrote these very brief words: “Feronia, Minerva, and the Novensiles came from the Sabines” (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, IV, p. 16; Arnobius, loc. cit., p. 122). Aelius, following Granius, believed them to be the Muses; Cornificius regarded them as the guardians of novelties. Cincius held that all gods customarily transported by conquerors, as we noted shortly before, into their own cities were invoked under this name Novensiles for the sake of brevity and to prevent any of them from being omitted. [Col. 0580A] When Decius devoted himself for the Roman legions, according to Livy’s testimony he invoked and adjured them together with many others as follows: “Divine Novensiles, Indigete gods, divine powers whose dominion extends over our people and the enemy” (Livy, VIII.9).

Arnobius also cites Manilius (Arnobius, loc. cit.), who, like Piso, believed these gods to be nine, but held that Jupiter had granted to them alone the power to cast his thunderbolt. Finally, some believed that they were human beings who had been made gods, such as, Arnobius says, Hercules, Romulus, Aesculapius, Liber, and Aeneas. This is confirmed by the following words of Servius: “The ancients indeed call those gods Novensiles upon whom the merits of their virtue conferred the dignity of divinity” (Servius on *Aeneid* VIII.187, [Col. 0580B] p. 498).

As regards Romulus, Aesculapius, and Liber, whom our author mentions there, we have discussed them above. Concerning that undoubtedly distinguished god Hercules, Cicero handed down the following: “As for those whom you say passed from humanity to the gods, you will explain how this could have happened or why it ceased to happen, and I shall gladly learn. As matters now stand, I do not see how he—Hercules, that is—reached his father’s eternal home” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, III, p. 245, line 38). But we discussed him above, together with his disastrous death, so utterly unworthy of a god (above, chap. 12, art. 2).

There remains the fifth figure named by Arnobius, Aeneas, whom Augustine testifies to have reigned in Latium for three years. [Col. 0580C] But when he later fell in battle, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Livy, an anonymous author, and Servius relate, and his body was not found, they proclaimed that he had departed to the gods. They built him a temple as a god upon the banks of the River Numicus, where he had been killed in battle, with this inscription: “To the Father God Indiges, who governs the waters of the River Numicus” (Augustine, *City of God*, XVIII.19 and 21, pp. 502–503; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, I, p. 52; Livy, *History*, I, beginning; anonymous author, *On the Origin of the Roman People*, p. 598; Servius on *Aeneid* XII, p. 702). For this reason Tibullus sang:

> Tireless Aeneas, brother of winged Love,  
> Who carries the Trojan sacred things in ships of exile,  
>   
> [Col. 0580D] Jupiter now assigns to you the fields of Laurentum;  
> The hospitable land now summons your wandering household gods.  
>   
> There you will be holy, when Numicus’ venerable wave  
> Has sent you to heaven as the god Indiges.

(Tibullus, II, Elegy 5.)

Ovid sings in accord with Tibullus, likewise celebrating the same Aeneas in verse:

> His mother purified his body and anointed it with divine perfume;  
> With ambrosia mixed with sweet nectar  
> She touched his mouth and made him a god. The people of Quirinus  
> Call him Indiges, and received him with temple and altars.

(Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, XIV, §13.)

But there Aeneas is placed by Tibullus and Ovid—as by Virgil (*Aeneid* XII.794) and the other writers already cited by us—not among the Novensilian gods, but among the Indigetes. [Col. 0581A] Arnobius himself certainly agreed with them elsewhere, where he ridicules the same Aeneas—although suppressing his name—and the other gods as follows: “Those Indigetes who crawl along the river and dwell in the channels of the Numicus with branches and little fish” (Arnobius, I, p. 20).

There seems, moreover, to be no doubt that those Indigetes were none other than the Novensilian gods. For, as Servius says, “The Indigetes are properly gods made from human beings, as though dwelling among the gods” (Servius on *Georgics* I, p. 94). Such were the Novensiles whom we have discussed. Servius adds: “By an extended usage, all gods may generally be called Indigetes, as though lacking nothing” (Servius on *Aeneid* XII, p. 702). But he explains these matters more fully elsewhere. Macrobius also confirms Servius’ former explanation by the authority of Hesiod: [Col. 0581B] “Hesiod,” he says (Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, I.8, p. 52), “an advocate of divine lineage, numbers the ancient kings among the gods; and, after the pattern of their ancient power, he assigns them even in heaven the office of governing human affairs. And lest anyone find it tedious if we insert the verses themselves as the Greek poet produced them, we shall repeat them as they have been translated from his words into Latin:

> These are the divine Indigetes by decree of highest Jupiter,  
> Once human beings, but now among the gods above, watching over human affairs,  
> Generous and bountiful, and still possessing the authority of kings.”

Our Arnobius, however, asserts that they were infamous for cruelty, sexual outrages, adulteries, sacrileges, and murders (Arnobius, II, p. 39). See Giraldi, Vossius, Lescalopier, and others (Giraldi, *Syntagma* I, p. 15; Vossius, *Etymologies*; Lescalopier on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, I, [Col. 0581C] §62). Who, therefore, could tolerate gods of this sort made by human beings, when neither their parents, their origin, nor their number had been ascertained? Is it within human power to confer divinity upon others?

## ARTICLE II. How varied were the pagans’ opinions concerning the Penates, Penetrales, Consentes, and Complices, and how their divinity is thereby overturned.

Source/review notes: The supplied Latin contains apparent textual corruptions or internal contradictions.
