In particular, “quod eorum nomina nemo nesciat” literally says that no one is ignorant of the Penates’ names, although the ensuing prose claims that Servius said their names were known to no one; “Servius non admonet” is likewise negative despite the surrounding argument treating it as affirmative.; The phrase “quidam aliorum testimonio fuiti” appears corrupt; the draft reasonably interprets it as though the text read “freti” (“relying on the testimony of others”).; The source cites the magical verses as Virgil, Eclogue 3, although they are conventionally located in Eclogue 8. Faithful translation requires preserving the supplied citation rather than silently correcting it.

If we proceed with our author to the Penates gods (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 123), we shall encounter no less quarrelling and controversy among the pagans concerning them. For he shows us that Nigidius’s opinion about them was altogether frivolous and inconsistent. He first maintained that the Penates were the gods Neptune and Apollo, who, under the terms of an agreement, built the walls of Troy, as we have seen elsewhere (above, [Col. 0581D] ch. 4, art. 1). Macrobius, however, asserts that this was the opinion not only of Nigidius but also of Cornelius Labeo and Virgil. For when discussing the Penates—or, as he calls them, the gods peculiar to the Romans—he writes:

> Nigidius, in the nineteenth book of his work *On the Gods*, asks whether the Penates are Apollo and Neptune of the Trojans, who are said to have built their walls for them, and whether Aeneas brought them into Italy. Cornelius Labeo, too, in his book *On Those Penates*, holds the same opinion. Maro follows this opinion when he says:
>
> Thus having spoken, at the altars he slaughtered the honors they deserved:
>
> A bull for Neptune, and a bull for you, beautiful Apollo.
>
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. III, v. 118.)

Servius likewise makes the following observation on these verses: [Col. 0582A]

> Certainly in this passage Virgil, following the opinion of the ancients, named only Neptune and Apollo. For these are said to have been the Penates whom Aeneas brought with him, although in various passages the poet, following other opinions held by other men, said different things about the Penates.

(Servius, p. 272.) See the same Servius discussing many other matters elsewhere concerning these same Penates (ibid., on bk. I, v. 384; and on bk. III, vv. 148 and 168).

Nigidius’s second opinion concerning these gods—which our author called inexplicable—was that there were four classes of Penates: some belonging to Jupiter, others to Neptune, others to the underworld, and the last to mortal men. However obscure this opinion of Nigidius may appear to Arnobius, let us nevertheless see [Col. 0582B] whether some light can be shed upon it. These are the verses of Virgil concerning the Penates that were cited shortly before:

> An exile, I am borne out upon the deep
>
> With my companions, my son, the Penates, and the great gods.
>
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, bk. III, v. 12.)

But let us attend for a moment, if you please, to what Servius observes concerning these verses:

> Some think that the “great gods” are Heaven and Earth, and thereby Jupiter and Juno. The Penates gods, taken by Aeneas from Samothrace, were brought into Italy; hence the Samothracians are said to be kindred to the Romans. Among other reasons, they call them “great” because, after they had been transferred from Lavinium to Rome, they twice returned to their own place; because emperors intending to depart for the provinces first offered sacrifice before them; because no one is ignorant of their names; [Col. 0582C] and because their presence is perceived. . . . They hold them in extraordinary veneration. No one except the priest was permitted to see them. They are therefore called Penates because they sit in the innermost chambers (*penetralia*) of the heavenly dwelling; for the inner chamber (*penetral*) itself is also called *penus*. . . . Varro calls them the Penates and the great gods. For upon their pedestal, too, was written: “TO THE GREAT GODS.” This may, however, also have been said as a mark of honor. For Jupiter, Juno, Minerva, and Mercury, who were worshipped at Rome, are also great gods; but the Penates were worshipped at Laurentum-Lavinium, from which it is apparent that they are not one and the same.

Although rather lengthy, we have transcribed this entire passage because it makes clear how greatly pagan writers differed concerning the Penates. Moreover, certain things reported by Arnobius are expressly affirmed here. The more common opinion, however—endorsed not only by Varro [Col. 0582D] but also by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Augustine, and others—was that the Penates were those gods whom Aeneas brought with him into Italy (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. IV, p. 35; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, bk. I, p. 54; Augustine, *City of God*, bk. X, ch. 16, p. 252). Dionysius further adds that Greeks who rendered the Latin word into Greek called these gods Πατρῴους (*Patrōous*, “ancestral”) according to some, γενεθλίους (*genethlious*, “gods of birth or lineage”) according to others, κτησίους (*ktēsious*, “gods of possessions”) according to some, and μυχίους (*mychious*, “gods of the inner recess”) or ἑρκίους (*herkious*, “gods of the enclosure”) according to others. Cassius Hemina, moreover, as quoted by Macrobius, states that these same Penates of the Romans were properly called θεοὺς μεγάλους (*theous megalous*, “great gods”), θεοὺς χρηστοὺς (*theous chrēstous*, “good gods”), and θεοὺς δυνατούς (*theous dynatous*, “mighty gods”) (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, bk. III, ch. 4, p. 321).

Who, from what has been said, cannot readily understand why Nigidius, [Col. 0583A] as cited by Arnobius (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 123), thought that Jupiter or Neptune was one of the Penates? For who does not see that Servius calls these “great gods”? Nor should anyone find it surprising that Nigidius adds that there are other Penates of the underworld and of mortal men, although this cannot be demonstrated quite so clearly. For Servius openly declares that the names of the Penates were not fully known to anyone. And indeed, who could have known the names and number of the gods whom Aeneas brought with him? To this may be added that, according to the testimony of Servius himself, no one except a priest was permitted to see them. They could therefore have been known to only a few.

Servius then does not inform us that they are called Penetrales because they sit in the innermost chambers of heaven. Cicero expresses the following opinion concerning this etymology:

> Nor are [Col. 0583B] the Penates gods far removed from this power, whether their name is derived from *penus*—for everything that human beings make use of is *penus*—or from the fact that they dwell deep within (*penitus insident*), whence they are also called Penetrales by the poets.

(Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. II, p. 224, line 15.) What could be more suitable and appropriate than these words for explaining and confirming what our author afterward reported?

> Varro believes that the gods of whom we are speaking are those who dwell within and in the deepest inner chambers of heaven; neither their number nor their names are known.

(Arnobius, bk. III, p. 123.)

In addition to these, Arnobius writes that there were some who thought Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva to be the Penates, without whom we can neither live nor breathe, since they govern us by reason, heat, and breath [Col. 0583C] (ibid.). In defense of this opinion, one may appropriately cite the following statement preserved by Macrobius:

> Those who investigate the truth more carefully have said that the Penates are those through whom we breathe inwardly, through whom we possess a body, and through whom we possess reason.

(Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, bk. III, ch. 4, p. 321.)

Caesius, however, cited afterward by our author, appears to disagree utterly and completely with those writers (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 123). For he held that the Penates were Fortune, Ceres, the Jovial Genius, and a certain Pales, Jupiter’s minister and steward. We have discussed Pales above. But what is surprising if, since the Penates and their names were known to no one, as we have said (above, ch. 14, art. 2), certain men, relying upon the testimony of others, [Col. 0583D] attempted somehow to identify them, or fabricated them according to their fancy?

Finally, Arnobius teaches that the Penates were called Consentes and Complices by the Etruscans (ibid.), and that there were six males and as many females, though their names were unknown; nevertheless, they were Jupiter’s counsellors, and they both arose and fell together. Augustine afterward says:

> They say that the Consentes gods are summoned to Jupiter’s council.

(Augustine, *City of God*, bk. IV, ch. 32, p. 104.) Varro, at the beginning of his work *On Agriculture*, invokes these and other gods as follows:

> And since, as they say, the gods who bring things about assist us, I shall invoke them first—not the Muses, as Homer and Ennius do, but the twelve Consentes gods; and not, indeed, those urban gods [Col. 0584A] whose gilded images stand at the Forum, six male and six female, but those twelve gods who are especially the guides of farmers.

(Varro, *On Agriculture*, bk. I, ch. 1.)

He calls each of these individually by name: Jupiter, Tellus, the Sun, the Moon, Ceres, Liber, Robigus, Flora, Minerva, Venus, Lympha, and Bonus Eventus. From this list of names alone, however, it is easy to conclude that Arnobius was speaking of the former rather than the latter. Those first Consentes gods are also called by some the gods of the greater nations; their names are expressed in these two verses of Ennius:

> Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars,
>
> Mercury, Jupiter, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo.

See Giraldi and Vossius, who made numerous observations concerning the Consentes gods [Col. 0584B] (Giraldi, *Syntagma* 7, ch. 18; Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, bk. I, chs. 14 and 17).

But, you will say, why did Arnobius state that these were called not only Consentes but also Complices? Does Heraldus not rightly suspect that this latter name is a superfluous gloss by which some ignorant person sought to explain the earlier word *Consentes*? Yet Heraldus himself added that Arnobius could have employed the name *Complices* to signify that these gods, who arise and perish together, are joined and bound together by the closest ties. Quite so. For Arnobius indicates clearly enough that this very fact was the reason why these gods were surnamed Complices by the Etruscans. Ambrose uses the word in this sense when he writes:

> Advantage is always intertwined (*complex*) with honorableness, [Col. 0584C] and honorableness with advantage.

(Ambrose, *On the Duties of Ministers*, bk. III, ch. 14, p. 130.) Should these considerations not therefore have sufficed to induce Heraldus to abandon his suspicion that our author’s text was corrupt?

For the rest, we suppose that no one is so slow-witted as not readily to perceive by now what must be concluded from the pagans’ many different and contradictory opinions concerning these gods. For who does not see that one completely overturns another? Moreover, even if one of them contained some truth, no one would ever be able to discover it. No one, therefore, will judge those Consentes and Penates gods worthy of divine honors, since all were compelled frankly to admit that they had no certain knowledge of what those gods were like, how they could render assistance to mortals, or what true [Col. 0584D] divinity—which can only be one—existed in them.

## ARTICLE III. How Great the Disagreement of the Pagans Was Concerning the Lares; Why They Were Called Grundules, and Why Summanus Was Set over Them; and How Evidently It Is Demonstrated That Neither These Nor the Other Gods Mentioned Above Possess Any Divinity

The pagans were no more in agreement concerning the Lares than they were concerning their other gods. The common opinion, as Arnobius says (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 124), was that they were the gods of streets and journeys, because a street is called λαύρα (*laura*) in Greek. Casaubon and many others have sufficiently confirmed this meaning of the Greek word (Casaubon on bk. XII; Athenaeus, ch. 10). Vossius, however, suspects that the name *Lares* was derived from the Etruscan word *Lar*. [Col. 0585A] Be that as it may, it is certainly established that in the common opinion of the pagans they were regarded as gods of streets. For concerning Lara, the mother of the Lares, we read in Ovid’s celebrated account that, when she was being led to the shades at Jupiter’s command, her own guide violated her after she had been rendered mute and speechless, and that thereafter:

> She becomes pregnant and gives birth to twins, the Lares,
>
> Who guard the crossroads and keep constant watch within our house.
>
> (Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. II, v. 703.)

Tibullus likewise asserts that they were guardians of the fields:

> You too, guardians of an estate once prosperous, now poor,
>
> Receive the offerings that are yours, O Lares.
>
> (Tibullus, bk. I, elegy 1, v. 23 ff.)

Yet, according to our author, Nigidius displayed great variability and inconsistency concerning those [Col. 0585B] gods. For he first asserted that they were the guardians of roofs and houses. We have seen this expressed by Ovid; Tibullus, too, accords with him in the following words:

> But preserve me, Lares of my fathers, you who likewise reared me
>
> When, still a tender child, I ran before your feet.
>
> And be not ashamed that you were fashioned from an ancient stump:
>
> Thus you have inhabited the dwelling of my forefather of old.
>
> (Ibid., elegy 11, v. 15 ff.)

Then the same Nigidius, as Arnobius relates (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 124), said that they were the Curetes who concealed the child Jupiter. Finally, he at one time reported that these same Lares were identical with the Idaean Samothracians, or Idaean Dactyls, whom we have discussed elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, bk. III, diss. 2, ch. 19, art. 2, p. 1163 ff.). But if Arnobius’s account is true, [Col. 0585C] we may conclude from it that Nigidius was one of those who distinguished the Curetes from the Idaean Dactyls, and that he did not know who the Lares were.

Varro’s uncertainty was similar. For our author informs us that Varro wrote somewhere that they were the Manes, and that for this reason their mother was Mania. Indeed, in one of his books we read the following in Varro’s own words:

> We see that Mania, the mother of the Lares, and Lucia Volumnia are named in the songs of the Salii.

(Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. VIII, p. 126.) Nor was this opinion his alone, but also that of Caecina, from whom Macrobius reports the following:

> For some time the practice was observed that boys should be sacrificed to the goddess Mania, mother of the Lares, for the safety of households or families.

(Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, bk. I, ch. 7, p. 207.) He indicates, however, that this sacrifice was afterward [Col. 0585D] changed into another.

But since this opinion did not entirely please Varro himself, elsewhere he defined the Lares as aerial gods and heroes; in another place, however, he followed the opinion of the ancients and pronounced them to have been Larvae—that is, certain spirits and souls of the dead. From Augustine we learn that Plotinus, who is said to have understood Plato more excellently than others, taught that demons are the souls of human beings, and that from these same human beings Lares arise if they have deserved well, Lemures if they have deserved badly, and Manes if it is uncertain what they have deserved (Augustine, *City of God*, bk. IX, ch. 10, p. 226).

Apuleius likewise, when discussing the god of Socrates and the various kinds of demons (Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*, p. [Col. 0586A] 295 ff.), clearly explains that certain men believed that the human soul after death was commonly called a Lemur in the old Latin language; that among the Lemures, the one who, as a peaceful and kindly divinity—doubtless because of the merits of his former life—possesses a house is called a household Lar; that one who lived badly is called a Larva; and that if his merits are doubtful, he is named a god of the Manes.

We have more than once discussed the error by which men asserted that demons were the souls of dead human beings. Concerning the Lares, however, one may consult Lilio Giraldi, Salmasius, Natale Conti, and Vossius, and concerning the Manes, Servius (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 537 and 993; Giraldi, *History of the Gods*, *Syntagma* 15, p. 480 ff.; Salmasius on Solinus, pp. 64, 412, and 913; Natale [Col. 0586B] Conti, *Mythology*, bk. IV, chs. 2 and 4; Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, bk. I, ch. 11, p. 43 ff.; Servius on *Aeneid* III, p. 166).

But what, someone will ask, does Arnobius mean when he reproaches the pagans for worshipping the Grundule Lares (the Royal manuscript reads *Grunulios*)? He should remember that many have already observed that the Lares were surnamed Grundules from the ancient verb *grundio*, later *grunnio*, “to grunt,” and that a shrine was built for them in memory of a sow that had given birth to thirty piglets. They establish this on the authority of Diomedes, who cited Cassius Hemina in confirmation of his opinion (Arnobius, bk. I, p. 15; Diomedes, *On the Doubtful Meaning of Words*, bk. II; Hemina, *Histories*, bk. II). See Vossius’s *Etymologicon* under the words *grunnio* and *suggrunda*.

[Col. 0586C] But why, another will ask, did our author insert a mention of the god Summanus among these gods? The answer is easy and obvious. For Summanus was regarded as the supreme king of the Manes. Accordingly, Arnobius himself, when later discussing Proserpina’s abduction by Pluto, says: “The king of the Manes, springing forth, carries away the abducted maiden with him.” Elsewhere Arnobius mentions his temple, and Cicero his earthenware image. Pliny, moreover, teaches that nocturnal thunderbolts were attributed to him:

> The writings of the Etruscans hold that nine gods send thunderbolts. . . . The Romans retained only two of these, assigning the thunderbolts of the day to Jupiter and those of the night to Summanus.

For this reason the pagans once paid greater honors to Summanus than to Jupiter, as Augustine attests. He relates, however, that these honors were afterward so diminished that scarcely anyone could any longer be found who remembered having read [Col. 0586D] the name of Summanus. Nevertheless, the pagans considered him a god, as Varro attests. But who, from this and from everything discussed throughout this chapter, cannot very readily understand that the pagans possessed no certain and established knowledge concerning the Lares, Penates, Novensiles, and other gods? Who, therefore, will deny that they were altogether false and fictitious? (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 125; Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. IV, pp. 18 and 19; Arnobius, bk. V, pp. 173 and 183; bk. VI, p. 191; Cicero, *On Divination*, bk. I, p. 257, line 41; Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. II, ch. 52, p. 206; Augustine, *City of God*, bk. IV, ch. 23, p. 105.)

But Arnobius presses the matter and argues [Col. 0587A] in the following manner (Arnobius, bk. III, p. 125). Whoever makes supplication to a god, implores his aid, or expressly asks to be relieved by him of some illness, must first know who that god is and whether the things he requests can be obtained from him or from another. It must be no less clear to him in what words the god is to be addressed and by what rite sacrifice is to be offered. But since opinions concerning a single god exhibit such great variation and contradiction, no one can ever know this. Thus a person laboring under this ignorance will rashly invoke some god, often mistaking one for another—Summanus for Janus, Neptune for Apollo, or the Curetes or Penates for the Lares. So far, therefore, will he be from obtaining through sacrifices and prayers the things he asks of that god that he will find the god’s ears blocked and stopped [Col. 0587B], or incur his displeasure and hatred.

## ARTICLE IV. Another Argument of Arnobius Against the Gods of the Nations Is Considered, Drawn from the Multiplication of the Number of These Same Gods—Namely, Three Jupiters, Five Suns, the Same Number of Mercuries and Minervas, Four Vulcans, Three Dianas and Aesculapiuses, Six Herculeses, and Three Classes Each of Castors and Muses

Arnobius further proves with the greatest clarity how false the gods of the pagans were, from the multiplication of one and the same god, undertaken not only by certain ignorant men but also by their ancient and more learned theologians. But I would have you hear how Arnobius demonstrates this by examples not merely of the lesser gods, but also of those whom the pagans vaunted as greater gods. He writes:

> Your theologians [Col. 0587C] and the founders of the lore of hidden antiquity say that there are three Jupiters in the natural world: one of them was begotten by Aether as father, another by Heaven, while the third was begotten by Saturn and committed to burial on the island of Crete.

(Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 133.) That this was taken from Cicero is sufficiently proved by these very words of the Latin Orator:

> To begin with, those who are called theologians enumerate three Jupiters. Of these, the first and second were born in Arcadia, the one having Aether as his father . . . the other having Heaven as his father . . . while the third was the Cretan, the son of Saturn, whose tomb is shown on that island.

(Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. III, p. 247, line 34.) That these were fictions of the ancient Greeks can readily be inferred from Cicero’s preceding words:

> For in the ancient writings of the Greeks [Col. 0587D], he says, we also find several Jupiters.

(Ibid., p. 245, line 45.) We have discussed these and still other Jupiters elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 752).

Arnobius next objects that the same pagans produced five Suns:

> The first, he says, is called the son of Jupiter and is held to be the grandson of Aether; the second likewise the son of Jupiter, with Hyperion given as his mother; the third was born to Vulcan—not the Lemnian Vulcan, but the one who was the son of the Nile; the fourth was the father of Ialysus, whom Acantho bore on Rhodes in the heroic age; the fifth is held to be the son of a Scythian king and of the shape-shifting Circe.

(Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 135.) These statements, too, were drawn from Cicero, who had said earlier:

> How many Suns are themselves brought forward by the theologians! One of them was born of Jupiter and was the grandson of Aether; [Col. 0588A] another was born of Hyperion; the third of Vulcan, the son of the Nile. . . . The fourth is he whom Acantho is said to have borne on Rhodes in the heroic age, and who was the grandfather of Ialysus, Camirus, and Lindus; the fifth is he who is said to have begotten Aeëtes and Circe in Colchis.

(Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. III, p. 247, line 45.)

Nor should one object that Arnobius here varied slightly from Cicero, since Arnobius said that the second Sun was born of Jupiter and Hyperion, whereas Cicero says only that he was born of Hyperion. For although one might reply that Arnobius perhaps read the name of Jupiter in Cicero’s text, this very slight discrepancy—whereby Cicero names only the mother of Apollo, while Arnobius names both father and mother—will persuade no one that Arnobius did not excerpt this passage from Cicero.

You will insist that Arnobius calls the fourth Sun the father of Ialysus, [Col. 0588B] whereas Cicero calls him his grandfather. But can the word “father” never signify a grandfather? Finally, as to the fifth Sun being called by Cicero the father of Aeëtes and Circe, and by Arnobius the son of a Scythian king and Circe, the two disagree only verbally. For what prevents us from understanding by “Scythian king” Aeëtes, king of the Colchians, who were once reckoned among the Scythians?

No one, however, will ever call into doubt that what Arnobius next says concerning the five Mercuries was extracted from the same Cicero. The mere reproduction of the wording makes this most evident to everyone. These are Arnobius’s words:

> The first Mercury, who is said to have neighed lustfully at Proserpina with his genitals erect, is the offspring of highest Heaven. The second is beneath the earth and is vaunted as being Trophonius. The third was begotten of Maia as mother and the third Jupiter. [Col. 0588C] The fourth is the offspring of the Nile, whose name the Egyptian nation shrinks from and reveres too greatly to utter. The fifth is the slayer of Argus, a fugitive and exile, and the transmitter of letters among the Egyptians.

(Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 135.) Cicero, however, speaks as follows:

> One Mercury was born of Heaven as father and Day as mother; his sexual organ is traditionally said to have been indecently aroused because he was excited at the sight of Proserpina. Another was the son of Valens and Phronoris; he is held to dwell beneath the earth and is identical with Trophonius. The third was born of the third Jupiter and Maia. . . . The fourth had the Nile as his father, and the Egyptians hold it unlawful to name him. The fifth, whom the Pheneatae worship, is said to have slain Argus and for that reason to have ruled Egypt and given laws and letters to the Egyptians.

(Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. III, p. 248, line 4.) You see [Col. 0588D] that these statements were undoubtedly taken by our author, who rendered them in his own words—more briefly, indeed, but less elegantly.

He continues and lists as follows the five Minervas likewise asserted by the pagans:

> The first was not a virgin, but by Vulcan became the mother of Apollo. The second was the offspring of the Nile and is said to be Egyptian. The third was of the stock of Saturn and devised the use of weapons. The fourth was the offspring of Jupiter, whom the Messenians call Coryphasia. The fifth was she who killed her father Pallas when he sought an incestuous union with her.

(Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 135.) Cicero, however, writes:

> The first Minerva is she whom we said above to be the mother of Apollo. The second arose from the Nile and is worshipped by the Egyptian Saites. The third is she whom we said above to have been begotten [Col. 0589A] by Jupiter. The fourth was born of Jupiter and Coryphe, daughter of Ocean; the Arcadians call her Coria [variant: Coryphasia] and hold her to have invented four-horse chariots. The fifth was the daughter of Pallas and is said to have killed her father when he attempted to violate her virginity; to her they attach winged sandals.

(Cicero, loc. cit., line 31.)

Clement of Alexandria likewise enumerates the same number of Minervas (*Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 17), so that our author appears to resemble him no less closely than Cicero:

> There are some who posit five Athenas: the first the daughter of Hephaestus, the Athenian; the second, daughter of the Nile, the Egyptian; the third, daughter of Cronus, the inventor of war; the fourth, daughter of Zeus, whom the Messenians surnamed Coryphasia after her mother; and, last of all, the daughter of Pallas and Titanis, daughter of Ocean, who, after impiously sacrificing her father, [Col. 0589B] was adorned with her father’s skin as though with a fleece.

“Some also invent five Minervas: one, indeed, the daughter of Vulcan, the Athenian; another, the daughter of the Nile”—[concerning whom Plato is afterward cited by Arnobius himself (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 137; Plato, *Timaeus*, vol. III, p. 21)]—“the Egyptian; the third, daughter of Saturn, the inventor of war; the fourth, daughter of Jupiter, whom the Messenians surnamed Coryphasia after her mother; the last, daughter of Pallas and Titanis, daughter of Ocean, who, after impiously sacrificing her own father, was adorned with her father’s skin as though with a fleece.”

We have quoted the passages of both Cicero and Clement of Alexandria in full because they shed light upon one another and upon Arnobius. Thus anyone may more readily judge whether Arnobius himself had one rather than the other in view, or both, or borrowed something from one and something else from the other. [Col. 0589C]

Furthermore, although Arnobius agrees with both Cicero and Clement of Alexandria in asserting that Minerva Coryphasia’s name was formed from that of her mother, Coryphe (Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 137), he afterward nevertheless warns us that it could also have been derived from the fact that she was said to have issued armed from the crown of Jupiter’s head. Perhaps this was not altogether without reason. For some have observed that the Greek word κορυφή (*koryphē*) signifies the crown, the highest middle part of the head between the forehead and the back of the skull. Yet there are some who maintain that she was so named from Mount Coryphasium.

Arnobius similarly excerpted from Cicero what he related about the other gods, though in fewer words. For, weary of recounting at greater length so many foolish pagan fables concerning them, [Col. 0589D] he briefly passes over the rest as follows:

> The same theologians say that there are four Vulcans, three Dianas, as many Aesculapiuses, five Dionysuses, six Herculeses, four Venuses, three classes of Castors, and the same number of Muses; teams of three winged Cupids, and fourfold sets bearing the name of Apollo.

(Arnobius, bk. IV, p. 136.) Cicero, however, enumerates all these individually, as he did the earlier gods. In him, therefore, you will find both an exposition and a demonstration concerning all of them. We have touched upon some of these elsewhere (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. III, pp. 245, 247, and 248; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 851).

Cotta, under whose name Cicero explains all these matters, concludes without hesitation that the traditions collected from ancient Greece [Col. 0590A] must be resisted altogether, lest religion be thrown into confusion. But our Arnobius clearly shows precisely how religion is completely confounded by them. For if, he says, there are several gods bearing the same name but distinct from one another, human religion will hesitate in confusion, since people will be unable to know to which one they should direct their vows and prayers. What, moreover, if some sacrifice is offered to Minerva, Jupiter, or another god? Will not each of them think that it was offered to himself alone? If one contends against another that it was made for him, will he not immediately quarrel with him, so that the two fight one another?

Arnobius does not permit anyone to answer him that it is unknown whether the pagan theologians wrote things certain and established, or things fictitious and false according to their fancy. It is quite enough for us, he says, to have shown that they speak about [Col. 0590B] public and commonly known matters, each of which discloses itself and is manifest to everyone. If, however, these theologians lied, the pagans must demonstrate from what source they learned anything certain about their gods. Yet how will they demonstrate this except from the writings of those same theologians of theirs, from whom they learned what was ordained or done in ancient times concerning the gods and divine matters? Finally, if the books of the theologians, pontiffs, or philosophers teem with lies and fables, they must be rejected entirely and utterly abolished, and all their religions exterminated.

# CHAPTER XVIII. How Clearly Arnobius, from the Serious and Weighty Histories of the Pagans Whose Memory Was Celebrated on Annual Festivals, Destroys Their Absurd Errors Concerning the Gods

[Col. 0590C]

## ARTICLE I. An Examination of the First History, in Which Numa Pompilius Was Said to Have Learned the Expiation of Thunderbolts from Jupiter, Who Had Been Summoned by the Arts of Faunus and Picus; and of Another History Concerning Cybele, Agdestis, and Attis, Celebrated on Annual Festivals; Including the Stupor and Madness of the Abderites

Arnobius most plainly demonstrates by another argument how false and superstitious the religion of the pagans was (Arnobius, bk. V, p. 154). He draws this argument from their serious and weighty histories, which they were so thoroughly persuaded to be true that they celebrated them in annual festivals as matters confirmed by daily practice and represented them through various images.

Arnobius therefore excerpted the first history from the second book of Antias, [Col. 0590D] that is, from the second book of his *Annals*. There Antias related that Numa, in order to be instructed in the knowledge of expiating thunderbolts, followed Egeria’s counsel and had the rustic gods Faunus and Picus—when they had come to a certain spring to quench their thirst—made drunk by cunningly and artfully giving them wine, and that after they had fallen asleep they were bound by twelve young men whom Numa himself had placed in ambush. He refused to have them released until they had extorted from Jupiter—summoned down to earth and deceived by various verbal evasions—the method of averting or expiating thunderbolts that King Numa wished to know. For to “attend to” (*procurare*) a thunderbolt is the same as to expiate it by that solemn rite and sacrifice through which it was believed that the thunderbolt could be warded off and removed. Hence Seneca says:

> They believe that thunderbolts must be expiated, [Col. 0591A] and they do not doubt that expiations are sometimes effective in removing dangers, sometimes in mitigating them, and sometimes in postponing them.

(Seneca, *Natural Questions*, bk. II, ch. 36, p. 422.)

This history was described not only by Antias but also by Ovid and Plutarch—the latter more briefly, the former at greater length. Livy, however, transmitted the following in writing concerning Numa:

> And concerning which prodigies sent by thunderbolts or by any other visible sign were to be undertaken and expiated: to elicit this knowledge from the divine mind, he dedicated an altar to Jupiter Elicius on the Aventine.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. III, § 3, p. 529 ff.; Plutarch, *Life of Numa*, vol. II, p. 70; Livy, bk. I, ch. 20.)

Arnobius, however, proves that this history is credible to no one [Col. 0591B] by various forceful arguments, as Plutarch also admits (Plutarch, loc. cit.). For who, he asks, could ever be persuaded that Faunus and Picus came to a spring to quench their thirst; that wine was given them there in place of water, so that they became drunk and were overcome by sleep; that bonds were then cast upon them; and that the expiation of thunderbolts could have been learned from no one except Jupiter? Nor will anyone be more readily persuaded that this same Jupiter was summoned by incantations to furnish remedies against his own thunderbolt; that he conversed with petty mortals on a *verricula*, as Arnobius calls it, or small *verruca*—that is, on a raised and rugged place, as Gellius teaches from Cato—and that he was deceived by their ambiguous words (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, bk. III, ch. 8, p. 224). Finally, it surpasses all belief that Jupiter, as they said, wished a thunderbolt to be expiated by the cruel sacrifice of a human head, which we discussed above (above, [Col. 0591C] ch. 4, art. 1).

Arnobius further notes that the incantation was performed with spurious sacrificial meal, incense, blood, the fumigation of sacred herbs, and the muttering of dreadful—that is, magical—words. You will see some of these things expressed in the following verses of Virgil:

> Bring water, and bind these altars with a soft fillet;
>
> Burn rich sacred herbs and male frankincense,
>
> So that by magical rites I may attempt to turn aside
>
> My spouse’s sound understanding; nothing is lacking here but spells.
>
> (Virgil, *Eclogue* 3, v. 64 ff.)

We have already made some observations elsewhere concerning magical deceptions and arts (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1239). Augustine nevertheless relates that Numa practiced hydromancy and cites Varro as his witness. According to Varro, Numa was said to have taken the nymph Egeria as his wife because he had drawn out or carried away the water from which he practiced hydromancy [Col. 0591D] (Augustine, *City of God*, bk. VII, ch. 35, p. 188). Valerius Maximus, Florus, Aurelius Victor, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and others report that he pretended to perform all his sacred rites at the admonition and counsel of his wife, the nymph Egeria (Valerius Maximus, ch. 2, § 1; Florus, bk. I, ch. 2; Aurelius Victor, *On Illustrious Roman Men*, ch. 2; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, bk. II, p. 122). But we shall discuss these matters in the following dissertation (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 30, art. 2).

For the rest, you see with what powerful arguments Arnobius demonstrates the foolishness with which the pagans celebrated at annual festivals events that bore no appearance of truth whatsoever. But if they believed them to be true, they utterly disgraced their own supreme and omnipotent Jupiter. [Col. 0592A] For they openly acknowledged that he had been summoned by magical spells, compelled to yield to them, and forced to teach the expiation of thunderbolts.

The second history—that of the Great Mother of the gods, or Cybele, and Attis—is then taken up by Arnobius, to the eternal glory of the pagans (Arnobius, book V, p. 157 ff.). He says that he drew it from its very origins out of Timotheus, a theologian of no mean reputation, as well as from other recondite books of antiquities and the innermost mysteries; and he describes it as follows. Within the borders of Phrygia there was a rock of unheard-of size, to which the inhabitants of that region gave the name Agdus. From it were taken the stones which Deucalion and Pyrrha cast at the command of Themis, and from which the Great Mother, together with the rest of humankind, was brought forth. [Col. 0592B] Jupiter was afterward seized with love for her; but when he was unable to obtain what he desired, he discharged his lust upon the rock, from which, in the tenth month thereafter, a boy was born, surnamed Agdestis. He possessed invincible strength and a spirit so fierce that he had regard neither for human beings nor for gods, but acted entirely according to his caprice and innate ferocity. Consequently, after the gods had deliberated about breaking his insolence, he was at last deprived of his virility through the devices of Liber, who had given him wine to drink in place of water. Then, from his flowing blood, a pomegranate tree was born. Nana, daughter of King Sangarius, admired the beauty of its fruit, and, after placing some of it in her bosom, became pregnant; as though she had been violated, she was cast into prison to be starved to death. Sustained, however, with fruit by the Mother of the gods, she gave birth to a little child, whom Sangarius ordered [Col. 0592C] to be exposed. But because he was nourished by Phorbas on goat’s milk, he was named Attis. When he grew up, the Mother of the gods and Agdestis loved him wickedly and desperately. Midas, king of Pessinus, in order to free the boy from so infamous a passion, resolved to give him his daughter in marriage. To prevent anything disastrous from happening to them on the appointed wedding day, he ordered the city gates to be closed. But the Mother of the gods, lifting up the city walls with her head, entered the city. Then, when everyone had been driven into frenzy and madness by the enraged Agdestis, “the daughter of Gallus’s concubine,” says Arnobius, “cuts off her own breasts, while Attis beneath a pine tree amputates his genitals and dies.” From the blood of the genitals, which the Mother of the gods had wrapped in the dead man’s garment and cast upon the ground, a violet was born. The bride of Attis, [Col. 0592D] whom the pontiff Valerius calls Ia, shed tears together with Agdestis, killed herself, and her blood was changed into violets. When the Mother of the gods sprinkled these, an almond tree arose from them. She then carried the pine tree, mentioned by us shortly before, into a cave; there she and Agdestis wept and wounded their breasts by beating them. Afterward Agdestis asked Jupiter to restore Attis to life. But he obtained nothing from him except that Attis’s body should not decay, that his hair should always grow, and that his little finger should remain alive and be agitated with perpetual motion.

Such, then, is the manner in which Arnobius describes this history of Cybele and Attis. Yet although he indicates that he culled it from recondite and intimate monuments of antiquity, it is nevertheless [Col. 0593A] certain that it is narrated very differently by other writers whom we have cited elsewhere (Dissertation on Minucius, chap. 20, art. 2). But lest anyone accuse him of having too readily trusted the secret records of the ancients and Timotheus, another and very ancient witness must be brought forward: Pausanias, who came closer than all the rest to Arnobius’s account. Since, however, it would take too long to transcribe his words both in Greek and in Latin, we shall present them in a form intelligible to everyone:

> “Another account concerning Attis,” he says, “is preserved in their own tradition”—that is, among the Greek inhabitants of Pessinus called Galli. “They tell that Jupiter, in a dream, spilled his seed upon the earth. From the earth’s conception a spirit came forth into the light, human in form indeed, but of ambiguous sex, and called Agdestis. The gods, terrified by the monster, cut off his male part; from it an almond tree [Col. 0593B] grew. When the daughter of the river Sangarius desired its ripe fruit and concealed it in her bosom, the fruit vanished, but the girl became pregnant and gave birth to a boy. Exposed in the forest, he was reared by a she-goat; and when he grew up, his beauty was extraordinary and far surpassed human beauty. Agdestis was therefore seized with love for him. When he had reached manhood, his relatives sent him to Pessinus. There, when he was about to marry the king’s daughter and the wedding song was already being sung, Agdestis intervened and inflicted such madness upon Attis that he cut off his own genitals. His father-in-law did the same. Agdestis repented of what had been done. He therefore obtained from Jupiter that no part of Attis’s body should decay or waste away.”

You readily perceive that much there resembles Arnobius’s account of Attis [Col. 0593C] and Agdestis, while some things differ, especially the complete silence concerning the Mother of the gods. But the points on which they agree certainly prove that Arnobius was neither rash nor unjustified in confronting the pagans with the authority of Timotheus and the others whom he followed.

From all the circumstances of this history, which he takes up one by one and which we need not repeat, he demonstrates with the greatest clarity that nothing could possibly be invented more insulting—not only to any god, but even to any honorable and self-controlled human being—and that nothing could more thoroughly overthrow and uproot the whole pagan religion. Indeed, the mere account of the birth and love of the Mother of the gods and of the obscene deeds of the others invincibly proves that she and the other gods once had a beginning and were infamous human beings, [Col. 0593D] who therefore could never have possessed either an eternal or a divine nature.

Our author therefore exclaimed with perfect justice:

> “O Abdera, Abdera, what ample opportunities for ridicule you would give mortals if such a tale, thus concocted, existed among you!”  
> (Arnobius, book V, p. 164.)

Abdera was a city of Thrace, the native city of the philosopher Democritus and other distinguished men. But some of its citizens were notorious for stupidity and madness. Hence the proverb discussed by Erasmus, *An Abderite mind* (*Abderitica mens*) (Erasmus, *Adages*, chiliad 4, century 6, adage 28, p. 877), and this verse of Martial:

> You have the heart of the populace of Abdera.  
> (Martial, book XX, epigram 25.)

Arnobius’s meaning, therefore, is that the Abderites, however [Col. 0594A] stupid and insane, would never have allowed such old wives’ tales—utterly unworthy of the gods and concocted to mock them—to be circulated and proclaimed among them without ridicule. Indeed, Cicero, after explaining the absurd opinion of that Abderite Democritus concerning the nature and images of the gods, added in a manner not wholly dissimilar:

> “All these things are indeed more worthy of Democritus’s native city than of Democritus himself.”  
> (Cicero, book I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 212.)

Nor, indeed, was there any room for the pagans to reply that absolutely no truth underlay that entire history. For Christians have no interest in whether it is said to be false or true. If the things narrated in it are true, the gods certainly ought not to be angry with Christians, who neither disclosed such great disgraces of theirs in any writings [Col. 0594B] nor ever disseminated them anywhere. But if they are false, the pagans have indeed provoked the gods’ just anger by daring to commit these things, to their reproach, both to writing and to everlasting memory. But tell me at last, I beg you: by what reasoning could they maintain that these and the many other things like them were false, when, as Arnobius says and as we have noted elsewhere, they celebrated them with annual festivals and rites, and with solemn abstinence from food, as Apuleius, Tertullian, and Jerome attest? Augustine attacks these matters at greater length; you will not regret reading his words in his books, though they are far too numerous to be quoted here. (Arnobius, book I, p. 54; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 759; Dissertation on Minucius, chap. 20, art. 2; Apuleius, book II of the *Metamorphoses*, pp. 206 and 209; Tertullian, *On Fasting*, chap. 2; Jerome, Letter [Col. 0594C] 7, to Laeta, and book II *Against Jovinian*, p. 91; Augustine, book VII of *The City of God*, chap. 26, p. 172.)

## ARTICLE II. An Examination of Other Commonly Circulated Histories: Fauna Fatua, or the Bona Dea, Beaten with Myrtle Rods, and the Most Shameful Origin of King Tullius

Arnobius acknowledges that both the nature of the subject he was treating—true and false religion—and the undertaking he had assumed of defending the Christian religion required him to pursue other similar histories represented in the sacred mysteries and festival days of the pagans (Arnobius, book V, p. 168). But lest he and others be contaminated by the exposition of their most shameful contents, he judged that many should be passed over in prudent silence. [Col. 0594D] By a rhetorical figure, therefore, he pretends to omit what he nevertheless relates briefly, though sufficiently for his purpose: namely, that Fauna Fatua, or the Bona Dea, was beaten with myrtle rods, according to Sextus Clodius, because, without her husband’s knowledge, she had drunk a jar full of wine. In memory of this deed, a covered wine amphora is placed in her mysteries, and no one is permitted to bring sacred boughs into them.

Macrobius, however, related these matters somewhat more explicitly, though not without some variation, in the following manner (Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, chap. 12). Fauna, he says, also called Fatua by some, and particularly by Cornelius Labeo and in the books of the Pontiffs, is said to be the same as Maia, the Bona Dea, Ops, Earth, and the Great Mother, for whom [Col. 0595A] divine worship is performed in the month of May, on the very Kalends of that month. Others, however, consider her to be the daughter of Faunus. When she resisted the will of her father, who was desperately in love with her, she was beaten by him with a myrtle rod. He then adds:

> “As evidence for all these things, they point out that it is forbidden for a myrtle rod to be kept in the temple; that a vine extends over her head, by which her father especially tried to deceive her; that wine is not customarily brought into her temple under its own name, but that the vessel into which the wine has been placed is called a honey-jar, while the wine is called milk; and that snakes appear indiscriminately in her temple, neither frightening nor frightened.”

Plutarch, meanwhile, in answer to the question why matrons, when adorning the domestic shrine of the female deity whom they called the Bona Dea, [Col. 0595B] do not include myrtle, says that the reason for that rite is not evident. Nevertheless, if any credence is to be given to the tale, the custom arose because they believed that the wife of a certain Faulius—perhaps Faunus—a soothsayer, after secretly drinking wine, was beaten by her husband with myrtle rods (Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, vol. II, p. 268).

Clodius, however, as quoted by Lactantius, reports that Fauna Fatua, the wife of Faunus, secretly drained a jar of wine contrary to custom and royal decorum and became intoxicated; she was consequently beaten to death by her husband with myrtle rods. But when he later repented of what he had done and could not endure the loss of his wife, he bestowed divine honors upon her. For this reason a wrapped wine amphora is offered in her rites. You may consult L. Giraldus [Col. 0595C] and Vossius for more about her, as well as the others cited by us shortly before (Lactantius, book I, *On False Religion*, chap. 22, p. 127; Giraldus, *History of the Gods*, syntagma 4, p. 137 ff.; Vossius, book I, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, chap. 12; above, chap. 11, art. 5).

Moreover, from this account by various writers anyone will be able to understand what Arnobius had earlier said in mockery of the pagans:

> “Fauna Fatua, the wife of Faunus, is called the Bona Dea—the Good Goddess—but she is better and more praiseworthy at drinking wine.”  
> (Arnobius, book I, p. 20.)

Who, then, after hearing these things, would not laugh with him, or rather lament the insane rashness of the pagans, who did not hesitate to ascribe divinity to such a woman and to others like her? But he demonstrates this still more clearly by another example.

[Col. 0595D] For he turns to the most shameful origin of Servius Tullius, king of the Romans (Arnobius, book V, p. 169); and although he indicates that he wishes to omit it, he nevertheless describes in a few words matters amply sufficient to demonstrate the infamy of this history. Dionysius of Halicarnassus related the entire affair as it had been handed down by many writers of Roman history (Dionysius of Halicarnassus, beginning of book IV of the *Roman Antiquities*, p. 207). Ovid, moreover, sang of it in the following verses, which confirm both the account of Arnobius and that of Dionysius:

> For Vulcan was the father of Tullius, Ocresia his mother,  
> A woman of striking beauty, born at Corniculum.  
> Tanaquil, when the customary rites had been prepared,  
> Ordered her to pour wine with her into the decorated hearth.  
> There amid the ashes either was, or seemed to be,  
> The shape of a man’s obscene member—but rather it truly was.  
> [Col. 0596A] At command, the captive woman warms it at the hearth;  
> Servius, conceived by her, has the seed of his race from heaven.  
> His father then gave signs, when with gleaming fire  
> He touched his head, and a fiery crest burned in his hair.  
> (Ovid, book VI of the *Fasti*, § 13.)

Who but thoroughly impious and criminal people could have worshiped these gods—or rather, these monstrosities of gods? But this impiety of theirs was revealed no less clearly by the solemn festivals and mysteries that they were accustomed to perform every year in their honor and in memory of their deeds. These must now be examined.

# CHAPTER XIX. How the Mysteries and Festivals Instituted and Celebrated by the Pagans in Honor of the Gods and in Memory of Their Deeds Demonstrated the Falsity of Their Divinity

[Col. 0596B]

## ARTICLE I. How Clearly the Bacchanalia, or Omophagia, the Initiations of Cyprian Venus, the Sabazia, Thesmophoria, Eleusinia, and Alimontia Demonstrate That the Gods of the Pagans Are False

Among the most shameful mysteries and festivals of the pagans, no insignificant place was occupied by the monstrous Bacchanalia, as Arnobius calls them, which were known by the Greek name *Omophagia* (“raw-flesh eating”). Anyone may recognize how great and execrable was the obscenity with which they were performed from what we discussed about them in the first volume of our *Apparatus*. From there one will also readily understand that the matters related by our Author were excerpted [Col. 0596C] from the books of Clement of Alexandria (Arnobius, book V, p. 169; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation I, chap. 9, art. I, p. 756; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 11).

From the same source, undoubtedly, he also drew the things he says about other Bacchanalia, in which Liber, or Bacchus, was celebrated as having been cut limb from limb by the Titans, as he himself had said elsewhere and as Diodorus Siculus and Macrobius record (Arnobius, book V, p. 169, and book I, p. 23 ff.; Diodorus Siculus, book III of the *Library*, p. 137; Macrobius, book I of the *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, chap. 12). If anyone wishes to read more about these Bacchanalia and Omophagia than what we have said (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, passage cited), let him consult Livy, Augustine, Castellanus, Johann Nicolai, and Meursius, who published books concerning them (Livy, book XXXIX, § 11 ff.; [Col. 0596D] Augustine, book VII of *The City of God*, chap. 21, p. 177; Castellanus, under the word Διονύσια, “Dionysia”).

The things our Author next relates about the hidden initiations and rites of Cyprian Venus and their founder Cinyras were likewise taken from the same book of Clement of Alexandria. Julius Firmicus speaks of them as follows:

> “I hear that Cinyras of Cyprus presented a temple to his mistress, a prostitute whose name was Venus. He also initiated very many people into the rites of Cyprian Venus and assigned them to various consecrations. He further ordained that anyone who wished to be initiated, after the secret of Venus had been handed over to him, should give the goddess a bronze coin in his hand as payment. What sort of secret this is we must all understand, since because of its obscenity we cannot explain the matter itself. [Col. 0597A] Cinyras serves well as a lover under the laws of prostitution: he ordered that a contribution be given by her own priests to the consecrated Venus, as to a harlot.”  
> (Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 15.)

Theodoret, however, committed the following to writing concerning Cinyras:

> Τὴν δὲ γε Ἀφροδίτην οὐδὲ εὐεργεσίας τινὸς ἄρξασαν, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἀκολασίας γεγενημένην διδάσκαλον· χαμαιτύπην γὰρ αὐτὴν καὶ ἑταίραν γεγενῆσθαί φασι καὶ ἐρωμένην Κινύρου, θεὰν ὠνομάκασι.
>
> “Venus, though she was the author of no benefaction, but rather became a teacher of licentiousness—for they say that she was a street-walking prostitute and courtesan, and the mistress of Cinyras—they nevertheless called a goddess.”  
> (Theodoret, vol. IV, discourse 3, *On Angels and Demons*, p. 511.)

Consult Vossius, if you wish, concerning Cinyras and Venus (Vossius, book VI, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, chap. 17, p. 71). We have discussed them elsewhere (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, [Col. 0597B] pp. 729 and 1176; Arnobius, book V, p. 169). But who does not see that by these most shameful and cruel mysteries and festivals the divinity of those in whose honor—or rather, to whose eternal disgrace—they were performed is uprooted entirely?

Our Author then briefly touched upon the Corybantic rites, in which the death of a brother slaughtered by his brother was customarily represented. But we discussed these in the first volume of our *Apparatus*; and if anyone wishes to read that discussion, he will immediately discover that here Arnobius once again follows in the footsteps of Clement of Alexandria (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 635 and 758; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 12).

He next explains at greater length the most foul mysteries by which the Phrygians were initiated, although, because [Col. 0597C] Jupiter’s name occurs in them, he does so unwillingly (Arnobius, book V, p. 170 ff.). Thus, in order to shame the pagans for branding Jupiter and their other gods with the disgrace of the most obscene crimes, he briefly explains how in these mysteries they represented the unbridled lust of Jupiter, who by various devices first violated Ceres and then Proserpina, who had been born from his adultery with Ceres. If you compare what he relates there with the already cited book of Clement of Alexandria, you will readily perceive that it was drawn from that source (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 10 ff.). We have discussed these mysteries in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 759 ff.), where we cited several writers who attempted to elucidate them.

[Col. 0597D] One point, however, must not be passed over without some observation: Clement of Alexandria gives these mysteries the name Σαβαζίων μυστηρίων, “mysteries of the Sabazia,” while our Author says: “which bear the name Sabadia” (Arnobius, book V, p. 171). Many have noted that Bacchus is called Sabasius, and his mysteries Sabazia. For we read in Cicero:

> “The third Dionysus, or Bacchus, they say, was born of the father Caprius and ruled as king over Asia; the Sabazia were instituted for him.”  
> (Cicero, book II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 248, l. 23.)

Diodorus Siculus likewise writes (Diodorus, book III, p. 148) that another Dionysus, or Bacchus, is brought forward, born of Jupiter and Proserpina, τὸν ὑπό τινων Σαβάσιον ὀνομαζόμενον, “who is called Sabasius by some”; and his birth, [Col. 0598A] sacrifices, and worship were introduced only at night and in secret because of their obscenity. Hence Cicero again says:

> “Aristophanes, the wittiest poet of Old Comedy, so ridicules new gods and the nocturnal vigils devoted to their worship that in his work Sabasius and certain other foreign gods, after being put on trial, are expelled from the city.”  
> (Cicero, book II, *On the Laws*, p. 337, l. 44.)

Finally, to omit Strabo and others, Suidas explicitly declares that Sebasius, Σαβάσιον, is the same as Dionysus, or Bacchus (Strabo, book XX of the *Geography*, p. 470 ff.; Suidas, under the word σεβάσιος, “Sebasius”).

[Col. 0598B] Nor should you object that the text of our Arnobius reads *Sabadiis*, or, as some think, *Sebadiis*. For in Apuleius we read *Saint Sabadius*, undoubtedly Bacchus. In Macrobius, however, we read:

> “We learn that in Thrace the Sun and Liber are regarded as the same; calling him Sebadius, they celebrate him with magnificent religious observance.”  
> (Apuleius, book VIII of the *Metamorphoses*, p. 140; Macrobius, book III of the *Saturnalia*, chap. 18, p. 264.)

You therefore see that Bacchus was called by them both Sebadius and Sabadius, and his mysteries Sabadia. Why, then, you will ask, are the mysteries in which Jupiter above all was worshiped likewise called Sabazia? Was it because Jupiter too bore the surname Sabasius? Gruter indeed presents various inscriptions reading **TO JUPITER SABASIUS** (*JOVI SABASIO*). Yet some, like Vossius, think that Jupiter is the same as Bacchus or Liber (Vossius, book II, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry*, chap. 14, p. 241). What wonder, then, if those most shameful mysteries in which [Col. 0598C] Jupiter’s twofold adultery was celebrated were called Sabazia? To this may be added that, as Clement of Alexandria noted, the Corybantes and Bacchus were mentioned in these mysteries (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 11).

What Arnobius subsequently relates concerning other mysteries, which the Greeks called *Thesmophoria*, he again drew from Clement of Alexandria and rendered in his own words (Arnobius, book V, p. 173; Clement of Alexandria, passage cited). He nevertheless added a few remarks of his own, by which he thought the obscenity of these mysteries and the blindness and shamelessness of the pagans who celebrated them ought to be assailed. We discussed them in the first volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation I, chap. 9, art. 2, p. 759 ff.). It is therefore enough to note that certain verses are cited there from a [Col. 0598D] Greek poet whom Clement of Alexandria calls Orpheus, while our Author calls him the son of Calliope—undoubtedly because Orpheus, as Virgil sings, was held to have been born of the Muse Calliope (Virgil, *Eclogue* 4, at the end). Clement presents those verses in Greek, while Arnobius gives them only in Latin; but who would dare determine whether Arnobius himself was the translator? It is certain, however, that the royal manuscript incorrectly reads *sanguinibus* (“blood”), while the printed editions have the better reading *inguinibus* (“groins”), though this is less decorous than the Greek verse: οὐδὲ πρέποντα τύπον, “nor a seemly form.”

Once again Arnobius borrowed from the same Clement the matters he appended concerning the Eleusinian mysteries (Arnobius, book V, p. 175; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 13). But if anyone asks us why [Col. 0599A] each of them there mentioned the Erechthids, we shall reply, following Diodorus Siculus, that during a time of sterility an enormous quantity of grain was brought to the Athenians by Erechtheus the Egyptian, whom they made king in return for so great a benefaction (Diodorus Siculus, book I of the *Library*, p. 17). Having obtained supreme power, he instituted the Eleusinian mysteries, or mysteries of Ceres, with rites transferred from Egypt. For this reason the Athenians are called Erechthids, or the people of the Erechthids, by Clement of Alexandria, Arnobius, and others. We treated those Eleusinian mysteries in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, book cited, p. 760).

Finally, Arnobius—[Col. 0599B] still the intermediary and interpreter of Clement of Alexandria—attacks as they deserve the execrable Alimontian mysteries, which can never be sufficiently detested (Arnobius, book V, p. 176 ff.; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, pp. 21–22). We have discussed elsewhere these most foul rites, which ought to be condemned to everlasting oblivion except when used to refute the pagans and lead them away from the superstitious worship of the gods to true religion (same vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 774 ff.).

Moreover, what person of sound mind can hear the account of so many and such horrifying mysteries without immediately concluding with our Author that the pagans displayed the height of injustice and madness when they attempted, by every kind of torture, [Col. 0599C] to compel Christians to worship gods infamous for such great and abominable crimes, and to perform mysteries so obscene and detestable? For what could be more unjust than to condemn them for this reason as persons convicted of atheism? Were not the pagans themselves more justly to be called atheists, since, having rejected the worship of the true God, they worshiped at public festivals and mysteries fictitious gods who, because of their execrable offenses, were not even worthy of the name of human beings?

## ARTICLE II. How Arnobius Utterly Overthrows the Pagan Reply That Those Mysteries and the Most Shameful Histories of Their Gods Must Be Interpreted Allegorically

The pagans perceived with no slight agitation of mind how clearly the festivals, mysteries, and even the histories of their gods, which we reviewed in the preceding chapter, [Col. 0599D] demonstrated the falsity of their divinity (Arnobius, book V, p. 179). They therefore attempted, by whatever means they could, to weaken the arguments derived from them. Accordingly, they replied that the things brought against them—which they could neither deny nor conceal—the shameful crimes of their gods represented in the mysteries, ought by no means to be understood literally, but in a higher, allegorical sense. For their more learned men taught that in all these things, however shameful and obscene they might appear, were contained physical, mystical, marvelous explanations known to few. Jupiter’s intercourse with Ceres, they said, or with his daughter, the rape of Proserpina, and any other similar events signified nothing but rain, earth, a rainstorm, seeds, and other [Col. 0600A] natural things, which their authors, and later Natalis Comes and Vossius following them, attempted to elucidate.

Indeed, we learn from Cicero that this was precisely the opinion and reply of Chrysippus and other philosophers called physicists. For in the second book of his *On the Nature of the Gods*, Balbus, speaking on behalf of the Stoics, attempts to extract and explain the physical and allegorical meaning concealed in those histories and mysteries. After clearly explaining there what was physically and allegorically signified by the binding of Saturn by Jupiter and by other deeds of the same kind, he concludes in this manner:

> “Do you see, then, how reasoning was drawn away from physical things, well and usefully discovered, toward fabricated and fictitious gods? This gave rise to false opinions, turbulent errors, and superstitions almost worthy of old women.”  
> [Col. 0600B] (Cicero, book I, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 223 ff.; and book I, p. 201.)

He therefore maintains that physical and natural things were transferred, through the utmost license of poets and others, to false and fictitious gods, and perversely transformed into them. Eusebius, however, argues the contrary (Eusebius, book II of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chap. 6, p. 74), relying on the authority of Diodorus Siculus and Clement of Alexandria. He contends that those most shameful opinions concerning their gods—or rather, monstrosities and prodigies of opinion—were first disseminated by the most ancient pagans. Afterward, when more recent people were ashamed, he says, of such great obscenities so shamefully expressed in them, yet were unable either wholly to reject or deny them, they were compelled to take refuge in a physical and allegorical sense.

[Col. 0600C] But however the matter may stand, it is certainly evident that these replies and empty explanations of the pagans are uprooted entirely by our Arnobius and the other Fathers of the Church. For in what way, asks our Author, can these interpretations prevent the things we read written concerning the gods, as the words themselves declare them, from being disgraceful and altogether impious? (Arnobius, book V, p. 180 ff.) And who will be able to prove that they must be explained only in an allegorical sense? For if this sense is hidden, as they said, who revealed it to the pagans? Can several explanations not also be offered for one and the same history—for example, the story of Jupiter and Ceres? Who, then, will establish for us with certainty that one rather than another is the true and genuine explanation?

Come now: must all the parts of the same history [Col. 0600D] be understood in an allegorical sense? (Ibid., p. 189 ff.) But who has ever explained to us, or could explain, what Brimo, what Baubo, what the grove and flowers of Henna, what the fire and torches of Etna, what the region of Attica, what the village of Eleusis, and other nearly countless details of that sort signify allegorically?

This fact, however, is especially worthy of attention: festivals and mysteries were performed in memory of those events by all pagans on annual and certain fixed days (Ibid., p. 184 ff.). Just as the origin of those festival days had to be certain and established, and founded upon some notable deed, so the things customarily displayed in them represented something that had actually occurred earlier. It was therefore necessary that at least some [Col. 0601A] parts of those histories should have a natural, and by no means an allegorical, meaning. But if some parts are to be understood in a natural sense and others in an allegorical sense, who will distinguish them correctly? For there is no mark or sign by which one may be separated from another.

Arnobius, however, presses the pagans still more sharply. Freely and generously he grants them that these histories and the things done in the mysteries can by no means be explained in a literal sense, but only allegorically. Yet from this, he argues, no less disgrace redounds upon the gods. For with what more grievous insult could they be scourged than to call them by names that most plainly signify outrages and crimes, simply because many people babbled that natural things were thereby indicated in a mystical sense?

[Col. 0601B] What could be more insulting to those same gods than the wish, by proclaiming and representing their most shameful deeds openly and everywhere, to signify serious and honorable realities? For by such an utterly absurd manner of speaking, the obscenity strikes the mind before the allegorical meaning and the authority of religion can do so. Who would also dare deny that it would have been far better to call each natural thing by its own natural name than by the name of some obscene or cruel crime of the gods? Then the matter would have been easy to understand, and the dignity of the heavenly powers would have remained unharmed.

No further hearing, therefore, should be given to the pagans, who still objected that the gods did not wish their mysteries to be known and that for this reason both the mysteries and their histories were veiled in allegorical circumlocutions (Ibid., p. 187). For who could know that this had pleased the gods? We know with certainty, however, [Col. 0601C] that the gods never wished shameful things to be said and proclaimed about them. What, for example, have the sun, the earth, and other natural things—if they are divine powers—done to deserve being named by the pagans after Attis, that is, a castrated and half-male human being, and after other criminal people? Finally, not only are the gods themselves to be worshiped, but even their names are worthy of veneration and honor; and those names should certainly not be imposed upon other earthly and contemptible things, much less upon things shameful and foul. Who, then, after duly weighing these arguments, does not see how correctly Arnobius proved that those who explained the histories and mysteries of their gods in an allegorical and mystical sense did no more to safeguard their religions than those who thought they should be understood in their literal and obvious sense? [Col. 0601D] For both groups do equal injury to their gods and, without realizing it, strip them of all divinity.

## ARTICLE III. How the Same Reply of the Pagans Is Thoroughly Weakened and Destroyed by Other Writers

We have set forth, as briefly and clearly as we could, all Arnobius’s arguments against the allegorical and mystical interpretations that the pagans gave of their gods and mysteries, so that everyone may more easily understand that he refutes them all the more plainly because the pagans so often resorted to them as to the greatest bulwark of their religion. Yet Arnobius was not alone: other writers too, both Christian [Col. 0602A] and pagan, drove them from this flimsy defense.

For Cicero, in the third book of *On the Nature of the Gods*, refutes Balbus, who was defending Stoic opinions through these explanations, in the person of the Academic Cotta:

> “But why,” he says, “does that explanation of myths and elucidation of names so delight you? … Zeno first, then Cleanthes, and afterward Chrysippus undertook a great and wholly unnecessary labor: to account for fabricated myths and to explain the reasons why each thing was designated by a particular name. In doing this, you certainly acknowledge that the matter stands very differently from common human opinion; for those who are called gods are the natures of things, not figures of gods. [Col. 0602B] So great was this error that not only was the name of gods bestowed even upon harmful things, but sacred rites were also instituted for them. There is, for example, a shrine of Fever on the Palatine.… Let every such error, therefore, be expelled from philosophy, so that when we discuss the gods, we may say things worthy of the immortal gods. I have my own view concerning them, but I have no reason to agree with you.”  
> (Cicero, book II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 248 ff.)

Do you hear how rightly Cicero rejects these Stoic interpretations as an utterly absurd error to be expelled from philosophy? You have perceived with no less ease how clearly he demonstrates that they advance nothing worthy of the immortal God, as Arnobius likewise contends.

Eusebius, and Theodoret after him, by transcribing [Col. 0602C] Plato’s own words from the *Timaeus*, show that he taught expressly and explicitly that those commonly circulated myths, or histories, concerning the gods, together with all their allegorical meanings, which the pagans thought adapted to philosophy, must be utterly excluded and restrained (Eusebius, book II of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, chap. 7, p. 76 ff.; Theodoret, discourse 3, *On Angels and Demons*, vol. IV, p. 512 ff.). Moreover, the same Eusebius, using the words of Dionysius of Halicarnassus taken from the second book of his *Roman Antiquities*, proves that the ancient Romans decreed that all such Greek natural theology should be cast out and banished from every domain of theology as wholly useless and internally inconsistent.

Source/review notes: The source citation “libr. XXVIII, cap. 12” is internally anomalous; it is retained and briefly marked uncertain rather than silently replaced with an unsupported conjecture.

It is therefore no wonder that the most ancient Fathers of the Church [Col. 0602D] attacked these same allegorical interpretations with such ardor. For, to say nothing of the author of the *Recognitions* inscribed with the name of Clement and of the *Clementines*, who assails them with arguments similar to those employed by our Arnobius, Athenagoras clearly demonstrates that the pagans—and specifically the Stoics—gain not the slightest advantage from these allegories in defending their religion. For it must be certain that divinity is attributed only to things that are created and corporeal. But the true God can have only one unbegotten, incorporeal, and eternal substance. From this it plainly follows that Saturn, Jupiter, and others of that kind were never gods (Clem., *Recogn.*, book X, ch. 35 ff., p. 517; *Clement.*, hom. 4, ch. 24 ff., p. 607, and hom. 6, [Col. 0603A] ch. 17 ff., pp. 625 ff.; Athenag., *Legation for the Christians*, pp. 22 ff.).

In the same manner Tatian, as we have noted elsewhere, rebukes the Gentiles, and especially Metrodorus of Lampsacus, who attempted to reduce all the gods and their histories to an allegorical meaning (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 522 and 550; Tatian, *Oration against the Greeks*, p. 160).

But Eusebius restrains this new and, as he calls it, insolent obstinacy of the pagans with still other arguments (Euseb., *Preparation for the Gospel*, book II, ch. 6, p. 74). For even after those allegorical and physical interpretations had been devised, the same pagans did not alter their ancestral rites for worshiping the gods. Indeed, they continued to honor livestock, human beings, and even those parts of the human body [Col. 0603B] which modesty forbids us to name, with the same divine honors, hymns, sacrifices, and other religious rites. Julius Firmicus employs almost the same weight of argument against the pagans (Jul. Firm., *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 4).

Hence Augustine acutely teaches that anyone who, by means of criminal and shameful things, worships other things that are natural sins twice (Augustine, *City of God*, book VII, ch. 27, p. 183): first, because he does not worship the true God; and second, because he does not worship Him in the manner in which He ought to be worshiped. Elsewhere he rejects the allegorical and physical explanations of shameful gods advanced by the more learned, because it makes little difference whether, as he says, “the one thing instructs religious people in truthful books, while the other delights impure demons in deceitful spectacles—demons whom those religious people [Col. 0603C] nevertheless worship as gods. And when they deny these things concerning them, they cannot clear them of every charge, since they present them with spectacles in their rites in which those deeds are shamefully performed which are, as it were, wisely denied. These gods are pleased by things false and shameful; and although the fable sings of a false crime committed by the divine powers, nevertheless to take delight in a false crime is itself a true crime” (Idem, ibid., book XXVIII [source reading; uncertain], ch. 12, p. 497).

Moreover, the pagans could not object to us that our sacred Scriptures also possess obscure, hidden, and allegorical meanings. For these differ wholly and completely from their interpretations, as Gregory Nazianzen explains most clearly in these words:

> “Among us also,” he says, “there are indeed hidden and obscure discourses; for I shall not deny it. But what is the principle of their twofold meaning [Col. 0603D], and what are its force and capacity? Their outward appearance is neither indecorous nor dishonorable; and what is concealed is admirable and, to those admitted into the innermost sanctuary, wondrously splendid. Like a most beautiful body, it is covered by a garment that deserves no contempt. For in my judgment it is fitting that not even the indications and outward forms of divine things should be dishonorable or unworthy of the things signified, nor, finally, of such a kind that human beings themselves would find it exceedingly painful if they were predicated of them. They should possess true, or indeed the highest, beauty—or at least be free from extreme ugliness—so that they may both delight the more educated and in no way unsettle the minds of the common people. Among you, by contrast, neither does what is proposed for understanding deserve belief [Col. 0604A], and what is outwardly presented to the eyes is deadly and destructive.”

(Greg. Naz., oration 39, or 1 against Julian, p. 250.)

Earlier, however, Origen, in his dispute against Celsus, skillfully showed that the allegories of Christians and Gentiles differ from one another in this respect: the latter offend the majesty of God (Origen, *Against Celsus*, book IV, p. 196), whereas the former are excellently suited to everyone—whether unlearned or learned—and to all who desire to investigate the true meanings of sacred Scripture. As we heard from Augustine, they do not prevent the true God from being worshiped with the rite and in the manner appropriate to Him.

# CHAPTER XX  
## How Vainly the Pagans Attempted to Prove from Certain Miracles, or from Answers Concerning Some Future Event, That Their Gods Truly Existed

[Col. 0604B]

## ARTICLE I  
### With What Clarity Arnobius Refutes the Pagans’ Argument Drawn from Miracles: Whether the Plague Was Brought to an End, the Games Were Renewed at Jupiter’s Warning, or the Image of Aesculapius Was Transported to the Tiber Island
