Against so many arguments of the Christians—any single one of which overturned from its foundations the entire worship of the gods and their whole religion—the pagans had only one refuge remaining, which Arnobius utterly destroys and demolishes. For they alleged that many miracles had been performed by the gods, and that responses had been given concerning future events, by which they believed it had been demonstrated, neither merely once nor obscurely, that the gods truly existed, that they were appeased by human satisfaction and sacrifices.

[Col. 0604C] First, therefore, they related that a miracle had occurred when a plague was devastating the city because the circus games instituted in Jupiter’s honor had not been properly performed (Arnob., book VII, pp. 242 ff.). When these games were renewed at Jupiter’s warning in the manner we have explained elsewhere, the pestilence immediately ceased (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, ch. 17, art. 3).

The Gentiles boasted that another miracle had occurred when, after an image of Aesculapius had been transported from Epidaurus, a city of the Peloponnese, to the Tiber Island, the plague was again brought to an end (Arnob., book VII, pp. 248 ff.). The whole event, celebrated in Ovid’s verse, happened in the following manner—if any credence is to be given to it (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book XV, pp. 580 ff.). When a most dreadful plague was devastating Rome and the neighboring regions, [Col. 0604D] the Romans, after applying human remedies in vain, received from the Delphic oracle the response that Aesculapius must be summoned from Epidaurus to Rome. The Romans obeyed the oracle and sent ambassadors to Epidaurus. Some of the Epidaurians assented to their requests; others refused. But after the Romans had been instructed by Aesculapius, they carried him—transformed into the form of a serpent—to the Tiber Island. When this had been done, the pestilence was driven away.

So Ovid relates; and his account can be confirmed by the authority of Valerius Maximus, Livy, Plutarch, Aurelius Victor, Lactantius, and Augustine, although they report some of its circumstances either more briefly or somewhat differently (Val. Max., book I, ch. 8, § 2; Livy, at the end of book X and book XXIX, ch. 11; Plutarch, [Col. 0605A] *Roman Questions*, vol. II, p. 286; Aurel. Vict., *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 22; Lactant., book II, ch. 7, p. 175; Augustine, *City of God*, book III, pp. 12 and 17, and book X, ch. 16).

The pagans, therefore, were accustomed to derive from these and other narratives of the same kind their principal and, as it appeared to them, decisive argument in favor of their own religion and against the Christian religion. Arnobius does not deny that the crucial point—or, as he puts it, the hinge—of this whole case and question turns upon this matter (Arnob., book VII, p. 243). For that argument appears all the stronger because the events recorded in the pagans’ annals presented some appearance of truth and miracle. But if they are examined thoroughly, he says, you will then discover that they contain nothing appropriate to the gods [Col. 0605B], to their divine power, or to supreme majesty.

As regards the renewed games, is it not absurd to say, he asks, that Jupiter Optimus Maximus, whom they advertised as the creator of all things, came down from heaven with great delight to watch geldings—that is, castrated horses—competing in speed, repeating seven circuits, or going seven times around the turning-post of the circus, and then to watch men being overturned with their chariots or dragged away with broken legs? (Ibid., pp. 245 ff.) What prudent person would not despise these things as childish and theatrical mockeries?

What, moreover, could be more unworthy of Jupiter than for him to blaze with anger [Col. 0605C] because a slave had been scourged in the circus and subjected to the punishment of death? For if the man deservedly paid the penalty, Jupiter ought not to have become angry. But if he was innocent when killed, the master of the games was guilty, for although he could have rescued him from death, he failed to do so and announced that Jupiter had been offended by the man’s slaughter. But how could Jupiter have been injured by the death of this slave, when he is said to have watched with gladness the killing of many plainly innocent persons at these games?

Arnobius indeed admits that, if this had been done before the games out of contempt for religion, Jupiter might be excused, since he was unable patiently to endure being despised through sacrilege. But if it happened through error and accident, Jupiter, being supremely good, ought certainly to have pardoned human frailty and imprudence. Moreover, although the deed, however it happened, ought not to have been left unpunished, nevertheless, on account of the offense of a single man, the whole population [Col. 0605D] of the city—all its women, children, infants, and countless other innocent persons—ought not to have been struck by the cruel punishment of plague. Is it not unjust that so many innocent people should be condemned and punished for only one guilty person?

Furthermore, if Jupiter wished the games to be restored, why did he inform a rustic rather than a consul, the chief pontiff, or his own Flamen Dialis, who were far better acquainted with these rites, of his will? Why did he not first induce the rustic’s mind to comply with his wishes before raging so bitterly against him? “But,” they said, “after he had completed the task of making the announcement, he was healed.” What is surprising, Arnobius replies, if the one who inflicted the evil also removed it? The restoration of health was undoubtedly a cruel benefit to that man, [Col. 0606A] since through it he felt the bereavement and death of his sons all the more bitterly.

The story of Aesculapius brought from Epidaurus to Rome had been fabricated no less foolishly and ineptly (Ibid., p. 249). For he cannot be called the son of Coronis, since that man perished after being struck by lightning. But whoever he may have been, they say that nothing else was brought from Epidaurus except a serpent of enormous bulk and immense length. Who could readily persuade himself that a god assumed the form of a most contemptible serpent crawling upon the ground, possessed organs necessary for eating and digestion, and required a ship in order to cross the seas? Why did he not present himself to be seen as he truly was? But if he wished to deceive and change his form, why did he assume no other than the horrifying likeness of a serpent? Did he not thereby give reason to doubt whether [Col. 0606B] it was truly he himself, or something entirely different from him?

Were the pagans not also obliged to offer at least some explanation why that serpent never appeared again after arriving at the Tiber Island? For the Christians—and undoubtedly the pagans themselves—knew nothing else concerning this fable beyond what was found handed down in the writings of those same Gentiles.

Finally, the pagans could not deny that this serpent was of an earthly species, “although,” says Arnobius (Ibid., p. 251), “it may have been monstrous and enormous, although in the length and strength of its body it surpassed the serpent slain by Regulus through the force of his army.” How enormous that serpent was may be judged from the report that, after it had been killed by the army of Atilius Regulus near the Bagrada River, where Regulus had pitched camp, [Col. 0606C] its skin, later sent to Rome, was 120 feet long. If you desire witnesses to this event, we shall give you Aulus Gellius, Livy as cited by Valerius Maximus, Pliny, Seneca, Florus, Orosius, and still others, if necessary (Gell., *Attic Nights*, book VI, ch. 3, p. 368; Val. Max., book I, final chapter, § 19, p. 77; Pliny, *Natural History*, book VIII, ch. 13, p. 153; Seneca, epist. 82, p. 156; Florus, book III, shortly after the beginning; Orosius, *History*, book IV, ch. 8). Who, then, would not marvel at the pagans, who declared a serpent of this kind to be a god and worshiped it?

They nevertheless insisted that, as soon as this serpent—or, as they said, Aesculapius—had been summoned to Rome from the books of fate, that is, the Sibylline books, and from the responses of the seers, that is, of Apollo, the plague was immediately driven away, and not without a great miracle [Col. 0606D] (Arnob., book VII, p. 251). But if Aesculapius, transformed into a serpent, was summoned, as Arnobius replies, in order to avert this calamity, where was he when the same city was subsequently afflicted so many times by the same disease, and when so many thousands of people perished in a similar plague? Why, after temples had been built for him, did he not prevent the pestilence from raging any longer?

Nor should you say that human morals were corrupted in the period that followed. For in great peoples and cities the good have always been intermingled with the wicked. We must therefore say either that the serpent’s force and power to bring later plagues to an end had been worn out, or that the fatal verses were false, since the serpentine remedy proposed by them did not prove beneficial in every age. What, then, is to be concluded from [Col. 0607A] all these things, except that the Gentiles went wholly astray when they claimed that miracles had truly been performed by Jupiter and Aesculapius?

## ARTICLE II  
### With What Clarity Arnobius Shows That the Miracles Which the Pagans Claimed Occurred When the Image of the Great Mother Was Brought to Rome from a Phrygian Mountain, and When Another Image of Jupiter Was Placed in a Higher Position Facing East, Were False

The argument of the pagans drawn from another allegedly great miracle was certainly of no greater weight (Arnob., book VII, p. 253). For they continually insisted upon the familiar claim that, by the divine aid of the Great Mother, or Mother of the Gods, after her image had been carried from the Phrygian mountain to Rome at the command of the seers, the exceedingly powerful enemy Hannibal [Col. 0607B] was driven from Italy; that through illustrious victories the City’s honor was restored; and that many other distinguished achievements at home and abroad established the name and majesty of the Roman people upon an invincible foundation. We have shown elsewhere which authors committed these things to writing (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 19, art. I).

But Arnobius refutes this argument with answers similar to those given above. Nothing true, he says, is contained in that whole story except that, as they reported, a small stone was sent by King Attalus from the Phrygian mountain and carried from there to Rome—a black, hard, rough stone, fashioned into the image of a statue whose form was not clearly expressed. But who will ever be convinced that Hannibal, under whom the Roman Republic had so long trembled in uncertainty over its fate, immediately [Col. 0607C] became wholly unlike himself once that stone had been brought, and was driven and put to flight from Italy? Was nothing accomplished at that time by human counsels, nothing by the military valor of the most distinguished commanders, nothing by the great strength of the armies? Did that stone, which could easily be carried by a single man, increase the strength of the Roman army, break and weaken Hannibal’s forces, and make him defeated and the Romans victorious? Whom, finally, will you readily persuade that the Mother of the Gods was truly present in a stone of this kind, or that some divine power dwelt in its veins, pieces, and fragments?

“In what manner, then,” the pagans asked, “was victory obtained through its arrival, if there was no divine power within that stone?” Arnobius replies that it should be attributed to the valor and courage of the combatants, or to the changeability and inconstancy of fortune. And indeed, in what part of the world was that illustrious divine power dwelling [Col. 0607D] when such great armies were cut down and the Romans came into the utmost danger?

If someone replies that the divine Mother was then very far away from Rome, he will immediately hear from Arnobius that a divine power is always present everywhere and always holds all things under its authority. Furthermore, why, I ask you, did that goddess entirely abandon her earlier Phrygian worshipers in order to migrate to the more powerful Roman people? Such great fickleness is not compatible with deity.

Nor could the Romans reply that this goddess passed over to their warlike nation because she loved military affairs. For it was not consistent with divine justice, says Arnobius, for her to involve herself in human conflicts [Col. 0608A] and, though no cause had been given her, to break the power of one people in order to display herself as the patroness of another; to take liberty from the former in order to raise the latter to the highest summit of dominion; to destroy the Phrygians so that the Roman state, born for the destruction of the human race, might place an innocent world beneath the most oppressive yoke of servitude.

The pagans pressed their case and again endeavored to prove, by another miracle wholly astounding in their own estimation, that their gods truly existed and that their power was infinite (Arnob., book VII, p. 245). For, they said, it had been handed down by witnesses most worthy of trust that, when the Capitol was struck by lightning, the statue of Jupiter was cast down from its place. But when, in accordance with the response of the haruspices, it had been placed on a higher site facing the rising sun, hidden matters were then disclosed and [Col. 0608B] crimes were uncovered and punished. For Cicero relates that the Romans still held clearly in their memory how, after many images of the gods had been cast from their places on the Capitol, the haruspices summoned from all Etruria

> “ordered that a larger image of Jupiter be made, placed in a lofty position, and, contrary to its former orientation, turned toward the east. They said that they hoped that, if that statue which you see looked upon the rising of the sun, the Forum, and the Senate-house, then those designs secretly formed against the safety of the City and the empire would be brought to light, so that they might be perceived by the Senate and People of Rome.”

(Cicero, third oration *Against Catiline*, p. 329.)

Nothing at all is found—either in the royal manuscript codex of Arnobius’ books, [Col. 0608C] in any edition of them, or elsewhere—concerning what Arnobius replied to this argument of the pagans. Some will perhaps suspect that he may have omitted it because it had been sufficiently refuted by his other replies to the objections mentioned above. But because we have already noted that a fragment was there improperly transposed by a careless copyist, it may be inferred that Arnobius replied individually to this argument of the Gentiles, as he did to the others, but that everything he had written on the matter was lost. Yet whatever that loss may have been, it is amply supplied by what we have thus far reported from his other replies and by what remains intact in his books.

If, however, he made any reply to this argument, we have no doubt that it was principally the one which Cicero—upon whom, as we have often said, he drew extensively—[Col. 0608D] left in writing. For immediately after the words cited by us, Cicero added:

> “Those consuls decided that the statue of Jupiter should be placed in that manner; but so great was the delay in the work that it was placed neither by the preceding consuls nor by us before the present day.”

(Ibid.)

Is not the whole exceedingly frivolous reasoning of the pagans plainly and completely weakened by these words alone? Does not the negligence of those consuls or of others most clearly prove how little the Gentiles valued the oracles and predictions of the haruspices and that statue of Jupiter?

Moreover, we have already shown that this entire argument, which the Gentiles considered most powerful, was overturned in another manner by Minucius Felix and our other ancient writers [Col. 0609A]. For by many strong supports of reasoning they demonstrate that, if anything unusual and outside the customary order of nature occurred in all these events, it must all be attributed to the deceptions and magical tricks of demons. Certainly no one should find it surprising if one and the same error of the Gentiles is assailed by several arguments and utterly destroyed (*Dissertation on Minucius’ Octavius*, ch. 19, arts. I and II).

# CHAPTER XXI  
## On the Temples of the Gentiles

## ARTICLE I  
### The Arguments by Which Arnobius Shows That Neither Temples, Huts, Rooms, nor Small Chambers Should Be Built for the Gods; on the First Temples of the Gods and Others Which Were Merely the Tombs of Dead Men; Likewise on the Hidden Tomb of Apis, the Capitol, Which Was Named from the Discovery of Tolus’ Head, and Polyandria

[Col. 0609B]

Since Arnobius demonstrated most conclusively, with so many and such weighty arguments, as we have seen, that the gods of the Gentiles were nonexistent and wholly fictitious, there was certainly no need for any other argument to prove that no temples should be built for them. Nevertheless, he proceeds further and demonstrates this clearly by certain particular arguments. For if temples, he says, can be of any use to the gods, why did they lack them through the many ages before temples were built? Arnobius says that the first builder of such structures “will be shown to you to have been either Phoroneus the Egyptian or Merops; or, as Varro relates in his *Marvels*, Aeacus, the offspring of Jupiter” (Arnob., book VI, pp. 189 ff.; ibid., p. 191). [Col. 0609C]

Earlier Clement of Alexandria had said:

> Whether it was that Phoroneus, or Merops, or someone else, who erected temples and altars for them.

But we have discussed elsewhere the first origin of temples and Aeacus (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 722 ff. and p. 1118).

At whatever time temples began to be constructed for the gods, however magnificent they may be and however much they glitter with gold and gems, it is certainly established that the true God can never be enclosed within any of them. Yet the pagans were persuaded that their gods were enclosed wholly within them, just as human beings are within their houses. To omit the very many witnesses to this false opinion, [Col. 0609D] what could be clearer than these words of Cicero?

> “I hold that the sanctuaries of the fathers—or, in another reading, of the gods—should be situated in cities. I do not follow the Persian Magi, on whose authority Xerxes is said to have burned the temples of Greece because they enclosed the gods within walls, although all things ought to lie open and free to them, and this whole world ought to be their temple and home. The Greeks and our own people acted better, for, in order to increase piety toward the gods, they wished them to inhabit the same cities as ourselves. For this belief introduces a religious reverence useful to states.”

(Cicero, *On the Laws*, book II, p. 335, line 44.)

But here we miss Cicero’s acuteness, for he did not know—or rather pretended not to know—that the true God is immeasurable and cannot be circumscribed by the extent of any place.

[Col. 0610A] Lucian therefore employs far better reasoning when he ridicules his fellow Gentiles, who asserted that they had built temples for the gods lest the gods should lack roofs or homes (Lucian, *On Sacrifices*, p. 185). Timaeus—or, as Plutarch relates, Hegesias of Magnesia—likewise joked freely when he said that the temple of Diana of Ephesus had burned down because Diana had wished to be present at the labor of Olympias, the mother of Alexander the Great, and was therefore absent from her home, that is, from her temple (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, p. 224, line 26; Plutarch, *Life of Alexander the Great*, p. 665). Although certain more knowledgeable pagans similarly ridiculed these things, all the rest were nevertheless wholly possessed by the opinion that their gods were not immeasurable and could therefore be enclosed and contained in a particular place.

For this reason they founded for these same gods not merely the most costly [Col. 0610B] temples, but also, as Arnobius says, huts, rooms, and small chambers—that is, small sanctuaries or certain private shrines within those magnificent temples, in which the image of a particular god was placed (Arnob., book VI, p. 191). From Aulus Gellius we learn that Scipio, namely Africanus, was accustomed to enter the Capitol at twilight “and order the chamber of Jupiter to be opened, and to remain there alone for a long time, as though consulting with Jupiter about the Republic” (A. Gell., *Attic Nights*, book VII, ch. 1, p. 396). This is confirmed by Livy, Valerius Maximus, and Aurelius Victor. Nor is mention of these chambers infrequent among other writers (Livy, book XXVI, ch. 19; Val. Max., book II, ch. 2, § 2; Aur. Vict., *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 49).

If, however, anyone proves that by “hut,” “room,” and “small chamber” Arnobius should also be understood as referring [Col. 0610C] to the small buildings customarily erected for lesser gods, we shall not entirely oppose him. But all must necessarily admit that those whom the Gentiles thought could be enclosed within either small or very great buildings and temples were not true gods.

Nor does Arnobius think that the Gentiles should be heard when they replied that they built temples for the gods so that, with the gods present there in some manner, they might speak to them face-to-face and at close range, and so that the gods might hear them speaking from nearby. For the true God, immeasurable and present everywhere, hears all people speaking and praying in every part of the world, and fully knows even all their thoughts. For [Col. 0610D] He does not, as Jupiter is imagined to do, go to dine among the Ethiopians; indeed, He can never change His location (Homer, *Iliad* I, p. 20; Lucian, *On Sacrifices*, p. 186; Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, book I, p. 62; Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, book VIII, p. 363; Greg. Naz., oration 1 against Julian, p. 263).

Arnobius insists that from this opinion of the pagans, who believed their gods moved from place to place, it follows that no hope would remain to human beings of being heard by them. For many temples had been erected to one and the same god in different and exceedingly distant regions of the earth, yet they believed him to inhabit only one of them. That god could therefore hear no others except those who prayed in that particular temple. Thus [Col. 0611A] other people prayed to him in other temples in vain, since, being absent from them, he could not hear them, much less grant any of their requests.

But let us follow our author as he presses the pagans further. The temples and sanctuaries of the gods, he says (Arnob., book VI, p. 193), are the tombs of dead human beings, or, as he himself puts it, “raised above the funeral pyres of the dead.” In these temples, therefore, the Gentiles either worshiped dead human beings as immortal gods, or, to the dishonor of the gods, associated dead human beings with them while they were alive, or believed that both alike were dead and buried. What greater insult could be offered to divine majesty?

Although Arnobius could have proved this by almost innumerable examples, he considered it sufficient for his purpose [Col. 0611B] to select several that were absolutely certain, which he presented as follows:

> “In the ninth book of his *Histories*, Antiochus records that Cecrops was committed to the earth at Athens, in the temple of Minerva. Again, Acrisius is written and indicated to have been buried in the temple of that same goddess situated on the citadel of Larissa; Erichthonius in the shrine of Athena Polias; the brothers Dairas and Immarus within the precinct of the Eleusinium below the city. What then? Are the daughters of Celeus not reported to have received burial rites in the temple of Eleusinian Ceres? Were not Hyperoche and Laodice—who are said to have been brought there from the lands of the Hyperboreans—buried in Diana’s sanctuary situated within that of Delian Apollo? Leandrius says that Clearchus received his final funeral rites in the Didymaeum at Miletus. Myndius declares, and [Col. 0611C] Zeno records, that the monument of Leucophryne is in the shrine of Diana at Magnesia. Is it not indicated by established writings that the seer Telmessus was buried beneath the small altar of Apollo which is seen near the town of Telmessus? Ptolemy son of Agesarchus, in the first book which he published concerning Philopator, declares on the authority of written records that King Cinyras of Paphos was laid to rest with his entire family—indeed, with all his descendants—in the temple of Venus.”

(Ibid.)

All these things were undoubtedly taken from the following Greek words of Clement of Alexandria:

> “In the temple of Athena at Larissa, upon the citadel, is the tomb of Acrisius. At Athens, on the Acropolis, is the tomb of Cecrops, as Antiochus says in the ninth book of his *Histories*. And what of Erichthonius? Was he not buried in the temple of Athena Polias? And were Immarus, son of Eumolpus and Daeira, not buried within the precinct of the Eleusinium below the Acropolis? Were the daughters of Celeus not buried [Col. 0611D] at Eleusis? Why should I enumerate for you the women of the Hyperboreans? They were called Hyperoche and Laodice; they were buried in the sanctuary of Artemis at Delos, which is within the sacred precinct of Delian Apollo. Leandrius says that Clearchus was buried at Miletus in the Didymaeum. Nor should we pass over the monument of Leucophryne, if we follow Zeno and Myndius: she was buried in the sanctuary of Artemis at Magnesia. Nor indeed should we omit the altar of Apollo at Telmessus, which historians report to be the monument of the seer Telmessus. Ptolemy son of Agesarchus, in the first book of his work concerning Philopator, says that at Paphos, in the sanctuary of Aphrodite, Cinyras and the descendants of Cinyras were buried.”

(Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Gentiles*, p. 29.)

We have presented this entire passage of Clement of Alexandria [Col. 0612A] and Arnobius so that everyone may readily understand that it was transcribed by our author and rendered into Latin in such a way that no other translation is needed. We have elsewhere elucidated the divergent readings occurring in the two texts and whatever is obscure and difficult in them (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 1, ch. 7, art. 3, pp. 725 ff.).

Arnobius adds two points. The first is this: “Nor does it require careful investigation to discover what punishment that Egyptian established for anyone who revealed where Apis lay hidden” (Arnob., book VI, p. 164), that is, where the tomb of Apis was situated. Apis, however, as Strabo and others testify, is the same as Serapis and Osiris. That Arnobius is speaking about his tomb is plainly demonstrated by what we have noted elsewhere [Col. 0612B] (Strabo, book XVII, p. 807; *Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 14, art. 4).

Second, Arnobius proves from the testimony of four authors—Sammonicus, Granius, Valerianus, and Fabius—that the name of the Capitol was derived from the head of Tolus, which had been dug up and discovered in its foundations after Tolus had been killed by his brother’s slaves and left unburied by his fellow citizens (Arnob., loc. cit., p. 194). This may readily be confirmed by many other witnesses. Varro writes: “The Capitol was so named because, when the foundations of the temple of Jupiter were being dug here, a human head is said to have been found.” Livy says: “Here is the Capitol, where, when a human head was once found, the response was given that in this place would be the head of the world and the supreme seat of empire.” These things are related more fully by Dionysius of Halicarnassus [Col. 0612C] and Pliny, whom anyone may readily and easily consult. By what reasoning, therefore, could Theodorus Canterus and certain others assert that no one besides Arnobius is found to have mentioned these matters? Moreover, what honor was it for Jupiter to possess the greatest of all temples, built and named not so much after himself as after a dead man? (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book IV, p. 10; Livy, book V, near the end, ch. 54; Dion. Halic., book IV, pp. 257 ff.; Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXVIII, ch. 2, p. 558; Canterus, *Various Readings*, book I, ch. 11.)

Finally, Arnobius asks: “In what temples are Varro’s *polyandria* enclosed?” (Arnob., ibid., p. 194). A *polyandrion*, as is clear from sacred and secular writers, was a place in which [Col. 0612D] the bodies of several human beings were buried. Arnobius’ meaning, therefore, is that the temples of the gods were shared with dead and buried human beings, whom the pagans had nevertheless not dared to enroll in the calendars of those same gods. In the preceding dissertation we showed that there were many temples in which the pagans openly proclaimed that their gods were buried (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 15, art. 2). Who, then, would not share Arnobius’ indignation that temples and sacred buildings were erected and consecrated to gods of this kind, although they are owed only to the living and eternal God?

## ARTICLE II  
### On Temples Impiously Consecrated to Human Affections or Virtues—Namely, Piety, Concord, Safety, Honor, Virtue, Happiness, Victory, Peace, and Equity—and, among the Egyptians, to Cats, Scarab Beetles, and Heifers; and How Correctly the Destruction of Temples Proves That None Should Be Built for False Gods

[Col. 0613A]

Temples were founded by the pagans not only for dead human beings, but also for the affections and fortunes of the living, as though these were true gods. At the beginning of his fourth book Arnobius censures their absurd and blind impiety—especially that of the Romans—in these terms:

> “I should like to ask you, and before all others the Romans themselves, the lords and rulers of the world, whether you believe that Piety, Concord, Safety, Honor, Virtue, Happiness, and the other divine powers of this kind, [Col. 0613B] for which we see that you have erected altars together with magnificent temples, possess divine power and dwell in the regions of heaven?”

(Arnob., book IV, p. 127.)

A little later he added that temples of Victory, Peace, and Equity had similarly been constructed by the same pagans. We must briefly inquire how true these statements are.

Famous and unknown to few is the story of a daughter—whether of plebeian or freeborn status—who nourished her mother with her own milk while the latter was confined in prison, lest she perish from hunger (Val. Max., book II, ch. 5, § 7, pp. 268 ff.); or, as others relate, she nourished her father. Pliny, and Solinus after him, relate that in memory of this deed a temple of Piety was founded in that same prison, in the consulship of Gaius Quinctius and Manius Acilius, at the place where the theater of Marcellus stood. Nor are there lacking those who believe that it [Col. 0613C] was the very temple which Manius Acilius Glabrio, according to Livy, established and dedicated in the Forum Holitorium (Pliny, *Natural History*, book VII, ch. 36, p. 57; Solinus, *Polyhistor*, ch. 1, p. 11; Livy, book XL, ch. 34).

From the same Livy we further learn that Gaius Flavius consecrated a temple of Concord in the precinct of Vulcan, and that another was established on the citadel by duumvirs appointed for that purpose (Idem, book IX, ch. 46, and book XXII, ch. 33). Cicero also attests that, during Cotta’s consulship, the temple of Concord was struck from heaven; mention of it is likewise made in Dio’s history and in the registers of the Roman magistrates (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, p. 223, line 5; and *On Divination*, book I, p. 252; Dio, *Roman History*, book XLIV, p. 275; and vol. XI [Col. 0613D] of *Roman Antiquities*, p. 189). Hence Ovid sang:

> You too, Concord, Livia dedicates in a magnificent temple,  
> which she bestowed upon her beloved husband.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, book VI, near the end.)

But Augustine ridicules and rejects these things as they deserve; the reader may consult him (Augustine, *City of God*, book III, ch. 25, p. 82).

Cicero, however, mentions the temples not only of Concord, but also of Virtue, Honor, Safety, and Victory, as though they were known to everyone. He also informs us that the temple of Honor had been restored by M. Marcellus (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, p. 223, line 6). Livy, moreover, has recorded that the temple of Safety, which [Col. 0614A] the consul had vowed during the Samnite War, was built by C. Junius Bubulcus and dedicated by him when he was dictator (Livy, IX, ch. 43, and X, ch. 1).

Livy further relates—and Plutarch agrees with him—that during the Gallic War at Clastidium Marcellus vowed a temple to Honor and Virtue, but that its dedication was prevented by the pontiffs, who maintained that a single sanctuary could not duly be dedicated to more than one god (Livy, XXVII, ch. 25; Plutarch, *Life of Marcellus*, p. 314). Valerius Maximus, however, testifies that this admonition from the pontiffs caused Marcellus to place the images of Honor and Virtue in separate temples (Valerius Maximus, I, § 8, p. 9). Vitruvius mentions both temples, as does Symmachus, who wrote the following to Ausonius: “Wisely [Col. 0614B] and properly did our ancestors—as they did other things in that age—place the twin temples of Honor and Virtue side by side, having conceived in thought what we have seen realized in you: that the rewards of honor are found where the merits of virtue are found.” Pliny, moreover, reports that this temple of Honor and Virtue was restored by the emperor Vespasian Augustus. Finally, we learn once again from Livy that another temple of Virtue was consecrated at the Capene Gate by M. Marcellus, son of the Marcellus whom we have mentioned (Vitruvius, III, ch. 1, and VII, Preface; Symmachus, I, epistle 14; Pliny, *Natural History*, XXXV, ch. 10, p. 224; Livy, IX, ch. 11).

As for Felicity, Pliny bears witness that Praxiteles made two statues which had been placed before the temple of Felicity (Pliny, *Natural History*, XXXIV, [Col. 0614C] ch. 8, p. 120). If Cicero is to be believed: “That L. Mummius,” as he says, “removed from Thespiae the statues now standing by the temple of Felicity, as well as the other secular statues from that town” (Cicero, fourth speech *Against Verres*, p. 160, line 39). We also read further references to the temple of Felicity in Dio, Augustine, and others (Dio, *Roman History*, XLIV, p. 278; Augustine, *City of God*, IV, chs. 18 and 23, pp. 100 and 104).

Postumius, moreover, if Livy is to be trusted, “dedicated the temple of Victory, whose construction, from money raised through fines, he had overseen while curule aedile” (Livy, X, ch. 33). In yet another book Livy mentions two different temples of Victory in these words: “M. Porcius Cato dedicated the shrine of Maiden Victory near the temple of Victory, [Col. 0614D] two years after he had vowed it” (ibid., XXXV, ch. 9). Pausanias and Dionysius of Halicarnassus also speak of the sanctuary of Victory (Pausanias, I, p. 20; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, I, p. 26). Elsewhere we also noted that Symmachus, after petitioning the emperor Valentinian to restore the altar of Victory in the senate-house, was refuted by Ambrose (*Observations on Ambrose*, epistle 18, and the *Memorial of Symmachus*, vol. II).

We further learn from Suetonius that the emperor Vespasian built the temple of Peace near the Forum, which Pliny, Xiphilinus, Josephus, and others mention. Moreover, according to the evidence of Pausanias, the statue of Chimene was transported to Rome, to the temple of Peace (Suetonius, [Col. 0615A] *Life of Vespasian*, ch. 9, p. 739; Pliny, *Natural History*, XII, ch. 19, p. 36, and XXXVI, ch. 15, p. 309, and elsewhere; Xiphilinus, *Epitome*, p. 221; Josephus, *Jewish War*, VII, ch. 24, p. 979; Pausanias, VI, p. 179).

Finally, by the name Equity Arnobius undoubtedly means Justice, concerning which Ovid appears to have composed these verses:

> No god is more moderate than our prince;  
> Through Justice he tempers his powers.  
> Caesar recently placed her in a temple made of marble,  
> Having long before placed her in the shrine of his own mind.

(Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, III, epistle 6, verses 23 ff.)

Some, however, judge that nothing concerning this temple is found in trustworthy authors, and that the poet therefore alluded to the temple of Mars the Avenger, since vengeance, [Col. 0615B] of which Ovid speaks, is one part of justice. But should Arnobius not be regarded as a sufficiently trustworthy witness, when he affirms that even in his own time Equity, like Victory and Peace, was honored with a temple by the Romans? Juvenal, moreover, includes in these two verses the temples of several gods whom our Author names individually:

> As Peace and Faith are worshiped, Victory and Virtue,  
> And Concord, who chatters when her nest is greeted.

(Juvenal, satire 1, verses 114 ff.)

We too have touched upon these matters elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 766).

Arnobius therefore rightly and deservedly assails the stupidity of the pagans, who had built temples for such fictitious divinities. Yet he undoubtedly [Col. 0615C] followed Cicero before him, who declares in the following words that these matters require no refutation:

> Do you therefore think that a more subtle line of reasoning is needed to refute these things? For we see that mind, faith, hope, virtue, honor, victory, safety, concord, and other things of this kind possess the efficacy of things, not of gods. Either they exist within ourselves—as do mind, faith, hope, virtue, and concord—or they are things to be desired by us, such as honor, safety, and victory. I see the usefulness of these things, and I also see that their images have been consecrated. But why divine power should reside in them I shall understand only when I have learned the reason.

(Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, III, p. 248, line 41.)

But if this impiety of the nations seemed to a pagan orator unworthy even of refutation, how much less worthy of refutation was the far greater madness of the Egyptians, [Col. 0615D] who, as Arnobius says, erected temples with lofty gables for cats, scarabs, and heifers, or young cattle (Arnobius, I, p. 15). Origen therefore rightly and deservedly rebukes the utterly demented rashness of Celsus, who, he says, even wishes to compare our religion with that of the Egyptians. To someone approaching the Egyptians, splendid sacred precincts with groves present themselves, as do temples with vestibules and porticoes, astonishing in their extraordinary size and beauty, along with exceedingly religious and mystical rites; but once inside, he will see a cat, an ape, a crocodile, a goat, or a dog being worshiped:

> Yet he wishes to compare the affairs of our faith with those of the Egyptians. Among them, someone approaching finds splendid sacred precincts and groves, gateways impressive in size and beauty, [Col. 0616A] marvelous temples, proud structures all around, and superstitious, mystic rites; but when he enters and proceeds farther within, he sees a cat, an ape, a crocodile, a goat, or a dog being worshiped.

(Origen, *Against Celsus*, III, pp. 120 ff.)

But we have discussed these matters in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* and elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 496–767, and the preceding *Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 12, art. 2).

We also examined another argument of Arnobius against the temples of the gods, drawn from their overthrow and ruin (ibid.). If, however, anything new concerning it presents itself, it will be weighed and elucidated in our customary manner in the following chapter, where we shall discuss the images of the gods, with which he connected that argument.

# CHAPTER XXII  
## On the Statues and Images of the Gods

[Col. 0616B]

## ARTICLE I  
### By what weight of reasoning Arnobius demonstrates that the images, statues, and representations of the gods were impiously worshiped and adored by the pagans; the face of a lion smeared with pure vermilion; and the earliest cult-images and others represented in human form

Arnobius turns to the images, statues, and representations of the gods, which, as we shall show a little later (Arnobius, VI, pp. 194 ff.), the pagans believed either to be their very gods themselves or at least to be inhabited by them (below, art. 4). By various kinds of argument he proves that those objects, which had been fashioned with much artistry, were worshiped and adored with an altogether impious and absurd religion. For, first, if the pagans had been persuaded that their gods existed and dwelt in heaven, they certainly ought to have directed their prayers to the gods themselves, not [Col. 0616C] to their images. If they doubted that the gods existed, it was ridiculous to fashion an image of something whose existence was uncertain.

Nor could they say that the presence of beings whom they were in no way able to see was manifested through images, and that those beings were then worshiped with greater devotion and dutiful services rendered to them. For how can someone who says this affirm that the gods truly exist when, as Arnobius says, “he needs to see something tangible, lest perhaps that which appears obscure should be empty” (ibid., p. 195)? That is, he reveals that he calls into doubt whether the gods exist, since he will not believe in their existence unless he sees their images.

“But,” the pagans said, “we honor our gods through their images.” Arnobius replies that this is wrong. For if there were no images of the gods, [Col. 0616D] they would never have worshiped them. Moreover, what could be more insulting to these gods than not to honor the very beings whom one believes to exist, but to worship them only through some likeness devoid of every faculty of sensation, as though through some kind of entrusted intermediary? Finally, this reply of the pagans was entirely futile and frivolous, since they believed that these likenesses and images were themselves gods.

Arnobius presses these idolaters still harder and makes it plain that they could not have known whether those gods of theirs, whom they had never seen, really were such as they represented them. But something that does not resemble another thing cannot be its likeness or image. Yet the pagans represented the sun as a man, the moon as a woman, and the winds as certain men blowing trumpets with puffed-out cheeks. [Col. 0617A] Who could ever have dared to say that these were true images of them?

Arnobius then immediately added:

> Among your gods we see the most savage face of a lion (the royal manuscript reads *leones*, “lions”), smeared with pure vermilion and called by the name Frugifer (“Fruit-Bearer”; the royal manuscript reads *frugiferio*).

(Ibid., p. 196.)

It is remarkable how severely this obscure passage has exercised the ingenuity of scholars. Latinus Latinius, however, seems to cut rather than untie the knot of this difficulty when he proposed correcting the words as follows: “Among the gods we see lions with an exceedingly savage face smeared with pure vermilion” (Latinius, *Sacred and Prophetic Library*, p. 98). But this is mere conjecture, founded on the authority of no manuscript. Accordingly, among those who wish nothing in ancient writings to be changed except upon the surest grounds, [Col. 0617B] some suspect that these words of our Author are to be understood of the Sun. Others refute them, however, because he had spoken separately of the Sun. It therefore appears more probable to some that he means the lions that were sometimes sculpted upon the gables of temples. But these seem to have been placed there as ornaments of the building rather than to represent the face of gods. We, therefore, shall more readily be persuaded that by these words our Author means the same thing that Minucius Felix said after Tertullian: “You consecrate as gods beings compounded of goat and man, and the faces of lions and dogs.” For after the words cited by us, Arnobius added: “It is a mask without the rest of the body, a face alone, with roaring jaws, savage mouth, and a blood-red coating of wax . . . [Col. 0617C] and weary dogs” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 16, and *To the Nations*, I, ch. 12; Minucius Felix, p. 261; Arnobius, passage cited, p. 196).

Who would not readily concede that both authors are speaking of images such as those of Pan, the Satyrs, and other beings of this sort, as we have shown in our dissertation on the book of Minucius Felix (Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 11, art. 3)? Arnobius’s addition in the same place—that the face was smeared with vermilion—plainly concerns that utterly ridiculous pagan custom by which they regularly coated the faces of images with vermilion. For we read in Pliny that “the face of the image of Jupiter himself was customarily smeared with vermilion on feast days” (Pliny, *Natural History*, XXXV, ch. 7, p. 56). Concerning the likeness of Pan, Virgil sings:

> [Col. 0617D] Pan, the god of Arcadia, came—whom we ourselves have seen  
> Red upon his cheeks with blood-red elderberries and vermilion.

(Virgil, *Eclogue* 10, verses 26–27.)

On these verses Servius observes: “*Ebulum* is a kind of plant resembling the elder. Vermilion is used because Pan is depicted with a red face, on account of his resemblance to the ether.”

Arnobius therefore concludes from this that it is the height of rashness to fashion a likeness and form of the gods that no one has ever been able to prove was truly theirs. Accordingly, Lucian wrote somewhere in the clearest terms:

> After erecting temples so that the gods supposedly might not be without houses or hearths, they portray their forms, summoning for the task Praxiteles, Polyclitus, or Phidias. But I do not know where these artists saw the likeness that they reproduce.

(Lucian, *On Sacrifices*, p. 185.)

That is: once sanctuaries [Col. 0618A] have been erected so that the gods may supposedly not lack roofs or homes, they fashion their forms, employing for the purpose Praxiteles, Polyclitus, or Phidias. Yet those artists represent a likeness of the gods that I do not know where they ever saw.

To restrain such audacity still further, our Author traces the matter back to its very origin:

> You laugh because in ancient times the Persians worshiped a river, as memorable writings indicate; the Arabs, a shapeless stone; the peoples of Scythia, a *cinaces* [acinaces, a short sword]; the Thespians, a branch in place of Cinxia; the Icarians, an unworked piece of wood in place of Diana; the people of Pessinus, a flint in place of the Mother of the Gods; the Romans, a spear in place of Mars, as Varro’s *Muses* indicate; and, as Aethlius records, before the practice and art of image-makers, the Samians worshiped a board in place of Juno.

(Arnobius, VI, pp. 196 ff.)

Here he follows Clement of Alexandria, [Col. 0618B] whose following Greek words he had undoubtedly read:

> Long ago the Scythians worshiped the *acinaces*, the Arabs a stone, and the Persians a river. Among the other peoples, those who were still more ancient set up conspicuous pieces of wood and erected pillars made of stone; these were also called *xoana* (ξόανα), because they were scraped and carved from their material. At Icarus, indeed, the image of Artemis was an unworked piece of wood; and at Thespiae the image of Hera Cithaeronia was a hewn tree trunk. The image of the Samian Hera, as Aethlius says, was at first a plank, but later, in the archonship of Procles, it was fashioned into the form of a statue. . . . In Rome, according to the author Varro, the ancient cult-image of Ares was a spear, before craftsmen had yet embarked upon this fair-faced but corrupt artistry.

(Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, pp. 29 ff.)

[Col. 0618C] The Scythians, then, in ancient times worshiped an *acinaces*; the Arabs, a stone; and the Persians, a river. Among other peoples, those who were still more ancient erected conspicuous pieces of wood and set up columns made of stones, which were also called *xoana* (ξόανα), because they were cut away and polished out of their material. At Icarus, certainly, the image of Diana was a piece of unworked wood, while that of Cithaeronian Juno at Thespiae was a hewn trunk. The image of Samian Juno, as Aethlius says, was at first a plank; afterward, during the archonship of Procles, it was fashioned into the form of a statue. . . . At Rome, however, Varro says that in ancient times the statue of Mars was a spear, when craftsmen had not yet arrived at this artistry, outwardly beautiful indeed, but morally corrupt.

You clearly see how Arnobius, when he excerpted these things from Clement of Alexandria, translated them into Latin, omitting certain details and adding something—[Col. 0618D] namely, what he said about a flint representing the likeness of the Mother of the Gods. We discussed this a little earlier (preceding chapter, art. 2), just as we discussed all the other matters in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I, *Apparatus*, book III, dissertation 1, ch. 18, art. 1, pp. 734 ff.). Let us also be permitted to add to all these things what Lucan sang in the following verses about the grove that Caesar ordered to be cut down during the siege of Massilia:

> The trees possess a horror of their own; then copious water falls  
> From black springs, and the mournful images of the gods  
> Lack all art, standing shapeless in hewn trunks.

(Lucan, III, verse 394.)

But if, says Arnobius, the pagans rightly laughed at these things, all the others were surely no less deserving of ridicule [Col. 0619A] when they supplicated immortal gods fashioned in human form (Arnobius, VI, p. 197). For who could ever have believed that gods were composed of human limbs? Therefore, he adds, if it were granted to us to look into the pagans’ innermost thoughts, we would certainly see that they held the same opinions as we do; yet they preferred stubbornly to defend what they had once done without reason rather than yield to acknowledged truth.

## ARTICLE II  
### How correctly Arnobius argues against these same images of false gods from the ridiculous representations of Ammon with ram’s horns, Saturn with a curved sickle, winged Mercury, Argiphontes with a *petasus*, Liber with soft limbs, naked Venus, Vulcan with cap and hammer, the Delian god with plectrum and lyre, the Muses with pipes and psalteries, Neptune with trident, Janus with a toothed key, Jupiter in a *ricinium* with a firebrand, Pallas with a military helmet, the Mother of the Gods with a drum, two-faced Janus, bearded Jupiter, Ceres with large breasts, and Diana with half-covered thighs

[Col. 0619B]

Our Author assails the deplorable blindness of the pagans more sharply (Arnobius, VI, pp. 197 ff.) and plainly shows that they represented the images and likenesses of their gods in a form that provoked in every sensible person a laugh all the greater for being so grim. Was it not the height of madness on the part of those by whom Ammon—or Jupiter, greatest of the gods—was portrayed with ram’s horns, as we have observed elsewhere (Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 15, art. 2)? Nor was the madness of Alexander the Great any less—indeed, it was perhaps greater—for, as Athenaeus, Clement of Alexandria (Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, XII, p. 537; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 36), and others testify, [Col. 0619C] he wished, as the son of this same Ammon, to be represented in the same fashion.

“Saturn,” says Arnobius, “with his curved sickle, is the guardian of the countryside, like some pruner of luxuriant branches” (Arnobius, VI, p. 197). Elsewhere he calls him “the sickle-bearer and planter of vines” (ibid., III, p. 117), and elsewhere again: “A reaping sickle is assigned to Saturn” (ibid., VI, p. 209). Since that remarkable figure of a rustic—or the god of rustics—is unknown to no one, it will suffice to transcribe in confirmation the following words of Macrobius:

> Janus ordered that Saturn be observed with the majesty of religious worship, as the author of a better life. His image bears witness to this, for Janus added to it a sickle, the emblem of the harvest. To this god they ascribe the arts of grafting shoots, cultivating fruits, [Col. 0619D] and raising all fertile things of this kind.

(Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, I, p. 205.)

If you wish, Ovid may be added here; he sang:

> An ancient tradition says that, when the land was called Saturnian,  
> Such words were spoken by the prophetic god:  
> “Offer sacrifice to the sickle-bearing old man; let the nations send  
> Two bodies.”

(Ovid, *Fasti*, V, § 13.)

Arnobius then continues: “The son of Maia with his *petasus*”—that is, Mercury (Arnobius, VI, p. 197). The *petasus*—Greek πέτασος—was a hat or cap, so called because it had broad brims. Athenaeus writes (Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, XII, p. 537) that Alexander the Great sometimes wore Mercury’s attire at banquets, “the *petasus* upon his head and [Col. 0620A] the herald’s staff in his hand.” That is: the *petasus* upon his head and the caduceus in his hands. Plautus introduces Mercury speaking as follows:

> I shall keep these little wings here on my *petasus*.

(Plautus, Prologue to the *Amphitryon*.)

If you please, consult Lambinus’s observations on this verse.

For the same reason our Author later said: “Winged Mercury Argiphontes” (Arnobius, VI, p. 209). The royal manuscript incorrectly reads *Argiforonites*. For *Argiphontes*—in Greek Ἀργειφόντης—is an epithet of Mercury, used more than once by Homer, among others, and rendered into Latin by his translator as “slayer of Argus and messenger” (Homer, *Iliad*, XVI, p. 296, and XXIV, p. 418). [Col. 0620B] Some maintain that Mercury was so surnamed because he killed Argus; others prefer to derive it from the speed and swiftness of speech, over which he was said to preside. On this matter see Macrobius and Lilius Giraldus (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, I, ch. 9, p. 268; Giraldus, *Syntagma on the Gods*, 9, pp. 291 ff.).

Arnobius proceeds:

> Liber with soft limbs, utterly enervated by the looseness of a womanish fluidity; Venus naked and exposed, as though you meant to display publicly and put up for sale the figure of a body available for hire.

(Arnobius, VI, p. 197.)

Concerning Liber—that is, Bacchus or Dionysus—Lucian says:

> All of you, I think, see how soft and womanish he is by nature, half-mad from sensual pleasures and breathing out unmixed wine from the first moment of morning.

(Lucian, *Council of the Gods*, p. 1096.)

[Col. 0620C] That is: “All of you, I think, see how soft and effeminate he is, half-mad with pleasures and breathing undiluted wine from the earliest morning.” Concerning Venus, Clement of Alexandria writes:

> And if someone sees a naked woman depicted, he understands her to be golden Aphrodite. . . . The statue was an image of Aphrodite, and it was naked.

(Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 38.)

That is: “If anyone sees a naked woman depicted, he understands her to be golden Venus. . . . It was an image of Venus, and it was naked.” Concerning her and Bacchus, Theodoret says:

> Venus, the teacher of these prostitutes, both statuaries and sculptors fashion naked, and they do not cover her even with a little tunic. . . . Dionysus too is fashioned by them with loosened limbs and naked.

(Theodoret, sermon 3, *On Angels and Demons*, vol. IV, p. 520.)

That is: “Statuaries and sculptors make Venus, the teacher of these prostitutes, naked, and do not even cover her [Col. 0620D] with a tunic. . . . The same artists also make Bacchus with soft and loosened limbs and an effeminate body.” Finally, Tertullian charges it as a fault against the pagans that they displayed Bacchus and Venus in the theaters under so shameful and infamous an appearance (Tertullian, *On the Shows*, ch. 10).

What more need be said? “Vulcan,” says Arnobius, “with cap and hammer”; or, as he said later, “Mulciber in a smith’s attire” (Arnobius, VI, pp. 197 and 209). For, as we read in Macrobius: “Mulciber is Vulcan, because he is fire and softens and subdues all things” (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, VI, ch. 7). He was represented in a smith’s attire because, as we have said elsewhere (*Dissertation*), they believed that he presided over the work of smiths.

[Col. 0621A] Because of a similar presidency, “the Delian god”—these are still Arnobius’s words—“with plectrum and lyre,” namely Apollo, and “the Muses with pipes and psalteries,” were seen (Arnobius, VI, pp. 197 and 209). This is sufficiently confirmed by Pausanias and others (Pausanias, III, p. 107, and VIII, p. 263). The king of the sea—namely, Neptune—was likewise depicted with a *fuscina*, as our Author calls it, that is, a trident (Arnobius, VI, pp. 197 and 209). The *fuscina*, a word also used by Cicero, or trident, is called Neptune’s scepter (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, I, p. 210, line 16). Even to children the following verses of Virgil, concerning Neptune addressing Aeolus, are surely familiar:

> Not to him was sovereignty over the sea and the savage trident  
> Given by lot, but to me.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, I, verses 142 ff.)

[Col. 0621B] Arnobius added: “As though he had to undertake a gladiatorial contest”; for gladiators, and especially net-fighters, were armed with a trident when they fought against murmillos. Hence Juvenal:

> The trident of Gracchus in his tunic defeated even this monster,  
> And in flight the gladiator traversed the middle of the arena, etc.

(Juvenal, satire 2, verse 143.)

See the observations of various scholars on these verses, and Lipsius, *Saturnalia*, II, ch. 8, vol. III, pp. 518 ff.

Furthermore, placed before everyone’s eyes was (Arnobius, VI, p. 209) Janus with a toothed key, plainly for opening the doors over which he was believed to preside. Thus Virgil sang:

> [Col. 0621C] Nor does Janus, their guardian, leave the threshold.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, VII, verse 610.)

And Ovid:

> He holds a staff in his right hand and a key in his left.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, I.)

Jupiter, Arnobius continues, was “clad in a *ricinium*, holding in his right hand a firebrand carefully carved in the likeness of a thunderbolt” (Arnobius, VI, p. 209). A person was called *riciniatus* from the *ricinium*, which Varro explains as follows:

> The *ricinium* was the garment worn by the most ancient people. It was so called because they used it doubled and cast half of it backward: from *reicere*, “to cast back,” it was called a *ricinium*.

(Varro, *On the Latin Language*, IV, p. 32.)

Servius, moreover, says: “A *ricinium* is so called because it is cast behind the back; it is what people commonly call a *mavorte*” (Servius on *Aeneid*, I, verse 286). Isidore endorsed this explanation (Isidore, *Origins*, XIX, ch. 25). Nonius [Col. 0621D] Marcellus, however, says that it is the same as a *masurtium*, a short female cloak. But Festus writes that a *ricinium* is any square garment (Festus, *On the Meaning of Words*). Sometimes, however, certain authors, such as Cicero, use it for a mourning garment (Cicero, *On the Laws*, II, p. 341). Arnobius undoubtedly employed the term here in the former sense.

A *fomes*, moreover, is dry and parched material that easily catches fire; the term may also signify the sparks struck from glowing iron. Hence Virgil:

> First Achates struck a spark from flint,  
> Caught the fire in leaves, placed dry fuel around it,  
> And swiftly seized the flame in the tinder.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, I, verses 178 ff.)

[Col. 0622A] Who, moreover, does not recognize the “little maiden hiding beneath a military helmet,” as our Author expresses it (Arnobius, VI, p. 209)? For no one would deny that this is Pallas, whom Ovid describes as painting herself in this way:

> But to herself she gives a shield and a spear with a sharp point;  
> She gives her head a helmet, while the aegis protects her breast.

(Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, VI, p. 201.)

“The Mother of the Gods with a drum,” Arnobius adds. Her image was indeed fashioned with drums around her to signify the roundness of the earth and its two hemispheres. Concerning her and the others mentioned above, see Cartari’s book *On the Images of the Gods*.

What Arnobius finally added (ibid.) concerning two-faced Janus, [Col. 0622B] bearded Jupiter Ammon, Ceres’ large breasts, and Diana’s half-covered thighs has been explained by us elsewhere (Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 15, art. 2).

By what folly and madness, then, could the pagans believe that their gods were such as they were fashioned in images and representations of this kind? For who could ever know the true form and figure of any god? Moreover, if through some deceit and fraud the features, clothing, attire, and ornaments of one god were assigned to another, would not pagans who were ignorant of the fraud receive and worship one god in place of another? What, then, could be more absurd or foolish than these images and representations of the gods? Yet this was surely all the more reprehensible because the pagans believed these objects truly to be their very gods [Col. 0622C] themselves, or believed the gods to dwell in them.

## ARTICLE III  
### Another argument of Arnobius against the images of the gods is examined, drawn from images of Mercuries represented in the likeness of Alcibiades, the Cnidian Venus and other Venuses represented in the likenesses of Cratina and Phryne, and also the Jupiter on whose finger Phidias inscribed “Pantarces is beautiful”; and what are called *sigilliola*

The more closely we investigate the superstitions of pagans who worshiped idols, the greater, certainly, do we find their impiety to have been. For it advanced so far that they substituted for the faces and likenesses of their gods images and statues of certain human beings—indeed, of notorious prostitutes. For, says Arnobius, “Who does not know that the Athenians fashioned those Hermae in the bodily likeness of Alcibiades?” (Arnobius, VI, [Col. 0622D] p. 198.) But he took this and what follows from Clement of Alexandria and reproduced it in the reverse order. For Clement wrote in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*:

> The stonecutters at Athens fashioned the Hermae in the likeness of Alcibiades.

(Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 35.)

That is: “Among the Athenians, stonecutters represented Mercuries in the likeness of Alcibiades.”

But Clement had previously said:

> Praxiteles, as Posidippus explains in his book *On Cnidus*, when fashioning the statue of the Cnidian Aphrodite, made her resemble the form of Cratina, the woman he loved.

(Ibid.)

That is: “Praxiteles, as Posidippus states in his book *On Cnidus*, when fashioning the image of the Cnidian Venus, expressed in it the form of Cratina, whom he loved.” Our Arnobius, [Col. 0623A] after the words of his already cited by us, translated this into Latin as follows:

> Who does not know that Praxiteles—if he rereads Posidippus—was compelled, through the rivalry of his skill, to fashion the face of the Cnidian Venus after the form of the prostitute Cratina, whom the unhappy man loved desperately?

(Arnobius, VI, p. 198.)

You plainly see that after the words “if he rereads” there is a lacuna, and that the words “these things in the book *On Cnidus*” are missing through the scribe’s incompetence or negligence; they must be supplied from Clement’s text.

After this, however, Arnobius (ibid.) considerably amplified what Clement had said very briefly:

> When Phryne, the Thespian courtesan, was in her prime, all painters modeled their images of Aphrodite after [Col. 0623B] Phryne’s beauty.

Arnobius narrates the matter as follows:

> That Thespian Phryne, as those who regularly wrote accounts of Thespian affairs report, when she was at the very summit of beauty, charm, and youthful bloom, is said to have served as the model for all the images of Venus held in high esteem, whether throughout the Greek cities or wherever affection and desire for such statues spread.

(Ibid.)

Concerning the gilded likeness of Phryne fashioned by Praxiteles, Pausanias recorded the following:

> Praxiteles fashioned a gilded image of Phryne—he too was one of the woman’s lovers—and the image was a dedication made by Phryne herself.

(Pausanias, X, p. 330.)

That is: “Praxiteles fashioned a gilded likeness of Phryne, being himself one of the woman’s lovers; Phryne herself dedicated the image.” If you wish to know more, you will find in Athenaeus an account not only of this image of Venus but also of another painted by Apelles. [Col. 0623C] You may further consult Plutarch and Aelian and, if you please, what we noted in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, XIII, ch. 6, pp. 590 ff.; Plutarch, *On the Fortune or Virtue of Alexander*, vol. II, p. 336; Aelian, *Various History*, IX, ch. 32; vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 150 and 744).

Indeed, our Author says:

> When Phidias had raised up the form of Olympian Jupiter in a work of immense scale, he inscribed upon the god’s finger, “Pantarces is beautiful.” This was the name of a boy whom he loved and desired with an obscene passion.

(Arnobius, VI, p. 199.)

He borrowed this too from Clement of Alexandria. For this most learned Greek writer had likewise reproached the pagans:

> The Athenian [Col. 0623D] Phidias inscribed upon the finger of Olympian Zeus, “Pantarces is beautiful.” For it was not Zeus who was beautiful to him, but the boy whom he loved.

(Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 35.)

That is: “The Athenian Phidias wrote upon the finger of Olympian Jupiter, ‘Pantarces is beautiful.’ For to him it was not Jupiter who was beautiful, but the one whom he loved.” But we have already treated all these matters in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 530, 737, and 744). We have related them all here so that everyone may see at a single glance what Arnobius excerpted from Clement of Alexandria and how he did so.

From this, together with Clement, he draws an especially powerful argument against pagan images and representations. For what, he asks, could be more impious and more [Col. 0624A] dreadful even to utter than that wanton and shameless statuaries and painters should have been permitted with impunity to inscribe upon the images and representations of the gods memorials of their execrable lusts? The pagans therefore deceived themselves through voluntary blindness: they venerated these images and refused to examine what they were, lest, once the darkness of their errors had been dispersed, they should be compelled to return to a sounder mind.

Arnobius presses them further and addresses them in these words:

> Do you refrain from laughter when, instead of immortal gods, you supplicate little images of human beings and human forms? Indeed, you regard the little figures themselves as gods and believe that nothing apart from these possesses divine power.

(Arnobius, VI, p. 197.)

A little later he rebukes them further in still sharper words:

> To such an extent is it a game and [Col. 0624B] a childish fancy to fashion those little figures, to worship them as gods, and to heap divine sanctities upon them.

(Ibid., p. 199.)

By *sigillaria* and *sigilliola* he means small images made by craftsmen, which represented their gods and were customarily sold publicly or sent to others. Spartianus indeed testifies that such little figures were freely given by the emperor Hadrian to clients and teachers, and that Caracalla gladly accepted them from friends and even sent them to people who were not expecting them (Spartianus, *Life of Hadrian*, around the middle, and *Life of Caracalla*, at the beginning). Macrobius, however, thinks that this custom derived its origin from the festival of the Saturnalia. If that is so, its origin is utterly corrupt; nor was it without the gravest sacrilege that the pagans, as Tertullian says, worshiped these little figures while sitting in chairs or upon benches (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, I, end of ch. 11; [Col. 0624C] Tertullian, *On Prayer*, ch. 12, p. 154).

## ARTICLE IV  
### By what reasoning Arnobius shows, from the material and craftsmanship by which the images of the gods had been made, that the pagans worshiped them with impious reverence and implored their aid; how vain and futile is the pagans’ reply that they venerated images only after their dedication; and an account of fillets, age-decayed trees, and the rite by which the pagans worshiped images

The pagans could not have been ignorant that the images of their gods—which they worshiped humbly, prostrate and bent forward upon their faces, as Arnobius says (Arnobius, VI, p. 200); to which they made trembling supplication; from which in adversity they sought aid, and in prosperity most submissively requested the continuation of love and favor—had been made by craftsmen from gold, silver, ivory, [Col. 0624D] and other earthly materials. Nor could they have been ignorant that these images were fashioned even from women’s ornaments—indeed, sometimes from prostitutes’ adornments—and from cooking pots, that is, little vessels in which stews were cooked, and from other vessels of the same sort, including still more obscene ones. How true these things are we have shown in the preceding dissertation (Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 21, art. 1). Who, moreover, can deny that this veneration of images, representations, and statues—of which we have treated more than once elsewhere—is most rightly and deservedly proscribed and repudiated by Arnobius?

But certainly it deserved condemnation all the more because the pagans sought and expected help, favor, and benefits from these images as though from gods who were present and [Col. 0625A] possessed divine force and power. Indeed, this foolish opinion was so deeply rooted in pagan minds that the Sicilians, according to Cicero, complained that “they no longer had even gods in their cities to whom they might flee, because Gaius Verres had removed their most sacred images from their most venerable shrines” (Cicero, *Against Verres*, Oration 4, opening, p. 46). According to Livy, the ambassadors of Ambracia likewise complained in the Roman senate:

> Our property has been taken away, and—what troubles us above all—the temples throughout the city have been stripped of their ornaments; the images of the gods, indeed the gods themselves, have been torn from their seats and carried away, leaving only bare walls and doorposts. No gods remain for the Ambracians to adore, to whom they may pray and make supplication.

(Livy, Book XXXVIII, ch. 43.)

Who, from these words, [Col. 0625B] does not perceive how plainly and seriously the most distinguished men among the pagans asserted before the Roman senate—and the Romans themselves likewise asserted—that these images truly were their gods, or that the gods inhabited them as their own dwellings, so that once these images had been removed they believed that they no longer had any gods?

If, however, someone excessively obstinate should still dare to deny this or call it into doubt, he will certainly be thoroughly refuted by the authority of our Arnobius, whom no one of sound mind can contradict. For openly, and not without the deepest grief of a contrite heart, he declares (Arnobius, Book I, p. 22) that when he was entangled in pagan errors, which were thoroughly familiar to him, he had been entirely persuaded that the images of the gods and the painted ribbons on age-decayed trees were the gods themselves, [Col. 0625C] whom he flattered, addressed, and from whom he sought benefits, as though, he says, the present power of the gods were inherent in them, or the gods truly dwelt within them.

What could be clearer or more explicit than this testimony? Who will deny that this opinion of Arnobius—or rather, as he himself admits, this most grievous error—was shared by him with other pagans? Hence Tertullian says of the time before images of the gods were manufactured: “A god himself was nowhere. For at that time the artistry of the Greeks and Etruscans had not yet flooded the City with manufactured images” (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25, p. 28). But we have briefly discussed that absurd pagan opinion and impiety in the first volume of our *Apparatus* (Apparatus, pp. 496 ff., 750 ff.). Tertullian, however, must be treated in his proper place. [Col. 0625D]

Moreover, Arnobius spoke of *taeniae*—Greek ταινίαι—that is, bands, or, as Servius observes (Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid*, Book V, p. 374), fillets or the ends of fillets, upon *veternosae* trees, that is, trees worn out by age or by a longstanding disease, as Donatus explains (Donatus on Terence, *Eunuch*, act 4, scene 4). Our author therefore means that, while he was still a pagan, he worshiped fillets and garlands upon trees consumed by great age—or rather, ancient trees wreathed with fillets and garlands. For the pagans of old worshiped trees dedicated to some god as though they were gods or the dwelling places of gods. Pliny says:

> These were the temples of divine powers, and, according to the ancient rite, even [Col. 0626A] now simple country folk dedicate an exceptionally fine tree to a god. We worship groves and the very silence within them no less than images gleaming with gold and ivory.

(Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XII, ch. 1, p. 4.)

Concerning the Phoenicians, Philo reported the following from Sanchuniathon, and Sanchuniathon from Taautus, if Eusebius is to be believed:

> Οὗτοί γε πρῶτοι ἀφιέρωσαν τὰ τῆς γῆς βλαστήματα, καὶ θεοὺς ἐνόμιζον, προσεκύνουν ταῦτα.

> They were the first of all to consecrate the growths of the earth—and consequently trees—and, regarding them as gods, rendered them worshipful adoration.

(Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book III, ch. 10, p. 34.)

Arnobius also mentions an anointed stone, which we discussed in our preceding dissertation, where we also touched upon trees (Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 19, art. 2). Arnobius therefore declares that formerly, [Col. 0626B] when he followed the foolish superstitions of the pagans, he worshiped and adored images, trees, and stones, sought benefits from them, and was falsely persuaded that these were the gods themselves and that divine force and power inhered in them.

Although, after becoming a Christian, he confesses with bitter sorrow and sincere repentance that he had worshiped the images of the gods (Arnobius, Book III, p. 101), such was nevertheless the obstinacy of the pagans that they regarded and venerated as gods the very objects which they could not have been unaware were made from the cheapest clay, once those objects had been placed in their temples. Truly blind men, in order to obtain something from them, as Arnobius says, “prostrated themselves before the faces of the gods”—that is, of the images—“and swept the very thresholds with their kisses” (ibid., Book I, [Col. 0626C] p. 29). This was indeed a rite of worshipers, as may sufficiently be gathered from Suetonius, Livy, Polybius, and others (Suetonius, Book VII, *Life of Vitellius*, shortly after the beginning; Livy, Book XXX, ch. 8; Polybius, Book XV, opening). Hence Tibullus sang:

> Nor am I unable, as a suppliant, to crawl upon the earth on my knees,  
> And to strike my wretched head upon the sacred ground.  
> Nor, if I have deserved it, would I hesitate to fall prostrate in temples  
> And give kisses to the consecrated thresholds.

(Tibullus, Book I, elegy 5.)

Lucretius, however, as quoted by Lactantius (Lactantius, *Institutes*, Book II, ch. 3, p. 150), denounces the impious worship of his fellow pagans in these verses:

> Nor is it any piety often to be seen with veiled head,  
> Turning toward a stone and approaching every altar,  
> Nor to fall prostrate upon the ground and spread one’s palms  
> [Col. 0626D] Before the shrines of the gods.

(Lucretius, Book V, vv. 1198 ff.)

Read also, if you wish, Plutarch, Lucan, and Brissonius, who recorded many details concerning these pagan rites (Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, p. 266; Lucan, Book II, vv. 128 ff.; Brissonius, *On Forms*, Book I, p. 46).

Arnobius next attacks this impiety most sharply, saying that “if it were possible to enter the inner recesses of some image,” or, as he states more clearly shortly afterward, “all its cavities and joints” (Arnobius, Book VI, pp. 201 ff.), nothing would be seen except its various parts, held together by iron chains, hooks, clamps, and poured lead. [Col. 0627A] Moreover, those images “whose feet and knees the pagans touched while praying” (Vegetius, Book II, ch. 44), being partly hollow and empty, and not in the least alive or breathing, rot and disintegrate through the ravages of time. Mice, lizards, and cockroaches also nest in them, while spiders and swallows defile them. Arnobius, therefore, like Minucius Felix and the other Fathers of the Church, as we have seen (Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 19, art. 2), rightly concludes from this that no divinity whatsoever can inhere in these images and representations.

To weaken somehow the force of this argument, by which they felt themselves overwhelmed, the pagans replied that they had never believed the images themselves to be gods, but that in them they worshiped and venerated only those gods “whom sacred dedication introduces and causes to inhabit the craftsmen’s images” (Arnobius, Book VI, pp. 203 ff.). [Col. 0627B] Our author, however, utterly demolishes and completely disperses this fabrication of a ridiculous opinion by various weighty arguments. For who of sound mind, he asks, will ever be persuaded that the gods are compelled by some ridiculous law of dedication either to inhabit earthly images or, having voluntarily abandoned their celestial seats, to migrate into them as often as a human being chooses to dedicate a statue? What of the fact that the gods cannot be compelled by any human force to remain in those images forever? Nothing is more wretched than such necessity, nor anything more unworthy of God. Furthermore, if they remain in them only for as long as they please, the images will certainly at some point cease to be gods when the gods depart from them. It will therefore remain uncertain [Col. 0627C] when sacrifices ought to be offered to them and when they ought to be adored. Moreover, Arnobius says, since many images of one and the same god are made, now small and now very large, do the gods either contract or extend themselves within them, adapting their bodies to the form and shape of the image? What could be more absurdly said or thought about God?

But come now: it is certain that very many images of one and the same god were placed in different regions, separated from one another by the greatest distances on earth. Could that god be present in all of them? Not in a divided state, because the true God cannot be divided. Nor whole and entire, for that god, as they believed, was corporeal and therefore could not be in several places at once.

Finally, if these images were either gods or [Col. 0627D] their habitations, should they not have protected themselves by their divine power against every mischance? Why, then, our author argues (ibid., p. 205), did the pagans close and fortify them with the strongest barriers, bars, and bolts, lest they suffer some injury?
