Why, lest they be secretly carried away by thieves at night, did they—these are his words—“protect them with a thousand temple-keepers and a thousand watchmen” (ibid.)? Tertullian argues in the same way and explains more clearly who those watchmen were:

> Surely they should first protect their own statues, images, and temples, which, as I understand it, Caesar’s soldiers preserve unharmed by keeping watch over them.

(Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 29, p. 29.)

Earlier, the author of the *Epistle to Diognetus* had addressed and rebuked the pagans as follows [Col. 0628A]:

> Do you not mock your gods when you venerate those made of stone and earthenware, leaving them without guards, but  
> Τοὺς δὲ ἀργυρέους καὶ χρυσοῦς ἐγκλείοντες ταῖς νυξὶ, καὶ ταῖς ἡμέραις φύλακας παρακαθίσαντες, ἵνα μὴ κλαπῶσι—  
> you lock up those made of silver and gold at night, and by day you station guards beside them so that they may not be stolen?

(*Epistle to Diognetus*, shortly after the beginning.)

Cyprian similarly pierces them with the no less sharp point of his pen:

> Thus, when they are injured, your vengeance defends them, just as, when they are shut away, your protection guards them lest they perish. You should be ashamed to hope for protection from those whom you yourself protect.

(Cyprian, *Treatise to Demetrianus*, p. 191.)

It was not enough for the pagans to protect the images—that is, their gods—with human guards and watches by day and night; for the same reason, Arnobius continues, [Col. 0628B] they also kept dogs and geese. Indeed, we read in Cicero: “Public contracts provide food for the geese, and dogs are kept on the Capitol so that they may give warning if thieves arrive” (Cicero, *For Roscius of Ameria*, Oration 2, §1, p. 24). This is also confirmed by the testimony of Livy, Pliny, Plutarch, Aelian, and others (Livy, Book V, near the end; Pliny, *Natural History*, Book X, ch. 22, p. 408; Plutarch, *Life of Camillus*, p. 142, and *Roman Questions*, p. 284; Aelian, *On Animals*, Book XII, ch. 33).

Yet these safeguards, Arnobius argues, were as useless as they were insulting to the gods. For if the gods themselves had at least inhabited the images, the task of protecting them against every mischance and injury should certainly have been entrusted to them and not to others. No pagan could ever have said that they either slept [Col. 0628C] or were unable to protect themselves. Hence Augustine likewise mocks and rejects these pagan gods by reference to the aforementioned guard of geese:

> At that time, when the whole city of Rome had been brought under enemy control, only the Capitoline hill remained; and it too would have been captured had not at least the geese kept watch while the gods slept. Hence Rome almost fell into the superstition of the Egyptians, who worship beasts and birds, when it celebrated solemn rites in honor of the goose.

(Augustine, *City of God*, Book II, ch. 22, p. 51.)

Who can deny that Arnobius rightly concludes from all these arguments that the pagan images, either before or after their consecration, are neither gods nor inhabited by gods, much less that gods can be compelled to abandon heaven and inhabit them? We have discussed elsewhere [Col. 0628D] the dedication of images (Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 19, art. 1).

## ARTICLE V

### Another argument of Arnobius against the images of the gods is examined, derived from the fact that the pagans themselves treated them with disgrace and dishonor and stripped them: namely, the image of Jupiter by Antiochus Cyzicenus and Dionysius the tyrant, that of Aesculapius by the same Dionysius, and those of Venus by Pygmalion and another young man; while other images were either demolished or burned. Here also concerning the several fires of the Capitol.

Arnobius’ final argument against the images of the gods is drawn from the fact that they were treated with the greatest dishonor and disgrace, ignominiously stripped, and finally, just like temples, cast down and utterly demolished. Who will deny that a statue of Jupiter was stripped by Antiochus Cyzicenus amid mockery and derision? To use Arnobius’ words:

> They report [Col. 0629A] that this Antiochus Cyzicenus removed from a shrine a golden Jupiter fifteen cubits high and substituted one made of bronze, superficially gilded with thin plates.

(Arnobius, Book VI, p. 205.)

This was undoubtedly taken from Clement of Alexandria. Listen, I ask, to his Greek words, and you will assuredly admit it:

> Ἀντίοχος ὁ Κυζικηνὸς, ἀπορούμενος χρημάτων, τοῦ Διὸς τὸ ἄγαλμα τὸ χρυσοῦν, πεντεκαίδεκα πήχεων τὸ μέγεθος ὂν, προσέταξε χωνεῦσαι, καὶ τῆς ἄλλης τῆς ἀτιμοτέρας ὕλης ἄγαλμα παραπλήσιον ἐκείνῳ πετάλοις κεχρυσωμένον ἀναθεῖναι πάλιν.

> Antiochus Cyzicenus, being in need of money, ordered the golden statue of Jupiter, which was fifteen cubits high, to be melted down, and ordered another statue like it, made from a less valuable material and gilded with thin plates, to be set up again.

(Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Pagans*, p. 34.) [Col. 0629B]

Arnobius also transferred the following into his book from the same Greek author:

> That Dionysius, the younger, when he stripped Jupiter of his golden covering and substituted a woolen one for it, also indulged in facetious jokes, saying that the former was cold in freezing weather but the latter warm, that the former was burdensome in summer but the latter airy under the heat.

(Arnobius, loc. cit.)

For Clement of Alexandria had said:

> Διονύσιος ὁ τύραννος, ὁ νεώτερος, τὸ ἱμάτιον τὸ χρύσεον περιελόμενος τοῦ Διὸς ἐν Σικελίᾳ, προσέταξεν αὐτῷ ἐρέουν περιτιθέναι, χαριέντως φήσας, τοῦτο ἄμεινον εἶναι τοῦ χρυσίου, καὶ θέρους κουφότερον, καὶ κρύους ἀλεεινότερον.

> Dionysius the younger, the tyrant, having taken away Jupiter’s golden garment in Sicily, ordered him to be clothed in wool, wittily [Col. 0629C] saying that it was better than the golden one, being lighter in summer and warmer in winter.

(Clement, loc. cit.)

We discussed both of these statues of Jupiter in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I, *Apparatus*, Book III, Dissertation I, ch. 8, arts. 2–3, pp. 737, 743). But if gods inhabited their images, Arnobius argues, neither Antiochus nor Dionysius would have done this with impunity, nor could Jupiter have endured so patiently such great insults inflicted upon him mockingly by feeble human beings. For, without waiting for anyone else’s assistance, as we said in the preceding article, he would himself have avenged them immediately.

Our author proceeds and relates that the same Dionysius likewise continued his joking when he stripped Aesculapius of his very large golden beard:

> For he said that it was truly an unseemly thing that a son begotten by Apollo, who was smooth-faced, [Col. 0629D] beardless, and very like a boy not yet of age, should be represented with such a beard that it was left uncertain which of them was the father and which the son—indeed, whether they were of one race and kin at all.

(Arnobius, Book VI, p. 206.)

Would anyone depart very far from the truth if he thought this had been taken from the following words of Cicero?

> The same Dionysius ordered the golden beard of the Epidaurian Aesculapius to be removed. For it was not fitting that the son should have a beard when in every shrine his father was beardless.

(Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book III, p. 252.)

Valerius Maximus, Lactantius, Aelian, and others related the same things about both impious acts of Dionysius (Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 2, §3, p. 20; Lactantius, Book II, ch. 4, p. 157; Aelian, [Col. 0630A] *Various History*, Book I, §8). Why, then, Arnobius presses, did neither god immediately avenge either of Dionysius’ audacious deeds, which were so disgraceful to them both? Why did they tolerate with such patience—the one the disfigurement of his face, the other his being so shamefully stripped of his ornament? Why did both gods fail, through well-deserved vengeance, to demonstrate that they were present in their images, as the pagans believed, and were their guardians and defenders? Ambrose says:

> They were held in such derision that Jupiter could not defend his garment, nor Aesculapius his beard; Apollo had not yet begun to grow a beard; and none of those who are called gods could draw back the offering-dishes that they held—not because they feared the guilt of theft, but because they possessed no sensation. Who, then, would worship those who can neither defend themselves like gods nor conceal themselves like human beings?

(Ambrose, *On Virgins*, Book II, ch. 5, §7, p. 172.) [Col. 0630B]

Nor is there any reason for some pagan, following Valerius Maximus, to object that although Dionysius did not pay the penalties he deserved, he nevertheless paid after death, through his son’s disgrace, the penalties he had escaped while alive. For the son suffered the penalties due not for his father’s cruelty but for his own, as is sufficiently proved from Athenaeus and Justin the historian (Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, Book XII, p. 541; Justin, *History*, Book XXI, chs. 2 and 5). Hence Ovid sang of him:

> He who lately was dreaded in the city of Syracuse  
> Scarcely drove off harsh famine by a humble trade.

(Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, Book IV, Epistle 3, p. 328.)

[Col. 0630C] What of the fact that Cicero himself, though a pagan, argues from the conduct of the elder Dionysius in precisely the same manner as our author and the other defenders of the Christian religion?

> Neither Olympian Jupiter, therefore, struck him with a thunderbolt, nor did Aesculapius destroy him by causing him to waste away through a wretched and protracted disease. He died in his own bed, was carried to the funeral pyre of Tympanis, and handed over to his son, as though it were a just and lawful inheritance, the power over his subjects which he himself had obtained through crime.

(Cicero, loc. cit.)

Nor does it help a pagan to reply that the gods completely disregard those insults and outrages which seem directed against their names and account them as nothing, so that they did not trouble to exact punishment for them. For with what countenance, Arnobius presses, and with what tranquility of mind—or rather, [Col. 0630D] with what stupidity—could the gods tolerate not only those impious acts of the two Dionysii and of Antiochus, but also other execrable outrages, not to be named without horror, which Philostephanus and Posidippus committed to writing? Our author says:

> In his *Cypriaca*, the former is our authority that Pygmalion, king of Cyprus, loved as a woman an image of Venus which was regarded among the Cypriots as possessing the sanctity of an ancient religious object … and that he was accustomed, after lifting the divine image onto his bed, to unite with it in embraces…. In a similar manner, Posidippus, in the book which he indicates was written about Cnidus and its affairs, recalls a young man of no undistinguished rank, but suppresses his name, who, seized with love for the Venus from whom Cnidus derives its fame, himself engaged [Col. 0631A] in amorous wantonness with the image of that same divinity, lying upon the marriage-bed and proceeding to the final consummation of the ensuing pleasures.

(Arnobius, Book VI [OCR reads VII], pp. 206 ff.)

But once again he borrowed this from Clement of Alexandria. For these are Clement’s very words:

> Ὁ Κύπριος ὁ Πυγμαλίων ἐκεῖνος ἐλεφαντίνου ἠράσθη ἀγάλματος· τὸ ἄγαλμα Ἀφροδίτης ἦν, καὶ γυμνὴ ἦν· νικᾶται ὁ Κύπριος τῷ σχήματι, καὶ συνέρχεται τῷ ἀγάλματι· καὶ τοῦτο Φιλοστέφανος ἱστορεῖ. Ἀφροδίτη δὲ ἄλλη ἐν Κνίδῳ, λίθος ἦν, καὶ καλὴ ἦν· ἕτερος ἠράσθη ταύτης, καὶ μίγνυται τῷ λίθῳ. Ποσίδιππος ἱστορεῖ· ὁ μὲν πρότερος ἐν τῷ περὶ Κύπρου, ὁ δὲ ἕτερος ἐν τῷ περὶ Κνίδου.

> That Cypriot Pygmalion fell in love with an ivory statue. The statue was an image of Aphrodite, and it was nude. The Cypriot was overcome by its form [Col. 0631B] and had intercourse with the image; Philostephanus relates this. There was another Aphrodite at Cnidus; it was made of stone, and it was beautiful. Another man fell in love with it and coupled with the stone. Posidippus relates this—the former story in his work *On Cyprus*, and the latter in his work *On Cnidus*.

(Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Pagans*, p. 38.)

See, if you wish, what we noted concerning these matters in the first volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I, *Apparatus*, Book III, Dissertation I, ch. 8, art. 4, p. 745).

Where in the world, then, Arnobius asks, was each of those two Venuses, who did not trouble to repel and restrain the unbridled and indomitable lust of these young men? Will the pagans reply that insults of this kind were highly pleasing to this goddess, the mistress of pleasure and lust? Yet the images of this goddess—whom the pagans admitted to be exceedingly lustful—and [Col. 0631C] their utterly criminal lovers should certainly have been delivered to avenging flames.

Moreover, even if soft and pleasure-loving goddesses had willingly permitted these things, did the other gods exhibit the same weakness and indolence? If, then, they possessed greater equanimity and fortitude, where, Arnobius asks (Book VI, p. 207), was Jupiter the Thunderer when devouring fire so often seized and consumed the Capitol and that Capitoline Jupiter himself, together with his wife and daughter? Where was Argive Juno when her temple burned together with her priestess Chrysis? Where were Egyptian Serapis together with Isis; Liber Eleutherius when Athens burned; Diana when Ephesus burned; Jupiter of Dodona when Dodona burned; and finally divine Apollo, when their temples and images were either plundered by robbers or consumed by fire? That these things too were taken from the already cited book of Clement [Col. 0631D] of Alexandria may be gathered from what we said in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I, *Apparatus*, ibid., pp. 729 ff.).

We shall therefore add nothing to this except that the Capitol was burned three times: once in the civil war when Scipio and Norbanus were consuls; a second time in the Vitellian war, after which the Capitol was restored by Vespasian; and a third time before the death of Titus Vespasian, Vespasian’s son, after which it was rebuilt by Domitian. Read Marlianus, Pancirolus, and Donatus on the city of Rome, together with the authors cited by them (vol. III, *Roman Antiquities*, pp. 77, 344, 577).

## ARTICLE VI

### It is shown how feeble is the pagans’ reply that images of the gods should be retained so that the ignorant common people might be kept in duty and religion through fear of them; and what is to be concluded from what has thus far been said.

[Col. 0632A]

The pagans’ final reply to the arguments we have thus far advanced against the images of the gods (Arnobius, Book VI [OCR reads IX], p. 208) was that they openly taught that the gods resided in them and that the images themselves were gods—not because they believed the matter truly stood thus, but so that, through this false persuasion and fear of present gods, the ignorant multitude of the common people, which formed the largest part of every state, might be kept in duty and religion. Cicero, indeed, held for the same reason, and contrary to the Persians’ opinion, that there ought to be temples in cities and sacred groves in the countryside (Cicero, *On the Laws*, Book II, p. 335). For the opinion [Col. 0632B] that the gods inhabit all cities and temples, and even their images, establishes religion, which is useful to every state, and makes individual persons more chaste and religious.

But what fear, Arnobius replies (Arnobius, loc. cit.), can the images of false gods inspire in the wicked, impious, and criminal, of whom the world has always been full? Did not these people, like everyone else, know perfectly well that tyrants, thieves, robbers, and others had attacked, stripped, plundered, carried away, cast down, and treated these images with the utmost disgrace and ignominy, as stated above, and had finally overthrown and utterly demolished them with impunity?

Furthermore, what did any human being have to fear from the images (ibid., p. 209)? Was it, our author asks, [Col. 0632C] Saturn’s harvesting sickle, the thunderbolt of Jupiter with his cloak drawn over his head, Juno’s girdle or belt, the drums of the Mother of the Gods, Pallas’ helmet, Mercury’s winged cap, Aesculapius’ staff, Ceres’ large breasts, the horn of Fortune—or of Amalthea, as Pausanias says—or, as others call it, the cornucopia, and finally the dog’s face of the ridiculous Anubis, as Diodorus Siculus, Macrobius, Lucian, and others declare (Pausanias, Book IV, p. 14, and Book VII, p. 234; Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, Book I, p. 55; Macrobius, *Metamorphoses* [sic], Book I, p. 201; Lucian, *On Sacrifices*, p. 186)? No one who was ever of sound mind could certainly have been persuaded that anything in these objects—which we explained a little earlier in this chapter and in the preceding dissertation [Col. 0632D] (Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 15, art. 2)—was to be feared or dreaded, or capable of deterring anyone from a wicked act.

So far were those and other images of the gods from turning wicked people away from any crime that neither the severity of the laws nor any kind of punishment has yet restrained their audacity. Indeed, they have frequently become even worse and more depraved because of them. It is therefore false that sincere religion is established or preserved through fear of images or of gods inhabiting them. Nor could this have been unknown to the pagans themselves, or at least to those who excelled among them in wisdom and learning. For Cicero somewhere made Cotta speak as follows:

> What of those who said that the whole belief concerning the immortal gods was invented by wise men for the sake of the commonwealth, so that religion might lead to duty those whom reason could not? Did they not utterly abolish all religion?

(Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, p. 212.) [Col. 0633A]

From everything discussed in this and the preceding articles, anyone may readily conclude that Arnobius proves by the strongest arguments that the images and statues of the gods must be utterly condemned and rejected. For the pagans had vainly persuaded themselves that, either before or after their dedication and consecration, these became gods and were capable of conferring help, favor, and benefits upon them. Nothing was in them except what was utterly alien to true divinity and, generally, because of its deformity, wholly unworthy of the true and perfect God. [Col. 0633B] These conclusions are further confirmed in a remarkable manner by what we have already observed more than once elsewhere, where, as we believe, we also plainly demonstrated to anyone not utterly blinded by preconceived opinions that no argument can be derived from this against the images which Christians are accustomed piously to venerate (Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 19, art. 2; vol. I, *Apparatus*, Book V, Dissertation I, ch. 9, art. 5, pp. 743 ff.). These matters, however, must be treated further in our subsequent dissertations.

# CHAPTER XXIII

## On the Sacrifices of the Pagans

## ARTICLE I

### By what arguments Arnobius demonstrates that no sacrifices should be offered to the gods of the pagans, and refutes the contrary arguments of those same pagans; here concerning the animate victim, *cnissa*, and the victim’s soul.

[Col. 0633C]

If the gods are fictitious and invented; if, consequently, no temples, shrines, or sanctuaries should be built for them; if their images are false and their representations and statues fabricated—does it not follow that no sacrifices whatsoever should ever be offered to them? But the first propositions, as we saw above, are proved invincibly by Arnobius. Therefore the final proposition has been demonstrated together with them so plainly that it appears to need not even the slightest further proof. Nevertheless, after refuting those preceding errors one by one, Arnobius judged that this subsequent error too should be attacked separately and with arguments peculiar to it.

First, therefore, he makes it evident that no reason whatsoever can be assigned by anyone for offering any sacrifice to the pagan gods [Col. 0633D] (Arnobius, Book VII, pp. 212 ff.). The gods, if any exist, could never derive from sacrifices any advantage, gain, or benefit. For it is false that they are fed and nourished by sacrifices. Whoever receives any food or nourishment must be mortal; but gods must be immortal.

Furthermore, what is brought to the gods’ altars is either inanimate or animate (ibid.). But the gods can be nourished by neither. They cannot be nourished by what is inanimate unless they are said to be corporeal, like human beings, and consequently not gods. Moreover, no one will deny that the animate is more suitable for them than the inanimate. The animate offering, as Arnobius says, is an “animate victim” (*hostia animalis*). What this means you may learn [Col. 0634A] from Macrobius, who, after citing Trebatius and Virgil, observes that the haruspices call that kind of victim of which only the soul is consecrated an *animate victim* (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book III, ch. 5, pp. 322 ff.). Strabo, while discussing Persian sacrifices, committed the following to writing: “They say that God desires nothing except the victim’s soul” (Strabo, *Geography*, Book XV, p. 732).

Yet the pagans vainly believed that the gods were nourished by animate things, or by a victim of this kind, “unless perhaps,” as Arnobius charges them with supposing, “a god devours the souls of victims, or seeks after the reek and smoke from burning altars, and feeds upon the *cnissae* exhaled by the burning entrails, still dripping with blood and moist with their former juices” (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 212). *Cnissa*—Greek κνίσσα or κνίσα—is the reek, [Col. 0634B] the fat and grease of animals, or the smoke which fire exhales when the victim is burned. Our author employs it here in this last sense.

That the pagans truly believed their gods to feed upon and be satiated by these *cnissae* may be gathered from the following words of Clement of Alexandria:

> Ζεὺς δὲ ὕστερον ἐπιφανείς, εἰ θεὸς ἦν, τάχα που τῆς κνίσης τῶν ὀπτωμένων κρεῶν μεταλαβών, ἧς δὴ τὸ γέρας λαχεῖν ὁμολογοῦσιν ὑμῶν οἱ θεοί.

> But Jupiter, when he appeared afterward—if indeed he was a god—perhaps partook of the *cnissa*, the savor of the roasting meat, which your gods acknowledge that they receive as their allotted honor.

(Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Pagans*, p. 12.)

This can be proved no less clearly by the authority of Lucian, who, although himself a pagan, nevertheless dared to mock his gods with this sarcasm (σαρκασμός; the source reads σαρκοσμῷ):

> The gods, seated beside Jupiter, look down upon the earth and, with their heads turned attentively in every direction, scan the scene to see whether anywhere they may perceive a fire rising upward, or a savor ascending into the air—ἢ ἀναφερομένην κνίσσαν—curling about the smoke. If someone happens to offer sacrifice, they all feast, gaping after the smoke and, like flies, sucking up the blood poured around the altars.

(Lucian, *On Sacrifices*, p. 185.) [Col. 0634C]

Arnobius refutes this utterly absurd opinion because nothing whatsoever from any sacrificed victim reaches the substance of the gods. Everything sacrificed by the pagans remained upon the earth or, after being lifted upward and dissolved into ashes, fell back to it. Hence the same Lucian says:

> Ἡ δὲ κνίσσα θεσπέσιος καὶ ἱεροπρεπὴς χωρεῖ ἄνω, καὶ ἐς αὐτὸν τὸν οὐρανὸν διασκεδνᾶται ἠρέμα.

> That sacred and divinely befitting savor rises upward and, carried into heaven itself, is gradually dispersed.

(Lucian, ibid., p. 186.) [Col. 0634D]

Hence Clement of Alexandria rightly concludes that Christians reject these things with the fullest justification:

> Εἰκότως ἄρα τῷ μὴ νικωμένῳ ἡδοναῖς θυσίαν οὐ προσάγομεν, κάτω που καὶ οὐδὲ μέχρι νεφῶν τῶν παχυτάτων, μακρὰν δὲ καὶ τούτων, τῆς διὰ τοῦ καπνοῦ ἀναθυμιάσεως φθανούσης, εἴ που φθάνει.

> Rightly, therefore, do we offer no sacrifice to him who is not overcome by pleasures, since the exhalation produced by the smoke remains below and does not reach even the densest clouds, but stops far short even of them—if indeed it reaches anywhere at all.

(Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book VII, p. 707.) [Col. 0635A]

He afterward refutes this foolish pagan opinion by another argument:

> Εἰ δὲ τῷ ὄντι ἡ κνίσσα γέρας ἐστὶ θεῶν τῶν παρ’ Ἕλλησιν, οὐκ ἂν φθάνοιεν καὶ τοὺς μαγείρους θεοποιοῦντες, οἳ τῆς ἴσης εὐδαιμονίας ἀξιοῦνται· καὶ τὸν ἰτμὸν αὐτόν [read ἰπνόν, or rather τὴν κάμινον αὐτὴν, προσκυνοῦντες] προσεχεστέραν γινομένην τῇ κνίσσῃ τῇ πολυτιμήτῳ.

> But if *cnissa* truly is the allotted gift of the gods worshiped among the Greeks, why do they not proceed first to deify the cooks, who are judged worthy of the same blessedness, and why do they not worship the oven itself, since it is closer to this highly honored *cnissa*?

(Ibid., p. 716.)

The pagans’ second reason for offering sacrifices to their gods was that victims should be slain for their pleasure, since the gods were thereby filled with joy and gladness [Col. 0635B] (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 213). For, as Lucian, already quoted by us, said:

> Τίς οὐκ ἂν εἰκάσειεν ἥδεσθαι ταῦθ’ ὁρῶντας τοὺς θεούς;

> Who would not readily suppose that the gods rejoice when they behold these things?

(Lucian, ibid., p. 186.)

But, Arnobius says, you will never persuade anyone who is not insane that the gods, like some kind of animal, are affected by pleasure and joy. For pleasure is perceived through the body’s five senses. But the gods, if they are immortal, must lack those senses.

Furthermore, what sort of joy is it by which anyone delights in the slaughter of innocent animals? Are not even savage human beings sometimes moved to compassion for them? How much more, then, should the gods be moved, whom the pagans represented as pious, gentle, [Col. 0635C] and exceedingly mild? Hence an ancient poet cited by Porphyry sang as follows (Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animals*, Book II, p. 230):

> Τίς ὧδε μῶρος, καὶ λίαν ἀνειμένος,  
> Εὔπιστος ἀνδρῶν, ὅστις ἐλπίζει θεοὺς,  
> Ὀστῶν ἀσάρκων, καὶ χολῆς πυρουμένης,  
> Ἃ καὶ κυσὶν πεινῶσιν οὐχὶ βρώσιμα,  
> Χαίρειν ἅπαντας, καὶ γέρας λαχεῖν τόδε;

> What man is so foolish, so utterly lax,  
> And credulous, as to hope that all the gods  
> Rejoice in fleshless bones and bile tried—or cooked—by fire,  
> Things that would not be edible even to starving dogs,  
> And that they receive this as their allotted prize?

Porphyry himself had said earlier that evil demons, who wish to appear as gods, are refreshed by κνίσσα and the [Col. 0635D] savor of sacrifices. Therefore, he says, the good and wise man will beware of sacrifices of this sort, lest he attract to himself such teachers of impiety. How much force there is in each and every one of the arguments we have expounded will, we think, be readily apparent to anyone. If anyone desires more, he will find it without great labor in Eusebius (Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, Book IV, ch. 22, p. 173; Book V, ch. 2, p. 182). We think there is no one who will not acknowledge that all Arnobius’ arguments, taken together, utterly overthrow the pagans’ absurd error (Arnobius, Book VI, p. 204).

## ARTICLE II

### How Arnobius refutes other arguments by which the pagans attempted to prove that sacrifices should be offered to their gods; here concerning the rite by which those pagans washed their bodies before entering temples, and an explanation of what are *bulba*, *immissulus*, *buteo*, *solipuga*, *natrix*, cumin, cress, *bulbus*, *cunila*, and wagtail.

[Col. 0636A]

Source/review notes: The supplied source itself ends in the middle of Ovid’s sentence (“Liba deo faciunt, succis quia dulcibus ille”), so a complete translation of the passage cannot be produced without the missing continuation. The draft appropriately remains incomplete at the same point.; Eight useful inline column boundaries were omitted; the edits restore them at the corresponding translated locations.; Varro’s “longius quam duo hila” was substantively mistranslated as “longer than those two”; the edit restores “longer than two strands” and retains *hila*.; The inherited boundary is intentional: source_to_cover ends with the incomplete Ovid fragment “succis quia dulcibus ille,” faithfully represented by the candidate’s terminal em dash. The following_context begins the next inventory chunk and is neither required nor assessed here.

The common opinion of the pagans—and what they considered a weighty argument for offering sacrifices to the gods—was founded upon the vain conviction that the gods were appeased by those who sacrificed and that their anger was thereby calmed. But Arnobius demonstrates the falsity of this belief with the utmost clarity (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 214). For no movement of anger can exist in the true God, since such a movement, closely akin to that of beasts, can belong only to those who are mortal and not yet blessed. But [Col. 0636B] the anger of God must be discussed more fully in the following dissertation (Dissertation on Lactantius, ch. 15, art. I ff.).

Yet suppose, if you wish, Arnobius says, that the gods really do become angry with human beings: you will still never thereby prove that they ought to be appeased by sacrifices. For a sacrifice should not be made to them before they have become angry. In that case, just as food is thrown before wild beasts to keep them from raging, so a sacrifice would restrain the gods’ future anger. Nor should sacrifice be offered to gods already inflamed with anger. For, apart from the fact that the gods cannot be injured by human beings, they certainly never established by any laws what sacred rite human transgressors were to perform in order to avoid paying the penalty for injuring the divine majesty. Moreover, it is wholly contrary to every appearance of probability that, when a pig, a hen, or other livestock has been sacrificed, they should lay aside their anger and forget injuries [Col. 0636C]. For if the hope were offered that crimes could be redeemed so easily, the multitude of wicked people would undoubtedly increase. Porphyry proves this point more fully (Porphyry, Book II, *On Abstinence from Animals*, p. 232 ff.): induced by this reasoning, any wicked person will believe that he has been given the power to act unjustly and wickedly; it would be otherwise if he believed that he would receive a reward from the gods solely for his good works.

Arnobius further adds that it seems entirely unjust for an innocent beast to be killed in place of a guilty and culpable human being. By a similar argument Porphyry shows that no animal should be sacrificed out of gratitude or in order to repay thanks to the gods (Idem, ibid., p. 163). For one who gives thanks for a benefit received ought not wrongfully to harm anyone who does not deserve it, nor sacrifice any innocent animal in place of a guilty person conscious of his crime [Col. 0636D].

The pagans, however, continued to insist, crying out even more loudly that victims must be sacrificed to each god so that he might grant us prosperity and avert adversity. But this argument does not appear to our author any firmer or more valid than the others (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 317 ff.). For the most learned pagan philosophers obstinately taught that all things occur, as we have seen elsewhere, by fate and fatal necessity. Yet it plainly follows from this that the gods can neither grant human beings anything at all nor prevent anything, and that they are therefore wearied in vain by offerings, victims, libations, and sacrifices (Dissertation on Minucius, ch. 6, art. 4).

Moreover, if the gods bestow prosperity and repel adversity, why have countless people—even those [Col. 0637A] who continually burden their altars with sacrifices—been reduced to the direst straits by bereavement, disease, shipwreck, and other evils and misfortunes? Would not the gods be the most ungrateful of all beings if, though able to prevent these things, they refused to do so and were unwilling to grant any of the requests of the pious?

“But first,” you will say, “the gods’ benefits must be procured and purchased with the blood of victims and with sacrifices.” What are you saying, my good man? What, I ask you, could be more unworthy of the gods than to make their benefactions objects of sale and to benefit no one without them? And what of the fact that, if sacrifices of this sort alone are effective, a rich man who slaughters for the gods numerous animals purchased at a price that is indeed considerable but, in relation to his wealth, small, ought to receive benefits from them correspondingly greater than those received by a poor man who offers something trifling, yet something of the greatest value to him [Col. 0637B] in his poverty? What greater injustice and inequity could there be than this? By the same reasoning, if two peoples at war with one another offer exactly the same sacrifices, the gods will never be able to bring them the aid which each equally deserves.

“But those sacrifices,” the pagans said, “were rightly instituted to honor the gods and magnify their dignity.” Arnobius plainly and explicitly denies this (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 220 ff.). For the attribution and increase of honors and dignities have a place only among human beings. God, however, can in no way whatsoever be increased in dignity, power, or honors. Indeed, Arnobius says, one who “is honored” with human honors—that is, according to Servius, Brissonius [Col. 0637C], and other interpreters, is thereby increased as though still further—is inferior to the one whose power is increased (Servius, on Book IV of the *Aeneid*, I, p. 316; Brissonius, Book I, *On Forms*, p. 21). But it is impious to say or even think this, or anything like it, of God (Cicero, *Fragments*, p. 16).

We therefore honor and worship God truly, supremely, and above all other things when we think of him worthily (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 222). For we believe that nothing exists in him which is proper only to mortals, or which comes to him from without and could disturb him. We also openly confess that by his own power he knows himself most perfectly, and that he is never agitated by any movement of anger, pleasure, ambition, desire, or anything else of that kind.

Who, then, would not hiss the pagans off the stage (ibid.) [Col. 0637D] for believing that they rendered no small honor to their gods if, before killing an ox or another animal before their faces and pouring out its blood, they first washed themselves in a certain sacred bodily ablution? Before entering the temples, they made themselves—or rather believed they made themselves—pure of every stain, *lauli*, that is, washed, and perfectly chaste, as Arnobius says (ibid.). Cicero wrote as follows concerning that pagan custom of cleansing themselves:

> “The law bids men approach the gods in purity—that is, purity of mind, in which everything resides. Nor does it dispense with bodily purity; but this must be understood as follows: since the mind is far more important than the body, and care is taken that one approach with a pure body, purity must be observed far more in the mind. For a bodily stain may be removed either by a sprinkling of water or by a prescribed number of days; but a stain of the mind [Col. 0638A] can neither vanish through length of time nor be washed away by any rivers.”  
> (Cicero, Book II, *On the Laws*, p. 335.)

Macrobius attests that this was a common pagan custom, but distinguishes sprinkling from washing:

> “It is agreed,” he says, “that one who intends to sacrifice to the gods above is purified by washing his body. But when sacrifice must be offered to the gods below, it is considered sufficient if only a sprinkling takes place.”  
> (Macrobius, Book III, *Saturnalia*, ch. 1.)

He cites many passages there from Virgil, while Brissonius cites far more from the same poet and other writers concerning this pagan rite. You will be able to consult these without great difficulty, as also Tertullian and Justin Martyr. Defending the Christian religion against the pagans, Justin writes that the demons [Col. 0638B], having learned of the washing enjoined by the prophet Isaiah, caused the pagans, when about to enter their temples, both to purify themselves by sprinkling with water and to wash their entire bodies (Brissonius, Book I, *On Forms*, p. 6 ff.; Tertullian, *On Baptism*, ch. 5; Justin, *Apology* II, or I, p. 94 ff.). Therefore Lactantius, as we shall see in the appropriate place, rebukes them because they imagined that they had sacrificed piously if they had washed beforehand (Lactantius, Book V of the *Institutes*, ch. 20, p. 512).

But this washing, ablution, or sprinkling performed before sacrifice did not cause the gods to be honored by the blood and stenches of slaughtered victims—stenches which even the sacrificers themselves could not endure, as our author rightly argues (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 222). Nor [Col. 0638C] should you say that the laws cited by Cicero require a pure mind together with bodily washing. For the pagans cared nothing about that. How could the minds of those be pure who offered the sacrifices we have described to gods whom they proclaimed to be defiled by every conceivable kind of utterly unbridled lust and shamelessness?

Moreover, if honor is rendered to the gods by sacrificed animals, why did the pagans not slaughter elephants, bears, dogs, and *belbae* for them? The royal manuscript reads *belluas*, with the letter *u* placed for *b* in the customary fashion (ibid., p. 223). *Belba* means the same as hyena, as Pseudo-Clement, the translator of the Epistle attributed to Barnabas, Capitolinus, and Cotelerius have observed (Barnabas, *Epistle*, no. 10; Clement, Book VIII of the *Recognitions*, §25; Capitolinus, near the end of *Gordian III*; Cotelerius [Col. 0638D], on the cited Epistle of Barnabas). Why, too, did the pagans not sacrifice the *Immissulus* and *Puteones*, which, according to Pliny, Aldrovandus, and others, were certain kinds of birds? Why not *solifugae* or *solipugae*, noxious little creatures that sting more sharply when the sun is hotter? Why not *natrices*, that is, water snakes that discharge venom into the water, concerning which see the same Pliny, Solinus, Lucan, Isidore, Cicero, Columella, and our discussion elsewhere (Pliny, Book XVIII of *Natural History*, chs. 7–8; idem, Book VIII, ch. 30; Book XXII, final chapter; Book XXIX, ch. 4; Solinus, ch. 4, p. 18; Lucan, Book IX, line 837; Isidore, Book XII of the *Origins*, ch. 4; Cicero, Book IV of the *Academic Questions*, p. 33; Columella, Book I, ch. 5).

The pagans replied that, in order to render the gods their due honor [Col. 0639A], those things should be sacrificed which the gods had supplied us for the sustenance of life. “Then,” says our author, “one ought to sacrifice to them cumin,” which Pliny mentions among others (Pliny, Book XIX of *Natural History*, ch. 8, p. 613); or cress, likewise mentioned by him and which, as Cicero attests, the Persians customarily ate; or bulbs, celebrated by Ovid and Martial (Pliny, ibid., p. 611; Cicero, *On Ends*, p. 66, and Book V of the *Tusculans*, p. 192; Ovid, near the end of the *Remedies for Love*; Martial, Book III, Epigram 34), whose nature, according to Pliny, is very close to that of skirret and parsnip; or *ocinum*, also called *ocymum*, *ocina*, and *ozina*, concerning which, in addition to the already cited Pliny, see Varro, Cato, and Theophrastus (Pliny, cited book, p. 591; idem, Book XIX, ch. 8, p. 611; Varro, *On Agriculture*, Book I, ch. 31 [Col. 0639B]; Cato, *On Agriculture*, ch. 54; Theophrastus, Book VII, *On Plants*, ch. 3); or *cunila bubula* (“ox savory”), whose many uses are described by Pliny, Columella, and Salmasius (Pliny, Book XIX, ch. 8, and Book XX, ch. 15; Columella, Book XVI, *On Agriculture*, ch. 13; Salmasius, on Solinus, p. 1275 ff.).

Arnobius presses the pagans further (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 224 ff.): if dogs, asses, pigs, wagtails—that is, birds which, according to Varro (Book IV, *On the Latin Language*, p. 19), are always moving their tails—and swallows were endowed with some measure of human understanding, believed that we were gods, and wished to perform sacred rites for us, would we regard it as an honor if they sacrificed to us flies, ants, dung, and the other things on which they feed? Yet the gods are no more honored by the slaughtered bodies of bulls and other [Col. 0639C] animals, which soon putrefy.

Someone, however, may detain us here and object that this argument of Arnobius carries no weight, since the Jews slaughtered sheep, oxen, and many other animals for the true God. Yet these sacrifices were pleasing to him—indeed, commanded by him—and therefore were made in his honor. But whoever raises this objection, by the very admission that those sacrifices were prescribed by God himself, unties whatever knot there may be in the difficulty he has proposed. For we have already shown above (above, ch. 8, art. 4), and it will be stated again shortly, that Arnobius rejects all the sacrifices of the pagans, whatever they offered to their gods, precisely because they had never been instituted by any law whatsoever of those gods—who, of course, did not exist [Col. 0639D]. The Jews, by contrast, honored the true God by sacrificing as he had commanded. For does not one who obeys a command thereby render the commander his due honor?

Moreover, many ancient Fathers of the Church and more recent theologians of our own have held that sacrifices were prescribed to the Jews by God, not principally so that he might be honored by them, but to prevent the Jews themselves from falling into the crime of idolatry, to which they were exceedingly prone. Finally, Arnobius chiefly refutes the pagans’ answers by attacking the grounds on which they boasted that they had been induced to sacrifice to their gods. Besides, even if particular arguments advanced by him on this or another subject might seem to some [Col. 0640A] not to possess equal force, no one will deny that, when all are set together and combined, they utterly and completely overthrow the superstitious sacrifices of the pagans. Let us therefore proceed, if you please, to examine the others.

## ARTICLE III. Another Argument of Arnobius Against Pagan Sacrifices Is Weighed, Drawn from the Fact That One Victim Was Sacrificed to One God and Another to Another; Here Also Concerning the Gods Below and the Pregnant Sow

To make it increasingly clear that pagan sacrifices must be rejected, Arnobius asks the pagans why they sacrificed a bull to one god, a kid to another, sheep to this one, and to that one an *inciens scrofa*—that is, a pregnant sow close to giving birth; why a particular victim was assigned to each individual god; why animals of the female sex were sacrificed to some, animals of the male sex to others [Col. 0640B], white or red animals to certain gods, and black ones to others. “By what law,” he asks, “was this ever established? And what difference does it make by the slaughter of which animal a human debt is discharged and the gods’ anger calmed? Is the blood of one more pleasing and acceptable to them than that of another?”

The pagans replied that the gods were male and female, some right-hand or favorable, others left-hand or unfavorable, some gods above and others gods below, and that victims of different kinds must therefore be slaughtered for them. They might perhaps have proved that this had been commanded by the gods through the following oracle of Apollo, delivered in Greek verse, which Eusebius excerpted from Porphyry (Eusebius, Book IV of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, ch. 9, p. 145 ff.). But because it is somewhat lengthy, we shall present only its Latin translation [Col. 0640C]:

> Remember to consecrate three victims to the Lares, and as many  
> To the heavenly gods, but with this distinction: let the victims  
> For the heavenly gods be white, while that for the Lares matches the earth in color.  
> Divide what is offered to the Lares into three parts,  
> And bury what belongs to the gods of Erebus deep in the earth;  
> Pour the steaming blood into hollow trenches.  
> Pour honey for the Nymphs and gentle gifts of Lyaeus.  
> For the wandering divinities that hover low around the earth,  
> Let blood overflowing all around fill the kindled altars,  
> And let an entire bird pass into the sacred flames.  
> But first, after moistening crushed barley and kneading it with honey,  
> Mix it with incense and cast salted grain upon it.  
> When you are about to sacrifice to Venus beside the slender sands  
> Of the dark-blue sea, cast the bird headfirst and hurl it whole  
> Into the deep waves. When these rites have duly been performed,  
> Turn your steps from there toward the great companies  
> Of the heavenly gods. The sacred honor is the same for all the celestial deities:  
> Let the blood poured upon the wheaten cakes stand in pools,  
> And set the consecrated limbs before the gods,  
> Placing the upper portions upon the flames and the rest upon tables. [Col. 0640D]

Thus he writes. Lilius Giraldus likewise rendered the same verses into Latin differently and treats the matter at greater length. Hence Servius observes:

> “Just as sacrifice must be offered to favorable gods so that they may assist us, so it must also be offered to adverse gods so that they may not harm us: for example, a black animal to winter, a white one to the kindly Zephyrs.”  
> (Giraldus, *History of the Gods*, Syntagma 17, p. 489 ff.; Servius, on Book IV of the *Aeneid*, p. 316.)

But apart from the fact that the falsity of the cited oracle was acknowledged by Porphyry himself, who reported it, as Eusebius attests (Eusebius, ibid., p. 148), our author certainly exposes and refutes with ease both this very oracle and the other inventions of the erring human mind adduced by the pagans. For it was false, as the wiser and more learned pagans acknowledged [Col. 0641A] and as he had demonstrated above, that the gods were male and female. No less clearly, as we have seen (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 228 ff.), he shows that the same pagans falsely asserted that certain gods were by their very nature evil and adverse, since the true God is of the most benevolent and beneficent nature. Finally, he denies that there are any gods below who dwell beneath the earth in Pluto’s realms (ibid., p. 226). Juvenal himself, though a pagan poet, likewise denies that any person believes this, unless perhaps he is a boy of so tender an age that he is not yet charged the bathing fee at the public baths. These are his very verses:

> That there are any Shades, and subterranean realms,  
> And Charon’s pole, and black frogs in the Stygian gulf,  
> And that so many thousands cross the ford in a single boat—  
> [Col. 0641B] Not even boys believe it, except those who do not yet pay to bathe.  
> (Juvenal, Satire 2, lines 149 ff.)

If the authority of a poet alone does not suffice for you, hear also a pagan orator whom you will doubtless not oppose—namely Cicero, who hisses and drives the infernal gods off the stage:

> “Tell me, please,” he says, “do those things frighten you: the three-headed Cerberus in the lower world? . . . Do you think me so utterly delirious as to believe that such things exist? . . . If, therefore, there are no wretched people in the lower world, then indeed there is no one at all in the lower world. That is exactly what I think.”  
> (Cicero, Book I of the *Tusculans*, p. 116, line 33.)

“But grant it,” Arnobius continues; “let us concede that there are gods below, presiding over sad and inauspicious affairs, and that a black victim must therefore be slaughtered for them” (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 226). “But how,” he asks [Col. 0641C], “can this be done? Do you not see that the victims’ teeth, bones, fat, cauls, and marrow are white?” “But the fleeces,” the pagans replied, “as well as the animals’ bristles—that is, their thicker and stiffer hairs—and certain other parts of them are dark and black.” “Quite so,” Arnobius says. “Then these parts alone, and not the whole animals, ought to be sacrificed to the gods below.” But what are we to make of those who offered the gods below many things which, like oil and blood, are not black? Does not that splendid religion thereby collapse?

Moreover, why is one particular victim slaughtered for Jupiter, Bacchus, or Mercury, and not another (ibid.)? The pagans indeed said that this had been established by ancient custom. But this custom, Arnobius argues [Col. 0641D], however ancient it may be, originated solely among human beings. To offer sacrifices to the gods, however, a heavenly and divine command is required.

By what law, too, was the apportionment of animals to be sacrificed to the gods made? On what grounds, for example, is a bull said to be appropriate for Jupiter rather than for another god? The pagans replied that a pregnant sow, mentioned by us shortly above, should be slaughtered for Tellus as mother, while for the virgin Minerva there should be slaughtered a virgin heifer that had never borne the yoke. But if that is how matters stand, Arnobius argues, musicians would have to be slaughtered for Apollo the musician, physicians for Aesculapius the physician, and smiths for Vulcan the smith. What more foolish or insipid notion could ever have been devised?

## ARTICLE IV. How Arnobius Demonstrates from the Very Things Employed in Sacrifices That Sacrifice Should Not Be Offered to the Gods; Here Are Explained the Meanings of *Farcimen*, *Apexabo*, *Hirciae*, *Silicernium*, *Longavo*, *Taedae*, *Taeniae*, *Polimina*, *Plasea*, *Siligo*, *Fitilla*, *Frumen*, *Africia*, *Gratilla*, *Catumeum*, *Conspolium*, *Cubula*, *Libum*, *Caro Strebula*, *Pulpamenta*, *Salsamina Quadrimis Copulata Frugibus*, *Far Pium*, *Feudicae*, *Rumae* or *Aerumnae*, *Gurgulio*, *Ruminatoria Saecula*, *Augmentum*, *Magmentum*, *Velamen Sanguinum*, and *Praesiciae*; and How Our Author Shows That These Things Are Burned in Sacrifices to No Purpose

[Col. 0642A]

Besides offerings and victims, nearly all the other things employed in sacrifices furnish Arnobius with another argument by which he demonstrates with the utmost clarity that sacrifices ought to be entirely abolished. For the pagans offered their gods various kinds of sausages, cakes, porridges, and *fitillae*. These were not merely unworthy of the gods, “but things [Col. 0642B] to which,” in the words of our author addressing them, “you gave obscure names and, by making them unfamiliar to the common people, made them appear more venerable,” and, as he had said shortly before, things “connected with the disciplines of the magicians” (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 229 ff.).

Scholars are not of one opinion concerning the meaning of these final words. Some think that those names are said to be connected with the disciplines of the magicians because they were dark and obscure, and similar to the names used by magicians. Salmasius, however, contends that nothing could be more contrary to Arnobius’s meaning (Salmasius, *Exercises on Solinus*, p. 128). He therefore judges that Arnobius is speaking about various kinds of sausages and cakes which he calls connected with the disciplines of the magicians because the magicians did not burn whole and unblemished entrails of bulls for the gods, but only portions [Col. 0642C] and cuttings of cauls. Consider, however, whether this opinion might be confirmed by the following words of Strabo on Persian sacrifice, which, in Xylander’s translation, read in Latin as follows:

> “They sacrifice in a clean place with prayers and set up a garlanded victim. When the Magus who explains the sacrifice has divided the meat into portions, each person takes his share and they depart, leaving no portion for the gods. . . . For they say that the god desires nothing except the victim’s soul; some, it is reported, place a part of the caul upon the fire.”  
> (Strabo, Book XV of the *Geography*, p. 532.)

But if in that sense these things were connected with the magical disciplines, what prevents us from supposing that Arnobius used these same words because their obscurity connected them with those same impious disciplines, since by that obscurity they were regarded as magical, or like magical things, and thus made more venerable in popular estimation?

[Col. 0642D] However the matter may stand, our author has woven together a long series of these terms. Since many of them may not be sufficiently familiar to many readers, we must not pass them over without some explanation and elucidation, if that can be achieved (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 229).

First he mentions *farcimen* (“sausage”), or, as Isidore says:

> “Meat cut up and minced; it is therefore called *farcimen* because an intestine is *farcitur*, that is, filled with it, together with an admixture of other ingredients.”  
> (Isidore, Book XX of the *Origins*, ch. 20.)

Varro, however, says:

> “From *fartum*, the sausages in the entrails were called *farcimina*; from this comes the name of that which is stuffed into the thinnest intestine.”  
> (Varro, Book IV, *On the Latin Language*, p. 28.)

Thus *farcimen* is an intestine packed and stuffed with finely minced meat and other filling. Apicius described various methods [Col. 0643A] of preparing it (Apicius, Book II, *On Cookery*, ch. 5).

*Apexabo*, or *Apexaones* as the royal manuscript reads (Arnobius, cited passage), was one portion of a sausage. The already cited Varro mentions it as follows:

> “Because in the top of this sausage something projects, just as an *apex* projects on the head, it is called *apexabo*.”  
> (Varro, ibid.)

*Hirciae*, or *Ircei* as Festus writes, were yet another kind of sausage employed in sacrifices (Festus, under the entry *IRCEI*).

Some believe that *silicernium* derives from *silex* (“flint”), and that the term designates a decrepit, stooped old man who looks down at the flints. But it also signifies a meal which, as Donatus says,

> “is brought to the Manes because they behold it [Col. 0643B] in silence—that is, the shades possess it—or because those who bring these things merely behold them and do not taste them. For whoever eats or drinks of things offered in libation to the gods below becomes polluted by death.”  
> (Donatus, on Terence’s *Brothers*, Act IV, scene 2, at the end.)

Nonius, however, rejects the first explanation and confirms the second in these words:

> “Those who understand *silicernium* very badly suppose that Terence used it because an old man, owing to his stooped posture, looks at the flints. Properly speaking, a *silicernium* is a funeral banquet offered to old men.”

Tertullian employs it in the same sense when he compares a *silicernium* with Jupiter’s banquet (Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 13; Festus, under the entry *SILICERNIUM*).

Thirdly and finally, Paulus and Verrius, whom Festus cites, observe that *silicernium* denotes a certain kind of sausage [Col. 0643C] with which a household was customarily purified after someone’s death. That Arnobius uses the term in this sense may be inferred from the fact that he is discussing various kinds of sausages.

*Longavi*—the royal manuscript corruptly reads *longaevi*—is better read *longavo* or *longano*. For in Apicius we read:

> “Stuffed pork *longanones*, cooked in Tarentine sauce and sliced.”  
> (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 229; Apicius, Book IV, *On Cookery*, ch. 2.)

Some believe that *longanon* is the rectum. But Varro considers the third kind to be “a stuffed item longer than two strands (*hila*)” (Varro, Book IV, *On the Latin Language*, p. 28). This is correct and sufficiently suited to the meaning of Arnobius, who declares that these four items mentioned by us are “kinds of sausage, some stuffed with the blood of a he-goat, [Col. 0643D] others with minced lungs,” that is, with these ingredients forcibly inserted and, as we have said, packed into them. You can see that among those four sausages there is certainly no great difference, and that the distinction lies in the name rather than the substance. For some, he says, were stuffed with goat’s blood, which some call *sanguiculus*, and others with minced lungs. He does not say from which animal the lungs came, unless he means us to understand a goat, whose blood he is discussing there. Perhaps he also left us to understand that the first two were made with the goat’s blood and the latter two with its minced lungs. Consult Turnebus besides, if you please and have the leisure (Turnebus, Book XXII of the *Adversaria*, ch. 6).

Arnobius continues:

> “What are *taedae*? What are *taeniae*—the manuscript reads *naeniae*? What are the morsels known not to the common people but by the recondite [Col. 0644A] designation *penitae*?”  
> (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 229 ff.)

But these and the following words have been disgracefully corrupted through a copyist’s incompetence. For this reason, someone wished to read *tuceta* there, a word which, according to Fulgentius, signifies royal foods (Fulgentius, *On Ancient Vocabulary*, near the end).

But this contributes nothing to our author’s purpose. Salmasius suspects that the text should be emended to “What are *taxiae*? What are *naeniae*?” He advises us there that *taxea* or *taxia*—from which he thinks the ignorant copyist wrote *taedae*—means the same as *arvina*, fat or lard (Salmasius, *Exercises on Solinus*, p. 128). Whether he has hit the mark you may infer from the following explanation of the term given there by Arnobius:

> “In the first,” he says, “the *arvina* is cut into tiny morsels in the customary manner of *catillamina*.”  
> (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 230.)

In [Col. 0644B] the royal manuscript we read *catillaminuam*; some editions have *at illa minutim*, others *et ilia minutim*. That the first reading is closer to the truth is evident from the ease with which a copyist ignorant of Latin might add one letter to a term unknown to him. *Catillamina*, however, and, in another book of Arnobius, “Lucanian *castellamenta*” (ibid.; Book II, p. 73), are still further kinds of sausage, which were also called by the far more familiar name *botuli*. The meaning, therefore, is that *arvina*, or the suet lying between an animal’s skin and entrails, was divided into the smallest pieces, fashioned into the form of sausages, and burned in sacrifice to the gods (ibid., p. 229). Martial speaks of Lucanian sausages more than once, and especially in this epigram:

> [Col. 0644C] A Lucanian sausage, daughter of a Picene sow, I come:  
> Hence a pleasing garland is given to snow-white porridge.  
> (Martial, Book XIII, Epigram 35; also Book IV, Epigram 46.)

But we shall say more about these near the end of this dissertation.

In the manuscript and old editions the second kind of *botuli*, or sausages of this sort, is called *naeniae* (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 229). But the editor of the latest edition, following Scaliger’s conjecture, preferred to write *taeniae*. Nevertheless, forgetful of this correction, shortly afterward he retained the term *naenias* with the other editions and our manuscript. But even if the reading were uncertain, the following explanation supplied by the author himself is certainly sufficient for us:

> “What is placed second is a length of intestine through which refuse is discharged, dried [Col. 0644D] of its vital juices,”

or, more briefly, the colon or rectum (ibid., p. 231). Some believe it possible to prove from the following verses of Plautus that the term *naenia* denotes this:

> If you have a sword, we too have a spit at home,  
> With which, if you provoke me, I shall make you  
> More perforated than a mouse’s *naenia*.  
> (Plautus, *Bacchides*, Act IV, scene 8.)

That is, according to the interpretation of certain scholars: “I shall make you more perforated than the intestine of a mouse caught in a mousetrap and pierced by some particular mechanism.”

Our author next mentions “the *offa penita*,” which, as he himself explains, “is a portion of entrail [Col. 0645A] cut off together with the animal’s tail” (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 230). But the ancients, as Festus and Paulus state, “called the tail *penis*; from that ancient usage even now, at sacrificial banquets, a piece of pork together with the tail is called an *offa penita*” (Festus and Paulus, under the entries *PENIS* and *PENITA*). Festus adds: “Naevius calls the *penita offa* a slice of meat together with the tail.” Plautus says:

> Take away that *offa penita*: this cold conger eel is excellent.  
> (Plautus, *The Braggart Soldier*, Act III, scene 1.)

But it is utterly absurd to say, Arnobius argues, that the gods take pleasure in these *naeniae* and *offae penitae*, and that “they do not lay aside their anger and resentment until they have seen *naeniae* prepared for burning before them and purchased morsels” (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 231). But what, you will ask, does he mean by the final word, *redemptas* (“purchased” or “redeemed”)? For he should rather have said [Col. 0645B] *redemptrices* (“redeeming”), since by these things, as he argues in that same place, the pagans imagined that they redeemed the gods’ favor. For there too he said that the gods “are bought off, so that they may benefit us, with the testicles of cattle.” But what reading can you establish against the sole surviving manuscript? Or what if Arnobius called those morsels “purchased” because almost everyone had bought them to offer them in libation to the gods?

But observe, please, how far pagan superstition proceeded. They offered their gods not only animals’ tails but also *polimina*. So that no one might be ignorant of what these were, or how unworthy they were to be offered to the gods, our author describes them as follows:

> “They are those things which we more modestly call the organs of generation, but which common people customarily designate by the name ‘testicles.’”  
> (Ibid., p. 220.)

They were therefore the same as *polimenta*, [Col. 0645C] which Verrius, Festus, and then Paulus explain in this manner:

> “The ancients called the testicles of livestock, when they castrated them, *polimenta*, from the trimming of crops or garments, because they are trimmed in a similar way.”  
> (Festus and Paulus, under the entry *POLIMENTA*.)

Scaliger indeed rejects this etymology and offers another, which is in turn rejected by someone else (Scaliger, on Book IV of *On the Latin Language*, p. 41). Since these matters contribute nothing to our purpose, it will be enough to note that *polimina* are nothing other than *polimenta*, which are mentioned in this verse of Plautus:

> Either pig’s *polimenta*, or something of that sort.  
> (Plautus, *Menaechmi*, Act I, scene 3.)

Arnobius further objects to the pagans’ offering of the caul, in Greek ἐπίπλοον (*epiploon*). It is a thin and [Col. 0645D] fatty membrane covering the lower portions of the belly and enveloping the coils of the intestines. Earlier he calls them “little membranes of cauls”; on these you may consult Persius, Pliny, and Isidore (Arnobius, cited passage, and Book III, p. 107; Persius, Satire 2, line 47; Pliny, Book II of *Natural History*, ch. 37, p. 574; Isidore, Book II of the *Origins*, ch. 1).

Our author next defines *palasea*, or, as some called it, *plasea*, as “an ox’s tail smeared with *siligo* and blood” (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 230). *Siligo* is flour made from the finest wheat and most thoroughly cleansed of bran. Hence this verse of Juvenal concerning bread:

> But the tender, snow-white bread, made from soft *siligo*,  
> [Col. 0646A] Is kept for the master.  
> (Juvenal, Satire 5, line 69.)

Seneca, Pliny, and Isidore say more about *siligo*. Thus a *plasea* was an ox’s tail smeared with the finest snow-white flour and blood (Seneca, Letters 119 and 123, pp. 226 and 232; Pliny, Book XVIII, ch. 8, p. 462; Isidore, Book XIX of the *Origins*, ch. 3).

Arnobius then asks: what assistance in sacrifices to the gods is provided by *fitilla* and *frumen*, which were different kinds of porridge? For Pliny indicates quite clearly that *frictilla*, or *fritilla* as others write, was a kind of porridge used in sacred rites. These are his very words:

> “Even today ancient rites and birthday observances are performed with *fritilla* porridge; and porridge seems to have been as unknown to Greece as pearl barley was to Italy.”

Jerome [Col. 0646B], however, reproaches Jovinian for resorting to cookshops and *fritillae*. By the term *fritillae*, if the reading is genuine, he means delicate porridges. See Scaliger’s observations on Varro (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 230; Pliny, Book XVIII of *Natural History*, ch. 8, p. 561; Jerome, Book I, *Against Jovinian*; Scaliger, on Book V of Varro’s *On the Latin Language*, p. 82).

*Frumen*, however, as Donatus, Servius, and Isidore teach, is the projecting or uppermost part of the throat through which the tongue sends food down into the stomach (Donatus, on Terence’s *Brothers*, Act V, scene 8, and *Phormio*, Act II, scene 2; Servius, on Virgil, Book I of the *Georgics*, p. 66, and Book I of the *Aeneid*, p. 181; Isidore, Book XX of the *Origins*, ch. 2). Donatus believes that the verb *fruor* was formed from *frumen*, while Servius believes the same of the noun *frumentum* [Col. 0646C]. What wonder, then, if others employed *frumen* to signify some kind of porridge? For further discussion of porridges, see Apicius (Donatus, on Terence’s *Eunuch*, Act IV, scene 7; Apicius, Book V, *On Cookery*, ch. 1).

But these things, Arnobius says, did no more good to the pagans sacrificing to their gods than did *africia*, *gratilla*, *catumeum*, *conspolium*, and *cubula*, which he signifies clearly enough to have been kinds of sacrificial cakes (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 239). Ovid sings in the following verses that *libum* was named after Liber, or Bacchus:

> Libations derive their name from their originator,  
> And so do *liba*, because a portion from them is given to the sacred hearths.  
> They make *liba* for the god because, with sweet juices, he—
He rejoices, and they relate that honey was discovered by Bacchus. (Ovid, *Fasti*, book III, § 10.)

But Varro, with whom others agree, thinks that this name was [Col. 0646D] derived from the fact that it is made for the purpose of offering a libation (*libandi causa*). Elsewhere, however, he wrote: “*Libum*, because it was offered in libation before it was—or they were—as it had been baked”; that is, because, once baked, it was first offered in libation before they ate it (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book VI, p. 80; ibid., book I, p. 26 ff.).

Servius explains what *liba* are, and from what ingredients they were made, as follows: “*Liba* are cakes made from spelt, honey, and oil, suitable for sacred rites.” He did not say this only once, but had previously asserted that *liba* were cakes (Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VII, verse 108; idem, on *Eclogue* 7, verse 33). Cato, however, distinguishes a *placenta* from a *libum*, and says that a *libum* is made from cheese, fine wheat flour or the finest flour, and one egg; after these have been thoroughly mixed, they are placed upon a leaf and gently baked (Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapters 54 and 76). [Col. 0647A] He then teaches how a *placenta* is made from fine wheat flour, first-grade *alica* soaked in water, fresh sheep’s-milk cheese, and good honey; these are mixed together and, with laurel leaves placed underneath, the *placenta* is formed and must be baked thoroughly and slowly. Yet, as you see, the difference between a *libum* and a *placenta* is not so great that they cannot be referred to one and the same class. Cato explains how they are made more than whether they actually differ from one another. Hence Isidore says: “*Placentae* are made from spelt; others call them *liba*, because they are pleasing (*libeant*) and agreeable (*placeant*)” (Isidore, *Origins*, book XX, chapter 2).

Nevertheless, although a *libum* and a *placenta* differed very little from one another, if Cato nevertheless distinguished them, there appears to be nothing whatever to prevent Arnobius [Col. 0647B] from having distinguished other kinds of *liba* that did not differ greatly from one another, which he calls *Africia*, *gratilla*, *catumeum*, *conspolium*, and *cubula* (Arnobius, book VII, p. 230). Indeed, the only difference among all these appears to have arisen from the material and the manner in which they were customarily made. They received their respective names either from these circumstances, from the place where they were first made, or from their differing form and shape. It matters little for our purpose to know whence these names were derived or what they really mean, but it does matter to know with what utter folly the pagans offered them in libation to their fictitious gods as though those gods were hungry.

Arnobius deliberately omits many other things that are equally ridiculous (ibid.), and says that he did not choose to name the *strebula* flesh removed from the hip-joints of bulls. [Col. 0647C] If we believe Festus, however, this name originated among the peoples of Umbria, because it was more commonly used among them than among the Romans (Festus, under *STREBULA*). For we read this observation in him:

> “*Strebula*. Plautus, using an Umbrian name, calls the hip-joints of sacrificial victims *strebulae*. The Greeks call them μηρία (*mēria*, ‘thigh-portions’). They were customarily placed upon altars, as Plautus says in the *Frivolaria*.”

No one, therefore, can doubt that this flesh was employed in pagan sacred rites. For Pollux also, when enumerating various expressions relating to sacrifices, mentions μηρία ἐπιθεῖναι (*mēria epitheinai*), “to place the thigh-portions upon the altar” (Pollux, *Onomasticon*, book I, § 14, chapter 1, p. 8). Some think that the following passage of Varro, although corrupted by copyists, bears upon this subject; there he cites various comedies of Plautus:

> “In the *Cestio*, *cerastibola*: ‘so that you may feast from the loin.’ [Col. 0647D] Opilius writes that *cerastibola* are what we call the regions around the hip-joints; the word is Greek, derived by a turning of this passage.”

(Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book VI, p. 83.)

They think that *caro strebula*, the subject discussed by our author, should be read there. See Scaliger’s notes on these words of Varro and, if you wish, Turnebus’ *Adversaria* (Turnebus, book XXIII, chapter 18).

Arnobius then says: “Nor do I choose to name the meat-portions that are not roasted, which are entrails upon spits, previously animated and scorched over coals” (Arnobius, book VII, p. 230). But the obscurity of this text sufficiently demonstrates that it was corrupted by an unskilled or inattentive copyist. Therefore, in order that some light may be shed upon it and it may become intelligible, it is helpful to observe that *pulpamentum* is undoubtedly derived from *pulpa*. According to Donatus, *pulpa* [Col. 0648A] “properly means the flesh that is chewed, because it is beaten and torn apart.” Isidore, however, says: “It is called *pulpa* because in ancient times it was eaten mixed with porridge (*puls*).” But elsewhere—and, as many think, more accurately—he writes: “*Pulpa* is flesh without fat, so called because it throbs (*palpitet*), for it often springs back. Many also call it *viscum*, because it is glutinous” (Donatus on Terence, *Hecyra*, act III, scene 4; Isidore, *Origins*, book XI, chapter 1, and book XX, chapter 2).

Once these points have been observed, the negative particle *non* appears to us to have been displaced from its proper position in Arnobius’ text. It should be restored before the noun *pulpamenta* and either understood before the word *exta* or placed there a second time, so that the passage may read as follows:

> “I do not choose to name the *strebula* flesh … [Col. 0648B] nor the roasted meat-portions that are upon spits; nor the previously animated entrails,” etc.

Arnobius’ meaning will then be clear: it is futile in sacrifices to burn meat-portions roasted upon spits—that is, the soft and delicate portions of flesh without fat, which quiver because of their softness. It is likewise futile to sacrifice the entrails of animals, previously alive and then scorched over coals, which could be roasted not upon spits but only over burning coals. If you doubt that these were offered to the gods, Festus will set you right. He believes that they received their name for this reason: “They are called *exta* because those parts which project (*extant*) and stand out most prominently are cut out for the gods” (Festus, under *EXTA*).

Arnobius adds: “Nor the salted preparations, which are a single mixture compounded from four kinds of produce” (Arnobius, [Col. 0648C] book VII, p. 230). Does he not mean by these words the salted grains that the pagans employed in sacrifices? For Sinon is represented as saying in Virgil:

> And now the accursed day had come,  
> When the sacrifice for me was being prepared,  
> And the salted grain.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, book II, verse 129.)

Pliny teaches that King Numa instituted the practice “of worshipping the gods with grain and making supplication with salted meal.” Servius, commenting on the cited verses of Virgil, observes that salt and spelt are called *mola salsa*, “salted meal,” which Pliny affirms was offered in every sacrifice and was the sole offering made by poor people (Pliny, *Natural History*, book XVIII, chapter 2, p. 473; prologue to book I, p. 5; and book XXXI, chapter 7, p. 809). But Tibullus sings that everyone frequently employed both spelt and salt:

> [Col. 0648D] And the fearful, credulous race of men appeases  
> All the terrors of the night with holy meal and crackling salt.

(Tibullus, book XIII, elegy 4.)

Servius describes how, by whom, and at what time the salted meal was prepared; consult him. Arnobius, moreover, declares it to be a mixture of four kinds of produce. Yet Virgil, in the verse already cited, mentions an indefinite plurality of grains (Servius on Virgil, *Eclogue* 8, p. 46).

Arnobius also wishes to reject the *fendicae*, or *feudicae*, as some think the word should be read (Arnobius, book VII, p. 230). Of the various names enumerated by him, some think that this alone is now unknown. [Col. 0649A] Others suppose that it was derived from the verb *findo*, “to split,” because the *fendicae* were made from pieces of split flesh. But the author himself explains what the *fendicae* are in these words:

> “They too are *hirae*”—the manuscript codex and other editions read *dirae*, but incorrectly—“which popular speech customarily calls *ilia* when it names them”—the manuscripts and certain editions read *illa*, but *hilla* should be read.

Festus defines *hira* as follows under that word:

> “A *hira*, called in the diminutive *hilla*, and called νῆστιν (*nēstin*, ‘the fasting or empty gut’) by the Greeks, is the intestine known as the jejunum.”

Macrobius, however, teaches that there are three intestines. The first is called *dissipium*, otherwise *disseptum*, and by the Greeks διάφραγμα (*diaphragma*, “partition”); the second, the middle intestine, is called μεσεντέριον (*mesenterion*, “mesentery”); and the third, which the ancients called the *hira*, is regarded as the principal one of all the intestines and carries away the refuse of food (Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, book I, chapter 6, [Col. 0649B] p. 44). Arnobius therefore said that the *fendicae* were the same as the *hirae*, which in popular language were called *hillae*, and that they were nothing other than the jejunum.

Just as Arnobius denies that *fendicae* and *hirae* should be employed in sacrifices, so too he rejects “the *oerumnae*, which,” he says, “are the first openings in the gullets by which nature enables ruminating species to send down and bring back their food” (Arnobius, book VII, p. 230). But it is certain that the word *oerumnae* has been corrupted there by an unskilled copyist and that *rumae* should be read. For when Arnobius himself repeats the same names shortly afterward (ibid., p. 231), *rumis* is consistently read in the royal manuscript and in all editions.

The word *ruma* is used in two senses by various authors. For, as Nonius Marcellus says, with the support of Varro, Festus, and Pliny, “the ancients called the breast *ruma*” (Nonius Marcellus, *On the Properties of Words*, chapter 2; Varro, *On Agriculture*, book II, chapters 1 and 11; Festus, under *RUMINALEM*; Pliny, *Natural History*, book XV, chapter 18, p. 198). [Col. 0649C] In Pliny’s text, however, we read *rumen* instead of *ruma*. In another sense, *ruma*, or *rumen* and *rumis*, signifies the hollow part of the throat, or, as our author puts it, the head of the gullet, by which certain animals bring their food back and ruminate. Hence Festus says: “The *rumen* is the part of the neck through which food is swallowed; hence *rumare* was used for what is now called *ruminare*, ‘to ruminate’” (Festus, loc. cit.). Servius writes: “*Ruminatio* is named from the *ruma*, the projecting part of the throat through which certain animals bring back food that has been swallowed” (Servius on Virgil, *Eclogue* 6, p. 33). [Col. 0649D] Isidore makes the following observations concerning the gullet and the *ruma* or *rumen*:

> “The *gurgulio* derives its name from the throat (*guttur*). Its passage extends to the mouth and nostrils, and it contains the channel through which the voice is transmitted to the tongue so that it can articulate words. Hence we also say *garrire*, ‘to chatter.’ The *rumen* lies next to the gullet and is the passage through which food and drink are swallowed. Hence beasts that bring their food back and chew it again are said to ruminate.”

(Isidore, *Origins*, book XI, chapter 1.)

Servius also says elsewhere: “*Curculio*. Varro says that this name arose through an interchange of letters, as though it were *gurgulio*, since it is almost nothing but a throat” (Servius on Virgil, *Georgics*, book I, p. 75).

Anyone may readily understand from what has been said that Arnobius’ words *ruminatoribus saeculis* signify all kinds of animals that ruminate. For Lucretius uses the noun *secula* or [Col. 0650A] *secla* in this sense more than once. In one place he sings:

> The races of wild beasts.

(Lucretius, book II, verse 1075.)

That is, the kinds of beasts. And shortly afterward:

> Indeed, very many beings of each race exist,  
> And belong to the same kind, especially among animals,  
> As the mind bears witness.

(Idem, verse 1078.)

But this noun is used in this sense so often by him and by others that the point requires no lengthier proof.

What, then, does our author say next? “Not the *magmenta*,” he says, “not the *augmina*, not the thousand varieties either of sausages or of *fitillae*” (Arnobius, book VII, p. 230). So the latest edition reads; but all the others, as well as the royal manuscript, have [Col. 0650B] *velamen sanguinum, vel fitillarum*, “a covering of bloods, or of *fitillae*.” What *magmentum* and *augmentum* mean may be learned from these words of Varro:

> “An *augmentum* is that which is cut from an immolated victim and placed upon the liver for the sake of increasing it. A *magmentum* is so called from *magis*, ‘more,’ because it has a greater relation to religion. Accordingly, for this purpose mountain shrines were established in fixed places, where it might be placed upon *matae*, from what the Greeks call μάτιας καὶ μάπιας [uncertain reading].”
