(Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book IV, p. 28.)

Commenting on this passage, Scaliger observes that a *magmentum* was a feast-offering consecrated by country people to Janus, Silvanus, Mars, Jupiter Dapalis, and others. Salmasius, however, warns us that Varro’s text is corrupt and should be emended from an ancient manuscript as follows:

> “Accordingly, for this purpose *magmentary cana* were established in fixed places, where it might be placed.”

[Col. 0650C] (Salmasius, *Exercises on Solinus*, p. 129.)

He thinks that the *magmentary cana* were baskets or dishes on which the *magmenta* to be carried to the altars were placed. See what Turnebus and Brissonius have noted concerning the *magmentum* (Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XXII, chapter 6; Brissonius, *On Formulae*, book I, p. 126 ff.).

Finally, as we have said, the editor responsible for the latest edition of Arnobius’ works replaced the corrupt words *velamen sanguinum* on his own authority with *vel farciminum*, “or of sausages,” undoubtedly because he thought that Arnobius was referring to the things mentioned shortly before. This conjecture could indeed have been recorded, but the text should not for that reason have been altered so boldly. Some think that the first word, *velamen*, should be divided as *vel amen*, and they tell us that *amen* there has the same meaning as [Col. 0650D] Hesychius’ εἶδος πλακοῦντος, “a kind of cake.” But what, I ask, would the following noun *sanguinum*, “of bloods,” mean there? What does it have in common with cakes? Others suppose that *amen* means the same as *amentum*, a strap or bond. But they ought to have shown what *amen*, or “bonds of bloods,” could contribute to Arnobius’ discussion of *magmenta*, *augmina*, and *fitillae*. It is therefore better to acknowledge frankly that these two words, *velamen sanguinum*, are corrupt, and that the true reading of our author must be sought from another and more accurate manuscript. If conjectures were permissible, however, we would suspect that he wrote *vel salsaminum*, “or of salted preparations.” For there he repeats what has already been said, and shortly before had mentioned *salsamina*. But we shall readily assent to more acute scholars [Col. 0651A] who discover a better reading.

Arnobius adds that it is futile to imagine that all those portions which they called *proficias*—*praesicias* in the manuscript—were pleasing to the gods (Arnobius, book VII, p. 231). But *prosiciae* or *prosicies*, and *prosicium*, were the cut-up entrails of animals, or the severed portions of them, that were carried to the altars. Solinus relates that when those who conduct rites on the hill of Vulcan have brought in the *prosiciae*, if the sacrifice is approved, even green twigs are kindled by the divinity itself, without any breath of flame being applied (Solinus, *Polyhistor*, chapter 5, p. 20). Salmasius discusses the *prosiciae* more fully in his commentary on this passage; he may be consulted, as may the learned Brissonius (Brissonius, *On Formulae*, book I, p. 28).

[Col. 0651B] Arnobius readily demonstrates that all the things thus far mentioned by us are offered to the gods or burned upon their altars in vain (Arnobius, book VII, p. 231). For no rational ground or cause—which, as has been said, is especially required in the performance of sacred rites—has ever been produced by anyone to explain why these things should be offered in libation to the gods. If the gods are true gods, they neither feast sumptuously, nor suffer from indigestion or hunger, nor seek the pleasures of flavors, so that foods now cooked, now half-raw, now roasted, and these or other kinds of animal flesh must be set before them. What, Arnobius asks, could they ever have taken for delightful *mateolae*, or, as Martial and Tertullian call them (Martial, book X, epigram 59; Tertullian, *On the Testimony of the Soul*, chapter 4), *mattyae*—that is, the most exquisite delicacies, concerning which see below (below, final chapter, article 3)? [Col. 0651C] What could be more absurd to say than that the gods are delighted, appeased, or rendered propitious by the testicles, tails, throats, dirges, morsels, and other similar things from cattle that are offered and poured out to them, all of which we have thus far enumerated?

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### On the Use of Incense and Wine in the Sacrifices of the Pagans, and on Certain Other Absurd Rites and Festival Days of Theirs

### ARTICLE I  
#### By What Arguments Arnobius Establishes That the Superstitious Use of Incense, or Panchaean Resin, Must Be Rejected in the Sacred Rites and Sacrifices of the Pagans; That It Was Unknown in the Heroic Age, in the Time of the Alban Kings, and Even to the Etruscans; and That Holy Spelt Was Then Employed. An Explanation of What “Male Incense” Is, and a Discussion of the Use of Incense in Pagan Funerals

[Col. 0651D] The pagans very frequently employed in their sacred rites and sacrifices not only the things enumerated in the preceding articles, but also incense and wine. Incense is called by Arnobius “Panchaean resin,” evidently after Panchaea, a region of Troglodytic Arabia adjoining the entrance of the Arabian Gulf (Arnobius, book VII, p. 231 ff.). Servius writes of it in his commentaries on Virgil:

> “Panchaea is a people of the Sabaeans, among whom incense grows, as in: ‘The Sabaeans alone possess the incense-bearing branch.’ Likewise: ‘And all Panchaea, rich in incense-bearing sands.’”

(Servius on Virgil, *Georgics*, book II, at verse 115, p. 101.)

Similarly Ovid writes:

> Let the Panchaean land bring incense  
> Sweated from the wood, and other flowers.

(Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book X, fable 9.) [Col. 0652A]

And Lucretius:

> And nearby the altar breathes forth Panchaean fragrances.

(Lucretius, book II, verse 417.)

Consult also, if you wish, Tibullus, Claudian, and others (Tibullus, book IV, elegy 2; Claudian, *On the Third Consulship of Honorius*, at the end).

Arnobius demonstrates that the use of Panchaean resin, or incense, in the sacred rites and sacrifices of the pagans was plainly foolish and superstitious from the fact that it was recent and newly introduced. For throughout many centuries after the creation of the world it was entirely unknown to the pagans. There occurs nowhere, he says, even the slightest mention of it in the heroic age, or in the time of the Trojans (Arnobius, book VII, p. 232). If you ask by whose authority this may be confirmed, we shall give you Pliny, [Col. 0652B] who recorded the following concerning perfumes: “Who first invented them is not reported. They did not exist in the time of the Trojan War, nor was incense used in supplication” (Pliny, *Natural History*, book II, chapter 1, p. 55).

Then Theophrastus—whose words were transcribed by Porphyry and Eusebius, not without variant readings—explains the same point more fully:

> Ἀνάριθμος μέν τις ἔοικεν εἶναι χρόνος, ἀφ’ οὗ τό γε πάντων λογιώτατον γένος, ὥς φησι Θεόφραστος, καὶ τὴν ἱερωτάτην ὑπὸ τοῦ Νείλου κτισθεῖσαν χώραν κατοικοῦν, ἤρξατο πρῶτον ἐφ’ ἑστίας τοῖς οὐρανίοις θεοῖς θύειν, οὐ σμύρνης, οὐδὲ κασίας, καὶ λιβανωτοῦ κρόκῳ μιχθέντων ἀπαρχάς· πολλαῖς γὰρ γενεαῖς ὕστερον παρελήφθη καὶ ταῦτα, καὶ πλάνης ἐρευνητὴς μαστὴρ ὁ ἄνθρωπος γιγνόμενος, τῆς ἀναγκαίας ζωῆς, μετὰ πολλῶν πόνων καὶ δακρύων, σταγόνας ἀπήρξατο τοῖς θεοῖς. [Col. 0652C] οὐ τούτων οὖν ἔθυον πρότερον, ἀλλὰ χλόης, οἱονεί τινα τῆς γονίμου φύσεως χνοῦν ταῖς χερσὶν ἀράμενοι.

> “There appears to have been an immeasurably long period since the people wisest of all, as Theophrastus says, who inhabited that most sacred land formed by the Nile, first began to sacrifice upon their hearths to the heavenly gods—not first-fruits of myrrh, cassia, and frankincense mixed with saffron. For these things were adopted many generations later, when humankind, becoming an investigator and seeker amid wandering, with many labors and tears, of the necessities of life, offered to the gods the resinous drops of the plants just mentioned. Thus in earlier times people did not sacrifice these things, but, taking blades of grass in their hands as though they were a kind of down from fertile nature, offered them.”

(Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animal Food*, book II, p. 124; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book I, chapter 9, p. 28.)



> An immeasurably long period indeed appears to have elapsed since the wisest of all peoples, as Theophrastus says—the people inhabiting that most sacred land formed by the Nile—first began to sacrifice to the heavenly gods within their private homes, without offering first-fruits of myrrh, cassia, or incense mixed with saffron. For many generations those later substances had not yet come into use. When humankind had become a traveler and, amid very many labors and tears, an investigator of the necessities of life, it offered to the gods drops from the plants I have mentioned. Thus people did not formerly offer such things, but grass, which they presented in their hands as a kind of primal down of fertile nature. [Col. 0652D]

Porphyry pursues these matters at greater length than would make it necessary for us to transcribe them all. Therefore, if you wish, consult his book, and you will recognize that he clearly asserts that the use of incense was unknown both in the heroic age and in the earliest times of the world. Nevertheless, Arnobius did not venture to affirm this without qualification, but added, “as is believed and reported” (Arnobius, book VII, p. 232). Certain persons therefore wrongly accuse him of error at this point.

Moreover, no one can deny the truth of what he added as an eyewitness, certainly one whose testimony in this matter is beyond all objection: the use of incense was recent and newly introduced in his own country. Even Etruria, he says—the progenitor and mother of superstition (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 1190)—[Col. 0653A] did not originally know it. Etruria is rightly called by him the teacher and mother of superstition, as is evident both from what we have noted concerning it elsewhere and from what Ovid, Servius, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, and Tertullian committed to writing (Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book XV, p. 577; Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid*, book II, p. 259; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book IX, p. 563; Tertullian, *On the Shows*, chapter 4). But among these writers Cicero must especially be cited; in his speech *On the Responses of the Haruspices* he speaks as follows:

> “For my part, I hold first as the authorities and teachers of the observance of religious rites … those who believed that explanations of portents were contained in the Etruscan discipline.”

(Cicero, Oration XXX, *On the Responses of the Haruspices*, p. 431.)

Our author demonstrates by two arguments that, in the earliest times of those same Etruscans, [Col. 0653B] no incense was employed in pagan sacred rites (Arnobius, book VII, p. 232). First, he says, this is shown by the rites of the shrines, where incense was not burned. Second, there was no use of it, he says, during the four hundred years in which the Alban state flourished, or for as long as Romulus and Numa—an architect of religious rites, as is sufficiently clear from the writers of Roman history—ruled the Romans. The kingdom of the Albans began with Aeneas, or rather with his son Ascanius, by whom Alba Longa was founded. Livy individually enumerates the others who reigned after him (Livy, book I, near the beginning); Sigonius, in his notes on Livy’s history, and other chronographers identify them from Livy himself, Ovid, Dionysius, and Eusebius.

[Col. 0653C] Arnobius says that no incense was offered in sacred rites down to those times. “This is shown,” he says, “by the holy spelt with which it was customary to perform the solemn duties of sacrifices” (Arnobius, loc. cit.). For in the ancient age, as Ovid reports, people, still rustic, made offerings and sacrifices to the gods with spelt and salt, or with *mola salsa*, salted meal, which we discussed above. He sang as follows:

> In former times, what could reconcile gods to man  
> Was spelt and a gleaming grain of pure salt.  
> No foreign ship, driven over the ocean waters,  
> Had yet brought myrrh wept from the bark.  
> Neither Euphrates nor India had sent incense or costus,  
> Nor were the red threads of saffron known.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, book I, § 8.)

After Varro, Pliny gave the reason for this custom: namely, that the ancients ate salt with bread. [Col. 0653D] Valerius Maximus, however, says that since porridge was more commonly used among them than bread, they employed *mola salsa*—that is, a composition of spelt and salt, not incense—in all their sacrifices (Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXI, chapter 7, p. 809 f.; Valerius Maximus, book II, chapter 5, § 5, p. 102).

Arnobius therefore argues from this as follows: if the gods are appeased by the burning of incense, ancient people, by whom that rite was omitted, sinned. But if incense either did not please the gods in former times or was a matter of indifference to them, then it is now employed futilely and wrongly (Arnobius, book VII, p. 233).

Nor should it be said that the gods are honored by the offering of incense. For the question is not whether human beings, but whether the gods, were persuaded of this. Yet who could ever [Col. 0654A] know it? Moreover, what sort of honor is paid to the gods by the odor of burned incense—that is, of a sticky resin flowing from the bark of trees? Why are they not honored by other odors and vapors as well? Is it perhaps because the smell of burning incense is more pleasing to them than any other? But the gods have no nostrils through which they might draw in breezes and airy breaths. For whatever breathes in that manner is mortal. Yet who does not acknowledge that the gods must be immortal? They are therefore captivated neither by incense nor by any other odor, “even if,” Arnobius says, “you burn a thousand pounds of male incense” (ibid., p. 234).

According to Pliny and Servius (Pliny, *Natural History*, book XII, chapter 14, p. 25; Servius on the cited verses of Virgil), “male incense” (*thus masculum*) is thought to be so named from its resemblance to testicles. In French it is called *encens mâle*, or *oliban*. Virgil sang of it:

> Bring water, and encircle these altars with a soft fillet;  
> Burn rich vervain and male incense.

(Virgil, *Eclogue* 8, verse 64 ff.) [Col. 0654B]

Moreover, even if it were conceded—although this is false—that the gods possess a sense of smell, by what reasoning, I ask, can it be proved that the odor of this incense is pleasant and agreeable to them? Is it because it is agreeable to human beings? Might it not readily happen that things which seem pleasant and delightful to human beings displease the gods—whose substance ought to be entirely different—and prove troublesome and disagreeable to them? See Gothofredus’ commentary on the edict of Theodosius the Great by which pagans were forbidden the use of incense, sacrifices, and all worship of the gods (vol. VI, *Theodosian Code*, law 12, p. 273 ff.).

[Col. 0654C] Finally, we may add one point correctly stated by our author: “Incense is very closely associated with the bodies of the dead in funeral rites” (Arnobius, book VII, p. 242). For it was customary among the pagans, when performing rites for their deceased relatives, to cover the bodies of the dead with incense, whether those bodies were cremated or committed to burial. Thus Virgil, when describing the funeral of Misenus and the manner in which his body was cremated, said:

> Heaped gifts of incense are burned,  
> Banquet-offerings and bowls of poured-out olive oil.

(Virgil, *Aeneid*, book VI, verse 224 ff.)

Festus wrote that an *acerra* was an altar customarily placed before the dead, upon which fragrances were burned, or a chest in which incense was stored (Festus, under *ACERRA*). Hence Cicero, when mentioning the laws concerning tombs and funerals, says, “Nor are the *acerrae* to be omitted” (Cicero, *On the Laws*, book II, p. 341). In Brissonius you may read various expressions used by the ancients concerning the offering of incense to the gods (Brissonius, *On Formulae*, book I, pp. 29–30). But it is certainly evident from what has been said that the use and custom of burning incense to the fictitious gods of the pagans was entirely useless and superstitious. We have, however, discussed it in our earlier investigations.

### ARTICLE II  
#### That the Custom of Offering Wine in Libation in Pagan Sacred Rites and Sacrifices, as the Companion of Incense, Was No Less Perverse; and an Explanation of *Bria*, *Simpuvium*, “Venerable Musks,” and “Be Thou Magnified by This Inferial Wine”

In the private and solemn sacred rites of the pagans, unmixed wine, [Col. 0655A] Arnobius says, was the companion of incense (Arnobius, book VII, p. 234). For they customarily poured wine upon incense given to the flames or, as Lactantius puts it, moistened the hearths by pouring out fragrant, aged wine (Lactantius, book VI, chapter 1, p. 542). Concerning this rite, besides the testimony of various authors, we read the following words of Horace:

> Boys, set down the sacred boughs and incense,  
> And a bowl of two-year-old unmixed wine.  
> With a victim sacrificed, [the deity] will come more gently.

(Horace, *Odes*, book I, ode 19.)

And Ovid:

> And with the bowl of unmixed wine stood the chest of incense.  
> Incense and wine were given to the hearths.

(Ovid, *Fasti*, book IV, near the end.) [Col. 0655B]

Elsewhere, when speaking of the celebration of the birthday of his wife, for whose welfare he prays, he writes:

> Give me incense, boy, to make the flames burn richly,  
> And unmixed wine that hisses when poured upon the holy fire.

In other books also he touches upon this custom, which is likewise discussed by Tertullian and at greater length by Brissonius (Ovid, *Tristia*, book V, elegy 5, p. 171; *Metamorphoses*, book XIII, fable 4, p. 485; *Fasti*, book II, § 15; Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 20; Brissonius, *On Formulae*, book I, p. 30 ff.).

But Arnobius demonstrates by various arguments that this depraved and perverse custom of offering wine in libation, like that of offering incense, must be rejected by everyone. First, no reason for this rite could ever be produced by anyone. For the gods, being immortal, never suffer thirst; nor must wine be served to them so that they may digest and process their food. By precisely the same reasoning Lactantius, the pupil of our Arnobius, assails this pagan error:

> “They slaughter choice and fat victims for the god as though he were hungry; they pour out wines as though he were thirsty.”

(Lactantius, book VI, chapter 2, pp. 542 and 547.)

He therefore argues:

> “Accordingly, they attribute to the gods not a heavenly but rather a human mode of sensation. They consequently believe that the things necessary and pleasing to us are also necessary and pleasing to them—to us who, when hungry, need food; when thirsty, drink; when cold, clothing; and, after the sun has set, light so that we may see. From no circumstances, therefore, can it be so clearly proved and understood that these supposed gods, who once lived, are dead as from the rite itself, which is wholly earthly.”

[Col. 0655D] Arnobius therefore attacks the pagans with both skill and wit:

> “Give the immortal gods cups from which to drink, I beg you; bring out goblets, *briae*, bowls, and *simpuvia*.”

(Arnobius, book VII, p. 235.)

A *bria* was a kind of measure, vessel, or drinking-cup suitable for holding wine. Hence in an old Latin–Greek glossary we read: “*Bria*, εἶδος ἀγγείου (*eidos angeiou*), ‘a kind of vessel’; a certain measure.” See Martinius’ lexicon and Du Cange’s glossary.

A *simpuvium* was likewise a wooden vessel, according to Nonius, or an earthenware vessel, as others hold. They maintain that it received this name because all the priests drank from it together (Nonius, *On the Properties of Words*, chapter 19, § 29). They infer from these verses of Juvenal that it was employed by Numa in sacred rites:

> [Col. 0656A] And who among men then despised the divine power?  
> Or who dared to laugh at Numa’s *simpuvium*,  
> His black dish, and the fragile little plates  
> Made upon the Vatican hill?

(Juvenal, *Satire* 6, verse 340.)

Would you like yet another witness to this custom? Hear Pliny:

> “In sacred rites, even amid today’s wealth, libations are poured not from vessels of murrhine stone or crystal, but from earthenware *simpuvia*.”

(Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 12, p. 245.)

They think that the *simpuvium* is the same as the *simpulum*, concerning which see Varro, Paulus, and others (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book IV, p. 31; Paulus, in the vocabulary under *SIMPULUM*). We have already offered some preliminary observations on it from our author himself and from Cicero (above, chapter 13, article 2).

Furthermore, as Arnobius says, the pagans, in honor of their gods, raised “venerable musks” after the coals [Col. 0656B] had been extinguished (Arnobius, book VII, p. 235). In the royal manuscript and the old editions, *muscas*, “flies,” is found instead of *muscos*, but seemingly without sense; other editions have *cnissas*, “the savor of burnt sacrifice,” with scarcely greater justification. Some added *suffitus*, “fumigations,” in the margin, undoubtedly only by way of explanation. We therefore prefer the word *muscos*, or *moschos*, by which some precious perfume is signified. For they cast a preparation made from incense and fragrant wine into the flames and burning coals, undoubtedly so that a pleasant odor might arise from it. Nevertheless, without the authority of some more accurate manuscript, we do not venture to affirm anything concerning the true reading of Arnobius’ text.

Whatever position one adopts concerning that reading, our author judges that no hearing at all should be given to the pagans, who [Col. 0656C] attempted to persuade everyone that this fragrant wine was rightly offered in libation to the gods as an honor and to render them propitious. For what honor, he asks, is paid to the gods when “you cast and sprinkle tiny drops of wine upon a glowing coal?” (ibid. ff.). What could be more opposed to right reason or more absurd to say than that the gods are honored, or induced to favor human beings, by wine poured out—wine that weakens the sinews of the virtues; that is hostile to modesty, chastity, and shame; and that, if you drink it too greedily, will plunge you into madness and frenzy?

But error had so thoroughly pervaded people deceived by the false appearance of religion that, in the solemn formulae with which they offered wine in libation to the gods, they professed that they were conferring great honor upon them. For they signified precisely this by the words that Arnobius reports in the same place:

> “Be thou magnified by this inferial wine” (*Mactus hoc vino inferio esto*).

(Ibid., p. 236.) [Col. 0656D]

Servius, and afterward Isidore, attest that this was written and prescribed in the Pontifical Books, or books of the pontiffs:

> “In the Pontifical Books, those performing sacrifice said to the god: ‘Be thou magnified by this inferial wine’” (*Macte hoc inferio vino esto*).

(Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid*, book IX, p. 564; Isidore, *Etymologies*, book X, under *MACTUS*; Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapters 132 and 134.)

The formula was recorded more than once by Cato and others. As may be learned from Festus, Scaliger, and Brissonius, *inferial wine* was wine poured below the rim of the bowl (Festus, under *INFERIUM*; Scaliger, conjectures on Varro, p. 80; Brissonius, *On Formulae*, book I, pp. 30 and 37). As we have already said, *mactus* meant “increased” or “magnified.” The meaning of these words was therefore: “You, Jupiter—or any other god—be magnified by this inferial wine, which, poured beneath the rim of the bowl, is offered to you in libation.”

Arnobius observes from Trebatius that the word *inferio* was added [Col. 0657A] lest the wine stored in cellars and storerooms, from which this wine had been drawn, should become sacred and be withdrawn from human use. Good heavens, how greatly that was to be feared!

But let us hear our author’s ensuing argument against the pagans. With what honor, he asks, can a god be magnified when the sacrificer imposes upon him a law that he must not demand more than that inferial wine? Was that exalted god so excessively voracious, such a glutton and gourmand, that his appetite had to be checked by this restriction? For the words *Mactus hoc vino inferio esto* meant nothing other than: “Be magnified—that is, increased and enlarged in honor—only to the degree I wish, and no more than I command. For you will not be honored beyond my pleasure, according as I will more or less wine to be poured below the rim of the bowl.” Thus this law and restriction affected with disgrace, not honor, a god who might have demanded more.

### ARTICLE III  
#### How Rightly Arnobius Attacks and Rejects Other Foolish Pagan Rites, by Which They Adorned Their Gods with Garlands and Crowns, Employed Cymbals, Drums, Concerted Music, and Foot-Clappers, and Greeted Them in the Morning; and How Ridiculous and Absurd Were the Washing of the Mother of the Gods, the Banquet of Jupiter, the Vintage Festival of Aesculapius, the Sacred Couches of Ceres and Others, and the Birthdays of Earth and Other Deities

There were other ceremonies [Col. 0657C] and various rites in the pagan sacred observances, no less useless, superstitious, and absurd than those thus far mentioned (Arnobius, book VII, p. 237). For they were accustomed to adorn their gods—or the images and statues of those gods—with garlands and crowns. But elsewhere, and more than once, we have shown how deservedly and justly Arnobius condemned this pagan custom (vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 802; and *Dissertation on Minucius*, chapter 19, article 2).

Arnobius further ridicules those same pagans who, in their mysteries, festivals, and solemnities, employed cymbals, drums, ensembles, and *scabilla*, which were a kind of rattle. They especially misused these and other musical instruments when, in celebrating the sacred mysteries and festivals of the Mother of the Gods, or Cybele, they carried her image through the cities. How ridiculous these practices were you may sufficiently [Col. 0657D] recognize from these verses of Ovid:

> The half-men shall go forth and beat their hollow drums,  
> And bronze struck upon bronze shall give a ringing sound.  
> (Ovid, *Fasti*, Book IV, § 3.)

And also from what he added shortly afterward:

> Imitating the ancient deed,  
> The goddess’s attendants shake their bronze and their hoarse hides.  
> Cymbals clash in place of helmets, drums in place of shields;  
> The pipe gives Phrygian notes, as it gave them long ago.  
> (*Ibid.*)

Lucretius similarly sang:

> Tight-stretched drums thunder beneath their palms, and hollow  
> Cymbals all around, while horns threaten with hoarse-sounding music;  
> And the hollow pipe excites their minds with a Phrygian rhythm.  
> (Lucretius, Book II, verses 618 ff.)

But we have already made certain observations about these matters elsewhere (*Dissertation* [Col. 0658A] *on Minucius*, ch. 19, arts. 2 and 3). Arnobius therefore jeers, not without wit, at these absurd rites of the pagans. For he asks those same pagans whether the gods, on hearing those crashes and noises, think themselves treated with honor; whether they are soothed and then truly lay aside their anger; or whether, like little children, they are frightened by them. If this was their belief, surely they could have devised nothing more rash than these ridiculous opinions, or more insulting to the divine majesty.

Our author then similarly assails their morning awakenings and vigils, by which they went to salute their gods in the morning just as they did in the evening (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 237). Apuleius speaks as follows about that customary practice of greeting the gods in the morning:

> I was awaiting the morning opening of the temple. [Col. 0658B] When the gleaming curtains had been drawn aside, each of us separately prayed before the venerable sight of the goddess; and the priest, going around the altars set in order, performed the divine service and, with solemn supplications, poured a libation of what had been drawn from the sanctuary’s spring [the word before *libat* is uncertain]. When the rites had now been duly completed, the worshippers loudly proclaimed the first hour with greetings to the dawning light.  
> (Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, Book II, p. 207.)

Seneca, however, declares in these very words that those morning salutations should be proscribed and forbidden:

> Let us forbid anyone to light a lamp on the sabbath, since the gods have no need of light, and not even human beings take pleasure in smoke. Let us prohibit the performance of morning salutations and sitting at the doors of temples. Human ambition is captivated by such attentions. He worships God who knows him.  
> (Seneca, Epistle 95, p. 191.)

[Col. 0658C] Yet the pagans, blinded by empty superstition, were accustomed to salute their gods not only morning and evening, but at every hour of the day, as Tertullian testifies: “Those who flatter them by grooming the idols, adorning the altars, and saluting them at every hour are said to perform their attendance” (Tertullian, *On Fasting*, ch. 16, p. 713).

What wonder is it, then, if Arnobius jokingly denounces these salutations, about which Brissonius has written at greater length?

> Do the heavenly gods fall asleep, so that they must return to wakefulness? What are those periods of sleep during which, so that they may fare well, you commend them with an auspicious greeting? Are the gods released by the repose of sleep, and, so that they may be occupied by it, must gentle lullabies be heard?  
> (Arnobius, loc. cit.; Brissonius, *Formulae*, Book I, pp. 38 ff.)

If you ask [Col. 0658D] what he intends by this last word, *naeniae*, we answer that it has several meanings. First, *naeniae* denotes intestine or food cut into very small pieces, which we discussed above. Second, it means a frivolous thing. Third, any useless song. Hence Horace:

> Tell me, Roscia, please: is the law better, or the children’s  
> Ditty that offers a kingdom to those who act rightly?  
> (Horace, Book I, Epistle 1, to Maecenas, verses 62–63.)

Fourth, it denotes a song in praise of the dead, or one used to entice children to sleep. The word *naenia* appears to be employed by Arnobius in this fourth or third sense. What, he asks, could be more absurd than imagining gods asleep and then awake after sleep?

He proceeds as follows to other, no less superstitious rites of the pagans: [Col. 0659A] “Today is the washing of the Mother of the Gods” (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 237)—that is, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, as we learn from these words of Ammianus Marcellinus:

> Before the sixth day before the Kalends, on which the annual processions of the Mother of the Gods are celebrated at Rome, and the carriage in which her image is conveyed is said to be washed in the waters of the Almo.  
> (Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXIII, ch. 3, p. 355.)

But not only her carriage but also her image itself was washed there, as Lucan sang in these verses:

> Then those who preserve the destinies of the gods and their secret songs,  
> And bring Cybele back after she has been washed in the little Almo.  
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, Book I, p. 124.)

Martial expresses it more briefly:

> The Capenian Gate, where the great drop falls,  
> [Col. 0659B] And where the Almo washes the Phrygian Mother’s iron.  
> (Martial, Book III, Epigram 47.)

“Iron,” that is, the sacred object. The place, therefore, where the Mother of the Gods was washed every year was where the river Almo flows into the Tiber before the Capenian Gate. See Ovid (*Fasti*, Book IV, p. 580), as well as the observations of Fulvius Ursinus on the rustic calendar and of Valesius on the cited words of Ammianus. Above all, however, Prudentius and Augustine should be read. They most sharply assail the utterly shameful rites of this washing, and Augustine finally concludes as follows: “What are acts of sacrilege, if these are sacred rites? Or what is pollution, if that is a washing?” (Prudentius, *On the Martyrdom of St. Romanus*; Augustine, *City of God*, Book II, ch. 4, p. 34.) Arnobius was therefore entirely right to maintain that it was ridiculous to say that the gods became dirty and required cleansing waters and the ancient rubbing with ashes in order to wash away their filth.

He then says: “Tomorrow,” [Col. 0659C] “is Jupiter’s feast” (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 238)—namely, on the Ides of November, as is recorded in the rustic calendar. Mention of this feast is by no means uncommon among various writers. Thus we read somewhere in Livy: “The Plebeian Games were repeated for two days, and Jupiter’s feast was held on account of the games” (Livy, Book XXV, ch. 2; Book XXVII, ch. 36; and Book XXXIII, ch. 42). He repeats the same statement elsewhere.

Cicero, moreover, teaches that this festal sacrifice and the three *epulones* who presided over it had been instituted by Numa:

> Because of the multitude of sacrifices, the ancient pontiffs wished there to be three men called *Epulones*, although they themselves had been instituted by Numa to perform, among other things, that festal [Col. 0659D] sacrifice associated with the games.  
> (Cicero, *On the Orator*, Book III, p. 187, line 30.)

Livy, however, reports that the Board of Three *Epulones* was first created at Rome by Romuleius, or Romulius (Livy, Book XXXIII, ch. 42). Valerius Maximus, Tertullian, and others have spoken of them and of Jupiter’s feast; but Gutherius has written more extensively on it, and you may consult him (Valerius Maximus, Book II, ch. 1, § 3, and Book IV, p. 2, § 3; Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 13; Gutherius, *On the Ancient Law of the Pontiffs*, Book IV, ch. 23).

Was not the blindness of the pagans therefore utterly deplorable, when they seriously said that Jupiter was filled with great banquets or, as Valerius Maximus says in the passage cited above, that Jupiter was invited to dinner upon a dining couch, while Juno and Minerva were invited to sit upon chairs? Therefore Lactantius, following his teacher Arnobius, [Col. 0660A] later mocked these absurd pagan rites as follows: “Indeed, they even prepare sacred banquets and elaborate feasts, offering them as though the gods were going to taste something from them” (Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book VI, ch. 1, p. 542).

Far more difficult, however, is what Arnobius adds: “The vintage-festival of Aesculapius is being performed and celebrated” (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 238). For he is not speaking there of the Wine Festivals, since Varro, Festus, Ovid, and others testify that the first of those was sacred to Jupiter and the later one to Venus (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book V, pp. 40 and 50; Festus, under the word *VENALIA*; Ovid, *Fasti*, Book IV, pp. 616 ff.).

It must be observed, however, that there were other festivals called the *Meditrinalia*, concerning which Varro says:

> The day was named from healing, because, as Flaccus, the Flamen of Mars, used to say, on that day it was customary to offer and taste both new and old [Col. 0660B] wine for medicinal purposes. Many still do this even now, saying: “I drink new and old wine; I remedy a new and old disease.”  
> (Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book V, p. 51.)

But Festus, who reported these last words, asserts that the *Meditrinalia* took their name from the goddess Meditrina (Festus, under the word *MEDITRINALIA*). Plutarch, however, relates that in former times those who tasted new wine made vows that its use might be harmless and a salutary medicine (Plutarch, *Table Talk*, Book III, question 7, p. 651). But he says that this was done on the day they called the *Pithoegia* (“Jar-Opening”). That festival, as Meursius teaches, was celebrated in honor of Bacchus (Meursius, *Greece at Festival*, Book I, p. 719; *Greek Antiquities*, vol. VII). Whether it was also sacred [Col. 0660C] to Aesculapius on account of its medicinal purpose is for others to judge. We are well aware that Theodoret mentions one festival of Aesculapius, which he calls the *Asklēpia* (Ἀσκλήπια) (Theodoret, Discourse 3, *On Sacrifices*, vol. IV, p. 583). But if you can rightly prove that this was the same as the vintage-festival of Aesculapius, we shall immediately agree with you.

Arnobius, however, clearly shows that these festivals of gods who were falsely believed to cultivate vineyards were celebrated as superstitiously as the lectisternium of Ceres (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 238). Indeed, there were, as Apuleius says, “preparations for public banquets, lectisternia of the gods, and feast days” (Apuleius, *On the World*, Book I, p. 409). For in the temples, says Augustine, “couches were spread in honor of the gods, from which this sacred rite—or rather sacrilege—received [Col. 0660D] its name” (Augustine, *City of God*, Book III, ch. 17, p. 74).

According to Livy, the first lectisternium was held at Rome to allay a plague raging during the summer, after the Sibylline Books had been consulted by decree of the Senate:

> For eight days, says he, the two commissioners for performing sacred rites sought to appease Apollo and Latona, Diana and Hercules, Mercury and Neptune, on three couches spread as magnificently as could then be managed.  
> (Livy, Book V, ch. 13.)

Who can be unaware that lectisternia were thereafter held very frequently? Of all of them, however, we shall mention only the one of which Livy speaks as follows. When Hannibal was laying waste the countryside of Italy, after the Sibylline Books had been consulted and a vow duly pronounced, [Col. 0661A] “a lectisternium,” he says, “was held for three days under the supervision of the ten commissioners for sacred rites. Six cushioned couches stood on display: one for Jupiter and Juno, a second for Neptune and Minerva, a third for Mars and Venus, a fourth for Apollo and Diana, a fifth for Vulcan and Vesta, and a sixth for Mercury and Ceres” (Livy, Book XXII, § 10).

You see clearly that in these lectisternia the gods were placed upon couches and cushions, and supplications were offered to them so that they might avert some evil. Arnobius mentions only Ceres, but by way of example. He does not mean that a lectisternium was held for her alone. He therefore rightly censures the madness of the pagans, since they imagined their gods reclining, in the manner we have described, upon soft couches and cushions spread out openly and publicly.

[Col. 0661B] Finally, in precisely the same manner, he jeers at and denounces other feast days which the pagans customarily celebrated as the birthdays of their gods. By the single example of Tellus, he shows that all the rest must likewise be condemned:

> It is Tellus’s birthday. For gods emerge from wombs and have joyous days assigned to them on which they began to draw the breath of life.  
> (Arnobius, Book VII, p. 238.)

Yet the ancient calendar records not only the birthday of Tellus but also those of various other gods, such as Mercury, Minerva, and Jupiter Ammon; on that calendar you may read the notes of Lambecius. Hence Lactantius says: “The celebrations of the games are festivals of the gods, since they were instituted on account of their birthdays or the dedications of new temples” (Lactantius, Book VI, ch. 19, p. 621).

[Col. 0661C] Arnobius was therefore right to attack that most foolish custom of the pagans with deserved ridicule. For, as he said, those who declared that the gods had once not existed and had been born from others necessarily confessed that these same gods were not true gods but false and fictitious ones, as we have demonstrated elsewhere, with our author himself, by irrefutable arguments. Who, then, after duly weighing everything discussed thus far, will not freely admit that the solemn festivals, sacred rites, and mysteries of the pagans utterly overthrow the divinity which those same pagans boastfully attributed to all those in whose honor they were performed?

# CHAPTER XXV. How Meager and Insignificant Human Knowledge Is

## ARTICLE I. How Little a Human Being Knows; That a Human Being Does Not Know What He Himself Is, How and When Dreams Occur, How Vision Takes Place and Taste Is Perceived, Why Hair Turns Gray and Oil Does Not Mix with Other Liquids, Why the Mind Is Sick in the Sick and Foolish or Delirious in Others, What the Arrangement of the Parts of Our Body Is, and to What End Arnobius Said These Things

[Col. 0661D]

Such was the wholly foolish opinion of the pagans by which, as we have seen (*Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 3, art. 1), they represented all Christians as entirely uneducated, ignorant, and illiterate, while boasting, as falsely as audaciously, that they themselves were thoroughly instructed in every branch of knowledge. Arnobius therefore beats down and crushes that empty ostentation with various supports of argument (Arnobius, Book II, p. 45).

From where, he asks, did that boast arise? Was it because they were able to inflect verbs and nouns through cases and tenses [Col. 0662A]—that is, because they knew the laws of grammar, rhetoric, or dialectic exceedingly well? (*Ibid.*, pp. 55–56.) But what results from this except an empty display of knowledge suitable for boys? Was it because their souls had, from their very origin, been imbued with every kind of knowledge and learning? But we have shown that this error was sufficiently refuted by Arnobius himself (above, ch. 9, art. 1). Was it because they had acquired the sciences and arts through labor and practice? Yet how meager human knowledge is may be inferred from the fact that, after so many ages have elapsed since the beginning of the world, human beings know with certainty not many things at all, but exceedingly few.

For does not “Socrates,” as our author puts it, “fail to comprehend in the *Phaedo* (Royal MS: *Phaedrus*) what a human being is, or whence he comes—ambiguous, variable, changeable, deceitful, manifold, multiform; [Col. 0662B] for what purposes he was brought forth, by whose ingenuity he was devised, what he is doing in the world, and why he experiences such great swarms of evils?” (*Ibid.*, p. 46.)

Why, however, *Phaedo* was printed there in place of *Phaedrus* is nowhere explained, either in the editions or in the notes. Yet in Plato’s *Phaedrus*, Socrates is represented (Plato, *Phaedrus*, vol. III, p. 230), while considering himself, as inquiring whether he is a beast more complex than Typhon, mad and furious, or some gentler and simpler creature, participating in a certain divine nature and destiny free from all pride and insolence. Whether our author paraphrastically (*paraphrastikōs*, παραφραστικῶς) expounded this passage of Plato or cited another one, consider, I ask, and decide.

[Col. 0662C] What of the fact that a human being is ignorant not only of these things but also of the ways in which, in Arnobius’s words, “dreams occur”? Indeed, “in the *Theaetetus* (MS codex: *Theaetone*—you see how corruptly), Plato doubts whether we are ever awake, or whether what is called wakefulness is itself a portion of a perpetual sleep, and whether what we seem to be doing when we say that we are dreaming is a dream” (Arnobius, Book II, p. 46). And indeed, in the cited book, that foremost of philosophers wrote that it is a very obscure question whether we sleep while awake or dream while thinking:

> Ὁρᾷς οὖν ὅτι τό γε ἀμφισβητῆσαι οὐ χαλεπὸν, ὅτε καὶ πότερόν ἐστιν ὕπαρ ἢ ὄναρ ἀμφισβητεῖται· καὶ δὴ ἴσου ὄντος τοῦ χρόνου ὃν καθεύδομεν, ᾧ ἐγρηγόραμεν, ἐν ἑκατέρῳ διαμάχεται ἡμῶν ἡ ψυχὴ, τὰ ἀεὶ παρόντα δόγματα παντὸς μᾶλλον εἶναι ἀληθῆ· ὥστε ἴσον μὲν χρόνον τάδε φαμὲν ὄντα εἶναι, ἴσον δὲ ἐκεῖνα· καὶ ὁμοίως [Col. 0662D] ἐφ’ ἑκατέροις διϊσχυριζόμεθα.  
> (Plato, *Theaetetus*, vol. I, p. 158.)
>
> You see, then, that it is not difficult to be in doubt about this matter, since it is disputed whether it is waking reality or a dream; and since the time during which we sleep is equal to that during which we are awake, in each state our soul contends that the opinions present to it at any given time are absolutely true. Thus for an equal length of time we affirm that these things are real, and for an equal length of time that those things are; and we maintain each claim with equal confidence.

Nor is it any better known, says Arnobius, whether “we see through the projection of rays and light, or whether images of things fly toward us and settle upon our pupils” (Arnobius, *ibid.*). Philosophers’ opinions concerning this matter indeed varied, and Aulus Gellius clearly explains them in these words:

> The Stoics say that the causes of vision are [Col. 0663A] the emission of rays from the eyes toward objects capable of being seen, together with a simultaneous tension of the air. Epicurus, however, thinks that certain images of the bodies themselves are constantly flowing from all bodies, that these enter the eyes, and that sensation is thereby produced. Plato believes that a certain kind of fire and light proceeds from the eyes; that, when joined and made continuous with the light of the sun or the brightness of some other fire, it relies upon both its own force and the external light, thereby enabling us to discern whatever it encounters and illuminates.  
> (Gellius, *Attic Nights*, Book V, ch. 16.)

Plutarch also reviews these and other opinions of the philosophers concerning the cause of vision (Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book IV, ch. 13, p. 901). Laertius reported the views of the Stoics and Pythagoras (Laertius, *Lives and Doctrines of the Philosophers*, Book VII, § 157, and Book VIII, § 29), while Lucretius reported the Epicureans’ view [Col. 0663B] in these verses:

> I say, then, that likenesses and slender shapes of things  
> Are emitted from the outermost surface of those things.  
> This should be called, as it were, a membrane or rind,  
> Because the image bears a form and appearance like that thing  
> From whose body, once shed, it drifts abroad.  
> Anyone, however dull of understanding, may learn this from what follows.  
> (Lucretius, Book IV, verses 46 ff.)

He strives to prove this opinion of Epicurus at greater length. Macrobius, however, refutes it and follows Plato (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book VII, ch. 14). Since Lactantius discusses these various philosophical opinions more fully, a more suitable opportunity to examine them carefully will be provided in the following dissertation (*Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 40, art. 2).

Our author further declares it uncertain [Col. 0663C] “whether taste resides in things or is produced by contacts with the palate”—that is, by contact with the palate (Arnobius, Book II, p. 46). This second opinion belonged to the Epicureans: namely, that pleasant and sweet taste arises from smooth and rounded atoms, which pleasantly affect the palate as they pass, whereas disagreeable and unpleasant taste arises from hooked and rough atoms, which injure the tongue and palate. Lucretius, a disciple of Epicurus, expressed this in the following verses:

> When these flowing bodies of juice are smooth,  
> They touch pleasantly and pleasantly stroke all  
> The moist regions of the tongue, sweating all around.  
> But, on the contrary, those that arise filled with greater roughness  
> Prick and lacerate the sense to a corresponding degree.  
> Then pleasure from the juice reaches its limit at the palate;  
> But once it has plunged downward through the throat,  
> There is no pleasure.  
> [Col. 0663D] (Lucretius, Book IV, verses 626 ff.)

He had said similar things elsewhere (Book II, verses 398 ff.). Alcmaeon, however, as Plutarch relates, thought that tastes were distinguished by the moisture and warmth of the tongue. Diogenes believed that tastes were diffused by the porosity and softness of the tongue and by contact with the nerves, as though drawn in by a sponge. But this question must be treated by us with Lactantius in the following dissertation (Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book IV, ch. 18; *Dissertation on Lactantius*, ch. 40, art. 3).

Arnobius says that no one has any surer knowledge of why hair gradually turns gray or why oil does not mix with any other liquids. We have shown elsewhere what certain philosophers thought about the cause of gray hair [Col. 0664A] (vol. I, *Apparatus*, Book III, dissertation 2, ch. 12, art. 1, p. 788). Plutarch explains that oil never mixes with other liquids because it is exceedingly moist and contains no dry parts, and consequently possesses no channels or spaces through which it might admit other liquid bodies. Elsewhere, however, he wished to warn us that others ascribed this property to its density, although Aristotle disagreed with them (Plutarch, *Table Talk*, Book VI, question 10, p. 696; Book VII, question 3, p. 702).

After this Arnobius added that those who taught that the human soul was immortal and a god could not explain to us why it is sick in the sick, foolish in infants, and itself delirious in the delirious old age of the body (Arnobius, Book VII [read: II], p. 47). No one can doubt that this ignorance arose from the various [Col. 0664B] opinions concerning the nature and immortality of the soul which Cicero, Plutarch, Theodoret, and others review (Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book I, pp. 123 ff.; Plutarch, *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, Book IV, chs. 2 ff., pp. 898 ff.; Theodoret, Discourse 5, *On Human Nature*, pp. 546 ff.). Their disagreement, as Justin Martyr says, is so great that they appear to agree on this point alone: that they deceive themselves and in turn accuse and convict one another of error. But we have treated these matters above and shall do so in the following dissertation (Justin, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, pp. 7–8; above, ch. 7, art. 1).

Moreover, as our author says, Cicero admits that human knowledge is so meager and that all things are so deeply hidden and surrounded by darkness that we do not know what our bodies are, how their parts are arranged, or what power each part possesses [Col. 0664C] (Cicero, *Academic Questions*, Book IV, p. 32).

But to what end, you will ask, is this entire discussion by our Arnobius concerning human ignorance directed? It is intended to demonstrate to everyone that the pagans were wholly unjustified in ridiculing the faith of Christians and the readiness with which they believed what Christ had taught. From what has been discussed thus far, he rightly concludes that we possess nothing entirely certain and established except what has been handed down to us by that same Christ, the Son of God, and by God himself.

Yet you should not imagine that Arnobius denied that human beings acquire knowledge through labor and practice. He maintained only that such knowledge is so meager and slight that the pagans could have no reason to boast of it. For there is nothing so certain and clear that they have not rendered it doubtful and uncertain [Col. 0664D] through their zeal for controversy and their disagreements. This point must now be examined further.

## ARTICLE II. How Rightly Arnobius Proved the Meagerness of Human Knowledge from the Disagreements of the Philosophers and the Various Opinions of Thales, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Archytas of Tarentum, Epicurus, and Democritus Concerning the First Principles of Things; of Plato Concerning the Soul; of Panaetius, Chrysippus, and Zeno Concerning the Conflagration of the World; of Carneades, Arcesilaus, and the Academics, Who Affirmed That Nothing Could Be Known; and Because Nothing Has Yet Been Established Concerning the Source of Truth, Why the Sea Is Salt, or Whether These and Other Similar Questions Should Be Abandoned

Arnobius demonstrates how little certainty, consistency, or stability human knowledge possesses by another argument, drawn from the philosophers’ various opinions [Col. 0665A] and disagreements concerning one and the same matter (Arnobius, Book II, p. 48). For while they fight among themselves with hostile obstinacy, and while each undermines and destroys the decrees and doctrines of another, they have rendered everything uncertain by these disputes and plainly show that they could know nothing with certainty. Indeed, none lacks arguments with which to assert and defend his own opinion (*ibid.*, pp. 82 ff.). Since these arguments are not devoid of plausibility, it consequently becomes impossible to distinguish truth from falsehood, and all things are therefore ambiguous and obscure to them.

Our author first sets before everyone’s eyes the philosophers’ various opinions concerning the first principles of things (*ibid.*, p. 48). He begins with Thales and Heraclitus, who respectively made water and fire the first origin of things, just as Pythagoras made numbers their origin. [Col. 0665B] But we have already discussed these matters (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 434 ff.; and the preceding *Dissertation*, on ch. 4, art. 1).

Arnobius rightly associated Archytas—undoubtedly Archytas of Tarentum—with this last philosopher. For, as we learn from Laertius, “he too was a Pythagorean” (Πυθαγορικὸς καὶ αὐτός). If you require another witness, Cicero is at hand, who records the following about him: “They say that Plato came to Italy in order to become acquainted with the Pythagoreans; that there he met, among many others, Archytas and Timaeus; and that he learned all the doctrines of Pythagoras” (Arnobius, Book II, p. 48; Laertius, *Lives and Doctrines of the Philosophers*, Book III, § 79; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, Book I, p. 121).

Arnobius then says that Epicurus, Democritus, and Metrodorus—whose opinion he had previously reported without naming them—believed that the first origin of things [Col. 0665C] consisted of atoms, or indivisible bodies, from which they dreamed that the world had been fashioned (Arnobius, Book II, p. 48, and Book I, p. 18). But we have also discussed these men, as well as Aristotle, of whom our author said that he added a fifth element to the primary causes (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 435, 436, and 770).

Other philosophers, he says, believed that the world had neither been born nor would perish, and was therefore eternal. Others, on the contrary, believed it had been generated and would perish; some held that it was made from four elements, others from fewer (Arnobius, Book II, p. 82). We have treated these various philosophical doctrines, along with their patrons and authors, both in the passages cited and elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, loc. cit., p. 1117).

Furthermore, Panaetius, Chrysippus, and Zeno, Arnobius says, [Col. 0665D] asserted that the world would one day burn. They followed the Stoic sect, of which Zeno was the founder. We have both demonstrated this and already observed that they maintained the doctrine of a conflagration of the world (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 1123, 1145, and 1117).

Moreover, as our author says, Plato “divides the soul and establishes incorporeal forms” (Arnobius, Book II, p. 48). For, as Theodoret astutely observes:

> Πλάτων καὶ Πυθαγόρας, τὸ μὲν λογικὸν αὐτῆς ἄφθαρτον εἶναι, φθαρτὸν δὲ τὸ ἄλογον.  
> (Theodoret, Discourse 5, *On Human Nature*, vol. IV, p. 546.)
>
> Plato and Pythagoras asserted that the rational part of the soul is incorruptible, but that the irrational part is corruptible. [Col. 0666A]

If you wish, consult Theodoret’s fuller discussion, as well as Plato’s own books in which he attempted to defend this opinion (Plato, *Timaeus*, vol. I, p. 59; *Phaedrus*, p. 244; and *Phaedo*, vol. III, pp. 99 and 106).

What more need be said? Carneades and Arcesilaus—or Arcesilaüs—and the adherents of the Second and Third Academies boldly affirmed that all things were enveloped in the deepest recesses of obscurity and that nothing could be comprehended. We demonstrated in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* that both Carneades and Arcesilaus were followers of the Academic school and defenders of this opinion (*ibid.*, pp. 1131 ff.).

Cicero writes at greater length about both men in his books of *Academic Questions*, where he says that Carneades composed four books [Col. 0666B] on withholding assent, and that there was nothing he accepted as certain (Cicero, *Academic Questions*, Book IV, pp. 29 and 37). Arcesilaus, as Cicero further relates,

> Denied that there was anything that could be known—not even the very proposition that Socrates had retained for himself. Thus they believed that all things lay hidden in concealment and that there was nothing that could be discerned or understood. For these reasons, no one ought to profess or affirm anything, or give approval by assent, but should always restrain rashness and hold it back from every lapse. Such rashness would be especially conspicuous when a false or unknown matter was approved; and nothing could be more disgraceful than for assent and approval to run ahead of knowledge and apprehension.

[The text shifts between the plural “they believed,” referring to the Academics, and a variant singular reading, referring to Arcesilaus.] Laertius, moreover, described the lives of Carneades [Col. 0666C] and Arcesilaus (Laertius, *Lives and Doctrines of the Philosophers*, Book IV, §§ 28 ff. and §§ 62 ff.).

Finally, the pagans had no greater agreement concerning their own gods. Some, says Arnobius, denied that they existed; others doubted; others affirmed their existence; some said that human affairs were governed by them, while others denied it. We have discussed these various opinions both above and in the first volume of our *Apparatus* (Arnobius, Book II, p. 82; above, ch. 9, art. 1; vol. I, *Apparatus*, Book III, dissertation 1, chs. 2 ff., pp. 781 ff.).

Arnobius enumerates many other questions—for example, whence wind arises and why the sea is salt—which human beings are unable to solve and explain. From these and all the other things that the pagans did not know, [Col. 0666D] he concludes that they most unjustly assailed the modesty of Christians, who freely admitted that they too did not know such things and did not wish to investigate them (Arnobius, Book II, pp. 85 ff.).

For Christ, the true Son of God, commanded his disciples to abandon these contentious and fruitless questions and disputes, so that with their whole mind, so far as possible, they might be raised toward the Lord of all things and adhere to him. He himself is indeed the one concerning whom no one could doubt unless he were mad or utterly stupid. To know him alone is sufficient, and knowledge of him is the highest knowledge.

# CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning the Illustrious Men, Poets and Seers, and Writers Cited by Arnobius, and the Barbarous, Obsolete, and Obscure Words He Used

[Col. 0667A]

## ARTICLE I. Concerning Pythagoras, Who Was Burned in a Temple; the Cruel Deaths of Socrates, Trebonius, Regulus, and Aquilius; Certain Magi; Zoroaster, Raised Up Through a Fiery Girdle; Armenius, Grandson of Zostrianus; Pamphilus of Cyrus; Apollonius; Damigeron; Velus; Julianus; and Bebulus

Arnobius cited in his books many men illustrious for both their deeds and their writings, by whose example or authority he supports and confirms his teachings. But because some of them may be wholly unknown, and others insufficiently known, to many readers of these books, we have decided to treat them separately [Col. 0667B] and in this place, so that the thread of our discourse would not be repeatedly interrupted in the preceding discussions. We shall begin with those by whose deeds and examples our author refutes and overcomes the pagans.

The first of these who presents himself to us is Pythagoras of Samos, who, Arnobius says, “was burned alive in a temple because of an unjust suspicion that he sought dominion” (Arnobius, Book II, p. 23). There were various opinions concerning the death of Pythagoras, which Laertius, Tzetzes, Suidas, and others have reported (Laertius, *Life of Pythagoras*, Book VIII, § 39; Tzetzes, *Chiliades*, XI, p. 443; Suidas, under the word Πυθαγόρας, “Pythagoras”).

The first is that, while he was in the house of Milo of Croton, the house was set on fire—either through the malice of one of those whom he had refused to admit there, or because the Crotoniates suspected and feared tyranny—and that he was suffocated in the flames. [Col. 0667C] Others report that, after escaping from there, he was overtaken in a field full of beans and gave his throat to his pursuers. Dicaearchus, however, believed that he hid for forty days in the shrine of the Muses at Metapontum and died of hunger and starvation. Laertius also relates other opinions of Heraclides and Hermippus concerning the death of Pythagoras (Laertius, loc. cit.).

Plutarch puts it more briefly:

> Τὸ μὲν τὰ τοιαῦτα συμπτώματα τῶν καλῶν καὶ ἀγαθῶν ἀνδρῶν, οἷον ἡ Σωκράτους καταδίκη, καὶ ὁ Πυθαγόρου ζῶντος ἐμπρησμὸς ὑπὸ τῶν Κυλωνείων.  
> (Plutarch, *On Stoic Self-Contradictions*, vol. II, p. 1051.)
>
> Such calamities befell noble and good men: for example, the condemnation of Socrates and the burning inflicted upon Pythagoras while he was still alive by the followers of Cylon.

But [Col. 0667D] he says nothing at all about whether Pythagoras was burned in a house or in a temple. We have, however, made certain observations concerning his death elsewhere (vol. I, *Apparatus*, pp. 1123 ff.). Consult also, if you please, Malchus Iamblichus, Tzetzes, and others on the life of Pythagoras, as well as the notes of Ménage and others on the cited passage of Laertius (Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras*, Book I, ch. 35; Tzetzes, *Histories*, *Chiliades* XI, verses 69 ff.).

Finally, Arnobius added that Pythagoras was burned alive “because of an unjust suspicion that he sought dominion.” This may be confirmed by the testimony of Tertullian, who unhesitatingly asserts that Pythagoras had aimed at tyranny (Arnobius, Book I, p. 23; Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 46). But we shall discuss this matter more fully in its proper place.

[Col. 0668A] Socrates too, says Arnobius, “was condemned by the judgment of his own city and suffered capital punishment” (Arnobius, Book I, p. 23). That he was condemned to death by his fellow citizens, the Athenians, and drank hemlock has been handed down by Laertius, Plato, and very many other writers; and we have made certain observations concerning his death elsewhere (Laertius, *Life of Socrates*, Book II, § 42; Plato, *Phaedo*, vol. I, p. 117; *Apology of Socrates* and elsewhere; *Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 6, art. 2). To gather further testimony would therefore be useless and superfluous.

Arnobius continues and asserts that Trebonius was killed by a similar kind of punishment. He was a man of consular rank, and, as Cicero says, an excellent citizen and a most moderate man, whom the treacherous Dolabella entrapped under the guise of a feigned friendship: “A man of consular rank”—[Col. 0668B] these are Cicero’s own words—“who, with consular authority, governed the province of Asia, he handed him over to Samarius, an exile. He did not wish to kill him immediately after capturing him, lest, I suppose, he appear too generous in victory. After he had mangled that excellent man with verbal abuse from his impure mouth, he subjected him for two days to scourging and torture in an inquiry concerning public money; afterward he severed his head from his neck, ordered the severed head to be fixed upon a pike and carried about, and cast the rest of the body, dragged and mangled, into the sea” (Cic., *Philip.* II, p. 644, line 30). He then joins and compares this Trebonius with Regulus, just as our author does: “Trebonius was tortured by Dolabella, and Regulus indeed by the Carthaginians. Since in the latter case the most cruel Carthaginians were condemned for their treatment of an enemy, what judgment must be passed upon Dolabella [Col. 0668C] for his treatment of a citizen?” (*Ibid.*, p. 645, line 13; Arnob., l. I, p. 23.) Among Cicero’s works there also survive the reciprocal letters of Trebonius to Cicero and of Cicero to Trebonius; and there too, in a letter addressed to the same Cicero, Lentulus calls it “the utterly undeserved murder of Trebonius” (Cicero, l. XII, ep. 15, p. 142). As for Regulus, whom, as was just said, our author couples with Trebonius, we discussed his cruel death as well in the preceding dissertation (*Dissert. in Minuc. Octav.*, c. 6, art. 3, and c. 19, art. 4).

The fourth person mentioned by Arnobius is Aquilius, who was killed by Mithridates with the most dreadful tortures; but we have discussed him too in that same preceding dissertation (*Ibid.*, c. 6, art. 3; Meursius, *Crit. Arnob.*, l. I, c. 10, p. 19). From that discussion, however, it is clear that Meursius’s conjecture is groundless: [Col. 0668D] in our author’s text, he suspects that *Acilius* should be read instead of *Aquilius*, and he wishes this to be the man who, as Juvenal—cited by him—sang, was removed from the world by Nero through a savage death. For from what was said there about Aquilius it is plainly gathered that nothing in Arnobius’s text should be changed.

When, moreover, our author demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion from Christ’s innumerable and hitherto unheard-of miracles, he rightly maintains that absolutely no similar deed was ever performed by the magicians of the pagans, either by themselves or through others. He proves this by the example of those who were said to have surpassed all others in magical art. He names them as follows: “Come now, I pray: let the magician Zoroaster come through the fiery zone from the inner [Col. 0669A] region of the world—a Bactrian, if we are to assent to Hermippus as our authority; and let that other man come whose exploits Ctesias sets forth in the first book of his histories: the Armenian, Zostrianus’s grandson and Cyrus’s familiar Pamphilus; Apollonius, Damigero and Dardanus, Velus, Julianus and Boebulus” (Arnob., l. I, p. 31). But very many complain that this passage has been grossly corrupted. First, Heraldus thinks that the words “through the fiery zone” were added by way of interpretation, and that the reference there is to Azonaces, who, according to Pliny, was a magician and Zoroaster’s teacher (Pliny, l. XXX, *Hist. nat.*, c. 1, p. 725). He therefore thinks that the text should be restored as follows: “Let some magician Azonaces come from the inner region of the world, if we are to assent to Hermippus as our authority. And let the Bactrian come”—that is, Zoroaster, who [Col. 0669B] was a Bactrian by birth. But these are mere conjectures, supported by the authority neither of the manuscript nor of any printed codex. Huet, however, formerly bishop of Avranches, appears to have cast his vote for Heraldus, and thinks that Arnobius means nothing other than that “Zoroaster came from inner Ethiopia through the fiery zone” (Huet, *Demonstr. Evang.*, proposition 4, c. 5, p. 89, D). For that learned man, as did many others, thought that Arnobius called Zoroaster an Ethiopian by birth (Arnob., l. I, p. 5; above, c. 4, art. 4). Yet why should we not believe that Arnobius calls him a Bactrian, since he had said above, as we observed, that Zoroaster ruled over the Bactrians and fought against Ninus by magical arts? It makes no difference that the name *Bactrianus* is placed last and at a considerable distance in our author’s text. For this is his peculiar manner of speaking, in which he employs hyperbaton everywhere and throughout.

[Col. 0669C]

Zoroaster, moreover, was not only a magician; some, as we have seen elsewhere, also attributed the invention of magic to him. But when Arnobius, in mockery of the pagans, summons him from the inner region of the world through the fiery zone (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 543 and 550), does he not appear to be alluding to what Suidas relates (Suidas, under the word Ζωροάστρης, *Zoroaster*), namely that Zoroaster prayed that he might depart by being consumed with fire? The author of the *Recognitions* inscribed with the name of Clement writes of Zoroaster in this manner: “He repeatedly attempted to produce those things”—that is, certain sparks from the stars—“until he was set alight and burned up by the very demon whom he importunately kept frequenting” (*Recognit.*, l. IV, c. 27). [Col. 0669D] For although that work is filled with fables, these things nevertheless appear to have been transmitted by its author because most people believed that Zoroaster had been consumed by fire. What, then, prevents us from thinking that Arnobius cast this in the pagans’ teeth with the sharp irony we have described?

Furthermore, Apuleius and Tertullian mentioned this magician Zoroaster and others cited there by Arnobius. Apuleius did so in these words: “If you prove even the slightest profit, let me be that Carimondas, or Hismoses, or Johannes, or Apollonius, or Dardanus himself, or any other man celebrated among magicians after Zoroaster or Hostanes” (Apuleius, *Apolog.* II, p. 375). Tertullian, for his part: “To use,” he says, [Col. 0670A] “the very names employed by magic, the originator of those beliefs: Hostanes, Typhon, Dardanus, Damigeron, Nectabis and Berenice” (Tertullian, *De anima*, c. 57).

Three, therefore, are mentioned by him and Apuleius, just as they are by our author: namely Apollonius, Damigero and Dardanus (Arnob., l. I, p. 31). But since several persons bore the name Apollonius, could this be said to be Apollonius of Tyana, who, according to Suidas, collected innumerable magical deceptions from the Egyptians, Babylonians and Arabs whom he visited? Could this not be confirmed from the books written by Philostratus on the life of this Apollonius, were it not that many learned men consider them to teem with old wives’ tales? We shall therefore not press their authority. Yet certainly no one, we think, will deny that the same [Col. 0670B] Apollonius is called a magician by Apuleius and by our author.

Furthermore, Pliny says: “Democritus brought Dardanus of Phoenicia to fame, after obtaining the volumes of Dardanus from his tomb” (Pliny, l. XXX, *Hist. nat.*, c. 1, p. 727). We have seen that Apuleius and Tertullian counted him among those devoted to magic. Indeed, for this reason magical arts are called “Dardanian” by Columella in these verses:

> But if no medicine has power to repel the plague,  
> Let Dardanian arts come to our aid.

(Columella, l. X, *De cultu hortorum*, verse 250.)

Who, then, will deny that Arnobius is speaking of this Dardanus? Elsewhere, following Clement of Alexandria, he addresses the Dardanus who was believed to have disclosed the mysteries of Phrygia, or of the Mother [Col. 0670C] of the Gods. But we discussed him in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (Clement of Alexandria, *Admonit. ad gent.*, p. 95; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 758).

Nor do the following words of Arnobius appear whole and uncorrupted: “the Armenian, Zostrianus’s grandson and Cyrus’s familiar Pamphilus.” For who can this Armenian Pamphilus be—evidently the son of Cyrus and the grandson of Zostrianus? It is still more difficult to say who this Zostrianus was. Some, however, suspect that the reading should be not *Zostriani* but *Ostanis*, or *Hostanis*, concerning whom Apuleius and Tertullian, cited a little above, spoke, and whom we discussed elsewhere (same vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 550). But although the name Zostrianus is obscure, the story of Er the Armenian was certainly known to very many: as was observed by Origen, [Col. 0670D] Cyril of Alexandria and ourselves, it was said that he returned to life on the eleventh day after his death (Origen, l. II *Contra Celsum*, p. 70; Cyril of Alexandria, l. VII *Contra Julianum*, p. 250; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 116). Concerning him, however, Clement of Alexandria has these very words, accurately copied by Eusebius: Plato, he says, “mentions Er the Armenian, Pamphylian by race, who is Zoroaster” (Ἡρὸς τοῦ Ἀρμενίου, τὸ γένος Παμφύλου, μέμνηται, ὅς ἐστι Ζωροάστρης) (Clement of Alexandria, l. V *Stromata*, p. 599; Eusebius, l. XIII *Praepar.*, c. 13, p. 675); that is, “He mentions Er, the son of Armenius, a Pamphylian by race, who is indeed Zoroaster.” If, therefore, Arnobius followed Clement of Alexandria there, as was his custom, he either confused these names through a lapse of memory, or they were corrupted by an unskilled copyist. But since he expressly cited his witness Ctesias [Col. 0671A] and the first book of his histories, which no longer survives, who would dare assert what Ctesias’s genuine words were?

They also judge the names that follow in his text, *Velus Julianus and Boebulus*, to be no less corrupt. Some therefore think that *Nilus and Vulcanus* should be written instead, since Laertius said: “The Egyptians relate that Vulcan was the son of the Nile and disclosed the precepts of philosophy” (Laertius, Proem, § 1). But no one has ever proved that magic should there be understood by the name of philosophy. Others therefore think that *Belus* should be substituted for *Velus*—and certainly not wholly without justification. For the initial letters B and V in both names are very frequently interchanged by copyists. Belus, moreover, as Diodorus Siculus relates, instituted priests who, [Col. 0671B] after the Egyptian custom, were exempt from public burdens and expenses (Diodorus Siculus, l. I, *Biblioth.*, p. 17). These men, whom the Babylonians call Chaldaeans, were accustomed in Egypt to observe the stars, like the priests who were natural philosophers and astrologers. Undoubtedly for this reason Pliny and Solinus call Belus the inventor of astronomical knowledge; and Jerome says that this same person is called *Bel* by the Hebrews and *Baal* by the Sidonians and Phoenicians, and that he was enrolled among the gods by his son Ninus (Pliny, l. VI, *Natur. hist.*, c. 27, p. 712; Solinus, c. 56, p. 87; Jerome, on Hosea c. 2, v. 16, p. 1251, new ed.).

Heraldus admits that he had discovered nothing about Julianus. Nothing concerning him occurs in the observations of others on the books of Arnobius either. Yet among the several men [Col. 0671C] bearing this name, two in particular are mentioned by Suidas. One was a Chaldaean and philosopher who had published four books concerning demons. The other, his son, wrote in verse works on theurgy, initiation, oracles and all the other secrets of this science. Although some may think that these things pertained more to the worship of the gods than to magic, if anyone should nevertheless prove that Arnobius was speaking of either the son or his father, we shall certainly not resist him greatly.

Finally, absolutely nothing has been noted by anyone about Baebulus. But what if *Babilus* should be read in Arnobius’s text instead of *Baebulus*? For Suetonius relates that during the reign of Claudius Nero, when a comet began to appear for several nights in succession: “Nero, anxious about this,” he says, “when he had learned from the astrologer Babilus that kings were accustomed to expiate such portents by some illustrious slaughter and to divert them from themselves onto the heads of their leading men, marked every eminent person for death” (Suetonius, l. VI, *Life of Nero*, c. 35).

Nevertheless, whether this man and the others reviewed by us were in fact the magicians whom Arnobius addresses, or whether anything in his text should be emended, and how, we certainly dare determine nothing without the aid of another, more complete codex. We therefore prefer to await the judgment of others on this matter rather than pronounce our own.

## ARTICLE II. On the Various Seers—Whether Human Beings, Namely the Sibyl, Bacis, Helenus and Martius, or Gods, Namely Jupiter of Dodona and Apollo Clarius, Pythius, Didymaeus and Philesius—Whom Arnobius Mentioned

[Col. 0672A]

By the fourfold example of the seers, Arnobius confirms that Christ’s human nature truly died, while his divine nature nevertheless remained unimpaired (Arnob., l. I, p. 38). For the beings who inspired those seers and spoke through them cannot be said to have been deprived of life when the seers themselves died.

The first of these seers named by our author is the Sibyl, whom we have discussed more than once (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, l. III, dissertation 2, c. 2, p. 20; art. 2, p. 1176). The second is called Bacis. We have also treated him elsewhere. Yet, if you have leisure and inclination, you may consult Dio Chrysostom as well (Dio, Oration [Col. 0672B] 13, *On Exile*).

Bacis is followed by Helenus, undoubtedly the son of Priam and Hecuba, who is deservedly included by Cicero among the other seers (Cicero, l. II *De natura deorum*, p. 214, line 41). For after he had foretold a shipwreck to Pyrrhus, Pyrrhus gave him Andromache as his wife in marriage, together with a share of the kingdom. Hence Virgil is read to have sung the following, which is confirmed by Pausanias (Pausanias, l. I, p. 10, and l. II, p. 66):

> Here an incredible report fills my ears:  
> That Helenus, Priam’s son, rules over Greek cities,  
> Having obtained both the bride and the scepters of Aeacides Pyrrhus,  
> And that Andromache has once more passed to a husband of her own people.

(Virgil, l. III, *Aeneid*, verses 294 ff.)

The same poet [Col. 0672C] later explains in these verses what knowledge of prophecy he possessed:

> Son of Troy, interpreter of the gods, who perceive the powers of Phoebus,  
> The tripods and Clarian laurels, and the stars,  
> The speech of birds, and the omens of a swiftly flying wing.

(*Ibid.*, verses 359 ff.)

Read, if you will, Servius’s notes on these verses.

The fourth and last is called Martius by our author; Livy and Ammianus Marcellinus call him a celebrated seer (Livy, l. XXV, c. 12; Ammianus Marcellinus, l. XIV, p. 5). Livy presents two of his verses. In the former, he says, Martius had foretold the disaster at Cannae; by the latter, as Macrobius also attests, he induced the Romans to vow and celebrate games for Apollo (Macrobius, l. I *Saturnalia*, c. 17, pp. 254 ff.).

Since, moreover, we have come to mention seers, [Col. 0672D] it will perhaps be neither useless nor wholly foreign to our purpose to say something about certain supposedly divine seers, prophets and utterers of divine oracles, whom Arnobius enumerates in this manner: “Trophonius . . . the Dodonaean, or Jupiter . . .; Apollo of Delos, or Clarius, Didymaeus, Philesius, Pythius—and he is to be regarded as divine” (Arnob., l. I, p. 14). So indeed the text stands in certain editions of these books. But in the older editions, instead of *Trophonius* we read *profanis* and *profanus*; in the royal manuscript, in the first hand, *profanius*. This name has been so grossly corrupted that it seems scarcely possible to restore it without another, better codex.

[Col. 0673A] But if it is rightly proved that Arnobius was speaking of Trophonius, this may be confirmed by the testimony of ancient writers, who recorded that his oracles were once delivered from a certain cave at Lebadea. Pausanias relates the rites by which those consulting Trophonius descended into this cave and the purifications they first had to undergo. On this oracle, besides Strabo, Cicero, Livy, Origen and Suidas, Erasmus should be read; he reported various opinions about it. Tertullian also dealt with it, as we shall see in its proper place. (Pausanias, l. IX, pp. 313 f.; Suidas, under the word Τροφώνιος, *Trophonius*; Strabo, l. IX *Geograph.*, pp. 414, 421, and l. XVI, p. 762; Cicero, l. I *Tuscul.*, p. 134, and l.
