III *De natura deorum*, p. 247; Livy, l. XLV, c. 27; Origen, [Col. 0673B] l. III *Contra Celsum*, p. 131; Erasmus, *Adagia*, chiliad, century 7, adage 77; *Dissert. in Tertullian.*, c. 7, art. 3.)

Arnobius then names Jupiter of Dodona and his oracles, which are mentioned, among others, by Pausanias, l. I, p. 15; Cicero, l. I *De divinatione*, p. 268; Pliny, l. IV *Hist. nat.*, at the beginning, p. 404; and Solinus, *Polyhistor*, c. 7. Servius, however, says more about him in his notes on Virgil’s poems, where he observes that cauldrons in the temple of Jupiter of Dodona, in the territory of the Aetolians, were consecrated by the ancients to him and to Venus (Virgil, l. III *Aeneid*, verse 446). Hence also came the Dodonaean bronze, which we discussed elsewhere (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, l. III, dissertation 1, c. 10; art. 1, pp. 770 f.), just as we did the Apollos [Col. 0673C] Clarius, Pythius and Didymaeus cited by Arnobius. Anyone wishing to know more about Apollo Clarius should consult Pliny, l. II *Natur. histor.*, c. 103, p. 254; Strabo, l. XIV *Geograph.*, p. 642; and Cornelius Tacitus, l. II *Annals*, past the middle, where he discusses Germanicus. On Didymaeus, see the same Strabo, in the book cited, p. 634; Pausanias, l. I, p. 15; Mela, l. I, where he treats Ionia; Apuleius, near the end of l. IV of the *Metamorphoses*, p. 70; Pliny, l. VI *Natural History*, c. 16, p. 678; and Sozomen, l. I, c. 7, p. 409. On Pythius, see Ovid, l. I *Metamorphoses*, around the middle; Diodorus Siculus, l. XVI *Biblioth.*, pp. 323 f.; Herodotus, l. I, § 65; Pausanias, l. X, pp. 320 ff.; Plutarch, *On the Oracles of the Pythia*, pp. 394 f.; Macrobius, l. I *Saturnalia*, [Col. 0673D] c. 17; and Origen, at the beginning of l. VII *Contra Celsum*.

Philesius is also named by our author. Macrobius committed the following concerning him to writing: “Ἀπόλλων Φιλήσιος, *Apollo Philesius*, because when his light rises, we greet it with the most affectionate reverence of our eyes” (Macrobius, l. I *Saturnalia*, c. 17, p. 259). Pliny, however, says: “Canachus made a nude Apollo, surnamed Philesius, at Didyma, in the Aeginetan alloy of bronze” (Pliny, l. III *Hist. nat.*, c. 3, p. 12, E). Pausanias undoubtedly mentions the same bronze Apollo at Branchidae, which Xerxes, son of Darius and king of the Persians, carried off and which Seleucus returned to the Milesians many years later (Pausanias, l. VIII, p. 275). Strabo further added that there was a precious grove there, [Col. 0674A] as well as other shrines containing the oracle and sacred rites of this Apollo. You will also be able, without much difficulty, to consult Giraldus if you are so inclined (Strabo, l. XIV, p. 634; Giraldus, *Syntagm.* 7 *De diis gent.*, p. 225). Finally, Statius sang the following concerning the various Apollos:

> Whatever you are, you will remain Phoebus’s eternal grief and ever-new disaster,  
> And for a long time you will be mourned at the silent Delphi.  
> This day will close Tenedos and Cirrha,  
> And Delos, bound fast at your birth, and the sanctuary of unshorn Branchus.  
> No suppliant inquirer shall on this day approach  
> The Clarian gates, the Didymaean thresholds, or Lycia.

(Statius, l. VIII, *Thebaid*, well after the beginning.)

## ARTICLE III. On the Various Writers Cited by Arnobius, Whose Names Are Presented in Alphabetical Order

Arnobius cited many writers in his books, [Col. 0674B] by whose testimony and authority he either establishes and confirms his own doctrines or refutes and destroys the errors of the pagans. We shall now name them in the order called alphabetical, which is easier and clearer than all others, and shall attempt briefly, and to the best of our ability, to set forth what other authors have handed down about them.

Aelius, then, is cited simply by that name by our Arnobius and is said to have adopted an opinion different from Piso’s, both concerning the Novensile gods and concerning the Muses. But there were two principal men named Aelius. The first was Gaius Aelius Stilo, whose disagreement with Piso concerning the Lacus Curtius is attested by Varro in these words: “It is agreed that the Lacus Curtius in the Forum was named after a Curtius. There are three versions of its history. For Procilius did not transmit [Col. 0674C] the same account as Piso, nor did Gaius Aelius Stilo follow the same account as Piso” (Varro, l. IV *De lingua Latina*, p. 36). Elsewhere Varro asserts that Aelius was well versed in Latin literature, and cites his interpretation of the songs of the Salii and another commentary by him; but in both places he is called Gaius Aelius (the same, l. VI, pp. 70, 76).

Suetonius, however, reports that Aelius had a double surname and records the following concerning him: “Lucius Aelius had a double surname. He was called both Praeconius, because his father had practiced the herald’s profession, and Stilo, because he was accustomed to write speeches for every eminent person. So great a supporter of the aristocratic party was he that he accompanied Quintus Metellus Numidicus into exile” (Suetonius, *De illustribus grammaticis*, c. 3). Pliny too wrote as follows concerning the surname Praeconinus: [Col. 0674D] “We find that even heralds commonly wore the broader purple stripe on their tunics, as did the father of Lucius Aelius Stilo Praeconinus, who was surnamed from that circumstance” (Pliny, l. XXXIII *Natural History*, c. 1, p. 16; and l. VII, c. 1, p. 358). Hence he is later cited by the surname Stilo Praeconinus alone. Aulus Gellius calls him Lucius Aelius, or simply Aelius, but calls him learned and elsewhere most erudite, as well as Varro’s teacher. In like manner he is sometimes called Aelius Stilo, or merely Aelius, by Festus (Gellius, l. II *Noctes Atticae*, c. 21, p. 158; l. III, c. 3, p. 218; l. V, c. 20, p. 357; l. XVI, c. 8; Festus, *De verborum significatione*). Is he not also the very man about whom Cicero wrote that philosophical doctrines “after the death of our Lucius Aelius could not even be obtained from Latin authors”? [Col. 0675A] (Cicero, l. I *Academica*, p. 4, line 44.)

Certainly the same Cicero committed the following concerning that Lucius Aelius Stilo to writing: “The speech of Cotta in his own defense”—some suspect that the words “in his own defense” should be deleted—“under the *lex Varia*, as it is entitled, was written by Lucius Aelius at Cotta’s request. He was altogether an excellent man and a Roman knight of the highest respectability; he was likewise exceedingly learned in both Greek and Latin literature, and literately versed in our antiquity—in matters discovered and deeds performed—and in the ancient writers. Our Varro received this knowledge from him and augmented it by his own efforts; being a man of outstanding ability and every kind of learning, he expounded it in writings more numerous and distinguished. But Aelius also wished to be a Stoic; as an orator, however, he never studied and never became one. Nevertheless, he wrote speeches for others to deliver, [Col. 0675B] as for Quintus Metellus, Quintus Caepio and Quintus Pompeius Rufus—although Rufus had himself written the speeches that he later used, but not without Aelius. I myself was present during the writing of these, when as a young man I was in Aelius’s company and was accustomed to listen to him with the greatest eagerness” (Cicero, *Brutus*, p. 229, line 16).

There was another Aelius, surnamed Tubero, who, as the same Cicero states in the same book, delivered speeches against Gracchus. But he was a harsh man, a Stoic by sect, middling in delivery, and highly learned in disputation. Aulus Gellius transcribes certain words of his reported by Cicero, and cites his books of histories and other scholarly works, as do Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Festus and others. You may also consult Vossius (*Ibid.*, p. 219, line 51; [Col. 0675C] Aulus Gellius, l. XIV *Noctes Atticae*, c. 2, p. 763; l. VI, c. 3, p. 368, c. 4, p. 370; l. X, c. 28, p. 573; l. XIV, c. 2, p. 763; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, l. I, pp. 6 and 67; Vossius, l. I *De historicis Latinis*, l. I, c. 9).

If you ask which of these two Arnobius cites, we shall reply that it is more likely the first Aelius, Stilo. In confirmation of this opinion one may adduce the words of Varro cited by us, in which he reported that this Aelius’s opinion differed from Piso’s, just as our Arnobius says. It is of little importance whether the same man is called Gaius Aelius by Varro or Lucius Aelius by others. For one letter could easily have been changed into another by copyists.

Arnobius, following Clement of Alexandria, [Col. 0675D] used the testimony of Aethlius, as we saw above. Vossius and we ourselves have already said something about him in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (Arnob., l. VI, p. 196; Vossius, l. III *De historicis Graecis*, p. 316; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 735).

Antias, or Quintus Valerius Antias, published an extensive work of annals. Its second book is cited by our author and by Macrobius (Arnob., l. V, p. 154; Macrobius, l. I *Saturnalia*, c. 13), while its twenty-fourth, forty-fourth and seventy-fifth books are cited here by Aulus Gellius. The author is also cited frequently by Livy and Pliny, and in one place by Dionysius of Halicarnassus and by the author of *The Origin of the Roman People* (Gellius, l. I *Noctes Atticae*, c. 7; l. VII, c. 9; [Col. 0676A] and elsewhere; Livy, l. XXXIII; Pliny, l. XIII, c. 13, p. 58; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, l. I, p. 6; author of *Orig. gent. Rom.*, p. 299).

Arnobius adduces Antiochus as a witness, but does so after Clement of Alexandria, as we have observed elsewhere, where an occasion arose to discuss this writer (Arnob., l. VI, p. 193; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 725 and 817).

Arnobius employs Apollodorus as a witness in precisely the same manner; but we have shown that several persons bore this name (Arnob., l. IV, p. 144; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 1192 and 1256).

Arrian had approved the teachings of Epictetus, as our author attests—and rightly so. For Arrian, a native of Nicomedia, historian and [Col. 0676B] philosopher, arranged the *Discourses* of Epictetus. Aulus Gellius cites their fifth book, but only four survive for us in print. See Vossius, Gesner and the notes on the cited passages of Gellius (Arnob., l. II, p. 90; Gellius, l. I, c. 2; l. XXVII, c. 19; l. XXIX, c. 2; Vossius, l. II *De historicis Graecis*, c. 11, p. 15).

Arnobius relates that Butas wrote in his *Causal Works* that women were not permitted to carry myrtle branches into the shrine of the Good Goddess. Some, however, suspect that *Plutarchus*, not *Butas*, should be read there—and perhaps not without reason (Arnob., l. V, p. 188; Plutarch, vol. II, p. 268). For Plutarch actually proposes and resolves that question in the *Roman Questions*, which bear the Greek title Ῥωμαϊκά (*Roman Matters*). [Col. 0676C] The reason Arnobius (l. I, p. 37) may have called this work *Causualia*—“Causal Questions”—is perhaps that Plutarch endeavors to supply the causes and reasons for the questions proposed. If anyone should nevertheless point out to us the *Causualia* of Butas, we shall immediately acquiesce.

Caesellius the grammarian published his highly celebrated commentaries on ancient readings, frequently cited by Aulus Gellius. Gellius attests that his surname was Vindex (Gellius, l. II *Noctes Atticae*, c. 16; l. III, c. 16; l. VII, c. 11; l. II, c. 14; l. XI, c. 15; l. XXVIII, c. 11; l. II, c. 2).

Two poets in particular bore the name Caesius (Arnob., l. III, p. 123). One of them was the tasteless and bad poet censured in these verses of Catullus to the orator Calvus Licinius: [Col. 0676D]

> For as soon as day breaks, I shall run  
> To the booksellers’ cases and gather the Caesii,  
> Aquini and Suffenus—all those poisons—  
> And repay you with these torments.

(Catullus, epigram 13.)

The other Caesius, surnamed Bassus, was a lyric poet who flourished in the age of Nero and whom Persius addresses as follows:

> Has winter already drawn you, Bassus, to your Sabine hearth?  
> Do your lyre and its strings now live within your austere breast,  
> Marvelous craftsman at fitting the primordial themes of the ancients  
> And their masculine resonance to the Latin lyre;  
> Then at stirring the sportive jests of youth,  
> And with an honorable thumb making distinguished old men your sport?

(Persius, Satire 6.)

Britannicus, however, observes in his notes on these verses that Fabius wrote as follows about him: [Col. 0677A] “Of lyric poets, Horace is almost the only one worthy to be read. For at times he rises to grandeur, is full of charm and grace, is varied in his language, and displays a most felicitous boldness. If you wish to add another, it will be Caesius Bassus, whom we saw recently.”

It is not easy to say which of these two—or of others, if there were any distinct from them—is cited by Arnobius. Yet if you prove that he is speaking of Caesius Bassus, we shall not resist. See Vossius on the Latin poets (Vossius, *Poetae Latini*, pp. 17 and 44).

Arnobius draws many things from the authority of Cincius. Dionysius of Halicarnassus numbers him among the most ancient historians in these words: “Histories not dissimilar were published by all those Romans who wrote the deeds of their city in the Greek language, the most ancient of whom [Col. 0677B] were Quintus Fabius and Lucius Cincius” (Λεύκιος Κίγκιος, *Leukios Kinkios*), “both contemporaries of the Punic Wars. Each of them carefully committed to writing the events in which he had himself participated, as matters thoroughly known to him. But as for the events that followed successively in early times after the city’s foundation, he was content to run through them summarily” (Arnob., l. III, p. 122; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, l. I, pp. 6 and 16). Cincius is later called by Dionysius a man of senatorial rank and by Livy “the greatest authority”—unless in this passage of Livy you think that *maxime*, “especially,” should be read instead of *maximus*, “the greatest,” as it is in certain printed editions (Livy, l. XXI, c. 38). Macrobius, moreover, cited his book *On the Fasti*, while Gellius transcribed various fragments from his book *On Military Affairs*. Vossius says more about him and may be consulted if you wish (Macrobius, l. I *Saturnalia*, c. 12; Gellius, l. XVI *Noctes Atticae*, c. 4; Vossius, [Col. 0677C] *De historicis Graecis*, l. IV, c. 13, and *De historicis Latinis*, l. I, c. 4).

Clodius, whose praenomen was Sextus, is cited by Arnobius as a witness for what he said concerning Faunus, in this manner: “Sextus Clodius states in the sixth book, *On the Gods*, written in Greek.” Some have suspected that the last word is corrupt and should be restored as “of the Greeks.” But they had not read the passage in Lactantius where he follows our Arnobius, his teacher, in these words: “Sextus Clodius, in the book that he wrote in Greek, relates that this woman was the wife of Faunus” (Arnob., l. V, p. 168; Lactantius, l. I, c. 22, p. 127). From this it is easily gathered that Arnobius’s text did not contain “of the Greeks,” but rather “written in Greek,” or something similar.

As regards Clodius, some think [Col. 0677D] that he was the man whose book entitled *Index of Times* is cited by Plutarch (Plutarch, *Life of Numa Pompilius*, p. 52). But no one has proved that this man’s praenomen was Sextus. Another man, however, to whom both this praenomen and nomen belong, is included by Suetonius among the distinguished rhetoricians: “Sextus Clodius,” he says, “of Sicily, a teacher of both Latin and Greek eloquence, with poor eyesight, and . . . a favorite of Antony, from whom, when he shortly afterward became consul, he also received an enormous grant, as Cicero reproaches Antony in the *Philippics*: ‘For amusement you employ as a teacher a rhetorician approved by your vote and that of your drinking companions. . . . You assigned two thousand iugera of the Leontine plain to the rhetorician Sextus Clodius, and exempted them from taxation, so that at so great a price you might learn nothing’” (Suetonius, *On Distinguished Rhetoricians*, § 5, p. 841). These very words of Cicero still occur in his Second *Philippic* (Cicero, *Philippic* II, p. 495). Yet, as you see, not only the name and praenomen mentioned by Arnobius apply to this rhetorician, but also the fact that he is said to have been learned in Greek. Consider, I pray, and decide whether he is the very man who is said to have published books *On the Gods* in Greek.

Arnobius reports Cornificius’s distinctive opinion concerning the Novensile gods (Arnob., l. III, p. 122). Macrobius has attested that Cornificius published several books of *Etymologies*, citing the third in these very words: “Cornificius, in book III of the *Etymologies*, says that Cicero derives the names not *Janus* but *Fanus* from *eundo*, ‘going’” (Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, c. 6, p. 212). Elsewhere Macrobius transcribed some verses concerning the Centaurs that Cornificius had sung in his *Glaucus* (*Ibid.*, l. VI, c. 4, p. 486). May it not be gathered from this that he is the very man of whom Eusebius speaks thus in his *Chronicle*: “The poet Cornificius, deserted by his soldiers, perished; he had often called them helmeted hares when they fled. His sister was Cornificia, whose distinguished epigrams survive” (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at the year 1576)? Vossius does not doubt that he is the same man as Virgil’s detractor, mentioned in Virgil’s life attributed to Donatus (Vossius, *On the Latin Poets*, p. 22). But he remains uncertain whether this was the man to whom an epigram of Catullus (Catullus, epigram 36) and letters of Cicero still extant were addressed, and whether the *Rhetoric to Herennius*, falsely ascribed to Cicero, proceeded from him. For our part, we can readily be persuaded that the Cornificius of whom Arnobius speaks is the very man whose books of *Etymologies*, as we observed just above, are cited by Macrobius.

Crates, also cited by our author, was undoubtedly the grammarian whom we discussed elsewhere (Arnob., l. III, p. 121; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 147 and 1259).

Cronius is named in the latest edition of Arnobius’s books, where Arnobius says: “You believe Plato, you believe Cronius, you believe Numenius” (Arnobius, book II, p. 49). But in the royal manuscript codex, *Crotonius* is read in place of *Cronius*. Since it is not known who this person was, scholars have thought the name corrupt. Yet each has conjectured according to his own judgment how it ought to be emended. [Col. 0678D] Canter, indeed, thinks that *Protonius*, or *Prothomus*, or rather *Prothomius*, should be read; concerning him Apuleius says: “There is sufficient distinction from Protomus, who was such a man that his grandson need not have been ashamed of him” (Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*, near the end). But how these words of Apuleius bear upon Arnobius’s purpose is certainly not clear to us. For this reason several others think that *Plotinus* should be written, and in support of this conjecture the following words of Theodoret may be adduced: Αὐτίκα τοίνυν τὴν Πλάτωνος διάνοιαν ἀναπτύσσοντες, καὶ ὁ Πλωτῖνος, καὶ ὁ Νουμήνιος, “Thus, for example, both Plotinus and Numenius, in expounding Plato’s thought” (Theodoret, Discourse 2, *On the First Principle*, vol. IV, p. 500). Are not these, they ask, the three more recent philosophers of whom [Col. 0679A] Arnobius made mention? Yet anyone who reads this passage attentively will acknowledge that he is speaking of philosophers of every kind. And, as we have often said, would it not also have been easier for an ignorant copyist to write *Crotonius* for *Cronius* than for *Plotinus*? But certainly, if the former reading, *Cronius*, is not altogether displeasing, it may be established by the authority of Eusebius. For he writes thus concerning Origen: “He also had daily in his hands the writings of Numenius and Cronius, Νουμηνίου καὶ Κρονίου, of Apollophanes and Longinus, and also of Moderatus and Nicomachus, and of others who are considered foremost among the Pythagoreans” (Eusebius, book VI of the *Ecclesiastical History*, ch. 19, p. 220). If, therefore, Cronius and Numenius were indeed foremost among the Pythagoreans, what prevents them from being identified as those in whom the pagans, as Arnobius says, placed their trust? [Col. 0679B] (Arnobius, book I, p. 31; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 1259.)

The first book of Ctesias’s *Histories* is also cited by him. We have discussed this author elsewhere. You will find various fragments of his books collected after the books of Herodotus.

We have also discussed elsewhere, and in this dissertation too, Diagoras of Melos, who, as Arnobius says, believed that the gods had been human beings (Arnobius, book IV, p. 147; above, ch. 9, art. 1; *Dissertation on Minucius*, ch. 10, final art.; and *Apparatus*, vol. I, p. 147).

Ennius is frequently mentioned by the most ancient writers, Livy and Aulus Gellius, and by the poets Ovid, Lucretius, and others, but still more often by Cicero. Arnobius, and after him Lactantius, relates that Ennius translated into Latin the books of Euhemerus of Acragas, [Col. 0679C] in which he demonstrated that the gods had been human beings (Lactantius, book I, ch. 11, p. 62, and *On the Anger of God*, ch. 11, p. 794). But this is excerpted from Cicero, who had said: “This argument was treated most fully by Euhemerus, whom our own Ennius, above all others, both translated and followed” (Cicero, book I of *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 212, line 34).

Arnobius reports what Ephorus thought about the number of the Muses. We have, however, discussed this writer more than once (Arnobius, book III, p. 12; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 545 and 1292).

Epicadius is praised by our Arnobius as an illustrious grammarian (Arnobius, book I, p. 37). Is he not the very man whom Suetonius placed among the celebrated grammarians in these words? [Col. 0679D] “Cornelius Epicadus, a freedman of the dictator Lucius Cornelius Sulla and an attendant in his augural priesthood, was also most highly esteemed by Sulla’s son Faustus; and for this reason he always styled himself the freedman of both. Moreover, he himself completed the final book that Sulla had left unfinished concerning his own achievements” (Suetonius, *On Illustrious Grammarians*, §12).

Arnobius, following Clement of Alexandria, as we saw above, confronts the pagans with Epicharmus’s opinion concerning Mars. But we have frequently discussed this poet and his various opinions and deeds in the first volume of our *Apparatus* (Arnobius, book IV, p. 143; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 861, 866, 867, 869, 1031, 1114, 1205; and Arnobius, book II, p. 90).

[Col. 0680A] The philosopher Epictetus was the teacher of Arrian, who arranged his discourses, as we observed a little earlier from Aulus Gellius. Suidas relates more concerning his life and writings (Suidas, s.v. ἐπίκτητος, “Epictetus”). Gesner, however, indicates which of these have been published and which remain unpublished (Gesner, in the *Bibliotheca*). Finally, Stobaeus copied down various opinions and memorable sayings of Epictetus and Epicharmus.

Ennius translated the books of Euhemerus concerning the gods into Latin, as we observed immediately above. But we have noted certain matters concerning this Euhemerus both above and in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus*. Lactantius states that he was a native of the city of Messana and that he composed his history from inscriptions and sacred institutions (Arnobius, book IV, p. 147; [Col. 0680B] above, ch. 9, art. 1; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 785; Lactantius, book I of the *Institutes*, ch. 11, p. 62, and *On the Anger of God*, ch. 16, p. 794).

Fabius is named by Arnobius as one of those who transmitted to posterity many things concerning Tolus’s father, homeland, and death (Arnobius, book VI, p. 194). But several men bore this name, two of whom are celebrated in these words of Cicero: “Servius Fabius Pictor was well versed in law, literature, and antiquity. Quintus Fabius Labeo was distinguished by almost the same accomplishments” (Cicero, *Brutus*, p. 214). There is also said to have been another, Fabius Maximus Servilianus, the pontiff, who, according to Macrobius, denied in his twelfth book that rites for the dead should be performed on an unlucky day (Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 16, p. 247). Some are charged with having confused him with Fabius [Col. 0680C] Pictor. There were also other Fabii, such as Fabius Caecilianus and Fabius Rusticus. Yet that Arnobius cited Fabius Pictor can be proved by the authority of Cicero, Pliny, and Aulus Gellius, who mention the *Annals* written by him. What is more, Dionysius of Halicarnassus calls him both the most ancient of the Roman writers and a composer of histories. Finally, Gellius had read these *Annals* of Fabius Pictor—books, as he says, of sound and genuine antiquity—which the bookseller boasted were free from errors. Dionysius excerpted from his first book the words that the Pontifex Maximus was required to speak when he selected a virgin. Elsewhere, however, he presents a long fragment of Fabius (Cicero, book I of *On Divination*, p. 269; Pliny, book X of the *Natural History*, ch. 4, p. 416, and book XIV, [Col. 0680D] p. 142; Gellius, book I of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 12, p. 60; book V, ch. 4, p. 322; and book X, ch. 5, p. 527; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book I of *Roman Antiquities*, p. 5, and book VII, p. 475).

Flaccus, whom Arnobius praised for his knowledge of grammar (Arnobius, book I, p. 37, and book V, p. 169), is Marcus Verrius Flaccus. Suetonius explains who he was and when he lived in these words: “Verrius Flaccus, a freedman, became especially renowned for his method of teaching. To exercise the abilities of his pupils, he regularly set those of equal attainment in competition with one another, proposing not only a subject on which they should write but also a prize for the victor. This was some ancient, beautiful, or rarer book. Accordingly, Augustus chose him as tutor [Col. 0681A] to his grandsons, and he moved to the palace with his entire school, on the condition that he should thereafter accept no additional pupil. He taught in the atrium of Catiline’s house, which was then part of the palace, and received one hundred thousand sesterces a year. He died at an advanced age under Tiberius. He has a statue at Praeneste, in the lower part of the forum opposite the Hemicycle, where he had publicly displayed the calendar arranged by him and engraved on marble tablets” (*On Illustrious Grammarians*, §17). Accordingly, Eusebius, in his *Chronicle* at the ninth year of Christ, when Augustus was still ruling the Romans, says: “Athenodorus of Tarsus, the Stoic philosopher, and Marcus Verrius Flaccus, the grammarian, are considered eminent.” Aulus Gellius cites the first book of Flaccus’s *Memorable Matters*, the fourth book *On the Meaning of Words*, and the second book [Col. 0681B] *On Obscure Expressions in Cato*, together with other passages taken from these works. He is also frequently praised by Pliny, and Macrobius transmitted some of his words (Gellius, book IV of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 5, p. 283; book V, ch. 17, p. 349; ch. 18, p. 351; book XVI, ch. 14; book XVII, ch. 18; book XVIII, ch. 17; book XX, ch. 7; Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 6, p. 198).

Granius, summoned two or three times by Arnobius as a witness, seems to be that very Granius Flaccus who, according to Macrobius, had written that divine rites were celebrated for Apollo and Liber on the same mountain (Arnobius, book III, pp. 118 and 122, and book VI, p. 194; Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 18, p. 263). Earlier, however, the same Macrobius had said that in the second book of Granius Licinianus the reason was given why market days were holidays (ibid., ch. 16, p. 248). [Col. 0681C] Yet there we read *Gaius* supplied in the margin in place of *Granius*. A certain Granius is also praised by Pliny, but since the discussion there concerns medicines, scholars believe that he was a physician (Pliny, book XXVIII of the *Natural History*, p. 572). It is therefore more probable that Arnobius should be understood as referring to the former, since he appears to have published some work concerning the gods. For Arnobius censures his opinion concerning the Muses and Tolus (Arnobius, book V, p. 177).

Laertius enumerates five men named Heraclitus, to whom Menagius added three others (Laertius, book IX, *Life of Heraclitus*, §17; Menagius, on this passage of Laertius). What our author reports from Heraclitus concerning the story of Liber and Prosymnus seems more appropriate either to Heraclitus, the author of the *Homeric Allegories*, or to Heraclitus [Col. 0681D] the lyric poet, who had sung the praises of the twelve gods (Arnobius, book III, p. 31).

Hermippus, who, as Arnobius notes, asserted that the magus Zoroaster was a Bactrian—is he not the man of whom Pliny says: “Hermippus, who wrote most carefully concerning the whole magical art and explained the two million verses composed by Zoroaster, also supplying indexes to his volumes”? Vossius has more concerning him; consult that author (Pliny, book XXX of the *Natural History*, ch. 1, p. 725; Vossius, book III of *On the Greek Historians*, ch. 16, pp. 102–103).

Hippo of Melos was numbered among the atheists; we have discussed him more than once (Arnobius, book IV, p. 147; above, ch. 9, art. 1; and vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 785).

[Col. 0682A] Arnobius, as we have said, adduced the testimony of Leander or Leandrius from Clement of Alexandria. But we have already mentioned him in the first volume of our *Apparatus* (Arnobius, book VI, p. 193; above, ch. 19, art. 1; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 870 and pp. 1218 ff.).

Leo of Pella, says our author, was reckoned by the pagans among the company of those who denied their gods. But we have discussed him both in this dissertation and elsewhere (Arnobius, book IV, p. 147; above, ch. 9, art. 1; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 785).

Arnobius cites the *Arch*, composed without doubt by the satirical poet Lucilius (Arnobius, book II, p. 45). He was a native of Aurunca, as is gathered from these verses of Juvenal:

[Col. 0682B] Yet why should I prefer to run across that field  
[Note: [Col. 0682D] That is, the field of satire.]

Through which the great son of Aurunca drove his horses?  
(Juvenal, Satire 1, verses 19–20.)

And later he sang the following concerning Lucilius’s satires:

Whenever fiery Lucilius, as though with sword drawn,  
Has thundered, the hearer whose mind is cold with crimes  
Blushes, and his heart sweats from unspoken guilt.  
(Ibid., near the end of the satire.)

Persius too:

Lucilius cut into the city—  
You, Lupus, and you, Mucius—and broke his back teeth upon them.  
(Persius, near the end of Satire 1.)

According to Pliny (Pliny, book I of the *Natural History*, p. 4), this Lucilius was the first to compose satire. Hence Horace:

[Col. 0682C] And Lucilius, who first dared  
To compose verses according to this form of work,  
And to strip away the skin beneath which each man, outwardly sleek,  
Moved among others, though inwardly foul.  
(Horace, book II, Satire 1, verse 93.)

Quintilian agrees with Pliny and Horace and gives this testimony concerning Lucilius and his manner of writing: “Satire, indeed, is entirely our own; in it Lucilius was the first to attain eminent praise, and even now he has certain admirers so devoted to him that they do not hesitate to prefer him not merely to authors of the same kind of work, but to all poets. I differ from them as much as I differ from Horace (book I, Satire 4, verses 6 ff.), who thinks that Lucilius flows muddily and that there is something one could remove. For in him there is remarkable learning and freedom, and hence pungency, and an abundance of wit” (Quintilian, book X of the *Institutes*, ch. 1, pp. 157 ff.). Nevertheless, although this same Horace said that Lucilius’s language was harsh and muddy, he still acknowledges that Lucilius was witty and possessed a discerning nose. Accordingly, he sings elsewhere:

Yet this same man, because with much salt  
He scoured the city, is praised on that very page.  
(Horace, book I, Satire 10, verses 30 ff.)

Cicero also recognized Lucilius’s wit (Cicero, book I of *On Ends*, p. 40, and book II of *On the Orator*, p. 12); he copied down some of Lucilius’s verses, and Aulus Gellius copied far more in his books of *Attic Nights*. Finally, Lucilius’s birth and death are recorded as follows in the Eusebian [Col. 0683A] *Chronicle*: “The poet Lucilius is born.” Then later: “Gaius Lucilius, writer of satires, dies at Naples and is carried forth in a public funeral in the forty-sixth year of his age” (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at the years 1869 and 1914).

Our Arnobius opposed Manilius’s opinion concerning the Novensile gods to those of other pagans. Is he not, therefore, the man whose views concerning Europa, Titanis, Cascus, and Casca we read as expounded by Varro? Is he not also the man whom Pliny calls the most diligent of the Romans, a senator, and, though he had no teacher, distinguished for the greatest branches of learning? Aulus Gellius numbers him among the most learned men, while Cicero places him among those versed in literature and skilled in speaking, answering, and conducting affairs (Arnobius, book III, pp. 129 ff.; Varro, book IV of *On the Latin [Col. 0683B] Language*, p. 10, and book VI, pp. 74 and 76; Pliny, book X of the *Natural History*, ch. 2, p. 389; Gellius, book XVII of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 7, p. 937; Cicero, *Brutus*, p. 118, and book I of *On the Orator*, p. 129).

Mnaseas, according to Arnobius, differed greatly from others concerning the parents and number of the Muses; but who he was may be called into question (Arnobius, book III, p. 122). Several men indeed bore this name. One of them, if Suidas is to be believed, was a native of Berytus and wrote *On the Art of Rhetoric* and on Attic names. Athenaeus praises another, Λοκρὸν καὶ Κολοφώνιον, “a Locrian or Colophonian,” who composed diversions entitled *Salpe* because of their variety (Suidas, s.v. Μνασέας, “Mnaseas”; Athenaeus, book VII of the *Deipnosophists*, p. 321). A third, much more celebrated than these and more frequently [Col. 0683C] cited by various writers, is Mnaseas of Patara or Patrae, whose books of *European History* are cited more than once by the same Athenaeus (ibid., book IV, p. 158; book VII, p. 296; and book XII, p. 530). He had undoubtedly undertaken a discussion of the gods in them. For Suidas gathered from that work that Praxidice was a goddess whose sister bore Ctesias (Suidas, s.v. πραξιδίκη, “Praxidice”). Moreover, as we also learn from Plutarch, Mnaseas equated Epaphus with Liber, Osiris, and Serapis. What, then, prevents us from believing that this is the man whom Arnobius attests to have discussed the Muses? You will find more concerning Mnaseas in Vossius and others (Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, vol. II, p. 365; Vossius, book I of *On the Greek Historians*, ch. 21, p. 134).

[Col. 0683D] Myrtillus or Myrsilus, says Arnobius, held a distinctive opinion concerning the Muses. But we have discussed this author and his opinion in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (Arnobius, book III, p. 121; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 785).

The pagans charged Nicagoras of Cyprus with atheism, as Arnobius relates. We have discussed him both in this dissertation and elsewhere (Arnobius, book IV, p. 147; above, ch. 9, art. 1; and vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 769 and 785).

Nigidius, praised three times by our author, flourished in Cicero’s age (Arnobius, book III, pp. 119, 123, and 124). He was a celebrated writer, a man of praetorian rank, and deeply versed in the humane arts, philosophy, astrology, and medicine. [Col. 0684A] A fragment of Cicero survives in which the learning of this Publius Nigidius is commended, as it also is by Macrobius, Aulus Gellius, and Servius (Cicero, fragments, p. 25; Macrobius, book VI of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 8, p. 495; Gellius, book XIX of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 14; Servius, on book X of the *Aeneid*, p. 585). The Latin orator wrote to this same man in these words: “At present I cannot even make a generous promise to Publius Nigidius, the most learned and upright man of all, once possessed of the highest influence, and certainly my closest friend” (Cicero, book IV, Letter 13). Aulus Gellius and others surname him Figulus (Gellius, book VI of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 6), and under that name Lucan greatly extols him in these verses:

But Figulus, whose concern it was to know the gods and heaven’s secrets,  
[Col. 0684B] Whom Egyptian Memphis, skilled in the stars, could not equal  
In observation or in the numbers that move the constellations.  
(Lucan, book I, verses 639 ff.)

Augustine explains in these words why this surname was given to him: “That famous contrivance involving the potter’s wheel is alleged in vain—the answer which Nigidius, when troubled by this question, is said to have given, and from which he was called Figulus” (Augustine, book V of *The City of God*, ch. 3, p. 116). If, moreover, you ask when and how he died, hear the author of the Eusebian *Chronicle*: “Nigidius Figulus, a Pythagorean and a magician, dies in exile” (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at the year 1973). Finally, his various books, and especially his grammatical commentaries, are very frequently cited by Aulus Gellius.

Nisus is placed by Arnobius among the grammarians. [Col. 0684C] Velius Longus is read as having mentioned him frequently, and Gesner records that he wrote books of *Calendars* (Arnobius, book I, p. 37; Velius Longus, *On Orthography*; Gesner, in the *Bibliotheca*).

Arnobius joined Numenius with Plato and Cronius. He was a Pythagorean and ἀνὴρ ἐπιφανής, “an eminent man,” as Eusebius attests. Theodoret, who frequently calls him a Pythagorean, wrote the following concerning him and Plutarch: Μετὰ γὰρ δὴ τὴν τοῦ Σωτῆρος ἡμῶν ἐπιφάνειαν αὐτοὶ γενόμενοι, τῆς χριστιανικῆς θεολογίας πολλὰ τοῖς οἰκείοις ἀνέμιξαν λόγοις, “For since they lived after the manifestation of our Savior, they mingled many things from Christian theology into their own writings.” But we have already spoken of him above and in the first volume of our *Apparatus* (Arnobius, book I, p. 49; [Col. 0684D] Eusebius, book II of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, ch. 9, p. 525; Theodoret, Discourse 2, *On Faith*, vol. IV, p. 500; above, s.v. CRONIUS; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 1115 and 1128 ff.).

The books of Orpheus—or, as Arnobius calls him, the Thracian seer—were reputed by the pagans to be of divine antiquity, doubtless because, according to Lactantius, they believed this Greek poet to have been contemporary with the gods themselves and to have sailed among the Argonauts together with Hercules (Arnobius, book V, p. 175; Lactantius, book I of the *Institutes*, ch. 5, p. 20).

Arnobius presents us with Panyassis’s testimony taken from Clement of Alexandria (Arnobius, book IV, p. 144). We observed this above and demonstrated elsewhere [Col. 0685A] who he was (above, ch. 12, art. 1; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 810).

Precisely the same must be said of Patrocles of Thurii and Philostephanus. Clement of Alexandria discussed them, and we did so after him (Arnobius, book IV, p. 144; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, pp. 817 and 1208).

Piso, whom Arnobius mentions, was called Lucius Calpurnius Piso Frugi (Arnobius, book III, p. 122). Concerning this man and his surname Cicero committed the following to memory: “He possessed such virtue and integrity that even in those best of times, when one could find no worthless man at all, he alone was nevertheless called *Frugi*, ‘the Honest’” (Cicero, Oration 11, *For Marcus Fonteius*, p. 223, line 43). Concerning Piso’s writings, the same Latin orator elsewhere left this statement: “Lucius Piso, tribune of the plebs, [Col. 0685B] was the first to propose a law concerning the recovery of extorted money, in the consulship of Censorinus and Manilius. Piso himself also pleaded cases and was either the proposer or opponent of many laws. He left speeches, which have now disappeared, and annals written in a decidedly meager style” (Cicero, *On Famous Orators*, or *Brutus*, p. 218, line 2). Gellius nevertheless asserts that in these same *Annals* (Gellius, book VI of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 9, p. 379, and book II, ch. 14, p. 698), which Cicero, Varro, Pliny, and Lactantius also cited, he employed the most unaffected charm in both subject matter and style, and that events were narrated there by him with great purity and elegance (Cicero, book IX, Letter 22, and book II of *On the Orator*, p. 144; Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, p. 36; Pliny, book II of the *Natural History*, ch. 53, p. 207; Lactantius, book I, ch. 6, p. 33). If you wish for more concerning him, consult Macrobius, [Col. 0685C] book I of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 12, p. 229; Cicero again, book III of the *Tusculan Disputations*, p. 156; Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, ch. 5; and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book II of *Roman Antiquities*, p. 105, and elsewhere.

Plutarch of Chaeronea is presented in the editions of our author’s books as a witness concerning the death of Hercules (Arnobius, book IV, p. 144). But in the royal manuscript codex, as we noted above (above, ch. 4, art. 4), “Hieronymus Plutarch” is written. Yet since Arnobius still appears to follow Clement of Alexandria there (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 19), a by no means slight conjecture may be drawn from this that the text should read “Hieronymus and Dicaearchus.” For both are cited by Clement. Nevertheless, [Col. 0685D] we think that nothing in Arnobius’s text should be altered rashly.

The testimony of Polemon concerning Minerva, who was killed by Ornytus, was cited by our author (ibid.) and was excerpted from the same Clement of Alexandria. No one (ibid.) who compares the words of the two writers with one another will be able to call this into doubt. See, if you please, what we noted in the preceding volume of our *Apparatus* (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 762).

“You preserve Pomponius’s *Marsyas* sealed in your memory,” says Arnobius (Arnobius, book II, p. 45). According to Pliny (Pliny, book VII of the *Natural History*, ch. 19, p. 38, and book XIV, ch. 4, p. 129), he was a man of consular rank and a poet. Pliny declares in the following words that he had written his life: “In relating the life of the poet Pomponius Secundus [Col. 0686A] and the dinner that he gave the emperor”—Gaius Caesar, son of Germanicus. Pliny the Younger mentions him; Quintilian, moreover, committed the following concerning him to writing: “Of those whom I have seen, Pomponius Secundus was by far the foremost. Though the old men considered him insufficiently tragic, they acknowledged that he excelled in learning and elegance” (Pliny the Younger, book III, Letter 5; Quintilian, book X of the *Institutes*, p. 748). Velleius Paterculus, however, writes that he “was distinguished in thought, rough in expression, and commendable for the novelty of the kind of work he invented” (Paterculus, book II of the *Histories*, well after the beginning). Eusebius teaches what that new kind of work was in his *Chronicle*: “Lucius Pomponius,” he says, “a native of Bononia and a writer of Atellan farces, is considered famous” (Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at the year 1826). From his skill in writing Atellan farces, which Macrobius asserts was revived by [Col. 0686B] Mummius after Nonius and Pomponius, there undoubtedly proceeded the plays *Maevia*, *The Temple Wardens*, *The Gauls*, *The Transalpines*, and *Porceta*, which are cited by Aulus Gellius (Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 10; Gellius, book X of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 14; book XII, ch. 10; and book XVI, ch. 6). Who, then, would not readily concede that the work our author called *Marsyas* was one of these?

Posidippus is praised once and again by Arnobius, who is still following in the footsteps of Clement of Alexandria. Suidas relates that Posidippus, a comic poet of Cassandreia and son of Cyniscus, first produced a play in the third year after Menander’s death and published thirty plays. But Vossius thinks that Arnobius and Clement of Alexandria cite a different Posidippus, whom he included in the register of Greek historians. [Col. 0686C] Certain verses by Posidippus concerning serpents are presented by Tzetzes. Whether he is the same man named by Arnobius is decidedly difficult to say. Gesner, however, does not appear to distinguish this Posidippus from the poet (Arnobius, book VI, pp. 198 and 206; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, pp. 35 and 38; Suidas, s.v. ποσίδιππος, “Posidippus”; Tzetzes, *Histories*, *Chiliad* 7, history 144, p. 184; Gesner, in the *Bibliotheca*).

Ptolemy was the son of Agesarchus. As we explained elsewhere, the first book of his work *On Philopator* is cited by our Arnobius following Clement of Alexandria (Arnobius, book VI, p. 193; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 29; above, ch. 9, art. 1), while its second and third books are cited by Athenaeus in these words: Πτολεμαῖος ὁ τοῦ Ἀγησάρχου, Μεγαλοπολίτης γένος, ἐν τῇ δευτέρᾳ [Col. 0686D] τῶν περὶ τὸν Φιλοπάτορα ἱστοριῶν, “Ptolemy, son of Agesarchus, a Megalopolitan by birth, in the second book of the *Histories concerning Philopator*” (Athenaeus, book VI of the *Deipnosophists*, p. 246). And again elsewhere: Πτολεμαῖος ὁ τοῦ Ἀγησάρχου ἐν τῇ τρίτῃ τῶν περὶ Φιλοπάτορα ἱστοριῶν, “Ptolemy, son of Agesarchus, in the third book of the *Histories concerning Philopator*” (book X, p. 425). Read Vossius, book I of *On the Greek Historians*, ch. 18, p. 117.

Sammonicus is frequently mentioned by various writers (Arnobius, book VI, p. 194). Macrobius writes as follows concerning who he was and the period in which he lived: “In the time of the emperor Severus, who made a display of austerity in his manners, Sammonicus Serenus, a man learned for his age, when writing to his emperor and undertaking [Col. 0687A] a discussion of this fish, prefaced it with the words of Pliny that I quoted above” (Macrobius, book III of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 16, p. 347). Elsewhere Macrobius also transmits his words and cites the fifth book of his *Hidden Matters* (ibid., ch. 9, p. 33, and ch. 17, p. 351). Capitolinus, however, in his account of Gordian Caesar, transmitted the following concerning Sammonicus to posterity: “Serenus Sammonicus, who had been his father’s closest friend and his own teacher, was exceedingly acceptable and dear to him—so much so that, when he died, he left to the younger Gordian all the books of Serenus Sammonicus, his father, which were estimated at sixty-two thousand. This raised Gordian to the heavens, for, endowed with so great an abundance and splendor of a library, he honorably achieved a reputation among learned men” (Capitolinus, p. 367). Spartianus attests that [Col. 0687B] many of Sammonicus’s books conducive to learning still existed in his own time, that he was among Antoninus Geta’s closest intimates, and that he was killed under Caracalla while dining with several others (Spartianus, *Caracalla*, p. 332, and *Antoninus Geta*, p. 335).

Our author rightly enrolled Scaurus among the illustrious grammarians (Arnobius, book I, p. 237). For Aulus Gellius calls him a most distinguished grammarian (Aulus Gellius, book XI of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 15, p. 599) and reports that he flourished during Hadrian’s reign: “Terentius Scaurus,” he says, “was a most distinguished grammarian in the time of the deified Hadrian.” Capitolinus agreed with Gellius; speaking of Emperor Verus, he indicates in the following words that another Scaurus, the former’s son and likewise a grammarian, was that emperor’s teacher: “He attended Scaurus, [Col. 0687C] a Latin grammarian, son of the Scaurus who had been Hadrian’s grammarian” (Capitolinus, *Life of Verus*, near the beginning). But Lampridius calls both men *Scaurinus*. For, when speaking of Alexander Severus, he says: “At Rome he had as grammarians Scaurinus, son of Scaurinus, a most celebrated teacher” (Lampridius, *Life of Alexander Severus*, near the beginning). Gesner noted certain works of his; you may consult him if you please (Gesner, in the *Bibliotheca*).

In addressing Sosibius, Arnobius follows Clement of Alexandria (Arnobius, book IV, p. 144; Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 23; vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 816). We have discussed him elsewhere (Arnobius, book IV, p. 147; above, ch. 9, art. 1; and vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 785).

[Col. 0687D] Theodorus of Cyrene was classed by the pagans among the atheists, together with others whom we named above. But we have more than once discussed him and the other impious men of this kind.

Arnobius calls Timotheus a theologian—that is, a pagan theologian—of no little distinction (Arnobius, book V, p. 157). But since this name was shared by several men, no one could readily say who this particular person was. One is cited by Plutarch: Τιμόθεος ἐν ιαʹ περὶ ποταμῶν, “Timotheus, in the eleventh book *On Rivers*” (Plutarch, *On Rivers*, p. 1151). Another was Timotheus of Pergamum, who, as we observed elsewhere, had composed a book *On the Courage of Philosophers* (vol. I of the *Apparatus*, p. 1270). A third was the Milesian poet, whose various works [Col. 0688A] and poems you will find cited by Athenaeus (Athenaeus, book III of the *Deipnosophists*, p. 122; book VI, p. 142; book VIII, p. 338; book XI, p. 465). A fourth was an Athenian who, as Laertius notes, published a book *On Lives*, περὶ βιῶν, doubtless the lives of philosophers. Menagius observes, however, that it is not easy to find anyone besides Laertius who mentions him. Vossius, on the other hand, thinks him to be the man whom Plutarch addresses in these words: Τιμόθεος ἐν τοῖς Ἀργολικοῖς, “Timotheus in the *Argolica*.” But he has not yet persuaded others of this. For Menagius doubts whether this is the same man whom we said was previously praised by the same Plutarch (Laertius, book II, *Life of Plato*, §5; book IV, *Life of Speusippus*, §4; book V, *Life of Aristotle*, §1; book VII, *Life of Zeno*, §1). Yet the same Vossius confidently affirms that this man is entirely different from the one whom [Col. 0688B] our author calls a pagan theologian (Vossius, book III of *On the Greek Historians*, p. 421, and *On the Greek Poets*, pp. 46–47). There Vossius reports from Suidas that there was another Timotheus, a contemporary of Euripides and Philip of Macedon, who added the tenth and eleventh strings to the lyre and composed several poetic works, which Suidas enumerates (Suidas, s.v. Τιμόθεοι, “Men named Timotheus”). He further identifies yet another Timotheus of Athens, a poet of Middle Comedy, and enumerates his writings. What more need be said? A certain Timotheus is also cited simply by name by Athenaeus; according to Casaubon, he was said to have provoked the laughter of witty men, being lacking in talent, frigid, and far too often foolish. Moreover, if poets, as Augustine says, were called theologians by the pagans because they composed poems concerning the gods, we may readily be persuaded [Col. 0688C] that our Arnobius cited one of these poets (Athenaeus, book VIII, p. 358; Casaubon, on the same book, chs. 5 and 11; Augustine, book XVIII of *The City of God*, ch. 14, p. 478; Arnobius, book VII, p. 236).

Trebatius, next summoned by Arnobius as a witness, undoubtedly seems to be the man whose first and ninth books *On Religious Rites* were cited by Macrobius, and whose fifth book was cited by Aulus Gellius. His name was Gaius Trebatius Testa, and he was one of Cicero’s closest and most intimate friends. For Cicero dedicated his *Topics* to him and addresses him as an interpreter of the law. To Atticus, moreover, he writes: “Although I do not disdain Trebatius’s letters, since I know that he has a singular affection for me” (Macrobius, book III of the *Saturnalia*, chs. 5 and 9; Gellius, book VI, ch. 12; Cicero, *Topics*, p. 276; the same, book VII, Letter 16, *To Atticus*, [Col. 0688D] p. 282; book VII, Letters 6 and 7, pp. 7 ff.; and book X, *To Atticus*, Letter 1, p. 313). But this is made still clearer by the many letters addressed to Trebatius that have been printed. Elsewhere Cicero calls him a good man and citizen; Horace addresses him thus:

Trebatius,  
Tell me what I should do.  
(Horace, book II, Satire 1, verses 4–5.)

Arnobius produced a certain Valerianus as a witness to his statements (Arnobius, book VI, p. 194). A man of that name is praised by Pliny: “Cornelius Valerianus, who recorded that the Phoenix flew down into Egypt” (Pliny, book X of the *Natural History*, ch. 2, p. 389); and elsewhere: “Valerianus Cornelius likewise considered it especially worthy of record that individual villas and houses were encircled by the tendrils of vines and [Col. 0689A] by clinging laurels” (book XIV, ch. 1, p. 111). Whether he is the same man as the one Arnobius mentions must be left to the judgment of others.

Our author relates what Valerius the pontiff committed to writing concerning Ia, the daughter of Midas and betrothed of Attis (Arnobius, book V, p. 160). But since very many men sprang from the most celebrated Valerian family, it may indeed appear doubtful and uncertain whom he calls “the pontiff.” Consider, however, whether he might be Marcus Valerius Messala, of whom Macrobius says: “Marcus Messala, the colleague of Gnaeus Domitius in the consulship and also an augur for fifty-five years, speaks as follows concerning Janus: ‘He who fashions all things and likewise governs them’” (Macrobius, book I of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 9). From the first book *On Auspices* by this Messala [Col. 0689B] the augur, Gellius also copied down a long fragment (Gellius, book XIII of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 15). It is therefore established that he wrote concerning the gods; why, then, could it not be said that he transmitted to memory something concerning the history—or rather the fable—of Ia that Arnobius cited? He is frequently commended to no small degree by Latin authors and extolled with great praises. On this subject one may readily consult Vossius, if time permits (Vossius, book I of *On the Latin Historians*, ch. 18, p. 81). If, nevertheless, you contend that Arnobius named some other Valerius the pontiff, show him to us, and we yield.

Varro Menippeus—or, as it is read in the royal manuscript codex and the early editions, *Setenipeus*, or, as others prefer, *in the Menippeans*—is one of the writers cited by our author. The first reading is supported by [Col. 0689C] Athenaeus, who appeals to Varro’s authority after prefacing it with these words: Οὔαῤῥον ὁ Μενίππος ἐπικαλούμενος, “Varro, surnamed Menippeus” (Athen., bk. IV, *Deipnos.*, p. 160). The last reading, however, is confirmed by Aulus Gellius, who cites him thus: “Varro, in the Menippean satire which he wrote *On the Duty of a Husband*” (Gell., bk. I, *Noct. Att.*, ch. 17, p. 80). Yet Gellius himself later introduced considerable obscurity into the matter when discussing slaves: “There were also,” he says, “not a few other slaves who afterward became distinguished philosophers; among them was that Menippus whose books Marcus Varro imitated in the satires which others call Cynic, but which he himself calls Menippean” (Idem, bk. II, ch. 18, p. 151). We find this written in precisely the same words by Macrobius (Macrob., bk. I, *Saturnal.*, ch. 11, p. 224). It may therefore quite reasonably be called into question [Col. 0689D] whether Arnobius is referring to Varro Menippeus or to the celebrated Roman Marcus Terentius Varro. If, however, you judge that he cited the latter rather than another—because he was a Latin author, incomparably more illustrious, and committed to writing more about the gods of whom our author speaks—we shall be all the less resistant, since, as we have seen, Arnobius’s genuine text was shamefully disfigured by an ignorant copyist.

The Verrius whom Arnobius made the repository and guarantor of his statements is Verrius Flaccus, whom we discussed above under the word *Flaccus* (Arnob., bk. I, p. 37).

What Arnobius brought forward from Zeno of Myndus (Arnob., bk. VI, p. 193), he had drawn from no source other than Clement of Alexandria. [Col. 0690A] We believe that we have sufficiently demonstrated this both in the present dissertation and elsewhere, where we treated the same Zeno of Myndus (above, ch. 9, art. 1; vol. I, *Apparatus*, p. 727 ff., and p. 817).

Finally, Arnobius mentioned certain other writers, namely Aristotle, Cicero, Euripides, Hesiod, Orpheus, Pindar, Plato, and Plautus. But since these celebrated writers cannot be unknown to anyone possessing even a moderate education, and their various works, whether Greek or Latin, have frequently been printed and are in everyone’s hands, we have judged that nothing needs to be said about them individually. To this must be added that, unless we are mistaken, in the first volume of our *Apparatus* we have discussed the Greek writers cited by our author sufficiently to make them known to everyone.

## ARTICLE IV. On the Barbarous, Obsolete, Unusual, or Obscure Words Used by Arnobius

[Col. 0690B]

We have already observed that Arnobius’s style and language are uncultivated and confused, and that in his books he employed obsolete, unusual, and barbarous words. So that these may not delay the reader, we must, in fulfillment of our duty, explain them to the best of our ability (above, ch. 2, art. 2). We have already explained very many of them when a suitable occasion presented itself above. But many no less obscure and difficult still occur, for the interpretation of which no sufficiently convenient place has offered itself. We have therefore judged that their interpretation and explanation should be deferred to [Col. 0690C] the end of the present dissertation. In this inquiry we shall follow the same “alphabetical,” as people like to call it, order as in the preceding article. Arnobius first said:

“Imitating the *ancillatrum* of a little slave with fearful tremblings”—that is, one who greets more powerful men with the utmost humility (Arnob., bk. VII, p. 221). This is indeed how we read it in the royal manuscript codex. But some, thinking the text corrupt at this point, wished it to be written: “of a maidservant or a little slave.” Yet this correction does not cohere with the words of Arnobius that follow. Others therefore conjecture that it should be restored as: “Imitating the fearful tremblings of maidservants’ little slave.” But they offer no evidence or even argument for this reading. What, however, if Arnobius used a new word to signify the servitude or obsequiousness of a little slave, which he calls *ancillatrum*, or rather *ancillatum*? [Col. 0690D] Let others weigh and decide whether this is the genuine reading of our author. For us, it is certainly enough to have disclosed its meaning.

Arnobius calls it the “grunting of geese,” because, as Festus says, “to grunt” (*grinnire*) is the proper term for the sound of geese (ibid., bk. VI, p. 205; Festus, under *GRUNNIRE*).

Arnobius calls the pine beneath which Attis deprived himself of his manhood an “arrested tree” (*arbor pausata*); around its trunk the Mother of the Gods, joining her lamentations with Acdestis, beats and wounds her breast (Arnob., bk. V, p. 160). Why it is called an “arrested tree,” however, all the commentators on these books of Arnobius confess themselves unable to discover. Some [Col. 0691A] therefore think that the word *pausatae* is corrupt, and that *lanatae*, *lausatae*, or *positae* should be read in its place. But others reject and hiss these suggestions off as sheer nonsense. For what prevents Arnobius from having used the word *pausatae* in imitation of Plautus, who said *Pausa*, that is, “Rest”? For our author writes there that the Mother of the Gods carried that tree into her cave, and there, around its trunk, now at rest—that is, resting and set down—joined her lamentations with those of Acdestis and beat and wounded her breast.

An “arched little chair” (*arquata sellula*) means one that is semicircular and fashioned in the likeness of an arch (Arnob., bk. I, p. 59). It is in this sense that Ovid sings:

> And Iris, marking the sky with her arching curve.  
> (Ovid, bk. II, *Metam.*, p. 418)

In the Phrygian language the animals that we call he-goats are called *attagi* [Col. 0691B] (Arnob., bk. V, p. 159). In Eustathius, however, says Bochart, ἄττηγοι are called αἶγες ἄῤῥηνες, “male goats,” or he-goats (Bochart, bk. II, *On the Animals of Sacred Scripture*, ch. 53, p. 647). Arnobius thinks that the name Attis was formed from this Phrygian word. Bochart, however, thinks it was derived rather from the Hebrew *athud*. Consult him if you wish.

Our author said *auctificari*; Ennius, however, as Nonius Marcellus notes, said *augificare*. It is an obsolete verb meaning the same as “to increase” (Arnob., bk. VII, p. 224; Nonius, *On the Properties of Speech*, ch. 2). In Lucretius, however, we read:

> And growth-producing motions  
> Can perpetually preserve created things.  
> (Lucret., bk. II, line 571)

[Col. 0691C] Arnobius similarly said *augustare*, “to render august” (Arnob., bk. VII, p. 201).

*Batiaca*; but in the royal manuscript codex it is most corruptly written *pastiocas* (ibid., bk. I, p. 59). For the Greek *batiaca*, βατιάκη, as we learn from Athenaeus, was a kind of drinking vessel (Athen., bk. II, *Deipnos.*, p. 486). Hence Plautus said somewhere:

> Those who have riches at home drink from little bowls,  
> tankards, and *batiola*.  
> (Plaut., *Stichus*, act V, scene 4)

But in some editions *Batiocis* is read there.

*Bigarii* is the word presented in the Roman edition of these books of Arnobius and in other later editions; in the royal manuscript codex, however, it is *Pigarii*, and in the latest edition, *cybiarii* (Arnob., bk. II, p. 70). But no [Col. 0691D] reason is given for this alteration. Why not rather read *Cibarii*, those who prepare or serve food? For Varro says in Nonius Marcellus: “Your own brother was Aristoxenus’s provisioner” (*cibarius*) (Non. Marcell., *On the Properties of Speech*, ch. 2, p. 536). “Why not,” someone will ask, “also read *Bigarii*, from which an ignorant copyist produced *Pigarii*?” For in the preceding line Arnobius had said *quadrigarii*, “four-horse charioteers.” Yet perhaps no one will be able to correct that corrupted word without the aid of another manuscript codex.

In our manuscript codex we read *Bolones*, for which some have incorrectly written *Volones* (Arnob., bk. II, p. 70). For, as Donatus says, fishmongers are those “who sell sea monsters—that is, large fish—and conduct *bolones*,” [Col. 0692A] that is, the fish trade (Donat., on Terence, *Eunuchus*, act II, scene 2, line 26). Others, citing Isidore, take the term to mean those who bought and sold various kinds of fish (Isidore, *Glosses*, p. 620). See Turnebus, bk. XIII, *Adversaria*, ch. 14.

According to Festus, *botulus* is a kind of sausage which, because of its links, is so named from *boli* (Arnob., bk. II, p. 73; Festus, under *BOTULUS*). Martial once sang:

> The sausage that came to you in midwinter  
> Had arrived seven days before Saturn’s feast.  
> (Martial, bk. XIV, epigram 72)

Hence Tertullian rebukes [Col. 0692B] the pagans in this fashion: “Among the trials you set before Christians, you also bring sausages swollen with blood, being perfectly certain that what you seek to use to make them transgress is unlawful among them” (Tertull., *Apology*, ch. 9, p. 11). Elsewhere, after he had defected from the party of the orthodox, whom he calls “Psychics,” he attacks them thus: “How am I to defend chastity and sobriety without censuring their opponents? Who these are I shall name once for all: the outer and inner sausages of the Psychics” (Idem, *On Fasts*, ch. 1, p. 701).

Some call the *buris* the rear part of the plough, others the upper part of the pole; both are curved (Arnob., bk. II, p. 59). Virgil used this term when he sang:

> At once in the woods, bent with great force, the elm is subdued  
> Into a *buris* and assumes the form of a curving plough.  
> [Col. 0692C] (Virgil, bk. I, *Georgics*, lines 169 ff.)

Servius makes the following observations on these lines: “‘Into a *buris*’ means ‘into a curved form.’ For *buris* is the curvature of a plough, so called as though from βοὸς οὐρά, ‘an ox’s tail,’ because it resembles the tail of an ox. Others call the upper curve of the pole the *buris*, and the part below it the *urvum*. For a *buris*, in order to be bent, is first softened by fire, that is, scorched (*amburitur*); hence things found naturally curved are so called. Varro says that the whole *buris* derives its name from *urbs*.” Isidore subscribed to the former opinion (Isidore, bk. XX, *Origins*, ch. 13; Arnob., bk. I, p. 24, and bk. VII, p. 222; ibid., bk. VI, p. 200).

*Busticeta*, as is noted in the glosses attributed to the same Isidore, were tombs in the countryside.

*Cacabulus* is undoubtedly the diminutive of *cacabus*, [Col. 0692D] which means a vessel in which a relish was cooked. See Martinius’s *Lexicon* and Vossius’s *Etymologicon*.

Arnobius says “to make the hair wave with curling irons” (*calamistris vibrare caesariem*) (ibid., bk. II, p. 72). A *calamistrum* was a fairly large needle or iron implement which was heated and used to twist and curl the hair. Hear Virgil:

> To defile in the dust her hair,  
> Damp with myrrh, though curled with a hot iron.  
> (Bk. XII, *Aeneid*, lines 90 ff.)

On these lines Servius says: “A *calamistrum* is a fairly large needle which, when heated and applied, curls the hair.” See Julius Pollux and Isidore (Pollux, bk. V, ch. 16; Isidore, bk. XX, *Origins*, ch. 13).

[Col. 0693A] Turnebus thought that by the name *caliendrum* Arnobius meant the mantle which he had previously called a *ricinium*. But after considering the matter more carefully, he judged that it meant a covering for the head. Horace uses it in this sense:

> . . . Sagana’s towering *caliendrum*.  
> (Horace, bk. I, satire 8, line 48)

On this poem Acro—or whoever else wrote under his name—noted that *caliendrum* means either an adornment for women’s heads, used to embellish their hair, or false hair adopted in place of natural hair. Tertullian also used this noun when inveighing against women: “But now, by procuring themselves in order that they may be approached more openly, they have renounced the matron’s robe, the *lupparum*, the little slipper, and the *caliendrum*, and by now even the [Col. 0693B] litters and chairs in which they used to be kept privately and secluded even in public” (Tertull., *On the Pallium*, ch. 4, p. 136).

“*Canacheni*, opening things barred up in the obscurity of *remedors*” (Arnob., bk. VI, p. 108). These are our author’s words, which quite reasonably appear to many to be plainly corrupt. Some therefore wish to restore *tenebrarum*, “of darkness,” in place of *remedorum*—but on what authority? They think that further inquiry must be made concerning the name *Canacheni*. But where is it to be investigated unless another, more reliable and complete manuscript codex is available? Yet it can certainly be obscure to no one that Arnobius is speaking of nocturnal robbers who either despoiled the statues of the gods or carried them away from the temples. Whether he means those who did this by magical art, however, we [Col. 0693C] leave to the judgment of others.

Arnobius uses *Chantharulus* (ibid., p. 209) for a small drinking vessel with which Bacchus was customarily depicted. For a few lines earlier he had written: “In the right hand of Liber, or Bacchus, hangs the drinker’s tankard.” If you seek the reason, Valerius Maximus will suggest it to you: “Father Liber, when leading his triumph from Asia, was said to have used this kind of cup” (Val. Max., bk. II, ch. 6, § 7). Following his example, as Valerius and Pliny have noted (Pliny, bk. XXXIII, *Natural History*, ch. 11, p. 73), Gaius Marius always drank from tankards after his victory over the Cimbri.

According to Julius Paulus, says Aulus Gellius, those were called *capite censi* who were assessed at no property or at exceedingly little, and paid little or no tax [Col. 0693D] (Arnob., bk. II, p. 63; Gell., bk. XVI, *Attic Nights*, ch. 10).

Arnobius uses *castus* in a special sense (Arnob., bk. V, p. 167), where he attacks the mysteries of the Mother of the Gods, or Cybele, in this manner: “What is abstinence from the nourishment of bread, to which you have given the name *castus*?” To understand this, it must be observed from Apuleius, Tertullian, Jerome, and others that in the celebration of these mysteries, besides many other superstitious rites, abstinence at least from ordinary foods was observed (Apul., bk. XI, *Metam.*, pp. 206 and 209; Tertull., *On Fasting*, ch. 2; Jerome, Letter 7 to Laeta, p. 59, and bk. II, *Against Jovinian*, p. 98). Some, however, such as Martinius and Vossius, [Col. 0694A] relying on the words and authority of Festus, think that the noun *Castus* signifies all these ceremonies. Tertullian, while arguing against the Catholics in defense of the fasts of his Montanists, says: “But it is well that, in heaping blasphemies upon our dry-food observances, you equate them with the *Castus* of Isis and Cybele” (Tertull., *On Fasting*, ch. 16). But if anyone would rather hear another writer arguing for the Catholics against the heretics, Jerome is at hand. In combating the errors of Jovinian, he wrote: “They pride themselves on abstinence from foods, as though even pagan superstition did not observe the *castus* of the Mother of the Gods and of Osiris” (Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, bk. II, p. 91). Later, more plainly and closer to the meaning of our Arnobius, he says: “Just as the imitation of virginity by the devil’s virgins does not prejudice true virginity, [Col. 0694B] so neither do the *castus* of Isis and Cybele and perpetual abstinence from certain foods prejudice true fasts—especially since among them a fast from bread was checked by a stuffing of meat” (ibid., p. 104). Is not that “fast from bread” the same as, in Arnobius’s words, “abstinence from the nourishment of bread”?

*Cimices* are foul-smelling little worms bred from wood, paper, and straw. Isidore says: “The *cimex* is named from its resemblance to a certain plant whose stench it possesses” (Arnob., bk. II, p. 75; Isidore, bk. XII, *Origins*, ch. 5).

“Our author,” he says, “brings forward the *cinnus*, which Greece calls the *cyceon*” (Arnob., bk. V, p. 174). Arnobius borrowed this and the many other things he relates there about the Eleusinian mysteries from Clement of Alexandria, as we noted above. [Col. 0694C] For that learned Greek had written: ἔπιον τὸν κυκεῶνα, “I drank the *cyceon*.” According to Nonius Marcellus, a *cinnus* was a kind of drink composed of many liquids (Clement of Alexandria, *Admonition to the Gentiles*, p. 13; Non. Marcell., *On the Properties of Words*, chs. 1 and 6). He further informs us that Cicero used this word. See Turnebus, bk. XII, *Adversaria*, ch. 8.

Those Roman citizens who were distributed into various classes were called *classici*. Livy and Dionysius of Halicarnassus described how they were so distributed (Arnob., bk. II, p. 63; Livy, bk. II, ch. 43; Dionys. Halic., bk. IV, pp. 221 ff.). In a special sense, however, as Aulus Gellius reports, only men of the first class were called *classici*: those assessed at one hundred and twenty-five [Col. 0694D] thousand asses or more (Gell., bk. VII, *Attic Nights*, ch. 13). Arnobius uses the noun *classicus* in that sense, if his text is complete and uncorrupted at that point, where no one can deny that many things have been shamefully disfigured. Arnobius had previously spoken of these same classes of Roman citizens (bk. II, p. 91), as we saw above. On them you may also consult Aulus Gellius, bk. X, *Attic Nights*, ch. 28, and Lipsius, bk. I, *On the Roman Military*, Dialogue 2, vol. III, p. 15.

If Nonius Marcellus is to be believed, *craterae* are wine vessels, while *crateres* are oil vessels; he attempts to prove both usages from the authority of Virgil (ibid., p. 56; Marcellus, ch. 19).

[Col. 0695A] A *cupa* is a vessel from which one drinks, or, as some prefer, a large wine vessel (Arnob., bk. II, p. 59).

The *curculio*, *curgulio*, or *gurgulio* is a small creature that gnaws grain (ibid., p. 75), as is evident from this verse of Virgil:

> And the weevil ravages the vast heap of spelt.  
> (Virgil, bk. I, *Georgics*, line 185)

If you wish, read the writers on agriculture: Varro, ch. 63; Cato, ch. 2; Columella, bk. I, ch. 6; and Palladius also, bk. I, title 19.

Arnobius says *defanata spatiola* (Arnob., bk. IV, p. 153), that is, “little profaned spaces.” For he seems there to allude to what Cicero, Valerius Maximus, and others record concerning Tiberius Gracchus (Cicero, bk. II, *On the Nature* [Col. 0695B] *of the Gods*, p. 215; bk. I, *On Divination*, p. 261; Val. Max., bk. I, ch. 1, § 3). When, they say, he had inadvertently taken his augural tent under a defect and had crossed the orchard without taking the auspices, the augurs therefore declared that the consuls had been defectively elected. If this is so, our author seems to call that tent and orchard “little profaned spaces.” If, however, you prove that he had another similar story in view, we shall certainly not oppose you; but the meaning of his words will always be the same.

“*Desultores*,” says Isidore, “were so named because in former times, as each reached the end of the course, he leaped down and ran; or because he leaped from horse to horse” (Arnob., bk. II, p. 70; Isidore, bk. XVIII, *Origins*, ch. 39). Livy uses the term in this sense [Col. 0695C] when discussing the agility of the Numidians: “Not all the Numidians were posted on the right wing, but only those who, after the manner of *desultores*, led two horses apiece and were accustomed, often amid the fiercest fighting, to leap fully armed from a tired horse onto a fresh one: such was their speed, and so tractable their breed of horses” (Livy, bk. XXIII, ch. 29). See Lipsius, bk. III, *On the Roman Military*, Dialogue 8, p. 95, vol. III; and Caelius Rhodiginus, bk. XXIII, *Ancient Readings*, ch. 30.

*Dibus* is read in the royal Arnobian codex (Arnob., bk. II, p. 60). But because the meaning of the word was unknown, the noun *cubus* was substituted for it in some printed editions. Salmasius, however, thinks that the reading he regards as genuine—*cubus*—was corrupted through the ignorance of copyists, who divided the second letter of this noun, *u*, [Col. 0695D] and, joining the first part of it to the initial letter *c*, produced *Dibus*. He attempts to prove this by another example, though one of no greater weight. Meursius, however, judged that the first reading, *Dibus*, which Agathias used and which signifies a pair, should be retained (Meursius, bk. II, *Critical Studies*, ch. 6; Salmasius, *Exercises on Solinus*, pp. 417 and 699). Others, nevertheless, would have wished him to confirm it with other examples. But is it not enough to prove this that Arnobius is there discussing numbers and immediately adds various numerical terms?

*Dynamis* is also recorded by him in the same passage, and in some editions *dymanis*, but incorrectly. *Dynamis* means a set of four, as Meursius [Col. 0696A] confirms from the testimony of Hierocles, and Elmenhorst from that of Hero of Alexandria.

Those who suffer from a descent of the intestine from its proper and natural place—that is, from a hernia—are called *enterocelici*. Pliny also used this Greek noun and naturalized it in Latin (Arnob., bk. VII, p. 240; Pliny, bk. XX, *Natural History*, ch. 4, p. 13).

Arnobius said “to discharge the gods themselves” (*exauctorare deos ipsos*) (same book, p. 236), meaning to take and strip authority from them.

*Fasciola*, the diminutive of *fascia*, means the same as a little strip of linen (Arnob., bk. II, p. 59), suitable for binding something, or specifically for binding wounds, as Isidore notes (Isidore, bk. XIX, *Origins*, ch. 33). Cicero used it in the first sense in a certain speech: “Publius Clodius,” [Col. 0696B] he says, “from the saffron robe, the mitre, women’s slippers, and little purple bands” (Cicero, Speech 30, *On the Response of the Haruspices*, p. 436). Horace, however, wrote in the second sense:

> Lay aside the tokens of disease,  
> The bandages.  
> (Horace, bk. II, satire 3, lines 254 ff.)

Arnobius uses the phrase “they might suck the breasts” (*fellitantes mammas exsugerent*) in an honorable sense (Arnob., bk. II, p. 70). For he is speaking of infants who sucked their mothers’ or nurses’ breasts. Solinus, however, said: “The mother by no means offers the chick breasts to suck” (Solinus, ch. 45, p. 74). Read Turnebus, bk. XXIV, *Adversaria*, ch. 13, and bk. XXIX, ch. 10.

We read *ferunculum* in the royal manuscript codex of Arnobius’s books (Arnob., bk. II, p. 47). But some, [Col. 0696C] thinking this word corrupt, have substituted *furunculum* in the text, though without good reason. For Isidore left it written: “A *furunculus* is a swelling rising to a point, so called because it burns (*ferveat*), as though *ferunculus*; hence in Greek it is called ἄνθραξ, ‘coal,’ because it is fiery” (Isidore, bk. IV, *Origins*, ch. 8). But whichever way it is read, it agrees very well with our author’s purpose. For he says that no philosopher has ever cured even the slightest *furunculus*, or *ferunculus*, with a single word. On the *furunculus*, however, see Pliny frequently in book XX, and others.

Our author said “to blow upon a reed” (*flatare calamo*) and “the blowings of the sky” (*coeli flaturas*) for blowing on a reed or flute and for the blast of the sky (Arnob., bk. I, p. 7, and bk. II, p. 69).

He also uses the word *fluor* more than once. We read that Festus [Col. 0696D] (Festus, under *FLUVIONA*), Apuleius, Solinus, and especially physicians also used this noun to signify a flow.

“Formation displaying various objects” (*formatura varia res spectans*) are Arnobius’s words (bk. II, p. 59); in his usual fashion, as we have seen elsewhere, he follows Lucretius:

> And in part shapes the formation of the lips  
> . . . . . . . . . . . . .  
> For it preserves the formation and preserves the figure.  
> (Lucret., bk. IV, lines 554 and 560)

Arnobius calls the stars “little fiery fragments” (*frustilla ignea*) (bk. II, p. 84), that is, tiny fiery pieces. For *frustillum* is formed as a diminutive from the noun *frustum*. Plautus likewise once said:

> [Col. 0697A] Now I shall make the ants carry you away from here bit by bit.  
> (Plaut., *Curculio*, act IV, scene 4)

That is, so that the ants may carry you off in different directions, cut into tiny pieces, and tear you apart.

According to Festus, *fulguritum* means the same as “struck by lightning” (Arnob., bk. V, p. 155; Festus, under *FULGURITUM*). A place struck by lightning immediately seemed to the pagans to be sacred and dedicated by the god to himself.

“To overshadow the eyes with soot” means to paint them black (Arnob., bk. II, p. 72). This is demonstrated by the following verses of Juvenal:

> With moist soot he extends his painted eyebrow  
> By an oblique needle, and paints, lifting up  
> His trembling eyes.  
> (Juvenal, satire 2, lines 93 ff.)

[Col. 0697B] We discussed that depraved custom in vol. I of the *Apparatus*, bk. III, dissertation I, ch. 12, art. I, p. 788.
