*Fuscinum* is sufficiently explained by the words of our author and Augustine (Arnob., bk. V, pp. 176 and 184, and bk. VII, p. 239; Augustine, bk. VII, *City of God*, ch. 9, p. 157).

In some editions of these books of Arnobius we read *gnariores*. In others, following Scaliger’s emendation, as it seems, *gnarures*. But the manuscript has *ignarores*, certainly incorrectly, as you can see. The sense of Arnobius, however, seems to require *gnarores* or *ignariores* (Arnob., bk. III, p. 115). For he immediately added: “and to possess branches of knowledge in which each excels.”

According to Varro, *grallator* derives from *gradus magnus*, “a great stride” (ibid., bk. II, p. 70; Varro, bk. VI, [Col. 0697C] *On the Latin Language*, p. 83). Festus, however, says: “*Grallatores* were pantomimes who, in order to imitate Aegipans in their dancing, attached poles fitted with little forks and, standing upon them, walked in imitation of the legs of that race, especially because of the difficulty of maintaining their balance. Plautus: ‘You would surpass in running both deer and the *grallator* in his stride’” (Festus, under *GRALLATORES*). This verse of Plautus is taken from his *Poenulus*, act III, scene 1. See also Nonius Marcellus, *On the Properties of Words*, ch. 2, under *Grallatores*.

A *hierophant*, Greek ἱεροφάντης, is one who taught sacred rites and ceremonies, and was the chief priest of the rites (Arnob., bk. V, p. 174).

“The duty of honor” (*honorationis officium*), that is, of honor and reverence [Col. 0697D] (ibid., bk. VII, p. 221).

*Jecusculum* is the diminutive of *jecur*, “liver.” Pliny also uses this noun: “It is said,” he says, “that the lobes of the little livers of mice correspond during the month to the number of the moon.” Earlier Cicero had said: “The little livers of mice are said to increase at midwinter” (ibid., bk. IV, p. 134; Pliny, bk. II, ch. 37, p. 571; Cicero, bk. II, *On Divination*, p. 283).

*Immoderatum* means without measure or end—that is, measureless and infinite (Arnob., bk. II, p. 97). Accordingly, Cicero translated a certain verse of Euripides (Cicero, bk. II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 223) into Latin thus:

> You see the ether aloft, outspread and measureless.

[Col. 0698A] Arnobius wrote *inequitare* more than once in the sense of harassing and pursuing.

Arnobius says “with winding inflections” (*inflexibus flexuosis*) (bk. II, p. 57), that is, by the turnings of a road, or by sinuous and curving reversals.

“Jupiter offering the fillet to elicit pity” (ibid., bk. V, p. 172; Varro, bk. VI, *On the Latin Language*, p. 76): that is, woolen coverings, as Varro and others teach, with which either his mother was to be adorned or, rather, his crime concealed. Examine the passage, and you will form your own judgment on the matter.

An *institor* was a person placed in charge of commerce and business (Arnob., bk. II, pp. 66 and 70). For Ovid sang:

> A loosely belted shopkeeper will come to the mistress eager to buy;  
> While you sit there, he will display his wares.  
> (Ovid, bk. I, *Art of Love*, line 425)

[Col. 0698B] Barbers, innkeepers, and cooks were also called *institores*, as some have observed on this verse of Martial:

> The reckless shopkeeper had appropriated the whole city,  
> And within his boundary no boundary remained.  
> (Martial, bk. VII, epigram 60)

Juvenal, however:

> A dealer in winter coverlets and snow-white Cadurcian cloth.  
> (Juvenal, satire 7, near the end)

On this verse, see the observations of the various commentators.

*Interibilis* means liable to destruction and mortal (Arnob., bk. II, p. 65).

*Isicia*, or *insicia*, says Varro, derives from the fact that the meat is cut up (*insecta caro*), as it is in the Hymn of the Salii; what in entrails [Col. 0698C] is now called the *prosectum*, the cut-off portion (ibid., p. 73; Varro, bk. IV, *On the Latin Language*, p. 28). Macrobius also informs us that *insicium* is derived from “cutting up” (*insectio*): “through the loss,” he says, “of a letter, it afterward acquired the name it now has” (Macrob., bk. VII, *Saturnalia*, ch. 8). Isidore, however, gave a different etymology for this noun in these words: “They call a certain fish *isox*, from which *isicia* were first made; and although they may be made from another kind of fish, the original fish nevertheless gave them their name” (Isidore, bk. XX, *Origins*, ch. 1). Lampridius further relates that Elagabalus was the first to make *insicia* from fish, oysters, and other similar shellfish. Apicius describes several kinds of *insicia* and the method of preparing them. See Casaubon on the books of Athenaeus, and the observations of the various commentators on the cited passage of Apicius [Col. 0698D] (Lampridius, *Life of Elagabalus*; Apicius, bk. II, *On the Culinary Art*, ch. 1; Casaubon on Athenaeus, bk. IX, ch. 5, p. 651).

Those who have large lips are called *labeones*. Pliny says: “From the lips (*labra*) some are called *Brocchi*, others *labeones*” (Arnob., bk. III, p. 108; Pliny, bk. XI, *Natural History*, ch. 37, p. 353).

*Lacernula* is undoubtedly derived from the noun *lacerna*. A *lacerna* was a cheaper and more common garment and, as Isidore says, “a fringed cloak which in ancient times only soldiers used. Hence, in distinguishing the military from the urban crowd, they called the latter toga-clad and the former *lacerna*-clad. *Lacernae* were so called as though the ends of their fringes had been cut off and were not as loose as those of hooded cloaks” [Col. 0699A] (Arnob., bk. II, p. 56; Isidore, bk. XIX, *Origins*, ch. 24). The noun is frequently used by various writers, particularly those who wrote about clothing.

A *laena*, Varro observes, is so called because it contains much wool (*lana*); for it is like two togas. As the very ancient *ricinium* of women was double, so was this garment of men (Arnob., bk. II, pp. 56 and 59; Varro, bk. VI, *On the Latin Language*, p. 33; Festus, under *LAENAE*). Festus adds that some handed down that it was so called in Etruscan, and others that it was called χλαῖνα in Greek. Nonius, however, says it is a military garment worn over all the rest (Nonius, ch. 13). In confirmation of his opinion, he cites the following verses of Virgil:

> And the *laena*, hanging from his shoulders,  
> Blazed with Tyrian purple.  
> (Virgil, bk. IV, *Aeneid*, line 262)

[Col. 0699B] On these verses Servius reports various opinions concerning the *laena* and its inventor. Some regard it as a doubled toga and the augural mantle in which, according to some, the filleted flamens sacrificed; others call it a circular mantle. You may read more in his commentaries.

“They pierce the lobes of their ears”—that is, the lowest parts of the ears, or their lower portions, so that they might insert gems or other objects into them (Arnob., bk. II, p. 72). See Vossius’s *Etymologicon* under *Lamina* and *Ligula*.

*Lancicula* appears to be the diminutive of *lanx* (ibid., p. 59), and therefore to mean the same as a small platter or lesser serving vessel, in which roasted or boiled meat was brought to the table. Plautus sings of a platter:

> [Col. 0699C] I must turn aside into a cookshop;  
> I shall wipe clean all the platters and drain all the ladles.  
> (Plaut., *Amphitryon*, act IV, scene 3)

When Varro discusses serving vessels, he says: “They coined *magida* or *langula*, the one from size, the other from breadth” (Varro, bk. I, *On the Latin Language*, p. 30). But if you believe Vossius, *langula* is said as though *lancula*. Consider, therefore, whether Arnobius wrote *lancula*, or whether *lancicula* was formed from it.

The Greek λαῦρα, *laura*, is correctly rendered in Latin as *vicus*, “street,” as Athenaeus notes and Casaubon sufficiently demonstrated; consult him if you please (Arnob., bk. III, p. 124; Casaubon on Athenaeus, bk. XII, ch. 10).

“The external smoothness renders the statues of the gods august through the seductive charm of their brilliance”: thus Arnobius speaks, and he calls radiance, beauty, and excellence *lenocinium*, [Col. 0699D] “seductive charm.” Cicero also speaks of “the seductive adornments of bodies”; and Suetonius, when describing the appearance of the emperor Augustus, says that it was free from all *lenocinium*, or acquired beauty (Arnob., bk. VI, p. 201; Cicero, bk. II, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 236, line 4; Suetonius, *Life of Augustus*, ch. 79).

*Lucanica* was a kind of sausage. Varro and Isidore think it was so called because it was first made in Lucania, or because soldiers learned from the Lucanians how it was made (Arnob., bk. II, p. 73; Varro, bk. IV, *On the Latin Language*, p. 28; Isidore, bk. XX, *Origins*, ch. 1). Martial wrote these verses about it:

> And Lucanian sausage with Filiscan tripe.  
> (Martial, bk. IV, epigram 46)

[Col. 0700A] And in another book:

> I, Lucanian sausage, come as the daughter of a Picene sow;  
> Hence a pleasing garland is given to snow-white porridge.  
> (Martial, bk. III, epigram 35)

On these verses some observe that Lucanian sausage was made from the minced meat of a sow born in the Picene territory. Cicero further writes to Papirius: “For formerly I used to take pleasure in your olives and Lucanian sausages” (Cicero, bk. IX, Letter 16, p. 102).

*Mantele*, *mantelium*, or *mantile* is so called from wiping the hands, as Servius notes on this verse of Virgil:

> And they bring towels with close-shorn nap.  
> (Virgil, bk. I, *Aeneid*, line 706)

Varro too had said: “*Mantelium*, as though *manuterium*, [Col. 0700B] where the hands are wiped” (Varro, bk. IV, *On the Latin Language*, p. 66). Isidore, however, while admitting that it was formerly used for this purpose, states that it is now employed to cover tables. Vossius collected more concerning it in his *Etymologicon*.

The Marsi, concerning whom see below under the word *Psylli* (Arnob., bk. II, p. 66).

The *mastruca*, or *mastruga*, was a garment of the Sardinians (ibid., p. 59), which Isidore explains thus: “A German garment made from the skins of wild beasts, concerning which Cicero says in defense of Scaurus: ‘Royal purple did not move him, since the Sardinians’ *mastruga* changed him.’ *Mastruga* is so called as though ‘monstrous,’ because those who put it on are transformed, as it were, into the appearance of wild beasts” (Cicero, Speech III, *On the Consular Provinces*, p. 509). See Turnebus, bk. X, *Adversaria*, ch. 3, and bk. XX, ch. 9.

[Col. 0700C] *Mateola* is a diminutive or, as others think, the same as *mattea*, or the Greek *mattya*, ματτύα or ματύη (Arnob., bk. VII, p. 231). It is a delicacy, or a choice selection of foods. Hence Martial:

> A rich dinner, furnished from the whole market,  
> Has been set before you, but *Mattya* alone delights you.  
> (Martial, bk. X, epigram 59)

And later:

> If any bird should compete, the thrush, in my judgment;  
> Among quadrupeds, the hare is the foremost *Mattya*.  
> (Martial, bk. XIII, epigram 92)

Read Athenaeus, bk. XIV, *Deipnosophists*, pp. 662–663.

Steeped and saturated with the unmixed draught of wisdom (Arnobius, book II, p. 47). *Meracum* is sometimes used adjectivally [Col. 0700D] and means “unmixed and pure”; sometimes substantivally, with the meaning “wine.” Pray hear Horace:

> He drove out the sickness with hellebore, and the bile with unmixed wine.  
> (Horace, book II, Epistle 2, verse 137.)

Arnobius used *micula* more than once (Arnobius, book II, p. 77, and book VII, p. 236). The noun is derived from *mica*, which signifies a tiny particle of some dry and parched substance. Thus by *micula* he means the smallest crumb or particle of a thing. In this manner, as we have now remarked rather often, he likes to use diminutive nouns.

For precisely the same reason he speaks of the *minimissimus digitus*, “the very smallest finger,” although it would have been enough for him to say *minimus*, “the smallest” (ibid., book V, pp. 260 and 266).

The *mitra*, as Servius teaches, was a curved cap [Col. 0701A] from which hung a covering adorned with pearls. It was worn by the Phrygians and Lydians, whom the Trojans imitated (ibid., book II, p. 57; Servius, on *Aeneid* IV.215 and IX.216). He adds that some regarded the *mitra* as the headgear of prostitutes and attributed it to persons charged with effeminacy. It was, however, a covering worn by Roman women, as is clear from these words of Pliny: “Polygnotus of Thasos was the first to paint women in shining garments and to cover their heads with multicolored *mitrae*.” Isidore, however, writes: “The *mitra* is a Phrygian cap protecting the head, like the head-ornament of women consecrated to religion. But the cap belongs to men, whereas the *mitra* belongs to women” (Pliny, book XXV of the *Natural History*, ch. 9, p. 197; Isidore, book XIX of the *Origins*, ch. 31).

Turnebus [Col. 0701B] and Vossius conjecture that Arnobius calls a *muccinium* the object with which we wipe away mucus, that is, the moisture of the nostrils (Arnobius, book II, p. 59; Turnebus, book XXIII of the *Adversaria*, ch. 14; Vossius, in the *Etymologicon*).

Cato teaches that *mustacium*, or *mustaceum*, is made from fine wheat flour moistened with must, anise, cumin, fat, cheese, and shavings from laurel twigs (Arnobius, book II, p. 59; Cato, *On Agriculture*, ch. 121). Juvenal sings:

> Nor is there any reason for you to waste the dinner and the *mustacea*.  
> (Juvenal, Satire 6, verse 201.)

On this verse the scholiast noted: “Sweet foods moistened with must, which were customarily served at the end of the banquet at wedding feasts.” See Erasmus, *Adages*, chiliad 4, century 9, adage 87, pp. 942 and 1215.

From *nasus*, “nose,” Arnobius calls those who, as he puts it, have “bursting nostrils,” or nostrils that make a sound, *nasicae* [Col. 0701C] (Arnobius, book III, p. 108, and book VI, p. 196).

Our author speaks of “the family of the *Nebridae*” when discussing the Eleusinian mysteries (ibid., book V, p. 185). Some think that *Nebridae* is a proper name. Others believe that Arnobius designated by this name a certain Athenian family, but that he was mistaken in doing so. Yet it seems to us that he does not stray altogether from the truth who says that Arnobius called by this very name those persons—or perhaps their priests—who celebrated the rites of Ceres and Bacchus. For they were clothed in the skin of a fawn or deer, called νεβρίς (*nebris*) in Greek. Hence Clement of Alexandria, from whom we have shown that Arnobius took many things, wrote in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*:

> ἧκε, ὦ παράπληξ, μὴ θύρσῳ σκηριπτόμενος, μὴ κιττῷ ἀναδούμενος, ῥίψον [Col. 0791D] τὴν μίτραν, ῥίψον τὴν νεβρίδα, σωφρόνισσον.  
> Come, madman, not leaning upon a thyrsus and not crowned with ivy; cast away the *mitra*, cast away the *nebris*, and become sober and self-controlled.  
> (Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 74.)

Statius, moreover, sang:

> Do you now behold the rites of Cadmus,  
> or did you suppose that Bacchus would drive ravenous mothers to crime,  
> and that they would bear fawnskins and fragile thyrsi  
> to an unwarlike din?  
> (Statius, book II of the *Thebaid*, shortly before the end.)

And elsewhere:

> Why have you purchased unwarlike thyrsi and cymbals  
> in the midst of cities, and brought hither Bacchic hides and *mitrae*,  
> and variegated fawnskins sprinkled with gold?  
> (Ibid., book I of the *Achilleid*, p. 234.)

[Col. 0702A] Arnobius says, “Let the whole sky be shut in by the cloudiness of the overflowing vapors,” that is, by the abundant fumes of burnt incense, by which the whole sky—or rather the whole air—is enclosed and covered as though by a cloud (Arnobius, book VII, p. 234).

Arnobius used the phrase “to set up nesting places” (*nidamenta ponere*) (ibid., book VI, p. 202), employing, that is, a Plautine word:

> Today he will heap up a thousand nesting places in the stocks.  
> (Plautus, *Rudens*, act III, scene 6.)

This word signifies a place where birds nest.

*Nitedula*; in the royal manuscript *Nitetula*, but incorrectly (Arnobius, book II, p. 75). The *nitedula*, or *nitella*, is in fact a field mouse, thought to be what in French is called a *mulot*. Hence Cicero says: “This too was the fate of the state: that the *nitedula* [Col. 0702B] dragged out of those little thorn-bushes should attempt to gnaw away the Republic” (Cicero, Speech 32, *For Publius Sestius*, p. 471). Servius thinks that Virgil calls it a “tiny mouse” (Servius, on book I of Virgil’s *Georgics*, p. 75). See Pliny, book VIII of the *Natural History*, ch. 58, p. 247; Gesner; and others.

Our author wrote *nominaliter* and *nominitare* in place of *nominatim*, “by name,” and *nominare*, “to name” (Arnobius, book II, p. 80, and book VII, p. 251).

He also uses *obsolefacere* in the sense of abolishing, destroying, removing from existence, and obliterating (ibid., book V, p. 160).

By “allegorical coverings” (*obtentiones allegoricae*) he means mystical and allegorical coverings and wrappings of words, or things that are concealed beneath allegories (ibid., p. 181).

We do indeed read *panchristiarii* in our author [Col. 0702C], but we suspect that an error lies beneath it (ibid., book IX, p. 70), arising from the copyist’s customary incompetence, which we have very frequently noted. We shall therefore readily subscribe to the opinion of those who think that it should be corrected to *panchrestarii*, rather than to *crustarii*, as Turnebus thought. The *panchrestarii* were so called because they prepared *panchrestum*, mentioned by Cicero and Pliny—that is, an exceedingly beneficial ointment, highly useful for curing many diseases (Turnebus, book XIII of the *Adversaria*, ch. 14; Cicero, Speech 3, *Against Verres*, p. 145; Pliny, book XXVI of the *Natural History*, ch. 20, p. 326). It matters little that Arnobius had previously mentioned perfumers. For it is not unusual for him either to repeat the same things or to follow no order in his enumerations.

[Col. 0702D] “A *papula*,” says Isidore, “is a very small raised area of skin, circumscribed by redness; and it is therefore called *papula*, as though *pupula sirimpia*” [uncertain corrupted reading]. Like our author, however, he distinguished it from a *pustula*, which he defined as follows: “A *pustula* is a swollen accumulation, as it were, on the surface of the body” (Arnobius, book I, p. 31; Isidore, book IV of the *Origins*, ch. 8). Virgil, however, spoke of “burning *pupulae*,” which Servius declares to be carbuncles. Read Celsus and other physicians (Virgil, book III of the *Georgics*, at the end; Celsus, book III, at the end).

Arnobius uses *partiliter* and *partilitas* in the sense of “partly” and “in some part” (Arnobius, book I, pp. 5 and 8; book I [apparently an OCR error], pp. 192 and 204).

He also used *passibilitas*, “capacity for suffering,” and *passivum*, “that which can undergo something.” Hence *passio* too signifies that which something suffers and endures, or endurance itself (ibid., book II, p. 61 ff.).

“I should like to see Liber [Bacchus] *peniculantem, decurtantem cantherios*” [Col. 0703A] (ibid., book V, p. 163): these are Arnobius’ words, but some have rightly regarded them as corrupt. Some conjecture that *peniculamenta* should be restored; others, *penicula decurtantem cantheriorum*. Martinius, who favors the former reading, thinks that *peniculamentum* signifies a fastening made from the bristles of geldings; Nonius, however, says that it means the hem of a garment, or the part of it that touches the ground (Nonius, ch. 2, under the word *PENICULAMENTUM*). But these explanations contribute little to Arnobius’ purpose, unless Bacchus himself is said to have tended the horses by which he was carried from heaven to earth. [Col. 0703B] Arnobius could indeed have reproached the pagans with this in a by no means witless irony; but without the aid of a more accurate manuscript we dare determine nothing with certainty.

For Arnobius, *pestilitas* is the same as *pestis*, “plague”; here, as often elsewhere, as we have observed, he imitated Lucretius in employing this word (Arnobius, book VII, p. 248; Lucretius, book VI, verses 1096, 1123, 1130).

Those who either decorate garments or weave designs into them are called *Phrygiones*. If you desire witnesses, we shall cite Servius, Nonius, and Isidore (Arnobius, book II, p. 70; Servius, on *Aeneid* III.484; Nonius, ch. 1, no. 10; Isidore, book XIX of the *Origins*, ch. 22). To these we shall further add Pliny, whose words are: “It is clear that embroidered garments [Col. 0703C] existed even in Homer’s time, from which triumphal robes took their origin. Or the Phrygians invented the making of them, and they were therefore called *Phrygionicae*” (Pliny, book VIII of the *Natural History*, ch. 48, p. 230). Plautus, however, often used the noun *Phrygio*:

> That cloak which you gave me some time ago—take it to the embroiderer,  
> so that it may be repaired and the embellishments I want may be added.  
> (Plautus, *Menaechmi*, act I, scene 8, and act III, scene 2.)

And elsewhere:

> There stand the fuller, the embroiderer, the goldsmith, and the wool-worker.  
> (Ibid., *Aulularia*, p. 176.)

Arnobius used “the fatty portions of the victims” (*pinguitiae hostiarum*) (book VII, p. 226) for their fat.

*Plani* are the same as sycophants, deceivers, seducers, [Col. 0703D] and impostors (ibid., book II, p. 66). Hear, if you please, Aulus Gellius: “Marcus Cicero left *planus* written in the sense of ‘sycophant’ in the speech he delivered for Cluentius” (Gellius, book XVI of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 7, p. 880; Cicero, Speech 14, p. 264). And indeed it is read in that speech. Horace too sang:

> Though mocked more than once, he is still concerned to raise  
> from the crossroads a *planus* with a broken leg.  
> (Horace, book I, Epistle 17, verse 52 ff.)

Pliny likewise uses the same word with the same meaning (Pliny, book XXXV of the *Natural History*, ch. 10, p. 210).

Arnobius says that the bodies of those who had been recalled from death to life by Christ’s divine grace were freed from the wrappings of the embalmers—that is, were loosened and released by the work of those who [Col. 0704A] washed dead bodies and tended them, from their burial bands and strips of cloth (Arnobius, book II, p. 26). Arnobius calls these bands *volumina*, “wrappings,” because the dead body was wrapped in them.

According to Festus, a *polubrum* is a vessel that we call a basin, or, as Nonius Marcellus says, a *trulleum* (ibid., book II, p. 59; Festus, under the word *POLUBRUM*; Nonius, ch. 19, no. 11). Consult them if you wish, and Turnebus, book XXVIII of the *Adversaria*, ch. 7.

*Porrina* is a kind of leek-like vegetable, and Arnobius does not appear to use it in any other sense (Arnobius, book II, p. 85, and book VII, p. 223). It is called “cut leek” (*porrum sectivum*) because, they say, it is cut repeatedly for use in the kitchen. Juvenal, however, wrote:

> And to enclose the counted fibers of the cut leek.  
> [Col. 0704B] (Juvenal, Satire 14, verse 133.)

See Pliny, book XIX, ch. 6, p. 595 ff., and Columella, book I of *On Agriculture*, ch. 3, and you will understand how the “cut leek” differs from the headed leek.

The “sunset behind the back” (*posterganeus ab sole occasus*) means that the rising sun is behind the person who faces west (Arnobius, book IV, p. 130).

Arnobius calls a governorship, or the office of a governor, overseer, or prefect, *praesidatus* (ibid., book III, p. 114, and book IV, p. 130).

*Priva*: a single thing, one and only. For, as Festus teaches: “The ancients used *privi* and *privae* for individual persons or things; for which reason those things that belong to each individual are also called *privata*” (Festus, under the word *PRIVUS*). Nonius indeed proves this by certain verses of Lucilius [Col. 0704C] (Nonius, ch. 2, no. 69), and by these lines of Lucretius:

> But if perhaps you believe that souls insinuate themselves from without  
> into worms and can enter their bodies one by one.  
> (Lucretius, book III, verse 722 ff.)

He employed that noun not only there but elsewhere as well (ibid., verse 390, and book IV, verses 261 and 570).

Aulus Gellius says that *protelarii*, or *proletarii*, was the name given to those who were the most insignificant and poorest among the Roman plebs and registered no more than five hundred thousand asses in the census (Arnobius, book II, p. 63). Paul and Nonius Marcellus, however, say that they were called *proletarii* because they provided only offspring (*proles*) for the Republic. Hence Augustine writes: “The proletarians received this name because, being unable through poverty to serve as soldiers, they devoted themselves to begetting offspring.” [Col. 0704D] Accordingly, “proletarian speech” in Plautus means cheap and plebeian speech (Paul, under the word *PROLETARIUM*; Nonius, ch. 1, no. 312, and ch. 2, no. 666; Augustine, book III of *The City of God*, ch. 17, p. 75; Plautus, *Miles Gloriosus*, act III, scene 1).

Where Arnobius mentions the Psylli and the Marsi (Arnobius, book II, p. 66), his text is corrupt. In its latest edition it is presented thus: “Against harmful blows and the venomous bites of snakes we often seek remedies and protect ourselves with plates, while Psylli and Marsi sell them, together with other peddlers and impostors” (*protegimus nos laminis, Psyllis Marsis vendentibus aliisque institoribus et planis*). The royal manuscript has *lamminis phyllis* for *laminis, Psyllis*, and *institutoribus* for *institoribus*. Theodorus [Col. 0705A] Canterus thinks the passage should be corrected thus: “We protect ourselves by the lips of Psylli or by the teeth of Marsi” (*Protegimus nos labiis Psyllis, Marsisve dentibus*). This would give excellent sense if *Psyllorum et Marsorum*, “of the Psylli and Marsi,” were read. Salmasius, however, wishes to emend it to *Psyllis labinis, Marsisve dentibus*, with precisely the same meaning. For those into whom serpents had infused deadly poison by biting were healed by the Psylli and Marsi through sucking.

There seems to be no room whatever for doubt that Arnobius is speaking of these peoples, the Psylli of Africa and the Marsi of Italy, who actually treated the venomous bites of serpents. For we read the following tradition in Pliny’s writings:

> Crates of Pergamum relates that on the Hellespont around Parium there was a race of men whom he calls Ophiogenes, who were accustomed to relieve snakebites by touch and, by laying on a hand, to draw the poison out of the body. Varro says that even now [Col. 0705B] there are a few there whose saliva remedies snakebites. A similar people in Africa were the Psylli, as Agatharchides writes, named after King Psyllus, whose tomb is in the region of the Greater Syrtes. Their bodies contained an inborn poison fatal to serpents, by whose odor they put them to sleep.... A similar race of Marsi survives in Italy; they preserve the tradition that they sprang from Circe’s son and therefore possess that natural power.  
> (Pliny, book VII of the *Natural History*, ch. 2, pp. 7–8.)

In another book he again reports the same thing and says that these peoples relieve those struck by serpents by mere touch or by slight suction (ibid., book XXVIII, ch. 3, p. 566). Hence elsewhere he calls the Marsi “tamers of serpents” (ibid., book XXV, ch. 2, p. 376). Finally, in yet another passage he records this same power of both the Marsi and Psylli (book XXI, ch. 13, p. 134).

[Col. 0705C] Aelian relates that a snakebite is cured by a Psyllus if he merely spits saliva upon it (Aelian, book I *On Animals*, ch. 57); or, when the body has been too deeply imbued with poison, if he gives the wounded person to drink a large quantity of water that has long been swished about in his mouth and between his teeth and then poured onto a mirror, after he has washed his hands with it. Finally, if the poison’s force gains still greater strength, the naked Psyllus lies upon the naked patient and heals him with his own body. Others further relate that the Psylli sucked out the poison with their own mouths and dulled serpents by incantations. Hence Lucan sang:

> A single people inhabits the earth unharmed  
> by the savage bite of serpents: the Marmarid Psylli,  
> whose speech is equal in power to potent herbs. Their very blood is safe  
> and can admit no poison, even when the chant  
> [Col. 0705D] has ceased: the nature of the region ordained that they,  
> dwelling among serpents, should be immune.  
> (Lucan, book IX, verse 891 ff.)

See Plutarch, *Life of Cato the Younger*, vol. I, p. 727; Strabo, book XVII of the *Geography*, p. 814; Suetonius, *Life of Octavian Caesar*, ch. 17; Solinus, ch. 27, p. 52; Jerome, preface to the prophet Joel addressed to Pammachius. Finally, concerning the Marsi, these verses of Lucilius are cited:

> Now let him be torn apart through the middle, just as the Marsian tears  
> snakes apart with a chant, when he has stretched every vein.  
> (Lucilius, book X of the *Satires*.)

These passages plainly enough show that Arnobius [Col. 0706A] was speaking, as we have said, about these Psylli and Marsi. But who would dare assert, without some complete and uncorrupted manuscript, whether the words *laminis* and *vendentibus* are genuine, or what should be substituted for them? Yet that *institoribus* was correctly restored in place of *institutoribus* can be inferred from what we said above under the noun *institor*.

*Pulticula*, that is, a small or very small porridge; this noun is employed by Pliny and Columella (Arnobius, book VI, p. 242; Pliny, book XXVI of the *Natural History*, ch. 8, p. 460; Columella, book VIII of *On Agriculture*, ch. 12).

*Pupulus* is a diminutive of the noun *pupus* and signifies a very small boy (Arnobius, book VII, p. 215). Catullus used it in this sense in an address to Cato:

> Just now I caught a girl’s little boy  
> thrusting.  
> [Col. 0706B] (Catullus, Epigram 57.)

Sometimes, however, it is used for an image with which infants and children commonly play, called in French a *poupée*, “doll.” Arnobius employs it in this sense.

*Querquera* is a fever attended by intense cold and trembling (Arnobius, book I, p. 28). Hence Aulus Gellius says: “Do you perhaps think that *morbus* here means a serious illness accompanied by a violent fever and *querquera*?” (Gellius, book XX of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 1, p. 1096). Read, if you wish, the various annotations on this passage, as well as Festus and Paul under the word *Querquera*.

“The streams of oil grow rancid” (*rancescere olearum fluenta*), that is, they become foul through rancidity and putrefaction (Arnobius, book I, p. 12).

“*Radius*, codex, book,” says Arnobius (ibid., book II, p. 59). *Radius* has several meanings, but [Col. 0706C] it is sometimes used for the instrument with which geometers and others draw lines. Virgil used it in this sense:

> Who with the rod traced out the whole world for the nations.  
> (Virgil, Eclogue 3, verse 41.)

And again elsewhere:

> The courses of heaven  
> they will trace with the rod, and name the rising constellations.  
> (And book VI, verse 844.)

Nevertheless, because Arnobius joined *radius* with “codex” and “book,” one might perhaps reasonably suspect that by this noun he designated the stylus with which the ancients customarily wrote.

According to Festus, *redivia*, or *reduvia*, and *reduvium* is the name given to the condition in which the skin comes loose around the nails (Arnobius, book I, p. 31). We read that Pliny used this word rather often [Col. 0706D] (Pliny, book VII of the *Natural History*, ch. 19, p. 38), and Cicero somewhere as well (Cicero, speech *For Sextus Roscius*, p. 34, line 2). Read Turnebus, book XVII of the *Adversaria*, ch. 8.

Our author calls *repetentia priorum*, “the recurrence of former things,” the act of repeating and resuming them (Arnobius, book II, p. 62). Indeed, he appears to have drawn this from the following verse of Lucretius:

> Once the recurrence of our being has been interrupted.  
> (Lucretius, book III, verse 868.)

We know, to be sure, that the editions already published read *repentia nostri*, “the creeping things of us”; but it may be conjectured, not altogether absurdly, that Lucretius wrote it in the manner we have stated, because Arnobius said in the same place: “Life was delivered to them for use, not as property” (*Usu est illis vita non mancipio tradita*). [Col. 0707A] For who would not readily persuade himself that Arnobius took this from the following other verse of Lucretius?

> Life is given to no one as property, but to all for use.  
> (Lucretius, same book, verse 984.)

Our author calls *runcina* the tool with which craftsmen smooth rough wood, called *rabot* in French, “a plane.” Pliny used it with the same meaning when he wrote somewhere of the fir: “Always rolling itself in a circular course, once pruned, under the rapid strokes of planes” (Arnobius, book VI, p. 200; Pliny, book XVI of the *Natural History*, ch. 42, p. 304).

“Let them derive their lineage from ballasted blood” (*saburato sanguine genus ducant*) is read in some editions of Arnobius (Arnobius, book V, p. 164); in the royal manuscript, “from blood *saburatio*,” but undoubtedly through a copyist’s error. Therefore the latest [Col. 0707B] edition printed “from more highly flavored blood” (*ex sanguine saporatiore*). But who does not see that this was emended by conjecture alone and ought to have been established by some evidence? The passage concerns the blood flowing from the amputated genitals of Acdestis, from which, according to the myth, the pomegranate arose. Arnobius therefore says that the fruits of that tree are moist and vinous because they derive their kind from that “more highly flavored,” or “flavored,” blood—that is, from blood that was tasty or imbued with flavor.

We are well aware that Plautus used the word *saburratae* when he sang:

> When we have been ballasted.  
> (Plautus, *Cistellaria*, act I, scene 2.)

That is, as the commentator notes, “laden with food and drink.” The metaphor comes from cargo ships: when entirely empty of cargo, they are loaded with ballast so that they may be firmer and more stable against storms [Col. 0707C] and waves. What then, someone may ask, if the text of Arnobius originally read that “the fruits, ballasted by blood”—that is, filled and laden with it—“derive their kind from it”? Yet this correction, even when explained in this way, will perhaps not commend itself to many. We therefore wish nothing to be altered without the authority of another manuscript or more certain evidence.

Arnobius said that the infant placed in its mother’s womb was “among the most obscene jars of *saccatum*” (Arnobius, book II, p. 69). But, as Isidore observes, “*saccatum* is a liquid made from water mixed with wine lees and strained through a sack” (Isidore, book V of the *Origins*, ch. 3). Yet Lucretius uses this word for urine. For he sings of dreaming boys:

[Col. 0707D]

> They believe that they lift their clothing  
> to pour out the *saccatum* moisture of their entire body.  
> (Lucretius, book IV, verse 1021 ff.)

*Seriae*, moreover, signify certain vessels in which water was kept. Hence Terence:

> I left all the casks, all the jars behind.  
> (Terence, *Heauton Timorumenos*, act III, scene 1.)

Furthermore, to demonstrate more plainly the lowly and abject condition of humanity, Arnobius wrote that, when a human being is formed in its mother’s womb, it lives amid phlegm and blood, “among these wineskins of excrement and the most obscene jars of *saccatum* moisture”—with “moisture” understood. Thus indeed it pleased our author to describe the womb of a pregnant woman.

Those who, as Elmenhorst observes after Papias, [Col. 0708A] made salt were surnamed *salinatores* (Arnobius, book II, p. 70); and he confirms this with an ancient inscription. Yet this name was also given to those who had imposed a new tax, as Livy puts it, upon the salt ration (*annona salaria*) (Livy, book XXVII, ch. 37). Arnobius appears to employ it in the former rather than the latter sense, although either sense seems to suit his purpose.

Arnobius calls the very smallest forms of knowledge and acquaintance with the arts *scientiolae*, “little bits of knowledge” (Arnobius, book II, p. 56). For, as we have remarked more than once, he is especially fond of using diminutive words.

“Lydia calls *scituli*,” says Arnobius (ibid., book V, p. 159), those, namely, who are nourished with goat’s milk. He later himself calls them “pretty little boys” (*scituli pusiones*) (ibid., p. 179). [Col. 0708B] There will perhaps be some who suppose that Arnobius wrote *scitali*, Greek σκίταλοι (*skitaloi*), a name applied to worthless and wicked men; for, as the *Suda* observes, Sciton was a fuller, a worthless man who was ridiculed by the comic poets because of his wickedness. Aristophanes writes in the *Knights*:

> Ἄγε δὴ σκίταλοί τε, καὶ φένακες, ἦν δ᾽ ἐγώ,  
> Βερέσχεθοί τε καὶ κόβαλοι, καὶ μόθωνες,  
> Ἀγορά τε ἐν ᾗ παῖς ὢν, ἐπαιδεύθην ἐγώ,  
> Νῦν μοι θράσος, καὶ γλῶτταν εὔπορον δότε,  
> Φωνήν τ᾽ ἀναιδῆ.  
>
> Come then, you *skitaloi* (“worthless fellows”) and deceivers, said I,  
> you rascals, rogues, and blackguards,  
> and you marketplace in which I was trained as a boy:  
> now grant me boldness, a fluent tongue,  
> and a shameless voice.  
> (Aristophanes, *Knights*, p. 823, vol. II, *Greek Poets*.)

These verses are indeed found in the cited comedy of Aristophanes [Col. 0708C]. Nevertheless, because Arnobius spoke of “pretty little boys, and adults formed with the loveliest contours,” the word *scituli*, “pretty,” should undoubtedly be retained. For Plautus sang of certain women:

> What do they look like? Pretty.  
> (Plautus, *Rudens*, act II, scene 7.)

And in this other passage:

> And both of them pretty in form and young in age.  
> (Act IV, scene 1.)

That is, of a somewhat elegant and charming appearance. Apuleius also uses this word often (Apuleius, book II of the *Metamorphoses*, pp. 19, 26, and elsewhere).

“An urbane little wit” (*scurrula urbanus*) is a diminutive of *scurra*, to which Plautus joined the adjective *urbanus*, just as Arnobius joined it to *scurrula* (Arnobius, book VII, p. 206). These [Col. 0708D] are Plautus’ verses:

> You truly are an urbane wit, the darling of the people,  
> yet you taunt me with the countryside.  
> (Plautus, *Mostellaria*, act I, scene 1, p. 521.)

And elsewhere:

> As the urbane citizens who are always about, whom they call *scurrae*.  
> (Ibid., *Trinummus*, act I, scene 2, p. 1022.)

The poet and other ancient writers called a witty and polished man, one who was in no way rustic, an “urbane *scurra*.” Arnobius similarly uses *scurrula* in this sense. Later, however, the word was employed in another and indeed contrary sense. On this matter see Turnebus, book XIX of the *Adversaria*, ch. 13; Vossius, in the *Etymologicon*; and others.

[Col. 0709A] Arnobius also uses the diminutive *securicula* for a small axe (Arnobius, book II, p. 56), as does Pliny, who somewhere reports: “An ingrafting hatchet should be at hand, with which the roots may be cut away” (Pliny, book XVIII of the *Natural History*, ch. 19, p. 493).

*Secus virile* and *secus femineum*, “the male sex” and “the female sex,” are read in our manuscript of Arnobius’ books and in several editions (Arnobius, book V, pp. 165 and 174), more correctly than the *sexus virile* found in certain others. For there the noun *secus* signifies the feature by which each sex is distinguished from the other. This meaning is supported by Festus; Martinius attempts to establish it from the testimony of Apuleius and Ammianus Marcellinus. Nonius reports that Sallust somewhere used *sexus* in the neuter gender, but others think that *secus* should be written there (Nonius, ch. 3, §198).

[Col. 0709B] The *sellularii* practiced plebeian and very lowly trades while seated (Arnobius, book III, p. 112). In this sense we read in Livy: “The common mass of craftsmen and the sedentary artisans, a class least suited for military service” (Livy, book VIII, ch. 20).

*Siliquastrum*, or *seliquastrum*; for some maintain that it is written both ways (Arnobius, book II, p. 59). “From sitting,” as Varro observes, “are named *sedes*, seat; *sedile*, bench; *sedum*; *sellae*, chairs; and *seliquastrum*.” Festus, however, says: “*Seliquastra* is the name for seats of an ancient kind, with the letter *d* changed into *l*, as also happened in *cella*, *subsellium*, and *solium*, which were no less named from sitting” (Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, p. 31; Festus, under the word *SELIQUASTRA*).

“To perish when the breathing passages”—that is, the faculties of breathing—“have been blocked” (Arnobius, book VII, p. 234). For Lucan sang:

> One cuts off the ears, another the breathing passages of the hooked nose.  
> [Col. 0709C] (Lucan, book II, verse 180.)

Statius too writes:

> It revives the breathing passages of the exhausted  
> fire and bursts turbulently upon the dreadful plains.  
> (Statius, book XII of the *Thebaid*, verse 69.)

*Spirula* is a diminutive of the noun *spira*, which has several meanings (Arnobius, book II, p. 73). First, it means the base of a column with one or two moldings; second, a kind of baked product; third, a nautical rope coiled into a circle. So Festus says (Festus, under the word *SPIRA*). Arnobius employs the noun in the second sense, [Col. 0709D] and it signifies a kind of cake, as may be gathered from Cato, who clearly explains how it should be made (Cato, *On Agriculture*, p. 77).

*Stragula* denotes either a garment or anything customarily spread over a bed, horse, or some other object. Our author uses it in the former meaning, as does Cicero in his speeches *For Sextus Roscius* and *Against Verres*, and other writers as well (Arnobius, book II, p. 58; Cicero, Speech IV, p. 34, line 45; book IV *Against Verres*, p. 170, line 3).

*Stribiligo*, or *stribligo*, comes from the Greek word στρεβλός (*streblos*), meaning “crooked, bent, twisted” (Arnobius, book III, p. 36). Among the older Latin writers, however, as Aulus Gellius says, a solecism was so called from the distortion and crooked perversity of twisted speech, as though *sterobiligo* (Gellius, book V [Col. 0710A] of the *Attic Nights*, ch. 20). Our Arnobius uses it with this same meaning.

According to Nonius, a *strophium* is a short band that restrains the maidenly swelling of the breasts, as he confirms from the testimony of Turpilius, Cicero, Plautus, and Varro (Arnobius, book II, p. 58; Nonius, ch. 14, no. 8). We may also add this verse of Catullus:

> Her milk-filled breasts not bound by a rounded breast-band.  
> (Catullus, *Argonautica*, verse 65.)

*Strophium* could also signify a garland. For Pliny, when discussing garlands, says: “The ancients used thinner ones, calling them *stropi*, whence arose *strophiola*” (Pliny, book XXI of the *Natural History*, ch. 2, p. 105). See Festus under the word *Stroppus*, and Hardouin’s notes on the cited passage of Pliny. Arnobius [Col. 0710B] employs it in the former sense.

“*Subscudes*,” says Festus, “is the name given to small boards by which planks are fastened together, because that into which they are inserted is struck from below” (Arnobius, book VI, p. 202; Festus, under the word *SUBSCUDES*). Cato used this word in book I of *On Agriculture*, ch. 18; by it, like Arnobius, he means fasteners.

“To pollute and profane the most sacred groves or holy places with substructures” (Arnobius, book VII, p. 217). Cicero used the word in the same sense:

> You Alban hills and groves, you, I say, I implore and call to witness, and you buried altars of the Albans, partners and peers of the sacred rites of the Roman people, which that man in his headlong madness overwhelmed with the monstrous masses of his substructures after cutting down and leveling the most sacred groves: then your [Col. 0710C] altars and your rites displayed their vigor, and your power prevailed—the power that he had polluted by every crime.  
> (Cicero, Speech 38, *For Milo*, p. 556 ff.)

Earlier, however, our author had said “supported by a bony substructure,” that is, upheld by bones built and placed beneath it (Arnobius, book III, p. 107).

Arnobius calls *subucula* a kind of garment worn beneath other clothing (ibid., book II, p. 56). Not only Varro and Nonius show that this is the meaning of the word, but Festus declares it manifest to everyone; he nevertheless adds that it also signifies a kind of sacrificial cake offered to the gods, made from spelt groats, oil, and honey (Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, p. 33; Nonius, ch. XIV, no. 36; Festus, under the word *SUBUCULA*). Yet it is clear that Arnobius takes it in the former sense, because he immediately [Col. 0710D] follows it with other kinds of garments.

In the royal manuscript we read *suaniminatam carmen* [an uncertain, corrupt reading] (Arnobius, book III, p. 73). But when the editors responsible for these books saw the copyist’s error, they corrected it by writing *suminatam*. If this correction is accepted, the word *suminata* is undoubtedly derived from *sumen*. Nonius Marcellus reports that the ancients used *sumen* for a woman’s breast (Nonius, ch. XV, §54). Others think that *sumen* is the part of the belly, specifically a sow’s belly, that contains the teats. Hence they say that Martial sang:

> Do you think it is not yet an udder? With the breast so full,  
> the teat overflows and swells with living milk.  
> (Martial, book III, Epigram 44.)

[Note: Col. 0710D. Another reading: “You can eat it bare.”]

[Col. 0711A] Arnobius calls that meat *suminata* which is taken from those parts of a pig’s belly, as can readily be understood from his preceding words.

Varro, cited shortly above, teaches that the *suppara* is a kind of garment worn over other clothing (Arnobius, book II, p. 56; Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, p. 28). Hence Lucan sang:

> Narrow *suppara* encircle their bared upper arms.  
> (Lucan, book II, verse 353.)

There are nevertheless some who think that *supparum* is the same as *subucula*, discussed a little above. But since our author distinguished them quite clearly, we have scarcely any doubt that he uses *supparum* in the meaning we have noted.

Arnobius calls “the *symplegmata* of mimes” their [Col. 0711B] embraces, entwining, and interlacings (Arnobius, book VII, p. 239). Martial sang:

> Let them perform—and keep silent—about which  
> entwining unites five pathic youths.  
> (Martial, book XII, Epigram 43.)

Our Arnobius also calls a girl *textricula*, using a diminutive noun (Arnobius, book V, p. 166), as though she were a very little weaver, who was weaving something with a hand not yet trained.

*Tiputa*; in the manuscript *hippula*, but incorrectly (ibid., book II, p. 84). The *tipula* is a species of worm or tiny spider with six legs, so light that it walks upon water; hence this verse of Plautus:

> Nothing has less weight than a water-strider—except a pimp’s good faith.  
> (Plautus, *Persa*, act II, scene 2.)

[Col. 0711C] The *trabea* was a garment of which there were three kinds. The first, made of purple, was consecrated to the gods (Arnobius, book II, p. 56). Another belonged to kings and was likewise purple, but had some white mixed into its color. The third was augural, with purple mixed with scarlet. It is frequently mentioned by good authors. See Suetonius’ book *On Types of Garments*, Isidore, book XIX of the *Origins*, ch. 24, and the works of others on clothing.

A *trapetum*, or *trapes*, is an olive mill (ibid., p. 59). For Virgil said:

> Winter comes; the Sicyonian berry is crushed in the olive mills.  
> (Virgil, book II of the *Georgics*, verse 519.)

On this verse Servius writes: “*Trapetis*: in olive mills; and *trapetum* is declined like *templum*.” Terentianus writes: “Seated above them, he regulates the markings upon the revolving mills.” [Col. 0711D] This meter is suited to men grinding olives. See Cato, *On Agriculture*, chs. 20 and 22, and Columella, book II of *On Agriculture*, ch. 50, and book III, ch. 2.

What a *tribula*, or *tribulum*, is (Arnobius, ibid.) is taught by the same Servius on this verse of Virgil:

> The threshing-sledges, the drags, and the harrow with its oppressive weight.  
> (Virgil, book I of the *Georgics*, verse 164.)

A *tribula*, he says, is “a kind of vehicle toothed on every side, with which grain is threshed; it was used especially in Africa.” Consult, if you wish, Varro, book IV of *On the Latin Language*, p. 6, and book I of *On Agriculture*, ch. 52; Columella, book I of *On Agriculture*, ch. 6, and book II, ch. 21.

[Col. 0712A] According to Isidore, *trilices vestes*, “triple-woven garments,” were so called from three sets of warp threads (*licia*) (Arnobius, book IV, p. 144). For we read in Virgil:

> A cuirass joined with hooks and triple-woven with gold.  
> (Virgil, book III of the *Aeneid*, verse 467.)

And in another book:

For him, [a cuirass] interlinked with smooth hooks and triple-woven with gold. (Book V, verse 259.) On the former verse, Servius says that *trilicem* means “woven in a threefold interlacing.”

Arnobius mentions the *trulla* and *trulleum* (Arnob., Book II, pp. 56 and 59). The *trulla*, however, as we learn from Varro, denotes both a large spoon or ladle and a wine vessel (Varr., Book IV, *On the Latin Language*, p. 29). He writes as follows: “*Trulla*,” he says, “from its resemblance [Col. 0712B] to a *trua*: because the latter is large and this one small, as though *truula*. Hence the Greeks have τρυβλίον (*tryblion*, bowl), and we have *trulla*. *Truae* are vessels that pour water from the kitchen into the washroom. *Trua* is so called because the water flies across (*travolat*) through it; from the same word *trulleum* is named. For it is similar in shape, except that it has a broader receptacle for water and its handle is not hollow—unless a wine-ladle is in question.” The word is taken in the former sense by Pliny, and in the latter by Cicero, where he inveighs against Verres as follows (Plin., Book XXXVII, *Natural History*, ch. 2, p. 362; Cic., Fourth Oration against Verres, p. 172): “There was also a wine vessel made from a single very large gemstone, hollowed out in the form of a ladle, with a golden handle. . . . He also sends and asks for the jeweled ladle, saying that he wishes to examine it more carefully; it too is sent to him.” Juvenal, however, signifies by the following verse that it is a drinking vessel:

[Col. 0712C] If the golden ladle gave a crack when its base was turned upward.  
(Juvenal, Satire 3, verse 108.)

And Horace likewise:

One accustomed to drink Veientine wine on feast days  
from a Campanian ladle, and sour wine on ordinary days.  
(Horace, Book II, Satire 3, verse 143 ff.)

See also Plautus, already cited by us above (*supra*, under the word LANCILULA), as well as Martial, Book IX, Epigram 98; Pliny, Book XXXIV, *Natural History*, ch. 2, p. 91; Cato, *On Agriculture*, chs. 10 and 11; and the annotations on Juvenal’s verse. Finally, *trulla* is the familiar tool of a mason; but Arnobius does not employ it in that sense (Arnob., Book II, p. 73).

If Fulgentius is to be believed, *tuceta* means royal dishes (Fulgent., *On Ancient Speech*, no. 4). Callimachus in the *Pisaean Poems*:

[Col. 0712D] The *tuceta* are fragrant with an ambrosial flavor.

But Johannes Britannicus, commenting on this verse of Persius:

Large platters and thick *tuceta*.  
(Persius, Satire 2, verse 40.)

observes that *tuceta* is a kind of sausage made from pork cut into small pieces. Nor will it be difficult for us to believe that Arnobius employs the term in this sense. Apuleius, moreover, said somewhere: “Whatever master was secretly preparing chopped mistletoe and flesh gathered piece by piece as poisonous feed—and indeed for my nostrils—I was already divining for myself a most exceedingly delightful *tucetum*.” Elsewhere, however: “He seasons fresh dishes with *tuceta*, the table being abundantly furnished” (Apul., Book II, *Metamorphoses*, p. 20).

[Col. 0713A] In the text of Arnobius we read “weavers of winnowing baskets and *sirpiae*” (Arnob., Book II, p. 70). Yet no one has made even the slightest annotation on these words of his, doubtless because the passage seemed too difficult, corrupt, and incapable of emendation. What, then, if someone, attempting to apply a healing hand to it, were to say that *sirpearum* should be read instead of *sirpiarum*? For in Varro we find written *sirpeas stercorarias*, “dung-carrying *sirpeae*,” and afterward *sirpeam stercorariam*, “a dung-carrying *sirpea*” (Varro, *On Agriculture*, chs. 10 and 11). Elsewhere he explains more clearly what a *sirpea* is: “A *sirpea*,” he says, “is something packed with rods, that is, woven together by binding, in which dung or some other thing is carried away.” A *sirpea*, therefore, is a kind of basket or hamper intended for carrying away dung and other things. Ovid, however, takes the word in another sense where he wrote:

[Col. 0713B] Without delay, the guests, their limbs reeling from strong wine,  
begin to move; their unsteady feet both stand and give way.  
But their host says, “Depart,” and lifted the lingering men  
onto a cart; on the cart was a broad *sirpea*.  
(Ovid, Book VI, *Fasti*, § 12.)

That is, a wagon or vehicle covered with a mat or coarse matting—in French, *natte*, “mat.” But if in Arnobius’s text you read *venditores*, “sellers,” instead of *vitores*, with only three letters either abbreviated or omitted through the copyist’s carelessness, Arnobius’s meaning will be plain and evident. For it fits his argument perfectly if sellers of winnowing baskets and *sirpeae* are mentioned there. Nor should you be surprised that three letters were omitted through an ignorant copyist’s drowsiness or incompetence. For on the same page, instead of *mentiri*, “to lie,” he had written merely *iri*, “to go.” We nevertheless leave these conjectures to the judgment of others.

[Col. 0713C] Arnobius said *vectitatus curru quadrijugo*, “conveyed in a four-horse chariot,” instead of *vectus* or *vectatus*, “carried” (Arnob., Book III, p. 183).

A *verrucula collis*, “little wart of a hill,” is more than once used by him to mean a more elevated and higher place on a particular hill (ibid., Book II, p. 77, and Book V, p. 156). Thus Cato, according to Aulus Gellius, calls a *verrula* an elevated and rugged place (Gell., Book VIII, *Attic Nights*, ch. 7, p. 224). But our author, according to his custom, employs a diminutive noun.

*Versuras in hujusmodi cogi* means “to be turned, transferred, and brought into meanings, interpretations, and explanations of stories or histories of this kind” (Arnob., Book V, p. 187).

To *vindicias justas dare* is to grant to someone who is disputing with another about [Col. 0713D] some matter his right and what belongs to him—to vindicate and affirm it [Col. 0714A] (ibid., Book IV, p. 128). See Festus and the authors cited by him, as well as Gellius and the various scholars’ observations upon him (Fest., under the word VINDICIAE; Gell., Book XX, ch. 10).

“Wine is suddenly changed *in perfidiam acoris*, into the treachery of sourness”; that is, wine becomes acidic contrary to its own nature (Arnob., Book I, p. 12).

Our author speaks of foul, whitish *vitiligines*, patches of vitiligo (ibid., pp. 26, 28, and 30). “But *vitiligo*,” says Festus, “is a white spot on a human body, which the Greeks call ἄλφος (*alphos*, a white skin-patch), from which we derive *album*, ‘white’; or it is so called from *vitium*, ‘blemish,’ even if it does no harm; or from a calf (*vitulus*), because of the whiteness of the membrane in which it is wrapped at birth. Lucilius: ‘This vitiligo is hateful to me.’ ‘It does not hurt,’ he says” (Fest., under the word VITILIGO). In Seneca, moreover, we read the following: [Col. 0714B] “It has been believed that certain waters cause scabies on the body, others vitiligo and an ugly mottling of white” (Senec., Book III, *Natural Questions*, ch. 26, p. 434). Some, however, think this vitiligo to be leprosy.

*Ulpicum* is a larger kind of garlic which the Greeks, as Columella reports, call ἀφροσκόδορον (*aphroskodoron*); some call it Punic or Cyprian garlic, as Pliny teaches, and others *antiscorodon* (Arnob., Book II, p. 85; Columell., Book XI, *On Agriculture*, ch. 3; Plin., Book XIX, *Natural History*, ch. 6, p. 597). Plautus wrote of it (Plaut., *Poenulus*, Act V, scene 5):

And then more full  
of garlic and *ulpicum* than Roman oarsmen are.

See also Palladius, *On Agriculture*, Book XII, [Col. 0714C] ch. 6.

*Volumina*: see above, *Pollinctores*.

An *ustrina* is described by Festus as follows: “When someone has merely been burned in one place but buried elsewhere, that place is called an *ustrina* from *urere*, ‘to burn.’” It is perfectly evident that Arnobius uses the term with this meaning (Arnob., Book VII, p. 222; Festus, under the word BUSTUM), since he writes there that the pagans’ altars, where animals were sacrificed, are the *ustrinae*, funeral pyres, and cremation grounds of the most unfortunate class of animals.

Still other unusual, obsolete, barbarous, and obscure words occur not infrequently in his books. But we have [Col. 0714D] briefly explained them in their appropriate places whenever a suitable occasion presented itself.

[Col. 0713]

# THE SEVEN BOOKS OF ARNOBIUS THE AFRICAN’S DISPUTATIONS AGAINST THE GENTILES

> **Note:** [Col. 0717A]
>
> *The Seven Books of Arnobius’s Disputations against the Gentiles.* This is the ἐπιγραφή (*epigraphē*, title) of these books in the Roman edition and in all the others derived from it. But they observe that the manuscript has *Against the Nations*. The matter is one and the same. Our author himself writes in Book III: “It has caused peoples [Col. 0717B] and nations utterly dissimilar in customs to converge with one mind upon assent to a single belief.” Book V, ch. 13: “What do you say, O peoples? What do you say, nations devoted to opinions of this kind?” In the books of the Old Testament all unbelieving peoples are called “nations,” and thence, in the apostolic books and the records of the evangelists, ἔθνη (*ethnē*, nations or Gentiles); namely, because apart from the people peculiar to God, enclosed within the boundaries of Judaea, and afterward apart from a few faithful persons, all other peoples and nations, ignorant of the true God, served idols. The ancient Church therefore retained those appellations until, with idolatry collapsing and Christian piety spreading far and wide, the face of affairs began to change. For then, when Christian emperors presided over the world and churches were established everywhere for Christ, while on the contrary the temples of idols were closed and overthrown, together with the reason for the designation that designation also changed; and instead of “nations,” “Gentiles,” and “ethnics,” they began to be called “pagans,” since they no longer occupied the whole world but were confined within narrow bounds and, as it were, enclosed only within certain villages (*pagi*) [Col. 0717C]. Nor do I doubt that this was the true reason for the name; and my judgment is usefully confirmed by a fact also observed by others: that this appellation was unknown before imperial power passed to Christian emperors. **HERALDUS.**
>
> From the fragment of Salmasius’s commentary on Arnobius, published by J. A. Fabricius at the end of the works of Saint Hippolytus, vol. II, pp. 122–134—where that man of immense learning discusses, according to his custom, the names and praenomina of the Romans at fairly great length, but learnedly—it will suffice to excerpt here the very few observations pertaining to the name of Arnobius. That most learned man begins by asking why the name Arnobius is inscribed here by itself, without praenomen or cognomen. Arnobius did this, of course, chiefly after the custom of the Greeks, who always retained their ancient usage of possessing a single name—although there can scarcely be any doubt that Arnobius had several names, since this was customary not only among Romans but also among Spaniards, Gauls, [Col. 0717D] and Africans living under Roman rule, down to Constantine, through whom the use of praenomina was almost abolished. That use had formerly been, of course, for a person to be called Titus, Marcus, Aulus, or Gnaeus before his other names. The custom of having several names was nevertheless retained, the first of which may each be regarded as occupying the place of a praenomen. From this very fact it may be inferred that this name was his proper personal name; for if, out of several names, one is selected in preference to the others while the rest are passed over, that seems to be the name most properly one’s own, by which alone the person is designated.
>
> Other writers of nearly the same period did the same, for example Agellius—so cited by Augustine, *The City of God*, Book IX, ch. 4, and by all the ancient books; from this the name “A. Gellius” was afterward disseminated through printed editions—and Apuleius, to whom the editions have assigned the praenomen Lucius, although it does not appear [Col. 0718A] at all in manuscript volumes, in which one reads only: “Here begins the first book of the *Metamorphosis* of Apuleius.” And so thereafter in his other writings as well. Certainly, as far as Agellius and Apuleius are concerned, it is likely that they repeatedly did this in imitation of Greek custom, for they display great affectation of it in every respect.
>
> But *Arnobius* too [Col. 0718B] is a purely Greek name: Ἀρνόβιος (*Arnobios*), like Ζηνόβιος (*Zenobios*), Μακρόβιος (*Makrobios*), and Πολύβιος (*Polybios*). For it is not a gentilicium, as *Apuleius* is; rather, although it is a harsh Greek-style designation, it belongs to the class of names customarily used as cognomina among freedmen, with their masters’ praenomen and nomen placed before them. For freedmen, after adopting their master’s praenomen and nomen, added as a third name their own personal and Greek name. Examples occur everywhere in authors and in ancient epigraphic monuments. Thus they styled themselves: **A. APPULEIUS, A. L. THYASUS**, that is, Aulus Appuleius, freedman of Aulus, Thyasus. Thyasus was the Greek name of the slave whose master was Aulus Appuleius, so designated by praenomen and nomen; his cognomen is unknown. After being manumitted by him, and having adopted his praenomen and nomen, he was called Aulus Appuleius Thyasus. This practice was perpetually and consistently observed in every case.
>
> The sons of freedmen, however, converted their father’s personal name—which in the father had served as a cognomen after his emancipation—[Col. 0718C] into a quasi-gentile name, and generally made a praenomen out of the patron’s gentile name, in this fashion: Flavius Sosipater Charisius. Sosipater is the personal name, Charisius the father’s. Sosipater, who was called Flavius, was manumitted by some patron from the Flavian clan. Thus, if that Thyasus had had a son named Epaphroditus, he would, according to this rule, have been called Appuleius Thyasus Epaphroditus. Sometimes the sons of freedmen also retained their father’s patron’s praenomen. But just as Arnobius seems to have had several names, so it is uncertain whether this appellation served him as nomen or cognomen. Thus Salmasius.

(C)

# BOOK ONE

## TABLE OF CHAPTERS

[Col. 0713D] Arnobius declares that he undertook this work in order to repel the frequently repeated calumny by which the pagans [Col. 0714D] falsely and rashly accused Christians of being the authors [Col. 0715A] of every public calamity, because Christians had renounced the worship of false divinities. Chs. 1, 2.

He therefore makes it plain that, since the beginning of the Christian religion, nothing in the natural world and nothing in people’s private or public affairs has either changed, slackened, or been dissolved. Chs. 2, 3.

He refutes the pagans’ objection that the gods, offended by the impiety of Christians, were overwhelming the world with pestilence and other calamities. From the histories of the Gentiles themselves, indeed, it is established that before the name of Christians had ever been heard, human beings were afflicted by either the same disasters or even more grievous ones. Chs. 3, 4.

He also demonstrates that it is just as certain that cruel wars were formerly waged by the Atlanteans, Assyrians, Bactrians, Persians, Greeks, Trojans, and Romans—by Ninus, Zoroaster, Xerxes, Alexander the Great, and others—as it is established [Col. 0715B] that those wars diminished after the birth of Christ. Chs. 5, 6.

He investigates why, according to the pagans’ opinion, the world is oppressed by so many and such great evils. He teaches that these events must either be referred to natural causes, or that things which are certainly useful to the whole of nature and to the world seem evil only to human beings, who measure everything by their own advantage. Chs. 7–12.

By various arguments he skillfully convicts the pagans of the perversity with which they clamored that all evils must be laid at the door of Christians, who had arisen only about three hundred years earlier. Chs. 13–16.

He demonstrates that it is absurd to say that anger can befall the immortal gods, and that there would at the same time be no equity in them if, because of injuries inflicted upon them by Christians, they exacted punishment for those injuries indiscriminately both from the Christians themselves and from innocent pagans, as the pagans claimed. He concludes [Col. 0715C] that these ridiculous accusations were fabricated solely by the avarice of soothsayers, diviners, and prophets. Chs. 17–24.

He replies to the pagans’ objection that the gods raged against human beings because Christians had introduced a new form of worship into the world. He thereby teaches in what, above all, the sum of the entire Christian religion consists. Chs. 25, 26, 27.

He then argues that the case of the Christians is better than that of those who revere false divinities. For they adore that Father from whom even the gods of the Gentiles themselves—if there are any—must have received whatever divinity and majesty they are believed to possess. Ch. 28.

Arnobius proves from his effects that this true God is the maker of all things, more ancient than Apollo, Mercury, and all other fictitious divinities, infinite, [Col. 0715D] unbegotten, immortal, and eternal. Chs. 29, 30, 31.

He asserts that it is implanted by nature in everyone to acknowledge him as the supreme King and governor of all things; indeed, even animals and the stones themselves, if by chance they could speak, would openly and publicly proclaim it. In vain, therefore, do the pagans proclaim Jupiter the supreme God, since they know that he was born in the ordinary human manner, whereas the supreme God is unbegotten and eternal. Chs. 31–35.

He meets the pagans’ accusation that Christians are culpable not because they venerate almighty God, but because they maintain that a man who was born and put to death by the infamous punishment of the cross is God. Chs. 36, 37.

But if, Arnobius says, it was permissible for the pagans to number certain persons [Col. 0716A] among the gods because of benefits which, as they supposed, those persons had conferred upon them, how much more ought Christ to be held in divine honor by human beings, since he bestowed upon them, in the greatest abundance, many far greater and boundless benefits? Chs. 38, 39.

“But he perished,” the pagans said, “fastened to the gibbet of the cross.” What follows from that? For the death of Christ—just like those of Pythagoras and Socrates—brought no injury to his teaching and excellent deeds. And what of the fact that the infamy of no manner of death can ever stain an innocent man, as Aquilius, Trebonius, and Regulus were? What, moreover, is more deserving of ridicule than this argument of the Gentiles, who honored with superstitious worship Liber, torn apart by the Titans; Aesculapius, struck by lightning; Hercules, burned alive; and others carried off [Col. 0716B] by violent death? Chs. 40, 41.

Furthermore, Christ, sent to us by the supreme King, is proved to be the true God as certainly as evidently by the innumerable miracles that he performed. A summary account is given of Christ’s miracles, from which his divinity is established. Chs. 42–47.

Nor could the recoveries from illness of certain persons treated by the pagans’ gods be set against these miracles. For even if this is provisionally conceded without proof, it is certain that no god of the Gentiles ever restored health to the sick, as Christ did, merely by applying his hand or uttering a word. Ch. 48.

Nor does the author allow it to be objected that the gods bring aid, not indeed to evil persons, but to good and pious ones. For Christ comes equally to the aid of all evil persons and good persons. Arnobius further shows that Christ’s miracles are genuine [Col. 0716C] from that wholly marvelous power which he gave even to persons of the lowest common rank: the power to perform prodigies of every kind merely through his name. Chs. 49–52.

And indeed, how great in dignity and power Christ himself is—God on high and from the deepest root—although formerly unknown to human beings, was demonstrated with the greatest possible clarity even by the miracles alone which occurred when he died. Ch. 53.

The truth of Christ’s miracles is established, first, from the most substantial witnesses, Christ’s disciples, who made them public and handed them down to posterity at the certain peril of their lives; and then from the fact that the Christian religion, founded and confirmed by those miracles, was received throughout the whole world in a very short time. Chs. 54, 55.

Finally, Arnobius proves that those miracles were neither [Col. 0716D] recorded falsely nor excessively exaggerated by our writers. Indeed, the things written about Christ in our books are as true as the traditions handed down by the Gentiles concerning their gods are false. Chs. 56, 57.

Arnobius rebuts the pagans’ insistence, on the one hand, that their own writings are more ancient and therefore truer, and, on the other, that ours were composed by uneducated men in crude and unpolished language. Chs. 58, 59.

The author answers the pagans who demanded of Christians why Christ, if he is God, assumed human form and was put to death in the human manner. Chs. 60, 61, 62.

He replies to the same people when they answer in turn that it is utterly incredible that Christ, being God and only appearing to be a man by virtue of a human nature, should have ended his life fastened to a gibbet. He shows [Col. 0717A] that, in order to heal and instruct human beings, Christ allowed himself, with as much gentleness as freedom, to be killed by the impious. Ch. 63.

Arnobius therefore sharply arraigns the pagans: although they rendered divine honors to tyrants, and exalted with the highest praises and awarded statues to others defiled by every kind of impiety and crime, they nevertheless persecuted Christ alone—the true, greatest, and supremely salutary messenger—with the most unjust and implacable hatred. Ch. 64.

[Col. 0718A] For what, he says, is more unjust and cruel than always to assail with the bitterest warfare the Lord of all virtues and destroyer of death, who, by permitting the death of the man whom he bore, gave everyone sure hope of the future salvation of our souls, if we live piously? Ch. 65.

> **Note:** [Col. 0718C]
>
> **I.—To rave, to be in a Bacchic frenzy.** That is, to affirm it like prophets filled with a god. Diviners and prophets, of course, were thought to be raving because of those motions by which they wheeled about as though impelled by divine force. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 445: “You will behold the raving prophetess”; and VI, 78: “The prophetess rages in Bacchic frenzy.” **HERALDUS and PRIOR.**—Likewise Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, ch. 27: “Even the prophets themselves, outside the temple, rave in this way, [Col. 0718D] rage in Bacchic frenzy in this way, and whirl about in this way.” Compare Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* III, p. 211. **ORELLI.**
>
> **And to speak as though delivering something ready-made from an oracle.** That is, boldly and grandly to pronounce something as though it were utterly certain and beyond doubt. For oracles were considered most august both for their majestic brevity and for the truth of their subject matter; and people thought that no doubt should be entertained concerning anything which a god had sung ἐκ τρίποδος (*ek tripodos*, “from the tripod”). Cicero, quoted by Augustine in *The City of God*, Book II, ch. 21, says of this verse of Ennius: “The Roman state stands by ancient customs and by men.” “That verse,” he says, “seems to me, by both its brevity and its truth, to have been uttered as though from some oracle.” The same author, *For Fonteius*, ch. 7: “If he thinks that whatever is said from that place is spoken from an oracle.” **HERALDUS and ELMENHORST.**—Compare Juretus on Symmachus, Book II, Epistle VII, p. 77, Le Lect’s edition. **ORELLI.**
>
> [Col. 0719B] **After the Christian people began to exist in the world, the world was ruined.** At that time they thus ascribed the causes of every evil to Christians, and said that the gods, provoked by Christian impiety, stirred up every evil whatsoever that afflicted the human race. Compare Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 40; Augustine, *The City of God*, Book II, chs. 2 and 3; Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, [Col. 0719C] etc. Later, when under the rule of Christian emperors the temples of the idols were closed and pagan superstition was prohibited, they also attributed the evils of the age to this cause; and from this arose the occasion given to Orosius to write his history. **HERALDUS and ELMENHORST.**
>
> **With which they formerly used to visit our affairs.** A very widespread belief among the ancients. See Catullus, *Epithalamium*, verse 382 ff.; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, 145–150; *Fasti* I, 247 ff. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Popular expressions.** That is, statements arising from popular ignorance, of a kind that it would have been utterly unworthy of men cultivated by learning to repeat. Similarly Augustine, *The City of God*, Book II, ch. 3: “Remember, however, that in recalling these things I am still arguing against the ignorant; from their ignorance also arose that common proverb: ‘The rain has failed because of the Christian name.’” **HERALDUS.**
>
> **That we deserve the hatred due to enemies.** For Christians were both regarded and called public enemies. **HERALDUS.**
>
> **The gods have been driven far away; such swarms of sorrows [Col. 0719D] have been brought upon the generations of mortals.** Stewechius restored this reading from the manuscript codex. The Roman edition has: “We have been driven away, while far off,” etc. Gelenius corrupted this in the following manner: “We must be driven away, if through us swarms,” etc., with Elmenhorst following him. Meursius, *Criticus Arnobianus*, p. 1, thinks it should read: “Let us be driven far away, while swarms,” etc., explaining “let us be driven away” as “let us be banished.” But if Arnobius had wished to repeat in other words what he had said immediately before—“that we deserve the hatred due to enemies”—he would undoubtedly have said, “We must be removed, we must be killed,” or something similar. For *exterminare* does not mean “to kill,” but “to send beyond the boundaries,” “to expel from the state.” See Nonius under this word, and Mercerus there, p. 98, a point which Heusinger rightly makes against Rothius in commenting on this passage of Cicero, *On Duties*, Book II, ch. 23: “And from that time such great dissensions followed that tyrants arose, the aristocrats were driven into exile, and the excellently constituted commonwealth of the Lacedaemonians fell apart.” Compare Bunemann on [Col. 0720B] Lactantius, *Institutes*, Book VI, ch. 19, pp. 810–811; Adriaan Behotius, *Apophoreta*, Book I, ch. 9, conjectures: “with the highest gods also driven far away, swarms,” etc. But the codex’s reading is sound. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Have been brought upon the generations.** See below, ch. 3. Thus Lactantius, *Epitome*, ch. 46, § 8: “In return for this God brought evils upon them,” on which verb Bunemann has much to say, [Col. 0720C] p. 1285. “The generations of mortals” means nothing other than the human race. See below, Book VII, ch. 24. **ORELLI.**

## I

Since I have discovered that certain persons, who by their own convictions believe themselves exceedingly wise, rave, rage in Bacchic frenzy, and pronounce as though delivering something ready-made from an oracle that, [Col. 0719A] after the Christian people began to exist in the world, the world was ruined; that the human race has been afflicted with manifold evils; and that even the heavenly beings, abandoning the customary concerns with which they formerly used to visit our affairs, have been driven away from the regions of the earth—I have resolved, according to the measure of my ability and the modest resources of my speech, to resist this odium and dissolve these calumnious accusations. My purpose is that they should not imagine themselves to be saying something important merely because they produce popular expressions, or, if we have abstained from disputes [concerning such matters], that they should suppose themselves to have won their case—a case defeated by its own fault, not abandoned through the silence of its defenders.

For I would certainly not deny that this accusation is exceedingly powerful, and that we deserve the hatred due to enemies, if it is established that among us lie the causes through which the world has strayed from its laws, the gods have been driven [Col. 0719B] far away, and such great swarms of sorrows have been brought upon the generations of mortals.

> **Note:** [Col. 0719B] The manuscript has *ab litibus*, “from disputes.”

> **Note:** [Col. 0720C]
>
> **II.—The meaning of that opinion.** Others read “the source.” But Arnobius immediately explains himself and what the expression means—what we express by the German *was daram sey, was dahinter steke*: “what there is to it, what lies behind it.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **Through zeal for contention.** Thus Augustine, *Confessions*, Book XII, ch. 18: “I do not wish to contend about words; for it is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear.” **ELMENHORST.**
>
> **So that it is not we who are more impious, but they themselves, etc.** Other writers likewise turn back upon the nations the charge concerning the alleged evils and impiety, for example Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 41; Lactantius, *Institutes*, Book V, ch. 8; Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*. **ELMENHORST.**
>
> **What unprecedented thing, what unknown thing, etc.** The Leiden edition has this reading from the correction of J. Meursius in the *Criticus*, p. 4. Others read “unusual.” But “unprecedented and unknown” means never previously known either by sight or by hearing; and in what follows Arnobius relates things which do not [Col. 0720D] merely depart from everyday experience—for that would be “unusual”—but which the human race has plainly never seen or heard at all. **ORELLI.**—That *invisitatum*, “unprecedented,” and *inusitatum*, “unusual,” are frequently confused has been noted by Lipsius, *Epistolary Questions*, Book II, ch. 26; the distinguished Hottinger on Cicero, *On Divination* I, p. 317; F.
