A. Wolf on Suetonius, vol. I, pp. 166–167; Oudendorp on the same passage of Suetonius; and Augustinus, ch. 13. Menkenius has taught the same at length in *Observations on the Latin Language*, entry 760, *invisitatus*. **JACOB OCHSNER.**
>
> **Contrary to the laws originally established.** That is, established at the very beginnings of things by God, the ruler and sovereign of all things. So it is used more than once in Tertullian. **HERALDUS.**
>
> **This rotation of the world.** That is, the world’s most rapid revolution, as Cicero says in *The Dream of Scipio*, ch. V: German *der Umschwung, die Kreisbewegung des Himmels*, “the revolution, the circular movement of the heavens.” Thus Pliny, *Natural History*, Book II, ch. 3, calls the world “a mass rotated in perpetual revolution.” **ORELLI.**—Arnobius uses “world” to mean “heaven,” as he does almost invariably in this work, and as do many [Col. 0721B] of the ancients, Manilius, Lucretius, and others. Festus: “The heaven, earth, sea, and air are called the world.” Macrobius on *The Dream of Scipio*, Book II, ch. 20: “It is perfectly certain that not only the earth but also heaven itself—which is properly called the world—is regulated by the sun.” Book II, ch. 20: “Whence it is also called ‘mundane,’ because ‘world’ properly means heaven.” Ennius in *Scipio*:
>
> —The vast world of heaven stood silent.
>
> **MEURSIUS.**
>
> **By whose light all things are clothed.** Thus Lucretius says of the sun, Book II, verse 145:
>
> How suddenly the rising sun is accustomed at such a time  
> to clothe all things, flooding them with its light,  
> we plainly and manifestly see before us.
>
> And Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 640:
>
> Here a more generous ether clothes the fields  
> [Col. 0721C] in purple light.
>
> (**CANNEGIETER**, Letter to J. D. Hortensius in van Hoven, *Literary Leisure*, p. 72.)
>
> **With heat, ceased burning, grew lukewarm.** The punctuation should be arranged in this way, so that “with heat” is connected with the preceding “are given life.” This also seemed right to the most learned Petrus Bertius. Arnobius used *exardere*, “to cease burning,” in place of *ardere desiit*, just as I have observed Martial using it, Book III, Epigram 66:
>
> Now, with Phaethon descending, Aethon sweats,  
> and the day has ceased blazing.
>
> **MEURSIUS**, p. 3.—“Grew lukewarm” means that, its burning heat having been reduced—having suffered a loss of heat—it grew cold, as Arnobius himself says below. For when *tepere*, “to be lukewarm,” is compared with cold it signifies warmth; if it is joined in contrast with heat, it signifies coldness, as Behotius shows with many examples in *Apophoreta*, Book III, ch. 3. **ORELLI.**
>
> **The tempering effects of its customary regulation.** That is, that mean between excessive heat and cold by which the sun regulates the earth. Thus *temperies* and *temperatura caeli*, “the temperateness of the sky,” are very frequently used among the ancients. **ORELLI.**
>
> [Col. 0721D] **Through the perpetual restoration of new growth.** Note the hyphenated compound ὑφ’ ἕν (*hyph’ hen*, “as one”), *semper-restitutione*, “perpetual-restoration.” Thus Lucretius, whom our Arnobius very frequently imitates, Book I, 125:
>
> From which he recalls that the image of ever-flourishing Homer  
> rose before him.
>
> So too *semper-lenitas*, “constant-gentleness,” in Terence, *Andria*, Act I, scene 2. **MEURSIUS**, p. 4.—But the passage of Lucretius proves nothing. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Have the moderate warmths perished through the intermingling of unequal seasons?** Meursius very badly reads “have occurred.” The “moderate warmths” are the warmths of spring and autumn, which perish amid unequal times or seasons of the year—namely, summer and winter—when they are intermingled with them. **ORELLI.**
>
> **The very late lights.** “Lights” here means daybreaks. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Have the winds breathed out their lives?** The ancient scholiast on those very well-known verses of Horace, *Odes* IV.12:
>
> Now the companions of spring, the Thracian breaths  
> that calm the sea, drive onward the sails,
>
> says: “It is customary for poets to call blasts ‘breaths’ or ‘souls,’ through a play upon the Greek word ἄνεμος (*anemos*, wind).” **ELMENHORST.**—Meursius cites several examples in his *Criticus*, p. 4, as does Caspar Barthius in *Adversaria*, Book III, ch. 12. **ORELLI.**
>
> **And with the blasts dead.** The ancients, in accordance with the Pythagoreans’ opinion, said that everything which failed or diminished “died,” because the Pythagoreans believed that everything which grew possessed a soul. Virgil, *Georgics* I, 107:
>
> And when the field swelters with its scorched, dying grasses.
>
> Servius should be consulted there. Persius, Satire 4:
>
> He sucks up the wrinkled dregs of dying vinegar.
>
> Cyprian, *Against Demetrianus*: “Although the vineyard disappoints, the olive deceives, and the sweltering field dries up as its grasses die from drought, what has this to do with the Christians?” Arnobius himself says below: “Reluctant rains cause the crops to die.” **MEURSIUS**, p. 5.
>
> **Is driven together.** Thus the Leiden editor, following the entirely correct conjecture of Fulvius Ursinus, which Elmenhorst supports with a cloud of examples in his booklet of variant readings, with Adriaan Behotius also approving it in his *Apophoreta*. *Coactare* is a frequentative of *cogere*, “to drive together,” an ancient and Lucretian verb—compare *On the Nature of Things* VI, verse 1120—such as must be restored in many places in Arnobius, a most devoted imitator of antiquity. Clouds are *driven together* in the sky, συνάγονται (*synagontai*, “are gathered together”), as is said hundreds of times among the ancients; they are not “compressed,” as the others, including the most recent editor Oberthür, read, unless the subject is things driven by winds into στενοχωρίας (*stenochōrias*, narrow places) and valleys between mountains. **ORELLI.**
>
> **And do fields drenched by the rains not follow?** This is the emendation of Thomas Canter, except only for the preposition *ex*, “by,” which we have added. The manuscript codex has: “nor do fields proceed to be drenched by the rains,” a reading defended by Heraldus, who thinks that *succedunt*, “follow,” was used for *pergunt*, “proceed.” [Col. 0722D] But *succedere* scarcely means simply “to proceed”; it means to proceed with work which another had begun. Meursius, p. 5, conjectures: “does it follow that the fields are drenched?” Gelenius printed: “nor do the fields, drenched by rains, take on moisture,” that is, acquire sap. Salmasius printed: “nor do the fields grow moist from the wetness produced by rains.” Behotius, *Apophoreta*, Book III, ch. 3, conjectures: “nor do the fields become accustomed to being drenched.” The preposition *ex* should not have offended Grotius, who reads: “nor do the fields proceed to be drenched by rains,” or Canter. For Arnobius is accustomed to use the prepositions *ex*, *de*, and *in* redundantly, in imitation of the Greeks, who employ ἐκ (*ek*, “from”) in the same way. **ORELLI.**
>
> **And the vine has changed in its fluids.** This is the entirely correct reading which J. Meursius extracted from the manuscript codex in his appendix. Sabaeus and Gelenius’s edition have “with its fluids burned out.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **They do not rut.** Thus the Leiden editor, following Fulvius Ursinus’s emendation. The manuscript codex has *non esuriunt*, “they do not hunger,” which Heraldus defends by taking *esurire* in place of *surire*, “to rut,” just as *egelidum* is used for *gelidum*, “cold.” Behotius [Col. 0723B] supports him in Book I, believing that the first and proper meaning of the verb *esurire* was “to desire sexual intercourse,” and that it was later transferred, for the sake of more decorous usage, to the appetite for food. But Arnobius below consistently has *surire*. *Surire* is properly used of female swine desiring the boar. See Festus under the word SUILLUM, and Scaliger there, and Nonius under the word CATULLIRE. But Apuleius uses it of males in the *Apology*: “Which of them are generated by mating, which coalesce from mud, how often and at what season of the year the females of each species are in heat and the males rut.” Our author himself does likewise below, Book V, ch. 28, concerning Bacchus: “Then, assuming the wantonness of one in rut, he twists his buttocks this way and that.” [Col. 0723C] So too Greek καπρᾷν (*kaprān*, “to be sexually excited”); κάπρος (*kapros*) means τὸ αἰδοῖον τοῦ ἀνδρός (*to aidoion tou andros*), “the man’s sexual organ,” as Meursius teaches in his *Criticus*, p. 6. Compare Behotius, who discusses this verb at length, and Pieter Burman the Younger in the *Latin Anthology: Epigrams*, vol. I, p. 629. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Taken in wombs.** Cannegieter prefers *sutos*, “sewn in,” that is, sewn into tunics or membranes within the mother’s body. *Sumptos in uteris*, “taken in wombs,” is badly used for *conceptos, assumptos in uteros*, “conceived, taken into wombs.” The ablative is used for the accusative, as we shall see later. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Inhabitable places**, with the prefix *in-* used without negative force, for the simple *habitable places*, just as *inhabitare* is used for *habitare*, “to inhabit.” **HERALDUS.** Elmenhorst wrongly takes it in a negative sense. **ORELLI.**
*Navitas* [activity, diligence]. Others read *nativitas* [birth, nature]. But in fact it is not *nativitas* but *navitas*, that is, industry and labor in seeking sustenance, which first dispersed mortals. Restore this word, therefore. CANNEGIETER.

“They do not contract marriages with the lawful solemnities of weddings.” Stewechius thinks that one should read “lawful marriages” . . . . . [Col. 0723D], just as jurists speak of “lawful weddings,” “lawful servitude,” and “lawful children.” But Heraldus rightly defends the manuscript’s reading. The *lawful solemnities of weddings* are the solemn rites of weddings, τὰ νομιζόμενα τῶν γάμων, “the customary observances of marriages.” *Justa* is, of course, used substantivally here. Thus Columella, *On Agriculture* VI.3, has “the due obligations of work and labor.” Compare Nic. Heinsius, *Adversaria*, p. 462, Burmann’s edition. ORELL.—So too Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II.627:

> . . . . . . And I performed unjust funeral rites.  
> OSCHNER.

“They direct their talents.” The manuscript prefixes *et* [and]. Not badly. For *dirigunt*, however, it has *derigunt*. But scribes habitually write *e* for *i*. MEURSIUS, in the *Appendix*.

“And reap the returns of diligent industry.” This is Fulvius Ursinus’ masterly emendation, deservedly received into the text by the Leiden editor. The common reading is “diligently reap the returns of birth,” which Stewechius changed to “the returns of diligent birth.” But I wish he had explained to us what “diligent birth” means. For I can scarcely believe that *nativitas* can be used for native disposition. One must therefore restore [Col. 0724B] *gnavitatis* or *navitatis* [industry], which alone is correct and could very easily have been corrupted by copyists into *nativitatis*. ORELL.

“To whom has the lot of such affairs been assigned? Do they not become more eminent,” etc. Meursius restored this from the manuscript in the *Appendix*. Previously it was printed: “has been assigned? To such persons,” etc. Gelenius V abuses his ingenuity by deleting *talium* entirely. Cannegieter prefers *talis*, referring to *sors*: “such a lot as to reign and command.” ORELL.

“Is equipped.” Properly said of arms with which the body is defended; hence, metaphorically, of any goods whatsoever, whether of mind or body. Thus Petronius, chapter V.21:

[Col. 0724C]

> . . . . . . Equip your mind with these goods.  
> ORELL.]

## II

Let us therefore examine the meaning of that opinion and the nature of what is being said; and, setting aside all contentious passions, by which contemplation of things is usually obscured and concealed, let us weigh with an impartial examination whether what is said is true. For the connected sequence of the arguments that follow will assuredly bring it about that it is not so much we who are found guilty of impiety [Note: [Col. 0720B] “Rather impious than we.” Fulv.], but those very men who profess themselves worshippers of the divine powers and devotees of long-established religions who are found guilty of that charge.

First, then, we inquire of them in familiar and peaceable language: after the name of the Christian religion began to exist upon earth, what unprecedented or unknown thing, what contrary to the laws originally established, has that very thing which is called and named nature either experienced or suffered? Have those primary elements, from which all things are agreed to have been compounded, been changed into contrary qualities? Has the structure of this mechanism and mass, by which we are covered and within which we are enclosed, been loosened or dissolved in any part? Has this revolution of the world exceeded the regulation of its primordial motion, or begun either to creep more slowly [Col. 0721A] or to be swept along with headlong rotation? Have the stars begun to rise from the western regions, and has the course of the constellations begun to be borne [Note: [Col. 0721A] Thus Sabaeus. Fulvius reads “to be carried toward their risings.”] toward their risings? Has the sun himself, prince of the heavenly bodies, by whose light all things are clothed and by whose heat they are animated, blazed up or grown lukewarm, and corrupted the temperate measures of his accustomed governance into contrary conditions? Has the moon ceased to restore herself and, through the perpetual renewal of her young light, to return to her former forms? Have cold, heat, and the intervening warmth perished through a confusion of the differing seasons? Has winter begun [Col. 0722A] to have long days, or a summer night to summon back the latest dawn? Have the winds breathed out their lives, so that, their blasts having died away, neither is the sky driven together into clouds nor do fields moistened by rains follow thereafter?

Does the earth refuse to receive the seeds entrusted to it, or do trees refuse to put forth leaves? Has the flavor of edible crops or the liquid of the vine changed? Is a foul gore pressed from the berries of olives and no longer supplied to a lamp whose flame has gone out? Do animals accustomed to the land and those living in the waters no longer feel sexual desire or conceive? [Col. 0723A] Do they not preserve the offspring conceived in their wombs according to their own customs and law? Finally, do human beings themselves, whom the earliest and incipient industry dispersed throughout the inhabitable regions of the earth, not contract marriages with the lawful solemnities of weddings? Do they not beget the sweetest lines of children; do they not conduct public business, private affairs, and household concerns? Do they not direct their talents, as each prefers, through the various systems of arts and branches of learning, and reap the returns of diligent industry? Do those to whom the lot of such affairs has been assigned not reign and command? Do they not daily become more eminent in offices and powers? Do they not preside over judicial disputes, interpret statutes and laws? Do not all peoples, in their respective nations, observe according to the institutions of their ancestral customs all the other things with which human life is equipped and sustained?

[Col. 0723B] [Note: [Col. 0724C]

## III.—“Has drawn apart the course . . . . . .”

That this must be the reading is shown by the words “with its continuity broken.” The manuscript has *deduxerit* [has led down], which Canterus defends in vain. On the force of the verb *irrumpere* [to break in], see the authors cited by Bunemann on Lactantius, book I, chapter 20, p. 126. ORELL.

“By which human affairs are assailed.” *Human affairs* means the same as “the circumstances of humanity.” Thus below: “both brings corruption upon bodies and weakens human affairs.” He uses *incursantur* [are assailed] as a highly expressive word. It is drawn from soldiers who ravage and devastate everything. The Greeks say εἰσβάλλειν, “to invade.” HERALD.

“Was granted the good fortune of this designation.” Heraldus interprets *meruit* as “began.” But *merere* or *mereri* does not have this meaning; rather, among writers of medieval Latin it is said of those who obtain something through the favor either of God, a prince, or someone more powerful. Thus Minucius Felix, chapter 6: “Those who, at the very birth of the world, *meruerunt* to have either propitious gods or kings” [Col. 0724D], that is, those to whom it was granted or fell by fortune that they should have them, etc. Spartianus, *Hadrian* 4: “Having been made consul for the second time through Plotina’s favor, he *emeruit* his entire expectation toward adoption.” Corte, on Pliny, *Letters* I.8, p. 32, Longolius’ edition, and on Rutilius, *Journey*, verse 6, p. 39, Kapp’s edition, teaches that in Roman writers the verb *mereri* always has attached to it the notion of one’s own merit or excellence, by which a person renders himself worthy of some benefit, whereas “to merit” without merit of one’s own, but by the sheer grace of God, has the flavor of ecclesiastical Latin. Compare Gierig on the same passage of Pliny, and Havercamp on Tertullian, *Apology* 33, p. 286. ORELL.

“And began to be harassed.” The manuscript has *infectari* [to be infected], which Stewechius defends in his note on book VII. ORELL.

“That these plagues broke in.” Stewechius suspects that one should read, in the old manner of speaking, “that these plagues broke themselves in,” and thinks that the same *se* [themselves] should be restored in three other passages. Yet it hardly seems likely that, if this had been Arnobius’ constant Latin usage, copyists would have omitted that *se* so many times. ORELL.

“A shortage, he says, of crops.” This is the reading of the first edition, which Fulvius Ursinus himself had altered. Yet Arnobius has quite often used *inquit* [he says] in this fashion—and not Arnobius alone, but many others as well, for example Tertullian, *Apology* 1: “But it is not therefore, he says, good,” etc. The reading is sound; those who wish to substitute *inquiunt* [they say] do so wrongly. HERALD.—Compare Bunemann on Lactantius, *On the Anger of God* 19, p. 1002, and below, on book III, chapter 6, the note of my dear Ochsner. ORELL.

“Distress in the grain supply”—an elegant expression, like Cicero’s repeated uses of “distress of the treasury,” “of public funds,” and “of private property.” ORELL.

“Devastation.” Cannegieter wishes to restore *egestate* [destitution]. But he himself adds: “I am well aware that devastation is brought upon regions by the calamities which our author enumerates.” Nothing, therefore, should be changed. On the verb *aggerare* [to heap up], see Oudendorp on Apuleius, p. 640. ORELL.

“They befall and have assailed everything.” Thus the manuscript and Sabaeus. Gelenius and Fulvius Ursinus changed this reading to *atterunt* [wear down], which is much more expressive and could very easily have been corrupted by copyists into *adierunt*. But the common reading can be defended from Virgil, *Aeneid* V.378:

> Nor does anyone from so great a company  
> Dare to assail the man.

Thus *adierunt* here is equivalent to “they attack,” εἰσβάλλειν, “to invade,” with the perfect used for the present. For that reason I would not venture to change this reading. Cannegieter thinks *accidunt* should be read with the middle syllable long, as derived from *ad* and *caedo* [strike]. But if we read *adierunt*, that verb cannot have a place here; *accidunt* instead means “they descend upon.” ORELL.

“Showers of stones have often shattered entire regions.” I do not see why this perfectly sound reading should be changed to *communisse*, as the Leiden edition has it. *Munire* and *communire* mean ὀχυροῦν, “to fortify”: to render something covered, firm, and level by means of stones built up and fitted together. Thus below, book II, chapter 17: “Do we not see some animals constructing dwellings for themselves in the most suitable sites for nests, while others cover and fortify them with overhanging stones and rocks?” But *communire* in the sense “to obstruct” is unusual among Latin writers. The correct reading is therefore *comminuisse*, that is, “to have broken apart,” referring, of course, to crops battered by hail. Compare Arntzenius on Pliny’s *Panegyric* 30, p. 134, Schwarz’s edition. On showers of stones, see Livy I.31; XXIII.3; XXVI.23; XXX.38; and Pliny, *Natural History* XX.24. ORELL.

[Col. 0726B] “They impose.” Thus the manuscript, excellently; consider this an idiom of Arnobius. Near the end of this same book: “It would be difficult for him to impose death upon whomever he wished”; and in book VII, chapter 42: “And he imposed pestilence, diseases, and slaughter upon mortality.” Indeed, I recall Manilius also speaking this way somewhere. MEURSIUS, in the *Appendix*.—Fulvius Ursinus reads *inducunt* [bring upon]. Yet *indicere* means to inflict, introduce, and prepare something which follows not immediately and on the spot but after some intervening period. Thus Suetonius, *Caligula* 26: “And sometimes, by closing the granaries, he proclaimed famine for the people.” ORELL.

“Dried up when their muds had become parched.” Fulvius Ursinus and Sabaeus read *inhorruisse* [to have become rough]; Stewechius, very badly, *induruisse* [to have hardened], for that is said only of rivers frozen by cold. *Inaruisse* [to have dried up] alone is correct. Thus Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV: “And marshy ground alike lies dry with parched sands.” Compare Elmenhorstius. For *limis* [muds], the manuscript has *limnis*, which Meursius in the *Appendix* thinks arose from *linsis lymphis* [uncertain reading: “drained waters”], and believes that this should be read. ORELL.

“They burn.” Lucretius IV.1160 ff. speaks similarly of plague. So too “to burn with scourges and blows,” and *urere* generally means “to afflict with evil.” See Nic. Heinsius, *Adversaria* IV.4, p. 591. ORELL.

“By locusts.” Compare Tacitus, *Annals* XV; Livy XLII; Orosius V.11; Augustine, *City of God* III.31. ELMENHORSTIUS.

“By locusts.” Compare Augustine, *City of God* III.31; Orosius, *Histories* V.11; Cornelius Tacitus, book XV, beginning; Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, chapter 1 ff. NOURRIUS.

[Col. 0726D] “By mice.” Compare Pliny, *Natural History* VIII.29. ELMENHORSTIUS.

0

“Is struck down and gnawed away.” Behotius and Cannegieter approve *occiditur* [is killed], which some early editions have. But nothing should be changed, since Arnobius likes to join together words with the same meaning. ORELL.

“Go through your histories.” This reading too comes from the manuscript; previously the text read, “Go through foreign histories.” HERALD.

“Cities . . . swallowed up by enormous chasms through the most violent movements of the earth.” Tertullian illustrates this in *Apology* 40: “We read that Hiera, Anaphe, Delos, Rhodes, and associated islands sank into the depths with many people. Plato also records that a landmass larger than Asia and Africa was torn away by the Atlantic Sea. The Corinthian Sea, moreover, was swallowed up by an earthquake, and the violence of the waves cut Lucania away from Italy and banished it under the name of Sicily.” ORELL.

“Cities totter to the point of destruction.” He uses *periculum* [danger] in a novel but proper sense for “destruction.” Thus below: “If they are born and begotten, they are certainly near to extinction and destruction”; and book VI: “Whatever is supported by external causes and things must be mortal and have a ready road to destruction whenever something by which it lives begins to be lacking.” I also find this common in Cyprian’s treatise *On the Dress of Virgins*: “Why does she go out adorned and coiffed, as though she had or were seeking a husband? Let her fear rather to please, if she is a virgin, and let her not seek her own destruction, she who preserves herself for better and divine things.” MEURSIUS, p. 6.]

## III

Since, therefore, these things are so, and no innovation has broken in to draw apart the perpetual course of things by breaking its continuity, what is the meaning of the claim that corruption was brought upon the earth after the Christian religion entered the world and revealed the mysteries of hidden truth? “But,” they say, “pestilences, droughts, wars, scarcity of crops, locusts, mice, hailstorms, and other harmful things by which human affairs are assailed are brought upon us by the gods, who have been exasperated by your injuries and offenses.”

If it were not foolish to linger any longer over matters that are evident and require no defense, I would certainly demonstrate, by reviewing earlier ages, that those evils of which you speak were neither unknown nor sudden; and that it was not after [Note: [Col. 0723B] “Before.” Fulv.] our people [Note: [Col. 0724B] “Our race.” Manuscript, wrongly.] were granted the good fortune of this designation that these plagues broke in and mortal affairs began to be harassed by a variety of dangers. For if we are the cause, and these scourges were devised as the recompense for our crime, how did antiquity come to know these names for miseries? How did it give a designation to wars? By what concept could it name pestilence and hailstorms, or adopt them among the words through which speech was expressed? For if these evils are new and derive their causes from recent offenses, how could antiquity form words for things which it did not itself know that it had experienced, and which it had not learned had repeatedly occurred in the times of its ancestors?

“A shortage,” he says, “of crops, and distress in the grain supply, confine us more tightly.” Were the ancient and most remote ages, then, ever without experience of this necessity? Do not the very names by which these evils are designated bear witness and cry aloud that no mortal has ever escaped them immune? If [Col. 0725B] the matter were difficult to believe, we could employ the testimony of authors to show how great and how frequent the famines were, what nations felt their horror, and what peoples perished amid accumulated devastation.

The most frequent occurrences of hail descend upon and have assailed everything. For do we not see it recorded and set down [Note: [Col. 0725B] “Placed.” Fulv.] in ancient writings that even showers of stones have often shattered entire regions? Difficult rains cause crops to die and impose sterility upon the earth. Was antiquity immune from these evils, when we have learned that even enormous rivers dried up when their muds had become parched? The contagions of pestilence burn the human race. Run through the annalistic records written in various languages, and you will learn that all nations have very frequently been desolated and bereaved of their inhabitants. By locusts and by mice every kind of crop is struck down and gnawed away. Go through your own histories, and from them you will be informed how often the former age was afflicted [Note: [Col. 0726B] “Was sorely afflicted.” Fulv.] by these scourges and fell into the miseries of poverty.

Cities shaken by the most violent movements of the earth totter to the point of destruction. What, did earlier times not see cities and their peoples swallowed up by enormous chasms, or did they possess fortunes secure from occurrences of this sort?

[Note: [Col. 0727B]

## IV.—“When was the world consumed by fire and dissolved into ashes and embers? Was it not before us?”

These words undoubtedly refer to the story of Phaethon, known from Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, beginning; Lucian, *Dialogues of the Gods* 25; Hyginus, *Fables* 154. Compare especially Plato, *Timaeus*, p. 291 [Col. 0727C], vol. IX, Bipontine edition. ORELL.

“Battles fought with lions.” Nourrius, p. 331, thinks that Arnobius is speaking of contests in which gladiators and athletes entered the arena to fight lions and other wild beasts. But the reference seems rather to be to African peoples harassed by lions. Thus Aelian, *On the Nature of Animals* XVII.27, relates that the Nomaei, a Libyan people, were utterly destroyed by lions. ORELL.

“By venomous snakes.” Thus Pliny, *Natural History* VIII.29, relates that Amyclae in Italy was destroyed by serpents. ORELL.

“May I say this with your peace and kind indulgence.” A formula prefacing a request for indulgence, familiar to the best writers, especially Velleius Paterculus I.7, 17; II.129. ORELL.]

## IV

When was the human race destroyed by floods of water? Was it not before us? When was the world consumed by fire and dissolved into embers and ashes? Was it not before us? When were the greatest cities covered by the waves of the sea? Was it not before us? When were wars waged with wild beasts and battles fought with lions? Was it not before us? When was destruction brought upon peoples by venomous snakes? Was it not before us?

For as to your customary allegation that we are the causes of frequent wars, of the devastation of cities, and of Germanic and Scythian incursions—may I say this with your peace and kind indulgence—you do not see, in your passion for calumny, what sort of claim this is.

[Note: [Col. 0727C]

## V.—“From the island said to be Neptune’s Atlantis, as Plato demonstrates.”

In the *Timaeus*, vol. IX, p. 296, Bipontine edition. ORELL.

“With Ninus and Zoroaster as their respective leaders.” Elmenhorstius collected many testimonies concerning [Col. 0727D] this war in his note on this passage. The chief is Jerome, vol. V, on Hosea 2: “All histories, both Greek and barbarian, relate that Ninus, son of Belus, was the first to reign over all Asia; among the Assyrians he founded the city of Nineveh after his own name”; and afterward: “He fought in a fierce contest against Zoroaster the magician, king of the Bactrians, and attained such glory that he represented his father Belus as a god.” Compare Diodorus II.6, who, however, calls the king of the Bactrians not Zoroaster but Oxyartes. The claim that the contest in this war was also conducted by magical arts is mentioned nowhere except in our author. Compare Scaliger on Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, p. 16. ORELL.

“But also by magic arts and from the secret disciplines of the Chaldaeans.” This is the reading of the first edition. Fulvius Ursinus, however, had removed the particle *ex* [from]. But we show a little below that in this author it very frequently παρελκεῖν, “is superfluously added.” HERALD.

[Col. 0728B] “That monstrous Xerxes.” *Immanis* is equivalent to φρενοβλαβὴς καὶ ἀτάσθαλος, “deranged and recklessly impious.” The Greeks use these terms for a man whose condition is hopeless and who is not merely accustomed to his evils but even delights in them—such as the Xerxes described by Herodotus in Book VIII. The same author, in Book II, says that Pheron, king of the Egyptians, ἀτασθαλίῃ χρησάμενον, “acting with reckless impiety,” dared to hurl a spear into the Nile as it flooded the fields and for that reason was deprived of his sight. Thus “monstrous Xerxes” means ἀτάσθαλος, “recklessly impious,” one who through excessive ἀτασθαλία, “recklessness,” despised gods and men and undertook deeds monstrous and beyond human capacity. By this term Arnobius therefore wished to signify in Xerxes a more-than-human madness and insanity [Col. 0728C], a πάθος θηριῶδες, “bestial passion,” by which name ἄγρια, “savage,” and extraordinary vices are called; just as, conversely, great virtues that surpass common examples have been called θεῖα, “divine,” as Aristotle observes in the *Nicomachean Ethics*. HERALD.—For *Xerxes*, P. Burmann II, on the *Latin Anthology*, vol. I, p. 191, thinks that *Perses* [the Persian] should be read, on the ground that the manuscript has *Xerxes*. But there is no reason for alteration: *x* and *s* are very frequently confused by copyists, but not *x* and *p*. ORELL.—These most celebrated deeds of Xerxes, piercing Mount Athos and joining the Hellespont, are recorded by ancient writers. Sylburgius, on Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* III.4, Potter’s edition, cited Lycophron, *Alexandra* 1414; Herodotus, *Polyhymnia*, p. 249; Thucydides IV, p. 156; Arrian, *Expedition of Alexander* V, p. 103. Add Isocrates, *Panegyricus* §25, repeated in Aristotle, *Rhetoric* III.9; *Historia Augusta*, vol. II, p. 365; B. Martin, *Various Readings*, p. 136; Ruhnken on Longinus, p. 250 ff. OCHSNER.

“Was brought about because of our name.” This is the manuscript’s reading [Col. 0728D], according to the testimony of Livineius on the *Ancient Latin Panegyrics*, p. 387, Arntzenius’ edition, and Markland on Statius, *Silvae* I, poem 1, note on p. 3; Gelenius rashly changed it, printing *injuria* [injury]. The Leiden editor printed *cura* [care]. Heinsius, *Adversaria* II.10, p. 276, prefers *culpa* [fault]. But the manuscript’s reading is excellent: “because of our name,” that is, because of us—namely, the Christians. Thus “the name of the wise” in Sulpicia’s *Satire*, verse 35, means the wise themselves, the philosophers. ORELL.

“Subjected to captivity and servitude.” I have printed *captivitati* in place of *captivitate*, following L. Bunemann’s emendation on Lactantius, *Institutes* VII.15. Examples of this construction occur throughout Lactantius, for example III.8, “to subject to dominion”; IV.10, “to subject to law”; *On the Anger of God* 13, “to subject to empire and dominion”; *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* 23, “to subject to the census.” ORELL.

“We can.” Thus the manuscript. Others read “we are able.” ORELL.]

## V

Was it because of us that, ten thousand years ago, a great host of men burst forth from the island said to be Neptune’s Atlantis, as Plato demonstrates, and utterly destroyed and extinguished countless nations? Was it due to our unpopularity that the Assyrians and Bactrians, with Ninus and Zoroaster as their respective leaders, fought not only with steel [Col. 0728A] and physical force but also by magic arts and from the secret disciplines of the Chaldaeans? Was it charged as a crime against our religion that Helen, carried off under the leadership and instigation of the gods, became a dreadful fate both to her own people and to future ages? Was it because of our name that the monstrous Xerxes brought the sea upon the land and crossed the sea on foot? Was it we who acted and aroused the causes by which a single young man, arising from the borders of Macedonia, subjected the kingdoms and peoples of the East to captivity and servitude? Was it we, of course, who drove the divine powers into such a fury that recently the Romans, like some raging river, submerged and overwhelmed every nation?

But if there is no one among humanity who would dare to impute to our times the events that occurred long ago, how can we be the causes of present miseries, when nothing new is happening, but all things are old and unheard-of in no period of antiquity?

[Note: [Col. 0728D]

## VI.—“Wars . . . . . after Christ was heard of in the world were not only not increased, but even diminished.”

[Col. 0729B] A very similar passage occurs in Tertullian, *Apology* 40: “And yet, if we compare former calamities, lighter ones occur now, since the world received Christians from God. For since then the innocence of the age has moderated its iniquities, and intercessors before God began to exist.” The ancient Fathers of the Church generally ascribe the peace of the world under Augustus and his successors to Christ’s appearance upon earth as its principal cause. See the passages of Jerome on Psalm 71 and Isaiah 2 cited by Elmenhorstius on this passage. ORELL.

“A kindred living being.” Thus Arnobius below, book II, chapter 16: “That we are living beings either similar to the rest or separated from them by no very great difference.” ELMENHORSTIUS.

“Who understand that they are human beings not through the form of their bodies . . . . .” Thus Fulvius Ursinus, Stewechius, and Meursius. The *se* [that they] is absent from the manuscript. ORELL.—And it can be absent, in the Greek manner, as below, chapter 28: “They perceive that they have obtained divinity”; Lipsius noted that passage in *Ancient Readings* II.7. Add Bentley on Horace, *Letters* I.7.22. In Latin one says either, “I understand that I am a human being,” or, by a Graecism, “I understand myself to be human.” OCHSNER.

“With the haughtiness of their insight.” The manuscript also confirms this reading. I would therefore be unwilling to alter it rashly. By *supercilium luminis* Arnobius perhaps means the arrogance through which someone believes himself more perceptive than others, καὶ ὀξυδερκέστατον, “and exceedingly keen-sighted.” HERALD.—Gelenius changed it to “with swollen haughtiness” (which Arnobius has below, book II, chapter 1), and Oberthür followed him. Meursius proposed “by the light of pride and haughtiness.” ORELL.

“With the uses of iron redirected toward gentler works.” Arnobius is referring to Isaiah 2:4. ORELL.]

## VI

Although it is not difficult to prove that those wars which you say are stirred up because of hostility toward our religion were, after Christ was heard of in the world, not only not increased but even, for the greater part [Note: [Col. 0729B] Thus Sabaeus. Others read “in part.”], diminished through the restraint of their furies. For since so great a multitude of people have learned from his teachings and laws that evil ought not to be repaid with evil, that it is nobler to suffer an injury than to inflict one, and that one ought rather to shed one’s own blood than to stain one’s hands and conscience with another’s blood, the ungrateful world has long possessed a benefit from Christ: through him the rage of savagery has been softened, and hostile hands have begun to refrain from the blood of a kindred living being.

But if [Note: [Col. 0729B] Thus Fulvius. Sabaeus reads “What if.”] absolutely all who understand that they are human beings not through the form of their bodies but through the power of reason were willing for a little while to lend an ear to his saving and peaceable decrees, and did not, out of pride and the haughtiness of their insight, trust their own perceptions rather than his admonitions, the entire world would long ago have redirected the uses of iron toward gentler works, would pass its life in the softest tranquility, and would unite in saving concord under unbroken stipulations of treaties.

[Note: [Col. 0729D]

## VII.—“Wretched mortality.”

Arnobius says *mortalitas* [mortality] in the sense of “the human race,” just as Minucius uses *humanitas* [humanity]. Thus below: “For Almighty God is known, by the one and common conviction of all mortality, neither to have been begotten,” etc.; and in book IV: “And after this do you dare to wonder whence arise these evils by which mortality is flooded and oppressed without any interruption?” HERALD.—So too Pliny, *Natural History* II.7: “frail and toilsome mortality”; and in the same chapter, §22, “improvident mortality.” ORELL.—Add Pliny the Younger, *Letters* VI.20: “Had I not believed that I was perishing with everyone and everyone with me—a great consolation of mortality, though a wretched one.” Of the same kind is Ovid’s “mortal evil,” *Metamorphoses* VII.525. OCHSNER.

“If the truth of the matter is made clear by fact and striking arguments.” [Col. 0730C] Jacques Cujas conjectures that one should read: “I shall do so, in order that the truth of the matter may be made clear by striking arguments.” HERALD.—Nothing should be changed: *facto* means “by examples consisting in fact,” *Thatsachen* [facts], as very frequently. Behotius thinks *si facto* entered the text from a gloss, since it is absent from the Royal Manuscript; he therefore deletes it with Meursius. ORELL.]

## VII

“But,” they say, “if through you no harm is done to human affairs, whence come these evils by which wretched mortality has long been harassed [Col. 0730A] and oppressed?”

You demand an explanation from me that is not at all necessary to this issue. For the present dispute [Note: [Col. 0730B] *Disceptatione*. Manuscript; *disputatio*, Fulvius, wrongly.], now before us, was not undertaken by me in order to show or prove by what causes and principles each particular thing occurs, but to show that the reproaches belonging to so grave a charge are far removed from us. If I establish this—if the truth of the matter is made clear by fact and striking arguments—I do not care whence these evils come or from what sources and first principles they flow.

[Note: [Col. 0730C]

## VIII.—“Contains them enfolded within its own principles.”

The manuscript reads, “contains them within its own irritations,” etc. This reading is to be preferred to the printed *in Rotationibus* [in rotations], which, after Gelenius, all have followed except Heraldus, because it signifies that something is hidden in matter which provokes and incites evils. If anything must nevertheless be changed, I would rather read *in rationibus* [within its principles]. (Justus Lipsius, *Stoic Physiology* I, dissertation XIV, p. 568, *Works*, vol. III, Wesel edition.) Thus *irritationes*, actively understood, is equivalent to “inciting forces,” *die bewegenden Kräfte* [the motive forces]. But I prefer Heraldus’ emendation—or rather Canterus’—*in rationibus*. Thus Lucretius V.1182 speaks of the *rationes* of the heavens, that is, their fixed motions, the fixed orders of the stars, and their courses, immutable from all eternity, as Lambinus explains it. Translate, therefore: *in ihren bestimmten, ewigen Gesetzen* [within their fixed, eternal laws]. *Rotationes* would mean rotating forces, *Schwungkräfte* [forces of rotation]. ORELL.

“Lines” (*lineis*), that is, constellations. ORELL.

“What if at fixed times?” The manuscript has, “What if in the times of summer?” From this Theodorus Canterus produced, “What if also at fixed times?” ORELL.

“Prosperity receding as evils return.” Properly, as though waves were drawing back and then returning. Thus Ennius’ *Andromeda*, quoted by Nonius: “Again the wild wave advances and recedes”; and in the same author, from another writer: “Draw back your spirit, I say, troublesome fellow,” where *animam* [breath] should be read. For “to draw back the breath” is altogether the proper expression, as below in this book. HERALD.—On the preceding words, “flow backward again,” Meursius observes that *rursus* in antiquity was used for *retrorsum* [backward], citing Donatus on Terence, *Hecyra*, act III, scene 1:

> I sense running about in alarm, backward and forward.

*Rursum* properly means backward; *prorsum*, forward. ORELL.

[Col. 0731B] “Plato, that sublime summit and mainstay of philosophers.” The Roman edition has “and light.” Stewechius proposes the archaic *colmen* for *culmen*. Wrongly, for *culmen* and *columen* differ somewhat, although they are very closely related and are frequently confused by ancient writers. *Culmen* properly means the highest part of a roof, from *culmi*, that is, the stalks or straw from harvested crops with which buildings [Col. 0731C] were covered. *Columen*, however, properly means the beam placed lengthwise at the highest point of the roof, from which all the roof’s connecting timbers extend as though born from it, just as all the other bones proceed from a fish’s principal spine: *Tragbalken* [supporting beam]. See Gesner’s *Thesaurus* under this word. Vitruvius, *On Architecture* IV.7: “The ridge-beam at the highest point of the roof”; from this, too, *columns* receive their name. Hence *columen* is often used for a column, for example in Cicero, *On Divination* I.11:

> Unless, fashioned with beauty upon the lofty column,  
> The sacred form of Jupiter should behold the bright east.

See there the distinguished Hottinger. *Columen*, therefore, signifies not only the summit, peak, or highest part of a thing, but also that which supports, sustains, and protects anything. Thus Curtius IX.6.8 calls Alexander “the mainstay and star of Macedonia”; and Plautus, *Epidicus*, act II, scene 2, verse 5: “who are called the mainstay of the senate,” on which see Taubmann. Catullus in the *Epithalamium*: “Peleus, mainstay of Emathia.” Aquila Romanus, *On Figures of Thought*: “guardian [Col. 0731D] and defender of the republic, the safety and mainstay of the state.” Compare Burmann on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I.689. Translate here, therefore: *das Haupt und der Grundpfeiler der Philosophen* [the head and foundational pillar of the philosophers]. Moreover, on the exceedingly high estimation of Plato among ancient writers, especially ecclesiastical ones, see J. Lipsius, *Introduction to Stoic Philosophy* I, dissertation 1, *Works*, vol. IV, p. 632. ORELL.

“Declared in his writings that it was a purification of the earth.” Arnobius is referring to these words of Plato in the *Timaeus*, p. 291, vol. IX, Bipontine edition: Ὅταν οἱ Θεοὶ τὴν γῆν ὕδασι καθαίροντες κατακλύζωσιν, “Whenever the gods purify the earth with waters by flooding it.” Other Fathers of the Church also cited this opinion of Plato, for example Origen, *Against Celsus* IV: Ἴσασι δὲ καὶ Ἕλληνες κατακλυσμῷ ἢ πυρὶ τὴν γῆν κατὰ περιόδους καθαιρομένην, ὡς καὶ Πλάτων που οὕτω λέγει, “The Greeks too know that the earth is purified at recurring intervals by flood or fire, as Plato also says somewhere.” HERALD.

“To call, and that through these a certain youthfulness is procured.” The manuscript has *et injuventutem*, which Theodorus Canterus thinks should be retained as a single archaic word, so that *injuventus* would mean “the height of youth.” But this is wholly unattested [Col. 0732B] and a monstrosity of a word. Stewechius reads, “For youthfulness,” an emendation that the Leiden editor received into the text. It is indeed satisfactory in sense, but unnecessary. There is here a syllepsis, a figure extremely frequent among ancient writers, in which a single verb is assigned to two different thoughts and objects although it does not properly suit both. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* II.258:

> Sinon secretly releases the Danaans enclosed within the womb  
> And the barriers made of pine.

Here *releases* cannot be applied to the Danaans; “lets out” must be understood. Similarly here, “is procured” does not depend upon the preceding “to call”; rather, the entire passage must be supplemented thus: “The prudent man did not fear . . . . . to call it—and to affirm that through these . . . . . a certain youthfulness is procured.” ORELL.]

## VIII

Yet, lest I seem, when questioned, to disclose absolutely nothing of what I think about matters of this kind, I can say:

What if the primary matter that has been divided into the four elements of the universe contains, enfolded within its own principles, the causes of all miseries? What if the movements of the stars, at definite signs, configurations, times, and positions, produce these evils and bring upon the things subject to them the necessities of various dangers? What if the vicissitudes of things occur at fixed times and, as with the tides of the sea, prosperity sometimes flows in, but sometimes flows backward again as evils return? What if this dross of matter, which we tread beneath our feet [Col. 0731A], has received as its law that it must breathe out the most harmful vapors, by which this air is corrupted and both brings corruption upon bodies and weakens human affairs? What if—and this is nearest to the truth—whatever seems adverse to us is not an evil to the world itself, and, because we judge everything according to our own conveniences, we charge the events of nature with guilt through misguided opinions?

Plato, that sublime summit and mainstay of philosophers, declared in his writings that those savage floods and conflagrations of the world were a purification of the earth. Nor did that prudent man fear to call the overthrow, calamity, ruin, destruction, and death of the human race a renewal of things, and to affirm that through them, when its powers have been restored, a certain youthfulness is procured.

[Note: [Col. 0732C]

### IX.—“What if someone accustomed to bake himself in the sun and to make his body dry?”

Elmenhorst collected, at this passage, many very well-known examples of this practice among the ancient gymnasts. The ancients called exposure to the sun *insolatio*, ἡλίωσις (*hēliōsis*, “sunning”), and ἡλιοκαΐα (*hēliokaïa*, “sun-burning”), and used it, on physicians’ prescription, to make the body dry. Compare Meursius, *Criticus*, p. 8; Isaac Casaubon, who discusses this subject extensively, on Persius, *Satire* IV, v. 32; and Ast on Plato’s *Phaedrus*, p. 262 ff. [Col. 0732D] ORELLI.

**“Blasts” (*flaturas*).** A rather unusual formation for *flatus*. Vitruvius nevertheless has it at II.7: “in the blowing of bronze” (*in aeris flatura*). ORELLI.

**“Idly to glow beneath the flames.”** Fulvius Ursinus conjecturally reads “idly to scorch himself” (*ocióse ustulare*). But nothing should be changed. For *rutilare* is the proper and precise verb in this matter: that is, “to impart a ruddy color to the skin.” Thus Persius, *Satire* IV, v. 15, speaks of “skin treated by the sun,” where the ancient scholiast says: “Treated, that is, by the *chromatiarii*; for those who apply color are called *chromatiarii*, either those who spend the whole day in the arena or those who remain in the sun. For the ancients used to anoint themselves and remain in the sun so that the body might absorb the oil.” ORELLI.

**“Our petty advantages” (*commodulis nostris*).** That is, advantages which may appear great to us but are nothing in comparison with the welfare of this whole universe, as Gesner correctly explains in the *Thesaurus*. *Commodulum* is a ἅπαξ λεγόμενον (*hapax legomenon*, a word occurring only once). ORELLI.

### IX

“The sky does not rain,” someone says, “and we are suffering from some inexplicable shortage of grain.” But why do you demand that the elements serve your necessities? And, so that you may live more comfortably and delicately, must the conditions of the seasons submit themselves to your conveniences? What if, in the same way, someone passionately fond of sailing were to complain that there had long been no winds and that the sky’s blasts had fallen still? [Col. 0731B; Col. 0732A] Must we therefore say that this calm of the world is harmful because it obstructs the wishes of travelers?

What if someone accustomed to bake himself in the sun and to make his body dry were similarly to complain that the pleasure of clear weather had been taken away by continual clouds? Must the clouds therefore be called hostile because they hang as a covering, since idle desire is not permitted to glow beneath the flames and prepare grounds for drinking bouts? All these events which occur and take place beneath this mass of the world must be weighed, not by reference to our petty advantages, but by the principles and ordinances of nature itself.

> **Note [Col. 0731B].** The manuscript inserts *sunt* (“are”), which is characteristic of Arnobius.

### X.—“Excessive moisture” (*uliginem nimiam*)

Servius on Virgil, *Georgics* II, v. 184: “*Uligo* is properly the natural moisture of the earth, never departing from it.” ELMENHORST.

**“How can you know whether it does not in this way remove what is excessive?”** [Col. 0733B] This stands for: “How do you know that it does not in this way remove what is excessive?” *Scio ut* or *ne hoc sit* in place of an infinitive belongs to earlier Latin. Plautus, *Asinaria*, Act III, scene 3, v. 154: “If your mother knows about the money—how it was done.” ORELLI.

**“So that through its own losses it may impose a limit upon things growing luxuriantly.”** Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 30: “We are a burden to the world; the elements scarcely suffice for us, our necessities grow more constricted, and complaint is everywhere, since nature can no longer sustain us. In truth, plagues, famines, wars, and the engulfing of cities must be regarded as remedies, like the pruning of an overgrown human race.” [Col. 0733C] ELMENHORST.

### X

Nor, if something occurs which has favored us personally or our affairs with less than happy results, is it therefore immediately evil and to be classed as a destructive thing. [Col. 0732B] The world rains or does not rain for itself. And, though you may perhaps not know it, either it bakes away excessive moisture with the heat of drought or tempers the aridity of a very long period by downpours of rain.

It produces pestilences, diseases, famines, and other destructive forms of evil. [Col. 0733A] How can you know whether it does not in this way remove what is excessive, so that through its own losses it may impose a limit upon things growing luxuriantly?

### XI.—“Whose origin or cause you are unable to explain or unravel”

*Dissolvere* (“unravel”), which has been added, comes from the manuscript codex. Arnobius is fond of piling up several verbs with the same meaning; this has led some to suppose that these books contain numerous glosses. Likewise, below, *constringere* (“constrict”) and *sustinere* (“endure”) were added from the same book. HERALDUS.

**“Perhaps obstructs your pleasures.”** So the manuscript codex has it. The reading “perhaps obstructs the happiness of your…” is exceedingly corrupt.

**“Freeze, constrict.”** So the manuscript codex. Gelenius should not have regarded *constringere* as a gloss, for our African author is exceedingly fond of accumulating synonyms, following the example of the ancients. See Aulus Gellius, Book XIII, ch. 23. MEURSIUS, in the Appendix.

**“Hellebore is poison to human beings.”** Lucretius, Book IV, v. 644:

> Therefore hellebore is a bitter poison to us,  
> But it increases the fat of goats and quails. [Col. 0733D]

Italy calls hellebore *veratrum*. Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XXV, ch. 5. ELMENHORST; ORELLI.

**“The wolf lies in wait for sheepfolds.”** Virgil, *Aeneid* IX:

> Just as a wolf that has lain in wait for a full sheepfold.

Arnobius has many passages from Virgil. HERALDUS.

**“Shall I curse, forsooth?”** The manuscript codex has *maledicam sc.*, that is, *scilicet*. Stewechius conjectures *Maledicam ilicet*, or rather *Maledicus ilicet*. The Leiden editor has *Maledicam sic*. But the received reading is excellent. For among Latin authors *scilicet* very frequently introduces an ironic question with a certain bitterness and mockery and prepares a negative answer. Gesner adduces several examples from Cicero in the *Thesaurus*; add Juvenal, *Satire* I, 122:

> You would, of course, shudder and regard it as a greater portent  
> If a woman bore a calf, or a cow produced a lamb? [Col. 0734B]

So the Germans say, “So? What do you suppose?” In his *Diatribe on Statius’ Silvae*, Addenda, p. 412, Gronovius defends the old reading *maledicam si*, for *an maledicam*, and supports it with several examples. But I admit that I have not yet found in Arnobius any such transposition of conjunctions in direct questions. I therefore prefer *scilicet*, arising from the abbreviation *sc.* [Col. 0734C] ORELLI.

**“Such savage portents” (*tum saeva prodigia*).** Balthasar Lydius, in Meursius, p. 9, prefers *tam saeva prodigia* (“such savage portents”), with the approval of Colvius on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* III, p. 198, Oudendorp’s edition, who discusses this word extensively. ORELLI.

**“Living creatures” (*genituris spirantibus*).** *Geniturae* here, in an altogether unusual sense, means “creatures” or “animals.” The commentators on this passage do not say so much as γρῦ (“a word”), nor do the lexicons recognize this meaning. Tertullian similarly uses it more than once of human beings; for example, *Against Marcion* IV.23, where he renders the words of the divine Savior, Luke 9:41, thus: “O unbelieving generation, how long shall I be among you? How long shall I endure you?” ORELLI.

### XI

Do you dare to say that this or that is evil in the world when you are unable to explain or unravel either its origin or its cause? And because it perhaps obstructs the pleasures of your delicacies and desires, do you call it harmful and harsh?

What then? Because cold is hostile to your limbs and is accustomed to freeze the heat of your blood, should there therefore be no winter in the world? And because you cannot endure the most scorching suns, must summer be removed from the year and nature be ordered anew under different laws?

> **Note [Col. 0733B].** “And because you cannot bear, endure.” So the manuscript. Correctly.

Hellebore is poison to human beings: should it therefore not have been born? The wolf lies in wait for sheepfolds: is nature at fault because it produced a beast exceedingly troublesome to wool-bearing animals? A serpent takes life with its bite: shall I, forsooth, curse the first beginnings of things because they added such savage portents to living creatures? [Col. 0733B; Col. 0734A]

### XII.—“To dictate a condition to those more powerful: to will that what you desire should happen”

The passage must be punctuated in this way, with Stewechius. Evidently the immoderate man demands that those more powerful should will and ratify what he himself has desired. ORELLI.

**“They do not occur for a particular part” (*non partiliter fiant*).** Thus it should be read, not *pariliter*. *Partiliter*, opposed to *generaliter*, occurs very frequently in Julius Firmicus’ *Mathesis*. [Col. 0734D] HERALDUS.—Compare the same author in *Adversaria* I.3, p. 6. *Partiliter* properly means “by parts.” Thus our author below, Book XI, ch. 4: “For this is proper to the gods: to fill all things with their power, not to be present in some particular part anywhere, but to be wholly present everywhere.” Here, however, it means “for the advantage or sake of some particular part or particular individuals,” as opposed to “the total reckoning of the whole,” as Fulvius Ursinus excellently corrected it. The manuscript had *sensus* (“sense”), with no sense. ORELLI.

### XII

It is an exceedingly arrogant thing, when you are not even your own master and are yourself situated within another’s possession, to dictate a condition to those more powerful: to will that what you desire should happen, rather than what you find established in things by ancient ordinances.

Therefore, human beings, if you wish your complaints to possess any validity, you must first show whence or who you are; whether the world was generated and fashioned for you, or whether you entered it as tenants from foreign regions. Since it is not within your power to say this, and you cannot explain for what purpose you dwell beneath this vault of heaven, cease to suppose that anything pertains especially to you. For the things that occur do not occur for a particular part, but return and are referred to the total reckoning of the whole.

### XIII.—“The gods bring all evils”

The text had: “they underwent all evils” (*mala omnia adierunt*). We have restored the entirely correct reading from the manuscript codex. HERALDUS.—*Ferunt* in the sense of *inferunt*, the simple verb for the compound. MEURSIUS.

**“That you are shamelessly making false accusations.”** That is, most impudently. Just as one who steals openly is called by the jurists a more shameless thief, so there is the expression “a shameless brow.” Accordingly he says *improbe*: “amid open and manifest lies.” For here the height of impudence consists in the fact that, although the lie is obvious and manifest, the false accusation is nevertheless obstinately and shamelessly pressed and defended. For, as Aristotle says in the *Rhetoric*, τὸ τὰ φανερὰ ἀρνεῖσθαι (“to deny evident facts”) is a feature of ἀναισχυντία (*anaischyntia*, shamelessness). [Col. 0735B] HERALDUS.

**“It is approximately three hundred years.”** Similarly in Book II he says: “Three hundred years ago your religion did not exist.” From these words it is evident that our author lived under Diocletian, approximately three hundred years after the Savior’s birth, and that he wrote this work, filled with varied learning, around the year of Christ 298, the year 1050 from the foundation of Rome—or at the end of 1049—during the consulship of Maximian and Gordian, as the most learned Joannes Meursius observes. ELMENHORST.

**“No immediate cheapness.”** Oudendorp, on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* V, [Col. 0735C] p. 348, prefers *prorsus* (“at all”) to *protinus*; but I would not alter *protinus*, meaning “soon, after a short interval,” as opposed to continual barrenness. ORELLI.

**“Without any holidays, as the saying goes.”** That is, without any intermixture of good things. Hence Philo says that God alone truly keeps festival, because he alone enjoys true joy and sincere peace, uninterrupted by even the semblance of war. His words in the commentary *On Cain* are:

> Μόνος ὁ Θεὸς ἀψευδῶς ἑορτάζει, καὶ γὰρ μόνος γήθει, καὶ μόνος χαίρει καὶ μόνος εὐφραίνεται, καὶ μόνῳ τὴν ἀμιγῆ πολέμου συμβέβηκεν εἰρήνην ἄγειν.

“God alone truly keeps festival; for he alone rejoices, he alone is glad, and he alone delights, and to him alone it belongs to maintain peace unmixed with war.” HERALDUS.

### XIII

“Because of the Christians,” they say, “the gods bring all evils, and destruction is prepared by the powers above for the crops.” I ask: when you say these things, do you not see that you are shamelessly making false accusations amid open and manifest lies? [Col. 0734B; Col. 0735A]

It is approximately three hundred years, a little less or more, since we began to exist as Christians and to be counted in the world. Throughout all these years, were there continual wars and continual barrenness? Was there no peace on earth, no immediate cheapness or abundance of goods? For this must first be established by anyone who accuses us: that these calamities were perpetual and unbroken, that mortals never drew breath at all, and that without any holidays, as the saying goes, they endured manifold forms of danger.

> **Note [Col. 0735B].** The manuscript wrongly has “not all” (*omnia non*).

### XIV.—“That innumerable victories were carried away from defeated enemies”

Cannegieter thinks that *de victis* should be read, which says something more than *victis*: namely, enemies who have been utterly conquered. ORELLI.

**“That the greatest yields of the grain supply very often occurred.”** Stewechius was the first to restore this reading from the manuscript codex. The Roman edition and others following it—for example Oberthür’s—have *proventus annorum* (“the yields of the years”). This is defended by N. Heinsius on Tacitus, *Dialogue on the Corruption of Eloquence*, ch. 19, p. 945, Oberlin’s edition, and *Adversaria* III.3, p. 923, by appeal to Pliny, *Natural History* XII.1: “From trees comes the liquid of oil, restoring the limbs, and the strength-giving drink of wine; finally, so many flavors of the year coming spontaneously,” where *venientes* stands for *provenientes*. But I would change nothing contrary to the authority of the manuscript codex. [Col. 0735D] ORELLI.

**“And all commerce stood stupefied, the authority of prices having been laid low.”** Nothing could have been expressed more precisely. Commerce is therefore said to “stand stupefied,” that is, to remain as though beset by stupor and torpor, just as the Greeks say λιθοῦσθαι (*lithousthai*, “to be turned to stone”) of those who stand thunderstruck after being struck by some stupor. From this arose the myth of the Gorgon’s head. HERALDUS.

**“For how could affairs be carried on, and how could the mortal race have endured until the present time?”** Fulvius Ursinus thinks *quiret durare* (“could endure”) should be read; with Cannegieter I prefer this, indeed regard it as uniquely correct. For *potest* (“it is possible”) is never understood by ellipsis unless *-ne* precedes, as, for example, “Am I, defeated, to desist from my undertaking?”—that is, “Is it possible?”—or unless in the second clause another *potest* has preceded in the first. One therefore cannot say absolutely, “Who to do?” or “Who to be done?” with *potest* or *possibile est* understood. ORELLI.

Ursinus’ correction *quiret durare* is good. But the observations adduced concerning an ellipsis of *potest* or *possibile est* contribute little. The completion of this kind of accusative-and-infinitive construction varies entirely according to the meaning of each sentence. It generally marks the emotion of someone wondering, indignant, or grieving, so that the proposed *potest* or *possibile est* is too vague and uncertain. For in Juno’s words, “Am I, defeated, to desist from my undertaking?” we must understand: “How grievous and unworthy of my majesty it is!” Thus the reason for the appended interrogative particle *-ne* becomes clearer: it has assuredly attached itself to *me* from some suppressed question in the other clause—“Is it to be endured that I should desist?” In such formulas, however, where emotion generally predominates, no precise account of each individual word is required; and the question itself, however it is to be understood, is a sign of an agitated mind.

Nor is it true that such a thought cannot be expressed without a question, which makes the prescribed rule—“Such an ellipsis never occurs unless *-ne* precedes”—still less probable. Consider Livy III.67, where the consul Quintus, filled with grief and indignation, speaks as follows: “That you should know this! That this should be handed down to posterity in memory!”—that is, “How shameful this is for me as consul!” You certainly see no interrogative particle, although *-ne* could be understood with *vos*: “Are you to know this?” But Greek examples demonstrate still more clearly that the alleged necessity of adding *-ne* is a vain invention.

Strepsiades cries in Aristophanes’ *Clouds*, v. 267:

> Τὸ δὲ μὴ κυνέην οἴκοθεν ἐλθεῖν, ἐμὲ τὸν κακοδαίμον᾽ ἔχοντα—

“And for wretched me to have left home without a dogskin cap!”

Here the scholiast says: Οὐ μωρὸν δηλονότι, οὐκ ἀνόητον—“Is it not foolish, evidently? Is it not senseless?”

Xenophon, *Cyropaedia* II.2:

> Τῆς τύχης, τὸ ἐμὲ νῦν κληθέντα δεῦρο τυχεῖν—

“What fortune, that I should happen to have been summoned here now!”

That is, οὐκ ἄθλιόν ἐστι (“is it not wretched?”), or ὡς δυνατόν ἐστι (“how can it be possible?”). [Cols. 0736B–D] OCHSNER.

### XIV

And yet do we not see that, amid these years and these periods, innumerable victories have been carried away from defeated enemies; that the boundaries of the empire have been extended; and that nations of previously unheard-of name have been reduced beneath its power? [Col. 0735B] Do we not see that the greatest yields of the grain supply have very often occurred, together with such cheapness and abundance of goods that all commerce stood stupefied, the authority of prices having been laid low? [Col. 0736A]

For how could affairs be carried on, and how could the mortal race have endured until the present time, if the fertility of things had not supplied everything that practical need required?

> **Note [Cols. 0735B–0736B].** “And yet” (*atqui*) is the manuscript reading; I think it should be retained and the question marks removed throughout this entire period. MEURSIUS.
>
> **Note [Col. 0736B].** The manuscript has: “as practical need required” (*usus ut posceret*).

### XV.—“And they were relieved by abundance”

Observe here the purely adversative use of *et* (“and”) for *at* (“but”), concerning which P. Burmann expresses doubt on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV, v. 613. ORELLI.

**“And were afterwards corrected by victories and successes.”** Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis* IV.14: “For then misfortunes and grievous calamities are corrected—διορθοῦνται (*diorthountai*)—by prosperous courses of events.” HERALDUS.

**“They are not angry and difficult.”** The opposite is “easy and propitious.” Those are called “difficult,” δύσκολοι and δυσέριδες, who possess a fastidious kind of irascibility, as Seneca says: people who do not readily accommodate themselves to the behavior of others but immediately grow angry if anything appears insufficiently harmonious with their disposition—or rather, with their disease. For this reason the Greeks also elegantly call them δύστροποι (*dystropoi*, ill-tempered). HERALDUS.

**“They always restore themselves to their original state by recollecting offenses.”** So the manuscript codex, and I do not see why this reading should be rejected. Fulvius Ursinus reads: “they restore themselves entirely through the recollection of offenses,” etc. Arnobius means that the gods are angry and difficult by nature, to such an extent that, even if they are at some time appeased by prayers or sacrifices, they immediately restore themselves to their original state at the very first recollection of offenses—that is, they return to the former disposition of wrath innate in them.

For “in playful alternations” (*vicibus ludicris*), Meursius, *Criticus* VII.9, suspects that *lubricis* (“slippery”) should be read. Not badly. [Cols. 0737B–C] ORELLI.

### XV

But there have sometimes been periods of some scarcity. And they were relieved by abundance. Again, certain wars were conducted contrary to our wishes. And they were afterwards corrected by victories and successes.

What, then, shall we say? That the gods are at one moment mindful of our wrongs and at another moment forgetful of them? If, whenever there is famine, they are said to be angry, it follows that in times of abundance they are not angry and difficult. Thus the matter is brought to this point: in playful alternations they both lay aside and resume their anger, and always restore themselves to their original state by recollecting offenses. [Col. 0736B; Col. 0737A]

### XVI.—“The Alamanni”

We should understand here not a particular German tribe but the German nation as a whole. Salmasius demonstrates this at length in commenting upon the words of Flavius Vopiscus in the *Life of Proculus*, *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. II, p. 761:

> For he crushed, with no slight splendor of glory, the Alemanni, who at that time were still called Germans.

Salmasius shows that the Alamanni were a populous nation of Germany and, as Aurelius Victor writes, fought remarkably well from horseback. When Caracalla defeated them near the Main, he assumed the surname *Alamannicus*. They subsequently gave their name to all Germany, which from them was called *Alamannia*, and is still so called among the French. This occurred not long before the time of Vopiscus, who lived contemporaneously with Arnobius under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian. Meursius’ conjecture *Alanos* (“Alans”) is therefore unnecessary. [Col. 0737D] ORELLI.

**“If among the Gaetulians and Tingitanians.”** This is the entirely correct emendation of Ludovicus Carrio, deservedly admitted into the text by the Leiden editor and approved also by Livineius on the *Latin Panegyrics*, p. 158, Arntzen’s edition. The old reading, “if among the Gaetulians, then the Aquitanians,” appears to have arisen from some pedantic copyist who intruded the Aquitanians here because Gaul had been mentioned in the preceding words and Aquitania was one of its provinces. But in the words “if among the Gaetulians,” etc., Arnobius begins a new sentence and speaks of the peoples of northern Africa afflicted by calamities of this kind. ORELLI.

**“Nothing joyful.”** The manuscript has the neuter *nihil laetum*. MEURSIUS, in the Appendix.

**“Enemies” (*duelles*).** That is, *hostes*. Gesner’s *Thesaurus* cites this as the only example of the word from Arnobius. The compound *perduellis* is much more frequent. It derives from the archaic *duellum* for *bellum* (“war”); see the commentators on Festus under *duellum*. [Col. 0738B] ORELLI.

**“Against favorable hopes.”** The manuscript has *in adversos*. I read *inadversus*, analogous to *inante* and *incoram*. [Col. 0738C] MEURSIUS.

**“By the foulness of an evil omen.”** Heraldus, in the *Second Studies* containing his observations on Salmasius’ *Attic and Roman Law*, prefers “of an evil name” (*mali nominis*). Stewechius conjectures “by the ill-omened character of an evil omen” (*mali ominis obscaevitate*), citing Nonius under *obcaevavit*, as though the word meant “he brought a *scaevum*, an evil omen,” *scaevus* meaning left or sinister and therefore unfavorable in the Greek sense; for among the Romans left-hand or sinister auguries were good and favorable.

But, as Heraldus correctly warns, nothing should be changed. *Obscenus* and *obscenitas* are properly used of all evil things, evidently because everything obscene and foul appeared mournful and ill-omened to the ancients, just as, conversely, pure and purified things appeared joyful and fortunate. Thus Virgil, *Georgics* I, v. 470, has “ill-omened dogs”; see Vossius there. Likewise Virgil, *Aeneid* III, vv. 242, 262, has “ill-omened birds”; and Festus, under *Alliensis*: “The Allian day was called by the Romans a day of the foulest omen.” Compare Festus under *Oscus* and Nonius under *Obscenus*. ORELLI.

### XVI

Yet the nature of this claim cannot be known by any intelligible conception. If the gods wished the Alamanni and Persians to be defeated precisely because Christians lived and dwelt among their peoples, how did they grant victory to the Romans, when Christians likewise lived and dwelt among their peoples?

If they wished mice and locusts to swarm portentously in Asia and Syria because Christians similarly lived among their peoples, why was nothing of the kind produced at the same time in Spain and Gaul, although innumerable Christians also lived in those provinces?

If for this reason they sent such drought and aridity among the Gaetulians and Tingitanians, why in that year did they grant the Moors and Numidians the most abundant harvests, although the same religion was also practiced in these regions? [Col. 0737B]

If, in any particular city, their aversion to our name caused very many people to die of famine, why in that same place did the high price of grain make not only people who were not of our body, but Christians as well, richer and exceedingly wealthy?

Either, therefore, everyone ought to have possessed nothing joyful, if we are the cause of evils—for we are present among every nation—or, since you see joyful circumstances mixed with hardships, cease to ascribe to us what injures your affairs, when we do nothing to obstruct joyful and prosperous circumstances.

For if I cause things to go badly, why do I not prevent them from going well? If my name is the cause of great scarcity, why do I do nothing to prevent the greatest fertility? If I am said to bring the fortune by which wounds are received in wars, why, when enemies perish, am I not regarded as a favorable, left-hand augury, nor denounced as opposing favorable hopes through the foulness of an evil omen? [Col. 0738A]

> **Note [Cols. 0737B–0738B].** The manuscript has “into adverse…” Fulvius reads: “nor do I oppose favorable circumstances.” Others: “nor do I oppose favorable hopes; nor am I denounced through the foulness of an evil omen.”

### XVII.—“The ministers of the divine powers”

*Antistites* means simply “priests,” nothing more. See the author of the extremely virulent refutation of Antonius Cercoetius’—that is, Denis Petau’s—observations on the notes of the distinguished Salmasius on Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, p. 147 ff., who discusses this subject extensively. Thus Livy, *History* I.7: “The Potitii, instructed by Evander, were for many generations the ministers of that rite.” Compare the passages cited by Elmenhorst. [Col. 0738D] ORELLI.

**“Why, just as…” (*cur ut*).** The Leiden editor restored *ut*, which is necessary to the sense. Behotus conjectures *qui irasci*, not badly. ORELLI.

**“For what else is it to be angry than to be insane, than to rage?”** Thus Horace, *Epistles* II.1: “Anger is a brief madness.” Seneca, *On Anger* I.1: “Some of the wise have called anger a brief insanity.” ELMENHORST.—Arnobius, moreover, speaks here according to the opinion of the Stoics, who attributed a benign and beneficent nature to God and denied that he could become angry. HERALDUS.

**“Toward the torments of another’s pain,” etc.** This is the reading required, since the manuscript codex has *crucis*, evidently for *cruces*. See Heraldus, *Second Studies: Observations on Salmasius’ Attic Law*, p. 600. Meursius, in the Appendix, suspects that it should read: “to revel amid another’s pains, in the estrangement of a savage and brutal heart.” ORELLI.

**“This, then, is what the great gods know.”** *Norunt* here means “experience” or “undergo,” Greek πάσχουσι (*paschousi*). *Scire* below has the same meaning. Thus even inanimate things—for example, wood—are said to “know” or “not know” woodworms. [Col. 0739B] HERALDUS.—By “the great gods,” Turnebus, *Adversaria* XV.21, understands those who possessed the greatest authority and divine power and were publicly worshiped, such as Jupiter, Juno, and so forth, whom Asconius calls the Lares of the city of Rome. ORELLI.

**“You assert that it experiences.”** Stewechius prefers *sentire* (“feels”) to *scire*, since *perpetiuntur* (“undergo”) and *sentiunt* (“feel”) preceded. But nothing should be changed. For *scire*, *nosse*, and similar verbs are not infrequently used by the ancients for “feel” or “experience.” See N. Heinsius, *Adversaria* III.3, p. 417. Arnobius speaks in the same sense below, ch. 23, saying that demons and heroes do not “know” heavenly things and remain involved in this coarser matter. [Col. 0739C] ORELLI.

**“Sparks flash forth.”** He describes the bearing of a man overcome by anger. Lucretius, Book III, v. 290:

> There is also that heat in the mind which it assumes in anger,  
> When it grows fierce and a sharp blaze flashes from the eyes.

Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, 101:

> He is driven by these furies, and from all his burning face  
> Sparks leap forth; a sharp fire flashes from his eyes.

Virgil imitated Lucretius. All these signs, moreover, are the same in madmen, as Seneca shows in his books *On Anger*. Thus Menaechmus in Plautus is shown to be insane by this sign also: “Look how his eyes flash!” HERALDUS.

**“Sparks flash forth, flames surge, the panting breast casts breath from the mouth.”** Fulvius Ursinus reads: “the panting breast surges with flames and casts foam from the mouth.” Salmasius in the Leiden edition reads: “Fiery sparks flash forth, the panting breast surges, foam is cast from the mouth.” Meursius reads: “is tossed from the mouth.”

For my part, I see no reason to abandon the ancient reading. “Flames surge” is properly said of the flames of anger which had previously been enclosed in the breast but now break forth and boil over. The following words are no less satisfactory: “the panting breast casts breath from the mouth.” Thus Seneca, *Medea*, vv. 387 ff.:

> Such a woman runs back and forth, and in her savage movement,  
> Bearing in her face the signs of maddened fury,  
> Her face aflame, she draws breath from deep within.

Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, vv. 101 ff.; Lucretius III.290; and Seneca, *On Anger* I.1, who lists constricted breathing among the signs of anger. [Col. 0739D] ORELLI.

Lactantius expresses the same thought most elegantly in *On the Anger of God*, ch. 1:

> But if anger is unbecoming to a human being who is otherwise wise and dignified—since, whenever it enters someone’s mind, it arouses such great waves, like a savage storm, that it changes the mind’s condition: the eyes blaze, the mouth trembles, the tongue falters, the teeth chatter, and now a spreading blush, now a whitening pallor alternately stains the face—how much more unbecoming to God is so foul a transformation?

HERALDUS.
