**“From his burning words the dryness of his lips grows white.”** Lactantius, *On the Anger of God*, ch. 5, similarly says of an angry person:

> The eyes blaze, the mouth trembles, the tongue falters, the teeth chatter, and now a spreading blush, now a whitening pallor marks the face with alternating stains.

Likewise I would prefer to interpret Virgil’s words about Dido, *Aeneid* IV.499, “At once pallor seizes her face,” as pallor of countenance revealing Dido’s anger against Aeneas, rather than, with Servius and Heyne, as consciousness of her intended death. Heraldus understands Arnobius’ words as referring to foam. Wrongly. [Col. 0740B] ORELLI.

### XVII

And yet, O great worshipers and ministers of the divine powers, why, just as you assert that those narrow-minded gods are angry with Christian peoples, do you not also notice and perceive what shameful emotions and what unseemly forms of madness you attribute to the divine powers? [Col. 0738B]

For what else is it to be angry than to be insane, to rage, to be swept into a lust for vengeance, and, in the estrangement of a brutalized heart, to revel amid the torments of another’s pain? This, then, is what the great gods know, undergo, and feel—what wild animals and beasts experience, and what deadly water-snakes hold in their poisoned fangs. [Col. 0739A]

That which is culpable as fickleness in a human being, as something earthly in a living creature, you assert that that surpassing nature, established in the steadfastness of perpetual virtue, experiences. And what necessarily follows except that sparks flash forth from their eyes, flames surge, the panting breast casts breath from the mouth, and from their burning words the dryness of their lips grows white?

### XVIII.—“Where passion is situated … disturbance follows; where there is disturbance, there are pain and distress”

Arnobius here follows the definitions of the Stoics, who distinguish emotion, passion, and disturbance. Seneca, *On Anger* II.2:

> So that you may know how emotions begin, grow, or become unrestrained: the first movement is involuntary, like a preparation for emotion and a kind of threat. The second is accompanied by a will that is not yet obstinate. The third movement is already beyond control and has defeated reason.

Arnobius accordingly calls the mind’s first movement “emotion” here, in the most restricted sense; the second, “passion”; and the third, “disturbance.” Compare J. Lipsius, *Introduction to Stoic Philosophy* III, Dissertation 7, p. 764 ff., *Works*, vol. IV, Wesel edition. [Col. 0740C] ORELLI.

**“Where there are pain and distress, there is already room for diminution and corruption.”** Similarly in Book II:

> But that which is exposed and open to passion is declared corruptible by the very fact that passibility intervenes.

And in Book VII:

> For whatever is vexed by the movement of some thing is evidently passible and fragile; and that which is subject to passion and fragility must necessarily be mortal.

ELMENHORST.

### XVIII

But if this is true, established, and known—that the gods grow hot with anger and that immortals are tossed by the disturbance of this kind of movement—then they are not immortal or everlasting, nor are they to be regarded as possessing any divinity.

> **Note [Col. 0739B].** So Sabinus correctly reads *fervescere* (“grow hot”). Fulvius has *effervescere* (“boil over”).
>
> **Note [Col. 0740B].** Fulvius has *aestimatione* (“valuation”) for *existimatione* (“estimation”).

For wherever there is any emotion, as the wise believe, passion must necessarily be present. [Col. 0739B] Where passion is situated, it is natural for disturbance to follow. [Col. 0740A] Where there is disturbance, there are pain and distress. Where there are pain and distress, there is already room for diminution and corruption. If these two afflict them, destruction is near at hand: death, which ends all things and takes life from every sentient being.

### XIX.—“They possess absolutely no proportion even of moderate fairness”

*Ratio* here means a proportion or due share. See Gesner’s index to the *Writers on Agriculture*. Hence also the German *die Ration*. [Col. 0740D] ORELLI.

**“To tear apart innocent crops.”** Cannegieter conjectures that *armenta* (“herds”) should perhaps be read instead. But nothing should be changed. For the ancients used *lacerare* and *dilacerare* not only of torn clothing and the mangling done by wild beasts, but also of any other things that were split, divided, or crushed. Thus Silius Italicus, *Punica* XIV, v. 14, speaks of Sicily being severed from Italy by an earthquake and an inrush of the sea:

> For once, through a hidden passage, the sea, driven blindly  
> By the force of a whirlwind, split apart the entrails  
> Of the lacerated earth.

Closer to our author is Columella, Book X, *On the Cultivation of Gardens*, v. 70:

> Banish sleep now, and with the curved plowshare’s tooth  
> Tear apart the green tresses.

Why, then, may crops broken and crushed by hail not properly be said to be torn apart by the gods? Meursius thinks it should be read: “So as to tear apart innocent crops—human beings, that is.” ORELLI.

**“To hate the Christian name and its worshipers.”** Cannegieter likewise thinks that *Christianum numen* (“the Christian divinity”) should be read, saying that *cultores* (“worshipers”) requires not *nomen* (“name”) but *numen* (“divinity”). Yet the received reading is sound: “its worshipers,” that is, Christ’s worshipers, which must be elicited from the preceding “Christian name.” Or, if anything is to be changed, I would prefer to read “the name of Christ” for Christ himself, just as “the name of God” stands for God. See Suicer, *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus of the Greek Fathers*, under ὄνομα (*onoma*, “name”). “The Christian name” means the Christians themselves, as we observed above at ch. V. [Col. 0741B] ORELLI.

### XIX

What of the fact that in this way you represent them not only as fickle and hot-tempered, but also—as ought to be kept far removed from gods—as inequitable and unjust, possessing absolutely no proportion even of moderate fairness?

For what is so unjust as to be angry with some and injure others, to complain about human beings and tear apart innocent crops? [Col. 0740B] To hate the Christian name and undermine their own worshipers with every kind of loss? [Col. 0741A]

### XX.—“Or is it perhaps?” (*an numquid*)

I know that Arnobius sometimes joins similar words, especially similar adverbs and particles; and *an* and *numquid* are similar. But we can dispense with that observation if we write *at numquid* (“but is it perhaps?”), changing a single letter. Must the same be said of the passage in Book II, ch. 5: “Or do you believe that these things happen everywhere and without purpose?” *Numquid*, without *an*, occurs frequently at Book I, ch. 2; Book V, ch. 24; and Book VII, ch. 9. CANNEGIETER, in Van Hoven’s *Literary Leisure*.

**“So that, stirred by wounds to their own persons.”** That is, by wounds belonging to themselves, οἰκείοις καὶ ἰδίοις (“their own and personal wounds”). The expression is Lucretian; Book II, v. 290:

> But lest the thing itself possess an inward necessity  
> In everything that is done.

Arnobius uses it frequently, and again a little below: “let them employ and test their own powers”; and below, ch. 36: “Venus, the lawful wife of the Trojan man and the revealer of an inward beauty”; and in Book II: “you trust that you become gods by your own inward effort”; and elsewhere. HERALDUS.

**“Therefore the gods seek human protection.”** Lactantius argues similarly, *Institutes* II.5:

> But when they punish those caught in sacrilege, they themselves distrust the gods’ power. For why do they not leave to the gods themselves the opportunity to avenge themselves, if they suppose that the gods have any power?

Moreover, the laws of the pagans demonstrate that they themselves elsewhere held this view: no penalties were established for perjurers if they had sworn falsely by the gods; by contrast, if they had sworn falsely by the emperors, penalties were ready and prepared. Compare law 11 of the Code, under the title *On Things Lent* (*De rebus creditis*). They therefore considered God the avenger of perjury and consequently believed that those who had violated the sanctity of an oath should be left to the judgment of the gods. “For wrongs done to the gods are the gods’ concern,” says Tiberius in Tacitus. [Col. 0741D] HERALDUS.

**“To repel, to ward off.”** Stewechius thinks *defendere* should be deleted as a gloss. Wrongly, for Arnobius loves to pile up terms of this kind having the same meaning. See Heraldus’ note above at the beginning of ch. XI. Moreover, *defendere* here means the same as “ward off” or “repel,” as Stewechius himself illustrates with several examples in his commentary on Vegetius, *On Military Matters* III.21, p. 260, Wesel edition. [Col. 0742B] ORELLI.—Compare Lipsius, *Various Readings* II.22. OCHSNER.

Or if it is an evil plan. Cannegieter maintains that *malum* should not be joined with the word *consilium*, but should be taken as an interjection expressing indignation or reproach. I, for my part, would not care to accept this explanation. For Arnobius is not so polished and refined a writer that absolutely nothing idle or superfluous occurs in him. Fulvius Ursinus conjectures that one should read: *sin alia consilium est aggredi nos via*, “but if the plan is to attack us by another way”; if this rested on the authority of the manuscript, I would not hesitate to admit it into the text. ORELLI.

*Indignationis.* Fulvius Ursinus, followed by the Leiden editor, emends this to *indicationis*; but *signum* and *indicium*, or *indicatio*, are plainly identical in meaning. I therefore see no reason why the ancient reading should be changed. ORELLI.]

## XX

Or is it perhaps for this reason that they rage against you as well, so that, provoked by inward wounds, you may rise up to avenge them? The gods, then, seek human protection; and unless they are protected by your championship, they are not themselves capable of repelling and defending themselves against the insults offered to them. Indeed, if it is true that they are burning with anger, allow them power over themselves; let them defend themselves. In vengeance for their offended majesty, let them display their inward powers and put their might to the test [Note: [Col. 0741B] Fulvius reads *expediantque*, “and deploy”]. If they wish, they can kill us by heat, by the most harmful cold, by pestilential winds, and by the most obscure causes of disease; they can consume us [Note: [Col. 0741B] This is absent from the manuscript] and utterly banish us from every society of mortals [Note: [Col. 0741B] Thus Fulvius. Sabinus incorrectly reads *mortalia*, “mortal things”]. Or, if it is an evil [Col. 0741B] plan to attack us by force, let them send forth [Note: [Col. 0741B] Fulvius reads *mittant*, “let them send”] some sign of their indignation [Col. 0742A], through which it may become clear to everyone that we dwell beneath the sky most unwillingly tolerated by them.

[Note: [Col. 0742C]

## XXI.—*Autumnitatem*

A word of ancient and approved Latin usage. Cato, *On Agriculture*, ch. 155: “At the beginning of autumn, when it is rainy, the danger from water is then greatest.” Here, however, Arnobius uses *autumnitas* for the produce of autumn, or of the vineyards. In the same sense Mamertinus, *Speech of Thanks to Julian*, ch. 22, uses *olivitas* for the yield of olives; see Livineius there, p. 183, vol. II of the *Panegyrici Veteres*, ed. Jaeger. Meursius has collected further examples in his *Criticus Arnobianus*, p. 16. ORELLI.

*At ex nostris exprimi unum prohibeant palmitis rorem* (“But from ours let them prevent even a single drop from the vine-shoot from being pressed out”). The commentators have obscured this perfectly sound passage with various conjectures. Some read *palmites*; the Leiden editor, *palmitibus*; Stewechius conjectures *vinum . . . rorem*, in the same sense in which Latin writers say *dies autumnos*, “autumn days,” for *autumnales*; *sexum marem*, “male sex,” for *masculinum*; and *verba oblivia*, “forgetful words,” for *obliviosa*. Nicolaas Heinsius, *Adversaria*, book I, ch. 10, p. 102, thinks one should read *udum rorem*, “moist dew.” Almost all these conjectures arose because learned men misunderstood the word *rorem*. For *ros* here is not that moisture which gathers on plants on clear nights—for that is wiped off, not pressed out—but the juice of the vine-shoots itself. Among Latin writers, *ros* is used of any liquid—water, wine, and so forth. Thus Sidonius, poem XXII, v. 25, has *ros meri*, “dew of unmixed wine,” for wine. By *unum rorem*, therefore, Arnobius means a single drop of wine or must. ORELLI.—Salmasius’ *palmitibus* seems to me more elegant; Heraldus also followed it, and the arrangement of the words is thoroughly Arnobian: “From your olive groves and vineyards . . . but from our vine-shoots.” Those who preferred *palmites* seem to have sought a nominative subject for the verb *prohibeant* corresponding to *fundi faciant* in the preceding clause. This is unnecessary, however, since the same nominative can readily serve as the subject of both clauses. OCHSNER.

*Et sub ipsis potum labris in acoris perfidiam vinum repente mutari* (“and let the wine, as it is being drunk at the very lips, suddenly be changed into the treachery of sourness”) [Col. 0743B]. Gelenius restored *potum* in place of the corrupt ancient reading *potu*; the Leiden editor changed it to *positum*, “placed,” for what reason I do not see. Arnobius elegantly called sourness, that is, vinegar, *perfidia*, “treachery”; for Latin writers apply *perfidus* and *perfidia* with particular aptness even to foods and drinks that disappoint the taster’s expectation. Thus Martial, book XII, epigram 48, in a passage very similar to ours:

> Let God himself charge nectar to my account: it will become vinegar,  
> And the wine-jar from the Vatican will become treacherous, worthless wine.

In the same sense Pliny, *Natural History* XIV.20, uses *nequitia*, “badness”: “In the badness of vinegar there lies a power useful for important purposes.” Compare the distinguished Nicolas Rigault on Artemidorus, *Oneirocritica*, book I, p. 45, vol. II, ed. Reiff. ORELLI.]

## XXI

Let them bestow favorable health upon you, but adverse and utterly wretched health upon us. Let them water your fields with timely rains, but drive away from our little plots every form of moisture that comes from rainfall. Let them see that your wool-bearing animals multiply through numerous offspring, but bring ill-omened sterility upon our flocks. Let them cause the full produce of autumn to pour forth from your olive groves and vineyards, but prevent even a single drop from the vine-shoot from being pressed out of ours [Note: [Col. 0742B] Fulvius reads: “any . . . drop”]. Finally and ultimately, let them command the produce in your mouths to retain its natural character; but in ours let honey become bitter [Note: [Col. 0742B] Fulvius reads “of oils” or “of the olive”], the flowing oil of olives grow rancid, and the wine, as it is being drunk at the very lips, suddenly be changed [Note: [Col. 0742B] Sabinus corruptly reads: “beneath the labor of the very drink”] into the treachery of sourness.

[Col. 0743A] [Note: [Col. 0743B]

## XXII.—*Neque ad vos plurimum*

*Plurimum* in place of *plus*. So below, book II, ch. 11, at the beginning: “And why is it that in this respect either you possess more or we less?” See Heraldus’ annotation on the words that follow. ORELLI.

*Quos in rebus tristissimis atque laetis* (“whom in the saddest and happiest circumstances”). It is customary for Arnobius and almost all writers of his age to interchange degrees of comparison and use the superlative for the positive, as “the children of the grammarians” (*οἱ τῶν γραμματικῶν παῖδες*) say. Hence we find Menander’s verse, “Bad associations corrupt good characters” (*φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί*), rendered among the ancient Doctors of the Church as: “The worst conversations corrupt good dispositions.” Such usages are countless in those writers. HERALDUS.]

## XXII

Since the facts themselves testify that this by no means occurs, and since it is evident that nothing less comes to us, nor anything more to you, from the benefits essential to life, what is this great passion for maintaining that the gods are enemies and foes of Christians, when you see that in the saddest and happiest circumstances Christians differ from you in no respect whatsoever? If you permit the truth to be spoken to you without any flattery: these are words, mere words—indeed, allegations believed through slander, not propositions established by the testimony of any knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 0743C]

## XXIII.—*Dii veri*

This is the excellent emendation of Fulvius Ursinus, deservedly admitted into the text by Oberthür. For how many of the pagans’ gods were free from the faults and passions that Arnobius lists below? The earlier reading was *dii vestri*, “your gods.” ORELLI.

[Col. 0743D] *Si se sibi aliquis adulatoria humilitate submittat* (“if someone subjects himself to him with flattering humility”). For this is what flatterers and those who wish to display great self-abasement are accustomed to do. Our author says below, book VII, ch. 13: “Then let him greet the god with bowed body, imitating the frightened trembling of a maidservant or a slave.” Tertullian elegantly calls this “diminishing oneself” in *On Repentance*, ch. 11: “Diminishing themselves at every encounter with any person of higher rank.” The Greeks call this *ταπεινοῦσθαι*, “to humble oneself,” *ὑποπίπτειν*, “to fall down before,” and *ὑποκύπτειν*, “to bow down”; Diodorus Siculus contrasts with these *ὑπερέχειν*, “to rise above” or “to be superior.” ORELLI.

*Quos jam dudum experientia doctorum daemonas appellat et heroas* (“whom the experience of learned men has long called demons and heroes”). The commentators have assailed this passage with various conjectures. The manuscript and the Roman edition have *appellat errores*, “calls errors,” which is manifestly corrupt; Gelenius changed this to *et hos*, “and these,” and later editors followed him down to Heraldus. Behotus, *Apophoreta*, book III, ch. 8, thinks one should read *et quos*, “and whom,” and, in the following words, *scit versari*, “knows to dwell.” Pontanus, as cited by Meursius, proposes *terrestres*, “earthly beings.” Stewechius proposes *errones*, “wanderers,” a term properly used of runaway slaves but also quite suitably applicable to demons wandering and flying about upon the earth; this does not seem wholly to be rejected. I have nevertheless preferred Fulvius Ursinus’ emendation, approved by Heraldus, *et heroas*, “and heroes,” since heroes are very frequently joined with demons—for example, by Augustine, *City of God*, book X, ch. 21: “They hold that heroes dwell with demons, by which name they call the souls of the dead who possess some merit.” Compare the commentators on the *Sayings of the Pythagoreans*, at the beginning. See more in Meursius, p. 17. ORELLI.

*Non nosse coelestia*, that is, not to know heavenly things through use and experience. See above, ch. 17, at the words “The great gods, therefore, know this,” and Heraldus’ note. ORELLI.]

## XXIII

But true gods, who are worthy to possess and bear the authority of this name, are neither angered nor indignant, nor do they devise through treacherous schemes anything that may harm another. For it truly [Col. 0743B] surpasses all impiety and sacrilege to believe that that wise [Col. 0744A] and most blessed nature considers it a great thing if someone subjects himself to it with flattering humility; and, if this is not done, that it believes itself despised and fallen from the pinnacle of the highest eminence. It is childish, petty, and paltry—scarcely appropriate even to those whom the experience of learned men has long called demons and heroes—not to know heavenly things and, though excluded from the nature proper to them, to dwell within this grosser material order of things.

[Note: [Col. 0744B]

## XXIV.—*Haruspices has fabulas, conjectores, arioli, vates . . . fanatici*

These same classes are joined together and rejected by Cicero as well, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.20, where Velleius says [Col. 0744C]: “Then follows your divination (*μαντική*) . . . by which we would be steeped in such great superstition, if we were willing to listen to you, that soothsayers, augurs, diviners, prophets, and interpreters would have to be worshiped by us.” The facts concerning the *haruspices*, or soothsayers who inspected entrails, are well known. *Conjectores* was the distinctive name for interpreters of dreams, *ὀνειροκριταί*. See Festus under this word, and Dacier there. *Arioli* were so called from altars (*arae*): they linger around altars, pray, and prophesy. See Isidore, *Origins*, book VIII, ch. 9. Donatus, on Terence, *Phormio*, act IV, scene 4, derives the term from *hari*, an ancient verb meaning “to speak.” Compare Havercamp on Tertullian, *Apology*, p. 227. *Fanatici* derives from *fana*, “temples” (the Glosses: *fanaticus*: *ἱερατικός*, “priestly”; *ἱερόδουλος*, “temple servant”); they were people who continually frequented temples to foretell the future. See Julius Firmicus Maternus, *Mathesis*, book III, ch. 13. By these terms Arnobius means impostors and itinerant charlatans who frequented public places, temples, forums, and streets, assailing foolish women and other ignorant persons with prophecies and similar vanities and extorting coins from their credulity. HERALDUS and ORELLI.

*Ac ne stipes exiguas consultoribus excutiant jam raris* (“and lest they shake out only meager coins from clients who are now few”). Cannegieter thinks one should read *stipes non exiguas*, “not meager coins.” But the words “clients who are now few” plainly show that this reading can by no means be admitted. The meaning is: fearing that their coins, already meager because of the scarcity of clients, may disappear altogether. ORELLI.

*Si quando vos velle rem venire in invidiam compererunt* (“if ever they discover that you wish their business to incur disrepute”). This passage has greatly tormented the commentators, who have tried to heal it with various conjectures. The Roman edition has *nos velle*, “that we wish,” and Thomas Canterus defends this, explaining *nos* as “we Christians,” who, inflamed with anger against those diviners, prophets, and so forth, wish their business to incur disrepute. Stewechius thinks one should read: *Si quando nos belle provenire compererunt, invident, indignantur, declamitantque*, “If ever they discover that we are prospering handsomely, they become envious and indignant, and declaim: ‘The gods are neglected,’” and so forth. Justus Lipsius, *Epistolary Questions*, book I, letter 20, proposes: *Si quando nos bellorum venire in invidiam*, and so forth, understanding this of the blame for wars and public calamity heaped upon Christians by those petty sacrificers. Cannegieter proposes *eos*, “that they wish,” namely those petty sacrificers. But they do not wish it; otherwise they would not seek consultation. The passage seems perfectly sound to me. Its meaning is: if ever they discover that you yourselves—that is, the pagans—wish their business to fall into disrepute. That such charlatans and petty sacrificers were despised and hated by the worshipers of the gods themselves because of their mendicancy and the wicked arts by which they deceived ignorant people is sufficiently clear from a great many ancient testimonies. Or, if something must be changed, I would much prefer simply to delete the pronoun *vos*, so that the phrase would be *velle venire in invidiam*, “to be inclined to incur disrepute,” equivalent to the simple *venire*. *Velle* with an infinitive is very frequently redundant in ancient writers. Thus in Petronius *velle* is several times used pleonastically; for example, ch. 70, §10: “Fortunata had now begun to want to dance,” where see Burmann and Antonius’ index. Particularly relevant to our passage is the author of the *Priapea*, poem LXXII, vv. 9–11:

> But from now on take care, in this place,  
> Not to deposit anything at all, lest a crowd  
> Of hungry dogs should want to come to me.

Here *velit venire*, “should want to come,” means simply *veniat*, “should come.” The sense of our passage would therefore be: “When they notice that their business—their tricks, their trade in oracles—is about to lose its credit” (*Wenn sie merken, dass ihre Sache, ihre Künste, ihr Orakelgewerbe, ihren Kredit verlieren wolle*). ORELLI.

*Negliguntur dii, clamitant, atque in templis jam raritas summa est* (“The gods are neglected, they cry, and there is now the greatest scarcity of worshipers in the temples”). Gelenius, with his usual passion for alteration, interpolated the perfectly sound manuscript reading as follows: “They become indignant and declaim: ‘In the temples,’” and so forth. The first edition corruptly has: “They are neglected, they declaim, and in the temples,” and so forth. Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “They cry,” and “the altars,” and so forth. But I see no reason for any change. ORELLI.

*Jacent . . . derisui caeremoniae* (“the ceremonies lie exposed to ridicule”). That is, they are despised and exposed or subjected to mockery. In the ancient writers *jacere*, “to lie,” is used hundreds of times of things neglected or despised, as is very well known. The construction of this verb with the dative, however, is rarer. Thus Silius Italicus, book XV, vv. 646–647:

> . . . Every commander who could inspire fear  
> In war lies fallen to his brother,

that is, has been slain and laid low by him. ORELLI.

*Occiderunt* (“have set”). Fulvius Ursinus thinks one should read *conciderunt*, “have collapsed.” But *occiderunt* is correct and much more expressive. The image is drawn from the stars, which set and disappear when the sun rises. ORELLI.

*Et merito humanum genus . . . tot laborum excruciatur aerumnis* (“And deservedly the human race . . . is tortured by the hardships of so many labors”). Stewechius thinks one should read *eo merito humanum genus . . . tot laborum exercetur aerumnis*, “and for that reason the human race is tried by the hardships of so many labors,” citing Virgil’s line, *Aeneid* III.182, “Son of Troy, sufficiently tried by suffering,” and Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book VI: “Psyche, tried by such great hardships.” This is indeed more elegant and more worthy of a good writer; but such elegance should not be demanded of Arnobius.

*Tot laborum excruciatur aerumnis.* Stewechius conjectures *exercetur aerumnis*, “is tried by hardships,” adducing two passages, one from Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book VI, “Psyche, tried by such great hardships,” and the other from Virgil, *Aeneid* III.182:

> . . . Son of Troy, sufficiently tried by suffering.

[Col. 0746C] But *excruciari aerumnis*, “to be tortured by hardships,” as well as “by grief,” “anxiety,” or “misery,” is no less frequent among Latin writers. Compare Terence, *The Self-Tormentor* I.2.4, and Cicero, *Letters to Friends* XIV.3. Nothing, therefore, should be changed. ORELLI.

*Et homines, brutum genus* (“And human beings, a brutish race”). Cannegieter thinks one should read *Ei homines*, “Those human beings”; not badly. ORELLI.—In a similar sense Horace, *Satires* I.3, called humanity “a dumb and shameful herd.” PRIOR.

*Furiosi* (“madmen”). See the remarks at the beginning of ch. I. ORELLI.]

## XXIV

These are your notions—irreverently conceived by you and still more irreverently believed. Indeed, to speak more truly, soothsayers devised these tales, along with dream-interpreters, diviners, prophets, and the invariably vain temple fanatics. Lest their arts perish and lest they shake out only meager coins from clients who are now few [Col. 0744B], whenever they discover that you wish [Col. 0745A] their business to incur disrepute, they cry: “The gods are neglected, and there is now the greatest scarcity of worshipers in the temples. The ancient ceremonies lie exposed to ridicule, and the once most venerable rites of sacred observance have set before the superstitions of new religions. Deservedly the human race is oppressed by the constraints of so many miseries and tortured by the hardships of so many labors.” And human beings—a brutish race, unable through innate blindness to see what lies beneath the light—dare in their madness to affirm what you, though sane, are not ashamed to believe.

[Note: [Col. 0746C]

## XXV.—*Mortalium . . . de saeculis*

That is, “from the race of mortals.” Lucretius very frequently uses *saeculum* for “race,” “offspring,” or “multitude”; for example, book III, v. 629: “the generations of earlier writers,” and book II, v. 77: “The generations of living creatures are changed in a brief space.” See Gesner in the *Thesaurus* and what we shall note below on book VII, ch. 24. ORELLI.

*Summitatem omnium summorum obtinentem* (“occupying the summit above all that is highest”). This God is presently called “the Highest,” the name by which the ancients designated that one supreme deity, the author [Col. 0746D] and governor of all things. Philosophers called God the Craftsman; others, eternal and most exalted Jupiter; the Greeks also called him *ὕψιστος*, “the Most High.” CANNEGIETER in Van Hoven, *Literary Leisure*.

*Temerariae vocis desperatione* (“with the desperate recklessness of a rash utterance”). Fulvius Ursinus thinks one should read *disparatione*, “separation”; others, incorrectly, *disceptatione*, “debate.” *Desperatio*, as Heraldus rightly explains, is the *ἀπόνοια*—the desperate recklessness—of those who have begun to despise divine anger and at the same time to cast aside all concern for salvation. *Desperatio vocis temerariae* therefore means the rash utterance of a wicked man who utterly despairs of his salvation: “a foolhardy, impious utterance” (*ein tollkühnes, ruchloses Wort*). ORELLI.

*In rebus fessis* (“amid exhausted circumstances”). Below, book III: “to bestow unexacted benefits upon exhausted and enfeebled circumstances.” He derives this from Virgil, *Aeneid* III.145:

> What end he brings to our exhausted circumstances, and whence  
> He bids us seek aid for our sufferings.

HERALDUS. Add Tacitus, *Annals* XV.50: “And a man had to be chosen who would bring aid to exhausted circumstances.” ORELLI.]

## XXV

Yet lest anyone, because of the lack of confidence in our reply, suppose that we ascribe gifts of tranquility to the gods, attach to them harmless minds [Note: [Col. 0745B] Sabinus incorrectly reads *affigere*], and represent them as removed from every disturbance, let us concede, as you have chosen to maintain, that they direct their anger against us, thirst for our blood [Col. 0745B], and have long desired to remove us from the generations of mortals. But if it is not troublesome or burdensome—if it is an act of common duty—to weigh the considerations in this dispute, not out of partiality but according to truth, we earnestly ask to hear from you [Col. 0746A] what principle or cause it is on account of which both the heavenly gods rage against us alone and embittered human beings blaze with fury.

“You practice impious religions,” they say, “and unprecedented forms of worship throughout the world.” What is this, you sharers in reason, that you, as human beings, dare to declare? What do you babble? What are you attempting to bring forth with the desperate recklessness of a rash utterance? Is it an accursed and ill-omened religion, full of impiety and sacrilege and contaminating ceremonies established in antiquity with the superstition of its own novelty, to adore the sovereign God, the Lord of all things that exist, who occupies the summit above all that is highest; to invoke him with reverent obedience; and amid circumstances of exhaustion to embrace, love, and venerate him with all our senses, so to speak?

[Note: [Col. 0747B]

## XXVI.—*Dilaceratis*

That is, with whips and iron claws, by which Christians’ sides were scraped and pierced. Among these lacerations we may also count the *ἑλκυσμοὶ θηρίων*, “dragging or mauling by wild beasts.” For Christ’s holy witnesses were sometimes given to beasts to be bitten, so that even by this means the greatest terror might be instilled into them. HERALDUS.

*Exuritis* (“you scorch”). I refer this not to burning alive, by which Christ’s soldiers were often “brought to their consummation” (*ἐτελειώθησαν*), but to the crosses and tortures that preceded their final “consummation” (*τελείωσις*). For Christians were tortured, lacerated, and scorched—that is, tested by fire and by heated plates brought close to them. The use of fire to extract the truth is a practice of the greatest antiquity. Arnobius rightly and appropriately places it last, for it was in fact very often the final *βασανισμός*, “torture.” Seneca, *On Anger*, book III, ch. 19: “He had tortured him by every means most dreadful in nature—with cords, plates, the spike, fire, and his own countenance.” [Col. 0747C] Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* X: “Nor were the wheel or rack, prepared after the Greek custom for his torture, now lacking. But, fortified by a marvelous determination, he yielded to no blows, not even to the fire itself.” Prudentius, *Martyrdom of Vincent*:

> Then, after hesitating a long while,  
> He decrees that the examination be conducted  
> by the most extreme means of all:  
> fire, the iron bed, and heated plates.

HERALDUS.

*Ad extremum nos feris et belluarum laniatibus objectatis* (“and finally you expose us to wild animals and the mangling of beasts”). Note the phrase “finally”: the punishments mentioned beforehand therefore came before the final contest. Hence Prudentius, in the first hymn *On the Crowns* (*περὶ στεφάνων*), vv. 54 ff.:

> They stand prepared to endure whatever final fate might bring:  
> Whether they must offer their necks to the public axe,  
> After the violence of cracking whips, after the fiery platforms;  
> Or whether their breasts must be offered to leopards or to lions.

They were exposed to beasts only when beast-hunts were being presented, since this was not permitted at other times. Hence, when people demanded that Polycarp be thrown to a lion [Col. 0747D], the proconsul replied that this could not be done because the beast-hunts had ended. Therefore that most steadfast and flourishing martyr was burned alive. HERALDUS.

*Is aut nomine appellandus est hominis, quamvis ille videatur sibi? aut Deus esse credendus est, quamvis ipse se esse mille profiteatur in vatibus? Trophonius nos impios*, etc. (“Should he either be called by the name of man, however much he may seem one to himself? Or should he be believed a god, though he himself professes himself such a thousand times through prophets? Does Trophonius call us impious,” etc.). This is the excellent emendation of Pierre Pithou, deservedly admitted into the text by the Leiden editor. The first Roman edition has, from the manuscript: “He should by no means be called by the name of man, however much he may appear one to himself; he should by no means be believed a god, however much he professes himself to be like one. Among the prophets, the profane one calls us impious,” and so forth. This is utterly false, for the oracles did not profess that those whom the nations worshiped were like gods, but that they were true gods; and in what follows, “the Dodonaean” would either lack “Jupiter” or have nothing to which it could refer. I therefore wonder that Oberthür removed this uniquely correct emendation from his text. Moreover, it may rightly seem strange to an attentive reader why Arnobius, while listing most of the Greek oracles, should have passed over the extremely famous oracle of Trophonius at Lebadeia in Boeotia. ORELLI.

*Clarius.* Clarian Apollo took his name from the grove of Claros near Colophon. Because this site seemed suitable to the priests for the construction of a temple, it eventually became famous through an oracle of Apollo founded by Manto, the daughter of the seer Tiresias, when she fled the Epigoni who had conquered Thebes, according to Pomponius Mela, *Description of the World* I.17. Its fame drew settlers there, by whose hands the town was built. It was the native city of Nicander. On the temple and oracle founded there, see Strabo, book XIV, p. 642; the scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius I.308; Pausanias, *Achaea*, ch. 3; and the authors cited by the distinguished Oberlin on Tacitus, *Annals* II.54, and on Vibius Sequester, p. 265, where he discusses the subject at length. ORELLI.—Compare the commentators [Col. 0748C] on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I.516. OCHSNER.

*Didymaeus.* Pomponius Mela, *Description of the World* I.17: “After the Basilicum, Ionia curves into several inlets; beginning its first bend at the promontory of Posideum, it encloses the oracle of Apollo, formerly called the Branchidae and now the Didymaean”; see Vossius there. Compare Strabo, book XIV, p. 634, ed. Casaubon, and Ernesti on Suetonius, *Caligula*, ch. 21. Apollo was called Didymaean from the name of the place, *Δίδυμα*; others derive the name from *δίδυμος*, “twin,” because he and Diana were born at a single birth. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.17, offers a third, philosophical explanation of the name and says that Apollo was worshiped under this name at Rome as well. ORELLI.

*Philesius.* Apollo was called *Φιλήσιος*, “lovable” or “friendly,” because, as Macrobius testifies in *Saturnalia* I.17, we greet his rising light as lovable and with the most affectionate veneration. There is no mention of this epithet elsewhere. ORELLI.

*Ab eo quod postulamus orare* (“to pray from him for what we ask”). Here *postulamus* is equivalent to “we desire”: the consequent is used for the antecedent. Nevertheless, Fulvius Ursinus’ conjecture, *ab eo, quo postulamus, ore*, “from that mouth from which we make our request,” seems by no means contemptible. ORELLI.

[Col. 0748D] *Vel auribus potuit scire, vel ipsius vocis sono* (“he could know either through his ears or from the sound of our very voice”). That is, “both from his ears and from the sound,” and so forth. For Arnobius often uses these disjunctive particles in place of copulatives, as does Julius Firmicus in countless passages. The remarks made on this passage in Fulvius Ursinus’ edition are entirely useless. HERALDUS.]

## XXVI

Is this, I ask, that audacious and monstrous crime [Col. 0746B] on account of which the greatest heavenly beings direct against us the stings of their anger and indignation? Is it on account of this that you yourselves, whenever a savage passion seizes you, strip us of our possessions, banish us from our ancestral homes, inflict [Col. 0747A] capital punishments upon us, torture us, lacerate us, scorch us, and finally expose us to wild animals and the mangling of beasts?

Whoever condemns this in us or thinks that it should be made a ground for any accusation—should he be called by the name of man, however much he may seem one to himself? Or should he be believed a god, though he himself professes himself such a thousand times through prophets? Does Trophonius, or the Dodonaean Jupiter, call us impious [Note: [Col. 0747A] Fulvius reads: “Does the Dodonaean Jupiter call us profane or impious in our rites” [Col. 0748A]], and will he himself be called a god and counted among the order of divine powers, when he either attaches the charge of impiety to those who serve the supreme king, or is tormented that the king’s majesty and worship are preferred to his own?

Is the Delian Apollo—or the Clarian, Didymaean, Philesian [Col. 0748A], or Pythian Apollo—to be regarded as divine, when he either does not know the supreme ruler or is ignorant that we supplicate him with daily prayers? Even if he did not know the secrets of our hearts or recognize what we contain in our innermost thoughts, he could nevertheless have learned through his ears, or from the very sound of the voice we employ in prayer, that we invoke the supreme God and pray to him for what we ask.

[Note: [Col. 0748D]

## XXVII.—*Cur ad Christi paveant mentionem*

Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, vv. 402 ff.:

> Apollo is tormented,  
> Struck by the name of Christ; he cannot endure the thunderbolts  
> Of the word. As many blows assail the wretch from the tongue  
> As praised miracles of God’s Christ resound.

Lactantius, book V, ch. 21: “When these contaminated spirits occupy human bodies and torment souls, they are adjured by these people and driven out in the name of the true God. On hearing it they tremble, cry aloud, and testify that they are being burned and beaten.” See Athanasius, *On the Humanity of the Word*. ELMENHORST.

[Col. 0749B] *Una pariter definitione figamus* (“let us establish by one common definition”). *Figamus* means “let us determine and set it down as firm and valid, beyond every hazard of doubt.” The metaphor is drawn from things fastened with nails. ORELLI.

*Aut amet substerni tot millium venerationem videre* (“or delights to see the veneration of so many thousands prostrated before him”). Stewechius thinks that *substerni*, “to be prostrated,” should be removed as a gloss. But Heraldus rightly defends it by a passage from Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 43: “How many among you are there—I do not now say who can cast demons out of you, nor do I say who can prostrate prayers for you also before the true God?” Meursius conjectures: *aut amet substerni tot millia in venerationem*, “or delights that so many thousands should prostrate themselves in veneration.” ORELLI.]

## XXVII

This is not yet the place for us to explain who all those beings that condemn us are, or where they come from; how much they can do or know; why they tremble at the mention of Christ; and why they regard his disciples as enemies and objects of hatred [Col. 0749A]. Yet for those who profess human understanding, let us establish the following by one common definition: we Christians are nothing other than worshipers, under Christ as our teacher, of the highest king and sovereign. If you examine it, you will find that nothing else is practiced in that religion [Note: [Col. 0749A] The manuscript has *isti*, “in that one.” Correctly, according to Meursius].

This is the sum of the entire activity; this is the appointed boundary of our divine duties, this their end. Before him we all prostrate ourselves according to custom; him we adore with our prayers united; from him we ask things just and honorable and worthy of being heard by him. It is not that he himself desires us to be suppliants or delights to see the veneration of so many thousands prostrated before him. This is for our benefit and has regard for our own advantage. For because, through the fault [Col. 0750A] of our innate weakness, we are inclined toward transgressions and the various appetites of passion, he allows himself always to be conceived in our thoughts, so that, while we pray to him and strive to deserve his gifts, we may acquire the will to innocence and cleanse ourselves of every stain by cutting away all our offenses.

[Note: [Col. 0749B]

## XXVIII.—*Quid dicitis, o sacri, quid divini interpretes juris?* (“What do you say, O sacred interpreters, O divine interpreters of law?”)

This is the absolutely certain reading proposed by Fulvius [Col. 0749C] Ursinus, in place of the old reading, “What do you say, divine interpreters, men?” HERALDUS.

*Grandules Lares.* Diomedes, book I, *On the Doubtful Position of Words*, p. 59, ed. Johannes Caesarius: “From this”—that is, from *grundio*, an ancient verb for *grunnio*, “to grunt”—“we understand that the Lares Grundules received their name; Romulus is said to have established them in honor of a sow that had given birth to thirty piglets.” He states this as follows. Cassius Hemina, in the second book of his *Histories*: “The multitude of shepherds, agreeing without dispute, placed Remus and Romulus equally in command, so that they were peers with one another in kingship. A portent occurred: a sow gave birth to thirty piglets. For this event they made a shrine to the Lares Grundiles.” Compare Nonius under *Grundules*. Elmenhorst. The manuscript corruptly reads *Grunduleos*. ORELLI.

*Aios, Locutios, Lementinos*, etc. The manuscript has *Locutios, Ajaceos, Boetios, Libentinos*, which is certainly very corrupt. Yet I believe that the name of some god charged with the care of cattle lies concealed in the word *Boetios*, and I would not rashly remove it from the text. I therefore conjecture that one should read: *Locutios, Ajos, Bubetios*—or *Bovicios*—*Limentinos*. Pliny, *Natural History* XVIII.3, mentions the Bubetian games [Col. 0749D]. Why should we not suppose that there were also Bubetian gods, since it is agreed that many names of lesser gods have perished through age, while others have been preserved only in the writings of the Fathers of the Church—Augustine, Minucius, Lactantius? Thus the goddess Bubona is mentioned by Augustine, *City of God* VI.3. ORELLI.

*Aios Locutios.* The classic passage on Aius Locutius is Livy, *History* V.50: “Mention was also made of expiating the nocturnal voice which, as a herald of disaster, had been heard and disregarded before the Gallic War; and orders were given that a temple to Aius Locutius be built on the New Road.” Compare Cicero, *On Divination* I.45 and II.32, and Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book XVI, ch. 17. ORELLI.

*Limentinos.* Our author says below, book IV, ch. 9: “Who is there who believes that Limentinus, or Lima, guards thresholds and discharges the duties of doorkeepers?” Augustine, *City of God* IV.8: “They assigned three gods: Forculus to doors, Cardea to hinges, and Limentinus to thresholds.” The manuscript incorrectly has *Libentinos*. Our author mentions below, book IV, ch. 1, Libentina and Liburnus, gods who preside over the protection of lusts. ORELLI.

*Rebus fessis languentibusque* (“for exhausted and failing circumstances”). See above, on ch. 25.

*Qui Faunos, qui fatuas.* Lipsius excellently emended the text thus in *Epistolary Questions*, book I, letter 20, and the reading is also confirmed by the manuscript, according to Meursius. The Roman edition has *statuas*, “statues.” But the dispute here is not with statues, but with the ridiculous names of gods. The classic passage concerning Faunus and Fatua is in Lactantius, book I, ch. 22:

> Just as Pompilius was among the Romans the founder of foolish religions, so before Pompilius there was Faunus in Latium. He both established impious rites for his grandfather Saturn and honored his father Picus among the gods; and he consecrated his sister Fatua Fauna, who was also his wife. Gavius [Col. 0750C] Bassus relates that she was named Fatua because she was accustomed to sing prophecies (*fata*) to women, just as Faunus did to men. Varro writes that she was a woman of such great chastity that, throughout her life, no male except her husband ever saw her or heard her name. Women therefore sacrifice to her in secrecy and call her the Good Goddess. Sextus Clodius, moreover, in the book he wrote in Greek, relates that she was the wife of Faunus; because, contrary to custom and royal dignity, she had secretly drunk a jar of wine and become intoxicated, her husband beat her to death with myrtle rods. Later, however, when he repented of his deed and could not bear his longing for her, he bestowed divine honor upon her. For this reason a wine amphora is placed, covered over, in her sacred rites.

Compare Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.12. ORELLI.—Varro (*On the Latin Language*, book VI) and Servius (on Virgil, *Georgics* I.10–11 and *Aeneid* VII.45 ff.) think that Faunus received his name from *fando*, “speaking”; or because, as Gaius Bassus says in Lactantius I.11, Fatua was so named because she was said to sing destinies to women, just as Faunus did to men. Virgil, indeed, praised the responses of Faunus in *Aeneid* VIII [Col. 0750D].103. But Cicero, although he said that the voices of Fauns had often been heard in battle lines and times of turmoil (*On Divination* I.45), nevertheless, when he introduced Cotta replying to Balbus in books II and III of *On the Nature of the Gods*, denied that he himself had ever heard such a voice of Faunus. NOURRY, p. 419.

*Civitatumque genios* (“and the guardian spirits of cities”). The matter of the guardian spirits of places is clear. Prudentius, in the second book *Against Symmachus*:

> Since you are accustomed to assign their own guardian spirits  
> To gates, houses, baths, and stables, and throughout every part  
> Of the city and every place to invent many thousands of spirits,  
> So that no corner may lack its own shadow.

But they believed such spirits to be specially assigned to individual cities and peoples, and that through their care and providence the respective cities were preserved. Symmachus, in his report on restoring the ancient worship of the gods, quoted by the same Prudentius, says: “Each has his own custom, each his own rite. The divine mind has distributed different guardians and forms of worship among cities. Just as souls are allotted to those who are born, so fateful guardian spirits are allotted to peoples.” Hence “THE GUARDIAN SPIRIT OF THE ROMAN PEOPLE” (*GENIUS POPULI ROMANI*) appears everywhere on ancient coins; Dio calls him *γένιος τοῦ δήμου*, “guardian spirit of the people,” and Ammianus Marcellinus calls him the “public guardian spirit.” HERALDUS.—Compare Caspar Barth on Rutilius, *Journey* I.328, where he discusses this matter at length. ORELLI.

*Pausos.* Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XV, ch. 21, thinks that Pausus was a god who brought pause and rest and was the adversary of wars. ELMENHORST.

*In sententiae suae perpetuitate defixum est* (“it is fixed in the perpetuity of his resolve”). That is, it remains unmoved and unchangeable, fixed and, as it were, established in God’s perpetual determination—that is, in his eternal decree. Similarly Cicero, *For Flaccus*, ch. 1: “We ask only this of you: that you consider all the resources of the commonwealth, the whole condition of the state, every memory of past times, the safety of the present, and the hope of what remains to be placed and fixed in your power, in your judgments, and in this single trial.” ORELLI.

*Crucem mereatur extremam* (“deserves the ultimate cross”). No punishment was more horrible, more degrading, or more detestable than this. HERALDUS.—For this reason the ancients called crucifixion “the supreme punishment,” “the ultimate penalty,” and *ἡ ἐσχάτη δίκη*, “the final punishment.” Here, however, the phrase may also be understood more broadly as pestilence or destruction, as Justus Lipsius rightly observes in *On the Cross*, book II, ch. 1, *Works*, vol. III, p. 1175, Wesel edition. ORELLI.

In the greatest cities . . . public rites are performed for paid prostitutes. The Athenians honored Leaena, a most notorious courtesan, and the Romans Acca, Laurentia, and Flora—shameless prostitutes—after their deaths with sacrifices and with the honor of annual funeral observances. Lactantius, book I, ch. 20; Gellius, book VI, ch. 7; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.10; Plutarch, *Roman Questions*. ELMENH.

**There is no swelling of indignation in the gods.** This was the entirely genuine reading of the manuscript codex and the first edition; in Gelenius’s edition, I believe, the printers corrupted it by changing a single letter. Minucius Felix, ch. 14: “For the onrush of his outpoured speech had relaxed the swelling of his indignation.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.40:

> . . . . . Every swelling and wrath  
> Of the gods subsided.

Hence Zeno of Verona, in Sermon VII, *On the Three Boys*, calls someone “inflated with anger”: “They despised the king himself, who, inflated with anger, ordered the furnace to be heated seven times more than usual.” The meaning, therefore, is: the gods contract no causes of indignation from this; they do not swell up on that account, nor are they “in a ferment” (*in fermento*), as the character in Plautus puts it. HERALD.—Oberthür’s edition incorrectly has *timor* (“fear”). ORELL.—Bentley, on Horace, *Art of Poetry*, v. 191, has shown with numerous examples how easy an error between *timor* and *tumor* was. OCHSNER.

**Temples for cats, scarabs, and heifers have been raised with lofty pediments.** He censures the superstition of the Egyptians. What he says about scarabs is known from Eusebius and others. Moreover, the temples that they established for those animals were proud and magnificent; hence Arnobius says that they were “raised with lofty pediments.” [Col. 0752C] The Epicurean Celsus also indicates this in Origen, when comparing Christian faith with Egyptian superstition. His words appear in Origen, book III:

> He wishes to compare the circumstances of our faith with those of the Egyptians, among whom, as one approaches, there are splendid sacred precincts and groves, gateways of great size and beauty, marvelous temples, proud structures all around, and rites that are highly superstitious and mysterious; but when one enters and goes farther inside, what is seen being worshiped is a cat, an ape, a crocodile, a goat, or a dog.

HERALD.—Isis (who was formerly Io), Apis, and even Venus were worshiped among the Egyptians in bovine form. See Joannes Meursius on Lycophron, *Alexandra*, v. 1292. ORELL.

**The powers of the divinities remain silent when mocked.** We have observed that complete iambic lines are sometimes found in this author. Here you have an example. HERALD.

**They perceive that they have obtained by allotment.** Perhaps this may appropriately be compared with the example “he perceived that he had fallen into the midst of the enemy” in Virgil, *Aeneid* II.377. Yet Arnobius seems to say something different. Others therefore read: “from whom they perceive that they themselves have obtained by allotment divinity itself, so to speak,” etc. I should nevertheless be unwilling to alter anything rashly. ORELL.—See J. Lipsius, *Antiquae Lectiones* II, ch. 7. OCHSN.

**By whose will and decision they both can perish and be dissolved, and cannot be dissolved or perish.** This is an altogether peculiar and unusual mode of expression for: “by whose decision they can both perish and be dissolved, and can be preserved from destruction and dissolution.” ORELL.

**It will consequently follow for you.** Thus I have edited the text following Meursius’s correction. Others read, “it will consequently follow for us.” ORELL.

**To derive the origin of their birth.** Such equivalent expressions—“beginning,” “birth of origins,” “origin of birth,” “commencement of nativity,” etc.—are very frequently combined by ancient authors, as Wopkensius demonstrates with numerous examples in his note on Justin, *Histories* II, ch. 1, in *New Miscellaneous Critical Observations*, fascicle II, p. 19. ORELL.

**Have merited.** See above on ch. 3; Meursius substituted *idem* for *idem* [an apparently identical reading in the printed text]. ORELL.

**Unstable.** *Labilis* is equivalent to *caducus*, “liable to fall,” a word familiar to Arnobius. See Olaus Borrichius, *Cogitationes*, p. 152. ORELL.]

## XXVIII

What do you say, O sacred ones? What do you say, O divine interpreters of law? Are those who worship the Grundule (“Grunting”) Lares, Aius Locutius, the Limentini, in a better position [Note: [Col. 0750A] “In a better position.” Fulvius] than all of us, who worship God, the Father of things, and ask him for protection for things that are weary and failing? And do those who revere Fauns, Fatuae, the guardian spirits of cities, Pausi, and Bellonae seem to you cautious, wise, supremely prudent, and liable to no reproach? But we, who have surrendered ourselves to God—by whose command and decision everything that exists subsists and remains fixed in the perpetuity of his decree—are pronounced dull, stupid, foolish, obtuse, and brutish.

Is this the judgment you declare? Is this the law you have established and promulgate: that whoever worships your servants should be accorded the highest honors, but whoever supplicates you yourselves, their masters, should deserve the final punishment of the cross? In the greatest cities and among the more powerful peoples, public rites are performed for women who were once paid prostitutes and exposed themselves to common lust, yet there is no swelling of indignation in the gods. Temples for cats, scarabs, and heifers have been raised with lofty pediments; the powers of the divinities remain silent when mocked, and are afflicted by no envy when they see the sacred honors of worthless animals placed on a level with their own. [Col. 0751B]

Toward us alone are the gods hostile; against us alone are they most bitter enemies, because we venerate their Father, through whom—if they exist—they began to exist and to possess the substance of their own divinity [Col. 0752A] and majesty; from whom they perceive that they have obtained divinity itself, so to speak [Note: [Col. 0751B] “They perceive themselves to have obtained it.” Fulvius], and recognize themselves as belonging to the number of existing things; and by whose will and decision they both can perish and be dissolved, and cannot be dissolved or perish.

For if we all concede that there is one sole first principle, whom no other thing precedes in temporal antiquity, then everything after him must necessarily have been born and brought forth, and have sprung into the nature belonging to its own name. But if this is fixed and certain, it will consequently follow for you that you must confess both that the gods are beings who came into existence and that they derive the origin of their birth from the first principle, the source of all things. If they came into existence and were begotten, they are surely near to destruction and its dangers. Yet they are believed to be immortal, everlasting, and never participants in any end. Therefore, it is the gift and bounty of God the Father that those same beings have merited to exist through endless ages, although by nature they are perishable and dissoluble.

[Col. 0752B]

[Note: [Col. 0753B]

**To be placed in the hearing of the human race.** Fulvius Ursinus and Gelenius corrected the text thus. The common reading is “to place,” which Heraldus attempts to defend in *Curae II*. But I wish he had given us examples of the expression “to place a speech in a hearing.” By contrast, people are properly said to be “placed in a hearing,” that is, in an assembly of hearers, an audience, as Caspar Barth explains well in *Adversaria*, book XXIII, ch. 3, p. 1121 ff. Compare Meursius, *Critica Arnobiana*, book I, ch. 10, p. 21. Thus the unknown author of the *Life of Lucan* prefixed to Grotius’s edition says: “He declaimed both in Greek and in Latin, to the great admiration of the audience.” ORELL.

**The head and mainstay of things.** This is written several times in Arnobius. Some have wished to rewrite *columen* as *culmen*, quite needlessly. For *columen* in this sense is known even to ancient writers. Servius, on *Aeneid* VIII: “Just as columns are placed over noble persons who have died, to exhibit their eminence.” Zeno of Verona calls Susanna “the mainstay of matrimony” in his sermon *On Chastity*. The glosses give: *columen*—*peristylion*, “colonnade.” HERALD.—See above on ch. 8. ORELL.

**Ill-omened.** That is, persons to be abominated and detested as some monstrosity and portent. *Infaustus*, “ill-omened,” “unfortunate,” was commonly used among the Romans of things of evil omen. ORELL.

**Atheists.** Christians were so called by the pagans because they abolished the long-established cults of the gods and thereby destroyed the gods themselves. Hence that customary cry in the amphitheaters, “Away with the atheists!” (*Αἶρε τοὺς ἀθέους*), which those who denied Christ and Christian piety were also ordered to utter. HERALD.

**More rightly.** See below, on book VII, ch. XVIII, the note of Heraldus. ORELL.

**Because we were either sent down or fell from him.** Pythagoras, Plato, and Origen raved that rational souls had existed in the heavens and, because of certain ancient sins, had fallen into bodies to undergo punishment. ELMENH. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.724–734, pertains to this. ORELL.

**In the blindness of this body.** Virgil, in book VI, says of human souls fallen from heaven:

> They possess a fiery vigor and a heavenly origin  
> In their seeds, insofar as harmful bodies do not impede them  
> And earthly limbs and mortal members do not dull them.  
> Hence they fear and desire, grieve and rejoice; nor, enclosed  
> In darkness and a blind prison, do they discern the heavens.

On this passage Heyne, V.S., remarks: “The body is compared to the soul’s chains and darkness, by which the soul is obscured and withdrawn from the free contemplation of things.” ORELL.

**To retain possession.** The manuscript codex has “possession in [Col. 0754B] the thing”; from this Stewechius judges that one should read “possession together with the thing,” thinking that these words allude to the formulas of the jurists who distinguish possession “with the thing” and “without the thing”: with the thing, when the person who receives it effectively retains the property; without the thing, when another can recover the inheritance by civil law. ORELL.

**He established the sun’s fires to serve the growth of things.** J. Meursius, p. 21, conjectures that one should read: “He established them to foster the growth of things,” from *foveo*, “I foster.” But nothing should be changed. *Esse ad rem* means “to remedy a thing, to be beneficial.” See Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. Thus Cato, *On Agriculture* XII: “It is good for [Col. 0754C] indigestion, for headache,” etc. ORELL.

**Since you believe the sun to be a god.** Thus *theos*, “god,” without any qualification, is not infrequently used by the Greeks to mean the sun; and “the god rising and setting” (*ἀρχόμενος καὶ δυόμενος θεός*) means the rising and setting sun. Themistius Euphrades, Oration XI:

> Those who ardently desire to gaze directly upon the god with their eyes first practice in water and test their eyes, training them to endure and remain fixed upon his appearance.

HERALD.—Compare Gisbert Cuper, *Harpocrates*, p. 113, Utrecht quarto edition. ORELL.]

## XXIX

And would that it were granted me, with the whole world gathered into the form of a single assembly, to employ this speech and to be placed in the hearing of the human race. Are we, then, charged by you with an impious religion and called—if we may use your abusive term—ill-omened atheists because we approach with reverent services the head and mainstay of things? And who could more rightly incur the odium of these names than one who, in preference to this God, knows, investigates, or believes in another?

Do we not all owe to him first of all the very fact that we exist, that we are called human beings, and that, whether sent down or fallen from him [Note: [Col. 0753B] “Sent down or fallen,” feminine plural. Incorrectly. Manuscript], we are confined within the blindness of this body? Does not the fact that we walk, breathe, and live come to us from him, and does not the very force of life cause us to exist and to be moved by animal activity? Do not the causes by which our well-being is supported through the bounty of various pleasures flow from him?

Whose is this world in which you dwell? [Col. 0753B] Or who has granted you its produce and allowed you to retain possession of it? [Col. 0754A] Who gave you that common light so that you might see, touch, and examine the things placed beneath you? Who established the sun’s fires as future means for the growth of things, lest the vital elements remain fixed and grow sluggish in the stupor of inactivity? Since you believe the sun to be a god, do you not inquire after his founder and maker? Since the moon is a goddess among you, do you not likewise take care to learn who her begetter and fabricator is?

[Note: [Col. 0754C]

**In whose possession you live? In whose property you are?** *Cujus, -a, -um* is a word of older Latin. Terence, *Andria*, act V, scene 4: “Tell me, whose boy did you put here?” Virgil, *Eclogue* III.1:

> Tell me, Damoetas, whose flock is this? Is it Meliboeus’s?

Nothing is more frequent than its feminine form in Plautus, Gellius, and others. See Olaus Borrichius, who collected a cloud of examples in *Cogitationes de Lingua Latina*, p. 78. ORELL.

**Which you draw back and forth by means of your vital breath.** Thus our author below, book II, ch. 16: “They receive breaths and return them in equal measure, drawn back and forth by breathing”; and book VII, ch. 28: “For whatever breathes and draws alternating breaths through channels accessible to air must necessarily be mortal.” Meursius judges that *aspiritu* should be read as one word, meaning “by aspiration”; but Arnobius very frequently employs the prepositions *a, in, de,* and *ex* redundantly (*περιττῶς*). ORELL.

**Whose springs you use abundantly.** *Abuti* is used here in a favorable sense, “to use greatly or to the utmost,” as it often is among the best authors. See Gronovius and Cortius on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* IX, Letter VI; Henmann on Cicero, *For Milo*, ch. 2; Davies on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, ch. 60; Jaeger on the *Panegyric of Nazarius*, ch. 30; Bunemann on Lactantius, *Institutes* I, ch. 6, p. 43; Ruhnken on Rutilius Lupus, p. 99. ORELL.

**Distinguished according to the particular nature of their principles.** Lucretius often uses *ratio* to mean a particular manner and nature. Arnobius does so in several passages. Shortly afterward: “Did Aesculapius, Hercules, or Diana fashion the principle of rains and storms?” HERALD.—Should we not read “fixed”? ORELL.

**Fashioned the principle of rains and storms.** We should write “fixed.” ORELL.]

## XXX

Does the thought not occur to you to consider and investigate in whose possession you live, in whose property you are? Whose is this earth that you wear out? Whose is this air that you draw back and forth by means of your vital breath? Whose springs do you use abundantly? Whose water? Who arranged the blasts of the winds? Who devised the billowing clouds? Who distinguished the fruitful powers of seeds according to the particular nature of their principles?

Does Apollo rain upon you? Does Mercury rain upon you? Did Aesculapius, Hercules, or Diana fashion the principle of rains and storms? And how can this be, when you profess that they were born within the world and at a definite time took hold of vital consciousness? For if the world preceded them in temporal antiquity, and before they were born nature already knew rains and storms, then those born later possess no right to cause rain, nor can they insert themselves into the principles [Note: [Col. 0755B] “Nations.” Incorrectly. Manuscript] that they found already operating here and being administered by a greater author.

[Note: [Col. 0755C]

**O you yourself, unseen and never comprehended by any created natures.** Thus the manuscript codex and Sabaeus’s edition. The others read *invise*, “O invisible one”; but there are many interchanges (*ἐναλλαγαί*) of this kind in these writers. “Never comprehended by any created natures” means “incomprehensible,” a word whose sense they prefer to convey rather than pronounce. Tertullian: “He is invisible, even if he is seen; incomprehensible, even if through grace he is represented.” This prayer should be compared with that of St. Augustine, *Confessions* I, chs. 3 and 4. *Invisus* means “not seen,” as it often does. See Bunemann on Lactantius, *Institutes* VII, ch. 16, p. 947 ff. *Natura*, moreover, here means “creature,” as in Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, Hymn X:

> He trod beneath his foot the waves of the liquid sea;  
> A fluid and tenuous creature coheres into solidity.

Meursius cited this passage. ORELL.

**To fall prostrate with knee bent.** It was a common custom of the ancient Christians in their prayers to fall prostrate upon the ground with knee bent. Origen, on Numbers ch. 4, Homily 5, [Col. 0755D] fol. 190: “We bend our knees when praying.” ELMENH.

**The place and space of things.** The ancient Peripatetics called God by this name, “the place of all things” (*τόπον πάντων*). Sextus Empiricus refutes them in *Against the Mathematicians*, book X, where Fabricius, p. 639, remarks:

> The Hebrews do not hesitate to call God, because he is contained by nothing but himself contains all things by his immeasurable power, [the Hebrew term is missing from the supplied text], or “place,” as frequently occurs in the little book of Passover rites edited by Rittangelius. Philo Judaeus, in *On Flight and Finding*, p. 360, explaining Exodus 21:13, says: “He now calls ‘place’ not a region filled by a body, but, through an implied meaning, God himself, since he contains but is not contained, and because he is the refuge of all things” (*Τόπον καλεῖ νῦν οὐ χώραν ἐκπεπληρωμένην ὑπὸ σώματος, ἀλλὰ δι’ ὑπονοιῶν αὐτὸν τὸν θεόν, ἐπειδὴ περιέχων οὐ περιέχεται, καὶ ὅτι καταφυγὴ τῶν ὅλων ἐστί*).

So too the Christian writers. Theophilus, *To Autolycus* II, p. 81: “For God is not contained in a place, but he himself is the place of all things” (*Θεὸς γὰρ οὐ χωρεῖται, ἀλλὰ αὐτὸς ἐστι τόπος τῶν ὅλων*). In the *Confession of the Greeks* edited by Normannus, p. 36, God is called “his own place” (*τόπος αὐτὸς ἑαυτοῦ*). Yet blessed Augustine rightly denies that God can properly be called a place, in *Eighty-Three Different Questions*, question 20: “All things are in God rather than he being anywhere; yet they are not in him in such a way that he himself is a place. For a place is in space, which is occupied by a body’s length, breadth, and height; and God is no such thing. Therefore all things are in [Col. 0756C] him, yet he is not a place.”

Thus Fabricius; to these references add Augustine, *Confessions* I, ch. 3. ORELL.

**No circumscription defines him; without quality or quantity.** Thomas Canterus, joining the word “quality” with “circumscription,” conjectures that one should read: “No circumscription of quantity defines him, who is without quality.” Incorrectly. Arnobius calls God “without quality or quantity,” because human beings can grasp or express in words neither his quality—that is, his powers—nor his quantity—that is, his supreme power and omnipresence. ORELL.

**Is capable.** The text used to read *potest*. But the royal manuscript has *potis est*, which reading we have reproduced. Elsewhere also we have very frequently restored *potis est* for *pote est* from the same manuscript. The ancients spoke in this way, using *potissum* for *possum*. Lucretius:

> Nor is it capable of being seen, because it is borne along devoid of light.

HERALD. [Col. 0756D] Compare Lipsius, *Variae Lectiones* I, ch. 14. OCHSN.

**Some deny that any divine power exists.** Namely Diagoras and Theodorus of Cyrene, who were therefore called atheists “preeminently” (*κατ’ ἐξοχήν*). See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I, ch. 23, and Lactantius I, ch. 2. ORELL.

**Some inquire whether it exists.** Protagoras of Abdera. See Cicero, book I. ORELL.

**By fortuitous accidents and random collisions.** Democritus was the author of this view, Epicurus its champion. Lactantius, book I, ch. 2. Compare Juvenal, Satire XIII.85; Pliny, *Natural History* II.7. ORELL.

**Fashioned by the impetus of diversity.** That is, by the violent collision of atoms, which the Epicureans held to be extremely diverse: some smooth, others rough; some round, others angular; some curved and, as it were, hooked. See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.24. “Diversity” is therefore equivalent to “diverse atoms,” and we have no need of J. Walker’s correction on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.38, p. 349 of Davies’s edition, where he reads “by the impetus” or “circuit of the universe.” In what follows, by contrast, [Col. 0757C] I approve the same Walker’s conjecture *opinatione*, “supposition,” for *obstinatione*, “obstinacy.” ORELL.]

## XXXI

O greatest and highest creator of invisible things! O you yourself, unseen and never comprehended by any created natures! Worthy, truly worthy are you—if indeed a mortal mouth should call you worthy—to whom every breathing and intelligent nature should never cease both to feel and to render thanks; before whom an entire lifetime should fittingly fall prostrate with knee bent and make supplication in unbroken prayers.

For you are the first cause, the place and space of things, the boundless foundation of all things whatsoever: unbegotten, immortal, everlasting, alone; defined by no bodily form [Note: [Col. 0755B] “Of a body.” Fulvius], determined by no circumscription, without quality or quantity, without position, movement, or condition. Nothing concerning you is capable of being said and expressed through the signification of mortal words. For you to be understood, one must remain silent; and so that wandering conjecture may be able to seek you out as though through a shadow, absolutely nothing must be uttered.

Grant pardon, supreme King, to those who persecute your servants; and, as is proper to your benevolence, forgive those who flee the worship of your name and religion. It is not remarkable if you are unknown; it would be a greater marvel if you were known. Unless, perhaps, someone dares—for this alone remains for frenzied madness—to hesitate and doubt whether this God exists or does not exist, and whether he is believed in because the truth of faith has been ascertained or merely through the supposition of an empty rumor.

For we hear that certain persons devoted to the study of philosophy partly deny that any divine power exists, while others inquire daily whether it exists. Some construct the totality of things from fortuitous accidents and random collisions, and hold that it is fashioned by the impetus of diversity. With these persons we shall at this time [Note: [Col. 0756B] “At this point in time.” Correctly; a Greek construction. Manuscript, Meursius] engage in no dispute whatever over such obstinacy. For people of sound judgment say that to contradict foolish propositions is an act of even greater folly.

[Col. 0757A]

[Note: [Col. 0757C]

**Let madness be averted.** Thus Lucilius in Nonius under *averruncare*: “May the gods have counseled better things and averted your madness.” ELMENH.—Our author perhaps had this passage before his eyes. ORELL.

**For it is as dangerous, etc.** Thus the Roman edition and the royal codex. Others read, “For it is so dangerous.” Lucretius sometimes couples these particles, using “thus—as” for “so—as.” HERALD.]

## XXXII

Our discourse is with those who, while agreeing that a divine race exists, entertain doubts about the greater beings, although those same people acknowledge the commoner and more humble ones to exist. Why, then, should we strive and labor to establish matters so great by arguments? Let this madness depart far away and, as the saying goes, be averted far from us.

For it is as dangerous to undertake by arguments to prove God, the first principle, as it is to wish to know by a method of this kind that he exists. Nor does it make any difference, nor is there any distinction, whether you deny him or affirm and confess that he exists, since the assertion of such a reality and its denial by an unbelieving opponent involve the same fault.

[Note: [Col. 0757C]

**Has entered the day of birth.** On the expressions “to enter,” “cross,” or “pass beyond” a year, day, etc., see Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* X, p. 679. ORELL.

**To him.** The manuscript codex has “to them,” which I prefer. ORELL.

**Were capable.** The first edition has “might have been capable,” which Heraldus and Salmasius defend, the latter in his note on Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, p. 67; this interchange of grammatical forms is extremely frequent in ecclesiastical writers, especially Tertullian and Cyprian. But *potis essent* came from the manuscript codex. Meursius, p. 22, conjectures *potissent*, from *potissum*, an archaic verb used by Lucretius. ORELL.

**If they were released into the facility of our languages; indeed, if trees, clods, and stones, animated with vital consciousness, could produce the sound of a voice and form the articulations of words—thus, without nature as their leader, etc.** Wakefield, in *Silvae Criticae*, vol. IV, p. 244, reconstructed the passage thus: “If they were released into the faculty of our languages—indeed, if trees, clods, and stones, animated with vital consciousness, could produce the sound of a voice and form the articulations of words, these things without nature as their leader,” etc. But I should be unwilling to change anything. “Facility” is much better suited to the verb “be released”; difficult things are released into facility, but not likewise into faculty. Nor should *ita* be changed to *ista*. Rather, *ita* means “thus” (*οὕτως*), that is, on this condition: if they were capable of opening their mouths, etc. ORELL.]

## XXXIII

Is there any human being who has not entered the day of first birth with a conception of that first principle? In whom is it not inborn, not fastened—indeed, almost impressed and implanted within the very generative organs of the mother—that there is a king and lord, the ruler of all things whatsoever?

Indeed, if mute living creatures themselves were capable of opening their mouths; if they were released into the facility of our languages; indeed, if trees, clods, and stones, animated with vital consciousness, could produce the sound of a voice and form the articulations of words, would they not, with nature as their leader and teacher and with the trust of uncorrupted simplicity, both understand that God exists and cry aloud that he alone is Lord of all?

[Note: [Col. 0758C]

**He says.** Others incorrectly read “you say.” See above on ch. III. ORELL.

**And have built enormous Capitols.** Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 25: “At that time, however, divine worship among the Romans did not yet depend upon temples or images: religion was frugal, its rites poor, and there were no Capitols rivaling heaven.” He calls them “enormous” after the example of Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.19:

> . . . . . And he built enormous temples.

HERALD.

**By introducing confusion.** Fulvius Ursinus reads “an ignorant confusion,” not badly. ORELL.

**Only recently formed in his mother’s womb.** “Only recently” corresponds to the Greek proverbial expression “yesterday and the day before” (*χθὲς καὶ πρώην*) for something done not very long ago, like the Latin “yesterday and the day before yesterday.” See Erasmus, *Proverbs*; [Col. 0758D] Gataker on Marcus Aurelius X.§7; J. C. Wolf on Libanius, Letter 270; Juretus on Symmachus I, Letter 3, p. 6 of Lectius’s edition. Arnobius calls Jupiter recent and newly formed in comparison with the true, supreme, eternal, and never-begotten God. HERALD and ORELL.

**Burst into.** This should be read following the correction of Fulvius Ursinus. The expression is used by the best authors. Terence, *Brothers*, act IV, scene 2, v. 11: “See that he does not burst straight in here.” Similarly, “to fling oneself into war,” in Cicero, *Letters* VIII.14. Others read “to have burst in,” with an ugly solecism. STEWECH. Compare Cortius on Cicero, loc. cit.]

## XXXIV

“But,” he says, “you assail and attack us in vain with a false and slanderous charge, as though we denied that there is a greater God, although Jupiter is both named by us and held to be Best and Greatest, [Col. 0757C] and although we have established for him the most august seats and built enormous Capitols.” [Col. 0758A]
