You are attempting to join dissimilar things and force them into a single form by introducing confusion. For by the single mind and common assent of all mortality, almighty God is known neither to have been begotten nor ever to have been brought forth into a new light, nor to have begun to exist at any time or in any age. He himself is the source of things, the sower of ages and times. For these do not exist of themselves, but proceed from his eternity in an everlasting and always infinite continuation.

Jupiter, by contrast, as you relate, has a father and mother, grandfathers, grandmothers, and brothers. Only recently formed in his mother’s womb, brought to full term and completed in ten months, he burst with vital consciousness into a light previously unknown to him. Therefore, if these things are so, how can Jupiter be a god, when it is agreed that God is eternal, while Jupiter is declared by you to be another being, to have had a birthday, and, terrified by the strange experience, to have raised a pitiable wail?

[Note: [Col. 0758D]

**If one religion is common to us and you, the anger of the heavenly beings ceases.** Meursius, p. 23, judges that one should read: “If there were one religion for us and you, the anger of the heavenly beings would be common.” ORELL.]

## XXXV

But let them, as you wish, be one, differing in no divine power or majesty. Why, then, do you persecute us with unjust hatred? Why do you shudder at the mention of our name as though it were the worst possible omen, if we worship the same God whom you worship? Or why do you maintain that, in the same case, the gods are intimate friends of yours but our most hostile and bitter enemies?

For if one religion is common to us and you, the anger of the heavenly beings ceases. But if they are hostile to us alone, it is manifest that both you and they are ignorant of God; and their very indignation as divinities makes it clear that God is not Jupiter.

[Note: [Col. 0758D]

**But because one born as a human being and—what is disgraceful for persons of low condition—killed by the punishment of the cross.** Lactantius, book IV, ch. 16: “For someone might perhaps say: Why, if he was God and wished to die, was he not at least subjected to some honorable form of death? Why especially the cross? Why an infamous kind of punishment, which appears unworthy even of a free person, however guilty?” HERALD.

**And whom you worship with daily supplications.** That is, whom you pray to and invoke, and approach with reverent services. For *adorare* means “to pray to,” “to entreat someone,” just as one speaks of “approaching the gods.” Tertullian, *On Prayer*: “John had also taught his disciples to pray.” And so throughout that writer. Livy likewise uses “to pray to” in book XXXVIII: “The very gods had at last been torn from their seats and carried away. The people of Ambracia had no one left whom they might worship, to whom they might pray and make supplication.” The words “had been carried away” have the flavor of a gloss, a kind of corruption with which, as we have observed, Livy’s manuscripts are contaminated in almost innumerable passages. HERALD.—Priorius explains *adorare* as “to kiss one’s own hand.” Incorrectly, for that was pagan, not Christian, adoration. See Salmasius on the *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. II, p. 685 ff. ORELL.

**But better and more praiseworthy in drinking wine.** This reading comes from the manuscript codex. The Roman edition had “but drunk with better and more praiseworthy wine,” a thoroughly corrupt reading. HERALD.—Stewechius judges that one should read: “drunk with better and more praiseworthy wine,” that is, intoxicated. But if we read it thus, the entire force of the irony vanishes. Arnobius is mocking the Good Goddess, whom he calls much better—and best of all—in drinking wine. Therefore the codex’s reading should not be abandoned. ORELL.

**Indigetes.** Servius says on Virgil, *Georgics* I.498, that the Indigetes are gods made from human beings, as though “living among the gods.” Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* I, ch. 9, confirms this explanation on Hesiod’s authority: “Hesiod,” he says, “the advocate of divine descent, numbers ancient kings among the gods and, following the model of their former power, assigns them even in heaven the office of governing human affairs. And lest anyone find it tedious, let us insert the actual verses as the Greek poet presented them; we shall reproduce them as they have been converted from his words into Latin words:

> These are the divine Indigetes by decree of supreme Jupiter,  
> Once human beings, but now among the gods watching over human affairs,  
> Generous and munificent, still possessing the right of kings.”

NOURR., p. 453.

**Those Indigetes who crawl along a river, etc.** A hero bears the inscription: “Son of the chthonic god, who governs the river’s stream” (*ΠΑΤΡΟΣ ΘΕΟΥ ΧΘΟΝΙΟΥ ΟΣ ΠΟΤΑΜΟΥ ΡΕΥΜΑ ΔΙΕΠΕΙ*). HERALD.—Arnobius alludes to the story of Aeneas, very well explained by Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.794:

> The story concerning Aeneas is as follows. After Turnus had been killed, Lavinia taken in marriage, and a city founded, he fell into the river Numicus—according to some while sacrificing, according to others while fleeing Mezentius, and according to still others Messapus—and his body was not found. Ascanius his son, together with the other Trojans, believed and proclaimed that he had been received among the divinities; or, wishing to consecrate his father, he established a temple which he ordered to be called the temple of the Indiges god.

Livy relates in *History* I.2 that he was called Jupiter Indiges. Compare Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIV.581 ff.; Tibullus, *Elegies* II.5.43; and Heyne, V.S., Excursus III on *Aeneid* XII. Moreover, “crawling” is used with particular force because of the reedy and muddy bed of the Numicus. [Col. 0760B] See Gierig on the cited passage of Ovid, second edition, p. 347. ORELL.

**Who crawl along a river.** He means Aeneas, concerning whom Tibullus, book II, Elegy V, says:

> Unwearied Aeneas, brother of winged Love,  
> Who carry Troy’s sacred objects in your fugitive ships,  
> Jupiter now assigns you the fields of Laurentum;  
> Now a hospitable land summons your wandering household gods.  
> There you will be holy, when the venerable wave  
> Of the Numicus has sent you to heaven as the god Indiges.

NOURR., p. 453.

**Of fair Maia.** He borrowed this from Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.138:

> Mercury is your father, whom fair Maia conceived  
> On Cyllene’s cold summit and brought forth.

Compare Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, ch. 12; Apollodorus, *Library* III. ELMENH.

**The bow-bearing Diana and Apollo carried about through their mother’s flights.** Meursius, p. 24, and in his *Hypocriticus Minutianus*, p. 258, wishes to correct this to “paraded about,” from *circulare*, which the glosses explain as “to wander about in the manner of a vagrant,” whence *circulator*, “vagrant” (*ἀγύρτης*). But if Arnobius had wished to use this verb, he would undoubtedly have written *circulantes*, not *circulati*; and all this is mere quibbling. ORELL.

**Venus, offspring of Dione.** This is the reading of the first edition. The royal manuscript has the meaningless *Loncia*. Venus was born of Dione and Jupiter, according to Hyginus. HERALD. Sciverius, in the appendix to Meursius, conjectures “Venus, offspring of the sea.” ORELL.

**The matron of the Trojan man.** He speaks of Venus’s intercourse with Anchises, from which Aeneas was subsequently born. See Servius on *Aeneid* I and Hyginus, *Fabulae* 94. ELMENH.

**The public vendor of her intimate beauty.** On the word *intestinus*, “intimate” or “inward,” see above on ch. 20, Heraldus’s note. *Decus* means beauty or charm, particularly that of women. Seneca, *Medea* v. 75:

> Her maiden beauty far surpasses  
> The daughters-in-law of Cecrops.

*Publicare* is properly used of prostitutes who make themselves publicly available. “To make her beauty public” therefore means: “to offer her charms publicly for sale.” Others read “disgrace.” ORELL.

**The Theban or Tyrian Hercules.** The Theban is the one Jupiter fathered by Alcmena. The Tyrian is the son of Jupiter and Asteria, Latona’s sister; he is worshiped especially at Tyre and is said to have had a daughter, Carthage. Thus Cicero writes in the classic passage *On the Nature of the Gods* III.16, where he distinguishes six persons named Hercules. Compare Herodotus II.44, who speaks of two: one an Olympian god and the other a hero. ORELL.

**The Tyrian Hercules.** Arrian, *Expedition of Alexander* II, ch. 16:

> For at Tyre there is a temple of Heracles, the most ancient of those whose memory human tradition preserves. It is not the temple of the Argive Heracles, the son of Alcmena; for Heracles was honored at Tyre many generations before Cadmus, setting out from Phoenicia, occupied Thebes, and before Semele, the daughter of Cadmus, was born, from whom Dionysus, the son of Zeus, was born, etc.

Mela, book III, ch. 6: “On the island of Gades is a temple of the Egyptian Hercules, renowned for its founders, cult, antiquity, and wealth; the Tyrians founded it. The bones deposited there are the reason why it is holy.” Here he incorrectly confuses the Tyrian Hercules with the Egyptian. Compare Pausanias V, ch. 25. See more in Nourrius, p. 431 ff. ORELL.

**The Tyndarid Castors.** “Castors” is very frequently used for the Tyndarid brothers Castor and Pollux. See Turnebus, *Adversaria* XV, ch. 21, and the authors cited by Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. ORELL.

**The Titans and the Moorish Bocchores.** The manuscript codex has *Tisianes et Bucures Mauri*. “As many words as there are, so many errors. Read: ‘The Titans and the Bocchores.’ The Titans were worshiped as gods in Africa, as was their mother Titaea. See Diodorus, book III. The Mauritanians, moreover, worshiped even their petty kings as gods. Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 24: ‘Every province and city has its own god . . . Africa has Caelestis, and Mauritania its own petty kings.’ Athenagoras reports that Juba was worshiped as a god by the Mauritanians. Before Juba, the Bogudes and Bocchores ruled in Mauritania: *Bogoi and Bokchoi* (*Βόγοι καὶ Βόκχοι*). Thus *Bocchor* and *Bokchos* (*Βόκχος*) are the same. *Bokchoris* (*Βόκχορις*) is also the name of an Egyptian king.” SALMASIUS, *Plinian Exercises on Solinus*, p. 199.—Gelenius conjectures “marine fires and flashes,” which the remaining editors followed, with the exception of Heraldus and the Lyon edition; even the latest editor, Oberthür, retained it, rejecting Salmasius’s uniquely correct emendation. Grotius, cited by Meursius, p. 25, suspects that one should read “Tisianira and those born of the Bull-horned one,” explaining this as persons born to Nemesis and bull-horned Jupiter, so called because he was once transformed into a bull. This is even farther from the truth. ID.]

And the Syrian gods, offspring of eggs. “Thus we have emended the text from an old book. For the printed reading, *Dioscuri*, is the work of correctors and entirely foreign to the author’s intention. Three lines earlier he named the Tyndarids, the Castors: why would he repeat here the Dioscuri, who are the same? By the Syrian gods he means the Syrian goddess, whom they believed to have been born from an egg. The anonymous author on Germanicus’ *Aratean Phaenomena* (v. 240) says: ‘Nigidius says that these fish—namely, those in the Zodiac—were in the river Euphrates, and that there they found an egg of wondrous size. By rolling it they cast it onto land; a dove then settled upon it and, after several days, hatched the Syrian goddess, who is called Venus.’ Lucius Ampelius, in his book addressed to Macrinus: ‘It is also said that, in the [Col. 0761D] river Euphrates, a dove sat upon a fish’s egg for many days and hatched a goddess kindly and merciful toward human beings, to lead them to a good life.’ Hence the Syrians did not even touch doves as food, because a dove had incubated the fish’s egg from which the Syrian goddess—whom they called Venus—was born. From these passages it is evident that the ‘Syrian gods,’ who are frequently mentioned in ancient inscriptions, must be understood as the Syrian goddess—that is, Venus—and her son Cupid, and perhaps also Adonis, who was Venus’ *paredros* (companion seated beside her) and was likewise worshipped by the Syrians. Arnobius calls the Syrian gods the offspring of eggs, as though not only Venus had issued from an egg, but her son too had been born in this manner. Hyginus certainly writes (*Fabulae* 117) that Venus came with her son to Syria, to the Euphrates, in fear of Typhon, and that they changed their form into the shape of fish: ‘And so,’ he says, ‘the Syrians who live nearest those places subsequently ceased to eat fish, because they fear catching them, lest for the same reason they appear either to attack the gods’ protectors or to capture the gods themselves. Eratosthenes, however, says that these were born from that fish.’ That is, these gods, Venus and Cupid. For this is how the [Col. 0762A] manuscripts read in that passage, where editors have printed, most absurdly, ‘human beings were born from that fish.’ If Venus and Cupid were born from a fish among the Syrians, they are plainly the offspring of eggs, [Col. 0762B] since fish are born from eggs. These, then, are the Syrian gods.” SALMASIUS. Add Hugo Grotius, *Annotations on Book I, §16, of The Truth of the Christian Religion*. ORELLI.—One of the Pierides in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V.331, also sings that Venus hid in a fish. OCHSNER.

Apis, produced in the Peloponnese. Apis was the son of Phoroneus by Laodice; concerning him, Apollodorus, *Library*, Book I, chapter 1:

> “Apis, having turned his power toward tyranny and being a violent tyrant, named the Peloponnese Apia after himself. He was plotted against by Thelxion and Telchin and died childless; being regarded as a god, he was called Serapis.”

There Heyne, the distinguished scholar, in his *Observations*, p. 97 of the new edition, rightly observes that this Apis was confused by the Greeks with the Egyptian Apis, whom Herodotus III.27 interpreted as Epaphus, while others interpreted him sometimes as Osiris and sometimes as Serapis. Augustine, *The City of God* XVIII.5, and Eusebius, *Chronicle* II, fol. 64, write that he was transported by ship to Egypt, died there, and was worshipped by the Egyptians under the name Serapis. Scaliger, however, rejects this tale as a fabrication of mendacious Greece in his *Observations*, p. 22.—Others, including Oberthür, read *Syriapis*, very badly. “Produced in the Peloponnese” means born in the Peloponnese. Sanctius shows by many examples in *Minerva* IV.4, p. 655, Perizonius’ edition, that this locative genitive occurs in the names not only of cities but also of regions, provinces, and islands. Thus Cornelius Nepos, *Miltiades* 2: “that he himself had a home in the Chersonese”; and chapter 8: “Throughout all the years he had lived in the Chersonese, he had not maintained uninterrupted dominion.” ORELLI and OCHSNER.

Isis, darkened by the Ethiopian suns, mourning her lost son and her husband mangled limb by limb. See Diodorus Siculus, *Library* I.21, and Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*. Moreover, the son and husband of Isis is the same Osiris. After Typhon had killed him and cut him into eleven parts, Isis sought out his scattered limbs everywhere and laid each one to rest in the very place where she had found it. Compare Lactantius I.21 and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX.690 ff., with Gierig’s note there. *Membratim*: “limb by limb” (*kata melē*). See Keuchen on Frontinus, p. 141.

[Col. 0762D] We pass over the royal offspring of Ops. Oudendorp’s conjecture on Apuleius V, p. 336, reading “excellent” (*egregias*)—ironically, of course—is not to be despised. Thus *egregius* is often used ironically to mean “very bad.” So Apuleius II: “The excellent wife takes courage and, with sacrilegious intent,” etc.; and likewise Book IX: “The excellent wife called down dreadful curses upon him.” So too our German expressions *fein, sauber, tugendsam*—“fine, respectable, virtuous.” ORELLI.

*Hice ergo* (“these, then”). Thus the Lyon edition; the others have *Hi*; the first edition of Sabaeus has *Hinc*. ORELLI.

They receive it with wounded ears. Whatever unpleasant and disagreeable things reach the ears are said to offend them and, by the proper term, to “wound” them. Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.582:

> Lest some more grievous message wound their ears.

Lactantius VII.1: “Their ears are wounded by the commandments of continence.” HERALDUS. Compare Reiff on Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams* I.24, p. 241. ORELLI.

[Col. 0763C] Of whose condition that which has been granted to themselves. *Cujus* (“of whose”) stands for *de qua* (“concerning which”). It is a partitive genitive, like the Franco-Gallic *dont*. ORELLI.

Is this not a kind of envy and greed? That is, *pleonexia* (covetous self-advantage). He could not express the Greek word with a single precise Latin term; he therefore employed several words. HERALDUS.

Is it not a certain sordid disparagement? In the strict sense. Gloss: “*Obtrectatio* (disparagement): jealousy, abuse, slander, malice.” Marcus Tullius Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* IV: “Emulation is distress felt when another possesses what one has desired while one lacks it oneself. Disparagement, however—which I wish to be understood as jealousy—is distress arising from the fact that another also possesses what one has desired for oneself.” HERALDUS.

That the fortunes of others should be crushed and trampled down in despised lowliness. Virgil, *Aeneid* XI:

> Do not cease to trouble them with fear and to exalt the strength  
> Of a twice-defeated people, while crushing in turn the arms of Latinus.

By the words “to be trampled down in despised lowliness,” moreover, he expresses [Col. 0763D] the Greek verb *tapeinousthai*, “to be humbled.” For *tapeinos* (“lowly”) is as though from *pateinos* (“trodden down”). Thus Plautus says “to crush contemptuously” in the *Poenulus*:

> Yet, however things may be, although we are rather poor,  
> There is something at home for us to eat; do not crush us so contemptuously.

HERALDUS.]

### XXXVI

“But,” he says, “the gods are not hostile [Col. 0758C] toward you because you worship the omnipotent God, but because [Col. 0759A] you maintain that a man who was born—and, in a manner disgraceful for persons of low station, was killed by the punishment of the cross—was also God; because you believe that he still survives and worship him with daily supplications.”

If it pleases you, friends, explain fully who these gods are who believe that our worship of Christ constitutes an injury to themselves. Is it Janus, founder of the Janiculum, and Saturn, founder of the city of Saturn? Fauna—[Note: [Col. 0759A] *Fenta*. Absurdly. Manuscript.] Fatua, Faunus’ wife, who is called the Good Goddess, but is better and more praiseworthy when wine has been drunk? Those Indigetes who crawl along the river and live among the frogs and little fish in the channels [Col. 0760A] of the Numicus? Aesculapius and Father Liber—the one born of Coronis, the other hurled by a thunderbolt from his mother’s genital parts? Mercury, poured from Maia’s womb—and, what is still more divine, from the womb of the fair Maia? Diana and Apollo, bearers of the bow, carried about during their mother’s flight and scarcely safe upon wandering islands? Dione’s daughter Venus, matron of a Trojan and advertiser of her intimate beauty; Ceres, born within the borders of Trinacria, and Proserpina, occupied in gathering flowers? The Theban or Tyrian Hercules—the one buried within the borders [Col. 0761A] of Spain, the other burned up in the flames of Oeta? The Tyndarids—[Note: [Col. 0761A] “The gods Tuno-dari, the Castors.” Manuscript and Sabaeus, most corruptly:] the Castors, one accustomed to taming horses, the other a good boxer and invincible with the rawhide cestus? The Titans and the Moorish Bocchores, and the Syrian gods, offspring of eggs? Apis, produced in the Peloponnese and called Serapis in Egypt? Isis, darkened by the Ethiopian suns, mourning her lost son and her husband mangled [Col. 0762A] limb by limb?

We pass over and move beyond the royal offspring of Ops; what sort of beings they were and what their characters were, your own authors have disclosed in their books for your instruction. These, then, receive with wounded ears the fact that Christ is worshipped by us, accepted, and regarded as a divine power? Forgetting what their own lot was a little earlier and of whose condition they were, [Col. 0763A] do they refuse to impart to another what has been granted to themselves? Is this the justice of the heavenly beings? Is this the holy judgment of the gods? Is this not a kind of envy and greed, a certain sordid disparagement—the desire that their own fortunes alone should stand preeminent, while the fortunes of others are crushed and trampled down in despised lowliness?

[Note: [Col. 0763D]

### XXXVII.—Not one and another? Not countless others?

Fulvius Ursinus reads, “Surely one or another?” and deletes “others.” Not badly. ORELLI.

Run through their writings, etc. Arnobius is referring to the writings of Euhemerus and of those whom he names below in Book IV, chapter 29. ORELLI.

In what region born. Do not read *innati* as one word. This transposition of prepositions is characteristic of Arnobius. ORELLI.

What they did, performed, endured, repeatedly enacted. Cannegieter, in his *Second Studies on Avianus*, Fable II, v. 6, in *Miscellaneous Critical Observations*, vol. VII, p. 200, thinks the text should read: “what they did, performed, and endured,” with “repeatedly enacted” deleted. But this sort of verbal abundance is characteristic of Arnobius. ORELLI.]

### XXXVII

We worship a man who was born. What then? Do you worship no man who was born? Not one and another? Not countless others? Indeed, have you not taken all those whom you now possess in your temples from the number of mortals and bestowed heaven and the stars upon them?

For if it has perhaps escaped your notice that they belonged to the human lot and shared the common condition, unroll the most ancient writings and run through the works of those who lived close to antiquity and, without any flattery, transmitted everything in transparent truth. You will then certainly learn from what fathers and mothers each was begotten, in what region they were born, from what nation, what they did, performed, endured, and repeatedly enacted; [Note: [Col. 0763B] What if the reading were “and tolerated”? Wopkens in *Miscellanies*.] and what adverse and favorable fortunes they experienced while undertaking their deeds.

But if, although you know that they were carried in wombs and sustained their lives on the fruits of the earth, you nevertheless reproach us for worshipping a man who was born, you are acting quite unjustly: you determine that to be condemnable in us which you yourselves habitually do, or you refuse to allow others in the same way what you permit to yourselves.

[Note: [Col. 0764C]

### XXXVIII.—But let us grant it for the present, yielding to your opinions

*Interdum* is used for *interim*, “for the present, meanwhile.” Thus Silius Italicus, *Punica* IV.491, concerning Hannibal:

> Meanwhile, from an alder seized in the neighboring woods,  
> He builds a river fleet in which to carry his ranks across.

Compare VI.30 and Drakenborch’s note there; Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* III, p. 174; and J. F. Gronovius, *Observations on Ecclesiastical Writers* XXII, p. 246. His expression “to give a hand” stands for the more usual “to give one’s hands.” The phrase arose from those who acknowledge themselves defeated and offer their hands to the victors to be bound. Hence metaphorically it means to submit to someone’s opinion and to acknowledge that one has been defeated by another’s argument. Thus Lucretius II.1042:

> If it seems true to you,  
> Yield your hands.

[Col. 0764D] See Lambinus there. Cicero, *Laelius* 26: “For the flatterer is not very easily recognized, since he often agrees even while opposing, fawns while pretending to quarrel, and at last yields his hands and allows himself to be defeated.” HERALDUS and ORELLI.

You have enrolled among the divine beings in heaven. The Royal manuscript has “enrolled in the register,” which is perhaps better. So below, Book IV, chapter 1. HERALDUS and STEWECHIUS.

From precipices and trackless places. “Broken-off places” are nothing other than precipices. Thus Lucretius VI.538: “To bear in its bosom crags and sheer rocks.” MEURSIUS, p. 25.

And his substance, never before anticipated by anyone’s knowledge. The substance of God—that is, his spiritual nature (*pneumatikē*). Arnobius, however, appears to be referring to the words of the Divine Savior at John IV.24: “God is spirit.” ORELLI.

The generative heat is summoned. Oudendorp, on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* IV, p. 312, shows that either *adsciscitur* or *arcessitur* should be read in place of *adscitur*, which the editions have. ORELLI.

[Col. 0765A] Why the moon is believed always to remain unharmed in its movement, continually recovering light and darkness through animate causes. Thus most editors, following Gelenius. The manuscript and the first Roman edition have: “always in motion, no one is believed,” etc., a most corrupt reading which commentators have attempted to repair in various ways. Stewechius reads: “in motion, that is, it is believed to be restless,” etc. Fulvius Ursinus: “is the same orbit restored?” Meursius: “is it believed with new forms?”—that is, shapes or appearances. The Leiden editor recasts the whole passage thus: “Why the moon, always amid reciprocal losses and increases, through annual causes”—that is, on account of the year, for the completion of the year—“continually recovers light,” etc. This emendation certainly provides a suitable sense, but it is extremely bold and too far removed from the manuscript reading.

If I too may attempt something, I would conjecture that instead of *idem ne is*, etc., one should read *in ter denis vicibus redditur*: “is restored in three times ten phases”—that is, is returned to its former state. There is a very similar passage below, Book VI, chapter 10: “The moon is always in motion and assumes three times ten appearances in its monthly restoration.” *Idem ne is* seems to have arisen when an ignorant scribe misheard *in ter denis* as another dictated it.

Moreover, I am led to regard this whole passage—from the words “From what source the sun’s fires,” etc., to “recovering darkness”—as a gloss that slipped into the text from the margin, where some pedantic [Col. 0765C] scribe had written down physical questions, especially by the indicative forms *adsciscitur* (“is summoned”) and *redditur* (“is restored”), which are out of place. For the preceding words, “by what father the world was established,” just as much as the following, “what the origin of living beings may be,” undoubtedly require the subjunctive.

The following words, “through animate causes,” seem perfectly sound to me. Stewechius alone partially saw the true meaning. “Animate causes” are living causes—the impulse of some force or intelligent nature, such as the Stoics attributed to the sun, moon, and other stars. Stobaeus, *Selections* I.26:

> “Zeno says that the sun, the moon, and each of the other stars is intelligent and rational and fiery, consisting of creative fire.”

Augustine, *The City of God* IV.11: “They—the Stoics—say that all the stars are parts of Jupiter, that they all live and possess rational souls, and that they are therefore indisputably gods.” Above all, Julius Firmicus Maternus, *Mathesis* I.3 (p. 7, Pruckner’s edition): “For the stars possess their own sensation and divine intelligence; animated by a pure conception of divinity, they obey with tireless accord that supreme and ruling God, who arranged everything according to the disposition of an everlasting [Col. 0765D] law, so that they may preserve the order of perpetual generation.”

The foremost Fathers also followed this opinion, as did Arnobius here and Origen, who, according to Jerome, *Letter to Avitus* 59, acknowledged souls in the sun, moon, and stars, yet held that they did not begin to exist when the world was made, but existed before they entered those shining and burning bodies. The ancient astrologers—Manilius, for example—accordingly called them:

> Stars conscious of fate,  
> Varying the diverse fortunes of human beings.

See J. Lipsius, *On Stoic Physiology* II, dissertation 14, *Works*, p. 933 ff., vol. IV, Wesel edition.

Moreover, someone might find it surprising that Arnobius here represented Christ as teaching about physics and atmospheric phenomena. But he did this after the fashion of many Fathers of the Church, who, representing the Divine Savior as the teacher of all wisdom, human as well as divine, attributed to him matters about which [Col. 0766A] he had not said so much as a word, just as Plato did to Socrates. ORELLI.

Who formed him. *Informare* has the same meaning as the simple *formare*. [Col. 0766B] Thus Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God* 8: “God the craftsman therefore did not wish to form those ears . . . with soft membranes.” See Bunemann there, p. 1165. ORELLI.

Established the very structure. Fulvius Ursinus conjectures “fashioned” (*conformaverit*), with the approval of Meursius and Stewechius. But “established” (*confirmaverit*) is preferable. For one may correctly speak of “fashioning a body,” but not of “fashioning the structure of a body”; rather, one “establishes” it—that is, renders it firm and solid in every respect. Besides, *conformaverit*, following the preceding *informaverit*, would produce a most disagreeable tautology. These two words are very frequently confused in manuscripts. See Graevius on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* I.8. ORELLI.

Whether it was sown together with the entrails themselves—that is, with the body itself, as often. ORELLI.

Whether we shall retain sensation . . . or shall possess no memory of our sensation and no recollection. Thus, with the Leiden editor, one must read *visuri* (“going to perceive”), not *victuri* (“going to live”). For Arnobius has just said, “whether the soul has been endowed with the perpetuity of immortality,” which would be exactly the same as asking whether we shall live. [Col. 0766C] Among Latin authors, however, “to see” is used of every form of sensation, so as to mean “to perceive” or “to know,” as when one says: “See what sound it makes; see what it smells or tastes like; see how hard it is.” See Saint Augustine, *Confessions* X.35, and Cortius on Sallust, *Catiline* 40, p. 247. Translate, therefore: “whether we shall still possess sensation after death, or whether all consciousness of sensation and recollection will cease.” ORELLI.

It is indeed true that words of seeing can be applied to all the senses, insofar as every sensation involves awareness. Many have commented upon this, including Ernesti on Callimachus, *Hymn to Apollo*, v. 4. But nearly all the examples cited are of such a kind that they include a particular class of sensations to which that verb is referred; “to see” is not used absolutely. It must therefore be investigated whether examples can be found in which “to see” embraces not this or that part of sensation but, as here, the entire faculty of sensation without qualification. OCHSNER.

Necks raised with pride. To raise the neck is characteristic of the proud; by contrast, those who think modestly of themselves are called “level” and are said to make themselves level. Cyprian, *On Mortality*: “Let the proud man bend his neck.” Lactantius V.23: “The same man, displaying no swelling or insolence, does not raise himself higher or lift a proud head, but is calm, harmonious, agreeable, and unassuming, because he knows his own condition.” ELMENHORST and HERALDUS.—Meursius emends this to “haughtily raised necks.” Others read “necks together with the eyebrow,” a reading defended by Janus Dousa on Catullus LXVIII.4, so that the meaning would be “both the raised eyebrow and the necks.” Petronius likewise writes in chapter 91, §7: “After he perceived that he was loved, he raised his eyebrow higher”; and our own author below, Book II, chapter 50: “Philosophers who suppose that they alone are supremely wise and, by the force of this title, have raised their eyebrows.” But “eyebrow” is also metaphorically used in general for haughtiness, pride, and arrogance. Juvenal, Satire 6.167:

> I would rather have a Venusian woman than you, Cornelia, mother  
> Of the Gracchi, if along with your great virtues you bring  
> A lofty pride and count triumphs as part of your dowry.

Accordingly, nothing should be changed. ORELLI.

[Col. 0767B] Who showed that we are shapeless living creatures. That is, imperfect and deformed, so that we should not boast of our beauty. I therefore think that nothing should be changed. HERALDUS.—Stewechius conjectures “weak.” ORELLI.

To have comprehended nothing, to know nothing, and not to see what lies before our eyes. Arnobius appears here to have wrongly transferred to the entire human race those words of Christ in Matthew XIII.15 which the Divine Savior spoke concerning the Jewish people:

> “For the heart of this people has grown dull, and with their [Col. 0767C] ears they have heard heavily, and they have closed their own eyes, lest perhaps they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn back, and I should heal them.”

ORELLI.

Lifeless images. Similarly below, Book II, chapter 39: “to make supplication to lifeless images.” Zeno of Verona, in his sermon *On Jonah*, calls images “stupid.” HERALDUS.]

### XXXVIII

But let us grant, for the present yielding to your opinions, that Christ was one of us—of the same mind, soul, body, frailty, and condition. Is he not worthy, in gratitude for such great gifts, to be called God by us and to be regarded as God?

For if you have enrolled among the divine beings in heaven Liber because he discovered the use of wine; Ceres, because she discovered the use of bread; Aesculapius, because he discovered the use of herbs; Minerva, because she discovered the olive; Triptolemus—[Note: [Col. 0763B] *Neoptolemus*. Wrongly. Manuscript.]—because he discovered the plow; and finally Hercules, because he overcame and subdued wild beasts, thieves, and serpents with many heads: with how great honors ought we to treat him who led us away from great errors by imparting the truth; who, when we were wandering everywhere like blind persons and without any guide, brought us back [Col. 0764B] from precipices and trackless places to smoother ground; who first showed what is fruitful and beneficial to the human race—namely, what God is, who he is, how great and of what kind; who allowed and taught us, so far as our limited capacity could grasp and understand them, to comprehend his profound and ineffable heights; who most kindly caused it to be known by what author and father this world was established and founded; who disclosed the manner of its birth and his substance, never before anticipated by anyone’s knowledge? [Note: [Col. 0764B] “Substance.” Wrongly, Sabaeus.]

From what source the generative heat is summoned to the sun’s fires; why the moon is believed always to remain unharmed in its movement, continually recovering light and darkness through animate causes; what the origin of living beings may be and what principles seeds possess; who fashioned man himself, who formed him, or from what kind of material he established the very structure of bodies; how sensation arises, what the soul is, whether it flew to [Col. 0766A] us of its own accord or was sown and engendered together with the entrails themselves; whether it lives subject to death or has been endowed with the perpetuity of immortality; what condition awaits us when we have departed from our dissolved limbs; whether we shall retain sensation or possess no memory of our sensation and no recollection.

Who restrained [Note: [Col. 0765A] “Restrains.” Sabaeus.] our arrogance and compelled necks raised with pride to recognize the measure of their own weakness; [Col. 0767A] who showed that we are shapeless living creatures, that we trust in empty opinions, have comprehended nothing, know nothing, and do not see what lies before our eyes; who—in an achievement surpassing and exceeding all his gifts—led us away from false religions to the true religion; [Note: [Col. 0767B] “Led away.” Others.] who raised us from lifeless images fashioned from the vilest clay to the stars and heaven, and enabled us to mingle words of supplication and the converse of prayer with God, the Lord of all things.

[Note: [Col. 0767C]

### XXXIX.—Gods fashioned upon anvils and by hammers

Fulvius Ursinus deletes “upon,” but nothing should be changed. “Upon” and “from” are very frequently redundant. See the note above on chapter 5, at the words “from the hidden teachings of the Chaldeans.” A passage very similar to ours occurs in Minucius Felix, *Octavius* 33: “A god of gold or silver is melted down from an unclean vessel—as was very often done for an Egyptian king—is beaten by hammers, and is shaped upon anvils.” HERALDUS and ELMENHORST.

Bands upon torpid old trees. He means trees upon which spoils were hung and consecrated to the gods. For on the votive offerings and dedications themselves there were bands—that is, fillets, ribbons, or the ends of ribbons, as Servius explains on Virgil, *Aeneid* I.374—and something depicted upon them. Plutarch, *Timoleon*:

> “For from the hanging votive offerings a certain ribbon slipped loose; as it was carried along, bearing wreaths and embroidered victories, it fell around Timoleon’s head.”

Passersby worshipped these trees with religious observance, and they remained inviolate for very many years; Arnobius therefore calls them “torpid with age.” Lucan describes such a tree most elegantly in Book I.136 ff. Testimonies concerning the worship and veneration of these trees are nearly countless elsewhere as well, and occur in especially explicit language in Apuleius’ first *Florida*. HERALDUS and NOURRY.—*Veternus* means lethargy, as Servius explains on Virgil, *Georgics* I.124; *veternosus* means sluggish or torpid. It was forbidden to pluck fruit from sacred trees; therefore they generally consecrated only trees that were aged and no longer fit for any use, a point Arnobius touches upon here. Tertullian expresses almost the same thought when he addresses the enemies of Christians in *Apology* 14: “I also wish to review your rites. I will not say what you are like in sacrificing, when you slaughter every creature that is worn out, diseased, and scabby.” Franciscus Odinus gives this excellent explanation of our passage in his *Critical Adversaria*, included in the *New Miscellaneous Critical Observations*, fascicle XXII, p. 458. ORELLI.

If ever I had seen a stone made slippery and befouled with olive oil. Thus Fulvius Ursinus. The manuscript has “a stone . . . arranged,” from which Theodorus Canter produced “perfumed,” and Stewechius “adorned.” Dempster, *Supplement to Rosinus’ Roman Antiquities* II.20, p. 184, Schrevelius’ edition, conjectures “watered”; Meursius, “consecrated”—that is, made divine. But “befouled” is preferable. The verb *sordidare*, “to befoul,” is not rare among ecclesiastical writers such as Lactantius, Cyprian, and Augustine.

He means an anointed stone, a *liparos lithos* (“greasy stone”). For so it is called in Greek, as may be seen from Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* VII:

> “These same people worship every piece of wood and every stone, especially the one called the ‘greasy stone.’”

Arnobius translated this passage, like many others from Clement, into Latin. Theophrastus’ *Character* XVI, “The Superstitious Man,” is not dissimilar:

> “And whenever he passes one of the greasy stones at the crossroads, he pours oil upon it from his flask.”

See Casaubon there. Apuleius calls it an “anointed stone” in the *Apology*, and in the *Florida* “a stone smeared with ointment.” PRIOR and ORELLI.

A block of wood. Prudentius, in *Crowns of Martyrdom*, calls it “a hewn post,” and in the *Apotheosis* a “pillar and figwood post.” ELMENHORST.

[Col. 0768D] To the divine name. Theodorus Canter reads “divine power,” with the approval of Stewechius and Meursius. But see the notes on chapter 20. ORELLI.]

### XXXIX

Only recently—O blindness!—I used to venerate images freshly brought out of furnaces, gods fashioned upon anvils and by hammers, elephants’ bones, paintings, and bands upon torpid old trees. If ever I had seen a stone made slippery and befouled with olive oil, I would fawn upon it as though a present power dwelt within it, address it, and ask benefits from a block of wood that perceived nothing. [Col. 0767B] I subjected [Note: [Col. 0767B] “I treated.” Manuscript.] to grievous insults those very divine beings whose existence I had persuaded myself to accept, since I believed them to be wood, stones, and bones, or to inhabit material of that kind.

Now, led onto the paths of truth by so great a teacher, I know what all those things are. I hold opinions worthy of worthy beings; [Note: [Col. 0768B] “Of divine beings.” Stewechius.] I inflict no insult upon the divine name; and I assign to each person or rank what is owed to it, according to distinct degrees and authorities.

Shall Christ, then, not be regarded by us as God? Shall he not—although otherwise the greatest of all that can be conceived—be honored with divine worship, when from him we have already received such great gifts while living and expect still greater ones when the day arrives?

[Note: [Col. 0768D]

### XL.—Pythagoras of Samos, because of an unjust suspicion of tyranny, was burned alive in a shrine

There were various opinions concerning Pythagoras’ death, reported by Laertius (VIII.§39), Tzetzes (*Chiliades* XI, p. 443), the Suda (under “Pythagoras”), and others. The first is that, while he was in the house of Milo of Croton, he was suffocated by flames when the same house was set on fire, either through the resentment of one of those whom he had refused to admit there or through the Crotoniates’ suspicion and fear of tyranny. Others report that he escaped from there but, in a field full of beans, surrendered his throat to his pursuers. Dicaearchus, however, according to Laertius in the cited passage, believed that Pythagoras hid for forty days in the shrine of the Muses at Metapontum and gave up his life through hunger and starvation. Laertius also relates further opinions of Heraclides and Hermippus concerning Pythagoras’ death.

Plutarch is briefer, *On Stoic Self-Contradictions*, vol. II, p. 1051:

> “Such events befell noble and good men—for example, the condemnation of Socrates and the burning of Pythagoras alive by the followers of Cylon.”

But he says nothing at all about whether Pythagoras was burned in some house or in a shrine. If desired, consult also Malchus, Iamblichus (*Life of Pythagoras* I.35), Tzetzes, and others on Pythagoras’ life, as well as the annotations of Menagius and others on the cited passage of Laertius. Finally, Arnobius’ following statement that Pythagoras was burned alive because of an unjust suspicion of tyranny may be confirmed by the testimony of Tertullian (*Apology* 46), who asserts without hesitation that Pythagoras had sought tyranny. NOURRY, p. 531 ff. Add Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 280, Rechenberg’s edition.

Moreover, Fulvius Ursinus conjectures *inusta* (“branded”) for *injusta* (“unjust”). Havercamp, on Tertullian, *Apology* 46, p. 391, reads “of unjust tyranny.” But nothing should be changed, for throughout this chapter Arnobius speaks of those who died innocent through the wrongdoing of their adversaries. Others read “in Samos” instead of “in a shrine.” Wrongly. ORELLI.

Aquilius. Meursius thinks the text should read Acilius, who was removed from the world by Nero through a savage death. But nothing should be changed. The most learned Casaubon rightly observed that Arnobius is speaking of Manius Aquilius, Oppius’ legate, whom Mithridates killed with extreme cruelty. After capturing Aquilius, Mithridates mocked him in extraordinary ways, paraded him about mounted upon an ass, and finally poured molten gold into his mouth, as Appian reports in *Mithridatic Wars* 21. Compare Pliny, *Natural History* XXXIII.3. Cicero also mentions him in *On the Manilian Law*. HERALDUS and NOURRY.

Lindner, in his index to Minucius Felix, understands Aquilius to be the duumvir appointed to inspect the Sibylline books who, because he was thought to have acted dishonestly and was denounced by an accomplice in the crime, was sewn into a sack and cast into the sea by King Tarquin the Proud. But wrongly: that man was Atilius, not Aquilius. See Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* IV, p. 239 ff., Sylburg’s edition. ORELLI.

Trebonius. This is the man whom Cicero, *Philippic* XI.1, and Appian, *Civil Wars* III.26, say was killed with extreme cruelty by Dolabella. HERALDUS, in his *Second Studies*.

By the cruelty. Thus L. Carrio emended the text in *Emendations* II.3, p. 134, in Gruter’s *Critical Torch*. It had previously read “the cruelty” in the accusative. ORELLI.]

### XL

“But he died fastened to a cross.” What bearing does that have upon the case? The character and hideousness of his death do not alter his words or deeds; nor will the authority of his teachings appear any less because he departed from the bonds of the body not through natural dissolution but died by inflicted violence.

Pythagoras of Samos, because of an unjust suspicion of tyranny, was burned alive in a shrine. Surely the things he taught did not lose their intrinsic force because he poured out his spirit not voluntarily but when assailed by cruelty? Similarly, Socrates, condemned by the judgment of his own city, suffered capital punishment. Surely his discussions of morals, virtues, and duties were not rendered void because he was driven from life by injustice?

Countless others eminent in glory, virtue, and reputation experienced the most bitter forms of death—Aquilius, Trebonius, and Regulus, for example. Surely they were not judged disgraceful after death because they perished not according to the common law of fate, but mangled and tortured by an extremely harsh kind of death? No innocent person ever becomes infamous because he has been wrongfully killed; nor is one stained with any mark of disgrace when he suffers grievous punishments not through his own deserts but through the cruelty of his torturer.

[Note: [Col. 0769D]

### XLI.—O you people!

This is a Greek idiom, *ō houtoi*, employed, of course, in contempt. See C. Barthius, *Adversaria* IX.10, p. 433, and XXVIII.2, p. 1311; and Viger, *On Greek Idioms* VII.11, where he cites our passage. C. Barthius also observes, *Adversaria* LIII.10, p. 2496, that Christian writers shrank from uttering the name “pagans” or “gentiles,” owing to a certain superstition by which the ancients thought that those against whom they were deservedly incensed should not even be named, since by the very act of naming them they might appear in some fashion to assent to them or to approve what had been done. Compare Heraldus, *Adversaria* I.3, p. 9. ORELLI.

Father Liber, torn limb from limb by the Titans. Thus the Leiden editor. Others read “scattered.” See below, Book V, chapter 19; Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, who discusses this myth at length; Hyginus, *Fabulae* 167; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* II.5; and Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*. ELMENHORST.

Magnified by the consecration of temples. This is the entirely correct reading of the Royal manuscript. Previously the text read “fitted for the consecration of temples.” Ludovicus Carrio was the first to recognize and restore the true reading, in *Emendations* II.3. Arnobius uses a parallel expression when he says that souls are “magnified by the condition of immortality,” Book II, chapter 28; and Book VII, chapter 14: “When God is said to be honored by a human being and magnified by the offering of some gift.” STEWECHIUS and HERALDUS.—Andreas Schottus illustrates this verb excellently in *Ciceronian Knots* IV.4, in *Humanistic Observations*, p. 371. *Mactare*, properly a term of sacred ritual, means the same as “to increase or magnify”; through euphemism it came to mean “to slaughter,” since according to ancient, savage superstition it was forbidden to utter ill-omened words, lest the rites be corrupted. Hence *mactare* came to mean “to kill.” ORELLI.

Surely great Hercules himself, etc. He calls him “great Hercules,” using a proper epithet. Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.102:

> By chance on that day the Arcadian king was rendering solemn honor  
> To great Amphitryon’s son and to the gods.

HERALDUS.

Invited by burned incense. Others, including Fulvius Ursinus, read “agitated,” wrongly. They invited the gods by sacrifices and even called upon them during the rite itself: “Be present,” etc. Virgil, *Georgics* II.529: “Pouring a libation, he calls upon you, Lenaeus.” The manuscripts have *tura* (“incense”), which was how people wrote in that age. Servius on *Georgics* I: “Certainly we now say *tus* without aspiration. For the ancients said *thus*, deriving it from the Greek *thyein* (‘to sacrifice’),” an explanation that found no favor. They preferred to derive *tura* from *tundere* (“to pound”), from the pounded lumps into which the substance flowing from the tree is said to congeal. HERALDUS.]

Burned alive, after his sufferings, and consumed by fire in death-polluted burial grounds. The words *after his sufferings* have slipped in from the preceding clause [Col. 0770D] and should therefore be deleted, unless one prefers: *through sufferings*. ADR. BEHOT., *Apophoreta*. Meursius, believing the whole passage to be dislocated, arranges it thus: “Did you not invite even great Hercules, after his sufferings, with sacrifices, victims, and burning incense—Hercules whom you yourselves report to have been burned alive and consumed by fire,” etc. These words seem to me to have originated with some pedantic copyist who wished by them to signify the labors (*ἆθλα*, “contests”) of Hercules. For *funestis* the Royal manuscript has *funestibus*, from which others have made *funebribus* (“funereal”), incorrectly. For *funestus* in this passage, in its proper and primary sense, means the same as “polluted by a corpse.” Thus *funesta busticeta* are “tombs full of dead men’s bones and every impurity” (*τάφοι γέμοντες ὀστέων νεκρῶν καὶ πάσης ἀκαθαρσίας*), as the divine Savior says, Matthew 23:27; or, as Arnobius himself says below, Book VII, chapter 15: “burial grounds constructed for a most loathsome purpose and fashioned as an abode of foul odors.” “*Busticeta*: tombs in the countryside,” in the Glosses of Isidore. Meursius, p. 28, defends *funestibus* by the practice of those writers, who very frequently confuse forms of the second and third declensions. Thus *diacones*, *subdiacones* in Augustine; *opipares* in Apuleius [Col. 0771B], *Metamorphoses* 1 and 2; Cyprian in his Letters has *presbyteres* and *diacones*; Festus has *patrimes*, *matrimes*, *heres* for *herus*, and *sacres*. Conversely, some place in the second declension words more commonly expressed in the third: Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, has *informus* and *elinguus*; Sallust, *inermus*; others, *imbecillus* also; Lucretius has *sterilus*, *hilarus*, *gracilus*, and *proclivus*. Gnaeus Matius said *acrum* in *Odyssey* XV, as Charisius notes from Caesellius Vindex; hence the Glosses: “*Acrum*: terrible, sharp” (*δεινὸν, δριμύ*). Thus Meursius. ORELL.

**Cut off and stripped of his manhood.** *Vir* is very frequently used for the genital organ—our German *Mannheit* (“manhood”). See Meursius and Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book IV, chapter 11, p. 158. ORELL.—Add Scaliger and Douza on Catullus 64.6. OCHSNER.

[Col. 0771C] **And you say that Quirinus is Martian.** I could readily believe that *Martium* (“Martian”) is a gloss. Indeed, unless I am greatly mistaken, that is how matters stand. For although Arnobius likes to couple several words, the example here nevertheless seems rather unsuitable. It is now universally known that the names of dead men who had been consecrated were customarily changed, lest anyone suppose that they had been human beings, as Lactantius observes. HERALD.—I wonder whether the reading should not be *Quirinum Martem* (“Mars Quirinus”). For Quirinus is properly an epithet of Mars. Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* I.292: “Mars, when he rages, is called Gradivus; when tranquil, Quirinus.” And it is well known that the Romans, as a mark of honor, attached the name of some god or goddess of the greater nations to human beings enrolled among the gods—for example, Juno Cleopatra, Juno Faustina, Venus Agrippina, Jupiter Serapis. See Lipsius and Oberlin on Tacitus, *Annals* V.2, pp. 467–68, and Musgrave on Sophocles, *Philoctetes* 929, p. 264, Erfurdt’s edition. Why, then, not Mars Quirinus as well? ORELL.]

### XLI

And yet, you people who ridicule us for worshiping a man who underwent an ignominious death—do you not yourselves honor Father Liber, torn limb from limb by the Titans, through the consecration of temples? Did you not appoint Aesculapius, the discoverer of medicines, after the pains and punishment of the thunderbolt, as guardian and presiding deity of health, well-being, and safety? Do you not invite even great Hercules with sacrifices, victims, and burning incense—Hercules whom you yourselves report to have been burned alive after his sufferings [Col. 0770B] and consumed by fire in death-polluted burial grounds? Do you not proclaim [Col. 0771A] that Attis the Phrygian, castrated and stripped of his manhood, is within the inner sanctuaries of the Great Mother a gracious god, a holy god, amid the acclamations of the Galli? Do you not say that Father Romulus himself, torn apart by the hands of a hundred senators, is the Martian Quirinus; do you not honor him with priests and sacred couches, worship him in most magnificent temples, and swear that after all this he ascended into heaven? Either, therefore, you too deserve ridicule, since you regard and worship as gods men who were killed by the most grievous torments; or, if there is a sound reason why you think you must do this, permit us also to know the causes and reasons for which we do the same.

[Note: [Col. 0771C]

### XLII.—**The things that have proceeded from him into us.**

A sound reading. So too Book II, chapter 2: “Who introduced true religion into the world” [Col. 0771D]. Zeno of Verona, in his sermon *On Susanna*: “Then the Holy Spirit entered into the holy boy Daniel.” The Greeks likewise spoke in this way, using *ἐν* (“in”) for *εἰς* (“into”). HERALD. This usage belongs not only to writers of the later age but also to those of the Golden Age. Ovid, *Fasti* III.664: “He goes onto the summit of the sacred mountain.” Phaedrus, Book V, fable 1: “Who is that debauchee who dares to come into my sight?” See Muncker on Hyginus, Fable 92, and Davies on Commodian, *Instructions* XIII. There is a twofold observation: first, that the ablative is put for the accusative; second, that the accusative is put for the ablative—a usage Lipsius affected everywhere in his critical works. It was especially noted by Beatus Rhenanus in the *Thesaurus of Tacitean Expressions*, Janus Gebhardus in his *Crepundia*, Oudendorp on Suetonius, *Augustus* 16, and others. Cannegieter, in opposition to Neveletus, has demonstrated the same in his *Dissertation on Avianus*, chapter 19, pp. 299 ff. OCHSNER.

**And without any ambiguity of doubt about anything.** *Rei* (“about anything”) is superfluous; accordingly I would read: “and without any ambiguity of renewed doubt” (*redubitationis*). [Col. 0772B] *Redubitatio* is formed like *repromissio* and similar words. HERALD. For my part, with Fulvius Ursinus, I consider *rei* to be deleted entirely. It is a gloss originating from the preceding *re certa* (“as a certain fact”). For there is no example among the ancients of the word *redubitatio*. ORELL.

**Angry and inflamed.** Fulvius Ursinus reads “inflamed with anger” (*ira percitus*). But nothing should be changed. Arnobius favors this expression. Below: “Would it not be a matter worthy of his being angry and inflamed on its account?” And in Book VII: “before they are angry and inflamed.” ELMENH.

**God of the inner powers.** A difficult passage, which I am greatly surprised none of the interpreters has addressed. I understand by “powers” those beings that in Sacred Scripture are called “the powers of the heavens” (*δυνάμεις τῶν οὐρανῶν*), “the host of heaven” (*στρατιὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ*) [Col. 0772C], that is, angels. It is well known that the Jews and the earliest Fathers of the Church—Judaizing in many respects—divided heaven into various regions or circles, each inhabited by its own powers, that is, intelligent natures most diverse in dignity and authority, which they called aeons. They assigned the middle and innermost place to God himself and to Christ sitting at the Father’s right hand; Christ himself is also called by the Fathers of the Church *κατ’ ἐξοχήν* (“preeminently”) an *ἄγγελος* (“angel”), or the Angel of the New Testament. See Suicer, *Ecclesiastical Thesaurus*, under *ἄγγελος*. They gave the next place to the Thrones, a more distant one to the archangels, followed by the Cherubim and Seraphim; finally, the outermost choir, farthest removed from God’s throne, is formed by the angels who preside over the stars and the guardian spirits of human beings. (On this subject see especially Dionysius the Areopagite, *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, or extracts from him in the distinguished Schröckh’s *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. XVII, pp. 546 ff.) This doctrine seems to have derived from the Chaldaeans, who similarly distributed heaven into various spheres or circles. See Michael Psellus’ *Summary of Chaldaean Doctrines* appended to the *Magical Oracles of Zoroaster* in Gallæus’ edition of the *Sibylline Oracles*. Arnobius therefore says [Col. 0772D] that Christ, as the being nearest to God, is God of the inner powers—German, *von den innersten (obersten) Himmelsmächten*, “of the innermost (highest) heavenly powers.” But let the more learned judge. Nourrius, p. 351, explains “God of the inner powers” as the ruler of our soul and all its faculties. But I very greatly doubt whether these words, used absolutely without the addition of “mind” or “soul,” can have this meaning. “God of hidden forces,” namely of nature—German, *Herr aller geheimen, verborgenen Kräfte*, “Lord of all secret, hidden forces”—would be more likely. Yet I still think that by these words Arnobius had in view some esoteric element of Gnostic doctrine. ORELL.

**Perhaps, having become still more insane and furious, he will demand proof that the matter stands so.** Should we not read: “Perhaps, still more insane and furious, he will demand that it be proved by facts (*factis*—that is, by matters embodied in fact, German *durch Tatsachen*) that the matter stands so”? ORELL.

**Conquered decrees.** *Victa* means “brought to completion” (*τελειωθέντα*), completed and consummated. ORELL.

**To be carried out beneath his own light.** This is Fulvius Ursinus’ correction. [Col. 0773B] The manuscript has *suo generis sub limine* (“beneath the threshold of its kind”), which does not seem rashly to be rejected, so that the sense would be: decrees of the divine power begun already from the first origins of the human race. ORELL.]

### XLII

You worship a man who was born. Even if that were true, nevertheless [Col. 0771B], as has been said in the preceding passages, because of the many and generous gifts that have proceeded from him [Col. 0772A] into us, he ought to be called and named God. But since he is God as a certain fact [Note: [Col. 0771B] “In truth.” Fulvius], and without any ambiguity of doubt about anything, do you suppose that we will deny that he is worshiped by us above all and is called the guardian of our body? “Then,” someone will say, raging, angry, and inflamed, “is that Christ God?” “God,” we shall answer, “and God of the inner powers; and—to torment unbelievers with the bitterest pains—sent to us by the supreme King for a matter of the greatest importance.” Perhaps, having become still more insane and furious, he will demand proof that the matter stands as we say. No proof is greater than the credibility of the deeds performed by him, than the unprecedented character of his miracles, than all the decrees conquered and the ordinances of fate dissolved, which [Col. 0772B] peoples and nations saw being carried out beneath his own light [Col. 0773A], with no one dissenting; deeds which not even those men dare to accuse of falsehood whose ancient or ancestral laws he showed to be utterly full of vanity and the emptiest superstition.

[Note: [Col. 0773B]

### XLIII.—**Perhaps he will confront us again with those many other slanderous and childish expressions.**

Stewechius prefers: “Perhaps another will confront us again with those many slanderous expressions,” etc., referring the pronoun back to the preceding words: “Perhaps, having become still more insane and furious, he will demand.” But nothing should be changed: “he will confront,” namely, my adversary—that is, the pagans, whom Arnobius, employing singular expressions of this kind, collectively embraces throughout his entire work. ORELL.

**He was a magician.** Celsus, in Origen, Book I: “In what follows he also accuses the Savior of having been able through sorcery to perform the deeds that seemed extraordinary” (*κατηγορεῖ δὲ ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς καὶ τοῦ Σωτῆρος, ὡς γοητείᾳ δυνηθέντος* [Col. 0773C] *ἃ ἔδοξε παράδοξα πεποιηκέναι*). ELMENH.

**From the inner sanctuaries of the Egyptians.** Horrendous are the blasphemies that in reckless desperation of speech they vomited against Christ. Since they had read that Christ was taken into Egypt because of Herod’s fury, they therefore said that in Egypt he practiced the magical arts, and that, furnished with them, he returned to his countrymen in Judaea and there arrogated to himself the name of God. This is what the most impure Celsus says in Origen (Book I, p. 30, Spencer’s edition): “And that, because of poverty, he hired himself out for wages in Egypt, and there made trial of certain powers on which the Egyptians pride themselves; he returned greatly elated by those powers and, because of them, proclaimed himself a god” (*καὶ ὅτι οὗτος διὰ πενίαν εἰς Αἴγυπτον μισθαρνήσας, κἀκεῖ δυνάμεών τινων πειραθεὶς, ἐφ’ αἷς Αἰγύπτιοι σεμνύνονται, ἐπανῆλθεν, ἐν ταῖς δυνάμεσι μέγα φρονῶν, καὶ δι’ αὐτὰς θεὸν αὑτὸν ἀνηγόρευσεν*). HERALD.

**From the inner sanctuaries of the Egyptians . . . he stole esoteric teachings.** The same Celsus in Origen, Book I: “And that, because of poverty, he hired himself out for wages in Egypt, and there made trial of certain powers on which the Egyptians pride themselves; he returned greatly elated by those powers and, because of them, proclaimed himself a god” (*καὶ ὅτι οὗτος διὰ πενίαν εἰς Αἴγυπτον μισθαρνήσας, κἀκεῖ δυνάμεών τινων πειραθεὶς, ἐφ’ αἷς Αἰγύπτιοι σεμνύνονται, ἐπανῆλθεν ἐν ταῖς δυνάμεσι μέγα φρονῶν, καὶ δι’ αὐτὰς θεὸν αὑτὸν ἀνηγόρευσεν*). Certain more recent interpreters of Holy Scripture, ill-employed in their leisure, have revived the same tale [Col. 0773D]. ORELL.

**Unknown and unfamiliar to you.** *Nescius* has a passive meaning, “unknown.” Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* V, concerning the pregnant Psyche: “Anxiously she counts the growing days and passing months, and wonders at the first beginnings of her unknown burden”; see Oudendorp there, p. 343. ORELL.

**The names of powerful angels.** He says “names” because in their incantations the Magi uttered barbarous and dreadful names of angels and powers, by whose force and efficacy they believed that any great and extraordinary (*παράδοξα*) deeds were performed. See Origen, Book I, *Against Celsus*. HERALD.

**O children.** Greek *ὦ νήπιοι*, “O infants.” HERALD.

**The games of magical arts.** In the proper sense. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter XXIII: “If they play at many miracles by tricks of street performers.” So too the Greeks call them the “tricks” (*παίγνια*) of magicians. Irenaeus, in Epiphanius, *Heresy* XXIV: “For by combining the tricks of Anaxilaus with the knavery of those called magicians, and by producing illusions and practicing magic through them, he cast those who saw him and believed him into amazement” (*Τὰ γὰρ Ἀναξιλάου παίγνια τῇ τῶν λεγομένων μάγων πανουργίᾳ συμμίξας, δι’ αὐτῶν φαντάζων τε καὶ μαγεύων, εἰς ἔκπληξιν* [Col. 0774B] *τοὺς ὁρῶντάς τε καὶ πειθομένους αὐτῷ περιέβαλεν*). Quintus Curtius therefore properly calls them the games of magicians, Book VII, chapter 4: “At that banquet was Cobares, a Mede by nationality, but renowned more for professing than for understanding the magical art—if indeed it is an art, rather than the mockery of every thoroughly foolish person.” The magicians themselves were also commonly called *vani*, “impostors.” HERALD.—Our German *Gaukelei, Gaukelspiel, Taschenspiel*: “jugglery, conjuring trick, sleight of hand.” ORELL.

**Who without any force of incantations**, etc.—namely, “did it,” which must be understood from what precedes. ORELL.

**Without any anxious observance whatsoever of sacred rites.** It is well known that certain rites were customarily observed most scrupulously by magicians. Victims were slain, male frankincense burned, and similar things repeatedly performed, about which writers speak everywhere. *Observatio* is that cautious circumspection which we must employ in sacred rites, lest we stumble in any respect [Col. 0774C] and offend the divine power. So below, in the following chapter: “Without the observance of any rite”; Book VI, chapter 8: “It follows that we should say something about the images and statues that you fashion with great art and tend with religious observance”; and Book VII, chapter 18: “Or—as is customary—through fear of some observance or religious scruple, one person abstains from goat’s flesh, another abominates contact with pork.” Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis*, Book VIII, chapter 6: “And, deprived of every favorable testimony of the stars, he will cause evildoers to be punished or sacrificed at the altar in observances of a religion that must be feared.” HERALD.

**Which necessarily come about according to their own arrangements, whether they wish it or not.** This is to be understood ironically. ORELL.

**To rupture the affections of households.** Fulvius Ursinus conjectured *familiarum* (“of households”), with the approval of Meursius and Heraldus in his *Second Cures*. But I see no reason for alteration. The sense is: those magicians rupture the bonds of households either by introducing some pestilential corruption into a person or by certain poisons through which, it was believed, enmity and deadly hatred could be instilled. ORELL.

[Col. 0774D] **Or to open without keys things that are locked.** Origen, Book II, *Against Celsus*: “And certain sorcerers loose bonds by incantations and open doors” (*Καὶ γόητές τινες ἐπῳδαῖς δεσμοὺς λύουσι, καὶ θύρας ἀνοίγουσιν*). HERALD.

**Or to disable horses in races.** An example of this power survives in Jerome’s *Life of Hilarion*. HERALD.

**The flames of forbidden love.** He means love potions (*φίλτρα*) and erotic spells, which were also called *ἀγώγιμα* (“attraction spells”) and *charitesia*. Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 20: “They employ exorcisms and incantations, love potions also and attraction spells, and those called attendant spirits and dream-senders, and whatever other subsidiary magical practices there are, are zealously cultivated among them.” Juvenal, Satire VI.608:

> One brings magical chants; another sells Thessalian  
> love potions with which she may torment her husband’s mind.

HERALD and CLEMENT.

**But by the power of those whom they invoke.** Heraldus in his *Second Cures* prefers “but of the gods” (*sed deorum*). Not badly. ORELL.]

### XLIII

Perhaps he will confront us again with those many other slanderous and childish expressions: “He was a magician; he accomplished all those things by secret arts; from the inner sanctuaries of the Egyptians he stole the names of powerful angels and esoteric teachings.” What are you saying, O children, babbling with the loquacity of reckless speech about matters unknown and unfamiliar to you? Then were the deeds that were performed illusions of demons and games of magical arts? Can you identify and point out to us anyone among all those magicians who have ever existed through the ages who accomplished even one-thousandth of anything comparable to Christ? [Col. 0773B] Anyone who acted without any force of incantations, without the juices of herbs and plants [Col. 0774A], without any anxious observance whatsoever of sacred rites, libations, and prescribed times? For we are not pressing the question or asking what things they promise that they will do, or within what classes of actions their entire teaching and experience is customarily contained. Who does not know that they either devote themselves to foreknowing imminent events, which necessarily come about according to their own arrangements whether they wish it or not; or send deadly corruption upon whomever they please; or rupture the affections of households; or open without keys things that are locked; or bind mouths to silence; or disable, spur on, or slow horses in races; or send the flames of forbidden love and frenzied passions into the wives and children of others, whether they are male or female? Or, if they appear to venture upon anything useful, who does not know that they can do it not [Col. 0774B] by their own power but by the power of those whom they invoke?

[Col. 0775A] [Note: [Col. 0775B]

### XLIV.—**By the capability of his name.**

Stewechius, following Fulvius Ursinus and Meursius, conjectures *numinis* (“divinity”) instead of *nominis* (“name”). But nothing should be changed. For *ὄνομα* (“name”) is frequently used in the New Testament for command, authority, and power; see Mark 16:17; Acts 3:6. *Possibilitas* here is used actively for power or capability. Thus Ammianus Marcellinus XIX.2: “Each person treated his wounds in accordance with his means and the availability of caregivers.” Gesner appears to have noted this in his *Thesaurus*. ORELL.

**Full of beneficial assistance.** So Fulvius Ursinus. The manuscript had *auxiliaribus plenum nobis*, from which Stewechius produced “full of assistance for us,” while others read “helpful, full for us.” ORELL.]

### XLIV

Yet it is established that Christ, without any material aids, without the observance or rule of any rite, performed all those deeds by the capability of his own name. And—as was proper, fitting, and worthy of the true God—he bestowed nothing harmful or injurious, but only what brought aid and health and was full of beneficial assistance, through the generosity of his beneficent power.

[Note: [Col. 0775B]

### XLV.—**O you, again—!**

This is an aposiopesis expressing the gravest indignation and reproach. Germans likewise say: *O ihr! ihr diese und jene!*—“O you! You such-and-such people!” ORELL.

**In ordinary, everyday words.** Apuleius calls these “common words” in *Metamorphoses* I [Col. 0775C]. This was also called “speaking in human fashion” (*ἀνθρωπίνως λαλεῖν*). Contrasted with such words are the mutterings of magicians, formulated in exotic and barbarous—even dreadful—expressions, as well as lofty and bombastic language such as that of tragic poets. HERALD.

**Illnesses.** So the manuscripts. I remember that I restored this word to Lucius Apuleius in Book IX, and I have observed that Cicero used it twice in *To Atticus*, Book VII, letters 2 and 5; I have also noted it in Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*. STEWECH.—The same word was also read in Justin, Book XIII, chapter 2, where Franciscus Modius deleted it. I have restored it to Arnobius, who favors such rarer and almost obsolete words. The remaining editions have *valetudines* (“ailments”). ORELL.

**Torments.** *Cruciamentum* for *cruciatio* is a rather rare word and almost neglected in lexicons, although Plautus used it several times, as did Cicero in *Philippic* XI, chapter 4. See Buenemann on Lactantius, *Institutes* IV, chapter 15, p. 482. ORELL.

[Col. 0775D] **Foul patches of vitiligo.** *Vitiligo* is properly a white spot on the human body, which the Greeks call *ἀλφός* (“white leprosy”), according to Festus under this word. Celsus writes at the end of Book V that it is indeed disfiguring and arises from an unhealthy bodily condition, but in itself brings a person no danger; he then says there are three varieties: *alphos*, *melas*, and *leuce*. Here, however, it means leprosy *κατ’ ἐξοχήν* (“preeminently”); for leprosy is said to be white “as snow” (*ὡσεὶ χιών*) in Exodus 4:6 and Numbers 12:10 [the printed “12:20” is evidently an error]. Justin uses it in the same sense, Book XXXVI, chapter 2, speaking of Moses: “But when the Egyptians were suffering from scabies and vitiligo, they were warned by an oracle and expelled him together with the sick from the borders of Egypt, lest the plague spread to a greater number.” See there Bongarsius and Elmenhorst’s notes on Apuleius. Compare Turnebus, *Adversaria*, Book XV, chapter 21, who distinguishes vitiligo from elephantiasis. ORELL.

**Their bodies stained.** Solinus uses *viscera* (“internal organs”) for the whole body, chapter 22: “There is also said to be there a nation of Panotii, whose ears are extended to such enormous size that they cover the rest of their bodies, and who have no other cloak than clothing their limbs with the membranes of their ears” [Col. 0776B]; and chapter XXV: “Part of the region is inhabited by barbarians upon whom craftsmen, from childhood onward, imprint various representations of animals through patterns of wounds; as their tattooed bodies grow, the pigmented markings grow with the person.” HERALD.—Here also *viscera* means the whole body, as above in chapter 38 and shortly below in “swollen bodies.” ORELL.

**At whose light touch.** Here too they wish to change *ex* (“at,” literally “from”) into *et* (“and”). But they should have observed what we noted earlier, at chapter 39: that this particle is often pleonastic. It is exceedingly frequent in Julius Firmicus, as in *Mathesis* III, chapter 5: “And those who receive wounds from iron.” Again: “But he frequently inflicts wounds with iron.” HERALD.

**Checked immoderate discharges.** The manuscript has “the immoderate discharges checked themselves,” which Meursius defends by taking *cohibere* in a passive sense, “to restrain themselves,” as in “the earth [Col. 0776C] moved” and similar expressions. ORELL.

**Discharges.** Arnobius likes to use this word frequently. Below, Book V, chapter 12: “with a discharge of blood,” etc.; chapter 14: “the genitals cut away amid discharges.” It also occurs frequently in Solinus. HERALD.

**From whose hand the sluggish waves of dropsy fled.** This is how it should be read; it is wrongly printed today: “from whose hand the dropsical persons, the dropsy” (*cujus manus intercutes, intercutis*, “of the dropsy,” *τοῦ ὕδρωπος*). One could also write: “From whose hand the dropsical waves of the sluggish disease fled,” that is, “the dropsical waves of the sluggish disease”; and this is more correct, for the condition was called *aqua intercus* (“water beneath the skin”), and *veternosus* meant *ὁ ὑδρωπικός* (“dropsical”). The Glosses: “*veternus*: dropsy” (*ὕδρωψ*). Servius on *Georgics* I says: “*Veternus* is the disease called subcutaneous dropsy, which makes people sluggish.” There he also cites these verses of Plautus from the *Addictus*:

> I work far more than I would rather sleep.  
> I fear the sluggish disease.

See Salmasius on Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, pp. 399–400. Gesner in his *Thesaurus* cites Boernavius as asserting that among the ancients *veternus* was used for leucophlegmasia, or white dropsy [Col. 0776D]. Most other editions have: “the dropsical persons and the sluggish waves fled.” But *et* (“and”) is absent from the manuscript. ORELL.

**It was also a task to be performed.** *Operis res* means simply *opus*, “a task,” and nothing more. *Res* is very frequently redundant among Latin writers. Sidonius, Book VII, Letter 6: “It is a matter of duty”; and Book V, Letter 20: “It is a matter of advantage”; see Savaron there, p. 172. ORELL.—The form of expression seems similar to our German *ein Stück Arbeit*, “a piece of work,” and the Greeks do not differ greatly; countless examples may be adduced of the word *χρῆμα* (“thing, matter”). Muretus, *Various Readings* VI.19, was the first to compare the Latin usages with the Greek. Add Valckenaer on Euripides, *Phoenician Women*, pp. 21–22; Mori’s index to Xenophon’s *Cyropaedia*, under *χρῆμα*; Verheyk on Antoninus Liberalis, p. 84. OCHSNER.

**And immobility of their joints.** We discussed above, at the beginning of chapter XV, the adversative force of the particle *et* (“and,” here “yet”). In the immediately following words read “and now” rather than “even,” the reading of a single Leiden editor; the former is more significant. *Immobilitates* (“immobility”) [Col. 0777B] is Stewechius’ correction. The manuscript and first edition have *mobilitates* (“mobility”). ORELL.

**Congenital.** In the proper sense: “blind, maimed from birth” (*τυφλός, κυλλὸς ἀπὸ γενετῆς*), as frequently in the New Testament. Stewechius therefore wrongly interprets it as “long-standing.” ORELL.]

### XLV

What are you saying, O you, again—! Was he, then, a mortal, or one of us, whose command, whose voice uttered [Note: [Col. 0775A] “Sent forth.” Fulvius] in ordinary, everyday words caused illnesses, diseases, fevers, and the other torments of bodies to flee? Was he one of us, whose presence and [Col. 0776A] sight that race of demons submerged within human bodies could not endure, but, terrified by a new power, withdrew from its possession of their limbs? Was he one of us, whose command the foul patches of vitiligo obeyed, being driven away immediately and leaving harmony of color in bodies formerly stained? Was he one of us, at whose light touch discharges of blood stopped and checked their immoderate flow? Was he one of us, whose hands the sluggish waves of dropsy fled and that penetrating fluid avoided [Note: [Col. 0775A] “Evaded.” Fulvius], while swollen bodies subsided into health-giving dryness [Note: [Col. 0776A] “Flowed away.” The same Fulvius]? Was he one of us who commanded the lame to run? There was also this feat: the maimed stretched out [Col. 0777A] their hands, and congenital immobility of the joints [Note: [Col. 0777B] “Unknown.” Incorrectly. Fulvius] gave way; those crippled in their limbs rose and presently carried back their own beds, though shortly before they themselves had been carried on others’ shoulders; those bereft of sight saw, and presently people born with no eyes beheld heaven and daylight.

[Note: [Col. 0777C]

### XLVI.—**One of us.**

“One of us,” that is, an ordinary, common man. Thus Petronius, *Satyricon*, chapter 44, §10: “And how kindly he was! He would return everyone’s greeting and remember all their names, just like one of us”; see Burmann there. ORELL.

**A hundred, or more than this.** The words “or more than this” seem to me suspicious as a gloss. For *centum* (“a hundred”) is very frequently indefinite, as a round number, like *sescenti* (“six hundred”).
