ORELL.—Yet this is not a sufficiently compelling ground for suspicion, and adding “or more than this” is no less customary. OCHSNER.

**At whose single utterance the raging and maddened seas grew calm.** *Ad simplicem vocem* (“at a single utterance”) means “at a word,” as in Lucretius IV.786; Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.547, “at the word”; Minucius Felix, chapter IV, “quicker than the word,” etc. Buenemann discusses these formulas fully on Lactantius, *Institutes* IV, chapter 15, pp. 489–90. ORELL.

**He trod upon the surface of the sea.** Prudentius, Preface to Book II *Against Symmachus*:

> He stops it and teaches one to walk  
> over the swollen surface of the sea.

[Col. 0777D] Virgil, *Georgics* I: “the backs that it raises from the sea”; on which Servius says: “*Terga*, the surface, as Homer says *νῶτα θαλάσσης*, ‘the backs of the sea.’” ELMENH.—Compare Schoettgen on Juvencus, *Evangelical History* I.637, p. 114, Reusch’s edition. ORELL.

**From loaves.** The preposition *e* is redundant (*παρέλκει*). See the beginning of the note on chapter 39. Meursius reads: “he satisfied five thousand with five loaves.” ORELL.

**To be released from the wrappings of the embalmers.** Here Arnobius calls the burial bands and bandages *volumina* (“wrappings”), because the dead body was wrapped in them. NOURR.—Ludovicus Carrio restored *voluminibus* from the manuscript in *Emendations* II, chapter 13, in Gruter’s *Lampas Critica*, vol. III, pp. 164–65, where he discusses this passage at length. Earlier editions printed *velaminibus* (“coverings”). Arnobius is referring to John 11:44 concerning Lazarus: “The dead man came out, his feet and hands bound with burial bands” (*Ἐξῆλθεν ὁ τεθνηκὼς δεδεμένος τοὺς πόδας καὶ τὰς χεῖρας κειρίαις*). On embalmers see Kirchmann, *On Roman Funerals*, Book I, chapter 9, and Muncker on Fulgentius, *On Ancient Speech*, in *Latin Mythographers*, vol. II, p. 169. It was the duty of the embalmers [Col. 0778B] to wash, anoint, wrap in bands, and crown the dead; that of the corpse-bearers to bury them. ORELL.

**He perceived in the hearts of silent persons what each was turning over . . . .** John 2:25: “He had no need that anyone should testify concerning man, for he himself knew what was in man” (*Οὐ χρείαν εἶχεν ἵνα τις μαρτυρήσῃ περὶ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου· αὐτὸς γὰρ ἐγίνωσκε τί ἦν* [Col. 0778C] *τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ*). ORELL.

**Through the immensity of his name being revealed.** See above, at the beginning of the note on chapter 45. Meursius conjectures *numinis* (“divinity”). ORELL.

**In the open light.** That is, in manifest, open, clear light, as opposed to what is hidden and, so to speak, veiled. Thus Lucretius VI.1265 calls places *prompta* when they are public and exposed to view. ORELL.

**Once, again, and more frequently.** Fulvius Ursinus and Meursius read “showed himself once” (*se semel*), correctly. *Se* cannot be absent or be understood from the preceding “revealed himself,” since the whole period “who spoke,” etc., has been inserted between them. ORELL.

**Those who loved him (*diligentibus sese*).** I think *se* should be read, namely Christ. *Diligentibus sese* would mean “those who loved themselves.” ORELL.—For my part, I would not lightly alter *sese*. Servius indeed noted somewhere, from Julius Caesar, that the simple *se* is used if something is said to have been done to another, but *sese* when done to oneself. Yet a passage identical with ours occurs in the *Historia Augusta*, II, p. 372: “with the soldiers imitating him” (*militibus sese imitantibus*), where Salmasius defends the doubtful reading, warning that *sese* is used for *ipsum* (“him”), as it often is among those authors, whose age was close to that of Arnobius [Col. 0778D]. OCHSNER.

**Not through empty dreams.** Dodwell, Dissertation II on Irenaeus, §57, p. 199, illustrates this passage by the example of Arnobius himself. For Jerome, in the Appendix to Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, Eusebian number 2342, relates that Arnobius was converted to faith in Christ through dreams—indeed, compelled by them. GALLAND.

**At the hearing of whose name silence is imposed upon seers.** Prudentius adorns this most elegantly in *Apotheosis* 438 ff. ELMENH.

**Boastful magicians.** That is, *ἀλαζόνες*, braggarts who promise and pledge things they cannot accomplish. For those whom the Greeks call *ἀλαζόνες*, Latin writers very frequently render *arrogantes*, “boastful.” HERALD. An example of such boasting in Simon Magus is described by Clement, *Recognitions* 2. ELMENH.

**By the privilege of a greater power.** That is, by force, “power and authority” (*δυνάμει καὶ ἐξουσίᾳ*). For this is how they appear to have rendered *ἐξουσία* (“authority”) [Col. 0779C]. Shortly afterward: “Was that, then, something human, or could such a right be conferred, such a privilege proceed from a mouth nourished on filth?” And in Book II: “For just as particular gods among you have particular guardianships, privileges, and powers, and you do not ask from any one of them something that does not belong to his power and privilege.” Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis* II, chapter 4: “They are of boundless power and privilege, and they designate the destinies of men by the authority of their power”; and Book IV, chapter 1: “He makes them great and powerful, formidable and effective among their own people, men who subjugate the greatest cities by the privilege of some power.” ELMENH.]

### XLVI

Was he, I ask, one of us who, by a single intervention, healed at one time a hundred persons—or more than this—afflicted by various disabilities and diseases? At whose single utterance did the raging and maddened seas grow calm, and the whirlwinds and storms subside? Who carried an unstained foot over the deepest abysses [Note: [Col. 0777B] “Unwashed.” Fulvius]? Who trod upon the surface of the sea while the waves themselves stood amazed and nature entered into servitude? Who satisfied five thousand followers from five loaves and, lest those unbelieving and hardhearted people think these things illusions, filled [Col. 0777B] the recesses of twelve baskets with a mound of leftover fragments? Was he one of us who commanded souls long since breathed out to return into bodies, those who had been buried to come forth from their mounds, and, on the third day after burial, to be released from the wrappings of the embalmers? Was he one of us [Col. 0778A] who perceived in the hearts of silent persons what each was turning over and what each concealed beneath obscure thoughts? Was he one of us who, when he uttered a single statement, was believed by different peoples speaking discordant languages to be employing familiar verbal sounds and each person’s own tongue? Was he one of us who, when he delivered the duties of a definite religion [Note: [Col. 0777B] “Definite.” Fulvius] to his followers, suddenly filled the entire world and, through the immensity of his name being revealed, showed how great and who he was? Was he one of us who, after laying aside his body, revealed himself to innumerable people in the open light? Who spoke and received replies, taught, reproved, and admonished? Who, lest they suppose themselves deceived by empty apparitions [Note: [Col. 0778B] “Regard through images.” Fulvius], showed himself once, again, and more frequently in familiar conversation? Who even now [Note: [Col. 0778B] “Even now.” Others] appears [Col. 0778B] to men of the greatest righteousness, unstained and loving him, not through empty dreams but in the form of pure simplicity? At the hearing of whose name harmful spirits flee, silence is imposed upon seers, soothsayers are rendered unable to respond, and the activities of boastful magicians are made ineffectual [Note: [Col. 0778B] “He causes.” Fulvius]—not, as you say, through dread [Col. 0779A] of the name, but through the privilege of a greater power?

[Note: [Col. 0779C]

### XLVII.—**For however great these things may be, they will be found mere trifles and sport.**

Ludovicus Carrio corrected the passage in this way from the manuscript in *Emendations* II, chapter 13, in Gruter’s *Lampas Critica*, vol. III, p. 165. Earlier editions read *reperirentur*. Adrianus Behotus, *Apophoreta* III, chapter 8, explains the sense of the words well: “However great and important these things that have been set forth may be, they will nevertheless be considered trifles [Col. 0779D] and games, matters of no weight or importance, if compared with,” etc. In this passage *vel* has an amplifying and intensifying force, as it often does; “or of what slightness?” means “of what slightness, I ask?” *Ludus* (“sport”) is elegantly used of something easy that we accomplish without any effort. Livy XXVIII: “Indeed, Publius Cornelius, when you behold Africa from the deep, your Spain will seem to have been sport and play.” The Greeks similarly use *παιδιά*, “play.” Elmenhorst’s Hanover edition has “trifles . . . for anyone.” ORELL and HERALD.

**If it is granted to be known.** Fulvius Ursinus: “if it is granted to know.” But this is explanation rather than emendation. ORELL.

**What the true God was.** For my part I would prefer “who he was,” or rather, in Arnobius’ manner, “who the true God was.” See below, the note of Heraldus on Book IV, chapter 9. ORELL.

**When he dissolved and conquered those things that had been bound fast by perpetual bonds and immutable necessity.** Stewechius wishes to restore “when these things are dissolved, he bound them,” because *devincta* (“bound fast”) follows. Incorrectly. Bonds are dissolved; necessity is conquered. ORELL.]

### XLVII

We have set forth these matters summarily, not on the ground that the greatness of their performer was to be discerned solely in these miraculous powers. For however great these things may be, they will be found mere trifles and sport if it is granted us to know from what kingdoms he came to us, and of what divine power [Note: [Col. 0779B] “Name.” Sab.] he came as minister. The deeds that he performed and repeatedly accomplished were done, not so that he might boast in empty ostentation, but so that hard and unbelieving people might know that what was promised was not false, and from the benevolence of his works might now begin to conjecture what the true God was. At the same time we also wish it to be known that, when—as has been said—a summary enumeration of his deeds was made, Christ was able not only to do the things he did but also to surpass the established ordinances of the fates. For if, as is evident [Col. 0779B] and established, disabilities and bodily sufferings—deafness, mutilation, muteness, contraction of the sinews, and loss of sight—occur and are imposed by decrees of fate, and Christ alone corrected, restored, and healed them, it is clearer than the sun itself that he was more powerful than the fates, since he dissolved and conquered things that had been bound fast by perpetual bonds and immutable necessity.

[Note: [Col. 0780C]

### XLVIII.—**That is, of some medicine.**

These words seem to Meursius to be a gloss. ORELL.

Querqueras. Festus interprets *querquera* as a cold fever accompanied by shivering. On this passage A. Dacier supplies the adjective *querquera* with *febris* [“fever”]. *Querquerus* comes from κερχαλέος (*kerchaleos*), which derives from κέρχω (*kerchō*). For Hesychius explains κερχαλέον (*kerchaleon*) as σκληρόν, ξηρόν, διψαλέον—“hard, dry, thirsty”—all of which are perfectly appropriate to a fever, which through dryness produces hoarseness and coughing. Hence Plautus, in a fragment of the *Frivolaria*, joins a cough with *querquera*:

> I had biliousness, dropsy, a cough, a fever, *querquera*.

Gesner discusses this word at length in the *Thesaurus*, under *Keuchen* [“to cough”]; see also his note on Sammonicus, v. 907, ed. P. Burmann, and Samuel Petit, *Miscellanies*, book I, ch. 23, pp. 63 ff. ORELLI.

“Which some importunate cruelty—I know not what—willed human bodies to endure.” In these words Arnobius seems to have followed [Col. 0780D] the opinion of the Gnostics, who attributed the creation of man and matter to a certain inferior principle whom they called the Demiurge. We shall discuss this below, in the note on book II. ORELLI.

“Attributed.” Thus Meursius in the *Appendix*, from the manuscript. Previously the reading was “or bestowed.” ORELLI.

“Or ordered some food to be taken.” The gods in whose shrines the sick slept prescribed and ordained (καὶ συνέταττον) particular remedies through their priests. For such commands (προστάγματα) proceeding from the gods were properly called prescriptions (συνταγαί). The emperor and philosopher Marcus Antoninus speaks of this in book I of his *Commentaries*: “Such is the meaning of the statement that Asclepius prescribed (συνέταξεν) for this person horseback riding, or cold bathing, or going barefoot.” HERALDUS.—Cf. Reiff on Artemidorus, vol. II, p. 452, and especially F. A. Wolf, “Contributions to the History of Somnambulism in Antiquity,” in *Philological Miscellanies*, where, at pp. 424 ff., he supplies several examples of such prescriptions (συνταγμάτων). ORELLI.

“To walk.” Meursius reads “or to walk.” ORELLI.

“Situated within a conjectural art.” A conjectural art—that is, [Col. 0781B] an art resting only upon suspicions and conjectures, rather than upon certain and indubitable truths: “an art based on mere conjectures and hypotheses.” Etc. Gesner cites *suspicabilis* in the *Thesaurus* as a *hapax legomenon* (ἅπαξ λεγόμενον), a word occurring only once. ORELLI.—Cicero, *On Divination* I.14: “Arts which consist in conjecture and are matters of opinion.” OCHSNER.

### XLVIII

“But in vain,” says someone or other, “do you arrogate so much to Christ, since we know, and have known, that other gods too have often given medicines to many sufferers and cured the diseases and infirmities [Col. 0780A] of many people.”

I do not inquire, I do not demand to know, what god, at what time, or whom he assisted, or what broken person he restored to health. I desire to hear only this: whether, without the addition of any material substance—that is, of any medicine—he ordered diseases to fly away from people at his touch; whether he commanded and caused the source of their ailments to die, and the bodies of the weak to return to their natural condition.

For Christ is known, either by placing his hand upon the afflicted parts or by the command of a simple utterance, to have opened the ears of the deaf, driven blindness from the eyes, given speech to the mute, loosened the bonds of the joints, and granted the power of walking to the crippled; and he was accustomed by a word and a command [Col. 0780B] to cure leukodermas, shivering fevers (*querquerae*), dropsical diseases, and every other kind of ailment which some importunate cruelty—I know not what—willed human bodies to endure.

What comparable thing was done by all those gods from whom, you say, assistance was brought to the sick and imperiled? If at any time, as report has it, they either attributed a medicine to certain persons, ordered some food to be taken, prescribed a drink of some particular quality, ordered the juices of herbs and grasses to be applied [Note: [Col. 0779B] “To apply over.” Manuscript.] to the troubling causes, or directed them to walk, rest, or abstain from something harmful, it is readily apparent, if you are willing to pay attention, that this is nothing great or worthy of any astonished admiration. Physicians too [Note: [Col. 0780B] “For.” Thus the Fulvius manuscript.] cure in this way, although they are creatures born from the earth and do not rely confidently upon the certainty of knowledge, but are situated within a conjectural art [Col. 0781A] that wavers among estimates founded upon inference.

But there is no power in removing harmful things by medicines: those benefits belong to the substances, and are not powers belonging to those who administer the treatment. And even if it is praiseworthy to know by what medicine or art particular people ought to be treated, the proper place for this praise is not in a god but in a human being. For it is no disgrace for a human being to have improved another’s health by employing external substances; but it is unworthy of a god not to be able to do this by himself, but to provide health and soundness through the assistance of external things.

[Note: [Col. 0781B]

### Note to XLIX

“They would prostrate themselves before the faces of the gods and sweep the very thresholds with kisses.” Below, book VI: “And the things which, prostrate and humbled, you worship in [Col. 0781C] every temple.” It was the custom of the ancients, during some great public or private calamity, to go as suppliants through all the temples, so that at last they might find some god favorably disposed. Indeed, they would sometimes fall upon the ground and make supplication (ἱκέτευον) in this posture. Lucretius, book V:

> Nor is it any piety often to be seen  
> Turning with veiled head toward a stone and approaching every altar,  
> Nor to fall prostrate upon the ground and spread one’s palms  
> Before the sanctuaries of the gods.

That is to say, immediately upon entering the temples and seeing the images of the gods, they would cast themselves upon the ground at the very threshold and sometimes kiss the threshold itself. This is what Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams* II.32, calls σαροῦν τὰ πρὸ τῶν νεῶν, “sweeping the ground before the temples.” Because this was considered rather abject and lacking in dignity, it was assigned almost peculiarly to women. For women, prostrate before the images with loosened hair, swept the ground with their hair. Claudian, *In Praise of Serena*, v. 224:

> [Col. 0781D] You devote yourself to divine powers and vows, and with suppliant hair  
> You sweep the ground.

(Heraldus; cf. Gesner on Claudian, book I.) Compare Tibullus, book I, elegy 2. MEURSIUS.

“With most wretched prayers.” Stewechius prefers: “most wretched in their prayers.” But nothing should be altered. “Most wretched prayers” means pitiable, lamentable appeals with which they implored the assistance of the gods—*klägliche Bitten*, “lamentable petitions.” ORELLI.

“Wore themselves away in expectation of compassion.” That is, while awaiting the compassion and mercy of the gods. For *pietas* bears this sense not only among writers of the later age but also among others. Hence, Spartianus says, the emperor Antoninus was called Pius because he was by nature most merciful; and this title afterward passed to other emperors. Thus Themistius Euphrades, in Oration IX, says that the Augusti were called εὐσεβεῖς, that is, φιλανθρώπους—“benevolent toward humanity.” *Pius*, therefore, means “merciful,” and *pietas* means “mercy,” *Gnade* [“grace, mercy”], even among polished writers. Claudian, *Panegyric on the Fourth Consulship of Honorius*:

> [Col. 0782B] Gentle toward petitions, abounding in mercy,  
> He was sparing in punishment.

And:

> Above all, be merciful; for although the gods surpass us  
> In every gift, mercy alone makes us equal to the gods.

(Heraldus; cf. Casaubon on Julius Capitolinus, *Antoninus Pius*, ch. 2, p. 249.)

[Col. 0782C] “Unless perhaps you say.” I venture to read: “Unless perhaps you will say.” *Nisi* has the force of “but.” Below in this book: “But perhaps you will doubt whether this is the emperor of whom we are speaking?” Likewise in the following book: “But perhaps the King of the world sent souls here for this reason.” Again in book V: “Unless some presumptuous man, knowing beforehand what Jupiter would say, prescribed it.” STEWECHIUS.

“Without considering who deserves it and who does not.” Nourry suspects that something is missing at this point, but wrongly, perhaps because he misunderstood the word *minime*. *Minime* stands for *non*, the superlative for the positive, as above in ch. XXII; see the note there. ORELLI.

“To place in the middle.” That is, to put something forward for discussion as though it were not sufficiently certain and decided. The Greeks also speak in this way. Herodotus, book VII: “So that I may not seem to you to take counsel privately, I place the matter in the middle (τίθημι τὸ πρῆγμα εἰς μέσον), bidding whichever of you wishes to declare his opinion.” Similarly, “to leave in the middle” means to leave something undecided. St. Augustine, *The City of God* III.4: “But whether Venus could have borne Aeneas through intercourse with Anchises, or Mars have begotten Romulus [Col. 0782D] through intercourse with Numitor’s daughter Silvia, let us leave in the middle.” Capitolinus, *Life of Verus*, near the end: “We do not leave this in the middle, but reject it as wholly cleared up and refuted.” HERALDUS. Similarly Tacitus, at the end of the *Germania*: “Which I shall leave in the middle as unascertained.” See Gellius, *Attic Nights* XVII.3, with Gronovius’s note; Cortius on Sallust, *Catiline* 19, p. 126; and Bunemann on Lactantius, *Institutes* VII.1, p. 852. ORELLI.

“Not because of guilt.” Nothing should be altered. Arnobius very frequently uses *meritum* for what we commonly call *demeritum*, that is, an offense or fault. And indeed *mereri* is neutral in meaning. Below, ch. 64: “For what guilt, I ask? Tell us. For the fault of what sin? What was committed by him?” And above: “For if we are the cause, and these plagues were devised as the punishment of our crime.” Solinus, ch. 1: “Valerius Soranus, finally, because contrary to the prohibition he had dared to disclose it, was put to death because of the guilt of his profane utterance.” Lactantius, book VII, ch. 20: “For he takes pleasure in having a man slaughtered in his sight, though the man has been condemned for his offenses.” Meursius’s proposed reading, “not for the sake of merit,” is therefore bad and would certainly be very harsh. ORELLI.]

### XLIX

And since you compare the benefits of health conferred by other divine powers with those conferred by Christ, how many thousands of disabled persons do you wish us to show you who, though afflicted with wasting diseases, obtained absolutely no remedy, even though they went as suppliants through every temple, prostrated themselves before the faces of the gods, and swept the very thresholds with kisses, [Col. 0781B] and, for as long as life remained to them, wearied and importuned Aesculapius himself, whom they proclaim the giver of health, both with entreaties and with the most wretched prayers?

Do we not know that some died together with their afflictions, that others grew old amid the torments of their diseases, [Col. 0782A] and that others began to fare still worse after they had worn away their days and nights in continual prayers and expectation of compassion [Note: [Col. 0782B] “Bestowed.” Incorrectly. Manuscript.]?

What advantage is there, then, in showing that one or perhaps two were cured, when no one came to the aid of so many thousands, and all the temples are full of the wretched and unfortunate? Unless perhaps you say that assistance is brought by the gods to the good, while the sufferings of the wicked are disregarded. Yet Christ came equally to the assistance of the good and the wicked, and no one was rejected by him who, in harsh circumstances, sought help against the assault and injuries of fortune.

For this is the distinctive quality of the true God and of royal power: to deny his kindness to no one and not to consider who deserves it and who does not, since natural weakness makes a human being a sinner, not a deliberate choice of will or judgment. Furthermore, to say that assistance is brought by the gods [Col. 0782B] to sufferers according to their merits is to place what you assert in the middle and make it doubtful, so that both the person who has been restored to health may appear to have been saved by chance, and the one who was not may be thought to have been unable to expel the ailment, not because of guilt but because of divine weakness.

[Col. 0783A] [Note: [Col. 0783B]

### Note to L

“With attachment to his name.” Meursius proposes *affictione* or *affixione*. Read, with Heraldus, *adjectione*, “by the addition,” or rather *affectatione*, “by invocation.” ORELLI. Nothing should be altered. Salmasius, on the *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, p. 40, observed that writers of the later age, including Tertullian, use *affectio* for *affectatio*, and *afficere* for *affectare*. Similarly, *trahere* is used for *tractare*, *tractus* for *tractatus*, *ostendere* for *ostentare*, and *ostensio* for *ostentatio*, as the same Salmasius notes on the *Augustan History*, vol. I, pp. 101, 442, 446, 453. OCHSNER.

“Permitted.” That is, he attributed power and ability. [Col. 0783C] He used this verb in the same way above, ch. 38: “Who permitted us to understand, and taught us, his profound and ineffable depths, insofar as our limited capacity could grasp them.” Below, ch. 52: “Let them permit one man from the people to articulate the mouths of the mute for the function of speech.” HERALDUS.

“Deniers.” This is the reading of the Leiden edition, from an emendation by J. Dousa cited by Meursius. The first edition has “claimants,” from the manuscript, which was undoubtedly corrupted from *arogatores*, an ancient spelling of *abrogatores*. See Stewechius. The other editors, following Gelenius, have “detractors.” ORELLI.

“So that there might remain no suspicion that he had bestowed those gifts and benefits through magical arts.” Compare Augustine, *The City of God* XVIII.53. STEWECHIUS.

“And they too, bearing themselves beneath the assaults inflicted by them, restored them to health and steadiness by no other command.” I have given the manuscript reading, although I am altogether doubtful and uncertain how the true reading of this extremely corrupt passage should be established. I shall place the conjectures of learned men in the middle, so that the benevolent reader may be free to judge.

Fulvius Ursinus conjectures that it should read: “And they too, when men were carried into their retreats”—that is, those of the apostles—“restored them by a bare command to health and steadiness.” *Successus* is the same as *secessus*, “a dwelling,” a sense in which Arnobius uses it several times, as in book VI, ch. 3, where he calls the temples of the Gentiles “certain small retreats and a kind of very narrow cavern.”

Stewechius approves: “And they too, carrying handkerchiefs to the afflictions, restored them by no other command,” etc., in the following sense: the apostles brought or applied handkerchiefs to the *casus*—that is, ulcers, scars, or, in general, the seats of diseases—and cured them by no other command. This would allude to Acts 19:11–12:

> God performed extraordinary miracles through the hands of Paul, so that even handkerchiefs or aprons taken from his skin were carried to the sick, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out.

Stewechius himself, however, immediately withdraws this conjecture and supports Ursinus. Heraldus reconstructs the passage thus: “And they too restored those whirled about beneath the attacks of the demons,” etc. Adrien de Behault, in *Apophoreta* III.8, alters it most boldly: “And they too restored to health and steadiness those placed beneath the power of the demons”—see the following chapter—“and dashed down by their assaults, by no command other than the invocation of Christ’s name.” Finally, the Leiden editor reads: “And they too restored those tortured beneath their assaults,” etc. Together with my very dear Ochsner, I especially approve this conjecture as the gentlest remedy for an extremely corrupt passage. Arnobius used “assaults of the demons” for “assaults inflicted by demons,” just as Virgil has “remnants of the Danaans” and “the wound of Ulysses.” ORELLI.

“Restored them to health and steadiness.” Entirely proper. For the frenzied and possessed are cast out of their condition and whirled about by various assaults. *Constantia*, “steadiness,” therefore exists when we remain in our own condition. The glosses give: “steadfast—σταθερός, εὐσταθής,” stable and well-balanced. Lactantius, book IV, ch. 27: “He restored the disturbed minds of human beings, driven to frenzy by evil assaults, to their former senses.” HERALDUS.—Compare Burmann on Velleius Paterculus II.29. OCHSNER.

“And by a contact hardly different from his, they restored the lineaments of bodies.” Behault, *Apophoreta* III.8, thinks that *laniamenta*, “mutilations,” should be read, a word which, although not recognized by lexicographers, could be tolerated, since Arnobius has several *hapax legomena* (ἅπαξ λεγόμενα), words occurring only once. But the subject here is not wounds or scars by which the body is mangled, but the pustules and warts of leprosy, which disfigure the body and deform its lineaments. *Conciliare* means συνάπτειν—“to join together, repair, restore.” Still less pleasing is Fulvius Ursinus’s conjecture *linimenta*, from *lino*, “to smear.” ORELLI.

“They arrested the wandering waters.” He used *statuere* in the unusual sense “to stop.” Thus Cyprian, *Against Demetrianus*: “If drought arrests the spring, if a pestilential vapor corrupts the air, if diseased health consumes human beings.” MEURSIUS, p. 32.—Writers of earlier Latin also use it in this way; for example Plautus, *Bacchides*, act II, scene 3, v. 57:

> … We immediately stopped the ship.

See J. F. Gronovius, who discusses this use of the verb at length in *Readings in Plautus*, pp. 173 ff. ORELLI.

“Through their own channels.” That is, through channels assigned to them by nature—“through their customary, natural channels.” ORELLI.

“Refusing to undergo healing.” That is, “desperate,” ἀπεγνωσμένα. For he wished to express the Greek word in Latin. HERALDUS.

“With continual feeding, he restrained them from feeding.” Behault explains it well: “He checked the ulcers from the erosion which they had long continued; he cured limbs long devoured by gnawing cancer and checked the destructive advance of the creeping disease.” But the same Behault should not be followed when he conjectures: “he restrained them by continuous *harpastus*,” which he explains as follows: “when the joining parts came together and the opening of the ulcer was closed.” But *harpastus* is no word. He ought to have written *herpestu*, from ἕρπειν, “to creep,” whence *herpes* in Lucretius VI.665 and *herpesticus* in Lucilius, quoted by Nonius.

Moreover, Wakefield, *Critical Miscellany*, part III, p. 139, aptly compares with our passage these words of John Chrysostom, Sermon 17, vol. I, p. 107, ed. Savile:

> But so that you may learn the Master’s benevolence toward humanity: he did not delay even momentarily, but immediately recognized what had happened and the magnitude of the ulcer, and hastened to the cure, lest the ulcer, after spreading, should render the wound incurable. Therefore, anticipating it, he checks it; immediately arriving, he stops the spread of the ulcer and does not leave it without care even for a short time, thereby imitating his own goodness.

ORELLI.—Hence Artemidorus writes that disease appears as a beast, evidently because of these kinds of diseases by which human bodies are devoured, *Interpretation of Dreams* II.12:

> But whenever the lion threatens or becomes savage, it both inspires fear and foretells disease; for disease resembles a wild beast.

HERALDUS.—Oudendorp discusses the word *pastus*, “feeding,” at length in his note on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* V, p. 353. ORELLI.

[Col. 0785C] “They compelled the stubbornness of the savage cancer to submit to scarring by circumscribing its unsheathings.” The cancer seems to have been compelled to submit to scarring insofar as it was prevented from spreading more widely through the limbs and was confined within the area circumscribed by the scar; thus it was forced, as it were, to withdraw from a broader field into a narrow space. OCHSNER.—“By circumscribing its unsheathings” therefore means the same as what he said above, “with its feeding restrained.” Nor should it be changed, with Gelenius, to *evagationibus*, “wanderings.” Arnobius evidently wrote *evaginationibus* after the manner of the ancients, who said *vager, vaginor; fruor, fruinor; nato, natino; domo, domino*, whereas *dominor* is now expressed deponentially. See Meursius in the *Appendix*. ORELLI.

“He recalled the dead to life.” This does not mean those slain and destroyed by external violence, but simply those entirely removed from the midst of life. For this is the meaning of *interimere*: to remove someone altogether from human affairs. *Emere* formerly meant “to take away,” and the force of the prefix *inter-* in such compounds—meaning “utterly, altogether”—was noted by the highly exact grammarian Aelius Donatus. *Interempti*, therefore, are those who are more often called simply *exempti*, “removed.” Solinus, [Col. 0785D] ch. 16: “Conversely, their funerals are joyful, so much so that they accompany those removed from life with rejoicing.” HERALDUS.

“And ordered the dead to return from their tombs through the reversal of their funeral processions.” Zeno of Verona—an imitator of Arnobius—in his sermon *On Hope, Faith, and Charity*: “And they often ordered even the dead themselves to return from their tombs together with their own funeral processions, so that everyone marveled that tears which had just been tears of bereavement became tears of joy.” HERALDUS.—A “reversal of a funeral procession,” therefore, occurs when those who followed the bier return and lead home the person raised from the dead. ORELLI.]

### L

What of the fact that he not only accomplished by his own power those mighty works which we have presented summarily, rather than as the magnitude of the subject demanded, but—what was still more sublime—permitted many others to attempt and perform them with attachment to his name?

For when he foresaw that you would become deniers of the deeds performed by him and of his divine work, then, so that there might remain no suspicion that he had bestowed those gifts and benefits through magical arts, he selected from that vast multitude of people who followed his grace in admiration fishermen, craftsmen, peasants, and men of that uneducated kind. Sent among various nations, they were to perform all those miracles without any tricks or auxiliary means.

By a word he checked the torment of worm-infested limbs, and by a word they too checked the vermin of frenzied afflictions. By a single command he drove demons from bodies and restored their own senses to the unconscious; and they too—[the text is corrupt: “bearing themselves beneath their assaults”]—restored them to health and steadiness by no other command. He wiped away with the touch of his hand the marks of whitening leukodermas; and by a contact hardly different from his, these men too restored the lineaments of bodies.

He ordered moist and swollen internal organs to recover [Note: [Col. 0783B] *Reciperare*. Manuscript.] their native dryness; and in the same manner his servants arrested the wandering waters and ordered them, to prevent the destruction of the body, to flow through their own channels. Within the brief interval of a single word, he restrained ulcers with boundless mouths, which refused to undergo healing, from their continual feeding; and in precisely the same way they compelled the stubbornness [Col. 0785A] of savage cancer to submit to scarring by circumscribing its unsheathings.

He gave the lame the power to walk, sight to blind eyes, and recalled the dead to life. No less did they too relax the contraction of sinews, fill with light eyes which had lost it, and order the dead to return from their tombs through the reversal of their funeral processions. Nor was anything done by him, while all looked on in astonished wonder, which he did not wholly grant those insignificant and rustic men the power to perform, subjecting it to their authority.

[Note: [Col. 0785D]

### Note to LI

“A ward-priest.” The *curiones* were priests of the wards who administered their sacred rites. The matter is very well known. ORELLI.

“Or rather the Flamen Dialis, through whom he is *Dius*.” I have admitted into the text this emendation proposed by Petrus Colvius in his notes on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VI, p. 408. It seems to me uniquely correct. The meaning is that Jupiter is understood to be *Dius* through the Flamen Dialis assigned to him—that is, the one from whom life was believed to be given to human beings, as Festus interprets the word *dialis*.

The previous reading was “which belongs to him,” [Col. 0786B] which could be tolerated in the sense “which is peculiar to him,” κατ’ ἐξοχήν, “preeminently.” For we know that Numa Pompilius established three flamens—the Dialis, Martialis, and Quirinalis—and that later, in the course of time, others were added until their number grew to fifteen. Since the Flamen Dialis far surpassed all of them in dignity, he was called “the Flamen” κατ’ ἐξοχήν, preeminently.

Canter thinks it should read “which is greater,” namely, than the Pontifex Maximus, undoubtedly referring to the passage in Festus under “Order of Sacred Offices,” where we read: “The greatest of the priests appears to be the King of Sacrifices, then the Flamen Dialis, after him the Flamen Martialis, in fourth place the Flamen Quirinalis, and in fifth the Pontifex Maximus. Accordingly, at banquets the King alone reclines above all; but the Dialis reclines above the Martialis and Quirinalis, the Martialis above the next in rank, and all of them above the Pontifex.”

Still less should Ludovicus Carrio be followed, who, in *Emendations* II.13, p. 164, vol. III of Gruter’s *Critical Lamp*, conjectures the reading “through whom he is a god,” as though Jupiter became a god only through the Flamen Dialis and would not have been numbered among the gods unless he possessed a flamen. Yet although, as we have said, even some of the lower gods—for example Vulcan, Furrina, Carmenta, and Pomona—had flamens, many other gods of the higher order, such as Neptune, Apollo, Juno, and so forth, had no flamen or priesthood of their own. See Stewechius on this passage and Rosinus, who discusses the subject at length in *Roman Antiquities* III.15–17. ORELLI.

“The condition of their limbs to the enervated.” This most certain emendation is owed to Gelenius. The manuscript’s *situs eruatis* is exceedingly corrupt. The error undoubtedly arose from the abbreviated spelling *eervatis*. MEURSIUS, in the *Appendix*.

“A pustule.” The glosses give: “pustule, φλύκταινα” [“blister, welt”]. ELMENHORST.—Cf. Turnebus, *Adversaria* XXIII.2, p. 270. ORELLI.

“A hangnail.” According to Festus, *reduvia* is the term used when the skin separates around the nails. We read that Pliny, *Natural History* VII.19, and Cicero, *For Sextus Roscius of Ameria*, used the word. See Turnebus, *Adversaria* XVII.8. NOURRY.—Cf. Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. ORELLI.

“A papule.” There are two kinds of papules. In the first, the skin is roughened by very small pustules and slightly eroded. The second is what the Greeks call ἀγρία, “the wild kind,” in which the skin is similarly, but more severely, roughened. Celsus, *On Medicine* V.28 §18. ELMENHORST.—Cf. Vossius on Virgil, *Georgics* III.566. These words, moreover, are miserably corrupted in the first edition, where the reading is: “but so that a doubtful papule might sprout.” ORELLI.

“Could such a right be given, could such authority proceed?” Arnobius uses *jus*, “right,” for power, and *licentia*, “authority,” in the same sense. Below: “Yet would that all the things either performed by him or brought to completion by his heralds with equal right and power could have been committed to writing.” The jurists use *jus* similarly. HERALDUS.—On the word *licentia*, see the note above on ch. 46. ORELLI.

“If the matter admits any superlative expression.” *Superlatio* means “hyperbole.” The word is Ciceronian: *On the Orator* III.53, “an elevation and transference of the truth”; see Harles there, p. 624 of the new edition. The author of the *Rhetoric to Herennius* I.6 calls such expressions *exsuperantia*, “exaggerations.” See Graevius there, p. 17 of Burmann’s edition, and Ch. Th. Ernesti, *Lexicon of Latin Rhetorical Terminology*, under *Superlatio*. ORELLI.

[Col. 0787A] “Power.” *Potentatus*, meaning “power” or “authority,” is an attested word of the best Latin usage, employed by Caesar, Livy, and others. See Meursius, p. 33; Olaus Borrichius, *Reflections*, p. 199; Johannes Vorstius, *On Select Latinity*, part IV, ch. 1, p. 241, ed. Gesner; and Cellarius on Lactantius, *Institutes* VI.17, p. 791, ed. Bunemann. ORELLI.

“For you will have done what you were capable of doing and what your power ought to have accomplished, so that the quality of the work and of the worker himself would be one and the same.” Thus Fulvius Ursinus and the Leiden edition. The manuscript and first edition read, “so that you will be able to be one,” etc., which makes no sense. Gelenius therefore printed “so that it would be one powerful quality.” Stewechius reads: “But what your power ought to have accomplished, so that it would be the one powerful quality both of the work and of the worker himself,” joining “to be able to transfer,” etc., to what follows. But the reading we have printed is preferable. The meaning is that the quality—that is, the force or power—should be discerned as one and the same, namely human, both in the work and in the worker himself. ORELLI.

“To transfer,” that is, to hand over or convey. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.422:

> And that your scepter should be transferred to Dardanian colonists.

On this Servius says: “Transferred—that is, handed over.” This expression is drawn from monetary transactions, for “to be entered in writing” means “to be given.” Isidore in the *Glosses*: “He transfers: he hands over by a written instrument.” See Savaro on Sidonius, poem II, v. 463, p. 32. ORELLI.]

### LI

What do you say, unbelieving, intractable, [Col. 0786A] and hardened minds? Did that Capitoline Jupiter give power of this kind to any mortal? Did he endow a ward-priest or the Pontifex Maximus—or rather the Flamen Dialis, through whom he is *Dius*—with this right?

I shall not say the right to raise the dead, or to restore light to the blind, or to restore the proper condition of their limbs to the enervated and disabled, but merely the right to reduce a pustule, a hangnail, or a papule by the command of his voice or the touch of his hand.

Was that, then, something human? Could such a right be given, could such authority proceed from a mouth nourished upon earthly refuse, and was it not divine and sacred—or, if the matter admits any superlative expression, more than divine and sacred?

[Col. 0787A] For if you yourself do what you are able to do and what accords with your strength and power, admiration has nothing at which to cry out. You will merely have done what you were capable of doing and what your power ought to have accomplished, so that the quality of the work and of the worker himself would be one and the same.

But to be able to transfer your right to a human being; to bestow upon the most fragile of creatures what you alone are able to do, and to impart to it the power to do the same—this belongs to a power established above all things, which contains beneath itself the causes of all things and the natures of their rational principles and capacities.

[Note: [Col. 0787B]

### Note to LII

“Come now: let some magician Zoroaster arrive from the inner world beyond the fiery zone.” There is great disagreement among scholars concerning this passage. Heraldus thinks that the words “beyond the fiery zone” were added as an explanatory gloss by some ignorant person, since none of the ancients knows of a Zoroaster from the fiery zone—that is, from inner Libya or Ethiopia, bordering upon τῆς κατακεκαυμένης, “the scorched region.” He therefore thinks the passage should read: “Let some magician Azonaces come from the inner world,” etc., so that it refers to the magician Azonaces, whom Hermippus, according to Pliny, *Natural History* XXX.1, reported to have been Zoroaster’s teacher.

Stanley, however, defends the common reading in his *History of Philosophy*, p. 1112, Leipzig edition. He thinks Arnobius was referring here to the story related by Dio Chrysostom in the *Borysthenitic Oration*, in which the Persian Zoroaster—who is confused with another of the same name—is said to have come to the people from a fiery mountain. Accordingly, the words “through the fiery zone” should be understood not of the arid regions of Libya, but either of that fiery mountain or of the dwelling of the divine powers assigned to the zones, which, according to Chaldean doctrine, lies above the Empyrean or corporeal heaven.

In the Leiden edition of Arnobius, Salmasius reads: “Let Zoroaster the magician, I ask, come through the fiery zone from the inner world.” He defends this conjecture in his *Plinian Exercises on Solinus*, p. 335, promising to demonstrate that Zoroaster was also regarded by the ancients as an Ethiopian or as a native of outer Libya—a promise which I wish he had fulfilled. Moreover, *quis super* was wrongly changed into *quaeso per*. For Arnobius very frequently uses *quis*, “someone,” *aliquis*, and *quidam*, “a certain person,” contemptuously. Thus below, book IV, ch. 26, “some Hercules or other”; see Heraldus’s note there. ORELLI.

“Come now: let some magician Zoroaster arrive from the inner world through the fiery zone,” etc. The ancients relate marvelous things about this founder of the Magi.

The Persians, according to Dio Chrysostom in the *Borysthenitic Oration* (vol. III, ed. Reiske, p. 93), say that in his pursuit of wisdom and justice he withdrew to some mountain or other, and that afterward the mountain was set ablaze by fire falling from heaven. While it continued to burn, the king and his companions approached it to worship; then Zoroaster suddenly appeared unharmed from the flames, with a kindly countenance, and commanded them to be of confident spirit and to perform certain sacrifices regularly, because the gods were present in that place.

Suidas and George Cedrenus report almost the same things about Zoroaster: namely, that, just as he had prayed to the immortal gods, he was burned by lightning, after first instructing the Persians to worship and preserve his ashes as a pledge that sovereignty would remain among them. Clement of Rome gives a somewhat different account in the *Recognitions*, Homily IX. Porphyry, drawing upon Eubulus, writes about Zoroaster’s cave in *The Cave of the Nymphs*.

To these may be added Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks* I, in these words:

> The firstborn son of Ham, son of Noah, was Cush. He passed over to the Persians, who called him Zoroaster—that is, “the living star.” From him they also became accustomed to worship fire; and because he himself was divinely consumed by fire, they worship him as a god.

There were, however, several men named Zoroaster, as is sufficiently established. The most ancient of all was the Bactrian, since he was a contemporary of Ninus, king of the Assyrians. See Arnobius above, ch. 5. Semiramis, queen of the Assyrians, defeated him in war, as Theon teaches in the chapter περὶ συγκρίσεως, “On Comparison,” of his *Progymnasmata*:

> For even if Tomyris was superior to Cyrus, or indeed—by Zeus—Semiramis to Zoroaster the Bactrian, it must not therefore be conceded that the female sex is more courageous than the male.

Another was Pamphylian by birth, the son of Armenius, whom Plato calls Er in book X of the *Republic*, as Clement of Alexandria writes in book V of the *Stromata*, and as our author does in this passage. There was also a Zoroaster of Proconnesus, slightly earlier than the time of Xerxes, according to Pliny, *Natural History* XXX.2. But the man who founded the practice of magic among the Persians is called the son of Oromazes by Plato in *First Alcibiades*. See Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus XXIII.6 §32. Compare Marsham, *Chronological Canon*, pp. 144 ff., and Salmasius on Solinus, p. 335. ORELLI.

Zoroaster—if we assent to Hermippus as our authority—the Bactrian; and let that one also come whose deeds Ctesias recounts in the first book of his *Histories*: the Armenian, grandson of Hosthanes; and Pamphylus, the intimate of Cyrus. These words admit entirely different interpretations according to how they are punctuated. If our punctuation is followed, Arnobius seems to mention four Zoroasters: the first a Chaldaean, also called an Assyrian by the *Suda*, who is said to have perished after being struck by lightning; the second the Bactrian, whom Arnobius mentioned above in chapter V and whose deeds Ctesias had recounted in the first book of his *Histories*; cf. Justin, book I, beginning; the third the Armenian, grandson of Hosthanes; and finally the fourth, the Pamphylian, otherwise named Er, whom Plato, at the end of book X of the *Republic*, asserts to have returned to life after ten days spent lying among [Col. 0788D] the corpses, and whom Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book V, p. 598, Frankfurt ed., attests was also called Zoroaster. (Cf. Paulus Leopardus, who discusses him at length, *Emendationes*, book IX, ch. 2, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, p. 170.)

Meursius and Salmasius, however, *On Solinus*, p. 335, read and punctuate our passage differently: “Zoroaster—if we assent to Hermippus as our authority—the Bactrian. And let that one also come whose deeds Ctesias recounts in the first book of his *Histories*: the Armenian, grandson of Hostanes” (in the Leiden edition of Arnobius it is *Zostrianus*; for what reason I do not see); “and Pamphilus, the intimate of Cyrus.” Accordingly, in Salmasius’s view there were only three Zoroasters: the first, according to some, from inner Libya, or from the vicinity of scorched Ethiopia (*tēs kekaumenēs*), or, if Hermippus is to be trusted, a Bactrian; the second an Armenian, grandson of Hostanes, whose deeds Ctesias wrote; the third, named Pamphilus, a friend of Cyrus.

Heinrich Ursinus, in his *Exercises on Zoroaster, etc.* [Col. 0789A], published at Nuremberg in 1661, infers from the same reading of Salmasius that Arnobius mentions only two and openly rejects the Bactrian, the Zoroaster of Hermippus; and that Ctesias, while refuting the fabulous history of Eudoxus, proves that Zoroaster lived in the time of Cyrus. But the words of Arnobius do not seem to require that alteration. For the Zoroaster whom Ctesias mentions seems to have been none other than the Bactrian: as Photius shows, codex 72, his first six books comprised only [Col. 0789B] Assyrian history and the events preceding Persian history.

Salmasius’s conjecture therefore seems false when he refers Arnobius’s citation of Ctesias to the grandson of Hostanes, since, according to Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXX, ch. 1, Hostanes lived under Darius Hystaspes. And the words “the Armenian, grandson and intimate of Hostanes; the Pamphylian of Cyrus,” in which they would have two Zoroasters mentioned, seem corrupt and should be restored thus: “the Armenian, grandson of Hostanes and his disciple; the Pamphylian Er,” where *familiaris* means the same as Greek *gnōrimos*, “disciple,” so that only one person is designated by those words.

Moreover, the Hostanes or Ostanes whom Arnobius mentions is the man of whom Pliny, *Natural History* XXX.1, says that, as Xerxes’ companion in the war he brought upon Greece, “he scattered, as it were, the seeds of his monstrous art, infecting in passing the world wherever he traveled.” Cf. Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, ch. 26. Hermippus, whom our author cites, according to the same Pliny, book I, explained the two million verses composed by Zoroaster and also supplied tables of contents for his volumes. We have excerpted these observations from Thomas Stanley, [Col. 0789C] *History of Philosophy*, part XIII, section I, ch. 2, p. 1111 ff., Leipzig ed.; he also mentions two other Zoroasters, a Medo-Persian and a Proconnesian, but they have no relevance to Arnobius. Cf. Marsham, *Chronological Canon*, p. 144 ff., Franeker ed., and Pastore, in the book entitled *Zoroaster, Confucius, and Mohammed*, pp. 6–7. ORELLI.

**Hermippo ut assentiamur auctori—“if we assent to Hermippus as our authority.”** On Hermippus of Smyrna, see Vossius, *On the Greek Historians*, book II, p. 102 ff. He wrote many works, among them *Bioi* (“Lives”—the last and most recent of these lives was the life of Theophrastus, from which it is inferred that he was Theophrastus’s contemporary) and *Peri Magōn* (“On the Magi”), according to Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXX, ch. 1: “Hermippus, who wrote most diligently about the whole art of magic and explained the two million verses composed by Zoroaster, also supplying tables of contents for his volumes.” Arnobius appears to have drawn his material from that book. NOURRY, p. 543, and ORELLI.

**Armenius Zostriani nepos—“the Armenian, grandson of Zostrianus.”** Valesius, on book I of Ammianus [Col. 0789D], takes *Armenius* to mean “son of Armenius,” Greek *ho Armeniou*. Incorrectly. For Arnobius—or rather Ctesias, whom he copied—seems to speak of another, Armenian Zoroaster and to distinguish him from the Bactrian. ORELLI.

**Et familiaris Pamphilus Cyri—“and Pamphilus, the intimate of Cyrus.”** The name Cyrus is suspect to me. For since Arnobius says that Ctesias mentioned this Magus in book I of his *Histories*, while it is certain that Ctesias wrote about Assyrian and Median affairs in his first six books and began Persian history in the seventh, I do not see how Ctesias could have mentioned Cyrus in book I. Perhaps, therefore, *Nini*, “of Ninus,” should be read in Arnobius. (Valesius on Ammianus, book I.)

Valesius seems to have read Arnobius’s words with too little attention. For what Arnobius cites from Ctesias refers only to the Armenian Zoroaster, grandson of Zostrianus—or, as others have it, Hostanes. Pamphilus is distinct from him (*Pamphilus* is the proper name of a man, not a designation of nationality), another Magus, a contemporary and intimate of Cyrus, of whom perhaps Hermippus made mention. ORELLI.

**Apollonius, Damigero et Dardanus—“Apollonius, Damigeron, and Dardanus.”** Apuleius also mentions these magicians [Col. 0790A] in the *Apology*, p. 331, Elmenhorst ed.; and Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 57. Apollonius is the famous man of Tyana, a Pythagorean philosopher and wonder-worker, whose life Philostratus wrote.

Johann Weyer thinks Damigeron is the same as Demogorgon. Adrianus Junius, however, believes the name to be a designation of Democritus in magical writings. Diogenes Laertius, in his life of Democritus, and [Col. 0790B] Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXX, preface, attest that Democritus heard the Chaldaeans and Magi and himself published books on magic. But the compiler of the *Geoponica* plainly distinguishes them, inserting into his work fragments of both Democritus and Damogeron or Damigeron. It therefore appears that some writer on magic or natural philosophy bore this name, though nothing definite is known about him. See P. Needham, *Prolegomena to the Geoponica*, p. 54, Niclas ed.

Dardanus was a Phoenician, a distinguished magician. Pliny, in the passage cited, records that Democritus became by far the most learned of men after obtaining from Dardanus’s tomb and carefully reading the books found there. Hence “Dardanian arts,” that is, magical arts, in Columella, book X, *On the Cultivation of Gardens*, verse 358, where see the commentators. Cf. Jean Brodeau, *Miscellanies*, book IV, ch. 10, in Gruter’s *Critical Treasury*, vol. II, p. 515; Jean Pamel, on Tertullian, book I; Savaron on Sidonius, book V, epistle IX, p. 342; and especially D. Tiedemann, who discusses him at length in his dissertation *On the Origin of the Magical Arts, etc.*, pp. 37 and 39. ORELLI.

**Velus, Julianus—“Velus, Julianus.”** Some scholars (Joseph Mercier) think we should read “Nilus, Vulcanus” (but on Julian, the author of the *Theurgica*, [Col. 0790C] see the following note. ORELLI), since Laertius, *Proem*, §1, said: “For Hephaestus was born the son of Nilus the Egyptian, and he began philosophy” (*Aigyptiou men gar Neilou genesthai paida Hēphaiston, hon arxai philosophias*). But no one has ever proved that *philosophy* there is to be understood as magic.

Others therefore think *Belus* should be emended for *Velus*, and indeed not wholly without justification. For the initial letters B and V of both names are very frequently interchanged by copyists. Belus, as Diodorus Siculus relates in book I, established priests who, after the Egyptian custom, were exempt from public burdens and expenses. These men, whom the Babylonians call Chaldaeans, used to observe the stars in the capacity of priests, natural philosophers, and astrologers. Doubtless for this reason Belus is called by Pliny and Solinus the inventor of astral science; and Jerome (*On Hosea*, ch. II) says that he is the same figure whom the Hebrews call Bel and the Sidonians and Phoenicians call Baal, and that he was enrolled among the gods by his son Ninus. NOURRY, pp. 534–535.

**Julianus—“Julian.”** Surnamed the Theurgist—he flourished under Marcus [Col. 0790D] Antoninus the Philosopher—he acquired a great reputation among magicians. Anastasius relates that he cured a plague at Rome by magical arts. The *Suda* and others write that he produced the rain which other authors attribute to Arnuphis. According to the same *Suda*, his father was Julian the Chaldaean, who wrote about demons and about *kyphi*, that is, a phylactery by which, through magical ceremonies, we may ward diseases away from the individual parts of the body. Julian the son wrote *Theurgica*, *Telestika* (“Works on Initiation”), *Logia di’ epōn* (“Oracles in Verse”), and other works pertaining to this secret discipline. Cf. D. Tiedemann, *Dissertation on the Origins of the Magical Arts*, p. 74. ORELLI.

**Baebulus.** No mention of him occurs among the ancients. Nourry therefore plausibly thinks that *Babilus* should be read, whom Suetonius mentions as a famous astrologer in *Nero*, ch. 36. There Casaubon thinks *Babylas* should be read, since *Babylas* is a common name in Greek histories and is very closely related to *Baebulus*. ORELLI.—Cf. Oudendorp on Suetonius, passage cited. OCHSNER.

[Col. 0791C] **In officium sermonis dandi—“for the function of giving speech.”** Arnobius uses *sermonem dare*, “to give speech,” in a rare but not improper expression. There is therefore no need to rewrite it as *in officium sermocinandi*, “for the function of speaking.”

**Surdorum auriculas reserare—“to unseal the ears of the deaf.”** The Leiden editor printed *returare*, meaning to open or unlock; its opposite is *obturare*, “to stop up”: see Nonius under this word. If it rested upon the authority of the manuscript, it would be especially suitable to Arnobius, a hunter after archaic and obsolete words. ORELLI.

**Ipse faciant, et cum suis ritibus faciant, quidquid malefici graminis, etc.—“Let them do it themselves, and do it with their own rites; whatever baneful plant, etc.”** Meursius deletes the second *faciant*. N. Heinsius, *Adversaria*, book II, ch. 9, p. 272, thinks we should read: “and with their own rites let them sharpen (*acuant*) whatever, etc.”—an ingenious proposal, certainly, but nothing should be changed. For the words “whatever baneful plant, etc.” belong to the following “let them add … let them gather,” and, as it seems to me, specifically to the latter. For a “roar of words” could scarcely be said to be gathered. ORELLI.

**Fremor ille verborum—“that roar of words.”** Arnobius properly calls a “roar of words” what others call magical muttering and magical whispering. Tibullus, I.2 [Col. 0791D], verse 47, calls it a magical shriek:

> Now with a magical shriek she summons the infernal hosts.

This is because those magical incantations were uttered more briefly and rapidly, and only with the very tips of the lips. Hence the Greeks too call them *psithyroi*, “whispers,” and *psithyrismoi*, “whisperings.” HERALDUS.—Cf. Savaron on Sidonius, poem II, verse 86, p. 12. ORELLI.

**Non interdicimus, colligant—“we do not forbid them; let them gather.”** *Interdicimus* is too imperious. I would therefore prefer *intercedimus*, that is, “we prevent,” a word Arnobius uses elsewhere more than once. It is transferred from the interventions of tribunes and others, whose formula when intervening was “I veto” or “I prohibit.” HERALDUS.

**Recognoscere—“to ascertain.”** Meursius conjectures *e re cognoscere*, “to know from the result.” ORELLI.]

### LII

Come now: let some magician come from beyond the fiery zone, from the inner region of the world—Zoroaster, the Bactrian, if we [Col. 0789A] assent to Hermippus as our authority; and let that other also come whose deeds Ctesias recounts in the first book of his *Histories*: the Armenian, grandson of Hosthanes [Note: [Col. 0789A] *Zostriani*, “of Zostrianus,” manuscript and Sab.], and Pamphylus, the intimate [Col. 0790A] of Cyrus; Apollonius, Damigeron, and Dardanus; Velus, Julian, and Baebulus; and anyone else who is said to have held the preeminence and a famous name in tricks of this kind.

[Col. 0791A] Let them enable any one man from the common people to make the mouths of the mute articulate speech, to unseal the ears of the deaf, to restore the natural powers of eyes created without the faculty of sight, and to bring sensation and life back into limbs long grown cold. Or, if this is an arduous task and they cannot grant others the powers required for such works, let them do it themselves, and do it with their own rites. Whatever baneful plant the recesses of the earth nurture, whatever power that roar of words and the accompanying constraints of incantations contain—let them add it; we do not begrudge them. Let them gather it; we do not forbid them. I wish to put it to the test and ascertain whether, with their gods, they can accomplish what Christian peasants have repeatedly accomplished by bare commands.

[Note: [Col. 0791D]

### LIII.—*Ut remini*

*Remini* was restored by Thomas Canter, *Variae Lectiones*, book II, ch. 17; previously the faulty reading was *memini*. ORELLI.

**Siquidem res anima pretiosa est, nec ipso se homini, etc.—“For the soul is a precious thing, nor to the man himself, etc.”** Meursius, p. 34, suspects that we should read *nec ipsa scilicet homini*, “nor, of course, the soul itself to man, etc.” ORELLI.

**Nihil fraudis delituit in Christo—“No fraud lay hidden in Christ.”** Thus Heraldus from [Col. 0792C] the manuscript. Previously the reading was: “There was no fraud, no offense in Christ.” ORELLI.

**Atque in lasciviam dissolvamini cachinnorum—“and abandon yourselves to the wantonness of guffaws.”** Prudentius, *Peristephanon*: “Why do you, holy man, dissolve into guffaws?” Petronius: “Meanwhile Giton stood there and with laughter was splitting his sides.” ELMENHORST. For *atque*, Meursius prefers *aeque*, just as incorrectly. ORELLI.

**Deus radice ab intima—“God from the innermost root.”** That is, God in every respect, God in his innermost power and nature, pure and sheer God—German *ganz und durchaus Gott, Gott nach seiner innersten Natur*, “wholly and thoroughly God, God according to his innermost nature.” In the following passage, for *ab incognitis regnis*, “from unknown kingdoms,” Stewechius prefers *inconditis*, “uncreated,” that is, eternal. ORELLI.

**Et merito. Exutus at corpore, etc.—“And rightly so. But, stripped of the body, etc.”** The Leiden editor most felicitously emended and punctuated the passage in this way. Previously it read *et merito exutus a corpore*, “and deservedly stripped of the body,” which rightly troubled Stewechius, as though Christ had deservedly been stripped of his body—that is, had died. He therefore conjectured that *at emerito*, “but when his service was completed”—that is, when his life was ended—should be read before *exutus a corpore*. But Salmasius’s emendation seems much better.

*Et merito*, “and rightly so,” must be joined to the preceding words, with this [Col. 0792D] sense: “Rightly did they not know him. It is not permissible to be surprised that they did not know him.” German: *Es ist natürlich, dass sie ihn nicht kannten*, “It is natural that they did not know him.” ORELLI.

**Postquam videri se passus est, cujus esset aut magnitudinis sciri—“after he permitted himself to be seen, to be known whose or of what magnitude he was.”** The passage is corrupt. Adrien Behotte, *Apophoreta*, book III, ch. 8, attempts to restore it by two conjectures: either, “after he permitted himself to be seen—who he was, or of what magnitude,” deleting the word *sciri*, “to be known,” as an inappropriate gloss; or thus: “after he permitted himself to be seen—who he was, or of what magnitude—to be known,” instead of “or to be known, of what magnitude he was.” I prefer the former. ORELLI.]

### LIII

Cease, you ignorant men, to turn [Col. 0791B] such great events into objects of abuse—abuse that will do no harm to him who performed them, but will bring danger upon you: danger, I say, not small, but situated among matters of the highest and foremost importance. For the soul is a precious thing, and nothing can be found dearer to a man than his own self.

As you should remember, nothing magical, nothing human, deceptive, or underhanded, no fraud lay hidden in Christ, though you may ridicule him according to your custom and abandon yourselves to the wantonness of guffaws. He was the sublime God, God from the innermost [Col. 0792A] root, God from unknown kingdoms; he was sent as God the Savior by the sovereign of all. Neither the sun itself, nor any stars—if they possess sensation—nor the rulers, nor the princes of the world, nor, finally, the great gods, nor those who frighten the whole race of mortals by pretending to be gods, were able to know [Note: [Col. 0791B] *Nosse*, “to know,” manuscript.] or even suspect whence or who he was. And rightly so.

But after he had been stripped of the body which he bore about upon a tiny part of himself, and after he permitted himself to be seen and his identity and magnitude to be known, all the elements of the world, terrified by the novelty of the events, were thrown into disorder: the earth was moved and trembled; the sea was poured back from its very depths; the air was enveloped in masses of darkness; and the fiery orb of the sun grew rigid as its heat cooled. For what else remained to happen after he had been recognized as God who had long been judged to be merely one of us?

[Col. 0792B] [Note: [Col. 0792D]

### LIV.—*Quinam isti sunt, fortasse quaeritis? Gentes, etc.*

“Who these are, perhaps you ask? Peoples, etc.” Here and in what follows I have adopted Meursius’s punctuation; and below I read *commodaret*, “would lend,” in place of *commodarent*, “would lend” in the plural. ORELLI.

**Numquam rebus ejusmodi credulitatis suae commodaret assensum—“It would never lend the assent of its credulity to matters of this kind.”** African writers very frequently use the imperfect tense for the pluperfect, as grammarians express it. This *enallagē*, “interchange,” occurs in many passages in Arnobius and [Col. 0793B] Tertullian, and indeed among ancient writers too, not rarely in Plautus, for example. Hence Augustine’s famous statement: “I would not believe the Gospel unless the authority of the Church moved me.” That is, “I would not have believed it at the time when I was a Manichaean.” So here *commodarent* is used for *commodassent*, “would have lent.” HERALDUS. Corte on Sallust, *Jugurthine War*, ch. 50, p. 681, and Gronovius on Livy, book XXXIV, ch. 4, have collected more examples of this interchange. ORELLI.

**Vanos, mendaces—“empty boasters, liars.”** Virgil likewise couples these terms, *Aeneid* II.79–80:

> Nor, if cruel Fortune has made Sinon wretched, [Col. 0793C]  
> will she also make him false and a liar.

Aulus Gellius, book XVIII, ch. 4, explains who are properly called *vani*: “We afterwards learned from Apollinaris that *vani* properly designates, not, as the common people said, foolish, dull, or senseless persons, but—as the most learned of the ancients had said—liars and the untrustworthy, who most cunningly fabricate frivolous and empty things in place of weighty and true ones.”

Gellius’s explanation is not entirely satisfactory. For the *vani* are rather those who lie from a kind of disease and an innate pleasure in lying, as Tertullian says, *Apologeticum*, ch. 7, than those who cunningly compose falsehoods. The *vani*, therefore, are those whom the Greeks call *mataioi*, because they lie *matēn*, “to no profitable purpose,” but merely to indulge their own disposition. HERALDUS.—In our language: *Aufschneider, Windbeutel*, “braggarts, windbags.” ORELLI.

**Aut puerili—“or by a childish.”** This is Heraldus’s correction; previously the text read *ut puerili*, “as by a childish.” ORELLI.

**Et execrabili haberentur in nomine—“and be regarded as accursed in their very name.”** Some scholars (Fulvio Orsini) thought *in omine*, “as an omen,” should be read, since Christians were regarded as unspeakably wicked. But precisely for this [Col. 0793D] reason the received reading had to be retained: namely, to signify that the very name of Christians was considered ill-omened and accursed. Above: “Why do you shudder at the mention of our name as though it were an omen of the worst kind?” And: “this accursed name.”

The glosses have: *Execramur*: *katarōmetha*, “we curse”; *apotropiazometha*, “we avert as ominous”; *bdelyttometha*, “we abhor.” Likewise: *Execrat*: *apagoreuei*, “he forbids”; *aphelpizei*—for which *aphierizei*, “he excludes from sacred things,” should be read—*apeuchetai*, “he curses”; *kataratai*, “he invokes curses upon.” The *execrabiles*, therefore, were those whom they barred from sacred rites as impious, polluted, and defiled by some great crime: the Greek *enageis*, “accursed.” If they released them from this condition, they were said *resecrare* them, “to remove the curse.” See Cornelius Nepos, *Alcibiades*, ch. 6. HERALDUS.]

### LIV

But you do not believe that these events occurred. Yet those who witnessed them being done and saw them enacted before their own eyes—the best witnesses and most trustworthy authorities—both believed them themselves and handed them down to us, their descendants, as things to be believed, with no slight confirmations.

Who these are, perhaps you ask? Peoples, populations, nations, and that incredulous human race which, unless the fact had been manifest and, as the saying goes, clearer than daylight itself, would never have lent the assent of its credulity [Col. 0793A] to matters of this kind.

Surely we shall not say that the people of that time were so thoroughly empty boasters, liars, stupid, and brutish that they pretended they had seen things they had never seen; disclosed through false testimony things that had never happened at all; or confirmed them with childish assertion? Although they could have lived harmoniously with you and maintained relations free from offense, would they have voluntarily incurred hatred for no reason and been regarded as accursed in their very name?

[Note: [Col. 0793D]

### LV.—*Coeli convexionibusque dimotae*

“Removed by the curvatures of the sky as well.” Obertus Giphanius thinks we should read *coelique convexionibus*, “and by the curvatures of the sky,” as Thomas Canter had proposed. But nothing should be changed. Arnobius is fond of this construction; for example, book II, ch. 2: “by whom all earthly things and all heavenly things are animated by motion and irrigated with vital power.” [Col. 0794B] Even the best writers use such a construction: Cornelius Nepos, for example, at the beginning of *Timoleon*: “Sicily, harassed for many years by war, and oppressed by barbarians”; Velleius Paterculus II.75: “bearing in her womb Tiberius Caesar, the future avenger of the Roman Empire and son of that same Caesar.” OCHSNER.

**Temeraria desperatione—“through reckless desperation.”** That is, *aponoia*, “desperate recklessness.” See above on chapter XXV. ORELLI.

**Beneficia patris munerandis animis hominibusque—“the Father’s benefits, to bestow gifts upon souls and human beings.”** This reading appeared corrupt to the commentators, who restored it in various ways. Gelenius: “And they carried gifts to human beings given by the gods.” Ludovicus Carrio: “And they carried gifts for healing souls and human beings,” followed by the Leiden editor. [Col. 0794C] Others: “gifts for women and men”; others: “gifts for devout souls and all”; others: “gifts for naked souls and bodies”; Heraldus: “They carried gifts as far as the boundaries of the world.”

Stewechius, however, rightly defends the ancient reading, in my judgment. For *homines*, “human beings,” here means the same as “bodies.” Thus below, book II, ch. 28: “souls situated outside and not yet joined to human bodies.” In the same sense, “men” are contrasted with “souls” in that very famous passage at the beginning of Homer’s *Iliad* I:

> And it sent many mighty souls of heroes down to Hades,  
> but made the men themselves prey for dogs, etc.

Cf. the scholia on Aristophanes, *Acharnians*, verse 397. And *munerare*, used absolutely, means German *beglücken, beschenken*, “to make fortunate, to bestow gifts upon.” Nor did absolutely all the miracles of Christ and the apostles consist in healings. ORELLI.]

### LV

But if that history of events is false, as you say, whence was the whole world filled with this religion in so short a time? Or how could peoples separated by regions [Note: [Col. 0793B] *Dissitae*, “situated far apart,” manuscript.], winds [Col. 0793B], and the curvatures of the sky come together in a single conviction?

Were they [Col. 0794A] enticed by bare assertions, led into empty hopes, and willing of their own accord to expose themselves to mortal dangers through reckless desperation, although they had seen nothing of such a kind as could, by its miraculous character, stir them to adopt these novel rites? On the contrary, because they saw all these things being performed both by him himself and by his heralds—who were sent throughout the whole world and carried the Father’s benefits to bestow gifts upon souls and human bodies [Note: [Col. 0793B] Thus the manuscript. Correctly. A learned man in *Miscellaneous Observations* VI, p. 309, compares Sallust, *Catiline*, ch. 52: “I, who have never granted indulgence for any offense to myself [Col. 0794B] or to my own spirit.” ORELLI.]—they were overcome by the power of truth itself and surrendered themselves to God. Nor did they count it a great loss to cast their limbs before you and offer their entrails to be mangled.

[Note: [Col. 0794C]

### LVI.—*Sed conscriptores nostri mendaciter ista prompserunt, extulere in immensum, etc.*

“But our writers falsely brought these things forward and raised them to immeasurable proportions, etc.” Justus Lipsius, *Epistolary Questions*, book III, epistle 15, p. 531, Wesel ed., thinks we should read: “But since our writers [Col. 0794D], etc.” Yet *conscriptores*, “writers,” is correct. These words contain a new objection by the pagans: “But,” they say, “our writers falsely brought these things forward.” *Conscriptor* is familiar to Arnobius. See the next chapter. So too *conscriptio*, “written account,” occurs throughout.

Nor would I wholly reject *promiserunt*, the reading of all editors before Salmasius. Arnobius appears to have taken this verb in its proper and primary sense of “putting forth, extending,” as one speaks of a “long-grown beard” or a “projecting peninsula.” Hence *rem gestam, historiam promittere*, “to extend an event or history,” is the same as to magnify, expand, or exaggerate it excessively. For Arnobius had already answered in the preceding chapter the opponents’ objection that all Christ’s deeds were wholly false and fabricated with lies. He now proceeds to a second objection: namely, that these events were true in part but had been excessively exaggerated and magnified by Christian writers. But since I sought in vain among the ancients for examples of the expression *promittere res, historias* in the sense “to magnify or expand events or histories,” I preferred to print *prompserunt*, “brought forward,” with the Leiden edition. ORELLI.

[Col. 0795C] **Aut apprehendere locum fortasse possetis, quo videretur esse simillimum veri—“or perhaps you might be able to seize upon a point by which it would appear most like the truth.”** Stewechius restored *quo videretur*, “by which it would appear,” from the manuscript in place of *quod videretur*, “which would appear,” while thinking the text should read: “or perhaps you might seize upon a false coloring by which it would appear.” I find this very pleasing and could scarcely restrain myself from admitting it into the text. ORELLI.

**Aut consimilium his hominum—“or of men resembling them.”** That is, heretics. ORELLI.

**Ut et prudentium tardaret fidem—“so that it might retard the belief even of the discerning.”** Fulvio Orsini: “so that they might retard the belief of those who accepted it.” But nothing should be changed. *Tardaret*, “might retard,” must be referred to *malevolentia*, “malice.” For *prudentium*, “of the discerning,” Meursius reads *prodentium*, “of those handing it down.” ORELLI.

**Sed numquam fuerit his bene, ut Christus qui fuerit litterarum testimoniis colligatur—“But may it never turn out well for them that who Christ was should be inferred from the testimony of writings.”** Thus I read and punctuate the text. *Fuerit* is equivalent to *erit*, “will be.” The future perfect is very frequently used for the indicative future, even when no *si*, “if,” has preceded, especially where a matter is under discussion whose outcome remains uncertain. Thus Cicero, *Academica* IV.36: “Come then, I shall have resisted the Peripatetics … I shall have withstood the Epicureans … what am I to do with Diodotus the Stoic?”

So here *numquam fuerit his bene* is equivalent to: “This matter will never—I hope, I believe—turn out for the benefit or advantage of those people,” namely the demons and men resembling them, “that Christ, etc.” Arnobius means that demons and heretics would have rejoiced if Christ’s deeds rested solely upon the reliability of writers, since writings can very easily be corrupted or mutilated. But, he continues, “may it never turn out well for them”; they shall never rejoice. German: *Es wird ihnen, hoffe, denke ich, nie zugute kommen; sie werden nichts dadurch gewinnen*, “It will never, I hope and believe, benefit them; they will gain nothing by it.” For Christian faith also rests upon many other proofs.

As for what the meaning of the usual punctuation could be—“But may Christ, whoever he was, never have turned out well for them; from writings, etc.”—I confess, with the most ignorant, that I do not know. ORELLI.]

### LVI

But our writers falsely brought these things forward: they raised insignificant deeds to immeasurable proportions and expanded narrow events with sufficiently ostentatious proclamation. Yet would that every deed could have been committed to writing, [Col. 0794B] whether performed by him himself or [Col. 0795A] accomplished by his heralds with equal authority and power! So great a force of miracles would have made you still more incredulous; or perhaps you might be able to seize upon some point by which it could be made to appear most like the truth that additions had been attached to the events and falsehoods inserted into the writings and records.

But not all the deeds performed among unknown peoples ignorant of the use of writing could either be written down or reach everyone’s ears.
