Or, if some were entrusted to writings and written accounts, the malice of demons—whose care and purpose it is to suppress [Note: [Col. 0795C] *Intercipi*, “that this truth be suppressed,” manuscript.] this truth—and of men resembling them interpolated some things and added others [Note: [Col. 0795C] “interpolated some things, and added some things,” Fulvio Orsini.], partly altered them, and removed words and syllables, so that this malice might both retard the belief even of the discerning and corrupt the authority of the deeds.

But may it never turn out well for them that Christ—[Col. 0795B] who he was—should be inferred from the testimony of writings. Writings about him have been handed down [Note: [Col. 0795C] *Est*, “has,” manuscript, with Meursius’s approval.] for this sole purpose: that, if it is established that the things we say are true, he may, by the confession of all, be shown to have been God.

[Note: [Col. 0795D]

### LVII.—*Compingimus*

“We patch together.” Stewechius restored this from the manuscript, and our author favors the word. Below, book IV: “you patch together disgraceful [Col. 0796C] fables”; and book VII: “to patch together obscene songs.” The others read *confingitis*, “you fabricate.” ORELLI.

**Edissertata—“expounded.”** This too we owe to Stewechius. African writers—Apuleius, Tertullian, and Arnobius—favor frequentative verbs in imitation of Plautus. Thus *edissertate et dicite*, “expound and tell,” occurs repeatedly in our author. Others read *edisserta*. ORELLI.

**Turpissimas diis notas—“most disgraceful stains upon the gods.”** Thus Meursius and Salmasius, entirely correctly. Previously *dii*, “the gods,” was read. ORELLI.

**Aut non simillimum veri est, fidem vicinis et finitimis, quam spatiorum inesse longinquitate distantibus—“Or is it not much more probable that credibility inheres in things near and close at hand than in things removed by the remoteness of distances?”** Note here the use of the superlative in place of the comparative where some greater degree of comparison is indicated. *Aut non simillimum veri est* means “Or is it not much more probable?” ORELLI.]

### LVII

You do not believe our writings; and we do not believe yours. We patch together falsehoods about Christ; and you proclaim empty and false things about your gods. For no god fell from heaven and recorded your affairs with his own hands, nor in like manner disparaged our affairs and religious observances. These things were written by men; and those things too were written by men and expounded in the speech of mortals. Whatever you have resolved to say about our writers [Note: [Col. 0796C] “written accounts,” Fulvio Orsini. Above: “if some were entrusted to writings and written accounts.”], take and hold as having been said about your writers also, with equal weight.

You wish the things contained in your writings to be true; then you must necessarily confess that the things recorded in our documents are true. You charge our accounts with falsehood; and we charge yours with falsehood.

“But ours,” you say, “are more ancient and are therefore utterly full of credibility and truth.” As though antiquity were not the mother most abundantly productive of errors, and had not itself given birth to those things that devised, in disgraceful fables, the most shameful stains upon the gods! Could falsehoods not have been both heard and believed ten thousand years ago? Or is it not much more probable that credibility inheres in things near and close at hand than in things removed by the remoteness of distances? For these things are established by witnesses, those by opinions; and it is far more plausible that there is less fabrication in recent things than in things withdrawn into ancient obscurity.

[Note: [Col. 0796D]

### LVIII.—*Sed ab indoctis hominibus et rudibus scripta sunt*

“But they were written by uneducated and uncultivated men.” This reproach against Scripture was repeatedly pressed by the pagans and was answered in the same way by Christian writers—for example, Clement of Alexandria in the *Protrepticus*, and Lactantius in book III, ch. 1 and elsewhere. HERALDUS.

**Numquam enim veritas sectata est fucum—“For truth has never pursued embellishment.”** Clement of Alexandria in the *Protrepticus*: “The divine Scriptures and sober rules of life are concise paths to salvation, bare of external ornament, elaborate eloquence, loquacity, and flattery” (*Graphai de hai theiai, kai politeiai sōphrones, syntomoi sōtērias hodoi gymnai kommōtikēs, kai tēs entos kalliphōnias, kai stōmylias kai kolakeias hyparchousai*). HERALDUS.—Moreover, *enim*, like Greek *gar*, indicates that something must be supplied from what precedes, as here: “And rightly so. For truth has never, etc.” ORELLI.

**Collectiones—“deductions.”** That is, *syllogismoi*, “syllogisms.” See Quintilian, *Institutes* IX.2, and J. C. T. Ernesti, *Lexicon of Latin Rhetorical Terminology*, under this word. ORELLI.

**Fides quaeritur assertionis—“credibility is sought for an assertion.”** Fulvio Orsini reads *assertioni*, “for the assertion”—not badly. ORELLI.]

### LVIII

“But they were written by uneducated and uncultivated men and therefore ought not readily to be believed upon hearing.” Consider whether this is not instead a stronger reason for regarding them as untainted by any lies: they were disclosed by a simple mind, ignorant of how to enlarge them through seductive embellishments.

“The language is commonplace and mean.” For truth has never pursued embellishment, nor does what has been investigated and established allow itself to be led circuitously through the more extended compass of an oration. Deductions, enthymemes, definitions, and all those ornaments by which credibility is sought for an assertion assist those who harbor suspicions; they do not display the outlines of truth. But a man who knows what the thing being discussed is neither defines nor deduces, nor does he pursue the other verbal artifices by which hearers are customarily captivated and compelled, by the constraining force of circumlocution, to assent to a proposition.

[Note: [Col. 0797C]

### LIX.—*Angusti pectoris reprehensio*

“A rebuke arising from a narrow mind.” Arnobius calls a narrow mind one that is *mikropsychon*, “small-souled,” and, as it were, *mikrologon*, “petty in speech.” HERALDUS.

**Quod cum spinis nascuntur et purgamentis aliis—“because they grow together with thorns and other refuse.”** *Purgamenta* here means useless plants, darnel, and so forth. Palladius, *On Agriculture*, book I, title 35: “When you see mists threatening, burn all at once the straw and refuse arranged in several places throughout the garden.” ORELLI.

**Utrumne quid glabre an hirsuta cum asperitate promatur—“whether something is expressed smoothly or with bristling roughness.”** This is a most felicitous emendation by Hugo Grotius, reported by N. Heinsius in *Adversaria*, book IV, ch. 8. The manuscript has *grave*, “heavily,” which is by no means opposed to bristling roughness. Others read *leve*, “lightly”; Fulvio Orsini, *lene*, “gently.” But *glabre*, “smoothly,” is best, and I did not hesitate to admit it into the text. Thus our author below, in book III, speaks of “the smoothnesses and baldness of bodies.” ORELLI.

**Inflectatur quod acui—“that what ought to be sharpened is inflected.”** [Col. 0797D] *Inflecti*, “to be inflected,” seems to be used here for *circumflecti*, “to be turned circuitously.” For the discussion here is not about delivery—which, if bad, certainly delays comprehension—but about style and the arrangement of letters. ORELLI.

**Deturque illis immo—“and let it rather be granted to them.”** Stewechius approves *deturque illis simiis*, “and let it be granted to those apes,” that is, to the ridiculous imitators of the best writers—for example, of Cicero. See Pliny, book I, epistle V; Sidonius, book I, epistle I. Meursius collected more examples in the appendix to his *Critical Arnobius*, on book III. ORELLI.

**Voluptatum delinimenta—“the softening enticements of pleasures.”** Others read *delenimenta*. But Oudendorp, on Apuleius, book III, rightly defends the received reading: pleasures are very properly called *delinimenta voluptatum*, as though they were an ointment that softens men, from *delino, -ere*, which means the same as *delibuo*, “to anoint.” ORELLI.

**Omne suum studium—“all their effort.”** The first edition reads: *Omnes unum studium*, “all one effort.” ORELLI.

**Trivialem studio humilitatem secutos—“deliberately pursuing commonplace lowliness.”** *Studio* means “deliberately.” Solinus, ch. 35: “These dolphins deliberately entice crocodiles to swim and, diving beneath them with deceitful cunning, cut open and kill them by swimming beneath [Col. 0798C] the tender parts of their bellies.” HERALDUS.

**Et sophistica se potius ostentatione jactarent—“and should instead parade themselves with sophistical ostentation.”** In that age the people especially called “sophists” were those who studied humane letters and devoted their effort to rhetoric and poetry—in short, to elegance of speech and the gathering of stylistic blossoms. These were the principal occupations of rhetoricians and grammarians. HERALDUS.

**Cum tibi sit ratio cum male se habentibus atque aegris—“when your business is with those who are unwell and sick.”** Others read *oratio*, “speech,” in place of *ratio*. But J. F. Gronovius, *Observations*, book II, ch. 10, rightly defends *ratio*: it means “business” and occurs several times in Cicero. ORELLI.

**Secus virile—“the male sex.”** Ludovicus Carrio restored this from the manuscript. The archaic *secus* occurs several times in Arnobius for *sexus*, “sex”—for example, book V, chapters 13 and 25. See the commentators on Festus under *sexus*. Thus Sallust, *Fragments of the Histories*, book II: “But Metellus, returning after a year to Further Spain, was seen amid great glory throughout all the streets and houses, as people of both the male and [Col. 0798D] female sex ran together from every direction.” See there Corte, p. 960; and J. F. Gronovius, who carefully collected every occurrence of this ancient and obsolete word, on Livy, book XXVI, ch. 47; and Lindenbrog on Ammianus Marcellinus, book XVI, ch. 11, §9. ORELLI.

**Applicetur—“let it be applied.”** Thus the Leiden editor from the manuscript. The others have the faulty *applicet*, “let him apply,” which Oberthür nevertheless retained in his usual fashion. Its subject is what follows, namely *haec*, “these things.” ORELLI.

“You accuse [our works] of the deformity of faults.” *Foeditate* (“by deformity”) is added from the manuscript by Meursius, very rightly. Lipsius emended the text to *vitio verborum criminamini* (“you accuse [them] of a fault in their words”), Bertius to *vi vitiorum* (“by the force of their faults”). ORELLI.

*Stribiligines.* The glosses: “*Stribiligo*: a solecism” (*σολοικισμός*). Gellius, book V, chapter 20: “A solecism is called *imparilitas* (‘inequality’) by Sinnius Capito and others of his age; by the older Latin writers it was called *stribiligo*, evidently from the twisting and crooked perversity of speech, as though it were a kind of *steribiligo*.” ELMENHORST.—It appears to be derived from *στρέφω*, “to turn,” *στρεβλός*, “twisted,” and *στρόβιλος*, “a whirling.” Hence in Gellius one should read *strebiligo* or *strobiligo* instead of *steribiligo*. ORELLI.

[Col. 0799B] “Does not one of you say *haec utria*, another *hos utres*?” I have printed this with the Leiden edition. The editors, however, differ. The manuscript has *aliud … aliud*, which is manifestly corrupt. For the sense of that reading would be that *utria* and *utres* are different things—that is, different in meaning—although Arnobius is here listing words with the same meaning but different endings and genders. Lipsius reads: “in one place *haec utria*, elsewhere … *hos utres*.” Heraldus, in his *Second Notes* against Salmasius, writes that the manuscript originally contained *alius*, but that it was later changed by another hand and in different ink to *aliud*; he himself thinks that one should read *alias—alias* (“at one time—at another”). For my part, I do not see why *alius … alius* should be changed. In place of *utria … utres*, Gronovius, on Aulus Gellius, book III, chapter 16, thinks that *utera … uteros* should be read, since Gellius has *uterus* in the passage cited. But here too nothing should be changed, for we know that many obsolete endings of this kind from older Latin have completely disappeared, while others have been preserved only in passages quoted by grammarians. And Nonius, under the word *utres*, expressly says that the neuter also was used by the ancients, citing a passage of Lucilius: “Andronius, Flacci’s man, needs *utria*.” ORELLI.

*Coelus* and *coelum.* See the same Nonius, under *coelum*, in his discussion of words of indeterminate gender, where he cites many examples. ORELLI.

*Filus* and *filum.* For some reason unknown to me, Fulvius Ursinus changes this to *hilus* and *hilum*. ORELLI.

*Crocus* and *crocum.* See the same Nonius, who under the word *crocum* cites the neuter from Sallust, *Histories* II: “He turned his course toward the city of Corcyra and took sustenance in a grove in which saffron (*crocum*) grows”; this fragment was overlooked by Cortius. So too Cornelius Fronto, in book I *On Orators*, among the works most recently discovered and edited by Angelo [Col. 0799D] Mai, p. 226: “You must repeatedly ensure that the saffron (*crocum*) is sprayed far and high in the theater.” ORELLI.

*Fretus* and *fretum.* Nonius supplies several examples of this. But where he quotes from Lucilius, “by the name of heaven and trusting in the salt sea” (*coeli nomine et salis fretus*), I would read, “the light of heaven and a strait of salt water” (*coeli lumen et sali fretus*). Lucilius thus meant that *coeli lumen* may elegantly be said for *coelum*, and *sali fretum* for *salum*. HERALDUS.

“This bread” (*hoc pane*) and “this bread” (*hic panis*). Charisius, *Grammatical Instruction*, book I, p. 69: “*Panis* is used in the masculine gender, although Plautus used it in the neuter in the *Curculio*:

> These are the supports of the belly: bread and roasted beef.”

Compare Nonius. ELMENHORST.

“This blood” (*hic sanguis*) and “this blood” (*hoc sanguen*). See Nonius under *sanguis*; Priscian, book VI, p. 708; Lucretius, book I, verse 837. ELMENHORST.

*Candelabrum, candelaber.* See Nonius under the word *candelabrum*. ELMENHORST.

*Epicadii.* Thus the manuscript and the Roman edition should be read; *Epicandeos* [Col. 0800B] is corrupt. Suetonius, *On Illustrious Grammarians*, chapter 12: “Cornelius Epicadus, a freedman of the dictator Lucius Cornelius Sulla and his attendant in the augural priesthood, was also a great favorite of Sulla’s son Faustus; for that reason he invariably described himself as the freedman of both. Moreover, he himself completed the last book that Sulla had left unfinished concerning his own achievements.” Compare Ludovicus Carrio, who discusses the man at length in *Ancient Readings*, book I, chapter 13. ORELLI.

*Caesellii.* Caesellius Vindex wrote highly celebrated commentaries entitled *Ancient Readings*, according to Gellius, book VII, chapter 2, who nevertheless calls him a man lacking understanding. He is also cited frequently by Charisius, books I and II, and Priscian, book X. ELMENHORST and ORELLI.

[Col. 0800C] *Verrii.* This means Marcus Verrius Flaccus, a distinguished grammarian of Augustus’s time, whom Suetonius discusses at greater length in *On Illustrious Grammarians*, chapter 17, and whose work *On the Meaning of Words* was abridged by Festus. ORELLI.

*Scauri.* Terentius Scaurus was perhaps the most distinguished grammarian in the time of the deified Hadrian, according to Aulus Gellius, book XI, chapter 24; see Gronovius there. His book *On Orthography*, edited by Putschius, survives. ORELLI.

“And Nisi.” Theodorus Canterus, *Various Readings* I.23, thinks one should read *Gnifones* (“Gnifos”; Marcus Antonius Gnifo is mentioned by Suetonius). But he himself retracts this opinion after being corrected by Carrio, *Ancient Readings*, book II, chapter 11, who discusses at length the grammarian Nisus, cited throughout Charisius, Velius Longus, Servius, and Priscian. Among other things, Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.12, attests that he wrote books of *Fasti*, information that escaped Carrio. ORELLI.]

### LIX

“Your works,” he says, “are beset with barbarisms and solecisms and polluted by the deformity of faults.” A childish criticism, certainly, and one proceeding from a narrow mind. If we were to admit [Note: [Col. 0797B] *Admittimus* (“we admit”). Fulvius.] that it is true, then let us cast away from our use certain kinds of fruit because they grow amid thorns and other refuse—things that cannot nourish us, yet do not prevent us from enjoying that which is principal and which nature intended to be most wholesome for us.

For what harm does it do, pray, [Col. 0797B] or what dullness does it impose upon understanding, whether something is expressed smoothly or with bristling roughness? Whether a word that ought to have the acute accent is inflected, or one that ought to be inflected is given the acute accent? Or how is what is said any less true if an error is made in number or case, preposition, participle, or conjunction?

Let this pomp of diction and speech conducted according to rules be reserved for public assemblies, lawsuits, the forum, and courts of law; or rather, let it be granted to those who, seeking the enticements [Note: [Col. 0798B] *Deliniamenta*. Fulvius.] of pleasure, have devoted all their zeal for words to rhetorical brilliance. When matters removed from ostentation are under discussion, one must consider what is said, not with what charm it is said; not what caresses the ears, [Col. 0798A] but what benefits it brings to its hearers. This is especially so since we know that even some men devoted to wisdom not only rejected cultivated speech, but, although they could have spoken more ornately and copiously, deliberately pursued a commonplace humility of style, lest they corrupt the austere rigor of seriousness and parade themselves instead through sophistical ostentation.

Indeed, it is the mark of a dissolute mind to seek pleasure in serious matters; and when your business is with those who are unwell and sick, to pour sweeter sounds into their ears rather than apply medicine to their wounds. Yet, if you attend to the truth, no form of speech is naturally correct, and likewise none is naturally faulty. For what natural principle or law written into the constitution of the world requires that one say “this wall” in the masculine (*hic paries*) and “this chair” in the feminine (*haec sella*)? They possess no sexes distinguished into female and male kinds, nor could even the most learned person teach me what *hic* and *haec* are in themselves, or why one of them denotes the male sex while the following noun [Col. 0798B] is assigned to the feminine gender.

These are human conventions, and they are certainly not necessary for everyone’s use in forming speech. For “this wall” in the feminine (*haec paries*) and “this chair” in the masculine (*hic sella*) might perhaps have been said without any fault if people had decided to speak so from the beginning and that usage had been maintained in common speech by succeeding generations.

And yet, you men who accuse our works of being polluted by the deformity of faults: do you not have these same *stribiligines*, these linguistic distortions, in those greatest and most admirable books of yours? Does not one of you say “these wineskins” in the neuter (*haec utria*), another in the masculine (*hos utres*)? *Coelus* and *coelum* for “heaven”? Likewise *filus* and *filum* for “thread”? Likewise *crocus* and *crocum* for “saffron”? Likewise *fretus* and *fretum* for “strait”? Do we not likewise find among you “this bread” in the neuter (*hoc pane*) and “this bread” in the masculine (*hic panis*), “this blood” as *hic sanguinis* and “this blood” as *hoc sanguen*? *Candelabrum* and *jugulum*, yet by the same principle *jugulus* and *candelaber*?

For if individual nouns cannot possess more than one gender each, and the same things cannot belong both to this gender and to that—for one gender cannot pass over into another—then a person who pronounces masculine things according to the rules of the feminine gender commits just as great an error as one who places masculine articles before feminine nouns. Yet we observe you expressing masculine things in the feminine, feminine things in the masculine, and things you call neuter in both this [Col. 0799B] and that fashion without any distinction.

Therefore, either there is no fault in using these forms indifferently, and you vainly call us disfigured by the obscenity of solecisms; or, if fixed principles determine how each word must be expressed, you too are entangled in similar faults, even though you have mastered every Epicadus, Caesellius, Verrius, Scaurus, and Nisus.

[Note: [Col. 0800C]

### LX.—“Which could receive the impact of the eyes”

Greek *τὴν ἐπίβλεψιν*, “the act of looking upon.” For Arnobius wished to render the Greek expression. HERALDUS.—Elmenhorst, in the Hanau edition, conjecturally reads *sustineret*, “could sustain.” ORELLI.

“Of most sluggish contemplation.” That is, of contemplation that is dull, obtuse, hindered, and because of human frailty incapable of beholding divine and heavenly things. In Greek, *μύωψ*, “short-sighted.” Others read *ineptissimae*, “most inept,” ineptly. For my part, I suspect that *intentissimae*, “most intent,” should be read. ORELLI.

“For who among mortals could see him, who discern him?” Stewechius was the first to restore this reading. Previously it was read, “Who would seek,” etc., which appears to have arisen because a copyist misunderstood the preceding words “of most sluggish contemplation.” But if we follow Stewechius, the latter clause should have been “who [could] discern,” or “who is there who [could] discern,” etc. I therefore prefer Heraldus’s proposal in his *Second Notes*: “For who among mortals could see him, who discern him?” deleting *est* (“is”). ORELLI.

“Primal nature.” Above: “the governance of the primal motion.” Book II: “It therefore possesses primal origins.” Martianus [Col. 0801B] Capella, book VII of *The Marriage of Philology*: “Jupiter, recognize the source of your unique and primal nature.” ELMENHORST.

[Col. 0801C] “Whether in quality or divine power.” “Quality” is the same thing as what Arnobius has just called his proper and primal nature; *numen*, “divine power,” is what they barbarously call “deity.” ORELLI.]

### LX

“But if Christ was God,” they say, “why was he seen in the form of a human being? And why was he killed in the human manner?” Could that invisible power, possessing no bodily substance, have entered and adapted itself to the world and participated in the assemblies of mortals in any other way than by assuming some covering of more solid matter, one that could receive the impact of the eyes and upon which the gaze of our most sluggish faculty of contemplation could fix itself?

For who among mortals [Note: [Col. 0799B] *Etenim*, “for indeed.” Fulvius.] could see him, who discern him, if he had chosen to enter the earth in the condition proper to his primal nature, and as he himself willed [Col. 0801A] himself to be [Note: [Col. 0801B] *Noluit*, “did not will.” Wrongly. Sabinus.] in his own quality or divine power? He therefore assumed the form of a human being and enclosed his power beneath the likeness of our race, so that he could be seen and perceived, could speak and teach, and could carry out all those things that he had come into the world to perform, while preserving [Note: [Col. 0801B] *Servatus*, “having been preserved.” Wrongly. Sabinus.] the command and ordinance of the supreme King.

[Note: [Col. 0801C]

### LXI.—“They lie thus wrapped in concealment”

Meursius emended the text thus in his appendix from the manuscript, which has *latentaliter involutae*. Previously *latenter involutae*, “secretly wrapped,” was printed, for which Fulvius Ursinus prefers *latentes, involutae*, “lying hidden, wrapped.” Stewechius: *latent altae, involutae*, “they lie deeply hidden, wrapped.” There is a very similar passage in Cicero, *On Divination* I.18: “Perhaps the cause lies hidden, wrapped in the obscurity of nature.” ORELLI.

“And had first shaped your brow for unbelief.” That is, for an obstinacy approaching shamelessness. He would, however, have spoken more clearly: “and had first shaped your brow for refusing belief”; or better still, *firmares*, “hardened,” rather than *formares*, “shaped,” as we say “to harden one’s brow.” HERALDUS.]

### LXI

“What then,” you say, “could the supreme King not accomplish the things he had decreed were to be done in the world without assuming a human disguise?” If it had been proper for them to be done in the way you describe, perhaps he would have done them so; because it was not proper, he did them otherwise.

Why he willed to do them in this manner and refused to do them in that—the reasons lie thus wrapped in concealment and are scarcely comprehensible to anyone. You might perhaps have been able to receive them, had you not long ago prepared yourself not to receive them, [Col. 0801B] and shaped your brow for unbelief before that which you were seeking [Note: [Col. 0801B] “That which was not.” Sabinus.] to know and hear had been explained to you [Note: [Col. 0801B] “Which you seek.” Fulvius.].

[Note: [Col. 0801C]

### LXII.—“But he was killed in the human manner. Not he himself,” etc.

Arnobius argues here from the doctrine of the Gnostics or Docetists, who maintained that the aeon—as they called him—Christ, having been joined to Jesus the son of Mary while he lived on earth, separated himself from him before Jesus [Col. 0801D] was fastened to the cross; accordingly it was not Christ the Son of God, but the man Jesus, son of Mary, who was killed upon the cross. This, evidently, was the doctrine of Cerinthus and the Ebionites. See Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book I, chapters 25–26, Erasmus’s edition. In this and several other passages we can readily recognize the Gnostic Arnobius, but especially in book II, in his discussion of the origin of souls. ORELLI.

“The man whom he had put on.” “Man” means human nature. Thus Lactantius, *Institutes* IV.10: “to the man whom he had put on, whom he bore”; see Bunemann there, p. 452. The concrete used for the abstract. ORELLI.

“If at any time the prophetic Sibyl, [pouring forth] those oracles,” etc. Thus Fulvius Ursinus, followed by all the other editors of Arnobius. The manuscript and Roman edition have: “If at any time the Sibyl [uttered] prophecies, oracles,” which Canterus deletes as a gloss; Heraldus defends it on the ground of Arnobius’s habit of accumulating several words of this kind with the same meaning. See above. ORELLI.

“If Bacis, if Helenus.” This is a most sagacious conjecture by Johannes Mercerus for the old reading: “if a seer, if [Col. 0802C] Helenus.” If we read the latter, the following words, “and other soothsaying seers,” would create a decidedly unpleasant repetition. Nor is it likely that Arnobius omitted Bacis from this list of the most celebrated prophets, particularly since Clement of Alexandria, whom our author follows most zealously and frequently reproduces word for word, mentions him in *Stromata* I, p. 398. The classic passage concerning Bacis, the Boeotian prophet, is in Pausanias’s *Boeotica*. Clement, in the passage cited, identifies two men of that name, one a Boeotian and the other an Arcadian. The scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Peace*, verse 1071, and Aelian, *Various History* XII.35, where the commentators should be consulted, teach that there were three Bacides. Compare Wesseling on Herodotus VIII.20 and Davis on Cicero, *On Divination* I.18. Who does not know Helenus from that very beautiful episode in Virgil’s *Aeneid* VIII.294? See the distinguished Heyne there, Excursus X. ORELLI.

“If Martius.” Livy XXV.12 calls him a famous prophet and cites two of his prophecies, one concerning the disaster at Cannae and the other concerning the games to be vowed to Apollo; Pliny, [Col. 0802D] *Natural History* VII.33, says: “Divinity and a certain fellowship with the inhabitants of heaven existed … among the Romans in Martius.” Servius mentions the brothers Martii on *Aeneid* VI.70, 72; so does Symmachus, book IV, letter 35, and above all Cicero, *On Divination* I.40, where see Davis. ORELLI.—Compare Festus under *Negumate* and *Ningulus*; Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV; Isidore, *Origins*, book VI; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.17; and many others. MEURSIUS.

“They disclosed the paths of events to those who asked.” Lycophron:

> … Unfolding the hard-to-utter  
> Paths of riddles.

(*… Διοίχνει δυσφάτους αἰνιγμάτων / οἴμους τυλίσσων.*) HERALDUS.

“It belonged to the humanity assumed, not to him himself; to the burden borne, not to its bearer.” Thus Fulvius Ursinus. The manuscript has: “the assumption of the man belonged to himself, to the burden borne,” etc., which makes no sense. ORELLI.

“Even to undergo that death he would not have submitted, had so great a deed not had to be accomplished.” Perhaps one should read: “He would have submitted to it, had so great a deed not had to be accomplished for his own people” (*succubuisset, suis tanta si non agenda res esset*). CANTERUS.]

### LXII

“But he was killed in the human manner.” Not he himself; for the fall of death cannot befall divine things, nor can that which is one and simple, and not compounded [Col. 0802A] by the aggregation of any parts, dissolve through the disintegration of destruction.

Who, then, was seen hanging upon the gibbet? Who died? The man whom he had put on and [Note: [Col. 0802B] *Sed*, “but.” Fulvius.] whom he himself carried with him.

“It is incredible to say and wrapped in blind obscurity.” If you wish it so; but it is not blind and closely approaches an intelligible analogy. If at some time the prophetic Sibyl, pouring forth those oracles while filled, as you say, with Apollo’s power, had been cut down and killed by impious brigands, would Apollo be said to have been killed in her? If Bacis, Helenus, Martius, and other similarly soothsaying prophets had been deprived of life and light, would anyone say that, subject to the law of humanity, those gods [Note: [Col. 0802B] Fulvius: “gods.”] had been extinguished who, speaking through the prophets’ mouths, disclosed the paths of events to those who asked?

The death of which you speak belonged to the humanity assumed, not to him himself; to the burden borne, not to its bearer. Even to undergo that death [Col. 0802B] he would not have submitted [Note: [Col. 0802B] Thus Gelenius and Fulvius; the manuscript has *occubuisset*, “would have died.”], had so great a deed not had to be accomplished, and had an inexplicable principle of destiny not had to be disclosed by mysteries being opened [Note: [Col. 0802B] The manuscript and Sabinus have *satis*, “sufficiently.”].

[Note: [Col. 0803B]

### LXIII.—“And admit them into the hidden recesses of the inner treasury”

Hesychius: “A treasury—a building for the storage of statues, valuables, and sacred objects” (*Θησαυρός—εἰς ἀγαλμάτων καὶ χρημάτων καὶ ἱερῶν ἀπόθεσιν οἶκος*). Correctly. Arnobius therefore means the sanctuary, “the hidden part of the temple” (*τὸ ἀπόκρυφον μέρος τοῦ ἱεροῦ*), the very “inner chamber of the sacred rites,” as Apuleius calls it, where the image and the other objects shown to initiates during their consecration were kept. He also appears to allude to the ancient philosophers’ “external discourses” (*λόγους ἐξωτερικούς*) and “internal discourses” (*εἰσωτερικούς*). The former were transmitted “to those outside” (*τοῖς ἔξω*), to whom the inner treasury was not yet open; the latter were entrusted “to the initiated” (*τοῖς μεμυημένοις*), those who had been duly initiated and sealed. HERALDUS.

[Col. 0803C] “Or by reversing their power.” This is a most successful emendation by the editor of the Leiden edition. The manuscript has “or by universal power” (*vel potestate universa*), which Stewechius changed to “or universal powers” (*vel potestates universas*). “Powers” evidently means those endowed with power, just as in the following chapter “nobilities” means noblemen. ORELLI.

“He who commanded the lame to walk.” The Roman codex reads *praeciebat*, from which Gelenius produced *faciebat*, “caused.” I prefer *praecipiebat*, “commanded.” For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Go and walk.” THEODORUS CANTERUS.

“To bind.” The manuscript incorrectly has *caligare*, “to darken.” Fulvius Ursinus reads *colligare*, “to bind together.” ORELLI.

“To pronounce death upon whomever he wished.” That is, to bring death by an utterance, a word, a bare command—as Arnobius says above. *Indicere* is used in a somewhat different sense above, chapter 3; see the notes there. ORELLI.

“Most brutal brigands.” Fulvius Ursinus reads “most dreadful.” ORELLI.

*Dissignasset.* Arnobius is fond of this verb. Thus below, book VII, chapter 6: “And let him regard it as an injury if a blind creature, always walking in the clouds of ignorance, has marked out or said anything by which their authority might be diminished.” Thus *dissignare* and *dissignator* occur throughout our author. Gesner, in his *Thesaurus*, thinks *dissignare* means the same as *designare*. I, however, would believe that there is some difference: *dissignare* is equivalent to “separate,” “distribute,” or rather “designate various and diverse things,” as here it denotes diverse and manifold tortures. Thus among the Romans the *dissignatores* were those who allocated seats to spectators in theaters. See the scholia on Horace, *Epistles* I.7.6, and Justus Lipsius, *On the Amphitheater*, chapter 15, p. 1033, Works, Antwerp edition, vol. III. ORELLI.—I do not know whether such subtle differentiation is futile in a writer of this kind, and Gesner’s judgment appears altogether more correct. Indeed, many copyists even in the Middle Ages affected the spellings *diffinire*, *diffinitio*, *dissignare*, etc., for *definire*, *definitio*, and *designare*. Nevertheless, the commentators on Plautus, *Poenulus*, Prologue, verse 19, could have been cited in support of that distinction. OCHSNER.

“For since, concerning the dangers of souls, many evils against those [souls] the revealer, teacher, and author,” etc. [Col. 0804B] The passage is wretchedly mangled and easily the most corrupt in all Arnobius; in the absence of more accurate manuscripts, one must apparently despair of restoring it. The commentators have contributed the following. Fulvius Ursinus reads: “For since concerning the dangers of souls [he was] the revealer of many remedies against them, their teacher and author,” etc. What this might mean, I confess myself as ignorant as the most ignorant. Heraldus and Stewechius, suspecting a gap in the discourse, printed the passage thus: “For since concerning the dangers of souls many things, many evils concerning their … against them the revealer,” etc.

The more recent Roman edition of 1583 restores the whole passage thus: “For since concerning the dangers of souls [he spoke] many things, many things concerning their nature, the revealer, teacher, and author directed them toward the limits, paths, laws, and ordinances of appropriate duties: did he not crush the arrogance of pride?” This reading could be accepted if only it were supported by ancient books.

I prefer Oudendorp’s emendation on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VII, p. 467, which reads: “For since, concerning the dangers of souls, he disclosed many things, many things concerning the nature of remedies, as teacher and author,” etc. Among writers of that age, *insinuare* frequently means “to indicate” or “to teach.” Thus Arnobius himself below, book II, chapter 19: “For what else do they promise that they can either disclose or transmit?” And book V, chapter 2: “To disclose them as truths and as something wondrous.” Dictys of Crete, *Trojan War* II.9: “For he then disclosed to the sorrowing Agamemnon what had happened concerning his son”; and V.14: “since they disclosed that it had been taken away through their own efforts.”

If I may venture a suggestion, several lines appear to have fallen out after the word *insinuator*, “revealer,” and the first member of the sentence might perhaps be restored thus: “For since he denounced many evils concerning the dangers of souls against the insinuators … teacher and author.” I think, namely, that in this passage Arnobius explained the causes of the Jewish people’s hostility and hatred toward Christ; and, if I perceive anything correctly, the particle *enim*, “for,” plainly declares that these words must be connected with what precedes, where he speaks of the savage and most brutal brigands who laid hands upon Christ.

The words “teacher and author,” etc., appear to me to form the conclusion of a new period in which Arnobius had treated Christ’s teaching in general, but whose beginning fell out through the copyists’ carelessness. I interpret *mala dissignare* as “to predict or threaten diverse and manifold evils”; see above on the same chapter. I explain *insinuatores* either as “teachers” or as men who ingratiate themselves with others by evil arts and court popular favor, such as the Pharisees among the Jews, against whom we know Christ inveighed most vehemently—for example, in Matthew 23, repeatedly saying, “Woe to you, Pharisees!” Moreover, the words that follow, “did he not crush the arrogance of pride?” appear to favor this conjecture. But let the more learned judge. ORELLI.]

### LXIII

“What,” you will say, “are those sealed and obscure mysteries which no human beings, nor even those who are called the gods of the world, can know or approach by any degree of conjecture and supposition, except those whom he himself has deigned to endow [Col. 0803A] with the gifts of so great a knowledge and to admit into the hidden recesses of the inner treasury?”

For you see [Note: [Col. 0803B] Thus Sabinus and the manuscript. Others: “For who …”], if he had been unwilling that anyone should lay hands upon him, that he would have had to strive with the greatest effort to keep his enemies away from himself, perhaps by reversing their power. He who had restored sight to the blind—could he not, if he needed to do so, make men blind? He who restored soundness to the disabled—did he find it difficult or laborious to make men disabled? He who commanded the lame to walk—did he not know how to bind the motion of their limbs by stiffening their sinews? He who drew the dead from their tombs—would it have been hard for him to pronounce death upon whomever he wished?

But because the principle by which those things were destined required that they be done, here in the world itself—and in no other manner than that in which it was carried out—that inestimable and incredible gentleness regarded human injuries against itself as childish follies, [Col. 0803B] and allowed hands to be stretched out against it by savage and most brutal [Col. 0804A] brigands. Nor did it think deserving of consideration [Note: [Col. 0804B] Thus Sabinus. Others: “to be imputed.”] what their audacity might devise, provided only that it showed its own people what they ought to expect from it.

For since, concerning the dangers of souls, [the text is corrupt: “many things, evils against them, the revealer”], as teacher and author he directed his own laws and ordinances toward the limits of appropriate duties. Did he not crush the arrogance of pride? Did he not extinguish the flames of lust? Did he not close the yawning mouth of greed? Did he not wrench weapons from men’s hands and cut away every seedbed of all viciousness?

Finally, was he himself not gentle, not calm, not easily approached, not familiar in conversation, not grieving over human miseries? Pitying with that unique kindness absolutely everyone afflicted by torments and bodily ailments, did he not return and restore them to health?

[Col. 0805A] [Note: [Col. 0805B]

### LXIV.—“Whom no human being could convict of guilt for any crime”

Christ himself bears witness to this concerning himself in John 8:46: “Which of you convicts me concerning sin?” (*Τίς ἐξ ὑμῶν ἐλέγχει με περὶ ἁμαρτίας;*) ELMENHORST.

“They despoil the votive offerings and plunder the temples.” Literally. Hence Sallust calls an inviolate temple an “unspoiled temple” (*inspoliatum*), or *ἄσυλον*, “a sanctuary,” and Julius Firmicus in countless passages calls plunderers of temples *ἱερόσυλοι*, “temple-robbers.” HERALDUS.

“Who, through proscriptions, exiles, and slaughters,” etc. Heraldus, in his *Second Notes*, and Salmasius, in the Leiden edition, restored the passage very well. Previously it read “and by their own slaughters,” for which Fulvius Ursinus preferred “and by savage slaughters.” ORELLI.

“Who overthrow the chastity of matrons and virgins by licentious violence.” Socrates, book I of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 2, numbers that shameful licentiousness among the tyrannical crimes of Maxentius: “Maxentius cruelly oppressed the Romans, treating them in a tyrannical rather than a royal manner, shamelessly committing adultery with the wives of freeborn men, killing many people, and committing the acts consequent upon these” (*Μαξέντιος δὲ κακῶς τοὺς [Col. 0805C] Ῥωμαίους ἐπέτριβε, τυραννικῷ μᾶλλον ἢ βασιλικῷ τρόπῳ χρώμενος κατ’ αὐτῶν, μοιχεύων ἀναίδην τὰς τῶν ἐλευθέρων γυναῖκας, καὶ πολλοὺς ἀναιρῶν, καὶ ποιῶν τὰ τούτοις ἀκόλουθα*). HERALDUS.

“You call them native gods and deified mortals.” Greek *ἥρωας*, “heroes.” Dio Cassius, book LI, says that Julius Caesar was enrolled by Augustus among the gods and called “the hero Julius” (*ἥρωα Ἰούλιον*), that is, “the deified Julius” (*Divum Julium*). Yet they sometimes called such figures “gods,” not “deified mortals,” and the Greeks often translated Latin *divi* as *θεοί*, “gods.” Lucian, *The Long-Lived*: “Apollodorus the Pergamene, rhetorician of the deified Caesar, teacher of Stephanus” (*Ἀπολλόδωρος δὲ ὁ Περγαμηνεὺς ῥήτωρ θεοῦ Καίσαρος, Στεφανοῦ διδάσκαλος*). HERALDUS.

“With ceremonial couches, altars, temples,” etc.—Prudentius:

> Posterity, following this custom of the ancients  
> In an age now receptive, worshiped Augustus with a month,  
> Shrines, a river, and altars; appeased him with calf and lamb;  
> And lay prostrate before his ceremonial couch.

This honor, therefore, was first bestowed upon Julius, then upon Augustus, and thereafter upon the rest. HERALDUS.

[Col. 0805D] “With games and the celebration of birthdays.” A transposition frequent in Arnobius, for “with the celebration of games and birthdays.” ORELLI. The triumvirs compelled everyone to celebrate Julius Caesar’s birthday—*τὰ γενέσια πάντας ἑορτάζειν*—an honor afterward extended to the other emperors. Dio Cassius, book XLVII. HERALDUS. Exactly so Velleius Paterculus II.68: “the Senate and by the authority of the consul”; see Ruhnken there. OCHSNER.

“They cut into your lives.” Fulvius Ursinus conjectured “your vices,” wrongly. Thus Julius Firmicus, *Astronomy* VIII.7: “They assail the lives of others with the license of bitter speech.” “To cut” is the proper expression for writers of satire. Persius, Satire I.115:

> Lucilius cut into the city—  
> You, Lupus, and you, Mucius—and broke his back tooth upon them.

HERALDUS and ELMENHORST.

“Who transmit to posterity the stains of their own age through the permanence of their writings.” Thus Fulvius Ursinus and Elmenhorst. The construction is: “who transmit the stains”—that is, the disgraces and infamies—“of their own age to posterity through the permanence of their writings.” The manuscript and Roman edition have: “who into the stains of later time … transmit.” But in that form the sentence is incomplete, for it lacks an accusative object to which *prolatant*, “transmit,” can refer. Stewechius reads: “who transmit stains into future time,” etc. Others read “prolong permanence.” ORELLI.

“Who urge that marriages should be held in common.” He censures Plato, who introduces this doctrine in the *Timaeus* and the *Republic*. ELMENHORST.

“Who lie with beautiful boys.” Arnobius appears here to be touching upon Socrates, against whom later writers, especially the Fathers of the Church, brought this charge, as did even pagans—for example, Lucian in *The Sale of Lives*, chapter 15. Compare J. M. Gesner’s little work, *Socrates the Holy Pederast*, and my very dear friend H. Bremi on Cicero, *On Fate*, chapter 5. ORELLI.

“Who declare that you are cattle,” etc. He here glances at certain doctrines of the Stoics. HERALDUS.

“You store them in the secret chambers of libraries.” Not only their books, but also their portraits and statues, as we observed on Martial. HERALDUS. I find that the ancients chiefly placed portraits in five locations: the atrium, entrance, bedroom, picture gallery, and library. Nor were the same kinds found in all of them. In the atrium stood family portraits and waxen likenesses of ancestors, arranged in order. Outside and at the entrance were placed bronze portraits, or portraits made of some other solid material, of those who had been especially illustrious and distinguished. Pliny discusses both kinds in book XXXIV, chapter 2.

In bedrooms were the household gods, and generally the portraits they called “bedroom portraits,” such as those of the people they held most dear. In picture galleries they kept portraits drawn freely rather than from life, or depictions of gods and heroes, or various myths and historical scenes. See Pliny, book XXXV, chapter 3, and Petronius, chapter 83, at the beginning.

There remains the library—Greek *μουσεῖον*, “museum”—in which were placed portraits of learned men, such as philosophers, orators, and poets, some drawn from life and others invented. Pliny in the passage cited and six hundred other authors attest this. Petavius on Synesius, *Praise of Baldness*, Commentary, p. 26. Meursius conjectures *in arcivis*, “in archives,” [Col. 0806D] instead of “in secret chambers.” ORELLI.

“You reward them with chariots and statues.” Namely, with chariot statues, which were erected not only for great heroes and men flourishing in military glory, but sometimes even for indolent and wholly “untrumpeted” men (*ἀσάλπιγκτοι*), such as pleaders. HERALDUS.

“Christ alone you can tear down and rend, if [he is] God; you desire,” etc. Thus the Leiden edition. *Convellere*, “tear down,” derives from Gelenius’s emendation. The manuscript and Roman edition have the corrupt and meaningless *compellere*, “compel.” Theodorus Canterus conjectures *compilare*, “plunder,” or the archaic verb *concipilare*, “seize and plunder.”

Mercerus reads what follows thus: “You can—that is, you dare—to rend him; if it be granted, indeed you desire only, if it be permitted,” etc. Fulvius Ursinus reads: “if you could [rend] God.” Theodorus Canterus: “You can rend him, if you wish,” or “if you wish him.” But nothing should be changed. “You can, if [he is] God” is said for “if you can rend him although he is God.” Above, Arnobius calls Christ God, indeed “the God of the inner powers,” and “God from his innermost root.” ORELLI.

[Col. 0807C] “To chew him with bloodstained mouths.” The precise verb. Lucretius, book IV:

> And as though being chewed by the bite of a panther  
> Or savage lion, they fill the whole place with mighty cries.

Ennius:

> In the woods a vulture was chewing a wretched man.

HERALDUS.]

### LXIV

What, then, drives you, what urges you to curse him, revile him, and pursue irreconcilable enmities against one whom no human being could refute or convict of guilt for any crime?

Your tyrants and kings, who, setting aside fear of the gods, despoil votive offerings and plunder temples; who, through proscriptions, exiles, and slaughters, strip cities of their nobility; who overthrow and wrest away the chastity of matrons and virgins by licentious violence—you call native gods and deified mortals. Those whom it would have been more fitting for you to assail with fiercer hatred you honor with ceremonial couches, altars, temples, and other forms of worship, with games and the celebration of their birthdays.

Moreover, all those who in writings of manifold kinds assail public morals with biting abuse; who cut into, scorch, and tear apart your extravagances and your lives; [Col. 0806A] who transmit to posterity the stains of their own age through the permanence of their writings; who urge that marriages should be held in common; who lie with beautiful, wanton, naked boys; who proclaim that you are cattle, fugitives, exiles, slaves of the vilest mark, mad and insane—you admire and applaud, raising them to the stars of heaven. You store them in the secret chambers of libraries; you reward them with chariots and statues and, so far as lies within your power, endow them with a kind of eternity through the testimony of immortal inscriptions.

Christ alone you can tear down and rend, though he is God; Christ alone, indeed, you desire, if only it were permitted, to chew with bloodstained mouths after the manner of wild beasts, and to swallow down together with his crushed bones.

For what service, pray, or for the guilt of what sin? Tell us: what did he commit that bent aside the course of righteousness and incited you, with the goads of the Furies, to bitter hatred? Was it because he declared that he had been sent by the sole King as guardian of your souls? Because he declared that he was bringing you immortality—the immortality which you are confident that you already possess, persuaded by the merely human assertions of a few men?

Even if you were certain that he spoke falsely and promised utterly vain hopes, I still do not see that you had any reason to hate him or condemn him with hostile punishment. Indeed, if your disposition had been merciful and gentle, for that reason alone you ought to have embraced him: because he promised you desirable [Col. 0807B] and prosperous things; because he was the messenger of good tidings; because he proclaimed things that harmed no one’s mind; indeed, because he filled it with the expectation of greater security [Note: [Col. 0807C] The manuscript has “made [you] more secure.”].

[Note: [Col. 0807C]

### LXV.—“Ready”

Thus Salmasius in the Leiden edition. The manuscript has *privatum*, “private.” Fulvius Ursinus conjectures *pronum*, “inclined.” ORELLI.

“You would nevertheless entrust yourselves.” A characteristic expression. Below, book II: “You entrust bodily illnesses to the hands of physicians.” Aulus Gellius, book I, chapter 15: “And so you hear them, but do not listen to them, as though to a drug-seller. For his words are heard, but no one entrusts himself to him when he is sick.” [Col. 0807D] HERALDUS.

Shone forth. Elegantly, like a flame suddenly bursting out. See Barth, *Adversaria*, book VI, chapter 5, p. 265. So too *relucessere* (“shone forth again”). Grattius, *Cynegetica*, v. 7:

> From this came every aid to life, and the right  
> Order shone forth again.

And Claudian, *On the Consulship of Stilicho*, book III, v. 64:

> Here, Stilicho, unexpected safety shone forth again for all,  
> When you were victorious. ORELLI.

*What inhumanity is so great?* Thus the Leiden editor, following Meursius’ emendation. Others read: “and so great an inhumanity.” ORELLI.

*The announcer of a gift and bearer of so great a thing.* Thus *portitor* (“bearer”) was already used in that age after this model. In this way St. Jerome calls letter-carriers *portitores litterarum*, whom elsewhere he calls *bajuli* (“bearers”). Papias: “*Bajulus*: a carrier, bearer, porter, nurse.” HERALDUS.—Compare Barth, *Adversaria*, book LIII, chapter 8, p. 2492; Savaron on Sidonius, book VI, epistle 4, p. 390, who cites a host of examples from writers of later Latin [Col. 0808C]; and J. F. Gronovius, *Observationes*, book III, chapter 20. The “gift” mentioned here is the proclamation of salvation and the preaching of truth. ORELLI.

*With ruins.* Scriverius preferred *runis*, “with darts” (*runa, -ae*, a kind of missile; see Festus), and not without reason, in the manner of Ennius’ line:

> The spearmen scatter spears; an iron rain arises.

But Cicero spoke similarly in book III of *On the Laws*: “Did not Gaius Gracchus, with the ruins and those knives which he himself said he had thrown into the Forum so that the citizens might fight one another, completely transform the condition of the republic?” And Seneca, Epistle IX: “How much more admirable is this man, who passed unharmed and uninjured through steel, ruins, and fires.” MEURSIUS, p. 37.—Thus *ruinae* here means stones, the rubble of demolished buildings. ORELLI.

*Who not only inflicted no evil upon no one.* Meursius prefers *ulli*, “upon anyone.” But Vechner, *Hellenolexicon*, chapter 35, p. 381, Heusinger’s edition, provides many examples of a double negative which does not affirm but, in Greek fashion, negates more emphatically. ORELLI.

*But equally kind to speak to enemies*, etc. This is the reading of the manuscript, rashly altered by Gelenius and F. Ursinus to: “but, equally kind, taught everyone”; that is, “was equally kind.” *Kind to speak* is a very common Graecism, πραῢς τὸ λέγειν, “gentle in speaking.” There is therefore no need to read *diceret*, “would speak,” with the Leiden editor. If anything must be changed, I should prefer *dixerit*, “spoke,” because *intulerit*, “inflicted,” precedes; or, with Stewechius on book II, chapter 1, *edixerit*, “declared fully.” The parchment glosses say: “*edicit*—he says the whole of it, or says it openly; hence *edictum*.” Nor should *hostibus*, “to enemies,” be changed to *omnibus*, “to everyone.” Arnobius seems to have had in mind those words of St. Paul to the Colossians 1:21: Καὶ ὑμᾶς ποτε ὄντας ἀπηλλοτριωμένους καὶ ἐχθροὺς τῇ διανοίᾳ ἐν τοῖς ἔργοις τοῖς πονηροῖς, νυνὶ δὲ ἀποκατήλλαξεν ἐν τῷ σώματι τῆς σαρκὸς αὐτοῦ διὰ τοῦ θανάτου, παραστῆσαι ὑμᾶς ἁγίους καὶ ἀμώμους καὶ ἀνεγκλήτους κατενώπιον αὐτοῦ: “And you, who were once alienated and enemies in mind through evil works, he has now reconciled in the body of his flesh through death, in order to present you holy, blameless, and irreproachable before him.” ORELLI.

[Col. 0810A] *His man.* That is, the man whom he had put on and assumed. See the notes on chapter 62. ORELLI.

*From the events that followed.* That is, from his resurrection. ORELLI.]

### LXV

O ungrateful [Note: [Col. 0807C] Canter transferred this passage, together with what follows on the next two pages [Col. 0808C], to the beginning of book II. The edition of Sabaeus and the manuscript condemn that transposition, as Stewechius observes.] and impious age! O age prepared for your own destruction by an incredible obstinacy of heart! If some physician had come to you from remote regions never known to you, promising a medicine of such a kind that it would ward off from your bodies absolutely every form of disease and ill health, would you not all run eagerly to him? Would you not receive him within your familiar walls, cherishing him with every kindness and honor? Would you not wish [Col. 0808A] that kind of medicine to be entirely certain and genuine, since it promised that you would remain free from such innumerable afflictions of the body to the utmost limits of life? And although the matter was uncertain, you would nevertheless entrust yourselves to him, nor would you hesitate to drink an unknown potion when the hope of health was set before you and you were inflamed with love of well-being.

Christ shone forth and appeared as the announcer of a matter of the greatest importance, bearing a favorable omen and a saving proclamation for believers. What is this cruelty, this so great inhumanity—or rather, to speak more truly, this disdainful arrogance—that you not only tear apart with verbal curses the announcer of a gift and bearer of so great a thing, but also persecute him with grievous warfare, with every discharge of missiles, and with stones from ruins? Do the things he says displease you, and are they heard by you with offense? [Col. 0808B] Count them as ridiculous prophecies. Does he speak the most foolish things and promise senseless gifts? Laugh at him, as the wise men you are, and leave his folly to wallow in its own errors.

What is this savagery—to repeat what has so often been said—what is this executioner-like lust to declare an implacable war upon one who has done nothing to deserve it from you? To desire, if the opportunity were given, to tear through the entrails of one who not only inflicted no evil upon anyone, but, equally kind even to enemies, spoke of what salvation was being brought to them from God the sovereign; of what had to be done so that they might escape destruction and obtain an immortality unknown to them? And when the novelty of the matter and the unheard-of promise [Col. 0809A] disturbed the minds of his hearers and made their belief hesitate, the Lord of all powers and destroyer of death itself permitted the man he had assumed to be put to death, so that from the events that followed they might know that the hopes concerning the salvation of their souls, which they had long since received, were secure [Col. 0810A], and that they could avoid the peril of death in no other way.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0809]

## INDEX OF CHAPTERS

[Col. 0809B] Arnobius asks the pagans why, after all, they hate Christ—who was guilty of no offense against them—so greatly that, merely upon hearing his name, they immediately blaze up with anger. Yet even if he were believed unworthy of anyone’s trust, he should at least not have been despised, because he showed everyone the way to heaven. Chapter 1.

The author answers the pagans when they reply that they pursue him with the utmost hatred because he abolished all worship of the gods. Chapters 2–3.

He shows that the pagans have absolutely no justification for disbelieving Christ’s words on the ground that he does not prove to us that he will ever actually give what he promises. For there are many by no means uncertain proofs of the things Christ has promised; and since these are readily available, there is no reason to doubt the fulfillment of the other things he has also promised. Chapters 4–5.

He checks the pagans’ boastfulness, since they gloried that they alone were adorned with wisdom and knowledge, while regarding all others throughout the whole world who had pledged themselves to Christ—even those endowed with great ability—as dull, obtuse, and foolish. Chapters 6–7.

There was therefore no reason for the pagans, who were no more learned than others, to reproach Christians for believing their divine teacher. For no undertaking at all is begun without prior faith. The pagans themselves believed the opinions of philosophers, who nevertheless advance nothing certain or established concerning the first principles of things and other matters, but are always fighting among themselves. Chapters 8–10.

Arnobius consequently concludes that it is more reasonable to believe Christ, who confirmed his teaching by such great miracles, than philosophers, however praiseworthy for moral integrity and wisdom, who could never perform anything even remotely similar. Chapter 11.

And certainly, if Christ had employed merely human arguments, no one would have trusted him; yet very many were compelled to do so because of the miracles performed by him and his disciples—performed, I say, everywhere in East and West, and especially at Rome, where Simon Magus is reported to have been cast down by Peter from high in the air to the ground. Chapter 12.

What more need be said? The faith of Christians certainly ought not to have been harassed by the pagans but praised by them, because Christians shared with the leading philosophers their opinions concerning God, the resurrection of bodies, the salvation of souls, and the future punishments of the impious, although the philosophers explained them differently from Christians. Chapters 13–14.

Arnobius takes this opportunity to explain the nature of our soul, the source from which it proceeds, and why it becomes subject to various passions and vices. He then refutes those who declared that our soul shares the same immortality and nature as God. Chapters 14–16.

“But the human soul is divine,” they said, “because man surpasses the other animals in reason.” “That would be entirely correct,” Arnobius replies, “if man always made good use of this reason of his.” Then, in answering certain objections, he sets forth and dispels common opinions concerning the excellence of the human soul. Chapters 17–18.

He continues to demonstrate that human souls are neither divine nor did they fly down from heaven into this world instructed in all knowledge; and from this falls that doctrine of certain philosophers according to which they imagined that the things we learn are recollections. Chapter 19.

He further proves by other considerations that this conjecture is false, especially by proposing the hypothesis of a child born in a most desolate and inaccessible wilderness and reared there in complete silence by a mute nurse. Chapters 20–21.

From this he plainly concludes that the human soul did not enter the world instructed in all knowledge. Chapters 22–23.

Arnobius then clearly refutes Plato’s contrary argument drawn from questioning a boy about numbers. Chapters 24–25.

He disposes of the objection of those who say that when the soul is joined to the body it forgets its former knowledge and, as they put it, changes from learned to elementary. Chapters 26–27.

He treats the same argument further. Chapter 28.

From what has been discussed, the author concludes that common man, utterly destitute as he is, should not be assigned to the first—that is, the divine—order, nor should the same immortality be attributed to him as to God. Chapters 29–30.

By the same reasoning Arnobius attacks the contrary opinion of Epicurus, who babbled that the human soul is mortal. Our author then maintains that the soul is a substance of an intermediate nature between the mortal and the divine. Chapters 30–34.

When the pagans press the question of how the soul can become immortal if it possesses that intermediate quality, Arnobius satisfies their objection. Chapters 35–36.

He then demonstrates that our soul was indeed created by some power of the lowest order, but is neither of divine offspring nor a daughter of the supreme God. Nor does the author permit it to be objected against him that the world would be imperfect without man, and that God therefore sent into the human body each individual soul begotten from himself. Chapters 36–38.

By a long induction he attempts to show that man was created not to complete the world—which could indeed exist without him—but for man’s own private benefit. From these considerations he concludes that the soul, supposedly sent by God into some body at a later time, is not divine. Chapters 39–43.

“But,” they say, “it came into the world by its own will, not at God’s command.” Arnobius answers this objection. Chapters 44–46.

The pagans pressed him by asking from what source the soul was begotten or brought forth. Arnobius replies to them, first, that we know this much: it is neither divine nor the offspring of God, since nothing could ever have been made by the supreme God unless it was perfect in every respect. He then adds that we know for certain that human beings are nothing other than souls bound to bodies, which are corrupted by every kind of vice. Chapters 47–48.

There are indeed some persons of excellent character, but these are assuredly very few. And what human beings are perfect? Therefore the human soul is not divine. Chapters 49–50.

Nor is there any reason for the pagans to laugh if we deny that we know how it was created. For if they think Plato rightly asserted that souls were created not by the supreme God but by certain lesser powers, why should we not be permitted to assert, with much greater certainty, that they possess an intermediate quality, though they may nevertheless be endowed with immortality by God? Chapters 51–53.

Nor should you say that absolutely nothing occurs without God’s will, or inquire too curiously whence evils arise and why God permits them. This alone must be held as certain: nothing evil, defective, or harmful is done by the true God, nor anything that is not beneficial to all and filled with the greatest love. Chapters 54–55.

No one should be surprised at our ignorance concerning so many other matters. For who does not know that human disputes about every subject are so extensive that nothing is asserted by one person which cannot immediately be demolished by another? Chapters 56–57.

Although Christians therefore did not know by whom and from what source the human soul was created, the pagans could accomplish nothing against them on that account, since far more things were unknown to the pagans themselves. Chapters 58–59.

Christ, the true God, therefore rightly spoke beneath a human form and commands us, leaving all questions aside, to be raised with our whole mind toward the Lord of all things. Although he cannot be comprehended, nevertheless no one but a madman doubts that he alone is God. Savage torments after death therefore await the pagans who do not acknowledge him. Chapters 60–62.

When the pagans press the question of what, then, became of the souls of those who died before Christ’s advent, and why all souls were not endowed with equal generosity, Arnobius replies, first, that divine benefits were equally poured out upon all; and second, that God equally calls everyone and has given everyone the ability to come to him, but imposes necessity upon no one. Chapters 63–64.

He explains why God does not compel unwilling people to believe his promises; then he shows that Christians alone obtain salvation through the aid and assistance of Christ, to whom this power was granted by God the Father. Chapter 65.

He passes to the pagans’ old complaint that the Christian religion was new and that ancient ancestral rites ought not to be exchanged for barbarous and foreign ones. Chapters 66–68.

Even if the Christian religion had been recently established, did not all human affairs—and especially, as the pagans themselves admitted, their gods—have a beginning? Chapters 69–70.

Therefore, if the Christian religion did not exist four hundred years ago, the pagans likewise could not deny that two thousand years ago none of their gods existed. In the end, the authority of a religion must be evaluated not by its age but by its divinity. Chapter 71.

Arnobius next demolishes the objection by which the pagans alleged that their religion was much older than Christianity and therefore truer. Chapters 72–73.

He answers the pagans themselves when they ask why Christ was sent by God so late. Chapters 74–75.

He satisfies the same people when they ask why the God whom Christians served allowed them to be afflicted and oppressed by every kind of persecution and punishment. Chapters 76–78.

[Note: [Col. 0811D]

### I—*If you consider it no insult to give some answer when questioned.*

For it does not appear entirely proper to question superiors and masters. Salvian, Epistle III: “Dearest fathers, most reverend fathers, we ask that we may be permitted to question you.” By contrast, proud men swollen with arrogance were accustomed to answer hesitantly or not at all. Cicero to Trebatius [Col. 0812D], book VII, epistle 16: “Those who come from your part of the world complain of your arrogance, because they say that you do not answer those who question you.” The same author, *Tusculan Disputations* I.8: “M. What? If I ask you something, will you not answer?—A. That would indeed be arrogant; but unless it is necessary, I prefer that you not ask.” HERALDUS and ELMENHORST.

[Col. 0813B] *Explain it to us and tell us.* See above, on book I, chapter 57. For *dicite*, “tell,” Stewechius thinks *edicite* should be read, that is: “tell clearly, openly, and fully; leave nothing unspoken”—*saget’s heraus* (“say it outright”). See on book I, final chapter. ORELLI.

*Or what offenses of his you retain.* That is, “you remember, hold in memory.” Below in this book: “Because you retain in memory the Lucilian arch and the Marsyas of Pomponius under seal”; and in book VII: “The gods,” he says, “are honored by these things, and if they retain any memories of offenses offered to them by human beings, they cast them aside.” So too κατέχειν, “retain,” among the Greeks; Lycophron: δεῖπνον οὐδὲν τοιοῦτο κατέχω δεδειπνηκώς, “I remember having eaten no such meal.” HERALDUS.

*Swollen with the haughty brow of arrogance.* See above, on book I, chapter 38. ORELLI.

*Injuries and insults.* Nonius: “An injury differs from an insult in this respect: an injury is a less serious matter.” Pacuvius: “I bear an injury easily if it is free of insult.” See Theophilus, *Institutes of Law*, book IV, chapter 3, περὶ ὕβρεως, “On Outrage.” ELMENHORST.—The Stoics maintain the contrary; for example, Seneca, Epistle 72, and in the book *That Injury Does Not Befall the Wise Man*, chapter 4. HERALDUS.

*Everywhere without any distinctions of person.* In these final words he explains what he had meant by “everywhere.” Thus *passim sine delectu*, “everywhere without selection,” occurs jointly several times in the body of Roman law. HERALDUS.—For what follows, Fulvius Ursinus corrects: “without any distinctions among persons.” ORELLI.

[Col. 0813D] *Who, even if he were not worthy of your having to listen to him.* Wopkensius, on Dictys of Crete IV.15, in *Miscellaneae Observationes Novae*, vol. II, p. 79, observes prolixity—μακρολογία—in these words, citing a very similar passage below, book V, chapter 27, at the end: “And the matter is altogether worthy of causing the gods utterly to abolish the entire race of mortals.” ORELLI.

*Should wish immortality for you.* These words are obscure, and I think them corrupt. I believe one should read: *et portas immortalitatis apertaret*, “and should open the gates of immortality.” Thus, shortly afterward: “Who opened the doors of piety to human beings who were blind and truly living in impiety.” *Apertare* would thus be formed like *opertare* in Festus. HERALDUS.—Meursius prefers *aptaret*, “should provide.” But nothing should be changed. *Vota immortalitatis optaret* means “should wish immortality for you, should seek it from God the Father by prayer.” Similarly Pliny, *Letters* X.20: “When the provincials had chosen me as their advocate against Marius Priscus,” that is, had requested me from the Senate. Arnobius has in view, unless I am mistaken, those words of Christ in John 17:24. ORELLI.

[Col. 0814B] *Even if he had not extended the light of life to all and removed the danger of ignorance.* These words, previously placed in a wholly inappropriate location—namely, above, after the words “inflicted everywhere without any distinctions of person”—were rightly transferred by Heraldus to the end of the chapter. The sense is: even if he had not extended the light of life to all, etc. [Col. 0814C], nevertheless he should not have been despised by you for this reason, that he showed you saving counsels, etc. Fulvius Ursinus should therefore not be followed when he conjectures *praetenderet . . . amoveret*, “were to extend . . . were to remove.” For *ignorationis*, “of ignorance,” Meursius, *Criticus*, p. 49, suspects that *interitionis*, “of destruction,” should be read. So our author in book VII: “Close to wild and savage beasts, he troubles those who endure with storms and leads them into the danger of destruction.” ORELLI.]

### I

If any opportunity could be granted in this place, I should like, briefly turning aside from the principal defense I have undertaken, to exchange the following words with all those to whom the name of Christ is hateful.

If you consider it no [Col. 0813A] insult to give some answer when questioned, explain it to us and tell us: what matter, what reason is there for your assailing Christ with such grievous wars? Or what offenses of his do you retain in memory, that at the mention of his name you boil over with the blazing passions of rabid hearts? Did he, claiming royal power for himself, occupy the whole world with fiercely hostile legions, destroy and eliminate some nations which had been peaceful from the beginning, and compel others to obey him after their necks had been placed beneath the yoke? Did he, burning with the fires of greed, claim as the chattel of his own possession all those riches with which the human race eagerly strives to fill itself? [Note: [Col. 0813B] “For his possession, as his property.” Fulvius.] Did he, exulting in lustful desires, violently break through the barriers of chastity or secretly lay snares for the marriages of others? Did he, swollen with the haughty brow of arrogance [Col. 0813B], inflict injuries and insults everywhere without any distinctions of person?

Even if he were not worthy of your having to listen to and believe him, he should at least not have been despised by you for the very reason that he showed you saving things, pointed out to you the paths to heaven, and wished immortality for you. Even if he had not extended the light of life to everyone and removed the danger of ignorance?

[Note: [Col. 0814C]

### II—*Who introduced true religion in the world.*

The Leiden edition reads “into the world.” But nothing should be changed. See above on book I, chapter 42. ORELLI.

*A religion more serviceable.* That is, one which more effectively serves the interests of the human race. So below, chapter 8: “Not believing that their chaste marriages and dutiful covenant toward their husbands would endure.” ORELLI.

*And is the source, and likewise the founder and creator, of perpetual things.* “Perpetual things,” that is, eternal things which will never perish. But I confess that I suspect a corruption in this passage. For not all things created by God are eternal and perpetual. I therefore read: “and is the perpetual source, and likewise the founder and creator, of all things.” Unless perhaps Arnobius expressed in these words the words of Paul in Hebrews 1:2, δι’ οὗ καὶ τοὺς αἰῶνας ἐποίησε, “through whom he also made the ages”—that is, this universe—having misunderstood them. ORELLI.

*Are watered with vital motion.* See above, on book I, chapter 55. ORELLI.

*Set up a boy as judge.* I did not hesitate to admit into the text this most felicitous emendation, which Heraldus proposed in his *Second Thoughts* and which accords perfectly with the following word *dubitabit*, “will doubt.” All editions read *da verum judicium*, “give a true judgment,” a phrase whose corruption Heraldus alone perceived. In his own edition he conjectured either *da naturae judicium*, “give the judgment of nature,” or *da verum animae judicium*, “give the soul’s true judgment,” as though the discussion here concerned the testimony of the soul, about which Tertullian wrote a separate book. Meursius conjectures *ad verum judicium*, “toward a true judgment.” But I greatly prefer *da*—that is, “set up, imagine for yourself”—“a boy as judge.” ORELLI.

[Col. 0815C] *And, as though he saw us, we raise our face to heaven.* Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter XVII: “Finally, when pronouncing these words, he looks not toward the Capitol but toward heaven. For he knows the dwelling place of the living God; from him and from there he descended.” HERALDUS.]

### II

“But he deserves hatred because he expelled religions from the world and forbade people to approach the worship of the gods.” Is he, then, charged as the destroyer of religion and the author of impiety who introduced true religion into the world? Who opened the doors of piety to human beings who were blind and truly living in impiety, and showed them the one to whom they should submit themselves?

Is there any religion truer, more serviceable, more powerful, or more just than to know God the sovereign, to know how to supplicate God the sovereign, who alone is the head and source of all good things and likewise the founder and creator of perpetual things; by whom all earthly and all heavenly things are animated and watered with vital motion; and without whom there would assuredly exist no thing bearing any name or substance?

Unless perhaps you doubt whether this one of whom we speak is the ruler, and believe rather that Apollo, Diana, Mercury, and Mars exist. Set up a boy as judge: as he surveys all these things which we see, he will sooner doubt whether the other gods exist than hesitate [Col. 0815A] concerning God, whose existence we all know naturally—whether when we exclaim, “O God!” or when we appoint him as witness against the wicked and, as though he saw us, raise our face to heaven.

[Note: [Col. 0815C]

### III—*But if elevation of mind and what the Greeks call typhus did not obstruct*, etc.

*Typhus*: τύφος—ἀλαζονεία, ἔπαρσις, κενοδοξία, “pretension, arrogance, vainglory”—occurs very frequently in Arnobius. See below, chapters 12, 19, 29, and 63 of this book. It is no less frequent in other later writers; for example, Augustine, *City of God* XI, penultimate chapter: “the one enjoying God, the other swollen with *typhus*.” ORELLI.

*What or why he forbade to be done.* We have already observed that in these writers disjunctive particles very frequently occur in place of conjunctive ones. HERALDUS.]

### III

“But he forbade human beings to supplicate the lesser gods.” Do you know who these lesser gods are, or where they are? Has even a suspicion or mention of them ever grazed you, so that you rightly take offense that worship has been withdrawn from them and they have been deprived of the bestowal of honor?

But if elevation of mind and what the Greeks call *typhus* (τύφος, “arrogant delusion”) did not obstruct and hinder you, you could long ago have learned what he forbade to be done, and why; within what limits he wished true religion to stand; how great a danger would arise for you from what you regarded as obedience; and from what evils you would emerge if you renounced your treacherous [Col. 0815B] error.

[Note: [Col. 0815C]

### IV—*When we have been carried altogether farther.*

Stewechius conjectures that *ulterius prorsius* should be read, taking *prorsius* from *prorsus, -a, -um*; hence *limites prorsi*, “forward boundaries,” in Festus. *Prorsum* means “turned onward, forward,” and is opposed to *rursum*, “backward.” Terence combines both in *Hecyra* III.1.35:

> I perceive a commotion, a running back and forth.

But although examples of *prorsus* used adjectivally occur in the older writers, the comparative *prorsior, -us* is entirely unattested; formations founded on no example should not be admitted. Moreover, *prorsus*, as an adverb of place meaning “onward” (see Festus), already contains a comparative force. ORELLI.

*But from the worst robbers.* Arnobius means false teachers, of whom Christ says in Matthew 7:15: Προσέχετε δὲ ἀπὸ τῶν ψευδοπροφητῶν, οἵτινες ἔρχονται πρὸς ὑμᾶς ἐν ἐνδύμασι προβάτων, ἔσωθεν δὲ εἰσὶ λύκοι ἅρπαγες: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves.” ORELLI.

*Impending and not yet void.* That is, not yet vain or ineffectual—κενά, “empty.” So very often in Tertullian and other ecclesiastical writers; for example, Minucius Felix, chapter 12: “How the empty hopes of a futile promise deceive you” [Col. 0816C] (where see Ouzel, p. 117, Gronovius’ edition).
