A little later: “If what is said to be impending should prove void and empty.” Below, chapter 12: “Or who would listen to one boasting of void and naked things?” Cujacius reads *passa*, interpreting it as “past,” but without precedent. HERALDUS.

*That is, the loss of salvation.* Meursius, p. 50, believes these words should be removed as a gloss and enclosed in brackets. ORELLI.]

### IV

But all these matters will be recounted more clearly and plainly when we have been carried altogether farther. For we shall show that Christ did not teach impiety to the nations, but rescued the ignorance of wretched human beings from the worst robbers.

“We do not believe,” you say, “that the things he says are true.” Why? Are the things which you deny to be true clear and established among you, when things still impending and not yet void cannot be refuted by any arguments?

“But he himself does not prove what he promises.” So it is. For, as I have said, no confirmation of future things can exist. Since, therefore, the condition of future things is such that they cannot be held or grasped by the touch of any anticipation, is it not the sounder reasoning, of two uncertainties suspended in doubtful expectation, to believe rather that which bears some hope than that which bears absolutely none? For in the former there is no danger if what is said to be impending should prove void and empty; in the latter there is the greatest loss—that is, the loss of salvation—if, when the time arrives, it is revealed that the statement was no lie.

[Note: [Col. 0816C]

### V—*Do not even these at least furnish you with grounds for belief?*

Although Arnobius sometimes links several expressions signifying one and the same thing, I nevertheless cannot persuade myself that the words “grounds for belief” are genuine. And the explanation is surely this: someone had written in the margin of his copy, “Grounds for belief.” For here are proposed arguments by which the Christian faith can be affirmed. HERALDUS.

*The solemn pledges of this immense name have been spread abroad.* [Col. 0816D] A little later in this same chapter: “to surrender the solemn pledges of saving military service.” Those who consecrated themselves to Christ are, of course, very often compared by ecclesiastical writers to soldiers who renounce father, mother, and every relative. Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*, chapter 11: “Do we believe that a human military oath may be superimposed upon the divine, that one may answer to another master after Christ and renounce father, mother, and every relative, whom even the law commands us to honor and to love next to God?” The same author, *To the Martyrs*, chapter 3: “We were called into the service of the living God at the very time when we pledged ourselves to the words of the sacrament.” Lactantius, book V, chapter 11: “He became a traitor to the sacrament he had received.” Compare Lipsius on Tacitus, *Annals* XV, and Stewechius on Vegetius, *On Military Matters* II.5, pp. 115 following, Wesel edition. HERALDUS, ELMENHORST, and ORELLI.

*Which, turned by love of him, has not.* Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “which, turned after his manner, has not.” Not a bad conjecture, certainly; but nothing should be changed. ORELLI.

*They seek these teachings.* That is, they seek to use the Christian religion as their teacher. On the force of the word *magisterium*, see Casaubon on Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 2, p. 179, Burmann’s edition. ORELLI.

*Whatever they may have decided.* Thomas Canter reads “whatever they may have decided upon.” But nothing should be changed: *quibus* here means “however great, of whatever kind,” as often. See Heinsius on Phaedrus, fable I.13. Fulvius Ursinus reads and punctuates the entire passage thus: “Slaves prefer to be afflicted by their masters with every torture they may have appointed; wives prefer to be released from their marriages.” ORELLI.

*Is roused to zeal for believing by the very spurs of prohibition.* [Col. 0817C] Similarly Tertullian, at the end of the *Apologeticus*: “Yet even your most exquisite cruelty accomplishes nothing; it is rather an enticement to our sect. We become more numerous whenever we are mown down by you: the blood of Christians is seed.” Compare the same author, *To Scapula*, chapter 4; Lactantius, book V, chapter 13; Minucius Felix, *Octavius*; Leo, Sermon 1 on Saints Peter and Paul. ELMENHORST.

*Or do you perhaps believe that these things occur indiscriminately and without cause?* That is, rashly and fortuitously, without selection—εἰκῇ, “at random.” Lactantius, book III, chapter 9: “When Anaxagoras was asked for what purpose he had been born, he replied, ‘To see the sun and heaven.’ Everyone admires this utterance and judges it worthy of a philosopher. But I think that, unable to find an answer, he poured this out at random rather than remain silent.” HERALDUS.—Compare Bünemann on Lactantius, book I, and Burmann on Phaedrus, Fables V.1.3, p. 238. So Quintilian, *Declamations* IV.13: “Do you believe that these things were arranged indiscriminately and by chance?” ORELLI.

*The executioner-hooks.* Others read “the executioner’s hooks.” But Arnobius uses *carnifex*, “executioner,” adjectivally, above in book I, the final chapter [Col. 0817D]: “What lust is so executioner-like?” The best writers do likewise. Horace, *Odes* I.15: “adulterous hair.” Tibullus I.11.46: “plowman oxen.” Silius XIII.375: “warrior sword.” See Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* II, p. 110. By “hooks” we should understand those two-pronged iron claws—or rather talons—which the ancients heated until glowing and used to torture and lacerate accused persons placed upon the rack. Prudentius, περὶ Στεφάνων (*On the Crowns*), hymn on Vincent the Martyr, vv. 173 following:

> He speaks these words, and once again  
> Is torn by screeching hooks.

See Maternus de Cilano, *Römische Alterthümer* (*Roman Antiquities*), who treats extensively of ancient Roman torture, and Joannes Durantius Caselius, *Variae* I.15, in Gruter, *Lampas Critica*, vol. III, part II, p. 211. ORELLI.

*As though seized by a certain sweetness and by love of all virtues*, etc. Gelenius reads: “As though drunk with a certain sweetness and nectar, they despise all things,” etc. Since the final words are found neither in the manuscript nor in the first Roman edition, Canter thinks Gelenius added them himself. And indeed the threefold repetition of *atque*, “and,” would be extremely disagreeable. ORELLI.

*Known reasons.* The same as what he called “grounds for belief” above. Fulvius prefers “unknown reasons.” ORELLI.

*Assent of belief.* *Credulitas*, “belief,” is used here and below, chapter 12, in a favorable sense for faith, as often in these writers. ORELLI.]

### V

What are you saying, O ignorant people, most worthy even of tears and pity? Are you not terrified that perhaps the things you despise and that furnish you with material for laughter are true? Do you not at least turn it over within yourselves, in the obscurity of your thoughts, lest a later time refute what you now stubbornly refuse to believe through your perversity [Col. 0816B], and irrevocable repentance punish you?

Do not even these at least furnish you with grounds for belief: that in so brief and short a time the solemn pledges of this immense name have already been spread throughout every land? That there is now no nation of such barbarous customs and so ignorant of gentleness that, transformed by love of him, it has not softened its harshness and, assuming tranquility, passed over into peaceful sentiments? That orators, grammarians, rhetoricians, legal experts, and physicians endowed with such great abilities—even those who investigate the secrets of philosophy—seek these teachings, despising the things in which they trusted shortly before? That slaves prefer to be afflicted by their masters [Note: [Col. 0815B] “By masters.” Fulvius.] with whatever tortures they may have decided upon [Col. 0817A], wives to be released from their marriages, and children to be disinherited by their parents, rather than break the Christian faith and surrender the solemn pledges of saving military service? That although you have set before those who follow the laws of this religion so many kinds of punishments, the movement increases all the more, and the people struggle more courageously against every threat and prohibition that inspires fear, and are roused to zeal for believing by the very spurs of prohibition?

Do you perhaps [Note: [Col. 0817B] “Or do you perhaps,” manuscript and Leiden edition.] believe that these things occur indiscriminately and without cause, and that these minds are seized by fortuitous impulses? Can it really be that this is not divine and sacred, or that such great conversions of their minds occur without God, so that although executioner-hooks and innumerable other tortures, as we have said, hang over [Note: [Col. 0817B] “May hang over.” Fulvius.] those who will believe, yet, as though seized by a certain sweetness and by love of all virtues, they accept known reasons and prefer friendship with Christ to all the things of the world [Col. 0817B]? [Note: [Col. 0817B] “Set before.” Sabaeus. Wrongly.] Unless perhaps those who now throughout the whole world agree and unite in assenting to this belief appear dull and foolish [Col. 0818A] to you.

[Note: [Col. 0818B] [The supplied source breaks off here.]

### VI.—“What then? Are you alone, stored away in wisdom and by the sheer power of intelligence, able to see some other, profound thing?”

I approve Stewechius’s conjecture: “What? Are you, then, alone, stored away in wisdom and by the sheer power of intelligence, able to see something deeper and more profound?” See the interpreters on Festus under the words *altum* and *profundum*. For *conditi* I read, with Oudendorp on Apuleius, book I, p. 8, *conditae*, that is, “stored away,” namely in literary studies. For one can scarcely say in Latin that a drunken man is “seasoned with wine” (*vino conditus*). For *mera*, Meursius in the Appendix prefers *in ea re*, “in that matter.” ORELLI.

**“Whence comes so much keenness and quickness?”** Here *vivacitas* means vigor and swiftness of intellect—our *Witz*. ORELLI.

**“Or to recognize it when it is unadorned.”** I would prefer to read: “Or when it is unstructured.” For properly speaking, unstructured expressions are opposed to rhythmical ones. Cicero, *On the Orator*, book III: “And Isocrates is said to have been the first to establish the practice of binding the unstructured mode of speech employed by the ancients into rhythms, for the sake of pleasure and of the ears.” HERALDUS.—Nothing should be changed. For Arnobius contrasts unadorned speech not with rhythmical speech, but with composed speech—that is, with the artful and elegant arrangement and disposition of words. The opposite of *incomptus* is *horridus*. See Cicero, *On the Orator* I.11; Quintilian, *Institutes* X.1.44; and, for an extensive discussion of this word, J. Ch. Th. Ernesti in the *Lexicon of Latin Rhetorical Terminology*, under *Compositio* and *Compositus*. ORELLI.

**“The *Brothel* of Lucilius.”** *Fornix* seems to have been the title of an unidentified book of Lucilius’s satires, apparently of an obscene subject. For *fornix* means the same as *lupanar*, “brothel.” Isidore, *Origins*, book X, p. 1075, in Godfrey’s edition of the *Authors on the Latin Language*: “A male or female fornicator is one whose body is public and common. Such women used to prostitute themselves beneath arches, places that are called *fornices*.” From this arose the later Latin words *fornicare* and *fornicatio*. See Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under *fornix*, and Oudendorp on Apuleius, p. 465. Thus Horace, *Satires* I.2.30: “standing in the stinking brothel.” Instead of *Lucilianum*, Meursius thinks *Caecilianum* should be read. But, so far as I know, no comedy of Caecilius with this title is cited by the ancients. Scriverius, in the same Meursius, p. 51, conjectures *Licinianum*. ORELLI.

**“The *Marsyas* of Pomponius.”** Two poets named Pomponius are celebrated: one is Lucius Pomponius of Bononia, the earliest author of Atellan farces—“celebrated for his ideas, rough in his language, and commendable for the novelty of the work he invented,” as Velleius Paterculus says; the other is Lucius Pomponius Secundus, a tragic poet and most distinguished citizen in the times of the emperors Gaius and Claudius, frequently mentioned by Seneca, Pliny, and Tacitus. I think the epigrammatist whom Varro names (*On the Latin Language*, book VI, p. 86, Bipont edition) was different from both. Perhaps the poem *Marsyas*, which Arnobius marks as indecent, should be attributed to him. It seems to have dealt with nocturnal debaucheries and the various forms of lust for which the statue of the god Marsyas was infamous. That statue stood in the most frequented part of the Forum, where lawsuits were conducted. Seneca, *On Benefits*, book VI, chapter 32, speaking of Julia, Augustus’s daughter: “After ranging throughout the city in nocturnal revels, she chose the Forum itself and the rostra—from which her father had promulgated the law against adultery—as the scene of her debaucheries; she made a daily gathering at the Marsyas and, transformed from an adulteress into a prostitute, sought the right to every kind of license under an unknown adulterer.” See Popma on the cited passage of Varro, p. 190, Bipont edition.

For my part, I do not see why that *Marsyas* should be denied to Pomponius, the writer of Atellan farces. Varro cites an epigram by Papinius, not Pomponius—the latter name being Scaliger’s conjecture—and I infer from Cicero, *Letters* IX.16, that those Atellan plays were of an especially obscene subject and corresponded to the Greeks’ satyric drama. Moreover, the title *Marsyas* itself seems to indicate a work of some length. That Pomponius, whom Arnobius appears to associate with his contemporary Lucilius, flourished in Sulla’s time, in the year 666 from the founding of the city. See Velleius Paterculus II.9 and Eusebius, *Chronicle*, at Olympiad 173.1. ORELLI.

**“What the constitutions are in lawsuits.”** Rhetoricians differ in their definition of *constitutions*. Cicero, *On Invention* I.8, generally calls a *constitution* the question from which the case arises. In the *Topics*, however, chapter 25, he says: “The rebuttal of an accusation, in which the charge is repelled, is called *stasis* (στάσις) in Greek and *status* in Latin; upon this the defense, having joined battle, first takes its stand, as it were, in order to resist.” Quintilian, *Institutes* III.6.13, cites this passage and adds: “What we call the *status*, some call the *constitution*, others the question, and others that which becomes apparent from the question.” See especially J. Th. Ernesti’s *Lexicon of Latin Rhetorical Terminology* under this word. ORELLI.

**“What is genus, what species.”** The second *what*, which is absent from the manuscript and the old editions, was added by Heraldus. ORELLI.

**“The wisdom of man is foolishness with God.”** These are the words of St. Paul, 1 Corinthians 3:19: Ἡ γὰρ σοφία τοῦ κόσμου τούτου μωρία παρὰ τῷ Θεῷ ἐστι, “For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.” Yet these words scarcely seem to have grazed the ears of pagans, who neither read nor listened to the sacred books of the Christians. ORELLI.

[Col. 0820B] **“And you proceed to unlock the secrets of nature.”** The phrase is Lucretian:

> I proceed to free men’s minds from the bonds of religions.

HERALDUS.

**“Their conjectures as things proved,” etc.** The reading *quod non agnoscunt*, “which they do not acknowledge,” absent from the manuscript and the old editions, derives from Stewechius’s correction. Here *suspiciones* means merely opinions, conjectures—*Hypothesen, Vermuthungen*—and nothing more. ORELLI.]

### VI

What then? Are you alone, stored away in wisdom and by the sheer power of intelligence, able to see some other, profound thing? [Note: [Col. 0817B] Fulvius gives the passage thus: “What then? Do you alone, by the sheer power of wisdom and intelligence, see something hidden and stored away?” More boldly than truly. See the Note.] Do you alone understand that all these things are trifles, mere words and childish absurdities—the things that we promise ourselves will come from the sovereign King? From where, I ask, was so much wisdom handed down to you? From where so much keenness and intellectual quickness? From what disciplines of knowledge have you been able to acquire so much understanding and draw so much power of divination?

Is it because you know how to decline verbs and nouns through cases and tenses; because you avoid barbarisms and solecisms; because you yourselves know how to deliver rhythmical, well-constructed, and carefully composed speech, or to recognize it when it is unadorned; because [Col. 0818B] you hold sealed in your memory the *Brothel* of Lucilius [Note: [Col. 0818B] Sabæus wrongly reads *Lucialinum*.] and the *Marsyas* of Pomponius; because you know what the constitutions are in lawsuits, how many kinds of causes and how many kinds of expression there are, what is genus and what species, and by what methods an opposite is distinguished from a contrary? Is it for this reason that you suppose yourselves to know what is false and what true, what can or cannot happen, and what the nature of the lowest and the highest things is?

Has that familiar saying never grazed your ears, that the wisdom of man is foolishness with God? First of all, whenever you discuss obscure matters and proceed to unlock the secrets of nature, do you yourselves thoroughly understand that you do not know the very things you say, assert, and frequently defend in a life-and-death struggle, and that each man, through stubborn opposition, protects his own conjectures as though they were proved and comprehended?

[Col. 0819B] [Note: [Col. 0820B]

### VII.—“For whether we perceive the truth … we can know by ourselves.”

*Si perspiciamus* means “whether” or “whether indeed we perceive,” as Stewechius correctly explains: *Könen wir aus uns selbst wissen, ob wir die Wahrheit erkennen*—“Can we know from ourselves whether we recognize the truth?” [Col. 0820C] The first edition has *si verum perspiciam*, “whether I perceive the truth,” enclosed in brackets, as though the author were speaking about himself. Wrongly. ORELLI.

**“Some envious agency, I know not what, has brought forth and fashioned.”** Arnobius means those evil natures hostile to God to which the Gnostics attributed the creation of souls; in this doctrine he followed them. Instead of *invidia*, “through envy,” the manuscript has *invida*, “envious,” modifying *res*, “agency”—not badly. ORELLI.

**“Of a somewhat swollen breast.”** I read *subinflati* with Meursius. The others separate the words, *sub inflati pectoris*. Heraldus defends that reading on the ground of Arnobius’s practice of using prepositions such as *in*, *sub*, and *ex* redundantly. But *subinflatus*, meaning “somewhat swollen,” also occurs in Caelius Aurelianus, *Acute Diseases* I.2; see Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. ORELLI.

**“That which the famous Socrates cannot comprehend in the *Phaedo*,” etc.** This is a lapse of Arnobius’s memory. For the passage is found not in the *Phaedo* but in the *Alcibiades*, p. 129 (p. 58, vol. V, Bipont edition):

> **Socrates:** Τί ποτ᾽ οὖν ὁ ἄνθρωπος;—“What, then, is man?”  
> **Alcibiades:** Οὐκ ἔχω λέγειν.—“I cannot say.”

ELMENHORST.—The manuscript has “in the *Phaedrus*,” from which Nourry suspects that Arnobius gave a paraphrastic account (*παραφραστικῶς*) [Col. 0820D] of a passage in Plato’s *Phaedrus*, second Stephanus edition, vol. III, p. 230 (Bipont edition, vol. X, p. 285), where Socrates himself says:

> Ὅθεν δὴ χαίρειν ἐάσας ταῦτα, πειθόμενος δὲ τῷ νομιζομένῳ περὶ αὐτῶν, ὃ νῦν δὴ ἔλεγον, σκοπῶ οὐ ταῦτα, ἀλλὰ ἐμαυτόν, εἴτε τι θηρίον ὢν τυγχάνω Τυφῶνος πολυπλοκώτερον, καὶ μᾶλλον ἐπιτεθυμμένον, εἴτε ἡμερώτερον καὶ ἁπλούστερον ζῷον, θείας τινὸς καὶ ἀτύφου μοίρας φύσει μετέχον.

> “Accordingly I leave these matters alone and accept the customary belief about them. As I was just saying, I investigate not these things but myself: whether I happen to be some beast more tangled and more swollen with pride than Typhon, or a gentler and simpler creature, naturally sharing in some divine and unassuming portion.”

This is much more probable. ORELLI.

**“Deceitful” (*pellax*).** Papias: “*Pellax*: a deceiver, crafty, fallacious.” Arnobius below, book V: “What shall we substitute for the showers of gold into which that same deceiver transformed himself by treacherous fraud?” ELMENHORST.—Compare Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* II.90. ORELLI.

**“Whether the earth, transformed by the putrefaction of some marshy moisture…”** Plato, in the *Timaeus*: Ἆρ᾽ ἐπειδὰν τὸ θερμὸν καὶ τὸ ψυχρὸν σηπεδόνα τινὰ λάβῃ, ὥς τινες ἔλεγον, τότε δὴ τὰ ζῷα συντρέφεται—“Is it then when heat and cold undergo a kind of putrefaction, as some used to say, that living creatures are generated together?” HERALDUS.—A doctrine taken from the Egyptians. See Diodorus Siculus I.7 and 10, and the commentators there. ORELLI.

**“And received the shape of the face.”** The reading is sound. [Col. 0821B] This is an interchange of number extremely common among ancient Greek and Latin writers. See Priscian, book XVII; Terence, *The Woman of Andros* IV.1.2:

> Can this be believed or even mentioned—  
> that such great madness should be innate in anyone:  
> that they should rejoice in evils and procure their own  
> advantages from another’s misfortunes?

But the same interchanges (*ἐναλλαγαί*) were frequent in Arnobius’s age. Julius Firmicus, book III, chapter 15: “It will cause the man who has the moon in that position to dwell sordidly in temples, and those who want something to announce it to men as though spoken by the gods”; and frequently elsewhere. HERALDUS.—Salmasius, in the Leiden edition, reads *acceperit*, “he received.” ORELLI.

**“A matter about which Plato is uncertain in the *Theaetetus*.”** The passage of Plato to which Arnobius refers is found in the *Theaetetus*, p. 158, vol. I of the Stephanus edition (p. 82, vol. II, Bipont edition). ORELLI.

**“Whether we see by the projection of rays and light,” etc.** Philosophers’ opinions on this matter certainly varied. Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* V.16, explains them clearly in these words: “The Stoics say that the causes of vision are the emission of rays from the eyes toward things capable of being seen, together with a simultaneous tension of the air. Epicurus, however, thinks that certain images of the bodies themselves continually flow from all bodies, that these enter the eyes, and that sensation thus occurs. Plato believes that a certain kind of fire and light goes forth from the eyes, and that this, joined and made continuous with the light of the sun or with the brightness of another fire, and relying upon its own force and an external one, enables us to perceive whatever it encounters and illuminates.” Compare Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers* IV.13; Diogenes Laertius I.157 and VIII.28; Lucretius IV.46 ff.; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VII.14. NOURRY, pp. 527–28.

**“Whether taste exists in things,” etc.** Compare Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers* IV.18; Lucretius IV.626 and II.398. NOURRY.

**“And settle in our pupils.”** Lucretius III.409–10:

> So, if the eye is wounded all around, but the pupil  
> remains unharmed, the living power of sight endures.

HERALDUS. An old Greek-Latin lexicon: “*Pupula*: ὀφθαλμοῦ κόρη, ‘the pupil of the eye.’” Papias: “*Pupula*: pupil, principal part.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.57: “The very point by which we see, called the pupil, is so small that it easily avoids things that might harm it.” See the commentators there. ELMENHORST.—Compare Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* III, p. 215. ORELLI.

**“For what causes hairs lose their innate blackness,” etc.** Alexander of Aphrodisias attempts to solve this question in *Problems* 1, 2, and 3. ORELLI.

**“Oil alone refuses,” etc.** See Plutarch, *Table Talk* VII, question 10, and VII, question 3. NOURRY, p. 528.

**“But is always visibly gathered together into its own impenetrable nature.”** I think it should be read: “But is always gathered visibly in its own impenetrable nature”; that is, “by its own nature.” For *in* is very frequently redundant in this author. HERALDUS.—I do not see why anything should be changed. The meaning is: whenever oil is mixed with other liquids, it gathers together—that is, collects itself at the top of the vessel—into its own nature, which other liquids cannot penetrate. *Perspicue*, “visibly,” means that it remains neither colored nor cloudy, but transparent. ORELLI.

**“Finally, the soul itself, which you declare to be immortal and a god.”** Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.26: “Therefore the soul—which, as I say, is divine, and which Euripides dares to call a god…” See Davies there. The same author, cited by Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* II.12: “Each person’s mind is that person himself.… Know, therefore, that you are a god, since a god is that which lives, feels, and remembers.” And Dionysius Cato, in that very well-known couplet:

> If the soul is a god, as poems tell us,  
> you must above all worship it with a pure mind.

The commentators have wrongly understood *animus*, “soul,” as a predicate dependent upon the word *Deus*, “god.” On the contrary, it is the subject, and the sentence must be construed: “If the soul is a god.” See Gisbert Cuper, who discusses this doctrine extensively in *Observations* II.17, p. 249, Leipzig edition. ORELLI.

**“Why it is sick in the sick, foolish in infants, and exhausted in old age.”** See Lucretius III.446–470. HERALDUS.

**“In old age exhausted, delirious, foolish, and insane.”** Some think that something is missing here. The discourse does indeed seem disordered and interrupted. Yet it depends on what precedes: “whom some agency, I know not what, brought forth so blind and proud and fashioned through envy that, although we know absolutely nothing, we nevertheless deceive ourselves and are exalted by the swelling of a somewhat inflated breast into the belief that we possess knowledge.” Then the following rightly succeeds: “whose delirious, foolish, and insane weakness,” etc. But a rather extended hyperbaton has intervened to prove the preceding statements. HERALDUS.—Yet the punctuation should by no means be changed, nor, as Meursius thinks, is anything missing. *Delira, fatua, insana* are ablatives and depend upon *senectute*: “in delirious, foolish, and insane old age.” [Col. 0822D] If anything must nevertheless be changed, I would prefer to follow N. Heinsius’s correction in *Adversaria* III.16, p. 530: *Deliret et fatue et insane*, “why it raves foolishly and insanely.” ORELLI.]

### VII

For even if all the ages of the world were spent in investigating things, how can we know by ourselves whether we perceive the truth—we whom some agency, I know not what, has brought forth so blind and proud and fashioned through envy that, although we know absolutely nothing, we nevertheless deceive ourselves and are lifted up into the belief that we possess knowledge by the swelling of a somewhat inflated breast?

To pass over divine matters and things submerged in natural obscurity, can any mortal explain what the famous Socrates cannot comprehend in the *Phaedo*: what man is, or whence he comes—ambiguous, changeable, unstable, deceitful, complex, multiform? For what purposes was he brought forth? By whose ingenuity was he devised? What does he do in the world? Why does he experience such swarms of evils? Did [Note: [Col. 0819B] Thus the manuscript.] the earth, transformed by the putrefaction of some marshy moisture, bring him to life like worms or mice? Or did these outlines [Col. 0820B] of body and the features of the face receive their shape by the hand of some fashioner and craftsman?

Can anyone, I ask, know these things, though they lie before us and are situated within the sphere of ordinary sensation: from what causes we sink into sleep, from what causes we awaken, in what ways dreams occur, and in what ways visions occur? Indeed, as Plato doubts in the *Theaetetus*, are we ever awake, or is that very state called waking merely a portion of perpetual sleep? And what [Note: [Col. 0821A] Stewechius reads *ecquid*, “whether anything.”] do we seem to be doing when we say that we are seeing a dream?

Do we see through the projection of rays and light, or do images of things fly toward us and settle in our pupils? Does taste exist in things, or is it produced through contact with the palate? For what causes do hairs lose their innate blackness and turn gray—not all at once, but by gradual addition? Why is it that all liquids [Col. 0822A] form one body when mixed, while oil alone refuses to admit immersion within itself, but is always visibly gathered together into its own nature, impenetrable by the others?

Finally, why is the soul itself—which you declare to be immortal and a god—sick in the sick, foolish in infants, and exhausted in delirious, foolish, and insane old age? Their weakness and pitiable ignorance is all the greater because, although it may happen that we sometimes say something true, even this very thing remains uncertain to us—whether we have said anything true.

[Note: [Col. 0822D]

### VIII.—“And since you are accustomed to ridicule our faith.”

The pagans mocked Christians as excessively credulous toward God and accused them of refusing either to provide or to receive a rational account of faith, but of saying simply, “At least believe.” The emperor Julian, cited by Gregory of Nazianzus in the *Invective*, p. 296:

> Ἡμέτεροι, φησίν, οἱ λόγοι καὶ τὸ ἑλληνίζειν, ὧν καὶ τὸ σέβειν θεούς· ὑμῶν δὲ ἡ ἀλογία, καὶ ἡ ἀγροικία, καὶ οὐδὲν ὑπὲρ τὸ, Πίστευσον, τῆς ὑμετέρας ἐστὶ σοφίας.

> “Discourse and Greek culture,” he says, “belong to us, and reverence for the gods is part of them; but irrationality and rusticity belong to you, and your wisdom amounts to nothing beyond ‘Believe.’”

Origen, *Against Celsus*, book I, pp. 9–10; Theodoret, discourse I, *On Faith against the Greeks*, pp. 12–13; Augustine, vol. VI, *To Honoratus, On the Usefulness of Believing*; and Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book I, demolish this slanderous charge with the strongest arguments and show that it is far removed from Christians. ELMENHORST.

[Col. 0823B] **“To lacerate.”** Above, book I, chapter 36: “Dark Isis mourning her lost son and her husband lacerated limb by limb.” On this word, which Catullus and Sallust also used, see Stewechius on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* IV, p. 298, Oudendorp’s edition. ORELLI.

**“Steeped in the unmixed wine of wisdom.”** That is, unmixed wine. [Col. 0823C] Thus Horace, *Epistles* II.2.137:

> He drove out the disease with hellebore, and the bile with unmixed wine.

NOURRY, p. 558.—*Meracus, -a, -um* is an archaic form for *merus*, “unmixed, pure.” See Lauremberg, *Antiquities*, under this word. ORELLI.

**“Do its agents undertake, take up, and embark upon it? You travel abroad.”** Thus Meursius and the Leiden editor. The manuscript has: “embark upon it. Do you travel abroad on land?” Scriverius, in Meursius’s Appendix, reads “do you travel abroad away from choruses?” Heraldus suspects that the text should read: “Do you travel abroad rashly?” from the very similar passage in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book I:

> Καὶ πλεῖ τις αὖθις εἰς ἄδηλον, οὐδ᾽ ἄλλην προβεβλημένος τῆς σωτηρίας ἄγκυραν, ἢ μόνην τὴν πίστιν, καὶ τὴν ἀγαθὴν ἐλπίδα.

> “And again, someone sails into the unknown, having cast out no other anchor of safety than faith alone and good hope.”

Fulvius Ursinus reads: “…let us undertake, take up, and embark upon it? Is it on land,” etc. But I prefer Salmasius’s correction to all these conjectures. Wasse, on Sallust, *Catiline* III, p. 34, Havercamp’s edition, declares himself uncertain whether *actores*, “agents,” should be corrected to *auctores*, “originators.” [Col. 0823D] ORELLI.

**“The partnership of marriage.”** Elegantly expressed. For marriage, as Modestinus says in Law 1 of the *Digest*, *On the Rite of Marriage*, is “the union of male and female, a partnership of all life, and a sharing of divine and human law.” Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* II, p. 95:

> Γυναῖκα γαμετὴν κατὰ νόμους ἱεροὺς συνελθοῦσαν ἀνδρί, κοινωνὸν ἁπάντων εἶναι χρημάτων τε καὶ ἱερῶν.

> “A lawfully wedded wife, united to a man according to sacred laws, is to share in all his property and sacred rites.”

ELMENHORST.]

### VIII

And since you are accustomed to ridicule our faith and to lacerate belief itself with humorous jokes, tell me, you witty men, steeped and saturated with the unmixed wine of wisdom: is there any laborious and active kind of work in life that its agents do not undertake, take up, and embark upon with faith going before them?

You travel abroad and sail: do you not believe that, once your business dealings have been completed, you will return home? You cleave the earth with iron and fill it with varieties of seed: do you not believe that you will receive a crop when the seasons have run their course? You enter into the partnership of marriage: do you not believe that wives will be chaste and faithful to their pledged duty toward their husbands? You undertake the begetting of children: do you not believe that your offspring will remain unharmed and, advancing through the stages of life, reach the boundaries of old age? You entrust bodily illnesses to the hands of physicians: do you not believe that diseases can be soothed and their severity alleviated? You wage wars against enemies: do you not believe that, through the successive course of battles, you will carry home victory? You venerate and worship the gods: do you not believe that they exist and incline favorable ears toward your supplications?

[Note: [Col. 0823D]

### IX.—“He who says that the origin of all things is fire or water—does he not believe Thales,” etc.

On these differing opinions of the philosophers, see Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians*, pp. 304–5, H. Stephanus’s edition; Calcidius on Plato’s *Timaeus*; Diogenes Laertius, book I; Tertullian, *Against Marcion*; Lactantius, *Institutes* I.5; Minucius Felix, *Octavius* 19; Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, book I; Cicero, *Academic Questions* IV [i.e. II], chapter 37, with Davies’s note there; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* I.5 and V.13; Hermias, *Mockery of the Pagan Philosophers*; Justin Martyr, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, pp. 3 and 5; Theodoret, *Against the Greeks*, discourse IV, *On Matter and the World*; and Nemesius, *On the Nature of Man* (*περὶ φύσεως ἀνθρώπου*), chapter 5. ELMENHORST.

**“He who locates the cause in numbers—does he not believe Pythagoras of Samos, or Archytas?”** Cicero, *Academics* II.37: “The Pythagoreans hold that all things proceed from numbers and the first principles of mathematics”—that is, points and lines. See the authors cited by Davies there. ORELLI.

**“He who divides the soul.”** That is, into rational and irrational parts. Theodoret, discourse V, *On the Nature of Man*, vol. IV, p. 546:

> Πλάτων καὶ Πυθαγόρας τὸ μὲν λογικὸν αὐτῆς ἄφθαρτον εἶναι, φθαρτὸν δὲ τὸ ἄλογον.

> “Plato and Pythagoras held that its rational part is incorruptible, but its irrational part corruptible.”

NOURRY, p. 530.—That is, into two parts, one participating in reason and the other devoid of reason. See Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* II.20, and Davies there. Other Platonists divided it into three parts: rationality, irascibility, and desire. See Apuleius, *On Plato’s Doctrine* II, p. 14, Elmenhorst’s edition, and the authors cited by Davies on Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.10. ORELLI.

**“He who adds a fifth element to the primary causes—does he not believe Aristotle,” etc.** Namely, *entelechy* (ἐντελέχεια), as though it were a kind of continuous and perpetual motion, as Cicero explains in *Tusculan Disputations* I.10; see Camerarius and Davies there. Compare Ernesti’s *Key to Cicero* and Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 30. ORELLI.

**“He who threatens the world with fire … does he not believe Panaetius, Chrysippus, and Zeno?”** See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.49; Theodoret, *Against the Greeks*, discourse V, *On the Nature of Man*; Justin Martyr, *Second Apology for the Christians*. ORELLI.

**“Arcesilaus.”** The Leiden edition has *Arcesilae*. Compare Grotius on Martianus Capella II, p. 46. This is the man whom Lactantius calls the teacher of ignorance, and of whom Cicero says that, through his doctrine of *incomprehensibility* (ἀκαταληψία), he utterly abolished all philosophy. ORELLI.]

### IX

What of those things removed from human cognition, about which you yourselves write and which you repeatedly read? Have you seen them with the inspection of your eyes and held them after touching them with your hands? Does not every one of you believe this or that authority [Note: [Col. 0823B] The manuscript has “authorities.”]? Does not each person, as though by a kind of pledge of faith, defend as true whatever he has persuaded himself another is saying?

He who says that the origin of all things is fire or water—does he not believe Thales or Heraclitus? He who locates the cause in numbers—does he not believe Pythagoras of Samos or Archytas? He who divides the soul and establishes incorporeal forms—does he not believe Plato the Socratic? He who adds a fifth element to the primary causes—does he not believe Aristotle, father of the Peripatetics? He who threatens the world with fire [Note: [Col. 0823B] Fulvius reads, “threatens fire against the world.”] and declares that, when the time comes, it will burn—does he not believe Panaetius, Chrysippus, and Zeno? He who continually constructs and destroys worlds from indivisible bodies—does he not believe Epicurus, Democritus, and Metrodorus? He who says that nothing can be comprehended by man and that all things [Col. 0824B] are wrapped in blind darkness—does he not believe Arcesilaus and Carneades, or, finally, some devotee of the Old or New Academy [Note: [Col. 0824B] Stewechius reads “or the more recent Academy.”]?

[Note: [Col. 0824D]

### X.—“Finally, the leading figures themselves.”

The manuscript has *Ipsi demus*, from which Heraldus, in his *Second Corrections*, conjectures *Ipsi demum*, against Salmasius. ORELLI.

**“Do they not say those very things?”** Thus Gelenius. The Roman edition has “Do they not among those things,” etc., from which Meursius produced “Or do they not say those things,” etc. ORELLI.

[Col. 0825C] **“Pythagoras, that things issue from number.”** I have admitted into the text the excellent correction of J. F. Gronovius, proposed in his letter to Salmasius, no. 289, in Burman’s *Collection of Letters*, vol. II, p. 529. Previously the text read, “Did Pythagoras know numbers?”—a completely false statement, for Pythagoras certainly knew numbers, though he did not know that the world issued from numbers. Heraldus reads: “that numbers come together.” Meursius: “Does he know numbers?” The Leiden edition: “that numbers proceed.” But *numero exire*, “that things issue from number,” is uniquely correct, *res*, “things,” being understood. ORELLI.

**“Common in our belief.”** Stewechius thinks it should be read: “with our belief.” But I am very pleased with Heraldus’s conjecture in the *Second Corrections*: “common in your belief”; that is, because you believe all those things, you share faith with us. ORELLI.]

### X

Finally, do not the leading figures themselves, the fathers of the sects just mentioned [Note: [Col. 0824B] Sabæus reads “opinions.”], say the very things they say because they believe their own conjectures? Did Heraclitus actually see things come into being through transformations of fire? Did Thales see them come from the condensation of waters? Did Pythagoras see things issue from number? Plato, incorporeal forms? Democritus, the collisions of indivisible bodies?

Or do those who maintain that absolutely nothing can be comprehended know whether what they say is true? Do they understand that the very proposition they define is a declaration of truth?

Since, therefore, you possess nothing ascertained or known, and assert all those things that you write and comprise in thousands of books under the guidance of belief, what sort of utterly unjust judgment is this—that you ridicule our faith, although you perceive that in our belief you yourselves share it in common with us? But, you say, you believe wise men instructed in every kind of discipline. Yes indeed—men who know nothing and pronounce no single settled judgment; who wage wars for their own opinions against those who oppose them [Col. 0825B] and always fight with hostile obstinacy; who, by undermining, destroying, and tearing away one another’s doctrines, have rendered everything uncertain and shown from their very disagreement that nothing can be known.

[Note: [Col. 0825C]

### XI.—“But let these things offer no obstruction and cause no hindrance.”

This is the entirely correct emendation of Johannes Meursius, deservedly admitted into the text by the Leiden editor. The manuscript has: “But let these things accomplish nothing and cause no hindrance,” a corrupt and meaningless reading. Gelenius printed: “But let these things depart and cause no hindrance.” Heraldus conjectures: “But let these things accomplish nothing, and cause no hindrance,” explaining *nihil efficiant* as “let them be fruitless and have no effect.” See C. Barth, *Adversaria* XXVIII.9, and Ruhnken on Rutilius Lupus II, p. 120. Heraldus himself, however, retracts this conjecture in his *Second Corrections*. ORELLI.

**“You believe Plato, you Cronius, you Numenius.”** I have printed this with the Leiden editor, following Fulvius Ursinus’s correction. The manuscript has *Crotonius*, a person nowhere mentioned among the ancients. Hugo Grotius nevertheless defends it in his note on Martianus Capella VI, p. 209, thinking it to be the ethnic adjective Κροτώνειος, “Crotonian,” from Κρότων, “Croton,” as Stephanus attests, and that Arnobius is alluding to Pythagoras. Cronius, however, was a Platonic philosopher and associate of Numenius, mentioned by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VI.19. Gelenius, whom most editors have followed, altered the text thus: “You believe Plato, you Plotinus, you Numenius.” Theodoret also joins these three in discourse II, *On First Principles*, p. 33:

> Αὐτίκα τοίνυν τὴν Πλάτωνος διάνοιαν ἀναπτύσσοντες καὶ ὁ Πλωτῖνος καὶ Νουμήνιος.

> “Accordingly, Plotinus and Numenius, unfolding the thought of Plato…”

Plotinus, leader of the Neoplatonists, is especially well known from the biography written by his disciple Porphyry. Thomas Canter thinks *Protomus* or *Prothomus* should be read, a figure mentioned by Apuleius in *On the God of Socrates*. Meursius, p. 53, thinks *Strato* should be read, citing Augustine, *City of God* VI.10; Scriverius, in the same Meursius, proposes *Crato*. Numenius of Apamea, a Syrian, was a Platonic and Pythagorean philosopher renowned for various writings, many fragments of which survive in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, books XI and XIII. Compare the *Suda* and Hesychius of Miletus in his biography. ORELLI.

**“Since both parties rely upon authorities.”** This is a highly discerning correction by Gelenius. The manuscript and the Roman edition have, absurdly and meaninglessly: “that with both authorities the time…” ORELLI.

**“You wish it to be granted to you that whatever is stated by them should be accepted, while you are unwilling to hear and examine the things advanced by Christ.”** Stewechius conjectures: “You wish it to be granted to you that whatever is said by them should be eagerly accepted, while you are unwilling to hear and examine the things advanced by Christ.” I think the words of Arnobius would be more closely preserved by reading: “You wish it to be granted to you that we should accept whatever is said by them; yet you are unwilling to hear and examine the things advanced by Christ.” Certainly the word *ita*, “thus,” is intrusive here and should plainly be deleted. ORELLI.

**“And confidently to judge.”** He uses *fideliter* in an unusual sense, for “confidently and boldly.” Prudentius likewise used *fidelis* to mean “credible and worthy of belief” in *On the Crowns*, hymn 10:

> If some madman regards these things as fabulous,  
> or if you yourself previously thought them insufficiently credible,  
> you may now recognize them as true.

MEURSIUS, p. 54.

**“A small inflamed swelling” (*fervunculum*).** Thus the Leiden editor, apparently from the manuscript. *Fervunculus* derives from *fervor*, “heat, inflammation.” See Flavius Caper, *On Doubtful Words*, p. 2248, in Putsch’s collection. Others read *furunculum*, which means the same thing. A *furunculus* is an acute swelling accompanied by inflammation and pain. Celsus, book V, final chapter. Our term is *Aisse*. ORELLI.

**“Flow in polished compositions.”** *Levigare* means “to make smooth and even”—*glatt machen, verebnen, glätten*. See Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* II, p. 236. ORELLI.

[Col. 0827B] **“Men whom one must necessarily believe concerning the most obscure matters.”** *Debeant* means “it is necessary.” Above, book I, chapter 63: “Could the man who had restored sight to the blind not, if it were necessary, make blind men?” Some wrongly wished to rewrite *deberet* as *liberet*, “if he wished.” HERALDUS.—Thus Petronius, *Satyricon*, chapter 33, near the end: “There must be something good here,” that is, “it is necessary that there be; it ought to be.” See Scioppius and Burman there. ORELLI.

**“To arrange their inductions consecutively.”** That is, to arrange them so that one induction follows from another—what we call *consequent*, “consecutive.” See Savaron on Sidonius VII.17, p. 477. ORELLI.

[Col. 0827C] **“Who uttered his discourse brightly.”** Should we not read *callidule*, “craftily,” with Heraldus in his *Second Corrections*? The immediately preceding discussion concerns syllogisms, enthymemes, and so forth, which the ancient philosophers used craftily to deceive their hearers and extort their assent against the truth. Thus our author below, chapter 68 of this same book, speaks of “crafty deception” (*fraus callidula*). ORELLI.

**“By the pledge.”** Meursius conjectures *responsione*, “by the answer.” Wrongly. ORELLI.]

### XI

But let these things offer no obstruction and cause no hindrance—certainly not enough to prevent you from believing and listening to them. What is it that, in this respect, either you possess in greater measure or we possess in less? You believe Plato, Cronius, Numenius, or anyone else you please; we believe Christ and rest satisfied in him.

How great is this injustice: although both parties rely upon authorities, and believing is one and the same thing shared by us and by you, you wish it to be granted to you that whatever is stated by those men should be accepted, while you are unwilling to hear and examine the things advanced by Christ? Yet if we wish to compare reasons with reasons and particular points with particular points, we are better able to show what we followed in Christ than you are able to show what you followed in the philosophers.

For our part, these are the things we followed in him: those magnificent works and most powerful acts of might that he produced and displayed in various miracles. By these anyone could be brought under the necessity of believing and confidently judge that the deeds being performed were not those of a man, but of some divine and unknown power.

What acts of might did you follow in the philosophers, such that it was more proper for you to believe them than for us to believe Christ? Which of them was ever able, by one word or by the command of a single order—not to say to restrain and subdue the madness of the sea or the fury of storms; not to restore sight to the blind or give it to those born without sight; not to recall the dead to life; not to dissolve long-standing afflictions—but, what is far easier, to heal by a single prohibition a small inflamed swelling, an itch, or a little thorn embedded in a callus?

I do not say this because we deny that those men were praiseworthy for the integrity of their character or thoroughly trained in every kind of study and discipline. For we know that they speak in the most splendid words and flow in polished compositions; that they construct syllogisms with the greatest acuteness; arrange [Col. 0827A] their inductions consecutively; supply formulas by means of definitions; separate and divide; say much about the kinds of numbers and much about music; and even explain geometrical matters according to their own rules and precepts.

But what does this contribute to the issue? Does their knowledge of enthymemes, syllogisms, and other similar things guarantee that they know the truth? Or does it make them worthy of being necessarily believed concerning the most obscure matters? A contest between persons is not to be decided by the powers of eloquence, but by the power of accomplished works. A good authority is not the man who has uttered his discourse brightly, but the man who supports what he promises with the pledge of divine works.

[Note: [Col. 0827C]

### XII.—“Who would promise him,” etc.

Others read *permitteret*, “would permit,” wrongly. *Promittere* means the same as *spondere*, “to pledge.” A little earlier: “Do syllogisms and other similar things guarantee the truth to them?” Juvenal:

> The stiff bristles across their breasts  
> promise a fierce spirit.

HERALDUS.

**“Who would promise that he judges anything openly.”** *Indicare*, “disclose,” should be read, as Meursius conjectured, with J. Davies’s support in his note on Caesar, *Gallic War* VI.42, p. 339, Oudendorp’s edition. ORELLI.

[Col. 0827D] **“Of foolish credulity.”** Thus Gelenius corrected the text, and all the other editors followed him. It previously read *solidae*, “solid,” which Prior defends and which perhaps should not be rejected altogether. *Facilitas solida* would mean complete credulity, so great that nothing can be added to it. Our *stock-dumm, stock-einfältig*—“utterly stupid, utterly simple”—corresponds to *facilitas stolida*, “foolish credulity.” ORELLI.

**“That force has subjected them.”** Gelenius reads *eas*, “them,” wrongly. *Ea* is feminine singular: understand *ea vis rerum*, “that force of circumstances,” etc. ORELLI.]

What was done in India. There the teaching of the Gospel is said to have been propagated by Pantaenus, about the year 196 after Christ. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, ch. 10, and Jerome’s *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 36. Here, however, “India” means Ethiopia above Egypt. ORELL.

In Arabia. See Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, ch. 19. ORELL.

In all the islands and provinces. Compare our author with Tertullian, book I, *Against the Jews*, ch. 7: “Christ’s kingdom extends everywhere; it is worshipped by all the nations enumerated above” (he had enumerated the Babylonians, Parthians, India, Ethiopia, Asia, Germany, Britain, the Moors, the Gaetulians, and the Romans); “everywhere it reigns, everywhere it is adored.” The same author, *Apologeticus*, ch. 37: “We are but of yesterday, and we have filled everything that belongs to you—cities, islands, fortresses, municipalities, meeting places, the camps themselves, tribes, wards, the palace, the senate, the forum. We have left you only the temples.” See Havercamp there, p. 311. Cf. Irenaeus, I, 3. ORELL.

In which, although there are people. For *sint* Stewechius prefers *essent*, and thinks that *sint* arose from a misunderstood scribal abbreviation, *hominESsent*. But the present tense is correct, for at the very time when Arnobius wrote this, Rome was full of worshippers of the gods. ORELL.

By the arts of King Numa. Stewechius conjectures that *ritibus* (“rites”) should be read, with Heraldus’s approval. ORELL.

Their ancestral affairs. Heraldus thinks *ritus patrios* (“ancestral rites”) should be read. But we must understand not only rites and public religious observances, but many other things as well, especially the business of the forum, to which those embracing the Christian religion bade farewell. ORELL.

For they had seen the chariot of Simon Magus, etc. We know, indeed, that this miracle is either called into doubt or wholly denied by some. For this story, drawn from books called pseudepigraphical—that is, undoubtedly, from the *Apostolic Constitutions* (book VI, ch. 9)—is variously narrated by various writers. Moreover, at Rome the report of that miracle was highly uncertain, and Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, and other very ancient writers maintained complete silence about it. The event was, however, committed to writing by Cyril of Jerusalem (*Catechesis* 6, p. 54); Ambrose (book IV of the *Hexaemeron*, ch. 8, § 33); Augustine (*On Heresies*, ch. 6); Isidore of Pelusium (book I, Epistle 13); Theodoret (book I of the *Compendium of Heretical Fables*, ch. 13); and Maximus of Turin (Homily V on the Feast of Saints Peter and Paul). NOURR. p. 299.—Likewise Augustine, *On Saints Peter and Paul*, sermon III, vol. X, fol. 268; Hegesippus, book III, ch. 2; Epiphanius, book I, *Against Heresies*, p. 31; Abdias, *On the Lives of the Apostles*, book I. ELMENH.—Add Sulpicius Severus, *Sacred History*, book II, ch. 42. ORELL.

And that the fiery four-horse chariot was blown away by Peter’s breath and vanished when Christ was named. Joan. Schefferus, in his work *On the Vehicles of the Ancients*, book II, ch. 34, proposes the reading: “but when Christ was named,” etc., taking *sed* in the sense of “and indeed,” or rather as introducing the author’s correction of himself. On this elegant use of the particle, consult P. Burmann on Petronius, ch. 128, and Schwabe on Phaedrus, book IV, fable 17, verse 19, p. 265. Thus our author below, book VI, ch. 12: “Vulcan with cap and hammer, his hand free—but his right hand, if the reading is sound”; and in the same book, ch. 11: “that Dionysius—but the younger.” ORELL.

Thereafter carried to Brunda. *Brunda*, or rather *Brenda*, is a poetic name for Brundisium. See Festus under the word *Brundisium* and the commentators there. Hegesippus, in the passage cited, writes that Simon Magus died at Aricia. Here too, however, Arnobius follows a different tradition. Meursius corrects the text to *Brendam*. ORELL.

For pouring darkness over. The construction is: “You gave them an opportunity for pouring darkness over.” ORELL.

## XII

You bring forward arguments against us, and ingenious suspicions. If Christ himself—with all respect to him, and, I would say, with his pardon—were to employ these in an assembly of the people, who would assent, who would listen, who would guarantee that he was making any clear judgment? Or who, however foolish and possessed of stupid credulity he might be, would follow one who cast about empty and naked assertions? The miracles set before their eyes, that unheard-of power manifested in deeds—whether performed openly by Christ himself or celebrated throughout the whole world by his heralds—kindled those flames of longing and caused nations, peoples, and communities utterly unlike in their customs to converge with one mind in assent to a single belief.

For it is possible to enumerate and bring into a reckoning what was done in India, among the Seres, Persians, and Medes; in Arabia and Egypt; in Asia and Syria; among the Galatians, Parthians, and Phrygians; in Achaea, Macedonia, and Epirus [*Epizo* in the text]; in all the islands and provinces traversed by the rising and setting sun; and finally in imperial Rome itself. Although its people were occupied with the arts of King Numa and with ancient superstitions, they nevertheless did not hesitate to abandon their ancestral affairs and unite themselves with Christian truth. [Col. 0828B]

For they had seen the chariot of Simon Magus and his fiery four-horse chariot blown away by Peter’s breath and vanish when Christ was named. They had seen him, I say, trusting in false gods yet betrayed by those same gods when they became afraid, hurled down by his own weight and lying with his legs shattered; and afterward, when carried to Brunda, exhausted by torments and shame, they had seen him once again throw himself from the summit of a very lofty roof.

You neither know that all these things occurred, nor wished to know, nor ever judged such knowledge necessary for yourselves. While trusting in your own hearts and calling conceit (*typhus*) wisdom, you gave deceivers an opportunity—those harmful beings, I mean, whose interest it is that the Christian name should disappear—to pour darkness over such great events and obscure them, to rob you of faith, and to implant contempt. Thus, because they foresee that an end befitting their deserts is approaching them, they sought to instill in you also a cause through which you might enter into danger and be deprived of divine benevolence. [Col. 0829B]

> **Note: [Col. 0829C]**
>
> **XIII.—To ride against.** Arnobius more than once uses this verb in the sense of “to attack” and “to persecute.” NOURRIUS. Some wrongly delete the following *to mock*. ORELL.
>
> **Have formed.** The manuscript has *secerunt*, which Stewechius defends as the past tense of the ancient verb *seco, -ere*, equivalent to *secare* (“to cut”), from which *secus* for *sexus*, *seculum*, *secius*, etc., appear to be derived. See Jo. Mellerus Palmerius, *Spicilegia on Plautus’ Miles Gloriosus*, in Gruter’s *Lampas Critica*, vol. IV, p. 676. But nothing should be changed. *Partes facere* is equivalent to “to establish distinct parties.” ORELL.
>
> **You who follow Mercury . . . .** This Mercury is Hermes Trismegistus, under whose name various writings—for example, the *Poemander* and *Asclepius* (translated by Apuleius)—were already read in the age of Arnobius. ORELL.
>
> **Does not your Plato in the Theaetetus . . . advise the soul to flee from the earth?** The passage of Plato is found in the *Theaetetus*, p. 173, second ed. of Stephanus (p. 116, vol. II, Bipontine ed.):
>
> “But in truth only his body—that of the wise man—lies within the city and resides there. His mind, regarding all these things as small and of no account and holding them in contempt, ranges everywhere, in Pindar’s words, measuring the regions beneath the earth and those upon its surface, studying the stars beyond the heavens, and investigating in every direction the whole nature of every existing thing in its entirety, never lowering itself to anything close at hand.”
>
> Similarly Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, book I, ch. 8: “The second virtues, which they call purificatory, belong to the man who is capable of the divine; they set free only the soul of the man who has resolved to purify himself from contamination by the body and, through a kind of flight from human things, to associate himself with divine things alone.” See Is. Pontanus there. ORELL.
>
> **You dare to ridicule us because we say that there will be a resurrection of the dead.** It was customary for philosophers and pagans to taunt Christians with humorous jests because they affirmed the resurrection of the flesh. Caecilius in Minucius says: “Not content with this mad belief, they construct and append old wives’ tales: they claim that after death they will be born again, ashes and embers alike; and with some inexplicable confidence they mutually believe their own lies. You would think they had already risen again.” Origen, *Against Celsus*, book I, p. 7: “And indeed, when the mystery concerning the resurrection is understood, it is continually mocked and ridiculed by unbelievers.” HERALD.
>
> **We indeed confess that we say this, but that you hear it otherwise than we mean it.** He appears to say this because he believed that the same bodies which had existed would not rise again—an opinion also held by certain others, such as Origen, who explains it himself in book V of *Against Celsus*. Here Arnobius discusses resurrection in such a way that he seems to be disputing only about the immortality of souls and to approach in some fashion the opinion of Marcion, who denied the resurrection of bodies; or at least he appears not yet to have held any certain or settled position concerning this doctrine. We do not say this as though we believed Arnobius to have been a follower of Marcion, but so that the reader may observe that Arnobius’s errors are those of a man not yet sufficiently instructed in the Christian faith and supported more by natural reasoning than by spiritual (*πνευματική*) teaching. See the various opinions of the ancients concerning resurrection in Athenagoras, Tertullian, and others. HERALD.—Here *audiri* (“to be heard”) is equivalent to “to be understood,” as it often is. ORELL.
>
> **What does the same Plato say in the Statesman?** The passage of Plato is found in the *Statesman*, p. 270, H. Stephanus ed. (p. 31 ff., vol. VI, Bipontine ed.). ORELL.
>
> **That human beings would burst forth again.** Stewechius conjectures the reading *rursus se erupturos* (“that they themselves would burst forth again”), in the manner of the ancients—Plautus, Terence, etc.—and of those who imitated the ancients, including Apuleius and Arnobius himself. ORELL.
>
> **They would end at the cradle of infancy.** The reading is sound and should not be tampered with. *Desinere* (“to end”) is used elegantly and vividly of things which gradually diminish, becoming from great things smaller and then very small, until at last they disappear entirely. Stewechius reads *defituros*; the Leiden edition, *exituros*. Wrongly. ORELL.
>
> **For what are human beings except souls, etc.?** Marcion, Basilides, and Origen, whom Arnobius follows here, distinguished the human being into an exterior and an interior person, and said that the interior person—that is, the soul—was properly the true human being. Tertullian argues against them in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 40. HERALD.
>
> **Fastened with beam-nails.** Beam-nails are the nails with which the beams of buildings were joined, so heavy and of such monstrous size that the expression is used metaphorically of immutable things which one is in no way permitted to escape. Horace, in that well-known passage, *Odes* I.35.15 ff.:
>
> “Before you ever walks savage Necessity,  
> bearing in her brazen hand  
> beam-nails and wedges.”
>
> See Cruquius and Mitscherlich there. Petronius, ch. 75: “You know that what I have once resolved is fixed with a beam-nail.” See the commentators there. ORELL.
>
> **And place no obstructing impediments before those returning to their ancestral homes.** For they believed that demons or genii were assigned to individual human beings coming forth into this life, as though they were guardians and governors of their entire lives; and that these same beings dragged their charges before the judgment-seat when they departed from this world, and that the judge’s sentence was delivered upon their testimony. This was Plato’s opinion, which he presents in the *Phaedo* and which Apuleius explains in his book *On the God of Socrates*. Cf. Augustine, *City of God*, book X, ch. 9; Servius on Virgil’s words, “Each of us suffers his own Manes” (*Aeneid* VI.743): “When we are born,” he says, “two genii are assigned to us by lot. One exhorts us to good; the other corrupts us toward evil. With these attending us, after death we are either admitted to a better life or condemned to a worse one; through them we merit either release or a return into bodies. He therefore calls the genii whom we receive by lot together with life ‘Manes.’” HERALD.

## XIII

Meanwhile, you people who admire and stand amazed at the doctrines of learned men and of philosophy—do you not regard it as grossly unjust to ride against us and mock us as though we were speaking foolish and brutish things, when you too are found saying either the very same things or things of the same kind as those which you ridicule when they are spoken and proclaimed by us?

My discussion is not with those who, dispersed through the various byways of sects, have formed this party and that through diversity of opinion. It is you, you whom I address: you who follow Mercury, Plato, and Pythagoras, and the rest of you who are of one mind and walk the same paths through unity of doctrine.

You dare to ridicule us because we venerate and worship the Father and God of all things, and because we surrender and entrust our hopes to him? What does your Plato say in the *Theaetetus*, to name him in particular? Does he not advise the soul to flee from the earth and always to dwell near God in thought and mind, as far as this can be done?

You dare to ridicule us because we say that there will be a resurrection of the dead? We indeed confess that we say this, but that you hear it otherwise than we mean it. What does the same Plato say in the *Statesman*? Does he not write that, when the world begins [Col. 0830B] to rise from the western regions and turn toward the pivot belonging to the rising sun, human beings will again burst forth from the bosom of the earth—old, white-haired, and decrepit—and that, as further years begin to accrue, they will pass downward through the same stages by which people now grow, until they end at the cradle of infancy?

> **Note: [Col. 0829B]** The manuscript wrongly reads *acceperit*.

You dare to ridicule us because we make provision for the salvation of our souls—that is, for ourselves? For what are we human beings except souls enclosed within bodies? Do not all of you likewise devote every care to their preservation—not in the sense that you abstain from every vice and desire, but because that fear possesses you, lest you should cling to bodies as though fastened to them with beam-nails?

What is intended by those rites of secret arts, in which you address certain powers unknown to me, asking them to be kindly disposed toward you and to place no obstructing impediments before you as you return to your ancestral homes?

> **Note: [Col. 0831B]** Fulvius reads *abstinetis* (“you abstain”).

> **Note: [Col. 0831D]**
>
> **XIV.—What does this same Plato of yours say in the volume he composed on the immortality of the soul? Does he not name Acheron, etc.?** See Plato, *Phaedo*, pp. 112–114, H. Stephanus ed. (pp. 251–258, vol. I, Bipontine ed.), and Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book XIII, ch. 7. ELMENH.—Compare Grotius on Martianus Capella, p. 37. ORELL.
>
> **He undertakes an insoluble problem, etc.** He therefore believes that souls, if they are devoid of matter, cannot be affected by bodily suffering and pain. This was also the opinion of Tertullian himself (*Apologeticus*, ch. 48) and others. Accordingly, Arnobius, together with Tertullian, believed souls to be corporeal—though composed of a subtler, spiritual (*πνευματικόν*) body—because he thought them capable of suffering. HERALD.
>
> **[Col. 0832B] And subjects them to the pains of the senses.** Thus Sabaeus. The manuscript has *doloris affici sensu* (“to be affected by the sensation of pain”), dependent upon “he says”; the Leiden editor, for some unknown reason, changed this to *doloris afficiat sensu*. Elmenhorst takes *sensus* as an accusative plural. ORELL.
>
> **To condemn.** Thus the manuscript. Others read “to be condemned.” ORELL.
>
> **For they are cast, etc.** Aeneas of Gaza expresses the same opinion in the *Theophrastus*, p. 52 (Barth ed.): “But the wicked, having fallen into Tartarus, from which they will never emerge, are no longer themselves benefited; but, having become an example of punishment, they will lie there forever. For these are the things Socrates confidently maintained in the *Phaedo* and the *Gorgias*.” ORELL.
>
> **They vanish.** Stewechius reads “they disappear.” ORELL.
>
> **For they are of an intermediate quality, as has been learned on Christ’s authority, and are capable of perishing.** These words savor of Valentinianism, as others too have observed. Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, ch. 32: “Among them the soul too is mortal, except the soul that has found salvation through faith.” Following them, therefore, Arnobius believed that the souls of the impious die—not, however, that they are immediately extinguished, but that they are consumed by the torments and pains of a very long period. ELMENH. and HERALD.
>
> **If they apply themselves to his threats and indulgences.** The manuscript reads *si ad ejus semina*, which makes no sense. In its place Gelenius reads *se minas*; others, *se misericordiam*; Heraldus, *se munia*. But *minas* is excellent: “to apply oneself to God’s threats” means to fear God’s threats—the destruction with which God threatens the wicked. Threats are therefore appropriately contrasted with indulgences. ORELL.
>
> **Souls not knowing God.** That is, souls unwilling to know or experience God and his mercy. See above, on book I, ch. 17, the words: “The great gods therefore know this.” ORELL.
>
> **With fierce fire.** Arnobius says *ignis ferus* (“fierce fire”), just as the Old Latin translator of the Bible says *feros fluctus*, in Greek ἄγρια κύματα (“wild waves”). Arnobius above: “inextinguishable fires.” Book IV: “the inextinguishable flames of Gehenna.” Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*, fol. 258: “burning Gehenna and living flames.” Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, ch. 48: “perpetual fire.” Lactantius, book VIII, ch. 21: “eternal fire,” etc. ELMENH.
>
> **Into which certain cruelly savage beings, unknown before Christ, will cast them, etc.** Yet long before the time of Christ, belief in demons that assail human bodies and serve as torturers of the wicked in the underworld had flourished among the Jewish people. Compare especially Westenius on the New Testament, vol. I, pp. 279 ff. We find a similar ignorance of Jewish doctrines in our author below, book III, ch. 12, at the beginning; see the notes there. ORELL.

## XIV

You dare to ridicule us when we speak of Gehenna and certain inextinguishable fires, into which we have learned that souls are cast down by their foes and enemies? What, then? Does this same Plato of yours, in the volume he composed on the immortality of the soul, not name the rivers Acheron, Styx, Cocytus, and Pyriphlegethon, in which he asserts that souls are rolled about, submerged, and burned? [Col. 0831B]

Yet this man of sound prudence and careful examination and judgment undertakes an insoluble problem: although he says that souls are immortal, everlasting, and devoid of corporeal solidity, he nevertheless says that they are punished and subjects them to the pains of the senses. Who among human beings does not see that what is immortal and simple can admit no pain, while that which feels pain cannot possess immortality?

And yet his authority does not depart very far from the truth. For although, as a gentle and benevolent man, he believed it inhuman for souls to be condemned by a capital sentence, he did not absurdly suspect that they are cast into rivers surging with balls of flame and hideous with muddy chasms. For they are cast into them and, reduced to nothing, vanish in the frustration of perpetual destruction. They are of an intermediate quality, as has been learned on Christ’s authority, and are capable of perishing if they remain ignorant of God, but of being freed for life and from exile if they apply themselves to his threats and indulgences.

And to make plain what is unknown: this is the true death of a human being, the death that leaves nothing remaining. For the death seen before our eyes is the separation of souls from bodies, not the final end of annihilation. This, I say, is the true death of a human being: when souls that do not know God are consumed through the torment of a very long period by fierce fire, into which certain cruelly savage beings, unknown before Christ and disclosed by him alone who knew them, will cast them.

> **Note: [Col. 0832B]** Sabaeus wrongly reads *ignifero* as a single word, “fire-bearing.”

> **[Col. 0833A] Note: [Col. 0833B]**
>
> **XV.—Which is said by certain new men.** This is Gelenius’s emendation, followed by all the other editors except Salmasius, who reads: “which is said to us by certain men,” etc.; Gallandius also admitted this into his text. But the conjecture of Fulvius Ursinus, “by certain good men,” etc., is much more pleasing—“good” being used ironically, as in Cicero, *On Duties* II.25: “the finest men sitting by the middle Janus”; and *For Roscius of Ameria*, ch. 8, “a most excellent man,” referring to T. Roscius, a thoroughly wicked person. ORELL.
>
> **And not tangible through any contact with the body.** *Contiguas* here means “capable of being touched,” “tangible,” an altogether unusual sense. See Barth on Grattius Faliscus, *Cynegetica*, verse 8. The dictionaries do not recognize this meaning. *Incontiguus* is used in the same sense below, book VII, ch. 3: “And he is untouchable by every kind of contact.” ORELL.
>
> **We live blamelessly and therefore irreproachably—good, just, etc.** These words must be understood ironically. ORELL.

## XV

Therefore there is no reason why what is said by certain new men, raised aloft by an immoderate opinion of themselves, should deceive us or promise us empty hopes: that souls are immortal, next in degree of dignity to the God and First Principle of all things; that they were brought forth by that Begetter and Father; that they are divine, wise, learned, and not tangible through any contact with the body.

Because this is true and certain, and because we were brought forth by the perfect one in a perfection incapable of improvement, we naturally live blamelessly and therefore irreproachably—good, just, and upright; guilty of no vice whatsoever; conquered by no desire and dishonored by no lust; preserving and maintaining intact the whole course of every virtue. And because the souls of all of us flow from one source, we therefore think one and the same harmonious thought: we do not differ in customs or opinions; we all know God; nor are there as many judgments as there are human beings in the world, judgments separated by infinite variety. [Col. 0833B]

> **Note: [Col. 0833B]** Sabaeus wrongly reads *sibi* (“for themselves”).
>
> **Note: [Col. 0833B]** The manuscript reads: “there are not as many judgments.”

> **Note: [Col. 0833C]**
>
> **XVI.—But while we slip down toward bodies.** See above, on book I, ch. 29. ORELL.
>
> **The causes by which we are evil and thoroughly wicked, seethe with desires and anger.** Thus Th. Canterus edited the text from the manuscript. Previously it read: “and with the worst desires,” etc. The Leiden editor reads “by which we are evil,” which would not be bad if the text had “by which we become evil,” since the following “we seethe” requires the subjunctive. ORELL.
>
> **We are condemned to lust.** That is, we are bound or destined by fatal causes. *Damnari* very often means “to be destined for some evil or misfortune.” Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.699:
>
> “And had condemned her life to the Stygian underworld.”
>
> And Petronius, *Satires*, ch. III: “What will this profit you . . . if, before the Fates demand it, you pour forth your uncondemned spirit”—that is, a spirit not yet destined for death? See Burmann there. ORELL.
>
> **By weaker causes.** Fulvius Ursinus conjectures *infimioribus* (“lower causes”), a comparative formed from the superlative *infimus*. Gesner, in his *Thesaurus*, adduces one example from the barbarous Latin translator of Irenaeus, book II, ch. 14. ORELL.
>
> **Disfigurements.** The glosses give: *dehonestamentum*, αἰσχύνη (“disgrace”). Gellius, book II, ch. 27: “That bodily disfigurement in which he especially delighted.” ELMENH.
>
> **Are you willing, human beings, to lay aside your settled pride and haughtiness?** This passage has been altered in various ways. Yet nothing should be changed. By *institutum* Arnobius means αὐθάδεια (“self-will”), or a σεμνοπρεπής (“solemnly dignified”) obstinacy. Thus Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis*, book VIII, ch. 6: “Whoever are born under this star promise one thing by their countenance but secretly conceal another in their character. They have a severe face, a long beard, and an obstinate brow, so that they seem altogether to imitate Cato’s established manner.” HERALD.—Fulvius Ursinus conjectures that the reading should be: “to lay aside the conceit of arrogance and your haughtiness.” The Leiden edition has “that conceit.” Meursius reads: “Are you people willing”—that is, ὦ οὗτοι (“O you people”)—“to lay aside your conceit and haughtiness?” For my own part, I determine nothing, since I do not know what the manuscript reads. ORELL.
>
> **You who claim God as your Father.** I had conjectured that *parem* (“equal”) should be read, but I retract that opinion. The meaning is: you who boast that you were created by God. Arnobius attempts to overthrow this opinion in what follows, asserting that human souls were created not by God but by certain inferior powers. ORELL.
>
> **Are you willing, after laying aside partiality.** Thus the first edition; others read “after laying aside arrogance.” The Leiden edition has “swelling pride.” But nothing should be changed. *Favore* means the favor with which you embrace your own opinion, what is barbarously called “partiality.” ORELL.
>
> **Similar to the other animals.** Thus most editors. The first edition reads “the other things similar,” which Heraldus vainly defends by explaining it as “the other living beings similar to us.” ORELL.
>
> **Or not separated from them by very great difference.** *Differitas* is a Lucretian word; *On the Nature of Things* IV.640: “So great in these matters are the distance and the difference.” Our author below, book IV, ch. 36: “Nor is there any sign inherent in the thing by which the difference between ambiguous and plainly expressed statements may be judged.” See Nonius under this word and Lud. Carrio, who discusses it at length, *Emendations*, book II, ch. 17, p. 177; vol. III, part II of Gruter’s *Lampas Critica*. ORELL.
>
> **Their bodies are founded upon bones.** A Lucretian phrase. Book V.925:
>
> “And founded within upon larger and more solid bones,”
>
> namely, the human race. HERALD.
>
> **Returned in turn through breathing.** Fulvius Ursinus reads *reciprocas*. See above, Heraldus’s note on book I, ch. 8. ORELL.
>
> **We too were fashioned into the same number of sexes.** Here too Stewechius restores the ancient form *secus*. See above, on book I, ch. 59, the words “the male sex.” ORELL.
>
> **They procreate through bodily unions.** *Concilium* in the sense of congress or intercourse is frequent in Lucretius; for example, book II.934:
>
> “No offspring can be produced unless union has first taken place”;
>
> and book I.184, “generative union.” See Creech there. ORELL.
>
> **We are poured forth and discharged from our mothers’ wombs. They are sustained by food and drink.** I read and punctuate thus with Meursius. Others read very badly: “We are poured forth and discharged from the wombs; we are sustained by our mothers’ food and drink.” For shortly afterward there follows: “We too are sustained by food and drink.” ORELL.
>
> **[Col. 0835D] They are all concerned to ward off deadly hunger.** A passage from Cicero, *On Duties* I, ch. 4, beginning, should be compared with our author. ORELL.
>
