> **That the souls of the wicked enter cattle and other beasts.** Plato presents this opinion both elsewhere and in the *Phaedo*, where he explains it at greater length. Tertullian treats the same matter in *On the Soul*, chapters 31, 32, and those following. HERALD.
>
> **Stripped.** Thus Gelenius. The manuscript reads *sumptae*, which Th. Canterus and Stewechius defend by a passage of Arnobius from book V: “How can you separate certain things from doubtful things?” There *sumere* is equivalent to *secernere*, “to separate”; nor does this reading seem altogether deserving of rejection. Salmasius, in the Leiden edition, reads *exemptae* (“removed”); Meursius, *summotae* (“taken away”). ORELL.

## XVI

But while we slip and hasten toward human bodies, causes from the cosmic spheres follow us, causing us to be evil and thoroughly wicked, to seethe with desires and anger, to spend our lives in shameful deeds, and to be condemned to public lust through the prostitution of bodies offered for sale. [Col. 0834A]

But how can bodies unite themselves with incorporeal beings? Or how can things made by God, the First Principle, be handed over by weaker causes to the disfigurements of vice?

Are you willing, human beings, to lay aside your settled pride and haughtiness—you who claim God as your Father and contend that you possess an immortality identical with his? Are you willing to inquire, investigate, and search out what you yourselves are, whose you are, by what father you are considered to have been begotten, what you are doing in the world, by what principle you are born, and in what manner you spring forth into life? Are you willing, after laying aside partiality, to perceive in silent reflection that we are living creatures, either similar to the others or at least not separated from them by very great difference?

For what indicates that we differ from their likeness? Or what distinction in us is so great that we disdain to be enrolled among the number of living creatures? Their bodies are founded upon bones and bound together by the interconnection of sinews; and in a comparable manner our bodies too are founded upon bones and bound together by the interconnection of sinews. They draw air through their nostrils and return it in turn through breathing; we too draw breath in the same way and exhale it through repeated passages. [Col. 0835A]

They are divided into female and male kinds; we too were fashioned by our maker into the same number of sexes. They bring forth offspring through wombs and procreate through bodily unions; we too are born through the conjunction of bodies and are poured forth and discharged from our mothers’ wombs. They are sustained by food and drink and discharge and cast out their superfluous filth through the lower, rear passages; we too are sustained by food and drink, and pour out through the same channels what nature has now rejected.

They are all concerned to ward off deadly hunger and must keep watch over the acquisition of sustenance. What else are we doing amid the countless occupations of life except seeking the things by which the danger of hunger may be avoided and unhappy anxiety laid aside? They suffer diseases and starvation, and finally are dissolved by old age. Are we immune from these evils? Are we not likewise broken by the afflictions of disease and destroyed by the wasting of old age?

And if what is said in the more secret mysteries is also true—that the souls of the wicked enter cattle and other beasts after they have been stripped of human bodies—then it is still more clearly established that we are neighbors to them and are not set apart by very long intervals. For the same single thing belongs both to us and to them, through which we are called living creatures and exercise the movement of life.

> **Note: [Col. 0834B]** Thus Sabaeus. Others read: “but to lust.”
>
> **Note: [Col. 0834B]** Fulvius reads “join.”
>
> **Note: [Col. 0835C]** Fulvius reads “similarly.”
>
> **Note: [Col. 0835C]** Others read *fossibilibus*.

> **Note: [Col. 0835D]**
>
> **XVII.—Rational.** Cf. Cicero, *On Duties*, ch. 4. ELMENH.
>
> **Speechless creatures.** Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I, § 133: “Speechless animals that understand nothing.” Accordingly, *brutorum* (“brutes”) should not be read, as had previously occurred to me. ORELL.
>
> **Would not undertake shameful occupations.** Thus the first edition from the manuscript. Others read “perform.” ORELL.
>
> **Through perversity of judgment.** The Roman edition reads “through littleness.” ORELL.
>
> **Yet I should like to know.** Meursius conjectures *vellem tam scire*, elliptically. ORELL.
>
> **To fortify.** See above, on book I, ch. III. ORELL.
>
> **With rocks and crags.** Others wrongly read “themselves with rocks and crags.” ORELL.
>
> **Serving hands.** Thus Seneca, *To Marcia*, ch. 25. Compare Bunemann on Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 16, p. 1201. ORELL.
>
> **Would hammer out works with ingenious novelty.** Fulvius Ursinus conjectured *navitate* (“with diligence”). But there is no need for this correction. “Ingenious novelty” is an exquisite and elegant designation for an art that is always devising something new and unprecedented. For *excuderent* Stewechius prefers *excluderent*, citing a passage from Apuleius, *Florida* I: “Alexander proclaimed throughout his whole world that no one should rashly reproduce the king’s likeness in bronze, color, or engraving, but that Polyclitus alone should fashion it in bronze, Apelles alone delineate it in colors, and Pyrgoteles alone cut it in engraving.” Elmenhorst’s edition, p. 344, however, has *excluderet*. Stewechius likewise prefers “ingenious novelties,” that is, new things never previously seen by anyone. ORELL.
>
> **Nevertheless.** Fulvius Ursinus reads “and nevertheless,” which is more pleasing and could very easily have been swallowed up by the preceding word *novitate*. ORELL.

## XVII

But we are rational, and in intelligence we surpass every kind of speechless creature. I would believe that this was said with perfect truth if all human beings lived according to reason and deliberation, maintained the course of their duties, abstained from unlawful acts, and did not undertake shameful occupations; and if no one, through perversity of judgment and the blindness of ignorance, sought things contrary and hostile to himself.

Yet I should like to know what this reason is through which we are superior to every kind of animal. Is it because we have made dwellings for ourselves in which we can escape the cold of winter and the burning heat of summer? What then? Do other living creatures lack foresight in this matter? Do we not see some constructing dwellings for themselves, their nests, in the most suitable places; others, hanging aloft, sheltering and fortifying themselves with rocks and crags; still others excavating the soil of the earth and preparing shelters and sleeping places for themselves in dug-out hollows?

If mother Nature had wished to grant them serving hands as well, there would be no doubt that they too would construct the lofty summits of walls and hammer out works with ingenious novelty. Nevertheless, in the very things they make with their beaks and claws, we perceive many representations of reason and wisdom that we human beings cannot imitate by any reflection, although we possess hands that are craftsmen, artistic in every kind of accomplishment.

> **Note: [Col. 0836C]** Fulvius reads “we may be able.”
>
> **Note: [Col. 0836D]**
>
> **XVIII.—Those things are not gifts of knowledge, but inventions of most impoverished necessity.** Theocritus, *Idyll* XXI.1:
>
> “Poverty alone, Diophantus, awakens the arts;  
> she herself is the teacher of toil.”
>
> Virgil, *Georgics* I.145:
>
> “Then the various arts arose: relentless labor conquered  
> everything, and want pressing amid harsh circumstances.” ORELL.
>
> **[Col. 0837A] Or an age not equipped by experience of things.** Thus the first Roman edition. “A well-equipped age” is very good Latin for an age abounding in all things. So too “a well-equipped province,” ἡτοιμασμένη (“prepared”). Others read *partum*, which makes no sense. Fulvius Ursinus reads *peritum* (“experienced”). ORELL.
>
> **It prepared and fashioned the petty sciences of the arts.** I have printed this following Oudendorp’s most felicitous emendation on Apuleius, book VII, p. 466. The others read: “It fashioned small petty sciences.” ORELL.
>
> **Jointly amended.** Thus the Leiden editor from the manuscript, taking the word as referring to the preceding “certain chance occurrences.” But the reading should rather be *coemendatas*, referring to the “petty sciences.” The manuscript has *commendatas*. Stewechius reads *commodatas* (“adapted”); Fulvius Ursinus, *commentatas* (“devised”), which Meursius defends and explains in a passive sense, like several deponent verbs in our author—for example, above, “impending and not yet suffered,” where, however, as we have seen, the reading is doubtful. Later in the same book *ingredi* is similarly used: “For what removes from things undertaken the repentance of earlier people.” Likewise *metiri*: “The sun may be larger than the world and be measured at the width of one foot.” But Meursius himself retracts this conjecture in his Appendix and prefers *coemendata*, which the manuscript has. Arnobius, moreover, is very fond of compounds of this kind: thus *conscriptores* in book I; *condignum* in the preceding chapter; *condiscere* in book VI, ch. 4; *confieri* in book V, ch. 39; *cohonestare* several times. It is enough to have mentioned this once. ORELL.

## XVIII

Those animals do not know clothing, nor how to construct chairs, ships, and plows, nor, finally, the rest of the household equipment demanded by ordinary use. Those things are not gifts of knowledge, but inventions of most impoverished necessity.

The arts did not fall together with souls from the inner recesses of heaven. Rather, they were all sought out and born here on earth, and with the passage of time were gradually compounded through reflection. For if souls possessed the kinds of knowledge that it is fitting for a divine and immortal race to possess, all human beings would have known everything from the beginning. There would have been no age ignorant of any art or unequipped by experience of things.

As matters stand, however, needy life, lacking many things, observed that certain chance occurrences turned out rather advantageously; and while it imitated, experimented, and attempted—while it went astray, corrected, and altered—it prepared and fashioned for itself, through continual correction, the petty sciences of the arts, and after jointly amending them over many ages brought them to a single finished outcome.

> **Note: [Col. 0837C]**
### XIX.—“But if human beings thoroughly knew either themselves.”

Stewechius’s conjecture, reading *penitius* from *penite*, is attractive; we find the latter in Catullus, *Epithalamium of Julia and Manlius*, verse 176:

> No less in that one than in you,  
> Deep within the inmost breast,  
> A flame is burning—but more deeply (*penite*).

Plautus certainly has the superlative *penitissime* several times, and Sidonius, book IV, epistle 9: “And I examined his daily actions most thoroughly (*penitissime*).” Compare Laurenberg, *Antiquar.*, under this word. ORELL.

**“That he is something magnificent.”** Thus the manuscript codex. Gelenius has *nosse*, followed by all the other editors except the Leiden edition—not badly. ORELL.

**“Little gratings.”** Arnobius uses the diminutive here, as below in “little cloaks” and “little axes,” by way of contempt. ORELL.

**“Basins” (*trulleos*).** Thus the manuscript codex. Others read *trullas*. But Varro distinguishes them in *On the Latin Language*, book IV, p. 34, Bipont edition: “The *trulleum* resembles the *trulla* in shape, except that it holds more water and its handle is not hollow—unless a wine-ladle (*vinaria trulla*) is meant.” See Turnebus’s note there, p. 86, and Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. Nonius, *On the Kinds of Vessels or Cups*, p. 547, Mercer edition: “A *trulleum*, in which the hands are washed” (basin). “We call its little pitcher an *aquaemanale*, because water is poured from it into the *tralleum*” (ewer). Pliny, *Natural History* XXXIV, 2, has the masculine *trulleus*. ORELL.

**“And mixing-bowls.”** If Nonius Marcellus, chapter 19, is to be believed, *craterae* are vessels for wine, whereas *crateres* are vessels for oil; and he attempts to prove both points from Virgil’s authority. NOURR., p. 554.—But *crateras* here is the Greek accusative of the noun *crater*, κρατήρ (*kratēr*, “mixing-bowl”). Fulvius Ursinus therefore made an excellent correction [Col. 0838A], for what follows—“undergarments,” etc.—requires a substantive here as well. The first edition and Gelenius read: “and made the other things.” ORELL.

[Col. 0838B] **“Undergarments” (*subuculas*).** The glosses: “*Subucula*, ὑποδύτης, ὑποχιτών”—an undergarment worn directly (*ἀμέσως*, “immediately”) against the body; it was also called an *interula*. The tunic was woolen, while the *interula* or *subucula* was linen. Horace, *Epistles* I, 1, verse 4:

> A worn undergarment lies beneath a freshly brushed tunic.

Nonius, under *subucula*, quoting Varro’s *On the Life of the Roman People*, book I: “After they began to have two tunics apiece, they established the practice of calling the lower one a *subucula* or *indusium*.” Compare Salmasius, who discusses this word at length, on Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, pp. 378 ff.; the distinguished Boettiger, in the work entitled *Sabina, or Morning Scenes in the Dressing Room of a Wealthy Roman Woman*, p. 375, distinguishes two kinds of *interula* or inner tunic: the *subucula* of men and the *interula* of women. Compare Ferrarius, *On Clothing* III, 1, p. 175; Rosinus, *Roman Antiquities* V, chapter 35; and G. J. Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under this word. ORELL.

**“Upper garments” (*suppara*).** Festus: “The *supparus* was the name of a linen garment for girls, which is also called the *subucula*.” See the interpreters there. Varro, however, clearly distinguishes them in *On the Latin Language*, book IV, p. 37, Bipont edition: “One garment is worn underneath (*subtus*), whence *subucula*; the other above (*supra*), whence *suppara*, except that this is the Oscan name for it.” See especially Gisbert Cuper, *Observations* IV, chapter 17, who most carefully compares every passage in the ancient authors concerning *suppara* and demonstrates that the *suppara* was a kind of tunic—indeed, an outer tunic—furnished with very short sleeves, which covered only the shoulders, or rested chiefly upon the shoulders, and was fastened by a brooch. Compare Salmasius on Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, p. 209, and Vossius, *Roman Etymology*. ORELL.

**“Mantles” (*laenas*).** Festus: “The *laena* is a kind of garment of double thickness. Some think its name Etruscan, others Greek, from what they call χλαῖνα (*chlaina*, ‘cloak’).” ELMENH.—The *laena*, then, was a toga thicker than other garments; hence Varro thinks it was so called from its abundance of wool (*lana*), since it was equivalent to two togas, *On the Latin Language*, book IV, p. 37—but incorrectly, for the word comes from the Greek χλαῖνα. See Popma on Varro, note, p. 94. ORELL.

**“Little cloaks” (*lacernulas*).** The *lacerna* was a close-fitting military garment resembling the *paenula*, encircling the body and, as it were, enclosing it tightly; it was dark-colored. See Festus under this word, and especially Justus Lipsius, *On the Pronunciation of the Latin Language*, chapter 3, p. 15, and *Selections* I, chapter 13, p. 683, vol. I, Wesel edition. It was a garment of the poor common people, and even of slaves. ORELL.

**“Robes of state” (*trabeas*).** “The *trabea* is the garment of senators,” says Papias. ELMENH. Rather, of the equestrian order. (Indeed, of the consuls themselves in Arnobius’s time. See the authors cited by Ph. Pareus in *Selections from Symmachus*, p. 64.) See Lipsius on Tacitus, *Annals* III, 2; Rubenius, *On the Broad Stripe* I, 5; Ferrarius, *On Clothing*, part I, book II, chapter 6. The *trabea* was a garment woven with purple stripes, to distinguish in the colonies a member of the equestrian order from a commoner. ORELL.

**“Raised up by conceit and arrogance.”** Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis* III, chapter 3: “He will also make them puffed up and raised aloft by a spirit of pride”; and VI, chapter 17: “They too are raised aloft by an exalted spirit of pride.” HERALD.

[Col. 0839B] **“Because they produced grammar, music, and rhetoric.”** Meursius, p. 57, conjectures that one should read: “Because they discovered grammar, music, and rhetoric,” since Arnobius immediately adds: “so that from their invention souls may be believed to be superior.” ORELL.

**“To surpass in dignity and substance.”** *Substantia* here is equivalent to “their spiritual nature,” or perhaps “stability” and “perpetuity.” Although I lack examples of this meaning, I do not doubt that writers of later Latin used *substantia* in this sense, since the verb *subsistere* frequently occurs in the sense of “to stand firm” or “to endure.” *Praeterire* is equivalent to “surpass,” as often; Martial XII, 36:

> There is no glory in surpassing little asses.

**“For what else do they profess either to be able to communicate or to impart?”** See above, on book I, chapter 63. ORELL.

**“So that we may measure the expanses of the lands.”** Here Arnobius uses *continentia* in the sense of περιοχή (*periochē*, “extent, compass”), as the Philoxenian Glosses interpret it, just as Lucretius uses *retinentia* for κατοχή (*katochē*, “retention”). Book III, verse 675: “So that all retention of past events has fallen away.” HERALD.—Among writers of that age *continentia* very often means “that which is contained.” Thus Fulgentius’s book is entitled *On the Content of Virgil*; see Muncker there, *Latin Mythographers*, p. 137, vol. II. Aptly for our passage, Aethicus, *Cosmography*, preface: “And thus within thirty-two years the whole circuit of the earth was traversed by surveyors, and a report concerning its entire contents was conveyed to the senate.” ORELL.

**“Nor that divine, learned souls.”** Thus the manuscript codex and the first edition. Fulvius Ursinus reads *divinitus eruditas*, “divinely instructed.” This is not bad, but *divinas* can stand if we explain it either as “proceeding from God” or as “immortal,” as below, chapter 62: “to become divine souls and to be removed from the laws of mortality.” We have observed above that Arnobius likes to place together adjectives of this kind without a conjunction. Thomas Canter conjectures *divine eruditas*, “divinely instructed.” ORELL.

**“That not all are learned, that not all can learn, and that there are among them....”** Thus Gelenius, followed by the other editors except Heraldus, who defends the old reading: “... can, so that they are,” or conjectures that *cur sint* (“why they are”) should be read, explaining *cur* as “because,” as in Sidonius I, epistle 1: “For this reason all the other members of Frontinianus’s family, imitating him as naturally belonging to his school, because they reproduced his drowsy style of speech, called him the ape of the orators.” But Gelenius is right, for copyists very frequently interchange *ut* and *et*. ORELL.

**“Dullards” (*bardi*).** Meursius and the Leiden editor have excellently restored this from the manuscript. The common reading is *tardi*, “slow.” Festus says: “A *bardus*, a fool, is so called from slowness of intellect.... It is derived from the Greek term βάρδεις (*bardeis*) used by them.” Compare Nonius. Thus Cicero, *On Fate*, chapter 5: “Zopyrus the physiognomist ... said that Socrates was stupid and dull (*bardum*).” See Turnebus there. ORELL.

**“For the pursuit of learning.”** I do not know what came into the mind of the Leiden editor, who not only maintained *discedendi* (“of departing”) in his booklet of variant readings, but even thrust it into the text. ORELL.

**“But if it were established that the things we learn are recollections.”** This was Plato’s doctrine: he asserted that human souls had lived before putting on bodies, and said that when they entered new bodies again, they did not learn anything new but merely recognized what they had already learned. See Plato in the *Meno* and *Phaedo*, p. 73, H. Stephanus edition; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I; Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 23. Augustine, *On the Trinity* X, chapter 15, and Theophilus, *To Autolycus* III, refute him. ELMENH.

**“But to learn things born here.”** Fulvius Ursinus reads “born to learn.” But nothing should be changed, for there follows “and, having become firmly established through conjectures,” that is, strengthened and confirmed by them. Thus Tacitus, *Annals* XIII, chapter 26: “disrespect firmly established together with liberty”; and XIV, 1: “boldness firmly established by the antiquity of their rule.” There Ernesti observes that the metaphor is taken from trees and plants, which are said to “become firmly established” (*coalescere*) when their roots have adhered to the earth and they cannot be torn out. ORELL.]

### XIX

But if human beings thoroughly knew either themselves or gained some apprehension of God from even the faintest breath of conjecture, they would never claim for themselves a divine and immortal nature. Nor would they think themselves something magnificent because they had made for themselves little gratings, basins, and mixing-bowls; undergarments, upper garments, mantles, little cloaks, robes of state, knives, cuirasses, and swords; rakes, little axes, and a plowshare.

Never, I say, raised up by conceit and arrogance, would they believe themselves to be the foremost [Col. 0839A] divine powers and equal to the supremacy of the ruler because they had produced [Note: [Col. 0839B] “discovered,” Fulvius] grammar, music, rhetoric, and geometrical formulas. We do not see what is so wonderful in these arts that, because of their invention, souls should be believed superior to the sun and all the stars, and to surpass in both dignity and substance this entire world, of which those things are parts.

For what else do they profess either to be able to communicate or to impart, except that we may learn the rules governing words and their distinctions; the intervals between vocal sounds; how to speak persuasively in lawsuits; and how to measure the expanses of the lands? If souls had brought these things with them from the divine regions, and if it were necessary to know them, everyone everywhere in the world would long ago have practiced them. No race [Col. 0839B] of human beings would be found that was not equally and uniformly instructed in all these things.

But as matters now stand, how few people in the world are musicians, dialecticians, or geometers; how few are orators, poets, or grammarians! From this it is apparent, as has been said rather often, that these things were invented under the compulsion of particular places and times, and that divine, learned souls did not fly down here. For not [Col. 0840A] all souls are learned; not all can learn; and among them there are very many whose intellectual sharpness is rather blunt, who are dullards, and who have to be driven to the pursuit of learning [Note: [Col. 0839B] “to learn thoroughly,” Fulvius. See the Note] by the coercion of beatings.

But if it were established that the things we learn are recollections, as was held in ancient systems of thought, then, since we all came from a single truth, it would be fitting for us all to know one thing and to recollect one thing, and not to hold differing, numerous, and mutually conflicting opinions. But since, as matters stand, each of us asserts one thing or another, it is clear and evident that we brought nothing down from heaven, but learn things born here and defend things that have become firmly established through conjectures.

[Note: [Col. 0840D]

### XX.—“Not excessively hot in heat.”

Thomas Canter corrected the passage thus. The manuscript codex reads: “Do not seethe excessively in heat.” Meursius conjectures that either *incalore* should be read as a single word, just as *injuventus* occurs in book I for *juventus*—although the reading there is suspect—or “not seething excessively in heat,” with the *in* being redundant, as it is more than once in Apuleius, for example “advanced in years” and “a jar of wine precious in age.” Fulvius Ursinus reads: “not seething with excessive heat.” ORELL.

[Col. 0841B] **“But let something spurious be produced.”** The meaning is that light should not be received plainly, but should creep in from elsewhere through little cracks, so that it cannot be called true light but counterfeit and νοθεῖον (*notheion*, “spurious”). Thus Lucretius, concerning the moon, book V, verse 575:

> And whether the moon is borne along, surveying places with borrowed light,  
> [Col. 0841C] Or casts forth her own radiance from her own body,  
> Whatever the case, she is borne along with no greater form.

And Catullus, poem 34, verse 15:

> You, powerful Trivia, are also  
> Called Moon from borrowed light.

PRIOR. Others read *novum*, “new.” The manuscript codex has *notum*, “known.” *Nothum*, “spurious,” is Scaliger’s emendation. ORELL.

**“By winding turns” (*inflexibus*).** Thus Stewechius, followed by the Leiden editor. It derives from *inflexus, -us*, used for *inflexio*, “a bending,” just as *commutatus* is used for *commutatio*. Lucretius I, verse 803, has *opinatus* for *opinio*; likewise IV, 466; *conjectus* for *conjectio*, book V, verse 417; *declinatus* for *declinatio* several times in Varro’s *On the Latin Language*; and *fissus* for *fissio* in Manilius, book I. See Tennulius on the preface to Frontinus’s *Strategems* I, p. 3, Oudendorp edition, where he has collected further examples. Others read “by inflections.” Arntzenius, on Nazarius’s *Panegyric to Constantine*, chapter V, §6, conjectures that one should read: “by circuitous bends.” ORELL.]

### XX

And to show you more clearly and plainly the value of a human being—whom you believe to be exceedingly similar to the higher power—form this image in your minds. By assuming a hypothetical case, let us regard something which could be done if we attempted it just as though we had actually attempted it.

Let us therefore have a habitable place excavated in the earth, constructed in the form of a sleeping chamber and enclosed by roof and walls. Let it be neither freezing with cold nor excessively hot in heat, but so temperate and moderate [Col. 0841A] that it experiences neither the sensation of winter cold [Note: [Col. 0841B] Fulvius adds “winter”] nor the fierce heat of summer.

Into this place let absolutely no sound of any voice penetrate: neither bird, beast, storm, human being, nor, finally, any crash whatsoever or the terrifying peal of the heavens. Let us next devise a way for it to receive light—not from fire brought inside, nor from a visible sun, but let something spurious be produced which, with darkness interposed, counterfeits the semblance of light. Let there not be a single door or a direct entrance; let it be approached by circuitous winding turns, and let it never be opened except when necessary reason requires it.

[Note: [Col. 0841D]

### XXI.—“Now, since we have prepared a dwelling for the imagined figure, let us next take someone just born into the lodging of that place, which contains nothing and is bare and empty, though he be of Platonic or Pythagorean stock, or descended from any of those said to have possessed divine intellectual acuteness or to have been declared wisest by responses of the gods.”

The passage is not only exceedingly dislocated but also mutilated. I restore and supplement it as follows: “Now, since we have prepared a dwelling for the imagined figure, let us next take someone just born, though he be of Platonic or Pythagorean stock, or descended from any of those said to have possessed divine intellectual acuteness or to have been declared wisest by responses of the gods, and shut him within the lodging of that place, which is bare and empty.” The sense demanded the final word, which I have added. MEURS., p. 58.—But everything was sound, provided that for *licet* (“though”) we read *scilicet* (“that is to say”). ORELL.

**“For the imagined figure” (*imagini*).** That is, for the human being conceived and fashioned in imagination—the ideal figure. ORELL.

**“And let her not part her mouth and lips to form any utterances.”** Thus Fulvius Ursinus, followed by the Leiden edition. This correction comes very close to the manuscript’s reading, “in the speech of someone,” which cannot stand, because no one except the single nurse was permitted to approach the infant. Gelenius reads: “to form any utterance.” Heraldus: “and let her not part her mouth ... for conversation.” ORELL.

[Col. 0842C] **“Let them be brought in.”** Thus Meursius and Salmasius. Others have: “let it be brought in.” ORELL.

**“But either *fitilla* made from millet.”** The Leiden editor restored this excellently. Previously the reading was “let it be that,” which agrees poorly with what follows, “or let there be bread made from spelt,” for bread is not the material from which food is made, but spelt or flour is. Moreover, the following substantives—bread, acorns ... and berries—seem to demand some substantive in the first member as well. One should therefore read *fitilla*, that is, a kind of porridge used in sacred rites. Our author uses it below, book VII, chapter 24: “What is *fitilla*? What is *frumen*?” etc. Pliny, *Natural History* XVIII, chapter 8: “Even today ancient sacred rites and birthday ceremonies are performed with *fitilla* porridge.” Compare Muretus, *Various Readings* XII, chapter 1, and Gesner in the *Thesaurus*, who discusses this word and its etymology at length. ORELL.

**“Acorns from hot ashes.”** That is, acorns roasted in hot ashes, according to the Greek construction. Homer, *Odyssey* XIX, verse 536:

> Χῆνές μοι κατὰ οἶκον ἐείκοσι πυρὸν ἔδουσιν  
> Ἐξ ὕδατος.

> “I have twenty geese about the house, and they eat grain  
> Out of the water.”

HERALD.

**“Untouched by the heat of fire.”** That hot water was customarily mixed with drinks is confirmed by the well-known passage of Horace, book III, ode 19:

> At what price shall we purchase  
> A jar of Chian wine? Who will temper water with fire?

On this the ancient commentator Acron writes: “For the Greeks were accustomed to temper their wines with warmed water.” Poorer people also, who drank water, were accustomed to heat the water itself. MEURS., p. 59.

**“Nor will appetite extend any farther, since it does not know that there is anything more to be sought.”** Thus Fulvius Ursinus and Meursius; the manuscript codex and first edition read “will be corrected.” “Since it does not know” refers to appetite; but it would, I think, be better to read “since he does not know,” referring to the boy. ORELL.

[Col. 0843B] **“Assumed on the basis of a deceptive expectation.”** *Frustrabilis* is equivalent to “deceptive,” possessing the active force “capable of frustrating.” The word is Arnobian. Thus below, book VI, chapter 22: “And to do other deceptive things in an empty imagining of desire.” ORELL.]

### XXI

Now, since we have prepared a dwelling for the imagined figure, let us next take someone just born into the lodging of that place, which contains nothing and is bare and empty—though he be of Platonic or Pythagorean stock, [Col. 0841B] or descended from any one of those said to have possessed divine intellectual acuteness or to have been declared wisest by responses of the gods.

Once this has been done, it follows that he must be nourished and raised with suitable sustenance. Let us therefore also employ a nurse who always approaches him naked and always silent, uttering no word and not parting her mouth and lips to form any utterances. After she has given him her breasts and performed the attendant duties, let her leave him to rest and remain day and night outside the closed doors. For the situation will often require nursing care to be present and to watch for his needs at the appropriate times.

But when the infant begins to need support from more solid foods, let them be brought in by the same nurse, with her clothing removed, as we have said, and her unbroken silence maintained. The food brought in must always be one and the same, differing in no respect in its substance and never renewed with varied flavors: either *fitilla* made from millet, bread made from spelt, or—so that we may imitate the ancient diet—acorns roasted in hot ashes or berries from wild branches.

Let a drink of wine remain wholly unknown. To quench his [Col. 0842B] thirst, let nothing be offered except pure liquid from springs, untouched by the heat of fire and, if possible, supplied in the hollow of the hands. For habitual practice will become familiar and, through custom, be transformed into nature; nor will appetite extend any farther, since it does not know that there is anything more to be sought.

[Col. 0843A] [Note: [Col. 0843B]

### XXII.—“And if it is true that he is so joyful a portion of the principal substance and lives here after being derived from the fountains of life.”

The manuscript’s reading was: “a portion now joyful,” incorrectly. Gelenius and most of the editors following him read: “a portion of the substance and from the fountains,” entirely deleting the words “now joyful.” The Leiden editor was the first to restore them to the text, reading “so joyful.” I am especially pleased, however, by Stewechius’s conjecture, “so choice a portion,” that is, in Horace’s words [Col. 0843C], “a particle of the divine breath.” *Principalis* means “divine,” proceeding from the supreme ruler, as it does several times in Arnobius. The omission of the conjunction *and*, which this writer often leaves out, should not trouble the reader. *Agere* here is equivalent to *degere*, “to live.” ORELL.

**“Lifetime” (*aevitatem*).** Nonius, under the word *aevum*: “*Aevum* is neuter; *aevitas* feminine.” Varro, in his *Tithonus: On Old Age*: “Where the final boundary of the allotted lifetime has touched the outermost limit.” Our author below, book V, chapter 8: “If confidence is to be placed in this statement, the Great Mother too must be said to have her lifetime enclosed within the limits of this number.” ORELL.

**“More obtuse than wood or stone.”** Plautus in the *Braggart Soldier*:

> My master is covered with an elephant’s hide, not his own,  
> And possesses no more wisdom than a stone.

“Stone” is therefore an insult common to Greeks and Latins, with which they assail stupid and intellectually obtuse people. Aristophanes in the *Clouds*: λίθοι, ἀριθμοί, πρόβατα—“stones, numbers, sheep.” HERALD.

**“An elephant or a mule.”** Thus the Leiden editor, following Stewechius’s highly probable correction. Only quadrupeds are named here, just as below in a very similar passage, chapter 52: “Whence come elephants, bulls, deer, mules, and asses?” Others read: “an elephant or a kite.” ORELL.]

### XXII

To what, then, do these things tend? Since souls have been believed to be divine and therefore [Note: [Col. 0843B] “and from God,” Sab., with the approval of the Leiden editor] immortal, and to fly into human bodies together with all branches of learning, let us test through the person whom we have chosen to raise in this manner whether the claim possesses credibility, or whether it has been lightly believed and assumed on the basis of a deceptive expectation.

Let the man, therefore, who has been raised in hidden solitude come forth before us at whatever age you wish. Do you wish him to be twenty? Thirty? Better still, when he has completed forty years, let him be brought into the society of mortals. And if it is true that he is so joyful a portion of the principal substance and lives here after being derived from the fountains of life, then, before he receives knowledge of anything or is instructed in human speech, let him answer when asked who he himself is, who his father is, in what regions [Col. 0843B] he was born, in what manner or by what means [Col. 0844A] he was nourished, and in the performance of what work or business he passed the lifetime already gone by.

Will he not stand there more obtuse and insensible than every beast, than wood or stone? When thrust among unfamiliar things never previously known to him, will he not, before all else, be ignorant of his very self [Note: [Col. 0843B] Thus the manuscript. Sabinus reads “to be”]? If you ask him, will he be able to indicate what the sun is, the earth, seas, stars, clouds, mist, rains, thunder, snow, or hail? Will he be able to know what trees, herbs, or grasses are; what a bull, horse, or ram is; what a camel, elephant, or mule is?

[Note: [Col. 0843D]

### XXIII.—“Must-cake” (*mustacium*)

Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 125, teaches that a *mustacium* or *mustaceum* is made from fine wheat flour sprinkled with must, together with anise, cumin, fat, cheese, and shavings from a laurel twig. Juvenal sings, Satire VII, 201:

> There is no reason for you to waste a dinner and must-cakes.

The scholiast annotates this verse as follows: “Sweet foods sprinkled with must, customarily served at the end of the banquet during wedding feasts.” See Erasmus, *Chiliades* IV, century 9, adage 87. NOURR., p. 559.—A *mustacius*, or rather *mustaceus*, was a cake or kind of pastry made from must. Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 121, teaches how to prepare it: “Make must-cakes as follows. Sprinkle one modius of fine wheat flour with must. Add anise, cumin, two pounds of fat, one pound of cheese, and shavings scraped from a laurel twig. When you have shaped them, place laurel leaves underneath them when you bake them.” Compare Palladius, October, chapter XXI, whose directions differ somewhat from Cato’s, and Schneider there. Hardouin, on Pliny, *Natural History* XV, chapter 30, observes that must-cakes were light foods customarily offered to those with rather weak stomachs. See also G. J. Vossius in the *Roman Etymological Dictionary*. ORELL.

**“Artichoke” (*carduum*).** The cultivated thistle or *cinara* (artichoke) is meant. The distinguished Schneider discusses it at length on Columella, book X, *On the Cultivation of Gardens*, verse 235, pp. 529 ff. ORELL.

**“In what condition each particular thing ought to be in order to serve as food.”** Thus the Leiden editor successfully emended the text. The sense is: in what condition each particular thing ought to be so that it can be eaten. The others read: “In what condition each particular thing ought to be. And for himself.” ORELL.

**“If you make a very large fire ... will he not go through the midst of the flames?”** Compare the very acute Kant in his *Anthropology*, p. 317, where he is in the closest agreement with Arnobius. ORELL.

**“Solifugae.”** Thus all editions, but with Stewechius one should rather read *solipugae*, mentioned by Pliny, *Natural History* XXIX, chapter 4 (29 in Hardouin’s edition): “There is also a kind of venomous ant, not generally found in Italy. Cicero calls them *solipugae*, while Baetica calls them *salpugae*.” Some codices there also have *solifugae*. The same author, book XXII, final chapter: “Venomous little creatures also breed in legumes, which sting the hands and endanger life, belonging to the genus of *solipugae*.” See Hardouin on Pliny VIII, 11, 88, p. 491; Lucan, *Pharsalia* IX, 837:

> What *salpuga* has feared to tread upon your hiding places?

Festus: “The *solipunga* is a kind of harmful little creature, so named because it becomes fiercer and more active through the heat of the sun.” Solinus, however, *Polyhistor*, chapter 4: “Sardinia is indeed free from serpents, but what the serpent is in other places, the *solifuga* is in the Sardinian countryside. It is a very tiny animal shaped like a spider and is called *solifuga* because it flees the sun.”

Salmasius, who discusses this little animal at length in *Plinian Exercises*, pp. 70–71, thinks it denotes the tarantula, peculiar to Apulia, which creeps unexpectedly from cavities in the ground and, at the height of summer, brings destruction upon harvesters. Vossius, *On Idolatry* IV, chapter 96, thinks that *solifuga* and *solipugna* mean precisely the same thing, the *p* having been changed to *f* according to ancient orthography. Thus Πύγελα (*Pygela*), from πυγή (*pygē*), becomes Latin *Fugela*; πείθω (*peithō*) becomes *fido*; from πόρος (*poros*) comes *forare*; *fungus* from σπόγγος (*spongos*); *figo* from πήγω (*pēgō*); *fere* from περί (*peri*); and so forth.

It seems to me that several different venomous little animals were designated by this name in ancient writers. By the *solifuga* of Arnobius, Solinus, and Pliny, as also the Baetican *salpuga*, I understand a venomous member of the spider family, of which the tarantula is one species. But the *solipugae* or φαλάγγια (*phalangia*, “venomous spiders”) which, according to Pliny, *Natural History* VIII, chapter 29; Aelian, *On the Nature of Animals* XVII, chapter 40; and Diodorus Siculus, *Library* III, chapter 29, destroyed an entire people on the nearer side of the Cynomolgi of Ethiopia, I take either, with the distinguished Schneider in his commentary on the cited passage of Aelian, to be that spiderlike *phalangium* very precisely described by the celebrated Pallas in *Zoological Miscellany*, fascicle IX, p. 37, which possesses crablike pincers at its mouth and with them injects an extremely potent venom into wounds; or, preferably, to be that little animal belonging to the ant family which Linnaeus calls *Termes fatale*, the scourge of both Indies, *die weisse Ameise* (“the white ant”), an excellent description of which may be found in E. A. W. Zimmermann’s *Almanac of Travels*, part I, pp. 163–182. ORELL.

**“Will he likewise be able, etc.?”** Should one not read: “Will he be capable of, etc.?” ORELL.

**“For the use of what function they are adapted? Let him indicate for what forms of dress....”** Salmasius punctuated the passage in this way, entirely correctly, for “let him indicate” must be connected with what follows. Others punctuate: “Let him indicate for the use of what function they are adapted?” Meursius reads: “Let him judge?” ORELL.

**“Covering cloth” (*vestis stragula*).** Livy XXXIX, 7: “For the origin of foreign luxury was brought into the city by the army from Asia. They first brought to Rome couches ornamented with bronze, costly covering cloths, hangings and other woven fabrics, and the objects then considered magnificent furniture—one-legged tables and sideboards.”

On this Marcellus Donatus, in Gronovius’s edition, p. 513, vol. III, writes: “When the term *stragulum* is used absolutely, I believe it includes not only bedcovers, but also tapestries and other kinds of woven cloth or fabric worked with various figures and colors of animals and plants. For this reason Plautus calls them *belluata*, ‘adorned with beasts,’ and Tibullus I, 2, verse 77 calls them *picta*, ‘pictured.’ But if we use the expression *vestis stragula*, with the additional word *vestis*, an article of dress or garment must undoubtedly be understood, though one of the same general kind.” ORELL.

**“Mitre” (*mitra*).** A band with which the hair was tied back. Its use was more frequent among barbarians than among Greeks. Among the Romans it was an ornament of old women and prostitutes, and sometimes also of men, though effeminate ones; hence it was an attribute of Bacchus. See J. G. Graevius, *Readings in Hesiod*, chapter 23; Turnebus, *Adversaria* IV, chapter 14; Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises on Solinus*, p. 392; Dempster, *Supplement to Rosinus’s Roman Antiquities* V, chapter 35; Ernesti, *Ciceronian Lexicon*, under this word; and Doering on Catullus, poem LXIV, verse 63. ORELL.

**“Breast-band” (*strophium*).** A little band with which women restrained their breasts, or rather a girdle or embroidered sash with which women bound up the chest and in which they often kept letters and other small articles. See Nonius under this word; Ernesti, *Ciceronian Lexicon*; Doering on Catullus, poem LXIV, verse 65; and especially the distinguished Boettiger, who discusses this word more fully in *Sabina*, pp. 73, 162, 172, and 376. ORELL.

**“Bandage” (*fascia*).** *Fasciae* or *fasciolae* were ornaments for the arms, legs, and joints. Among the Romans they were first used by the sick and weak, from whom their use was afterwards adopted by delicate and effeminate men. Horace, *Satires* II, 3, verse 254:

> Put away the emblems of disease—  
> Your little bandages, elbow-pad, and neck-wrap.

See Casaubon, who discusses them at length, on Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 82; and Dempster, *Supplement to Rosinus’s Roman Antiquities* V, chapter 35, pp. 927 ff., Schott edition. Here *fascia* seems preeminently to mean a band for the foot or lower leg, which among the Romans served in place of our stockings (*Strümpfe*). ORELL.

**“Handkerchief” (*muccinium*).** A nosecloth—that is, linen in which they caught the mucus from the nose. See Turnebus, *Adversaria* XIII, chapter 14; Barthius, *Adversaria* XIV, chapter 9, p. 2004 (*mouchoir*, “handkerchief”). ORELL.

**“Mantle” (*laena*).** See above, on chapter 19. ORELL.

**“Nightcap” (*calantica*).** Thus the manuscript. A covering for the head used by women. Boettiger, *Sabina*, p. 123, teaches that it was worn only in bed at night and was made from an ox’s bladder, adducing Martial VIII, epigram 23:

> [Col. 0846B] A stronger bladder preserves the curled hair.

Compare Salmasius on Solinus, p. 392. Hadrianus Junius interprets it as a woman’s head-covering hanging down as far as the shoulders, called *chaperon* by the French. Gelenius reads *tunica*. Others read *caletica*; Meursius, *calautica*. Compare Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under *Calantica*. Boettiger discusses the *calantica*, the Greek κεκρύφαλος (*kekryphalos*, “hair-net”), at length in the work entitled *The Aldobrandini Wedding*, pp. 79 and 150.—But that the correct spelling is *calautica*, not *calantica*, is evident from the recently discovered fragments of Cicero’s speech against Publius Clodius and Curio, edited by Angelo Mai at Milan in 1815. There, on p. 21, at the words “when a *calautica* was fitted to his head,” the ancient scholiast—Asconius himself, as Mai thinks—observes: “The *calautica* ... was the name given to a kind of covering with which women veiled their heads.” Afranius too mentions it in *The Female Cousins*, speaking as follows: “with mitres and *calauticae*.” Compare the very learned Mai’s note there. ORELL.

**“Towel” (*mantele*).** Virgil, *Georgics* IV, 376:

> In due order her sisters give him clear spring-water for his hands  
> And bring towels with their nap shorn.

See Heyne there, and Vossius, who discusses them at length, pp. 854 ff. *Mantelia* (χειρόμακτρα, *cheiromaktra*, “hand-towels”) were therefore cloths not of wool, as Heyne thought, but of linen; they nevertheless had a nap—*roh, zottig, gewalkt* (“coarse, shaggy, fulled”)—though the fluff upon the fabric’s surface was shorn, so that they were smooth and soft for drying the hands. Compare Boettiger, *Sabina*, p. 364. ORELL.

**“Mastruca.”** Isidore, *Origins* XIX, chapter 23, says: “The *mastruca* is a Germanic garment made from the small skins of wild beasts. Cicero says of it in his speech *For Scaurus*: ‘The man whom royal purple did not move was transformed by the *mastruca* of the Sardinians,’” etc. Cicero likewise, *On the Consular Provinces*, chapter 7: “An exploit was performed in Sardinia against little brigands clad in *mastrucae* by a propraetor with a single auxiliary cohort.” See Abramus there, who compares all the passages with the greatest care. Compare J. Lipsius on Tacitus, *Germania*, chapter 17, p. 546, Oberlin edition. Turnebus, *Adversaria* XX, chapter 9, and Ernesti, *Ciceronian Lexicon*, explain the *mastruca* as a garment sewn from the skins of *musmones* or *musimones* (mouflons). On this animal peculiar to Sardinia, see Aelian, *History of Animals* XVI, 34, and the distinguished Schneider there. ORELL.

**“Slipper, sandal, shoe.”** Salmasius explains the distinction excellently on Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, pp. 353–357 and 382 ff. Shoes (*calcei*) covered the whole foot, both below and above; sandals (*soleae*) covered only the sole of the foot, leaving the upper part bare; the *soccus* was a lower and looser kind of shoe, worn by women and also by men, though effeminate ones, and especially by comic actors—whence the proverb “from the slipper to the tragic buskin.” Compare Balduinus, *On the Shoe*, chapter 16; Boettiger, *Sabina*, pp. 372 ff.; and especially Rost and Wichmann, *The Antiquities of Greece and Rome in Pictures*, fascicle I, pp. 13 ff. ORELL.

[Col. 0847A] **“What a wheel is.”** Thus the first edition, followed by the Leiden edition. Others, following Ludovicus de la Cerda’s correction on Virgil, *Georgics* I, 160, read *traha*, “drag-sledge,” a reading which by no means deserves contempt. For Virgil joins the terms in *Georgics* I, verse 164: “Threshing-sledges and drags, and the rake with its unequal weight.” On this Servius comments: “The *traha*, as some say, is a plank customarily drawn by oxen across a threshing floor to gather fodder.” Compare Varro, *On Agriculture*, chapter 25; Columella II, chapter 21. ELMENH. and ORELL.

**“Threshing-sledges” (*tribula*).** Servius on the cited passage of Virgil: “The *tribula* is a kind of vehicle toothed on every side, by means of which grain is carried”—read “threshed”—“and which was used especially in Africa.” Vossius, p. 95, explains it very well: “The *tribulum*, or Punic *plostellum*, the threshing-frame, was a vehicle made from planks whose low wheels, according to Jerome on Isaiah 28:27, were fitted with iron teeth like a saw. The *trahea*, or drag-sledge, was a plank fitted with teeth of stone or iron and lacking wheels. Both, weighted down by the driver or by a load, as Varro I, 52 states, were drawn over the ears of grain by beasts of burden in order to crush them. Threshing is still performed in this way in Italy or in Eastern countries.”

Moreover, Latin authors use *tribula* and *tribulum* indiscriminately. Columella, like our author in the cited passage, has the feminine; Virgil and others use the neuter in the plural. Compare Gataker, *Critical Works*, vol. I, p. 270, who discusses this word at length. ORELL.

[Col. 0847C] **Cask (*cupa*).** *Cupae* were round wooden vessels for transporting wine (German: *Tanse, Kufe*, “vat, cask”). Since these vessels were rather large, they were set upright and covered with lids, which Nonius mentions from Varro. They stored not only wine in them but also wheat and similar commodities, as the jurists teach. Smaller vessels, resembling *dolia*, were closed at both ends and suitable for carrying wine from place to place. Thus Casaubon, on Julius Capitolinus’ *The Two Maximini*, *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. II, p. 52. Cf. Salmasius on the same authors; Vossius, *Roman Etymology*; the distinguished Schneider, *Observations on Palladius, On Agriculture*, book I, title XVIII, p. 25; and Gesner, in the *Thesaurus*. ORELLI.

**Oil-press (*trapetum*).** An olive mill or machine for crushing or pressing olives. For a lucid description and illustration of it, see the distinguished Schneider’s excursus on Cato, *On Agriculture*, vol. I, part II, pp. 610 ff. Compare Vossius, *Roman Etymology*. ORELLI.

**Plough-beam (*buris*).** The curved rear portion of a plough. See Servius and Vossius on Virgil, *Georgics* I.370. ORELLI.

**A curved little seat.** That is, one formed in the shape of an arch, [Col. 0847D] as semicircular seats are. They wrote *arquus* for *arcus*. Hence in book I, “Diana and Apollo, the bow-bearers” (*Arquitenentes*). These letters were, of course, frequently interchanged. Thus, conversely, *licet* occurs for *liquet* in Plautus and Tertullian. In this same African author we find *locuntur*; likewise *animaecus* for *animaequus*. The glosses give: *animecum*, ἰσόψυχον (“equal-souled”). So too *oblicum* for *obliquum*. HERALDUS.—Compare Lambinus on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III.20. ORELLI.

**Scraper (*strigilis*).** Thus the manuscript, correctly. It is an old nominative form, like *vulturis*, *sanguinis*, and similar forms. Hence the accusative *strigilim* in Lucilius, as cited by Charisius, book I, who had before his eyes the verse:

> A broken scraper, a worthless half of a sandal.

MEURSIUS, in the Appendix.—*Strigil, strigilis*: an instrument for scraping the body in baths; for its description and illustration, see Hieronymus Mercurialis, *On the Gymnastic Art*. Cf. Gonsalus on Petronius, chap. 91. The following word, *polubrum*, shows that it is this instrument, and not a currycomb for scraping horses, [Col. 0848A] that must be understood here. ORELLI.

**Washbasin (*polubrum*).** The glosses: *polubrum*—ποδόνιπτρον (“foot-basin”). Festus: “A *polubrum* is a *peluvium*, the vessel that we call a *pelvis*.” Thus Livius Andronicus, in his translation of *Odyssey* I.137:

> A maidservant brought water for the hands and poured it from a pitcher  
> Beautiful and golden, over a silver basin, [Col. 0848B]  
> For washing.

He rendered προχόῳ χρυσείῃ (“from a golden pitcher”) as *aureo gutto*, and ὑπὲρ ἀργυρέοιο λέβητος (“over a silver basin”) as *argenteo polubro*. Cf. Gesner, in the *Thesaurus*. ORELLI.

**Chair (*siliquastrum*).** Festus: “Seats of an ancient kind are called *seliquastra*, with the letter D changed into L, as also happened in *sella*, *subsellium*, and *solium*, which no less derive their names from sitting”: cf. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book IV. NOURRIUS.—Hyginus uses the word several times; for example, *Poetical Astronomy* II.10: “Cassiopeia … has been placed among the constellations, sitting upon a *siliquastrum*.” See there Muncker. Eratosthenes, *Catasterisms*, chap. 16, says of the same figure: ἐσχημάτισται δὲ ἐπὶ δίφρου καθεζομένη, “she is represented seated upon a chair.” Casaubon, on Suetonius, *Otho*, chap. VI, p. 228, vol. IV, Wolf’s edition, interprets it as an uncovered woman’s seat, used indoors rather than outside. Cf. Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, and Gesner, in the *Thesaurus*. Others, not understanding this word, wished the text to read “a basket, a rake.” ORELLI.

[Col. 0848C] **Dipper (*trulla*).** A vessel for water, smaller than a *trulleum*, used for washing the hands. See above on chap. 19. ORELLI.

**Drinking vessel (*batiaca*).** Greek βατιάκη or βατιάκιον in Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, book XI, p. 484, Casaubon’s edition, was a kind of drinking cup called *batiola* in Latin. See Nonius; Plautus, *Stichus*, act V, scene IV:

> Those who possess wealth at home drink from bowls and tankards  
> And little *batiolae*; we drink from our little Samian cup.

There Turnebus, *Adversaria* XVI.11, thinks that *batiocis* should be read. See Taubmann on this passage of Plautus; Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under *batiola*; Bekmann on Aristotle, *On Marvellous Things Heard*, chap. 50, p. 100; and especially the distinguished Creuzer, who discusses this word at length in *Academic Dissertation* I, *On the Causes of Bacchic Phenomena*, p. 59. ORELLI.

**Codex … book.** A *codex* differs from a book or scroll in that it is a mass or body composed of several tablets laid one upon another; these could be made of wood, ivory, parchment, or papyrus. Thus the form of a *codex* is that of modern books, whereas a scroll—or *liber*, as Arnobius calls it here—has sheets joined lengthwise to other sheets, which are then rolled into a single roll or cylinder. (Gesner, in the *Thesaurus*.) Cf. Rost and Wichmann, *The Antiquities of Greece and Rome in Pictures*, fascicle I, pp. 10 ff. ORELLI.

**Pointer (*radius*).** Virgil, *Eclogues* III.40:

> In the middle are two figures: Conon—and who was the other  
> Who with his pointer traced the entire globe for humankind?

Servius there: “A *radius* is the rod of philosophers, with which geometers indicate lines.” It was an instrument peculiar to mathematical demonstrations. See Barthius, *Adversaria* XLIX.3, pp. 2282 f. Nourrius understands it as a stylus with which the ancients wrote, but without any supporting example. ORELLI.

**Not after the manner of an ox, or ass, or pig.** Thus Meursius and Salmasius. Others: “not after your manner,” etc. ORELLI.

[Col. 0849B] **Or any animal still slower.** Νωθέστερον (“more sluggish”). For this is how the Greeks use the word of people with slower intelligence, transferring the epithet from those animals. Indeed, this is almost the ass’s distinctive epithet, ὡς ἐστερημένου τοῦ θέειν, “as being deprived of the ability to run.” Homer:

> As when an ass, approaching a field, overpowers the boys—  
> A sluggish beast, around whose sides many sticks have been broken.

Aeschylus transferred the term to human beings in *Prometheus*:

> … so that,  
> Though a sophist, he may learn that he is duller than Zeus.

HERALDUS.

[Col. 0849C] **He will indeed observe these things, regarding their various forms.** Thus Fulvius Ursinus, with Heraldus’ approval in his *Second Notes*. The manuscript: “various forms, observing things.” The Leiden editor: “observing things of varied form,” that is, things formed in different ways. *Formatura* is a Lucretian word; for example, book IV, verse 560:

> For it preserves its formation and preserves its shape.

ORELLI.

**But without knowing what the individual things are.** Thus the Leiden edition, very well, so as to correspond with the preceding “indeed.” The others: “and what they are,” etc. ORELLI.]

## XXIII

If you give a hungry man a grape, a must-cake, an onion, a thistle, a cucumber, or a fig, will he know that his hunger can be appeased by all of these, or in what manner each ought to be eaten? And if you make a very large fire for him, [Note: [Col. 0844B] The manuscript wrongly has “for himself.”] or place venomous beasts around him, will he not [Col. 0844B] go through the midst of the flames, vipers, and venomous ants, [Col. 0845A] not knowing that they are harmful and not even knowing what fear is?

Again, if you set out in the middle clothing and furnishings, both urban and rustic, will he be able to distinguish the purpose for which [Note: [Col. 0845A] The manuscript adds a word. “To distinguish—to discern—for what purpose” is sound. MEURSIUS.] each object is suitable, or the function for whose use it is adapted? Let him indicate for what forms of dress the following have been made: a coverlet, a turban, a breast-band, a bandage, a cushion, a handkerchief, a cloak, a head-covering, a towel, a fur garment, a slipper, a sandal, and a shoe.

What if you add [Col. 0847A] the question [Note: [Col. 0847A] The manuscript has: “add the question, what a wheel is.”] what a wheel is, or a threshing-sledge, winnowing fan, jar, cask, olive-press, ploughshare, sieve, millstone, plough-beam, or hoe? What if you ask about a curved little seat, needle, bath-scraper, washbasin [Note: [Col. 0847A] The manuscript corruptly has “snake.”], chair, dipper, small dish [Note: [Col. 0848A] Fulvius wrongly reads “lentil.”], lampstand, [Col. 0848A] drinking vessel, broom [Note: [Col. 0848A] Others read “barmaids.”], cup, or sack? What if you ask about a lyre, flute, silver, bronze, codex, pointer, or scroll? What, finally, if you ask about all the other instruments with which human life is equipped and sustained?

As we have said, will he not observe these things after the manner of an ox, [Col. 0849A] ass, pig, or any still slower animal, indeed regarding their various forms, but without knowing what the individual things are or for what purpose they are possessed? If compelled by some necessity to utter a sound, will he not—as is customary with the mute—open his mouth and shout some inarticulate thing or other?

[Note: [Col. 0849C]

## XXIV—“Why in the *Meno*, Plato, do you question a certain boy by applying principles of number?”

See Plato, *Meno*, pp. 82–84, H. Stephanus’ edition (Bipontine edition, vol. IV, pp. 353–357). Cf. Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.24. But Meursius’ conjecture on p. 60 is highly attractive: “with the principles of number removed from the boy.” ORELLI.

**Within the bounds of humanity.** Others: “to be within [Col. 0849D] the bounds of humanity.” But Meursius and Salmasius quite rightly delete the verb as an erroneous repetition. ORELLI.

**Obscure (*involutum*).** Here in an unusual sense: the same as “enigmatic,” αἰνιγματῶδες. ORELLI.

**What a cube or a power is; lastly, what a sesquioctave or a sesquitertian ratio is.** I read thus with Fulvius Ursinus, Theodorus Canterus, Salmasius in the Leiden edition and in his *Exercises on Solinus*, pp. 297 and 492, where he admirably illuminates this extremely difficult passage:

> Arnobius appropriately joins “cube” and “power.” An ancient Greek author, *On Numbers*, says: “All these numbers are called squaring: three times three, 9, is a power; three times 9, 27, a cube; three times 27, 81, a power of a power; three times 81, 243, a power-cube; three times 243, 729, a cube of a cube” (Τετραγωνισμὸς καλεῖται οἱ ἀριθμοὶ οὗτοι ἅπαντες· τρὶς τρεῖς θʹ δύναμις· τρὶς θʹ κζʹ κῦβος· τρὶς κζʹ παʹ δυναμοδύναμις· τρὶς παʹ σμγʹ δυναμόκυβος· τρὶς σμγʹ ψκθʹ κυβόκυβος).
>
> “Cube” and “power,” therefore, were names for numbers commonly used by Greeks and Latins alike. Thus, among geometers, what receives measurement in a straight line is called a number; what receives it in a plane, a power; and what receives it in a solid, a cube. Among numbers, the dyad corresponds to a line, which has length alone. It is the principle of even numbers, [Col. 0850B] and hence is called both ἀρχή (“beginning”) and γένεσις (“generation”). Two times two is the first square, which possesses breadth as well as length and corresponds to an *embadon*, or area, and is called δύναμις, “power.” Martianus Capella calls it *potentia*; see Grotius there, p. 23. Two times four is the first cube, a number equated with a στερεόν, or solid.
>
> Similarly, the triad is the principle of odd numbers. Three times three is a power; three times nine is a cube. Learned men should also cease asking what “the final sesquitertian” may be, for the text should read: “or, finally, a sesquioctave or sesquitertian ratio.”

Thus far Salmasius. In place of *cubus*, the other editors have *dibus*, which Meursius [Col. 0850C] defends by taking it to mean “a pair” and citing a passage from Agathias, epigram 72 (Brunck’s *Analecta*, vol. III, p. 60), concerning Zenon’s τάβλα, that is, gaming board or gaming tray, where verses 10–11 read:

> And the piece beside the *summus* had two; but another single  
> Piece, the last one, the *dibus* encompassed.

But δῖβος, or *dibus*, is not a pair, as Meursius thinks. Rather, as the distinguished Jacobs teaches in his *Observations on the Analecta*, vol. III, part I, p. 122, and as Salmasius explains—at greater length—in his *Observations on Julius Vopiscus’ Proculus*, *Augustan History*, vol. II, p. 753, it is a Latin name formed from *divus*, just as σοῦμμος is formed from *summus*. It signifies the place or line on one side of the gaming board for counters or dice that was called *divus*, δῖβος, as though it were the seat of a Roman king or emperor. For everyone knows that Roman emperors were called *Divi*, “deified ones,” after death. Opposite and contrary to it on the other [Col. 0850D] side was the *Antigonus*, the name of a Macedonian king, since it is well known that Macedonian kings were always adversaries and opponents of the Romans. Such a board game was devised entirely in the image of war; hence it was called “the contest of the board.” In it black or reddish counters contended against white ones. But this has nothing to do with our passage, which concerns numbers, not gaming counters. Therefore *cubus* must be read. ORELLI.

**Whether he can resolve the question put to him.** Stewechius conjecturally reads: “whether he can resolve a question sought out from all sides,” citing Festus’ authority: *anquirere*, “to seek all around.” But nothing should be changed. *Inquisitam* is used for the simple *quaesitam*, “asked.” ORELLI.

**Will perceive.** Theodorus Canterus conjectures “will hesitate,” that is, “will be in doubt.” But nothing should be changed. ORELLI.

**Marpesian rock.** He took this from Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.471–472:

> Nor is her countenance moved any more by the words begun  
> Than if she were hard flint or stood as a Marpesian crag.

[Col. 0851B] Servius there: “By the Marpesian crag he means Parian marble. For Marpesus is a mountain on the island of Paros.” ELMENHORSTIUS.

**Whether you are conversing with another or with himself.** I agree entirely with Meursius, who deletes these words as a gloss and an idle repetition of what immediately preceded. ORELLI.]

## XXIV

Why in the *Meno*, Plato, do you question a certain boy by applying principles of number, and strive from his answers to prove that what we learn we do not really learn, but return to the memory of things we knew long ago? If he answers you truly—for it does not befit us to deny credibility [Note: [Col. 0849B] Sabæus has “assign credibility.”] to the things you say—he is guided not by knowledge of the subjects but by understanding; and because he knows certain numbers from everyday use, [Col. 0849B] it comes about that he follows when questioned, while the very process of multiplication continually [Col. 0850A] leads him onward.

But if you truly trust that souls fly here immortal and full of knowledge, stop questioning that young boy, whom you see to be ignorant of things and still within the bounds of humanity. Call that forty-year-old man to you and ask him—not something recondite, not something obscure, not about triangles, not about squares, not what a cube or a power [Note: [Col. 0849B] Thus Meursius. Others: *Dynamus*.] is, or, finally, what a sesquioctave or sesquitertian ratio is—but ask him what total twice two and twice three, matters lying in plain view, produce. We wish to see; we wish to know what answer he gives when questioned and whether he can resolve the question put to him.

Thus he will perceive, although his ears are open, whether you are saying something, asking something, or requesting that something be answered by him [Note: [Col. 0850B] The manuscript has: “whether something be answered to you by himself.”]; and will he not stand like a log or, as the saying goes, a Marpesian [Col. 0850B] rock, speechless and mute, ignorant and unaware even of this: whether you are speaking with yourself or rather with another, whether you are conversing with another or with himself; whether what you utter is discourse, or merely the sound of a voice, signifying nothing but drawn out in an empty sequence? [Col. 0851A]

[Note: [Col. 0851B]

## XXV—“The soul … occupying the fourth place after God, the sovereign of things, and after the twin intelligences.”

These words must be explained from the doctrine of the Platonists. They assigned the highest and sovereign place in the natural order to θεὸς πρῶτος (“the first God”), Ζεὺς μέγας (“great Zeus”), the δημιουργός (“Demiurge”); the second [Col. 0851C] to the θεοὶ γεννητοί (“generated gods”), created by the supreme God and subject to him; the third to the δαίμονες (“daemons”); and finally the fourth to human souls, created by the same supreme God. For they maintained that the lesser gods formed bodies from the elements. See Alcinous, *Introduction to the Philosophy of Plato*, chap. 17.

Plato, *Phaedrus*, p. 247, second edition of Stephanus (Bipontine edition, p. 321):

> Now the great leader in heaven, Zeus, drives his winged chariot and proceeds first, ordering and caring for all things; and behind him follows an army of gods and daemons, arrayed in eleven divisions.

Alcinous, book I, chap. 15, p. 105, Fischer’s quarto edition, in the *Platonic Dialogues*: “For God himself is the creator both of the universe and of the daemons” (Ὁ μὲν γὰρ Θεὸς τοῦ τε παντὸς ὑπάρχει ποιητὴς αὐτὸς καὶ τῶν δαιμόνων).

Accordingly, by “twin intelligences,” that is, similar or equal intelligences—see Servius on *Aeneid* I.165—Arnobius means θεοὺς καὶ δαίμονας, “gods and daemons,” in whose place Platonizing Jewish and Christian teachers substituted ἀγγέλους καὶ δυνάμεις, “angels and powers.” See Wettstein on Matthew 24:29, *New Testament*, vol. I, p. 503. ORELLI.

**From living bowls.** That is, ποταμὸς ὕδατος τῆς ζωῆς, “a river of the water of life.” See Revelation 22:1. ORELLI.

[Col. 0851D] **What is called the lesser world.** Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* II.12: “The natural philosophers said that the world is a great human being, and a human being a small world.” Calcidius on Plato’s *Timaeus*, p. 126: “There is in our bodies a portion of water and likewise of air, as well as of fire and earth; hence, I think, the ancients called man a small world, κόσμου συντομή (‘an epitome of the cosmos’).” Cf. Nemesius, *On Human Nature*, chap. 1. ELMENHORSTIUS and ORELLI.

**Let him remain inactive; let him prosper in money, though he live for countless years.** I have printed this from the very slight and felicitous emendation of Caspar Barthius in *Adversaria* XLIV.1, p. 1987. The passage’s meaning is evidently: place a man in solitude; make him as healthy as you please; make him immortal; give him the sum of all wishes in this life—namely, that he may prosper *in aere*, that is, abound in money and wealth. The manuscript and first edition have *valeat in aere*, “let him prosper in money,” which the annotator nevertheless says has no meaning. Fulvius Ursinus and Gelenius boldly give: “let him remain inactive like a boy, though,” etc. Stewechius proposes reading either “let the inactive man whimper lovingly,” or, closer to the manuscript’s wording and with a term transferred from sheep, [Col. 0852B] “let the inactive man lovingly bleat”—both most badly. For the thirty-year-old man whom Arnobius imagines emerging among human beings from the dark prison in which he had been confined will no longer whimper like an infant; nor, since he has thus far seen no sheep and has beheld nothing except his nurse, will he bleat like one.

Johannes Meursius thinks that the text should read: “let him remain extremely inactive and ignorant, though,” etc. Heraldus, in his *Second Notes*: “as though in the air,” that is, as if he were a bird living in the air, as we say in German: *Er lebt, es ist ihm wohl, wie dem Vogel in der Luft* (“He lives and fares as happily as a bird in the air”). The Leiden editor: “he will likewise be inactive; though he may have strength to remain alive for countless years,” [Col. 0852C] which is bolder and further removed from the manuscript’s wording.

Nor should another conjecture of the same Caspar Barthius, in the passage cited, be despised: “let him prosper, though in a citadel,” that is, in the safest possible place, situated beyond every hazard and every human danger, as the expression occurs very often in the ancients. I have nevertheless preferred the former. *Demoretur* is used for *demorabitur*, “he will remain,” in accordance with Arnobius’ custom of very frequently placing the present subjunctive for the future indicative. ORELLI.

**Bodily knots.** Bodily knots are equivalent to the bonds of the body, which detain the soul within it during life. See Caspar Barthius, *Adversaria* XII.15, p. 694. ORELLI.

**Through compulsion of practice and habituation.** Perhaps “through the teaching of habituation.” MEURSIUS, p. 63.

**To recognize the turns on the racecourse.** Arnobius very frequently uses *noscere*, “to know,” *scire*, “to understand,” and their compounds of things that one learns through practice and experience. See above on book I, chap. 23. ORELLI.

**To fly back to its master’s dwelling.** Thus Gelenius. The manuscript has “to recall.” Arnobius perhaps wrote *revolgare*, an archaic [Col. 0852D] form for *volare*, “to fly.” Lucretius II.163:

> At the time when the sun’s rays fly across the heavens.

Pacuvius: “Like a halcyon, I am borne flying along the shore.” HERALDUS.—For “dwelling,” Ursinus reads “house.” ORELLI.

**The crow to bring forth names.** The royal manuscript has *corsus*. Some interpret this as ὡς ἀπὸ τῆς καρδίας, “as though bringing them forth from the heart,” and refer it to the parrot; but anyone can be persuaded that *corvus*, “crow,” is the genuine reading. Apuleius, *Florida*, book II, says: “But in truth both the crow and the parrot utter nothing except what they have learned.” In that book the author reports many obscure details about the nature and identifying characteristics of parrots. As for the crows that uttered greetings and were purchased by the emperor Augustus, Macrobius, *Saturnalia* II.10, should be consulted. HERALDUS and STEWECHIUS.—For *expromere*, “bring forth,” Fulvius Ursinus reads *exprimere*, “express.” Wrongly. Virgil, *Aeneid* II.280: “To bring forth sorrowful words.” ORELLI.]

## XXV

What are you saying, gentlemen, who attribute to yourselves more than is enough from another’s nobility? Is this that learned soul which you call immortal, perfect, divine, occupying the fourth place after God, the sovereign of things, and after the twin intelligences, and flowing abundantly from living bowls? Is this that precious human being, endowed with the most august rational faculties, who is called the lesser world and has been fashioned and formed in the likeness [Note: [Col. 0851B] Fulvius reads “and likeness.”] of the whole?

As has become apparent, he is no better than any beast, duller than wood or stone: a man who does not know human beings and always lives in mute solitudes; [Col. 0851B] let him remain there inactive, let him prosper in money, though [Col. 0852A] he live for countless years and never be freed from bodily knots. But when he has reached schools and been educated by the instruction of teachers, he becomes intelligent and learned and lays aside the ignorance he possessed a short while before.

An ass and an ox likewise learn, through compulsion of practice and habituation, [Note: [Col. 0851B] The manuscript has “of those to be compelled.”] to plough and grind; a horse, to submit to the yoke and recognize the turns on the racecourse; a camel, to lower itself both when taking up burdens and when setting them down; a released dove, to fly back to its master’s dwelling; a dog, when it has found prey, to check and restrain its barking; a parrot, to complete words; and a crow, to utter names.

[Note: [Col. 0852D]

## XXVI—“To come here from earlier ages.”

Fulvius Ursinus conjectures “from their dwelling places,” but nothing should be changed. [Col. 0853B] Arnobius uses *saeculum*, “age,” in the sense of stock, offspring, and multitude, after Lucretius’ manner. Consult Gifanius’ index. ELMENHORSTIUS.—See above on book I, chap. 25, and below on [Col. 0853C] book VII, chap. 24. ORELLI.

**To become elementary.** That is, to require instruction in the first elements. Seneca, *Epistle* XXXVI: “An old man learning his letters is a shameful and ridiculous thing.” ELMENHORSTIUS and NOURRIUS.—German: *Eine ABC-Schülerin*, “an ABC schoolgirl.” ORELLI.

**Recovery of what came before.** The glosses: *Repetentia*—ἐπανάληψις (“recovery, resumption”). Below, chap. 28: “For that which removes from beings that have entered bodies the recovery of what came before,” that is, ἀνάμνησιν (“recollection”). Lucretius III.863–865:

> Once our recovery has been interrupted,  
> What we were before now has no relevance to us.

Likewise *retinentia*, “retention,” occurs in Lucretius for the faculty by which we retain, and as it were draw back, the fleeing memory of past things, III.674–675:

> For if the power of the mind has been changed so greatly  
> That all retention of deeds done has escaped it—

HERALDUS and ELMENHORSTIUS.

**That incorporeal souls do not possess substance.** Thus the Leiden edition, following Stewechius’ correction. The earlier reading was “the incorporeal soul,” but *incorporalis* in the manuscript is a plural accusative for *incorporales*. Others: “an incorporeal substance of souls.” ORELLI.

**Be induced.** Fulvius Ursinus thinks “be seen” should be read. But nothing should be changed. “Be induced to lose,” that is, be affected so as to lose it. Thus *suadere*, “to induce,” and *imperare*, “to command,” are very frequently used even of inanimate things in the sense of impelling or prompting. Lucretius I.174–175:

> We see grain brought forth at the prompting of heat,  
> And vines at the prompting of autumn.

Others, however, read “as the vines sweat.” See Lambinus, p. 35. ORELLI.

**In bodies.** Fulvius Ursinus: “incorporeal.” Wrongly. ORELLI.

**The joinings of bodies.** Others read “the bindings,” wrongly. Arnobius below in the same book: “Who is the author of the joining?” In book III: “With the difference in the joining of the multitude preserved.” In book VI: “To coalesce into a joining of images.” ELMENHORSTIUS.

[Col. 0854B] **Through the intervention of passibility.** *Passibilitas*, “passibility,” is a word of declining Latin. See Vossius, *On Faults of Speech*, and Olaus Borrichius, *Reflections*, p. 189. Similarly *passibilis*, “passible,” below in book VII: “For whatever is distressed by the motion of some thing is established to be passible and fragile.” [Col. 0854C] ORELLI.]

## XXVI

But when I hear the soul called some extraordinary thing or other, neighboring and closest to God, knowing [Note: [Col. 0852B] Fulvius reads: “and knowing.”] all things and coming here from earlier ages, [Col. 0852B] I do not want it to learn but to teach; nor, though said to be learned, to become elementary, [Col. 0853A] but to bind itself about with earthly bodies while still retaining its own knowledge.

For unless matters stand in this way, how will anyone be able to discern whether it recollects what it hears or learns it—especially since it is much easier to believe that it learns what it does not know than that, having forgotten what it knew shortly before, it loses through the body’s obstruction the recovery of what came before?

And what becomes of the claim that an incorporeal soul possesses no substance? For that which belongs to no body is not obstructed by the opposition of another, nor can it be induced to lose anything, since it cannot sustain the contact of an opposing thing. For just as a number established in bodies remains untouched and inviolate, though it be buried beneath a thousand bodies, so souls, if they are incorporeal, as is asserted, must suffer no forgetfulness of what came before, though the most solid joinings of bodies bind them about.

What is more, the same line of reasoning indicates not merely that they are not incorporeal, but also deprives them entirely of immortality and brings them to the boundaries at which life is accustomed to end. For whatever, when some cause assails it, is so changed and transformed that it cannot retain its integrity must necessarily be judged passible by nature. But that which is readily open and exposed to passion is declared corruptible through the very intervention of passibility. [Col. 0854A]

[Note: [Col. 0854C]

## XXVII—“If only it thinks itself everlasting.”

The text should undoubtedly read “if only it thinks *itself* everlasting.” ORELLI.

**For every passion is a gateway to death and destruction.** Below: “But if souls, in turn, approach the gateways of death.” He imitates Lucretius V.374:
