> Therefore the gateway of death has not been barred against heaven.

HERALDUS.

**Bringing inevitable dissolution upon things.** *Functio*, “discharge, completion,” is used for death, just as *fungi*, “to discharge,” is used for dying—an expression familiar to Arnobius. Thus below, chap. 57: “He thinks that souls are everlasting and survive the dissolution of mortals.” Similarly, “having discharged death,” that is, “having died,” in book I, chap. 41. See Vorstius on Sulpicius Severus I.7 and Bünemann on Lactantius, *Institutes* VII.10, p. 914. ORELLI.

**Life has been given to them for use, not conveyed as ownership.** That is, life has been given to them for use, not so that they may possess it perpetually and eternally. Lucretius III.984:

> Life is given to no one as property, to everyone for use.

Seneca, *Epistle* LXXII: “Fortune gives nothing as property.” ELMENHORSTIUS.

**Although some argue otherwise.** That is, reason or conclude otherwise. This expression is not infrequent in Tertullian and Apuleius, but is also used by more approved writers—for example, Quintilian, *Institutes* V.14 and VIII.4. Bünemann collected several examples in his note on Lactantius, *Institutes* VII.13, pp. 927 f. ORELLI.]

## XXVII

Therefore, if souls lose everything they knew when confined by bodily bonds, they must necessarily undergo something that causes them to put on [Note: [Col. 0853B] Others read “to introduce.”] the blindness of forgetfulness. For if they underwent absolutely nothing, or preserved their integrity, they could not lay aside their knowledge of things or pass into other conditions without mutability of their own.

Yet we consider that whatever is one, immortal, and simple must necessarily always retain its own nature, in whatever thing it may be; and that it ought not and cannot undergo anything, if only it thinks itself everlasting and remains within the boundaries of its own immortality.

For every passion is a gateway to death and destruction, [Col. 0854B] a road leading to death and bringing inevitable dissolution upon things. If souls experience this and yield to its contact and assaults, then life too has been given them for use, not conveyed as ownership, although some argue otherwise and in their arguments place confidence in a claim of such magnitude.

[Note: [Col. 0854D]

## XXVIII—“Yet, lest we depart without fuller instruction, let us hear from you how, as you say, souls, when they have been enveloped in earthly bodies, possess no recollection of what came before.”

Thus all editions except the first and the Leiden edition following Gelenius’ correction. The manuscript and first edition have: “let us depart, lest we seem to you”; from this Heraldus, in his *Second Notes*, suspects that the text should read: [Col. 0855B] “Yet, lest we be regarded and appear to you as not more fully instructed, how, as you say, souls, when they have been enveloped in earthly bodies, possess recollection of what came before,” with *non* deleted.

This is utterly false. For Arnobius refutes those who maintained that human souls are divine and eternal, and would therefore retain recollection of their previous existence were they not obstructed by the bonds of the body. He wishes to show them that if souls had lived a life before this human one, the body would not obstruct their recollection of what they did while situated outside and not yet joined to human beings. In this way he prepares his demonstration that human souls are neither eternal nor derived from God, but come from natures far inferior.

The Leiden editor reads: “let us depart; we desire to know,” which amounts to the same as Gelenius’ “let us hear.” Meursius, p. 63, conjectures: “let us depart, lest you laugh at us; how, as you say, … they possess no recollection.” ORELLI.

**And rendered almost insensible through intermixture with them.** The reading is sound. Those who wish to correct *perfectae*, “rendered,” to *effectae*, “made”—as Fulvius Ursinus does—are mistaken. *Perficere* was used in this sense. Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis* VII.16: “They will render the women virgins and sterile”; and often elsewhere. ORELLI.

**From recalling their ancient arts.** The manuscript codex has: “from their ancient arts and recalling,” from which Meursius conjectures “from recalling their ancient arts equally.” Others: [Col. 0855D] “their arts and ancient things.” ORELLI.

**Honored with the condition of immortality.** See above on book I, chap. 41. ORELLI.

**It is not a sign of memory lost, but proof and evidence of memory preserved.** Johannes Schefferus of Strasbourg, in his book of *Adversaria*, chap. 20, cited in *Miscellaneous Critical Observations*, vol. IX, p. 163, thinks that “evidence” was added by a glossator. Wrongly: Arnobius is fond of joining nouns that signify the same thing. ORELLI.]

## XXVIII

Yet, lest we depart without fuller instruction, let us hear [Note: [Col. 0854B] Fulvius reads: “we desire to hear.”] from you how, as you say, souls, [Col. 0855A] when they have been enveloped in earthly bodies, possess no recollection of what came before, although, when situated within those very bodies and rendered almost insensible through intermixture with them, they tenaciously and faithfully retain what, many years before—say eighty years, or even more—they either did, suffered, said, or heard.

For if the body’s obstruction prevents them from remembering things that they knew long ago, before becoming human, they ought all the more to forget what they did when enclosed within bodies than what they did while situated outside and not yet joined to human beings. For whatever removes from beings that have entered bodies the recovery of what came before ought also to destroy, by an obliteration beyond recall, the things performed within itself.

One cause cannot produce two effects [Note: [Col. 0855B] Thus the manuscript. Sabæus has “contrary effects.” Others: “different effects.”] contrary to one another, so as to lull memories of some things to sleep [Col. 0855B] while allowing other things done by the agent to return to recollection.

But if the souls of which you speak are obstructed by the hindrance of bodily members from recalling their ancient arts, how, while established within those very bodies, do they remember and know that they are souls, that they possess no bodily substance, and that they have been honored with [Col. 0856A] the condition of immortality? How do they know what rank they hold among existing things, at what degree they are set apart from God the Father, by what means they arrived at these lowest regions of the world, and what qualities they drew from which circles as they fell down into these places?

How, I ask, do they know that they were most learned and lost what they knew through the bodies’ obstruction? For they ought not to have known even this, if bodily conjunction had introduced any such thing into them. To know what you were and what you are not today is not a sign of memory lost, but proof and evidence of memory preserved.

[Note: [Col. 0855D]

## XXIX—“Of slight weight.”

Although the commonly accepted reading “of slight name” can be tolerated, I nevertheless prefer, with others, including Meursius, “of slight weight” (*exigui mominis*). Thus our author below, chap. 35: “of no weight with the ruler,” that is, of no importance; and book VI, chap. 20: “under the very impulse (*momine*) of the theft and deed.” He imitates Lucretius, as often elsewhere, III.189:

> So that, when impelled, they can be moved by a slight impulse.

HERALDUS and GALLANDIUS.

**Cease assigning man—since he is a proletarian—to the first orders of the first class, though he is assessed merely by the head.** The manuscript has, absurdly: [Col. 0856B] “since he is a proletarian, a man of the first class”; for proletarians were beneath the classes. Gelenius therefore emended it well. MEURSIUS, in the Appendix.—Livy II.43 and Dionysius of Halicarnassus IV, p. 221, relate that Roman citizens were divided into various classes. Yet, according to Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* VII.13, only men of the first class, whose assessed property amounted to 125,000 asses or more, [Col. 0856C] were called *classici* in the strict sense.

It is in this sense that Arnobius here contrasts men of the first class with proletarians, who, being very poor, furnished only offspring (*proles*) to the republic. Those assessed merely by the head, as the author calls them, were people assessed as possessing no property or very little and who paid little or no tax, according to Aulus Gellius XVI.10. NOURRIUS.—Cf. Isaac Pontanus on Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.15, and Johann Nicolaus Funck on the Twelve Tables, pp. 77 f. ORELLI.

**And never deserving to be called a man of patrician distinction.** “Distinction” (*claritas*) properly belonged to senators and patricians, who under the emperors were called “most distinguished men” (*viri clarissimi*). While the republic flourished, only men of the highest rank were marked by that title, which also implied praise of them as good citizens. Hence Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* XIV.11, is indignant that Antony publicly bestowed this title upon Caesar after his death; and in speeches delivered before the senate he always addresses them as “Conscript Fathers,” [Col. 0856D] never simply as “Fathers” or “most distinguished men.”

The senate as a body was indeed called “the most distinguished order,” but individual senators were not, until the imperial period. See Schwartz on Pliny’s *Panegyric* 90. In a later age even senators’ wives were called “most distinguished women”; see Salmasius on Aelius Lampridius’ *Heliogabalus*, *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, p. 797.

Arnobius, therefore, in this passage employs a rather bold metaphor in calling a human being derived and created from God “a man of patrician distinction.” We consequently have no need of the Leiden editor’s correction: “nor to call him the offspring of so distinguished a father, despite such great merits.” The first edition reads “of the fatherland,” etc. ORELLI.

**By whose evils we are all raised aloft.** Thus the first Roman edition and all the others. But Fulvius Ursinus offers the ingenious conjecture: “By whose wings we are all raised aloft”; and similarly in the words that follow: “you have refused merely to clip those creatures’ wings” (German *beschneiden*, “to clip”), in place of the common reading, “you think that these evils merely befall them.” ORELLI.]

We are swollen with the vanity of empty things. Fulvius Ursinus thinks one should read *inani* [“empty”], etc.—wrongly. “The vanity of empty things” means a vain opinion, an estimation of things that are empty. ORELLI.

“However much he may be of a disposition that always flees disgrace and what is ignominious,” etc. A point of philosophy. Some abstain from wrongdoing through fear of punishment; others execrate and detest the vices themselves; still others fear disgrace and unfavorable reports about themselves, and for that reason abstain from shameful acts. These are men of sensitive conscience, ἐπιεικεῖς (“decent, equitable”) and αἰδήμονες (“modest, sensitive to shame”), whom the wicked consider δειλούς (“cowardly”) and inert, just as, conversely, they regard τοὺς ἀναισχύντους (“the shameless”) as steadfast and ἀνδρείους (“courageous”). By these words, therefore, Arnobius describes an αἰδήμων, a person sensitive to shame. For an αἰδήμων is one who fears τὰ εἰς ἀδοξίαν φαινόμενα φέρειν, “to incur things that appear to lead to disrepute,” as Aristotle defines it—that is, one who flees disgrace and what is ignominious, as Arnobius puts it. HERALDUS.

“Should rush headlong into every shameful act.” This is the old reading, which Gelenius ought not to have altered. For this verb is very frequently used ἐνεργητικῶς, “actively.” HERALDUS. Thus in Book I, chapter 34, he used *irruere* actively. Plautus, Apuleius, and others similarly use *penetrare*, [Col. 0857D] *emergere*, and other verbs. MEURSIUS, in the Appendix.

“Of the power above.” Thus Salmasius, following Meursius’ emendation. Others read “proud”; others, “higher.” ORELLI.]

## XXIX

Since these things are so, cease, I beg you—cease to value small matters, things of trifling importance, at enormous prices. Cease to enroll among the classes and first ranks a man who, though a proletarian [Col. 0856B] and assessed by the head, is destitute, poor in household possessions, the occupant of a poor hut, and has never deserved to be called a man of patrician distinction.

For when it was incumbent upon you, as men who profess rectitude and integrity, to break down the conceit and arrogance by whose evils we are all puffed up, and are swollen with the vanity of empty things, you judge not merely that these evils occur, [Col. 0857A] but—what is much more serious—you have added causes by which both the vices might increase and incorrigible wickedness might persist.

For what man is there, however much he may be of a disposition that always flees disgrace [Note: [Col. 0857B] Fulvius reads *infamiae*; the Leiden edition has *infamia*, which should be adopted.] and what is ignominious, who, when he hears it said especially by wise men that souls are immortal and are not subject to the laws of fate, would not rush headlong into every shameful act, would not fearlessly [Note: [Col. 0857B] The manuscript has *securus* (“secure, unconcerned”). The Leiden edition adds both readings.] undertake and attempt unlawful things? Who, finally, would not grant his desires everything that ungovernable lust commanded, fortified besides by the freedom of impunity?

For what will prevent him from doing these things? Fear of the power above, and divine judgment? And who could be terrified by the horror of any fear if he had been persuaded that he is just as immortal as the primal God himself, and that God can pass no judgment upon him, [Col. 0857B] since immortality is the same in both, and, given their equality of condition, the immortality of the one cannot be afflicted by the other?

[Note: [Col. 0857D]

### XXX.—“But the punishments spoken of in the underworld, manifold in their kinds of torment?”

We must repeat from the preceding words: “And who could be terrified by the horror of any fear?” ORELLI.

“Or the revolutions of rolling wheels.” Thus, even in those times when they fashioned these stories, the penal wheel was already in use. For they modeled the torments of the underworld on ordinary punishments. The penal wheel, concerning which Cujacius’ *Observations*, Book III, should be consulted, was once a punishment reserved for slaves; later, however, it was employed during interrogations to extract confessions of crimes. The victims were bound to the wheel and stretched out; and as it was turned, they were beaten with scourges. Hence στρεβλοῦσθαι properly means “to be tortured.” The scholiast on Aristophanes, at *Peace*: Οἱ δοῦλοι σφαλλόμενοι [Col. 0858C] ἐπὶ τοῦ τροχοῦ δεσμούμενοι καὶ συρόμενοι ἐτύπτοντο ἀνακλώμενοι ἐν αὐτῷ: “Slaves, when subjected to punishment, were bound upon the wheel, dragged around, and beaten as they were bent backward upon it.” HERALDUS.

“Though it be surrounded by flames.” Should one not read *amburatur*, “though it be scorched”? That is the proper verb for those who are tormented by fire but not completely killed, which is what *comburere* means. ORELLI.

“It must remain unharmed and untouched, and must not experience any sensation of death-dealing suffering.” The reading is sound. Those who think *assumat* should be written are entirely mistaken. African writers delight in these changes of mood. Below: “Accordingly, when you charge us with abandoning the religion of our predecessors, it is proper that you examine the cause, not reproach us with the mere fact or with what we abandoned, but chiefly consider what we have followed.” HERALDUS.—The manuscript, instead of *illibatum*, which is due to Gelenius’ correction, nevertheless has *illaesum* (“unharmed”). ORELLI.—Compare the commentators on Livy XXI.49. OCHSNER.

“But it also removes the very rationale of philosophy.” This is explained in the next chapter in these words: “Thus a certain intermediate and doubtful, ambiguous nature of souls gave philosophy its place and furnished the reason why it should be sought.” HERALDUS.

“And, unbridled, to scatter the heat of boundless desire through every kind of lust.” From the similarity of the letters, I think that a verb has been lost which could contribute considerably to the embellishment of the trope; I therefore restore: “unbridled, to roam in the heat of boundless desire.” There is a parallel passage in Book IV of this author, and it should therefore be adduced: “that God loved”—I believe he means Jupiter Optimus Maximus—“and drove the seductiveness of his incestuous desires through every form of lust.” Marcus Cato used *spatiator* (“wanderer”) for *errator*, as Pompeius Festus and Macrobius, Book VII, attest. I have also seen this word in Petronius: “He saw,” he says, “certain persons wandering about together.” STEWECHIUS.—There is no need for this conjecture. The metaphor is drawn from ships that are scattered over the seas by the winds. ORELLI.

“If souls approach the gates of death, as Epicurus’ doctrine determines.” Epicurus, of course, maintained that the mind is born, grows, ages, and perishes together with the body. See Lucretius, Book III, verses 418–840. ORELLI.

“That souls are purified by it.” This is how it should be read, following Meursius’ emendation, not “that these souls are purified.” They considered philosophy to be ζωῆς ἀνθρωπίνης κάθαρσιν καὶ τελειότητα, “the purification and perfection of human life.” See Plato in the *Phaedo* and Hierocles on the *Golden Verses of the Pythagoreans*. HERALDUS.

“In their very bodies their vital sensation perishes and is extinguished.” Some wish to read “together with their bodies.” Wrongly. Arnobius is touching on the arguments by which they attempted to establish that the soul is mortal. Among other things, they especially insisted that within the body itself the soul diminishes, becomes corrupted, and at last is extinguished together with it. For, they said, it is sick in the sick, weary in those exhausted by age, and when the body perishes, it is extinguished together with the very parts that first sink into unconsciousness, and so forth. All these points are discussed by Lucretius in Book III and refuted by Lactantius in Book VII, chapter 12. HERALDUS.]

## XXX

But what of the punishments spoken of in the underworld, manifold in their kinds of torment? Is there anyone so brutish and so ignorant of the consequences of things as to believe that Tartarean darkness can do any harm to incorruptible souls, or fiery rivers, or marshes with muddy depths, or the revolutions of rolling wheels?

For that which cannot be touched and has been removed from the laws of dissolution—even though it be surrounded by all the flames of rushing rivers, rolled in mud, overwhelmed by falling rocks hanging above it, and covered by the ruins of enormous mountains—must remain unharmed and untouched, [Col. 0858A] and must not experience any sensation of death-dealing suffering.

What is more, that conviction not only incites people to vice through the very freedom it gives them to sin, but also removes the very rationale of philosophy and declares that it is undertaken in vain, with the difficulty of a needless [Note: [Col. 0858B] Thus Fulvius; the manuscript and Sabaeus have “needless work.”] labor.

For if it is true that souls have no share in any end and advance through all ages in everlasting perpetuity, what danger is there, after virtues have been despised and neglected—virtues by which life is made more constrained and austere—in devoting oneself to pleasures and, unbridled, scattering the heat of boundless desire through every kind of lust? Is it feared that the soul might grow feeble from indulgence and be corrupted by the softness of vice? By what means could that be corrupted which is immortal, which exists forever, and which is subject to no suffering? Is it feared that it might become filthy and be polluted by the foulness of shameful deeds? And how could that which has no corporeal substance be polluted? Or where could contamination establish its seat, when there is no space in which the mark of that very contamination could fasten itself [Note: [Col. 0858B] Fulvius reads “be affixed”]?

Conversely, if souls approach the gates of death, as Epicurus’ doctrine determines, not even then is there an adequate reason why philosophy should be sought, even if it is true that souls are purified by it and rendered clean from every vice. For if they perish without exception, and in their very bodies their vital sensation perishes and is extinguished, [Col. 0859A] it is not only the greatest error but foolish blindness to restrain innate appetites, confine life within narrow bounds, grant nothing to nature, and refrain from doing whatever desires have commanded and urged, when no rewards for so great a labor await you once the day of death arrives and you are released from the bonds of the body.

[Note: [Col. 0859C]

### XXXI.—“Thus a certain intermediate and doubtful, ambiguous nature of souls gave philosophy its place.”

This was the doctrine of the Stoics. Accordingly, what Arnobius has written here about the intermediate state of souls he derived partly from the Stoic school and partly from Scripture wrongly understood. Compare Lactantius, Book VII, chapter 20. HERALDUS.

“Nor can degenerate within a mortal nature.” The editor of the Leiden edition, following Meursius’ emendation in the Appendix, reads “degenerate into a mortal nature.” Wrongly. See the observations on Book I, chapter 42, and the words in Book II, chapter 2: “He introduced true religion into the world.” ORELLI.]

## XXXI

Thus a certain intermediate and doubtful, ambiguous nature of souls gave philosophy its place and furnished the reason why it should be sought: one man, naturally, fears the danger arising from evils he has committed; another conceives good hopes if he commits no crime and passes his life in duty [Col. 0859B] and justice.

Hence it is that among learned men endowed with excellence of intellect there is a dispute about the quality of souls. Some say that they are mortal in nature and cannot sustain a divine substance; [Col. 0860A] others, however, say that they are everlasting and cannot degenerate within a mortal nature. That this [Note: [Col. 0859B] Sabaeus reads “What is this?”] should be so is brought about by the law of their intermediate condition: the former have arguments available by which souls are found to be subject to suffering and perishable, while the latter, conversely, do not lack arguments by which souls are shown to be divine and immortal.

[Note: [Col. 0859D]

### XXXII.—“For knowledge of him is a kind of leaven of life.”

Arnobius has in view the words of the Divine Savior in John 17:3: Αὕτη δέ ἐστιν ἡ αἰώνιος ζωή, ἵνα γινώσκωσί σε τὸν μόνον ἀληθινὸν Θεόν, καὶ ὃν ἀπέστειλας, Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν: “And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom you have sent.” ORELLI.

“Then, having laid aside savagery and inhumanity, let them resume gentler dispositions, so that they may be prepared for that which will be given.” By these words Arnobius signifies both regeneration through baptism and the Eucharist, but in such a way that he adapts the language of the Gentiles to Christian rites. For the Gentiles believed that the mysteries had been instituted so that human beings might be cultivated and transferred from a rustic and savage life to civilized humanity; hence they were called “initiations.” See Cicero, *On the Laws* II.14. This is the παλιγενεσία (“regeneration”) of the nations. But baptism is called λουτρὸν ἀναγεννήσεως, “the washing of regeneration,” by the Apostle at Titus 3:5.

In this passage Arnobius briefly and obscurely touches upon what was observed πρὸ τοῦ βαπτίσματος, “before baptism.” In the preceding words he says, “provided only that they attempt and meditate upon knowing him.” Thus he intimates the order of catechumens. For catechumens, before they were baptized, κατηχοῦντο, “were catechized,” and were instructed in the first principles of Christian teaching and taught to know Christ. They then professed their faith, and afterward devoted themselves to prayers and fasts and performed penance, laying aside savagery and inhumanity, so that they might be prepared for that which would be given—that is, for communion in the body of Christ. For immediately after they had been baptized, they were led into the assembly and there participated in the Eucharist.

Previously, when that sacrament was celebrated, the catechumens were not even present, a practice also customary in profane mysteries, from which those who had not been initiated and consecrated were excluded. Hence the formula: Ἑκὰς ἑκὰς ἔστε, βέβηλοι, “Far away, far away, you profane!” Even the words “that which will be given,” etc., seem to have been transferred from the mysteries of the Gentiles, in which certain tokens and memorial objects were given. Arnobius, therefore, because he had heard that bread and wine were given to the faithful but did not possess a sufficiently clear understanding of the nature of this mystery, speaks about it rather obscurely and in language that is not sufficiently precise. Thus it appears that he had seen something only confusedly, [Col. 0860D] and nothing as yet distinctly. HERALDUS.—Nourry refutes Heraldus, thinking that in this passage Arnobius is discussing generally the blessed immortality of our soul, which we cannot obtain unless we acknowledge the true God and lay aside inhumanity of conduct. But the words “that which will be given” seem to me to indicate something singular and μυστηριῶδες (“mysterious” or “pertaining to the mysteries”), which Arnobius appears to have withheld deliberately and prudently, not, as Heraldus thinks, because of ignorance of the matter, but lest he offend the minds of Gentiles who did not understand such things. Therefore, with this one exception, I agree with Heraldus.

Yet after reading these words again and being better instructed, I now adhere entirely to the opinion of the most learned Nourry. “That which will be given” is eternal life, for which souls ought to be ready—that is, prepared and rendered worthy to receive it, naturally through virtue and good works. ORELLI.

“We have surrendered and bound ourselves over.” Fulvius Ursinus reads “we bind ourselves over”—wrongly. ORELLI.

[Col. 0861B] “We protect ourselves with tablets, the Psylli and Marsi selling them.” Thus reads the Leiden edition. In the royal codex the reading is “with tablets, leaves.” Theodorus Canterus thinks the passage should be corrected as follows: “We protect ourselves by the lips of the Psylli or by the teeth of the Marsi”—with an excellent sense, certainly, if it read “of the Psylli and the Marsi.” Salmasius, however—in his note on Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, page 239, and on Solinus, page 246, Orelli—wishes to emend it thus: “by Psyllian lips or Marsian teeth.” The sense is certainly the same. (Yet I have searched in vain for the formation *labinum, -i*, in place of *labium*. Orelli.) For those into whom serpents had wickedly infused venom by biting them were cured by the Psylli and Marsi through suction.

There seems no room for doubt that Arnobius is speaking of these peoples, the Psylli of Africa and the Marsi of Italy, who did in fact cure the venomous bites of serpents. They are mentioned by Pliny, *Natural History* VII.2; XXI.13; XXV.2; XXVIII.3; Aelian, *On the Nature of Animals* I.57; Plutarch, *Cato the Younger*; Strabo, Book XVII, page 814; Casaubon on Suetonius’ *Augustus*, chapter 17; Solinus, chapter 27; and Jerome, Preface to Joel. Lucan wrote most elegantly of the Psylli in the *Pharsalia* IX.891 and following:

> One nation alone inhabits the lands,  
> unharmed by the savage bite of serpents:  
> the Psylli of Marmarica, whose speech is as powerful as herbs.  
> Their very blood is safe and can admit no venom,  
> even when their incantation ceases; the nature of their country  
> has ordained that they should be immune while dwelling among serpents.

Finally, the following verses of Lucilius are cited from Book X of the *Satires* concerning the Marsi:

> Now let him be torn apart through the middle, just as a Marsian  
> tears serpents apart by song, when he has made every vein swell.

(Compare Aulus Gellius XVI.11; Firmicus, *Astronomy* VIII.6, etc.; and Cornelius Fronto, *On the Parthian War*, *Works*, page 322, in Angelo Mai’s edition: “If anyone born of a Marsian father feared vipers, lizards, and water snakes, would he not appear to have degenerated?”) ORELLI.—These passages indeed show clearly enough that Arnobius spoke, as we have said, of these Psylli and Marsi. But whether the words “tablets” and “selling” are genuine, or what should be substituted for them, who would dare assert without some complete and uncorrupted codex? NOURRY, pages 562–563.—For my part, I think that absolutely nothing should be altered. What prevents us from believing that magical tablets—amulets—were sold by impostors of this sort? Moreover, the following words, “and other peddlers and impostors,” seem to require the participle “selling”; and the construction “We protect ourselves by the lips of the Psylli or the teeth of the Marsi and by other peddlers,” etc., would certainly be exceedingly harsh.

And I now rejoice that, in explaining the passage and defending the codex’s reading, Johannes Schefferus of Strasbourg agrees with me. In a book of *Adversaria* included in *Miscellaneous Critical Observations*, volume IX, page 163, he cites Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* III, concerning these magical tablets: “She—Pamphile—equipped her deathly workshop with every kind of spice and with inscribed tablets bearing unintelligible writing.” We should understand inscribed bronze tablets marked with particular magical signs or names—for example, ΑΒΡΑΞΑΣ ΜΙΘΡΑΣ (“Abraxas Mithras”)—as protection against poisons. Images of these may be seen in Montfaucon’s *Antiquities*, plates 80 and 81, and the abridgment by Schatz. Compare Johannes Selden, who treats them extensively, *On the Syrian Gods* I.2. ORELLI.

“Peddlers.” The royal codex wrongly has “instructors.” *Institores*—here, “hawkers”—are those who retail either their own wares or those of others, and who have their wares, or even their services, for sale. Thus below, in chapter 38, Arnobius uses this word to include cooks, procurers, muleteers, prostitutes, and others whom he had previously named. Ovid, *The Art of Love* I.25:

> The loose-robed peddler will come to a mistress eager to buy,  
> and while you sit there he will display his wares.

NOURRY and ORELLI.]

## XXXII

Since these things are so, and since we hold it as a teaching handed down by the highest authority that souls are not situated far from the chasms and jaws of death, but can nevertheless be made long-lived by the gift and beneficence of the supreme Prince, provided only that they attempt and meditate upon knowing him—for knowledge of him is a kind of leaven of life and a bond that glues together what would otherwise fall apart—and then, having laid aside savagery and inhumanity, resume gentler dispositions, so that they may be prepared for that which will be given: why are we judged by you to be brutish and foolish if, because of these fears, we have surrendered [Note: [Col. 0860B] Thus Sabaeus; others read “have given.”] and bound ourselves over to God as our Liberator?

Against harmful blows and the venomous bites of snakes, we often seek remedies, [Col. 0861A] and protect ourselves with tablets sold by the Psylli and Marsi, and by other peddlers and impostors. And lest cold and the scorching sun cause us discomfort, with the anxious diligence of precaution we prepare the defenses of houses and clothing.

[Note: [Col. 0862C]

### XXXIII.—“What are we doing that does not proceed from common sense?”

Arnobius uses “common sense” to mean wisdom and judgment. Below, in Book IV: “Unless you take away and rob us of common sense”; and “that common sense which is present in all mortals.” Horace, *Satires* I.3: “He is entirely devoid of common sense.” Phaedrus I, fable 7:

> This is said of those to whom Fortune has granted  
> honor and glory, but has taken away common sense.

ELMENHORST.—Compare Schefferus on Phaedrus, Book I. The Roman edition wrongly has “from a sense of advantage.” Meursius restored the true reading, just as in what follows we read “prefer” in place of “set before.” ORELLI.

“Provided that the exchange is equitable.” Meursius conjectures that one should read “provided that this relation is necessary”—wrongly. The sense is: if a thing of such trifling value as the human soul admits of any comparison and exchange with Christ. ORELLI.

“By your own inward effort.” See above on Book I, chapter 20. ORELLI.

“You think that, as soon as you have departed, released from the knots of your limbs, wings will be supplied to you,” etc. Thus Gelenius. The first edition reads “you will have departed *senodes*,” which makes no sense. Cicero speaks in a manner suited to this thought in his *Consolation*, as quoted by Lactantius III.19: “For those same wise men did not think that the same path into heaven lies open to all. They taught that those polluted by vices and crimes are cast down into darkness and lie in mud; but that souls which are chaste, pure, whole, uncorrupted, and further refined by honorable studies and arts fly by a light and easy movement to the gods—that is, to a nature like their own.” Compare Euripides, *Suppliants*, verses 532–536. HERALDUS.

“To fly to the stars.” Stewechius prefers “to fly away to the stars.” ORELLI.

“To seek the abodes above.” Thus the Leiden edition and Oberthür, following Stewechius’ conjecture; others read “things above.” ORELLI.

“May deserve.” See above on Book I, chapter 3. ORELLI.]

## XXXIII

When fear of death—that is, the destruction of souls—is set before us, what are we doing that does not proceed from the common sense by which we all love ourselves, when we retain and embrace the one who promises to deliver us from such a danger, and prefer him even to our very souls, provided that the exchange is equitable?

You place the salvation of your souls within yourselves and trust that you will become gods by your own inward effort. We, however, promise ourselves nothing on the basis of our weakness, considering that our nature possesses no powers and is overcome by its own passions in every struggle with circumstances. You think that, as soon as you have departed, released from the knots of your limbs, wings will be supplied to you by which you can proceed to heaven and fly to the stars. We shrink from such audacity and do not regard it as lying within our power to seek the abodes above, since we are uncertain even of this very thing: whether we may deserve to receive life and to be removed from the law of mortality.

You presume that you will return of your own accord to the Lord’s court as though to your own home, with no one preventing you. We, however, neither hope that this can happen without the Lord of things nor judge that so great a power and freedom can be attributed to any human being.

[Col. 0863A] [Note: [Col. 0863C]

### XXXIV.—“Can be fulfilled.”

Fulvius Ursinus prefers “can confer,” but nothing should be altered against the authority of the codex. ORELLI.

“If we prostrate ourselves before his name.” Meursius and Stewechius wrongly conjecture “divinity.” “The name of Christ” is equivalent to Christ himself, just as “the name of God” stands for God. See above on Book I, chapter 20. ORELLI.

“To be endowed with the eternity of life.” Thus Salmasius. Others read “to be endowed with life by eternity.” Meursius conjectures “to be endowed with life in eternity.” Perhaps Arnobius, imitating his Lucretius, wrote *vitai aeternitate*, “with eternity of life,” using the archaic genitive. ORELLI.]

## XXXIV

Since these things are therefore so, what injustice can be so great that we should appear to you foolish for believing them, when we see that you both believe similar things and live in the same expectation? If we are judged worthy of ridicule because we promise ourselves a hope of this kind, the same ridicule awaits you, who appropriate to yourselves the hope of immortality. If you possess and follow some rational principle, grant us too some share in that same principle.

If Plato in the *Phaedo* [Note: [Col. 0863C] The manuscript here too has “in the *Phaedrus*.”], or another from this company, had promised us these joys—that is, the way of escaping death—and could provide it and bring his promise to fulfillment, it would have been fitting for us to adopt the worship of one from whom we expected so great a gift and benefit.

Now, since Christ has not only promised it but has also shown by such mighty works that it can be fulfilled, [Col. 0863B] what inappropriate thing are we doing, or on what grounds do we incur the charge of folly, if we prostrate ourselves before his name and majesty, from whom we hope for both things: to escape a tormenting death and to be endowed with the eternity [Note: [Col. 0863C] Stewechius reads “everlastingness.”] of life?

[Note: [Col. 0863C]

### XXXV.—“If we say that we do not know this,” etc.

The construction is: “Where will our belief appear to have gone astray, if we say that we do not know this … if we have believed that nothing is difficult or arduous for the omnipotent King?” *Credulitas* here has a favorable sense, equivalent to “faith.” See Caspar Barth’s index to Claudianus Mamertus, *On the State of the Soul*, under this word, and Conrad Rittershausen on Salvian, *Against Avarice* III, §518, page 160 of the Bremen edition. ORELLI.

“And of no importance before the Prince.” Thus Meursius, the editor of the Leiden edition, and Oberthür. Others read “of no name,” which could also be defended in this passage. ORELLI.

“For if we all concede that there is one Father of things,” etc. This was indeed the opinion of the ancient sages: that there is one God, the ruler and father of all things, and even of the gods themselves. This was the opinion of Hermes Trismegistus, as the blessed Augustine also teaches in *The City of God* VIII.23: “That Egyptian, however, says that some gods were made by the supreme God, and others by human beings,” etc. The Pythagoreans afterward commonly followed this opinion. See Hierocles. Compare Lactantius I.6. Hence Valerius Soranus:

> Jupiter almighty, himself the King of kings and God,  
> progenitor and mother of the gods; the one God and all.

[Col. 0864C] HERALDUS.—On this subject compare the special work of the distinguished Meiners, *History of the Doctrine concerning the True God*, Lemgo, 1780, in two volumes. ORELLI.

“Mutable.” The Roman edition has “liable to fall,” which Stewechius wrongly defends. ORELLI.

“And nothing whatsoever is found before him that possessed any designation.” That is, nothing that could be named, none of the things that exist: *kein einziges von allen nennbaren Dingen*, “not a single one of all nameable things.” *Vocamen* (“designation, appellation”) is a Lucretian word, Book II, verse 656:

> And prefers to misuse the name of Bacchus  
> rather than utter the liquid’s proper designation.

Solinus and Arnobius use it frequently—for example, Book I, chapter 3: “Our nation deserved to be endowed with the felicity of this designation”—and elsewhere. HERALDUS and ORELLI.

[Col. 0864D] “Brought forth.” “If they have been brought forth and begotten,” etc. Thus the Leiden edition. The earlier reading was: “if they have been brought forth. Brought forth and begotten.” Meursius reads: “brought forth; if they have been brought forth and begotten.” ORELLI.]

## XXXV

“But if souls,” they say, “are mortal [Note: [Col. 0864C] Fulvius omits these words.] and of an intermediate quality, how can they be made immortal from intermediate qualities?”

If we say that we do not know this and have merely believed what we heard from one more powerful, where will our belief appear to have gone astray, if we have believed that nothing is difficult, nothing arduous, for the omnipotent King? If what is impossible for us to do is possible for him and entirely ready for execution [Note: [Col. 0864C] The manuscript reads “obedience.”]? Is there anything that can obstruct his will, or does it not necessarily follow that whatever he has willed to exist comes into being?

Or shall we infer from our own classifications what can or cannot come into being, without considering that our rational powers are as mortal as we ourselves are, and of no importance before the Prince?

And yet, you who do not believe that souls are of an intermediate quality and are confined upon the middle boundary between life and destruction: are not absolutely all those beings whom opinion imagines to exist—gods, angels, demons, or whatever other name they bear—themselves also of an intermediate quality, mutable and in a condition of ambiguous fortune?

For if we all concede that there is one Father of things, who alone is immortal and unbegotten, and if nothing whatsoever is found before him that possessed any designation, [Col. 0864B] it follows that all those whom opinion has believed to be the gods of mortals were either begotten by him or brought forth at his command. If they were brought forth and begotten, they belong to a later order and time. If they belong to a later order and time, they must necessarily have an origin, and beginnings of birth and life. But that which has an entrance and a beginning of commencing life must necessarily also have a setting and an end.

[Note: [Col. 0864D]

### XXXVI.—“In what way, then, is the bestowal of immortality a gift of God, certainly to beings brought forth,” etc.

Thus, following Gelenius’ emendation, all editors down to the Leiden edition. The manuscript codex and first edition have: “He bestowed immortality; the gift of God is certain to those brought forth,” which makes no sense. Heraldus therefore suspects that the words “gift of God” are a gloss that crept into the text from the margin, where “Immortality is a gift of God” had been written, and that the passage should read: “In what way, then, has he”—that is, God—“bestowed certain immortality upon beings brought forth?” Wrongly. For Arnobius expressly denies that God has bestowed immortality upon beings brought forth; he says only that God can bestow it. Souls, just like bodies, are by their own nature perishable and mortal; if they attain immortality, it must be credited to God. I therefore think nothing should be altered. The Leiden edition recasts the sentence: “In what way, then, is immortality a gift of God the bestower in relation to beings brought forth and to souls,” etc.—excellent in sense, certainly, but too bold. ORELLI.

“Plato … in that discourse and book entitled the *Timaeus*,” etc. The passage occurs in Plato’s *Timaeus*, page 41 of Henri Estienne’s edition, volume III; volume IX, page 323 of the Bipont edition. Cicero translates it thus in *On the Universe*: “Then the God who begot all things speaks to the gods: ‘Attend to these words, you who have arisen from the stock of gods. The works of which I am the father and maker cannot be dissolved against my will, although everything that has been bound together can be dissolved. But it is by no means characteristic of one who is good to wish to dissolve what has been rationally bound together. Yet because you have come into being, you cannot indeed be immortal and indissoluble. Nevertheless, you shall by no means be dissolved, nor shall any fate of death destroy you, nor any power stronger than my purpose, which is a greater bond for your perpetuity than those bonds with which you were fastened when you were begotten.’” ELMENHORST.

“And cannot be dissolved by anyone other than him who bound it.” Thus Fulvius Ursinus, with the approval of Meursius and the Leiden edition. The manuscript codex and the first Roman edition read, nonsensically, “nor by anyone of abolition by him who bound it”; Gelenius therefore produced: “and the bond by abolition from him who bound it.” Stewechius reads: “nor by anyone except him who bound it.” But, as Stewechius himself admits, Fulvius’ emendation comes closer to the manuscript codex’s reading. ORELLI.

“And be endowed with a saving bond.” I have printed this with the Leiden edition. The others read “release.” But the subject of this passage is not the release of souls from corporeal bonds—which would be *missio*—but that “bond for perpetuity,” as Cicero calls it in the passage quoted above from Plato’s *Timaeus*: in other words, the binding by which souls, mortal by their own nature, are held together by God so that they are not dissolved. The Roman edition has “command,” which Theodorus Canterus approves: namely, the command that they remain safe and eternal. ORELLI.

“That souls are not daughters of the supreme King,” etc. Arnobius drew these ideas from the doctrine of the Neoplatonists—or rather of the Gnostics: Simon, Basilides, Saturninus, Carpocrates, and others—who maintained that the world was created not by God but by angels, and that the human being was likewise fashioned by them. Irenaeus, Book I, chapter 21, page 32 of Erasmus’ Paris edition: “Saturninus, like Menander, presents one Father unknown to us, who made angels, archangels, powers, and authorities. The world and everything in it, however, were made by seven particular angels. The human being was also a work of angels. When a luminous image appeared from above, from the supreme Power, and they could not retain it because it immediately returned upward, he says that they exhorted one another, saying: ‘Let us make a human being in our image and likeness.’ When he had been made, the modeled form was unable to stand upright because of the angels’ weakness, but wriggled about like a worm. Then the Power above, taking pity on him because he had been made in its likeness, sent forth a spark of life, which raised the human being upright, articulated his limbs, and made him live. Saturninus therefore says that after death this spark of life returns to things of its own kind, while the rest, from which those other elements were made, are dissolved,” etc.

The same author, chapter 24, concerning Carpocrates: “Carpocrates and his followers say that the world and the things in it were made by angels far inferior to the unbegotten Father.” [Col. 0866C] Compare Tertullian, *On Prescription against Heretics*, chapters 46 and 48; the same author, *On the Soul*, chapter 23; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, Book I, page 32; Philastrius, *On Heresies*, chapters 29, 31, 36, and 38.

Moreover, Arnobius speaks of all these matters only covertly and obscurely, deliberately and prudently, as it seems to me, lest, if he had discussed them more distinctly and named the Gnostic creators of the world—the Demiurge, Logos, Phronesis, Sophia, Dynamis, and the others whom they called aeons—he himself should be accused by the Gentiles of the polytheism that he wished to refute and destroy. ORELLI.

“And be predicated in the essence of his own name.” Meursius defends the codex’s reading, “in the meaning of his own name,” by reference to a parallel passage in Arnobius, Book I: “We have surrendered ourselves to God, by whose command and judgment everything that exists subsists and remains fixed in the perpetuity of his determination”; and, in the same book: “when the former has been removed, to transfer it into the form and meaning of others.” Thus *sententia* in this passage would be equivalent to αἴσθησις, “perception” or “sense.” Although Arnobius could use it absolutely in that sense, “the meaning of a name” is nevertheless novel and without parallel. ORELLI.

“Quite numerous.” In place of “quite many.” The superlative is used in place of the positive, as frequently in Arnobius. See above on Book I, chapter 22. (*Satis multus*, moreover, was used to mean “excessively numerous.” See Barth, *Adversaria* XXIX.13, page 1380.) Thus *satis pulcherrima*, “quite most beautiful,” occurs in Pomponius, *On the Origin of Law*: “There survives a quite most beautiful speech of his—Cicero’s—entitled *For Quintus Ligarius*.” STEWECHIUS and ORELLI.]

### XXXVI

But the gods are said to be immortal. They are immortal, then, not by nature, but by the will and gift of God the Father. Since, therefore, the bestowal of immortality is a gift of God—certainly to beings already brought forth—he will in the same way deign to endow souls with immortality, although savage death may seem able to extinguish them, reduce them to nothing, and destroy them by an irreversible annihilation.

That divine Plato, who held many conceptions worthy of God and far from those common among the multitude, says in the discourse and book entitled *Timaeus* that the gods and the world are corruptible by nature [Note: [Col. 0866B] The manuscript correctly has “corruptible”], and are not altogether exempt from dissolution, but by the will of God, their king and prince, are held forever in a bond. For what has been rightly bound and fastened with the most perfect knots is preserved by God’s goodness; and it can be dissolved by no one other than him who bound it—if circumstances require—or be endowed with a saving bond.

Therefore, if the matter is so, and no other view is fitting either to entertain or to believe, why are you surprised that we call souls beings of an intermediate quality, when Plato says that the very divine powers themselves possess intermediate natures, but that continuous and unfailing life is granted to them by the benevolence of the supreme ruler? For if perhaps you do not know this, and it was previously unknown to you because of the novelty of the matter, receive it even at this late hour and learn from him who knows and has brought it into the open through Christ: souls are not daughters of the greatest King; nor, as is said, did they begin, after being begotten by him, to know themselves and to be designated according to the essence of their own name [*praedicuri*, materially uncertain; probably *praedicari*]. Rather, they have some other progenitor, separated from the Emperor by very many degrees of dignity and power, yet noble through his place in the Emperor’s court and through the loftiness of his eminent birth.

[Note: [Col. 0864C] The manuscript has *largiter*, incorrectly.]

[Note: [Col. 0865B] Fulvius reads “to the gods.”]

[Note: [Col. 0866D]

### XXXVII—*Habuissent*

Fulvius Ursinus reads *hausissent*.

ORELLI.

“And the most obscene vessels of strained liquid.” This is taken from Lucretius, book IV, verse 1020:

> Little boys often believe that beside a basin or a broken jar,  
> Fast bound in sleep, they lift their clothing  
> And pour out the strained moisture of their whole body.

HERALDUS.

Because the ancients filtered wine through a sack—an operation they also called *saccare*, “to strain”—an analogy, not without charm though applied to a rather indecent subject, caused urine, as liquid passed through a filter, to be called “strained piss,” since the bladder has the appearance of a wine-strainer or sack.

TURNEBUS, *Adversaria*, book XXIII, chapter 14, and ELMENHORST.

Similarly, Sammonicus, *On Medicine*, verse 77:

> Therefore it helps to apply mud to limbs rubbed raw,  
> Which the body’s strained moisture produces from an ass.

See there Kenchen and Ackermann, as well as Morgagni, Epistle I, in the Vulpian edition of Celsus, vol. II, p. 283.

ORELLI.

“And what benefit do human beings bring to the world?” The view that the world was not created for the sake of human beings belonged to the Epicureans. Lactantius, book VII, chapter 5: “What advantage,” Epicurus asks, “does God derive from the human being, that he should make him for his own sake? What, then, does human worship contribute to God, who is blessed and in need of nothing?” Arnobius follows this opinion here—though elsewhere, when philosophizing, he is a Stoic—in order to demonstrate that human souls cannot have proceeded from God. Lactantius refutes it in book VII, chapter 4, and in the *Epitome*, chapter 7; Origen, book IV, *Against Celsus*; Clement, *Recognitions*, book I, p. 13, and book VI, p. 101.

ELMENHORST and HERALDUS.

“This totality of the universe is imperfect and lame.” Here *claudus* means the same as *mancus*, “defective, mutilated”—Greek κυλλός (*crooked, maimed*)—not χωλός (*lame*). Thus Livy, book XXXVII, chapter 24, speaks of “disabled and mutilated ships.”

ORELLI.

“The blasts of the winds will fall silent.” So above, book I, chapter 2: “Surely the winds have not breathed out their souls,” etc. Lactantius uses “spirits of the winds” in the same sense, *Institutes*, book VII, chapter 6; see Bunemann there, p. 893.

ORELLI.

“From gathered clouds.” See the note on book I, chapter 2.

ORELLI.

“For the perfection of the world.” Fulvius Ursinus would prefer to read: “For a world of perfection.” I do not know why.

ORELLI.]

### XXXVII

For if souls were, as report has it, the offspring of the Lord, and their generation derived from the supreme power, nothing would have been lacking to their perfection, since they had been produced by the most perfect excellence. They would all have possessed one understanding and one agreement; they would always have inhabited the royal court. Nor would they, after abandoning the abodes of blessedness in which they had known and retained the most august teachings, have foolishly sought these earthly regions, become enveloped in dark bodies, and lived amid phlegm and blood—amid these bags of excrement and most obscene vessels of strained urine.

But these regions too had to be inhabited, and for that reason almighty God sent souls here as though into certain colonies. And what benefit do human beings bring to the world? For the sake of what purpose are they necessary, so that they may be believed to have been obliged, not in vain, to live in this part of it and to be tenants of an earthly body? Do they contribute some part toward completing the integrity of this vast structure, so that, unless they are added, this totality of the universe is imperfect and defective?

What, then? If human beings do not exist, will the world cease performing its functions? Will the stars not complete their revolutions? Will there be no summers [Col. 0867B] and winters? Will the blasts of the winds fall silent? Will rains no longer fall to earth from gathered, suspended clouds, bringing relief to its aridity? Yet all things must necessarily proceed through their courses and must not depart from the continuity of their native order, even if the name of humanity is never heard in the world and this earthly sphere falls silent in the stillness of an empty solitude.

How, then, can it be vaunted that an inhabitant had to be added to these regions, when it is clear that nothing from the human being contributes to the perfection of the world, and that all human pursuits always look to private advantage and never pass beyond the limits of personal utility?

[Note: [Col. 0867B] The manuscript incorrectly has *pigarios*, from which others produced *bigarios*. See the note.]

[Note: [Col. 0867D]

### XXXVIII—“Why pantomimes, why little mime-actors,” etc.

Mimes and pantomimes differ in this respect: pantomimes, while a boy sang and a flute-player accompanied responsively, performed songs through dance while themselves mute and silent; mimes, however, also sang and spoke onstage. See Salmasius, who discusses them at length, on Flavius Vopiscus, *Carinus*, chapter 19, *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. II, p. 828 ff.; and Rigaltius on Artemidorus, book I, chapter 78, p. 75, Reiff’s edition.

ORELLI.

“Those blowing upon trumpet, pipe, and reed.” Festus: “*Flator*: a flute-player.” The Glosses of Philoxenus: “*Flat*, φυσᾷ, ‘he blows’; *flator*, αὐλητής, ‘flute-player.’”

HERALDUS.

Stewechius prefers the frequentative *flatitantes*, incorrectly. *Flo* becomes *flato*, just as *no* becomes *nato*.

ORELLI.

“Trick-riders.” Those who drove two horses without saddles and repeatedly leapt from one to the other with astonishing speed were called *desultores*. Compare Gesner in the *Thesaurus*; Scaliger on Manilius V, verse 85; and Muncker on Hyginus, fable LXXX, p. 133.

ORELLI.

[Col. 0868C] “Stilt-walkers.” According to Festus, these were pantomimes who, in order to imitate goat-Pans in their dancing, attached poles with small forks and, standing upon them, walked in imitation of that creature’s legs—obviously because of the difficulty of keeping their balance. See the commentators there and on Varro, *On the Latin Language*, VI, p. 94; Notes, p. 225, Bipont edition; and Muretus, *Various Readings*, book XIII, chapter 19.

They were called *grallatores* from the *grallae*, the stilts upon which they mounted and walked. *Grallae* is a contraction of *gradulae* and means the same as *colobathra*; French *des échasses*, German *Stelzen*, “stilts.” In Greek these men were called γύπωνες. Pollux, *Onomasticon*, book IV, chapter 14, section 104:

> The γύπωνες, mounting upon wooden legs, danced while clad in transparent Tarentine garments.

See Jungermann there, p. 410, vol. I, Hemsterhuis’s edition. Compare Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under *grallae*, and Bulenger, *On Theatres*, I.32. Translate it, therefore, *Stelzenläufer*, “stilt-walkers.”

J. F. Gronovius, who discusses these people extensively in *Plautine Readings*, p. 284 ff., observes:

> These people appear to have acquired by frequent practice the ability even to dance and leap upon stilts, unlike those whom we see walking on stilts today, who take long strides rather than swift ones.

I also remember reading in some itinerary—whose title has escaped me—that, because of the sandy soil, inhabitants of the French province bordering Spain near Bayonne, in the département of Landes, run, travel, and even carry burdens while standing upon stilts.

ORELLI.

“Rope-walkers.” Barth discusses the skills of the ancient rope-walkers at length in *Adversaria*, book V, chapter 19, p. 248.

ORELLI.

“Why sellers of salted tuna.” Salmasius made this excellent correction in the Leiden edition and in his note on Solinus, p. 174. The manuscript had *quibiarii*, which is the same as *cybiarii*. Thus manuscripts have *Quinegion* and *Quizicus* for *Cynegion* and *Cyzicus*; and in an ancient codex of Paulinus’s letters Paulinus writes to Ausonius *triquinon*, that is, τρίκυνον, “a threefold greeting.”

From *quibiarii*, others who did not understand the force of the word produced *bigarii*, which would be wholly out of place here, for above Arnobius grouped chariot-drivers with runners and boxers. By contrast, *cybiarii*—that is, those who sell *cybia*—are appropriately joined with salters and fishmongers. *Cybium* was a square-cut kind of salted fish or *tarichos*, named from Greek κύβος, which among geometricians denotes a square or cubical figure. *Cybium* was made from pelamys, or young tuna, which is also called κύβεια by Oppian, *Halieutica* I, verse 183. Compare Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXII, chapter 11, Hardouin’s major note there, p. 599, and the commentators on Festus under this word. Accordingly, *cybiarii* were those who salted and sold *cybia*, that is, τεμάχη θύννων, “cuts of tuna.”

Nourry, p. 551, prefers *cibarios*, meaning those who prepare and serve food—French *traiteurs*, “caterers”—citing Varro’s words in Nonius, chapter 2: “Your own brother was Aristoxenus’s food-provider.”

ORELLI.

“Salt-workers.” That is, salters. The Glosses of Philoxenus: “*Salitor*, ταριχευτής, one who salts or pickles.”

HERALDUS.

Papias: “A *salinator* is one who makes salt.” An ancient inscription on p. MCXIV of Gruter reads:

> THE SALT-WORKERS OF THE COMMUNITY OF THE MENAPII  
> TO LEPIDUS PROCULUS, SON OF LUCIUS,  
> FOR HIS SERVICE. SEPTIMINA  
> SAW TO ITS RESTORATION AT PUBLIC EXPENSE.

ELMENHORST.

Compare Nourry, p. 564 ff. German *Salzbereiter*, “salt-preparers.”

ORELLI.

[Col. 0869C] “Fishmongers.” So the Leiden edition, following the emendation of A. Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XIII, chapter 14, p. 11, vol. II. The manuscript has *bolones*, from which others produced *volones*, the name given during the Punic War to volunteer soldiers drawn from slaves. But that meaning has no relevance here.

Could they instead be men who voluntarily hired themselves out to sword and steel? I might think so, were they not preceded by salt-workers. We should therefore read *bolones*, or with a Greek ending *bolonas*, from *boli* of fish, for this was the name given to the shops of fishmongers. See Donatus on Terence, *Eunuch*, act II, scene II, verse 26. I have also found in an ancient lexicon from the library of Pierre Daniel that *bolonas* is expressly explained as μεταπράτας καὶ παλιγκατήλους, that is, “middlemen and retail-dealers.” Thus fishmongers who sold *boli* were also called by this name. Βόλον ὠνεῖσθαι, “to buy the cast,” from fishermen, was a familiar proverb among the ancients. So Turnebus, book I; Gesner in the *Thesaurus*; and Vossius in *Roman Etymology*.

ORELLI.

“Weavers of winnowing baskets and wicker cart-baskets.” Salmasius demonstrates at length in his note on Solinus that this is the correct reading. *Vitores* are οἱ πλέκται, “the plaiters,” those who bind or weave, from the ancient verb *vio* or *vieo*; Greek μίω. The Aeolians said βίω, meaning “I bind, I plait.” Festus: “*Viere*: to bind,” whence *vimina*, “withies,” and *vasa viminea*, “wicker vessels.” See the commentators there and Columna on the fragments of Ennius, p. 293—or p. 184 in Hesselius’s edition.

Hence *vitor* or *vietor* in Plautus, *Rudens*, act IV, scene III, verse 50, and in Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXV, chapter 11, concerning the painter Pausias: “In his youth he loved Glycera, a weaver of garlands”; for by Salmasius’s conjecture *vitricem* should be read instead of *inventricem*. Nourry is therefore wrong to think that *venditores*, “sellers,” should be read.

Moreover, *sirpiae*, *sirpeae*, or *scirpeae* were baskets woven from withies and placed on carts. See Graevius on Justin XLIII, chapter 4, p. 716, Abraham Gronovius’s edition; and Junius, who discusses this word at length, on Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* II.4, p. 199, Graevius’s edition. Others explain them as dung-crates; but Varro, *On Agriculture* I.23, expressly distinguishes them from crates. See the distinguished Schneider in his *Lexicon to the Agricultural Writers* under this word. Compare Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under *sirpare*.

ORELLI.

[Col. 0870A] “Why fullers and wool-workers.” Plautus likewise joins them in *Aulularia*, act III, scene V, verse 34:

> There stands the fuller, the embroiderer, the goldsmith, the wool-worker.

Our author perhaps had this passage before his eyes. The *lanarii* are ἐριουργοί, workers in wool, who cleanse it of dirt and prepare it for spinning and weaving—German *Wollkämmer*, “wool-combers.” Julius Firmicus, *Astronomy*, book III, chapter 9: “Their trades are dirty and filthy or foul-smelling, such as those of leather-dressers, fullers, wool-workers, painters, and cooks.” A fuller is, as Ovid says, one “who removes stains from damaged garments.”

ELMENHORST and ORELLI.

“Embroiderers.” These are people who decorate and interweave garments with a needle, for the Phrygians were the first to invent that kind of textile-work. See Pliny, *Natural History*, book VIII, chapter 48. Compare Servius on *Aeneid* III, verse 484; Nonius, chapter I, no. 10; Isidore, *Origins*, book XIX, chapter 22. Plautus frequently mentions embroiderers—for example, in *Aulularia* at the passage just cited, and in *Menaechmi*, act I, scene III, and act III, scene II.

NOURRY.

Compare Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under this word, and G. F. Gronovius, *Plautine Readings*, p. 214 ff.

ORELLI.

“Confectioners of *panchrista*.” Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XIII, chapter 14, offers various explanations of this word. He thinks that either *panchrestarios* should be read, from the all-purpose ointment *panchrestum* mentioned by Cicero, *Against Verres* III.65, so that they would be druggists and pharmacists who prepare medicines and remedies for every kind of illness; or else “bread-making pastry-cooks,” that is, makers of pastries or small cakes.

Johannes Wowerius, on Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, chapter 14, p. 132, Jacob Gronovius’s edition, conjectures that “bread-sellers, pastry-cooks” should be read. The Glosses have: “*Panarius*, ἀρτοπώλης, a bread-seller.”

But nothing should be changed. *Panchristarii* or *panchrestarii* were makers of cakes and *panchresta*—that is, sweets, confectionery, and small cakes, Greek γλυκάσματα. These were called χρηστά and πάγχρηστα μελιττώματα, “fine” and “universally pleasing honey-confections,” by the Greeks, and *panchrista* by the Latins, since they were made of honey and poppy-seed. See Salmasius on Aelius Lampridius, *Heliogabalus*, chapter 32, *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, p. 873. Salvian, *On Providence*, book VI:

> Nearly all little children who are disobedient, whom threats and rods do not make compliant, are sometimes drawn to obedience by πάγχρηστα—sweetmeats—and caresses.

ORELLI and HERALDUS.

“Contribute.” So Heraldus and the Leiden edition. The manuscript incorrectly has *conferre*; Meursius reads *confert*.

ORELLI.

[Col. 0870D] “Unless the contained addition of a wretched animal … were joined to it.” So the manuscript and the Leiden edition; the latter has *conditio*. Others read *completio*. But Heraldus rightly defends the ancient reading. *Contentio* is the same as *continentia* above in chapter 19 of this book, where the notes may be consulted. Here, then, *contentio* has a passive sense: “that which is contained.” The meaning is: “Unless there were joined to it something contained within it—namely, a wretched and superfluous animal.”

ORELLI.]

### XXXVIII

For what benefit does it bring to the world—to begin with serious matters—that there should be here mighty kings? What benefit do tyrants bring, or masters, or countless other and very extensive powers? What benefit do commanders highly experienced in warfare and skilled in capturing cities, or soldiers steadfast and utterly invincible in cavalry engagements or infantry combat?

What benefit do orators, grammarians [Col. 0868B], and poets bring? What benefit do writers, dialecticians, and musicians? What benefit do pantomimes, little mime-actors, stage-players, singers, and those who blow upon trumpet, pipe, and reed? What benefit do runners, boxers, chariot-drivers, trick-riders, stilt-walkers, rope-walkers, and conjurers bring?

What benefit do sellers of salted tuna [Note: [Col. 0867B] The manuscript incorrectly has *pigarios*, from which others produced *bigarios*. See the note], salt-workers, fishmongers [Col. 0869A], perfumers, goldsmiths, bird-catchers, and weavers of winnowing baskets and wicker cart-baskets bring? What benefit do fullers, wool-workers, embroiderers, cooks, confectioners, muleteers, pimps, butchers, and prostitutes bring? What benefit do the other kinds of retailers bring?

What do the systems of the learned professions and of the arts—which an entire lifetime is too short to enumerate—contribute to the ordering and constitution of the world, so that it should be believed that the world could not have been established without human beings and would not have attained its integrity unless the contained addition of a wretched and superfluous animal were joined to it?

[Note: [Col. 0870D]

### XXXIX—“Exempt from bodily contact and earthly circumscription”

So Gelenius. The manuscript and the Roman first edition have “rash circumscription,” whose meaning is not easy to divine. Heraldus conjectures that we should read: “exempt from bodily contact, elemental circumscription,” in Arnobius’s customary manner of omitting conjunctions. The Leiden edition reads “exempt from circumscription by boundaries” (*metariae circumscriptionis expertes*).

For my part, I suspect that *terrariae*, “terrestrial,” should be read, since it is closer to the manuscript’s reading; on this word see the same Salmasius on Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, p. 413 ff. Thus the Romans called birds raised in aviaries *aves terrariae*, “land-birds,” as distinguished from “birds of the air,” which enjoy the free air; or, more generally, birds content with land alone, such as thrushes, peacocks, and turtledoves, and which do not also require water, as geese, ducks, and teal do.

ORELLI.

“Would spring forth.” In the same sense the Greeks say προτορεῖν, ἐκπροθορεῖν, and ἐκθορεῖν, “to leap or issue forth.” See Hemsterhuis on Lucian, *Prometheus*, §4, p. 212, vol. I, Bipont edition.

ORELLI.

“Utterly senseless wailing.” *Ineptissimos* means “least fitting for beings regarded as goddesses, utterly unworthy of divine souls”; or, better, in a general sense, ἀνοήτους, “mindless”—German *verstandloses Gewimmer*, “senseless whimpering”—as below in a very similar passage in book VII: “Little infants are frightened out of their senseless wailing when they hear rattles.”

ORELLI.

“Would drain the breasts by sucking.” The Glosses of Isidore: “*Fellitat* … sucks.” Thus Solinus, *Polyhistor*, chapter 45: “A mother never offers her udder to be sucked by a foal,” concerning mares from which the *hippomanes* had been snatched away. θηλᾷν means “to suck the breast”; in Aeolic, φηλᾷν. From this comes Latin *felare*. Thus Varro: “to suck human milk”; and elsewhere: “Once the fosterlings sucked the she-wolf.” From it also come the frequentatives *felitare* and *fellitare*.

SALMASIUS, on Solinus, *Plinian Exercises*, book I, p. 662.

Meursius collected more examples, p. 66 ff.

ORELLI.

“So that they might be brought to silence by the movements of a frightened nurse and by hearing rattles.” Some, including Meursius, wish to read *vocibus*, “voices.” But the common reading can be defended. Arnobius therefore says “by the nurse’s movements,” namely, those by which she rocks the cradle in order to bring the children to silence. Thus *motus* here means German *das Wiegen, Schaukeln*, “rocking, swinging.”

For *pavidae*, “frightened,” the manuscript has *pavidi*, referring to the infants—that is, “crying from fear”—which I prefer. *Crepitacula* were small instruments shaped like a sistrum, toys for infants, whose inventor is said to have been Archytas—German *Kinderklapper*, “children’s rattle.” Martial, *Epigrams* XIV.54, “On a Little Rattle”:

> If some crying little household slave hangs upon your neck,  
> Let him shake these chattering sistra with his tender hand.

Here too, moreover, Arnobius imitates his Lucretius, book V, lines 228 ff.:

> But the varied flocks, herds, and wild beasts grow,  
> Nor have they need of rattles, nor does any require  
> A kindly nurse’s coaxing, lisping speech.

HERALDUS, ELMENHORST, and ORELLI.

The Greeks call those rattles πλαταγώνια. Julius Pollux, *Onomasticon*, book IX, section 127:

> The πλαταγώνιον was played with by lovers, whether male or female; for both the castanet and the sistrum which nurses shake while lulling and amusing children who have difficulty sleeping are so called.

Meursius, p. 68. Compare Hugo Grotius on Martianus Capella, book I, p. 4.

ORELLI.

“Who had been guileless.” *Simplices* means harmless in goodness, as Arnobius himself explains extremely well in the words that follow. Thus open-hearted people, in whom there is no deceit and no malice, are called “guileless and good.” So Marcus Tullius Cicero, *On Duties* I.30:

> There are others very unlike these: guileless and open, who think that nothing should be done covertly or through ambush—devotees of truth and enemies of deceit.

In Greek, εὐηθεῖς, ἁπλοῖ, ἁπλοϊκοί, “simple, sincere,” or even ἀκέραιοι, “innocent, unmixed,” as the Divine Savior calls them in Matthew 10:16; see Grotius there.

HERALDUS and ORELLI.

“To pretend … to conceal.” Thus Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 5—whom Arnobius appears to imitate throughout this passage—calls Catiline “a pretender and concealer of whatever he pleased.” See Cortius there, p. 32. The Wolfenbüttel Glosses explain: “I pretend that which I do not wish to do; I conceal that which I do wish to do.” Aurelius Victor, *Epitome*, chapter 14, concerning Hadrian:

> He cunningly concealed an envious, gloomy, wanton disposition, insolently inclined to self-display, pretending to clemency and, conversely, concealing the passion for glory with which he burned.

ORELLI.

“To seek gain through flattering abasement.” Arnobius uses *captare*, “to seek to obtain,” significantly, because the flatterer’s end is κερδαίνειν, “to make a profit.” Otherwise he is judged and designated by the milder name ἄρεσκος, “one eager to please,” whom in Latin we may call *blandus*, “ingratiating.” Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* IV.14:

> The person who aims merely at being pleasant, and not at anything else, is an ingratiating person; but the one who does so in order that some benefit may accrue to him in money, or in things obtainable through money, is a flatterer.

Themistius Euphrades likewise says in Oration III that the flatterer’s object is κερδαίνειν, ἢ γαστρίζεσθαι ἐκ τοῦ ἔργου, “to profit or fill his belly from the business”; and Lucian says in his discourse *In Defense of the Portraits*: τὸν κόλακα ἐπαινεῖν τῆς χρείας ἕνεκα τῆς ἑαυτοῦ, “the flatterer praises for the sake of his own advantage.”

HERALDUS.

[Col. 0872C] “To entertain one thing in the mind and promise another in the face.” Similarly Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 10: “To keep one thing concealed in the breast and have another ready upon the tongue.” The Latins called such people “double-tongued”; for example, Virgil, *Aeneid* I, “the double-tongued Tyrians,” and Horace, *Odes* I.6.7, “the duplicitous Ulysses.” Thus also among the Greeks διπλοῦς, “double,” is opposed to τῷ ἀληθευτικῷ, “the truthful person.”

HERALDUS.

Compare our observations on Jacob Balde, *Selected Poems*, III, *Lyrics*, Ode VI, verse 21.

ORELLI.

“To gather the poisons of malice.” So the Leiden editor punctuates the passage. Heraldus, however, punctuated the whole as follows: “to deceive the unsuspecting through frauds and snares, by the countless arts of malicious practices; to seek out poisons.” But I prefer the former, because below, in chapter 42, we read: “Did he send souls for this reason, that they might prepare poisonous draughts?” If we follow Heraldus, that would be an idle repetition of our passage. Moreover, “the poisons of malice” is an entirely appropriate designation for cunning deceptions and frauds that creep secretly like poisons. Thus Catullus, poem LXXVII, calls Rufus, a treacherous and deceitful man, “the poison and plague of friendship.”

ORELLI.

“With deceitful changeability.” So Fulvius Ursinus. Sabaeus’s first edition has “with the changeability of deceitfulness.” On the word *pellax*, “deceitful,” see above, the note on chapter 7.

ORELLI.

“Would oppress and enslave themselves beneath the yoke of servitude.” In this way Arnobius reveals the infancy—indeed, the very birth—of slavery. Those captured in war were enslaved to their conquerors. Slavery was afterward propagated in this manner. On the causes of slavery, see Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 20.

HERALDUS.

“And finally, after the condition of their birth had been changed, each would come under the power of another.” Meursius prefers: “different ones under different powers,” not badly, as below in chapter 41: “different ones would seize different things.”

ORELLI.

“After the condition of their birth had been changed.” Because all are born free. Accordingly, since freedom is natural, slavery is contrary to nature and is an institution of the law of nations. Digest, book IV, *On the Status of Persons*, etc.

HERALDUS.

[Col. 0873B] “Of consummate truth.” That is, of perfect and utterly complete truth, which admits no further doubt. In our language, literally, German *ausgemachte Wahrheit*, “established truth.”

ORELLI.

“Would ask them for aid.” Latin very frequently uses *poscere*, “to ask,” with two accusatives, after the Greek manner αἰτεῖν τινά τι, “to ask someone for something.” Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 50:

> Only ask the gods for pardon.

See more examples in Gesner’s *Thesaurus*. Others omit “them.”

ORELLI.

“Or would utterly deny that anything exists.” “That anything exists” means the existence of all things. Arnobius alludes to the ἀφασία (*aphasia*, suspension of assertion) of the Pyrrhonists.

ORELLI.

“And, as though bereft of the lights of their eyes.” Meursius reads: “so that, as though,” etc.

ORELLI.]

### XXXIX

Unless perhaps the King of the world—though it is the height of rashness for a human mouth to utter such a thing—sent souls begotten from himself into this world for the following purpose: that those who had been goddesses in his presence, exempt from bodily contact and earthly circumscription, might be plunged into human seed, spring forth from women’s genitals [Col. 0871A], utter and continue the most senseless wailing, drain breasts by sucking them, and smear and drench themselves with their own discharge; and that they might be brought to silence by the movements of a frightened nurse and by hearing rattles.

[Note: [Col. 0871A] The manuscript has “and then,” which should not be changed, according to Meursius.]

Did he send souls for this reason: that those who had been guileless and, until recently, harmless in their goodness might learn among human beings to pretend, to conceal, to lie, to overreach, to cheat, to seek gain through flattering abasement, to entertain one thing in the mind and promise another in the face; to ensnare and deceive the unsuspecting through frauds and ambushes [Col. 0872A], to gather the poisons of malice through countless devices, and to adapt them to the needs of the moment with deceitful changeability?

Did he send souls for this reason: that, though they had lived in peaceful and tranquil serenity, they might take from bodies the causes by which they would become savage and monstrous, maintain quarrels and hostilities, wage wars against one another, storm and overthrow cities, oppress and enslave themselves beneath the yoke of servitude, and finally, after the condition of their birth had been changed, each come under the power of another?

Did he send souls for this reason: that, forgetful of consummate truth [Col. 0873A] and oblivious to what God is, they might make supplication before lifeless images, address pieces of wood, bronze, and stone as divine powers, seek aid [Note: [Col. 0873B] Sabaeus reads “might be asked”] through the blood of slaughtered animals, and make no mention of themselves; indeed, that some of them might even doubt their own existence, or utterly deny that anything exists?

Did he send souls for this reason: that those who in their own abodes had been of one mind, with equal understanding and knowledge, should, after putting on mortal forms, be divided by differences of opinion; that one thing should seem just to some, and another useful and right to others; that they should dispute over things to be sought and avoided; that different souls should establish different boundaries of good and evil; that the obscurity of things should confront those desiring to know the truth [Note: [Col. 0873B] Fulvius reads “to know”]; and that, as though bereft of the lights of their eyes, they should perceive nothing with certainty and be led astray along the ambiguous paths [Col. 0873B] of conjecture?

[Note: [Col. 0873C]
