### XL—“Would seek for themselves the protection or covering of clothing”

Stewechius prefers *velamina*, “coverings,” in keeping with Arnobius’s practice of imitating the ancients, especially Lucretius.

ORELLI.

“Would procure various household furnishings for the poverty of their daily necessities.” The same Stewechius conjectures that we should read: “would procure their daily needs amid a poverty of things”—that is, amid a daily lack of necessities. But nothing should be changed. Arnobius used the neuter plural *diurna* in the rarer sense of things necessary for daily sustenance:

> Things whose denial causes human nature pain.

German *die täglichen Bedürfnisse*, “daily necessities.” I have nevertheless searched in vain for examples of this meaning in other writers.

ORELLI.

“By crop-rust.” Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 150:

> … so that harmful rust  
> Might consume the stalks.

Servius comments there:

> Rust is a kind of blight by which stalks perish, which country people call a calamity. This kind of blight generally arises from mist, when the crops blacken and are consumed. Hence there is also a god Rubigus, and his rites, held on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, are called the Rubigalia.

ELMENHORST.

As the distinguished Vossius teaches in his note on this passage of Virgil, the ancients designated two different plant diseases by that name: one white, which the Germans call *Mehltau*, “mildew,” and the other red, *der Rost im Getreide*, “rust in grain.” Elsewhere it is called *aerugo*, “verdigris”; by Cyprian, *comestura*, “devouring”; and by the Greeks, βρῶσις, “corrosion.” See Davis on Lactantius, *Epitome*, chapter 65, p. 1333, Bunemann’s edition.

ORELLI.

[Col. 0874B] “And in their zeal for possessing would burn with an insatiable appetite of the heart.” Here *habere*, “to possess,” is used absolutely, as it is by the best writers. Juvenal, quoting Ennius:

> No one asks where you got it; but you must possess.

And *habentia*, “possessions,” means πλοῦτος, “wealth.” Quadrigarius in Nonius: “Possessions had inflated their spirits.” So too Greek ἔχειν means “to possess.” Sophocles in *Ajax*:

> For envy creeps toward the possessor.

So too in the Gospel:

> To the one who possesses, it shall be given.

HERALDUS.

Add Ruhnken on Rutilius Lupus, p. 78.

OCHSNER.

“Would penetrate hidden nations at the risk of their lives.” The abstinence of the faithful at that time was remarkable. They condemned avarice and an excessive desire for possessions so strongly that they condemned dangerous commercial voyages on this very ground. See Lactantius, book V, chapter 18; Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chapter 11.

HERALDUS.

“And, after transporting their merchandise, would always seek high prices and low prices.” Zeno of Verona, Sermon I, *On Avarice*:

> Another man watches for the market-price of all commodities and lies in wait for the time to sell: smaller in measure, greater in price. He denies that he possesses what he intends to sell, so that he may be begged, so that he may cut the buyer’s throat—and would that the product were at least sold unadulterated! Moreover, he groans if the year is barren, and much more if it has been fertile: in the former case because he sells too little, in the latter because he is not the only seller. Do you wish to know in what deep darkness he knows himself to be enveloped? He is angry with God if he is not always enriched by public misfortunes.

HERALDUS.

Meursius therefore wrongly conjectures that “and would seek profit” should be read.

ORELLI.

“Would practice greedy and utterly unjust usury.” Christians of that age, whose charity was more fervent, believed that every form of interest-taking was ἀθέμιτον, “unlawful,” and alien to humanity itself. Hence Miltiades, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.19, where he attacks the Montanist prophets:

> Tell me: does a prophet dye his hair? Does a prophet paint his eyes? Does a prophet love adornment? Does a prophet play at gaming boards and dice? Does a prophet lend money at interest?

HERALDUS.

So too did pagans—for example Cato, who said that lending at interest was the same as killing a human being.

ELMENHORST.

“And from the blood of the wretched would be tormented by sleepless calculations. They would continually extend the boundaries of their estates for thousands…” I have printed the text this way following Heraldus’s emendation. The codex has: “they would increase sleeplessnesses by calculating,” from which Gelenius and those who followed him produced: “they would torment themselves with the madness of calculating.” Stewechius reads: “they would increase their sleeplessness by calculating sums.”

It should rather be the singular *insomniam*, for the subject here is not dreams but the wakefulness of the miser. Salmasius, in the Leiden edition, reads: “And from the blood of the wretched they would torment themselves sleeplessly in calculating accounts. Of estates…”

The conjunction “and” appears to me to have been put in the wrong place, and the words “from the blood of the wretched” should be joined to the preceding phrase, “would practice greedy and utterly unjust usury.” I therefore think the passage should be established as follows: “They would practice greedy and utterly unjust usury from the blood of the wretched, and would be tormented by sleepless calculations. They would continually extend the boundaries of their estates for thousands…”

ORELLI.

“From the blood of the wretched.” For possessions are regarded as though they were a person’s blood—αἷμα καὶ ψυχὴ βροτοῖς, “blood and life to mortals.” Thus Plautus, *Bacchides*, act III, scene I, verse 5, concerning prostitutes:

> Away with those sisters from me, who suck human beings’ blood!

Compare Rigaltius on Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams*, book I, chapter 35, p. 23, Reiff’s edition; and J. F. Gronovius, who illustrates the matter with many examples, *Observations*, book IV, chapter 24, p. 796, Platner’s edition. Similarly, the ancients call an estate a person’s entrails, sinews, and strength. For, as Hesiod sings:

> Wealth is indeed life to wretched mortals.

ORELLI.

[Col. 0875C] “Would be tormented by sleepless calculations.” With these words Arnobius graphically depicts moneylenders keeping watch and calculating the money owed to them. Lucian, *The Cock*:

> Do you see this man too, keeping watch amid his anxieties, calculating the interest, with fingers hardened by counting—although before long he will have to leave all these things and become a cockroach, a gnat, or a fly?

Hence Prudentius also, in the battle of Avarice and Mercy:

> For her swift right hand scrapes away plunder  
> And exercises brazen talons upon the spoils.  
> Care, hunger, fear, anxiety, perjuries, pallor,  
> Corruption, fraud, contrivances, sleeplessness, filth—  
> The Eumenides and Furies—march as the monster’s retinue.

HERALDUS.

“They would continually extend the boundaries of their estates for thousands.” In place of “thousands,” the Leiden edition gives “accounts” and joins it to the preceding phrase: “they would torment themselves sleeplessly in calculating accounts. Of estates…” “Calculating accounts” means calculating sums owed to them—German *das Berechnen ihrer Capitale*, “the calculation of their capital.”

But nothing should be changed. To extend the boundaries of estates “for thousands” is the same as to extend them by thousands of paces, by miles—German *ganze Meilen weit ausbreiten*, “to spread them out for whole miles.” *Millia*, “thousands,” is frequently used absolutely for milestones or thousands of paces. Compare Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* I.16, and Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. Thus Aurelius Victor, *Epitome*, chapter 40: “His body—that of Severus—is carried into the tomb of Gallienus, which is nine miles from the City along the Appian Way.”

ORELLI.]]

### XL

For this reason did he send souls: so that, while the other living creatures were nourished on things growing spontaneously [Note: [Col. 0873B] Others read *mata*.] and produced without any sowing [Note: [Col. 0874B] Others read *prolata*.], and sought for themselves neither the protection nor the covering of houses or clothing, a pitiable necessity might be imposed upon these souls—so that, at the greatest expense and with unremitting [Col. 0874A] toil, they might build [Note: [Col. 0874B] Others read *constituerent*, “establish.”] houses for themselves, fashion coverings for their limbs, accumulate varied furnishings to meet their daily need, borrow from mute animals aids for their own weakness, and do violence to the earth, so that it would not furnish its own grasses but would raise the crops commanded of it; and so that, after pouring out all their blood in subduing the soil, they might lose the hope of their labor through blight, hail, or drought, and at last, under the violence of hunger, fall upon human corpses and, disfigured by wasting emaciation, be severed from the forms of human beings?

For this reason did he send souls: so that those which, while dwelling with him, had never felt any desire for possession might here become utterly avaricious and burn, in their zeal for ownership, with the insatiable appetite of the heart; might excavate lofty mountains and transform the unknown entrails of the earth into materials bearing another name and serving another use; might penetrate hidden nations at the risk of their lives and, by transporting merchandise, continually seek what was dear in one place and cheap in another; might conduct greedy and grossly unjust moneylending and torment themselves, drawing up accounts from the blood of the wretched, with sleepless nights; might continually extend [Col. 0875A] the boundaries of their possessions by thousands [of paces]; and, although they had made entire provinces into a single farm, might wear out the courts with lawsuits over one tree or one furrow and undertake irreconcilable feuds with friends and brothers?

> **Note: [Col. 0875D]**
>
> **XLI—Markets.** Savaro, on Sidonius, book I, epistle V, p. 39, understands amphitheaters. But what follows shows that the word must be taken in its proper sense. **ORELLI.**
>
> **And establish amphitheaters.** I do not know what came into the minds of those who wished to change this reading and substitute *construerent*, “construct.” For this Latin usage occurs several times [Col. 0876A] in this author. Below in this book: “and when you establish sacred buildings for them,” and elsewhere. Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, verse 194:
>
> > The Trojans shall establish walls for me.
>
> Solinus: “Then Long Alba and Fidenae were established by Ascanius.” Lactantius: “For it was in the time of Jupiter, [Col. 0876B] when temples first began to be established and new forms of worship of the gods began to exist.” And it occurs everywhere in the best Latin authors. **HERALDUS.**
>
> **For the gratification and pleasure of the spectators.** Thus Jacques Cujas excellently corrected the extremely corrupt reading of the manuscript, *In gratam voluptatemque sensorum*. From this Gelenius had made: *In gratam voluptatem consessorum*, “for the welcome pleasure of those sitting together.” But I prefer Cujas’s correction, which the Leiden editor also admitted into the text. **ORELLI.** Relevant here is what Julius Firmicus writes, *Mathesis* VIII.12: “Such men sell themselves, at the cost of their blood, for the pleasure”—read *voluptatem*, “pleasure,” instead of *voluntatem*, “will”—“of another’s gratification, for a spectacle of death.” **HERALDUS.**
>
> **Some from others.** Thus Gelenius. The manuscript reads “other things from others.” **HERALDUS.**
>
> **Would live as blessed and fortunate.** They correct this to “would regard them as blessed.” But perhaps nothing should be changed. If any change were necessary, I should prefer to read *veherent*, “would carry,” rather than *eveherent*, “would extol.” **HERALDUS.**
>
> [Col. 0876C] **For this reason did he send souls: so that, forgetful of divine weight and dignity, they might purchase gems, precious stones, and pearls at the cost of chastity; bind their necks with them; pierce the lobes of their ears; diminish their foreheads with bands; seek cosmetics for bodies to be made up; and shadow their eyes with soot.** Heraldus arranged these words excellently in this way in his *Second Investigations*, and the Leiden editor agrees with him, except that, with Meursius, he placed “diminish their foreheads with bands” after the words “seek cosmetics for bodies to be made up.” In the manuscript and in every edition except that of Salmasius, the passage is dislocated, and the words “seek cosmetics for bodies to be displayed” stand in a wholly inappropriate place—namely, immediately after “purchase at the cost of chastity.” Even the latest editor, Oberthür, retained that arrangement, very badly. But we shall now examine each point.
>
> The corrupt manuscript reading produced various conjectures among the commentators. In particular, the words “bind their necks with them,” wrongly placed after “seek cosmetics for bodies,” were deservedly suspected by learned men. [Col. 0876D] Accordingly, Fulvio Orsini conjectured: “bind their necks with chains”; Stewechius: “bind their necks with ribbons”; while Heraldus, most acutely, printed in his edition: “bind their necks with threads.” The Romans called the strings on which pearls were inserted *lina* or *lineae*, “threads.” Thus Tertullian writes in *On the Dress of Women*: “Ten million sesterces are strung upon a single thread”; and Jerome in the *Life of Paul the Hermit*: “The prices of whole estates hang upon a single strand.” There is also the classic passage in Cornelius Fronto’s speech *On the Inheritance of Matidia*, *Works*, p. 285, Mai’s edition: “Who will buy that famous and celebrated string, and the other ornaments worth so much money? If your wife buys them, she will be said to have seized the spoil and carried it off for a trifling sum, and for that reason less will have reached those to whom it was bequeathed. Will Faustina not buy those ornaments? Who, then, will buy the pearls bequeathed to your daughters? Will you strip your daughters’ [Col. 0877A] necks of these pearls so that whose swollen gullet, pray, may be adorned?”
>
> These strings were sometimes single, sometimes double or triple; hence *monolinum*, *dilinum*, and *trilinum*. See Casaubon and Salmasius on the *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. II, p. 63, and the distinguished Böttiger, *Sabina*, p. 405. But we have no need of these conjectures if the words are read in the order in which we have printed them: “bind their necks with these”—that is, with the gems, stones, and pearls, which were inserted on those strings or threads in such a way that each individual pearl was followed by a gem. Hence Tertullian, *On the Dress of Women* 11, calls such gems “the lights of the stones by which necklaces are varied.” See Scheffer, *On Necklaces* 10, p. 47, and Böttiger, *Sabina*, p. 405.
>
> Arnobius says that women purchase these gems, stones, and pearls at the cost of chastity, in accordance with the opinion of Christians of that age. Jerome, in his *Letter to Laeta*: “Take care not to pierce her ears, not to paint with white lead and rouge a face consecrated to Christ; do not weigh down her neck with gold and pearls, adorn her head with gems, dye her hair red, or give her any omen drawn from the fires of Gehenna.” Compare Tertullian in the work cited and Cyprian, *On the Good of Chastity*.
>
> Our author continues: “They might pierce the plates of their ears.” The glosses: “*Lamna*, λοβὸς ὠτίου—the lobe, the lowest part of the ear.” Sidonius, book I, epistle II, calls them “the tongues or little strips of the ears”; see Sirmond there, p. 13. Compare Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under *Lamina* and *Ligula*.
>
> In place of “diminish the forehead with bands,” Heraldus prefers “diminish the forehead with *nimbi*.” According to Isidore, *Origins* XIX.31, in Godefroy’s collection, p. 1307, a *nimbus* is “a transverse band of gold sewn onto the linen worn upon women’s foreheads.” Plautus: “The more I look at her, the more *nimbata*—adorned with a nimbus—she is.” But the received reading is sound. For the linen onto which that *nimbus* was sewn was itself called a *limbus*, “band.” Statius, *Achilleid* II:
>
> > Or they bind their brows with jeweled bands.
>
> And Prudentius, *Psychomachia*:
>
> > From her neck flows a border of delicate fabric.
>
> Elmenhorst cited these passages. “Diminish the forehead with bands” is also correctly expressed. For Heraldus on this passage and J. F. Gronovius, *Disquisition on Statius’ Silvae* II.1.17, p. 94, teach us that the ancients prized a slender, very small, compressed forehead. [Col. 0877D]
>
> The following words, as they are read in the Leiden edition, “seek cosmetics for bodies to be made up,” can indeed be defended, if *conficiendis* either means the same as *perficiendis*, “perfected, adorned,” or is taken in a bad sense as “wasting, killing” bodies, since cosmetics are extremely harmful to bodily health. But I am wonderfully pleased by Oudendorp’s correction, reported by Pieter Burman on the *Latin Anthology* III, epigram 132, vol. I, p. 587: “for bodies deserving to be spat upon”—that is, because of their ugliness or deformity, so that they may cover nature’s faults with cosmetics—especially since the manuscript has *conspiendis*, from which Gelenius made *conspiciendis*, “to be displayed.” Stewechius proposed *compingendis*, “to be fitted together”; Heinsius, *conliniendis*, “to be smeared.”
>
> “Soot,” as Elmenhorst rightly explains, is the black powder by which the outlines of the eyes are extended. Juvenal, Satire II, verses 93–95:
>
> > One, touching his eyebrow with moistened soot,  
> > Lengthens it with a slanting needle, and paints his trembling  
> > Eyes while raising them.
>
> The Greeks called this powder στίμμις (*stimmis*, antimony), whence στιμμίζειν and ὑποστιβίζειν, “to paint the eyes with antimony,” in Nicolaus of Damascus; see Valesius there, pp. 175–76 of our edition. In Latin it was *stibium*. [Col. 0878A] Compare Grotius, *Annotations on the Old Testament*, at 2 Kings 9:30 [correcting the source’s apparent OCR error, “CXI, 30”], and the distinguished Böttiger, *Sabina*, p. 49. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Nor, while in male forms, be ashamed to make their hair quiver with curling irons.** I do not know what came into the mind of the very learned Scaliger, in his notes on the *Priapea*, poem XLII, when he altered a perfectly sound passage. He thought it should read: “Nor would they be ashamed to make their hair quiver with male curling irons heated hot,” so that *formis calamistris* would mean “with glowing iron,” since among the ancients *formus* meant “hot.” Stewechius proposed *informis calamistris*, “with very hot curling irons,” taking *in-* as an intensive prefix and *formus* as “hot.”
>
> But *in formis*, “in the forms,” must be joined with *masculorum*, “of males,” so that the sense is: “when the souls have assumed the forms or bodies of males.” Arnobius is, of course, censuring men who submitted to womanly practices and curled their hair with irons after the fashion of women. Scaliger also wrongly changed *in* to *ii*, “they,” since what preceded was not “human beings” or “men,” but “souls.” A *calamistrum*, as Servius explains on Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, verse 100, is “a rather large needle which, when heated and applied, curls the hair”; in Greek, κάλαμις (*kalamis*). See Böttiger, *Sabina*, p. 124. *Vibrare* means the same as *crispare*, “to curl.” Compare Virgil in the passage cited. **ORELLI.**
>
> **To smooth the skin of the temple.** This was done by effeminate men who divested themselves of virility, as we observed on Martial. Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis* VIII.7: “These men too, after removing their hair, will transform their bodies into the likeness of the female body; even their clothing will be embellished in imitation of women’s attire. Walking softly, they suspend their steps with a certain dainty restraint.” And Athenaeus, book XII, portraying the softness of Sardanapalus, says that he was “painted with white lead, wearing a woman’s dress, with his beard shaved off, and polished smooth with pumice” (*ἐψιμμυθιωμένον, γυναικείαν στολὴν ἔχοντα, καὶ κατεξυρημένον τὸν πώγωνα, καὶ κατακεκισσαρισμένον*). **HERALDUS.**
>
> **To walk with the backs of their knees bare.** Varro in the *Meleagris*: “Walking not only with his calves uncovered, but almost with his nostrils uncovered.” **HERALDUS.**
>
> **Both to expose the vigor of manhood.** Fulvio Orsini proposed “and to lay aside”; Stewechius, “and to set aside,” which is more pleasing. In the following clause the Leiden edition has “to be softened” instead of “to soften.” But nothing should be changed. **ORELLI.**

### XLI

For this reason did he send souls: so that those which had formerly been gentle and knew nothing of being stirred by savage passions might establish for themselves meat markets and amphitheaters, places of bloodshed and public impiety; so that in one of them they might see human beings eaten and torn to pieces by the mangling of beasts, and others killing one another for no cause of any desert, but for the gratification and pleasure of the spectators; and so that they might count the very days on which so great an outrage was committed among their public rejoicings and consecrate them with festive merriment; while in the other they might tear apart the entrails of wretched animals, snatch portions from one another, as dogs and vultures do, crush them with their teeth, and deliver them to a most cruel stomach; and, amid customs so savage and dreadful [Note: [Col. 0875A] Others read *oribus*, “mouths.”], might lament their own lot when the constraints of poverty rescued them from such tables, yet live as blessed and fortunate while such cruel provisions polluted their mouths and faces [Note: [Col. 0876A] Fulvio Orsini reads *fauces*, “throats.”]?

For this reason did he send souls: so that, forgetful of divine weight and dignity, they might purchase gems, [Col. 0877A] precious stones, and pearls at the cost of chastity; bind their necks with them; pierce the lobes of their ears; diminish their foreheads with bands; seek cosmetics for bodies to be made up; shadow their eyes with soot; and, while in male forms, not be ashamed to make their hair quiver with curling irons, to smooth the skin of the body, to walk with the backs of their knees bare, and through every other form of adornment both to expose the vigor of manhood and soften it into the dress and refinements of women?

> **Note: [Col. 0878C]**
>
> **XLII—Substitute false wills.** This was virtually an established custom in those times. Lactantius, book V, chapter 9: “And, to mention matters that are trivial and commonplace: they hunt for inheritances, substitute false wills, and either remove or exclude the rightful [Col. 0878D] heirs.” **HERALDUS.**
>
> **To break into houses by night.** The Philoxenian Glosses: “Burglars, θυρεπανοῖκται”; “housebreaker, θυρεπανοίκτης.” By a milder name, “opener.” The reading “by night” is sound and correct, for it is precisely at that time that such men carry on their activities. The proposal of Meursius and Scriverius to substitute “with crowbars” is therefore false. Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis* VI.31: “When placed in fixed signs, they will make notorious housebreakers—men who, armed with a sword, while people are asleep, inflict both the loss of property and the peril of life.” Compare Savaro on Sidonius IX, epistle VII, p. 575. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Entice.** The reading is sound. Those who think something is missing are mistaken. Here *sollicitare*, “entice,” means to lure away another man’s slaves—a grave crime of kidnappers. Hence the Philoxenian Glosses: “*Sollicitare*, πλαγιάζειν—to kidnap.” Papias: “A kidnapper is one who leads boys astray and entices the slaves of others.” Hesychius: “A *psychagōgos* … is an enslaver, a deceiver, and one who leads souls down into Hades” (*ψυχαγωγὸς . . . ὁ ἀνδραποδιστὴς, καὶ ὁ ἀπατεὼν, καὶ ὁ κατάγων τὰς ψυχὰς εἰς ᾅδου*). The *psychagōgoi*, of course, are those who entice the slaves of others with flattering, honeyed words and lure them to themselves. **HERALDUS.**
>
> **Drive away.** Arnobius means cattle rustlers or [Col. 0879A] even slave-stealers—German *Seelenverkäufer*, “soul-sellers.” Those who wish to read *ambirent*, “canvass,” are therefore mistaken. **HERALDUS and ORELLI.**
>
> **Betray their clients’ cases.** In Latin, *praevaricatores* denotes advocates who assist the opposing party by betraying their own case. See Catanaeus on Pliny, book I, epistle 20, p. 71, Longolius’s edition. Compare C. A. Duker, who amassed a cloud of examples in his *On the Latinity of the Ancient Jurists*, pp. 167ff. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Birds.** Fulvio Orsini reads “fattened birds.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **To make little coils and sausages.** *Spirula* is a diminutive of *spira*, a kind of pastry whose preparation is taught by Cato, *On Agriculture* 77, where the distinguished Schneider compares the *spirae* with the Greeks’ στρεπτοί (*streptoi*, twisted pastries) in Demosthenes and Pollux VI.77. Festus: “*Spira* is the name … both of a kind of baker’s product and of a ship’s rope wound into a coil.”
>
> A *botulus*, according to the same Festus, is a kind of sausage, so called from *boli* because of the way it is joined—or, rather, a Lucanian sausage stuffed with balls of pork. Tertullian, *Apology* IX: “Finally, among the tests imposed upon Christians you even place before them sausages distended with blood.” This kind of food was already known in Homer’s time, as is clear from the vivid description in *Odyssey* XVIII, verses 44ff.:
>
> > Here lie goats’ stomachs upon the fire; for supper  
> > We filled them with fat and blood and set them down.
>
> German *Blutwürste*, “blood sausages.” The manuscript and older editions very corruptly have *boletos*, “mushrooms,” for this kind of fungus is not prepared by art but grows in forests. Hence N. Heinsius, *Adversaria*, p. 621, suspects that the text should read *botellos*, “little sausages,” *bottellus* being a diminutive of *botulus*. Thus Sidonius Apollinaris, epistle XI:
>
> > Where amid chains scented with thyme  
> > A red little sausage smells of paired berries, etc.
>
> See Savaro there, p. 533, and Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under *botulus*. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Minced dishes.** *Isicium* or *insicium* is derived from *insectio*, “cutting up,” as Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, p. 28, and Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VII.8, teach. The classic passage is Apicius, *On the Art of Cookery* II.1–2, where there are numerous recipes for *isicia* made from fish, meat, caul fat, small mushrooms, and so forth. Everywhere one finds food cut up, pounded, ground, seasoned with spices, sometimes wrapped in leaves, dried, and then moistened again with sauce. **NOURRY and GESNER, in the *Thesaurus*.** Compare Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under this word; Lindenbrog, *Observations on Donatus’ Commentary on Terence’s Eunuch*, act II, scene II, verse 26, vol. II, p. 522, Zeune’s edition; and especially Salmasius on the *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, p. 831. The *isicium* seems to correspond to the dish the English call “pudding.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **Lucanian delicacies.** Thus Salmasius printed in the [Col. 0879D] Leiden edition and in his *Plinian Exercises on Solinus*, p. 90. The others read *castellamenta*, which Heraldus interprets as certain kinds of sausage called πυραμίδες (*pyramides*, “pyramids”) in Greek from their distinctive shape, citing Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus*, p. 19, Potter’s edition: “Are not these sesame cakes and pyramids, balls of wool, many-bossed sacrificial cakes, grains of salt, and the serpent, the sacred emblem of Dionysus Bassareus?” (*οὐ σησάμαι ταῦτα καὶ πυραμίδες, καὶ τολύπαι, καὶ πόπανα πολυόμφαλα, χόνδροι τε ἁλῶν, καὶ δράκων, ὄργιον Διονύσου Βασσάρου*).
>
> Johannes Wower agrees with Heraldus in his notes on Minucius Felix, *Octavius* XIV, p. 133, Gronovius’s edition, judging that the text should read “*castellamenta*, Lucanian sausages.” But in the passage cited from Clement the subject is not kinds of sausage but kinds of sacrificial cakes [read *liborum* for the printed *librorum*]. In any case, it seems that one should read *catillamenta* with Salmasius, a correction also defended by N. Heinsius, *Adversaria* IV.9, p. 621.
>
> That correction seems to be confirmed by a very similar passage of Arnobius below, VII.24: “The fat is cut up, according to custom, into tiny morsels for *catillamina*.” *Catillamenta* and *catillamina*, as Salmasius and [Col. 0880A] Heinsius explain in the cited works, are therefore dainties and delicious delicacies. Properly speaking, however, they seem to have called sausages, or links stuffed with finely chopped meat, by this name because they were eagerly sought by *catillones*, “dish-lickers.” *Catillamentum* comes from *catillare*, the same as *ligurrire*, “to lick greedily,” which is derived from *catillus*, a diminutive of *catinus*, “dish.” Hence gluttons were called *catillones* from licking dishes—German *Tellerlecker*, “plate-lickers.”
>
> **Lucanian sausages.** The Glosses: “*lucanica*, ἀλλάντια—sausages.” This is a kind of sausage stuffed with pork and first invented by the Lucanian peoples. See Apicius, *On the Art of Cookery* IV.2, and Paulus Manutius on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* IX.17. Charisius: “*Lucanicum* is understood to mean a dish; and *Lucanicus* an intestine, with ‘sausage’ or ‘preparation’ understood. The feminine *Lucanica* is understood with *hira*, that is, ‘intestine.’” Compare Meursius, who treats this word at length, pp. 70–71. **ORELLI.**
>
> [Col. 0880B] **Suckling pork along with these.** *Suminata caro* is the flesh of a *suminata* sow—that is, one giving milk. *Suminatus* comes from *sumen, -inis*, the udder of a sow that has given birth and is full of milk, a kind of food among Roman delicacies. See Casaubon and Salmasius on Aelius Lampridius’s *Alexander Severus* 22, *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, pp. 914ff.
>
> Moreover, I am greatly pleased by N. Heinsius’s very acute conjecture in the *Adversaria*, p. 621: “suckling pork with intestines.” A *hira* properly denotes the intestine called the jejunum, Greek νῆστις (*nēstis*), German *Leerdarm*. Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* I.6, in describing the three principal intestines, says: “The third, which the ancients called the *hira*, is regarded as the chief of all the intestines and conveys away the refuse of food.” Compare Festus under this word. Nonius, however, teaches under *Hilae* that it was also used for the other intestines: “The ancients said that *hillae*, a diminutive of *hirae*, were intestines; hence the town Bohilla in Italy, because an ox reached that place dragging its intestines from a wound.” Compare Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under *Hillae*. Hence Plautus, *Curculio*, act I, scene I, verses 21ff.:
>
> > The spleen kills me, the kidneys ache,  
> > The lungs are torn apart, the liver is tortured,  
> > The roots of the heart perish; all the intestines ache.
>
> The word *hira* was used especially in sacrificial contexts. Below, VII.24, our author lists many kinds of sausage used in sacrifices: “Not likewise the *fendicae*, which are themselves *hirae*, although the speech of the common people customarily calls them *ilia* when referring to them.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **Tuceta prepared under icy conditions.** The Glosses: “*Tucetum*, ζωμὸς παχύς—thick broth.” Isidore’s Glossary: “*Tucetum*: seasoned beef among the Cisalpine Gauls.” Nonius calls *tuceta* royal foods; and Fulgentius, *On Archaic Speech*, citing a fragment of *Gallimorphus*: “And among the Pisaeans … *tuceta* exhale an ambrosial flavor.” Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* II, calls it a most savory dish; see Oudendorp’s notes there, p. 104. The scholiast on Persius, Satire II, verse 42, on the words “great dishes [Col. 0880D] and rich *tuceta*,” says: “Among the Cisalpine Gauls, *tuceta* means beef coated and marinated with certain thick seasonings; it therefore lasts throughout the year. Pork seasoned in the same fashion is also customarily preserved, or used for the gravies of mixed dishes.”
>
> Compare Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under this word. From Arnobius’s phrase “under icy conditions”—that is, by an icy method of seasoning—I would conjecture that *tucetum* was a broth of beef or pork congealed with snow or ice, with small pieces of the same meat mixed into it, or with that meat finely chopped, like our jellies and gelatins, German *Sülzen, Gallerten*. We certainly learn very often from Seneca, *Letters* LXXVII and *Natural Questions* IV, final chapter, that snow and ice were mixed into the foods and drinks of the luxurious. Compare Martin Lister on Apicius, *On the Art of Cookery* IV.1, p. 107.
>
> But the words of the scholiast on Persius, “and therefore it lasts throughout the year,” stand in the way. When compared with our passage, they seem to indicate a kind of sausage preserved from decay both by certain seasonings and by snow [Col. 0881A] and ice in underground chambers. In his Appendix, Meursius suspects that one should read “slender” or “icy *tuceta* by preparation,” explaining *tuceta* whose udder was hardened like ice. **ORELLI.**
>
> **So that they might distend their cheeks by blowing into pipes.** This seems especially ugly and deforming. Alcibiades therefore rejected pipes on the ground that they puffed out the cheeks and distorted the whole face, “so that even close acquaintances would recognize the face only with the greatest difficulty” (*ὡς τοὺς συνήθεις ἂν πάνυ μόλις διαγνῶναι τὸ πρόσωπον*), as Plutarch says in his *Alcibiades*. Christians of that age vigorously rejected all instruments of luxury and pleasure, especially if any appearance of idolatry seemed mixed with them. For this reason they also condemned the use of pipes, since pipes were played in the rites of the pagans. Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus* II.4: “Let the shepherd’s pipe, then, be assigned to shepherds, and the flute to superstitious people hastening toward idolatry. For in truth these instruments must be banished from a sober banquet, since they are more suited to beasts than to human beings—and, among human beings, to the more irrational” (*Σύριγξ μὲν οὖν ποιμέσιν ἀπονενεμήσθω· αὐλὸς δὲ ἀνθρώποις δεισιδαίμοσι εἰς εἰδωλολατρείας σπεύδουσιν. Καὶ γὰρ ὡς ἀληθῶς ἀποπεμπτέα τὰ ὄργανα ταῦτα νηφαλίου συμποσίου, θηρίοις μᾶλλον ἢ ἀνθρώποις κατάλληλα, καὶ ἀνθρώπων τοῖς ἀλογωτέροις*), and what follows, pp. 192ff., Potter’s edition. **HERALDUS and ORELLI.**
>
> **So that they might rhythmically lead obscene songs and accompany them with the resounding clatter of foot-clappers.** By an elegant but wholly unnecessary alteration, the Leiden editor printed this passage as follows: “So that they might lead obscene songs; might repeat numerous sounds with the clatter of foot-clappers.” *Sonores* is the same as *sonos*, “sounds,” as occasionally in Virgil and Tacitus; for example, *Annals* IV.48: “But so that, with each man intent upon shouting, missiles, and his own danger, he could not perceive the sound of the other battle.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **With the clatter of foot-clappers.** *Scabilla*, special instruments of mime performers, were clappers made of iron—Lucian, *On Dancing* §85: σιδηροῦν ὑπόδημα, “an iron shoe”—or of wood—Pollux VII.22 and 28: ξύλινον ὑπόδημα, “a wooden shoe.” They were shaken by the feet to which they were fastened and made a clattering sound, as an ancient statue in which a *scabillum* appears demonstrates, and as Rubenius, *On Clothing* II.17, confirms. This is Ernesti in the *Key to Cicero*, under this word.
>
> Compare Salmasius on Vopiscus’s *Carinus* 19, vol. II, p. 838. He refutes Casaubon on Suetonius, *Caligula* 54, who thought *scabillum* a foreign word, although it is thoroughly Latin and must be derived from *scamnum*, whence the diminutives *scamellum* and *scamillum*, *scabellum* and *scabillum*. Compare Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under *Scamna*; Gesner in the *Thesaurus*; and especially *Explanation of Various Remarkable Monuments*, pp. 47ff., where an ancient monument displaying *scabilla* is explained. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Dance.** Dancing and leading dances were forbidden to Christians. Paul, Romans 13:13: “Let us walk becomingly, as in the day, not in revelries and drunkenness” (*Ὡς ἐν ἡμέρᾳ εὐσχημόνως περιπατήσωμεν, μὴ κώμοις καὶ μέθαις*); likewise Galatians 5:21 and 1 Peter 4:3. In connection with these, Cyril’s Glosses and another old manuscript lexicon have: “κῶμος—a dance accompanied by song and drunkenness”; Suidas gives the same explanation.
>
> The same rule was therefore enacted in the *Apostolic Canons* and at the Council of Laodicea, canon 53, p. 23: “Christians going to weddings must not leap or dance” (*Οὐ δεῖ χριστιανοὺς εἰς γάμους ἀπερχομένους βαλλίζειν ἢ ὀρχεῖσθαι*). The old translator: “Christians going to weddings ought neither to dance nor to leap, but to dine or breakfast chastely, as befits Christians.” See the *Abridgment of the Canons* of Bishops Ferrandus and Cresconius, the ancient *Corpus of Canons*, and Charlemagne’s *Capitularies* in many passages; Ambrose, *On Fasting* 18 and *On Virgins* III; Augustine, vol. X, *On the Christian Name*, sermon I, p. 234. **F. LINDENBROG, in Elmenhorst.**
>
> **Turn circles in the dance.** Cicero, *Against Piso* X: “Not even then, when he was turning that dancing circle of his, did he fear the wheel of fortune.” **ELMENHORST.**
>
> **Sway with a rippling of the loins.** Below, VII: “and sway with their buttocks rippling.” The description is graphic, for waves gently stirred are properly called rippling and swelling. Minucius Felix, *Octavius* 3: “And as the sea is always restless even when the winds have subsided, although it did not rush upon the shore in white and foaming breakers, nevertheless it did so in rippling, swelling waves.” Thus walking “in a wavelike manner” was said of those who gently wriggle their buttocks as they walk. Afranius in Nonius: “I wish to go to him magnificently, in a swaying gait.” Gloss: “*Crispat*—κραδαίνει, σείει, ‘shakes, sways.’” **HERALDUS.**
>
> Similarly Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* II: “Gently sliding her own limbs, with her loins softly quivering and her mobile spine moving placidly, she undulated gracefully.” Here “undulated” is the same as “swayed.” See Oudendorp’s note, p. 105. Compare Alciphron I, epistle XXXIX; Juvenal, Satire XI, verse 164; Martial V, epigram 80; Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXIII.20, p. 1540; and Scioppius on the *Priapea*, poem XVIII. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Debauchees.** The Glosses: “*Exoletus*, ὑπέρακμος, τριβανός—past the prime of youth, hardened.” [Col. 0882C] **ELMENHORST.** The Romans called *exoleti* shameless men who submitted to the woman’s role—men certainly older and past the boyish age suited to that abuse. See Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Sambuca-players, harpists.** *Sambucistriae* derives from *sambuca*, a triangular musical instrument constructed from strings unequal in length as well as thickness, as Porphyry describes in his commentary on Ptolemy’s *Harmonics*. Compare Isidore, *Origins* III.20; Festus under this word and his interpreters; Barthius, *Adversaria* LV.9; and Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. Moreover, it is sufficiently well known from the comic poets that such women made a profit not only from their art but also from their bodies. There is no need to follow Stewechius in taking this passage as referring to stage shows polluted by every kind of obscenity, since crimes of this sort are also notoriously associated with women who sang at private tables. **ORELLI.**
>
> **So that they might lay their bodies out for sale.** The reading is sound, and those who wish to correct it to “prostitute” should not be heard. Diocletian and Maximian on the *Lex Julia, Concerning Adultery and Debauchery*: [Col. 0882D] “the utterly foul wickedness of those women who lay their modesty prostrate before the lusts of others.” **HERALDUS.**
>
> **Publicly advertise their own cheapness to the people.** Some replace “cheapness” with “virility”; others, including Meursius, with “usefulness,” meaning “use.” Thus Zeno of Verona in his sermon *On Chastity*: “It always delights and repents in varied exchanges of lusts, never attaining satiety through its slippery utility”—that is, through slippery use. This is the word’s proper and ancient meaning. Thus Varro, *On the Life of the Roman People* I: “And so they placed or hung up for themselves only what utility demanded: a dipper, chamber pot, basin, and water pitcher.” Later, because whatever offers its use also brings advantage and benefit, *utilitas* came to be used for those things. *Publicare* means “to prostitute.” Hence victims of public lust are called “public women” by Tertullian and, following him, Jerome; likewise by Zeno of Verona. In our author above, I.36, Venus is called “the publisher of inward beauty.” The Greeks too call them κοιναὶ γυναῖκες, “common women.” **HERALDUS.**
>
> Stewechius attacks stage shows and female performers, in which there was great madness and still greater obscenity, since they publicly exhibited or—as Minucius Felix says—even displayed acts of adultery. On the prostitutes customarily laid publicly upon the stage at Rome after the games had ended, consult Justus Lipsius, *Selections* I.2. On the term “cheapness,” another pair of Arnobius’s passages is ready to hand: book IV, “Venus is represented dancing as a lover, and through every passion of a harlot’s cheapness she is shown raging in shameless imitation”; and book V, “to burst out into obscene cheapness.” **STEWECHIUS.** Meursius prefers “usefulness,” equivalent to χρῆσις, “use”—wrongly. Compare Bunemann on Lactantius, *Institutes*, at V.20, p. 121. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Bound in brothels.** Thus the manuscript. Fulvio Orsini and the Leiden editor changed it to “available”; Scaliger, as reported by Meursius, to “forgotten”—wrongly, in my opinion. They were bound either to pimps or to the shameless men who abused them. On the meaning of *fornix*, see above on chapter 6 of this book and Scioppius on the *Priapea*, poem XIII. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Prepared for violation of the mouth.** Thus Gelenius and Fulvio Orsini. The manuscript has “prepared for comparison with a sacred mouth,” which makes no sense. From this Canter produced “prepared for sacrifice of the mouth.” Stewechius proposed “matched in comparisons of the accursed mouth,” with the same meaning as Gelenius’s reading; for the Romans said that legions or gladiators were “joined,” “matched,” or “paired” with one another.
>
> Salmasius, however, in the Leiden edition printed: “matched for the violation of an accursed mouth”—that is, a mouth to be abominated and devoted to curses, as in “accursed hunger for gold.” But Lindenbrog rightly defends Gelenius’s correction in his notes on the *Priapea*, poem XII. Arnobius is referring to that monstrous and most unnatural crime which the Greeks called λεσβιάζειν and λεσβιασμός, “to practice Lesbianism” and “Lesbianism,” after the Lesbians among whom this obscenity was practiced. The Latins called people of this kind *Opici*, as Meursius teaches. See Aulus Gellius I.21 and XI.16, and Pliny, *Natural History* XXXIX [sic; the book number is materially uncertain]. You may consult the mass of examples collected on this passage by Elmenhorst and Lindenbrog in the places cited. For my part, I do not transcribe obscenities. **ORELLI.**

### XLII

For this reason did he send souls: so that some might infest the passages of the roads, others ensnare the unwary, substitute false wills, prepare poisoned drinks, break into houses by night, entice away slaves, drive off livestock or persons, betray their clients’ cases, and turn traitor; so that they might drive disgust with flavors from the palate, learn how to retain the escaping fat when birds were being cooked, and make little coils, [Col. 0880A] sausages, minced dishes, delicacies, Lucanian sausages, suckling pork along with these, and *tuceta* prepared under icy conditions?

For this reason did he send souls: so that beings bearing a holy and most august name might here practice the arts of ensemble-music and pipe-playing; so that they might distend their cheeks by blowing into pipes, rhythmically lead obscene songs, and accompany them with the resounding clatter of foot-clappers, at which another wanton multitude of souls might dissolve into disordered bodily movements, dance, [Col. 0882A] and sing, turn circles in the dance, and finally, with buttocks and hip joints raised, sway with a rippling of the loins?

For this reason did he send souls: so that among males they might become debauchees, and among females prostitutes, sambuca-players, and harpists [Note: [Col. 0881A] The manuscript wrongly reads *psalteriae*.]; so that they might lay their bodies out for sale, publicly advertise their own cheapness to the people, stand ready in brothels, be bound in vaulted dens, refuse no treatment, and be prepared for violation of the mouth?

> **Note: [Col. 0883D]**
>
> **XLIII—Were those wise, then?** For some reason unknown to me, the Leiden edition changed these words to: “Were those the souls of wisdom, then?” etc. **ORELLI.**
>
> **That they might carry them about.** Isaac Pontanus, in his notes on Macrobius’s *On the Differences between the Greek and Latin Verb*, p. 693, thinks one should read *generent*, “generate,” from the ancient verb *geno, -ere*, which is the same as *gignere* or *generare*, “beget.” But nothing should be changed. [Col. 0884B] Here *gerere* means “to carry with oneself,” as messengers and bearers do, and is therefore appropriately joined with “celebrate everywhere.” In the same sense, above at the end of book I, Arnobius calls Christ “the bearer of so great a gift.” **ORELLI.**

### XLIII

What are you saying, O offspring and progeny of the primal divinity? Were those souls, then—wise souls brought forth from primary causes—acquainted with these kinds of shameful acts, crimes, and wicked deeds? And were they commanded to inhabit these regions and to be clothed with the enclosing covering of a human body so that they might practice, carry about, and celebrate these evils everywhere?

Is there anyone among mortals who has received any degree of rational understanding who would think that the world was set in order through these souls, rather than that a seat and dwelling was established in which every outrage might daily be perpetrated, every evil deed accomplished—ambushes, frauds, deceits, avarice, robberies, violence, crime, audacity, obscenity, dishonor, infamy, and all the other [Col. 0883B] evils which human beings throughout the whole world bring forth from a harmful mind and contrive to inflict as mutual corruption?

> **Note: [Col. 0884B]**
>
> **XLIV—By command.** The manuscript and Fulvio Orsini read *missione*, “by sending,” which I do not know why all the editors changed. **ORELLI.**
>
> [Col. 0884C] **Depart.** The manuscript wrongly reads *abscondere*, “hide.” *Abscedere*, “depart,” means to turn aside from the way of salvation. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Or that something would come upon them from outside.** These words must be referred back to the preceding clause: “For if he knew that they would degenerate through changes of place, or that something from outside,” etc. I have therefore enclosed the words “and he ought to have known … as the establisher of all causes” within brackets as a parenthesis. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Of all things.** That is, of all vices and crimes—though out of reverence for God Arnobius does not dare to state this explicitly. I would translate: German *von allem, was begegnet*, “of everything that happens.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **Through inaction made the crime his own.** “For he in whose power it lies to prevent a thing commands it to be done if, when it is committed, he does not prevent it,” says Salvian, book VII. Hence below, in book III, Arnobius calls this inaction “hostile”: “And why, through hostile inaction, do they not take care to avert fierce contagions and pestilential diseases from summer?” **HERALDUS.**
And through neglect of restraint, he had previously permitted it. That is, by inaction, because he was unwilling to restrain it. For we have observed that this word [Col. 0884D] is sometimes used in this sense by these writers. Vegetius, *On Military Matters*, book I, chapter 8: “Accordingly, once the recruits have been marked down, the science of arms must be demonstrated to them through daily exercises. But the neglect born of security has abolished the practice of this.” Hence also Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book V, chapter 5: “For there is no grace except after an offense, nor peace except after war. Moreover, both the people, through transgression of discipline, and the entire human race, through neglect of nature, had sinned and rebelled against the Creator.” Here “neglect of nature” is, as it were, a cessation of nature, whereby human beings suppress in unrighteousness the knowledge implanted in them by nature. HERALD.]

### XLIV

“But,” you say, “they came of their own will, not at the king’s command.” Yet where was the almighty Father? Where was the authority of his royal majesty, that he might prevent them from departing [Col. 0884A] and not permit them to plunge headlong into pleasures? For if he knew that through changes of place they would become degenerate—and, as the maker of all causes, he ought to have known—or that something would come upon them from without that would make them forget their own dignity and beauty, then, though I should beg pardon a thousand times, the cause of all these things is none other than he himself. For he allowed those whom he foresaw would not preserve the condition of their integrity to possess an unrestricted right to wander [Note: [Col. 0883B] The manuscript has *providebat*, “foresaw”]. Thus it comes to this: it makes absolutely no difference whether they came voluntarily or obeyed his command, since, by not preventing what ought to have been prevented, he made the offense his own through inaction, and had already permitted it through neglect of restraint.

[Note: [Col. 0884D]

**XLV.—“To have begotten souls so changeable, possessing no seriousness, weight, or constancy.”** Stewechius conjecturally reads *tam nobiles animas*, “souls so noble,” which is indeed not a bad reading. But the received reading can also be defended, with the sense: “to have begotten souls so changeable that they possess no seriousness, constancy,” etc. ORELL.

[Col. 0885B] **“To have ordered them to enter bodies.”** Thus Gelenius. The manuscript has *jussisset*, “had ordered,” which Heraldus vainly attempts to defend as an interchange of mood and tense for *jusserit*, “ordered.” For if we read the entire passage in that way, it becomes obscure and tangled. ORELL.

**“Clothed in whose prisons.”** Stewechius reads *inclusae*, “confined”; the Leiden edition, *inductas*, “led into.” But nothing should be changed. *Indutae*, “clothed,” must of course be referred to “bodies,” which is to be understood with “prisons,” so that the sense is: “clothed in which, as though in prisons, they would live . . .” ORELL.

**“At one time they would suffer obscenities.”** Meursius prefers: “at one time, being obscene, they would suffer.” ORELL.

**“Some would suffer mangling by wild beasts, while others would perish from the poison of flies.”** I have printed this with the Leiden editor. The manuscript has: “some would suffer the mangling of infernal mice,” corruptly and without any sense. For what are “infernal mice”? Fulvius Ursinus reads: “some would suffer the mangling of their internal muscles,” which is not bad—namely, the internal muscles of the body (*die innersten Muskeln*, “the innermost muscles”). Stewechius, emending the text to “some would suffer the mangling of misshapen mice,” thinks that this passage alludes to that kind of torture in which mice or dormice were placed upon the bare chest of those being tortured and were then covered with a basin; unable to endure the fire subsequently placed above it, they would begin to tear the chest to pieces. He therefore interprets “misshapen mice” as “very hot mice,” deriving the word from intensive *in-* and *formus*, which Festus and the ancient glossaries attest was formerly used for “hot.” See above on chapter 41.

But it is most improbable that Arnobius, who here is enumerating not kinds of torture or torment but the commonest forms of calamity and death encountered everywhere, should have mentioned this rarer and more unusual torture. Others read: “some would suffer the mangling of those below, while others, the mice, would perish from poison.” But mention of the inhabitants of the underworld or of Gehenna is wholly foreign to this passage, while “the poison of mice” could mean nothing other than poison prepared and suited for killing mice—*Mausegift*, “mouse poison”—and would have to be understood as aconite, which, according to Pliny, book XXVII, chapter 3, kills mice from far away by its odor and whose use in poisoning among the ancients is very well known. Compare Pliny at the passage cited, and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, verse 147:

> Ghastly stepmothers mix livid aconite.

For the use of arsenic was unknown to the ancients. But I very much doubt whether “the poison of mice” could be said in Latin with this meaning. Indeed, the practice of killing mice with poison seems to have been entirely unknown among the ancients and throughout much of the Middle Ages. I infer this from the verses of Manuel Philes in his poem *On the Nature of Animals*, chapter 89, “On Mice,” verses 8 following:

> Οὔς καὶ γαλῆ τρίζουσα, καὶ πλὰξ, καὶ βρόχος,  
> Καὶ παγὶς ἐξέτριψε, καὶ βραχὺ στέαρ.

> A squeaking cat, a slab, a noose,  
> a trap, and a little fat have destroyed them. [Col. 0886B]

There is no mention of poison there.

It therefore remains for us to follow Salmasius’s emendation, which I consider uniquely correct: “some would suffer mangling by wild beasts, while others would perish from the poison of flies.” *Venenum muscularum*, “the poison of little flies”—*muscularum* being the diminutive of *musca, -ae*—means the poison of blister beetles, which Pliny calls winged little worms, that is, flies, in *Natural History*, book XI, chapter 35 (41 in Hardouin’s edition). The ancients used them not only for blistering plasters but also for poisoning, as is attested by the same Pliny, book XXVIII, chapter 9 (33 in Hardouin’s edition); Cicero, *Letters to Friends* IX, letter 21, with Manutius’s note there; and Ovid, *Ibis*, verse 308:

> May you drink the juices of blister beetles, given you by your father.

Valerius Maximus, book VI, chapter 2, Foreign Examples no. 3: “For when the king Lysimachus threatened him with death, he—that is, Theodorus of Cyrene—said, ‘Truly, you have achieved something magnificent, since you have acquired the power of a blister beetle.’” Compare G. J. Vossius, who treats these and other poisonous insects at length, *On Idolatry*, book IV, chapter 96, page 599. ORELL.

**“Unhappy and pitiable mortality.”** *Mortalitas* has the same meaning as *mortales*, “mortals.” See above on book I, chapter 7. ORELL.

**“And tear one another with the savagery of cruel teeth.”** This is characteristic of those who curse and slander *ἄδην καὶ ἀδιαλείπτως*—“to excess and without ceasing.” Thus Persius says that Lucilius, a most vehement and biting satirist, broke his eyetooth upon those whom he tore to pieces; by these words he meant to express the frenzy of abusive speech:

> . . . Lucilius slashed the city—  
> you, Lupus, and you, Mucius—and broke his eyetooth upon them. HERALD.]

### XLV

But far be from us the monstrosity of that wicked belief: that almighty God, the sower, maker, and progenitor of great and invisible things, should be believed to have begotten souls so changeable, possessing no seriousness, weight, or constancy—liable to fall into vices, prone to every kind of sin—and, although he knew them [Col. 0885A] to be such and of this character, to have ordered them to enter bodies, clothed in whose prisons they would live beneath the daily storms [Note: [Col. 0885A] Fulvius reads: “would be driven by storms.”] and tempests of fortune; at one time committing shameful deeds, at another suffering obscenities; perishing through shipwrecks, collapsing buildings, and the conflagrations of fires; some being crushed by poverty, others by beggary; some suffering mangling by wild beasts, others perishing from the poison of flies; some walking lame, others losing their sight; some sitting with their joints bound; and, finally, being exposed to all the diseases that unhappy and pitiable mortality endures through the rending inflicted by diverse torments.

Then, having forgotten that they came from one source, one progenitor, and one head, they would rend and break apart the bonds of kinship; overthrow their own cities; ravage lands as enemies; make slaves out of free persons; violate virgins and the marriages of others; hate one another; envy the joys and good fortune of others; and then curse, revile, and tear one another with the savagery of cruel teeth.

[Note: [Col. 0886C]

**XLVI.—“That God, the preservation of all things.”** *Salus rerum*, “the preservation of things,” means the preserver of all things. Those [Col. 0886D] therefore err who wish to substitute, as Meursius does: “That God, the sower of all things.” ORELL.

**“The head of all virtues, and the pillar of benevolence.”** See above on book I, chapter 10. ORELL.

**“Abodes preserving their own integrity.”** Thus the Leiden edition. Others read *mensiones*, “measures,” which can be defended if it is used for *mensura*, meaning the proper share of integrity assigned to them. Thomas Canter prefers *conservans mentiones* or *dimensiones*, “preserving measurements,” as in book III: “But in your case it is too little that you embrace the gods by a measurement of their forms.” Here I am at a loss. ORELL.

**“Should have made anything defective.”** See above on chapter 37 of this book. ORELL.

**“Which was far removed from what is right.”** Thus all the editors except the Leiden editor, who, for some reason unknown to me, restored the manuscript reading “which was less than right” to the text. “Less than right” is equivalent to “less right.” But I much prefer “far removed.” ORELL.

[Col. 0887B] **“An unhappy and pitiable thing.”** This belonged among the arguments of those [Col. 0887C] who denied that the human being was created by God. See Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*. HERALD.

**“A latent power and a cruelty hostile to humanity, whatever it might be, would feed upon their torments.”** Franciscus Modius restored this passage most excellently, with the approval of Stewechius and Salmasius. The manuscript has: “however latent it might be, I do not know.” This is corrupt. By these words Arnobius undoubtedly describes the devil, whom he called cruelly savage above. ORELL.]

### XLVI

But far be from us—so that we may repeat the same point yet again and more insistently—so monstrous and wicked a conviction: that he, the preserver of all things, God of all, the head of all virtues, the pillar of benevolence, and, to extol him with human praises, the supremely wise and just being who makes all things perfect and makes abodes that preserve their own integrity, should either have made anything defective and far removed from what is right, or have been the cause of miseries or dangers to any creature, or have ordained and commanded the very activities through which human life is lived and conducted, and decreed that they should flow [Col. 0887A] from his own ordering [Note: [Col. 0887B] The manuscript has *ab*, “from,” rather than *a*.].

These things are beneath him and destroy the power of his greatness. So far is he from being believed the author of such things that whoever supposes that the human being was born from him incurs the charge of sacrilegious impiety: the human being, an unhappy and pitiable thing, who grieves that he exists; who detests and laments his condition; who understands that he was created for no other reason than that evils might not lack material through which to spread themselves, and that there might always be miserable beings upon whose torments a latent power and a cruelty hostile to humanity, whatever it might be, could feed.

[Note: [Col. 0887C]

**XLVII.—“Likewise, we confess that we do not know this.”** I think *iterum*, “again,” should be read instead of *item*, “likewise.” ORELL.

**“And who have appropriated for themselves the status of deities through the opinions of mortals.”** *Usurpare* here means to claim something for oneself against right and divine law, without any merit—Greek *σφετερίζεσθαι*, “to appropriate”; German *usurpieren*, “to usurp.” Thus Suetonius, *Claudius*, chapter 25: “He executed with the axe those who usurped Roman citizenship.” See Casaubon there. ORELL.

**“But those whom we deny to be God’s.”** Thus Stewechius and the Leiden editor from the manuscript. The others read: “But because we deny them to be God’s.” The same.

**“For if we deny that flies, beetles, bedbugs,”** [Col. 0887D] etc. The belief that God did not create the tiny animals was a delusion of Marcion, Valentinus, and Apelles, as we learn from Jerome, volume IX, page 211, in the proem to *Philemon*. Augustine refutes them in *The City of God*, book XI, chapter 15, and book XII, chapter 25. ELMENH.

**“Nitedulae.”** Servius, on *Georgics* I, verse 181, interprets *nitedula* or *nitela* as a reddish field mouse. Papias: “The *nitedula* is an animal shining like fire, a small mouse, which in Greek is called *lamparis*.” Cicero, *For Sestius*, chapter 33: “so that that little field mouse, dragged out from the brambles, might attempt to gnaw at the commonwealth.” ELMENH.—Compare Pliny, *Natural History* VIII, chapter 57, with Hardouin’s note there; R. Bentley on Horace, *Epistles* I.7, verse 29, where he restores *nitedula* for *vulpecula*, “little fox”; and Salmasius on Solinus, pages 223 following, where he discusses this little animal at length. From the gloss of Philoxenus, in which *nitela* is explained as *δενδροβάτης*, “tree-climber,” he conjectures that it is the same as the squirrel (*das Eichhorn*). But the words of Servius and Papias seem to fit better the little animal that the French call *mulot*, the field mouse (*die Feldmaus*), or rather the larger hazel dormouse or oak dormouse, with a reddish back, which very frequently climbs trees and sleeps through the winter—the large hazel dormouse (*die grosse Haselmaus*). Nourry, page 560, thinks it means the woodland mouse that the French call *le mulot*. Compare also Ernesti, *Ciceronian Lexicon*, under this word. ORELL.

**“And maintain that they were not brought forth by the higher God.”** The one whom Arnobius here calls “higher” he calls above the “first God.” For Marcion this is the better God and the Father of Christ. See Tertullian, *On Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 7; Irenaeus, Epiphanius, and others. ELMENH. and HERALD.]

### XLVII

“But,” you say, “if God is not the parent and also [Note: [Col. 0888B] The manuscript has *et*, “and,” which is better. Meursius; already Fulvius.] the progenitor of souls, [Col. 0887B] by whose agency were they begotten, and by what principle were they brought forth?”

If you wish to hear an unvarnished answer, one not derived from any ostentation of eloquence, we likewise confess that we do not know this and have no knowledge of it. We consider knowledge of so great a matter to surpass not only our own weakness and frailty but also that of all the powers that exist in the world and have appropriated for themselves the status of deities through the opinions of mortals.

But must we demonstrate whose those are whom we deny to belong to God? That does not follow by any necessity. For if we deny that flies, beetles, bedbugs, *nitedulae*, weevils, and moths are the work of the almighty king, it does not logically follow that we must be required to say who made and established them. We may, without blame, be ignorant of who gave even them their origin, while maintaining that things so superfluous, so vain, so irrelevant to every rational purpose—and indeed sometimes harmful and productive of serious injuries—were not brought forth by the higher God.

[Note: [Col. 0888C]

**XLVIII.—“Since we refuse to acknowledge that souls are the offspring of God the sovereign.”** Similarly, Lucretius uses *renutare*, “to refuse,” for “to deny,” book III, verse 351:

> For the rest, if anyone denies that the body possesses sensation, etc. HERALD and ORELL.

**“Truer than everything true, and more certain than everything certain.”** This is a Hellenism. Seneca, *Natural Questions*, book II, chapter 36: “Nothing is truer than the truth.” Martial, *Epigrams* VI.30, to Paetus:

[Col. 0888D]

> Do you want me to tell you things truer than truth?  
> You have lost six hundred thousand sesterces, Paetus. ELMENH.

The superlative is also used for the comparative in the Greek manner. Thus Euripides, *Andromache*, verse 6:

> Νῦν δ᾽ οὔτις ἄλλη δυστυχεστάτη γυνὴ  
> Ἐμοῦ πέφυκεν, ἢ γενήσεταί ποτε.

> Now no other woman has been born more unfortunate than I,  
> nor ever will be.

Homer, *Odyssey* XI, verse 481:

> . . . σεῖο δ᾽, Ἀχιλλεῦ,  
> Οὔτις ἀνὴρ προπάροιθε μακάρτατος, οὔτ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ὀπίσσω.

> . . . than you, Achilles,  
> no man before was more blessed, nor will any be hereafter.

See Clarke and Hermann there; the distinguished commentator on Viger, *On Greek Idioms*, page 715; and compare Gataker, *On the Style of the New Testament*, chapter 25. Moreover, Bremi, the distinguished scholar, most correctly observes in our *Supplement to Nicolaus of Damascus*, pages 51 following, that this form of expression occurs only in comparisons and never absolutely. ORELL.

[Col. 0889B] **“By the incalculable perversity of their vices.”** Thus Fulvius Ursinus, most correctly. The glosses give: “*Scaevitas* . . . wickedness.” Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* IX, page 221 in Elmenhorst’s edition: “Behold,” they say, “the outrageous perversity of the deed.” Hence *scaeva*: “left-handed, perverse, [Col. 0889C] contrary.” See above on book I. ORELL.

**“Weak-willed.”** Arnobius seems to use this term for those whom the Greeks call *ἀκρατεῖς*, “lacking self-control.” HERALD.

**“The distinctions of their birth.”** This means more than “honorable birth,” which properly denotes the freeborn and those of liberal status, just as “honorably born” means freeborn and of the status of a freedman. Thus Livy, book XXVI, says that Gnaeus Fulvius imbued an army of Roman citizens, honorably born and liberally educated, with servile vices. Here, however, the meaning is the greatest nobility that can possibly be expressed—*εὐγένεια ἡ πάνυ*, “nobility in the fullest sense,” the divine nobility of souls. It is equivalent to what Arnobius had just called “sovereign nobility,” that is, nobility proceeding from God, the source and sovereign of all things. HERALD.]

### XLVIII

Similarly here also, although we refuse to acknowledge that souls are the offspring of God the sovereign, it does not immediately follow that we must explain from what parent they were produced or by causes of what kind they were begotten. For who prevents us either from not knowing whence they arose and came forth, or from knowing that they are not God’s offspring?

“By what reasoning,” you ask, “and by what method?”

Because it is truer than everything true, and more certain than everything certain, that nothing is done, made, or established by the sovereign of all things, as has often been said, except what ought and is fitting to be made—except what is complete, unimpaired, and perfected in the full realization of its own integrity.

Yet we see human beings—that is, the souls themselves; for what are human beings except souls bound [Col. 0889A] to bodies?—revealing through the incalculable perversity [Note: [Col. 0889B] Thus Fulvius. The manuscript has *servitute*, “slavery”; others wrongly read *savitate*.] of their vices that they themselves are not of patrician stock but were born from families of middling rank. For we see some who are merciless, criminal, audacious, rash, headlong, blind, deceitful, dissembling, lying, proud, arrogant, avaricious, greedy, lustful, inconstant, weak-willed, and incapable of preserving even their own resolutions. They assuredly would not be such if sovereign nobility vindicated them as its own and they derived the distinctions of their birth from descent from the source of all things.

[Note: [Col. 0889C]

**XLIX.—“Of thoroughly faultless character.”** That is, of the most perfect and unblemished character, polluted by no crime. Juretus illustrates the expression at length in his note on Symmachus, book I, letter 26, page 40 in Lectius’s edition; Johannes Wowerius on Petronius, page 143 in Lotichius’s edition; J. F. Gronovius on Seneca, *On Anger* I, chapter 5; and Cortius on Pliny, book III, letter 3, page 187. ORELL.

**“Good men . . . among humanity, wise men.”** Others remove the comma after “men,” so that the sense becomes “wise in human affairs.” But wrongly: “among humanity” means among the human race as a whole—*in der Menschheit*, “in humankind.” ORELL.

**“In whom integrity itself . . . would find nothing wanting.”** The Leiden editor restored this most excellently from the manuscript, so that the sense is: “in whom integrity itself”—virtue personified—“would find nothing wanting,” *an denen die Tugend selbst nichts auszusetzen hatte*, “in whom virtue itself found nothing to criticize.” The other editions have: “integrity would in no respect be found wanting.” ORELL.

**“Limited in number.”** Juvenal, Satire XIII, verses 28 following, is apposite to our author:

> The good are indeed rare; their number is scarcely as great  
> as the gates of Thebes or the mouths of the rich Nile.

[Col. 0890B] ELMENH.—The manuscript has *diffiniti*. ORELL.

**“Be weighed.”** Thus the manuscript. Fulvius Ursinus reads “be suspended,” for some reason unknown to me. ORELL.

[Col. 0890C] **“Upon the little protuberance of a single hill.”** There is a parallel passage in book V: “Shall we also believe that a god of such mighty divinity was drawn down to earth and, standing upon the little protuberance of a single hill with a puny man, entered into an argumentative conversation?” Arnobius has adapted this from Cato’s *Origins*: “I judge that, if you wish to save the situation, you should order some four hundred soldiers to go to that protuberance and command them to occupy it.” See Aulus Gellius, book III, chapter 7, and Nonius under the word *verruca*. MEURS.—The same words occur below in book V, chapter 3. According to Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* III, chapter 7, Cato called an elevated and rugged place a *verrucula*. But our author employs the diminutive noun according to his custom. NOURRY.

**“Tiny particles.”** He says *miculae*, “tiny particles,” in imitation of Lucretius I, verses 839 following:

> And it is evident that gold may consist of particles of gold,  
> and that earth may grow together from tiny particles of earth. [Col. 0890D] HERALD.

**“Its capacity to inspire wonder is acquired through accumulation.”** These words are altered in various ways. Fulvius Ursinus reads “by observation, by accumulation”; Stewechius, “its enumeration,” etc. But the received reading can be approved. Arnobius therefore speaks of the wonder inspired by gold, because the brilliance of gold dazzles the eyes and draws them into contemplating and admiring it. HERALD. I would therefore translate: “Only through the heaping together of the tiny particles of gold does it become the metal that the world admires” (*Erst durch Zusammenhäufung der kleinen Goldstäubchen wird es zum Metall, das die Welt bewundert*). ORELL.

**“For this minuteness is consumed by the immense.”** That is: that small quantity of river water immediately passes into the sea’s saltiness and, because of its smallness, cannot alter the sea. PRIOR. Fulvius Ursinus reads “in the immense.” ORELL.

**“It must be considered of no weight.”** Here too *mominis*, “weight,” should be read instead of *nominis*, “name.” HERALD.]

### XLIX

“But,” you will say, “there are also good men among humanity—wise and just men, of blameless and thoroughly faultless character.” We raise no question as to whether there have ever been any such persons, in whom integrity itself, as it is called, would find absolutely nothing wanting. Grant that they are thoroughly honorable and have been praiseworthy; that they have attained the highest summit of perfection; and that their lives have never limped through any fault. Yet we demand to hear how many they are or have been, so that from the magnitude of their number we may measure whether a fair counterweight has been produced and whether it has been balanced by an equivalent compensation [Note: [Col. 0889B] The manuscript adds “and whether.”].

One, two, three, four, ten, twenty, a hundred—certainly limited in number, and perhaps confined within the compass of a list of names. Yet the human race ought to be judged and weighed not from the few good people but from all the rest. For the part is contained in the whole; the whole is not contained in the part. The totality must draw its portions to itself; the totality must not be assimilated to its portions.

What if you were to say that a person crippled in every limb and wailing from bitter torments was healthy merely because the nail of one finger suffered no pain? Or that the earth was made of gold because, upon the little protuberance of a single hill, there were tiny particles which, when melted together, produced gold, and whose capacity to inspire wonder was acquired through accumulation?

The entirety of the soil [Note: [Col. 0890B] Fulvius reads: “of the earth.”] establishes the nature of its material, not fixed specks of dust. Nor is the sea immediately sweet if you add and pour into it some number of drops of milder water, for this minuteness is consumed [Col. 0890B] by the immense [Note: [Col. 0890B] Fulvius reads: “in the immense.”]. What is diffused throughout the whole, vanishes, and is swallowed up in the vastness of a great body must be considered not merely of little weight but of no weight at all.

[Note: [Col. 0891C]

**L.—“And by the power of this name have raised their brows.”** Thus Heraldus and the Leiden edition instead of “in this name,” etc. Janus Dousa, on Catullus, poem LXVIII, verse 45, page 549 in Graevius’s edition, suspects that something has fallen out after the word “name.” Meursius, page 74, supplies: “And in the good fortune of this name have raised their brows.” But everything will be clear if we read: “by the power . . . of the name.” ORELL.

**“To drive out, to expel.”** *Proturbare*, “to drive out,” means to cast down from or out of a place, to expel. See Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* IX, page 668. ORELL.

**“So that they may remove from themselves the causes of falling.”** Thus the manuscript. Others, unaware that *aferre* and *afore* were ancient customary spellings for *auferre* and *abfore*, and joining the phrase with the preceding words “lest they be capable of being driven into vices,” etc., altered it to: “and bring upon themselves causes of falling.” STEW.

[Col. 0891D] **“It does not demand to be amended or corrected.”** Thus the Leiden edition, in accordance with Arnobius’s custom of combining several words of this kind with the same meaning. The manuscript has *corripi*, “to be rebuked,” which Heraldus defends by observing that writers of that age used *corripere*, “to rebuke,” for *corrigere*, “to correct,” although he adduces no example. ORELL.

**“If the form of each kind intends to persist in its own integrity.”** *Cogitat*, “intends,” is equivalent to “wishes,” for the form of a kind has no intelligence. Thus *cogitare* is used even of things lacking intelligence, for example in Virgil, *Georgics* I, 462:

> The sun will give you signs of what the rain-bearing south wind intends. ORELL.

**“Therefore, he who struggles to correct the inborn perversities of souls most plainly shows himself to be imperfect, although he strives with every effort and all persistence.”** Thus all the editors [Col. 0892C] except the Leiden editor. In place of *imperfectum*, “imperfect,” the manuscript has *improbabilem*, “unapproved,” which Stewechius correctly demonstrates should by no means have been altered. The noun is evidently derived from the inspectors of public works, whom ancient inscriptions and Roman writings mention countless times. See Janus Guilielmus, *Verisimilia* II.8; Franciscus Modius, *Novantiquae Lectiones*, letter 39; and Ludovicus Carrio, *Emendations* II.5.

Yet even so the sentence is mutilated and gaping, for the following *contendat*, “strives,” has nothing to which it can refer. Therefore, following traces of the manuscript, the Leiden editor printed the passage thus: “He most plainly shows himself to be imperfect, approved though he strives with every effort and persistence.” For my part, I suspect that we should read: “He most plainly shows himself to be unapproved, although with every effort and persistence he strives to prove the contrary.” The word “contrary” has either fallen out or been absorbed by the preceding *contendat*. [Col. 0892D] For *animorum*, “souls,” Meursius prefers *animarum*, since this is Arnobius’s consistent form. ORELL.]

### L

You say that within the human race there are good men who perhaps acquire the appearance of goodness through comparison with the very worst. Who are these people? Tell us.

The philosophers, I suppose, who consider themselves alone to be supremely wise and who, by the power of this name, have raised their brows. They, of course, are the very men who daily fight against their own desires and undertake, through the virtues’ obstinate struggle, to drive out and expel the passions implanted in their souls [Note: [Col. 0891C] The manuscript has *pertinacium*, “of obstinate things.”]. Lest they be capable of being driven into vices by the impulse of any opportunity, they flee estates and riches, so that they may remove from themselves the causes of falling.

But when they do this and make it their concern, they demonstrate most plainly that their souls are unstable and, through weakness, prone to vice. In our judgment, however, that which is good by nature does not demand to be amended or rebuked. Indeed, it ought itself to be ignorant of what evil is, if the form of each kind intends to persist in its own integrity. For a contrary cannot be implanted in its contrary [Note: [Col. 0892C] The manuscript has *potis est*, “is capable.”], nor equality be contained in inequality, nor sweetness in bitterness. [Col. 0891B]

Therefore, he who struggles to correct the inborn perversities of souls most plainly shows himself to be imperfect, although he strives with every effort and all persistence.

[Note: [Col. 0892D]

**LI.—“A projection of the mind directed at a nothing set before it.”** A “nothing set before it,” that is, set before the mind in thought: a nonexistent thing that you nevertheless conceive and represent to yourselves as though it truly existed—*ein Non-ens, etwas, das nicht wirklich existiert, das bloss Ideal ist*, “a nonbeing, something that does not actually exist but is merely ideal.” There is a similar proverbial expression among the Germans: *gegen einen Strohmann fechten*, “to fight against a straw man.” ORELL.
