**“That is, souls descending from the seat and region above.”** I would very much like to cast out these words as a gloss, were they not supported by a style that somehow has the flavor of Arnobius. MEURS.]

### LI

But our answer is an object of ridicule to you because, although we deny that souls are royal offspring, we do not state in reply from what causes and origins they were created. Yet what sort of offense is it either to be ignorant of some matter or, without any concealment, to profess oneself ignorant of precisely what one does not know?

Which of the two seems more deserving of your ridicule: the person who lays claim to no knowledge of some obscure matter, or the person who thinks that he knows perfectly clearly what surpasses human understanding and is enveloped in blind darkness?

If the nature of each matter is examined thoroughly, you stand in the same position that you condemn in us. For when you say that souls descend from the king himself and enter into human forms, you are not stating something ascertained and placed in the light of perfectly manifest truth. You conjecture; you do not know. You suspect; you do not possess certain knowledge.

For if knowledge means retaining what you yourself have seen or apprehended with the mind, you cannot say that you have ever seen any of the things you assert—that is, souls descending from the seat and region above. You therefore rely upon suspicion, not upon the assurance of explicit knowledge.

But what is suspicion except an uncertain opinion about things and a projection of the mind directed at a nothing set before it? Therefore, one who suspects does not possess certain knowledge [Col. 0892B] and does not walk in the light of understanding. And if this is true and firmly established among upright and supremely wise judges, then that suspicion of yours in which you trust must also be regarded as ignorance.

[Note: [Col. 0892D]

**LII.—“And what or whence are the souls of all the things that live?”** Thus Fulvius Ursinus. The manuscript has “of those who live,” which cannot stand, for “panthers” precedes. “The things that live” therefore means animals in general. ORELL.

[Col. 0893A] **“As though from that Platonic mixing bowl which Timaeus prepares and mixes.”** Plato, *Timaeus*, page 41 (volume III of H. Stephanus’s edition, page 326 of volume IX of the Bipont edition):

> Ταῦτ᾽ εἶπε, καὶ πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸν πρότερον κρατῆρα, ἐν ᾧ τὴν τοῦ παντὸς ψυχὴν κεραννὺς ἔμισγε, τὰ τῶν πρόσθεν ὑπόλοιπα κατεχεῖτο μίσγων, τρόπον μέν τινα τὸν αὐτόν, ἀκήρατα δ᾽ οὐκέτι κατὰ ταῦτα ὡσαύτως, ἀλλὰ δεύτερα καὶ τρίτα.

> Having said this, he returned to the former mixing bowl in which he had blended and mixed the soul of the universe. He poured into it the remnants of the previous ingredients and mixed them in approximately the same manner, though they were no longer equally pure, but of second and third grades.

Calcidius: “Again he sets forth the mixing bowl and the mixing and combination of those powers from which the soul of the world had been combined, and from their remnants he fashions our souls—namely, from that twofold nature consisting of the same and the different, and from divisible substance. These were not, as before, of unmixed purity. For a soul fashioned from the purest elements could not fall into the vices of so great a material forest, nor be compatible with the frailty of a mortal body. He mixed them, Timaeus says, in almost the same manner, yet the same purity and serenity of products did not result.” ELMENH.—Moreover, “which Timaeus prepares and mixes” is elegantly used for “which Timaeus says was prepared and mixed.” So in Aristotle, *οἱ γεννῶντες τὸν οὐρανόν*, “those who generate the heavens,” [Col. 0893C] stands for *οἱ τὸν οὐρανὸν γεννητὸν εἶναι λέγοντες*, “those who say that the heavens were generated.” HERALD.—Similarly Minucius Felix, chapter 22: “Homer wounded Venus, bound Mars, wounded and put him to flight,” etc. See Gronovius there, page 226, and J. F. Gronovius, *Diatribe on Statius’s Silvae*, chapter 22. ORELL.

**“Shrew.”** A small animal of the mouse family, although smaller and more shrill in its squeaking, as Donatus says on Terence, *Eunuch*, act V, verse 23. Others interpret it as a woodland mouse, or rather as the species that Linnaeus calls *Sorex araneus*, and we call *die Spitzmaus*, “the shrew.” Pliny, *Natural History* XI.37, and others confuse it with the house mouse, whence French *la souris* for the common mouse. Yet Columella distinguishes them, as does our author, in book XII, chapter 13: “If a snake, mouse, or shrew falls into the must,” and elsewhere. ORELL.

**“Centipede.”** Pliny describes it in *Natural History* XXIX, chapter 6: “The millipede, called by others the centipede or multipede, is an animal belonging to the little worms of the earth, hairy, possessing many feet, crawling in a curved manner, and contracting itself when touched. The Greeks call it *oniskos*, others *tylon*. They report that it is effective against pain of the ears.” See Hardouin there, volume II, page 516. ORELL.

**“And to live, because they have the same cause and origin of birth from the elements themselves—if, for the generation of living beings . . .”** Thus the Leiden editor corrected the corrupt reading of the earlier editions: “And indeed the cause and origin of their birth and life comes to them from the elements themselves, if, for the generation of living beings,” etc. Heraldus wished to alter this to: “Even if the true cause and origin of their birth comes to them from the elements themselves, if, for the generation of living beings,” etc. But I greatly prefer the Leiden editor’s emendation.

These words must evidently be joined to what precedes, so that the sense is: “For it is not credible that from that same Platonic mixing bowl . . . all these animals derived life and souls together with the human being, merely because all have the same cause and origin of birth from those very elements by which they live”—that is, because they are composed in a similar manner from the elements themselves: earth, water, and air.

A new [Col. 0894A] sentence then begins with the words: “If, for the generation of living beings,” etc. Moreover, *animalia* must here be understood in its proper and primary sense, *die belebten Wesen*, “animate beings,” which dwell, of course, in the forms or bodies of shrews, centipedes, and so forth. [Col. 0894B] ORELL.

**“For we also see some of the sages saying that earth is the mother of human beings; others, earth together with water; others joining to them an airy spirit.”** Here too I have followed the emendation of the Leiden editor. In the first edition these words are extremely corrupt and read thus: “For we see some of the sages saying that earth is the human being, water the mother; then others air, others joining spirit to these.” From this Stewechius had produced: “Then others adding air as spirit to these,” citing the words of Pacuvius from the *Chryses*: “Earth is the mother; she gives birth to the body; let ether add the soul.”

But the manuscript has *aerium*, “airy,” rather than *aerem*, “air.” Hence Heraldus suspects that the passage should read: “that earth is the mother of human beings; then others water; others joining to them an airy spirit.” The remaining editors followed him [Col. 0894C] except for the Leiden editor, who changed “then others water” into “others, water together with it,” etc. Arnobius is plainly repeating here, more briefly, the diverse opinions of the ancient philosophers about the causes of things, which he treated at greater length above in chapter 9. I have therefore enclosed this entire passage—from “For we also see,” etc., to the words “moved by its life-giving agitation”—in parentheses. ORELL.

**“That earth is the mother of human beings.”** Orpheus:

> ΓΑΙΑ Θεὰ μὴτηρ μακάρων θνητῶν τ᾽ ἀνθρώπων.

> Earth, goddess and mother of the blessed gods and mortal human beings.

Lactantius, book II, chapter 10: “Certain erring philosophers say that human beings and the other animals arose from the earth without any maker; hence that line of Virgil:

> Earth-born offspring raised its head from the hard fields.” ELMENH.

**“Others, earth together with water.”** Above, chapter 10: “Did Thales see things come into being through a combination of waters?” Censorinus, *On the Natal Day*, [Col. 0894D] chapter IV: “Anaximander of Miletus believed that either fish or animals resembling fish arose from heated water and earth; that within these human beings developed, and the offspring were retained inside until puberty; and only then, when those creatures burst open, men and women emerged who were already capable of feeding themselves.” See Lindenbrog there, page 19 of Havercamp’s edition. ORELL.

**“Others, however, that the sun is their maker, and that creatures animated from its fires are moved by its life-giving agitation.”** Compare the same Censorinus, chapter 8, page 36, who attributes this doctrine to the Chaldeans, and Diodorus Siculus, *Library of History* I, chapter 7. ORELL.

**“And since he did not wish the souls of the human race to be of the same purity of mixture.”** Thus Heraldus, in his *Second Observations*, admirably emended the extremely corrupt reading of the earlier editions: “and since he wished the mixtures—the souls of the human race—to be of the same purity.” Gelenius, Elmenhorst, and the Leiden editor, however, printed the passage thus: “and since he did not wish the mixtures of the human race’s souls to be of the same purity.” ORELL.]

## LII

And yet, lest you think that you alone are permitted to employ conjectures and suspicions, we too can do the same, since the question you ask is one that anyone may put forward. “Whence,” you say, “are human beings, and what are the souls of human beings, or whence do they come? Whence are elephants, bulls, deer, mules, asses? Whence lions, horses, dogs, wolves, panthers—and what are the souls of these living creatures, or whence do they come?” For the matter does not admit the belief [Col. 0893A] that either their souls have come from that Platonic mixing-bowl which Timaeus fashions and blends, or that the locust, mouse, shrew, cockroach, frog, and centipede are believed to be animate and alive because the elements themselves furnish them with the cause and origin of birth—if, that is, hidden and profoundly obscure principles for generating the animals that dwell in each of these elements are contained within them. (For we also see some of the wise saying that the earth is the mother of human beings; others, that water is their mother together with earth; still others join the airy spirit to these; while some hold the sun to be their maker, and say that beings animated from fire are set in motion by its life-giving activity.)

What if these things too are untrue, and there is some other reality [Col. 0894A], another cause, another principle, another power—in short, something unheard of by us and bearing an unknown name—which fashioned the race of human beings and fitted it into the constitutions of things? Is it not possible that human beings arose in this way, and that the authorship of their birth is not to be referred to the First God?

[Note: [Col. 0893A] Thus the manuscript. Others read *pote est*.]

For what reason do we suppose that the great Plato, that pious, holy, and wise man, had when he removed the fashioning of the human being from the supreme God and transferred it to certain lesser beings of whom I know nothing? Or when he refused to allow the souls of the human race to be a mixture of the same purity as that from which he had made the soul of this universe? Surely it was because he judged the fabrication of the human being unworthy of God, and thought that the fashioning of so feeble a thing was incompatible with His greatness and exalted rank. [Col. 0895A]

[Note: [Col. 0895B]

**LIII.—“Of small and failing powers; to be endowed with perpetuity, if they direct their hope for so great a gift toward God the sovereign.”** Thus the Leiden editor published and punctuated the passage. In the earlier editions *si* (“if”) is absent. Heraldus, in his *Second Notes*, also agrees with the Leiden edition, except that he removes the punctuation after *virium* (“powers”), [Col. 0895C] so that the sense would be: “the souls of human beings, being of small and failing powers, are endowed with perpetuity.” But these words are better joined to what precedes: “the souls of human beings are of an intermediate quality, since they were produced by beings that are not primary, subject to the law of death, and of small and failing powers; they are, however, endowed with perpetuity if they direct their hope for so great a gift toward God the sovereign.” In his own edition the same Heraldus had conjectured that the text should read *ut spem*, etc. For *conferant*, the Elmenhorst-Hanover edition has *conferimus*. ORELL.

**“But do we believe this foolishly? What is that to you? Most absurdly, foolishly. Where do we harm you?”** I think this should be read in place of the corrupt text: “What is that to you? Most absurd, foolish women? Where do we harm you?” Here, therefore, he says: “What concern is it of yours whether we believe this foolishly or not? Indeed, suppose that we believe it most absurdly and foolishly: what injury do you suffer from it?” HERALD.—Fulvius Ursinus reads *ineptissimi, fatui* (“most absurd, foolish men”). Meursius: *ineptissime fatui*, just as Plautus says in the *Mostellaria*: “At times he is absurdly foolish”; and Lactantius, book I, chap. [Col. 0895D] 18: “Who is so foolishly absurd?” etc. But I by far prefer Heraldus’ correction. ORELL.

**“And to be rescued, as the saying goes, from the jaws of Orcus.”** Note the words “as the saying goes.” For this was expressed proverbially, and they said that a person had been snatched from the jaws of Orcus when he had been delivered from some immediate and deadly danger. The Greeks too have their own proverbial expressions (*φράσεις παροιμιώδεις*) in this connection. Thus they speak of drawing someone out and “bringing him back into the sunlight from the gates of Acheron” (*καὶ ἐπαναγαγεῖν εἰς τὸν ἥλιον ἐκ τῶν πυλῶν τοῦ Ἀχέροντος*), and similar things. Titus Livy, book IX, chap. 6, says of the Romans who were surrounded at the Caudine Forks and were at last released after suffering disgrace: “When they had escaped from the defile under the eyes of the enemy, although, as if drawn up from the lower world, they seemed then for the first time to behold the light, nevertheless that very light, as they looked upon so disfigured a column, was more grievous than any death.” This manner of speaking was customary among both Latins and Greeks. Artemidorus, book II, chap. 60: “In ordinary speech we say that a person saved contrary to expectation has come back up from Hades” (*Φαμὲν ἐν τῇ συνηθείᾳ τὸν παρὰ προσδοκίαν σωθέντα ἐξ ᾅδου ἀναβεβηκέναι*). Florus, book II, chap. 6 [Col. 0896B]: “Meanwhile the Roman began to breathe again and, as it were, to emerge from the lower world.” HERALD.—Compare Reiff on Artemidorus, book I, p. 398, and Wetstein on Ephesians 4:9. ORELL.]

## LIII

Since, therefore, these things are so, it is neither irrationally nor idly that we believe the souls of human beings to be of an intermediate quality, since they were produced by beings that are not primary, subject to the law of death, and of small and failing powers; but that they are endowed with perpetuity if they direct their hope for so great a gift toward God the sovereign, who alone has the power to bestow such things beyond the reach of corruption.

But do we believe this foolishly? What is that to you? Most absurdly, foolishly. Where do we harm you, or what injury do we do or inflict upon you, if we trust that almighty God will take account of us when we begin to depart from our bodies, and that we shall be rescued, as the saying goes, from the jaws of Orcus?

[Col. 0895B]

[Note: [Col. 0896B]

**LIV.—“And must be examined with no slight care.”** Greek: *Οὐκ ὀλιγώρως*, “not negligently.” HERALD.

[Col. 0896C] **“So that all evils too are understood to arise by His will.”** Augustine, *The City of God*, book XX, chap. 1: “No human being acts rightly unless aided by divine assistance; no demon or human being acts wickedly unless this is permitted by the divine and wholly just judgment of God Himself.” Compare Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book I, chap. 8; Augustine, *Tractates on John*, tractate XLII, chap. 8. ELMENH.

**“Conscious of and progenitor of no evil.”** Sextus, in the *Sentences*: “God is the author of no evil.” Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*:

> God is not the inventor of vice;  
> a degenerate angel conceived it in his infamous mind and created it.

Arnobius becomes entangled in the discussion of the nature of evil and is unable to extricate himself with sufficient clarity from this difficult question. Evil is named in two ways in Holy Scripture: namely, the evil of guilt and the evil of punishment. According to the Fathers of the Church, the devil is the author of the former, [Col. 0896D] God of the latter. See Augustine, *Against Adimantus the Manichaean*, vol. VI, chap. 46, and *On Free Choice of the Will*, book I, chap. 10; Chrysologus, sermon 9; Lactantius, book IV, chap. 6; Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, chap. 57. ELMENH.

**“At every single point.”** That is, of time. Thus the Leiden edition; the manuscript has *cuncta per singala*, from which Gelenius and the others produced *cuncta per saecula* (“all things throughout the ages”). ORELL.

**“And crimes.”** Thus Gelenius corrected the text. Previously it read *et favoribus* (“and favors”). HERALD.

**“For what more empty stupidity can be found?”** Thus the first edition and the others that followed it, except the Leiden edition, which has, from Salmasius’ conjecture, “what greater stupidity can be found?” The manuscript has *immanior* (“more monstrous”), which can be said of savagery, cruelty, and similar vices, or at least of foolishness and stupidity combined with cruelty, but not of simple stupidity. See above, on book I, chap. 5, the words *immanis ille Xerxes* (“that monstrous Xerxes”), and Heraldus’ note. ORELL.]

## LIV

“Can anything, then,” someone will say, “possibly happen without the will of God?”

[Note: [Col. 0895B] Thus the manuscript.]

We must consider this carefully and examine it with no slight care, lest, while we think that by such a question we are honoring the Lord, we fall into the contrary impiety and destroy the exalted majesty of His being.

“In what way, and for what reason?”

Because, if all things are accomplished by His will, and [Col. 0896A] nothing in the world can either arise or occur without His nod, it necessarily follows that all evils too are understood to arise by His will. But if, on the contrary, we should wish to say—while removing from Him the causes of the worst things—that He is conscious of and progenitor of no evil, then the worst things will begin to seem to happen either against His will or—what it is monstrous to say—without His knowing, while He is ignorant, and—I know not what else.

Again, if we should wish to say that there are no evils, as we find that some have thought and maintained, every people and every nation will protest, displaying to us their sufferings and the manifold forms of danger by which, at every single point, the human race is scorched and torn. They will then ask us why, if there are no evils, you abstain from certain deeds and crimes. Why do you not do everything that impatient lust has ordered and commanded? Why, finally, do you establish terrible punishments in your laws for the guilty? For what more empty stupidity can be found than to contend that there are no evils, and yet to destroy and condemn offenders as though they were evil? [Col. 0896B]

[Col. 0897A]

[Note: [Col. 0897C]

**LV.—“By name.”** The author uses *nominaliter* for *nominatim*; below, in book VII, he likewise says *nominitamus* for *nominamus*. NOURRIUS.

**“Indeed, rather—more truly.”** On this accumulation of two comparatives, see below on book VII, chap. 18. ORELL.

**“Than to say that nothing happens without God (by His will).”** That is, without God’s will. Thus, when he says “by His will,” he explains what he meant by “without God.” I therefore think that nothing should be altered. HERALD.—The Leiden edition has: “Than to say that nothing happens without the will of God.” [Col. 0897D] To me, the words “by His will” seem to be the gloss of some pedantic copyist, written in the margin to explain what “without God” means; I have therefore enclosed them in parentheses. ORELL.

**“Nor do we regard it as a matter of great weight.”** Thus Meursius corrected the text. Previously it read *duximus* (“we regarded”). To “regard something among matters of great weight” means the same as to “regard it as a great matter”: Greek *ἐν μεγάλῳ τίθεσθαι*, “to esteem highly,” and *ποιεῖσθαι περὶ πολλοῦ*, “to make much of.” See Casaubon on Suetonius, *Caesar*, chap. 23, p. 130, vol. III, Wolf’s edition. ORELL.]

## LV

When, overcome by the evidence, we have agreed that these things exist, and have acknowledged that all human affairs teem with them individually and by name, the question will follow: Why, then, does almighty God not remove these evils, but allow them to exist and to continue through every age in an obstinate succession?

If we possess an understanding of God the king and sovereign, and are unwilling to wander through impious insanities of suspicion, we must answer that we do not know these things; that we have never sought or attempted to know what could be comprehended by no powers of ours; and that we consider it better—indeed, rather, far better—to remain within the bounds of unknowing and ignorance than to say that nothing happens without God (by His will), so that it would simultaneously be understood both that He supplies the causes of evils and that He is the creator of innumerable miseries.

“Whence, then,” you will say, “are [Col. 0897B] all these evils?”

“From the elements,” say the wise, “and from their inequality.” But how things that possess neither perception nor judgment can be declared malicious and harmful—or whether the malicious and harmful one is not rather he who undertook to bring things destined to be most evil into the completed effect of some work—is for those who make this assertion to discern.

What, then, do we say? Whence do they come? We are under no necessity to answer. For whether we can state the answer or whether we are less capable and cannot, both alternatives are of little importance to us; nor do we regard either ignorance or knowledge of this as a matter of great weight, content to establish this one thing alone: nothing harmful and destructive proceeds from God the sovereign. This we hold, this we know; upon this single truth of knowledge and understanding we take our stand: [Col. 0897C] nothing is done by Him except what is beneficial to all, what is sweet, what is filled to overflowing with love, joy, and gladness, what contains infinite and incorruptible pleasures, what each person would seek with all his prayers to obtain for himself—and would regard being excluded from these things as destructive and deadly. [Col. 0898A]

[Note: [Col. 0897D]

**LVI.—“Some of the wise think that the world was neither born nor will perish at any time.”** Heraclitus of Ephesus in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book VI, p. 255 (711 in Potter’s edition, where see his note); Aristotle in Lactantius, book II, chap. 10; Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book I, 29; and Pliny, *Natural History*, book I, chap. 1. Compare Junius Philargyrius on Virgil, *Georgics* II.6; Plutarch, *Opinions of the Philosophers*, book II, chap. 4; Ambrose, *Hexaemeron*, book I, chaps. III and V. ELMENH. On this entire passage compare Antonius Delrio on the *Syntagma of Latin Tragedy*, Part III, p. 532 ff. ORELL.

[Col. 0898C] **“Some describe it as immortal, although they write that it was born and generated.”** A doctrine of Plato. “For although it is in itself perishable, insofar as it has come into being, it will not be dissolved nor meet the lot of death, because of the will of God” (*Ὅτι αὐτὸς μὲν φθαρτός ἐστιν, ᾗ γέγονεν, οὐ λυθήσεται δὲ οὐδὲ τεύξεται θανάτου μοίρας διὰ τὴν βούλησιν τοῦ θεοῦ*), he writes in the *Timaeus*. Hermes Trismegistus agrees, in the *Poemander*, chap. 8: “The Father is Himself eternal through Himself; but the cosmos, through the Father, has become ever-living and immortal” (*Ὁ πατὴρ αὐτὸς ἑαυτοῦ ἀΐδιος· ὁ δὲ κόσμος ὑπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς ἀείζωος καὶ ἀθάνατος γέγονε*). Compare Apuleius, *On Plato’s Doctrine*, and especially J. Lipsius, *Stoic Physiology*, book II, dissertation XX, p. 951 ff., *Works*, vol. IV, Wesel edition. ORELL.

[Col. 0898D] **“Both born and generated, and destined to perish by ordinary necessity.”** The Stoic view. Seneca, *Consolation to Polybius*, chap. 20: “So it is: nothing is everlasting; few things are long-lasting. One thing is fragile in one way, another in another; the endings of things vary. But whatever has begun also comes to an end. Some threaten the world with destruction, and—if you think it right to believe it—some day will disperse this universe, which embraces all things divine and human, and plunge it into its ancient confusion and darkness.” Compare his *Natural Questions*, book III, chap. 29, and J. Lipsius, *Stoic Physiology*, dissertations XXI and XXII, p. 952 ff., who carefully collected all the passages. ORELL.

**“Undermine and weaken the doctrines of others.”** The manuscript has *subrupiant*, which Meursius defends in his *Appendix*, though I wish he had given us an explanation of this word. Fulvius Ursinus and Modius read *subruant* (“undermine”). For *scita* (“doctrines”) all the books have *secreta* (“secrets”), which seems to have arisen from a copyist misreading the abbreviation *v. scita* as an abbreviation of *secreta*. See J. F. Gronovius on Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, book II, chap. 17, p. 185. ORELL.

[Col. 0899B] **“Others hand down and declare that this same world consists of four elements; others, of two; a third group, of single elements.”** See Lipsius, *Stoic Physiology*, book II, dissertation XI, p. 922 ff., vol. IV, Wesel edition. Yet there we read not even a grunt—*ne γρὺ quidem*—about philosophers maintaining more or fewer than four elements, apart from one corrupt passage of Seneca in which three are posited: water, earth, and spirit. Arnobius therefore seems in this passage to have wrongly confused the parts from which ancient philosophers defined the world as consisting with its elements: to have said that those who divided the world into heaven and earth posited two elements; and to have affirmed that others, who said that the world was matter, posited a single element. *Stare* means “to consist,” as often in Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chap. IV, §22: “You see, therefore, that the whole condition of humanity consists especially in this: that man is born naked and frail, is afflicted by diseases, and is punished by premature death.” See Bunemann there. Here, moreover, *singula* does not mean “one after another,” but “one, a single thing,” absolutely; yet I have sought in vain for examples of this meaning in other writers. I therefore wonder whether the text should read *ex singulo tertii* (“a third group, of a single element”). The singular number with the adjective *singuli* is customary among the earlier writers—see Gesner in the *Thesaurus*—of whom Arnobius is a most devoted imitator. ID.

**“Others, of two.”** In common speech earth and water, or earth and sea, were called “the two elements.” Thus Ammianus Marcellinus, book XVII, chap. 13, §19: [Col. 0899D] “Thus, across both elements, the anger and valor of the victors destroyed the Sarmatians.” See Wagner there, p. 294. And Chariton, book VII, chap. 5, §10, at the beginning: “For the war is at its height in both elements” (*ἐν ἀμφοτέροις γὰρ τοῖς στοιχείοις ὁ πόλεμος ἀκμάζει*). There d’Orville, p. 579 of the Leipzig edition, cites a cloud of examples from writers of later Latin and Greek. Arnobius, however, speaking here about the doctrines of philosophers, seems to mean those who posited two first principles of things, dry and moist, assigning earth and fire to the former and water and air to the latter. ORELL.

**“Indivisible bodies.”** The atoms of the Epicureans. ORELL. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II.37. OCHSNER.

**“Thus some also deny that gods exist.”** For example, Diagoras of Melos and Theodorus of Cyrene. ORELL.

**“Or none of these is certain.”** Meursius reads “so that none,” etc. Wrongly. ORELL.

**“Others say that they are wholly uncertain whether gods exist anywhere.”** Protagoras in Diogenes Laertius, IX, section 51: “Concerning the gods, I am unable to know either that they exist or that they do not exist; for many things prevent knowledge—the obscurity of the matter and the brevity of human life” (*Περὶ θεῶν οὐκ ἔχω εἰδέναι οὔθ’ ὡς εἰσίν, οὔθ’ ὡς οὐκ εἰσίν· πολλὰ γὰρ τὰ κωλύοντα εἰδέναι, ἥ τε ἀδηλότης καὶ βραχὺς ὢν ὁ βίος τοῦ ἀνθρώπου*). See those whom Menagius cites there, p. 420, vol. II, Meibom’s edition. Compare Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, chap. 23, and Davies there. HERALD and ORELL.

**“Others, however, say that they exist but do not concern themselves with human affairs.”** The Epicureans. ORELL.

**“Indeed, others declare that they take part in mortal affairs,”** etc. Plato and the Stoics. ORELL.]

## LVI

As for all the other matters customarily debated in inquiries and controversies—by what progenitors they arose, or by what agents they are brought about—we neither contend that we know them nor care to inquire into or investigate them. We leave them all to their own causes and judge that they are neither connected nor relevant to what we seek.

For what is there that human intellects, through eagerness for contradiction, do not dare to weaken and dissolve, although what they attempt to undermine is pure and clear and fortified with the seal of truth? [Col. 0898B] Or, conversely, what are they unable to maintain with plausible arguments, although it is most plainly false, although it is an evident and manifest lie? For when someone has persuaded himself that something exists or does not exist, he loves to defend what he believes and to surpass others in acuteness—especially if the matter under discussion is remote, hidden,

[Note: [Col. 0897C] The manuscript wrongly has *abditae*.]

and enveloped in the darkness of nature.

Some of the wise think that the world was neither born

[Note: [Col. 0898C] The manuscript wrongly has *siccatum*.]

nor will perish at any time. Some describe it as immortal, although they write that it was born and generated. A third group has taken it into its head to say both that it was born and generated and that it will perish by ordinary necessity. And although one of these three opinions must necessarily be true, none of them lacks arguments by which its advocates may both confirm their own decrees [Col. 0898C] and undermine and weaken [Col. 0899A] the doctrines of others.

Others hand down and declare that this same world consists of four elements; others, of two; a third group, of single elements. Some say that it consists of none of these, and that indivisible bodies are its matter and first origin. And although one of these opinions is true

[Note: [Col. 0899B] The manuscript has *versa sunt*.]

—or none of them is certain—here likewise arguments are available to all, by which they may establish as true what they say and refute the falsehoods contained in the opinions of others.

Thus some also deny that gods exist; others say that they are wholly uncertain whether gods exist anywhere; others, however, say that they exist but do not concern themselves with human affairs; indeed, others declare both that they take part in mortal affairs and that they administer earthly concerns.

[Note: [Col. 0900C]

**LVII.—“The latter does not believe that they survive, but that they perish together with the bodies themselves.”** The opinion of the Epicureans and of Dicaearchus the Peripatetic. See Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations*, book I, chap. 21. ORELL.

**“But after the human being has been laid aside, some further life is granted to them, and afterward they fall under the laws of mortality.”** This was the Stoic opinion. Marcus Tullius, *Tusculan Disputations*, book I, chap. 31: “The Stoics, however, grant us only a lease, as though we were ravens; they say that souls will remain for a long time, but deny that they will remain forever.” He speaks of “laying aside the human being” as others speak of “putting off the human being,” that is, the body. HERALD.—One might also explain *post hominem positum* as “after the human being has been laid to rest,” that is, buried and placed in the tomb. Thus Lucretius, book III, lines 883–884:

> And so, when a man sees himself lamenting himself,  
> thinking that after death he will rot when the body has been laid aside.

See Lambinus there. On this Stoic opinion, moreover, see Justus Lipsius, *Stoic Physiology*, book III, chap. 11; Thomas Gataker on Antoninus IV.21; and Davies on Cicero, book I. [Col. 0900D] ORELL.

**“Discordant.”** Others read “to be discordant.” ORELL.

**“Or to wish to contend that one knows.”** More clearly: “or to wish to contend that one knows” (*behaupten wollen, dass man es wisse*). But Arnobius is fond of such transpositions. HERALD. Thus we have no need of Meursius’ twofold conjecture: “to wish to put forward something and contend that one knows,” or “to contend that one knows it perfectly.” ORELL.

**“You may see that it can be destroyed.”** Thus the manuscript, a wholly correct reading that Gelenius wrongly changed to “that it can be established.” Nor do I see what difficulty Meursius found in these words. “To be destroyed” means nothing other than “to be denied,” or “to be maintained not to exist.” ORELL.

**“Of those who hallucinate.”** Fulgentius explains *hallucinari* as “to dream vain dreams,” deriving it from *allucitae*, which we call *κώνωπες* (“gnats”). According to Nonius, however, it means “to wander, not to remain steady.” STEWENH. Aulus Gellius, book XVI, chap. 12, derives it from *ἀλύειν* (“to wander in mind”); see Gronovius and Vossius, *Roman Etymologies*, there. ORELL.

**“But we weigh and measure them by human reasonings.”** [Col. 0901B] This is the old reading, in place of which Gelenius also gives *commetamur*. I would not alter anything rashly. For perhaps Arnobius uses *commetari* archaically—*ἀρχαίως*—for *commetiri*, “to measure.” *Metari* was formerly used for *metiri*. Hence *castra metari*, “to measure out a camp,” which the Greeks interpret as “to measure out areas for an encampment” (*διαμετρεῖν χώρας τῷ στρατοπέδῳ*) and “to measure and mark out places suitable for camps” (*στρατοπέδοις ἐπιτήδεια χωρία ἀναμετρεῖν καὶ διαγράφειν*). HERALD.—The Leiden edition gives *conjectamus* (“we conjecture”); Stewechius, *commetimur* (“we measure”). ORELL.]

## LVII

Since, therefore, these things are so, and it cannot be otherwise than that one opinion among all of them is true, nevertheless all parties contend with arguments, and no individual lacks [Col. 0899B] something plausible to say, whether they are defending their own positions or contradicting the opinions of others. The condition of souls is [Col. 0900A] discussed by them in no different or dissimilar fashion. For one man thinks both that they are everlasting and that they survive the completion of mortal life; another does not believe that they survive, but that they perish together with the bodies themselves. A third holds that nothing happens to them immediately, but that after the human being has been laid aside, some further life is granted to them, and afterward they fall under the laws of mortality.

And although all these views cannot share in truth, nevertheless all parties conduct their cases with such strong and extremely powerful proofs that you cannot discover what should seem false to you, although you see that statements diverse in every respect are being made, discordant because of the contradictions between the facts. This certainly would not happen if human inquisitiveness could grasp anything certain, or if what seemed to have been discovered were confirmed by the agreement of everyone else.

It is therefore an utterly empty thing and a superfluous labor to put forward something as though you knew it; or to wish to contend that you know something which, even if true, you may see can be destroyed; [Col. 0900B] or to accept as true something that perhaps is not true and is advanced in the manner of those who hallucinate. And rightly is the matter so. For we do not weigh and measure divine things by divine, but by human reasonings; [Col. 0901A] and just as we suppose that something deserved to come about, so we contend that it must be so.

[Note: [Col. 0901C]

**LVIII.—“This world which contains us.”** Fulvius Ursinus: read “which surrounds us.” But nothing should be altered. ORELL.

**“Whether it was not generated, or was established at some point in time.”** Thus the Leiden edition. The manuscript has: “whether it was generated or at some point in time,” which Meursius corrected to: “whether it was generated or established at some point in time.” But *utrumne* (“whether”) seems to require *an* (“or”) in the following clause. ORELL.

**“Or was established at some point in time.”** Meursius corrects this to “or at some point in time,” or “and at some point in time,” because he had read “whether it was generated” in the preceding words. ORELL.

[Col. 0901D] **“In a circular movement.”** Nonius: “*orbicum*—the edition of Mercerus has *orbitum*—means ‘in a circle.’” Varro, *Know Thyself* (*γνῶθι σεαυτόν*): “As the stars of the gods’ heaven, which revolve around the earth and the axis, move in a circular movement.” Others wrongly read “throughout the whole sphere.” ORELL.

**“Whether it turns itself around by its own impulse and will.”** Thus the Leiden edition from the manuscript. In the others *se* (“itself”) is absent; Heraldus attempts to defend this as a passive usage, like “turn,” “turn away,” “move,” “the earth moved,” and similar expressions. Others read “whether it is turned around.” ORELL.

**“To make plain.”** Lucretius, II.933:

> For him it will be sufficient to make this plain and prove it.

ELMENH.

**“What secretly opens out snow into feathery flakes.”** This is indeed elegantly expressed, as is the later phrase: “What spread out rains and feathery snows . . .” Martial too, when treating snow in book IV, epigram 3, writes:

[Col. 0902C]

> See what a dense fleece of silent waters  
> falls upon Caesar’s breast and into his folds.

Note “fleece of waters.” For the ancient Greeks called snow periphrastically “woolly water” (*ἐριῶδες ὕδωρ*). Eustathius on Dionysius Periegetes, line 678, p. 91, H. Stephanus’ edition: “The ancients wittily call snow ‘woolly water,’ taking their cue from the wise King David when he says, ‘He gives His snow like wool’” (*τὴν χιόνα ἐριῶδες ὕδωρ ἀστείως οἱ παλαιοὶ φασι, τοῦ σοφοῦ βασιλέως Δαβὶδ ἀφορμὴν ἐνδόντος αὐτοῖς, ὅτε εἴπῃ· διδόντος χιόνα αὐτοῦ ὡσεὶ ἔριον*). Psalm 147. MEURS.—Herodotus, book IV, chap. 31, similarly reports that the Scythians compare falling snow to birds’ feathers; there Wesseling, p. 294, aptly cites our passage. The region called Pterophoros, mentioned by Pliny, *Natural History*, book IV, chap. 12, must likewise be understood in this way. For *subaperiat*, Stewechius thinks *suboperiat* should be read, so that it means the same as “condenses”; he adduces a passage from Apuleius, *On the Cosmos*: “It is agreed that snow is collected through the tossing together of dense clouds.” But nothing should be altered. In verbal compounds *sub-* very often denotes some obscure and hidden cause. “What secretly opens out snow into feathery flakes” [Col. 0902D] therefore stands for: “What hidden cause, unknown to us, opens snow out into feathery flakes”—that is, displays or reveals it to us in the form of feathery flakes. ORELL.

**“These little fiery fragments.”** Arnobius so calls the stars—that is, tiny fragments of fire. For the diminutive *frustillum* is formed from the noun *frustum*, “fragment.” See Plautus, *Curculio*, act IV, scene IV. NOURRIUS.

**“It was fitting and necessary that they should be fixed.”** Fulvius Ursinus made this correction, with Heraldus’ approval. The manuscript and first edition have *oportuerit figura* (“it was necessary—a figure”), which makes no sense; hence the Leiden editor produced *figurari* (“to be fashioned”). ORELL.]

## LVIII

What, then? Are we alone ignorant and unknowing of who the creator and establisher of souls is?

[Note: [Col. 0901B] Others read *qua causa*, “by what cause.”]

What cause fashioned the human being? Whence evils burst forth? Or why the supreme King allows them both to exist and to be committed, and does not drive them away from human affairs? Do you have anything concerning these matters that has been ascertained and known?

If you wish to set forth the boldness of your suspicions, can you explain and declare whether this world which contains us was not generated, or was established at some point in time? If it was established and made, by what kind of operation, or for the sake of what thing? Can you introduce and unfold the reason why it does not remain fixed and immovable, but is always carried around in circular motion? Whether it turns itself around by its own impulse and will, [Col. 0901B] or is driven round by the impulses of some power? What is the place and space itself in which it is situated and revolves? Infinite

[Note: [Col. 0901B] Fulvius supplies “or finite.”]

or finite? Empty or solid? Does an axis support it, resting upon pivots at its extremities, or does it rather uphold itself by its own force and remain suspended by an inner spirit?

[Col. 0902A] Can you, when questioned, make it plain and demonstrate with perfect knowledge

[Note: [Col. 0902B] The manuscript wrongly has “with utter ignorance.”]

what secretly opens out snow into feathery flakes? What principle and cause there was that the first day should not rise from the western regions and end its light in the east? How the sun, by one and the same contact, produces such diverse—indeed, contrary—effects? What the moon is, and what the stars are? Why the moon does not remain in one form, or why it was fitting and necessary that these little fiery fragments should be fixed throughout the whole body of the world? Why some of them are small and others broader and larger; why some possess a dull light, while others have a keener and brilliantly shining radiance?

[Note: [Col. 0902D]

**LIX.—“What spread out feathery snows and lightning flashes.”** I printed this with Salmasius in the Leiden edition and in the commentary on Solinus, p. 137. The manuscript has *et foliora dilatarit*, which Gelenius, not understanding it, absurdly changed to *Aeoli ora dilatarit*, “spread open the mouths of Aeolus.” [Col. 0903A] For who ever said that Aeolus emits the winds from his own mouth? On the contrary, as Virgil says, *Aeneid* I.56 ff.:

[Col. 0903B]

> In his vast cavern King Aeolus  
> restrains the struggling winds and roaring storms  
> under his command, and bridles them with chains and prison walls.

Moreover, the following words, “whence the wind arises,” would be a mere repetition of “what spread open the mouths of Aeolus.” Stewechius suspects that the text should read: “What spread rains and snows into little feathers and little leaves” (*plumulas et foliola*—German *Blüttchen, Flöckchen*). Nicolaus Heinsius, in P. Burmann’s *Latin Anthology*, book V, epigram 93, p. 378, vol. II, corrects it to: “What spread out rains to be generated, snows and frosts from the dew of heaven.” But Salmasius’ emendation alone seems true. For in ancient manuscripts *fulgora* (“lightning flashes”) is often reproduced as *foliora*, just as *toja* occurs for *toga* and *Ilycias* for *Glycias*. Arnobius uses “feathery snows” in the same sense as Aeschylus’ “winged snow” (*πτεραίη χιών*), and Solinus, chap. 15: “Beyond these people—the Arimaspi—and the Riphaean ridge lies a region beset by continual snows. They call it Pterophoros, ‘Feather-bearing,’ because the fall of the continuous frosts there presents something like feathers.” [Col. 0903C] See Salmasius, book I.—Yet I now have the gravest doubts about the truth of this reading. For Arnobius is speaking here of watery, not fiery, phenomena. Moreover, I can scarcely believe that lightning flashes can be said to be “spread out.” I therefore think the text should read: “What spread snows into feathers”—or, with Stewechius, “little feathers”—“and little leaves.” ORELL.

**“Or of the lands.”** Fulvius Ursinus, for some reason unknown to me, changes this to “of the other waters.” “Of the lands” means “the waters of the lands,” which must be mentally supplied from the preceding word “seas,” as though Arnobius had said “the waters of the sea.” Yet the correction of the most learned Wakefield, in *Critical Miscellanies*, vol. III, section 145, p. 132, seems very slight—indeed, uniquely correct and deserving admission into the text: “Or the sweet waters of the earth,” etc. ORELL.

[Col. 0903D] **“What made the channels hollow like pipes and passable.”** I think *fecerit* (“made”) was an error by Arnobius himself, writing hastily and slipping from a direct into an indirect question; I therefore think nothing should be altered. The context would demand *fecit*. In the preceding words Meursius likewise substitutes the subjunctive *sint* for *solidata sunt*, and reads what follows thus: “What are owls doing in the world?” etc. ORELL.

**“Immussuli.”** Festus: “The *immustulus* is a bird of the eagle kind, but of less strength than an eagle. This bird rarely appears, and generally only in spring, because it fears heat and cold. It is so called because it suddenly and unexpectedly swoops down.” The same author: “The *immusculus* . . . is a kind of bird that some call the wren, others the osprey.” There the commentators demonstrate that the *immusculus* and *immustulus* of Festus and the *immusulus* or *immussulus* of Arnobius and the ancient glossaries are one and the same, namely, a species of eagle. Pliny, *Natural History*, book X, chap. 7: “The Roman augurs regard the *immussulus* as a matter of great uncertainty. Some think it the young of a vulture, but Masurius the young of an eagle before its tail turns white.” G. J. Vossius carefully examines the etymology of the word under this entry in his *Roman Etymologies*. ORELL.

[Col. 0904A] **“Buzzards.”** The buzzard is an augural bird of the hawk family. Pliny, *Natural History*, book X, chap. 8: [Col. 0904B] “We have discovered sixteen kinds of hawk . . . The *triorches*, named from the number of its testicles, to which Phemonoe assigned first rank in augury: the Romans call this bird the *buteo*. A family too”—that is, from the Fabian clan—“received its surname from it, when it settled upon the commander’s ship under favorable auspices.” Hardouin there thinks it is the same bird that Gallic fowlers call the *Milan*, not to be confused with the kite, the Greek *ἰκτίνος*, which is tawny, whereas the buzzard is black. Aristotle, *History of Animals*, book IX, chap. 36: “The *triorches* is the strongest of the hawks” (*Τριόρχης κράτιστος τῶν ἱεράκων*); see Scaliger there. Festus: “The following were regarded as winged birds that gave auspices by their flight: the buzzard, *sanqualis*, *immusculus*, eagle, and vulture.” Compare the same author under *Buteo*, and G. J. Vossius, who treats this bird at length in *Roman Etymologies*; in German it is called *Bushard*. Inventius, in the *Elegy on Philomela*, line 42:

> And in the marsh-bearing waters the bittern booms,

[Col. 0904C] seems by *buteo* to mean some marsh bird, perhaps the bittern, German *die Rohrdommel*. ORELL.

**“What the winged augural birds and the other birds are.”** Among the Romans, *alites* were birds that gave omens by their wings and flight, while *oscines* gave omens by singing with their mouths. See Festus under *alites* and *oscines*; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II.64, and *Letters to Friends*, book VI, letter 6, with Manutius’ extensive discussion there; and Vossius, *Roman Etymologies*, under *ales*. Here, therefore, Arnobius seems to distinguish *alites*, augural birds, from the other birds that had no role in auspices. ORELL.

**“What the shameless flies are.”** Below, book VI: “With which they might entangle the flight of chirping and heedless flies.” HERALD.

**“Shrews.”** See above on chap. 52. ORELL.

[Col. 0904D] **“Water striders.”** Festus: “The *tippula* is a kind of tiny creature with six feet, but of such lightness that, when running over water, it does not sink.” Plautus, *Persa*, act II, scene II:

> A water strider’s weight is no lighter than a pimp’s good faith.

See the commentators there. German *die Schnake*. ORELL.

**“What are wild oats, and what is darnel?”** Virgil also joins the two, *Georgics* I.153:

> Barren darnel and sterile oats hold sway.

See Völlius there. Servius on Virgil, *Eclogues*, line 37: “He called oats sterile according to conditions in Italy, for in Thrace they are fruitful.” From this passage Salmasius, on Solinus, p. 153 ff., conjectures and demonstrates at length that the Romans knew no oat other than this sterile variety, which sprang up spontaneously and was counted among the blights of grain. Accordingly, nothing is read in the ancient agricultural writers about its sowing. [Col. 0905B] Thus the oat in this passage is the Greek *αἰγίλωψ*, wild or barren oat—German *wilder, tauber Hafer*—which must be carefully distinguished from *βρόμος*, the fruitful, cultivated oat. Servius, in the passage cited, says that the latter was sown by the Thracians; Pliny, *Natural History*, book XVIII, chap. 17, records that it was sown by the peoples of Germany and that they lived on no other porridge. ORELL.]

Or seeds that are unpleasant in their odors. Stewechius conjectures that one should read [Col. 0905C] “seeds unpleasant in their fumes” (*tristia nidoribus semina*), wrongly: for *nidor* signifies only the smell of things burned or scorched, never the scent of flowers or herbs. Guilielmus Canter, *Variae Lectiones*, II, 22, p. 584, thinks that *inodoribus* should be read as one word—that is, “with no odors” or “with bad odors”—just as Lucretius supposedly used *intactus* for *nullus tactus*, “no touch.” But I confess that I have searched in vain for the substantive *intactus* in Lucretius, and nothing should be changed, for we have observed above that the prepositions *in*, *ex*, and *sub* are very often pleonastic (*παρέλκειν*) in Arnobius. Moreover, in the preceding words Salmasius printed *suaveolentia* (“sweet-smelling”) in place of *redolentia* (“fragrant”). But nothing should be changed. For *redolere*, when used absolutely, nearly always signifies some mild and pleasant odor. Thus in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII, verse 675:

> And apples fragrant in broad baskets.

Others have attempted in vain to read “breathing fragrance” (*halantia*), others “smiling” (*ridentia*). ORELLI.

**Melo.** Thus the manuscript. Others read *inula* (“elecampane”). We now call it *enula*, perhaps from the Greek ἐλένιον (*helenion*). Elecampane (*inula*; German *Alant*) stimulates [Col. 0905D] the stomach and excites the appetite. It is of two kinds: some varieties are sour, others bitter. See Pliny, book XIX, chapter 5; Horace, *Satires* II.2:

> And prefers sour elecampane.

And in Satire VIII of the same book:

> . . . I was the first to show  
> That bitter elecampane should be cooked in.

PRIOR.

**Porrina.** Cato also used this feminine form in place of *porrum* (“leek”) in *On Agriculture*, chapter 47, just as *cepina* is used for *cepa* (“onion”) in Columella, XI, chapter 3, §36, Schneider’s edition. ORELLI.

**Ulpicum.** A larger kind of garlic, which the Greeks, as Columella reports (*On Agriculture*, book XI, chapter 3), call ἀφροσκόροδον (*aphroskorodon*); some call it Punic or Cyprian garlic, as Pliny teaches (*Natural History*, book XIX, chapter 6), while others call it *antiscorodon*. Plautus sang of it (*Poenulus*, Act V, Scene 5):

> [Col. 0906B] . . . Then, moreover, fuller  
> Of garlic and *ulpicum* than Roman oarsmen are.

See also Palladius, *On Agriculture*, book XII, chapter 6. NOURRY, p. 570.

**“Flavor, I mean, insofar as it is flavor, and the rest.”** Meursius and the Leiden edition corrected the text in this way: *ut est sapor*, namely, “as it exists in each individual thing,” which must be understood from what precedes. The manuscript has *id est sapor*, which makes no sense. For my part, however, I entirely agree with Heraldus, who suspects these words of being a gloss and reads, “flavor, I mean, and the rest.” Besides, at this point Arnobius reproduced a verse of Lucretius, book III, verse 268:

> There are odor, a certain heat, and flavor; yet from all  
> Of these is formed the body’s single, complete growth.

ORELLI.

**“They possess some odor or *olor*.”** This reading was approved by the most learned men: Meursius in his *Appendix*; Caspar Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXXVII, chapter 6, p. 1684; Colvius and Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book I, p. 57. Arnobius plainly contrasts odor with *olor*, just as he contrasts sweet things with bitter ones—that is, a good and pleasant odor with one that is bad and foul. *Olor*, namely, is a bad smell, a stench. Isidore’s Glosses: “*Olacitas* . . . foulness, *olor*.” Apuleius, at the passage cited: “But [Col. 0906D] he, struck by the *olor* of that otherwise most filthy liquid with which those Lamiae had drenched me, recoils violently.” Thus in Virgil, *Georgics* IV.49, several manuscripts have: “Or where the heavy *olor* of mud,” etc., in place of *odor*. The Leiden editor gave from the manuscript: “They possess some odor or color.” This could indeed be defended, so that the sense would be: “They possess some odor or color, either pleasant or disagreeable,” which must be understood from the words immediately following. This reading also agrees exceedingly well with the foregoing: “Was there some necessity that they should possess no flavors, odors, or colors other than those which the individual things possess?” Consequently, I am uncertain which reading should be preferred here. ORELLI.

## LIX

If whatever one might wish to know is readily available, and knowledge of things has been set openly before us, explain and tell us [Note: [Col. 0902B] “And proclaim it to us” (*et nobis edicite*) in the manuscript; correctly. MEURSIUS] by what methods and principles rains are produced. How is water held suspended in the upper regions and here in the midst of the air, although it is by nature fluid and always so prone to flowing and falling downward? Explain, I say, and tell us what causes hail to be hurled; what makes rain fall drop by drop; what disperses showers, feathery snows, and lightning flashes; whence wind arises and what it is; why alternations of seasons were established, when a single season could have been fixed and there could have been one unvarying condition of the sky, without the completeness of creation lacking anything.

What cause, what principle makes the seas salt, [Note: [Col. 0903A] “Alone” (*sola*) in the manuscript.] while some of these waters on land are fresh, others bitter or cold? From what kind of matter were the internal organs of human bodies compounded [Note: [Col. 0903A] *Concreata* in the manuscript; wrongly.] and stabilized? Whence were the bones made solid? What made the intestines, and what made the hollow, traversable veins? Since it would have been more advantageous to furnish us with numerous eyes against the danger of blindness, why have we been confined to the narrow resources of two?

[Col. 0904A] For what purpose were the virtually infinite and innumerable species of beasts and snakes formed or brought forth? What do owls, screech owls, and buzzards do in the world? What of the other winged creatures and birds? What of the kinds of ants and worms born to cause various kinds of corruption and destruction? What of fleas? What of shameless flies, spiders, shrews, mice, leeches, and crane flies? What of thorns and brambles, oats and darnel? What of the seeds of herbs or shrubs—some fragrant [Note: [Col. 0904A] Thus Sabaeus; others read “sweet-smelling” (*redolentia*).] [Col. 0905A] to the nostrils, others unpleasant in their odors?

Indeed, if you believe that anything can be known or comprehended, tell us what wheat is: spelt, barley, millet, chickpea, bean, lentil, little melon, cumin [Note: [Col. 0905B] Correct to: *melo, inula, cuminum*—“melon, elecampane, cumin.” The manuscript corruptly has: *melo, cuminum*.], leek, *ulpicum*, onion. For although they are useful to you and have been placed among the principal classes of foods, it is not therefore easy or readily possible to know what each one is. Why were they fashioned in such forms? Was there some necessity that individual things should possess no flavors, odors, or colors other than those which they possess, or could they have assumed others as well?

Then what are these very things themselves—I mean flavor insofar as it is flavor, and the remaining differences of qualities—and from what principles are they derived? “From the elements,” you say, “and from the primary origins of things.” Are the elements, then, bitter or sweet? Do they possess some odor or *olor*—that is, a pleasant scent or a stench—so that we may believe that, through their combination, qualities have been apportioned among generated things, qualities by which either delight is produced or offense is given to the senses?

> [Note: [Col. 0906D]
>
> **LX.—“Let their hearing burst and be torn apart.”** Cicero, *For His House, to the Pontiffs*: “Let that madman burst apart, if he will, and let him hear this from me.” ELMENHORST. Virgil, *Eclogue* VII.26:
>
> > So that Codrus’s entrails may burst with envy.
>
> ORELLI.—Hemsterhuis on Lucian, *Timon*, §40. OCHSNER.
>
> [Col. 0907B] **“Yet to fashion for oneself certain indefinable breaths of contemplation of him.”** Arnobius used *auras* (“breaths,” “breezes”) here for certain faint shadows or insubstantial images that one fashions for oneself. Thus Lactantius, *Institutes*, book III, chapter 17: “But if he—Lucretius—had been able to gather even the faintest breath of truth, he would never have said that the latter demolished his own house”; see Bünemann there. And Jerome, *Letter to Marcella* 141: “He had received a faint breath of Greek learning.” In the same sense appears αὔρα συνέσεως, “a breath of understanding,” in Epiphanius. Thus the ancients call every force [Col. 0907C] that passes from one person to another a “breath” or “inspiration,” as when, for example, through association with wise men we become wise, and through association with learned men, learned. See Isaac Casaubon on Persius, Satire I, verse 123, p. 157. But the expression “to fashion for oneself breaths of contemplation” is rather unusual here; and I do not know whether it might be more correctly read: “yet, through contemplation of him, to fashion for oneself certain indefinable breaths”—namely, of the memory of him. ORELLI.
>
> **“That he alone is indubitable.”** Meursius, believing the passage mutilated, suspects that one should read: “that he alone is indubitable—it is indubitable.” Wrongly: these words depend upon the preceding “Christ commanded,” etc. It then continues: “For, among all things,” etc.; that is, “Christ said,” which must be supplied by syllepsis, a very familiar figure. ORELLI.
>
> **“Fixed upon God, the head and knowledge of things.”** Either something has fallen out before the word “knowledge,” perhaps “in mind and knowledge,” or—as I prefer—we should read: “fixed upon God, the head and summit of things,” an expression familiar to Arnobius. See above on book I, chapter 8. ORELLI.]

## LX

Since, therefore, the origins, causes, and principles of so many and such great things escape even you yourselves, and since you cannot explain what was made, or why, [Col. 0906A] or why it ought not to have existed, you tear apart and mangle our modesty because we confess that we do not know what cannot be known. Nor do we care to seek out or investigate things which, it is perfectly clear, cannot be comprehended, although conjecture may stretch and strain itself through a thousand human hearts.

And therefore Christ—God, though you object; Christ is God, I say, for this must often be repeated so that the hearing of unbelievers may burst and be torn apart—speaking in human form by command of God the sovereign, knew that the nature of mortals is blind and incapable of comprehending any truth, even concerning things placed before their eyes; that it regards as discovered and known whatever it has persuaded itself to be so; and that it is utterly [Note: [Col. 0906B] The manuscript has “and not utterly” (*nec prorsus*).] entangled in conjectures, sowing and pressing contentious questions. He therefore commanded us to abandon [Col. 0906B] and disregard all such matters, and not to cast fruitless thoughts upon things set far beyond our knowledge.

Instead, as far as can be done, we are to advance toward the Lord of all things with our whole mind and spirit; to rise above these regions; to direct toward him the expectant turnings of the heart; and to keep perpetual remembrance of him. [Col. 0907A] Although he can be given form by no image, we are nevertheless to fashion for ourselves certain indefinable breaths of contemplation of him. For, among all the things encompassed by the darkness of his august divinity, he alone is indubitable, alone true, and one about whom no one could doubt unless he were insane and possessed by a mad despair. It is enough to know him even if you know nothing else; and thus you will have attained true and supreme knowledge, fixed upon God [Note: [Col. 0907B] “Upon God’s” (*in Dei*) in the manuscript; wrongly.], the head and knowledge of things.

> [Note: [Col. 0907D]
>
> **LXI.—“Whether the sun is larger than the world or measures one foot in breadth.”** See Cicero, *Academic Questions*, book II, chapter 26, and Davies there. *Metiatur* is passive. Thus Curtius, book V, chapter 1, at the end: “The infantrymen’s pay was fixed at two hundred [denarii]”; and Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 23: “The fields were measured clod by clod”; see Bauldri there, p. 169. ORELLI.
>
> **“Whether the moon shines with light of its own.”** Meursius restored *an* (“whether”) to Arnobius. Previously the text had *ac* (“and”). ORELLI.
>
> **“Whether anything has always existed.”** This must be read with Fulvius Ursinus and the Leiden edition. Heraldus should not be followed when he attempts to defend, with logical subtleties, the old and corrupt reading *supernatum*, which arose from *spernatum*, itself the result of misunderstanding a scribal abbreviation. ORELLI.
>
> **“Your own concern is placed in jeopardy—I mean the salvation of your souls.”** Thus the Leiden edition. Others read: “The salvation of your souls is placed in jeopardy.” Meursius, Fulvius Ursinus, and Stewechius delete the words “of your souls” [Col. 0908B] as a gloss. Perhaps Arnobius wrote: “Your own concerns are placed in jeopardy—the salvation of your souls.” ORELLI.]

## LXI

“What business is it of yours,” he says, “to investigate and inquire who made humanity, what the origin of souls may be, who devised the causes of evils, whether the sun is larger than the world or measures one foot in breadth, whether the moon shines by borrowed light or by light of its own?” There is no advantage in knowing these things and no loss whatsoever in not knowing them.

Leave these matters to God, and concede that he himself knows [Col. 0907B] what a thing is, why it is, or whence it comes; whether it ought to have existed or not; whether anything has always existed or has primordial beginnings; whether it ought to be abolished or preserved, [Col. 0908A] burned away and dissolved, or restored with its integrity renewed. Your circumstances do not permit you to entangle yourselves in such matters and concern yourselves uselessly [Note: [Col. 0907B] The manuscript has “things remote through uselessness” (*remota inutilitate*). I read: “to concern yourselves uselessly with remote [Col. 0908B] things. Your own concern,” etc. MEURSIUS.] with such distant things.

Your own concern is placed in jeopardy—I mean the salvation of your souls. Unless you attach yourselves to the knowledge of God the sovereign, a savage death awaits you when you have been released from bodily bonds: not bringing sudden extinction, but consuming you over a long course of time through the bitterness of tormenting punishment.

> [Note: [Col. 0908B]
>
> **LXII.—“An airy hope.”** That is, an empty and vain hope, as Meursius explains. Compare Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. ORELLI.
>
> **“What is said by certain petty scholars who are exceedingly presumptuous.”** Gelenius corrected the text thus, with the approval of the Leiden edition. The manuscript has “by certain schools” (*a scholis nonnullis*), that is, by certain philosophical sects, a reading defended by Heraldus; but I prefer “by petty scholars” (*a sciolis*). ORELLI.
>
> [Col. 0908C] **“If they have lived more strictly.”** Nazarius, *Panegyric of Constantine*, chapter 15: “Those celebrated ancient regulators of life, who lived strictly and contentedly by restraining their desires”—that is, sparingly and contentedly, as Pacatus says in the *Panegyric of Theodosius*, chapter 18. Lactantius, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 20: “Why, then, someone will ask, are sinners often happy, while those who live piously are often wretched? Because fugitives and disowned sons live freely, whereas those under the discipline of a father or master live more strictly and frugally.” See Bünemann there, p. 1004. ORELLI.
>
> **“And after the completion of one’s human function.”** Our author likes to use *functio* (“completion of a function”) for death. See above, chapters 27 and 57 of this book. Gesner rightly observes in the *Thesaurus* that the term is a euphemism (εὐφημία), indicating the necessity of dying and discharging that final duty. ORELLI.
>
> **“Ancestral” (*patritam*).** Thus the manuscript, correctly. For the ancients said *patritus*, “ancestral,” just as they said *avitus*, “inherited from one’s grandfather.” Varro, *Manius*: “Moved by a death in the family, we prayed according to ancestral custom, inherited from grandfather and father.” [Col. 0908D] The same author, *On the Commonwealth*, book XX: “Had he lived according to ancestral laws.” Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I, chapter 19: “That paternal and ancestral philosophy, as Theophrastus says.” MEURSIUS, in the *Appendix*. Others read *patriam* (“native”), as Davies also printed in the cited passage of Cicero. ORELLI.
>
> **“In the Acherontic books.”** Tages was believed to have written the Acherontic books concerning Acherontic rites and ceremonies. Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.399: “It should be known that, according to the books of haruspicy and the Acherontic rites said to have been composed by Tages, the fates can by a certain method be deferred for ten years; Vulcan now says that this could have been done,” etc. HERALDUS. Censorinus calls them the “Books of Fate” in *On the Birthday*, chapter 14; see Lindenbrog there, p. 66, Havercamp’s edition. The reference is evidently to books containing ceremonies for summoning the spirits of the dead from Acheron. Others think that “in the Aruntic books” should be read, doubtless understanding by these the books which Dionysius [Col. 0909C] of Halicarnassus, Gellius, Lactantius, and others report that a Tarquin bought from the Sibyl for a great price. But the buyer of those books is nowhere called Arruns Tarquinius: some call him Tarquinius Priscus, others Lucius Tarquinius Superbus. See Bünemann on Lactantius, *Institutes* I, chapter 6, p. 41. Nor can “Aruntic books” mean books concerned with averting evils and expiating unfavorable omens. For the contracted form of *Averruncus* is *Arruncus*, *Arrungus*, or *Arruncicus*, not *Arunticus*. Accordingly, *Acheronticis* alone is correct. ORELLI.
>
> **“That souls become divine.”** That is, immortal. See below [Col. 0909D] on chapter LXIV. ORELLI.
>
> **“Who can make them long-lived and provide a spirit of perpetuity.”** Salmasius printed and punctuated the manuscript reading in this way, entirely correctly. Editors vary at this point. Fulvius Ursinus and Gelenius read, “can make them of long-lived perpetuity, and provide a spirit,” with Stewechius’s approval. Canter and Heraldus, in his *Second Thoughts*, read, “can make them of long-lived perpetuity,” etc. But “of perpetuity” must be joined to the following “spirit,” and I do not see what “provide a spirit,” said absolutely, could mean. ORELLI.
>
> **“Let the wise deny themselves everything human.”** Fulvius Ursinus prefers “claim for themselves” (*arrogent*), wrongly. This refers to the fasts and abstinences by which the ancient magicians believed that they could secure for themselves the appearance and assistance of the gods. ORELLI.
>
> **“Unless this has been granted to souls.”** Arnobius regularly uses *animi* for *animae*, “souls”; it is enough to have noted this once. See Bünemann on Lactantius, *Institutes* VII, chapter 2, p. 860. ORELLI.
>
> **“When one begins to approach awareness of destruction.”** Thus Gelenius, acutely. The manuscript has *cum absens cum*, etc., which makes no sense. MEURSIUS, in the *Appendix*.]

## LXII

Nor should that thought creep in or flatter you with an airy hope which is advanced by certain petty scholars [Note: [Col. 0908B] The manuscript has *ab sciolis*.] who are exceedingly presumptuous: that they are God’s offspring and not subject to the laws of fate; that, if they live more strictly, his court lies open to them, and after the completion of their human function they will, with no one barring them, be carried back as though to their ancestral home.

Nor should you trust what the Magi promise: that they possess commendatory prayers by which certain indefinable powers, once softened, provide easy paths for those striving to fly upward to heaven. Nor should you trust what Etruria promises in the Acherontic books: that, when the blood of particular animals is given to particular divine powers, souls become divine and are withdrawn from the laws of mortality.

These allurements are empty and merely foster vain wishes. No one except almighty God can preserve souls. Nor is there anyone besides him who can make them long-lived and provide a spirit of perpetuity, except the one who alone is immortal and everlasting, bounded by no limitation of time. For since all the gods—either whatever true gods there may be or those said by rumor and opinion to exist—are immortal and everlasting by his will and through the gift of his favor, how is it possible for them to bestow upon others what they themselves are, when they possess it as something belonging to another [Note: [Col. 0909C] Thus the manuscript; alternatively, “when others possess it.”], loaned by a greater power?

Let Etruria slaughter victims as numerous as it pleases; let the wise deny themselves everything human; let the Magi soften and mollify [Col. 0909B] all powers. Unless the Lord of all things has granted to souls what reason requires, and has granted it through his command, they will afterward deeply regret having been objects of mockery [Note: [Col. 0909C] The manuscript has *me risui*. I read *derisui*, “objects of mockery.” MEURSIUS.], when they begin to approach awareness [Note: [Col. 0909C] Thus Gelenius. The manuscript has *absens cum*.] of their destruction.

> [Note: [Col. 0910C]
>
> **LXIII.—“Indeed, who was the maker of man himself?”** The manuscript has *Quinimmo potiuse*. “Binding” in the preceding sentence is owed to Meursius. Others read “joining.” ORELLI.
>
> **“Put aside these concerns.”** The Leiden edition, following the manuscript, has “set forth these concerns” (*exponite*). ORELLI.
>
> **“If self-exaltation were absent from you, you could long ago have learned it from him as your teacher.”** Meursius and Fulvius Ursinus think [Col. 0910D] that *potuissetis* should be read. But Cortius, on Sallust, *Jugurtha*, chapter 85, §48, and *Fragments of the Histories*, book III, p. 967, teaches that Latin authors speak in this way in order to make the statement more definite. Thus Livy, book II, chapter 10: “The pile bridge nearly gave the enemy a passage, had there not been one man, Horatius Cocles.” Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.112:
>
> > Nor would I have come, had events not afforded a place and dwelling.
>
> And, appositely to our passage, Curtius, book IV, chapter 12: “But if Mazacus had fallen upon them while they were panic-stricken, a great disaster could have been suffered.” ORELLI.]

## LXIII

“But,” they say, “if Christ was sent by God for this purpose, to deliver unhappy souls from the ruin of destruction, what had the former ages done to deserve their fate—those consumed under the condition of mortality before his coming?”

Can you know what was done with the souls of the ancient and most remote mortals? Can you know whether aid was given to them as well by some means, whether provision and care were made for them? Can you, I say, know what could have been learned through Christ’s teaching: whether the ages since the human race began to exist on earth are infinite or finite; when souls were first bound to bodies; who was the author of that binding—indeed, who was the maker of man himself; where the souls of those who came before departed; in what parts or regions [Col. 0910A] of the world they existed; whether they were corruptible or, on the contrary, incorruptible; whether they could have incurred the danger of dying if Christ the preserver had not come to meet them at the necessary time?

Put aside these concerns, and leave questions unknown to you alone. Royal compassion was bestowed upon them as well; divine benefits ran equally through all; they were preserved and delivered, and laid aside the lot and condition of mortality.

By what means? Which of them? When? If arrogance, conceit, and self-exaltation were absent from you, you could long ago have learned it from him as your teacher.

> [Note: [Col. 0910D]
>
> **LXIV.—“The fountain of life,” he says, “lies open to all,” etc.** Arnobius appears to be referring to Christ’s words in John 6:35 and 37: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς. Ὁ ἐρχόμενος πρὸς μὲ οὐ μὴ πεινάσῃ· καὶ ὁ πιστεύων εἰς ἐμὲ οὐ μὴ διψήσῃ πώποτε . . . Πᾶν ὃ δίδωσί μοι ὁ Πατήρ, πρὸς ἐμὲ ἥξει· καὶ τὸν ἐρχόμενον πρὸς μὲ οὐ μὴ ἐκβαλῶ ἔξω—“I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me shall certainly not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall certainly never thirst. . . . Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I shall certainly not cast out.” ORELLI.
>
> **“For no one’s choice of his lot in life,” says Plato, “is God responsible.”** Plato, *Republic*, book X, p. 617, H. Stephanus’s edition; Bipont edition, vol. VII, p. 330: Ἀρετὴ δὲ ἀδέσποτον, ἣν τιμῶν καὶ ἀτιμάζων, πλέον καὶ ἔλαττον αὐτῆς ἕκαστος ἕξει· αἰτία ἑλομένου· θεὸς ἀναίτιος—“Virtue has no master; according as each person honors or dishonors her, he will possess more or less of her. The responsibility belongs to the chooser; God is blameless.” The same author, *Republic* [Col. 0911C] II, p. 379; Theodoret, *On Providence*, Discourse VI, *Against the Greeks*, p. 95; Tertullian, *Exhortation to Chastity*, chapter 2; Justin Martyr, *Second Apology for the Christians*, p. 36. ELMENHORST.
>
> **“You will have deprived yourself of the advantage of the gift.”** Thus the Leiden edition, following Fulvius Ursinus’s correction. The manuscript has, “you will have proved the advantage of the gift for yourself,” which Heraldus attempts to defend in his edition, explaining: “See whether accepting that gift is advantageous for you or not.” But in his *Second Thoughts* he withdrew his own opinion and approved Ursinus’s emendation. ORELLI.
>
> **“Whether he makes us gods.”** Gelenius corrected the text thus in place of the earlier reading, “whether God makes us.” Correctly. By “gods,” therefore, Arnobius means immortals. The pagans called the dead gods. Marcus Tullius Cicero, *On the Laws* II: “Let the rights of the divine dead be sacred. Let them regard those given over to death as gods.” See Pliny, *Natural History*, book VII, chapter 55: hence the *Di Manes*, “divine dead,” and δαίμονες (“spirits”) throughout funerary inscriptions. From this Prudentius proves that the dead were regarded as gods by the nations, in the first book *Against Symmachus*:
>
> > See—why do you deny that the divine dead are regarded as gods?  
> > The monuments of our fathers themselves prove it: “To those divine spirits”  
> > I read upon the carved marbles wherever Latin antiquity  
> > Guards the ashes, and along the Salarian Way crowded with tombs.
>
> The *Di Manes*, therefore, are also the δαίμονες, “spirits,” of a single dead person. Livy, book III: “When peace had been secured, the tribunes then pressed the senators to fulfill the pledge of Publius Valerius; they pressed Claudius to free the divine spirit of his colleague from breach of faith and to permit the law to be put forward.” He calls the divine spirit of his colleague τοὺς τοῦ συνάρχοντος δαίμονας, “the spirits of his fellow magistrate.” HERALDUS.]

## LXIV

“But,” you say, “if Christ came as the preserver of the human race, why does he not deliver absolutely everyone with equal generosity?”

Does he not deliver equally when he calls everyone equally? Does he repel or reject [Col. 0910B] anyone from the sovereign’s favor when he uniformly gives to the high and lowly, slaves, women, and children the power to come to him?

“The fountain of life,” he says, “lies open to all, and no one is forbidden or driven from the right to drink.” If your disgust is so great that you reject the benefit of the proffered gift—indeed, if you are so mighty in wisdom that you call the things offered by Christ a joke and foolishness—how does the one who invites you sin against you [Note: [Col. 0910C] The manuscript corruptly has “awaits” (*exspectat*).], when his sole role is to place the fruit of his kindness at your disposal, under the free decision of your own right?

“For no one’s choice of his lot in life,” says Plato, “is God responsible”; nor can another’s will rightly be imputed to anyone, since freedom of will has been placed in the power of the person who exercised that will. Or must you perhaps be begged to deign to accept the benefit of salvation [Col. 0910C] from God? Although you spurn it and flee far away, must the grace of divine benevolence be poured into your lap?

Do you wish to take what is offered and turn it to your own use? You will have looked after your own interests. [Col. 0911A] Do you spurn, scorn, and despise it? You will have deprived yourself of the advantage of the gift. God imposes necessity upon no one and terrifies no one with imperious fear. For our salvation is not necessary to him, as though he would thereby experience some gain or loss, whether he makes us gods or permits us to be reduced to nothing through corruption and dissolution.

> [Note: [Col. 0911D]
>
