> **LXV.—“I do not wish it,” he says, “and I do not have the will.”** This must be read with Fulvius Ursinus and the Leiden edition. “I do not wish it,” he says—that is, “to do it”—“nor do I have the will,” namely, to accept the good things, which must be understood from what precedes. Some defend the old reading, “I wish it, he says, and I do not have the will,” as follows: “I am in conflict with myself; now I wish it, now I do not.” But those words cannot signify this. Perhaps [Col. 0912C] it might more suitably be read: “I do not wish it,” he says, “and I have no desire for the will” (*voluntatem non aveo*). *Aveo* and *habeo* are very often interchanged in the manuscript. ORELLI.
>
> **“But rename them in contrary terms.”** “In contrary terms” (*in alia verba*) means in opposite terms, namely, by disparaging and accusing God’s gifts. Thus the expression “to go over entirely to the other side” (*in alia omnia abire*), which is familiar even to beginners. ORELLI.
>
> **“Rights and powers.”** See above on book I, chapter 46. ORELLI.
>
> **“It is Christ’s sole pontifical office.”** We owe this entirely correct emendation, recovered from the manuscript, to Ludovicus Carrio, *Emendations*, book I, chapter 9—in Gruter’s *Critical Thesaurus*, vol. III, p. 108. Previously the text read: “It belongs to Christ, the sole pontiff,” etc. Arnobius therefore uses *pontificium* for a right, power, and office, in a sense very familiar among these authors. Thus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book I, chapter 13: “By the one whose business and official charge [Col. 0912D] it was.” Symmachus, book III, Letter 17: “Though increased by the official charge of a renewed honor, you gave me no indication of our common joy.” Arnobius the Younger on Psalm 58: “These receive the official charge of judging”; and on Psalm 113: “He will give the official charge of ruling to the priests of the temples.” STEWECHIUS and HERALDUS.—Compare Meursius in the *Appendix* and Juretus on Symmachus, book VII, Letter 27, p. 195, Lectius’s edition, where he discusses this word at length. ORELLI.
>
> **“Through him alone is there an entrance to the light.”** Meursius prefers “through this,” namely, through this gate. But nothing should be changed. “Through him,” namely, through Christ. Arnobius is evidently referring to the Savior’s words in John 10:7: Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα τῶν προβάτων—“I am the gate of the sheep.” But if we read “through him,” then in what follows *alias*, “by other ways,” rather than *alia*, “by another,” will have to be written. ORELLI.
>
> **“Nor has it been granted to creep or force one’s way in by another.”** I have printed this on the basis of Franciscus Oudendorp’s entirely correct emendation on Frontinus, *Stratagems*, book II, chapter 5, p. 271 of the new edition. “By another,” namely, by another way or gate. All editions have “nor has it been granted to creep or force one’s way in by other ways.” ORELLI.]

## LXV

“Indeed,” he says, “if God is powerful, merciful, and a preserver, let him turn our minds and make us believe his promises against our will.”

That would be force, then, not grace; not the sovereign God’s generosity, but a childish and empty contest arising from eagerness to prevail. For what is so unjust as to wrench the wills of resistant and unwilling people toward the opposite course, to force upon their minds what they do not want and what they reject—to harm them before benefiting them, and, after removing their former disposition, to transfer them into an alien habit and conviction?

You who desire to be changed and to suffer force, so that under compulsion you may do and seize upon what you do not wish—why do you refuse willingly to accept what you desire to do once you have been turned and altered?

“I do not wish it,” he says, “and I do not have the will.”

Why, then, do you accuse God as though he were failing you? You want him to bring you aid, although you not only spurn and flee from his gifts and favors, but rename them in contrary [Note: [Col. 0911B] Fulvius reads “empty” (*inania*).] terms and pursue them with mocking jests.

“Then, unless I become a Christian, [Col. 0912A] I shall be unable to possess any hope of salvation?”

It is as you yourself state. For he alone has received from God the Father the assigned and entrusted role of giving salvation and of conferring upon souls what it is fitting and necessary for them to receive, the more remote and inward causes being as they are. For just as particular gods among you have particular guardianships, rights, and powers, and you do not ask any of them for something that does not belong to his power and authority, so it is Christ’s sole pontifical office to give salvation to souls and to confer upon them the spirit of perpetuity.

For if you believe that Father Liber can grant a vintage but cannot grant medicine; that Ceres can grant crops, Aesculapius health, Neptune one thing, and Juno, Fortune, Mercury, and Vulcan another; and that each is the giver of certain particular things, then [Col. 0912B] you must also accept this from us: souls can receive the force of life and preservation from no one except him whom the supreme king has appointed to this gift and office.

The almighty sovereign willed this to be the way of salvation, this, so to speak, the gate of life. Through him alone is there an entrance to the light; nor has it been granted to creep or force one’s way in by another, since all the rest are closed and fortified with an impregnable stronghold.

> [Col. 0913A] [Note: [Col. 0913B]
>
> **LXVI.—“Lest they close the roads against him as he returns to heaven.”** *Ne*, “lest,” which is absent from the manuscript and earlier editions, was restored by Heraldus because the sense demands it. Thomas Canter restored from the manuscript the archaic verb *cludant* in place of *claudant*, which had been printed. Thus below, book VII: “Not even if you burn a thousand measures of male frankincense and this whole sky is closed by the cloudy mass of billowing vapors”; and Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chapter 11: “He hastened, I suppose, and once and for all closed heaven”; see Havercamp’s edition, p. 122. Meursius collected further examples. ORELLI.
>
> [Col. 0913C] **“Lest they close the roads.”** This must be read from the Roman edition with *cludant*, not *claudant*, which Gelenius introduced by interpolation. For the ancients said *cludere* instead of *claudere*, “to close.” See Meursius on this passage, and especially Johannes Rhodius, who cites a cloud of examples in his *Scribonian Lexicon*. Thus Arnobius himself below, book VII: “Not even if you burn a thousand measures of male frankincense and this whole sky is enclosed by the cloudy mass of billowing vapors.” ORELLI.
>
> **“Nor that you could abandon your ancient ancestral religion and be transferred to barbarous and foreign rites.”** The nations most obstinately maintained and defended the religion handed down to them by their ancestors. No arguments could bring them to abandon their long-established ancestral religion and embrace new forms of worship. Cotta, in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II: “No speech by anyone, learned or unlearned, will ever move me from the belief concerning the worship of the immortal gods which I received from my ancestors.” Pseudo-Clement, *Recognitions*, book V: “It is impious if we do not worship what has been handed down to us by our fathers and if we betray the religion [Col. 0913D] given by our ancestors.” See Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animal Food* (περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψύχων), book II; Lactantius, book II, chapter 6, and book V, chapter 19; Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chapter 6; Isocrates, *Address to Nicocles, On Kingship* (περὶ βασιλείας); Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book I, chapter 1; and our notes on Minucius. ELMENHORST.
>
> **“That, when grain had been discovered, they scorned acorns and rejected arbutus berries.”** Arnobius takes this from Lucretius. For Lucretius writes as follows in book V, verses 937 ff., where he describes the manner of life of the earliest human beings:
>
> > Among acorn-bearing oaks they generally tended their bodies,  
> > And the arbutus berries which you now see in wintertime  
> > Ripen to a scarlet color, the earth then bore  
> > In far greater numbers and of greater size.
>
> HERALDUS.
>
> “To eat acorns after grain has been discovered” appears to be a proverb in Cicero, *Orator*, chapter 9. OCHSNER.
>
> **“That they ceased to be covered with bark and clothed in skins after woven clothing had been devised.”** For they related that the first coverings of the earliest human beings were made of bark, [Col. 0914B] the next of skins, and that woven clothing succeeded these. Lucretius V.951 ff.:
>
> > Not yet did they know how to handle things with fire, or how  
> > To clothe the body in the skins and spoils of wild beasts;  
> > But they inhabited groves and hollow mountains and forests,  
> > And hid their filthy limbs among bushes, compelled  
> > To escape the lashes of winds and the rains.
>
> HERALDUS.
>
> **“Habitations” (*successibus*).** That is, houses or dwellings. See above on book I, chapter 50, and Meursius, *Critica*, p. 80. ORELLI.
>
> [Col. 0914C] **“Nor preferred to remain beneath rocks and in caves like beasts.”** Juvenal, Satire VI.2 ff.:
>
> > . . . when the cold cave  
> > Furnished a little home and enclosed fire, hearth,  
> > Flock, and masters beneath a common shadow.
>
> ELMENHORST.
>
> **“Was established” (*constiterit*).** Thus Fulvius Ursinus. Others read “they established” (*constituerint*). ORELLI.]

## LXVI

Therefore, although you may be pure and cleansed from every contamination of vice, and although you may have won over and bent those powers so that they do not close the roads and obstruct the passage against you as you return to heaven, you will be unable by any exertions to attain the reward of immortality unless, through Christ’s bestowal, you receive that which produces immortality itself and are admitted to true life.

For the objection you customarily make against us—that our religion is new and was born almost only a few days ago, and that you could not abandon your ancient ancestral religion and be transferred to barbarous and foreign rites—is urged without any rational basis.

For what if we wished, in this same way, to cast blame upon those former and most ancient ages because, when grain had been discovered, they scorned acorns and rejected arbutus berries [Note: [Col. 0913B] The manuscript wrongly has *arbusta*, “shrubs.”]? Or because they ceased to be covered with bark and clothed in skins after woven clothing, more convenient in use and practicality, had been devised? [Col. 0913B] Or because, after houses had been built [Col. 0914A] and more elegant habitations established, they did not cherish their ancient huts or prefer to remain beneath rocks and in caves like beasts?

It is common to everyone, and a disposition handed down almost from the cradle itself, to prefer good things to bad, to place useful things before useless ones, and more gladly to pursue and seek what has been established as more valuable—and to fix upon it the hope of salvation and of benefits conducive to salvation.

### LXVII.—You who, by condemning the practices of your forefathers, have passed over to other customs and other rites.

Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, book II, verse 303 ff.:

> Ancient Rome does not remain consistent with herself, transformed through the ages  
> And altered in rites, attire, laws, and arms.  
> She worships many things which she did not worship under King Quirinus.  
> Some practices she established for the better; others she abandoned.  
> Nor did she cease to vary her custom, and the laws  
> Which she had formerly enacted she reversed into their contraries.  
> Why, Roman senator, do you cast customary rites in my teeth,  
> When the frequently changing judgment of an unstable decision  
> Has altered the decrees of the Fathers and the people?  
> [Col. 0914D] Even now, how often is it advantageous to depart from established practices  
> And to condemn former habits by adopting a recent observance?

HELMENH.

**Do you still keep the people divided into five classes?** Why Arnobius numbers only five classes, although it is clear from Livy, book I, and Aulus Gellius, book X, chapter 28, that there were six, is explained by the fact that the sixth or lowest class, into which the poorest citizens—the *proletarii* and those counted merely by head—were thrust, was regarded as no class at all. Hence Livy, book I, and Charisius mention only five classes, as Meursius correctly observes in *Criticus*, book II, chapter 16, p. 81, against Justus Lipsius, who wished to emend the text to “six classes.”

Moreover, Heinrich Valesius admirably elucidated this passage in his note on Ammianus Marcellinus, *History*, book XIV, p. 11, on the words: “And although the tribes are now inactive and the centuries at peace”; his entire comment may be transcribed here:

> Marcellinus calls the centuries inactive because at that time there were, of course, no tribes and no centuries. The centuries had indeed ceased to exist long before the age of Marcellinus, as Arnobius bears witness in our passage. [Col. 0915A] The tribes likewise gradually collapsed under the rule of the Caesars. At last, in my opinion, they disappeared entirely shortly after the time of Antoninus Caracalla, when he had granted citizenship to everyone dwelling within the Roman world. Certainly after the period I have mentioned, references to the tribes become rare or virtually nonexistent in ancient inscriptions, whereas previously we see a man’s tribe commonly appended before his cognomen. Nor am I troubled by the fact that the emperor Julian, in his third Oration to the empress Eusebia, mentions at Rome *τῶν φυλῶν ἐπιστάτας*, “superintendents of the tribes.” For he means not prefects of tribes but curators of the city’s regions, as I have also very often found Libanius speaking.

Thus Valesius. ORELL.

**Do you appoint magistrates through the people?** See J. Lipsius, *On the Magistracies of the Ancient Romans*, [Col. 0915B] chapter 3. ELMENH.

**Do you know what the military, urban, and common assemblies are?** Turnebus explains this passage excellently in *Adversaria*, book XIII, chapter 14, vol. II, p. 11, and Gesner follows him in the *Thesaurus*, under the word *comitium*. Even beginners know that there were three kinds of assemblies among the Romans: the centuriate, curiate, and tribal assemblies. Looking, therefore, to this diversity of assemblies, Arnobius calls the centuriate assemblies “military,” because the people were organized by centuries in military fashion; the curiate assemblies “urban,” because the curiae belonged to the urban populace; and the tribal assemblies “common,” because they were formed from the tribes of the entire people and belonged not only to the urban population but also to the rural and suburban population. Elmenhorst is therefore mistaken in interpreting “common assemblies” from Livy, book IV, as the joint assemblies of the Fathers and the plebs. Livy’s passage has nothing to do with ours. ORELL.

**Do you observe the heavens, or render official proceedings idle through adverse announcements?** *Servare* means to report something on the basis of an observation of the heavens. [Col. 0915C] What *obnuntiare* means, however, you may learn from these words of Donatus on Terence (*The Brothers*, act IV, scene 4): “One who announces bad news *obnuntiat*; one who announces good news *annuntiat*.” For augurs who had seen something of evil and grim omen were properly said to *obnuntiare*. Thus *obnuntio* means “I report an impending evil,” as though “I report an omen.” From this comes the *ἐτυμολογία* (“etymology”) of the word. Cicero uses both words, and the first more frequently, especially when he writes to Atticus (book IV, letter 3) as follows:

> He gave notice that on every assembly day he would observe the heavens.

Yet the substance of the matter is this:

> Unless Gaius Appius had made an adverse announcement against Milo, the assembly would have taken place.

And in book II of *On Divination*, chapter 35:

> As for observing the heavens, surely you do not think that those who took the auspices used to do so in person? Now they give orders to the keeper of the sacred chickens, and he reports back.

Even before our Arnobius, Lucan complained in the following verses that this earlier custom had been utterly neglected or had already become obsolete, *Pharsalia*, book VI, verse 426 ff.:

> I have no wish to ask what nurturing Dodona may declare concerning the first crops  
> [Col. 0915D] From the mouth of Jupiter; who can discern the fates in entrails,  
> Who disclose them through birds, who observe the lightning of heaven,  
> And who scrutinize the stars with Assyrian care?

NOURR., p. 312.

**When you prepare for war, do you display the signal from the citadel? Or do you administer fetial law? Do you demand the return of stolen property through *clarigatio*?** Arnobius here mentions three practices connected with declaring war.

1. The signal or standard displayed from the citadel, concerning which Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 16, says:

   > I would not distinguish days preliminary to battle from lawful days. For lawful days are the continuous thirty days during which, once the army has been levied, a russet-colored standard is set up on the citadel—that is, on the Capitol. Days preliminary to battle, however, are all those on which it is lawful to demand restitution and challenge an enemy.

   Compare Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, verse 2; Stewechius on Vegetius, *On Military Matters* I, chapter 6; and especially J. Lipsius, *On the Roman Army* I, dialogue III, *Works*, vol. III, p. 26 ff., Wesel edition.

2. Fetial law, because the fetials declared war in the name of the Roman people, as we learn from Livy I, chapter 32; [Col. 0916A] Gellius XVI, chapter 4; and others. On the fetials there is a special dissertation by Johannes Jensius in *Ferculum litterarium*, Leiden, 1717, octavo.

3. He names the *clarigatio*, concerning which Servius writes on *Aeneid* IX, verse 53 ff.:

   > When they wished to declare war, the *Pater Patratus*, that is, the chief of the fetials, went to the enemy’s borders and, after reciting certain solemn formulas, declared in a loud voice that he was announcing war for specified reasons: either because they had injured allies, or because they would return neither stolen animals nor persons liable to surrender. This was called *clarigatio* from the loudness (*claritas*) of the voice. After the *clarigatio*, a spear cast into their territory signaled the beginning of combat.

Yet the same Servius, on *Aeneid* X, verse 14, derives *clarigatio* [Col. 0916B] *ἀπὸ τῆς κλήρου*, “from the lot,” since they invaded the enemy’s lands by the lot of war. Brissonius gives further information on the *clarigatio* and the fetials in *On Formulas*, book III, p. 383. HERALD., ELMENH., and NOURRIUS. Compare Abramus on Cicero, *Speech for Publius Sestius*, chapter 26. ORELL.

**Do you assume the hope?** Similarly Virgil, *Aeneid* X, verse 18:

> Prepare your weapons in your hearts, and anticipate the war in hope.

Others—for example, the Leiden edition—read: “Do you take up the hope of battle?” In the preceding text Stewechius prefers *subeuntes* (“entering upon”) to *obeuntes* (“undertaking”). ORELL.

**Do you take auspices from points?** What “auspices from points” were is uncertain. Gesner, in the *Thesaurus*, approves Cerda’s opinion on Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 199, that the points of beaks are meant, which were observed in the “full dance” of the sacred chickens. Others think that the points were mountain summits, which it was customary to climb in order to obtain auguries. Yet both opinions [Col. 0916C] appear to conflict with Cicero’s words in *On Divination* II, 36, where he asserts that auspices from points were entirely military. See the distinguished Hottinger there, p. 252.

Others suspect that what is meant is the points of darts, swords, and javelins shining more or less brightly than usual. Nourrius appropriately cites concerning these a passage of Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* V, p. 312, Sylburg:

> “From the javelins planted beside the tents—for these are Roman missiles which they take into their hands when they join battle and cast—… from the tips of the small iron heads of these javelins flames began to kindle, and throughout the whole camp there was a radiance as though from torches, which occupied much of the night. From this apparition they understood—as the interpreters of portents declared, and as it was not difficult for anyone to infer—that the divine power signified for them a swift and brilliant victory, since everything yields to fire and there is nothing that is not destroyed by fire.”

Nourrius himself ultimately inclines to the opinion of those who understand the points of military standards, which, mounted on longer poles, [Col. 0916D] ended in iron tips. If, when camp was struck, the standard-bearer could easily pull these from hostile ground, this gave a favorable omen and promised certain victory; but if he had difficulty drawing them out, this foreshadowed an adverse outcome and impending disaster.

Moreover, *auspicare* is an archaic form for *auspicari*, “to take the auspices.” See Nonius, *On Contrary Genders of Verbs*, p. 468, Mercer edition, citing many examples; likewise Festus under *prohibere*, and Stewechius on this passage. Thus Naevius, *The Punic War* IV:

> When the man arrives as praetor, he takes a favorable auspice.

Plautus, *The Rope* III.4.12:

> Today I did not take the auspices for that business, so as to converse with a gallows-bird.

ORELL.

**In undertaking offices, do you observe the age laws?** The *annariae* or *annales leges* prescribed the age at which each person was permitted to seek a magistracy. If someone was elected at the prescribed age—for example, as consul—he was said to have become consul “in his proper year.” Ambition produced these laws, so that there would be successive stages in seeking office. Villius, tribune of the plebs, first enacted a more precise law, when Aulus Postumius Albinus and [Col. 0917A] Quintus Fulvius Flaccus—or, according to others, Gaius Calpurnius Piso—were consuls, in the year 571 from the founding of the city. It was therefore called the *Lex Annalis*, and that name adhered to the family. Livy, *History* XL, chapter 44.

This law established the ages of thirty-one for the quaestorship, thirty-seven for the aedileship, forty for the praetorship, and forty-three for the consulship. Cicero, *On the Orator* II, 65, states that Marcus Pinarius Rusca, tribune of the plebs, enacted another law, but nothing from it survives and its date is not sufficiently certain.

Arnobius in this passage testifies that those laws had been abolished. For under the emperors we find men younger than twenty made consuls. Indeed, we see even the boys Gratian, Valentinian, and Honorius designated consuls. See Antonius Augustinus, *On Laws and Decrees of the Senate*, title *Villia Annalis*, p. 152 ff.; Manutius, *On Laws*, chapter VI; and J. A. Ernesti, *Key to Cicero*, Index of Laws, [Col. 0917B] title *ANNALES*. ORELL.

**In gifts and presents, do you observe the Cincian laws?** The Cincian law was proposed by Marcus Cincius Alimentus, tribune of the plebs, in the year 549 from the founding of the city, when Cornelius and Sempronius were consuls, and was advocated by Quintus Maximus. Cicero, *On Old Age*, chapter 4. It concerned gifts and presents, “lest anyone receive them for pleading a case,” in the words of Tacitus, *Annals* XI, 5; hence Plautus called it the *Muneralis*, “Law of Presents.” Augustus revived it when it was disappearing through age and confirmed it by a new decree of the Senate. Claudius limited the amount to ten thousand sesterces. Ulpian writes in book VIII, *On All Tribunals*, that a hundred gold coins were permitted. Although all these provisions were sometimes in force, they were annulled by custom. See Antonius Augustinus, *On Laws*, p. 47; Lipsius on Tacitus, book I; Ernesti, *Key to Cicero*. ORELL.

**In restraining expenditure, do you observe the censorial laws?** The censorial laws, also called sumptuary and dietary laws, checked excessive expenditure on dinners and banquets. See Aulus Gellius II, [Col. 0917C] chapter 24—the classic passage on them; Pliny, *Natural History* VIII, chapter 15; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* II, chapter 13. Many laws belonged to this class, for example the Fannian, Licinian, Cornelian—which Sulla enacted—Aemilian, and Antian laws; likewise the edict of Capito Ateius; and finally the Julian law, introduced by the emperor Augustus. See Stewechius on this passage and, for each particular law, the cited book of Antonius Augustinus. ORELL.

**Do you keep perpetual hearth-fires burning in the inner chambers and *colignae*?** Some printed editions read “in the inner chambers of Vesta.” In the Leiden edition the conjunction “and” is removed. But no one has told us on what authority these things were done. Lipsius (*Treatise on Vesta and the Vestals*, chapter 10), having been alerted by Rosweyd, observes that one manuscript reads: “in almost in-inner-chambers and *colignae*.” Certainly the royal manuscript simply has: “in-inner-chambers and *colignae*.” It is therefore no wonder that this corrupt passage has caused learned men no little torment.

Lipsius thinks it can be explained in two ways. First, Arnobius’s words should not be referred to Vesta, but to a certain private rite [Col. 0917D] by which fire was anciently preserved and tended in the interior part of houses and in the kitchen. To confirm this conjecture, he adduces these words of Varro: “It is called *culina* because there they tended (*colebant*) the fire.”

Second, he says that the words might still be understood of the public Vesta, and that one should write *in culignis*, so that Arnobius’s meaning would be: “Fire was formerly kept in *culignae* and earthenware vessels, just as even now it is commonly preserved beneath ashes.” But the first explanation is opposed by the fact that Varro is speaking of the ordinary and common use of fire, whereas Arnobius is speaking of a sacred fire, or at least of one whose use the pagans had abolished. Against the second stands the fact that, as Lipsius himself acknowledges, the noun *culigna* in Varro, Festus, and Livy rather means a drinking vessel in which wine was offered during sacrifices. Besides, why would Vesta be mentioned there, when there is no trace of her in Arnobius’s text?

The entire difficulty of this obscure Arnobian saying lies chiefly in the single word *coliginis*. We learn that there were “inner-chamber hearths” [Col. 0918A] from Catullus’s verses (*Epigram to Marcellus*) concerning Troy:

> Toward which you hasten, it is said that the Greek youth  
> From every side abandoned their inner-chamber hearths.

Servius too, on *Aeneid* VI, verse 71, observes that Virgil calls the secret parts of temples *penetralia*, in the following verse:

> Great inner sanctuaries also await you in our kingdoms.

Who would not readily believe that perpetual hearth-fires existed within them?

It remains only to determine what, if anything, should be restored in place of *coliginis*. But, you will say, why not read *in culinis*, “in kitchens”? Vossius, following Scaliger, shows [Col. 0918B] from an ancient inscription that there were kitchens in shrines of Hercules where those about to travel abroad sacrificed. The conjecture might be sound, if you could prove that perpetual fires were once preserved there.

Might one not nevertheless add in support of this conjecture that pagans regarded the hearths of the *genii* as gods, and that for their worship and honor fire was once preserved in kitchens and hearths, as the cited Varro noted, but that later generations neglected this custom when it became more troublesome and burdensome to them?

There are also some—for example Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, pp. 370, 587, and 914—who wish to retain the word *coliginis*, which they believe was derived from the verb *colo*, “I inhabit.” They accordingly thought that *coligo* in our author means the same as “house,” “dwelling,” or “habitation.” But the conjunction “and” would have to be removed from Arnobius’s text, and it would be necessary to prove by at least one example who used the noun *coligo* in that sense. Consider, therefore, [Col. 0918C] whether the word *culinis*, “kitchens,” appears better suited to Arnobius’s purpose. For without the assistance of a more accurate manuscript, we do not venture to establish anything certain on the matter. NOURR., p. 315 ff.

**Do you keep perpetual hearth-fires burning in the inner chambers of the dwelling (*coliginis*)?** This passage has greatly tormented learned men. The royal codex has: “In-inner-chambers and *colignae* do you keep perpetual hearth-fires burning?” The Limpurg manuscript cited by Rosweyd in Burmann’s *Collection of Letters*, vol. II, p. 141—apparently a copy of the royal codex—has: “in almost in-inner-chambers and *colignae*, etc.” All these readings are manifestly corrupt.

Gelenius published: “In the inner chambers of Vesta’s fire do you keep perpetual hearth-fires burning?” The other editors followed him, except Salmasius in the Leiden edition, Nourrius, and Gallandius, though Fulvius Ursinus thinks that the word *ignis*, “fire,” should be deleted. But if we read thus, as Lipsius correctly observes in *Treatise on Vesta and the Vestals*, chapter XIV, *Works*, vol. III, p. 1109, Arnobius would contradict himself by this question. For below, book IV, chapter 35, where he affirms that Vesta’s fire and the Vestal virgins still enjoyed the highest honor, [Col. 0918D] he says in the plainest words:

> The chaste virgins sit at the spectacles, the perpetual nourishers and preservers of the fire.

Lipsius therefore reads with Meursius and Scaliger: “In the inner chambers and *colinae*—the same as *culinae*, ‘kitchens’—do you keep perpetual hearth-fires burning?” He understands this of a private rite within houses, where in ancient times they preserved and tended fire in the interior section and kitchen, in private honor of the Lares or Vesta. But who would believe that this custom was altered and the fire moved from the most convenient part of the house to another?

Heribert Rosweyd, letter 823 to J. Lipsius, in Burmann’s *Collection*, vol. II, p. 141, thinks Arnobius does not mean that Vesta’s fires had been entirely abolished, but merely that the manner of preserving that fire had been altered, or that it had been transferred from its former location. He therefore proposes two conjectures. The first is: “In the inner chambers and *culignae* do you keep perpetual hearth-fires burning?” Only one letter is changed, and the sense would be that Vesta’s fire, formerly kept on a bare altar, was afterward preserved in an earthenware vessel. [Col. 0919A] For according to Festus and the Glossary, *culigna* is a kind of small vessel.

His second conjecture is that Arnobius means only that this fire was no longer preserved in the inner sanctuaries of Lavinium and Alba, and that the Romans had thus departed from ancient rites. Accordingly, one should read, close to the writing of the Limburg manuscript: “In the inner chambers of *Penenium* and the *colliginae*, do you keep perpetual hearth-fires burning?” *Colligina* might perhaps be understood of the hills of Alba, and the inner chambers of *Penenium* of Lavinium. But I wish he had given us examples of these meanings.

N. Heinsius, letter 115 to Graevius in the same Burmannian *Collection*, vol. IV, p. 155, conjectures that the text should read: “in the Trojan-born inner chambers,” that is, Trojan chambers; for Vesta was a Trojan divinity. [Col. 0919B] Lucan:

> Alba worships the Trojan fire and the lesser Vesta.

Isaac Vossius, *Notes on Catullus*, p. 377, proposes two conjectures: either one should read, “In the inner chambers do you keep perpetual hearth-fires burning for the heaven-born?”—the heaven-born being, of course, the Lares, who in the ancient inscription in Tertullian cited immediately below are called “powerful in the dwelling”; or, as he prefers, one should write: “In the store-room, in the inner chambers, and in the kitchens, do you keep perpetual hearth-fires burning?”

The *penus* is the innermost place both in Vesta’s temple and in private houses. Hence the Penates are the same as the Lares. For protection, their images, covered with dogskin, were placed in the *penus*, in kitchens around the hearth, and finally in atriums and inner chambers through which smoke escaped (*Rauchgange*, “smoke-passages”), or wherever their guardianship was believed to be beneficial.

The reading we have printed, “in the inner chambers of the dwelling” (*in penetralibus coliginis*), comes from Salmasius’s correction in the Leiden edition and in his notes on Solinus, p. 641 ff. The ancients used *colo, -ere* absolutely in the sense “to inhabit”; hence *colium, -ii* means “habitation” or “house.” [Col. 0919C] Tertullian, *On the Shows*, chapter 5:

> Even now an altar to that Consus is buried in the circus with an inscription of this kind:  
> **CONSUS, POWERFUL IN COUNSEL; MARS, IN WAR; THE LARES, IN THE DWELLING.**

For thus the old books read, *COLIO*, rather than *COMITIO*. The Lares “powerful in the dwelling” are therefore the same as the Greek *θεοὶ οἰκίδιοι, πατοικίδιοι*, “household gods” and “ancestral household gods,” whom Solinus calls by the Greek term *Icidii*. Arnobius, however, uses a different formation here: *coligo, -inis*, for “habitation” or “house”; and “the hearths of the dwelling” means “the hearths of the Penates.” Compare the same Salmasius on Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, p. 430. Gesner also approves this reading in the *Thesaurus*, under *Coligo*.

Heinsius, however, finding no examples of this meaning, reshapes the phrase in *Adversaria* IV, chapter 12, p. 629, Burmann edition, as: “in smoke-darkened inner chambers,” that is, smoky chambers, like Ovid’s “ash-covered halls” in the *Fasti*. But we find many such *ἅπαξ λεγόμενα* (“words occurring only once”) in Arnobius, and I admit that, of all the conjectures we have presented, that of Salmasius pleases me most.

Arnobius is therefore saying that [Col. 0919D] the pious custom of the ancients—keeping a perpetual fire burning in the inner parts of houses, through which, in ancient belief, homes were made sacred just as tables were by saltcellars—had been neglected. ORELL.

**Do you make tables sacred by setting saltcellars and images of the gods upon them?** A *salinum* was a small vessel in which salt was customarily kept for use at the table and in sacrifice. Porphyrio, on Horace II, Ode 16, says: “Properly speaking, a *salinum* is a dish in which first-fruits were offered to the gods with salt.”

How sacred and precious it was to the ancients is clear from these words of Livy XXVI, chapter 36:

> Those who have a wife or daughters shall retain one ounce by weight of gold for each; and of silver, those who have sat in a curule chair shall retain their horse’s ornaments and a pound by weight, so that they may possess a saltcellar and a dish for the sake of the gods.

Valerius Maximus IV, chapter 4, §3, infers that there was silver in the houses of Gaius Fabricius and Quintus Aemilius Papus because each possessed a dish for the gods and a saltcellar. Hence also that irony of Persius, *Satires* III, verse 25:

> You have a little meal and a saltcellar pure and without blemish:  
> [Col. 0920A] Why should you be afraid?—and a dish that securely tends the hearth.

More on the saltcellar in J. Lipsius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 2. NOURR., p. 316.

**When you enter into marriage, do you spread the couches with a toga and invoke the husbands’ guardian spirits?** The reference is to the bridal bed, the *γαμήλιος* (“nuptial bed”), such as Lucan describes, II, verse 356 ff.:

> Rising upon sloping ivory steps  
> Stands the couch, and painted gold distinguishes its rails.

This bed was called “genial” either because it was sacred to the Genius and Juno, or, as a favorable omen, from *gignere*, “to beget.” [Col. 0920B] The brides themselves spread it with magnificent adornment, and while spreading it they invoked their husbands’ guardian spirits, asking them to be present and make their offspring fruitful. See especially J. Lipsius, who discusses the subject extensively, *Selections* I, chapter 17, p. 695, vol. I, Wesel edition. ELMENH. and HERALD.

**Do you stroke the hair of brides with the celibate spear?** *Caelibaris* means “pertaining to a bachelor.” In ancient times it was a custom among the Romans for the husband to part the bride’s hair with the point of a spear which, as Festus relates under *celibaris*, had remained lodged in the body of a defeated and slain gladiator. Festus, book I, and Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, chapter 87, Hutten edition, vol. VIII, p. 362, calling it *αἰχμὴν δορατίου*, “the point of a little spear,” give various explanations of this custom. Ovid too mentions this spear in *Fasti* II, verse 558 ff.:

> Nor shall the curved spear dress your maiden hair,  
> You who will appear ripe for an eager mother.

Compare B. Brissonius, *On the Rite of Marriage*, p. 218. [Col. 0920C] NOURRIUS and ORELL.

**Do you carry the little togas of girls to Maiden Fortune?** For girls the time of marriage was the equivalent of the day on which boys began military or public life. At that time women laid aside the bordered toga before Maiden or Virginal Fortune, who was worshiped as a kind of goddess of chastity. Her temple stood outside the Capenian Gate and, according to Plutarch in *Roman Questions*, was built by Servius Tullius.

Augustine, *City of God* IV, chapter 11, calls this goddess *Virginensis*: “To her virgins untied their girdle.” Festus, however, calls Juno *Cinxia*, from the loosening of the girdle with which the new bride had been bound. See Ausonius Popma on the fragments of Varro, p. 308, Zweibrücken edition, and Scaliger on Festus under *Cinxia*.

They also dedicated their hair to the virgin goddess under whose guardianship they had previously been. Statius, *Thebaid* II:

> … They approached at the threshold  
> Unwedded Pallas, to whom, throughout the Argive cities,  
> Larissa was not ranked behind the Munychian hills. Here, by ancestral custom,  
> [Col. 0920D] The daughters of Inachus [*Inachides*; source reading uncertain], whenever chaste youth ripened for marriage,  
> Were accustomed to dedicate their maiden hair  
> And obtain pardon for their first bridal beds.

Nourrius, p. 317, understands the temple of Maiden Fortune built by Servius Tullius, mentioned by Plutarch in *Roman Questions*, chapter 74 (p. 354, vol. VIII, Hutten edition). HERALD. and ORELL.

**Do your matrons work in the atriums of their houses, bearing witness to their industry?** In former times Roman women, to prove their diligence, performed all women’s work in the front part of the house, that is, the atrium. Cornelius Nepos, Preface:

> For what Roman is ashamed to bring his wife to a banquet? Or whose matron does not occupy the foremost place in the house and appear publicly there?

See the interpreters on that passage. Compare Livy I, 57; Cicero, *For Milo*, chapter 5, with Asconius there; Festus under *Andron*; Stewechius on Vegetius, *On Military Matters* I, chapter 7; and especially J. Lipsius, *Selections* I, chapter 17, *Works*, vol. I, p. 696 ff., Wesel edition. ELMENH. and ORELL.

[Col. 0921B] **Do they abstain from drinking wine?** The use of wine was formerly forbidden to Roman women and was even a capital offense. Pliny XIV, chapter 13; Dionysius of Halicarnassus II, p. 96; Gellius X, chapter 23; Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chapter 6; Valerius Maximus II, chapter 1; Servius on *Aeneid* I, verse 738. ELMENH. and STEWECH. Compare Ausonius Popma on the fragments of Varro, p. 306 ff., Zweibrücken edition. ORELL.

**Do their relations by marriage and blood have the right to kiss them, etc.?** See Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chapter 6; Pliny, *Natural History* XIV, chapter 13; Juvenal VI, verse 1; Gellius [Col. 0921C] X, chapter 23; Plautus, *Stichus*, act I, scene II. ELMENH.—Compare Plutarch, *Roman Questions*, chapter 6. ORELL.]

### LXVII

Accordingly, when you charge us with having turned away from the religion of our predecessors, you ought to examine the reason, not merely the deed; you ought not to object to what we have abandoned, but above all to consider what we have chosen to follow. For if changing one’s judgment is any fault or crime, and if it is criminal to migrate from ancient institutions to other, new things and convictions, that accusation also concerns you, who have changed your life and customs so often—you who, by condemning the practices of your forefathers, have passed over to other customs and other rites.

[Col. 0914B] Do you still keep the people divided into five classes, [Col. 0915A] as your ancestors once did? Do you appoint magistrates through the people? Do you know what the military, urban, and common assemblies are? Do you observe the heavens, or render official proceedings idle through adverse announcements? When you prepare for war, do you display the signal from the citadel? [Col. 0916A] Or do you administer fetial law? Do you demand the return of stolen property through *clarigatio*? Or, when undertaking the ordeal of war, do you take up the hope of battle and take auspices from points?

In undertaking offices, do you observe the age laws? In [Col. 0917A] gifts and presents, the Cincian laws? In restraining expenditure, the censorial laws? [Col. 0918A] Do you keep perpetual hearth-fires burning [Col. 0919A] in the inner chambers of the dwelling? Do you make tables sacred by setting saltcellars and images of the gods upon them?

When you enter into marriage, do you spread the couches with a toga and invoke the husbands’ guardian spirits? [Col. 0920A] Do you stroke the hair of brides with the celibate spear? Do you carry the little togas of girls to Maiden Fortune? Do your matrons work in the atriums of their houses, [Col. 0921A] bearing witness to their industry? Do they abstain from drinking wine? Do their relations by marriage and blood have the right to kiss them, so that the women may prove themselves sober and abstinent?

[Note: [Col. 0921C]

### LXVIII.—Surely under King Tullius you began to offer entrails that were half-raw and only lightly kindled?

Giraldus, as cited by Thomas Canter, reads: “lightly scorched.” Isaac Casaubon, on Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 1, p. 233, vol. III, Wolf edition: “lightly deprived of life.” But nothing should be changed. *Animare*, as Elmenhorst correctly explains, is the same as to kindle, scorch, or soften with fire. Thus below, book VII, chapter 24:

> Those things which have been roasted on spits, first kindled and toasted over coals;

and Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpina* III, 386 ff.:

> As grim Megaera rushes to kindle the deadly yew trees  
> For her crimes.

See Heinsius and Gesner there.

Heraldus is therefore wrong to interpret this of entrails still quivering or palpitating, which—having been torn, of course, from the wombs of victims while they were still alive—were a favorable sign in sacrifices. See Virgil, [Col. 0921D] *Aeneid* IV, 64, and Seneca, *Oedipus*, 353 ff. For the subject here is not the inspection of entrails; rather, *exta* must be taken in the wider sense of everything covered by the hide, including the flesh.

*Porricere*, the same as “to present to the gods,” is a technical term of sacrifice. See Macrobius, *Saturnalia* III, chapter 2; Varro, *On Agriculture* I, 29: “When they gave the entrails to the gods, they called it *porricere*.” Virgil, *Aeneid* V, verse 237:

> … and the entrails I shall offer  
> To the salt waves.

See Servius and the distinguished Heyne there, as well as Brissonius, *On Formulas* I, p. 27, and J. F. Gronovius, who cites a cloud of examples in *Readings in Plautus*, p. 254 ff.

For *Tullio*, the first edition has *Tullo*. Wrongly: Servius Tullius, not Tullus Hostilius, is meant. ORELL.

**And did you not likewise alter this custom by a clever little deception and an ambiguity of names?** The ancient Latins long appeased Dis with human heads and Saturn with male victims. [Col. 0922B] See Dionysius of Halicarnassus I, p. 30; Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, chapter 30. At last Hercules persuaded them to exchange ill-omened sacrifices for favorable ones and to offer, in place of human heads, small masks fashioned in human likeness. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 7; Lactantius I, chapter 21; Dionysius of Halicarnassus I. ELMENH. Compare book V, beginning. ORELL.

**Contrary to common sense and judgment:** that is, contrary to common sense and common judgment. ORELL.]

### LXVIII

In ancient times, on Mount Alban, it was permissible to sacrifice no bulls except those of snow-white color. Surely you changed that custom and religious observance, and the Senate established by decree that reddish bulls might be offered?

When, in the reigns of Romulus and Pompilius, entrails thoroughly cooked and soaked were burned for the gods, surely under King Tullius [Note: [Col. 0921B] The manuscript has *Tullus*.] you began to offer them half-raw and only lightly kindled, in contempt of the ancient observance?

Before Hercules came to Italy, when, at Apollo’s command, Father Dis and Saturn were propitiated with human heads, did you not likewise alter this custom by a clever little deception and an ambiguity of names?

Since, therefore, you yourselves have followed now those customs, now other laws, and have rejected and despised many things either upon recognizing their errors or upon perceiving better alternatives, [Col. 0922A] what have we done contrary to common sense and judgment if we have chosen greater and more certain things, and have not allowed ourselves to be held fast by false religions?

[Note: [Col. 0922C]

### LXIX.—For philosophy, music, and all the other arts by which the common life has been cultivated and refined, etc.

I would not venture, with the other editors, to expunge *etenim* (“for”), which is in the manuscript codex. Arnobius seems to have used this particle in the sense “for example.” The Leiden edition has: “Tell me, were philosophy, etc.”

For *exculta* (“cultivated”), which is Fulvius Ursinus’s correction, the manuscript codex has *exstructa* (“built up”), which Stewechius attempts to defend. But the examples he adduces have no bearing on our passage. For it is indeed possible to speak of “fashioning a man,” “building up children,” or “constructing and putting together offspring”; but I confess that I have sought in vain for examples of the expression “to build up life by the arts.” ORELL.

**Tages, the Etruscan.** Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 4:

> Moreover, in the territory of Tarquinii a boy named Tages is said to have been divinely ploughed up (*hervorgepflügt*), who proclaimed the discipline of inspecting entrails; the Lucumones, then the rulers of Etruria, wrote it down.

See the authors cited there by Lindenbrog, p. 24, Haverkamp edition. Ovid likewise writes of him, *Metamorphoses* [Col. 0922D] XV, 553 ff.:

> He was no less astonished than when the Tyrrhenian ploughman  
> Saw in the midst of his fields a fateful clod  
> First move of its own accord, with no one stirring it,  
> Then assume human form and lose the form of earth,  
> And open newly made lips to reveal the coming fates.  
> The natives called him Tages, who first taught  
> The Etruscan people to disclose future events.

Compare Davies on Cicero, *On Divination* II, chapters 23 and 38, and especially Dempster, *Etruria Regalis* III.1. ORELL.

**Reached the shores of light.** A Lucretian phrase, for example book I, verse 23 ff.:

> Nor without you does anything rise into  
> The divine shores of light, nor does anything become joyful or lovely.

And very frequently elsewhere. ORELL.

**In the fall of thunderbolts, etc.** If a thunderbolt had struck anything, it was regarded as a portent of no slight importance, and to appease the wrath of the gods [Col. 0923B] a *bidental* was consecrated where the lightning had flashed. They therefore buried the thunderbolt there, consecrated the place, and brought sacrificial victims to it, as Lucan elegantly describes, book I, verse 608 ff.; see Burmann there. Consequently they were unwilling even to approach such places, as Artemidorus observes, book II, chapter 8, since they had been sealed with divine awe.

Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIII:

> And the books dealing with lightning pronounce that places struck in this manner ought neither to be looked upon nor trodden.

HERALD.

[Col. 0923C] **Genethliacal calculation.** *Ratio* means “calculation.” See above on book I, chapter 59. ORELL.

**The Egyptian Theuth.** Theuth—called Theutis or Thoth by others—is Hermes Trismegistus, concerning whom Plato writes in the *Phaedrus*, p. 274, H. Stephanus edition, vol. III; Zweibrücken edition, vol. X, p. 379:

> “I have heard, then, that near Naucratis in Egypt there was one of that country’s ancient gods, whose sacred bird is the one they call the ibis, and that the name of the divinity himself was Theuth. He was the first to discover number and calculation, geometry and astronomy, and also games of draughts and dice, and, in particular, letters,” etc.

Compare Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* I, 9, and the classic passage concerning him, Lactantius I, chapter 6, with the interpreters there.

For *Thentin*, the first Roman edition has *Theutatem*, which was the name of Mercury among the Gauls, according to Lucan I, verse 444, and Lactantius, *Institutes* I, chapter 21. See Bunemann there, p. 135, and Gronovius on Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, chapter VI, p. 53 ff. ORELL.

**The prop of heaven.** That is, Atlas the heaven-bearer, as Statius says in the *Thebaid*, book V. *Destina* is a rather rare word, [Col. 0923D] meaning “support” or “prop.” Corippus the African, *Panegyric on the Praises of Justin the Younger* I, verse 18 ff.:

> And Thomas, the prop of tottering Libyan land,  
> Who restored it after its fall and gave the Africans hope of life.

See Ruiz and Rittershausen there, in *Latin Panegyrics*, Jaeger edition, p. 481, vol. II.

Isidore, *Sentences* II, chapter 40:

> The ruin of adultery is caught by the supporting prop of marriage.

Braulio, *Life of Isidore*:

> I believe that God raised him up after so many disasters of Spain in these last times to restore the monuments of the ancients, lest we grow utterly old in rustic ignorance, setting him in place, as it were, as a supporting prop.

ELMENH. and MEURSIUS.—P. Wesseling restored the same word from a manuscript of Vitruvius V, chapter 12, in *Observations* II, chapter 13, p. 198; see him there. Compare Cujacius, *Observations* XXI, chapter 28. ORELL.]

### LXIX

But ours is a new name, and the religion we follow was born only a few days ago. Even if, for the moment, I grant that the charge brought against us is not falsely intended, what is there in human affairs—whether accomplished by bodily labor [Note: [Col. 0921B] Fulvius deletes “bodily.”] and by the hands, or maintained solely by mental training and knowledge—that did not begin at some point in time and pass into the use and experience of mortals? For did philosophy, music, and all the other arts by which our common life has been cultivated and refined arise together with humankind, rather than only recently—indeed, almost just a short while ago—beginning to be practiced, understood, and celebrated? Before Tages the Etruscan reached the shores [Note: [Col. 0922B] The manuscript wrongly reads “with the mouth.”] of light, did any human being know, or take care to learn and master, what was signified in the occurrence of lightning strikes or in the veins of entrails? When did knowledge of the movements of the stars, or of the principles of natal astrology, begin? Was it not after Theuth the Egyptian, or after Atlas, as some report—the bearer, carrier, buttress, and prop of heaven?

[Note: [Col. 0923D]

### LXX.—“Jupiter both supreme and Stygian”

“Stygian Jupiter” means Pluto. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 638:

> [Col. 0924B] The rites for Stygian Jove, which I duly began and prepared,  
> I intend to complete.

Silius VIII.116 calls him “Black Jupiter”; the same author, II.674, calls him “Tartarean Jupiter,” as does Valerius Flaccus, *Argonautica* I.730. He is called Ζεὺς χθόνιος, καταχθόνιος, “subterranean, underworld Zeus,” in Orpheus, *Hymn* LXX (Hermann’s edition), Homer, *Iliad* I.457, and Sophocles, *Oedipus at Colonus*, verse 1606. Similarly Proserpina is called “infernal, Avernian, Stygian Juno” in Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.137, and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIV.114. These appellations appear to have arisen from the teaching of the most ancient philosophers, [Col. 0924C] who posited two hemispheres, an upper and a lower, and assigned its own gods to each, according to Lactantius—or Lutatius—on Statius, *Thebaid* IV, p. 192 of Crucaeus’s edition; for Neptune is nowhere called “Jupiter of the seas.” Compare C. Barth, *Adversaria* XXII.10, p. 1091, and his commentary on Statius, *Thebaid* II.49, vol. II, p. 278, where he treats this subject at length. ORELLI.—But Pausanias, on the authority of Aeschylus, proves that the name Jupiter was also added to Neptune, although more rarely; Hemsterhuis cited the passage in his commentary on Lucian, II, p. 520, Bipontine edition. OCHSNER.

### “Lord of the salt sea”

Others read “lord of the soil,” so as to express Ἐνοσίχθων, Ἐννοσίγαιος, “Earth-shaker.” But that is wholly foreign to our passage. ORELLI.

### “By a Saturnian progenitor”

This is the correct reading of the parchment manuscripts. I take “the Saturnian progenitor” to be the same as Jupiter, since he was born of Saturn as his father; and the conjunction “and” here signifies nothing other than “that is.” Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* IV:

> [Col. 0924D] Near Ocean’s end and the setting sun.

STEWECH.—Others read “with Saturn having been begotten,” wrongly. ORELLI.

### “Before Memory, Alcmena, etc.”

The word “than” before *Alcmena* is plainly superfluous and obstructs the sense; I therefore judge that it should be deleted and have enclosed it in parentheses as a gloss. In place of *Alcmena*, Fulvius Ursinus prefers *Camena*, wrongly. ORELLI.

### “From intercourse with Jupiter”

Here *intercourse* is the same thing as what our author above, chapter 16, called “bodily unions.” ORELLI.

### “Diespiter”

Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV (p. 20, Bipontine edition): “This same point is shown still more clearly by the ancient name of Jupiter. For formerly he was called *Diovis* and *Diespiter*, that is, ‘father of the air and day’; from him were named the gods, who come from there, and also *dies* (‘day’), *dius* (‘divine’), and *divus* (‘god’).” ELMENHORST.—The name *Diespiter* for Jupiter must be carefully distinguished from *Dispiter* or *Dis Pater*, the name of Pluto. See Cellarius and Bünemann on Lactantius, *Institutes* I.14, p. 90. ORELLI.

### [Col. 0925B] “Established in existence”

Stewechius judges that *in essentiam*, “into existence,” the reading of the manuscript, should be adopted, in accordance with Arnobius’s usual practice of putting the accusative for the ablative and vice versa. See above. ORELLI.

### “Consecrated by an inviolable religious sanction”

Strictly so. For, as Servius says on Virgil, *sancire* means to render something sacred and inviolable by the shedding of a sacrificial victim’s blood. Hence Lucan, book VII:

> They will wish to sanction the Roman laws with this blood.

[Col. 0925C] And Livy, book XXIII: “‘Now,’ he said, ‘I shall sanction the Roman treaty with Hannibal’s blood.’” Religions were therefore said to be sanctioned in this way, and the divine powers themselves to be thus consecrated, because for that reason it was sacrilege to violate them, and anyone who had violated them atoned for the offense with his life. Similarly, laws and “sanctions” were said to be sanctioned because anyone who transgressed them was punished capitally, as Ulpian observes in book IX, *On the Division and Nature of Things*. Hence things defended and protected from human injury were called “sacred,” Digest VIII, under the same title. Thus ambassadors were sacred and inviolable; and the tribunes of the plebs were sacred, or rather sacrosanct—ἱεροὶ καὶ ἄσυλοι, “holy and inviolable,” as Dionysius of Halicarnassus translates it in book VI of the *Roman Antiquities*. They were called sacrosanct because it had been sanctioned that, if anyone violated them, his head should be sacred to Jupiter. Titus Livy, book III: “By sanctioning that, if anyone harmed the tribunes of the plebs, the aediles, judges, or decemvirs, his head should be sacred to Jupiter, and his household should be sold at the temple of Ceres, Liber, and Libera.” Anyone could kill persons thus consecrated and devoted ἄνευ κρίσεως, “without trial,” and with impunity. [Col. 0925D] They were devoted especially to the infernal gods, θεοῖς καταχθονίοις, “the gods beneath the earth.” Hence “sacred gods” and “sacred temples of the gods,” consecrated with blood and slain victims; but the term also applied to gods whose majesty, if someone violated and diminished it, he satisfied with his own blood and expiated his crime. Arnobius therefore says with strict propriety that a deity is “consecrated by an inviolable religious sanction,” because the deity had thus been sanctioned as sacred and inviolable; and if its majesty had been violated, the offense was expiated with the life τοῦ ἀσεβήσαντος, “of the impious offender.” HERALDUS.]

### LXX

But why do I speak of these minor matters? According to what is handed down in your writings and opinions, did not the immortal gods themselves—whose temples you now enter and whose divine powers you worship in supplication—begin at definite times to exist, to become known, and to be designated by names imposed upon them? For if it is true that Jupiter, together with his brothers, was begotten by Saturn and his wife, then before Ops’s marriage and childbirth there was nowhere any Jupiter, either supreme or Stygian; nowhere a lord of the salt sea, nowhere Juno—indeed, no other being at all, apart from the two parents, dwelt in the habitations of heaven. Rather, they were conceived through their intercourse, [Col. 0923B] were born, and drew the breath of life.

At a definite time, therefore, Jupiter began to be a god, at a definite time to deserve worship and sacrifices, and at a definite time [Col. 0924A] to be placed above his brothers in authority. Again, if Liber, Venus, Diana, Mercury, Apollo, Hercules, the Muses, the Tyndarid Castors, and fire-powerful Vulcan were brought forth by father Jupiter—that is, begotten by the Saturnian progenitor—then, before Memory, (than) Alcmena, Maia, Juno, Latona, Leda, Dione, and Semele as well became pregnant through the embraces of Diespiter [Note: [Col. 0923B] The manuscript has *fetiae*, absurdly.], they too existed nowhere among the nations [Note: [Col. 0923B] The manuscript wrongly reads “to have existed.”] or in any part of the natural order. Rather, they were inseminated through intercourse with Jupiter, were born, and began to possess some awareness of themselves. Therefore these too began to exist at a definite time and to be invoked, among the number of sacred divine powers, in religious ceremonies.

The same statement may likewise be transferred to Minerva. For if, as you assert, she burst forth from Jupiter’s brain without the discharge of any seed, then before Diespiter was begotten and received the outline of his form in the womb of his bodily [Col. 0924B] mother [Note: [Col. 0924B] Thus the manuscript and Fulvius; Sabaeus reads “in a body.”], it is certainly clear that Minerva did not exist, was not counted among existing things, and had no being in any substance. But from the moment [Col. 0925A] when she was born from Jupiter’s head, she began to be something, established in existence. She therefore has a first origin, and from a definite time began to be called a goddess, to be set up in sacred buildings, and to be consecrated by an inviolable religious sanction.

Since this is so, when you speak about the novelty of our religions, do your own not come to mind? Do you not care to examine when your gods arose, what origins and causes they have, or from what roots they broke and burst forth? What sense of shame—or rather, what degree of shamelessness—is it to rebuke another person for what you see yourself doing, and to present as grounds for abuse and accusation things that can be turned back against you in reciprocal exchange?

[Note: [Col. 0925D]

### LXXI.—“One should consider not on what day you began to worship, but what you began to worship”

*What* is Gelenius’s correction; previously the text read *who you began*, a reading Heraldus attempts to defend by taking *who* in the sense of “how,” so that the meaning would be that it is not the age of a religion that should be considered, but its rationale. I prefer *what*, so that it corresponds to the preceding “divine power.” ORELLI.

### “‘Four hundred years ago,’ you say, ‘your religion did not exist’”

It is needless to say that the passage is corrupt. For from what Arnobius wrote in book I, chapter 13—“It is about three hundred years, more or less, since Christians began to exist and to be counted in the world”—one can readily see that the pagan’s objection, when he says “four hundred,” involves a considerable error in the numerical signs. One must also take into consideration that our author shortly afterward adds that, when he was writing this, approximately 1,050 years had passed since the foundation of Rome; and he repeats and reckons there the two thousand years mentioned above. When I examine the Roman consular lists and, in addition to the other matters that must be brought into this calculation, consider the reign of Diocletian—under whom Saint Jerome and others testify that Arnobius lived—I find that year 1,050 from the foundation of Rome, namely the consulship of Anicius Faustus and Gallus, falls only in the year of Christ 298. We should therefore restore Arnobius’s text to: “‘Three hundred years ago,’ you say, ‘your religion did not exist.’” For this alludes to the preceding ironic concession: “But ours is a new name, and the religion we follow was born only a few days ago.” STEWECH.

Nothing should be changed, for others have already observed that our author is not entirely consistent with himself in calculating years—for example Baronius at *Annals* 302, §17; Dodwell, *Dissertations on Irenaeus* II, §56; and Pagi at *Annals* 302, §15. From his words cited above by Stewechius, book I, chapter 13, and from those occurring below in our chapter—“The city of Rome counts 1,050 years, or not much fewer”—they rightly inferred that Arnobius wrote these words around the year of Christ 297 according to the Varronian reckoning, or 298 [Col. 0926D] according to the Capitoline reckoning of years from the foundation of Rome.

Yet words that we read below, in book IV, chapter 36, appear to conflict with this calculation: “Why did our writings deserve to be given to the flames? Why were our meeting places demolished with impunity?” As Baronius noted in the passage cited, these words do not appear to have been written before the year 303 after Christ’s birth, when the Diocletianic persecution began to rage. Moreover, we have no precise information either about when Arnobius wrote his books or about the year in which he died, except that scholars infer from Jerome’s words in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 79, that he lived until the year 326 after Christ’s birth. If, therefore, the author wrote this one year after the three-hundredth year, the pagan adversary whom he introduces here could have said in round numbers: “‘Four hundred years ago’ your religion did not exist.” Compare Schoenemann’s *Literary Notice*, §1. ORELLI.

### “Who fathered Picus, the father of Faunus and grandfather of Latinus? Saturn, etc.”

On Saturn’s reign, his arrival in Italy as a fugitive, Picus, Faunus, and so forth, see especially Aurelius Victor, *On the Origin of the Roman People*, chapters III and IV, and the commentators there. ORELLI.

### [Col. 0927C] “Do you wish Faunus, Latinus, and Picus to have lived one hundred and twenty years each? For it is denied that human life can be extended beyond that”

Note the story of the death of great Pan and the passing of other spirits in Plutarch, *On the Obsolescence of Oracles*. Statius clearly makes the condition of the Fauns inferior to that of the Nymphs in *Thebaid* VI.96, when he says that their companies perished while that woodland endured. Servius on *Aeneid* I.372: “The Nymphs do not know everything, for according to Aristotle they too die, as do the Fauns and Pans.” Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpina* III.379:

> . . . Together they suffered ruin,  
> And together laid down their foliage; upon the field lies low  
> The grief of Fauns and Dryads.

BARTH, on Statius, vol. III, p. 382.

### “Aeneas. Whose father was he? Of the founder of the town of Alba”

I have printed this from Freinsheim’s emendation in the index to Florus under the word *Iulus*. The manuscript and the editions that followed it [Col. 0927D] have: “Aeneas, father of Latinus. Of whom? Of the founder of the town of Alba”—a thoroughly corrupt reading contrary to all historical authority. Obertus Gifanius reads: “Aeneas’s father? Of whom? etc.,” with Thomas Canter’s approval. Fulvius Ursinus reads: “Aeneas, father of Ascanius, founder of the town of Alba.” Salmasius, in the Leiden edition, printed and punctuated it: “Aeneas. He was the father of Ascanius. Of which Ascanius? The founder of the town of Alba,” so that Ascanius the founder of Alba is distinguished from other men named Ascanius—for example, the leader of the Phrygians in the Trojan War, whom Homer mentions in *Iliad* II.862 and XIII.792. But how many of Arnobius’s readers would have thought of any Ascanius other than Aeneas’s son, the founder of Alba? Finally, Meursius recasts it as: “Aeneas. Of the Latin race.” ORELLI.

### “It counts one thousand and fifty years”

*Counts*, that is, “calculates, reckons,” as J. F. Gronovius correctly interprets it in *Observations* II.10, pp. 130–31, refuting some scholar, I do not know whom, who explained it as “endures.” *Ducere* is a verb proper to arithmetic and calculation, not merely to addition, as Ernesti maintains in [Col. 0928B] his *Key to Cicero* under this word, but to every kind of calculation. Thus Gellius, book I, chapter 20: “Among numbers likewise a cube is calculated when every side of the same number is resolved equally into itself, as happens when three times ten are multiplied.” ORELLI.

### [Col. 0928C] “Or fully”

The following words, “to make an allowance for their age,” show that this should be read with Fulvius Ursinus. The manuscript has “not fully.” ORELLI.

### “The religion … which you practice”

That is, “which you worship.” Thus below, book III, chapter 5: “You do not perform the duties owed to the other gods,” in place of: “You do not render duties to the other gods.” ORELLI.

### “You supply them, at the risk of decay”

*Decay* is very often used of disease that attacks the body. Thus “the black fluid of the corrupted body” in Lucretius III.502. In place of *suggeritis*, “you supply,” Fulvius Ursinus prefers *oggeritis*, “you heap up,” as the more ancient form. But nothing should be changed. Statius too speaks of supplying food to someone, *Thebaid* IX.740. ORELLI.]

### LXXI

But what we do is new, whereas what you do is ancient and of extreme antiquity. And how does that [Col. 0925B] either help you or impair our cause and argument? What we practice is new; at some point it too will become old. What you practice is old; but at the time when it began, it was new and sudden. The authority of a religion, however, is not to be evaluated by time but by its divine power; one should consider not on what day you began to worship, but what you began to worship.

“Four hundred years ago,” you say, “your religion did not exist.” And your gods did not exist two thousand years ago. By what arguments or calculations can that be established? Not by difficult or obscure ones, but by arguments that anyone who wishes can see and, as the saying goes, touch with his hands.

Who fathered Jupiter and his brothers? Saturn, united with the generative organs of Ops [Note: [Col. 0925B] The manuscript reads “with the marriage-bed of Ops joined.”], as you report, himself begotten by Caelus and Hecate. Who fathered Picus, the father of Faunus and grandfather of Latinus? Saturn, as you yourselves likewise hand down in your writings and authorities. Therefore, if these things are so, it follows that Picus and Jupiter are united to one another by the right of brotherhood, since they were begotten from one blood and one seed. The statement is consistent.

From Jupiter and Picus down to [Col. 0927A] Latinus, how many generations are there? Three, as the succession shows. Do you wish Faunus, Latinus, and Picus to have lived one hundred and twenty years each? For it is denied that human life can be extended beyond that. The estimate is fair and clear. There are therefore a full three hundred and sixty years after them; the matter stands as the calculation indicates.

Whose father-in-law was Latinus? Aeneas’s. Whose father was Aeneas? The founder of the town of Alba’s. For how many years was kingship exercised at Alba? Four hundred and nearly twenty. What age is assigned to the city of Rome in the annals? It counts one thousand and fifty years, or not much fewer. Therefore, from Jupiter, who is Picus’s brother and the father of the younger and remaining gods, down to the present time there are nearly two thousand years—or fully two thousand, to make an allowance for their age.

Since this cannot be refuted, the religion [Col. 0927B] which you practice is shown not only to have been born recently, but the very gods to whom you supply bulls and other victims, at the risk of decay, are shown still to be infants and little children, who ought even now to be nourished at the breast and with milk expressed drop by drop.

[Note: [Col. 0928C]

### LXXII.—“And yet, lest we appear to betray our cause by so prolonged a concealment”

I have printed this from Thomas Canter’s emendation, which the editor of the Leiden edition and Freinsheim, in his index to Florus under the word *veteres*, approve. The manuscript and the Roman first edition have: “And yet, lest we appear to betray so lengthy a cause, etc.” Heraldus attempts to defend this reading, thinking that Arnobius is excusing himself for dwelling rather long on this argument and therefore saying that he deliberately did so lest, by treating it more briefly and keeping silent about matters pertinent to the subject, he should appear to have wished to betray the cause he had undertaken to defend.

But the matters Arnobius had previously discussed in this book—for example, the origin of souls—have very little relevance to that cause and are entirely foreign to the work’s purpose. He therefore says precisely the contrary: namely, that he is now returning to the proposed subject of the work, lest by dwelling too long on less necessary matters he appear to have wished to betray his cause; for until now he had deferred bringing forth the strength of the true argument. The reading should therefore be: “by so prolonged a concealment.” *Concealment* and *to conceal* are used of those who deliberately suppress the truth and omit matters pertinent to a case. See above on chapter 44. Gelenius printed: “Lest we appear to betray so good a cause by concealment.” Wrongly. ORELLI.

### “Which is called eternity”

Thus Meursius and the editor of the Leiden edition. Others read: “By which eternity is named.” ORELLI.

### “Where it is fitting, etc.”

Thus Fulvius Ursinus. The manuscript [Col. 0929B] has “where it is fitting to come together.” The Leiden editor restored this to the text, so that the meaning is: “where it is fitting for human beings to come together,” words that must be supplied from the preceding passage. Meursius prefers: “where it would be fitting.” ORELLI.]

### LXXII

But your religions precede ours by many years and are truer for that reason, because they are fortified by the authority of antiquity. Yet what advantage is it for them to precede ours by very many years, when they began at a definite time? Or what is a span of two thousand years when compared with so many thousands of ages?

And yet, lest we appear to betray our cause by so prolonged a concealment, tell us, if it is not troublesome: does the almighty and first God seem to you a recent thing, and do those who honor and worship him appear to practice and introduce unheard-of, unknown, and suddenly arisen religions? Is there anything more ancient than he? Can anything be found that precedes him in reality, time, or name? Is he not alone unbegotten, alone immortal and everlasting? Who is the head or source of all things? Is it not he? To whom does eternity owe the very fact that it is called eternity? Is it not to him? Is it not from his perpetuity that infinite ages are brought into being?

This is indubitable and true. What we follow, therefore, is not new; rather, we learned late what we ought to follow and worship, or where it is fitting to fasten our hope of salvation and place the means that bring salvation. For he who would show the way to those who wandered had not yet shone forth, to cast the light of knowledge upon those established in the deepest darkness and disperse the blindness of ignorance.

[Col. 0929A] [Note: [Col. 0929B]

### LXXIII.—“But are we alone subjected to criticism in matters of this kind?”

Thus, as the sense demands, the editor of the Leiden edition emended the text extremely well. The manuscript and Elmenhorst’s edition read: “But is the cause in a matter of this sort turned alone?”—a thoroughly corrupt and meaningless reading. Hence Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “Is it turned on ground of this sort?” But the Leiden editor’s emendation alone is true, as what follows demonstrates. ORELLI.

### “What? Did you not enroll the Egyptian divine powers named Serapis and Isis among your gods only after the consulship of Piso and Gabinius?”

Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter VI: “Serapis, Isis, and Harpocrates, together with his Cynocephalus, were forbidden to be brought into the Capitol”—that is, they were driven from the senate-house of the gods. “Piso and Gabinius, who were certainly not Christians, repudiated them, even overturning their altars, thereby restraining the vices of shameful and idle superstitions. Once they had been restored, you conferred the highest majesty upon them.” HERALDUS and ELMENHORST.—Compare the same Tertullian, *Against the Nations* I.10. The consulship of Aulus Gabinius and Lucius Calpurnius Piso fell in year 696 from the foundation of Rome, 58 before Christ’s birth. See Almeloveen, *Consular Fasti*, p. 99.

In that year, and more than once, the Senate ordered the shrines of these divinities that certain private persons had erected to be demolished, because it did not esteem those divine powers highly. But shortly afterward, when the popular faction prevailed, their worship was restored. At first their temples were located outside the *pomerium*, according to Dio Cassius XLII.47; see Reimarus there, vol. I, p. 252. Finally, during the consulship of Hirtius and Pansa, in year 711 from the foundation of Rome, the triumvirs Caesar Octavian, Antony, and Lepidus decreed a new temple for the same divine powers, as Dio likewise records in XLVII.15, p. 501, Reimarus’s edition. Compare Augustine, *City of God* XI.14; Lucan, *Pharsalia* VII.83; the distinguished Böttiger in *Sabina*, pp. 199 ff.; and Gijsbert Cuper, who explains the whole history of those rites fully and learnedly in *Harpocrates*, pp. 149 ff. ORELLI.

### “What? The Phrygian Mother, whose rites are said to have been founded by either Midas or Dardanus”

Here Arnobius follows Clement of Alexandria, in whose *Exhortation to the Greeks* 5, p. 12, Potter’s edition, we read:

> Let him therefore perish who first introduced this deception among humankind—whether Dardanus, who displayed the mysteries of the Mother of the Gods; or Eetion, who instituted the orgies and initiatory rites of Samothrace; or that Phrygian Midas, who learned the contrived deception from the Odrysian [Orpheus] and then transmitted it to his subjects.

Compare Diodorus III.58, with Wesseling’s commentary there; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* I, p. 55. ELMENHORST.—Add Justin XI.7: “After him [Gordius], his son Midas reigned. Initiated by Orpheus into the solemn rites, he filled Phrygia with religious observances, by which he was kept safer throughout his life than by weapons.” Compare Perizonius on Aelian, *Various History* III.18. On Dardanus see above, on book I, chapter 52. For “is indicated,” the Leiden edition has “is judged.” ORELLI.

### “When Hannibal the Carthaginian was ravaging Italian affairs … you began both to recognize and to know her”

Cicero, *On the Response of the Haruspices*, chapter 13 (p. 344, F. A. Wolf’s edition): “Long ago, therefore, on the advice of this prophetess [the Sibyl], when Italy was exhausted by the Punic War and harried by Hannibal, our ancestors imported these rites from Phrygia and established them at Rome. They were received by the man judged the best man of the Roman people, Publius Scipio, and by the woman considered the chastest of the matrons, Claudia Quinta.” ELMENHORST.

—“To ravage affairs” is an established expression. Virgil, *Aeneid* X.14:

> Then it will be permitted to contend in hatred, then to have ravaged affairs.

[Col. 0930C] On this passage Servius says: “The ancients used ‘to ravage affairs’ to mean ‘to injure,’ even if no charge of plunder existed; similarly, they said ‘to give satisfaction’ to mean ‘to restore possessions.’” Thus “to demand restitution” is τὰ δίκαια αἰτεῖν and τὰς δίκας αἰτεῖν, “to demand one’s rights” and “to demand penalties,” as Dionysius of Halicarnassus translates it. HERALDUS.—“To ravage affairs” corresponds to the Greek ἄγειν καὶ φέρειν, “to carry off and plunder.” ORELLI.

### “As for the sacred rites of Mother Ceres … it was arranged that they should be called Greek, etc.”

Cicero, *For Balbus*, chapter 24: “Our ancestors wished the sacred rites of Ceres to be performed with the highest reverence and ceremonial observance. Since they had been adopted from the Greeks, they have always been administered by Greek priestesses, and everything connected with them has been called Greek.” Compare Valerius Maximus I.1 and Festus under *Greek rites*, with Dacier’s commentary there. ORELLI.

### “The Pompilian indigitamenta do not know the name of Apollo”

Servius on Virgil, *Georgics* I.21:

> And all the gods and goddesses whose concern it is to guard the fields.

“These names,” he says, “of divine powers are found in the *indigitamenta*, [Col. 0930D] that is, in the pontifical books, which contain both the names of the gods and the account of the divine powers themselves.” The *Glosses of Philoxenus*: “*Indigitamenta*: ἱερατικὰ βιβλία, ‘priestly books.’” HERALDUS.—Meursius, pp. 85–86; Ole Borch, *Reflections*, p. 129. Compare G. J. Vossius, *Roman Etymologies*, and Joseph Scaliger on the Hymns of Orpheus in his *Poems*, p. 186.
