What Arnobius writes of Apollo, Macrobius writes of Venus in *Saturnalia* I.12: “Varro also agrees with Cincius, affirming that not even under the kings was the name of Venus found among the Romans or Latins, either in Latin or Greek, and that a month therefore could not have been named after Venus. Nor, unlike the other heavenly deities, is any praise of Venus celebrated in the songs of the Salii.” Compare the commentators on Varro, p. 136, Bipontine edition. ORELLI.

### “But afterward, at some time”

The first edition of Sabaeus reads: “but somewhat afterward.” Nothing should be changed, however. The sense demands “at some time,” that is, at some indefinite time. For the cults of those divine powers were instituted at differing intervals, some shorter and others longer. ORELLI.

### [Col. 0931C] “Who would call us away from conjectural things to his worship”

“Conjectural things” means empty things founded solely upon human opinion. Fulvius Ursinus prefers “true worship.” ORELLI.]

### LXXIII

But are we alone subjected to criticism in matters of this kind? What? Did you not enroll the Egyptian divine powers named Serapis and Isis among your gods only after the consulship of Piso and Gabinius? What of the Phrygian Mother, whose rites are said to have been founded by either Midas or Dardanus? Did you not begin both to recognize and to know her, and to consecrate her with a memorable religious sanction, only when Hannibal the Carthaginian was ravaging Italian affairs [Note: [Col. 0929A] Thus Sabaeus; others read “Italy’s affairs.”] and demanding dominion over the lands?

Although the sacred rites of Mother Ceres were not unknown to you but had been imported a short while before, was it not arranged that they should be called “Greek,” so that their very epithet attested their novelty? Is it not recorded in the writings of the learned that the Pompilian *indigitamenta* [priestly invocation-books] [Col. 0930A] do not know the name of Apollo? From this it is apparent and clear that he too was unknown to you, but afterward, at some time, began to be known.

If, therefore, someone were to ask you why you adopted the worship of the divine powers we have just mentioned so late, you would certainly answer either that until recently you did not know that they were numbered among the gods, or that you have now been warned by prophets, or that in extremely harsh circumstances you were saved by their benefits and assistance. If you judge that this can rightly be said by you, then consider that a similar answer, based on similar reasoning, has been given on our side.

Our religion was born only now, because only now was he sent and arrived who would show it to us, lead us into its truth, reveal what God is, and call us away from conjectural things to his worship [Note: [Col. 0931C] Fulvius reads “to true worship.”].

[Note: [Col. 0931C]

### LXXIV.—“Savior”

Arnobius is fond of this title for Christ. See the following chapter and book I, chapter 53: “God the Savior was sent from unknown realms and by God the prince of all.” Compare Lactantius IV.26. ELMENHORST.

### “Autumn”

See above on book I, chapter 21. ORELLI.

### “Cannot by any”

Thus Fulvius Ursinus. The manuscript reads “powerful by none,” which Stewechius attempts to defend. But then the sentence gapes and lacks a finite verb. ORELLI.

### “Attain. What ought to be done, when, or in what manner, the father, governor, and Lord of all things himself alone knows”

Thus all the editors except the Leiden editor, who reads and punctuates as follows: “Attain what ought to be done, when, or in what manner. The father, governor, and Lord of all things himself alone knows it.” For my part, I see no reason for making a change. ORELLI.

### “Which has been shown to be indubitable by such great kinds of mighty works and powers”

The parchment manuscripts favor: “Which, by such great kinds of mighty works and powers, has been shown to possess indubitable power.” I found this more attractive: “Which, by such great kinds of mighty works, and such great powers, has been shown to possess indubitable power”; or should it rather be: “Which, by such great kinds of mighty works and by powers of powers, has been shown to be indubitable”? STEWECH.]

### LXXIV

“And what,” someone says, “seemed good to God, the king and prince, that only a few hours ago, as the saying goes, Christ the Savior should be sent to you from the heights of heaven?”

We ask you in reply [Note: [Col. 0931C] Sabaeus reads “we ask ourselves.”]: what cause, what reason is there that the seasons are sometimes not restored to their proper months, but winter comes late, summer late, and autumn late? Why, after the crops have dried up and the grain has died, do rains sometimes fall that ought to have descended while the crops were still unharmed and to have ministered to the opportune needs of the season?

Indeed, we ask this instead: if Hercules had to be born, and Aesculapius, Mercury, Liber, and certain others who would both be admitted to the councils of the gods and bring some benefit [Col. 0931B] to mortals, why were they brought forth by Jupiter so late that only posterity knew them, while earlier antiquity remained ignorant of them? You will say that there was some reason. There was therefore also a reason here why the Savior of our race came not recently, but today.

What, then, was that reason? We do not deny that we do not know. For it is not readily possible for anyone to see the mind of God or the ways in which he has ordered his affairs. A human being, a blind animal ignorant even of itself, cannot by any reasoning attain to it. What ought to be done, when, or in what manner, the father, governor, and Lord of all things himself alone knows.

Nor, if I have been unable to set forth for you the reasons [Col. 0931C] why something occurs in this way or that, [Col. 0932A] does it immediately follow that what has been done becomes undone, or that a fact loses the credibility which has been shown to be indubitable by such great kinds of mighty works and powers.

[Note: [Col. 0931D]

### LXXV.—“In infinite and everlasting ages, absolutely nothing should be called late”

This is an excellent emendation by Thomas Canter, deservedly adopted into the text by subsequent editors. The manuscript reads: “Nevertheless it should be called true,” a thoroughly corrupt reading. Moreover, the reason why the Savior was sent so late is excellently explained by Theodoret, *Against the Greeks*, Discourse VI; Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel* VI.10; Gregory of Nyssa, *Catechetical Oration* 39; Leo, Sermon III, *On the Nativity of the Lord*; and Chrysologus, Sermon XVIII, p. 73. ELMENHORST and ORELLI.

### “The boundless continuation of the ages”

A Lucretian expression, which he uses rather often. Lucretius I.1012:

> Or again, unless one of the two limits the other  
> By its simple nature, and only the boundless lies open, etc.

Similarly Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.25, translates a verse of Euripides from an uncertain tragedy as follows:

> You see the lofty, outspread, boundless ether.

“Boundless ether,” that is, “immeasurable,” τὸν ἄπειρον αἰθέρα, “the infinite ether.” HERALDUS and NOURRY.

### “Human beings were once demigods—heroes—with monstrous and enormous bodies”

See the materials collected by Girolamo Maggi, *Miscellanies* II.4. ORELLI.

### “You read that they uttered Stentorian wails”

An expression drawn from Stentor, the loudest-voiced of the Greeks, who is mentioned in Homer, *Iliad* V.785 ff., and from whom the proverb “louder than Stentor” arose. Juvenal, Satire XIII.112:

> In your misery you shout, so that you might surpass Stentor.

Compare Dio Chrysostom, *First Tarsian Oration*. The manuscript has: “that they uttered centenarian wails,” from which Meursius produced: “that they certainly uttered varied wails.” ELMENHORST.

### “Their bones, dug up in various regions, etc.”

See Herodotus I.68; Aulus Gellius III.10; Solinus, chapter 15; Phlegon of Tralles, *Marvels*; Servius on *Aeneid* IX, p. 578; Juvenal, Satire XV; Glycas, p. 370. ELMENHORST and STEWECH.

### “Made it credible”

Fulvius Ursinus conjectures “would make it credible,” not badly. ORELLI.]

### LXXV

You may object and demand in reply: “Why was the Savior sent forth so late?” In infinite and everlasting ages, absolutely nothing should be called late. For where there is no end and no beginning, nothing is delayed. Time is known by its boundaries and endpoints, which a succession and boundless continuation of ages cannot possess.

What if the very circumstances to which aid had to be brought required this opportune moment? What if ancient things were of one condition and subsequent things of another? What if aid had to be given to the people of old in one way, and provision made for later people in another? Do you not hear your own writings record that human beings were once demigods—[Col. 0932B] heroes—with monstrous and enormous bodies? Do you not read that infants beneath their mothers’ breasts uttered Stentorian wails, and that their bones, dug up in various regions, scarcely made their discoverers believe that they were the remains of human limbs?

It is therefore possible that almighty God, the one God, sent forth Christ only when our race of human beings began to be weaker and our nature more feeble. If what has been done today could have been done [Note: [Col. 0932C] Thus Sabaeus; others read “ought to have been done.”] thousands of years ago, the supreme king would have done it then. Or if what has been done today ought to have been accomplished after an equal number of thousands of years, nothing compelled God to fail to await the necessary [Col. 0932C] measures of time. His affairs are carried out according to fixed principles, [Col. 0933A] and what has once been decreed to happen cannot be altered by any novelty.

[Note: [Col. 0933B]

### LXXVI.—“Since, therefore, you say that you serve the almighty God, why does he permit you to endure such great persecutions?”

The nations made very extensive use of this argument, as is clear from the ecclesiastical writers, who answered it abundantly. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.2:

> But the more moderate among the pagans, who appeared to sympathize to some degree, repeatedly reproached them, saying: “Where is their God, and what benefit did they gain from the religion that they chose even in preference to their own lives?”

Compare Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, chapter XII; Justin Martyr, *First Apology for the Christians*, p. 34; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* II [printed “XI”], pp. 216–17; Gaudentius, Preface to Benevolus, pp. 46–47; Eusebius, *Demonstration of the Gospel* X.8; Lactantius V.12. HERALDUS and ELMENHORST.]

And that you establish sacred abodes for them. So the manuscript and the Leiden edition. Others, following a conjecture of Fulvius Ursinus, read: “sacred temples . . .” ORELLI.

And consume all the incense-boxes upon altars full of incense. [Col. 0933C] For *conficiatis* (“consume”) I think we should write *conjiciatis* (“cast”), that is, that you pour the incense-boxes themselves onto the altars, and do not merely sprinkle incense with the tips of your fingers. For those who wished to venerate the gods more religiously heaped incense upon the altars and poured it out not merely by the incense-box, but by the full platter; and everything that others did moderately in the worship of the gods, these people performed extravagantly—ὑπερβολικῶς (“to excess”)—and lavishly. They therefore slaughtered hecatombs, piled incense upon the altars, and poured out wine most abundantly. Or one might also read, “all the heaps of incense,” a form of expression he employs below, Book VII; Tibullus, IV, Elegy VI, 1:

> Natal Juno, receive these sacred heaps of incense  
> Which a tender, learned maiden gives you with her hand.

Martial:

> I have consumed the salted meal and heaps of incense;  
> The flock allotted them to me, while lamb after lamb was falling.

HERALDUS. The editor of the Leiden edition admitted the emendation into the text. [Col. 0933D] Yet Heraldus himself, in his *Second Observations*, thinks that the reading should be: “all the incense-boxes full of incense,” etc. Ancient grammarians differ no less than modern scholars in determining the meaning of the word *acerra*. Festus: “An *acerra* is an altar which used to be placed before a dead person and on which perfumes were burned; others say that it is an incense-chest, namely one in which incense was stored.” G. J. Vossius also agrees with Festus in his *Roman Etymology*, interpreting *acerra* as a small altar or bronze vessel in which perfumes were burned; and in this sense *acerra*, denoting the censer itself, may be read in Martianus Capella, *On the Marriage of Philology*, Book II, p. 46, Bern edition: “The maiden’s hands are burdened with an *acerra* heavy with many spices and itself glowing.” Note that the *acerra* is glowing—that is, with fire. So too in the Twelve Tables, Table X, law 12: *Nei loncai coronai, neive acerai preferuntor* (“Let neither long garlands nor acerras be carried before”); what is meant is undoubtedly not incense-chests but the burning and smoking censers or braziers themselves, customarily carried in front at funerals. See Funccius’s note, p. 453. If this [Col. 0934B] interpretation is correct, *conficiatis* seems to me perfectly sound. For *conficere* here is the same as *consumere*, “to consume,” namely by burning or fumigation: *ganze Rauchfässer ausbrennen* (“to burn out entire censers”). Thus Cicero, *On Divination* II.57: “What age is there that can consume the divine power?” But Jani and Mitscherlich, on Horace III, Ode VIII, 2 ff., and the recent editor König, on Persius, Satire II.5, interpret *acerra* as a square incense-box, generally fashioned elegantly from bronze, from which incense was taken and cast into the fire (*das Weihrauchkästchen*, “the little incense-box”); it must be carefully distinguished from the censer in which incense was burned. If we follow that explanation, then in our passage the reading must certainly be *conjiciatis* (“cast”). ORELLI.

“By which they daily drive you,” etc. Since *agimus* (“we conduct”) preceded, Stewechius, to avoid the disagreeable repetition of *agere*, thinks that one should read *vos subigunt* (“they subdue you”), or, in the more ancient form, *subagunt*. What if we read *vos angunt* (“they distress you”)? Nothing should be changed: *agunt* means “they agitate, harass.” Thus [Col. 0934C] the Greeks say ἄγειν καὶ φέρειν, “to drive and carry off.” ORELLI.

“The loss of loved ones.” *Pignora* refers not only to children but also to parents. Thus Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chapter 12: “It was demonstrated to us even then that both loved ones and crafts and occupations must be abandoned for the Lord, when James and John, called by the Lord, left both their father and their boat.” The reference, of course, is to the man who declined to take time to bury his father in order that he might come to Christ. PRIOR.—Quintilian, *Institutes* VI.1.24: “In these matters age, sex, and loved ones also carry weight; by ‘loved ones’ I mean children, parents, and relatives.” ORELLI.

“While enclosed in the little skin of this morsel of flesh.” Nonius: “Lucilius used *folliculus* (‘little skin’ or ‘bag’) for the body” (Book XXVI): “What I am, if indeed I am anything, and what skin I am clothed in—I cannot [the quotation breaks off].” Arnobius, on Psalm 149: “In the expansion of our bodily bellows.” Tertullian, *Apology*, final chapter: “Pound, pound the skin of Anaxarchus.” ELMENHORST.—A familiar expression of the Stoics. See Gataker on Marcus Antoninus, *Commentaries* VIII.37, p. 309 ff., London edition, and the distinguished Böttiger, *Sabina*, p. 318. ORELLI. The Greeks similarly use θύλακος, “sack.” Theodoret, [Col. 0934D] *On the Martyrs*, Book VIII: “Nor even that Anaxarchus who, while being pounded with iron pestles, said, as they report: ‘Pound the sack of Anaxarchus; for it is not Anaxarchus that you are pounding.’” He took this from Diogenes Laertius, Book IX, in the life of Anaxarchus, where it reads: “Pound the sack of Anaxarchus; for it is not Anaxarchus that you are striking.” Tertullian rendered it word for word in the final chapter of the *Apology*: “When Anaxarchus was being pounded to death with a barley-pounding pestle, he said: ‘Pound, pound the skin of Anaxarchus; for it is not Anaxarchus that you are pounding.’” And just as these writers said “skin,” so Varro used “bark” in his *Tithonus, or On Old Age*: “Thus the mature soul, though reluctant, easily left its bodily bark.” SCALIGER, on the *Virgilian Catalepton*, p. 301. Compare Petavius on Themistius, Oration XVII, p. 724. Compare especially C. A. Duker, *On the Latinity of the Jurists*, p. 233, and C. Rittershausen on Salvian, Book III, *Against Avarice*, §497, p. 153. ORELLI.

“Indeed, we have been taught to regard and esteem lightly all the threats of Fortune, whatever they may be.” The passage is perfectly sound, though some have vainly attempted to interpolate it. For Arnobius says this: “Indeed, we have been taught to regard and esteem lightly all the threats of Fortune, whatever those threats may ultimately be.” The obscurity of this passage was therefore produced by the displacement of the word *Fortunae* (“of Fortune”), from which the corruption of the following words arose. HERALDUS.—Meursius punctuates it thus: “to regard and esteem lightly. Of Fortune, and if ever . . .” Incorrectly. ORELLI.

“And if at any time some more grievous violence should assail us, which the end must necessarily follow, not to fear or flee from it, so that more easily,” etc. [Col. 0935C] Heraldus has arranged the passage excellently in this way. In earlier editions it is most corruptly printed: “. . . to attain; to ascribe it to misfortune; pleasure neither to fear nor flee.” Here the words “to ascribe it to misfortune” undoubtedly arose when a copyist incorrectly interpreted the preceding words *aestimare Fortunae* in the margin, taking *Fortunae* as dative rather than genitive; and then, beside the following words, “nor will torment inflict punishment,” wrote in the same margin: “but pleasure.” The Leiden editor recasts the passage: “which must necessarily bring about the end of life; not to fear it,” etc. But *finis* used absolutely means death, as it very often does. The meaning is therefore: “If at any time some more grievous violence should assail us, which must necessarily be followed or attended by the end—that is, death.” ORELLI.]

### LXXVI

“When, therefore,” you say, “you serve almighty God and trust that he takes care of your salvation and safety, why does he allow you to undergo such great persecutions and to endure every kind of punishment and torture?”

Let us ask you in return why, although you worship so many and such innumerable gods, establish sacred temples for them, fashion images out of gold, slaughter herds of living creatures, and consume all the incense-boxes upon altars full of incense, you do not live immune from the many dangers and storms by which destructive and manifold misfortunes daily [Col. 0934A] harass you. Why, I ask, do your gods refrain from turning away from you the many kinds of diseases and infirmities, shipwrecks, collapses, fires, pestilences, barrenness, the loss of loved ones, the confiscation of property, dissensions, wars, feuds, the capture of cities, and, once free birth has been taken away, slavery?

“But neither does God assist us in cases of this kind.” The reason is ready and evident. Nothing has been promised to us for this life, nor, while we are enclosed in the little skin of this morsel of flesh, has any aid been pledged or assistance decreed to us. Indeed, we have been taught to regard and esteem lightly all the threats of Fortune, whatever they may be. And if [Col. 0935A] at any time some more grievous violence should assail us, which the end must necessarily follow, we have been taught not to fear or flee from it, so that we may be more easily stripped of our bodily bonds and escape the blindness of darkness.

[Note: [Col. 0935C]

### LXXVII.—“A man committed to prison, with tortures,” etc.

Fulvius Ursinus corrected it thus, excellently. The manuscript has, corruptly: “a man born for prison, an entrance of tortures,” etc.; for *ingressum* (“entrance”) is plainly a gloss. HERALDUS. Others—for example Elmenhorst [Col. 0935D] in the Hanover edition—read: “a man condemned in prison.” As Arnobius calls this bodily dwelling in which the soul is detained a “prison,” so Empedocles, in Aeneas of Gaza’s *Theophrastus*, calls it a “cave”; Arrian, in Epictetus I.9, calls it “bonds,” δεσμά; Nemesius, *On the Nature of Man*, chapter III, calls it a “tunic” or “garment”; and so forth. See C. Barth, *Adversaria* XLII.12, p. 1873 ff. ORELLI.

“Destructive blindness.” Thus Virgil, *Georgics* II.256: “to seek out destructive cold,” that is, harmful and exceedingly troublesome cold; and Rutilius, *Itinerary* I.53:

> May accursed oblivion sooner overwhelm the sun.

See the commentators there. Compare C. Barth, *Adversaria* XXV.15, p. 1246. ORELLI.

“Mangled and violently maltreated.” The glosses: *Lancino*, θυννάζω, “I cut or mangle.” Papias: “*Lancinate*: to butcher, to tear apart.” Prudentius, *On the Crowns of Martyrdom*: “All this for which we are mangled causes no pain.” ELMENHORST. [Col. 0936B] See above, on chapter 8 and on Book I, chapter XLI. For *divexatis* (“violently maltreated”), the Leiden edition, following the manuscript, gives *diu vexatis* (“long maltreated”). ORELLI.

“The more you press upon us . . . the more you relieve us of tight and heavy bonds.” Stewechius thinks it should read: *quanto instatis . . . tanto artis*, that is, “the more you press . . . the more you relieve us of tighter bonds.” “More,” “to a greater degree,” “better,” and similar expressions are frequently omitted by Latin authors after the custom of the Greeks. Thus Book I, chapter LVII: “faith in neighbors and those living nearby, rather than in those separated [Col. 0936C] by remoteness of distance.” Stewechius likewise seems to have read *telis* (“weapons”) for *vinculis* (“bonds”). If that reading came from the manuscript, I do not think it should be rejected outright, since it could derive from *tela, -ae* (“web”). Elmenhorst aptly compares our passage with Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I: “But if anything of this kind should happen to us, so that it seems to have been announced by God, let us cheerfully depart from life, obeying and giving thanks, and let us consider that we are being released from custody and relieved of our bonds.” ORELLI.]

### LXXVII

Accordingly, that harshness of persecution of which you speak is our liberation, not persecution; the torment will not inflict punishment but will lead us forth into the light of freedom. It is as though some brutish and foolish person should suppose that he could never subject a man committed to prison to severe and monstrous tortures unless he vented his rage upon the prison itself—breaking up its material, burning its roof, stripping away its wall, doors, and the other parts of the structure, tearing them down and battering them apart—unaware that by this very act he was giving light to the man whom he thought he was harming and taking away his destructive blindness.

In just the same way, with the flames, exiles, [Col. 0935B] tortures, and wild beasts by which you mangle [Note: [Col. 0935B] Fulvius reads “tear.”] and violently maltreat our bodies, you do not take life from us, but relieve us of our little skins and hides. You do not know that the more [manuscript: “so much”] you press upon these images and outward forms of ours and persist in raging against them, the more [manuscript: “so much”] you relieve us of tight and heavy bonds and, once our restraints have been cut away, enable us to fly forth into the light. [Col. 0936A]

[Note: [Col. 0936C]

### LXXVIII.—“Something must also be done without a rational account.”

That is, where reason fails, action must proceed through trust placed in God alone and through obedience subjected solely to his will as declared by himself. Compare *Enchiridion* XXXII.3, where Epictetus teaches that God must be consulted concerning those matters in which we must act but in which no reason or human art enables us to discover what decision to make: οὔτε ἐκ λόγου, οὔτε ἐκ τέχνης τινὸς ἄλλης, ἀφορμαὶ δίδονται πρὸς τὸ συνιδεῖν τὸ προκείμενον, “no starting points are supplied, either by reason or by any other art, for discerning the matter before us.” SCHWEIGHÄUSER, on Epictetus, Fragment 181.

“As Arrian attests that Epictetus said.” [Col. 0936D] Arnobius appears to have had in view Arrian’s *Commentaries* I.12, where Epictetus teaches that a person ought to follow God in all things and submit himself to God’s will, even if he has not fully perceived God’s purposes and the usefulness of the things God has commanded. ORELLI.

“Of the name.” Fulvius Ursinus reads “of the divinity,” incorrectly. ORELLI.

“What we are unwilling should be true, and strive against.” The Leiden edition reads: “what we are unwilling should be true, and deny.” But nothing should be changed. *Adnitimur* means that we strive for it “not to be,” an expression to be understood from the preceding “we are unwilling that it should be.” Examples of this kind of anacoluthon in our author have already been noted above. It is preferable, however, to read *obnitimur* (“strive against”), with Gesner in his *Thesaurus*, who cites this example from Arnobius as a ἅπαξ λεγόμενον, a unique occurrence. ORELLI.

“Be found in the jaws of hostile death.” See above, at the end of chapter 53 of this book, and C. Barth on Statius, *Achilleid* II.176, vol. III, p. 1729. ORELLI.]

### LXXVIII

Therefore, people, cease obstructing your own hopes with empty questions. Nor, if something is otherwise than you suppose, ought you to trust your own opinions rather than an august reality. Times full of danger press upon us, and deadly punishments hang over us; let us flee for refuge to the saving God, and let us not demand a rational account of the gift offered to us.

When the salvation of souls and concern for us are at stake [Note: Others read *agitur* for *agatur*.], something must also be done without a rational account, as Arrian attests that Epictetus said. We doubt, we hesitate, and we suspect that what is said is not wholly credible. Let us commit ourselves to God, and let not our own unbelief have greater weight with us than the greatness of his name and power, lest, while we search out arguments for ourselves by which what we are unwilling should be true, and strive against, may appear false, the final day steal upon us and we be found in the jaws of hostile death.

# BOOK III

[Col. 0937]

## INDEX OF CHAPTERS

[Col. 0937A] The Christian religion has long since been more than sufficiently defended by distinguished men; nevertheless, being entirely unshaken in itself, it has no need whatever of any defender. Chapter 1.

Resuming the defense that had been interrupted, Arnobius answers the pagans’ question why Christians neither worshiped nor adored the gods. In God, the creator of all things, Christians worship and adore whatever ought to be worshiped and adored. Therefore, if there are any gods, they derive their origin from him and are worshiped in him. Chapters 2–3.

But the pagans could never prove that those beings truly were gods, since it always remained unknown to them either whence the gods had received their names or how great their multitude was. Chapters 4–5.

The author proceeds further and, from what the pagans proclaimed about [Col. 0937B] their gods, demonstrates with complete clarity that no such gods exist. First, they worshiped male and female gods; but it is shown that the divine nature is incapable of either sex. Furthermore, if the gods of the nations could beget and be begotten, then, since they are imagined to be immortal, their number would by now be infinite. Chapters 6–9.

In addition, the gods would be polluted by shameful desires and pleasures. There is therefore no reason for the pagans to take offense when Christians reject gods of this kind who beget and are begotten. Chapters 10–12.

Arnobius next censures the Gentiles because, like the Sadducees, they were persuaded that the gods were shaped and constituted in bodily and human form. Chapters 12–13.

Once this has been admitted, however, the gods would have to be said either to resemble or to differ from one another. Both alternatives are absurd. [Col. 0937C] Chapters 14–15.

Arnobius demonstrates that neither should those be heard who replied that human form was assigned to the gods solely for the sake of honor. Chapter 16.

Therefore, although God hears, sees, and understands, he can possess no outward form or figure. We know one thing: there is nothing bodily and nothing belonging to human passions in God, whose nature can be explained by no mortal speech. Chapters 17–19.

Arnobius ridicules the pagans because they introduce gods presiding over human duties, occupations, and other affairs, whether good or bad. Chapters 20–21. [Col. 0937D] [Col. 0938A]

The author confirms his position by completing an enumeration of the duties over which the gods preside. Chapters 22–25.

He pursues the same argument and concludes that opinions of this kind will never persuade Christians, however much they are called impious and atheists. Chapters 26–28.

Arnobius further demonstrates clearly that the gods of the Gentiles are wholly fictitious, from the various opinions circulated about those same divinities: first concerning Janus, Saturn, Jupiter, and Juno. Chapters 29–30.

Next concerning Minerva, Neptune, Mercury, the Great Mother, Liber, and Apollo; in addition, concerning Diana, Ceres, and others, as well as the World, which some have vainly supposed to be the eternal God. From this variety of utterly ridiculous opinions, the falsity of the remaining gods is most clearly demonstrated. [Col. 0938B] Chapters 31–36.

Arnobius proves the same thing no less effectively from the absurd disagreements among those same pagans concerning the origin and number of their gods: first concerning the Muses, Chapter 37; the Novensiles, Chapters 38–39; the Penates, Chapter 40; and the Lares, Chapters 41–42.

Amid such great disagreements, no pagan was ever able to discern which of them was the true God, or which was to be honored, invoked, and entreated. Chapters 43–44.

[Note: [Col. 0937D]

### I.—“For the Christian religion cannot fail to stand without defenders.”

In this passage *stare* means “to remain and endure,” as in Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.539:

> And among those who remember, gratitude for an ancient deed securely endures.

Suetonius, *Otho*, chapter 5: “For he did not conceal the fact that he could not remain standing unless he became emperor, and that it made no difference whether he fell before the enemy in battle or beneath his creditors in the Forum.” The Old Latin translator of the Book of Ecclesiasticus (Jesus son of Sirach), chapter XL: “Faith will stand forever.” ELMENHORST.—The manuscript has: [Col. 0938D] “For neither can the Christian religion remain without defenders,” etc. Meursius attempts to defend this reading in his *Appendix*, as does Salmasius in his *Plinian Exercises on Solinus*, p. 21, maintaining that *restare* is an ancient verb meaning “to stand” or “remain,” on the basis of Propertius III, Elegy VIII.31:

> While the Danaans prevail, while barbarian Hector stands against them.

Yet Salmasius appears afterward to have withdrawn this opinion, for in the Leiden edition he prints the passage thus: “For neither can a thing stand without defenders, and the Christian religion,” where *et* would be equivalent to *id est*, “that is.” See Stewechius’s note on Book II, [Col. 0939C] chapter 70. And that passage of Propertius proves absolutely nothing. For there “Hector stands against them” means that he resists, strives against, and fights back. What Heraldus advances on this passage is mere sophistry. Others punctuate: “For neither . . . the Christian religion?” Incorrectly, for *neque enim* can never stand at the beginning of a question. ORELLI.

“To abolish faith in it.” The manuscript has: “to arrogate its end.” Very corruptly. MEURSIUS, in the *Appendix*.]

### I

Long since, indeed, all these accusations—or rather slanders, to speak the truth—have been answered sufficiently, fully, and carefully by distinguished men [Col. 0938C] on this side who have deserved to know that truth. Not a single point of any question has been passed over that was not refuted in a thousand ways and by the most powerful arguments. It is therefore unnecessary to linger any longer over this part of the case.

For surely the Christian religion cannot fail to stand without defenders? Or will it be proved true only if it has many supporters and derives its authority from human beings? It is content with its own powers and rests upon the foundations of its own truth. Nor is it stripped of its force even if [Col. 0938D] it has no defender at all—indeed, even if every tongue speaks against it, [Col. 0939A] strives in opposition, and conspires with the passion of united agreement to abolish faith in it.

[Note: [Col. 0939C]

### II.—“For the present we can say.”

Here *interim* is equivalent to the Greek τέως, “for now,” “for the present” (*für jetzt, für einmal*). Thus Tacitus, *Annals* I.5: “And besides, two young men who for the present weigh down the state, and will one day tear it apart.” See Oberlin there. ORELLI.

“The first God.” Nourry thinks that Arnobius called God the Father “first” with reference to God the Son, that is, Christ. But “the first God” means nothing other than God as the beginning, fountain, and origin of all things. ORELLI.]

### II

Let us now return to the sequence from which we were compelled to digress a little while ago, lest the defense, interrupted for too long, be said to have conceded to our slanderers the victory due to a proven charge. For they next raise this objection: “If divine religion is dear to you, why do you not worship and adore the other gods together with us? Why do you not participate in the sacred rites common to your peoples and join in the ceremonies of their religions?”

For the present we can say: for fulfilling the worship of divinity, the first God is sufficient for us—the first God, I say, the Father and Lord of all things, the founder and governor of everything. In him we worship everything that is to be worshiped; we adore everything that ought to be adored; and whatever claims the obedience of reverence, we seek to merit by our acts of reverence. For since we possess the very head of divinity, from whom the divinity of all divine beings, whatever they may be, derives, we consider it superfluous to go through each one individually—especially since we do not know either who they are or what names they possess, and cannot obtain any clear, comprehended, or established knowledge of their number. [Col. 0939B]

[Note: [Col. 0939C]

### III.—“To adore by name together with the rulers.”

“Together with the rulers” means beside or near the rulers, with honor equal to theirs. Thus Statius, *Achilleid* I.13:

> And Thebes recalls me among the ancient names  
> Of her forefathers, together with her Amphion.

See C. Barth there, vol. III, p. 1590 ff., and vol. I, p. 20. ORELLI.

Adoration was also offered to kings; hence the frequent expression, “to adore the sacred purple.” HERALDUS.—Compare Elmenhorst on this passage and Arntzen on Mamertinus, *Birthday Panegyric for Maximinus*, chapter XI, in *Ancient Panegyrics*, vol. I, p. 142. “By name” means by addressing the name of each individual. On the adoration of the sacred purple, see especially Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus XVI.5.18, p. 132 ff., Wagner edition. ORELLI.

“And this, indeed, may have been stated by us in this way, provided it is clear and established that besides the king and ruler himself there are still other individual beings.” I have followed the emendation of the Leiden editor. The manuscript has “that there are other, not heads,” [Col. 0940C] a reading rightly regarded with suspicion by scholars. Gelenius prints, “that there are no other heads.” Meursius, p. 87: “that there are some heads.” Others: “that there are other new heads.” Heraldus, however, defends the manuscript reading, thinking that by “other non-heads” Arnobius means the common people of the gods, apart from their head and ruler. It seems to me that *non* arose from a copyist’s misunderstanding of the word *capita*. For *capita* here by no means signifies rulers or the foremost gods, but, on the contrary, gods of the lesser nations, the common people of the gods, as he says in what follows—as though they were proletarians and persons counted only by the head. Thus among the Romans *caput* is very often used with a certain contempt and mockery, as in “shameful creature” and “charming creature.” Likewise the “heads of a flock” are not the rams, but the individuals that constitute the entire flock. See Gesner’s *Thesaurus*. C. Barth’s proposal in *Adversaria* XLIII.6, p. 1935 ff., should therefore be dismissed: he reads *monoptota*, as though Arnobius were alluding to the grammarians’ “monoptotes,” that is, nouns possessing only one case, such as *sponte*—a notion wholly foreign to this passage. ORELLI.

“And that you should wish to show us those images also.” The construction is thoroughly Arnobian, for he often mixes and transposes those particles. HERALDUS.—The Leiden edition reads: “and those images,” etc. ORELLI.

“Which you too understand, but refuse and decline to confess.” I have printed this with Heraldus in his *Second Observations*, who thus corrected the manuscript, where *ses* is read instead of *sed recusatis* (“but you refuse”). Others read merely “and decline,” omitting “refuse,” which Stewechius was the first to restore to Arnobius from the Royal manuscript. Heraldus, however, in his own edition suspects it of being a gloss—incorrectly, in my opinion, for he himself has observed that Arnobius very frequently joins words with the same meaning. In that edition Heraldus thinks it should read “and do not decline,” because, he says, the Gentiles themselves by no means denied that those images had been fashioned by craftsmen from bronze, clay, or silver. But, as we have seen, he withdrew this opinion in his *Second Observations*. Salmasius printed: “but you refuse and decline,” etc.; this should be adopted if it came from the manuscript, as Stewechius and Meursius attest. ORELLI.

“Of the name.” Meursius conjectures “of the divinity.” ORELLI.]

### III

Just as in earthly kingdoms we are under no necessity to adore by name, together with the rulers, those established in royal households, but whatever is attached to the kings silently feels itself embraced by honor in the worship of the kings themselves [Note: Sabaeus reads: “feels itself embraced by the silent force of honor.”], so by no different principle, whoever these gods may be whom you set before us as existing—if they are a royal offspring and spring from the sovereign head—even if they receive no worship from us by name, nevertheless understand that they are honored collectively together with their king and included in the reverence paid to him. [Col. 0940A]

And this, indeed, may have been stated by us in this way, provided it is clear and established that besides the king and ruler himself there are other individual beings which, arranged and distinguished by number, constitute, as it were, a people drawn from a plebeian multitude. Nor, in sacred temples, should you wish to show us as gods effigies and those images which you too understand, but refuse and decline to confess, to be forms of the cheapest clay and childish fabrications of craftsmen. [Col. 0940B]

When we discuss a divine matter with you, what we demand that you show is that there are other gods by nature, power, and name—not those set before us in images, which we see, but gods existing in that substance in which the power belonging to so great a name must properly be judged to reside. But it is not our purpose to linger longer over this part of the case, lest we appear intent upon stirring up the greatest disputes and engaging in tumultuous contests.

[Col. 0941A] [Note: [Col. 0941B]

### IV.—“We assent, acquiesce, and connive.”

Heraldus and Stewechius added “connive” from the manuscript. ORELLI.

“We transfix this doubtful and ambiguous matter.” Meursius prefers *conficimus*, “we settle.” But *configimus*, “we transfix,” as though with weapons, is more expressive. ORELLI.

“Or whether they themselves gave themselves these names on their days of purification.” Thus Meursius and Heraldus, with the approval of the Leiden editor. Correctly. The “day of purification” was the day on which infants were purified and received their name. Among the Romans it was the ninth day for males and the eighth for females, according to Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.16, Festus, and Plutarch. Among the Greeks it was the tenth day, as is clear from Harpocration, the Suda, Hesychius, the author of the *Proverbs*, the scholiast on Aristophanes, and others; sometimes [Col. 0941C] it was also the seventh. See Meursius, p. 87. The manuscript has “on days . . . of mockery,” which Stewechius alone defends, taking it to mean “festive days,” just as “autumn days” can be used for “autumnal days.” See above, on Book I, chapter 21. Gelenius reads “on festive days,” a reading defended by C. Barth, *Adversaria* XLIII.6, who understands by “festive days” the days on which games and sacred rites were held for each god. Fulvius Ursinus reads: “from matters . . . of amusement.” But Meursius’s emendation alone is correct. ORELLI.

“You used to see.” Meursius and Heraldus think one should read “you had seen,” because “you had known” follows. But such alternations of tense, ἐναλλαγαί, are frequent in Arnobius. ORELLI.]

### IV

Let there be, as you proclaim, this common people of divinities; let there be innumerable nations of gods. We assent, acquiesce, and connive, and we do not transfix this doubtful and ambiguous matter as part of any dispute.

Nevertheless, we demand and ask to hear this from you: whence did it become known to you, or by what reasoning was it ascertained, that those whom you suppose to exist and worship are in heaven, rather than some other beings of whom neither opinion nor name has ever been heard? For it may be that those whom you do not think to exist do exist, while those in whose existence you trust are found in no part of nature. You have never flown up to the stars of heaven and seen the faces and countenances of each. Nor, remembering which gods were there, did you establish the worship of those same gods here as beings known and seen. [Col. 0941B]

But we also desire once again [Col. 0942A] to hear from you whether they merely have these names by which you call them imposed upon them, or whether they themselves gave themselves these names on their days of purification. If these names are divine and heavenly, who transmitted them to you? But if the designations they bear were applied by you, how could you give names to beings whom you had never seen and whose nature or identity you had not known through any acquaintance whatsoever [Note: Sabaeus reads “through no acquaintance”]?

[Note: [Col. 0941C]

### V.—“Let them also be called by those names under which popular opinion causes them to be enrolled as gods of the people.”

Some remove the word *populares* (“gods of the people”), regarding it as superfluous and useless. But this reading is also supported by the Royal manuscript, where *popularem* is incorrectly written. The preceding words explain it clearly: “that there are other individual beings which, arranged and distinguished by number, constitute, as it were, a people drawn from a plebeian multitude.” Hence he calls them *populares*, as though they were plebeians and did not occupy that first rank. Lactantius, Book I, chapter 5: “Antisthenes held that there were indeed many gods of the people, but one natural God, that is, the maker of the whole universe.” HERALDUS.—C. Barth, *Adversaria* XLIII.6, p. 1937, thinks it should read: “Let them also be called by those names under which popular opinion causes them to be enrolled collectively.” Not badly. ORELLI.

“Yet how do you know which beings complete the register under these names?” Heraldus printed this from the Royal manuscript, except that he changed *sensum* (“meaning”), the reading in the parchment, to *censum* (“register”). But, as C. Barth rightly observes in the passage cited from his *Adversaria*, the word *quae* (“which things”) has no antecedent unless we say that Arnobius, writing hastily, had “divinities” in mind, although he had written “gods” immediately before. Fulvius Ursinus therefore gives the better reading: “who complete the register of this name,” that is, who are worthy to be entered in the census-roll of this name—namely, that of the gods. Arnobius is evidently alluding to the Roman census. Thus someone who possesses enough wealth to be enrolled on the roll of patricians or knights is said to “complete the census” [Col. 0942B] of the senators or knights. Not understanding this form of expression, Sabaeus and Gelenius printed: “which complete the meaning of this name.” C. Barth, in the passage cited from the *Adversaria*, thinks one should read: “Yet whence, I ask, do they complete the register under these names?” Meursius: “Yet whence, I ask you, do they complete the register of this name?” Stewechius reads: “Yet whence do they complete for you the register of this cognomen?” The Leiden editor recasts the passage thus: “Yet whence have you the ability to know how many complete the meaning of this name?” The words “to you” seem to me to produce a disagreeable repetition with the following words, “whether any are known to you,” etc. If conjecture is permissible, I would alter the passage thus: “Yet how do you know which or how many complete the register with their names?” By *census* I understand a roll in which the names of the gods are entered, *das Götterregister* (“the register of gods”). I would therefore translate: *Woher wisst, kennt ihr alle diejenigen, die mit ihren Namen das Götterregister anfüllen?* (“Whence do you know—are you acquainted with—all those who fill the register of gods with their names?”) Or *his* (“under these”) can stand, referring to the plebeian names of the gods of the lesser nations, with which Arnobius had dealt in the preceding passage. ORELLI.

“Whether their total population is without any total.” *Populositas* means “abundance” or “numerousness,” like *populosus*; these are terms from the declining period of the Latin language, used by Apuleius, Solinus, Vegetius, and Ammianus Marcellinus. See Vossius, *On Faults of Speech*, and Olaus Borrichius, *Reflections*, p. 197. The construction is: “whether their numerousness is without any total,” that is, cannot be expressed in numbers, as he says in what follows: “The total number of gods may have no total and may not be bounded by a numerical limit.” ORELLI.

“Or are there any whose names are unknown to you, who have at some time been brought into customary use and recognition?” I have admitted into the text this exceedingly acute and, as it seems to me, entirely correct emendation of C. Barth, *Adversaria* XLIII, [Col. 0942D] chapter 6, p. 1937:

> Arnobius asks his adversaries whence they know that they themselves know all the names of the gods; whence it is established for them that there are not more gods than they worship; and whether the number they had established was ever increased by any gods previously unknown by name. Those foolish babblers could not escape the argument by any means. For whenever individual nations had been conquered, new divinities were consecrated by the Romans. Nor was it possible for them to provide a definite number even of the gods whom they worshiped, much less of all gods, whose number, according to them, could be infinite. This sense is clearly confirmed by what follows. The manuscript had *in cognitione*: from this we produced *incogniti nomine*. For *one* is an ancient abbreviation for *nomine*. And the entire question here concerns the names of the gods, as well as their number.

So far Barth. Correctly. “Gods unknown by name” are therefore those of whom some knowledge reached human beings, but concerning whose name, number, power, and so forth there was uncertainty, such as the Novensiles, Penates, Consentes, Lares, and others, whom he discusses below, chapter 41 ff. Such also [Col. 0943B] was that θεὸς ἄγνωστος, “unknown god,” of the Athenians, whose altar Saint Paul saw. See Acts of the Apostles XVII.23.

*In cognitione*, the manuscript reading, is much better than *in cognitionem*, which Meursius and the Leiden editor wished to substitute; for *in cognitione* would depend on the preceding “are.” Thus “they are known to you” is equivalent to “you know them.” But “to be brought into cognition” and “to be brought into recognition” are plainly one and the same thing. We know, indeed, that Arnobius very frequently joins words of the same meaning. But in this passage, if I see correctly, the words “brought at some time into customary use and recognition” are manifestly separate from the preceding “known.”

Stewechius suspects that the reading should be: “or are any brought to your knowledge rather than to customary recognition?”—with the particle “rather” suppressed, which, as Stewechius himself shows above on Book II, chapter 77, is frequently omitted by Arnobius. On this reading *cognitio*, that is, full and perfect knowledge of the gods, is distinguished from merely obscure [Col. 0943C] acquaintance with them. For *in usum* (“into customary use”), Meursius and Heraldus in his *Second Observations* prefer *in visum* (“into sight”), incorrectly. “Use” is equivalent to “worship.” ORELLI.

“Let us suppose that you worship a thousand gods.” Orpheus, in Theophilus, *To Autolycus* III, acknowledges 360 gods. Varro, in Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter XIV, acknowledges three hundred Joves or Jupiters. ELMENHORST.

It is possible that there are more than this. “More than this,” namely, in number. Above, Book II, chap. 28: “many years ago, if you wish to say eighty, or more than this,” where “in time” must be supplied. On this ellipsis see Sanctius, *Minerva*, Book IV, chap. 4, and Bunemann on Lactantius, *Institutions*, Book VII, chap. 14, p. 931. ORELLI.

For a corresponding part. That is, in place of the one true God whom we worship. ORELLI.]

## V

But, as you wish and believe, and as you are persuaded, let these be gods [Note: [Col. 0941B] “Let them be” in Sabaeus; “Let them be absent” in the manuscript]; and let them also be called by those names under which popular common opinion holds that they are commonly registered [Note: [Col. 0942B] Fulvius deletes this word. The manuscript has the singular “common”]. Yet how can you know how many complete the register of this name, even though some have been brought within your knowledge [Col. 0942B] and at some time brought into use and acquaintance? [Col. 0943A] For it is not easy to know whether the multitude constituting their number is definite and fixed, or whether their population is without any total and bounded by no method of computation.

Let us suppose that you worship a thousand gods—or rather five thousand. Yet perhaps it may be the case in the nature of things that there are a hundred thousand gods; perhaps there are more than this; indeed, as we said shortly before, perhaps the total number of gods is unlimited and not confined within any countable boundary. Therefore either you too are impious, because apart from a few gods you do not perform your duties toward the rest; or, if you ask pardon for your ignorance of the others, you will procure the same pardon for us, if in a corresponding case we abstain from the religious observances of beings whose very existence [Col. 0943B] we do not know at all.

[Col. 0944A] [Note: [Col. 0943C]

### VI.—To be unwilling to undertake the oath of allegiance to the other gods, etc.

He appropriately uses a military term. Vegetius, Book II, chap. 3: “They hasten to undertake the military oath of allegiance.” The glosses: *Sacramentum*—ὅρκος στρατιωτικός, “military oath.” ELMENHORST.—Heraldus thinks that Arnobius is alluding here to the custom [Col. 0943D] of pricking soldiers’ skin, so that by this means they might know themselves to have been consecrated and devoted to military service. Those marks were, as it were, memorials of the military oath, just as οἱ μεμυημένοι, “those initiated into the mysteries,” were also marked with certain signs—what Prudentius, in the *Martyrdom of Romanus*, calls “receiving seals.” But see above, on Book II, chap. 5. ORELLI.

For devoted minds. In the strict sense. Soldiers devoted themselves and consecrated their entire selves to the commonwealth or to Caesar. Vegetius: “They swear by God, Christ, and the Holy Spirit, and by the majesty of the emperor, which, second only to God, must be loved and revered by the human race. For when the emperor has received the title Augustus, faithful devotion must be shown to him as to a God present in bodily form, and vigilant service must be rendered.” Hence those men in Dio, Book LIII, say σοὶ καθοσιώμεθα, “let us be consecrated to you.” For *devovere*, “to devote,” is καθοσιοῦν, “to consecrate,” as the ancient glosses rightly interpret it. HERALDUS.—Compare Lipsius on Tacitus, *Annals*, Book XV, chap. 67, p. 1005, Oberlin’s edition.

[Col. 0944B] “Devoted minds” means the same as pious or religious minds. Thus Lactantius, Book VII: “Let us all follow him, hear him, and obey him with the utmost devotion”; and Juvencus, *History of the Gospels*, Book I, verse 407:

> So that, devoted, the righteous man may worship the Lord of heaven.

Here Koenig, p. 80 of Reusch’s edition, citing our passage, observes that *devotus*, “devoted,” in the sense “pious,” is a word of ecclesiastical Latin. ORELLI.

And we stretch out suppliant hands. I certainly think this is a gloss. For what purpose does “suppliant” serve? Someone added this word because he did not understand the source from which these expressions had been transferred. Thus soldiers, when summoned and wishing to declare themselves ready for the oath, stretched out their hands. I therefore think the text should read: “And we stretch out our hands.” HERALDUS.

Nor do we disdain to go wherever you invite us. This too is taken from military service. Soldiers swore that they would follow [Col. 0944C] their commanders wherever they might lead. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book XI: Ὁ στρατιωτικὸς ὅρκος, ὃν ἁπάντων μάλιστα ἐμπεδῶσι Ῥωμαῖοι, τοῖς στρατηγοῖς ἀκολουθεῖν κελεύει, ὅποι ποτ’ ἂν ἄγωσιν, “The military oath, which the Romans observe more steadfastly than anything else, commands them to follow their generals wherever they may lead.” Horace was alluding to this in *Odes* II.17.9 ff.:

> I have not sworn  
> A faithless oath. We shall go, we shall go,  
> Wherever you lead the way, prepared  
> As companions to travel the final road.

HERALDUS.

“Saturn,” he says, “and Janus.” “He says,” namely the opponent whom Arnobius imagined as pleading the pagans’ case. See above on Book I, chaps. 3 and 34. To these passages one may add what my very dear friend Jacob Ochsner communicated to me: “Besides Ernesti’s *Clavis Ciceroniana*, the following remarks of Bentele on Horace, *Satires* I.4.79 illustrate Heraldus’ observation concerning *inquit*, ‘he says,’ used for *inquiunt*, ‘they say’: ‘*Inquit* is the regular form whenever we imagine that something is being objected and set against us, whether this is done by one person or several, [Col. 0944D] by someone absent or present. Similarly Horace, *Epistles* I.19.43, uses *ait*, “he says” (like Greek φησί), indefinitely.’” Fulvius Ursinus and Johann Scheffer of Strasbourg, therefore, needlessly disturbed this passage in a book of *Adversaria* included in *Miscellaneous Critical Observations*, vol. IX, p. 163, wishing to read *inquiunt*, “they say.” ORELLI.

Aesculapius and the other remaining gods. This should be written instead of “others and the remaining gods,” following Meursius’ correction. “Other remaining” is an Arnobian expression. Below, Book VI, chap. 11: “The hocks, ankles, and other remaining limbs, and wood, stones, and bones, and the other remaining materials of which statues and images of divine powers are customarily composed.” HERALDUS.—Compare Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VII, p. 489. The Leiden edition has: “Aesculapius and the rest.” ORELLI.

You would invent, in place of “you would have invented.” We have already discussed this interchange of forms, common among writers of this kind. HERALDUS.—See above on Book I, chap. 54. ORELLI.

Which would not merely defile their dignity, but would prove from the qualities attached to them that they did not exist at all. [Col. 0945B] I have printed this following Heraldus’ correction. Others read: “you would prove.” ORELLI.

One part to be males and the other part females. Prudentius, *On the Crowns of Martyrdom* [Col. 0945C]:

> You order me, abandoning the sacred rites of the Father and Christ,  
> To worship with you a thousand females and males,  
> Gods and goddesses, and offspring of a double sex—  
> Sons, grandsons, great-grandsons—  
> And the filthy progeny of so many acts of debauchery, etc.

Compare Lactantius, Book I, chap. 16. ELMENHORST.

Men of lively intelligence. That is, men of penetrating intellect and independent judgment. Thus Pliny, *Panegyric*, chap. 44, §6: “You love steadfastness in citizens, upright and vigorous minds”; see Arntzen there. Likewise, *Letters* VIII.6, at the end: “I know how lively and independent your mind is,” although the recent editor Gierig prints “true” instead of “lively.” J. F. Gronovius collected further examples in *Observations*, Book III, chap. 4. ORELLI.

Tullius, the most eloquent man of the Roman race, etc. Catullus, Poem XLIX.1:

> Most eloquent of Romulus’ descendants,  
> Of all who are, and all who ever were, Marcus Tullius.

ELMENHORST. Moreover, Davies, at the end of his edition, p. 325, assigns this quotation to a lost chapter of Cicero’s third book *On the Nature of the Gods*. ORELLI.

The brilliance of words. That is, the ornaments, elegance, and splendor of words, as Gesner explains in his *Thesaurus*. Citing our passage, he records the word as a ἅπαξ λεγόμενον, “a word occurring only once.” ORELLI.

This case would have been fully argued. Others read: “This case also would have been fully argued.” But I follow Davies, who deletes the conjunction “also,” which was produced by the repeated ending of the preceding word. ORELLI.

Nor would it demand from us, infants as we are, what are called second speeches. Τὴν δευτερολογίαν, “the second speech,” in which ὁ δευτεραγωνιστῶν ἤγουν δευτερολογῶν, “the second performer, that is, the one delivering the second speech,” added anything omitted by the first speaker, ὑπὸ τοῦ πρωταγωνιστήσαντος. HERALDUS.—“From us, infants as we are,” namely, if we are compared with Cicero, the most eloquent of the Romans. ORELLI.

Thus infancy. We also read it in its strict sense in Cornelius Fronto, *On Speeches*, Book I, *Works*, p. 223, Angelo Mai’s edition: “Then, if a choice must be made, I prefer eloquence far, far above infancy.” ORELLI.]

## VI

And yet, lest anyone obstinately suppose that we refuse to undertake the oath of allegiance to all the other divine powers, whatever they may be—for we offer devoted minds and stretch out suppliant hands, nor do we disdain to go wherever you invite us—let us only learn who these gods are whom you thrust upon us and whom it is proper to join in the worship of the supreme King and Prince.

“Saturn,” he says, “and Janus; Minerva, Juno, Apollo, Venus, Triptolemus, Hercules, Aesculapius, and the other remaining gods, to whom religious antiquity has consecrated magnificent temples in almost every city.” You might perhaps have been able to invite us to worship these divine powers, had you yourselves not been the first, through the foulness of shameful opinions, [Col. 0944B] to invent such things about them as would not [Col. 0945A] merely defile their dignity, but would prove from the qualities attached to them that they did not exist at all.

For, first of all, we cannot be induced to believe that that immortal and supremely excellent nature is divided by sex, with one part male and the other female. Men of lively intelligence have long since explained this subject fully in both Roman and Greek literature; and before them all Tullius, the most eloquent man of the Roman race, fearing no accusation of impiety, openly, steadfastly, and freely disclosed—with the greater piety—what he thought about such an opinion. If you were willing to take from him the matters he wrote with soundness of judgment, rather than the brilliance of his words, this case would already have been fully argued, nor would it demand from us, infants as we are, what are called second speeches.

[Col. 0945B] [Note: [Col. 0945D]

### VII.—On account of this

That is, “because of this,” as often. See Tursellinus, *On the Particles of the Latin Language*. ORELLI.

[Col. 0946B] It ought to be decreed by the Senate that these writings be abolished, etc. For this was done by authority of the Senate. See Valerius Maximus, Book I, chap. 4, §12; Lactantius, *Institutions* I, chap. 22; St. Augustine, *City of God*, Book VII, [Col. 0946C] chap. 34, with Ludovicus Vives there; and Elmenhorst on this passage. ORELLI.—It is therefore possible that we owe the mutilated state of the third book *On the Nature of the Gods* to these superstitious pagans. Perhaps, however, certain fearful Christians were not free of this fault. Certainly no others than these rendered many manuscripts defective from Book II, chap. 6 to chap. 33. DAVIES, on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, in the passage cited.

Convict Cicero of error; refute, disprove, reject what he has said as rash and impious. So the Leiden editor prints from the manuscript, except that the parchment has “refute” in the indicative where Gelenius altered it to: “Refute, disprove, reject the rash and impious things he has said.” Stewechius, however, believing the passage corrupt, arranged it thus: “Convict Cicero of error, refute him, disprove him; prove that he makes rash and impious assertions.” I find this highly attractive and could scarcely restrain myself from admitting it into the text. ORELLI.]

## VII

But why should I say that elegant refinements of language and splendor of style are sought from him, when I know that there are not a few who turn away from and shun his books on this subject, and refuse to admit to their ears a reading that overcomes their preconceived opinions? And when I hear others muttering indignantly and saying: “It ought to be decreed by [Col. 0946A] the Senate that these writings be abolished, writings by which the Christian religion is confirmed and the authority of antiquity crushed”?

Indeed, if you are confident that what you say about your gods has been thoroughly ascertained, convict Cicero of error; refute, disprove, and reject what he has said as rash and impious. For to suppress writings and to wish to bury a published work is not to defend the gods, but to fear the testimony of truth.

[Note: [Col. 0946C]

### VIII.—For you are accustomed to say in your prayers, “whether you are a god or a goddess”

L. Carrio corrected the text thus, [Col. 0946D] *Emendations*, Book I, chap. 3, in Gruter’s *Critical Lamp*, vol. III, p. 110. The Romans used this formula, “IF A GOD, IF A GODDESS,” in prayers when, for example, the earth had moved or some other event had occurred and it was uncertain by what cause and by the power and divine agency of which god it had been brought about. See Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, Book II, chap. 28, and Gronovius there. It was also the solemn formula by which the tutelary gods of cities under siege were summoned out of them, using the ambiguous expression “IF A GOD, IF A GODDESS,” lest, by naming one instead of another or confusing their sex, they should bind the people through a mistaken religious observance. See Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book III, chap. 9, and Brissonius, *On the Formulas and Solemn Expressions of the Roman People*. Moreover, concerning the frequent confusion of the gods’ sex among the ancients—for example, Venus as male and female, and Lunus and Luna—see Casaubon and Salmasius on Aelius Spartianus, *Caracalla*, chap. 7, *Augustan History*, vol. I, pp. 720 ff.; and Selden, who refutes them, *On the Syrian Gods*, Syntagma II, chap. 2, pp. 149 ff. The manuscript wrongly has, “whether you are a god, or whether you are a goddess.” ORELLI.

For bodies, if they are male and female, must be marked by the distinction of sex. [Col. 0947B] This is the manuscript reading defended by Fulvius Ursinus, which others altered for some reason unknown to me. Gelenius and the remaining editors down to Salmasius read: “If they are male and female, bodies are indicated by the distinction of sexes.” Heraldus defends this reading, thinking that Arnobius meant: “For if the gods are male and female, they must have bodies, which are thereby indicated and demonstrated, because different kinds, or different sexes, of gods are established.” Stewechius conjectured: “For bodies must exist, if they are male and female, [Col. 0947C] marked by the separation of sexes.” Meursius: “For bodies, if the gods are male and female, must be indicated,” etc.; yet he himself retracts this conjecture in his Appendix, reading “must have been indicated.” Finally, the Leiden editor has: “to be in signification by distinction of sex.” I prefer the manuscript reading to all the others as the simplest and best: “to be marked by the distinction of sex,” that is, by those parts through which sex is distinguished. ORELLI.]

## VIII

Yet, lest some thoughtless person bring an accusation against us as though we believed the God whom we worship to be male—simply because, when we speak, we refer to him using the masculine gender—let him understand that this designation and its significance arise not from sex, but from the usage and familiarity of speech [Note: [Col. 0945B] “Signification” in the manuscript]. For God is not a male; rather, his name is of the masculine [Col. 0946B] gender. You cannot say the same in your religion. For in your prayers you are accustomed to say, “whether you are a god or a goddess”; and this reservation expressing doubt makes it clear that, by the very separation, you assign sex to the gods.

We therefore cannot be induced to believe that the gods possess bodies. For [Note: [Col. 0946B] Fulvius reads “But”] bodies, if they are male and female, [Col. 0947A] must be marked by the distinction of sex. For who, even with the smallest degree of understanding, does not know that the Creator formed earthly living creatures with different sexes for no other reason than so that, through copulation and the union of bodies, the perishable and transitory order of things might endure through the perpetual renewal of succession?

[Note: [Col. 0947C]

### IX.—So that they might supply offspring

Virgil, *Georgics* III.64–65:

> Release the males; be first to send the herds to Venus,  
> And by generating one from another supply new offspring.

Lucretius, Book III, verse 704:

> …It supplies another nature from itself.

Apuleius, *Florida*, p. 79: “Human beings, subject to change, as offspring must successively be supplied.” ELMENHORST.

[Col. 0947D] And as each new brood arises. So Elmenhorst and the Leiden edition most correctly. Others read “a new brood also.” ORELLI.

A renewed replacement. Papias: “Renewed … things born again.” Servius, on *Aeneid* IV.337 and X.54, at the words, “And they seek a Troy renewed”: “*Recidivum* is something which, after being cut down, is born and sprouts again.” Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, Book II:

> It begets, nourishes, and restores, and preserves the seeds renewed.

The author of the *Poem on Sodom* transmitted among Cyprian’s works:

> But the renewed impiety of humankind, together with a second race,  
> And once again a new age of evil, sprouts forth.

Thus Tertullian calls a recurring year *recidivus*, that is, παλίνδρομος, “returning,” which is why the Greeks call it ἐνιαυτός, “a year completing its circuit.” ELMENHORST and HERALDUS.—From this Tertullian formed the noun *recidivatus*, “restoration,” in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, chap. 1: “They certainly foretold the bodily restoration of the soul”; and chap. 30: “The restoration of the Jewish state is represented through the re-embodiment and [Col. 0948B] reunion of the bones.” See Lindenbrog on the *Moretum* in the *Virgilian Minor Poems*, p. 303. ORELLI.

If through these laws of sex they experience themselves. “Sex” is in the genitive and must be joined with “laws.” But I prefer Heraldus’ correction in his *Second Observations*: “And in addition they undergo laws of sex.” ORELLI.

Since they themselves too continually reproduce. So Meursius, followed by the remaining editors. Earlier editions read: “Since, if they themselves too continually reproduce.” But “if” disrupts the sense. ORELLI.

Why they have been marked with these regions. What Arnobius here calls “regions” he calls “parts” below. He means those organs which we cannot decorously name. Pliny, *Natural History*, Book X, chap. 37: “What in a human being they call the ‘regions’ is in other animals the womb.” See also the other examples amassed by Heraldus and Elmenhorst on this rather indecorous subject. ORELLI.

Or that improvident nature wished sweetly to sport in their case. I have printed this following the Leiden editor’s correction. The manuscript reads: “Or that nature wished to sport with its own improvidence in their case.” But “to sport with,” that is, “to deceive,” its own improvidence has no place here; hence Gelenius corrected it to: “Or that nature wished its own improvidence to shine in them.” Meursius: “Or that nature wished to sport with its own providence in them.” ORELLI.

Which are not to be used. Fulvius Ursinus reads “which were not to be used.” Not badly. ORELLI.

For just as, etc. So Stewechius. Earlier editions incorrectly read: “But as, then,” etc. This perhaps arose from the Royal manuscript’s spelling *seicut*, an ancient form of *sicut*, “just as,” as Stewechius himself shows in *Apuleian Questions*, Book II. Salmasius printed simply: “As.” ORELLI.]

## IX

What, then, shall we say? That gods procreate? That gods are born? That for this reason genital organs were added, so that they might supply offspring, and, as each new brood arose, a renewed [Note: [Col. 0947B] Fulvius wrongly reads “revived”] replacement might substitute whatever the preceding generation had removed?

Therefore, if this is so—that is, if the heavenly gods procreate, if through these laws of sex they experience themselves, and if they are immortal and are not rendered infertile by the coldness of old age—it follows that everything must be filled with gods, and that not even countless heavens could contain [Col. 0947B] their multitude, since they themselves too continually reproduce, and an always multiplying incalculable host increases through the offspring of offspring. [Col. 0948A]

Or, if the obscenity of copulation is, as is fitting, absent from the gods, what cause or reason can be shown why they are marked with those regions by which the sexes are accustomed to recognize themselves through the promptings of their own lusts? For it is not probable that they possess these things to no purpose, or that improvident nature wished sweetly to sport in their case by burdening them with parts which are not to be used. For just as hands, feet, eyes, and the remaining structure of the limbs have each been established for definite uses and their respective functions, so it is proper to believe that these parts too were fashioned for the discharge of their own office; otherwise, one must confess that something in the bodies of the gods is purposeless, fashioned vainly and to no end.

[Note: [Col. 0948D]

### X.—Ministers of religious rites

That is, priests. See above on Book I, chap. 17. To the passages cited there add Cornelius Nepos, *Lysander*, chap. III, §3: “When he had set out with this hope, the ministers of Jupiter greatly deceived him.” ORELLI.

Which it is disgraceful even for modest mouths to utter by their proper names. For when modesty forbade the ancients to name certain things, they customarily indicated them either by other respectable terms—for example, “regions,” “parts,” or “things”—or by some elegant circumlocution. Thus the Greeks called those parts τὰ ἀναγκαῖα, “the necessary parts” (see Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams*, Book I, chap. 47); the Latins called them *necessaria*, “the necessities.” Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis*, Book IV, chap. 12: “It causes defects around the natural and necessary parts”; and chap. 18: “But from the necessary and female regions it indicates a grave danger to health.” See below, Book V, chap. 27, and the extensive discussion by the distinguished Ruhnken on Rutilius Lupus, *Figures of Thought*, [Col. 0949B] Book I, chap. 18, p. 61, where he also cites our passage. ORELLI.

To rush with raging desires into mutual embraces, etc., etc. Appropriately, in *Critical Letter* I, p. 156 of the latest edition of the *Homeric Hymn to Ceres*, Ruhnken compares these words with the very similar passage in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* II, p. 26: “Until, exhausted in mind and with our limbs grown faint, we both collapsed together amid mutual embraces, gasping out our breath.” ORELLI.

And at last, their bodies broken and dissolved, to languish from pleasure’s enervation. So Salmasius. Others read “so that at last,” etc., which could be tolerated if we understand from the preceding words “we are to believe.” Moreover, Tertullian elegantly expresses the same thought in *On the Soul*, chap. 27: “In that very final heat of pleasure, in which the generative fluid is expelled, do we not feel that something of the soul too departs, so that we wilt and grow feeble, with a loss of vitality?” ELMENHORST and ORELLI.

To miscarry. That is, to have an abortion, used actively. ORELLI.

To carry to term. That is, to bear until due maturity, *austragen*. [Col. 0949C] Thus Nemesianus, *Eclogue* III.23, concerning Bacchus:

> The almighty father, provident of the age to come,  
> Carried him and brought forth the offspring at the proper time.

In most editions, however, “brought forth” is read instead of “carried.” Pliny, *Natural History*, Book VII, chap. 11: “But when a short interval of time has elapsed between two conceptions, both are carried to term, as was apparent in the case of Hercules and his brother Iphicles.” See Hardouin there. Add Salmasius on Solinus, p. 21, and Oudendorp’s extensive discussion of this verb in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, Book VI, p. 398. ORELLI.

The mind longs and burns, etc. Gelenius most correctly amended the manuscript reading, “It possesses even now and burns,” which Th. Canter and Heraldus vainly try to defend by saying that *habere*, “to possess,” was anciently written for *avere*, “to long.” But that meaning of the verb was altogether obsolete in Arnobius’ age, and *habere*, meaning to possess or inhabit, is very far removed from *avere*, meaning to desire. Moreover, if we read the text thus, we have no subject to which τὸ *habet*, “it possesses,” can refer. C. Barth, *Adversaria*, Book XLIV, chap. 24, pp. 2036–37, failing to understand the force of the irony, conjectures: “Even Numa possesses and burns,” as if the discussion concerned Numa’s intercourse with the gods; but this is wholly foreign to the passage. “The mind longs” is also read below in Book V. Davies too, on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book II, chap. 1, p. 102 of the first edition, shows that *avere* and *habere* are very frequently confused in manuscripts. ORELLI.

In those great Chalcidica. Gelenius wrongly printed *chalcaeica*. For below, Book IV, chap. 33: “Your gods are represented as dining in heavenly dining rooms and in golden Chalcidica,” etc. We know little about what kind of building the *Chalcidicum* was; Festus reports that it was named after the city of Chalcis. Ausonius, in his summary of *Odyssey* I, writes “Penelope descended from the Chalcidicum,” and in Book XXIII:

> The nurse passed beyond the Chalcidicum with an old woman’s gait.

He undoubtedly rendered the Homeric term ὑπερῷον, “upper chamber,” a room in the upper part of the house where women customarily remained. The Romans, however, called that part of the house a *cenaculum*, because they dined there. See the interpreters on Ausonius in the passage cited, p. 755 of Tollius’ edition. Hyginus too uses *Chalcidicum* in the same sense in *Fabula* 185; see Muncker there, and our author here. It occurs in another sense, however, in the Monumentum Ancyranum: “THE SENATE HOUSE AND THE CHALCIDICUM ADJOINING IT, AND THE TEMPLE OF APOLLO ON THE PALATINE”; and in Dio Cassius, Book LI, chap. 22. There it seems to mean a surrounding portico or exterior walkway encircling a building. See Reimar, vol. I, p. 655; Scaliger on Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, p. 203; Turnebus, *Adversaria*, Book XVIII, chap. 34; and Vossius, *Roman Etymologies*. ORELLI.

Ceres, full-breasted because of Iacchus, as the Muse of Lucretius proclaims. Ludovicus Carrio most correctly amended the manuscript reading in *Emendations*, Book II, chap. 17, p. 179, in Gruter’s *Critical Lamp*, vol. III, replacing the formerly printed “in the presence of Iacchus.” Arnobius is alluding to Lucretius, Book IV, verse 1162:

> But she with twin breasts—Ceres herself—is full-breasted because of Iacchus.

“Ceres because of Iacchus” is Ceres ἡ τοῦ Ἰάκχου, “the Ceres of Iacchus,” Ceres beloved by Iacchus, whom Iacchus loved, as Lambinus and Thomas Creech explain; or, as Salmasius more correctly interprets it on Solinus, p. 528, she was full-breasted when she nourished the boy Iacchus with her milk. *Mammosa* means “having large breasts,” as Arnobius calls Ceres below in Book VII, chap. 25. Compare Gisbert Cuper, *Apotheosis of Homer*, p. 255. ORELLI.

Hellespontine Priapus. Priapus was called Hellespontine after Lampsacus, a city on the Hellespont, from which, after being expelled, he became a god. See Antonius on Petronius, *Satyricon*, chap. 139, p. 462. Ovid, *Tristia* I.9.26:

> And you, Lampsacus, kept safe by your rustic god.

Moreover, the classic passage on the worship of Priapus is in Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, Book I, verses 102 ff.:

> Behold, a Greek man, fashioned in bronze, stands among the gods  
> And shines in Numa’s august citadel.  
> He was once a vigorous lord of a cultivated field,  
> An excessive fornicator, accustomed with abundant lust  
> To molest rustic prostitutes and, among the willow beds  
> And dense hedges, to enter obscene couches.  
> Straining an untamed spirit, always ready  
> For wickedness, he never granted rest to his heated veins.  
> This god, highly renowned from his native Hellespont,  
> Came as far as Italian gardens with his shameful rites.  
> Each year he receives this bowl of milk and these sacrificial cakes,  
> And guards the vineyards of the Sabine countryside—  
> One whom anyone would blush to behold with that branch disgracefully affixed.

ELMENHORST and ORELLI.
