Those things. “Things” in an obscene sense, referring to the male organs. Thus below, in the translation of an Orphic poem, Book V, chap. 26:

> And he cast before his eyes the things formed upon the groin.

And Martial:

> Refrain, then, from giving masculine names to your things.

See Janus Dousa, *Preliminary Notes on Tibullus*, chap. XV, [Col. 0951B] p. 448, Graevius’ edition. This was a respectable expression for a shameful thing. Thus in Latin: “these many things,” “those many things,” “these numerous matters”; in Greek: πάντα ταῦτα, “all those things,” for forbidden pleasures and the sport of Venus. See Heraldus on this passage. Similarly the distinguished Wieland, in his translations, circumlocutes things that cannot decorously be uttered with the words [Col. 0951C] *Was ihr wisst*, “you know what.” ORELLI.

Ready for the expedition of battles. “Battles” in an indecent sense, referring to sexual intercourse. Thus Virgil, *Georgics* III.98, concerning an exhausted horse:

> …If ever it has come to battle.

See the distinguished Heyne there and Ausonius Popma on the fragments of Varro, p. 327, Bipontine edition. ORELLI.

Through the troublesome burden of their inward weight. “Inward weight” is what Tertullian, *To His Wife* I, chap. 5, calls “the womb’s burden.” Here *morositas*, “troublesomeness,” is the same as discomfort, or is used actively of that which makes pregnant women slow and fretful. I do not remember reading the word elsewhere in this sense. ORELLI.

Pierced by other heavy shafts … Stewechius conjectures “difficulties,” as below, chap. 21: “the difficult complications of childbirth.” But nothing should be changed here. Who does not know the shafts of Lucina, χαλεπὸν βέλος Εἰλειθυίας, “the grievous shaft of Eileithyia,” from Theocritus, *Idyll* XXVII.28? ORELLI.

To be tortured. So the Leiden edition, following Th. Canter’s very successful correction of the unsuitable “to be encouraged,” which was formerly read. The word is Lucretian, Book III, verse 661:

> You will then see all the parts separately, severed by a fresh  
> Wound, writhing in torment and sprinkling the earth with gore.

Nonius: “*Tortor* … for *torqueor*, ‘I am tortured.’” Pomponius, *The Fuller’s Decuma*: “And when I leaped upon the spiral-shaped rack, there I writhe at a gallop.” ORELLI.

To implore the aid of Juno Lucina. “Juno Lucina, I appeal to your protection!” Plautus, *The Pot of Gold*, Act IV, scene VII, verse 10. See below, chap. 21. ORELLI.]

## X

What are you saying, holy and undefiled ministers [Col. 0948B] of religion? Do the gods, then, possess sexes and carry about the foulness of genital organs, which it is disgraceful even for modest [Col. 0949A] mouths to utter by their proper names? What, then, remains except that we believe them, after the fashion of unclean quadrupeds, to be driven frantic by the madness of lust, to rush with raging desires into mutual embraces, and at last, their bodies broken and dissolved, to languish from pleasure’s enervation?

And since certain experiences are peculiar to the female sex, it follows that we must also believe the goddesses to discharge their laws as their months come round; to undergo and endure nauseating pregnancies; to miscarry [Note: [Col. 0949A] Fulvius wrongly reads “to abort”], to carry to term, and sometimes, through premature labor, to bring forth seven-month offspring. [Col. 0950A]

O pure, holy divinity, separated and set apart from every stain of shame! The mind longs and burns to behold, in those great Chalcidica and in the palaces of heaven, the gods and goddesses with their bodies uncovered and naked: Ceres, full-breasted because of Iacchus, as the Muse of Lucretius proclaims [Note: [Col. 0950A] Others read “Lucretian”; the manuscript, “Lucretia”], and Hellespontine Priapus carrying about among virgin goddesses and mothers those things, always ready [Col. 0951A] for the expedition of battles.

The mind longs, I say, to see pregnant goddesses, goddesses who have given birth, lingering as their bellies swell day after day through the troublesome burden of their inward weight; some laboring through a long-drawn delivery and seeking midwives’ hands; others pierced by heavy shafts and the sharp points of pain, wailing, being tortured, and amid all this imploring the aid of Juno Lucina. Is it not much more proper to curse the gods, revile them, and heap other insults upon them than, under a pious pretext [Note: [Col. 0951B] The manuscript wrongly reads “than so that, under a pretext”], to presume such monstrous opinions about them in so degrading a manner?

[Note: [Col. 0951D]

### XI.—And you dare to assign to us the cause of the gods’ displeasure, although, if judgment were held, it would most certainly be found to lie with you, and not to consist in the insult which you suppose

I have printed and punctuated the passage thus, following J. Freinsheim’s very certain correction on Florus, Book IV, chap. 2, p. 765, Duker’s edition. It was formerly printed: “Although, if a most certain judgment were held, it would be found to lie with you and to consist in the insult which you suppose.” This is wrong, for the sense is: If judgment were held, the gods’ displeasure would most certainly be found to lie with you, but not to consist in the insult which you suppose—namely, the insult which you believe us to have inflicted upon the gods. [Col. 0952B] ORELLI.

To endure reluctantly and most fiercely. There is necessarily a corruption, for, unless my memory most extraordinarily deceives me, no Latin author ever said “to endure most fiercely” in the sense “with the utmost distress.” I read: “To endure reluctantly and with the utmost reluctance.” [Col. 0952C] This is our Arnobius’ genuine form of expression. Similarly, Book II: “Through which we are bad and very bad—desires,” etc.; and frequently in this work. MEURSIUS, p. 89.

If indeed it pertains to their care. So the Leiden edition. Others read: “If indeed it pertains to care for them.” Stewechius added the preposition “to” from the manuscript. ORELLI.

To think and believe much more honorably than you concerning the dignity of their name. So the Leiden edition, in accordance with Arnobius’ habit of very frequently omitting the conjunction. The manuscript has: “To think than to believe,” which Stewechius defends in vain. Gelenius reads: “And also to believe.” Others: “And to believe.” ORELLI.]

## XI

And you dare to assign to us the cause of the gods’ displeasure, although, if judgment were held, it would most certainly be found to lie with you, and not to consist in the insult which you suppose. For if the gods, as you say, are affected by anger and grow hot with indignation of mind, why should we not think that they endure reluctantly and most fiercely your assigning to them the sexes with which dogs and pigs were formed, and that, when you believe such things, they resent being fashioned in no other way and put on display with an ignominious ostentation?

Therefore, since this is so, you are the cause of all calamities. You impel the gods and provoke them to assail the earth with every evil and to devise ever-new disasters each day, by which, exasperated by so many injuries and curses from you, they may avenge themselves. Curses, I say, and injuries, which your theologians, your poets, and you yourselves celebrate in dishonorable rites, partly through shameful fables and partly through indecorous opinions. You will find human affairs ruined and the gods to have abandoned the helm—if indeed it pertains to their care to rule and administer the fortunes of mortals.

For they have no reason to be angry with us, whom they see and perceive neither to worship them nor, as the saying goes, to ridicule them, but to think and believe much more honorably than you concerning the dignity of their name.

[Note: [Col. 0952C]

### XII.—And let no one at this point set against us Jewish stories and stories of the Sadducean kind, as though we too attributed a form to God

The reading is sound and, as it seems to me, was wrongly altered by Salmasius, who printed: “As though they attributed forms and a face to God.” For the pagans confused Christians with Jews, or regarded them as a particular Jewish sect, and charged them with many things which were indeed peculiar to the Jews but wholly foreign to the Christian religion—for example, hatred of the human race. Accordingly, on hearing in the writings of Jewish teachers that bodily form was attributed to God, they also fastened such absurdities upon Christians. That this is the meaning of our passage is made perfectly clear by the words that follow: “which either have nothing to do with us and possess nothing in common with us in any respect; or, if they are, as is believed, shared,” etc.

Moreover, Arnobius here touches upon those utterly absurd inventions of the Rabbis, who attributed human shape and countenance, and even bodily dimensions, to God. These are discussed at greater length by the most learned citizen ὁ νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις, “who is now among the saints,” Heinrich Corrodi, in the book entitled *Critischte des Chiliasmus*, vol. I, pp. 79 ff. Arnobius seems altogether to have confused the Sadducees—who rejected every tradition of the elders and were therefore regarded as unbelievers—with the Pharisees and other Jewish teachers who originated such stories. ORELLI.]

*And as though by an established fact*, etc. So the manuscript codex reads; Heraldus defends this reading in his *Second Critical Notes*, and I do not see [Col. 0953B] why it should be changed. Fulvius Ursinus: *and read, “by an established fact and authority.”* Leiden edition: *and as though even by an established fact*. Meursius recasts the entire passage thus: *in their writings: it is said as though it were an established fact*—without any necessity. ORELL.

*Or, if they are, as is believed, shared.* So the Leiden editor. Sabaeus’ first edition: *or, if they are believed to be associated*; Fulvius Ursinus: *or, if the associates are believed*. But *shared* is sound, namely *the stories*—that is, stories common to us as well, so that what is said in them might seem to apply also to us, as Heraldus rightly interprets it. ORELL.

*To loosen the clouds and wrappings of those writings.* Similarly Claudianus Mamertus, *On the State of the Soul*, book II, [Col. 0953C] chap. 12: “But in this dark cloud of obscure matters, let us seek answers from the inner sanctuaries of supercelestial teachings.” See there Gasp. Barth in the *Glossary*. ORELL.]

## XII

So much for sex. Let us now come to the appearance and forms in which you believe the heavenly gods to have been delineated—indeed, fashioned in these forms and placed in the most spacious seats [Col. 0952B] of temples. Nor let anyone confront us here with Jewish stories of the Sadducean kind, as though we too attributed forms to God. For this is thought to be stated in their writings and to be confirmed as though by an established fact and by authority. Yet these stories either have no bearing [Col. 0953A] upon us and share nothing with us in any respect; or, if they are, as is believed, shared, you must seek teachers of a higher understanding, through whom you may learn the ways in which the clouds and wrappings of those writings ought to be loosened.

Our judgment on this matter is as follows. The whole divine nature, which neither began to exist at some point nor will at some point thus come to the end of its life, is without bodily outlines and possesses no representations of forms by which an exterior boundary ordinarily encloses and terminates the joined structure of limbs. For whatever is of this kind we judge to be mortal and perishable; nor do we believe that what is confined within outer limits and enclosed by a necessary boundary can possess perpetual eternity.

[Note: [Col. 0953C]

### XIII.—*By an outline bounded according to the human form*

Arnobius uses *filum* (“outline”) for the lineaments and outer boundaries of bodies. Thus Lucretius, II, 341:

> To be of equal outline and endowed with a similar shape.

See Creech there. A. Gellius, book XIV, chap. 4: “Chrysippus fashions an image of Justice . . . with the form and outline of a maiden.” The same author, book I, chap. 9: “To investigate the characters and natural dispositions of human beings by a kind of inference from the cast of the face and countenance, and from the outline and bearing of the whole body.” HERALD. and HELMENH.—So too Plautus, *The Merchant*, act IV, scene IV, verse 15:

> A sufficiently fine outline for a woman.

Salmasius, on Solinus, p. 465, shows by many examples that *filum* is used generally of the outer lines of any body whatsoever. In the same sense Petronius, [Col. 0953D] *Satyrica*, chap. 126, uses *scriptura* (“delineation”): “Eyebrows running as far as the delineation of the cheeks, and again almost meeting at the boundary of the eyes.” See the interpreters there. ORELL.

### *Outer contour*

*Circumcaesura* (“circumcision, outer contour”), Greek *περικοπή* (*perikopē*, “cutting around”). It is the same thing he has just called *filum*, “outline.” Lucretius, III, 220:

> Yet the outer contour of the limbs  
> Preserves itself unharmed, nor is one whit of the body lost.

Compare IV, 651. HERALD.—Compare Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XIII, chap. 20. ORELL.

### *By the joinings of the little vertebrae*

I have printed this from the wholly correct emendation of F. Dousa on the *Fragments of Lucilius*, p. 295, Havercamp’s edition. *Verticum*, which is read in all editions, cannot be tolerated here. One must read *verticularum*, or *verticulorum*, which Solinus has in chap. 34. *Verticulae* are the joints by which the spine is connected with the head. Others read *vertebrarum* in the same sense. See Salmasius on Solinus, book I, p. 406. ORELL.

### *It follows that they also have ears pierced through with winding passages* [Col. 0954B]

Zeno of Verona, in his sermon *Attend to Yourself*, speaks of “uneven windings”: “The ears, moreover, opened through certain uneven windings, receive with distinct modulation the sound of air when it is struck.” A little later he calls them “curving windings,” just as Arnobius below calls them “curving passages.” HERALD.

### *Movable little spheres of the eyes*

“Orbs” and “little orbs of the eyes,” as the Greeks say *κύκλοι* (*kykloi*, “circles”). Solinus, chap. 30: “It never checks the gaze of its orbs.” Seneca in the *Oedipus*:

> Eagerly he probes his eyes with hooked hands;  
> Torn utterly from their deepest roots,  
> [Col. 0954C] he rolls out both orbs together.

Sophocles had said in the same play: “Lifting it, he struck the joints of his own eye-circles”; and in the *Antigone*: “the circles of the eyes.” HERALD.—Compare Keuchen on Sammonicus, verse 669, in P. Burmann’s *Minor Latin Poets*, vol. II, p. 319; Bünemann on Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chap. 10, p. 1168. ORELL.

### *The suspended gutter-tile of the nostrils*, etc.

Arnobius elegantly compares the nostrils with an *imbrex*, that is, a hollow tile fitted to roofs so that water may flow down through it: German *Dachrinne, Dachtraufe* (“roof gutter, eaves”). Moreover, Aristotle’s *History of Animals*, book I, chap. 11, should be compared with our passage:

> Further, one part of the face is the nose, a passage for breath; for through it one both inhales and exhales, and through it sneezing occurs—a sudden expulsion of breath, an omen-bearing sign and the only sacred one among the movements of breath.

Add Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, chap. 57. Compare Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chap. 10. ORELL.

### *For the working down of food, teeth of three kinds*, etc.

Namely: [Col. 0954D] 1. *οἱ τομεῖς* (*hoi tomeis*, “the cutters”), called *front teeth* by Pliny, but *incisors* by Isidore, *Origins* XI, chap. 1, and *seizing teeth* in draft animals; 2. *κυνόδοντες* (*kynodontes*, “dog-teeth”), the canine teeth, called *little columns* by Isidore, loc. cit., because of their length and roundness, and *columnar teeth* in horses; 3. *γόμφιοι* or *μύλοι* (*gomphioi* or *myloi*, “pegs” or “millstones”), called molars by Isidore, jaw-teeth by Pliny, and *genuine teeth* by Cicero. See especially Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams*, book I, chap. 31, and Rigaltius’ note there, pp. 20 ff., vol. II, Reiff’s edition. Cicero likewise puts the point elegantly in *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, chap. 54: “Food is chewed by the teeth set in the mouth, and by them it is broken down and ground. The sharp front teeth divide food by biting, while the innermost teeth, which are called the *genuine teeth*, complete the process.” ORELL.

### *But if the things that are exposed are carried, it is consistent that those things also are carried*

This is the manuscript codex’s reading, wrongly changed by some to “it is consistent also to carry those things,” and by others to “it is consistent also to suppose those things.” The sense is: if the things that are exposed—that is, readily visible—are carried by the gods (which must be supplied from the following *are carried*), it is consistent that those things also should be carried by them, etc. OR.

### [Col. 0955B] *Beneath their ribs and beneath their framework*

Here *crates* (“framework”) means the joined structure of the ribs. Similarly Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, VIII, 805:

> Where once a belly was, there was a belly’s empty space; you would think  
> The breast hung loose and was held only by the framework of the spine.

And Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chap. 5: “The internal organs are covered by the ribs, so that those which had to be made soft and less robust might be protected by the embrace of that solid framework.” See Bünemann there, p. 1147. ORELL.

### *The little membranes of the omenta*

The *omentum*, Greek *ἐπίπλοον* (*epiploon*), is a thin and fatty membrane that enfolds the windings of the intestines and covers the lower parts of the abdomen (German *das Darmfell*, “the intestinal membrane”). ORELL.—Hence Pliny, *Natural History*, book II, chap. 37, says: “The stomach and intestines are covered with a fatty and thin omentum, except in egg-laying animals.” Compare Isidore, *Origins*, book II, chap. 1. NOURR., p. 405.

### *Windpipes*

Lactantius, *On the Workmanship of God*, chap. 11, [Col. 0955C] §6: “Breath, by contrast, which is incorporeal and subtle, because it could not make room for itself, received an open passage called the windpipe.” German *Luftröhre* (“windpipe”). ORELL.

### *Stomachs, spleens*

So Gelenius and the Leiden edition. Stewechius: “stomachs, kidneys.” The manuscript codex has “stomachs, veins,” which cannot stand, because there immediately follows: “and veins of purple blood passing through all the internal organs.” Meursius prefers “stomachs, kidneys.” ORELL.

### *Joined with the breath-bearing arteries*

Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book XVIII, chap. 10, sheds light on these words: “A vein is a receptacle for blood, which physicians call an *ἀγγεῖον* (*angeion*, ‘vessel’), mingled and blended with natural spirit, in which there is more blood and less spirit. An artery is a receptacle for natural spirit mingled and blended with blood, in which there is more spirit and less blood.” More briefly, Pollux, *Onomasticon*, book II, §216 (Hemsterhuis): “The heart has cavities for both blood and breath; the latter it sends out through the arteries, while the former it sends upward through the veins.” Compare the great [Col. 0955D] Hippocrates, who admirably explains the nature of the arteries in *On the Heart*, vol. I, p. 269, Foesius’ Geneva edition, and Gorrhaeus in *Medical Definitions*, s.v. *Ἀρτηρία* (*Artēria*, “artery”). ORELL.]

## XIII

But as for you, it is not enough that you confine the gods [Col. 0953B] within a measurement of forms, within an outline bounded according to the human form [Note: [Col. 0953B] So Sabaeus; others read *determined*], [Col. 0954A] and—what is far more degrading—within the outer contour that limits earthly bodies.

What, then, are we to say? That the gods bear a head gathered into a smooth roundness, fastened to the back and chest by the ligaments of sinews, and supported for the necessary movements of the neck by the joinings of little vertebrae and by a bony substructure? If we accept this as true, it follows that they also have ears pierced through with winding passages; movable little spheres of the eyes, shaded by the borders of the eyebrows; the suspended gutter-tile of the nostrils, passable both for discharges of mucus and for the passage of breath; teeth of three kinds for the working down of food, arranged for three functions; hands as servants of labor, made manageable by joints, fingers, and the mobility of the elbows; and feet for supporting their bodies, extending their steps, and enabling the forward movement of their journeys. [Col. 0954B]

But if the things that are [Col. 0955A] exposed are carried, it is consistent that those things also should be carried which, beneath the ribs and their framework, the skins and the little membranes of the omenta cover: windpipes, stomachs, spleens, lungs, bladders, livers, the tracts of the winding intestines, and veins of purple blood passing through all the internal organs, joined with the breath-bearing arteries.

[Note: [Col. 0955D]

### XIV.—*Toothless*

Nonius: “It was decided that *edentulus* should be used as though meaning ‘without teeth.’” Statius Caecilius: “Do you then dare to love, toothless old man fit for the bier?” The glosses: “*Edentulus*: *νωδός* (*nōdos*, ‘toothless’).” ELMENH.

### *To hang through the emptiness of swollen bodies*

We have no need of the shameful word *pedere* (“to fart”), which Stewechius wishes to force upon Arnobius here. *Pendere* (“to hang”) is elegantly used of bodies that are hollow, empty, and wasted by hunger, and therefore readily collapse. See the passage of Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII, 805, cited on the immediately preceding chapter. ORELL.

### *Therefore one must say that some are big-headed*, etc.

Arnobius here appears to have imitated a passage of Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I, chap. 29: “I return to the gods. Do we suppose any of them to be, if not positively cross-eyed, at least slightly squinting? Do any have a mole? Are any snub-nosed, flap-eared, large-browed, or big-headed, as some of us are? Or are all such things perfected in them?” etc. [Col. 0956B] *Capitones* are those who have a large, or dense and sturdy, head. Hence Plautus, *The Persian*, act I, scene II, verse 8, calls parasites who can endure slaps and chamber-pots hurled at their heads “hard-headed.” It was also a Roman cognomen in the Fonteian family. The glosses: “*Capito*: *κεφαλίων* (*kephaliōn*, ‘big-headed man’).” HERALD. and ORELL.

### *Little high-browed men*

This is the old reading, confirmed by the royal manuscript. Others substituted *little snub-nosed men*. But the former reading is entirely correct. For after the mention of big-headed men, *cilones*, or its diminutive *cilunculi*, “high-browed men,” follow more suitably than *sili, silones, silunculi*, “snub-nosed men.” In the glosses of Philoxenus, *sili* are *σιμοί* (*simoi*, “snub-nosed”); according to Festus, they are people whose noses bend backward and upward. Isidore also calls them *silones* in his *Glosses*, although according to Nonius Marcellus *silones* are people with prominent eyebrows. But *cilones* are those whose forehead is more prominent and appears, as Festus says, to have been cut away on the right and left. A *cilo*, namely, is a person whose forehead seems to rise, move upward, and stand out; for *cellere* is Greek *κέλλειν*, that is, *κινεῖν* (“to move”), [Col. 0956C] and transitively *κινεῖσθαι καὶ κλίνειν* (“to be moved and to incline”). Hence *excellere* and *recellere*, the latter meaning, as Festus rightly interprets it, “to bend back”; from the same root comes *incellere*, that is, “to assail with abuse,” for which *incilare* was said in antiquity. Lucretius, book III, 975 ff.:

> . . . . . . . . . . it must  
> Proceed justly, I think, justly rebuke and assail.

A *cilo*, therefore, is *προκέφαλος* (*prokephalos*, “with a projecting forehead”), as the glosses of Philoxenus explain it. HERALDUS. Compare Meursius in the *Appendix* and Lipsius on Tacitus, *Annals* XII, 21, p. 652, Oberlin’s edition. I fully agree with Heraldus. For immediately afterward there follows “those with upturned noses,” which is nothing other than *silunculi*. By contrast, *cilunculi* are most aptly joined with *frontones*, “large-browed men”: the former have a high and convex forehead, German *von hoher, gewölbter Stirne* (“with a high, arched forehead”); the latter a large and more extended one, *von hoher, langer Stirne* (“with a high, long forehead”). I am greatly surprised that the Leiden editor restored *silunculos*, a word imported into Arnobius from Cicero, who has *sili*. [Col. 0956D] Moreover, on this and other cognomina derived from parts of the body, consult Carolus Sigonius’ book *On Roman Names*, in Godfrey’s *Writers on the Latin Language*, pp. 1439 ff. ORELL.

### *Thick-lipped men*

Those whose lips—or rather *labiae*—are large. Charisius, in Godfrey’s *Authors of the Latin Language*, p. 1361: “Moderate lips are *labra*, immoderate lips *labia*, and from these come *Labiones*.” Among the Romans this was a cognomen of the Fabian clan, and likewise of the Antistian and other clans. ORELL.

### *Men with birthmarks*

*A naevus*, that is, a natural mark on the body, German *Muttermal, Mutterflecken* (“birthmark”). Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book I, chap. 28: “But it is a blemish, a mole, upon the body; yet to him it seemed an ornament.” And Solinus, chap. 5: “For sometimes the causes of resemblance look back to the stock and pass through offspring into a family, just as many little children bear now moles, now scars, now marks of whatever kind indicating their origin.” Compare Pliny, *Natural History*, book VII, chap. 11. Aristotle, *History of Animals*, book VII, chap. 6: “And in general they often resemble one another in unnatural features as well, possessing hereditary marks and scars.” [Col. 0957B] The glosses: “*Naevi*: *ἀκροχορδόνες* (*akrochordones*, ‘skin growths’).” Likewise: “*Naevus*: *φακὸς προσώπου* (*phakos prosōpou*, ‘a lentil-like spot on the face’).” Others: “*Naevus*: *ὑπερσάρκωσις* (*hypersarkōsis*, ‘fleshy excrescence’).” MEURS., in the *Appendix*, and Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 28.

### *Men with spreading noses*

Arnobius himself explains below, book VI, chap. 10, who the *Nasicae* are: “That he should bear flared nostrils, whom you make and depict as broad-nosed.” ELMENH.

### *With flared nostrils*

That is, opened and widened. Lucretius, VI, 129 ff.:

> Nor is it strange, since a little bladder full of breath  
> Often suddenly bursts and gives forth a sound in just this way.

HERALD.

### *Those with upturned noses*

Upturned nostrils, Greek *ἀνάσιμοι* (*anasimoi*), are drawn back and upward. See Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. ORELL.

### *By the swelling of their cheeks*

I very much approve P. Colvius’ conjecture on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book XI, p. 758, Oudendorp’s edition, reading “by the tubular swelling of their cheeks,” that is, by the puffing out of the cheeks; for *tuber, tubus,* and *tubulus* derive from *tumere*, “to swell.” ORELL.

### [Col. 0957C] *Pouch-cheeked men*

I have followed Salmasius’ emendation in the Leiden edition and in his note on Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, p. 298. The manuscript codex has the meaningless *sacrivoces*, from which Gelenius made *acrivoces*, “sharp-voiced men.” But that has no place here, since sharpness of voice by no means depends upon inflated and swollen cheeks. C. Barth, in his *Adversaria*, proposes two conjectures. In book IV, chap. 19, p. 197, he thinks one should write *artivoces*, that is, persons whose voice passes constrictedly from swollen cheeks. In book XLIII, chap. 6, p. 1936, however, he suspects that one should read *Satyriones*, so called from the deformity of a gaping mouth and a certain discordant laugh of the kind with which Satyrs were represented. Hence Phurnutus, *On the Nature of the Gods*, chap. 30, in Gale’s *Mythological Opuscula*, derives *Σατύρους* (“Satyrs”) from *σεσηρέναι* (“to grin”). But I greatly prefer *saccibucces*, which comes closest to the manuscript reading. [Col. 0957D] *Saccibucces*: *ἀσκογνάθοι, φυσιγνάθοι* (*askognathoi, physignathoi*: “bag-jawed, puff-cheeked”). ORELL.

### *Dwarfs, tall men, men of medium height*

A perfectly sound reading, ineptly disturbed by C. Barth in the *Adversaria*, p. 197, where he conjectures *moldy men*, which is entirely foreign to this passage. Others read *moderately sized*. But *men of medium height* is correct: that is, intermediate between dwarfs or pygmies and tall men or giants. Thus “medium stature” in military terminology means intermediate between lofty or elongated stature and short stature. See Stewechius on Vegetius, *On Military Science*, book I, chap. 5, p. 18, Wesel edition. On dwarfs, see A. Gellius, book XVI, chap. 5. ORELL.

### *Dark-complexioned*

*Aquilus* is a dusky color, intermediate between white and black. Festus falsely derives the word from *aqua*, “water,” although it comes from *aquila*, “eagle,” whose color this is. See Scaliger and Dacier on the cited passage of Festus. The glosses: “*aquilum*: *μέλαν, ὡς Λουκίλλιος* (‘black,’ as Lucilius uses it).” Isidore’s *Glosses*: “*aquilum* . . . dusky, black.” See Hugo Grotius on Martianus Capella, book II, p. 40. Moreover, as Gesner rightly observes in his *Thesaurus*, Arnobius here seems chiefly to have the color of the eyes in view. ORELL.

### [Col. 0958B] *Blue-gray-eyed*

Terence, *The Mother-in-Law*, act III, scene IV, verse 26:

> Tall, ruddy, curly-haired, stout, blue-gray-eyed.

Donatus there: “*Caesius* means having blue-gray eyes, as though possessing the blue-gray eyes of a cat.” Hence blue-gray-eyed Minerva, *γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη* (*glaukōpis Athēnē*, “bright- or gray-eyed Athena”). See A. Gellius, book II, chap. 26. ORELL.

### *Tawny-eyed*

Festus: “Those are called *ravi* in color who fall between yellow and blue-gray, whom Plautus calls *ravistelli*.” See the interpreters there. Thus *ravus* here refers to a color of the eyes, such as Varro, *On Agriculture*, book II, chap. 2, §4, praises in rams, and book II, chap. 9, §3, in dogs; see the note there by the distinguished Schneider, vol. I, part II, p. 471. Thus grain is *rava*, Greek *μελανόπυρρα* (*melanopyrra*, “dark-fiery”), French *du roux ardent* (“fiery russet”); and Cicero, *Academics* IV, chap. 33: “The sea . . . because to us it appears blue just now, but tawny in the morning,” as the text reads in Davies’ edition, who restored *tawny* for *yellow* from Nonius. ORELL.

### *Covered by the casting over them of flowing garments*

A most exact expression. Thus he calls the longer garments which were cast over the other clothes to prevent discomfort from the cold; the Greeks also call this *ἐπαναβάλλειν* (*epanaballein*, “to throw on over”). Herodotus: “Over these they wear white woolen garments cast loosely about them.” This is also called *ἐπιτιθέναι* (*epitithenai*, “to put upon”). HERALD.]

## XIV

Or is it perhaps the case that the bodies of heavenly beings are free from these deformities? And because they abstain from mortal foods [Note: [Col. 0955B] The manuscript has “are kept from”], must we believe them to be toothless like infants and bereft of all internal organs, so that, like inflated skins, [Col. 0955B] they hang through the emptiness of their swollen bodies?

What of the fact that, if these things are so, you will have to consider whether all the gods are alike or are contained within dissimilar configurations of form? For if all have an equal and single kind of likeness, it is not absurd to believe that they go astray and are deceived when attempting to recognize one another. But if they exhibit differences in their faces, it follows that their dissimilarities must be understood to have been given to them for no other reason than that they might individually recognize one another by the distinctive characteristics of differentiating signs.

Therefore one must say that some are big-headed, high-browed, large-browed, or thick-lipped; that among them some have projecting chins, birthmarks [Note: [Col. 0956B] Manuscript *Maevinos*; Sabaeus *naevimos*], or spreading noses. [Col. 0956B] These have flared nostrils, [Col. 0957A] those upturned ones; some have swelling cheeks or are pouch-cheeked from the puffing out of their cheeks; some are dwarfs, tall, or of medium height, lean, fat, or stout; these have little curls from the twisting of their hair, while others are stripped bare by baldness and smoothness.

Nor is our supposition shown to be false: your own workshops disclose and confirm it. For when you make and fashion gods, you represent these as long-haired and others as smooth-faced, some as old men [Note: [Col. 0957B] Manuscript: “light, gentle, old”], young men, or boys; some as dark-complexioned [Note: [Col. 0958B] Sabaeus: *Aquilios*], blue-gray-eyed, or tawny-eyed; some as half-naked or uncovered, while others—lest the cold discomfort them—as covered by the casting over them of flowing garments.

[Note: [Col. 0958C]

### XV.—*Is there anyone among human beings touched by some taste of reason?*

That is, lightly smeared and imbued with it. Lucretius, book VI, verse 1186:

> Thin spittle, scanty, tinged with the color of saffron.

HERALD.

### *Of forest-growing hair*

Just as forests are said by the ancients *τριχοφυεῖν* (*trichophyein*, “to sprout hair”), so, conversely, hair is said “to grow into a forest.” See F. Lindenbrog on the *Virgilian Catalecta*, p. 324. ORELL.

### *Decent*

That is, touched by some sense of shame and modesty; by contrast, *shameless* is *τολμηρὸς καὶ ἀναίσχυντος* (*tolmēros kai anaischyntos*, “audacious and without shame”). HERALD.

### [Col. 0958D] *With which you spit upon us as uncultivated*

The pagans reproached Christians with ignorance and *ἀπαιδευσία* (*apaideusia*, “lack of education”), because few among them engaged with secular literature and very many were sedentary artisans and *βάναυσοι* (*banausoi*, “mechanical laborers”). Minucius Felix: “For this reason everyone must be indignant—indeed, must grieve—that certain people, and these unversed in scholarship, strangers to literature, and ignorant even of sordid crafts, dare to pronounce anything certain about the highest order of things and about majesty.” Justin Martyr, Origen, and others frequently discuss this accusation.

Certainly, because Christians were excluded from honors and magistracies and lived private lives, they neglected even those branches of learning especially necessary for discharging forensic or political duties with distinction. Furthermore, because sophists and philosophers were the principal enemies of the Christian name, many rejected philosophy itself for that very reason. The ancient and learned teachers of the Church nevertheless attempted to correct this error, and some went so far as to ascribe more than was proper to philosophy, as is evident from Clement of Alexandria alone. The judgments of the early Christians were even harsher concerning the more humane and ornate branches of literature. They despised and condemned tragedies and comedies and the rest of the poets’ writings, because they considered them to contribute nothing to solid learning, and furthermore believed them to teem with wantonness and obscenity and to constitute a storehouse of fabulous idolatry.

Hence Tertullian, in his book *On Idolatry*, judges schoolmasters and the other professors of literature to be allied with idolatry in its many forms, since they must proclaim the gods of the nations and expound their names, genealogies, myths, and every honorific distinction, etc. And Origen, in the third book *Against Celsus*, expressly says that Christian teachers reject those who expound comedies and wanton poems, but not those who expound serious philosophy. HERALD.

### *Because they inserted the forms of mute animals into divine principles*

Perhaps one might more appropriately read: “inserted them into divine registers.” But I dare change nothing. *Divine principles* appear here to mean the same as *divine powers*, German *die Göttermächte* (“the powers of the gods”). ORELL.

### *And because they receive those same forms with much incense*

Below, book VII, chap. 22: “And because Earth is a mother, she must likewise be received with pregnant sows.” Thus the Greeks frequently speak of *θεοὺς ὑποδέχεσθαι* (*theous hypodechesthai*, “receiving the gods”). Artemidorus, book III, chap. 14: “For those who have fallen into distress both sacrifice to the gods and receive them.” HERALD.]

## XV

Is there anyone among human beings touched by some taste of reason who believes that hairs and down grow upon the bodies of gods? Who believes that distinctions of age exist in them? Who believes both that they go about clothed in the highly varied forms of coverings and garments and that they protect themselves from heat and cold?

Whoever holds this to be true must necessarily accept this also as true: that the gods are fullers and barbers, who either wash the sacred garments or shorten the hair wrapped in fleeces of forest-growing locks.

Is it, then, not shameful and not full of impiety and insult to give the gods the outlines of a mortal and perishable creature? To mark them with those parts which no decent person would dare enumerate or trace in detail, or even conceive in the imagination without horror at their supreme foulness? Is this that disdain of yours, this the arrogant wisdom with which you spit upon us as uncultivated and suppose that all knowledge [Col. 0958B] of divine things lies open to you?

You laugh at the enigmas of the Egyptians [Col. 0959A] because they inserted the forms of mute animals into divine principles, and because they receive those same forms with much incense and the rest of the apparatus of ritual. You venerate images of human beings as though they were divine powers, and you are not ashamed to impose upon them the faces of an earthly animal—to condemn others for error and folly, yet be caught in the likeness and fault of that same error.

[Note: [Col. 0959D]

### XVI.—*For form’s sake*

Thus J. Lipsius corrected it. *Dicis causa*, that is, *προφάσεως ἕνεκα, λόγου χάριν* (*prophaseōs heneka, logou charin*: “for the sake of a pretext, for name’s sake”): in word, not in reality; for appearance’s sake, German *zum Scheine* (“for show”). See A. Bosius’ index to Cornelius Nepos; A. Schott, *Humanistic Observations*, book V, chap. 33; Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XI, chap. 20, who derives it not from *dico, dicis* (“say”) but from *dico, dicas* (“dedicate”), so that it would mean “as though for the sake of dedication”; and Ernesti’s *Ciceronian Key*. The Roman first edition has the very corrupt *for the sake of a dowry*. ORELL.

### *To have attributed to divine formations*

So the manuscript and Fulvius Ursinus. The Roman edition wrongly has “the form of the mind.” *Formamentum* (“formation”) is a Lucretian word, II, verse 518:

> . . . . . . All the formations  
> Of the first elements can exist in any brightness.

HERALDUS and ELMENHORST.

### *Not what you judge to exist in reality and in the truth itself*

So the manuscript, a reading rashly altered by others and restored by the Leiden edition. There is a transposition of words, namely for: “not what you judge to exist in reality and what exists in the truth itself.” We have seen above [Col. 0960B] that Arnobius favors such transpositions. Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “What you judge actually to exist in truth,” with Heraldus approving in his *Second Critical Notes*. ORELL.

### *If little asses, dogs*, etc.

These words appear to have been modeled upon verses of Xenophanes of Colophon preserved in Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book V, p. 256, and Theodoret, *Against the Greeks*, oration III, p. 49. I shall reproduce them here as emended by Joseph Scaliger, that foremost master of genius and of all refined literature:

> But if cattle or lions had hands,  
> And could draw with their hands and accomplish works such as men do,  
> They too would draw the forms of gods and fashion their bodies  
> In shapes like the bodily form that they themselves possessed:  
> Horses like horses, and cattle like cattle.

ELMENH.

### *What flames of anger, I say, they would pour over us and arouse*

Fulvius Ursinus conjectures “pour forth.” But J. F. Gronovius, *Diatribe on Statius*, p. 401, properly defends “pour over,” citing Silius, book IX, 491:

> . . . . . . Blood had overspread  
> His face, and flames rose from his grim eye.

And book XI, 218:

> Then the maiden, blazing inwardly and suddenly violent,  
> Overspread her face with flames.

And Claudian, *On the Consulship of Mallius*, verse 21:

> [Col. 0960D] . . . . . Nor does passion make his eyes  
> Fierce, or suffuse his raging veins with blood.

ORELL.

### *If the holy Pompilius*

I do not know what those who read “if Ancus Pompilius” mean. Yet Numa Pompilius is rightly called holy, both because of the integrity of his life and because of his reputed intercourse with the gods. ORELL.

### *Except for what some author or other wished to be shared also with the tailless animal*

Salmasius was the first to restore to the text this excellent and uniquely correct reading of the manuscript codex, deservedly commended by Heraldus. The *clurine animal* is the ape. Papias: “*Clura*, or the *clurine animal*, is the name for the ape.” *Clura* is evidently contracted from the Greek *κόλουρα* (*koloura*), just as *glans* is from *γάλανος* (*galanos*). *Κόλουρος* (*kolouros*) means one who lacks a tail or has a mutilated tail. See the interpreters on Festus, s.v. *Cluna*. Compare Salmasius on Solinus, p. 267; Savaro on Sidonius, p. 4; and especially Keuchen on Sammonicus, *On Medicine*, verse 825, in P. Burmann’s *Minor Latin Poets*, vol. II, p. 345.

Failing to understand this, the first editor Sabaeus and all others who followed him, except [Col. 0961C] Salmasius, printed the very bad reading “with draft animals.” For *draft animals*, as Lambinus shows at length on Lucretius, book V, verse 863, p. 673, are all animals capable of carrying something—cattle, horses, mules, asses, etc.—none of which bears more than a minimal resemblance to a human being. Moreover, as Nourrius teaches, that “author or other” is Ennius, whose well-known verse is quoted by Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I, chap. 35:

> How like us is the ape, that ugliest beast!

Nor should Meursius be heard when he suspects in the *Appendix* that “with the buttocked animal” should be read. Compare Savaro on Sidonius, book I, letter 1, p. 4. ORELL.]

## XVI

Unless perhaps you will say that the gods indeed possess other forms, and that you have fitted the appearances of mortals to them as a mark of honor and for form’s sake [Note: [Col. 0959B] Others read “exist”; the manuscript, “existed”]. Yet this is a far greater insult than committing some error through ignorance.

For if you admitted that you had attributed to divine formations what your own conjecture had led you to believe, it would be less injurious to have erred through a preconceived opinion. But now, since you believe one thing and fashion another, you are insulting toward those to whom you attribute what you confess they are not; and you are shown to be irreligious, since you worship what you fashion, not what you judge to exist in reality and in the truth itself.

If little asses, dogs, and pigs possessed some measure of human understanding and had the arts of representation; [Col. 0960A] and if they likewise wished to honor us with some form of worship and with the consecration of statues, what flames of anger, what whirlwinds of indignation would they arouse in us if they wished our images to bear and retain the forms of their own bodies? What flames of anger, I say, they would pour over us and kindle if Romulus, the founder of the city, stood with an ass’s face; if the holy Pompilius stood with a dog’s; if the name of Cato or Marcus Cicero were inscribed beneath the form of a pig!

Do you therefore suppose that your stupidity is not laughed at by your divine powers, if they do laugh? Or, since you judge them susceptible to anger, do you suppose that they do not grow mad or rage, that they do not wish to avenge such great injuries and insults, hurling against you those things which pain is accustomed to cast and the bitterness of offense to devise?

How much more proper it would have been [Col. 0960B] to endow them with the forms of elephants, panthers, tigers, bulls, and horses! For what is beautiful in a human being, what, I ask, is admirable or comely, except for what some author or other wished to be shared also with the tailless animal?

[Col. 0961A] [Note: [Col. 0961D]

### XVII.—*We are prevented*

So Gelenius. The first edition wrongly has “we prevent.” ORELL.

### *Or formed into a globe and fashioned from fragile earthenware*

Stewechius reports that this is the reading of the manuscript codex, and Salmasius was the first to restore it to the text. Correctly, in my judgment. For “formed into a globe” agrees far better with fragile earthenware than *shaped by cutting*, which the other editors have from Gelenius’ correction. Fragile earthenware is not fashioned by carving, but is manufactured from soft clay or mud, then fired and baked in a kiln. Moreover, I greatly doubt whether the compound *condolare* (“to shape by cutting”) can be proper Latin; I have sought the word in lexicons in vain. For *con-* in compounds suggests some joining, addition, or composition; but nothing is added by cutting—rather, something is removed or cut away from wood, stone, or metal.

Fulvius Ursinus therefore conjectures: “coalesced and fashioned from fragile earthenware,” followed by Elmenhorst. Stewechius reads: “shaped from fragile wood, or fashioned from earthenware,” perhaps with an eye [Col. 0962C] to Martial, book VI, epigram 49: “Priapus carved from a fragile elm.” But I greatly prefer the codex’s reading, “formed into a globe,” which is also supported by the closely similar passage in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, chap. 39: “And first let the whole earth be perceived, situated at the center of the universe, solid and spherical, and gathered from every side into itself by its own natural tendencies, clothed with flowers.”

Moreover, Lactantius imitated his teacher Arnobius in *On the Workmanship of God*, chap. 17, §9: “If someone were to tell me that the sky is bronze, or glass, or—as Empedocles says—frozen air, should I agree at once merely because I do not know the material from which the sky is made?” See Bünemann there, pp. 1207 ff. ORELL.]

## XVII

“But,” they say, “if our opinion displeases you, then you must show and tell us what form God possesses.”

If you wish to hear the true judgment: either God has no form, or, if he is formed in some way, we certainly do not know what it is. For we do not consider it shameful not to know what we have never seen; nor are we thereby prevented from refuting the opinions of others because we ourselves put forward no opinion of our own on this subject.

For just as, if the world were said to be made of glass, silver, or iron, or to have been formed into a globe and fashioned from fragile earthenware, we would not hesitate to contend that this was false, although we did not know what its material was; so, when the appearance of God is at issue, we prove that it is not the one you assert [Note: [Col. 0961C] Sabaeus wrongly has “you assert” in another form], even if we are less able to explain what it is.

[Col. 0961B] [Note: [Col. 0962D]

### XVIII.—*Placed over the pupils*

So the manuscript and the Leiden edition. Others read “little girls.” But *pupula* is an older, Lucretian form of the kind Arnobius favors. ORELL.

### *The many-fold tongue articulates sounds*

Stewechius’ conjecture is more pleasing: “the tongue articulates manifold sounds.” ORELL.]

## XVIII

“What then?” someone will say. “Does God not hear? Does he not speak? Does he not see the things placed before him? Does he not look upon them?”

Perhaps in a mode proper to himself, not in ours. For in so great a matter we can know nothing true or investigate it by conjectures, which among us [Note: [Col. 0962C] Fulvius reads “among you”] are plainly unstable, slippery, and like empty dreams.

For if we say that he sees by the same means by which we see, it follows that he must be understood to have little membranes placed over his pupils, to close and blink his eyes, to perceive by rays or images, or—something common to all eyes—to see absolutely nothing without the admixture of another light.

The same must likewise be said about hearing, the mode of speech, and the utterance of words. If he hears through ears, he must [Col. 0961C] also have ears pierced with winding passages through which [Col. 0962A] a voice may creep in to report the meaning of speech. Or, if words are poured forth from a mouth, he must have lips together with teeth, by whose impact and movement the many-fold tongue articulates sounds and shapes the voice into words.

[Note: [Col. 0962D]

### XIX.—*Who . . . directs?*

So the manuscript codex and the Leiden edition. Others prefer “to direct,” because the infinitives “to know,” “to understand,” and “to foresee” preceded it. But anacolutha of this kind are frequent among the best authors. ORELL.

### *By the majesty of the name*

Others read “of the divine power.”]

### XIX

If you do not refuse to hear the thought of our mind, so far are we from attributing bodily features to God that we are afraid to ascribe to so great a being even the ornaments of the mind and those very virtues in which scarcely a few have been permitted to excel. For who would call God brave, steadfast, temperate, or wise? Who would call him upright? Who sober? Who, indeed, would say that he knows anything, understands anything, foresees anything, or directs the decisions governing his actions toward fixed ends of duty? These are human goods, and they have deserved to be esteemed praiseworthy by contrast with vices. But who is so dull-witted, [Col. 0962B] so brutish, as to say that God is great by reason of human goods, or that he excels in the majesty of his name because he is free from the foulness of vice? Whatever you say about God, whatever you conceive in the reflection of your silent mind, passes over into human meaning and is corrupted by it; and whatever is expressed in our words—words devised for human affairs—does not bear the mark of its own proper significance. The one most certain human understanding of the nature of God is this: to know and perceive that nothing about him can be brought forth in mortal speech.

> **Note: [Col. 0962D]**
>
> **XX.—Wool-workers.** Should we not read *wool-manufacturers*? For there is no mention of gods who are wool-cleaners—that is, those who cleanse wool of dirt (see above, on Book II, chapter 38)—but there is mention of wool-manufacturers. Thus the Fates are “the wool-working sisters.” But perhaps Arnobius was less precise in distinctions of this kind. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Sailors.** Nonsense! There are no sailor-gods; for even Neptune, [Col. 0963B] because he holds dominion over the sea, could be called a sailor only in the most inept fashion. I restore *naccas*. Among the ancients, however, fullers were called *naccae*. Festus: “Fullers are commonly called *naccae*, as Curiatius says, because they are of no account (*nauci*).” Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* IX: “For, as it happened, her husband was dining out at the house of a neighboring fuller (*nacca*).” He had in fact previously called the gods fullers—as here he calls them *naccae*—when he said: “There are gods who are fullers, and others who are shearers, to wash even the sacred garments,” etc. **MEURSIUS**, p. 91 ff.—Meursius’s correction is certainly ingenious. Yet I would not venture to alter the received reading; for gods may be called “sailors” as patrons of sailors and helpers of seafarers—for example, the Dioscuri and [Col. 0963C] Portumnus, whom Arnobius mentions below in chapter 23. **ORELLI.**
>
> **And, what remained, farmers.** So Janus Guilielmus restored the text in *Questions on Plautus’ Curculio*, chapter IV (in Gruter’s *Lampas Critica*, vol. III, part II, p. 365). For the Latins customarily speak in this way when, after recounting many shameful acts committed by someone, they finally add that it only remains for him to commit this or that further offense against himself. That this conjecture is correct is guaranteed by the manuscript and by the verse of the scourger of Virgil:
>
> “He who has said ‘barley’ has only to go on and say ‘wheat.’”
>
> **STEWECH.** Others read: “And what surpasses farmers.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **A diviner.** The glosses: “*Divinus*, μάντις”—“a seer.” Thus Cicero, *On Fate*: “The struggling Chrysippus hopes that the Chaldeans and the other diviners are mistaken.” **ELMENHORST.**—The meaning is extremely familiar. See nevertheless Graevius on Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, Book X, letter IV, and Bunemann on Lactantius I, chapter 11, p. 64. **ORELLI.**
>
> **For the others are not gods, and through want of skill they do not know how to foretell what is to come, and through ignorance of the future they know nothing of it.** Fulvius Ursinus [Col. 0963D] conjectures: “For the others are not diviners.” But I think nothing should be changed. For certainly, if they are not *divini*—that is, if they cannot know and foretell the future—they should not be considered gods either. Lactantius, Book I, chapter 11: “First, in this there was foolishness, not divine providence; for unless Themis had told him the future, he himself would not have known it. But if he is not a diviner, neither indeed is he a god; hence the very word *divinity* is formed, just as *humanity* is formed from *human being*.” **HERALDUS.**
>
> **Ready in sequences of words.** Fulvius Ursinus prefers: “ready in harmonious arrangements of words.” But nothing should be changed. “Sequence of words” is a Ciceronian expression, whereas *concinnatio* is a barbarous word found nowhere. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Bards.** See above, on Book II, chapter 19. **ORELLI.**

### XX

And this, indeed, is the first insult to your divine powers, an insult for which you, as their virtuous and religious defenders, have made yourselves responsible by assigning them forms and sexes. But what are we to make of what follows—that among your gods you introduce [Col. 0962C] some as craftsmen, others as physicians, others as wool-workers or sailors, [Col. 0963A] lyre-players, flute-singers, hunters, shepherds, and, what remained, farmers? “That one,” you say, “is the god of music, while this other is a diviner.” For the others are not gods, and through want of skill they do not know how to foretell what is to come, and through ignorance of the future they know nothing of it. One has been trained in the arts of midwifery; [Col. 0963B; ms. *obstetriciis*; others *obstetricis*] another has been instructed in the disciplines of physicians. Do individuals, then, possess power only in their own particular field and, when called upon for help, are they unable to give assistance in departments belonging to others? This one is eloquent in speech and ready in sequences of words; others, after all, are bards and cannot utter anything polished when a speech must be delivered.

> **Note: [Col. 0963D]**
>
> **XXI.—Lowly workshop artisans know and possess them.** He calls those craftsmen who practice dirty and lowly trades *sellularii*, “sedentary workshop artisans.” Below, in the following chapter: “Since among the heavenly beings there is no place for these arts, and neither their employment nor their nature demands that they know anything ingenious or belonging to a lowly workshop.” Hence in Gellius, Book III, chapter 1, and Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXX of the *Histories*, p. 452, *quaestus sellularius* means a disgraceful and contemptible occupation. **ELMENHORST.**
>
> **Workshop artisans.** They were held in the greatest contempt among the ancients. Livy, Book VIII, chapter 20: “The common mass of craftsmen and sedentary artisans, who are least fit for military service.” **NOURRY**, p. 566.
>
> **There are forests on the mountains of the stars, there are wild-beast lairs, etc.** Meursius reads: “There are mountains among the stars, there are forests.” Caspar Barth, *Adversaria*, Book IV, chapter 5, p. 266, proposes that one should read: “There are mountains and forests in the starry abodes; there are wild-beast lairs.” Yet the same scholar, in Book LVII, chapter 17, p. 2714 of that work, defends the manuscript reading, which Salmasius also restored to the text: “There are forests amid the starry motions,” etc.—that is, among the stars driven in perpetual motion. Thus Arnobius would be expressing his astonishment here: “How can the stars, which wheel about with perpetual motion and unceasing revolution, nourish forests and sustain groves?” With this question he reproaches his opponents. *Montibus*—“on the mountains”—comes from Gelenius’s correction. Heraldus thinks that this passage alludes to the opinion that there are mountains and forests on the lunar sphere, an opinion attributed by some to Anaximenes and by others to Xenophanes—for example, by Cicero, *Academica* II, chapter 39, where see Davies; Diogenes Laërtius, however, Book II, section 88, attributes it to Anaxagoras. Compare Plutarch, *On the Face in the Moon*, chapter 35; and, on the mountains of the moon and the other planets according to the opinion of more recent astronomers, J. E. Bode, *Allgemeine Betrachtungen über das Weltgebäude* (“General Reflections on the Structure of the Universe”), p. 59 ff. **ORELLI.**
>
> **He is pressed and driven by the power of a greater divinity.** Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 78:
>
> “The prophetess rages, to see whether she can  
> Shake the mighty god from her breast; all the more  
> He wears out her frenzied mouth, subdues her wild heart,  
> And shapes her by pressing upon her.”
>
> [Col. 0964D] **ORELLI.**
>
> **So that Juno may soothe the troublesome delays of childbirth and Lucina hasten them.** *Corripiat*—“hasten”—namely the *tricas*, the entanglements or delays; that is, hasten the birth. Similarly Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX, lines 281 ff.:
>
> “May the divine powers at least favor you,  
> And hasten the delays when, at the appointed time,  
> You call upon Ilithyia, guardian of frightened women in labor.”
>
> **ORELLI.**
>
> **Flame-mighty Vulcan.** I know that the Roman codex—that is, the first printed edition—is corrupt, since in it they substituted *flammis potens*, “powerful through flames.” The other form must be retained, since elsewhere Arnobius also called Vulcan *ignipotens*, “fire-mighty”; by a similar compound Apuleius, Books I and VII, calls a witch *divinipotens*, “divinity-mighty.” In the same fashion Diana is called by the poets:
>
> “Woodland-mighty goddess, a goddess known to the woodland nymphs.”
>
> **STEWECH.**
>
> **Forge swords for them.** So the manuscript. The printed editions gave *fabricetur*, “let him fashion.” Yet both forms were used by good authors, including Marcus Tullius Cicero, father of the Latin language. **STEWECH.**—Thus in Cicero, *On Duties*, Book I, chapter 41, most manuscripts have “those who fashion statues,” although Heusinger printed *fabricantur*, “are fashioned”; see him at p. 344. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Three-heddled tunics.** That is, tunics made with three heddles. *Licia*, from *lacere*, “to catch or entangle,” are threads with which women weaving on looms interlace the strands of the warp; by their aid these can be separated and the weft inserted with the shuttle. French *lisse*; German *die Litze, Kammlitze, das Geschirr* (“the heddle, comb-heddle, harness”); Greek μίτοι (*mítoi*, “warp-threads”). Various kinds of garments receive their names from the number of heddles used in weaving; these names designate some particular nature and form belonging to each—for example, two-heddled and three-heddled cloth, our German *Zwillich, Drillich*, etc. See the distinguished Schneider, who discusses ancient weaving at length in the index to the *Writers on Agriculture*, under *Tela jugalis*, vol. IV, part II, pp. 371–372. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Or make them from silk.** I have followed Meursius’s emendation. The earlier reading was “or put them on from silk.” But one may correctly say “compose garments” in the sense of “fashion” them; one cannot similarly say “put on.” Salmasius printed: “or place them upon them from silk and without burden.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **So that the offspring of Atlas may carry off first place in eloquence, etc.** Gallandus is amusing when he interprets “the offspring of Atlas” as Calypso, Atlas’s daughter. Was eloquent Mercury, the grandson of Atlas, unknown to him from Horace, Book I, Ode X? **ORELLI.**

### XXI

But I ask: what rationale, what such harsh necessity, what cause is there that the heavenly beings should know and possess these crafts like lowly workshop artisans? Is there singing and harp-playing in heaven, so that the nine elegant sisters may join together and modulate the intervals and measures of voices? [Col. 0964A] Are there forests on the mountains of the stars, are there wild-beast lairs and groves, so that Diana may be regarded as supreme in hunting expeditions? Do the gods not know what is imminent, and do they live by lots and undergo the decrees of fate, so that the Latonian prophet may explain and disclose what tomorrow or the next hour will bring to each? Is he himself filled by another god and pressed and driven by the power of a greater divinity, so that he may deservedly be called and regarded as a diviner? Are the gods seized by diseases, and can they be wounded or afflicted by something, so that, when circumstances demand it, the helper from Epidaurus may come to their assistance? Do they go into labor and give birth, so that Juno may soothe the troublesome delays of childbirth and Lucina hasten them? Do they engage in agriculture or attend to military duties, so that flame-mighty Vulcan may forge swords for them or hammer out farming tools? Do they need the covering of clothing, so that the Tritonian virgin may carefully spin thread for them [Col. 0965A] and, according to the character of the season, make either three-heddled tunics or garments of silk? Do they bring accusations and refute charges, so that the offspring of Atlas may carry off first place in eloquence acquired through diligent practice?

> **Note: [Col. 0965C]**
>
> **Things to be learned.** Meursius corrects this to *sciendas*, agreeing with *artes* (“arts”). **ORELLI.**
>
> **And to make this man skillful.** So Ursinus and Salmasius. The old reading is: “and to make him skillful in these things.” Meursius: “and to make him skillful.” Stewechius: “and skillful in this way.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **He himself must first know what he has determined that another should cultivate.** This is the manuscript reading. Heraldus interprets it by taking *colere* as equivalent to *docere*, “to teach,” and as similarly construed by Arnobius with a double accusative: “to cultivate someone in something,” like “to teach someone something.” I have, however, searched in vain for examples of this construction. Yet the manuscript reading can be accepted if we interpret it thus: “The man himself must know what he has determined that another should cultivate”—that is, he himself must know the art that he places before another to be learned. This agrees very well with the preceding words: “But anyone who places some discipline before an ignorant and unknowing person and strives to make him skillful through knowledge of some work.” Here Arnobius properly said “places a discipline before him.” For the gods did not laboriously educate and instruct human beings in arts and disciplines; they merely introduced them into human life—that is, they pointed out the arts to human beings, as though with their fingertips, so that human beings themselves might learn them. I therefore think that nothing should be changed. For *colere artem*, “to cultivate an art,” in the sense of “to learn it,” occurs hundreds of times among the ancients. Fulvius Ursinus conjecturally reads: “what he has determined that another should master,” with Stewechius’s approval; Salmasius printed: “what he has determined to teach another.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **The gods, therefore, are craftsmen; they are the first—whether because, etc.** Heraldus thinks that some corruption lies in these words and that the second *sunt* should be removed, so that the sentence may proceed smoothly. The Leiden edition has: “Therefore let the gods be craftsmen; first let them be.” But nothing should be changed. “The gods, therefore, are craftsmen” is the conclusion drawn from the preceding argument. Arnobius then continues: “indeed, they are the first,” which he demonstrates in what follows. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Why you say that different gods are more knowledgeable in different branches of understanding.** Canterus and the Leiden edition printed *gnarures*, following Joseph Scaliger’s emendation in his note on Festus under the word *gnarigavit*. The manuscript has the corrupt *ignariores*, from which Gelenius had produced *gnariores*. But *gnarures* must be read. *Gnaruris* is the archaic form of *gnarus*, just as *gnaruro* is used for *gnarum reddo*, “I make known.” Plautus, *Mostellaria*, Act I, scene II: “At the same time I want you to know this matter along with me.” See the commentators on Festus at the passage cited; on Ausonius, Letter XXII, line 20, p. 671 of Tollius’s edition; Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* I.15, p. 64; and especially G. J. Vossius, who discusses this word at length in his *Roman Etymologies*, under *gnarus*. In place of *perceptionibus* (“branches of understanding”), the first edition has *praeceptionibus* (“precepts”), which could be accepted as meaning the precepts of the arts. Meursius conjectures *ignarures*, “more ignorant.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **And possess skills in which individuals surpass one another.** Fulvius Ursinus, with Meursius’s approval, emended this closer to the manuscript reading—*in quibus singulis evincant*—as “in which individuals surpass one another.” Stewechius prefers: “in which individuals flourish.” The Leiden edition has: “in which individuals are preeminent.” **ORELLI.**

### XXII

“You are mistaken,” he says, “and deceived; [Col. 0965B: but the manuscript has, ‘But you are mistaken.’ Correctly. Meursius and Sabinus read, ‘And you are mistaken.’] For the gods are not themselves craftsmen; rather, they place these arts before human minds and, so that life may be better equipped, hand down to mortals the things they must learn.” But anyone who places some discipline before an ignorant and unknowing person and strives to make him skillful through knowledge of some work must himself first know what he has determined that another should cultivate. For no one can hand down any body of knowledge without knowing the precepts of what he transmits and possessing its method in a thoroughly mastered form. The gods, therefore, are the first craftsmen: either because, as you yourselves say, they implant [Col. 0965B] knowledge in human minds, or because, being immortal and never born, they precede the whole earthly race in antiquity of time. [Col. 0966A] This, then, is what is being asked: since among the heavenly beings there is no place for these arts, and neither their employment nor their nature demands that they know anything ingenious or belonging to a lowly workshop, why do you say that different gods are more knowledgeable in different branches of understanding and possess skills in which individuals surpass one another, being distinguished by their knowledge of particular sciences?

> **Note: [Col. 0966D]**
>
> **And that their providence ensures that they turn out well and successfully.** Why should *cadant*, “turn out,” be used here? As though *cedere* were not said in precisely the same way! Thus “to turn out well and successfully” corresponds to the Greek εὐροεῖν and εὖ πλεῖν, “to flow prosperously” and “to sail well.” A thing is similarly said to ὁδῷ βαδίζειν, “proceed along its road,” when it advances well and successfully toward its end, delayed by no obstacles. Plutarch, *Pyrrhus*: “Thinking that the plot was proceeding along its road, he could not contain himself, but in his joy disclosed it to his friends” (καὶ τὴν ἐπιβουλὴν ὁδῷ βαδίζειν οἰόμενος οὐ κατεῖχεν, ἀλλ’ ὑπὸ χαρᾶς ἐξέφερε πρὸς τοὺς φίλους). Thus also Ovid, *Fasti* I:
>
> “She rejoices; drawing the garment away from her feet,  
> She had begun to proceed toward her desires upon a fortunate road.”
>
> **HERALDUS.**
>
> **That the gods remain over us as guardians.** *Superesse* means “to preside over.” Thus below, chapter 25: “Unxia,” he says, “presides over anointings, Cinxia over the unfastening of girdles”; and Book IV, chapter 9: “Who appointed Libentina, who Liburnus, to preside over the protection of lusts?” So very frequently among the jurists. In the same sense, above, *supra rem aliquem esse* means “for someone to preside over a matter” in Vitruvius’s preface to Book VII: “The king referred the matter to those who had been placed over the library” (Caspar Barth, *Adversaria*, Book XXIV, chapter 11, p. 1193). Similarly Tacitus, *Annals* III.47: “The legates had contributed loyalty and courage, he himself counsel”—that is, he had been present and rendered assistance. See Ernesti, p. 318 of Oberlin’s edition. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Portunus provides the safest voyages over the seas for travelers.** “The safest” is correct. Hence people also offered prayers and sacrifices to Ποσειδῶν Ἀσφαλεῖος, “Poseidon the Giver of Safety.” Thus those about to sail invoked not only Neptune but also Portunus and the other gods of the sea. **HERALDUS.** The classic passage concerning Portunus or Portumnus—for both forms are written—is Ovid, *Fasti* VI, 541 ff.:
>
> “Rejoice, Ino, your labors ended,”  
> He said, “and always favor this people with your right hand.  
> You shall be a divinity of the sea; the sea shall also possess your son.  
> Take other names in your waters.  
> You will be Leucothea to the Greeks and Matuta to our people.  
> Your son shall possess every right over harbors.  
> Our tongue will call him Portumnus, his own Palaemon.  
> Go, I pray, and both be gracious to our lands.”
>
> Portunus, of course, derives his name from *portus*, “harbor.” See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.26. [Col. 0967C] **ELMENHORST and ORELLI.**
>
> **Consus.** Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, 636: “The Sabine women were carried off at the Consualia—that is, in the month of March. Consus, moreover, is the god of counsels; for this reason his temple is under a roof, to show that counsel ought to be covered. Hence sacrifice was also offered to Fides with the hand covered by a cloth, because faith ought to be covered and veiled. They carried off the Sabine women before the image of Consus so that the plan adopted for the abduction might be concealed. This Consus is also called equestrian Neptune; hence circus games are also celebrated in his honor.” Compare Asconius Pedianus on Cicero’s preface to the *Action against Verres*; Plutarch, *Romulus*, chapter XIII; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, Book II, p. 100, Sylburg’s edition; Augustine, *City of God*, Book IV, chapter 11; and Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chapter 5. **ELMENHORST and ORELLI.**—Compare Rittershausen on Salvian, p. 69, Bremen edition.
>
> **Pales and Inuus as guardians.** According to Macrobius (*Saturnalia* I.22), Inuus was the same as Pan; or, as Servius observes (*Aeneid* VI, line 776), Inuus is his name in Latin and Πάν, “Pan,” in Greek. He is also ἐφιάλτης, “the nightmare-demon,” in Greek, and *Incubo*, “the incubus,” in Latin. He is also Faunus, Fatuus, and Fatuellus. He is said to derive his name from *ineundo*, because he mates indiscriminately with all animals. (Nourry, p. 410.) He is also Faunus, Fatuus, and Fatuellus. Inuus is said to derive his name from going indiscriminately among all animals. Aurelius Victor agrees with Servius in *Origin of the Roman People*, chapter IV; see there Joannes Arntzen, who carefully collected all the ancient passages concerning Inuus, p. 11. Compare Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.22; Rutilius, *Itinerary* I, line 232; and the commentators in P. Burman’s *Minor Latin Poets*, vol. II, pp. 77–78. **ORELLI.**
>
> **To avert them from the summer pastures.** Varro noted these summer pastures in *On Agriculture* II.1.16: namely, that the Romans drove their livestock to winter in one place and summer in another, much as their soldiers had winter quarters in one place and summer quarters in another. **STEWECH.**
>
> **Through hostile inaction.** Stewechius thinks one should read: “through theatrical inaction.” Meursius: “through rainy inaction”—that is, inaction caused by rain. But the received reading, “hostile,” is sound: it is equivalent to “unwelcome, troublesome,” as Schwarz correctly explains in his note on Pliny’s *Panegyric*, chapter XVI, p. 85. *Cessatio* means the failure to hinder or avert an evil one could avert—German *das Zusehen, Zulassen, Geschehenlassen* (“looking on, permitting, allowing to happen”). See above, on Book II, chapter 44. **ORELLI.**
>
> **That prostitute Flora.** So all editors before Salmasius, who gave *genetrix*, “mother,” in the Leiden edition. But if *meretrix*, “prostitute,” derives from the manuscript, it should not be eliminated. Thus Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, chapter 25: “Indeed, Acca Laurentia and Flora, shameless prostitutes, must also be reckoned among the diseases and the gods of the Romans”; see Elmenhorst there, p. 257 of Gronovius’s edition. Lactantius, *Institutes* I.20: “When Flora had acquired great wealth through prostitution, she named the Roman people as her heir and left a fixed sum of money, from the annual interest on which her birthday was to be celebrated by presenting games called the Floralia.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **The most destructive frost scorches the budding grasses.** *Urere* and *adurere*, “to burn” or “scorch,” are very frequently used of cold by the best authors. Thus Ovid, *Fasti* I, 680:
>
> “Nor let the new grass be scorched beneath the freezing snow.”
>
> [Col. 0968C] And Virgil, *Georgics* I, line 93:
>
> “Or let the fiercer power of the swift sun,  
> Or the piercing cold of Boreas, scorch it.”
>
> See Servius there. Compare Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* II.16, and Davies there; Heinsius and Drakenborch on Silius IV.68; Savaron on Sidonius, poem V, line 528; Valckenaer on Theocritus’s *Adonis*, p. 224; and Oberlin on Tacitus, *Annals* XIII.35, p. 782. **ORELLI.**
>
> **By the murderous struggles of labor.** Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 25: “Yet even while still in the womb the infant is slaughtered by necessary cruelty when, twisted sideways at the exit, it refuses delivery—a matricide unless it is to die.” **HERALDUS.**
>
> **And portions of cities.** So the manuscript and the Leiden edition. Others read *potiores*, “the more important,” from a conjecture of Gelenius. But nothing should be changed. “Portions of cities” are the districts and neighborhoods of cities, which are rather frequently consumed by fire; entire cities very rarely. **ORELLI.**
>
> **He allows them to collapse into ashes through the voracity of flames.** [Col. 0968D] The expression is exact, for fire is said to devour like some savage beast. Accordingly, the Egyptians were unwilling to cremate bodies because they believed that fire “is a living beast and eats everything it catches” (θηρίον εἶναι ἔμψυχον· πάντα δὲ αὐτὸ ἐσθίειν, τάπερ ἂν λάβῃ), as Herodotus writes in Book III. Pindar likewise calls the fire erupting from Etna a ἑρπετόν, “creeping creature,” for precisely the same reason, in the First *Pythian Ode*. And Aeschylus in *Prometheus*:
>
> “Rivers of fire, devouring with savage jaws  
> The fair-fruited fields of Sicily.”
>
> (Ποταμοὶ πυρὸς δάπτοντες ἀγρίαις γνάθοις  
> Τῆς καλλικάρπου Σικελίας λευρὰς γύας.)
>
> Hence *to lick*, which is properly attributed to serpents, is often said of fire by Virgil and others, and *to taste* by Lucretius II, 192. **HERALDUS.**
>
> **Twisted, doubtful.** So the manuscript, and I would not venture to change the reading. For we have already shown rather often that Arnobius likes to join such epithets without connective particles. In the same sense Statius, *Thebaid* III.382, spoke of “twisted prayers,” when someone does not ask directly but says things that possess the force of prayers. “Twisted answers,” therefore: German *gewundne geschraubte Antworten* (“winding, convoluted answers”). In the same sense Pacuvius once used *flexa*, “bent”:
>
> “At Delphi the utterance is accustomed to pronounce things bent, not false.”
>
> [Col. 0969B] Thus Virgil says of the Sibyl filled with Apollo in *Aeneid* VI: “She chants dreadful riddling circumlocutions.” Hence Apollo is called Λοξίας, “the Oblique One,” among the Greeks. Fulvius Ursinus reads: “why oblique and submerged in obscurity,” omitting the word “doubtful.” Salmasius and Oberthür read: “Why oblique and doubtful.” **HERALDUS and ORELLI.**
>
> **And submerged in a cloud of obscurity.** The manuscript has “and submerged in obscurities, in a cloud,” which Heraldus defends, placing punctuation after *submersa*—“submerged, in a cloud”—in keeping with Arnobius’s custom of joining several terms without a conjunction. But one may doubt whether Arnobius departed here from the customary expression *obscuritatis caligo*, “a cloud of obscurity.” I therefore follow the emendation of Stewechius and the Leiden editor. Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “submerged in a cloud of obscurities.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **He very often gives and supplies answers.** So the Leiden edition, following the conjecture of Meursius and Stewechius, which Heraldus also approved in his *Second Thoughts*. The manuscript has: “He points out answers.” Both readings, I think, can be accepted. Apollo “points out” answers to those consulting the oracles; he “supplies” them to the priests who prophesy. **ORELLI.**
>
> **Aesculapius presides over the duties and arts of healing.** Stewechius conjectures “workshops,” etc., thinking that *officia* used absolutely in an obscene sense would suit Priapus better than Aesculapius. But nothing should be changed. This is, of course, Arnobius’s familiar transposition for “the duties and arts of healing.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **Indeed, do they not become more terrible beneath the very hands of those treating them? Mercury oversees, etc.** I have printed this from the extremely felicitous and, as I think, entirely correct emendation of the Leiden editor. The manuscript reads: “Indeed, beneath the very hands of those treating them they become more terrible. Treatments. Mercury,” etc. Fulvius Ursinus and Heraldus rightly suspected the word “treatments” and deleted it; Stewechius read “treatment.” But Salmasius’s correction is much better: he restored *curat*, “oversees,” and joined it to the words that follow. **ORELLI.**
>
> **The *ceroma*.** This word has two meanings. A *ceroma* is an ointment made from oil, softened wax, and clay, with which athletes and others were anointed; Martial, Book XIV, epigram 19; Pliny, *Natural History* XXVIII.4 and XXIX.1; and Juvenal, Satire VI, line 247, mention it.
