In another sense, however, *ceroma* signifies the place where those same athletes were anointed. Pliny, *Natural History* XXXV.13: “They adorn wrestling schools with images of athletes and their own *ceromata*.” Seneca, *On the Shortness of Life*, chapter 1: “In the *ceroma* … he sits as a spectator of boys quarreling.” The word appears to have this second sense in our passage. **NOURRY**, p. 414. The formation of the accusative as though it belonged to the first declension is, however, rather unusual here, since in all the cited passages the form is *ceroma, -atis*, neuter. Compare Gorraeus, *Medical Definitions*, under Κήρωμα (*kḗrōma*).
>
> **He presides over boxing and wrestling.** Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II, §4:
>
> “Then the Etruscan soldier fought with scourge-bearers  
> And with boxers anointed with oil and gymnastic art;  
> Nor could Mercury, distinguished by his broad-brimmed hat,  
> Save his own wrestling schools when Sparta was captured.”
>
> **NOURRY**, p. 415.
>
> [Col. 0970A] **Why the presidency rests in the office of one.** Below, Book IV: “And what, I ask, is he to do, since this god has received the presidency over hearths?” **ELMENHORST.**—A prefecture, or the office of a president, superintendent, or prefect. **NOURRY**, p. 561. See the following chapter. The word belongs to declining Latin. Aurelius Victor, *On the Caesars*, [Col. 0970B] chapter 29: “He governed the Macedonians with the office of governor.” Vopiscus, *Carinus*, chapter 17, p. 812: “He administered the governorship of Dalmatia,” etc. Compare Ole Borch, *Cogitationes*, under this word. **ORELLI.**
>
> **He makes these possessors of victory, but allows others to be mocked because of their disgraceful weakness.** Note the construction in passing. Thus Homer, *Iliad* I:
>
> “She then  
> Leapt into the deep sea from gleaming Olympus,  
> But Zeus toward his own house …”
>
> Supply “went.” And in tragedy:
>
> “And do not send me dishonored from this land,  
> But make me rich in authority and master of the house.”
>
> Supply “establish me.” So here understand *perficit*, “he makes”: “he makes these possessors of victory, but allows others,” etc. The verb must be taken as common to both clauses, ἀπὸ κοινοῦ (*apo koinou*). **HERALDUS.** This zeugma occurs everywhere. Stewechius, therefore, should not be followed when, both in his edition and in his notes on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* XI, p. 800 of Oudendorp’s edition, he conjectures *compotit*, “makes possessors.” The verb is otherwise well attested and ancient. **ORELLI.**
>
> **To be mocked because of their disgraceful weakness.** Nothing here should be altered either. Why “because of weakness” here? In this way, then, those who perform their roles ineptly are mocked by the spectators. Horace, *Epistles* I.1, lines 8–9:
>
> “While sound, release the aging horse in good time, lest  
> He stumble at the finish, be mocked, and heave his flanks.”
>
> Such was the fate of that fat runner, slow because of his excessive corpulence, whom Aristophanes in the *Frogs* describes as mocked and prodded by the spectators. **HERALDUS.**

### XXIII

“Unless perhaps you say that the gods are not craftsmen but preside over and take care of these arts; indeed, that everything we administer and perform has been placed under their guardianship, and that their providence ensures that our undertakings turn out well and successfully.” This could indeed deservedly and plausibly be said if the things we undertake and perform, or hazard in human affairs, always proceeded according to our will and intention. But since events daily turn out in the opposite direction, and the ends of our actions do not correspond [Col. 0966B] to the purpose of our will, it is mere sport to say that the gods remain over us as guardians—gods fashioned by our suspicion, not apprehended by verified truth. [Col. 0967A]

Portunus provides the safest voyages over the seas for travelers; but why has the raging sea presented such frequent scenes of destruction from cruel shipwrecks? Consus suggests beneficial and trustworthy counsels to our thoughts; but why does the unforeseen reversal of our decisions constantly turn toward opposite outcomes? Pales and Inuus preside as guardians over herds of cattle and flocks of livestock; but why, through hostile inaction, do they not take care to avert savage contagions and pestilential diseases from the summer pastures? That prostitute Flora, through the sacred obscenity [Col. 0968A] of her games, takes good care that the fields blossom; but why does the most destructive frost daily scorch and kill the buds and budding grasses? Juno has been appointed over childbirth and assists pregnant mothers; but why do thousands of mothers die each day, destroyed by the murderous struggles of labor? Fire is under Vulcan’s protection, and its substance has been placed under his governance; but why does he so frequently allow sacred buildings and portions of cities to collapse into ashes through the voracity of flames? Pythian Apollo grants the science of divination to soothsayers; but why does he so often give and supply answers that are twisted and doubtful, submerged [Col. 0969A] in a cloud of obscurity? Aesculapius presides over the duties and arts of healing; but why can so many kinds of diseases and ailments not be brought to health and soundness—indeed, why do they become more terrible beneath the very hands of those treating them? Mercury oversees the *ceroma* [Col. 0969A: Fulvius reads *ceromast*] and presides over boxing and wrestling; but why does he not make all those over whom he presides invincible? Why, within the function of a single presidency, does he make these possessors of victory but allow others to be mocked because of their disgraceful weakness?

> **[Col. 0970A] Note: [Col. 0970C]**
>
> **XXIV.—And unless they see their little altars smeared with the blood of livestock.** Yet elsewhere *arulae* are called ἐσχάραι περιφορηταί, “portable hearth-altars,” as the scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Acharnians* teaches. The Latins call them *foculi*, “small hearths,” a term general in name but specifically assigned to this object. Thus what Livy, in the story of Scaevola, and Seneca, Letters XXIV and LXVII, call an “ignited *foculus*,” Plutarch in *Publicola* calls ἐσχαρίδα πῦρ ἔχουσαν, “a small hearth containing fire.” **HERALDUS.**—But *arula* in this passage undoubtedly means an altar. For livestock were never offered on such portable hearths, but only produce or smaller living creatures—for example, doves—or else spices were burned on them. Moreover, the guardian gods named by the author were not always lesser gods or spirits, but also gods of the major order, to whom accordingly sacrifice was made with larger victims—for example, Juno Sospita. **ORELLI.**
>
> **And that unexpected gifts of benevolence flow voluntarily from them.** Where had the minds of those scholars gone—for example, Fulvius Ursinus—who wanted *inexpetita*, “unsought,” to be restored here? Yet the received reading is excellent and extremely appropriate. For people believed so firmly that unexpected benefits flowed from the gods that they credited the gods with whatever turned out prosperously and successfully beyond expectation. Hence they called such things θεόπεμπτα (*theópempta*), “god-sent”—for example, Artemidorus, Book I, chapter 7. They likewise said that these happened κατὰ θεῖον, “through divine agency”; κατὰ δαίμονα, “through a divine power”; κατὰ τύχην or ἀπὸ τύχης, “by chance.” The Latin expression is *divinitus*, “by divine agency.” **HERALDUS.**
>
> **He supplies them equally to all—to good, evil, just, freeborn, and enslaved persons.** I approve Fulvius Ursinus’s conjecture: “He supplies them equally to all—to good, evil, just, unjust, freeborn, and enslaved persons.” Stewechius, following the traces of the manuscript, which reads “evil, unjust, enslaved,” corrects it to “just, enslaved”; he thinks that “just persons,” in opposition to slaves, should be understood as freedmen who, according to the jurists’ definition, had obtained lawful or greater liberty, or indeed Roman citizenship—namely, those who had been manumitted by the rod, by enrollment in the census, or by testament. *Ingenuis*, “freeborn,” comes from Gelenius’s correction. **ORELLI.**
>
> **To weary and powerless beings.** See above, on Book I, chapter 25. **ORELLI.**
>
> [Col. 0971C] **And always hedged in by manifold harshness.** Thus he renders the Greek περίστασις (*perístasis*), “distressing circumstance.” **HERALDUS.**
>
> **After sacrifices have been offered.** In his *Second Thoughts*, Heraldus prefers: “after sacrifices have been rendered.” **ORELLI.**
>
> **The magnificence of the name.** Stewechius prefers “of the divine power.” But Arnobius likes to say “the name of God” for “God.” See above, on Book I. **ORELLI.**

### XXIV

“No one,” he says, “offers supplication to the guardian gods, and therefore they individually withhold their familiar services and assistance.” Unless they receive incense and salted grain, are the gods unable to confer benefits? Unless they see their little altars smeared with the blood of livestock, do they desert and abandon the offices over which they preside? Yet I had believed a little while ago that the kindnesses of the divine powers were spontaneous, and that unexpected gifts of benevolence flowed voluntarily from them. For is the king of heaven coaxed by some libation [Col. 0971A] or sacrificial victim into granting the races of mortals all these advantages by which they live? Does not God equally supply to everyone—the good, the evil, the just, the freeborn, the enslaved, the poor, and the rich—the generative heat of the sun, the seasons of the night, the winds, the rains, and the crops? For this is proper to a powerful and true God: to furnish benefits without being entreated to weary and powerless beings always hedged in by manifold harshness. To grant what you request only after sacrifices have been offered is not to assist those who ask, but to put the bounty of one’s own benevolence up for sale. We human beings play and behave wantonly in a matter of such importance; and, forgetting what God is and what the magnificence of that name entails, we arrogate to guardian divinities every vile or sordid thing that we have been able to invent through credulous suspicion. [Col. 0971B]

> **[Col. 0972A] Note: [Col. 0971C]**
>
> **XXV.—Unxia, he says, presides over anointings, Cinxia over the unfastening of girdles.** Martianus Capella, *The Marriage of Philology*, Book II, p. 37 (p. 61 of Bernhard’s edition): “Mortal maidens must invoke you, Juno, at weddings as Interduca and Domiduca, Unxia and Cinctia, so that you may protect their journeys, lead them into the homes they desire, fasten a favorable omen upon them when they anoint the doorposts, and not abandon them in the bridal chambers when they lay aside the girdle.” Compare Festus under *Cinxia Juno*. **ELMENHORST.**—Cinxia was called by the Greeks Εἰλήθυια λυσίζωνος, “Ilithyia who loosens the girdle.” Theocritus, *Idyll* XVII, line 60:
>
> “For there she called upon Ilithyia, loosener of the girdle.”
>
> (Ἔνθα γὰρ Εἰλήθυιαν ἐβώσατο λυσίζωνον.)
>
> **NOURRY**, p. 412.
>
> [Col. 0971D] In place of *replicationi*, “the unfastening,” Stewechius suspects that one should read *explicationi*, “the untying”; for the girdle was bound with a Herculean knot—that is, an extremely tight one—according to Festus. See G. J. Vossius, *On the Idolatry of the Gentiles*, Book II, chapter 26, p. 161. **ORELLI.**
Victa and Potua, most holy. These elegant divinities are found designated in such various ways that one might readily suppose their majesty was neither great nor very celebrated. HERALD.—Augustine, *City of God*, book IV, chapter 11: “She is called Potina, who ministers drink; Educa, who provides food.” Cato, *On the Education of Children*, in Nonius, calls Edusa and Potina goddesses who preside over infant children. Varro, in Donatus on Terence, *Phormio*, Act I, scene 1, verse 11, reports that boys were initiated into the rites of Edulia, Potica, and Cuba, goddesses of eating, drinking, and lying down; see Lindenbrog there, p. 593, Zeune’s edition. Compare Ausonius Popma on the *Fragments of Varro*, p. 400, Bipont edition, who judges that in our author *Victua* should be read for *Victa*, with Fulvius Ursinus. Meursius: *Victa and Pota*. ORELLI.

Unless the doorposts of the husbands were smeared with fatty ointment [Col. 0972B] by the brides. Servius on *Aeneid* IV, verses 457 ff.: “Dido,” he says, “desired her husband’s temple to possess the character of a true and venerable temple. For temples are marked as sacred by coverings, and it had been customary that, as soon as brides arrived at their husband’s threshold, before entering they should, as an omen of chastity, adorn the doorposts with woolen bands—whence Virgil says ‘with snowy fleeces’—and anoint them with oil. From this wives (*uxores*) were so called, as though ‘anointers’ (*unxores*).” A little later: “Those who are said to have written about weddings report that, when a new bride is led into her husband’s house, the doorposts are customarily smeared with wolf’s fat, because both the claw and the limbs of this beast are remedies for many conditions. Others say that this was instituted in the time of Romulus, because Romulus and Remus were nourished on a she-wolf’s milk.” HERALDUS.—Compare Brissonius, *On the Wedding Rite*. ELMENHORST.

Unless the husbands, already burning and pressing upon them, loosened the virginal bonds. Festus: “A new bride was girded with a belt made from sheep’s wool, which the husband loosened in bed, so that, just as that wool, gathered into balls, was joined together, so her husband might be girded and bound together with her. The husband loosened this belt, tied with the Herculean knot, for the sake of the omen: that he might be as fortunate in begetting children as Hercules, who left seventy children.” Compare Ernesti on Callimachus, *Hymn to Diana*, verse 16, and Döring on Catullus, poem II, final verse. Furthermore, “pressing husbands” means husbands most eagerly seeking a woman’s embrace, as though just about to loosen the reins of appetite. Thus Catullus, poem LXI, verse 171:

> Look within, how, reclining,  
> Your husband upon the Tyrian couch  
> Presses wholly upon you.

See there Achilles Statius, p. 213, Graevius’s edition, and C. Barth, *Adversaria*, book XLVI, chapter 20, p. 2172. ORELLI.

You attribute to them natures delighting always in evils, and in the devastation of the human race. Thus Fulvius Ursinus, with the approval of Meursius, Heraldus, and Salmasius. The manuscript: “you have attributed devastation.” ORELLI.]

### XXV

“For anointings,” he says, “there remains Unxia; for the unfastening of belts, Cinxia; most holy Victa and Potua provide for food and drink.” O splendid interpretation of the gods, and extraordinary interpretation of their powers! Unless the doorposts of husbands were smeared with fatty ointment by brides; unless husbands, already burning and pressing upon them, loosened virginal bonds; unless human beings drank and ate—would the gods have no names? What of the fact that, not content to have subjected and entangled the gods in such shameful concerns, you also attribute to them savage, ferocious, monstrous natures, always delighting in evils and in the devastation of the human race?

[Note: [Col. 0972D]

### XXVI.—The goddess Laverna of thieves

Hence the thief’s prayers to Laverna in Horace, *Epistles* I.16, verses 60 ff.:

> Lovely Laverna,  
> Grant me the power to deceive; grant that I may seem just and holy;  
> Cast night over my sins, and a cloud over my frauds.

Here Acro says: “Laverna has a grove on the Salarian Way. She is a goddess of thieves, called Laverna from *lavare*, ‘to wash,’ for thieves are called *lavatores*, ‘washers.’” An example occurs in Petronius, chapter 140, §15; see Antonius there. Compare G. J. Vossius, *On Idolatry*, book VIII, chapter 17, and book IX, chapter 30, and his *Roman Etymology*, under *Laverniones*. ORELLI.

Bellonae, Discords. Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.701:

> And the grim Furies from the sky;  
> And Discord strides exultantly, her robe torn apart;  
> Bellona follows her with bloodstained whip.

[Col. 0973B] Compare Augustine, *City of God*, book IV, chapter 21. HERALDUS and ELMENHORST.

And those sinister divinities which you establish. “Sinister divinities” is used here in the Greek sense: divinities more powerful in harming than in helping. Thus below, book VII, chapter 23: “For to say that the gods are most benevolent, that their natures are gentle, is holy, religious, and true; but that they are evil and sinister must by no means be admitted to one’s ears.” And in the same chapter: “Thus it is of no benefit to wish to win over sinister gods by sacrifices.” Compare Gellius, *Attic Nights*, [Col. 0973C] book V, chapter 12. In the opposite sense, among Romans “sinister divinities” are favorable and propitious, as in Virgil, *Georgics* IV.7:

> . . . . . . . . . if the favorable  
> Divinities permit him, and Apollo hears when called.

See Vossius, the distinguished scholar, pp. 733 ff. ORELLI.

With the silence of taciturnity. Meursius should not be heeded when he conjectures: “with silence sufficiently taciturn.” Writers of the later period liked to speak in this way. Aldhelm, *On the Praise of Virginity*, quoted by Elmenhorst: “If that most celebrated kind of spectacle, renowned throughout every quarter of the world, should decline in value, stopped up by the silence of taciturnity.” In the same sense, “taciturn silences” occurs even among the best writers; for example, Ovid, *Art of Love* II.505:

> Let him who pleases in conversation break the taciturn silences.

We shall place Mars himself in the midst. The Greeks speak in this way. Arrian, book III, *Discourses of Epictetus*: “Come into the midst and tell us: when did you sleep more tranquilly—now, or before you became Caesar’s friend?” HERALD.

For if he is the queller of military madness. Mars Quirinus. See above on book I, chapter 41. ORELLI.

But if he is their founder. Mars Gradivus. See above on book I, chapter 41. ORELLI.

And impose the condition of slavery. This expression is used precisely and in the jurists’ manner of speaking. Zeno of Verona, second sermon *On Avarice*: “But this does not apply to you, brothers, whose generosity is known throughout all the provinces. Many have been redeemed by you; many freed from deadly decrees; many released from their conditions give thanks. Your houses stand open to all strangers,” etc. Hence *conditionales*, those who hired out their labor under specified conditions. Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chapter XII: “I was both a laborer and a conditional servant.” HERALD.

Through the parricidal slaughter of brothers dying together. He alludes to the story of Eteocles and Polynices. Meursius conjectures “through parricidal slaughter.” ORELLI.

With the parricidal horror of their encounter. A transposition not uncommon among Latin writers, for “with the horror of their parricidal encounter,” as Fulvius Ursinus wished, unnecessarily, to correct it. ORELLI.]

### XXVI

We shall not mention here the goddess Laverna [Col. 0972B] of thieves, the Bellonae, Discords, Furies, and those sinister [Col. 0973A] divinities which you establish; we shall pass them over with the silence of taciturnity. We shall place Mars himself in the midst, together with that beautiful mother of the Cupids: of these you set the one over battles, the other over loves and the heat of desire.

“Mars,” one says, “possesses power over wars.” Is it so that he may suppress them once they have been stirred up, or so that he may stir them up when they have ceased and are at rest? For if he is the queller of military madness, why are wars never absent from day to day? But if he is their founder, shall we therefore say that, for the sweetness of his own pleasure, a god makes the whole world collide; that he sows causes of discord and crisis among nations separated by vast distances of land; draws together from opposing sides so many thousands of mortals; and within the brief interval of a single word heaps fields with corpses, sends torrents of blood rushing down, destroys the most firmly established empires, levels cities [Col. 0973B] with the ground, abolishes the freedom of the freeborn and imposes the condition of slavery; delights in civil dissensions, [Col. 0974A] in the parricidal slaughter of brothers dying together, and finally in the parricidal horror of encounters between sons and fathers?

[Note: [Col. 0974B]

### XXVII.—Whatever stain and crime proceeds from such madness must be imputed to wounds inflicted by Venus

Thus the printed editions, following the correction of the Leiden editor. The manuscript: “must be imputed to such venereal wounds”; from this Gelenius had made: “proceeds from such, must be imputed to Venus,” etc. Heraldus: “proceeds from such, so that it must be imputed to Venus,” etc. ORELLI.

Are torn apart. The same as “are divided” or “are severed.” [Col. 0974C] See Salmasius on Solinus, p. 797. Others read “are unstitched,” not badly. ORELLI.

Into incestuous lusts. Stewechius restored this from traces in the manuscript, where there stood “incestuous lusts”; the Leiden edition followed him. Previously it read: “with incestuous lust.” ORELLI.

Wise and brave men dissolve the settled resolutions of constancy. He speaks in Stoic terms. Among the Stoics, those who master their spirit and suppress their vices are called brave, rather than those who excel in military glory. From the same source come “settled resolutions,” *ta kekrimena* (τὰ κεκριμένα), “the things decided,” from which arises an unconquered *prohairesis* (προαίρεσις), “moral choice,” and thence constancy, *to bebaion tou ēthous* (τὸ βέβαιον τοῦ ἤθους), “firmness of character,” when virtue has been fully consummated and founded upon the strongest roots. HERALD.

When the vigor of manhood has been softened. Meursius, p. 95, and Drakenborch on Silius Italicus, book VI, verse 275, p. 307, suspect that “when the rigidity of manhood has been softened” should be read. But Wopkens, *Tullian Readings*, book I, chapter 11, p. 63, ably defends the received reading. Thus [Col. 0974D] Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, chapter IV: “unless long softened and deprived of vigor,” where Salmasius, p. 253, notes that Tertullian and other writers of their time frequently use “vigor” for “rigidity” and whatever is opposed to softness. Thus the same Tertullian, in *On the Soul*, called the rigid doctrine of the Stoics and that “Stoic impassibility” (*apatheian tēn Stōikēn*, ἀπάθειαν τὴν Στωϊκήν) “vigor”: “According as it is Plato’s distinction and Zeno’s vigor, Aristotle’s tension, Epicurus’s stupor, or Heraclitus’s sorrow.” Similarly, he speaks of “the vigor of discipline” and of “giving vigor to discipline,” that is, making it more rigid. Cyprian likewise says, “rebuking with the vigor of a censor and judge,” for “with the severity of a censor,” etc. These observations are from Salmasius, in the place cited. ORELLI.

Nooses are fastened to necks. R. Bentley, on Horace, *Epodes* XVII.72, demonstrates from many examples that the expression “and in vain you will fasten chains to your throat,” like “to fasten nooses to necks,” is entirely contrary to good and approved Latin usage. One should instead have said “to fasten the throat with chains” and “to fasten necks with nooses.” He therefore proposes that Horace should read: [Col. 0975B] “and in vain you will bind chains to your throat,” and perhaps our author as well: “nooses are bound to necks.” Nevertheless, as that greatest of critics himself admits, something of this kind may perhaps be tolerated in Arnobius, since he was a less exact writer of a later age. ORELLI.

Blazing pyres are mounted. An allusion to Dido’s fate. ORELLI.

And, hurled headlong, they cast themselves everywhere from vast and towering cliffs in voluntary leaps. Arnobius is undoubtedly referring [Col. 0975C] to that famous leap from the Leucadian rock, from which despairing lovers seeking a cure for their madness cast themselves into the sea. See Ovid, *Heroides* XV.164 ff., and especially the very full discussion of this subject by the illustrious Barthélemy in *Voyage of the Young Anacharsis*, chapter 36. ORELLI.]

### XXVII

The very same argument may be transferred to Venus by an equal and identical line of reasoning. For if, as you report and believe, she implants the flames of love in human thoughts, it follows that whatever stain and crime proceeds from such madness must be imputed to wounds inflicted by Venus.

Is it, then, under the compulsion of a goddess that even nobles so often betray their dignity to prostitutes of the vilest repute; that the bonds of enduring [Note: [Col. 0973B] The manuscript is thoroughly corrupt: *Disuriuntur tanacium*.] marriages are torn apart; that blood relationship is inflamed into incestuous lusts; that mothers become mad for their children; that fathers turn their virgin daughters’ desires toward themselves; that, contrary to the dignity of their age, old men groan with shameful youthful passions; [Col. 0974B] that wise and brave men dissolve the settled resolutions of constancy when the vigor of manhood has been softened; that nooses are fastened [Col. 0975A] to necks, blazing pyres are mounted, and, hurled headlong, they cast themselves everywhere from vast and towering cliffs in voluntary leaps?

[Note: [Col. 0975C]

### XXVIII.—Is there any human being endowed with the rudiments of any reason?

P. Burmann restored the passage thus from the manuscript in his commentary on the *Latin Anthology*, book III, poem LXXIV, verse 10, p. 514, vol. I. The other editions have “imbued.” But “to put on” virtues and vices occurs among the best writers. Thus Tacitus, *Annals* XV, chapter 45: “He had not put on a character formed by good arts.” Livy, book III, chapter 33: “So completely had he put on a character new to himself.” So too Homer uses *epieimenos* (ἐπιείμενος), “clothed in,” in *Iliad* I.149 and frequently; and the New Testament, Gospel of Luke, final chapter, verse 49: *Endysēsthe dynamin* (Ἐνδύσησθε δύναμιν), “You shall be clothed with power.” Compare Arntzenius on Pliny’s *Panegyric*, chapter 81. ORELLI.

That in the united totality of virtue retains the summit of perfection and the very height of wisdom. “In the united totality of virtue” is correct: that is, in the whole and complete chorus of the virtues, in the entire sum of virtue, so that no part of virtue can be lacking. Those who wish to alter this are therefore mistaken. HERALD.—Fulvius Ursinus conjectures “unique”; Stewechius, “of the single virtue.” For “retains,” Gelenius printed “retain,” followed by the Leiden editor—wrongly, in my judgment. The sense is that being calm, gentle, and mild retains the summit of perfection. In the same sense St. Paul, Colossians III.14: *hētis agapē esti syndesmos tēs teleiotētos* (ἥτις ἀγάπη ἐστὶ σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος), “which love is the bond of perfection.” ORELLI.]

### XXVIII

Is there any human being endowed with the rudiments of any reason who would pollute or contaminate the constancy of divinity with such shameful behavior? Who would attribute to the gods natures of a kind that human gentleness has often soothed and softened even in wild beasts?

Where, I ask, is that doctrine that the gods are far removed from every passion of disturbance? That they are gentle, calm, and mild? That this quality, in the united totality of virtue, retains the summit of perfection and the very height of wisdom? Or why do we pray to them to repel from us adverse and hostile things, if they themselves are found to be the authors of all the evils by which we are daily afflicted?

Call us irreverent, irreligious, or atheists as much as you please; [Col. 0975B] you will never make it credible that there are gods of love, gods of war, gods who sow discord, gods who disturb minds with the goads of the Furies. For either they truly are gods and do not do the things you have mentioned; or, if they do the things you say, then beyond all doubt they are not gods. [Col. 0976A]

[Note: [Col. 0975D]

### Chapter XXIX.—One of you says one thing about the same matters, another something else

Thus Meursius. Previously, “about the matter of the same,” etc. The Leiden editor, by a bolder conjecture, changes it to “one of you says that there are some gods in the same things, another that there are others,” rashly, in my opinion; for not everything in Arnobius is perfectly exact and in accordance with the precepts of logicians. For my part, with Stewechius, I think the word “matters” should be deleted as a copyist’s gloss, so that the sense is: “one says one thing about the same beings, another something else”—that is, about the gods. ORELLI.

Whom some among you have declared to be the world, others the year, and some the sun. See Ovid, *Fasti* I.117 [Col. 0976B] ff.; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 9; Vossius, *On Idolatry*, book II, chapter 16; and especially John Lydus, *On the Months*, chapters 1 and 2, pp. 55 ff., Schow’s edition. ORELLI.

Founder of the town of Janiculum. Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.358:

> Father Janus founded this citadel, and Saturn that one;  
> This was named Janiculum, that Saturnia.

Compare Ovid, *Fasti* I.241 ff. ORELLI.

[Col. 0976C] Father to Fontus. Thus the manuscript. I write “father of Fontus.” Martianus Capella lists this god among the gods of the second region of heaven. Varro also mentions him in *On the Latin Language*, book V, and Cicero in *On the Laws*, book II, chapter 22, when speaking of burial: “For the body is returned to the earth and, when placed and laid there, is, as it were, covered by the covering of its mother. By the same rite, we have learned that our king Numa was buried in that tomb not far from the altars of Fontus.” These altars stood on the Janiculum, near which was Numa’s tomb; Fontus also had a shrine near the Capene Gate. His sacred festival, the Fontinalia, was celebrated on the day before the Ides of October. MEURSIUS, pp. 96–97.—Compare Reinesius, *Inscriptions*, p. 102; Davies on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, chapter 20; and Hugo Grotius on Martianus Capella, book I. Wagner, the most recent editor of the books *On the Laws*, citing our passage at the place in Cicero praised above, judges that it should read “near the altars of Fontus.” Vaillant, cited by Eckhel in *Doctrine of Ancient Coins*, vol. V, p. 214, conjectures that the Fonteian clan derived its name from this Fontus or Fonto—whom we know to have been Janus’s son from Arnobius alone. He bases this on a coin of that clan depicting the double head of Janus covered with down in the usual fashion. Raschius, however, in his *Lexicon of Numismatics*, under *Fonteia*, calls the clan’s divine founder Fonton. Gelenius, failing to understand this, printed “father of Faunus,” very badly. For who could believe that Arnobius contradicted himself so sharply, having above, in book II, chapter 70, made Faunus the son of Picus, and here, with only a few pages intervening, the son of Janus? ORELLI.

Son-in-law of Vulturnus. Vulturnus is a river of Campania, discussed at length by the distinguished Oberlin on Vibius Sequester, pp. 210–11. Arnobius alone, so far as I know, makes the nymph Juturna his daughter. ORELLI.

Husband of Juturna. The classic passage concerning this goddess is Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.139: “Juturna is a most health-giving spring in Italy, near the river Numicus, whose name was derived from *juvare*, ‘to aid.’ For although all water is naturally harmful to foreign bodies, this spring is most healthful to everyone. Water from this spring was customarily brought to Rome for all sacrifices. Lutatius Catulus was the first to build a temple to this Juturna in the Campus Martius; for those whose craft is practiced with water also celebrate Juturna’s festival, and call that feast day the Juturnalia. Varro, in the fourteenth book of *Divine Matters*, says: ‘Juturna is placed among the particular gods and nymphs.’” Thus Servius. Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.785, represented Juturna as an indigenous goddess of Latium, daughter of Daunus and sister of Turnus. See the distinguished Heyne, Excursus III on *Aeneid* VI, p. 125, vol. III, and Vulpius, *Ancient Latium*, vol. I, pp. 346 ff. But Arnobius follows another genealogy of the goddess by some unknown author. ORELLI.

Whom you place first in all your prayers, etc. Ovid, *Fasti* I.171 ff.:

> Then I said: “Why, though I appease the divinities of others,  
> Janus, do I first offer incense and unmixed wine to you?”  
> “So that through me, who guard the thresholds,” he replied,  
> “You may gain access to whichever gods you wish.”

Servius on *Aeneid* VII: “Some say that Janus was called Eanus from *eundo*, ‘going,’ and that he is Mars; and because he possesses the greatest power among the Romans, he is therefore named first in worship. Others believe Janus to be the air; and because he is regarded as the progenitor of the voice, our prayers are therefore entrusted to him to be conveyed to the gods.” Compare Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 9, and B. Brissonius, *On Formulae*, book I, pp. 45–46. HERALDUS and ELMENHORST.

To open the way for you. Thus Meursius and the others who follow him. Previously: “to open the way for us.” ORELLI.

So that what is *Chronos* is taken as *Cronos*. Cujacius thinks that “is taken as Cronos” should be deleted as a copyist’s gloss, on the theory that the scribe had written in the margin, in Greek, “is taken as *chronos*” (χρόνος); the passage would then read: “For if time is signified by this name, as the Greek interpreters maintain, that which is *chronos* has no existence.” But I see nothing to change. The sense is: so that what among the Greeks is *Chronos* (χρόνος), “Time,” is taken as *Cronos*, that is, Saturn. Furthermore, on the name Cronos see Lactantius, *Institutes* I.12; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.22; Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.25; Apuleius, *On the World*, p. 135; Athenagoras, *Apology for the Christians*; Augustine, *City of God* IV.10; and others cited by Elmenhorst and Nourry. ORELLI.

The divinity Saturn. Salmasius printed this from the correction of Obertus Gifanius. Others: “the name Saturn.” ORELLI.

Vine-planter. The glosses: “Vine-planter, *ampelophytēs* (ἀμπελοφύτης).” Accius in Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VI.5:

> Dionysus, best father, vine-planter, born of Semele.

Virgil, *Aeneid* VII.179:

> The vine-planter, preserving beneath his image the curved sickle.

ELMENHORST.

Sickle-bearer. Below, book VI, chapter 12: “Saturn, with his hooked sickle, like some guardian of the countryside, a pruner of luxuriant branches.” ELMENHORST.

[Col. 0978B] Handed down to the age of their descendants. “Descendants” means the same as “posterity.” Lactantius, *Institutes* II.7: “But this deceives them: because the name ‘ancestors’ is applied, they do not think it possible either that they themselves should possess greater wisdom, since they are called ‘descendants,’ or that the former should have been foolish, since they are called ‘ancestors.’” See Bünemann there, p. 208. Virgil uses the word in this sense very frequently. ORELLI.]

### XXIX

And yet we might somehow accept from you these ideas, utterly filled with irreverent fabrications, were it not that, by producing so many mutually contrary assertions about the gods—assertions that destroy one another—you compel the mind to withhold its assent. For when each of you contends that he surpasses every other in the distinction of deeper knowledge, you abolish the very gods whom you suppose to exist; you substitute others whose nonexistence is manifest; one of you says one thing about the same matters, another something else; and you record as innumerable those whom human consensus has always accepted as single beings.

Let us therefore begin, as is customary, with Father Janus—and let us begin with him too: some among you have declared him to be the world, others the year, and some the sun. But if we accept this as true, it follows that we must understand there never to have been any Janus [Col. 0976B] who, they report, was begotten by Caelus and Hecate, first reigned in Italy, founded the town of Janiculum, was father to Fontus, son-in-law of Vulturnus, and husband of Juturna. Thus, through your own teaching, the name of a god is erased—the god whom you place first [Col. 0977A] in all your prayers and believe opens the way for you to obtain a hearing from the gods.

Again, however, if Janus is the year, not even in that way can he be a god. For who does not know that a year is a fixed circumscription of time, and that something bounded by intervals of months and a counting of days does not possess divine power?

The same argument may be transferred to Saturn by a not dissimilar line of reasoning. For if this name signifies time, as Greek interpreters maintain, so that what is *Chronos* (χρόνος, “Time”) is taken as *Cronos* (Κρόνος, “Saturn”), there is no divinity Saturn. For who is so insane as to call time a god, when it is the measure of a certain interval enclosed within the continuous succession of eternity? And so this god too will be removed from the order of heavenly beings: [Col. 0977B] the one whom primeval antiquity declared to have been born of Caelus as his father, to have begotten the great [Col. 0978A] gods, to be a vine-planter and sickle-bearer, and whom it handed down to the age of its descendants.

[Note: [Col. 0978B]

### XXX.—For what?

Meursius conjectures: “Now what?” etc. ORELLI.

Jupiter, whom the wise have repeatedly declared to be the sun. Orpheus, *Hymn to the Sun* VIII, verse 13, Hermann’s edition:

> Blazing, undefiled, father of Time, immortal Zeus.

Likewise the fragment of the *Hymn to Zeus* preserved by Stobaeus, *Physical Eclogues* I.1, and by Proclus in his commentary on the *Timaeus*:

> Zeus is the breath of the winds; Zeus the impulse of the tireless air;  
> Zeus the root of the sea; Zeus the sun and the moon.

Compare Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.23; Sanchuniathon in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* I.7; G. J. Vossius, *On Idolatry* II.13, p. 138; and especially Gisbert Cuper, *Harpocrates*, p. 88, Utrecht quarto edition, and Columna on the *Fragments of Ennius*, pp. 326–27, Hessel’s edition p. 209. ORELLI.

Driving winged chariots, etc. This is drawn from the very celebrated passage of Plato’s *Phaedrus*: “The great leader in heaven, Zeus, drives his winged chariot and proceeds first; the host of gods and spirits follows him.” Compare the authors cited by Toup on Longinus, section XV, §4, p. 322, Weiske’s edition. ORELLI.

Some declare him to be the ether blazing with fiery force. See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.15 and II.26; Servius on *Aeneid* I.47; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.4; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* V; Germanicus, *Aratean Phenomena*, p. 86; Augustine, *City of God* IV.11 and III.4; Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV. ELMENHORST.—Compare Vossius, *On Idolatry* II.84, p. 268. ORELLI.

With the inextinguishable immensity of its heat. Thus the Leiden edition. Others: “of inextinguishable heat.” ORELLI.

He is recorded as having been concealed within the territory of the Cretans. Origen, *Against Celsus* III, p. 141; Athenagoras, *Apology*, p. 38; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* III. ELMENHORST.

If she is the air. According to the Stoic view. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.26: “The air, however, as the Stoics argue, lying between sea and sky, is consecrated under the name of Juno, who is both Jupiter’s sister and wife, because it resembles the ether and is most closely united with it. They made the air female and assigned it to Juno because nothing is softer than it.” Compare Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* I.17 and *Saturnalia* III.3; Porphyry in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* III.11; Augustine, *City of God* IV.10 and VII.16. NOURRY, p. 441. Athenagoras, *Apology*; Servius on *Aeneid* VII.311. ELMENHORST.—Add Cornutus, *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 3. ORELLI.

[Col. 0979A] By repeating the Greek name in inverted order. That is, as Gesner explains in his *Thesaurus*, by repeating the name *Hēra* (Ἥρα) in such a way that in the end one cannot tell whether it is said as *Hēra* (Ἥρα) or *aēr* (ἀήρ), “air.” Furthermore, the word “inversion” is a *hapax legomenon* (ἅπαξ λεγόμενον), occurring only once. Others read “through the harshness of the Greek name,” wrongly; for I do not see what is harsh in this word. ORELLI.

[Col. 0979B] No Fluvionia. Read *Fluonia*. Festus: “Women worshiped Juno Fluonia because they thought that she restrained the flow of blood during conception.” MEURSIUS. Augustine confirms this nomenclature on Varro’s authority in *City of God* VII.2: “The goddess Mena presides over menstrual flows; although Jupiter’s daughter, she is nevertheless obscure. Yet in his book on the select gods the same author, Varro, assigns this province of menstrual flows to Juno herself, who is queen even among the select gods and here, as Juno Lucina, presides over the same blood together with Mena, her stepdaughter.” Compare the same work, chapter 3, and Vossius, *On the Origin and Progress of Idolatry* VI.26. NOURRY, pp. 441 ff.

No Pomona. Pomona, goddess of gardens, is familiar even to beginners; Varro, *On the Latin Language* VI, p. 74, Dordrecht edition, says that the origin of her name is obscure. Yet it is not easy to see how she could have been identified as Juno. Some therefore suspect—Meursius among them—that this name was corrupted through a copyist’s carelessness and that *Sororia* should be substituted for it, since Juno was said to be Jupiter’s [Col. 0979C] sister and wife. In confirmation of this opinion, one may add that a temple was built at Rome for Juno beside the Sister’s Beam (*tigillum sororium*), and was therefore called the temple of Juno Sororia.

But if it is permissible to add another conjecture to one unsupported by any manuscript evidence, we shall say that, because apples and fruits belong to the earth or ground, it may have happened that Juno—who was believed to be the earth and to govern earthly things—was called Pomona, just as she was called by so many other names. Augustine, *City of God* VII.16, reminds us that Juno was regarded as the earth through these words of Varro, *On the Latin Language* VI, p. 19: “Juno is the wife of Jupiter; he is the sky, she the earth, which is likewise Tellus. She is called Juno because together with Jupiter she gives aid; and queen because she governs all these earthly things.” But let others judge this conjecture of ours. NOURRY, p. 442. Scriverius, in Meursius, thinks *Covona* should be read, from *covum*, an ancient word for “sky.” Thus Juno Covona—or, as Varro said, *Covella*, *On the Latin Language* V, p. 49—is the same as *Ourania* (Οὐρανία), “the Heavenly One.” ORELLI.

[Col. 0979D] No Ossipagina. Some—again Meursius, with Heraldus’s approval—thought this name of Juno corrupt and proposed the correction: “no Ops, Opigena.” Festus says of her: “Married women worshiped Juno Opigena because they believed that she brought aid to women laboring in childbirth.” But this does not establish clearly enough whether she is the same as Ossipagina, who, as Arnobius later wrote, was believed to harden and solidify infants’ bones. Vossius, however, in his etymological work under the word *os*, “bone,” supports Stewechius, who thought that *Ossipaga* or *Ossipanga* should be restored. He judges that she was so named because she “fixed” (*pangat*)—or, as the ancients said, *paget*—children’s bones. NOURRY, p. 442.

No Februtis. Februtis, or Februlis—as Janus Dousa emended it in Meursius; ORELLI—was a Roman name for Juno, as Festus still observes under *Februarius*: “The month of February was so called because at that time—that is, in the final month of the year—the people were *februated*, that is, purified and cleansed by the Luperci; or from Juno Februata, whom others call Februalis and the Romans Februlis.” Read Varro, *On the Latin Language* V.§3; Augustine, *City of God* VII.7; and Lilius Giraldus, *Syntagma* III, p. 119. NOURRY, p. 442, and ORELLI.

Populonia. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* III.2, mentions Juno Populonia and a temple dedicated in her honor. Publius Tertius said: “For in the Papirian law it is explicitly reported that a dedicated table can serve in place of an altar: ‘as,’ it says, ‘a table was dedicated in the temple of Juno Populonia.’” They report that this name was given to her because they believed Juno presided over the union of male and female, from which new peoples are created. On this Juno and likewise Juno Februtis, Martianus Capella, *Marriage of Philology*, book II, should be read. NOURRY, ibid.

Caprotina. Women once sacrificed to Juno Caprotina—or Capratina, as others prefer—in gratitude for the chastity of girls and married women having been preserved and for the defeat of the people of Fidenae, who wished to violate it. Varro, *On the Latin Language* V, p. 47, Dordrecht edition, speaks of this sacrifice as follows: “The Nones are called Caprotine because on that day in Latium women sacrifice to Juno Caprotina; they do so beneath a wild fig tree and employ a branch from the wild fig tree.” Macrobius relates the cause and institution of this sacrifice and festival, called the “festival of the female slaves,” in *Saturnalia* I.11. Plutarch [Col. 0980C] also mentions it in *Parallel Stories*, vol. II, p. 313, as do others. Furthermore, Juno had still more names, as Servius says on *Aeneid* I.12–13, including Curis and Lucina; since Arnobius had already mentioned enough of them, he preferred to pass these over in silence. NOURRY, p. 443.]

### XXX

For what shall we say of Jupiter himself, whom the wise have repeatedly declared to be the sun, driving winged chariots while a multitude of divinities follows him? Or whom some declare to be the ether, blazing with fiery force and with the inextinguishable immensity of its heat?

But if this is clear and established, then, on your own authority, there is no Jupiter at all: no Jupiter who, born of Saturn as his father and Ops as his mother, is recorded as having been concealed within the territory of the Cretans so that he might escape his father’s fury.

Does not a similar theory now remove Juno too from the number of the gods? For if she is the air, as you are accustomed [Col. 0978B] to jest and repeatedly assert [Note: [Col. 0977B] The manuscript reads: “you assign.”], by reversing the Greek name, [Col. 0979A] then there will be found no sister and wife of almighty Jupiter; no Fluonia, no Pomona, no Ossipagina, no Februtis, Populonia [Note: [Col. 0979A] The manuscript reads *Populona*.], Cinxia, or Caprotina. Thus the fabrication of that name will be found utterly empty, disseminated by the renown of a groundless belief.

[Note: [Col. 0980C]

### XXXI.—Granius

Granius Flaccus Licinianus, a grammarian cited by Festus under *Ricae* and by Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.16 and 18. Among other works, he wrote a book *On the Indigitamenta* addressed to Caesar, as Censorinus attests in *On the Birthday*, chapter 3, p. 13, Havercamp’s edition. Compare G. J. Vossius in the appendix to book III of *On the Latin Historians*, *Works*, vol. IV, p. 261. ORELLI.

He explains with plausible arguments that Minerva is the moon. Porphyry in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* III.11: “What Apollo is in the sun, Athena is in the moon; for she is a symbol of understanding, being a kind of Athena.” NOURRY, p. 443.—Add Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.17. ELMENHORST.—The ancients referred all gods to the sun and all goddesses to the moon—which the Greeks called *anthēlion* (ἀνθήλιον), that is, “the sun’s deputy,” according to Hesychius. Thus Minerva, Diana, Ceres, Juno, Isis, Hecate, Proserpina, Rhea, Caelestis, Astarte, the Fates, Enyo, and others were regarded as the moon, as Gisbert Cuper demonstrates from Porphyry in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* III.11, and many other authors, in *Harpocrates*, p. 108. ORELLI.

The ethereal summit. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* III.4: “Minerva is the highest summit of the ether.” The same author, *Saturnalia* I.17; Augustine, *City of God* VII.16. ELMENHORST.—See especially G. J. Vossius, *On Idolatry* II.42. ORELLI.

Minerva, as though a certain Meminerva. Festus: “Minerva is so called because she advises well.” Isidore, *Origins* VIII.11; Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.17. ELMENHORST.—Cicero follows another etymology in *On the Nature of the Gods* II.26: “Minerva, moreover, because she would diminish or threaten.” But falsely, as Vossius demonstrates, book I, p. 199. Minerva—or rather Menerva—comes from *menos* (μένος), “force of mind,” whence Latin *mens*, “mind,” and the ancient verbs *meneo* and *meno* for *moneo*, “I advise”; whence *mentio*, “mention,” *memini*, “I remember,” *memor*, “mindful,” and *reminiscor*, “I recall.” ORELLI.

There is therefore no daughter of Mind. Meursius rewrites this as “daughter of Metis.” When Jupiter, at the prompting of Heaven and Earth, had swallowed Metis while she was pregnant and about to give birth to Minerva, he became pregnant in the head and, after summoning Vulcan and having his skull split open, himself gave birth to Minerva, as Hesiod attests in the *Theogony*, verses 885 ff.

But Vossius, *On Idolatry* II.42, demonstrates from a fragment of Afranius in Aulus Gellius XIII.8 that “daughter of Mind” is correct:

> Experience fathered me; Memory, my mother, gave me birth.  
> The Greeks call me *Sophia*; you call me Wisdom.

Minerva is therefore the same as Prudence, which is the daughter of Memory or Mind. Arnobius himself says below, chapter 37: “Others declare that Jupiter fathered the Muses by his wife Memory, or Mind.” ORELLI.]

No daughter of Victory. It is difficult to prove on what grounds Minerva is said by Arnobius to be the daughter of Victory. For Dionysius of Halicarnassus relates (*Antiquities*, bk. I, p. 26, Sylb.):

> “The Arcadians tell the myth that Victory (*Nikē*) was the daughter of Pallas, son of Lycaon, and that she received from human beings the honors which she still possesses today, by the will of Athena, because she had been brought up together with the goddess. For they say that Athena, immediately after her birth, was given by Zeus to Pallas, and was reared in his household until she reached maturity.”

By these words he certainly makes it clear that Minerva [Col. 0981C] was not the daughter of Victory, but was merely brought up together with her. Arnobius nevertheless had Pausanias as an earlier advocate of his opinion, for Pausanias had said (bk. I, p. 40, Sylb.):

> “And another sanctuary has been built there for Athena, who is called Victory.”

Moreover, in a certain hymn ascribed to Orpheus (no. 32, ed. Hermann), she is called “victory-bearing divinity” (*nikēphore daimōn*). Yet Arnobius’ account would be fully supported by this if his text read: “There is therefore no daughter of Mind [*Mens*]” (or of Metis, as Meursius wished; cf. Hesiod, *Theogony*, vv. 885 ff.), “no Victory.” But if the reading must be “no daughter of Victory,” consider, I pray, whether this opinion gained currency because she received her surname from her own temple, in which she was called Victory, or because combatants were said to win victory through her aid. NOURR., p. 445.

Gisb. Cuperus, in *The Apotheosis of Homer*, p. 173, believes that the reading should be “no Victory,” and offers the following:

> “Phurnutus, or Cornutus, *On the Nature of the Gods*, ch. 28 (p. 187, ed. Gal.), attests that Victory was called *Nikē*: ‘They call her Alalcomeneis and Ageleis, deriving the former name from *alalkein*, “to ward off” [Col. 0981D]—for she is capable of giving aid and coming to one’s assistance, from which she is also called Victory (*Nikē*)—and the latter from her leading (*agein*) the peoples.’ And a little below, p. 189: ‘She is represented with wings because of the swift tendency and unchangeable character of actions.’ Indeed, Meursius, *Attic Readings*, bk. I, ch. 20, proves from Aristophon the Pythagorean, Aristophanes, and Eustathius that on the citadel at Athens there was an image of Athena Victory adorned with golden wings. Nonnus, bk. XXXII, calls her ‘the helpful female Athena, whom they call Victory,’ and Euripides also mentions her (*Ion*, v. 1528; see ibid., v. 457). And just as Minerva sprang from the head of Jupiter, so too did Victory, according to Philo Judaeus (*On the Creation of the World*): ‘The number Seven alone, as I said, is by nature neither generative nor generated; for this reason the other philosophers liken this number to motherless and virgin Victory, who, according to the story, sprang from the head of Zeus,’ etc.”

Thus Cuperus. ORELL.

**Sprung from Jupiter’s brain.** So the Leiden edition. Others read “born.” The first edition has “raised up.” ORELL.

[Col. 0982A] **Because water covers the earth, he was called . . . Neptune.** Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. IV: “Neptune, because the sea covers (*obnubit*) the lands as a cloud (*nubes*) covers the sky, from *nuptu*, that is, covering.” ELMENH.—Stewechius conjectures that *Neptunus* should be read, but it appears rather to be derived from the Greek *nephos*, “cloud,” or *nephoō*, “to cover with clouds.” Scaliger, on Theophrastus, *On the Causes of Plants*, derives it from *niptō*, “to wash.” See Voss., *On Idolatry*, bk. II, ch. 77, p. 259. [Col. 0982B] Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II, ch. 26, derives it from swimming (*nando*); see Davies there. Lipsius, who discusses this etymology at length in *Saturnalian Discourses*, bk. I, ch. 2, believes that in the passage of Cicero one should read “from covering” (*a nubendo*). In any event, *nubere* here, in its proper and primary sense, means the same as “to veil” or “to cover.” See Weitz. on *The Vigil of Venus*, v. 22. ORELL.

**There is no god Neptune at all.** In the Leiden edition, perhaps through a printer’s error, the text reads “the god of no one,” etc. But “there is no” is correct, as above: “There is no sister and wife of Jupiter, no Fluvionia,” etc. ORELL.

**Brother of Stygian Jupiter.** See above, on bk. II, ch. 70. ORELL.

**Lord of sea-monsters.** According to Nonius, the *pistrix* is a marine creature with a long but narrow body. The word appears to have been used of various sea-monsters. Festus interprets it as a whale. But Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. IX, chs. 3 and 4, clearly distinguishes the whale from the *pristis*, which is the same as the *pistrix*. There the most recent editor of that book, Laur. Theod. Gronovius, p. 6, interprets the *pristis* [Col. 0982C] as a fish inhabiting the Ocean, especially the Arctic Ocean, belonging to the shark family, with a pointed, bony, flat snout toothed on both sides, called by Linnaeus *Squalus pristis*, German *Sagehay*, *Sagefisch* (“saw-shark,” “sawfish”). Cf. Jan. Dousa on the *Fragments of Lucilius*, p. 199, ed. Haverc. ORELL.

**Maenae.** N. Heinsius discusses this despised and inexpensive little fish at length in his note on Ovid, *Fasti* II, v. 578; see him there. The Greeks call it *mainis*, for example Plutarch in *Numa*, ch. 15, where Kaltwasser translates it as *sardelle*. Hardouin, on Pliny, *Natural History*, bk. XXXII, ch. 11, understands it as the little fish which the French call *la mendole* and the Romans *menola*, German *Hautling*, *Sparfisch*. ORELL.

**King of the salty depths and shaker of the trembling ground.** So Meursius. Others read “of the salt,” apparently from a manuscript. But I prefer “shaker of the ground,” that is, *Seisichthōn* (“Earth-shaker”) and *Enosigaios* (“Earth-shaker”). Moreover, these words seem to me to have been borrowed by Arnobius, for the sake of mockery, from some ancient comic or tragic poet. ORELL.]

### XXXI

Aristotle, as Granius records, a man mighty in intellect [Col. 0980A] and pre-eminent in learning, explains with probable arguments, and demonstrates by the authority of literature, that Minerva is the moon. Others have said that this same goddess is the summit of the ether and the highest point of its very height; some have said that she is memory, from which the name *Minerva* itself was formed, as though it were *Meminerva*. [Col. 0981A] But if this account is accepted as credible, there is therefore no daughter of Mind, no daughter of Victory, no inventor of the olive sprung from Jupiter’s brain, no goddess instructed in the mastery of the arts and in the varieties of the disciplines.

Because water covers the earth, they say, he was called and surnamed Neptune. If, therefore, the covering of liquid is signified by the application of this name, there is no god Neptune at all; and thus the brother of Stygian Jupiter and sibling of Olympian Jupiter is removed and taken from our midst: he who is armed with the iron trident, lord of sea-monsters and *maenae*, king of the salty depths, and shaker of the trembling ground. [Col. 0982A]

[Note: [Col. 0982C]

### XXXII.—Mercury was also named as though he were a certain *Medicurius*

Isidore, *Origins*, bk. VIII, ch. 11: [Col. 0982D] “Mercury is said to have been so named as though he were ‘running in the middle’ (*Medius currens*), because speech runs in the middle between human beings.” Cf. Augustine, *The City of God*, bk. VII, ch. 14. ELMENH.—Festus derives the name from merchandise (*merces*). ORELL.

**Because discourse runs as an intermediary between two speakers and passes back and forth.** This is the true and genuine reading of the manuscripts in place of the published text, “between two speakers” with *duos*. In my note on Flavius Vegetius, *On Military Matters*, I showed that the ancients used *duo* in the accusative in place of *duos*, and restored that expression to him twice, in bk. II, ch. 6, and bk. III, ch. 15. If you desire examples, see Cicero, *Letters to Friends*, bk. VII, ep. XXV: “Apart from us two,” he says, “no one speaks in that fashion.” Prudentius, *Apotheosis*: “He orders bread and two fish to be brought.” Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, ch. 19, in the tribunician decree: “The urban praetor who now holds office, and whoever shall hold it hereafter, shall keep two lictors with him.” The common editions commonly give “two lictors” with *duos*, incorrectly. I recall that Sosipater the grammarian also made a note on this matter. STEWECH.—Cf. Manutius on the cited passage of Cicero. ORELL.

[Col. 0983B] **That Cyllenian herald, poured forth upon the summit of the icy mountain.** This construction is familiar to Arnobius, in place of “poured forth upon the summit of the icy mountain,” with *mountain* placed in the genitive. See above, on bk. I, ch. 36. Birth is elegantly described as “being poured forth” or “being poured out.” Thus above, bk. I, at the cited passage: “Mercury, poured forth from Maia’s womb.” Bk. II, ch. 16: “We are poured forth and emitted from our mothers’ wombs.” Below, bk. IV: “And why do they marvel at Jupiter, whom you proclaim to have been poured forth from a woman’s womb?” Lactantius, bk. III, ch. 16: “For neither walls nor the place in which anyone was poured forth from the womb procures wisdom for a human being.” The same author, *On the Workmanship of God*, ch. 3: “They complain . . . that man, naked and unarmed, is cast and driven, as if from shipwreck, into the miseries of this life; unable either to move himself from the place where he was poured forth, to seek the nourishment of milk, or to withstand the assault of the weather.” See Bunemann there, p. 1127. HERALD. and ORELL.

**Exchanger of merchandise and commercial dealings.** Festus: “Mercury was named from merchandise (*merces*), for they considered him the god of all business dealings.” Plautus, in the Prologue [Col. 0983C] to the *Amphitryon*:

> As you wish me gladly, in your own trading,  
> By buying and selling, to enrich you with profits  
> And to assist you in every undertaking.

Cf. G. J. Voss., *Roman Etymology*, s.v. *merces*. ELMENH. and ORELL.

**Some of you have said that Earth is the Great Mother because she supplies all living creatures with nourishment.** Lucretius, bk. II, vv. 995 ff.:

> Since she provides the food by which all creatures nourish  
> Their bodies, lead a pleasant life, and propagate their offspring,  
> She has therefore deservedly acquired the name of mother.

HERALD.

**Because she bears a crop of health-giving seeds, they declare her to be Ceres.** This is the view of Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. II, ch. 26: “Her mother”—that is, Proserpina’s—“is Ceres, from her bearing crops (*a gerendis frugibus*), as though she were *Geres*”; and of Varro, *On the Latin Language*. Varro notes that just as C is used here for G, so the reverse occurs elsewhere, writing in book IV: “*Gladius* comes from *clades*, with C changed into G.” Festus likewise forms *Orcus* from *urgere*, “to press,” and *prodigium* from *praedicere*, “to foretell.” These letters were also interchangeable among copyists in antiquity; hence *Gaius* and *Caius*, and a thousand other words, are so often confused in manuscripts. Indeed, everyone knows that this sort of play is also found among different languages. We say *ciconia* in Latin; but the French, Italians, and Spaniards write the second syllable with *g* and pronounce it more softly. STEWECH.—But the great Scaliger, on Varro, p. 31, Dordrecht ed., shows at length that this etymology is false and that the name Ceres must be derived either from the ancient verb *cereo*, meaning *creo*, “I create,” or from the most ancient Greek name of Ceres, *Gērys*.—Sainte-Croix, in *Researches on the Mysteries of Paganism*, p. 523, derives it from *Cerus*, the name by which the ancient Etruscans signified the creator (“*Cerus mannus* means ‘the good creator.’” Festus, bk. XI, p. 237; Isidore, *Origins*, bk. VIII, ch. 10); des Brosses derives it from the Egyptian or Hebrew word *Erets*, “earth.” Cf. N. Ignarra’s very learned discussion of the etymology of the Latin name Ceres and the Greek *Dēō* [Col. 0984B] in *Emendations on Homer’s Hymn to Ceres*, in the latest edition of that hymn by Ruhnken, pp. 493 ff. ORELL.

**Some, however, say that she is Vesta, because she alone stands still in the world, while its other parts have been set in perpetual motion.** Plato, *Phaedrus*, p. 247 (vol. III, ed. H. Steph.):

> “For Hestia alone remains in the house of the gods.”

Ovid, *Fasti*, bk. VI, v. 299:

> The earth stands by its own power; from standing by power Vesta takes her name,  
> And the reason for her Greek name may be the same.

Cf. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, bk. II; Isidore, *Origins*, bk. VIII, ch. 11; Augustine, *The City of God*, bk. IV, ch. 10; G. J. Voss., *On Idolatry*, bk. II, ch. 59, p. 231; and J. Lipsius, *Treatise on Vesta and the Vestals*, ch. 1. This statement, of course, arose from the false opinion of the ancients. Modern astronomers from Copernicus onward maintain precisely the opposite. ORELL.

[Col. 0984C] **Whom Nigidius supposes to have been married to Saturn.** Below, bk. IV: “His Great Mother was married to him.” HERALD.—On P. Nigidius Figulus, Cicero’s contemporary and associate in suppressing the Catilinarian pestilence, the most learned of the Romans after Varro and a Pythagorean, see Harles, *Major Introduction* and *Survey of Roman Literature*, p. 165; Ernesti in the *Ciceronian Key*; and especially Jan. Rutgers, who collected, arranged, and explained his fragments in *Various Readings*, bk. III, ch. 16, pp. 246 ff. ORELL.—There is a separate dissertation on this writer by Burigny in the book entitled *Memoirs of the Academy of Inscriptions*. OCHSNER.

**She is indicated by these predicates alone.** Fulv. Ursinus, for some reason unknown to me, changes “by these” to “by those,” etc. ORELL.]

### XXXII

Mercury also was named as though he were a certain *Medicurius*; and because discourse runs as an intermediary between two speakers and passes back and forth, the character of this name was fashioned accordingly. [Col. 0983A] Therefore, if this is so, Mercury is not the name of a god, but of speech and voice passing back and forth; and in this manner [Note: [Col. 0983A] Sabaeus incorrectly reads “by this act.”] that Cyllenian herald is abolished and extinguished: he who was poured forth upon the summit of the icy mountain, the inventor of words and names, and the exchanger of market wares, merchandise, and commercial dealings.

Some of you have said that Earth is the Great Mother because she supplies all living creatures with nourishment; others declare this same Earth to be Ceres because she bears a crop of health-giving seeds; some, however, say that she is Vesta, because she alone stands still in the world, while its other parts have been set in perpetual [Col. 0984A] motion. But if this is advanced and affirmed upon certain reasoning, the three names alike, according to your interpretation, have no reality: neither Ceres nor Vesta will be reckoned in the registers of the gods; finally, not even the Mother of the Gods herself, whom Nigidius supposes to have been married to Saturn, can properly be called a goddess. For all these are names of the one Earth, and she is indicated by these predicates alone. [Note: [Col. 0984A] Fulvius reads “those.”]

[Note: [Col. 0984C]

### XXXIII.—Avoiding excess

That is, excessiveness. For *satis* is repeatedly used for *nimis*, “too much,” by these writers. HERALD.—Thus Julius Capitolinus, in the *Life of Marcus Antoninus the Philosopher*, ch. 24: “Antoninus, for his part, was not *satis* moved by Cassius’ revolt,” that is, greatly or excessively moved; [Col. 0984D] see Salmasius there, in *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, p. 385. Nothing is more frequent in Cyprian. Thus our German *genug* very often signifies abundance or, to use a barbarous expression, a certain excessiveness: for example, *ich habe genug Arbeit*, that is, *mehr als genug, überflüssig*—“I have more than enough work, work in excess.” In this sense Cicero and other writers of the golden age of Latin say *satis superque*, “enough and more”; by contrast, they use *satis* by itself of a certain middling quantity that falls short rather than exceeds, like our *so so, nicht allzuviel*—“so-so, not very much.” See Heusinger on Cornelius Nepos, *Cimon*, ch. II, and on Cicero, *On Duties*, II, ch. 25, p. 363, as well as Bunemann on Lactantius, *Institutes*, bk. VI, ch. 13, p. 774. ORELL.

**Whom you all declare to be fire, etc.** See Isidore, *Origins*, bk. VIII, ch. 10; Augustine, *The City of God*, bk. VII, ch. 16. ELMENH.

**Venus, because she comes to all.** Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. II, ch. 26: “The goddess who came to all things was named Venus by our people.” ELMENH. Others, [Col. 0985B] however, have held a different view of this word’s etymology. For Varro (*On the Latin Language*, bk. VI, p. 12) derives it from the ancient verb *viere* (see above, on bk. II, ch. 38), that is, “to bind,” because Venus herself wishes not indeed to conquer (*vincere*), but to bind and to be bound (*vincire, vinciri*), namely by shameful bonds. Isidore, however, *Origins*, bk. VIII, ch. 11, says: “Venus was so called because without force”—another reading has “without a man”—“a woman does not cease to be a virgin.” Yet Cicero’s opinion perhaps not undeservedly appeared more probable to Arnobius. NOURR., p. 449.—Add Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, p. 223. The passage of Cicero led Fulv. Ursinus to change the text to “because she came to all things.” ORELL.

**Proserpina.** See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, bk. II, ch. 26; [Col. 0985C] Isidore, *Origins*, bk. VIII, ch. 11. ELMENH.—Add Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. IV, p. 20, Bipontine ed. For “creep forth” (*proserpant*), Fulv. Ursinus conjectures “crawl forth” (*prorepant*), incorrectly. ORELL.

**The name of an insentient power.** So Gelenius, which I approve. *Potestas*, “power,” is repeatedly used for a divine being. HERALD.—Thus below, bk. IV, ch. XI, beginning: “What do you say, O fathers of new religions, what do you say of the powers?” The first Roman edition reads “an insentient name of power,” a reading which the Leiden editor restored for some reason unknown to me. ORELL.

**Movements of crops springing up.** *Motio*, “movement,” is used for growth, and *moveri*, “to move,” for growing, very frequently. Columella, bk. XI, ch. 2: “Accordingly, from the Kalends of March until the tenth day before the Kalends of April is an excellent time for pruning vines, provided that the buds have not yet begun to move.” Ovid, *Tristia*, bk. III, elegy XII, v. 13:

> And wherever there is a vine, the bud moves forth from the shoot.

In the same sense the Greeks use *kinein kai blastanein*, “to move and sprout,” for example Theophrastus, *On the Causes of Plants*, bk. I, ch. 7. J. Fr. Gronovius collected further examples [Col. 0985D] in *Observations*, bk. III, ch. 1, p. 335, ed. Platner. ORELL.

**What of your contention that Liber, Apollo, and the Sun are one divine being?** Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, bk. I, chs. 17–18; Augustine, *The City of God*, bk. VII, ch. 16; Servius on Virgil, *Georgics* I, v. 7. ELMENH.—See especially Gisb. Cuperus, *Harpocrates*, pp. 106 ff. ORELL.

**The Semeleian; the Pythian.** Fulv. Ursinus and others rewrite “Semeleian” as “Smintheus” because of what follows: “the other, destroyer of the Sminthean mice.” But just as the statements made about Bacchus do not pertain to the epithet “Semeleian,” so what is added here perhaps does not pertain to the epithet by which Apollo is called “Pythian,” but points to another designation of his. HERALD.—For *Semeleius*, which Meursius restored, the first edition has *Semelius*. ORELL.

**The one, giver of lees-filled merriment.** Varro in Nonius: “No one drinks anything more pleasant than this. They discovered it as a cure for sorrow; it is the sweet seed-bed of merriment; it is the bond that holds banquets together.” Here Varro was assembling the virtues of wine, concerning which Athenaeus draws material from various authors in book II. HERALD.

**The other, destroyer of the Sminthean mice.** Lactantius, bk. I, ch. 7, mentions Apollo Smintheus—see Cellarius and Bunemann there—as do Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, ch. 17, and Ammianus Marcellinus, bk. XXII, ch. 11. ELMENH.—Eustathius on the *Iliad*, bk. I, v. 39:

> “Smintheus is an epithet of Apollo. Some say that he is so called from Sminthe, a city near Troy; others say it is from the *sminthoi*, which means mice. For he is believed once to have become the destroyer of mice that were harming the people there; for this reason a temple was founded for him and he himself was called Smintheus, because of the mice that had been driven away, which the inhabitants called *sminthoi*. For the account says that at Chryse there is a sanctuary of Smintheus and that a mouse lies beneath the foot of the wooden cult-image,” etc. [Col. 0986C]

Cf. Gisb. Cuperus, who discusses this name at length in his *Commentary on Unpublished Ancient Monuments*, appended to *Harpocrates*, pp. 212 ff., Utrecht ed.; and Bunemann on Lactantius, p. 47. ORELL.]

### XXXIII

We pass over Vulcan here, avoiding excess, whom you all unanimously declare to be fire; Venus, because she comes to all; [Col. 0985A] and Proserpina, who was so surnamed because things that have been sown creep forth into the light. [Note: [Col. 0985B] Fulvius reads “crawl forth.”] In this part of your account you once again remove three divine beings: since the first is the name of an element, the designation of an insentient power; the second belongs to lust diffused throughout all living creatures; while the third signifies shoots raising themselves and the movements of crops springing up.

What of your contention that Liber, Apollo, and the Sun are one divine being enlarged by three names? Is not the register of the gods diminished by your doctrines, and does not the proclaimed opinion [Note: [Col. 0985B] Fulvius reads “prejudged opinion.”] fall apart? For if it is true that the Sun is identical with Liber and identical with Apollo, it follows that in the nature of things there is neither any Apollo nor any Liber; and thus, through you yourselves, the Semeleian and the Pythian are abolished and erased: the one the giver of lees-filled merriment, the other [Col. 0985B] the destroyer of the Sminthean mice.

[Col. 0986A] [Note: [Col. 0986C]

### XXXIV.—Men among you who are not unlearned

Here Arnobius undoubtedly had the Stoics in view. Servius says of them, on Virgil, *Georgics* I, v. 7: “The Stoics say that the Sun is likewise . . . and similarly that the Moon is the same as Diana, the same as Ceres, the same as Juno, and the same as Proserpina; following them, Virgil invoked Liber and Ceres in place of the Sun and Moon.” NOURRIUS.

**Not babbling whatever caprice has prompted.** That is: not rashly chattering myths and nonsense through intemperance of speech and a kind of sickness. For the Latins often call *libido*, “caprice,” what the Greeks call *nosos*, “disease,” when we are carried toward something by a natural and blind impulse without reason. [Col. 0986D] The Greeks also express this natural and rash inclination toward anything by the verb *philein*, “to be fond of.” Thus they say *philomythous*, “fond of myths,” *philopseudēs*, “fond of falsehood,” *philoneikous*, “fond of strife,” and similar expressions. HERALD.

**By a threefold sisterhood** (*triviali germanitate*). That is, by triple sisterhood. Arnobius is, of course, alluding to Diana’s title *Trivia*. ORELL.

**Differences.** The manuscript reads “disagreements.”

**And thus, if.** So Meursius, in place of the former reading, “and thus itself to be.” Others read “and thus to be.” ORELL.

**Be stripped of.** Fulv. Ursinus reads “and be despoiled.” Stewechius conjectures *despolietur*, a verb frequently used by Cicero, Plautus, and Apuleius. For my part, I see no reason for a change. ORELL.

**That antlered hunter.** Actaeon, who was transformed into a stag. See Apollodorus, *Library*, III, ch. 4, §4; Hyginus, *Fable* 180; Fulgentius, *Mythologies* III.3; and especially Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III, vv. 131, 252, with Gierig, the distinguished scholar, p. 188 of the new edition. ORELL.]

### XXXIV

Men among you who are not unlearned and who do not babble whatever caprice has prompted [Note: [Col. 0986B] Others read “dictated.”] declare that Diana, Ceres, and the Moon constitute a single deity in a threefold sisterhood, and that, although the names are three and dissimilar, there are not three distinct persons. They say that in all these the Moon is named, and that the sequence of the remaining surnames has been heaped upon her designation.

But if this has been ascertained, if it has been fixed, and if the truth of the matter shows that it is so, the name of Ceres is once more empty, and that of Diana empty. The matter is thus brought to the point that the goddess who, as you report, discovered crops has no existence, with you as our guides and authorities; and Apollo is stripped of his sister, whom that antlered hunter once watched as she washed the impurities from her limbs in pure springs—and found the punishment of his curiosity.

[Col. 0986B] [Note: [Col. 0986D]

### XXXV.—Memorable in the study of philosophy

The first [Col. 0987B] edition reads the singular *memorabili*, through a misunderstanding of the manuscript’s spelling, where *memorabilis* is written in the old manner for the plural *memorabiles*. HERALD., in *Second Corrections*.

[Col. 0987C] **Pillar.** Others read “summit.” Arnobius, however, prefers the former word. See above, on bk. I, ch. 8. ORELL.

**One living creature, wise and rational.** Plato, *Timaeus*, p. 30 (vol. III, ed. H. Steph.):

> “Accordingly, following the probable account, we must say that this cosmos truly came to be a living creature, endowed with soul and intelligence, through the providence of God.”

Cicero translates it in *On the Universe*: “For this reason we must not hesitate to profess, if anything can be discovered through conjecture, that this world is a living creature, intelligent, and established by divine providence.” See Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*, bk. III, ch. 11. ELMENH.—For “rational,” the Roman edition and Gelenius have “capable of reasoning”—incorrectly. For “living creature” the manuscript has *animas*, which Meursius defends in his Appendix as an ancient expression for *animans* or *animal*, citing Ennius:

> The race adorned with feathers is accustomed to lay eggs,  
> Not living creatures.

Thus *Cosules*, *praegnas*, *damnas*, *Cesores*, and *istita* were written without *n*. But it is not probable that Arnobius wrote in this fashion, [Col. 0987D] since throughout this entire work he consistently writes *animal*, never *animas*. ORELL.

**Prudent.** The same as “wise.” Nothing more. ORELL.

**If their opinion is true and fixed, certain.** Perhaps it should read: “if their opinion is true, fixed, and certain.” TH. CANTER.—Nothing should be changed, but punctuation is needed: “and fixed, certain.” Arnobius likes to join words in this way without a conjunction. HERALD.

**Nor, conversely, can many human beings, while the distinction created by their separation is preserved.** So Meursius and the others who followed him, down to the Leiden edition, which corrects it to “through the disagreement of their separation.” The earlier reading was: “nor, conversely, can human beings, while the distinction created by the conjunction of a multitude is preserved.” Everyone sees that “of a multitude” is corrupt. But I think that “the distinction of their conjunction” was incorrectly changed to “the distinction of their separation.” “The distinction of their conjunction” means the difference or discord between parts that have been joined. Thus Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, v. 9:

> The discordant seeds of things not properly joined.

[Col. 0988B] Such is the monster Horace imagines at the beginning of the *Art of Poetry*: “To a human head,” etc. Accordingly, it seems that the text should read: “many, while the distinction within their conjunction is preserved,” that is, if, within the union, they preserve the difference between their minds and characters. The following words recommend this reading: “nor, if its individual parts are gods, can they be forced and converted into the consciousness of a single living creature.” [Col. 0988C] ORELL.

**Into the simplicity of a single consciousness.** Fulv. Ursinus prefers: “into the register of a single simplicity.” This conjecture is unnecessary if we understand the preceding “conjunction” as the conjunction of diverse parts of the mind. ORELL.

**So that neither the Sun is a god, nor the Moon, etc.** Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, and Lactantius, *Institutes*, bk. II, ch. 5, teach this abundantly. ELMENH.]

### XXXV

Men memorable in the study of philosophy, and raised by your praises to the pinnacle of that title, define with probable assurance that this entire mass of the world—by whose embrace we are all surrounded, sheltered, and sustained—is one living creature, wise, rational, and prudent. [Col. 0987A] If their opinion is true and fixed, certain, then those whom a little earlier you were locating in its parts under altered names will immediately cease to be gods.
