For just as one human being cannot, while the integrity of his body remains intact, be divided into many human beings, nor, conversely, can many human beings, while the distinction created by their separation is preserved, be fused into the simplicity of a single consciousness, so, if the world is one living creature and is moved by the activity of one mind, it cannot be dispersed into a plurality of divine beings; nor, if its individual parts are gods, can they be forced and converted into the consciousness of a single living creature.

The Moon, [Col. 0987B] the Sun, the Earth, the ether, and the stars are members and parts of the world. But if they are parts and members, they are certainly not living creatures in their own right; for in no case can parts be the very thing that the whole is, or possess wisdom and sensation on their own, since they are affected by no motions of their own without the agreement of the whole living creature.

Once this has been established and granted, the whole conclusion returns to this: neither the Sun nor the Moon nor the ether, the Earth, and the rest is a god. For they are parts of the world, not distinct names of divine beings. And thus, through your confusion and intermingling of all things divine, it is brought about that the world is established as the one God in the nature of things, while all the others are rejected—or rather [Note: [Col. 0987B] Fulvius reads “altogether.”] established emptily, vacuously, and without any substance.

[Note: [Col. 0988C]

### XXXVI.—With which you are accustomed to drench your thirst

Virgil, *Aeneid* I, v. 739:

> . . . And drenched himself from the full golden cup.

Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, bk. I:

> Greedy for wine, he drenched himself with a mighty draught.

HERALD. and ELMENH.

[Col. 0988D] **Indeed.** So Meursius. The first edition of Sabaeus incorrectly reads “certain persons.” ORELL.

**And that they do not exist in any one part of nature.** So the manuscript, a reading correctly defended by Th. Canter and Heraldus, taking it as equivalent to “and that they do not exist in any part of nature,” Greek *en oudeni physeōs merei*. Gelenius published “and that they do not exist in any,” etc. ORELL.]

### XXXVI

If we were to undermine belief in your gods by as many methods and as many doctrines, no one would doubt that, inflamed with anger and frenzy, you would demand fires, wild beasts, swords, and other kinds of punishment against us, with which you are accustomed to drench your thirst through craving for our blood.

But when almost the entire race of divine beings is removed by you yourselves under the display of intellect and learning, you dare to charge that human affairs are oppressed by the gods on account of our name. Yet, indeed, if it is true that those gods exist anywhere and grow hot with the flames of anger, they could have no more just reason for raging against you than that you deny that they have any real existence or that they exist in any one part of nature.

[Note: [Col. 0988D]

### XXXVII.—Mnaseas

He was from Patara, a city of Lycia. Athenaeus cites the third book of his *European History*, bk. IV, p. 158; the second book of his *On Asia*, bk. VIII, p. 346; and finally his *Periplus* in the same book, p. 331. Columella, bk. XII, ch. 4, calls him a writer of the Greek nation who was not obscure, and, together with Varro, commends him among the writers on agriculture, bk. I, ch. 1. He must not be confused with Mnaseas of Berytus, who, according to the Suda, wrote on the rhetorical art and Attic names, or with another Mnaseas, of Locris or Colophon, who—as the same Athenaeus relates—composed written entertainments which, because of their variety, were called *Salpē*. Cf. Nourr., p. 544; Voss., *On Greek History*, [Col. 0989B] bk. I, ch. 21, pp. 134 ff.; and Hardouin, under this word in the index to Pliny’s *Natural History*. ORELL.

**They were daughters of Earth and Heaven.** In the genealogy of the gods prefixed to his *Fables*, p. 31, ed. Muncker, Hyginus says that Moneta—that is, Mnemosyne, mother of the Muses—was born from Ether and Earth. ORELL.

**Ephorus, then, declares that they are three in number.** On Ephorus, the very well-known historian of Cyme, a pupil of Isocrates and fellow student of Theopompus, see the Suda and G. J. Voss., *On Greek History*, p. 30. Moreover, this is a classic passage concerning the disputed number of the Muses. See also Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* I, v. 12, and *Eclogue* VII, v. 21; and Muncker on Hyginus, *Fable* CCXXII, p. 288. In the most ancient times only three were recognized; Pausanias preserved their names in his *Boeotica*: *Meletē* (“Practice”), *Aoidē* (“Song”), and *Mnēmē* (“Memory”). [Col. 0989C] Ausonius, *Riddle of the Number Three*, vv. 30–31:

> And the lyric poets equal the Mnemonides in number,  
> Of whom Phoebus’ right hand once possessed only three.

See Tollius there, p. 458. Tzetzes, *Commentary on Hesiod’s Works*, p. 6, ed. Heinsius:

> “But Eumelus of Corinth says that there are three Muses, daughters of Apollo: Cephisō, Apollonis, and Borysthenis.”

Add G. J. Voss., *On Idolatry*, bk. VIII, ch. 12, p. 752. ORELL.—See Tzetzes on Hesiod, *Works and Days*, v. 1; Phurnutus, *On the Nature of the Gods*, p. 157; G. Creuzer, *Symbolism*, vol. III, pp. 295–296; Hug, *On Myth*, etc., pp. 222–223. Varro offered the following reason why there were three Muses (in Augustine, *The City of God*, XVIII, and A. Popma, *Fragments*, p. 459): because it was easy to observe that every sound, which is the material of songs, is threefold by nature. Ruhnken, *Critical Letter* II, p. 309 of the new edition, presented a passage from the Paris manuscript, where the text reads:

> “Eumelus”—so it is to be read—“of Corinth says that there are three Muses, daughters of Apollo: Cephisō, Apollonis, and Borysthenis.” [Col. 0989D]

MARX on the fragments of Ephorus, p. 264.

**Mnaseas, whom we have mentioned, says four.** Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III, ch. 21: “Next come the first four Muses, born from the second Jupiter: Thelxiope, Aoede, Arche, and Melete.” On the disputed reading there, see Davies. Aratus likewise recognized four Muses in the fifth book of his *Astrica*, according to Tzetzes on Hesiod at the passage cited. ORELL.

**Myrtilus.** The name is written in various ways. Besides our author, Clement—whom Phrynichus excerpted under the word *kataphagai*—and the scholiast on Apollonius call him Myrtilus; Athenaeus, however, bk. XIII, p. 617, calls him Myrsilus. He was a Lesbian, a contemporary of Alcaeus and Sappho, and wrote a *History of Lesbos*, according to Antigonus of Carystus, chs. 5, 17, and 129. Under his name Jo. Annius of Viterbo published a spurious book *On the Origin of Italy and the Tyrrhenians*. See Voss., *On Greek History*, bk. III, p. 591, and Hardouin, *Index to Pliny*. ORELL.

**Myrtilus introduces seven.** Epicharmus likewise did so, according to the same Tzetzes at the cited passage:

> “Epicharmus, in *The Marriage of Hebe*, says that there are seven, daughters of Pierus and the nymph Pimpleis: Neilō, Tritōnē, Asōpō, Heptapolis, Achelōïs, Tipoplo, and Rhodia.” [Col. 0990B]

ORELL.

**Crates affirms that there are eight.** Crates of Mallos, the very well-known grammarian and interpreter of Homer, must undoubtedly be understood. Moreover, the grammarians’ fiction concerning eight Muses seems to have arisen from Plato’s invention concerning the eight Sirens seated on the whorls of the adamantine spindle of the Fates, which is found in *Republic* X, p. 616, ed. H. Steph. (Bipontine ed., vol. VII, pp. 327–328). ORELL.

**Finally Hesiod presents nine, together with their names.** I have punctuated the text in this way. For the sense is: Hesiod presents nine Muses together with their names, from *prodo, prodere*, “to bring forth,” not: “he proceeds,” from *prodeo, prodire*, “with nine names.” [Col. 0990C] The passage of Hesiod occurs in the *Theogony*, vv. 75 ff.:

> These things the Muses sang, who possess Olympian dwellings,  
> Nine daughters born from mighty Zeus:  
> Clio, Euterpe, Thalia, Melpomene,  
> Terpsichore, Erato, Polymnia, Urania,  
> And Calliope, who is the foremost of them all.

ORELL.

**For if it were clearly known what the truth is, the voice of all would be unanimous.** So Oberthür published the text. The manuscript omits “would be,” incorrectly. The Leiden edition gives: “there would be one,” etc. Th. Canter believes that the text should read: “For if it were clearly known, the voice of all would have been unanimous.” But I would not venture to eliminate the words “what it is”; *quid sit* is used absolutely, as we say in German, *was an der Sache sei*—“what the truth of the matter may be.” Grotius, in Meursius, conjectures “that it is,” etc. ORELL.

**And the agreement of all would proceed and converge upon the conclusion of the same opinion.** *Pergere* here has its proper and primary meaning, “to go” or “to tend toward.” Thus Terence uses *huc pergo*, “I proceed here,” and *horsum pergo*, “I proceed in this direction.” ORELL.]

### XXXVII

Mnaseas is our authority that the Muses were daughters of Earth and Heaven. The others proclaim that they were born to Jupiter from Memory [Col. 0989A] as his wife, or from Mind. Some write that they were virgins, others that they were mothers. For it is now pleasing to touch briefly upon those matters as well in which the diversity of your opinions shows you saying different things about the same subject.

Ephorus, then, declares that they are three in number; Mnaseas, whom we have mentioned, says four; Myrtilus [Note: [Col. 0990B] Fulvius reads *Myrsilus*; the manuscript, *Murcylus*; Sabaeus, *Myrtilis*.] introduces seven; Crates affirms that there are eight; finally Hesiod presents nine, together with their names, enriching heaven and the stars with gods.

Unless we are mistaken, this disagreement belongs to people who know nothing of the truth; it does not descend from the truth of the matter. For if it were clearly known what the truth is, the voice of all would be unanimous, and the agreement of all [Col. 0989B] would proceed and converge upon the conclusion of the same opinion.

[Col. 0990A] [Note: [Col. 0990D]

### XXXVIII.—How, then, can you restore the full force of religion to completeness?

*Integrare* means to bring something to integrity or perfection. Thus above, bk. II, ch. 15: “We preserve and maintain intact the tenor of all the virtues.” *Integrator* has the same sense in Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. XLVI, at the end: “How, then, are the philosopher and the Christian alike—the disciple of Greece and the disciple of heaven, the broker of reputation and the broker of salvation . . . the falsifier of error and restorer of truth, its thief and its guardian?” ORELL.

**Or the former erases and destroys six divine Muses.** Heraldus wishes to delete “Muses” as a gloss. But such redundancies (*perittologiai*) are not uncommon in Arnobius. Moreover, *interficere*, “to destroy,” is elegantly used for removing or taking away. In the same sense Tertullian uses “destroyer of the truth” in *On the Flesh of Christ*, ch. 4. ORELL.

**Piso believes that the Novensiles are nine gods established among the Sabines near Trebia.** This too is a classic passage concerning the Novensile gods, containing much that you would seek elsewhere in vain. Cf. Jac. Nicol. Loensis, *Miscellaneous Epiphyllides*, [Col. 0991B] bk. IV, ch. 15, in Gruter’s *Critical Lamp*, vol. V, pp. 421–422; he carefully examined every passage in the ancient authors concerning those gods. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, bk. IV, p. 22, Bipontine ed., likewise agrees with Piso. Moreover, on L. Calpurnius Piso Frugi, consul in the year 520 from the founding of the City, sponsor of the Calpurnian law on extortion, and writer of *Annals*, see G. J. Voss., *On Latin History*, bk. I, ch. 6. ORELL.

Bringing his view into agreement with Aelius. This is Aelius Stilo, who had explained the *Carmen Saliare* and written other works, mention of which occurs throughout the grammarians, Varro, Aulus Gellius, and Festus. Aelius Gallus is a different man. HERALDUS.

Varro gives the number nine, because it is always regarded as the most powerful and greatest number for setting things in motion. Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 14: “Most astrologers have carefully distinguished these two numbers (7 and 9), saying that seven pertains to the body, nine to the [Col. 0991C] soul; that the former is assigned to the medicine of the body and to Apollo, the latter to the Muses, because music is accustomed to soothe and cure the maladies of the soul, which they call πάθη (*pathē*, ‘passions’).” Compare Ausonius, *Idyll* XI. In place of *movendis* (“setting in motion”), Fulvius Ursinus prefers *innovandis* (“renewing”), wrongly: *movendis* is equivalent to *promovendis* (“advancing”). ORELLI.

Cornificius. A grammarian rather than a historian, cited several times by Festus and Macrobius, the latter of whom praises his books of *Etyma*. Vossius, *On the Latin Historians*, book III, in the appendix on writers about whom it is uncertain whether they wrote historical works, Amsterdam edition of the *Works*, vol. IV, p. 260, says that he flourished in the time of Augustus. He must not be confused with the rhetorician Lucius Cornificius, to whom letters of Cicero survive. ORELLI.

Manilius says that they are nine gods, etc. Titus Manilius, cited by Varro, *On the Latin Language*, books IV and VI, as well as by Pliny, *Natural History*, book X, chapter II, who praises him as the earliest and most diligent of Roman writers. He flourished in the time of Marius and Sulla. See G. J. Vossius, *On the Latin Historians*, book I, chapter IX. [Col. 0991D] Or Manilius Chrestus may be meant, who wrote a book *On the Hymns of the Gods*, according to Fulgentius, *On Ancient Speech*. See “yoked oxen,” several fragments of which Johannes Mydus included in his little work *On the Months*, edited by Schow. ORELLI.

To whom alone Jupiter granted the power of hurling his thunderbolt. A passage of Pliny, *Natural History*, book II, chapter LII, sheds light upon ours: “The Etruscan writings hold that nine gods cast thunderbolts, and that these are of eleven kinds; for Jupiter hurls three kinds. The Romans retained only two of them, assigning those of the day to Jupiter and those of the night to Summanus,” etc.; see Hardouin there. Compare Seneca, *Natural Questions*, book II, chapter 41: “Jupiter, indeed, is especially armed with the thunderbolt, and was thought to send only red thunderbolts, while the other gods hurled white or black ones, as Meursius observes from Horace, Claudian, and Acro in his notes on Lycophron. This is perhaps why we read in Livy, book XXXII, that a golden thunderbolt weighing fifty pounds was made as a gift for Jupiter, but gifts of silver for Juno and Minerva. Besides Jupiter, however, I find that the ancients commemorated as thunder-wielding gods Summanus, [Col. 0992B] Saturn, Mars, Hercules, Vulcan, Minerva, Juno, the Mother of the Gods, Apollo or the Sun, and Zagreus or Bacchus.” So writes Gisbert Cuper, who discusses these gods learnedly and at length in his *Harpocrates*, pp. 99 ff., Utrecht quarto edition. ORELLI.

Cincius. Lucius Cincius Alimentus, a contemporary of Fabius Pictor and praetor of Sicily after the disaster at Cannae, wrote in Greek a *History of Hannibal*, and in Latin a history concerning Gorgias of Leontini, books *On Military Affairs*—from which Vegetius drew a great deal—*On the Fasti*, and *On Ancient Words*, from which the present material appears to have been taken. Livy praises him as a diligent authority on ancient records, *History*, book VII, beginning. See G. J. Vossius, *On the Greek Historians*, book IV, chapter III, and *On the Latin Historians*, book I, chapter IV. ORELLI.

For the Romans were accustomed to distribute the religious rites of conquered cities partly in private among families, etc. Thus the Leiden edition, following the emendation of Franciscus Modius from traces in a manuscript, [Col. 0992C] which has *regiones* (“regions”); from this Gelenius had made *omnes deos* (“all the gods”). That the Romans were accustomed to summon the gods away before storming cities and invite them to Rome is very well known. See the formula employed for that purpose in Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book III, chapter 9; Pliny, book XXVIII, chapter 2; Livy, etc. Hence Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, book II:

> Thereafter, from cities subdued by valor, Rome  
> Begot innumerable gods for herself out of glorious triumphs.  
> Amid the smoking ruins of the temples,  
> The armed right hand of the conqueror seized the enemy’s images  
> And, revering the captives as though divine powers, carried them home.

ORELLI, STEWECHIUS, and HERALDUS.

And lest any of the gods should be passed over because of their multitude or through ignorance. I have printed this following Heraldus’s emendation in his *Second Series of Critical Notes*. The others have: “and lest anything belonging to the gods,” etc. ORELLI.]

### XXXVIII

How, then, can you restore the full and unimpaired force of religion when you are mistaken about the gods themselves? Or how can you invite us to venerable forms of worship when you teach us nothing certain about the apprehension of those divine powers? For, to pass over the authorities who stand between the two extremes, either the first of them erases and destroys six divine Muses, if it is established that there are nine; or the last and final authority adds six which do not exist, when only three truly exist. Thus it is impossible either to know or to apprehend which should be added and which removed, and the undertaking of religion itself is brought into danger, either by worshipping what does not exist or perhaps by passing over what does. [Col. 0990B]

Piso believes that the Novensiles were nine gods established among the Sabines [Col. 0991A] at Trebia. Granius considers them the Muses, bringing his view into agreement with that of Aelius. Varro gives the number nine, because it is always held to be the most powerful and greatest in setting [Note: [Col. 0991B] Fulvius reads “renewing.”] things in motion. Cornificius calls them the guardians of novelties, because under their care everything is renewed by novelty and maintained. Manilius says that they are nine gods to whom alone Jupiter granted the power of hurling his thunderbolt. Cincius declares that they are foreign divinities named from novelty itself; for the Romans were accustomed to distribute the religious rites of conquered cities partly in private among families, [Col. 0991B] and partly to consecrate them publicly. And lest any [Col. 0992A] of the gods should be passed over because of their multitude or through ignorance, they were all invoked together, for the sake of brevity and economy, under the single name *Novensiles*.

[Note: [Col. 0992C]

### XXXIX

There are, besides, some who say that human beings who had been made gods were designated by this title. Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, verse 187: “Indeed, certain ancient writers say that the Novensiles are gods upon whom the merits of their valor conferred the dignity of divine power.” Compare Martianus Capella, *The Marriage of Philology*, book I, p. 27, Bern edition. [Col. 0992D] ORELLI.

Who attaches to things possessing substantial existence the emptiest and most insubstantial things. This is the old reading, which can be tolerated and explained. For Varro was saying that the Novensile gods were the number nine; and in this way he attached utterly empty and insubstantial things—for what is emptier than numbers?—to things possessing substantial existence. The obscurity of this passage arose from the transposition of the conjunction, in place of “attaches empty and insubstantial things.” HERALDUS.—The transposition of a conjunction is familiar in Arnobius. Thus book I, chapter 64 has “of the games and the celebration of birthdays,” in place of “the celebration of games and birthdays”; see the notes there. Accordingly, in this passage we do not need the correction of the Leiden editor: “attaches an utterly empty thing, and one without substance,” much less Fulvius Ursinus’s conjecture, “attaches utterly empty arguments,” or that of Meursius, “attaches empty and insubstantial things.” For *in substantia* (“in substantial existence”), Modius fashioned *in essentia* (“in essential existence”). But the manuscript has *instantia*, perhaps written in abbreviation as *in stantia* for *in substantia*. ORELLI.

[Col. 0993B] Cornificius is proved to be wavering. I have restored to Arnobius this entirely authentic manuscript reading, most suitable to the context, and well defended by Stewechius and P. Colvius in his notes on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book V, p. 368, Oudendorp edition. Sabaeus in the first Roman edition printed *balare* (“to bleat”), which the other editors retained and Heraldus also defended, thinking that Arnobius intended through this word to make sport of the name Cornificius. Bleating, of course, is the sound of sheep; and since the sheep is a very simple animal, that designation was applied by the ancients to people who were not very shrewd and were somewhat foolish, for example by Aristophanes in the *Clouds*: Λίθοι, ἀριθμός, πρόβατα, “stones, a mere number, sheep.” Accordingly, those who foolishly blurt something out rather than speak may also correctly be said to “bleat.” [Col. 0993C] Yet it must be observed that in this passage Arnobius refutes the learned men whom he had listed with the utmost moderation, without any harshness or malice, saying that they err, are found imprudent, speak falsely, and so forth. Therefore “bleat” is wholly out of place here. Guilielmus Canterus, *New Readings*, book III, chapter 22, in J. Gruter’s *Critical Lamp*, vol. III, p. 584, conjectures that *halare* should be read, a word which the ancients, according to Festus, used for “to lie.” But *labare* (“to waver”) is preferable. Thus in the following chapter: “The opinions waver”; and in chapter 41: “since from one account and another it becomes manifest and evident that you hesitate, waver, and know nothing certain about these matters which you assert.” ORELLI.

Because of the novelty of the honor. The Leiden edition reads: “from the novelty of the honor.” Meursius: “in honor of novelty,” looking back to the view of Cornificius, who said that they were guardians of novelties. ORELLI.

Thus, when we say “Novensiles,” it is a name for gods who, though human, earned the right to be gods. Gelenius restored the passage in this form. The manuscript reads corruptly: “thus, when we say Novensiles all if there are nine of them.” Fulvius Ursinus: “we say all nine of them.” Meursius: “thus, when we say Novensiles, all who,” etc., deleting the words “if there are nine of them.” The Leiden edition: “thus, when we say Novensiles, if this is the name of gods,” etc. Whatever emendation of this extremely corrupt passage we choose, “nine” certainly cannot have a place in it, since those who, though human, earned the right to be gods number not nine but far more, and their number is uncertain. ORELLI.]

### XXXIX

There are, besides, some who proclaim that human beings who had been made gods were designated by this title, such as Hercules, Romulus, Aesculapius, Liber, and Aeneas. These opinions, as is evident, are all different; nor can it happen in the nature of things that those who differ in their opinions should be regarded as authorities for a single truth.

For if Piso’s opinion is true, Aelius and Granius [Col. 0992B] are lying. If what they say is certain, [Col. 0993A] the most learned Varro is in error, since he attaches to things possessing substantial existence the emptiest and most insubstantial things. If the number nine gives the Novensiles their name, Cornificius is proved to be wavering, for he grants a power belonging to another sphere to divinities who preside over novelty. But if Cornificius’s opinion is true, Cincius is found imprudent, since he endows the gods of conquered cities with the power of the Novensile divinities. If, however, the Novensiles are those whom Cincius proclaims, Manilius will be found to speak falsely, since under that title he includes the hurlers of another’s thunderbolt. But if what Manilius asserts is ascertained and true, those men are in the gravest error who suppose that mortals raised to divine honors and consecrated are called Novensiles because of the novelty of that honor.

But if the Novensiles are those who, after departing from the mortality of life, deserved to be raised to the stars, [Col. 0993B] there are, in an absolute sense, [Col. 0994A] no Novensile gods at all. For just as *slaves*, *soldiers*, and *masters* are not the names of the individual persons underlying them, but of offices, conditions, and functions, so, when we say that “Novensiles” is the name for gods who, though human, earned the right to be gods, it is manifest and evident that no specifically defined persons are being named; rather, novelty itself is designated by the title *Novensiles*.

[Note: [Col. 0993D]

### XL

Nigidius reported that the Penates were the gods Neptune and Apollo. Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book III, chapter 4: “Nigidius, in the nineteenth book of *On the Gods*, asks whether the Penates of the Trojans are Apollo and Neptune, who are said to have built their walls for them.” Compare Servius on *Aeneid* III, verse 12. ELMENHORSTIUS.

Caesius, himself following these. I would maintain without any hesitation that it must be read thus: “following these,” namely the Etruscan teachings; for these had been mentioned shortly before. THEODORUS CANTERUS. The manuscript has the meaningless *assequens*. [Col. 0994B] Others read “following them”; the Leiden edition, “following it.” But Canterus’s emendation comes closest to the manuscript’s wording. For *Caesius*, the same Canterus suspects that *Caelius* should be read, undoubtedly understanding Lucius Caelius Antipater, who flourished in the time of the Gracchi and wrote a history of the Punic War and other works. Compare Livy, book XXI, chapter 38. G. J. Vossius, however, understands Caesius Bassus, a lyric poet and, according to some, the author of commentaries on Aratus’s *Phaenomena* as translated by Germanicus; he lived in the time of Nero and Galba. See *On the Latin Historians*, book I, chapter 22, and the appendix. M. Delrio, in *Survey of Latin Tragedy*, part III, [Col. 0994C] p. 377, where he discusses these gods at length, corrects the name to *Cassius* from Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book III, chapter 4: “Cassius Hemina, however, says that the Samothracian gods, who are also properly called the Penates of the Romans, are θεοὺς μεγάλους, θεοὺς χρηστούς, θεοὺς δυνατούς—‘great gods, beneficent gods, powerful gods.’” Yet, as we see, this Cassius of Macrobius differs very greatly from the Caesius of Arnobius. ORELLI.

The Jovial Genius. A very obscure god, information about whom you will seek elsewhere in vain. C. Barthius, in a rather lengthy *Disputation on Genii* appended to Rutilius’s *Journey*, verse 328, tries to prove from inscriptions that the pagans assigned special divine powers and certain genii to their gods, and therefore interprets the Jovial Genius as “a divinity who stood in the place of a genius to Jupiter.” Joannes Clericus, *Critical Art*, part II, section II, chapter 5, teaches that this is utterly false. For the Genius of Jupiter, Juno, or Pluto would be nothing other than genii begotten or sent by those gods. He therefore thinks that the Jovial Genius is the name of a household Lar, so called because it was believed to have been given to the family by Jupiter. For my part, I agree with neither of them, but [Col. 0994D] would rather believe that Arnobius is indicating here that first and greatest of the genii, who was called “the Genius” κατ’ ἐξοχήν (“par excellence”) by Martianus Capella in a no less obscure passage, where he treats the regions or circles of heaven and the abodes of the gods, *The Marriage of Philology*, book I, p. 16; see Grotius there: “From the next, or sixth, region, after the dwellings of the royal consorts have been passed, Ceres, Tellurus, Vulcan the father of Earth, and the Genius are summoned.” I conclude that the Jovial Genius is intended here from Martianus’s words following shortly afterward: “But the Genius of Juno Hospita is summoned from the ninth region”—as though inferior to that former Genius. The genii, therefore, are, as it were, the ministers and messengers of Jupiter and Juno. But let the more learned judge. ORELLI.

And Pales . . . but some minister and steward of Jupiter of the masculine sex, I know not whom. Martianus Capella mentions Pales as a god of the masculine sex in the passage cited above, book I, p. 27: “You too, Pales and Favor, sons of Jupiter, together with Celeritas, daughter of the Sun, are summoned from the sixth region of heaven”; and shortly afterward: “But Liber and Secundanus Pales are also summoned from the seventh”; see Grotius there and at p. 16. [Col. 0995A] And Servius on Virgil, *Georgics* III, verse 1: “Pales, however, is the goddess of pasture, whom some call Vesta, others the Mother of the Gods. Virgil refers to her in the feminine gender; others, including Varro, in the masculine, as *this Pales*.” Compare C. Barthius on Statius, *Thebaid* VI, verse 111, vol. III, p. 386. ORELLI.

*Vulgaritas*. The same as *vulgus*, “the common people.” A word peculiar to Arnobius, as Gesner observes in his *Thesaurus*. Thus below, “the common populace.” ORELLI.

He holds that the gods of whom we speak are, etc. Those words, “of whom we speak,” [Col. 0995B] seemed to conceal something ancient. If I were not afraid of departing too far from the common reading, I would write: “He holds that they are the Select Gods,” etc. Augustine, *The City of God*, book IV, chapter 23: “For who can tolerate,” he says, “the fact that Felicity has been placed neither among the Consenting Gods, whom they say are admitted to Jupiter’s council, nor among the gods whom they call Select?” The same author, in book VII, chapter 29, mentions these same Select Gods from Varro. STEWECHIUS.—To me the words “of whom we speak” appear to mean nothing other than “whom we have just mentioned,” namely the Penates. ORELLI.

The Etruscans say that these are the *Consentes* and *Complices*. I have read nothing about these *Complices* gods. I once thought the word was a gloss in this passage: that some unskilled person had tried to interpret *Consentes* by *Complices*, as though they were, of course, accomplices conscious of the same crime. Isidore in the *Glosses*: “An accomplice is one who is joined to another for evil in a single sin or crime; the term is never used with reference to good.” Prudentius, in the *Martyrdom of Romanus*:

> [Col. 0995C] “Why do I delay,” said he, “to destroy them both,  
> The boy and his teacher, accomplices in an impious sect?”

But Arnobius’s addition, “because they rise together and set together,” seems to confirm the reading, so that they are *complices* as though conjoined together and bound by the closest ties. They were called *Consentes*, however, rather because they were supreme Jupiter’s counselors, as he adds: presumably because *consere* means συμβουλεύειν (“to deliberate together”). Hence also the god Consus. HERALDUS.—Nourrius, p. 456, defends *Complices* against Heraldus, who wished to expunge it as a copyist’s gloss, explaining it to mean “most closely joined, bound by the closest bonds.” Ambrose uses it in this sense, *On the Duties of Ministers*, book III, chapter 14: “Advantage is always conjoined with honor, and honor with advantage.”

The question of the *Dii Consentes* is difficult. For illustration’s sake, I shall present the observations of Scipio Maffei in the *Museum of Verona*, p. 237, also drawing upon Stewechius’s observations on book V, chapter 18 of our author and adding some remarks of my own, such as they are. “Who the *Dii Consentes* were,” writes [Col. 0995D] Maffei, “is not evident. Whoever can explain the words of Arnobius that are cited concerning them as though decisive will be a great Apollo in my eyes. Varro (*On the Latin Language*, book VII, p. 121, Bipont edition): ‘The people say: the Penates gods, the Consenting Gods.’ They are commonly understood to be the gods of the greater nations, whom the Greeks call the twelve, θεοὺς δώδεκα καλουμένους (‘those called the twelve gods’). Μὰ τοὺς δώδεκα (‘By the twelve gods!’), says Aristophanes in the *Knights*. But their names are well known” from that distich of Ennius, preserved by Martianus Capella, *The Marriage of Philology*, book I, p. 26, Bern edition, and by Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*:

> Juno, Vesta, Minerva, Ceres, Diana, Venus, Mars,  
> Mercury, Jove, Neptune, Vulcan, Apollo.

The rustic marble Farnese Calendar also agrees with this, for in it the same gods are assigned as guardians of the individual months of the year: Juno to January, Neptune to February, Minerva to March, Venus to April, Apollo to May, Mercury to June, Jupiter to July, Ceres to August, Vulcan to September, Mars to October, [Col. 0996A] Diana to November, and Vesta to December. “Arnobius, on the contrary, says that neither their number nor their names are known. Hence Martianus, at the passage cited: ‘after Jupiter himself, the Consenting Gods’; and St. Augustine (*The City of God*, book IV, chapter 23): ‘the Consenting Gods, whom they say are admitted to Jupiter’s council.’” Thus Maffei.

Among the ancients, however, the number of the Consenting Gods is disputed. Martianus Capella at the passage cited, Plautus in the *Epidicus*—

> If Jupiter were to bring eleven gods besides himself—

[Col. 0996B] and others establish twelve together with Jupiter. But Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI, verse 72:

> Twice six celestials, with Jupiter in their midst, sit  
> In their lofty seats with august solemnity;

and Seneca, *Natural Questions*, book II, chapter 41: “For Jupiter summons twelve gods”—twelve excluding Jupiter as presiding deity, and thus they establish thirteen in all. Accordingly, commentators attempting to reconcile this disagreement add a thirteenth: some Bacchus, some Cupid, and some Cybele, the Mother of the Gods. All this, therefore, is uncertain and arbitrary. Anyone who wishes to learn more about the Consenting Gods should consult Ludovicus Vives on the cited passage of Augustine; Columna on the fragments of Ennius, p. 264 (164 ff. in Hessel’s edition); Salmasius on the *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, pp. 141 ff.; Burmann on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, verse 167; and above all G. d’Arnaud in his little book *On the Gods πάρεδροι* (*paredroi*, “assessors”), though he appears to have been wholly unaware of the classic passage in Arnobius. ORELLI.

Because they rise together and set together. We could restore the sense of the words by reading: “They are raised up together and sit together.” But *oriantur* (“rise”) can also be retained. For Pompeius Festus says: “*oriri* . . . means to be born or to rise”; and in Velius Longus, *On Orthography*, “a rising consul” means the same as “a consul taking office.” It is therefore perfectly sound to say that Jupiter’s counselors “rise together and sit together.” For that reason they are *Consentes*, that is, agreeing and harmonious, or *considentes*, sitting together. MAFFEI in the *Museum of Verona*, at the passage cited.—For my part, I would not venture to alter anything. Perhaps the foundation of this invention was the rising and setting of the planets, and this was accordingly attributed to all twelve, though it applies to only a few. ORELLI.

Six males and as many females. Varro also agrees with Arnobius, *On Agriculture*, book I, chapter 1: “First I shall invoke—not, like Homer and Ennius, the Muses, but the twelve Consenting Gods; yet not those urban gods whose gilded images stand by the forum, six males and as many females, but those twelve gods who are especially the leaders of farmers.” See Schneider’s notes there, p. 245; he also cites our passage. ORELLI.

And most sparing of compassion. These most difficult words [Col. 0996D] have been tortured in extraordinary fashion by commentators. Gelenius, indulging his passion for alteration, reshapes them as “of a most barbarous nation,” a reading defended by Andreas Delrio, *Survey of Latin Tragedy*, part III, p. 377, who thinks the Samothracians are so called, since from them originated the Phrygians, who are barbarians in the strict sense. Fulvius Ursinus reads “of very scant mention,” which can mean nothing other than that they are mentioned only rarely and are scarcely worthy of consideration—a number rather than gods, if compared with Jupiter. Joseph Scaliger reads “of very sparing sacrificial feasting,” with whom Meursius agrees, reading “of very little sacrificial feasting” (a superlative used by Lucretius, book I, verse 609). Thus gods “of very little” or “very sparing sacrificial feasting” would be gods to whom victims or sacrificial animals were to be slaughtered only sparingly. For *visceratio* is a banquet from the *viscera*, that is, the flesh of sacrificed victims, celebrated among the participants in a sacrifice, such as Virgil describes in *Aeneid* VIII, lines 179 ff. See Salmasius on Solinus, p. 55. Hence, in this passage, by a rather unusual usage in which the part stands for the whole, it refers to the sacrifices themselves.

Yet, if I may say so with all respect to these most learned men, I cannot at all persuade myself that Etruria, the mother of superstitions, held that victims should be offered to the other gods of the greater nations only sparingly and rarely. The manuscript reading, “most sparing of compassion,” can in some measure be defended, so that it signifies harsh and inhuman gods, possessing little mercy and difficult to sway by prayers and sacrifices. [Col. 0997A] But this too accords poorly with what precedes. [Col. 0997B]

Doubtful and uncertain about establishing the true reading, I nevertheless venture to propose three conjectures for the judgment of the learned. Either, by the slightest alteration—the omission of only one letter—we should read “most equal in compassion,” that is, equally disposed toward the human race and exercising the same care over human affairs. The superlative *parissimus* (“most equal”) occurs in Plautus, *Curculio*, act IV, scene II, verse 20, and Aulus Gellius XX, chapter 1: “the most exact retaliation.” Why should it not also occur in Arnobius, a most diligent imitator of antiquity?

Or we should read “most equal in sacrificial feasting,” which signifies gods equal in degree of honor and therefore to be propitiated by the same, or equally great, sacrifices. This would accord perfectly with what precedes: “Consenting and Conjoined . . . because they rise together and set together.”

Or finally, if we wish to retain “most sparing,” it seems that we should read “of most sparing government,” that is, gods who have care of scarcely anything, [Col. 0997C] to whom dominion over the fewest matters has been entrusted, but who are purely and simply Jupiter’s counselors—according, of course, to the Etruscans’ opinion. *Moderatio* is used for “rule” or “government” in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III, chapter 35: “There is certainly no divine government of the world over human beings if it makes no distinction between good and evil.” But let the more learned judge. ORELLI.

Counselors and chief men of supreme Jupiter. That is, senators, as Martianus Capella also calls them, *The Marriage of Philology*, book I, at the passage cited. HERALDUS.

Nor were there lacking those who wrote that Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva were the Penates. Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book III, chapter 4: “Varro, in the second book of *Human Antiquities*, relates that Dardanus carried the Penates from Samothrace into Phrygia, and Aeneas from Troy into Italy. Who the Penates are Varro does not state in the book just mentioned; but those who investigate the truth more carefully have said that the Penates are those through whom we breathe inwardly, through whom we possess a body, and through whom we possess the rational faculty of the soul; that Jupiter is the middle ether, Juno the lower air together with the earth, and Minerva the highest summit of the ether. As an argument they employ the fact that Tarquinius, son of Demaratus of Corinth, who had been mystically initiated into the Samothracian rites, united the divinities just mentioned in a single temple and beneath the same roof.” [Col. 0997D] HERALDUS.—Compare Servius on *Aeneid* III, 12. ORELLI.

And here too nothing harmonious is said. The trifling peddlers of nonsense who act as textual correctors—Gelenius among them—raved when they caused *continens* (“continuous”) to be printed, although the manuscripts have *concinens* (“harmonious”); Cicero used the same word more than once. He says, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, 8: “the parts of the world harmonizing with one another.” Again elsewhere, *On Ends* V, 28: “Do you see how these things harmonize?”—that is, fit together and agree. Martianus Capella, book II of *The Marriage*: “Therefore,” he says, “the number of the aforesaid names harmonized.” Our manuscript glosses read: “*concinens*: consonant.” STEWECHIUS.—Grotius had already made the same observation in Meursius. The Greek συνᾷσαι (“to harmonize”) is used in the same sense. See Heraldus on Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, chapter I, p. 5, Gronovius’s edition. ORELLI.

[Col. 0998A] Nothing is settled by a single declaration. I prefer Fulvius Ursinus’s conjecture, *finitum* (“settled”), so that it refers to what precedes: “nothing harmonious is said.” ORELLI.

[Col. 0998B] Nor is there anything trustworthy on which the mind can take its stand. The same Fulvius prefers: “Nor is there anything solid,” etc. But *fidus* (“trustworthy”) has the same sense, as, for example, in Virgil, *Aeneid* II, 281:

> . . . O most trustworthy hope of the Trojans,

where others wrongly read “bravest,” and others “firmest.” ORELLI.]

### XL

Nigidius reported that the Penates were the gods Neptune and Apollo, who once surrounded the city of Ilium with walls under an agreed condition. [Note: [Col. 0993B] The manuscript has, most corruptly, “of the immortals.”] The same author, following the Etruscan teachings, explains again in his sixth and tenth books that there are four classes of Penates: some of Jupiter, others of Neptune, a third class belonging to the lower world, and a fourth to mortal human beings—saying some inexplicable thing or other.

Caesius, himself following these teachings, considers Fortune [Col. 0994B] and Ceres, the Jovial Genius, and Pales to be the Penates; [Col. 0995A] not, however, the female Pales accepted by the common people, but some minister and steward of Jupiter of the masculine sex, I know not whom.

Varro holds that the gods of whom we speak are those who dwell farther within, in the innermost recesses of heaven, and that neither their number nor their names are known. The Etruscans call these the *Consentes* (“Consenting”) [Col. 0996A] and *Complices* (“Conjoined”), because they rise together and set together: six males and as many females, of unknown names and most sparing of compassion; but they are believed to be the counselors and chief men of supreme Jupiter.

Nor were there lacking those who wrote that Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva were the Penates, without whom we cannot live or understand, but who govern us inwardly by reason, heat, and breath.

As you see, here too nothing harmonious is said; nothing is settled by a single declaration. Nor is there anything trustworthy on which the mind can take its stand and draw a conclusion by a conjecture very close to the truth it seeks. For the opinions waver so greatly, and one view is so completely torn down by another, that either none of them is true, [Col. 0998A] or, if the truth is stated by someone, it cannot be known amid so many divergences.

[Note: [Col. 0998B]

### XLI

Whom the common people consider gods of neighborhoods and roads. They believed the Lares to be, as it were, the particular genii of places, specifically assigned to individual families and houses. Hence Priscian and Philoxenus interpret *Lares* as θεοὺς κατοικιδίους (“household gods”), whom Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book IV, calls τοὺς κατ’ οἰκίαν ἥρωας (“the household heroes”). Ausonius in the *Technopaegnion*:

> Nor the Genius of houses, the Lar begotten by Larunda.

For this reason they also regarded the same gods as gods of neighborhoods and roads; hence the *Lares Viales*, “Lares of the roads,” in Plautus’s *Merchant*. For that reason Lares were also established at crossroads and worshipped there, and were called *Compitales*. HERALDUS.—Suetonius, *Augustus*, [Col. 0998C] chapter 31: “He instituted the adornment of the Lares Compitales twice a year.” An ancient inscription:

> TO FORTUNA REDUX, THE LAR OF THE ROAD, AND ETERNAL ROME, QUINTUS AXIUS AELIANUS.

ELMENHORSTIUS. Compare Andreas Delrio, *Survey of Latin Tragedy*, part III, p. 374. ORELLI.

Because the Greeks call neighborhoods *laurae*. Fulvius Ursinus prefers the Greek word λαύρας (*lauras*, “lanes”). See Pollux, *Onomasticon*, book IX, chapter 5, section 38, p. 1002, Hemsterhuis’s edition. ORELLI.

Guardians of roofs and houses. Hence Ausonius calls them “genii of houses,” as we observed just above. And because they were guardians and, as it were, protectors of houses, they stood covered with dogs’ skins, while an animal φυλακτικόν (“fit for guarding”) stood beside them. Lares represented in this way were called *Praestites*, as though προεστῶτες (“those standing before as protectors”), says Plutarch—more correctly [Col. 0998D] than Ovid, *Fasti* V:

> Yet the reason that title was given to them  
> Was that through their watchful eyes they keep all things safe.

HERALDUS. An ancient inscription, p. 106 of Gruter:

> TO THE LARES, FOR THE SAFETY AND SECURITY OF THE HOUSE OF QUINTUS SERTORIUS.

Plautus, *The Pot of Gold*, prologue, and *The Rope*, act IV, scene VI; Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*, p. 91. ELMENHORSTIUS.

At another time those Curetes who are said once to have concealed Jupiter’s crying with bronze instruments. Lucretius, book II, lines 633 ff.:

> They relate that the Curetes of Dicte once concealed  
> In Crete that crying of Jupiter,  
> When, as armed boys around a boy, in swift dance  
> They struck bronze upon bronze in measured rhythm,  
> Lest Saturn should seize him and commit him to his jaws,  
> And inflict an eternal wound beneath his mother’s breast.

[Col. 0999B] Ovid, *Fasti* IV, lines 207 ff.; Lactantius, book I, chapter 21; Minucius in the *Octavius*; Cyprian, *On Idols*; Hyginus, *Fables* 139. ELMENHORSTIUS.—Festus: “Cato used *aeribus* in the plural from *aes*, that is, bronze.” See Charisius, book I; Phocas, *On Heteroclite Nouns*; Priscian, book VII; and Meursius. ORELLI.

At another time the Samothracian Fingers. This is the manuscript’s excellent reading in place of the earlier printed *Indigetes of Samothrace*. Salmasius rightly restored it to the text in the Leiden edition and in his notes on Solinus, chapter II, p. 46. For this is how the Latins translated Δακτύλους Ἰδαίους (“Idaean Dactyls,” literally “Idaean Fingers”). In the judgment of the same Salmasius, the same word must also be restored in Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, chapter 16, where in place of “Idaean Dactyls” or “Idaean natives,” as others have it, we should write [Col. 0999C] “Idaean Fingers”; Joannes Davies and Ernesti also followed this reading.

Moreover, Macrobius too agrees with our author, *Saturnalia*, book III, chapter 4: “Cassius Hemina says that the Samothracian gods, who are also the Penates of the Romans, are properly called θεοὺς μεγάλους, θεοὺς χρηστούς, θεοὺς δυνατούς—‘great gods, beneficent gods, powerful gods,’” etc. The distinguished Sainte-Croix discusses the worship of those gods extensively in *On the Ancient Mysteries*, translated by Lenz, book II, chapters 1, 2, and 3.

“I think that the Praenestines called them ‘Fingers’ or *Digitii* because they indicated the way to travelers, as though with a finger. Perhaps they were even sculpted with a finger extended, just as even now, in many provinces, iron or wooden hands are fixed to crosses or pillars at ambiguous turns in the roads, directing the course of the roads with the index finger extended.” This and much else is found in M. A. Delrio, who discusses the gods called Lares at length in his *Survey of Latin Tragedy*, part III, pp. 373 ff. ORELLI.

Whom the Greeks indicate to be five and to be called the Idaean Dactyls. This is a sound reading, nor do I know what those intended who wished to substitute *quosque* (“and whom”) for *quinque* (“five”), as Fulvius Ursinus did. Julius Pollux, *Onomasticon*, book II, chapter 4, section [Col. 0999D] 156: Καὶ τοὺς Ἰδαίους δακτύλους κεκλῆσθαι λέγουσιν· οἱ μὲν κατὰ τὸν ἀριθμόν, ὅτι πέντε, οἱ δὲ κατὰ τὸ τῇ Ῥέᾳ πάνυ ὑπουργεῖν, ὅτι καὶ οἱ τῆς χειρὸς δάκτυλοι τεχνῖταί τε καὶ πάντων ἐργάται—“They say that they were called the Idaean Dactyls: some say because of their number, since they are five; others because they rendered very great service to Rhea, since the fingers of the hand too are craftsmen and workers of all things.” HERALDUS.—Compare Isaac Casaubon on Athenaeus, book I, chapter 5, p. 20. ORELLI.—Lucian, vol. V, p. 455. OCHSNER.

At another time, [he says,] they are the Manes, and that Mania was therefore called the mother of the Lares. Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chapter VIII: “Games were held throughout the city at the crossroads, having been restored, of course, by Tarquinius Superbus, in honor of the Lares and Mania, in accordance with an oracle of Apollo. By this oracle it was commanded that heads should be offered in supplication; and for some time this was observed in such a way that, for the safety of families, boys were sacrificed to the goddess Mania, mother of the Lares,” etc. “Mother Mania” is also mentioned by Martianus Capella, *The Marriage of Philology*, book II, p. 65, Bern edition. ORELLI.

He says that the Lares are specters, as though they were certain genii and the souls of the dead who have completed life. I suspect that *animas* (“souls”) is a gloss and interpretation of *genios* (“genii”). [Col. 1000B] On this subject Apuleius writes in *On the God of Socrates*: “Let the second designated class of daemons be the human soul, stripped of and released from the obligations of life after renouncing its body. I find that in the old Latin language this was commonly called a *Lemur*. Of these Lemures, therefore, the one that has been allotted the care of its descendants and possesses their house with a peaceful and tranquil divine power is called the household Lar. But one which, because of the evil deserts of its life, is punished by wandering upon the earth as though in exile, having no blessed dwelling place—an empty terror to good people but harmful to the wicked—is commonly called by most people a *Larva*.”

They called these “gods originating from souls.” Servius on *Aeneid* III, verse 168: “Labeo, in the books entitled *On the Gods Whose Origin Is from Souls*, says that there are certain rites by which human souls are transformed into gods, who are called *animales* (‘soul-derived’), because they are made from souls.” [Col. 1000C] HERALDUS.—Martianus Capella also agrees with Apuleius, *The Marriage of Philology*, book II, p. 65, Bern edition, adding: “Greek classification records the Manes as ἀγαθοὺς καὶ κακοὺς δαίμονας—‘good and evil daemons.’”

“And of those who have completed life” is due to Stewechius’s correction. The manuscript corruptly has *effunctorum*, from which Gelenius made *defunctorum* (“of the deceased”). P. Burmann II, on the *Latin Anthology*, book IV, epigram 394, vol. II, p. 285, prefers to delete “of the dead” as a gloss, since *functus* is very frequently used absolutely for *defunctus* (“dead”), for example in Prudentius, Hymn X, *Peristephanon*, verse 1081:

> Then, when the spirit has left him lifeless,  
> And the funeral procession bears him to the tomb;

and Claudian, Epigram XLVIII, 20:

> And you bring escaped souls back into lifeless bodies.

And you bid life return. With this I wholly agree. Canter considers both [Col. 1000D] words, *animas mortuorum* (“souls of the dead”), to be deleted. ORELL.]

### XLI

We may, if it seems appropriate, also say something briefly about the Lares, whom the common people suppose to be the gods of villages and roads, because the Greeks call streets *laurai* (λαῦραι). In different writings Nigidius identifies them now as guardians of roofs and houses; now as those Curetes who are said once to have concealed [Col. 0999A] the wailing of Jupiter with bronze instruments; now as the Samothracian Fingers, whom the Greeks indicate to be five [Note: [Col. 0999B] Fulvius wrongly reads *quosque*.] and call the Idaean Dactyls. Varro, similarly wavering, declares at one time that they are the Manes, and that Mania was therefore called the mother of the Lares; at another, that they are gods of the air and are called heroes; and again, following the opinions of the ancients, he says that the Lares are specters (*larvae*), as though they were certain guardian spirits—the departed souls of the dead.

[Note: [Col. 1000D]

### XLII.—Concerning whom you have not brought forth ambiguous and conflicting opinions, with a thousand variations of belief

The Leiden edition did not place *non* before *ambiguas*. But the commonly received text seems more consistent with Arnobius’s style. ORELL.

*We do not know personally who the Lares are.* That is, we do not know the persons, the true names, of the Lares, etc. Borrichius too, in *Cogitationes*, p. 191, would like another example of the adverb *personaliter* in this sense. Elsewhere this word is used by writers of medieval and late Latin, in curial style, to mean “in person,” “by oneself, not through another.” Aulus Gellius, Book XV, chapter 13: “*Personaliter* means by persons.” ORELL.

*That they nevertheless exist, the very consensus of the authorities confirming it.* Thus I have printed the text following Salmasius’s emendation. The others read: “That they nevertheless exist, the very consensus of the authorities confirms,” which could indeed be tolerated if the statement were direct discourse. But Salmasius’s reading is much more elegant. ORELL.

*And possess among the ranks of the heavenly beings a form peculiar to their kind.* [Col. 1001B] Ἐν τοῖς τάγμασι τῶν οὐρανίων, “among the orders of the heavenly beings.” Or he is alluding to a Greek idiom. HERALD.

*Not all gods can furnish all things.* I think the word *praestare* (“furnish”) could be absent. Virgil: “We cannot all do all things.” STEWECH. But Arnobius likes such redundancies. ORELL.

*You report that the dispositions and displeasure of the several gods are appeased.* *Animos* means “anger.” Thus below, Book VII: “Sacrifices are made to the gods above for this reason, that they may lay aside their wrath and anger”; and Apuleius speaks of “the anger of dogs,” *Metamorphoses* VIII, p. 554, Oudendorp’s edition. See C. Barth, *Adversaria*, Book XXXIII, chapter 22, p. 1543. Compare Savaro on Sidonius, [Col. 1001C] Poem VII, p. 82. ORELL.]

### XLII

It would be endless and immeasurable to pass through each individual class, and an easy matter to fill entire books by showing that there is no god acknowledged or believed in by you concerning whom you have not brought forth ambiguous and conflicting opinions, with a thousand variations of belief. But [Col. 0999B] for the sake of brevity and to avoid weariness, it is enough to have said what [Col. 1000A] has already been said. It is excessively laborious to heap [Note: [Col. 0999B] The manuscript reads *coadunare*, “bring together.”] many things into one, when from one example and then another it becomes manifest and evident that you waver and say nothing certain [Note: [Col. 0999B] The manuscript wrongly reads *certe*, “certainly.”] about the matters you assert [Note: [Col. 1000B] Thus the manuscript and Sabaeus; others read *scire*, “know.”]—unless perhaps you say that, although we do not personally know who the Lares, the Novensiles, or the Penates are, they nevertheless exist, the very consensus of the authorities confirming it, and possess among the ranks of the heavenly beings a form peculiar to their kind.

But how can it be known whether someone is a god, if it remains unknown and unascertained what he is? Or how can the very request for benefits be effectual if it has not been investigated and settled which god ought to be called upon in each consultation [Note: [Col. 1000B] The manuscript wrongly reads *consolationem*, “consolation.”]? For everyone who seeks to obtain a response from some divine power must [Col. 1000B] necessarily know to whom he is making supplication, whom he is imploring, and from whom [Col. 1001A] he is demanding assistance in human affairs and necessities—especially since you yourselves report both that not all gods can furnish all things and that the dispositions and displeasure of the several gods are appeased by dissimilar rites.

[Note: [Col. 1001C]

### XLIII.—For if this god desires a black hide and that one a white

White victims were customarily offered to the gods above, while black or dusky ones were offered to the gods below. The matter is very well known. See the scholiast on Horace, *Odes* III.8, and Servius on *Aeneid* VI.244. ORELL.

*Sacrifice must be made to this god with the head covered, to that one with it bare.* Those greeting the gods kept their heads covered, lest some hostile and ill-omened sight should present itself and disturb the omens—see Virgil, *Aeneid* III.405 ff.—with the exceptions, however, of Saturn and Hercules, to whom they performed rites with uncovered heads, as Festus, under “Saturn” (where see the commentators), Macrobius, *Saturnalia* III.6, and Servius on *Aeneid* I attest. HERALD and HELMENH.

*That god is consulted about marriages.* Although marriages had their own presiding deities, people nevertheless approached Apollo to learn his oracle whenever they intended to contract a marriage; or they consulted augurs, soothsayers, and the other vain followers of Apollo. Apuleius, *Milesian Tale* II: [Col. 1001D] “For even now at Corinth among us a certain visiting Chaldaean is throwing the whole city into confusion with his marvelous responses and, for payments of small coins, discloses the secrets of fate: what day will sanction a marriage union; what day will make the foundations of walls endure,” etc. Aristophanes also teaches that marriages were contracted only after birds had been consulted. For thus he says in *The Birds*:

> We are for you Ammon, Delphi, Dodona, Phoebus Apollo.  
> For you first go to the birds, and only then turn to every undertaking—  
> To commerce, to the acquisition of a livelihood, and to a man’s marriage.

Hence Marcus Tullius Cicero also says in *On Divination* I.46: “I myself heard Lucius Flaccus the flamen say that Caecilia, the wife of Metellus, when she wished to give her sister’s daughter in marriage, went out to a certain shrine in order to obtain an omen, as was customarily done according to the practice of the ancients.” HERALD.

*Be present, stand near, gods of the household.* Servius on *Aeneid* VIII: “Thus Tiberinus is invoked in prayers: ‘Stand near, Tiberinus, with your waters.’” Hence gods who are present and propitious. HERALD.—Compare B. Brisson, *De formulis*, Book I, pp. 70–71. ELMENH.

*I burn, I am scorched, I am tormented.* *Torreor* (“I am scorched”) comes from an emendation by Ob. Gifanius approved by Th. Canter and the other editors. The manuscript reads *terreor* (“I am terrified”). For *vexor* (“I am tormented”), Stewechius prefers *versor*, citing Janus Guilielmus, *Quaestiones Plautinae*, on the *Persa*, chapter 4, who discusses this verb at length. But nothing should be changed. Jerome similarly writes in the preface to Habakkuk: “If a sick man, burning with fevers, asks for cold water and says to the physician, ‘I am suffering violence, I burn, I am exhausted,’” a passage cited by Elmenhorst. *Versari*, moreover, as Guilielmus shows, is properly said of fish that [Col. 1002C] are turned about while being cooked. ORELL.

*Those Samothracian Fingers.* Here too Stewechius and the Leiden editor restored *digitos* (“fingers”) from the manuscript. See above, chapter 41. ORELL.

*So greatly does the matter require that the gods be known specifically.* Lucretius, whom our author greatly delights in, says *propritim*, which I too would prefer; but I think nothing should be changed rashly. TH. CANTER.—The passage of Lucretius occurs in Book II, verse 974:

> What then? The human race, of what specifically was it made?

Lambinus, however, when citing our passage, printed and defended in his notes *propriatim* or *proprietim*, that is, “properly” or “specifically.” Thus *propriatim deos scire* means to know which beings are properly gods. ORELL.

*Have their ears blocked.* This is the same as *obstructas*, “stopped up”; no other example of this meaning occurs to me. Should we not read *surdas*, “deaf”? ORELL.]

### XLIII

For if this god desires a black hide and that one a white; if sacrifice must be made to this god with the head covered, to that one with it bare; if that god is consulted about marriages, while this one supplies remedies for afflictions—it cannot be a matter of no consequence whether the one is a Novensilis or the other, since ignorance of the facts and confusion of the persons offend the gods and necessarily cause ritual guilt to be incurred.

Suppose, for example, that because of some affliction and in order to avert a danger I make supplication to some one of these divine powers, saying: “Be present, stand near, gods of the household—you, Apollo, and you, Neptune—and by the mercy of your divine power avert all these evils by which I burn, am scorched, and am tormented.” Will there be any hope [Col. 1001B] of obtaining assistance from them if Ceres, Pales, Fortuna, [Col. 1002A] Jovialis, or a Genius—not Neptune and Apollo—are the Penates? Or if I invoke as Lares the Curetes whom some of your authorities assert to be the Samothracian Fingers, how shall I be able to enjoy their assistance and favor when I have imposed on these gods names that are not their own, and on the others names belonging to strangers [Note: [Col. 1001B] Fulvius reads *nomina*, “names.”]?

So greatly does the matter require that the gods be known specifically, and that there be neither uncertainty nor doubt concerning the power and name of each one, that if they have been invoked with rites and appellations belonging to others, they both keep their ears blocked and hold us bound by ritual offenses that cannot be expiated.

[Note: [Col. 1002C]

### XLIV.—You ought to stand within the limits of a single proposition

Below, Book V, chapter 3: “The utterance is still incomplete and is not yet a full or completely delimited proposition.” And in the same book, chapter 37: “I again see this openly set forth in common propositions.” Gellius, *Attic Nights* XVI.8: “Marcus Varro, in the twenty-fourth book of *The Latin Language*, addressed to Cicero, defines it most clearly as follows: ‘A proposition is a statement in which nothing is lacking....’ For example: ‘Hannibal was a Carthaginian’; ‘Scipio destroyed Numantia’; ‘Milo was condemned for murder’; ‘Pleasure is neither good nor evil’; and in general, whatever is expressed as a full and complete verbal statement such that it must necessarily be either true or false is called an ἀξίωμα (*axiōma*, “proposition”) by the dialecticians, a *proloquium* by Marcus Varro, as I have said, and a *pronuntiatum* by Marcus Cicero (*Tusculan Disputations* I.7). Cicero nevertheless testified that he would use this word only ‘until,’ he says, ‘I find a better one.’” Compare C. Barth, *Adversaria* IV.13, p. 2610. Compare also his *Glossary* to Claudianus Mamertus, *On the State of the Soul*. ORELL.

*To detract from the credibility of the very matters that you construct.* Thus Lactantius, [Col. 1003A] *Epitome*, chapter 50: “For if he does not do so, he will detract from the credibility of his own precepts.” See there Bunemann, who illustrates the expression *fidem derogare* with numerous examples, p. 1290. For *struitis*, Meursius prefers *adstruitis*. ORELL.

*If Summanus.* Martianus Capella, *The Marriage of Philology* II, p. 65, Bern edition: “Pluto ... who is also called Summanus, as though ‘the highest of the Manes.’” ORELL.

*To remain fixed in an assured knowledge of the matter.* I have followed Meursius’s emendation. Others read: “To remain fixed assuredly....” Whether that can be said in Latin I very much doubt. One does indeed say that a person remains constantly or firmly fixed upon or attached to something, but not “assuredly.” ORELL.

[Col. 1004A] *No, rather, they are the Trebian gods.* Above, chapter 38: “Piso believes there are nine gods established among the Sabines at Trebia.” Nothing, therefore, should be changed. HERALD.—Th. Canter’s *Trebianis* (“for the Trebians”) is therefore wrong. ORELL.

*Or rather guardians of overthrown cities.* The Leiden editor added *vel* (“or”), though it is uncertain whether from the manuscript or by conjecture, merely to heighten the force of the discourse. This is, however, a transposition familiar to Arnobius, for: “or rather guardians of overthrown cities.” ORELL.

*And bring matters into this danger.* Others read *adducere*; the Leiden editor has *perducere*, which derived from the manuscript, according to Meursius in his Appendix. ORELL.]

### XLIV

Therefore, if it is clear to you that this multitude whom you enumerate as gods dwells and abides in the lofty palaces of heaven, you ought to stand within the limits of a single proposition and not, distracted among various and mutually contradictory opinions, detract from the credibility of the very matters that you construct. [Col. 1002B] If he is Janus, let him be Janus; if he is Liber, let him [Col. 1003A] be Liber; if Summanus, let him be Summanus. For this is what it means to have confidence, to hold fast, and to remain fixed in an assured knowledge of the matter—not to speak after the manner of the blind and wandering: “The Novensiles are the Muses”; “No, rather, they are the Trebian gods”; [Col. 1004A] “No, the number nine”; “Or rather, the guardians of overthrown cities”—and to bring matters of such importance into this danger: that while you remove some gods and substitute others, it may rightly be doubted of them all whether they exist anywhere at all.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 1003]

## TABLE OF CHAPTERS

[Col. 1003B] Arnobius continues the argument begun against the gods of the pagans and shows that Piety, Concord, Safety, and other divine powers of this kind cannot, either in jest or seriously, be said to possess divine power and be included in the register of the gods, since it is agreed that all these things reside in human actions and affections. Chapters 1–2. [Col. 1003C] No less perversely, because of certain supposed acts of beneficence, the pagans brought forth numerous gods—such as Luperca, Praestana, Panda or Pantica, Pellonia, and other troops of unknown divine powers. Chapters 3–4. The pagans further prattled that certain gods presided over the regions on the left and were hostile to those on the right. Chapter 5. The same pagans also quite foolishly imagined certain gods appointed over certain matters and no others; Arnobius lists some of them. Chapters 6–7. He proceeds to enumerate and ridicule other divine powers of this kind. Chapters 8–11.

Nor may anyone object that they are gods because, when summoned by soothsayers, they immediately come and return definite [Col. 1003D] answers. Arnobius refutes this objection. Chapters 11–13. But the author presses his case and makes clear that the pagans produce utterly absurd monstrosities among their gods: namely, three Jupiters, five Suns, the same number of Mercuries, Minervas, and Dionysuses, and so forth. Chapters 13–15. Yet all these gods of the same name cannot be genuine, or else which among them is the true god is utterly unknown. Arnobius confirms this by the example of Minerva. Chapters 15–17.

He then answers the pagans’ insistence by saying that it is unknown whether the theologians or others wrote in their books about the gods things known and ascertained, or things made up and fabricated according to their pleasure. Chapters 18–19. He demonstrates that no truth can be indicated in [Col. 1004B] books in which those same gods are everywhere indiscriminately said to have been subjected to the gravest insults. Chapters 19–22. Pursuing the same argument, he concludes that the public calamities of the human race must be attributed to the pagans themselves, who impiously worship these monstrous divine beings, and not to the Christians, who abhor them with the horror they deserve. [Col. 1004C] Chapters 22–24.

He recalls other shameful things attributed by the pagans to their gods. Chapters 24–25. Nor does he pass over the gods’ insane lusts and raging wantonness. Chapters 26–27. Yet all these stories are either false or true. If the former, the gods ought to have avenged such great and shameless slanders; if the latter, those same gods are proved to have been wretched, infamous, and utterly criminal human beings. Chapters 27–28. That gods of this sort were human beings is most manifestly established. Arnobius declares, however, that he has not undertaken to demonstrate this point—which would otherwise have been easy—but only that the gods are treated more insultingly by no one than by the pagans. Chapters 29–31. [Col. 1004D] He clearly demonstrates that these stories are not inventions of the poets. Chapters 32–34.

But the pagans’ injustice was all the greater because they punished with the utmost severity of the laws the authors of any defamatory saying, poem, or pamphlet, while they endured with the greatest patience the writing and public recital of such great disgraces concerning the gods. Chapters 34–35. Nor does their guilt end there: for they bestowed praises and rewards upon those who wrote such things, and even upon actors and mimes who represented them in the theaters. Therefore, if the gods are inflamed by anger, as the pagans supposed, they ought to have been angry not with the Christians but with the pagans themselves, who set the gods’ disgrace before the eyes of everyone. If, however, they are free from anger, they are said in vain to be angry with the Christians. Chapters 35–37.

[Col. 1005A] [Note: [Col. 1005A]

### I.—Piety

Lactantius, Book I, chapter 20. Ancient inscriptions collected by Gruter, p. 86. ELMENH.—The story is famous and unknown to few: a woman, whether plebeian or [Col. 1005B] freeborn, nourished with her own milk either her mother—as Valerius Maximus, Book II, chapter 5, §7, relates—or, as others report, her father, who had been confined in prison, lest the prisoner perish from starvation. Pliny, *Natural History* II.36, and after him Solinus, chapter 1, relates that in memory of this deed a temple of Piety was established in that same prison, during the consulship of Gaius Quinctius and Marcus Acilius, where the Theater of Marcellus stood. Nor are there lacking those who believe that it was the very temple which, as Livy says, Marcus Acilius Glabrio dedicated in the vegetable market. NOURR., p. 483.

*Concord.* Augustine mentions the goddess Concord in *The City of God* III.25; Varro, *The Latin Language* IV; Martianus Capella, *The Marriage of Philology* II; *Ancient Inscriptions*, p. 100; Pliny, *Natural History* II.7. ELMENH.—According to Livy, Book IX, chapter 46, a shrine of Concord was consecrated by Gaius Flavius in the precinct of Vulcan; and, Book XXII, chapter 33, there was another, which the two commissioners appointed for that purpose established on the citadel. Cicero likewise attests, in *On the Nature of the Gods* II, that while Cotta was consul, [Col. 1005C] the temple of Concord was struck by lightning; mention of it is also made in Cassius Dio, Book LXIV, and in the Roman *Fasti*. Hence Ovid sang near the end of *Fasti* IV:

> You too, Concord, Livia dedicates in a magnificent shrine—  
> Livia, whom she rendered dear to her husband.

NOURR., p. 483.

*Safety.* See Augustine, *The City of God* III.25; Varro, *The Latin Language* IV, p. 22, Bipontine edition; an ancient inscription, p. 100, in Gruter: “DEDICATED TO PERPETUAL SAFETY.” ELMENH.

*Honor.* Augustine, *The City of God* IV.21: “To the god Honorinus, so that they might be honored.” Lactantius, Book I, chapter 20; *Book of Inscriptions*, p. 100; Pliny, *Natural History* II.7; Plutarch, *The Fortune of the Romans*, p. 318; Valerius Maximus, Book I, chapter 1. ELMENH.

*Virtue.* Augustine, *The City of God* IV.22: “They also made Virtue a goddess.” Varro, *The Latin Language* IV, p. 22, Bipontine edition; Valerius Maximus, Book I, chapter 1; [Col. 1005D] Lactantius, Book I, chapter 20; *Ancient Inscriptions*, p. 102; Plautus, prologue to the *Amphitryon*. ELMENH.

*Happiness.* Augustine, *The City of God* IV.18 and 33; *Ancient Inscriptions*, p. 101. ELMENH.—I have taken care to print all these names with capital initials. For Arnobius, as Meursius rightly observes, sets them down not as the names of virtues but as the names of gods and goddesses. ORELL.

*And the other names of this kind.* The reading is sound. For he calls them empty names without any substance, as he sufficiently shows shortly afterward in these words: “For if, thinking these to be empty words and names without any substance....” Meursius and those who wish to rewrite *nomina* (“names”) as *numina* (“divine powers”) are therefore mistaken. HERALD.

*Or, as is customary, merely for form’s sake, because*, etc. Thus the manuscript, a reading defended by Th. Canter. Something is said to be done *dicis causa* when it is done negligently and carelessly, and solely with the intention of seeming to have discharged one’s duty—not accurately, but perfunctorily, insofar as that is sufficient to avoid [Col. 1006A] reproach. Hence Varro, *The Latin Language* VI, near the end: “And certain things were done merely for form’s sake, neither done nor spoken in the same way.” So Canter; compare what we noted above on Book III, chapter 16. I wholly agree with Canter and do not see why *dicis causa* cannot stand here. The sense is: “Although you do not believe these names to be genuine divine powers, you have nevertheless included them among the heavenly beings merely for form’s sake—that is, by way of honor—because you both value the good things signified by them and wish those things to befall you.”

Sabaeus and Gelenius printed: “or, as it is customary to say, for the reason that,” etc., which is plainly corrupt. The Leiden editor: “or, as it is customary to say, for the reason from that.” Herald: “or, as it is customary to say, because,” etc., deleting *causa* as a gloss and interpretation of the words “because,” etc. To me, however, the words “as it is customary to say” seem to prepare for some proverbial expression in what follows. I therefore conjecture that the text should be written: “Or, as it is customary to say, merely for form’s sake, because,” etc. I think *dici* was swallowed up in the manuscript by the following words *dicis causa*. But let more learned persons judge. ORELL.

*Because we desire and wish these good things to befall us, you have included them in the register of the heavenly beings.* [Col. 1006C] The ancients, however, gave several reasons for consecrating these names, including the one proposed by the blessed Augustine in the words of the pagans in *The City of God* IV: “Since they knew that such things were granted to no one unless some god bestowed them, and could not discover the names of those gods, they called the gods by the names of the things they felt were given by them,” etc. They saw, moreover, that the human heart was sometimes stirred by some blind and unusual power, and therefore believed those impulses to be divine. Marcus Tullius Cicero touches on this reasoning in *On the Nature of the Gods* II: “The thing itself in which some greater power inheres is then named in such a way that the power itself is called a god, as Faith, Mind,” etc. The Greeks call such things δαίμονες and θεοί, “divine spirits” and “gods.” Thus Euripides calls ambition (φιλοτιμία) “the worst of divine spirits” and caution (εὐλάβεια) “the most useful of gods,” and says similar things. HERALD.

*Or of your divine powers.* With Meursius I read *ac vestrorum numinum*, “and of your divine powers.” ORELL.

*You nevertheless consecrate them with divine rites.* Thus the Leiden edition. Others read: “you nevertheless consecrate them in divine regions,” that is, in sanctified abodes. I remain uncertain which reading should be preferred. ORELL.

*With which you equate and associate them.* Fulvius Ursinus prefers: “to which you adapt and join them.” ORELL.

*But if, from the more settled judgment of your mind, you have thought that these too are gods, and have burdened them with temples and sacred couches*, etc. Meursius wrongly transposes the words thus: “If, having thought these to be gods, you have burdened them also with temples and sacred couches,” etc. ORELL.

*You have burdened.* Thus the manuscript, and Stewechius very rightly defends this reading against Gelenius and the other editors who rashly altered it to “you have honored.” “For we are said to be burdened,” says Johannes Vorstius in *De Latinitate selecta*, p. 129, M. Gesner’s edition, “not only with things that are heavy and troublesome, but also with things that are pleasing and agreeable, if there is a certain multitude of them.” Thus Justin, *Histories* V.5, aptly says with reference to our passage: “They therefore burden him, Alcibiades, with every honor, not only human but also divine.” Acidalius thinks “they honor” should be read there. Wrongly. Tacitus, *Histories* I.25: “After he recognized in their varied conversation those who were cunning and bold, he burdened them with payments and promises, money being given to test the inclinations of a larger number”; and Book IV, chapter 13: [Col. 1007B] “to burden with immoderate praises.” Phaedrus, Book V, Fable 5, line 20: “They burden him with many praises.” See there Burmann, pp. 249 ff. Add Drakenborch on Silius, Book III, verse 15, and Cortius on Sallust, *Jugurtha* 12, p. 458. Petronius similarly says in his poem on the Civil War, verse 156:

> ... And you, Saturnian land,  
> Once rejoicing in my arms of war and burdened with triumphs.

Others wrongly read “adorned” or “to be adorned.” ORELL.

*Victory.* See Varro, *The Latin Language* IV; Augustine, *The City of God* IV.14, 15, 17, and 21; the prologue to Plautus’s *Amphitryon*; *Ancient Inscriptions*, p. 100: “DEDICATED TO THE GODDESS VICTORY.” ELMENH. Postumius, if Livy is to be believed, Book X, chapter 33, dedicated the Temple of Victory, which, as curule aedile, he had commissioned with money from fines. In another book, XXXV.9, Livy records further shrines to twofold Victory in these words: “Marcus Porcius Cato dedicated a small shrine of Maiden Victory near the Temple of Victory, two years after he had vowed it.” Pausanias, Book I, p. 20, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* I, p. 26, also speak of a sanctuary of Victory.
