We have likewise noted elsewhere that when Symmachus asked the emperor Valentinian to restore the altar of Victory in the senate house, Ambrose prevented it. NOURR., p. 484.

*Peace.* An ancient inscription, p. 239:

> SACRED TO THE ETERNAL PEACE OF THE HOUSE OF THE EMPEROR VESPASIAN CAESAR AUGUSTUS AND HIS CHILDREN. TRIB. SUC. THE YOUNGER.

Juvenal, *Satires* I.115:

> As Peace and Faith, Victory and Virtue are worshiped.

ELMENH.

*Equity.* An ancient inscription, p. 76:

> TO PRIMIGENIAN FORTUNE. THE IMAGE OF EQUITY. NIGRINA AUXESIS, WITH FELIX, FREEDMAN OF AUGUSTUS, AND HER FAMILY, D. D. D. D.

ELMENH.

[Col. 1007D] By the name Equity, Arnobius undoubtedly means Justice, of whom Ovid sang in *Letters from Pontus* III.6.23 ff.:

> No god is more moderate than our prince;  
> With Justice he tempers his power.  
> Recently Caesar placed her in a temple made of marble;  
> Long ago he had placed her in the shrine of his own mind.

Some nevertheless think that nothing concerning that temple is found in trustworthy authors, and that the poet therefore alluded to the Temple of Mars the Avenger, since vengeance, of which Ovid speaks, is a certain part of Justice. NOURR., p. 484.]

### I

I should like to ask you—and before all others the Romans themselves, the lords and rulers of the world—whether [Note: [Col. 1005A] The manuscript wrongly reads *verumne*.] you think that Piety, Concord, Safety, Honor, Virtue, Happiness, and the other names of this kind, for which we see that you have constructed altars together with magnificent sanctuaries, possess divine power and dwell in the regions of heaven; or whether, as is customary, merely for form’s sake, because we desire and wish these good things to befall us, [Col. 1006A] you have included them in the register of the heavenly beings.

For if, thinking them to be empty words and names without any substance, you nevertheless consecrate them with divine rites, you will have to consider whether this is a childish game or whether it aims at mocking your divine powers, with which you equate and associate the fabrications of empty words. But if, from the more settled judgment of your mind, you have thought that these too are gods and have burdened them with temples and sacred couches, we ask you to instruct our ignorance: by what reasoning and by what means can Victory, Peace, Equity, and the other things mentioned above be understood to be gods and to belong to the council of the heavenly beings?

[Note: [Col. 1007D]

### II.—Unless perhaps you abolish and wrest away from us our common faculty of perception

The man whom Arnobius chiefly imitates, Lucretius, attributed the greatest importance to this faculty, since he was a follower of Epicurus, who regarded the knowledge furnished by the senses as the most certain and secure of all. Lucretius therefore says in Book I, lines 423 ff.:

[Col. 1008A]

> For the common faculty of perception makes clear that body exists  
> By itself; unless our primary trust in this faculty remains firmly grounded,  
> There will be no standard to which we may refer matters hidden from sight

[Col. 1008B]

> And thereby establish anything through the reasoning of the mind.

HERALD.

*The virtue of a man.* Stewechius prefers “the virtue of a virtuous man.” Wrongly. For no other virtue is meant here than physical courage, which Varro calls manliness and the strength of a man, and for which a temple was established at Rome, as the contrast with “cowardice of heart” in the words that follow shows. See Herald’s following note. ORELL.

*The honor of an honored person.* Varro, *The Latin Language* IV: “*Honos* comes from honoring what is honorable; accordingly, someone is called *honestus* because he has been honored.” ELMENH.

*Cowardice of heart.* He contrasts cowardice of heart with virtue, which he has said is named from *vir* (“man”) and is proper to a man. By these words he revealed the primary meaning of *virtus* and employed the term specifically (εἰδικῶς), although not courage alone but the other virtues as well were consecrated. The ancients certainly called strength and steadfastness of spirit in warfare *virtus*, as Plutarch too observes in his *Coriolanus*. Hence Lucan, Book VI, line 147:

> Headlong toward every crime, and one who did not know, amid civil arms,  
> How great a crime courage could be.

By *virtus*, Lucan meant courage, ἀνδρεία. The Romans certainly worshiped Virtue as the goddess specifically of this quality, whom they otherwise called Bellona. Lactantius, Book I, chapter 21: “Among rites of this kind, those of Virtue, whom they also call Bellona, must be judged no less insane ... in which the priests sacrifice not another’s blood but their own.” HERALD. Compare the authors cited by Bunemann on Lactantius, Book I, p. 140. ORELL.

*For as these things occur and are situated in human actions and accidental affections.* Thus the text should be read instead of: “For as these things may occur, which are situated in human actions, accidental affections,” etc. That is: just as these are accidental qualities that befall human beings and are situated or located either in human actions—such as inequity and cowardice of heart—or in accidental affections and events that occur by chance, such as unhappiness, illness, and the like; so the more favorable qualities—Equity, Happiness, and so forth—befall a human being and, after being received by him, acquire these names properly belonging to them. HERALD.—Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “which are situated in the accidental actions of human beings,” deleting *affectibus*. Stewechius reads: “which are situated in human actions, accidental effects,” etc. The Leiden editor: “in actions and accidental effects.” I do not approve. For *affectus* means a passion or disease in Celsus, while the adjective *affectus, -a, -um* means sick or afflicted. Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* IV, p. 314, Oudendorp’s edition: “The entire community also lamented the sorrowful fate of the afflicted house.” Ovid, *Amores* II, Elegy 2, speaks of an “afflicted beloved,” that is, one who is sick. The omission of the conjunction also agrees with Arnobius’s style, as has already been observed several times above. ORELL.

[Col. 1009B] *This formation of names has been conceived.* Meursius prefers “of divine powers.” ORELL.]

### II

For unless perhaps you abolish and wrest away from us our common faculty of perception, we perceive and discern that none of these things possesses divine power or is contained within some form peculiar to its own kind. Rather, virtue belongs to the man, safety to the safe person, honor to the honored, victory to the victor, [Col. 1008A] concord to the concordant, piety to the pious, and memory to the mindful; happiness, moreover, belongs to one who lives happily and without any misfortunes.

That this is most truly said by you can readily be learned from the contrary terms opposed to them [Note: [Col. 1007A] Fulvius reads “and from oppositions.”]: unhappiness, discord, forgetfulness, inequity [Note: [Col. 1008A] Sabaeus wrongly reads *inquietate*, “disquiet.”], impiety, cowardice of heart, and a less fortunate condition of the body. For just as these things occur and are situated in human actions and accidental affections, so that which is opposed to them receives its name from the more favorable qualities and must inhere in other persons [Col. 1009A]; and from those persons, once they have been qualified in this manner, this formation of names has been conceived.

[Note: [Col. 1009B]

### III.—For as to your introducing to us other troops of unknown gods

Gelenius was the first to emend the text thus; the other editors followed him, and Herald too approved it in his second *Critical Observations*. The first Roman edition reads “troops of designated gods.” ORELL.

*The goddess Luperca.* Lactantius, Book I, chapter 20: “Romulus’s nurse, the she-wolf, was accorded divine honors”; Ovid, *Fasti* II; *Book of Inscriptions*, p. 105, inscription XI; Plutarch, *Romulus*; Juvenal, *Satires* XI. ELMENH.—Onzelius, on Minucius Felix, chapter 25, pp. 257–58, Gronovius’s edition, shows that the goddess Luperca was the same as Acca Larentia. Compare Livy, *History* I.4. ORELL.

*From the outcome of events, therefore*, etc. That is, ἐκ συμβεβηκότος τοῦτο συνέβη, “this occurred by accident.” Thus above, Book I, chapter 14, he spoke of “the outcome of the grain supply,” and in Book II used *provenire*: “Nor, without his command, can anything in the world either occur or pass away.” HERALD.—*Proventus* means “success,” or simply “outcome,” in the best writers. Thus Caesar, *The Gallic War* VII.80: “The minds of all the soldiers intently awaited the outcome of the battle”; and chapter 29: “They err if they expect every outcome of affairs in war to be favorable.” See there Davies and Morus in the index. Compare Bentley on Manilius, Book I, line 410; Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* X, p. 728; Bunemann on Lactantius, *Institutes* VI.4 §9, p. 715. ORELL.

*She herself began to exist.* Meursius and Herald restored this entirely correct reading from the manuscript. Previously the text read: “She herself began to be this.” ORELL.

*And derived the signification of that very name.* The glosses: “*Significantia*: σημασία, ‘signification.’” Fabius Victorinus, in the preface to Book I of Cicero’s *On Invention*: “An art is something that does not possess a full signification of itself.... This word ‘kind’ has a threefold signification.” Lactantius, *Institutes* IV.26: “For none of the things he suffered were empty, but they possessed a figure and great signification”; and in the same chapter, §17: “Just as his works also possessed the signification of a greater power.” HERALD and ELMENH.—Compare Bunemann on Lactantius, Book I, p. 535, and Mercier on Nonius Marcellus, p. 82. ORELL.

*Praestana.* I have sought in vain for mention of this goddess in other authors. ORELL.

*The goddess Panda.* The glosses: “Panda, εἰρήνης θεά, ‘goddess of peace.’” ELMENH.—Varro mentions this goddess in a fragment of the *Shadow-Fight* (Σκιομαχία), cited by Aulus Gellius, Book XIII, chapter 21:

> You, Anna Perenna, Panda, and broad Pales,  
> The Neriones, Minerva, Fortune, and Ceres.

The same Varro, *On the Life of the Roman People* I, in Nonius, under *pandere*: “Aelius thinks that this goddess, Panda, is Ceres; but because bread was given to anyone who fled for refuge into the asylum, her name was formed from the giving of bread.” See Ausonius Popma on Varro, Book I, vol. II, pp. 307 and 381, Bipontine edition; and G. J. Vossius, *On Idolatry* II.36, p. 186. ORELL.—Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book II, p. 105, records that the maiden who was said to have opened the way for Titus Tatius to capture the Capitoline hill was honored with burial where she had fallen, and that funeral offerings were rendered to her annually by the Romans. Is it not therefore probable that for this reason she was enrolled among the goddesses under the name Panda [Col. 1010C] or Pantica? NOURR., p. 417.

*Or Pantica. Before these events, therefore, they had never been divine powers.* Thus the Leiden editor. The first edition reads, most corruptly: “or Pantica revealed. And therefore these,” etc. Gelenius deletes “revealed.” Th. Canter punctuates: “or Pantica. These things too having been revealed, therefore....” Stewechius: “or Pantica, and these therefore....” Herald, however, deletes *et* (“and”) as superfluous. The manuscript reads: “made by you, and these therefore,” etc., which is plainly a corruption of “before these events.” ORELL.

*Nor if.* This should be read with Gelenius in place of *neque* (“and not”), which was formerly printed. *Neque* would introduce an apodosis wholly out of place here. ORELL.

*Designation.* Above, Book I, chapter 3: “Our nation deserved to be endowed with the good fortune of this designation.” ORELL.]

### III

For as to your bringing forward against us other troops of unknown gods, we cannot determine whether you do this seriously and in reliance upon a fact ascertained to be true, or whether, playing with empty fictions, you indulge in the wanton extravagance of your imaginations. Because a she-wolf, though not gentle, spared the abandoned infants, she was called the goddess Luperca, Varro says. Was this goddess, then, revealed by the outcome of events, and not by the power of her nature? And only after the savage beast restrained its ferocious bites did she herself begin to exist and acquire the meaning expressed by her name? Or, if she had long been a goddess before Romulus and his brother were born, disclose what name and designation she then possessed.

Praestana, as you relate, was so called because Quirinus surpassed the strength of everyone in casting the javelin [Col. 1009B]; and because permission was given to open and disclose a way for Titus Tatius [Col. 1010A] to capture [Note: [Col. 1009B] “might capture,” Fulvius] the Capitoline Hill, a goddess was called Panda, or Pantica. Before these deeds were performed, then, these were never divine beings; and if Romulus had not secured the Palatine by the flight of his missile, and if the Sabine king had not been able [Note: [Col. 1009B] “had gained possession of,” or “had begun,” Fulvius] to take the Tarpeian Rock, there would have been no Pantica and no Praestana? And if you say that these goddesses existed before the causes of their surnames, indicate—as was asked in the preceding chapter—what designation they then possessed.

> **Note: [Col. 1010C]**
>
> **IV.—Pellonia, the powerful goddess who drives away enemies.** Augustine, *On the City of God*, IV.21: “For the goddess Fessonia had to be invoked on account of the weary, and the goddess Pellonia on account of enemies who had to be driven away.” ELMENH.—Compare Vossius, *On Idolatry*, VII.18, p. 763. ORELL.
>
> **[Col. 1010D] “If it is not troublesome.”** I think that the manuscript reading should be redeemed even at the price of gold in preference to the commonly printed one: *si ne molestum est*. The words *si ne*, written separately, are no less correct than Titinnius’ and Plautus’ *nevis, nevult* for *non vis, non vult* (“you do not wish,” “he does not wish”). Festus has *nepurus* for *non purus* (“not pure”). Similarly, the very learned Janus Mellerus Palmerius, in his *Spicilegia*, p. 39, correctly interpreted Catullus’ *ne funera* from Plautus. Elsewhere, for the benefit of the young, I have shown that Cicero, Plautus, Terence, and Caesar used *si non* for *nisi*. STEWECH.
>
> **“Or to whose favor will she yield?”** That is: to whom will she grant her favor and goodwill? For this phrase should not be explained otherwise. We ought not to take *concedere* in the sense of *cedere* (“withdraw” or “yield”), since Pellonia is under discussion here, not Cedonia—to make a play upon the words. I therefore once thought that the text should read: “Or into whose battle line will she advance?” Nor have I yet regretted that conjecture. HERALD.—These are mere subtleties. Pellonia does indeed yield—that is, give way—in favor of those whom she favors and whose enemies she repels. ORELL.
>
> **[Col. 1011C] “But if she should in any case do so.”** I have printed this with the Leiden editor. The common reading is *utrimque* (“on both sides”), which is altogether idle and superfluous, since precisely the same thing is said both in the immediately preceding and in the following words. ORELL.
>
> **[Col. 1011C] “Which was formed from the repulsion exercised by one side.”** Thus the Leiden editor, very correctly. The others print the single word *impulsione* (“assault”), which is wrong. For Pellonia is not the goddess of enemies who are to be impelled—that is, attacked—but of those who are to be driven away, that is, put to flight. Fulvius Ursinus: *Ex impulsione*. It would have been better to say *e pulsione*. But it has already been observed above, in the notes on Books I and II, that Arnobius very frequently interchanges these prepositions. ORELL.
>
> **“At the Caudine Forks.”** Augustine, *On the City of God*, III.17: “At the Caudine Forks both consuls, besieged by the Samnites together with their army, were compelled to make a shameful treaty with them: six hundred Roman knights were given as hostages, while the rest, having lost their arms, been stripped of their other possessions, and deprived of their coverings, were sent beneath the enemy’s yoke wearing only one garment apiece” [Col. 1011D]. ELMENH.—Livy relates the story at length from the beginning of Book IX. ORELL.
>
> **“At Lake Trasumenus.”** Thus the manuscript. Others: “Trasimene.” Valerius Maximus, I.7: “At Lake Trasimene fifteen thousand Romans were slain, six thousand captured, and ten thousand put to flight.” ELMENH.
>
> **“The fields of Diomedes.”** By the River Aufidus, where Cannae stood, a village made famous by the Roman disaster. Hence the prophetic Marcius in Livy, XXV.12:
>
> > Roman, son of Troy, flee the River Canna,  
> > lest foreigners compel you to join battle  
> > on the field of Diomedes.
>
> Compare Festus under this word, and Dacier there. ORELL.

### IV

Pellonia is the powerful goddess who drives away enemies. Tell us, if it is not troublesome, whose enemies she drives away [Note: [Col. 1010B] “whose, then?” Sabinus]. Two sides come into conflict and decide the issue between themselves at close quarters by the clash of arms: this side is hostile to that one, and that one hostile to this. Whom, then, will Pellonia drive away when the fighting takes place on both sides? Or to whose favor will she yield [Col. 1010B], when by virtue of her name she is bound to furnish both sides with her power and service [Col. 1011A]? But if she should in any case do so—that is, if she grants favor and support to both sides—she will lose the force of her name, which was formed from the repulsion exercised by one side.

Unless, perhaps, you say: “This goddess belongs to the Romans alone, and, siding only with the Quirites, she is always at hand with gracious assistance.” Because we favor the name of Rome, we certainly wish this to be so; but the matter raises no small question. For why should the Romans possess gods peculiar to themselves, who do not belong to other nations? And how can they [Note: [Col. 1011B] “could they,” Sabinus] be gods unless they display the impartiality of their divine power to every nation everywhere? And where, I ask, was this Pellonia in former times, when the honor of the state was made to pass beneath the yoke at the Caudine Forks; when torrents of blood ran at Lake Trasumenus; when [Col. 1011B] the fields of Diomedes were heaped with Roman corpses; when a thousand other wounds of war were received in countless disasters? Was she sleeping, snoring, or—as worthless persons are accustomed to do—had she fled for refuge [Note: [Col. 1011B] “taken refuge,” others] into the enemy’s camp?

> **Note: [Col. 1011D]**
>
> **V.—“Male gods and female gods of the left.”** This excellent reading of the manuscript must not be altered. Here *dii* (“gods”) includes both gods and goddesses through a very common zeugma of gender: when the sex of several persons is indeterminate, the masculine gender is generally employed as the more dignified. See Sanctius, *Minerva*, IV.10, p. 718, Perizonius’ edition. Stewechius is therefore wrong: “Male gods of the left, female gods of the left.” The Leiden edition reads: *Dii laevia laeva*, what that may mean I confess myself as ignorant as the most ignorant, and I think it a printer’s error; the very learned Salmasius probably wrote: *Dii laevi a laeva* (“gods of the left, from the left”—understand “hand”). ORELL.—Perhaps the simple reading should be: “Gods of the left.” For if the substantive “gods” includes both sexes, why should the adjective not do so as well? OCHSNER.
>
> **“By what possible reasoning this is said.”** A phrase worthy of attracting an attentive reader. The pronoun *istud* is elegantly redundant. So shortly afterward: “Yet these very regions that we call left, and the others right, possess in relation to us nothing permanent.” It is a Hellenism. Luke, Acts 3:13: “The God of our fathers glorified his servant Jesus, whom you delivered up and denied” (*Ὁ Θεὸς τῶν πατέρων ἡμῶν ἐδόξασε τὸν παῖδα αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦν, ὃν ὑμεῖς μὲν παρεδώκατε καὶ ἠρνήσασθε αὐτόν*). HERALD.
>
> **“For, first of all, the world in itself has neither right nor left,” etc.** See Hadrianus Junius, who discusses this subject at length, *Observations*, III.3, in J. Gruter’s *Lampas Critica*, vol. IV, p. 384. ELMENH.
>
> **“Neither front nor rear regions.”** Varro, *On the Latin Language*, VI, p. 81, Bipontine edition: “The sky where we observe the omens is called a *templum*. Thus: ‘The great temple of high-thundering Jupiter trembled.’ [Col. 1012D] That is—as Naevius says in the *Hemisphere*—‘where the earth stands enclosed by the blue.’ That temple has four parts: the left from the east, the right from the west, the front toward the south, and the rear toward the north.” Festus differs slightly: “A rear door is said to be in the back part of a house. Moreover, the ancients also called a neighbor living at the rear of a house by this name. In short, the things before us are called ‘front,’ and those behind us ‘rear’; and we speak of the front right and the rear left. Likewise, that part of the sky illuminated by the sun toward the south is called the front, while that toward the north is called the rear; these are in turn divided into two parts, east and west.” See the interpreters there, and especially J. F. Gronovius, who discusses this word at length in *Readings in Plautus*, p. 332. ORELL.
>
> **“The pivot of cold.”** That is, the Arctic Pole. Statius, *Thebaid*, VII.38:
>
> > …gliding down from the pivot of the northern gate.
>
> ORELL.
>
> **“The south wind and the South pass under the designation ‘left.’”** Thus, from the manuscript, where *Meridus transit* is written, Stewechius and Heraldus restored the passage. The others: “The south wind and the South will draw the designation ‘left.’” Meursius: “will draw,” in the plural. ORELL.
>
> **“That neither right nor left exists by nature.”** Stewechius restored this from the manuscript. I am surprised that subsequent editors neglected it and omitted the words “neither right.” ORELL.
>
> **“But of position and time.”** I write: “and by reason of time.” For something of this kind is missing; or the ablative should be used: “by position and time.” MEURSIUS, p. 121.
>
> **“Which they have declared to be favorable and always accompanied by prosperous omens” [Col. 1013C].** Mark the expression: for *prospera omnia* means all good and favorable omens, in the most idiomatic usage. The Glosses of Philoxenus: “Favorable, *αἴσιον* (‘auspicious’). Favorably, *εὐτυχῶς, κατὰ προαίρεσιν, αἰσίως, εὐμενῶς, κατὰ γνώμην* (‘successfully, according to one’s wish, auspiciously, propitiously, according to one’s intention’).” Pliny calls “favorable names” those that Cicero calls “good names”: “Why,” he says, “in public purifications do we also choose favorable names for those leading the victims?” Festus: “The ancients employed certain favorable names—that is, names inflected so as to counteract the evil eye.” Hence “a favorable day” and “a good day.” Ovid, *Fasti*, I.71:
>
> > A favorable light arises: grant favor with tongues and hearts!  
> > Good words must now be spoken on a good day.
>
> For *prosperum* is that which suggests and holds forth good hope. HERALD.—Others: “always with all prosperous things.” ORELL.

### V

The male and female gods of the left preside only over regions on the left and are enemies of those on the right. By what possible reasoning this is said, or with what conception in mind, we ourselves cannot comprehend; nor do we trust that you can bring it into any light of common understanding [Col. 1012A].

For, first of all, the world in itself has neither right nor left, neither upper nor lower regions, neither front nor rear. For whatever is spherical and enclosed on every side by the convexity of a solid globe has no beginning and no end; and where there is neither end nor beginning, there can be no portion bearing either of those names. Accordingly, when we say [Note: [Col. 1012B] “shall say,” Sabinus], “This region is right and that one left,” we do not speak in relation to the form of the world, which is everywhere wholly like itself, but refer the terms to our own position and location. For we are so formed that some things are said to be on our right and others on our left. Yet these very regions that we call left, and the others right [Col. 1012B], possess in relation to us nothing permanent or fixed; rather, according as chance and the circumstances of the moment place us, they take their configurations from our sides.

If I face the rising sun, the pivot of cold and the North lie to my left; but if I turn my face toward the North, the sunset, which will be situated behind the sun, will be on my left. Again, if I direct my eyes toward the western quarter, the south wind and the South pass under the designation “left” [Col. 1013A]; but if the necessary conditions of the moment turn me toward the South, then, through the changed orientation of my body, the East comes to be called left. From this it can very readily be recognized that neither right nor left exists by nature, but only by position and time, and according to the way in which the situation of our body has been placed in relation to surrounding things.

Since this is so, by what reasoning or in what manner can there be gods of the left-hand regions, when it is established that those same regions become now right and now left? Or what wrong have the regions on the right done to the immortal gods, that they should live without any guardians, although they have been declared favorable and always accompanied by prosperous omens?

> **Note: [Col. 1013C]**
>
> **VI.—Lateranus.** This god is mentioned nowhere else. ORELL.
>
> **“And called by this name.”** Thus Salmasius. The manuscript has “and added”; Gelenius, “and enlarged”; Meursius in the Appendix, “and added”; Scriverius, “and enrolled.” For no other name is given for that god to which the name Lateranus might have been added. Others read “and endowed,” which pleases me more. ORELL.
>
> **“What, then, if the hearths were made of baked clay,” etc.** Furnaces were often built from unbaked bricks, as Pliny also shows, and sometimes from tiles; Arnobius therefore does not raise this objection rashly. For the tube surrounding *ἡ ὀπή*, that is, the *κάπνη*—the opening through which smoke passed and was exhaled—was sometimes made of baked clay; hence the Greeks called it *ὀπαία κεραμίς*, “a vent-tile.” HERALD. The Roman edition read “if that”; from this Gelenius arbitrarily refashioned “if of clay.” Stewechius and Heraldus restored “baked clay” from the manuscript. ORELL.
>
> **“Has not been constructed from earthen molds.”** In the proper sense; hence “formwork walls,” which Pliny describes. HERALD.
>
> **“And what, I ask, is he to do?”** Stewechius prefers, “What, then, is he to do?” But nothing should be changed. *Et* is adversative, as frequently in our author. ORELL.
>
> **“Kitchens.”** Papias: “*Coquina*: a kitchen.” ELMENH.
>
> **[Col. 1014B] “He imparts soundness to earthen vessels, lest, overcome by the violence of the flames, they burst apart.”** The same function was also attributed to Vulcan, according to Varro, *Fragments*, p. 265, Bipontine edition: “He prays three times to Vulcan that the new jars of the pots may not burst.” See Ausonius Popma there, p. 325. ORELL.
>
> **“He takes care that the flavors of unspoiled ingredients reach the palate with their proper delights.”** Stewechius conjectures, “with the greatest delights.” Nicolaas Heinsius, Letter 257 to J. G. Graevius, in Burmann’s *Sylloge*, vol. IV, p. 329, prefers: “with refined delights.” The manuscript corruptly has “to palates with delights.” But the words “of unspoiled ingredients” lead me to prefer the received text [Col. 1014C]. ORELL.
>
> **“He performs and tests the function of a preliminary taster.”** Yet this is properly the cook’s function. Elsewhere the preliminary tasters, *προγεῦσται*, are those who taste food after it has been served, a custom later transferred from the Persian court elsewhere. Hesychius: “*ἐδέατρος* … a king’s preliminary taster, the supervisor of the meal” (*προγεύστης βασιλέως, ἐπιμελητὴς δείπνου*). HERALD.—Meursius recasts the whole passage more elegantly, though less in accordance with Arnobius’ habit of joining words of this kind even when they fit less aptly: “and he tests whether the dishes have been properly seasoned and performs the function of a preliminary taster.” ORELL.

### VI

Lateranus, as you say, is the god and genius of hearths, and is called by this name because that kind of furnace is built by human beings from unbaked bricks [Col. 1013B]. What, then, if hearths have been made of baked clay or any other material whatever—will they have no guardian spirits? And will this Lateranus, whoever he is, withdraw from his protective duty because the possession within his kingdom has not been constructed from earthen molds [Col. 1014A]?

And what, I ask, is this god to do, now that he has obtained the guardianship of hearths? Does he run through the kitchens of humankind, inspecting and investigating from what kinds of wood the heat is kindled in his little hearths? Does he impart soundness to earthen vessels, lest, overcome by the violence of the flames, they burst apart? Does he take care that the flavors of unspoiled ingredients reach the palate with their proper delights, and does he perform and test the function of a preliminary taster to determine whether the dishes have been properly seasoned?

Is it, then, not shameful—indeed, to speak more truly, not insulting and impious—to introduce certain imaginary gods solely for this purpose: beings whom you do not honor with worthy rites, but appoint over shameful things and an infamous activity?

> **[Col. 1014B] Note: [Col. 1014C]**
>
> **VII.—Military Venus.** Mention of a Military Venus is rather rare among the ancients. Nevertheless, Pausanias mentions an armed, and therefore military, Venus more than once, II, p. 48, and III, pp. 95 and 103. Nonnus too, where he sings that Venus is mightier than Mars, *Dionysiaca* XXXV.175:
>
> > Do not set foot in Sparta, where the warlike citizens  
> > bear the brazen image of Aphrodite under arms.
>
> (*Μὴ Σπάρτης ἐπίβηθι, μαχήμονες ᾗχι πολῖται  
> Χάλκεον εἶδος ἔχουσι κορυσσομένης Ἀφροδίτης.*)
>
> [Col. 1014D] Compare Lactantius, *Institutes*, I.19. Finally, Hesychius mentions “Spear-bearing Aphrodite among the Cypriots” (*Ἔγχειος Ἀφροδίτη, Κυπρίοις*). NOURR., p. 424. Venus also was believed, as it were through love for her Mars, to assist in war; hence she was called *Symmachia* (Συμμαχία, “Ally”) and was worshiped under that name by the Mantineans, according to Pausanias in the *Arcadica*. So Vossius, *On Idolatry*, VIII.18, p. 762. ORELL.
>
> **“Presides over abductions in the camp.”** The manuscript and old editions read “crimes of the camp.” NOURR.
>
> **Perfica.** This impure goddess too is mentioned by no other author. Turnebus, *Adversaria*, XI.20, does indeed cite Lucretius II.1115:
>
> > Until at last creative Nature, the perfecter,  
> > brought all things to the utmost limit of their growth.
>
> But there *perfica* is an adjective, equivalent to “perfecting,” as Nonius explains. Compare Lambinus and Creech on Lucretius, Book I. Julius Capitolinus uses *perficere* in an obscene sense in *Maximinus*, chapter 4; see Salmasius, *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. II, p. 18. ORELL.
>
> **“Muddy pleasures.”** “Muddy,” that is, most shameful and contemptible, worth less than mud. Thus Plautus, *Truculentus*, IV.4.1:
>
> > A prostitute is as worthless as beet and mud.
>
> See the interpreters there. Plautus similarly uses “dung-like” in *The Braggart Soldier*, II.1.12:
>
> > My master, the soldier,  
> > who has gone from here to the forum—boastful, shameless,  
> > dung-like, full of perjury and adultery.
>
> ORELL.
>
> **Pertunda.** Tertullian, *Against the Nations*, II.11: “And the goddess Pertunda, and Subigus, and Prema … Spare us, shameless gods! No one intervenes when married couples are struggling.” Augustine, *On the City of God*, VI.9: “For there are present the goddess Virginiensis, Father Subigus, Mother Prema, the goddess Pertunda, Venus, and Priapus, and what follows is assuredly obscene and shameful.” ORELL.
>
> **“The virginal furrow.”** Thus Euripides, *Phoenician Women*, verse 18: “to sow the furrow of children” (*σπείρειν τέκνων ἄλοκα*). ORELL.
>
> **Tutunus.** Thus Salmasius printed from the manuscript in the Leiden edition and in his note on Solinus, chapter 26, p. 219. Others: Mutunus. On this most shameful god, see below at chapter 11. ORELL.
>
> **“Upon whose monstrous genitals,” etc.** Compare Augustine, *On the City of God*, XI.9 and XII.24; Lactantius, *Institutes*, I.22 §36. ELMENH. and HERALD.
>
> **“But if the facts themselves do not in the least direct you toward an understanding of the truth.”** The sense is: If the facts themselves—that is, the enormity of the shameful things over which your supposed gods or goddesses are believed to preside—do not, I say, direct you toward an understanding of the truth, meaning toward understanding the true condition of your gods (*was an der Sache sei; was an euren Göttern sei*—“what the real state of the matter is; what your gods truly are”), then at least from the absurdity of their names themselves you can know this, etc. “Direct,” the reading of Gelenius and Salmasius, appears to derive from the manuscript. Fulvius Ursinus conjectures “move,” with Heraldus’ approval. But it matters little or nothing which reading we adopt. Believing the passage dislocated, Meursius thinks that the words “But if they do not in the least direct you … and imaginary representations of false gods” should be moved to the end of the chapter, after “caring for and guarding the sweetness of honey.” ORELL.
>
> **Puta … Peta … Nemestrinus.** These gods are unknown elsewhere. See Vossius, *On Idolatry*, p. 236. ORELL.
>
> **“Patellana is a divinity, and so is Patella.”** Papias: “The pagans speak of the goddess Patellana when the husks of the crops open or the grain emerges from the ears.” ELMENH.—Augustine calls her Patelena in the passage that we shall cite shortly. ORELL.
>
> **“For things that are to be opened.”** Should we not read “for seeds that are to be opened”? For Patellana is a goddess of the fields. See the passage of Papias just cited. ORELL.
>
> **Nodutis.** Augustine, *On the City of God*, IV.8: “They therefore appointed Proserpina over the sprouting grains; the god Nodotus over the joints and knots of the stalks; the goddess Volutina over the coverings of the husks; the goddess Patelena when the husks open so that the ear may emerge; the goddess Hostilina when the crops are made level with new ears, because the ancients called leveling *hostire*; the goddess Flora over the grains in flower; the goddess Lacturtia over those filling with milk; the goddess Matura over those ripening; and the goddess Runcina when they are weeded—that is, removed from the earth.” The name is variously written: Nodotus, Nodutus, Nodutis. ORELL.
>
> **“And the one who presides over the threshing of crops, Terensis.”** Grotius, as cited by Meursius, restored “threshing” for “bearing,” which was formerly read. Elmenhorstius and Stewechius printed: “and because Noduterensis presides over the threshing of crops.” I would not venture to decide anything in a matter wholly uncertain and doubtful. ORELL.
>
> **Vibilia.** By conjecture I read Vehilia. For *veha* meant “road” in old Latin, according to Varro, *On Agriculture*, I.2. Or perhaps Venilia, whom the same Varro mentions in *On the Latin Language*, IV. MEURSIUS.
>
> **Orbona.** Pliny, *Natural History*, II.7: “There is a shrine of Orbona beside the temple of the Lares.” There, however, Orbona is not the protectress of the bereaved, but rather the goddess who brings bereavement. For she is joined with diseases, plagues, fever, and bad fortune, all of which were enrolled among the gods. Tertullian likewise uses the name in this sense in *To the Nations*, II.14: “the goddess Orbona, who destroys offspring and produces bereavement.” See Hardouin on Pliny, vol. I, p. 72, and G. J. Vossius, *On Idolatry*, VIII.17, p. 759. Moreover, as Stewechius correctly observes, the ancients called both a father who had lost his children and children who had lost their father *orbus*. See Festus under *Orba*. Pliny’s words appear to have been copied from Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, III.25; see Davies there. ORELL.
>
> **Naenia.** A shrine outside the Viminal Gate was consecrated to the goddess Naenia, who presided over the end of life or over funerals, as we learn from Paulus and Festus. Augustine, *On the City of God*, VI.9, says of her, following Varro [Col. 1016D]: “Varro began to mention and enumerate the gods from the conception of a human being, and continued the sequence down to the death of a decrepit person; and he concluded the gods pertaining to the human being himself with the goddess Naenia, whose song is sung at the funerals of the aged.” NOURR., p. 426.
>
> **“Now she who hardens.”** I have printed this from Meursius’ correction of “For she who hardens.”
>
> **Ossilago.** We should read either Ossipago with Canterus or Ossipanga with Stewechius. See above on Book III, chapter 30. ORELL.
>
> **Mellonia.** Augustine, *On the City of God*, IV.34: “Crops without Segetia, cattle without Bobova, honey without Mellona, fruit without Pomona.” ELMENH.—Meursius reads Mellona. ORELL.

### VII

Does a Military Venus also preside over abductions in the camp and the violation of boys? Is Perfica also one [Col. 1015A] of the common throng of divine beings—she who brings those obscene and muddy pleasures to completion and causes them to proceed to their consummation with their sweetness unimpaired? Is there also Pertunda, who stands by in bedchambers when husbands excavate the virginal furrow? Is there also Tutunus, upon whose monstrous genitals and bristling phallus you consider it auspicious for your married women to ride, and even desire them to do so?

But if the facts themselves do not in the least direct you toward an understanding of the truth, can you not at least recognize from the names themselves that these are fabrications of utterly empty superstition and imaginary representations of false gods?

Puta, you say, is present at the pruning of trees; Peta, when things are sought. Nemestrinus is the god of groves [Col. 1016A]. Patellana is a divinity, and so is Patella, one of whom has been appointed over things opened, the other over things that are to be opened. A god is called Nodutis because he brings planted things to the stage of forming knots; and the one who presides over the bearing of crops is Terensis. The goddess Vibilia [Note: [Col. 1015A] Vipibilia, Sabinus] frees people from wandering astray on roads. Parents bereaved of children are under Orbona’s protection; those whose time has reached its end [Note: [Col. 1015A] The manuscript adds this; Sabinus omits it] are under Naenia’s. Now she who hardens and strengthens the bones of little infants [Note: [Col. 1016A] “to be,” manuscript; “she herself,” Sabinus] is herself recorded as Ossilago. The goddess Mellonia is powerful and mighty among bees, caring for and guarding the sweetness of honey.

> **Note: [Col. 1016D]**
>
> **VIII.—“Tell me, I beg you, and may Peta, Puta, and Patella thus favor you propitiously.”** Thus the first edition. But Fulvius Ursinus eliminated the particle *ut*, which certainly ought to have been retained. It is used in this way everywhere, as in: “May the gods and goddesses destroy that old man,” and similar expressions. The most diligent grammarian Aelius Donatus observes that *ut* in such passages is used for *utinam* (“may it be so”). Elsewhere *ita* and *sic* are very frequent. HERALD.
>
> **“Or if we human beings were born without bones, like certain worms.”** Heraldus and the Leiden editor very correctly restored “human beings,” which is absent from the earlier editions. ORELL.
>
> **“Although it was similarly unknown to you.”** Here “unknown” has a passive sense: “that which is not known.” See Aulus Gellius IX.12, who says this passive use of the word is uncommon. Thus in Book I: “What are you saying, little men, babbling with the loquacity of a reckless tongue about things unascertained and unknown to you?” MEURSIUS.

### VIII

Tell me, I beg you—and may Peta, Puta, and Patella thus favor you propitiously [Col. 1017A]—if there were no bees at all on earth, or if we human beings were born without bones, like certain worms, would there be no goddess Mellonia? Or would Ossilago, the strengthener of bones, have no proper name?

For I ask and repeatedly inquire whether, in your judgment, the gods are older in nature, time, and antiquity than human beings, bees, crops, shoots, and all other things. No one will doubt that you declare the gods to precede everything that exists by countless ages and generations. But if this is so, how can it occur in the natural order that beings earlier in time should receive their names from things created afterward? Or that gods should obtain guardianship over things that had not yet been born or assigned for mortal use?

Or were the gods perhaps formerly without names, and only after things began to come into existence and to be present upon the earth did they deign to be designated by you with these signs and appellations [Col. 1017B]? And how could you know what names to give each of them, when you were altogether ignorant that they existed or that these particular powers resided in them [Col. 1018A]? For it was similarly unknown to you which of them could do what, and over what thing each ought to be set in accordance with the power of his divinity.

> **Note: [Col. 1017C]**
>
> **IX.—“Judged, but falsely.”** Thus the Leiden edition. Others: “and false things.” ORELL.
>
> **“Which is the perception common to all mortals.”** Fulvius Ursinus: “which is the perception implanted in all mortals.” Not badly. ORELL.
>
> **“For who is there who believes,” etc.** This is the old reading, which they altered rashly. For *qui* is often used for *quis* by writers of this kind. Cyprian, III, Letter 24: “What vigor of a victorious conscience is now yours, dearly beloved brothers?” And elsewhere, from Scripture: “Who are you, who judge another’s servant?” HERALD.
>
> **“That there are gods of profit.”** Gregory Nazianzen, Oration 2 against Julian, p. 308: “If I see your Profit-maker, and your patron of eloquence and contests, I cover my eyes and run past the god” (*Ἄν ἴδω σου τὸν Κερδῷον, καὶ τὸν λόγιον ἐναγώνιον, συγκρύπτω τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς, καὶ παρατρέχω τὸν θεόν*). And Oration 3 against Julian: “How, then, will their Profit-maker be set up, and his purse put on display, and the god’s power of theft be honored?” (*πῶς οὖν ὁ κερδῷος αὐτοῖς σταθήσεται, καὶ τὸ σακέλλιον προβληθήσεται, καὶ ἡ κλεπτικὴ δύναμις τοῦ θεοῦ τιμηθήσεται;*) ELMENH.—*Kerdōos* (Κερδῷος, “Profit-maker”) is properly Mercury; see the *Suda* under Κερδῷος. But Lycophron, *Alexandra* 208 [Col. 1017D], applies the name to Apollo because of the oracles by which he served both others’ advantage and his own, saying:
>
> > Beside the caves of the Delphinian, profit-making god.
>
> (*Δελφινίου παρ᾽ ἄντρα Κερδῴου θεοῦ.*)
>
> See Meursius there. ORELL.—The *Suda*, under κερδῷος, teaches us who these gods were: “The god Kerdōos is Hermes, because he produces profit. They also call him messenger and thief; therefore they represent him carrying a purse. They make him overseer of speech, theft, and trade—that is, overseer of profit” (*Κερδῷος θεὸς ὁ Ἑρμῆς, ὡς κέρδους ποιητικός· καὶ ἄγγελον δὲ αὐτὸν καλοῦσι καὶ κλῶπα· διὸ καὶ μάρσυππον αὐτὸν ποιοῦσι βαστάζειν· καὶ ἔφορον αὐτὸν τοῦ λόγου, καὶ τῆς κλοπῆς, καὶ ἐμπολείων, ἤγουν κέρδους ἔφορον*).
>
> Nonnus says the same in his commentary on Gregory Nazianzen’s Oration against Julian, p. 148, Montagu’s edition: “The Greeks call Hermes the god Kerdōos, because he procures profit. Hence Aristophanes the comic poet, in the play *Wealth*, being at a loss what Hermes ought to be called, says: ‘Let us establish him as Empolaios,’ that is, as overseer of profit” (*Κερδῷον θεὸν καλοῦσι οἱ Ἕλληνες τὸν Ἑρμῆν, ὡς κέρδους περιποιητικόν· διὸ καὶ Ἀριστοφάνης ὁ κωμικὸς ἐν τῷ δράματι τῷ Πλούτῳ, ἀπορῶν τίνα δεῖ καλέσαι τὸν Ἑρμῆν, φησίν· Ἐμπόλαιον αὐτὸν ἱδρυσώμεθα, τουτέστι κέρδους ἔφορον*).
>
> Apollo too is *kerdōos*. Julian is witness in the same Oration, p. 77: “How, then, will their Profit-maker be set up, and his purse put on display, and the god’s power of theft be honored, together with the claim that Phoebus does not prophesy without bronze and that nothing is more precious than an obol?” (*πῶς οὖν ὁ κερδῷος αὐτοῖς σταθήσεται, καὶ τὸ σακέλλιον προβληθήσεται, καὶ ἡ κλεπτικὴ δύναμις τοῦ θεοῦ τιμηθήσεται, καὶ τὸ ἄνευ χαλκοῦ Φοῖβον [Col. 1018B] μὴ μαντεύεσθαι, μηδὲ εἶναί τι τοῦ ὀβολοῦ τιμιώτερον;*) NOURR., p. 422, and ORELL.
>
> **Libentina.** Augustine, *On the City of God*, IV.8: “They dare assign certain functions to the goddess Cloacina, or to Volupia, who was named from pleasure, or to Libentina, whose name derives from lust.” ELMENH.—Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II.23: “From this class the names of Cupid, Pleasure, and Venus Libentina have been consecrated—names of vicious and not natural things,” etc.; see Davies there, p. 153. Nonius under *Prolubium* … Varro, *On the Latin Language*, V: “*Prolubies* and *prolubido* are said from that which pleases; hence also the grove of Venus Lubentina.” See Mercerus there. For in all editions of Varro—for example, the Bipontine, p. 63—the passage is defective and corrupt. See Antonius Augustinus’ note, vol. II, p. 138. Venus Libentina must therefore be carefully distinguished from Venus Libitina, who presides over funerals. ORELL.
>
> **“Who Liburnus?”** [The lemma is elliptical in the source.] This name appears corrupt. The Royal manuscript has *Burnum*. Because scribes apparently suspected that this was corrupt, they rewrote it as *Liburnum*. Meursius therefore thought that *Liberum* (“Liber”) should be read; Augustine, *On the City of God*, VI.9 and VII.2, attests that the pagans placed Liber over lust. NOURRIUS.—Nevertheless, I would change nothing. We read many names of such unknown gods in our author. On the verb *superesse* (“to exist”), see above at Book III, chapter 23. ORELL.
>
> **“Attempts.”** Thus the manuscript. Others: “is carried through,” which Heraldus defends in vain. Elmenhorstius: “seeks.” ORELL.
>
> **[Col. 1018D] “Who Limentinus, and who Lima?”** I shall say what I think. I do not know who the goddess Lima is, nor do I think she should be tolerated here. Arnobius subsequently says: “Who brought into being the Limi, guardians of oblique paths?” Augustine, *On the City of God*, IV.8, ridiculing the folly of pagans who entrust a whole house to one doorkeeper but appoint three gods over a single door, says: “They set three gods there: Forculus over the doors, Cardea over the hinge, and Limentinus over the threshold.” Tertullian presents those same three in his *Scorpiace*, though “Cardus” is read there. Again, in *The Soldier’s Crown*, “they named Carda” is read. Finally, in *On Idolatry*, “Cardea” is regularly read. What if we suppose that they worshiped Cardeus and Cardea, and likewise Limentinus and, instead of this Lima, the goddess Limentina—just as they worshiped both Robigus and Robigo? STEWECH.—The manuscript reads “who Luna,” most corruptly. Heraldus suspects that “who Janes” should be read, using the ancient spelling for Janus, and cites Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chapter 15, “Janes from *janua* (‘door’)”; and *Apology*, chapter 10: “Saturn … was received by Janus or Janes, as the Salii maintain.” I leave the reading doubtful and uncertain. ORELL.—Lima is nowhere mentioned by the ancients. They therefore suspect that the name is corrupt and that we should read Limentina [Col. 1019B] (Stewechius), Janus, Jana, or Janes (Heraldus). What if Cardea were read, the goddess appointed over door hinges, whom Tertullian mentions in *To the Nations*, II.15, and *On Idolatry*, chapter 15—or Carna, about whom Ovid sang at greater length in *Fasti*, Book VI? NOURR., p. 421.
>
> **“When every day we see temples,” etc.** Meursius’ conjecture, “when every day we see a thousand temples,” is unnecessary. The thresholds of temples—supplied from what precedes—are undermined and torn away by thieves and the sacrilegious. ORELL.
>
> **“And that without them there can be no shameful visits to brothels.”** The wording is exact. Lactantius, III.15: “What difference, then, did it make with what intention the philosopher frequented the most notorious prostitute, when the people and his rivals saw that he was more depraved than every abandoned man?” See Bunemann there, p. 347. “Shameful” is likewise used precisely. Cicero: “But as for acts of debauchery and crimes, shame deters me from recounting his impious lusts.” These words agree perfectly with what precedes. The conjecture that they should be transposed is therefore groundless. HERALD. Meursius wished to transpose these words to follow “practices and exercises disgraceful obscenity”—which he also wrongly changed to “seeks”—because this is the function of Liburnus and Libentina, not of Limentinus and Lima. Arnobius, however, appears to have in mind lovers keeping watch at the doors of prostitutes; on this familiar subject see the interpreters on Propertius I.16. Moreover, for Liburnus, who is nowhere else mentioned, Meursius thinks Liber should be read, citing Augustine, *On the City of God*, VI.9. They claim that Liber was named from “release,” because through his beneficence males are released in intercourse by the emission of seed. ORELL.
>
> **“Who brought into being the Limi, guardians of oblique paths?”** Hyginus, *On Establishing Boundaries*, p. 151, Goes’ edition: “Boundaries were called *limites* from *limus*, an ancient word meaning ‘transverse.’” See Rigault there, p. 262. The old glosses: “*Limes*: a path, an oblique road” (*τρίβος, πλαγία ὁδός*). Compare Servius on *Aeneid* XII.120; hence *limis oculis*, “with sidelong eyes.” Moreover, as far as I know, the gods called Limi are mentioned nowhere else. ORELL.
>
> **[Col. 1019D] “Saturn as presiding over things sown.”** I have followed Canterus’ correction as the closest to the manuscript’s corrupt reading *Latinis*. Others—for example, Gelenius and Salmasius—printed “presiding over sowing.” But “presiding over things sown” appears more elegant, like “prefect over the city.” ORELL.
>
> **“Who Montinus of the mountains?”** Mountains were once held in great veneration, and—as is abundantly clear from both sacred and secular history—altars and temples were built upon them for very many deities. The Indians in Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*, I.2, call the Caucasus “the dwelling of the gods” (*θεῶν οἶκον*). The Persians in Herodotus I.131, “ascending to the highest parts of the mountains” (*ἐπὶ τὰ ὑψηλότατα τῶν οὐρέων ἀναβαίνοντες*), sacrifice victims to Jupiter. Montinus, a god who presides over mountains, occurs in Arnobius. In Lactantius’ *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 11, the mother of Galerius Maximianus is called a worshiper of the mountain gods and an exceedingly superstitious woman. “THE MOUNTAIN GODS” (*DII MONTENSES*) are celebrated in an inscription in Gruter, p. 21. Since this inscription was found at Rome, the words seem to denote the gods who presided over the seven hills [Col. 1020A], in whose honor perhaps the festival of the Septimontium was instituted. This was celebrated by the *montani*, that is, the inhabitants of the hills, not by the whole people, as may be seen in Varro, *On the Latin Language*, V; and, according to Festus, they offered sacrifice in seven places, to the gods, as I suppose, who presided over the hills [Col. 1020B] (Gisbert Cuper, *Apotheosis of Homer*, p. 15). Johannes Columbus supplies more in his note on Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, pp. 284 ff., Bauldri’s edition; and Bernart on Statius, *Thebaid*, I, p. 4, Crucaeus’ edition. ORELL.

Who [would believe] Murcia [the goddess] of the sluggish? Augustine, *City of God*, IV.16: “They called Murcia the goddess who would not stir beyond measure, and who would make a person, as Pomponius says, *murcidus*, that is, excessively idle and inactive.” ELMENH.—Murcia was a surname of Venus, who, according to Festus, had a shrine beneath the Aventine Hill. Learned men disagree, however, about the etymology of the name. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, IV, p. 43, Bipontine ed., reports that some derived it from *urcei* (“pitchers”), because that place was among the potters, while others derived it from *murtetum* (“myrtle grove”), because one had stood there. See the note of Ausonius Popma, p. 105; Scaliger and Dacier on Festus, p. 253. Salmasius, however, on Solinus, p. 637, and G. J. Vossius, *Roman Etymologies*, derive it more correctly, as it [Col. 1020C] seems to me, from the Greek μαλακός (*malakos*, “soft, weak”), Aeolic μαλκός (*malkos*), μολκός (*molkos*), or μυλκός (*mulkos*), and, in the Syracusan dialect—as Hesychius attests—μυρκός (*murkos*). Hence the Latin *marcer*, *marcidus*, and *murcus*, *murcidus*. See Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus, XV, p. 98. Moreover, this same divinity is also mentioned by Pliny, *Natural History*, XV.29, and by Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, who calls Murcia the goddess of languor (*marcoris*) according to Turnebus’ correction. Some read “of love” (*amoris*), others “of marble” (*marmoris*). The Leiden edition reads *Murcidam*, owing, I believe, to a compositor’s error. For Salmasius himself, on Solinus, p. 1, where he discusses this name at length, determines that *Murciam* should be read. ORELL.

The goddess Money. Augustine, *City of God*, IV.20: “To the goddess Money, so that they might be wealthy”; chapter 24: “Money was called the goddess who gives money.” VII.4: “The goddess Money has been obscured.... Why was the goddess Money not preferred to Minerva?” Juvenal, however, thinks differently, *Satires* I.114:

> [Col. 1020D] Although death-dealing Money does not yet  
> Dwell in a temple, and we have erected no altars to coins.

ELMENH.

To bestow gold rings. That is, equestrian rank. And such indeed was the case:

> If six or seven thousand are lacking from the four hundred thousand,  
> You will be one of the common people.

There is another observation concerning the right to wear gold rings. HERALDUS.

The highest platforms of honors. Meursius conjectures: “Honor, the highest platforms.” ORELL.

Leisure made secure through wealth. Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis*, V.5, calls it “repose accompanied by an abundance of possessions”: “For before this time they will be vicious, gluttons and drunkards, who, having set aside all care for their property, seek nothing other than to live, in Epicurean fashion, without labor, in repose and an abundance of possessions.” HERALD.—Stewechius, who everywhere scents something ancient and recondite, thinks that *per pollentias* (“through powers”) should be read. Incorrectly. ORELL.]

## IX

What [Note: [Col. 1017B] “Because others.”], then, you say? Do you judge that these gods exist nowhere among the nations, but have been established by false opinions? It is not we alone who say this, but truth itself, and reason, and that common sense which exists in all mortals. For who is there who believes that there are gods of Gain, and that they preside over the acquisition of profits, when profits very frequently arise from shameful causes and always consist in other people’s losses? Who believes that Libentina or Liburnus watches over lusts, which wisdom commands us to flee, and which shameless obscenity both experiences and practices in a thousand forms? [Col. 1018B] Who believes that Limentinus or Lima guards thresholds [Note: [Col. 1018B] “Lights,” Sabaeus, ineptly.] and performs the duties of doorkeepers, when every day we see the thresholds both of temples and of private houses torn up and demolished, and when, without them, the disgraceful traffic to brothels could not exist? Who believes the Limi [Note: [Col. 1019A] *Limones* in the manuscript.] to be supervisors of oblique courses? Who believes Saturn to be patron of things sown; Montinus, of mountains; Murcia, of the sluggish; or, finally, the goddess Money to exist, whom your literature declares, as though she were the greatest [Col. 1020A] divinity, to bestow gold rings, front seats at games and spectacles, the highest platforms of honors, the grandeur of public office, and—what the indolent love most—leisure made secure through wealth?

[Note: [Col. 1020D]

## X.—If you insist that bones, honey, etc., have their own particular patrons

I have followed Salmasius’ correction, which is most perfectly suited to the context. The manuscript and all the other editors read: “But what if they had their own particular patrons in their seats?” What the words “in their seats” are supposed to mean here, I confess that I am utterly unable to understand. Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “What if they had their own divine patrons within themselves?” Yet the things of which Arnobius speaks—bones, honey, and so forth—certainly did not have gods enclosed within themselves, but gods placed over them, that is, gods who attended to their care. ORELL.

Excessiveness. Below: “While we accuse you of excessiveness.” VII.26: “It follows that we should say something about incense and unmixed wine without any excessiveness.” Apuleius uses this word, *Apology*, p. 461; Pliny, *Natural History*, XIV.6; Columella, IV.24; Ammianus Marcellinus, XIX, p. 179. ELMENH.—Eutropius also, X, final chapter: “Some think that Jovian [was killed] by an excessive quantity of coals, which he had ordered to be burned in great numbers because of the severe cold.” [Col. 1021C] ORELL.

Savory. Scribonius Largus, chapter 124: “*Cunila*, which some call *Satureja*”; see Rhodius there in his *Lexicon*. German *Pfefferkraut* (“savory”). ORELL.

Not figs. Stewechius, on the authority, as he says, of a manuscript, restored *non ficubus*. In his observation he adduces much concerning the distinction between *ficus, -i*, meaning a disease of the extremity of the rectum caused by excessive friction, and *ficus, -us*, meaning the tree and its fruit. Gesner, however, teaches in his *Thesaurus* that this distinction does not hold: the word *ficus*, with either declension but in the feminine gender, was used indiscriminately for the tree and its fruit, especially by writers of earlier Latin; whereas *ficus, -i*, in the masculine gender, denoted a bodily defect. But J. G. Graevius, in Letter 259 to N. Heinsius, Burmann’s *Sylloge*, IV, p. 334, attests that the same manuscript reads *ficiis*, and rightly wonders that figs are mentioned here among herbs and vegetables. Accordingly, he thinks *coepitiis* should be restored in place of *non ficiis*. For my part, I think that with a slighter change—the alteration of only one letter—we should write *non* [Col. 1021D] *viciis*, “not vetches.” Vetches (*Wicken*) are a kind of legume mentioned by Virgil, *Georgics* I.75, and by others. ORELL.

Beet-roots, cabbages. Thus Salmasius most correctly edited the text from the manuscript. *Betaceis*, with *pedibus* (“feet”) understood, means the roots and fibers of beets. So too *malvacei* and *rapicii*, with *pedes* understood, mean mallow-roots and turnip-roots. See the same Salmasius on Solinus, chapter 40, p. 583. The other editors, not understanding this, changed it to “beets, cabbages.” We can also omit the comma and read “beet-stalks,” that is, the stalks or stems of beets from which the leaves grow. But I would rather insert the comma and understand *caulibus* of cabbage, in which sense the word is used by the Latins κατ’ ἐξοχήν (*kat’ exochēn*, “par excellence”). See Davies on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, II.47, p. 217, second ed.; and Joseph Scaliger on Varro, *On Agriculture*, I.16. Hence the French *le chou* and our German *Kohl*. *Beta* or *betacei*, Greek τεῦτλον (*teutlon*), Italian *bietola*, is our German *Mangold*, *Beisskohl*. See its description in Pliny, *Natural History*, XIX.8. Add Schneider’s index to the *Writers on Agriculture*, under this word. ORELL.

[Col. 1022B] In parts, and are liable to very many accidents. Meursius suspects that the text should read: “In parts? These are, etc.” I would prefer: “which are.” ORELL.]

## X

But if you insist that bones, honey, thresholds, and the other things which we have either [Col. 1021A] touched upon cursorily or failed to approach from weariness at the excessiveness of it all [Note: [Col. 1021A] “We approach,” Sabaeus.] have their own particular patrons, then by similar reasoning you may introduce a thousand other gods who would have to provide their care and protection for innumerable things. For why should a god preside only over honey, and not over gourds or turnips, not over savory or cress, not over figs, beet-roots, or cabbages? Why should bones alone have deserved protection, while nails, hairs, and all the other things situated in obscure places and in the more modest parts of the body have not deserved it, although they are liable to very many accidents and have greater need of the gods’ care and attention? Or, if you say that these parts too conduct their affairs under their own guardian [Col. 1022A] gods [Note: [Col. 1021A] “Protecting gods,” Sabaeus, incorrectly.], then there will begin to be as many gods as there are things; nor will it be possible to explain why divine care does not preside over all things, if you say that there are certain things over which divine powers preside and for which they provide.

[Note: [Col. 1022B]

## XI.—What do you say, fathers of novel religions, what of the powers?

“Do you cry out and complain that these are the gods whom we violate and neglect through sacrilegious contempt?” Thus I have edited the text according to the correction of the Leiden editor. The manuscript and the first Roman edition have: “What do you say, fathers of novel religions, who obscenely of powers cry out that the gods are violated and sacrilegiously neglected by us, and complain that they are despised,” etc., which makes no sense. Friedrich Lindenbrog recasts it: “What do you say, fathers of novel religions? What do you protest?” Heraldus, offended for some reason by the phrase “fathers of novel religions,” thinks that the passage should be restored thus: “What do you say, fathers of great religions and powers? Do you therefore cry out that the gods are sacrilegiously violated and neglected by us, and complain that they are despised?” etc. For my part, I think that *quid* should be deleted before *potestatum*, and that one should read: “What do you say, fathers of novel [Col. 1022C] religions—of powers?” This is a genuinely Arnobian construction. In all else I follow the Leiden editor. The “fathers of novel religions,” etc., are not priests or prelates, as Heraldus interprets them, but the Romans in general, whom Arnobius addresses at the beginning of this book and who were introducing new and previously unheard-of divinities and their cults. *Potestates* (“powers”) means the same as gods or divine powers. See above, on III.33. ORELL.

Fathers of religions, that is, authors or inventors—a frequent metaphor. See Petavius on Synesius, Letter I, note, p. 44. Thus Philo of Byzantium, *On the Seven Wonders of the World*, chapter III: “Cronus is the father of Zeus in heaven, but Phidias is his father in Elis” (Διὸς Κρόνος μὲν ἐν οὐρανῷ, Φειδίας δ’ ἐν Ἤλιδι πατήρ ἐστι). See there Allatius’ notes and our own, and our notes on *Letters of Socrates* VI, p. 168. Compare Boissonade on Marinus, *Life of Proclus*, p. 75 ff. ORELL.

Lateranus, the Genius of hearths. Meursius restored this from the manuscript. Previously the text read: “the Lar, the Genius of hearths.” Although that reading could be defended, it cannot stand here, where Arnobius repeats the names of the gods whom he mentioned above: Limentinus, Pertunda, Perfica, Nodutis, Terensis, and Lateranus. ORELL.

Nodutis, Terensis. Thus the Leiden editor punctuates the passage. Others, following the manuscript, read *Noduterensem*. See above on chapter 7. ORELL.

Because we do not fall as suppliants before Mutunus and Tutunus. This correction by Gelenius is entirely true and comes closest to the monstrous reading of the manuscript: “Because we do not fall as suppliants before one and it is one,” from which Sabaeus in the first Roman edition had fashioned: “Because we do not fall as suppliants—that is, to the ground—before Tutunus.” Meursius: “Because we do not fall equally as suppliants before Futinus.” Salmasius, in the Leiden edition, retained both corrections and presented the passage thus: “Because we do not fall as suppliants on the ground before Mutunus and Tutunus.” “To fall on the ground” is a Lucretian phrase. V.1299:

> Nor to fall prostrate upon the ground and spread out one’s hands.

Moreover, Salmasius discusses at length the etymology of the names Mutunus and Tutunus in his notes on Solinus, chapter 24, p. 219. His words are as follows:

> “The Greek is μυττός (*muttos*) ... τὸ γυναικεῖον (*to gunaikeion*, ‘the female organ’), Hesychius; and μυττών, -ῶνος (*muttōn, -ōnos*), whence *muttonus* and *muttunus*, although among the Latins this is almost always used of the male member. Lucilius, however, appears to have understood the female organ in a fragment of *Satire* IV, in Nonius V, under *lurcare*:
>
> > For what need has this *moetunus*—  
> > (for that is how it must be read, not *moetinus*)—  
> > Of this erect sign?
>
> Here both organs are under discussion. *Tutunus*, however, comes from πόσθη (*posthē*, ‘penis’) and πόσθων (*posthōn*), one who has a huge male member; in Aeolic, πόθθων, πόθθωνος (*potthōn, potthōnos*). Hence the Latin *puttunus* and *tuttunus*. For T and P were interchanged both by the Aeolians and by the ancient Latins. Muttunus Tutunus, therefore, was a Priapic (πριαπῶδες) divinity [Col. 1023C] worshiped by Roman matrons—see above, chapter 7, and Augustine, *City of God*, IV.11: ‘Mutunus and Tutunus, who among the Greeks is Priapus.’ It appears to have borne the obscene designation of each and the genitals of both sexes, or at least an image of each sexual organ was consecrated in the same shrine, which, according to Festus, stood on the Velia opposite the Mustelline wall. For among the ancients each was used ἀντὶ τοῦ προβασκανίου (*anti tou probaskaniou*, ‘as an amulet against the evil eye’) and to ward off bewitchment. Hence the ancient glosses: ‘*Mutonium*: προβασκάνιον (*probaskanion*, ‘protective amulet’), as in Lucilius.’”

(For Varro attests that representations of the genitals were hung from children’s necks as amulets.) Thus Salmasius. Compare Turnebus, *Adversaria*, XVII.33; Janus Guilielmus, *Verisimilia*, I.23, in Gruter’s *Lampas Critica*, III, p. 274; Scioppius and Scaliger on *Priapeia* 73; the commentators on Festus under this word, p. 256, Dacier’s ed.; Douza on Lucilius, *Fragments*, p. 286, Havercamp’s ed.; J. Lipsius, *Electa*, II.19, *Works*, I, p. 822 ff., Wesel ed.; Bunemann on Lactantius, I.20, [Col. 1023D] p. 132; and P. Burmann the Younger, in the *Latin Anthology*, II, p. 544. ORELL.

Lest, while fashioning such monsters and contriving such things. The manuscript adds: “such things and contriving.” The same word has incorrectly been repeated. For we should write: “Lest, while fashioning such monsters and contriving them.” MEURSIUS, in the Appendix.

Grow. Gelenius most properly gives *inolescant* in place of *insolescant*. *Inolescere* means to grow or increase and is a Virgilian word. ORELL.—After “grow through daily additions,” something is necessarily missing. For the pagans appear to have wished to prove the truth of their religion from the inspection of entrails and from auguries; Arnobius begins to refute that part of their defense with the words: “Why, then,” etc. MEURSIUS, p. 129.

Why, then, someone among you may perhaps have said, do you maintain that it is false that those are gods? And when invoked, etc. Thus Salmasius edited the manuscript. Gelenius: “Why, then ... do you maintain that those gods are false? If, when invoked,” etc. But nothing should be changed. It is, namely, a transposition, by no means uncommon in Arnobius, for: “Why, then, someone among you may perhaps have said, do you maintain that it is false [Col. 1024B] that those are gods?” The following *et* (“and”) is adversative. See above on I.15. ORELL.

Or because the whole matter is exceedingly full of suspicions. Thus the manuscript. Fulvius Ursinus and Sabaeus printed “superstitions.” ORELL.

Or, expectation being disappointed, be twisted into contrary outcomes. Thus Gelenius, Elmenhorst, and Salmasius. But in Theodore Canter’s edition one reads “the undertaking being frustrated”; if this came from the manuscript, I would not think it should be rashly rejected. *Expeditio* must then be taken in its proper and primary sense, in which it signifies ἄνυσις (*anusis*), the successful completion of a work, its accomplishment and perfection. In this sense accounts are called *expeditae*, “settled.” ORELL.]

## XI

What do you say, fathers of novel religions—what of the powers? Do you cry out and complain that these are the gods whom we violate and neglect through sacrilegious [Note: [Col. 1022A] “You complain,” Sabaeus.] contempt: Lateranus, the Genius of hearths; Limentinus, patron of thresholds; Pertunda; Perfica; Nodutis; Terensis? And because we do not fall as suppliants before Mutunus and Tutunus, do you say that affairs have sunk toward destruction and that [Col. 1023A] the world itself has changed its laws and established ordinances?

But indeed take care and consider whether, while fashioning such monsters and contriving such things, you may have offended the truest gods—if, that is, there are any who deserve to bear and possess the exalted dignity of that name—and whether, for no other reason, those evils of which you speak are raging and growing through daily additions.

“Why, then,” someone among you may perhaps have said, “do you maintain that it is false that those are gods [Note: [Col. 1023A] Fulvius deletes this.]? And yet, when invoked by haruspices, they obey; when summoned by their own names, they come; and they give trustworthy answers to those who inquire.”

We can establish that what is said is false, either because the whole matter is exceedingly full of suspicions, or because we see many predictions every day either turn out differently or, expectation being disappointed, be twisted into contrary outcomes. [Col. 1024A]

[Note: [Col. 1024B]

## XII.—You will nevertheless produce the same assurance

This is the old reading, in place of which others—Gelenius among them—give “never, however.” Mercerus’ conjecture pleases me: “At last, however, you will produce assurance.” I had suspected: “Will you, however, produce that assurance?” HERALD.—Salmasius [Col. 1024C], in the Leiden edition, gave: “Will the same persons, however,” etc.; and in the preceding words: “But let them be true, as you assert,” namely, the predictions, instead of the singular “let it be true,” which was previously read. Fulvius Ursinus: “Who, however, will produce assurance?” The manuscript’s reading seems entirely sound to me, in this sense: “But let us grant you that these predictions are true. Will you nevertheless produce the same assurance for us—that is, persuade us in a similar manner,” as Meursius correctly interprets it in his Appendix, “by saying that these divinities, Mellonia for example, insert themselves into the fibers?” ORELL.

Significations. See Elmenhorst’s note above on chapter 3 of this book. ORELL.

Little livers. Similarly Sidonius, V, Letter XVII: “For frequent pains stabbed him because a fiber of his little liver was swollen”; see Savaron there, p. 366. Thus *bonuscula* appears in the *Theodosian Code*; *specula* for “a slight hope” in Plautus’ *Rope*; and *mercedula*, “a trifling fee,” and *bibliothecula*, “a little library,” in Symmachus, IV, Letter XVIII. See there Juretus, who discusses such diminutives at length, in Lectius’ edition, [Col. 1024D] p. 145. ORELL.

Cannot it happen or come about, although you artfully conceal it? This is Gelenius’ excellent correction. Others give from the manuscript: “Cannot it happen (although you conceal that it comes about in actuality)?” Heraldus eliminates “comes about in actuality” as a gloss and interpretation of *happen*, and reads: “Cannot it happen (although you conceal it)?” But I much prefer Gelenius’ correction, which is perfectly consistent with Arnobius’ style of joining such verbs without a conjunction. ORELL.

Summonings. Thus the Leiden edition. The manuscript and first edition have “in actions.” Others read “in incantations.” But *accire* (“to summon”) and *accitio* (“summoning”) are proper terms concerning magicians, although no other examples of this noun occur to me. ORELL.

*Antitheoi* often creep in in place of those summoned. Stewechius was the first to extract this entirely correct reading from the manuscript, where “in place of *accis*” was read, which Gelenius incorrectly changed to “in place of the true ones.” Meursius: “in place of others.” Concerning the *antitheoi* (ἀντίθεοι), that is, evil spirits who oppose the good and obstruct their works and benefits, see Iamblichus, *On the Egyptian Mysteries*, section 3, chapter 31, p. 102, Gale’s ed.; and D. Tiedemann, *Dissertation on the Origin of the Magical Arts*, etc., p. 14. Hence Lactantius, *Institutes*, II.9 §13, calls the devil an *antitheos*, that is, an adversary of God; see Bunemann there, p. 238. Moreover, *obrepere* (“to creep in”) is the proper word for everything that approaches covertly and deceitfully and deceives the senses—for example, demons, specters, and dreams. See Gesner in the *Thesaurus* and C. Barth on Rutilius, *Itinerary* I.305, p. 233, Jansson’s ed. Thus Cicero, *On Divination*, II.67: “No images, therefore, creep from outside into the minds of those who sleep.” ORELL.

Why should we not believe by equal reasoning? Fulvius Ursinus: “Why should we not believe the gods by equal reasoning?” The Leiden edition: “Since we believe by reasoning that is not dissimilar.” ORELL.]

## XII

But let them be true, as you assert: will you nevertheless produce the same assurance that Mellonia, for example, or Limentinus inserts himself into the fibers and adapts himself to signify the matters about which you inquire? Have you ever seen their mouth, bearing, or face? Or can these same features be discerned in lungs or little livers? Cannot it happen or come about, although you artfully conceal it, that one being takes the place of another, deceiving, mocking, misleading, and presenting the appearance of the one invoked?

If magicians, the brothers of haruspices, record that in their summonings *antitheoi* often creep in in place of those summoned [Note: [Col. 1024A] “Certain,” Fulvius; etc.; see the Note.], and that these are certain spirits composed of grosser matter, who pretend to be gods and mock the ignorant through lies and impersonations, why should we not believe by equal reasoning that here too others substitute themselves for those who do not exist, both to confirm your opinions and to rejoice that victims are slaughtered to themselves under alien names? [Col. 1025A]

[Note: [Col. 1025B]

## XIII.—Submitting himself to all parts of places and their divisions, etc.

I can by no means be deprived of the conviction that I have scented the true restoration of this passage, and that students of Arnobius will be grateful for it: “Submitting himself to all parts of livers and their divisions,” [Col. 1025C] perhaps with *jecorum* as an old inflection of *jocinorum*. That the entire matter concerns the inspection of entrails is indicated by these words introduced not long before: “You will never, however, produce assurance that Mellonia, for example, or Limentinus inserts himself into the fibers,” etc. Nor will you deny that the following also supports me: “Have you ever seen their”—that is, the gods’—“mouth, bearing, or face? Or can these same features be discerned in lungs or little livers?” Moreover, Festus attests that the fibers belong to livers. That these were customarily examined above all in inspections of entrails cannot be unknown to those who have tasted with the tips of their lips the study of antiquity and the delicacies of ancient learning. Whoever has the leisure may read Labeo’s fragment from Book XV, *On the Etruscan Disciplines*, in Fulgentius Planciades’ *Manales*, and Apuleius’ first *Apology for Himself*. STEWECH.—I cannot agree with Stewechius. For in the immediately preceding passage the discussion is no longer about haruspices but about their brothers the Magicians, and about the gods themselves who appear. Therefore these words must be referred to the same beings: “Submitting himself to all parts of places [Col. 1025D] and their divisions.” They are a hendiadys (ἓν διὰ δυοῖν) for “all parts of divided places,” that is, places separated by even the greatest interval. This figure, very common among poets, is admittedly more unusual in prose writers, but must nevertheless be tolerated in Arnobius, an imitator of ancient poets such as Lucretius and Virgil. ORELL.

Who is this single being? someone will ask. Perhaps we can, etc. Fulvius Ursinus and Stewechius wish to restore “you will ask.” “Someone will ask” is perhaps legitimate, as he says, concerning which we spoke on I.3. HERALD.—Meursius punctuates thus: “Someone will perhaps ask. We can,” etc. The same scholar thinks that no small amount has fallen out after the words “present to you the appearance of many divinities and powers,” concerning the unity of God and those who pretend to be gods. In my judgment, however, everything coheres perfectly well. ORELL.

Perhaps we can name him on the authority of truthful authors. The manuscript reads: “Perhaps we can name the established one with true names,” which Stewechius defends. ORELL.

[Col. 1026B] Egyptians. Cudworth and Jablonski attempt to demonstrate that the priests among the Egyptians possessed some knowledge of the supreme and true God, from that famous inscription of the temple at Sais preserved by Proclus in his commentary on Plato’s *Timaeus*, p. 30:

> I am all that has come to be, all that is, and all that shall be,  
> And no one has yet uncovered my veil.

(Ἐγώ εἰμι πᾶν τὸ γεγονὸς καὶ ὂν καὶ ἐσόμενον,  
Καὶ τὸν ἐμὸν πέπλον οὐδείς πω ἀπεκάλυψεν.)

They also rely upon a passage of Porphyry in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, III.12. The distinguished Meiners establishes the contrary with numerous arguments in his *History of the Doctrine of the True God*, I, section 1, p. 31 ff. ORELL.

Persians. See Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, I, concluding chapter; Stanley, *History of Philosophy*, part XIV, chapter VI, p. 1163; and, above all, the distinguished Meiners in four dissertations included in the *Transactions of the Göttingen Society of Sciences*. ORELL.

Chaldaeans. See Stanley, *History of Philosophy*, part XIII, section II, chapter 32, p. 1150, Leipzig ed.; and Meiners, *History of the Doctrine of the True God*, part I, section III, p. 74 ff. [Col. 1026C] ORELL.

Indians. See Meiners, in the work cited, part I, section IV, p. 91 ff. ORELL.
