And all those others who, through the more inward arts, have seen and learned these things. He calls those arts “more inward” which elsewhere he calls arcane and secret. Above, II.61: “What is the meaning of those rites of the secret arts, by which you address I know not what powers?” HERALD.

At a point where not only little boys and the impudent cannot restrain their laughter. The Royal manuscript has *puericuli* (“little boys”). From this some, including Meursius, conjecture “ridiculous boys.” The received reading can be retained, so that Arnobius thus indicates the sauciness and impudence of household-born slaves. It is sufficiently well known that saucy little boys, often brought from Alexandria, were among the ancients’ favorite luxuries. Papinius:

> I have not purchased from a Pharian ship insolent  
> Darlings, or an infant skilled in the insults of his own Nile,  
> Shameless alike in tongue and wit.

HERALD. [Col. 1026D] J. G. Graevius, in Letter 239 to N. Heinsius, in Burmann’s *Sylloge*, IV, p. 335, thinks one should read either “impudent home-born slaves” or, preferably, “home-born slave-boys and the impudent.” Thus Martial has “a god of home-born slaves, livid with gall.” Heinsius approves this conjecture in Letter 241, p. 337. ORELL.

But even serious men hardened into the grim harshness of their character. I have given Salmasius’ correction. The manuscript has: “but even serious men and males hardened by grim harshness.” Following the traces of this reading, Stewechius thinks it should read: “but even serious males, hardened by grim harshness,” supposing that males are here contrasted with little boys. Incorrectly: males are contrasted with females, men with boys. Gelenius printed: “and hardened by harshness into grim characters.” Canter: “and hardened by grim harshness into their characters.” Defending this reading, Heraldus explains *mores* as a confirmed and deeply ingrained disposition (ἐγκεχρωσμένον ἦθος), in which sense Greek philosophers use ἦθος absolutely. Julius Firmicus describes such people in *Mathesis* VIII.15: “All who are born when this star is rising will be grave and austere, fearsome for every kind of savage severity, always fashioning their countenance in accordance with the integrity of their character; they may also follow the Stoic school with genuine conviction.” Such were the Catos among the ancients. For my part, however, I prefer Salmasius’ correction. ORELL.

Communicated and handed down. See above on I.73. ORELL.

The specific character of each name could not. (“For by the nature of things it is impossible that what is one should become two, and that unity should pass into different things, divided despite its innate simplicity.”) [Col. 1027C] I have ventured to insert here these words, which in all editions are read at the end of this book, but which most editors enclose in brackets as badly dislocated and placed in an entirely inappropriate location; this seems to be their proper and most suitable place. Nevertheless, they appear to me to have originated with some pedantic glossator. I have therefore enclosed them in parentheses and arranged for them to be printed in what are called italic letters. ORELL.

And with recollection of their elementary lessons laid to rest. This is the old reading, for which Gelenius rashly substitutes “set aside”; others more appropriately give “lulled to sleep.” Yet the old reading can also be explained, if *composita* means virtually “buried,” since *componere τοὺς νεκρούς* properly means “to lay out the dead.” “I have laid them all to rest.” “Happy ones.” HERALD.—Salmasius follows Heraldus. I would myself prefer “lulled to sleep,” all the more readily if, as Elmenhorst notes in the variant readings, that is the reading of the manuscript. ORELL.

Men of acute judgment and penetrating intelligence. Others read: “men acute in judgment,” etc. The Leiden edition and Gallandi’s edition, which follows it, read: “and through penetrating intelligence.” I do not know whether this arose through a compositor’s error or whether *per* was deliberately introduced into the text from the manuscript, since no variant reading is recorded at these words. If we follow that reading, there is tmesis in *per ingenio perspicaci*, meaning “with an exceedingly penetrating intelligence.” Thus the intensifying *per* is not infrequently separated by tmesis from its word; for example, Cicero, *On the Orator*, I.49: “It seemed exceedingly [*per*] strange to me”; II.67: “It seems exceedingly [*per*] clever to me.” I confess, however, that neither *perperspicax* nor any similar compound with a double *per* has so far occurred to me. ORELL.

This matter could have provided us with a shortcut. That is: “This matter could have allowed us to discharge the subject in very few words.” *Dare compendium*, “to provide a shortcut,” is a rather unusual manner of speaking. ORELL.]

## XIII

Or, if because of its novelty you refuse to understand the matter in this way, how do you know whether there is not some single being who takes the place of all those whom [Note: [Col. 1025A] “Into whom,” manuscript. Meursius conjectures “of those whom.”] you invoke, submitting himself to all parts of places and their divisions and presenting to you the appearance of many divinities and powers?

“Who is this single being?” someone will ask. Perhaps we can name him on the authority of truthful authors; but lest you refuse to believe us, let him ask [Note: [Col. 1026A] Thus Sabaeus; others, “ask them.”] the Egyptians, Persians, Indians, Chaldaeans, Armenians, and all those others who, through the more inward arts, have seen and learned these things. Then you will certainly learn who the one God is, or who the many beings beneath him are who pretend to be gods and make sport of the ignorance of the human race.

For some time now we have been ashamed to come to a point where not only little boys and the impudent cannot restrain their laughter, but even serious men hardened into the grim harshness of their character. For [Col. 1027A] since we have all received it as communicated and handed down by our teachers that, in the declensions of the gods’ names, there are no plural numbers, because the gods are each single beings, and the specific character of each name could not pass collectively through many beings [Note: [Col. 1027B] “Because they are,” Fulvius.]—for by the nature of things it is impossible that what is one should become two, and that unity should pass into different things, divided despite its innate simplicity—you have become forgetful, with recollection of your elementary lessons laid to rest, and have placed several gods beneath the same names. Although you are otherwise more restrictive about their number, you have again made them multiple through shared surnames.

Long ago, indeed, men of acute judgment and penetrating intelligence explained this part of the subject in both Latin and Greek. And this matter could have provided us [Col. 1027B] with a shortcut, if we did not see that some people are unacquainted with those writings, and if the discourse we have undertaken did not itself compel us to bring forth something concerning these matters, even though borrowed from and already related by those writers. [Col. 1028A]

[Note: [Col. 1027D]

## XIV.—Your theologians therefore say, etc.

Arnobius borrowed this and what follows from Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, III.21 ff. Compare with these L. Ampelius, *Book of Memorials*, chapter 9, and Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation to the Greeks*, p. 24, Potter’s ed. ORELL.

[Col. 1028B] That there are three Jupiters in the universe. Cicero, in the passage cited: “To begin with, those who are called theologians enumerate three Jupiters. Of these, the first and second were born in Arcadia: one with Aether as father—this Jupiter, they also say, fathered Proserpina and Liber—and the other with Heaven as father; he is said to have fathered Minerva, whom they declare to be the originator and inventor of war. The third is the Cretan Jupiter, son of Saturn, whose tomb is shown on that island.” Clement speaks somewhat differently in his *Exhortation*, p. 24: “There are,” he says, “some who record three Zeuses: one, the son of Aether, in Arcadia; the other two, sons of Cronus, one of these in Crete and the other again in Arcadia” (Εἰσὶν οἳ τρεῖς τοὺς Ζῆνας ἀναγράφουσιν· τὸν μὲν Αἰθέρος ἐν Ἀρκαδίᾳ· τὼ δὲ λοιπώ, τοῦ Κρόνου παῖδε· τούτοιν τὸν μὲν ἐν Κρήτῃ· θάτερον δὲ ἐν Ἀρκαδίᾳ πάλιν). Ampelius agrees with him; see the most recent editor, Tzschuck, there, p. 103 ff. Compare Lactantius, I.11. ORELL.

Both born on the island of Crete and consigned to burial there. Callimachus, *Hymn to Zeus*, verses 8 ff.:

> Cretans are always liars; for the Cretans, O Lord,  
> Even fashioned a tomb for you. But you did not die, for you exist forever.

(Κρῆτες ἀεὶ ψεῦσται· καὶ γὰρ τάφον, ὦ ἄνα, σεῖο  
Κρῆτες ἐτεκτήναντο, σὺ δ’ οὐ θάνες· ἐσσὶ γὰρ αἰεί.)

See Spanheim there. Compare Lactantius, I.22; Minucius Felix, *Octavius*; Augustine, *City of God*, VII.4. ELMENH. and ORELL.

Five Suns ... of whom, as they report, the first Sun is called the son of Jupiter and is held to be the grandson of Aether. Cicero, in the passage cited: “How many Suns themselves are produced by the theologians? One of them was born from Jupiter and was the grandson of Aether.” Compare Ampelius, chapter 11. ORELL.

The second was likewise the son of Jupiter and is reported to have Hyperiona as his mother. Thus the manuscript. Cicero: “The other Sun was born from Hyperion.” Hence Sabaeus, the first editor, recast the passage on his own judgment thus: “The second was produced from Regina and Hyperion as father.” Theodore Canter, in *Various Readings*, II.11, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, III, p. 748 ff., defends this reading against Gelenius’ alteration, “the second was produced from Rhea and Hyperion as father,” demonstrating that the Great Mother is called Βασίλεια (*Basileia*), that is, “Queen,” by Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, III, p. 190, and by Augustine, *City of God*, II.4. But the manuscript reading, first restored to Arnobius by Stewechius and followed by Heraldus and the Leiden editor, is confirmed by a parallel passage in Arnobius himself below, chapter 22 of this book: “From Hyperiona as mother, you say, and from Jupiter, hurler of the thunderbolt, the golden and most blazing Sun was born.” Our author therefore followed a tradition different from Cicero’s.

Moreover, all authors except Arnobius agree that Hyperion was the father of this second Sun. They do not similarly agree concerning his mother: Hesiod calls her Theia in the *Theogony*, verse 371, as does Pindar at the beginning of *Isthmian* V; Apollodorus, I.2 §2, calls her Euryphaessa; Homer likewise in the *Hymn to the Sun*, verse 4. See Tzschuck on the passage of Ampelius cited above, p. 107. ORELL.

The fourth, father of Ialysus. Cicero adds: “of Camirus and Lindus.” [Col. 1029A] Tzetzes on Lycophron, verse 922: “Lindus, Ialysus, and Cameirus are cities of Rhodes, named after the descendants of Helios and Rhodos, or of Rhodos and Poseidon” (Λίνδος καὶ Ἰήλυσος καὶ Κάμειρος πόλεις εἰσὶ Ῥόδου, ἀπὸ τῶν ἐγγόνων Ἡλίου καὶ Ῥόδης, ἢ Ῥόδης καὶ Ποσειδῶνος). Davies on the passage of Cicero cited above, p. 303, second ed.

Whom Acantho bore at Rhodes in the heroic age. Should we not read: “Whom Rhodos bore to Acanthus in the heroic age”? For in the preceding passages not only the mothers but also the fathers of the gods are mentioned; and Rhodos, though as Neptune’s wife, is mentioned in the passage of Tzetzes just cited, whereas Acanthus occurs nowhere among the ancients as a woman’s name. Yet I would not venture to decide anything in a matter wholly uncertain and doubtful.—Thus ORELL. at first. But he later added:—Our annotation on these words should be deleted. For Cicero’s passage, *On the Nature of the Gods*, III.21, demonstrates that the received reading “whom Acantho bore at Rhodes” is entirely sound: “The fourth Sun is he whom Acantho is said to have borne at Rhodes in the heroic age, the grandfather of Ialysus, Camirus, and Lindus.” In copying this, however, Arnobius erred by calling that Sun the father, rather than the grandfather, of Ialysus. Compare Johannes Meursius, *Rhodes*, I.4, p. 10 ff. ORELL.

The fifth is held to be [the son] of the Scythian king and [the father] of the shape-shifting Circe. “Scythian king,” that is, king of Colchis. Ampelius, chapter IX: “The fifth was the son of Colchus, from whom Circe, Medea, and Phaethon were born.” Cicero, however—whom our author copied throughout almost this entire chapter—in agreement with most other [Col. 1029C] genealogies of the gods, makes the Sun the father of Circe, saying: “The fifth, who is said to have begotten Aeëtes and Circe in Colchis.” Hence I suspect that our passage should be recast thus: “The fifth is held to be the son of the Scythian king and the father of the shape-shifting Circe.” Moreover, Pliny, *Natural History*, book VII, chapter 57, mentions yet another Sun, a son of Ocean, to whom Gellius had attributed the invention of medicine from honey. See Tzschucke on Ampelius, book I, p. 109. ORELLI.

Now the first Mercury, who is said to have neighed lustfully after Proserpina with his genitals erect, is the offspring of highest Heaven. Cicero, book I, chapter 22: “One Mercury was born of Heaven as father and Day as mother; his sexual organ is said to have been aroused because he was stirred by the sight of Proserpina.” Moreover, *adhinnire* properly means “to neigh after.” Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*:

> For he, that adulterer under the guise of a god,  
> Was the first to neigh after Tuscan girls.

And Arnobius himself below, book V, chapter 22: “Did he neigh after even his mother, even his daughter, with the desires [Col. 1029D] of a savage heart?” ELMENHORST. Oudendorp illustrates this construction with many examples in his note on Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 70, p. 281, and in the Addenda, p. 1022. Thus Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* I, p. 7: “to feel Venus toward someone”; and Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, chapter 22: “He relates that Jupiter . . . . . enticed by the thong of Venus, lay with his wife Juno more ardently than he was accustomed to lie with adulteresses.” Meursius correctly restored “Now the first Mercury” in place of “For,” which was previously read. ORELLI.

The other is beneath the earth, the one proclaimed to be Trophonius. Cicero, book I: “The other, the son of Valens and Phoronis—or, as Davies suspects it should be read, Coronis—is the one believed to be beneath the earth, namely Trophonius.” ELMENHORST. Ampelius: “The second was the son of Jupiter and Cronia, or of Proserpina.” Servius on *Aeneid* IV, 877, represents him as the son of Liber and Proserpina. Pausanias in the *Boeotica*, p. 785, and Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*, book VIII, chapter 19, make Trophonius the son of Apollo. See Davies on Cicero, book I. ORELLI.

The third was born of Maia as mother and of Jupiter—but the third Jupiter. [Col. 1030A] Cicero: “The third was born of the third Jupiter and Maia; from him and Penelope they say that Pan was born.” ELMENHORST.—Ampelius: “The third was the son of Cronus and Maia, and was the inventor of the lyre.” ORELLI.

The fourth is the offspring of the Nile, whose name the Egyptian nation shrinks from and reverentially avoids uttering. Cicero: “The fourth had the Nile [Col. 1030B] as his father; the Egyptians consider it impious to name him.” ELMENHORST.—Davies, on Cicero, book I, observes an equal superstition among the Jews concerning the divine name. Ampelius does not recognize this fourth Mercury, but confuses him with the following one. ORELLI.

The fifth is the slayer of Argus, a fugitive and exile, and the transmitter of letters in Egypt. Cicero: “The fifth, whom the people of Pheneus worship, is also said to have slain Argus and for that reason to have fled to Egypt, where he gave the Egyptians laws and letters. The Egyptians call him Thoth. The first month of their year is called by the same name.” Ampelius: “The fourth was the son of Cyllenius, who taught the Egyptians letters and number.” Compare Diodorus Siculus, *Library* I, chapter 16. “Slayer of Argus”: Ἀργειφόντης (*Argeiphontēs*, “Argus-slayer”). ORELLI.

But there are also . . . . . five Minervas. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, chapter 23: “The first Minerva is the one whom we said above to be the mother of Apollo; the second was born of the Nile and is worshipped by the Egyptian people of Sais; the third is the one whom we said above to have been begotten by Jupiter; the fourth was born of Jupiter and Coryphe, daughter of Ocean, and the Arcadians call her Coria and say that she invented the four-horse chariot; the fifth was the daughter of Pallas, and is said to have killed her father when he attempted to violate her virginity; they attach winged sandals to her.” Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus* (p. 24, ed. Potter):

> There are also some who posit five Athenas: the Athenian one, daughter of Hephaestus; the Egyptian one, daughter of the Nile; the third, daughter of Cronus, the inventor of war; the fourth, daughter of Zeus, whom the Messenians have surnamed Coryphasia after her mother; and last of all, the daughter of Pallas and Titanis, daughter of Ocean, who impiously sacrificed her father and is adorned with her father’s skin as though with a fleece.

CANTER.—Compare Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, chapter 17, p. 436, ed. Gronovius, and L. Ampelius, chapter 9. ORELLI.

The first was not a virgin but, by Vulcan, became the mother of Apollo. Ampelius, Julius Firmicus in book I, and Clement make her the daughter of Vulcan who founded Athens. ORELLI.

The second was the offspring of the Nile and is said to be the Egyptian Sais. Davies, on Cicero, book I, ably defends this entirely correct reading of the manuscript against the Leiden editor, who wrongly removed the word *Sais*. From Pausanias’ *Boeotica*, book IX, chapter 12 (p. 560, Frankfurt ed.), he shows that Sais was the name not only of an Egyptian city but also of the Minerva worshipped there. Compare Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XI, chapter 16, vol. II, p. 214. Plato in the *Timaeus*, and our author below in chapter 16, nevertheless relate that the proper name of Minerva among the Egyptians was Neith (Νῆϊθ). Moreover, on the worship of the Minerva of Sais, see Herodotus, book II; Plutarch, *On Isis and Osiris*, chapter 36; Origen, *Against Celsus*, book III, p. 256; Athenagoras, *Apology for the Christians* (p. 26, ed. Rechenberg). Julius Firmicus: “There was another in Egypt, the daughter of King Nile and mistress of the art of weaving.” ORELLI.

The third is the offspring of Saturn and devised the use of arms. Julius Firmicus: “The third, however, was begotten by Saturn as her father. But they record that she was a warrior-woman; for she never confined herself within the modesty of the female sex, but pursued arms, the din of battle, and the bloody pursuits of war.” Ampelius, however: “The third was the daughter of Jupiter, who exercised herself in the business of war.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1031B] The fourth is the offspring of Jupiter, whom the Messenians call Coryphasia. This has been translated word for word from Clement. Julius Firmicus gives a different account: “The fourth was the daughter of the Cretan king Jupiter, and she reported to her father that Liber had been killed.” And Ampelius: “The fourth was the daughter of the Sun and yoked four-horse chariots.” ORELLI.

And the fifth is the one who killed her father Pallas when he sought an incestuous union with her. Thus Gelenius and the other editors. The first Roman edition, from the manuscript, has *Corypallantem*, from which Fulvius Ursinus reconstructed *Corya Pallantem*. But, as Heraldus rightly observes, the first syllables appear to have been transferred here from the preceding passage, where he names Minerva “Coryphasia.” For the other [Col. 1031C] authors whom we have cited agree on the name Pallas. Julius Firmicus, book I: “The fifth was born of Pallas as father and Tritonis as mother. Because she was called Pallas after her father’s name, she was named Pallas by humankind. In parricidal madness, at the instigation of furious frenzy and insane recklessness, she butchered her father Pallas in a cruel death. Not content with the mere death of her father, so that she might enjoy her evils for longer and triumph more cruelly over her father’s death, she adorned herself with the spoils of his body, so as to make the crime of her parricide public through this cruel display. The Palladium—horrible to say!—was consecrated in her name.” Ampelius more briefly: “The fifth was the daughter of Pallas and Titanis. She killed her father in defense of her virginity, because he lusted after her. Hence she was also called Pallas.” The name Pallas is nevertheless better derived ἀπὸ τοῦ πάλλειν τὸ δόρυ, “from brandishing the spear.” Compare Dresen on Joseph of Exeter, book II, verse 272. ORELLI.]

## XIV

Your theologians, therefore, and the compilers of accounts concerning hidden antiquity, say that there are three Jupiters in the natural order: one of them was begotten by Aether as his father, another by Heaven, and the third by Saturn; this last was both born and committed to burial on the island of Crete [Note: [Col. 1027B] Fulvius wrongly reads “brought forth.” Below: “The third was born of Maia and begotten [Col. 1028B] by Jupiter.”]. They say that there are five Suns and five Mercuries. Of the Suns, as they relate, the first is called the son of Jupiter and is held to be the grandson of Aether; the second is likewise the son of Jupiter [Note: [Col. 1028B] The manuscript omits this. Otherwise see the Note.] and is represented as having Hyperiona for his mother; the third was born of Vulcan—not the Lemnian Vulcan, but the one who [Note: [Col. 1028B] Unless the manuscript is corrupt.] was the son of the Nile; the fourth, whom Acantho bore on Rhodes [Col. 1029A] in the heroic age, was the father of Ialysus; the fifth is held to be [the son] of the Scythian king and [the father] of the shape-shifting Circe.

Now the first Mercury, who is said to have neighed lustfully after Proserpina with his genitals erect, is the offspring of highest Heaven. The other is beneath the earth, the one proclaimed to be Trophonius. The third was born of Maia as mother and was begotten by Jupiter—but the third Jupiter. The fourth is the offspring of the Nile, whose name the Egyptian nation [Col. 1030A] shrinks from and reverentially avoids uttering. The fifth is the slayer of Argus, a fugitive and exile, and the transmitter of letters in Egypt.

But, they say, just as there are five Suns and Mercuries, so there are also five Minervas. Of these, the first was not a virgin but, by Vulcan, became the mother of Apollo; the second was the offspring of the Nile and is said to be the Egyptian Sais. The third is the offspring of Saturn and devised the use [Col. 1031A] of arms; the fourth is the offspring of Jupiter, whom the Messenians call Coryphasia; and the fifth is the one who killed her father Pallas when he sought an incestuous union with her.

[Note: [Col. 1031C]

## XV

“And lest it seem lengthy and excessive to wish to proceed little by little through every individual heading.” This reading comes from the royal manuscript. Previously the text read “and excessively minute.” *Minutatim* (“little by little”) is a Lucretian word: II, verse 1130; V, 708, 724; [Col. 1031D] and several other places. HERALD.

“There are four Vulcans.” See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III, chapter 24, and Ampelius, chapter IX. ORELLI.

“Three Dianas.” Cicero, book I, chapter 23; Ampelius, book I. ORELLI.

“The same number of Aesculapiuses.” Cicero, book I, chapter 22; Ampelius. ORELLI.

“Five Dionysuses.” Cicero, book I, chapter 23; Ampelius. Diodorus Siculus, however, mentions only three in *Library* III, p. 207. ORELLI.

“Three pairs of Herculeses.” Cicero, book I, chapter 16; Ampelius, in the passage cited. Herodotus, book II, chapters 43–44; Diodorus Siculus, *Library* III, pp. 207–208; and Arrian, *Expedition of Alexander*, book II, chapter 16, count only three. See Davies on Cicero, book I. ORELLI.

“Four Venuses.” Cicero, book I, chapter 23, and Ampelius enumerate the same number. Plato, in the *Symposium* (p. 182, vol. X, Bipontine ed.), posits only two. ORELLI.

“Three races of Castors.” Cicero, book I, chapter 21. ORELLI.

“And the same number of Muses.” Cicero, book I, chapter 21, where [Col. 1032B] see Davies, p. 301, second edition. Compare our observations above on book III, chapter 37. ORELLI.

“Triads of winged Cupids and four-horse teams of Apollonian names.” Τριάδας καὶ τετράδας, “groups of three and four.” On this manner of speaking, many observations were made formerly by Cujas and Scaliger, and recently by Isaac Casaubon on Vopiscus. HERALD. Joseph Scaliger, on Propertius, book III, elegy 21, verse 15, observes that the Greeks use συνωρίδα (“a pair of horses”) and τετρωρίδα (“a team of four”) in the same sense, and illustrates this form of speech with many examples. Moreover, Cicero, book I, chapter 23, enumerates four Apollos with our author; Ampelius, chapter 9, however, enumerates five, following Aristotle as his authority, as does Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus*, p. 24, ed. Potter. Clement notes that Didymus the grammarian adds a sixth, the son of Magnes. Cicero relates similar things about the triad of Cupids in the same chapter. ORELLI.

“Or, if one of these is he, it will be unknown and unknowable, because he has been blinded by the confusion of similar names.” Thus all editors before the Leiden editor, who recast the passage as follows: “Or, if one of these is he, it will be unknown and unknowable what he is, blinded by the confusion of similar names.” I do not approve of this correction. For the context seems to require “who he is,” namely, which god; and I greatly prefer the old reading, with the following sense: “Or, if one of these is he”—a god—“it will be unknown and unknowable, because he has been blinded by the confusion of similar names”; that is, obscured, so that he cannot easily be distinguished. Cicero uses “blind” in the same sense of speech that is “blinded by its rapid speed” in *Brutus*, chapter 76. The reading there, however, is doubtful, since others read “driven.” In the same sense the ancients use “blind” countless times for something hidden or difficult to recognize. See Gesner in the *Thesaurus* and Semler’s index to Tertullian. But our passage could perhaps be more conveniently recast by a very slight change: “Or, if one of these is he, it will be unknown and unknowable who he is, since such persons are blinded by the confusion of similar names”—a Greek construction in place of “by the blinding confusion of similar names.” ORELLI.]

## XV

And lest it seem lengthy and excessive to wish to proceed little by little through every individual heading, these same theologians say that there are four Vulcans and three Dianas, the same number of Aesculapiuses, five Dionysuses, three pairs of Herculeses and four Venuses, three races of Castors and the same number of Muses, triads of winged Cupids, and four-horse teams of Apollonian names. In the same way they identify their fathers and mothers and the places in which they were born, and display the origin of each together with his lineage.

But if this is true and certain, and is demonstrated by an affirmation based on knowledge of the facts, either they are not all gods—since, as [Col. 1031B] we have learned, several cannot exist under the same name—or, if one [Col. 1032A] of these is he, it will be unknown and unknowable, because he has been blinded by the confusion of similar names. And thus, through your own doing, however unwilling you may be to bring it about, religion is left disturbed and wavering, with no certain goal toward which it can direct itself, mocked by errors of ambiguity that admit no end.

[Note: [Col. 1032D]

## XVI

“Suppose, then, that we have been moved either by adequate authority or by the force of the terror you inspire.” This is Gelenius’ most felicitous correction of the manuscript reading, “or moved for that reason by authority.” I certainly do not know what moved the Leiden editor to alter this to “or moved by authority.” Yet “adequate authority” is sound, that is, authority that is sufficient, just as among legal writers “adequate resources” means sufficient resources, and “adequate persons” means persons to whom money may properly and safely be entrusted. See Stewechius. ORELLI.

“Minerva, for example.” Lucretius, III, 423 following:

> And when, for example, I proceed to speak of the soul,  
> Teaching that it is mortal.

HERALD.

“To render at blazing altars the offerings appointed for her.” This is the proper term. Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 194:

> [Col. 1033B] On platters broad we render smoking entrails.

Servius notes there that “render” is a sacrificial term. Thus “to render incense,” “to render wine,” and similar expressions. HERALD.—Compare C. Barth on Statius, *Thebaid* IV, 466, where he discusses this verb at length, and Voss on Virgil in the passage cited. ORELLI.

“The name of Minerva, together with her divine power, is mine.” I printed this following the correction of the Leiden editor. Previously the reading was: “My name is Minerva’s, then the divine power.” But *tum* as a connective is never used unless either another *tum* or some other corresponding word has preceded it. Fulvius Ursinus therefore conjectured that one should read “and the divine power.” ORELLI.

“The fifth Minerva will say.” Thus Gelenius and the others. In the first edition “the fourth” was read, through an obvious error. ORELLI.

“You are merely clanging.” Thus the Leiden editor very shrewdly corrected the manuscript’s *tutunis*, from which Stewechius made *tutun’ es*. Gelenius conjecturally reconstructed “you may be,” and most of the later editors followed him. But I greatly prefer *tu tinnis*: “you clang,” that is, “you chatter; you speak empty things.” Thus Plautus, *Pseudolus*, act III, scene II:

> Do not be excessively troublesome; now you are clanging, and I do not like it.

See Lambinus and Gronovius there. The metaphor is drawn from bronze vessels, bells, and casks, which are properly said to “clang” or “ring”; hence also *tintinnabulum*, “bell.” ORELLI.

“You have been diminished in the sanctity of pure chastity.” These words are exceedingly explicit—καὶ ἐμφατικώτατα (“and most emphatic”). By “pure chastity” he means virginity. For a virgin is pure and intact, and chaste, because she has not known the works of Venus. Below, book VII: “because she is pure in untouched virginity.” And “to diminish virginity” is the proper expression—that is, to violate that integrity. Plautus, *Cistellaria*, act I, scene I: “Nor has anyone else diminished my chastity”; and Arnobius himself, book V: “by which he might diminish in chastity his mother, who feared nothing of the sort.” Hence Ausonius, in the *Nuptial Cento*, used “diminution” for first intercourse. “The sanctity of chastity” is also correct. For chastity and virginity are sacred and inviolable even among restrained enemies. Accordingly Scipio, in Livy, when he hands down to posterity a great example of self-restraint and has not violated even with his eyes the integrity of the captive maiden who was brought to him, says: “For my own sake and that of the Roman people I would act so that nothing which has hitherto been sacred among you should be violated. Now your own excellence and dignity also cause me to take greater care of the matter.” HERALD and ELMENHORST.—Similarly Curtius, book III, chapter 12, §21, on Alexander: “He treated virgins of outstanding beauty as sacredly as if they had been born of the same parent as himself”; and book IV, chapter 10, §53: “The queen was treated chastely and sacredly.” Bunemann supplies more examples in his note on Lactantius, *Institutes* VI, chapter 24, pp. 844 following. Joseph Scaliger explains at length the force [Col. 1034B] of the verb “diminish” in his note on *Priapea*, poem XXXII, line 2, in P. Burmann’s *Latin Anthology*, vol. II, p. 505. ORELLI.

“Do you not see that in all Capitolia the images of the Minervas are virginal?” Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book III, and Vitruvius, *On Architecture* I, chapter 7, attest that there were three shrines—σηκούς—in the Capitol, belonging to Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva; this arrangement was also imitated in the colonies. Hence Arnobius said “in all Capitolia.” [Col. 1034C] Therefore, when Cicero, Aurelius Victor, and Tertullian call the Capitol the dwelling place of all the gods, this must be understood not of the temple but of the Capitoline hill itself, which everywhere, and almost in its entirety, was occupied by altars, statues, and temples of the gods. See Justus Lipsius, *On the Greatness of Rome* III, chapter 5, *Works*, vol. III, p. 770, Wesel ed.; and Justus Rycquius, *Commentary on the Roman Capitol*, chapter 9, p. 107. ORELLI.

“Among whom I am called Neith in their language, as Plato’s *Timaeus* testifies.” Plato, *Timaeus*, p. 21, ed. H. Stephanus:

> There is in Egypt, he said, in the Delta, around the point at which the stream of the Nile divides, a district called the Saite district. The greatest city of this district is Sais, from which King Amasis also came. The city’s founder-goddess has the Egyptian name Neith, but in Greek, according to their account, Athena.

Chalcidius translates it thus: “There is a region of Egypt called the Delta, at whose apex the streams of the Nile divide; near these is a great city named Sais, governed by an ancient custom called the Saite law. From this city came the emperor Amasis; the divine founder of the city is designated Neith in the Egyptian language and is called Athena in Greek.” ELMENHORST.—Chalcidius most absurdly interprets νομός, that is, the Saite *nome* or district, as “law.” ORELLI.

“Whose name is Coryphasia,” etc. On this name see P. Victorius, *Various Readings* XI, chapter 15. ORELLI.

“Or will the one who is third patiently surrender the name?” Canter restored the passage in this form. The manuscript corruptly reads “will surrender the name to patience.” The Leiden editor rewrites it “will patiently yield in respect of the name,” which is more elegant. But “to surrender something” is by no means uncommon. Thus in P. Burmann’s *Latin Anthology*, book IV, epigram 154, p. 112, vol. II:

> And learned Pedana surrendered the pleasing lyre.

“Do you, Sais, born from mud, dare to appropriate to yourself the majesty of my name?” I have not hesitated to restore to Arnobius the entirely correct reading of the manuscript. For Minerva had two names among the Egyptians, Neith and Sais. See above on chapter 14. Gelenius, failing to understand this, conjecturally printed: “to appropriate, she who was born from mud.” Others read: “To appropriate. If it is true, from mud.” Meursius in the Appendix: “to appropriate the uncorrupted majesty, from mud,” etc. Salmasius: “to appropriate, from mud.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1035B] “But as for you, assume another dignity for yourself.” These are the words of the third, Saturnian Minerva to the fourth, Coryphasian Minerva. This correction by Salmasius is therefore excellent. Previously the text read: “or you assume for yourself a dignity belonging to another.” In what follows it had “and concerning,” etc., in place of “the goddess who.” Meursius, in the Appendix, thinks it should read: “You assume the dignity of the goddess who, from the crown,” etc. Scriverius, in the same place: “You assume the dignity and from the crown,” etc. ORELLI.

“Does he beget sons conceived from his head?” Nothing should be changed. For he asks whether Jupiter conceives sons in his head and begets them. The other proposals are therefore pointless. HERALD.—Others read: “Were you conceived from Jupiter’s head?” Meursius conjectures “daughters conceived.” Incorrectly. “Sons” means children, sons and daughters, just as “brothers” includes brothers and sisters, and “gods” gods and goddesses. See Burmann on Quintilian, *Institutes* IX, chapter 3, §63, p. 517. ORELLI.

“Tongs.” Thus Elmenhorst and Salmasius, entirely correctly. Others read “shears.” The first edition has “arches.” ORELLI.

“Offering-wines (*inferia vina*) to be poured from golden bowls.” From the manuscript Ludovicus Carrio admirably restored the passage thus in *Emendations* II, chapter 3, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, part II, pp. 134 following, where he discusses these words extensively; see also Meursius, p. 131. Previously the text read, “wine to be poured into a jar.” Arnobius himself below, book VII, chapter 31, drawing on Trebatius, gives an excellent explanation of what *inferia vina* are. *Inferium vinum* was namely wine that is brought in or offered—a χοή (“libation”) in Greek. Festus, however, deriving the term from *infra* (“below”), says that *inferium vinum* was the wine placed below the lip of the bowl during sacrifice. See the commentators there and on the word *Calpar*. Hence the formula of libation: “Jupiter, be increased and honored by this inferial wine.” Had this formula not been employed, all the wine was withdrawn from human use and made sacred to Jupiter. See Paulus Leopardus, *Emendations* XVIII, 16, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, part I, p. 338; Nicolaus Loensis, *Epiphyllidean Questions* III, chapter 12, in vol. V of the same work, p. 358; Schneider, the distinguished scholar, on Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 132, p. 167; Johannes Saubertus, *On Sacrifices*, chapter 25, [Col. 1035D] p. 590, ed. Crenius; and Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. ORELLI.

“Arbitrator.” The glosses: “arbitrator,” διαιτητής. Festus: “An arbitrator is said to be a judge who has decision and power over the whole matter. He is appointed by the praetor or chosen by agreement of the litigants.” ELMENHORST.

“Will have such a mighty neck.” That is, will be so strong, bold, and shameless. The phrase is Ciceronian, from *Against Verres* III, chapter 59: “What recuperators will have necks so mighty that they dare, in a province and in the praetor’s presence, to judge not only against his wishes but even against his interests?” Our Arnobius undoubtedly imitated that passage. As Hotman rightly observes there, the metaphor is taken from oxen, of which those with the stoutest necks are judged the strongest. ORELLI.

“To award rightful provisional possession.” Asconius on Cicero, *Against Verres* III: “A dispute over provisional possession occurs when litigation before the praetor concerns a thing whose rightful possessor is uncertain,” etc. [Col. 1036B] Thus “to award provisional possession” was the act of a praetor assigning the disputed object to the claimant, that is, decreeing possession to him. Compare Festus under this word; Gellius, *Attic Nights* XX, chapter 10, with the notes there and Gronovius’ excursus; Heineccius, *Antiquities of Roman Law*, on the *Institutes* IV, title VI, vol. II, pp. 225 following; Vincenzo Gravina, *On the Origin of Law*, p. 183; and Adams, *Handbook of Roman Antiquities*, vol. I, pp. 411 following. ORELLI.

“Or attempt to pronounce the sacramental stakes unjust.” Varro: “The money brought into court in lawsuits is called *sacramentum* from *sacer*, ‘sacred.’ In some cases both claimant and denier deposited five hundred asses with the pontiff; in other cases each deposited a fixed, different number of asses. The man who prevailed at judgment recovered his own sacramental stake from the sacred fund. That of the defeated party reverted to the treasury.” The plaintiff therefore challenged the defendant by a formal wager, so that he must either acknowledge the debt or make a counter-stipulation. The custom is extremely ancient. Aristophanes in *Wealth*:

> What penalty, then, shall I enter against you in the suit [Col. 1036C] if you are convicted?  
> **Answer:** Whatever you please.

But this passage can be understood of a simple wager. Yet the man who summoned a debtor to law at the same time deposited the πρυτανεῖα, that is, the sacramental stakes, and compelled the debtor to do likewise. Aristophanes in the *Clouds*:

> For everyone to whom I happen to owe money is swearing.  
> He says that I shall lose the court-fees for your sake and be utterly destroyed.

Here the scholiast writes at greater length: “By depositing with the prytaneis a tenth of the debt, they brought the debtors into court; the *prytaneia* are what are now called *sportulae* among the Romans.” Later: “It was a sum of money deposited by both litigants, both the defendant and the prosecutor.” HERALD.—Festus, agreeing with Varro, adds: “The bronze money began to be called by the name *sacramentum* because, both on account of the treasury’s poverty and the great number of public rites, it was expended on divine matters.” See the commentators there and on Valerius Maximus VII, chapter 7, §2; Heineccius, *Antiquities of Roman Law*, vol. II, pp. 231 following. ORELLI.

“Will he not rather go home?” Like Blepharo in Plautus’ *Amphitryon*:

> Settle it between yourselves; I am going away. I have business elsewhere.

HERALD.

“Incur the charge of stupidity.” Similarly Lactantius, *Institutes* II, chapter 7, at the end: “I shall incur the charge of loquacity.” Bunemann, p. 214, illustrates with many examples that this expression is customary among the sacred writers, Jerome, Ambrose, and others. ORELLI.]

## XVI

Suppose, then, that we have been moved either by adequate authority or by the force of the terror you inspire, and have resolved, for example, to worship Minerva according to your solemn rites and the customary ritual. If, when we prepare the divine ceremonies and proceed [Note: [Col. 1031B] Sabinus reads “and should proceed.”] to render at blazing altars the offerings appointed for her, all the Minervas fly to us and, contending over possession of that name, each demands that the sacrificial provision be rendered to herself, what shall we, frail creatures, do in their midst? Or to which side [Col. 1032B] shall we preferably transfer the duties of our pious service?

For perhaps that first Minerva whom we mentioned will say: “The name of Minerva, together with her divine power, is mine—I who gave birth to Apollo and Diana, and through the fruit of my womb increased heaven’s divine powers and multiplied the number of the gods.”

“No indeed,” the fifth Minerva will say; “you are merely clanging, you who have been married and have given birth so many times, and have thereby been diminished in the sanctity of pure chastity. Do you not see that in all Capitolia the images of the Minervas are virginal, and that none of the artists gives them the forms of married women? Cease, therefore, from claiming for yourself the name of a right that is not yours. For the entire chorus of poets, which calls me Pallas, deriving my surname from my father, bears witness that I am Minerva, begotten by Pallas as my father.”

“What are you saying?” the second will ask upon hearing this. “Do you, then, bear [Note: [Col. 1033B] Sabinus reads ‘will you bear.’] the name of Minerva, you wanton parricide, polluted by the contamination [Note: [Col. 1033B] The manuscript deletes ‘by.’] of incestuous love? While you painted yourself and adorned yourself with the arts of a prostitute, you aroused your father’s mind toward you, filling it [Col. 1034A] with frenzied lusts [Note: [Col. 1033B] Fulvius reads ‘entirely full.’]. Go on, then; seek [Note: [Col. 1034B] Others read ‘to seek.’] another designation for yourself. For this title is my property: I whom the Nile, greatest of rivers, generated from its liquid waters and condensed into a virginal form through the coagulation of its dew. If you seek assurance of the fact, I too shall offer the Egyptians as witnesses; in their language I am called Neith, as Plato’s *Timaeus* testifies.”

What, then, do we suppose will happen? Will that one whose name is Coryphasia cease to call herself Minerva, whether from the designation of her mother Coryphe or because she flashed forth from the very crown of Jupiter’s head, bearing a shield and girded with the terrors of arms? Or will the one who is third patiently surrender the name, without taking account of herself in words of this kind and refuting the arrogance of the first claimants?

“Do you, Sais, born from mud [Note: [Col. 1034B] Fulvius reads ‘since from mud.’ See the Note.] [Col. 1034B] and produced from swirling depths, coagulated out of slime, dare to appropriate to yourself the majesty of my name? But as for you [Col. 1035A], assume another dignity for yourself—you goddess who falsely claim to have been begotten from Jupiter’s crown and persuade the supremely foolish mortals that you are Reason. Does he beget sons conceived from his head? So that the weapons you carry could be forged and manufactured, was there a smith’s workshop in the hollow of that very crown—anvils, hammers, furnaces, bellows, charcoal, and tongs? Or, if what you assert is true and you are Reason, cease from claiming for yourself that name which is mine. For the Reason of which you speak is not a definite form of divine power, but the understanding of obscure causes.”

If, therefore, as we have said, when we approach to perform religious duties, five Minervas present themselves and, quarrelling over the exclusive ownership of this name, each desires either that incense-smoke be offered to herself or that offering-wines (*inferia vina*) [Col. 1036A] be poured for her from golden bowls, by what umpire, by what judge, shall we settle controversies so great? What investigator, what arbitrator, will have a neck mighty enough to attempt, between persons of this kind, either to award rightful provisional possession or to pronounce the sacramental stakes unjust? Will he not rather go home and, keeping himself apart from affairs of this sort, judge it safer to have nothing to do with any of these matters, lest by giving to one what belongs to all he make enemies of the rest, or incur the charge of stupidity if he assigns to all what ought to have belonged to one alone?

[Note: [Col. 1036D]

## XVII

“Whose numbers you stretch and multiply.” Stewechius corrects this to “whose numbers you extend, you multiply,” which accords with Arnobius’ habit [Col. 1037C] of omitting conjunctions. I nevertheless would not venture to change anything. Stewechius also alters the preceding words “about all the others” to “about all the other divine powers.” ORELLI.

“Excess.” See above on chapter 10. ORELLI.

“Worthy of the estimation attaching to so great a name.” Here too Meursius wishes to restore “so great a divine power.” ORELLI.]

## XVII

We can set forth the same arguments concerning the Mercuries and Suns—indeed, concerning all the others whose numbers you stretch and multiply. But it is enough to know from one example that the same reasoning applies to the rest; and lest excessive length perhaps produce disgust in our audience, we shall cease to proceed through the individual cases, so that, while accusing you of excess, we ourselves may not incur the fault of immoderate loquacity.

What do you say, you people who invite us to the worship of the gods by the mutilation of our limbs, and compel us to undertake the worship of your divine powers? We can refrain from being difficult, provided only that something worthy of the estimation attaching to so great a name is shown to us. Show us Mercury—but one Mercury. Give us Liber—but one Liber; one Venus, and likewise one Diana. For you will never persuade us that there are four Apollos or three Jupiters—not even if you summon Jupiter himself as a witness or appoint the Pythian Apollo as your authority.

[Note: [Col. 1037C]

## XVIII

“As it seemed good and became settled.” *Sedere* means “to be pleasing,” or “to be fixed and firmly resolved.” Virgil, *Aeneid* V, 418:

> And this resolution is pleasing to pious Aeneas; its sponsor Acestes approves;

and VII, verse 611:

> When the fathers’ fixed decision for war is settled.

Florus, book II, chapter 15, §4: “When war was resolved upon, negotiations concerning the end of the war were undertaken.” See Duker there, and Freinsheim in his Index, where he also cites our passage. [Col. 1037D] Compare Perizonius on Sanctius’ *Minerva* IV, chapter 4, p. 114; and Savaro on Sidonius, book IV, letter 15, p. 276. ORELLI.

“Have produced a licentious fiction.” Thus all editions. The manuscript has “have produced it through licentious fiction,” which, with Stewechius, I would prefer to the common reading. ORELLI.

“That which has been placed in the midst.” That is, what has been made public, as Lucretius had just expressed it, book V, verse 1159:

> And to bring into the midst sins long concealed.

So also the Greeks. Heraclitus, quoted somewhere by Plutarch: “It is not better to conceal ignorance, but to place it in the midst and cure it.” Similarly εἰς μέσον φέρειν, “to bring into the midst”; εἰς μέσον ἕλκειν, “to drag into the midst”; and like expressions. HERALD.

“From human writings about them.” Thus Salmasius. The manuscript has “from things described by men.” Fulvius Ursinus reads “things described by men,” omitting “from,” which Stewechius approves. ORELLI.

“That no mortal had ever written anything about the gods.” This too is a correction by the Leiden editor. The manuscript and first edition have, very corruptly: “that no mortal at any time, that there is nothing concerning the gods.” From this Gelenius reconstructed “remembered anything concerning the gods.” Heraldus prefers “made anything known concerning the gods,” that is, φανερῶσαι, γνωρίσαι, “to reveal, to make known.” But I prefer Salmasius’ correction because of what follows: “whom no acquaintance with any writing had formed in your minds.” ORELLI.]

## XVIII

But someone, taking the opposite side, says: “How do we know whether the theologians wrote down things investigated and known, or whether, as seemed good and became settled in their minds, they produced a licentious fiction?” That has no bearing on the case. The point of the present argument does not rest on whether matters are as the theologians’ writings indicate, or whether they stand otherwise and are separated from them by a great difference. For it is sufficient for us to speak about things that have been made public, and not to inquire what accords with truth, but to refute and disprove that which has been placed in the midst and which human opinion has embraced.

But if those writers are liars, then you must explain what the truth is and disclose the irrefutable secret. And how can that possibly be done [Note: [Col. 1037C] Thus the manuscript; others read “how is it possible?”] once the instruction supplied by literature has been removed? What can be said about the immortal gods that has not reached human understanding from human writings about them? [Col. 1037C] Or can you yourselves relate anything concerning their rites [Col. 1038A] and ceremonies that has not been committed to writing and made public in authors’ commentaries?

Or, if you judge these writings to have no weight, let all the books you possess about the gods—books composed by theologians, pontiffs, and even some devotees of philosophy—be abolished. Indeed, rather let us suppose that, from the beginning of the world, no mortal had ever written anything about the gods. We wish to make the experiment and desire to know whether you could mutter or open your mouths when the gods are mentioned, or form in your minds conceptions of gods whom no acquaintance with any writing had formed in your souls.

But since it is established that you learned their names and powers from the books that supplied them to you, it is unjust to detract from the credibility of those writings by whose testimony and authority you confirm the very things that you say.

[Col. 1038B] [Note: [Col. 1038C]

## XIX

“Both being human.” Thus Meursius and the Leiden editor. Gelenius reads “on both sides.” ORELLI.

“To charge it with caprice and falsehood.” Some, including Meursius, rewrite this as “with capricious falsehood,” in the same way that he said above “a licentious fiction.” I would not rashly change anything. Arnobius therefore means a fiction arising from the poets’ caprice and pleasure: because, evidently, it pleased them to fabricate and devise the things that they afterward committed to writing. HERALD.—Elmenhorst [Col. 1038D] thinks it should read: “to charge it with falsehood capriciously.” ORELLI.]

By the rights shared by the human race and by the fellowship of mortality itself. This manner of adjuring or entreating is highly elegant: intact, indeed, in this passage, but elsewhere interpolated more than once, as I have shown in the *Apuleian Questions*. STEWECH.—We have a splendid example in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book VI, at the beginning: “By that fruit-bearing right hand of yours, I beseech you; by the harvest rites that bring gladness; by the silent mysteries of the caskets; and by the winged chariots of the dragons that serve you,” etc., etc., “come to the aid of the soul of pitiable Psyche, your suppliant.” See the interpreters there, p. 385, Oudendorp’s edition, and Elmenhorst in the Index. ORELLI.

Or when you suppose that you exist in this way. Fulvius Ursinus prefers “that they exist.” But nothing should be changed. “That you exist in this way,” that is, that you have arisen from the lowliness of an earthly stock. ORELLI.—*Arbitrari* (“to suppose”) is used here in the sense of “to judge,” a meaning frequent in the writings of Apuleius and Plautus. STEWECH.

Lest you incur any offense in the eyes of the gods themselves. Book V: “Although you could incur a single fault.” ELMENHORST.

[Col. 1039B] By the services of obscenity. *Obscoenitas* here means the obscene male member. See Bunemann on Lactantius, *Epitome*, ch. 23, p. 1240. ORELLI.

Of that name. Meursius: “of that divinity.” ORELLI.

Or gods exempt from birth, etc. I do not know what came into Stewechius’ mind when he corrupted this thoroughly sound—indeed, uniquely correct—reading by substituting *expertos* (“having experienced”), from a manuscript. Yet it is clear that *expertes* (“exempt”) must be read from the opposition immediately following: “Or, if they have any origins.” ORELLI.]

### XIX

Unless, perhaps, these things are false, while those which you say are true. By what argument? By what sign? For since both groups were human beings—those who devised these accounts and those who devised the others—and since each side has disputed about uncertain matters, it is arrogant to say that what pleases you is true, while accusing whatever offends your mind of wanton invention and falsehood.

By the rights shared by the human race and by the fellowship of mortality itself: when you hear and read, “From that father and that mother this god was born,” does not some awareness stir within your minds that something human is being said, something proceeding from the lowliness of an earthly stock? Or, when you suppose that you yourselves came into being in this way, do you feel no anxiety lest you incur some offense [Col. 1038C] in the eyes of the gods themselves, whoever they may be, [Col. 1039A] because you believe that through shameful intercourse and the emission of seed they emerged into a light previously unknown to them, through the service of the obscene male member?

For our part—lest anyone perhaps suppose that we are ignorant and do not know what befits the dignity of that name—we certainly judge that gods ought to be exempt from birth. Or, if they have any origins, we hold and believe that they were sent forth by the Lord and sovereign of all things, according to principles known to him alone: unstained, utterly chaste, pure, knowing nothing of that foulness of copulation, with primary generation ending at their own level.

[Note: [Col. 1039B] Fulvius reads *emissos*, “sent forth.”]

[Note: [Col. 1039B]

### XX.—And enter into marital covenants after terms have first been sought

So the manuscripts and other witnesses commonly read. Hence the formula: “I do not accept your terms.” Thus in Quintus Curtius, book IV, ch. 5, where Darius offers his daughter to Alexander in marriage and, as dowry, whatever lies between the Hellespont and the Euphrates, Parmenion says: [Col. 1039C] “It is an excellent thing that a kingdom can be acquired by an agreement, not by war.” HERALD.—Compare G. Cortius on Pliny, book I, letter 10, and book VI, letter 32, pp. 42 and 472 of Longolius’ edition. ORELLI.

By use, spelt-cake, or purchase. According to Servius on Virgil’s *Georgics*, book I, verse 30, all these belonged to the ancient rites of marriage. Among the ancients, he says, marriages were contracted in three ways: BY USE, if, for example, a woman had lived with a man for a year, even without legal formalities; BY SPELT-CAKE, when they were joined through the chief pontiff and the Flamen Dialis by means of grain and salted meal—whence it was called *confarreatio*—and children with both parents living were born from such marriages; but BY PURCHASE and the convention of coming under the husband’s authority, when the woman came into the position of a daughter and the husband into that of a father, so that, if either died first, the other would inherit. See Brissonius, *On the Ancient Rite of Marriage*, in Graevius’ *Thesaurus of Roman Antiquities*, vol. VIII, pp. 1016–1128; he explains these ancient rites and what Arnobius presently adds concerning women hoped for, covenanted, betrothed, and Fescennine verses. NOURRIUS.

[Col. 1039D] They mutually stipulate the sacred rites of the bridal bed. The common edition reads “they bring together,” whose absurdity Ursinus also perceived, as did our Modius; both agree with me. Not much farther below Arnobius calls them “the covenants of the bridal bed”; Apuleius, in book IX of *The Ass*, speaks of “the covenant of the bridal couch.” There is an allusion to the nuptial formula by which mutual fidelity was pledged: “Where you are Gaius, I am Gaia.” That formula had the following origin. The wife of Tarquinius Priscus, king of the Romans, was named Gaia Caecilia; afterward her name was frequently used at weddings for the sake of a good omen, according to Festus, to whom Plutarch in the *Roman Questions* should be added. On the bridal bed, after Guilielmus Canterus and Joseph Scaliger, consult Justus Lipsius, *Selections*, book I, ch. 17, and Plutarch, *Roman Questions* 2. STEWECH.—He properly said “sacred rites.” The aforesaid ceremonies were employed to ratify and confirm the marital covenant. They were therefore like certain mystical signs and, furthermore, as it were, sacred bonds of mutual fidelity. HERALD.

[Col. 1040B] They have women hoped for; they have women covenanted. Nonius, p. 439, Mercer’s edition: “The distinction between a woman hoped for, one formally named, one covenanted, and one betrothed is this: before a maiden is sought in marriage, she is called ‘hoped for.’” Plautus, *Amphitryon*:

> Amphitryon gladly greets his hoped-for wife.

Thereafter she may be called promised, formally named, covenanted, or betrothed. Virgil, *Aeneid*, book II:

> To whom I, once named as your bride by father and husband, am abandoned.

And likewise elsewhere (*Aeneid* X, 79):

> And tear the covenanted brides from their embraces.

Titinius in *Quintus*: “When, at the appointed age, the bride has been formally betrothed.” Compare Juretus on Symmachus, book IX, letter 40, p. 216, Lectius’ edition. Among the ancients a girl was called *pacta* (“covenanted”) when [Col. 1040C] agreement had been reached about the marriage on definite terms; but when formal stipulations had been exchanged and the betrothal celebrated, she was then called *sponsa* (“betrothed”). See Reuschius on Juvencus, *Gospel History*, book I, verse 139, p. 34. ORELLI.

They have betrothed women after stipulations have been exchanged. Plautus in the *Curculio*:

> Do you pledge this woman to me as wife, soldier?  
> **SOLDIER:** I pledge her.

In the *Trinummus* (Act II, Scene IV):

> Without a dowry I ask your sister for my son—  
> May the matter turn out well. Do I have her covenanted? Why are you silent?  
> **S.** By the immortal gods! What sort of proposal is this?  
> **PH.** Come, speak! May the gods make it turn out well.  
> **S.** I pledge her.

Later:

> Now I ask your sister for my son—  
> May the matter turn out well. What? Are you still deliberating?  
> **L.** What is this? Since you wish it so, may the gods make it turn out well: I pledge her.

Here you have a complete stipulation and, once the stipulation is exchanged, [Col. 1040D] the betrothal pledge. HERALD.

And because they had not taken part in the Fescennine verses. Fescennine verses were customarily sung by boys and consisted of shameful words, full of every kind of wantonness and obscenity; hence Chrysostom calls such jests ῥήματα αἰσχρὰ καὶ ἀσχημοσύνῃ γέμοντα, “shameful words filled with indecency.” They were called Fescennine either from Fescennium, a town of Etruria, or from *fascinum*, “the phallus.” PRIOR.—Lucan II, 368:

> The customary jests were not exchanged, nor, in Sabine fashion,  
> Did the gloomy husband endure the festive taunts.

HERALD.

They threw everything into turmoil with their quarrels, etc. Arnobius alludes to the exceedingly famous golden apple of Eris and the resulting dispute among Juno, Minerva, and Venus, disastrous for the Trojans. ORELLI.

And against the human race thereafter? etc. Should we not read: “And sowed inhuman hazards of destruction against the race thereafter”? ORELLI.

Sowed. So Meursius and all who follow him, entirely correctly. Previously *saevisse*, “raged,” was printed. ORELLI.]

### XX

But you, on the contrary, forgetful of their majesty and such great sublimity, attach to them such births and ascribe to them [Col. 1039B] origins which people of somewhat refined intelligence [Col. 1040A] would regard with both execration and horror. From their mother Ops, you say, and their father Saturn, Jupiter was born together with his brothers.

Do gods, then, have wives, and do they enter into marital covenants after terms have first been sought? Do they mutually stipulate the sacred rites of the bridal bed by use, spelt-cake, or purchase? Do they have women hoped for, women covenanted, women betrothed after formal stipulations have been exchanged? And why do we speak of the unions themselves, when you say that certain gods even celebrated weddings and held festive gatherings, and that goddesses played at these; and that, because they had not taken part in the Fescennine verses, they threw everything into turmoil with their quarrels and sowed hazards of destruction [Col. 1040B] against the human race thereafter?

[Col. 1041A] [Note: [Col. 1041B]

### XXI.—Father of gods and human beings

Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, ch. 25: “But Jupiter himself—that is, the helping father, whom, by an interchange of cases, we call Jove from ‘helping’—is called by the poets the father of gods and human beings.” ELMENHORST.—This expression is taken from Homer, in whom Jupiter is repeatedly called πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε, “father of both men and gods.” See Dio Chrysostom, orations XII and LIII; Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras*, §39; Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*, book IV, §30; Davis on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, ch. 2, p. 112. ORELLI.

Making the whole heaven move and tremble with his brow and nod. This too is taken from Homer, *Iliad* I, 528 ff. [Col. 1041C] Compare Davis on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, 2. ORELLI.

And immediately preserved the life entrusted to him by nourishment from another’s breast. Varro in Nonius: “Having food placed before him, sitting high at another’s expense.” Lactantius too, a most eloquent writer, used this word. *Institutes* VII, ch. 4: “The world, therefore, was made by God, certainly not for the sake of the world itself; for, since it lacks sensation, it needs neither the sun’s heat, nor the moon’s light, nor the blowing of winds, nor the moisture of rains, nor the nourishment of crops.” And ch. 5: “So that, by the abundance of crops and living plants, it might provide nourishment for each kind according to its nature and use.” HERALD.—See Bunemann on Lactantius at the passage cited; he illustrates the rather rare word *alimonia* with numerous examples, p. 874. “From another’s breast,” that is, not his mother’s. Arnobius is referring to the goat Amalthea, who fed Jupiter with her milk. ORELLI.

Thundering, flashing, hurling thunderbolts, and gathering terrifying clouds. Βροντητής, ἀστεροπητής, ἀστράπτης, νεφεληγερέτης: “Thunderer, lightning-flasher, wielder of the lightning, cloud-gatherer.” Apuleius, *On the World*: “Jupiter is called both the producer of lightning, the thunderer, and the hurler of thunderbolts.” HERALD and ELMENHORST.—*Fulgurans*, “flashing,” [Col. 1041D] which appears in the Leiden edition, is Stewechius’ correction. Previously the text read *fulgens*, “shining.” ORELLI.

In order to cease his exceedingly prolonged crying. *Exponeret*, found in the manuscript, was first restored to Arnobius by Thomas Canterus, whom the Leiden editor followed. Others read *poneret*. But among writers of that period *exponere* not infrequently means *deponere*, “to put down, cease.” See Salmasius on Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, p. 352, and Semler’s *Index of Latinity in Tertullian*. Thus a toga is *exponitur*, “laid aside”; in the fragments of Hilary, *exponere episcopos* means “to depose bishops”; and Arnobius himself below, ch. 26, says: “to lay aside the name of virginity.” For “exceedingly prolonged,” Stewechius thinks we should read “exceedingly tossed,” or rather “exceedingly touched”—namely by mothers or nurses, so that they may soothe children and induce sleep. Plautus alludes to this in the *Amphitryon*:

> But if I stroke him continuously, so that he sleeps.

Burmann, in the Addenda to Claudian, p. 1019, conjectures “exceedingly broken crying”; but that would [Col. 1042B] produce an unpleasant repetition with the following words, “broken tones.” Nor can an infant’s cry, which is always the same and nearly of a single note, be called “broken.” Nothing at all should be changed: *tractus fletus* means the same as “prolonged, continuous crying.” Thus in Cicero, *On the Orator* II, §159, sustained and flowing speech is contrasted with speech that is tightly wound and sharp. ORELLI.

And soothed by broken tones. This comes from Lucretius V, 231:

> The gentle and broken speech of the nurturing nurse.

That is, when affectionate nurses babble in imitation of babbling little children. For “broken” properly describes [Col. 1042C] the speech of infants. Minucius Felix, ch. 2: “And—what is especially lovable in children—while their years are still innocent and they are still attempting half-formed words, their speech is made sweeter by the very brokenness of their stumbling tongue.” Saint Jerome to Salvina, *On Preserving Widowhood*: “Let her chattering and babbling speech be sweeter through the stumbling of her tongue.” HERALD.—Thus Philo too, in his book *On Agriculture*, calls theatrical music κεκλασμένην μουσικήν, “broken music,” that is, soft and effeminate, unworthy of masculine ears. HERALD, likewise, on the cited passage of Minucius, p. 11, Gronovius’ edition.

Is born. So the manuscript. See above on book II, ch. 43. Lucretius uses this verb in book III, verse 798:

> That the whole can endure outside the body and be born.

Varro, *On Agriculture* I, ch. 40: “The first seed, which is the principle of begetting, is twofold.” Likewise II, ch. 6: “Because they are born resembling their parents,” etc.; and Censorinus, ch. 3: “Whether because he ensures that we are born, or because he is born together with us, or because he receives and protects us once born, the Genius is certainly so called from begetting.” [Col. 1042D] These passages were cited by Meursius in his Appendix. Others read “is begotten.” ORELLI.]

### XXI

But perhaps in the other cases the foulness of this disgrace is less conspicuous. Was that ruler of the firmament, then—the father of gods and human beings, who makes the whole heaven move and tremble with his brow and nod—formed from a man and a woman? And unless both sexes, their bodies coupled, had surrendered themselves to obscene pleasures, would that greatest Jupiter never have existed? Would the divine powers down to this very day have had no king, and heaven have stood without a lord?

And why should we marvel that you repeatedly declare Jupiter to have poured forth from a woman’s womb, when your authors write that he even had a nurse and immediately preserved the life entrusted to him by nourishment from another’s breast? What are you saying, men? Was he, then—I ask again—the god who thunders, shines, hurls thunderbolts, and gathers terrifying clouds, one who sucked streams from breasts, uttered an infant’s wail, crawled, and, in order to cease his exceedingly prolonged crying, [Col. 1041B] fell silent [Col. 1042A] upon hearing rattles; one who was lulled to sleep while lying in the softest cradle and soothed by broken tones?

O religious defense of the gods! O exposition and commendation of the venerable dignity of their awe-inspiring grandeur! Is this, I ask, how the eminence of the heavenly powers is born among you? Do your gods come forth into the light through the same processes of generation by which asses, pigs, and dogs—by which this whole unclean flood of earthly beasts—is conceived and born?

[Note: [Col. 1042D]

### XXII.—These unions

This too is an excellent correction from the manuscript in place of *coitus*, “acts of intercourse,” as formerly read. Following the old manuscript, we shall restore *coetum*, “union,” to Arnobius at least three times; and besides Lucretius, whose phrasing this author seems especially to have loved, it will be shown below that Cicero himself spoke in the same way. STEWECH.

You proclaim that he begot children more shamefully than he himself was born and brought forth. Stewechius restored this most certainly correct manuscript reading to Arnobius, and the Leiden editor followed him. Others, including the most recent editor Oberthür, follow Gelenius’ interpolation: “You proclaim that he begot children, was born, and was brought forth.” Others: “You proclaim that he begot the one whom you say was born and brought forth.” Both are wrong. ORELLI.

Bow-bearing. Thus above, book II, ch. 23: “a bow-shaped chair,” where see Herald’s note. ORELLI.

Diana, driver of the woods. Stewechius prefers [Col. 1043B] “dweller in the woods.” But the received reading, which came from the manuscript, is well defended by Burmann on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V, verse 605, vol. II, p. 371. “To drive wild beasts” is a very familiar expression for hunters. Hence, by a bolder metaphor, Arnobius called Diana “the driver of the woods,” that is, a huntress who drives the wild beasts in the woods. ORELLI.

And from the same father the Castors, whose Greek name is Dioscuri. Gelenius’ edition reads: “From the same father those whose Greek name is Dioscuri.” In the Roman manuscript “those” is absent, and there is a gap in its place. Yet to fill it we should apparently read not “those,” but rather “the Castors.” For in antiquity Castor and Pollux were called “the Castors,” and in Greek they are called Διόσκουροι, “sons of Zeus.” Thus our author in book I, ch. 36: “the Tyndarid Castors”; and in this same book, ch. 15: “three classes of Castors.” Minucius, *Octavius*, ch. 21: “The Castors die by turns so that they may live.” THOMAS CANTERUS. Compare Turnebus, *Adversaria* XV, ch. 21, p. 467. Salmasius quite correctly admitted Canterus’ emendation into the text. ORELLI.

Who is also called Bromius. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV, 11 ff.:

> They offer incense and call him Bacchus, Bromius, and Lyaeus,  
> Fire-born, twice-born, and the only one with two mothers.

ELMENHORST.—Βρόμιος, ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ τὴν γένεσιν αὐτοῦ γενομένου βρόμου, “Bromius, from the roaring that occurred at his birth,” as Diodorus Siculus says, book III, p. 149, and in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* II, ch. 2, p. 54. NOURRIUS, p. 394.

From the thigh. So Meursius in the Appendix and Stewechius from the manuscript, in place of “from seed,” which was formerly read. ORELLI.

Bearer of tractable snakes. “Tractable snakes” means tame, gentle, harmless snakes. ORELLI.

And, with the ardor of his inflamed heart, grew hot for female objects of desire. Below, ch. 26: “What shall I say about those passions by which, according to the account preserved in your writings and authors, the holy celestials grew hot for women?” [Col. 1043D] Ovid, *Tristia* III:

> That two goddesses grew hot with passion for their guest.

Horace, *Odes* IV.11.32:

> Hereafter I shall burn  
> For no other woman.

ELMENHORST.

When such great nobility commended her, her appearance, and the dignity of her countenance. Stewechius’ conjecture is clever but unnecessary: “when nobility commended her, and her splendid appearance”; no more necessary is Meursius’ “when such great nobility of appearance commended her.” For “the dignity of her countenance,” the manuscript has “countenance, dignity,” which is not bad. ORELLI.

The snow-white, marble gleam of her arms. Λευκώλενος Ἥρη, “white-armed Hera.” He has therefore reproduced Homer’s epithet. HERALD.

Not content with one wife. Quintilian, *Declamation* XIV: “I have always been content with one and the same courtesan.” Petronius: “Content with a widow, and a chaste one, for the night.” ELMENHORST.—The Greeks use ἀγαπᾶν, “to be content with,” in the same sense. ORELLI.

Mistresses. Thus the Greeks speak of ἐρωμέναι, “beloved women” or “mistresses,” and distinguish them from a lawful wife. Plutarch in the *Antony*: “For Octavia had united herself with him [Col. 1044B] for reasons of state, because of her brother, and enjoyed the title of lawful wife; but Cleopatra, though she ruled so many people, was called Antony’s mistress.” Thus Diogenes Laertius says that Lamia was the ἐρωμένη, “mistress,” of Demetrius of Phalerum—that is, his female companion and concubine—but calls Conon’s sister his wife. HERALD.

He scattered his incontinence everywhere. Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* II, p. 171: “Showing my uncontrollable desire for my Fotis.” ELMENHORST.—By *impatientia* he means the dishonorable irritation of lust. Elmenhorst explains this meaning with many examples in his index to Apuleius under this word; so too J. F. Gronovius, who treats the word at length in *Observations* IV, ch. 25, p. 817, Platuer’s edition. ORELLI.

As *babecali* young men are accustomed to do. Salmasius was the first to restore this uniquely correct reading to Arnobius from the manuscript. The same word also occurs in Petronius’ [Col. 1044C] *Satyricon*, ch. 37, at the end: “In short, she will toss any one of those *babaecali* onto a rue leaf”; there, however, it is variously printed, by some as *babaceli*, by others as *babaeculi*. If we read *babaceli*, it seems to derive from the Greek βαίκηλος or βάκηλος, and thence, by reduplication, βαβαίκηλος, just as βαβάζειν derives from βάζειν. Βάκηλος denotes a man of great stature but foolish or effeminate. Yet I prefer *babecalis*, a compound of βαβαί and καλοί, “ah, handsome!” And so it should be read in our author, yielding the sense “fine young gentlemen—if it please the gods.” It is, of course, spoken ironically: *unsere schönen, feinen jungen Herren*, “our handsome, refined young gentlemen.” Other interpreters, failing to understand the word, wrongly altered our passage. Gelenius, for example, prints “as young men are accustomed to revel,” a reading Herald defends and supports with many examples. “To revel” means to wander about with a certain wantonness and impudence, to scatter one’s lasciviousness, to roam and run about insolently, and, as it were, to frisk; it occurs in this sense in Lucretius V, 821 ff.:

> [Col. 1044D] At nearly a fixed season it poured forth every animal  
> That roams wildly everywhere upon the great mountains.

And Lampridius in *Commodus*: “He reveled in the palace amid banquets and baths.” Meursius conjectures “as young men are accustomed to roam,” in the same sense, with the approval of Rigaltius on Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams* II, ch. 53, p. 97, Reiff’s edition. But the manuscript reading *babecali*, in the sense we have explained, is preferable. ORELLI.

From innumerable bodies. Salmasius substituted “from finite bodies,” that is, mortal bodies. But nothing should be changed. “From infinite bodies” means “from innumerable bodies.” Meursius conjectures “from innumerable bodies entered,” that is, violated—not badly; *initis* could very easily have been swallowed up by the final letters of the preceding word. ORELLI.]

### XXII

Not content with attributing these unions to the august daughter of Saturn, you proclaim that even the king of the world begot children more shamefully than he himself was born and brought forth. From the mother Hyperiona, you say, and Jupiter the Hurler of the Thunderbolt, were born the golden, blazing Sun; from Latona and the same father, the bow-bearing Delian Apollo [Col. 1042B] and Diana, driver of the woods; from Leda and the same father, [Col. 1043A] the Castors, whose Greek name is Dioscuri; from Alcmena and the same father, that Theban Hercules, protected by his club and skin; from Semele and Jupiter himself, Liber, who is called Bromius and was born a second time from his father’s thigh; again from Jupiter himself and Maia, Mercury, eloquent in speech and bearer of tractable snakes.

Can any graver insult be inflicted upon your Jupiter? Is there anything else that could shake or destroy the authority of the chief of the gods more than your belief that he was at some time conquered by lustful pleasures and, with the ardor of his inflamed heart, grew hot for female objects of desire? And what business had the Saturnian king with other men’s marriages? Was Juno not enough for him? Was he unable to calm the violence of his desires upon the queen of the divine powers, when she was commended by such great nobility, [Col. 1043B] her beauty, the dignity of her countenance, and [Col. 1044A] the snow-white, marble gleam of her arms?

Or, not content with one wife and delighted by concubines, mistresses, and favorites, did that lustful god scatter his incontinence everywhere, as dandified young men are accustomed to do, and, though white-haired, restore from innumerable bodies the ardor of his flagging pleasures? What are you saying, impious people? What foul conceptions do you fabricate concerning your Jupiter? Do you not notice, do you not see, with what disgrace you brand him, of what crime you make him the author, or what stains of shameful acts and how great a mass of infamies you heap upon him?

[Note: [Col. 1044D]

### XXIII.—Yet they punish adultery by law and subject offenders to capital penalties

Here he makes adultery a capital offense, as do the author of the *Querolus*, p. 11; Ammianus Marcellinus, *History* XXVIII, p. 397; and Theodoret, discourse III *Against the Greeks*, p. 45. [Col. 1045B] At Rome it was punished not by death but by relegation. The emperor Tiberius was the first to increase the penalty: deportation for men, and deportation with confiscation of property for women. Constantine the Great was the first to punish the crime of adultery capitally and to punish by the sword those sacrilegious violators of marriage. See Cujacius, *Observations* VI, ch. 11; Brissonius on the Julian Law concerning adultery, p. 91; Theodorus Marcilius on Justinian’s *Institutes*, p. 755.
