ELMENHORST.—But intercourse with low-born women and public prostitutes went unpunished, [Col. 1045C] because they considered that no one was properly injured by it. Plautus, *Curculio*:

> No one here prohibits or prevents you  
> From buying what is openly for sale, if you have the money.  
> No one prevents anyone from walking on the public road,  
> Provided he does not make a path across enclosed land.  
> So long as you abstain from wife, widow, maiden,  
> Youth, and freeborn boys, love whatever you please.

Thus, provided they abstained from the bodies of others and of the freeborn, they could pour out their lust everywhere without any fear of disgrace. Therefore, concerning Sossianus, who had violated slave women, the emperors Diocletian and Maximian ruled that his reputation had been burdened rather than afflicted with infamy. From this alone, therefore, it is evident how blind human wisdom is. HERALD.

By the storming of another’s bridal bed. Saint Cyprian: “That assailant of another man’s marriage.” Zeno of Verona, in his sermon *On Patience*: “Yet in the very enjoyment of his deed, in which he is accustomed to rejoice over the stain of another’s violated chastity, he is always unhappy.” Nor did Arnobius say “bridal bed” without purpose. For he thus signifies that even the γαμήλιον θεόν, “god of marriage,” is violated. Apuleius, [Col. 1045D] *Milesian Tale* II: “And certainly refrain from a sexual bond with your hostess, and religiously respect the bridal couch of the honorable Milo.” HERALD.

The character of a prowler and adulterer. *Subsessores* are those who lie in wait for women in order to commit adultery. Valerius Maximus II, ch. 1, §5: “For at that time no one feared the eyes of those lying in wait for other men’s marriages.” See the interpreters there and Taubmann on Virgil, *Aeneid* XI, p. 974. ORELLI.

Of what stigma. Glosses: “*Nota*: ψόγος, σπῖλος”—“reproach, stain.” Papias: “*Nota*: sin, disgrace, stain.” Nonius: “*Nota* means reproach.” Lucilius, book XXX:

> Whom you know to know all your stains and stigmas.

ELMENHORST.

*Amissis* (“lost”). So Meursius and Salmasius, excellently, in place of *amissi*. ORELLI.

Maltreatment. Below, book V: “Even so, however, you are not free from maltreatment of the gods.” HERALD.—Compare Turnebus, [Col. 1046B] *Adversaria* XI, ch. 20, and Pontanus on Macrobius, *Saturnalia* V, ch. 17, p. 543, Zeunius’ edition. ORELLI.

That could turn Jupiter’s eyes toward itself. Meursius excellently restored the passage in this form. Previously it read: “that could turn Jupiter’s eyes away from there.” ORELLI.

O splendid reward of guilt. Because the manuscripts had *o gra merces*, I thought it might be read “O great reward.” Plautus similarly has “a great sum of money.” See the *Commentaries on Vegetius* on book III, ch. 7, p. 289, Wesel edition. STEWECH.]

### XXIII

Though human beings are prone to lust and, through the weakness of nature, inclined toward the enticements of pleasure, they nevertheless punish adultery by law and subject to capital penalties those whom they discover to have flung themselves against another’s marital covenant by storming the bridal bed. Did the greatest of kings not know how shameful was the character of a prowler and adulterer, or what stigma it bore? And did that observer, as report has it, of both good deeds and very evil ones fail—after losing the counsels of his mind—to perceive what it was proper for him to desire?

Perhaps even this maltreatment could be tolerated if at least you joined him with persons of equal rank, and if you represented him as the adulterous lover of immortal goddesses. But in human bodies, I ask, what beauty was there, what comeliness that could arouse Jupiter and turn his eyes toward itself? Skins, entrails, phlegm, and that entire discharge of the intestines enclosed beneath their coverings—something at which not only Lynceus, with his penetrating vision, might recoil in horror, but which anyone else would avoid even in thought.

O splendid reward of guilt! O worthy and precious delight, for whose sake [Col. 1045B] Jupiter the Greatest became a swan and a bull—and the begetter of gleaming white eggs!

[Col. 1046A] [Note: [Col. 1046B]

### XXIV.—To look upon the truth in its own form

[Col. 1046C] Stewechius’ conjecture “the manifest truth” is wonderfully attractive—that is, truth laid open and exposed to the eyes of all. See above on book II, ch. 57. ORELLI.

The afflictions of the human race. *Labores* here means calamities or hardships, as it very often does. ORELLI.

That certain gods were born from eggs. This was most correctly restored by the Leiden edition. Previously the reading was: “were born from Jupiter.” Arnobius is alluding either to the Castors or, more probably, to the Syrian gods, whom above, book I, ch. 36, he called the offspring of eggs. ORELLI.

That the whiteness of Cytherean Venus took shape and congealed. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, ch. 8: “They say that he”—Saturn—“cut off the genitals of his father Caelus; when they were cast into the sea, Venus was born, and from the foam out of which she congealed she received the name Aphrodite.” See Pontanus there. ORELLI.

Surely it was not we who said that Saturn was bound on a charge of parricide and relieved of the great weight of his bonds only on his own festival days. J. Lipsius, *Epistolary Questions* III, letter 15, *Works*, vol. I, p. 532, Wesel edition, restored the text by this elegant conjecture. For the ancient belief was that during his own days—that is, the Saturnalia—[Col. 1046D] Saturn again became, as it were, master of his kingdom, but spent the rest of the year in chains. Lucian, *Cronosolon*: “He was neither shackled nor full of squalor, as the painters represent him … but held his sickle, very sharply honed; in all other respects he was cheerful and vigorous and was equipped like a king.” The first edition was exceedingly corrupt: “Saturn, and from these days to be raised by such great weights of bonds.” From this Gelenius produced: “and on his own days to be relieved of such great weights of bonds.” Meursius, however: “and on some days to be relieved of such great weights of bonds.” The manuscript has: “and to be washed clean on so many days,” etc. Salmasius defends this in the Leiden edition and on Solinus, ch. 15, p. 132, recasting the passage thus: “And on fixed days to be washed clean, released from and relieved of the weights of his bonds.” Salmasius thinks *ablui*, “to be washed clean,” was used for *absolvi*, “to be released,” just as Cicero, *On Friendship*, ch. 21, uses *dilui*, “to be dissolved”: “friendships should be gradually dissolved rather than torn apart.” To this may be added another almost identical passage of Cicero, *On Duties* II, [Col. 1047A] ch. 33: “Wise men think that friendships which are less pleasing and less approved should be gradually dissolved rather than suddenly cut off.” But since in both passages of Cicero the best manuscripts and most reliable editions have “unstitched” and “to be unstitched,” and since *ablui* is nowhere else found in the sense “to be released,” [Col. 1047B] I have preferred to follow Lipsius’ correction. “On his own days” is also much more expressive of the Saturnalia than “on fixed days.” ORELLI.

That Jupiter was saved from destruction through the service of the Curetes. See above on book III, ch. 41. ORELLI.

Surely it was not we who said that he drove his father from the throne, etc. Minucius Felix, ch. 22: “Saturn, a fugitive from Crete, came to Italy in fear of his raging son. Received as a guest by Janus, he taught those rude and rustic people many things—as a refined little Greek would—such as imprinting letters, striking coins, and making implements. Accordingly, he preferred his hiding place to be called Latium because he had safely lain hidden there, and he gave the name Saturnia to a city from his own name … His son Jupiter reigned in Crete after expelling his father.” Compare Lucian, *Saturnalia*; Cyprian, *On Idols*; Lactantius I, chs. 13–14; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* III, ch. 3; Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 10. ELMENHORST.

Surely it was not we who said that the expelled old man lay hidden within the territory of the Italians, etc. So the parchment manuscripts, though the reading is undoubtedly corrupt. Gelenius and Elmenhorst read “expelled by Jupiter,” with Herald’s approval. Heinsius, letter 257 to J. G. Graevius, [Col. 1047C] in Burmann’s *Collection*, vol. IV, p. 329, corrects it to “expelled through Jupiter’s fault,” which Graevius approves in the next letter, p. 331. I think the passage can be healed merely by transposing one word and punctuating thus: “Surely it was not we who said this: that the expelled old man lay hidden within the territory of the Italians.” “Surely it was not we who said this” must be repeated from the words a little earlier: “Surely it is not said by us that certain gods were born from eggs, like storks or wood pigeons?” This emendation agrees equally well with what immediately follows: “Surely it is we who say that Jupiter himself contracted an incestuous marriage with his sister?” ORELLI.

And gave Latium its name in return for the service. See the passage of Minucius Felix just cited, and Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII:

> And preferred it to be called Latium,  
> Since he had lain safely hidden on these shores.

Compare Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I. ELMENHORST.

Surely it is we who say that Jupiter himself contracted an incestuous marriage with his sister? Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 14: [Col. 1047D] “Jupiter foully rutting upon his sister.” Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*: “As for Juno, they maintain—lest Jupiter should lack even incest—that she, his sister, was made his wife.” ELMENHORST.

Or that, invited to the privilege of the table, he unwittingly feasted upon Lycaon’s offspring in place of pork entrails. The manuscript has “in place of those entrails,” from which Stewechius thinks we should read “in place of sausage entrails.” We explained above, on book II, ch. 42, what *hirae* and *hillae* are. *Suillis*, “pork,” is Gelenius’ emendation. The story of Lycaon is well known, though related in various ways by the ancient mythographers. Compare Apollodorus, *Library* III, ch. 8, section 1, pp. 302 ff., Heyne’s new edition, where see the notes; Hyginus, fable 176, with Muncker’s commentary; Nicolaus of Damascus, p. 446; the *Suda* under Λυκάων; the scholiast on Lycophron, verse 481; and Ovid, who set it forth in most elegant verses, *Metamorphoses* I, 214 ff. Our author, however, follows Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation*, p. 11 (31, Potter’s edition): “Zeus himself also partook of a human table among the Ethiopians, [Col. 1048A] and of an inhuman and lawless one when entertained by Lycaon the Arcadian. At any rate, he gorged himself on human flesh, though not knowingly; for the god was unaware that Lycaon the Arcadian, his host, had slaughtered his own son—whose name was Nyctimus—and served him to Zeus as meat.” ORELLI.

Surely it was not we who said that one of them was lame in one foot, etc. [Col. 1048B] Clement mentions this matter as follows in the *Exhortation*, p. 8 (25, Potter’s edition): “Hephaestus, whom Zeus hurled from Olympus, ‘from the divine threshold,’ fell upon Lemnos and worked as a smith, crippled in both feet … ‘and beneath him his slender legs moved nimbly’” (Homer, *Iliad* XVIII, 410). THOMAS CANTERUS. These words remind me of the old custom of jokingly calling lame people “sons of Vulcan.” I note from the *Argonautica* of Orpheus, verse 211:

> Among them came Palaemonius, Lerna’s illegitimate son;  
> Both ankles were injured, and he was not sound in his feet;  
> Therefore everyone used to call him the offspring of Hephaestus.

MEURSIUS, p. 133.

Surely it was not we who said that, on account of desire and avarice, as the Boeotian Pindar sings, Aesculapius was pierced by the missile of a thunderbolt. The same Clement, p. 1: “You have among the gods not only a smith but also a physician. The physician, however, was avaricious; his name was Asclepius. And I shall set before you your own poet, Pindar the Boeotian” (*Pythian Ode* III, antistrophe 3).

[Col. 1048C]

> Gold, appearing in his hands,  
> turned even him aside with a splendid fee,  
> to bring back from death  
> a man already taken captive by it.  
> But the son of Cronus, hurling  
> with both hands, swiftly  
> struck the breath from his breast,  
> and the blazing thunderbolt  
> drove death into him.

Thus he lies there, struck by lightning, within the territory of Cynosuris.

And Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 14: “There is also that lyric poet—I mean Pindar—who sings that Aesculapius was condemned by the thunderbolt because of the greed with which he practiced medicine criminally.” CANTER and ELMENHORST. Tertullian likewise, *Apologeticum*, ch. 14: “There is also,” he says, “that lyric poet—I mean Pindar—who sings that Aesculapius was condemned by the thunderbolt because of the greed with which he practiced medicine criminally. Jupiter is evil, if the thunderbolt is his: irreverent toward his grandson and envious of the craftsman.” NOURRIUS, p. 398.

[Col. 1048D] **Deceived by the ambiguity of an answer.** See Lucian, *Dialogues of the Gods* XVI, “Juno and Latona”; Cicero, *On Divination* II, ch. 56; Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. XXII; Jerome, *On Isaiah*, ch. 41. ELMENHORST. Arnobius is referring to the story of Croesus and Pyrrhus, who were deceived by Apollo’s oracle. ORELLI.

**Have we publicly branded Mercury a thief?** That is, have we declared it publicly and shown no regard for his reputation? Below, in this same book (ch. XXXVI): “You should instead dismantle these theaters, in which the gods’ disgraceful deeds are daily exposed publicly in scandalous plays.” Tertullian, *Against the Jews*, ch. 10: “Except that here he was setting forth the Lord’s cross, by which the serpent, the devil, was publicly exposed.” That is, he was publicly displayed and marked out—just as the fate of those who are put to death in that way is made more public than if they were removed by some other kind of death. St. Ambrose, commentary 13 on Galatians ch. 3: “Because everyone who hangs upon a tree is accursed; so that it was sufficient for one condemned to death that he died suspended upon a tree, lest, if he remained suspended longer, his death should bring him greater disgrace than was fitting and become a stain upon his family, if his death were given still greater publicity.” There is therefore no reason to tamper with the passage of Tertullian, which he repeats in the same words in Book III *Against Marcion*. HERALD.—Compare Semler, *Index of Tertullian’s Latin*. [Col. 1049B] ORELLI.—Moreover, concerning Mercury the thief, Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*:

> Mercury, Maia’s son, initiated humankind,  
> previously inexperienced in stealing, into this art; now he  
> is held to be a mighty god, whose expertise produced thieves.

Compare Fulgentius, *Mythologies*, p. 171; Suidas, under Ἑρμῆς (*Hermes*) and Κερδῷος (*Giver of Gain*); Phurnutus, *On the Nature of the Gods*. ELMENHORST.

**That we are Laverna.** Salmasius printed, “that you are not Laverna”? For my part, I see no reason for alteration. ORELLI.

**Is Myrtilus an authority from among us, who declares that the Muses were the maidservants of Megaclo, Macar’s daughter?** Theodorus Canter restored our passage in this way, in *Various Readings* I, ch. 1, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, p. 712 ff., from Clement of Alexandria, who pursues this story at greater length in his *Protrepticus*, p. 9 (27, Potter ed.):

The Muses, whose descent Alca(n)der traces from Zeus and Mnemosyne, and whom [Col. 1049C] the other poets and prose writers deify and worship—indeed, entire cities now establish shrines of the Muses for these very Muses—were maidservants purchased by Megaclo, the daughter of Macar. Macar was king of the Lesbians, but he was continually quarreling with his wife. Megaclo was distressed on her mother’s behalf—and how could she not have been? She therefore purchased these maidservants, as many in number as they were, and called them *Mysae* in the Aeolian dialect. She taught them to sing and to accompany harmoniously on the lyre the deeds of ancient times. By continually playing the lyre and beautifully charming Macar with their songs, they delighted him and brought an end to his anger. In gratitude for this service to her mother, Megaclo dedicated bronze statues of them and ordered them to be honored in every sanctuary. Such, then, were the Muses; the story is found in Myrsilus of Lesbos.

Thus Clement. The earlier reading was: “Who declares that the Muses were Macar’s daughters and Megaclo’s maidservants”—a corrupt reading which, for some reason unknown to me, the Leiden editor retained. On Myrtilus [Col. 1049D] of Lesbos, see above on Book III, ch. 37. ORELLI.]

### XXIV

If you are willing to open the eyes of your minds and contemplate the truth itself without any private partiality, you will discover that the causes of all the miseries by which, as you say, the human race has long been afflicted [Note: [Col. 1045B] *Flictatur* in the manuscript] flow from such beliefs as you held in ancient times concerning your gods, and which, though the truth was set before your eyes, you refused to reform for the better.

For what improper thing have we ever thought about them, or published in shameful writings, so that the sufferings of the human race and the diminished resources by which life is sustained should be laid to our charge? Is it we who say that certain gods were hatched from eggs, like storks or doves? Is it we who say that the gleaming whiteness of Cytherean Venus congealed and took form from the foam of the sea and the severed genitals of Heaven? Is it we who say that Saturn was bound for parricide and is released from the great weight of his chains only on his own festival days? Is it we who say that Jupiter was saved from destruction through the kindness of the Curetes? Is it we who say that he expelled his father from his kingdom and held dominion belonging by right to another through violence and fraud? Is it we who say that the banished old man hid within the borders of the Italians and, because he had been safe from his son, bestowed upon Latium its name as a reward? Is it we who say that Jupiter himself contracted an incestuous marriage with his sister, or that, when invited to the privilege of the table, he unknowingly dined on Lycaon’s offspring in place of pigs’ entrails? Is it we who say that Vulcan, lame in one foot, practiced his smith’s craft on the island of Lemnos? Is it we who say that, because of lust and greed, Aesculapius was pierced by a thunderbolt, as the Boeotian Pindar sings? Is it we who say that Apollo, after becoming wealthy, deceived by the ambiguity of his answer those very kings whose treasures and gifts had enriched him? Have we publicly branded Mercury a thief? Do we say that we are Laverna [Col. 1049A] and that together with him we preside over furtive frauds? Is Myrtilus [Note: [Col. 1049A] *Myrsilus*, Fulvius] an authority from among us, who declares that the Muses were the maidservants of Megaclo [Note: [Col. 1049A] *Meglaco*, incorrectly in the Sabine manuscript], daughter of Macar?

[Note: [Col. 1049D]

### XXV—Who consecrated among the number of the gods Venus, a little prostitute enriched by a Cyprian king whose name was Cinyras?

Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus*, p. 5 (12, Potter ed.):

“For Cinyras, the Cyprian islander, will never persuade me—the man who, in his wantonness, dared to hand down by daylight the nocturnal orgies associated with Aphrodite, in his ambition to deify a prostitute who was his fellow citizen.”

Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 425, Gronovius ed.: “I hear that the Cyprian Cinyras gave a temple to his mistress, a prostitute; her name was Venus. He also initiated very many into the rites of the Cyprian Venus and assigned them to empty consecrations. He further ordained that anyone who wished to be initiated, once the secret of Venus had been imparted to him, should place a bronze coin in his hand as a fee for the goddess.” ELMENHORST.—See our author below, Book V, ch. 19; Lactantius I, ch. 20; and Lucian, *On the Syrian Goddess*. ORELLI.

**Who disclosed that the Palladium was constructed from the remains of Pelops?** Clement, Book I, p. 14 (41, Potter ed.):

“Many would perhaps be astonished if they learned that the Palladium called ‘fallen from Zeus,’ which Diomedes and Odysseus are said to have carried away secretly from Ilium and entrusted to Demophon for safekeeping, was fashioned from the bones of Pelops, just as the Olympian statue was made from other bones belonging to an Indian beast. And I refer anyone who wants an account of the matter to Dionysius, in the fifth part of his *Cycle*.”

Compare Julius Firmicus, who recounts the matter more fully in *On the Error of Profane Religions*, and Joseph Scaliger’s note there, p. 434 ff., Gronovius ed. ORELLI.

**Who said that Mars was a Spartan? Is not Epicharmus the authority?** etc. This passage too is taken from Clement, *Protrepticus*, p. 8 (24 ff., Potter ed.):

Ares, at any rate, who has been honored by the poets as highly as possible—

> Ares, Ares, bane of mortals, bloodstained, stormer of walls—

this fickle and accursed being was, according to Epicharmus, a Spartan; Sophocles knows him as a Thracian, while others call him an Arcadian.

CANTER.

**Who says that he was born within the borders of Thrace? Is it not the Attic Sophocles, with every theater expressing its assent?** Vegetius, *On Military Matters* I, final chapter, is also a witness, having been induced by the poets’ fables to say that Mars was born among the Thracians. I know that Euripides is among them, for I recall that he calls Thrace the dwelling place of Mars. Homer does likewise: in *Odyssey* VIII he sang that Mars, once released from Vulcan’s chains after being caught by him in adultery, immediately departed for Thrace. Mars certainly was a god of the Thracians, as Lycophron’s commentator attests, and was especially worshiped in the city named Crestone. Stephanus of Byzantium, *On Cities*, and Lycophron likewise, line 937:

> I shall swear by the god of Crestone.

Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XXVII, attests further that the Thracians customarily appeased Mars and Bellona with captives as sacrificial victims. On their ferocity, their greatness of spirit, and their contempt for life itself, consult Mela, Solinus, Herodotus, Florus, and others. Florus even records that those men were so warlike that they became accustomed to the standards, weapons, and even the discipline of the Romans. STEWECHIUS, on Vegetius I, p. 87, Wesel ed.; Hadrian Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus XXI, p. 420. ORELLI.

**Who says that he was bound for thirteen months in Arcadia? Is it not the son of the river Meles?** Clement, *Protrepticus*, p. 8 [Col. 1050D] (26, Potter ed.): “Homer says that he was bound for thirteen months” (*Iliad* V, 385 ff.):

> Ares endured it, when Otus and mighty Ephialtes,  
> the sons of Aloeus, bound him in a powerful chain.  
> For thirteen months he lay bound inside a bronze jar.

Arnobius therefore calls Homer the son of the river Meles, *Melesigenes* (Μελησιγενής), though he has understood this epithet differently from Herodotus, Plutarch, and Proclus in their *Lives of Homer*. They report that Homer was so named because the nymph Critheis, pregnant through a secret union, gave birth to him ἐπὶ τὸν ποταμὸν τὸν καλούμενον Μέλητα, that is, beside the river Meles near Smyrna. An uncertain author of an epigram in Brunck’s *Analecta*, vol. III, p. 255, nevertheless agrees with our author:

> Homer, son of Meles, etc.

Compare C. Barth on Statius, *Silvae* III, vol. I, p. 312. From this Meleager derived the phrase Μελητείους χάριτας, “Melesian Graces,” meaning Homer’s Graces or Muses; and Tibullus, in the *Panegyric to Messalla*, derived “Melesian pages.” See N. Heinsius, *Adversaria* I, ch. 8, p. 78 ff. Among the Greeks the name is therefore consistently Μέλης, genitive Μέλητος. Elmenhorst accordingly thinks that *Meletis* should be read. Moreover, John Jortin, in the work entitled *Philological, Critical and Miscellaneous Tracts*, London, 1790, vol. II, p. 139, most successfully restored this passage, badly dislocated in every edition, as follows: “Who says that he was in Arcadia? Is it not you? Who says that he was bound for thirteen months? Is it not the son of Meles,” etc. For here Arnobius copied Clement and followed him closely. Nor does Homer say that Mars was bound in Arcadia, but only that he was bound for thirteen months, without specifying a place. ORELLI.

**Who says that dogs were sacrificed to him by the Carians, and asses by the Scythians? Is it not chiefly Apollodorus, together with the others?** Clement, Book I, continues thus:

“May the Carians enjoy many blessings, since they sacrifice dogs to him; and let the Scythians never cease sacrificing asses, as Apollodorus and Callimachus say:

> Phoebus delights in the Hyperboreans’ sacrifices of asses.

And the same poet elsewhere:

> The rich sacrifices of asses delight Phoebus.”

On such sacrifices of dogs and asses, see C. Barth on Statius, *Thebaid* XII, 70, vol. III, p. 1440; J. Saubert, *On Sacrifices*, ch. 23, p. 518 ff., Crenius ed., who diligently collected every passage in the ancients; Verheyk on Antoninus Liberalis, ch. 20; Potter on Clement, Book I, p. 25; Bentley and Hemsterhuis on Callimachus, fragments 187 and 188, p. 511, Ernesti and Heyne ed.; and Heyne’s observations on the fragments of Apollodorus, p. 394 f., new ed. THE SAME.

**Who says that, while he violated another man’s marriage bed, he was caught entangled in snares?** Thus the manuscript most correctly. He means marriage couches. Arnobius speaks similarly in Book V: “Who committed those sweetest thefts in another’s marriage bed? Is it not you?” Others read *genitalibus*, “genital parts,” incorrectly. For *genitalia* are the sexual organs, which may not be named without first begging pardon. Arnobius writes of Attis in Book V: “He cuts off his own genitals.” Above, in Book II: “Saturn joined to Ops in their genital parts,” although there the manuscripts favor “joined to Ops in marriage.” Again, the correct reading in Book VI is: “When, together with the image of that same divinity, he was spread out upon marriage couches.” Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* II: “Abstain from sexual intercourse with your hostess, and look with greater reverence upon the marriage bed of the honorable Milo.” On the marriage bed, which they also called the “opposite bed,” consult J. Lipsius, *Electa* I, ch. 17, and Joseph Scaliger, *Corrections on Festus*, under the word *Plutus*. STEWECHIUS.

**Was it ever written by us that gods performed hired servitude?** etc. This too is taken from Clement, *Protrepticus*, p. 22, Potter ed.:

“Such gods of yours, then, having become slaves to their passions, naturally submitted even to a yoke of servitude like the so-called Helots among the Lacedaemonians. Apollo served Admetus at Pherae, and Heracles served Omphale at Sardis; Poseidon and Apollo worked for wages under Laomedon, like a worthless household slave who had evidently been unable to obtain his freedom from his former master. It was then, too, that the two of them rebuilt the walls of Ilium for the Phrygian.”

TH. CANTER.—Arnobius says “hired servitude” with perfect precision, since those persons performed servile duties and were obligated to those who hired them by the same bond by which freedmen were obligated to their patrons. HERALD.—Compare Tertullian, *Apologeticum* [Col. 1052A] ch. 14; Lactantius, *Institutes* I, ch. 10; Cyprian, *On Idols*; Minucius Felix. ELMENHORST.

**As Hercules, because of sordid love and wantonness.** I restore: “as Hercules at Sardis to Omphale.” A hurried copyist omitted this phrase. The history and the sequence of the discourse—ἀκολουθία—cry out for it. Furthermore, if Arnobius had omitted the masters of Hercules and Neptune whom they served, I could believe that he also wished silently to pass over Hercules’ mistress. Someone might think the reading should be “as Hercules to Eurystheus,” since he served him too; but the former correction is confirmed by Clement, whose passages Arnobius reproduces extensively in these final books. Clement writes: “Apollo submitted to the yoke of slavery under Admetus at Pherae, Heracles under Omphale at Sardis,” etc. MEURSIUS.—Fulvius Ursinus, following Clement, refashions the text as: “as Hercules at Sardis, because of love and wantonness,” and Salmasius admitted this correction into the text. But nothing should be changed. Arnobius does not mention the places in which Hercules and Apollo performed their servile duties. ORELLI.

**Minerva as attendant of the light and governess of the lamps.** Thus Theodorus Canter corrected the text. The first edition reads “composer of the lamps.” C. Barth defends that reading in his note on Statius, *Thebaid* III, 661, vol. II, p. 856, thinking that there is here a simultaneous allusion to study by lamplight and to the olive. Stewechius prefers *inoleatricem*, “oiler.” Clement, Book I: “Homer is not ashamed to make Athena appear beside Odysseus, saying that she held a golden lamp in her hands” (*Odyssey* XIX, 33 f.). ORELLI.

**Is not that poet one of yours who represented Mars and Venus as wounded by mortal hands?** etc., etc. Clement, Book I, p. 23 (31, Potter ed.):

“Homer establishes the point with great precision by introducing Aphrodite as uttering a shrill, loud cry over her wound, and by relating that Diomedes wounded the supremely warlike Ares in the flank. Polemon says that Athena too was wounded by Ornytus; indeed, Homer says that Hades was shot with an arrow by Heracles; Panyassis also records the rays of Helios [as struck], and the same Panyassis records that Hera the patroness of marriage was wounded by that same Heracles at sandy Pylos; and Sosibius says that Heracles himself was wounded in the hand by the sons of Hippocoon.”

CANTER and ORELLI.

**Panyassis.** This is how the Roman manuscript reads instead of *Panyasis*, and it appears that here our Arnobius followed the Greeks, who spell it with a double consonant; Latins otherwise spell it with one for the sake of euphony. But our author sometimes delights in writing in Greek fashion. CANTER.—Panyassis flourished around the 78th Olympiad. Suidas attests that even the ancients did not agree about his city or parentage. Duris reported that he was a Samian and the son of Diocles; others called him a Halicarnassian and the son of Polyarchus, and still others Herodotus’s maternal uncle. He flourished around Olympiad 78. He wrote the *Antiquities of Greece*, though in verse; also a *Heracleid* in fourteen books and nine thousand verses—from which poem the material that Clement and Arnobius report from him appears to have been taken—and an *Ionica* in pentameter verse. See Suidas and G. J. Vossius, who treats him at length in *On the Greek Historians* IV, ch. 6. ORELLI.

**Slain by Ornytus.** Meursius prefers “injured,” because it would be absurd to say that an immortal goddess was killed by a mortal man, and Clement, whom our Arnobius follows, has τρωθῆναι, “to be wounded”; I approve this. For although *caedo, caedere* is very frequently used for “to beat” or “to wound,” I do not recall reading the participle *caesus* used absolutely, nor the noun *caedes*, with this meaning. And C and L could very easily have been confused by copyists. ORELLI.

**Of Polemon.** Polemon, son of Evegetes and surnamed Helladicus, an Ilian by birth, was a contemporary of Aristophanes the grammarian and a pupil of Panaetius. He flourished under Ptolemy Epiphanes, around Olympiad 168. Athenaeus and Suidas cite various writings of his: on the origins of cities; geographies of Phocis, Pontus, and Laconia; three books *On the Course of the Sun*; a *Greek History*; and so forth. Above all others, G. J. Vossius, *On the Greek Historians* I, ch. 18, should be consulted concerning him. ORELLI.

**Sosibius declares that Hercules himself reported being tortured by the sons of Hippocoon, and suffering both the inflicted wound and its pain.** Our author copied this from Clement’s *Protrepticus*. Hyginus, however, states in Fable 31 that Hercules killed Hippocoon together with his ten sons. Apollodorus says the same in Book II of the *Library* (ch. 7, §3). ELMENHORST. See Heyne’s observations on Apollodorus, Book I, p. 188, new ed. On Sosibius the Laconian, a grammarian and contemporary of Callimachus, see Suidas; Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, ch. 21; J. Lipsius on Tacitus, *Annals* XI.1; and G. J. Vossius, *On the Greek Historians* I, ch. 15. ORELLI.

**Has it been published by us that Jupiter was committed to burial on the island of Crete?** etc. Clement, *Protrepticus*, p. 24 (32, Potter ed.):

“Search for your Zeus; investigate not heaven but earth. The Cretan will tell you, in whose land he also lies buried. Callimachus in his *Hymns*:

> For the Cretans, O lord,  
> constructed even a tomb for you.”

See above on Book III, ch. 30. ORELLI.

**Do we say that the brothers were buried within the borders of Sparta and Lacedaemon, and that they grew up together in their cradles?** etc., etc. This and what follows are again from Clement, Book I, p. 19 (26, Potter ed.):

“Philochorus says that Poseidon is honored on Tenos as a physician, and that Cronus lies upon Sicily and is buried there. Patrocles of Thurii and Sophocles the Younger, in three tragedies, tell the following about the Dioscuri: these two Dioscuri were mortal men subject to death, if Homer is sufficient to confirm what has been said” (*Iliad* III, 243):

> But the life-giving earth already held them  
> there in Lacedaemon, in their beloved native land.

“Let the author of the *Cyprian Poems* also come forward:

> Castor is mortal, and the doom of death has been allotted him;  
> but Polydeuces, the scion of Ares, is immortal.

This, however, he falsely asserted in poetic fashion. Homer is more trustworthy than he, having spoken of both the Dioscuri.”

Arnobius therefore calls the sons of Tyndareus, the Castors, “the brothers” par excellence in this passage. ORELLI.

**Patrocles of Thurii is indicated in the titles of writings.** Stewechius conjectures *indigitatur*, “is designated in the titles,” in the same sense. Against him, Olaus Borrichius rightly observes in *Reflections*, p. 129, that among Latin authors *indigitare* does not mean “to indicate” or “enumerate upon the fingers,” but “to invoke.” Thus Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, ch. 17: “The Lindians worship Apollo λοιμίος, ‘the Averter of Pestilence,’ who was given this surname when a plague ended. The same conception of a healing and medical god is fostered in our own rites, for the Vestal Virgins invoke him thus: ‘Apollo the Physician, Apollo Paean.’” Hence the *indigitamenta*, or ceremonial books. See above on Book II, ch. 73. Tertullian appears to use this verb for “to proclaim” in *On Fasting*: “When the sky is stagnant and the year is parched, barefoot processions are announced, the magistrates lay aside their purple, turn the fasces backward, proclaim prayer, and renew the sacrifice.” Yet there *indigitant* could also be explained as “they commence the prayers” or “prepare themselves for the festival with prayers.”—On Patrocles of Thurii, see Vossius, *On the Greek Historians* III, *Works*, vol. IV, p. 184, Amsterdam ed. ORELLI.

**Plutarch of Chaeronea**, etc. Thus the printed editions. But the royal manuscript presents: “Hieronymus, Plutarch.” Yet if Arnobius is following Clement of Alexandria here as elsewhere, the text should have read: “Hieronymus and Dicaearchus,” or “Hieronymus the philosopher.” Clement’s words, p. 19, Sylburg ed., are:

“Homer himself, then, knows Heracles as a mortal man. Hieronymus the philosopher even describes the condition of his body: he was short, bristly-haired, robust, broad-shouldered, sinewy, dark, hook-nosed, somewhat blue-eyed, and straight-haired. This Heracles, then, after living fifty-two years, ended his life by being cremated upon the pyre on Oeta.”

ORELLI.—For both authors are cited by Clement, *Protrepticus*, p. 19. Yet we think nothing in Arnobius’s text should be rashly altered. NOURRIUS.—Indeed, nothing at all should be changed. For in this passage Arnobius, leaving Clement aside, seems to have followed Plutarch, who wrote a book *On the Life of Hercules*, as Lamprias and Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* I.1, attest. The distinguished Wyttenbach collected some fragments of it in his edition of Plutarch’s *Moral Works*, without omitting our passage. Moreover, on Hercules’ death on Mount Oeta compare Minucius Felix; Lactantius I, ch. 9; Augustine, *City of God* XVIII, ch. 4; Servius on Virgil, *Eclogue* VIII; Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*; and Hyginus, Fable 36. ORELLI.]

### XXV

Who consecrated among the number of the gods Venus, a little prostitute enriched [Note: [Col. 1050A] *Dictatum*, wrongly in the Sabine manuscript] by a Cyprian king whose name was Cinyras? Who disclosed that the Palladium was constructed [Col. 1050A] from the remains of Pelops? Was it not you?

Who said that Mars was a Spartan? Was it not Epicharmus, an authority of yours? Who said that he was born within the borders of Thrace? Was it not the Attic Sophocles, with every theater expressing its assent? Who said that he was in Arcadia? Was it not you? Who said that he was bound for thirteen months? Was it not the son of the river Meles [Note: [Col. 1050A] From Plutarch I read *Meletis*. Elmenhorst]? Who says that dogs were sacrificed to him by the Carians, and asses by the Scythians? Is it not chiefly Apollodorus, together with the others? Who says that, while [Col. 1051A] he violated another man’s marriage bed, he was caught entangled in snares? Is it not your commentaries and your stage?

Was it ever written by us that gods performed hired servitude: Hercules because of sordid love and wantonness; Delian Apollo under Admetus; Jupiter’s brother under Laomedon of Troy; the Pythian god under that same man, but together with his uncle; and Minerva as attendant of the light and governess of the lamps when married couples mingled in their secret chamber? Is not that poet one of yours who represented Mars and Venus as wounded by mortal hands? Is not Panyassis one of you, who records that Pluto the Father and Queen Juno were wounded by Hercules? Do not the writings of your Polemon indicate that the warrior-maiden was struck, bloodied, [Col. 1053A] and maltreated by Ornytus? Does not Sosibius declare that Hercules himself reported being tortured by the sons of Hippocoon and suffering both the inflicted wound and its pain?

Has it been published by us that Jupiter was committed to burial on the island of Crete? Do we say that the brothers were buried within the borders of Sparta and Lacedaemon and grew up together in their cradles? Is that authority ours who is indicated in the titles of writings as Patrocles of Thurii, and who records that the tomb and remains of Saturn are contained in Sicilian soil? Is Plutarch of Chaeronea shown to belong to our side—the man who disclosed that Hercules, broken down by the ravages of epilepsy upon the heights of Oeta, was reduced to ashes?

[Note: [Col. 1054C]

### XXVI—Is it we who accuse the king of the sea of depriving Amphitrite, Hippothoe, Amymone, Menalippe, and Alope of their virginal chastity in the heat of frenzied lust?

Salmasius printed *Alopes* in place of *Alcyones*. Here too Arnobius has reproduced Clement almost word for word. Clement’s words in the *Protrepticus*, p. 20 (27, Potter ed.), are:

“Call Poseidon for me, together with the chorus of women corrupted by him: Amphitrite, [Col. 1054D] Amymone, Alope, Melanippe, Alcyone, Hippothoe, Chione, and the countless others. Yet even though they were so very numerous, your Poseidon’s passions still felt themselves confined.”

Julius Firmicus likewise appears to have drawn from the same source, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 427, Gronovius ed.: “It is difficult to enumerate all their adulteries. Who corrupted Amymone? Who Alope? Who Menalippe? Who Chione and Hippothoe? Your god, of course, is recorded as having done these things.” Here Johannes Wowerius thinks that *Chiones* should be restored in Arnobius in place of *Alcyones*. But it is not certain which of the two he omitted, since Clement mentions both. On Chione, see Apollodorus, *Library* III, ch. 15, section 4, p. 368, Heyne’s new ed.; on Amymone, the same author II, ch. 1, section 4, p. 121; Hyginus, Fable 169, with Muncker’s note; and the scholia on Euripides, *Phoenician Women*, line 195. In place of *Menalippas*, the same Wowerius, commenting on Firmicus, Book I, thinks *Melanippas* should be restored from Clement. But the form *Menalippe* also occurs in Juvenal, Satire VIII, 229; Varro, *On Agriculture* II; and Aulus Gellius XII, ch. 11, where see A. Thysius, as well as Muncker on Hyginus, Fable 186, where her story is set out at length. On Hippothoe, see Apollodorus, *Library* II, ch. 4, section 5, p. 147; on Alope, mother of Hippothoon by Neptune, Pausanias I, ch. 39, Facius ed., and Hyginus, Fable 187; on Alcyone, whom our author omitted but Clement adds, the same author, Fable 157 [Col. 1055B], and the authorities cited there by Muncker. For “virginal chastity,” Meursius prefers “chastity and virginity,” or “the chastity of virginity.” ORELLI.

**Arsinoe, Aethusa, Hypsipyle, Marpessa, Zeuxippe, Prothoe, Daphne, and Sterope.** Clement, in the passage cited, continues:

“Call Apollo for me as well. This is Phoebus, the pure prophet and good counselor. Sterope, however, tells a different story, as do Aethusa, Arsinoe, Zeuxippe, Prothoe, Marpessa, and Hypsipyle. Daphne alone escaped both the prophet and corruption.”

Julius Firmicus, Book I, p. 428: “The one whom they wish to correct the sins of erring people through stern oracles loves Sterope, carries off Aethusa, violates Zeuxippe, seeks Prothoe, and flatters Arsinoe with adulterous desire. Yet from that flock of corrupted women, one girl both escaped and defeated the god who loved her. For the prophetic god, who foretold the future, could neither find nor violate Daphne.” On Arsinoe, the mother of Aesculapius, see above all the scholiast on Pindar, *Pythian* III.14; Apollodorus, *Library* II, ch. 10, section 3, with Heyne’s observations, p. 176, new ed. Meursius and Stewechius restored *Aethusas* from Clement. Previously the reading was *Chrysas*. See the same Apollodorus III, ch. 10, beginning. No one, so far as I know, mentions Hypsipyle as Apollo’s beloved except our author and Clement. Apollodorus has preserved for us the story of Marpessa, *Library* I, ch. 7, section 8, p. 49; I have sought in vain elsewhere for mention of Zeuxippe and Prothoe. Ovid embellished the tale of Daphne in most elegant verses, *Metamorphoses* I, 452 ff. Compare Hyginus, Fable 203. ORELLI.

**Is the aged Saturn indicated in our poems as having been caught in adultery by his wife?** etc. Junius Philargyrius on Virgil, *Georgics* III.93: “When Saturn had fallen in love with Philyra, daughter of Ocean, in Thessaly and was coupling with her, upon the approach of his wife he transformed himself into a stallion and her into a mare, and thus they both escaped disgrace.” ELMENHORST.—Compare Hyginus, Fable 138, and the authorities cited there by Muncker. ORELLI.

**Assumed the form of a beast**, that is, a horse. Virgil, *Aeneid* II.51:

> And into the curved belly of the beast, compacted with joints,  
> he hurled it.

Accius, *Medea*:

> Skillfully placing bridles upon the beasts in the stalls.

HERALD. These examples come from Nonius. Compare Livineius on Nazarius’s *Panegyric*, ch. 29, p. 79, vol. II, Jaeger ed.; Cassiodorus on Psalm 31: “For *frenum* (‘bridle’) was so called from restraining a beast—*ferum retinendo*—since the ancients called a horse *ferum*. Hence Centaurs were called *semiferi*, that is, half-horses.” Compare Savaro on Sidonius, Poem XI, p. 135, who supplied several examples. ORELLI.

**Was not Jupiter himself, king of the world, disgraced by you as having passed through innumerable forms?** I have printed this following J. G. Graevius’s correction in Letter 258 to N. Heinsius, Burmann’s *Sylloge*, [Col. 1056A] vol. IV, p. 331. The earlier reading was “is infamous.” But the infinitive *isse*, “to have gone,” requires a participle, not an adjective. ORELLI.

**Veiled under servile deceptions.** N. Heinsius, in Letter 257 to Graevius, thinks the reading should be either *pervilibus*, “utterly worthless,” or *versipellibus fallaciis*, “shape-shifting deceptions”; but in Letter 259 he prefers [Col. 1056B] *vernilibus fallaciis*, “slavish deceptions.” For they called everything *vernile* that was considered less than worthy of a freeborn person. Yet *servilis* is also used in the same sense, as Graevius rightly maintains in Letter 258. Who does not know the deceptions and tricks of the Davuses and Getas in comedy? ORELLI.

**Was it written?** See above on Book I, ch. 56. THE SAME.

**At one time transformed into gold**, etc. Clement, *Protrepticus*, p. 24 (32, Potter ed.): “For Zeus is dead—do not be distressed—as Leda, as a swan, as an eagle, as an amorous man, as a serpent.” Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 427: “Someone delights in adultery: he looks to Jupiter and seeks from him fuel for his own lust; he approves, imitates, and praises the fact that his god deceives as a swan, abducts as a bull, sports as a satyr, and—so that he may become lavish in his debaucheries—corrupted an imprisoned royal maiden with gold flowing abundantly.” ELMENHORST and ORELLI.

**At another time into a sportive satyr, into a serpent.** N. Heinsius, in Letter 257 to J. G. Graevius, Burmann’s *Sylloge*, vol. IV, p. 329, thinks the reading should be: “at another time into Satyra” (a Greek accusative), “slippery, into a serpent”; Oudendorp approves this in his note on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* I, p. 22. To me the old reading seems sound and by no means to be altered. “Sportive” is a most fitting epithet for satyrs, who are very frequently called dancing, playful, lustful, and wanton by the poets. Nor have I been able to find *Satyr, Satyris* anywhere as a third-declension noun. ORELLI.

**Into a tiny ant, so that he might make Clitor’s daughter the mother of Myrmidon among the Thessalians.** Gelenius most correctly restored the passage thus from Clement, who says in the *Protrepticus*, p. 25 (34, Potter ed.):

“What? Are not the Thessalians again said to worship ants because they learned that Zeus, having assumed the likeness of an ant, coupled with Eurymedusa, the daughter of Cletor, and begot Myrmidon?”

The first edition was extremely corrupt: “So that he might, of course, produce Clitor’s daughter as Mirdon’s mother among the Thessalians.” ORELLI.

**Who made him remain awake with Alcmena for nine continuous nights?** Arnobius here follows Clement, whose words in the *Protrepticus*, p. 9, are:

“To what a degree of wantonness did that Zeus proceed, who indulged in pleasure with Alcmena for so many nights? For not even those nine nights were long to that unrestrained being; on the contrary, his whole life was too short for his incontinence, so that he might beget for us the god who averts evil.”

Here Potter, p. 28, annotates:

“Most authors report that Jupiter lay with Alcmena for three nights. Hence Lycophron calls Hercules, born from that union, τριέσπερος, ‘born of three evenings,’ *Alexandra* 33, as does Justin in the *Exhortation*. Statius in *Thebaid* XII spoke of ‘Hercules’ threefold night.’ Seneca in the *Agamemnon* reports two nights; that number is also found in Propertius II, elegy XXII.25; Martianus Capella II; Hyginus, Fable 29; Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, ch. 4; and Ovid, *Amores* I, elegy XIII. Plautus, in the prologue to the *Amphitryon*, says one night, but a longer one. Cyril agrees with Clement and Arnobius in *Against Julian* VI, p. 196: ‘Let Alcmena also be recorded, with whom the one who never had his fill even of the most shameful acts passed nine whole nights.’”

Compare M. A. Delrio, *Syntagma of Latin Tragedy*, Part II, p. 286. ORELLI.

**The holy god Hercules.** “Holy” means chaste and upright in life. See above on ch. 16 of this book. Arnobius thus calls Hercules *holy* ironically, as C. G. Schwarz rightly observes on Pliny’s *Panegyric*, ch. I, p. 3. Stewechius should therefore not be followed when he substitutes “Hercules Sancus the god.” Sancus was indeed a name for Hercules among the Sabines. See Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, and Cellarius on Lactantius, *Institutes* I, ch. 15, p. 95, Bunemann ed. But this is wholly foreign to our passage. ORELLI.

**The fifty daughters born to Thestius.** Others read “to Thespius.” But Pausanias in the *Boeotica*, p. 302; Athenaeus XIII, p. 556, Casaubon ed.; Gregory Nazianzen, *First Oration against Julian*; Suidas under Θεστιάδες (“daughters of Thestius”); and above all Clement of Alexandria, whom our author followed, agree on the name Thestius. Clement’s words in the *Protrepticus*, p. 28, Potter ed., are:

“Heracles, son of Zeus—truly Zeus’s son, since he was begotten during a long night—completed his twelve labors with great suffering over a long period, but corrupted the fifty daughters of Thestius in a single night.”

Compare Fronton du Duc on Tatian’s *Oration to the Greeks*, p. 78, Worth ed. [Col. 1057C] ORELLI.

**And expose the name of virginity.** J. G. Graevius, in Letter 258 to N. Heinsius, Burmann’s *Sylloge*, vol. IV, p. 331, thinks the reading should be: “lay aside the name of virginity.” Gelenius printed “set down.” But see what we noted above on ch. 21 of this same book. “To expose the name of virginity” therefore means to prostitute virginity, just as *the name of a little field* means “a little field,” and *the name of one’s fatherland* means “one’s fatherland” in Justin. See above on Book I, ch. 5. ORELLI.

**What of the fact that, not content to attribute to the gods passions for the female sex—** Stewechius prefers the punctuation: “What? The fact that.” But it matters little or nothing how we punctuate it. The same Stewechius correctly interprets *cares* as “loves,” citing the familiar opening of Virgil, *Aeneid* IV:

> But the queen, long wounded by a grievous passion,  
> feeds the wound within her veins and is consumed by hidden fire.

Festus says: “*Cura* (‘care’ or ‘passion’) is so called as though it eats the heart, or because it burns the heart”; see Dacier there. ORELLI.

**You also add males of their own sex as objects of their love.** The word *sexus*, “of their own sex,” is absent from the manuscript. ORELLI.

**Someone or other loves Hylas.** That is, Hercules. *Someone* is sometimes used in this manner. Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 11: “Yet how many worthier men have you left in the lower regions—some Socrates distinguished for wisdom, some Aristides for justice?” And ch. 12: “O impious words! O sacrilegious insults! Gnash your teeth, foam at the mouth! You are the same people who censured some Seneca for arguing more fully and forcefully against your superstition.” In this way the Greeks sometimes elegantly say τινά, “someone,” when they are making a veiled thrust at a person. Aristophanes in the *Frogs*: κακὸν ἥκει τινί, “evil has come upon someone,” and ἥκει τῷ κακόν, “evil has come upon the fellow,” etc.:

> ἀγορεύω τινὶ  
> ἐμὲ μὴ βασανίζειν ἀθάνατον ὄντα.
>
> I tell someone not to torture me, since I am immortal.

“I tell someone”—ἀγορεύω τινί—that is, “you yourself.” Similarly, in the same play: ἤλγησέ τις, “someone felt pain,” and repeatedly elsewhere. So Plautus in the *Amphitryon*: “A certain man smells trouble for himself.” This is the correct reading: *quidam*, not *quidem*. HERALD.—Arnobius again borrowed this and what follows from his Clement, p. 28, Potter ed.:

“For your gods did not even abstain from boys: one loved Hylas, another Hyacinthus, another Pelops, another Chrysippus, and another Ganymede.”

Julius Firmicus writes similarly, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 427, Gronovius ed.: “Someone delights in the embraces of boys: let him seek Ganymede in Jupiter’s lap; let him see Hercules seeking Hylas with impatient love; let him learn that Apollo was seized by longing for Hyacinthus; let one look at Chrysippus, another at Pelops, so that he may say that whatever is now punished most severely by Roman law is permissible to him through the example of his gods.” ORELLI.

**Another is absorbed in Hyacinthus.** Ovid transmitted in most elegant verses the story of Hyacinthus, beloved by Apollo, *Metamorphoses* X, 162 ff. Compare Hyginus, Fable 271. ORELLI.

**That one burns with desire for Pelops.** Neptune, namely; Tatian, *Oration against the Greeks*, and Pindar, *Olympian* I.38, write that Pelops was loved by him:

> Pelops, whom mighty Poseidon, holder of the earth, loved.

ORELLI.

**This one sighs more ardently for Chrysippus.** Aelian, *Various History* XIII.5, and Apollodorus, *Library* III, ch. 5, section 5, transmit the story of Chrysippus, son of Pelops, abducted by Laius; see Heyne’s observations there, p. 237, new ed., and Boettiger in Wieland’s *Attic Museum*, vol. I, p. 346 ff. Hyginus, Fable 271, reports that he was abducted by Theseus during the games, if the reading is sound; see Muncker. Praxilla of Sicyon, in Athenaeus XIII, p. 603, Casaubon ed., says that he was abducted by Jupiter himself. ORELLI.

**Catamitus.** Festus: “They used *Catamitus* for Ganymede, who was Jupiter’s male bedfellow.” Papias: “Catamitus … Ganymede. Ganymede was effeminate; hence effeminate men are called *catamites*.” Thus our author below: “The boy Catamitus was stripped of the honor of his modesty.” C. Barth, *Adversaria* XXIII, ch. 7, p. 1128; L. Bunemann on Lactantius, *Institutes* I, ch. 11, p. 67; and P. Burmann II, *Latin Anthology* III, epigram 92, vol. I, p. 547, collected several examples of this name. ORELLI.

**Destined to become his darling and keeper of his cups.** I have printed this according to the entirely correct correction of the Leiden editor. Others read: “destined to become the keeper of his delights and cups.” But “keeper of his delights” has no relevance to Ganymede; nor is it part of the scandalous fable. C. Barth, *Adversaria* I, suspects that the reading should be *deliciarium futurus*, “destined to become the repository of Jupiter’s greatest delights.” But I have sought the word *deliciarium* in vain in the lexicons. ORELLI.

Source/review notes: The supplied source ends at an incomplete [Note: [Col. 1068C] opening; the translation explicitly marks this inherited source boundary.

And so that he might be called Jupiter’s “chick,” Fabius is burned in his tender parts and stamped upon his buttocks. Festus: “Quintus Fabius, whose surname was Eburnus because of his fair complexion, was called Jupiter’s chick, because his buttocks had been struck by lightning. The ancients, moreover, called a boy whom someone loved his ‘chick.’” HERALD.—On this passage of Festus, Dacier makes the following annotation: “Understand that Fabius who was surnamed Ambustus, and who thereafter gave that surname to the whole family. For *ambusti* properly means those whom Jupiter has grazed with the blasts of his thunderbolt and touched with its fire. From *puer* come *puerus*, *puerulus*, *pullus*. Unless one prefers *pullus* to derive from πῶλος (*pōlos*, ‘foal’), which pleases me even more. For among the Greeks πῶλος means a catamite and a courtesan. Hesychius: ‘Πῶλος … ἑταίρα. πώλους γὰρ αὐτὰς ἔλεγον οἷον Ἀφροδίτης πώλους, ἢ τοὺς νέους καὶ τὰς νέας καὶ παρθένους—*Pōlos*: a courtesan; for they called such women *pōloi*, as though “the foals of Aphrodite,” or else young men, young women, and maidens.’” ORELL.

## XXVI

For what am I to say about those love affairs in which, according to the record preserved in your writings and authorities, the holy celestial beings burned with passion for women? Is it we who accuse the king of the sea of having, in the heat of furious lust, deprived Amphitrite, Hippothoe, Amymone, Melanippe, and Alope of their virginal chastity? Is it we who say that Apollo, son of Latona—that spotless, most chaste, [Col. 1055A] and pure god—desired Arsinoe, Aethusa, Hypsipyle, Marpessa, Zeuxippe, Prothoe, Daphne, and Sterope with the ardors of an ungoverned heart? Is it in poems of ours that the aged Saturn, long since covered with white hair and already chilled by the passage of the years, is reported to have been caught by his wife in adultery, to have assumed the form of a beast, and to have fled away under the appearance of a farm animal, uttering neighs?

Has not Jupiter himself, the king of the world, been defamed by you as one who passed through countless shapes and [Col. 1056A] concealed the flame of wanton love beneath servile disguises? Was it ever written by us that, to accomplish his lustful thefts, he was transformed now into gold, now into a sportive satyr, into a serpent, a bird, a bull, and—to surpass every species of disgrace—into a tiny ant, so that he might make Clitoris’ daughter the mother of Myrmidon among the Thessalians? Who made him remain awake with Alcmena for nine consecutive nights? Was it not you? Who made him lie idle in his love affairs [Col. 1057A] after abandoning his station in heaven? Was it not you?

And indeed you add no small benefits: for through you the god Hercules was born, who in matters of this kind would exceed and surpass the prowess of his father. Jupiter could scarcely hammer out, fashion, and put together a single offspring in nine nights; but Hercules, the holy god, thoroughly taught the fifty daughters of Thestius in a single night both to surrender the name of virginity and to bear the burdens of motherhood.

And what of the fact that, not content with assigning to the gods passions for the female sex, you also add [Col. 1058A] males as objects of their love? Someone or other loves Hylas. Another is engrossed by Hyacinthus; one burns with desire for Pelops, another sighs more ardently for Chrysippus. Catamitus is carried off to become a darling and keeper of the cups. And so that he might be called Jupiter’s “chick,” Fabius is burned in his tender parts and stamped upon his buttocks.

> **Note: [Col. 1058D]**
>
> **XXVII.—“Has it not been provided in your writings?”** The passage [Col. 1059A] is undoubtedly faulty and corrupt, yet it may easily be healed and restored by changing a single letter. For our author means to say: [Col. 1059B] “Is it not contained and celebrated in your writings?” It is sufficiently clear that the present word does not admit that meaning. Therefore, by the smallest alteration, as I have said, I conjecture that this is the true and genuine reading: for *cautum* (“provided”) read *cantum*, that is, “sung.” TH. CANTER.—For my part, I regard the commonly received reading as entirely correct. These words plainly refer back to the preceding statement: “The sanctity belonging to the female sex has been preserved.” Yet Arnobius continues: “Has it not been provided in your writings”—that is, provided that the sanctity belonging to the female sex should not be preserved? Thus there is here a zeugma or syllepsis, a very familiar figure in which one verb is referred to two different propositions, though it properly fits only one. See Julius Rufinianus, *On Figures of Speech*, in the lexicon appended to Rutilius Rufus, p. 228, ed. Ruhnken. The sentence here is therefore to be supplemented as follows: “Has not this—namely, that the sanctity of women should not be preserved—been provided in your writings (and handed down): that Tithonus was loved by Aurora,” etc. ORELL.
>
> **“That Tithonus was loved by Aurora,” etc.** [Col. 1059C] Arnobius borrowed these points from his Clement, who says as follows in the *Protrepticus*, p. 28 ff., ed. Potter:
>
> “Ἀλλ’ οἱ μὲν ἄρρενες αὐτοῖς τῶν θεῶν ἴσως μόνοι ἅπτουσι περὶ τὰ ἀφροδίσια·  
>   
> Θηλύτεραι δὲ θεαὶ μένον οἴκοι ἑκάστη,  
>   
> φησὶν Ὅμηρος· αἰδούμεναι αἱ θεαὶ διὰ σεμνότητα Ἀφροδίτην ἰδεῖν μεμοιχευμένην· αἱ δὲ ἀκολασταίνουσιν ἐμπαθέστερον ἐν τῇ μοιχείᾳ δεδεμέναι· Ἠὼς ἐπὶ Τιθώνῳ, Σελήνη ἐπὶ Ἐνδυμίωνι, Νηρηῒς ἐπὶ Αἰακῷ, καὶ ἐπὶ Πηλεῖ Θέτις· ἐπὶ δὲ Ἰάσωνι Δημήτηρ, καὶ ἐπὶ Ἀδώνιδι Φερεφάττα· Ἀφροδίτη δὲ ἐπ’ Ἄρει κατῃσχυμμένη, μετῆλθεν ἐπὶ Κινύραν, καὶ Ἀγχίσην ἔγημεν, καὶ Φαέθοντα ἔλαχεν, καὶ ἤρα Ἀδώνιδος.”
>
> “But perhaps only the male gods among them engage in sexual matters?
>
> ‘But the goddesses, each of them, remained at home,’
>
> says Homer—the goddesses, in their modest dignity, being ashamed to see Aphrodite caught in adultery. Yet they behave even more wantonly, bound fast in adulterous passion: Dawn for Tithonus, the Moon for Endymion, a Nereid for Aeacus, and Thetis for Peleus; Demeter for Iasion, and Persephone for Adonis. Aphrodite, disgraced over Ares, passed on to Cinyras, married Anchises, obtained Phaethon, and fell in love with Adonis.”
>
> Compare Apollodorus, *Library* III, ch. 12, §4, and Heyne’s observations there, p. 300 ff., new ed.; also the classic passage, *Homeric Hymn to Venus* 219 ff. ORELL.
>
> **“The Moon for Endymion.”** A very well-known tale. See Apollodorus I, ch. 7, §5, and the authorities cited there by Heyne, pp. 43 ff.; Hyginus, *Fabulae* 261; Fulgentius, [Col. 1059D] *Mythologies* II.19. ORELL.
>
> **“A Nereid for Aeacus.”** Apollodorus III, ch. 12, v. 9: “Μίγνυται δὲ αὖθις Αἰακὸς Ψαμάθῃ τῇ Νηρέως εἰς φώκην ἠλλαγμένῃ διὰ τὸ μὴ βούλεσθαι συνελθεῖν, καὶ τεκνοῖ παῖδα Φῶκον—Again Aeacus couples with Psamathe, the daughter of Nereus, after she had changed herself into a seal because she was unwilling to have intercourse with him; and he fathers a son, Phocus.” The tale of the loves of Peleus and Thetis is very well known. ORELL.
>
> **“Proserpine for Adonis.”** The classic passage on the loves of Venus and Proserpine for Adonis is in Apollodorus, *Library* III, ch. 19, §4; see there Heyne’s observations, p. 326, new ed., and Méziriac on Ovid’s *Epistles*, pp. 357 ff. Hence Adonis is called τριφίλατος (*triphilatos*, “thrice-beloved”) by Theocritus, *Idyll* XV.86, where the scholiast says: “τριφίλατος, ὁ πολυφίλατος, ὡς καὶ παρ’ Ὁμήρῳ Ἀσπασίη τριφίλητος· ἢ ὅτι ὑπὸ τριῶν ἐφιλήθη, Διὸς, Ἀφροδίτης καὶ Περσεφόνης ἐν ᾅδῃ—*Triphilatos* means ‘much beloved,’ as Homer also calls Aspasia *triphilētos*; or else it means that he was loved by three: Zeus, Aphrodite, and Persephone in Hades.” Moreover, on the two forms *Adon, -is* and *Adonis, -idis*, see Oudendorp on Apuleius’ *Metamorphoses* II, pp. 155 f. ORELL.
>
> **“Her mother Ceres for Iasion.”** The passage was most correctly restored in this form by L. Carrio, *Emendations* II, [Col. 1060A] ch. 17; *Lampas* of Gruter III, part II, p. 180; and M. A. Delrio, *Syntagma of Latin Tragedy* III, p. 260, with the approval of Salmasius in the Leiden edition and in his notes on the [Col. 1060B] *Writers of the Augustan History* I, p. 440. Previously it read: “Adonis, her male; Ceres for Iasion.” This is utterly corrupt, for it is not easy to explain how Adonis could be called the “male of Venus,” either in good Latin or in accordance with fact. By contrast, even beginners know that Ceres was Proserpine’s mother. The classic passage concerning Iasion is Homer, *Odyssey* V.125 ff.:
>
> “Ὡς δ’ ὁπότ’ Ἰασίωνι εὐπλόκαμος Δημήτηρ  
> Ἑῷ θυμῷ εἴξασα μίγη φιλότητι καὶ εὐνῇ,  
> Νειῷ ἐνὶ τριπόλῳ· οὐδὲ δὴν ἦεν ἄπυστος  
> Ζεύς, ὅς μιν κατέπεφνε βαλὼν ἀργῆτι κεραυνῷ.”
>
> “As when fair-haired Demeter, yielding to her desire, mingled with Iasion in love and bed in a thrice-plowed field; nor was Zeus long unaware of it, and he slew Iasion by striking him with a blazing thunderbolt.”
>
> Compare Apollodorus, *Library* III, ch. 12, beginning, and Heyne’s observations there, p. 292; Hyginus, *Fabulae* 270, with Muncker’s note; Heraclides, *Homeric Allegories*, pp. 203 f., ed. Schow; and above all Sainte-Croix, *On the Ancient Mysteries*, translated by Lenz, ch. III, pp. 66 f. ORELL.
>
> **“For some rustic named Iasion.”** Iasion, whom our author calls a rustic of unknown origin, is called by Nonnus (*Dionysiaca* XLVIII.969) a husbandman and [Col. 1060C] the spouse of Ceres; by others he is said to have been the son of Jupiter and Electra, and by some the son of Menoeus and Phronia. Hesiod, however (*Theogony* 969), reports that he fathered Plutus by Ceres:
>
> “Δημήτηρ μὲν Πλοῦτον ἐγείνατο δῖα θεάων  
> Ἰασίῳ ἥρωϊ μιγεῖσ’ ἐρατῇ φιλότητι.”
>
> “Demeter, divine among goddesses, bore Plutus after mingling with the hero Iasion in lovely union.”
>
> Consult further, if you wish and have leisure, Theocritus, *Idyll* III.50, and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX. NOURR., p. 402.
>
> **“Phaethon.”** Th. Canter restored this reading from the first edition and from Clement, book I, in *Various Readings* I, ch. 19, in Gruter’s *Lampas* III, part I, p. 730. Previously the text read *Phaeon*. But J. Potter’s conjecture is very attractive: he thinks *Phaon* should be read in both our author and Clement, since Athenaeus II, near the end, p. 69, ed. Casaubon, testifies that Venus had relations with him:
>
> “Κρατῖνος δέ φησι, Φάωνος ἐρασθεῖσαν τὴν Ἀφροδίτην ἐν καλαῖς θριδακίναις αὐτὸν ἀποκρύψαι, Μαρσύας δ’ ὁ νεώτερος ἐν χλόῃ κριθῶν.”
>
> “Cratinus says that Aphrodite, having fallen in love with Phaon, hid him among beautiful lettuces; but Marsyas the Younger says that she hid him among young barley.”
>
> See also Aelian, *Various History* XII, ch. 18, with Perizonius’ note, pp. 744 f., ed. A. [Col. 1060D] Gronovius. By contrast, no ancient author records either Phaeon or Phaethon as having been loved by Venus. ORELL.—I nevertheless also believe that Arnobius wrote *Phaethon*, and that in his own day he read the same text in Clement that we now read. Did that excellent man, most learned in ancient matters, err in recounting these love affairs of the goddesses? I certainly think so; and therefore the passage should not be emended, but rather excused for errors that, at least in our own day, are of no importance. He thus appears to have said Phaethon when he ought to have said Phaon. VALCKENAER, on Callimachus, *Elegiac Fragments*, p. 119.
>
> **“Into marriage with Anchises.”** See Hyginus, *Fabulae* 94. ELMENHORST.
>
> **“Which you gather together for reviling them.”** The reading is sound. That is: “which you scrape together in order to assail them with abuse.” Nothing, therefore, should be changed. *Conducere* is often used in this sense by Lucretius and others. HERALD.—Fulvius Ursinus’ reading is therefore bad: “Which your abusive speech scrapes together against them.” ORELL.

## XXVII

But among you only males fall in love, and the sanctity belonging to the female sex has been preserved! Has it not been provided in your writings that Tithonus was loved by Aurora, [Col. 1059A] that the Moon burned for Endymion, a Nereid for Aeacus, Thetis for the father of Achilles, Proserpine for Adonis, and her mother Ceres for some rustic named Iasion; and that, after Vulcan, Phaethon, and Mars, Venus herself—the mother of the descendants of Aeneas and founder of Roman dominion—entered into marriage with Anchises?

Since, therefore, you hurl such disgraces and shameful monstrosities not against some one god by name, but equally against the entire race of heavenly beings which you suppose to exist, without any exception, do you dare, while preserving a straight face, [Col. 1060A] to say either that we are impious or that you are pious, when the gods suffer far greater affronts from you through all the scandals you gather together for reviling them than they receive grandeur and honor from the rite and duty of worship?

For either all those tales readily produced about each god, tales injurious to their reputation and majesty, are false—in which case the matter is altogether one for which the gods ought utterly to destroy the entire race of mortals—or, if they are verified and true and established beyond all doubt, the matter is brought to this final conclusion: that, [Col. 1061A] however unwilling you may be, we must believe that they belonged not to the heavenly but to the human race.

> **Note: [Col. 1061B]**
>
> **XXVIII.—“Crafts.”** Either the arts of midwifery are to be understood, or Arnobius is referring to what he said above, II.18: “Those things—crafts—are not gifts of knowledge, but inventions of the poorest necessity.” ORELL.
>
> **“Civil status.”** That is, freedom; for only free persons are considered to possess a legal personality or “head” [Col. 1061C] in the state, whereas slaves are regarded as being without one. TURNEBUS, *Adversaria* XI, ch. 20, p. 341.
>
> **“And deprived him of his royal right.”** On the expression *abstinere aliquem aliqua re*, “to deprive someone of something,” as good and approved Latin, see J. Lipsius, *Epistolary Questions* II, Epistle V, *Works* I, p. 488, Vesalius ed. ORELL.
>
> **“Retreats.”** The same as secluded places, in the proper and primary sense. ORELL.
>
> **“To excel in the stratagems of theft.”** Thus the manuscript. The Roman first edition, apparently through a printer’s error, has “to excel in the gifts of theft,” a reading nevertheless defended by Heraldus, who understands it of Mercury as favoring thieves and offering men gifts carried off by theft. Gelenius, indulging here too his passion for alteration, published “to excel in the ranks of thieves.” Stewechius prefers “to excel in stolen loves.” For my part, I see no reason to abandon the manuscript reading, most correctly restored by Meursius and the Leiden editor; it agrees perfectly with what Arnobius said above, ch. 24, about Mercury: “to preside over thievish frauds.” ORELL.
>
> [Col. 1061D] **“Allurement” (*pellacia*).** So below, ch. 35: “to alter faces by allurement” (see the notes there); and V.21: “the records of Jovian allurement.” Lucretius V.1002:
>
> “Nor could the deceitful allurement of the placid sea  
> entice anyone into peril with its smiling waves.” ELMENHORST.

## XXVIII

For where there are weddings, marriages, childbirths, nurses, crafts, bodily weaknesses; where there are civil status and the condition of slavery; where wounds, slaughter, and blood; where loves, desires, pleasures; where there is every passion of the mind arising from restless disturbances—there can necessarily be nothing divine there. Nor can what is peculiar to a mortal race and earthly frailty adhere to a superior nature.

For who, if only he recognizes and understands the force of that divine power and what it is, could believe either that a god possessed generative [Note: [Col. 1061B] The manuscript reads “genitable.”] organs and was deprived of them by a most hideous mutilation; or that he at some time destroyed offspring produced from himself and was restrained by the punishment of chains; [Col. 1061B] or that he in some fashion waged civil war with his father and deprived him of his royal right [Note: [Col. 1062B] Sabaeus reads “petty royal right.”]; or that, terrified by fear of an inferior and overcome, he turned his back and hid like a fugitive and exile in secluded retreats?

Who, I ask, could believe that a god reclined at human tables, was murdered for the sake of gain, deceived suppliants through the ambiguity [Col. 1062A] of an oracle, excelled in the stratagems of theft, committed adultery, served as a slave, was wounded, fell in love, and carried his seductive allurement through every form of lust and incestuous desire? Yet you assert both that all these things happened and that they exist in your gods; nor do you omit any form of vice, crime, or degradation which, through the wantonness of your opinions, you do not heap upon the divine beings as an insult.

Either, therefore, you must seek other gods to whom none of these things applies—for those to whom they do apply belong to the human and earthly race—or, if these are the only gods whose names and characters you have made public, you abolish them by your own opinions. For everything you relate is mortal.

> **Note: [Col. 1061D]**
>
> **XXIX.—“Euhemerus of Acragas.”** Lactantius, *Institutes* I.11: “The ancient author Euhemerus, who belonged to the city of Messene, collected the deeds of Jupiter and the others who are regarded as gods, and composed a history from sacred titles and inscriptions preserved in the most ancient temples.… Ennius both translated and followed this history.” Compare Minucius Felix, *Octavius* 21; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.42; Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians* IX.17, with Fabricius’ note, p. 552; Augustine, *City of God* VI.7 and VII.26; Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* II.4; and, among more recent authors, G. [Col. 1062B] J. Vossius, *On the Greek Historians* I.11; Columna on the *Fragments of Ennius*, p. 311; Brucker, *Critical History of Philosophy*; and above all our countryman J. J. Zimmermann, *Defense of Euhemerus against the Charge of Atheism*, included in his *Theological Essays* II, pp. 1052 ff.
>
> Moreover, here too Arnobius had Clement of Alexandria before his eyes, [Col. 1062C] who says as follows in the *Protrepticus*, p. 20, Potter’s edition:
>
> “Ὧν δὴ χάριν θαυμάζειν ἔπεστί μοι, ὅτῳ τρόπῳ Εὐήμερον τὸν Ἀκραγαντῖνον, καὶ Νικάνορα τὸν Κύπριον, καὶ Διαγόραν, καὶ Ἵππωνα τὸν Μήλιον, τόν τε Κυρηναῖον ἐπὶ τούτοις ἐκεῖνον, ὁ Θεόδωρος ὄνομα αὐτῷ, καί τινας ἄλλους συχνούς, σωφρόνως βεβιωκότας καὶ καθεωρακότας ὀξύτερόν που τῶν λοιπῶν ἀνθρώπων τὴν ἀμφὶ τοὺς θεοὺς τούτους πλάνην, ἀθέους ἐπικεκλήκασιν.”
>
> “For this reason I may well wonder how they came to call Euhemerus of Acragas, Nicanor of Cyprus, Diagoras, Hippo of Melos, and, besides these, that Cyrenian whose name was Theodorus, together with many others—men who lived temperately and perceived more keenly than the rest of mankind the error surrounding these gods—‘atheists.’” ORELL.
>
> **“Nicanor of Cyprus.”** I write *Nicanore Cyprio*. Clement, Lactantius, and no few others give his name in this form. MEURSIUS.—Arnobius should be emended thus from Clement. Others read “Nicagoras of Cyprus.” Perhaps he means Nicanor, the disciple of Epicurus mentioned by Diogenes Laertius X.20. POTTER, on Clement I.
>
> **“Leon of Pella.”** Arnobius added this man on his own; Clement omitted him. Nor, so far as I know, does any other author mention him. See Vossius, *On the Greek Historians* III, *Works* IV, p. 179, Amsterdam ed.—Orellius originally wrote the foregoing, but afterward added: “The opening words of our annotation [Col. 1062D] must be deleted entirely. For Clement does mention this Leon in *Stromata* I, p. 322 (Sylburg):
>
> ‘Λέων δὲ, ὁ τὰ περὶ τῶν κατ’ Αἴγυπτον θεῶν πραγματευσάμενος, τὴν Ἶσιν ὑπὸ τῶν Ἑλλήνων Δήμητρα καλεῖσθαί φησιν—Leon, who treated the subject of the gods of Egypt, says that Isis is called Demeter by the Greeks.’
>
> “So too Tatian, *Address to the Greeks* 44:
>
> ‘Λέοντος κεκτημένοι τὰ ὑπομνήματα πρὸς τοὺς ἀφ’ ἡμῶν ἐλέγχους δυσχεραίνετε—Although you possess the memoirs of Leon, you take offense at the refutations that come from us.’
>
> “Thus this Leon—whom we learn from Arnobius alone to have been a native of Pella—wrote *Aegyptiaca*, or a book about the Egyptian gods, in which he appears to have transmitted material refuting pagan superstition and false religion concerning their gods. Compare W. Worth’s extensive discussion of this Leon and others of that name, the Alabandan and the Byzantine, in his notes on Tatian, l.c., p. 96.” ORELL.
>
> **“Theodorus of Cyrene.”** He is mentioned by Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.1, and Diogenes Laertius II.86, 101. See Ernesti’s *Key to Cicero*. ORELL.
>
> **“Diagoras.”** See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I.1 and 23; the Suda; Lactantius I.2, with Bunemann’s note, p. 14. ORELL.
>
> [Col. 1063B] **“The care of scrupulous diligence.”** *Scrupulosus* means μικρολόγος (*mikrologos*), one who investigates every smallest detail. Thus Frontinus, [Col. 1063C] *On Aqueducts* II, beginning: “with scrupulous inquiry preceding”; see Keuchen’s note there, p. 383. ORELL.
>
> **“To bring forth the wars of Minerva, the virgin, and of Diana.”** Meursius, p. 136, punctuates thus: “and to bring forth the wars of the virgin Minerva, and of Diana,” thinking that Arnobius wished to express Minerva’s epithet Παρθένος (*Parthenos*, “Virgin”), under which name she was worshiped by the Athenians. ID.
>
> **“What Venus’ condition was, what her occupation, what her trade.”** All these terms—*conditio*, *opera*, *quaestus*—are used with the greatest precision. We commented previously on *conditio*. *Opera* (“occupation”) is likewise exact. Thus they say ἐργάζεσθαι (*ergazesthai*, “to work”), courtesans are called ἐργάσιμοι (*ergasimoi*, “working women”), and their sale and trade is called ἐργασία (*ergasia*, “business”). The observation about *quaestus* (“trade” or “earnings”) is elementary. But beginners should note this passage of Plautus’ *Asinaria*:
>
> “Mother, that is my trade:  
> my tongue demands it, my body seeks it, my heart asks for it, necessity counsels it.” HERALD.
>
> [Col. 1063D] Compare Oudendorp on Apuleius’ *Metamorphoses* VIII, p. 578. ORELL.
>
> **“By the handsome Attis.”** The glosses give *speciosus*, εὐειδής (*eueidēs*, “good-looking”). Chirius Fortunatianus, *Rhetoric* III, p. 109: “I have a beautiful wife.” Servius on *Aeneid* IX.539: “Attis, a beautiful boy.” ELMENHORST.

## XXIX

And indeed at this point we could show that all [Col. 1062B] those whom you introduce and call gods were human beings. We could do so by unfolding Euhemerus of Acragas, whose little books Ennius translated into the Italian language so that the matter might become clear to everyone; or by appealing to Nicanor of Cyprus, Leon of Pella, Theodorus of Cyrene, Hippo and Diagoras of Melos, or [Col. 1063A] a thousand other authorities who, with the care of scrupulous diligence and the freedom of freeborn men, brought hidden matters to light.

We could, I say, if it pleased us, bring forth both the deeds of Jupiter and the wars of Minerva, the virgin, and of Diana; the stratagems by which Liber sought the kingdom of the Indians; what Venus’ condition was, what her occupation, what her trade; whose marriage the Great Mother entered into; what hope, what pleasure she conceived from the handsome Attis; whence came the Egyptian Serapis, whence Isis, and from what causes the very appellation of their names was devised.

> **Note: [Col. 1063D]**
>
> **XXX.—“For it is not the man who carefully reviews.”** Arnobius alludes to the etymology of *religio*: “Those who diligently considered and, as it were, reviewed (*relegerent*) everything pertaining to the worship of the gods were called *religiosi*,” says Marcus Tullius Cicero (*On the Nature of the Gods* II.28). Arnobius followed this view. His pupil Lactantius (*Institutes* IV.28), however, more correctly held that *religio* was named from *religare*, “to bind.” For just as *postulio* comes from *postulo*, so *religio* comes from *religo*. Yet he does not seem to have understood the rationale of the derivation sufficiently, although he quoted a verse of Lucretius excellently suited to elucidating the whole matter (I.931):
>
> “I proceed to release minds from the knots of religions.”
>
> [Col. 1064B] And this is indeed so. For *religio* properly signifies the dread which divine things and powers surpassing human strength [Col. 1064C] inflict upon us, with the result that we are held as though bound and do not dare turn the mind’s attention elsewhere. Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII:
>
> “Even then the place’s dreadful sanctity  
> terrified the fearful country folk.”
>
