> Hence *religio* very often means a dread which, when presented to us by some sign, restrains us and holds us as though bound. Examples are innumerable. Particularly noteworthy, however, is the passage from Plautus’ *Merchant* which we cited above for another purpose:
>
> “Look here to the right, Charinus. Do you not see opposite us  
> a black cloud and rain threatening? Now look to the left.  
> Do you see how the sky opposite is filled with brightness?”
>
> CHARINUS: “It has put a religious scruple in my way; I shall turn back at once.”
>
> Here you see a man who had already set out on his journey, yet, when a religious scruple was presented to his mind, was as though bound and prevented from pursuing the journey he had undertaken. Arrian likewise says explicitly, [Col. 1064D] *Discourses of Epictetus* II.7:
>
> “Νῦν δὲ τρέμοντες τὸ ὀρνιθάριον κρατοῦμεν, καὶ τὸν θεὸν ἐπικαλούμενοι δεόμεθα αὐτοῦ, Κύριε ἐλέησον, ἐπίτρεψόν μοι ἐξελθεῖν—But now, trembling, we cling to the diviner by birds, and, calling upon God, we beg him: ‘Lord, have mercy; permit me to go out.’” HERALD.
>
> —So too a certain ancient writer quoted by Aulus Gellius IV.9:
>
> “One ought to be a careful reviewer, not entangled by religious scruples.” MEURSIUS, p. 137.
>
> **“Things which are not merely far removed and distant from their nature.”** Thus Meursius in the appendix and the Leiden editor from the manuscript. They therefore wrongly altered it to: “Things which are not merely far removed from their divine and surpassing nature.” ORELL.

## XXX

But in the discourse we are conducting, we have undertaken neither the small task nor the intention of showing and making public who all these beings were. Our purpose is this: since you call us impious and irreligious, while maintaining that you, by contrast, are pious [Note: [Col. 1063B] Thus Fulvius; “we,” Sabaeus, wrongly.] and [Col. 1063B] worshipers of the gods, we intend to demonstrate and set plainly before all that they are treated more disgracefully by no human beings than by you.

But if it is evident from the very slanders themselves that the matter stands so, it follows that you must be understood to stir up in the heavenly beings the goads of furious indignation, since you either hear or believe such foul and disgraceful things about them, or yourselves fabricate such stories.

For it is not the man who carefully reviews the ritual [Col. 1064A] and slaughters spotless victims, who provides heaps of incense to be burned in the fire, who should be judged [Note: [Col. 1063B] Sabaeus reads “agreed,” but wrongly.] to worship the divine powers or alone to fulfill the duties of religion. True worship lies in the heart and in an opinion worthy of the gods. Nor does the offering of blood and gore accomplish anything if you believe about them things which are not merely far removed and distant from their nature, but which also attach some stain and disgrace to their majesty and dignity.

> **Note: [Col. 1064D]**
>
> **XXXI.—“In your ceremonies and divine rites there is a place for *postuliones*.”** This is the entirely correct reading of the manuscript, first restored to Arnobius by Salmasius. A *postulio* occurs when offended gods demand expiation through the voice of the soothsayers. Thus Cicero, *On the Response of the Haruspices* 31: “By the same portent it is said that a *postulio* is owed to Tellus”—although both other editions and the most recent edition of Fr. A. Wolf read *postulatio*. Still more pertinent to our passage is Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, [Col. 1065A] p. 41, Bipontine ed.: “Procilius records that at that place the earth opened; and when the matter was referred by decree of the senate to the haruspices, the response was that the god of the Manes—Summanus—demanded a *postulio*, that is, that the bravest citizen be sent into the same place.” See there the many discussions of this word; Joseph Scaliger and Ausonius Popma II, pp. 100 ff.
>
> Gutherius, *On the Law of the Manes* IV, distinguishes *postulationes* from *postuliones*. He says that *postulationes* were made to the gods above, [Col. 1065B] but *postuliones* to the gods below, in which they sought to have a human being devoted to them. Gelenius and the other editors read *postulationibus*. Compare Turnebus, *Adversaria* XI.20. ORELL.
>
> **“And it is said that the commission of an offense requiring expiation has been incurred.”** See above, col. 1064. The ancient scholiast on Horace, *Odes* I.28: “*Piacula* were the victims by which a committed crime was expiated.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.569:
>
> “He deferred until a late death the offenses requiring expiation that he had committed.”
>
> Servius comments: “Committed *piacula* are offenses for which expiation is owed; in Greek, ἄγος (*agos*, ‘pollution’). The opposite is *impie commissum*, an offense committed impiously.” Cicero, *On the Laws* II.9: “A sacred offense that cannot be expiated has been committed impiously; one that can be expiated is to be expiated by the public priests.” ELMENHORST and HERALD.—*Piaculi* is from Meursius’ correction. In the first edition and that of Gelenius we read *piaculis*. Stewechius conjectures *piacularis commissio*, “the commission of an expiatory offense.” Justus Lipsius, *Ancient Readings* IV.3, *Works* I, p. 400, Vesalius ed., deletes the conjunction *et* and reads and punctuates the whole passage thus: “In your ceremonies and divine rites there is a place [Col. 1065C] for *postuliones*, for expiatory offenses. A commission is said to have been incurred,” etc. This is an excellent emendation and thoroughly consistent with Arnobius’ style, which very frequently omits connective particles. ORELL.
>
> **“If through an inadvertent slip someone errs in a word.”** In divine rites even the smallest details were observed with awestruck religious care; hence the commands for εὐφημία (*euphēmia*, reverent silence) and similar things, discussed elsewhere. There were fixed formulas to which they adhered scrupulously, and if at any time they erred in them through an inadvertent slip, it was believed that an enormous offense requiring expiation had been incurred. HERALD.
>
> **“Or errs with the *simpuium*.”** It is variously written: *sympinium* from συμπίνειν (*sympinein*, “to drink together”), *simpuvium*, or *simpulum*. Festus: “A *simpulum* is a small vessel not unlike a ladle, with which wine is poured as a libation in sacrifices. Hence women devoted to divine rites are called *simpulatrices*.” See the commentators there.
>
> Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, p. 35, Bipontine ed.: “A vessel by which they dispensed wine so as to pour it drop by drop was called a *guttum* from *guttae*, ‘drops’; and the vessel by which they took it little by little was named a *simpulum* from *sumere*, ‘to take’”—that is, to drink; see Meursius. [Col. 1065D] See there Joseph Scaliger, who discusses this word extensively in his *Observations*, p. 89, vol. II. Deriving *simpulum* from *simpo*, which is the Greek σίφων (*siphōn*, “tube” or “siphon”), he says that it was a small vessel with a slender tube or narrow neck, used for tasting wine, and that the sole difference between the *simpulum* and the Greek σίφων was that the Romans used their *simpulum* only in sacred rites, whereas the Greeks used τῷ σίφωνι (“the siphon”) to taste wine in a tavern.
>
> Compare Stewechius on this passage; Hadrianus Junius, *Critical Observations* II.10, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, p. 370; Hardouin on Pliny, *Natural History* XXXV.12.46; Gesner in the *Thesaurus* under this word; Ruperti on Juvenal, *Satires* VI.343; and Saubert, *On the Sacrifices of the Ancients* 17, p. 349, Crenius ed. We see different forms of such small vessels illustrated in Schatz’s compendium of Montfaucon’s *Antiquities*, plate LIV, figs. 5–9; and Nonius, under this word, teaches that they were made of earthenware as well as wood. To “err with the *simpuvium*,” therefore, means nothing other than to err in the proper pouring or dispensing of the libation wine.
>
> Moreover, this entire passage is drawn from the pseudo-Ciceronian *Speech on the Response of the Haruspices* 23: “Or if an actor came to a halt, or a flute-player suddenly fell silent, [Col. 1066A] or that boy whose father and mother were both living failed to keep hold of the ground, or let go of the sacred car or its strap, or if the aedile erred in a word or with the *simpulum*, the games were not duly performed; those errors were expiated, and the minds of the immortal gods were appeased by repeating the games.” For more on the *simpuvium*, see Meursius IV.12. ORELL.
>
> **“Or if someone strays from the proper course at solemn games and sacred races; everyone at once cries out that an offense…”** Salmasius most correctly punctuated the passage [Col. 1066B] in this way. For the words “or if during the procession,” etc., are to be referred to what precedes: “there is a place for *postuliones*, and it is said that the commission of an offense requiring expiation has been incurred,” etc. By contrast, a new clause begins with “everyone at once cries out that an offense,” etc.
>
> Heraldus therefore wrongly reads and punctuates: “Or if again, in solemn praises and divine races, everyone at once cries out that an offense,” etc. *Cursu* (“in the course” or “procession”) in place of *rursus* (“again”), which stood in the manuscript, is a most successful emendation by Gelenius. The “divine races” are the chariot games held in honor of the gods.
>
> Theodorus Marcilius, on Horace, *Odes* I.21, most admirably restored the damaged and mishandled passage by reading: “Or erred with the *simpulum*; or if again, at solemn games and divine races, an actor came to a halt or a flute-player suddenly fell silent; or if that boy who is called *patrimus* omitted his place through ignorance, or was unable to hold the sacred car: everyone at once cries out that an offense against the sacred religious rites,” etc. ORELL.
>
> **“If an actor came to a halt.”** The matter is familiar even from the proverb: “All is safe while the old man dances.” A *ludius* is an ὀρχηστής (*orchēstēs*, dancer). Plautus, *Aulularia*:
>
> [Col. 1066C] “…If you are wise, you will make that cock  
> smoother for me than a plucked dancer.”
>
> Plautus is speaking of these dancers because they were plucked smooth, with beardless, depilated faces. Julian, in the *Misopogon*, mentions:
>
> “μίμους, ὀρχηστὰς, κιστα ἥαἰσχυνομένας γυναῖκας, παιδάρια περὶ κάλλους ἁμιλλώμενα ταῖς γυναιξὶν, ἄνδρας ἀποψιλουμένους οὔτι τὰς γνάθους μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἅπαν τὸ σῶμα, λειότεροι τῶν γυναικῶν ὅπως φαίνοιντο τοῖς ἐντυγχάνουσιν—“mimes, dancers, κιστα ἥαἰσχυνομένας [corrupt in the supplied source] women, boys competing with women in beauty, and men removing the hair not merely from their jaws but from their entire bodies, so that they might appear smoother than women to those who encountered them.”
>
> Tertullian likewise speaks of them in *On the Shows* 23: “And will that man be pleasing who alters his face with a razor, unfaithful to his own countenance, which, not content to make it resemble those of Saturn, Isis, and Liber, he furthermore exposes to the insults of slaps, as though he were mocking the Lord’s command?” HERALD.
>
> —Servius on *Aeneid* VII: “When the Circus games were being celebrated for Apollo, and it was reported that Hannibal was bearing down upon the city near the Colline Gate, everyone seized weapons and rushed together. When they later returned, fearing that an offense requiring expiation had been incurred, they found a certain old man dancing in the Circus. When questioned, he said that he had not interrupted his dance; [Col. 1066D] hence the proverb arose: ‘All is safe: the old man is dancing.’” Compare Festus under “All is safe.” ELMENHORST. See Salmasius on Trebellius Pollio, *Claudius* 5, II, p. 632, and on Vopiscus, *Carinus*, p. 843; Burmann on Ovid, *Art of Love* I.112; and Ernesti’s *Key to Cicero*, under *Ludius*. ORELL.
>
> **“Or if that boy who is called *patrimus* let go of the strap through ignorance.”** Asconius interprets this passage in his commentary on the first *Against Verres* 59: “Some think that *thensae* are so called from their divine character, because straps are stretched before them; those who conduct them delight to hold and touch these straps with their hands.” Learned men think Asconius took this from Virgil, who sings in *Aeneid* II.238 of the Trojan horse as it was being led into the city:
>
> “…Around it boys and unwed maidens  
> sing sacred songs and delight to touch the rope with their hands.”
>
> It therefore appears that boys whose fathers and mothers were both living, and who conducted—that is, accompanied—each sacred car, held in their hands both the *thensa* and the strap by which the horse drew it; and if any of them happened to let go of that [Col. 1067B] strap, an offense requiring expiation was committed. GRAEVIUS, on Cicero, *On the Response of the Haruspices* 11.
>
> Fulvius Ursinus, following the cited passage of Cicero, recasts the text: “Or if that boy who is called *patrimus and matrimus*,” etc. But perhaps nothing should be changed, for Arnobius seems to have copied his Cicero somewhat carelessly, also omitting the following words: “or the *thensa* or…”
>
> Concerning the *thensae*, sacred vehicles made of ivory and [Col. 1067C] silver in which images of the gods were carried, the matter is familiar. See nevertheless Lipsius, *On the Vestals* XI; Vossius, *On Idolatry* II.10; and Saubert, *On Sacrifices* 19, pp. 402 f. ORELL.
>
> **“Or was unable to keep hold of the ground.”** Heraldus admits that he does not know what “to keep hold of the ground” means and thinks these words should be deleted as a gloss from Cicero and Arnobius. Salmasius and Fabrettus, cited by the distinguished Fr. A. Wolf on Cicero, l.c., p. 339, conjecture: “if he was unable to hold the incense-box.” Lipsius, however, *Ancient Readings* IV.3, proposes: “or was unable to hold the *siserra*.” The glosses define *siserra* as πρόβατον μεῖζον ἐνιαυτοῦ, “a sheep more than a year old.”
>
> But Varro, *On Agriculture* I.2, and Macrobius, *Saturnalia* III.9—cited by Turnebus, *Adversaria* XVI.10—show that “to keep hold of the ground” means to touch the ground with one’s hands. Graevius and the distinguished Wolf approve this explanation, while deleting with Ernesti and Garatoni the words “or the *thensa*” as spurious additions from Cicero. Meursius, by contrast, expands the text to read: “or was unable to hold either the *thensa* or the ground.”
>
> Joannes Saubertus, *On Sacrifices* 19, pp. 398 f., [Col. 1067D] Crenius ed., disagrees. He thinks the words allude to a special ritual observed by the attendants of victims, or by boys whose fathers and mothers were both living and who conducted the victims: they never had one foot raised except in the act of stepping forward. This, he argues, is what “to keep hold of the ground” means.
>
> Whichever explanation we follow, the sense of the passage will be this: if that boy, the ἀμφιθαλής (*amphithalēs*, one whose parents are both living), fell and touched the ground with his hands or feet. For it is generally agreed that every fall was an evil omen. Hence even new brides were forbidden to touch the threshold with the sole of the foot as they crossed it, but were lifted over it, lest they stumble at the beginning and by this sign vitiate the auspices of the marriage.
>
> Those who insert “ground” here too and read “or was unable to hold either the sacred car or the ground” are mistaken. Cicero, and Arnobius after him, rightly joined the sacred car and its strap. For to let go of the strap—namely, the strap of the sacred car—is plainly the same as being unable to hold the car. The man who conducted the sacred car held it by the strap, or held the car’s strap, as is clear from the passage of Asconius cited above.
>
> There were various sacred cars. The first of all belonged to Jupiter; [Col. 1068B] the emperor himself was accustomed to conduct it, as in Suetonius, *Augustus* 43 and *Vespasian* 5. Under the old republic this was the consul’s role, as in Juvenal, *Satires* 10, and Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown* 13. The remaining sacred cars, both of gods and of heroes, were conducted by boys whose fathers and mothers were both living. If one of these failed to keep hold of the sacred car’s strap, or let go of it, those Circus games had not been duly [Col. 1068C] performed; the error had to be expiated and the games repeated. THEODORUS MARCILIUS, on Horace, *Odes* I.21, p. 26. ORELL.

## XXXI

For I should like to question you and summon you to answer a brief argument: which do you consider more serious—to slaughter no victims for the gods because you think that so exalted a nature neither desires nor seeks them, or to conceive such disgraceful beliefs about them that they could drive anyone’s mind into a frenzy of vengeance?

If the weight of the matters is assessed, you would find [Col. 1064B] no judge so prejudiced as not to consider it more criminal that a person’s reputation should be torn apart by conspicuous slanders than that he should be passed over by someone in silence. For the latter might perhaps be regarded and believed to arise from reason; the former belongs to a sacrilegious mind and to blindness beyond hope in its fabrications.

In your ceremonies and divine rites there is a place for *postuliones* [Note: [Col. 1064B] The manuscript reads *postilionibus*; Fulvius, *pollutionibus*; Sabaeus and the other editors, *postulationibus*; see the note.], and it is said that the commission of an offense requiring expiation has been incurred if, through an inadvertent slip, someone errs in a word [Col. 1065A], or with the *simpuvium* [Note: [Col. 1065A] Thus the manuscript; Sabaeus reads *sympivium*.], or in the course or procession at solemn games and sacred races. Everyone immediately cries out that an offense against the sacred rites has been committed if a dancer comes to a halt or a flute-player suddenly falls silent; or if that boy who is called *patrimus* missed the proper place through ignorance [Col. 1066A], or was unable to keep hold of the ground.

And do you dare deny that in offenses so grave the gods are always violated by you, when you yourselves confess that in less serious matters they frequently become angry even to the destruction of the state?

[Col. 1067A]

> **Note: [Col. 1068C]**
>
> *The supplied source ends here with this note incomplete.*
### XXXII.—“For pleasure.”

The first edition of Sabaeus reads: “At will.” ORELLI.

**“Less brutish.”** Fulvius Ursinus prefers: “not at all brutish.” ORELLI.

**“Of unrestricted right.”** The Glosses: *licentiosus*, παρρησιαστής, “one who speaks freely.” It is a sound word of approved Latinity, used also by Quintilian, *Institutes*, book I, chapter 6. ELMENHORST and ORELLI.

**“To confront so great a rashness.”** Thus Canter and the Leiden editor reconstructed the text from the manuscript codex and the first edition. Gelenius printed *itis*. ORELLI.

### XXXII

“But,” they say, “all these things are inventions of the poets, playful compositions devised for pleasure.” It is certainly not credible that men who were less brutish and investigators of the most remote antiquity either inserted into their poems tales that survived in human conceptions and had taken their place in people’s ears, or wished to claim for themselves a right so unrestricted that in their folly they fabricated things that were not far removed from madness and could bring upon them fear from the gods and danger from human beings.

But let us grant, as you say, that the poets were the contrivers and inventors of such great deformities. Even so, you are not free from the charge of mistreating the gods, since you either fail to punish such offenses or have not enacted laws and, by severity of penalties, confronted [Col. 1067B] so great a rashness, establishing that henceforth no human being should utter anything approaching obscenity or unworthy of the majesties of the gods. For whoever allows a wrongdoer to do wrong supplies strength to his audacity; and it is a matter of graver insult to brand and stigmatize anyone with false accusations than to cast true offenses in his teeth and charge him with them. [Col. 1068A] For to be told what you are, and what you know yourself to be, has a lesser sting, blunted by the testimony of tacit acknowledgment. But that wounds most bitterly which brands the innocent and brings the honor of their name and reputation into disrepute.

[Note: [Col. 1068C]

### XXXIII.—“In golden Chalcidian halls.”

See above, on book III, chapter 10. ORELLI.

**“Most patient ears.”** Stewechius prefers *patientissimas*; but nothing should be changed. “Patience of the ears” is found also in Lactantius, book I, chapter 1, and this seems more fitting in view of the words immediately following: “Nor do you judge [Col. 1068D] it unworthy,” etc. ORELLI.

**“By which earthly bodies are sustained.”** What could be more contrary to common sense than this? Bodies are enervated and broken by pleasures; so far are they from being strengthened by them. I emend: “by which earthly bodies are soothed,” and *quas aures expetant*, “which ears seek,” for *expetunt*. MEURSIUS. But Arnobius here understands not sexual pleasures, but those of which he spoke before—banquets and drinking parties—which, provided they do not exceed due measure, may rightly be said to sustain human bodies. ORELLI.

**“You exalt with the incentive of praise.”** Heraldus and Salmasius restored this reading from the manuscript codex. Previously the text read: “incentives … with praise.” *Incentivum* means the same as incitement or stimulus, a word of later Latinity. Thus the anonymous *Panegyric on Constantine* VIII, chapter 1, p. 480, and Jaeger: “For if in military affairs and battles themselves not only trumpets and horns, but even Spartan flutes, are said to have supplied some incentive.” And Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV, at the beginning, concerning Gallus: “His wife had been added as a powerful incentive to his cruelty, swollen beyond measure by her kinship with the Augustus.” Zosimus, speaking of the same man, expresses it thus: ἔχοντος καὶ τὴν ὁμόζυγον πρὸς τοῦτο αὐτὸν ἐρεθίζουσαν, “since he also had his wife inciting him to this very thing.” The Greeks called it ἐνδόσιμον, “an incitement.” Compare Rittershusius, who discusses this word at length, on Salvian, *On the Governance of God*, p. 8, Bremen edition. ORELLI.

**“The wounds of his mutilation,” etc.** Thus Meursius and Salmasius, quite correctly, for “those wounds.” ORELLI.

**“What ought utterly to have been removed from the fellowship of the human race.”** Gesner, in the *Thesaurus*, explains the word *coalitus* thus: “What ought utterly to have been removed, lest it coalesce—that is, become prevalent [Col. 1069C] and established among human beings.” But it seems preferable to interpret it: “What ought utterly to have been removed from the society and fellowship of the human race.” Livy uses the verb *coalescere* in this sense, book I, chapter 8: “And the multitude was summoned to an assembly, since it could coalesce into the body of one people by nothing except laws.” And chapter 11: “Thus the state could coalesce through concord.” Lambinus, however, on Lucretius II.1129, p. 282, and VI.1066, p. 852, endeavors to prove that *coalescere* and *coalitus* are insufficiently Latin and that in all those passages *coolescere* and *coolitus* should be substituted. Our passage is the sole example of the noun *coalitus*, fourth declension, cited in the lexicons. Hence Elmenhorst and others proposed *coetu*, “from the assembly.” ORELLI.

**“You review them, you learn them by heart.”** Stewechius was the first to restore *ediscitis*, “you learn by heart,” from the manuscript codex. So shortly afterward, chapter 36: “You both recite encomia of abuse every day and learn them by heart every day.” ORELLI.]

### XXXIII

Your gods are represented as dining and drinking in heavenly dining rooms and golden Chalcidian halls, and finally as being soothed by the lyre and the modulation of voices. You lend them most patient ears; nor do you judge it unworthy that those pleasures should be attributed to the gods by which earthly bodies are sustained and which ears softened by the enervation of a debilitated heart eagerly seek.

Some of them are introduced as lovers and adulterers against chastity, joining not only with women but even with men in shameful and disgraceful intercourse. You have no concern for what is said about [Col. 1068B] matters so grave, nor do you restrain the audacity of licentious literature even by the threat of punishment. Others, in fits of insanity and frenzy, mutilate themselves and, as though with an enemy’s blood, stain themselves with their own through murderous violence against their own persons. You marvel at those sacrileges when they are loftily elevated in style; and that which deserved to be punished with every penalty, you exalt with the incentive of praise, so that its audacity may rise more spiritedly. [Col. 1069A] Those others groan over the wounds of their mutilation and, with unseemly wailings, accuse the cruelty of fate [Note: [Col. 1069B] Sabaeus wrongly reads *facta*, “deeds.”]; you stand amazed at the powers of eloquence, and what ought utterly to have been removed from the fellowship of the human race you review and learn by heart, taking care that it should not perish through any forgetfulness.

They are recorded as being wounded and tormented and as waging wars among themselves in the furious heat of deadly conflicts; you take pleasure in that description, and, to defend so great an audacity on the part of the writers, you falsely claim that these things are allegories and doctrines of natural science.

[Note: [Col. 1069C]

### XXXIV.—“Whose name it was fitting for you to utter.”

Thus Meursius for “whose divinity it was fitting for you to utter.” ORELLI.

**“He is described as a lover captivated by his wife and confessing his offenses.”** [Col. 1069D] Thus the manuscript. Gelenius printed *amasius*. But Apuleius also uses the comparatively unusual form *amasio, -onis*, *Metamorphoses* III, p. 216, and VII, p. 488, Oudendorp’s edition, where see the notes; so too Prudentius, poem X, Περὶ στεφάνων (*On the Crowns*), verse 182:

> Girls marry; they are often made sport of by the tricks  
> Of lovers and are violated by their deceits.

For the rest, as Canter notes, Arnobius is referring here to the Homeric passage, *Iliad* XIV.312–328. ORELLI.—So too *pusus, pusio, pumilus, pumilio*, and other forms. MEURSIUS, in the Appendix.

**“Hardened in shamelessness, to publish.”** He calls a man “hardened in shamelessness” when he has become wholly hardened into impudence and has so hardened his face and brow—that is, all those features through which shame ordinarily betrays itself—that no sign of modesty remains in them. Hence Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams* I.24, uses χάλκεον, σιδήρεον, λίθινον μέτωπον, “a brazen, iron, or stone forehead,” of the shameless; and σιδηροῦς, “iron,” of a person who cannot be moved by any force of shame, as, for example, in [Col. 1070B] that verse of Sophocles quoted by Aristotle, *Rhetoric* II.23:

> Σαφὼ σιδηρὼ καὶ φοροῦσα τοὔνομα.  
> “Manifestly iron-hearted, and bearing the very name.”

HERALDUS.

**“You declare them to be most sacred heads.”** This follows a Greek mode of expression which the Latins also frequently used with equal elegance. Seneca in the *Oedipus*:

> O head sacred to the gods, second only to Phoebus.

HERALDUS.

**“So that words carry greater weight among you than the violated sublimity of the heavenly beings.”** Others—for example, Meursius—prefer: “by which the sublimity of the heavenly beings is violated.” ORELLI.

**“Indiscriminately … utter.”** *Passim* means without choice or distinction. [Col. 1070C] See above, on book II, chapter 1. ORELLI.

**“Utter. Nor did they earn from you even that honor,” etc.** Stewechius restored the passage thus from the manuscript codex, followed by the Leiden edition. Previously it was printed: “utter, and so that they might earn from you at least that honor.” But these words depend not upon those immediately preceding, but, as Stewechius rightly notes, must be referred to what Arnobius said a little earlier: “Therefore it was fitting,” etc. In what follows, Meursius restored *expellitis* for *expelletis*. The same scholar conjectured *expelleretis*, very badly. *Expellitis* is equivalent to “you are accustomed to repel.” ORELLI.

**“Among you those are guilty of treason who have muttered something rather disparaging about your kings.”** We owe this very correct reading also to Stewechius, who restored it to the text from the manuscript codex. Previously *secus*, “otherwise,” was read. But *sequius*, “rather worse” or “disparagingly,” is far superior. Thus Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VIII: “Thrasyllus approved the form of the funereal wedding and suspected nothing untoward.” Varro, quoted by Nonius under the verb *Ruminare*: [Col. 1070D] “Not only will he, in your absence, think nothing disparaging about you, but he will also reflect upon your kindness.” Stewechius cited these passages.

For the rest, Paul, *Sentences* V, title 29, speaks thus concerning the crime of treason: “Under the Julian Law of Treason, a person is liable if, through his aid or counsel, arms have been taken up against the emperor or the commonwealth and the emperor’s army has been led into an ambush; or if, without the emperor’s command, he has waged war, held a levy, raised an army, solicited it, or deserted the emperor. Formerly such persons were permanently denied fire and water; now, however, those of lower rank are thrown to beasts or burned alive, while those of higher rank are punished by beheading. This crime is aggravated not only by deeds, but especially by impious and abusive words.” See Fr. Lindenbrog on the sole law in the Code, *If Anyone Has Spoken Ill of the Emperor*. ORELLI and ELMENHORST.

**“Or assail a senator with abuse.”** The emperors Arcadius and Honorius wished senators to be preserved so inviolable that they declared them to be a part of their own body, and condemned anyone who killed them or injured them by word or deed to be struck down by the sword [Col. 1071B] as guilty of treason, all his property being assigned to the treasury. See Law V in the Code, on the Julian Law of Treason. STEWECHIUS and ELMENHORST.

**“To compose an abusive poem,” etc.** The law of the Twelve Tables was framed thus:

> IF ANYONE SHALL CHANT, REHEARSE, OR COMPOSE A SONG WHICH BRINGS DISGRACE OR INFAMY UPON ANOTHER, LET IT BE A CAPITAL OFFENSE.

Cicero discusses this law in *On the Republic* IV, quoted by Augustine, *City of God* II.9: “Although our Twelve Tables made very few offenses capital, they nevertheless thought that this one should also be made so: if anyone performed or composed a song that brought infamy or disgrace upon another.” And chapter 12: “The Romans, as Scipio boasts in that discussion on the republic, did not wish life to be exposed to the reproaches and injuries of poets, and enacted that anyone who dared to compose such a song should even be punished capitally.”

A similar [Col. 1071C] provision occurs in Law X of the Theodosian Code, *On Defamatory Pamphlets*: “Let all who have hurled defamatory pamphlets at their enemies like some poisoned weapon—and also those who, upon recognizing an impudent defamatory composition, have not immediately torn it up, burned it in the flames, or disclosed the reader whom they know—fear the avenging sword upon their necks.” ELMENHORST.

An “abusive poem,” therefore, is a defamatory, accusatory, or slanderous poem, the writing of which was prohibited on pain of death and beating with rods, as Horace testifies, *Epistles* II.1.152ff.:

> Indeed, a law and penalty were also enacted  
> Which forbade anyone to be portrayed in an abusive poem;  
> And, through fear of the cudgel, poets changed their tune  
> And were brought back to speaking well and giving pleasure.

See the ancient scholiast there. Compare Savaron on Sidonius I.11, p. 78; Fornerius on Cassiodorus, *Variae* XI.11, p. 707, Geneva edition; Lipsius on Tacitus, *Histories* IV.45; Funccius on the Twelve Tables, Vinc.; and Gravina, *On the Origin of Law*, p. 167ff. ORELLI.

**“Against whom the right has been granted by you.”** Thus Fulvius Ursinus and Gelenius corrected the text. The first edition has: “In anyone [Col. 1071D] it has been granted by you.” ORELLI.

**“Has fashioned.”** Thus Meursius. Previously *confixerit*, “has pierced,” was printed. ORELLI.

**“Forms.”** The same Meursius, *Criticus* VII.9, suspects that *forias*, “refuse, dung,” should be read. Nonius: “*Foriae* … more liquid dung, whence *foricae*, ‘latrines.’ *Forire*, to relieve the bowels. *Forioli*, persons whose bowels are loose and excessively soft.” But we have no need of this ugly word. ORELLI.]

### XXXIV

But why do I complain that the insults offered to the divinities of others are neglected? Jupiter himself, whose name it was fitting for you to utter only with fear and a trembling of the whole body, is described as a lover captivated by his wife, confessing his offenses, and, like a madman unaware of what he is doing, hardened in shamelessness, publicly declaring which little mistresses and which concubines he had preferred to his spouse and wife. [Col. 1069B] Yet you commemorate those who brought forth such monstrosities [Col. 1070A] as the chiefs and kings of poets, endowed with divine genius, and as most sacred heads. You have flown so far from the duty of the religions you introduce that words carry greater weight among you than the violated sublimity of the heavenly beings.

Therefore, if there were among you any fear of the gods, or if with the confidence of certain conviction [Note: [Col. 1069B] The manuscript reads “most certain.”] you believed that they existed anywhere, it would surely have been fitting to intervene by legislative proposals, plebiscites, and the intimidating decrees of the senate—to prohibit and ordain that no one should choose to utter indiscriminately anything concerning the gods unless it were full of reverence. Nor did they earn from you even that honor: that by the same laws with which you repel injuries from yourselves, you should ward injuries away from them.

Among you those are guilty of treason who have muttered something rather disparaging about your kings. You have decreed that to call a magistrate to order [Col. 1070B] or assail a senator with abuse [Col. 1071A] is most perilous under your penalties. You were unwilling to allow anyone to escape unpunished under the decrees of the decemvirs for composing an abusive poem by which another’s reputation and life are defiled; and, lest anyone strike your ears with insolent abuse, you established legal formulas concerning aggravated injuries.

The heavenly gods alone are dishonored, contemptible, and worthless among you. Against them you have granted everyone the right to say whatever he pleases, and to fling at them whatever forms of obscenity lust has fashioned and devised. Yet you do not blush to charge us with neglect of such infamous divinities, although it is far more proper not to believe that gods exist than to believe them to be such as these and to think of them with such an estimation.

[Note: [Col. 1071D]

### XXXV.—“What of the actors?”

There is a very similar passage in Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 15: “The writings of the actors also depict all their foulness. The Sun mourns his son cast down from heaven while you rejoice, and Cybele sighs after her disdainful shepherd while you do not blush. And you endure encomia of Jupiter being sung and Juno, Venus, and Minerva being judged by a shepherd.” ELMENHORST.

**“Do they not abuse your gods for the purposes of their own profit, while pandering delights are drawn from injuries and insults to the gods?”** Thus the manuscript. Gelenius printed the singular *abutitur*, referring it, like the following *attrahit*, to the preceding words “that multitude of the debauched class.” Heraldus thinks *attrahit* is used impersonally [Col. 1072B] for *attrahunt*. “Draws”;  that is, some person does so, as above he says “someone will ask.” The manuscript reading seems to me entirely correct, and *attrahit* must certainly be referred to “the multitude of the debauched class.” I understand this expression, however, not of theatrical performers and actors, although he calls them by that name in the following chapter, but rather of the soft and effeminate multitude of spectators, who most eagerly seize every enticement of pleasure. For we showed above, on book II, chapter 43, that such persons were called *exoleti*, “debauched” or “worn out by vice.”

The sense of our passage, therefore, will be this: “Do not those pantomimes, actors, and mimes abuse your gods for the purposes of their own profit, while the multitude of the debauched class draws pandering delights from injuries and insults to the gods?” I would not deny that this is somewhat harsh; nevertheless, such things must be pardoned in Arnobius, a writer insufficiently polished. ORELLI.

**“The fifteen laurel-crowned men.”** The quindecimvirs were guardians of the Sibylline [Col. 1072C] books. Although they eventually numbered sixty, the designation “fifteen” nevertheless remained among them, as Servius observes. They were laurel-crowned because, when they attended the games wearing various crowns, it was surely most appropriate that the quindecimvirs who handled the Sibylline lots should be crowned with laurel. HERALDUS.

**“Kings nearest to the gods and most august.”** In those times the Roman emperors and their sons were called “kings.” Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chapter 30: “So many kings are watching, who were reported to have been received into heaven after consecration”—that is, emperors enrolled among the divine. And Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 19, concerning Diocletian: “Then he comes down, and the veteran king is conveyed through the city in a carriage, carried outside, and dismissed to his native land.” Compare Ezechiel Spanheim, who discusses the matter extensively in *On the Excellence and Use of Coins*, dissertation 12, vol. II, p. 399, Amsterdam edition. ORELLI.

**“Of the ruler and the people.”** Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.852:

[Col. 1072D]

> You, Roman, remember to rule the peoples with sovereign power.

ORELLI.

**“Venus is danced … and the Great Mother too is danced.”** *Saltare*, “to dance,” means ἐπιδεικτικῶς ὑπορχήσασθαι, “to represent dramatically in dance,” and is said of mimes and pantomimes, who by gesticulation and the movement of hands and feet, through manifold figures and postures accompanied by song, imitated a history or tale. Thus Horace, *Satires* I.5, says “to dance the Cyclops,” and Juvenal, satire VI.63:

> While soft Bathyllus dances Leda with expressive gestures,  
> Tuccia no longer commands her bladder.

See Ruperti there. Concerning such a dancer, an ancient epigram in the *Latin Anthology*, P. Burmann II, book III, no. 178, vol. I, p. 622, says:

> The man has as many tongues as limbs: wondrous is the art  
> Which makes his joints speak while his mouth is silent.

See Rigaltius, who discusses this subject extensively, on Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams* I.76, vol. II, p. 57f., Reiff’s edition. ORELLI.

[Col. 1073B] **“Adorned with sacred fillets.”** The Glosses: *Infulae*, στέμματα, “bands” or “crowns.” Virgil, *Aeneid* X.538:

> Whose temples a sacred fillet encircled with its band.

Servius comments there: “An *infula* is a band in the form of a diadem, from which ribbons hang down on both sides.” Compare Festus, under *Infula*. ELMENHORST.

**“In the embrace of a single herdsman … to be in transports.”** Oudendorp prefers “into the embrace,” on Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 70, Addenda, p. 1022. See above, on chapter 14, the words: “Who is said to have neighed lustfully after Proserpina with erect genitals.” ORELLI.

**“Of Sophocles in the *Women of Trachis*.”** Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* II.8: “But let us consider Hercules himself, who was then being broken by pain when he sought immortality itself through death. What [Col. 1073C] cries does he utter in Sophocles’ *Women of Trachis*? When Deianira had clothed him in a tunic stained with the Centaur’s blood, and its poisonous force had adhered to his entrails, he says:

> O many things grievous to tell and harsh to endure,  
> Which I have borne in body and in mind,” etc.

ELMENHORST. The manuscript has “Sophocles in the *Women of Trachis*,” incorrectly; hence Gelenius reconstructed “by Sophocles in the *Women of Trachis*.” Salmasius: “of Sophocles in the *Women of Trachis*.” N. Heinsius, Letter 257 to Graevius, in Burmann’s *Sylloge*, vol. IV, p. 329, reads: “in the Sophoclean *Women of Trachis*,” which I prefer. Arnobius is referring to *Women of Trachis* 1063ff. ORELLI.

**“Ensnared in a hunting net.”** Janus Guilielmus restored the text thus in *Plautine Questions on the Curculio*, chapter 5, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, part II, p. 366. This correction is also confirmed by the manuscript codex, according to Stewechius and N. Heinsius in the letter to Graevius just cited. *Circumretitus*, “ensnared,” corresponds excellently to *indago*, “hunting net,” whose proper setting is hunting and nets. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.121:

[Col. 1073D]

> And they encircle the glades with a hunting net.

Arnobius uses it in the same way below, book V, chapter 41: “When we say that Mars and Venus were ensnared in adultery by Vulcan’s skill.” Previously *circumpetitus*, “assailed on every side,” was read. ORELLI.

**“Wasting.”** Meursius prefers “by the laceration of his entrails.” But “wasting” is correct: Arnobius is evidently indicating that the entrails—that is, the flesh, whatever lies beneath the skin—were eaten away and dissolved by poison. ORELLI.

**“Indeed, even that greatest ruler of heaven himself in the tales.”** Prudentius, *Martyrdom of Romanus*:

> The swan-shaped ravisher sins upon the stage;  
> An actor dances the thunderer as a horned bull.  
> You, chief pontiff, sit as spectator of these things  
> And laugh yourself; nor do you absolve yourself by denial  
> When the fame of so great a deity is defiled.

HERALDUS.

**“Without any fear of the name….”** Meursius reads “of the divinity,” correctly. ORELLI.

**“To deceive chastity.”** Fulvius Ursinus conjectures that “to destroy chastity” should be read. Wrongly. “To deceive chastity” is, of course, to destroy it—[Col. 1074B] to subvert chastity by tricks and deceptions. ORELLI.

**“Mothers of families.”** This rather unusual transposition for *matresfamilias* should be noted. Among the Latins, a *materfamilias* is a lawful wife, as opposed to a concubine. ORELLI.

**“To alter his face by trickery.”** Stewechius showed that this should be read from the manuscript codex, which has *ellacia*. Compare N. Heinsius, Letter 257 to Graevius. Previously the text read “to alter his face deceitfully.” But see what we observed above on chapter 28. ORELLI.

**“And, through the simulation of a substituted body, to assume the appearance of their husbands.”** This alludes to Plautus’ *Amphitryon*. For *subditivi*, “substituted,” others read *subdititii*, “supposititious.” But Plautus uses the same form, *Amphitryon* I.2.25:

> Look, the substitute Amphitryon is coming out.

ORELLI.]

### XXXV

But did you intend that poets alone should be permitted to invent unworthy tales and shameful mockeries concerning the gods? [Col. 1071B] What of your pantomimes? What of your actors? What [Col. 1072A] of that multitude of mimes and of the debauched class? Do they not abuse your gods for the purposes of their own profit, while the multitude draws pandering delights from injuries and insults to the gods?

At the public spectacles sit the colleges of all the priests and magistrates: the chief pontiffs and chief curiones; there sit the fifteen laurel-crowned men, and the Flamen Dialis and the other flamens with their pointed caps; there sit the augurs, interpreters of the divine mind and will, as well as the chaste virgins, the perpetual nurses and preservers of the fire. The whole people and senate sit there; fathers who have held consulships; kings nearest to the gods and most august. And—what would be impious even to hear—that progenitress of the martial nation, the loving Venus, mother of its ruler and people, is danced upon the stage and, through every passion of harlot-like degradation, is represented by an indecent imitation as raving in frenzy. [Col. 1072B]

[Col. 1073A] The Great Mother too is danced, adorned with sacred fillets; and, contrary to the dignity of her age, that Pessinuntian Dindymene is represented as writhing with shameful desire in the embrace of a single herdsman. So too that offspring of Jupiter, the Hercules of Sophocles’ *Women of Trachis*, ensnared in the hunting net of his pestilential garment, is introduced uttering pitiable wails, broken by the violence of his pain, and consumed to utter dissolution by the wasting of his liquefying entrails.

Indeed, even that greatest ruler of heaven himself is introduced in the tales, without any fear of his name or majesty, playing the role of adulterers and, so that he may deceive the chastity of other men’s lawful wives, altering his face by trickery and, through the simulation of a supposititious body, [Col. 1073B] assuming the appearance of their husbands.

[Col. 1074A] [Note: [Col. 1074C]

### XXXVI.—“The divinities are assailed with jocular taunts.”

Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 15, beginning: “Other products of licentious ingenuity also minister to your pleasures through the dishonoring of the gods. Examine the witticisms of the Lentuli and Hostilii, and ask whether in their jokes and tricks you are laughing at the mimes or at your gods: Anubis the adulterer, the male Moon, Diana scourged, the testament of the dead Jupiter recited, and three hungry Herculeses mocked.” HERALDUS.—*Cavillatio*, “taunting jest,” and *cavillari*, “to taunt,” are terms proper to mimes. Solinus, chapter 2, concerning Sicily: “Here comedy was first invented; here too mimetic jesting took its place upon the stage.” *Cavillatio* is said to derive from *calvere*, which means to frustrate and deceive, as Priscian writes in book VIII. Nonius Marcellus says that the verb *calvere* itself was derived from bald-headed mimes, because they serve to deceive everyone. See Henricus Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus XXX, p. 406. ORELLI.

**“The theaters shout together and rise to their feet.”** For when the mimes and other actors pleased them, the spectators testified by acclamations, applause, [Col. 1074D] and exultation to the pleasure they received from them. Cicero notes this ἐπισημασία, “demonstration of approval,” in *Letters to Atticus* XIV.3: “If you have anything πραγματικόν, ‘of practical importance,’ write to me about it; if not, give me a full account of the people’s ἐπισημασία, ‘demonstration of approval,’ and the sayings of the mimes.” They therefore rose and leaped up, an action for which the Greeks use the particular verb ἀναπηδᾶν, “to spring to one’s feet,” as, for example, Arrian, *Discourses of Epictetus* III.4, and Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.30, speaking of the pride and insolence of Paul of Samosata, by which he courted—indeed, purchased—applause in the church as though in a theater. HERALDUS.

**“Gifts and rewards are established for the debauched men who mock the divinities.”** Besides the prizes that existed before the games, actors also received certain gifts and rewards, sometimes costly ones. Cato of Utica attempted to correct this extravagance by his example when he supervised Favonius’ games at Rome. See Plutarch, *Life of Cato* 46. HERALDUS.

**“Leisure from public duties, immunity, and exemption, together with [Col. 1075A] crowns.”** Theodoret, *On Providence*, Discourse IX, p. 205:

> Καὶ τραγῳδίας μὲν καὶ κωμῳδίας ὑποκριταὶ ἔχουσιν, εἰς ὃ βλέποντες τὴν τέχνην μετίασι, καὶ τῇ τῶν στεφάνων ἐλπίδι τῶν πόνων ἀνέχονται·  
> “Actors in tragedy and comedy have a goal with a view to which they practice their art, and in the hope of crowns they endure their labors.”

Philo, *Embassy to Gaius*:

> ὅταν παρατυγχάνῃς σκηνικοῖς ἀγῶσιν, ἢ γυμνικοῖς [Col. 1075B] ἢ τοῖς κατὰ τὰς ἱπποδρομίας, λάμβανε τὸν τοιοῦτον λογισμόν· Εἰ τὰ μηδὲν ὠφελοῦντα τὸν ἀνθρώπινον βίον, τέρψιν τε μόνην καὶ ἡδονὴν παρέχοντα θεαταῖς, ἐκπονοῦσιν οὕτω τινὲς, ὡς ἐπαινεῖσθαί τε καὶ θαυμάζεσθαι, καὶ γέρα καὶ τιμὰς καὶ στεφάνους μετὰ κηρυγμάτων λαμβάνειν, τί χρὴ πράττειν τὸν τῆς ἀνωτάτω καὶ μεγίστης τέχνης ἐπιστήμονα;  
> “Whenever you happen to attend dramatic contests, athletic contests, or those held at horse races, adopt this reflection: If some people labor so hard at things that bring no benefit to human life but provide spectators with mere amusement and pleasure, in order to be praised and admired and to receive prizes, honors, and crowns proclaimed by heralds, what ought the person skilled in the highest and greatest art to do?”

Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis* VIII.20: “If the third portion of Taurus is found in the horoscope, it will produce celebrated actors who, when placed in sacred contests, obtain the most splendid insignia of crowns.” These crowns were made from little leaves of gold and silver. Crassus initiated this extravagance, as Pliny teaches, *Natural History* XXI. But Cato of Utica attempted to moderate it at the games of Favonius, and afterward Alexander Severus did the same, as Lampridius writes in his *Life*. ELMENHORST and HERALDUS.

**“Encomia of abuse.”** Papias: “*Elogium* … the heading of any matter.” Arnobius below, book V, chapter 26: “The records of ancient writings bring forth the shameful marks and origins of your Eleusinian rites.” Calpurnius Flaccus, *Declamations* [Col. 1075C] 17: “I shall place you among the tombs of your ancestors, and inscribe your name in the epitaph you desired.” Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 2: “To speak from your own indictments”; and chapter 17: “And you endure encomia of Jupiter being sung,” etc. ELMENHORST.—Compare Havercamp on Tertullian, at the passages cited, pp. 22 and 150, and Valesius on Ammianus XIV, p. 15. ORELLI.

**“And whenever you wish the idle mind to be occupied with idle delusions.”** Thus Salmasius. Gelenius and others read: “And if ever,” etc. ORELLI.—*Hallucinatio*, “delusion” or “wandering,” is the proper term. By it they signify a sort of dissolution and drowsiness of the mind. Aulus Gellius IV.20: “As though that indication belonged to a wandering and hallucinating mind.” And elsewhere: “But he, yawning and resembling one who hallucinates.” HERALDUS.—J. F. Gronovius, on the cited passage of Gellius, p. 375, Leipzig edition, teaches that *allucinantis* should be written, deriving it from the Greek ἀλύκη, which denotes languor accompanied by yawning. ORELLI.

**“You demand that days be given to you.”** Elmenhorst is mistaken in understanding *dies* here as volumes of daily records, a meaning on which we shall comment below. For the following words, [Col. 1075D] “and be presented without any interruptions,” clearly show that “to demand days” means nothing other than demanding whole, continuous days for watching those theatrical games. ORELLI.

**“You ought long ago to have burned these books and rather to have demolished and destroyed these theaters.”** Heraldus and the Leiden editor emended the passage thus. Previously it read: “You ought long ago to have burned these books, to have demolished those,” etc.—incorrectly, since *demoliri*, “demolish,” cannot be said of books, but must refer to the following “theaters.” For my part, I would prefer to delete the pronoun “those” as a gloss rather than, with Heraldus in his *Second Notes*, read: “the books, then to demolish,” etc. ORELLI.

**“For why did our writings deserve to be given to the flames?”** Eusebius describes this persecution thus, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.2:

> Τῶν μὲν προσευκτηρίων τοὺς οἴκους ἐξ ὕψους εἰς ἔδαφος αὐτοῖς θεμελίοις καταρριπτομένους, τὰς δ’ ἐνθέους καὶ ἱερὰς γραφὰς κατὰ μέσας ἀγορὰς πυρὶ παραδιδομένας αὐτοῖς ἐπείδομεν ὀφθαλμοῖς, etc.  
> “With our own eyes we saw the houses of prayer cast down from their full height to the ground, foundations and all, and the inspired and sacred Scriptures surrendered to the fire in the middle of the marketplaces,” etc.

[Col. 1076A] HERALDUS.—The manuscript codex has *meruerunt*, “did deserve.” The first edition, from which the others flowed, reads *meruerint*, “may have deserved.” ORELLI.

**“Why were the meeting places savagely demolished?”** This was the name given to the places where Christians assembled to pray, to receive the interpretation of the divine word, and to hold sacred gatherings. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVII: “It is established that, [Col. 1076B] in the Basilica of Sicininus, where the Christian rite has its meeting place, 137 corpses of slain persons were found in a single day.” Lactantius, book V, chapter 11: “Some rushed headlong into killing, as did one man in Phrygia who burned the entire population together with the meeting place itself.” HERALDUS.

**“In which the supreme God is entreated.”** Cyril of Jerusalem states this more fully, *Mystagogical Catechesis* 5:

> παρακαλοῦμεν τὸν Θεὸν ὑπὲρ κοινῆς τῶν ἐκκλησιῶν εἰρήνης, ὑπὲρ τῆς τοῦ κόσμου εὐσταθείας, ὑπὲρ βασιλέων, ὑπὲρ στρατιωτῶν καὶ συμμάχων, ὑπὲρ τῶν ἐν ἀσθενείαις, ὑπὲρ τῶν καταπονουμένων, καὶ ἁπαξαπλῶς ὑπὲρ πάντων βοηθείας δεομένων.  
> “We beseech God for the common peace of the churches, for the stability of the world, for kings, for soldiers and allies, for those afflicted by illnesses, for those undergoing hardship, and, in a word, for all who need help.”

NOURRY, p. 376.—Ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεός, “the God over all”: the supreme God, the God of angels. For in this manner the writers of the ancient Church designate the God of the angels, whom Scripture sometimes calls gods because of their power, etc. HERALDUS.—See on book I, chapter 25. ORELLI.

**“Peace for all and pardon are sought for magistrates, armies, [Col. 1076C] kings,” etc.** Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 30: “Looking up toward heaven, we Christians pray with hands outspread because they are innocent; with head uncovered because we are not ashamed; finally, without a prompter because we pray from the heart. We all pray always for all emperors, asking for them a long life, a secure reign, a safe household, brave armies, a faithful senate, an upright people, a peaceful world, and whatever else a human being or a Caesar desires.”

Dionysius of Alexandria testifies to the same:

> ἡμεῖς τοίνυν τὸν ἕνα Θεὸν καὶ δημιουργὸν τῶν ἁπάντων, τὸν καὶ τὴν βασιλείαν ἐγχειρίσαντα τοῖς θεοφιλεστάτοις Οὐλεριανῷ καὶ Γαλιήνῳ σεβαστοῖς, τοῦτον καὶ σέβομεν καὶ προσκυνοῦμεν· καὶ τούτῳ διηνεκῶς ὑπὲρ τῆς βασιλείας αὐτῶν ὅπως ἀσάλευτος διαμείνῃ, προσευχόμεθα.  
> “We therefore revere and worship the one God and Creator of all, who entrusted the imperial power to the most God-loving Augusti Valerian and Gallienus; and to him we pray continually on behalf of their reign, that it may remain unshaken.”

Thus they offered supplications even for their rulers who persecuted them and were enemies of the Church: for Christ commanded them to pray even for their persecutors (Matthew 5:44), and the Apostle commanded prayers to be poured forth for all human beings, but especially ὑπὲρ βασιλέων καὶ πάντων τῶν [Col. 1076D] ἐν ὑπεροχῇ ὄντων, “for kings and all who are in high position” (1 Timothy 2:2), to whom he also wishes πᾶσαν ψυχὴν ὑποτάσσεσθαι, “every soul to be subject” (Romans 13:1). HERALDUS.

**“For those still passing their lives here, and for those released from the bonds of their bodies.”** Certainly, supplications for the dead were presented to God not only in Arnobius’ age, but also in the preceding century. This is established by several very celebrated passages of Tertullian; for example, *On Monogamy*, chapter 10: “Indeed, she also prays for his soul, asks meanwhile for refreshment for him and participation in the first resurrection, and makes an offering on the anniversaries of his falling asleep.”

Zeno of Verona, in his sermon *On the Resurrection*: “Hence a wife declares that she cannot endure the desolation caused by the loss of her husband, and complains of her cold side in a bed grievously widened by his absence. With odious cries she seeks to make God an object of odium; with profane wailings she sometimes disrupts those very divine rites by which the priests of God are accustomed to commend those at rest. Disfiguring her whole appearance with filthy neglect, she embraces the corpse amid loud lamentation and warms its cold lips with repeated kisses.”

[Col. 1077B] Dionysius the Areopagite describes this entire rite in the final chapter of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. He says that the following observances were practiced: the deceased brother was carried by his relatives to the bishop, as if to receive a crown; they then sang hymns of thanksgiving to God, τῷ τῆς νίκης αἰτίῳ, “the author of the victory,” by whose grace and aid the brother had departed victorious; afterward the priest rendered thanksgiving to God for the same benefit; certain passages of Scripture concerning the resurrection were read and hymns adapted to the same theme were sung; the catechumens were then dismissed; the saints at rest were next named and proclaimed aloud as victors; the priest again offered a prayer for the deceased; the substance of the prayer was that God should grant the deceased forgiveness of sins and receive him into the place of the living. [Col. 1077C] He was afterward greeted with a kiss, anointed, and finally buried.

Later, when the condition of the Christians had become more prosperous, ceremonial funeral processions were added. Hymns and psalms were sung at funerals, even by choirs, and candles were carried before them, pagan rites having been converted to better uses, as they believed. The words of Jerome will explain this matter abundantly. Thus he writes to Eustochium in the epitaph of her mother Paula: “Then there was no wailing, no lamentation, such as is customary among worldly people; instead, companies chanting psalms in different languages resounded. She was carried upon the hands of bishops, who placed their necks beneath the bier, while some prelates carried lamps and candles before her and others led choirs of psalm-singers; and she was placed in the middle of the Church of the Savior’s Cave.” Here you see psalms sung by those who followed the funeral, while choirs of clergy additionally modulated the chants of the psalms. HERALDUS.

[Col. 1077D] **“In which nothing is heard except what makes human beings,”** etc. Pliny the Younger writes to the same effect concerning Christians, book X, letter 97: “They affirmed that by their oath they bound themselves not to any crime, but not to commit theft, robbery, or adultery, not to break their word, and not to deny a deposit when called upon to restore it.” Compare Augustine, *City of God* II.28. ORELLI.

**“Those who share in a common matter as intimates.”** Janus Guilielmus restored the text thus in *Plautine Questions on the Curculio*, chapter V, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, part 2, p. 366. Previously it read “intimates who share in the matter.” That corruption arose because *familiares* had been written in the codex as *familiareis* in the genitive case, by an archaism. Thus Lucilius has *fur, fureis, furei* for *furis*. Heraldus thinks it should read: “intimates and those who share in the matter,” deleting the following “and.” For my part, however, I prefer Guilielmus’ correction. ORELLI.]

And joined by the bond of relationship with all whom brotherhood unites. I have printed the passage thus, following Stewechius’ correction, which is partly derived from the manuscript, where *cupulatos* is clearly read. Previously it was printed: “And with all whom [Col. 1078B] the joining together of brotherhood unites by the bond of relationship.” But this makes the sentence broken and disjointed, for *et* has nothing to which it can refer. Salmasius printed: “and joined with all by the bond of a consolidated brotherhood,” that is, bound to all by the name and affection of brothers and sisters. But I have searched the lexicons in vain for the adjective *consolidus*. ORELL.]

### XXXVI

Nor is this offense enough: even in mimes and farcical entertainments the persons of the most holy gods are brought upon the stage. And so that laughter and merriment may be aroused in idle spectators, the divine beings are assailed with jocular taunts; the theaters shout aloud and rise to their feet, and every tier resounds with uproar and applause [Note: [Col. 1074B] The manuscript has *plausu*; Sabaeus, *plausis*].

And—an offense that no acts of atonement could expiate—gifts and privileges are established for effeminate performers and mockers of the gods: exemption from public duties, immunity, and release from service, together with crowns. And after this do you dare to wonder where these evils arise from, by which mortality is flooded and oppressed without any interruption, when every day you recount and every day learn by heart all those things in which are contained the disgraces [Col. 1075A] of the divine beings and their records of condemnation; and when you wish your indolent minds to be occupied with idle delusions, you demand that days be granted you and that such shows be presented without interruption?

But if you felt any indignation on behalf of your religions, it is these writings and these books that you should long ago have burned; it is these theaters that you should rather have demolished and destroyed, in which the infamies of the divine beings are daily made public in shameful [Col. 1076A] plays. For why, indeed, did our writings deserve to be given to the flames? Why were our meeting places savagely torn down? In them the supreme God is entreated; peace and pardon are sought for all—for magistrates, armies, kings, relatives, enemies, those still passing their lives here, and those released from the bonds of their bodies. In them nothing is heard except [Col. 1077A] what makes people humane, except what makes them gentle, modest, self-restrained, pure, sharers of their private property, and joined by the bond of relationship with all whom brotherhood unites.

[Note: [Col. 1078B]

### XXXVII.—“And to be dutiful toward the gods”

Meursius’ reading is very bad: “And that they themselves are in place of gods.” ORELL.

### “And because certain spaces had been desecrated”

That is: spaces had been profaned. For Arnobius seems here to have in view what Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, §215; Valerius Maximus, book I, chapter 1, §3; and others recorded concerning Tiberius Gracchus. When he, they say, [Col. 1078C] had inadvertently taken his augural station and had crossed the *pomerium* without taking the auspices, the augurs accordingly declared that the consuls had been elected under a defect in the auspices. NOURR.

### “Desecrated spaces”

The same as profaned spaces. For Arnobius seems to allude to the events concerning Tiberius Gracchus mentioned by Cicero (*On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, and *On Divination*, book I), Valerius Maximus (book I, chapter 1, §3), and others. When he, they say, had inadvertently taken his augural station under a defect in the auspices and had crossed the *pomerium* without taking the auspices, the augurs therefore declared that the consuls had been elected under a defect in the auspices. NOURR., p. 554.

### “Had corrupted”

Thus Thomas Canter most felicitously emended the text. Previously it read: “had collapsed.” ORELL.

### “That, in consequence of the opinions stated above, they contain no slight fits of anger”

So the manuscript codex reads, according to Canter and Stewechius; Salmasius admitted this reading into the text of the Leiden edition. Gelenius and the rest who followed him printed: “That, in consequence of the opinions stated above, they conceive them.” I confess that this pleases me more. “To contain anger” or “wrath” [Col. 1078D] may indeed be said in two senses: it means either to foster anger in one’s breast and persist in wrath, or to restrain and check anger so that it does not break forth. But *concipere*, “to conceive,” is much better suited to the context. For *opinionibus* Canter prefers *opinationibus*. ORELL.

### “From furies of this kind”

Heraldus most excellently restored this from the manuscript codex. Previously the text was printed: “from wicked persons of this kind.” ORELL.

### “And they are free from its conception and commingling,” etc.

These words and those that follow have tormented the interpreters, who enclosed them in brackets as though they were a lacuna placed in a wholly inappropriate location. This is entirely true of the following words and the final words of this book: “For by the nature of things it cannot happen that what is one should become two, and that unity should pass into different things, divided though endowed with an innate simplicity.” I have therefore ventured to transfer them to a much more appropriate position in chapter XIII of this book; see the notes there. But the earlier words of this lemma, “and they are free from its *comptus* and commingling,” seem to require connection [Col. 1079A] with the preceding words: “who do not know what anger is.”

Everyone can see that *comptu*, which stands in the manuscript, is corrupt. Sabaeus and Gelenius printed *contenta*, an entirely new and unheard-of word meaning “containment” (*κατοχή*, *holding*), as our author said above in book II, chapter 19; Cujacius and Meursius approve it. Similarly one finds *remissa* in Cyprian, *deducta* in Cicero, *On the Laws*, book II, *condita* in Censorinus, chapter IV, and *abscissa* and *resona*, in place of *remissio*, *deductio*, *conditio*, *abscissio*, and *resonatio*. Stewechius thinks that *contentu* should be read in the same sense; Fulvius Ursinus, *contactu*. I think that *conceptu* should be read. From this, when abbreviated as *c—tu*, the faulty reading *comptu* could very easily have arisen. Thus Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis* V, chapter 12, used “conceptions of the mind” for designs entertained in the mind; and “to conceive anger” occurs very frequently in the best [Col. 1080A] writers—for example, Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* IV, chapter 9: “Discord is a more bitter anger, conceived in the inmost mind and heart.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, 166:

> In his mind he conceives mighty wrath, worthy of Jove.

Valerius Flaccus, *Argonautica* I, 747:

> . . . . . . Arms  
> The king prepares, and conceives the savage fires of wrath.

Nor do I doubt that Arnobius could have spoken of a “commingling” caused by the force of passions disturbing the mind’s tranquility, in the same sense in which Cicero said of Pericles in *The Orator*, chapter 9: “If he had used an unadorned style, the poet Aristophanes would never have said that he flashed lightning, thundered, and threw Greece into confusion.” ORELL.]

### XXXVII

But the truth is that, because you possess very great power through swords and armed force, you also judge yourselves to take precedence in knowledge of the truth, and to be dutiful toward the gods whose powers you were the first to defile by the obscenity of your beliefs.

At this point, if your ferocity permits and your madness allows, we ask you to answer us this: do you think that anger falls within the nature of the gods, or that divine blessedness is far removed and separated from these passions? For if they conceive these flames and are goaded by movements of anger, as your beliefs assert—for you often say that because games were conducted with insufficient care, because unacceptable presiding officials were appointed, because certain spaces were desecrated, and [Col. 1078A] because ceremonies were not duly completed, they roared through the tremors of earthquakes and corrupted the atmosphere with the contagion of pestilence, accompanied by the grievous devastation of the people—it follows that they must be understood, in consequence of the opinions stated above, to contain no slight fits of anger.

But if this is granted, the necessary consequence is also granted: that all these miseries with which the human race has long been overwhelmed flow from fictions of this kind. And if the divine beings’ indignation arises from these causes, you are the authors of such great miseries—you who never cease offending the minds of the heavenly beings and provoking them to the frenzy of vengeance.

But if the race of gods is immune from furies of this kind, and the gods have absolutely no knowledge of what it is to be angry, then they are also said without any reason to be angry with us, since they do not know what anger is and are free from its conception and commingling.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1079]

## TABLE OF CHAPTERS  
[Hebrew Text]

[Col. 1079B] Arnobius passes to another argument against the gods of the pagans, and derives it from their histories. Since the heathen preserved these in daily use and celebrated them in annual festivals, they plainly believed them to be entirely true.

The first is the story of Numa Pompilius, who is said to have obtained from Jupiter Elicius, after deceiving him through tricks and stratagems, the means of averting the effects of lightning. Chapters 1, 2. From all the circumstances of this story, however, the author makes it clear that nothing could be invented more alien to truth and divinity. Chapters 3, 4.

The second is the story of Acdestis and Attis, which is found to have been notorious for the utterly shameful crimes [Col. 1079C] of Jupiter, the Mother of the Gods, Nana, and Ia; for the disgraceful castration of Attis and the deaths of Attis and Ia; and for the other incidents connected with it. Chapters 5, 6, 7. Arnobius therefore argues against it just as he does against the other stories. He presses the heathen hard and mocks their insanity. Chapters 8, 9. He examines other incidents in the same story that are utterly full of absurdities. Chapters 10, 11.

He nevertheless shows that the heathen cannot convict the story of falsehood, since it was transmitted by their most ancient writers [Col. 1079D] and was customarily celebrated by the heathen themselves in the annual festival of the Mother of the Gods. Chapters 12–17. Arnobius declares that, deterred by their execrable foulness, he will pass over several other similar stories. He nevertheless briefly touches upon Fauna Fatua, or the Good Goddess, beaten with rods; the shameful origin of Servius; and the abominations customarily committed in the Omophagia, the rites of the Corybantes, the Bacchanalia, and the Phrygian rites and mysteries. Chapters 18, 19.

Taking occasion from these, he reproaches the heathen with Jupiter’s incest with his mother Ceres and his daughter Proserpina. Chapters 20, 21. Having set these matters forth, he shrewdly observes that so many and such great adulteries and other crimes of Jupiter are related [Col. 1080B] that he appears to have been born for no other reason than that the whole flood of infamy might be channeled into him. Chapters 22, 23.

He next pursues other sacred rites, namely the Thesmophoria and the Eleusinian rites. Chapters 24–27. He also discusses the Halimuntian rites, in which there was no less wantonness and insolence than in the others. Chapters 28, 29. Having related these, he asks the heathen whether Christians ought to be compelled by every kind of torture to perform these sacred rites; and at the same time he declares that it seems astonishing to him that anyone who denies or doubts that these are gods is called an atheist and a sacrilegious person [Col. 1080C] by them. Finally, he concludes that gods of this kind ought to have been hostile not to Christians, who reject them, but to the heathen, who proclaim such great crimes of theirs. Chapters 29, 30, 31.

He rejects with contempt the pagans’ reply that all these stories must be understood only in an allegorical sense. Chapters 32, 33. He presses more forcefully the absurdity of such an evasion. Chapters 34, 35, 36. He proves the same point still more fully by examining the stories of Summanus and Proserpina, and also of Jupiter and Ceres. [Col. 1080D] Chapters 37, 38, 39.

Yet grant, if you wish, that in the description of any story something altogether different from what its words express is signified: it will certainly rebound no less to the dishonor and insult of the gods. Chapters 40, 41, 42. Finally, Arnobius shows that many things are regularly read in the histories of the gods which cannot be explained in an allegorical sense. From these he concludes that it is utterly impious for the gods to be called by the heathen—if they were truly persuaded that the gods existed—names that are most shameful and wholly unworthy of divine majesty. Chapters 43, 44, 45.

[Note: [Col. 1079D]

### I.—“Grant that they were composed by playful poets,” etc.

The sense is: I grant you that the things previously set forth were fabricated by poets engaged in play and wantonness. But how, then, will you excuse those things disclosed by grave and serious histories, and those things handed down in what you regard as your most holy mysteries, though they are no less ridiculous? He therefore rightly contrasts grave and serious histories [Col. 1080D] with things written in jest and for amusement by playful authors, with no definite purpose proposed. For this is what “to play” means; in the same sense the Greeks also use *παίζειν* (*paizein*, “to play”) of those who do nothing seriously but act *μάτην* (*matēn*, “idly, without purpose”), and call such intellectually feeble men *ματαίους* (*mataious*, “idle” or “frivolous”).

For example, Herodotus, Book II, chapter 173, speaking of Amasis:

> Ἐχρᾶτο δὲ καταστάσει πρηγμάτων τοιῇδε· τὸ μὲν ὄρθριον, μέχρι ὅτου πληθώρης ἀγορῆς, προθύμως ἔπρησσε τὰ προσφερόμενα πρήγματα· τὸ δὲ ἀπὸ τούτου ἔπινέ τε καὶ κατέσκωπτε τοὺς συμπότας, καὶ ἦν μάταιός τε καὶ παιγνιήμων.

> He followed this ordering of his affairs: from early morning until the marketplace was full, he energetically attended to the business brought before him; but after that he drank, mocked his drinking companions, and behaved frivolously and playfully.

A little later Herodotus says that the same man was *φιλοπότην καὶ φιλοσκώμμονα καὶ οὐδαμῶς κατεσπουδασμένον ἄνδρα*—“a man fond of drinking and joking, and in no respect serious.” Thus *σκώπτειν* (“to jest”) and *σπουδάζειν* (“to be serious”) are very frequently opposed, [Col. 1081C] just as are *παίζειν* (“to play”) and *σπουδάζειν* (“to be serious”). Eunapius says in his preface:

> Εἰ γὰρ τὸ παίγνιον τῆς ἀρετῆς ἄξιον λόγου, ἀσεβοῖτο ἂν πάντως τὸ σπουδαζόμενον σιωπώμενον.

> For if the playful manifestation of excellence is worthy of mention, it would surely be impious to pass over in silence what was done seriously.

Arnobius calls the same mental fault “wantonness,” a word that properly denotes a dissolute *διάθεσις* (*diathesis*, “disposition”) of the mind, by which we do something for the mind’s amusement, *μάτην* (“idly”), with no definite goal proposed. Thus above, in book IV, “to play” means “to indulge in wantonness”: “We cannot determine whether you do this seriously and from confidence in a fact you have ascertained, or whether, playing with empty fictions, you indulge in wantonness through the extravagance of your inventions.” HERALD.

### “Nor would you retain certain things in their own use”

Thus Gelenius and the others. The first edition and manuscript codex read *quodam suo*, “in a certain use of their own.” The Leiden edition has: “Nor would you retain them in daily use,” which pleases me more. Nevertheless, I would not venture to alter anything. ORELL.

### “The due restraint of moderation”

See above, on book I, chapter 2. Thus in this passage “the due restraint of moderation” means a mean between excessive prolixity and excessive brevity in the narrative. ORELL.

### “In the second book of Antias”

On Gaius Valerius Antias, a very ancient writer of annals mentioned by Livy, Pliny the Elder, Aulus Gellius, Macrobius, and others, see G. J. Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, book I, chapter 10. ORELL.

### “Knowledge of how to avert the lightning”

“To attend to” or “avert lightning” means to turn it aside, to expiate it, and to cause Jupiter, seeing his will satisfied, to avert the harmful force of an angry storm. See C. Barth, *Adversaria*, book LV, chapter 13, and our observations above on book II, chapter 49. ORELL.

### “At Egeria’s prompting, twelve chaste young men,” etc.

For this narrative, compare with our author Plutarch, *Life of Numa*, chapter XV, and Ovid, *Fasti* III, 259–350, a most elegant passage. ORELL.

### “Mars’ Picus”

“Martian” is an allusion to the transformation of Picus by Circe into the woodpecker—a bird sacred to Mars—because he had spurned her love. Compare Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIV, 319 ff.; Virgil, *Aeneid* VII, 187, and Servius there; Pliny, *Natural History* X, chapter 18 (20), and Harduin there, vol. I, p. 552; and Plutarch, *Roman Questions*. ORELL.

### [Col. 1082B] “To that place”

That is, on the Aventine Hill. Plutarch, *Life of Numa*, chapter 15:

> Μυθολογοῦσι γὰρ εἰς τὸν Ἀβεντῖνον λόφον οὔπω μέρος ὄντα τῆς πόλεως, οὐδὲ συνοικούμενον, ἀλλ’ ἔχοντα πηγάς τε δαψιλεῖς ἐν αὐτῷ καὶ νάπας σκιερὰς, φοιτᾶν δύο δαίμονας, Πῖκον καὶ Φαῦνον, etc.

> For they relate in myth that two divinities, Picus and Faunus, used to visit the Aventine Hill, which was not yet part of the city or inhabited, but had abundant springs and shady glens upon it, etc.

Compare Ovid’s most elegant description, *Fasti* III, 295 ff. ORELL.

### “The king filled large cups with unmixed wine and honeyed wine”

I have not hesitated to restore to Arnobius the old reading which Elmenhorst attests to have come from the manuscript codex. All the other editors follow Gelenius’ interpolation: “The king filled cups, not few in number, with wine and honeyed wine.” *Merum vinum* is wine not diluted with water: Plautus, *Amphitryon*, act I, scene I, calls it [Col. 1082C] “wine as it was born from its mother.” ORELL.

### “According to their usual custom”

The preposition *de* is very frequently redundant in Arnobius and other writers of his age. Thus below, book VI, chapter 10: “Thrusting his tongue out from his open mouth in his eagerness to drink”; and Nemesianus, *Cynegetica*, verse 17:

> Who does not know Semele and the bridal fire,  
> Fatal too through a mistress’s cunning?

See Burmann there, p. 333, and C. Barth, *Adversaria*, book XVII, chapter 17, p. 884, who cites many examples. We have already remarked several times above on Arnobius’ abundance of such particles. ORELL.—Compare Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI, 80. OCHSNER.

### “But when they encountered cups fragrant with aromatic liquors”

Ovid, *Fasti* III, 300 ff.:

> Here Numa came, and to the Spring the king  
> Sacrificed a sheep. He set out cups filled  
> With fragrant Bacchus for the gods, then hid  
> Himself with his companions in the cave.
>
> [Col. 1082D] The woodland deities came to their accustomed springs  
> And relieved their parched breasts with abundant unmixed wine.

Juretus, on Symmachus, book I, letter 26, p. 39 of Lectius’ edition, understands this as wine seasoned with fragrances, according to the Greek custom. See Fischer on Aristophanes, *Plutus*, verse 808, where he discusses the matter at length. This is wrong.
