Cups fragrant with aromatic liquors and cups full of fragrant Bacchus are nothing other than cups of wine naturally very fragrant because it was old and of fine quality, such as Phaedrus describes in book III, fable I:

> An old woman saw an emptied wine jar lying there,  
> Which still, from noble clay and Falernian lees,  
> Spread its delightful fragrance far and wide.

See Burmann in his commentary, p. 118. ORELL.

### “They fell asleep, made heavy”

Ovid, in the passage cited: “Rest follows wine.” ELMENH.

### “They put bonds upon the drunken men”

*Madidatis* means “drunken.” See N. Heinsius, *Adversaria*, book I, chapter 10, [Col. 1083B] p. 102, and the interpreters on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VIII, p. 558, Oudendorp’s edition. Thus below: “to be soaked with abundant unmixed wine.” ORELL.

### “Could be drawn down”

Ovid, *Fasti* III, 327:

> They draw you down from heaven, Jupiter; and hence  
> Posterity even now invokes you as Elicius.

ELMENH. The verb is used particularly of sacrifices and the summoning forth of the shades and gods. Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter XXVIII: “For we know that magicians, in order to investigate hidden things, call forth attendant and divining spirits.” See C. Barth, *Adversaria*, book IV, chapter 12, p. 180. ORELL.

### “He drew down”

Priscian’s observation, book X, p. 381 of the Basel edition, is thus frustrated in this passage: namely, that the past tense of *elicio, -ere* is never *elexi*, but *elicui*. ORELL.

### “You will expiate, he said, the places struck by lightning with a head”

Meursius, in his Appendix, and the editor of the Leiden edition restored from the manuscript codex the ancient form *dixe* in place of *dixisse*. *Fulgurita* means places marked out by religious awe. Festus says: “A thing struck by lightning is called *fulguritum*. The place is immediately regarded as having become sacred, because the god appeared to have consecrated it to himself.”

The old glosses on the following verse of Persius, satire II—

> You lie there, grim and shunned within the grove, a *bidental*—

explain: “A *bidental* is a place struck by sacred lightning, which is consecrated by the soothsayers with the sacrifice of a two-year-old sheep, and which it is impious to tread upon.” Indeed, the books on lightning even forbade people to look upon such places. The soothsayers therefore carefully enclosed them and placed there a covered water jar, as Ammianus Marcellinus attests, book XXIII, p. 246. See H. Valesius’ extensive discussion there, in his notes, p. 259 of the Paris edition. [Col. 1083D] Compare Rigaltius on Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams*, book II, chapter 9, p. 73, vol. II of Reiff’s edition, and the interpreters on Festus under *bidental*. ORELL.

### “The king replied, ‘an onion’s’; Jupiter again, ‘a human—’” etc.

Ovid, in the passage cited:

> “Cut off a head,” he said. The king replied,  
> “We shall obey: an onion from my garden  
> Must then be dug up and beheaded.”
>
> “Of a man,” he added. “His topmost hairs,”  
> Said Numa. He demands a life. “A fish’s,”  
> Numa replies.
>
> The god laughed: “Use these, then, to avert  
> My weapons, O man not to be dismissed from converse with me!”

ORELL.

### “The god in reply, ‘a living—’; Pompilius supplied, ‘fish’s’”

I have printed the text thus, following the emendation of Gelenius and Salmasius in the Leiden edition. The word “fish’s” is absent from the manuscript codex and the first edition, where the reading is: “The god in reply, ‘with a living creature’; Pompilius supplied . . .” There follows a mark indicating a lacuna, which Gelenius filled with “fish’s,” while Heraldus supplied “a sprat’s,” following Plutarch, who has:

> Ἀποκριναμένου δὲ τοῦ Διὸς ἐμψύχοις, ἐπαγαγεῖν τὸν Νουμᾶν, μαινίσιν.

> When Zeus replied, “with living creatures,” Numa added, “with sprats.”

On the *maena*, or sprat, see above on book III, chapter 31. Stewechius thinks the text should read: “The god in reply, ‘with an *animal*’—that is, with something animate—Pompilius supplied, ‘with a *pompilus*.’” This is also the conjecture of Fulvius Ursinus, so that there would be a play on the ambiguity of a word that was both the king’s name and the name of a fish.

Pliny, *Natural History* IX, uses *pompilus* of two kinds of fish. One is a species of tuna, chapter 15; the other a shelled animal of the nautilus family, chapter 29. See Laurentius Theodorus Gronovius there, and Rittershusius on Oppian, *Halieutica* I, 186. But I fear that this conjecture is more ingenious than true. Nor do I see why the word “fish’s,” which Ovid also has, should be eliminated, since he appears to have drawn from the same source as our author, namely Valerius Antias.

With Salmasius, I would prefer [Col. 1084C] to place “fish’s” before “supplied,” which better suits the extremely rapid course of the speech. We must understand that all these words were uttered with the greatest possible speed. Numa did not allow Jupiter to explain his intention in several words, but intercepted each word of his as soon as it “escaped the barrier of his teeth” and, as it were, parried it with another word better suited to his own designs.

Plutarch also indicates this by saying *ὑπολαβόντος τοῦ Νουμᾶ*—“when Numa took him up”—which Kaltwasser translates, “quickly interrupting his speech.” The cunning of Numa, as Jupiter calls it, consisted in nothing other than the speed and presence of mind with which, interrupting each of Jupiter’s words when it had scarcely left his mouth, he twisted it by a most fitting reply into senses different from those the god had intended. It was evidently regarded as unseemly for the gods and unworthy of their majesty to explain the words they had pronounced, often brief and ambiguous, or to interpret their meaning to those who consulted them—something especially well known in the case of oracles. ORELL.

### [Col. 1084D] “Not with an onion’s hair”

Thus Gelenius and the others. The manuscript codex and Sabaeus’ edition have: “Numa, with an onion’s hair.” From this Heraldus suspects that the reading is: “Not, however, with an onion’s hair.” Revising this conjecture in his *Second Thoughts*, he proposed: “Not with a sprat’s or an onion’s hair.” ORELL.]

### I

Grant that all those disgraceful things concerning the immortal gods were disclosed [Col. 1081A] by poets at play. What of the things contained in grave, serious, and painstaking histories, and those handed down in secret mysteries? Were these too devised by the poets’ wantonness? If you regarded them as fables consisting of such absurdities, you would neither retain certain of them in customary use [Note: [Col. 1081B] Others read: “and which”], nor celebrate rejoicings at yearly intervals as festivals, nor preserve them in sacred rites as representations of events that had actually occurred.

From these many stories I shall for the present set forth one, observing the due restraint of moderation—a story in which Jupiter himself is represented as foolish and improvident, outwitted through ambiguities of language. In the second book of Antias, lest anyone perhaps think that we fabricate accusations by calumny, the following tale is recorded.

When the king Numa had no knowledge of how to avert the effects of lightning, but desired to learn, he concealed, at Egeria’s prompting, twelve chaste young men with bonds beside the water. His purpose was that when Faunus and Mars’ Picus came to that place to drink—for their customary route to water led there—the young men should attack, restrain, and bind them.

But so that the affair might be accomplished more readily, the king filled large cups with unmixed wine and honeyed wine and placed a treacherous snare for the approaching visitors around the approaches to the spring. Seized, according to their usual custom, by a desire to drink, they came to their familiar resort. But when they encountered cups fragrant with aromatic liquors, they preferred these new things to what they had previously known, fell upon them greedily, and, captivated by the sweetness of the drink, swallowed far too much. They fell asleep, made heavy by it.

Then the twelve young men set upon them as they slept, put bonds upon the drunken pair, and, when they awoke, the two immediately instructed the king fully concerning the means and sacrifices by which Jupiter could be drawn down [Col. 1083A] to earth. Having received this knowledge, the king performed a divine rite on the Aventine, drew Jupiter down to earth, and asked him for the rite by which lightning was to be expiated.

After hesitating for a long time, Jupiter said: “You will expiate the places struck by lightning with a head—”

“An onion’s,” the king replied.

Jupiter continued: “A human—”

“But only its hair,” the king answered.

The god replied: “With a living—”

“Fish,” Pompilius supplied.

Then Jupiter, caught by these ambiguous proposals, cried out: “You have deceived me, Numa! For I had determined that places struck by lightning should be expiated with human heads, not with an onion’s hair. Yet because your cunning has outmaneuvered me, retain the custom you have chosen; and with the objects for which you have bargained, you shall always undertake the expiation of places struck by lightning.”

[Note: [Col. 1084D]

### II.—“For everything has been contrived and arranged to provoke ridicule”

Plutarch, in the passage cited:

> Ταῦτα μὲν οὖν μυθώδη καὶ γελοῖα τὴν τῶν τότε ἀνθρώπων ἐπιδείκνυται διάθεσιν πρὸς τὸ θεῖον, ἣν ὁ ἐθισμὸς αὐτοῖς ἐνεποίησεν.

> These mythical and ridiculous tales display the attitude toward the divine that custom had produced in the people of that time.

HERALD.

### “Are we to believe that Faunus”

Meursius conjectures: “Shall we believe,” etc., and similarly in the following lines. ORELL.

### “Bound by sleep”

Fulvius Ursinus prefers “conquered.” Wrongly. Lucretius IV, 455:

> Finally, when sweet sleep has bound his limbs;

and verse 1021:

> Bound by sleep, they believe they lift up their garment.

ORELL. Compare F. A. Wolf on Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter XVI, vol. I, p. 127. OCHSNER.

### [Col. 1085B] “Did they disclose to the inquirer”

Should we not read “did they declare”? This would be more expressive. ORELL.

### “Or was Jupiter alone acquainted with the knowledge of this matter?” etc.

Meursius wishes the entire passage to be read thus: “Or was Jupiter alone acquainted with the knowledge of this matter—for the thunderbolts fall from him—so that, when they threaten, they must be averted by the discipline of someone’s special knowledge?” ORELL.

### “He knew—for the thunderbolts fall from him—that the discipline of some special knowledge must avert what threatened”

This is a sound reading and should not have been disturbed. For it is not threatening thunderbolts themselves that are ritually averted, but the things that thunderbolts signified were threatening. Shortly afterward: “And if at any time I signify through lightning that something threatens.” HERALD.—Fulvius [Col. 1085C] Ursinus conjectures: “For thunderbolts threaten from him.” Meursius reads and punctuates the entire passage thus: “He knew—for they fall from him—that thunderbolts, when threatening, must be averted.” ORELL.

### “That it is the task of others to know”

Stewechius thinks “the task” should be deleted as a gloss and a copyist’s explanation. ORELL.

### “That he himself knew the remedies”

*Scire*, “to know,” is undoubtedly corrupt. For there is nothing at all ridiculous in the same Jupiter who sends human beings omens through thunderbolts also knowing the remedies for averting what the thunderbolts signify. What Arnobius calls absurd is that Jupiter himself instructed mortals by what means his power could be reduced to nothing, and even established rites and ordained ceremonies by which he was bound so as to be unable afterward to carry out his indignation.

We should therefore read either, with Heraldus in his *Second Thoughts*, *remedia sciscere*, “to ordain remedies,” or, with C. Barth, *Adversaria*, book LV, chapter 13, pp. 2618 ff., *remedia sancire*, “to sanction remedies.” From the latter, written in abbreviation, *scire* [Col. 1085D] could very easily have arisen. ORELL.

### “My anger”

Thus Salmasius, following Meursius’ emendation in the Appendix. The first edition has: “these things of mine”; Gelenius, “these threats.” But shortly before: “By what means his anger and temper ought to be moderated.” ORELL.

### “And if at any time I signify through lightning that something threatens”

*Significare* is used in its proper sense, like the Greek *σημαίνειν* (“to give a divine sign”); and shortly afterward there are *significationes*, or *διοσημεῖαι* (“signs from Zeus” or “weather portents”). HERALD.

### “And vanish through the power of the rites”

Cujacius restored this from the manuscript, where it reads: “and the rites vanish.” The first edition has, incorrectly: “and the sacred thing vanishes.” C. Barth, *Adversaria*, book LV, chapter 13, p. 2619, reads: “and it vanishes through the power of the sacred rite”—*sacrum* being the rite itself as handed down by Jupiter. Heraldus, in his *Second Thoughts*, proposes: “vanishes through the rite.” Elmenhorst reads: “and the ineffectual fate vanishes,” deleting the preceding words “empty and void.” Meursius, in his Appendix, thinks that after “of the rites” some word such as “performance” has fallen out. L. Bünemann illustrates with many examples the use of the simple verb *vanescere* in place of *evanescere*, on Lactantius, *Institutes* IV, [Col. 1086B] chapter 8, p. 449. ORELL.]

### II

It is not easy to say whether the mind should first pursue one point or the last, [Col. 1083B] or should fall silent; nor can the problem be resolved by any process of reflection. For everything has been contrived and arranged to provoke ridicule, so that you must strain to have these things believed false, even if they are [Note: [Col. 1083B] Sabaeus reads: “are”] true, rather than wish to maintain them as true and, as though they were something marvelous, insinuate them at the cost of contempt for the divine being himself.

For what do you say, you people? Are we to believe that Faunus and Mars’ Picus, if they belong to the number of the gods and to that eternal and immortal nature, were at some time parched by dry thirst and went to the streams of springs so that they might moisten the heat of their veins? Are we to believe that, captivated by unmixed wine and enticed by the sweetness of honeyed wine, they gorged themselves from the treacherous cups so long that they came even to the danger point of drunkenness? Are we to believe that, bound by sleep and submerged in the oblivion of deepest slumber, [Col. 1084B] they gave earthly creatures the opportunity to bind them? On what parts of their bodies, then, were those interlacing bonds imposed? Did they possess any solidity? Were their hands formed of hard bones, so that they could be restrained by snares and confined by the fastening of knots?

For I do not inquire or demand whether they could utter anything while staggering in the derangement of drunkenness; whether, against Jupiter’s will—or, rather, without his knowledge—anyone could disclose the rite for drawing him down to earth. I desire to hear only this: if Faunus and Picus are of divine race and power, why did they not themselves disclose to the inquiring Numa what he more perilously desired to hear from Jupiter himself?

Or was Jupiter alone acquainted with the knowledge of this matter—for thunderbolts fall from him—so that the discipline of some special knowledge must avert what threatens? Or, since he himself hurls these fires, is it the task of others [Col. 1085B] to know by what means his anger and temper ought to be moderated?

For it is truly most foolish to believe that he himself ordained the remedies by which the things he had determined to bring about in human affairs through the hurling of a thunderbolt could be averted. For this amounts to saying: “By that kind of rite you will appease my anger; and if at any time I signify through lightning that something threatens, do this and that, so that what I have resolved should happen may become empty and void and vanish through the power of the rites.”

[Note: [Col. 1086B]

### III.—“Had ordained remedies”

*Scisse* is from *scisco, sciscere*, “to ordain.” We therefore see that in the preceding chapter, instead of “to know remedies,” we should read: “to ordain remedies.” Thus above, book II, chapter 19: “It was ordained in ancient beliefs.” Some wrongly conjecture there: “it was sanctioned”; for *scitum* is from *sciscere*. ORELL.

### “On the little prominence of a single hill”

See above on book II, chapter 49, and, concerning the expression “to join discourse,” Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* V, p. 349. ORELL.

### “And what divine force, I ask, compelled Jupiter to be summoned away from so great a dominion over the universe?”

I have printed the passage thus, following the most felicitous emendation of J. G. Graevius in letter 258 to N. Heinsius, in Burmann’s *Sylloge*, vol. IV, p. 332. [Col. 1086C] Previously the text was printed: “from so great an impulse of events.” But what could this “impulse of events” be? ORELL.

### “To present himself at the summonses of mortals”

*Denunciatio* is properly a summons by which someone is called into court through the officers of a magistrate. Paulus the jurist, *Sentences* V, title V; Brisson, *On the Meaning of Words*, book IV, p. 173. ELMENH.—In this passage, as Priorius rightly observes, *denunciatio* is the same as *condictio* among the augurs, which occurs when notice is given that someone must be present for an inauguration before the third day. See Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 117, and Gesner’s *Thesaurus*, under *condictio*. The following word *sistere*, “to present oneself,” is likewise forensic. Cicero, *On Duties* III, chapter 10: “The other became surety that he would present him.” ORELL.

### “Salted meal, incense, blood, fumigation with sacred boughs”

The very learned Scaliger’s conjecture is ingenious but unnecessary: “incense, sacred herbs, fumigation with sacred boughs.” Festus says: “They called the sacred herbs *sagmina*, because they were plucked from a sacred place for envoys setting out to make a treaty.” [Col. 1086D] See the interpreters there. Livy therefore joins them with sacred boughs in book I, chapter 24. But in our passage “blood” seems much more appropriate because of what precedes: salted meal and incense.

The use of sacred boughs is extremely well known not only in the rites of the fetial priests but in all other rites as well. The classic passage is Servius on *Aeneid* XII, 120: “Properly, *verbena* is a sacred herb—rosemary, as many suppose, that is, *λιβανωτίς* (*libanōtis*)—taken from a sacred place on the Capitol, with which the fetial priests and the *pater patratus* were crowned when about to make treaties or declare wars. By an extended use, however, we also call all consecrated foliage *verbenae*, such as laurel, olive, or myrtle.”

Compare Donatus on Terence, *The Woman of Andros*, act IV, scene III, verse 11; Vossius on Virgil, *Eclogues* VIII, 65:

> Burn rich sacred boughs and male frankincense;

and Johannes Saubert, *On Sacrifices*, chapter 24, pp. 541 ff., who most diligently collected nearly all the passages from the ancients. Meursius approves the reading: “the substitution of sacred boughs.” ORELL.

### “The mutterings of terrifying names”

“Terrifying names” means magical names. See above on book I, chapter 52. ORELL.

### “Voluntarily to surrender himself to deceptions”

Thus the manuscript, quite correctly. Fulvius Ursinus conjectured: “to deceptions that had been handed down”; Gelenius, “that he surrendered.” ORELL.

### [Col. 1087C] “Complete in expression”

See above on book III, chapter 44. ORELL.

### “Whether with the head of a ram, or a pig, or an ox, or any other creature”

I have restored the reading of the manuscript codex. What induced all the editors to banish the words “or an ox,” I certainly do not know. *Vervecino*, “of a ram,” in place of the thoroughly corrupt *cervicino* found in the manuscript codex, comes from Gelenius’ emendation. ORELL.]

### III

But let us grant, as is said, that Jupiter himself ordained remedies against himself, and devices by which his own signs could be counteracted. Are we also to believe that a god of such great divine power was drawn down to earth and, standing with a petty mortal on the little prominence of a single hill, joined him in a disputatious conversation?

And what divine force, I ask, compelled Jupiter to be summoned away from so great a dominion over the universe and to present himself at the summonses [Col. 1086B] of mortals? Salted meal, incense, blood, fumigation with sacred boughs, and the mutterings of terrifying names? Were all these things more powerful than Jupiter, so that they compelled him against his will to obey commands, or voluntarily to surrender himself to deceptions?

What of the next part? Will anyone believe that the son of Saturn was so improvident that he either proposed expressions by whose ambiguities he himself would be caught, or did not know beforehand the methods by which mortal cunning and cleverness would make sport of him?

“You will expiate,” he says, “the places struck by lightning with a head—”

The utterance is still incomplete, not yet a complete expression, and the meaning has not been fully defined. For one must necessarily know whether Diespiter ordains that this expiation be carried out with the head of a ram, or a pig, or an ox, or any other creature.

Since he had not yet specified this in particular, and the statement was still suspended and not yet brought to a conclusion, how could Numa know that Jupiter was about to say “a human head,” so that he might anticipate and forestall him and divert the uncertainty of that ambiguity toward the head of an onion [Note: [Col. 1087B] Sabaeus reads *coepitii*]?

[Note: [Col. 1087C]

IV.—That they are petty inventions of childish minds. *Ingeniolum* is a diminutive of *ingenium*, here used for a thing fashioned and invented by ingenuity, εὕρημα (“invention”), a sense especially frequent in Tertullian, in whom the three words *ingenium*, *artificium*, and *argumentum* are synonymous, as Salmasius observes on the *De Pallio*, p. 79. Compare Semler, *Index Latinitatis Tertullianeae*. This usage is also found, however, in the better writers of the Silver Age; for example, Tacitus, *Annals* XVI.20, *noctium ingenia*, “ingenious contrivances of the nights,” referring to cleverly devised nocturnal debaucheries; and Pliny, *Panegyric* 49: *Exquisita ingenia coenarum*, “elaborate inventions for banquets,” where see Gierig, p. 147. ORELLI.

The quickness of Numa’s mind. *Numae* is the third case, that is, the dative. [Col. 1087D] ORELLI.

The greatest lack of foresight is attributed to Jupiter. Stewechius prefers *imputatur* (“is imputed”), which he suspects arose from the old spelling *impoutatur*, changed by copyists who did not understand it into *importatur*. But *importatur impudentia alicui*, “imprudence is brought upon someone,” may be said no less properly than Cicero and others speak of bringing sickness, anxiety, grief, or suspicion upon someone. See G. Cortius on Cicero, *Ad Familiares* XVI, Epistle 21, p. 847, and M. Gudius—who discusses this verb at length—on Phaedrus I, fable XXVIII, verse 6, p. 247, Burman’s edition. ORELLI.

To confess that you have been caught. F. Ursinus: “To confess that God has been caught.” But in that case it would have had to be written: “to confess that God has himself been caught”; nor can *te* (“you”) be absent in view of the following words, “when you grieve that you have been deceived,” for which the same Ursinus substitutes: “when he grieves that he has been deceived.” Elmenhorstius: “When you grieve that God has been deceived.” ORELLI.

And to relinquish the remedy which you had offered. Shrewd, but by no means necessary, is the conjecture of Maureius and Heraldus in the [Col. 1088B] *Second Corrections*: “and to bring forth the remedy which you had concealed.” Jupiter *ponit* it, that is, lays it aside or grants it to Numa—the remedy he had previously offered for expiating those struck by lightning—by permitting a head of onion (*caput caepicium*) to be offered to him instead of a human head. [Col. 1088C] ORELLI.

A lustful craving for human blood. *Libidinose* means “cruelly.” For among the ancients *libido* is used of any passion or desire whatsoever. See C. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXIX.14, p. 1382. ORELLI.

Why, moreover, it could have been undertaken by Numa even with an onion. I have printed this from the emendation of the Leiden editor. The manuscript has: “that Numa could be undertaken for him by an onion,” which makes no sense. The first edition reads: “that Numa said it could be undertaken by an onion,” which can be tolerated if we understand “said” from the words that follow, and here supply: “that Numa said that it could be undertaken by an onion.” Scriverius, cited by Meursius, prefers: “that it could have been undertaken by Numa with an onion.” Meursius himself, in the Appendix: “that Numa understood it to be undertaken from an onion” (supplying “said” or “understood”). Stewechius, finally: “that Numa thought—or may have thought—it could be undertaken with an onion.” ORELLI.]

IV. Unless perhaps you will say that the king was divine: surely he could not have been more divine than Jupiter himself? Unless the man, by anticipating what Jupiter was going to say, outwitted him, God could not know the ways in which the man was preparing to outwit him. Thus it is plain and manifest [Col. 1088A] that these are petty inventions of childish minds: while through them quickness of mind is acquired for Numa, the greatest lack of foresight is attributed to Jupiter. For what could be more imprudent than to confess that you have been caught by the cleverness of a human mind and, while grieving that you have been deceived, to yield to the victor’s will and relinquish the remedy which you had offered? For if there was some rationale and natural fitness by which the expiation of a person struck by lightning had to be undertaken with a human head, I do not see why the king redirected the reference to an onion; but if the matter could also be settled with an onion, then the craving for human blood was wanton and cruel. And so each side is driven into the contrary position: Numa is not shown to have wished to know what he did wish to know, while Jupiter is demonstrated to have been cruel, because he said that he wished what Numa could have discharged even with an onion to be expiated with human heads.

[Col. 1088B] [Note: [Col. 1088C]

V.—In Timotheus, a man of no mean standing among theologians. Apart from our author, no ancient writer mentions Timotheus the Theologian. See G. J. Vossius, *De Historicis Graecis* III. C. Barthius, *Adversaria* [Col. 1088D] LV.13, thinks that he is identical with the lyric poet and highly skilled musician under Philip of Macedon, famous for inventing the tenth and eleventh strings of the lyre; concerning him see the *Suda*. Wrongly, in my opinion. For what Arnobius reports from him appears to have been taken from some historical work about the gods and their mysteries. Concerning that Timotheus whom Plutarch also calls an ἐξηγητής, that is, a hierophant, mystagogue, interpreter of the Eleusinian rites—or, as Tacitus says, a superintendent of ceremonies—Gisbert Cuper should be consulted in the Appendix to the *Apotheosis of Homer*, p. 277. In place of *virum* (“a man”), Fulvius Ursinus prefers *unum* (“one”). But nothing should be changed. ORELLI.

Concerning the Great Mother of the Gods and her rites, the following account of their origin is given. Compare with this narrative Pausanias in the *Achaica*, p. 430, Sylburg’s edition, who describes the same history or fable, though somewhat more briefly. ORELLI.

Drawn from the innermost mysteries—as he himself writes and relates. Stewechius suspects that we should read: “drawn from the innermost mysteries and—as he himself writes—imparted to them.” But we have already read several times in our author: *tradit insinuatque*, “he transmits and relates”; for *insinuare* is equivalent to “transmit, teach.” See above, on Book I, chapter 63. ORELLI.

Whose name is Agdus, from the region so called by its inhabitants. From it.... Stewechius and Meursius prefer: “so called. From it.” Wrongly. *Sic vocatae* is a Greek construction. ORELLI.

As Themis had commanded in prophetic utterance. This passage recalls to my mind a remarkable error by Acro on Horace, *Odes* I.2, when he says: “When the flood had occurred and only Parnassus projected above the waters, Deucalion and Pyrrha consulted Apollo about how they might restore the human race. When he replied that they should cast the bones of their mother, they then understood that the earth was called their mother; and consequently, when Pyrrha cast stones, girls were born, and when Deucalion did so, males.” For the oracle consulted was not Apollo’s but [Col. 1089C] Themis’s. This is clear from the present passage of Arnobius and from Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I.320:

> They worship the divinities of the mountain  
> And prophetic Themis, who then possessed the oracle.

And certainly Themis had a temple in Boeotia beside the Cephisus before Apollo did. See the *Etymologicum* under θεμιστεύων (“delivering oracles”), the *Suda* under θεμιστεύειν (“to deliver oracles”), and the interpreter of Juvenal on Satire I (Placidus Lactantius on Statius, *Thebaid* III, p. 109, Lindenbrog’s edition). Indeed, Orpheus, in his hymn to Themis, sings that she first revealed oracles to humankind and instructed Apollo. Thus he says:

> She first revealed the holy oracle to mortals,  
> Pronouncing divine judgments in the Delphic recess,  
> Upon the Pythian ground, when she reigned at Pytho;  
> She also taught Lord Phoebus the ordinances of justice.

The interpreter of Pindar, however, attributes this to Pan, contrary to the sense of Orpheus. MEURSIUS, Book V, chapter 2.—Earth first presided over the Delphic oracle, afterward Themis, and finally [Col. 1089D] Apollo. See Aeschylus, *Eumenides*, opening lines; Pausanias, *Phocica*, p. 809; scholia on Euripides, *Orestes*, verse 163. ORELLI.

Was given form. *Informari* means “to be brought into life, to be compelled to assume a form,” as C. Barthius explains in *Adversaria* LV.13, p. 2619. By contrast, *informis* (“formless”) is that which lacks a form by which it can be recognized. Hence Apuleius, Book V, concerning Psyche: “hearing formless voices,” that is, hearing voices whose source she could not identify. ORELLI.

When she had surrendered herself to rest and sleep, the wanton Jupiter assailed her with incestuous desires. I have printed this according to the very slight and elegant emendation of C. Barthius in *Adversaria*, at the passage cited and at XXIX.14; for *nequam* very often means “lustful, wanton.” Thus Martial I.109:

> She is more wanton than Catullus’s sparrow.

*Nequitia* has the same sense in Petronius, *Satyrica* LXXXVII: “But he was not displeased by my wantonness.” It was formerly printed: [Col. 1090B] “whom Jupiter assailed with incestuous desires”; if this is sound, *quam* can mean nothing other than “very, exceedingly incestuous,” since *quam* joined to a positive adjective sometimes performs the function of a superlative. See Tursellinus, *De Particulis Linguae Latinae*. Thus the unknown author of *The Spanish War*, chapter 33: “He ordered a most sumptuous dinner to be brought.” But this is excessively harsh in the present passage. I have therefore preferred to follow C. Barthius’s correction. ORELLI.

Defeated, he discharged his lust upon the stone. *Voluptas* here refers to the physical effect of lust, namely generative seed. Similarly Hyginus, *Poetic Astronomy* II.13, concerning Vulcan’s assault upon Minerva: “And when, full of desire, he rushed toward her to join himself to her in an embrace, he was repulsed and discharged his lust upon the earth.” ELMENHORSTIUS.

After many bellowing sounds had first been emitted, etc. The first edition and Gelenius read: “Having first been produced with many bellowing sounds,” etc.; from this C. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXIX.14 and LV.13, suspects that the text should be restored as: “After he had first been heard amid many bellowing sounds, Acdestis was born.” A shrewd conjecture. Nevertheless, I would not venture to change anything. ORELLI.

An insane and frenzied lust, and one belonging to both sexes. Thus Fulvius Ursinus and Gelenius. The first edition reads: “and from either sex,” which makes no sense. Meursius reads: “of both sexes,” so that the meaning is that Acdestis was androgynous; Pausanias also attests this:

> While sleeping he discharged seed upon the ground; in the course of time the earth sent forth a divine being possessing two sets of genitals, those of a man and those of a woman. They gave this being the name Agdistis.

Heraldus, overturning the author’s entire sentence and joining it to what follows, thinks it should be read: “and indeed from the womb of the stone came a power fitted to devastate and destroy.” C. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXIX.14, p. 1383, defends Gelenius’s emendation and thinks *sexu* is an old nominative form for *sexus*, citing Festus: “*Sexus*, alternatively *sexu*, is natural condition and constitution, from the Greek,” etc.; on this see Joseph Scaliger. Thus Sallust, *Histories* II, fragment: “Everywhere persons of masculine and feminine sex were seen throughout the streets and on all the roofs”; and Sisenna, *Histories* IV: “Then upon the wall were persons of masculine and feminine sex, the entire multitude of the people having assembled.” Others, however, read *secus*, which Stewechius also wishes to restore in our passage. But what prevents us from taking *sexu* here as an ablative, so that the meaning is that Acdestis, being androgynous, experienced the sexual drive (*Geschlechtstrieb*) of both sexes? [Col. 1090D] ORELLI.

Wherever the savagery of his disposition led him. See above, on Book I, chapter 5, the words: “As that savage Xerxes.” Salmasius printed: “To go wherever the savagery of his disposition led.” But the old reading seems to me much more expressive: “to devastate everything, to destroy it, wherever the savagery of his disposition led him.” ORELLI.

And to believe that nothing was more powerful than himself. Fulvius Ursinus prefers *prae se*, “in comparison with himself.” ORELLI.]

V. In Timotheus, a man of no mean standing among theologians, and likewise in other equally learned authors, the following account of the origin of the Great Mother of the Gods and of her rites is given, drawn from recondite books of antiquity and—as he himself writes and relates—from the innermost mysteries. Within the borders of Phrygia, he says, there is a certain rock of entirely unparalleled vastness, whose name is Agdus, from the region so called by its inhabitants. [Col. 1089A] From it Deucalion and Pyrrha took stones and, as Themis had commanded in prophetic utterance, cast them into a world empty of mortals. From these stones, together with the others, the one who is called the Great Mother was given form and divinely animated.

When she had surrendered herself to rest and sleep upon the very summit of the rock, the wanton Jupiter assailed her with incestuous desires. But although he struggled for a long time, he was unable to obtain what he had promised himself; defeated, he discharged his lust upon the stone. From this [Note: [Col. 1089A] *Hanc*, according to Sabaeus.] the rock conceived; and after first emitting many bellowing sounds, in the tenth month it gave birth to Acdestis, named after his mother. He possessed unconquerable strength and [Col. 1090A] an untamable ferocity of disposition, an insane and frenzied lust belonging to both sexes, and a violence that used force to devastate and destroy whatever the savagery of his disposition drove him toward; he cared nothing for gods or human beings, believed nothing more powerful than himself, and despised earth, heaven, and the stars.

[Note: [Col. 1090D]

VI.—Aroused by play and hunting. *Ludus* here seems to signify sexual activity, τὰ ἀφροδίσια (“the affairs of Aphrodite”). ORELLI.

At the time of necessity. This is the reading of the manuscript [Col. 1091A] and the first edition. Others read: “in the summertime.” ORELLI.

With the other end he catches the testicles together with the genitals themselves. Our author several times uses *proles* (“offspring”) for the testicles. Thus below, chapter 23 of this book: “tearing away the membranes surrounding the generative organs”; and Book VII, chapter 24: “The *polimina*, moreover, are what we have more modestly called the generative organs.” See C. Barthius, *Adversaria* LV.13, and Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. ORELLI.

When the power of the wine had evaporated from him. Thus the Leiden editor, following Joseph Scaliger’s highly successful emendation. The manuscript has: “when he had been raised up by the power of the wine,” which Stewechius defends as referring to the highest degree of drunkenness (“when his drunkenness had reached its highest degree”). Wrongly. For the effect of extreme drunkenness upon Acdestis was a very deep sleep, from which he awoke only after his intoxication had at last passed off. We should therefore read *exhalata*, “evaporated,” with Scaliger; Heraldus also approves this. “Freed from the power of the wine,” which was formerly read, comes from Gelenius’s correction. The first edition reads: “having been raised up,” etc. Canterus: “having been rendered powerless.” ORELLI.

He deprives himself of the sex which he had possessed. The sense requires that we read with Fulvius Ursinus: “he deprives himself of the sex by which he had been a man.” For Acdestis was androgynous, as we have just seen. ORELLI.

With the tearing apart of the organs. Theodorus Canterus shows that, following the emendation of Obrecht Gifanius, *discidio* must be read instead of the formerly printed *dissidio*. For *discidium*, a word extremely common in Lucretius, signifies διαχωρισμός, διάλυσις (“separation, dissolution”), the violent separation and rupture of two things joined together, from *discindo*, “tear apart”; *dissidium*, by contrast, from *dissideo*, denotes a kind of discord and disagreement of minds. See Faernus and Bentley on Terence, *Andria* IV.2.14; Gesner in the *Thesaurus*; and especially the eminent Valckenaer on Callimachus, *Elegiac Fragments*, p. 102. C. Barthius prefers *decidio*, which is equivalent to *discidium*. Here, however, *partes* (“parts, organs”) is used κατ’ ἐξοχήν (“pre-eminently”) for the male genitals, a sense that occurs repeatedly in the *Priapea*, for example epigrams 8, 29, and 48, passages which modesty forbids me to transcribe. Compare Erhard on Petronius, chapter 112, and P. Burman II on the *Latin Anthology*, vol. II, p. 513. C. Barthius, failing to understand this, thinks in *Adversaria* LV.13 that we should read: “with the tearing away of the fathers,” asserting that *patres* (“fathers”) and *fratres* (“brothers”) are used in Latin in the same obscene sense as *proles* and *soboles* (“offspring”); yet he has supplied no example of this meaning. [Col. 1091D]

The reading *discidio patrum*, “with the tearing away of the fathers,” is also approved by Lindanus on Hesychius, under Ἑλέσθε, p. 1172, vol. I, Alberti’s edition. He explains that the Greeks likewise call the testes or testicles κύαμοι (“beans”) in the same sense; for example, in the following verse of Empedocles cited by Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* IV.11:

> Wretches, utter wretches, keep your hands away from beans.

As Gellius explains, the Pythagoreans called them κύαμοι in a concealed and symbolic fashion because they are “powerful for generating and causes of generation.” But the distinguished Alberti preferred the received reading. ORELLI.

A pomegranate tree suddenly sprang from them, together with its fruits. I have printed this according to Meursius’s entirely certain emendation. Others read: “a Punic apple.” But *malum* and *pomum* mean the fruit of a tree, not the tree itself. See Salmasius on Solinus, p. 674. ORELLI.

Nana, the daughter of King Sangarius—or of the river—looked upon its beauty. *Vel* (“or”), omitted by the earlier editors, was first restored from the manuscript by Stewechius, with Salmasius’s approval in his notes on Solinus, p. 618. Concerning the Sangarius, a river of Asia, Arrian, *Expedition of Alexander* I.29, says:

> The sources of the Sangarius are in Phrygia; the river itself flows through the land of the Bithynian Thracians and empties into the Euxine Sea.

Latin writers, such as Ovid, call it *Sagaris*. On its bank dwelt the Berecyntian Phrygians, famous in the time of the Trojans; from them Cybele, who was worshipped in this region, received the name Berecyntian, as an ancient epigram in Brunck’s *Analecta*, vol. I, p. 495, concerning a Gallus, a priest of Cybele, teaches:

> And shouting aloud  
> Beside the river Sangarius, he invoked the Mother.

See Oberlin on Vibius Sequester, pp. 187–88. In place of *Nana*, Salmasius, citing our passage in his notes on Solinus at the place cited, printed *Nava*; I do not know whether this was a printer’s error. Pausanias treats the same story in the *Achaica*, p. 430, Sylburg’s edition, though more briefly than our author:

> The gods, fearing Agdistis, cut off the male genitals belonging to him. When an almond tree sprang from them and bore beautiful fruit, they say that the daughter of the river Sangarius took some of the fruit. When she placed it in her bosom, that fruit immediately vanished, and she became pregnant. After she gave birth, a he-goat tended the exposed child.

Nonnus, *Dionysiaca* XV, p. 422, Hanover edition, and Memnon in the *Excerpts*, chapter 41, call her Nicaea, following another tradition: namely, that the daughter of Sangarius became pregnant not from the genitals of Acdestis cut off by Bacchus, but because Bacchus himself made her drunk and violated her. See our notes on Memnon, p. 241. ORELLI.

With little staffs. Joseph Scaliger thinks that *pabulis*, “with food,” should be read. ORELLI.

Some Phorbas or other takes the discovered child and nourishes him with goat’s milk. I have followed the correction of the Leiden editor. Although no mention of this Phorbas survives among ancient authors, it is likely that Arnobius wrote this, since he adds “some ... or other,” thereby suggesting that several shepherds of this name were mentioned by the ancients. The other editors read: “someone or other takes him and gives him form,” etc. This is undoubtedly corrupt, though C. Barthius vainly defends it in *Adversaria* LV.13, p. 2619, explaining it as: “He takes care that the boy should not become misshapen and twisted in his limbs.” But I wish this man of vast learning had given us examples of such a meaning. For a child is already formed in its mother’s womb; education and care do not acquire a human being’s form but preserve it. [Col. 1092D]

Heraldus thinks that the word *format*, “gives form,” should be deleted as a gloss, since the manuscript reads *formas*. He believes this originated with an ignorant copyist who found *formosos* (“beautiful”) written in the margin of the manuscript he was copying, beside the word *scitulos* occurring shortly afterward, and inserted *formas* into the text in its place. In his *Second Corrections*, however, Heraldus retracts this opinion and recommends reading: “someone or other takes him, cherishes him, and nourishes him with goat’s milk.” For my part, in a doubtful reading I have preferred to follow Salmasius. ORELLI.

*Scitulos*, that is, “beautiful, handsome, elegant.” Thus Plautus, *The Rope* IV.1.2–3:

> Now I have found my clients,  
> Both pretty in form and youthful in age.

So *scitus* and *scitulus* are used more than once by Plautus of things desirable and pleasing to see or hear, and correspond to our German *artig* (“pretty, charming”). See Gronovius on Plautus, *Bacchides* II.2.31, and Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VII, p. 486. Fulvius Ursinus is therefore wrong to emend it to *citulos*. ORELLI.

Or because in their own manner of speech the Phrygians call goats *Attagi*. Bochart departs from Arnobius’s view in *De Animalibus Sacrae Scripturae* I.53, p. 647; consult him if you wish. GALLANDIUS.

Or because in their own expressions the Phrygians use *Attagi* for goats, it followed that he received the name Attis. Hesychius: “Ἀδαγοούς ... a certain hermaphroditic god among the Phrygians.” Hesychius’s interpreters, Sopingius and Biel, teach that he is identical with our Attis. Drusius, *Animadversions* I.25, thinks that *Atasos* or *Atysos* should be read instead of *Attagos*, so that it may be inflected after the Hebrew word for “goat,” as *Lais*, λῖς, means “lion.” He even continues: “I think it comes from [word missing in the supplied text], whence [word missing]: larger goats.” Eustathius on *Odyssey* I, p. 1625, Roman edition, teaches that the Ionians called a goat ἀττηγός. Bochart, *On the Arrival of Aeneas in Italy*, p. 1075 of his *Works*, conjectures that this is the same being who, according to the myths, was born from Mercury and Venus (Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV.288), and thinks that in Hesychius we should read Ἀδαγύους, as though it were a Phrygian corruption of the Greek Ἀνδρόγυνος (“androgynous”). Biel defends the reading Ἀδαγοούς as derived from *Atagus*, with *t* changed to *d* through dialectal variation and with the ending *-ους*, customary in Phrygian proper names [Col. 1093C] (as above we had *Agdus*, the Phrygian name of that enormous rock from which the Great Mother was formed). He thinks that from *Attagus*, “goat,” that Phrygian god was called Ἀδαγοούς by Hesychius and Attis by our author—that is, “goat-like”—perhaps because he was either worshipped as κριοπρόσωπος (“ram-faced”), like Jupiter Ammon (concerning whom see Spanheim, *De Usu et Praestantia Numismatum*, pp. 349 ff.), or was κριοφάγος (“goat-eating”), that is, a god to whom goats were sacrificed. Compare Hesychius under κριοφάγος. Similarly Apollo was called Μαλόεις on Lesbos, ἀπὸ τῶν μήλων, “from the sheep,” because sheep were sacrificed to him. See Salmasius on Solinus and the interpreters of Hesychius under Ἀδαγοούς.

The Mother of the gods loved him uniquely because he possessed a face of surpassing beauty. Ovid, *Fasti* IV.423 ff.:

> A Phrygian boy, remarkable for beauty in the lofty woods,  
> Bound the tower-crowned goddess in a chaste love.  
> She wished him to be kept for herself and to guard her temples,  
> And said, “See that you always wish to remain a boy.”  
> He pledged his fidelity to her command and said, “If I prove false,  
> May that Venus whom I deceive be my last.”  
> He proves false, and in the nymph Sagaritis ceases to be  
> What he had been. For this the goddess’s anger exacts punishment.

ELMENHORSTIUS.

And, in the only way he could be, he was bound by improper flatteries. Salmasius most rightly, as it seems to me, restored to the text this manuscript reading, which alone is genuine. The meaning is that Acdestis, being a person of insane and frenzied lust—as our author described him above—could be won only by *minus rectae*, that is, shameful and disgraceful flatteries. For some reason unknown to me, this offended the other editors. Gelenius altered it, with his customary boldness, to: “and, as alone a lover could be, he was bound by concealed flatteries.” Theodorus Canterus: “and, as only a mime could be, he was bound by concealed flatteries”; this is approved by P. Colvius on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* X, p. 688, Oudendorp’s edition. Partly following Canterus, Meursius recasts the entire passage thus: “The Mother of the gods loved him uniquely because he possessed a face of surpassing beauty. Acdestis also loved him ... and, as only a mime could be, by concealed flatteries,” etc. It is certainly true that copyists very frequently interchange *mimus* and *minus*. But how could a lover of untamable ferocity of disposition, such as Acdestis was, be called a “mime” or “mimic”? Stewechius is no more worthy of a hearing when he recasts it as: “and, by the only means possible, defeated by touches and flatteries.” Isaac Pontanus, on Macrobius, *Saturnalia* V.17, recommends: “and, loving in the only way he could, from his very depths,” etc.; *imitus* would be an adverb like *stirpitus* and *medullitus*. Yet soon afterward, among his omissions, he himself retracts this conjecture. C. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXIX.14, thinks it should read: “joined from afar by concealed flatteries,” with this meaning: from afar, as though at a distance, since neither courage nor opportunity was available, Acdestis pursued the young man and courted his affections by covert blandishments. But such modesty is utterly foreign to Acdestis, the despiser of gods and human beings. More acceptable is Heraldus’s conjecture, which comes very close to the manuscript’s wording: “bound by flatteries that were insufficiently concealed”—*durch allzuoffenbare Gunstbezeugungen*, “through excessively open demonstrations of favor.” Nevertheless, I prefer the manuscript reading, deservedly restored by Salmasius. ORELLI.

Hence it is forbidden for persons polluted by wine—which betrayed the secret—to enter his sanctuary. This too is the manuscript reading, deservedly restored to the text by the Leiden editor, with the following meaning: it is forbidden for those polluted by wine to enter Attis’s sanctuary, because, overcome by wine, he betrayed the secret. Gelenius rashly altered this reading to: “Hence it is forbidden to bring into his sanctuary the wine which betrayed the secret, when polluted,” namely by Venus, lust, or unlawful love. Stewechius thinks we should read: “Hence concerning wine,” etc., taking *de* as pleonastic, as below in Book VI, chapter 10: “from a blood-colored wax-plaster,” where see Heraldus’s note. *Sanctum* for *sanctuarium*, “sanctuary, temple,” occurs below in the same book, chapter 39: “That pine which is ceremonially carried into the sanctuary of the Mother Goddess.” Aelius Lampridius, however, used it for an image in *Heliogabalus* 7; on this see Salmasius, *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, p. 807. Others think that *polluctis*, “consecrated, devoted,” should be read instead of *pollutis*, “polluted.” Thus below, chapter 12, opening: “consecrated through belief in the gods.” If we follow this reading, however, the preceding words must certainly be rewritten: “Hence it is forbidden to bring wine ...,” etc., with *sese* deleted. ORELLI.]

VI. Since the gods had repeatedly deliberated and asked by what means his audacity could be weakened or restrained, while the others hesitated Liber undertook responsibility for this task himself. He strongly infused with the power of unmixed wine a spring familiar to Acdestis, at which he had been accustomed to allay the heat and burning of his thirst when aroused by play and hunting. [Note: [Col. 1090A] Thus Sabaeus. Others read *validissimi*, which is acceptable.] At the time of necessity [Col. 1091A] Acdestis hurried there to drink and, with his veins gaping, swallowed the draught too immoderately. The result was that, overcome by an unfamiliar influence, he was plunged into the deepest sleep.

Liber came to lay his trap. From bristles most skillfully intertwined he cast one noose around the sole of Acdestis’s foot; with its other end he caught the generative organs together with the genitals themselves. When the power of the wine had evaporated from him, Acdestis sprang up violently; and as the bond pulled upon his foot, by his own strength he deprived himself of the sex which he had possessed. With the tearing apart of the organs, an immense quantity of blood flowed. The earth absorbed and drank it in. [Col. 1092A] From it a pomegranate tree suddenly sprang up, together with its fruits.

Nana, the daughter of King Sangarius—or of the river—looked admiringly upon its beauty, plucked one of the fruits, and placed it in her bosom. From this she became pregnant. Her father shut her away as though she had been violated and arranged for her to die of starvation; but she was sustained by the Mother of the gods with fruits and other little staffs [probably corrupt], and gave birth to a little boy. Sangarius, however, ordered the child to be exposed. Some Phorbas or other discovered and took him, and nourished him with goat’s milk. And because the Lydians call handsome boys by this name, or because in their own manner of speech the Phrygians call goats *Atagi*, it followed that he received the name Attis.

The Mother of the gods loved him uniquely because he possessed a face of surpassing beauty. Acdestis too became the grown youth’s flattering companion and, in the only way he could be, was bound by improper flatteries, leading him through wooded and mountainous groves and presenting him with many gifts of wild game. At first the boy Attis claimed that these were the product of his own labor and achievement, boasting of them. Later, under the influence of wine, he confessed both that Acdestis loved him and that Acdestis honored him with gifts from the woods. Hence it is forbidden for persons polluted by wine—which betrayed the secret—to enter his sanctuary.

[Note: [Col. 1094C]

VII.—He destines his own daughter for him in marriage. Thus Meursius. Previously: “He destines his daughter for his marriage.” Perhaps we should read: “He now destines his daughter for marriage to him.” [Col. 1094D] ORELLI.

And lest some ill-omened person should interrupt the wedding joys. That is, σκαιός, ἐπαρίστερός τις, “some sinister and inauspicious person.” In unions and covenants of this sort, people sought to secure the most favorable auspices for themselves and to avoid everything contrary. Hence Seneca, *Controversies* V of Book X: “Dread omens encounter those newly married, and mournful omens encounter public rites; especially on holidays, solemn festivals, and days dedicated to gladness, those half-dead troops confront them.” For this reason newlyweds were not permitted to attend funerals. Synesius, Epistle III: “For it is not, I think, customary for brides to go to a funeral procession.” HERALDUS.—Thus *scaevus* means “sinister,” that is, perverse, in the Greek sense. Compare Fr. Juretus, who discusses this word at length, on Symmachus I, Epistle XXV, pp. 35 ff., Lectius’s edition. ORELLI.

He caused the town to be closed. That is, he ordered it, in our French idiom, *faire fermer*. We have observed *fecit fieri*, “he caused to be done,” in Aelius Spartianus, and similar expressions in Cassiodorus, Chrysologus, and others. HERALDUS.

[Col. 1095B] The terrified Phrygians immediately cry out. Salmasius corrected this most successfully in the Leiden edition and in his notes on Solinus, p. 232. *Ad horam* means the same as *ad praesens*, “at once, on the spot,” παραχρῆμα, αὐθωρεί. Thus Quintilian, *Institutes* XII: “And so I would not wish him—the orator—if he should happen to stand up on the spot,” that is, if he is compelled to speak extemporaneously and plead the case immediately, “to be unskilled in taking testimony.” The meaning, therefore, is: as soon as Acdestis presented himself to the banqueters, the Phrygians immediately cried out. The manuscript has *ad orandum*, “for praying,” which makes no sense; nor does the reading *adorandorum* in Sabaeus and Gelenius. Fulvius Ursinus reads: “before the faces of the gods.” Meursius: “before the faces—that is, in the sight—of both,” which Heraldus approves. Elmenhorstius, on Apuleius X, p. 302, Frankfurt edition: “The Phrygians, terrified by the Dorian mode.” Stewechius: “The Phrygians, terrified by the things being prepared,” explaining this as “moved by the crimes which they saw the banqueters preparing against them”; and he cites the Plautine phrase “to be deceived in speech.” [Col. 1095C] Soon afterward, however, retracting this conjecture, he attempts to defend Gelenius’s reading *adorandorum* in the same sense, as equivalent to “things to be done or performed.” Festus says: “Among the ancients *adorare* meant ‘to conduct an action’; and in the laws of the Twelve Tables: ‘If he prosecutes a theft which is not manifest, let him pay double.’” But this is as exceedingly harsh as it is unusual. Others, finally, read: “before the faces of such mighty beings.” ORELLI.

The daughter of a Gallus’s concubine cuts off her own breasts. Festus says: “At present those who submit to another are called *pellices* (‘concubines’), not only women but also men”; on this see Dacier. The passage concerns the daughter of some unspecified Gallus, that is, a priest of Cybele. For what follows prevents us from taking this as referring to the daughter of Midas, king of Pessinus, who was betrothed to Attis. ORELLI.

Attis snatches up the pipe which the very instigator of the madness was carrying. I have preferred to follow Salmasius here as well. The others read: “Attis snatches up a potsherd,” a reading defended by Meursius in the Appendix, Galland on this passage, and Ramirez, *Pentecontarchus* 4, p. 30. On the basis of Pliny, *Natural History* XXXV.12, Ramirez teaches that the priests of the Mother of the Gods, called Galli, used a Samian potsherd to cut off their virility. But *fistula*, “pipe,” is much better suited to the words that follow: “which the very instigator of the madness was carrying”—that is, which he carried to incite the banqueters to madness. For the frenzy of Bacchants or Galli is incited not by potsherds but by trumpets, pipes, drums, and other instruments of that kind. Vossius and Gronovius, on Minucius Felix 21, p. 204, teach us that the cutting or castration of the Galli was performed to the music of a pipe, because the pipe both added a stimulus of furious frenzy to the act of cutting and afterward lessened the pain of those castrated. We should therefore accept *fistulam* with Salmasius. ORELLI.

And beneath a pine tree he cuts off his own genitals, etc. Pausanias also relates all these events in the *Achaica*, p. 430, Sylburg’s edition, though more briefly:

> When, as he grew, he possessed beauty greater than was natural for a human form, Agdistis thereupon conceived a passion for the boy. When Attis had grown up, his relatives sent him to Pessinus to marry the king’s daughter. The wedding song was being sung when Agdistis appeared, and Attis, driven mad, cut off his genitals; the man who was giving him his daughter did so as well. But Agdistis was seized with remorse for what he had done to Attis. He obtained from Zeus the concession that no part of Attis’s body should decay or waste away. These are the best-known traditions concerning Attis.

ELMENHORSTIUS.

Even now the sacred pines are veiled and crowned. It is very well known that the pine was under the protection of the Mother of the Gods. HERALDUS.

Valerius the pontiff. It is certainly doubtful and uncertain which pontiff Arnobius means. Consider, however, whether he might be Marcus Valerius Messala, concerning whom Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.9, says: “Messala, the colleague of Gnaeus Domitius in the consulship and likewise an augur for fifty-five years, thus speaks concerning Janus: ‘He who fashions all things and governs them.’” Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* XIII.15, also transcribed a long fragment from the first book of this same augur Messala’s work *On Auspices*. It is therefore established that he wrote about the gods; why, then, should he not have written about the history of Ia? NOURRY, p. 549.—There is no mention of this man elsewhere. See G. J. Vossius, *De Historicis Latinis*, in the Appendix. The following *Iam* comes from the manuscript. Others read *Ion*. ORELLI.

He sheds tears together with Acdestis. This is a distinctive expression, for one “gives tears” to the deceased as though they were some service owed to him. Immediately after someone had expired, the weeping and wailing of relatives and friends followed; then the body was laid upon the ground, at which point it was said “to be upon the earth,” as Servius teaches. After it had been kept for several days, arranged, and prepared for the funeral procession, the deceased was called upon for the last time. Finally, when the body was placed upon the fire, it was mourned for the last time. Compare Servius on *Aeneid* VI.218 ff. HERALDUS.

The Mother of the Gods also poured forth such tears. Thus the Leiden editor emended the text, correctly in my opinion. *Et has* means “such tears also.” The manuscript and first edition read, most absurdly: “The Mother burrowed beneath herself, a goddess.” Gelenius: “The Mother, a goddess, buried her.” Here this can bear no meaning other than “dug her into the ground, buried her.” Yet, so far as I know, *suffodere* is nowhere used for *defodere*, “to bury.” Fulvius Ursinus altered the text more boldly: “The Mother took her up and buried her.” But I have preferred to follow Salmasius’s correction, which is far less drastic and exceedingly well suited to the context. ORELLI.

From this an almond tree arises, signifying the bitterness of the funeral. It appears that either Arnobius himself or that theologian Timotheus whom he transcribes throughout this narrative derived the word ἀμύγδαλος, “almond tree,” from ἀμύσσειν, which means “to prick,” and metaphorically “to cause mental pain or grief”; for example, Homer, *Iliad* I.243:

> ... and inwardly you will tear your heart,  
> Grieving, etc.

The bitter almond—*die bittere Mandel*—must be understood here. ORELLI.]

[Col. 1097B] **Around the strength of the rested tree.** This extremely obscure passage has proved a torment to interpreters. Heraldus, confessing that he does not know what *a rested tree* means, thinks it should be rewritten: “and rhythmically wounds his breast around the strength of the tree”; *rhythmically* (*pausate*), that is, τακτῶς, “in measured fashion,” with pauses and in a fixed manner—namely, when the lamentation was performed to the accompaniment of a dirge, after genuine and raw lamentations had already been poured forth. Thus the hired mourning women (*praeficae*) “set the measure of mourning for the others,” says Festus under *Praeficae*. Stewechius thinks that either *lanatae*, “wrapped in woolen fillets,” or *lausatae* should be read—though I frankly confess that I do not know what this novel and unheard-of word is supposed to mean. Salmasius, on Aelius Spartianus, *Pescennius Niger*, ch. 6, vol. I, *Writers of the Augustan History*, p. 661, thinks the reading should be: “around the strength of the rested tree,” that is, ἀναπαυομένη, “at rest.” [Col. 1097C] The Leiden editor restored the reading of the manuscript, which C. Barthius ably defends on Statius, *Thebaid* X.168, vol. III, p. 1145 ff. Arnobius therefore calls the tree “rested,” meaning that it was consecrated in such a way that, although everything in that cavern and shrine was raging, the tree nevertheless remained at rest and was shaken by no wind or tumult—according, that is, to the belief of Cybele’s worshippers. Claudian describes such a tree in most elegant verses, *The Rape of Proserpine*, book I, line 200 ff.:

> And the sacred stone  
> Of the temple that must be worshipped, which a pine shades  
> With dense foliage; and, though no storm disturbs the groves,  
> It modulates shrill songs through its cone-bearing branches.  
> Within, the terrible companies and the frenzied sanctuaries  
> Groan with mingled harmony. Ida revels in howling cries;  
> Gargara bows down its fearful forests.

Or, as Nourrius interprets it more truthfully, *pausatam* means “resting and placed within the cavern,” and therefore safe from the force of winds and storms. *Pausare*, “to rest,” [Col. 1097D] is an ancient word found in Plautus. ORELLI.

**Let it decay.** Thus the first edition reads from the manuscript. Gelenius, however, reads “let it rot,” followed by Salmasius. But *putescere*, or *putiscere*, is a word of the earlier Latin language, used several times by Cato in *On Agriculture* and by our author below, book VII, ch. 24: “since these things themselves, if they are not yet dung, will nevertheless soon become so, and after the intervention of a short period of time will decay.” See Gesner, *Thesaurus*, and Schneider, *Index to the Writers on Agriculture*. ORELLI.

**So that the very smallest of his fingers may live.** A superlative formed from a superlative. So below, ch. 14. Similarly ἐλαχιστότατος, “very smallest,” occurs among the Greeks, for example in Sextus Empiricus, *Against the Mathematicians*, book IX; see Fabricius there, p. 627. The same formation occurs in *pessimissimus*, “very worst,” in Seneca, *Epistle* 81, and *postremissimus*, “very last,” in Apuleius, Tertullian, and Aulus Gellius, book XV, ch. 12. Compare Vossius, *On Analogy*, book II, ch. 26. ORELLI.

**And alone be stirred with perpetual motion.** This is characteristic of Arnobius’s style, which favors such transpositions. The old reading is: “And alone be stirred and with perpetual motion.” Gelenius removed the final [Col. 1098B] conjunction. HERALDUS.

**And honored it with the testicle-less priests.** This is Salmasius’s splendid emendation in the Leiden edition and in his notes on Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, p. 155: *intestibus*, that is, “those who lack testicles.” Previously *antistitibus*, “chief priests,” was read, most incorrectly, for *antistes* and *sacerdos* mean one and the same thing, as the same Salmasius demonstrates at length in his exceedingly vitriolic *Refutation of Antonius Cercoetius* (Denis Pétau), p. 146 ff. Isaac Vossius, in his notes on Catullus, p. 164, defends the old reading *antistitibus* against Salmasius by citing Dio Chrysostom, Oration XXXV, on Celaenae in Phrygia:

> Ἄλλους σοφοὺς ὑμῖν ἀποδεικνύουσιν τρεῖς ἢ τέτταρας κομήτας, καθάπερ τοὺς ἱερέας τῶν παρ’ ὑμῖν τοὺς μακαρίους λέγω τοὺς ἁπάντων ἄρχοντας τῶν ἱερέων, τοὺς ἐπωνύμους τῶν δύο ἠπείρων, τῆς ἑσπέρας ὅλης.

> “They point out to you as other wise men three or four long-haired persons, like your blessed priests—I mean those who rule over all the priests, those renowned throughout the two continents and the whole West.”

[Col. 1098C] Here he understands ἱερέας, “priests,” as the Galli, and τοὺς ἁπάντων ἄρχοντας ἱερέων, “those who rule over all the priests,” as the Archigalli—the same persons whom Arnobius here calls “chiefs of the priests.” ORELLI.

## VII

Then Midas, king of Pessinus, wishing to estrange the youth from so infamous a union, appoints his own daughter to marry him; and, lest some ill-omened person interrupt the wedding festivities, he had the town closed. But the mother [Col. 1095A] of the gods, knowing the young man’s fate and that he would remain safe among human beings only so long as he was free from the marriage bond, entered the closed city, lifting its walls with her head, lest anything sorrowful should occur. For this reason she first came to be represented as turret-crowned.

Acdestis, seething with rage because the youth had been torn away from him and diverted toward desire for a wife, instilled frenzy and madness into everyone at the banquet. Terrified, the Phrygians immediately raised a united cry. The daughter of Gallus’s concubine cut off her own breasts. Attis seized the pipe which the very instigator of the madness was carrying; and he too, now filled with frenzy, raving and tossing wildly, at last flung himself down and beneath a pine tree cut off his own genitals, saying: “Keep these, Acdestis, for whose sake you stirred up such great upheavals of frenzied danger.” [Col. 1096A] His life flew out with the stream of blood. But the Great Mother of the gods gathered up the severed parts and cast earth upon them, after first covering and wrapping them in the dead man’s garment. From the flowing blood a violet flower sprang, and with it the tree was wreathed. From this arose the custom, still observed today, of veiling and crowning the sacred pines.

The maiden who had been his bride—whom the pontiff Valerius records as having been named Ia—covered the lifeless man’s breast with softer wool, shed tears together with Acdestis, and killed herself. The slain girl’s blood was transformed into purple violets. The Mother of the gods also covered these [with earth], whence an almond tree arose, signifying the bitterness of the funeral. Then she carried into her cavern the pine tree beneath which Attis had deprived himself of his manhood, and, joining her lamentations [Col. 1097A] with those of Acdestis, beat and wounded her breast around the strength of the rested tree.

Acdestis asked Jupiter to restore Attis to life. He did not permit this; yet he readily granted whatever fate allowed to be done: that his body should not decay, that his hair should always grow, that the very smallest of his fingers should live, and that it alone should be stirred with perpetual motion. Satisfied with these favors, Acdestis consecrated the body at Pessinus and honored it with annual rites and with testicle-less priests.

[Note: [Col. 1098C]

## VIII.—“You rewarded it with the honor of perpetuity.”

See above, on book I, ch. 41. ORELLI.

**You would be guilty of insult and injury.** The manuscript has “and injuries,” incorrectly; hence Meursius in his *Appendix* thinks the reading should be “and injurious.” ORELLI.

**The Mother of the gods, because of the flood, existed in no part of nature.** I have restored the manuscript reading, although it is utterly false and corrupt, since the true and genuine reading appears uncertain and has not yet been clearly established. “At the time of the flood,” which most editions have, is an interpolation by Gelenius. Fulvius Ursinus conjectures “by the occurrence of the flood,” which comes closest to the manuscript’s wording, for *causa*, “cause,” and *casus*, “occurrence,” are very often confused by copyists. But although it is very well known that the best authors use *casus* for something that happens or eventuates, whether favorably or unfavorably, I nevertheless greatly doubt whether *diluvii casu* can be said in Latin to mean “at the time when the flood occurred.” I therefore prefer Salmasius’s emendation: “The Mother of the gods, before the occurrence of the flood, existed in no part of nature.” Heraldus suspects that the reading should be: “The Mother of the gods, at the cessation of the flood, existed in no part of nature.” *Diluvii pausa*, “the cessation of the flood,” means “at the flood’s end, when the flood was over.” Thus a little later, in the following chapter: “Since you have been unable to make any pause in the slanders against Jupiter himself, even for the interval of a very short time.” Yet Arnobius says precisely the contrary: that the Mother of the gods did exist after the flood ended, but not before the flood. ORELLI.

**And owes it to the benefactions of Pyrrha.** C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXIX, ch. 14, prefers “owes it to beneficent Pyrrha.” ORELLI.

**Because she sees herself worshipped in the character of some substance.** The same Barthius, *Adversaria*, at the place cited, suspects that the reading should be “because she sees herself continuing in the character of some substance,” since the discussion is not about worship but about substance, or τὸ εἶναι, “being,” as people say today. On the contrary, the discussion is indeed about worship, and [Col. 1099B] the common reading is entirely sound, with this meaning: because she—the Mother of the gods, that is—sees herself worshipped as some actual substance, that is, as a truly existing thing or person, not as something fabricated by human imagination—*as a real being*. ORELLI.

**One of us.** See above, on book I, ch. 45. [Col. 1099C] ORELLI.

**And by the same manner of throwing.** Meursius and Stewechius were the first to see that this should be read in place of “manner of making,” which had previously been printed. Nor is the conjecture “would be produced” in place of “would be established” displeasing, given the words that follow. ORELLI.

**Down to the consulship of Hirtius and Pansa**, which fell in the year 711 from the foundation of the city, 43 before Christ. See Janssonius, *Consular Fasti*, p. 101. ORELLI.

**With whom, if the authority stands, the Mother too must be said...** This is Heraldus’s very slight and highly successful correction in *Curae Secundae*. The sense is: “with that same Varro—if his authority stands,” that is, “according to this statement of his, if it may be accorded credibility.” The first edition reads: “With whom the authority stands.” Gelenius printed: “If his authority is established.” The Leiden edition: “If the authority of this statement is established.” ORELLI.

**They have obtained by perpetual continuance.** Stewechius was the first to restore this most authentic manuscript reading to Arnobius. Previously the text read: “They have obtained in perpetual cognition”; Meursius conjectures: “in their condition.” ORELLI.]

## VIII

If some despiser of the divine powers, frenzied with the savagery of a sacrilegious heart, had directed his mind toward reviling your gods, would he dare to say anything more outrageous against them than the things disclosed by this story—a story which you have reduced, as though it were something marvelous, to the formal scheme of written records, and which, lest the force of time and the long duration of antiquity render it obsolete, [Col. 1097B] you rewarded with the honor of perpetuity? [Col. 1098A]

For what is set down or recorded in it concerning the gods that, if you said it of a human being brought up amid shameless morals and particularly brutal practices, would not make you guilty of insult and injury, and expose you to the hatred of offense requited by implacable enmities?

“You say that the Mother of the gods was begotten from the stones thrown by Deucalion and Pyrrha.” What are you saying, theologians? What are you saying, high priests of the powers above? Did the Mother of the gods, then, because of the flood, exist in no part of nature? And if the violence of the rains had not destroyed the whole race of mortals, would the cause and origin of her procreation have failed? That she perceives herself to exist is therefore a human gift; and she owes it to the benefactions of Pyrrha that she sees herself worshipped in the character of some substance.

If this is true, then the following too must necessarily be no falsehood: that she was a woman, not a goddess. For if it is certain that human beings derive the origin of their birth from that throwing of stones, then she too must necessarily be believed to have been one of us, procreated through causes of the same kind. For it cannot come to pass through an inherent contradiction that, from one kind of stones and by the same manner of throwing, some should be established as possessing the lot of immortals, while others should be established as possessing the human condition.

The Roman Varro, eminent [Note: [Col. 1099B] The manuscript reads *multiformis*.] in manifold branches of learning and a searching investigator of antiquity, teaches through careful calculations, in the first of the four books he left written *On the Race of the Roman People*, that from the time of the flood mentioned above down to the consulship of Hirtius and Pansa there were not yet two thousand years. If his authority stands [Note: [Col. 1099B] Meursius: “If, as to this, his authority...” See the Notes], then the Great Mother too must be said to have the duration of her life enclosed within the limits of this number. The matter is thus brought to the point that she who is said to be the mother of all the divine powers is not their mother but their daughter—indeed, an infant and a little child, if we grant that the gods have obtained neither beginnings nor ends of their ages, but perpetual continuance.

[Note: [Col. 1099D]

## IX.—“But why do we say that you have sullied the Mother of the gods with earthly filth?”

Thus I read in place of *obsolvisse*, which the manuscript has. For Arnobius used *obsolere* actively, just as Terence, Virgil, Plautus, and Apuleius used *irruere*, “rush upon”; *proruere*, “overthrow”; *ruere*, “cast down”; *penetrare*, “penetrate”; and *emergere*, “bring forth.” MEURSIUS, in the *Appendix*. Fulvius Ursinus reads “wrapped”; Salmasius, *obsolvisse*. ORELLI.

**Make a pause.** Lucilius, book I of the *Satires*:

> When he had spoken these words, his mouth made a pause from speaking.

Plautus, *The Rope*, act V, scene VI; Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book IX, p. 365; Nonius under *Pausa*. ELMENHORST.

**When the Mother of the gods was sleeping on the summit of Mount Agdus, then... to creep upon her.** Meursius arranges the words thus: “When the Mother of the gods was sleeping on the summit of Mount Agdus, then... to creep upon her,” etc. ORELLI.

**Even against his mother...?** Augustine, *City of God*, [Col. 1100B] book II, ch. 4: “Human modesty preserves even toward parents something that wickedness itself cannot take away.” ELMENHORST.

**But nature itself has subjected even some animals to it.** [Col. 1100C] Varro, *On Agriculture*, book II, ch. 7: “When a horse could not be induced to mount his mother, the driver covered his head, brought him to her, and compelled him to enter his mother. When, as he dismounted, the driver removed the veil from his eyes, the horse attacked him and bit him to death.” ELMENHORST and HERALDUS.

**Or did regard for filial duty and decency fail the guardian of the Capitol?** I have followed this very slight emendation of Salmasius, which comes closest to the manuscript’s *depuit*. This could very easily have been corrupted by copyists from *defuit* written in capital letters. Gelenius printed: “it is spat upon by the guardian.” The second Roman edition: “he spat upon the protection,” which is no freer of error. Meursius in the *Appendix* prefers *depuvitur*, citing Festus, who explains *depuvere* as “to beat.” Franciscus Modius conjectures: “did shame depart from the guardian?” Stewechius defends this by citing Ovid, *Heroides* IV.155:

> Shame departed, and fugitive modesty abandoned its standards.

But in that case *praesidem*, not *praesidi*, would have to be written. For *pudet* or *depudet mihi hujus rei*, “I am ashamed of this matter,” is no more a Latin construction than *depudet mihi respectus, pudor*, “respect, shame departs from me.” In the passage of Ovid one must supply *me*: “shame departed from me,” that is, as Heinsius correctly explains, “I cast aside all shame.” I have therefore preferred Salmasius. ORELLI.

**He was feeling her intimate parts.** *Res*, “things,” is used obscenely for the genitals. See above, on book III, ch. 10. ORELLI.—The manuscript reads *pellabat*. Perhaps *fellabat*, “he performed oral sex.” MEURSIUS, in the *Appendix*.

**Testing the depth of the sleeper’s...** That is, testing how deeply and profoundly she slept. Or we may interpret it as “the majesty of the sleeper.” Meursius’s transposition, “testing the depth of his sleeping mother and her endurance,” is therefore unnecessary. ORELLI.

**O foul posture of Jupiter!** Thus the Leiden editor from the manuscript. Others read “of the foul Jupiter.” ORELLI.

**When, being hasty, he had been repelled from his furtive attempt to creep upon her.** Thus Fulvius Ursinus, entirely correctly. For shortly before we read: “the son endeavored treacherously to creep upon the modesty of her as she rested.” The first edition reads [Col. 1101C] “from the theft of an objection,” incorrectly. Stewechius: “of subjugation.” Meursius: “of pleasure.” ORELLI.
