**Separated.** Thus Meursius and the Leiden edition. Others read “bound.” ORELLI.]

## IX

But why do we say that you have sullied the Mother of the gods with earthly filth, when you have been unable to make any pause in the slanders against Jupiter himself, even for the interval of a very short time? When the Mother of the gods was sleeping on the very summit of Mount Agdus, her son, you say, attempted treacherously to creep upon the modesty of her as she rested.

After innumerable virgins and matrons stripped of their chastity, did Jupiter conceive the hope of an unspeakable lust even against his mother? Nor could he be turned away from the heat of that desire by the horror which nature itself, and that universally implanted sense, has subjected not only to human beings but even to some animals? Or did regard for filial duty and decency fail the guardian of the Capitol, so that, his mind confounded by madness, he could neither reconsider nor perceive what crime he desired?

But however the matter stands [Note: [Col. 1100B] Fulvius reads: “But however the matter stands”], forgetful of his dignity and majesty, he went creeping toward those shameful, furtive acts, fearful and trembling, holding back the breath of his mouth, his steps suspended through dread; and, placed midway [Col. 1100B] on the frontier between anxiety and hope, he felt her intimate parts, testing the depth of the sleeper’s slumber and his mother’s [Note: [Col. 1100B] Fulvius: “his mother’s and...”] endurance.

O indecent image of the affair! O foul posture of Jupiter, made ready for the prosecution of an obscene contest! Therefore, when that king of the world, acting incautiously and hastily, had been repelled from his furtive attempt to creep upon her, did he turn to violent assault and, when he could not seize pleasure through treacherous fraud, attack his mother by force and openly begin to undermine her venerable chastity? Did he therefore struggle for a very long time with her against her will, and then, defeated, broken, and overcome, give up? And did discharged lust separate him when filial duty had been unable to sever him from his unspeakable desire for his mother?

[Note: [Col. 1101C]

## X.—“The human race avoids and abhors a union of this kind.”

Thus Salmasius printed from Heraldus’s emendation. Previously the reading was: “of union into an undertaking of this kind.” Janus Guilielmus, *Questions on Plautus’s Curculio*, ch. 5, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, part II, p. 366, suspects that the reading should be: “intercourse directed toward a coupling of this kind,” that is, τὰς συνουσίας εἰς ἀφροδισιασμόν, “sexual intercourse directed toward copulation.” For *convenire* means to engage in the begetting of children. Thus below, book VII: “They love their offspring and come together to beget children”; and *conventus* and *conventio* mean sexual intercourse above, book II, ch. 70: “They were inseminated and born from intercourse with Jupiter.” *Coetus* has the same meaning, as was noted above. Thus Lucretius, book III, lines 857–858:

> Yet this is nothing to us, who are constituted as one,  
> Fitted together through the union and marriage of body and soul.

[Col. 1101D] And Juvenal, *Satire* VI:

> Bold enough to endure the intercourse of men.

Even *colloquium*, “conversation,” was used in the same sense. See Moeris Atticista under διαλέγεσθαι, “to converse,” and Pierson there, p. 131 ff. I confess that I prefer Guilielmus’s emendation to that of Heraldus. Fulvius Ursinus thinks *conventionis*, “union,” should be deleted as a gloss. But such redundancies are characteristic of Arnobius. ORELLI and STEWECHIUS.

**Eagerly to satisfy the incitements of his desire.** Thus Salmasius, following Meursius’s emendation. The others read “of eager desire.” Fulvius Ursinus prefers “of his desired longing.” ORELLI.

**The flint, he says...** The reading must certainly be “they say.” For the preceding words are “men of great self-restraint,” etc., with no following verb to which they may be referred. Unless we prefer to supply the words thus: “he says”—that is, the adversary—“men of great self-restraint say: it drank in,” etc.; but that would certainly be exceedingly harsh. ORELLI.

[Col. 1102C] **Drank in the seed that had been discharged.** On the authority of the old book this must be written in the feminine, rather than in the masculine, for *sementis*, “seed,” is feminine. Marcus Tullius used the noun *sementis* in more than one passage. In his speeches it was first written thus: “when sowing had been prevented and the harvest lost.” In his philosophical works the same author uses “a sowing of evils.” STEWECHIUS.—Thus Stewechius corrected the text from the manuscript, quite rightly; for *sementis, -is* is feminine. Others read it in the masculine. Meursius conjectures: “drank in the discharged semen; then, when the period was completed,” etc.; and in what follows “bore” instead of “raised.” ORELLI.

**And, already bellowing his father’s thunder, reproduced it in imitation.** This is the old reading, which I would not alter, although Salmasius’s extremely acute correction pleases me wonderfully: “and reproduced it from deep within”—*imitus* being an ancient adverb used by Aulus Gellius, book XVII, ch. 10, and Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* V: “tell us from deep within what happened,” that is, from the depths of the breast; see Oudendorp there, p. 266. Compare above, on ch. 6. Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “he imitated and reproduced.” Stewechius: “when provoked, he reproduced it,” [Col. 1102D] very badly, for that would mean that Acdestis reproduced bellowing whenever he was provoked, presumably by the rock in which he had been enclosed being struck. ORELLI.

**From the region of heaven.** Stewechius suspects the reading should be: “from the governance of heaven.” Not badly. ORELLI.

**That most harmful virus of the seed.** Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 27: “In the very heat of the final pleasure, when the generative virus is expelled.” Papias, on the *Eunuchus*: “Some of these copulate and emit virus.” ELMENHORST.—Compare Caspar Barthius on Statius, *Silvae* I.4.104, vol. I, p. 128, and Gesner, *Thesaurus*. ORELLI.]

## X

Unless perhaps you will say: “The human race avoids and abhors a union of this kind; among the gods no relationships are incestuous.” Then why did the mother resist her son so fiercely [Note: [Col. 1101B] The manuscript reads “fight”] when he offered her violence? Why did she flee from his embraces, avoiding his touches as unlawful? For if there were no evil in the act, she ought to have complied with him without any hesitation, just as he eagerly wished to satisfy the incitements of his desire.

And indeed, at this point, lest those holy seeds should seem to have been poured forth in vain, men of great self-restraint and sparing even in matters of shameful conduct say that a flint drank in the foul discharge of Jupiter’s incontinence. What followed next, I ask? Tell us. In the middle hollow of the stone, within that hardness of whetstone, an infant was formed and endowed with life, destined to be the offspring of great Jupiter.

It is not easy to contradict conceptions so prodigious and marvelous. For since, according to you, the human race arose and was begotten from stones, [Col. 1102A] it must be believed both that stones possessed genital receptacles and drank in the seed discharged upon them, and that, when the periods were completed, they bore heavy wombs and at last gave birth, straining with the difficulty customary among females.

One point compels our curiosity to inquire further. Since you say that the offspring was delivered after ten months, during the time in which he was enclosed in the stone’s womb, by what nourishment and juices was he sustained? Or what nutriment could he derive from stony hardness, as offspring customarily derive it from their mothers?

“He had not yet reached the light,” someone says, “and already, bellowing his father’s thunder, reproduced it in imitation.” And [Note: [Col. 1101B] Others read “But.”] after he had been permitted to behold heaven and daylight, he attacked and ravaged everything he encountered, and promised himself that he could drive the gods themselves from [Note: [Col. 1102B] The manuscript reads “from.”] the region of heaven.

O cautious [Col. 1102B] and provident Mother of the gods! Lest she incur the ill will occasioned by so insolent a child, or lest the bellowing fetus disturb her dreams or interrupt her rest, she withdrew herself and transmitted that most harmful virus of the seed far away from herself, offering it as a draught to the roughness of the rocks.

[Note: [Col. 1102D]

## XI.—“By what means that untamable force of savagery could be subdued.”

Thus the best manuscripts read *edominari*, that is, *edomari*, “be subdued.” For the ancients said *domo, domino*, as was explained above on book I, ch. 50; the passive of this verb is now used deponentially. Certainly this passage of Arnobius and an old poet—whether Ennius or another—testify that the ancients employed it actively, since the poet used *dominari* passively:

> O ancient house, alas, by how different a master are you mastered!

MEURSIUS, in the *Appendix*. N. Heinsius therefore wrongly changes it to *edomitari* in *Adversaria*, book I, ch. 6, p. 73. Sabaeus and Gelenius have *edomari*. In place of “could,” the first edition has “was,” which Canterus defends as a Greek construction, ἦν δαμᾶσθαι, “it was possible to subdue,” for ἐξῆν. ORELLI.

**That he should be drenched with much unmixed wine.** Stewechius added “much” from the manuscript. ORELLI.

**And be deprived of his powers by their being cut off.** Nothing should be changed here. For a eunuch’s masculine powers are plainly removed together with his virile parts; hence eunuchs are also called *enervati*, “unmanned.” Claudian, *Against Eutropius*, book I, line 315:

> The eunuch Tiresias and the unmanned Melampus.

Moreover, Arnobius plays wonderfully upon the names of this part. For at one moment he calls it “the man,” at another “the pair,” as though translating διδύμους, “twins”; then “offspring”; and sometimes “flowers.” C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXIX, ch. 14, p. 1383.—*Vis*, “force,” has the same meaning in the following chapter: “when that force was covered in the bosom of the earth”; see Heraldus’s note there. *Virilibus*, “virile parts,” which the others have, is an interpolation by Gelenius. ORELLI.

**Those who have reaped away these parts from themselves.** Horace, *Satires* I.2.45:

> It happened that they reaped away with iron  
> A certain man’s testicles and lustful tail.

[Col. 1103C] Lactantius, *Institutes*, book V, ch. 9: “Those who reap away their virile parts with iron and, what is more criminal, do so that they may become chiefs of religion.” HERALDUS.—Compare Bünemann on Lactantius at the place cited, p. 617. ORELLI.

**Become more wanton.** True indeed; nevertheless they cannot beget offspring. Papias: “Some eunuchs copulate and even emit virus, but it is empty and powerless for procreation.” Firmicus, *Astronomy*, book III, ch. 7: “It makes eunuchs, castrated men, archigalli, or hermaphrodites, and men who do not perform these acts but instead undergo the treatment women customarily undergo, roused by the swelling of a womb through perverse fires of lust.” And ch. 11: “It makes eunuchs, or men without seed, who cannot copulate—infamous, immodest catamites.” Compare Terence, *Eunuchus*, act IV, scene III, and Juvenal, *Satire* VI, line 364 ff. ELMENHORST.—Muretus, *Various Readings* X.11. OCHSNER.

**Yet I should like to see.** Meursius conjectures: “I should so like to see,” explaining it as an ellipsis. ORELLI.

**If it had been granted me to be born in those times.** Stewechius correctly restored “those” in place of “these,” which had previously been read. For Arnobius is speaking about the times in which Father Liber performed this deed. ORELLI.

**After the most august councils of the gods.** I restore: “after the most august concerns of the gods.” For Arnobius is rightly astonished that the composers of poetic fables were so forgetful of the dignity that ought especially to be preserved in relation to the gods that they dared summon down to earth, for affairs not merely worthless but utterly filthy and shameless, those who are occupied in heaven with great matters and the most august concerns. Arnobius, book III: “What of the fact that, not content to subject and entangle the gods in such disgraceful concerns...” The same author in the final book: “that the terrors of the celestial gods had come to rest, and that they were recalled to concern for and familiarity with human beings.” STEWECHIUS.—Stewechius’s conjecture does not please me, and the common reading seems far more elegant. “After the most august councils of the gods” is equivalent to “after a most august senate of the gods had been convened.” Thus [Col. 1104A] Cicero uses *curia*, “senate-house,” metonymically for *senatus*, “senate,” *Letters to Atticus* XII.21: “For what have I to do with the forum without law courts, without a senate-house?”—that is, after losing the senate, since there is no senate. See Manutius there. Nor should it be doubted that Arnobius wrote this. For above, ch. 6, he had said: “Since it had often been asked in the deliberation of the gods by what means his audacity could be weakened or restrained”; and shortly before: “There was great agitation in the councils of the gods over the means by which that untamable force of savagery could be subdued.” He is therefore ridiculing the convening of a full senate of the gods over so vile and contemptible a matter. ORELLI.

**Cutting short the tail-hairs of geldings.** I have followed the emendation of Joseph Scaliger on Virgil’s *Moretum*, line 23, in the *Catalecta*, p. 162: *peniculamentum* derives from *peniculus*, a diminutive of *penes, -is*, in its ancient and primary sense. Festus says: “The ancients called the tail *penis*. From this ancient usage, even now, a piece of pork with its tail is called *offa penita* at sacrificial banquets; and the brushes with which shoes are wiped are called *peniculi*, because the ancients made the brushes used for wiping them from the tips of tails. The word was perhaps derived from hanging.” Cicero, *Letters to Friends* IX.22: “The ancients called the tail *penis*, whence, because of the resemblance, comes *penicillus*, ‘brush.’ Today, however, *penis* is used of the obscene parts.” See Manutius there.

*Peniculamentum* is used in the same sense here for “tail”; hence it is also used metaphorically for a kind of coarse, shaggy garment. See Nonius and Columna on the *Fragments of Ennius*, p. 97, Hessel’s edition. “To cut short the *peniculamenta* or *penicula* of geldings”—the latter being another form proposed by Scaliger—therefore means to pull or cut the hairs from horses’ tails. *Cantherius* properly means a castrated horse whose testicles have been removed; secondly, it means a horse in general. The first edition has “tailing the cuttings geldings,” which makes no sense. Gelenius, reshaping this into “tailing the cuttings of geldings,” seems to have understood *decuramenta* as an invented word from Greek κουρά, “a cutting of beard, hair, wool, or sausages”; but there is no authority for this word. In the Leiden edition Salmasius gave “tailing and cutting short geldings.” I would not have hesitated to receive this correction into the text as the slightest alteration and one highly consistent with Arnobius’s style of repeating the same thing in several words, had I not, with Gesner in the *Thesaurus* and Vossius in *Roman Etymology* under *penis*, desired another example of the extremely rare verb *peniculare* or *peniculari*, which they explain as “to pluck a tail.” I have therefore preferred Scaliger’s emendation, also approved by [Col. 1104D] Stewechius and Heraldus. Meursius, p. 158, badly changes the following words, “cutting short the geldings,” to “cutting with a cautery.” ORELLI.

**Fastening movable nooses.** Stewechius’s conjecture “knot-forming nooses” is by no means contemptible: that is, nooses which can be drawn together and constricted into knots—“closing, running ropes.” For a little later Arnobius says, “so that the surrounding bites of the nooses might encircle everything.” ORELLI.

**Violating the harmless purity of the waters with the great force of unmixed wine.** *Sauciantem*, “violating,” means changing or defiling them by imparting to them the power of causing intoxication. See C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book VIII, ch. 3, p. 365. Thus *saucius*, “wounded,” very often means “drunk.” Petronius, *Satyricon*, ch. 67: “Meanwhile the drunken women laughed together and joined inebriated kisses.” Justin, book I, ch. 8: “They are conquered by drunkenness before they are conquered in war. For when Cyrus learned this, he returned by night, surprised them while drunk, and killed all the Scythians together with the queen’s son.” See the commentators there, p. 40, A. Gronovius’s edition. ORELLI.

[Col. 1105B] **Then to have applied the cares of craftsmanship to things destined to perish.** Stewechius prefers “to have applied craftsmanship’s carefulness to things destined to perish,” deriving *curatum* from *curatus, -us*, a fourth-declension noun for which, however, I have searched elsewhere in vain. I think nothing should be changed, since Arnobius very often uses such particles περιττῶς, “redundantly.” The Leiden edition has: “thus then to have applied the care of craftsmanship to things destined to perish.” The “things destined to perish” are Acdestis’s genital parts, for whose destruction Liber employed every kind of contrivance. ORELLI.]

## XI

There was great agitation in the councils of the gods over the means by which [Note: [Col. 1102B] Sabaeus reads “could.” Correctly.] that untamable force of savagery might be subdued; and when no way remained, recourse was had to the single expedient of drenching him with much unmixed wine and depriving him of his powers by cutting them off.

As though those afflicted with such bodily losses became less daring, and as though we did not see every day that those who have reaped away these parts from themselves become more wanton, cast aside every restraint of shame and modesty, and rush into obscene degradation, publicly proclaiming their disgraceful practices.

Yet I should have liked to see—had it been granted me to be born in those times—Father Liber, vanquisher of Acdestis’s ferocity, after the most august councils of the gods, gliding down from the heights of heaven, cutting short the tail-hairs of geldings, fastening movable nooses, and violating the harmless purity of the waters with the great force of unmixed wine; and, after drunkenness had arisen from the drink, cautiously inserting his hands, handling [Col. 1105A] the sleeper’s virile parts, and then, so that the surrounding bites of the nooses might encircle everything, applying the cares of craftsmanship to things destined to perish.

[Note: [Col. 1105B]

## XII.—“Consecrated according to their opinion.”

I embrace this entirely correct emendation of Salmasius: *polluctus*, “imbued and, as it were, consecrated.” See above, on ch. 7 [Col. 1105C] of this book, and Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XI, ch. 7. Others read *pollutus*, “polluted,” incorrectly. ORELLI.

**Or at least reckoned him among mortals.** Thus the first edition, entirely correctly; for a little later Arnobius asks: “For if Acdestis was regarded as belonging to our lot and human condition, why did he inspire so much terror in the divine powers?” Those who wish to correct “mortals” to “immortals” should therefore not be heeded. ORELLI.

**Whose obscenity was amputated.** See above, on book IV, ch. 19. ORELLI.

**Or that anything should be cut from a divine body.** The old reading is: “or that anything should be cut off from out of a divine body.” We have a similar pleonasm in book IV, ch. 18: “For what can be said about the immortal gods which has not arrived at human conceptions from out of accounts written by men?” HERALDUS.—This passage, printed corruptly, proves nothing, as we have shown in the notes. Nowhere in Arnobius do we find two prepositions governing one and the same case of a noun, although he very often uses prepositions, like other particles, redundantly. ORELLI.

**From a flow of blood, and from the amputated genitals, a pomegranate tree arose.** Perhaps the reading should be: “Did a violet flower also spring from the flow of blood, and from the genitals,” etc.? For so above, ch. 7: “From the flowing blood a violet flower sprang, and with it the tree was wreathed.” THOMAS CANTERUS.—But Canterus is mistaken, for the cited passage concerns not Acdestis but Attis. The words “from a flow of blood” must be understood of the blood bursting from Acdestis’s genitals when they were constricted by the noose. Concerning this we read above, ch. 6: “when the parts were torn away, blood flowed without measure.” On the form *fluor, -oris*, frequently used by Arnobius, see the notes on book I, ch. 45. In place of “pomegranate tree,” Meursius prefers “Punican apple tree.” ORELLI.

**When that force was covered in the bosom of the earth.** That is, that “man,” that member, that part. Above, ch. 11: “that he should be deprived of his powers by their being cut off.” HERALDUS.

**With balaustia.** Pliny, *Natural History*, book XIII, ch. 19 (34 in Hardouin’s edition): “In the region of Carthage the Punic apple claims a surname from the place; some call it the pomegranate.... Its flower is called *balaustium* and is suitable both for medicines and for dyeing garments, whose color has taken its name from it.” See Hardouin there. Dioscorides, book I, ch. 155: βαλαύστιόν ἐστιν ἄνθος ἀγρίας ῥοιᾶς, “the *balaustion* is the flower of the wild pomegranate.” ELMENHORST.—Compare Ezekiel Spanheim, who discusses this word at length in *On the Excellence and Use of Coins*, dissertation VI, vol. I, p. 315 ff., and the commentators on Alciphron, book I, Epistle II, p. 20 ff., Wagner’s edition. From this arose the word *Balluster*, by which we Swiss designate this same flower of the pomegranate tree when cultivated in gardens. ORELLI.]

In the space of a moment. Thus Fulvius Ursinus, from the manuscript; the Leiden edition follows him. The first edition reads: “In points the reasoning,” which makes no sense; from this Gelenius produced *in punctistitio*. *Punctum* means a point of time, as it does several times in Lucretius. ORELLI.

[Col. 1106C] Therefore their color is yellowish beneath a suffusion of purple light. This is the old reading, for which Salmasius substituted “through an obstruction of the light.” *Sufficere*, a dyers’ term, means to lay down a color over which another is subsequently applied. See Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. Nonius therefore interprets it incorrectly as “to dye.” Seneca, *Natural Questions*, book I, chapter 5: “Moreover, when you are told that a cloud has been suffused by the sun, you are not being told that color has been mixed into it as into a hard, stable, and enduring body, but as into something fluid and shifting, which receives nothing more than a very fleeting appearance.” Thus “eyes suffused with death,” “eyes suffused with blood,” “cheeks suffused with spots,” and so forth. *Suffectio* therefore has the same sense here, so that the meaning is “yellowish, in such a way that a purple light—that is, a purple color—shines through the suffusion”: “yellowish with a translucent purple color” (*gelblich mit durchscheinender Purpurfarbe*). Yet “through an obstruction of purple light—or color” is an equally good reading, signifying that the purple light is hindered or intercepted by the interposition of another body, namely the rind or shell of the pomegranate. Thus Lucretius, book V, verses 772 following, on eclipses of the sun and moon:

[Col. 1106D] That we might know the varied courses of the sun  
And the moon’s paths, what force and cause impelled them,  
And how they commonly set with their light obstructed.

I nevertheless dare decide nothing, since I do not know whether the reading derives from the manuscript. Instead of “purple light,” Meursius prefers “by a suffusion of the purple stream,” because the preceding words were: “from an effusion of blood a violet is born.” ORELLI.

That they derive their origin from ballasted blood. Here too, still doubtful and uncertain about the true reading, I have printed the commonly received text. The manuscript has “from blood ballast,” corruptly. Salmasius printed “from more savory blood,” that is, from blood having a better, sharper flavor than that of other human beings: “from more flavorsome, more highly seasoned blood” (*von schmackhafterm, gewürzhasterm Blute*). Constantine the African, *On Fevers*, chapter IV—cited by Gesner in the *Thesaurus*—says in the same sense: “Blood is more flavorful than all the elements.” N. Heinsius, *Adversaria*, book I, chapter 10, p. 102, defends the received reading and teaches that one should read either *saburrato*, *saburratiore*, *saburralitio*, [Col. 1107B] or finally *saburracco*, from *saburra*, that is, a stuffed crop, a “full load” (*πλήρωμα*), or a ship’s ballast (*τῆς νεὼς ἕρμα*). See Scaliger on Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book VI, p. 151. Hence in Plautus, *The Casket*, act I, scene II, women satiated with food and drink are called *saburratae*, “ballasted.” Hence “ballasted” or “more ballasted blood” means the blood of a drunken man, such as Acdestis was, who, as was said above in chapter 6, “had immoderately drawn into his gaping veins a drink kindled by Liber with the most potent strength of unmixed wine.” This corresponds perfectly to the preceding words, “moist, and therefore vinous.” Nourrius thinks one should read: “because those fruits, ballasted—that is, filled and laden—with blood, which were said in the fable to have sprung from Acdestis’ flowing blood, derive their origin from it.” Nevertheless, I confess that the received reading pleases me more, in the sense we have stated. ORELLI.

O Abdera, Abdera, how many opportunities for mockery you would give mortals. Stewechius restored the text thus from the manuscript, where it reads: “O Abdera, Abdera, how many opportunities for mockery you would give mortals”; Salmasius added the words required by the sense. Sabaeus and Gelenius print: “O Abdera, Abdera, how you would become an object of mockery to mortals.” Meursius conjectures: “how you yourself would become an object of mockery to mortals.” Grotius: “to what extent you would become one.” *Quanti … tanti* in place of *quot … tot* occurs not infrequently even in the best authors. See Broukhusius on Propertius, book I, elegy V, verse 10, p. 21, and Duker, *On the Latinity of the Jurists*, p. 358. Among ecclesiastical writers—Tertullian, Ambrose, Augustine, and others—nothing is more frequent. Compare Havercamp on Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter I, p. 8, and Bünemann on Lactantius, *Institutes*, book I, chapter 4, p. 22. The madness and stupidity of the people of Abdera were exceedingly notorious and became proverbial for every sort of fool and dullard. Hence Cicero, *To Atticus*, book IV, letter XVI, says of the Roman Senate: “You will say that this is Abdera, and not because I have kept silent. Yet will you not stop? Forgive me; I scarcely can. But what could be more ridiculous?” Compare Worth on Tatian, *Address to the Greeks*, p. 63. ORELLI.

All the fathers tell it. Fulvius Ursinus conjecturally reads “learn it,” and so forth. But I certainly prefer the received reading. [Col. 1107D] “Tell” means that all the fathers of the religions—that is, the priests and pontiffs—teach that fable. Instead of “all,” Stewechius prefers “wise.” ORELLI.

Haughty cities read it through. G. J. Vossius, *On Faults of Speech*, condemns the word *superciliosus* as barbarous; Ole Borch defends it in his *Reflections*, p. 249, from Seneca, Letter CXXIII: “Do not value at a penny those grim and haughty censors of another’s virtue, enemies of their own, public schoolmasters.” But this word was more frequently used in Arnobius’ time. Thus, for example, Sidonius, book VII, letter X: “the Catonian judgment of a haughty brow”; and Martianus Capella, book VIII: “You used to rebuke me more haughtily.” ORELLI.]

## XII

Would anyone have said this about the gods if he were imbued with even the slightest favorable opinion of them? Or, if they are occupied with such affairs, thoughts, and concerns, would any wise person either believe them to be gods or reckon them even among mortals? This Acdestis, I ask, whose severed obscenity was to bring security to the heavenly beings—was he one of the creatures of the earth, or some god endowed with the honor of immortality? For if he belonged to our lot and to the human condition, why did he inspire such terror in the divine powers? But if he [Col. 1106A] was a god, how could he be deceived, or how could anything be cut away from a divine body?

Yet we raise no question on this point. Let him have belonged to the divine race, or have been one of us, if you think it more correct to say so. But did a pomegranate tree actually spring from the effusion of blood and the amputated genitals? Or, when that force was covered in the bosom of the earth, did it clasp the soil with a root, shoot up into the strength of a trunk, put forth branches laden with pomegranate blossoms, and in the space of a moment bear ripe fruits, completed by the maturity proper to them? And because these arose from red blood, is their color therefore yellowish beneath a suffusion of purple light? Add also that they are moist for this reason, vinous for this reason, because they derive their origin from [Col. 1106B] ballasted blood, and fill out the fable consistently [Note: [Col. 1107A] “You have filled it out,” manuscript; better, according to Meursius].

O Abdera, Abdera, how many opportunities for mockery you would give mortals if such a fable, composed in this fashion, existed among you! All the fathers tell it, and haughty cities read it through; yet you are judged foolish and possessed of the most benumbed stupidity.

[Note: [Col. 1107D]

### XIII.—The reasoning follows itself

Meursius corrects this to: “the reasoning, of course, follows,” supposing that *se* arose from an abbreviation of *scilicet*. Not badly. ORELLI.

Fruits there must be in heat. Salmasius deservedly admitted into the text this most felicitous correction by Fulvius Ursinus. *Surire* means “to be in sexual heat” (*καπρᾷν*). See above, on book I, chapter [Col. 1108B] 2. The old reading is “must arise,” which Heraldus and Elmenhorst defend in vain. ORELLI.

Berecyntia nourished her in confinement. I would prefer “in banishment.” Above, chapter 6: “As though she had been violated, her father shuts her up and takes care that she die of starvation; she is sustained by the mother of the gods with fruits and other little berries.” HERALDUS.—Nothing should be changed. She was “confined,” namely shut up in prison at her father’s house; “banished” would mean sent away into exile, or shut up and guarded in some other, more remote place. ORELLI.

He disdained to call him the offspring of his own child. Thus Heraldus in *Corrections II* and Stewechius emended the text. The manuscript reads: “Having been designated, and to be called the offspring of his own child,” which Gelenius changed to: “and if he were his son, to be called the offspring of his own child”; the Leiden edition follows him. *Pignora* means children. See above, on book II, chapter 76. ORELLI.

The male sex. Thus the manuscript, as Heraldus and Stewechius attest. See above, on book I, chapter 59. ORELLI.

[Col. 1108C] But even livestock become mothers from males. I have printed the very slight emendation of Fulvius Ursinus, which comes closest to the manuscript reading: “but even livestock become males from males,” which makes no sense. Gelenius and most who followed him read: “Livestock … become non-males.” Meursius conjectures: “mothers without mothers,” that is, “having no mothers” (*μητέρας μὴ ἔχοντας*), like *exos* and similar forms; but this is plainly the opposite of what Arnobius wished to say. He is, of course, ridiculing the goat that offered its udders to Attis, as an utterly absurd fable. Among the Romans, just as among our own people, “to milk a he-goat” is a proverb for something altogether absurd and impossible, as the very familiar verses of Virgil, *Eclogue* III, verses 90 following, attest:

Let him who does not hate Bavius love your songs, Maevius,  
And let that same man yoke foxes and milk he-goats.

Stewechius, confusing everything, thinks one should read: “but virgins also become breastless,” as though the discussion here concerned Gallus’ daughter cutting off her own breasts, of whom [Col. 1108D] Arnobius speaks a little later. Salmasius printed: “But livestock also come from males,” deleting the word “mothers” or “males.” He explains the basis of his conjecture in his notes on Aelius Lampridius’ *Commodus*, chapter 7, *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, p. 493, interpreting *ex maribus* as “those who have lost their male organs,” as in Plautus’ *Amphitryon*: “He has been made a woman from a man,” that is, he has lost his manhood. In the same sense the Greeks call the blind “men away from their eyes” (*ἐξ ὀμμάτων*), and the Latins “men without eyes” (*ab oculis*), or in a single word *aboculi*. But if we follow this explanation, “livestock come from males” would mean only that livestock are castrated by excision of their testicles, not what Arnobius wishes to indicate: that male animals are transformed into females, he-goats into she-goats. I have therefore preferred to follow Fulvius Ursinus. ORELLI.

Goatish stench. We can readily dispense with Elmenhorst’s annotation. The subject here is not the stench of the armpits, which the Latins call “the goat” (see Horace, *Epode* XII, 5), but the stench contracted from nourishment with goat’s milk. ORELLI.

[Col. 1109B] But it is not easy even for conjecturers to surmise what Midas dreaded. Rather: “it is not difficult.” For he dreaded Acdestis’ detestable passive lust. HERALDUS.

[Col. 1109C] We certainly admire. Meursius: “We certainly do not admire.” ORELLI.

Because, though mindful of the law and fate, he exposed an insufficiently guarded city to its enemies. This is the entirely correct emendation of Heraldus in *Corrections II*. The manuscript reads: “From you he made it for the enemies,” and so forth, from which Gelenius produced: “When Attys, mindful of the law and fate, made it for the enemies,” and so forth. But—not to mention that, by raising the walls with his head, as was said above in chapter 7, Berecyntia made the inhabitants of the city not less provident but more cautious—one would have had to write “of Attis’ fate.” For this is Arnobius’ declension of that name: above, in book I, chapter 41, we have the accusative “the mutilated Phrygian Attis,” and in book IV, chapter 29, the ablative “by the beautiful Attis.” For this reason we should not listen to Fulvius Ursinus either, when he corrects the text to: “When Attys, mindful of the law and fate, made the city far too accessible to its enemies.” Arnobius calls the city insufficiently guarded because of the joys of the wedding, which King Midas did not wish to have interrupted and therefore ordered the town closed. Consequently neither the conjecture [Col. 1109D] of the Leiden editor, “less provident,” nor that of Meursius, “less well provided for,” is necessary. ORELLI.

Unless the boy had thrown the severed parts before the offended company. Thus I have printed the text following the exceedingly acute emendation of Heraldus in *Corrections II*. The old reading is: “unless the boy had thrown the severed things of satiety before the offended man.” Gelenius printed: “had offered an offense,” and the others followed him, except Salmasius, who in the Leiden edition more boldly recast it as: “unless the boy had thrown these severed parts before the offended one.” Meursius: “unless the mutilated boy Attys had offered an offense.” ORELLI.]

## XIII

Nana, he says, conceived a son through her bosom from a fruit. The reasoning follows itself: for where crags and hard rocks give birth, fruits there must necessarily be in heat. Berecyntia fed the imprisoned woman with acorns and figs—consistently and correctly; for she who had become a mother [Col. 1108A] from a fruit was obliged to live on fruits.

After the offspring had been delivered, Sangarius ordered it to be cast far away. Though he had long believed it to have been conceived by divine agency, he disdained to call it the offspring of his own child. The infant was reared on goat’s milk. O fable, always hostile and utterly inimical to the male sex! In it not only do human beings lay aside the male sex [Note: [Col. 1108A] Read “the male sex.” See the Note], but even livestock become mothers from males.

He was distinguished by renowned beauty and celebrated comeliness. It is marvelous enough that a goatish stench did not make him repellent and someone to be avoided. The Great Mother loved him. [Col. 1109A] If she loved him as a grandmother loves a grandson, the matter is innocent; but if she loved him as the theaters loudly proclaim, the love was infamous and shameful. Acdestis also loved him and enriched him with hunting gifts. There could certainly be no danger to his chastity from a half-man; but what Midas dreaded is not easy for those conjecturing to judge [Note: [Col. 1109B] “To assess,” Fulvius].

The Mother herself entered together with the city walls. We certainly admire [Note: [Col. 1110B] “We used to admire,” manuscript] the divine power and courage in this matter; but we fault the king’s negligence [Note: [Col. 1110B] “Again,” manuscript], because, though mindful of the law and fate, he exposed an insufficiently guarded city to its enemies.

While the marriage vows were being celebrated, Acdestis inflicted frenzy and madness upon them. If King Midas had given offense by binding the young man to a wife, what had Gallus done, or the concubine’s daughter, that the former should deprive himself of manhood and the latter of the honor of her breasts? “Take these for yourself,” he says, “on account of which you have stirred up such great events through the overthrow of minds.” We would all still be ignorant of what the Acdestian madness had desired in the adult’s body if the boy had not thrown the severed parts before the offended company. [Col. 1109B]

[Note: [Col. 1109D]

### XIV.—What do you say, O peoples … nations?

See above Heraldus’ note on the title of the work. ORELLI.

Male genitals. Glosses: “*Veretrum* … the sexual organ” (*αἰδοῖον*). Below, book VI: “the sizes of their genitals were made public.” Papias: “*Veretrum*.” Suetonius, *Tiberius*, chapter 62. ELMENHORST.

Those severed genitals, together with their discharges. Thus Fulvius Ursinus, entirely correctly; the others follow him. Previously the text read: “those scattered genitals.” Instead of “discharges,” others read “flowers”; Meursius, “offspring.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1110B] Mourning by herself. I think the words “by herself” should be deleted as the explanatory gloss of some petty schoolmaster. MEURSIUS.

[Col. 1110C] And lest they lie naked and dissolve in the bosom of the soil in this way. I think one should read “namely, of the soil.” It would have been clearer: “and lest, namely, they lie naked,” and so forth. Perhaps, however, the abbreviation *sc.* had been written, from which *sic* arose. HERALDUS.

Before she veiled and covered them with clothing. On the custom of clothing corpses after they had been washed and anointed, see H. Columna on the *Fragment of Ennius*, p. 54, Hessel edition:

A good woman washed and anointed the body of Tarquin.

See also the authors cited by Savaro on Sidonius, book III, letter III, p. 191. ORELLI.

For how could fragrant violets have arisen unless that application of perfumes had moderated the member’s putrefaction? Thus Salmasius printed the text. The old reading is: “For how could violets have arisen, by fragrance, unless,” and so forth. On *putor* and other nouns of this kind ending in *-or*, see C. Barth on Statius, *Thebaid* V, 147, vol. III, p. 99. ORELLI.

Do you not seem to yourselves to be listening either to little weaving girls, and so forth? Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV, 36 following:

[Col. 1110D] One of them, drawing out the thread with nimble thumb, said:  
“While the others cease work and attend invented rites,  
Let us too, whom Pallas, a better goddess, keeps occupied,  
Lighten the useful work of our hands with varied talk.  
And in turn let us bring something to our unoccupied ears  
That will not allow the time to seem long.”

HERALDUS.

For credulous infants. Fulvius Ursinus’ conjecture “for fretful infants” is plausible; since it better suits the following “diversions,” Scioppius also approves it on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* IV, p. 299, Oudendorp edition. ORELLI.

Diversions. The word is significant. *Avocare* means to draw and call the mind away elsewhere. Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book IV, p. 299: “But I shall at once divert you with charming stories and old women’s tales.” See Oudendorp there. In the same sense Tertullian calls a mountebank or itinerant charlatan a “diverter of men.” ORELLI.

And lest he be altogether extremely harsh. Should one not read: “But lest he be,” and so forth? ORELLI.

[Col. 1111B] The very smallest. See above, on chapter 7. ORELLI.

A hair to grow on a dead man. Yet pupils of the physicians affirm this; experience itself bears witness that it occurs in those who have been hanged. See Tertullian, *On the Soul*, chapter 51. ELMENHORST.—What Arnobius denies can happen, Aristotle affirms in *History of Animals*, book III, chapter 11: [Col. 1111C] “Hair grows more in certain illnesses, such as consumptive diseases, and in old age, and also on the dead; and it becomes harder instead of soft” (*Αὔξονται δὲ τρίχες ἔν τε νόσοις τισὶν, οἷον ταῖς φθισικαῖς μᾶλλον, καὶ ἐν γήρᾳ, καὶ τεθνεώτων, καὶ σκληρότεραι γίνονται ἀντὶ μαλακῶν*). Petavius on Synesius, *Praise of Baldness*, note, p. 32. Alexander of Aphrodisias explains the cause in *Problem* 145. ORELLI.

The part not to have perished. Fulvius Ursinus was the first to add “not,” which the sense requires. ORELLI.

Mortal. Thus the Leiden edition, following Meursius’ entirely correct correction. Others read “immortal,” which is plainly the opposite of what Arnobius wishes to say. ORELLI.]

## XIV

What do you say, O peoples? What do you say, nations devoted to opinions of this kind? When these things are brought forth, are you not seized by shame and embarrassment at such great obscenities? We long to hear or learn from you something worthy of the gods; but what you bring forth for us are excisions of breasts, amputations of male genitals, wrath, blood, frenzies, the voluntary deaths of maidens, and flowers and trees produced from the blood of the dead. [Col. 1110A]

Tell us, I ask once more: did the mother of the gods, then, herself mourning, collect those severed genitals together with their discharges in dutiful solicitude? Did she herself touch and lift with her holy hands, with her divine hands, the instruments of that disgraceful and foul deed? Did she even order them to be hidden in the earth? And lest they lie naked and dissolve in this way in the bosom of the soil, did she, before veiling and covering them with clothing, of course wash them with balsams and anoint them? For how could fragrant violets have arisen unless that application of perfumes had moderated the member’s putrefaction?

When you read through such stories, I ask you, do you not seem to yourselves to be listening either to little weaving girls, beguiling the delays of their tiresome work, or to long-lived old women seeking diversions for credulous infants and bringing forth varied inventions under the appearance of truth? [Col. 1110B]

Acdestis spoke with Jupiter so that he might restore his beloved to life. Jupiter refused to consent because he was restrained by more powerful fates. But lest he be altogether extremely harsh, he granted one favor: that the body should not be dissolved by any putrefaction, that the hair should always continue growing, and that the very smallest of the fingers alone should live upon the body and alone exhibit perpetual movements. Would anyone accept this, or confirm it with the assent of credulity—that a hair grows on a dead man; that the part did not perish; and that a mortal body, exempted from the law of decay, has endured even until now? [Col. 1111A]

[Note: [Col. 1111C]

### XV.—Comparison

Perhaps “confirmation” should be read. CANTER.

Unless it were part of folly even to learn such things. C. Barth, *Adversaria*, book XXIX, chapter 44, p. 1383, prefers: “Unless it were equal to folly.” Instead of “to learn,” Stewechius suspects that “to open one’s mouth” should be read, citing book I, chapter 23: “Finally, if dumb animals themselves were able to open their mouths,” and book IV: “We wish to test whether you can mutter or open your mouths at the mention [Col. 1111D] of the gods.” But nothing should be changed. Arnobius says that it is part of folly even to learn—that is, to read—such absurd fables, much less to compare them and investigate them more deeply. ORELLI.

Banished. See on book I, chapter 1. ORELLI.

That it exists among actual events, and so forth. Thus the first edition, which the others have followed. Fulvius Ursinus, however, conjectures “in the records of the days,” that is, in daybooks, daily proceedings, or journals. Elmenhorst approves this. Thus below, book VII, chapter 9: “So many things that scarcely ten thousand volumes either of annals or of daily records could unfold them.” See the notes there. If the received reading is sound, “that it exists among actual events” means that it exists or is handed down as a fact actually accomplished: “that it is founded upon facts” (*Sie sei auf Tatsachen gegründet*). Heraldus suspects: “that it exists in the rites,” that is, in the sacred ceremonies, which pleases me greatly. Meursius refers “it” to the preceding “cause of offense.” For he reads this in the singular instead of “causes of offense,” and more boldly recasts [Col. 1112B] what follows as: “entered by you into books and commentaries.” ORELLI.

For the instruction of future time. I have followed the emendation of the Leiden editor. The old reading is “through construction,” which makes no sense. Fulvius Ursinus printed “by prior construction”; I wish he had explained to us what he intended this to mean. [Col. 1112C] ORELLI.

Nor have we sent them into public attestation through the celebrations of your rites. The same Fulvius reads “inserted,” incorrectly. For if we understand “through the celebrations of your rites” in the ablative case, I do not see why the construction “to send something into public attestation” should be disturbed. ORELLI.]

## XV

We could long ago have pressed you to compare the evidence on this matter, were it not part of folly both to learn such things and to demand proofs of matters of this kind. But this story is false and contains no element of truth in itself. It is of no concern to us whether the story for whose sake you contend that the gods have been banished from the earth is consistent and supported by the firmness of reliable testimony, or, on the contrary, has been composed deceitfully through some fictitious falsehood.

For it is enough for us, whose purpose today is to demonstrate [Col. 1111B] that those divine powers whom you bring forward—if they exist anywhere among the nations and grow hot with the fervors of anger—receive the causes of their furious offense no more from us than from you; that the story exists among actual events, has been entered by you into commentaries, is read through daily by those who desire to do so, and is handed down in due succession for the instruction of future time.

If it is indeed true, we see no underlying reason why the heavenly gods are said to be angry with us, since we have neither disclosed such great obscenities of theirs [Note: [Col. 1111B] “Since we have not disclosed,” manuscript], nor committed them to any writings, nor sent them into public attestation through the celebrations of your rites. [Col. 1112A] But if, as you suppose, the story is false and adulterated with deceitful lies, no human being can doubt that you are the cause of the offense, since you either allowed certain persons to write such things or permitted what had been written to endure in the memory of the ages.

[Note: [Col. 1112C]

### XVI.—To be true

Meursius prefers “that this writing is true.” Well said. ORELLI.

Of proven reliability. Thus Fulvius Ursinus, from the manuscript; excellently. Sabaeus and Gelenius print: “of explained reliability.” ORELLI.

For what is the meaning of that pine tree which you always introduce into the sanctuary of the Mother of the Gods on appointed days? This was done on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, as is noted for that day in the Roman Calendar of Constantine the Great: “The Tree enters,” which must be understood of the pine tree’s introduction into the sanctuary of the Mother of the Gods. The days that follow were dedicated to various solemnities of that same Mother of the Gods: the Day of Blood is marked on the ninth day before the Kalends of April in the same Calendar, the Hilaria on the eighth, the Rest on the seventh, and the Washing on the sixth. SALMASIUS, in the *Appendix to Solinus*, *On Medical Matter*, p. 3.

Valesius, on Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIII, p. 255, thinks one should read: “which … you introduce into the sanctuary of the Mother of the Gods.” But nothing should be changed. “To introduce in the sanctuary” can be said no less properly than, above in book II, chapter 2, “to bring true religion into the world,” and in book I, chapter 42, “the gifts which, proceeding from him, exist in us,” where we illustrated this mode of expression with several examples. Moreover, we learn from Julian’s *Oration* V that in the course of time these ceremonies were altered and the days consecrated to the Mother of the Gods reduced to only three. Compare Sainte-Croix’s book *On the Mysteries of the Ancients*, translated into German by Lenz, chapter 4, pp. 72 following. ORELLI.

With which Ia also covered him as he was dying. Stewechius has shown, entirely correctly, that this should be read instead of the received: “with which she also covered him as he was now dying.” For it was not the Great Mother [Col. 1113A] but the maiden who had been his bride—whom the pontiff Valerius records as having been named Ia—who covered the breast of the lifeless Attis with softer wool. Moreover, so far as I know, this maiden is mentioned nowhere else; Stewechius is egregiously mistaken in thinking that Homer mentions her. This conjecture rests solely upon a corrupted transcription of the Homeric verse, *Odyssey* XIV, 435. [Col. 1113B] ORELLI.

Why do the Galli, with hair disheveled, strike their palms against their breasts? Ovid, *Fasti* IV:

This madness became their model, and the effeminate ministers  
Beat their worthless limbs while tossing their hair.

ELMENHORST.—Apuleius, *Milesian Tale* VIII: “An old, effeminate debauchee, bald indeed, yet wearing his half-gray, curling locks long and dangling: one of the common dregs of the mob who, clashing cymbals and castanets through the streets and towns and carrying the Syrian goddess about, compel [him] to beg.” Again in the same book: “For a long time they lowered their heads, twisted their necks in sinuous movements, and whirled their hanging hair in a circle; sometimes they even bit their own muscles, and finally each cut his arms with the double-edged blade he carried.” Thus all fanatics, soothsayers, and itinerant charlatans of that kind wore long hair, as is sufficiently well known from the ancient authors. Hence Arrian, *Discourses of Epictetus*, book IV, chapter 8: “This man is a philosopher. Why? Because he has a cloak and long hair. But what do the itinerant charlatans have?” (*οὗτος φιλόσοφος. Διὰ τί; τρίβωνα γὰρ ἔχει καὶ κόμην, οἱ δὲ ἀγύρται τί ἔχουσιν;*) [Col. 1113C] HERALDUS.

Why is there abstention from the sustenance of bread, to which practice you have given the name *Castus*? See how dangerous it is to emend anything by conjecture and without manuscripts, and to depart from the ancient traces. Although the Roman manuscript correctly read “abstention from the sustenance of bread,” Gelenius emended it to “bread compounded with the nourishment of beans.” But ignorance of the meaning of *temperatus* provided him with the occasion for error. For *temperatus* is not used here of mixture, as he supposed, but of temperance and abstinence. We discussed this passage more fully in *Various Readings*, book II, chapter 21, in Gruter’s *Lamp*, vol. III, pp. 766 following. TH. CANTER.

The priests of Cybele and Isis abstained from bread. St. Jerome, *Letter to Laeta on the Education of Her Daughter*: “Let the worshipers of Isis and Cybele do this: with gluttonous abstinence they devour birds from the Phasis and steaming turtledoves, lest, of course, they contaminate the gifts of Ceres.” They called this abstinence—and, as Arnobius says, *temperatus*—*castus*. St. Jerome, book II, *Against Jovinian*: “Their abstinence from foods pleases them, as though the superstition of the Gentiles did not observe the *castus* of the Mother of the Gods and of Isis.” The text had incorrectly read *cessum*. This same word must be restored later in the same book: “Just as the imitation practiced by the devil’s virgins does not prejudice true virginity, so neither do the *casta* of Isis and Cybele, and perpetual abstinence from certain foods, prejudice true fasts—especially since among them fasting from bread is compensated by stuffing themselves with meat.”

Tertullian, *On Fasting*: “But it is well that, when heaping abuse upon our dry fasts, you equate them with the *castus* of Isis and Cybele.” The *castus* therefore belonged properly to Isis and Cybele, but also to other gods; people were “in the *castus*” of these gods on certain appointed days—that is, they abstained from particular foods, or even from sexual intercourse, as did those who were “in the *castus* of Ceres.” Festus: “Private mourning is diminished when one is in the *castus* of Ceres.”

Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 23: “For the image of the Heliopolitan God is carried on a litter, as the images of the gods are carried in the procession of the Circus games; provincial nobles, their heads shaved and purified by the chastity of a long period, generally shoulder it.” Here he calls abstinence from sexual acts “chastity” (*ἁγνεία*). Apuleius uses *castimonia* in the plural in *Milesian Tale* XI: “For I had learned by careful inquiry that obedience to the religion was difficult, the abstinence imposed by its rules of chastity arduous enough, and that a life subject to many vicissitudes had to be guarded with cautious circumspection.” Here by “the abstinence imposed by rules of chastity” he means rigid abstinence from every pleasure of food, from animals, from wine, and at the same time from those other activities.

He explains it later in the same book: “Before all witnesses he plainly commanded that during those ten consecutive days I should restrain my pleasure in food, eat no animal, and drink no wine.” Thus *castus* comes from *careo*, “I lack,” and *cassum*, “empty”; hence *cassus*, and, by a change of letters (*μεταβολή*), *castus*. Festus: “Those who spend the entire month in religious observances for the sake of sacred rites were said to be pure for the month; that is, they are pure by abstaining from certain things.” The same author: “They were called ten-day and thirty-day ceremonies, because those about to approach the rites were required to abstain from certain things for ten or thirty consecutive days.” THE SAME AUTHOR.

Accordingly, both *castum*, neuter, and *castus*, masculine, were used, as in the present passage. See Nonius under *Castus*; Ausonius Popma on the *Fragments of Varro*, p. 303, Bipontine edition; Meursius, *Graeco-Barbarian Glossary*, under *Καστεῖα*; D. Petavius on Julian’s *Oration* V, p. 88, Leipzig edition; and especially Kühn on Aelian, *Various History* II, 33, pp. 152 following, Gronovius edition. The Greeks used the term similarly. Marinus, *Life of Proclus*, p. 45 (16, Boissonade edition): “He observed in purity the monthly rites of abstinence belonging to the Mother” (*Τὰς δὲ Μητρῳακὰς … καστείας ἑκάστου μηνὸς ἥγνευεν*). Here the learned Boissonade restored *καστείας* from the manuscripts in place of *ἁγιστείας*, which Fabricius’ edition has. See his note, pp. 105 following. ORELLI.]

## XVI

And yet how can you charge that account with falsehood, when the rites themselves—which you perform in their yearly cycles—bear witness both that you believe the account to be true and that you judge it to be of proven reliability?

For what is the meaning of that pine tree which you always introduce [Note: [Col. 1112B] “Omit,” manuscript] into the sanctuary of the Mother of the Gods on appointed days? [Col. 1112B] Is it not the likeness of that tree beneath which the frenzied and unfortunate young man laid violent hands upon himself, and which the mother of the gods consecrated as a consolation for her wound?

What is the meaning of the fleeces of wool with which you bind and envelop the tree’s trunk? Are they not a repetition of that wool with which Ia covered him as he failed, believing that she could impart some warmth to his cooling limbs? [Col. 1113A]

What is the meaning of the tree’s branches, adorned and wreathed with crowns of violets? Do they not indicate how the Mother adorned the pine with the first flowers, as the token and testimony of her pitiable misfortune?

What is the meaning of the Galli striking their palms against their breasts with hair disheveled? Do they not call to mind those acts of mourning with which the turret-crowned Mother, together with Acdestis, attended the boy with tearful wailing?

What is the meaning of abstention from the sustenance of bread, to which practice you have given the name *Castus*? Is it not an imitation of that time when the divine power, in the violence of her grief, abstained from the grain of Ceres? [Col. 1114A]

[Note: [Col. 1114C]

### XVII.—Why, in the manner of mourners, do they beat both their breasts and arms?

Above: “Joining her lamentations with those of Acdestis, she beats and wounds her breast around the strength of the felled tree.” The matter of this mournful beating of breast and arms is clear. Hence Artemidorus, book I, chapter 43, writes that women in mourning strike and disfigure their breasts: “for in mourning they themselves also mutilate their breasts” (*αὐταὶ γὰρ ἐν πένθει καὶ τοὺς μαζοὺς λωβῶνται*).

All these things, however, were interpreted allegorically: the Mother of the Gods signified the earth, while the Galli lacerated their arms and removed their male organs on account of [Col. 1114D] plowing and harvest. For this is what those acts signified. Tertullian observes this in *Against Marcion*, book I, chapter 13, in an obscure passage which the interpreters understand in no way:

“Common superstition too, shared by ordinary idolatry, when it is ashamed of the names and fables of ancient dead persons embodied in its images, takes refuge in an interpretation based upon natural things and conceals its disgrace beneath ingenuity. It represents Jupiter as a fiery substance and his Juno as air, in accordance with the sound of the Greek words; likewise Vesta as fire, the Camenae as waters, and the Great Mother as earth—reaped in her reproductive parts, plowed in her arms, and watered by washings.”

He adds “watered by washings” because the Mother of the Gods was washed in the Almo on a solemn day. HERALDUS.—Julian likewise explains these rites allegorically in *Oration* V. Add Sainte-Croix, *On the Mysteries*, chapter 4, p. 77 of Lenz’s translation. C. Barth collected a mass of examples of the custom of beating the arms in his notes on Statius, *Thebaid* VI, verse 133, vol. III, p. 400. ORELLI.

[Col. 1115B] What is the meaning of the crowns? Of the violets? Why did they wrap coverings of soft wool around it? I did not hesitate to admit into the text this excellent emendation of J. F. Gronovius in his *Disquisition on Statius’ Silvae*, book I, poem VI, chapter 20, p. 110. The old reading is: “What is the meaning of the crowns? Of the violets? Why the winged coverings of soft wool?” The Leiden editor reads: “and the coverings of soft wool.” Elmenhorst thinks the word “coverings” should be deleted as a gloss and interpretation of the word “winged.” ORELLI.

Which the vile Galli initiate. Thus the Leiden editor. [Col. 1115C] The manuscript has, very corruptly: “gape after.” Gelenius: “enter upon.” Fulvius Ursinus: “initiate themselves,” and in what follows, “complete.” Heraldus in *Corrections II*: “begin.” But in these writers *initiare* is not infrequently used for “to begin” or “commence,” and *initiari* for “to take a beginning.” Tertullian, *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 15: “You have heard of grief and fear. From these the other things took their beginning.” Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis* II, chapter 12: “Spring begins when the sun has entered the first part of Aries.” ORELLI.

Worn-out debauchees. See above, on book II, chapter 42, and book IV, chapter 35. ORELLI.]

XVII. Or if the things we say are not so, do you explain them; do you tell us: what business, concern, or care do those emasculated and effeminate men—whom we see taking part with you in the rites of that divinity—have there? And why, after the manner of mourners, do they beat both their breasts and their arms, and imitate the plight of those placed in a lamentable [Col. 1115A] lot? What are the garlands for? What the violets? What was intended by the coverings of soft wool? Why, finally, is the pine itself—which a little before was a most lifeless piece of wood nodding among the thickets—established in the dwelling of the Mother of the gods as though it were some present and most august divinity? For either this is the explanation which we find in your writings and commentaries, and it is evident that you are not performing divine ceremonies [Note: [Col. 1115B] The manuscript has “complaints” (*querimonias*).], but reenacting an image of mournful events; or, if there is some other explanation which the obscurity of the mystery has denied to us, that explanation too must necessarily share in the disgrace of some shameful act. For who could believe that there is anything honorable in a rite which is initiated by contemptible Galli and performed by effeminate debauchees?

[Note: [Col. 1115C]

XVIII.—Or those mysteries contain sacred things from which they take the name “initiations.” Cicero, *On the Laws* II, chapter 14: “For although your Athens seems to me to have produced and introduced into human life many excellent and divine things, it produced nothing better than those mysteries by which we were cultivated and softened into humanity from a savage and brutish way of life. And as they are called ‘initiations’ (*initia*), so in very truth we have learned from them the beginnings (*principia*) of life.” HERALDUS.—Livy, book XXXIX, chapter 8, on the Bacchanalia: [Col. 1115D] “There were initiatory rites which at first were transmitted to a few; afterward they began to be spread among men and women.” In Greek they were called *teletai* (τελεταί), “initiations.” ORELLI.

“And which are transmitted not indiscriminately to all, but under the pledged silence of a few.” Thus the Leiden editor; the manuscript has: “but to have transmitted them under the pledged silence of a few.” Gelenius printed: “are transmitted.” Others: “transmit.” The scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Frogs*, and Suidas following him: “Mysteries (*mystēria*), from the fact that those who hear them close (*myein*) their mouths and explain these things to no one.” HERALDUS and ORELLI.

“Prevents us from treating them all bodily.” Here *corporaliter* means the same as “member by member,” “part by part,” *en détail*. No other examples of this meaning occur to me. ORELLI.

“Fauna Fatua, therefore, who is called the Good Goddess.” Thus Ursinus printed it. But in the first edition and the royal manuscript the reading was: “Foul Fatua, therefore” (*Foedam igitur Fatuam*). Nor ought this reading to have been changed rashly and without manuscript authority. For perhaps, contrary to expectation (*para prosdokian*, παρὰ προσδοκίαν), he calls Fatua “foul” rather than “Fauna,” because of the foul acts which he presently censures. [Col. 1116B] HERALDUS.—For my part, I agree entirely with Heraldus. For above, book I, chapter 28, we read: “Those who revere the Fatuas, the guardian spirits of cities, the Pausi, and the Bellonae”; there in the notes we cited the classic passage of Lactantius on the Good Goddess, *Institutes*, book I, chapter 22. ORELLI.

“Had drunk a jar full of unmixed wine.” See N. Heinsius, *Adversaria*, book IV, chapter 9, p. 624. ORELLI.

“Sextus Clodius states in the sixth book of his work *On the Gods*, written in Greek.” Fulvius Ursinus printed: “in the sixth book *On the Gods of the Greeks*,” incorrectly. For Fatua was a goddess not of the Greeks but of the ancient Latins, [Col. 1116C] and Lactantius, at the passage cited, expressly says that Sextus Clodius’ book *On the Gods* was written in Greek. Bosius and Graevius, on Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, book IV, letter XV, p. 412, maintain that this Sextus Clodius is the same person as the rhetorician of the same name and surname, a Sicilian and a teacher of both Latin and Greek eloquence, whose life Suetonius describes in *On Famous Rhetoricians*, chapter 1. Compare Burmann on Suetonius, vol. 2, p. 183; Bünemann on Lactantius at the passage cited, p. 152; and G. J. Vossius, *On the Greek Historians*, book IV, part III, p. 511. Stewechius thinks that Cloatius Verus is meant; quite a few fragments from his books on sacred rites occur in Pompeius Festus. On myrtle rods, see Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 7. ORELLI.

“When women perform a divine rite for her.” That is, offer sacrifices. See Savaro on Sidonius, book V, letter XVII, p. 365, who discusses this form of expression at length. ORELLI.

“A covered amphora of wine is set out.” Lactantius: “For that reason a wrapped amphora of wine is placed in her rites.” Plutarch writes in the *Roman Questions* that the wine brought into the rites of the Good Goddess was called “milk”; Macrobius writes that the vessel in which the wine was placed was called a “honey jar.” HERALDUS.

“As Butas writes in his *Aitia*.” Plutarch mentions this writer in *Romulus*, chapter 21: “A certain Butas recorded in elegiac verses the explanations of Roman customs.” HERALDUS, in the Addenda.—The manuscript and first edition have *Putas*, from which they produced “Plutarch,” because the same question is expounded in Plutarch’s *Roman Questions*. Incorrectly. The title of the work was undoubtedly *Aitia* (Αἴτια, “Causes”), such as were written among the Greeks by Plutarch, Butas, and Callimachus. ORELLI.

“The inseminating gods” (*deos conserenteis*). Salmasius, on Solinus, chapter II, p. 46, showed that this is how the passage should be read, as the Leiden edition has it. Those “inseminating” Lares, therefore, who impregnated Ocrisia at the hearth, were so called from “sowing” or “inseminating,” in precisely the sense in which Lucretius says, book IV, verse 1101:

> And in this lies the power of Venus: to sow the fields of womanhood.

[Col. 1117A] The old reading “assisting” (*Conferentes*) must therefore be eliminated, as must the much worse conjecture of Meursius and Stewechius, “the Consenting Gods” (*Consentes*). For those gods are wholly foreign to this passage. See above on book III, chapter 40. ORELLI.

“Flaccus.” Either the Granius Flaccus whom we discussed above on book III, chapter 31, must be understood, or, more probably, Verrius Flaccus, the celebrated grammarian who lived under Augustus and wrote, among other things, books on memorable matters cited by Aulus Gellius, book IV, chapter 5, and several times by Pliny the Elder. Pompeius Festus abridged this same writer’s books *On the Meaning of Words*. [Col. 1117B] See Suetonius, *On Illustrious Grammarians*, chapter 17, and G. J. Vossius, *On the Latin Historians*, book I, chapter 20. Compare the annotations on book I, chapter 59. ORELLI.

“Had buried themselves in the ash.” Thus Meursius and Salmasius. Others: “had buried themselves in ash.” ORELLI.

“A little pot of entrails.” Johann Friedrich Gronovius, on book XXV, chapter 16, thinks the reading should be “an entrail-pot” (*ollula extari*). An old glossary: “*Extar* . . . a pot in which entrails were cooked.” But Gronovius himself cites “a pot of gold” (*aula auri*) from Plautus. Why not likewise “a pot of entrails” (*olla extorum*)? ORELLI.

“When Tanaquil, skilled in Etruscan lore, moved it aside,” etc. Dionysius of Halicarnassus relates the same story more fully at the beginning of book IV of the *Roman Antiquities*:

> Another account of this same man—Servius Tullius—is preserved in the native records, elevating the circumstances surrounding him into the realm of myth. We found it in many Roman histories; it says that he was dear to gods and divine spirits, and runs approximately as follows. From the hearth of the kings, at which the Romans perform [Col. 1117C] various other sacred rites and consecrate the first portions taken from their meals, they say that a male sexual organ rose up above the fire. Ocrisia, who was bringing the customary sacrificial cakes to the fire, was the first to see it, and she immediately went and told the king and queen. Tarquinius, after hearing of it and subsequently seeing the prodigy himself, was filled with wonder. But Tanaquil, who was wise in other matters and no less skilled than any Etruscan in divination, told him that from the royal hearth a child greater than ordinary human nature was destined to be born from a woman who coupled with the apparition. When the other interpreters of prodigies declared the same thing, the king resolved that the woman to whom the prodigy had first appeared should have intercourse with it. The woman was then adorned in the customary bridal fashion and shut up alone in the room where the prodigy had been seen. One of the gods or spirits coupled with her and vanished after the union—either Hephaestus, as some suppose, or the household hero, that is, the family Lar. [Col. 1117D] She became pregnant and gave birth to Tullius at the proper time.

ELMENHORSTIUS.

“The gods raised themselves up” (*surrexisse se deos*) derives from *subrigo, -ere*, for which the ancients said *surgo* by syncope. Thus in the final verse of Plautus’ *Epidicus* some manuscripts read:

> Applaud and farewell; raise and lift your loins,

where the editions have “move your loins.” See Taubmann, p. 458, and Scioppius, *Suspect Readings*, book IV, letter XVII. ORELLI.

“Thereupon commanded the captive woman of Corniculum.” I have printed this following the correction of Meursius and Fulvius Ursinus, which Arntzenius also approves on Aurelius Victor, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 7, p. 79, as does Gesner in the *Thesaurus*, under “Inseminating Gods.” Ocrisia is called “the woman of Corniculum” by Ovid, *Fasti* VI, verse 627:

> For Vulcan was Tullius’ father; his mother Ocrisia,  
> Remarkable for beauty, came from Corniculum.

[Col. 1118A] She was so called from Corniculum, of course, a city captured by Tarquinius Priscus, according to Livy, book I, chapter 38. ORELLI.

“Ocrisia, a most prudent woman.” The name of Servius’ mother is written in various ways: Ocresia, Ocrisia, Oclisia. See Arntzenius on Victor at the passage cited, and Antonius Augustinus on Festus at the passage cited. Dionysius of Halicarnassus also attributes to her the praise of beauty and chastity at the beginning of book IV of the *Roman Antiquities*: “In Corniculum, a city of the Latin nation, a man of royal lineage lived with a woman named Ocrisia, the most beautiful and most virtuous of the women in Corniculum.” After her husband was killed in battle, Tarquinius Priscus carried her off, pregnant and captive, [Col. 1118B] to Rome. But when Tarquinius’ wife Tanaquil learned that she was pregnant, she exempted her from servitude and kept her in her home; and because she understood from the prodigy that kingship was portended for the boy, she persuaded her husband to accept him as a son-in-law. Compare Livy, book I, chapter 36; Pliny, book XXVI, chapter 27; Valerius Maximus, book III, chapter 4; and Dionysius at the passage cited. Moreover, doubts were repeatedly entertained concerning Servius Tullius’ parentage, so much so that Seneca writes in his letters that this king was believed to have been born without a father. Some make his father Spurius Turnus of Corniculum (see Festus under *nothus*, “bastard”), others Vulcan; hence arose this shameful and absurd tale. STEWECHIUS and ORELLI.—For “most prudent” (*prudentissimam*), Meursius prefers “most modest” (*pudentissimam*). Not badly. ORELLI.

“Then the sacred and fervid divinities vomited forth the *vis* of Lucilius.” This ridiculous conception of the boy leaves the meaning obscure unless one understands that *vis* in Lucilius’ sense. Marcus Terentius Varro will serve us as interpreter; he says in book IV of *The Latin Language* (p. 19, Bipontine edition): [Col. 1118C] “The poets say that fiery seed fell from heaven into the sea and that Venus was born from the foam, thereby signifying the power produced by the conjunction of fire and moisture, from which power (*vis*) life (*Vita*) was named, as in that line of Lucilius: ‘Power is life, you see—the force that compels us to do everything.’” STEWECHIUS.—Compare Scaliger on Manilius, *Astronomica*, book II, p. 187, Heidelberg edition, published by Commelin; Ausonius Popma on the cited passage of Varro, in the notes, p. 43, who correctly explains *vis* as “generative seed” (*gonēn, thoron*, γονήν, θόρον); and, appositely, F. Dousa on the *Fragments of Lucilius*, p. 207, Havercamp edition, adduces a little Greek verse expressing the same thought:

> It is called life (*bios*) because it is procured by force (*bia*).

“Sacred divinities” is ironic, as above, book IV, chapter 26: “Hercules, the sacred god.” ORELLI.]

XVIII. The magnitude of the subject and the duty imposed by the defense do indeed demand that we pursue in the same manner the other forms of shameful conduct [Col. 1115B]—whether those disclosed [Col. 1116A] by the histories of antiquity, or those contained in the sacred mysteries that are called initiations and are transmitted not indiscriminately to all, but under the pledged silence of a few. Yet the countless rites of your cults, and the ugliness attached to each one, prevent us from treating them all member by member [Note: [Col. 1115B] Fulvius reads “individually”]. Indeed, to express the truth [Note: [Col. 1116B] The manuscript reads “more truly.” Not badly. Meursius], we ourselves deliberately and rationally turn away from certain of them [Note: [Col. 1116B] Thus Fulvius. Others read: “by which”], lest, while striving to explain everything, we be polluted by the very defilements involved in their exposition.

Let us therefore pass over Fauna Fatua, who is called the Good Goddess. Sextus Clodius, in the sixth book of his work *On the Gods*, written in Greek, states that she was beaten with myrtle rods because, without her husband’s knowledge, she had drunk a jar full of unmixed wine. He states that a sign of this is still displayed: when women perform a divine rite for her, a covered amphora of wine is set out, and it is unlawful to bring in myrtle branches, as Butas writes in his *Aitia*. But let us likewise [Col. 1116B] pass over in silence and concealment the inseminating gods, whom, together with the others, [Col. 1117A] Flaccus writes were transformed into the likeness of a human penis and buried themselves in the ash which had formed beneath a little pot of entrails. When Tanaquil, skilled in Etruscan lore, moved it aside, the gods raised themselves up and grew rigid with divine sinews. Thereupon they commanded the captive woman of Corniculum to ascertain and recognize what they wanted of her. [Col. 1118A] Ocrisia, a most prudent woman, inserted the divine organs into her genital passage and performed certain movements. Then the sacred and fervid divinities ejaculated what Lucilius calls *vis*—generative power—and Servius, king of Rome, was born.

[Note: [Col. 1118C]

XIX.—“Let us also pass over the monstrous Bacchanalia.” Gelenius most correctly substituted “monstrous” (*immania*) for “empty” (*inania*). Moreover, this passage is again drawn from Clement [Col. 1118D] of Alexandria, *Protrepticus* (p. 11, Potter edition): “The Bacchants celebrate raving Dionysus in orgies, conducting their sacred frenzy with raw flesh, and, crowned with serpents, consummating their allotments of flesh from the slaughter while crying ‘Euan!’” C. Barthius treats these Bacchanalia at length on Statius, *Thebaid* II.74, vol. II, pp. 294–299; and M. A. Delrio, *Syntagma of Latin Tragedy*, part III, p. 324 ff. ORELLI.

“Which have the Greek name Omophagia.” C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XI, chapter 15, thinks the reading should be *Ophiophagia*, “snake-eatings,” because the Bacchants supposedly sometimes tore serpents apart with their teeth without suffering injury. He supports this by the authority of Prudentius, in whose first book *Against Symmachus*, verse 130, we read:

> With their mouths they tear apart green water-snakes,  
> Those who wish to appease Bromius.

But Ch. G. Schwarz very correctly defends the received reading in his *Academic Essays*, chapter 3, [Col. 1119A] *On an Ancient Gem Depicting a Sacrifice to Bacchus*, p. 82, Harles edition. For Arnobius and Clement could rightly have called “Omophagia,” or “Raw-Eatings,” those rites in which the Bacchants customarily tore apart raw flesh and the entrails of calves, cows, bulls, and especially goats—a fact clear even from Euripides’ *Bacchae*, act III. [Col. 1119B] In the same sense Homer, *Iliad* XXII.592, calls wolves *ōmophagoi* (ὠμοφάγοι), “eaters of raw flesh,” because they tear apart and devour the raw flesh of other animals. And in Hesychius we read: “Raw-flesh banquets . . . those who divide up and eat raw meat.” These are the words of the most learned Schwarz. Compare Gisbert Cuper, *Harpocrates*, p. 60. ORELLI.

“With soundness of mind set apart.” *Sequestrata* means separated, divided, removed. Later writers used this word, derived from *sequester*, a term very familiar to the jurists; for example Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, book II, prose V: “But if they are beautiful by nature, what concern is that of yours? For these things would have pleased in themselves even if separated from your possessions.” There see Sitzmann, p. 79, Leiden edition with variorum notes, and C. Barthius, who discusses this word at length, on Statius, *Thebaid* II.425, vol. II, pp. 499 ff. ORELLI.

“With snakes wound about you.” Demosthenes, *On the Crown*: “Squeezing the thick-cheeked snakes, lifting them above your head, and shouting ‘Euoi Saboi!’” HERALDUS.—Compare [Col. 1119C] Clement at the passage cited; Euripides’ *Bacchae*; Plutarch’s *Alexander*; Horace, book II, ode XIX, and his scholiast there; Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*; and Schwarz in the book cited. ELMENHORSTIUS and ORELLI.
