“With bloodied mouths you scatter the entrails of bleating goats.” Martial, book III, epigram 34:

> A goat guilty of harming the vine stood at your altars, Bacchus,  
> About to die, a victim welcome to your rites.

Servius on Virgil, *Georgics* II.380: “Victims are sacrificed to divinities either through similarity or through opposition. Through similarity, as a black animal to Pluto; through opposition, as a sow, which harms crops, to Ceres, and a he-goat, which harms vines, to Liber. Likewise a she-goat to Aesculapius, who is the god of health, although a goat is never without fever. . . . A he-goat was sacrificed to Liber everywhere because it ate the vines that were held in his honor. In anger Bacchus caused it to be killed and its hide removed to make a wineskin, into which he caused wine to be put as punishment for it.” Compare [Col. 1119D] Varro, *On Agriculture*, book I, chapter 2, and Ovid, *Fasti* I.357. Although the he-goat was Bacchus’ regular sacrificial victim, we nevertheless find that sheep and bulls were also sometimes sacrificed to him. SCHWARZ, *On an Ancient Gem Depicting a Sacrifice to Bacchus*, §8, *Academic Essays*, p. 79.—Thomas Gataker, *Posthumous Miscellanies*, chapter 43, *Works*, vol. I, p. 885, suspects that in the cited passage of Clement Arnobius read “allotments of kid flesh” (*kreonomias eriphōn*) in place of “allotments of flesh from the slaughter” (*kreonomias phonōn*). ORELLI.

“And also those hidden initiations of Cyprian Venus,” etc. These things too come from Clement, whose words we transcribed above on book IV, chapter 5. ORELLI.

“Those receiving them.” “To receive initiations” is a proper expression. Thus “to undertake initiations” in Spartianus’ *Hadrian*: “After this he sailed through Asia and the islands to Achaea, and undertook the Eleusinian rites after the example of Hercules and Philip.” Likewise, “to receive sacred rites” in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* XI: “Day by day my desire to receive the sacred rites grew more and more.” Arnobius below, chapter 26: “Finally, the very tokens which, when questioned at the reception of the rites, you give in reply: [Col. 1120A] ‘I fasted,’” etc. So too the Greek *mystēria paralambanein*, “to receive mysteries.” Suidas: “Those who receive the mysteries are called initiates.” HERALDUS.—Johann Wowerius therefore needlessly disturbed a perfectly sound passage in his note on Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 426, Gronovius edition, conjecturing: “in which they receive bronze coins.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1120B] “And in return receive phalli given as tokens of the propitious divinity.” Clement, *Protrepticus* (p. 13, Potter edition):

> The foam-born and Cyprus-born goddess, the beloved of Cinyras—I mean Aphrodite, “lover of the genitals,” because she sprang from genitals, those lustful, severed genitals of Uranus which, after their cutting, violated the sea-wave—Aphrodite thus becomes for you, in the initiations, a fitting fruit of lewd organs. As a token of this sea-born pleasure and its seed, a lump of salt and a phallus are given to those being initiated into the adulterous art. Those initiated contribute a coin to her, as lovers do to a courtesan.

A learned man whose name has escaped me discussed at greater length the display of phalli in the mysteries of Ceres, Bacchus, Venus, and so forth, in Wieland’s *Der Deutsche Merkur*, at the passage cited, year 1806. ORELLI.

“Let the Corybantian rites also be given over to oblivion,” etc. Clement treats these somewhat more fully (pp. 15 ff., Potter edition):

> If you also wish to behold the Corybantes’ orgies, these two, after killing their third brother, covered the dead man’s head with a purple cloth, crowned it, and buried it beneath the foothills [Col. 1120C] of Olympus, carrying it on a bronze shield. And these are the mysteries—to sum them up in a word: murders and burials. Their priests, whom those concerned with naming them call “Anactotelestae,” aggravate the calamity further by absolutely forbidding that celery be placed on the table; for they believe that celery sprang from the blood that flowed from the Corybantian victim.

CANTER.—Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, p. 426, Gronovius edition: “In the rites of the Corybantes, fratricide is worshiped. For one brother was killed by two others; and lest any evidence disclose the murder of their brother, he was consecrated by his fratricidal brothers beneath the roots of Mount Olympus. The foolish superstition of the Macedonians worships this same figure. He is Cabirus, to whom the Thessalonians once made supplication with bloody hands.” Compare Sainte-Croix, translated by Lenz, *On the Ancient Mysteries*, chapter 4, p. 69. ORELLI.

“Was slaughtered.” Others: “is slaughtered.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1120D] “Celery.” Greek *selinon* (σέλινον); German *Milchpetersilie*. Concerning this plant—which was particularly used in crowns and garlands even among the Romans, who believed that something sacred and mysterious inhered in it, and which was called “the blood of the Corybantes”—see especially the celebrated Boettiger in the work cited, *Sabina, or Morning Scenes in the Dressing Room of a Wealthy Roman Woman*, and in the essay entitled “Further Observations on the Garden Art of the Greeks and Romans,” in Wieland’s *Neuer Deutscher Merkur*, March 1800, p. 100. ORELLI.

“But we also refrain from proclaiming those other Bacchanalia,” etc. [Col. 1120D] Clement speaks thus of these Bacchanalia in the *Protrepticus* (p. 15, Potter edition):

> For the mysteries of Dionysus are utterly inhuman. While he was still a child and the Curetes were dancing around him with armed movement, the Titans slipped in by stealth, deceived him with childish toys, and then tore him apart while he was still an infant, as Orpheus the Thracian, the poet of the rite, says:
>
> A cone and a spinning-top, and jointed dolls,  
> And beautiful golden apples from the clear-voiced Hesperides.
>
> Nor is it useless, for their condemnation, to set before you the useless tokens of this initiation: a knucklebone, a ball, a spinning-top, apples, a whirligig, a mirror, and a fleece. [Col. 1121B] Athena secretly removed the heart of Dionysus and was called Pallas from the “palpitating” of the heart. The Titans, who had torn him apart, set a cauldron upon a tripod, threw Dionysus’ limbs into it, and first boiled them down. Then, piercing them with little spits, they “held them over Hephaestus.” Zeus later appeared—if he was a god, perhaps after receiving his portion of the savor of the roasting flesh, the honor which your gods acknowledge as their allotted share—and maltreated the Titans with his thunderbolt. He entrusted Dionysus’ limbs to his son Apollo for burial. Apollo—for he did not disobey Zeus—carried the dismembered corpse to Parnassus and laid it to rest there.

CANTER.—Compare Elmenhorstius’ observation on book I, chapter 41. ORELLI.

“By the sweetness of the cooking-smell.” Others read: “of the odor.” Whether this came from a manuscript is uncertain to me; the sense is the same. ORELLI.

“Uninvited,” that is, not called, not asked, as Stewechius correctly explains. ORELLI.

[Col. 1121C] “The Thracian prophet recorded in his poems, as testimony to this event and evidence of the fate: knucklebones, a mirror, spinning-tops, rolling little wheels, smooth balls, and golden apples taken from the maiden Hesperides.” It is too late today to inquire what each of these symbols signified. On the mystical mirror of Bacchus—or of the sun—see the most learned Creuzer, essay I, *On the Causes of Bacchic Rites*, pp. 39 ff. For “spinning-tops, rolling little wheels,” N. Heinsius, *Adversaria*, book III, chapter 11, p. 477, suspects the reading should be “the rolling little wheels of a top,” thinking these words designate hoops, which Virgil and Tibullus called “tops.” But that the hoop differs from the top is shown at length by Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under *trochus*, and Arntzenius on Dionysius Cato, *Distichs*, p. 34 of the latest edition. For my part, I would venture to change nothing. Perhaps the rolling little wheels symbolize the wheels of punishment in Tartarus. And I agree entirely with the most learned Salmasius, who, in the appendix to Solinus, *On Medical Matter*, p. 3, interprets the “spinning-tops” in our author and the *kōnoi* and *strobiloi* in Orpheus and Clement [Col. 1121D] as pinecones, citing an old glossary: “*Kōnoi*: the pinecones and the thyrsi. Diogenianus.” Pinecones, that is, were symbols of the Bacchic initiations and were carried by the Bacchants at the tops of their thyrsi. For the Bacchic rites were akin to the rites of the Mother of the Gods, and the initiations of both were the same; hence also the pine, the tree under Cybele’s protection. See above on chapter 16. Apples are enumerated *par excellence* among the symbols of the Bacchic mysteries because the discovery of fruits and other tree-fruits was attributed to Bacchus, according to Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, book III, chapter 7, p. 82, Casaubon edition. Hence “the apples of Dionysus” are celebrated among the poets; for example, Theocritus, *Idylls* II, verse 120:

> Guarding apples in the folds of Dionysus’ robe,  
> And bearing on his head a white poplar, Heracles’ sacred branch.

The same Athenaeus, a little later in the same chapter: “Timachidas says in his fourth book that certain apples are called ‘apples of the Hesperides’ . . . and Pamphilus says that in Lacedaemon these are set before the gods, that they are fragrant but inedible, and that they are called apples of the Hesperides.” Here Dalechamp [Col. 1122B] understands our golden apples (*Goldäpfel*), which have a most delightful fragrance and were believed to possess exceptional power in love, since they enticed girls to intercourse and drew them toward love. See Joseph Scaliger and Pieter Burman the Younger on the *Latin Anthology*, book VII, epigram LXX, vol. II, pp. 544 ff. Boettiger also shows, in *Sabina*, p. 219, that apples in general were employed by the ancients as symbols of love; and N. Ignarra, on the *Homeric Hymn to Ceres*, verse 372, p. 501 of Ruhnken’s latest edition, shows that the ancients regularly played upon the allegorical notion of a garden and its fruit when they wished something somewhat obscene to be understood. Moreover, Sainte-Croix, *On the Ancient Mysteries*, chapter 5, [Col. 1122C] pp. 128 ff., shows at length that in these Bacchic mysteries the Theban son of Semele was confused with Iacchus, or the Egyptian Horus, whom Diodorus, *Library* I, chapter 25, reports to have been torn apart by the Titans but restored to life by his mother Isis. ORELLI.]

XIX. Let us also pass over the monstrous Bacchanalia, which have the Greek name *Omophagia* (“Raw-Eatings”). In these rites, with feigned frenzy and soundness of mind set aside, you wind snakes about yourselves and, in order to demonstrate that you are filled with the divine presence and majesty, tear apart with bloodied mouths the entrails of bleating goats. Let us also pass over those hidden initiations of Cyprian Venus, whose founder is said to have been King Cinyras. Those receiving them contribute fixed payments as to a prostitute [Col. 1120A] and in return receive phalli given as tokens of the propitious divinity.

Let the Corybantian rites also be given over to oblivion, in which that sacred mystery is transmitted: a brother was slaughtered by his brothers; celery sprang from the murdered man’s blood; and that vegetable was forbidden to be placed upon tables, lest an inexpiable offense be contracted from the dead man’s hands.

But we also refrain from proclaiming those other Bacchanalia [Col. 1121A] in which a secret matter, of which one must not speak, is disclosed and intimated to the initiated: how Liber, preoccupied with childish toys, was torn apart by the Titans; how he was cut limb from limb by them and thrown into little pots to be cooked; how Jupiter, enticed by the sweetness of the cooking-smell, flew uninvited to the meal; and how, when he learned what had happened, he overwhelmed the marauders with a thunderbolt and hurled them down into the lowest abodes of Tartarus. As testimony to this event and evidence of the fate, the Thracian prophet recorded in his poems: knucklebones, a mirror, spinning-tops, rolling little wheels, smooth balls, and [Col. 1122A] golden apples taken [Note: Sabaeus reads “assumed”] from the maiden Hesperides.

[Note: [Col. 1122C]

XX.—“It was our intention to pass over these things.” Thus the editions read with Salmasius, so that a new chapter begins with these words. Others joined them to the preceding passage and printed: “Knucklebones, a mirror . . . and golden apples taken from the Hesperides for maidens—it was our intention to pass over.” But the words “knucklebones,” etc., undoubtedly depend upon the words: “As testimony to this event and evidence of the fate, the Thracian prophet recorded in his poems,” as we see from the passage of Clement and the Orphic verses just cited. Salmasius therefore added “these things” most correctly. What must be understood is not the symbols but the mysteries themselves. ORELLI.

“Briefly” (*strictim*). That is, briefly, swiftly, and cursorily, as though merely grazing the outer skin and surface of the subject. Thus Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* II.1: “The book which you touched on briefly at Corcyra”; there see Manutius and Ernesti in the *Clavis*. Likewise Sallust, *Catiline*, chapter 4: “I resolved to write briefly”—for so some manuscripts read instead of “selectively”—“of the achievements of the Roman people, insofar as each seemed worthy of remembrance.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1122D] “To ride upon.” The same as “to insult” or “trample upon.” Below, book VII, chapter 30: “But in vain,” he says, “you ride upon us.” We likewise say in German, *auf einem herumreiten*. ORELLI.

“Once, they say, Diespiter, when he lusted after Ceres his mother,” etc. Thus Clement, *Protrepticus* (p. 13, Potter edition):

> The mysteries of Deo, Zeus’ amorous embraces with his mother Demeter, and the wrath—I no longer know what I should call Deo: his mother or his wife. It is on account of this wrath that she is said to have been called Brimo. There are Zeus’ supplications, the drinking of bile, the tearing out of hearts, and deeds of which one must not speak. The Phrygians consummate these rites for Attis, Cybele, and the Corybantes. They have spread the story that Zeus tore the paired testicles from a ram and cast them into the midst of Deo’s lap, thereby paying a false penalty for his violent coupling, as though he had actually castrated himself. I know that the symbols of this initiation, if added for good measure, will provoke laughter in you—if indeed you are still inclined to laugh after these exposures: “I ate from the drum; I drank from the cymbal; I carried the sacred vessel; I slipped beneath the bridal chamber.” Are these symbols not an outrage? Are these mysteries not a mockery? But what if I should add what remains? [Col. 1123B] Demeter becomes pregnant, and the Maiden is reared; and then this same Zeus who fathered her couples with Pherephatta, his own daughter, after coupling with her mother Deo, forgetful of his former pollution. Zeus is both father and ravisher of the Maiden; he couples with her after becoming a serpent—his identity was thus exposed.

And a little later: [Col. 1123C] “Pherephatta also becomes pregnant with a bull-shaped child. Indeed, an idolatrous poet says . . . ‘the bull’:

> The father of the serpent was a bull, and the serpent the father of the bull.

CANTER. The manuscript has *inicere Cererem* instead of “lusted after Ceres” (*in Cererem*), whence Joseph Scaliger suspects the reading “to have intercourse with Ceres” (*inire Cererem*). Meursius in the Appendix proposes *inigere Cererem*. ORELLI.

“For this goddess is held by the inhabitants of that region to be Jupiter’s mother.” Ceres, of course—as even her Greek name indicates—is the same as Earth, Vesta, and Cybele, and hence was also regarded as Jupiter’s mother. Proclus, *Platonic Theology* V.11, p. 267: “According to Orpheus, when she consorts with Cronus she is called Rhea; but when she brings forth Zeus and, together with Zeus, manifests both the universal and the particular orders of the gods, she is called Demeter.” Compare Ezechiel Spanheim, *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, dissertation 6, vol. I, p. 312. ORELLI.

“Violate his mother’s chastity.” Thus book IV, chapter 16: “You have been deprived of the sanctity of pure chastity.” See the notes there. ORELLI.

“An ambusher.” See above on book IV, chapter 23. ORELLI.

[Col. 1123D] “He conducts his incestuous business.” Thus Salmasius. Others: “the incestuous one conducts his business.” ORELLI.

“Foams.” The manuscript has “foams forth.” See on book I, chapter 17. ORELLI.

“From her unremitting anguish she afterward assumed the name Brimo.” William Canter, *New Readings*, book I, chapter VI, p. 519, most successfully corrected Arnobius from Clement in this way. This correction, approved by P. Leopardus, *Emendations*, book XVI, chapter 11, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, pp. 331 ff., as Heraldus attests, is also confirmed by the authority of the manuscript. Brimo (Βριμώ)—from *briman* (βριμᾶν), “to rage” or “roar”—is a name applied sometimes to Ceres, sometimes to Proserpina, and sometimes also to Hecate, by Apollonius Rhodius and Lycophron, verse 1176; there see Meursius. Compare C. Barthius on Statius’ *Silvae*, vol. I, p. 221. The earlier reading was: “From her unremitting anguish, first afterward,” etc., which has no meaning. Adrianus Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XI, chapter 16, restored the same word in Propertius, book II, elegy II, verse 11, reading:

[Col. 1124B]

> Brimo is said, beside the sacred waters of Lake Boebeis,  
> To have joined her maiden body to Mercury,

where the earlier reading was:

> Sais is said, beside the waters of Lake Boebeis,  
> First to have joined her maiden body to Mercury.

“Be called” is Meursius’ emendation. The manuscript has “was called.” [Col. 1124C] Sabaeus reads “is called,” incorrectly. ORELLI.]

XX. It was our intention to pass over these things, and also to pass by those mysteries into which Phrygia and that entire nation are initiated, had the name of Jupiter, inserted among them, not prevented us from passing briefly over the wrongs and disgraces attributed to him. This is not because it is pleasant for us to trample upon such foul mysteries, but so that it may become readily evident to you, again and again, what insults you heap upon those whose guardians, champions, and worshipers you profess yourselves to be.

Once, they say, Diespiter was inflamed with wicked lusts and forbidden [Col. 1123A] desires toward Ceres his mother—for this goddess is held by the inhabitants of that region to be Jupiter’s mother. Yet he did not dare to seek by open violence what he had conceived in his wanton appetite, and so devised ingenious stratagems by which he might violate the chastity of a mother who feared nothing of the kind. The god became a bull and, concealing the mind and audacity of an ambusher beneath the appearance of cattle, suddenly rushed in fury upon her while she was unsuspecting and unaware. He conducted his incestuous business and, once his deceit was exposed through his lust, flew away after being recognized and identified.

The mother blazed with fury and indignation; she foamed, panted, and seethed. Unable to restrain the roar and tempest of her anger, she afterward assumed the name Brimo from her unremitting anguish. Nothing else was dearer to her heart than to pursue her son’s audacity with every punishment in her power.

[Col. 1123B]

[Note: [Col. 1124C]

XXI.—“With very large testicles.” *Bene* in the sense of “very” (like the French *bien*) occurs even in the best authors—for example Cicero—and this is very well known. See Horatius Tursellinus, *On Latin Particles*, under this word. Nothing is more frequent in our author and in later writers. ORELLI.

“Upon seeing the manhood of her offspring.” Quintilian, book V, chapter 17: “Dealers in slaves pander to the beauty of boys by cutting away their manhood.” Pliny, book VII, chapter 4: “Soon afterward his beard and manhood developed.” Martial:

> He mourns the loss of the manhood taken from him.

So too Greek *andreia* (ἀνδρεῖα), as Artemidorus teaches, *Interpretation of Dreams*, book I, chapter 47. ELMENHORSTIUS and HERALDUS.

“And her care for the child already conceived is restored.” Fulvius Ursinus printed it thus, with the approval of Stewechius and subsequent editors. The earlier reading was: “And she conceives; her care for the child is restored.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1124D] “Libera.” The name of Proserpina among the ancient Latins. See Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book II, chapter 23, and the commentators on Livy III.55. ORELLI.

“Ram-like Jupiter.” Compare “ram’s head” in Plautus’ *Poenulus*. See Colvius and Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book VII, p. 491. ORELLI.

“He returns to his former acts.” “Acts,” namely those of incest and adultery, which were mentioned a little before. We can therefore readily dispense with the conjecture of Meursius and Stewechius, who rewrite the phrase: “He returns to his former wiles.” ORELLI.

“Under a savage guise.” I would write: “And under a savage gaze,” or, if preferred: “under the guise of a savage beast.” For the preceding words are before my eyes: “he changes into the terrifying form of a serpent.” He calls a wild, grim, and forbidding appearance an *obtutus*, “gaze,” from *obtuendo*. Apuleius speaks no differently in book I of the *Florida*, concerning Socrates: “He thought,” he says, “that men should be considered not by the sight of the eyes but by the keenness of the mind and the gaze of the soul.” STEWECHIUS.—Nothing should be changed. *Obtentus* is a pretext or guise, where something false is presented in place of the truth. ORELLI.

[Col. 1125B] “Deceit.” See above on book IV, chapter 35. ORELLI.

“Then we shall cite that well-known Tarentine senarius: ‘A bull,’” etc. This was an iambic senarius by some Tarentine poet. For Clement of Alexandria too makes its author “a certain idolatrous poet”; no one should therefore suppose that the verse circulated anonymously. Hence I would not substitute “commonplace,” as some—including Meursius—do, for “Tarentine.” The author of this verse may perhaps have been Rhinthon of Tarentum, the very celebrated comic poet, “founder of the so-called hilarotragedy,” as Suidas says. HERALDUS.—Meursius and Elmenhorstius, that is, think the reading should be: “One will require an authority for so great”—that is, so atrocious—“an event; then we shall cite that commonplace verse,” etc. ORELLI.

“A bull begot a serpent, and a serpent a bull.” Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*, chapter 27 (p. 453, Gronovius edition): “There follows yet another formula, which is transmitted as something momentous to the credulous ears of wretched men: ‘A bull is the father of a serpent, and a serpent of a bull.’” [Col. 1125C] ELMENHORSTIUS.—Compare the passage of Clement cited on the preceding chapter, and Sainte-Croix, *On the Ancient Mysteries*, section VI, chapter 4, p. 286, Lenz’s translation. ORELLI.

“Which are called Sebadian.” Thus the manuscript. Others read “Sabazian.” The Leiden edition has “Sabadian.” But Julius Firmicus too, *On the Error of Profane Religions* (p. 426, Gronovius edition), when speaking of the same matter, writes “Sebazius.” His words are: “Those who worship Sebazius Jupiter, when they are initiated, draw a snake through the fold of their garment.” There see Johann Wowerius. “Sebadius” also occurs in Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I.18: “Likewise, we learn that in Thrace the Sun and Liber are held to be the same god; calling him Sebadius, they celebrate him with magnificent worship.” In Greek, *Sabazios* (Σαβάζιος). Clement, at the cited passage: “The token of the Sabazian mysteries for those being initiated is ‘the god through the fold’; this is a serpent drawn through the fold of the initiates’ garment, an exposure of Zeus’ incontinence.” For numerous examples showing that the Greek *z* was rendered by the Latins as *d*, see Valesius on Harpocration, p. 100; Salmasius on Julius Capitolinus’ *Antoninus Pius*, chapter 9, [Col. 1125D] *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, p. 269; Meursius, *Criticism of Arnobius*, book V, chapter 8; and the commentators on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VIII, p. 574. Thus the glosses have *trapedias*, “tables,” for *trapezas*; Isidore has *obridtum aurum* for *obryzum*, “refined gold”; *Ladi* for *Lazi*; and so forth. On the god Sabazius and his cult compare Selden, *On the Syrian Gods*, chapter 3; Sainte-Croix, *On the Ancient Mysteries*, at the passage cited; and the celebrated Ast on Theophrastus, *Characters* XXVII, p. 233. ORELLI.

“Is sent down.” Fulvius Ursinus prefers *demittitur*, “is lowered,” to *dimittitur*, “is sent away.” ORELLI.

“The consecrated.” These are the people whom he earlier called “the initiated”: “in which a secret matter, of which one must not speak, is disclosed and intimated to the initiated.” Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* XI: “Morning came, and when the solemn rites had been completed, I proceeded forth, consecrated with twelve robes.” And: “Those consecrated call this the Olympian robe.” Likewise *sacrari*, “to be consecrated,” means *teleisthai* (τελεῖσθαι), “to be initiated.” The old translator of Irenaeus, book I, chapter 18: “And they perform what is, as it were, a mystic rite for those being consecrated, accompanied by certain profane utterances.” Irenaeus’ words were: “And they perform a mystagogical rite for those being initiated, accompanied by certain invocations.” And a little later: [Col. 1126B] “These words are uttered by those who consecrate; the person being consecrated replies.” Irenaeus had written: “These words are spoken by those who initiate; the initiated person replies.” HERALDUS.]

Source/review notes: The supplied source itself ends mid-note and mid-quotation at Virgil, Georgics I.203; the draft faithfully preserves that inherited truncation.

### XXI

Jupiter, broken by fear, exerts himself, but cannot discover by what remedies he might soothe the feelings of the violated goddess. He pours out prayers and makes supplication; the ears of the grieving woman are closed. The entire order of the gods is brought forward, but no one’s authority is great enough to gain a hearing. At last her son, seeking ways to make satisfaction, devises the following remedy. He selects a noble ram [Col. 1124A] with very large testicles, cuts these off himself [Note: [Col. 1123B] Sabaeus reads *ipsi*], and strips them of their woolly covering. Approaching his mother in grief and submission, as though he himself had condemned himself by his own sentence, he throws them into her lap and casts them before her. At the sight of her child’s virility she assumes a gentler disposition and is recalled to concern for the offspring she has conceived. After the tenth month she gives birth to a daughter of splendid bodily form, whom a later generation of mortals called sometimes Libera and sometimes Proserpina.

When the ram-like Jupiter saw that she was very vigorous, blooming, and full of richer vitality, he forgot what evil and crime, and how much recklessness, he had attempted a little before, and returned to his former conduct. Because it appeared sufficiently abominable for a father to unite bodily with his daughter in marital intercourse, he changed into the terrible [Col. 1124B] form of a dragon, bound the terrified maiden in his enormous coils, and beneath that savage guise sported and dallied with her in the tenderest embraces. Thus she too was impregnated by the seed of most mighty [Note: [Col. 1123B] Fulvius wrongly reads *summi*, “highest”] Jupiter, though not with the same result as her mother: the mother produced a daughter fashioned in her own lineaments, whereas from the maiden’s delivery there issued the form of a bull [Note: [Col. 1124B] Fulvius reads *species est*, “the form is”], [Col. 1125A] a memorial of Jupiter’s deceit.

Someone will demand an authority for this account. We shall then cite that Tarentine author and the familiar senarius which antiquity recites in the words:

> The bull begot a dragon, and the dragon a bull.

Finally, the sacred ceremonies themselves and the rites of initiation, which are called the *Sebadia*, will be able to bear witness to the truth: in these a golden snake is let down into the bosom of the initiated and is drawn out again from their lower and nether parts.

> **Note: [Col. 1126B]**
>
> **XXII.—“And how great the disgraces.”** Fulvius Ursinus edited *quantumque ignominiae*, “and how much disgrace.” But nothing should be changed. *Quantas* is used for *quot*, “how many,” as shortly before: “and how many springs of shameful deeds and enormities are contained in the depraved parts,” where I myself suspect that for *pravis*, “depraved,” one should read *parvis*, “small,” that is, in the smallest parts of those mysteries: *In den kleinsten Theilen derselben*—“in their smallest parts.” And above, chapter 12: “O Abdera, Abdera, how many opportunities you would give mortals for feeling envy,” where see the notes. ORELLI.
>
> **“The gods bear.”** Thus Meursius and the others who followed him. Previously *differant* was printed. ORELLI.
>
> **“There is no infamous kind of disgrace, no adultery.”** Stewechius suspects that one should read: “There is no kind of disgrace, of infamy, no adultery,” Heraldus approving this as closer to the Arnobian [Col. 1126C] style. ORELLI.
>
> **“Europa hastened to the designation ‘woman.’”** She became a woman, although she had been a maiden. Thus “woman” is distinguished from “maiden”; we employ this usage not only in our own language, but the Greeks also formerly employed it in theirs. Thus, in Theocritus (*Idyll* XXVII), that country girl, after being deflowered, says that she came as a maiden and will return home as a woman, *γυναῖκα*:
>
> > I came here a maiden, but I shall go home a woman.
>
> This distinction was properly and frequently observed by ordinary people and virtually sanctioned by everyday usage. Tertullian, *On the Veiling of Virgins*: “But since they employ the designation ‘woman’ in such a way that they do not think it applicable except to her alone who has experienced a man, we must prove that the proper meaning of that term pertains to the sex itself, not to the stage of the sex, so that virgins too are commonly included under it.” Arnobius below, chapter 24: “At one time, they say, when Proserpina, not yet a woman and still a maiden, was gathering purple flowers in the meadows of Sicily.” Optatus of Milevis, book II: “Returning from there, Urbanus of Formiae [Col. 1126D] and Felix of Idica found mothers whom they turned from women under vows of chastity into women in the sexual sense.” HERALDUS. Compare Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VII, p. 486. ORELLI.
>
> **Electra.** Electra was a nymph, the daughter of Oceanus and Tethys. Violated by Jupiter, she gave birth to Dardanus, according to Ovid (*Fasti* IV, verse 49), or, as Dionysius of Halicarnassus (*Antiquities*, book I, p. 49) believes, to Dardanus and Iasus. NOURRY, p. 595.—The daughter of Atlas, who bore Dardanus to Jupiter. Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, 135 ff.:
>
> > Dardanus, first father and founder of the city of Ilium,  
> > Born, as the Greeks relate, of Electra, daughter of Atlas,  
> > Came to the Teucrians; mighty Atlas begot Electra,  
> > Atlas who supports the heavenly spheres upon his shoulder.
>
> ORELLI.
>
> **Laodamia.** The daughter of Bellerophon, by whom Jupiter fathered Sarpedon, king of Lycia, as Homer sings in *Iliad* VI, verses 197–198:
>
> > With Laodamia Zeus the counsellor lay,  
> > And she bore godlike Sarpedon, helmeted in bronze.
>
> NOURRY, ibid.
>
> [Col. 1127B] **Catamitus.** See above, on book IV, chapter 26. ORELLI.
>
> **“In which you do not combine his name with associated lusts.”** This is the old reading, in place of which others give *consecratis*; Salmasius, in the Leiden edition, gives *inseratis*. It seems to me that, with the slightest alteration and transposition, one should read: *quod non ejus in nomen consociatis libidinibus congeratis*—“which you do not heap upon his name with associated lusts.” Thus shortly before: “There is no adultery which you do not heap upon his head, as upon some cheap and earthen figure.” ORELLI.
>
> **“So that it may appear that there is absolutely no cause that does not exist.”** Meursius thinks one should read: “that there is no cause whatsoever.” But we have shown above, on the final chapter of book I, that a double negative sometimes intensifies the negation after the Greek manner. ORELLI.
>
> [Col. 1127C] **“A crop of crimes.”** Thus Meursius corrected the text in *Criticus Arnobianus*, book V, chapter 8. “A crop of crimes,” that is, a field, as it were, from which a countless multitude of crimes sprouts. In the same sense Prudentius has “a crop of wicked deeds” in the *Hamartigenia*, and Plautus “a crop of goads” in *Aulularia*, act I, scene 1, verse 6, where see Taubmann, p. 142. Previously “a seat of crimes” was read. ORELLI.
>
> **“Into whom all obscenities might flow from the polluting streams of the stage.”** The editor of the Leiden edition changed this to “from the polluting streams of bilge-water.” Wrongly; for Arnobius is referring to what he said above, book IV, chapter 35, about Jupiter and his adulteries being represented in the theatres by actors through mimetic dance. ORELLI.
>
> **“But the injury caused by ill-treatment would be tolerable.”** The first edition of Arnobius has *malectionis*; from this Gelenius printed *maleactionis*. Since the manuscripts support it, I think it should be retained, and those—for example, Theodor Canter—who substitute the word *maledictionis*, “cursing,” should not be followed. For *maledictio*, *maleactio*, and *maletractio* are equally Latin and are equally employed by our author. [Col. 1127D] STEWECHIUS.—Fulvius Ursinus edited *maletractationis*. ORELLI.
>
> **“He neighed after his daughter.”** See above, on book IV, chapter 14. ORELLI.

### XXII

I do not think it necessary here to proceed in a lengthy discourse through every individual part and demonstrate how many springs of shameful deeds and enormities are contained in the depraved parts. For what mortal possessing even a slight sense of humanity does not perceive for himself [Col. 1126A] what all these things are like, how criminal, how foul, and how great the disgraces the gods bear from the sacred ceremonies of the mysteries themselves and from the shameful origins of those rites?

“Jupiter,” they say, “burned with passion for Ceres.” What so great a wrong, I ask, has this Jupiter of yours, whoever he is, done to you, that there is no infamous kind of disgrace, no adultery, which you do not heap upon his head, as upon some cheap and earthen figure? Leda betrayed the law of marriage: Jupiter is said to have caused her guilt. Danaë could not preserve her virginity: the theft is related as Jupiter’s. Europa hastened to the designation “woman”: the same Jupiter is vaunted as the conqueror of her chastity. Alcmena, Electra, Latona, Laodamia, a thousand other maidens, [Col. 1127A] and a thousand mothers, and together with them the boy Catamitus, were stripped of the honor of their chastity. Everywhere the story is the same—Jupiter—and there is no kind of obscenity in which you do not combine his name with associated lusts. Thus that pitiable being seems to have been born for absolutely no other reason than to be a crop of crimes, material for curses, and a kind of exposed place into which all obscenities might flow from the polluting streams of the stage.

Yet if you were to say that he had intercourse with women who were strangers to him, it would indeed be an impious matter, but the injury caused by ill-treatment would be tolerable. Did he also neigh, with the desires of a maddened heart, after his mother and even after his daughter? Could neither the sacredness and reverence owed to his mother, nor even horror at the child begotten from himself, draw him away from the image of so foul a thought?

> **[Col. 1127B] Note: [Col. 1127D]**
>
> **XXIII.—“That father of the gods, Jupiter, the eternal power over things and human beings.”** He derives this from Virgil, in whose *Aeneid*, book X, verse 18, Venus says:
>
> > O father, O eternal power of men and gods!
>
> Here *potestas*, “power,” stands for *potens*, “the powerful one,” the abstract for the concrete. Arnobius, however, seems to have read—as one still reads in certain manuscripts and editions:
>
> > O father, O eternal power of men and things!
>
> See the very learned Heyne in the *Variant Readings*. HERALDUS and ORELLI.
>
> **“Chewing pale grasses.”** Virgil, *Eclogue* VI, 54:
>
> > Beneath a dark holm-oak he chews pale grasses.
>
> HERALDUS.
>
> **“His hocks and ankles smeared with soft dung.”** This is an outstanding correction by Fulvius Ursinus. The first edition reads, without sense, “his hock, smeared with a very soft ankle,” for which Gelenius gave “smeared with the softest ankles.” Stewechius read “his ankles smeared with the softest dung.” The *suffragines* are the bends of the legs in animals, “whose legs bend backward,” as Aristotle says. See Pliny, *Natural History* XI, chapter 45. ORELLI.
>
> **“Then probing the hidden parts with a heated knife.”** Thus Gelenius. The Roman manuscript reads *ferventi nullas*. Neither reading pleases me; but what ought to be substituted I leave for more learned men to decide. CANTER.—Stewechius approves Gelenius’s conjecture and explains *ferventi smila* as a *smila*—that is, a knife or graving tool, “a sharp-cutting blade”—heated, as it were, by excessive sharpening ([Col. 1128C] *samiare* was the old word for “to sharpen”). The Latins called it a *sicila*. See Casaubon on Suetonius, *Vitellius*, chapter 2, p. 235, vol. III, Wolf’s edition. Salmasius, in the Leiden edition, more boldly printed “probing those hidden parts,” deleting *ferventi*. I prefer Heraldus’s correction in his *Second Notes*, recasting it as “probing the ram’s hidden parts.” Perhaps Arnobius wrote “probing the ram-like hidden parts,” or “probing the ram’s farthest parts,” that is, its innermost and most deeply concealed parts, beyond which nothing could be found. But let more learned men decide. ORELLI.
>
> **“And, after dismissing witnesses, tearing away the little membranes wrapped around the offspring.”** Meursius thinks one should read: “and, after dismissing the ram’s … around the offspring,” which accords with Arnobius’s fondness for transposing words in this fashion. Nevertheless, I would rather retain the common reading and understand *prolibus* in the dative. What *proles* means we have explained above, on chapter VI of this book. For *diripientem*, Stewechius, after his custom [Col. 1128D] of hunting for extremely ancient and obsolete words, suspects that one should read *diribentem*, which the ancients used for “dividing.” From this came *diribitorium*, that part of a house in which the boys were separated from the rest of the household, or else the place in which soldiers’ pay was distributed. See Stewechius. ORELLI.
>
> **“Like certain fillets.”** That is, coverings used by suppliants. The Greeks called them *stemmata* (στέμματα), as, for example, Homer in the famous verse of *Iliad* I:
>
> > Holding in his hands the fillets of far-shooting Apollo.
>
> Ovid, the finest interpreter of Homer, writes in the *Art of Love*:
>
> > He had heard that Chryses, bearing laurel and ribbons in his hand,  
> > Had not prevailed on behalf of his daughter.
>
> For the laurel or olive branch and the ribbons—or the ribboned laurel—formed a suppliant’s covering. Hence Aeschylus in the *Suppliants* speaks of “white-garlanded suppliant branches.” Here, therefore, the *infulae* in Arnobius are *stemmata*, coverings. The glosses give: “*infulae* … *stemmata*.” HERALDUS.
>
> **“Presenting.”** That is, holding out. For suppliants stretched out their coverings toward the knees of those whom they entreated; [Col. 1129B] indeed, they sometimes laid them down. Euripides, *Iphigenia at Aulis*, 1216:
>
> > I fasten my suppliant branches to your knees.
>
> They even covered the very altars to which they had fled, so as to render them still more sacred and inviolable in this manner. The same poet in the *Children of Heracles*:
>
> > These children of Heracles sit here as suppliants,  
> > Having wreathed the altar, as you see, my lord.
>
> HERALDUS.
>
> **“Or can any nation be found endowed with such irreligious beliefs?”** [Col. 1129C] Stewechius deletes *tam*, “such,” though there are indeed many examples of its omission in writers of that age. Nevertheless, I would not wish to change anything. ORELLI.
>
> **“Indeed, he would reduce all things to the form of their ancient unity.”** That is, uniformity, as they barbarously call it, in which no parts of differing shapes could be distinguished. In this passage Arnobius appears to have had in mind that famous passage of Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, verse 6, where Chaos is described in the same manner:
>
> > Throughout the whole world Nature had but a single face,  
> > Which men called Chaos.
>
> ORELLI.

### XXIII

I should therefore like to see that father of the gods, [Col. 1128A] Jupiter, the eternal power over things and human beings, adorned with bovine horns, twitching shaggy ears, chewing [Note: [Col. 1127B] Thus Sabaeus. The manuscript reads *rumigantem*] pale grasses with feet contracted into hoofs, and, on his hindquarters, his tail, hocks, and ankles smeared with soft dung, and his body befouled by intestinal discharge.

I should like, I say—for it must be said repeatedly—to see him who whirls the stars and who terrifies and casts down pallid nations with the thunder’s crash pursuing flocks of rams, inspecting rams’ testicles, and seizing them with that censorial and divine hand with which he is accustomed to brandish flashing fires and rage with thunderbolts. Then I should like to see him probing the hidden parts with a heated knife, dismissing witnesses and tearing away the little membranes wrapped around the offspring, and presenting them like certain fillets intended to elicit pity to his mother, who was still seething; cast down, pale, wounded, feigning [Col. 1128B] the torments of pain and, to lend credence to the deed, [Col. 1129A] stained with a ram’s blood and covering the false appearance of a wound with woollen bandages and strips of linen.

Can such a thing be heard and read beneath this vault of heaven, while those who discuss these matters wish themselves to be regarded as pious, holy, and guardians of religion? Is there any sacrilege greater than this? Or can any nation be found endowed with such irreligious beliefs [Note: [Col. 1129B] A manuscript reads *praedicata*, “proclaimed”] as one which believes or accepts such things, or discloses them within the innermost mysteries of its sacred rites?

If that Jupiter, whoever he is, perceived that he existed, or if he were affected by any awareness of the injury done to him, would this not be a matter worthy of making him, in wrath and fury, withdraw the earth from beneath our steps, extinguish the lights of the sun and moon, and indeed reduce all things to the form of their ancient unity?

> **Note: [Col. 1129C]**
>
> **XXIV.—“But these rites,” he says, “do not belong to our commonwealth.”** Heraldus most correctly restored *inquit*, “he says,” from the first edition in place of *inquiunt*, “they say,” which Fulvius Ursinus conjectured. We have already commented several times above on this form of expression. ORELLI.
>
> **The Thesmophoria.** Concerning these rites, which women alone were permitted to celebrate, men being excluded, see Meursius, *Graecia Feriata*, and Sainte-Croix, *Über die alten Mysterien*, [Col. 1129D] section VI, chapter I, pp. 236 ff. Moreover, here and in what follows Arnobius confuses the Thesmophoria with the Eleusinian rites. For everything he reports in the following chapters about the origin and entire apparatus of those mysteries pertains to the Eleusinian religion, as Salmasius demonstrates at length on Solinus, p. 527. Clement, by contrast, whom Arnobius has copied almost word for word throughout this passage, correctly distinguishes “the Eleusinian rites from the Thesmophoria,” as we shall presently see. ORELLI.
>
> **“Sacred vigils and solemn all-night observances were consecrated.”** Thus Gelenius corrected the monstrous reading of the first edition, *et phanniciis migrave*, which has no sense. Nor is this correction foreign to Arnobius’s style of expressing one and the same thing with several words. For *privilegium* [sic], “a privilege,” and *pannychismus*, “an all-night observance,” are one and the same. The glosses give: “vigil—*pannychismos*, an all-night period of wakefulness.” Thus “solemn all-night observances” would mean sacrosanct all-night rites, *die heiligen, mystischen Nächte*—“the holy, mystical nights.” See Sainte-Croix, the passage cited, section V, chapter IV, p. 203. Fulvius Ursinus [Col. 1130B] edited: “Sacred vigils and all-night rites were consecrated. Is it burdensome? Do you wish…?” That is: “Unless it is burdensome, do you wish…?” Heraldus conjectures that one should read: “Sacred vigils were consecrated, and all-night observances migrated,” that is, they departed from the Attic people. But if we read thus, the resulting sense is entirely foreign to what Arnobius intended to say—namely, that other nations borrowed these nocturnal rites from the Attic people. Moreover, “the all-night observances migrated” would mean that they went into exile, were abolished among the Attic people, and were transferred elsewhere; but this conflicts with history. For it is well known that the Eleusinian rites endured down to the time of Theodosius. [Col. 1130C]
>
> The extremely corrupt manuscript reading *phannyciis migrare* has raised in my mind the question whether Arnobius may perhaps have written: “through which those holy vigils and phallic spectacles were consecrated among the Attic people,” that is, the shameful exhibition of phalluses. *Miraculum*, “spectacle,” occurs in this sense in the following chapter: “she resolved to cheer her with spectacles of mockery,” as we shall presently see. The public exhibition of phalluses in the Eleusinian rites is very well known. See Sainte-Croix, the passage cited, p. 194 of Lenz’s translation. ORELLI.
>
> **“Athens … flourishing in the arts and pursuits of civilization.”** Propertius, book II, elegy VI:
>
> > But let it be worth so much to me to know learned Athens.
>
> Book III, elegy XXI:
>
> > I am compelled to undertake the long journey to learned Athens.
>
> Valerius Maximus, book IV, chapter 3: “Although Athens may glory in her learning.” ELMENHORST. Savaro, on Sidonius, book V, letter 1, p. 318, illustrates the expressions “to flourish in learning, studies, and eloquence” with numerous examples.
>
> [Col. 1130D] Here Arnobius also had before his eyes the words of Clement:
>
> > And what wonder is it if the Tyrrhenians, who are barbarians, are initiated by such shameful experiences, when among the Athenians and throughout the rest of Greece—the shame-filled mythology concerning Deo makes me blush to tell it …
>
> ORELLI.
>
> **“As others repeatedly say.”** Thus Stewechius gives the manuscript reading, most correctly. Others read “as others say.” ORELLI.
>
> **“At one time,” they say, “when in the meadows of Sicily,” etc.** See Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions* (pp. 419 ff., Gronovius’s edition); Apollodorus, *Library*, book I; Hyginus, fable 146; Diodorus Siculus, *Library*, book I, p. 287 (Rhodomann); Ovid, *Fasti* IV, 420–620, a most elegant passage. ELMENHORST.
>
> **“Not yet a woman … and still a maiden.”** From the manuscript Stewechius restored *virago*, “a manlike or heroic woman.” Not badly. Thus below, chapter 37: “In the grove of Henna,” he says, “Proserpina once used to gather flowers.” And in the same chapter: “the *virago* who had long been occupied in gathering flowers.” *Virago* properly means a strong woman who resembles a man and [Col. 1131A] performs manly deeds, in Greek *antianeira* (ἀντιάνειρα), a distinctive epithet of Minerva and Diana. See Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, 468. But Arnobius also applies it to Proserpina, [Col. 1131B] who is called by the ancients “the Maiden,” *Korē* (κόρη), par excellence. Meursius prefers: “but still a maiden.” ORELLI.
>
> **“Through a cavern of profound depth.”** Lactantius similarly writes in *Institutes* VI, chapter 4: “So that no one can perceive the deception before he has been hurled down and fallen into a profound depth.” L. Bünemann illustrates this expression with numerous examples, pp. 713–714. Others read: “through a cave of profound depth.” ORELLI.
>
> **“Recesses.”** See on book I, chapter 50. ORELLI.
>
> **“She takes up two torches kindled by the flames of Etna.”** Thus Fulvius and Gelenius corrected the text. Below, chapter 35: “Why was fire taken from Etna, and why were torches kindled from it?” The first edition reads, without sense: “two torches weighed down by a burden of Etnaean flames.” HERALDUS. Compare Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V, 438. ORELLI.

### XXIV

“But these rites,” he says, “do not belong to our commonwealth.” [Col. 1129B] Who says this, or who makes this answer? A Roman, Gaul, Spaniard, African, German, or [Col. 1130A] Sicilian? And how does it help your case if these rites are not yours [Note: [Col. 1129B] Sabaeus reads *sint*, “are”], when those who perform them belong to your own peoples? Or what difference does it make whether you approve them or not, when the rites peculiar to you are found either to possess similar foulness or an even greater kind of obscenity?

Would you like us, then, to consider those divine mysteries which the Greeks call the Thesmophoria, through which those sacred vigils and solemn all-night observances were consecrated among the Attic people? Would you like us, I say, to examine their origins and causes, so that we may also prove that Athens herself, flourishing in the arts and pursuits of civilization, says things about the gods just as insulting as others continually say, and that under the guise of religion no lesser disgraces are publicized by the Athenians than those which you impute to other peoples?

“At one time,” they say, “when Proserpina, not yet a woman and still a maiden, was gathering purple flowers [Col. 1130B] in the meadows of Sicily, and while her eagerness to gather them drew her here and there indiscriminately through the flowering harvest, [Col. 1131A] the king of the dead leapt forth through a cavern of profound depth, carried off the abducted maiden with him, and was hidden once more in the recesses of the earth.

“When Ceres did not know that this had happened and could not conjecture where in the world her daughter was, she resolved to search for the lost girl throughout the entire world. She took up two torches kindled by the flames of Etna and, lighting the way before herself with them, proceeded to search through every region of the earth.”

> **Note: [Col. 1131B]**
>
> **XXV.—“In the wandering of this search she is carried even to the territory of Eleusis,” etc.** Clement (*Protrepticus*, p. 16, Potter’s edition):
>
> > For Deo, wandering in search of her daughter Korē, grows weary near Eleusis—this is a place in Attica [Col. 1131C]—and sits grieving beside a well. This is forbidden to the initiates even to this day, lest those who have completed the mysteries should appear to imitate her in her lamentation. At that time the earthborn inhabitants occupied Eleusis; their names were Baubo, Dysaules, and Triptolemus, and also Eumolpus and Eubuleus. Triptolemus was an oxherd, Eumolpus a shepherd, and Eubuleus a swineherd. From them the hierophantic families of the Eumolpidae and the Ceryces sprang and flourished at Athens.
>
> CANTER.
>
> **“The earthborn inhabitants who occupied these parts at that time,” etc.** It appears that one should read: “And at that time.” “At that time the earthborn inhabitants occupied Eleusis,” says Clement of Alexandria. HERALDUS.
>
> **Baubo.** Nicander, *Alexipharmaca* 130 ff., and Antoninus Liberalis, *Metamorphoses*, chapter XXIV, where see Verheyk, p. 107 of Teucher’s edition, call her Misme. The author of the *Hymn to Demeter* attributed to Homer says that Ceres was first revived by a drink offered by Metanira, wife of Celeus of Eleusis, after she had been cheered by Iambe, Metanira’s maidservant, verses 197–208. Compare [Col. 1131D] Schott on Proclus’s *Chrestomathy of Poetry*, p. 30, and Gierig on Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V, 447. ORELLI.
>
> **“Triptolemus, the yoker of oxen.”** The classic passage concerning Triptolemus is Xenophon, *Hellenica* VI, 3, §6:
>
> > For our ancestor Triptolemus is said to have been the first to reveal to foreigners the ineffable rites of Demeter and Korē—to Heracles, the founder of your Spartan people, and to the Dioscuri, your fellow citizens—and also to have given the Peloponnese the first seed of Demeter’s crop for sowing.
>
> Servius on *Georgics* I, 19: “Triptolemus distributed grain. Ceres gave him this duty because of the kindness of his father Icarius”—read “Rharus,” following Ruhnken’s correction on the Homeric *Hymn to Demeter*, p. 53—“who received her hospitably in Attica while she was searching for Proserpina after the latter had been carried away to marry Pluto.” Compare Pausanias, *Attica*, p. 13 (Sylburg); Hyginus, fable 227; Hesychius, s.v. *Rharon*; Suidas, s.v. *Rharias*. ORELLI.
>
> **“Triptolemus, Eubuleus, Dysaules, Eumolpus: Triptolemus, the yoker of oxen; Dysaules, keeper of goats; Eubuleus [Col. 1132A], keeper of pigs; Eumolpus, keeper of the wool-bearing flock.”** Salmasius supplied these words from the manuscript. These names were extremely celebrated in the Eleusinian mysteries. See Sainte-Croix, [Col. 1132B] pp. 108–109 of Lenz’s translation. For *Eubuleus* (Εὐβουλεύς), which Meursius restored, earlier editors wrongly have *Euboleus*. Eubuleus was Triptolemus’s brother and Dysaules their father, according to Pausanias, book I, chapter 14. Pausanias relates that they received from Ceres the method of sowing grain because she first learned from them of her daughter’s abduction. ORELLI.
>
> **“From whom the family of the Eumolpidae also descends.”** The Roman manuscript reads “the family also flows”; from this I suspect that one should read *gens effluit*, “the family flows forth.” Thus below: “the causes and origins flow forth.” CANTER. Fulvius Ursinus reads the same. Hesychius: “Eumolpidae … those descended from Eumolpus were so called, from the first man to perform the office of hierophant. For there were many men of the same name, Eumolpus.” HERALDUS. Compare Meursius, *Eleusinia*, chapter 13. ORELLI.
>
> **“And the caduceus-bearers, hierophants, and heralds who later flourished.”** He appears to call the *kērykes* (κήρυκες) both “caduceus-bearers” and “heralds,” wishing to express the Greek word by these two Latin terms. But since he inserts “hierophants” between them, there is certainly reason to suspect that he wished to distinguish the caduceus-bearers [Col. 1132C] from the heralds. I therefore think that here “caduceus-bearers” designates those who were called *spondophoroi* (σπονδοφόροι) in these rites, whom Pollux likewise joins with the heralds: “hierophants, torch-bearers, heralds, and libation-bearers.” And *spondophoroi* certainly are caduceus-bearers. Clement of Alexandria in the *Protrepticus*: “The Word is our libation-bearer, reconciler, and savior.” HERALDUS. Yet *spondophoroi* are priests who offer libations, as is clear from the cited passage of Pollux, book I, chapter 1, section 35. Compare Sainte-Croix, p. 145 of Lenz’s translation. The former explanation therefore seems preferable. ORELLI.
>
> **Hierophants.** Hesychius: “A hierophant … a mystagogue, a priest who displays the mysteries.” That is, “the one who reveals the sacred objects,” who displayed the rites and symbols to those being initiated. Plutarch in *Alcibiades*: “Imitating the mysteries and displaying them to his companions in his own house … wearing a robe such as the hierophant wears when displaying the sacred objects.” He was the chief of the other priests. [Col. 1132D] Plutarch says in *Numa Pompilius* that the *Pontifex Maximus* among the Romans held the same position among the priests as the *prophētēs*, “prophet,” or *exēgētēs*, “interpreter”—or rather, he says, the *hierophantēs*, “hierophant”—held among the Greeks: “The greatest of the pontiffs holds the rank of an interpreter and prophet, or rather of a hierophant.”
>
> Therefore, the prophet and the hierophant had the same office. But this seems to have been the distinction: insofar as the hierophant was “the one who displayed the sacred objects” while discharging his office, he was also a “prophet,” insofar, namely, as he explained the mystical religion. But he also had subordinate “prophets and interpreters,” whose services he sometimes employed and whose office it was to draw back the curtains, show the image to the initiates, and interpret what was obscure in the mysteries. HERALDUS. Compare Sainte-Croix, the passage cited, section IV, chapter 1, p. 132. ORELLI.
>
> **Heralds.** Harpocration: “The Ceryces are an Athenian family named after Ceryx, the son of Hermes.” Diodorus Siculus, book I, says that the Ceryces correspond to the Egyptian *pastophoroi*, while the Eumolpidae correspond to the Egyptian priests, [Col. 1133A] and that the institution was transferred from Egypt to Athens. The Ceryces, therefore, constituted a kind of sacrosanct college, while the Eumolpidae were priests. HERALDUS.—Arnobius undoubtedly means the *Hierokērykes*, “sacred heralds,” whose rank in the Eleusinian rites was third, after the hierophants and the *dadouchoi*, “torch-bearers.” See Sainte-Croix, book I. [Col. 1133B] ORELLI.
>
> **“Accordingly, that Baubo,” etc., etc.** Our Arnobius rendered this passage almost word for word from Clement of Alexandria. Clement’s words are as follows (*Protrepticus*, p. 17, Potter’s edition):
>
> > And indeed—for I shall not refrain from speaking—after Baubo had received Deo as her guest, she offered her a *kykeon*. But when Deo refused to take it and was unwilling to drink, for she was full of grief, Baubo, deeply distressed at apparently being slighted, bared her private parts and displayed them to the goddess. Deo was delighted by the sight and only then, at last, accepted the drink, pleased by the spectacle. These are the secret mysteries of the Athenians; these indeed are also recorded by Orpheus.
>
> CANTER.
>
> **“She offers the thirsty goddess a drink of spelt, a *cinnus*.”** Thus Salmasius edited the passage according to the traces of the manuscript, which reads *sitienti adori*. From this others produced *sitienti ardori*, “to her burning thirst.” Salmasius explains the basis of his correction in his *Plinian Exercises on Solinus*, p. 232. A “drink of spelt” is the *kykeon*, into which *ador*—that is, groats or flour made from roasted barley—was mixed. See [Col. 1133C] Festus and Nonius under this word. This correction is also confirmed by passages of Ovid and Antoninus Liberalis in which the same story is treated. Thus Ovid, *Metamorphoses* V, 449–450:
>
> > An old woman came forth, saw the goddess, and, when she asked for water,  
> > Gave her a sweet drink that she had previously cooked with roasted groats.
>
> Antoninus Liberalis, *Metamorphoses*, chapter 24:
>
> > When she was suffering from intense heat, Misme received her and gave her water to drink, putting pennyroyal and barley meal into it.
>
> See Verheyk there. Compare the scholiast on Euripides, *Orestes*, at verse 962. The common reading *sitienti ardori* could indeed be defended from the following words in chapter II of this book, concerning Faunus and Picus: “At one time, parched by burning thirst, they went to the streams of springs so that they might water the heat in their veins.” Nevertheless, I greatly prefer Salmasius’s correction, supported by such authorities. ORELLI.
>
> **“A *cinnus*, which Greece calls a *kykeon*.”** Nonius, under *concinnari*: “A *cinnus* is commonly said to be a kind of drink compounded from many liquids. The Greeks call the *cinnus* a *kykeon*.” Hesychius and Suidas under *kykeon*; Eustathius on Homer, *Iliad* XI. ELMENHORST.—[Col. 1133D] A drink made from roasted groats, honey, wine, flowers, and various herbs. See Heinsius and Burmann on Ovid, book I; Munker on Lactantius’s *Argument*; Delrio on Seneca, *Hercules Oetaeus*, verse 1097; Fischer’s index to Theophrastus under this word; Verheyk on Antoninus Liberalis at the cited passage; and especially the most learned Creuzer, commentary I, *On the Causes of Bacchic Rites*, p. 50. Tertullian calls it *cocetum* in *Against the Valentinians*, chapter 12. Canter restored *cinnum* from the manuscript. Others wrongly read *cynum*. ORELLI.
>
> **“Nor does circumstance permit her to remember their shared condition of health.”** Thus Gelenius and Heraldus in his *Second Notes*, followed by the remaining editors. The first edition reads *fortunam*, “fortune,” without sense. ORELLI.
>
> **“Lest disgust.”** The manuscript reads *ane*. Perhaps one should read *anus ne*, “lest the old woman.” HERALDUS, in his *Second Notes*.
>
> [Col. 1134A] **“An unalterable determination.”** One from which a person cannot be moved, as Caspar Barth correctly explains on Statius, *Thebaid* V, 45, vol. III, p. 30. ORELLI.
>
> **“She resolved to cheer her with spectacles of mockery.”** Festus: “Things worthy of admiration we call *miracula*; the ancients used the word of obscene things.” See the commentators there. Compare [Col. 1134B] our observations on the preceding chapter and Meursius, book V, chapter 9. ORELLI.
>
> **“That part of the body through which the female sex is accustomed both to produce offspring and to acquire a name for its kind, she frees from long neglect.”** Ludovicus Carrio restored this from the manuscript. Previously the text read: “through which the female sex…” See above, on book I, chapter 59. Behotius, in *Apophoreta* III, chapter 5, thinks one should read: “With that part of her body … she frees her”—that is, Ceres—“from prolonged despondency” (*athymia*, ἀθυμία). Wrongly, as we shall presently see. I have given the words “and is accustomed to acquire a name for its kind, she frees it from prolonged neglect” according to Gelenius’s correction. The manuscript has: “for its kind, when with prolonged…” Stewechius printed “generic; with prolonged…”; Salmasius: “a name for its kind, then with prolonged…”
>
> Stewechius admits that he does not know what it means “to free that part from neglect,” and substitutes *interula*, “undergarment,” for *incuria*, “neglect.” But Artemidorus explains it for us in a very similar passage, *Interpretation of Dreams* I, chapter 41: [Col. 1134C]
>
> > Hairiness … foretells widowhood for women; for they live more negligently and become hairy when the man for whose sake they tend their bodies is not present.
>
> See Rigault there, p. 25, vol. II of Reiff’s edition. Thus Baubo frees that part from neglect—that is, “from hairiness”—by either plucking out the hairs growing wild upon it or shaving them off with a razor. Behotius is therefore very greatly mistaken in referring the words “she frees it … from neglect” to Ceres. For if we interpret them thus, everything is dislocated and the order of the words becomes extremely confused.
>
> “That part … it” is a graceful pleonasm. Similarly Plautus, *Pseudolus*, act I, scene 5, verse 114: “That flute-girl whom your son desperately loves, I shall cleverly trick the procurer out of her.” Livy, book I, chapter 19: “Having thus gained the kingship, he prepared to found anew through justice, laws, and customs the new city that had been established by violence and arms.” Again, concerning Lucretia, book I, chapter 58: “The knife which she had beneath her garment, she drove into her heart.” These passages were cited by Gronovius, *Observations* I, chapter 22. I noticed with great joy, after I had already committed these observations to paper, that this most learned man agreed with me in illuminating [Col. 1134D] and explaining this entire passage. Dresemius, on Joseph of Exeter, *Trojan War* I, verse 7, p. 4 of Perizonius’s edition, discusses at length the verb *sylvescere*, “to grow wild,” and similar verbs ending in *-asco*, *-esco*, and *-isco*. But now I withdraw my hand from these obscene and shameful matters. ORELLI.
>
> **“She causes it to assume a cleaner appearance.”** Behotius thinks one should read: “she goes to assume an appearance,” understanding the words of clothing. But the following words, “and to be smoothed into the appearance,” plainly show that these words must be joined with those preceding them. The sense, therefore, is: “she causes it”—that is, that part—“to assume a cleaner appearance,” *habitus* here meaning aspect or look. ORELLI.
>
> **“And to be smoothed into the appearance of a little boy not yet hard and bristly.”** “Hard,” that is, rough and hairy. Thus Juvenal, *Satire* II, 11:
>
> > Shaggy limbs indeed, and coarse bristles upon the arms,  
> > Promise a fierce spirit.
>
> [Col. 1135A] And Sidonius Apollinaris, book I, letter 2: “hard arms,” [Col. 1135B] that is, rough with bristles; see Savaro there, p. 12. In place of *striculi*, Meursius restores *istriculi* from the glosses of Philoxenus, where *istriculus* is explained as *dasyprōktos* (δασύπρωκτος), “hairy-buttocked.” But just as *Spanus* stands for *Hispanus*, *Spalis* for *Hispalis*, and *strio* for *histrio*, so too *strix* stands for *hystrix*—see Grotius on Martianus Capella, book VI, p. 201—and *striculus* for *hystriculus*, a diminutive of *hystrix*, “porcupine,” an animal distinguished for the thickness and roughness of its quills. In the same sense Varro, as cited by Nonius, uses *ericium* for a shaggy and bristly person. A boy who is “not yet *striculus*” is therefore one not yet covered with hair. See Salmasius, who discusses this word at length, on Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, pp. 244–245, and on the *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, pp. 219 and 288. ORELLI.
>
> **“She returns to the goddess.”** The manuscript reads *redita*, from which Stewechius produced: “Thus she returns to the goddess,” not badly. ORELLI.
>
> **“And at once the goddess fixes her eyes upon the pubic region.”** [Col. 1135C] I demonstrated in book I of *On the Particles of the Latin Language* that among the ancients *atque* could mean “at once, immediately,” with temporal force. There I explained the following words from Plautus’s *Menaechmi*: “For after I gave her to you a short time ago, immediately I went to the forum.” Cicero, *On the Laws* II: “If he summons him to court, immediately let him go.” Virgil, *Georgics* I, 203:
>
> > … If by chance he has relaxed his arms,
And the channel sweeps him headlong away in the plunging stream. If you wish, see also Nonius and Aulus Gellius, book X, chapter 29. STEWECH.—Compare J. F. Gronovius on Livy, book XXVI, chapter 39; Heyne, *Variae lectiones*, on Virgil, book I. The repetition of *atque* (“and”), to be sure, is extremely disagreeable, but it must readily be forgiven in Arnobius, a rather unpolished writer—unless, in the preceding words *atque omnia illa pudoris loca*, etc., we prefer to read *adeoque* for *atque*. *Pubes* means the private part, as often. Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 427:

> The first appearance was human, and a maiden with a beautiful body  
> Down to the groin. ORELL.]

## XXV

In the wandering course of this search she is carried even to the borders of Eleusis [Col. 1132A]—that is the name of a village situated in the region of Attica. The earthborn inhabitants then dwelling in those parts bore these names: Baubo, Triptolemus, Eubuleus, Dysaules, and Eumolpus. Triptolemus was a yoker of oxen, Dysaules a keeper of goats, Eubuleus of pigs, and Eumolpus of a wool-bearing flock. From Eumolpus both the clan of the Eumolpidae descends and that celebrated name among the Cecropians is derived, as are the Heralds, Hierophants, and Sacred Criers who afterward flourished. [Col. 1133A]

Accordingly, that Baubo, whom we have said to have been an inhabitant of the village of Eleusis, receives Ceres into her home when the goddess is worn down by manifold misfortunes. She seeks to win her over with gentle attentions and urges her to take thought for restoring her body. To quench her thirst she offers her a drink made from spelt, the *cinnum* that Greece calls *cyceon* (*κυκεών*). The mourning goddess turns away and rejects these offices of kindness, and her condition does not allow her to remember the ordinary needs of health. Baubo, in turn, begs and exhorts her, as is customary in such circumstances, not to disdain her hospitality. [Col. 1134A] Ceres persists with the utmost obstinacy and retains the stubbornness of her unconquered rigidity.

When this happened repeatedly, and her inescapable resolve could not be weakened by any attentions, Baubo changed her methods. Since she could not entice her by serious means, she determined to cheer her with astonishing mockeries. That part of the body by which the female sex is accustomed both to bring forth offspring and to acquire its name as a sex, she frees from the neglect of long standing, causes it to assume a cleaner condition, and makes it smooth in the likeness of a boy not yet hard or bristly. She returns to [Col. 1135A] the sorrowing goddess and, amid those ordinary devices by which griefs are customarily broken and moderated, uncovers herself. With her groin exposed, she displays all those parts belonging to modesty. The goddess fixes her eyes upon Baubo’s pubic region and feeds upon the sight of this unheard-of consolation. Then, growing more expansive through laughter, she takes and drinks the beverage she had rejected; and what Baubo’s modesty had long been unable to elicit, the obscenity of a shameful deed extorted.

[Note: [Col. 1135C]

### XXVI—The Thracian seer

Orpheus, whom Arnobius calls a seer [Col. 1135D], thereby signifies not merely a poet but also a *mystagogue* (*μυσταγωγός*), because he is said to have instituted *τὰς Θεῶν τελετάς*, “the rites of the gods,” according to the testimony of Pausanias in his *Boeotica*, Tatian at the beginning of his *Address to the Greeks*, and others. ORELL.

**And by singing published them through the ages to the human race.** *Cantando* is a dative gerund in place of *ad cantandum* (“for singing”), unless we prefer to read: “which were to be sung through the ages,” etc. ORELL.

**Having thus spoken**, etc. Arnobius translated these verses from Clement of Alexandria, in whose *Protrepticus*, p. 17, Potter’s edition—and in almost the same words in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book II, chapter 5—they read as follows:

> Having thus spoken, she drew up her robes and displayed everything,  
> A form of the body by no means seemly; and the child Iacchus was there,  
> And, laughing, kept tossing it with his hand beneath Baubo’s bosom.  
> Then, when the goddess smiled, and smiled within her heart, [Col. 1136A]  
> She accepted the gleaming vessel in which the *cyceon* was contained.

In determining either the reading or the meaning of these verses [Col. 1136B], learned men have labored greatly, and perhaps more than enough—for example, Daniel Heinsius on Clement; Paulus Leopardus, *Emendations*, book VI, chapter 25 (in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, p. 125 ff.); Salmasius on Solinus, p. 527 f.; J. C. de Pauw on Anacreon, p. 181; and J. M. Gesner on Orphic Fragment XVI, p. 475, Hermann’s edition. Since we aim at brevity in a foul and obscene matter, we shall offer only what most directly concerns the elucidation and correction of Arnobius.

First of all, it must be observed that Arnobius gave a paraphrase rather than a strict translation of this Orphic poem—or, rather, that he read those verses differently from the Greek texts of Eusebius and Clement. For Iacchus, whom Orpheus mentions in verse 2, is not mentioned at all in our author. In every respect, moreover, the Orphic verses sound much more modest and decent than Arnobius’ version. Hence Daniel Heinsius’ opinion is probable: religious men, ashamed of the words [Col. 1136C], interpolated these verses, whereas Arnobius read the true and genuine words of the Greek poet thus:

> Having thus spoken, she drew up her robes and displayed everything,  
> A form of the body by no means seemly, a childish bloom.  
> Baubo kept tossing it with her own hand beneath her bosom.  
> Then the softened goddess smiled, and smiled within her heart,  
> And accepted the gleaming vessel in which the *cyceon* was contained.

But we shall now examine the details. ORELL.

**Having thus spoken, she gathered up her garment from the bottom of her lap.** Thus reads the Leiden edition, following Dionysius Lambinus’ correction on Lucretius, book VI, p. 784. Others read: “Having thus spoken, at the same time,” etc. ORELL.

**And presented to her eyes the parts fashioned at her groin.** Arnobius thus rendered the Greek poet’s words, *σώματος οὐδὲ πρέποντα τύπον*, “a form of the body by no means seemly.” For such *παρατιλμός*—depilation—which, according to the *Suda*, was prized as a refinement among the ancient Athenians, is the mark of a shameless [Col. 1136D] woman. See Aristophanes, *Lysistrata*. On *res* (“things” or “parts”) in an obscene sense, see above on book III, chapter X, and book V, chapter 11. ORELL.

**Which Baubo, shaking them in her hollow hand.** Learned men have attempted by various conjectures to remedy the neglect of syllabic quantity in this verse. Daniel Heinsius thinks one should read: “Which Baubo, shaking them in her hollow hand,” etc., with *manu* as a nominative, a form used very frequently by Lucretius for *manus*. Jean Dorat prefers: “Which, shaking them with Bacchus’ hollow hand,” wishing to reproduce the words of the Orphic poem, “and the child Iacchus was there; and with his hand he kept tossing it,” etc. The meaning would then be that the boy Iacchus, or Bacchus, whom Ceres had nursed, handled Baubo’s private parts. But, as Heraldus very correctly teaches, nothing should be changed. Innumerable examples of neglected meter occur in the poets of that age. What Orpheus expresses by the single word *ῥιπτάσκειν* (“to keep tossing”), Arnobius rendered by three verbs: “shake,” “pat,” and “handle.” ORELL.

[Col. 1137B] **For those parts had the appearance of a boy.** Heraldus very correctly restored this from the royal manuscript. *Ollis* means “those things” or “those parts” which Baubo had caused “to assume a cleaner condition and to become smooth in the likeness of a boy not yet hard or bristly.” Previously *olli* was read. ORELL.

**Handles them fondly.** That is, gently strokes them. ORELL.

**Softened.** In Greek, *ἠπίη*. This must be read in verse 410 of the Orphic poem in place of *Ἡ δ᾽ ἐπεί*. *Ἤπιος* is equivalent to *πρᾶος*, “gentle,” according to Hesychius. DAN. HEINS.

**Cup (*poclum*).** So too Virgil has *gubernaclum*; and *serracla, vernacli, fiblae, fiblatoria* stand for *serracula, vernaculi, fibulae*, etc., with six hundred other examples. See Salmasius on the *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, p. 871. ORELL.

[Col. 1137C] **Joyfully drains all the liquid of the cyceon.** *Perducit* means “drinks it down.” Juvenal, *Satires* VI, 427:

> From which another pint  
> Is drunk before the meal.

And Plautus, *Amphitryon*, act I, scene I:

> **MERCURY:** There was a jar; from it I filled a pitcher.  
> **SOSIA:** It went in.  
> **MERCURY:** I drained it of pure wine just as it had been born from its mother.

STEWECH. and ELMENH.—They used not only *ducere* and *perducere* in this sense, but also *trahere*. Seneca in *Agamemnon*:

> And they drink pure wine from the gold of ancient Assaracus.

So too Greek *ἕλκειν* and *σπᾶν*, for example in Aristophanes and Athenaeus. HERALD.—Compare Lambinus on Lucretius, book VI, p. 784; L. Bunemann on Lactantius, *Institutes* VII, chapter 27, p. 993; and J. Rhodius under this verb in his lexicon of Scribonius. ORELL.

**What say you, offspring of Erechtheus?** This is the old reading, which I would not dare alter against the manuscripts. Salmasius printed, from a correction by François Pithou: “What say you, sons of Erechtheus, O wise men?” [Col. 1137D] Similarly Apuleius, book X: “Why, moreover, was that judgment held among the lawgiving Athenians, those wise men and masters of every branch of knowledge?” See the notes there, p. 747, Oudendorp’s edition. ORELL.

**Citizens of Minerva.** That is, Athenians. Hyginus, *Fables* 275; Servius on *Georgics* I, p. 60, and *Aeneid* III, p. 494. ELMENH.

**So thoroughly pierced.** Thus Livy, book V, chapter 11: “And yet that they, pierced through by so many judgments and already condemned, should come before the judgment of the people.” See Doering there. The metaphor is drawn from gladiators. ORELL.

**That is no false suspicion.** J. Lipsius thus emended the passage in *Epistolary Questions*, book III, letter XV, and the reading is also confirmed by a manuscript. Previously *susceptio* was printed. Fulvius Ursinus printed *suspicio*. But *suspectio* has the same meaning. See P. Burmann on Quintilian, *Declamations* I, 2; Stewechius on Vegetius, *On Military Matters* III, chapter 6, p. 253 f., Wesel edition; F. Oudendorp on Frontinus, *Stratagems* I, [Col. 1138B] chapter 8, p. 105; Muncker on Fulgentius, *Mythologies* III, preface. The Leiden edition gave *subscriptio*. ORELL.

**The shameful testimonies of ancient writings set forth the marks and origins of your Eleusinian rites.** I would write: “the marks of your Eleusinian rites”; or: “I shall set forth the marks and origins.” MEURS., p. 169.—Meursius evidently failed to notice that *elogia* is the subject here. ORELL.

**Finally, the tokens themselves.** Clement, *Protrepticus* (p. 18, Potter’s edition):

> The watchword of the Eleusinian mysteries: “I fasted; I drank the *cyceon*; I took from the chest; after performing the rite, I placed it in the basket, and from the basket into the chest.” Fine sights indeed, and worthy of a goddess!

ELMENH.—What Arnobius here calls a *symbolum* (“token”), Clement of Alexandria calls a *σύνθημα* (“watchword”). Initiates had certain tokens and signs by which they recognized one another. Apuleius, *Apology*: “To all others, however, I declare in the clearest voice: if anyone who shares the same rites with me happens to be present, let him give the sign, and then he may hear what I preserve. For no danger whatever could compel me to disclose to the profane what I received under obligation to keep silent.”

Just as in military service there were two kinds of signs, spoken and mute, so too in these rites. The one we have here is spoken; in Apuleius certain others are mute—namely, those that the initiated received from priests. Apuleius in the same *Apology*: “I have participated in the initiatory rites of many cults in Greece. Certain signs and memorial objects from them, handed down to me by the priests, I carefully preserve. I say nothing unusual, nothing unknown.
