You fellow-initiates of Father Liber alone who are present know what you keep hidden at home and silently venerate, apart from all profane persons.” He calls them “signs and memorial objects,” obviously [Col. 1138D] because initiates recognized one another by them, as I just observed, and because by them they also recalled those secret rites to memory. Hence in the same book he also calls them *memoracula*, “reminders,” and, for the former reason, *crepundia*, “recognition tokens,” that is, *γνωρίσματα*, as the older scholars have excellently interpreted the word. HERALD.

Murrius, in his commentary on the Herculaneum Tablets, vol. V, tablet 8, appropriately cites our passage and compares these tokens with the signs by which members of certain secret societies still recognize one another (*Freimaurerzeichen*, “Freemasons’ signs”). ORELL.

**I fasted and drank the cyceon; I took from the chest**, etc. Hadrianus Junius, *Observations* VI, chapter 23, emended the passage thus from Clement’s words. Previously it read, most corruptly, “I took the entrails.” Anyone wishing to see a fuller description of these ceremonies should consult J. Meursius, *Eleusinia*, chapter 10, and Sainte-Croix, *On the Mysteries of the Ancients*, section V, chapter 1. ORELL.]

## XXVI

If anyone should happen to suspect that we are dishonestly slandering them, let him take up the books of the Thracian seer, which you affirm to belong to divine antiquity. He will find that we neither cunningly [Note: [Col. 1135A] *Calide*, Sab.] fabricate [Note: [Col. 1135A] *Effingere*, Fulv.] anything nor seek and contrive means by which the sacred majesties of the gods may be brought into ridicule. For we shall place before you the very verses that the son of Calliope uttered in Greek and, by singing, published through the ages to the human [Note: [Col. 1136A] “to the law,” Sab., very badly.] race:

> Having thus spoken, she gathered up her garment from the bottom of her lap,  
> And presented to her eyes the parts fashioned at her groin,  
> Which Baubo, shaking them in her hollow hand [Note: [Col. 1136A] “Shaking which things Baubo in her hollow hand,” Fulv.]—for those parts  
> [Col. 1137A] Had the appearance of a boy—pats and handles fondly.  
> Then the goddess, fixing upon them the orbs of her august eyes,  
> Softened a little, lays aside the sorrows of her heart.  
> Next she takes the cup in her hand and, with laughter following,  
> Joyfully drains all the liquid of the *cyceon*.

What say you, offspring of Erechtheus? What say you, citizens of Minerva? My heart longs to know by what arguments you will defend such perilous affairs, or what devices you possess to bring safety to persons, wounds, and causes so thoroughly pierced. That is no false suspicion, nor are you being assailed by a slanderous accusation. The shameful testimonies of ancient writings set forth the marks and origins of your Eleusinian rites [Note: [Col. 1137B] Thus Sab.; “cities betray,” Fulv.]. Finally, there are the very tokens with which you reply when questioned at the reception of the rites:

> I fasted and drank the *cyceon*. I took from the chest and put into the basket; I took it back again and transferred it into the little chest.

[Col. 1138A]

[Note: [Col. 1138D]

### XXVII—Badges of the wretched

The first edition has “of miseries.” Terence describes such a man in *Eunuch*, act II, scene II, verse 5:

> I see him unkempt, filthy, sick, buried beneath rags and years. ORELL.

**Which it is impious to name before chaste ears without first begging pardon and paying due respect.** A person “prefaces a mark of respect” when, being about to say something indecent, he uses words that beg pardon by way of excuse, such as “Forgive me,” “With your leave I shall say it,” and the like. See P. Manutius on Cicero, *Letters to Friends* IX, letter XXII: “If, however, we say in jest, ‘He strangled his father,’ we do not preface a mark of respect; but if we say something about Aurelia or Lollia, a mark of respect must first be offered.” Quintilian, *Declamation* III, has preserved for us the formula for prefacing respect in obscene matters: “May due respect be paid to your most sacred ears.” It corresponds to our phrase *mit Respect zu melden*, “with respect be it said.” ORELL.

**What, I ask, in such a sight**, etc. Thus the Leiden edition, following Stewechius’ very slight and felicitous correction. *Spectus*, fourth declension, is an old word of the kind Arnobius loves. [Col. 1139C] Festus: “Pacuvius used *spectu* without a preposition in *Dulorestes*, when he said: ‘Fierce, with a more ruddy color and insolent appearance.’” See Dacier there. Compare G. J. Vossius, *Roman Etymology*, under *specio*, and Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. The first edition has *specu*, from which others reshaped *spectaculo*. ORELL.

**Parts of shame (*verendisque*).** Thus Theodor Canter emended the formerly printed *reverendisque*. *Verenda* means *αἰδοῖα*, “private parts,” a word used several times by both Pliny the Elder and Pliny the Younger. ORELL.

**Could we have brought forth in ridicule and mockery**, “deriding it like mimes.” Prudentius, *Martyrdom of Lawrence*:

> Do you think, gallows-bird, that you have with impunity  
> Woven so many tricks  
> Through mimetic mockery,  
> While, as a buffoon, you dance a play?

The glosses: *cavillatio*, *κακοήθεια*, *εἰρωνεία*—“mockery, spitefulness, irony.” HERALD.—See above on book IV, chapter 36. ORELL.]

## XXVII

Is it then true, as those holy and secret mysteries disclose, that your gods are abducted and abduct others? That they enter marriages sought by furtive frauds? That the honor of virginity is torn from those who resist and are unwilling? That impending outrages pass unnoticed, and what happened to those abducted is unknown? That the lost are sought like human beings, and in the brightest sunlight the vastness of the world is traversed with lamps and torches? That they are afflicted, fall sick, assume the filth of mourners and the badges of miseries; and that, to enable them to apply their minds to nourishment and the taking of food, no reasoning, no consideration of time, no serious speech, no earnest affability is employed, but the shameful obscenity of bodies is displayed, and those parts are thrust before them which common modesty commands to be hidden, which the law of natural shame bids be concealed, and which it is impious to name before chaste ears [Col. 1138B] without first begging pardon and paying [Col. 1139A] due respect?

What, I ask, was there in such a sight—what was there in the shameful parts (*pudenda*) and “reverend” parts (*verenda*) of Baubo—that could turn a goddess of the female sex, fashioned with a similar member, to amazement and laughter? What was there which, when set before divine light and sight, could bring forgetfulness of miseries and transform her condition into a happier one through sudden merriment? Oh, what things and how many could we have brought forth in ridicule and mockery, had not respect for the nation [Note: [Col. 1139A] “of the one who knows us,” ms., absurdly.] and the authority of literature forbidden us!

[Col. 1140A]

[Note: [Col. 1139C]

### XXVIII—To gape about

That is, to look around with gaping mouth, as Gesner correctly explains in the *Thesaurus*. [Col. 1139D] The word, however, is a *hapax legomenon* (*ἅπαξ λεγόμενον*), occurring only once. ORELL.

**To double, as the saying goes, the Tellenian entanglements.** Varro in Nonius (under *tricae*): “Do you think they will not sooner unravel Atellan entanglements than disentangle that?” “Atellan entanglements” appear to mean the tricks of mimes by which they customarily evaded and escaped. But scholars observe that certain manuscripts of Nonius read “Tellenian entanglements”; this reading of Arnobius is thus confirmed, and the proverb may perhaps have been drawn from Greek sources, among whom *τὰ τοῦ Τέλληνος ἀείδειν*, “to sing the songs of Tellen continually,” is said of those who repeatedly force an inept ditty upon their hearers. HERALD.—Ausonius Popma, in his notes on the fragments of Varro, vol. II, p. 350, Zweibrücken edition, explains this proverb differently and, in my judgment, more correctly than Heraldus and Hadrianus Junius in the *Supplement to Erasmus’ Adages*, century V, proverb 68: “‘Tellenian entanglements,’” he says, “are proverbially (*παροιμιωδῶς*) used for obstructed and intricate affairs, from Tellena, an ancient city of the Latins which Ancus Marcius, the sixth king, captured.” Compare A. Turnebus, *Adversaria* XVII, 21, and Ruhnken, *Critical Letter* I, on the Homeric *Hymn to* [Col. 1140B] *Ceres*, p. 203, latest edition. ORELL.

**While shame restrains me from disclosing those mysteries of Halimus**, etc. Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus* (p. 29, Potter’s edition):

> But as for the mysteries at Sagra and those at Halimus in Attica, their disgrace has been confined to Athens; yet a disgrace to the whole world are the contests and phalli celebrated for Dionysus, which have perniciously spread throughout life.

Salmasius printed *Alimontia* following the traces of the manuscript, which, according to Canter, has “to disclose those things of Halimonia”; from this Gelenius made “to disclose those nurturing mysteries.” Pithou first understood the true meaning of the passage, correcting it to “those mysteries of Halimus,” etc. Halimus was a village of Attica. ORELL.

**In which Greece erects ithyphalli in honor of Father Liber.** Lucian, *The Syrian Goddess*, chapter XVI:

> The Greeks erect phalli for Dionysus; upon them they also carry something of this kind: small men made of wood, having large private parts. These are called puppets. There is also this in the sanctuary, on the right side of the temple: a small bronze man sits there, having a large private part.

There the ancient scholiast says:

> When the Greeks celebrated a festival for Dionysus, they honored him with phalli. A phallus is a representation of a man’s private part made from red leather. They put it around themselves, both upon their necks and between their thighs, and danced in honor of Dionysus by means of it.

The *Suda* agrees: “Phalli … a private part made of fig wood, and later of red leather, had the form of a man’s private part,” etc. ELMENH.—In those pomps and, so to speak, processions, the basket-bearer (*ἡ κανηφόρος*) went first; the phallus-bearer (*ὁ φαλλοφόρος*) followed; and after him came those singing the phallic song (*οἱ ᾅδοντες τὸ φαλλικόν*). You have the complete mime of this abominable superstition in Aristophanes’ *Acharnians*. HERALD.—Janus Guilielmus, *Questions on Plautus’ Curculio*, chapter V (in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, part II, p. 367), most correctly restored *subrigit*, “erects,” to Arnobius. For this emendation is confirmed by what he says below in the next chapter: “Let him question all Greece as to what these phalli mean, which ancient custom erects and venerates throughout countryside and towns.” The old glosses: *subrigit*, *ὑπορθοῖ, ὑποστηρίζει*, “raises, supports”; *subrigo*, *ἀναβιβάζω, ἀνορθῶ*, “raise up, set upright.” Virgil says of Rumor, “raises so many ears,” meaning the same as Terence’s “Prick up your ears, Pamphilus.” Previously *subrugit* was read, which scholars explained as referring to men singing ithyphallic songs in a hoarse, masculine voice.

Salmasius printed *phallos* for *ithyphallos*, but I would not dare change anything. For Lucian’s scholiast, in the passage cited, expressly distinguishes phalli from ithyphalli: “All these are phalli; but they are ithyphalli when bound straight along the thighs.” The phallic and ithyphallic meters were likewise different, as Joseph Scaliger teaches on *Priapea*, poem 36. The meaning of our passage will therefore be: Greece erects ithyphalli—namely, “upon the thighs”—in honor of Liber, and all territories flourish with little images of this kind placed throughout villages and towns. ORELL.

**Territories.** Meursius wrongly suspects that “buildings” should be read. For below we find: “which custom erects throughout countryside and towns.” ORELL.

**And, having marveled at such great things, preserve them always in pure minds with scrupulous observance.** They believed that those secret rites had to be held in the mind with the highest religious devotion and most cautious reverence (*εὐλάβεια*), and must not be divulged without great fear of sinning. Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis* IV, chapter XVI:

> Now that I am about to explain the venerable secrets of this doctrine, which the divine ancients uttered with the utmost trepidation and left wrapped in the circumlocutions of obscurity, lest divine knowledge, once published, should reach the awareness of profane people, let whatever they said be imparted in this treatise through the simplest explanations to an attentive and tranquil mind, unoccupied by other considerations.

Such great dread and such awestruck reverence prevailed especially in the mysteries. More generally, however, some fear and awestruck reverence attended every sacred rite. Hence participants were commanded *εὐφημεῖν*—to observe reverent silence—and not merely to restrain their tongues but silently to guard the mind itself. Quintilian in the *Declamations*: “But in a temple, where we spare our words, where we compose our minds, where we guard even our silent thought, it is intolerable to strike someone as though in a solitude, as though in some private place.” HERALD.

**While the Nysian and Semeleian Liber was still among men, they say.** I think the name *Liber* has been imported here by an interpolating hand, because I observe that this writer gladly uses epithets of this kind alone, without adding a noun. He calls Bacchus “the Semeleian” from his mother, concerning which we have commented above; similarly, he called Jupiter “the Saturnian” more than once. He also calls Liber “the Nysian,” from the city Nysa, whether it is the one in Arabia or India where, as the story goes, he was raised by nymphs. STEWECH.—“Nysian” is not derived from the Arabian city of Nysa, but rather from Nysus, his father. For Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III, whom our author follows in enumerating five Dionysi or Libers, expressly asserts: “The fifth was born of Nysus and Thione.” NOURR., p. 394.—The standard passages concerning Nysa and Nysian Bacchus are in Diodorus, *Library* I, chapter 15—see Wesseling there—and book III, chapters 57–60. ORELL.

**He desired to know the lower world**, etc. Our author likewise borrowed this passage from Clement (p. 29 f., Potter’s edition):

> Dionysus, desiring to descend into Hades, did not know the road. A man named Prosymnus promises to show it to him, but not without payment. The payment was not honorable, though it was agreeable to Dionysus: the fee Dionysus was asked to pay was a sexual favor. The request was made to the willing god, and he promises to grant it if he should return, confirming his promise by oath. Having learned the road, he departed; he returned again but did not find Prosymnus, for he had died. Dionysus, intent upon fulfilling his religious obligation to his lover, hastens to the tomb and lusts for passive intercourse. Cutting off a chance branch of a fig tree, he shapes it in the manner of a male organ and sits upon the branch, fulfilling his promise to the dead man. As a mystic memorial of this passion, phalli are erected to Dionysus throughout the cities; “for if they did not hold a procession for Dionysus and sing a hymn to the private parts, most shameless deeds would have been done.” “Hades and Dionysus are the same, for whom they rave and celebrate the Lenaea”—not so much, as I think, because of bodily drunkenness as because of the disgraceful revelation of licentiousness.

CANTERUS.

**Prosumnus.** The authors who relate the same story vary in the name. Gregory of Nazianzus, *Invective* II [Col. 1142B], as well as our author and Clement, calls him *Πρόσυμνος*, Prosumnus. Pausanias in the *Corinthiaca*, p. 80, and Nonnus in the *Explanation of the Pagan Stories Mentioned by Gregory* call him *Πόλυμνος*, Polymnus. Theodoret, *Cure of Greek Affections*, and sermon VIII, *On the Martyrs*, together with Tzetzes on Lycophron, verse 212, call him *Πολύϋμνος*, Polyymnus. Phavorinus, under *Ἐνόρχης*, calls him *Πολύσυμνος*, Polysymnus. Finally Hyginus, *Poetic Astronomy* II, chapter 5, corruptly has Hypolipnus or Hypolymnus, for which Muncker and J. Wowerius think Polyhypnus should be written, and *Πολύϋπνος* in Tzetzes. ELMENHORST and D. HEINS., on Clement. Wowerius on Firmicus, *The Error of Profane Religions*, p. 428, Gronovius’ edition. Meursius reads Polymnus. ORELL.

**More than sufficiently inclined.** *Satis* means “too much,” as we observed above on book II. ORELL.

**Expedition.** Stewechius restored this from the parchment manuscripts. The word is familiar to Arnobius, borrowed, of course, and transferred in different ways from military affairs. Above, in book III: “that Diana may be regarded as supremely powerful over hunting expeditions.” Previously *expetitionis* (“seeking”) was read. ORELL.

[Col. 1142C] **That guide departs from the number of the living.** Gelenius and Stewechius thus emended the passage. The old reading was, “the guide then falls from the number of the living,” which Heraldus defends after removing only the particle “then,” repeated from the preceding word *index*. ORELL.

**Evius.** Acron on Horace, *Odes* II, 11, 17: “Father Liber was so called because, when the gods waged war against the Giants, he was the first to change into a lion and killed a Giant. From this deed Jupiter praised him thus: ‘Euhye,’ that is, ‘good son’; for in Greek *υἱός* means ‘son.’ This cry was also prolonged in the rites of Bacchus, as in Virgil, ‘Euhye.’” Compare H. Columna on the fragments of Ennius, p. 407; Hessel’s edition, p. 265. ORELL.

**In order to fulfill the pledge of his bargain and free himself from the religious obligation of his oath.** Yet he had been freed from the religious obligation of his oath by the death of the man to whom compliance had been promised. Nevertheless, behold: the religious god wishes to add something even beyond his duty. Although Arnobius says this ironically (*εἰρωνικῶς*), he nevertheless shows how religiously the ancients observed an oath. To avoid polluting themselves by even the slightest deviation, when formulating an oath they attentively considered and weighed their words; and lest they nevertheless be susceptible to some captious alternative interpretation, they declared that they swore by their mind rather than their tongue—that is, that they formulated the oath only according to what they intended, and that the words were not to be taken strictly. Hence the customary formula, “If I knowingly deceive.” And because only *what is possible* (*τὸ δυνατόν*) is guaranteed, they sometimes mentioned this condition too. Furthermore, lest even after death the shades of those persons appear to remain bound by an unspoken force, they also made an exception for death. Hence Achilles in *Iliad* I, verses 88–89:

> No one, while I live and look upon the earth,  
> Shall lay heavy hands upon you beside the hollow ships.

HERALD.—Observe here the unusual tmesis and transposition of the words: “free himself from the religious obligation of the right of swearing,” in place of “free himself from the religious obligation of an oath.” We have already observed a similar example above. ORELL.

**And, cutting a very sturdy branch from a fig tree [Col. 1143C], hews, planes, and smooths it**, etc. Minucius Felix, chapter XXIII: “For a wooden god, perhaps a piece of a funeral pyre or an ill-omened log, is hung up, cut, hewn, and planed.” See Wowerius there, p. 239, J. Gronovius’ edition. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter VII: “Yet axes, planes, and rasps bear down all the more strongly upon every limb of your gods.” The *runcina* is a carpenter’s tool—the half-barbarians called it a plane—by which boards or planks are scraped or smoothed. In Greek, *ῥυκάνη*; French *rabot*; German *Hobel*. Hence *runcinare*, “to polish with a plane.” ORELL.

**Places it beneath himself, sits upon it.** Stewechius wrongly prefers *subsidit*, “sits down,” since “to sit down” and “to sit upon” mean one and the same thing here. By contrast, *subdo*, “place beneath,” namely beneath oneself: *sich etwas unterschieben*, “to slide something underneath oneself.” ORELL.

**Then assuming the wantonness of one in heat.** The same Stewechius restored to Arnobius this entirely correct manuscript reading. On the verb *surire*, “to be in heat,” see above on chapter 3 and book I, chapter 2. Previously the text read: “Then assuming extravagant wantonness.” ORELL.

**Twists his buttocks this way and that.** Namely, to submit to violation. The glosses: “buttocks, *πυγαί*.” Juvenal, *Satires* II, [Col. 1143D] verse 20:

> And, after speaking about virtue,  
> They wag the buttock.

*Priapea*, epigram XVIII:

> She who, with no tunic covering her buttock,  
> Moves it more aptly and deeply for your entrails.

ELMENH. Compare P. Burmann II, in the appendix of notes to the *Latin Anthology*, vol. I, p. 743. ORELL.

**What he had long before promised in reality.** That *veritas*, “reality,” is pointedly opposed to fictitious persons or things, pretense, and empty display has been illustrated by many examples: Gronovius, *Observations* IV, chapter 7; Markland on Statius, *Silvae* V, 39; Salmasius on the *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, p. 821; Ernesti, *Key to Cicero*, under *veritas*; and Ruhnken on Rutilius Lupus, p. 92. Thus our author below, book VI, chapter 10: “How can this man here be fair-haired, when in reality he has blue-gray eyes?” ORELL.]

## XXVIII

I confess that for some time now I have been hesitating, gaping about, seeking evasions, and doubling, as the saying goes, the Tellenian entanglements, while shame restrains me from disclosing those mysteries of Halimus in which Greece erects ithyphalli in honor of Father Liber, and all its territories blossom with images of male organs. Perhaps it is unclear what this means, and one may ask by what reasoning it is done. Whoever you are who do not know it, learn; and, having marveled at such great things, preserve them always in pure minds with scrupulous [Col. 1141A] observance.

While the Nysian and Semeleian Liber was still among men, they say, he desired to know the lower world and to investigate what was going on beneath the abodes of Tartarus. But this desire of his was obstructed by certain difficulties, because in his ignorance of the route he did not know where to go or how to proceed. A certain Prosumnus appears, a dishonorable lover of the god and more than sufficiently inclined to impious lusts. He promises to point out the gate of Dis and the approaches to Acheron if the god will comply with his desire and allow him to pluck from him the pleasures of a wife.

The accommodating god swears that he will place himself at Prosumnus’ power [Col. 1142A] and disposal, but only after he has returned from the lower world with his wish and expedition accomplished. Prosumnus courteously explains the road and sets him down at the very threshold of the lower world. Meanwhile, while Liber inspects the Styx, Cerberus, the Furies, and all the other things [Note: [Col. 1141A] “every thing,” ms.] with inquisitive curiosity, that guide departs from the number of the living [Note: [Col. 1142A] “falls,” others.] and is buried according to human custom.

Evius emerges from the lower world and learns that his guide is dead. In order to fulfill the pledge of his bargain and free himself from the religious obligation of his oath, he proceeds to the place of burial. Cutting a very sturdy branch from a fig tree, he hews, [Col. 1143A] planes, and smooths it, and fashions upon it the likeness of a human penis. He fixes it above the mound of the tomb and, baring himself from behind, approaches it, places it beneath himself, and sits upon it. Then, assuming the wantonness of one in heat, he twists his buttocks this way and that, and attempts to suffer from the wood what he had long before promised in reality.

[Note: [Col. 1144B]

### XXIX—Heraclitus as witness

Thus the Leiden edition. Previously: “Heraclitus as though a witness.” See the passage of Clement cited above. ORELL.

[Col. 1144C] **What these phalli mean**, etc. Stewechius printed this from the manuscript, which has “these ramparts.” Earlier editors read “ithyphalli.” See the preceding chapter. Moreover, the scholiast on Aristophanes’ *Acharnians*, verse 245, explains for us what induced Greece to erect phalli in honor of Liber. Philosophical interpreters of the mysteries—Plotinus, Iamblichus, and Eusebius—offer other, physical causes. See Sainte-Croix, the passage cited, p. 208 ff., Lenz’s edition. ORELL.

**He will find the causes to be those we have stated.** Salmasius printed: “He will find both the causes and the facts to be those we have stated.” ORELL.

**Those wearing the bordered toga.** That is, boys still wearing the *toga praetexta*. Thus Juvenal, *Satires* IV, verse 78: “an adulterer in the bordered toga.” See Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 6, the standard passage on this subject. ORELL.

**What bargains Liber entered into with his lovers.** Similarly Julius Firmicus—who should be compared throughout this chapter with our author—*The Error of Profane Religions*, p. 428: “Does someone submit to a woman’s role and seek consolation for an effeminate body? Let him look upon Liber, who even after his lover’s death represents the reward of the lust he had promised by imitating disgraceful intercourse.” ORELL.

**Brothers from the same seed.** R. Bentley, on Horace, *Satires* I, 1, 100, teaches that the masculine gender, as the more dignified, very frequently includes the feminine under itself. Thus *Digest* II, 10, 38: “Lucius and Titia, brother and sister.” Tacitus, *Annals* XII, 4: “And he distorted the love of the siblings”—namely Silanus and Junia Calvina—“which was not incestuous but merely unguarded, into infamy.” Livy XXXVII, 3: “Envoys from Ptolemy and Cleopatra, kings of Egypt.” ORELL.

**Intercourse, beds.** Meursius and Heraldus think *concubitus*, “intercourse,” should be deleted as a gloss. I would be unwilling to delete it in Arnobius, who loves such redundancies of expression. ORELL.

**The entire faculty of hearing must be closed.** *Audientia*, “hearing,” stands for “ears,” as above, book III, chapter 29: “Janus, whom you place first in all your prayers and believe opens for you a way to the hearing of the gods.” ORELL.

**For when the first and perfect nature**, etc., etc. [Col. 1145B] Arnobius seems to have in view that very well-known passage of Terence’s *Eunuch*, act III, scene V, verse 38 ff.:

> [Col. 1145C] Looking up at a certain painted panel, upon which was this picture: Jupiter  
> Sending, as they say, a shower of gold into Danaë’s lap long ago.  
> I too began to look at it; and because he had already played  
> A similar game in former times, my heart rejoiced all the more—  
> That a god had changed himself into money and, through another man’s roof,  
> Had secretly come through the rain to deceive a woman.  
> But what a god! The one who shakes the highest temples of heaven with his thunder.  
> Should I, a mere little man, not do it? Indeed I did it—and gladly. ORELL.]

## XXIX

But lest anyone perhaps suppose that matters so impious have been fabricated by us, we do not ask him to believe Heraclitus as a witness, nor do we wish him to believe the mysteries; let him learn from reading Heraclitus himself what he thought about such things. Let him question all Greece as to what is meant by those phalli which ancient custom erects and venerates throughout the countryside and towns: he will discover that their causes are those which we state. Or, if shame has prevented the truth from being plainly explained, what advantage will there be in obscuring and concealing the cause and origin [Col. 1143B] of the rite, when the very charge against the religion lies in the deed itself?

What are you saying, O peoples, O nations engrossed in and devoted to the veneration of temples? Is it to these sacred rites that you compel us by fires, exiles, slaughter, and every other [Note: [Col. 1143B] Fulvius added *cum*.] kind of punishment, and by fear of your cruelty? Are these the gods whom you bring upon us, insinuate into us, and force upon us—gods whom neither you yourselves nor anyone connected with you [Col. 1144A] by degree of blood and right of kinship would wish to resemble?

Can you tell your boys, still under age and wearing the bordered toga, what bargains Liber entered into with his lovers? Can you urge your daughters-in-law—or rather, the women joined to you in marriage—to imitate the modesty of Baubo and the chaste pleasures of Ceres? Do you wish your young men to know, hear, and learn what sort of person Jupiter himself proved toward one mother and another? Do you wish grown maidens and fathers still vigorous to learn by what device that same god sported with his daughter? Do you wish brothers now in the heat of youth, sprung from the same seed, to hear once more that he did not disdain his sister’s bed of intercourse? [Note: [Col. 1144B] The manuscript absurdly reads: *aspernaturos*.]

Must one not, therefore, immediately flee far from gods of this sort and, lest the obscenity of so impure a religion creep into the mind, close one’s hearing [Col. 1144B] entirely? For what mortal has been trained in morals so chaste that the examples of the gods do not incite him to frenzies of this kind? Or who can restrain his desires from relatives and persons deserving reverence, when he sees that among the heavenly beings nothing sacred has been preserved amid the confusion of lusts? For when the first and perfect nature has not succeeded in restraining its desire within [Note: [Col. 1144B] Sabaeus reads *inter*.] proper bounds [Col. 1145A], why should a human being not pour himself out into indiscriminate appetites—both driven headlong by his innate frailty and aided by the teaching of holy divinity?

[Note: [Col. 1145C]

## XXX.—“Who [say] that there are gods”

Stewechius conjectures: “Who [say] that these are gods.” ORELLI.

“When, if a true examination of the matter is made and maintained.” Meursius prefers: “When, if an examination of the facts is made,” etc. ORELLI.

“Than if you had imbibed the purpose of doing this openly, with avowed curses.” *Combibere* here means to induce something deeply into one’s mind. In the same sense Lucretius uses *imbibere*, III, 1009:

> Who has imbibed the desire to seek from the people the fasces and cruel axes.

And VI, 70:

> …Not because the supreme power of the gods  
> Can be violated, so that it should imbibe the desire, in anger, to exact bitter penalties.

HERALDUS.

The Leiden edition has *coimbibissetis*; I do not know whether this comes from a manuscript. Compounds of verbs with *con-* are indeed familiar to Arnobius, as was shown above at Book II, chapter 18. But I would not venture to change anything here, since the figurative use of *combibere* also occurs in Cicero, *On Ends*, III, chapter 18. For *confessis*, Stewechius prefers *contextis*. The manuscript codex has *contestis*. It is well known that copyists very frequently interchange the letters *st* and *x*. ORELLI.

“He does not grant credence to matters wrapped in obscurity.”

> For many things prevent knowledge: both obscurity and the shortness of human life  
> (*Πολλὰ γὰρ τὰ κωλύοντα εἰδέναι, ἥ τε ἀδηλότης καὶ βραχὺς ὢν ὁ βίος τοῦ ἀνθρώπου*).

[Col. 1146B] He is alluding to the opinion of Protagoras. HERALDUS.

“Yet heaps incidental praises upon them.” Canterus restored this reading, with confirmation from the manuscript codex, in place of *subcisivis*, which stood in the printed editions. Surveyors called *subsicivum* or *subsecivum* that which remains outside the normal line—that is, the line closing the side of a square. For land division was reduced to quadrature. See W. Goes, *Antiquitates Agrariae*, chapter 12, in *Scriptores Rei Agrariae*, p. 102 ff. Shoemakers likewise called *subseciva* those pieces which, in cutting the material, they discarded as though superfluous, from *subseco, -are*, for which the ancients said *subsico, -are*. See G. J. Vossius, *Etymologicon Romanum*, s.v. *subsicivum*, and the commentators on Cicero, *Second Philippic*, chapter 8, p. 244, vol. VI, ed. Graevius. Hence, by transference, Cicero in the passage cited speaks of *subsecivae horae, operae*—“spare hours” and “spare efforts,” that is, times and studies—and here we have *subsicivae laudes*, “incidental praises”: praises that are not reckoned here, but are other and different from those which you either attribute to your gods or expect or demand should be attributed to them—*anderweitige Lobsprüche*, “praises of another kind.” ORELLI.]

## XXX

I confess that for a long while, as I have reflected within my mind upon monstrosities of this sort, I have habitually wondered that you dare call any of these people atheistic, irreligious, and sacrilegious—those who either deny altogether that there are gods or doubt their existence, or those who maintain that they were human beings and, because of some power or merit, were admitted into the number of the gods. For if a true examination is made and maintained, no one [Note: [Col. 1145B] Sabaeus reads *nullius*.] deserves such designations more than you do: under the guise of worship, you heap more curses and crimes upon them than if you had imbibed the purpose of doing this openly, with avowed curses.

The person who doubts that there are gods, or who denies altogether that they exist, although by the audacity of his opinion he may seem to follow monstrous doctrines, nevertheless attacks no person but merely declines to grant credence to matters wrapped in obscurity. And the person who asserts that they were of earthly stock, although he deprives them of the sublimity of heavenly beings, nevertheless heaps incidental praises upon them [Col. 1146A], since he believes that through benefactions and the admiration of their virtues they were raised to the rank of divinity.

[Note: [Col. 1146C]

## XXXI.—“Promoters”

Fulvius Ursinus printed “defenders.” ORELLI.

“Any one of these.” Gelenius and Salmasius printed: “Any single one of these.” [Col. 1146D] ORELLI.

“Or at least restrained by the authority of their name.” Meursius conjectures: “Or by the authority of their divinity,” etc. ORELLI.

“Pretty little boys.” See above, at chapter VI of this book, and Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, Book VII, p. 486. ORELLI.

“With most graceful lines.” *Lineae* means the lines or contours of bodies, *Gesichtszüge*, “facial features.” The metaphor is drawn from painters. See Salmasius on Solinus’ Proem, *Exercitationes Plinianae*, p. 5, and what we observed above at Book III, chapter 13. ORELLI.

“Dishonorably.” Thus Elmenhorstius and the Leiden edition, following Meursius’ emendation. Previously the text read “unjustly.” ORELLI.

“Castrated”—that is, in respect of the genitals (*κατὰ genitalia*). ORELLI.

“Even obtained earthly burials”: “to obtain earthly tombs” (*γηΐνων τάφων τυχεῖν*). For this is what *mereri* means here and in countless other passages. HERALDUS.—See the note at Book I, chapter 3. ORELLI.

“Crimes to the dishonor of the gods.” Thus Canterus from the manuscript. Previously: “among dishonors.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1147B] “Because of our name.” This passage confirms that above, [Col. 1147C] Book I, chapter 5, the reading should be: “It has come about because of our name.” ORELLI.]

## XXXI

But you, who have maintained that you are their champions and promoters of their immortality—have you passed over any one of them and left him unscathed by your curses? Or is there any kind of disgrace so condemnable in common estimation that you have feared to fasten it upon them, restrained at least by the authority of their name?

Who has declared that the gods loved perishable and mortal bodies? Was it not you? Who has said that they committed those sweetest thefts in the marriage beds of others? Was it not you? Who has said that sons engaged in intercourse with their mothers, and unfortunate fathers in turn with their own maiden daughters? Was it not you? Who has said that pretty little boys, and grown men of the most graceful bodily contours, were dishonorably sought after [Col. 1146B]? Was it not you? Who has said that some were castrated, some worn out by debauchery, some shape-shifters, some thieves, some held in bonds and chains; who, finally, has said that some were struck by thunderbolts, some wounded, some met their final day, and even obtained earthly burials? Was it not you?

Why, then, when so many and such great crimes have been fabricated by you to the dishonor of the gods, do you dare object that because of our name [Col. 1147A] the minds of the divine powers have been offended, when it has long been clear that you yourselves are guilty of such great wrath and are the authors of divine indignation?

[Note: [Col. 1147C]

## XXXII.—“In the pursuit of the subjects”

For my part, I think it should be written as a single word: “in the persecution of the subjects” (*rerum*—that is, “of our religions”—*in insectatione*). ORELLI.

“Nor such as just anyone can readily understand by intellectual vigor.” Arnobius often calls readiness and strength of mind *vivacitas*, “vigor,” just as he speaks of a “living intellect” above, Book III, chapter 6, where the notes may be consulted. Conversely, slow people seem virtually dead. Servius, on Book VI of the *Aeneid*: “For in a healthy body the mind possesses one degree of vigor; in a sick body it is more sluggish.” HERALDUS.—See J. F. Gronovius, *Observationes*, Book III, chapter 4, p. 352, Platner’s edition. ORELLI.

“But through allegorical meanings,” etc. See Plato, *Cratylus*; Theodoret, *Discourse III Against the Greeks*, pp. 44–45; Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*; Clement, *Recognitions*, Book X, p. 163. ELMENHORSTIUS.

“The embraces of Venus.” Meursius wished to correct this to: [Col. 1147D] “the embraces of Ceres.” Wrongly: “embraces of Venus” means Venus-like, amorous embraces—“prostitute couplings” (*περιπλοκαὶ πορνικαί*)—and nothing more. ORELLI.

“He calls Jupiter the rain and Ceres the earth.” C. Barthius, on Statius, *Thebaid*, IV, 758, p. 1256, conjectures that “Rhea” should be read, since mention of the daughter—namely Ceres—immediately follows. But above, chapter 20, we read: “When Diespiter burned with improper lusts and forbidden desires for Ceres, his own mother—for this mother of Jupiter is said by the inhabitants to belong to that region.” Nothing, therefore, should be changed. ORELLI.

“The man who says that Proserpina was carried off by her father Dis.” Firmicus, in the passage cited: “They claim that Proserpina signifies the substance of crops, because crops benefit (*prosunt*) human beings when they begin to be sown.” ELMENHORSTIUS.

“Not, as you suppose, for the vilest appetites.” Thus Fulvius Ursinus from the manuscript codex. The first edition has the thoroughly corrupt “Not as [the appetites] of Ceres”; Gelenius has “not by the force of Ceres.” ORELLI.]

## XXXII

“But you are mistaken,” he says, “and going astray; and by your very pursuit of the subjects you demonstrate sufficiently that you are inexperienced, unlearned, and rustic. For all those stories which appear shameful to you and injurious to the divine dignity contain within themselves holy mysteries and wonderful, profound explanations—not such as just anyone can readily understand by intellectual vigor. For what has been written and placed upon the first surface of the words is not what is meant and stated; rather, all those things are understood through allegorical senses and hidden, substituted meanings.

“Accordingly, the man who says [Note: [Col. 1147B] Sabaeus reads *dicet*, ‘will say’.] that Jupiter slept with his own mother does not mean incestuous or shameless embraces of Venus [Col. 1147B], but calls Jupiter the rain and Ceres the earth. And the man who reports in turn that he practiced wantonness with his daughter says nothing about foul pleasures, but uses Jupiter to signify rain and the daughter to signify seed. So too the man who says that Proserpina was carried off by her father Dis does not say, as you suppose, that the vigorous maiden was abducted for the vilest appetites. Rather, because we hide seeds in clods of earth, he signifies that the goddess went beneath the earth and contracted with Orcus the covenants of generative fertility.

“In the same way, in the remaining stories one thing is stated but another is understood; beneath the common simplicity of the language lies a secret explanation and the veiled profundity of a mystery.” [Col. 1148A]

[Note: [Col. 1147D]

## XXXIII.—“For since one is ashamed and disgraced to accept the straightforward readings, recourse has been had to this course”

Thus [Col. 1148B] Salmasius. The manuscript codex has: “It is unseemly into this course,” which makes no sense. Sabaeus and Gelenius corrected it to: [Col. 1148C] “there has been an inclination toward this course.” Stewechius supplies: “one is ashamed, disgraced, it is unseemly; this course has been taken.” Heraldus reads: “hence provision has been made”—using the old *cotum* for *cautum*—“for this course”; and in his *Second Corrections*: “this course is taken.” Following the traces of Salmasius’ emendation, but adhering more closely to the manuscript reading, I would emend it thus: “hence recourse has been had to this course.” Here “readings” means the opinions of writers, a sense in which Tertullian uses this word several times. ORELLI.

“In the signification of the prominent words.” Stewechius conjectured “of the words issuing forth,” wrongly. For “prominent words” are properly opposed to the obscure meaning of the ideas. ORELLI.

“And yet, lest we appear unwilling to examine what sort of thing this is that is being said.” Construe: “And yet, lest we appear unwilling to examine what sort of thing this is that is being said.” ORELLI.

“If only you are willing to grant us a patient hearing.” Meursius thinks the reading should be *parientiam*, “obedience.” But since this word is supported by the authority of no ancient writers, but only of critics who restore it in Aulus Gellius, Cassiodorus, Salvianus, the Pandects, and so forth, I would not, contrary to the evidence of the codices, alter *patientiam*, meaning “patient ears.” ORELLI.

“First, in the allegorical mode.” The word “first” is altogether redundant here, since “first we ask this of you” has preceded. ORELLI.

“How did this become known to you, or how was it disclosed to you? The writers summoned you into their counsels, of course? Or were you then hiding within their breasts,” etc. I printed this following the punctuation of Heraldus and Oberthür. The old reading was: “How did this become known to you, or how was it disclosed to you that the writers summoned you into their counsels? You, of course, were then hiding within their breasts,” etc. ORELLI.

“Disclosed.” The glosses: “To disclose … to make known” (*γνωρίσαι*). Martianus Capella, *On the Marriage of Philology*, Book VI, p. 192: “What I taught even to them—something that scarcely ever happens—I shall disclose as well as I can in Roman words.” Book VII, p. 136: “He disclosed everything to his ears.” Apuleius uses this word [Col. 1149C], as do Firmicus, *Astronomy*, Book VI, chapter 12; Prudentius, *Martyrdom of Romanus*; and Aelius Spartianus, *Pescennius Niger*, chapter 7. ELMENHORSTIUS.—“Known” and “disclosed” differ. *Intimare* means “to make known, reveal, manifest” (*γνωρίσαι, ἐμφανίσαι, φανερῶσαι*); therefore, “what has been disclosed” is *τὸ φανερωθέν*, while “what has become known” is *τὸ γνωσθὲν δι’ ἡμῶν*, “what has been learned through our own agency.” Thus in the same book Arnobius distinguishes “to know” and “to learn.” See Heraldus—who discusses this verb at length—*Adversaria*, Book I, chapter 3, p. 7 ff.; and Casaubon and Salmasius on the *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, p. 405 ff. ORELLI.

“With the truth intercepted.” This is a tmesis familiar to Arnobius, standing for “with the truth intercepted” (*intercepta veritate*). Others emend it, wrongly. Similarly, he has *adquaesitum* for *adquisitum*, *aedifacere* for *aedificare*, and so forth. STEWECHIUS.

[Col. 1149D] “So that you wish to understand what they did not wish [you to understand]; you wish to know,” etc. Meursius transposes these words thus: “So that what they did not wish you to understand, you wish yourselves to know,” etc. Not badly. ORELLI.]

## XXXIII

These are all, as is evident, sophistries and ingenious subtleties of the sort commonly employed to support bad cases in court. Or rather, to speak more truly, they are the rhetorical colors of sophistical disputations, by which not truth but always an image, appearance, and shadow of truth is sought.

For since one is ashamed and disgraced to accept the straightforward readings, recourse has been had to this course: one thing is substituted for another, and an interpretation of shamefulness is forced into the appearance of decency. But what concern is it of ours whether other meanings and other opinions underlie these empty compositions? For to us, who contend that the gods are treated criminally and impiously by you, it is enough to accept what is written [Col. 1148B] and what is heard, and not to trouble ourselves about what may lie hidden beneath it, since the insult to the divine powers lies not in the obscure meaning of the ideas but in the signification of the prominent words.

And yet, lest we appear unwilling to examine what sort of thing this is that is being said, first, if only you are willing to grant us a patient hearing, we ask you this: how did it become known to you, or how was it disclosed to you, that these writings either were composed in the allegorical mode or ought to be understood in that same way? The writers summoned you into their counsels, of course? Or were you then [Note: [Col. 1148B] The manuscript has *utrum*, “whether,” correctly, according to Meursius.] hiding within their breasts [Col. 1149A], when, with the truth intercepted, they substituted one thing for another?

Next, if through fear arising from some principle and from religion they wished to wrap those mysteries in shadowy obscurity, how great is your audacity, that you wish to understand what they did not wish you to understand; that you wish to know and lay open to the knowledge of all what [Note: [Col. 1149C] Sabaeus reads *quid*, “what”.] they concealed—to no purpose—in words that did not signify the truth?

[Note: [Col. 1149D]

## XXXIV.—“Hinds are said in place of Iphigenias”

A proverbial expression: “Hinds in place of Iphigenias,” or “A hind in place of a maiden” (*ἔλαφος ἀντὶ παρθένου*). Achilles Tatius, *The Loves*, Book VI, chapter 2:

> And he, naturally enough, when he beheld the most extraordinary spectacle—the proverb of the hind in place of a maiden—was astonished and stood in silence.  
> (*Κᾀκεῖνος, ὡς τὸ εἰκός, θέαμα ἰδὼν παραδοξότατον, τῆς κατὰ τὴν ἔλαφον ἀντὶ παρθένου παροιμίας, ἐξεπλάγη καὶ ἔστη σιωπῇ.*)

See Boden on that passage, p. 506 ff. The proverb was applied to those who either, after being disappointed in a great hope, obtain some trifling thing; or who, though accused of a crime, are acquitted because innocent of the matter; or finally, as here, when one thing is fraudulently substituted for another, falsehood for truth. See Hadrianus Junius, *Adagia*, century VI, no. 2.

Its basis is the well-known story of Iphigenia, daughter of Agamemnon. When at Aulis she had already been placed by her father upon the altar to be sacrificed for the safety of the Greeks, she is said to have been snatched away by Diana and a hind substituted in her place [Col. 1150C]. See Euripides, *Iphigenia at Aulis*, verse 1585 ff.; Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, XII, 34; Hyginus, *Fables* 78 and 261. ORELLI.

“You disclose.” The Leiden and Catana editions read: “You unfold.” ORELLI.]

## XXXIV

But let us grant you that in all these stories hinds are spoken of in place of Iphigenias. How, nevertheless, is it clear to you, when you unfold or disclose these allegories, that you are interpreting and understanding [Note: [Col. 1150C] Fulvius reads *sentiri*, “were understood”.] the same things that the historians themselves conceived in their unspoken thoughts, but expressed not by the proper words but through other significations?

You say that the intercourse of Jupiter and Ceres signifies rain falling into the bosom of the earth. Another person can fabricate something else by ingenious reasoning and conjecture something else possessing a likeness to truth. A third can propose one thing and a fourth another; and according as the qualities of the conjecturing intellects incline them, so each individual matter can be explained by infinitely many interpretations.

For since this whole so-called allegory is derived from matters that are closed up, and possesses no definite limit in which the meaning of the matter under discussion is fixed and immovable, everyone is free to draw the reading toward whatever he wishes and to affirm that the author meant whatever his own suspicion and conjectural inference has led him to. Since this is so, how can you derive certain matters from doubtful ones and attach a single signification to a statement which, as you can see, may be drawn through innumerable paths by a diversity of explanations?

[Note: [Col. 1150C]

## XXXV.—“If you consider it suitable”

*Accommodus* is the same as the simple *commodus*, “suitable.” Virgil, *Aeneid*, XI, 522–523:

> There is a valley with a winding bend, suitable for an ambush  
> And for the stratagems of war.

ORELLI.

“All the stories about the gods.” Thus Salmasius, following an emendation of Meursius. Previously the reading was “all the stories about these.” Heraldus, in his *Second Corrections*, prefers: “All these stories?” ORELLI.

[Col. 1150D] “That is, every one of them.” Meursius deletes these words as a gloss on “all.” ORELLI.

“Wholly two-sided.” Thus Gelenius emended the text and the remaining editors followed him. The manuscript codex has: “whether two-sided,” which Stewechius defends. ORELLI.

“And, for Libera and her father Dis, the sinking and casting of the seed.” Meursius deletes this very sound emendation. Libera is Proserpina, as was shown above. Previously the reading was: “and, for Liber and for father Dis,” which prompted Fulvius Ursinus to correct the following words to: “the sinking of the seed and the pouring of wine.” ORELLI.

“Brimo.” Thus Th. Canterus restored the text from the manuscript, as above at chapter 20, where the notes may be consulted. ORELLI.

“And the torches kindled by that fire.” “That” means the fire just mentioned; this manuscript reading is confirmed by the words preceding in chapter XXIV: “She takes twin torches kindled by the flames of Aetna.” Previously the text read: “and those kindled torches.” STEWECHIUS and ORELLI.

“What the shaving means.” Stewechius rashly disturbed this entirely correct manuscript reading, conjecturing that it should be “what the stripping means.” Salmasius rightly defends it on Aelius Lampridius, *Heliogabalus*, chapter 31, *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. I, p. 871.

Latin writers elegantly use *novare* for “to polish” and, as it were, “make new.” Valerius Flaccus:

> Here, with crimson salt and living water,  
> He refreshes his gleaming limbs.

Hence “to renew the beard” means to smooth it and, as it were, make it new; a *novaculum* is an instrument by which the beard is renewed and shaved and the skin smoothed. Thus *novatio* appropriately means the smoothing of the genitals, which caused her to assume a purer appearance, as he said above in chapter 25. ORELLI.

“Nor can you substitute.” Thus Meursius, very correctly, for “oppose.” For he had previously said: “what ought to be substituted.” The letter *s* had adhered to the end of the preceding word, and the copyist, as usual, had written *o* for *u*. ORELLI.

“Nor summon a different context of events.” I have restored to the text this reading of the first edition, which comes closest to the corrupt wording of the codex: “nor either … context.” *Alterum* means “different, changed,” as in Horace, *Odes*, II, 10, 14:

> A heart well prepared  
> Hopes in adversity and fears in prosperity  
> A changed fortune.

[Col. 1155D] *Vocare* stands for *advocare*, “to summon,” namely, to your cause. A “context of events” is the continuity of events, when all things agree with and fit one another. Thus Cicero, *On Ends*, Book V, chapter 28: “And, by Hercules, their interconnection of matters is remarkable: the conclusions correspond to the premises, the intermediate points to both, and everything to everything.”

The meaning of our passage will therefore be: “unless you can summon to your cause a context and connection of events entirely different from the true one”—*wenn ihr nicht einen ganz andern Zusammenhang der Dinge annehmen könnet*, “unless you can assume an entirely different connection of events.” Failing to understand this, Gelenius changed it to: “Nor summon individual things into the context of events”; Stewechius: “Nor summon them into a different context of events”; Heraldus and Meursius: “Nor summon them into the true context of events”; the Leiden editor: “Nor summon them into a different meaning of events.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1152B] “Why, by obscure allegories, do you make respectable what is dishonorable?” Without doubt, “dishonorable” must be read. For the stories Arnobius adduces are shameful and obscene. ORELLI.]

## XXXV

Finally, if you consider it suitable, we seek an answer from you to this further question, repeated once again [Col. 1149C] [Col. 1150A]: do you consider all the stories about the gods—that is, every one of them—to be wholly two-sided, double-speaking, and written in shape-shifting modes? Or do some parts of them state nothing ambiguous, while others are manifold and veiled by the superimposition of an allegorical covering?

For if the entire text and sequence of the exposition, from beginning to end, are enclosed by allegorical veils, explain and show what we ought to substitute for each individual subject described by every story, what we ought to bring forth from it, and to what other subjects and meanings we ought to refer them. For just as you wish Jupiter, for example, to be understood as rain and Ceres as earth, and Libera and her father Dis as the sinking and casting of seed, so you must tell us what we ought to understand by the bull; what by the indignation and wrath of Ceres; what the word *Brimo* means; what Jupiter’s anxious supplication means; what the heavenly beings who were called upon but did not listen mean; what the castrated ram means; what the offspring of the castrated ram means; what the satisfaction made to them means; and what is meant by the things once again enacted with the daughter in still more obscene lust.

Likewise, in the other story, what are the grove of Enna and the flowers? What is the fire taken from Aetna, and the torches kindled by that fire? What is the journey throughout the world with them? What is the region of Attica? What is the Eleusinian village? What are Baubo’s hut and rustic hospitality? What does the drinking of the *cyceon* signify? What does the rejection of the drink mean? What do the shaving and exposure of the genitals mean? What is the shameful delight of the spectacle, and what the oblivion of bereavement obtained through such remedies?

If, by transforming the subjects, you show what ought to be substituted for all these things, we shall then be able to grant our assent to your assertion. But if you cannot substitute something for every individual item or summon a different context of events, why, by obscure allegories, do you make respectable what was stated plainly and published for common understanding?

[Note: [Col. 1152B]

## XXXVI.—“But that some parts were written commonly”

That is, plainly and for common understanding. I therefore do not know why they wished to interpolate this passage. HERALDUS.—Fulvius Ursinus printed: “written in a unified manner” [Col. 1152C]. The Leiden edition has: “commonly composed,” though I do not know whether on the authority of a manuscript codex. Here, therefore, *communiter* has the same meaning as what we call “popular.” ORELLI.

“That is an urbane subtlety, one accessible to any brute.” C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book XXIX, chapter 14, thinks the reading should be: “That is an urbane subtlety—but one accessible to any Brutus.” The learned man evidently thinks Arnobius is joking and playing upon words: because he had spoken of an “urbane” subtlety, he introduces with a double meaning the name of Brutus, ruler of the city and first consul, since in one sense it denotes a wise man, but in the other a stupid one.

But there is no need for this emendation if we interpret “urbane subtlety” not as witty and elegant cleverness, but as a trifling, jocular subtlety—*gemeine, abgedroschne Subtilität*, “commonplace, hackneyed subtlety.” See Victorius, *Variae Lectiones*, IV, 12; J. F. Gronovius, *De Sestertiis*, Book IV, chapter 9, p. 318 ff.; and Ernesti, *Clavis Ciceroniana*, s.v. *urbanus*. ORELLI.

“Difference” (*differitas*). Thus L. Carrio restored the reading from the manuscript. Others have *differentia*. See above, at Book II, chapter 16. ORELLI.]

## XXXVI

Unless perhaps you say that these allegories do not extend throughout the entire body of a story, but that some parts were written commonly and others in a double sense, veiled by a two-sided covering. That is an urbane subtlety, one accessible to any brute. For since it is exceedingly difficult for you to transfer, invert, and redirect everything that has been written, you select certain things that accord with your wishes and, on their basis, strive to maintain that spurious and adulterated readings have been superimposed upon an inner truth.

Yet even if we grant you that matters stand as you say [Col. 1151B], how do you know, or from what source do you learn, which part of the story was written with a plain meaning, and which is covered by discordant and alien significations? For it is possible that what you suppose to be one way is in fact another, or that what you believe to be otherwise was expressed according to different and contrary conceptions.

For when it is said that within the body of a single composition one part was written allegorically and another in unmistakable [Col. 1152A] and straightforward language, while the matter itself contains no sign by which the difference between ambiguous and plainly stated things can be judged, it is just as possible to suppose that what is plain was spoken ambiguously as to believe that what was written ambiguously has been stripped of its coverings. We confess that we are utterly unable to understand either how this can happen or how it can be believed possible.

[Note: [Col. 1152D]

## XXXVII.—“Proserpina, the vigorous maiden, was gathering flowers”

J. Meursius added “the vigorous maiden” from the manuscript, with Heraldus’ approval. ORELLI.

“For the four-horse team, the chariot.” Meursius conjectures: “What is the four-horse chariot?” taking “four-horse” adjectivally. But such redundancies of expression are far from uncommon in Arnobius. ORELLI.

“Summanus.” See above, at Book III, chapter 44, and J. F. Gronovius, *Lectiones Plautinae*, p. 87. Plautus, *Curculio*, III, 46, coined from it the verb *summanare*, “to steal, seize greedily.” ORELLI.

“So that the story was suddenly transformed into something else.” Canterus was the first to restore “suddenly,” absent from the earlier editions, to the text from the manuscript codex. The manuscript has *aliud*, an old form defended by Meursius as archaic and Lucretian. See Doering on Catullus, poem LXVI, verse 28. But it is scarcely credible that Arnobius used this archaic and obsolete form in this one passage when it occurs nowhere else in his entire work. ORELLI.

“These expressions are used here in accordance with their own characters and conditions.” That is, according to the characters and conditions proper to those gods. Stewechius therefore disturbed the passage to no purpose by conjecturing the reading: “These expressions are used here with their own notions and distinctions,” as above in Book I: “By what conception could he designate pestilence and hailstorms?” Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “by names and distinctions.” ORELLI.

“To the real Jupiter.” Meursius conjectures that the reading should be: “to the word Jupiter.” Wrongly. ORELLI.]

## XXXVII

Let us examine what is said in this fashion.

“Once, in the grove of Enna,” he says, “Proserpina, the vigorous maiden, was gathering flowers.” Up to this point the account is intact and expressed in straightforward language; for what a grove and flowers are, what Proserpina is, and what a vigorous maiden is, are undoubtedly known to everyone.

“Summanus flashed forth from the earth, borne in a four-horse chariot.” This too is equally plain [Col. 1152B], for the four-horse team, the chariot, and Summanus require no interpretation.

“Appearing unexpectedly, he seized Proserpina and carried her away with him beneath the earth.” “The hiding of seed,” he says, “is designated by the abduction of Proserpina.” What happened, I ask, so that the story was suddenly transformed into something else and Proserpina was called seed? Why did she who had long been regarded as a vigorous maiden engaged in gathering flowers begin, after she was taken away and abducted, to signify [Col. 1153A] seed for sowing?

“Jupiter,” he says, “was transformed into a bull and sought intercourse with his mother Ceres.” As was explained above, by these names are designated earth and falling rain. I see the allegorical rule explained through shadowy ambiguities.

“Ceres became angry and blazed with rage, and received the offspring of a ram as punishment and vengeance.” Here again I see matters readily expressed in common forms of speech; for anger, testicles, and satisfaction are expressions used here in accordance with their own characters and conditions. What happened here, then, so that the subject passed from Jupiter, who is rain, and Ceres, who was called the earth, to the real Jupiter and to the plainest possible statement of events?

[Note: [Col. 1153C]

## XXXVIII.—“Cannot be led by transformation into the allegorical”

Thus Canterus restored the text from the manuscript codex. Previously the reading was: “into an allegory.” What if, with Elmenhorstius, we read: “cannot by transformation be led into an allegory”? [Col. 1153D] ORELLI.

“A proscription can indeed, as Tullius jokes, be called and termed a battle of Cannae.” Cicero, *For Roscius of Ameria*, chapter XXXII: “The battle of Cannae made you a sufficiently good prosecutor. We saw many men slain, not at Lake Trasimene, but at the Servilian Lake.” ELMENHORSTIUS.

“But the battle which was fought long ago cannot be that same thing, the very same proscription.” Fulvius Ursinus and Stewechius conjecture: “but the battle which was fought long ago cannot be a battle,” etc. ORELLI.]

## XXXVIII

Therefore, either everything must have been written and set down in the allegorical mode, and the whole must be demonstrated to us [Col. 1153B]; or nothing was composed in that mode, since what is believed to exist, as though in only part of a story, does not appear to exist at all.

“All these things were written in the allegorical mode.” That by no means appears certain. Do you ask for what reason and on what ground? Because everything that has been done and has been established in the manifest reality of some action [Note: [Col. 1153C] Sabaeus adds *est*, “has been”.] cannot be transformed into an allegory. For what has been done cannot become undone, nor can the nature of an accomplished event degenerate into an alien nature.

Surely the Trojan War cannot be transformed into the condemnation of Socrates? Or that battle of Cannae into a proscription and the cruelty of Sulla? A proscription can indeed, as Tullius jokes, be called and termed a battle of Cannae [Col. 1153C] [Col. 1154A]. But the battle which was fought long ago cannot be that same thing, the very same proscription. For, as I said, what has been done cannot be anything other than what was done; nor can that which is fixed in its own proper force and in the quality of its own kind migrate into an alien substance.

[Note: [Col. 1153D]

## XXXIX.—“From what source, then, do we prove that these histories are written accounts of accomplished events?”

Here too a word is missing. I write: “that all are allegorical accounts of events,” etc. Read what precedes, and you will see. MEURSIUS.

“Or what the peoples transmit in secrecy.” Salmasius’ conjecture, “or what is secretly handed down to the initiated,” is bold and unnecessary. ORELLI.

[Col. 1154C] “That pine which is solemnly carried into the sacred precinct of the Mother-goddess.” Here too Stewechius wishes to correct “sacred precinct” to “sanctuary.” Wrongly. See above at chapters VI and XVI of this book, and Ezechiel Spanheim, *On the Use and Excellence of Coins*, dissertation VI, vol. I, p. 313. ORELLI.—Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religion* (p. 457, ed. J. Gronovius): “In the Phrygian rites, which they call the rites of the Mother of the Gods, every year a pine tree is cut down, and in the middle of the tree an image of a young man is fastened.” ELMENHORSTIUS.—Meursius prefers “into the sacred precinct … of the Mother of the Gods,” correctly; for our author consistently calls her by that title. ORELLI.

“Attis deprived himself of his manhood.” *Virum*, “man,” means the genital organs, as we observed above. ORELLI.

“Of the phalli.” Thus the manuscript. Others read: “of the ithyphalli.” ELMENHORSTIUS.]

A fawnskin conferred distinction upon the family of the Nebridae. [Col. 1154D] I do not remember reading anywhere that there was any family of this name in Attica. But Arnobius—or the author from whom he took this—having read of a family of the Νεβριδῶν (*Nebridae*) on the island of Cos (see Stephanus of Byzantium, s.v. Κῶς, “Cos”), transferred it to Attica, because those initiated into the rites of Ceres were girded with the skin of a fawn, which the Greeks call a νεβρίς (*nebris*). Bacchus, or Iacchus, was worshiped together with Ceres in those Attic initiations, and his attendants and the Bacchants wore νεβρίδες (*nebrides*, “fawnskins”), as is clear from countless testimonies of authors. Accordingly, in the Eleusinian mysteries, which belonged jointly to Ceres and Iacchus, νεβρίδες were also employed by the initiates. They called this νεβρίζειν (*nebrizein*, “to wear a fawnskin”) and νεβρισμός (*nebrismos*, “the wearing of a fawnskin”). See Harpocration under that word. He therefore confused τοὺς Νεβρίδας, the Coan Nebridae—so named after Nebrus, the grandfather of Hippocrates the Great, as L. Holstenius teaches in his note on Stephanus, at the place cited, p. 184—with τοὺς νεβρίζοντας, those in Attica who wore the fawnskin. SALMASIUS, *Exercitationes Plinianae in Solinum*, p. 607. Heraldus thinks that the initiates of Ceres were called Nebridae because Ceres, while seeking her daughter and wandering through the wastes of the earth, was covered with a fawnskin [Col. 1155C]—of which circumstance, so far as I know, there is no mention among the ancients. But the fawnskin was the emblem of Bacchus and the Bacchants. Clement of Alexandria, in the *Protrepticus*: “Come, you madman, without leaning upon the thyrsus, without being crowned with ivy; cast away the headband; cast away the fawnskin; come to your senses.” For *hinnulae* (“of a fawn”), Fulvius Ursinus printed *hinnulea*. ORELLI.

*If from actual events*, etc. The same Fulvius reads: *si e rebus actis?* (“if from actual events?”), etc. ORELLI.

*Who have fastened upon themselves a religious rite.* Meursius: *affinxerint* (“have fabricated”). Incorrectly. For Arnobius uses the same expression below, Book VI, chapter 1: “You are accustomed to fasten upon us the gravest charge of impiety.” And chapter 26: “He would be fixed in perpetual numbness.” There Meursius incorrectly reads: “would be afflicted.” ORELLI.]

### XXXIX

From what, then, do we prove that all these narratives are written accounts of actual events? From the solemn rites, of course, and the mysteries of initiation—whether those performed at fixed times and on fixed days, or those which nations transmit in secrecy [Note: [Col. 1153C] Sabaeus incorrectly reads *Genitis*.]—while preserving the continuity of their own custom. For it must not be believed that these practices exist without origins of their own, are performed vainly and without meaning [Note: [Col. 1154C] Thus Sabaeus. Others read *inaniter*, “idly.”], or have no causes connected with their first institution.

That pine tree [Col. 1154B] which is solemnly carried into the sanctuary of the Mother Goddess—is it not an image of the tree beneath which Attis, after cutting off his genitals, deprived himself of his manhood, and which, as tradition relates, the goddess consecrated as a consolation for her grief? That erection of phalli and representations of shameful deeds, which Greece adores and celebrates in annual rites—does it not reproduce the deed by which Liber freed himself from his obligation? Those Eleusinian mysteries and the hidden rites of the sacred ceremonies—of what event do they preserve the memory? Is it not of that wandering in which the weary Ceres, while searching for her daughter, came to the shores of Attica, brought crops of wheat, honored the family of the Nebridae with a fawnskin, and laughed at that extraordinary spectacle in Baubo’s groin? [Col. 1154C] [Col. 1155A] Or, if there is some other cause, that makes no difference to us, provided that all these things arise from some cause. For it is not credible that these practices were adopted with no preceding causes; nor should the Athenians be judged insane for having fastened upon themselves a religious rite formed from no grounds whatever.

But if it is clear and established—that is, if the causes and origins of the mysteries flow from actual events—they cannot by any transformation be converted into allegorical forms. For what has been done and enacted cannot become undone, since the nature of things forbids it.

[Note: [Col. 1155D]

### XL.—*A fall of rain from heaven*

Here *labes* means the same as *lapsus*, “a fall.” Nothing more. ORELLI.

*Moisture.* See the note on Book I, chapter 2. ORELLI.

*To speak about the work of agriculture.* Stewechius was the first to recover this entirely correct reading from the manuscript, although he prefers: “to speak about the work.” Previously the text was absurdly printed: “with the disgrace of Dis the Father, the God of agriculture, to declare.” For who ever called Dis the Father the God of agriculture? ORELLI.—I write: “with the disgrace of Dis the Father and of the God of agriculture,” taking *Dei* (“God”) for *Deae* (“Goddess”). Thus in Book III: “They declare Diana, Ceres, and Luna, by commonplace sisterhood, to be the head of one God.” Thus Virgil:

> I descend, and with a god as my guide, pass through flame and foes.

Compare Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book III, chapter 8. MEURSIUS, p. 174.—But in his appendix the same scholar adopts the manuscript reading. ORELLI.

*And to lose that gush of voice and din of foul loquacity*, etc. The manuscript has: “than to emit that gush of voice [Col. 1156C] and din of foul loquacity”; from this Stewechius restored the passage accordingly. Not badly. ORELLI.]

### XL

And yet, even if we grant you that these matters stand as you say—that is, that the narratives sound like one thing in their words but, after the manner of soothsayers, mean some other thing or other—do you not notice, do you not see, with how much dishonor and insult to the gods this claim is made? Can any more serious affront [Col. 1155B] be found than to say and call the intercourse of Jupiter and Ceres “earth and rain”—or whatever else it may be, for it makes no difference into what interpretation it is converted—and by the crimes of the gods to signify the fall of rain from heaven and the moisture of the soil? Can anything be considered or believed more irreligious than to call seeds buried in the earth—or anything else, for here likewise it makes no difference—the abduction of Proserpina, and to speak about the work of agriculture with the disgrace of Dis the Father attached to it? Would it not have been a thousand times preferable [Col. 1155C] to become speechless and mute, and to lose [Col. 1156A] that gush of voice and din of foul loquacity, rather than to call utterly shameful things by the names of the gods—or, still worse, to signify commonplace processes by the gods’ shameful deeds?

[Note: [Col. 1156C]

### XLI.—*Formerly it had been customary to veil allegorical expressions with thoroughly honorable meanings, and to clothe things shameful and foul to utter in the dignity of honorable things*

I have given the old reading, which has a sound and straightforward sense: namely, that it was customary to veil allegorical expressions—obscene ones, evidently—with thoroughly honorable meanings or explanations. Meursius prefers *obumbrari* (“to be veiled”), which I too prefer because of the following *convestirier* (“to be clothed”). Salmasius, however—whether relying upon the authority of the manuscript I do not know—printed the passage thus: “Formerly it had been customary, in allegorical discourse, [Col. 1156D] to veil with thoroughly honorable meanings things shameful and foul to utter,” etc. ORELLI.

*Are mentioned.* Thus Meursius and Salmasius, very correctly, for *commorantur* (“linger”). ORELLI.

*So that what formerly—the depravity of foul things—was covered by modesty is now expressed slavishly and shamefully, the language of worthy things having been changed.* I have given the manuscript reading, deservedly restored by Salmasius; except for the final words “of worthy things,” etc., it is entirely sound. The first editor, Sabaeus, altered everything with extreme boldness, printing: “So that what formerly—the depravity of a foul thing—was covered by modesty is now expressed scurrilously and shamefully, the worthy thing having been changed in expression.” In this reading, to say nothing of other matters, *verniliter* (“slavishly, buffoonishly”) was very badly changed into *scurriliter* (“scurrilously”). But the whole text was sound, provided that after “of worthy things” we insert a single word, *gravitas* (“dignity”), so that “the dignity of worthy things” may be opposed to “the depravity of foul things.” ORELLI.

*You had wished … you indicated.* Thus the Leiden edition. Others: “he had wished … he indicated.” ORELLI.

*Did it entail any danger?* I read thus with Meursius, instead of: “Did it entail no danger?” ORELLI.

[Col. 1157C] *The image of a foul thing.* Here too the manuscript has “of foul things.” HERALDUS.

*Should subject.* Thus Gelenius. The first edition: *subeat* (“should enter”). ORELLI.]

### XLI

Formerly it had been customary to veil allegorical expressions with thoroughly honorable meanings, and to clothe things shameful and foul to utter in the dignity of honorable things. But under your authority grave matters are expressed through obscenity, and things powerful in purity are mentioned in obscene words; so that what formerly—the depravity of a foul thing [Note: [Col. 1155C] Write: “of foul things.” Notas reads this. The manuscript incorrectly has *foederum*, “of treaties.”]—was covered by modesty is now expressed scurrilously and shamefully, the language of worthy things having been changed.

“When we say,” he states, “that Mars and Venus were ensnared in adultery by Vulcan’s art, we mean desire and anger, [Col. 1156B] subdued by the force and counsel of reason.” What prevented or hindered you from expressing each thing in its own words and with its own meanings? Indeed, when you wished to indicate some matter or other through treatises and writings, what compelled you to refuse to have understood the very thing you indicated, and instead to undertake two contrary purposes at once in a single exposition: the zeal of one wishing to teach and the ill will of one unwilling to disclose? Did calling the gods adulterers entail any danger? Would the utterance of “desire” and “anger” have polluted your tongue and mouth by obscene contact? If [Col. 1156C] that had in any case been done and the veil of allegorical blindness removed, [Col. 1157A] the matter would have been easy to learn and the dignity of the gods would have been preserved unharmed.

But now, when it is said that the binding of Mars and Venus signifies the restraint of vices, two utterly perverse effects occur at the same time: the image of a foul thing subjects an honorable meaning to itself, and obscenity strikes the mind before the authority of any religious meaning does.

[Note: [Col. 1157C]

### XLII.—*Or why do you take pains to unravel these things in the explanation of allegories?*

Thus the Leiden edition, entirely correctly. Others read: “into an explanation.” ORELLI.

*You number among them and say.* Perhaps one should read: “you mention.” CANTER.

*For whom, amid the sacred observances, we see specifically annual and expressly divine rites performed.* This is a transposition of words familiar to Arnobius, for: “for whom, amid the sacred observances, we see annual divine rites performed specifically and by name”—that is, in the name of Attis himself, not merely by invoking the sun’s name. ORELLI.

[Col. 1157D] *But if it is a goat-name and Phrygian.* Above, chapter 6: “Or because the Phrygians in their own speech call goats *attagi*, from that it came about that he received the name Attis.” ORELLI.

*From the mutilated man.* Meursius suspects that the text should read: “from the surname of the mutilated man.” Incorrectly. For he had just said: “Was the name Attis transferred from the man to the sun?” ORELLI.

*Should be deemed worthy to be called.* Stewechius’ conjecture is plausible: “should be deemed a god and be called.” Elmenhorst reads: “more worthy.” ORELLI.]

### XLII

Unless perhaps you will say—for this alone remains as something you might think can be raised in opposition—that the gods do not wish their mysteries to be known by human beings, and that this is why the narratives were written in allegorical circumlocutions. But how is it clear to you that the gods above do not wish their mysteries to be made public among human beings? How do you know those mysteries, or why do you take pains to unravel them in the explanation of allegories? [Col. 1157B] Finally and ultimately, what do the gods mean by this: that, while unwilling to have honorable things said of them, they permit utterly shameful and indecent things to be said?

“When we name Attis,” one says, “we signify and mean the sun.” But if Attis is the sun, as you number him among them and say, who will that Attis be whom your writings report and declare to have been born in Phrygia, to have suffered certain things and likewise to have performed certain things; whom every theater knows from dramatic shows; for whom, amid the sacred observances, we see specifically annual and expressly divine rites performed? Was this name transferred from the sun to the man, or from the man to the sun?
