For if this name has its original source [Col. 1157C] in the sun, what, pray, did the golden sun [Col. 1158A] do to deserve from you that you should make this name common to it and to a half-man? But if it is a goat-name and Phrygian, what offense did the father of Phaethon, the source of this light and brightness, commit, that he should be deemed worthy to be called after a mutilated man and should be made more august by being designated with the name of an emasculated body?

[Note: [Col. 1157D]

### XLIII.—*In the coupling of Jupiter and Ceres*

Others read *coitu* (“intercourse”), incorrectly. See above. ORELLI.

*The concealment of the seed.* I restore *occultatio* (“concealment”) for *occupatio* (“seizure”), a correction which immediately suggests itself to anyone reading the passage. ORELLI.]

### XLIII

But what the truth of the matter is has now become obvious to everyone. Because you are ashamed of writings and narratives of this sort, and see that you cannot abolish what has once been shamefully recorded in written accounts, you strive to dignify shameful things; by every kind of clever device you substitute other matters for them and overturn and corrupt the natural meanings of words. And, as commonly happens to the mentally deranged, whose turbulent violence of disease has driven away perception and understanding, you utter confused and uncertain things [Col. 1158B] and rave amid fictions concerning empty matters.

Granted: in the coupling of Jupiter and Ceres, let the irrigation of the earth be signified; in Dis’s abduction, the concealment of the father’s seed; in the tearing apart of Liber’s entrails, wines scattered over the earth; and let the binding together of the adulterers Venus and Mars be called the restraint of desire and rashness.

[Note: [Col. 1157D]

### XLIV.—*Transformations*

That is, changes, τρόπους (*tropous*, “turnings” or “figures”), in the proper and primary sense. Thus *foliorum versura* (“turning of the leaves”) in Varro, *On Agriculture*, I.46; see Schneider’s index there. ORELLI.

[Col. 1158C] *For what shall we substitute for those clubs?* By “clubs” Arnobius means that very stout fig-tree branch which Liber fashioned into the form of a human penis and planted over the mound of the tomb beneath which Prosumnus had been buried, as we read above in chapter 48. I therefore do not see what moved Salmasius to change *fustibus* (“clubs”) into *fluctibus* (“waves”). ORELLI.

*The lust of Semele’s offspring twisted.* Stewechius and Salmasius, in his notes on Solinus, pp. 28 and 628, have shown that *urigo* (“lust”) must be read instead of *origo* (“origin”), which the first edition has. Fulvius Ursinus and Heraldus correct it to *prurigo* (“itch, lust”). But *urigo* signifies the same thing, namely the itching for intercourse, καυθμός, κραῦσις (“burning desire”; German *die Brunst*). Thus Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, I: “She, soon aroused by lust, draws me onto her couch.” See Stewechius [Col. 1158D] and Oudendorp there, p. 35. Meursius, p. 475, has collected further examples. The ancient poets use *uri* (“to burn”) in the same sense of a most ardent passion—for example, Virgil: “Unhappy Dido burns,” etc. Ovid:

> I burn, as waxen torches burn when sulfur is applied,  
> As pious incense burns when placed upon smoking pyres.

Gesner’s *Thesaurus* lacks the noun *urigo*. *Contorquere* (“to twist”) is used in an obscene sense, as is the simple *torquere* above, chapter 28: “She twists her buttocks this way and that.” ORELLI.

*And what for those abducted Ganymedes?* Canterus restored the text thus from an emendation by L. Fruterius. Previously it read: “Ganymedes obtained.” ORELLI.

*Appointed as masters of lusts.* If the reading is sound, the sense will be that Ganymede was appointed to teach Jupiter his lusts. Thus above, chapter 29: “A man … assisted by the instruction of sacred divinity”—which is utterly false. I therefore embrace C. G. Schwarz’s conjecture in his note on [Col. 1159B] Pliny’s *Panegyric*, reading: “appointed to the services of lusts.” See Burmann on Valerius Flaccus VII.536, and Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 11. ORELLI.

*Seductive.* See above, the note on Book IV, chapter 36. ORELLI.

*By such an account concerning the gods above.* Fulvius Ursinus incorrectly printed: “to such an account,” etc. ORELLI.

*You added, as the saying goes, the picarel to the garum.* This manuscript reading, which Meursius produced in his appendix, was restored to Arnobius as entirely correct and elegant [Col. 1159C] by N. Heinsius, *Adversaria*, Book VI, chapter 8, p. 619 in Burmann’s edition, and by Salmasius in the Leiden edition. “To add a picarel to garum” was a proverb applied to those who defile the most precious and august things and deprive them of their honor by joining the vilest and most abject things to them. (A similar proverb, admittedly filthy and rather indecent, remains in use among common people: *D . . . . . in die Milch machen* [“to s— in the milk”].) For *garum*, an exquisite sauce prepared from the entrails of fish—especially mackerel, the best of which were caught in Spain—and macerated with salt, was counted among the most costly foods. See Apicius Caelius, Book I, chapter 7, and Lister there; the interpreters on Petronius, chapter 36; Gesner in the *Thesaurus*; and especially the *Geoponica*, Book XX, chapter 46, with Niclas there, p. 1270; likewise the distinguished Heindorf on Horace, *Satires* II.7.46, p. 437. By contrast, Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XXXII, chapter 53—see Harduin there, p. 594, vol. II—and Martial, Book III, epigram 76, mention *gerres* (“picarels”) as exceedingly cheap little fish:

> And picarels delight you, and melandrya with gray skin.

And Book XII, epigram 32:

> That they were picarels, or worthless *maenae*,

[Col. 1159D]

> The shameless odor of the jar confessed.

Ausonius, in the preface to *Idyll* XI, p. 448 in Tollius’s edition: “And so I have sent you trifles more worthless than Sicilian picarels, so that, when you are doing nothing, you may read them, and, lest you do nothing, defend them.” The glosses: “*Gerres*: μαινίδες (*mainides*, picarels).” See Turnebus, *Adversaria*, Book XXIV, final chapter.

Not understanding this, [Col. 1160B] Sabaeus—and all the remaining editors after him down to Salmasius—printed: “You have added, as the saying goes, gangrene.” Hadrianus Junius, in the supplements to Erasmus’s *Adages*, century VIII, proverb 5, explains this as: “You have doubled the evil; you have aggravated an old fault by adding a new offense.” For gangrene is a kind of cancer. Lucilius in the *Satires*:

> So that it might spread through the evil like gangrene and creeping herpes.

[Col. 1160C] But the manuscript reading is far more elegant and expressive; I am greatly surprised that Oberthür did not admit it into his edition. ORELLI.

*You have defiled.* Stewechius prefers *coinquinavistis*, “you have polluted,” as above, Book IV, chapter 34: “To compose a malicious song by which another’s reputation and life are polluted.” He observes from Festus that *inquinare* and *coinquinare* are derived from the old verb *cunire*, which means “to make dung.” But Victorinus, *On Orthography*, p. 2467 in Putsch’s collection, maintains that *conquino* is both said and written. Compare Scaliger and Mercerus on Plautus, *Pseudolus*, Act III, scene 2, verse 75. ORELLI.

*Indubitable.* Others: *indubitabile*.]

### XLIV

But if you wish these tales to have been written in allegorical fashion, what is to become of the others, which we do not see can be forced into transformations of this kind? For what shall we substitute for those clubs which the lust of Semele’s offspring twisted over the mound of a tomb? And what for those abducted Ganymedes, appointed as masters of lusts? What for that transformation into an ant, into [Col. 1158C] which Jupiter the Greatest compressed the outlines [Col. 1159A] of his immensity? What for the swans and satyrs? What for the golden showers into which that same seducer clothed himself by deceit, playing treacherously with varieties of form?

And lest we seem to have wished to speak of Jupiter alone: what things in the love affairs of the other divine beings can be allegories? What allegories are there in their service for wages and their enslavements? What in their bonds, bereavements, and lamentations? What in their tortures, wounds, and tombs? In this matter, although you could have incurred a single fault by such an account concerning the gods above, you added, as the saying goes, the picarel to the garum: you called shameful things by the names of gods, and in turn defiled the gods with the names of infamous things.

But if you believed with indubitable certainty that they were present here or existed anywhere, fear would strike you whenever you made mention of them; you ought to have believed and kept it fixed in your thoughts that they were listening to you and receiving your words. For among people devoted to dutiful religious observance, not only the gods themselves [Col. 1159B] but also the gods’ names [Col. 1160A] should be treated with reverence. As much dignity as belongs to the beings thought to bear these names ought likewise to belong to the names by which they are called.

[Note: [Col. 1160C]

### XLV.—*Give the true form of the judgment*

Stewechius emended the text thus from the manuscript, citing the parallel passage in Book II, chapter 2: “Give a true judgment”; there, however, one should read with Heraldus: “Give a boy as judge.” Others read: “According to the true form of judgment.” For *formam* (“form”), Meursius conjectures *normam* (“standard”). ORELLI.

*But speech is sordid if it has been polluted with such words. Modesty worthy of praise*, etc. The manuscript has: “Modest and worthy of praise,” from which Stewechius suspects that one should read: “As befits modest and refined persons, you blush,” [Col. 1160D] etc., explaining “refined persons” as people trained in the pursuit of dignity, in which sense the expression occurs in Book VII. Meursius, in the appendix, thinks one should read: “This modesty is worthy of praise.” The Leiden edition: “But speech is sordid if it has been polluted with such words; modest and worthy of praise”—ironically, of course. For my part, I would not alter anything against the manuscript’s authority. ORELLI.]

### XLV

Give the true form of the judgment, and you are liable to censure in this respect also: in your customary speech you use “Mars” for battle, “Neptune” for water, “Father Liber” for wine, “Ceres” for bread, “Minerva” for yarn, and “Venus” for obscene lusts. [Note: [Col. 1159B] Thus the manuscript, correctly. Sabaeus reads the singular, “lust.”] For what reason is there that, although things can be designated by their own names, they should instead be called by the names of gods, and that the divine beings should receive an insult which not even we human beings would endure, if anyone were to take our names and transfer and distort them into names for trivial objects?

But [Note: [Col. 1160B] Others: “And.”] speech is sordid if it has been polluted with such words. What modesty, worthy indeed of praise! You blush to name bread and wine, [Col. 1160B] yet you are not afraid to say “Venus” in place of sexual intercourse.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 1161]

## INDEX OF CHAPTERS

[Col. 1161A] In this and the following book Arnobius refutes another accusation made by the pagans: that Christians were guilty of the greatest impiety because they had no temples or images of the gods and never offered them any sacrifices. Chapters 1–2.

He begins with the temples of the gods and acknowledges that Christians indeed have none—not out of contempt for the gods, if any such beings exist, but because they despise temples as incapable of being of any use to the gods, and because, moreover, it is more insulting to the gods rashly to assert that any god can be enclosed within a temple. Chapter 3.

When the pagans reply that temples are erected for the gods so that people may converse with them as though they were in some manner present, Arnobius answers that the true God knows even the silent thoughts of our minds, hears all things equally, and is absent nowhere—in a word, that by his immensity he is present everywhere. [Col. 1161B] Chapters 4–5.

He adds that many temples of the gods are nothing other than tombs of the dead. From this Arnobius concludes that temples have been constructed for the gods in vain and contrary to their dignity. Chapters 6–7.

There is certainly no better reason for worshiping their images. For if the gods are in heaven, prayers should be poured out to them rather than to their images. The author adds further arguments against the images of the gods. Chapters 8–10.

The ancients who worshiped as gods a river, a scimitar, a stone, a shapeless piece of wood, or anything similar were deservedly mocked by the pagans. Arnobius shows, however, that those very pagans who invented no less absurd things about the gods deserve mockery just as much. Chapters 11–12.

Nor did the pagans merely give their gods ornaments unworthy of them; [Col. 1161C] they also gave them the form and features of certain human beings and prostitutes. Chapter 13.

Arnobius therefore exhorts the pagans to return to a sounder frame of mind and at last understand that the images which they worshiped with such honor are bones, stones, bronze, silver, gold, and very often the cheapest material. Chapters 14–15.

To this is added the fact that, if anyone were to enter the innermost parts of the image of Olympian Jupiter or of any other god, what would he see except plates, or pieces of wood and stone, fastened together with poured lead or with chains, hooks, [Col. 1162A] and rings? Would he not see the head, belly, and other parts of the image hollow and empty within? And whatever appears on the exterior becoming discolored, collapsing, and being polluted? Chapter 16.

By various arguments Arnobius demolishes the pagans’ opinion that it is not the material of the images that is worshiped, but the gods who dwell within the images. Chapters 17–19.

He presses the question: why, then, do they protect the images and guard them carefully against injury? Chapters 20–21.

If you say that the gods care nothing about such things, nevertheless they at least should have preserved unharmed the images and shrines in which they lived from the insolence of depraved persons, from fire, and from other accidents. Chapters 22–23.

Finally, Arnobius destroys the pagans’ last refuge: their repeated assertion that certain people had not been ignorant of all these facts, but had nevertheless thought the uneducated multitude ought to be kept dutiful and religious by the worship of images. [Col. 1162B] Chapters 24–27.

[Note: [Col. 1161D]

### I.—*What impious disgraces of opinions you have established concerning your gods*

This is a sound reading. For he shows that there was no kind of disgrace which they did not proceed to attribute to their gods. Why, then, read *insanias* (“madnesses”)? HERALDUS.—Fulvius Ursinus’s conjecture *insanias* can be defended from the parallel passage in Book II: “Nor should we have wished to wander through the impious madnesses of suspicions.” ORELLI.

*To fabricate against us the gravest charge of impiety.* Sabaeus, Gelenius, and Salmasius printed *affigere* (“to fasten upon”). But in Book I, chapter 26, we read: “Who fabricates a charge of impiety against those who serve the supreme King?” Nothing, therefore, should be changed. ORELLI.

[Col. 1162D] *Because we neither construct sacred buildings*, etc. Thus in Minucius Felix, chapter 10, Caecilius asks: “Why do Christians have no altars, no temples, no recognized images?” See the interpreters there. Compare Heraldus’s note below on chapter 3 of this book. ORELLI.

*By rash despair.* See above, the notes on Book I, chapters 25 and 55. C. Barthius, therefore, *Adversaria*, Book XXIX, chapter 18, p. 1390, should not be followed when he conjectures: “By rash disdain.” For disdain and contempt are one and the same. ORELLI.

*But because we suppose them.* Stewechius restored this from the manuscript. Others: “But because we suppose the gods.” ORELLI.]

### I

Now, since we have shown in summary what impious disgraces of opinions you have established concerning your gods, it follows that we should speak about temples, images, and sacrifices, and about the further series of matters attached to them and connected with them by close association.

For on this point you are accustomed to fabricate against us the gravest charge of impiety: because we neither construct sacred buildings for the duties of worship, nor set up an image or representation of any god; because we make neither altars nor sacrificial hearths; because we offer neither the blood of slaughtered animals, nor incense, nor salted grain, nor, finally, [Col. 1162C] liquid wine in libations poured from bowls. We refrain from constructing or performing these things, not because we possess impious and criminal minds, or because in rash despair concerning the gods we have adopted contempt for them, but because we suppose and believe that, if indeed there are any true gods endowed with the eminence of that name, they either regard such forms of honor as ridiculous, if they are capable of laughter, or endure them with indignation, if they can be provoked by movements of anger.

[Col. 1163A]

[Note: [Col. 1163B]

### II.—*So that the same things may be said again and to satiety*

The edition of Gelenius has “jointly.” ORELLI.

*Nor devote themselves to external aids.* Thus the Leiden edition. The manuscript has: “Nor devote to external aids [Col. 1163C].” Stewechius reads: “Nor devote themselves to external aids.” Gelenius and Fulvius Ursinus ingeniously reconstructed: “To need aids.” Heraldus conjectures *addigere*, a word for which I have searched the dictionaries in vain. ORELLI.

*Of untroubled blessedness.* Thus in Gellius, Book II, chapter 1: “untroubled health”; Solinus, chapter IV: “untroubled happiness”; Ovid, *Tristia* I, elegy VIII: “an untroubled life”; Pliny the Younger: “untroubled pleasure”; Tacitus: “an untroubled journey.” ELMENHORST.

*Not to hold them liable and bound by obligations arising from vows.* Horace, *Odes* II.8.5 ff.:

> But you, as soon as you have bound  
> Your faithless head by vows, etc.

HERALDUS.

*Expiatory victims.* By this he means purificatory expiations which possessed the power to avert portents. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book V: “The praetor who then pronounced the formula, if he did so unknowingly, is purified by an expiatory pregnant victim.” Compare Book I, chapter 26: “Others call them victims carried about the streets,” because, [Col. 1163D] evidently, the victims by which the threats of portents were expiated were carried around, and all places were thus fortified against the divine being’s anger. Apuleius, *Milesian Tales* IV: “At last, after being led through every street, in the manner of those who with purificatory expiations avert the threats of portents by victims carried about the streets, I am conducted by an angular route through the forum and stationed beside its tribunal.” ELMENHORST and HERALDUS.

*To support their prosperity.* That is, to increase their happiness. Fulvius Ursinus therefore incorrectly conjectures: “to support their adversity.” ORELLI.

*To suffer, feel pain, and be diminished.* That is, to be corrupted, φθείρεσθαι (*phtheiresthai*). Above, Book I, chapter 18: “Where there is disturbance, there are pain and sickness. Where there are pain and sickness, there is already room for diminution and corruption.” HERALDUS. Thus the manuscript, Ursinus, and the Leiden editor. Gelenius: “to suffer pain, to be diminished.” Stewechius: “to suffer, through pain to be diminished.” ORELLI.

*Heavenly beings.* Thus Salmasius; the manuscript: “from heaven”; Gelenius: “of the heavenly beings.” Others: “celestial beings.” ORELLI.]

### II

So that you may know what we think about this designation and what judgment we hold, we believe that, if indeed there are any true gods—to say the same things once again and to satiety—they ought to be wise, just, grave, and possessed of every perfect virtue, provided that there is no fault in heaping human praises upon them. They ought to abound in inward goods and not devote themselves to external aids, since through those inward goods the completeness of untroubled blessedness is fulfilled in them. They ought to be free from every emotion and every disturbance: not to blaze up in anger, not to be aroused by any desires, not to inflict calamity upon anyone, not to derive a cruel will from human wickedness, not to terrify by portents, not to display prodigious horrors, not to hold people liable and bound by obligations arising from vows, and not to demand expiatory victims through threatening signs [Col. 1163B]; not to bring pestilences and diseases through corruption of the air, not to scorch crops with drought, not to take part in the slaughters of wars or the destruction of cities, not to wish adversity upon these people or support the prosperity of those. Rather, as befits [Note: [Col. 1163B] Others read: *esset* (“it was”).] [Col. 1164A] great minds, they ought to weigh everyone in an equal balance and display an inseparable benevolence toward all.

For the doctrines and pronouncements of the wise define it as belonging to a perishable nature and to human weakness to need contrary conditions, and for those touched by emotion to suffer, feel pain, and be diminished. Nor can it be otherwise than that those enslaved to any disturbances are bound by the laws of mortality. Since this is so, how can we be judged to hold the gods in contempt, when we deny that those who are not upright and admirable for the greatness of their minds exist as gods at all, or can be counted among the powers of heaven?

[Note: [Col. 1164B]

### III.—*To whom the gods, together with us, owe*

I have printed this following the emendation of Johannes Meursius, which Johannes Walker also approved in his note on Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, Book I, chapter 13, p. 335 in Davis’s edition. The manuscript and all editions [Col. 1164C] have: “To whom divine things, together with us, owe.” Heraldus thinks the word *divina* (“divine things”) should be deleted as a gloss. C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book XXIX, chapter 18, p. 1391, suspects that one should read: “To whom the vain gods, together with us, owe”; but a little later, retracting this conjecture, he defends the common reading and argues that *divina* can be used for “gods” from the example of Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*, Book II, chapter 2: “But if the gods cannot be absent—because, since they are diviners, wherever in the world they may be, they see and hear all things.” He also cites Cyprian, *Poem on Sodom*:

> Although ignorant of the divine ones, of his own accord  
> He calls upon and addresses them, revering them with a father’s honor.

But, apart from the fact that in these two passages the gods are called *divini* in the masculine, not *divina* in the neuter, the passage of Lactantius proves nothing, since there they are called *divini* because they are endowed with the faculty of divination. I have therefore preferred to follow Meursius’s correction. ORELLI.]

Do we honor him with shrines or with the construction of temples? [Col. 1164D] If temples are magnificently constructed places in which images of a god are set up and where a god is thought, as it were, to dwell, just as we have buildings for use as dwellings, then in the earliest periods of the Church Christians had no temples. But if every place in which the faithful assemble, invoke God with united prayers, and perform the other offices of religion is to be called a temple, then Christians certainly always had their own temples: namely, private houses and whatever parts of houses were available, cemeteries, and even woods and caves in which they assembled when persecutions were raging. Once the violence of the persecutions had subsided, however, they did erect meetinghouses (*οἴκους, οἴκους ἐκκλησιῶν*, “houses, houses of churches”); not for display, nor as places where some image of a god might be approached as though it were a divinity present there, but humble buildings differing in humility not at all from private houses. For this reason the Gentiles, who valued the outward appearance of things more highly than the inner recesses of the heart, repeatedly insisted that Christians had no temples and no shrines. [Col. 1165B] Christians freely admitted this; indeed, they asserted that the use of temples was not merely superfluous but even impious, and that God was to be consecrated not in *ναοῖς χειροποιήτοις* (“temples made by hands”), but in our own minds. See Minucius Felix, chap. XXXII; Origen, *Against Celsus*; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, book VII; Lactantius, *On the Wrath of God*, final chapter. What is more, Christians rejected the very designation “temple” as though it had arisen from idolatry. Hence Zeno of Verona, in his sermon *On Continence*: “Let us suppose, therefore, as often happens, that on one and the same day the observances of different religions coincide, so that you must go to church, and he to the temples.” He calls the Christians’ meetinghouse a church, but assigns temples to the Gentiles. Hence also blessed Jerome, in his letter to the priest Riparius against Vigilantius: “They kept vigils for a dead and polluted corpse, so that after many centuries one who slept might dream—or rather belch forth his most unclean drunkenness—and, together with Julian the persecutor, either destroy the basilicas of the saints [Col. 1165C] or convert them into temples.” Thus, even when Christian affairs were flourishing and their basilicas were no less splendid than many temples of the Gentiles, they nevertheless abstained from that designation and left it to the nations. HERALDUS.—Already among the ancients there were differing opinions about *delubra* (“shrines”). The classic passage is Asconius on Cicero’s *Divination against Caecilius*: “Some say that *templa* are places assigned individually to particular gods, while *delubra* are complexes of many chambers beneath a single roof, protected from the flooding of rain. Others call those temples *delubra* in which there are basins for washing bodies, such as those of Jupiter at Dodona or Apollo at Delphi, in whose shrines cauldrons and tripods may be seen. There are also those who suppose that *delubra* were pieces of wood that had been *delibrata*, that is, stripped of their bark, and set up as images of the gods in the ancient manner; but this is wrong.” Servius, on *Aeneid* II.225, explains a *delubrum* as a temple consecrated to several gods. Compare G. J. Vossius, *Roman Etymologies*; Gesner in the *Thesaurus*, under this word; and J. Rycquius, who treats the matter at length in his book *On the Capitol*, chap. XII, p. 140 ff. Christian writers, however, use the words *delubrum* and *templum* interchangeably. [Col. 1165D] ORELLI.

“Do we also slaughter victims?” Thus the Leiden edition; the manuscript: “Do we slaughter victims?” Fulvius Ursinus: “Do we slaughter victims for him?” ORELLI.

“More powerful.” Manuscript: “more excellent,” a reading defended by Stewechius. ORELLI.

“Or for the necessity of what thing.” The word “or” is supplied by Gelenius; the manuscript omits it. ORELLI.

“You say.” Stewechius prefers: “you consider.” ORELLI.

“Certain slight elevations.” See the note on book I, chap. 50. Meursius conjectures: “upon certain slight elevations.” ORELLI.

“Of a poverty-stricken mind.” *Paupertinus* means poor and needy. See Nonius under this word, and Savaron on Sidonius, book II, epist. 10, p. 155, and book VII, epist. 17, p. 475. Thus “poverty-stricken letters” in Gellius, book IV, chap. 6; “poverty-stricken elements” in Tertullian, *Against Marcion*, book I, chap. 14; “ragged and poverty-stricken little possessions” in Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book IV. ORELLI.

[Col. 1166B] “If you ask to hear who was their first builder,” etc., etc. Clement, in the *Protrepticus*, p. 13 (38 in Potter’s edition):

> “Hence it occurs to me to wonder by what imaginings the first men to go astray were led away when they proclaimed superstition to humankind and ordained that accursed demons should be worshipped—whether that man was Phoroneus, or Merops, or someone else—those who erected temples and altars to them; and they are also mythically reported to have been the first to institute sacrifices.”

CANTER.

“Either Phoroneus, an Egyptian, or Merops.” It must be punctuated thus, rather than: “either Phoroneus the Egyptian, or Merops.” Arnobius likes to transpose and interweave that particle in this manner. HERALDUS.—Heraldus’s punctuation is uniquely correct. For Phoroneus was not an Egyptian, but a king of Argos. Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, translated by Jerome, no. 211: “Phoroneus, son of Inachus and Niobe, first established laws and courts. Some think that Niobe was his daughter.” See there Joseph Scaliger, [Col. 1166C] p. 19; Lutatius on Statius, *Thebaid* I.541 and IV.589: “This man, Phoroneus, is said to have been the first to sacrifice to Juno, as Dardanus was to Jupiter. Phoroneus, moreover, was the son of Inachus and the first of mortals to reign; Jupiter is said to have been the first to violate his daughter Niobe among mortal women, since there is another Niobe, the daughter of Tantalus.” The same man established a temple for his younger brother Phegeus after his death, where cattle were sacrificed to him as to a god, according to Augustine, *City of God*, book XVIII, chap. III. Compare Hyginus, fables 143, 225, and 274, and Muncker there, pp. 211 and 327; Pausanias, book II, p. 112; Tatian, *Against the Greeks*; Marsham, *Chronological Canon*, p. 83 ff., Franeker edition; and C. Barthius on Statius, vol. III, p. 1502. Meursius thinks one should read: “Phoroneus the Argive.” But everything will be sound if Heraldus’s punctuation is restored. ORELLI.

“An Egyptian, or Merops.” In book II, preface, of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* translated by Jerome, we read: “Now this man is Cecrops Diphyes, a native, under whom the olive first sprang up on the citadel and the city of the Athenians received its name from Minerva. He was the first of all men to name Jupiter, devise images, set up an altar, and sacrifice victims, since nothing of this kind had previously been seen anywhere in Greece.” Joseph Scaliger therefore, in his notes, p. 13, alters Clement, from whom Arnobius adapted his material, by substituting *Κέκροψ* (“Cecrops”) for *Μέροψ* (“Merops”). But since our author too has “Merops,” this appears to be an error of Clement himself rather than of a copyist. Cecrops, the first king of Attica, must certainly be understood. Some, for example Apollodorus, *Library* III.14, make him *αὐτόχθονα* (“autochthonous”); others make him an Egyptian, as does the scholiast on Aristophanes, *Plutus* 773:

> “Cecrops, who was Egyptian by birth, settled Athens; hence the Athenians are called Cecropidae.”

Suidas repeats this verbatim, as does Tzetzes, *Chiliades* V, History 18:

> “After that flood in the time of Ogygus,  
> Cecrops came from Sais, a city of Egypt,  
> to Athens in Greece.”

Compare Meursius, *On the Kings of Athens*, book I, chaps. 8–12. ORELLI.

[Col. 1167A] “Or, as Varro relates in his *Marvels*.” The words “or, as” were added by Canter. The title of Varro’s book was *Gallus Fundanius, On Wonders, or On Marvels*. See *Fragments of Varro*, [Col. 1167B] p. 253, Zweibrücken edition. ORELLI.

“Aeacus, offspring of Jupiter.” See Hyginus, fables 52 and 155. ELMENHORST.

“Or gleam with golden coffered ceilings.” Pliny, *Natural History* XXXIV.3: “Coffered ceilings, which are now covered with gold even in private houses, were first gilded on the Capitol after the destruction of Carthage, during the censorship of Lucius Mummius; from there the practice passed to vaulted ceilings, and also to walls, which are now themselves gilded like vessels.” ELMENHORST. Ovid, *Fasti* I.223:

> Temples delight us too, though we approve the ancient ways;  
> golden magnificence is fitting for a god.

And verse 77:

> The flame strikes the gold of the temple with its brilliance  
> and scatters a trembling radiance through the summit of the shrine.

Not only coffered ceilings but also doors and other parts of temples were gilded, and because of these ornaments the temples were called “golden.” HERALDUS.

“Here let gems shine.” Ovid, *Fasti* I.201 ff.:

> Jupiter could scarcely stand at his full height in the narrow shrine,  
> and in Jupiter’s right hand was a thunderbolt of clay.  
> They adorned with foliage the Capitol now adorned with gems,  
> and the senator himself pastured his sheep.

Hence Lactantius, *Institutes* V.8: “His temple is not stones or clay, but the human being himself, who bears the image of God. That temple is adorned not with gold and gifts of gems, but with the eternal gifts of virtues.” HERALDUS.

“And, diversified by patterned inlay, pour forth starry radiance.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.619:

> He marvels, and turns over in his hands and arms  
> the helmet terrible with crests and breathing flames.

ORELLI.

“Nor refuse or disdain to be enclosed.” [Col. 1167D] That is: “and no less refuse and disdain these dwellings,” etc. An Arnobian turn of phrase. HERALDUS.

“And be confined and shut in by the barriers they present.” This is the genuine reading of the manuscripts. He speaks similarly in book VII: “behind whose obstruction and opposition he had screened himself.” STEWECHIUS.—Others read “by obstructions,” as shortly before in this same chapter: “to protect them by an obstruction of stones.” ORELLI.

“‘This,’ he says, ‘is the temple of Mars,’” etc. Hence they even inscribed the name of the particular god upon the doors of temples. Iamblichus, *Life of Pythagoras* I.2:

> “When Mnesarchus returned to Samos from Syria with very great profit and abundant wealth, he built a sanctuary to Apollo and inscribed upon it: ‘OF PYTHIAN APOLLO.’”

Note the form of the inscription *Πυθίου*, “of Pythian Apollo,” for the genitive case is used absolutely in this way. Accordingly, this passage should have been rendered: “He constructed a temple to Apollo with this inscription: OF PYTHIAN APOLLO.” This was the customary form of inscription. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* I:

> “And the Latins construct for him a hero-shrine adorned with the following inscription: ‘OF THE FATHER, THE CHTHONIAN GOD WHO GOVERNS THE STREAM OF NUMICIUS.’”

[Col. 1168A] Plutarch, *Eroticus*:

> “And Belestiche, by Zeus, was not some barbarian woman from the marketplace; the Alexandrians have sanctuaries and temples of hers which, through love for the king, they inscribed: ‘OF APHRODITE BELESTICHE.’”

Thus Pliny, *Natural History* VIII.18: “For this reason Elpis dedicated a temple on Samos to Father Liber, which the Greeks, after that event, called ‘of gaping Dionysus.’” That is, they inscribed it *κεχηνότος Διονύσου*, “OF GAPING DIONYSUS.” And book X, chap. 3: “For this reason the inhabitants made what they call a hero-shrine in that place, named ‘of Jupiter and the Maiden’”—*Διὸς καὶ Κόρης*, “OF ZEUS AND KORE.” Marcus Tullius Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III.34: “Dionysius now ordered the silver tables to be removed from all the shrines; since they bore the inscription ‘of the good gods,’ in accordance with the custom of ancient Greece, he said that he wished to make use of their goodness.” Zosimus, book II:

> “An altar was found which bore the inscription: ‘OF HADES AND PERSEPHONE.’”

Servius on book III of the *Aeneid*: “Others say that in the temple of Apollo there was an altar inscribed: ‘OF ANCESTRAL APOLLO.’” Other monuments too were inscribed in this absolute fashion. Plutarch, *Otho*:

> “When I was at Brixellum, I saw a modest tomb and an inscription which, if translated, would signify: ‘OF MARCUS OTHO.’”

In *Marcellus*:

> “In his honor and memory, Octavia his mother dedicated the library, while Caesar dedicated a theater, inscribing it: ‘OF MARCELLUS.’”

[Col. 1168C] Hence, then, arose the constructions “at the temple of Tellus,” “at that of Diana,” and so forth. HERALDUS.

“This is Hercules’, Apollo’s, Dis’s: what else is this than to say, ‘This house is Mars’, this one Juno’s and Venus’?” These words, absent from the earlier editions, were supplied by Stewechius from the manuscript. Meursius corrects “this is Venus’” to “that is Venus’,” not implausibly. ORELLI.

“Apollo dwells here.” Temples, then, were regarded as dwellings of the gods, and therefore as sacred buildings. Thus *ναός* (“temple”) is said to derive *παρὰ τὸ ναίειν* (“from dwelling”), because the god for whom a temple was constructed was believed to *ναίειν*, “dwell,” in it. Hesychius is therefore correct: *ναός … οἶκος ἔνθα θεὸς προσκυνεῖται*, “temple: a house where a god is worshipped.” Hence the expressions “sacred houses” and “holy houses” occur everywhere in the ancient poets, and “houses of the gods” often in Herodotus, just as does “sacred buildings.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II.27: “Timaeus neatly remarked—as he did many things—that when, in his history, he had stated that the temple of Diana of Ephesus burned down on the night when Alexander was born, he added that this was not at all surprising, because Diana, wishing to attend Olympias in childbirth, had been away from home.” Lucian too censures the construction of temples under this name in his little work *On Sacrifices*:

> “Then they erected temples so that the gods themselves might supposedly not be without houses or hearths.”

HERALDUS.

“Thus is it not,” etc. Stewechius most correctly restores this from the manuscript. Previously it was printed: “Is that not,” etc. Arnobius likes to begin his rebukes with the particle “thus.” So in book V: “Thus do you not perceive, do you not see, with how much ignominy this is said to be done?” Likewise in book VI, in a similar rebuke: “Thus do you not see that these statues whose feet and knees you touch and handle as you pray are breathing?” ORELLI.

“To keep the gods confined within dwellings.” *Distringere* is used here in the rarer sense of binding or constraining—or, more precisely, of enclosing and confining on every side. Thus Cicero, *On Duties* III.32: “For fraud constrains, but does not dissolve, perjury”; see the commentators there. Heusinger, however, printed “binds.” Statius, *Achilleid* II.422:

> [Col. 1169B] … might constrain the air within a circle.

See C. Barthius there, vol. III, p. 1760, and L. Bünemann, who treats this verb extensively, on Lactantius, *Institutes* V.19, p. 669 ff. ORELLI.

“To build chambers and cells.” For the images of the gods were kept in cells. Vitruvius describes those cells in book IV. Thus there were several cells on the Capitol, the meeting-place of all the demons. Livy, book XXXVII, says that the people had once been reproved by him because they wished to make him perpetual consul and dictator; he had forbidden statues of himself to be placed in the Comitium, on the Rostra, in the Senate-house, on the Capitol, or in the cell of Jupiter. In Greek it was called *σηκός*. Hesychius: *σηκός … ἐνδότερος τόπος τοῦ ἱεροῦ*, “*sekos*: the innermost place of the sanctuary.” Diodorus Siculus, book I, speaking of Isis:

> “Likewise, after her departure from humankind, she obtained immortal honors and was buried near Memphis, where to this day her *sekos* is shown within the sacred precinct of Hephaestus.”

[Col. 1169C] Pollux, book I, §6:

> “The place in which we worship the gods is called a sanctuary and a temple; the place where we establish their images is called a *sekos* or sacred precinct. The more precise writers call that of heroes a *sekos*, but the poets use the word also for that of gods, as do the tragedians: ‘Into the god’s holy *sekos*.’”

(See Kühn there, p. 5.) A *sekos*, then, properly belonged to heroes and heroines. Euripides, *Bacchae*:

> I praise Cadmus, who once made that ground  
> inviolable, as his daughter’s sacred enclosure.

A *sekos* of this kind was plainly not some magnificent temple of the sort customarily erected in cities for the greater gods, but rather a chapel than a temple, especially one erected in the countryside—just as we still call those small buildings customarily set up in fields for certain saints “chapels.” The temples of heroes and lesser gods were therefore lower and narrower: chapels and little cells rather than true temples. [Col. 1169D] Hence blessed Augustine, *City of God* IV.23: “For who can bear the fact that Felicity was included neither among the Consentes, whom they say Jupiter calls into council, nor among those gods whom they call select, so that some temple might be made for her which surpassed the others both in the elevation of its site and in the dignity of its workmanship?” HERALDUS. “Little cells,” that is, chapels or certain private little structures within those magnificent temples, in which an image of some particular god was placed. From Aulus Gellius (*Attic Nights* VII.1) we learn that Scipio Africanus was accustomed to enter the Capitol at twilight, order the cell of Jupiter to be opened, and remain there alone for a long time, as though consulting with Jupiter about the Republic. This is confirmed by Livy XXVI.19, Valerius Maximus II.2.2, and Aurelius Victor, *On Illustrious Men* 49. Yet if anyone establishes that by “little hut,” “chamber,” and “cell” Arnobius should also be understood as speaking of the small buildings customarily constructed for lesser gods, we shall not entirely oppose him. [Col. 1170B] NOURRY, p. 480.]

### III

But we erect no temples for them, nor do we adore their images; we do not slaughter sacrificial victims or pour libations of incense and wine. And what [Note: [Col. 1163B] Others: “Is there anything?”] more can we attribute to them, whether of honor or of dignity, than that [Col. 1164B] we place [Note: [Col. 1164B] Others: “we do place.”] them in that rank in which we place the Head and Lord of things, the supreme King himself, to whom the gods, together with ourselves, owe their awareness that they exist and are contained within a living substance? For do we honor him with shrines or with the construction of temples? Do we also [Col. 1165A] slaughter sacrificial victims? Do we give him other things whose offering and outpouring is not a matter of rational expenditure, but merely a custom perpetuated by habit? For it is utter madness to measure beings more powerful than yourself by your own necessities, to give to the gods who bestow them the things that are useful to you, and to consider this an honor rather than an insult.

For what uses of the gods, then, do we seek temples? For the necessity of what thing do you say they were constructed, or think that they should now be built again? Do they feel the cold of winter or burn beneath the summer sun? Are they drenched by rainstorms, [Col. 1166A] or harassed by whirlwinds? Are they in danger of suffering a hostile assault or the rabid attacks of wild beasts, so that it would reasonably be fitting to shut them within the fortifications of roofs or protect them by barriers of stone?

For what are these temples? If you ask human weakness, they are something immense and spacious; if you measure them against the power of the gods, they are certain slight elevations—and, to speak more truly, an extremely cramped species of cave, suspended aloft by the contrivance of a poverty-stricken mind. If you ask to hear who was their first builder [Note: [Col. 1166A] The manuscript aptly adds: “Who was their founder, who their builder”], you will be shown that it was either Phoroneus, or an Egyptian, or Merops; or, as Varro relates [Col. 1167A] in his *Marvels*, Aeacus, offspring of Jupiter.

Let them, if you wish, be constructed of masses of marble, or gleam with golden coffered ceilings; let gems shine there and, diversified by patterned inlay, pour forth starry radiance. All these things are earth, compounded from the lowest dregs of inferior matter. For even if you value them at very high prices, one should not therefore believe that the gods take delight in them, or that they do not refuse and disdain to be enclosed and, shut in, confined by the barriers they present.

“This,” one says, “is the temple of Mars; this one belongs to Juno and Venus; this one to Hercules, Apollo, and Dis.” What else is this than to say, “This house is Mars’; this one Juno’s and Venus’; Apollo dwells here; Hercules remains in this one, Summanus in that one”? Thus is it not the first and greatest insult to keep the gods confined within dwellings [Note: [Col. 1167A] Manuscript: “broken down,” wrongly]? To give them little huts, [Col. 1169A] to build chambers and cells for them, and to suppose that they require things required by human beings, cats, ants, lizards, and timid, fleeing, insignificant mice?

[Note: [Col. 1170B]

### IV.—“But not,” he says, “for that reason”

At this point Fulvius Ursinus wishes to read “you say,” wrongly, as has already been shown several times above. ORELLI.

“But so that we may behold them face-to-face and at close quarters.” The Gentiles advanced this as the principal reason for temples: namely, that they constructed temples so that they might place images of the gods there and address the gods from nearby. Lucian’s *Demonax* ridicules this superstition:

> “When one of his companions said, ‘Let us go, Demonax, to the Asclepieion and pray for my son,’ he replied: ‘You must think Asclepius very deaf, if he cannot hear us praying from here.’”

And Seneca, *Epistle* XLI: “We need not raise our hands toward heaven, nor beg the temple-attendant to admit us to the ear of the image, as though we could be heard better that way.” HERALDUS.

“To address them from nearby.” Properly, “to address” and “speak to the gods.” [Col. 1170C] Plautus in the *Amphitryon*:

> Just now it came into my mind  
> to thank the gods upon my arrival for their favors, and to address them.

Thus the Greek *προσειπεῖν*, “to address.” Euripides, *Heracles*:

> Having at last returned from the sunless recesses  
> beneath Hades and Kore, I shall not fail  
> first to address the gods beneath this roof.

HERALDUS.

“To mingle conversations of worship.” Above, book I: “And to mingle words of supplication and conversations of prayer with God, the Lord of all things.” HERALDUS.

“For this is proper to gods: to fill all things with their power,” etc. See J. Lipsius, *Physiology of the Stoics*, book I, dissertation XXI, *Works*, vol. IV, p. 892 ff., Wesel edition. ORELLI.

“Not to go to dine among the Ethiopians.” Homer, *Iliad* I.423 ff.:

> For Zeus went yesterday to Ocean among the blameless Ethiopians  
> to attend a feast, and all the gods accompanied him;  
> but on the twelfth day he will return again to Olympus.

Compare Nazianzen, *Oration against Julian*, p. 300, and his scholiast there, Elias of Crete; Lucian, *On Sacrifices*, p. 72. ELMENHORST. Compare Statius, *Silvae* IV, “On Domitian’s Banquet.” Eustathius, on this passage of the *Iliad*, records that at Diospolis, a city of Egypt, there was a very great temple of Jupiter, from which the Ethiopians took images of Jupiter and the other gods and, at a certain time, carried them throughout all Libya for twelve continuous days, because that was the number of gods among them. The scholiast on Nicander’s *Theriaca* also mentions this and adds that the Ethiopians customarily proceeded in this solemn procession crowned with tamarisk. MEURSIUS, p. 184.]

### IV

“But,” he says, “we assign temples to the gods not for the purpose of warding off from them damp showers, winds, rains, or the heat of the sun, but so that we may behold them face-to-face and at close quarters, address them from nearby, and, as it were, mingle conversations of worship with beings who are present. For if they are invoked beneath the bare vault of heaven and beneath the covering of the ether, they hear nothing; and unless prayers are brought near to them, they will stand blocked and motionless, as though nothing were being said.”

Yet we think that every god without exception—provided that he truly possesses the power signified by this name—ought to hear, from whatever part of the world, whatever [Col. 1170A] each person has said, just as though he were present; indeed, he ought to anticipate in advance, by his knowledge, whatever anyone has conceived beneath the obscurity of the senses. And just as the stars, the sun, and the moon, when they pass above the earth, are immediately and everywhere present to absolutely everyone who sees them, so too it is fitting that the hearing of the divine powers should be closed to no tongue but always present, even though voices flow toward it from distant regions.

For this is proper to gods: to fill all things with their power; to be present not partially in some place, but wholly everywhere; neither to be present nor to be absent; not to go to dine among the Ethiopians and return after twice six days to one’s private dwelling.

[Note: [Col. 1170D]

### V.—“That you may be heard”

This must be read according to Meursius’s emendation because of the following “you perform.” The first edition of Sabaeus has “that we may hear”; Gelenius, “that we may be heard.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1171B] “Whenever you perform sacred rites in accordance with the dues of ceremonies.” He calls them “dues of ceremonies,” as elsewhere “religious duties” and “the duty of worship.” Below, book VII, chap. 21: “If a goat is slaughtered for Jupiter, though it is customary for one to be sacrificed to Father Liber or Mercury; or if a barren cow is sacrificed to Unxia according to the rite and observance by which you assign it to Proserpina—what crime will there be in this? What evil or guilt will have been incurred, when it makes no difference to the act of homage from the head of which animal that honorary due is discharged?” HERALDUS.—“To perform sacred dues” and “to discharge them” are used in the same sense. For human beings are regarded as debtors to the gods by nature, law, or their own vow; they therefore appease and propitiate them by sacrifices, as though the gods were the givers of all goods and their creditors. See Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises on Solinus*, p. 9. ORELLI.

“Let us posit, for the sake of understanding the matter.” Stewechius thinks the word “sake” should be deleted and adduces a cloud of examples in which the ablatives *causa*, *gratia*, and *nomine* (“for the sake of”) are omitted by ellipsis. Thus Priscian, book XVIII, says that the Latins frequently use “he labors to save the people,” and “he puts himself in danger to defend the republic.” Sallust freely uses this construction. *Catiline* VI.7: “The royal government, which at first had been established for the preservation of liberty and the enlargement of the republic.” And *Jugurtha* LXXXVIII.4: “When he learned that these were merely glorious but did not bring the war to completion.” See Cortius there, pp. 46 and 818. Our author too, above, book V, chap. 23: “Offering to his mother, while she was still raging, what were, as it were, certain fillets intended to elicit pity.” Sanctius, *Minerva* IV.4, and Perizonius and Heusinger there, in the additions to p. 133, as well as Vechner’s *Hellenolexia*, will supply more examples. Yet I would not alter anything against the testimony of the manuscripts. ORELLI.

“Among the Canary Islands.” Pliny, *Natural History* VI.33; Solinus, chap. 60. ELMENHORST.

“Near furthest Thule.” Our author is imitating Virgil here, although, according to ancient custom, *y* has been used for *u*. Hence the two letters are everywhere confused in old manuscripts: *gyla* and *gula*—about which I recall Sosipater Charisius also speaking—*Capya* and *Capua*, *Sylla* and *Sulla*, and six hundred similar cases. Virgil’s verse is *Georgics* I.30:

> Let furthest Thule serve you.

Likewise Claudian, *Gothic War* 203 ff.:

> And with the unaccustomed din of war  
> he made distant Thule, far removed from our sky, tremble.

STEWECHIUS. See Solinus, chap. XXV; Mela, book III, chap. 6, and Isaac Vossius there; Mannert, *Geography of the Greeks and Romans*, vol. I, p. 78, and vol. II, part II, p. 265 ff. ORELLI.

“The four cardinal points.” The four cardinal points of the world. ORELLI.

“Compels each to consider.” Meursius suspects that one should read: “compels each to ask.” ORELLI.

“And thus,” etc. Thus the manuscript. Others: “But thus.” ELMENHORST.

“The others have accomplished nothing.” “To accomplish nothing” means to strive in vain, to labor in vain, and here to pray in vain. See C. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXVIII.9, p. 1327. ORELLI.]

### V

But if this is not so, all hope of assistance is removed, and it will be doubtful whether or not you are heard by them whenever [Col. 1171A] you perform sacred rites in accordance with the dues of ceremonies.

Let us posit, for the sake of understanding the matter, that a temple of some divine power exists among the Canary Islands; another of the same divinity near furthest Thule; another among the Seres; another among the dark-skinned Garamantes; and still others, if there are any, whom seas, mountains, forests, and the four cardinal points separate from knowledge of one another. If all of them, at one and the same time, perform divine rites and ask of the divine power whatever each person’s own necessity compels him to consider, what hope will all of them have of a benefit being granted in return, if the god does not hear the voice sent to him from every quarter, and if there is any distance into which the prayer of one requesting assistance cannot penetrate?

For either he will be present in no regions, if it is ever possible for him not to be somewhere; or he will be present [Col. 1172A] only to certain people, since he cannot offer his hearing commonly and without distinction. And thus it follows that either the god will aid no one at all, if, occupied with some matter, he has been unable to fly swiftly to hear their voices; or only one person will depart with his prayer heard, while all the others have accomplished nothing.

[Note: [Col. 1172B]

### VI.—“With golden domes”

Statius, *Thebaid* II:

> … and I shall fasten the arms  
> upon the lofty domes.

Lactantius Placidus: “The *tholus* is the central vault of a temple, the place in which the first fruits offered by those making vows were suspended.” ELMENHORST.—But *tholi*, not *thola*, are the more elevated domes customarily added to temples or other buildings, in which images of gods or goddesses were placed. See Philander’s *Lexicon of Vitruvius* and Gesner’s *Thesaurus* under this word, and our note on Jacob Balde, *Lyric Poems* IV, ode XLV, verse 25. ORELLI.

“Is it not clear and evident from this either that you worship dead men as immortal gods,” etc. Our author likewise borrowed this passage from Clement, whose words are as follows (*Protrepticus*, p. 39 ff., Potter’s edition): [Col. 1172C]

> “It is therefore natural that superstition, once it had taken its beginning from somewhere, became a fountain of senseless wickedness. Then, because it was not checked but advanced and flowed forth abundantly, it became the creator of many demons, sacrificing hecatombs, celebrating public festivals, erecting images, and building temples. These too—for I shall not keep silent about them either—I shall expose: they are euphemistically called temples, but are actually tombs; that is, tombs have been given the name of temples. But you—even now, at least—forget your superstition and be ashamed to honor tombs. In the temple of Athena at Larissa, on the citadel, is the tomb of Acrisius; and at Athens, on the citadel, is that of Cecrops, as Antiochus says in the ninth book of his *Histories*. And what of Erichthonius? Is he not buried in the temple of Athena Polias? And Immarus, son of Eumolpus and Daeira—is he not buried within the precinct of the Eleusinium beneath the citadel? Are not the daughters of Celeus buried at Eleusis? Why should I enumerate for you the women of the Hyperboreans? They are called Hyperoche and Laodice, and they are buried in the Artemision [Col. 1172D] on Delos, which lies within the sanctuary of Delian Apollo. Leandrius says that Clearchus was buried at Miletus in the Didymaeum. Here too, following Zeno of Myndus, one should not pass over the monument of Leucophryne, who is buried in the sanctuary of Artemis at Magnesia; nor indeed the altar of Apollo at Telmessus, which historians report to be itself a monument of Telmesseus the seer. Ptolemy son of Agesarchus, in the first book of his work *Concerning Philopator*, says that at Paphos, in the sanctuary of Aphrodite, Cinyras and the descendants of Cinyras were buried. But if I were to go through the tombs that you worship, not even all of time would suffice for me.”

CANTER.—The same material, in almost the same words, is found in Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* II.6. Compare Cyril, *Against Julian* X, and Athenagoras, *Embassy for the Christians*, p. 258, Rechenberg edition. ORELLI.

“Upon whose burial-places the shrines and temples of the dead have been erected.” Stewechius thinks one should read: “have been swollen up with burial-places,” the word having been transferred to the mounds of those who were interred. [Col. 1173A] Wrongly. For below in the same chapter: “those common burial-grounds of Varro over which temples are placed, and what masses of overlying weight they bear upon themselves.” Thus, “temples have been erected upon the burial-places of the dead” means that temples were built over the burial-places of the dead. ORELLI.

“Antiochus in the ninth book of his *Histories*.” Antiochus of Syracuse must undoubtedly be meant. He flourished in the ninetieth Olympiad, or in the year 330 of the city of Rome, and wrote a Sicilian History in nine books. Concerning it Diodorus says, book XII, chap. 71:

> “Among historians, Antiochus of Syracuse concluded his history of Sicilian affairs with this year—the first year of the eighty-ninth Olympiad—having begun with Cocalus, king of the Sicanians, in nine books.”

See Wesseling there, p. 528, vol. V, Zweibrücken edition, and G. J. Vossius, *On the Greek Historians* IV.7. ORELLI.

“Again, in her temple which is on the citadel at Larissa.” Barthius, on Statius, *Thebaid* I.382, vol. II, p. 132, thinks one should read: “on the citadel Larissa,” supposing that Larissa, the acropolis of the city of Argos, is meant. Strabo describes it, book VIII, p. 370, Casaubon’s edition:

> “The city of the Argives is situated for the most part on level ground; but it has an acropolis called Larissa, a hill of moderate strength. Near it flows the Inachus, a torrent-like river whose sources are in Mount Lyrceium, on the Cynurian borders of Arcadia.”

But he is mistaken. For, apart from the fact that Strabo mentions a temple not of Minerva but of Jupiter on the citadel Larissa, Pausanias expressly relates in his *Corinthiaca*, book II, that Acrisius, of whom the discussion here treats, withdrew to Larissa in Thessaly beside the river Peneus. See the following note. ORELLI.

[Col. 1173C] “Acrisius is recorded and identified as buried there.” Pausanias, in the passage cited, p. 112, Sylburg’s edition:

> “The sons of Abas son of Lynceus divided the kingdom. Acrisius remained at Argos itself, while Proetus possessed the Heraeum, Midea, Tiryns, and the parts of Argolis by the sea.… Much later, when Acrisius learned that Perseus himself was still alive and was accomplishing notable deeds, he withdrew to Larissa on the Peneus. Perseus, since he wished above all to see his mother’s father and to receive him graciously in both words and deeds, came to him at Larissa. Being in the prime of life and taking pleasure in his invention of the discus, Perseus displayed his skill before everyone. By divine intervention Acrisius unwittingly came beneath the impetus of the discus. Thus the god’s prediction concerning Acrisius was fulfilled, and the devices employed against his daughter and his daughter’s son—Danae and Perseus—did not turn aside his fate.”

Some therefore very wrongly make this Acrisius the grandfather of Ulysses; Stewechius shows that the latter was Arcesius, not Acrisius. ORELLI.

[Col. 1173D] “Erichthonius in the shrine of Polias.” At Athens, King Erichthonius—famous for the invention of the four-horse chariot—was buried in the temple of Minerva Polias, an extensive description of which may be seen in Pausanias, book I, p. 48 ff., Sylburg’s edition; Virgil, *Georgics* III.113, and Pliny, *Natural History* VII.56, bear witness to his invention. ORELLI.

“The brothers Daeiras and Immarus.” Salmasius emended the text thus from Clement. The manuscript has “Immaranchus”; the first edition, “Immarnachus.” Writers vary in this name. Pausanias, book I, p. 49, and Cyril, *Against Julian* X, p. 349, call him *Ἰμμάραδον παῖδα Εὐμόλπου*, “Immaradus, son of Eumolpus.” In Eusebius he is called Ismarus. Arnobius, however, appears either not to have understood his Clement, to have read him differently, or even to have drawn from different sources. For Clement writes: *Ἴμμαρος δὲ ὁ Εὐμόλπου καὶ Δαείρας*, which means: “Immarus, son of Eumolpus and Daeira.” Arnobius, however, taking *Δαείρας* as masculine, makes Daeiras the brother of Immarus. Pausanias, book I, p. 71, Sylburg’s edition, mentions Daeira, daughter of Oceanus, who was violated by Mercury [Col. 1174A] and bore the hero Eleusis. ORELLI.

“Within the Eleusinian enclosure.” Thus the Leiden edition, from the Royal manuscript. Sabaeus and Gelenius printed: “within the enclosure at Eleusis.” Others: “within the enclosure of the Eleusinium.” From Clement’s words *ἐν τῷ περιβόλῳ τοῦ Ἐλευσινίου*, “within the precinct of the Eleusinium,” Heraldus conjectures that our author wrote “within the enclosure of the Eleusinium”—that is, of the temple of Eleusinian Ceres. But, as Salmasius correctly observes on Solinus, p. 8, Arnobius seems to have read Clement’s passage differently, namely *ἐν τῷ περιβόλῳ τῷ Ἐλευσινίῳ*, “within the Eleusinian precinct,” translating it as “within the Eleusinian enclosure” rather than “the Eleusinium.” Thus shortly afterward he says “of Eleusinian Ceres” instead of “Eleusinian,” and Virgil, *Georgics* I.163:

> And the slowly rolling wagons of the Eleusinian mother.

The Greeks call an enclosure *περίβολος*: a definite extent of land left open around temples, planted with vines or trees and enclosed by a wall, dedicated to the god whose temple it was, and serving the uses of the priests. Pollux, book I, §10:

> “Places set apart for gods are groves and sacred precincts and enclosures, and the circuit surrounding them is a *peribolos*.”

Aelian, *On the Nature of Animals* XVII.16:

> “He says, then, that many domesticated birds are raised within the temple precinct.”

Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* XI: “Having rented lodgings within the temple enclosure, I establish a temporary household there for myself.” Daeiras and Immarus, therefore, were buried not inside the temple but within its enclosure. See Heraldus on this passage; Salmasius on Solinus at the cited place; and Keuchen on Sammonicus, verse 936, in P. Burmann’s *Minor Latin Poets*, vol. II, p. 362. ORELLI.

[Col. 1174C] “Which lies below the city.” Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “which lies below the citadel.” ORELLI.

“What of the daughters of Celeus? Are they not said to have received the offices of burial in the sanctuary of Eleusinian Ceres?” This reading, deservedly received into the text, is owed by Salmasius to Heraldus. The manuscript and first edition have: “are said to have offices in burials,” which makes no sense. From this Gelenius produced: “when buried, they are said to receive offices,” which can mean nothing other than: “when buried there, they are said to be honored by sacrifices and funeral offerings.” Whether “to receive offices” can be used absolutely in that sense is highly doubtful. Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “are said to have obtained the offices of burial.” Meursius: “when buried, they are said by everyone to be treated dutifully.” Stewechius: “the buried man is said to have offices,” explaining this to mean that those maidens had discharged the function of undertakers. Wrongly; for one thing is “to receive offices,” and another “to perform offices.” “To receive offices” means to receive a service or kindness from another. Pliny, *Letters* VII.19: “I cherished both, loved both; which one more, I do not know, nor did they wish a distinction to be made. They received my services in prosperity and received them in adversity.” “To have received the offices of burial,” therefore, is the same as to have been buried and interred—*τετάφθαι*, as Clement writes.

The daughters of Celeus, king of Eleusis, are meant. His son Triptolemus, after Ceres had been received as a guest, received from her the art of sowing crops. See Apollodorus I.5.1. Pausanias, book I, p. 71, Sylburg’s edition, gives their names from Homer and Pamphos as *Διογένειαν καὶ Παμμερόπην καὶ τρίτην Σαισάραν*, “Diogeneia, Pammerope, and a third, Saisara.” Fulvius Ursinus therefore very wrongly restores: “What of the maidens of Elea?” deriving them from the village Elaeum in Argos, whose inhabitants Stephanus says were Eleusinians. But “the maidens of Celeus” are *Κελεοῦ θυγατέρες*, “the daughters of Celeus.” Thus “the maiden of someone” means “his daughter” in the best writers—for example Cornelius Nepos, *Epaminondas* 3.5: “For whenever any of his fellow citizens had been captured by the enemy, or a marriageable daughter of a friend could not be given in marriage because of poverty, he convened a council of his friends and prescribed how much each should give according to his means.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1175A] **Were not Hyperoche and Laodice, who are said to have been brought there [Col. 1175B] from the territories of the Hyperboreans, in Diana’s shrine, which is situated within Apollo’s at Delos?** Gentianus Hervetus, in his commentary on Clement’s *Protrepticus*, book I, conjectures that this Hyperoche and Laodice were the wives of those Hyperboreans whom Pausanias, book I, p. 7, reports as having brought aid at Delphi against the Gauls—namely Hyperochus and Hamadocus, whom Pyrrhus, son of Achilles, joined as a third. Moreover, *delubrum* here seems to mean a smaller temple, or rather a chapel of Apollo situated within the larger Artemision. See above on chapter 3. ORELLI.

**In the Milesian Didymaeum.** The Didymaeum in which Clearchus was buried was a temple of Apollo, who was called Didymus; concerning him Orpheus says in *Hymn* XXXIII, verse 7:

> Βράγχιε καὶ Διδυμεῦ, ἑκάεργος, Λοξία, ἁγνέ.  
> O Branchian and Didymaean, far-working, Loxias, pure one.

GENTIANUS HERVETUS, on Clement, at the passage cited. Mela, book I, chapter 17, attests that Apollo was worshipped at Miletus under both names, Branchian and Didymaean. See there Isaac [Col. 1175C] Vossius. Compare Ruhnken on the cited passage of Orpheus, in Hermann’s edition, p. 295. ORELLI.

**Clearchus.** Thus Ursinus, from Clement. The first edition has *Cleomachus*, as does Eusebius, Κλεόμαχον. Who he was is uncertain. Gentianus Hervetus thinks that Clearchus the sculptor of Rhegium is meant; Pausanias mentions him in book VII, p. 350, ed. Sylburg. ORELLI.

**Leandrius.** Leander, or Leandrius, of Miletus, a writer of uncertain date, left a commentary on Miletus and the Milesians. See Laertius, book I, section 28, and the interpreters there; Meursius on Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 17; and G. J. Vossius, *On the Greek Historians*, book III. Others read: *Leandrus*. ORELLI.

**Leandrius says that he received the final rites of burial.** That is: that he was laid away and buried, τετάφθαι (“to have been buried”), which is the final duty of a funeral. He uses *suprema* absolutely, “the last rites.” Solinus, chapter 15: “Not content to attend his last rites at the expense of the funeral, he cut off his hair.” HERALDUS.

[Col. 1175D] **The monument of Leucophryne.** Who she was is uncertain. Gentianus Hervetus thinks that from this Leucophryne the Magnesian Diana herself received the epithet Λευκοφρύνης Ἀρτέμιδος (“Artemis Leucophryne”). See Pausanias, book I, p. 47, and book III, p. 196. Lipsius discusses this epithet at length on Tacitus, *Annals* III, chapter 62, p. 338, ed. Oberlin. Compare especially Joannes Selden, *Commentary on the Arundel Marbles*, pp. 176 ff. ORELLI.

**Zeno of Myndus.** Stephanus of Byzantium, s.v. Μύνδος: “Ἀπολλώνιος καὶ Ζήνων Μύνδιοι γραμματικοί”—“Apollonius and Zeno, grammarians of Myndus.” VIGERUS, on Clement.

**Beneath the little altar of Apollo, which is seen near the town of Telmessus, is it not indicated by consistent written testimony that Telmessus the seer was buried?** Cicero, *On Divination*, book I, chapter 41: “Telmessus is in Caria, a city in which the discipline of the haruspices is pre-eminent”; see Davis there. Arrian likewise bears witness concerning the Telmessians in *The Expedition of Alexander*, book II, chapter 3. Yet among the ancients there is no mention of a seer Telmessus, from whom perhaps [Col. 1176A] the town took its name. ORELLI.

[Col. 1176B] **Ptolemy son of Agesarchus, in the first book he published concerning Philopator, etc.** Canter restored this from the first edition in *Various Readings*, chapter 2. Gelenius corrupted it very badly, joining the first word to what preceded and rewriting the entire passage in his edition as follows: “Is it not indicated by the consistent writings of Agesarchus? Ptolemy Philopator, whom he first produced,” etc. He was evidently unaware that Ptolemy son of Agesarchus wrote a history concerning Philopator—something Athenaeus alone could amply have taught him, since he cites this author several times, for example in the *Deipnosophists*, book VI, p. 246, and book X, p. 425, ed. Casaubon. Compare the passage of Clement from which Arnobius took these statements, and Vossius, *On the Greek Historians*. ORELLI.

**Cinyras, king of Paphos.** See above on book IV, chapter 24, and book V, chapter 19. ORELLI.

**To record who are in which shrines throughout the whole world.** Stewechius’ conjecture is not to be despised: *toto siti in orbe*, “situated throughout the whole world.” Thus shortly before: “to be situated in the temple [Col. 1176C] of Venus with his entire line”; and *hic situs est*, “here he lies,” that is, buried, laid away in a tomb, occurs hundreds of times in inscriptions. ORELLI.

**What punishment the Egyptian established for anyone who disclosed in which [shrines] Apis lay concealed.** C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXIX, chapter 18, p. 1391, thinks that *quibus* should be read as *ubi suus*. But the passage is perfectly sound. *Quibus* means “in which shrines,” *fanis* being supplied from the preceding words: “It is infinite and immeasurable to describe who are in which shrines throughout the whole world.” Moreover, Augustine casts light upon our passage in *The City of God*, book XVIII, chapter 5: “It was also decreed concerning him—Apis or Serapis—that whoever said he had been a man should pay the capital penalty. And because in almost all the temples where Isis and Serapis were worshipped there was also an image which, with a finger pressed to its lips, seemed to admonish that silence be kept, Varro thinks this signified the same thing: that it should not be said that they had been human beings. [Col. 1176D] But that bull which Egypt, deceived by marvellous vanity, nourished amid abundant luxuries in his honor—because they worshipped it alive without a sarcophagus—was called Apis, not Serapis.” For *is Aegyptius*, which Salmasius fashioned, others have *Aegyptus*. For my part, I determine nothing. ORELLI.

**Those polyandria of Varro, etc.** Papias: “*Polyandrion* … a mound of the dead.” The glosses: “Slaughter … πολυάνδριον, σωρὸς νεκρῶν”—“a mass grave, a heap of corpses.” Lactantius, *Epitome of the Divine Institutes*, final chapter: “And the bodies of the dead will be heaped together in that valley, and its name will be called *Polyandrion*.” An ancient inscription:

> TRAVELER, BRING YOUR EYES CLOSER HERE; THEN SPEAK WITH ME. WHILE ALIVE I WAS WITHOUT LOVE; LOVING, ALAS, I DIE. TELL, I BEG YOU—PLEASE—MY STORY [the reading *REM. MEN.* is uncertain]. I GAVE MYSELF IN DEATH TO THIS MASS GRAVE BECAUSE OF THE BURNING LOVE OF A YOUTH IN THE FLOWER OF HIS AGE, MOST BEAUTIFUL. “WHY ARE YOU MAD? YET YOU LIVED AS A LOVER.” INDEED, WHEN I HAD BEGUN TO LOVE TO MY HURT, THE YOUNG MAN, REJECTING LOVE’S GIFT, REFUSED ME. I WASTED AWAY; SNATCHED OFF BY DEATH, HERE I AM, A MASS GRAVE FOR THE PITIFUL CORPSES OF THOSE DRIVEN MAD BY LOVE.

Pausanias, *Boeotica*, p. 289; *Corinthiaca*, pp. 65, 67; Aelian, *Various History*, book XII, chapter 21; the biblical commentator on Ezekiel, chapter XXXIX. ELMENHORSTIUS.]

### VI

What of the fact that many of these temples, which have golden domes and rise upon lofty pediments, are proved by the written accounts of authors to cover ashes and bones and to be burial places for the bodies of the dead? Is it not plain and obvious that either you worship dead men as immortal gods, or else an inexpiable insult is inflicted upon the divine powers whose shrines and temples have been raised over the funeral pyres of the dead?

In book IX of his *Histories* [Col. 1173A], Antiochus records that Cecrops was committed to the earth at Athens in the temple of Minerva; again, Acrisius is written and stated to have been laid away in her temple situated on the citadel of Larissa; Erichthonius, in the shrine of Athena Polias; [Col. 1174A] the brothers Dairas and Immarus, in the precinct of Eleusis lying below the city. What of the daughters of Celeus? Are they not said to have received the rites of burial in the temple of Eleusinian Ceres? Were not Hyperoche and Laodice—[Note: [Col. 1175A] Sabaeus reads: *Elaudice*.] who are said to have been brought there from the territories of the Hyperboreans—buried in Diana’s shrine, which is situated within Apollo’s at Delos? [Col. 1175A]

Leandrius says that Clearchus received the final rites of burial in the Milesian Didymaeum. Zeno of Myndus declares and records that Leucophryne’s monument is in Diana’s shrine at Magnesia. Beneath the little altar of Apollo which is seen near the town of Telmessus, is it not indicated by consistent written testimony that Telmessus the seer was buried? Ptolemy son of Agesarchus, in the first book he published *On Philopator*—[Note: [Col. 1175A] Others read *Brimo*. Absurdly.]—declares on literary authority that Cinyras, king of Paphos, together with his entire household—indeed, with his whole line—lies in the temple of Venus. [Col. 1176A]

It would be an infinite and immeasurable task to describe who are in which shrines throughout the whole world; nor does it call for scrupulous inquiry to ask what punishment the Egyptian established for anyone who disclosed in which [shrines] Apis lay concealed; which temples cover those mass graves of Varro; and what masses of weight raised above them they contain.

[Col. 1177A] [Note: [Col. 1177B]

### VII—In the Capitol of the ruling people

The reading of the old manuscript is not to be despised: *in … Capitolium*. The well-known expression in Terence’s *Andria* is *in memoriam habeo*, “I hold it in remembrance,” and likewise Plautus has *in mentem est*, “it is in mind.” See [Col. 1177C] Aulus Gellius, book I, chapter 7, and also book XVII, chapter 2. STEWECHIUS.

**That it is the tomb of Olus of Vulci.** Servius on *Aeneid* VIII, verse 345, teaches us that this should be read with the Lyon editor as *Oli*, not *Toli*, as was previously printed:

> Some say that when the foundations of the Capitol, where it now stands, were being laid, a human head was found which was said to belong to Olus. Alarmed by this omen, the founders sent to Etruria to a noted haruspex of that time. He had already informed his son Argus that fate had granted dominion to the place in which that head had been found. Those who had been sent therefore met Argus and asked where his father was. When he learned the reason for their journey, he disclosed his father’s entire answer and warned them to take care not to be deceived by his questioning. But when the envoys reached the haruspex and asked about the significance of the discovered head, he wished to assign the dominion of the world to his own homeland instead. Pointing out a place of his own, he asked whether they had found it “here.” [Col. 1177D] When they denied it, he suspected that his answer had been betrayed and asked whether they had met anyone. They candidly admitted that they had encountered a young man. The haruspex then mounted a horse, pursued Argus, and killed him in the place where Rome now stands; from his slaughter the Argiletum took its name.

Dionysius of Halicarnassus recounts the same story in *Roman Antiquities*, book IV, p. 257, ed. Sylburg, as does Pliny, book XXVIII, chapter 2, though he suppresses the name of the man whose severed head it was and derives the word *Capitolium* not from Olus but from *caput*, “head,” κεφαλή. See Suidas, s.v. Καπιτώλιον. From Pliny we learn that the Etruscan haruspex was named Olenus Calenus. Compare Justus Rycquius, *On the Capitol*, chapter 10, pp. 113 ff. ORELLI.

**Or alone, or with the remaining parts.** It seems that *sine partibus caeteris*, “without the remaining parts,” should be read. ORELLI.

**Sammonicus.** This must mean Quintus Sexenus Sammonicus the elder, killed by Caracalla, author of many learned books and praised by Aelius Spartianus in his *Life of Caracalla*. A poem of his [Col. 1178B] on medicine still survives. Macrobius praises his books of arcane matters—from which our author doubtless excerpted these statements—in the *Saturnalia*, book III, chapter 9; see Meursius there and especially the celebrated Ackermann in the preface to his edition of Sammonicus. ORELLI.

**Granius.** See above on book III, chapter 31. ORELLI.

**Valerianus.** Fulvius Ursinus conjectures *Valerius Antias*. But perhaps this means the Cornelius Valerianus whom Pliny cites in *Natural History*, book III, chapter 12, and book XIV, chapter 2. ORELLI.—A Cornelius Valerianus is praised under that name by Pliny (*Natural History*, book X, chapter 2); he reported that the Phoenix had flown down into Egypt. Elsewhere too (book XIV, chapter 1): “Valerianus Cornelius also considered it especially worthy of remembrance that country houses and dwellings were encircled by the tendrils of individual vines and by clinging laurels.” Whether he is in fact identical with the man Arnobius records must be left to the judgment of others. NOURRY, p. 159. Vossius says the same in *On the Latin Historians*, p. 700. It therefore appears that this Valerianus composed books [Col. 1178C] *On Sacred Matters* or *Antiquities*. ORELLI.

**Whose son Aulus was.** From these words we see that *Oli*, not *Toli*, must be read in the preceding passage. For *Olus* and *Aulus* are the same name. The ancient Latins, like the French today, pronounced *au* as *o*. See Keuchen on Frontinus, p. 414, and Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* V, pp. 536 f. ORELLI.

**How he was deprived of life and light by his brother’s slaves.** Thus the Leiden edition. The first edition has: *ut a germani servuli*. Gelenius and the others: *ut a germani servulo*, etc. ORELLI.

**Or in what part the curious matter was enclosed in obscurity.** Canter restored this from the first edition. Others omit *rei* and read: “in what part it was curious.” Moreover, I freely confess that I do not understand these words. ORELLI.
