**So that, namely, the immovable and fixed perpetuity of the sealed omen might stand.** For whenever favorable omens presented themselves, they revered the gods so that the gods might confirm them; and they themselves religiously contributed everything they could toward confirming them. Silius Italicus, book IV, 127:

> I recognize you, highest of the gods.  
> Be present, Father, and confirm the omen of your bird.

Accordingly, they also attempted to confirm such omens by sacrifices. Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIII: “When this had been shown, he cried out more joyfully, while everyone applauded, that Babylon had fallen to the ground, stripped of all its ornaments; and after being detained for a short while so that he might confirm the omen by making propitiation through victims, he came to Davana.” HERALDUS.

**Cast into the midst.** Εἰς μέσον ἔρριψεν, “he cast it into the midst,” that is, made it public. See above on book IV, chapter 18. HERALDUS.

**Worshipper of all divine powers.** The Romans—as Caecilius says in Minucius, chapter 6—worshipped the gods of every nation, sought foreign gods everywhere and made them their own; they even erected altars to unknown divine powers and shades. ELMENHORSTIUS.

[Col. 1179B] **When it gave the temple its designation.** *Vocabulum* means the same as *nomen*, “name.” Thus Tacitus, *Annals* III, chapter 56: “Augustus devised the designation of that highest rank.” Cicero, *Letters to Friends*, book X, letter 6: “Believe me, therefore, Plancus: all the degrees of distinction you have so far attained … will bear the titles of offices, not the insignia of true dignity, unless you unite yourself with the liberty of the Roman people and the authority of the senate.” See Corte there, p. 494, and Sitzmann on Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, book II, meter VII, p. 99, Leiden edition. ORELLI.]

### VII

But why do I speak of these trifles? Who among men does not know that in the Capitol of the ruling people is the tomb of Olus of Vulci? Who, I ask, does not know that not so very long ago a human head was dug out from the foundation beds—either alone, without the remaining parts, as some report, or having received the rites of burial together with all its limbs?

If you demand that this be made plain through the testimony of authors, Sammonicus, Granius, Valerianus, and Fabius will tell you whose son Olus was, to what race and nation he belonged, how he was deprived of life and [Col. 1178A] light by his brother’s slaves, and what he deserved from his fellow citizens such that burial in his native earth was denied him. [Note: [Col. 1177A] The manuscript wrongly reads *Patientiae*.]

You will also learn—even though they pretend to be unwilling to make it public—what was done with the severed head, or in what part the curious matter was enclosed in obscurity, so that, namely, the immovable and fixed perpetuity of the sealed omen might stand. Although it would have been proper for this to be suppressed and concealed through the oblivion of antiquity, the formation of the name cast it into public view and caused it, together with its grounds, to advance through the ages granted to it with testimony that could never be extinguished. Nor was that greatest city, worshipper of all divine powers, ashamed, when giving the temple its designation, to call it *Capitolium* from the head (*caput*) of Olus rather than to name it from Jupiter.

[Col. 1179A] [Note: [Col. 1179B]

### VIII—Temples have been built for the immortal gods either uselessly for them

The *iis* (“for them”) is an elegant redundancy. It occurs frequently [Col. 1179C] in these writers. HERALDUS.—Salmasius was therefore right to restore *iis* to the text. Gelenius and others delete it. ORELLI.

**It follows that we should say something about statues and images.** He calls every likeness (*πᾶν ὁμοίωμα*) a *simulacrum*, “image.” *Forma* is what the Greeks call εἶδος, from which comes the diminutive εἴδωλον; hence *idolum* means the same as *simulacrum*. Tertullian, *On Idolatry*, chapter 3:

> For this purpose an interpretation of the word is necessary. In Greek εἶδος means “form”; the diminutive εἴδωλον derived from it has likewise produced among us the word meaning “little form.” Every little form or form, therefore, requires that it be called an idol.

The Greeks, however, sometimes used εἴδωλα for unreal things, which appear rather than subsist in nature, such as the apparitions, φάσματα, that sometimes appear in the air. In the same sense the Latins too used *simulacra*, *species*, and *imagines*. From this arose the utterly false observation of Suidas and other grammarians who distinguish εἴδωλα, “representations of things that do not subsist, such as Tritons, Sphinxes, and Centaurs,” from ὁμοιώματα, [Col. 1179D] “likenesses of things that do subsist, such as animals or human beings.” Yet εἴδωλον indiscriminately signifies every form, both of things existing in nature and of things not existing. Thus Plutarch, in *Sulla*:

> It is said that the women brought him such a quantity of spices that, apart from those being carried in 210 burdens, a large image of Sulla was fashioned, and a lictor too was fashioned, from costly frankincense and cinnamon.

HERALDUS.

**And tend with religious observance.** θεραπεύετε, “you tend/worship.” He reproduces the Greek verb. HERALDUS.

**Are amusing yourselves in childish delusion.** See above on book IV, chapter 36. ORELLI.

**For if it is certain among you that the gods whom you suppose to exist, etc.** This is the first argument by which he proves that images are empty. If the gods really exist, he says, to what purpose do you establish images before which to pour out prayers? His argument, therefore, is as follows: either you believe that the gods exist or you do not. If you believe it, there is no need [Col. 1180B] for images, since you have the gods themselves in reality, before whom you may pour out your prayers. If you doubt it, to what purpose do you establish images of doubtful beings? This argument is general and applies to images of every kind. HERALDUS.

**Even so.** That is, even when the matter is thus: *auch in diesem Fall*, “even in this case.” This fullness of expression is characteristic of Arnobius. ORELLI.

**Or do you perhaps say that a certain presence of the divine powers is displayed to you beneath these images?** This was the pagans’ rejoinder: images are not empty, because in them are worshipped the gods whose presence they display, as it were, [Col. 1180C] in some fashion. Thus Phidias in Dio Chrysostom, Discourse XII:

> For no one would say that it was better for no shrine or image of the gods to be exhibited among human beings, on the ground that one ought to look only upon the heavenly bodies. For the intelligent person reveres all these together, since he believes that he beholds the blessed gods not from afar; and because of the disposition toward the divine, all human beings possess a powerful longing to honor and worship the deity from close at hand, approaching and touching it, etc.

HERALDUS.

**That they are thus worshipped.** Thus the Leiden edition. The first edition has the thoroughly corrupt and meaningless *eos insolidi*. Gelenius reads *eos ita coli*. ORELLI.

**And to them dutiful services.** Heraldus added *iis*, followed by Salmasius. ORELLI.]

### VIII

We have therefore, I think, sufficiently shown that temples have either been built uselessly for the immortal gods, or else have been constructed, contrary to their supposed dignity and power, on the basis of insulting notions. It follows that we should say something about the statues and images which you fashion with great artistry and tend with religious observance.

In this matter, if there is any good faith at all, we can establish within ourselves, by reflection, whether you do this seriously and with a weighty purpose, or whether, in laughing, you are amusing yourselves with the very matters themselves in childish delusion. For if it is certain among you that the gods whom you suppose to exist do indeed exist and dwell in the highest regions of heaven, what cause, what reason is there for these images to be fashioned by you, when you possess definite realities to whom you can pour out your prayers and from whom you can request aid in circumstances of need? [Col. 1179B]

But if you do not believe—or, to put it more moderately, if you are doubtful—even so, what reason is there to fashion and establish images of doubtful beings, and to form by an empty imitation what you do not believe exists? [Col. 1180A] Or do you perhaps say that a certain presence of the divine powers is displayed to you beneath these images and that, because it has not been granted to you to see the gods, they are thus worshipped and dutiful services rendered to them? Whoever says and maintains this does not believe that the gods exist. He is proved to have no confidence in his own religions, since he needs to see something that he may grasp, lest perhaps what is obscure because unseen should be empty.

[Note: [Col. 1180C]

### IX—“We worship the gods through images,” you say

Thus the first edition, lest anyone think this reading was transferred from other authors. HERALDUS.

**Through certain entrusted commissions.** A *fideicommissum* is a form of testamentary disposition by which an heir or another person is requested to give or do something. See Brissonius, *On Formulas* VII, p. 669, and Heineccius, *Roman Antiquities*, book II, title XXIII. Arnobius therefore means that the gods receive human acts of worship through the images as though through trustees, since human beings impose upon those images, as it were, the duty of carrying their prayers to the gods. ORELLI.

**And what could be done that is more injurious, etc.** Thus Stewechius from the manuscript. Others have *fieri pote est*. In place of *et quid*, this same Stewechius here and in chapter III of this book—“And what more could we do?”—as well as in all other passages where editions of Arnobius read *et quid*, substituted *ecquid*. ORELLI.

**And to supplicate another thing.** The manuscript has *et rei alterae supplicare*, which Stewechius defends, proving by many examples in his note on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VIII, p. 531, ed. Oudendorp, that in antiquity the forms *alia, aliae; una, unae; illa, illae; neutra, neutrae; utra, utrae*, etc., were declined in this manner. See Priscian, book VI. ORELLI.

[Col. 1181B] **To strike the smith when you mean to hit the fuller.** Others read *cadere*. This is a proverb concerning those who punish and lash an innocent person in place of the guilty one. See Hadrianus Junius’ supplement to Erasmus’ *Adages*, century VI, proverb 84. The Greek proverbs are very similar: πταίσαντος ὑφάντου ἠπήτης ἐτύφθη, “when the weaver stumbled, the tailor was beaten”; and μαγείρου ἐξαμαρτάνοντος τύπτεται αὐλητής, “when the cook makes a mistake, the flute-player is beaten.” See Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, book IX, chapter 7, p. 381, ed. Casaubon, and Dalechamp there; and Paulus Leopardus, *Emendations*, book X, chapter 5, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, p. 193. ORELLI.

**To ask for judgments about what should be done.** C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXIX, chapter 18, p. 1319, explains *sententias* as “oracular lots,” citing a passage from Plautus’ *Rudens*:

> That I might endure both my master’s poverty  
> And my own lot.

But *sententiae* here means counsels concerning actions to be undertaken. ORELLI.]

### IX

“We worship the gods through images,” you say. What then? If these images do not exist, are the gods unaware that they are worshipped, and will they think that no honor is being imparted to them by you? Through certain pathways, therefore, and through certain entrusted commissions, as the expression goes, they take and receive your acts of worship. Before those to whom that homage is owed become aware of it, you first propitiate the images and then, as though they were some remnants, transmit your worship to the gods on another’s authority. [Col. 1180B]

And what could be done that is more injurious, insulting, or cruel than to recognize one being as a god and supplicate another thing; to hope for aid from a divine power and to direct entreaties toward an image devoid of all sensation? [Col. 1181A] Is this not, I ask, what is said in common [Note: [Col. 1181B] The manuscript wrongly reads *vulgariis*.] proverbs: to strike the smith when you mean to hit the fuller? Or, when you seek a human being’s counsel, to ask little asses and piglets for judgments about what should be done?

[Note: [Col. 1181C]

### X—Who is fashioned by you as smooth-faced

The manuscript has *effigitur*. I therefore think *effigiatur* should be read. Apuleius: “a trunk shaped by carving.” Minucius speaks similarly when treating images in *Octavius*, chapter III: “stones shaped, anointed, and crowned.” STEWECHIUS.—Compare Wower on Minucius, at the cited passage, p. 20, ed. Gronovius. For *levis* one must write *laevis*, that is, beardless. Thus below, chapter 12: “for each of them—the Sun and Mercury—is fashioned by you as smooth and with a beardless face.” See Bunemann, index to Lactantius, s.v. ORELLI.

**Who in truth has blue-gray eyes.** See above on book V, chapter 28, and book III, chapter 14. ORELLI.

**To carry splayed nostrils, though you represent and shape him as snub-nosed.** See the note on book III, chapter 14. ORELLI.

[Col. 1181D] **Because it does not carry lines corresponding to the original face.** That is, because it does not reproduce lines equal to the face of its original, namely the divinity it represents. *Lineare*, *lineae*, and *lineamenta* are painters’ terms for the outer contours (*die Umrisse*) of a body, which they sketch with their brush. See Salmasius, who discusses this matter at length, on Solinus, pp. 4–5. *Filum* has the same sense above in book III, chapter 13: “with a human contour and boundaries”; see the notes there. ORELLI.

**That the sun is spherical.** *Teres* in its proper sense: like a globe, identical with itself on every side, even, smooth, polished, *von allen Seiten gleich abgerundet*, “equally rounded on every side.” Thus Horace, in the very well-known passage *Satires* II.7.86, concerning the wise man: “whole in himself, smooth and round.” See Lambinus and the celebrated Heindorf there. ORELLI.

**We all understand that the winds are a flowing of air driven and stirred by cosmic causes.** Stewechius restored this entirely correct reading from the manuscript. Previously the text read: “that the winds are a flowing of air, driven and stirred by cosmic causes.” Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “flowings driven … and stirred.” *Mundanae rationes* means cosmic—that is, celestial—causes. Thus Avienus, *Aratea*, verse 47: “a mind forgetful of the cosmic source.” ORELLI.

**Through you, human forms give life to the coils of trumpets.** Excellent: for the *buccina* is twisted and bends back upon itself in a bronze circle, and differs from the straight trumpet, as Vegetius teaches in book III, *On Military Affairs*, chapter 5. This is the Greeks’ στρογγύλη σάλπιγξ, “curved trumpet.” HERALDUS.—See an illustration of a wind blowing a curved trumpet in Montfaucon, *Antiquities*, plate LI, figure 9, ed. Schatz. ORELLI.

**With internal and domestic blasts.** τοῖς οἴκοθεν, “with those from within.” Thus the character in Plautus says that he has a back of his own at home, lest he seek one abroad. HERALDUS.

**Among your gods the most savage face of a lion** (the manuscript has *leones*, “lions”) **is smeared with pure vermilion and called by the name Fruit-Bringer** (the manuscript has *frugiferio*). It is remarkable how greatly this obscure passage has exercised the ingenuity of scholars. Latinus Latinius (*Sacred and Profane Library*, p. 90) seems to cut rather than untie the knot of this difficulty when he wishes to correct the words as follows: “Among the gods we see lions with a most savage face smeared with pure vermilion.” But this is mere conjecture, supported by the authority of no manuscript.

Accordingly, some of those who wish nothing in ancient writings to be altered without the surest reasoning conjecture that these words of our author should be understood of the Sun. They are refuted, however, because he has already spoken of the Sun separately. Others therefore think it more probable that he means the lions sometimes carved upon the pediments of temples. Yet these seemed to have been placed there as ornaments of the building rather than to express the face of gods.

We will therefore more readily be persuaded that by these words Arnobius means the same thing that Minucius Felix said after Tertullian (*Apology*, chapter 16; *To the Nations* I, chapter 12): “You consecrate gods blended from goat and lion, and the faces of lions and dogs.” For after the quoted words Arnobius added: “Without the rest of the body it is a mask and a face alone, with roaring gapes and savage jaws, its bloody wax-paint scraped away … and weary dogs.” Who would not readily grant that each author is speaking of images such as those of Pan, the Satyrs, and others of that kind?

Arnobius’ additional statement that the face was smeared with vermilion plainly refers to the utterly ridiculous pagan custom of smearing the faces of images with vermilion. For we read in Pliny (*Natural History*, book XXXV, chapter 7): “The face of Jupiter’s own image was customarily smeared with vermilion on festival days.” Of Pan’s image Virgil says, *Eclogue* X.26:

> Pan, god of Arcadia, came, whom we ourselves saw  
> Red with blood-colored elderberries and vermilion.

[Col. 1183A] Servius makes the following observation on these verses: “Dwarf elder is a kind of plant resembling the elder tree. He is painted with vermilion because Pan is represented with a red face, owing to its likeness to the ether.” NOURRY, pp. 486 f.

**Among your gods we see the most savage face of a lion, smeared with pure vermilion and called by the name Fruit-Bringer.** In this extremely vexed passage I have followed Salmasius’ emendation. The manuscript reads as follows, according to N. Heinsius in his letter to Gisbert Cuper, no. 428, in Burmann’s *Sylloge*, vol. II, p. 714: “Among the gods we see [Col. 1183B] your lions, the newest face, smeared with pure vermilion and from the name frug… called seriously.” From this Sabaeus produced: “And to be called by the name ‘upright’ in earnest.” Gelenius: “Smeared with excessive pure pigment and called by the name ‘upright’ in earnest.” J. Lipsius, *Epistolary Questions*, book I, letter XX, conjectures: “And to be called by a savage name in earnest,” with Thomas Canter’s approval. Heraldus reads: “And by the name of a savage beast”; Meursius, “of an upright beast”; others, “of an upright wild creature.” Fulvius Ursinus reads “smeared with excessively pure pigment,” following Sabaeus in the rest. C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXIX, chapter 18, p. 1391: “And to be called by a name derived from an upright wild creature,” that is, by those who are upright.

N. Heinsius, in the letter just cited, reads: “Among the gods we see your lions, with a most savage face, smeared with pure vermilion, and commonly called by the name of the Phrygian goddess”; or: “called by command of the Lady Phrygia,” so that *domina* or *dea Frugia* would be an archaism characteristic of Arnobius for *dea Phrygia*, that is, Cybele, just as *dea Suria*, “the Surian goddess,” stands for *dea Syria*, Venus. He nevertheless withdrew this conjecture in letter 260 to J. G. Graevius, in the same [Col. 1183C] Burmann *Sylloge*, vol. IV, p. 335. Graevius had conjectured in the preceding letter: “the most savage face of a lion and mouths smeared with vermilion, to be named under the dominion of the Lady Phrygia.” Heinsius instead altered the entire passage thus: “the most savage face of a lion, smeared with vermilion wax-paint, and the divine power named from its bestial roar”; or “named after its bestial roar.”

Graevius, however, recast it in his reply, p. 337, as follows: “the most savage face of a lion, smeared with waxen vermilion, and the divine power named according to a bestial rite.” To say nothing else, I greatly doubt that *cereum minium*, “waxen vermilion,” can be used for wax mixed with or coated in vermilion—*rothes Wachs*, “red wax.”

The explanations of the passage are no less diverse:

> Laurentius Pignorius and Elmenhorstius think that the author is speaking of gods represented with lions’ heads, such as Minucius Felix (chapter 28, p. 292) and Tertullian (*Apology*, chapter 16) display and describe, which were worshipped among the Egyptians as signifying the rays of the sun. Desiderius Heraldus condemns this, turning now in one direction and now in another and establishing nothing certain; I shall not examine that most learned man’s reasons, lest I seem to seek glory by laboriously refuting the errors of others. Either, then, a man with a lion’s face is described, or the animal lion, through which the Greeks, Romans, Egyptians, and others represented the Sun, although Heraldus wrongly denies it; and the entire passage must be interpreted from that superstition. Hence I think its face was customarily filled with vermilion so that it might reproduce the Sun’s red color and fiery rays; for the same reason, according to Pausanias, book VII, a statue of Bacchus among the Achaeans was anointed with cinnabar. Hence too it is called “Fruit-Bringing,” because the Sun is the father of crops and the principal cause and source of fertility. Thus, on Albinus’ coin, Mercury appears radiate—an emblem of the Sun—with the inscription *Saeculo Frugifero*, “To the Fruitful Age”; and Statius, *Thebaid* I, calls Osiris, or the Sun, “Fruit-Bringing.”

These are the words of Gisbert Cuper in letter 426 to Nicolaas Heinsius (Burmann’s *Sylloge*, vol. II, p. 713). Salmasius agrees with him in his note on Flavius Vopiscus, *Aurelian*, chapter V, thinking that Arnobius means the Sun Mithras, whom the Persians worshipped [Col. 1184A] represented with a lion’s face and a tiara—see Montfaucon, *Antiquities*, plate XLI, figures 6 and 7, ed. Schatz—as does Rigaltius on Artemidorus, *Oneirocritica*, book II, p. 101, ed. Reist. For my part, I think the name “Fruit-Bringing Lion” originated among the Egyptians, whose region the Nile flooded when the Sun entered the sign of Leo in the Zodiac, according to John Lydus, *On the Months*, under July, chapter II, p. 121, ed. Schow:

> Κατὰ τὸν ἐν λέοντι ἥλιον ἀναχεῖται ὁ Νεῖλος.  
> The Nile overflows when the Sun is in Leo.

But I leave this most difficult passage [Col. 1184B] to more learned men to explain. ORELLI.

**If all these images are representations of the divine powers above.** Thus Meursius, followed by Salmasius. Previously *superiorum*, “of the higher beings,” etc., was read. ORELLI.

**Without the rest of the body it is a mask, and a face alone, roaring through savage gapes.** It is merely a mask, because just as only the lion’s face is depicted, so too there—in heaven, that is—there must be only a face, and thus, as it were, merely a mask. *Persona*, “mask,” is apt, since theatrical masks too roar through savage gapes. Thus Tatian, *Against the Greeks*:

> Τί μοι συμβάλλεται πρὸς ὠφέλειαν ὁ κατὰ τὸν Εὐριπίδην μαινόμενος, καὶ τὴν Ἀλκμαίωνος μητροκτονίαν ἀπαγγέλλων; ᾧ μηδὲ τὸ οἰκεῖον πρόσεστι σχῆμα· κέχηνέ τε μέγα καὶ ξίφος περιφέρει.  
> What benefit does the actor driven mad according to Euripides and recounting Alcmaeon’s murder of his mother contribute to me? He does not even possess his own proper appearance: he gapes enormously and carries a sword about.

I omit other passages cited by others. Because of this deformity, Greek poets sometimes called the face ῥύγχος, “snout.” Athenaeus, book III, chapter 15, p. 95, ed. Casaubon:

> ὅτι δὲ κυρίως λέγεται ῥύγχος ἐπὶ τῶν συῶν, προείρηται, ὅτι δὲ καὶ ἐπ’ ἄλλων ζῴων, Ἄρχιππος Ἀμφιτρύωνι [Col. 1184C] δευτέρῳ κατὰ παιδιὰν εἴρηκε καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ προσώπου, etc.  
> It has already been stated that “snout” is properly said of pigs; that it is also said of other animals, however, Archippus in the second *Amphitryon* applied jestingly even to the face, etc.

HERALDUS.—Others read: “and with a face alone.” Compare W. Worth on the cited passage of Tatian. ORELLI.

**Roaring through savage gapes, dreadful.** In the Leiden edition Salmasius rather boldly refashioned this as: “with roaring gapes and savage jaws.” But *torvidus* in place of *torvus*, “savage,” was already read above. Nothing, therefore, should be altered. ORELLI.

Terrible in his blood-red *cerotum*. This is the highly perceptive emendation of N. Rigault in his notes on Artemidorus, *Oneirocritica*, book II, p. 100, Reiff’s edition, approved also by Heraldus, since it is very close to the corrupt reading of the manuscript codex and the first edition: *Dirus sanguineo decoroto*. From this, with his customary rashness, Gelenius produced *sanguineo de guttare*. Meursius, p. 186, conjectures *sanguine decolorus* (“blood-discolored”), a plausible error arising from the abbreviated writing of *decolor*. Thus *unicolorus*, *versicolorus*, and *multicolorus* occur in Prudentius. Canterus suspects that one should read *sanguineo de colore* (“terrible in his blood-red coloring”). J. G. Graevius, in Letter 261 to N. Heinsius, Burman’s *Sylloge*, vol. IV, p. 337, reads *sanguineo decolor* [Col. 1184D] *ore* (“with blood-discolored face”). Salmasius printed *sanguinea*—namely, *facies* (“the face”)—*de ceroto*. By “blood-red *cerotum*” (*κηρωτόν*) Arnobius means pure vermilion, with which lions’ faces were smeared. Indeed, human beings too were painted with white lead and vermilion, and with, as it were, a blood-red and crimson *cerotum* or wax-salve—for *ceratum* and *cerotum* are the same thing. Thus Pliny, *Natural History*, book 33, chapter 7, attests that Camillus celebrated his triumph painted with vermilion. Compare what we observed on Jacob Balde, *Lyric Poems* III, Ode 31. The expression, moreover, is sound and customary among these writers: *Dirus sanguineo de ceroto*. Thus Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter 5: “Domitian too had made the attempt, a portion of Nero in cruelty”; and chapter 9: “O Christian Jupiter, and his father’s only son in cruelty.” Heraldus cited these examples. ORELLI.

Crushing an apple with his teeth. Like a *manducus*, a grotesque figure with snapping jaws. See Festus. HERALDUS.—C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXIX, chapter 18, p. 1391, thinks that *dentibus saevis* (“with savage teeth”) should be read. ORELLI.

And, like weary dogs, thrusting his tongue out from his gaping mouth in eagerness for drink [Col. 1185A]. I have followed the highly probable emendation of the Leiden editor. Previously the text read: “And, as once weary dogs, thrusting his tongue out from his gaping mouth because of phlegm.” But the particle *olim* (“once”) is entirely out of place here, and *pituitas, -atis* is not a Latin word. ORELLI.

And to say that it is an image of God. Scriverius made this emendation in Meursius’s Appendix, and Salmasius followed him. The manuscript codex has *accidere*. Gelenius printed: “And to believe that it is an image of God.” ORELLI.]

## X

And, finally [Note: [Col. 1181B] *Notissime* in Sabaeus], how do you know that all these images, which you fashion as substitutes standing in for the immortal gods, reproduce their likeness and possess a divine resemblance? For it may be that the being whom you represent as smooth-faced is bearded in heaven; that the one to whom you assign the age of a boy is rather advanced in years; that the one depicted here as fair-haired actually has blue-gray eyes; that the one whom you make and represent as large-nosed bears widely flaring nostrils. For it is not right to call or name something [Col. 1181B] an image if it does not carry over corresponding lines from the original [Col. 1182A] countenance. That this is plain and certain may be recognized from manifest facts.

For although, by the indisputable observation of our eyes, we all see that the sun is spherical, you bestow upon it a human face and the features of mortal bodies. The moon is always in motion and assumes thirty forms in its monthly renewal; under your guidance and representations it is a woman with a single countenance, though it changes through a thousand appearances in its daily instability. We all understand that the winds are currents of air set in motion and stirred by the workings of the world [Note: [Col. 1182B] *Lationibus*. Wrongly]; through you they become human forms, giving life to the coils of trumpets with breath from within themselves. Among your gods we see the most savage face of a lion, smeared with pure vermilion and called by the name of “Fruit-Bearer” [Col. 1182B].

If all these images are representations [Col. 1183A] of the gods above [Note: [Col. 1182B] *Superiorum* in Sabaeus], then one must say that a god of the very same kind also dwells in heaven, to whose shape and appearance the likeness of this image has been conformed. And of course, just as this one is here, so that one is there: a mask without the rest of a body, a face alone, roaring through grimly gaping jaws, terrible in his blood-red wax-paint [Col. 1184A], crushing an apple with his teeth, and, like weary dogs, thrusting his tongue out from his gaping mouth in eagerness for drink. But if he certainly does not exist—and we all believe that he does not—what tremendous audacity is this, to devise for yourself whatever form you please and to declare it to be the image [Col. 1185A] of a god whom you cannot prove to exist in any part of nature?

[Note: [Col. 1185B]

### XI.—You laugh that in ancient times the Persians worshiped a river, etc.

The following sequence has once again been taken from Clement, *Protrepticus*, p. 40, Potter’s edition:

> Long ago, then, the Scythians worshiped the *acinaces*, the Arabs a stone, and the Persians a river. Still earlier members of the other nations set up conspicuous pieces of wood and erected pillars of stone, which indeed were called *xoana* because the material had been scraped down. Certainly, in Icaria the image of Artemis was a piece of unworked wood, while that of Cithaeronian Hera at Thespiae was a hewn tree-trunk; and the image of Samian Hera, as Aethlius says, was at first a plank, but later, during the archonship of Procles, it became anthropomorphic. Once the *xoana* began to be made in the likeness of human beings, they acquired the name *brete* from mortals, *brotoi*. At Rome, Varro the author says, the ancient *xoanon* of Mars was a spear, before craftsmen had yet rushed into this fair-faced malpractice.

CANTERUS.

The Persians worshiped rivers. Herodotus, book I, chapter 138:

> They neither urinate nor spit into a river, nor wash their hands [Col. 1185C] in it, nor do anything else of that kind; rather, they venerate rivers above all things.

ELMENHORST.—Compare J. F. Gronovius, *Observations*, book IV, chapter 10, p. 638 ff., Platner’s edition, who illustrates this Persian religious practice with numerous examples. ORELLI.

As memorable writings indicate. “Memorable writings” are records or memorials in Aulus Gellius and repeatedly in Tertullian. Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis*, book VI, chapter 26, speaks of “ancient records of readings.” HERALDUS.

The Arabs, a shapeless stone. Clement says simply “a stone.” Maximus of Tyre calls it a square stone:

> The Arabs venerate a square stone; precisely which one, I do not know. But the image I saw was a square stone.

Arnobius, however, does not add “shapeless” without reason. Dio Chrysostom likewise speaks of “unmarked stones” in Discourse XII:

> Consequently many barbarians, through poverty and lack of artistic skill, call mountains gods, as well as unworked trees and unmarked stones.

HERALDUS.—Similarly, in the *Suda* under “The god Ares,” this god’s image is called “a black, square, unshaped stone, four feet high and two wide,” which it records as having been erected at Petra in a most beautiful temple [Col. 1185D]. But J. Davies, on Maximus of Tyre, loc. cit., Dissertation VIII, § 8, p. 142, Reiske’s edition, and Samuel Bochart, who discusses the matter at length in *Phaleg*, book II, chapter 14, p. 126, Frankfurt edition, show that the *Suda* errs in supposing Mars to be meant, and that instead of “the god Ares” one should read “Dusares,” the name of Bacchus among the Nabataeans. Even today at Mecca the Arabs worship the black stone in the Kaaba and kiss it out of reverence. See Bochart, loc. cit.; Nerreter, *The Newly Opened Mohammedan Mosque*, p. 282 ff.; and Gisbert Cuper, who discusses the ancient worship of stones with great learning in his notes on Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, vol. II, p. 154, Bauldri’s edition. ORELLI.

The nations of Scythia, the *acinaces*. Although *acinaces* is a Persian word meaning a sword, as Herodotus relates in the *Polyhymnia*:

> And they call the Persian sword an *acinaces*,

the Greeks nevertheless also commonly use it for the Scythian sword, which that nation revered and worshiped as a kind of god. Clement:

> Among the Scythians, the Sauromatae venerate an *acinaces*.

Ammianus Marcellinus, book 31:

> No temple or shrine is seen among them, not even a hut roofed with thatch; instead, according to barbarian custom, a naked sword is planted in the ground, and this they worship with exceptional reverence as Mars, the guardian of the regions through which they range.

BRODAEUS, *Miscellanies*, book V, chapter 5, in Gruter’s *Lampas Critica*, vol. II, p. 533.—Herodotus relates the same thing in book IV, chapter 62, the classic passage, as do Lucian in [Col. 1186B] *Zeus Tragoedus*, chapter 42, and *Toxaris*, chapter 38. ORELLI.

The Thespians, a branch in place of Cinxia. Janus Guilielmus very successfully restored this from the manuscript codex in place of the extremely corrupt words of the first edition, *Ramum procinexia Thespios*, from which Gelenius, with his persistent rashness, made: “The Thespians, the branch of Procne.” Lilius Gyraldus cites our passage in his book *On the Gods of the Gentiles* as *Ramum proconnesii Athespios*, which makes no sense. From Clement’s passage cited above—“and the hewn trunk of Cithaeronian Hera at Thespiae”—Canterus suspects that one should read: “The Thespians, a branch in place of Cithaeronian Hera.” Gentianus Hervetus, in his notes on Clement, proposes: “The Thespians, a pruned branch in place of Juno.” But *pro Cinxia* alone is correct, as Salmasius also proves in his notes on Solinus, p. 14. Cinxia is Juno, worshiped by the Romans under that name because she presided over the bridal girdle of the newly married woman. See above, on book III, chapter 25. ORELLI.

The Icarians, an uncarved piece of wood in place of Diana. This must be read with Clement instead of “the Carians.” For Strabo, book XIV, p. 639, Casaubon’s edition, attests that there was a temple of Diana among the Icarians:

> [Col. 1186C] Near Samos lies the island of Icaria, from which the Icarian Sea takes its name. The island itself is named after Icarus, son of Daedalus. They say that when he shared his father’s flight, at the time when both took wing and departed from Crete, he fell here because he could not control his course.

And shortly afterward:

> There is a headland stretching toward the west wind; and on the island there is also a sanctuary of Artemis called the Tauropolium.

CANTERUS.—C. Barthius therefore errs in his notes on Statius, *Thebaid* IV.225, vol. II, p. 978, in thinking that one should read “the Caryans,” from Caryum, a town of Laconia, from which Diana was called Caryatis because she was worshiped there. ORELLI.

Aethlius. I read this with Clement instead of *Ethedius*, for I have found no mention anywhere of an Ethedius. Athenaeus, however, in addition to Clement, mentions Aethlius in book XIV of the *Deipnosophists*, p. 650, Casaubon’s edition:

> Aethlius, in the fifth book of the *Boundaries of the Samians*—if the writings are genuine—calls them *homomelides*.

And shortly afterward in the same book, p. 653:

> What marvel, then, does Aethlius of Samos appear to report when, in the fifth book of the *Seasonal Produce of the Samians*—Casaubon reads *Boundaries*—he says: “The fig, the grape, the *homomelis*, apples, and roses came forth [Col. 1186D] twice in the year”?

What especially supports this reading is Athenaeus’s testimony that Aethlius was a Samian and wrote about Samian affairs. CANTERUS. The *Etymologicum Magnum* also mentions him under *Νένωται*. See Vossius, *On the Greek Historians*, book III, under Aethlius. ORELLI.

Before the practice and art of sculptors. *Fictorum* comes from *fictor*, “sculptor” or “maker of statues,” whom Arnobius below calls a *signifex*; in Greek, *πλάστης* (“modeler”). Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, chapter 29: “We know the other gods with whatever face painters and sculptors have chosen to give them.” ORELLI.

The Samians, a plank in place of Juno. This most certain and very slight emendation is owed to Obrecht Gifanius and Theodore Canterus, who proposed it in *Various Readings*, book II, chapter 25, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, p. 771. The earlier reading was: “The Samians, a well in place of Juno.” But Eusebius and Clement, who discuss the same matter and express it by *σανίς* (“plank”), make it clear that *pluteum*, “plank,” alone is correct. Gentianus Hervetus wrongly prefers “an unadorned board in place of Juno.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1187B] Indeed, you believe that the statues themselves are gods. Arnobius uses *sigillaria* here, like the preceding *sigilliola*, in the unusual sense of life-sized statues, as Gisbert Cuper demonstrates at length in *Harpocrates*, p. 86. For *ipsa* the manuscript has *illa*. ORELLI.

And all the other limbs. See above, on book III, chapter 6. ORELLI.

Though fully aware, you plead the bad cause of a living being. There is some corruption here. *Scientissimi* means “knowing,” but the sense is not “you assert a bad cause in ignorance.” Should *animantis* therefore be *argumentis*, so that the text reads, “You maintain it with arguments,” etc.? HERALDUS.—Meursius conjectures: “Madmen, you maintain,” etc. I myself conjecture: “You maintain it resolutely” [Col. 1187C], that is, with the utmost zeal and exertion. ORELLI.]

## XI

You laugh that in ancient times the Persians worshiped rivers, as memorable writings indicate; that the Arabs worshiped a shapeless stone; the nations of Scythia, the *acinaces*; the Thespians, a branch in place of Cinxia [Col. 1186A]; the Icarians, an uncarved piece of wood in place of Diana; the people of Pessinus, a flint in place of the Mother of the Gods; the Romans, a spear in place of Mars, as Varro’s *Muses* indicate; and that, as Aethlius records, before the practice and art of sculptors, the Samians worshiped a plank in place of Juno. Yet you refrain [Col. 1187A] from laughter when you supplicate little human statues and human forms as immortal gods.

Indeed, you believe that the statues themselves [Note: [Col. 1187B] *Illa* in the manuscript] are gods, and you believe that nothing apart from them possesses divine power. What are you saying, you people? Do the heavenly gods, then, have ears and temples, necks, the backs of their heads, spines, loins, flanks, knees, buttocks, hocks [Note: [Col. 1188B] *Suffraginem* in Sabaeus], ankles, and all the other limbs of which we are constructed and which were stated somewhat more fully in the first part and presented in a more expansive discussion?

If only it were possible to look within your thoughts and into the very recesses of your minds, where you turn over various and embark upon most obscure reflections! We would discover that you yourselves think the same things as we do and entertain no different opinions about the representation of the divine powers. But what can we do against obstinate passions, against men who threaten us with swords [Col. 1187B] and devise novel punishments? Though fully aware, you plead the bad cause of a living being [Col. 1188A; text uncertain]; and because you once acted without reason, you defend your act lest you ever appear to have been ignorant. You think it better not to be defeated than to yield and assent to acknowledged truth.

[Note: [Col. 1187C]

### XII.—From causes of this kind, with your connivance, this consequence too has followed, etc.

There now follows the classic passage concerning the insignia and attributes of the gods, containing many details that one would search for elsewhere in vain. ORELLI.

Which could be an object of ridicule to any solemn man. “Any solemn man,” that is, any grave, severe, austere man or philosopher—a grim old sourpuss—such as Heraclitus and Cato, for example. Thus Lucilius in Nonius, under the word *TRISTIS*: “A solemn and severe philosopher.” See there Dousa, p. 404 of Havercamp’s edition of Censorinus, who aptly cites a verse from Afranius’s *The Stepson*:

> I did not know you as solemn, severe, and serious.

ORELLI.

Thus Ammon is now shaped and fashioned with ram’s horns. The classic passage concerning the horned gods of the chief nations occurs in Porphyry, *On Abstinence*, book III, p. 250, de Rhoer’s edition:

> Thus the Greeks attached ram’s horns to the image of Zeus and bull’s horns to Dionysus, while they fashioned Pan from a man and a goat.

[Col. 1187D] The horns attributed to river-gods are a very familiar matter. Compare the interpreters on Minucius Felix, chapter 21, and Ezekiel Spanheim, who discusses these gods learnedly and at length and reproduces a splendidly engraved image of Jupiter Ammon in *On the Use of Coins*, Dissertation VII, p. 389 ff. ORELLI.

The son of Maia with a *petasus*, as though preparing to set out upon the roads. Martianus Capella, *The Marriage of Philology*, book I, p. 2: “Mercury, however, began to lead the way, his *petasus* and winged sandals set in motion.” Compare Xiphilinus in the *Life of Commodus* and Plautus, *Amphitryon*, Prologue 143. ELMENHORST. For the *petasus* and cap were used on journeys, though at other times people rarely wore caps, as highly learned men observed long ago—for example, J. Lipsius, *On the Amphitheater*, chapter 19. HERALDUS. The *petasus*, Greek *πέτασος*, was a brimmed cap or hat, so called because it had broad edges. Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, book XII, p. 537, writes that Alexander the Great sometimes wore Mercury’s costume at banquets, “with the *petasus* upon his head and the herald’s staff in his hand” [Col. 1188B]. Plautus, however, in the prologue to the *Amphitryon*, introduces Mercury speaking thus:

> I shall keep these little wings here on my *petasus*.

If you wish, consult Lambinus’s observations on this verse. NOURRY, p. 489. The *petasus* was a covering for the head very much like a brimmed cap; see its illustration in Montfaucon’s *Antiquities*, plate LXXXV, figures 9 and 10, Schatz’s edition. ORELLI.

Liber with soft limbs and utterly relaxed through the looseness of womanly fluidity. For Bacchus is *λυσιμελής*, “limb-relaxing,” as is Venus. Most elegant is the phrase: “utterly relaxed through the looseness of womanly fluidity.” Women are thus called soft [Col. 1188C] and, as it were, melting and flowing away; hence their gait is looser and more relaxed. Apuleius, *Milesian Tales* II: “By his flowing gait he pretended to be a woman.” The Greeks call this *ὑγρὸν βάδισμα*, “a fluid gait.” Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book III:

> For they should not, like some women emulating the acting of comedy and carefully observing the broken movements of dancers, strut theatrically through social gatherings by their very dainty motions, their fluid gait, and their affected voices, looking languorously about them, trained as a lure for pleasure.

Dio Chrysostom, in Discourse IV, *On Kingship*, contrasts “the fluid and soft appearance” with “the manly and dignified”:

> Does a manly and dignified appearance, then, befit such a divinity, or rather one that is fluid and soft?

Hence the Greek *ὑγρὸς βίος*, “fluid life,” corresponds to the Latin “a life steeped in and overflowing with pleasures.” Arnobius’s phrase is therefore excellent and most elegant: “utterly relaxed through the looseness of womanly fluidity.” *Dissolutus* means *διαλελυμένος*, “dissolved,” and one who flows with pleasures. Tertullian, *On the Shows*, chapter X:

> In the theatrical arts too there is the patronage of Liber and Venus, in those things that are private and peculiar to the stage, involving gesture and the flowing movement of the body. For they sacrifice softness to Venus and Liber: to her through sex, to him—for so one should read instead of “to her”—through the flowing movement of the dissolute. [Col. 1188D]

HERALDUS. Contrast dry bodies, to whose “meager, dried-out bones,” as Catullus says, “the ravenous skin clings.” Compare J. F. Gronovius, *Disquisition on Statius’s Silvae*, chapter XXV, p. 151 f., who illustrates our passage with numerous examples, and Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XXIII. Meursius therefore wrongly tampered with this perfectly sound passage by reading *liquoris seminei*, “seminal fluid,” because the ancients placed Liber over male seed; still worse, C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book LVIII, chapter 15, interprets “womanly fluidity” as wine. ORELLI.

As though you were to say that she displays and puts up for sale the beauty of her hireable body. That is, *τὴν ὥραν ὥσπερ τι ὤνιον πιπράσκειν*, “to sell her beauty as though it were merchandise.” For here *formam* means *τὴν ὥραν*, “beauty in its bloom.” Julius Firmicus expresses the same idea in *Mathesis*, book VI, chapter 31: “But if this should be a woman’s nativity, it will make her a public and notorious prostitute, marketing her modesty.” [Col. 1189B] HERALDUS.—Arnobius alludes to Venus Vulgaris, *πάνδημος* (“common to all”), of whom Eugraphius writes on Terence, *Eunuch* I, scene II, line 5: “Menander plainly said that prostitutes customarily had, near their homes or in their courtyards, an altar of Venus Vulgaris, to whom they sacrificed daily.” Compare Murr, on the *Herculanean Tablets*, vol. VII, p. 4, plate 16. ORELLI.—A hireable body. Hence they also call the brothel itself a *meritorium*, a “place of hire,” Greek *ἐργαστήριον*, “workshop.” Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis*, book IV, chapter 25: “But if the star of Venus approaches them, a woman taken from a notorious brothel is joined in marriage to eminent men.” HERALDUS.

Vulcan with cap and hammer, balancing it in his right hand. I have admitted into the text this entirely correct emendation by Cannegieter, who also proposes another correction [Col. 1189C]: “Vulcan with cap and hammer, balancing the hammer in his right hand.” But I greatly prefer the former because of the disagreeable repetition of *malleus*, “hammer.” Previously the text was printed: “Vulcan with cap and hammer, free but in his right hand,” which appears corrupt—unless perhaps Arnobius had in view such an image as Montfaucon presents in *Antiquities*, plate 11, figure 4 of Schatz’s abridgment: namely, Vulcan’s right hand free, but his left wrapped in his cloak. Meursius conjectures, “disabled; but free in his right hand.” I cannot discern what that could mean unless *mancus* might express the Greek *χωλός*, “lame,” as Vulcan was; but I lack examples of that meaning. For *mancus* properly means lacking a hand, not limping on a twisted foot. ORELLI. Others, including Heraldus, have already observed from Arrian’s *Discourses of Epictetus*, book IV, chapter 8, that smiths wore caps. ELMENHORST.

And girt for smith’s work. That is, *περίζωμα περιθέμενος*, “wearing an apron.” Arrian, in the same chapter:

> No one will say, “I am a musician,” if he buys a plectrum and a lyre; nor, “I am a smith,” if he puts on a cap and apron.

[Col. 1189D] HERALDUS.—I am doubtful about the word *expeditione*. It denotes what in our language we call a leather apron. Perhaps the Greek *περιζώματι*, “with an apron,” was written, and a copyist ignorant of Greek altered it. One could nevertheless call *expeditio fabrilis* the means and method by which a craftsman carries out his work, although it must also be said that the word *succinctum*, “girt,” is not very suitable to that meaning. CANNEGIETER. This sense of *expeditio* is extremely unusual, nor is it likely that Arnobius wrote *περιζώματι*, since no Greek word is read anywhere in the entire work. But everything will be sound if with Stewechius we read: “girt for smith’s work,” that is, equipped for carrying out his craft. You may see Vulcan thus girt in Montfaucon’s *Antiquities*, plate 14, figures 2 and 3, Schatz’s edition. ORELLI.

The Delian god with plectrum and strings, maintaining the bearing of a lyre-player and of an actor about to sing dirges. This is the reading of all editions except the Leiden edition, which has “the Delian lyre-player,” perhaps through a printer’s error [Col. 1190B]. For if we read it in that way, the following *et* has nothing to which it can refer. Taubmann, on Plautus, *Bacchides*, act 4, scene 8, and Gesner in his *Thesaurus* show that *naeniae* denotes not only funeral songs but any commonplace, childish, or trifling utterances. Thus below, in book VII, chapter 32, nurses’ songs by which they lull children to sleep are called *naeniae*: “For they are freed in the quiet of sleep, and, so that they may be overcome by it, they must hear gentle lullabies.” ORELLI.

The king of the sea with a trident, as though he had to enter a gladiatorial contest. For net-fighters used a trident in gladiatorial games. Juvenal, Satire II, verse 143:

> [Col. 1190C] Even this monstrosity was surpassed by the trident of tunic-clad Gracchus.

See Lipsius, *Saturnalia*, book II, chapter 8. ELMENHORST. Gladiators, and especially net-fighters, were of course armed with a trident when fighting *murmillones*. Hence Juvenal, Satire II, verse 143:

> Even this monstrosity was surpassed by the trident of tunic-clad Gracchus,  
> As the gladiator swept the arena’s center in his flight.

You may consult the observations of various commentators on these verses, as well as Lipsius, *Saturnalia*, book II, chapter 8. NOURRY, p. 490.

A clever, urbane king should remove the Sun from his doorway. I should never have imagined that anyone—Gelenius, who conjectures “from his shrine.” ORELLI.—could doubt this reading. The Sun is properly stationed at the doorway, whence he was called *προστατήριος*, “guardian of the entrance.” Sophocles, *Electra*, verse 637:

> Now may you hear, Phoebus who guards the entrance,  
> My secret utterance.

The scholiast explains *προστατήριε*: “because he is established before the doors” [Col. 1190D]. Pausanias says the same. Tertullian, *On Idolatry*: “Among the Greeks too we read of Apollo *θυραῖος*, ‘of the doorway,’ and of the Antelian spirits as guardians of entrances.” Aristides, in his hymn to Minerva, speaks of “Apollo before the gate.” HERALDUS.

Since it is costume that indicates your gods, etc. Prudentius:

> Fortune’s fashioned costume, with its simple horn.

Tertullian calls these “insignia” in *On Idolatry*: “For it makes no difference whether you build or adorn, if you have furnished his temple, altar, or chapel, if you have embossed a gold leaf, fashioned insignia, or even built a house.” HERALDUS.

Distinction. Here *interstitio* is equivalent to *discrimen*, “distinction,” from *intersto, -are*, “to stand between”; I lack another example of this meaning. Elsewhere *interstitio* means a cessation or interval. Others read *interstinctio*, “differentiation,” which we encountered above in chapter 3: “And they pour forth starry gleams in variegated differentiation.” ORELLI.

To assign them names as though those were proper to them. Meursius wrongly prefers *numina*, “divine powers,” to *nomina*, “names.” ORELLI.]

## XII

From causes of this kind, with your connivance, this consequence too has followed: artists’ wanton fancy has sported with the bodies of the gods and given them forms that could be an object of ridicule to any solemn man. Thus Ammon is now shaped and fashioned with ram’s horns; Saturn with a hooked sickle, like some guardian of farmland and pruner of luxuriant branches; the son of Maia with a *petasus*, as though preparing to set out upon the roads and shield himself from sun and dust; Liber with soft limbs and utterly relaxed through the looseness of womanly fluidity; Venus naked and exposed, as though you were to say that she displays [Col. 1188B] and puts up for sale the beauty of her hireable body; Vulcan [Col. 1189A] with cap and hammer, balancing it in his right hand and girt for smith’s work; the Delian god with plectrum and strings, maintaining the bearing of a lyre-player and of an actor about to sing dirges; the king of the sea with a trident, as though he had to enter a gladiatorial contest. Nor can any representation of any divine power be found that does not bear a particular costume bestowed upon it by the generosity of craftsmen.

Suppose now that, without your knowledge or awareness, some clever, urbane king should remove the Sun from his doorway and transfer him to Mercury’s shrine; then seize Mercury in turn and make him move into the Sun’s temple—for both are constructed by you as beardless and smooth-faced—and should give Mercury rays while placing a little *petasus* [Note: [Col. 1189B] The manuscript has the absurd *petajoculum*] upon the Sun’s head. By what means could you distinguish [Col. 1189B] whether this one is the Sun or Mercury, since it is costume [Col. 1190A], not the distinctive character of the face, that ordinarily indicates your gods?

Again, by a similar transference, suppose he were to tear the horns from naked Jupiter and attach them to Mars’s temples, strip Mars of his weapons, and with them encircle Ammon in turn. What distinction could be made among the several gods, when the one who had been Jupiter could be regarded as Mars, and the one who had been Mavors could assume the appearance of Jupiter Ammon? To such an extent it is mere play to fabricate those images and assign them names as though the names were proper to them; for if you take away their costume, all recognition of the individual gods disappears. One god can be believed to be another and one appear in place of another—indeed, either may be regarded as either.

[Note: [Col. 1191B]

### XIII.—For who does not know that those Athenian Herms, etc.

Clement, *Protrepticus*, p. 47, Potter’s edition:

> In the same way, the stonecutters at Athens modeled the Herms after Alcibiades.

CANTERUS.

Who does not know that Praxiteles, etc. The same Clement, on the same page:

> Praxiteles, as Posidippus explains in his work [Col. 1191C] *On Cnidus*, when fashioning the statue of Cnidian Aphrodite, made her resemble the appearance of Cratina, his beloved, so that the wretched men might have Praxiteles’s mistress to worship.

CANTERUS.

If he rereads Posidippus. In the Roman codex—the first edition—the reading is “if he rereads the writings of Posidippus.” CANTERUS.—If the reading of the Leiden edition, “if he rereads Posidippus,” is sound, something has fallen out after “rereads,” perhaps “his book *On Cnidus*.” For Clement, whom Arnobius has copied here too, says: “As Posidippus explains in his work *On Cnidus*.” The older editions, such as Elmenhorst’s earlier one, have “if he rereads Posidippus.” On this Posidippus see Vossius, *On the Greek Historians*, book III. ORELLI.

Concentrated through a contest of artistic skills. That is, with the utmost diligence and a rivalry of artistic abilities, as though all the artistic skills he possessed—the *Kunstfertigkeiten, Geschicklichkeiten*—had been summoned into competition. Fulvius Ursinus’s conjecture, “through a skillful rivalry with other women,” is therefore utterly false. ORELLI.

[Col. 1191D] That Thespian Phryne. Clement, loc. cit.:

> But when the Thespian courtesan Phryne was in her bloom, all the painters modeled their images of Aphrodite after Phryne’s beauty.

CANTERUS.—Compare Pausanias in the *Boeotica*, pp. 302 and 330. ORELLI.

Those who repeatedly wrote about Thespian affairs. That is, “Thespian events,” as we showed on book I, chapter 3. Fulvius Ursinus therefore wrongly inserts the Greek article *τό* before *negotia*. HERALDUS.

When she stood at the very peak of beauty. “At the peak,” that is, *ἐν ἀκμῇ ὥρας, κάλλους*, “in the prime of bloom and beauty.” See the interpreters on Achilles Tatius, *The Adventures of Leucippe and Clitophon*, book III, chapter 8, p. 260, Boden’s edition. Others therefore make the dreadful alteration *culmine*, “summit.” ORELLI.

Model. *Exemplarium* has the same meaning as *exemplar*. This is a rarer formation, though it occurs in the *Digest*. See Brissonius, *On the Meaning of Words*, under this word. ORELLI.

Or wherever love for such statues flowed. I have printed this according to Meursius’s highly satisfactory emendation. The others read: “or whether this one to whom love flowed.” ORELLI.

To whom truthfulness in reproducing likenesses awarded first place [Col. 1192B]. Fulvius Ursinus suspects that *navitas*, “industry,” should be read in place of *veritas*, “truthfulness.” Wrongly. We encountered a similar expression above in book II: “in whom completeness itself lacked nothing.” ORELLI.

The lineaments of a prostituted head. See above, on the beginning of book III, chapter 13. ORELLI.

[Col. 1192C] The artists’ conceptions burned. A difficult passage. I understand *scita* as referring to the forms conceived in the artists’ minds, *die Ideale der Künstler*, “the artists’ ideals.” The Leiden edition has: “The decisions of artistry burned.” “They burned,” namely with love for Phryne: “They were full of fire and life.” I believe this is a printer’s error, for “to burn for someone” can mean nothing other than to love that person passionately. ORELLI.

Among the statue-makers. *Signifex*, “statue-maker,” is a word of the Latinity of the Bronze Age, used in addition to our author by Apuleius, Martianus Capella, and Sidonius; see Savaron on Sidonius, book VI, Letter XII, p. 403. Compare C. Scioppius, *Verisimilia*, book I, chapter 7, p. 33, and Colvius on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* I.22, p. 92. ORELLI.

Among the statue-makers, the famous Phidias was the foremost, etc. Clement, loc. cit.:

> Phidias the Athenian wrote upon the finger of Olympian Zeus, “PANTARCES IS BEAUTIFUL.” For to him it was not Zeus who was beautiful, but his beloved.

CANTERUS.

[Col. 1192D] Upon the god’s finger he inscribed, “PANTARCES IS BEAUTIFUL.” Both the passage of Clement just cited and Pausanias, book VI, p. 362, Sylburg’s edition, make it clear that this is how the text must be read, according to Theodore Canterus’s emendation in *Various Readings*, book II, chapter 14, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, p. 752:

> After Iccus, there stands Pantarces of Elis, who defeated the boys in wrestling and was the beloved of Phidias.

Compare p. 306. Previously the text was printed “Pantauches.” ORELLI.

He inscribed “beautiful.” The *Suda*, under *καλοί*, says that lovers inscribed the names of their beloveds on walls or the leaves of trees, adding the caption “So-and-so is beautiful.” Its words are:

> “Aristophanes is beautiful.” The Athenians used to write “beautiful” on walls. It was characteristic of lovers to write the names of their beloveds on walls, trees, or the leaves of trees in this form: “So-and-so is beautiful.”

ELMENHORST.—Compare Boettiger, who discusses this subject extensively, in *Sabina*, pp. 322 and 346, and the same author’s *Explanations of Ancient Vase Paintings*, vol. III, p. 66 ff. ORELLI.

To jest and sport wantonly. See above, on book V, chapter 1. ORELLI.

[Col. 1193B] The forms given to them by himself, fashioned in the likeness of limbs. This is the ancient reading, deservedly restored to the text by the Leiden editor. Nor do we need Fulvius Ursinus’s emendation, “with form given to them by himself,” which is indeed more elegant, but the other is more consistent with Arnobius’s rather unpolished style. Still less do I understand what Heraldus intends by his punctuation: “forms given to them by himself? In the likeness of limbs,” etc. For the words “the forms given to them by himself,” etc., depend upon the preceding “he knew.” ORELLI.

Was worshiped. Fulvius Ursinus reads “was marked”; others, “was adorned.” Both wrongly. ORELLI.]

## XIII

But why do I laugh at the gods’ false endowments and artificial supports? Why at horns, hammers, and caps, when I know that certain images [Col. 1190B] are the forms of particular human beings and [Col. 1191A] the features of infamous prostitutes? For who does not know that those Athenian Herms were fashioned in the likeness of Alcibiades’s body? Who does not know, if he rereads Posidippus, that Praxiteles concentrated all his artistic skills in competition to make the face of the Cnidian Venus conform to the appearance of the prostitute Cratina, whom the unhappy man loved to distraction?

But is this the only Venus whose borrowed beauty was enhanced from a harlot’s face? That Thespian Phryne, as those report who repeatedly wrote about Thespian affairs, when she stood at the very peak of beauty, charm, and youthful bloom, is said to have served as the model for all the Venuses held in esteem, whether throughout the Greek cities or wherever love and desire for such statues flowed. And so all the artists living at precisely that time, to whom truthfulness in reproducing likenesses awarded first place [Col. 1191B], strove with every care and effort to transfer the lineaments of a prostituted head into statues of the Cytherean goddess. The artists’ conceptions burned; each sought to surpass the other in contentious rivalry—not so that Venus might become more august, but so that Phryne might stand in place of Venus [Col. 1192A].

Thus matters were brought to the point that sacred rites were performed for prostitutes in place of the immortal gods, and the unhappy region was deceived by the manufacture of statues. Among the statue-makers, the famous Phidias was the foremost. After he had raised up the form of Olympian Jupiter in a work of immense scale, he inscribed upon the god’s finger: “PANTARCES IS BEAUTIFUL.” This, however, was the name of a boy whom he loved and cherished with an obscene passion. No fear or religious scruple moved him against calling the god by the name of a male prostitute—indeed, against consecrating Jupiter’s divine power and image to a sexually degraded youth.

To such an extent it is mere play and childish emotion to fashion those little statues, worship them as gods, and heap divine sanctity upon them, when we see the artists themselves jesting as they make them and consecrating memorials of their own lusts. For why, one may ask, should Phidias have hesitated to jest and sport wantonly [Col. 1192B], when a little earlier he had known that the Jupiter he had made was itself merely gold, stones, and shapeless bones—separate and confused—and that he himself was the assembler and binder [Note: [Col. 1191B] The manuscript has “joiner”] of all these materials; that the forms given to them by himself [Col. 1193A] were fashioned in the likeness of limbs; and, what comes first among all these points, that it was the benefaction of his own craft that Jupiter had been born through him and was worshiped in human affairs?

[Note: [Col. 1193B]

### XIV.—Those images that terrify you, etc.

He returns to the discussion of images in general [Col. 1193C] and argues from the material of which they are made. This, therefore, is a general argument against all images. On the formula of worship touched upon by Arnobius, we have spoken in our note on book I. HERALDUS.

Or glue mixed with gypsum. Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I:

> If a pliant sheet of gold has covered gypsum,  
> It gradually disintegrates as the treacherous glue fails.

HERALDUS.

Of the Indian animal. The elephant. ORELLI.

From cooking-pots. Havercamp teaches, in his note on the very similar passage of Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter XIII, p. 132, that the spelling should be *caccabulis*, not *cacabulis*:

> The household gods whom you call Lares you treat with household authority, pawning, selling, and altering them—sometimes turning Saturn into a cooking-pot, sometimes Minerva into a ladle, etc.

There *caccabulum* and *trulla* denote filthy implements used to receive the burden of the belly and the bladder. But since *caccabula* are here joined with little pots, candlesticks, and so forth, and shortly afterward other, more obscene vessels are mentioned [Col. 1193D], Gesner in his *Thesaurus* more correctly interprets *caccabulum* here as a kitchen utensil—a kitchen cauldron or pot—a sense in which Apicius also uses it several times. *Caccabulum* is therefore the diminutive of *cacabus*, Greek *κάκκαβος*, a vessel in which food was cooked, a *χύτρα* or cooking-pot, as Varro explains in *On the Latin Language*, book IV. It was also a baker’s vessel. See Casaubon on Aelius Lampridius, *Heliogabalus*, chapter 19, p. 828 f. ORELLI.

Or from other, more obscene vessels. Minucius Felix, chapter XXIII, p. 240, Gronovius’s edition:

> A bronze or silver god is cast from a filthy vessel for an Egyptian king, as has very often happened; it is beaten with hammers and shaped upon anvils.

ELMENHORST.

And issued forth into the forms you behold. In the strict sense. Horace, *Art of Poetry*, verse 22:

> A wine jar was begun;  
> Why, as the wheel turns, does a pitcher emerge?

HERALDUS.

“Scraped with *grosfis*.” Gelenius thus emended *grossis*, which had previously been read without any sense. *Grosfus* or *grosphus*, [Col. 1194B] *-i* (γρόσφος), is explained by Gesner in the *Thesaurus* as the point of a spear. In this passage it seems to signify the instrument which in Pollux, *Onomasticon* VII.113 and X.146, is called ἀρίς, “a borer,” akin to a file. But I would like another attestation of this word. In the Leiden edition Salmasius printed: “Scraped on lathes”; *tornus*, German *Dreheisen, Drechslereisen* (“turning iron, lathe tool”), on which Heyne, most learned scholar, treats at greater length in the passage cited: *Antiquarische Aufsätze*, part II, p. 143 ff. ORELLI.

“Filed down from files.” This is the old reading, for which Gelenius gave: “Filed down with files.” Yet we observed above that these particles are often pleonastic (πλεονάζειν) in these writers. Servius on *Aeneid* X: “According to Roman custom, on account of the pig which is struck with a stone.” HERALDUS. *Descobinare* [Col. 1194C] derives from *scobs, scobis*, ῥίνημα, “the scrapings abraded by a file.” *Descobinatum*, ἀποριναθέν, “filed down.” Hence a file was called *scobina*, because by rubbing it produces filings, Glosses of Isidore. See Salmasius on Solinus, p. 758, and Meursius, *Criticus*, p. 188. ORELLI.

“With drills, with axes.” Salmasius, on Solinus, p. 774, shows that this is how the passage should be read. The manuscript and first edition have, most corruptly: “with bran, spikes, axes.” Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “with pincers, with axes.” Others: “with perforators and axes.” But *furfuraculis* is the true reading and comes closest to the manuscript’s spelling. *Furfuraculum* and *perforaculum* mean one and the same thing, namely τὸ τρύπανον, a kind of drill, called either *perforaculum* from perforating, or, among writers of later Latin, *furfuraculum* because in boring wood it produces *furfures*, that is, filings resembling bran. The Glosses: “*furfuraculum* … τρύπανον, drill.” It makes not the slightest difference that augers are mentioned immediately afterward, for augers are different from *furfuracula* or perforators. Thus the Greeks also distinguish τέρετρα, “augers,” and τρύπανα, “drills.” A Greek epigram on craftsmen’s tools:

[Col. 1194D] “Well-whirling drills and swift-cutting augers.”

An auger is τέρετρον; a *perforaculum* or *furfuraculum* is τρύπανον. So Salmasius. ORELLI.

“Hollowed out by the rotating whirl of augers.” *Vertigo* here means simply a circular turning, German *das Umdrehen* (“the turning around”), nothing more. Thus Propertius, Book III, elegy VII.65:

> The wave, twisted in a whirl, snatches this swimmer away.

And Arnobius himself above, Book I, chapter 2: “this rotation of the world”; see the note there. ORELLI.

“Smoothed by the planes of smoothing-tools.” On *runcina*, “plane,” see above on Book V, chapter 28, and Turnebus, *Adversaria*, Book XXIII, chapter 28. *Planis* comes from *plana, -ae*, an obsolete word whose diminutive *planula* is explained in the Glosses as *runcina*, “plane.” Arnobius therefore combines, in his usual manner, two words having the same meaning—unless we prefer to understand *planis* as the part of the plane that smooths the wood. *De* is redundant here, as it often is. ORELLI.

[Col. 1195B] “The workmanship of your fingers.” The first edition has “the part.” Meursius conjectures “the product.” ORELLI.—Lactantius: “For those things are the playthings and fragile fabrications of mortal fingers.” And: “A human being must therefore be regarded as, so to speak, their parent: through his hands they were born; through him they began to possess appearance, shape, and beauty.” HERALDUS.

“And in adversities and harsh times to come to your aid through the favor of a propitious divinity.” This is the old reading, for which Gelenius gives: “for favors to hasten to your aid.” But perhaps nothing should be changed. These words may depend on the verb “ask.” Thus the gods are asked, in adverse circumstances, “to come to one’s aid and bring help through the favor of a propitious divinity”—that is, that they should come to one’s aid and bring help. And indeed a “propitious divinity” is one which comes to one’s aid and is close at hand; to this corresponds the Greek ἵλεως, “gracious,” namely ὁ πρόθυμος ἐποπτεύειν τοὺς δεομένους, “one eager to watch over those in need.” For, as Eustathius says, ἱλάω means τὸ ἵεμαι λάειν, ἤγουν ἐφίεμαι καὶ ὁρμῶ ἐπιβλέπειν, “I hasten to look—that is, I desire and press forward to watch over.” Arnobius therefore could not have expressed himself more precisely. HERALDUS.—The construction is Greek, namely αἰτεῖν, ἀλεξεῖν, “to ask someone to defend.” Thus Virgil, *Eclogue* II.43:

> Long has Thestylis been asking me to take them away.

For more examples, see Vechner, *Hellenolexia*, p. [Col. 1195D] 354, and Cortius on Sallust, *Catiline* LII.24, Leiden edition: “for the favor of the propitious divinity to come to one’s aid.” Meursius conjectures: “to acquire favors.” There is no need. ORELLI.]

## XIV

At this point I should like, as though all the nations from the whole world were present, to deliver a single public address and bring forth into the ears of all these things that all must hear alike. What is this, human beings, that in matters so evident and manifest you willingly deceive and circumvent your own selves through voluntary blindness? Dispel the darkness at last, return to the light of the mind, look more closely, and see what kind of thing this is that is being done—provided only that you retain your proper faculty and remain within the bounds [Note: [Col. 1193B] Thus Sabaeus. Others: “within the bounds given to you,” which I prefer.] of the reason and judgment granted to you.

These images [Col. 1193B] which terrify you, and which you prostrate yourselves and humbly adore in every [Col. 1194A] temple, are bones, stones, bronze, silver, gold, earthenware, wood taken from a tree, or glue mixed with gypsum. Perhaps they have been assembled from prostitutes’ ornaments or women’s finery, from camels’ bones or an Indian animal’s tooth, from cooking-pots, little jars, [Note: [Col. 1194B] Sabaeus also has “and.”] candlesticks and lamps, or from other, more obscene vessels; they have been melted down, drawn into these shapes, and have issued forth into the forms which you see. They have been fired in potters’ kilns, born from anvils and hammers, scraped with *grosfis*, filed down from files, sawn, drilled, and cut with axes, hewn, dug out and hollowed by the rotating whirl of augers, and smoothed by the planes of smoothing-tools.

Is this, then, not error? Is it not, to call it by its proper name, madness to believe that something is a god when you yourself have fashioned it? To fall trembling in supplication before a thing manufactured by you; [Col. 1195A] and although you know and are certain that it is your own work and the workmanship of your fingers, [Note: [Col. 1195B] Sabaeus reads “father.”] to cast yourself face-down, humbly beg for aid, and ask it, in adversities and harsh times, to come to your aid through the favor of a propitious divinity?

[Note: [Col. 1195D]

## XV.—“Masses of untamed silver”

He calls silver not yet subdued by fire or engraving, not yet forced into a form, “untamed”; it is elsewhere called “unworked.” On the word *massa*, see Savaro on Sidonius, Book VI, Epistle I, p. 383. ORELLI.

“Unwrought gold.” Isidore, *Origins*, Book XV, chapter 17: “There are three kinds of silver, gold, and bronze: stamped, wrought, and unwrought. Stamped is what exists in coins; wrought is what exists in vessels and statues; unwrought is what exists in masses and is also called ‘heavy.’” Compare Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* X.527, and J. F. Gronovius, who treats the matter extensively in *On Sesterces*, Book I, chapter VII, p. 33 ff. ORELLI.

“Little ears.” That is, ears. The poet says: “King Midas has an ass’s little ears”; and Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter XXXVI, at the end: “And so the confessors’ eyes were gouged out, their hands amputated, their feet cut off, and their noses and [Col. 1196B] ears sliced away.” See there Gisb. Cuper, p. 214, Bauldri edition. ORELLI.

[Col. 1196C] “Does it change bronze into gold, or compel the cheapness of a potsherd to degenerate into silver material?” Stewechius excellently restored the passage thus. Previously it was read most corruptly: “Into gold, bronze having been changed so that a potsherd may compel cheapness to degenerate into silver material.” Heraldus conjectures: “into gold, bronze, or the cheapness of a transformed potsherd, compel it to degenerate into silver material,” explaining: “What is it that compels gods to pass into these materials?” Wrongly, for “changes” and “compels” depend upon the preceding “fashioning of novelty.” ORELLI.

“Which were insensate a little before.” Thus Stewechius and the Leiden edition. Others read “insensible.” But *insensilia*, which the manuscript has, is a Lucretian word, II.865 ff.:

> Yet you must confess that all things consist  
> Of insensate first beginnings; nor do the manifest facts,  
> Those known and ready to hand, refute or oppose this.  
> Rather, they themselves lead us by the hand and compel belief  
> That living creatures are born from insensate things, as I say.

[Col. 1196D] And verse 887:

> Unless you believe that a sentient thing is born from insensate things.

Elmenhorst cited these passages. ORELLI.

“Causes them to be alive.” “Causes,” namely, “the fashioning of novelty.” Fulvius Ursinus therefore wrongly reads “may cause.” ORELLI.

“To be moved.” Stewechius conjectures “to stir.” ORELLI.]

## XV

Look: suppose someone were to place before you raw bronze, not cast into any work, masses of untamed silver, unwrought gold, wood, stones, bones, and all the other materials of which customary statues and images of divinities consist. Better still, suppose someone were to place before you the battered faces of gods, images melted down and reduced, and then order you to slaughter sacrificial victims to those pieces and fragments and to bestow sacred rites and divine services upon shapeless masses. We demand to hear from you whether you would do this or refuse to comply with the command. [Col. 1195B]

Perhaps you will say: “For what reason? Because no one in human affairs is so foolishly blind as to place silver, bronze, gold, gypsum, ivory, or clay among the gods and declare that these things possess and retain divine power in themselves.”

What, then, is the reason why, if all these materials remain untouched and unwrought, they lack divine power and heavenly authority, but if they receive human forms—if they receive little ears, noses, [Col. 1196A] cheeks, lips, eyes, and eyelids—they immediately become gods and are enrolled in the order and census of the inhabitants of heaven? Does the fashioning of novelty add something to these materials, so that by that very addition you are compelled to believe that something of divinity and majesty has been conferred upon them? Does it change bronze into gold, or compel the cheapness of a potsherd to degenerate into silver material? Does it cause things which were [Note: [Col. 1195B] Fulvius reads “had been.”] insensate a little before to become alive and to be moved by a stirring of spirit?

If, once incorporated in the bodies [Note: [Col. 1196B] The manuscript reads “corporeal things.”] of images, they retain all the natures which they possessed outside them, what stupidity is so great—I shrink from calling it blindness—as to suppose that the natures of things are changed by the character of their forms, and that something receives divinity from its outward appearance when in its original material it was inert, brutish, and deprived of the mobility of sensation?

[Note: [Col. 1196D]

## XVI.—“And so, unmindful and forgetful of what the substance and origin of the images is”

In his second book of *Critical Observations*, Heraldus suspects that one should read: “And so, unmindful and forgetful of what the substances and origins of the images are.” ORELLI.

“Human beings, a rational animal.” The Glosses: “Animal, ζῷον λογικόν, ἄνθρωπος—human being, a rational living creature.” ELMENHORST.

“You adore sheets of bronze.” That is, you prostrate yourselves and pray to them, for *adorare* means “to pray to,” Book I, chapter XXXVI. HERALDUS.

“Acquisitions, profits.” Meursius reads: “acquisitions of profit,” contrary to Arnobius’ custom of heaping together words of the same meaning. ORELLI.

“And although it is patent and evident that words are being addressed to senseless objects.” [Col. 1197B] Thus Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book III: “For according to us, all who address lifeless objects as though addressing a god are drunk. And why do I say ‘drunk’? They are rather insane when they hurry into temples and worship statues as gods.” ORELLI.

“Empty credulity.” Fulvius Ursinus prefers “foolish credulity.” But *vacuus* here is the same as “vain, empty.” Thus below: “empty imagination.” ORELLI.

“Interior cavities.” *Pendigines* are the hollow interstices of an image. See Gesner and Schneider on Vegetius, *Veterinary Medicine*, Book III, chapter 44.1. Others explain them as the coverings of an image. Salmasius, on Solinus, p. 268, interprets them as the joinings and connections of its parts, τὰ πήγματα. [Col. 1197C] See Gesner’s *Thesaurus* for more on this word. ORELLI.

“To pull them apart, resolved into their members.” J. G. Graevius, in Letter 261 to N. Heinsius (*Sylloge* of Burmann, vol. IV, p. 337), showed that this should be read instead of “to lead them down.” I have not hesitated to admit this very certain correction into the text. ORELLI.

“Dowels.” Festus says that *subscudes* are “little boards by which boards are fastened to one another, because the place into which they are inserted is struck from beneath.” Cato used the word in his *On Agriculture*, chapter 18, where, as in Arnobius, it signifies fasteners. NOURRY, p. 566.—*Subscudes* was the name for wedge-shaped wooden pieces used to join beams and other objects.
