See Festus under this word, the interpreters there, and Schneider on Cato, *On Agriculture*, chapter 18. Haynisch translates it in the index as German *Zungen* (“tongues”). Greek πελεκῖνοι; German *Döbelhölzer* (“dowels”). ORELLI.

“Clamps.” *Ansulae* properly denoted the hooks or rings of sandals, through which the inserted straps bind the foot. See Gesner in the *Thesaurus* and Boettiger, *Sabina*, p. 275. Here they seem to signify the iron bands [Col. 1197D] by which images are secured, German *eiserne Bänder, Klammern* (“iron bands, clamps”). ORELLI.

“Even if, to be sure, they could not be discerned because of the sculptor’s art of concealment.” Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “because they were concealed by art.” Wrongly. The “art of concealment” is an artful concealment—namely, the sculptor’s art, which conceals those things and hides their defects from the spectators’ eyes. ORELLI.

“That you accomplish nothing.” See above on chapter 5 of this book. ORELLI.

“To expend the vanities of ritual services.” Fulvius Ursinus prefers “energies,” wrongly. “Vanities of services” are vain and fruitless services by which nothing is accomplished. ORELLI.

“These breathing statues.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.848:

> Others will more softly hammer out breathing bronze.

HERALDUS.

“Whose soles and knees you touch and handle while praying.” That suppliants touched the gods’ knees is a commonplace observation. But they grasped not only their knees, but sometimes their very feet and soles, as Arnobius says, and their footprints, and often kissed them. Hence Prudentius, *Against the Jews*:

> To bow the imperial head before Minerva’s feet,  
> To lick the sandals of earthen Juno, to cast oneself  
> At Hercules’ soles, to bend before Diana’s knees.

Note: “to lick Juno’s sandals.” Apuleius, *Milesian Tale* VI: “Then Psyche, casting herself at her feet and drenching the goddess’s footprints with abundant weeping, sweeping the ground with her hair”; and *Milesian Tale* XI: “Then the people, steeped in joy and carrying palm shoots, sacred boughs, and garlands, kissed the footprints of the goddess, which had been fashioned in silver and adhered to the steps, and departed for their homes.” The Greeks call this τοῖς ἴχνεσι τοῦ ἀγάλματος προσφῦναι, “to cling to the footprints of the statue.” [Col. 1198C] Heliodorus, *Aethiopian History*, Book V: “Entering the sanctuary, he finds her clinging to the footprints of the statue.” And Book VII: “Clinging to the footprints of the statue and remaining thus for a very long time, he came close to dying.” So too sometimes in supplication to human beings. Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XVII: “Casting aside the protection of their weapons, they bound behind their backs the hands made ready for battle; and seeing that their sole remaining hope of safety lay in prayers, they threw themselves at the feet of the merciful Augustus.” But more on this elsewhere. HERALDUS.

“Steeped in smoke.” Thus Sidonius, Book II, Epistle XIII: “From there the dining room, perfumed with cinnamon and incense, would scatter foreign fragrances to the nostrils.” See there Savaro, p. 173, who treats this word extensively. ORELLI.

“Lose their appearance through neglect and be wounded and eaten away by rust.” Thus I have printed with Fulvius Ursinus. The old reading is thoroughly corrupt: “may lose neglect in appearance.” Heraldus, transposing the words, thinks it should read: “may lose their appearance, and be wounded by neglect and eaten-away rust.” The Leiden edition has: “may lose their positions, appearances,” etc., so that “to lose position” would mean “to collapse, to be displaced from its base and foundation.” ORELLI.

“Within the hollows of those images.” This most certain correction is owed to Gelenius. Previously “causes” was read, without any sense. Stewechius prefers “cages,” understanding the cases and cabinets in which images of the gods were customarily enclosed like birds in a cage. But from the very similar passages in Minucius Felix, chapter XXIV, beginning, it is evident that the images themselves are to be understood as gnawed by such little creatures: “How truly the dumb animals judge your gods by nature! Mice, swallows, and kites know that they have no sensation; they recognize this, trample upon them, and sit upon them; and unless you drive them away, they build nests in the very mouth of your god. Spiders weave over his face and suspend their threads from his head. You wipe, clean, and scrape them, and you protect and fear those whom you make.” And Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, chapter XII: “Therefore, if we do not worship statues and cold images closely resembling their dead originals—which kites, mice, and spiders understand—did not the rejection of a recognized error deserve praise rather than punishment?” ORELLI.

[Col. 1199B] “Shrew-mice.” See on Book II, chapter 59. ORELLI.

“To establish nesting-material.” A Plautine expression, *Rudens*, Act III, scene VI:

> Today he will heap up a thousand nestings in the stocks.

NOURRY, p. 560.

“Bones dragged into a hedge.” I have admitted into the text this masterly emendation of C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book [Col. 1199C] XXIX, chapter 18, p. 1391. Everyone knows that those animals use bones as defenses for their nests. The common reading is: “bones dragged away in hope,” which Heraldus defends in vain. He thinks the sense to be that mice, shrew-mice, and so forth, although unable to gnaw bones, nevertheless drag them away, hoping, of course, that they may be able to eat them, since they have not yet sufficiently tested the strength of their teeth or matched it against the hardness of the bones. I very much doubt that such a subtlety entered Arnobius’ mind. Fulvius Ursinus thinks it should be read: “bones dragged into tow.” *Stupa, stipa* is that with which nests are stuffed and strengthened. See Vossius, *Roman Etymology*. Meursius conjectures: “hard pieces of bread shaped like bone in appearance … for softness,” etc., in the ancient manner of speech. *Os, osse, ossum, ossu*, like *testum, testu*, in Ovid, *Fasti* II.645 and V.519. Salmasius printed: “bones of hunger dragged away in hope,” that is, bones dragged into the nest in expectation of hunger. *Spes*, “hope,” means expectation or fear, as it does a hundred times in the ancients. But I greatly prefer Barthius’ correction. Yet now I prefer the old reading: “dragged away in hope”—that is, in hope of the future, so that they may have something to eat. [Col. 1199D] Thus Horace, *Satires* I.1.35:

> Fly over there; for the ant, an example of great industry,  
> Draws in its mouth whatever it can and adds it to the heap  
> Which it builds, neither ignorant nor heedless of the future.

ORELLI.

“For the softness of their little nests, of course, and as warm bedding for their wretched chicks.” Thus the Leiden edition. The manuscript has: “solicitously for the softness of their little nests, and as warm bedding for their wretched chicks.” The first edition: “solicitously in the softness of their little nests,” etc. The other editors delete “solicitously.” ORELLI.

“Webs to be begun by spiders.” *Ordiri* here has a passive sense, which should be noted. *Ordiri*, or the old form *ordire*, is a term proper to weaving and the work of the loom. See Nonius and Festus under this word, the interpreters there, and Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. ORELLI.

“Finally, do not swallows,” etc. Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus*, p. 46, Potter edition: “Swallows and most birds fly into the temples and defile the statues themselves, paying no regard to Olympian Zeus, Epidaurian Asclepius, Athena Polias, or Egyptian Sarapis.” [Col. 1200B] ORELLI.

“Flying about among the very domes of the buildings.” *Tholus* means a vault—that is, a round, convex chamber, German *Kuppel* (“dome”). See Lindenbrog and Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus XXVIII.4.9, p. 241, Wagner edition. ORELLI.

“To discharge themselves when full of dung.” The interpreters [Col. 1200C] commend Joannes Auratus’ conjecture “patches of dung,” citing Martial II.29.10:

> Do you not know who he is? Remove the patches, and you will read it;

see the interpreters there. The sense would be that swallows discharge *splena* or *splenia* of dung, that is, plasters or patches. But I have sought *splena, -ae* in the lexicons in vain; and for *splen, splenis*, whose accusative might be the Greek form *splenas*, I have found no meaning other than the spleen, the seat of laughter and sadness, German *die Milz*. See Vossius, *Roman Etymology*. Nor do I see why the common reading should be disturbed. Its sense is: swallows, being full of dung, discharge themselves—that is, empty the bowels. Arnobius uses “to discharge” absolutely, an honorable word for a dishonorable act. Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “to discharge missiles of dung.” ORELLI.

“To drop obscenities.” This is Fulvius Ursinus’ masterly emendation of the manuscript’s defective reading “to say obscenities,” from which Gelenius had made “to do obscenities.” Stewechius prefers: “to digest obscenities.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1200D] “Impelled by the truth of nature.” The manuscript and first edition read “distinguished,” wrongly. “Impelled by the truth of nature” means by nature’s true and proper instinct. Meursius’ conjecture is therefore unnecessary: “impelled by the severity”—that is, necessity—“of nature.” ORELLI.]

## XVI

And so, unmindful and forgetful of what the substance and origin of the images [Col. 1196B] is, you human beings—a rational animal endowed with the gift of wisdom and judgment—prostrate yourselves before baked potsherds, adore sheets of bronze, and ask from elephants’ tusks good health, magistracies, commands, powers, victories, acquisitions, [Note: [Col. 1196B] Sabaeus reads the singular “acquisition.”] profits, rich harvests, and most abundant vintages. Although it is patent and evident that words are being addressed to senseless objects, do you suppose that you are heard, and do you willingly expose [Col. 1197A] your own selves to ridicule through the deception of empty credulity?

If only it were possible to enter into the innermost cavities of some image! Better still, if only it were possible to pull apart those Olympian and Capitoline Jupiters, resolved into their members, and to examine separately and individually all those parts by which the totality of their bodies is enclosed! You would long ago have seen that those gods, whose smooth outer surface is rendered august by the allure of its brilliance, are lattices of beaten metal plates, assemblages of misshapen particles held together by dowels, chains, hooks, and clamps against the accidents of collapse and the danger of dissolution; that lead runs, poured in, through all their recesses and the junctions of their seams and supplies salutary delays to prolong the statues’ endurance.

You would long ago have seen, I say, faces alone without backs to their heads, half-complete hands without arms, bellies [Col. 1198A] cut in half together with their sides, incomplete traces of soles, and—what especially provokes laughter—figures pieced together by an uneven construction of bodies, wooden on one side and stone on the other. Even if, to be sure, these things could not be discerned because of the sculptor’s art of concealment, at least the things lying openly before you should themselves have taught and warned you that you accomplish nothing and expend the vanities of ritual services upon empty objects.

Do you therefore not see that these “breathing” statues, whose soles and knees you touch and handle while praying, now collapse under falling drops of water, now come apart through rotting decay; that, steeped and discolored by odors and smoke, they grow black; that through the neglect [Note: [Col. 1197B] Fulvius reads “injury.”] of a longer age they lose their appearance through grime and are wounded and eaten away by rust? Do you not see, I say, within the hollows [Note: [Col. 1198B] Fulvius reads “huts.”] of these images, geckos, [Col. 1199A] shrew-mice, and light-shunning cockroaches establishing nesting-material and taking up residence? Do you not see them bringing there every kind of filth and other things suited to their uses—half-gnawed hard pieces of bread, bones dragged into a hedge, rags, down, and scraps of paper, for the softness of their little nests, of course, [Note: [Col. 1199B] Sabaeus reads “solicitously in softness.” Wrongly.] and as warm bedding for their wretched young?

Are webs and treacherous nets not sometimes begun by spiders in the mouth of an image, so that they may ensnare in them the flight of shrill little insects and shameless flies? Finally, do not swallows, flying about within the very domes of the buildings, discharge themselves when full of dung, painting now the faces themselves, now the countenances of the divinities—their beards, eyes, noses, and all the other parts whatsoever upon which the outpouring from an emptied anus happens to fall?

Blush, then, though late, and learn paths and principles from dumb animals. Let those very creatures teach [Col. 1199B] you that no divinity is present in the images—images upon which animals following their own laws and impelled by the truth of nature neither fear nor refrain from dropping obscenities.

[Note: [Col. 1200D]

## XVII.—“Whom sacred dedication introduces”

Minucius, chapter XXIII, at the end: “When, then, is this god born? Look: it is cast, fabricated, and carved. It is not yet a god. Look: it is soldered with lead, assembled, and erected. It is still not a god. Look: it is adorned, consecrated, and prayed to. Only then, at last, is it a god, once a human being has so willed and dedicated it.” HERALDUS.

“Union.” Others read “bondage.” ORELLI.

“Under imposed necessities.” The first edition has “one subjected to necessities,” wrongly. ORELLI.

“If they do this unwillingly.” Fulvius Ursinus deletes “if,” because in the other member of the sentence, “if by the assent of voluntary compliance,” “if” was absent from the manuscript. But with Salmasius it is better added in both places. ORELLI.

[Col. 1201B] “Are compelled into some necessity …” The manuscript has “are compelled in some necessity,” which Heraldus defends in his second book of *Critical Observations* as an example of Arnobius’ manner of placing the ablative [Col. 1201C] for the accusative, which we have already observed several times, for example on Book II, chapter 2. ORELLI.

“And what?” Here Stewechius reads “surely?” ORELLI.

“Practically bound together by the force of bondage.” Thus the Leiden edition. The others: “all bound and practically tied together.” ORELLI.

“Ennoble the potsherds.” Thus the Leiden edition in place of *nobilitatis*, a scribal error which arose in the manuscript from *nobilitantis*. Meursius and the other editors read: “may ennoble the potsherds.” Heraldus: “so that they may ennoble the potsherds.” ORELLI.

“If we grant that they prefer them to heaven and their abodes among the stars, they will have lost the power of their divinity.” These words, which are shamefully mangled in the other editions and are read only in the following chapter after the words “when it is fitting and proper to abstain from them,” were restored by the Leiden editor to this place as by far the most suitable. Meursius, [Col. 1201D] however, transferred them after the words in the following chapter: “when it is fitting and proper to abstain from them.” In my judgment, however, they smack of a gloss; for that reason I have enclosed them in brackets. ORELLI.]

## XVII

“But,” he says, “you are mistaken and go astray. For neither bronze, nor the substances of gold and silver, nor the other materials from which statues are made do we determine to be gods in themselves and divine objects of worship. Rather, in them we worship and venerate those whom sacred dedication introduces and causes to inhabit images made by craftsmen.” [Col. 1200A]

This is not an improper or contemptible line of reasoning, by which any dullard—and even the wisest person—might be able to believe that the gods, after abandoning their proper abodes, that is, heaven, do not refuse or shrink from entering earthly dwellings; indeed, that when impelled by the right of dedication they merge into union with images.

Do your gods therefore dwell continually in gypsum and potsherds? Or rather, are the gods the minds, spirits, and souls of potsherds and gypsum? And so that the cheapest objects may be rendered more august, do they allow themselves to be enclosed and to lie hidden under the confinement of an obscure abode?

In this connection, therefore, this is the first thing we desire and request to hear from you: do they do this unwillingly—that is, when drawn by the right of dedication do they enter the dwellings of images? Or are they ready and compliant, with no necessities imposed upon them? If they do this unwillingly, how can it be that, with their majesty diminished, they are compelled into some necessity? [Col. 1201A] But if they do so by the assent of voluntary [Note: [Col. 1201B] Sabaeus omits “if.” Fulvius punctuates: “are compelled. By voluntary …”] compliance, what do gods seek in potsherds, that they should prefer them to their abodes among the stars and, practically bound together by the force of bondage, ennoble the potsherds and the other materials from which statues are made? If we grant that they prefer them to heaven and their abodes among the stars, they will have lost the power of their divinity.

[Note: [Col. 1201D]

## XVIII.—“Or do they have freedom to go,” etc.

Correctly. For *liber*, “free,” comes ἀπὸ τοῦ λύειν, “from releasing”; ὁ λελυμένος, “the one released,” is ἐλεύθερος, “free,” among the Greeks, because he has freedom to go. Plautus, *Menaechmi*. Messenio:

> Then allow me, since you deny that I belong to you, to go away free.

Menaechmus:

> For my part, by Hercules, be free, and go wherever you wish.

Hence ἀφεῖναι and *amittere liberum*, “to release and let go free.” In the same play:

> Because I saved you, you have let me go free.

Then Menaechmus:

> I ordered you to go away free.

[Col. 1202B] And:

> Are you delaying me at all from going away free, as you ordered?

[Col. 1202C] Menaechmus:

> Be free.

HERALDUS.

“Sacred rites should be rendered.” See above on Book IV, chapter 16. ORELLI.

“But in vast images,” etc. Thus Meursius and Salmasius, excellently. The others read “or indeed.” ORELLI.

“To extend themselves to maximum size.” The first edition reads “in maximum size,” which can be defended by Arnobius’ style, fond as he is of putting the ablative in place of the accusative, as we have already observed several times. *Maximitas*, “maximum size,” is a Lucretian word, II.497:

> Lest you be compelled to suppose that some things are of monstrous maximum size,  
> Beyond the limit which I have already shown cannot be established.

“And in seated statues it must be said that the god sits.” For, as Porphyry says in Eusebius, they represented their gods ἀνετύπουν σχήμασι διαφόροις καὶ ἡλικίαις, καθέδραις τε καὶ στάσεσι καὶ ἀμφιάσεσιν, “in differing forms and ages, in seated and standing postures and in differing modes of dress.” HERALDUS.]

## XVIII

What, then? Do the gods always dwell in materials of this kind and never depart anywhere, even if some very great circumstance demands it? Or do they have freedom to go whenever they please, to depart wherever they wish from their abodes and images?

If they endure the necessity of remaining, what could be more pitiable or unhappy than they, if hooks and leaden bonds hold them so fast upon their bases? But if they fly away whenever they wish and possess an unrestricted right to abandon the empty images, [Col. 1201B] then at some time the statues will cease to be gods, and it will remain uncertain when sacred rites ought to be rendered and when it is fitting and proper to abstain from them.

We often see these statues made by craftsmen, now very small and compressed into a size measurable by the palm, now raised to an immense height and elevated to an astonishing magnitude. By this reasoning, therefore, it follows that we must understand the gods to contract themselves within tiny figurines and be compressed into conformity with a body not their own; but in vast images [Col. 1202A] to stretch themselves farther and extend themselves to maximum size.

Therefore, if this is so, it must be said both that the god sits in seated statues and stands in standing ones, [Note: [Col. 1202B] Sabaeus reads “in those pressing on.” Wrongly.] runs in those depicted running, discharges missiles in those hurling weapons, shapes and adapts his face to theirs, and accommodates himself to the likeness of all the other postures of the represented body.

[Note: [Col. 1202D]

## XIX.—“Because things which are individual and singular by nature”

Thus Fulvius Ursinus and Meursius, with Stewechius’ approval. Others read “private and singular.” But Festus, Nonius, and Aulus Gellius, Book X, chapter 20, teach us that the ancients called those things *priva* which we call individual, and that *privata*, “private things,” and *privilegia*, “privileges,” were formed from it. See Scaliger and Dacier on Festus under this word, p. 374. Moreover, *privus* is also a Lucretian word, and Arnobius is a diligent imitator of Lucretius. Thus *On the Nature of Things* III.722:

> But if by chance you believe that souls slip in from outside  
> Into worms and can enter their bodies individually.

And V.732:

> And that, on each individual day, each created thing passes away.

And so more often elsewhere. ORELLI and STEWECHIUS.

“All reasoning and the integrity of truth perish.” Thus Sabaeus and the Leiden edition. Others read “the integrity of the truth.” ORELLI.]

## XIX

The gods inhabit images: does each god inhabit each image in his entirety, or only partially, divided into members? For neither can one god be present in numerous images at one time, nor, conversely, can he be divided into parts through the intervention of a severing.

Let us suppose, for example, that there are ten thousand images of Vulcan throughout the whole world. Can one Vulcan, as I have said, be present in all ten thousand at one time? I do not think so. For what reason? Because things which are individual and singular by nature cannot become many [Col. 1202B] while the integrity of their simplicity is preserved; and still less can they do so if the gods possess human forms, as your belief declares.

For neither can a hand separated from a head nor a foot divided from a body furnish the totality of the whole; nor must it be said that portions can do the same as the whole, since the whole cannot exist unless it has been formed by the aggregation of its parts.

But if the same god is said to exist in all images, all reasoning and the integrity of truth perish if it is assumed that one being can remain [Col. 1203A] in all of them at one time. Or each of the gods must be said so to divide his own self from himself [Note: [Col. 1203B] Thus the manuscript; Sabaeus better: “himself from his own self.”] that he is both himself and another—not separated by any distinction, but the very same self and yet another.

Since nature refuses, rejects, and disdains this, either it must be said and confessed that there are innumerable Vulcans, if we wish him to dwell and be present in every image, or he will be in none, because nature forbids him to be divided among many.

[Note: [Col. 1203B]

## XX.—“You guard, preserve, and keep them shut in”

Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*: “Thus, when they are harmed, your vengeance defends them, just as your protection guards them when they are shut in, lest they perish. Be ashamed to worship those whom you yourself defend; be ashamed to hope for protection from those whom you protect.” HERALDUS.

“You protect them with a thousand temple-keepers and a thousand watchmen.” Tertullian, *On the Soldier’s Crown*: “Will he now also perform guard duties for anyone more readily than for Christ? Or even on the Lord’s Day, when he will not do so for Christ? And will he stand guard before the temples which he has renounced?” They kept watch both over the shrines and images of the gods and also over the riches which were very often preserved there. Plautus, *Bacchides*:

> Why, it has itself been deposited there in Diana’s temple;  
> They guard it there at public expense.

HERALDUS. *Aeditui* were those to whom the care of a temple had been entrusted and who kept watch in it at night. Varro, *On Agriculture*, Book I, testifies that the ancients said *aeditimus* and later writers *aedituus*. Compare Petrus Daniel on Pseudo-Plautus’ *Querolus*, p. 64, and Duker, *On the Latinity of the Jurists*, p. 28. ORELLI.

“Why do you provide the geese with sustenance and nourishment?” The manuscript has *alimonia*, from *alimonium, -ii*, which is the older form and was used several times by Varro in his books *On Agriculture*. On dogs and geese as guards, see Cicero, *For Roscius of Ameria*, chapter XX; Augustine, *City of God*, Book II, chapter 22; Vegetius, *On Military Matters*, Book IV, chapter 26; and Stewechius’ collected notes there. ORELLI.

[Col. 1203D] “Under the very pressure of the work.” Fulvius Ursinus and Meursius emended the text thus, entirely correctly. Others read “under the very name of the work.” See above on Book II, chapter 28. ORELLI.

“May fasten sacrilegious persons with adequate punishments.” I emend this to “may strike sacrilegious persons with adequate punishments.” *Fligere*, “to strike,” is an ancient verb; today its compounds are more commonly used. Livius, in *Aegisthus*:

> Wounded, he himself strikes himself against the earth as he falls.

Accius, *The Battle at the Ships*:

> Nor does he grieve deeply that his comrades are struck down in death  
> And that the fields are covered with them.

And in *Aegisthus*:

> Alas, whose stock does he strive to strike down root and branch?

Lucretius, Book II.85:

> … For when swiftly from above  
> They have struck what meets them, it happens that suddenly in different directions …]

Burst apart. MEURSIUS. Stewechius thinks the reading should be *subsigant*, that is, “fasten them to the cross [Col. 1204B] or gibbet,” which Justus Lipsius, *On the Cross*, book I, chapter 13, shows to have been the punishment peculiar to sacrilegious persons. ORELLI.

“To entrust the guardianship of the highest divinities to the anxious care of dogs.” For these watchmen display great and intense vigilance; for that reason they are ordered to sleep during the day, so that they may keep watch at night. Varro, *On Agriculture*, book I: “It is better to keep a few dogs of good quality and fierce disposition than many. You should accustom them particularly to keep watch at night and to sleep shut up [Col. 1204C] during the day.” Hence in Phaedrus the dog says, fable XLVI (book III, fable VII):

> They tie me up during the day,  
> So that I may rest in daylight and keep watch when night has come.

Thus the watchman in Aeschylus, at the very opening of the *Agamemnon*, complains that he has stood watch through successive nights like a watchdog:

> I ask the gods for release from these labors,  
> From this year-long watch, during which, lying  
> On the roof of the sons of Atreus, resting on my elbows like a dog,  
> I have come to know the nightly assembly of the stars.

HERALDUS.

“With their honking” (*gingritibus*). Festus: “*Gingrire*—is the verb proper to the cry of geese”; see Scaliger there, who cites our passage. The Glosses: “*Gingriunt*: geese cry out” (*χῆνες ἐκβοῶσι*). “*Gingrum*: the cry of a goose” (*φωνὴ χηνός*). Hence *γιγγράζειν* and *γίγγρίζειν*, “to honk.” See Salmasius on Solinus, p. 87, and Schneider in his Lexicon under this word. Indeed, the cry of geese is expressed in various ways by the ancients: *gingrire, trinnire, graccitare, gratitare*. [Col. 1204D] See Wernsdorf on Juventius’s *Elegy on the Nightingale*, verse 19, in *Minor Latin Poets*, vol. VI, p. 391.

Columella calls the cry of geese *clangere*, “to clang.” The Greeks say *χηνίζειν*, “to cry like a goose.” On geese as guards, Aelian, *History of Animals*, book XII, chapter 33, writes: “Dogs, as it turns out, are less useful than geese for keeping guard, and the Romans discovered this” (*Φυλάττειν δὲ ἄρα χηνῶν κύνες ἀχρειότεροι, καὶ τοῦτο κατεφώρασαν Ῥωμαῖοι*). See Gonsalo de Salas on Petronius, pp. 424–425. ORELLI.]

### XX

And yet, you people! If it is evident and perfectly clear to you that gods live within the bodies of statues and that heavenly beings dwell there, why do you guard them beneath the strongest keys and enormous locks, behind bars, bolts, and other things of this kind; why do you preserve them and keep them shut in? And lest some thief or [Col. 1203B] nocturnal robber happen to creep in, why do you protect them with a thousand temple-keepers and a thousand sentries? Why do you feed dogs on the Capitols? Why do you provide food and sustenance for geese? [Col. 1204A] Indeed, if you trust that the gods are there and never depart from their statues and images, allow them to take care of themselves. Let the sanctuaries always be unlocked and open; and if anything is stolen by anyone’s reckless deceit, let them display the power of divinity and, at the very moment of the theft and deed, [Note: [Col. 1204B] Fulvius reads “crime.”] transfix the sacrilegious with appropriate punishments. For it is an unworthy thing, destructive alike of their power and authority, to entrust the guardianship of the highest divinities to the anxious care of dogs; and, when you seek some terror with which to deter thieves, not to obtain it from the gods themselves, but to place and locate it in the honking of geese.

[Note: [Col. 1204D]

### XXI—“They say that Antiochus Cyzicenus,” etc.

Clement, in the *Exhortation* (p. 46, Potter’s edition), writes:

> Antiochus Cyzicenus, being short of money, ordered the golden statue of Zeus, which was fifteen cubits high, to be melted down, and another statue resembling it, made from cheaper material and gilded with gold leaf, to be dedicated again in its place.

(*Ἀντίοχος δὲ, ὁ Κυζικηνός, ἀπορούμενος χρημάτων, τοῦ Διὸς τὸ ἄγαλμα τὸ χρυσοῦν, πεντεκαίδεκα πηχῶν τὸ μέγεθος ὂν, προσέταξε χωνεῦσαι, καὶ τῆς ἄλλης τῆς ἀτιμοτέρας ὕλης ἄγαλμα παραπλήσιον ἐκείνῳ, πετάλοις κεχρυσωμένον, ἀναθεῖναι πάλιν*.)

CANTER.—Meursius was the first, following Clement, to restore “fifteen cubits” in place of “ten cubits,” which had previously been read and which even the most recent editor, Oberthür, very badly retained; see Meursius, p. 195, followed by the Leiden edition. ORELLI.

[Col. 1205B] “That Dionysius—but the younger,” etc. Clement, on the page cited:

> For Dionysius the Younger, the tyrant, stripped off the golden cloak of Zeus in Sicily and ordered that a woolen one be put upon him, wittily saying that this was better than the golden one: lighter in summer and warmer in winter.

(*Διονύσιος μὲν γὰρ ὁ τύραννος ὁ νεώτερος, θοιμάτιον τὸ χρύσεον περιελόμενος Διὸς ἐν Σικελίᾳ, προσέταξεν αὐτῷ ἐρεοῦν περιτιθέναι, χαριέντως φήσας, τοῦτο ἄμεινον εἶναι τοῦ χρυσίου, καὶ θέρους κουφότερον, καὶ κρύους ἀλεεινότερον*.)

CANTER.—Stewechius and Heraldus are therefore wrong in thinking that the words “but the younger” should be deleted as a gloss, although Heraldus himself later retracts his opinion in his *Second Critical Notes*. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, III, chapter 34; Lactantius, *Institutes*, book II, chapter 4; and Aelian, *Various History*, book I, chapter 20, attribute this witticism to Dionysius the Elder; see Kühn there. Compare Petrus Victorius, *Various Readings*, book XXI, chapter 10. ORELLI.

“When he stripped Jupiter of his golden covering.” Marcus Tullius says that the tyrant Gelo had adorned him with it from the spoils of the Carthaginians. [Col. 1205C] The gods had their own coverings and mantles with which they were clothed and adorned. Suetonius, in *Caligula*: “In the temple stood a golden portrait-statue, which was dressed every day in clothing of the kind that he himself wore.” Lactantius, book II, chapter 4: “Thus to these playthings, ornamented and enormous puppets, they bring ointments, incense, and perfumes. To them they sacrifice rich and fat victims, although they have mouths devoid of any use of teeth; to them they offer robes and precious garments, although they have no use for covering,” etc. Philo elegantly observes in his exposition of the Decalogue that the makers of statues and images are very often afflicted by every kind of misery, while the images fashioned and formed by them are adorned with purple, gold, and other precious ornaments. Philo’s words are:

> And the craftsmen themselves have often grown old in poverty and obscurity and died amid successive misfortunes, while the things they fashioned are made objects of reverence with purple and gold and the other costly things that wealth supplies.

(*Καὶ οἱ μὲν τεχνῖται πολλάκις ἄποροι καὶ ἄδοξοι κατεγήρασαν, ἀτυχίαις ἐπαλλήλοις ἀποθανόντες· τὰ δὲ τεχνιτευθέντα πορφύρᾳ καὶ χρυσῷ καὶ ταῖς ἄλλαις πολυτελείαις, ἃς πλοῦτος χορηγεῖ, σεμνοποιεῖται*.)

Thus these ornaments were often exceedingly precious. See [Col. 1205D] Lactantius, book II, chapters 4 and 7, and book VI, chapter 13. HERALDUS.

“Joking” (*ludens*). Fulvius Ursinus conjectures *lusit*, “he joked.” ORELLI.

“Cold amid the chills.” Meursius, p. 195, prefers “cold amid the cold” (*in frigoribus algidum*), which is very attractive. For *rigor* is a condition of bodies caused by cold. ORELLI.

“Warm” (*vaporum*). So the Leiden edition. The manuscript wrongly has *vaporem*, from which some made *vaporeum*, others *vaporosum*. *Vaporum* means “emitting much warm vapor.” Nemesianus, Eclogue IV, 63:

> Three times with fillets, three times with sacred foliage, three times with steaming incense  
> He purified it.

ORELLI.

“An urbane wit.” Plautus, *The Haunted House*, act I, scene I:

> You truly are an urbane wit, the darling of the people.

In the *Three-Coins*, act II, scene I:

> Surely nothing is more foolish or more stupid,  
> More mendacious, more scheming,  
> More brazen in speech, or more perjured  
> [Col. 1206B] Than those ever-present city-dwellers whom they call wits.

ELMENHORST. The poet and other ancient writers called a clever and polished man who was in no way rustic an “urbane wit” (*scurra urbanus*). Arnobius similarly uses *scurrula* in this sense. Later, however, the word was certainly employed with another and contrary meaning. See Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XIX, chapter 13; Vossius in his *Etymological Dictionary*; and others. NOURRY, p. 565.

“That the dignity of Aesculapius was mocked by him.” See Lactantius, book II, chapter 4; Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, chapter 34; Valerius Maximus, book I, chapter 1, foreign example 3. ORELLI.

“Philosophical thickness.” Philosophers were bearded. Prudentius, book II, *Against Symmachus*: “the bearded sophist.” [Col. 1206C] In the *On Crowns*, “bearded Plato.” Juvenal, Satire XIV, verse 12: “bearded teachers.” Tatian, *Against the Greeks*, p. 287; Theodoret, *On Providence*, discourse 1. ELMENHORST.—Such a philosopher is graphically depicted by Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* XI: “One who, with cloak, staff, sandals, and goatish little beard, would counterfeit a philosopher.” STEWECHIUS.

“Indeed, whether they are.” So all editors after Canter, from Meursius’s emendation. Previously the text read “whether he is.” ORELLI.

“Joked” (*jocaretur*). Sabaeus reads “spoke” (*loqueretur*). Wrongly. ORELLI.

“Why did he not punish the insult of having his face made smooth,” etc. The plucking out of a beard was connected with the greatest disgrace. Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*, book VII, chapter 14; Procopius on Isaiah, p. 120; Herodian, on Maximinus and Balbinus. ELMENHORST.—Persius, Satire I, 132–133:

> The crafty fellow knows how to laugh and is ready to rejoice greatly  
> If an impudent streetwalker should tug a Cynic’s beard.

This was a cruel insult, which Hanun, king of the Ammonites, [Col. 1206D] also inflicted upon the ambassadors sent by David: 2 Samuel, chapter X. Women, however, had their hair cut round. Lucian, in the *Dialogues of the Courtesans*:

> But if a man, Chrysis, is neither jealous nor angry, and has never slapped you, cut your hair, or torn your clothes, is he still your lover?

(*Εἴ τις δὲ, ὦ Χρυσί, μήτε ζηλοτυπεῖ, μήτε ὀργίζεται, μήτε ἐρράπισέ ποτε, ἢ περιέκειρεν, ἢ τὰ ἱμάτια περιέσχισεν, ἔτι ἐραστὴς ἐκεῖνός ἐστιν;*)

HERALDUS.

“Their own temples” (*suas aedes*). So Salmasius from the manuscript. Others read “their own seats” (*suas sedes*). ORELLI.]

### XXI

They say that Antiochus Cyzicenus removed from its sanctuary a golden Jupiter fifteen cubits high and substituted for it one made of bronze and disguised with gold leaf. If the gods are present in their own images and dwell within them, [Col. 1204B] what business, what concerns, held Jupiter fast and prevented him from prosecuting his private injuries and avenging the substitution of himself [Col. 1205A] for himself in a cheaper material?

That Dionysius—but the younger—when stripping Jupiter of his golden covering and substituting a woolen one for it, also played with joking pleasantries: he said that the former was cold amid the chills and the latter warm; that the former was burdensome in summer, while the latter, by contrast, was airy beneath the heat. Where, then, was the king of heaven, that he might prove himself present by inspiring some fear and recall this urbane wit to seriousness through torture?

For why should I mention that the dignity of Aesculapius was mocked by him? When he stripped Aesculapius of a very ample beard, substantial in weight and philosophical in thickness, he said that it was an unworthy thing for the son begotten of Apollo—a father who was smooth and beardless, and very like a boy not yet of age—to be represented as so heavily bearded that one was left in doubt which of them was the father and which the son—indeed, whether they were of one [Col. 1205B] stock and kin at all.

While all these things were being done, and while the robber [Col. 1206A] joked with sacrilegious mockery, if a divine power lay beneath the statue consecrated to its name and majesty, why did it not pursue with just and deserved vengeance the insult of having its face made smooth and its countenance dishonored? Why did it not demonstrate by this act that it was present and that with persistent vigilance it guarded its own temples and images?

[Note: [Col. 1206D]

### XXII—“In which, though scorned, they do not care to show themselves through some act of vengeance.”

Fulvius Ursinus added “themselves” (*se*), as the sense requires. ORELLI.

“Philostephanus, in his *Cyprian History*, records that Pygmalion,” etc. Clement, in the *Exhortation* (pp. 50–51, Potter’s edition):

> Thus the famous Cypriot Pygmalion fell in love with an ivory statue. The statue was of Aphrodite, and it was naked. The Cypriot was overcome by its form and had intercourse with the statue; Philostephanus records this. Another Aphrodite at Cnidus was made of stone and was beautiful. Another man fell in love with her and coupled with the stone; Posidippus records this. The former author tells the story in his work *On Cyprus*, the latter in his work *On Cnidus*.

(*Οὕτως ὁ Κύπριος ὁ Πύγμαλίων ἐκεῖνος ἐλεφαντίνου ἠράσθη ἀγάλματος. Τὸ ἄγαλμα Ἀφροδίτης ἦν, καὶ γυμνὴ ἦν· νικᾶται ὁ Κύπριος τῷ σχήματι, καὶ συνέρχεται τῷ ἀγάλματι· καὶ τοῦτο Φιλοστέφανος ἱστορεῖ. Ἀφροδίτη δὲ ἄλλη ἐν Κνίδῳ λίθος ἦν, καὶ καλὴ ἦν· ἕτερος ἠράσθη ταύτης, καὶ μίγνυται τῇ λίθῳ· Ποσίδιππος ἱστορεῖ. ὁ μὲν πρότερος, ἐν τῷ περὶ Κύπρου· ὁ δὲ ἕτερος, ἐν τῷ περὶ [Col. 1207B] Κνίδου*.)

CANTER.—Others report that Pygmalion was not a king but a sculptor, and that he burned with love for a statue he himself had made. Compare Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X, verses 245 following. Philostratus mentions the sculptor Pygmalion in the *Life of Apollonius*, book V, chapter 5. On the love affairs involving the Cnidian Venus, see Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXVI, chapters 4 and 5; Valerius Maximus, book VIII, chapter 11; Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*, book VI, chapter 40. Aelian records several other examples of similar loves in *Various History*, book IX, chapter 39. POTTER, on Clement, at the passage cited.—He was Callimachus of Cyrene’s compatriot and *σύγχρονος*, or contemporary, [Col. 1207C] and his friend, as Athenaeus attests, book VIII, p. 331. Athenaeus also relates that he wrote *On the Cities of Asia*, book VII, p. 297; Clement of Alexandria mentions his *On Discoveries* (*περὶ εὑρημάτων*), *Stromata* I, p. 308; Harpocration, under “Stryme,” his *On Islands* (*περὶ νήσων*); and the scholia on Pindar his *On Cyllene* (*περὶ Κυλλήνης*). HARDUIN, Index to Pliny.—On Philostephanus of Cyrene, the friend of Callimachus, see G. J. Vossius, *On the Greek Historians*, book I, chapter 15. Among other works he wrote an *On Islands* (*περὶ Νήσων*), of which that book on Cyprus appears to have been a part. ORELLI.

“Mind” (*animo*). The first edition and Gelenius read “soul” (*anima*). ORELLI.

“As though it were a conjugal possession” (*uxoria res*). Fulvius Ursinus reads “a wife’s” (*uxoris*). ORELLI.

“Posidippus.” See above, at chapter 13 of this book.

“Which he identifies as written on Cnidus.” Meursius, p. 196, thinks *indigitat*, “expressly identifies,” should be read. But no change is necessary. For *indicat* means “entitles,” and the title of books is *ἐπιγραφή*. This story is also narrated by Lucian in the *Amores*. HERALDUS.

“And concerning its affairs.” This is Gelenius’s emendation. The first edition reads: “and concerning the thing by himself of it” (*superque re a se ejus*). From this [Col. 1207D] Canter produced “and concerning the actual matter” (*superque reapse*), a conjecture confirmed by the Royal manuscript. HERALDUS.—Stewechius conjectures “and concerning his guilt” (*superque reatu ejus*), that is, his crime. The word is extremely frequent among the jurists. For my part, I prefer Gelenius’s reading, “concerning its affairs” (*super rebus ejus*), that is, the affairs of Cnidus, *περὶ τῶν ἐν Κνίδῳ*. ORELLI.

“Suppresses” (*obscurat*). That is, leaves in obscurity, omits. Nothing more. ORELLI.

“On whose account Cnidus is renowned.” *Ὀνομαστός ἐστιν*, “it is famous.” Above, in chapter 13, he said “held in repute”: “It is said to have been the model for all the Venuses that are held in repute” (Heraldus). So too “in fame,” like the Greek expressions *ἐν φήμῃ* and *ἐν ὀνόματι*. See Salmasius on Tertullian, *On the Pallium*, p. 39. ORELLI.

“Used the marriage-bed and reached the consummation of the pleasures that followed.” I have followed Meursius’s highly probable emendation. Previously the text read “poured out upon the marriage-bed” (*genialibus fusum toris*). But *fusum* agrees badly with the following *finibus*, although it might nevertheless be defended as zeugma or syllepsis. The “consummation of pleasures” is *τὰ τέλη τῶν ἀφροδισίων*, “the satisfaction of sexual desire” (*die Befriedigung des Wollustriebes*). ORELLI.

“Where in the world were the one and the other Venus, that they might repel the young men’s shameless wantonness,” etc. I think the reading should be: “that they might not repel the shameless wantonness.” ORELLI.

“How little would it have taken for them to extinguish the poor men’s frenzied pleasures.” Meursius conjectures: “They should have taken care to extinguish,” deleting the question mark after “senses.” Wrongly. *Quantum* here means *quantillum*: “how little,” “how small,” “how easy,” as it does a hundred times among the ancients. Thus Phaedrus, book II, fable VIII, verse 23:

> [Col. 1208C] How much labor is it to remove  
> These cobwebs!

That is, how little labor. And Lucan, *Pharsalia* III, 392:

> How little is that by which the fates are held!

See Burman there, p. 192, and Ernesti on Tacitus, *Agricola*, chapter 15. So too Martial:

> How little would it have cost, unhappy man, to cheat two rags—  
> Why refuse?—not you, Naevolus, but the moths?

Heraldus aptly cites this passage. ORELLI.]

### XXII

Unless perhaps you say that the gods disregard these losses and do not consider them a sufficient reason to reveal themselves and inflict upon the guilty the penalty for violated religion. Therefore, if this is so, they do not even desire to possess the images themselves, since they allow them to be torn down and carried off with impunity. Indeed, on the contrary, they thoroughly demonstrate that they despise those objects in which, although scorned, they do not care to show themselves through some act of vengeance.

Philostephanus, in his *Cyprian History*, records that Pygmalion, king of Cyprus, loved as a woman a statue of Venus which [Col. 1206B] among the Cypriots was regarded as possessing the sanctity of an ancient object of worship. [Col. 1207A] His mind, soul, and light of reason and judgment were blinded; and in his madness he was accustomed, as though the image were a conjugal possession, to lift the divine figure onto his couch, join it in embraces and kisses, and perform other acts of lust, rendered futile by the empty [Note: [Col. 1207B] So Sabaeus. Others read “empty.” Better.] imagination.

In a similar manner Posidippus, in the book that he identifies as written on Cnidus and concerning its affairs, relates that a young man of no obscure birth—though he suppresses his name—was seized with love for the Venus on whose account Cnidus is renowned. He too mingled in amorous wantonness with the image of that same divinity, used it upon the marriage-bed, and reached the consummation of the pleasures that followed.

So that I may again ask the same sort of question: if the powers of the heavenly beings lurk within bronze and the other materials from which statues are formed, where [Col. 1207B] in the world were the one and the other Venus, that they might repel the young men’s shameless wantonness far [Col. 1208A] from themselves and punish their impious contact with tormenting chastisement? Or, since the goddesses are gentle and of rather tranquil dispositions, how little would it have taken for them to extinguish the poor men’s frenzied pleasures and restore their mad minds by bringing their senses back to health?

[Note: [Col. 1208C]

### XXIII—“Which they knew was offered by themselves.”

Fulvius Ursinus conjectures “that they subjected themselves” (*quod se subdi*). Wrongly. ORELLI.

“When devouring fire so often consumed the Capitol,” etc., etc. Arnobius borrowed this passage too from Clement. Clement’s words are these, in the *Exhortation*, pp. 46–47, Potter’s edition:

> But fire and earthquakes certainly cannot be bribed, nor do they fear or stand in awe of demons or statues any more than the pebbles piled upon the seashore by the waves. I know a fire that exposes falsehood and cures superstition. If you wish to cease from folly, fire will illuminate your way. This fire burned down the temple in Argos together with the priestess Chrysis; also the temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the second after the Amazons’ temple; and it has often overrun the Capitol at Rome. Nor did it spare the temple of Sarapis in the city of the Alexandrians. At Athens it demolished the temple of Dionysus Eleuthereus; and at Delphi a storm first seized the temple of Apollo, after which a chastening fire destroyed it. This presents to you a prelude to what the fire promises.

(*Ἀλλ’ οὔτι γε τὸ πῦρ καὶ οἱ σεισμοὶ κερδαλέοι, οὐδὲ μὴν φοβοῦνται ἢ δυσωποῦνται, οὐ τοὺς δαίμονας, οὐ τὰ ἀγάλματα, οὐ μᾶλλον ἢ τὰς ψηφίδας τὰς παρὰ τοῖς αἰγιαλοῖς σεσωρευμένας τοῖς κύμασιν· Οἶδα ἐγὼ πῦρ [Col. 1208D] ἐλεγκτικὸν καὶ δεισιδαιμονίας ἰατικόν. Εἰ βούλει παύσασθαι τῆς ἀνοίας, φωταγωγήσει σε τὸ πῦρ. Τοῦτο τὸ πῦρ καὶ τὸν ἐν Ἄργει νεὼν σὺν καὶ τῇ ἱερείᾳ κατέφλεξεν Χρυσίδι· καὶ τὸν ἐν Ἐφέσῳ τῆς Ἀρτέμιδος, δεύτερον μετὰ Ἀμαζόνας, καὶ τὸ ἐν Ῥώμῃ Καπιτώλιον ἐπινενέμηται πολλάκις· οὐκ ἀπέσχετο δὲ οὐδὲ τοῦ ἐν Ἀλεξανδρέων πόλει Σαράπιδος ἱεροῦ. Ἀθήνῃσι γὰρ τοῦ Διονυσίου τοῦ Ἐλευθερέως κατήρειψε τὸν νεών· καὶ τὸν ἐν Δελφοῖς τοῦ Ἀπόλλωνος πρότερον ἥρπασεν θύελλα, ἔπειτα ἠφάνισε πῦρ σωφρονοῦν. Τοῦτό σοι προοίμιον ἐπιδείκνυται, ὧν ὑπισχνεῖται τὸ πῦρ*.)

CANTER.—Compare Lactantius, book III, chapter 17, §§12–13. ORELLI.—The histories attest that the Capitol was burned more than once. It was burned during the Servile War, as may be seen in St. Augustine, *City of God*, book III, chapter 17, and was afterward restored by Sulla. Suetonius and Cornelius Tacitus also record that it was burned during the revolt of Vitellius. See Alexander ab Alexandro, *Days of Geniality*, book V, chapter 11. GENTIANUS HERVETUS, on Clement, at the passage cited.

[Col. 1209A] “Where was Juno the queen, when the same violence of flame destroyed her renowned shrine and the priestess Chrysis in the city of Argos?” Thucydides, *History* IV, chapter 133:

> In the same summer the temple of Hera was burned down. Chrysis the priestess had placed a lighted lamp close to the garlands and then fallen asleep; consequently the whole structure caught fire and was consumed without her noticing it. Chrysis, fearing the Argives, immediately fled that night to Phlius; and they appointed another priestess according to the prescribed law, named Phaeinis.

(*Καὶ ὁ νεὼς τῆς Ἥρας τοῦ αὐτοῦ θέρους κατεκαύθη, Χρυσίδος τῆς ἱερείας λύχνον τινὰ θείσης ἡμμένον πρὸς τὰ στέμματα, καὶ [Col. 1209B] ἐπικαταδαρθούσης· ὥστε ἔλαθεν ἁφθέντα πάντα καὶ καταφλεχθέντα. Καὶ ἡ Χρυσὶς μὲν εὐθὺς τῆς νυκτὸς δείσασα τοὺς Ἀργείους, ἐς Φλιοῦντα φεύγει· οἱ δὲ ἄλλην ἱέρειαν ἐκ τοῦ νόμου τοῦ προσκειμένου κατεστήσαντο, Φαεινίδα ὄνομα*.)

Pausanias, book II, chapter 59, p. 113, and book III, chapter 86, p. 167, Sylburg’s edition, relates the same story but records that this Chrysis fled to Tegea, to the altar of Athena Alea. Clement and Arnobius therefore followed another tradition. Compare Paulus Leopardus, *Emendations*, book VI, chapter 11. This fire occurred in the second year of the eighty-ninth Olympiad, the ninth year of the Peloponnesian War and, according to Varro’s reckoning, [the year is omitted in the supplied source] from the foundation of Rome. ORELLI.

“Where was the Egyptian Serapis,” etc. Concerning the burning of the temple of Serapis—the one, I mean, that occurred before Clement’s time—I have not read even a word. For its destruction after Clement’s time, however, see the ecclesiastical historians. GENTIANUS HERVETUS.

“Where was Liber Eleutherius, when at Athens?” For the origin and description of this temple, see Pausanias’s *Attica*, p. 72, Sylburg’s edition. No mention of its burning survives. GENTIANUS HERVETUS.

“Where was Diana, when at Ephesus?” So Sabaeus, Meursius, etc., quite correctly. Gelenius reads “from Ephesus.” Herostratus burned that temple for no other reason than to obtain everlasting fame for himself by this deed. The story is extremely familiar and known even to beginners. ORELLI.

“Where was Dodonaean Jupiter, when at Dodona?” Arnobius added this on his own. It is uncertain when this temple burned. Others read *Dodone*. ORELLI.

“Where, finally, was divine Apollo,” etc. On the destruction of the Delphic temple, Pausanias, book X, p. 618, Sylburg’s edition:

> Yet I found no account stating in what manner this temple happened to be destroyed. For they say both that it fell into a chasm in the earth and that it was melted by fire. The fourth temple was built by Trophonius and Agamedes, and they record that it was made of stone. It burned when Erxicleides was archon at Athens, in the first year of the fifty-eighth Olympiad, in which Diognetus of Croton was victorious.

(*Οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ τρόπον ὅντινα ἀφανισθῆναι συνέπεσε τῷ ναῷ κατὰ ταῦτα εἰρημένα εὕρισκον. Καὶ γὰρ ἐς χάσμα γῆς ἐκπεσεῖν αὐτὸν καὶ ὑπὸ πυρὸς τακῆναι λέγουσιν. Τέταρτος δὲ ὑπὸ Τροφωνίου μὲν εἰργάσθη καὶ Ἀγαμήδους, λίθου δὲ αὐτὸν ποιηθῆναι μνημονεύουσι. Κατεκαύθη δὲ Ἐρξικλείδου μὲν Ἀθήνησιν ἄρχοντος, πρώτῳ δὲ τῆς ὀγδόης ὀλυμπιάδος ἔτει καὶ πεντηκοστῆς, ἣν Κροτωνιάτης ἐνίκα Διόγνητος*.)

[Col. 1209D] The same author recounts the many vicissitudes of this temple on pp. 620 following. ORELLI.

“Did not possess even one *scripulum*.” The manuscript reads *scrypulum*. The ancients said *scriptulum* to express the Greek word *γράμμα*, “gram”; later writers used *scripulum* without the *t*. Sosipater Charisius, book I: “*Scriptulum*, which the common people now pronounce without the *t*.” Rhemnius Fannius, *On Weights*, verse 9:

> What our people call a *gramma*, the earlier writers called a *scriptlum*.

The Glosses: “*Scripulum* … *γράμμα, σταθμός*,” “gram, weight.” Why it is called *γράμμα* is explained by the same Rhemnius, verse 24:

> … From this one should suppose  
> That they are called *grammata*, because an ounce contains  
> Twenty-four of them.

Or perhaps one should read: “did not possess even one *scrupulum*.” Vitruvius uses that form in book VII, chapter 8: “When a weight of one hundred [units] has been removed, if a *scrupulum* of gold is placed there, it floats on the surface.” [Col. 1210A] Valerius Maximus, book IV, chapter 4: “That same nation possessed not a single *scrupulum* of silver before Paulus, after defeating King Perseus, gave his son-in-law Quintus Aelius Tubero five pounds of silver from the booty.” And I am indeed led to believe that Arnobius wrote *scrupulum*, not *scripulum*, since he speaks in Varro’s words. Varro likewise used this form in the *Plutophthoryne* and the *Annals*, in a fragment preserved by Charisius, book I: “They say that silver coinage was first minted by Servius Tullius; it was four *scrupuli* heavier than the coins.” MEURSIUS, *Critical Notes on Arnobius*, pp. 197–198.—*Scriptulum, scripulum, scrypulum,* and *scrupulum* are the same. We say *ein Gran*, “a grain.” Compare Petrus Daniel on the pseudo-Plautine *Querolus*, p. 69, Padua edition, where there is extensive discussion of this word. Cornelius Fronto likewise speaks of *scripuli* of hours in a letter to Marcus Caesar, II.1, p. 69, Angelo Mai’s edition: “At each tiny fraction of an hour it becomes colder, warmer, or more wintry.” ORELLI.

“For guest swallows” (*hirundinibus hospitis*). Nothing abstruse should be sought here, as Heraldus thinks. Swallows are called “guests” because they build their nests in temples, houses, and other buildings inhabited by human beings, and therefore are creatures dear to the household gods. Thus the stork too is called in Petronius, *Satyricon*, chapter 55, “welcome, foreign, hospitable”; see the commentators there. Others read “for dwellings” (*hospitiis*); others, [Col. 1210C] “for hosts” (*hospitibus*). ORELLI.

“Varro the Menippean, as he says.” So the Leiden edition, following the correction of L. Carrio, *Emendations*, book II, chapter 17. Varro is called “Menippean” because of the Menippean satires that he wrote. See Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book II, chapter 18. The manuscript and the Roman edition have the meaningless words: “Varro, as he says, might show himself a Thenipeus” (*Varro ut dicit se Thenipeus ostenderet*); from this Gelenius produced “Varro, as he says in the *Menippeans*.” Meursius, p. 197, proposes “Varro, as he says in the Menippean satires,” or: “that he might finally show himself”—that is, Apollo—or even: “that the god might then show himself.” But Carrio’s emendation is preferable to all of them. ORELLI.

“And the priests themselves stripped them, having diverted suspicion.” Stewechius prefers *suspectione*, “suspicion,” with the same meaning: namely, so that they themselves diverted every suspicion from themselves, there being no suspicion that such holy men had turned out to be sacrilegious. ORELLI.

“And the Canacheni, opening what was locked by the obscurity of their devices.” This is the reading of the manuscript. Because the true reading of this very obscure passage is uncertain, we have preferred [Col. 1210D] to retain it with Salmasius. What are the *Canacheni*? Gesner, in his *Thesaurus*, interprets the word as “crafty thieves,” perhaps so called from Canachus, the ingenious artist concerning whom Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXIV, chapter 8, writes: “Canachus made the nude Apollo surnamed Philesius, in the Didymaeum, from bronze alloyed according to the Aeginetan method; and with it a stag so poised upon its footprints that a thread may be drawn beneath its feet, its toes and heel alternately holding the ground, the teeth of each section being so articulated that they spring back in turn when pushed.” He also made boys called *Celetizontes*—that is, *κελητίζοντας*, “riding single horses,” trick-riders. Perhaps the *Canacheni* are thieves and temple-robbers of the kind vividly represented by Canachus in some anciently celebrated relief. Heraldus, however, in his *Second Critical Notes*, regarding the word *Canacheni* as suspect, conjectures that the reading should be “Saracens,” promising a fuller explanation of the passage in his more extensive commentary; that commentary, however, never appeared.

It is certain that the Saracens were already known to the Romans before Arnobius’s time. [Col. 1211B] They are first mentioned under Marcus Antoninus. See Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV, chapter 4, who describes them as follows:

> The Saracens, who have never been desirable either as friends or as enemies, ranged here and there and in a brief moment devastated whatever could be found, like rapacious kites which, if they spy their prey from on high, seize it in swift flight, or, if they have obtained it, do not linger.… Among these peoples, whose territory begins with the Assyrians and extends to the cataracts of the Nile and the borders of the Blemmyae, all are warriors of equal status, half naked, clad to the groin in dyed cloaks, roaming through various regions in peaceful or troubled times with the aid of swift horses and slender camels. Not one of them ever takes hold of a plow handle, [Col. 1211C] tends a tree, or seeks his livelihood by cultivating fields; rather, they wander constantly over spaces stretching far and wide, without hearth, fixed homes, or laws—

and what follows is especially worthy of reading. Compare the notes of Valesius; Reitemeier on Zosimus IV.22, p. 638; and Gothofredus on the ancient description of the world under Constantine the Great, p. 9. Thus that nation’s speed and skill, not only in plundering but also in secret thefts, housebreaking, etc.—as with the Gypsies (*Cingarorum; der Zigeuner*) today—might have become proverbial.

For my part, I would not rashly alter the preceding words, “and opening what was locked by the obscurity of their devices,” nor read with Heraldus “opening what was locked after the obscurity had been removed,” nor with Fulvius Ursinus “through the darkness of night,” nor even correct *remedorum* to *remediorum* with Gesner. Arnobius could have said *remedorum* according to an orthographic practice employed by earlier writers, who carefully avoided the meeting of two vowels and wrote, for example, *alis* for *alius* and *alimodi* for *aliusmodi*, as Meursius explains in the *Critical Notes on Arnobius*, book II, chapter 17. But let more learned men judge.—[Col. 1211D] If, following Heraldus in his *Second Critical Notes*, we read “with all obscurity removed” in place of “by the obscurity of their devices,” the word *Canacheni* may perhaps be tolerated. For Arnobius then appears to use the name for robbers who break into houses and smash doors and their locks, not by secret theft and guile but by open force, from *κάναχος*, “din, clatter.” They are opposed to thieves who enter houses silently and covertly. Our equivalent for *Canacheni* is *Bramarbas, Eisenfresser*—“swaggering bully, iron-eater.” Finally, Nourry too understands the term as meaning robbers who—if we read “through the darkness of night”—stripped the images of the gods or carried them away from the temples at night; or—if we prefer “by the obscurity of their devices”—did so by magical arts. *Remedorum* for *remediorum* is archaic. They likewise said *vulturus* for *vulturius*, and so forth. ORELLI.

“Covered by indwellings.” So Stewechius restored the text, followed by the Leiden edition. Others read “inhabitants.” ORELLI.

“Subjected” (*subjecta*). Sabaeus reads “exposed” (*objecta*). ORELLI.]

### XXIII

Unless perhaps, as you maintain, the goddesses of lust and pleasure regarded those insults as extremely gratifying, and did not think the deed worthy of corresponding vengeance because it soothed their own minds as well, and because they knew that it was offered by themselves to human desires.

But if the goddesses called Venuses, being endowed with rather placid dispositions, judged that allowance should be made for the misfortunes of the blind, then when devouring fire so often consumed the Capitol and seized Capitoline Jupiter himself together with his wife and daughter, where was the wielder of the thunderbolt at that time, that he might ward off [Col. 1208B] that criminal conflagration and deliver his possessions, himself, and his whole family from the destructive calamity?

Where was Juno the queen [Col. 1209A] when the same violence of flame destroyed her renowned shrine and the priestess Chrysis in the city of Argos? Where was the Egyptian Serapis when, in a similar disaster, he lay dissolved into ashes together with all his mysteries and Isis? Where was Liber Eleutherius when this happened at Athens? Where was Diana when it happened at Ephesus? Where was Dodonaean Jupiter when it happened at Dodona? Finally, where was divine Apollo when he was so plundered and burned by pirates and sea-robbers that, out of all the masses of gold which countless generations had accumulated, [Col. 1210A] he did not possess even one *scripulum* to display to the guest swallows, as Varro the Menippean says?

It would be a task of endless labor to describe throughout the whole world which temples have been torn down by earthquakes and storms; which have been burned by enemies, which by kings and tyrants; which their own chief priests and priests have stripped after diverting suspicion from themselves; and, finally, which have been stripped by thieves and by the Canacheni, who opened what was locked under cover of the obscurity of their devices. Yet these temples would surely have remained safe and exposed to no accidents if guardian gods were present or had, as is said, any concern for their temples. But as things now stand, because they are empty and covered by no indwelling presences, fortune possesses her own rights over them, and they are just as subject to every accident [Col. 1211A] as are all other things deprived of inner motion.

[Note: [Col. 1211D]

### XXIV—“But on account of the untamed and ignorant multitude.”

This is another defense of images. [Col. 1212B] Some said that wise men indeed knew there was no divinity in images, but that images had been invented so that, through contemplating and looking upon them, the ignorant multitude might be kept to its duty, as though the gods were present everywhere. Marcus Tullius presents this same doctrine in book II of *On the Laws*:

> The Greeks did better, as did our ancestors, who, in order to increase reverence toward the gods, wished them to inhabit the same cities that we inhabit. For this belief produces a religious reverence useful to states. That saying too is sound which was uttered by Pythagoras, a most learned man: religion and reverence are especially present in our minds when we attend to divine rites. So too is the statement of Thales, who was the wisest of the Seven, that human beings ought to believe that everything they saw was full of gods; for all would then be [Col. 1212C] more chaste and, as if they were in sanctuaries, especially religious. For by a certain belief the form of the gods is before our eyes, not only within our minds.

They said, moreover, that images were like books for the common people and that their use was therefore necessary on account of the ignorant multitude. Porphyry says this in Eusebius, book III of the *Preparation for the Gospel*:

> In presenting the conceptions of theological wisdom, men disclosed both God and the powers of God through images akin to sense-perception, imprinting invisible things in visible forms, for those who have learned to read from statues as if from books the written teachings concerning the gods. It is therefore no wonder that the wholly uneducated regard sacred images as wood and stones, just as those who are ignorant of writing see the inscribed monuments as stones, writing tablets as wood, and books as woven papyrus.

(*Σοφίας θεολόγου νοήματα δεικνὺς, οἷς καὶ τὸν Θεὸν καὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ τὰς δυνάμεις διὰ εἰκόνων συμφύλων αἰσθήσει ἐμήνυσαν ἄνδρες τὰ ἀφανῆ φανεροῖς ἀποτυπώσαντες πλάσμασι, τοῖς καθάπερ ἐκ βίβλων τῶν ἀγαλμάτων ἀναλέγειν τὰ περὶ θεῶν μεμαθηκόσι γράμματα. Θαυμαστὸν δὲ οὐδὲν ξύλα καὶ λίθους ἡγεῖσθαι τὰ ξόανα τοὺς ἀμαθεστάτους· καθὰ δὴ καὶ τῶν γραμμάτων οἱ ἀνόητοι, λίθους μὲν ὁρῶσι τὰς στήλας, ξύλα δὲ τὰς δέλτους, ἐξυφασμένην δὲ πάπυρον τοὺς βίβλους*.)

HERALDUS.

“The multitude, which is the largest portion in states.” L. Bunemann illustrates this very familiar construction with many examples in his commentary on Lactantius, book IV, chapter 16, p. 496, as does Corte at several passages in Sallust. ORELLI.

“Change” (*mutatione*). Gelenius reads “transformation” (*immutatione*). ORELLI.

[Col. 1212D] “Nor for any other reason,” etc. Lactantius, book II, chapter 7: “The more ornate the temples and the more beautiful the images, the more majesty they are believed to possess. Thus the religion of the gods is nothing other than that which human desire admires.” HERALDUS.

“Which might perhaps appear to be said with some reason.” So Canter, following the Roman edition, for “for some reason,” which Gelenius had interpolated. Thus in book VII: “Which might perhaps have been both heard and said with some reason.” ORELLI.

“The very name of innocence has almost perished.” Thus the Greeks elegantly say that not even the name of a thing survives when they mean that it has been utterly abolished. Theocritus, in the *Hiero*:

> And over their weapons may spiders spread  
> Their delicate webs; and may not even the name of the battle-cry remain.

(*ἀράχνια δ’ εἰς ὅπλ’ ἀράχναι  
λεπτὰ διαστήσαιντο· βοᾶς δ’ ἔτι μηδ’ ὄνομ’ εἴη*.)

HERALDUS.

“Are brought forth” (*pariantur*). I do not know what came into Stewechius’s mind when he derived this from *pario, -are*. The context plainly shows that *pariantur* is the subjunctive of *pario, -ere*, dependent upon [Col. 1213B] the preceding *cum*, and that the apodosis follows only in the words “how is it fitting to say,” etc. ORELLI.

“By sacrilegious violations.” Stewechius prefers “by sacrileges and violations” (*sacrilegiis violationibus*), which is not alien to Arnobius’s style of piling up such synonyms. ORELLI.]

### XXIV

In this same part of the argument, defenders of images also customarily say that the ancients were not unaware that statues possess nothing divine and have absolutely no sensation within them; rather, on account of the untamed and ignorant multitude—which forms the largest portion of peoples and states—they fashioned them with salutary and deliberate purpose. By setting before such people what was, as it were, some visible form of the divine powers, they meant to cast off the multitude’s savagery through fear; so that, believing themselves to conduct their affairs beneath the eyes of gods who were present, they might abandon impious deeds and, through a change of character, pass over to the duties of humanity. [Col. 1211B]

Nor, they say, were venerable forms of gold and silver devised for them [Col. 1212A] for any other reason than that some power might be believed to be present within their splendors—a power which would not only dazzle the faculty of sight but would also terrify the minds themselves with the rays of its most majestic light.

This might perhaps appear to be said with some reason if, after temples had been built for the gods and images instituted, no evil person existed in the world and no wickedness at all; if justice, peace, and good faith possessed mortal hearts; and if no one on earth were called guilty or innocent, because everyone was ignorant of criminal deeds. But as things now stand, when, on the contrary, everything is full of evils, when the very name of innocence has almost perished, and at every moment and every instant new swarms of crimes are brought forth by the depravity of the guilty—how is it fitting to say that images were instituted to strike fear into the multitude? For besides innumerable forms of crimes [Col. 1212B] and wicked deeds, we see the temples themselves attacked through sacrilegious violations [Col. 1213A] by tyrants, kings, robbers, and nocturnal thieves; and we see those very gods whom ancient tradition fashioned and consecrated in order to inspire fear carried off into the caves of brigands, together with their own golden and supposedly fearsome splendors.

[Note: [Col. 1213B]

### XXV—“Janus with a two-faced brow, or that serrated key by which [Col. 1213C] he is distinguished.”

Ovid, *Fasti* I, 95:

> Then sacred Janus, wondrous in his two-faced form.

And verse 99:

> He held a staff in his right hand and a key in his left.

ELMENHORST.

“Jupiter wearing a *ricinium*.” This does not mean manfully clad in a toga, as some explain it, but with his head covered by a *caliendrum*, as though with a *ricinium*, or with a fold of the toga drawn back over his head. That this is the true explanation of the passage is shown by what follows later: “little sickles, keys, *caliendra*, fire-starters,” etc. The Glosses: “*Rica*: *μίτρα*,” “headband.” Isidore, in the Glosses: “It was called *ricinius* from the crown of the head, because it was drawn back from the toga onto the crown.” There is some corruption in these words. The same author, in the *Origins*, book XIX, chapter 25:

> The *stola* is a matron’s covering, which, with head and shoulder covered, is cast from the right side onto the left shoulder. It is called *stola* in Greek because it is put on over the body. The same garment is called *ricinium* in Latin because half of it is thrown back, which commonly [Col. 1213D] is called a *mavors*. They say that *mavors* is named as though from Mars. For in it lies the sign of marital dignity and authority.

Thus Jupiter wearing the *ricinium* is, as it were, Jupiter wearing a matron’s robe. HERALDUS.—Compare Varro, *On the Latin Language*, book IV, p. 37, Bipont edition. The commentators on the Twelve Tables distinguish two kinds of *ricinium*, one female and the other male. See Theodorus Marcilius in S. Leuw’s *Authors of Roman Civil Law*, p. 300. ORELLI.

“Fire-starter” (*fomitem*). *Fomes* is dry and arid material that easily catches fire, or else the sparks struck from glowing iron. NOURRY, p. 490.—Thus here it means *Feuerkiel*, “a fire-kindler.” ORELLI.

“That girdle of Juno.” The girdle (*caestus*) is attributed not only to Venus but also to Juno. Martial:

> Let Juno ask a girdle from you, and Venus herself as well.

TURNEBUS, *Adversaria*, book XIII, chapter 27.

“A little maiden hiding beneath a military helmet.” Prudentius, book II, *Against Symmachus*:

> [Col. 1214B] Neither armed Venus nor then shield-bearing Minerva  
> Came to their aid.

ELMENHORST.

“The Muses with psalteries.” Arnobius here appears to have used “psalteries” in a general sense for musical instruments fitted with strings, and therefore for the lyres and citharas [Col. 1214C] attributed to the Muses. Strictly speaking, however, the psaltery, which consists of ten strings, differs from the cithara. See Isidore, *Origins* II, chapter 2; Gesner in the *Thesaurus*; and Graevius on Cicero’s speech *On the Response of the Haruspices*, chapter 21. ORELLI.

“Aesculapius with his staff.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV, 654 following:

> … But such as in his temple  
> He is accustomed to appear, holding a rustic staff in his left hand  
> And with his right smoothing the hair of his long beard.

ELMENHORST.

Source/review notes: The supplied title “contra Unionitas” appears corrupt; because the source does not support a secure reconstruction, the uncertain reading is retained and marked.

Or Fortune with a horn, etc. On the fruit-bearing horn attributed to Fortune, see the very learned discussion of Ezekiel Spanheim, *On the Excellence and Use of Coins*, dissertation 13, vol. II, p. 536 ff. ORELLI.

Anubis with a canine face. Prudentius, *Against Unionitas* [title uncertain in the supplied text]:

> What superstition could be so foul as that which places  
> Dog-shaped, barking Anubis upon heaven’s throne? ELMENHORST.]

## XXV

For if you examine the matter truthfully and without any partiality, what great power do those images, as they call them, possess in themselves, such that antiquity might reasonably have hoped and believed that at the sight of them human vices could be broken and men’s conduct restrained from wrongdoing? The reaping-hook, of course, which is attributed to Saturn, was going to strike such fear into mortals that they would wish to lead peaceful lives and cast aside malicious intentions; or Janus with his double face; or that toothed key with which he is distinguished; Jupiter [Col. 1213B] wearing a *ricinium* and a beard, holding in his right hand a firebrand carefully fashioned in the likeness of a thunderbolt; that girdle of Juno; or the little girl hiding beneath a military helmet; the Mother of the Gods with her tambourine; the Muses with pipes and stringed instruments; Mercury, the winged slayer of Argus; [Note: [Col. 1213B] The manuscript has *Argiforonites*. Absurdly.] Aesculapius with his staff; Ceres with her great breasts; or the drinking-cup hanging from Liber’s right hand; [Col. 1214A] Mulciber in a craftsman’s dress; Fortune with a horn full of apples, figs, or autumn fruits; Diana with thighs half uncovered; naked Venus arousing lust; Anubis with a canine face; or Priapus, inferior to his own genitals.

[Note: [Col. 1214C]

### XXVI.—*Would be fastened in perpetual stupor*

Meursius prefers *affligeretur*, “would be afflicted.” But *affigi*, “to be fastened,” is far more expressive and especially appropriate to stupor. ORELLI.

### *Caliendra*

This should be read instead of *caliendria*, which the Roman edition has. The glosses: “*Caliendrum*: κόσμιον κεφαλῆς, an adornment of the head.” Horace, book I, Satire VIII, 48:

> Canidia’s teeth and Sagana’s lofty *caliendrum*  
> Fell out.

On this passage Acro says: “*Caliendrum* is the name given to an adornment of women’s heads, or to false hair, which they used in place of natural hair.” MEURSIUS, p. 198.—Compare Ausonius Popma on the fragments of Varro, p. 396, Bipont edition, who explains *caliendrum* as a head-covering, tall and raised like a cap. Here, however, Arnobius seems to have meant the *ricinium*, which the Greeks called κρήδεμνον (*krēdemnon*, head-covering) or θέριστρον (*theristron*, summer veil), since in the preceding chapter he mocked Jupiter for wearing a *ricinium*. See Baxter on the cited passage of Horace; G. Cuper, *Observations*, book III, chapter 14; and Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book VII, chapter 20. ORELLI.

[Col. 1215B] *Were empty of understanding.* Meursius conjectures: “had been empty of understanding.” ORELLI.

### *By the most monstrous grimness of masks they would also be constrained by mocking faces and bogeys*

I have followed the very felicitous emendation of Salmasius. The first edition, following the manuscript codex, has, in a thoroughly corrupt form: “the most monstrous grimnesses; for years even they would be constrained, and hands”; the manuscript has “yearly” in place of “for years,” which makes no sense. From this Gelenius and Fulvius Ursinus produced: “By the most monstrous grimness both their minds and their hands would be constrained.” In his appendix Meursius thinks the text should read: “By the most monstrous grimness they would also be constrained in their minds and hands.” (On the forms *monstruosus* and *monstrosus*, *hirtuosus* and *hirtosus*, see Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* V, p. 350.) But the emendation of Salmasius is at once the truest and the slightest; Salmasius himself, the best interpreter of his own meaning, explains it in his commentary [Col. 1215C] on Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, p. 300, adducing the following:

> Learned men know from Festus that *maniae* are ugly and misshapen figures, or masks, with which nurses threaten children. *Sannae* are ridiculous or even horrible distortions of the face, which we commonly call grimaces (*Fratzengesichter*), by which little children are frightened. Hence *sanniones*, those who are ridiculous more through their faces than through their wit.

This most felicitous correction is also approved by the late Ruhnkenius, “the blessed” (ὁ μακαρίτης), on Timaeus’ *Platonic Lexicon*, s.v. μερμορύττει (*mermoryttei*, “makes a bogey-face”), p. 181 of the new edition, except that in place of *sannis* he prefers to read *Lamiis*, “Lamias,” citing Casaubon on Strabo I, p. 36, who lists such terrors for children: Lamia, Gello, Gorgon, and Mania. For my part, however, I much prefer *sannis*, which is the true reading of the manuscript codex—the only error being that its first letter was drawn back into the preceding word *torvitate* by an ignorant scribe—and is exceedingly well suited to the context. *Sannae* has the same sense in Persius, Satire V, verse 91:

> Learn—but let anger fall from your nose, and the wrinkled grimace.

[Col. 1216B] As regards the thought, our passage deserves comparison with Seneca, *On the Firmness of the Wise Person*, chapter 4:

> Thus we are troubled not only by pain, but by the idea of pain, in the manner of children, into whom fear is struck by a shadow, the ugliness of masks, and a distorted face.

Compare Ruhnkenius on the cited passage of Timaeus. ORELLI.

### *Nor would such diverse crosses, etc.*

We had *crosses* above, book I, chapter 17, in the general sense of punishments. ORELLI.

### *Even fixed and settled condemnation*

Stewechius restored this from the manuscript codex in place of *affixa*, “attached,” which had previously been read; *fixa* means established, certain, indubitable. ORELLI.]

## XXVI

O dreadful shapes of fear and terrifying horrors, because of which the human race [Note: [Col. 1214B] Thus Sabinus. Others: “humankind.”] would be fastened in perpetual stupor, undertake nothing, and, thunderstruck, restrain itself from every criminal and shameful act! Little sickles, keys, head-coverings, firebrands, winged sandals, staffs, little tambourines, pipes, stringed instruments, breasts displayed and enormous, little cups, tongs, fruit-bearing horns, women’s naked bodies, and the publicly exhibited sizes of male organs! Would it not have been better to dance and sing than, under the name of gravity and severity, and beneath that pretext, to recount images so insipid and absurd, supposedly fashioned by the ancients to restrain sins and to terrify the guilty and impious?

Were the mortals of that age and time so empty [Col. 1215A] of understanding, so devoid of reason and perception, that, like tiny little children, they would be restrained from wicked actions by the most monstrous grimness of masks, and even by mocking faces and bogeys?
