And how has the matter been reversed to the contrary, so that, although in the cities there are so many temples filled with images of all the gods, it is impossible, by so many laws and by such great varieties of punishment, to check the multitude of criminals; no remedies can cut short their audacity; and wicked deeds, doubled over and over, multiply all the more, the more exertion is made through laws and judgments to diminish cruel acts and to suppress them by the restraint of punishments?

For if images inflicted any fears upon mortals, the enactment of laws would cease, nor would such diverse crosses be established against the audacity of criminals. But now, since it has been established and proved by the fact itself that the belief in the fear said to flow from images is empty, recourse has been had to the sanctions of laws, [Col. 1216A] from which fear might be utterly certain, and condemnation fixed and settled. To these laws even the images themselves owe the fact that they still stand unharmed and are protected by the concession of some measure of honor.

[Note: [Col. 1216B]

### XXVII.—*Circumlocutions*

Fulvius Ursinus conjectures *circumlationibus*, “circuitous procedures.” Wrongly. ORELLI.

### *We attribute*

Thus Meursius from the manuscript. Others: “we ascribe.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1216C] ### *To call us atheists*

Christians, of course, were compelled to offer sacrifices because there was no more evident sign of worshipping the gods. Hence PIETAS too is seen upon coins with the instruments customarily employed in sacrifice; because Christians refused to do this, they were called atheists. Gisbert CUPER, on Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 10, p. 152, Bauldri’s edition.

### *Even to impose capital punishments*

That *irrogare*—“to impose”—is used in ecclesiastical Latin with punishments, tortures, war, arms, hands, violence, death, etc., in place of “to inflict,” is shown by J. F. Gronovius, *Monobiblos on Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 1, p. 15, and P. Bauldri on Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 1, p. 13. ORELLI.

### *This indeed we acknowledge*

Thus Meursius, following the Leiden edition. Previously: “This indeed we do not acknowledge.” ORELLI.

### *The powers of this name*

Meursius: “of this divine power.” Wrongly. ORELLI.]

## XXVII

But since, so far as the matter allowed, it has been sufficiently shown how vainly images are made, the order of our argument may next speak, in as few words as possible and without any circumlocutions, about sacrifices, the slaughter and immolation of victims, wine, incense, and all the other things performed in this department. For it is on this point that you are accustomed to arouse the most violent hostility against us, to call us atheists, and, because we attribute almost nothing to the gods, even to impose capital punishments upon us with the savagery of wild beasts.

This indeed we acknowledge that we do, not from contempt for and rejection of the divine, but because we believe [Col. 1216B] that the powers belonging to this name demand nothing of the kind and are not held captive by desires for things of this sort.

# BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 1217]

## INDEX OF CHAPTERS

[Col. 1217] In this book Arnobius proves, whether by authority or by reason, that no sacrifices are to be made to the gods. For they are not nourished by these sacrifices, since everything that is nourished is mortal. Chapters 1, 2, and 3. Nor are victims slaughtered for the gods’ pleasure, for whoever is affected by delight of this sort is still mortal. Chapter 4.

Arnobius then demolishes the common belief which maintained that the anger of the gods is appeased by sacrifices. For the agitation of anger, which is unworthy of the gods, cannot enter an immortal mind. Chapters 5, 6, and 7. Furthermore, no one will be persuaded that, when some animal has been slaughtered and offered, the gods lay aside their anger or forget their injuries; or that, through such sacrifices, as though a stipulated payment had been made, they grant pardon for sins committed against them. Chapters 8 and 9.

Nor is there any basis for someone to argue that victims are sacrificed to the gods so that they may grant prosperity [Col. 1217B] and remove adversity. For even if we leave aside for the moment that opinion of the philosophers that all things are governed by fate, certainly, if it rests with the gods to grant favorable and adverse circumstances to human beings, they show an ungrateful spirit when they allow those who burden their altars with victims to be reduced to the utmost distress. Chapters 10 and 11. Moreover, it is absurd to say that the gods sell their benefits for the price of sacrifices. Chapter 12.

Nor is there any stronger reason for asserting that sacrifices are made to the gods to honor them and magnify their power. Chapters 13 and 14. Arnobius nevertheless acknowledges that honor should be shown to the true God, who, just as he does not blaze with anger, neither rejoices at honor conferred nor is indignant when it is withheld, nor believes that he is made greater by the services of others. Moreover, no honor accrues to the gods from slaughtered animals, by whose smoke the images, and by whose blood and stench the temples and altars, are polluted. Chapters 15 and 16. [Col. 1217C]

But if you maintain that the gods are honored by the blood of animals, why are elephants, camels, lions, and very many other animals not sacrificed to them? And do not say that the gods are honored only by those things which they benignly provide for our nourishment; for cumin, cress, turnips, and the other things useful to us would then also have to be offered to those same gods. Chapters 16 and 17.

Arnobius further presses the point that, just as the gods form a single class, so they ought to have a single judgment: “Why,” he asks, “is one victim sacrificed to one god, and another to another?” Chapters 18–21. Nor does it help to answer that different victims have long been slaughtered for different gods by ancient and established custom. For the question is not whether human beings, but whether the gods, decreed that one victim was more appropriate for one god than for another. Chapters 21 and 22.

To the pagans’ objection that sacrifices must be offered to the good gods so that they may benefit us, and to the evil gods so that they may not [Col. 1218] harm us, Arnobius replies that all gods [Col. 1218A] ought by nature to be good, and thus, even if human beings show them no honor, they still cannot harm them on that account. Furthermore, if this opinion of the pagans is true, it follows from it that a good god becomes evil if the victim owed to him is not slaughtered; while, conversely, an evil god becomes good once the sacrifice has been performed. Chapter 23.

Furthermore, even if it could lawfully be permitted for bulls and other animals to be sacrificed to the gods, of what advantage to them could the varieties of sausages, porridges, and cakes employed in pagan rites be? Chapters 24 and 25.

There is no better rationale for burning incense upon their altars. For that rite is recent and was unknown in ancient times. It must accordingly either be judged useless, or the people of old, among whom it is established that it was never practiced, must have sinned. Chapters 26 and 27. [Col. 1218B]

And what of the boast that by offering incense some honor is bestowed upon the gods? Incense is nothing but a sticky substance flowing from the bark of certain trees. Why, then, is a substance congealing from other trees not similarly burned for them? Is it because its smell is not so pleasant? Are some odors, then, pleasant to the gods, as they are to human beings, while others are distasteful and disagreeable? Yet, as the philosophers acknowledge, the gods are incorporeal and therefore cannot be soothed by incense or any other odor. Chapters 27 and 28.

They also poured pure wine in their rites as a companion to incense, uselessly and likewise without any supporting reason. For the gods suffer neither thirst nor hunger, so the use of wine is entirely useless. The pagans were also mistaken in supposing that it was poured either to honor the gods or to make them propitious. Chapters 29 and 30.

For what could be more senseless than to pour a little wine as a libation with a fixed formula, lest every other wine become sacred and be withdrawn from human [Col. 1218C] use? Chapter 31.

Arnobius shows that it is no less ridiculous to believe that the gods are delighted by garlands, wreaths, cymbals, tambourines, and musical ensembles. In addition, he mocks their festival days and attacks the games instituted in their honor. Chapter 32.

He proves that nothing is more alien to right reason than the belief that the gods are delighted and lay aside their anger because of the disgraceful comedies and tragedies then being performed. Chapter 33. He then demonstrates that so many such monstrous beliefs arose because the pagans did not know what the nature of the true God is and falsely persuaded themselves that their gods were of the same substance as themselves. Chapter 34.

Next he proceeds to overthrow the pagans’ final and supposedly stronger bulwark, by which, from various accounts of prodigies, as they called them, they attempted to prove that the gods, offended by human sins, had blazed with anger but had afterward been appeased by human satisfaction. First, he examines the restoration of the Circus games in honor of Jupiter, after the proper performance of which the pestilence was said to have ceased. Chapters 35, 36, and 37. He next passes to the story of the Capitol struck by lightning and the image of Jupiter cast down from its seat; when, in accordance with the responses of the haruspices, it was finally placed on a higher site facing the rising sun, they believed that hidden matters had then been disclosed. By recounting these things, he makes it plain that nothing can ever be imagined more unworthy of the supreme majesty, or even of the very name, of the gods. Chapters 37–41.

He next subjects to examination the story of Aesculapius’ image being transferred to the Tiber Island, as a result of which they believed that the dreadful plague then raging in the republic’s troubled circumstances was suddenly calmed. [Col. 1219B] Chapters 41–45.

He takes up the image of the Mother of the Gods brought to Rome from Pessinus in Phrygia. They repeatedly declared that at that time the enemy had been driven out of Italy, the city’s former splendor restored, the boundaries of empire extended far and wide, and other benefits conferred upon the Roman people. After bringing these claims forward, Arnobius demonstrates that nothing exists, or can even be invented, which is more opposed to truth or less deserving of belief. Chapters 46–48.

Finally, he compares and contrasts the beliefs of pagans and Christians and concludes from this that the Christians are pious, while the Gentiles are themselves truly guilty and conscious of the insane impiety which they imputed to the Christians. Chapters 49, 50, and 51.

[Col. 1219C] [Note: [Col. 1219C]

### I.—*The opinion of your Varro*

Varro taught these things from the doctrines of the Stoics. To this belongs that excellent passage of Persius, Satire II, 71 ff.:

> Let us rather give the gods what the bleary-eyed offspring  
> Of great Messala could not give from a great platter:  
> Justice and divine law harmoniously composed within the soul,  
> The mind’s holy inner recesses, and a heart steeped  
> In generous honor. Give me these to bring to the temples,  
> And I shall make an acceptable offering with meal.

There the most recent editor, Koenig, cites in support of the same thought Plato, *Alcibiades II*, vol. V, p. 99, Bipont edition; Horace III, Ode XXIII, 17 ff.; Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII, 102; Propertius III, Elegy III, 17; Ovid, *Tristia* I.II, 75; *Letters from Pontus* IV.VIII, 29; Valerius Maximus II.V.5. Add Lucretius V, 1197 ff. See more in Elmenhorst and Johann Saubert, *On Sacrifices*, chapter I, p. 3 ff., Crenius’ edition. ORELLI.

### *More irreproachable, truer*

Thus Meursius and the Leiden edition from the manuscript. Others omit the final word. ORELLI.

### *Scaevus*

This is the correct reading, not *saevus*, “savage.” *Scaevus* means σκαιός, ἐπαρίστερος: “awkward, left-handed,” one who apprehends things slowly and perversely. Athenaeus, book IV, couples ἀγροῖκον, “boorish,” with ἐπαρίστερον, “left-handed,” and treats them as equivalent. HERALDUS.

### *And most difficult to grasp*

*Occupare*, “to grasp,” is used for the simple *capere*, “to comprehend.” *Difficilis*, “difficult,” is active in sense—ἐνεργητικῶς—meaning someone who apprehends matters only with difficulty; or simply one who is persuaded with difficulty even by things closely resembling truth and who does not readily surrender. HERALDUS.

### *For who is so dull of heart?*

Thus Lactantius, [Col. 1220C] *Divine Institutes*, book II, chapter 5, §4: “Some man of sluggish and dull understanding.” The opposite is *cordati*, “men of understanding,” the wise. See Bünemann, p. 375. ORELLI.

### *Separated*

The same as “disjoined.” A ἅπαξ λεγόμενον, a word occurring only once. See C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XLV, chapter 8, p. 2071. ORELLI.]

## I

“What then,” someone may say, “do you judge that no sacrifices at all should be performed?” To answer you with the opinion not of one of our people but of your own Varro: none. [Col. 1220A] “Why so?” “Because,” he says, “the true gods neither desire nor demand them; while those made from bronze, earthenware, plaster, or marble care much less about such things, for they lack sensation. Nor is any guilt incurred if you do not perform them, or any favor gained if you do.”

No opinion can be found more irreproachable or truer, or one which anyone could comprehend, however awkward and exceedingly difficult to convince he might be. For who is so dull of heart that he would slaughter victims and sacrificial animals either for things possessing no sensation, or believe that they ought to be given to beings who are far separated from these [senseless images] in nature and blessedness?

[Note: [Col. 1220C]

### II.—*And to be counted in the list of names*

Thus the Leiden edition. Others: “in the list of divine powers.” Fulvius Ursinus: “to be counted as a list.” ORELLI.

### *As Terentius believes*

Marcus Terentius Varro.

### *Insofar as he is God*

Thus the Leiden edition from the manuscript. Others: “in that he is God.” ORELLI.

### *Earthly pleasures drawn from the resources of matter*

Thus the Leiden edition, following the Roman edition. Others: “Earthly, from the resources of matter,” etc. ORELLI.]

## II

“Who,” you ask, “are the true gods?” To answer you with an ordinary and straightforward word: we do not know. For how can we know who those are whom we have never seen? We are accustomed to hear from you that the gods [Col. 1220B] are exceedingly numerous and are counted in a list of names. If they exist somewhere, as you say, and if, as Terentius believes, they are true gods, it follows that they resemble the name they bear—that is, that they are such as we all perceive they ought to be, and such as should be designated by the title of this name.

Indeed, to bring the matter briefly to an end, they must be of the same nature as the Lord of all things and the Almighty himself, whom we all know and understand that we mean when, upon mentioning his name, we call him the true God. For one god does not differ from another in any respect insofar as he is a god; and what belongs to one class cannot exist to a lesser or greater degree in its individual members, provided the uniformity of its proper quality is maintained. Since this is not doubtful, it follows that they ought never to have been born, that they ought to be everlasting, to desire nothing from outside themselves, and not to pluck any earthly [Col. 1220C] pleasures from the resources of matter.

[Note: [Col. 1220C]

### III.—*And settle to their advantage*

Others: “may settle.” Stewechius corrects the phrase to “may settle into their advantages,” explaining it as “may reach the substance of the divine powers.” For my part, however, I have preferred to follow Salmasius’ reading. We have already seen several times above that Arnobius uses the ablative in place of the accusative. Virgil uses the verb *subsido* in the same sense at *Aeneid* XII, 835:

> Mingled into so great a body,  
> The Trojans will settle.

That is, “they will remain concealed,” as Servius explains it. The verb properly refers to things which, when mingled, occupy the lowest place. Arnobius therefore means: “I ask what profit and what perpetual and enduring advantage flows from these sacrifices to the gods.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1221B] ### *And have a downward path toward destruction*

*Periculum* here means destruction, as above in book I, chapter 3: “Cities totter even toward destruction,” where see Meursius’ note. ORELLI.

### *For either incense is given*

Here you have a classification of sacrifices. And this is indeed how matters stand. Either animate or inanimate victims are offered to the gods. Arnobius discusses the latter before the former because they are believed to be more ancient, as Eusebius shows from Theophrastus, Porphyry, and others. “Incense is given” is a distinctive expression. Ovid:

> I gave pious incense on your behalf, and I alone  
> Added my own prayers to all the public vows.

Thus they sometimes gave incense by itself, without adding any animal victim. Certainly they scarcely prayed to the gods without burning incense to them as well, if they had the means. Ovid, book IV of the *Letters from Pontus*:

> To them I offer words of prayer with incense as often  
> As day rises from the eastern world. HERALDUS.

### *Or the victim is an animal*

Macrobius, differently, says that an “animate victim” is one whose soul alone is consecrated to God, an observation which is certainly not free from vanity. HERALDUS.

### *Dissolved into ash, it collapses*

See Bünemann on Lactantius, *On the Anger of God*, chapter 13, p. 1061. ORELLI.

### *And feeds upon the knisai*

The glosses: “Κνίσσα: the smell of roasting meat.” Κνίσσα or κνίσα is the burning and smoke of meat in sacrifice. Homer used the word in *Iliad* I, 66. Arnobius employed many Greek words in this work which he delights in giving citizenship both in Latium and in the city of Rome. Thus in book II he used *plani* for “sycophants”; in book VI he said that images were scraped with *grosphi*; and in book VII he called flute-players *salpinctae*—though we read *salapittae*. The learned reader will easily observe similar instances in Arnobius for himself. STEWECHIUS.—Compare Lindenbrogius on *Priapea*, Epigram LXXII, in P. Burmann’s *Latin Anthology*, vol. II, p. 542. ORELLI.

### *Which the burning entrails vomit forth*

Arnobius likes this verb in a metaphorical sense. Thus book VI, chapter 3: “They vomit forth starry radiance in variegated patterns.” ORELLI.

### *Still wet with blood*

The first edition has “still *suda* with blood,” which Salmasius restored; it makes good sense if we understand *sudus, -a* as *subudus*, “somewhat wet,” as Servius explains it on *Aeneid* VIII, 529. For my part, I decide nothing. ORELLI.

### *And moistened with its former fluids*

Perhaps: “and moistened with streams of gore.” Yet I would not wish to alter the text rashly. MEURSIUS, p. 205.

### *How can it be possible?*

Thus the manuscript. Others: “can it be.” ORELLI.

### *This rationale*

The manuscript has “this” here, not inappropriately. MEURSIUS.

### *Can be*

Thus the manuscript. MEURSIUS.

### *And are sustained from feeding upon them*

Stewechius added “from” from the manuscript. This is the usual redundancy of prepositions in our author. ORELLI.]

## III

Therefore, if these things are so, the first thing we ask to know from you is what cause, what rationale, leads you to perform those sacrifices; and then, what profit from them reaches the gods themselves and settles to their advantage. [Col. 1221A] For everything that is done ought to have a cause for its being done, and ought not to be so divorced from reason that it is carried into futile activities and plays amid the empty delusions of vanity.

Are the heavenly gods perhaps nourished by these rites, and is some supply of material required to maintain their bodily structure? Who among human beings is so utterly ignorant of what a god is that he believes the gods are sustained by some kind of nourishment, and that it is the function of food to make them live and endure throughout immeasurable eternity? For whatever is supported by causes and things external to itself must necessarily be mortal and have a downward path toward destruction whenever something by which it lives begins to be lacking.

Moreover, we see that nothing from the things brought to the altars reaches or penetrates the substances of the divine powers. For either incense is given and, liquefied upon the coals, [Col. 1221B] disappears; or the victim is an animal and its blood is lapped up greedily by dogs; or, if some entrail has been delivered to the altars, it burns away in the same manner and, dissolved into ash, collapses—unless perhaps the god devours the souls of the victims, pursues the smell and smoke rising from the burning altars, and feeds upon the *knisai* (κνῖσσαι, sacrificial fumes) which the burning entrails vomit forth while still wet with blood and moistened with their former fluids.

But if God, as is said, has no body and is beyond contact with every touch, how can it be possible for what is incorporeal to be nourished by corporeal things; for what is mortal to support what is immortal; for it to preserve the well-being [Col. 1222A] of a thing it cannot touch and to furnish it with the motions of life?

This rationale for the rites therefore fails, as is evident. No one can say that sacrifices are celebrated because the divine powers are nourished by them and sustained by feeding upon them.

[Note: [Col. 1222C]

### IV.—*And are placed upon kindled altars*

Stewechius suspects that the text should read: “and incense is placed upon kindled altars.” ORELLI.

### *Fleeting sweetness*

A fleeting sweetness is one that quickly perishes and vanishes. The glosses: “Fleeting, … εὐόλισθον, readily slipping away.” Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVII, chapter 10: “slippery mud.” OUDENDORP, on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* IV, p. 243.

### *For what is dissolved by pleasure, etc.*

Boethius, *Consolation of Philosophy*, book II, meter VII:

> All such pleasure has this quality:  
> It drives its fevered victims with goads,  
> And, like the flight of bees,  
> Once it has poured out pleasing honey,  
> It fixes its sting and strikes the wounded heart  
> With an exceedingly tenacious bite. ELMENHORST.

### *Which trembles with delight*

Persius, Satire I, 20:

> To make the enormous Tituses tremble, etc.

Arnobius thus expresses a more unrestrained movement, one unworthy of a steadfast person. This is why he says “delight” rather than “joy.” HERALDUS.—Compare Casaubon on the cited passage of Persius, and Barthius on Statius, *Thebaid* II, 476, vol. II, p. 522. ORELLI.

### *Is lifted up by the frivolities of joys*

He does not say “of joy” in the singular, because joy is a milder πάθος (*pathos*, emotion). “Is lifted up” is likewise correct. For the Stoics said that delight and joy were both forms of elevation, ἔπαρσις; but delight was an irrational elevation, ἔπαρσις ἄλογος, while joy was a rational elevation, ἔπαρσις μετὰ λόγου. See Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* IV, chapter 6; and Augustine, *Commentary on Galatians*, chapter 5. HERALDUS.

[Col. 1223B] ### *And the intestines roll out together with the dung*

The reading is sound, for this conjunction *et*, “and,” is often genuinely redundant in these writers and is woven into the syntax indirectly. HERALDUS.—Fulvius Ursinus is therefore wrong to remove *et*. ORELLI.

### *And the trembling veins quivering among the entrails*

[Col. 1223C] Nothing should be changed here either. For Arnobius likes to join συνώνυμα (*synōnyma*, synonymous expressions) in this way, as we observed above. HERALDUS.—Fulvius Ursinus and Stewechius conjecture: “with the trembling veins.” ORELLI.

### *Or rather, to express ourselves*

Thus Salmasius. Previously: “first.” The first edition is clearer. ORELLI.

### *Because, abandoning the law of humanity, we have broken our fellowship in a common natural origin*

These words were spoken by Arnobius in a thoroughly philosophical spirit. For since human beings properly share no community of law with brute animals, Arnobius does not say simply “having broken the law” or anything similar, but “having abandoned the law of humanity.” He means the law of humanity because the human being, an animal gentle by nature, seems bound to abstain from other living creatures; this was the opinion of the Pythagoreans and afterward of certain others. The Greeks call this humanity χρηστότης (*chrēstotēs*, kindness). For they acknowledge that human beings are bound to brute animals by no community of law, but say that there is a certain χρηστότης, kindness, which takes the place of justice toward those weaker animals.

Plutarch, in his *Cato the Elder*, where he censures that aged censor for holding that slaves who were infirm and worn out by age should be sold, says:

> Καίτοι τὴν χρηστότητα τῆς δικαιοσύνης πλατύτερον τόπον ὁρῶμεν ἐπιλαμβάνουσαν· νόμῳ μὲν γὰρ καὶ τῷ δικαίῳ πρὸς ἀνθρώπους μόνον χρῆσθαι πεφύκαμεν· πρὸς εὐεργεσίας δὲ καὶ χάριτάς ἐστιν ὅτε καὶ μέχρις ἀλόγων ζῴων.

> And yet we see that kindness occupies a broader sphere than justice; for by nature we employ law and justice only toward human beings, but beneficence and gracious treatment sometimes extend even as far as irrational animals.

Please see what follows there. HERALDUS.

### *Does anyone believe that the gods are compassionate?*

He calls the gods *pii*, “compassionate” or “merciful,” as we showed on book I, chapter 49. On this point one should note St. Augustine’s observation in *The City of God* X, chapter 1:

> *Pietas* is also properly understood as the worship of God, which the Greeks call εὐσέβεια. Yet the word is also used of dutiful conduct toward parents. In common usage, moreover, this name is frequently employed for works of mercy. I think this came about because God especially commands such deeds and declares that they please him either as sacrifices or more than sacrifices. From this customary usage it has come about that God himself is called *pius*; the Greeks, however, never call him εὐσεβής in their own established usage, although even their common people employ εὐσέβεια in the sense of mercy. Consequently, in certain passages of Scripture, to make the distinction more certain, they preferred to say not εὐσέβεια, which signifies good worship, but θεοσέβεια, which signifies the worship of God.

Yet Greek writers, though more recent ones, have sometimes also called God εὐσεβής. Thus Themistius Euphrades, Oration V:

> Οὐδεὶς γὰρ ἐν ταῖς ἐπικλήσεσι τοῦ Θεοῦ τὸν νικητήν, ἤτοι θριαμβευτὴν ἀνακαλεῖται, ἢ τὸν Γερμανικόν, ἢ τὸν Σκυθικόν, ἀλλὰ τὸν φιλάνθρωπον, καὶ τὸν εὐσεβῆ, καὶ τὸν σωτῆρα.

> For no one, among the invocations of God, calls upon him as the Victor or Triumphant, or as the Germanicus or Scythicus, but as the Lover of Humanity, the Compassionate, and the Savior.

Thus God is here εὐσεβής in the sense of *pius*, compassionate, and φιλάνθρωπος, humane—a word by which Themistius wished to express *pius*. HERALDUS.

### *Beneficent*

They often coupled εὐεργέτας, “benefactors,” with σωτῆρας, “saviors.” HERALDUS.

### *If at any time they fall beneath them*

That is, before their eyes and beneath their altars, as Arnobius says below. Nothing should therefore be changed. HERALDUS.

### *And, as we see, pleasure too is no cause for sacrifices*

Salmasius edited and punctuated the passage in this way, very correctly. Previously it read: “and by pleasure. Therefore,” etc. ORELLI.]

## IV

If perhaps this is not the reason, are victims slaughtered for the gods and placed upon kindled altars for the sake of some pleasure and gratification, as it is called? Is there anyone among human beings who persuades himself that the gods grow soft through the outpouring of pleasures, leap with delight into lustful joy, and, like some base animal, are affected by flattering sensations and soothed by the swift titillation of fleeting sweetness?

For what is dissolved by pleasure must necessarily be constricted by its opposite, sorrow; nor can that which trembles with delight and is lifted up [Col. 1222B] by the frivolities of joys remain immune from the anguish of grief. The gods, however, must be free from both emotions if we wish them to be everlasting and exempt from the frailty of mortals.

Furthermore, every pleasure is, as it were, a certain flattery of the body and is received through those familiar five senses. If the gods above experience it, they too must necessarily partake of bodies, through which there is a path to the senses and a doorway for receiving pleasures.

Finally, what kind of joy is it to delight in the slaughter of harmless living creatures; often to hear their pitiful lowing; to see streams of blood and souls escaping with the gore; and, once their hidden parts have been laid open, to see the intestines roll out [Col. 1223A] together with the dung, hearts still leaping from the remnant of breath, and the trembling veins quivering among the entrails?

We human beings are half-wild—or rather, to express what is truer and plainer to say, wholly wild—for unhappy necessity and evil custom have taught us to take food from these creatures. Yet at times we are moved to pity for them; we reproach ourselves and, once the event has been thoroughly seen and examined, condemn ourselves because, abandoning the law of humanity, we have broken our fellowship in a common natural origin. [Note: [Col. 1223B] Sabinus reads: “we have found.” Wrongly.]

Does anyone believe that the gods are compassionate, beneficent, and gentle, yet take pleasure in the slaughter of cattle and overflow [Note: [Col. 1223B] Sabinus: “are split apart.”] with delight whenever animals fall beneath their eyes and pitifully breathe their last? And, as we see, pleasure too is no cause for sacrifices, nor is there any rationale for their performance, since there is no pleasure involved; [Note: [Col. 1223B] Sabinus: “not one.”] or, if perhaps there is some pleasure, it has been demonstrated that it cannot by any reasoning fall upon the gods. [Col. 1223B]

[Note: [Col. 1224C]

### V.—*So that they may lay aside their anger and resentment*

See above, on book V, chapter 2, at the end. ORELLI.

### *Definition*

Others read *diffinitionem*, a spelling very frequently interchanged by scribes with *definitionem*. So too *designare* and *dissignare*. ORELLI.

[Col. 1224D] ### *Which we ought always steadfastly to remember*

*Pertinaciter* is used here in a favorable sense, meaning “steadfastly.” Thus Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* IV, chapter 18, §16:

> Likewise, concerning his—that is, Christ’s—silence, which he steadfastly maintained even unto death, Isaiah again spoke as follows, etc.

See Bünemann there, p. 509. Compare Pitiscus on Curtius V.9.4. Similarly, *contumax*, “unyielding,” is used for “steadfast” in Prudentius, *Peristephanon* X, 714, and Mamertinus, *Birthday Oration*, chapter 11, where see Schwarz, p. 183, vol. II, Jaeger’s edition. ORELLI.

### *It follows that we should believe*

Thus Stewechius and Salmasius from the manuscript, in place of “it is reasonable that we should believe.” ORELLI.

### *Leads toward the danger of destruction*

*Interitio*, “destruction,” is an ancient word. See Nonius and the passage above, book II, chapter 62:

> Much later there will be regret that it was an object of mockery, when one begins to approach the experience of destruction. ORELLI.

### *For whatever is agitated, etc., etc.*

He argues in the same way above, book I, chapter 18. ORELLI.]

### V

It follows that we should also examine that argument which we hear commonly bandied about and which circulates in popular belief: that sacrifices are offered to the gods above for this reason, that they may lay aside their wrath and resentment and become gentle and placid once the indignation of their heated breasts has subsided. [Col. 1224A] But [Note: [Col. 1224B] “And,” which the Lyon ed., B, adopts.] if we retain that definition which we ought always steadfastly to remember—namely, that all emotions of the mind are unknown to the gods—it follows that we must believe that the gods are never angry; indeed, that no emotion is further removed from them than that which, being most akin to wild and brute beasts, disturbs those who experience it with tempestuous agitation and brings them into danger of destruction. For whatever is disturbed by the motion of some thing is plainly susceptible to suffering and fragile; what is subject to suffering and fragility must necessarily be mortal. Anger, however, disturbs and unhinges those who experience it; therefore that which is subject to the passions of anger must be declared mortal. But surely we know that the gods must be everlasting and possess an immortal nature. If this is established and clear, anger is far removed from them and wholly alien to their condition. There is therefore no rational ground for wishing to appease among the gods above something which, as you can see, cannot be compatible with their blessedness. [Col. 1224B]

### VI

But let us concede, as you wish, that a disturbance of this kind is natural to the gods, and that divine rites are performed and sacred ceremonies celebrated for the purpose of appeasing it. When, then, is it proper [Note: [Col. 1224B] Thus Sab. Others: “will it be proper.”] for these offerings to be employed, [Col. 1225A] or at what time should they be given? Before the gods are angry and aroused, or after they have been moved and are already in a state of indignation? If they must be forestalled beforehand so that they do not become resentful, you are setting wild beasts before us, not gods—beasts to which it is customary to throw food so that, once roused, they may not rage and shatter the bars of their cages, but may vent their frenzy upon the food and divert their desire to inflict harm. But if this satisfaction of sacrifices is heaped before them when they are already heated and blazing with indignation, I neither inquire nor demand whether that joyful and exalted magnanimity of the divine powers can be moved by an offense committed by paltry human beings, or can regard as a wound anything which a blind creature, forever walking amid the clouds of ignorance, may have done or said to diminish their authority.

[Note: [Col. 1224D]

**VI.—For the purpose of appeasing it.** I have printed this with Meursius, in place of *placandique ejus causa*. ORELL.

[Col. 1225B] **That joyful and exalted magnanimity.** Fulvius Ursinus would have *lauta*, “splendid,” restored. I do not approve. I think one should read *elata*, “exalted.” Thus he interprets μεγαλοφροσύνην, “magnanimity.” [Col. 1225C] And so he denies that exacting vengeance for an offense befits the gods’ μεγαλοφροσύνη, “magnanimity.” Indeed, as Plutarch says in his *Pelopidas*, μέγα μέρος μεγαλοψυχίας ἀνεξικακία, “forbearance under wrong is a great part of magnanimity.” Hence Lactantius, in *On the Anger of God*, ch. V: “It is an attractive and popular argument that this pettiness of mind cannot befall God, so that he should suppose himself injured by one who cannot injure him.” HERALD.—Nothing at all should be changed. Arnobius is referring to the gods’ life, which is spent in perpetual joys. ORELL.

**Or can regard as a wound.** That is, as an offense or a most grievous injury. So Eutropius, Book X, ch. 16: “For there were some who inflicted wounds upon his glory.” See C. Barth, who discusses this expression at length, on Claudianus Mamertus, *On the State of the Soul*, p. 302 ff. One could also interpret it as “regard as a crime or offense,” in which sense *vulnus*, “wound,” frequently occurs in ecclesiastical writers; for example, Juvencus, *Gospel History* IV, 114:

> If amid these things anyone can keep his breast  
> Protected from a wound until the end, he will depart  
> Crowned with the lofty garlands of eternal life and light.

[Col. 1225D] And ibid. II, 434 ff.:

> . . . May not merely seven offenses,  
> But wounds multiplied tenfold beyond them, be forgiven a brother.

See Omeis there, p. 305, ed. Reusch. ORELL.

**May have devised (*dissignaverit*).** Others: *designaverit*. See above, at Book I, ch. 63. ORELL.]

### VII

But neither do I insist that the following be said or heard: what causes the gods have for anger [Col. 1225B] against human beings, such that an offense they have incurred must be soothed with sacrifices. Have they ever enacted any laws for mortals? Has it ever been established by them what human beings ought or ought not to do, what they should pursue and what avoid, or at least by what rites the gods wished themselves to be worshiped, so that acts committed otherwise than they commanded might be pursued with the punishments [Col. 1226A] of their wrath, and so that, when treated with contempt, they might wish to avenge themselves upon the audacious and the transgressors? In my opinion, they have never either established or ordained anything, since they have never appeared, and even whether any such beings exist could not be learned with the clearest certainty. What justice is there, then, in the heavenly gods’ becoming angry for some reason with people to whom they have never deigned to reveal that they exist, and to whom they have neither given nor imposed any laws which they wished them to observe and preserve with inviolable obedience?

[Note: [Col. 1225D]

**VII.—What causes the gods have for anger against human beings.** Thus Gelenius, acutely. The first edition reads: “in which, if too little,” etc. HERALD.

**And even whether any such beings exist could not be learned with the clearest certainty.** Thus the manuscript codex, according to Stewechius; I, for my part, would not rashly alter this reading. Meursius punctuates it thus: “And, if there are any, none could with the clearest,” etc. All editions read: “Nor, if they have been seen.” *Si*, “if,” stands for *an*, “whether,” as it very often does. ORELL.

**To whom they have never revealed that they exist, etc.** Stewechius added *esse*, “exist,” from the manuscript. Others read: “to whom they have not revealed themselves.” *Se* in place of *sese* [Col. 1226B] is Salmasius’ emendation. ORELL.]

### VIII

But this, as I have said, I pass over and allow to depart unchallenged in silence. One point above all I ask: why, if I kill a pig, does a god change his disposition and lay aside his resentment and fury; and if I burn a hen or calf before his eyes and altars, [Col. 1226B] why does he forget the injury and wholly abandon his sense of offense? What from this act passes over to relieve his pain? Or of what remedial value is a goose, a goat, or a peacock, that medicine should be applied to an angry god from its blood? Do the gods, then, sell redress for their injuries and, like little children, receive sparrows, dolls, [Note: [Col. 1225B] Read *pupulas*, “dolls.” See the Note.] hobbyhorses, and little Pans [Col. 1227A] so that they may spare their tempers, cease crying, and have something with which to distract themselves? Do the immortal gods likewise accept these appeasing gifts, so that they may lay aside their wrath and resentment and become reconciled with those who have offended them? Yet I had thought that the gods—if indeed it is right to believe that they are agitated by movements of anger—laid aside their wrath and resentment without any rewards or payments, and freely forgave sinners their offenses. For it is proper to divine beings to grant generous pardons and gratuitous forgiveness. But if this cannot be done, it is far wiser for them to remain obstinately fixed in their offense than to be softened by the corruption of gifts. For the number of sinners increases when hope is offered that sin may be redeemed, and people readily proceed to wrongdoing where the favor of those who forgive is for sale.

[Note: [Col. 1226B]

**VIII.—Allow to depart unchallenged in silence.** The manuscript codex and first edition have *obire*, which Heraldus defends on the basis of the ancients’ custom of very frequently interchanging the prepositions *ab* and *ob*. Perhaps from this arose the meaning of *obire*, “to die.” ORELL.

**If I burn a hen or calf before his eyes and altars.** Below: “What kind of honor is this—to burn a wether, ram, or bull beneath the god’s face and kill it before his eyes?” For statues stood at the altars, and the victims were slaughtered facing them. Lucretius II, 352:

> For often before the gods’ splendid temples a calf  
> Falls slaughtered beside the incense-burning altars.

Hence Euripides in the *Phoenician Women* calls statues θεῶν δεξίμηλα ἀγάλματα, “the gods’ images that receive the sheep,” παρὰ τὸ δέχεσθαι τὰ μῆλα, “from receiving the sheep,” just as in the *Andromache* he calls a house δεξίμηλον δόμον, “sheep-receiving,” and a hearth δεξίμηλον ἐσχάραν, “sheep-receiving.” HERALD.—For “calf,” Fulvius Ursinus conjectures that “chick” should be read. ORELL.

**Peacock (*pavus*).** This is the more ancient form, used by Varro in Gellius, Book VII, ch. 16; writers of the Golden Age of Latin instead said *pavo, pavonis*. Besides our author, Tertullian also has the ancient form in *On the Soul*, ch. XXXIII: “a most beautiful peacock, and most splendidly adorned with whatever color it desires.” ORELL.

**Like little children, so that they may spare their tempers and cease crying.** Thus Heraldus emended the text. The first edition reads: “and like little children spare their tempers,” etc.; Gelenius: “and like little children, in order that they may spare their tempers,” etc.; the Leiden edition: “so that they may spare the high-spirited,” etc. Colvius, on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VIII, p. 448, ed. Oudendorp, thinks one should read: “That they may spare their tears,” or “that they may feed their tempers.” Wrongly. “To spare their tempers” means the same as the earlier expression “to lay aside wrath and resentment,” as G. J. Vossius rightly observes in *On Idolatry*, Book III, ch. 98, p. 464. ORELL.

**They receive sparrows, dolls, hobbyhorses, and little Pans, etc.** Pliny, Book IV, Letter 2, and Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VIII, p. 448, also mention such children’s toys. ORELL.

**Dolls.** It is well known that *pupus* and *pupa* mean little boys and girls; Varro in Book VI uses *pusa*. From these forms, *pupulus* and *pupula* are diminutives formed in the same way in Catullus, Apuleius, and others. In antiquity these terms also denoted εἰκόνια, “little images,” small figurines still used today by nurses and children; and from them they are still called *Puppen* in our vernacular. Of them comes the line of Persius, Satire II, 70:

> . . . Dolls dedicated by a maiden to Venus.

One may therefore write the word with two *p*s, or with one if preferred. Varro, *Origins*: “A large part fell into longing for dolls and little figures.” STEWECH.

**Little Pans.** These should be understood, as Heraldus quite rightly observes, not as ἄρτων κλάσματα, “pieces of bread,” but as little figurines fashioned in the likeness of Pans. These were boys’ toys, just as dolls—which were also called νύμφαι, “nymphs”—were girls’ toys. I have therefore written *Panes* with a capital letter. ORELL.

**To grant gratuitous forgiveness.** Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “to bestow gratuitous forgiveness.” But nothing should be changed. The sense is that the gods possess favors which they grant without payment. ORELL.]

### IX

Suppose that some ox, or any one of those animals [Col. 1227B] which is killed to appease and mitigate [Note: [Col. 1227B] The manuscript has “and mitigate toward.”] the furies of the divine powers, were to assume a human voice and speak in these words:

“Is this, then, O Jupiter—or whatever other god you may be—humane and right, or to be regarded as possessing any justice: that when another has sinned, I should be killed, and that you should permit satisfaction to be made to you with my blood, although I have never injured you, never knowingly or unknowingly violated your divinity [Note: [Col. 1227B] Sab.: “name.”] and majesty? I am, as you know, [Note: [Col. 1228B] Manuscript: “as you know,” plural.] a dumb animal, following the simplicity of my nature [Col. 1228A] and not unstable amid the varieties of multiform conduct. Have I ever performed your games with insufficient sanctity and care? Have I ever paraded before you any presiding official who had offended your divinity? Have I ever sworn falsely by you? Have I ever carried off your possessions through sacrilegious thefts and plundered your treasuries? Have I ever uprooted most sacred groves, or polluted and profaned any holy places with private buildings? What cause is there, then, that another’s crime should be expiated with my blood and that my life and innocence should be brought into a wickedness foreign to me? Is it because I am a worthless animal, sharing neither reason nor counsel, as those creatures who call themselves human beings declare, although in savagery they surpass the beasts? Did not the same nature produce and fashion both me and them from the same beginnings? Is there not one breath that governs both [Col. 1228B] them and me? Do I not breathe and see in the same manner and experience the other senses? They have livers, lungs, hearts, intestines, and stomachs; has not the same number of bodily parts also been assigned to me? They love their offspring and come together to beget children; do I not likewise possess concern for perpetuating my young, and sweetness in them when they have been born?

“But they are rational and utter articulate sounds. How do they know whether I too perform what I do according to reasons of my own, and whether this sound [Col. 1229A] which I utter constitutes the words of my kind, understood by us alone? Ask piety whether it is more just that I should be killed and destroyed, or that a human being should be granted pardon and impunity for his crimes. Who shaped iron into the sword? Was it not a human being? Who brought destruction upon peoples, who imposed slavery upon nations? Was it not a human being? Who secretly administered and compounded deadly potions for parents, brothers, wives, and friends? Was it not a human being? Who invented evil deeds, or devised so many that they could scarcely be recounted in ten thousand annals or days? Was it not a human being? And so is it not savage, monstrous, and cruel? Does it not appear unjust and barbarous to you, O Jupiter, that I should be killed and slaughtered so that you may become placid and criminals may obtain impunity?”

[Col. 1229B] It is therefore established that sacrifices performed for this reason—that angry divine powers may be appeased—are performed in vain, since reason has taught us both that the gods never become angry and that they do not wish one being to be destroyed and slaughtered for another, nor the obliteration of offenses to be purchased through the blood of the innocent.

[Note: [Col. 1227D]

**IX.—Suppose that some ox, etc.** There now follows the victim’s address to Jupiter, a most beautiful passage. ORELL.

**Which is killed to appease and mitigate the furies of the divine powers.** *Furies* has the same sense above, at the end of Book IV: “But if the race of the gods is immune from furies of this kind.” ORELL.

**Although I have never injured you.** This reading of the old codex is more pleasing to the ear than the editors’ “because I have never injured you.” STEWECH.—Others read: “since I have never,” wrongly. ORELL.

**Have I ever paraded before you any presiding official who had offended your divinity?** Thus Stewechius most correctly emended the text. The manuscript codex has: “paraded before,” for which Gelenius reads: “or paraded you.” Arnobius is evidently referring to the story of the slave condemned to the fork who was paraded through the middle of the circus, which he narrates below in ch. 36 of our edition. ORELL.

**Have I ever uprooted most sacred groves?** By this crime—indeed, by this more-than-sacrilege—it was believed that the gods’ inappeasable wrath and offense were incurred. Therefore, when Caesar’s soldiers were ordered to cut down the grove at Massilia, rendered most sacred by the awe of its ancient religion, for engines of war and the other equipment of the siege, they stopped fearfully before beginning the deed, fearing that their own axes would rebound against them. Lucan depicts this superstition of the soldiers in vivid colors in Book III:

> He orders this forest to fall beneath the invading iron;  
> For, close to the work and untouched in the previous war,  
> It stood, the densest growth amid the stripped hills.  
> But their strong hands trembled; shaken by the place’s  
> Awful majesty, they believed that, if they struck  
> The sacred oaks, their axes would return upon their limbs.  
> When Caesar saw the cohorts gripped by profound paralysis,  
> He was the first to dare seize and swing an axe  
> And cleave an airy oak with iron, etc.

HERALD.

**Polluted and profaned with private buildings.** To pollute groves consecrated to the gods—like all other places θεοῖς ἀνειμένα, “dedicated to the gods”—with buildings or any other profane use was a grave act requiring expiation. HERALD.—Cicero spoke in the same sense (*For Milo*): “You Alban mounds and groves, you, I say, I implore and adjure; and you buried altars of the Albans, partners and equals in the sacred rites of the Roman people, which that man in his headlong madness overwhelmed with insane masses of buildings after cutting down and leveling the most sacred groves: then your altars and religious powers flourished, your force prevailed—the force which he had polluted with every crime.” NOURRY, p. 567.

**Should be expiated with my blood.** Fulvius Ursinus introduces the preposition *e*, “with/from,” wrongly. ORELL.

**Should be surrendered.** Thus the Leiden editor from the manuscript. Others: “should be brought.” ORELL.

**Utter articulate sounds.** I have printed this from the correction of Fr. Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* X, p. 711. Others: “express.” But to “express a sound” is either to extort it from another or to reproduce it by imitation and so represent it, which is foreign to our passage. ORELL.

**How do they know, etc., etc.** Abr. Willet, on Galen’s *Exhortation to the Arts*, ch. I, p. 60 ff., shows through many examples that the ancient philosophers, especially the Stoics, held that animals share reason and speech imperfectly with human beings. ORELL.

**Who shaped iron into the sword, etc.** Juvenal, Satire XV, v. 160:

> Yet it was not enough that man, upon an accursed anvil,  
> Produced death-dealing iron, though the earliest smiths,  
> Accustomed to forging only rakes and hoes, exhausted  
> By mattocks and plowshares, had not learned to hammer out swords.

ELMENH.

**And compounded potions.** Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, 147:

> Terrible stepmothers compound livid aconite.

HERALD.

[Col. 1229D] **Devised so many.** Fulvius Ursinus prefers *commentus est tanta*, from *comminiscor*, “devise.” ORELL.

**So many that they could scarcely be recounted in ten thousand annals or daily records.** That is, μυριάσιν, “in tens of thousands.” But his use of *dies*, “days,” to mean “daily journals” is novel, and I fear it is spurious. HERALD.—J. G. Graevius, in Letter 258 to N. Heinsius, Burmann’s *Sylloge*, vol. IV, p. 332, emends the text to “or daily records,” understanding the urban *Acta Diurna*, in which crimes and misdeeds were recorded. The common reading could be defended by the very similar passage in Book V, ch. 15: “That it exists in the daily records and was entered by you in the registers.” But here *diebus*, “days,” seems to have flowed from an interpolation by Fulvius Ursinus, not from the manuscript codex. I therefore decide nothing. For “could,” Gelenius printed “could not,” in accordance with the Greek construction of a more emphatic negative. ORELL.

**Offenses (*dissignationibus*).** Thus the manuscript. Others: *designationibus*, in the same sense. See the note of my very dear Ochsner on Book I, ch. 63: *dissignationibus*, namely, “offenses committed by the victims.” ORELL.]

### X

But perhaps someone will say: “We expend victims and other offerings upon the gods so that, having in some way been made friendly by our supplications, they may grant us prosperity and avert evils from us; so that they may cause us always to live amid joys, while driving away sorrows and the threats arising from chance misfortunes.”

This passage requires no little care, nor is what is said easy to hear or believe, accustomed though people are to it. For immediately that entire company of the most learned will swoop down; affirming and proving that whatever happens occurs by fate, it will snatch this belief from your hands and press you with the charge that you trust in empty [Col. 1229C] convictions.

“Whatever,” it will say, “has been done, is being done, or will be done in the world was long ago determined and fixed. It possesses immutable causes through which events, linked to one another, weave an unassailable necessity connecting the past with what is to come. [Col. 1230A] If it has been determined and fixed what evil or good must befall each person, it is already certain. But if it is certain and fixed, all assistance from the gods is useless; useless are their hatreds, useless their kindnesses. For they are no more able to provide what cannot happen than to prevent from happening what must necessarily come to pass.” Indeed, if they wish, those learned men will be able to press this doctrine more forcefully, so that they may even declare that you worship the gods themselves in vain and adore them with superfluous supplications. For since the gods cannot overturn the order of things or change what fate has established, what point or reason is there in wishing to weary and deafen the ears of beings upon whose aid you cannot rely in your greatest necessities?

[Note: [Col. 1229D]

**X.—Cause us to live amid joys.** χαίρειν, εὖ πράττειν, “to rejoice, to fare well.” [Col. 1230C] A pure and unmistakable Graecism. ORELL.

**And the threats arising, etc.** The word *et*, “and,” is absent from the manuscript, with Meursius approving the omission as an elliptical manner of speaking. ORELL.

**If they wish.** Thus Gelenius, as the sense demands. The first edition has “if they do not wish,” incorrectly. ORELL.

**So that they may even declare that you worship the gods themselves in vain.** Lucian ties this argument together with many knots in *Zeus Tragoedus*. HERALD.]

### XI

Finally, if the gods drive away sorrowful and troublesome things, [Col. 1230B] and if they bestow those which are joyful and favorable, whence come so many countless wretched people in the world? Whence so many unhappy persons living a pitiable life in the lowest condition? Why are those not free from calamities who at every moment and every instant load and heap their altars with sacrifices? Do we not, they say, see that some of these people are abodes of diseases; that, with their eyes extinguished and their ears stopped, they are unable to walk; that they live as trunks without hands; that they are submerged, crushed, and destroyed by fires, shipwrecks, and collapsing buildings; that, cast down from immense estates, they sustain themselves by hired labor; that they beg for the smallest coins in the extremity of want; that they are banished and proscribed; that they are always in mourning, broken by the loss of their children; and that they are harassed by all the other misfortunes whose kinds and forms no enumeration could define? [Col. 1230C] This surely would not happen if the gods, bound by the merits of sacred rites, could repel or turn aside these evils. [Col. 1231A] But as things now stand, because chance has no place in these affairs, but everything comes to pass by inescapable necessity, the prescribed order runs its course [Note: [Col. 1231C] Sab.: “the order set down in writing.”] and completes what has once been decreed.

[Note: [Col. 1230C]

**XI.—Finally, if the gods drive away sorrowful and troublesome things.** Meursius rashly tampered with this entirely correct reading, conjecturing “sorrows and misfortunes.” ORELL.

[Col. 1230D] **Living a life in the lowest condition.** Bünemann illustrates the very familiar phrase *vitam ducere*, “to lead a life,” with many examples on Lactantius, Book VII, ch. 9, p. 909 ff. ORELL.

**They say.** Fulvius Ursinus: “they will say.” ORELL.

**Submerged, crushed, and destroyed.** Stewechius arranged the words in this order, followed by Salmasius. Others: “crushed, submerged, and destroyed.” ORELL.

**Cast down from immense estates.** *Evolutos* means “thrown down, dislodged.” Thus Tacitus, *Annals* XIII, 15: “He resolutely began a song signifying that he had been cast down from his ancestral seat and supreme position.” And Seneca, *Letters* 75: “You will encounter men driven into exile and stripped of their goods.” ORELL.

**They beg for the smallest coins in the extremity of want.** This is the utmost and most extreme misery. Julius Firmicus, *Astronomy*, Book V, ch. 8: “They will at some time reach such destitution that they will be compelled miserably to ask others for the necessities that sustain life.” ELMENH.

[Col. 1231C] **But everything comes to pass by inescapable necessity.** Thus Canterus. Sab.: “they accomplish”; Fulvius Ursinus: “they may accomplish.” *Confieri*, “come to pass,” is a verb very frequently used by Arnobius, as we observed above. ORELL.

**Runs its course.** Fulvius Ursinus reads “or it runs,” connecting this with the following words: “Or they must be called ungrateful,” etc. Not badly. ORELL.]

### XII

Or the heavenly gods must be called ungrateful if, although they possess the right to prevent it, they allow the unhappy race to become entangled in so many punishments and calamities. And perhaps they might say something weighty, something which ought not to be received by deceitful, frivolous, and contemptuous ears. Yet because the matter requires an excessively long and extended discussion, we pass rapidly over these aspects without explaining or touching them, content merely to have established this point: you attach dishonorable reputations to your gods if you deny that they can bestow good things and turn aside hostile ones unless they have first been purchased with the blood of she-goats and sheep and with the other things [Col. 1231B] brought to the altars.

For, first, it is unworthy that the power of the divine beings and the sublimity of the heavenly ones should be believed to hold their favors for sale—first to take payment and only then to provide them. Then, what is far more shameful, unless they have received payment they benefit no one, and they permit the most wretched people to undergo perilous fortunes, although they could prevent them and come to their aid.

Suppose that of two men performing sacred rites, one is well-born and wealthy, while the other possesses a humble household but is praiseworthy for his innocence and integrity. Let the former slaughter a hundred oxen and as many mother sheep with their lambs; let the poor man burn a little incense and a single clod of some aromatic substance. If the divine powers provide nothing without preceding rewards, will it not follow that they must be believed to extend their favor and assistance to the wealthy man but turn their eyes away from the poor fellow, whom not his disposition but the necessity of his household circumstances has made parsimonious? [Col. 1231C] For where the giver is venal and works for hire, favor must necessarily be bestowed in proportion to the size of the gift, and his vote must incline toward the source from which a much greater payment and a more disgraceful bribe have flowed to the one who provides the favor. [Col. 1232A]

What if, again, two peoples at variance and engaged in hostile warfare enrich the altars of the gods above with equal sacrifices, and each asks that strength and assistance be lent to it against the other? If the gods are induced by rewards to render help, must we not once again believe that they hesitate between both sides, remain fixed in indecision, and cannot discover what to do, since they understand their favor to have been obligated by the acceptance of sacred offerings? For either they will furnish assistance on both sides—which cannot happen, since they would then be fighting against themselves, opposing their own favors and inclinations—or they will cease to supply aid to both peoples, which, after receiving the payment that was expended, is a great crime.

Therefore this whole disgrace must be driven far away from the gods. It must not be said at all [Col. 1232B] that rewards and payments entice them to confer good things and remove their opposites—if indeed they are true gods and deserve to be placed within that designation. For either whatever happens occurs by fate, in which case partiality and favor have no place among the gods; or, if fate is excluded and cast out, it does not befit the dignity of the beings above to put up for sale their favor toward a good deed [Note: [Col. 1232C] Manuscript: “favors.”] and the acts of generosity which they bestow.

[Note: [Col. 1231D]

**XII.—Although they possess the right to prevent it.** That is, ἐξουσίαν, “authority,” as we observed at Book I. HERALD.

**One is well-born and wealthy.** Thus jurists use *honestus* to mean wealthy, opposing it to the poor, Digest, Book XLVII, title *On Thefts*, law 52, §15. It is opposed to a common person in Digest, law 5, title *On Statutory Guardians*. HERALD.—Here *honestus* means one born in a good social position and of respectable parents. For I used to observe that *honestas* and *honestus*, “respectability” and “respectable,” are commonly set virtually as ἀντίθετα, “opposites,” to *humilitas* and *humilis*, “low status” and “lowly,” especially as the purity of Latin declined. The emperor Justinian says: “The same law imposes a penalty upon ravishers: if they are respectable, confiscation of half their goods; if of low status, corporal punishment together with relegation.” Cicero uses *honestus* for a man of rank in more than one letter, as does Vegetius, *Military Science*, Book I, ch. VII. STEWECH.

**Hesitate, remain fixed in indecision.** *Defigi* is most explicitly used of those who stand motionless, inclining to neither side. Hence *figere* and *defigere*, Greek πῆξαι, “to fix,” mean “to bind, tie, or render immovable.” Those who, from amazement, are brought into a stupor and remain rooted to the spot are said to be “fixed by astonishment.” Compare Salmasius, who discusses this verb at length in his work on Solinus, p. 765. ORELL.

**If indeed they are true gods and deserve to be placed within that designation.** That is, if they are worthy of this designation as true gods. Those who would restore *acceptione*, “acceptance”—for example, Fulvius Ursinus—are therefore mistaken. HERALD.

**Partiality and favor have no place among the gods.** Here *ambitio* means favor or partiality. I would certainly not note this if I did not see that men who dare to emend the best authors are disgracefully ignorant of it. Cornelius Tacitus, at the beginning of the *Agricola*: “Thus each man most celebrated for his talent was led to publish the memory of virtue without favor or partiality, solely by the reward of a good conscience”; that is, οὐδενὶ χαριζόμενος, καὶ μηδεμίαν αὐτὸς χάριν μνώμενος, “showing favor to no one and himself remembering no favor.” Thus *ambitio* denotes excessive ἀρέσκεια, “obsequiousness,” by which we trim our sails to the popular breeze and desire to stand well with every social order. Livy, Book XLIII: “The consul’s army was under strength because furloughs had commonly been given out through favoritism.” In the same place: “The levy was difficult not for consuls, but for popularity-seeking consuls.” Elsewhere: “And such songs were sung by the soldiers against the commander that it was apparent they were directed at an indulgent and favor-seeking general.” There are also *decreta ambitiosa*, that is, decrees bestowed out of favor: Digest, Book IV, title *On Minors*, law 3. HERALD.]

### XIII

We have sufficiently shown, I think, that victims and their accompanying rites are brought before the immortal gods in vain: for the gods are neither nourished by them nor derive any pleasure from them; they neither lay aside wrath or resentment because of them, nor on their account bestow favorable circumstances, nor drive away and avert their opposites.

It follows that we should also [Col. 1232C] examine that argument which certain people customarily assert and connect with ceremonial reasons. For they say that these sacred rites were instituted to honor the heavenly beings, that they perform them for the sake of honor, and that by them they increase the powers of the divine beings. What if they were similarly to say that they keep themselves awake and sleep, walk about and stand still, write something and read, in order to show honor to the gods and render them greater in dignity? For what is added to the gods by the blood of cattle? What increase in substance comes from the performance of the other sacred rites? What is added or annexed to their power?

[Col. 1233A] For every honor which is said to be shown by one person and attributed as an act of superior reverence is relational to another and consists of two parts: the concession made by the giver and the exaltation of the recipient. Thus, if someone, upon seeing a man of most powerful name and authority, moves out of his way, rises, uncovers his head, and gets down from his carriage, and then, bowing low, greets him, imitating with fearful trembling the servile condition of a slave, I see what is accomplished in an act of veneration of this kind: through one person’s abasement, a great deal is bestowed upon the other; [Col. 1233B] and the man whom an inferior’s reverence has exalted and placed above his own concerns is made to appear great.

[Note: [Col. 1232D]

**XIII.—That victims and their accompanying rites are brought before the immortal gods in vain.** The expression is precise. Above: “Unless they have first been purchased with the blood of she-goats and sheep, [Col. 1233C] and with the other things brought to the altars.” Lucan I, 608:

> Then to the sacred altars he brings  
> A male victim with neck erect.

The Greeks say θυσίαν βωμῷ προσάγειν, “to bring a sacrifice to an altar.” HERALD.

**Keep themselves awake.** Oudendorp, on Suetonius, *Vespasian* ch. 21, p. 559, suspects that *vigilare*, “remain awake,” should be read. But we saw above that our author sometimes uses compounds in place of simple verbs. ORELL.

**If someone, upon seeing a man of most powerful name, moves out of his way, rises, uncovers his head, and gets down from his carriage, etc.** Sallust in Nonius: “For these reasons Sulla, when dictator after his victory, was accustomed to dismount from his horse before him, rise from his seat, and uncover his head.” HERALD. It was evidently customary, when a magistrate or prince approached, to rise, uncover the head, and dismount from horse or carriage; to do so whether one was seated alone or with one’s wife; to lay aside one’s sword; and to transfer from the right hand to the left the switch used for striking the horse. See Seneca, *Letters* LXX; Apuleius, *Florida* III; and the authors cited by Stewechius on this passage; [Col. 1233D] also Justus Lipsius, who discusses the matter at length in *Electa*, Book I, ch. 23, *Works*, vol. I, p. 725, Wesel ed. A separate book on ancient forms of greeting was published by Jacobus Claudius at Utrecht in 1702, in small format. ORELL.

**Rises.** Virgil, *Georgics* II, 97 ff.:

> There are also Aminean vines, producing the most steadfast wines,  
> Before which Tmolus rises, and King Phanaeus himself.

Servius here says: “The metaphor is taken from seated persons, who are accustomed to rise in honor of someone.” ORELL.

**And then, bowing low, greets him.** Thus Stewechius corrected the earlier reading *acclivis*, “sloping upward,” to *acclinis* from the manuscript codex. *Acclinis* is equivalent to “bent forward, supported upon the knees.” ORELL.

**Imitating with fearful trembling the servile condition of a slave.** I have followed this entirely correct emendation of Tiberius Hemsterhuis on Lucian’s *Timon*, ch. 5, vol. I, p. 344, Bipont ed., and of Gesner in the *Thesaurus*, under *ancillatrum*. The manuscript codex and first edition have: “imitating the fearful tremblings of maidservants belonging to a slave”; [Col. 1234C] from this Gelenius, with his customary freedom in making alterations, produced: “imitating the fearful tremblings of a maidservant or slave.” Salmasius, in the Leiden edition and in his work on Solinus, p. 804, printed: “imitating a slave’s maidservile conduct with fearful tremblings,” explaining *ancillatrum* as *ancillatio*, “maidservile conduct,” from *ancillor, -ari*, “to serve as a maid.” But I wish he had given us examples of this form. I have therefore preferred *ancillatum*, which Arnobius uses emphatically to indicate the status and condition of maidservants, which was humbler and more abject than the condition of male slaves. ORELL.

**With fearful trembling.** Elegantly expressed. Thus Plutarch in his *Nicias* calls it τὸ ἀθαρσὲς καὶ καταπεπληγμένον, “timidity and terror”: ὑποδηλοῖ δὲ καὶ Φρύνιχος τὸ ἀθαρσὲς αὐτοῦ καὶ καταπεπληγμένον ἐν τούτοις·

> Ἦν γὰρ πολίτης ἀγαθὸς ὡς, εὖ οἶδ’ ἐγώ,  
> Κοὐχ ὑποταγεὶς ἐβάδιζεν ὥσπερ Νικίας.

“And Phrynichus too indicates his timidity and terror in these lines:

> For he was a good citizen, as I well know,  
> And did not walk submissively like Nicias.”

HERALD.

**Whom the respect.** Thus Salmasius from Meursius’ emendation, entirely correctly. For *suspicere* properly denotes looking up to someone in veneration. Others read *susceptio*, “reception.” ORELL.]

[Note: [Col. 1234D]

**XIV.—To rejoice in lofty rank.** The preposition *de*, “in,” is redundant, as it very often is in our author. ORELL.

**Or what eminences accrue to them.** Thus Fulvius Ursinus. Others read “are added,” wrongly. ORELL.

**From the performance of sacred rites.** This is Meursius’ entirely correct emendation and comes very close to the codex’s reading, “from conjectures.” Others read “from contributions.” Scriverius, cited by Meursius in the Appendix, prefers “from collections.” ORELL.

**To be honored by the offering of some gift.** See above, at Book I, ch. 41. ORELL.

**But the human being more exalted, etc.** Meursius added these words from the royal manuscript. ORELL.]

## XIV

But this entire concession and attribution of honor of which we are speaking has its place among human beings alone. Natural weakness and the desire to stand in higher positions teach them to rejoice in rank and to be preferred to others by comparison. But I ask [Note: [Col. 1233B] Thus the manuscript and Sabaeus. Others: “But rather.”], among the heavenly beings where is there room for honor, or what eminences are found to accrue to them [Col. 1234A] [Note: [Col. 1234B] Fulvius reads “to be added.”] from the performance of sacred rites? Do they become more august and powerful when animals are slaughtered? Is anything thereby added to them, or do they begin to be gods to a greater degree because their divinity has been enlarged [Note: [Col. 1234B] The manuscript reads “they conceive.” Wrongly.]? Yet I judge it very nearly an insult—indeed, a complete insult—when a god is said to be honored by a human being and magnified by the offering of some gift. For if honor increases and augments the dignity of the one to whom it has been attributed, it follows that a god is made greater by a human being, from whom he has received a gift and a bestowal of honor. And so the matter is brought to this point: the god who is magnified by human honors is inferior, while the human being who increases the power of the divine being is superior.

[Note: [Col. 1234D]

### XV.—“Since we have also learned, under more powerful commands, to honor human beings.”

Fulvius Ursinus prefers: “Since we have also learned to honor human beings belonging to a more powerful command.” Wrongly. The sense is: since we Christians have learned under more powerful commands—that is, under the command or bidding of one more powerful, namely God or Christ—that human beings of every kind are to be honored. ORELLI.

[Col. 1235B] “Tell us, you say, what conception of the gods is worthy, right, and honorable, and not blameworthy through the deformity of any disgrace. First, that you should not believe them...” The Leiden editor excellently restored this lacunose and corrupt passage from the traces of the manuscript. The first edition and that of Gelenius have: “Tell us, you say. Let the conception concerning them not be blameworthy through deformity, so that neither...” The manuscript reads: “Tell us, you say. Let the conception concerning them first be worthy, right, and honorable, and not blameworthy through the deformity of any disgrace, so that neither...” Meursius defends this reading in the *Appendix*, taking *ne sit* as *sitne* (“whether it is”), as often among these writers. Stewechius reads and punctuates the words thus [Col. 1235C]: “What conception concerning them is, first, worthy, right, and honorable, and not blameworthy through the deformity of any disgrace: that neither...” ORELLI.

“That which is outside itself and comes from without.” The passage is correctly punctuated with a comma after “outside”; that word must by no means be joined with the following “coming.” Things that are outside us are external things, gifts of fortune—*τὰ οὐκ ἐφ’ ἡμῖν* (“the things not within our control”), according to the Stoic doctrine. ORELLI.

“Not to be incited by rewards so that they do no harm.” I have admitted into the text this highly probable correction by Thomas Canter. Others read: “not to be incited by rewards so that they may do harm,” which would mean: not to be incited by rewards to harm, namely, our foes and enemies. ORELLI.

“And not to be affected when it is not given.” Fulvius Ursinus thinks that the text should read “and not to be afflicted.” Wrongly. *Affici* means generally “to be changed, moved.” ORELLI.

“Of the divine reality.” Fulvius Ursinus suspects that the reading should be “of the divine nature,” since *res divina* elsewhere means “sacrifice.” But Arnobius appears here to have rendered the Greeks’ *τὸ θεῖον* (“the divine”). ORELLI.

“To bind beneath the face of the god.” Meursius prefers *convertere*, “to turn,” that is, to turn its face toward heaven, to bend it back—what Homer calls *αὖ ἐρύειν* (“to draw back again”), *Iliad* I.459. For my part I decide nothing, since the question whether victims were ever tied before the altars is still disputed among scholars. See Saubert, *On Sacrifices*, ch. XIX, p. 404 ff., Crenius’s edition. It might perhaps also be explained as “to be encircled with fillets, headbands, and garlands,” with which sacrificial victims were customarily adorned. See the same Saubert, ch. XVIII, p. 385. But I lack examples of the verb *connectere* used absolutely in this sense. ORELLI.

“With burning piles of wood.” Thus Meursius and the Leiden edition; the manuscript has *structibus*. Others read *struitibus*. But *struicibus*, from *struix, -icis*, should be restored. Similarly *instruix*, from *instruere*, is read in Solinus, ch. XXVIII. See Salmasius there, p. 268. ORELLI.

“Cremation grounds” (*ustrinae*). The glosses: *ustrina, καύστερα νεκρῶν* (“places for burning the dead”). Servius on *Aeneid* III.22: “The preparations for the dead are commonly called the funeral; the construction of the wood, the pyre; the placing of the fire beneath it, the funeral fire; the cremation of the corpse, the *bustum*; the place, the cremation ground.” ELMENHORST.—*Ustrina*—“Where someone has merely been burned, but has been buried elsewhere, that place is called an *ustrina* from the act of burning.” Festus, s.v. *Bustum*. This is the meaning found here in Arnobius. NOURRY, p. 570.

“Places of burial” (*busticeta*). See above on Book I, ch. 41. ORELLI.

“And fashioned as an abode for stenches.” Meursius, p. 207, suspects that the text should read “and fashioned as an abode for cattle.” But immediately afterward he himself retracts this entirely unnecessary conjecture. ORELLI.]

## XV

What then, someone will say: do you think that absolutely no honor at all should be given to the gods? If you set before us [Col. 1234B] gods such as they ought to be if they exist, and such as we all understand ourselves to mean when we utter that name, how could we fail to accord them even the greatest honor—since under more powerful commands we have learned to honor human beings also, whatever their rank and whatever their fortune?

And what is this greatest honor? It is far more dutiful than the honor paid by you, and is situated within a more powerful category.

Tell us, you say, what conception of the gods is worthy, right, and honorable, and not [Note: [Col. 1236B] [[Col. 1236] This note is printed at the foot of column 1236, but its callout letter, *b*, does not appear in the text.] The manuscript reads “to be esteemed.”] [Col. 1235A] blameworthy through the deformity of any disgrace. First, that you should not believe that they have anything resembling a human being, or that they expect anything which is outside themselves and comes to them from without. Then [Note: [Col. 1235B] Sabaeus reads “Then.”]—as has been said repeatedly—that they do not blaze with the flames of anger, do not exult in bodily pleasure, are not solicited with entreaties to confer benefits, are not incited by rewards so that they do no harm, do not hold their kindness and favor for sale, do not rejoice in honor bestowed, and do not become indignant or affected when it is withheld; but, as is proper to the divine reality, know themselves by their own power and do not measure themselves by the flatteries of others.

And yet, so that we may examine the true character of what is being asserted: what sort of honor is it to bind a wether, a ram, or a bull beneath the face of a god and kill it in his sight? What sort of honor is it to invite a god to blood, when you see him take it in company with dogs [Col. 1235B] and share it with them? [Col. 1236A] What sort of honor is it to cover the sky with smoke by setting piles of wood alight, and to darken the images of the divine beings with funeral soot? But if you are willing to assess what is done by its own intrinsic character, without first adopting preconceived valuations, those things you call altars, those beautiful raised altars, are cremation grounds for the most unfortunate race of animals, pyres and burial grounds constructed for a most hideous purpose and fashioned as an abode for stenches.

[Note: [Col. 1236B]

### XVI.—“From the woolly fleeces of lambs.”
