*Lanitium* denotes both wool itself, as here, and wool-bearing livestock, as in Book I, ch. 11: “Is nature somehow at fault because it has raised up the most troublesome beast among wool-bearing animals?” And ch. 21: “Let your wool-bearing animals be multiplied by numerous offspring.” See Turnebus, *Adversaria*, Book XV, ch. 21, and Taubmann on Virgil, *Georgics* III.384. ORELLI.

“And are they honored by this?” See on Book I, ch. 41. ORELLI.

“You present yourselves as pure, washed, and perfectly undefiled from every stain.” This includes bodily stain. “Pure” and “undefiled” are joined together and often employed of one and the same thing: what is called “undefiled” is elsewhere called “pure,” *καὶ ἐξ ἀντιστρέφοντος* (“and conversely”). Hence “pure, undefiled, and washed.” For this reason the Greeks also call those “washed” (*λελουμένοι*) for the sake of sacred rites “holy” (*ἁγνοί*). Thus, just as the Latins combine “undefiled” and “pure,” the Greeks combine *ἁγνούς, καθαρούς* (“holy, pure”). And these are likewise the washed, *λελουμένοι*, etc. HERALDUS.—In these words Arnobius alludes to the custom of the ancients, who washed themselves before approaching temples and making vows. There is a notable passage on this subject in Justin Martyr, *Apology* II: *Τὸ λουτρὸν δὴ τοῦτο* [Col. 1236D] *ἀκούσαντες οἱ δαίμονες διὰ τοῦ προφήτου κεκηρυγμένον, ἐνήργησαν καὶ ῥαντίζειν ἑαυτοὺς τοὺς εἰς τὰ ἱερὰ αὐτῶν ἐπιβαίνοντας, καὶ προσιέναι αὐτοῖς μέλλοντας, λοιβὰς καὶ κνίσας ἀποτελοῦντες. Τέλεον δὲ καὶ λούεσθαι ἀπιόντας, πρὶν ἐλθεῖν ἐπὶ τὰ ἱερὰ, ἔνθεν ἵδρυνται, ἐνεργοῦσι* (“When the demons heard that this washing had been proclaimed through the prophet, they contrived that those entering their temples and intending to approach them while making libations and burnt offerings should sprinkle themselves; and they even cause them to wash themselves completely before departing to the temples where they are established”). Likewise in Lactantius, Book V, ch. 20: “But those wretched people do not even understand from their own crimes how evil the thing they worship is, since they come to pray defiled by every shameful deed; and they suppose that they have sacrificed piously if only they have washed, as though any rivers could wash away lusts enclosed within the breast, or any seas purify them.” And so throughout. MEURSIUS, p. 207 f. Compare Brissonius, *On Formulae*, Book I, pp. 6–7. ELMENHORST.

“More defiled, more ill-omened, filthier.” Meursius conjectures: “more defiled, more fetid, filthier.” But Heraldus correctly explains *infelicius* as “of worse omen.” ORELLI.

“Than if their own nature has made them such.” Thus the editors have printed the passage following the emendation of Fulvius Ursinus. The first edition has: “than if the nature of their perception has made them such.” If this reading derives from the manuscript, I would be reluctant to eliminate it rashly—“their perception,” that is, the gods’ perception. ORELLI.

“Why do you not sacrifice mules, elephants, and asses to them as well?” Yet the Romans did sacrifice mules at the Consualia, rites sacred to the god Consus. See Plutarch, *Problems* XLVIII, with Boxhorn’s note. Asses were sacrificed to Priapus, according to Ovid, *Fasti*, Book I, line 391. Elephants, too, were sometimes sacrificed. See Juvenal, Satire XII, line 111, and Johannes Saubert, *On Sacrifices*, ch. 23, p. 513 ff. ORELLI.

“Why not dogs, bears, foxes, and camels as well?” “It is certain that a dog was sacrificed to Hecate on Samothrace, in Greek rites of expiation, at Rome during the Lupercalia in February—which received its name from *februare*, that is, ‘to purify’—to Genita Mana, the goddess presiding over generation, and finally in purificatory rites. This has been demonstrated from Lycophron, Plutarch, [Col. 1237C] Pliny, Livy, and others by Bochart, Book II of the *Hierozoicon*, ch. 56, and Reinesius, *Various Readings*, Book I, ch. 15. To these may be added the Suda under the entries *Ζηρυνθία* (‘Zerynthia’), *Ἀλλ’ εἴ τις* (‘But if anyone’), *Σαμοθράκη* (‘Samothrace’), and *Ἱππαρικόν* (‘Equestrian’), as well as Ovid, *Fasti*, Book I, line 389:

> I have seen the Sapaeans offer the entrails of dogs to Trivia,  
> And all who dwell beside your snows, Haemus.

“But since those rites relate not so much to the heavenly gods as to the gods below, Arnobius may be considered to have taught the truth, especially because Plutarch writes in the *Roman Questions* that the ancients thought this animal wholly incapable of purification and that it was therefore sacrificed to *Ὀλυμπίων οὐδενὶ θεῶν* (‘none of the Olympian gods’). Certainly we shall find that a dog was very rarely, if ever, sacrificed among the Greeks and Romans to the twelve greater gods.” These and many other observations are made by Gisbert Cuper, who discusses this matter at length in *Harpocrates*, p. 67 ff. Gyraldus, *Syntagma* XVII, p. 493, teaches that the Arabs sacrificed fat and well-fed camels upon the altar of the Unknown God. ORELLI.

[Col. 1237D] “And hyenas” (*belbas*). Thus I have printed the word with the Leiden editor. Others read “and wild beasts” (*belluas*), which when used absolutely is applied properly and *κατ’ ἐξοχήν* (“preeminently”) to elephants. See Graevius on Florus, Book II, ch. 6, p. 348, Duker’s edition. Yet this is inappropriate here, since elephants have just been mentioned. We should therefore write *belbas* or *belvas* with a single *l*. The glosses have: *ὕαινα, ζῶον bellua* (“hyena, an animal: *bellua*”). Write *belva* or *belba*. Both forms, *belbus* and *belba*, are used, just as *merulus* and *merula*, *luscinius* and *luscinia*, *simius* and *simia*, *ferus* and *fera*. Julius Capitolinus, *Gordian*, ch. 33: “Under Gordian there were at Rome thirty-two elephants, of which he himself had sent twelve and Alexander ten; ten elks, ten tigers, sixty tame lions, thirty tame leopards, ten *belbi*—that is, hyenas—etc.” See Salmasius there, who discusses this word at length in *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. II, p. 133. Clement of Rome, *Recognitions*, Book VIII, p. 124, calls them *benuae*: “But lest, as human beings suppose, these things should appear to occur through some order of nature and not by the Creator’s dispensation, he commanded a few creatures, as an indication and proof of his providence, to preserve their kind upon earth with the order changed: for example, the raven was to conceive through its mouth and the weasel to give birth through its ear; certain birds, such as hens, were sometimes to lay eggs conceived from wind or dust; and some other animals were alternately to change the male into the female and alter their sex every year, as hares and hyenas, which they call *benuae*.” Elmenhorst cited this passage. From *belbus* or *belba*, *belva*, seem to have flowed the words in more recent languages signifying a wolf, for example Anglo-Saxon *hwelp, hwylp*, Frankish *welf*, English *whelp*, Swedish *hwalp*, German *Wolf*. See Wachter, *German Glossary*, s.v. *Wolf*. On the variant spelling *belba, benua*, compare the distinguished Schneider on Aristotle, *History of Animals*, Book VIII, ch. 7, vol. II, p. 605. ORELLI.

“And lions.” Julius Capitolinus, in the *Life of Maximinus*, attests that such animals were sacrificed by Maximinus. See Saubert, *On Sacrifices*, XXIII, p. 515. We have no certain knowledge, however, of bears and foxes being sacrificed. ORELLI.

“Merlins, buzzards.” See above on Book II, ch. 59. The buzzard was sacred to Diana, but it is uncertain whether it was ever sacrificed. ORELLI.

“Solifugae.” See on Book II, ch. 23. ORELLI.

“Thistles.” That is, cultivated thistles, artichokes. See on Book II, ch. 23. ORELLI.

“Roots.” The radish is called this *κατ’ ἐξοχήν* (“preeminently”). RETTIG. See Schneider, *Lexicon of Agriculture*. ORELLI.

“Basil.” A herb with a sharp scent, which the Greeks also called *βασίλειον* (“royal herb”). See Casaubon on Persius, Satire IV.22; Gesner and Schneider on Varro, *On Agriculture*, Book I, ch. 31, and in the *Agricultural Lexicon*, s.v. ORELLI.

“Cut leek.” That is, a leek cut for culinary use (*Schnittlattich*). Juvenal, Satire XIV.133:

> And to lock away the counted stalks of cut leek.

Consult Pliny, *Natural History*, Book XIX, ch. 6, and Columella, [Col. 1238D] *On Agriculture*, Book I, ch. 3, and you will understand how the cut leek differs from the headed leek. NOURRY, p. 561.

“The same gods.” Thus Gelenius, entirely correctly. The Roman edition has “the same god.” ORELLI.

“And to sprinkle cow-oregano over all these things.” *Cunila bubula* means wild oregano; it is called *bubula* because it kept oxen free from mange. See Bodaeus à Stapel on Theophrastus, *History of Plants*, Book VI, ch. 2, p. 564; the distinguished Schneider on Columella, Book VI, ch. 31, p. 355, and in the *Agricultural Lexicon*; Ast on Theophrastus, *Characters* 10, p. 115; and above all Salmasius on Solinus, ch. 56, p. 900 f., who discusses this plant at length. Our people call it *Wohlgemuth*. ORELLI.]

## XVI

What are you saying, you people? Is that stench, then, which rises and exhales from burning hides, from bones, from bristles, from the woolly fleeces of lambs, and from the feathers of hens—is this a gift and honor to a god? And are those whose temples you intend to enter honored by this, though you present yourselves as pure, washed, and perfectly undefiled from every stain?

And what could be more defiled, more ill-omened, or filthier for them [Col. 1236B]—if their own nature has made their senses such that they hold such savage things among the objects of their love and take delight in stenches which neither the sacrificers themselves can bear nor well-bred nostrils, when they are drawn in through the breath, endure? [Col. 1237A]

But if you think that the minds of the heavenly beings are honored and affected by the blood of living creatures, why do you not sacrifice mules, elephants, and asses to them as well? Why not dogs, bears, foxes, camels, hyenas, and lions? And since you also include birds among the kinds of animals, why not vultures, eagles, storks, merlins, buzzards, ravens, hawks, and owls—and, along with them, salamanders, water snakes, vipers, and solifugae? Surely these too contain blood and are animated in the same manner by a vital spirit. What greater workmanship is there in the former, or less skill in the latter, that these should not increase, while those enhance, the dignity of the heavenly beings?

“Because,” he says, “it is right to honor the heavenly beings with those things by which we ourselves are nourished, sustained, and kept alive, and which in the kindness of their divine power they have deigned to grant us for our subsistence.”

But the same gods also granted you cumin, cress, turnips, bulbs, parsley, thistles, radishes, gourds, rue, mint, basil, pennyroyal, and cut leek, and commanded that these should form part of the foods you use. Why, then, do you refrain from offering these also upon your altars, sprinkling cow-oregano over all these things, and mixing in the pungency of onions?

[Note: [Col. 1238D]

### XVII.—“If chattering swallows.”

Virgil, *Georgics* IV.307:

> . . . . . . . . Before  
> The chattering swallow hangs her nest from the rafters.

The Greek proverb is *χελιδόνος λαλίστερος* (“more talkative than a swallow”). HERALDUS.

[Col. 1239B] “And undertook to perform rites for you for the sake of honor.” The very acute Guilielmus, in *Plautine Questions* on *Curculio*, ch. V, in Gruter’s *Lampas*, vol. III, part II, p. 367, thus emended the extremely corrupt old reading: “And undertook rites for you; therefore they performed honors.” He says that Arnobius had here too written *honoreis* in the genitive case, which ignorant copyists took as accusative and therefore changed the other words to agree with it. Nothing is more customary than the formula “to perform rites for the sake of honor”; but “to undertake rites, to perform honors” is not even Latin. Cato, in his book *On Agriculture*, says to Janus: “For the sake of the same matter, be thou magnified with sacrificial wine”; and our author says below: “To give wine to the gods for the sake of honor.” STEWECHIUS.

“By natural apposition.” Fulvius Ursinus reads “by natural appetite.” ORELLI.

“They killed.” Thus the Leiden edition. Gelenius reads “they yielded.” ORELLI.

“When asses gave hay to your altars and offered straw.” This is the proper fodder of asses. Hence Philemon, in the excerpts of Athenaeus, says *ὄνος βαδίζεις εἰς ἄχυρα τραγημάτων* (“like an ass you make your way toward the straw of sweetmeats”) of a glutton who can no more be deterred by blows from delicacies than an ass from straw and pasture. For the Greeks had a proverb: *ὄνος εἰς ἀχυρῶνας ἀπέδρα* (“an ass has escaped into the straw-barns”). HERALDUS.

“And you would reckon being treated with dung among grievous insults.” The jurist in Digest 47.11.1, *On Extraordinary Crimes*: “An injury is committed contrary to good morals, as, for example, if someone has drenched another person with befouling dung.” Add Digest 9.2.27 §17, *On the Lex Aquilia*. Thus Florus says that the envoys of the Roman people were sprinkled with urine by the Tarentines in a vile insult too obscene to relate. This insult was afterward atoned for by enormous disasters. Strabo writes that the same insult was the cause of the Achaean War, in which the most noble and flourishing city of Corinth was destroyed. HERALDUS. Compare Valerius Maximus, Book II, ch. 2; Livy, Book XII; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, excerpts *On Embassies*, p. 21. ELMENHORST. On the verb *accipere*, see above on Book III, ch. 15, and C. Barth, *Adversaria*, Book XIX, ch. 15. ORELLI.

“Begin to stink” (*putescant*). Thus the manuscript, Sabaeus, and Salmasius. Gelenius and others read “begin to rot” (*putrescant*). But, as Stewechius correctly observes, *putesco* is the inchoative of *puteo*. See above on Book V, ch. 12. ORELLI.

“You will perceive.” Others read “you perceive.” ORELLI.

“To be increased” (*auctificari*). *Auctificare*, or—as Nonius has it—*augificare*, is equivalent to *augere*, “to increase,” and is an ancient and obsolete verb. Ennius, *Andromeda*: “What is it? Is the uprising wasting away, or is it increasing its numbers?” And *auctificus* (“productive, increasing”) occurs in Lucretius II.571:

> Nor furthermore can the generative and productive  
> Motions of things preserve created beings forever.

NOURRY, p. 551.

“If the gods commanded you to take these into your care and turn them to the preservation of your health.” This is Salmasius’s excellent emendation and, as it seems to me, the only true one. The old reading is: “If the gods commanded you to turn this care, yours, to the preservation of health”; but the word “care” has nothing in the preceding text to which “this” can refer. By contrast, “these” is excellent—that is, those spoiled entrails. Fulvius Ursinus corrects it to: “If the gods commanded us to turn the cultivation of you into pleasure”—more audaciously than truthfully. ORELLI.

“You honor them with the odors and juices.” Meursius, p. 208, suspects that the reading should be: “you honor them with odors and smoke,” since Arnobius had previously said, “or pursues the smoke from the burning altars.” But nothing should be changed. “Juices” are the vapors from roasting meat. ORELLI.

“Those things which nourish you.” Thus Meursius and the rest who followed him. Earlier editions printed “and these nourish you,” which Oberthür too retained, wrongly. ORELLI.

[Col. 1240D] “And repeatedly fawn upon those who hold it out.” *Alludere* means to coax, to win over with blandishments, *προσπαίζειν* (“to play up to”); of dogs it is Homer’s *σαίνειν* (“to fawn”), *Odyssey* X.216 f.:

> Around their master the dogs . . . fawn,

which the scholia interpret as *κολακεύωσιν* (“they flatter”). In our language, *wedeln* (“to wag the tail”). Thus Lactantius, *Institutes*, Book III, ch. 10: “The supreme good of the human being therefore lies in religion alone. For the other faculties, even those believed to be peculiar to the human being, are also found in other animals. For since they distinguish and recognize their own voices among themselves by signs peculiar to them, they seem to converse. Some capacity for laughter also appears in them when, with ears caressed, mouths drawn back, and eyes relaxed in playfulness, they either fawn upon a human being or each upon its own mates or offspring.” See Bünemann there, pp. 319 and 1021. ORELLI.]

## XVII

Suppose, then—since some things must be imagined so that the matter can be perceived more clearly—that dogs and asses, wagtails together with them, chattering swallows, and pigs along with these, having acquired some degree of human understanding, thought and believed [Col. 1239A] that you were gods. Suppose that they undertook to perform sacred rites for you for the sake of honor, not from other materials and other kinds of things, but from those by which they are customarily nourished and sustained through natural apposition. We ask you to tell us whether you would judge this to be honor or rather the greatest possible insult: when swallows killed flies for you and wagtails slaughtered and consecrated ants; when asses gave hay to your altars and offered straw; when dogs placed bones upon them and burned an outpouring of human excrement; and when, finally, piglets poured out before you mud taken from bristling wallows and filthy pools.

Would you therefore not become inflamed because your dignities had been spat upon, and would you not reckon being treated with dung among grievous insults? Yet you honor your gods with the bodies of bulls and the slaughter of other living creatures. [Col. 1239B] And how does this differ from the other, when these things themselves, though not yet dung, will nevertheless soon become dung and, after the intervention of only a brief span of time, begin to stink?

Finally, cease placing fire beneath your altars: then you will certainly perceive those sacred entrails of bulls, by which you increase the honor of the gods, boiling with worms and seething, corrupting and befouling the condition of the atmosphere, and afflicting neighboring regions with their diseased odors. If the gods commanded you to take these things [Col. 1240A] into your care and turn them to the preservation of your health—to prepare lunches or dinners from them according to solemn custom—you would flee far away; and after cursing that kind of smell, you would seek pardon from the heavenly beings and swear that you would never again perform such rites for them.

Is this, then, not to mock, not to confess, not to disclose that you do not know what a god is, nor to what power the force of this name ought to be subordinated and its designation applied? You increase the gods with novel foods and honor them with odors and juices; and because the things which nourish you are pleasant and agreeable to you, you also believe that the gods rush eagerly toward the enjoyment of them, lay aside their savagery over a bone in the manner of barking dogs, and repeatedly fawn upon those who hold it out?

[Note: [Col. 1240D]

### XVIII.—“So that one god is honored with bulls.”

“God” is used here collectively of gods and goddesses. ORELLI.

“This one with virgin heifers.” Thus Fulvius Ursinus. The first edition reads “with bovine animals.” Stewechius thinks that “with calves” should be written, since Arnobius says below in ch. 22: “For the virgin Minerva a virgin calf is slain, never exercised or touched by any goads or any labor.” ORELLI.

“With pregnant sows.” This excellent emendation, the only true reading, is owed to Fulvius Ursinus and Scriverius in Meursius. *Incientes scrophae* are sows about to give birth. Below, ch. 22: “For Mother Earth, they say, a pregnant and gravid sow is sacrificed.” Festus, under *gravida*: “*Inciens* means near to giving birth, because its offspring has been set in motion.” Compare the distinguished Schneider on Varro, *On Agriculture*, Book II, ch. 2, p. 408, and the *Agricultural Lexicon*, s.v. The first edition has “with enormous sows.” ORELLI.

“That one with dark victims.” Thus the manuscript, correctly. Similarly, a little later in ch. 20: “Why do you not take care that all the other things which it is customary to bring to their sacrifices should be black and smoke-darkened, and so colored gloomily?” Others read: “that one with black victims.” MEURSIUS.

“Or is the blood of one kind less agreeable and pleasant to one god than to another?” I have followed this entirely correct emendation by Gelenius. Others read: “Or is the blood of one animal more agreeable and pleasant to another?” In conjunction with the following words, “while the blood of another pours pleasure into another,” this would produce a mere tautology. Fulvius Ursinus added “animal,” which was most correctly absent from the manuscript. ORELLI.

“Less agreeable.” The particles “more” and “less” are very often redundant in these writers. Thus Book I, ch. 19: “a more stronger argument”; and Book IV: “more ignominious.” Zeno of Verona, Sermon I, *On Psalm 130*: “Our God, brothers, is humble of heart; and that ineffable force of wisdom and power of might lies within the humanity he assumed, more admirable because he is so great and of such a kind.” And in his sermon *On Chastity*: “If, therefore, his glory often exults among the nations, how much more ought it to be more glorious among the Christian people?” But examples of this pleonasm are not uncommon among the ancients. Plautus, *Stichus*, Act V, scene IV, line 21: “No indeed, this one is more sweeter”; and frequently elsewhere. Among the Greeks *μᾶλλον* (“more”) is very often *πλεονάζει* (“redundant”) in this way, as in *μᾶλλον ὀλβιώτερος* (“more happier”) in Aristophanes and similar expressions. HERALDUS.—Vechner gives more examples in the *Hellenolexicon*, p. 166 f. Similarly “less” is redundant in Florus, Book IV, ch. 2 §47: “Nor was the outcome of this war less more admirable.” See Duker there, Freinsheim in the index, and Mercier on Nonius Marcellus, p. 88. ORELLI.

“From fear of some observance or religious scruple, that one abstains from goat’s flesh.” Spartianus, *Didius Julianus*: “For Julianus is said to have been so frugal that he divided a suckling pig over three days and a hare over three days if anyone happened to send him one; but often, although there was no religious scruple, he was content with vegetables and legumes and dined without meat.” Thus *religio* is used here in its proper sense. We discussed “observance” at Book I, ch. 43. HERALDUS.]

## XVIII

And since our discussion of sacrificial victims is now before us, what cause, what rationale is there that—although the immortal gods (for let them exist, even with our permission, whoever they are believed to be) are of one mind, or ought to be of one nature, one kind, and one quality—not all are propitiated by every kind of victim, but particular gods by particular victims according to the laws of sacred rites [Col. 1240B] [Note: [Col. 1239B] The manuscript reads “from the laws.”]?

For what cause is there, I ask again, that one god should be honored with bulls, another with kids or sheep; this one with suckling piglets, another with unshorn lambs; this one with virgin heifers, that one with horned goats; this one with barren cows, but that one with pregnant sows; this one with white victims, that one with dark; one with living creatures of the female sex, another with males? [Col. 1241A]

For if victims are slaughtered for the gods for the sake of honor and reverence, what difference does it make, or what does it matter, from the head of what animal this debt is discharged and whose anger and displeasure are laid to rest? Or is the blood of one kind less agreeable and pleasant to one god than to another, while the blood of another pours pleasure and delight into another? Or—as commonly happens—does that one abstain from goat’s flesh through fear of some observance or religious scruple, while another abhors contact with pork? Are the entrails of sheep noisome to this one, while that one avoids the toughness of beef so as not to weary his feeble stomach, and chooses the tenderness of suckling animals so that he may digest it more easily?

[Note: [Col. 1242B]

### XIX.—“If reason proves victorious.”

Thus the manuscript. Sabaeus reads “has commanded”; Fulvius Ursinus, “has conclusively proved.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1242C] “To be approved, to be found.” Fulvius Ursinus prefers “to be adopted” instead of “to be found.” ORELLI.

“What principle is there in colors, such that white victims should rightly be sacrificed to these gods, but dark and utterly black ones to those?” Arnobius plainly distinguishes black, dark, white, and bright-white victims. Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* III.118: “The principle governing sacrificial victims follows the character of the divine beings. For either creatures harmful to their gifts are sacrificed to them, such as the pig to Ceres because it harms the crops, or the he-goat to Liber because it injures the vines; or victims are chosen by resemblance, so that black animals are sacrificed to the gods below and white ones to those above; likewise dark victims to stormy weather, bright-white ones to serenity.” C. Barth, therefore, on Statius, *Thebaid* IV.445, vol. II, p. 1086, suspects that the text should read: “that white victims should be sacrificed to these gods, dark ones to those, and black ones to others.” Yet I would not venture to alter the received reading, since Arnobius commonly accumulates expressions with the same meaning, and a little later, in the next chapter, we read: “that grim victims of the blackest color should be brought to them.” ORELLI.

“And to those powerful in the propitiousness of omens.” Learned men—Meursius, Grotius, and Canter—long ago demonstrated [Col. 1242D] that this should be written instead of “and of human beings.” HERALDUS.—For favorable and prosperous omens—that is, right-hand omens—were taken from the gods above; they believed that the gods below and the shades presided over unfavorable and left-hand events. Festus teaches us further how an omen differs from an augury: “An *omen* is as it were an *oremen*, because it occurs by speech (*ore*); an augury is what occurs through birds or in some other manner.” On dark victims, consult Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, Book III, ch. 4, and Festus under the word *furvum*. STEWECHIUS.

“Unpropitious gods.” See above on Book IV, ch. 5. Compare Aulus Gellius, Book V, ch. 12. ORELLI.

“A dusky color” (*furvus*). Valerius Maximus, Book II, ch. 4 §5: “Black victims were anciently called *furvae*.” It is a standing epithet of things belonging to the underworld. See Broukhusius on Propertius, Book IV, Elegy I.5, p. 477, and Mitscherlich on Horace, *Odes* II.13.17. ORELLI.

“That there are no kingdoms beneath the earth and no Plutonian dwellings.” Juvenal, Satire II.149:

> That there are shades and kingdoms beneath the earth  
> Not even boys believe, except those still too young to pay at the baths.

ELMENHORST.]

## XIX

But you are mistaken, he says, and have gone astray; for there is a hidden and deeper rationale, removed from the knowledge of the common people, for sacrificing female victims to female gods and males to male gods. [Col. 1241B]

I do not inquire, I do not demand to know what the rites prescribe or what their laws contain. But if reason proves victorious and truth prevails—that there is no distinction of sexes among the gods and that they are not differentiated by any sex [Col. 1242A]—must not all these rationales necessarily be dissolved and be approved and found to rest upon the most foolish suppositions?

I shall not invoke the opinions of wise men, who cannot restrain their laughter when they hear distinctions of sex attributed to the immortal gods. I ask each person among humankind whether he himself inwardly believes and persuades himself that the race of gods is divided, that some are males and others females, and that they have been formed with a suitable arrangement of organs for generating offspring.

But if the laws of sacrifice prescribe that corresponding sexes be sacrificed to each sex—that is, females to female gods and male victims to male gods [Note: [Col. 1241B] Thus Fulvius and Sabaeus. The manuscript reads “describe.”]—what principle is there in colors, such that white victims should rightly be sacrificed to these gods, but dark and utterly black ones to those?

“Because,” he says, “a cheerful color, fortunate in the joyousness of its whiteness, is acceptable to the gods above and to those powerful in the propitiousness of omens. [Col. 1242B] But a dusky color, dyed with gloomy pigments, is more pleasing to unpropitious gods who inhabit the regions below.”

But if reason again prevails—that the name of the underworld is utterly empty and void, and that there are no kingdoms beneath the earth and no Plutonian dwellings—then the opinion you hold concerning black cattle and the gods beneath the earth must likewise prove false. [Col. 1243A] And if there is no underworld, there must likewise be no gods of the shades. For how can there be any inhabitants of places that do not exist?

[Note: [Col. 1243C]

### XX.—“And victims of the blackest color should be brought near.”

Thus Meursius and the others who followed him. Earlier editions printed “colors.” ORELLI.

“What then? Do you not see...?” Stewechius punctuates: “What? Do you therefore not see...?” ORELLI.

“To settle upon pastures.” *Pastus* is used here for the pastures themselves, as in Tacitus, *Annals*, Book IV, ch. 25: “With the Numidians’ horses hampered or wandering through different pastures”; and Solinus, ch. 29: “If they direct their faces straight toward the pastures.” OUDENDORP, on Apuleius, Book V, p. 353.

“And so colored gloomily.” Salmasius made this excellent emendation. Previously: “both grim and colored.” ORELLI.

“So that those things may be corpse-yellow, pour in soot together with the ashes.” Meursius changes “corpse-yellow” (*lurida*) to “dusky” (*furva*), very badly. For corpse-yellow is properly the color of decaying corpses and is most aptly opposed to the purple-red blood of healthy bodies. ORELLI.

“But if you have no religious scruple about bringing certain white things.” Thus the manuscript. Those who wish to read “bringing in”—Fulvius Ursinus and Stewechius—are mistaken. The best authors used the simple verb “to bring” in this connection. Thus “to bring incense” in Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, Book I, letter V:

> And I remember bringing with worthy hand to the true gods  
> Incense owed to the Caesars, together with a spouse worthy of Caesar.

And Book II, letter IX:

> Why should I bring Neptune ineffectual incense?

Book III, elegy I:

> Bring incense and pure wine to the mighty gods.

Book IV, elegy VIII:

> Finally, I shall bring the customary incense to the devouring flames.

Likewise “to bring prayers.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII.60:

> Duly bring prayers to Juno, and overcome her anger  
> And threats with suppliant vows.

[Col. 1244C] Servius there: “Thus ‘bring prayers,’ in the same manner as we speak of sacred offerings being brought.” HERALDUS.]

XX. But let us grant, as you wish, both that there is an underworld and that there are spirits of the dead, and that in those regions dwell certain gods—I know not who—less favorable to human beings and set over the more sorrowful circumstances of life. Yet what cause, what reason is there that victims of a repulsive appearance and the blackest color should be brought before them? Because black things suit black beings, and gloomy things are pleasing to those like themselves. What, then? Do you not see that, along with you, we too are speaking foolishly and in the same fashion, since the flesh, bones, teeth, fat, entrails together with the brains, and the soft marrow [Col. 1243B] within the bones of the victims are white? But their fleeces are black, and black too are the animals’ bristles. Therefore sacrifice to the gods only the wool and the little hairs plucked from the victims; leave the most unfortunate creatures, stripped and shorn though they are, to draw the breath of heaven [Note: [Col. 1243C] *Heaven* (*coelo*), Meursius.] and, wholly innocent, to lie upon their pastures.

But if you suppose that things which are black and dark-hued are pleasing to the gods below, why do you not arrange that all the other things which it is customary to introduce into their sacrifices should be black, smoke-stained, and foully colored? Dye the incense, if incense is offered; dye the salted grain and every kind of libation. Pour soot mixed with [Col. 1243C] ashes into milk, oil, and blood, so that the blood may present a purple color and the others may become corpse-pale. But if you feel no religious scruple about bringing certain white things [Col. 1244A] that retain their own brightness, you yourselves dissolve your religious principles and rationales, since in the performance of your rites you preserve no single consistent and enduring rule.

[Note: [Col. 1244C]

XXI.—**“Which it is customary to sacrifice to Father Liber, to Mercury.”** Thus the Leiden edition, from the manuscript. Gelenius’ correction, *and to Mercury* (*Mercurioque*), is therefore unnecessary; for we have already observed several times that our Arnobius is fond of omitting the conjunction. The sacrifice of goats to Liber is very well known. But I do not recall reading elsewhere that they were also consecrated especially (*κατ’ ἐξοχήν*, “preeminently”) to Mercury. ORELLI.

**Unxia.** See above, on Book III, chapter 25. ORELLI.

**That due honorarium.** Book IV: “If ever you perform sacred rites with the ceremonies that are due.” ELMENHORST.

**To confuse the duties of the rites and their expiatory administration.** In my judgment *and their expiatory administrations* (*procurationumque*) would be more correct. For the *procuratio*, that is, the expiation, is not always and everywhere the same, nor directed toward only one end. The words of a Roman senatorial decree are found in Aulus Gellius: “The consul was to make expiation to Jupiter and Mars with full-grown victims.” Book IV of the *Attic Nights*, chapter 6, where more may be seen. Similarly Arnobius repeatedly uses *procuratio* of a thunderbolt to mean its expiation in Book V alone, and there sets forth the rite by which it was expiated. STEWECHIUS.—Meursius also agrees with Stewechius. ORELLI.

**“And that prescribed acts of supplication are performed.”** Thus the Leiden edition, correctly, from the manuscript; for Arnobius uses not only particles but also the auxiliary verb redundantly. Others read: “And prescribed acts of supplication” (*Certa et supplicamenta*). Meursius: “And that prescribed acts of supplication are performed” (*certaque supplicamenta praestari*). ORELLI.

**“Or something fallen from heaven.”** That is, something entirely certain and about which no one can any longer be in doubt. Book I: “For no god has fallen from heaven or devised your affairs with his own hands.” Lactantius, Book III, chapter 19: “For no one has descended from heaven to pronounce judgment upon the opinions of individuals.” ELMENHORST.

[Col. 1245C] **Settlement.** *Transactio* is a forensic term for an agreement by which one withdraws from litigation already begun or about to be begun after something has been given, retained, or promised: *ein gütlicher Vergleich*, “an amicable settlement.” See Brissonius, *On the Meaning of Words*, under this word, and Heineccius, *Roman Antiquities on the Institutes*, Book VI, title VI, vol. II, p. 217 following. ORELLI.

**“It was agreed by compact that,” etc.** Thus the Leiden edition. Others punctuate: “by compact? Was it agreed that,” etc. ORELLI.

**“That this one should cease to exercise rights over another’s blood.”** Thus Gelenius, with Heraldus approving in *Curis*, II. Others read *should desire* (*desideret*). ORELLI.]

XXI. But it is also appropriate at this point to learn [Note: [Col. 1244C] The manuscript has “to learn” (*discere*).] the following from you. If a goat is slaughtered for Jupiter, though it is customary to sacrifice it to Father Liber, to Mercury; or if a sterile cow is slaughtered for Unxia, though you assign it to Proserpina—by what rite and observance is this prescribed?—what crime will there be in this, what evil or guilt will have been incurred, since it makes no difference, as regards the act of homage, from the head of which animal that due honorarium is discharged?

“It is not lawful,” someone says, “for these things to be confused, nor is it a small offense to confuse the duties of the rites and their expiatory administration.”

Please explain the cause.

“Because it is lawful to consecrate victims of a specified kind to specified divine powers, [Col. 1244B] and prescribed acts of supplication are to be performed.”

And once again, what is the cause that it should be lawful to consecrate victims of a specified kind to specified divine powers and to perform prescribed acts of supplication? For this law itself must have its own cause and must arise and be derived from definite reasons.

Are you going to cite antiquity and custom? You are proclaiming to me decrees made by human beings and inventions of a blind animal. But when I ask that the cause be produced for me, I desire to hear either something fallen from heaven or—what the matter more urgently demands—what affinity Jupiter has with a bull’s blood, such that it ought to be sacrificed to him but not to Mercury or Liber. Or what is there in the nature of a goat that makes it in turn suitable for these gods but unfitting for sacrifices to Jupiter?

Was a division of animals made among the gods? Was it agreed by the compact of some settlement that one god should abstain from another’s victim, [Col. 1244C] and that this one should cease to exercise rights over another’s blood? Or, like jealous little boys, are they unwilling to share in tasting one another’s livestock? Or is it as report says is the highly diverse custom among nations: the very things considered edible among some are rejected from the diets of others? [Col. 1245A]

[Note: [Col. 1245D]

XXII.—**“The rationale of sacrifices is itself empty.”** The manuscript codex has *the giving* (*datio*), which Stewechius approves. ORELLI.

**“For how can it be possible?”** Thus the manuscript. Others: “can it be” (*pote est*). MEURSIUS.

**“To Mother Earth, they say, a pregnant and fecund sow is sacrificed.”** Thus Salmasius and Vossius, *Institutes of Oratory*, Book V, chapter 2, section 4. Others omit *and*. The manuscript: “as fecund” (*ut foeta*). Meursius in the Appendix: “as to the fecund” (*ut foetae*). Antonius Augustinus, on Festus under *plena sue*, suspects that one should read: “A pregnant sow and a *forda*, namely a cow, are sacrificed.” Ovid, *Fasti* IV.631:

> A *forda* is a cow carrying young, and she is called fecund from carrying.

Festus, Book I, moreover explains the reason why a sow was sacrificed to Earth: “A pregnant sow was sacrificed to Mother Earth because that kind of livestock, when seed is sown, is sufficiently hostile to it, since it ruins the seed by digging with its snout.” For *pregnant* (*inciens*), which is owed to Fulvius Ursinus, the manuscript, Sabaeus, and Gelenius have *large* (*ingens*), which Heraldus defends from a passage of Virgil, *Eclogues* I.50:

> Unaccustomed pastures will not trouble the heavy mothers.

[Col. 1246C] There Servius explains *foetas* as both pregnant animals and those delivered of offspring, but incorrectly. See above on chapter 18. ORELLI.

**Pregnant and fecund.** Antonius Augustinus: “pregnant and *fordae*.” See the preceding note. ORELLI.

**“Which we all seek.”** Thus the Leiden edition, from the manuscript. Others: “because we all seek” (*quoniam cuncti expetimus*). ORELLI.

**“Similarly she must receive pregnant sows.”** See above on Book III, chapter 15. ORELLI.

**“Of untouched virginity.”** That is, of unimpaired virginity. In Euripides untouched virgins are *ἄζυγες κοῦραι*, “unwed maidens.” ELMENHORST.—Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “And of untouched virginity.” ORELLI.]

XXII. Therefore, if these things are empty and possess no rational firmness, the rationale of sacrifices is itself empty. For how can what follows possess an adequate cause when the very first principle from which the second derives is found to be utterly empty and void, established upon no solidity?

“To Mother Earth,” they say, “a pregnant and fecund sow is sacrificed; but to the virgin Minerva a virgin heifer is slaughtered, one never [Col. 1245B] trained by any goads or by the exertion of any labor.”

Yet we think that neither should a virgin have been slaughtered for a virgin, lest virginity be violated in the animal—the very quality in which the goddess is preeminent—nor should pregnant and fecund animals have been slaughtered to Earth in honor of that fertility which we all seek and desire always to continue with an inextinguishable virginity.

For if, because the Tritonian is a virgin, it is therefore fitting that virgin victims be sacrificed to her, and because Earth is a mother, she must similarly receive pregnant sows, then, because Apollo is musical, musicians ought to be slaughtered to him; physicians to Aesculapius, because he is a physician; craftsmen to Vulcan, because he is a craftsman; and the eloquent and most accomplished speakers to Mercury, because he is eloquent.

But if saying this is insane—or, to pronounce upon it moderately, brutish—it is far more demented to cut the throats of pregnant animals [Col. 1245C] for Earth because she is heavy with offspring, and of chaste and virgin victims for Minerva [Col. 1246A] because she is pure, of untouched virginity.

[Note: [Col. 1246D]

XXIII.—**“And whatever is naturally gentle and placid is far removed from the practice of harming.”** Canterus restored this from the manuscript codex. Others omit *from* (*ab*). ORELLI.

**“This one, contracted, may plant its sting.”** This is the entirely correct reading, which Gelenius rashly altered; for he wrote *touched* (*contactus*). Fulvius Ursinus, however, thinks that the word should be removed altogether. They are all egregiously mistaken. A scorpion, when contracted, certainly does plant its sting. Tertullian describes it vividly in the *Scorpiace*: “Accordingly, that jointed succession forming the scorpion, venomous with a fine vein within it, rises in an arched thrust and draws back the hooked point at its extremity after the manner of a siege engine. Hence they also call ‘scorpion’ the military engine that propels missiles by recoil.” HERALDUS.

**“And that coaxing may do no good.”** By such coaxing, of course, he made play with and caressed those wild beasts. The expression is taken from dogs. Above, chapter 18: “After the manner of barking dogs, to lay down morsels before their savagery and repeatedly play with them as they stretch them out.” Thus what he had previously called stroking and caressing with the hand he now denotes by the word *coaxing* (*allusio*). *Mulcere* means *πράως ἅπτεσθαι*, “to touch gently,” as Plutarch interprets it in the *Camillus*. From this comes *multare* also: namely, to soften someone with fists or cudgels, as the comic poets joke. Those who think one should write *mulcare* are therefore mistaken. For *multo* comes from the supine *mulsum*, just as *confuto* comes from *confusum*, and similarly in other cases. HERALDUS.

**“Since neither creature is driven to harm by the goads of anger.”** This is the old reading, which they altered in the other editions, printing *may be driven* (*exagitentur*). Certainly the particle *cum* has sometimes assumed this force. Lucretius VI.129:

> Nor is it strange, since the little bladder of breath, when full,  
> Often suddenly bursts and gives forth a sound in just this way.

Marcus Tullius, *For Quinctius*: “Since this is so, the property was not possessed in accordance with the edict.” Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter IX: “Since Saturn did not spare his own children, he assuredly persisted in not sparing those of others”—*Τῶν ἀλλοτρίων μηδὲν φειδόμενος διετέλει*, “he continued to spare none of those belonging to others.” It is a Hellenism. The same author, chapter XXII: [Col. 1247C] “Since, therefore, both sides concur in the confession that denies they are gods, recognize that they are a single kind,” etc. In all these passages *cum* means “since.” Nothing, therefore, should be altered in this passage of the same author, *Apology*, chapter II: “Since, therefore, in every respect you treat us differently”—*Ἡμᾶς ἄλλως διατίθεσθε*, “you dispose of us otherwise.” Nor, therefore, should the following passage of the same Tertullian, *On Patience*, chapter X, be emended: “I make no place for shame, since I gain more from its loss: since he himself in some fashion exhorts the man, saying, ‘Pay no regard to me.’” HERALDUS.

**“Driven by the goads of anger.”** Virgil, *Aeneid* XI.452:

> Their anger roused by no gentle goads.

And XI.728:

> He incites their anger with no gentle goads.

HERALDUS.

**“Thus it does no good to wish to earn the favor of evil gods through victims.”** Compare Lactantius, Book VI, chapter 19, at the end: “Let us obey this God and serve him with the greatest devotion; let every action, concern, and effort be devoted to earning his favor.” See there Bunemann, who discusses this verb at length, p. 743. ORELLI.

**“And toward those things for which they were made.”** *Πρὸς ἃ ἐγενήθησαν, πρὸς ἃ ἔφυσαν*, “toward those things for which they came into being, toward those things for which they were naturally constituted.” For it was for this reason that he said, “they act according to their nature.” It is therefore a Hellenism, and nothing should be changed. HERALDUS.—Canterus suspects that one should read: “toward those things for which they were made”; I myself much prefer this. For the construction “toward those things which they were made” in place of “toward those things for which they were made” is exceedingly harsh, and I do not recall finding another similar example in our author. ORELLI.]

XXIII. As for the claim which we hear you make—that some of the gods are good, but others evil and more prone to a lust for harming, and that the solemn rites of sacrifice are performed so that the former may benefit us while the latter may not harm us—we confess that we cannot understand by what rationale this is said [Note: [Col. 1245C] The manuscript has “that we cannot” (*nos non posse*). Correctly. Meursius.].

For it is both sacred, religious, and true to call the gods supremely benevolent and to hold that they possess gentle natures; but that they are evil and sinister is something that the ears should by no means admit, because that divine power is by nature far removed and separated from doing harm. Whatever, however, is capable of introducing the cause of calamity must first be examined to determine what it is and must, by the widest possible difference, be separated from the name of god.

And so, even if we grant your assertion that there are gods who favor fortunate and unfortunate circumstances, there is still no reason why you should entice some toward favorable actions, while soothing others with sacrifices and rewards so that they will not harm you. First, good gods cannot do evil even if they have been accorded no honor; for whatever is naturally gentle and placid is far removed from the practice and thought of harming. [Col. 1246B] An evil being, however, does not know how to restrain its savagery, though it be enticed by a thousand herds and a thousand altars. For bitterness cannot transform itself into sweetness, nor dryness into moisture, nor the heat of fire into cold; nor can what is contrary to any given thing assume and transform into its own nature that which is contrary to itself.

Thus, if you stroke a viper with your hand or caress a venomous scorpion, the former may attack you with its bite, the latter, contracted, may plant its sting; and that coaxing may do no good, [Col. 1246C] since neither creature is driven to harm [Col. 1247A] by the goads of anger but by a certain property of its nature. In the same way it does no good to wish to earn the favor of evil gods through victims, since whether you have done this or, on the contrary, have not done it, they act according to their nature and are led toward those things for which they were made by inborn laws and a certain necessity.

What of the fact that, on this reasoning, both classes of gods cease to exist within their own powers and to remain within their own qualities? For if divine worship is performed so that the good gods may benefit us, while others are supplicated by the same means so that they may not harm us, it follows that we must understand that the favorable gods will provide no benefit if they receive no gifts, while the evil gods, if they receive gifts, will abandon their intention of doing harm and thereby become good. The matter is thus brought to the point that neither are the former favorable nor the latter sinister—or, what cannot happen, that both classes are themselves favorable and both again sinister. [Col. 1248A]

[Note: [Col. 1247D]

XXIV.—**“But if it appears magnificent and splendid.”** That is, *μεγαλοπρεπὲς καὶ μεγαλόψυχον*, “grandly magnificent and high-minded.” Sallust, *The Conspiracy of Catiline*: “Magnificent in offerings to the gods, frugal at home.” They believed that their magnificence ought to shine forth especially in this honor paid to the gods. Aristotle, Book VI of the *Nicomachean Ethics*: *Καὶ ἔστιν ἀρετὴ ἔργου, μεγαλοπρέπεια ἐν μεγέθει· ἔστι δὲ τῶν δαπανημάτων, οἷα λέγομεν τὰ τίμια, οἷον τὰ περὶ τοὺς θεοὺς ἀναθήματα, καὶ κατασκευαὶ καὶ θυσίαι*—“Magnificence is an excellence of a work on a grand scale; and it concerns those expenditures which we call honorable, such as dedications, constructions, and sacrifices relating to the gods.” HERALDUS.

**“If the victims’ entrails are burned whole and undiminished.”** [Col. 1248B] Undiminished, whole entrails are entire entrails from which nothing has been removed—*ὁλόκαυστα*, “whole burnt offerings”—as opposed to *proficiae*, *θυμάτων ἀπαρχαί*, “first portions of sacrificial victims.” See Taubmann on Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, p. 502; Salmasius on Solinus, p. 90; and P. Colvius on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, Book X, p. 707, Oudendorp’s edition. *Viscera*, “entrails” or “flesh,” properly means whatever lies between the bones and skin, as is very well known. ORELLI.

**“What is intended by all these remaining things, which accord with the disciplines of the Magi?”** “These remaining things” means the *proficiae* and the various kinds of sausages and cakes that were customarily offered to the gods and burned upon the altar. Arnobius says that they accord with the disciplines of the Magi, who did not burn for the gods the entire, undiminished flesh of bulls, but only a portion of the omenta and the *proficiae*. Learned men, however—Heraldus among them—take Arnobius’ words as though those names of the *proficiae* enumerated below were obscure and barbarous, like the terms used by the Magi. Nothing could be more contrary to Arnobius’ meaning. Catullus, Poem XC, on the discipline of the Magi:

> So that, having received the chant, the son may worship the gods,  
> Melting the rich omentum in the flame.

“If it is splendid,” says Arnobius, “and magnificent to sacrifice bulls to the gods and burn their entire flesh for them, what is intended by all these remaining things, which accord with the disciplines of the Magi—namely, these small portions of the entrails and flesh which you offer separately to the gods and place upon the altar?” SALMASIUS, on Solinus, p. 90.

**Apexanes.** Salmasius so printed. The manuscript codex has *apexabones*. Others: *apexabo*. But just as *longanones*—see Elmenhorst’s note immediately below—so too *apexabones*, *apexaones*, and *apexanes* derive from *apexabo*. Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book IV, p. 32, Bipontine edition: “The *hila* are named from *hilum*, that is, the smallest thing.… Because something projects at the top of this sausage, it was called *apexabo* from the *apex* upon a head.” ORELLI.

**Hirciae.** Thus the Leiden edition from the manuscript. Earlier editions printed *isicia*, on which see above at Book II, chapter 42. Meursius [Col. 1248D] in the Appendix and Stewechius correct it to *hircei* or *ircei*, a kind of sausage used in sacrifices, according to Festus. But Salmasius, on Solinus, p. 90, defends *hirciae*, explaining it by Arnobius’ own words immediately following: “a kind of sausage stuffed with goat’s blood.” Compare N. Heinsius, *Adversaria*, Book IV, chapter 9, p. 621. ORELLI.

**Silicernia.** The glosses: “*silicernium*—*περίδειπνον*, ‘funeral meal.’” Festus: “The *silicernium* was a kind of sausage by which the household was purified from mourning.” See the interpreters there. ELMENHORST.

**Longavi.** Thus Salmasius, following the traces of the manuscript codex, which has the meaningless *longaevi*. Gelenius: *longavo*. Others: *longabo*; still others: *longano*. This word is variously written. The glosses: “*longano*—*κωλέντερον*, ‘large intestine.’” Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book IV: “The third stuffed item is the *longabo*, so called because it is longer than two *hila*.” Apicius, Book IV, chapter 2: “pork *longanones*.” Vegetius, *Veterinary Medicine*, Book I, chapter 14: “The intestine through which dung is expelled is called the *longanon*.” See Schneider, that distinguished scholar, there and in the *Rural Lexicon*. Caelius Aurelianus, *On Chronic Diseases*, Book II: “The *longanon* [Col. 1249B] together with the sphincter and anus.” Our author, finally, forms *longavus*. Compare Jansson, *Lexicon to Caelius Aurelianus*, and Martin, *Etymological Lexicon*. ORELLI.

**“What are the taedae?”** This is the old reading, for which Gelenius rashly substituted *tuaeta*. For why would *tuceta* occur here among obscure terms peculiar to sacred rites? It is not yet clear, however, how the word should be stated. HERALDUS. Meursius in the Appendix conjectures that one should read: “What are the *codae*?”—the archaic form of *caudae*, “tails.” Salmasius, on Solinus, in the passage cited, refashions it as: “What are the *taxiae*?” This, he says, arose from the corrupt spelling *taeciae* or *tacciae*, from which the unlearned produced *taedae*. *Taxia* or *taxea* is fat or lard. Afranius in *Prosa*:

> A cloaked Gaul fed on rich *taxia*.

ORELLI.

[Col. 1249C] **“What are the naeniae?”** Festus, under this word: “Some say that the name *naeniae* was derived from the word for the end of the intestine.” To prove this, he employs the testimony of Plautus, *Bacchides* IV.8.48:

> And when you have provoked me, I shall assuredly turn you  
> Into a mouse-like *naenia*, riddled with stabs.

Scaliger, however, there interprets *naenia* as the cry emitted by a mouse when stabbed. Dacier, on the cited passage of Festus, defends the meaning “intestine.” Salmasius in the Leiden edition printed: “What are the *taeniae*?” But since in a parallel passage of the next chapter he himself printed, “unless they see *naeniae* prepared to be burned in their honor,” I have preferred to retain it here as well and leave the matter intact for the judgment of the more learned. ORELLI.

**“What are the morsels—not ordinary ones, but those whose name and designation is penitae?”** Festus: “The ancients called the tail *penis*, and from this ancient usage a piece of pork with the tail, served at pure feasts, is still called the *offa penita*.” The same author: “Naevius calls the *offa penita* a segment of flesh with the tail. For the ancients called the tail *coda*, a portion cut into the shape of a ball, like porridge rolled by hand.” This *offa penita*, moreover, was also served apart from sacrifices; hence Plautus in the *Miles Gloriosus* numbers it among the delicacies of a banquet. HERALDUS.

**“The fat is cut, after the manner of catillamina, into tiny crumbs.”** This is a transposition of words, very frequent in our author, for: “the fat is cut into tiny crumbs after the manner of *catillamina*.” *Catillamen* comes from *catillo, catillare*, first conjugation, meaning generally “to lick up eagerly” dainties and delicious delicacies. But they seem properly to have given the name to sausages or small puddings stuffed with minced meat, because they were eagerly sought by gluttons (*catillones*); see Salmasius on Solinus, p. 90. Above, Book II, chapter 42, he called them *catillamenta*; see the notes there. This excellent emendation by Meursius and Salmasius rests on the following manuscript reading: “the fat is into tiny crumbs *catilla minuam* cut according to custom.” Sabaeus: “But it is cut up into small pieces according to custom.” Gelenius: “Or the entrails are cut up into small pieces according to custom.” Heraldus: “Or the *hila* are cut up into small pieces; then in the order in which the second is situated.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1250B] **“Among these, what bears the name of omentum is a certain part,” etc.** That is: “Among these, a certain part bears the name of omentum,” or, to speak more clearly, “of their number the omentum is a certain part.” Those who did not understand this wished to alter the text. HERALDUS.—It should rather be interpreted thus: “Of these, the thing we have named, the omentum, is a certain part.” Fulvius Ursinus therefore wrongly deletes the word *name* (*nomen*). ORELLI.

**“Polimina, moreover, are the things that we have more modestly called offspring.”** Festus says that pigs’ testicles are called *polimina*. I think they were so called not from *polire*, “to polish,” as he prefers, but from *pellis*, “skin”; for *poliones* stands for *pelliones*, “furriers.” Plautus also mentions pigs’ *polimenta* in the *Miles Gloriosus*. HERALDUS.

[Col. 1250C] **“What are fitilla, frumen, africia, gratilla, catumeum, conspolium, and cubula?”** On *fitilla*, see above on Book II, chapter 21. For *frumen*, Meursius conjectures *frama*, in place of *forma*, a porridge made from honey and millet, according to Festus; similarly, as Quintilian testifies in *Institutes of Oratory* I.5, many ancients regularly said *Tharsomenos* for *Thasymenos*, while Tinra of Placentia said *precula* for *pergula*. Since Arnobius himself explains the remaining terms, which are mentioned by none of the ancients, we shall be content with this Cato. *Cubula* was perhaps so called from its cubic shape. ORELLI.

**Strebula flesh.** *Caro strebula*, *κρέας στρεβλόν*, “twisted flesh,” is the flesh around the hip joints of cattle, so called from its curvature and turning. For *στρεβλός* means “curved” and “crooked”; hence *stribligo*, “corrupt speech,” *ὁ σολοικισμός*, “a solecism.” See Varro, *On the Latin Language*, Book VI, p. 93, Bipontine edition, and Scaliger there. Festus, however, says that in the *Frivolaria* Plautus used the Umbrian word *strebulas* for portions of sacrificial meat. ORELLI.

**Pulpamenta.** *Pulpamentum* here means the same as *pulpa*, that is, boneless flesh; the word derives from its quivering, since it is soft and tremulous. See Casaubon on Persius, Satire II.63. ORELLI.

**“The entrails that are on spits.”** Meursius thinks one should read: “not those that are on spits,” etc. A repeated *not* could easily have dropped out. ORELLI.

**“Previously alive.”** See above on Book II, chapter 68, and Semler’s *Latin Index to Tertullian* under this word. ORELLI.

**“Nor likewise fendicae, which are themselves also hirae.”** Scriverius, Meursius, Heraldus, and Salmasius most correctly emended the text thus. Festus: “The *hira*, called *hilla* in the diminutive, is the intestine which the Greeks call *νῆστιν* and which they name the jejunum.” See above on Book II, chapter 42, the words: “flesh with udders along with these.” Earlier editions read, nonsensically: “which are themselves dreadful.” I have searched elsewhere in vain for the word *fendicae*. Gesner derives it in his *Thesaurus* from *findo*, “to split,” because they were made from pieces of split flesh. ORELLI.

**“Which the speech of the common people, when it speaks of the entrails, customarily calls by name.”** Thus Scriverius, quite correctly. Earlier editions read: “which that speech of the common people customarily,” etc. Scaliger conjectures *illas* in place of *hillas*, with Heraldus approving. But *hilla*, a diminutive of *hira*, is not a common word but one used in sacred rites. *Hillae* are the inner fleshy parts suitable for stuffing—*des tripes*, “tripe.” See Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* II.25, p. 102. ORELLI.

**Aerumnae.** Thus the Leiden edition from the manuscript codex. Canterus: *rumae*. The *ruma* is the projecting part of the throat through which certain animals bring back the food that has descended, as Servius explains on Virgil, *Eclogues* VI.54. Festus and Isidore, *Origins* XI.1 and XII.1, call it *rumen*. Compare G. J. Vossius, *Roman Etymologies*. I do not recall reading *aerumnae* elsewhere in this sense, but I would not eliminate it on that account; for this seems to have been an obscure, sacred name, whereas *ruma* and *rumen* were common terms. ORELLI.

**“Ruminating races.”** L. Carrio, *Emendations* II.17, most correctly restored this from the manuscript codex. The “ruminating races” are ruminant animals, nothing more. In this sense *saecula* means the stock, kind, or multitude of any thing—*γενεά*, “race”—very frequently in Lucretius, whom Arnobius imitates throughout this work. Thus Book V.864:

> At once the wool-bearing flocks and horned races;

and I.38:

> And in a brief span the races of living things are changed.

See above on Book I, chapter 25; Stewechius on the present passage; and especially Vechner, *Hellenolexia* II.5, p. 494. Away, therefore, with Gelenius and his “calf among the ruminating creatures.” ORELLI.

**“Neither magmenta nor augmina.”** See the next chapter. ORELLI.

**“Not a thousand kinds either of sausages or of fitillae.”** In this exceedingly obscure and corrupt passage I have followed Salmasius’ emendation. The old reading is: “not a thousand kinds, a covering of blood or of *fitillae*,” where Fulvius Ursinus thinks the words should be separated: “not a thousand kinds, or an *amen* of blood, or of *fitillae*.” Meursius and Heraldus candidly admit that they do not know what “an *amen* of blood” could mean. Elmenhorst understands it as some kind of cake or pastry, citing Hesychius: *Ἄμεν … εἶδος πλακοῦντος*, “amen: a kind of cake.” Gesner in his *Thesaurus* interprets it as a bond or connection of blood, from *ἅμμα*, “knot,” and *ἅπτω*, “to fasten,” whence also *amentum*. “An *amen* of blood” would thus be thickened, coagulated blood of the sort found in blood sausages. But a nominative cannot stand here because of the preceding *kinds* and the following “or of *fitillae*,” which require a genitive. I therefore read “or of sausages,” unless one prefers “either of *catillamina* or of *fitillae*.” For *fitillarum*, Meursius and Scaliger think *fritillarum* should be read. ORELLI.]

XXIV. So be it. Let it be granted that the most unfortunate animals are not slaughtered at the temples of the gods without some religious function and that what has arisen from customary practice contains some rational cause. But if it appears magnificent and splendid to slaughter bulls for the gods, if the victims’ entrails are burned whole and undiminished, what is intended by all these remaining things, which accord with the disciplines of the Magi and which the pontifical mysteries established in the hidden laws of the rites and inserted into divine worship?

What, I ask, is intended by these *apexanes*, *hirciae*, *silicernia*, and *longavi*? These are names [Col. 1249A] and kinds of sausages, some stuffed with goat’s blood, others with minced lungs. What are the *taedae*? What are the *naeniae*? What are the morsels—not ordinary ones, but those whose name and designation is *penitae*? Of the first of these, the fat is cut, after the manner of *catillamina*, into tiny crumbs. The second is a length of intestine [Note: [Col. 1249B] “A cutting” (*prosectio*). Petrus Daniel.], through which the discharge is expelled, dried entirely of its vital fluids. An *offa penita*, however, is a morsel containing a portion of entrail together with the animal’s severed tail.

What are the *polimina*? What are the *omenta*? What is the *palasea*, or, as some call it, the *plasea*? Among these, what bears the name of *omentum* is a certain part by which the enmeshed coverings of the stomachs are enclosed. The *plasea* is an ox’s tail smeared with fine wheat flour [Col. 1249B] and blood. The *polimina*, moreover, are what we more modestly call “offspring,” [Col. 1250A] though in common usage they are customarily designated by the term “testicles.”

What are *fitilla*, *frumen*, *africia*, *gratilla*, *catumeum*, *conspolium*, and *cubula*? Of these, the first two are names for porridges, but of different kinds and qualities. The series that follows, however, contains terms for cakes, and these too do not all have one and the same preparation.

They do not choose to call the flesh removed from the hip joints of bulls *strebula flesh*; nor the entrails set upon spits, previously alive and then scorched over coals, roasted *pulpamenta*; nor, finally, a single mixture compounded from four kinds of grain *salsamina*. Nor do they similarly call *fendicae*—which are themselves also *hirae*—what the speech of the common people customarily calls *ilia* (“guts”). [Col. 1250B] [Col. 1251A] Nor, by the same rationale, do they so call the *aerumnae*, the foremost parts in the gullets which are naturally formed to send food down and bring it back up for the ruminating races. Nor the *magmenta*, nor the *augmina* [Note: [Col. 1251B] *Augmenta*, Fulvius.], nor the thousand kinds either of sausages or of *fitillae*, upon which you have bestowed obscure names and which, so that they might appear more venerable to the common people, you have made august.

[Note: [Col. 1251D]

XXV.—**“What has it to do with various stuffings?”** Thus the Leiden edition. [Col. 1252B] Sabaeus has *fratribus*, that is, “offspring” or “testicles”—see above on Book V—with Heraldus approving. Fulvius Ursinus prefers *frattibus*, a new and unheard-of word derived from the Greek *φράττειν*, “to stuff.” ORELLI.

**“By the method of preparation.”** Oudendorp, on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* II, p. 103, prefers “by the method of cutting up” (*consectionis jure*). ORELLI.

**“Seasoned with a variety of fillings.”** *Impensa* means any stuffing or filling. Apicius frequently uses it in this sense, as in: “then add the prescribed *impensa*,” that is, the stuffing. Palladius, *On Agriculture*, Book I: “The walls are to be packed with a filling of pumice,” that is, filled with a mixture of crushed pumice. SCALIGER, on Varro, *On the Latin Language* IV, p. 118, Bipontine edition.—Compare the interpreters of Festus under *Impensa*. Theodorus Marcilius, however, on Horace, *Epistles* I.19, p. 135, interprets it as a seasoning for foods. ORELLI.

**“So that one must devise innumerable banquets for them.”** The manuscript codex has “so that numbered banquets,” etc., which Stewechius approves, explaining it as “counted out.” ORELLI.

**“Do they suffer from aversions of the stomach?”** Similarly Petronius, chapter 141: “For no flesh is pleasing in itself, but is corrupted by some art and made agreeable to averse stomachs.” See there Gonsalo de Salas, p. 249, Burmann’s edition. Galen, *On the Composition of Medicines*, Book VIII, chapter 3, calls that aversion of the stomach *ἀπεψίαν*, “indigestion.” ORELLI.

**“Which you call prosiciae.”** This reading requires no defense. He says that the gods “love to receive” them because these were the portions offered to the gods. Hence the pimp in Plautus’ *Poenulus*, when he saw that he could not obtain favorable omens, forbade the entrails to be cut off as offerings, since he was angry with the goddess whom he had been unable to appease and render favorable to himself:

> For today, unhappy man that I am, I sacrificed  
> Six lambs to my most angry gods, yet still  
> I could not make Venus favorable to me.  
> [Col. 1252D] Since I cannot obtain favorable omens, I left at once,  
> Angry, and forbade the entrails to be cut off as offerings.  
> I was unwilling even to look at them, since the soothsayer  
> Said they were unfavorable; I judged the goddess unworthy.

HERALDUS. *Prosicias* derives from an emendation by Adrianus Turnebus. Earlier editions printed *praesicias*. Festus: “A *prosicium* is what is cut off and thrown forward.” See Dacier there and the following note. Compare Grotius on Martianus Capella, Book I, p. 5. ORELLI.

**“What cause, what reason is there that the strebula flesh should be set apart, the ruma, tail, and plasea set apart, the hirae alone and the omentum alone, and that they should be added for the purpose of augmenta?”** The passage should be corrected and punctuated thus. Therefore the *strebula* flesh, *ruma*, tail, *plasea*, *hirae*, and *omentum* were all placed upon the altars, together with the liver of the sacrificed victim, for the purpose of providing *augmenta*. All these parts, cut beforehand from the victim, were called *prosiciae* or also *praesiciae*. If anything more was added, it was called a *magmentum*, as though it were a greater *augmentum*, just as *mactus* means *magis auctus*, “more greatly increased.” Varro, Book IV of *On the Latin Language*: “*Magmentum* comes from *magis*, ‘more,’ because it pertains more closely to religion. For this reason *magmentaria cana*”—that is, baskets—“were established in specified places, because that substance was placed upon them.” SALMASIUS, on Solinus, p. 91.—Scaliger, however, on the cited passage of Varro and on Festus under this word, interprets *magmentum* as a feast consecrated by country people to Janus, Silvanus, Mars, and Jupiter Dapalis, though that meaning is foreign to our passage. For *cauda*, “tail,” the manuscript codex has the archaic *coda*. For “the omentum alone and for the purpose of augmenta,” etc., the Leiden edition reads: “and the name alone of the augmenta.” Meursius conjectures “and the *omen* alone”—*omen* in place of *omentum*. Nicolaus Heinsius, *Adversaria* IV.10, p. 620: “and the abdomen alone.”

“They maintain that this sacrificial custom took its origin from Prometheus. According to it, people were accustomed to cast part of the victim into the fire and to appropriate part for their own food, whereas previously the entire, undiminished flesh of the victims was consumed by fire. They therefore placed the portion cut from the entrails upon the altar and burned it for the gods; the persons participating in the sacrifice ate the other part. They ate the entrails before the remaining flesh. Hence the story of the Pinarii, who arrived for the rest of the feast after the entrails had already been eaten in the sacrifice of Hercules. See Livy. It was consequently ordained that thereafter the Pinarii should be excluded from sharing in the entrails but admitted to the remaining distribution of the meat.”

Thus Salmasius in the cited passage. ORELLI.

**“They take these tiny little pieces for delicious delicacies.”** Fulvius Ursinus: “these pieces, even though tiny,” etc. *Mateola*, *macteola*, *mattea*, and *mactea*—Greek *ματτύα*—mean every delicacy and every sumptuous, costly food. See the interpreters on Varro, pp. 78 following, Bipontine edition; Bentley on Aristophanes, *Clouds* 450; and Turnebus, *Adversaria* XXII.6. ORELLI.

**“But so that they may rouse the palate from idleness.”** We have emended the text thus from the royal codex. The common editions print the meaningless: “That they may bring idleness to palates.” *Admonere* means to spur or warn with a goad and a certain sensation of pain. Thus Martial: “To urge horses with the whip.” SALMASIUS, on Solinus, p. 21. Compare Cortius on Rutilius’ *Itinerary* I.20 and Gronovius, *Diatribe on Statius’ Silvae* V, ode II, pp. 322 following. Thus Lucan IV.241:

> Their throats swell, roused by the taste of blood.

And Cicero, *Against Verres* I.24: “As his shameful lusts had prompted him to do,” where other codices incorrectly read “had moved.” We therefore have no need of Heraldus’ correction in *Curis* II, “that they may remove the palate’s idleness,” nor of Passeratius’ “that they may bring appetite to the palates.” ORELLI.

**“May stimulate.”** Stewechius conjectures *may inflict* (*infligant*) or *will inflict* (*infligent*). Incorrectly. ORELLI.]

[Col. 1254B] **And breasts.** Stewechius, following Nonius, interprets *rumae* as breasts. But see the preceding chapter. ORELLI.

**Dirges.** Here too Scaliger restored *taenias* (“bands”). ORELLI.

**And purchased morsels.** “And hidden morsels.” HERALDUS.

**Salted offerings.** These must be understood, as Arnobius himself explains in the immediately following words, as salted grain or *mola salsa* (“salted meal”), which they employed in sacrifices—not, as the word elsewhere signifies, meat or fish preserved in salt, *τάριχοι* (*tarichoi*). ORELLI.]

## XXV

For if everything done by human beings—and especially in sacred matters—must have its own causes, and nothing in any undertaking or form of administration is to be done without reason, explain to us fully and tell us what cause, what reason, there is for these things also to be given to the gods and burned upon sacred altars. For we linger, dwell, and fasten upon this point at greater length because it is especially necessary to the present case, desiring [Col. 1251B] to learn what God has to do with porridges, what with [Col. 1252A] sacrificial cakes, what with various stuffings seasoned according to a manifold art of preparation [Note: [Col. 1252B] The manuscript has, absurdly, “by method and manifold.”] and with a variety of costly ingredients.

Are the divine powers treated to sumptuous dinners or luncheons, so that countless dishes must be devised for them? Do they suffer from aversions of the stomach, and is a variety of flavors sought to banish their distaste, so that at one time roasted foods are set before them, at another raw, and at another half-cooked and half-raw? But if the gods love to receive all these portions which you call *praesiciae*, and if they find them pleasing through some sensation of pleasure or sweetness, what intervenes, what prevents you from bringing all these things before them at once together with the entire animals? What cause, what reason, is there for the *strebula* flesh to be offered separately, the breast, tail, and *plassea* separately, the entrails alone, the caul alone, and the organs of increase [Col. 1252B] to be added to the proceeding?

Are the gods of heaven delighted by varieties of relishes, so that—as is customary after the surfeit of rich and wealthy dinners—they take these tiny [Note: [Col. 1253B] Fulvius reads “and.”] little fragments as agreeable delicacies, not to settle their hunger, but to rouse the idleness of the palate and stimulate themselves to appetite with renewed voracity? O wondrous majesty of the gods, comprehended by no human beings, understood by no human natures! For, if they are to benefit us, they must be bought off with the testicles and breasts of cattle; nor do they lay aside their anger and resentment until they have seen dirges prepared to be burned for them, and morsels purchased for them.

[Note: [Col. 1254B]

## XXVI

**Are mingled.** Thus Meursius emended the text. Previously: “Are produced as mingled.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1254C] **You could have come to know.** Thus Fulvius. Previously, “you will be able,” which Heraldus and Meursius defend as an archaism. Thus Pacuvius said *moneris* and Plautus *tetinero*. So too *voleris* occurs in an ancient formula used in taking auspices: “May you have favored the betrothed well and auspiciously.” ORELLI.

**In heroic times.** That in the age of Troy—as also among the Romans in the time of Romulus and Numa—the use of incense was unknown, and that sacred grain, that is, roasted grain sprinkled with salt, was used in its place, is taught, besides our author, by Festus under *mola*, *ador*, and *immolare*, and by Pliny, *Natural History*, book XIII, chapter 1. STEWECHIUS.—Pliny likewise bears witness, *Natural History*, book XIII, chapter 1: “Who first invented perfumes is not recorded, nor was supplication made with incense in the age of Troy.”

And Theophrastus, as quoted by Porphyry, *On Abstinence*, book II, and Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel*, book I, chapter 9:

> An incalculable span of time seems to have elapsed since the race most endowed with reason of all, as Theophrastus says—the race inhabiting the most sacred land founded by the Nile—first began to sacrifice upon the hearth to the heavenly gods. They did not offer first-fruits of myrrh, cassia, and frankincense mixed with saffron; for these too were adopted many generations later, when humanity, becoming an inquisitive hunter after error and acquiring the necessities of life through many toils and tears, offered drops of them as first-fruits to the gods. Thus they did not formerly sacrifice these substances, but grass: taking in their hands, as it were, a kind of down from fertile nature.

NOURRY, p. 518.

**Etruria, the begetter and mother of superstition.** For it was from Etruria that the first haruspices were summoned, together with those capable of interpreting prodigies successfully. Cicero, *On Divination*, book I, and *On the Responses of the Haruspices*; Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chapter IV; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book IX; Livy, book I. ELMENHORSTIUS.

**Sacred grain.** Virgil, *Aeneid* V, 744:

> The Lar of Pergamum and the sanctuary of hoary Vesta  
> he worships suppliantly with sacred grain and a full censer.

ELMENHORSTIUS. Horace, *Odes* III.23.19:

> No costly victim has more persuasively softened  
> [Col. 1255C] the estranged Penates  
> than sacred meal and crackling salt.

HERALDUS.

**Should take the first place in the ceremonies.** That is how the matter stands. They kindled the fire; then placed incense upon the altar; afterward they slaughtered the victims. Seneca, *Oedipus*:

> **M.:** [Col. 1255D] A choice victim stood before the sacred altars.  
> **Tiresias:** Invoke the gods above; call them with uplifted voice,  
> and heap the altars with an offering of eastern incense.  
> **M.:** I have now cast incense upon the sacred hearths of the gods, etc.

HERALDUS.]

## XXVI

It follows that we should say something, without any excess, about incense and unmixed wine. For these kinds of ceremonial observance also are joined and mingled together, and are very widely employed in worship.

First, concerning incense itself, we ask and inquire of you this: whence or [Col. 1253B] at what time could you have come to know or understand it, so that you might rightly judge either that it should be given to the gods or that it is [Col. 1254A] especially agreeable to their will? For it is virtually a new thing, and no incomprehensible series of years has elapsed since knowledge of it flowed into these regions and it earned a place in divine temples.

For neither in heroic times, as is believed and reported, was it known what incense was—as is confirmed by the ancient writers, in whose books no mention of it is found—nor did Etruria, the begetter and mother of superstition, know its reputation or even hear of it, as the rites of its shrines indicate. Nor during the four hundred years in which the Alban state flourished did it come into anyone’s use when sacred rites were performed.
