Neither Romulus himself nor Numa, that craftsman in devising religious observances, knew either that it existed or that it grew, as is shown by the sacred grain with which it was customary to discharge the duties of solemn sacrifice.

From what source, then, did its use begin to be adopted? Or what novelty burst into ancient and long-established custom, so that something which throughout so many ages [Col. 1255A] had not been necessary should take the first place in the ceremonies? For if religious observance limps without incense, and if its power is necessary to render the heavenly gods favorable and gentle toward human beings, the ancients sinned—indeed, their entire life was filled with acts requiring expiation—because through negligence they failed to offer what was especially suited to the pleasure of the gods. But if in ancient times neither human beings nor gods desired the substance of this incense, it is thereby established that even today it is supplied vainly and to no purpose: antiquity did not believe it necessary, and novelty desired it without any reasons.

[Note: [Col. 1255D]

## XXVII

**Or what accrues to their minds.** Thus Gelenius, correctly. The first edition has “happens.” ORELLI.

**Why they desire these things so familiarly.** Should we not read, “why they desire them so ardently,” or even “why they desire them so hungrily,” or something similar? ORELLI.

**Congealing through a tear-like distillation.** That is, congealing from liquids or juices that drip like tears. Thus one speaks of the “tears” of plants—the vine, the poppy, and so forth. “Tears” means the sap these plants exude. Compare Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 30: “grains of incense worth a single as, tears of an Arabian tree”; see Havercamp there, [Col. 1256C] p. 278. ORELLI.

**That little Panchaean resins should burn for them.** Lucretius, book II, verse 417:

> And the altar close by breathes forth Panchaean scents.

Servius on Virgil, *Georgics* II.115: “Panchaea is a people of the Sabaeans, among whom incense grows.” ELMENHORSTIUS. That is, from Panchaea, a part of Troglodytic Arabia adjoining the mouth of the Arabian Gulf. Servius, in his commentary on Virgil’s *Georgics* II.115, says of it: “Panchaea is a people of the Sabaeans, among whom incense grows,” as in:

> The Sabaeans alone possess the incense-bearing bough,

and likewise:

> And all Panchaea, rich in incense-bearing sands.

Similarly Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book X, fable 9:

> Let the Panchaean land bear incense  
> sweated from the wood, and other flowers.

And Lucretius, book II, verse 417:

> And the altar close by breathes forth Panchaean scents.

Consult also, if you wish, Tibullus, book III, elegy 2, and Claudian, *On the Third Consulship of Honorius*, at the end. NOURRY, p. 517.]

## XXVII

Finally, so that we may always maintain that rule and definition by which it has been demonstrated and established that whatever is done by a human being must have its own [Col. 1255B] causes, we shall retain it in this matter too, and ask you what cause, what reason, there is for incense to be cast upon the altars before the very images of the divine powers, and for them to be thought, through its burning, to become friendly and gentle. What is acquired for them by an act of this kind, or what accrues to their minds, so that we may rightly judge that these things are properly paid out and are not consumed vainly and to no purpose?

For just as you must show why you give incense to the gods, so it follows that you must also disclose some reason possessed by the gods why they do not reject it—indeed, why they desire it so familiarly. “We honor the gods by these things,” someone will perhaps say. But we are asking about the perception of the divine powers, not yours. We inquire not what is done by you, but at what value they assess what is given as the price of their favor.

Yet, O piety, how great or what sort of honor is this, which is produced from the odor of fire [Note: [Col. 1255C] Fulvius reads “heat.”] and procured from the resin of a tree? For, lest you happen not to know what this incense is or whence it comes: it is a viscous substance flowing from bark, as from the almond or cherry tree, and congealing through a tear-like [Col. 1256A] distillation. Is it this, then, that honors and augments the dignities above? Or, if offense has ever been incurred, is it dissolved by the vapor of incense, and is indignation soothed and moderated?

Why, then, do you hesitate to burn indiscriminately the resin of any tree, without any distinction? For if the divine powers are honored by this and do not regard it as unworthy that little Panchaean resins should burn for them, what difference does it make from what source smoke is produced upon the sacred altars, or from what kind of resin clouds of fumigation boil upward?

[Note: [Col. 1256D]

## XXVIII

**Fumigations.** The manuscript codex has *suffectionibus*. Incorrectly. ORELLI.

**For the judgments of the gods are diverse.** Fulvius Ursinus deletes the word “of the gods.” Incorrectly. ORELLI.

[Col. 1257C] **So that things which delight some.** Thus the Leiden edition. The first edition has “and things which delight some,” which could be defended as a shift of gender and mood of a sort not uncommon in these writers. Gelenius reads “so that things which delight them.” ORELLI.

**But each is affected according to the constitution he possesses for contact with a thing arriving from outside.** Thus Gelenius and Salmasius printed the text, entirely correctly. The first edition has “contact thus produces,” which makes no sense. ORELLI.

**Nor be raised up by the eminence of any strength.** This is the old reading, for which Gelenius wrongly substituted “nor by any solidity,” etc. Soon afterward: “For that which has no strength or corporeal substance,” etc. HERALDUS.—Others read: “nor by the eminence of any scent-producing quality.” ORELLI.

**Not even if you burn a thousand measures of male incense.** Virgil, *Eclogues* VIII.65:

> Burn rich vervain and male incense.

HERALDUS. The ancients called the best and most excellent incense “male”; the same was called *stagonias*, being round like a drop, as is clear from Dioscorides and Pliny, *Natural History*, book XII, chapter 14. It was assigned a sex on religious grounds, lest the other sex be employed. See Heyne and Vossius on the cited passage of Virgil. ORELLI.]

## XXVIII

But will someone perhaps say that incense is given to the gods above because its smell is sweet and soothes the sense of their nostrils, whereas other substances are harsh and therefore excluded because they cause offense? Do the gods, then, possess nostrils [Col. 1256B] through which they draw in airy breaths, receiving and releasing the air, so that the qualities of differing odors may penetrate them?

But if we grant that this happens, we attach them to the law of mortality and exclude them from the bounds of divinity. For whatever breathes and draws alternating breaths through passages permeable to the air must be mortal, because it is sustained by feeding upon the atmosphere. And whatever is sustained by feeding upon the atmosphere—if you remove the recurring movements by which the vital alternation is restored and drawn back—must have its life crushed out and its principle of living overthrown and destroyed.

Therefore, if the gods also breathe and draw scent toward themselves wrapped in accompanying currents of air, it is not irrelevant to say that they live on fumigations supplied by others and could perish if their breathing passages were obstructed. And how, finally, do you know that, if they are captivated by sweetness of scent, the same things are pleasant to them as to you, and that they soothe and affect [Col. 1256C] your natures with an identical sensation? Is it not possible that things which give you pleasure may, on the contrary, seem harsh and disagreeable to them?

For since the judgments of the gods are diverse and their substances are not all one, by what reasoning can it be brought about that what differs in quality should experience and receive a single kind of contact? Do we not see every day, even among living creatures born upon the earth, that the same things are bitter to some and sweet to others; that things deadly to these are not naturally destructive to those; and that the same things which delight some with pleasant scents breathe pestilential exhalations upon the bodies of others?

But the cause of this event and occurrence does not lie in the things themselves, which cannot simultaneously be deadly and wholesome, sweet and bitter. Rather, each is affected according to the constitution he possesses for contact with a thing arriving from outside. He does not receive a quality born from the impact of the things, but one arising from the nature of his own sense and contact [Note: [Col. 1257B] Fulvius reads “structure.”].

Yet this entire account is far removed from the gods, and separated from them by no narrow interval. For if it is true, as [Col. 1257B] wise persons believe, that they are incorporeal and are not [Note: [Col. 1258B] Sabaeus reads “nor.”] raised up by the eminence of any strength, scent is an empty thing in relation to them, nor can the breeze of any odor affect them perceptibly—not even if you burn a thousand measures of male incense and this whole heaven is enclosed by the cloudiness of overflowing vapors.

For that which has no strength or corporeal substance cannot be touched by corporeal substance. Odor, however, is a body, as is shown by its contact with the nostrils. It therefore cannot be perceived by a god on any principle, since he lacks corporeal reality and is devoid of every sense and faculty of thought.

[Note: [Col. 1257D]

## XXIX

**Unmixed wine is incense’s companion.** That is so: after incense had been cast upon the kindled altar, wine was immediately poured and shed upon it. Ovid, *Tristia* V, elegy 5:

> Give me, boy, incense that makes the flames grow rich,  
> and unmixed wine that hisses when poured upon the sacred fire.

HERALDUS. They were accustomed, of course, to pour wine upon incense given to the flames—or, as Lactantius expresses it, to wet the hearths by pouring out fragrant, aged wine. On this rite Horace, *Odes* I.19:

> Set down, boys, vervain and incense,  
> together with a bowl of two-year-old unmixed wine;  
> once a victim has been sacrificed, she will come more gently.

NOURRY.

**Why it is poured over that burning.** Meursius, p. 213, conjectures: “why it is poured over its burning.” Not badly. ORELLI.

**Their dryness.** Fulvius Ursinus reads “their dryness” in the singular. ORELLI.

**After solid meals of cakes and porridges.** Meursius and Stewechius, entirely correctly, restored “solid” from the manuscript codex in place of “customary,” which was formerly read. But Stewechius is mistaken in thinking that by these words Arnobius refers to the ancient belief that nothing ought to remain from the cakes, porridges, and other foods offered. Rather, *solid foods* means firm, substantial, nourishing foods—*feste, nahrhafte Speisen*. Nothing more. ORELLI.

**And slaughtered victims.** For they poured wine not only at the beginning of the sacrifice, when the altar had been kindled and incense placed upon it, but also after the victims had been slain and brought forward. Homer, *Iliad* III:

> He spoke, and with pitiless bronze cut the lambs’ throats,  
> then laid them upon the ground, gasping,  
> deprived of life, for the bronze had taken away their strength.  
> Drawing wine from the mixing bowl in cups,  
> they poured it out and prayed to the everlasting gods.

HERALDUS.

[Col. 1258D] **Brias.** The glosses: “*bria* … a kind of vessel” (*εἶδος ἀγγείου*). HERALDUS.—A *bria* was a certain liquid measure, or a kind of vessel and cup. An old Latin-Greek glossary: “*Bria*, a kind of vessel, a certain measure.” See, if you please, Martini’s *Lexicon* and Du Cange’s *Glossarium*. NOURRY, p. 521.—From this word grammarians derive *ebrius* (“drunk”) and *sobrius* (“sober”). See Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. ORELLI.

**And sympuvia.** The manuscript has *sympubiaque*. Sabaeus reads *sympiniaque*. See above, on book IV, chapter 31. ORELLI.

**Lest some piece of flesh badly swallowed should remain lodged in the passage of the stomach.** C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book IV, chapter 1, p. 2576, interprets this very badly. He understands *viscus* as a glutinous substance, a sluggish and tenacious fluid of the sort that blocks passages. But *viscus*, genitive *visci*, or *viscum*, genitive *visci*, properly signifying a kind of gum and birdlime, must be distinguished from *viscus*, genitive *visceris*, of the third declension, which means flesh—whatever lies between the bones and skin—whence the plural *viscera*. See Oudendorp, who discusses these words at length, on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* II, p. 103. ORELLI.

[Col. 1259B] **Heaven deprived of its administrators.** Stewechius suspects that one should read “heaven deprived of its administration,” because the passage concerns only Jupiter’s obstruction or crushing, and he alone is the administrator of heaven. *Administratus*, fourth declension, indeed appears nowhere in the lexicons; but formations of this kind are not uncommon in our author. See [Col. 1259C] the note on book II, chapter 20. ORELLI.]

## XXIX

Unmixed wine is incense’s companion, and we similarly demand an explanation of why it is poured over that burning. For if the reason why it is done is not shown and the practice has no disclosed cause of its own, it must no longer be charged merely to ludicrous error but—to speak more plainly—to insanity, madness, and blindness. For, as has now been said rather often, everything that is done must have a clear cause of its own, not hidden beneath the obscurity of some darkness.

If, then, you have confidence in the act, disclose and show why this liquid is given—that is, why wine is poured over the altars. Do the bodies of the divine powers feel parching thirst, and must their dryness be moderated by some fluid? Is it their custom, as it is ours as mortals, to mix drinks with their dinners? In the same way, after solid meals of cakes, porridges, and slaughtered victims, so that their food may decay and be digested more easily, do they wash it down and take copious quantities of wine?

Give the immortal gods cups to drink from, then, I beg you: bring out goblets, *briae*, bowls, and *sympuvia*. And since they stuff themselves with bulls, rich banquets, and sumptuous foods, come to their aid and hurry, lest some piece of flesh badly swallowed should remain lodged in the passage of the stomach. Give unmixed wine to Jupiter Best and Greatest, lest he choke! He wishes [Col. 1259A] to belch but cannot. Unless that obstruction slips away and is dissolved, there is the greatest danger that his breath may be cut off by the crushing blockage, and heaven may remain widowed and deprived of its administrators.

[Note: [Col. 1259C]

## XXX

**And we rouse venerable fragrances with extinguished coals.** I have given the passage according to Salmasius’ emendation, for which he himself supplies the reasoning in his *Commentaries on Solinus*, p. 232, in these words:

> The Royal manuscript has *et venerabiles miscus*, from which they produced *venerabile miscus*. What that might be, I should like someone to explain to me. It is beyond controversy that the reading must be: “and we rouse venerable fragrances with extinguished coals.” Here *muscus* means *εὐωδία* (“fragrance”) and a fragrant odor. In its place *miscus* had been written, just as *Thile* for *Thule*, *Bitiae* for *Bituae*, and *Titinus* for *Tutunus*. Our glosses have: “*muscus*, fragrance” (*εὐωδία*). Other glosses have: “*muscus*: moss, seaweed, musk” (*βρύον, φῦκος, μοῦσχος*). By *μοῦσχος* is meant what we have stated. The Greek-Latin glosses have: “*μοῦσχος*, *muscus*.”
>
> Apuleius, much earlier than Arnobius, also used this word. His words from the tenth *Milesian Tale* must be read thus: “And by Hercules, he cleansed Orchium’s smoothly turned chariot with washes of fragrant musk and Chian rosewater.” In the Florentine manuscripts the incorrect *hyaci* is read instead of *mysci*, whence Elmenhorstius added those words. Oudendorp, p. 717, emends it to *Lyaei*.
>
> Since both Arnobius here and Apuleius—to say nothing of Jerome—employed *muscus* for fragrance, it is sufficiently clear from this that the animal which produces musk was known to the ancients. If they did not know the animal itself, they must at least have known the perfume. Aëtius and Paulus call it *μόσχος*, whence also *μόσχατα*, compounds made from it.
>
> Very learned men hold that the *muscus* which Saint Jerome mentions among perfumes is not the aromatic substance (*ἄρωμα*) of any animal, but fragrant moss, which the Greeks call *βρύον* and *βρύον ἀρωματικόν* (“aromatic moss”). Hermolaus so judges in his *Corollarium*. If his opinion is correct, who would not judge that the word in Arnobius and Apuleius must also be understood of this moss?
>
> Jerome’s words, from book II *Against Jovinian*, are these: “the sweetness of scent, the various incenses, amomum, *cyphi*, grape-blossom, moss, and the skin of a foreign mouse.”
>
> Pliny, *Natural History*, book XII, chapter 28, enumerating aromatic species from which perfumes are made: “To the same class belongs *bryon*, the cluster of the white poplar, best around Cnidus or Caria, in thirsty, dry, and rough places; the second-best grows upon the cedar of Lycia. To the same class belongs *oenanthe*.” *Βρύον* is *muscus* in Latin. The glosses have: “*muscus*: moss, seaweed” (*βρύον, φῦκος*). Thus *oenanthe* and *muscus* are similarly joined in Jerome, as *bryon* and *oenanthe* are in Pliny. Dioscorides records that *bryon* is added to perfumes made from balanus oil and to aromatic substances used for fumigation, which the Greeks call *θυμιάματα* (“incenses”).
>
> Yet in those passages of the authors *muscus* is not *βρύον*, but *μόσχος* or *μοῦσχος*: a perfume extracted from an animal similar to a gazelle in India. Because it is extremely fragrant, Arnobius and Apuleius used *muscus* for any fragrance or sweetness of scent, etc., etc.

Thus Salmasius. Gelenius printed: “and venerable odors of roasting fat,” etc.; all subsequent editors except Salmasius follow him, with Stewechius also approving. ORELLI.

**Drops of a little wine.** Gelenius reads “a drop.” ORELLI.

**Obviously because among you greater force belongs to.** Thus Gelenius and the others. The first edition has “first because,” etc. “Greater” is absent from the manuscript, with Stewechius approving the omission. ORELLI.

**A thing closely connected with sexual acts.** Thus the first edition. Others wrongly altered this very sound reading to “a thing closely connected with Venus”; others to “a thing close to Venus”; and the Leiden edition to “for Venus, he in a closely connected matter,” where I confess, along with the profoundly ignorant, that I do not know what the word “he” is supposed to mean. Arnobius very aptly calls wine a thing closely connected with sexual acts—that is, *τοῖς ἀφροδισίοις* (“the things of Aphrodite”). Valerius Maximus expresses the same opinion, book I, chapter 1:

> The use of wine was formerly forbidden to Roman women, evidently lest they should fall into some disgrace, because the next step from the intemperance of Father Liber has commonly been toward illicit sexual intercourse.

Elmenhorstius appropriately cited this passage. ORELLI.

**To cashier.** That is, to remove or wrest authority from the gods. NOURRY, p. 553.—Should we perhaps read “to be cashiered”? Arnobius is evidently mocking drunken gods assailing one another with curses. ORELLI.

**And the reproach of a ruined man.** He rightly says “ruined.” For the Greeks call such persons *ἄσωτοι* (“profligates,” literally “past saving”) because their prospects are desperate. Aristotle says that the *ἄσωτος* perishes because his resources perish. Thus in the *Nicomachean Ethics*, book IV:

> For a man who has one particular vice, that of destroying his substance, is intended by the term “profligate”; for the profligate is one who is ruined through his own agency.

HERALDUS.]

## XXX

“But unfairness is imputed to us in vain,” he says. “For we do not pour out unmixed wine to the gods above for those reasons, as though we thought that they thirsted, drank, or rejoiced in the pleasure it affords. It is therefore given to honor them, so that their sublimity may thereby be made loftier, greater, and more august. We pour libations over the very altars and rouse venerable fragrances with extinguished coals.”

And what more serious insult can be inflicted upon the gods than to believe that they are rendered favorable by receiving unmixed wine, or to suppose that they are shown great honor if only you cast and drip a few drops of wine upon a glowing ember? [Col. 1259B] We are not speaking with people devoid of reason or lacking the common truth of understanding. Wisdom is present in you too; perception is present, and you yourselves know by your inward judgment that we speak the truth.

But what can we do with people unwilling to consider the things themselves deeply and to converse with themselves? [Col. 1260A] For you do what you see being done, not what you trust ought to be done. Obviously, among you irrational custom has [Note: [Col. 1259B] “Greater” is absent from the manuscript.] greater force than the nature of things, examined and weighed by an inquiry into truth.

For what has God to do with wine? What or how great is the power in its substance, that when wine has been poured out, God’s sublimity increases and his authority is thought to have been honored? What, I ask, has God to do with wine—a thing closely connected with sexual acts, weakening the sinews of every virtue, and an enemy of modesty, shame, and chastity? It has frequently hurled excited minds into madness and frenzy, and has compelled them to strip those very gods of authority with frenzied curses.

Is it not, then, an impiety and a crime full of sacrilege to present as an honor that which, if you consume it too greedily, leaves you unaware of what you are doing and ignorant of what you are saying, [Col. 1260B] until at last you earn the reproach and disgrace of a riotous, dissolute, and ruined man?

[Note: [Col. 1260D]

## XXXI

**Be honored with this wine now being offered.** See above, on book IV, chapter 16. Compare Cujacius, who discusses this formula at length in *Observations on the Law*, book II, chapter 12, pp. 52 ff. ORELLI.

[Col. 1261C] **Trebatius.** A writer of uncertain date. His ten books on religious matters are cited by Macrobius. See G. J. Vossius, *On Latin Historians*, book III, under this name. ORELLI.

**Nor will the remainder be bound by religious consecration. What sort of honor, then, etc.** Gelenius, followed by the other editors, punctuated the passage in this entirely correct manner. Previously it was read: “Nor will it be bound by religious consecration. But what sort, then…” ORELLI.

**Who is compelled to receive honor subject to a condition.** When the ancients consecrated anything, they spoke cautiously and precisely and always expressly added laws and conditions, lest they bind themselves by some unspoken religious obligation. This is evident from several inscriptions, for example:

> JUPITER BEST AND GREATEST, WHEN I GIVE AND DEDICATE THIS ALTAR TO YOU TODAY, I SHALL GIVE AND DEDICATE IT UNDER THOSE LAWS AND WITHIN THOSE BOUNDS WHICH I SHALL HERE AND TODAY DECLARE OPENLY.

HERALDUS.]

## XXXI

It is worthwhile to set forth the very words which it is customary to use in supplication when wine is given:

> Be honored with this wine now being offered.

Trebatius says that the word “being offered” was added for this reason and is uttered with this intention: so that absolutely all the wine stored in the cellars and storerooms, from which the wine being poured out was taken, should not begin to be sacred and be withdrawn from human use. Thus, with this word added, only what is actually offered will be sacred, nor will the remainder be bound by religious consecration.

What sort of honor, then, is this, in which something like a law is imposed upon a god, lest he seek more than has been given? Or how greedy is the god himself, if, unless barred by the limitation of a word, he would extend his desire farther and deprive his suppliant of his stores?

> Be honored with this wine now being offered.

This is an injury, not an honor. For what if the divinity wants more than this and is not content with what has been offered? Must he not be said to suffer a notable affront, when he is compelled to receive honor subject to a condition? For if, without the addition of the restrictive phrase, absolutely all the wine in the cellars must become sacred, it is clear both that an insult is done to the god, because a limit is set for him against his will, and that you yourselves violate the ceremonial duties of sacred observance, because you do not bestow as much wine as you see that the god wishes to have supplied to himself.

> Be honored with this wine now being offered.

What else is this than to say: “Be honored only as much as I wish; be magnified only as much as I command; assume only as much honor as I decree you should possess and define by a circumscription of words”?

O mighty sublimity of the gods, [Col. 1262A] which one ought to venerate and worship with every ceremonial duty: the worshiper imposes a law upon it, adores it with conditions and formulas, and restrains it from immoderate desires for wine through fear of a single word!

[Note: [Col. 1261C]

## XXXII

**Are the gods also treated with garlands, wreaths, and flowers?** That the gods were adorned with wreaths, garlands, and flowers is an observation made everywhere. [Col. 1261D] This was done especially when something prosperous had occurred, when some evil had been driven away, or during great festive solemnities. Lactantius, book II, chapter 1:

> After fear has deserted them and the dangers have receded, they then hurry eagerly to the temples of the gods: to these they pour libations, to these they sacrifice, and these they crown.

Hence Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams*, book II, chapter 34:

> To crown gods with the flowers and branches appropriate and customary to them signifies good for everyone, though the outcome will not be without anxieties.

And for this reason wreaths were once condemned among Christians. HERALDUS.

**Also by the ringing of bronze.** In the rites of Isis especially, cymbals, drums, and instruments of that kind were employed. HERALDUS.

**Also by the ringing of bronze and the clashing of cymbals? Also by drums?** Lucretius likewise joins these together, II.618 ff.:

> Tight-stretched drums thunder beneath their palms, and hollow cymbals ring around;  
> horns threaten with their harsh-sounding music,  
> and the hollow pipe excites their minds with a Phrygian rhythm.

[Col. 1262B] And Ovid, *Fasti*, book IV:

> [Col. 1262C] The half-men will go and beat their hollow drums,  
> and bronze struck by bronze will give forth ringing sounds.

NOURRY, p. 523.

**What do the rattlings of the scabella accomplish?** See above, on book II, chapter 42. ORELLI.

**Are they soothed by the shrilling of pipes?** When sacrifices were offered to the gods and prayers were formulated, pipes and various musical instruments sounded noisily at the same time. More particularly, however, there were the pipes used to lead the music and the lyres customarily played before the gods’ couches, as no one, I think, is unaware. Hence we also showed, in the note on book II, chapter 42, that pipes were once rejected by Christians. HERALDUS.

**What is the purpose of those awakenings, etc.?** Awakenings of this kind were especially customary in the rites of Isis and Serapis. At the first hour the priests of Isis opened the temple, an act called the “opening”; they then greeted the goddess, which was called the “greeting” and the “awakening.” Afterward they begged for contributions throughout the day. Then, at the eighth hour, they returned, settled the goddess for sleep, and closed the temple. Witnesses are Apuleius, *Milesian Tale*, book XI—see Oudendorp there, [Col. 1262D] p. 795—and Porphyry, *On Abstinence from Animals*. Joseph Scaliger, on Tibullus I, elegy III, verse 31, and J. Lipsius, *Select Discussions*, book II, chapter 18, collected further material. ORELLI.

**Puttings to sleep.** Thus the manuscript codex and first edition. Gelenius printed *domuitiones* (“bringings home”), which Canterus and Stewechius approve as an ancient and entirely reputable word employed by Pacuvius, Lucilius, Plautus, Apuleius, and even Cicero, *On Divination*, book I: “that a near return and homecoming be granted to the fleet.” I would not, however, venture to alter anything. The distinguished Boettiger discusses at length the “puttings to sleep”—that is, the songs by which the great goddess Isis was invited to take sleep—and the “awakenings” by which she was roused from sleep early in the morning, in his work *The Evening of Isis*, included in *Minerva: Pocketbook for the Year 1809*, pp. 131 and 136. ORELLI.

**The Washing of the Mother of the Gods is today.** That is, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, as we learn from these words of Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXIII, chapter 3:

> On the sixth day before the Kalends, when the annual processions for the Mother of the Gods are celebrated at Rome and the carriage in which her image is borne is said to be washed in the waters of the Almo—[Col. 1263A]

that is, at the place before the Capene Gate where the river Almo flows into the Tiber. The very learned Valesius, p. 10, vol. III, Wagner’s edition, makes these observations there:

> The festival of the Great Mother lasted six days. [Col. 1263B] On the first day, which was the ninth day before the Kalends of April, the Galli, tossing their hair, bloodied their arms with repeated blows; and that day was called the Day of Blood, according to Tertullian in the poem *To a Senator*, Trebellius Pollio in *Claudius*, and Augustine in Tractate VII on John. The following day was celebrated with great universal rejoicing and was therefore called the Hilaria, according to Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I. On the third day they rested. Finally, on the fourth day, which was the sixth day before the Kalends of April, they placed the image of Cybele upon a carriage and washed it in the water of the Almo. This day was called the Washing, the preceding one the Rest, as is taught by the Roman calendar drawn up in the age of Constantine, which we owe to Georg Herwart:
>
> Tenth day before the Kalends: The Tree Enters.  
> Tenth day before the Kalends: Purification of the Trumpets.  
> Ninth day before the Kalends of April: Blood.  
> Eighth day: Hilaria.  
> Seventh day: Rest.  
> Sixth day: Washing.

Moreover, Ovid sang of this rite in *Fasti* IV.337 ff.; Martial, book III, epigram 47; and Prudentius, *Martyrdom of Saint Romanus*. Compare Augustine, *City of God*, book II, chapter 4. NOURRY, p. 54, and ORELLI.

**There is need of waters that wash.** Thus the first edition, undoubtedly from the manuscript codex, and entirely correctly. For the ancients conjugated *lavere* according to the third conjugation, as Meursius teaches, p. 213. Examples occur in Lucretius, Plautus, Virgil, Horace, and countless others. See Nonius Marcellus. Gelenius printed “washing waters.” Canterus prefers “flowing waters.” ORELLI.

**And with the added rubbing of ancient ash.** I would rewrite: “of old ash,” or “with an ancient rubbing of ash.” Nonius Marcellus, citing Caesar, Catulus, and Calvus, notes that the ancients used *cinis* (“ash”) not only as masculine but also as feminine; so too Charisius, book I, adducing two passages from Calvus. No one, I think, is unaware that old ash is used in making lye. Pliny called it “lye-producing ash,” while Scribonius called it “lye ash.” STEWECHIUS.—Fulvius Ursinus corrects it to: “with some rubbing of ash.” ORELLI.]

Jupiter’s banquet is tomorrow. I have observed that it fell precisely on the Ides of November. The Roman rustic calendar expressly places the **BANQUET OF JUPITER** in that month. The calendrical fasti assign it to those very Ides and call it [Col. 1263D] the **PROCLAIMED BANQUET** (*EPULUM INDICTUM*). Festus will teach us what this was and whence it received its name. He says that the ancients called those men *epolones* whom they afterward called *epulones*; they were given this name because they possessed the authority to proclaim banquets for Jupiter and the other gods. STEWECH.—That is, on the Ides of November, as is recorded in the rustic calendar. Mention of this banquet is by no means uncommon among various writers. Livy, book XXV, chapter 2: “The Plebeian Games were repeated for two days, and a banquet of Jupiter was held on account of the games.” Cicero, moreover (*De oratore*, book III), teaches that this banquet-sacrifice and the three *epulones* who presided over it were instituted by Numa: “The ancient pontiffs,” he says, “because of the multitude of sacrifices, desired that there be three men as *epulones*, although they themselves had been instituted by Numa to perform also that banquet-sacrifice connected with the games.” Livy, however, book XXXIII, chapter 42, relates that the triumvirs called *Epulones* were first appointed at Rome by Romuleius or Romulius. Valerius Maximus, book II, chapter 1, §3; Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, [Col. 1264A] chapter 13; and others have discussed them and Jupiter’s banquet. For more about them, see Gutherius, *De veteri jure pontificio*, book IV, chapter 23. NOURR., p. 524.

**The vintage of Aesculapius is conducted and celebrated.** The passage is obscure and difficult. Arnobius is not speaking here of the festivals called the Vinalia, of which Varro (*De lingua Latina*, book V), Festus (s.v. *Vinalia*), Ovid (*Fasti*, book IV), and others attest that the earlier were sacred to Jupiter and the later [Col. 1264B] to Venus. It must be observed, however, that there were other festivals called the Meditrinalia. Concerning them Varro (*De lingua Latina*, book V, p. 48, Dordrecht ed.) says: “The day was called *Meditrinalia* from healing (*medendo*), because, as Flaccus, the Flamen Martialis, used to say, on this day it was customary to offer as a libation both new and old wine and to taste it as a medicine.” Many people still do this even now, while saying: “I drink new and old wine; I remedy a new and old disease.” But Festus (s.v. *Meditrinalia*), who reports these last words, asserts that the Meditrinalia received their name from the goddess Meditrina. Plutarch, moreover, records (*Table Talk*, book III, 9) that in former times those tasting new wine made vows that its use might be harmless and a salutary medicine. Yet he says that this was done on the day they called *Pithoegia* (“Jar-Opening”). But this festival, as Meursius teaches (*Graeciae feriatae*, book I), was celebrated in honor of Bacchus. Whether it too was sacred to Aesculapius because of its medicinal character is for others [Col. 1264C] to judge. Nor, furthermore, are we unaware that Theodoret (*On Sacrifices*, discourse 3) records one festival of Aesculapius, which he calls the Ἀσκληπία (*Asklēpia*). But if you can properly prove that it was identical with the vintage of Aesculapius, we shall immediately agree with you. NOURR., p. 525.

**And gathered for their own uses.** This is a most discerning emendation by Salmasius in the Leiden edition and in his notes on Solinus, p. 176. *Usio* in the sense of *usus* (“use”) is frequent in Cato, Varro, and others. The Royal manuscript has *et ad suasionibus contractis*, which makes no sense; from it Gelenius produced *et ab suasionibus contracti*, whose meaning I understand no better. Stewechius thinks one should read *et longis ab vasionibus (id est itionibus) contracti*, “and gathered after long journeyings.” ORELL.

**There will be a lectisternium for Ceres on the coming Ides.** Livy, book XXII, chapter 10, records such a ceremony: when Hannibal was laying waste the fields of Italy, after the Sibylline books had been consulted and a vow duly pronounced, a lectisternium was held for three days under the supervision of the decemvirs in charge of sacred rites. Six ceremonial couches were displayed: one for Jupiter and Juno, [Col. 1264D] a second for Neptune and Minerva, a third for Mars and Venus, a fourth for Apollo and Diana, a fifth for Vulcan and Vesta, and a sixth for Mercury and Ceres. NOURR., p. 525. He means the Cerealia, which were celebrated at Rome on the seventh day before the Ides of April. See Ovid, *Fasti* IV, 395 ff. Lectisternia are a familiar subject. ORELL.

**It is Earth’s birthday.** An ancient calendar: “On the seventeenth day before the Kalends of May” (15 April), “a pregnant cow is sacrificed to Earth.” ORELL.]

### XXXII

But let it be, as you wish, that honor consists in wine and incense, and that the wrath and displeasure of the divine powers are appeased by the immolation and slaughter of victims. Are the gods also honored with garlands, wreaths, and flowers? With the ringing of bronze and the clashing of cymbals as well? With drums too? With musical ensembles too? What do the clatterings of the stage-clappers accomplish, so that when the divine powers hear them they should consider themselves honorably treated and lay aside their inflamed passions through forgetfulness of their anger? Or is it perhaps that, just as tiny children are frightened out of their foolish wailing when they hear rattles, [Col. 1262B] so in the same way the omnipotent divine powers are soothed by the shrilling of pipes and, their indignation softened to the rhythm of cymbals, grow languid?

What is the meaning of those “awakenings” that you sing in the morning, joining your voices to the pipe? Do the gods above fall asleep, so that they must return to wakefulness? What are those “puttings to sleep,” with which, under an auspicious salutation, you bid them fare well? Are they relaxed by the repose of sleep, and must soothing lullabies be heard so that they may be overtaken by it?

“Today,” someone says, “is the washing of the mother of the gods.” The gods, then, become dirty, and to wash away their dirt [Col. 1263A] they require cleansing waters together with the ancient practice of rubbing with ashes.

“Jupiter’s banquet is tomorrow.” Jupiter, then, eats dinner and must be filled with great dishes, for he has long been ravenous from want of food and has fasted throughout the intervening year.

“The vintage of Aesculapius is conducted and celebrated.” The gods, then, cultivate vineyards, and after gathering grape-harvesters for their own uses, they press out wine.

“There will be a lectisternium for Ceres [Col. 1264A] on the coming Ides.” The gods, then, possess beds, and the indentation of the cushions is raised and plumped up so that they may recline upon softer coverings.

“It is Earth’s birthday.” The gods, then, issue from wombs and have festive days assigned to them on which they first made use of the breath of life.

[Note: [Col. 1264D]

### XXXIII.—The Floralia

In the ancient Roman calendar we see that these games fell on the fourth day before the Kalends of May; Pliny appears likely to support this. Ovid, however, writes:

> The festival of Flora extends also into the Kalends of May.

The licentiousness of the Floralia is described by Augustine, *The City of God*, book II, chapter 26, and Lactantius, book I, chapter 20. Compare Lipsius, *Electa*, book I, and Justinian’s Novel 105. STEWECH.—The Florales or Floralia, as Macrobius observed (*Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 4), were games and festivals that derived [Col. 1265B] their name and origin from a notorious prostitute. She was first called Chloris and wished these games to be instituted from the money she had accumulated through the shameful sale of her body. But so that the memory of such an infamous origin could more readily be effaced, they changed her name to Flora and invented the story that she presided over flowers. Compare Ovid, *Fasti*, book IV, 946. They were held, as is clear from Pliny (*Natural History*, book XVIII, chapter 19), on the fourth day before the Kalends of May. In the calendrical fasti, however, they are recorded on the sixth day before the Kalends of June, and in the rustic calendar toward the end of May. See more in Varro, *De lingua Latina*, book IV, p. 18; Cicero, the fourth oration *Against Verres*; Suetonius (*Galba*, chapter 6); Martial [Col. 1265C] (book I, epigrams 3 and 36); Valerius Maximus, book II, chapter 10, §8; and especially Lactantius. NOURR., p. 436.

**And the Megalensian Games.** Festus: “They call the games of the Great Mother the Megalesia.” Inscription 133 in Gruter. Augustine, *The City of God*, book II, chapter 4. ELMENH.—These games, celebrated by the Romans on the second day before the Nones (4 April), Cicero calls exceptionally chaste, solemn, and religious according to ancestral custom and ordinance, in his oration *On the Response of the Haruspices*, chapter XII; see the commentators there. ORELL.

**And if they retain any memories of offenses inflicted by human beings, they cast them away.** Thus the editor of the Leiden edition restored the text, excellently. The old reading is: “if they retain any memories of offenses inflicted by human beings.” But Meursius correctly teaches that “to inflict a memory of offenses” is not admissible Latin usage, and emends it: “memories of offenses—they cast those away.” Juretus, on Symmachus, book I, epistle XL, p. 50 of Lectius’s edition, wishes to heal the passage merely by changing the punctuation, dividing it as follows: “and if they [Col. 1265D] retain any memories of offenses committed by human beings, they cast them away,” etc. For my part, I prefer Salmasius’s emendation. ORELL.

**Lays aside his passions**—that is, θυμούς, “anger, wrath.” Seneca uses this expression in another sense, that of boldness, in *Troades*, line 745:

> Father himself would have laid aside his proud spirit after Troy.

ORELL.

**The ancient story reenacted by actors.** *Refricare* means “to repeat” or “revive.” See Colvius and Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book IV, p. 292. ORELL.

**If she sees a pantomime, in the costume of Adonis, perform the role through movements of dance.** Cicero (*De oratore* II, chapter 57): “Yet I often marvel at the impudence of those who perform gesture on the stage while Roscius is watching.” Thus *gerere* may stand alone in this sense. Apuleius: “This man, girded with a belt, played the soldier.” HERALD.—*Gestus*, therefore, is the same as σχῆμα, “pose” or “figure.” See Ernesti, *Clavis Ciceroniana*. ORELL.

**Or does Flora think herself honorably treated?** I printed this following Meursius’s emendation. Others read: “Is she thought,” etc. But what follows demands an active form. Heraldus conjectures: [Col. 1266B] “Will she think.” Stewechius: “Flora is thought to be honorably treated.” ORELL.

**And whose performers your law has judged to be dishonorable and to be numbered among persons marked by infamy.** Augustine, *The City of God*, book II, chapter 14: “The Romans exclude theatrical performers from all public honors”; and chapter 27: “This most wanton, most impure, most wicked, and most unclean propitiation of such divine powers—its performers the character of praiseworthy Roman virtue deprived of honor, removed from their tribe, recognized as base, and rendered infamous.” Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, chapter 51, calls mimes “ignominious and notorious persons.” ELMENH.—Arnobius says: “whose performers [Col. 1266C] are dishonorable.” Charioteers are likewise called dishonorable persons in Code IV, *De spectaculis*, although they are said to be exempt from infamy in Digest IV, *De his qui notantur infamia*. Similarly, on this very subject Aemilius Probus (Cornelius Nepos), in his preface, distinguishes dishonor from infamy: “But to appear upon the stage and be a spectacle to the people was a disgrace to no one among those same nations; all these things among us are regarded partly as infamous, partly as lowly and remote from respectability.” HERALD.—Valerius Maximus, book II, chapter 9, teaches, however, that performers of Atellan farces were exempt from this mark of dishonor. Compare Meursius, *Critica*, book II, chapter 9, and Samuel Petit, who treats this matter extensively in his *Commentary on the Laws of Attica*, p. 75 ff., Paris ed. ORELL.

**In whose many *symplegmata* they know themselves to be intermingled**, etc. He appears to call the contrivances of mimes *symplegmata*, which they συμπλέκουσιν and συστρέφουσιν—that is, “weave together” and “twist”—in various ways. HERALD.—Rather, this appears to mean the gestures, dances, and obscene couplings of actors representing the incestuous loves of the gods: obscene, [Col. 1266D] indecent groupings (*unanständige Gruppierungen*). Such scenes seem to have been depicted and described in those notorious booklets of Elephantis, the τύποις Ἐλεφάντιδος, “figures of Elephantis.” See the distinguished Boettiger in *Sabina*, p. 329. ORELL.

**As the fact is.** A formula by which they denote the present state of affairs. See Schwarz on Mamertinus’s *Panegyric*, chapter 9, p. 171, Jaeger ed., and Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book II, p. 169. Here, therefore, it should be translated: *comme chez nous*, “as among us.” ORELL.

**The shaven heads of the Stupidi.** The heads of mimes and γελωτοποιοί (“jesters”) were shaven; hence μωρὸς φαλακρός, “bald fool,” in the epigrammatists. Artemidorus, *Interpretation of Dreams*, book I, chapter 23: “To dream that one’s whole head is shaved is good only for priests of the Egyptian gods, jesters, and those who customarily shave; for everyone else it is bad.” Hence Juvenal, Satire V:

> If you can and must endure all things, someday  
> you will offer your shaven head to be struck;  
> nor will you fear to suffer the cruel [Col. 1267A] lash,  
> worthy of these dinners and such a friend.

In this context, however, they were properly called *stupidi*. For among the γελωτοποιοί some played the parts of fools: they feigned dullness and for that reason were sometimes reprimanded with slaps. Capitolinus, in his *Marcus Antoninus*: “It was alleged against him as a crime that he promoted his wife’s adulterers—Tertullus, Vitilius, Orphitus, and Moderatus—to various honors, although he had even caught Tertullus dining with his wife. Concerning him, while Antoninus was present, a mime said on stage that, when [Col. 1267B] the fool asked a slave the name of his wife’s adulterer and the slave said three times, ‘Tullus,’ and the fool still kept asking, the slave replied: ‘I have already said it three times: he is called Tullus.’” In this mime a *stupidus* played his proper role, as in nearly all mimes. Hence Arnobius here calls those buffoons and clowns *stupidi*. HERALD.—For my part I have written *Stupidi* with a capital letter, following the very learned Maffei in *Museum Veronense*, p. 137. For such stage performers applied this title to themselves with pride, as the designation of the profession they practiced; they correspond exactly to our Harlequins and Hanswursts. The inscription in Maffei, loc. cit., reads:

> D. M. AEMILIAE IRENE QUAE VIXIT ANN. XXVI DIEBUS XIIII  
> AURELIUS EUTYCHES STUPIDUS [Col. 1267C] GREG. URB.  
> CONJUGI KARISSIMAE.

“To the spirits of the dead. To Aemilia Irene, who lived twenty-six years and fourteen days. Aurelius Eutyches, Stupidus of the urban troupe, to his dearest wife.”

Here *Stupidus gregis urbani* means the *Stupidus* of the urban stage performers. ORELL.

**At the sound of slaps.** Joseph Scaliger, on Virgil’s *Catalepton*, p. 1302, Masvicius ed., teaches that *salapittarum sonitu* should be read instead of *salpinctarum sonitu*: “For,” he says, “we must understand not σαλπικτῶν, ‘trumpeters,’ but *salapittarum*, that is, ῥαπισμάτων, ‘slaps,’ as the ancient glosses explain. To provoke laughter, actors allowed their faces to be cut and beaten with slaps. Martial:

> Your face has been cut more than Latinus himself  
> strikes the cheap cheeks of Panniculus with a resounding blow.

The same author:

> Oh, how worthy you were, Marianus, of Latinus’s slaps!  
> I believe that you will succeed Panniculus.

Tertullian, in *On the Shows*: “In addition, he offers his face to the insults [Col. 1267D] of slaps, as though making sport of the Lord’s precept.” Cyprian likewise intimates in *On the Shows*: “The wretched face is hired out for blows.” From this flowed the proverbial manner of speaking, “to offer one’s face to someone”—that is, to be compliant with him—in Terence and Livy.” Thus Scaliger, with the approval of Heraldus and Salmasius. Others, including even the most recent editor, Oberthür, prefer the old reading *salpictarum*, as the manuscript has it, corruptly for *salpinctarum*—that is, “of trumpeters,” τῶν σαλπιγκτῶν. Thus Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis*, book VIII: “It will produce trumpeters, if some should die pierced through in war.” ORELL.

**If they see men unman themselves into feminine indecencies.** Columella, *On Agriculture*, book I: “Astonished, we marvel at the gestures of effeminate men because, by feminine movement, they counterfeit the sex denied to men by nature and deceive the spectators’ eyes.” Cyprian graphically writes in book II, epistle II: “Their morals are emasculated. All the dignity and vigor of their sex is softened by the disgrace of an enervated body; and whoever has more thoroughly broken a man into a woman pleases them more.” Most elegantly, [Col. 1268A] Clement of Alexandria, *Paedagogus*, book II, chapter 10: “Nor of those broken creatures—those dancers, indeed, who bring voiceless pathic obscenity onto the stages,” etc. See, if you please, Lucian, *On Dance*. HERALD.—Compare Rittershausen on Salvian, *The Governance of God*, book VI, §193, p. 58, Bremen ed. ORELL.

**These shouting to no purpose.** He indicates tragic actors, whose principal concern was to bellow with a vast voice rather than speak. Hence Crantor used to say that they had ἀπελέκητον φωνὴν καὶ φλοιοῦ μεστήν, “a voice unhewn and full of bark,” as [Col. 1268B] Diogenes Laertius writes. Hence Demosthenes also reproaches Aeschines with a φωνασκίας ἐπίδειξιν, “display of vocal training”; the same author teaches in *On the Crown* and *On the False Embassy* that Aeschines had been an actor and a τριταγωνιστής, “third actor.” Tertullian, *On the Shows*: “But when the tragic actor bellows, that man recalls the exclamations of some prophet.” Dio Chrysostom, discourse IV, *On Kingship*, says that they βοᾶν ὀξὺ καὶ διάτορον, “shout in a shrill and penetrating voice.” HERALD.—N. Heinsius, on Petronius, chapter XL, p. 176, Burman ed., conjectures that one should read: “to shout here to no purpose.” Wrongly; for if we read thus, the following “others” has nothing to which it can refer. ORELL.

**Others running about without cause.** Thus Gelenius. The manuscript has “others running about without fault,” doubtless corrupt; from this N. Heinsius, on Petronius, loc. cit., very shrewdly conjectures: “others running about on the stage.” I nevertheless prefer Gelenius’s emendation because of the preceding “these shouting to no purpose.” Arnobius evidently appears to refer to his own times, when the dramatic art had long since degenerated from its former simplicity into [Col. 1268C] excessive affectation and an empty din of words. Meursius conjectures: “others crying out like citizens without cause.” Wrongly. ORELL.

**And maiming themselves with raw boxing-gloves.** The manuscript has “from boxing-gloves,” which N. Heinsius, loc. cit., defends because *se* (“themselves”) has just preceded. We have already several times observed such redundancy of prepositions. ORELL.

**These competing in breath.** Heinsius, loc. cit., conjectures the reading: “constricting the mouth with breath,” which happens when the veins are inflated. But I think nothing should be changed. “To compete in breath” is, unless I am mistaken, to compete in speaking or singing with an uninterrupted, unbroken breath: *wetteifern, wer es länger aushalten könne, in einem Atem fortzureden oder fortzusingen*—“vie to see who can continue speaking or singing longer in a single breath.” ORELL.

**And resounding with empty vows.** The Royal manuscript reads: “and resounding with monstrous vows.” “Salmasius (where, I do not know) reads: ‘and clapping with hollowed hands.’ But hands are mentioned immediately afterward, so that they have no place here. One may suspect that Arnobius wrote ‘and with empty *stlopi*,’ in imitation of Persius, Satire V, 13:

> Nor do you stretch your swollen cheeks to bursting with a *stlopus*.

[Col. 1268D] (A *stlopus* is the sound that bursts forth from puffed-out cheeks.)” Thus Heinsius. Perhaps, with the change of one letter, one should read: *volisque immanibus concrepare* (“resound with mighty palms,” *vola* being the middle part of the hand or, as supposedly here, of the foot), and translate: *mit mächtigen Fersen stampfen*, “stamp with mighty heels.” Better: *mit gewaltigen Händen klatschen*, “clap with powerful hands,” for Arnobius is speaking of the din made by applause. ORELL.

**They raise their hands to heaven**, etc. Heraldus, thinking it absurd that gods who are in heaven should raise their hands to heaven, believes that the whole passage must be rearranged as follows: “resounding with empty vows, raising their hands to heaven, leaping up when moved by astonishing events, shouting aloud; they return to friendship with human beings.” Wrongly, in my opinion. For those gods of whom Arnobius speaks are not remaining in heaven but descending to earth to watch the theatrical games, and so can raise their hands to heaven—which is the gesture of people expressing astonishment. Thus below, chapter XXXVIII of our edition, Jupiter departs from heaven to watch horses repeating their seven circuits. Indeed, even if [Col. 1269C] they were watching those performers from heaven, it would be most biting irony and a witty jest, like that by which Lucian in *Zeus Tragoedus* represents Jupiter praying on behalf of Timocles, the defender of the gods, against the atheist Damis. Nor do the words “moved by astonishing events, they leap up” suit the actors; they suit the gods who are watching. ORELL.

**If from comedies, Atellan farces, mimes**, etc. I was inclined to write *comoedis*, “comic actors.” Atellan farces were rather austere plays, and their actors—called Atellani—are accordingly believed not to have removed their masks. See Festus, author of the entry *Personata*. They were certainly exempt from the infamy attaching to other stage performers, which has already been discussed. Elsewhere I have shown from Livy and Valerius Maximus that all actors apart from Atellani were excluded from military service. STEWECH.

**And undulate with twitching buttocks.** A thoroughly sound reading. See our notes on book II, chapter 42, at the words “undulate with a twitching of the loins.” You may see an image of such a dancing-girl in the Herculanean plates, vol. IV, plate 26, where Murrius observes that this obscene dance was called ἀπόκινος (*apokinos*) by the Greeks. ORELL.]

### XXXIII

But the games that you conduct, which are called the Floralia [Col. 1265A] and the Megalensia, and all the other games that you have determined should be sacred and numbered among the duties of religion—what rationale, what cause do they possess, such that they had to be instituted and established and designated by the names of divine powers?

“The gods,” someone says, “are honored by these; and if they retain any memories of offenses inflicted by human beings, they cast them away, banish them, and, with friendship restored, become our supporters once again.”

And what cause, in turn, makes them tranquil, placid, and gentle? Is it that foolish actions are performed and idle people make sport while a crowd watches? Does Jupiter lay aside his passions if Plautus’s *Amphitryon* has been performed and declaimed? Or does he restrain the agitation of his anger if Europa, Leda, Ganymede, or Danaë has been represented in dance? Does the Great Mother become calmer and more gentle if she sees [Col. 1265B] the ancient story of Attis reenacted by actors? Will Venus forget an offense if she sees a pantomime, in the costume of Adonis, perform the role through movements of dance? [Col. 1266A] Will Alcides’ indignation grow faint if Sophocles’ tragedy called the *Trachiniae*, or Euripides’ *Hercules*, is repeatedly performed? Or does Flora think herself honorably treated if she sees disgraceful acts performed at her games, and sees the brothels transferred into the theaters?

Is this not to diminish the dignity of the gods—to dedicate and consecrate to them the basest deeds, deeds that a censorious mind would reject and whose performers your law has judged to be dishonorable and to be numbered among persons marked by infamy? The gods, of course, delight in mimes, and that transcendent power, which no human nature can comprehend, most willingly lends its ears to listen to men in whose many *symplegmata* [Note: [Col. 1265B] The manuscript has *implegmatibus*, corruptly.] the gods know themselves to be intermingled as material for mockery. They take pleasure, [Col. 1266B] as among us, in the shaven heads of the Stupidi, in the sound [Col. 1267A] and applause of slaps, in indecent deeds and words, and in the redness of enormous phalluses.

And then, if they see men unman themselves into feminine debaucheries; these shouting to no purpose; others running about without cause; others, while preserving the pledge of friendship, pounding one another and maiming themselves [Col. 1268A] with raw boxing-gloves; these competing in breath and distending their cheeks with air; and resounding with empty vows—then the gods raise their hands to heaven, leap up when moved by these astonishing spectacles, shout aloud, and return to friendship with human beings.

If these things bring the immortal gods forgetfulness of their quarrels, if from comedies, Atellan farces, [Col. 1269A] and mimes they derive the most joyful pleasures, why do you delay, why do you hesitate to say that the gods themselves play, frolic, dance, compose obscene songs, and undulate with twitching buttocks? For what difference or distinction does it make whether they do these things themselves or regard their performance by others as objects of love and delight?

[Note: [Col. 1269D]

### XXXIV.—Flowed

Thus Scriverius and all the other editors, as the sense demands. Previously: *fluxi*. ORELL.

**Substance, quality.** The Leiden edition has: “substance of what kind.” ORELL.

**Cessation.** Thus the manuscript. Sabaeus reads “cession”; Fulvius Ursinus, “sitting.” ELMENH.

**And because they see themselves rejoicing and being glad, and becoming sorrowful from more melancholy causes.** This may not appear to be corrupt, yet on thorough consideration the corruption will readily become apparent. For why should he omit the causes of joy but supply those of sorrow, when he afterward passes over neither, saying: “they suppose both that the divine powers rejoice in more cheerful things and that from less joyful things,” etc.? I therefore emend: “and because they rejoice at a joyful event and become sorrowful,” etc. MEURS.—This emendation of Meursius is excellent and deservedly should be admitted into the text. ORELL.

**To be contracted: they think themselves affected by games**, etc. “Affected” depends on the preceding words, “because they see.” Salmasius’s punctuation is therefore bad: “to be contracted. They think themselves affected by games,” etc. ORELL.

**Suffering from enteroceles.** The glosses: “*ramex* . . . ἐντεροκήλη, ‘intestinal hernia.’” An *enterocele* [Col. 1270C] is said to be a kind of hernia in which the blind intestine descends into the scrotum, just as an *epiplocele* occurs when the omentum descends, and a *hydrocele* when fluid flows into one of the testicles. See Celsus, *On Medicine*, book VII, chapter 18. Compare Muncker on Fulgentius, *Mythologies*, book III, chapter 7, p. 122, and Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. ORELL.

**And rendered heavy by the size of enormous hernias.** *Ponderosi* (“heavy”) derives from the weight of the genitals; it is commonly called *gravedo* from the heaviness of the burden. Augustine, in the final book of *The City of God*, chapter 8: “A certain man was cured of a deformed weight of the genitals.” Juvenal calls this a hernia. And Moses, Leviticus, chapter XXI, where he describes what sort of person a minister of God ought to be: “Nor may he approach the ministry if he is heavy.” So the ancient translator in the manuscript; for this the Old Latin version has “herniated.” A hernia, moreover, is called a “weight” because of the rupture caused by a burden, when the intestines descend into the bladder after the membrane is ruptured. Catullus also used *pondera*, “weights,” for the testicles (*Poem* LXIII, 5):

> [Col. 1270D] He himself cast down his weights with a sharp flint.

And Martial, book VI, epigram:

> No foreskin covers a Jewish “weight.”

For this reason Juvenal calls the testicles “two-pounders.” Ovid, however, used “burden of the groin” for “weight” in *Fasti*, book IV. RETR. DANIEL, in the Pseudo-Plautine *Querolus*, p. 59, Padua ed.

Following the conjecture of an anonymous French scholar (see above, in Schoenemann’s *Literary Notice*), we have relegated to the end of our edition the following rather extensive passage, from the words “Come now, in summary” through “they are food for fires and very closely connected with funeral offerings for the dead.” This passage, in which Arnobius must be thought to have brought his work to an apt and elegant conclusion, occupies chapters XXXV–XXXVII of Oberthür’s edition of this book. Accordingly, the following chapter, beginning with the words “But if the immortal gods,” is chapter XXXV in our edition and XXXVIII in Oberthür’s.]

### XXXIV

From what source, then, has this perversity of opinions flowed, or from what causes has it arisen? Chiefly, of course, from this: human beings are unable to know what a god is, what his power, nature, substance, and quality are; whether he possesses a form or is bounded by no bodily outline; whether he does anything or does nothing; whether he remains perpetually awake or is sometimes released into sleep; whether he runs, sits, and walks, or is free from movements and cessation of this kind.

Because, as I have said, they are unable [Col. 1269B] to know any of these things or perceive them through any rational process, they have fallen into such notions that they fashion gods from themselves and give them a nature of actions, circumstances, and desires like the nature they themselves possess. But if they perceived themselves to be animals of no value, and that there was no very great difference between themselves and an ant, they would assuredly cease to suppose that they have anything in common with the gods above, and would confine their modesty within the limits of their own lowliness.

As matters stand, however, because they see that they themselves possess faces, eyes, heads, cheeks, [Col. 1270A] ears, noses, and all the other parts of limbs and internal organs, they suppose that the gods too are fashioned in the same manner and that the gods contain their own form within a corporeal structure. And because they see themselves rejoicing and being glad, and becoming sorrowful from more melancholy causes, they suppose both that the divine powers rejoice in more cheerful things and that, from things less joyful, they are brought into contraction of spirit. They think that they themselves are affected by games, and that the minds of heaven’s inhabitants are soothed by the pleasure of games.

And because they find it a pleasure to warm themselves in the heat of baths, they conclude that the cleanliness afforded by washings is pleasing to the gods above. We human beings gather grapes, and they suppose and believe that the gods too conduct and carry on vintages of their own. We have birthdays, and they assert that the celestial powers and gods have natal days. If they could ascribe states of health, illnesses, and bodily [Col. 1270B] diseases to the gods, they would not hesitate to call them sufferers from diseased spleens, inflamed eyes, and enteroceles, because they themselves are often splenetic and bleary-eyed and rendered heavy by the size of enormous hernias. [Note: [Col. 1269B] The manuscript has *gruenarum*, a thoroughly corrupt reading.]

[Note: [Col. 1270D]

### XXXV.—But if the immortal gods

Thus Fulvius [Col. 1271B] Ursinus, entirely correctly. Others read: “But the gods.” Heraldus conjectures: “If the gods,” omitting “but.” ORELL.

**And changed the condition of the sky and [Col. 1271C] of the weather into a more cheerful state.** Thus the Leiden edition. Previously the reading was: “changed the condition of the sky, the weather”—a construction genuinely characteristic of Arnobius, rashly altered by Meursius to “the settled weather of the sky.” ORELL.

**And certain statues and images were erected upon loftier columns.** For they used to place upon columns images of those whom they wished to be held in the highest honor. Suetonius, in *Galba*: “As soon as it was permitted, the senate had decreed to him a statue standing atop a column adorned with ships’ beaks in the part of the Forum where he had been slain.” Writers report that in the earliest times columns were erected in place of images and worshiped as substitutes for images. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I: “Before the forms of statues had been accurately perfected, the ancients erected pillars and worshiped them as representations of the god.” Eusebius likewise observes this in book I of the *Preparation for the Gospel*. HERALD.

**All the heat and indignation of the divine powers grow cold.** Here *calor* (“heat”) means anger or wrath, as it often does. See C. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book VII, chapter 19, p. 351. ORELL.

**Do not occur without the will of heaven’s inhabitants.** Meursius prefers: [Col. 1271D] “without the pleasure of heaven’s inhabitants.” ORELL.

**And are censured with complete ignorance.** Μετὰ πάσης ἀπειρίας, “with complete inexperience.” HERALD.]

### XXXV  
*(Oberthür XXXVIII)*

“But if the immortal gods,” someone says, “cannot grow angry, and if their nature is neither shaken nor convulsed by any passions of mind, what do the histories mean, what do the annals mean? In their accounts we read that the gods, moved by certain offenses, [Col. 1271A] brought pestilences, barrenness, scarcity of crops, and other dangers upon cities and nations; and that, once appeased in turn by the satisfaction afforded by sacred rites, they laid aside the heat of their indignation and changed the condition of the sky and of the weather into a more cheerful state.

“What is the meaning of those tremors and movements of the earth which, we have learned, occurred because games had been conducted carelessly and had not been performed according to their proper form and prescribed conditions? Yet when these games had been restored and repeated with scrupulous observance, the terrors sent by the gods above subsided, and they were recalled to concern and friendship for humankind.

“How often, at the commands of prophets and the responses of haruspices, after a divine rite was performed, certain gods were summoned from overseas nations, temples were built for them, and certain statues and images were erected upon loftier columns! Then both the fear of imminent [Col. 1271B] dangers was turned aside, the gravest enemies were driven away, and the commonwealth was enlarged by frequent joys of victory and by the possession of numerous provinces. This assuredly would not happen if the gods spurned sacrifices, games, and all other forms of worship, and did not consider themselves honored by the performance of such observances.

“If, therefore, when these things are given, all the heat and indignation of the divine powers grow cold, and the things that appeared to bring terrors are turned to prosperity, it is manifest that all these events do not occur without the will of heaven’s inhabitants, and that our rendering of these observances [Col. 1272A] is censured emptily and with complete ignorance.”

[Note: [Col. 1271D]

### XXXVI.—To the very crux of the case

“The crux of the case” is the same as “the principal point of the case or matter.” See Olaus Borrichius, *Cogitationes*, p. 49. ORELL.

**We have come to the true and most closely connected question.** This is the old reading, deservedly restored to the text by Salmasius. The cause is “most closely connected,” namely, with the aim and design of the work. There is a very similar passage in Cicero, *For Cluentius*, chapter 10, which Gesner aptly compares with ours in his *Thesaurus*: “I shall now state the remainder in a mass, judges, so that I may come to those matters that are nearer and more closely connected with the present case.” Gelenius therefore wrongly interpolated: “and closely joined”; Fulvius Ursinus: “and most just”; Meursius: “and most unassailable.” ORELL.

**Once the fear of superstition has been removed.** Excellent. For superstition arises from an enormous dread of divinity, whereby we recoil from a god as excessively harsh and savage, and [Col. 1272B] therefore zealously pursue every minute detail of divine worship that enters our minds and omit nothing. The Greeks accordingly call this πάθος (“passion”) δεισιδαιμονία (“superstitious dread”), which Plutarch defines as “an emotionally charged belief and a fear-producing conception that abases and crushes the person who believes that gods exist but that they are grievous and harmful.” [Col. 1272C] Cicero calls this dread “an empty fear of the gods” in book I of *The Nature of the Gods*: “For the opinions of all these men remove not only superstition, in which there is an empty fear of the gods,” etc. Hence Varro, as quoted by the blessed Augustine, says that God is revered by the religious person but feared by the superstitious person. Plutarch says, following the judgment of ancient sages, that this dread “abases and crushes” a human being; Lucretius expresses this in book VI, lines 49 ff.:

> The other things that mortals behold occurring  
> on earth and in heaven, while often they hang upon them  
> with frightened minds, render their spirits low  
> through dread of the gods and press them down to earth, etc.

Maximus of Tyre therefore says elegantly in Discourse IV that the pious person is God’s friend, while the superstitious person is God’s flatterer: “The pious man is a friend to God; the superstitious man is God’s flatterer.” [Col. 1272D] HERALD.

**And of the name.** Meursius prefers: “and of the divine power.” ORELL.

**With games and sacrifices.** Fulvius Ursinus added “with games.” ORELL.

**We both read and know it to have been recorded that once, during the Circus Games themselves**, etc. The same story is told by Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 11; Augustine, *The City of God*, book IV, chapter 26; Livy, book II, chapter 36; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book VII, p. 742 (Sylburg); Plutarch, *Coriolanus*; Lactantius, book II, chapter 7; and Valerius Maximus, book I, chapter 8. ELMENH.—Add Cicero, *On Divination*, book I, chapter 22, and Minucius Felix, *Octavius*, chapter VII. In place of “and to have been recorded,” Fulvius Ursinus reads: “and that these same things were recorded.” ORELL.

**Punished him afterward with the penalty of the forked gibbet.** Thus Canterus restored the text from the first Roman edition. Previously it read “the penalty” in the accusative, very badly. In place of *multasse* (“punished”), the manuscript has *mulcasse* (“maltreated”). ORELL.]

To go to the consuls, show that the leader of the dance had displeased him, and that matters could go better for the state, etc. [Col. 1273C] Lipsius thus emended the text in *Epistolary Questions*, Book III, Letter XV. Previously it read: “to advise the consuls,” etc., which makes no sense. Meursius wishes to retain both verbs, reading: “to go to the consuls, advise them, show that the leader of the dance had displeased him, and that matters could go better for the state,” etc. ORELLI.—**Leader of the dance.** Livy (Book II, ch. 36) has *praesultatorem*; Valerius Maximus and Lactantius, in the passages just cited, have *praesultorem*. Plutarch and Dionysius of Halicarnassus have ὀρχηστήν, “dancer.” The Glosses: *praesultor* . . . ὁ ἐν τοῖς ἱεροῖς ὀρχούμενος, “one who dances in sacred rites.” ELMENHORST.—The demon, however, called this fork-bearing slave the leader or foremost dancer because those who are beaten with rods turn about and tremble after the manner of dancers, and are therefore sometimes said, by analogy, to dance. Hence Artemidorus writes that many blows are portended for a slave if he dreams that he is dancing. Thus he says in *Interpretation of Dreams*, Book I, ch. 78: Ὅπως δ’ ἂν ὀρχήσεται δοῦλος, καὶ ὅπου ἂν πολλὰς λήψεται πληγάς. Καὶ ὁ πλέων ἤτοι ναυαγήσει, ἢ καὶ μόνος ἐκπεσὼν κολυμβήσει. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ παιόμενος, ὁ δὲ νηχόμενος κινηθήσεται δι’ ὅλων τῶν σωμάτων: “However and wherever a slave dances, he will receive many blows. A man at sea will either be shipwrecked or, falling overboard alone, will swim; for both the man being beaten and the man swimming will be moved throughout his whole body.” HERALDUS.

**For the hesitating man.** Thus Fulvius Ursinus. Previously: *contatori*. ORELLI.]

### XXXVI. (Oberthür XXXIX.)

Thus, as we speak, we have come to the very point of the case, to its hinge, to the true and most closely pertinent question. We must look into it after removing the fear of superstition and laying aside partiality: whether these are gods whom you assert become savage when offended and are rendered gentle by sacrifices, or whether they are something altogether different and ought to be separated from both the force and the designation of this name.

For we do not deny that all the things you have advanced in opposition are contained in the written annals. We too, according to our measure and the capacity of our intelligence, have read and know it to be recorded that once, at the very circus games held in honor of Jupiter Greatest, [Col. 1272B] before the proceedings had begun, a certain head of a household led across the middle of the circus arena a slave who had behaved very badly, after having him beaten with rods, and in the customary manner afterward punished him with the penalty of the fork. Then, when the games had ended and the races had been completed, not long afterward the city began to be devastated by a plague. And as each day added a more grievous evil to the last and the people died in crowds, Jupiter told a certain rustic—obscure by the lot of his lowly station—in a dream that he should go to the consuls, show that the leader of the dance had displeased him, [Col. 1273A] and declare that matters could go better for the state if due religious observance were restored to his games and they were conducted afresh with scrupulous care.

When the man took no trouble to do this—either because he suspected that the dream was empty and would gain no credence among those who heard it, or because, mindful of his innate lowliness, he fled from and feared an approach to so great an authority—Jupiter became hostile to the hesitant man and inflicted the deaths of his sons as punishment. Soon, when Jupiter threatened the man himself with death unless he proceeded as messenger of the rejected leader, the man was terrified by fear of dying. Since he himself was now also burning with the fever of the plague, on the advice of his relatives he was carried to the senate house. When he had explained the vision of his dream, the flames of the contagion flew from him. The restoration of the games was then decreed, [Col. 1273B] painstaking care was devoted to the spectacles, and the people’s former health was restored.

[Note: [Col. 1273D]

### XXXVII.—Contagion

*Contages* is an archaic form of *contagium*, “contagion.” Lucretius IV, 337:

> Which by their own contagion color everything with pallor.

ORELLI.

**When the Capitol had been struck by lightning.** See Livy, Book XXVII, ch. 4. ELMENHORST.—Oudendorp, in his notes on Julius Obsequens, *On Prodigies*, ch. 122, p. 209, shows by numerous arguments that this Jupiter was different from Capitoline Jupiter and stood upon a column outside the temple of Capitoline Jupiter. He writes that the event occurred in the consulship of Marcus [Col. 1274C] Cicero and Gaius Antonius, in the 690th year from the founding of the City. ORELLI.

**That savage and most grievous events were portended.** Meursius and Stewechius think one should read: “the ill-omened event,” etc. See above, Book I, ch. 16. ORELLI.

**But that these things could be averted—indeed, that the criminal plans could not otherwise be exposed.** Meursius, believing that *posse*, “could,” has been wrongly repeated twice, corrects the text to: “But that these things could be averted—indeed, otherwise,” etc. I approve. ORELLI.

**With the summit raised higher.** Thus Guilielmus for *subrepto*, which was previously read, very badly; according to Stewechius, the manuscript also confirms this correction. *Subrectum culmen* means “a summit erected higher.” Thus Virgil says of Rumor:

> [Col. 1274D] She pricks up so many ears.

ORELLI.]

### XXXVII. (Oberthür XL.)

Nor, again, shall we deny that we know the following: once, in harsh times for the city and the commonwealth, either a hostile plague was destroying the people by wasting them away in continual contagion, or powerful enemies, through success in battle, were already close to the danger of depriving them of their liberty; then, at the commands and admonitions of seers, certain gods were summoned from nations overseas and honored with magnificent temples. They both calmed the fury of the plague and, after the enemies’ strength had been broken, brought victory in triumph very frequently; the boundaries of the empire were enlarged, and innumerable provinces fell beneath the laws of your dominion.

Nor [Col. 1273C] has this escaped our notice: it is read and recorded [Col. 1274A] that, when the Capitol had been struck by lightning, along with many other things within it, even the statue of Jupiter that stood high upon the summit was cast down from its place. The haruspices then issued a response that savage and most grievous events were portended: fires, massacres, the destruction of the laws, and the extinction of justice, but above all danger from domestic enemies and the impious band of conspirators. Yet these things could be averted—indeed, the criminal plans could not otherwise be exposed—unless Jupiter were again set upon a higher summit, turned toward the eastern quarter and facing the rays of the sun. The prediction was confirmed by the event: for when the summit had been raised and the statue turned toward the sun, hidden matters came to light, crimes were disclosed, and punishment was exacted.

[Note: [Col. 1274D]

### XXXVIII.—But if you wish to examine thoroughly the things done, the persons, etc.
