I punctuate and restore: “But if you wish to examine thoroughly the matters, deeds, and persons.” I think a similar passage in Book II of Arnobius, written in a similar way, should be corrected: “But if men knew themselves thoroughly, or if a breath of suspicion received the understanding of God,” where one should read “knew themselves more deeply”; likewise above in this book, “the matter having been examined more deeply,” instead of “thoroughly.” STEWECHIUS.—This correction by Stewechius is also approved by the very learned Oudendorp in his notes on Julius Obsequens, *On Prodigies*, ch. 118, p. 194, Kapp’s edition. *Penitius*, however, is derived not from *penitus* but from *penite*, which Catullus used in *The Wedding of Julia and Manlius*, verse 178:

> No less than you,  
> he burns in his inmost breast  
> with flame, but still more deeply.

ORELLI.

**To the appearance of this name.** Meursius prefers *numinis*, “divinity.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1275B] **Geldings competing in speed and completing seven circuits.** That the ancients favored an odd number as more auspicious, even in military matters, I have shown in more than one passage of my *Commentary on Vegetius*. Yet it is clear that, besides the number three, seven too was regarded as especially suitable for religious observance, from the words of Apuleius in Book II of *The Ass*: “And immediately, in my eagerness for purification, I entrusted myself to a sea-bath, plunging my head beneath the waves seven times, because the divine Pythagoras declared that number especially appropriate to religion.” The seven circuits of the charioteers are very well known. For at top speed they went seven times around the turning posts established in the Circus. Sidonius Apollinaris, in praise of the city of Narbonne, sings as follows among many other things:

> You, redoubled by the very effort,  
> press hard upon the four-horse teams and, with consummate skill,  
> reserve your strength well for the seventh circuit.

STEWECHIUS. Hence Plautus in the *Persian*:

> Come, boy,  
> inaugurate these games from the top with seven cups; move your hands, make haste.

And Lactantius, concluding his work: “Since, having set out, we have run through the proposed work’s seven laps to the finishing post.” HERALDUS.

**Fall headlong.** *Cernuus* means “falling upon the head.” Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, Hymn VII:

> He pressed the moistened dust with his face bowed to the ground.

See Elmenhorst, who discusses this word at length in the index to Apuleius, and Oudendorp on Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* I.15, p. 62 ff. ORELLI.

**To be dragged by the legs and limp with them shattered.** See Sophocles’ *Electra*, where Orestes’ fictitious death is described. HERALDUS.—Fulvius Ursinus reads: “disabled in their legs,” etc. Wrongly. ORELLI.

**Regarded.** Meursius conjectures *habuisset*, “would have regarded,” and in the preceding words *eos tamen gauderet*, “would nevertheless rejoice that they,” instead of *gaudere*. Very badly. ORELLI.

**Which any cheerful man.** Thus the manuscript. This reading is confirmed by the following words: “not trained in the pursuit of complete seriousness and weightiness.” Gelenius’ correction is therefore unnecessary: “which any refined man,” that is, λαμπρόβιος, ἐπαινετὴς μέγας, “one living splendidly, a great man worthy of praise,” as the Glosses explain it. See Elmenhorst. ORELLI.

**Seriousness and weightiness.** *Pondus*, “weight,” is the same as seriousness or authority, in Greek τὸ βάρος, βαρύτης, ὄγκος, “weight, gravity, dignity.” Thus Silius Italicus, verses 428 ff.:

> Upon his brow, beneath his unkempt hair, there rested  
> a terrible beauty and a venerable weight of spirit.

And VIII.609:

> A cheerful gravity in the man and a lovable weight of mind.

So too Trebellius Pollio, *The Thirty Tyrants*, ch. 5: “But distinguished by personal virtue, they lived without the weight of nobility.” See Salmasius there, who discusses this word at length, in *Writers of the Augustan History*, vol. II, p. 263, Hackius’ edition. Ammianus Marcellinus uses it for pride or arrogance joined with disdain in Book XXVII, ch. 9: “The ancient inventors of law, mitigating their bluster and oppressive arrogance, decreed that even some innocent persons should occasionally be eliminated by capital punishments.” See Wagner there, vol. III, p. 198. ORELLI.]

### XXXVIII. (Oberthür XLI.)

All the things that have been said certainly have [Col. 1274B] the appearance of miracles—indeed, they are believed to have it—if they reach human ears just as they are put forward. We do not deny that there is something in them which, when placed, as the saying goes, upon their outer face, can strike [Note: [Col. 1273C] Fulvius reads *praestringere*, “dazzle.”] the ears and deceive through its resemblance to truth. But if you wish to examine thoroughly the events, the persons, and the intentions of the persons, [Note: [Col. 1274C] The manuscript has *voluptates*, “pleasures,” wrongly.] you will find nothing worthy of gods or, as has often been said already, anything that can be related to the appearance and dignity of this name.

For, first, who would believe that he was a god who took pleasure in little horses running to no purpose and considered it most delightful to be summoned by this form of entertainment? Indeed, who would agree that he was [Col. 1274C] that Jupiter whom you call the chief god [Col. 1275A] and the creator of all things that exist—a Jupiter who would set out from heaven to watch geldings competing in speed and completing seven circuits; who nevertheless delighted to see animals he himself had willed to be unequal in bodily swiftness pass and be passed; fall forward and headlong; be overturned backward with their chariots; be dragged by their legs or limp after those legs had been shattered; and who regarded foolishness mixed with trifles and cruelties as the highest pleasures—things that any cheerful man, even one not trained in the pursuit of complete seriousness and weightiness, would consider childish and disdain as mere sport?

Who, I ask—let us repeat this phrase continually—would believe that he belonged to the divine race who, because a man destined to pay the penalties and punishments for his conduct was led through the arena during the games, became inflamed with rage and girded himself [Col. 1275B] for the forces of vengeance? For if the slave was guilty and deserved to be punished by that correction, why should Jupiter have been moved by any indignation, when nothing unjust was being done and, indeed, a guilty person was being chastised with fitting penalties? But if the slave was free from wrongdoing and liable to no charge, Jupiter himself was responsible for the defective leader of the dance: though able to aid him, he did not do so. Indeed, he himself contrived both that what he disapproved should be suffered and that penalties for his own permission should be exacted from others. And why [Col. 1276A] did he afterward complain and announce that he had been injured in the person of that leader because the man had been led through the middle of the circus to the punishment of the cross, torn by rods and whips?

[Note: [Col. 1276C]

### XXXIX.—We ought to pardon

Thus the first edition, approved by Canterus and the Leiden editor. Gelenius and others read: “there is reason why we ought to pardon.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1276D] **By a pardonable concession.** That is, by the granting of pardon, with pardon granted. ORELLI.

**Breaths of air.** A very similar passage occurs in Vegetius, *On Military Matters*, Book III, ch. 2: “If, in autumn or summer, a multitude of soldiers remains too long in the same places, then from polluted drafts, through contamination of the waters and the foulness of the very odor, and from corrupted air, a most destructive disease arises.” N. Heinsius collected further examples in *Adversaria*, Book I, ch. 17, p. 183. ORELLI.

**He declared plague, disease, and a massacre of mortality.** Fulvius Ursinus conjectures *induxit*, “introduced.” Wrongly. See the note on Book I, ch. 3. N. Heinsius, *Adversaria*, p. 183, prefers: “he declared a massacre against mortality,” that is, against mortals. The correction is unnecessary, for in Arnobius’ age the use of *mortalitas*, “mortality,” for a mass death was not novel. Thus Salvian, *On the Governance of God*, Book VII, p. 153, Bromius’ edition—a passage aptly cited by Meursius: “Just as the people fell because of Achar’s theft, just as plague arose from Saul’s jealousy, just as mass death arose from holy David’s census.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1277C] **Took less care to ascertain.** The reading is entirely sound and should by no means be altered. Here *ediscere* means “to inquire, ask.” The consequent stands for the antecedent, as very frequently. Pighius and Stewechius therefore wrongly conjecture *edicere*, “to proclaim,” interpreting it of the proclamation by the man who presented the games, or the notice specifying for what god, goddess, or purpose the coming games were to be held. That does not fit here at all. ORELLI.

**Whom the condition of their weakness has excluded from public business.** [Col. 1277D] Ulpian, Book I, *On Sabinus*: “Women are removed from all civil or public duties.” Livy, Book XXXIV, ch. 2, in Cato’s speech: “Our ancestors did not wish women to conduct even any private business without a guardian; they were to be under the authority of parents, brothers, and husbands.” ELMENHORST.]

### XXXIX. (Oberthür XLII.)

And what stain or foulness could have flowed from this deed, so as either to render the circus less pure or contaminate Jupiter, when at every brief instant and point of time he beheld so many thousands throughout the world perish in various kinds of death and under different tortures? “He was led across,” you say, “before the games began to be performed.” If this was done with a sacrilegious heart and in contempt of religion, we ought to pardon Jupiter for being indignant that he was despised and that insufficient care was devoted to his own circus games. But if through error or accident that hidden defect was not noticed and recognized, would it not have been right and fitting for Jupiter to pardon human [Col. 1276B] lapses and grant the blindness of ignorance a pardonable concession?

But the matter had to be avenged. And after this will anyone believe that he was a god who avenged and punished neglect of a childish entertainment with the destruction of a city? Will anyone believe that he possessed any firmness of seriousness, weight, or constancy, when, so that races might be run afresh for his pleasurable delight, he turned the air they breathed into poisonous destruction and, through the disease of pestilence, decreed mass death? If the magistrate presenting the games [Col. 1277A] took insufficient care to ascertain who had been led through the middle of the circus that day, and guilt was contracted from this, what had the unfortunate people deserved, that they should pay for another’s offenses with punishments upon their own lives and be cruelly driven from life by pestilential contagions? Indeed, what had the race of women done, whom the condition of their weakness has excluded from public business? What had grown [Note: [Col. 1277C] Sab.’s manuscript has “adulterous.”] virgins done? What had tiny boys done? What, finally, had infants still being nourished under the care of nurses done, that one and the same savagery should be sent against them and that they should experience the bitterness of death before any sweetness of the light?

[Note: [Col. 1277D]

### XL.—If Jupiter himself

Thus Meursius in his Appendix and the Leiden edition. The manuscript has: “Jupiter himself.” Gelenius and the others: “If Jupiter.” ORELLI.

**Restore.** The first edition has: “restored.” ORELLI.

**Be prolonged further and increased.** Thus Stewechius from the manuscript. The first edition has: “prolonged . . . increased”; others: “to prolong . . . to increase.” In his Appendix Meursius understands *augere*, “increase,” passively, as *movere*, “move,” may mean “move oneself.” ORELLI.

**That the consul should come to him.** Others: “the consul or to him.” ORELLI.

**Would it not have been more direct?** Meursius suspects one should read: “would it not have been more upright?” But the received reading is sound. *Pronius* means “easier,” *leichter, weniger gewaltthätig*—“less violent.” ORELLI.

**Subdue his will.** Meursius and Stewechius prefer: [Col. 1278C] “subject his will.” But “subdue” is stronger and more expressive. ORELLI.

**But he also caused the man himself to be seized by the savagery of the pestilence.** The word is ancient. Lucretius VI, 1096:

> And all that force of diseases and pestilence.

And verse 1123:

> This sudden new disaster and pestilence, therefore.

HERALDUS.

[Col. 1278D] **And his disobedient delay.** Thus Salmasius from the manuscript and in his notes on Solinus, p. 24. *Obaedio*, *obaedus*, *inobaedus*: “one who does not obey.” The dictionaries, however, recognize no other authority for this adjective besides our passage. In his Appendix Meursius thinks one should write *in obedientia cessatio*, “delay in obedience,” which, when abbreviated by copyists, gave rise to the erroneous *inobeda*. Gelenius and the others printed *in obeundo cessatio*, “delay in carrying it out.” ORELLI.

**What savagery, what cruelty was so great that...** Thus Meursius and the Leiden edition. Others read: “What was that savagery of cruelty? What so great...” Wrongly. Stewechius prefers: “What was that savagery? What cruelty so great?” ORELLI.

**Removed.** Thus Gelenius and those who followed him, very rightly. The first edition has: “returned.” ORELLI.

**In empty display.** This most correct emendation too is owed to Gelenius. The manuscript has: “in another display.” Fulvius Ursinus: “in a display of evil.” Meursius: “in an evil display.” ORELLI.]

### XL. (Oberthür XLIII.)

If Jupiter desired games to be conducted more scrupulously for himself and restored; if he wished faithfully to restore the people’s health and not to prolong further and increase the evil he had caused, [Col. 1277B] would it not have been more proper for him to go to the consul himself, to one of the public priests, the chief pontiff, or his own Flamen Dialis, and through a dream disclose to him both the defect in the leader of the dance and the cause of that deadly season? What reason was there for him to choose as the messenger of his will and the agent of the satisfaction he demanded a man accustomed to the countryside, unknown because of his obscure name, ignorant of urban affairs, and perhaps not even knowing what a leader of the dance was? [Note: [Col. 1278C] Sab.’s manuscript has *diligeret*, “esteem.”]

If, provided only that he was divine, he certainly knew this man would prove evasive in obeying him, would it not have been more direct and fitting for a god to change the man’s mind and subdue his will to obey rather than enter upon more savage courses and rage indiscriminately, like a robber, without any principle? For if the rustic, being old and ill-equipped for carrying out affairs, hesitated over the commanded matter because he was hindered by the reasons given above, what had his unfortunate children deserved, that anger and indignation should be turned against them [Col. 1278A] and that they should pay for another’s offenses by the deprivation of their own lives? Is there anyone among men who would believe that he was a god when he was so unjust, so impious, and did not even observe the ordinances of mortals, among whom it would be regarded as a great abomination for one person to be punished for another and for the offenses of some to be avenged upon the necks of others?

“But he also caused the man himself to be seized by the savagery of the pestilence.” Would it not therefore have been better—indeed, more just—if this seemed necessary, for the terror of coercion to begin with the father himself, in whom lay the cause of so great a disturbance and the disobedient delay, rather than to do violence to his children to cause him pain and to burn up and destroy innocent persons? What savagery, what cruelty was so great that, after his offspring had been destroyed, the father was afterward frightened with dangers to his own life? If Jupiter had long before wished to do this—that is, in the first place—innocent siblings would not have been destroyed, and the offended will of the divine power would have become known.

“But when the duty of reporting had been fulfilled, the illness immediately vanished and the man was at once restored to health.” And what is marvelous about this, if Jupiter removed the evil he had inspired and vaunted himself in an empty display? If you weigh the matter thoroughly, that was cruelty rather than the benefit of health, since he preserved the wretched man, who desired to die after his sons, not for the joys of life, but so that he might come to know his loneliness and feel the torments of bereavement.

[Note: [Col. 1278D]

### XLI.—Lest disgust be produced by excess

After [Col. 1279C] these words, the Roman edition and the manuscript insert an entire page. With Stewechius, Nourry, and others, we have arranged for it to be printed after the end of Arnobius’ text, as spurious and a mere repetition of what precedes. ORELLI.

**Aesculapius, you say, from Epidaurus, etc.** Lactantius, Book II, ch. 7: “Equally marvelous is the report that, when a plague was raging, Aesculapius was summoned from Epidaurus and freed the city of Rome from a protracted pestilence.” Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 8; Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV.622; Augustine, *City of God*, Book III, ch. 17; Livy, Book X; Orosius, Book III, ch. 22. ELMENHORST.

**A snake of great bulk.** Meursius plausibly corrected this [Col. 1279D] from Lucretius, who uses *augmen* for bodily mass in Book I, 434 ff.:

> For whatever it may be, it must itself be something,  
> of great or little bulk, at any rate, while it exists.

Likewise Book III, 269:

> And yet from all these  
> there arises the single bulk of the completed body.

And in other passages. Yet the received reading *agminis*, “train,” can be defended from Ausonius, *Moselle* 138, cited by Meursius himself:

> Thus through the straits in greatness  
> you glide, and scarcely unwind the trains of your long body.

Here *agmina*, “trains,” are what Virgil and Apuleius call *volumina*, “coils.” ORELLI.

**What, then, shall we say?** Thus the manuscript, as below: “What, then, shall we say? That famous Hannibal,” etc. Others have “do we say?” STEWECHIUS.

[Col. 1280C] **Dragging itself along in winding coils.** Germanicus, in the *Phaenomena* of Aratus, verses 48 ff.:

> Between these, like a broken river,  
> a monstrous serpent twists its winding coils.

ELMENHORST. Zeno of Verona, in his sermon *On Patience*: “Yet, recoiling in the pale curve of its outermost coils, as though acknowledging the earth’s right and avoiding its violation, it breaks against itself with marvelous patience and is checked by the same waves by which it is driven.” HERALDUS.]

### XLI. (Oberthür XLIV.)

By a similar method it will be possible to proceed through other histories and show that in them too something far different from what gods ought to be is said of these very beings and indicated in the exposition of those histories. Consider this very account, which I shall set out next together with one or two others, lest disgust be produced by excess.

“After certain gods had been brought,” you say, “from nations overseas, after temples had been founded for them [Col. 1279A] and altars heaped with sacrifices, the sick people revived and recovered, and pestilential diseases fled when health was restored.” Which gods, please tell us? “Aesculapius,” you say, “a god presiding over good health, brought from Epidaurus and established on the island in the Tiber.”

If it were our intention to treat these matters more scrupulously, we would establish from your own authorities that he was certainly no deity, since he was conceived and born from a woman’s womb, and advanced through the stages of years to that end of life at which the force of a thunderbolt, as your writings relate, expelled him both from life and from the light. But we leave that question aside. Let the son of Coronis be, as you wish, one of the immortals and endowed with everlasting heavenly sublimity.

Nevertheless, what else was brought from Epidaurus but a snake of great bulk? If we follow the authority of the annals and attribute established truth to them, nothing else, as it is written. What, then, shall we say? Is this Aesculapius whom you proclaim an eminent god, a holy god, a giver of health, the repeller, restrainer, and destroyer of the worst diseases, bounded by the shape and outline of a serpent? Does he crawl over the earth; scrape the ground with chin and breast, as worms born in mud are accustomed to do; drag himself along in winding coils; and, so that he may make any forward progress at all, draw the hindmost part of himself onward by the efforts of the foremost?

[Note: [Col. 1280C]

### XLII.—Relieving bodies of filth whose foulness is to be abhorred

Th. Canterus very correctly restored this passage from the Roman edition. [Col. 1280D] Others have: “the bodies having been relieved.” ORELLI.

**So that he could disguise who he was, or observe what sort of men they were.** The final phrase is certainly feeble and false. What, then? Could he not see what sort of men they were, so that he had for that reason to put on the form of a snake? Nor is there anything of that kind in what follows. I emend: “so that he could disguise himself, and who or what he was might thereby be less discernible.” *Intueri*, “to discern,” is passive, as Lucretius more than once uses *tueor*. MEURSIUS, p. 219.—Meursius’ conjecture is ingenious. The reading we have given derives from Gelenius. The first edition has: “who he was or what sort men to behold,” which makes no sense. Fulvius Ursinus conjectures: “nor could men behold who or what he was.” ORELLI.

**He ought not to have denied himself to the sight of their eyes.** For my part, I think these words should be deleted. They were perhaps stitched in by an ignorant copyist who wanted some antithesis to the preceding words, “nor ought he to have wished to be seen in the form of a serpent.” Certainly everything flows better when they are omitted. ORELLI.]

### XLII. (Oberthür XLV.)

And since we read that he also consumed foods by which life is prolonged in bodies, he has gaping jaws with which to swallow foods sought through the openings [Col. 1279C] of his mouth. He has the receptacle of a belly [Col. 1280A] and entrails in which to digest what has been chewed and swallowed, so that blood may be supplied to the body and renewed strength furnished. He also has terminal passages through which unclean refuse departs, relieving bodies of filth whose foulness is to be abhorred.

Whenever he changes places and prepares to pass from one region to another, he does not, like a god, fly unseen through the stars of heaven and in a moment of time stand wherever the occasion requires. Rather, like a brute animal, he seeks a vehicle to support him. He avoids the waves of the sea and, so that he may be kept safe and unharmed, boards a ship with human beings; and that god of public health entrusts himself to fragile wood and the joining of planks.

We do not think you can prove and establish that this serpent was Aesculapius, unless you wish to introduce the pretext that the god transformed himself into a snake so that he could disguise who he was, or observe what sort of men they were. If you say this, the very inconsistency of the facts will show how weakly and ineffectually it is said. [Note: [Col. 1279C] Sab.’s manuscript has “are proclaimed.”] For if the god sought to avoid being seen by human beings, he ought not to have wished to be observed in the form of a serpent, since in any form he would be no one other than himself, but would still be himself. But if he intended to make himself visible, he ought not to have denied himself to the sight of their eyes. Why did he not allow himself to be seen as he knew himself to be and as he knew himself to be contained within the power of his own divinity? For this would have been more appropriate, far more excellent, and fitting to majestic dignity than becoming a beast, being transformed into the likeness of a fearsome animal, and providing an opportunity for doubtful contradictions as to whether he was a true god or some other thing, far removed from heavenly sublimity. [Col. 1280C]

[Col. 1281A] [Note: [Col. 1281C]

### XLIII.—Had concealed himself

Thus Canterus from the Roman edition. Others: “concealed himself.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1281D] **If the functions of particular persons among you are assigned to particular persons. Since the matter stands thus.** I punctuate in this way with Meursius. Others punctuate: “if the functions of particular persons are assigned to particular persons among you. Since the matter stands thus.” ORELLI.

**And your religion.** Meursius deletes “and.” Wrongly. ORELLI.

**This snake, of course.** Meursius conjectures: “this snake, nevertheless, if the word is permissible.” This is good, for there follows: “or, if this name is sordid,” from which we infer that the Latin designation *colubra* or *coluber*, “snake,” was considered more sordid and contemptible than *anguis* or *serpens*, “serpent.” ORELLI.

**But supported on his belly.** Thus the manuscript. Others use a variant spelling of “supported.” ORELLI.

**A back covered with scales.** Thus Fulvius Ursinus. The manuscript and earlier editions have: “smeared.” ORELLI.

**That serpent slain by Regulus with the force of an army.** See Florus, Book II, ch. 2, §20; Livy’s *Epitome*, Book XVIII; Aulus Gellius, Book VI, ch. 3; Valerius Maximus, Book I, ch. 8, no. 19 in the text; Pliny, *Natural History* VIII, ch. 14; Obsequens, *Prodigies*, ch. XXIX. ORELLI.

**Surpassed in length of body and strength.** “Length of strength” offends Meursius, who prefers to correct it either to “surpassed in length of body and magnitude of strength” [Col. 1282C] or “surpassed in length of body and in strength.” The received reading can, however, be defended as zeugma or syllepsis, [Col. 1282D] a figure frequently employed by the best writers. ORELLI.

**What.** Thus the first edition from the manuscript. Others: “who.” ORELLI.

**Had concealed himself.** Thus Canterus from the Roman edition. Others: “concealed himself.” ORELLI.

**Passageways.** See above on Book VI, ch. 52. ORELLI.]

### XLIII. (Oberthür XLVI.)

“But if he was not a god,” someone says, “why, after he had brought himself out of the ship, did he crawl to the island in the Tiber, immediately disappear, and cease to be seen as before?” Can we know whether there was some obstacle behind whose obstruction and barrier he concealed himself, or some opening? You must pronounce upon it; you must say what that thing was or to what class of things it should be assigned, if among you the functions of particular persons are assigned to particular persons.

Since the matter stands thus, and since it is your divine power and your religion that are under discussion, it is rather for you to teach and show what that thing was than to wish to hear our opinions and await our judgments. For what else can we say except what actually occurred and was seen—what all the histories have handed down and what was grasped by the senses of the eyes?

[Col. 1281B] We nevertheless call this, of course, a snake of exceedingly powerful body and immense length; or, if this name is sordid, we call it an *anguis*, a serpent; or we designate it by any other name that usage supplies us or amplification of speech fashions. For if he crawled like a snake, not conveying himself on feet or unfolding strides of his own, but supported on belly and breast; if, formed from the material of flesh, he extended his length in a slippery mass; if he had a head and tail, a back covered with scales, variegated with colored spots, and a mouth bristling with teeth and equipped to inflict bites—what else can we do but say that he belonged to an earthly kind, however monstrous and enormous he may have been, and however much he may have surpassed in length of body and strength that serpent slain by Regulus with the force of an army?

But we suppose something else, and we undermine and destroy the truth. It is therefore for you to explain what he was, of what kind, of what name, and of what quality. For how could he be a god when he possessed the features we have described, which gods ought not to possess if they think that they are gods and possess the eminence belonging to this designation?

“After he crawled to the island in the Tiber [Col. 1282A] he immediately appeared nowhere; from this it is shown that he was a divine power.” Can we know whether there was some obstacle belonging to some object there, behind whose obstruction and barrier he concealed himself, or some opening, or passageways and arches among masses piled unevenly, into which he rapidly carried himself after escaping the spectators’ line of sight? What if he leapt across the river? What if he swam across it? What if he took himself into the dense woods [Note: [Col. 1281C] Fulvius Ursinus thus supplies the words.]? It is a feeble argument to suspect for this reason that the serpent was a god—because with the utmost haste he withdrew himself from their eyes—when by the very same argument it can in turn be shown that he was not a god.

[Note: [Col. 1282C]

### XLIV.—If from the books of fate

When the Romans were oppressed by misfortunes or entangled in diseases, they consulted the books of fate. Livy, Book V: “It was found in the books of fate that the gods had to be appeased in order to ward off the plague”; and several times elsewhere. ELMENHORST.

**Was afflicted by the disasters of this evil? Was so often torn and harassed at one time after another, and diminished by the slaughter of countless thousands of citizens? For since, etc.** Thus Meursius and Stewechius, followed by the other editors, supplement the text from the manuscript. Previously it read: “was afflicted by thousands of this evil? For since,” etc., which makes no sense. Others read “kinds” for “times.” ORELLI.

**Allowed deserving cities to suffer the plague for a longer time.** This reading is, at least in my judgment, entirely sound. For some unknown reason the Leiden editor changed it to: “allowed the plague of the deserving city to continue for a longer time.” ORELLI.]

### XLIV. (Oberthür XLVII.)

“But if that serpent was not a present god, why after his arrival was the force of the pestilence [Col. 1282B] broken and health restored [Note: [Col. 1281C] The manuscript has: “health was restored.”] to the Roman people?”

We answer in turn: if, on the authority of the books of fate and the responses of seers, the god Aesculapius was ordered to be invited to the city so that he might preserve it safe and unharmed from the contagion of plague and pestilential diseases; and if, as you say, he came without disdain, transformed into the shape of a snake, why was the Roman [Note: [Col. 1282C] Sab.’s manuscript has “Rome.”] state so often afflicted by the disasters of this evil? Why was it so often torn and harassed at one time after another and diminished by the slaughter of countless thousands of citizens?

For since the god is said to have been summoned for this purpose, that he might wholly avert all the causes by which pestilence was generated, it followed that the city ought to have remained untouched and always to have been preserved immune and unharmed by its destructive breath. Yet we see, as was said above, that these diseases very often brought it courses of life that ended in death, [Col. 1282C] and that the people’s strength was broken and enfeebled by no slight losses.

Where, then, was Aesculapius? Where was he who had been promised by the venerable oracles? After temples had been founded and sanctuaries built for him, why did he allow deserving cities [Note: [Col. 1282C] The manuscript has “the deserving city.”] to suffer the plague for a longer time, when he had been summoned for this purpose: both to remedy the evils already pressing upon them [Col. 1283A] and not to permit anything of this kind that might be feared to creep in during the future?

[Note: [Col.

[Col. 1283C]

XLV.—“If either in ancient times,” etc. Thus the Leiden edition. [Col. 1283D] Others delete *in*. ORELLI.

**To merit.** Thus the manuscript. Others read *merere*, a form used by earlier writers. ORELLI.

**Assumed the renown of Preserver.** Σωτῆρος, “Savior.” For he wished to express the Greek appellation by which either gods or men who were believed to have warded dangers away from others were distinguished. Thus Castor and Pollux are called εὐεργέται ἀνθρώπων καὶ σωτῆρες, “benefactors and saviors of humankind,” by Plutarch in his *Theseus*. But on this more fully elsewhere. HERALDUS.

**To have strayed.** Thus the Roman edition. Others: “to have wandered.” CANTER.]

### XLV. (Oberthür XLVIII)

Unless perhaps someone will say that, in later and succeeding ages, the protection of such a god was lacking because people were by then living with impious and reprehensible morals, whereas he brought aid to earlier generations because they were innocent and removed from every contagion of wickedness. This might perhaps have been said and heard with some reason if, in ancient times, either everyone without exception had been good, or the succeeding ages had produced everyone evil and without any differentiation among them.

But since the fact is that among great peoples and nations—indeed, even in every city—the human race is mixed in its dispositions, wills, and morals, and good and evil persons alike could have existed both in earlier centuries and in more recent [Col. 1283B] ages, it is foolish enough to say that, because of their wickedness, later mortals did not merit the assistance of the divine powers. For if, because of the evil people of succeeding ages, the good people of later times were not protected, then because of the evil people of antiquity the good among the ancients likewise ought not to have merited the benevolence of the divine powers. But if, because of the good ancients, the evil ancients too were preserved, then because of the later good people, the succeeding age too, although reprehensible, ought to have been protected.

Either, therefore, after the force of the disease had already been broken and rendered harmless, that serpent which was brought over assumed the renown of Preserver, although it had brought no benefit whatsoever; or it must be said that the oracular verses of fate strayed far from truthful predictions, since the remedy given by them is found to have assisted, not all generations thereafter, but only a single [Col. 1283C] age.

[Note: [Col. 1283D]

XLVI.—“But the Great Mother also,” he says, “was summoned from Phrygian Pessinus.” Livy, book XXIX, chs. 11 and 14; Augustine, *The City of God*, book III, ch. 12; Tertullian, *Apologeticum*, ch. 25; Minucius Felix; Lactantius, book II, ch. 7; Cicero, *On the Response of the Haruspices*. ELMENHORSTIUS and ORELLI.

**Of a dusky and black color.** Prudentius, περὶ Στεφάνων (*On the Crowns*), called it “a blackish stone.” ELMENHORSTIUS.—Compare Bronkhusius on Propertius, p. 477. ORELLI.

[Col. 1284C] **Uneven with projecting little corners.** Stewechius restored Arnobius’ diminutive *angellis* (“little corners”) from the manuscript, followed by the Leiden edition. Others read *ungulis* (“little claws”). ORELLI.]

### XLVI. (Oberthür XLIX)

“But the Great Mother also,” he says, “summoned from Phrygian Pessinus in accordance with the prophets’ commands, brought salvation to the people and was the cause of great rejoicing. For a powerful enemy of long standing was driven from possession of Italy; [Col. 1284A] the city’s former glory was restored by glorious and illustrious victories; the boundaries of its empire were extended far and wide; the right to liberty was wrested from innumerable nations, cities, and peoples, and the yoke of servitude imposed upon them; and many other accomplishments abroad and at home established the nation’s name and majesty with unassailable firmness.”

If the histories speak the truth and introduce no falsehoods into their records of events, they state that nothing else at all was brought from Phrygia and sent by King Attalus except a certain stone, not large, which could be carried in a person’s hand without any exertion: dusky and black in color, uneven with projecting little corners [Note: [Col. 1283C] Thus Sabaeus. The manuscript has *angallis*, wrongly]; and today we all see that very stone placed in the image at the position of the face, unworked and rough, giving the statue, through mere imitation, a face insufficiently represented. [Col. 1284B]

[Note: [Col. 1284D]

XLVII.—**To the pinnacle of empire.** Thus Stewechius. Others read “summit.” See above, the note on book I, ch. 8. ORELLI.

**Sooty in color and black in body.** Fulvius Ursinus deletes *corporis* (“in body”). ORELLI.

**And who among men.** Sabaeus reads *qui*, which, as we showed above, is sometimes used by these writers in place of *quis*. ORELLI.

**That something subject to some divine power dwelt in the fragments of flint in the manner and was hidden in its veins.** This is the manuscript’s reading, restored to the text by Stewechius and Salmasius. But what it means I frankly confess that I do not know. Gelenius printed: “That a mass subject to some divine power dwelt in fragments of flint.” Stewechius prefers “the underlying moisture,” or rather, “matter.” But what is the moisture or matter of a divine power? I prefer Fulvius Ursinus’ emendation: “the underlying majesty.” What if we read: “That the power of some divine being dwelt, wonderfully (θαυμαστῶς), implanted in fragments of flint,” etc.? ORELLI.

[Col. 1285C] **And hidden in its veins.** He takes this from Virgil, *Georgics* I.135:

> That from the flint’s veins he might strike out the hidden fire.

HERALDUS.

**Why did she not bravely present herself to the threatening danger?** The sentence was inverted and the words distorted by inept pedants, whose rashness and ignorance are exposed by the manuscripts, since they read: “Why did she not present herself to threatening *forti*?” Among the ancients *fors, fortis, forti* was declined with the meaning “fortune, chance.” Nor is it in Arnobius alone, to my knowledge, that this word has been corrupted: I observe that it must be restored in at least three passages of the Justinian Code, and I note this on the law *Si cum*, Code, *On Gifts before Marriage*. On ancient stones and coins this inscription presents itself everywhere: FORTI FORTUNAE, “To Mighty Fortune.” Terence, *Phormio*: “What chance (*fors*) brings, we shall bear with an untroubled mind.” From the noun *fors* the grammarians form adverbs of various shapes, such as *forsan, forsitan, fortasse,* and *fortassis*, although *fors* itself is also used adverbially, as in Virgil, *Aeneid* V.232:

> And perhaps, with prows abreast, they would have won the prize.

See Nonius, Charisius, and others. STEWECHIUS.

**Never demands to be asked.** That is, wishes or desires. Thus Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII.707:

> We ask to be priests and to guard your shrines.

The comic poets familiarly use *postulare* in the same sense. See J. F. Gronovius on Gellius IV.1 and Ruhnken on Rutilius Lupus, p. 134. ORELLI.]

### XLVII. (Oberthür L)

What, then, shall we say? Was it a stone that drove from Italy that Carthaginian Hannibal, that powerful and formidable enemy beneath whom the Roman state, uncertain and precarious, trembled, and its greatness quaked with fear? Was it a stone that broke him, a stone that made him a frightened fugitive unlike himself? And when the state again sprang up to the pinnacle of empire and royal supremacy, was nothing accomplished by planning, nothing by human strength? Did the military knowledge or practical experience of so many great commanders contribute nothing to the recovery of its ancient eminence?

Did a stone give some men strength and others a weakness of vigor? Did it drive these men from prosperity and raise up the fortunes of others when they lay prostrate in despair? And who among men [Col. 1284C] would believe [Note: [Col. 1283C] Sabaeus reads “believes”] that a stone taken from the earth, responsive to no sensation, sooty in color and black in body [Note: [Col. 1283C] Fulvius deletes this word], was the mother of the gods? Or who, again, would accept—this being the only possibility left—that something subject to some divine power dwelt in fragments of flint in the manner [Note: [Col. 1284C] Fulvius reads “a mass”], hidden in its veins? [Col. 1285A]

And from what source was victory obtained if no divine power was present in the Pessinuntine stone? We may say that it came from the diligence and courage of the combatants, from practice, opportunity, planning, and reason; we may even say that it came from fate and the alternating vicissitudes of fortune. But if affairs were improved by the stone’s assistance and a happy victory was recovered [Note: [Col. 1285C] The manuscript has the older spelling *reciperata*], where was that Phrygian Mother at the time when, after so many great armies had been slaughtered, the whole state was brought low and reached the danger of utter ruin? Why did she not bravely present herself to the threatening danger? Why did she not break and repel the immense assaults of war before those monstrous blows fell, by which all blood was poured out and life itself almost collapsed when its vital powers had been drained?

“For she had not yet been brought over, nor had she been asked to bestow her favor” [Note: [Col. 1286C] Sabaeus reads “fear”]. But a good helper never demands to be asked, always coming to the rescue through spontaneous assistance. “Separated as she still was by a vast extent of sea and habitable lands, she could not drive out and put the enemy to flight.” But for a god, if god she is, nothing at all is distant: to such a being the earth is a point, and all things are placed beneath her command. [Col. 1285B]

[Note: [Col. 1286C]

XLVIII.—**Slaughters.** The new sense of the word *mortalitas* as “slaughter” should be noted, although it was not new in that age. It occurs also in Salvian, book VII: “As the people fled because of Achan’s theft, as a pestilence arose because of Saul’s jealousy, as mortality arose from David’s censuses.” So too *mortalis* means “deadly, pestilential” in Cyprian, book I, epistle 7: “Nor should they listen to those who deceive them through false and deadly circumvention.” And in *On the Good of Patience*: “Adultery, fraud, and murder are mortal crimes.” MEURSIUS, p. 221.—Here, therefore, *mortalitas* means what in German we call *ein Sterben*, “a dying-off.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1286D] **Believe.** Fulvius adds *credat*, “believe,” as the sense requires. ORELLI.

**Raised others to the pinnacle of dominion.** A sound reading, as we showed in the note on book II, just now: “And when it again sprang up to the pinnacle of empire and royal supremacy.” That is, “raised”

> The Romans, lords of all things, and the toga-clad nation.

HERALDUS.

**Subjugated the innocent world.** With these words the entire work is concluded in the other editions. Because this ending of the book is excessively abrupt, Fulvius Ursinus concludes that the book is mutilated and incomplete. By relegating chapters XXXV–XXXVII of the other editions to the end, however, we shall give the book an entirely suitable conclusion, most worthy of this excellent work. See what we noted above before ch. XXXVIII. ORELLI.]

### XLVIII. (Oberthür LI)

But let the divine power have been present in that very stone, as you demand that we believe. Is there any mortal, however credulous he may be and however readily he may lend an ear to any fictions whatsoever, who would judge that she either was a goddess at that time or ought today to be spoken of and called one—she who now covets this and now demands that; who abandons and disdains her worshippers; who migrates from humbler provinces and attaches herself to more powerful and wealthier peoples?

“But she loves military affairs and desires to be amid battles, slaughter, carnage, [Col. 1285C] and bloodshed.” If it is proper to the gods—provided that they are genuine gods and deserve to be designated by the force of that word and by divine power—to do nothing maliciously, nothing unjustly, and to offer themselves to all human beings with one and equal favor, without any partiality, [Col. 1286A] let no one among men believe that she was of divine stock or possessed an equity worthy of the gods: for she inserted herself into human conflicts, shattered the resources of some, and offered and presented herself to others as their patroness; took liberty from these and raised others to the pinnacle of dominion; and, so that one city might tower above all others, was born for the destruction of the human race and subjugated the innocent world.

[Note: [Col. 1286D]

XLIX.—**Let us compare them by setting the individual parts in opposition.** I read: “the individual pairs.” HERALDUS.

**And which.** Others: “which.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1287C] **We swear with unhesitating assurance.** Fulvius Ursinus prefers “we confirm” or “we judge.”

**Because we hold and think that arts are not necessary to the gods, and it is established and clear that they were devised as an aid to poverty.** This is how I read from the Roman edition in place of: “and we think that these are not; it is established and clear,” etc. It would, however, be far more elegant if, with our Lipsius (*Epistolary Questions*, book III, epistle XV), we read *quas* (“which”) in place of *et eas* (“and these”); and perhaps the author wrote it so. [Col. 1287D] CANTER.—Meursius also approves Lipsius’ emendation. ORELLI.]

### XLIX. (Oberthür XXXV)

Come now: since our discourse has been extended and brought to this point, let us briefly compare the individual parts by setting them in opposition, to determine whether you hold better opinions concerning supernatural things, [Col. 1286B] or whether we, rather, think about them far more honorably and correctly, and in a way that gives and assigns divine reality its proper dignity.

First, you profess that the gods whom you either think or believe to exist in the universe, and whose images and forms you have erected in all your temples, were born and were begotten from the seeds of males and females according to the law of sexual unions. We, by contrast, hold that if there truly are gods, possessing the authority, power, and dignity of this name, they are either unbegotten—for this is the reverent belief—or, if they have a beginning through birth, it belongs to the supreme God to know by what principles he made them, or how many ages have passed since he granted them the perpetual existence of their divine nature.

You hold that the gods possess sexes, some of them being male and others of the female [Col. 1286C] kind. We deny that heavenly powers are divided by sex, [Col. 1287A] because a distinction of that sort was given to earthly living creatures, which the Creator of things wished to copulate and reproduce so that offspring might replace them through sexual desire.

You believe that they bear the likeness of human beings and were fashioned with mortal countenances. We think that bodily shapes are far removed from them, since bodily form is mortal; and if perhaps they possess any form, we swear with unhesitating assurance that no one can comprehend it.

You claim that each of them practices a craft after the manner of artisans. When we hear such things, we laugh, because we judge that arts are not necessary to the gods, and it is established and clear that they were devised as an aid to poverty. [Note: [Col. 1287C] The manuscript reads “are, and it is established.”]

[Note: [Col. 1287D]

L.—**Some of them, you say, belong to discords.** I write: “Some of them, you say, are Discord.” MEURSIUS.—Perhaps Arnobius had it in mind to write: “Some of these, you say, are authors of discords for others.” Fulvius Ursinus prefers “Discords.” ORELLI.

**But we, by contrast.** Others: “But these things we, by contrast”; and in what follows, “separate” in the neuter rather than the feminine. ORELLI.

**Undergoing.** Thus Gelenius, entirely correctly. Previously: “for those undergoing”; Meursius prefers the singular, “of one undergoing.” ORELLI.

**And you think that, when offenses have been laid to rest, they return to favor with human beings.** Gelenius rashly corrupted this entirely genuine reading of the manuscript and first edition by printing: “and you think that, when offenses have been forgiven, they return to favor with human beings.” ORELLI.

**Believe.** Sabaeus: “believes.” ORELLI.

**Or from tiny drops of wine.** Properly expressed. Silius Italicus, book XI, vv. 299 ff.:

> Before all others the commander, in honor  
> Of the august name, pours wine from goblets according to the rite;  
> The rest of the throng follows him and, in Bacchus’ fashion,  
> Sprinkles the tables with liquor and grows warm with Lyaeus.

HERALDUS.

[Col. 1288C] **You are convinced that the gods are affected by the ringing of bronze and the sounds of pipes, by horse races**, etc. Livy repeatedly, Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, ch. 12, Valerius Maximus, book II, ch. 4, and others testify that games, among other things, were instituted as means of appeasing heavenly wrath. See Stewechius on Vegetius, *On Military Affairs*, book II, ch. 24. ORELLI.

**And are delighted.** I added “and” with Stewechius. ORELLI.

**To be softened.** Thus the manuscript and first edition. Others: “to soften.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1288D] **That they count these things among their pleasures and delights.** Thus I printed from the emendation of Stewechius and Heraldus. Others: “that these things are counted among their pleasures and delights.” The word *esse* (“are”) is absent from the manuscript. ORELLI.]

### L. (Oberthür XXXVI)

You say that some of them belong to discords, others that they inflict pestilences, others that they cause [Col. 1287B] loves or frenzies, while still others preside over wars and rejoice in the shedding of blood. We, by contrast, judge such things to be foreign to the dispositions of divine powers; or, if there are beings who bring and impose these evils upon wretched mortals, we maintain that they are far removed from the nature of gods and must not be placed under the designation of that name.

You judge that the divine powers grow angry and agitated and are enslaved and subject to the other passions of the mind. We consider movements of this sort foreign to them, since they are functions belonging to savage kinds and to beings undergoing mortality.

You believe that they rejoice and delight in the blood of cattle, in the slaughter and butchery of sacrificial victims, and that, when their offenses have been laid to rest, they return to favor with human beings. We hold that heavenly beings possess no love of blood and are not so cruel that they cast aside their anger only after it has been satiated by the slaughter of wretched animals. [Col. 1287C]

You think that honor is added to the gods by unmixed wine and incense and that their dignity is increased thereby. [Col. 1288A] We judge it monstrous and prodigious that any person believes either that a god becomes more august through smoke, or that from tiny drops of wine he considers himself to have been entreated by human beings with sufficient sanctity and honor.

You are convinced that the gods are affected and delighted by the ringing of bronze and the sounds of pipes, by horse races and theatrical games, and that their anger, once conceived, is sometimes softened by the satisfaction these provide. We deem this incongruous; indeed, we judge it incredible that beings who have surpassed every kind of virtue by a thousand degrees through the summit of perfection should count among their pleasures and delights things at which a wise person would laugh and which appear to contain some charm for no one except tiny children and persons trained in commonplace and popular tastes.

[Col. 1288B] [Note: [Col. 1288D]

LI.—**From the judgments of the parties.** That is, from their opinions and doctrines. ORELLI.

**So that you believe they desire nothing contrary to the honor of their assumed sublimity.** The manuscript had *promperae sublimitatis*. Ursinus’ Roman edition retained *promptae sublimitatis*, “manifest sublimity.” In this same author such expressions are common: “it is plain and manifest”; “it is evident and manifest”; “it is manifest from the books to do,” etc. STEWECHIUS.

**For gruels and incense together with flesh are food for devouring flames and are most closely associated with funeral offerings to the dead.** This is because, just as these things were thrown upon the funeral pyre, so in sacrifices they were placed upon the kindled altar to be consumed. Concerning these funeral offerings at rites for the dead, I shall say something briefly, because I see that the matter has not yet been sufficiently explained.

First, therefore, when a dead person was cremated, a funeral meal was carried to the pyre. For this is what they called those funeral offerings. Apuleius, *Florida* IV: “Let them therefore drive the torches [Col. 1289A] far away; let them remove the fires far away; let them carry the funeral meal back from the tomb to the table.” Catullus, LIX, calls it simply a “meal”:

> The wife of Menenius, whom you have often seen  
> In graveyards snatching a meal from the very pyre,  
> When, as she pursued bread that had rolled from the fire,  
> She was beaten by the half-shaven cremator.

Tertullian too must be understood as referring to this funeral meal in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, ch. 1: “But I shall laugh still more at the populace even then, which burns the dead themselves with the utmost cruelty, and afterward feeds them with the utmost gluttony, both propitiating and offending them with the same fires.” Very learned men wrongly refer this passage to the ninth-day meal. Thus, when the deceased was cremated, the meal was burned and thrown upon the pyre. But this was also done afterward during the Parentalia.

Ovid explains the whole matter in book II of the *Fasti* (v. 533). We shall set out his words and briefly elucidate them:

[Col. 1289B]

> Honor is due even to tombs. Appease your fathers’ souls,  
> And bring small offerings to the constructed pyres.  
> The Manes ask little; piety pleases them in place of a costly  
> Gift. The lowest Styx holds no greedy gods.  
> A roof tile veiled with outstretched garlands is enough,  
> With scattered grain and a small crumb of salt,  
> Grain softened in unmixed wine and loose violets:  
> Let these be left in a potsherd in the middle of the road.  
> I do not forbid greater gifts. But a shade is appeased even by these:  
> Add prayers and the proper words at the erected hearths.  
> Aeneas, a fitting author of piety,  
> Brought this custom into your lands, righteous Latinus.  
> He carried solemn gifts to his father’s spirit;  
> From him the people learned these pious rites.

Ovid is treating the rites for the dead that were performed annually in February and to which the souls of the departed were believed to be summoned. By these words, therefore—“Honor is due even to tombs. Appease your fathers’ souls”—he shows why these rites were called *parentationes*: namely, [Col. 1289C] because they were performed by descendants for their forebears (*parentes*), whose Manes were thus appeased.

For this reason tombs were inscribed, so that everyone might know where the person whom he wished to appease was laid. Lucan, book VIII (vv. 771 ff.):

> Meanwhile let us mark the shore with a little stone,  
> So that the burial-place may be known. If anyone should perhaps wish  
> To appease the slain man and pay the full honors due to death,  
> Let him find the headless body’s ashes and recognize the sands  
> To which, Magnus, he may return your head.

For they sometimes marked the burial-place itself with a wooden stake; and to prevent the stake from being moved, they inscribed upon it the name of the person cremated. Hence, in the same book, v. 791:

> And lest a sailor move the burial marker when tying up his rope,  
> He inscribed the sacred name upon a half-burned stake:  
> “Here lies Magnus.”

They therefore inscribed the names of the dead upon tombs so that their Manes might be appeased there. Another purpose was added to this one: that their memory might thereby be preserved and transmitted to posterity. For this reason their deeds, [Col. 1290A] honors, and other things of this kind were added. Lucan, in the same book (vv. 806 ff.):

> But if you deem the stone worthy of so sacred a name,  
> Add his mighty deeds and the greatest monuments of his achievements;  
> Add the savage uprisings of Lepidus and the Alpine wars, etc.

And at v. 816:

> What tomb can contain these things? The pitiable grave rises  
> Filled with no titles, no such sequence  
> Of triumphal records—records customarily read upon the lofty summits  
> Of the gods and on arches built high with enemy spoils.  
> Not far away, on the lowest sand, is Pompey’s name,  
> Depressed beneath a mound, which no passing stranger would read,  
> Which even a Roman guest would pass unless it were pointed out.

To come closer to the present matter: in February they performed rites for the Manes of the dead and invited the souls of their relatives to those banquets. Hence Artemidorus writes that the memory of a man who had taken his own life by hanging was condemned and afflicted with such disgrace that he was not even named among his other relatives at the funeral rites. These are Artemidorus’ words, *Interpretation of Dreams*, book I, ch. 5:

> Ἄτιμός τε καὶ φυγὰς γενόμενος, ἀναρτήσας ἑαυτὸν, ἐτελεύτησε τὸν βίον, ὡς μήδ’ ἀποθανὼν ἔχειν ὄνομα. Τούτους γὰρ μόνους ἐν νεκρῶν δείπνοις οὐ καλοῦσιν οἱ προσήκοντες.

> “Having been dishonored and become an exile, he hanged himself and ended his life, so that even after death he had no name. For these alone their relatives do not summon at banquets of the dead.”

Thus, during the Parentalia, relatives passed over the names of those who had polluted themselves by so shameful a death; for the others were then summoned to the feasts, and their names were called aloud, as Ausonius says in the penultimate of his *Poems on the Professors*, where he treats the first funeral offerings:

> Those in the study of grammar, or rhetoric, or both,  
> Whom it is enough for me to have remembered after death—  
> Elaborate praise belongs to the living; it will suffice  
> Merely to summon their names aloud at their own tombs.

Artemidorus therefore rightly says of those who were passed over that they ὄνομα οὐκ ἔχειν, “have no name.”

Ovid adds: “And bring small offerings to the constructed pyres.” For pyres were also constructed during the Parentalia, into which offerings to the dead were cast, as Lucian too teaches most explicitly in his *Episkopousin* [title uncertain]. Hence the Glosses: “He performs funeral rites—ἀποκαίει νεκροῖς νεκύσια, ‘he burns funeral offerings for the dead.’”

Thus Arnobius says in this passage that gruels and incense together with flesh, when heaped upon a kindled altar, are most closely associated with the funeral rites of the dead. Incense, therefore, was also cast upon pyres. There is no doubt whatever that this was done upon the original funeral pyres, but the present passage shows that it was also customarily done at the Parentalia. But enough of this. HERALDUS.—Compare Lipsius on Tacitus, *Annals* VI.5, pp. 486 ff., Oberlin edition. ORELLI.

**Incense together with flesh**, etc. For the ancients had the custom, when performing funeral rites for their relatives, of covering the bodies of the dead with incense, whether they were cremated or committed to burial. Virgil is a witness, where he describes Misenus’ funeral, *Aeneid* VI.224 ff.:

> …Heaped-up gifts of incense are burned,  
> Banquet fare, and bowls of poured-out olive oil.

LE NOURRY, p. 520.]

### LI. (Oberthür XLII)

Since these things are so, and since there is so great a difference between our opinions and yours, how are either we impious or you pious, when the reckoning of piety and impiety must be weighed according to the judgments of the respective parties?

For a person is not to be regarded as devoted to divine things merely because he fashions for himself an image to venerate as a god, or slaughters innocent cattle and burns them upon sacred altars. Opinion constitutes religion, as does a correct understanding of the gods, so that you believe they desire nothing contrary to the honor of their assumed sublimity.

For since we see all the things given to them consumed here before our eyes, what else must we say reaches them from us except opinions worthy of the gods and most appropriate to their name? These are the surest gifts; these are the true sacrifices. For gruels and incense together with flesh are food for devouring flames and are most closely associated with funeral offerings to the dead. [Col. 1288C]

[Col. 1291]

## APPENDIX TO THE SEVEN BOOKS OF ARNOBIUS AFER’S DISPUTATIONS AGAINST THE NATIONS, BY J. CONRAD ORELLI

[Col. 1291A] Benevolent reader, the following encomium upon this work of Arnobius, of which I offer you this new edition, appears in what has hitherto been its fullest edition, the Leiden edition:

> “This repository of profound wisdom, by which the foolish religion of the pagans is demolished and the true religion confirmed, is greater than all praise. For who, on reading through the vigor of its eloquence, the weight of its arguments, and its exquisite thoughts, is not swept away into love and longing for so great an author? Everywhere his most flourishing style triumphs, and even the pagans themselves are slain with their own sword. That pen pierced through and destroyed all the silent gods of the pagans at once. The gods themselves, if such beings were gods, would blush upon hearing here of their crimes and the foolish fables invented about them.
>
> “In the second book, indeed, our author follows the Gnostics’ opinion concerning the immortality of souls, and in other passages he departs somewhat from Christian truth. But this must be forgiven in one who had only recently come from the darkness of paganism to Christian truth. The same thing happened to this author that commonly happens [Col. 1291B] to those who, when brought from a dark prison into the light, still have uncertain vision. In all else he is subtle and eloquent, powerful in intellect and expression, and a most valiant conqueror of paganism.”

If perhaps you think this praise excessive, overstepping the boundaries of truth and proceeding from an editor driven almost mad by love for his author, then, I beg you, ἔρχου καὶ βλέπε, “come and see”: read through the entire work, as learned as it is eloquent. You will admire this Varro of the Latin Church—the most accurate title by which learned men honor Arnobius.

Or read only its more luminous sections: for example, what he discusses in book I concerning Jesus Christ, his character, conduct, and miraculous works, and you will understand that absolutely no ancient and very few recent authors have spoken more truthfully and excellently about the divine Savior (*Soter*). Indeed, you will think yourself to have read, not a writer of the ancient Church still wavering and faltering between truth and superstition, but one of the wisest theologians of the present day.

Or survey what he says most eloquently in book II about the weakness of the human mind [Col. 1291C]; or in book III about the evils of Mars and Venus, that is, of wars and sensual pleasure; or what in that book and those following he produces in mockery of the pagan gods and goddesses, in a manner worthy of Lucian’s genius; or what he splendidly discusses concerning the empty magnificence of temples and idols and the vanity-filled apparatus of sacrifices. You will admit that, even in intellect and eloquence, hardly any ecclesiastical writer deprives him of the palm—if perhaps you except Origen alone in his books against Celsus.

You will admit also that, by as much as his pupil Lactantius, the “Cicero of the Fathers,” as he is called, surpasses his master in the elegance of pure and polished Latin style, by so much is he surpassed by that same master in intellect, learning, and genuine eloquence—not borrowed from elsewhere but flowing from his very heart.

And this is no small part of his praise: he is a wise and sober writer. Here there are no subtle sophistries, no idle exercises of ingenuity, no dreams of an imagination running riot, [Col. 1291D] no foolish and far-fetched metaphors and allegories in which other Fathers of the Church, even the most celebrated—such as Tertullian, Jerome, Ambrose, and Origen in his exegetical works—take extraordinary delight. Nor did even the divine John, whose words flow from a golden mouth, preserve himself altogether pure and free from them. [Col. 1292A]

As for the fact that in his second book he has certain things contrary to the truth and drawn from the doctrine of the Gnostics, to which he was attached—for example, that brute animals derive their origin from a source other than the supreme Creator of the universe, and that the human soul itself, on account of its weakness and depravity, was not created by God Most Good and Most Great, but only sanctified by him and adorned with the gift of immortality—I hope that you will readily forgive this in a man who had only recently emerged from the darkness of paganism into Christian light, remembering that, in the doctrine of the best possible world, most philosophers, even those of the greatest reputation, groped blindly before Leibniz.

Eight years ago, therefore, when I first began to read this most excellent writer, I conceived an almost incredible love for him. The thought then occurred to me to test upon him whatever abilities I possess and to prepare a new edition. This edition would both select what earlier interpreters had accomplished in correcting and explaining him, [Col. 1292B] and elucidate what they had left untouched, thereby making the path to understanding an admittedly difficult writer of profound learning more accessible to students of both sacred and secular literature.

I was particularly moved by discovering that, with the sole exception of Oberthür’s edition—which nevertheless lacks all the interpretive aids that are especially necessary in this author—most of his other editions were extremely rare and expensive. Nor, to tell the truth, did any one of them seem to me to satisfy the reasonable expectations of readers.

Some, such as the Leiden edition, were burdened by an excessive mass of commentary: although the notes explained many things well and learnedly, they left wholly untouched no fewer matters that appeared to stand in the greatest need of elucidation, while treating other trifling matters that were either known even to beginners or were so ἀπροσδιόνυσα, “irrelevant and indeterminate,” that they pertained to almost anything rather than Arnobius. Others, such as Priorius’ edition, I found suffering from a lack of those same commentaries.

[Col. 1292C] And, if one excepts Heraldus alone, none of all those who labored to correct and explain Arnobius appears to have discharged the interpreter’s duty fully in every respect. Gelenius, for example, who after the first Roman edition—stained with the most hideous errors—was the first to revise Arnobius’ text, abused his confidence in his own ability and in very many passages corrupted rather than corrected his author, giving us an Arnobius utterly unlike himself.

Theodore Canter, a man of exact judgment and meticulous diligence, accomplished more. He both acutely corrected and learnedly elucidated quite a few passages, but passed over far more, including the most difficult. It is much to be wished that this most learned man had fulfilled his promise to prepare a second and fuller edition of Arnobius.

Fulvius Ursinus also made some excellent corrections. In his *Criticus*, Meursius corrected Arnobius on his own initiative and with youthful boldness and, as he himself admits, not infrequently wandered beyond his intended limits. [Col. 1292D] Nevertheless, he brought a remedy to several passages and restored from the manuscript several entirely genuine readings neglected by the first editor, Faustus Sabaeus. His chief merit is that he learnedly illustrated from Plautus, Lucretius, and others the older Latinity which Arnobius, like Apuleius and other African writers, deliberately affected. [Col. 1293A]

Godescalcus Stewechius indeed offers quite a few learned and valuable observations, but he sails far beyond measure under the banner of archaism. Carried away by an excessive passion for the ancient manner of speaking, whenever he imagined that he had found some archaic and obsolete word or expression originating in the infancy of the Latin language—in fragments of Ennius or Pacuvius, or in inscriptions or ancient glossaries—he attempted, whether Arnobius would have it or not, to thrust it into his author.

Although Elmenhorstius admits that he pursued brevity in his critical observations, it is nevertheless clear that his commentary contains much that is wholly superfluous and useless. He frequently explains and supports the clearest and best-known matters without any necessity, and includes still more that lies outside the course and beyond the author’s purpose.

This man seems to have taken the greatest pleasure in explaining obscene and shameful subjects. If Arnobius touches upon anything of that kind—for example, in book II, ch. 42, in the words “prepared for violation of the mouth”—Elmenhorstius often fills several pages with it. [Col. 1293B]

But Desiderius Heraldus must readily be called the foremost of all Arnobius’ interpreters and his true rescuer. That most learned man acutely corrected many things, learnedly explained more, and was the first to disclose the true sense of most of the most difficult passages.

Nor should Nicolaus le Nourry be despised: a man of outstanding learning and consummate knowledge of antiquity, who most learnedly explained many matters relating to mythology and ancient customs and was the first to shed light upon quite a few passages that earlier interpreters had left untouched.

It is, however, greatly to be regretted that Salmasius’ commentary, with which that man of immeasurable learning had wished to elucidate Arnobius, was scarcely begun, much less completed, and that nothing from so great a man on this writer survives for us except certain corrections of inestimable value, which Thysius incorporated into his very full edition printed at Leiden in 1651.

[Col. 1293C] Accordingly, from the commentaries of these interpreters I diligently excerpted everything of sound value that seemed to me to be found in them concerning Arnobius. At first, indeed, my plan was to give all of Heraldus’s annotations in full, since they were exceedingly learned and both admirably emended and elucidated many passages of other writers. But I changed my plan, fearing that in this way the size and price of the book would be increased excessively, especially since I had learned that almost everything—or at least most of what, in his observations, concerns other writers, particularly Lucian, Artemidorus, and Titus Livy—had already been put to use by the editors of those authors, Reitzius, Drakenborch, and Reiffius. I therefore gave some of those annotations in full and abridged others; a few others I omitted entirely where other interpreters had offered something better.

Yet even with everything that could be culled from Arnobius’s earlier interpreters, scarcely half the labor had been completed. Very many passages remained either to be emended or elucidated, which they had passed over in the profoundest silence. Light for Arnobius therefore had to be sought elsewhere. [Col. 1293D] A great many other authors had to be read who, while treating other subjects in passing, cast some light upon him. The treasuries of Salmasius’s learning in his works on Solinus, Tertullian’s *On the Pallium*, and the writers of the *Augustan History* had to be thoroughly examined, since many knots in Arnobius are admirably untied there. The editions of ancient writers by Heinsius, Burman, Gronovius, Davies, and Oudendorp, and other philological works, had to be surveyed—for example, Burman’s collection of letters, the works of Justus Lipsius, the *Adversaria* of Barthius and Heinsius, Gronovius’s *Observations* on sacred as well as secular writers, and so forth—in which there is no small amount concerning Arnobius, and that by no means contemptible.

But even so, very many passages remained either obscure or corrupt, upon which light had to be cast or a remedy applied by my own efforts. It was necessary to range over almost the entire field of learning wherever it extends; and all the manifold arts and disciplines touched upon in his work by this most learned writer had to be summoned to our aid: philosophy, both the ancient philosophy [Col. 1294A] of nearly all schools and sects and the Gnostic philosophy of the earliest Christians; mathematics, arithmetic, astronomy; then history, geography, mythology, archaeology, jurisprudence, medicine, physics, natural history, agriculture and botany, the theatrical art, and sometimes even the culinary art itself. Authors had to be read from the archaic and obsolete period of Latin, whom Arnobius, like Apuleius, imitates, as well as from the later and ecclesiastical period, whose faults he occasionally adopted. In short, six hundred books of every kind had to be turned over until an edition might emerge which I could hope would meet with the approval of learned men, at least in some degree.

At last, after two full years—that is, in the summer of 1808—the work was completed, composed during no few nights of study; but it immediately began to struggle against adverse storms and for more than seven years was attended by so hostile a star. For the fair copy, journeying through almost every province of Germany and seeking for itself some publishing house from which it might issue into the light in print, [Col. 1294B] was repeatedly cast back, as it were, upon the shore and returned, its purpose unfulfilled, to the ancestral home of its editor. The disturbances of war that raged in Germany for so many years, and the unfavorable conditions of the book trade, prevented it from finding a purchaser who would undertake the care of printing it.

What is more, an utterly false opinion seems to have done my Arnobius no little harm: namely, that this writer should not be counted among the classical authors but rather among the Fathers of the Church, and that, since interest in the latter had long since cooled in Germany, he would consequently find very few readers. Yet this delay, however tedious it may have seemed to the editor, was of no little benefit to Arnobius himself. For whenever the fair copy returned to me—as it did more than six times—it gave me an opportunity to reconsider my author, to correct many things either wrongly conjectured or annotated beside the point, and to augment the work with the many aids to interpretation that I was able to obtain in the meantime. Foremost among these were [Col. 1294C] the most learned annotations of Nourry, whose *Apparatus*, after I had sought it in vain in almost every library in Switzerland, I finally received on loan through the kindness of two most humane men: Januarius Frey, abbot of the monastery of Rheinau in the canton of Zurich, a man deserving of the highest veneration, and Blasius Hautinger, the most reverend librarian of the same monastery.

At last, when I had entirely abandoned every hope of seeing my Arnobius in print, and had begun to console myself with the exceptional benefit that I myself had derived from studying him, with the not inconsiderable increase he had brought to my modest knowledge of ancient literature, and with the very sweet recollection of the labors bestowed upon so excellent a writer—behold, through the kindness of the distinguished G. H. Schaefer, whose proofs of humanity and truest friendship toward me I can feel but cannot express in words or proclaim with worthy praises, there was found a man willing to undertake the care of printing it: Frederick Christian William Vogel, a most honorable man who, through the many classical authors issued by his [Col. 1294D] publishing house, both most accurately edited and elegantly printed, has rendered the highest service to humane letters.

Now receive in a few words an account of what has been accomplished in this edition. I have given chiefly the text of Oberthür’s edition, whose division into chapters I have also followed, though in many places I have rendered it more correct, principally from Salmasius’s corrections presented in the Leiden edition and from those of other learned men, wherever the matter seemed to require it. As I have said, out of concern for the expense to readers, I wished to present only a selection of annotations, not a complete Arnobian apparatus—such as, only after my edition had at last been completed, I learned from a friend was at some time to be expected from the most learned Willem Te Water, professor at Utrecht. Such an apparatus would easily have caused this edition, which consists of two fairly substantial volumes, to grow to six or seven volumes of the same size.

I prefixed both the fullest literary account of Arnobius [Col. 1295A] from Schoenemann’s *Library of the Latin Fathers* and a synopsis of the work, with a summary of each chapter, from Gallandi’s *Collection of the Fathers of the Church*, printed at Venice in 1765 and following years. Finally, I added three very full indexes: of the authors cited by Arnobius, of subjects, and of words—or rather, I enlarged with many terms the indexes appended to the Leiden edition.

A most welcome supplement to this edition is provided by learned and acute annotations on Arnobius’s first book, which were most generously shared with me by my fellow citizen Jacob Ochsner, professor of catechetics and sacred history at the Zurich gymnasium, a most learned man whose exact knowledge of the Latin language places him among the very few, and one who has already rendered the highest service to my Nicholas of Damascus. To him, and to another very dear fellow citizen, Leonhard Keller, professor of mathematics at the Zurich school of arts—who, while staying at Göttingen, most kindly excerpted for my use Heraldus’s observations on Salmasius’s *Attic and Roman Law*, containing his second thoughts on Arnobius, Behotius’s *Apophoreta*, and other rarer books not to be found [Col. 1295B] in our nurturing homeland—may I be permitted on this occasion to testify to the feelings of my most grateful heart.

But I do not wish to detain you with a longer preface, kindly reader. Whatever good and perhaps pertinent material you find in this new edition of Arnobius, I ask that you receive it favorably.
