Wherever errors have been made—and I greatly fear they are very numerous—I hope that you will pardon them, remembering how easy it is to slip even in writers far easier than this one, who is among the most difficult, has in very many passages been treated abominably by copyists, and of whom, so far as I know, only one manuscript exists in the whole world, in the Royal Library at Paris, from which every one of all the editions has descended.

Above all, I should like to ask the learned men who intend to devote their efforts to reviewing my Arnobius in the literary journals to pass a fair and just judgment upon it and—what I should desire most of all—to state frankly their opinion concerning two exceptionally difficult passages about whose [Col. 1295C] true reading and interpretation I still remain in doubt. The first is Book III, chapter 40:

> “The Etruscans say and call these gods *Consentes* and *Complices*, because they rise together and set together: six males and as many females, of unknown names and of most sparing compassion.”

The second is Book VI, chapter 23:

> “And the Canacheni, opening what has been barred through the obscurity of remedies” [reading and sense uncertain].

If this new specimen of my labor in this branch of literature should not displease them, then at some time—if God Most Excellent and Most Great grants me life and strength—I shall publish the remaining [Col. 1296A] Latin defenders of the Christian faith as well: Minucius Felix, Julius Firmicus, Cyprian, Tertullian’s *Apologeticum* and his two books *Against the Nations*, and perhaps also the foremost Greek writers, Clement of Alexandria, Justin Martyr, Tatian, Athenagoras, and Hermias, critically revised and elucidated with the same care.

Written in the month of November 1815, at Zurich in Switzerland.

**ORELLIUS**

I do not remember finding mention anywhere of translations of Arnobius other than the Dutch version, translated by Joachim Oudaen, Harlingen, 1677, octavo, cited by Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina*, Book IV, chapter 3, p. 291, Venice edition.

Only a single manuscript has thus far been discovered, from which Arnobius was first derived and repeatedly emended; it now exists in the Royal Library at Paris. It would, however, be desirable for some learned man who has access to this royal manuscript to describe it accurately, [Col. 1296B] to establish by sound arguments in what century it appears to have been written, and above all to determine whether it was copied in characters or scribal abbreviations so hideous that it could repeatedly occupy men of outstanding learning—whom we name in the appropriate places—and never without yielding a fresh harvest of variant readings.

For although we by no means despise Gelenius’s judgment concerning the editors of the first Roman edition, neither should those editors be thought to have wished to deceive us. Indeed, what they testified universally concerning this manuscript book may well be true:

> “Arnobius previously abounded in as many errors as it contains letters. We removed countless ones; some we deliberately passed over, because they either could not be understood in any way or were entirely missing. For it would be the mark of an arrogant disposition to wish to restore things of which one is wholly ignorant.”

As for the manuscript of Flacius Illyricus, afterward Petraeus’s, which Franciscus Modius collated for the use of Stewechius, I do not know whether I read somewhere that it was nothing other than a copy [Col. 1296C] of the Royal manuscript, or whether I was the first to notice it. I am certainly now fully persuaded of it, after comparing more carefully the readings of this manuscript, which Stewechius expressly presented in the margin of his edition, with the readings excerpted by Scaliger from the Paris manuscript at the end of Meursius’s *Arnobian Critic*. In this comparison we discovered a remarkable agreement between the two, although it also appeared that Modius and Meursius had not selected and excerpted precisely the same passages, but different ones according to their different judgments—and Modius far more sparingly.

# ADDENDA

[Col. 1319]

## PREFACE

[Col. 1319] Kindly reader, learn in a few words what occasioned this appendix to my edition of Arnobius and what has been accomplished in it. When, at the spring book fair of the preceding year, I received my edition of Arnobius, issued from the press of the most honorable Vogel, from that time onward I considered nothing more pressing or more important than to read through both the text of this edition and the annotations appended to it once again and with closer attention, noting for myself every error committed or omission made [Col. 1320] in them. At the same time, either personally or through friends, I diligently sought out everything scattered through other philological books that might contribute to the correction or elucidation of an author rendered exceptionally difficult by his recondite learning, but which had escaped my notice while I was occupied in editing Arnobius.

After I had done this for several months, no very abundant harvest of serious errors presented itself, [Col. 1321A] unless one chooses to count among them twelve to fifteen entirely correct emendations by earlier interpreters which, though approved in my annotations, I had forgotten to admit into the text; these are now recorded in the list of errors appended to the end of this supplement. Yet, as I searched, a correspondingly greater abundance of new aids that had not previously been available to me presented itself. This happened especially after I had examined for this purpose certain splendid works, some of them rarely encountered, containing monuments of ancient art—as the one critic of my Arnobius hitherto known to me, and a most fair-minded one, had desired in the Leipzig Literary Gazette. Such works were, for example, Visconti’s *Museo Pio-Clementino* and *Musée de Clermont*, Gori’s *Museum Etruscum*, the antiquities and paintings excavated at Herculaneum—of which, while editing Arnobius, I had been able to use only the edition printed at Augsburg and furnished with a few rather meager notes by Murr—[Col. 1321B] and, further, Zoëga’s profoundly learned work on ancient reliefs discovered at Rome (*Li Bassirilievi antichi di Roma*). I also consulted the new edition of Winckelmann’s works prepared by three profoundly learned men: Fernow, whom a cruel fate took from humane letters some years ago, though he had been their distinguished glory and ornament; Meyer; and Schulze.

I acknowledge with the deepest gratitude that the labors of these most learned men, highly skilled in antiquity, have now restored light to more than thirty—and those among the more difficult—passages of my Arnobius. [Col. 1321C] Not content with these resources, however, I read once again the commentaries of Arnobius’ earlier interpreters, especially Heraldus, Stewechius, and Elmenhorstius, as well as Nourry’s *Apparatus*. Through the kindness of the same most courteous men whom I praised in the Preface to Arnobius, the latter was again made available to me; previously, since the manuscript of my Arnobius had already been sent to Leipzig, I had been able to glean from it only a few scattered ears, as it were. My purpose was that, if I found in those works anything of value which had either escaped my diligence while I was editing Arnobius, or which I myself had judged should be passed over in silence because it seemed to contain something long familiar to me and I did not suspect that it might be unknown to others, I might now include it in these second thoughts. [Col. 1321D]

In addition, I consulted some editions of ancient authors which I had not yet used in editing Arnobius, as well as various philological books of the most diverse kinds: [Col. 1322A] for example, Casaubon’s *Ecclesiastical Exercises*; Salmasius’ *Letters*; Philipp Karl’s by no means negligible *Observations on Aulus Gellius and Quintus Curtius*; Christoph Cellarius’ little book *On the Barbarisms of the Latin Language*, exceptionally rich in valuable material; and Schelling’s dissertation *On the Samothracian Gods*, brief indeed, but filled with varied and recondite learning. To this last work, as it seems to me at least, I owe the uniquely correct explanation of that most difficult passage of all, Book III, chapter 40, concerning the Consenting Gods, about which I had solicited the judgments of learned men in the Preface to Arnobius. I also consulted the excellent work of Creuzer—a man whom merely to name is to praise—entitled *Symbolism and Mythology of the Ancient Peoples*, [Col. 1322B] and many other books.

Finally, no unwelcome addition was supplied by several conjectures of the late Heumann. These had been written in the margin of a copy of Elmenhorstius’ edition printed at Hamburg in 1610 and preserved in the very extensive Georgia Augusta Library. They were communicated to me by Beneke, professor at Göttingen, a man as profoundly learned as he is courteous, who has already rendered excellent service to my editions both of the *Socratic Letters* and of Memnon of Heraclea and Chion.

Accordingly, after all these materials had been excerpted, collected, arranged, and fitted to the individual pages of my edition, and after such contributions of my own as they are had been added, and, finally, after all the errors both of a wandering pen and of typography that repeated reading had enabled me to discover had been corrected, [Col. 1322C] there at last emerged this final gleaning for my Arnobius, which I now offer to you, kindly reader. I hope that in it, although it is brief and consists of only a few sheets, you will nevertheless find several things not altogether negligible and not, as they say, picked up at the crossroads; and that, if you compare it with my edition, you will no longer find very many things lacking that could assist either the textual criticism or the explanation of Arnobius.

To him I now bid a final farewell, as to a most welcome friend with whom I have enjoyed the closest intimacy for no few years. I earnestly hope that this author, most worthy of reading, powerful in learning and acuteness, and second to none among the Fathers of the Latin Church, may find very many readers among devotees [Col. 1322D] of sacred and humane learning.

Written at Zurich in Switzerland, February 11, 1817.

[Col. 1321]

## FRAGMENT

Which the Royal Arnobian manuscript, and from it the Roman edition, has attached to the text at the beginning of chapter 41 of Book VII, after the words in our edition: “lest distaste be produced through excess.”

[Col. 1321D] We do not deny that all these things which you have advanced in opposition are contained in the written annals; for we ourselves also, in proportion to our abilities and to the capacity of our understanding, have read these same accounts and know that they are recorded. But the essence of the question lies in this: are these the gods whom you emphatically assert become savage when offended and are rendered mild again by games and sacrifices? [Col. 1322D] Or are they something entirely different, and ought they to be separated from the force both of this name and of this power?

For, first of all, who could suppose that they are gods, or believe that those beings exist, who are released into pleasurable joys by theatrical motions and dances and by geldings running to no purpose, and who journey down from heaven to watch foolish and insipid performances? [Col. 1323A] Who could believe that they are distressed at being offended and at having their honors diminished if a performer stops for a little while, or if a weary flute-player takes a short rest? Or that they declare a presiding official displeasing to them if some guilty person, on his way to pay the penalties and punishments deserved by his actions, proceeds through the middle of the circus?

If all these matters are considered thoroughly and without any indulgent partiality, they will be found not only alien to gods, but even to any cultivated human being, though not trained to the highest summit of dignity and weightiness.

For, first of all, who could suppose that those beings were gods, or believe that they exist, who possess a nature inclined to harm and cruelty, but cast that nature aside again, appeased by a single cup of blood and a fumigation with incense? Who could believe that they spend festal days amid theatrical motions and the dances of actors, and pleasures utterly filled with merriment; that they journey down from heaven to watch geldings running to no purpose and without any reason; [Col. 1323B] and that they rejoice to see some of these animals pitch forward and fall headlong, some overturned backward together with their chariots, and others dragged along disabled [Col. 1324A] and limping on shattered legs? Or that they declare a presiding official displeasing to them if some guilty person, on his way to pay the penalties and punishments deserved by his actions, proceeds through the middle of the circus? Or that they are distressed at being offended and at having their honors diminished if a performer stops for a little while, a weary flute-player takes a rest, or that boy whose mother is living falls accidentally after slipping because someone was unsteady?

If all these matters are weighed thoroughly and without any partial indulgence toward either side, they will be found not only far, far removed from gods, but commonplace in the judgment of any thinking human being, even one who has not been educated toward devotion to truth through knowledge of rational principles.

> **Note:** [Col. 1324A] In this fragment several things which had previously been said in scattered passages are copied again in precisely the same words. Why the copyist ventured to thrust this accretion into Arnobius’ text is not easy to say. [Col. 1324B] However that may be, it is enough to warn that these words are not Arnobius’. —NOURRY.

[Col. 1323]

# SUPPLEMENT OF ANNOTATIONS ON THE SEVEN BOOKS OF ARNOBIUS AFRICANUS *AGAINST THE NATIONS*

## BOOK I

[Col. 1323B]

Col. 718, at the note *And as though something . . .*, add:—Even the emperor Maximinus, most hostile to the Christians, in the letter which he wrote in reply to the cities requesting their persecution, and which Eusebius [Col. 1323C] has preserved for us, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IX, chapter 7, asserts that the more bitter calamities occurred “because of the destructive error of the hollow vanity of those impious men, when it prevailed in their souls and, one might almost say, oppressed the whole inhabited world everywhere with its shame” (*διὰ τὴν ὀλέθριον πλάνην τῆς ὑποκένου ματαιότητος τῶν ἀθεμίτων ἀνθρώπων ἐκείνων, ἡνίκα κατὰ τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν ἐπεπόλαζε, καὶ σχεδὸν εἰπεῖν τὰ πανταχοῦ τῆς οἰκουμένης αἰσχύναις ἐπίεζε*). Later still, Symmachus (in Ambrose, vol. II, pp. 631 ff.) did not hesitate to ascribe the barrenness of the earth and the general famine to the abolition of the privileges of the Vestals and pagan priests: “Let no one suppose that I alone am defending the cause of the religions: from deeds of this kind have arisen all the misfortunes of the Roman race. . . . This deed was followed by a general famine, and a sickly harvest disappointed the hopes of all the provinces. These are not defects of the lands. . . . The year withered through sacrilege; for it was inevitable that everything should perish which was being denied to the religions.” NOURRIUS, p. 324.

Col. 719, at the note *Worthy of hostile . . .*, add:—Moreover, *condignus* is an ancient word [Col. 1323D] used several times by Plautus. See J. F. Gronovius on *Casin.*, act I, v. 43. ORELLI.

Col. 721, at the note *With heat, it blazed up . . .*, add:—Heumann conjectures *aut intepuit* (“or grew lukewarm”). But such connective particles are very frequently omitted by Arnobius. ORELLI.

Col. 722, at the note *Nor drenched . . .*, add:—The most learned Jena reviewer of my Arnobius (*Jenaische Litteraturzeitung*, January 1817, nos. 11–12), whose judgment a friend communicated to me after the autograph manuscript of this Appendix had already been sent to Leipzig, conjectures that the reading should be *arva succrescunt* (“the fields grow up”). ORELLI.

Col. 723, in the note *Uninhabitable*, after HERALDUS, insert the following:—Thus below, book VII, chapter 47, at the end (col. 1285, line 17 of our edition): “and separated by uninhabitable lands” (*terrisque inhabitabilibus discreta*). For this is how the text must be restored from the manuscript codex and the Roman edition, [Col. 1324B] in place of *habitabilibus* (“habitable”). Heumann therefore should not be followed when he conjectures the reading *per habitabiles oras* (“through habitable regions”).

Col. 723, at the note *And devoted . . .*, add:—But now, having been better instructed by the most learned Jena reviewer, I change my opinion and consider the received reading, *studiosae nativitatis*, the only true one. Arnobius is evidently referring [Col. 1324C] to the opinion of Plato and other ancient philosophers, who maintained that the seeds of the arts and disciplines are not received from without, but, implanted in the human mind from its first birth by the supreme Creator, grow and increase with it, or even degenerate. A notable passage expressing this view occurs in Tertullian’s book *On the Soul*, chapter 20, at the beginning: “And from this, therefore, we conclude that all the soul’s natural properties, as belonging to its substance, are inherent in it and advance equally with it, from which the soul itself takes its origin. So also Seneca, often one of our own: ‘Implanted within us are the seeds of all arts and ages, and God, the hidden master, brings forth our abilities’—from seeds, that is, implanted and hidden throughout infancy, which are also the seeds of understanding. For from these our abilities are brought forth. Moreover, just as the seeds of crops possess a single form for each kind, yet have varying courses of development—some emerge in an unimpaired state, others produce even better results, and others degenerate according to the condition of the sky and soil, according to the manner of labor and care, according to the [Col. 1324D] outcome of the seasons, and according to the freedom of accidents—so too we may understand the soul as uniform in seed but multiform in offspring”; and what follows is most worthy of reading. In chapter 24 of the same book we read: “And if we acknowledge the soul as immortal, so that this belongs to its divinity, we nevertheless acknowledge it as capable of suffering, so that this belongs to its birth” (that is, to its native disposition). Arnobius therefore says *studiosae nativitatis usuras*: “the fruits of pursuits implanted in human beings from their first birth.” ORELLI.

Col. 724, after the note *Tenor . . .*, insert the following:

*He disclosed the mysteries of hidden truth.* *Sacramenta*, that is, “mysteries” (*μυστήρια*). Nothing more. For ecclesiastical writers use this word not only of the Christians’ sacred rites, but of all the secrets of religion. Thus Zeno of Verona, in his sermon *On Judah*, speaks of “the mystery of the ternary number” (the Trinity); and Fulgentius, [Col. 1325A] *On the Incarnation of Christ*, of “the mystery of redemption.” See Isaac Casaubon, who discusses this word at length, *Exercises on Baronius’s Annals* XVI, section 43, pp. 478 ff. ORELLI.

Col. 724, at the note *To whom affairs . . .*, in place of the word HERALDUS, add:—For the much-celebrated *βωμολόχευμα* (“buffoonery”) found in Plautus (*Asinaria*, act I, scene 1, v. 21) was taken from the same source:

> Among cudgel-beaten and iron-shackled islands,  
> Where dead oxen assail living men.

HERALDUS.

Ibid., in the note *By good fortune . . .*, at the end, in place of “Kapp’s edition. Compare Gierig,” read:—Kapp’s edition, and Muncker on Fulgentius, *Mythologies*, book II, chapter 5, p. 672, Van Staveren’s edition. Compare Gierig.

Ibid., after the note *By good fortune . . .*, insert the following:

*For if we are the cause.* Thus Cicero, book I, letter 1 to Lentulus: “these things are the cause” (*in causa haec sunt*). ELMENHORST.

Ibid., after the note *To have burst in . . .*, add the following:

*Habitually performed in the times of their ancestors.* Heumann [Col. 1325B] thinks *in* should be deleted. But Arnobius likes to use such prepositions superfluously (*περιττῶς*). See below, at chapter 5, Heraldus’s note on the words *from the hidden disciplines of the Chaldeans*. ORELLI.

Col. 725, after the note *Devastation*, add the following:

*How many peoples, how often, and which peoples have experienced dreadful famine.* Very many examples of this occur in the ancient historians. Thus Livy, book IV, chapter 12, relates that, when Proculus Geganius and Lucius Menenius Lanatus were consuls, there was so great a scarcity of grain at Rome that many of the plebeians, having abandoned hope, wrapped their heads and threw themselves into the Tiber rather than suffer torment by prolonging their lives. Eusebius likewise records in the *Chronicle*, under the year 2022 [from Abraham] and the eighth year after the birth of Christ, that so great a famine occurred at Rome that five modii were sold for twenty-seven and a half denarii. Yet at that time the Christian name had not yet been heard either there or elsewhere. Compare Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, book I, p. 21, Sylburg’s edition, and Augustine, *City of God*, book III, chapter 17. NOURRIUS, p. 327.—*Quantae gentes* (“how great peoples”) in place of *quot gentes* (“how many peoples”). See the Annotation on book V, chapter 12, vol. II, p. 290. ORELLI.

[Col. 1325C] Ibid., in the note *Befall . . .*, after *adierunt*, insert the following:—Still less should Heumann be followed when he wishes to correct it to *adurunt* (“scorch”), a word which, although in the sense of “injuring” (see the next column) Virgil applied even to rain by a very daring zeugma, *Georgics* I, vv. 93–94:

> Lest fine rains, or the power of the scorching sun,  
> Grown fiercer, or Boreas’ piercing cold should scorch them.

Yet I very much doubt whether it can also be said of hail beating down plants by its force and violence.

Col. 726, in the note *They impose*, in place of “Fulvius Ursinus reads *inducunt*,” read:—Fulvius Ursinus and Heumann read *inducunt*.

Ibid., after the short note *History . . .*, insert the following:

*How often the former age was afflicted.* Compare Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 40; Augustine, *City of God*, book III, chapter 1, and book IV, chapter 2; Sextus Aurelius Victor, *Trajan*. ELMENHORST.

Col. 727, after the note *When . . .*, insert the following:

[Col. 1325D] *Wars with wild beasts.* See Gellius, *Attic Nights*, book VI, chapter 3, on Regulus’s battle near the Bagrada River in Africa with a serpent of immense size. ORELLI.

Ibid., at the note *From the island . . .*, add:—Compare Pliny, *Natural History*, book II, chapter 10; Strabo, *Geography*, book II, p. 101; Casaubon on Seneca, *Natural Questions*, book VI, chapter 24; Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 40; *Against the Nations*, chapter 9, and *On the Pallium*, chapter 2; Ammianus Marcellinus, book XVII, chapter 7. NOURRIUS, p. 330.

Col. 728, at the note *To captivity . . .*, in place of the word ORELLI, add:—Moreover, Cellarius, in his *Later Observations on Barbarisms of the Latin Language*, published at Jena in 1687, pp. 126 ff., notes the very verb *subjugare* (“to subjugate”) as a word belonging to declining Latinity. ORELLI.

Ibid., after the short note *We may be able*, insert the following:

*But all things are old.* Heumann reads: *sed sint*, etc. (“but let them be”), which is more pleasing because of the preceding words, “since nothing new occurs.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1326A] Ibid., after the note *Wars . . .*, add the following:

*That evil ought not to be repaid with evil.* Our Savior himself commands this in Matthew 5:38–39. ELMENHORST.

*That it is better to suffer injury than to inflict it.* Matthew 5:39 ff. Compare Lactantius, *Institutes*, book VI, chapter 22. ELMENHORST.

*Hostile hands.* Heumann, without any necessity, wishes to correct this to the singular *hostilis manus*, so that the following *cohibere* would stand for *cohibere se* (“to restrain oneself”). ORELLI.

Col. 732, after the note *To call . . .*, insert the following:

IX.—*Because it obstructs the wishes of travelers.* Heumann prefers: *Quia vectoris*, etc. (“because it obstructs the traveler’s wishes”). ORELLI.

Ibid., after the note *What if by the sun . . .*, insert the following:

*We must say that the clouds hang as enemies by their covering.* He imitated those words of Virgil, *Georgics* I, v. 214:

> While the earth is dry and allows it, while the clouds are hanging.

ELMENHORST.

Ibid., after the note *Small advantages . . .*, insert the following:

[Col. 1326B] X.—*Fovit* (“cherished”). Heumann: *fovet* (“cherishes”). ORELLI.

Col. 734, after the note *To those hoping for offspring . . .*, add the following:

*Why did they add such savage prodigies to those hoping for offspring?* Why God created harmful animals is explained by Augustine, *On Genesis Against the Manichaeans*, vol. II, book II, chapter 16; Lactantius, *Institutes*, book VII, chapter 4; and Basil, Homily IX on the *Hexaemeron*. ELMENHORST.

Col. 735, after the note *Without any . . .*, insert the following:

*That mortals have never had any respite at all.* Dionysius of Alexandria: “When both we and they had obtained the briefest respite, this disease descended upon us” (*Βραχυτάτης δὲ ἡμῶν καὶ αὐτῶν τυχόντων ἀναπνοῆς, ἐπικατέσκηψεν ἡ νόσος αὕτη*). HERALDUS.

Col. 736, in the note *In what manner . . .*, in place of the word ORELLI, insert:—Meursius conjectures: *Quemadmodum enim res aliae, et usque ad hoc tempus genus qui duraret mortalium* (“For in what manner other things, and a race of mortals that might endure to this time”). ORELLI.—*It is a good . . .*

Col. 737, after the note *If among . . .*, add the following:

*And they sent drought.* I recommend that we write *ariditatemque immiserunt* (“and they inflicted drought”), which Arnobius himself confirms in this same [Col. 1326C] book, chapter 43: “Or to inflict a deadly wasting disease upon whomever they pleased”; and in the same chapter: “To inflict the flames of forbidden love and frenzied desires.” The doubling of the syllable was overlooked. STEWECHIUS.—Moreover, Muncker, on Hyginus, *Fables* 29, shows that *mittere* in place of *immittere* is extremely frequent among writers both of the Silver and of the Bronze Age. ORELLI.

Col. 738, at the note *Why, in order that . . .*, add:—Canter reads *ut irasci*, etc., omitting *cur*, and compares the very similar passage of Arnobius below, book V, chapter 40, at the beginning: “And yet, in order that we may grant you that these matters are as you say—that is, that the stories express one thing in their words but, after the manner of soothsayers, mean some other thing—do you not thus perceive, do you not see how great,” etc. But here the construction is different: *ut* is joined to the subjunctive, whereas it is joined to the indicative in our passage. ORELLI.

Ibid., at the note *What is . . .*, add:—Moreover, Heumann deleted the words “For what else is it to be angry . . . to rave like a Bacchant?” as a gloss. ORELLI.

[Col. 1326D] Col. 742, in the note *But from . . .*, in place of “From which almost all the conjectures arose,” read:—From which some of the conjectures arose.

Col. 744, after the note *Not to know . . .*, insert the following:

*And to move in this grosser material realm, excluded from their proper condition.* Apuleius speaks thus of these demons in his book *On the Doctrine of Plato*: “They move,” he says, “in the regions of the air bordering upon the earth and no less adjoining heaven, just as in every part of nature there are its own proper animals—those flying in the ether and those walking upon the earth.” And Minucius Felix, chapter 25: “They are impure and wandering spirits, weighed down from heavenly vigor by earthly stains and desires.” Lactantius, book II, chapter 25, should also be consulted. STEWECHIUS.—Augustine expresses the same view in *City of God*, book VII, chapter 6: “Between the orbit of the moon and the summits of clouds and winds there are aerial souls, but they are seen by the mind, not by the eyes, and are called heroes, Lares, and Genii.” The divine Paul calls them [Col. 1327A] “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (*Τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν ἐπουρανίοις*) at Ephesians 6:12; see Wetstein there. ORELLI.

Col. 748, in place of “on Vibius Sequester, p. 265, who discusses this matter at length. ORELLI,” read:—on Vibius Sequester, p. 265, and Schneider on Nicander, *Alexipharmaca*, v. 11, pp. 80 ff., who discusses this matter at length. ORELLI.

Ibid., at the note *Philesius*, in place of the word ORELLI, add:—Indeed, it occurs in Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXIV, chapter 19: “Canachus made a nude Apollo, who is surnamed Philesius, in the temple at Didyma, in bronze of Aeginetan composition.” Here Hardouin considers this Apollo to be the same as the Apollo among the Branchidae, where his oracle was located, made in bronze by Canachus, whom Pausanias mentions in *Boeotia* IX, p. 557, Sylburg’s edition. Compare Nourrius, p. 537. ORELLI.

Col. 749, note *Or loves . . .*:—in the veneration of so many thousands. ORELLI.—Read:—in the veneration of so many thousands. Heumann: “Or loves to have people prostrate themselves, and to see the veneration of so many thousands.” ORELLI.

[Col. 1327B] Col. 751, at the note *Pausi . . .*, add:—“*Pausus* among the Etruscans was *Pase*. Among the Greeks *παῦσος* signifies a cessation, which in Latin is also *pausa* (‘pause’). Under this name, however, the Romans understood a principal god, the companion of Peace, or Peace itself. Yet Etruscan religion appears to have distinguished Pausus from Peace.” These are the words of the most learned Gori in his *Dissertation on the Hellenism of the Etruscans*, *Symbolae Literariae*, vol. II, p. 65. The ancient Etruscans therefore appear to have assigned to Pausus guardianship over armistices, but to Peace guardianship over a stable peace established by solemn treaties. ORELLI.

Ibid., after the note *Pausi . . .*, add the following:

*Bellonas.* At Rome, near the Carmental Gate, a temple was built for this warlike goddess by Appius, as Augustine relates in *City of God*, book III, chapter 25, and book IV, chapter 11; it was dedicated on the day before the Nones of July. Ovid, *Fasti* VI, vv. 198 ff., sang of it as follows:

> On this day Bellona is said to have been consecrated  
> [Col. 1327C] During the Etruscan war, and she is ever favorable to Latium.  
> Appius was its founder; he who refused peace to Pyrrhus  
> Saw many things in his mind, though deprived of sight.  
> From the temple a small open space overlooks the far end of the Circus.  
> There stands a small column of no small renown.  
> From here a spear, the herald of war, is customarily cast by hand  
> Against a king and peoples whenever it is resolved to take up arms.

Frequent mention is made of this temple and of the Senate convened within it in Livy X, 19; XXVI, 21; XXVIII, 9; and in other writers, especially the poets Horace, Lucan, and Tibullus. NOURRIUS, p. 413.

Col. 752, after the note *Have obtained . . .*, add the following:

*And they recognize them as belonging to the number of existing things.* Elmenhorst’s edition has “and they know them as belonging to the number of existing things” (*et in rerum numero cognoscunt*). Heumann prefers “and among the number of the gods,” etc. But that would merely repeat the preceding words: “from whom they think that they have obtained divinity itself.” The received reading *in rerum numero* is entirely sound: that is, “among the number of existing things,” or, as it is barbarously phrased, “among the number of beings” [Col. 1327D] (*in der Zahl, Reihe der existierenden Wesen*). The sense, therefore, is: if your gods are such, they owe to that supreme God both their very divinity and their existence. ORELLI.

Ibid., after the short note *By whose will . . .*, add the following:

*That there is one sole ruler.* The manuscript has *Solem* (“Sun”), an obvious error. STEWECHIUS.

Ibid., after the note *Of their origin . . .*, insert the following:

*Destructions* (*interitionibus*). An attested word of Golden-Age Latin. Thus Cicero, *Against Verres* III, chapter 54: “the destruction of the farmers” (*aratorum interitio*). We learn from Nonius Marcellus that this is the proper reading in place of *internecio*; compare Victorius, *Various Readings*, book III, chapter 2. The same word is also used by the uncertain author of the *Spanish War* appended to Caesar, chapter 24: “Thus, on the day before, the destruction of two centurions was expiated by this punishment of the enemy.” See Morus there, p. 760, Oberlin’s edition; and our author below, book II, chapter 63: “When an awareness of destruction begins to be approached.” ORELLI.

Col. 753, at the note *Blindness . . .*, add:—[Col. 1328A] I restored the reading *hujus in corporis* (“of this body,” in the surrounding construction) from the Roman copy in place of *hoc in corpore* (“in this body”), which was previously read. CANTER.

Col. 754, after the note *The Sun a god . . .*, insert the following:

*Since the Moon is a goddess among you.* Orpheus, *To the Moon*:

> Hear me, royal goddess, light-bearing, divine Selene  
> (*Κλῦθι θεὰ βασίλεια, φαεσφόρε, δῖα Σελήνη*).

Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book III, chapter 20: “If the Moon is a goddess, then the Morning Star and the other wandering stars will also be included among the gods.” An ancient inscription:

> TO THE UNCONQUERED SUN AND THE ETERNAL MOON.

Compare Lactantius, book II, chapter 5. ELMENHORST.

Col. 756, at the note *The place of things . . .*, add:—Tertullian likewise expresses the same view in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 16: “God is omnipotent, who grasps the whole world in his hand as though it were a nest, whose throne is heaven and whose footstool is the earth; in him is every place, while he himself is not in a place, he who is the outermost boundary of the universe.” NOURRIUS, p. 341.

Ibid., after the note *None . . .*, add the following:

[Col. 1328B] *Concerning whom nothing can be spoken or expressed through the signification of mortal words.* Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration 49 on Faith*, in Rufinus’s translation: “God is that which, when spoken of, cannot be spoken; when conceived, cannot be conceived; when defined, grows beyond the very definition.” ELMENHORST.

Col. 757, before the note *May it be averted . . .*, insert the following:

*Common and more humble.* Supply “divinities.” HEUMANN.

Ibid., at the note *If in the lang— . . .*, add:—Stewechius conjectures that the reading should be: “With animal sensation they would seek the sound of the voice,” etc., since below, chapter 38, Arnobius said: “Ever recovering light and darkness by animal causes.” But there is absolutely no need for alteration. ORELLI.

Col. 760, after the note *Who the river . . .*, insert the following:

*That son born of Coronis.* Hyginus, *Fable* 202: “Apollo struck and killed the pregnant Coronis” (because of adultery, namely, committed with Ischys, son of Elatus. ORELLI), “and reared Aesculapius after he had been cut from her womb.” ELMENHORST.—Compare Apollodorus, *Library* III, chapter 10, §§7–10, and Heyne’s observations there, p. 277 of the new edition. ORELLI.

[Col. 1328C] Ibid., note *Bow-bearing . . .*:—“But if Arnobius had wished to use this word, he would undoubtedly have written *circulantes*, not *circulati*,” etc.—These words should be deleted. For Seneca also uses the verb *circulor, -ari* in the sense “to wander about,” Epistle 88: “Appion the grammarian, who under Gaius Caesar wandered throughout all Greece”; see Lipsius there. Elsewhere *circulari* means to stand in groups for the purpose of conversation, as in Caesar, *Civil War* I, 64: “Throughout the whole camp the soldiers were gathering in groups and complaining that the enemy was being allowed to escape from their hands and that the war was being unnecessarily prolonged.” See Oberlin’s Index there. Compare P. Victorius, *Various Readings* VIII, 13. ORELLI.

Col. 761, after the note *The Tyndarids . . .*, add the following:

*And unsurpassed with the rawhide boxing glove.* Below, book VII, chapter 33: “while preserving the bond of friendship, some pound one another and mutilate themselves with rawhide boxing gloves.” Virgil, *Georgics* III, v. 20:

> . . . and Greece will contend with the rawhide glove.

HERALDUS. Servius: “Hard, because the boxing gloves are made of hard hide.” ORELLI.

Col. 764, after the note *But let us grant . . .*, insert the following:

[Col. 1328D] *Because bread—Ceres.* Lucretius, book V, v. 14:

> For Ceres is said to have established grain for mortals,  
> And Liber the juice of vine-born liquor.

An ancient inscription: “SACRED TO CERES THE FRUIT-BEARER.” Thus ELMENHORST.

*If Triptolemus, because of the plow.* Virgil, *Georgics* I, v. 19:

> . . . and the boy who revealed the curved plow.

Servius there: “Some understand Triptolemus, others Osiris, which is more likely.” ELMENHORST.—Compare especially Böttiger, who most learnedly explains the myth of Triptolemus in *Vasengemälde*, vol. I, part II, pp. 193 ff. ORELLI.

Col. 765, note *Why the moon . . .*:—“He is always believed to be in motion lest anyone . . .” Read:—“The same one is always believed to be in motion lest anyone . . .”

[Col. 1329A] Ibid., in the same note, after “ill-spoken of,” insert the following:—(But now, having been better instructed by rereading this passage, I withdraw this conjecture and, approaching most closely the emendation of Gelenius, judge that the text should read: “Why is the moon always restored in motion and unharmed?” etc.)

Col. 766, note *Raised . . .*, at the end, in place of “Therefore nothing should be changed,” read:—And it is altogether clear from a very similar passage in Zeno of Verona’s sermon *On the Precept, Attend to Yourself*—a passage cited by Heraldus—that nothing in our passage should be changed: “Look for me at some ambitious man, raised up with a vast brow of respectability, wearing in his outward demeanor a certain image of sobriety.” ORELLI.

Col. 768, after the short note *From the trunk*, insert the following:

*And those very divinities whom I had persuaded myself to exist.* The punctuation should follow Meursius: “and those very beings—divinities whom I had persuaded myself to exist.” ORELLI.

*I think things worthy of the worthy.* Meursius prefers: “I think things worthy of the gods” (*digna de divis sentio*). But the received reading is much more expressive. ORELLI.

[Col. 1329B] Col. 770, note *Living . . .*:—“These words seem to me to have proceeded . . .” Read:—“The words following *punishments* seem to me to have proceeded . . .”

Col. 771, at the note *Which from . . .*, add:—Ph. Carolus collected several such forms of expression—for example, *in memoriam habere* (“to keep in memory”), *in potestatem habere* (“to hold in power”), *in possessionem esse* (“to be in possession”), *in fugam esse* (“to be in flight”), *in servitutem remanere* (“to remain in slavery”), and so forth—from ancient writers in his *Critical Observations on Aulus Gellius’s Attic Nights*, published at Nuremberg in 1663, book VI, chapter 14, p. 350. ORELLI.

Col. 775, note *Of the name . . .*, at the end:—“in the *Thesaurus*.” Read:—“in the *Thesaurus*, and especially Muncker on Fulgentius’s *Mythologies*, book II, fable VI, p. 675, Van Staveren’s edition.” ORELLI.

Col. 777, after the note *Whose voice . . .*, add the following:

[Col. 1329C] *He was carrying his foot unwetted.* Heumann conjectures *in tutum* (“into safety”). Wrongly. Both *illotus* and—though indeed more rarely—*illutus* are used; *inlutus* properly means “dirty,” but here, in its primary sense, “untouched by water, unwetted, not wet” (*unbenetzt, nicht nass*). Thus we find *illutibilis* in Plautus and *illutibarbus* in Apuleius, *Florida* I, 3. ORELLI.

Ibid., at the note *He trod . . .*, after ELMENHORST, add:—Compare Schoettgen on Juvencus, *Gospel History* I, v. 637, p. 114, Reusch’s edition. ORELLI.

Col. 779, at the note *What it was . . .*, after HERALDUS, add:—Heumann conjectures “that he was the true God,” namely Christ. ORELLI.

Ibid., at the note *When those things . . .*, after ORELLI, add:—Moreover, Arnobius is here referring to the Stoic doctrine that the decrees of fate can in no way be altered. Ammianus Marcellinus, *History*, book XXIII, chapter 5: “No human power or virtue has ever been able to deserve that what the order of fate has prescribed should not occur.” Compare Augustine, *City of God*, book V, chapter 8, and Firmicus, *Astronomy*, book I, chapter 3. ELMENHORST.

Col. 782, after the note *Nor to consider . . .*, insert the following:

*Since natural weakness makes a human being a sinner, [Col. 1329D] not the choice of will or judgment.* Thus the Leiden edition. Previously the text read “but of judgment” (*sed judicationis*), for which Heumann substituted “and of judgment” (*et judicationis*). Heraldus attempts to defend the received reading *sed judicationis* by annotating as follows: “Arnobius says that we sin through human weakness, not by a choice of will but by a choice of judgment, because in reality we neither will nor choose evil; rather, through natural blindness we judge that to be good which is nevertheless evil in reality. This was the opinion of certain thinkers, which Aristotle refutes in the third book of the *Nicomachean Ethics*. And it is certainly most false that we sin not by a choice of the will but solely through the blindness of judgment—an opinion Arnobius had drawn from the Platonic school, being not yet sufficiently versed in Christian teaching. Lactantius, book V, chapter 14: ‘Accordingly, they say that those who appear evil do not sin of their own accord or prefer to choose evil; rather, deceived by the appearance of good, they fall into evil because they do not know the distinction between good and evil.’ [Col. 1330A] Arrian moreover defends this opinion most vigorously in several passages of the *Discourses of Epictetus*, especially book I, chapter 27. The entire chapter is devoted to this argument.” Thus Heraldus. But Arnobius here appears to contrast natural weakness, through which we are blinded by our passions and, as though carried away, slip into vice, with the choice of will or judgment—“the choice of a free and independent will and of examining and judging reason” (*der Wahl des freien selbständigen Willens und der prüfenden und urteilenden Vernunft*). ORELLI.

Ibid., after the note *Not through merit . . .*, add the following:

*But through weakness.* This entirely correct emendation is owed to Thomas Canter. Previously the text most wrongly read “but through firmness” (*sed firmitate*). ORELLI.

Col. 783, after the note *Lest any . . .*, add the following:

*The torments of verminous limbs . . . the gnawing pains of sufferings.* *Verminare* and *vermina* are words of ancient and approved Latinity. Festus: “*Vermina* are bodily pains accompanied by a certain minute movement, as though one were being torn apart by worms.” See Scaliger there, p. 588, Dacier’s edition. Lucretius V, 995:

> Until savage gnawing pains deprived them of life.

[Col. 1330B] Hence *verminari*, “to suffer griping torments.” See Nonius, *On the Proper Meaning of Words*, p. 40, Mercer’s edition. ORELLI.

Col. 791, note *Let them themselves make . . .*, at the end:—“and indeed, as it seems to me, with the latter. For it could scarcely be said that they ‘collect the roar of words.’ ORELLI.”—These words, which were produced through carelessness, should be deleted. For the construction is: “let them add . . . let them collect everything—whatever harmful plant the recesses of the earth nourish, whatever power that roar of words contains,” etc.

Col. 792, note *Never . . .*, at the end, in place of the word ORELLI, read:—*Credulitatis*, that is, “of faith.” See the *Corrections and Additions* to vol. II, p. 462. ORELLI.

Col. 793, after the note *Or childish*, insert the following:

*That you might live unanimously.* *Unanimiter* is an adverb of the Middle Ages, used especially by Christian writers; Vopiscus also uses it in *Tacitus*, chapter 4: “Because you unanimously chose me”—that is, with one mind and one voice. [Col. 1330C] Compare Cellarius, who collected several examples in *On the Latinity of the Middle and Lower Ages*, p. 103. ORELLI.

Col. 794, note *But the co-authors . . .*:—“*Conscriptor* is characteristic of Arnobius. See the following chapter.” *Conscriptor* is characteristic of Arnobius in this passage. (“*Conscriptores*: ‘the authors,’ *οἱ συγγραφεῖς*, as Heumann correctly notes in the margin.”) See the following chapter.

Col. 795, note *Or appreh— . . .*, after “from admitting it into the text,” add:—Heumann wishes to delete the passage as a gloss. ORELLI.

Col. 796, after the note *But from . . .*, add the following:

*See whether this is not the stronger reason.* Heumann reads: “See,” in the plural (*Videte*), etc. He likewise—once it has been noted, it is enough—consistently wishes to replace *inquit* (“he says,” namely, the opponent) with *inquiunt* (“they say”). Wrongly, as has already been observed repeatedly in our Annotations. ORELLI.

*To enlarge.* Heumann: “unknown writings to be enlarged” (*ignara [scil. scripta] ampliari*). Correctly. ORELLI.

Col. 797, after the note *May be bent . . .*, add the following:

[Col. 1330D] *That pomp of speech.* Thus Cassiodorus, book XI, letter 1: “The splendor of Roman eloquence shines forth”; and Minucius Felix, who perhaps had our author before his eyes, *Octavius*, chapter 16, at the end: “Indeed, the less skillful the discourse, the more illustrious the reasoning, since the standard of righteousness is upheld as it truly is, without being adorned by the pomp of eloquence and charm.” See Cellarius there, p. 49. ORELLI.

Col. 798, before the note *And sophistical . . .*, insert the following:

*Lest, of course, they corrupt the sternness of gravity.* Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I: “For one who has chosen the true life must practice not only a frugal manner of living but also speech that is simple and unaffected, if indeed we reject luxury as both deceitful and ruinous” (*εὐτελῆ γὰρ οὐ μόνον δίαιταν, ἀλλὰ καὶ λόγον ἀσκητέον ἀπέριττον καὶ ἀπερίεργον τῷ τὸν ἀληθῆ βίον ἐπανῃρημένῳ, εἴγε τὴν τρυφὴν ὡς δολεράν τε καὶ ἄσωτον παραιτοίμεθα*), etc. Please see there many more passages expressing the same view. Seneca, moreover, treats this argument expressly in several letters. HERALDUS.

Col. 799, at the short note *This blood . . .*, after ELMENHORST, [Col. 1331A] add:—Thus Ennius also, as quoted by Cicero, *On Ends* V, chapter 11:

> Let the blood retreat in fear and grow pale from dread.

Compare Ph. Carolus, who collected several examples in his *Critical Observations on Aulus Gellius’s Attic Nights*, book III, chapter 7, p. 200. ORELLI.

Col. 800, note *Most intense . . .*, before ORELLI, add:—Heumann agrees with me. ORELLI.

Col. 801, before the note *Or by quality . . .*, insert the following:

*He therefore assumed the form of a human being.* Arnobius enumerates reasons for “the incarnation of Christ” (*ἐνσαρκώσεως τοῦ Χριστοῦ*), but omits the true and principal cause—an ignorance that must indeed be attributed to Arnobius, not to the teaching of his age. Origen therefore speaks excellently against Celsus when he says [Col. 1331B] that a human body was assumed by Christ so that he might dwell upon the earth, suffer death for our redemption, and, as true man, satisfy divine justice on behalf of the human race: “But we say that he assumed a human body, as one born of a woman, and came into this life, a body capable of undergoing human death” (*Ἀλλ᾽ ἡμεῖς σῶμα αὐτὸν λέγομεν ἀνειληφέναι, ὡς ἀπὸ θηλείας, τῷ βίῳ ἐπιδημήσαντα, ἀνθρώπινον, καὶ θανάτου ἀνθρώπου δεκτικόν*), etc., book I. HERALDUS.—But Arnobius by no means omits the true cause “of the incarnation” (*τῆς ἐνσαρκώσεως*) of the divine Savior, for it is contained in the following words: “and should accomplish all those things,” etc.; he is referring both to his divine deeds and to the death which he suffered for the salvation of human beings. ORELLI.

Ibid., note *Lie hidden . . .*:—“hidden, enveloped.” Stewechius.—Read:—“hidden, enveloped.” Bertius, as quoted by Meursius: “and was unwilling in that form? Enveloped obscurely.” Stewechius.

Ibid., after the note *A human being . . .*, add the following:

*It is not blind.* That is, it is not hidden, with its cause unknown. *Caecus* (“blind”) is very often used in this sense by the best writers; for example, Cicero, *On the Orator* II, chapter 87: “Things hidden and removed from the judgment of sight.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IX, 174:

> And by a hidden wasting disease  
> His marrow melted away.

ORELLI.

[Col. 1331C] *And placed very near to a likeness.* That is, it approaches very near to the following likeness—namely, the analogy with the Sibyl, Bacis, and Helenus; “it has a great resemblance to the following examples” (*es hat große Ähnlichkeit mit folgenden Beispielen*). ORELLI.

Col. 803, note *And in . . .*, after “and were sealed,” add:—Thus in Pythagoras’s school some were merely “hearers” (*ἀκούοντες*), while to others the mysteries of philosophy were disclosed in the inner treasury. Origen, in book I *Against Celsus*: “That there should be a certain teaching beyond the external doctrines, which does not reach the multitude, is not peculiar to Christian doctrine alone, but belongs also to the philosophers, among whom there were external teachings and others that were internal. Some were hearers of Pythagoras and received only ‘he himself said it,’ while others were taught in secret matters that were not fit to reach profane and not yet purified ears” (*Τὸν δ᾽ εἶναί τινα οἷον μετὰ τὰ ἐξωτερικὰ, μὴ εἰς τοὺς πολλοὺς φθάνοντα, οὐ μόνον ἴδιον τοῦ Χριστιανῶν λόγου, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν φιλοσόφων, παρ᾽ οἷς μὲν ἦσαν ἐξωτερικοὶ λόγοι, ἕτεροι δὲ ἐσωτερικοί· καί τινες μὲν ἀκούοντες Πυθαγόρα, ὡς αὐτὸς ἔφα, ἄλλοι δ᾽ ἐν ἀπορρήτῳ διδασκόμενοι τὰ μὴ ἄξια φθάνειν εἰς ἀκοὰς βεβήλους, καὶ μηδέπω κεκαθαρμένας*). HERALDUS.

Ibid., after the note *And most harsh . . .*, add the following:

*Nor did he think it should be imputed.* In the Roman codex the reading is *haec reputandum*. I read *nec reputandum putavit*. CANTER.

Col. 807, after the note *Bloodstained . . .*, add the following:

[Col. 1331D] *Nor if I see the cause.* Stewechius, on book VII, p. 142 of the Leiden edition, conjectures the reading *nec hic* (“nor here”), etc. ORELLI.

*Nay rather, he would fill it with a more secure expectation.* Should the reading perhaps be *implerent* (“they would fill”)? Moreover, *implere* with the genitive is extremely common among the best writers, the construction being Greek. Thus Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 219:

> They are filled with aged wine and rich venison.

And Cicero, *Letters to Friends*, book IX, letter 19: “to fill a pot with denarii”; see Cortius there, p. 467. Compare Vechner, who amassed a cloud of examples in the *Hellenolexicon*, book I, part II, chapter 24, pp. 324 ff., Heusinger’s edition. ORELLI.

## BOOK TWO

Col. 814, at the note *So that not in . . .*, in place of the word ORELLI, add:—The earlier reading was: “So that, from love of all, he did not also extend the light of life over everyone.” But the words *omnium virtutum amore* (“through love of all virtues”) appear to have been deliberately struck out as a gloss by the editor of the Leiden edition and, after him, by Oberthür—quite correctly, as it seems to me. For Christ cannot properly be said to have removed from human beings the danger of ignorance “through love of all virtues,” which he instilled into their souls, but rather through his saving precepts concerning God and divine matters. [Col. 1332A] But if we read “the danger of destruction” (*periculum interitionis*), then those words are appropriate and should not be disturbed. ORELLI.

Ibid., at the note *And the source . . .*, in place of the word ORELLI, add:—The Jena reviewer defends the received reading *res perpetuas*, explaining it as “things following one another in a continuous and uninterrupted order,” since he believes that Arnobius is speaking here of that creation which theologians call the second creation. ORELLI.

Col. 815, before the note *What if . . .*, insert the following:

III.—*Deprived of a share in honor.* Thus all the editions except the Leiden edition, [Col. 1332B] where we read *impertitione*. But both forms are used, *impartior* (or, in the archaic form, *impartio*) and *impertior*; hence also *impartitio* and *impertitio* (“imparting”). The latter word is cited as a *hapax legomenon* (*ἅπαξ λεγόμενον*) in Gesner’s *Thesaurus*. ORELLI.

Col. 816, before the note *That is . . .*, insert the following:

*So that they cannot be grasped and comprehended by the touch of any preconception.* Salmasius correctly restored the plural *possint* (“they can”), followed by Heumann, in place of the singular *possit* found in the old editions. *Anticipatio*, Greek *πρόληψις*, is “the faculty of preliminary cognition” (*das Vorerkennungsvermögen*). See Ernesti’s *Key to Cicero*, under *Πρόληψις*. ORELLI.

Ibid., after the note *Of the immeasurable . . .*, insert the following:

*Because there is no nation of so barbarous a character.* Origen, *Against Celsus*: “And after proving stronger than so many opponents, he prevailed to an even greater degree over barbarism and transformed countless multitudes of souls toward the worship of God according to his teaching” (*Καὶ γενόμενος τοσούτων ἀνταγωνιστῶν ἰσχυρότερος, ἐπὶ πλέον δὲ τῆς βαρβάρου ἐκράτησε, καὶ μετεποίησε μυρίας ὅσας ψυχὰς ἐπὶ τὴν κατ᾽ αὐτὸν θεοσέβειαν*). HERALDUS.

Col. 817, after the note *For whom they determined . . .*, insert the following:

*Since the kinds of punishments are so great*, etc. In the [Col. 1332C] margin Heumann takes *tanta* (“so great”) as equivalent to *tot* (“so many”). See the Annotations on book V, chapter 12, p. 290. But here *tanta* appears to mean “punishments so atrocious in their kind.” ORELLI.

Col. 818, before the short note *Whence . . .*, insert the following:

*Those things which we promise ourselves.* Should the reading perhaps be “which we promise you” (*quae vobis promittimus*)? ORELLI.

Ibid., note *Marsyas . . .*, at the end, in place of ORELLI, put:—Marsyas was worshiped by the ancients as the champion of liberty, according to Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 20: “In free cities there was an image of Marsyas, who is under the protection of Father Liber.” And on *Aeneid* IV, 58: “Liber is appropriately the god of liberty in free cities; hence Marsyas too, his attendant, is placed in the forum of cities as an emblem of liberty, testifying with his raised hand that the city lacks nothing.” The ancient Romans therefore appear to have attached to the statue of Marsyas in the Roman Forum written notices filled with witticisms (*σκώμμασι*), or even abusive verses—pasquinades—just as modern Romans do to the statue of Pasquino. Hence the *Marsyas* of Pomponius mentioned by Arnobius appears to have been some poem filled with obscene jokes. Moreover, the very well-known myth of Marsyas flayed [Col. 1332D] by Apollo is explained at greater length by the commentators on the *Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. II, plate XIX, pp. 122 ff. ORELLI.

Col. 819, after the note *Wisdom . . .*, insert the following:

*First, even they themselves.* The Roman edition reads: “First, and what they themselves,” etc. Perhaps, if we follow the traces of the ancient reading, it should be: “First, therefore, they themselves.” CANTER.—The Leiden edition has: “First, whether they themselves,” etc. ORELLI.

Col. 820, at the note *Natural . . .*, after HERALDUS, add:—Thus Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV, 145: “I shall reserve the oracles of the august mind”; and Valerius Flaccus, *Argonautica* II, v. 437:

> The priest Thyotes meets the Minyans as they land  
> And receives them in the sanctuary, revealing secrets to his guests.

ELMENHORST.

Col. 822, note *He himself . . .*, after ORELLI, add:—[Col. 1333A] Besides these, Pythagoras, as cited by Minucius (*Octavius*, chapter 19), Plato, *Laws*, chapter 5, and Augustine, *City of God*, book VII, chapter 5, maintain that the mind is God. ELMENHORST.

Source/review notes: The supplied source ends with a dangling insertion instruction; this section faithfully marks that inherited source boundary.

Ibid., at the brief note *Why in . . .* after the word HERALD., add:—Similarly Servius on Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, verse 724: “Bodies, according as they are either vigorous or sluggish, make the minds correspondingly so; this can be demonstrated even in one and the same body. For in a healthy body the mind has one sort of vigor, in a sick body it is more sluggish, and in the insane it is feeble and devoid of reason, as we see in the delirious. Thus, when the soul has entered the body, it does not act according to its own nature but is altered by the body’s quality.” See Galen in his most elegant treatise, *That the dispositions of the soul follow the temperaments of the body* (*ὅτι τὰ τῆς ψυχῆς ἤθη ταῖς τοῦ σώματος κράσεσι ἕπεται*). ELMENH.

Col. 825, after the note *But may hinder . . .* insert the following:

*Very greatly [hindering] you from having [it].* Although *very greatly* can be tolerated, it is nevertheless not free from suspicion. Indeed, it certainly appears to be an incomplete gloss. Someone had perhaps noted [Col. 1333B] in the margin of his copy the striking expression that follows immediately, *to have very much*; from this *very much* remained and was eventually added to the text. And the expression *to have very much*—that is, “more,” in Arnobius’ manner; see above in this Appendix of Notes, on vol. I, p. 300, line 12, ORELL.—and *to have less* is indeed noteworthy and translated from a Greek idiom. For the Greeks say *πλεῖον ἔχειν* (“to have more”) and *μεῖον ἔχειν* or *ἔλαττον ἔχειν* (“to have less”). Arrian, book II, *Discourses of Epictetus*, ch. 6: “Do not even be indignant if certain others have more than you in those respects” (*Μηδ’ ἀγανακτῇς, εἴ τινες ἄλλοι πλεῖόν σου ἔχουσιν ἐν ἐκείνοις*). HERALD.

Col. 826, after the note *And to judge . . .* insert the following:

*And what is by far the lightest.* In place of *and what is by far lighter*. The superlative is used for the comparative, as happens not infrequently among these writers. Thus Trebellius Pollio in *The Thirty Tyrants*, ch. 11: “I shall now see to it that Gallienus, the most contemptible of all women, understands his father’s commanders.” See Casaubon there. Compare G. J. Vossius, *On Construction*, p. 382. ORELL.

Col. 828, at the note *Ancestral institutions . . .* after the word ORELL. [Col. 1333C] add:—Numa’s laws concerning sacrifices, auspices, burials, and so forth are preserved even today in the fragments of the Twelve Tables. Lactantius, book I, ch. 22, has recorded that Numa’s books on pontifical law were discovered and burned by decree of the senate during the consulship of Cornelius Balbus and Baebius. I read *rites* in place of *arts*. For anyone who does not know that the word *rite* is peculiar to sacred matters, and that the Etruscans’ “ritual books” took their name from it, should read Pompeius Festus. STEWECH.

Col. 829, after the note *Of pouring over . . .* insert the following:

*Of wresting faith from you.* Heumann conjectures that the reading should be *of wresting faith from us*. But the received reading is sound. The sense is: “You have given them—the deceivers—an opportunity to prevent you from believing, from placing faith in the Christian religion.” Moreover, the fact that this must be the reading is also shown by the following words, *of subjecting to contempt*, which plainly refer to pagans, not Christians. ORELL.

[Col. 1333D] Ibid., after the brief note *To ride upon . . .* insert this:

*Which you laugh at as being said and declared by us.* Heumann conjectures *which you laugh at as being said by us*, etc. But the received reading can be tolerated, namely as a Greek construction of the kind our Arnobius favors. ORELL.

Col. 830, at the note *Which indeed . . .* in place of the word ORELL., add:—For *to say*, Heumann prefers *to teach*. But *to say* means “to affirm that something is,” Greek *φάναι*. ORELL.

Ibid., after the brief note *To the cradle . . .* insert this:

*That is, to ourselves.* Heumann reads *to our very selves*. ORELL.

Col. 831, note *With beam-nails . . .* at the end, in place of the word ORELL., add:—Elmenhorst, together with Cruquius on Horace, book I, Ode XXXV, interprets *beam-nails* as sharpened stakes driven through the bodies of criminals from the lowest part of the body to the highest, but without any example. ORELL.

Ibid., after the note *With beam-nails . . .* insert the following:

[Col. 1334A] *What do those rites of secret arts mean?* Below, ch. 62: “Nor because the Magi promise that they possess commendatory prayers by which certain powers, once appeased, furnish easy paths for those striving to fly upward to heaven.” HERALD.

Ibid., after the note *What Plato . . .* insert the following:

*And a man of no corrupt wisdom.* Canter reads *of no small wisdom*. Wrongly. Arnobius is contrasting Plato’s true wisdom with the false or corrupt wisdom of the Sophists. ORELL.

Col. 833, after the note *Because by . . .* insert the following:

*And uplifted by an immoderate opinion of themselves.* This entirely correct emendation is owed to Gelenius. Previously the text read: *and uplifted by an immoderate opinion toward themselves*. Herald conjectures *and uplifted under an immoderate opinion*, citing the words of Arnobius quoted above, ch. 7: “and that we may be raised into an opinion of knowledge under the opinion of an inflated breast.” But this example proves nothing. For there *under* is not redundant (*παρέλκει*); rather, as we have printed it, *inflated* must be read as a single compound word. Arnobius calls their opinion immoderate—as the same [Col. 1334B] Herald correctly explains—because he believes that they extend the dignity of the soul farther than was proper. ORELL.

*Of a dignity next in rank to the true God and first principle*, etc. The Manichaeans taught that the human soul is part of the divine nature and of the same essence as God; Augustine refutes them in *Against the Manichaean Adimantus*, ch. 22, and *Against Faustus the Manichaean*, book III, ch. 6. ELMENH.

Ibid., note *Disfigurements . . .* after the word ELMENH., add:—*Dehonestamentum* (“disfigurement, disgrace”) is a good word, attested by the best writers. Sallust, *Histories*, book I, in the *Speech of Lepidus*, §21: “Fufidius, a shameful slave-girl, the disgrace of every office.” Apuleius used *inhonestamentum* in the *Apology*: “I take diligent care not to admit any stain or disgrace into myself.” Compare Ph. Carolus, who cites a cloud of examples in his *Observations on Aulus Gellius*, book II, ch. 26, p. 168. ORELL.

Col. 834, note *Or not . . .* after the word Gruter, in place of [Col. 1334C] ORELL., put:—*Or not* in place of *so that not* derives from Herald’s correction. ORELL.

Ibid., after the brief note *With bones . . .* insert this:

*By a comparable rationale.* We also read the very rare form *comparilis* for *compar* (“comparable”) in Ausonius, *Eclogue* II, 38:

> It does not know how to shape comparable outlines of flanks.

ORELL.

Col. 835, after the note *Concern for them . . .* insert the following:

*With the afflictions of diseases.* *Incommoditas* is very frequently used for “disease” among ecclesiastical writers; for example, Hegesippus, *On the Destruction of Jerusalem*, book I, ch. 45: “He was nearly yielding now to the torments of so great an illness.” See Gronovius, *Monobiblos on the Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 1, p. 15. In German, *Unpässlichkeit* (“indisposition”). ORELL.

Col. 836, note *Artful . . .* in place of the passage “activity. But there is no need,” read: “activity, with Heumann’s approval; but there is no need.”

Col. 837, after the note *Or of things . . .* insert the following:

[Col. 1334D] *From continual error.* *Reprehensio* here appears to be taken in the unusual sense of the error itself or an act deserving censure—German *Fehlgriff, Missgriff* (“misstep, blunder”)—not of the act of censuring. The consequence is used for the antecedent. ORELL.

Col. 828, at the note *Suppara . . .* in place of the word ORELL., add:—Lucan speaks thus of the *suppara*, *Pharsalia* II, 362:

> And narrow *suppara*, clinging to the tops  
> Of the shoulders, encircle the naked upper arms.

The Herculanean Paintings teach us that the *supparum* was a woman’s garment; in vol. I, plate XXII, we see a woman dressed in a *supparum* depicted with the greatest elegance. See the commentators there, p. 118, and vol. IV, p. 260. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note *Trabeae*, in place of the word ORELL., add:—John Lydus describes the *trabea* in *On the Magistracies of the Romans*, book I, ch. 7, ed. Hase: “The *trabaia*, however, belonged to the king alone as a *paratoura* (*la pariture* [a border or trimming?]), [Col. 1335A] that is, as a distinctive robe. It was a tunic and a semicircular mantle, which Agathocles, the tyrant of Sicily, is said to have invented first” (*Ἡ μέντοι τραβαία μόνου τοῦ ῥηγὸς ἐτύγχανε παρατοῦρα, οἱονεὶ στολὴ ἐπίσημος. Χιτὼν δὲ ἦν καὶ περιβόλαιον ἡμικύκλιον, ὃ πρῶτον Ἀγαθοκλέα τὸν Σικελίας τύραννον ἐξευρεῖν λόγος*). ORELL.

Col. 839, before the note *Because grammar . . .* insert the following:

*Supremacy.* Thus book I, ch. 25: “To worship God, who holds the supreme place among all supreme things.” On this word belonging to declining Latinity, see Ch. Cellarius, *Later Studies on the Barbarisms and Idioms of the Latin Language*, p. 155. ORELL.

Ibid., after the note *As of the lands . . .* insert the following:

*Uniformly.* Thus below, ch. 64 of this book: “Who uniformly grants to the exalted and the lowly, to slaves, women, and children, the right of coming to him.” Compare Cellarius, *Later Studies on Latin Barbarisms*, p. 233. ORELL.

Ibid., note *Nor divine . . .* in place of the passage “divinely learned. ORELL.,” read: “divinely learned, or even *divine, learned*—that is, neither divine nor learned. ORELL.”

Col. 840, after the note *But if those things . . .* insert the following:

[Col. 1335B] *It is manifest and evident.* This too comes from Lucretius’ storehouse. Book II, 246:

> For this we see to be evident and manifest.

HERALD.

Col. 842, at the note *From ash . . .* after the word HERALD., add:—Compare Pliny, *Natural History* V, 16; and Broukhusius on Tibullus II, verse 138, p. 215. ORELL.

Col. 843, note *Aevitatem*, in place of the word ORELL., add:—*Aevitas*: Greek *ἡλικία*, “age,” and *χρόνος*, “time.” From this, by syncope, comes *aetas*. See Heraldus, *Adversaria*, book I, ch. 1, p. 2. ORELL.

Col. 844, note *Sun-fleeing*, at the end, in place of the word ORELL., add:—The Jena Reviewer defends the received reading *solifugas* (“sun-fleeing”) as an epithet of vipers, as below, book VII, ch. 16: “and with them salamanders, water-snakes, vipers, sun-fleeing snakes.” ORELL.

[Col. 1335C] Col. 845, at the note *Mitra*, in place of the word ORELL., add:—The *mitra*, as Servius teaches (on *Aeneid* IV, verse 215, and IX, 216), was a curved cap from which hung a covering of beads; the Phrygians and Lydians used it, and the Trojans imitated them. He adds that some regarded the *mitra* as belonging to prostitutes and ascribed it to those accused of effeminacy. Yet it was a woman’s head-covering, as is clear from these words of Pliny, *Natural History* XXXV, ch. 9: “Polygnotus of Thasos was the first to paint women in shining garments and to cover their heads with multicolored *mitrae*.” Isidore, however, *Origins* XIX, ch. 31: “The *mitra* is a Phrygian cap protecting the head, such as is the head ornament of consecrated women. But the cap belongs to men, whereas the *mitra* belongs to women.” NOURR., p. 559.—Compare the *Commentary on the Herculanean Paintings*, vol. II, plate XVIII, p. 116; and Visconti in the *Pio-Clementine Museum*, vol. III, p. 29. ORELL.

Col. 846, at the note *Manete*, in place of the word ORELL., add:—You may see such a *mantele* depicted with the greatest elegance in the *Herculanean Paintings*, vol. V, plate LXVXV [sic]. Compare the [Col. 1335D] commentary there, p. 372. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note *Mastruca*, in place of the word ORELL., add:—Compare Dempster, *On Royal Etruria*, vol. I, book III, ch. 54; also H. Meyer and J. Schulze in their *Observations on the Works of Winckelmann*, vol. III, p. 463. ORELL.

Col. 847, after the note *Threshing-sledge*, insert the following:

*Winnowing-fan.* Servius, on Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 166, makes the following observations on the words “and the mystic fan of Iacchus”: “They understand the ‘mystic fan’ as follows: they say that the fan is a broad wicker vessel into which countrymen, because of its capacity, customarily gather the first fruits of the crops and consecrate them to Liber and Libera.” The shape of the fan among the ancients differed somewhat from that used by farmers today; see the *Herculanean Paintings*, vol. II, plate XXVIII (Commentary, p. 170), and vol. V, plate LXXV (p. 335). ORELL.

Col. 848, at the note *Polubrum*, in place of the word ORELL., add:—A Herculanean plate, vol. III, no. XXXV, contains a splendid image of Cupid pouring water with a ladle into a *polubrum* or washbasin; see the commentary there, [Col. 1336A] p. 168. Compare Nourry, p. 561. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note *Radius*, in place of the word ORELL., add:—You may see most splendidly depicted in the *Herculanean Paintings*, vol. II, plate VIII, a woman—perhaps the Muse Urania—holding a *radius* or pointer in her right hand and a solid sphere in her left, such as Martianus Capella describes in *The Marriage of Philology*, book II; see the commentary there, pp. 50–51. ORELL.

Col. 849, at the note *What a . . . may be*, in place of the word ORELL., add:—Joseph Scaliger, in his book *On Coinage*, p. 8, thinks that in book V, by *dibus*, Arnobius meant a *deunx* or *dibussis*, that is, two thirds of an as divided into three parts. The Jena Reviewer defends *dibus* because of the following words, “twice two, twice three.” For my part I would prefer *cubus* (“cube”), because *or a power* immediately follows, to which *dibus* would correspond less well. ORELL.

Col. 851, at the note *With another . . .* after the word ORELL., add:—The author of *On the Differences of Words*: “We converse when we engage in speech with someone.” ELMENH.

[Col. 1336B] Ibid., note *From mixing bowls . . .* Delete the note on these words and insert the following in its place:—Arnobius is referring to those words of Plato in the *Timaeus*: “Again to the former mixing bowl, in which, while blending the soul of the universe, he mixed it” (*Πάλιν ἐπὶ τὸν πρότερον κρατῆρα, ἐν ᾧ τὴν τοῦ παντὸς ψυχὴν κεραννὺς ἔμισγε*). Cicero translates them thus: “To the former blending, in which God, while blending the entire soul of universal nature, mixed it together.” Compare Tennemann’s *History of Philosophy*, vol. II, p. 416 ff.; and the note on ch. 52, p. 78. ORELL.

Ibid., note *May linger . . .* in place of the passage “*aere*, without any sense,” read: “*aerio*, without any sense.”

Ibid., same note: in place of “in the *Second Corrections*: as though in the air,” read: “in the *Second Corrections*: may prevail as though in the air.”

Col. 855, before the note *It is not . . .* insert the following:

*What rank they occupy among things.* The Roman edition has “what rank they occupy,” etc., which Canter defends in vain. For the construction is: “How do they know . . . what rank they occupy,” etc. The question marks that follow in the text must therefore be deleted, except for the one after *they have drawn*. ORELL.

[Col. 1336C] Ibid., at the note *Cease . . .* in place of the word ORELL., add:—Canter punctuates the passage thus: “Cease to enroll man . . . among the orders, since he is destitute of the foremost things”—“foremost,” namely, “goods”: German, “since he lacks the first and most important thing”; as in Cicero, *Brutus*, ch. 70: “not slow in ideas, not poor in words.” Or, since *inops* is usually construed with the genitive, one may take *primis* in the dative case: “since he is destitute in relation to the foremost”—namely, “orders”: German, “since he is too poor for the first classes.” But I prefer the received reading. ORELL.

Col. 857, at the note *Although . . .* in place of the word HERALD., add:—Arnobius also speaks both precisely and philosophically when he says *of disposition*. For the sense of shame by which we are restrained from disgraceful acts is not properly the virtue of a steadfast man grounded by firm roots in his resolve for virtue. It belongs rather to a youth of good natural disposition (*εὐφυής*) and a mind inclined toward virtue, and is more a passion (*πάθος*) than a settled disposition (*ἕξις*). Aristotle teaches this in the final chapter of book IV of the *Nicomachean Ethics*. You may also read Plutarch’s *On Excessive Bashfulness* (*περὶ Δυσωπίας*). HERALD.

Ibid., at the brief note *Of the powers above . . .* after the word ORELL. add:—Thus [Col. 1336D] Arnobius below, book IV: “Is it thus, I ask, that among you the eminence of the powers above comes into being?” ELMENH.

Ibid., after the same note insert the following:

*Nor can the one be afflicted in the other*, etc. Meursius conjectures: “nor can the one be afflicted by the force of the other,” etc. Wrongly. The construction is: “nor, amid equality of condition, can the one”—namely, soul, to be understood as supplied from the common context (*ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ*)—“be afflicted by the other”—soul. ORELL.

Col. 859, after the note *Nor in . . .* insert the following:

*He is found to regard them as capable of suffering and perishable.* Should we not read: “and he is found to regard them as perishable”? *To be* appears to have been absorbed by the final syllable of *perishable*. Moreover, *interibilis* (“perishable”) is a word of ecclesiastical Latin, used several times by Tertullian. See Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. ORELL.

Col. 861, at the note *We protect . . .* add:—“Some suspect that the Greeks gave the African Psylli their name from fleas, *ἀπὸ τῶν ψύλλων*, [Col. 1337A] because they sucked out blood in the manner of fleas—namely, to heal in this way those struck by snakes. Celsus speaks of them as follows in book III, ch. 27, where he discusses snakebite: ‘A person must be employed to suck out the wound; and, by Hercules, those called Psylli do not possess any special knowledge, but rather boldness confirmed by practice itself.’” So writes Bochart in the *Hierozoicon*, book IV, ch. 19, vol. II, p. 477, ed. Rosenmüller. ORELL.

Col. 862, after the note *Dealers . . .* insert the following:

*And impostors.* *Plani* are the same as sycophants, deceitful seducers, and impostors—German *Gaunerstreichenpack*, “a pack of swindling rogues.” Cicero, *For Cluentius*, ch. 26: “Here was that utterly wicked impostor, nourished by profit from the courts”; and Horace, book I, *Epistles* 17, verse 52:

> Nor, though mocked more than once, does he trouble  
> To lift from the crossroads an impostor with a broken leg.

Compare Aulus Gellius, book XVI, ch. 7. NOURR., p. 561.—The glosses: “*planus*, a deceiver”; from *πλανᾶν*, “to lead astray,” the Greeks also say *πλάνος*, “impostor.” See Salmasius on Julius Capitolinus, [Col. 1337B] *Antoninus the Philosopher*, ch. 13; and Ernesti’s *Ciceronian Lexicon* under this word. ORELL.

Ibid., after the note *Why not . . .* insert the following:

*Because he who promises us.* The first edition has, most corruptly: “than when he who promises us.” Meursius: “when he,” etc. Fulvius Ursinus: “indeed, him.” Herald: “because he,” etc. ORELL.

Ibid., note *When you . . .*: in place of “you will have departed, *senodes*, without any sense. But to this,” read: “you will have departed, *senodes*, without any sense. Stewechius reads *you will have departed senodes*, that is, ‘released from knots.’ But to this.”

Col. 863, note *If of him . . .*: in place of “Meursius and Stewechius,” read: “Meursius and Stewechius together with Heumann.”

Col. 865, at the note *Not to be . . .* after the word ORELL., add:—But Arnobius seems chiefly to have followed the heresy of Carpocrates, which was partly composed from those earlier doctrines and partly possessed its own peculiar monstrosities. This is manifest and evident from Tertullian, *On Prescription*, ch. 48: “Carpocrates, furthermore, introduced the following sect. He says that there is one principal power in the realms above; [Col. 1337C] that from it angels and powers were brought forth; that these, standing far apart from the higher powers, established this world in its lower regions; that Christ was not born of the Virgin Mary but was begotten from the seed of Joseph, being merely a man, though certainly better than others in his cultivation of justice and integrity of life; that he suffered among the Jews, and that his soul alone was received into heaven because it was firmer and stronger than the others. From this he would infer, since only the salvation of souls was retained [the printed *tentata*, “attempted,” is probably an error], that there are no resurrections of the body.” Arnobius therefore received this from the Carpocratians, Marcionites, and other heretics of that kind. Seleucus and Hermias, and later the Messalians, likewise attributed the creation of souls to angels. See Philastrius. HERALD.

Col. 868, at the note *Leapers from horse to horse . . .* in place of the word ORELL., add:—*Desultores* are called *κέλητες* in Greek; Homer already described their skills in most elegant verses, *Iliad* XV, 679. Compare Livy XLIII, ch. 29, and Suetonius, *Caesar*, ch. 39. The *Herculanean Paintings*, vol. III, plate XXIV, also show an image of such a rider. See the commentary there, [Col. 1337D] p. 229 ff., and Nourry, p. 554. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note *Rope-walkers*, in place of the word ORELL., add:—Manilius speaks most elegantly of rope-walkers in *Astronomica* V:

> And if perhaps his spirit rises toward some art,  
> He will devote his zeal to sheer heights and conquer  
> Danger by skill; or, daring narrow steps with no boundary,  
> He plants unerring footprints upon outstretched ropes  
> And, having rehearsed a path through heaven, will lose the ground beneath his feet.

See Scaliger there, p. 421, Boecler’s edition. Moreover, on the skills of rope-walkers, springboard acrobats, and other people of this kind, consult the commentary on the *Herculanean Paintings*, vol. III, plate XXXII, which displays two rope-walkers wearing broad-brimmed hats and standing upon a rope, pp. 158 ff. ORELL.

[Col. 1338A] Col. 870, at the note *Why fullers . . .* after ELMENH. and ORELL., add:—Juvenal, *Satire* VII, verses 224 ff.:

> Because from the middle hour of night  
> You sat there, when no craftsman, when no one would sit  
> Who teaches how to draw out wool with a slanting iron.

That is, a wool-worker, as the ancient scholiast interprets it. HERALD.
