Ibid., at the note *Phrygiones*, in place of the word ORELL., add:—See below in the *Corrections and Additions*, p. 463. Compare the commentary on the *Herculanean Paintings*, vol. V, plate LXVIII, p. 303, and especially Salmasius on Flavius Vopiscus, *Carinus*, ch. 20, *Augustan History*, vol. II, p. 850 ff. ORELL.

Col. 871, after the note *They would drain dry . . .* insert the following:

*They would smear and drench themselves with their own discharge.* The glosses: *Proluvies*—“an excessive evacuation of the belly” (*κοιλίας ὑπερέκτρωσις*). Below, book VI, ch. 16: “Into whatever places the discharge of the emptied anus has carried itself.” Virgil, *Aeneid* III, 217:

[Col. 1338B]

> The birds have maidens’ faces, but the foulest  
> Discharge of the belly.

HERALD.

Ibid., note *So that at . . .*: in place of “Some wish to read—Meursius—*with voices*. But the received reading,” read: “Some wish to read differently: Meursius, *with voices*; Heumann, *with nods*. But the received reading.”

Col. 873, after the note *With rust . . .* insert the following:

*Through the violence of hunger they would fall upon human corpses.* Petronius, *Satyrica*, ch. 141: “The Saguntines, besieged by Hannibal, ate human flesh and did not wait for an inheritance. The Petavians did the same in the extremity of famine. . . . When Numantia had been captured by Scipio, mothers were found holding in their laps the half-eaten bodies of their children.” Compare Seneca, *Controversies* IV, 27, and Juvenal, *Satire* XV, with the interpreters there. ORELL.

Col. 876, at the note *For the sake of . . .* add the following:

Let it be permissible to append, in support of the same view, a most elegant passage from Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II, [Col. 1338C] verses 189 ff. (on a Vestal Virgin watching gladiatorial games):

> Then to the public seating of the arena goes nurturing modesty  
> And piety free from blood, to see men’s bloody  
> Encounters, deaths, and wounds sold for sustenance—  
> A spectacle for sacred eyes. She sits there, distinguished  
> By the venerable ornaments of her fillets, and delights in the trainers.  
> O tender and gentle spirit! She rises at the blows;  
> And whenever the victor drives his sword into a throat, she  
> Calls it her delight, and with inverted thumb the modest  
> Virgin orders the fallen man’s breast to be torn apart,  
> Lest any portion of life lie hidden deep within the lowest  
> Vitals while it still throbs beneath the pursuer’s more deeply driven sword.

Compare Cyprian, *Epistle II, to Donatus*. ELMENH.

Col. 878, at the note *Vigor . . .* in place of the word ORELL., add:—*Exponere* in the sense of *deponere* (“to lay aside”) is extremely common among ecclesiastical writers and in our Arnobius. See the note on book IV, ch. 21, p. 221. ORELL.

Col. 879, at the note *Like little coils*, add the following:

[Col. 1338D] In an inset image in the *Herculanean Paintings*, vol. V, plate XIV, the commentators believed that they recognized a fine sausage; and on p. 383 they derive the word *botulus* from *botones*, that is, swellings raised by heaped-up earth—the *Glosses of the Land-Surveyors* in Rigault—as though from *botonuli*. Apicius, *On the Art of Cookery*, book II, ch. 3, teaches us the method of making sausages: “You will make a sausage thus: from cooked egg-yolks and chopped pine kernels; add onion, chopped leek, and mix in uncooked sauce”—that is, with well-pounded and rubbed meat, which must be supplied from the preceding section on the *vulvula*—“and ground pepper; then stuff the intestine, add fish sauce and wine, and cook it thus.” See Hummelberg there, p. 65, Jansson’s edition. ORELL.

Ibid., note *Catillamenta . . .* after the words “from licking little dishes”—German *Tellerlecker*, “plate-licker”—add:—Mazocchi, on the *Herculanean Paintings*, vol. V, p. 382, prefers *castellamenta* and compares those little castles that children build while playing by placing three nuts below and one above [Col. 1339A]—we Swiss call this *ein Hoc Nüsse*; Italian *casteletto*.

Ibid., in the same note, at the end, in place of the word ORELL., add:—Apicius, at the place cited: “Preparation of Lucanian sausages. . . . Pepper, cumin, savory, rue, parsley, seasoning, laurel berries, and fish sauce are ground, and well-pounded meat is mixed in, so that it is again thoroughly rubbed with the ground mixture, together with added fish sauce, whole peppercorns, abundant fat, and kernels. You will stuff an intestine drawn out exceedingly thin, and then hang it in the smoke.” Compare Nourry, p. 558, and Rader on Martial XIII, epigram 35, p. 859. ORELL.

Col. 881, at the note *Of the scabilla . . .* in place of the word ORELL., add:—Compare *The Ancient Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. IV, plate XIII, p. 62, and *The Bronzes of Herculaneum*, vol. II, plate XLI, p. 155. ORELL.

Col. 882, at the note *Female sambuca-players . . .* in place of the word ORELL., add:—Livy also joins these together when, after the defeat of Antiochus, king of Syria, commonly called “the Great,” he says in book XXXIX, ch. 7: “For the origin of foreign luxury was brought into the City by the army from Asia. . . . [Col. 1339B] Then came female harpists and sambuca-players, and entertainments provided at banquets.” Doering there says that the *sambuca* was an instrument almost similar both in shape and use to what we call a harp. Compare Spanheim on Callimachus, *Hymn to Delos*, verse 253 (p. 541, Ernesti’s edition), and the commentators on the *Herculanean Paintings*, vol. II, plate VI, pp. 35–38, who discuss these and other similar musical instruments with the greatest learning. ORELL.

Col. 885, note *As of wild beasts . . .* at the end: in place of “*On Idolatry*, book IV, ch. 96, p. 599. ORELL.,” read: “*On Idolatry*, book IV, ch. 46, p. 599; and Schneider, the very distinguished scholar, on Nicander’s *Alexipharmaca*, verse 115, pp. 114 ff., who most diligently collected the testimony of ancient and modern physicians concerning blister beetles and their poison. ORELL.”

Col. 887, at the note *For not . . .* after the word ELMENH., add:—These are Jerome’s words in book I: “But if they do not think that small things belong to those to whom great things belong, [Col. 1339C] they must, in accordance with Valentinus, Marcion, and Apelles, introduce for me one creator of ants, worms, gnats, and locusts, and another of heaven, earth, sea, and the angels.” BOCHART, *Hierozoicon*, book IV, ch. 6, vol. II, p. 325, ed. Rosenmüller.

Col. 888, after the note *And to obtain . . .* add the following:

*So vain*, that is, of no use. ORELL.

Col. 889, note *With perversity . . .*: in place of “See above on book I. ORELL.,” read: “See above on book I, ch. 22. Stewechius prefers: ‘Through servitude to innumerable vices.’ ORELL.”

Ibid., after the note *With perversity . . .* insert the following:

*Bold, rash, headlong, blind.* Here Arnobius, in his customary manner, heaps up several expressions which, although they appear to signify one and the same thing, nevertheless differ in some respect, and each possesses certain properties not present in the others. Boldness is the source and head of rashness; for from the fact that someone is undaunted in the face of dangers and somewhat too bold, rashness arises—that is, *προπέτεια*, “precipitancy,” as the ancient glosses correctly interpret it. [Col. 1339D] Rashness also has blindness attached to it, and so Arnobius rightly combines “rash, headlong, blind.” For when we are borne headlong in some direction, we cannot fix the gaze of our eyes upon things; consequently we see some things imperfectly and others not at all. Hence Seneca the tragedian also pronounced rashness blind in the *Agamemnon*, verse 145. HERALD. So too in German we say: *kühn, verwegen, blind und tolldreist*—“bold, reckless, blind, and foolhardy.” ORELL.

Ibid., after the brief note *Feeble . . .* insert the following:

*Primal nobility*, that is, original nobility. HEUMANN. Rather, nobility proceeding from God, the first principle of all things, as Herald correctly explains. See the following note. Thus below, ch. 64: “Or does he repel anyone from primal favor?” ORELL.

Col. 894, after the note *And since . . .* insert the following:

*Of that purity of which he had made the soul of this universe.* Meursius, p. 75, regards these words as mutilated. But everything coheres perfectly. The sense is: Plato did not wish the souls of the human race to possess the same purity of mixture—or the same pure mixture—[Col. 1340A] whose purity he had made, or taught in his *Timaeus* to belong to, the soul of this universe, that is, the world-soul. ORELL.

Col. 895, before the note *Of small things . . .* add the following:

LIII.—*As having been brought forth by things that are not primal.* Tertullian reduced to a brief compendium, in *On the Soul*, ch. 23, the various opinions of different Gnostics concerning the origin of souls which Arnobius follows throughout this entire discussion. Since the passage sheds light upon our author, let it be permissible to transcribe it here in full:

> “Some,” he says, “believe that human beings descended from the heavens, with as much conviction as they confidently promise that they will return there. Thus Saturninus, a disciple of the Simonian Menander, introduced the doctrine that man was made by angels: at first, as a futile, feeble, and unstable work, he writhed upon the earth like a worm because he lacked the strength to stand; then, through the mercy of the supreme power, in whose image—though one not fully perceived—he had rashly been constructed, [Col. 1340B] he received a tiny spark of life, which awakened and raised him, animated him with stability, and after his departure from life was to carry him back to his mother-source. Carpocrates, too, claims so much for himself from the realms above that his disciples make their own souls already equal even to Christ, let alone to the apostles, and, when they wish, prefer them—souls which they have in turn conceived from a sublime power that despises the ruling principalities of the world. Apelles reports that souls, enticed by earthly foods, were brought down from supercelestial abodes by the fiery angel—the God of Israel and ours—who thereafter fashioned sinful flesh around them. The Valentinian swarm instilled the seed of Sophia into the soul, through which they recognize the histories and Milesian tales of their aeons in the images of visible things. I am genuinely grieved that Plato has been made the provider of seasoning for all heretics,” etc.

See Pamelius there. ORELL.

Col. 896, after the note *Of evil . . .* insert the following:

*Unknowing, ignorant, and I do not know.* I would prefer *unaware*, since *I do not know* follows. ORELL.

Ibid., after the brief note *Points . . .* insert this:

[Col. 1340C] *It is burned and torn.* See the note on book I, ch. 3, vol. I, p. 284. In place of *is torn*, Stewechius prefers *is mangled*. ORELL.

Col. 897, at the note *Than without . . .* after the word ORELL., add:—Should I read: “Indeed, far better to remain rather within the bounds of unawareness and ignorance than knowingly to declare that nothing is done by God except in accordance with his will”? MEURSIUS, p. 75.

Col. 899, note *Or none . . .*: in place of *so that none*, read *but none*.

Col. 900, before the brief note *The world . . .* insert this:

LVIII.—*What cause fashioned man.* Meursius, p. 76, prefers *for what cause*. Wrongly. *What cause* is equivalent to “what author or creator.” ORELL.

Col. 903, after the note *Why the veins . . .* insert the following:

*To illuminate us by means of the eyes.* Heumann reads *for us to be illuminated*. Excellent. ORELL.

*To the danger of blindness.* The same Heumann reads *because of the danger*. ORELL.

Col. 906, note *Taste . . .*: in place of “sense. For my part, however, with Herald,” read: “sense; from this Stewechius rather boldly refashioned the entire passage thus: ‘Then what are these things themselves—taste, smell, that same taste, and the other differences among qualities—and from what principles are they derived?’ For my part, however, [Col. 1340D] with Herald.”

Col. 907, after the note *Breezes . . .* insert the following:

*For from all the things which the obscurity of august divinity contains.* If the reading is correct, the sense will be: “from all the things which august divinity keeps enveloped in darkness—or obscurities”—German, “from all those things which the most exalted being keeps hidden from mortals, wrapping them in darkness.” But I think the reading should be: *For from all the things which the obscurity of narrow divination contains*, in this sense: “from all the things which our narrow reason—that is, reason circumscribed within confined limits—can comprehend while divining the truth rather than clearly perceiving it.” But let the more learned judge. ORELL.

Col. 909, after the note *Who is the vessel of long . . .* insert this:

[Col. 1341A] *So that others may be able to bestow that which they themselves are.* This entirely correct emendation is owed to Stewechius. Previously the text read, “so that others may bestow, or what they themselves are,” etc., without any sense. ORELL.

Col. 910, brief note *Lay aside . . .*: in place of “*exponite*, from the manuscript. ORELL.,” read: “*exponite*, from the manuscript, a reading which, with Canter also approving it, ought to have been adopted. See on book IV, ch. 21, the words *ut fletam exponeret*, an expression most ineptly introduced. ORELL.”

Col. 911, after the note *If either . . .* add the following:

*For what is so unjust*, etc. Horace, *Art of Poetry*, verse 467:

> He who saves a man against his will does the same as one who kills him.

ELMENH.

Col. 914, after the brief note *Will have stood*, insert this:

*More joyfully.* Heumann reads *more excellently*. Not badly. ORELL.

Col. 919, after the note *Sacred . . .* insert the following:

*And to images of the gods.* That is, images of those gods under whose protection, beyond doubt, were either sacred tables or the other tables at which the pagans reclined after first invoking the gods. Is not one of these gods the one of whom [Col. 1341B] Statius sings, *Silvae* IV.6, verse 32:

> . . . the guardian spirit and protector of the chaste table?

And shortly afterward, verse 50:

> . . . the Pallaean ruler will possess it,  
> A divinity venerable at joyful tables.

But the pagans afterward rejected these practices as old women’s superstitions. NOURR., p. 317.

Col. 920, at the note *Mothers . . .* after ELMENH. and ORELL., add:—From Suetonius we learn that women not merely of the lowest or middle rank, but even of the highest, were trained in this fashion, not only in the period of the nascent republic but also when the republic was yielding to the rule of a single person. In ch. 64 he relates the following concerning Augustus: “He trained his daughter and granddaughters so that he even accustomed them to wool-working, and forbade them to say or do anything except openly and of a kind that could be entered in the daily record.” Likewise, ch. 73: “He rarely wore any clothing other than that made at home by his wife, daughter, and granddaughters.” [Col. 1341C] NOURR., p. 318.—Compare Ph. Carolus, *Observations on Quintus Curtius*, p. 613. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note *Drinks . . .* after the word ORELL., add:—Valerius Maximus, book I, gives the reason for the prohibition of wine: namely, that women might not lapse into some disgrace, because the step nearest to intemperance under Father Liber has customarily been toward illicit sexual intercourse. For the rest, see Ph. Carolus, who discusses this subject at length in his *Observations on Aulus Gellius*, book X, ch. 23, pp. 435 ff. Athenaeus, *Deipnosophists*, book X, ch. 13, relates that wine was forbidden to women because, when Hercules asked for a drink, a woman offered him water instead of wine. ORELL.

Ibid., before the note *Is it not beneath . . .* insert the following:

[Source boundary: the supplied section ends here; no text to insert follows.]

LXVIII.—On Mount Alban in ancient times, etc. Livy, namely, relates in Book I, chapter 31, that under Servius Tullius, king of the Romans, stones rained down on Mount Alban; and then, he says, they seemed to hear a mighty voice from the summit, commanding the Albans to perform their rites according to their ancestral custom—rites which they had [Col. 1341D] consigned to oblivion, as though they had abandoned their gods together with their homeland. The same author, Book V, chapter 52, represents Camillus addressing the Romans in these words: “Observe the difference between us and our ancestors. They left certain rites to be performed by us on Mount Alban and at Lavinium.” We likewise read it recorded by Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book IV, p. 250, that, in order that the treaty struck by Tarquin with the Volscians and Hernicans might be perpetual, it was decreed by the unanimous consent of all that holidays should be celebrated annually on the lofty mountain overlooking Alba, where rites were performed for Jupiter Latiaris and a bull was slaughtered as the common victim of them all. Does Arnobius not imply that this bull was white, and complain of an alteration in this rite? NOURR., pp. 318–19.—Propertius, Book II, elegy 19, and Pliny, *Natural History*, Book II, chapter 3, attribute to the Clitumnus, a river of the Faliscans, the power of turning reddish cattle snow-white; Dausqueius, on Silius Italicus, Book VIII, p. 359, thinks that, when this power vanished, reddish bulls began to be sacrificed. ORELL.

[Col. 1342A] Ibid., at the note *And this one . . .* after the word ORELL., add:—Macrobius, in the passage cited, exposes and explains this entire deception in these words:

“When for a long time they believed that they were appeasing Dis with human heads and Saturn with male victims, because of the oracle which ran:

> Καὶ κεφαλὰς Ἀΐδῃ καὶ τῷ πατρὶ πέμπετε φῶτα.  
> And send heads to Hades, and lights—or men—to the Father.

they say that Hercules, later returning through Italy with Geryon’s cattle, persuaded their descendants to exchange ill-omened sacrifices for auspicious ones: they should offer Dis, not human heads, but little masks (*oscilla*) fashioned in imitation of the human form, and should honor Saturn’s altars, not by slaughtering men, but by lighting lamps, because *phōta* (φῶτα) signifies not only ‘a man’ but also ‘lights.’ From this arose the custom of sending candles as gifts during the Saturnalia.” NOURR., p. 319.

Col. 923, after the note *Theutin . . .* insert the following:

**Flute-player or support (*tibicinem*).** According to Paulus (in Festus, s.v. *tibicines*), *tibicen* is sometimes used for a pillar or support by which some building, house, or [Col. 1342B] other object is propped up. Juvenal certainly used it in this sense, Satire III, verse 203:

> We inhabit a city propped up by a slender support.

Ovid likewise, *Fasti* IV, verse 695:

> She had only just been sweeping the villa that stood supported by a prop.

NOURR., p. 321.—The Glosses: “. . . *tibicines* . . . ἀντηρίδες, δοκοί,” “buttresses, beams.” Festus explains the reason for the name: it derives from the resemblance to flute-players, who support themselves as they play, just as these props support buildings. Compare the *Commentary on the Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. V, plate LXX, p. 314, and Heraldus, *Adversaria*, Book I, chapter 8, p. 43. ORELL.

Col. 926, at the note *Who [is the father] of Picus . . .* after the word ORELL., add:—Virgil sang in these most elegant verses in *Aeneid* VII, verses 45 ff.:

> . . . King Latinus, now advanced in years,  
> Was ruling fields and cities, tranquil in a lengthy peace.  
> Him we understand to have been born to Faunus and the Laurentian nymph Marica;  
> [Col. 1342C] Picus was Faunus’s father, and he traces you, Saturn,  
> As his parent: you are the ultimate source of his bloodline.

Col. 927, after the note *You wish . . .* insert the following:

**Therefore, fully three hundred and sixty years have elapsed since these men.** In Eusebius’s *Chronicle* this interval is compressed much further in these words (at the year 838): “The first king of the Romans after Troy’s capture was Aeneas. Before him Janus, Saturn, Picus, and Faunus reigned for approximately 150 years”—that is, at least as many years fewer than Arnobius freely conceded to the pagans. On these earliest kings of the Latins, see Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities*, Book I, pp. 24 and 34; Lactantius, Book I, chapter 22; Augustine, Book XVIII, chapter 15; and others. NOURR., p. 312.

Ibid., after the note *Of Aeneas . . .* insert the following:

**Founder of the town of Alba.** The hitherto unknown history of the kings of ancient Latium from Aeneas down to Amulius has very recently been brought to light by a notable fragment of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. It survives complete in an Armenian manuscript preserved [Col. 1342D] at Milan in the Ambrosian Library, and the most learned Angelo Mai published it in Latin translation, together with several other works, as a foretaste of this greatly desired publication, in the book entitled *Unpublished Works of Philo the Jew, Porphyry the Philosopher, and Eusebius Pamphilus*, Milan, 1816, octavo. Since the fragment occupies only a few sheets, it may be permissible to transcribe it here in full, pp. 65–69.

### On the Founding of Rome

“There is very great controversy concerning the City’s foundation, namely its date and its founders; and, in my opinion, no historian has related the matter satisfactorily. Since the relevant facts have been ascertained, however, it will suffice to indicate them. Cephalion of Gergis [read: of Gergetha], an excellent author and man, says that in the second generation after the Trojan War the City was built by those who survived safely at Ilium and joined themselves to Aeneas as companions, etc.”

[Col. 1343A] Four pages, whose publication we await in the complete work. From Book VII of Diodorus, *On the Origin of the Ancient Romans*:

“Certain historians have thought that the Romuli—that is, Romulus and Remus, who founded Rome—were born of Aeneas’s daughter. This, however, is far removed from the truth, for an immense succession of years intervenes between the reigns of Aeneas and Romulus, by whom Rome was founded in the second year of the third Olympiad. The building of the city, therefore, occurred more than 433 years after the Trojan War. For in the third year after Troy’s capture Aeneas obtained the kingdom of the Latins, which he held for three years, until he was removed from human sight and received divine honors. His son Ascanius succeeded to his rule and founded Alba, now called Longa. He named this city after the river then called Alba, which is now the Tiber.

“As regards the name of that city, however, Fabius, a historian of Roman affairs, invents other tales. [Col. 1343B] He says that an oracle was delivered to Aeneas declaring that some quadruped would show him beforehand the place where the city was to be founded. Now, when Aeneas happened to bring a pregnant white sow forward for sacrifice, she escaped from the sacrificer’s hands and fled to a certain hill, where she gave birth to thirty young. Aeneas, struck with wonder and eager to carry out the oracle, then resolved to found a city on that spot. In a dream, however, he was deterred from this undertaking and instructed to build the city after thirty years, corresponding, of course, to the number of offspring. Aeneas therefore refrained from populating the city with inhabitants.

“After Aeneas was taken from life, Ascanius, his son and heir to the kingdom, occupied the hill with buildings thirty years later and named the city Alba after its color. For in their language the Latins call ‘white’ *album*, which we call λευκόν (*leukon*, ‘white’). He added the name Longa because its breadth was very slight, while it extended to an excessive length. He [Fabius] adds that Ascanius chose Alba as the seat of his kingdom and [Col. 1343C] destroyed many neighboring peoples. Ascanius became famous through these successful deeds and died in the thirty-eighth year of his reign.

“After Ascanius’s death, a popular disturbance arose because two men were contending to seize the kingdom. Julius, Ascanius’s son, claimed his father’s rule for himself, while Silvius, Ascanius’s brother, born to Aeneas and Silvia, Latinus’s first wife, sought the same kingdom. (For when Aeneas died, Ascanius had abandoned in the mountains the boy whom he wished to destroy; yet shepherds raised him there, and he accordingly acquired the name Silvius from the place.) At last, after prolonged contention between the factions, Silvius obtained the kingdom by popular vote. Julius, cast down from his hope of rule, was nevertheless elevated to the dignity of chief pontiff and ranked second to the king. From him, they say, descended the Julian clan, which survives at Rome to this very day.

“King Silvius accomplished nothing memorable and died in the forty-ninth year of his reign. His son Aeneas succeeded him and received the additional name Silvius; he ruled for [Col. 1343D] more than thirty years. Latinus then reigned, likewise surnamed Silvius, for fifty years. He became renowned for his many achievements and battles. He both destroyed neighboring towns and founded eighteen ancient cities of the Latins: Tibur, Praeneste, Gabii, Tusculum, Cora, Pometia (the Armenian manuscript has *Comedia*), Lanuvium, Labicum, Scaptia, Satricum, Aricia, Tellenae, Crustumerium, Caenina, Fregellae, Cameria, Medullia, and Boilum, which others call Bola. (Compare Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 768 ff.) After Latinus’s death, his son Alba Silvius was made king and held the kingdom for thirty-eight years. Next came Capetus Silvius for twenty-six years, succeeded by Capys for twenty-eight years; then his son Calpetus for thirteen years; then his son Tiberinus for eight years. Tiberinus attacked the Tyrrhenians in arms, and, while leading his army across the river Alba, was drowned; from this event the river acquired the name Tiber. Agrippa then ruled the Latins for forty-one years, followed by Aulus Silvius for nineteen. Aulus is said to have been so swollen with pride that he opposed [Col. 1344A] and threatened Jupiter himself. Once, indeed, in the season of the crops, when tremendous thunderclaps were repeatedly sounding, he commanded all his soldiers simultaneously, at a single signal, to strike their shields with their swords, so that the crash of thunder might be surpassed by that noise. The gods did not permit his arrogance to go unpunished: he was destroyed by lightning and submerged together with his entire household in Lake Alban. As evidence of the event, the Romans who live beside the lake still point out a column projecting above the water’s surface at the place where the royal family was submerged. (See Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Antiquities* I, 71, who calls that king Ἀγρίπαν Ἀλλάδην or Ἀλλώδιον, *Agrippas Allades* or *Allodios*, according to the variant readings. Compare also Syncellus, p. 185, ed. Goar.) Aventinus followed him and reigned for thirty-seven years. Defeated in war by the neighboring peoples, he was forced to flee to the Aventine Hill, which then first took that name from him. Proca Silvius was next appointed to rule for thirteen years. After his death, Amulius, his younger son, usurped the tyranny while Numitor, the elder brother, was traveling far away. This Amulius reigned [Col. 1344B] for more than forty-three years, until he was killed by Romulus and Remus, who founded Rome.”

Thus Eusebius. They therefore reigned at Alba:

| King | Years |
|---|---:|
| Ascanius | 37 |
| Silvius | 49 |
| Aeneas Silvius | 30 |
| Latinus | 50 |
| Alba Silvius | 38 |
| Capetus Silvius | 26 |
| Capys | 28 |
| Calpetus | 13 |
| Tiberinus | 8 |
| Agrippa | 41 |
| Aulus Silvius | 19 |
| Aventinus | 37 |
| Proca Silvius | 13 |
| Amulius | 43 |
| **Total** | **432** |

[Col. 1344C] This somewhat exceeds Arnobius’s calculation. ORELL.

Col. 929, at the note *What? Do you . . .* replace the word ORELL. with:—Compare H. Meyer and J. Schulz, *Notes on Winckelmann’s History of Art*, Book II, no. 399, *Works of Winckelmann*, vol. III, p. 349. ORELL.

Col. 930, at the note *Of Apollo . . .* replace the word ORELL. with:—Compare Aulus Gellius XIII, 22; Vossius, *On Idolatry* I, 12; Gutherius, *On the Ancient Law of the Pontiffs* I, 20; Brissonius, *On Formulas* I, 103; and the *Commentary on the Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. IV, plate XVII, p. 84. The *Indigitamenta*, therefore, were Ritual Books which Numa Pompilius had received from the Etruscans; in them, as Festus says, it was prescribed by what rite cities were to be founded and altars and temples consecrated, with what sanctity walls were invested, under what law gates were established, and in what manner tribes and centuries were distributed, etc. ORELL.

Col. 933, after the note *Since, therefore . . .* insert the following:

**Let us, in turn, inquire, etc.** Augustine, *City of God*, Book I, chapter 29: “Let the pagans who [Col. 1344D] insult the integrity of Christians and say to them, whenever they happen to fall into some temporal misfortunes, ‘Where is your God?’ themselves tell us where their gods are when they suffer the very things to avoid which they either worship those gods or maintain that they ought to be worshiped.” ELMENH.

Ibid., at the note *Incense-boxes . . .* replace the word ORELL. with:—I now incline to the latter explanation, “an incense chest.” Nothing need be changed. *Conficiatis*, that is, “consume” (“why you pour out, empty, all your incense-boxes upon the full altars”). In the *Painting of Herculaneum*, vol. II, plate XXXIII, a woman is seen carrying an *acera*, that is, an incense-bearing chest, together with laurel. See the most learned commentators there, p. 197, and Visconti in the *Pio-Clementine Museum*, vol. IV, p. 5. ORELL.

Col. 934, after the note *The loss . . .* insert the following:

**When the privileges of free birth had been removed.** Among the Romans, *ingenuitas* was the status of those born to free parents; [Col. 1345A] hence the “right of free birth,” whose insignia for men were the plain toga and for boys the *bulla* and purple-bordered toga. For a freeborn man was a citizen with full legal rights. Cicero, *Against Verres* I, chapter 58: “For no one was disturbed by the clothing which custom and the right of free birth granted him,” namely, the purple-bordered toga. Compare Sigonius, *On the Ancient Law of the Roman People* I, chapter 6, vol. I, p. 75, Leipzig edition. ORELL.

## BOOK THREE

Col. 937, before the first note place the following:

I.—**By now, indeed, all these accusations—or rather, curses.** He calls the charges “accusations,” which can exist without curses and abusive language. Since, therefore, the pagans’ charges were not simple, unadorned accusations but were stained with all the gall of bitterness, he adds “or rather, curses.” Similar are these words of Origen against Celsus, Book III: Ἤρκει μὲν οὖν καὶ ταῦτα πρὸς τὰς Κέλσου λοιδορίας μᾶλλον ἢ κατηγορίας, “These things, then, would have sufficed against what are Celsus’s abusive attacks rather than accusations.” HERALD.

Col. 939, before the short note *To belief . . .* insert this:

[Col. 1345B] **Or thereby it will be proved true.** *Aut* (“or”), that is, “neither,” by *apo tou koinou* (ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ), the construction in which a shared word is supplied from the preceding clause. HEUMANN., in the margin.—Thus Cicero, *Letters to Friends* II, final letter: “The letter indicated neither where nor on what day it had been dispatched, or at what time I should expect you.” ORELL.

Ibid., after the same short note add the following:

**Of united agreement.** *Unire* (“to unite”) and *unitus* (“united”) are words of ecclesiastical Latin. In Nero’s age they were not yet in use, except in philosophical circles. Seneca, *Natural Questions* II, chapter 2: “I could not have extricated myself if I had wished to employ the philosophers’ language and call them ‘united bodies.’” See Cellarius, *On Barbarisms in the Latin Language*, p. 148, and the *Addenda*, p. 156. Nothing is more frequent in our author. ORELL.

Ibid., after the note *We can . . .* insert the following:

**All the divine beings, whoever they may be.** Heumann conjectures *quicumque* (“whoever”), taking *divinorum* as masculine. But Arnobius uses the same expression for the gods in Book VI, chapter 3: “what the divine beings owe in common with us.” [Col. 1345C] I wish I had not already changed this to “what the gods owe in common with us.” ORELL.

Col. 941, in the note *Whether these . . .* after the words “But Meursius’s correction is uniquely true,” add:—Heumann conjectures *an ipsi haec sibi diebus imposueritis lustricis* (“whether you yourselves imposed these things upon them”—that is, upon the gods themselves—“on days of purification”). Wrongly. ORELL.

Col. 944, after the note *Nor . . .* add the short note:

**Who are those divinities?** Heumann reads *sint* (“are”), correctly. ORELL.

Col. 945, at the short note *Of words . . .* add:—Heumann reads *luculentia* (“splendor”). But nothing should be changed. See *Corrections and Additions*, p. 466. ORELL.

Ibid., final note:—For “**Concerning this.** That is, ‘because of this,’ as often. See—” read:—“**From this.** That is, ‘because of this,’ as often (Heumann conjectures *ob hoc*). See—”

Col. 946, note *Of error . . .*: for *dictave* read *dictare*.

Ibid., after the note *Of error . . .* insert the following:

VIII.—**We pronounce it in the masculine gender.** Jerome, *Letter 143 to Pope Damasus*: “Nor should sex be thought to exist in the powers of God, since even the Holy Spirit himself is expressed, in accordance with the properties of the Hebrew language, in the feminine gender, *ruaḥ* (רוּחַ); in Greek, in the neuter, τὸ πνεῦμα (*to pneuma*); and in Latin, in the masculine, *spiritus*. From this it must be understood that, when higher things are discussed and something masculine or feminine is used, sex is not so much being signified as the idiom of the language is sounding; for the invisible and incorruptible God himself is expressed in the masculine gender in almost all languages, although sex does not apply to him.” ELMENH.

Ibid., in the note *For you have been accustomed . . .* after the middle portion, for “and the solemn words of the Roman people. Moreover,” read:—“and the solemn words of the Roman people, as well as Phil. Carolus, *Observations on Aulus Gellius*, in the passage cited, pp. 171 ff., who treats this matter at length. Moreover,”

Col. 949, at the short note *To be miscarried . . .* after the word ORELL., add:—Papias: “*aboriri* . . . to be born badly.” Nonius: “*aboriatur*, *abortiat* . . . Varro . . . wine produced there in a certain place, if a pregnant woman drinks it, causes her to miscarry.” ELMENH.

[Col. 1346A] Col. 950, at the note *Hellespontian*, after the word ORELL., add:—*Etymologicum Magnum*, s.v.:

“Ἀβαρνὶς πόλις Λαμψάκου. ὠνομάσθη δὲ ἀπὸ τοιαύτης αἰτίας. Διονύσου ἐρασθεῖσα Ἀφροδίτη, ἐμίγη αὐτῷ· ἀναχωρήσαντος δὲ τούτου εἰς τὴν Μηδικὴν [read Ἰνδικὴν, ‘India,’ as in the scholiast on Apollonius], ἐγαμήθη Ἀδώνιδι· ὕστερον δὴ ἐπανελθόντος Διονύσου, στέφανον πλέξασα ἡ Ἀφροδίτη ἀπήντησεν αὐτῷ· ᾐτεῖτο δὲ ἀκολουθῆσαι αὐτῷ διὰ τὸ ἤδη γεγαμῆσθαι· εἰς δὲ Λάμψακον ἀναχωρήσασα, τὸν ἐξ αὐτοῦ κυοφορούμενον ἐβούλετο ἀνελεῖν. Ἡ δὲ Ἥρα ζηλοτυπήσασα μεμαγευμένῃ τῇ χειρὶ ἐφήψατο τῆς γαστρὸς αὐτῆς, καὶ ἐποίησεν αὐτὴν τεκεῖν παῖδα· ὃν Πρίηπον ὀνομασθῆναι, ἄσχημον καὶ βαθυαιδοῖον· καὶ τοῦτον ἀπαρνηθῆναι αὐτὴν τὴν Ἀφροδίτην· καὶ ἀπὸ τούτου Ἀπαρνίδην κληθῆναι, κατὰ δὲ ἐναλλαγὴν τοῦ στοιχείου Ἀβαρνίδην.”

“Abarnis, a city of Lampsacus. It was named for the following reason. Aphrodite fell in love with Dionysus and had intercourse with him. When he departed for Media [read: India, as the scholiast on Apollonius has it], she married Adonis. Later, when Dionysus returned, Aphrodite wove a garland and went to meet him; but she declined to accompany him because she was already married. Withdrawing to Lampsacus, she wished to destroy the child she had conceived by him. Hera, moved by jealousy, touched Aphrodite’s belly with an enchanted hand and caused her to give birth to a child, who was named Priapus and was ugly and possessed of an enormous sexual organ. Aphrodite disowned him; and from this he was called *Aparnides* (‘the disowned one’), or, through an interchange of letters, *Abarnides*.”

The scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius I, 932, has the same account in almost the same words. Compare Zoëga’s most learned illustration of this shameful tale in the work entitled *The Ancient Bas-Reliefs of Rome*, vol. II, plate LXXX, pp. 165 ff. ORELL.

Col. 951, at the note *To torture*, replace the word ORELL. with:—Heumann [Col. 1346B] conjectures *plorare* (“to bewail”). Wrongly. ORELL.

Col. 953, after the note *Or if . . .* insert the following:

**Joints (*coagmenta*).** Nonius should be corrected at this word: “*Coagmenta* are so called because they are close and matching unions [read: *compages*, ‘joinings’], from *cogere*, that is, ‘to bind tightly.’” MEURS., p. 93.

Col. 955, at the note *With arteries*, replace the word ORELL. with:—Heumann reads *spiralibus* (“with spirals”). Wrongly. ORELL.

Col. 956, at the note *Cilunculi*, replace the word ORELL. with:—Compare Dausqueius on Silius Italicus, p. 2, who prefers *silunculos* and compares the word σιμιχίδας (“the snub-nosed”) in Theocritus; this, however, is more appropriate to those whom Arnobius shortly afterward calls “those with upturned noses.” ORELL.

Col. 963, at the note *The others*, after the word HERALD., add:—Heumann construes it: “For the other gods are not [divine],” “divine” being supplied from what precedes. ORELL.

Col. 964, at the note *There are in . . .* replace the word ORELL. with:—Andrea Cirino, in his *Discourse on the City of Rome*, chapter 24, [Col. 1346C] included in Sallengre’s *Thesaurus of Roman Antiquities*, vol. II, p. 266, thinks that either C. Barth’s conjecture *in sidereis sedibus* (“in the starry abodes”) should be adopted, or that the text should read: “in the starry abodes, forests on mountains” (in Arnobius’s usual manner of omitting a conjunction). He observes:

“He follows, in fact, the opinion of Anaxagoras and Democritus, who, according to Plutarch in *On the Face in the Moon’s Orb* and *Opinions of the Philosophers*, taught that the moon is a fiery firmament containing plains, mountains, and valleys. Heraclitus thought the earth was dark and covered with cloud; Philolaus and the Pythagoreans utter similar nonsense. Perhaps they show symbolic embodiments of powers placed at the summit of the heavens; and since Orion is prominent among the constellations, the hunter and the hare displayed this abode to hunters as the end of illustrious labors and immortal glory.” ORELL.

Ibid., at the note *As difficult*, replace the word ORELL. with:—Heumann conjectures *corrigatque* (“and may correct”). Wrongly. ORELL.

Col. 965, before the short note *Things to be known*, insert this:

[Col. 1346D] XXII.—**And that life may be better equipped.** I read: “and that life may be better equipped with these things.” MEURS., p. 93.

Col. 970, before the note *And unless . . .* insert the following:

XXIV.—**Tutelary gods.** Arnobius below, Book IV: “If you say that these parts too perform their functions under their own tutelary divinities.” Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Roman Antiquities* IV, p. 220: Βωμοὺς ἐκέλευσεν αὐτοῖς ἱδρύσασθαι, θεῶν ἐπισκόπων τε καὶ φυλάκων τοῦ πάγου, “He ordered them to establish altars to the gods who oversee and guard the hill”; Book VI, p. 393: Καπιτώλιε Ζεῦ, καὶ θεοὶ πόλεως ἐπίσκοποι, “Capitoline Zeus, and gods who oversee the city.” Jerome, vol. IV, on Isaiah 58: “Rome, mistress of the world, venerates in every apartment and house, with candles and lamps, an image of Tutela, whom they call by this name because of the protection [read *ob* for *ad*] of the buildings.” An ancient inscription:

> TO THE TUTELARY GOD, AEMILIUS SEVERIA, MIME-WRITER, SET THIS UP.  
> TO MERCURY AND MINERVA, THE TUTELARY GODS.

ELMENH.

[Col. 1347A] Col. 971, in the note *With anointings . . .* at the end, for the passage “the girdle was bound with the Herculean knot (that is, the tightest knot),” read:—“the girdle was bound with the Herculean knot (that is, the tightest knot, which the distinguished Boettiger discusses at length in *Greek Vase Paintings*, vol. I, part II, p. 103).”

Col. 975, before the note *Another . . .* insert the following:

XXIX.—**And things dissolving themselves.** *Se* is absent from Heraldus’s manuscript: “things dissolving themselves” [*dissolventia ipsa se*]. ORELL.

**Whom [you say] are always individual, etc.** Arnobius seems here to have used *singulos* in the rather unusual sense of “defined by number” (“of a definite, limited number”), as opposed to “innumerable.” ORELL.

**By Janus . . . the father, etc.** Servius on *Aeneid* VIII, verse 605: “Some hold that Janus is called the lord in whose domain are sunrise and sunset. . . . Others call him lord of the entire year, which is acknowledged to be divided into four seasons. That he is god of the year is proved by the fact that the first part of the year is named after him: January (*Januarius*) is named from Janus. Others understand Janus as the world, whose doors are therefore closed in peacetime because the world is closed on every side; in wartime they are opened so that they may stand open for seeking aid.” [Col. 1347B] He adds that some, including Cicero, say that Janus or Eanus is named from *eundo* (“going”) and that he is Mars; others call him Clusivius, Patulcus, Janonius, and even Quirinus. Macrobius, however, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 9, says that certain persons, such as Nigidius, identify him with the Sun and Apollo, while some identify him with the world and the sky; others call him by the same names Servius lists, especially Janonius, “as though,” he says, “he controlled the entrance not only of January but of all the months.” Compare Augustine, *City of God* VII, chapter 7. NOURR., p. 140.—Compare John Lydus, *On the Months*, pp. 55 ff., and especially the very learned Creuzer in the work entitled *Symbolism and Mythology of the Ancient Peoples*, vol. II, pp. 450 ff. ORELL.

Col. 976, at the note *Father*, after the word ORELL., add:—The Etruscans called the Latins’ god Fontus or Fontinalis *Fontir*, from φυτεύω (*phyteuō*), “to produce and send forth”; from this the Latins had *fons* (“spring”), just as [Col. 1347C] among them *scaturigo* (“gushing spring”) is formed from *scateo* (“to gush”). GORIUS, *Dissertation on Etruscan Hellenism*, in *Literary Symbols*, vol. II, p. 66.

Ibid., at the note *Of Juturna*, near the end, after the word ORELL., add:—According to Virgil, *Aeneid* XII, 138, she was the goddess of lakes among the ancient Latins:

> At once the goddess thus addressed Turnus’s sister,  
> A divinity who presides over pools and sounding rivers:  
> The lofty king of heaven, Jupiter, consecrated this honor to her  
> In return for the virginity he took away.

Compare the observations appended to the *Commentaries on the Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. I, p. 171. ORELL.

Col. 980, at the note *Aethereal*, replace the word ORELL. with:—This is a doctrine of the Egyptians, according to Diodorus Siculus, Book I, chapter 12. Since his words, also preserved by Eusebius in *Preparation for the Gospel* III, chapter 3, are classic evidence on this matter, it is worthwhile to transcribe them in full:

“Τὸν δ’ ἀέρα προσαγορεῦσαί φασιν Ἀθηνᾶν, μεθερμηνευομένης τῆς λέξεως, καὶ Διὸς θυγατέρα νομίσαι ταύτην, καὶ παρθένον ὑποστήσασθαι διά τε τὸ ἄφθορον εἶναι τῇ φύσει τὸν ἀέρα, καὶ τὸν ἀκρότατον ἔχειν τόπον τοῦ σύμπαντος κόσμου· διόπερ ἐκ τῆς κορυφῆς τοῦ Διὸς μυθολογηθῆναι ταύτην γενέσθαι· ὠνομάσθαι δὲ αὐτὴν Τριτογένειαν ἀπὸ τοῦ τρὶς μεταβάλλειν αὐτῆς τὴν φύσιν κατ’ ἐνιαυτόν, ἔαρος καὶ θέρους καὶ χειμῶνος· λέγεσθαι δ’ αὐτὴν καὶ Γλαυκῶπιν, οὐχ, ὥσπερ ἔνιοι τῶν Ἑλλήνων ὑπέλαβον, ἀπὸ τοῦ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ἔχειν γλαυκούς (τοῦτο μὲν γὰρ εὔηθες ὑπάρχειν), ἀλλ’ ἀπὸ τοῦ τὸν ἀέρα τὴν πρόσοψιν ἔχειν ἔγγλαυκον.”

“They say that, when the term is translated, they call the air Athena; they regard her as a daughter of Zeus and represent her as a virgin both because air is by nature incorruptible and [Col. 1347D] because it occupies the highest region of the entire cosmos. For this reason she was mythically said to have been born from Zeus’s crown or head. She was named Tritogeneia because her nature changes three times during the year—in spring, summer, and winter. She is also called Glaukopis (‘bright-eyed’ or ‘blue-gray-faced’), not, as some Greeks have supposed, because she has blue-gray eyes—for that is a foolish notion—but because the air has a blue-gray appearance.” NOURR., pp. 443–44.

Col. 981, at the note *There is none . . .* replace the final word ORELL. with:—I know, indeed, that Mind and Victory were regarded as goddesses. Of these, Victory was first consecrated by Atilius Regulus and afterward by Aemilius Scaurus, while Mind was consecrated during the Samnite War by Atilius’s consular colleague, M. Postumius Megellus. But this occurred at Rome, not in Greece, where this goddess was born. Nevertheless, Victory was also worshiped at Athens, where she had a wingless image. MEURS., p. 99.

[Col. 1348A] Col. 982, at the short note *Stygian . . .* add:—Heumann conjectures: “Neptune is the name of no god.” ORELL.

Col. 983, at the note *Of wares . . .* add:—Goods and commercial dealings (“trade and commerce”). ORELL.

Col. 984, at the note *Whom Nigidius . . .* after the word OCHSN., add:—He was a celebrated author, a man of praetorian rank, and highly knowledgeable in the liberal arts, philosophy, astrology, and medicine. A fragment of Cicero survives (p. 25) in which the learning of this Publius Nigidius is praised, as it also is by Macrobius, *Saturnalia* VI, chapter 5; Aulus Gellius XIX, chapter 16; and Servius on *Aeneid* X, 583. Compare Cicero, *Letters to Friends* IV, letter XIII. Aulus Gellius, Book VI, chapter 6, surnames him Figulus (on this surname see Augustine, *City of God* V, chapter 3); Lucan likewise calls him by this name in Book I, verse 693:

> But Figulus, whose concern it was to know the gods  
> And the secrets of heaven—whom Egyptian Memphis  
> Could not equal in observing the stars  
> And the numbers that move them.

[Col. 1348B] Eusebius, in the *Chronicle* at the year 1973: “Nigidius Figulus, a Pythagorean and magician, dies in exile.” NOURR., p. 545.

Ibid., at the note *Whom [they say] to be . . .* add:—Varro too, *On the Latin Language* IV, p. 18: “Vulcan was so named from the greater force and violence of fire.” Servius is still more explicit on *Aeneid* VIII, verse 414: “Vulcan, as we have said, is fire; and he is called Vulcan, as though *Volicanus*, because he flies (*volet*) through the air. For fire is born from the clouds; hence Homer too says that Vulcan was cast down from the air to earth, because every thunderbolt falls from the air.” NOURR., p. 449.

Col. 985, at the note *Proserpina*, replace the word ORELL. with:—Hence Proserpina was included among the divinities of agriculture. The same Varro, in Augustine, *City of God* VII, chapter 24: “They believe Earth to be Ops because she is improved by labor (*opera*); Mother, because she gives birth to many things; Proserpina, because crops creep forth (*proserpant*) from her; Vesta, because she is clothed (*vestiatur*) with grass.” Compare Graevius, *Readings in Hesiod*, chapter 11, and Muncker’s extensive treatment of this goddess in his commentary on Fulgentius, *Mythologies* I, chapter 9, p. 635, ed. van [Col. 1348C] Staveren. ORELL.

Col. 988, after the note *Of one . . .* insert the following:

**Is affected by no movements of its own.** The *e* is redundant, as above, Book I, chapter 39, “gods fashioned on anvils and from hammers,” where see Heraldus’s note, vol. I, p. 323. ORELL.

Ibid., after the short note *So that neither . . .* add the following:

**The world is established as the one God.** Heumann wishes to delete the word *world*. Wrongly, for Arnobius is speaking of those who maintained that the world, or the world-soul, was God. ORELL.

Col. 990, note *Novensiles . . .* for the passage “shook out. With Piso,” read:—“shook out. Compare the distinguished Creuzer in the work entitled *Symbolism and Mythology*, vol. II, p. 476. With Piso,”

Col. 991, before the note *Granted . . .* add the following:

**Stationed at the Trebia.** The Trebia is a river not far from Placentia which, as Strabo wrote in Book V, p. 217 (Casaubon), flows from the Apennines into the Po. Moreover, beside this river Hannibal defeated the consul Scipio with very great slaughter, [Col. 1348D] as Polybius relates, Book III, pp. 220 ff. (Casaubon). Hence this passage of Lucan, Book II, verse 448:

> O wretched fate, that we were not born  
> For the Punic age of Cannae, nor as the youth of Trebia!

(NOURR., p. 452.)

Ibid., at the same note, after the word HERALD., add:—See more in Nourry, pp. 537 ff. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note *Cornificius . . .* add:—Perhaps he is the same man of whom Eusebius speaks as follows in the *Chronicle* at the year 1576: “The poet Cornificius, abandoned by his soldiers, whom, when they fled, he often called helmeted hares, was killed. His sister was Cornificia, whose distinguished epigrams survive.” NOURR., p. 540.

Col. 993, at the note *Nigidius . . .* add:—Compare the *Commentary on the Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. IV, plate XXXI, p. 147, and especially the distinguished Creuzer in the work entitled *Symbolism and Mythology*, [Col. 1349A] vol. II, pp. 306 ff. and 439. ORELL.

Col. 994, at the note *Genius . . .* add the following:—The most learned Creuzer has explained this extremely difficult passage particularly well in the aforementioned work, vol. II, p. 441, where he treats the religion of the ancient Etruscans—for Arnobius here refers to their doctrine concerning genii. It may be permissible to transcribe his words in full:

“According to this doctrine, every god, every human being, every house, and every city had its own Genius. Those of the gods were called Penates, and there were in all four classes of Genii: those of Tina (Jupiter), those of Neptune, those of the underworld gods, and those of human beings. It was a system of beings who, in descending order, connected the higher gods with the lower and the deity with humankind: a great pyramid, as it were, whose apex vanished into Tina (Jupiter), the world-governing center, and whose broad base rested upon the earth toward all four quarters of the world.”

Thus Creuzer. This observation is altogether essential. Among the Greeks there are no traces of gods who are omnipresent or who act [Col. 1349B] simultaneously in two places—unless one might perhaps refer here Homer’s words about Hercules in the *Nekyia*, *Odyssey* XI, verses 600 ff.:

> Τὸν δὲ μετ’ εἰσενόησα βίην Ἡρακληείην,  
> Εἴδωλον· αὐτὸς δὲ μετ’ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσι  
> Τέρπεται ἐν θαλίῃς, καὶ ἔχει καλλίσφυρον Ἥβην.

> After him I perceived mighty Heracles—  
> His phantom; but he himself among the immortal gods  
> Delights in feasts and possesses fair-ankled Hebe.

Whenever the gods resolved either to reward the good or to punish the wicked, they left Olympus and visited the earth. (See the tales of Deucalion, Lycaon, and Philemon and Baucis.) The Etruscans held a different view. According to their doctrine—which had its source in Egypt and was received from them by the Romans and other Italian peoples—Jupiter and the other gods never leave their abode, heaven, but each has his own genii, at once companions and servants, through whom they communicated with humankind. The highest of these was the Genius of Jupiter mentioned by our Arnobius and in the inscription in Muratori, p. 587:

[Col. 1349C]

> TO JUPITER LIBER, OR TO THE GENIUS OF JUPITER.

Indeed, Gorius, *Etruscan Museum*, vol. II, p. 319, teaches that the Etruscans assigned three genii to Jupiter. Thus, in the *Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. I, plate XI, we behold the genius of Minerva most elegantly depicted in the form of a winged boy with the aegis; and the genius of Diana—a winged boy offering food to a doe on a dish—in the same work, plate LX, where see the commentators’ most learned discussion of the matter, pp. 263 ff. Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* II, 370 ff., sang as follows concerning the genii, or Penates, of peoples, cities, and individual human beings:

> But the skillful orator says that because the city  
> Obtained its allotted span by fate, it claims a Genius of its own:  
> “For every people or walled city,” he says, “is assigned  
> Either a Fate or a Genius, in the manner of our souls,  
> Which by differing lot enter new bodies.”

ORELL.

Ibid., at the note *And Pales . . .* replace the word ORELL. with:—Servius on *Aeneid* III, 325: “The Etruscans call Ceres, Pales, and Fortune the Penates.” You will see the image of Cales, [Col. 1349D] her head crowned with ears of grain, in the *Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. V, plate V. Compare the most learned Mazocchi there. ORELL.

Col. 995, at the note *These Consentes . . .* replace the final word ORELL. with:—Salmasius discusses the *Di Consentes* most learnedly in his *Letter to Ménage*, appended at the end of Book I of his *Letters*, published after his death at Leiden in 1656, p. 15. ORELL.

Col. 996, at the note *Because together . . .* add:—Rather, the rising and setting of the twelve signs of the Zodiac. But even this has no place there: “to rise” and “to set” mean nothing more than “to be born” and “to die.” See the words of the most learned Schelling which we shall presently cite. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note *And in compassion . . .* replace the final word ORELL. with the following:—Light has now been shed on this exceedingly corrupt passage by the distinguished Schelling in the work entitled *On the Deities of Samothrace*, Stuttgart, 1815, octavo. The most learned man therefore reads, with F. Ursinus, *memorationis parcissimae* (“of the scantiest mention”), [Col. 1350A] in this sense: there was no, or only scant, mention of them among the Etruscans in prayers and sacrifices, since they possessed absolutely no power, not even the least, over human affairs, but were attached to supreme Jupiter as counselors.

“A divine council, therefore” (these are his words, p. 59, compared with p. 115), “a coherent whole composed of gods, is found among the ancient Etruscans. Their individual names were unknown; collectively, however, they were called *Consentes* and *Complices*, which is merely an explanation—indeed, a literal translation—of the name of the Cabiri. There were six male and six female beings, in addition to the one to whom they were collectively subordinate: Jupiter, called Tina in the Etruscan language. (Accordingly, they were only intermediary beings whom Jupiter employed as his male and female servants in governing the world.) Though different gods, they are nevertheless united as one. Pelasgian settlers, as is historically known, had brought their gods there into the Etruscan country; on the coast of Lavinium Aeneas disembarked the Trojan Penates. [Col. 1350B] And concerning these very Etruscan gods Varro asserts that they were called *Complices* because they could live only together and die together. It would be impossible to add anything to this expression or to characterize more aptly the true conception of those united gods.”

Moreover, the most learned Schelling considers the Etruscans’ *Di Consentes* identical with the Cabiri, the gods of Samothrace. Even the name *Consentes*, he argues, signifies this, since it corresponds most exactly to the name of the Cabiri: “associated,” “companion,” “companions”; for example, Index XX, 11, “all associated into one,” “united, all as one man.” Hence Greek Κάβειροι and Κάβιροι: *Consentes*, *Complices*. See Schelling, ibid., pp. 107 ff. The distinguished Creuzer agrees with him in explaining Arnobius’s words, in the work entitled *Symbolism and Mythology*, vol. II, pp. 439 ff. ORELL.

Col. 999, at the note *Now to be . . .* add:—Schelling, in the passage cited, pp. 93 ff., thinks that these gods were anciently called Fingers, Δάκτυλοι (*Daktyloi*), because of the [Col. 1350C] extremely small, finger-sized stature in which the Samothracians represented them. “Fingers,” as though “dwarfs, pygmies, thumb-men, Lilliputians, little mountain-men.” He also cites an old gloss in Scherz’s *Glossary of Medieval German* II, p. 2011: “little wights, wights, little goblins; Penates.” ORELL.

Ibid., note *Ghosts . . .*: for “they call it a ghost. These,” read:—“they call it a ghost. (If it was uncertain what they deserved, they were called *Manes*. See Augustine, *City of God* IX, chapter 10, and Nourry, p. 458.) These . . .”

## BOOK FOUR

Col. 1005, at the note *Salus*, after the word ELMENH., add:—Livy, Book X, chapter 1: “Gaius Junius Bubulcus . . . dedicated as dictator the temple of Salus which he had vowed as consul during the Samnite War and contracted for as censor” (in the consulship of Lucius Genucius and Servius Cornelius, in the year 451 from the City’s foundation).

ORELL.

Ibid., after the note “Virtue,” insert the following:

**Honor, Virtue.** Livy, book XXVII, chap. 25—supported by Plutarch—states that, during the Gallic War at Clastidium, Marcellus [Col. 1350D] vowed a temple to Honor and Virtue. Its dedication was prevented by the pontiffs, who maintained that a single sanctuary could not properly be dedicated to more than one god. Valerius Maximus, however, book I, chap. 8, testifies that, as a result of that warning by the pontiffs, Marcellus erected the images of Honor and Virtue in separate temples. Vitruvius mentions both temples, book III, chap. 1, and book VII, in the preface; so too does Symmachus, who wrote as follows to Ausonius in book I, Epistle 14: “Wisely and rightly did our ancestors—as in other matters belonging to that age—place the twin temples of Honor and Virtue side by side, having devised in advance what we have seen realized in you: that the rewards of honor are found where the merits of virtue are found.” Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXV, chap. 10, records that this temple of Honor and Virtue was restored by the emperor Vespasian. Finally, from Livy, book XXIX, chap. 11, we learn further that another temple of Virtue was consecrated at the Porta [Col. 1351A] Capena by M. Marcellus, son of the Marcellus whom we have mentioned. NOURR., pp. 483–84.

Col. 1007, at the note “Peace,” after the word ELMENH., add:—We learn furthermore from Suetonius (*Vespasian*, chap. 9) that the emperor Vespasian built a temple of Peace near the Forum; Pliny, *Natural History*, book XII, chap. 19; Xiphilinus; Josephus, *Jewish War* VII.24; and others mention it. Moreover, according to Pausanias, book VI, p. 179, the statue of Chimenes was transported to Rome, to the temple of Peace. NOURR., p. 484.

Col. 1008, after the last line insert this short note:

**Which is opposed to them.** Canter supplied *Est* from the Roman edition. The other editions, including the Leiden edition, do not have it. ORELL.

Col. 1009, after the note “Luperca,” insert the following:

**He says.** Heumann reads *you say*. It seems that this reading must certainly be restored in this passage. For here Arnobius is not, as before, addressing the opponents of the Christian faith in general, but specifically the Romans, masters of the world, whose goddess Luperca was. ORELL.

Col. 1013, after the note “And was called,” add the following:

[Col. 1351B] **Because it was made from unbaked bricks, etc.** See Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXV, chap. 14. ORELL.

Ibid., in the note “What then,” in place of the word HERALD., insert:—The Greeks called it thus: “This is the one that, they say, has the chimney” (*ἔστι δὲ αὕτη, ἡ τὴν κάπνην, φασὶν, ἔχουσα*), says Eustathius. Thus *κεραμίς* means something made either from pottery or from bricks; for in reality the difference is slight. HERALD.

Ibid., at the short note “Kitchens,” after the word ELMENH., add:—Nonius: “The ancients called a kitchen (*culina*) a *coquina*.” Yet the examples he adduces there seem to show that he wrote *colina*, not *coquina*. HERALD.

**Small hearths.** Plautus in the *Persian*: “For already within, my belly’s little hearths are smoking.” The same author, *Captives*, act IV, scene II, line 65:

> Do you order—or do you not order—the cauldrons to be set up? The dishes washed?  
> The bacon and the feast kept hot upon the blazing hearths?

But a *foculus* is a small altar, a matter we discussed above (at book III, chap. 24). HERALD. and ORELL.

Col. 1014, at the note “Taster,” after the word ORELL., [Col. 1351C] add:—A *praegustator* is one who samples the first portions of food. Suetonius, *Claudius*, chap. 44: “And it is generally agreed that he was killed by poison. Some relate that, while he was dining in the citadel with the priests, it was administered by the eunuch Halotus, his taster” (see Burmann there, p. 805. ORELL.). An ancient inscription:

> A VOW TO SILVANUS: T. F. DIADUMENUS LURNESIANUS,  
> TASTER OF THE EMPEROR, FREELY AND DESERVEDLY FULFILLED IT.

ELMENH.

Col. 1016, before the note “And those things,” insert this short one:

**Because at the knots.** With Meursius one should write: “who at the knots.” ORELL.

Col. 1018, at the note “Libentina,” add:—Nourrius thinks that *Libera* should be read in place of *Libentina*. According to Augustine, *City of God*, book VII, chap. 2, Libera too was regarded as presiding over sexual desire. ORELL.

Col. 1022, at the note “Fathers,” add:—Compare also the distinguished Hottinger on the words of the Epistle of St. James, chap. I, verse 17: “From the Father of lights” (*Ἀπὸ τοῦ πατρὸς τῶν φώτων*), p. 31. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note “Because not,” after the final word ORELL., add:—Compare the very learned commentators on the *Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. III, plate 39, pp. 178 ff., and on the *Antiquities of Herculaneum* (Bronzes), vol. II, plate 94, p. 382. ORELL.

Col. 1024, before the note “Or because,” insert the following:

**And, when invoked by the haruspices, they obey.** Julius Firmicus, *Mathesis*, book II, final chapter: “This consideration also confounds the haruspices. For whatever is invoked by them, because its power is less than the power residing in the emperor, will be unable to disclose the substance.” HERALD.

Col. 1031, at the note “The fourth Jupiter,” after the word ORELL., add:—She is also called *Hippeia* (“Equestrian,” *Ἱππεία*) by the Greeks. The name Coryphe is also corrupted in Suidas: “Athena Hippeia: they say that she was the daughter of Poseidon and Coryphe”—for so one must read in place of *Polyphe*—“the daughter of Ocean; and that, because she was the first to construct a chariot, she was therefore called Hippeia” (*Ἱππεία Ἀθηνᾶ, ταύτην Ποσειδῶνος εἶναί φασι θυγατέρα καὶ Κορύφης [sic enim legendum pro Πολύφης] τῆς [Col. 1352A] Ὠκεανοῦ· ἅρμα δὲ πρώτην κατασκευάσασαν διὰ τοῦτο Ἱππείαν κληθῆναι*). MEURS., p. 100.—See Küster there, vol. II, p. 141. ORELL.

Col. 1032, after the note “Or if,” add the following:

**So that religion, thrown into confusion, may be left in doubt.** This uniquely correct reading is owed to Salmasius. The first Roman edition reads: “so that this too may be religion thrown into confusion.” Gelenius: “so that this may be religion,” etc. ORELL.

Col. 1034, at the note “Of whom,” add:—Moreover, concerning this and the other names of Minerva among the ancient Egyptians, Greeks, Etruscans—among whom she was called Tana and Menerva—Romans, etc., and concerning their etymology, the very learned commentator on the *Antiquities of Herculaneum*, vol. VI (*Bronzes* II), plate V, pp. 17 ff., has much to say. ORELL.

Col. 1039, at the note “By usage,” after the word NOURRIUS., add:—The manuscript reads “by the usage of spelt.” Stewechius conjectures “by usage, by confarreation,” citing Ulpian in the *Fragments of the Institutes*, title 8, and Boethius in the *Topics*. The opposite is *diffareatio*. ORELL.

Col. 1040, at the note “And because,” after HERALD., [Col. 1352B] add:—Franciscus Modius furnished me from an old book with this reading: “and because they were participants, and why they were not participants in the Fescennine verses.” I restore: “and because they were equally participants in the Fescennine verses.” STEWECH.

Col. 1046, after the note “Because to bend,” insert this:

**That Lynceus.** Lynceus is very well known from the story of the Argonauts. Valerius Flaccus says of him, book I, lines 462 ff.:

> But Lynceus, the brother of Idas, is preserved for mighty purposes—  
> He whom Arene bore could pierce the earth  
> And, sending his gaze through it, discern the silent Styx.

Compare the *Orphic Argonautica*, line 175; Hyginus, *Fables* XIV; and P. Burmann, who most diligently collected all the ancient testimony concerning him in the *Catalogue of the Argonauts* prefixed to Valerius Flaccus. ORELL.

Col. 1048, in the middle of the note “Surely of desire,” delete the words printed twice:—“And Tertullian . . . judged by lightning.”

Col. 1051, at the end of the note “Who to him”:—For “*Fragment*, pp. 394 ff., new ed. ORELL.,” read:—*Fragment*, pp. 394 ff., new ed.; and Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, book II, chaps. 19 and 56. There, from Plutarch, *Roman Questions* 111, he demonstrates that the Spartans too imitated the example of the Carians; indeed, that all the Greeks sacrificed a dog in rites of expiation; and that, according to Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXIX, chap. 4, at Rome too the Luperci slaughtered a dog in February, a month named from *februare*, “to purify”; p. 798, Rosenmüller’s edition. ORELL.

Col. 1055, after the note “Arsinoë,” insert the following:

**To have sought it in the passions of an unadvised heart.** He says this because Apollo is called “the Counselor,” *σύμβουλος*, as Clement of Alexandria calls him in this very passage, which Arnobius reproduced. HERALD.

Ibid., at the note “Jupiter,” in place of the final word ORELL., add:—Moreover, concerning Jupiter’s love affairs, see the most elegant passage in Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI.102–114, and Gierig there. ORELL.—Gregory of Nazianzus also sang of them, vol. II, poem 61, p. 152 (Bill.):

> Look first, then, at all the shapes he assumed in his lusts:  
> Bull, swan, gold, serpent, husband, bear—everything  
> Swift Love—a feeble boy—commanded him to become.  
> So at least they themselves relate, the fabricators of powerless gods.

NOURR., p. 395.

Col. 1056, after the note “Now into,” add the following:

**Into a sportive satyr.** Namely, when having intercourse with Antiope, daughter of Nycteus, by whom the twins Amphion and Zethus were born. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI.110–11:

> She added how Jupiter, concealed beneath a satyr’s form,  
> Filled the beautiful daughter of Nycteus with twin offspring.

Compare Hyginus, *Fables* VIII; Apollodorus III, chap. 5; scholia on Apollonius Rhodius IV.1090; Lactantius Placidus on Statius, *Thebaid* IX.423. ORELL.

Col. 1057, at the note “Hercules,” after the word ORELL., [Col. 1353A] add:—These are Varro’s words in the passage cited: “Aelius Gallus said that Dius Fidius was the son of Diovis, that Castor was *Dioscurus* (*Διόσκουρον*), and thought that this figure was called Sanctus in the Sabine language and Hercules in Greek.” MEURS., p. 136.

Ibid., at the note “Hylas,” after the final word ORELL., add:—On Hylas see Valerius Flaccus III.530 ff.; Hyginus, *Fables* 270; Prudentius, book I, *Against Symmachus*. ELMENH.

Col. 1059, at the note “Mother,” in place of ORELL., add:—Compare especially the very learned Creuzer in the work entitled *Symbolik und Mythologie*, vol. II, pp. 319 ff., and vol. III, pp. 566 ff. ORELL.

Col. 1063, after the note “With a splendid,” insert the following:

**XXX.—Or a little task.** *Operula* is a rather rare diminutive form in place of *opella*. Yet Apuleius also has it in *Metamorphoses*, book I, p. 105, Elmenhorst’s edition: “I even devoted to her the little earnings that, while still vigorous, I made by working as a maker of soldiers’ cloaks.” See Elmenhorst there in the Index and Gesner in the *Thesaurus*, s.v. ORELL.

[Col. 1353B] **More . . . more disgracefully.** A double comparative, in Arnobius’ manner. Moreover, *ignominiose*, in place of which writers of approved Latinity said *cum ignominia* (“with disgrace”), is an adverb of declining Latinity. Eutropius, book IV, chaps. 24 and 26: “he fought disgracefully”; and Orosius, book VII, chap. 7, concerning Nero: “fleeing most disgracefully.” See Cellarius, *Curae Posteriores de Barbarismis Linguae Latinae*, p. 146, and the Index to Eutropius. ORELL.

Col. 1070, beginning of the note “Of majesty”:—For “restored. Previously it was read:” read:—“restored. Likewise, *obministraverit* from the manuscript, incorrectly. Previously it was read:”

Ibid., in the same note, after the final word ELMENH., add:—Theodosius the Great subsequently mitigated this law. See in the Justinian Code, book I, titles 7 and 8, and in the Theodosian Code, vol. III, p. 41, the laws concerning curses directed against the emperor, together with Gothofredus’ observations upon them. NOURR., p. 433.

Ibid., before the note “A senator,” insert the following:

**To reduce a magistrate to the ranks.** Others use *to compel into the ranks* in the same sense—that is, to diminish his authority or dignity, *demütigen, herabsetzen* (“humiliate, abase”). ORELL. Livy, book XXV, chap. 4: “Postumius had dissolved the assembly of the plebs and compelled the tribunes into the ranks”; and book XLIII: “The tribune complained that by this act the assembly had been taken away from him and that he had been compelled into the ranks, and departed.” Compare Pliny, book I, Epistle XXVIII (GUIL. RONCHINUS, *Various Readings*, book I, chap. 12, in vol. I of Hermann Schminkius’ *Critical Collection of Various Authors*, published at Marburg in 1717, p. 23).—Compare Doering on Livy, book VI, chap. 38, p. 93. ORELL.

Col. 1072, after the note “Fifteen,” insert the following:

**And also chaste virgins, etc.** Prudentius, in the second book *Against Symmachus*:

> From there, to the assembled audience in the theater, nurturing modesty . . . .

HERALD. We cited this passage above in this Appendix. ORELL.

Col. 1074, at the note “From official duties,” in place of the final word [Col. 1353D] ORELL., add:—*Elogium*, in the unfavorable sense of an account of an offense, occurs very frequently among ecclesiastical writers. Tertullian, *The Soldier’s Crown*, chap. 5: “an account of sacrilege”; *Apology*, chap. 24: “an account of irreligion”; *Monogamy*, chap. 9: “an account of adultery.” Jerome, *Selected Epistles* (edited by Canisius) I.8: “He had deferred the account of the accursed man.” The glossator cited by Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXXVII, chap. 12: “*Elogium* . . . the text of evil deeds accompanied by disgrace.” Compare Casaubon on Vulcatius Gallicanus, *Historia Augusta*, vol. I, p. 470; especially Muncker and van Staveren on Fulgentius, *Mythologies*, book I, chap. 1, p. 623; and Perizonius on Aelian, *Various History* XIV.43. ORELL.

Col. 1076, at the note “Why savagely,” after the word HERALD., add:—Concerning these Christian gatherings before dawn, Pliny the Younger’s letter to Trajan, book X, Epistle 97, is particularly worth reading; Orosius, book VII, Tertullian in the *Apology*, and Eusebius [Col. 1354A] in the *Chronicle* mention it. Indeed, I recall that the emperors Arcadius and Honorius also forbade all heretics to assemble in profane gatherings, by night or day, to perform a litany. From this constitution it is clear that, when Pliny in the aforesaid letter wrote that they “sang a hymn to Christ as to a god,” he meant nothing other than the Christians’ public litanies (*λιτανείας*) and supplications. An ancient law in the Twelve Tables pertains both to Pliny’s letter and to the imperial constitution: “LET NO ONE HOLD NIGHTTIME ASSEMBLIES IN THE CITY.” Porcius Latro mentions it in his *Speech against Catiline*. Nor was it without reason that the ancients called the dead of night *intempestiva*, as Varro notes from Brutus and Aelius in book V of *The Latin Language*, because at that time there was no time available for action; Censorinus made the same observation in *The Birthday*, chap. 10. STEWECH.

Col. 1077, at the note “And when,” after the word ORELL., add:—It was customary for Christians gladly to hear themselves called—or to be spoken of as—brothers. Witness the Epistles of St. Paul and of others; likewise Minucius Felix in the *Octavius*, where, among other things, he says: “And indiscriminately they call one another brothers and sisters.” STEWECH.—Arnobius the Younger on Psalm CXXXIII: “Now tell me: why have you assembled together, you who are called brothers, or on what grounds are you all brothers? Explain. From one Father, he says, Christ, and from one mother, the Church.” ELMENH.—Compare also Tertullian, *Apology*, chap. XXXIX, p. 324, Havercamp’s edition. ORELL.

Col. 1078, before the note “And because of,” insert the following:

**Because of unapproved leaders.** Among the Romans *praesul* properly designated the chief of the Salii, “the leader of the dance” (*ὁ ἐξάρχων τοῦ ὀρχεῖσθαι*), who was responsible for the Salian hymns and *axamenta*. See Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XIX, chap. 10, and especially Casaubon and Salmasius on Capitolinus, *Antoninus the Philosopher*, chap. 4, in the *Historia Augusta*, vol. I, p. 302. Here, however, it must be understood generally as *praesultor*, or, as the ancient glosses call him, *prosaltor*, “leader of a dance.” Arnobius is undoubtedly referring to the story he tells below, book VII, chap. 36 of our edition, about the slave whom [Col. 1354C] his master drove with rods around the circus. ORELL.

Ibid., after the short note “To have corrupted,” insert the following:

**The breezes of the seasons.** A monstrosity! I read: “the breezes of the winds.” MEURS., p. 143.—The commonly received reading seems preferable to me. By “the breezes of the seasons,” Arnobius means winds occurring in periodic succession—that is, the four seasons of the year blowing over the earth. ORELL.

## BOOK V

Col. 1081, at the note “Of Egeria,” add the following:

**At Egeria’s warning.** Augustine, *City of God*, book VII, chap. 35, relates that Numa practiced hydromancy, and cites Varro as his witness. Varro says that Numa took the nymph Egeria as his wife because he had drawn out or carried out the water from which he performed hydromancy. Valerius Maximus, book I, chap. 2; Florus, book I, chap. 2; Aurelius Victor, *Illustrious Men*, chap. 2; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, *Antiquities*, book II, p. 122; and others, however, record that he pretended to do everything [Col. 1354D] at the warning and according to the counsels of his wife Egeria. NOURR., p. 463.

Col. 1082, after the note “But when,” insert the following:

**Eagerly.** In archaic fashion (*Ἀρχαϊκῶς*). Thus *duriter* (“harshly”) in Terence, *The Woman of Andros*, act II, scene I, line 47; *blanditer* (“flatteringly”) in Plautus, *The Asses*, act I, scene 3, line 69; *praeclariter* (“splendidly”) in Quadrigarius, *Fragments of the Annals*: “And thus, when affairs have been splendidly conducted, we shall return home”; *duriter* in Catullus, poem LXXV.19, where see Vulpius, p. 441. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note “To have cast upon,” in place of ORELL., add:—Compare also Broukhusius on Tibullus I, Elegy II, line 45, p. 45. ORELL.

Col. 1083, in the note “You will expiate”:—For “the Leiden editor. *Fulgurita*,” read:—“the Leiden editor. (Thus *cresse*, *cesse*, for *crevisse*, *cessisse*, in Lucretius III.683 and I.1104. Likewise *divisse*, *produxe*, *promisse*, *sumpse*, *consumpse*. See Ausonius Popma, *On the Use of Ancient Speech*, book I, chap. 12, p. 770, Messerschmid’s edition. And perhaps Valerius Antias, from whom Arnobius drew his material, wrote it in this way.) *Fulgurita*,”

[Col. 1355A] Col. 1085, at the note “And of the sacred rites,” in place of the final word ORELL., add:—This usage is especially familiar to ecclesiastical writers. See Muncker on Fulgentius, *Mythologies*, book II, chap. 6, p. 674, van Staveren’s edition. ORELL.

Col. 1087, at the note “Childish,” in place of the final word ORELL., add:—For “it is ready to hand.” Stewechius prefers “it is ready,” in the manner of the ancients. ORELL.

Col. 1090, after the note “With lowings,” insert the following:

**Acdestis, surnamed from his mother’s name.** That is, from the rock Agdos, upon which Jupiter discharged his lust. But Strabo, book XII, p. 567 (Casaubon), attests that the mother of the gods herself was called Agdistis among the Phrygians: “Pessinus is one of the greatest trading centers of that region and has a sanctuary of the Mother of the Gods, which enjoys great reverence. They call her Angidistis”—read *Agdistis*—“In ancient times the priests were a kind of rulers, enjoying a great priesthood; but now their honors have been greatly diminished, though the trading center continues,” etc. (*Πεσσινοῦς δ᾽ ἐστὶν ἐμπορεῖον τῶν ταύτῃ μεγίστων, ἱερὸν ἔχον τῆς μητρὸς τῶν θεῶν σεβασμοῦ μεγάλου τυγχάνον· καλοῦσι δ᾽ αὐτὴν Ἀγγιδίστην [sic leg. Ἀγδίστιν]. Οἱ δ᾽ ἱερεῖς τὸ παλαιὸν δυνάσται τινὲς ἦσαν, ἱερωσύνην καρπούμενοι μεγάλην· νυνὶ δὲ τούτων μὲν αἱ τιμαὶ πολὺ μεμείωνται· τὸ δ᾽ ἐμπορεῖον συμμένει*, etc.).

Hesychius agrees: “Agdistis . . . the same as the Mother of the Gods” (*Ἀγδίστης . . . ἡ αὐτὴ τῇ μητρὶ τῶν θεῶν*). See the interpreters there, [Col. 1355B] p. 39, Alberti’s edition, and Nonnus on Gregory of Nazianzus, *Stelita* I.59: “The Mother of the Gods among the Phrygians had her genital organ cut off by the Corybantes because of her many acts of fornication” (*Ἡ παρὰ Φρυξὶ μήτηρ τῶν θεῶν ἀπετμήθη παρὰ τῶν Κορυβάντων τὴν κύστην διὰ τὰς πολλὰς αὐτῆς πορνείας*).

Pausanias, *Achaica*, or book VII, chap. 17, does not diverge from this. We gave his words in full, although dispersed over three passages, at pp. 273, 275, and 279 (cols. 1090, 1092, and 1095), though he does not expressly say that Agdistis was the same as the Mother of the Gods. Our Arnobius therefore follows another basis for the story. Furthermore, see the distinguished Creuzer, *Symbolik und Mythologie*, vol. II, pp. 37 ff.; and especially Zoëga, who most learnedly illustrated all the ancient testimonies and monuments concerning the Mother of the Gods and her cult in the work entitled *Li Bassirilievi antichi di Roma*, vol. I, note on plate XIII, pp. 100 ff. ORELL.

Col. 1091, at the note “Exhaled,” after the word ORELL., add:—I correct it: “Exulting, he violently seizes,” etc.; or even: “Roused, he seizes,” etc. For *ci* could easily have changed into *a*, and *l* arisen from the doubling of *t*. MEURS., p. 153.—But Scaliger’s emendation alone is correct.

[Col. 1355C] Col. 1092, at the note “Found,” in place of the final word ORELL., add:—Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, book II, chap. 53, thinks one should read: “Someone—I know not who—found him and nourished him with molds of goat’s milk,” that is, cheeses. There Rosenmüller, vol. I, p. 741, cites in a note Ménage’s *Origines de la langue française*, under *Fromage*. The same Bochart derives the name Attis from the Hebrew *athoud*. ORELL.

Col. 1093, at the note “Or because,” after the word *Ἀδαγοούς*, add:—Compare Jablonski, *On the Lycaonian Language*, p. 64, Te Water’s edition. ORELL.

Ibid., after the note “And by which,” insert the following:
