**And to be honored by him with woodland gifts.** Properly and accurately expressed, for gifts are a sign of honor. The Philosopher elegantly says in *Rhetoric*, book I, chap. 5: “Among every people gifts are held in honor; for a gift is both the bestowal of a possession and a sign of honor. Hence both lovers of wealth and lovers of honor desire gifts, since gifts contain what both need: a gift is a possession, which lovers of wealth desire, and it carries honor, which lovers of honor desire” (*Δῶρα παρ᾽ ἑκάστοις τίμια· καὶ γὰρ τὸ δῶρόν ἐστι κτήματος δόσις, καὶ τιμῆς σημεῖον· διὸ καὶ οἱ φιλοχρήματοι, καὶ οἱ φιλότιμοι ἐφίενται αὐτῶν· ἀμφοτέροις γὰρ ἔχει ὧν δέονται· καὶ γὰρ κτῆμά ἐστιν, οὗ ἐφίενται οἱ φιλοχρήματοι· καὶ τιμὴν ἔχει, οὗ οἱ φιλότιμοι*). HERALD.

Col. 1094, at the note “And lest ill-omened,” in place of the final word ORELL., [Col. 1355D] add:—Thus Orosius, *Histories*, book IV, chap. 6: “Just as among us too it often happens that, in the eyes of enemies, those whom they detest do nothing that is not depraved, nothing that is not shameful, nothing that is not somewhat ill-omened”—for thus, with Havercamp, one must read *subscaevum* in place of *subsicivum*—“nothing, whether in word or deed, that does not wound those enemies”; see Havercamp there, p. 231. ORELL.

Ibid., after the note “He made,” add the following:

**For this reason it began to be turreted.** The classic passage concerning the turreted Mother of the Gods is in Lucretius, book II, lines 599 ff.:

> Therefore she alone was named the mighty Mother of the Gods,  
> The mother of wild beasts, and the parent of our body.  
> The ancient and learned poets of the Greeks sang that she,  
> Raised aloft in a chariot, drove a pair of yoked lions  
> . . . . . . . . . . . . .  
> . . . . . . . . . . . . .  
> And they encircled the summit of her head with a mural crown,  
> Because, fortified in distinguished places, she sustains cities.

[Col. 1356A] Compare Cornutus, *On the Nature of the Gods*, chap. 6, and Zoëga, who treats the matter most learnedly in *Bassirilievi antichi*, vol. I, pp. 93 ff. ORELL.

Col. 1095, at the note “He snatches,” in place of ORELL., add:—Zoëga, in the passage cited, vol. I, p. 104, demonstrates from many sources that pipes, flutes, and other instruments of that kind, together with cymbals and drums, were extremely common in the rites of Cybele. ORELL.

Col. 1097, at the note “Having come to rest,” in place of ORELL., add:—Heumann explains in the margin: “fixed so firmly in the earth that it stood securely.” ORELL.

Ibid., at the note “Of the fingers,” in place of ORELL., add:—Philippus Carolus, in his *Observations on Aulus Gellius*, book II, chap. 30, pp. 178 ff., collected many examples of such rather unusual superlatives—for example, *assiduissimus* (“most constant,” Suetonius, *Augustus*, chap. 71), *parissimus* (“most equal,” Plautus, *Curculio*, act IV, scene II), *noxiissimus* (“most harmful,” Seneca, *On Clemency* I.26), *celerissimus* (“most swift,” Ennius in Priscian), *egregiissimus* (“most outstanding,” in Pacuvius), *postremissimus*, *piissimus*, and *crebrissimus*—as well as comparatives such as *idoneior*, *Poenior*, *Neronior*, *necessarior*, *tenuior*, *extremior*, *noxior*, etc. ORELL.

[Col. 1356B] Col. 1099, at the note “A pause,” after the word ELMENH., add:—Compare Cellarius, *On Barbarisms of the Latin Language*, p. 252. ORELL.

Col. 1106, at the note “Therefore,” in place of ORELL., add:—“*Sufficere*, *officere*, *inficere*, and *conficere*,” says Salmasius in Epistle CVIII to J. F. Gronovius, *Posthumous Letters*, p. 24, “are dyers’ terms, though they refer to different kinds and degrees of dyeing; we have minutely explained them all in our notes on Arnobius.” Since the commentaries of that most learned man have not yet seen the light, we shall attempt to explain these terms to the best of our ability. *Inficere*, therefore, is the general verb used when we dye cloth any color whatever. *Sufficere*, as we explained above, means to lay down an underlying color upon which another is afterward applied; for example, white cloths that are to be coated with red are first dyed blue, so that the red color may adhere more firmly. *Conficere* seems to mean coating cloth with two [Col. 1356C] or more colors in such a way that all appear together upon the surface (*meliert, mélange*—“mottled, blended”). *Officere*, by contrast, means coating cloth simultaneously with two colors in such a way that, according as one looks at it in sunlight or in shadow, one color obscures the other (*Schillerfarbe*—“iridescent color”). ORELL.

Ibid., at the note “Which from,” in place of ORELL., add:—Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, part II, book IV, chap. 12, reads “from flavored blood.” On this occasion he demonstrates that, besides our author, Tertullian and Ammianus Marcellinus also used *saporatum* to mean “seasoned,” but no writer of the Augustan age did. ORELL.

Col. 1110, after the note “Before,” insert the following:

**He certainly washed him with balsams and anointed him.** Meursius, p. 161, prefers: “He certainly washed him and anointed him with balsams.” But such a transposition of particles is familiar in Arnobius. ORELL.

Col. 1112, at the note “For what,” in place of the final word ORELL., add:—Compare the authors cited by the very learned Zoëga in *Li Bassirilievi antichi*, vol. I, p. 102, note no. 117. ORELL.

Col. 1114, before the note “Why in the manner,” insert the following:

**By which the divinity itself—from the grain of Ceres . . .** I write: “by which the divinity itself—from Ceres’ grain . . .” [The source excerpt is syntactically incomplete.] MEURS., p. 162.

Col. 1115, at the note “Fauna,” after the final word ORELL., add:—Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chap. 12, related these matters somewhat more clearly than Arnobius—though not without some difference—in the following manner. Fauna, he says, who is also called Fatua by some, especially Cornelius Labeo and in the books of the pontiffs, is the same as Maia, the Good Goddess, Ops, Earth, and the Great Mother; a divine rite is performed for her in May, on the Kalends of that very month. Others, however, regard her as the daughter of Faunus. When she resisted the will of her father, who was desperately in love with her, he beat her with a myrtle rod. Macrobius then adds: “As evidence for all these things they put forward the fact that it is forbidden to keep a myrtle rod in her temple; that a vine is extended over her head, with which her father chiefly attempted to deceive her; that wine is not customarily brought into her temple under its own name, but the vessel in which the wine has been placed is called a honey-pot, and the wine is called milk; and that serpents appear in her temple without being afraid.” [Col. 1357A] NOURR., p. 466.—Compare Gierig on Ovid, *Fasti* V.148 and the Index, s.v. *Bona Dea*, and the very learned Creuzer, *Symbolik und Mythologie*, vol. II, p. 488. ORELL.

Col. 1117, at the note “When he,” after the word ELMENH., add:—Ovid too recounts the same shameful story in most elegant verses, *Fasti* VI.627–636; see Gierig there, p. 358. ORELL.—Compare Pliny, book XXXVI, chap. 27. MEURS., p. 164.

Col. 1118, at the note “By which,” after the word ORELL., add:—The very learned Visconti has much to say concerning these Omophagia and Ophiophagia in the work entitled *Museo Chiaramonte*, vol. I, p. 96. He explains that, because in antiquity human heads had been sacrificed to Bacchus in memory of Pentheus, who was torn apart by the Maenads, after that savage sacrifice was abolished it was ordained that, on fixed days, Bacchus’ initiates should eat raw flesh from young bulls in commemoration of it. He cites the most elegant lines of Catullus, poem LXIV, *The Marriage of Peleus and Thetis*, lines 255 [Col. 1357B] ff.:

> Then they, rejoicing everywhere, raged with frenzied minds,  
> Crying “Evoë!” in Bacchic ecstasy, “Evoë!” as they tossed their heads.  
> Some of them shook thyrsi with their points concealed;  
> Some snatched limbs from a bullock torn asunder;  
> Some girded themselves with writhing serpents;  
> Some celebrated obscure rites with hollow chests—  
> Rites that the uninitiated vainly desire to hear.

Compare Seneca, *Phoenician Women*, line 365; *Trojan Women*, line 674. The distinguished Creuzer illustrates the subject no less learnedly in *Symbolik und Mythologie*, vol. III, p. 341. ORELL.

Col. 1121, after the note “Invoked,” insert the following:

**Assailants.** Gloss: “A *grassator* . . . is one who plots slaughter either from wantonness or for the sake of rewards.” Among the Romans this was the name of a class of robbers who occupied the streets in the city and beat, despoiled, and threatened with death those whom they encountered when circumstances made them vulnerable to injury: *Banditen, Strassenräuber* (“bandits, highway robbers”). Cicero, *On Fate*, chap. 15: “For in this way even a well-dressed traveler would be said to have been the reason why an assailant robbed him”; and Petronius, *Satyricon*, chap. 82: “A soldier noticed me—whether he was an impostor or a nocturnal assailant.” See the interpreters there, p. 406, Burmann’s edition. Compare Torrentius and Casaubon on Suetonius, *Augustus*, chap. 32, and Ernesti’s *Key to Cicero*, s.v. Here, however, Arnobius seems to have used *grassatores* generally for evildoers: *Frevler, Bösewichte* (“malefactors, villains”). ORELL.

Ibid., in the middle of the note “Of which matter”:—For “The Bacchants wore. For the rites,” read:—“The Bacchants wore. (See the commentary on the *Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. III, plate XXXVIII, p. 190.) For the rites.”

Col. 1124, after the note “With very large,” insert the following:

**He throws [them] into his lap and casts these things of his [reading uncertain].** The words “and casts” seem to me to require deletion as a gloss. Yet perhaps something of this kind must be tolerated in Arnobius. ORELL.

Col. 1125, at the note “By which,” after the word ORELL., add the following:—An ancient inscription:

> SI. METIUS. ZETUS. [Col. 1357D]  
> TO JUPITER SEBAZIUS. D. L. D.
>
> TO JUPITER SEBAZIUS. Q. NUNNIUS ALEXANDER  
> FULFILLED HIS VOW FREELY AND DESERVEDLY.

ELMENH.—Many have observed that Bacchus was called Sabazius and his mysteries Sabazia. For in Cicero (*On the Nature of the Gods* III.23) we read: “They say that the third Dionysus—or Bacchus—was born of the father Caprius and ruled as king over Asia; his are the rites called Sabazia.” Diodorus Siculus also writes (book IV, chap. 4) that another Dionysus, or Bacchus, is represented as the offspring of Jupiter and Proserpina: “whom some call Sabazius; they introduce his birth, and his sacrifices and honors as nocturnal and secret, because of the shame resulting from the intercourse. They say that he excelled in ingenuity and was the first to attempt to yoke oxen and, through them, to accomplish the sowing of crops; for this reason they also represent him with horns” (*τὸν ὑπό τινων Σαβάσιον ὀνομαζόμενον, οὗ τήν τε γένεσιν καὶ τὰς θυσίας καὶ τιμὰς νυκτερινὰς καὶ κρυφίους παρεισάγουσι, διὰ τὴν αἰσχύνην ἐκ τῆς συνουσίας ἐπακολουθοῦσαν· λέγουσι δὲ αὐτὸν ἀγχινοίᾳ διενεγκεῖν καὶ πρῶτον ἐπιχειρῆσαι βοῦς ζευγνύειν, καὶ διὰ τούτων τὸν σπόρον τῶν καρπῶν [Col. 1358A] ἐπιτελεῖν, ἀφ᾽ οὗ δὴ καὶ κερατίαν αὐτὸν παρεισάγουσι*). (See *Paintings of Herculaneum* V, plate V. ORELL.)

Hence Cicero again says (*On the Laws* II.18): “Aristophanes, that most witty poet of Old Comedy, so attacks the new gods and the nocturnal vigils practiced in their worship that, in his work, Sabazius and certain other foreign gods are tried and expelled from the city.” Finally, to omit Strabo and others, Suidas, s.v. *Σεβάσιος*, expressly declares Sebazius to be the same as Dionysus or Bacchus.

Why then, you will ask, are the mysteries in which Jupiter was especially worshiped themselves called Sabazia or Sebazia? Surely because Jupiter too bore the surname Sabazius; for Gruter presents various inscriptions reading: “TO JUPITER SABAZIUS.” Some, however—Vossius, for example, *Origins of Idolatry*, book II, chap. 14—consider Jupiter to be the same as Bacchus or Liber. What wonder, then, if those most shameful mysteries, in which Jupiter’s twofold adultery was celebrated, were called Sabazia? To this must be added the fact that, as Clement of Alexandria observed, mention was made in these mysteries of the Corybantes and Bacchus. [Col. 1358B] NOURR., p. 469.—It is useful to adduce on this subject the words of the very learned Goerenz on Cicero, *On the Laws*, at the passage cited, p. 159:

> Not enough inquiry has yet been made concerning this god. For the statements scattered throughout the ancient authors concerning him and his cult are, as it were, dismembered parts; they require a hand capable of assembling them into a single body, and one exercising mature judgment. The origin of this god’s cult is traced both to the Phrygians and to the Thracians (see the scholia on Aristophanes, *Wasps*, line 9. ORELL.), both to King Caprius and to Jupiter. As for his name, he is called sometimes Jupiter and sometimes Iacchus; for anyone who weighs the matter more carefully cannot regard these as distinct. Finally, the surname Sabazius is said to have originated sometimes among the Thracians and sometimes among the Phrygians, among whom a considerable number of grammarians and scholiasts attest that *σαβάζειν* has the same meaning as *εὐάζειν*, “to cry *Evoë*.” Yet there is scarcely any doubt that this god’s rites passed from the Phrygians to the Thracians. His differing origin and name seem to arise from the fact that the Greeks and Romans, who customarily adapted the names of their own gods to foreign ones, discovered in this god the attributes [Col. 1358C] of both Jupiter and Bacchus and therefore called him now by the one name, now by the other.

Thus Goerenz. Compare the commentary on the *Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. III, plate XXXVIII, p. 190, and the distinguished Creuzer, who illustrates the matter most learnedly in the work entitled *Symbolik und Mythologie*, vol. III, pp. 360 ff. ORELL.

Col. 1126, after the note “Which kind,” insert the following:

**And a clay mask.** That is, utterly worthless and of no value. Plautus, *The Churl*, act IV, scene 4, line 1: “A prostitute is insipid and worthless unless, over wine, she knows how to advance her own interests.” The same author in *The Little Carthaginian*, act IV, scene II, line 3:

> Nowhere among all peoples is there another more perjured or worse  
> Than my master, nor one so worthless or so smeared with filth.

Cicero, *Against Verres* III, chap. 14: “Then this worthless fellow also wishes to appear crafty and an old hand.” See Hotman there, p. 28, Graevius’ edition. ELMENH. and ORELL.

Col. 1129, beginning of the note “All-night vigils”: for “For privilege,” read:—“For an all-night vigil.”

[Col. 1358D] Ibid., in the middle of the same note, for *Novimum*, read *Novimus* (“We know”).

Col. 1133, at the note “Of mockeries,” after the word ORELL., add:—Hence also the prostitutes are called *Miraculae* in Plautus’ *Nervolaria*:

> Two-obol women, perfumed girls, miracle-women.

MEURS., p. 168.

Col. 1137, after the note “I fasted,” insert the following:

**I fasted.** It is not evident who used the verb *jejunare* (“to fast”) outside the Church. Tertullian, *On Fasting*, chap. 2: “One should fast indifferently, by choice, not by command of the new discipline.” Jerome, Epistle XXII, chap. 13: “When I was going to read Cicero, I fasted.” Prudentius, *Hymn of Those Who Fast*, line 177:

> Long ago, when burdened with failing limbs,  
> Jesus fasted with a consecrated heart.

Although Arnobius here transfers this word to the Eleusinian [Col. 1359A] rites, it should not thereby be removed from the class of ecclesiastical vocabulary, because, as a Christian, he translated in his own way into Latin the Greek expressions belonging to a Greek rite. In place of this verb Cornelius Nepos elegantly said “to abstain from food,” *Atticus*, chap. 22. CELLAR., *Antibarbarus*, p. 47, and *Curae Posteriores*, p. 266.

**I took from the chest.** Concerning the mystic chest or casket that was carried around in the Eleusinian rites by the Cistophori, and in which—besides other frivolous objects to be handled by initiates alone—there was principally concealed the phallus, to which the worshipers sang the *phallic hymn* (*τὸ φαλλικόν*), see Spanheim on Callimachus, *Hymn to Ceres*, line 3; Wesseling on Diodorus Siculus I.22; Ernesti, *Key to Cicero*, s.v. *Cistophorus*; Doering on Catullus, poem LXIV, line 260; the commentary on the *Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. II, plate XXVIII, p. 270; and Visconti in the work entitled *Museo Chiaramonte*, vol. I, plate XXXIV, p. 83. ORELL.

**I placed it in the basket.** Concerning the basket carried upon the head by the noblest virgins during the festival of Eleusinian Ceres, see Spanheim on Callimachus, *Hymn to Ceres*, line 1, [Col. 1359B] pp. 735 ff., Ernesti’s edition, where we see a very finely engraved image of it, and the commentary on the *Paintings of Herculaneum* at the passage cited. Moreover, as is clear even from this passage of Arnobius, that basket must by no means be confused with the mystic chest. For the basket was not among the secret things (*ἐν ἀπορρήτοις*). ORELL.

Col. 1141, at the note “Prosumnus,” in place of ORELL., add:—Compare Verheyk on Antoninus Liberalis, chap. 41, p. 282, and Creuzer, *Symbolik*, vol. IV, p. 43. ORELL.

Col. 1444, at the note “To Heraclitus,” after the word ORELL., add:—Laërtius lists five men named Heraclitus in book IX, to whom Menagius added three others. What our author related from Heraclitus concerning the story of Liber and Prosumnus seems better suited either to Heraclitus, author of the *Homeric Allegories*, or to Heraclitus the lyric poet, who had sung the praises of the twelve gods. NOURR., p. 543.

Col. 1143, after the short note “Or of the name,” insert the following:

[Col. 1359C] **With their virgins . . . fathers.** *Virgins* in place of *daughters*, as in Cornelius Nepos, *Epaminondas*, chap. 3: “For whenever any of his fellow citizens had been captured by the enemy, or a marriageable daughter of a friend could not be given in marriage because of poverty, he summoned a council of his friends,” etc. ORELL.

Col. 1154, at the note “Of fawnskins,” in place of the final word ORELL., add:—*Nebris* (*Νεβρίς*), the distinctive emblem of the Bacchants. Seneca, *Oedipus* 435:

> Now among the Cadmean  
> Mothers, the impious Maenad . . . .

A companion came to Ogygian Iacchus,

His flank girded with the sacred fawnskin.

(See Delrio there, p. 109.) Sidonius, *Epithalamium for Ruricius*, Preface, verse 15:

Then Alcides sported with his club, Mavors with his spear,

Arcas with his wand, and Bromius with his fawnskin.

See *Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. III, plate XXXVII, where a Maenad is clothed in a fawnskin [Col. 1359D]; see also the most learned commentators there, p. 183 ff. ORELL.

Col. 1155, at the note “And a bubbling spring . . .,” after the word ORELL., add:—Thus Prudentius, *On the Crowns* (*περὶ στεφάνων*):

Let the very place be rent apart,

So that the loquacity of gushing speech

May lose its breath. ELMENH.

Col. 1160, at the last note, in place of ORELL., add:—The reading *Pro sed oratio sordida est* is corrupt. The old editions have: “And let the speech be sordid” (*Et oratio sordida sit*); Heumann corrected this to: “And the speech becomes sordid” (*Et oratio sordida fit*). Excellent. ORELL.

## BOOK SIX

Col. 1161, at the note “Charge . . .,” in place of the word ORELL., add:—Valesius and Gronovius, however, in their note on Ammianus Marcellinus, book XIV, ch. 1, prefer *affigere* (“to affix”), a word exceedingly frequent in ecclesiastical writers—Jerome, Facundus, Boethius [Col. 1360A], and others. Thus Macrobius too, book VII of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 2, says that marks of censure are “affixed” to someone or “have been affixed.” ORELL.

Col. 1163, after the note “Unimpaired . . .,” insert the following:

**Not to display portentous terrors.** Nothing could have been said more expressively, for he thus embraces both prodigies and portents together. He says “portentous terrors” because signs and monstrosities are never announced or presented without fear thereby slipping into human minds. And such is the case that, although portents are not invariably ill-omened, they nevertheless seem more often to foreshadow pestilence and calamity. Cedrenus: “It is said that these things signify no good for the cities in which they occur” (*Λέγεται δὲ σημαίνειν μὴ ἀγαθὰ ταῖς πόλεσιν, ἐν αἷς γίνεται ταῦτα*). HERALD.

Col. 1170, after the note “That is . . .,” insert the following:

**Nowhere by portions.** The Glosses of Isidore: “By portions” (*partiliter*)—dividedly, in parts, distributively. Thus Firmicus, *Astronomy*, book II, ch. 18, has “set forth by portions”; and Fulgentius, *Mythologies*, book III, ch. 2: “For it is better to be instructed portion by portion through a more secure course of labor than to be suddenly terrified by an approaching necessity [Col. 1360B]”; see Muncker there, p. 707, van Staveren’s edition. In the same way, a later age used *partile* in the sense of “divisible.” Claudianus Mamertus, *On the State of the Soul*, book I, ch. 18: “Then you will persuade me that this same soul is localized or divisible”; see C. Barth in the Index. ORELL.

Ibid., note “Not having dined . . .”: for “The scholiast adds to the *Theriaca*:—l.—The scholiast adds to the *Theriaca*, verse 612,” read: “The scholiast on the *Theriaca*, verse 612, adds.”

Col. 1172, at the note “Domes . . .,” in place of ORELL. add:—Hesychius: “A *tholos* (*Θόλος*) is properly a vaulted roof, but, by an extended use, a building constructed with a roof terminating in a point” (*κυρίως μὲν καμάρα, καταχρηστικῶς δὲ οἶκος εἰς ὀξὺ ἀπολήγουσαν ἔχων τὴν στέγην κατεσκευασμένος*). Thus the earliest use and meaning of *tholi* appears to have referred to a round roof placed upon and supported by columns (*la cuppola*, “the cupola,” as the most learned commentators on the *Paintings of Herculaneum* correctly interpret it, vol. III, plate LX, p. 315, and vol. I, plate XLIV, p. 231). Servius on *Aeneid* IX, verse 408, says: “A *tholus* is properly like a small shield at the center of a roof, where the beams meet; gifts were customarily suspended from it. Others say that a *tholus* is a kind [Col. 1360C] of structure belonging to sacred buildings, like those of Vesta and the Pantheon. They also say that round temples ought to be made for three gods: Vesta, Diana, and Hercules or Mercury.” Later, however, the term *tholi* seems to have been applied to the gabled roofs of temples, whether round or square. Nor did temples alone possess *tholi*, but other buildings did also—for example, baths. See Valesius on Ammianus Marcellinus XXVIII, ch. 4, vol. III, p. 241, Wagner’s edition; and above all Schneider, the distinguished scholar, who discusses this word most learnedly in his note on Vitruvius, book IV, ch. 8, p. 294 ff. ORELL.

Col. 1184, before the note “If the images . . .,” at the preceding note, in place of ORELL., add:—Jan Broukhusius offered another explanation of this exceedingly obscure passage in his note on Tibullus, book II, elegy 1, verse 55, p. 219 f.:

> “Arnobius,” he says, “alludes to the myth in which Bacchus is said to have fought against the Giants in the form of a lion and to have torn them apart with his claws and teeth. See Horace, book II, Ode XIX, verse 21, where an unpublished scholiast writes in the margin of the Graevius manuscript: ‘He touches upon the myth. When [Col. 1360D] the Giants sought Jupiter’s kingdom by piling mountains upon mountains, Father Liber, Jupiter’s son, put on a lion’s skin, seized one of the Giants, named Rhoetus, with his claws and jaws, twisted him backward, and hurled him down. That skin is said to have belonged to the Nemean lion and to have been given to him by Hercules.’ Why he called Bacchus ‘Fruit-Bearing’ is clear from Diodorus Siculus, book I, ch. 11, whom Virgil follows in the *Georgics*, as does Tibullus I, elegy VIII, 29. Yet if anyone prefers to refer Arnobius’ words to the Sun, I shall not stubbornly resist: for the masters of ancient wisdom teach us both that the Sun is identical with Bacchus and that he is sometimes represented in the form of a lion. (See Diodorus, in the passage cited. ORELL.) At Phelloe a wooden statue of Bacchus could be seen coated with vermilion; the people of Phigalia had another likewise colored with vermilion, according to Pausanias in his *Achaica* and *Arcadica*.”

Thus Broukhusius. On the ancients’ practice of coloring statues of the gods with vermilion—especially those of agricultural deities, Bacchus, Pan, and Priapus [Col. 1361A]—see Dalecampius and Harduin on Pliny, *Natural History*, book XXXIII, ch. 7 (36 in Harduin), and the commentary on the *Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. IV, plate LII, p. 253. On the Sun worshipped by the Persians in the form of a lion, see Muncker on Albricus, *On the Images of the Gods*, ch. 5, p. 901, van Staveren’s edition. ORELL.

Col. 1187, at the note “Accordingly, Hammon,” add the following:

**Hammon.** The classic passage on the form and attire of Jupiter Hammon is found in Curtius, book IV, ch. 7, §23: “The object worshipped as the god does not have the same appearance that artists have commonly assigned to the gods: down to the navel it resembles a ram, and its attire is set with emeralds and gems.” See the interpreters there and the images of Jupiter Hammon represented on coins in Snakenburg’s edition, p. 215 f. Compare Silius Italicus, book III, verse 8 ff.:

Ancient faith has long been preserved within the shrine,

Where, sitting aloft, a rival to the caves of Cyrrha,

Horn-bearing Hammon among the panting Garamantes

Unfolds the coming ages from his prophetic grove. [Col. 1361B]

See Dausqueius there, p. 101. Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, ch. 21, held that Hammon was the setting sun. Compare the *Corrections and Additions*, p. 476. ORELL.

Col. 1188, after the note “Liber . . .,” insert the following:

**Venus naked and exposed.** Clement of Alexandria, *Exhortation*, p. 38: “Even if someone sees a painted woman, he thinks of golden Aphrodite” (*Κἂν ἴδῃ τις ἀνάγραπτον γυναῖκα, τὴν χρυσῆν Ἀφροδίτην νοεῖ*). Concerning her and Bacchus, Theodoret, Discourse 3, *On Angels and Demons*, vol. IV, p. 520, says: “Both painters and sculptors fashion Aphrodite, their teacher, naked and do not cover her even with a little tunic . . . and Dionysus too, the limb-loosener, is fashioned by them naked” (*Ἀφροδίτην τὴν τούτων διδάσκαλον γυμνὴν καὶ οἱ ἀνδριαντοποιοί, καὶ οἱ ἀγαλματογλύφοι κατασκευάζουσι, καὶ οὐδὲ χιτωνίσκῳ καλύπτουσι . . . καὶ μέντοι καὶ ὁ Διόνυσος λυσιμελής τε καὶ γυμνὸς ὑπὸ τούτων κατασκευάζεται*). NOURR., p. 489.

Col. 1197, after the note “To separate . . .,” insert the following:

**Makes august** (*Augustat*). That is, “renders august.” A verb occurring only once (*ἅπαξ λεγόμενον*). See Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. ORELL.

Col. 1198, after the note “Under those men’s . . .,” insert the following:

**Geckos** (*Stelliones*). The *stellio* is an animal of the lizard family that nests in buildings [Col. 1361C]; in Greek, *askalabōtēs* (*ἀσκαλαβώτης*). Phavorinus: “The *skalabōtēs* is a little creature resembling a lizard, which crawls up the walls of houses” (*Σκαλαβώτης . . . ζωΰφιον ἐοικὸς σαύρᾳ ἐν τοῖς τοίχοις τῶν οἰκημάτων ἀνέρπον*). Bochart also discusses it at length throughout book IV, ch. 7 of the *Hierozoicon*, where Rosenmüller, vol. II, p. 515, adds in a note a description of this little animal from Hasselquist’s *Itinerary*. The Italians call it *Gekko*. Compare Schneider on Nicander’s *Alexipharmaca*, p. 260 f. ORELL.

Col. 1202, before the note “Sacred . . .,” at the preceding note, after HERALD., add:—*Itus, -us* (“going”) is also an ancient, Lucretian word; for example, III, verse 389 f.:

Nor do we perceive the movement of any creeping creature,

Nor each separate footprint of its feet.

Suetonius nevertheless also uses it in *Tiberius*, ch. 38. Compare Lauremberg, *Antiquities*, under this word. ORELL.

Col. 1203, note “Under the very . . .”: for “Others read *nomine*. See above—” read: “Others read *nomine*; Heumann reads *molimine*. See above.”

Col. 1206, after the note “Why the affront to his face . . .,” insert the following:

[Col. 1361D]

**Why did he not pursue with just vengeance the affront of his shaven face . . .?** Ambrose expresses the same thought in book II, ch. 5 of *On Virgins*: “The gods,” he says, “have been subjected to such mockery that neither could Jupiter defend his garment, nor Aesculapius his beard, nor Apollo even begin to grow a beard; nor could all those who are called gods draw back the bowls they held—not because they feared the charge of theft, but because they lacked sensation. Who, then, would worship beings that cannot defend themselves like gods or hide themselves like men?” NOURR., p. 498.

Col. 1208, after the note “When the Capitol . . .,” insert the following:

**And had seized Capitoline Jupiter himself together with his wife and daughter.** Besides the temple dedicated to Juno by Camillus on the Aventine, and besides the one erected to Juno Moneta, there was another on the Capitol shared with Jupiter and Minerva, where the three divinities were worshipped in separate chambers but were jointly invoked, as in Silius Italicus, book X [Col. 1362A], verse 433 ff.; Cicero, *Speech on His House*, ch. 57, and *Against Verres* V.72; Valerius Maximus V.10, example 2. Compare Lactantius, book I, ch. 11, and Augustine, *City of God* IV.10. For more, see Dausqueius on Silius in the passage cited, p. 435, and Ruperti, vol. II, p. 89. ORELL.

Col. 1210, at the note “Varro . . .,” in place of the final ORELL., add:—Symmachus likewise calls Varro “Menippean” in a letter first published by Carrio in book I: “You indeed imitate the scholarly zeal of Menippean Varro, but surpass his genius.” Compare Havercamp on Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 14, p. 146. ORELL.

Col. 1211, before the note “In dwellings . . .,” at the preceding note, in place of ORELL., add:—“Perhaps *Chanabeni* should be read. *Chanabeni* is an eastern word corrupted from the Hebrew for ‘thieves.’ Arnobius could also have said *Saraceni* in the same sense, from the Arabic *sarak*, ‘he stole, carried off.’” Thus the most learned Jena reviewer. The Leipzig reviewer likewise thinks that Arnobius intended by this word to signify secret thieves, not robbers who break the bars of doors by force and violent assault. ORELL.

[Col. 1362B] Col. 1213, at the note “Wearing a *ricinium* . . .,” in place of the final ORELL., add:—Cicero, *On the Laws* II.23, attests that the *ricinium* was a woman’s cloak worn in adversity and mourning. Compare Ernesti in his *Key*, under this word, and Salmasius—who, in his customary fashion, elucidates the subject most learnedly—on Vopiscus, *Aurelian* 45, *Augustan History*, vol. II, p. 541 ff. ORELL.

Col. 1214, before the note “With psalteries . . .,” insert the following:

**The Mother of the Gods with a drum; the Muses with pipes and psalteries.** I wonder whether the punctuation should be: “The Mother of the Gods with a drum, with pipes; and the Muses with psalteries,” so that the pipes are assigned to the Mother of the Gods. The pipe was, indeed, a Phrygian invention. Pollux, book IV, §74: “The kinds of pipes are: the transverse pipe; the lotus-wood pipe, an invention of the Libyans . . . the *elymos*, which is made of boxwood but was invented by the Phrygians; a horn curving upward is attached to each of the two pipes, and it is played for the Phrygian goddess” (*Αὐλῶν δὲ εἴδη, πλάγιος, λώτινος, Λιβύων τὸ εὕρημα . . . ἔλυμος τὴν μὲν ὕλην πύξινος, τὸ δὲ εὕρεμα Φρυγῶν· κέρας δὲ ἑκατέροις τοῖς αὐλοῖς ἀνανεῦον πρόσεστιν, αὐλεῖ δὲ τῇ Φρυγίᾳ θεῷ*). Pipes were exceedingly common in the rites of Cybele. Ovid, *Fasti* VI.189, on the festival of the Idaean Mother:

[Col. 1362C] I would like to ask many things, but the sound of shrill bronze

Terrifies me, as does the curved flute with its dreadful tone.

Compare Zoëga, who elucidates the matter most learnedly in *Ancient Bas-Reliefs*, vol. I, p. 104 (and on Cybele’s drum, p. 94), and the commentary on the *Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. II, plate XXIX, p. 175. What of the fact that Cybele herself is sometimes seen in ancient monuments furnished with a pipe—for example, in Montfaucon’s *Antiquities*, plate I, figure 5, Schatz’s abridgment? Yet because Arnobius used *tibiis* in the plural, I would be reluctant to abandon the received reading. ORELL.

Ibid., at the same note, “With psalteries . . .,” in place of the final ORELL., add:—It is worthwhile to transcribe Isidore’s words on the difference between the psaltery and the cithara, *Origins* III.21: “The psaltery,” he says, “which is commonly called a song, is named from playing the psaltery, because the chorus responds to its sound in harmony. It resembles a foreign cithara in the shape of the letter Δ. But this is the difference between the psaltery and the cithara: the psaltery has the hollow wooden body from which [Col. 1362D] the sound is produced at the top; the strings are struck from below and sound above. The cithara, by contrast, has the hollow of its wooden body below,” etc. We see a most elegantly portrayed Muse with a cithara in the *Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. II, plate V, and a Muse with a psaltery in plate VI; see there the annotations—or rather dissertations—of the most learned Mazocchi, p. 33 ff. Furthermore, Arnobius here seems to have included under the term *psalteries* the lyre, cithara, and other instruments of that kind attributed to the Muses. Compare the commentators on the *Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. II, plate VI, p. 34 ff., who discuss these instruments most learnedly. ORELL.

Ibid., after the note “Aesculapius . . .,” insert the following:

**Or the drinking-cup called a *cantharus* hanging from Liber’s right hand.** The *cantharus* was a kind of large, handled drinking vessel from which wine was poured into smaller cups or bowls. On its shape, see Scaliger on Ausonius, Epigram XXX, p. 26, Tollius’ edition, and Drakenborch on Silius Italicus VII [Col. 1363A], verse 196. To drink “from full *canthari*” (as we say, *aus vollen Humpen trinken*, “to drink from brimming tankards”) was the practice of heavy drinkers, as is clear from Plautus, *The Persian*, Act V, scene II, verse 40:

Come, pass the honeyed wine around; give us drink from *canthari* filled to the brim.

Hence the *cantharus* is the constant emblem of Bacchus and Silenus. Virgil, *Eclogue* VII.17:

And a heavy *cantharus* hung from its well-worn handle.

Macrobius, book V of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 21: “The *scyphus* is Hercules’ drinking-cup, just as the *cantharus* is Father Liber’s.” See, if you please, an image of Bacchus with a *cantharus* in Montfaucon’s *Antiquities*, plate XXVIII, figure 9, Schatz’s abridgment. ORELL.

Ibid., after the note “Anubis . . .,” insert the following:

**Or Priapus, smaller than his own genitals.** *Inferior* means smaller, shorter. HEUMANN., in the margin.

Ibid., after the note “*Caliendra*,” insert the following:

**Winged sandals** (*Talaria*). The winged footwear of Mercury is called *talaria* par excellence (*κατ’ ἐξοχήν*). Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.249 ff.:

[Col. 1363B] He prepared to obey his great father’s

Command; and first he binds golden sandals to his feet,

Which bear him aloft on wings, whether over sea

Or land, as swiftly as the rushing wind.

I recall having read a most learned discussion of them in the distinguished Voss’s *Mythological Letters*, a book I do not now have at hand. ORELL.

Col. 1215, note “Masks . . .,” after the quoted verse of Persius, insert the following:—The scholiast on Satire I says there: “There are three kinds of mocking gesture: using the hand to represent a stork; placing the thumb against the temples to make asses’ ears; or sticking out the tongue like a thirsty dog. A *sanna* is a distorted mouth and expression, such as we make when ridiculing others. Hence those who do not have a straightforward expression are called *sanniones*, buffoons.” Compare the commentary on the *Antiquities of Herculaneum*, book VI (*Bronzes*, vol. II), p. 379.

## BOOK SEVEN

Col. 1221, before the first note, “And to possess . . .,” insert [Col. 1363C] the following:

**With some kind of nourishment** (*alicujus alimonii genere*). Above, book IV, ch. 21, and below, book VII, chs. 16 and 39, we have *alimonia, -ae*. Both forms, however, already occur in the earliest writers—Plautus, Lucretius, and others. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note “Or animal . . .,” after ORELL., add:—These are the words of Macrobius, book III of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 5: “Trebatius, in book I of *On Religions*, teaches that there are two kinds of sacrificial victims: one in which the will of the god is sought through the entrails; the other in which the soul alone is consecrated to the god, whence the soothsayers also call these victims ‘animate’ (*animales*).” Thus Strabo too, book XV, p. 732 Casaubon, says of the Persians: “For they say that the god requires the sacrificial animal’s soul and nothing else” (*Τῆς γὰρ ψυχῆς φασι τοῦ ἱερείου δεῖσθαι τὸν Θεόν, ἄλλου δὲ οὐδενός*). NOURR., p. 501.—But in this passage an “animal victim” means simply a victim, or an offering taken from a slaughtered animal, nothing more. ORELL.

Col. 1223, at the note “The gods . . .,” after the final HERALD., add:—Should *credat* perhaps be read in place of *credit*? “Could anyone possibly believe it?” (*Sollte jemand wohl glauben können?*) ORELL.

Col. 1226, at the note “In silence . . .,” in place of ORELL., add:—Heumann [Col. 1363D] conjectures: “In silence I allow it to depart condemned” (*silentio patior abire damnatum*). Incorrectly. Arnobius means that he wishes to grant his opponents the concession of letting these matters pass and silently passing them over. Accordingly, *donatum* (“granted”) should by no means be disturbed. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note “Peacock . . .,” in place of ORELL., add:—Ausonius likewise uses the feminine *pava* several times; for example, Epigram LXIX, verse 4:

And the peahen stood before the eyes of the peacock.

And Letter XX.10:

Your hundred eyes, royal peacock, he surpasses.

In the same manner they also used both *capo* and *capus* for “capon.” See Muncker on Fulgentius, *Mythologies* II.3, p. 668, van Staveren’s edition. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note “Little sparrows . . .,” add the following:

**Little sparrows.** Little sparrows were a very common plaything for children among the ancients. Mention of this is already made in [Col. 1364A] the Old Testament, Job 40:24: “Will you play with it as with a bird, or bind it like a sparrow for a child?” (*Παίξῃ δὲ ἐν αὐτῷ ὥσπερ ὀρνέῳ, ἢ δήσεις αὐτὸν ὥσπερ στρουθίον παιδίῳ*). And who does not know Catullus’ most delightful verse:

Sparrow, my girl’s darling.

Compare Bochart, who discusses this subject extensively in the *Hierozoicon*, part II, book I, ch. 22, vol. II, p. 727 f., Rosenmüller’s edition. ORELL.

Col. 1227, at the note “Surely . . .,” in place of ORELL., add:—Heumann conjectures: “who would reveal your divinity, or I have exposed you” (*tuum numen qui ostenderet, aut te traduxi*). Very badly. ORELL.

Col. 1229, note “Misdeeds . . .”: delete the words “Misdeeds, namely those of the victims,” and add:—Arnobius used *dissignationes*, as Heumann correctly explains in the margin, in the wholly unusual sense of “sins,” which shortly before he had called “offenses.” Furthermore, *dissignatio* is a word occurring only once (*ἅπαξ λεγόμενον*). See Gesner in the *Thesaurus*.

Col. 1230, after the note “And from . . .,” insert the following:

**That entire company of most learned men.** He means the Stoics. See J. Lipsius, *On Constancy* I.18; *Works* [Col. 1364B], vol. IV, p. 553 ff., Wesel edition. ORELL.

**Hatreds are idle.** *Vacant* means “are of no use.” Thus Tertullian, *Apology*, ch. 2: “And now, if confessions anticipate them, the tortures will be idle.” See Havercamp there, p. 41, who also cites our passage. ORELL.

Ibid., after the note “If they wish . . .,” insert the following:

**They will be able** (*Quibunt*). I do not recall reading this future form elsewhere. Lucretius I.380 has *nequibunt* (“they will not be able”):

Where, moreover, will the waters be able

To withdraw, when the fish will not be able to go?

Col. 1231, at the note “But by an inescapable . . .,” in place of ORELL., add:—See Ernesti’s *Key to Cicero* under this word; Oudendorp on Suetonius, *Caesar*, ch. 20, who shows that *confici* and *confieri* are very frequently confused by copyists; and van Staveren on Hyginus, *Poetic Astronomy* IV.1, p. 545. ORELL.

Ibid., after the note “If with . . .,” insert the following:

**Deceptive** (*Frustratoriis*). *Frustratorius* is African usage. Thus Tertullian, *On the Soul*, ch. 47, calls dreams “vain and [Col. 1364C] deceptive and shameful and mocking and unclean.” Compare Cellarius, *Antibarbarus*, p. 41. ORELL.

Col. 1232, at the note “If only . . .,” after HERALD., add:—Heumann conjectures: “Nor should they be included under the exception attached to this name” (*Neque in hujus nominis exceptione ponendi*). Incorrectly. The sense is: “If they are worthy of being excepted by those whom you call gods, but who are not true gods.” ORELL.

Col. 1233, note “As if . . .,” near the end: for “Wesel. Peculiar—” read: “Wesel, and Ph. Carolus on Aulus Gellius, book II, ch. 2, p. 114 ff. Peculiar . . .”

Ibid., after the same note, “As if . . .,” insert the following:

**Let him leave the road.** The lictors walking before the consul instructed the people to do this with the formula preserved for us by Plautus, *The Pot of Gold*, Act III, scene I:

Make way for the consul; see that the streets lie open.

Compare Seneca, Letter XCIV. See Phil. Carolus, *Observations on Aulus Gellius*, p. 115, and Brissonius, *On Formulae* VIII.34, p. 700. ORELL.

[Col. 1364D] Col. 1234, at the note “Since even . . .,” in place of ORELL., add:—Arnobius may perhaps be referring to those words of Christ in Mark 10:42–43. ORELL.

Col. 1236, at the note “From every . . .,” after the final HERALD., add:—On this ablution Macrobius, book III of the *Saturnalia*, ch. 1, says: “It is agreed that one who intends to perform sacred rites for the gods above is purified by washing the body; but when sacrifice must be offered to the gods below, it appears sufficient if only a sprinkling takes place.” NOURR., p. 509.

Col. 1238, after the note “*Immussuli* . . .,” insert the following:

**Salamanders.** Entecnius speaks thus of salamanders in his paraphrase of Nicander’s *Theriaca*, verse 818: “The creature called the salamander is also dangerous. Yet it is not harmed at all by fire; rather, it lives in fire, remains beside it, and passes through unharmed, and the salamander has its entire skin mottled” (*Χαλεπὸν δέ ἐστι θηρίον καὶ ἡ καλουμένη σαλαμάνδρα· ἀδικεῖται δ’ οὖν ὑπὸ πυρὸς οὐδέν, ἀλλὰ ἐν τούτῳ διαιτᾶται, καὶ μένει παρὰ τῷ πυρί, καὶ διέρχεται ἀβλαβῶς, καὶ τὸ δέρμα ἡ σαλαμάνδρα πᾶν κατάστικτον ἔχει*). The scholiast adds: “Its entrails remove hair; the animal resembles a lizard, has four feet, and a short tail” (*Τὰ δὲ ἔντερα αὐτῆς ψιλοῖ τὰς τρίχας· ἔστι δὲ τὸ ζῶον ὅμοιον σαύρᾳ, τετράπουν, βραχύκερκον*). See Schneider there [Col. 1365A], p. 267, and his note on the *Alexipharmaca*, verse 538, p. 260 f., where he has collected the testimony of ancient physicians concerning this poisonous little creature. ORELL.

**Sun-fleeing vipers.** As the most learned Jena reviewer very correctly judges, *solifugas*, not *solipugas*, should be read. For here, as in book II, ch. 23, the subject is amphibians, not insects; and Arnobius is fond of epithets of this kind. Thus in book VI, ch. 16, he called beetles “light-fleeing” (*lucifugas*). ORELL.

Ibid., before the note “Thistles,” insert the following note:

**Bulbs.** Properly speaking, all round, layered roots were called *bulbi*, such as those of the lily, crocus, narcissus, colocasia, and reeds. See Gesner in the *Thesaurus*. Here, however, Arnobius appears to designate a particular kind used by the ancients as food, especially at wedding banquets, because they stimulated sexual desire, as Martial attests in book XIII, Epigram 34, and Apicius, who gives the method of preparing bulbs for food in *The Art of Cooking* VII.12. There M. Lister, p. 207 of Jansson’s edition, understands either a kind of orchid or tulip roots, which are edible and exceedingly pleasant bulbs [Col. 1365B], very common in Asia and Greece and used as food. Compare the distinguished Schneider in the *Agricultural Lexicon*, under this word. ORELL.

Ibid., after the note “Roots,” add the following notes:

**Gourds.** Gourds were among the ancients’ most agreeable foods. One must understand, however, as M. Lister observes on Apicius III.4, p. 79, those very long and slender varieties still widely and commonly used in Italy and warmer regions, but entirely unknown to our gardeners. According to the same Apicius in the passage cited, their seasonings among the Romans were mint, celery, and pennyroyal, which our Arnobius discusses here. ORELL.

**Rue.** Rue—especially the rue berry, that is, the seed capsule—is repeatedly praised by Apicius as one of the most common seasonings for food; for example, in book VI, ch. 2. ORELL.

**Mint.** *Menta* or *mentha*. Dioscorides, book III, ch. 41, *menthē* (*μένθη*). Pliny, book XIX, ch. 8: “The sweetness of its scent changed its name [Col. 1365C] among the Greeks, although it had otherwise been called *Mintha*, from which our ancestors derived its name.” That is, the Greeks called it *hēdyosmos* (*ἡδύοσμος*, “sweet-smelling”). Julius Pollux, *Onomasticon* VI.10, following Strabo VIII, notes that mint was named after Mintha, Pluto’s concubine, who was transformed into this plant. Jo. RHODIUS, in the *Lexicon of Scribonius*, under this word.—The same Pliny, book XX, ch. 14, says: “Mint is beneficial to the stomach and is employed in many ways as a seasoning.” There were two kinds of mint, namely wild and garden mint. The latter, which the Jews especially used for sprinkling the floors of houses and synagogues, is also mentioned under the name *hēdyosmon* (*ἡδύοσμον*) by the Divine Savior in Matthew 23:23. See Schleusner, who discusses this word extensively in his *Lexicon of the New Testament*, and Lister on Apicius I.29, p. 44. In our language, *Münze, Gartenmünze*—“mint, garden mint.” ORELL.

Ibid., after the note “Basil,” insert the following:

**Pennyroyal.** *Puleium* or *pulegium*—see Rhodius, *Lexicon of Scribonius*—in our language *Poley, Poleymünze*, is an officinal plant today, but among the ancients it was food, or rather a very common seasoning [Col. 1365D] for foods, especially olives, as Palladius, November, ch. 22, attests. See the distinguished Schneider in the *Agricultural Lexicon* and Lister on Apicius III.5, p. 79. ORELL.

Col. 1240, after the note “Those things which . . .,” insert the following:

**To lay aside their savagery through morsels.** Should we perhaps read, “to lay aside their savagery when morsels have been offered” (*offis oblatis saevitias ponere*)? ORELL.

Col. 1242, at the note “A dusky color,” add the following:

Furthermore, concerning the different kinds of victims to be sacrificed to the gods above and below, and the manner in which sacrifice ought to be offered to each, there survives a celebrated oracle of Apollo preserved for us from Porphyry by Eusebius in *Preparation for the Gospel* IV.9. Since Eusebius’ work is in few people’s hands, it may be permissible to transcribe it in full. Apollo speaks as follows:

Proceed, friend, once you have entered this god-given path,

And do not forget, as you sacrifice, the offerings due the blessed ones:

Which are for those upon the earth, which for those in heaven, and which at times

[Col. 1366A] For the very rulers of the upper air and of the moisture-bearing atmosphere,

For the gods of the sea, and for all those beneath the earth;

For all the fullnesses of nature are contained within these.

I shall sing how, as is right, the rites involving living creatures are to be completed;

And inscribe my oracle upon tablets.

Three victims are for the gods upon the earth, and three for the gods of heaven.

Choose bright-colored victims for the heavenly gods, but for the earthly ones

Victims resembling the earth in color; divide the offerings for the earthly gods into three,

Bury those for the gods below, and cast the blood into a pit.

Pour honey for the nymphs and the gifts of Dionysus.

For all those who continually fly around the earth,

Fill an altar brimming on every side with the blood of slaughter;

After sacrificing, cast into the fire the body of a winged creature,

And, mixing honey with grain scorched by hostile fire,

Add there the vapors of frankincense and whole barley-grains.

When you go upon the sands, pour out the gray-blue salt sea,

Sacrifice a victim from the head downward, and into the deep wave of the sea

Cast the whole living creature. When you have completed all these things,

Proceed to the broad choir of the heavenly beings of the air.

Then, for all the astral and ethereal gods,

Let blood stream from the victims’ throats in fountains around the altar

And pool there; let the limbs be prepared for the gods’ feast.

Give the extremities to Hephaestus, but partake of the rest,

Filling the whole flowing air with savory vapors;

And send up prayers to those gods together with them. [Col. 1366B]

NOURR., p. 507, and ORELL.

Col. 1243, after the note “And foully . . .,” insert the following:

**With milk, oil, to blood** (*Lacte, oleo sanguini*). It seems that we should read: “With milk and oil, the blood” (*Lacte, oleo sanguinem*). The sense is: “Stain everything you offer the gods—the incense, salted grain, libations, and blood: the blood, indeed, with milk and oil, so that it acquires a purple color; but pour soot mixed with ashes into the former offerings, which are yellow in color, so that they become black.” The somewhat difficult and involved construction gave occasion for the error. ORELL.

Col. 1244, at the note “And prescribed . . .,” in place of ORELL., add:—Furthermore, *supplicamentum*—in place of which the early Romans, such as Livy XXII.57 and Sallust, *Catiline* 9, used *supplicium*—is a word of declining Latinity, especially common among African writers, Apuleius (*Metamorphoses* XI, p. 265) and Tertullian. It designates victims and sacrifices as well as prayers and supplications [Col. 1366C], and in general the entire apparatus of ceremonies by which the gods are rendered propitious. ORELL.

Col. 1245, after the note “Here, just as . . .,” insert the following:

**Those same things are rejected from the diets of other nations.** Meursius, p. 211, conjectures “those same things belonging to other people,” etc. Incorrectly, for the preceding statement was: “as report says is the practice among nations with widely differing customs.” ORELL.

Col. 1246, after the note “Which all . . .,” insert the following:

**The Tritonian Virgin.** They relate that Minerva acquired the name Tritonia because she was first seen on the bank of Lake Triton in Africa in the time of King Ogyges, as Festus noted. STEWECH.—Pomponius Mela, book I, ch. 8: “Beyond the Greater Syrtis, an immense lake receives the river Triton. The lake itself is called Tritonis, from which Minerva too received her surname, since, as the inhabitants believe, she was born there. The myths lend some credence to this, because they celebrate what they consider her birthday with contests in which maidens compete against one another in games.” See the interpreters there. Compare Servius on *Aeneid* II.171 and Broukhusius on Lucan, *Pharsalia* IX.354, p. 699, Oudendorp’s edition. ORELL.

[Col. 1366D] Col. 1247, at the note “And toward . . .,” in place of the final ORELL., add:—Now, after rereading these words and being taught better, I reject Canter’s conjecture, “the things they have declared” (*quae fati sunt*), which would mean “the things they have threatened.” But our Arnobius is speaking here not of the gods’ threats but of their nature, which is prone to anger and vengeance. Nor could he properly have said that the gods are driven by irresistible necessity toward that which they had threatened. Therefore, until the Greek idiom assumed by Heraldus can be established by examples, I prefer to follow Heumann’s reading: “toward those things for which they were made” (*ad ea, ad quae facti sunt*). ORELL.

Col. 1249, after the note “What are the morsels?” insert the following:

**The first of these.** Namely, the *taeda*, for Arnobius is now explaining individually the items he had named before. Accordingly, *taedae* were small sausages stuffed with lard or fat chopped into tiny pieces—*Speckwürste*, “bacon sausages.” ORELL.

Ibid., after the note “Into tiny . . .,” insert the following:

**Thoroughly dried of its vital juices.** [Col. 1367A] Arnobius is now describing the *naenia*, which was the intestine through which excrement is discharged—the rectum (*der Mastdarm*)—stretched out either by a press or in some other manner and then dried in smoke, so that, after losing all its vital moisture, it would remain untouched by decay for a long time. ORELL.

Col. 1250, at the note “Of which . . .,” in place of ORELL., add:—The omentum, in Greek *epiploon* (*ἐπίπλοον*), is a thin, fatty membrane by which the lower parts of the abdomen are covered and the coils of the intestines enveloped. Above, book III, ch. 13, he spoke of “the little membranes of the omenta.” Compare Pliny, *Natural History* IX.37, and Isidore, *Origins* II.1. NOURR., p. 512.—In German, *das Netz*, “the caul.” ORELL.

Ibid., after the same note, “Of which,” insert the following:

**The cow’s tail is a *palasea*, smeared with fine wheat flour and blood.** *Siligo* is flour from the finest wheat, most thoroughly purified of bran (*Semmelmehl*, “fine white flour.” ORELL.). Hence Juvenal’s verses here concerning bread, Satire V.69:

But the tender, snow-white loaf, made from soft fine flour,

Is kept for the master. [Col. 1367B]

NOURR., p. 512.

Ibid., at the note “What is a *fitilla*? . . .,” in place of ORELL., add:—Under these unknown names Arnobius describes various kinds of sacrificial cakes or pastries whose use belonged to sacred rites, for the ancients called these *liba*. It is fully established that many kinds of *liba*, differing in both material and shape according to the gods to whom they were offered, were employed in sacrifices in antiquity. Thus among the Greeks we find *popana, pelanoi, psaista, phthois*, and so forth (*πόπανα, πέλανοι, ψαιστά, φθοῖς*), on which see Spanheim on Aristophanes, *Wealth*, verse 660. Thus Pollux, *Onomasticon* VI, §76:

> “*Pelanoi* are common to all the gods and are named from their shape, as is the ‘ox’; for it is a baked cake made with projecting horns, offered to Apollo, Artemis, Hecate, and Selene. The *melittouta*, however, is offered to Trophonius, as are the *arester*—a name that appears to bear some resemblance to Arnobius’ *gratilla*—and the *hygieia*; for the *hygieia* too is a kind of barley-cake” (*Πέλανοι δὲ κοινοὶ πᾶσι θεοῖς, κέκληνται δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ σχήματος, ὥσπερ ὁ βοῦς· πέμμα γάρ ἐστι κέρατα ἔχον πεπηγμένα, προσφερόμενον Ἀπόλλωνι, καὶ Ἀρτέμιδι, καὶ Ἑκάτῃ, καὶ Σελήνῃ, μελιττοῦτα μέντοι Τροφωνίῳ, καὶ ἀρεστὴρ καὶ ὑγίεια ὁμοίως· καὶ γὰρ ὑγίεια μάζης ἐστὶν εἶδος*).

Likewise, Athenaeus’ *Deipnosophists* XIV.14, where he enumerates several kinds of pastry, establishes that cakes fashioned in the form of a phallus were offered to Priapus and cakes fashioned in the form of female genitalia, called *mylloi* (*μύλλοι*), were offered to Ceres [Col. 1367C]. Compare also the most learned commentators on the *Paintings of Herculaneum*, vol. III, plate XXXVI, p. 178. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note “Flesh . . .,” in place of ORELL., add:—These are the words of Festus: “Plautus uses the Umbrian name *strebula* for the thighs of sacrificial victims, which the Greeks call *mēria* (*μηρία*) and which were customarily placed upon altars, as Plautus says in the *Frivolaria*: ‘Hold the ranks of *strebulae*.’” See Dacier there, p. 529 f. ORELL.

Ibid., after the note “Choice pieces of flesh,” add the following:

**Choice pieces of flesh, not roasted, which are entrails on spits, etc.** The obscurity of this text sufficiently demonstrates that it was corrupted by an unskilled or careless copyist. Therefore, so that some light may be cast upon it, if possible, it is useful to observe that *pulpamentum* is undoubtedly derived from *pulpa*. Properly speaking, however, *pulpa*, as Donatus remarks on Terence, *The Mother-in-Law*, Act III, scene IV, is flesh [Col. 1367D] that is chewed, because it is beaten and torn apart. Isidore, *Origins* II.1, says: “It is called *pulpa* because it was eaten mixed with porridge”; elsewhere, however, in XX.2, he says—as many think, more correctly: “*Pulpa* is flesh without fat, so called because it quivers (*palpitet*), for it often springs back. Many also call it ‘birdlime,’ since it is sticky.”

Given these observations, the negative particle *non* appears to have been displaced from its proper position in Arnobius’ text. It should be restored before the noun *pulpamenta*, and before the word *exta* it must either be understood or be placed there a second time, so that the passage reads: “He does not care to name the flesh called *strebula* . . . nor roasted choice pieces placed on spits, nor formerly living entrails,” etc.

Arnobius’ meaning will then be clear: it is futile in sacrifices to burn roasted choice pieces on spits—that is, soft and delicate portions of flesh without fat, which quiver because of their softness—and equally futile to offer animals’ entrails, formerly alive and roasted over coals. These could not, indeed, be roasted on spits, but only over burning coals. [Col. 1368A] If you doubt that such things were offered to the gods, Festus, under the word *exta*, will assure you; he thinks that they received their name for this very reason: “They are called *exta* because those parts which stand out and project most prominently are cut off for the gods.” NOURR., p. 514.

**Finally, not the salted mixture, which is a single compound formed by combining four kinds of grain.** He undoubtedly means salted grain, or *mola salsa*, whose use in sacred rites is very well known. From Servius on Virgil, *Eclogue* VIII.81, we learn that preparing this meal for sacred uses was the duty of the Vestal Virgins:

> “Sacred grain,” he says, “that is, pure salted meal, is prepared as follows. From the Nones of May until the day before the Ides of May, on alternate days, the three chief Vestal Virgins place ears of spelt in harvesting baskets. The virgins themselves parch, pound, and grind these ears and store what has thus been ground. From this grain the virgins make the meal three times a year—at the Lupercalia, the Vestalia, and the Ides of September—adding prepared salt and hard salt.”

Thus Servius. Our Arnobius differs from him somewhat, saying that those salted mixtures, or portions of *mola salsa*, were made not only from spelt [Col. 1368B] but from a mixture of four kinds of grain (*quadrinis*, that is, of four distinct kinds)—perhaps spelt, emmer, wheat, and barley. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note “Not likewise,” after ORELL., add:—Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* I.6, teaches that there are three intestines. The first is called *dissipium*, otherwise *disseptum*, and by the Greeks *diaphragma* (*διάφραγμα*); the second, the middle intestine, is called *mesenterion* (*μεσεντέριον*); and the third, which the ancients called the *hira*, is regarded as the principal one of all the intestines and carries away the refuse of food. Arnobius therefore says that the *fendicae* are identical with the *hirae*, which were called *hillae* in popular speech, and are nothing other than the jejunum. NOURR., p. 515.

Col. 1252, at the note “Ingredients,” in place of the final ORELL., add:—Compare the *Corrections and Additions*, p. 479, beginning. But Th. Marcilius’ explanation must certainly be approved. Thus Apicius, book XIII, ch. 8, has “ingredients for hare” (*impensam in leporem*), where he enumerates its components—pepper, date, silphium, fish sauce, and so forth. The subject here, therefore, is seasoning [Col. 1368C], for he next adds “for stuffed hare” and explains how to prepare it. In Arnobius too the word must be understood as “seasoning,” since immediately before he had mentioned stuffings. ORELL.

Col. 1253, at the note “Little pieces . . .,” in place of ORELL., add:—Furthermore, *frustillum* as a diminutive of *frustulum* is peculiar to our Arnobius. Thus above, book II, ch. 58, he said “these little fiery pieces.” ORELL.—We read *frustillatim*, “in little pieces,” in Plautus, *Curculio*, Act IV, scene IV:

Now I shall make the ants carry you off from here piece by piece.

NOURR., p. 555.

Ibid., after the note “But so that . . .,” insert the following:

**Through an appetite of voracity.** *Voracitas* (“voracity”), in place of *edacitas* (“gluttony”), is a word of Silver Latin. Eutropius, book VII, chapter 18, concerning Vitellius: “He ruled with great disgrace and severe cruelty, being especially notorious for his gluttony and voracity.” There Grosse, in the Index, cites Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* VII, near the end, and Pliny, *Natural History* II.107, beginning, as having used this word. Cellarius adduces further examples [Col. 1368D] in his *Later Observations on the Antibarbarus of the Latin Language*, p. 130. ORELL.

Col. 1255, before the note “The passage . . .” insert this brief note:

**Through such storms.** That is, through storms of such long duration. ORELL.

Ibid., after the same note “The passage . . .” also add this brief note:

**Novelty.** Here it means “the later, more recent age,” in a highly unusual sense. ORELL.

Col. 1256, after the note “With fumigations” insert the following:

**Breathing passages.** That is, the organs or faculties of breathing. Thus Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book II, verse 180:

> One man cuts off the ears, another the breathing passages  
> Of the hooked nose.

And Statius, *Thebaid* XII, verse 269:

> The stormy blast restores the breathing passages  
> Of the exhausted fire and bursts upon the dreadful fields.

NOURR., p. 566.

Col. 1257, at the note “Not if . . .,” in place of the final words of ORELL., [Col. 1369A] add:—The anonymous author *On Frankincense*, in Salmasius, *Plinian Exercises*, p. 1151: “The male kind is called *chalkolibanos* (χαλκολίβανος), sunlike—read ‘bronze-like’ (*chalkoeidēs*, χαλκοειδής)—and fiery-red, that is, yellow.” Compare Bochart, *Hierozoicon*, part II, book VI, chapter 16, vol. III, p. 895, Rosenmüller’s edition. ORELL.

Ibid., after the note “Let it not be . . .” insert the following:

**Cloudiness.** That is, the overflowing vapors of burning incense, by which the whole atmosphere is enclosed and covered as though by a cloud. NOURR., p. 560.—*Nebulositas* (“cloudiness”) is a *hapax legomenon* (ἅπαξ λεγόμενον), a word occurring only once. ORELL.

Col. 1258, after the note “And of the victims . . .” insert the following:

**Give, let them drink.** Heumann conjectures, “Give, so that they may drink.” But *ut* (“so that”) is omitted according to Greek construction (*elleipei*, ἐλλείπει). ORELL.

Col. 1262, after the note “Sleepings” add the following:

**Gentle dirges are to be heard.** See the Annotations on book VI, chapter 12, col. 1190: “It should be noted, namely, that *naenia* is also used of a joyful subject, as of the songs sung at the Trojan Games. Varro, book IV, *On the Life of the Roman People*, in Nonius, with Scaliger’s correction and combination of the text: ‘There a woman who possessed the finest voice used to praise Pergamum; [Col. 1369B] then a *naenia* used to be sung to the flute and the lyres of those who had taken part in the Trojan Games.’ For, as I suppose, those who had fallen at Troy were praised, or perhaps others; at any rate, it was a song of praise. And because much frivolous material was sung in these *naeniae*, the word consequently also came to be used of a childish and unpolished song. Horace, *Epistles* II.1.62 ff.:

> Tell me, if you please: is the Roscian law better, or the children’s  
> Ditty that offers a kingdom to those who act rightly?

“These and many other observations are given by Gisbert Cuper, who discusses this word at length in his *Observations*, book I, chapter 1, pp. 6 ff., Leipzig edition. Concerning the word’s etymology, John Lydus writes as follows in *On the Magistracies of the Romans*, book I, chapter 33, end, p. 56, Fuss’s edition: ‘Among them—the Romans—the funeral song is called *nenia* (νηνία), by an etymology derived rather from Greek, because the Greeks call the last of the strings on a lyre the *nētē* (νήτη).’” ORELL.

Ibid., at the note “The washing . . .,” after the final words of NOURR., add:—Dausqueius, on Silius Italicus, book VIII, p. [Col. 1369C] 345, aptly compares with this solemn washing of the Mother of the Gods the very similar rite of the ancient Germans recorded by Tacitus in *The Customs of the Germans*, chapter 11: “Afterward the vehicle of the goddess Hertha and her garments—and, if one is willing to believe it, the deity herself—are washed in a secluded lake.” Moreover, Augustine, *The City of God* II.4, complains that many unspeakable and shameful things were sung and performed at this festival: “We delighted in the most shameful games that were presented to gods and goddesses. Before the litter of the Heavenly Virgin and Berecynthia, the mother of all, on the solemn day of her washing, such things were publicly sung by the vilest stage-players as it would have been improper, I will not say for the Mother of the Gods, but even for the mother of the stage-players themselves, to hear.” Compare Zoëga’s highly learned elucidation of the matter in *Ancient Bas-Reliefs*, vol. I, on plates XIII and XIV, note 109, p. 103. ORELL.

Col. 1264, at the brief note “Of Earth,” after ORELL., add:—Yet the birthdays not only of Earth alone, but also of various other gods, such as Mercury, Minerva, and Jupiter Ammon, are recorded in the ancient Calendar, on which one may read Lambecius’s notes. [Col. 1369D] Hence Lactantius, *Institutes* VI.19, says: “The celebrations of games are festivals of the gods, since they were instituted either for their birthdays or for the dedication of new temples.” NOURR., p. 526.

Col. 1265, at the note “And at the Megalesian Games,” after ORELL., add:—In the Praenestine Calendar, in Foggini, *Fasti of Verrius*, p. 108, under the day before the Nones of April: “Games of the Idaean Great Mother of the Gods. They are called *Megalesia* because that goddess is called *migale* (*megalē*, μεγάλη, ‘great’).” In another ancient Calendar, in Graevius’s *Thesaurus*, vol. VIII: “The day before the Nones . . . the fifth day before the Ides of April: the Megalesian Games,” that is, from the fourth to the ninth day of April. See more in Zoëga, *Ancient Bas-Reliefs*, vol. I, p. 91. ORELL.

Col. 1267, before the note “Of the salapittae,” at the preceding note, in place of the final words of ORELL., add:—The highly learned commentator on the *Herculanean Antiquities*, vol. VI (*Bronzes*, vol. II), plate XCII—where we see such men depicted with the greatest elegance—p. 370, seeks to prove that fools were kept for amusement among the ancients and that their heads were shaved, on the basis of [Col. 1370A] an epigram of Lucian, *Anthology* II.3.6; Brunk’s *Analecta*, vol. II, p. 311:

> If you see a hairless head, breast, and shoulders,  
> Ask nothing: you are looking at a bald fool.

Jacobs, a most learned man, more correctly interprets this, however, as a jest (*skōmma*, σκῶμμα) directed against a certain Cynic. ORELL.

Ibid., after the same note “Of the salapittae . . .” add the following:

**With the redness of enormous fascina.** By *fascina* he means phalluses, which the ancients hung around boys’ necks as amulets for warding off the evil eye. Varro, *On the Latin Language* VI, p. 80, Dordrecht edition: “A certain indecent object is hung around boys’ necks, so that nothing may harm them, for the sake of a favorable omen.” There see Scaliger, p. 152. (“For the sake of a favorable omen,” that is, for the sake of a good sign. For, according to Festus, *scaeva* was a neutral word. The common people indeed use *scaeva* of both good and bad things when they speak of a good and an evil *scaeva*; writers, however, customarily use it in a bad sense. *Scaevus* derives from the Greek *skaios* [σκαιός, “left”]; hence a *bona scaeva* was what the Romans regarded as the left hand, whereas among the Greeks and barbarians the right hand was auspicious [Col. 1370B], as Dacier correctly explains.)

Suidas: “A *phallos* (φαλλός) . . . is a leather likeness of the genitals [Greek reading *aidoion skytipon*, αἰδοῖον σκύτιπον, uncertain]; later it was made from red leather and had the form of the male organ. Wearing this around their necks and between their thighs, they danced in honor of Dionysus while celebrating the Dionysia.” Compare Gonsalo de Salas on Petronius, chapter 138, p. 243, Burman’s edition, and the commentary on the *Herculanean Antiquities*, vol. VI (*Bronzes* II), plate XCVII, p. 398. ORELL.

Col. 1269, at the note “If from . . .,” after ORELL., add:—The passage of Livy is book VII, chapter 2: “The young men retained this kind of entertainment, which they had received from the Oscans, and did not allow it to be debased by professional actors; and the rule remains that performers of Atellan farces are neither removed from their tribe nor excused from military service as though they were professional stage-players.” There Doering writes: “The Atellan farce was a dramatic and witty kind of entertainment, broadly similar to what we call, by a word borrowed from the French, a *farce*. It took its name from Atella, a town of Campania situated between Capua and Naples.” NOURR., p. 348.—He considers Atella to be the same place that is today called Aversa. ORELL.

[Col. 1370C] Ibid., at the note “And with their buttocks . . .,” in place of ORELL., add:—Canterus thinks the text should read, “and to undulate with their buttocks thrusting obscenely,” citing Juvenal, *Satires* VI.322:

> She herself worships the undulation of Medullina’s obscene thrusting.

Wrongly. See the note on book II at the passage cited. ORELL.

Ibid., at the note “And because . . .,” in place of ORELL., add:—Heumann conjectures, “to rejoice in more cheerful things.” ORELL.

Col. 1274, after the brief note “But to be bent . . .” insert the following:

**That it might be fixed upon a higher summit.** See Cicero, *Third Oration against Catiline*, chapter 8. ORELL.

Ibid., after the final line add this note:

**And that he is summoned away by this kind of amusement.** I read *avocarique* (“and that he is diverted”), etc. Thus above, in the same book, chapter 8: “Just as very small children receive little sparrows, dolls, toy horses, and figures of Pan with which they may divert themselves.” Jerome, *Letter to Laeta*: “Let her first learn the Psalter. Let her divert herself with these songs, and let her be instructed for life in the Proverbs of Solomon.” The same author, *To Marcellus*: “The sweating reaper diverts himself with psalms, and the vine-dresser, pruning [Col. 1370D] the vine with his curved sickle, sings something from David.” The ancient glosses: “*Avocat*—distracts (*perispāi*, περισπᾷ; read in place of *peristia*, περιστία), leaves idle (*katargei*, καταργεῖ), diverts from occupation (*aposcholei*, ἀποσχολεῖ).” Plutarch, in his *Life of Solon*, used *to paragein* (τὸ παράγειν, “diversion”) in the same sense. HERALDUS, *Adversaria* I.3, pp. 8 ff.—This is an outstanding correction by Heraldus and rightly deserves to be admitted into the text. ORELL.

Col. 1275, after the note “Geldings . . .” insert the following:

**Yet that they rejoice to pass by.** Consider whether the text should read: “that he—namely Jupiter—upon seeing them rejoice, nevertheless passes by,” etc. ORELL.

Col. 1276, after the note “Pestilence . . .” add the following:

**Presenter of the games.** That is, the sponsor of the games. Cellarius marks the word *exhibitor* as barbarous in his *Antibarbarus of the Latin Language*, p. 37, and *Later Observations*, p. 209. ORELL.

Col. 1278, before the note “What sort . . .” insert this:

**To consume.** Namely, with pestilence; see the Annotation on book II, chapter 3. ORELL.

[Col. 1371A] Col. 1279, after the final line add these brief notes:

**Holy God.** An ancient inscription found at Rome, in Gruter, p. LXX:

> TO HOLY AESCULAPIUS, DECIMUS JUNIUS AGATHOPUS AND TERENTIA RUFINA, GIVING THANKS TO YOUR DIVINE POWER, GAVE AND DEDICATED THIS.

ORELL.

**One who restrains.** A word of declining Latin. Apuleius, *On the God of Socrates*, p. 52: “Socrates never had need of anyone to encourage him, but occasionally did have need of someone to restrain him.” ORELL.

Col. 1280, after the note “By which to lie . . .” insert the following:

**How feebly and weakly it is said.** *Infirmiter*, in place of *infirme*—the latter of which Cicero used in *Letters to Friends* XV.1—is an adverb of doubtful Latinity. See Cellarius, *Antibarbarus*, p. 57. ORELL.

Col. 1282, at the note “Flint . . .,” after ELMENH., add:—By the books of fate—that is, the Sibylline books—and by the responses of the prophets and of Apollo. NOURR., p. 477.

[Col. 1371B] Col. 1283, before the brief note “Of the color . . .” insert this:

**From King Attalus.** Attalus—namely, the king of Phrygia—had entered into an alliance with the Romans against Philip of Macedon, [Col. 1372A] who was Hannibal’s ally. See Livy, book XXIX, chapter 11. ORELL.

Ibid., at the same note “Of the color . . .,” in place of ORELL., add:—Prudentius, *Roman Martyrdom* 206:

> A darkish stone, to be carried upon a carriage,  
> Sits enclosed in silver shaped as a woman’s face.

And Martial, book III, epigram 41, alluding to its dusky color, calls the object of the Phrygian Mother *ferrum* (“iron”). Compare Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpina* I.200 ff., and the classic passage in Herodian, *History* I.11.7. Zoëga, moreover, has most diligently collected all the testimonies of the ancients in *Ancient Bas-Reliefs*, vol. I, pp. 88 ff. ORELL.

Col. 1284, after the note “With little angles . . .” insert the following:

**And presenting to the statue, through mere semblance, a face that was less distinctly formed.** Zoëga, at the passage cited, thinks that the stone sent by Attalus to Rome had been cut from a particular rock in [Col. 1372B] Phrygia which, when viewed from a distance by superstitious people, displayed a certain semblance of a human face. ORELL.
