## OVERVIEW OF THE COMPLETE EDITION
First Dissertation on the Eighth Epistle of Saint Cyprian, by Dodwell: On Visions, and How the Ancients Established the Credibility of Their Visions, etc. 9

§ 1. Visions and prophetic gifts continued from the time of the Apostles down to Cyprian, as shown by the author of the Apocalypse and by Hermas.—§ 2. By Clement of Rome and the author of the apocryphal Esdras.—§ 3. By Ignatius.—§ 4. By Quadratus, Philip’s daughters, Ammia of Philadelphia, and Polycarp.—§ 5. By Justin Martyr.—§ 6. By Melito of Sardis, Alexander the Phrygian, Attalus, and others.—§ 7. By Irenaeus.—§ 8. By Perpetua and Saturus. They were not Montanists.—§ 9. It is not true that the Church left to the Montanists the claim to prophecy.—§ 10. On the contrary, after the reign of Commodus, Catholics refuted the Montanists’ prophecies by this very argument: that the gift of true prophecy was to remain perpetually in the Church, whereas the Montanists’ gift had already become extinct.—§ 11. Thus Asterius Urbanus and Epiphanius.—§§ 12, 13. The author of the Acts of Perpetua and Felicity.—§ 14. The visions of Natalis and Potamiena, and concerning the appointment of Alexander at Jerusalem and Fabian at Rome as bishops.—§ 15. Origen acknowledges prophecies.—§ 16. The testimony of Gregory of Nyssa concerning Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus is set aside.—§ 17. A vision of Dionysius of Alexandria.—§§ 18, 19, 20, 21. Visions of Cyprian himself.—§ 22. Another vision of Dionysius of Alexandria.—§ 23. Visions were customarily announced publicly, and indeed before the event.—§ 24. How provision was made against fraud committed under the pretext of visions.—§§ 25, 26, 27. On the arguments by which the credibility of visions was established, especially intrinsic arguments. The gift of disclosing thoughts.—§§ 28, 29, 30. The gift of predicting future events. According to the principles of that age, future events which would not otherwise exceed created powers nevertheless could not be predicted by anyone other than God.—§ 31. It comes to the same thing whether they were revealed immediately by God himself or through the mediation of some creature.—§ 32. The agreement of this hypothesis with the phenomena is an argument for its truth.—§ 33. How they established the credibility of some prophecies from the credibility of others.—§ 34. Not everything belonging to true prophets was prophetic.—§§ 35, 36, 37. Certain errors in prophets are compatible with true prophecy, and which errors these are.—§ 38. The truth of a prophecy was established from the unity of the communion to which the prophet had joined himself.—§ 39. The credibility of those whose prophecies had all been obscure could not be commended in any other way than by the unity of communion.—§ 40. Visions were peculiar to the young.—§§ 41, 42. What is to be thought of those who held those ancient prophecies up to ridicule. 9

Second Dissertation on the Twenty-Fourth Epistle of Saint Cyprian, by Dodwell: On Presbyter-Teachers, the Teacher of the Hearers, and Ecclesiastical Embassies. 33

§ 1. Presbyter-teachers, older than Cyprian, held a dignity of the first rank in the Church.—§ 2. They were contemporaries of the Apostles and derived from the Jewish scribes and teachers. [Col. 1372]—§ 3. Their office was founded upon an extraordinary gift.—§§ 4, 5, 6. Contrary to the common belief, that duty of teaching did not belong to all presbyters.—§ 7. In approving a teacher of the hearers, Cyprian consulted only the presbyter-teachers.—§ 8. The hearers were the same as the catechumens.—§ 9. They also used the word “catechumens.” From what the name “hearers” was derived.—§ 10. The instruction of catechumens corresponded to the mysteries.—§ 11. In Cyprian, the teacher of the hearers was a subdeacon. On Pantaenus, Clement of Alexandria, and Origen as catechists in the Alexandrian school.—§ 12. In Cyprian, ministers of the lower orders are sometimes included under the common name of the clergy and sometimes excluded.—§ 13. All Cyprian’s embassies, and others mentioned in his Epistles.—§ 14. In Cyprian’s time embassies were conducted by clerics, generally in pairs, who rarely held a rank above the subdiaconate.—§ 15. Other embassies older than Cyprian: those of Clement of Alexandria and Irenaeus.—§ 16. The embassies of the Church of Smyrna, associated with Polycarp and Ignatius, were more honorific than those of Cyprian.—§ 17. Embassies of the apostolic age.—§ 18. They were modeled upon the customs of the law of hospitality.—§ 19. Traveling Apostles were received by the Churches in the same manner in which provincial governors were customarily received by their provincials.—§ 20. The embassies of that age were highly honorific. 33

Third Dissertation: On the Second Baptism of Martyrdom, by Dodwell. 47

§ 1. Why we devote a separate dissertation to this subject.—§ 2. This opinion has continued from the earliest times of the Church down to our own.—§ 3. Baptism by water and external union with the Church were prerequisites for the baptism of martyrdom by blood.—§ 4. The ancients preferred baptism by blood to baptism by water.—§§ 5, 6. A passage of Cyprian concerning this matter is explained.—§ 7. This position of the ancients is defended.—§ 8. From which passages of Scripture they derived it.—§ 9. First observation: legitimate argumentation proceeds from the Lord’s deeds, especially deeds of the kind employed by the ancients in this matter.—§§ 10, 11. Second observation: it is established not merely from deeds but from the Lord’s own words that martyrdom is to be regarded as a baptism.—§ 12. Third observation: the affinity between baptism and martyrdom is not merely one of words but of the realities themselves. The circumstances of the passages in which the ancients believed baptism by blood to be discussed were those of martyrdom. The Lord’s baptism was his martyrdom, and that in the ecclesiastical sense.—§§ 13, 14, 15, 16. Heretics contemporary with the Apostles denied martyrdom. Saint John refuted their pseudo-Christs with an argument drawn from the true Messiah’s coming through water and blood. That entire argument is explained.—§ 17. Fourth observation: in the very rite of initiation and expiation to which the ancients attributed the cleansing of sins, the use of blood was as frequent among them as that of water—and indeed the initiates’ [Col. 1373] own blood.—§ 18. This practice obtained not only in initiations but also in covenants, according to the most ancient customs.—§ 19. Just as they readily assigned the principal part to blood in this work of expiation, so they recognized that human blood possessed by far the greatest power, even in comparison with other kinds of blood.—§ 20. Fifth observation: this baptism by blood belongs to the sacrament of baptism itself, and belongs to it in such a way as to complete its principal part.—§ 21. First, the baptismal covenant must be explained according to the customs governing covenants among the ancients.—§ 22. Second, in our baptismal covenant, as in other covenants, two duties belonging to different parties must be distinguished from one another: God’s duties and ours.—§ 23. Third, every legal right which we obtain by the benefit of the covenant must be derived from God’s promises upon the fulfillment of our duty.—§ 24. Fourth, the conditions incumbent upon us in this baptismal covenant and to be fulfilled on our part must be inferred from the meaning of its solemn symbols.—§ 25. Fifth, in the solemn symbols of our sacramental baptism, not only baptism by water but also baptism by blood is signified, and each is signified in such a manner that both are understood to belong to one and the same baptism.—§ 26. Such is the fact.—§§ 27, 28. The reason for the fact is given.—§§ 29, 30. Sixth, baptism by blood is foreshadowed in the very symbol of baptism by water in such a way as plainly to imply that baptism by water has no efficacy unless it is referred to baptism by blood.—§§ 31, 32. Seventh conclusion: not only under the law of the baptismal covenant, but also according to its equity, all the benefits which Christ is to furnish as his part of the baptismal covenant may be claimed in baptism by blood.—§§ 33, 34. Eighth conclusion: full pardon of all preceding sins is to be granted to martyrdom just as it is to baptism.—§ 35. It is in no way foreign to the nature of baptism that baptism by water and baptism by blood should be separated from one another by an interval of time.—§ 36. Ninth, the ancients regarded the martyrs’ blood as Christ’s blood.—§ 37. Tenth, especially if, following Christ’s example, it had been shed for the public cause of souls.—§ 38. The ancients are defended.—§ 39. We pledge ourselves to martyrdom also in the other sacrament, the Eucharist.—§ 40. In martyrdom we obtain a right both to the privative and to the positive benefits of baptism. Ibid.

Chapter II.—On the author and date of these books, and the manner in which they were composed by him. 390

Article II.—On the true title and subject of these books; whether the subject is properly treated by Arnobius; on his style and learning; and on the division of the entire work into books and chapters. 393

Chapter III.—New Observations on the Books of Arnobius; first, an examination of the arguments by which Arnobius demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion. 405

First Article.—How Arnobius vindicates the truth of the Christian religion—which had previously been asserted by many and needed no defender—by various miracles of Christ and his disciples. Ibid.

Article II.—How Arnobius disposes of the arguments by which the pagans attempted to discredit all the miracles of Christ and his disciples. 408

Article III.—How absurdly the pagans objected that the same or similar miracles had been performed by their gods as by Christ. 412

[Col. 1376] Article IV.—How this entire disputation overthrows the foolish arguments of the Socinians and atheists against the miracles of Christ and his disciples. 414

Chapter IV.—Other arguments of Arnobius by which he demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion are examined. 416

First Article.—How Arnobius demonstrates the truth of the Christian religion by the most dreadful and hitherto unheard-of torments, steadfastly endured for the confession of Christ down to life’s final breath by almost innumerable martyrs of every sex, age, and condition. Ibid.

Article II.—How Arnobius further vindicates the truth of the Christian religion from the fact that its doctrine was very rapidly embraced throughout the whole world by innumerable people previously devoted to the worship of the gods. 418

Chapter V.—The pagans’ arguments against the truth of the Christian religion are examined. 420

First Article.—How absurdly the pagans objected that the Christian religion should be rejected because it was new, while ancestral and hereditary rites should be preserved—rites which they themselves had altered or abolished in the classes of the people, in omens observed from the sky, in adverse auspices, assemblies, signals from the citadel, the fetial rites, the formal declaration of war (*clarigatio*), pointed instruments used in taking auspices, the Annarian, Cincian, and Censorian laws, and the innermost sanctuary of *coligo* [uncertain reading]. Ibid.

Article II.—On other pagan alterations in arranging the bridal couches of those marrying and invoking the guardian spirits of husbands; and on dressing the brides’ hair with the spear of celibacy; on the little robes of girls carried to Maiden Fortune, women’s wool-working and abstinence from wine; on white bulls sacrificed upon the Alban Mount, entrails thoroughly cooked or half raw being offered, and human heads being sacrificed. 427

Article III.—That same pagan argument is further weakened because, just as the Christian religion had a beginning in novelty, so too did disciplines, arts, and sciences: haruspicy after Tages—where the Acherontic Books are discussed—and astrology after Theutis and Atlas, the flutist and prop of heaven; likewise because the gods were born, because things ancient were once new, and because the Roman religion did not exist before two thousand years ago, just as the Christian religion did not exist before four hundred years ago—where the first kings of the Latins are discussed—and finally because Christians worship nothing new. 431

Chapter VI.—Another argument of the pagans against the Christian religion, drawn from public calamities, is answered. 434

First Article.—The pagans’ argument against the truth of the Christian religion, drawn from the various disasters and calamities by which the human race was afflicted in former times, is presented; and it is shown by which writers it was formerly dissolved and refuted. Ibid.

Article II.—Each of Arnobius’s arguments is considered, by which he utterly overthrows the foolish accusations of the pagans, who incessantly proclaimed Christians to be the cause of all public disasters and calamities; and how clearly he demonstrates that from the very beginning of the Christian religion down to his own age nothing had changed contrary to the fixed laws of nature, either in heaven or on earth, whereas before the Christian era nations had more frequently been exhausted by famine, and there had occurred destructive falls of hail, showers of stones, dried-up rivers, most deadly plagues, crops consumed by mice and locusts, and immense chasms and earthquakes. 437

Article III.—By what other examples Arnobius shows that before the rise of the Christian religion there occurred numerous public calamities, conflagrations, and floods—where Atlantis and the computation of the years from the beginning of the world are discussed—as well as battles with wild beasts and very great wars between the Assyrians and Bactrians under the leadership of Ninus and Zoroaster, other wars of Alexander and the Romans, and that after Christ’s birth events had proceeded far more prosperously. 441

Article IV.—An answer is given to the pagans asking what the cause of evils or public calamities may be; it is proved that what is good for one may be evil for another; that it is futile to object that the Alemanni were defeated and the Getulians and Tingitanians killed by famine because Christians lived among them; and that it is much more absurd to assert that the gods were angry with those same Christians, and that this lie was fabricated by certain mendicant pagans. 446

Chapter VII.—The evidences for the Christian religion advanced by Arnobius are examined; first, concerning God. 451

First Article.—By what weighty arguments Arnobius demonstrates that God exists; what he held concerning God’s nature; how clearly he demonstrates that it is wholly incorporeal; and that a certain reply of his has been undeservedly criticized by some. Ibid.

Article II.—How correctly Arnobius asserts that God’s form cannot be explained; how he teaches what God’s immensity and infinite knowledge are; and that God has nothing resembling human beings. 454

[Col. 1377] Article III.—Whether Arnobius’s position concerning the wrath of God is sound. 456

Article IV.—Whether Arnobius believed that God is the author of all evils, both of punishment and of guilt. 458

Article V.—Whether Arnobius believed that certain animals were not created by God, that the human being is not exposed to evils through natural weakness, and that he does not sin by the choice of his own will. 461

Chapter VIII.—On Christ’s supreme divinity and the mystery of his incarnation. 464

First Article.—By what powerful arguments Arnobius asserts and vindicates Christ’s supreme divinity. Ibid.

Article II.—How clearly Arnobius taught that Christ was as truly God as he was human. 469

Article III.—Why Christ became human; why he did so late and not much earlier; what happened to people who died before his birth—where people of gigantic body and the Stentorian wailing of infants are discussed. 471

Chapter IX.—On the human soul. 475

First Article.—Which false opinions of the ancients concerning the nature, origin, and immortality of the human soul Arnobius recounts, and whether he refutes them correctly. Ibid.

Article II.—Whether Arnobius rightly said that the origin of the human soul is uncertain; whether he fell into the error of Simon Magus, Saturninus, Carpocrates, and the Seleucians, who affirmed that it was created by someone other than God; and whether original sin was unknown to him. 480

Article III.—What Arnobius’s true opinion concerning the nature and immortality of the human soul was, and whether he fell into some error concerning it. 484

Article IV.—Whether Arnobius taught that the souls of the impious would eventually be reduced to nothing, or denied the future resurrection of our bodies. 488

Chapter X.—On the Christians’ faith, hope, churches, Holy Scriptures, altars, images, assemblies, and prayers, including prayers for the dead. 490

First Article.—On the Christians’ faith and its necessity; on their certain hope of the future life; and how strongly it is opposed to the opinions of the pagans. Ibid.

Article II.—On the Christians’ churches, Holy Scriptures, and assemblies; the rite by which they prayed to God in them; and what they asked of him. 492

Article III.—On the Christians’ prayers for the dead. 494

Article IV.—On the Christians’ altars, sacrifices, and use of incense; whether Arnobius spoke of catechumens, the sacraments of Baptism and the Eucharist, and the necessity of divine grace. 497

Chapter XI.—The earlier arguments of Arnobius by which he demonstrates that the pagan religion is false are examined. 499

First Article.—The arguments drawn by Arnobius against the pagan religion from the pagans’ inability to explain where their gods lived, by whom their names had been imposed, and how great their number was are investigated; also from Cicero’s books, especially *On the Nature of the Gods*, concerning which Arnobius’s judgment is examined; and finally from the testimony of Euhemerus, Nicagoras, Leo of Pella, Theodorus, Hippo, and others. Ibid.

Article II.—How Arnobius demonstrates the false divinity of those who were declared gods either because they bestowed benefits upon humanity—as Liber for the invention of wine, Ceres of bread, Aesculapius of herbs, Minerva of the olive, and Triptolemus of the plow—or because of certain illustrious deeds, as in the case of Hercules and Romulus, who was torn to pieces by the hands of the senators. 503

Article III.—Another argument of Arnobius against the pagan religion is considered, drawn from the pagans’ assertion that their gods were male and female and, after celebrating marriages in the human manner, or by another and more shameful means, begot children; here are discussed seven-month offspring, *chalcidica*, Priapus of the Hellespont, the large-breasted Ceres, marriages of the gods celebrated by *usus*, spelt, and *coemptio*, betrothals, Fescennine songs, the royal offspring of Ops, the infamous birth of the Cytherean Venus, and Venus the little prostitute enriched by the king of Cyprus. 506

Article IV.—How Arnobius demonstrates the false divinity of Jupiter from his adulteries: with Hyperion, whence the golden Sun; with Latona, whence the bow-bearing Apollo and Diana upon the wandering islands; with Leda, whence the Tyndarid Castors, or Dioscuri, offspring of eggs, of whom one was a tamer of horses and the other a boxer invincible with the *caestus*; likewise from Jupiter’s other adulteries: with Alcmena, whence Hercules; with Semele, whence Bacchus—also called Bromius, Nysius, and Evius—struck by lightning in his mother’s genital region and born again from his father’s seed; likewise Jupiter with Maia, whence Mercury; with Electra, whence Dardanus; and with Laodamia, whence Sarpedon; here are discussed Minerva born from Jupiter’s brain, Jupiter’s transformations into various animal forms, and these words: “Tisianes, and Bocores, Moorish and *babecali* youths” [the final term is uncertain]. 509

[Col. 1378] Chapter XII.—How Arnobius shows the pagan religion to be false from the adulteries and crimes of other gods and goddesses. 516

First Article.—How invincibly Arnobius proved the absurdity of the pagans’ opinions concerning their gods from Saturn’s adultery with Philyra; Mars’s with Venus; Hercules’ with the fifty daughters of Thestius; Neptune’s with Amphitrite, Amymone, and Alope; and Apollo’s with Arsinoe, Arethusa, Hypsipyle, Marpissa, Zeuxippe, Prothoe, Daphne, Sterope, and also Coronis, whence came Aesculapius, who was struck by lightning because of his greed. Ibid.

Article II.—How clearly Arnobius further proved that the pagans’ gods were false from the boys Catamitus, or Ganymede, Hylas, Hyacinthus, Pelops, and Chrysippus, whom those gods most shamefully loved and violated. 518

Article III.—How Arnobius shows the gods’ divinity to be false from the goddesses’ unchaste love for men: Aurora’s for Tithonus, Luna’s for Endymion, the Nereid’s for Aeacus, Thetis’s for the father of Achilles, Proserpina’s for Adonis, Ceres’ for the rustic Jasion, and Venus’ for Vulcan, Phaethon, Mars, and Anchises; and why Venus is called Dioneia and the mother of the Trojan man. 521

Chapter XIII.—How clearly Arnobius proves that the pagans’ gods are false and nonexistent from their homeland, form, appearance, disciplines, and arts, to which the pagans boasted that they had devoted themselves or over which they presided. 524

First Article.—How invincibly Arnobius demonstrates the false divinity of the gods from the homeland, form, and appearance assigned to them by the pagans. 524

Article II.—How fictitious are the gods whom the pagans proclaimed to be skilled in, or placed in charge of, various arts; here are discussed Apollo the seer who foretells the future, Aesculapius the physician, Vulcan the smith, Tritonia or Tritogenia and Arachne the weavers, and the offspring of Atlas—namely Calypso, more eloquent than the rest; also others imagined to preside over arts or sciences, such as Portunus over navigation, Pales over herds and flocks—whence the Palilia—Innuus or Pan over animals, Pythius over soothsayers, enriched with the treasures of kings, and the Tutelary Gods appointed to guard human beings. 529

Article III.—On other gods similarly placed over particular matters: Juno Lucina over childbirth, Unxia over anointings, Cinxia—or the Virginensian goddess—over the loosening of girdles, and Victua and Potua over food and drink. 533

Article IV.—On other fictitious gods no less absurdly placed over other matters, such as Bellona over wars, Discord and the Furies over dissensions, Mars over battles, and Mercury over contests with oil and dust, boxing, and wrestling; Pellonia over driving off enemies—although the battles at the Caudine Forks and Lake Trasimene, and the disaster at Cannae, prove that she did not favor the Romans; nor can it be said that the gods preside over the left-hand side and oppose the right; likewise on Pausus, the opponent of wars; on Praestana and Panda, or Pantica; and on Titus Tatius, brought into the Capitol. 535

Article V.—How Arnobius pursues his argument and demonstrates that the pagans wrongly imagine the god Lateranus to preside over unbaked bricks, the Genius over the hearth and other places, Aius Locutius over Rome’s protection, Fauns and Fatuae over predicting future events, Puta over pruning trees, Peta over things to be sought, Nemestrinus over groves, Patellana and Patellus over things disclosed or to be disclosed, Nodutis over the knots of fruit, Terensis over threshing crops, Saturn over sowing, Flora over flowers, Montinus over mountains, Vibilia over wanderings from the road, Limentinus over thresholds, Lima over their protection, Limi over oblique positions, the Lucrii over the acquisition of profits, and the goddess Pecunia over wealth. 539

Article VI.—On other gods and goddesses whom the pagans asserted to preside over human vices and other matters; here are discussed Laverna, goddess of thieves, and Murcida, goddess of the slothful; Venus Militaris and the most shameful crimes; Perfica, Pertunda, and Tutinus or Mutinus over obscene pleasures; Libentina and Liburnus as guardians of lusts; Orbona and Naenia as ridiculous divinities presiding over life’s end and funerals; and also the prostitutes for hire Acca Larentia, Flora, and Leaena. 546

Chapter XIV.—Another argument of Arnobius against the pagan gods, drawn from their servitude, bonds, wounds, death, and tombs, is investigated. 551

First Article.—How powerful Arnobius’s argument for destroying the pagans’ belief concerning their gods is, being drawn from the servitude of Hercules, Apollo, and Neptune; Minerva’s shameful service; the servitude of the Muses; the bonds of Mars and Saturn and Saturn’s expulsion from his kingdom; and the wounds of Mars, Venus, Pluto, Juno, Minerva, and Hercules. Ibid.

How the same is proved by the examples of Jupiter, who unknowingly ate human flesh; from his death and burial; from the tombs of the brothers Castor and Pollux, Saturn, and the Tyrian Hercules; and from the Theban Hercules’ destruction by fire. 553

[Col. 1379] Chapter XV.—How Arnobius proved that the pagans wrongly cast upon the poets all the things related about the gods, and that the gods are disgraced and stripped of the divinity attributed to them by the games instituted in their honor. 556

First Article.—It is shown that all the things said about the gods are wrongly laid at the door of the…
the poets, and that the pagans ought to have passed judgment against them as against men who murmured against the sovereign power and were slanderers, and together with them to have proscribed actors, mimes, and pantomimes; with a discussion of the fifteen Laureati. Ibid.

Article II.—How Arnobius demonstrates that the gods of the pagans are false from the solemn games presented in their honor, especially the Floralia and the Megalensia, and from the restoration of certain games; on the comedies, tragedies, and Atellan farces performed at those same games; on the shaven heads of fools, the sound of the *salepitae*, and the redness of phallic charms (*fascina*). 559

Chapter XVI.—How varied were the pagans’ opinions concerning each of their gods, and how rightly Arnobius demonstrates from this that the divinity of each is false. 564

Article I.—Arnobius’ argument against the gods of the pagans is examined, drawn from the fact that a god whom some said had been begotten by parents was affirmed by others to be some natural entity; especially Janus, Saturn, Jupiter, Juno, Fluviona, Pomona, Ossipagina, Februtis, Populonia, Cinxia, and Caprotina. Ibid.

Article II.—How Arnobius shows, from the pagans’ various opinions about her—namely, that she sprang from Jupiter’s brain and that she was the daughter of Mind and Victory—that Minerva is not truly a goddess; with a discussion of the etymology of the name Minerva. 569

Article III.—How Arnobius further shows the same from Neptune, brother of Styx, lord of sea-monsters, and mover of sea-fish and whirlpools; likewise from Mercury the Caduceus-Bearer, the Cyllenian inventor of words and names, and regulator of markets, merchandise, and commerce; and also from Ceres, who was called Earth, the Great Mother, Vesta, Ops, and Saturn’s wife; with a discussion of the etymology of the names Neptune, Mercury, Ceres, and Vesta. 572

Article IV.—By what reasoning Arnobius shows the divinity to be false of Vulcan, who was said to be fire; of Venus, who was said to be Proserpina; of the Sun, who was called Liber and Apollo; of Diana, who was called Ceres and the Moon; and of all the other divinities, because many pagans considered the world to be a kind of living being and a god; with a discussion of the etymology of the names Vulcan and Venus, and of Apollo as the destroyer of mice. 575

Chapter XVII.—How Arnobius further overturns the vain fabrications of opinion concerning the pagans’ gods from their other disagreements about those same gods. 578

Article I.—Arnobius’ argument is examined, drawn from the pagans’ diverse and contradictory opinions concerning the parents, status, and number of the Muses, and concerning the Novensile and native gods; with a discussion of the death of Aeneas. Ibid.

Article II.—How varied were the pagans’ opinions concerning the Penates, Penetrales, Consentes, and Complices, and how their divinity is thereby overturned. 581

Article III.—How great was the disagreement among the pagans concerning the Lares, why they were called Grundules, and why Summanus was set over them; and how plainly it is demonstrated that neither they nor the other gods previously mentioned possess any divinity. 584

Article IV.—Arnobius’ argument against the gods of the nations is considered, drawn from the multiplication of the number of the same gods: namely, three Jupiters, five Suns, the same number of Mercuries and Minervas, four Vulcans, three Dianas and three Aesculapiuses, six Herculeses, and three sets each of Castors and Muses. 587

Chapter XVIII.—How clearly Arnobius destroys their absurd errors concerning the gods from the pagans’ serious and weighty histories, whose memory was celebrated on annual feast days. 590

Article I.—The first history is examined, according to which Numa Pompilius was vaunted as having learned from Jupiter—summoned through the arts of Faunus and Picus—how to expiate a thunderbolt; and another history, concerning Cybele, Agdestis, and Attis, celebrated on annual feast days; with a discussion of the stupidity and madness of the Abderites. Ibid.

Article II.—Other widely circulated histories are considered: concerning Fauna Fatua, or the Good Goddess, beaten with myrtle rods, and concerning the most shameful origin of King Tullius. 594

Chapter XIX.—How the pagans’ mysteries and festivals, instituted and celebrated in honor of the gods and in memory of their deeds, demonstrated the falsity of their divinity. 596

Article I.—How plainly the Bacchanalia, or Omophagia, the initiatory rites of Cyprian Venus, the Sabazia, Thesmophoria, Eleusinia, and Alimontia demonstrate that the pagans’ gods are false. Ibid.

Article II.—How Arnobius utterly overturns the pagans’ reply, in which they maintained that those mysteries and the most shameful histories of their gods were to be explained allegorically. [Col. 1380] 599

Article III.—How the same reply of the pagans is thoroughly weakened and destroyed by other writers. 601

Chapter XX.—How vainly the pagans attempted to prove that their gods truly existed from certain miracles or from responses concerning some future event. 604

Article I.—With what clarity Arnobius refutes the pagans’ argument drawn from miracles: whether when a plague was brought to an end, when the games were restored at Jupiter’s warning, or when the image of Aesculapius was conveyed to the Tiber Island. Ibid.

Article II.—With what force of evidence Arnobius shows that the miracles which the pagans maintained had occurred were false: when the image of the Great Mother was brought to Rome from the Phrygian mountain, and when another image, of Jupiter, was placed in a more elevated location facing east. 607

Chapter XXI.—On the temples of the pagans. 609

Article I.—By what arguments Arnobius shows that neither temples, little huts, chambers, nor cells should be built for the gods; with a discussion of the first temples of the gods and of others that were merely the tombs of dead men; likewise, of the hidden tomb of Apis; of the Capitol, said to have been named from the discovered head of Tolus; and of mass graves. Ibid.

Article II.—On temples impiously consecrated to human affections or virtues—namely, Piety, Concord, Safety, Honor, Virtue, Felicity, Victory, Peace, and Equity—and, among the Egyptians, to cats, scarabs, and heifers; and how rightly it is proved from the destruction of temples that none should be built for false gods. 613

Chapter XXII.—On the statues and images of the gods. 616

Article I.—By what weighty arguments Arnobius demonstrates that images, representations, and statues of the gods are impiously worshiped and adored by the pagans; the meaning of a lion’s face smeared with pure vermilion; and a discussion of the earliest statues and of others represented in human form. Ibid.

Article II.—How rightly Arnobius argues against these same statues of the false gods from their ridiculous images: Ammon with ram’s horns; Saturn with a curved sickle; winged Mercury; Argiphontes with a broad-brimmed hat; Liber with effeminate limbs; naked Venus; Vulcan with cap and hammer; the Delian god with plectrum and lyre; the Muses with pipes and psalteries; Neptune with a trident; Janus with a toothed key; Jupiter wearing a *ricinium* (mantle or veil) and carrying tinder; Pallas with a soldier’s helmet; the Mother of the Gods with a drum; Janus with two faces; Jupiter with a beard; Ceres with large breasts; and Diana with her thighs half covered. 619

Article III.—Another of Arnobius’ arguments against the statues of the gods is examined, drawn from images of Mercury represented in the likeness of Alcibiades, of the Cnidian Venus, and of other Venuses represented in the likeness of Cratina and Phryne; and also from the statue of Jupiter, upon whose finger Phidias inscribed, “Pantarces is beautiful”; and what are called *sigilliola*, or little images. 622

Article IV.—By what reasoning Arnobius shows, from the material and craftsmanship from which the statues of the gods had been made, that the pagans adored them with impious worship and implored their aid; and how vain and futile is the reply of those same pagans, in which they professed that they venerated the statues only after their dedication; with a discussion of fillets, decaying old trees, and the rite by which the pagans adored statues. 624

Article V.—Another argument of Arnobius against the statues of the gods is examined, drawn from the fact that the pagans treated them with disgrace and dishonor and stripped them: namely, the statue of Jupiter by Antiochus of Cyzicus and by the tyrant Dionysius, that of Aesculapius by the same Dionysius, and that of Venus by Pygmalion and another young man; while other statues were either demolished or burned; with a discussion of the several fires at the Capitol. 628

Article VI.—It is shown how weak is the pagans’ reply that statues of the gods should be retained so that the ignorant populace might be kept in duty and religious observance by fear of them; and what conclusion is to be drawn from what has thus far been said. 632

Chapter XXIII.—On the sacrifices of the pagans. 633

Article I.—By what arguments Arnobius demonstrates that no sacrifices should be made to the pagans’ gods, and refutes the opposing arguments of those same pagans; with a discussion of the animal victim, the *cuissa*, and the victim’s life-breath. Ibid.

Article II.—How Arnobius overturns other arguments of the pagans by which they sought to prove that sacrifices ought to be made to their gods; with a discussion of the rite by which those same pagans washed their bodies before approaching the temples; and an explanation of what *bulba*, *immissulus*, *buteo*, *solipuga*, *natrix*, cumin, cress, bulb, savory, and wagtail are. 636

Article III.—Another argument of Arnobius against the sacrifices of the pagans is weighed, drawn from the fact that some victims were sacrificed to one god and others to another; with a discussion of the infernal gods and the pregnant sow. 640

[Col. 1381]

Article IV.—How Arnobius demonstrates from the very things employed in sacrifices that sacrifice should not be offered to the gods; with explanations of what *farcimen*, *apexabo*, *hirciae*, *silicernium*, *longavo*, torches, fillets, *polimina*, *plasea*, fine wheat flour, *fitilla*, *frumen*, *africia*, *gratilla*, *catumeum*, *conspolium*, *cubula*, sacrificial cake, *caro strebula*, pieces of meat, salted provisions combined with four-year-old crops, consecrated spelt, *feudicae*, *rumae* or *aerumnae*, throat, ruminating animals, *augmentum*, *magmentum*, the covering of blood, and *praeciciae* are; and how our Author shows that these things are burned in sacrifices to no purpose. 642

Chapter XXIV.—On the use of incense and wine in the sacrifices of the pagans, and on several other absurd rites and feast days of theirs. 651

Article I.—By what weighty arguments Arnobius concludes that the superstitious use of incense, or the little resin of Panchaia, in the sacred rites and sacrifices of the pagans must be rejected; that it was unknown in the heroic age, in the time of the Alban kings, and even to the Etruscans; and that consecrated spelt was then employed; with an explanation of what male frankincense is, and a discussion of the use of incense at pagan funerals. Ibid.

Article II.—That the custom of pouring libations, the companion of incense, was no less perverse in the sacred rites and sacrifices of the pagans; and an explanation of what *bria*, *simpuvium*, *musci venerabiles*, and “Be honored with the wine poured below” (*Mactus inferio vino esto*) mean. 654

Article III.—How rightly Arnobius assails and rejects other foolish rites of the pagans, by which they adorned their gods with garlands and crowns, employed cymbals, drums, ensembles, and foot-clappers, and greeted them in the morning; and how ridiculous and absurd were the washing of the Mother of the Gods, Jupiter’s banquet, the vintage festival of Aesculapius, the ceremonial couch-feasts of Ceres and the other gods, and the birthdays of Tellus and the others. 657

Chapter XXV.—How meager and scanty human knowledge is. 661

Article I.—How few things a human being knows, and how it remains unknown to him what he himself is; how and when dreams arise; how vision occurs and taste is perceived; why hair turns gray and oil does not mix with other liquids; why the mind is diseased in the sick, and foolish or delirious in others; what the arrangement of the parts of our body is; and to what end Arnobius said these things. Ibid.

Article II.—How rightly Arnobius proved that human knowledge is meager, both from the disagreements among philosophers and from the various opinions of Thales, Heraclitus, Pythagoras, Archytas of Tarentum, Epicurus, and Democritus concerning the first principles of things; of Plato concerning the soul; of Panaetius, Chrysippus, and Zeno concerning the conflagration of the world; of Carneades, Arcesilaus, and the Academics, who affirmed that nothing could be known; and because it still remains unknown whence truth arises, why the sea is salty, and whether these and other similar questions ought to be abandoned. 664

Chapter XXVI.—On the illustrious men, seers, and writers whom Arnobius cited, and on the barbarous, obsolete, and obscure words that he used. 667

Article I.—On Pythagoras, who was burned in a shrine; on the cruel deaths of Socrates, Trebonius, Regulus, and Aquilius; and on certain magicians: Zoroaster, summoned by means of a fiery zone; Armenius, grandson of Zostrianus; Pamphilus of Cyrus; Apollonius; Damigeron; Velus; Julianus; and Bebulus. Ibid.

Article II.—On the various seers mentioned by Arnobius: whether human beings—namely, the Sibyl, Bacis, Helenus, and Marcius—or gods—Dodonaean Jupiter and Apollo Clarius, Pythius, Didymaeus, and Philesius. 672

Article III.—On the various writers cited by Arnobius, whose names are presented in alphabetical order. 674

Article IV.—On the barbarous, obsolete, unusual, or obscure words used by Arnobius. 690

THE SEVEN BOOKS OF ARNOBIUS AFRICANUS’ DISPUTATIONS AGAINST THE NATIONS. 713
## BOOK I.—INDEX OF CHAPTERS

Arnobius declares that he undertook this work in order to repel the repeatedly urged slander by which the pagans falsely and rashly accused Christians of causing every public calamity because they had renounced the worship of false divinities. Chs. 1, 2.—He therefore makes it clear that, from the beginning of the Christian religion, nothing in the natural world and nothing in the private or public affairs of humankind has either changed or become weakened and disordered. Chs. 2, 3.—He refutes the pagans’ objection that the gods, offended by the impiety of the Christians, overwhelm the world with pestilence and other calamities; for it is established from the histories of the pagans themselves that, before the name of Christians had ever been heard, human beings were afflicted by the same disasters or even more grievous ones. Chs. 3, 4.—He also demonstrates that it is as certain that cruel wars were formerly waged by the Atlanteans, Assyrians, Bactrians, Persians, Greeks, Trojans, and Romans, and by Ninus, Zoroaster, Xerxes, Alexander the Great, and others, as it is established that such wars diminished after the birth of Christ. Chs. 5, 6.—He investigates why, according to the pagans’ view, [Col. 1382] the world is oppressed by so many and such great evils. He teaches that either these things must be referred to natural causes, or that things which are certainly useful to the whole of nature and to the world merely seem evil to people, who measure everything by their own advantage. Chs. 7–12.—By various arguments he skillfully exposes how perversely the pagans clamored that all evils must be laid at the door of Christians, who had arisen only about three hundred years before. Chs. 13–16.—He demonstrates that it is absurd to say that immortal gods can be subject to anger, and that they possess no equity at all if, on account of injuries inflicted upon them by Christians, they exact punishment for those injuries without distinction both from the Christians themselves and from innocent pagans, as the latter claimed. He concludes that these ridiculous accusations were fabricated solely by the greed of haruspices, soothsayers, and seers. Chs. 17–24.—He answers the pagans’ objection that the gods rage against human beings because the Christians had introduced a new form of worship into the world. From this he explains wherein the chief substance of the entire Christian religion consists. Chs. 25, 26, 27.—He then argues that the case of the Christians is better than that of those who revere false divinities. For Christians adore that Father from whom the gods of the pagans themselves—if there are any such gods—must have received whatever divinity and majesty they are believed to possess. Ch. 28.—Arnobius proves from His effects that this true God is the maker of all things: older than Apollo, Mercury, and every other fictitious divinity; infinite, unbegotten, immortal, and eternal. Chs. 29, 30, 31.—He asserts that it is implanted by nature in everyone to acknowledge Him as supreme King and ruler of all things; indeed, even animals and stones themselves, if they should happen to speak, would openly and plainly proclaim it. The pagans therefore proclaim Jupiter the supreme God in vain, since they know that he was born in the ordinary human manner, whereas the supreme God is unbegotten and eternal. Chs. 31–35.—He confronts the pagans who accused Christians, not because they worshiped Almighty God, but because they maintained that a man who had been born and put to death by the infamous punishment of the cross was God. Chs. 36, 37.—But if, Arnobius says, the pagans were entitled to enroll certain persons among the gods on account of benefits which they believed had been conferred upon them, how much more ought Christ to be accorded divine honor by human beings, since He bestowed upon them, in the greatest abundance, benefits far greater and without number? Chs. 38, 39.—But He, the pagans said, perished after being fastened to the gibbet of the cross. What follows from that? For Christ’s death, just like that of Pythagoras or Socrates, brought no detriment to His teaching and outstanding deeds. And what of the fact that the infamy of no form of death can ever dishonor an innocent man, as in the cases of Aquilius, Trebonius, and Regulus? Furthermore, what is more deserving of ridicule than this argument of the pagans, who honored with superstitious worship Liber, torn apart by the Titans; Aesculapius, struck by lightning; Hercules, burned alive; and others carried off by violent death? Chs. 40, 41.—Moreover, Christ, sent to us by the supreme King, is proved as certainly as He is manifestly to be true God by the countless miracles He performed. A summary account of Christ’s miracles, from which His divinity is established. Chs. 42–47.—Nor could the cures of certain persons’ infirmities by the pagans’ gods be set against these. For, even if this is provisionally conceded without proof, it is certain that no pagan god ever restored health to the sick, as Christ did, merely by the application of His hand or by His voice. Ch. 48.—Nor does the author allow it to be objected that the gods bring assistance, not to evil persons, but to the good and devout. For Christ aids all the evil equally with the good. Arnobius further shows that Christ’s miracles are genuine from that altogether marvelous power which He granted even to persons of the lowest common rank: the power to perform all manner of wonders by His name alone. Chs. 49–52.—Indeed, how great in majesty and power Christ Himself is—God exalted and from His innermost root, although once unknown to human beings—was most manifestly demonstrated even by the miracles alone that occurred at His death. Ch. 53.—The truth of Christ’s miracles is proved, first, from the most trustworthy witnesses, Christ’s disciples, who published them and handed them down to posterity at certain peril of their lives; and then from the fact that the Christian religion, established and confirmed by those miracles, was embraced throughout the whole world in a very short time. Chs. 54, 55.—Finally, Arnobius proves that these miracles were neither falsely recorded nor excessively exaggerated by our writers. Indeed, what was written about Christ in our Books is as true as what the pagans handed down about their gods is false. Chs. 56, 57.—Arnobius rebuts the pagans who insisted, on the one hand, that their writings were older and therefore truer, and, on the other, that ours had been composed by uneducated persons in rude and unpolished language. Chs. 58, 59.—The author answers the pagans who demanded of the Christians why Christ, if He is God, assumed human form and was put to death in the human manner. Chs. 60, 61, 62.—He answers the same pagans when they rejoin that it is altogether incredible that Christ, being God and man, appeared only in human nature and ended His life fastened to a gibbet; and he shows that, in order to heal and instruct human beings, Christ allowed Himself to be killed by the impious with as much gentleness as freedom. Ch. 63.—Arnobius therefore sharply arraigns the pagans, who nevertheless rendered divine honors to tyrants and extolled with the highest praises and honored with statues others defiled by every kind of impiety and crime, [Col. 1383] yet persecuted Christ alone—the true, greatest, and most salutary messenger—with the most unjust and implacable hatred. Ch. 64.—For what, he says, is more unjust and cruel than always to assail with the bitterest warfare the Lord of every virtue and destroyer of death, who, by permitting the death of the man whom He bore, gave everyone a sure hope of the future salvation of our souls, if we live devoutly? Ch. 65. 718–810.

## BOOK II.—INDEX OF CHAPTERS

Arnobius asks the pagans why, after all, they hated Christ, who was guilty of no offense against them, so greatly that, even upon hearing His name, they immediately blazed up in anger; yet even if He were not believed worthy of anyone’s trust, He should at least not have been spurned, because He showed everyone the way to heaven. Ch. 1.—The author meets the pagans’ reply that they pursued Him with the greatest hatred because He had overthrown all worship of the gods. Chs. 2, 3.—He shows that the pagans were wholly unjustified in refusing to believe Christ’s words on the ground that He does not prove to us that He will ever actually give what He promises. For there are many by no means uncertain factual proofs of the things Christ promised; and since these are readily available, there is no reason to doubt the fulfillment of the other things He has promised. Chs. 4, 5.—He rebuts the boastfulness of the pagans, who gloried that they alone were adorned with wisdom and knowledge, while regarding all others throughout the world who had pledged themselves to Christ—even those endowed with great ability—as dull, obtuse, and foolish. Chs. 6, 7.—The pagans, therefore, being no more learned than others, had no grounds for reproaching Christians for believing their divine Teacher. For certainly no undertaking is commenced without antecedent faith. The pagans themselves believed the opinions of philosophers, who nevertheless offered nothing certain and established concerning the first principles of things and other matters, but were always at war among themselves. Chs. 8, 9, 10.—From this Arnobius infers that it is more equitable to believe Christ, who confirmed His teaching by such great miracles, than philosophers, however highly they may be praised for integrity of character and wisdom, who were never capable of anything even remotely similar. Ch. 11.—And certainly, if Christ had employed merely human arguments, no one would have trusted Him; yet very many were compelled to believe on account of the miracles performed by Him and His disciples—performed, I say, everywhere in East and West, and especially at Rome, where Simon Magus is said to have been cast down by Peter from high in the air to the ground. Ch. 12.—What more need be said? The faith of the Christians certainly ought not to have been harassed by the pagans, but rather praised, because Christians shared with the foremost philosophers views concerning God, the resurrection of bodies, the salvation of souls, and the future punishments of the impious, although these matters are explained by the philosophers differently from the Christians. Chs. 13, 14.—From this Arnobius takes occasion to explain the nature of our soul, from what source it proceeds, and why it becomes subject to various passions and vices. He then refutes those who declared that our soul shares the same immortality and nature as God. Chs. 14, 15, 16.—But the human soul, they said, is divine, since by reason a human being excels the other animals. Quite so, Arnobius replies, if a human being always made good use of this reason. Then, meeting several popular objections, he sets forth and dispels common opinions concerning the excellence of the human soul. Chs. 17, 18.—He proceeds to demonstrate that human souls are neither divine nor did they fly down from heaven into this world already furnished with knowledge of everything; and from this collapses that doctrine of certain philosophers whereby they imagined that the things we learn are recollections. Ch. 19.—He proves this conjecture false by still other weighty arguments, but chiefly by proposing the hypothetical case of a child born in the most deserted and inaccessible wilderness and reared there in utter silence by a mute nurse. Chs. 20, 21.—From this he manifestly concludes that the human soul did not come into the world instructed in all knowledge. Chs. 22, 23.—Arnobius then lucidly refutes Plato’s contrary argument drawn from the boy who was questioned about numbers. Chs. 24, 25.—He resolves the objection of those who say that the soul, when joined to the body, forgets its former knowledge and, as they put it, goes from learned to elementary. Chs. 26, 27.—He treats the same argument further. Ch. 28.—From what has been discussed, the author concludes that a human being of the commonest rank, altogether destitute, must not be assigned to the first—that is, the divine—order, nor be granted the same immortality as God. Chs. 29, 30.—By the same reasoning Arnobius attacks the contrary opinion of Epicurus, who prattled that the human soul is mortal. Our author then determines that the soul is a substance of a certain intermediate nature between the mortal and the divine. Chs. 30–34.—Arnobius answers the pagans when they press him as to how the soul can become immortal if it is of that intermediate quality. Chs. 35, 36.—He then demonstrates that our soul was indeed created by some power of the lowest order, but is neither divine offspring nor a daughter of the supreme God. Nor does the author allow it to be objected that the world would be imperfect without the human being, [Col. 1384] and that God therefore sent into a human body the soul of each individual, begotten from Himself. Chs. 36, 37, 38.—By a lengthy induction he attempts to show that the human being was created, not for the perfection of the world, which could indeed exist without him, but for the private advantage of the human being himself. From this he concludes that the soul is not divine and was not subsequently sent by God into some body. Chs. 39–43.—But it came into the world, they say, by its own will, not at God’s command. Arnobius meets this objection. Chs. 44–46.—The pagans pressed the question from what source, then, the soul was begotten or brought forth. Arnobius replies to them that this, first of all, is established for us: it is neither divine nor the offspring of God, for nothing could ever have been made by the supreme God unless it were perfect in every respect. He then adds that we know this with certainty: human beings are nothing other than souls bound to bodies, and these souls are corrupted by every kind of vice. Chs. 47, 48.—Some, indeed, possess excellent morals, although they are certainly very few. Yet which human beings are perfect? The human soul, therefore, is not divine. Chs. 49, 50.—Nor is there any reason for the pagans to laugh if we deny that we know how it was created. For if they consider Plato right in asserting that souls were created, not by the supreme God, but by certain lesser powers, why should we not be permitted to assert, with far greater certainty, that they are of an intermediate quality, although they may nevertheless be endowed with immortality by God? Chs. 51, 52, 53.—Nor should you say that absolutely nothing occurs without God’s will, or inquire too curiously whence evils arise and why God permits them. This one thing must be held certain: nothing evil, defective, or harmful is ever done by the true God, nor anything that is not salutary for all and filled with the greatest love. Chs. 54, 55.—No one should find our ignorance concerning so many other matters astonishing. For who does not know that human disputes over every subject are so extensive that nothing is asserted by one person which cannot immediately be demolished by another? Chs. 56, 57.—Therefore, although Christians did not know by whom or from what source the human soul was created, the pagans could accomplish nothing against them on that account, since far more things were unknown to the pagans themselves. Chs. 58, 59.—Rightly, therefore, Christ, true God, speaking under human form, commands us to abandon all such questions and be raised with our whole mind to the Lord of all things; and although He cannot be comprehended, no one but a madman doubts that He alone is God. Savage torments after death consequently await the pagans who do not acknowledge Him. Chs. 60, 61, 62.—When the pagans press the questions what, then, became of the souls of those who died before Christ’s advent, and why all souls were not endowed with equal generosity, Arnobius replies, first, that divine benefits were poured out upon all equally; then, that God equally calls everyone and has given everyone the ability to come to Him, but compels no one. Chs. 63, 64.—He explains why God does not cause people to believe His promises against their will; and then that Christians alone obtain salvation through the aid and assistance of Christ, to whom this power was granted by God the Father. Ch. 65.—He passes to the old complaint of the pagans, by which they protested that the Christian religion was novel and that ancient, ancestral rites ought not to be exchanged for barbarous and foreign ones. Chs. 66, 67, 68.—Even if the Christian religion had been recently instituted, did not all human institutions have a beginning—and above all, as the pagans themselves admitted, did not their gods begin to exist? Chs. 69, 70.—If, therefore, the Christian religion did not exist four hundred years ago, the pagans could not deny that two thousand years ago their own gods likewise did not exist. Ultimately, however, the authority of a religion must be assessed not by time, but by divinity. Ch. 71.—Arnobius next demolishes the objection by which the pagans alleged that their religion was far older than the Christian religion and therefore truer. Chs. 72, 73.—He answers the pagans themselves when they demand why Christ was sent by God so late. Chs. 74, 75.—He answers the same people when they ask why the God whom Christians served allowed them to be harassed and oppressed by every kind of persecution and punishment. Chs. 76, 77, 78. 809–936.

## BOOK III.—INDEX OF CHAPTERS

The Christian religion was long ago defended more than sufficiently by distinguished men; yet it has no need whatever of a defender, being in itself altogether unshaken. Ch. 1.—Resuming his interrupted defense, Arnobius answers the pagans as to why Christians neither worshiped nor adored the gods. Whatever is to be worshiped and adored is worshiped and adored by Christians in God, the creator of all things. If, therefore, there are any gods, they derive their origin from Him and are worshiped in Him. Chs. 2, 3.—But the pagans were never able to prove that they were gods in reality, since it always remained unknown to them either whence their gods received their names or how great their multitude was. Chs. 4, 5.—The author proceeds further and demonstrates most openly, from the very things the pagans proclaimed about their gods, that no such gods exist. For first they worshiped male and female gods, yet it is proved that the divine nature is capable of neither sex. Moreover, if the gods of the nations could beget and be begotten, then, since they are imagined to be immortal, their number would already be infinite. Chs. 6, 7, 8, 9.—In addition, the gods would be polluted by foul desires and pleasures. There is therefore no reason why the pagans should take offense when gods of this kind, begetting and begotten, are rejected by Christians. Chs. 10, 11, 12.—Arnobius then censures the pagans because, like the Sadducees, they held the conviction that the gods were fashioned and constituted in bodily and human form. Chs. 12, 13.—Once this is admitted, however, the gods would have to be described as either like or unlike one another. Both alternatives are absurd. Chs. 14, 15.—Arnobius proves that those who replied that human form was assigned to the gods solely for honor’s sake ought not to be heard. Ch. 16.—Although God hears, sees, and understands, He can therefore possess no appearance or shape. We know one thing: there is nothing bodily or pertaining to human passions in God, whose nature cannot be explained by any mortal language. Chs. 17, 18, 19.—Arnobius ridicules the pagans because they introduce gods presiding over human duties, occupations, and other affairs, whether good or evil. Chs. 20, 21.—The author confirms his view by enumerating these functions over which the gods preside. Chs. 22, 23, 24, 25.—He pursues the same argument and concludes that no one will ever persuade Christians of doctrines of this kind, however much they may be called impious and atheistic. Chs. 26, 27, 28.—Arnobius further demonstrates lucidly that the gods of the pagans are altogether fictitious, from the various opinions current concerning these same divinities: first concerning Janus, Saturn, Jupiter, and Juno. Chs. 29, 30.—Then concerning Minerva, Neptune, Mercury, the Great Mother, Liber, and Apollo; in addition, concerning Diana, Ceres, and others, as well as the World, which certain persons vainly supposed to be an eternal God. From this variety of altogether ridiculous opinions, the falsity of the remaining gods is most manifestly demonstrated. Chs. 31–36.—Arnobius establishes the same point no less effectively from the absurd disagreements of those same pagans concerning the origin and number of their gods. Here he deals first with the Muses. Ch. 37.—The Novensiles. Chs. 38, 39.—The Penates. Ch. 40.—The Lares. Chs. 41, 42.—Amid such great disagreements, no pagan was able to discern which of them was a true god or which ought to be honored, invoked, and entreated. Chs. 43, 44. 937–1003.

## BOOK IV.—INDEX OF CHAPTERS

Arnobius continues the argument begun against the gods of the pagans and shows that Piety, Concord, Safety, and other divinities of this kind cannot, either in jest or in earnest, be said to possess divine power and be enrolled among the gods, since all these things are demonstrably situated in human actions and dispositions. Chs. 1, 2.—No less perversely did the pagans, on account of certain benefits which they imagined had been rendered, bring forth numerous gods such as Luperca, Praestana, Panda or Pantica, Pellonia, and other troops of unknown divinities. Chs. 3, 4.—The pagans further prattled that certain gods presided over regions on the left and were hostile to those on the right. Ch. 5.—The same pagans also imagined, altogether foolishly, certain gods appointed over particular things and no others; Arnobius lists some of them. Chs. 6, 7.—He proceeds to enumerate and ridicule other divinities of the same kind. Chs. 8–11.—Nor may anyone object that they are therefore gods because, when summoned by haruspices, they come at once and give definite replies. Arnobius refutes this objection. Chs. 11–13.—But the author presses on and makes it plain that the pagans produced the most absurd monstrosities among their gods: namely, three Jupiters, five Suns, the same number of Mercuries, Minervas, and Dionysuses, and so forth. Chs. 13, 14, 15.—Yet all these gods of the same name cannot be genuine, or else it is altogether unknown which of them is the true god. Arnobius confirms this by the example of Minerva. Chs. 15, 16, 17.—He next confronts the pagans when they press the point that it is unknown whether theologians or others wrote in their books things about the gods that were known and established, or facts and fictions composed according to whim. Chs. 18, 19.—He demonstrates that no truth can be disclosed in books in which the same gods are everywhere and indiscriminately reported as having suffered the gravest insults. Chs. 19–22.—Pursuing the same argument, he concludes that the public calamities of the human race must be ascribed to the pagans themselves, who impiously worshiped these monstrous divinities, and not to Christians, who detested them with the horror they deserved. Chs. 22, 23, 24.—He recalls other shameful things attributed by the pagans to their gods. Chs. 24, 25.—Nor does he pass over the gods’ insane lusts and raging wantonness. Chs. 26, 27.—Yet all these things are either false or true. If the former, the gods ought to have avenged such great and shameless slanders; if the latter, those same gods are proved to have been wretched, infamous, and utterly criminal human beings. Chs. 27, 28.—That gods of this kind were human beings is most manifestly proved. Arnobius explains, however, that he did not undertake to demonstrate this point, which was otherwise easy, but only that the gods were treated more insultingly by no one than by the pagans. Chs. 29, 30, 31.—He manifestly demonstrates that these things were not inventions of the poets. Chs. 32, 33, 34.—But the injustice of the pagans was all the greater because they punished with the utmost severity of the laws the authors of some defamatory remark, poem, or pamphlet, while very patiently allowing such great disgraces of the gods to be written and [Col. 1386] sung. Chs. 34, 35.—Nor does their guilt end there: for they enhanced with praises and rewards those who wrote such things, and even actors and mimes who represented the same things in the theaters. Therefore, if the gods are inflamed with anger, as the pagans supposed, they ought to have been angry, not with Christians, but with the pagans themselves, who publicly displayed their disgrace before everyone’s eyes. But if they are exempt from anger, they are vainly said to be angry with Christians. Chs. 35, 36, 37. 1003–1080.

## BOOK V.—INDEX OF CHAPTERS

Arnobius passes to another argument against the gods of the pagans, deriving it from their histories; since the pagans retained these histories in daily practice and celebrated them in annual festivals, they clearly considered them entirely true. The first is the story of Numa Pompilius, who is said to have obtained the rite for averting lightning from Jupiter Elicius after deceiving him by stratagems and artifices. Chs. 1, 2.—From all the circumstances of this story, however, the author makes it manifest that nothing more alien to truth and divinity could be invented. Chs. 3, 4.—The second is the story of Acdestis and Attis, which is found to have been notorious for the most shameful outrages of Jupiter, the Mother of the Gods, Nana, and Ia; for the disgraceful castration of Attis; for the deaths of Attis and Ia; and for the other circumstances appended to it. Chs. 5, 6, 7.—Arnobius therefore argues against it just as he does against the other stories. He presses the pagans and ridicules their madness. Chs. 8, 9.—He examines other elements in the same story that are exceedingly full of absurdities. Chs. 10, 11.—He nevertheless shows that the pagans could not convict it of falsehood, since it had been handed down by their most ancient writers and was customarily celebrated by the pagans themselves at the annual festival of the Mother of the Gods. Chs. 12–17.—Arnobius declares that, deterred by their abominable foulness, he passes over many other stories similar to these. Yet he briefly censures Fauna Fatua, or the Good Goddess, beaten with rods; the shameful birth of Servius; and the unspeakable acts customarily performed in the Omophagia, the rites of the Corybantes, the Bacchanalia, and the Phrygian rites and mysteries. Chs. 18, 19.—On occasion of these matters he reproaches the pagans with Jupiter’s incest with his mother Ceres and his daughter Proserpina. Chs. 20, 21.—Having set these matters forth, he skillfully observes that so many and such great adulteries and other outrages of Jupiter are related that he seems to have been born for no other reason than that the whole cesspool of infamy might be channeled into him. Chs. 22, 23.—He then proceeds to other sacred rites, namely the Thesmophoria and Eleusinia. Chs. 24–27.—And the Alimontia, in which there was no less lewdness and wantonness than in the others. Chs. 28, 29.—Having related these matters, he asks the pagans whether Christians ought to be compelled by every kind of torture to perform such rites; at the same time he declares that it seems astonishing to him that anyone who denies or doubts that these are gods should be called an atheist and sacrilegious person by those very pagans. Finally, he concludes that gods of this kind ought to have been hostile not to Christians, who rejected them, but to pagans, who proclaimed such great crimes of theirs. Chs. 29, 30, 31.—He blows away the pagans’ answer that all these stories must be understood solely in an allegorical sense. Chs. 32, 33.—He presses the absurdity of this evasion more forcefully. Chs. 34, 35, 36.—He proves the same still more fully by examining the stories of Summanus and Proserpina, and those of Jupiter and Ceres. Chs. 37, 38, 39.—Yet grant, if you wish, that in the description of any story something altogether different from the words’ apparent meaning is signified: it will assuredly redound no less to the disgrace and insult of the gods. Chs. 40, 41, 42.—Finally, Arnobius shows that many things are commonly read in the histories of the gods which cannot be explained allegorically. From these he concludes that it was altogether impious for the gods to be called by the pagans by names most disgraceful and plainly unworthy of divine majesty, if the pagans were genuinely convinced that they existed. Chs. 43, 44, 45. 1080–1160.

## BOOK VI.—INDEX OF CHAPTERS

In this and the following book, Arnobius refutes another accusation made by the pagans, by which they charged Christians with the greatest impiety because they had no temples or images of the gods and never offered them any sacrifices. Chs. 1, 2.—He begins with the temples of the gods and declares that Christians do indeed have none—not out of contempt for the gods, if any such beings exist, but because they disregard temples, since these can be of no use to the gods, and because it is moreover more insulting to the gods rashly to assert that any god can be confined within a temple. Ch. 3.—To the pagans’ rejoinder that temples are erected for the gods so that people may converse with them as though they were somehow present, Arnobius replies that the true God knows even the silent thoughts of our minds, hears all things equally, is absent from no place—in a word, is present everywhere in His immensity. Chs. 4, 5.—Furthermore, a great many temples of the gods are nothing other than tombs of the dead. From this Arnobius establishes that temples were constructed for the gods in vain and contrary to their dignity. Chs. 6, 7.—There is certainly no stronger reason for worshiping their images. For if the gods are in heaven, prayers should be poured forth to them rather than to their images. The author also gathers additional arguments against the images of the gods. Chs. 8, 9, 10.—The ancient people who worshiped a river, a scimitar (*acinaces*), a stone, an unshaped piece of wood, or something similar as gods were rightly and deservedly ridiculed by the pagans. Yet Arnobius demonstrates that those very pagans were no less deserving of ridicule, since they fabricated things no less absurd concerning the gods. Chs. 11, 12.—Nor did the pagans merely give their gods ornaments unworthy of them, but also the form and features of certain human beings and prostitutes. Ch. 13.—Arnobius therefore exhorts the pagans to return to a sounder mind and at last understand that the images which they adored with such great honor were bones, stones, bronze, silver, gold, and very often the cheapest material. Chs. 14, 15.—To this is added the fact that, if anyone were to enter the innermost parts of the image of Olympian Jupiter or of another image, what would he see except plates or little pieces of wood and stone held together with poured lead or with chains, hooks, and small rings? Would he not see the head, belly, and other parts of the image hollow and empty within? Whatever appears on the exterior, moreover, becomes discolored, decays, and is defiled. Ch. 16.—By various arguments Arnobius demolishes the pagans’ opinion that it was not the material of the images that was worshiped, but the gods dwelling within the images. Chs. 17, 18, 19.—He presses them: why do they protect the images and guard them carefully lest they suffer any injury? Chs. 20, 21.—If you say that the gods care nothing about these things, they ought at least to have preserved unharmed the images and shrines in which they dwelt from the insolence of depraved people, from fire, and from other accidents. Chs. 22, 23.—Finally, Arnobius overthrows the pagans’ last refuge: their repeated assertion that certain persons had not been ignorant of all these facts but had nevertheless judged that, through the worship of images, the uneducated populace must be kept to duty and religious observance. Chs. 24–27. 1161–1216.

## BOOK VII.—INDEX OF CHAPTERS
In this book Arnobius proves, whether by authority or by reason, that no sacrifices should be offered to the gods. For they are not nourished by these sacrifices, since whatever is nourished is mortal. Chs. 1, 2, 3.—Nor are victims slaughtered for the gods’ pleasure, since anyone affected by pleasure of this kind is still mortal. Ch. 4.—Arnobius also demolishes the common opinion that the anger of the gods is appeased by sacrifices. For a movement of anger, unworthy of the gods, cannot enter an immortal mind. Chs. 5, 6, 7.—Furthermore, no one will be persuaded that, when some animal has been slaughtered and offered, they lay aside their anger or forget the wrongs done to them; or that through these sacrifices, as though for an agreed payment, they grant pardon for sins committed against them. Chs. 8, 9.—Nor, certainly, is there any reason for someone to argue that victims are sacrificed to the gods so that they may bestow prosperity and avert adversity. For, setting aside for the moment the philosophers’ opinion that all things are governed by fate, certainly, if it lies within the gods’ power to bestow favorable and adverse circumstances upon human beings, they show an ungrateful disposition in allowing those who load their altars with victims to be reduced to the direst straits. Chs. 10, 11.—Moreover, it is absurd to say that the gods sell their benefits for the price of sacrifices. Ch. 12.—Nor is there any stronger basis for asserting that sacrifices are made to honor the gods and magnify their power. Chs. 13, 14.—Arnobius nevertheless acknowledges that honor should be rendered to the true God, who, just as he does not blaze up in anger, neither rejoices when honor is bestowed nor takes offense when it is withheld, nor considers himself made greater by the services of others. Moreover, nothing is added to the gods’ honor by slaughtered animals, whose smoke fouls their images, and whose blood and stench pollute their temples and altars. Chs. 15, 16.—But if you contend that the gods are honored by this bloodshed of animals, why are elephants, camels, lions, and a great many other animals not sacrificed to them? And do not say that the gods are honored only by those things which they graciously supply for our nourishment; for cumin, cress, turnips, and the other things useful to us ought then likewise to be offered to those same gods. Chs. 16, 17.—Arnobius further presses the point that, just as the gods are of one kind, so they ought to have one judgment: “Why,” he asks, “is one victim sacrificed to one god, and another to another?” Chs. 18–21.—Nor is it helpful to reply that different victims are slaughtered for different gods by ancient and long-standing custom. For the inquiry is not whether human beings, but whether the gods, decreed that one victim was more appropriate to one god than to another. Chs. 21, 22.—When the pagans object that sacrifices must be made to good gods so that they may benefit us, and to evil gods so that they may not harm us, Arnobius replies that all gods [Col. 1388] ought by their very nature to be good and therefore, even if human beings show them no honor, they cannot harm them on that account. Furthermore, if this pagan opinion is true, it follows from it that a good god becomes evil if the victim owed to him is not slaughtered, while, conversely, an evil god becomes good once the sacrifice has been performed. Ch. 23.—Yet even if it could lawfully be done that bulls and other animals were sacrificed to the gods, how could the various kinds of sausages, porridges, and cakes employed in pagan mysteries be of any benefit to them? Chs. 24, 25.—There is no better reason for burning incense upon their altars. For that rite is recent and was unknown in ancient times. It must therefore either be judged useless, or else ancient people, who certainly never practiced it, must have sinned. Chs. 26, 27.—What, moreover, of the boast that by offering incense some honor is rendered to the gods? For incense is nothing other than a gum exuding from certain kinds of bark. Why, then, is gum formed on other trees not likewise burned for them? Is it because its scent is not so pleasant? Are some odors, then, agreeable to the gods, as they are to human beings, and others unpleasant and disagreeable? Yet, as the philosophers acknowledge, the gods are incorporeal and therefore cannot be soothed by incense or any other odor. Chs. 27, 28.—In their rites they also poured out undiluted wine as incense’s companion, uselessly and without any reason. Since the gods suffer neither thirst nor hunger, the use of wine is plainly useless. The pagans were likewise mistaken in thinking that it was poured out either in honor of the gods or to make them favorable. Chs. 29, 30.—For what could be more senseless than pouring out some wine with prescribed words, lest any other wine whatsoever become sacred and be withdrawn from human use? Ch. 31.—Arnobius shows it to be no less ridiculous that the gods should be delighted by garlands, wreaths, cymbals, drums, and musical ensembles. In addition, he ridicules their feast days and assails the games instituted in their honor. Ch. 32.—He proves that nothing is further removed from right reason than to suppose that the gods are delighted and appeased by the shameful comedies and tragedies performed at that time. Ch. 33.—He demonstrates that so many and such monstrous opinions arose because the pagans did not know the nature of the true God and falsely persuaded themselves that their gods were of the same substance as themselves. Ch. 34.—He next proceeds to demolish the pagans’ last and, as it was thought, stronger bulwark, by which they attempted to prove from various accounts of prodigies, as they maintained, that the gods, offended by human sins, had blazed up in anger but were afterward appeased by the satisfaction offered by those human beings. First, he examines the restoration of the Circus games in honor of Jupiter, upon whose proper celebration the plague was said to have ceased. Chs. 35, 36, 37.—He then passes to the account of the Capitol struck by lightning and the image of Jupiter cast down from its seat. When, finally, in accordance with the soothsayers’ responses, it had been placed on higher ground facing the rising sun, people believed that hidden matters had thereby been disclosed. After relating these things, Arnobius makes it plain that nothing could ever be imagined more unworthy of the supreme majesty, or even of the very name, of the gods. Chs. 37–41.—He next calls back for examination the narrative concerning the image of Aesculapius transferred to the Tiber Island, by whose coming, they believed, the dreadful plague then raging amid the troubled circumstances of the commonwealth was suddenly quelled. Chs. 41, 45.—He begins a discussion of the image of the Mother of the Gods brought to Rome from Phrygian Pessinus. At that time, they repeatedly claimed, the enemy was driven from Italy, the city’s former glory was restored, the boundaries of the empire were extended far and wide, and other benefits were bestowed upon the Roman people. Having brought these claims forward, Arnobius demonstrates that nothing exists, or could be invented, that is more contrary to truth or less deserving of belief. Chs. 46–48.—Finally, he compares the opinions of the pagans and Christians with one another and sets them in opposition; from this he concludes that the Christians are pious, whereas the pagans themselves are truly guilty and conscious of the insane impiety with which they reproached the Christians. Chs. 49, 50, 51. 1217–1388.

**END OF VOLUME FIVE.**
